title: Mahābhārata
text:
Ugraśravā, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, a sūta versed in the Purāṇas, came once to the twelve-year sacrificial session of Śaunaka, lord of the kula, in the Naimiṣa forest.
The son of the sūta approached the brahmarṣis who were seated there, those of sharpened vows, bowing humbly before them.
When he arrived at that hermitage, the ascetics dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest gathered around him, eager to hear his wondrous tales.
Having saluted all those sages with palms joined, he enquired after the progress of their austerities, and was in turn warmly greeted by those good men.
When all the ascetics had taken their seats, Lomaharṣaṇi humbly took the seat that had been indicated for him.
Seeing him comfortably seated and rested, a certain ṛṣi then asked him a question, setting the conversation in motion.
"From where have you come, O Sauta? And where has this time been spent by you? O lotus-eyed one, tell me this, for I am asking."
The sūta said: "I was in the presence of the royal sage Janamejaya, son of Parīkṣit, that great-souled lord among the Pārthas, at his snake sacrifice."
"The highly meritorious and various tales spoken by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana were duly recited there by Vaiśaṃpāyana as well."
"Having heard those stories of varied meaning, rooted in the Mahābhārata, and having visited many tīrthas and sacred shrines in pilgrimage,"
"I went to that holy place frequented by the twice-born, named Samantapañcaka, where in former times the great battle of the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus, and all the kings of the earth, took place."
"Wishing to see you, I have come from there to your presence. O long-lived ones, you are all, in my view, become Brahman itself."
"O highly fortunate ones, blazing with the splendour of the sun and fire, purified by ritual baths, pure, having completed your mutterings and fed the fires — you sit here at ease. What shall I speak to you, O twice-born ones?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Sacred tales rooted in the Purāṇas, or tales rooted in dharma, the histories of kings and of great-souled ṛṣis —"
The ṛṣis said: "That Purāṇa proclaimed by Dvaipāyana, the supreme ṛṣi, which the gods and the brahmarṣis heard and honoured —"
"— that which is foremost among narratives, with its varied words and cantos, endowed with subtle meanings and reasoning, adorned with the purport of the Vedas —"
"— the holy Bhārata itihāsa, united with the meaning of its text, elevated by refinement, spoken in the language of Brahmā, enriched by various śāstras —"
"— which Vaiśaṃpāyana, that ṛṣi, recited duly and with joy to King Janamejaya at the sacrifice, by the command of Dvaipāyana —"
"— we wish to hear that saṃhitā of Vyāsa of wondrous deeds, equal to the four Vedas, righteous and removing the fear of sin."
The sūta said: "Having made obeisance to the primal Puruṣa, the Lord, invoked by many and praised by many, who is the Truth, the one-syllabled Brahman, both manifest and unmanifest, the eternal —"
"— who is both the unreal and the real, who is this universe, who transcends both being and non-being, the creator of the high and the low, the ancient, the supreme, the imperishable —"
"— having bowed to Viṣṇu, the auspicious source of all auspiciousness, the most excellent, sinless, pure, Hṛṣīkeśa, Hari, the teacher of all that moves and does not move —"
"— I shall now fully declare the teaching of Vyāsa of boundless splendour, that great-souled maharṣi honoured throughout all the world."
"Some poets have told this itihāsa on earth; others are telling it even now; and yet others will tell it likewise in the future."
"This great knowledge is established in the three worlds; it is preserved by the twice-born both in its expanded and its condensed forms."
"Adorned with auspicious words, with divine and human usages, furnished with various metres and verses, it is dear to the learned."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In this state when there was no lustre, no light, when all was enveloped in darkness on every side, there arose the single great Egg, the imperishable seed of all creatures."
"At the beginning of the age, that great divine cause is proclaimed; within it is heard the true light, the eternal Brahman."
"That which is wondrous and unthinkable, which has attained equality everywhere, unmanifest, subtle, the cause — that is of the nature of both being and non-being."
"From that arose the Grandfather, the one Lord, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the teacher of gods, Sthāṇu (Śiva), Manu, Ka, and Parameṣṭhin."
"Then Dakṣa Prācetasa, and the seven sons of Dakṣa — from these arose the twenty-one lords of creatures."
"And the Puruṣa of immeasurable self, whom all the ṛṣis know, the Viśvedevas, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins as well —"
"— the Yakṣas, Sādhyas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and the Pitṛs — from these sprang the learned, the well-conducted, the spotless brahmarṣis."
"And many royal sages endowed with all virtues; water, sky, earth, wind, the intermediate regions, and the directions —"
"— the year, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, days and nights in succession — and whatever else came into being that is witnessed by the world —"
"— whatever is seen here, whether stationary or moving — all this universe is drawn back again at the end of the age."
"Just as the many and varied marks of the seasons appear again and again in their cycle, so too do conditions recur at the beginnings of each age."
"Thus this wheel, without beginning or end, causing the dissolution of all beings, without beginning or cessation, revolves in the world."
"Thirty-three thousand, thirty-three hundred, and thirty-three — such, in brief, is the count of the creation of the gods."
"Bṛhadbhānu, son of Divas; Cakṣus; Ātmā; Vibhāvasu; Savitā; Ṛcīka; Arka; Bhānu; Āśāvaha; Ravi —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"All these are sons of Vivasvat; among them the youngest was Mahya; Devabhrāṭ was Mahya's son; and from him is born one known as Subhrāṭ."
"Subhrāṭ had three sons, bearers of offspring and greatly learned: Daśajyoti, Śatajyoti, and the self-possessed Sahasrajyoti."
"The great-souled Daśajyoti had ten thousand sons; the sons of Śatajyoti here numbered ten times that many."
"And the sons of Sahasrajyoti were ten times greater still; from them arose this lineage of the Kurus, of the Yadus, and of Bharata."
"And the lineages of Yayāti and Ikṣvāku, and of royal sages in every direction — many dynasties and the detailed creation of beings arose from them."
"All the abodes of beings, the threefold secret, the application of the Vedas together with its knowledge, dharma, artha, and kāma as well —"
"— the śāstras of dharma, kāma, and artha, the various other śāstras, and the ordinances for the conduct of worldly life — all this the ṛṣi saw and set down."
"Itihāsas with commentaries, and the various śrutis as well — all of this is traversed here; such is declared to be the scope of this text."
"Having expanded this great knowledge, the ṛṣi also stated it in condensed form; for in the world, both the expanded and the condensed forms are cherished by the learned."
"Some brāhmaṇas study the Bhārata beginning from the Manu episode, others from the Āstīka episode, and still others from the Uparicara episode — each according to his tradition."
"The wise illuminate the various knowledge of the saṃhitā; some are skilled in expounding the text, others in preserving it."
"By austerity and celibate study, having arranged the eternal Veda, the son of Satyavatī composed this holy itihāsa."
"The learned son of Parāśara, the brahmarṣi of sharpened vow, righteous of soul, at the bidding of his mother and of the wise Gāṅgeya —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"— the mighty Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana formerly fathered, in the field of Vicitravīrya, three offspring of the Kuru line, like three sacred fires."
"Having begotten Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura, the wise one returned once more to his hermitage for austerities."
"When those three were born, had grown up, and had gone to the highest state, that great ṛṣi proclaimed the Bhārata in this human world."
"Being asked by Janamejaya and by thousands of brāhmaṇas, he instructed his disciple Vaiśaṃpāyana, who was seated nearby."
"Seated together with the officiants, Vaiśaṃpāyana caused the Bhārata to be heard, being urged again and again during the intervals of the sacrifice."
"Dvaipāyana properly told of the full extent of the Kuru lineage, the righteousness of Gāndhārī, the wisdom of Kṣattṛ (Vidura), and the fortitude of Kuntī."
"The blessed ṛṣi told of the greatness of Vāsudeva, the truthfulness of the Pāṇḍavas, and the evil conduct of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
"He composed the Bhārata saṃhitā of twenty-four thousand verses; without the subsidiary tales, that much is called the Bhārata by the learned."
"After that, the ṛṣi further made a condensed version of one hundred and fifty verses, the index chapter that summarises the contents along with the parvans."
"Dvaipāyana first taught this to his son Śuka; thereafter the lord gave it to other fitting disciples as well."
"Nārada caused the gods to hear it; Asita Devala caused the Pitṛs to hear it; and Śuka caused the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas to hear it."
"Duryodhana is a great tree made of wrath; Karṇa is its trunk; Śakuni its branches; Duḥśāsana its abundant flowers and fruit; and the unwise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra is its root."
"Yudhiṣṭhira is a great tree made of dharma; Arjuna is its trunk; Bhīmasena its branches; the twin sons of Mādrī its abundant flowers and fruit; and Kṛṣṇa, Brahman, and the brāhmaṇas are its root."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Pāṇḍu, having conquered many lands by warfare and valour, lived in the forest devoted to hunting, along with his people."
"By killing a deer in the act of mating, he incurred a terrible calamity; and it was there that the Pārthas were born and the sequence of their customs and conduct began."
"And the assistance of the two mothers with regard to the mystery of dharma — the approach of Dharma, Vāyu, Śakra, and likewise of the two divine Aśvins —"
"— growing up together with ascetics, protected by their mothers, in sacred pure forests and in the hermitages of the great ones —"
"— and the children, handsome, with matted hair, living as celibate students, were then personally brought by the ṛṣis to the Dhārtarāṣṭras —"
"— and saying 'These are your sons, brothers, disciples, and friends — these are the Pāṇḍavas,' the sages then vanished."
"Seeing the Pāṇḍavas presented by them, the Kauravas at that time, and the well-born citizens of all the classes, cried out repeatedly in great joy."
"Some said, 'These are not his sons'; others said, 'They are indeed his.' Still others said, 'Since Pāṇḍu died long ago, how can they be his?'"
"Voices were heard everywhere saying: 'Welcome — by good fortune we behold the offspring of Pāṇḍu! Let welcome be declared!'"
"When that noise died down, a tumultuous sound arose from unseen beings, filling all the directions."
"At the entry of the Pārthas there was a rain of flowers, auspicious fragrances, and the sound of conches and drums — it seemed wondrous."
"And out of the joy of all the citizens, a great joyous sound arose there that touched the sky and magnified their glory."
"And those Pāṇḍavas, having studied all the Vedas and the various śāstras, dwelt there honoured and without fear from any quarter."
"The subjects were gladdened by the purity of Yudhiṣṭhira, by the steadfastness of Bhīmasena, and by the valour of Arjuna —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By Kuntī's devoted service to her elders and by the humility of the twin sons, the whole world was pleased — as also by their quality of valour.
Then, at the assembly of kings gathered for the princess's self-choice of a husband, Arjuna won Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) by performing a most difficult feat.
From that time onward, he was honoured in this world as the foremost of all bowmen, blazing like the sun and hard to behold even in battle.
Arjuna, having conquered all kings and all great confederacies, brought back to the king (Yudhiṣṭhira) the tribute needed for the great Rājasūya sacrifice.
The great Rājasūya sacrifice performed by Yudhiṣṭhira was endowed with abundant food and rich sacrificial fees, adorned with every auspicious quality.
Through the wise counsel of Vāsudeva and through the might of Bhīma and Arjuna, Jarāsaṃdha and the Cedi king (Śiśupāla) — who was proud of his strength — were slain.
Then tribute and homage — jewels, gold, precious gems, cattle, elephants, horses, and wealth — came from every quarter to Duryodhana.
Seeing that great and thriving prosperity of the Pāṇḍavas, an immense rage born of envy arose in him (Duryodhana).
Seeing the assembly hall of the Pāṇḍavas — built with consummate skill by Maya and resembling a celestial palace — presented to them, he was consumed with anguish.
There he had been laughed at by Bhīma — before the very eyes of Vāsudeva — as he stumbled in his confusion, like one of base birth.
Though enjoying varied pleasures and divers jewels, when reported to Dhṛtarāṣṭra he had grown pale, wan, and emaciated.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, doting on his son, consented to the dice game. Hearing of this, Vāsudeva's anger was greatly aroused.
He (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) was not greatly pleased in his heart, yet he approved the quarrels, and looked on while horrible unrighteous acts born of gambling and the like grew and spread.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Setting aside Vidura, Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat — in that tumultuous conflict, the kṣatriya warriors destroyed each other.
When the sons of Pāṇḍu were victorious, having heard the most grievous ill tidings and knowing the counsel of Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, Dhṛtarāṣṭra reflected for a long time and then addressed these words to Saṃjaya.
"Hear everything from me, Saṃjaya — do not find fault with me. You are learned, intelligent, wise, and esteemed by the discerning."
"My mind does not desire this conflict, nor do I rejoice in the destruction of the Kurus. I make no distinction between my own sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu."
"My sons, given over to rage, bear malice toward me in my old age. But I, being blind, endure it out of wretchedness and love for my sons — and I follow foolish, senseless Duryodhana in his delusion."
"Having witnessed the splendour of the mighty Pāṇḍava at the Rājasūya, and then having endured that mockery at the sight of the assembly hall —"
"— burning with indignation yet unable to conquer the Pāṇḍavas in battle, and incapable of winning their prosperity by valiant means like a true kṣatriya, together with the king of Gāndhāra he devised treacherous gambling."
"In that matter, hear from me, Saṃjaya, everything as I came to know it. Having heard my words, which are informed by wisdom and truth, you will then recognise me, O Sūta's son, as one who sees with the eye of understanding."
"When I heard that the wondrous target had been pierced and brought down to earth with a drawn bow, and that Kṛṣṇā had been won before the eyes of all the assembled kings — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Subhadrā, the Mādhavī lady, had been carried off by force by Arjuna at Dvārakā, and that the two heroes of the Vṛṣṇi clan had gone to Indraprastha — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When I heard that Indra the king of gods had been repelled by Arjuna with divine arrows, and that Agni had been satiated in the Khāṇḍava forest — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Yudhiṣṭhira, his kingdom seized, had been defeated by Śakuni in the dice game, yet was followed into exile by his immeasurable brothers — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Draupadī, weeping in her throat, was dragged in grief to the assembly hall wearing but a single cloth, in her menses, though she had protectors, treated as if she had none — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard of the manifold endeavours of those righteous ones — the Pāṇḍavas — who set out for the forest and suffered hardship out of loyalty to their eldest brother — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the Dharma-king, dwelling in the forest, was followed by thousands of high-souled brāhmaṇas who were snātakas living on alms — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Arjuna had propitiated the god of gods — three-eyed Tryambaka (Śiva) in the form of a Kirāta — in battle and obtained that great weapon the Pāśupata — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Dhanaṃjaya, dwelling in the heavens, properly received divine weapons from Indra in person — he of firm truth being thus extolled — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Bhīma and the other sons of Pṛthā had met with Vaiśravaṇa (Kubera) in that region inaccessible to mortals — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that those who came on the cattle-tour had been captured by the Gandharvas, and were released by Arjuna — the very sons of mine who had set their minds on following Karṇa's counsel — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When I heard that Dharma in the form of a Yakṣa had met the Dharma-king, O Sūta, posing questions and answering them all correctly — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the foremost of my warriors had been routed single-handedly by the great-souled Dhanaṃjaya while he dwelt in the kingdom of Virāṭa — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the king of Matsya honoured and gave his daughter Uttarā to Arjuna, and that Arjuna accepted her for his son (Abhimanyu) — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that seven akṣauhiṇī armies had rallied to Yudhiṣṭhira — he who had been vanquished, stripped of wealth, banished, and separated from his kinsmen — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Nārada declared of those two — Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, who are Nara and Nārāyaṇa — 'I have seen them eternally in the world of Brahmā' — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Mādhava Vāsudeva had committed himself wholly to the Pāṇḍavas' cause — he of whom they say a single stride of his encompasses this earth — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Karṇa and Duryodhana had resolved to seize Keśava, and that he thereupon revealed his own self in manifold forms — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that, as Vāsudeva was departing, he stood in front of his chariot, and Pṛthā (Kuntī) in her anguish was comforted by Keśava — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Vāsudeva was their counsellor, that Bhīṣma son of Śaṃtanu was likewise on their side, and that Droṇa son of Bharadvāja was uttering blessings for them — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Karṇa said to Bhīṣma, 'I shall not fight while you are fighting,' and thereupon abandoned the army and withdrew — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When I heard that those two — Vāsudeva and Arjuna — and likewise the bow Gāṇḍīva of immeasurable power — these three of fierce valour — had come together — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Arjuna, overwhelmed by despondency, was sinking down on the chariot floor, and that Kṛṣṇa revealed the worlds within his own body — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Bhīṣma, crusher of enemies, was slaying ten thousand charioteers in the battle, and that none of these (Pāṇḍavas) of visible form was being killed — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Bhīṣma — supremely heroic and unassailable in battle — had been felled by Pārtha (Arjuna) after placing Śikhaṇḍin in front — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the aged hero Bhīṣma, having reduced the Somakas to a handful, lay on his bed of arrows, brought down by shafts with beautiful feathering — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that as Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, lay (on his arrow-bed) and asked for water, Arjuna, urged to provide it, pierced the earth and there satisfied Bhīṣma's thirst — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that both Venus (Śukra) and the Sun were favourably aligned for the sons of Kuntī toward victory, and that beasts of prey always cried out against us — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When Droṇa, a wondrous warrior, displaying manifold paths of his weapons in battle, still could not slay the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the great warriors on our side, the Saṃśaptakas who had pledged themselves to bring about Arjuna's death, were slain by Arjuna — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the heroic son of Subhadrā (Abhimanyu) alone had broken and entered the battle-array, impenetrable to others, guarded by Droṇa son of Bharadvāja who had taken up his weapons — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When all the great warriors together surrounded and slew that young Abhimanyu — rejoicing in their faces as they did so — because they were unable to face Pārtha (Arjuna) — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that, after Abhimanyu was slain, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who shouted in foolish exultation had the wrath of Arjuna unleashed upon the Sindhu king (Jayadratha) — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the vow taken by Arjuna to slay the Sindhu king had been fulfilled — true to his word, accomplished in the midst of his enemies — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that as Dhanaṃjaya's horses were exhausted, Vāsudeva unharnessed them, watered them, let them recover, then reharnessed them and proceeded — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that while the horses were recovering, Arjuna, standing on the chariot platform, held back all the warriors with his Gāṇḍīva bow — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Yuyudhāna (Sātyaki), having crushed Droṇa's army — hard to overcome as it was with the strength of elephants — went to where those two Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha were, following the Vārṣṇeya — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Bhīma, having encountered Karṇa and been spared from death, was struck with the tip of Karṇa's bow and taunted with words of reproach by that hero Karṇa — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When Droṇa, Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, Karṇa, Droṇa's son (Aśvatthāman), and the valiant king of Madra could not bear watching the Sindhu king being slain — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the divine Śakti spear given by Indra had been deflected by Mādhava — spent instead against Ghaṭotkaca the Rākṣasa of terrifying form — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When I heard that in the battle between Karṇa and Ghaṭotkaca the sūta's son (Karṇa) had released the Śakti — by which Savyasācin (Arjuna) would have been slain in combat — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the teacher Droṇa alone, having set aside his weapons on the chariot floor in preparation for death, was slain by Dhṛṣṭadyumna in transgression of dharma — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the son of Mādrī, Nakula the heroic Pāṇḍava, engaged in equal single-chariot combat with Droṇa's son, fighting bravely before the eyes of the world — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When Droṇa was slain and Droṇa's son unleashed the divine Nārāyaṇa weapon, yet could not bring about the end of the Pāṇḍavas — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Karṇa — supremely heroic, unassailable in battle — was slain by Pārtha in that conflict of brothers, a secret known to the gods — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Droṇa's son, Kṛpa, Duḥśāsana, and fierce Kṛtavarman were unable to overpower Yudhiṣṭhira who stood virtually alone — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the valiant king of Madra — he who always rivalled Kṛṣṇa in battle — was slain in combat by the Dharma-king, O Sūta — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that sinful Śakuni — son of Subala, the root of the quarrel and the dice game, relying on his power of illusion — was slain in battle by the Pāṇḍava Sahadeva — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Duryodhana — exhausted, chariotless, his pride shattered — had gone to a lake and stilled its waters to hide within it, lying there alone — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the Pāṇḍavas, standing together with Vāsudeva on the bank of the Gaṅgā lake, were provoking my wrathful son — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When I heard that, as he circled through the various paths of mace-fighting, he was wrongfully struck down through the stratagem of Vāsudeva — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Droṇa's son and the others slew the Pāñcālas and the sons of Draupadī while they slept — a gruesome, inglorious act — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that Aśvatthāman, pursued by Bhīmasena, in his fury unleashed the supreme weapon — the Aiṣīka — by which he struck the embryo in the womb — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that the Brahmaśiras weapon fired by Arjuna was peacefully neutralised weapon-against-weapon by Aśvatthāman, and that Aśvatthāman gave up the jewel-gem from his head — then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory."
"When I heard that as Droṇa's son unleashed the great weapon against Uttarā's womb, Dvaipāyana and Keśava cursed Droṇa's son with mutual imprecations — then (I had no hope of victory)."
"Pitiable is Gāndhārī, bereft of sons and grandsons; so too are the daughters-in-law (widows) bereft of fathers and brothers. The Pāṇḍavas have accomplished a most difficult task and have regained a kingdom free of rivals."
"Alas — in the war I have heard that ten survived: three of our side and seven of the Pāṇḍavas'; and eighteen less two akṣauhiṇī armies were destroyed in that great conflict, that slaughter of kṣatriyas."
"I am covered over by darkness; delusion seems to enter me. I cannot recover my senses, O Sūta — my mind seems to reel."
Having said this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra lamented and fell into a swoon in his great grief; then, having recovered his senses, he addressed these words once more to Saṃjaya.
O Sañjaya, now that things have come to this pass, I wish to give up my life without delay, for I see not even the slightest benefit in continuing to live.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
To that king, despondent and lamenting thus, the wise son of Gavalgaṇa — Sañjaya — spoke these weighty and momentous words.
You have heard, O king, about those rulers of immense enterprise and great might, as recounted by the sage Dvaipāyana and the wise Nārada.
Born in the greatest of royal lineages, distinguished by every virtue, versed in celestial weapons, and equal in splendour to Indra himself —
— having conquered the earth by righteousness, having performed sacrifices with lavish gifts of honour, having won glory in this world — they too in the end came under the dominion of time.
Vainya the great warrior, heroic Sṛñjaya foremost among conquerors, Suhotra, Rantideva, Kakṣīvān the son of Uśij —
— Bāhlika, Damana, Śaibya, Śaryāti, the unconquerable who was yet conquered, Viśvāmitra the slayer of enemies, mighty Ambarīṣa —
— Marutta, Manu, Ikṣvāku, Gaya, and Bharata himself, Rāma the son of Daśaratha, Śaśabindu, Bhagīratha —
— Yayāti of auspicious deeds, for whom the gods themselves served as officiating priests, and whose whole earth became marked with sacrificial posts and filled with the sounds of soma-pressings —
— these twenty-four kings were thus enumerated long ago by the divine sage Nārada to Śaibya, who was consumed by grief for his son.
And before them still others passed away — kings even mightier, great warriors, noble souls, endowed with every virtue.
Pūru, Kuru, Yadu, Śūra, Viṣvagaśva, Mahādhṛti, Anenā, Yuvanāśva, Kākutstha, Vikramī, Raghu —
— Vijitī, Vītihotra, Bhava, Śveta, Bṛhadguru, Uśīnara, Śataratha, Kaṅka, Duliduh, Druma —
— Dambhodbhava, Para, Vena, Sagara, Saṃkṛti, Nimi, Ajeya, Paraśu, Puṇḍra, Śambhu, Devāvṛdha the sinless —
— Devāhvaya, Supratima, Supratīka, Bṛhadratha, Mahotsāha, Vinītātmā, Sukratu, Nala the lord of Niṣadha —
— Satyavrata, Śāntabhaya, Sumitrā, Subala the mighty lord, Jānujaṅgha, Anaraṇya, Arka, Priyabhṛtya, Śubhavrata —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— Balabandhu, Nirāmarda, Ketuśṛṅga, Bṛhadbala, Dhṛṣṭaketu, Bṛhatketu, Dīptaketu, Nirāmaya —
— Avikṣit, Prabala, Dhūrta, Kṛtabandhu, Dṛḍheṣudhi, Mahāpurāṇa, Saṃbhāvya, Pratyaṅga, Parahā, Śruti —
These and countless others are heard of — hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, and still more counted in the hundreds of millions.
Wise and mighty kings who had renounced the most vast pleasures — they too met their deaths, surpassing even your sons in greatness.
Whose deeds were celestial, whose valour and generosity, whose nobility of soul, reverence for the sacred, truthfulness, purity and straightforwardness —
— are celebrated in the world by scholars, by ancient sages and the greatest of poets — even those endowed with the full wealth of all virtues passed away.
Your sons were evil-minded, consumed by wrath, greedy, and predominantly ill-behaved — you should not grieve for them.
You are learned, O Bhārata, intelligent and wise, esteemed by the wise; those whose understanding follows the scriptures are not deluded.
Both punishment and favour are well known to you, O lord of men; it is taught that one should not be utterly indulgent in shielding one's sons.
What had to be has come to pass — you should not grieve over it. Who, however superior his wisdom, is able to turn back fate?
None transgresses the path ordained by the Creator. All this — existence and non-existence, pleasure and pain — has time as its root.
Time ripens all beings; time dissolves all creatures; and time again pacifies that same time which burns the people to ashes.
Time transforms all conditions in the world, both auspicious and inauspicious; time contracts all creatures and once more releases them; time moves among all beings, unobstructed and impartial.
Past conditions, future ones, and those which exist at present — understanding that all are fashioned by time, you should not abandon your composure.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Sūta said: Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana declared this holy secret teaching here — that even one who studies with faith a single verse of the meritorious Bhārata is purified of all sins without remainder.
For in this text are celebrated the holy divine sages, as well as the brahmarṣis and rājarṣis of auspicious deeds, and likewise the yakṣas and great serpents.
The eternal Lord Vāsudeva too is celebrated here; for he is truth and righteousness, the pure and the holy.
He is the eternal Brahman supreme, the unchanging and everlasting light, whose divine deeds the wise declare.
From that God proceed the non-existent, the existent, and also both the existent and non-existent together — the continuity of creation, its ongoing activity, birth, death, and rebirth.
And what is heard regarding the Self — that which consists of the qualities of the five elements, and that supreme reality beginning with the Unmanifest — he alone is hymned as all of that.
That which the best of ascetics, intent in meditation and possessed of the power of yoga, behold as dwelling in the self — like a reflection in a mirror — is he.
A person who is faithful, ever diligent, devoted to truth and righteousness, and who regularly studies this chapter is freed from sin.
The believer who continually hears this table-of-contents chapter of the Bhārata from the beginning never sinks in adversities.
Reciting even a little of it at both twilight junctions, one is immediately freed from whatever transgression has been accumulated through the day and the night.
For this is the very body of the Bhārata — both true and immortal; as butter is the essence of curds, so is the brahmin the essence among two-footed beings —
— as the ocean is supreme among lakes and the cow is the highest among four-footed beings, so in the same way the Bhārata is called the most excellent.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whoever causes even a single verse of it to be recited to brahmins at a śrāddha ceremony — inexhaustible food and drink stands ready for his ancestors.
One should supplement the Veda with the Itihāsa and Purāṇa; the Veda fears the poorly-learned, thinking: 'This person will cross me over wrongly.'
The learned one who causes this Veda of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana to be recited attains its fruit, and sheds even the sin incurred by the slaying of an embryo — without doubt.
Whoever, with a pure heart, recites this chapter at every fortnightly occasion — by him the entire Bhārata may be considered as having been studied, in my judgement.
The person who daily hears this seer-composed text with faith will attain long life, fame, and passage to heaven.
On one side were placed the four Vedas together, and the Bhārata alone on the other side, when the divine sages assembled and weighed them of old; in greatness and in weight the Bhārata was found to be the heavier.
Because of its greatness and because of its weightiness, it is called the Mahābhārata; one who knows its true etymology is freed from all sins.
Austerity is not impurity, nor is study impurity; the natural observance of Vedic duty is not impurity, nor is forceful acquisition of wealth impurity — but those same acts, when tainted by evil intention, become impurity.
The sages said: O son of the sūta, you have mentioned a place called Samantapañcaka — we wish to hear all about it fully and in due order.
The Sūta said: If you, O brāhmaṇas, desire to hear my words and these auspicious tales, then listen, O best of the twice-born, to the account called Samantapañcaka.
At the junction of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, Rāma — the foremost of those who bear arms — driven by wrath, repeatedly slaughtered the earthly warrior class.
Having extirpated all the kṣatriyas by his own might, blazing like fire, he made five lakes of blood at Samantapañcaka.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In those blood-filled lakes, overcome with rage, he satisfied his ancestors with blood — so we have heard.
Then the ancestors, headed by Ṛcīka, came to that bull among brāhmaṇas and restrained him saying: 'Forgive, forgive!' — and thereupon he desisted.
The holy region near those blood-filled lakes is celebrated as Samantapañcaka.
The wise declare that the region which is identified and distinguished by a particular mark should be named according to that very mark.
And in the interval that arrived between the Dvāpara and Kali ages, the great battle of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies took place at Samantapañcaka.
In that supremely righteous land, free from any taint of the earth, eighteen akṣauhiṇī armies assembled, eager for battle.
Thus, O twice-born, has the name of that region come about; and that holy and delightful land has now been described to you.
All this has been told to you by me, O best of sages — how that region has become renowned and celebrated in the three worlds.
The sages said: O son of the sūta, you have used the word 'akṣauhiṇī' — we wish to hear all about that in full and exactly as it is.
Tell us precisely the measure of an akṣauhiṇī in terms of chariots, horses, men and elephants — for all of this is known to you.
The Sūta said: One chariot, one elephant, five foot-soldiers and three horses — this unit, by those who know, is called a patti.
This patti multiplied by three is called a senāmukha by the wise; three senāmukhas together are called one gulma.
Three gulmas constitute a gaṇa; three gaṇas are remembered as a vāhinī; and three vāhinīs are called a pṛtanā by those with discernment.
Three pṛtanās make a camū; three camūs make an anīkinī; and ten anīkinīs, the learned declare, constitute an akṣauhiṇī.
The precise count of chariots in an akṣauhiṇī, O best of the twice-born, as reckoned by those who know the truth of number and calculation, is twenty-one thousand —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— and eight hundred and seventy more; and the count of elephants is exactly this same number.
The number of men, O sinless ones, is to be known as one hundred thousand plus nine thousand and three hundred and fifty.
For horses they give the count, accurately reckoned, as sixty-five thousand and six hundred and ten.
This is what those who know the truth of enumeration call an akṣauhiṇī — which I have now described to you in full detail, O best of the twice-born.
By this reckoning the combined forces of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies, O best of the twice-born, were in total exactly eighteen akṣauhiṇīs.
They assembled in that very region and met their destruction there, the Kauravas being made the instrument by time of wondrous deeds.
Bhīṣma, the supreme master of weapons, fought for just ten days; Droṇa then commanded and protected the Kuru army for five days.
Karṇa, crusher of enemy forces, fought for two days; Śalya held command for half a day; after that came the mace-fight.
At the close of that very day, Kṛtavarman son of Hṛdika, Aśvatthāman son of Droṇa, and Kṛpa son of Gautama slaughtered the army of Yudhiṣṭhira while it slept trustingly in the night.
At the sacrifice of Śaunaka I shall narrate the extensive tale of the Bhārata; there also, before it, I shall first tell the story called Pauloma.
That tale of diverse meanings and varied metres, approached by wise men as the liberated approach dispassion — that is the one I shall tell.
Just as the self is the most worthy of all things to be known, and life the most dear of all beloved things, so this history is the foremost in purpose and the greatest among all scriptural traditions.
In this supreme history, the finest intellect has been employed; the entire range of vowels and consonants, all speech rooted in the world and the Veda, finds its home here.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of this history of the Bhāratas, rich in wisdom, adorned with varied words and divisions, let the summary of the parvas now be heard.
First comes the Index of Parvas; second, the Parva-Compendium; then the Pauṣya, the Pauloma, the Āstīka, and the Descent of the Primeval Lineage.
Then is recounted the Sambhava Parva, wondrous and fashioned by the gods; within it is the burning of the house of lac, and the Hiḍimba Parva is also told.
Then the parva of the slaying of Baka; then the Citraratha Parva; and then is told the parva of the svayamvara of the princess of Pāñcāla.
Having won her by the law of warriors, the Marriage Parva follows; then the parva of Vidura's arrival, and likewise the parva of the obtaining of the kingdom.
The forest sojourn of Arjuna; then the abduction of Subhadrā; after the abduction of Subhadrā comes the parva known as Haranahārika, of gifts for the bride.
Then the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest, and within it the appearance of Maya; then the Sabhā Parva is narrated, and after it the Council Parva.
The parva of the slaying of Jarāsandha; likewise the Digvijaya Parva of conquest of the quarters; after the Digvijaya, the Rājasūya Parva is spoken.
Then the offering of the arghya and the slaying of Śiśupāla; the Dice Parva is then narrated, and after it the Subsequent Dice Parva.
Then the Āraṇyaka Parva, and within it the slaying of Kirmīra; the battle between the Lord Śiva and Arjuna, known as the Kirāta Parva.
Next to be known is the parva of the journey to Indra's world; then the pilgrimage parva of the wise king of the Kurus.
The parva of the slaying of Jaṭāsura; then the combat with the Yakṣa; and right after it is to be known the Ajagara Parva of the great serpent.
The Mārkaṇḍeya Dialogue Parva is told after that; then the parva of the conversation between Draupadī and Satyabhāmā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the Ghoshayatra Parva; then the fear arising from the dream of the deer; then the tale known as Vrihidraounika is narrated immediately after.
The parva of the abduction of Draupadī from the forest by the Sindhu king; then, next here, is told the parva of the theft of the earrings.
Then the Araneya Parva; immediately after, the Virāṭa Parva; the parva of the slaying of the Kīcakas; and then the parva of the cattle-raid.
The marriage of Abhimanyu with the princess of Virāṭa is remembered as a parva; from here onward is to be known the great and wondrous Udyoga Parva.
Next to be known after that is the parva known as the Journey of Sañjaya; then the Prajagara Parva, arising from Dhṛtarāṣṭra's anxiety.
The Sanatsujāta Parva, with its secret vision of the inner self; then the Yamasandhi Parva and the journey of the Lord himself.
Here is to be known the Vivada Parva concerning also the great-souled Karṇa; and then the parva of the setting out of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies.
Then the parva of the enumeration of the great chariot-warriors; then the parva of the arrival of Ulūka as envoy, which heightens the fury.
Then the Ambā Episode Parva is to be known after this; the Bhīṣma Installation Parva is to be known as wondrous in its cause.
The creation of the Jambūdvīpa is told as a parva immediately after; then the Bhūmi Parva is to be known, with its account of the extension of the islands.
The Bhagavad Gita is told as a parva; then the fall of Bhīṣma; the installation of Droṇa is told as a parva; and then the slaying of the Saṃśaptakas.
The parva of the slaying of Abhimanyu; and the Vow Parva is recounted; the parva of the slaying of Jayadratha; and then the slaying of Ghaṭotkaca.
Then the parva of the slaying of Droṇa, to be known as hair-raising; the release of the Nārāyaṇa weapon is told as the next parva.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the Karṇa Parva is to be known; then the Śalya Parva follows; then the parva of entry into the lake; and after it the mace duel.
Then the Sārasvata Parva, endowed with accounts of pilgrimage sites and lineages; above that, the horrific Sauptika Parva is recounted.
The Aishika Parva is indicated here, exceedingly terrible; then the parva of the water libation; and after that the Stri Parva.
Then is to be known the Śraddhā Parva, the post-mortem rites of the Kurus; then the Installation Parva of the wise king of righteousness.
The parva of the suppression of Charvaka, the demon in brahmin form; and the distribution of houses is told as a parva immediately after.
Then the Śānti Parva, where the duties of kings are expounded; the law in times of distress is told as a parva, and after it the law of liberation.
Then the supreme Anushasanika Parva is fully to be known; then the Svargароhаnika Parva of the wise Bhīṣma.
Then the Aśvamedha Parva, which destroys all sins; after it the Anugita Parva is to be known, which speaks of the inner self.
The parva known as the Forest Hermitage sojourn, and the sight of the sons; then here is told the parva of Nārada's arrival.
Then the terrible Mausala Parva is fully described; then the Mahaprasthana Parva, and after it the Svargarohana Parva.
Then the Harivamsha Parva, a Purāṇa known as a supplement; and the Bhavishya Parva too is told, wondrous and great, also among the supplements.
This full hundred of parvas was spoken by the great-souled Vyāsa, and repeated faithfully by the son of Sūta, Lomaharṣaṇa.
It was narrated in the Naimiṣa forest; the parvas number eighteen in all; this summary of the Bhārata was there set forth as the Parva-Compendium.
In the Pauṣya Parva the greatness of Utanka is described; in the Pauloma Parva the full expansion of the lineage of Bhṛgu is celebrated.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the Āstīka Parva: the birth of all serpents and of Garuḍa; the churning of the milk-ocean; and also the birth of Uccaiḥśravas.
And the story of King Parīkṣit's son performing the serpent sacrifice, through which this tale of the great-souled Bhāratas came to be told.
The various births of kings are told in the Sambhava Parva, and also those of other brahmins and of the sage Dvaipāyana.
And here is celebrated the descent of portions of the gods, of the daityas, of the danavas, and of the mighty yakshas.
The origins of nagas and serpents, of gandharvas and of birds, and of other diverse beings as well.
The re-birth of the great-souled Vasus in the Gaṅgā, their residence in Śaṃtanu's house, and their ascent once more to heaven.
And also here the birth of Bhīṣma through the combined energy of divine portions; his renunciation of the kingdom; and his steadfast vow of celibacy.
The keeping of his vow; and the protection of Citrāṅgada; and upon Citrāṅgada's death, the protection of his younger brother.
The installation of Vicitravīrya in the kingdom; and the birth of Dharma among humans, arising from the curse of the sage Aṇīmāṇḍavya.
And the begetting by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, born of a boon; the births of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and the Pāṇḍavas.
The journey to Vāraṇāvata; the conspiracy of Duryodhana; and by Vidura's counsel, the construction of the escape tunnel.
In the terrible forest, the Pāṇḍavas' encounter with Hiḍimba; and the birth of Ghaṭotkaca is celebrated right here.
The incognito wandering of the Pāṇḍus; their dwelling in a brahmin's house; the death of Baka; and the amazement of the townspeople.
Having defeated Angarparna on the bank of the Gaṅgā, Arjuna then, together with all his brothers, journeyed toward the Pāñcālas.
Then the Tapatī legend, the Vasiṣṭha legend, and the excellent Aurva legend; the wondrous sub-tale of the five Indras is also told here.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The deliberation of Drupada regarding the five having one wife; and the divinely ordained, superhuman marriage of Draupadī.
The arrival of Vidura; the sight of Keśava; and the dwelling at Khāṇḍavaprastha; and likewise the rule over half the kingdom.
And by Nārada's injunction, the regulation concerning Draupadī; and the sub-tale of Sunda and Upasunda is celebrated there.
The forest sojourn of Pārtha; his meeting on the road with Ulūpī; the journey to holy pilgrimage sites; and the birth of Babhruvāhana.
In Dvārakā, the lovely Subhadrā, enamored of the lover's approach, was won by the diadem-wearer with Vāsudeva's consent.
Taking her away, when Kṛṣṇa the son of Devakī had arrived, the obtaining of the discus and the bow; and the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest.
The birth of Abhimanyu, of supreme radiance, from Subhadrā; the rescue of Maya from the fire; the liberation of the serpent; and the birth of the sharika offspring of the great sage Mandapāla.
Thus this first Adi Parva has been told, vast in its scope; it is reckoned by the supreme sage as two hundred chapters, with eighteen additional chapters set down by the radiant Vyāsa.
Seven thousand shlokas, and nine hundred shlokas, and eighty-four shlokas besides — thus the text was measured by the great-souled one.
The second, the Sabhā Parva, is described as rich in many accounts: the building of the assembly hall by the Pāṇḍavas, and the sight of the servants.
The account of the halls of the world-guardians, from Nārada's sight of those divine abodes; the commencement of the Rājasūya; and likewise the slaying of Jarāsandha.
The liberation by Kṛṣṇa of the kings imprisoned in Girivraja; and at the Rājasūya, during the dispute over the arghya, the slaying of Śiśupāla.
Having seen that splendor of the sacrifice, Duryodhana, seized by grief and indignation, was mocked by Bhīma right there on the floor of the assembly hall.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Where his fury arose, through which he caused the dice game to be played; where the gambler Śakuni defeated the son of Dharma at dice.
Where Draupadī, like a ship on the ocean of dice, rescued them who were drowning; and King Duryodhana, knowing they had crossed over, summoned the Pāṇḍavas once more to the dice game.
All this Sabhā Parva has been recounted by the great-souled one; its chapters are to be known as seventy, plus two more in the count.
Two thousand shlokas, and five hundred shlokas, and eleven shlokas besides — these are to be known as celebrated in this parva.
After this, the third is to be known as the great Āraṇyaka; and also the following of the citizens after the wise son of Dharma.
Where the Vṛṣṇis come and the Pāñcālas in their entirety; where the tale of the slaying of Saubha is told, and likewise the slaying of Kirmīra; and the exile of the boundlessly radiant Pārtha for the sake of weapons.
The battle with Mahādeva in his guise as a Kirāta hunter; the sight of the world-guardians; and indeed the ascent to heaven.
The sight of the great sage Bṛhadaśva, whose soul is cultivated; and the lamentation of the afflicted Yudhiṣṭhira in his misfortune.
The Nala sub-tale right here, righteous and moving to compassion, where Damayantī holds firm during Nala's time of misfortune.
And the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, gone into forest exile — their passage to heaven is narrated by Lomaśa to Arjuna.
The pilgrimage of the great-souled Pāṇḍavas is likewise described here, and the slaying of Jaṭāsura is narrated in that same context.
Bhīmasena, commissioned by Draupadī on the Gandhamādana mountain to fetch mandāra flowers, there assaulted that lotus lake.
There his great battle took place with the rākṣasas and also with the mighty yakṣas headed by Maṇimat.
The tale of Agastya is also there — the devouring of Vātāpi, and the sage's approach to Lopāmudrā for the sake of offspring.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Next in succession comes the tale of the hawk and the pigeon, where Indra, Agni, and Dharma tested King Śibi.
The story of Ṛśyaśṛṅga, a celibate from boyhood, and the deeds of Rāma Jāmadagnya of great splendour.
The slaying of Kārtavīrya and the destruction of the Haihayas are described there, and likewise the tale of Sukanyā, where the sage Cyavana of the Bhārgava line appears.
At Śaryāti's sacrifice the Nāsatya twins made him a drinker of soma, and there that sage was restored to youth by them.
Here too is the tale of Jantu, where King Somaka sacrificed his son to gain offspring and thereby obtained a hundred sons.
Here too is the story of Aṣṭāvakra, where the sage, having defeated Bandin in debate and recovered him from the ocean, regained his father.
Having obtained divine weapons for the sake of his teacher, the left-handed archer fought the Nivātakavacas, the dwellers of the golden city.
Pārtha's reunion with his brothers on the Gandhamādana mountain, and the Ghoṣayātrā, where Kirīṭin fought with the gandharvas.
Their return again to the Dvaitavana lake, and the abduction of Draupadī from her hermitage by Jayadratha.
Where Bhīma, swift as the wind, pursued him; and the tales told in portions within the Mārkaṇḍeya conversations.
The vision of Kṛṣṇa and his dialogue with Satyā, the tale of the grain and the heron, and likewise the story of Indradyumna.
The story of Sāvitrī and of Uddālaka's line, and the tale of the son of Vena, and here too the Rāmāyaṇa episode narrated at great length.
Here the theft of Karṇa's earrings by Purandara; and the tale of the forest-dweller, where Dharma instructed his son; where the Pāṇḍavas, having obtained their boons, went westward.
This third parvan is celebrated as the Āraṇyaka; the great sage has enumerated in it two hundred chapters plus sixty-nine chapters further declared.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Eleven thousand verses, six hundred more, and sixty-four additional verses — such is this parvan as enumerated.
Now understand in detail this expansive Virāṭa parvan: going to Virāṭa's city and seeing the great śamī tree in the cremation ground, the Pāṇḍavas deposited their weapons there.
Where, having entered the city, they lived in disguise; and where the wicked Kīcaka was slain by Vṛkodara.
Where the Kurus were defeated in battle by Pārtha at the cattle raid, and where the cattle wealth of Virāṭa was rescued by the Pāṇḍavas.
Where Uttarā was given by Virāṭa as a daughter-in-law to Kirīṭin, pledged to Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadrā, the slayer of foes.
This extensive fourth parvan, the Virāṭa, has been described; here too the great soul has counted up the chapters.
Sixty-seven chapters complete — now hear from me the count of verses too: two thousand verses and fifty more are declared in this parvan by the reckoning of the supreme sage.
The Udyoga parvan is to be known as the fifth; hear what follows: when the Pāṇḍavas were encamped at Upaplavya intent on victory, both Duryodhana and Arjuna came before Vāsudeva.
Having said, 'You should render us assistance in this war,' the great-minded Kṛṣṇa then spoke thus.
'Shall I give to which of you my own self who will not fight but will serve as counsellor, O best of men, or an entire akṣauhiṇī of troops?'
The dull-witted Duryodhana of wicked mind chose the army, while Dhanaṃjaya chose Kṛṣṇa, who would not fight, as his counsellor.
Where the mighty Mahārāja Dhṛtarāṣṭra dispatched Saṃjaya as an emissary to the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of peace.
And where, upon hearing of the Pāṇḍavas with Vāsudeva at their head, sleeplessness overtook Dhṛtarāṣṭra from his anxious brooding.
Where Vidura caused King Dhṛtarāṣṭra the wise to hear words of varied import and wholesome counsel.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Likewise where the king, afflicted with mental anguish and consumed by grief, was made to hear the supreme teaching on the Self from Sanatsujāta.
Where, at the royal assembly at daybreak, Saṃjaya proclaimed before the king the unity of Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
Where Kṛṣṇa of great glory, moved by compassion and desiring peace, himself came to the city of Nāgasāhvaya to make reconciliation.
And the rejection of Kṛṣṇa, who was beseeching on behalf of the good of both sides, by King Duryodhana.
Having perceived the wicked plotting of Karṇa, Duryodhana, and their allies, Kṛṣṇa there displayed his sovereignty as lord of yoga before the kings.
Where Karṇa, mounted on the chariot, was persuaded by Kṛṣṇa through counsel; yet from his own valour and pride, he refused.
Then also the march forth of chariots, horses, men, and elephants from the city of Hāstinapura, and the enumeration of the forces.
Where the king sent Ulūka as a harsh-spoken emissary to the Pāṇḍavas on the eve of the great battle; the enumeration of maharathas and rathas; and likewise the tale of Ambā.
This fifth parvan of the Bhārata, the Udyoga parvan, is designated as containing very many accounts and pertaining to peace and war.
In terms of count, one hundred and eighty-six chapters are noted here, and six thousand verses, and likewise that many hundreds.
And ninety verses are declared, and likewise eight more, by the great-souled Vyāsa of noble mind in this parvan, O sages rich in austerity.
From this point on the Bhīṣma parvan of manifold import is told; the formation of the Jambū continent is described there by Saṃjaya.
Where a terrible, exceedingly dreadful battle raged for ten days; where the army of Yudhiṣṭhira fell into the deepest despondency.
Where the great-minded Vāsudeva destroyed Pārtha's faintness born of delusion through the reasoned arguments of the teaching of liberation.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Where Pārtha the great archer, placing Śikhaṇḍin in the van, struck Bhīṣma down from his chariot with sharp arrows.
This great sixth parvan of the Bhārata is celebrated; one hundred chapters are declared, and seventeen further.
Five thousand verses, eight hundred more, and eighty-four verses are proclaimed in this parvan — so counted by the Veda-learned Vyāsa in the Bhīṣma parvan.
Then is told the Droṇa parvan, varied and full of many accounts, where the Saṃśaptakas lured Pārtha away from the battlefield.
Where Mahārāja Bhagadatta, equal to Śakra in battle, was slain by Kirīṭin together with his elephant Supratīka.
Where many great warriors of the world, led by Jayadratha, slew Abhimanyu, the young hero who had not yet reached full youth.
Abhimanyu being slain, where the enraged Pārtha in battle, having killed seven akṣauhiṇīs, slew King Jayadratha; and the destruction of the remaining Saṃśaptakas in the combat was accomplished fully.
Alambusa, Śrutāyu, the valiant Jalasandha, Saumadatti, Virāṭa, the great warrior Drupada, Ghaṭotkaca and others were slain in the Droṇa parvan.
And here too Aśvatthāman, when Droṇa had fallen in battle, in his fury released the terrible Nārāyaṇa weapon.
This great seventh parvan of the Bhārata is declared; it is here that those protectors of the earth, those heroic bulls among men designated in the Droṇa parvan, met their end for the most part.
One hundred and seventy chapters are declared, and eight thousand verses and nine hundred more.
And nine verses likewise are here counted by the sage Pārāśarya, the seer of truth, having pondered the Droṇa parvan.
From this point on the supremely marvellous Karṇa parvan is told; the appointment of the wise king of Madra as charioteer; and the ancient legend of the destruction of the triple city is narrated there.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And here during the march the harsh dialogue between Karṇa and Śalya; and the tale of the swan and the crow, full of reproach, is here as well.
And the mutual anger between Yudhiṣṭhira and Kirīṭin; and where the great warrior Karṇa was slain by Pārtha in single chariot combat.
This eighth parvan has been designated by the scholars of the Bhārata; sixty-nine chapters are declared in the Karṇa parvan, and four thousand verses, and nine hundred verses more.
From this point on the Śalya parvan of manifold import is celebrated; when the foremost warriors of the army were slain, the lord of Madra became its leader.
The episodes of chariot battles are celebrated there in parts; the destruction of the chief Kurus is celebrated in the Śalya parvan.
And here the death of Śalya at the hands of Dharmarāja the great warrior; and the tumultuous mace battle is celebrated here as well; and the sanctity of the tīrthas of the Sarasvatī is also celebrated.
This ninth parvan, marvellous and full of meaning, is designated; fifty-nine chapters are counted there by those skilled in enumeration.
Many accounts are enumerated and the verse total is here celebrated: three thousand verses, two hundred and twenty more, composed by the sage in honour of the glorious Kauravas.
From this point I shall speak of the dreadful Sauptika parvan, where the wrathful King Duryodhana lay with his thigh broken.
When the Pārthas had withdrawn, three chariots approached — Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and Drauṇi — at evening, drenched in blood.
Where Drauṇi the great warrior, with firm anger, vowed: 'Without killing all the Pāñcālas headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and the Pāṇḍavas together with their counsellors, I will not remove my armour.'
Where those bulls among men, led by Drauṇi, slaughtered the Pāñcālas along with their retinue in the night as they slept unsuspecting.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Where those five Pārthas were saved through the protection of Kṛṣṇa's might, and the great archer Sātyaki too, while the rest met their deaths.
Where Draupadī, tormented by grief for her sons and afflicted by the slaughter of her father and brothers, having resolved to fast unto death, sat before her husbands.
Where Bhīma of terrible valour, at Draupadī's words, furiously pursued the son of Bharadvāja, the teacher's son.
Where Drauṇi, driven by fate and in fear of Bhīmasena, released his weapon in rage with the intent 'Let there be no Pāṇḍava offspring.'
'Not so,' said Kṛṣṇa, restraining his words; and there Phālguna appeased that weapon with a counter-weapon.
The mutual curses exchanged among Drauṇi, Dvaipāyana, and others; and the water-rite, the offering of water to all the kings.
And the tale of Karṇa, son of Pṛthā, born in secret — this is here called the tenth parvan, the Sauptika.
Eighteen chapters are declared in this parvan by the great soul; the verse count stated here is eight hundred.
And seventy verses are declared, duly counted, in the parvan comprising the Sauptika and the Aiṣīka together, by the one of boundless intellect.
After this, they speak of the Strī Parva, which arises from grief — where the lamentation of the wives of heroes is remembered as most pitiable, and the rage and subsequent composure of Gāndhārī and Dhṛtarāṣṭra are told.
There they beheld those brave kṣatriyas who had met their fated end without retreating — their sons, brothers, and fathers slain on the battlefield.
There the greatly wise king, foremost among all upholders of dharma, performed the cremation of those royal bodies in accordance with scripture.
This eleventh parva has been described — deeply moving and great; twenty-seven chapters are enumerated in this parva.
Seven hundred and seventy-five verses are said to be in it by count; the tale of the Bhārata composed here by that great-souled author moves the minds of good people to distress and to tears.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
After this comes the twelfth parva, the Śānti Parva, which increases wisdom — where king Yudhiṣṭhira, overcome with despair after having caused the slaughter of his elders, brothers, sons, in-laws, and kinsmen, finds peace.
In the Śānti Parva, the duties spoken from the bed of arrows are expounded — those duties which kings who rightly desire knowledge of statecraft ought to know.
There too are the duties in times of distress, which illuminate the causes relating to time — knowing which a person attains complete omniscience; and the varied, extensively elaborated dharmas of liberation are also told there.
This twelfth parva, dear to wise people, has been designated; to be known in this parva, O ascetics, are three hundred and thirty-nine chapters.
Fourteen thousand five hundred and twenty-five verses are said to be enumerated in it.
After this is to be understood the excellent Anuśāsana Parva, where the Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira, restored to his natural disposition, hears the authoritative determination of dharma from Bhīṣma, the son of the Bhāgīrathī.
Here all of civil conduct oriented toward dharma and artha is taught in its entirety, as are the various categories of merit arising from diverse kinds of gifts.
Likewise the special distinctions of worthy recipients, the highest rule of giving, the practice of rules of conduct, and the supreme course of truth are all set forth.
This Anuśāsana, containing many narratives and supreme, is where Bhīṣma's attainment of heaven is celebrated.
This thirteenth parva, which establishes the conclusions of dharma, contains one hundred and forty-six chapters and six thousand seven hundred verses.
Then comes the fourteenth parva named the Aśvamedhika; it contains the incomparable tale of Saṃvarta and Marutta.
The acquisition of the treasury of gold is told there, as is the birth of Parīkṣit — who had previously been burned by the fire of a weapon and was brought back to life again by Kṛṣṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
During the ritual progress, the horse released for the Pāṇḍava is followed, and battles with intolerant princes here and there are narrated.
There the peril of Dhanaṃjaya in battle against Babhruvāhana, son of Citrāṅgadā, born from a daughter given as an heir, is depicted; and the tale of Nakula in the great aśvamedha sacrifice is also told.
Thus this Aśvamedhika Parva, full of great wonders, has been described; one hundred and thirty-three chapters are named in it.
Three thousand three hundred and twenty verses have been counted by the seer of truth.
After that is remembered the fifteenth parva called the Āśramavāsa, where the king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having renounced his kingdom, together with Gāndhārī, went to his hermitage, and Vidura went with him.
Seeing him set forth, the virtuous Pṛthā also followed then, having given up the kingdom of her son, devoted to serving her elder.
There the king saw his slain sons, grandsons, and other princes — heroes who had gone to another world — returned once more.
By the grace of the ṛṣi Kṛṣṇa (Dvaipāyana), having witnessed that incomparable marvel, he relinquished his grief and together with his wife attained the highest perfection.
There, taking refuge in dharma, Vidura attained a good state; and Saṃjaya too, that great minister, the learned son of Gavalgaṇa, the self-controlled one.
There dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira saw Nārada, and from Nārada heard of the great destruction of the Vṛṣṇis.
This parva named the Āśramavāsa, described above, full of great marvels, is reckoned to contain forty-two chapters.
One thousand five hundred and six verses have been counted by the seer of truth.
After this, learn of the terrible Mausala Parva, where those tiger-like men, who could endure the touch of weapons in battle, were crushed by the rod of brahmic power, near the salt sea.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Intoxicated with drink in a drinking hall, driven on by fate, they struck one another with thunderbolts in the form of eraka reeds.
There, having wrought the total destruction, those two — Rāma and Keśava — did not transgress the time that had come, the time of universal dissolution, the equalizer.
There Arjuna, that bull among men, came to Dvāravatī emptied of the Vṛṣṇis and fell into profound despondency and great anguish.
Having duly honored Śauri, the best of the Yadus, his own maternal uncle, he witnessed the great carnage of the Yadu heroes in the drinking hall.
He performed the funeral rites for the body of Vāsudeva and of great-souled Rāma, and for the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis.
Taking the old and the young, the people from Dvāravatī, he then witnessed in that terrible calamity the failure of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
He witnessed the unresponsiveness of all the divine weapons, the destruction of the wives of the Vṛṣṇis, and the impermanence of all powers.
Having seen all this and overcome with dispassion, urged by the words of Vyāsa, he approached the dharma-king and resolved upon renunciation.
Thus this Mausala Parva, the sixteenth, has been celebrated; eight chapters are named in it and three hundred verses.
After that is remembered the seventeenth, the Mahāprasthānika, where the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men, having renounced their kingdom, together with the goddess Draupadī, attained the highest perfection.
In it three chapters are spoken and one hundred and twenty verses have been counted by the seer of truth.
After that is to be known the Svarga Parva, divine and superhuman; five chapters are counted in this parva, O ascetics, and two hundred verses are reckoned.
In this way eighteen parvas have been described in full; and among the supplements, the Harivaṃśa and the Bhaviṣyat are celebrated.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All of this Bhārata has been narrated through the summary of the parvas; eighteen akṣauhiṇī armies came together out of desire for battle, and that great and terrible war lasted eighteen days.
A twice-born who might know the four Vedas together with their ancillaries and Upaniṣads, but does not know this epic tale — he would not truly be called learned.
Having heard this narrative, nothing else that is fit to be heard pleases — just as after hearing the song of the male cuckoo, the harsh cry of the crow grates.
From this finest of itihāsas, the intellects of poets are born, just as from the five elements the three worlds come into being.
The Purāṇa exists within the domain of this narrative, O twice-born, just as the four kinds of beings exist within the domain of the sky.
This narrative is the refuge of all the qualities of action, just as the diverse activities of the mind are the refuge of all the senses.
Without taking refuge in this narrative, no story exists on earth — just as the sustaining of the body without taking recourse to food.
This narrative is what all the foremost poets live by, as servants seeking advancement live by a nobly born lord.
This immeasurable text issuing from the lips of Dvaipāyana — holy, purifying, sin-removing, and auspicious — whoever thoroughly studies the Bhārata as it is recited: what need has such a one of bathing in the waters of Puṣkara?
This supreme narrative of great meaning, here set forth in this great summary of parvas — hearing it first, people enter it easily, as one crosses the vast salt sea with a vessel.
The Sūta said: Janamejaya, son of Parīkṣit, was engaged in a long sacrifice at Kurukṣetra together with his brothers. His three brothers were Śrutasena, Ugrasena, and Bhīmasena.
While they were seated at that sacrifice, a dog born of Saramā came there; struck by the brothers of Janamejaya, it went crying to its mother.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His mother, seeing him crying, said: 'Why do you weep? By whom have you been struck?'
Thus addressed, he replied to his mother: 'I was struck by the brothers of Janamejaya.'
His mother replied to him: 'Clearly you must have done some wrong there, for which you were struck.'
He replied to her again: 'I have done no wrong at all — I did not look at the oblations, nor did I lick them.'
Hearing this, his mother Saramā, afflicted by grief for her son, went to that sacrifice where Janamejaya with his brothers was engaged in the long sacrifice.
He was addressed there by her in anger: 'My son has done no wrong — for what reason was he struck? Because he was struck though he had done no harm, an unseen fear will come upon you.'
Thus addressed by Saramā, the divine dog, Janamejaya was greatly agitated and distressed.
When that sacrifice was completed, he returned to Hāstinapura and, seeking a suitable purohita, made great effort, thinking: 'One who can cleanse my sin.'
One day, Janamejaya son of Parīkṣit, while out hunting, saw a hermitage in a certain district of his own realm.
There a certain seer named Śrutaśravā dwelt; his beloved son, named Somaśravā, also lived there.
Janamejaya, son of Parīkṣit, approached that son and solicited him for the office of purohita.
He bowed to that ṛṣi and said: 'Blessed one, let this your son be my purohita.'
Thus addressed, he replied: 'O Janamejaya, this son of mine was born of a serpent woman; he is a great ascetic, endowed with Vedic study, sustained by the power of my austerity, having grown in her womb which drank my seed. He is capable of cleansing all your sins — save for a deed against Mahādeva. But he has one secret vow: if any brahmin should ask him for anything, he must give it to that person. If you can accept this, then take him.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus urged, Janamejaya replied to him: 'Blessed one, so it shall be.'
Taking that purohita with him and returning, he said to his brothers: 'I have chosen this preceptor; whatever he says must be done without question.'
Thus instructed by him, his brothers complied. Having so enjoined his brothers, he set out toward Takṣaśilā and brought that region under his control.
Meanwhile, there was a certain seer named Āyoda Dhaumya. He had three disciples: Upamanyu, Āruṇi, and Veda.
He sent one disciple, Āruṇi of Pāñcāla, saying: 'Go and stop up the breach in the field embankment.'
Thus instructed by his teacher, Āruṇi of Pāñcāla went there but was unable to stop up that breach in the field embankment.
Struggling and finding no solution, he thought: 'Let it be — I will do it thus.'
He lay down there in the breach of the field embankment, and with him lying there, the water stopped.
Then one day the teacher Āyoda Dhaumya asked his disciples: 'Where has Āruṇi of Pāñcāla gone?'
They replied: 'He was sent by you yourself, saying: Go and stop up the breach in the field embankment.'
Thus addressed, he said to those disciples: 'Then let us all go to where he is.'
Going there, he called out to summon him: 'Ho, Āruṇi of Pāñcāla, where are you, my dear? Come here!'
Hearing the teacher's words, Āruṇi instantly rose from that field embankment, went to the teacher, and addressed him thus: 'Here I am, venerable sir — I had lain down in the embankment to stop the water that could not be restrained from flowing out. The moment I heard your revered voice, I broke through the embankment and have come to you. I salute you, reverend one; command me — what shall I do?'
The teacher said to him: 'Since you broke open the field embankment and rose from it, you shall henceforth be known by the name Uddālaka.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Blessed by the teacher, he was told: 'Because you have carried out my words, you shall attain the highest good, all the Vedas shall shine forth in your mind, and all the scriptures of dharma shall be manifest to you.'
Thus addressed by the teacher, he departed to the place he desired.
Now there was another pupil of that same Āyoda Dhaumya, by the name of Upamanyu.
The teacher sent him out, saying: 'Dear Upamanyu, go and tend the cows.'
Obeying the teacher's instruction, he tended the cows. Each day, having tended them until evening, he would return and stand before the teacher and make his obeisance.
The teacher saw that he was well-fed and spoke to him: 'Dear Upamanyu, by what means do you sustain yourself? You are indeed quite stout.'
He replied to the teacher: 'I sustain myself by begging alms.'
The teacher replied to him: 'You must not eat the alms you collect without first offering them to me.'
Agreeing with 'so be it,' he went again to tend the cows, and returning after tending them, he stood before the teacher just as before and made his obeisance.
The teacher, seeing him still just as stout, said: 'Dear Upamanyu, I take all your alms without remainder — by what means do you now sustain yourself?'
Thus addressed by the teacher, he replied: 'After offering the first portion to you, reverend sir, I beg a second round, and by that I sustain myself.'
The teacher replied to him: 'This is not proper conduct toward a teacher. By doing so you obstruct the livelihood of others as well — behaving thus you are greedy.'
Accepting this with 'so be it,' he tended the cows, and after tending them he came again to the teacher's house and stood before the teacher and made his obeisance.
The teacher, seeing him still just as stout, said again: 'I take all your alms, and you beg no second round — yet you are stout. By what means do you sustain yourself?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He replied to the teacher: 'Sir, I sustain myself on the milk of these cows.'
The teacher replied to him: 'It is not right for you to consume the milk — I have not given you permission for that.'
Accepting this with a promise of 'so be it,' he tended the cows and came again to the teacher's house and stood before the teacher and made his obeisance.
The teacher saw him still stout and said to him: 'You eat no alms, you beg no second round, you drink no milk — yet you are stout. By what means do you sustain yourself?'
Thus addressed, he replied to the teacher: 'Sir, I drink the foam that these calves spit out while suckling at their mothers' udders.'
The teacher replied to him: 'Out of compassion for you, these calves spit out a greater quantity of foam. Even so, by doing this you obstruct the calves' nourishment — behaving thus you have no right to drink even the foam.'
Having promised 'so be it,' he tended the cows without any food. Thus forbidden, he ate no alms, begged no second round, drank no milk, and took no foam.
One day, tormented by hunger in the forest, he ate the leaves of the arka plant.
The arka leaves he had eaten — caustic, pungent, and hot in their digestion — damaged his eyes and he became blind. Wandering about even in his blindness, he fell into a well.
When Upamanyu did not return, the teacher said to the other pupils: 'I have forbidden Upamanyu in every way — surely he is angry and that is why he has not come back; he has been gone a long time.'
Saying this, he went to the forest and called out for Upamanyu: 'Upamanyu, dear child, where are you?'
Hearing that summons from the teacher, he called back loudly: 'Here I am, teacher — I have fallen into a well!'
The teacher said to him: 'How did you come to fall into a well?'
He replied: 'After eating the leaves of the arka plant I became blind, and that is how I fell into the well.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The teacher said to him: 'Praise the Aśvins — those two divine physicians will restore your sight.'
Thus instructed by the teacher, he began to praise the two divine Aśvins with words and Rigvedic hymns.
I praise with my voice those two who go before all, who were born first, who shine with wondrous light — the blazing ones, boundless, divine, with beautiful wings, pure, glorious in their chariot, who dwell over all the worlds.
Golden birds, companions in battle, the Nāsatyas — the Dasras, fair-nosed, bearing the banner of victory — swiftly weaving brightness, with beautiful loom-work, wrapping around the dark Vivasvat.
The quail that had been seized by the power of the eagle — the Aśvins released her for good fortune; those two of beautiful form, bowing with their wondrous power, led up the dawn-red cows, the very best.
Sixty cows and three hundred milch-cows give birth to a single calf, and they milk him — distributed in various herds, arranged for a single milking — and those two Aśvins milk the warm oblation worthy of praise.
Seven hundred spokes rest upon a single hub; twenty other spokes are set in the felloes — the ageless wheel turns without a rim; with their wondrous power the Aśvins anoint the people.
One wheel turns with twelve spokes, six felloes, six hubs, one axle — the vessel of immortality in which all the gods are suspended on high — let not those two Aśvins who release it be downcast.
The Aśvins, having become more powerful than Indra with nectar, hid him; the Aśvins, lord of the slave woman — splitting the mountain and bringing forth the cow, that day of rain brought the fame of Vala's undoing.
You two give birth to the ten directions at the fore; at the common summit they part on their chariots — in the wake of their going the seers follow after; gods and men walk upon the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You two fashion colors in all their forms; they who dwell over all the worlds — their very rays too go following after; gods and men walk upon the earth.
We invoke you two, the Nāsatya Aśvins, and the garland of the lotus that you wear — you two Nāsatyas, growing strong wrapped in immortality; apart from the gods, she brings that forth by her foremost step.
May those two young ones receive the embryo in the mouth; the dead spirit brings it forth by the forefoot — the embryo, just born, devours the mother; those two Aśvins, release the cows to live.
Thus praised by him, the two Aśvins came and, being pleased, said to him: 'Here is a cake for you — eat it.'
Thus addressed, he replied: 'You two speak no untruth — yet I dare not eat this cake without first presenting it to my teacher.'
Then the two Aśvins said to him: 'Your teacher too praised us in exactly this way before you, and a cake was given by us who were pleased, and he ate it without presenting it to his teacher — you too should do just as the teacher did.'
Thus addressed, he replied once more: 'I respectfully decline, O Aśvins — I dare not consume it without presenting it to my teacher.'
The two Aśvins, being pleased, said to him: 'Well done — through this devoted service to your teacher, your teeth which were of black iron shall become of gold; you shall regain your sight and you shall attain the highest good.'
Thus spoken to by the Aśvins and having regained his sight, he came to the teacher's presence, paid homage to him, and reported everything; and the teacher was pleased with him.
He told him: 'Just as the Aśvins have said, so shall you attain the highest good, and all the Vedas shall shine forth in your mind.'
Such was the testing of Upamanyu as well.
Now there was another pupil of that same Āyoda Dhaumya, by the name of Veda.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The teacher instructed him: 'Dear Veda, you should stay here — you must spend some time serving me in my household. It will be for your highest good.'
