Agreeing with 'so be it,' he dwelt in the teacher's household for a long time wholly devoted to serving the teacher — like a draught ox, constantly yoked to the teacher's burdens, enduring the hardships of cold and heat, hunger and thirst, never resistant in any matter.
After a long time the teacher became fully satisfied, and from that satisfaction he bestowed upon him the highest good and omniscience. Such was the testing of Veda as well.
With the teacher's leave, having completed his residence at the teacher's house, he returned to the householder's stage of life. Even while he was dwelling in his own home, he too came to have three pupils.
He gave the pupils no instruction at all — neither 'do this task' nor 'attend upon the teacher' — for being well acquainted himself with the hardships of life in a teacher's house, he was unwilling to burden his pupils with such affliction.
In the course of time, the two Kṣatriyas Janamejaya and Pauṣya came to Veda the Brahmin and chose him as their officiating priest.
When he was once setting out on account of his priestly duties, he commissioned a pupil named Uttaṅka: 'Dear Uttaṅka, whatever may be lacking in my household — I wish that you see to it that nothing falls short.'
Having thus instructed Uttaṅka, Veda departed on his journey.
So Uttaṅka, devoted to service of the teacher and carrying out the teacher's command, continued to dwell at the teacher's household.
While he was staying there, the teacher's wives, gathered together, called him and spoke to him: 'Your teacher's wife is in her fertile season and the teacher is away — see to it that this season of hers does not pass barren; she is distressed.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed, he replied to those women: 'I cannot perform this improper act on the word of women — the teacher has not instructed me to do what ought not to be done.'
After some time the teacher came back home from that journey. Learning everything that had transpired — the full account — he was pleased.
He said to him: 'Dear Uttaṅka, what can I do to please you? You have served me in accordance with dharma, and therefore mutual affection between us has grown; I give you leave to go — you shall attain all accomplishment.'
Thus addressed, he replied: 'What shall I do to please you?' — for thus it is said:
He who speaks contrary to dharma, and he who asks contrary to dharma —
— one of those two perishes and the other acquires enmity. Therefore I, having received your leave, wish to bring you the teacher's gift that you desire.
Thus addressed, the teacher replied: 'Dear Uttaṅka, stay here for the present.'
One day Uttaṅka said to that teacher: 'Command me, reverend sir — what shall I bring as teacher's gift to please you?'
The teacher replied to him: 'Dear Uttaṅka, you press me many times saying "let me bring the teacher's gift." So go, enter here and ask the teacher's wife what you should bring — whatever she tells you, bring that.'
Thus instructed by the teacher, he asked the teacher's wife: 'Revered lady, I have been given leave by the teacher to go home — I wish to depart free of debt by first bringing the teacher's gift that you desire. So please command me: what shall I bring as the teacher's gift?'
The teacher's wife, thus addressed, replied to Uttaṅka: 'Go to King Pauṣya and beg from him — the earrings fastened on his Kṣatriya queen, bring those to me. The auspicious day falls four days from now; I wish to serve the Brahmins wearing them, adorned with those earrings — arrange for them on that day.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus instructed by the teacher's wife, Uttaṅka set out. As he was going along the road, he saw an enormous bull, and mounted upon it a man of equally enormous size.
That man addressed Uttaṅka: 'Uttaṅka, eat this dung of the bull.'
Thus spoken to, he was unwilling.
The man said to him again: 'Eat it, Uttaṅka — do not hesitate. Your teacher ate it before you as well.'
Thus addressed, he said 'very well,' and after eating the dung and drinking the urine of the bull, Uttaṅka set out toward the place where the Kṣatriya Pauṣya was.
Approaching him, Uttaṅka found him seated. Coming near, he greeted him with blessings and said: 'I have come to you as a petitioner.'
Pauṣya, paying him reverence, replied: 'Reverend sir, I am indeed Pauṣya — what may I do for you?'
Uttaṅka spoke to him: 'I have come seeking the earrings for the sake of my teacher. Those earrings that the queen wears — you ought to give them to me.'
Pauṣya replied to him: 'Enter the inner apartments and ask the queen herself.'
Told thus, he entered the inner apartments but did not see the queen.
He said to Pauṣya again: 'It is not right of you to deal with me falsely. The queen is not present in your inner apartments — I do not see her.'
Pauṣya, addressed thus, replied to him: 'Consider first whether you are in a state of having eaten without performing the ritual rinsing. The queen cannot be seen by one who has eaten and is impure; being a devoted wife, she does not come before the sight of one who is unclean.'
Addressed thus, Uttaṅka reflected and said: 'It is true — I did touch water while in a state of ritual impurity after eating, since I was walking hurriedly.'
Pauṣya replied to him: 'That is indeed so — water touched while walking does not count as the proper ritual contact; it must be done while seated still.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Uttaṅka, saying 'so be it,' sat facing east; with hands, feet, and face thoroughly washed, he performed the water-ritual with water that was soundless and pleasing to the heart — drinking three times and wiping twice — and then touched the orifices of the body with water. He entered the inner apartments and beheld the queen.
And she, upon seeing Uttaṅka, rose to receive him, offered him reverence and said: 'Welcome, venerable one. Command me — what shall I do?'
He said to her: 'These earrings have been requested by me for the sake of my teacher — please bestow them.'
She, pleased by that sincerity of his, thinking 'this man is a worthy recipient and one whose request cannot be refused,' removed the earrings and gave them to him.
And she said to him: 'Takṣaka, the king of the serpents, covets these earrings — carry them away with vigilance.'
Addressed thus, he replied to the queen: 'Be at ease, my lady. Takṣaka, the king of the serpents, is not able to assail me.'
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the queen, he returned to where Pauṣya was.
Seeing him, he said: 'I am pleased, O Pauṣya.'
Pauṣya replied to him: 'Reverend sir, a worthy recipient is encountered only after a long time, and you are a guest endowed with virtues. I shall perform the ancestral śrāddha ceremony — please wait a moment.'
Uttaṅka replied to him: 'The moment is already set for me — I wish whatever food is readily available to be served quickly.'
He said 'so be it' and fed him with whatever food was at hand.
But Uttaṅka, seeing the food was cold and contained a hair, considered it impure and said to Pauṣya: 'Since you give me impure food, you shall become blind.'
Pauṣya replied to him: 'Since you too condemn food that is not defiled, you shall be without offspring.'
Then Pauṣya proved the impure state of the food.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, the food having been brought by a woman with loosened hair, and being found to contain hair and to be cold and impure, he sought to appease Uttaṅka: 'Reverend sir, through ignorance this food was brought to you with hair in it and cold. I beg your forgiveness — may I not become blind.'
Uttaṅka replied to him: 'I do not speak falsely — you shall become blind and before long become sighted again. And let the curse you have uttered upon me also not come to pass.'
Pauṣya replied to him: 'I am not able to take back the curse, for my anger has not yet subsided. Moreover, do you not know this truth —'
'The heart of a brahmin is soft as butter, yet on his tongue is placed a razor sharp-edged. The opposite holds for the warrior: his speech is not soft as butter, but his heart is keen-edged.'
'Thus being so, I am not able to undo that curse, for my heart is sharp. Go your way.'
Uttaṅka replied to him: 'I have been shown the impure state of the food by you and have been propitiated. Yet earlier you said to me: "Since you condemn food that is not defiled, you shall be without offspring." Since the food was indeed defiled, this curse of mine shall not take effect.'
Saying 'Let us now complete our task,' Uttaṅka departed, taking the earrings with him.
On the path he saw a naked mendicant approaching, appearing and disappearing again and again. Then Uttaṅka set those earrings down on the ground and went in search of water.
In that interval, the mendicant swiftly approached, seized the earrings and fled. Uttaṅka pursued and caught hold of him. The mendicant, abandoning that form and assuming the form of Takṣaka, suddenly entered a great burrow that opened in the earth.
Entering the realm of the serpents, he went to his own abode. Uttaṅka followed him through that same burrow, and having entered, he praised the serpents with these verses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Those serpents who are kings descended from Airāvata, resplendent in assembly, like rain-clouds with lightning, stirred by the wind —'
'— beautiful and ugly alike, with dappled earrings, those born of Airāvata shone like the sun in the vault of heaven.'
'Many are the serpent-paths along the northern bank of the Gaṅgā — who would wish to move through the army of the sun's rays without Airāvata?'
'Eight hundred and eighty hundreds, and twenty thousands — so many multitudes of serpents proceed forth whenever Dhṛtarāṣṭra stirs.'
'Those who approach him and those who have gone far beyond — to the elder brothers of Airāvata I have made my obeisance.'
'Him whose dwelling was always in Kurukṣetra and in the Khāṇḍava forest — that son of Kadrū, Takṣaka, I now praise for the sake of the earrings.'
'Takṣaka and Aśvasena, those two who are constant companions, dwell in Kurukṣetra along the river Ikṣumatī.'
'The youngest-born of Takṣaka, known as Śrutasena, who is destined to eclipse great glory while seeking the foremost rank among the serpents — to that great-souled one I shall always give reverence.'
Even as he praised the serpents thus, when he still did not obtain the earrings, he then saw two women who, having placed cloth on a loom, were weaving fabric.
And in that loom were black and white threads. He also saw a wheel being turned by six youths, and he saw a handsome man.
He praised all of them with these verses of sacred incantation.
'Three hundred are set in the middle of it, and sixty move perpetually in this fixed wheel — joined in twenty-four segments — which the six youths turn.'
'And this loom of universal form — two young women weaving, perpetually drawing out threads, turning the black and white ones unceasingly — all beings and all the worlds are woven upon it.'
'The bearer of the thunderbolt, the protector of the worlds, the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of Namuci — that great-souled one who wears dark garments, who distinguishes truth from falsehood in the world —'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'— who has mounted the ancient embryo of the waters, the horse, whose vehicle is the fire of Vaiśvānara — homage always to him, the lord of the universe, the ruler of the three worlds, the destroyer of citadels.'
Then that man said to him: 'I am pleased with you by this hymn of praise. What that is dear to you shall I do?'
He said to him: 'May the serpents come under my control.'
That man said to him again: 'Blow into the lower aperture of this horse.'
He blew into the lower aperture of the horse. Then, as the horse was blown into, from all its orifices flames of fire with billowing smoke burst forth.
By those flames the serpent world was fumigated.
Then Takṣaka, in great agitation and terrified by the power of the fire, seized the earrings and swiftly emerged from his own abode and said to Uttaṅka: 'Please accept these earrings, reverend sir.'
Uttaṅka received those earrings. Having received them he reflected: 'Today is the auspicious day of my teacher's wife, and I have come from far away — how indeed shall I reach her in time?'
Then, even as he was thus reflecting, that man said to him: 'Uttaṅka, mount this horse — it will bring you to your teacher's household in a moment.'
Saying 'so be it,' he mounted that horse and returned to his teacher's household. The teacher's wife, having bathed and sitting with her hair being dressed, was about to resolve in her mind to curse Uttaṅka since he had not yet come.
Then Uttaṅka entered, paid his respects to the teacher's wife, and offered her those earrings.
She replied to him: 'Uttaṅka, you have arrived at the right place and time. Welcome, dear child. You are only barely not cursed by me. Good fortune attends you — may you attain fulfillment.'
Then Uttaṅka paid reverence to his teacher. The teacher replied to him: 'Welcome, dear Uttaṅka. Why were you delayed so long?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Uttaṅka replied to his teacher: 'Sir, an obstruction was caused in this undertaking by Takṣaka, king of the serpents — he carried me off to the serpent world.'
'There I saw two women who, having placed cloth upon a loom, were weaving, with black and white threads in that loom — what does that signify?'
'There too I saw a wheel with twelve spokes, and six youths turning it — what does that signify as well?'
'And I also saw a man — who then is he?'
'And a horse of extraordinary size — who is that also?'
'While going along the path I saw a great bull, and a man was mounted upon it. That man addressed me with courtesy: "Uttaṅka, eat the dung of this bull — your teacher has also eaten it." Then, upon his word, I consumed the dung of that bull. I wish to know what all of this means as explained by you.'
Addressed thus, the teacher replied: 'Those two women are Dhātā and Vidhātā; those black and white threads are night and day.'
'That wheel with twelve spokes that the six youths turn — those six are the seasons, and the wheel is the year. The man is Parjanya, the rain-god; the horse is Agni, the fire.'
'That bull you saw as you went along the path — that is Airāvata, king of the serpents. He who was mounted upon it is Indra. And that dung of the bull that you consumed — that is ambrosia, the nectar of immortality.'
'It is by that that you were not destroyed in that serpent abode. And Indra is also my friend.'
'By his grace you have returned having obtained the earrings. So, gentle one, you may go — I give you leave. You shall attain great good fortune.'
Given leave by his teacher, Uttaṅka, filled with anger and determined to retaliate against Takṣaka, set out for the city of Hāstinapura.
That foremost brahmin Uttaṅka, reaching Hāstinapura before long, came to meet King Janamejaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He saw him just returned from Takṣaśilā, undefeated, fully victorious, and attended on all sides by his ministers.
Having first offered him the customary blessings of victory, he addressed the king at the proper moment with words adorned with eloquent speech.
'While there is another duty to be done, O best of kings, you attend to something altogether different, as if out of childishness, O foremost of monarchs.'
Addressed thus by the brahmin, King Janamejaya replied, his mind serene, having duly honoured that sage.
'I protect my own warrior-dharma through the protection of these subjects. Or tell me, what is to be done, O lord among brahmins — today I am eager to hear your words.'
Addressed thus by that best of kings, the foremost brahmin, the most excellent among the meritorious, spoke to the king of undaunted spirit concerning the very duty that was the king's own.
'O lord among lords of men, retaliate against that serpent of evil soul, Takṣaka, by whom your father was slain.'
'And I consider this the proper time for the action enjoined by sacred ordinance. Therefore go, O king, and perform the act of vengeance for that great-souled father of yours.'
'For that king, though guiltless, was bitten by that one of wicked inner soul and passed away to the five elements, like a tree struck by a thunderbolt.'
Takṣaka, the vilest of serpents, swollen with the arrogance of power, acted wickedly — that sinful one who bit your father.
That evil-doer slew the king who was equal to the immortals and guardian of the royal-seer lineage, and also turned back Kaśyapa.
You should burn that sinner in the blazing fire of the oblation-carrier, O great king — for that very purpose is the serpent sacrifice ordained for you.
In this way you shall have fully avenged your father, O king, and you will have done something exceedingly dear to me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O protector of the earth, great king, O sinless one — an obstacle was made to my task by that evil-souled one, while I was performing my duty toward my teacher.
Having heard this, the king became furious at Takṣaka — kindled by the oblation of Uttaṅka's words as fire is kindled by clarified butter.
Deeply grieved, the king then asked his ministers — even in the very presence of Uttaṅka — concerning his father's passage to heaven.
That lord of kings was overwhelmed with grief and sorrow at that very moment when he heard from Uttaṅka of his father's fate.
Ugraśravās, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, a sūta skilled in the Purāṇas, attended upon the seers who had come together at the twelve-year sacrifice of the householder Śaunaka in the Naimiṣa forest.
That one well-versed in the Purāṇas, experienced in purāṇic lore, addressed them with joined palms: "What do you wish to hear? What shall I recite?"
The seers said: "O Lomaharṣaṇa, we shall ask you the highest matter, and you shall narrate to us who are eager to listen the connected narrative — but first, the venerable Śaunaka is presiding over the fire-sanctuary."
He knows the divine stories, the tales of gods and demons, the stories of men, serpents, and gandharvas — he knows them all in every detail.
And he, O sūta, is the learned head of the assembly, a brahmin, capable, firm in vows, wise, and a master in both the śāstra and the āraṇyaka.
He is a speaker of truth, devoted to tranquility, an ascetic, steadfast in his vows — he is deserving of reverence from all of us; let him be waited upon first.
When that teacher is seated on his most honored seat, then you shall narrate whatever that best of twice-born men asks of you.
The sūta said: "So be it — when that great-souled teacher is seated and has asked me, I shall narrate the sacred stories that touch upon various subjects."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That foremost brahmin then, having completed all his duties in proper order, having satisfied the gods with hymns and the ancestors with water, arrived there.
There the accomplished brahmin-seers were seated, firm in their vows, gathered at the sacrificial enclosure, with the sūta's son at their fore.
When the officiating priests and the assembly members had taken their seats, the householder Śaunaka seated himself and then spoke thus.
Śaunaka said: "My dear son, your father formerly studied the entire Purāṇa — have you too studied all of that, O Lomaharṣaṇa?"
"For in the Purāṇa are told divine stories and the primordial lineages of the wise — those were formerly heard by us from your father."
"Among those, I wish first to hear the lineage of Bhṛgu — narrate that story; we are fit and ready to hear from you."
The sūta said: "What was formerly studied thoroughly by the great-souled ones headed by the brahmin Vaiśaṃpāyana, and what was formerly narrated by them —
"What was studied by my father and in turn by me in full — hear first that lineage which is honored by the gods together with Indra, Agni, and the Marut hosts: the foremost lineage of the Bhṛgus, O delight of Bhṛgu."
"O brahmin, O great sage, I shall recite for you this lineage of Bhārgava accompanied by its narrative and grounded in purāṇic tradition."
The deeply beloved son of Bhṛgu was Cyavana of the Bhārgava line; Cyavana's heir was the righteous one named Pramati; and from Pramati was born a son in Ghṛtācī named Ruru.
From Ruru too was born a son who had crossed to the further shore of the Vedas — the righteous-souled Śunaka, born of Pramadvarā — your own great-grandfather.
He was an ascetic, illustrious, learned, the foremost knower of Brahman, most righteous, a speaker of truth, disciplined, with controlled senses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śaunaka said: "O son of the sūta, how the name 'Cyavana' became renowned for that great-souled Bhārgava — tell me that, as I ask."
The sūta said: "The dearly beloved wife of Bhṛgu was renowned as Pulomā; in her a child was conceived, born of Bhṛgu's seed."
"While that embryo was growing in Pulomā, O foremost of the Bhṛgu line — at that time, in the illustrious one's righteous wife who shared his disposition —"
"When Bhṛgu, the foremost of the upholders of dharma, had gone out to bathe, a rakṣasa came to his hermitage and approached Pulomā."
"Entering the hermitage and seeing the blameless wife of Bhṛgu, he was seized by desire and became bewildered, losing his senses."
"The beautiful-looking Pulomā then received that rakṣasa as a guest with forest offerings of fruits, roots, and the like."
"But that rakṣasa, O brahmin, tormented by desire upon seeing her, rejoiced there, wishing to abduct that blameless woman."
"Then he saw Jātavedas blazing in the fire-shrine; the rakṣasa then asked the blazing purifier Fire —"
"'Tell me, O Agni, whose wife is this? You have been truly asked — you are Truth itself; speak truth to me who asks, O purifier.'"
"'This fair-complexioned woman was first chosen by me for the purpose of marriage, yet afterward her father gave her to Bhṛgu, that doer of untruth.'"
"'If this fine-hipped woman is indeed Bhṛgu's wife who has come here alone, then tell me truly — I wish to take her away from this hermitage.'"
"'For rage burns as though scorching my heart today, since Bhṛgu took her — this slender-waisted one who was formerly my wife.'"
"Having thus addressed the blazing Jātavedas, the rakṣasa, uncertain about Bhṛgu's wife, asked again and again."
"'You, O Agni, dwell eternally within all beings as a witness to their virtuous and sinful deeds — speak truthfully, O wise one; utter words of truth.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'If this is she — my former wife, taken by Bhṛgu that doer of untruth — then you ought to tell me truly.'"
"'Having heard from you that she is Bhṛgu's wife, I shall carry her away from this hermitage — O Jātavedas, even as you look on, speak my true words to me.'"
"Hearing those words of his, the seven-flamed Fire was deeply troubled, fearful both of falsehood and of Bhṛgu's curse, and spoke softly —"
The sūta said: "Then, O brahmin, having heard the words of Agni, that rakṣasa seized her, taking the form of a boar and swift as mind and wind."
"Then that child dwelling in the womb — O foremost of the Bhṛgu line — fell from his mother's womb in anger, and by that falling he became known as Cyavana."
"Seeing him, blazing with the radiance of the sun, fallen from his mother's womb, that rakṣasa was reduced to ashes and fell, releasing her."
"Taking him, the beautiful-hipped Pulomā — the delight of Bhṛgu — O brahmin, walked on with Cyavana of the Bhārgava line, faint with sorrow."
"Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all worlds, saw her — Bhṛgu's blameless wife weeping, her eyes filled with tears — and the venerable grandfather Brahmā comforted that daughter-in-law."
"From the drops of her tears a great river flowed forth, following the path of that illustrious wife of Bhṛgu as she walked."
"Seeing that river flowing along her path, the grandfather of the worlds then gave that river its name — calling it Vadhūsarā — as it flowed toward Cyavana's hermitage."
"In this way the mighty Cyavana was born as the son of Bhṛgu; the father saw Cyavana there, and also that illustrious woman."
"Then the enraged Bhṛgu asked his wife Pulomā: 'By whom were you here pointed out to that rakṣasa who wished to abduct you? For that rakṣasa did not know you, my fair-smiling wife.'"
"'Tell me that — for I wish today to curse him in my anger. Who does not fear my curse? Whose transgression is this?'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Pulomā said: 'It was by Agni, O venerable one, that I was disclosed to that rakṣasa; thereupon the rakṣasa carried me off even as I cried out like an osprey.'"
"'I was freed by the radiance of this your son; that rakṣasa, reduced to ashes, fell releasing me.'"
The sūta said: "Having heard this from Pulomā, Bhṛgu was seized with utmost fury and, thoroughly enraged, cursed Agni: 'You shall become the eater of all things!'"
The sūta said: "Cursed by Bhṛgu, the fire became angry and spoke: 'What rash deed have you done now, O brahmin?'"
"'For one striving in dharma, speaking truth impartially, when asked, I spoke truth — what transgression is mine in this?'"
"'For a witness who, when asked, knowingly gives false testimony destroys seven of his own ancestors as well as seven in the opposing family.'"
"'And one who knows the truth of a matter yet does not speak when knowing — he too is tainted by that very sin; of this there is no doubt.'"
"'I too am capable of cursing you, yet brahmins are to be honored by me — even though knowing, I shall explain clearly to you; understand this.'"
"'By my power, dividing myself manifold, I dwell in many forms — in the agnihotras, in the sattras, in the ritual acts, and in the sacrifices.'"
"'Whatever oblation is offered into me according to the ordinance prescribed by the Vedas — by that the gods and ancestors become satisfied.'"
"'Water constitutes all the hosts of gods; water likewise constitutes the hosts of ancestors; the new-moon and full-moon rites belong to gods together with ancestors.'"
"'Therefore the gods are the ancestors and the ancestors too are gods; they are worshipped as one and also separately at the sacred occasions.'"
"'Whatever the gods and ancestors constantly offer into me — thus I am known as the mouth of the thirty gods and of the ancestors.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'On the new-moon day the ancestors, and on the full-moon day the gods, are invoked through my mouth alone and consume the offered oblation — how then shall I become the all-devourer and yet remain their mouth?'"
"Having reflected thus, Fire then withdrew himself from the agnihotras of the twice-born, from the sacrifices and from the satra rites."
"Without the oṃkāra and the vaṣaṭkāra, bereft of the svadhā and svāhā — without Agni, all creatures were then in deep distress."
"Then the seers, greatly agitated, went to the gods and spoke: 'O sinless ones, because of Agni's disappearance and the breakdown of rites, the three worlds are thrown into confusion — ordain what must be done here so that no time may pass in vain.'"
"Then the seers and the gods, approaching Brahmā, reported to him the curse upon Agni and the withdrawal of the ritual acts."
"'O greatly fortunate one, Agni has been cursed by Bhṛgu for another reason — how can he, who has become the mouth of the gods, the first receiver of the share of sacrifice, the consumer of oblations in all the worlds, now become the all-devourer?'"
"Hearing those words of theirs, the creator of the worlds summoned Agni and spoke a gentle word to him, the eternal nurturer of all beings."
"'You are here the maker and the very end of all the worlds; you uphold the three worlds and you set the ritual acts in motion — O lord of the world, act in such a way that the rites may not be cut off.'"
"'Why have you become so confused, O consumer of oblations, when you are the lord? You are the purifier in the world and you pervade all beings.'"
"'You shall not become the all-devourer with your whole body, O blazing one — those flames of yours that take up fuel shall burn everything.'"
"'Just as everything touched by the rays of the sun is perceived as pure, so everything burnt by your flames shall become pure.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'Therefore, O Agni, you are the great radiance that has issued forth from its own nature — by your own splendor fulfill the sage's curse as truth, O mighty one, and receive into your mouth the oblation that is the share of the gods and of yourself.'"
"So be it," replied Fire to the grandsire Brahmā, and went forth to carry out the command of the supreme lord.
The divine sages departed joyfully as they had come, and the rishis resumed all their rites as before.
The gods in heaven rejoiced, as did all the assemblies of living beings on earth, and Fire, his taint removed, attained the highest delight.
Such is this ancient tale born of Fire's curse — the destruction of Pulomā and the birth of Cyavana.
The Sūta said: That Cyavana of Bhṛgu's line, O brahmin, begot upon Sukanyā a son, the great-souled Pramati of blazing energy.
Pramati begot upon Ghṛtācī a son named Ruru; and Ruru begot upon Pramadvara a son named Śunaka.
Of that Ruru of great splendor, O brahmin, I shall recount the entire story in full — hear it without omission.
There was in former times a great rishi endowed with austerity and knowledge, known by the name Sthūlakeśa, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
In that very time, O brahmin-rishi, the king of the gandharvas known as Viśvāvasu had fathered a child upon Menakā.
Then the apsara Menakā, O son of Bhṛgu's line, abandoned that embryo in due time near the hermitage of Sthūlakeśa.
Having abandoned the embryo on the riverbank, she departed; the infant girl shone with the beauty of a celestial child, blazing as it were with radiant glory.
The great rishi Sthūlakeśa, that splendid one, saw her abandoned on the riverbank, alone, bereft of kin.
Seeing that girl, Sthūlakeśa, best of twice-born men, that foremost sage, filled with compassion, took her in and nurtured her; and she of lovely form grew up beautifully in his hermitage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
She was the most excellent among women, endowed with beauty and virtue in every way; and so the great rishi gave her the name Pramadvara.
Ruru, the righteous-souled one, on seeing Pramadvara at that hermitage, found his heart overtaken by the god of love.
Then that scion of Bhṛgu's line had his friends convey his wish to his father, and Pramati, having heard, went himself to the illustrious Sthūlakeśa.
Then the father gave that maiden Pramadvara to Ruru, having first fixed the wedding for the auspicious asterism presided over by Bhaga.
Then, a few days before the wedding arrived, that fair-complexioned maiden was playing with her companions,
when she did not notice a serpent lying asleep stretched across her path; she stepped upon it, driven by fate toward death.
The serpent, urged on by the law of time, drove its venom-smeared fangs deep into her body while she was careless.
Bitten, she instantly fell to the ground, her senses gone, her life departed — yet even lifeless her form was supremely beautiful to behold.
She lay upon the earth as if asleep, tormented by the serpent's venom; the slender-waisted one became even more heart-ravishing than before.
Her father and the other ascetics saw her fallen on the ground, her lotus-radiant form convulsed.
Then all the best of twice-born men gathered filled with compassion — Svastyatreya, Mahajanu, Kuśika, Shankhamekhala,
Bharadvaja, Kaunakutsa, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Gautama, Pramati with his son, and other forest-dwellers as well.
Seeing that maiden lifeless, afflicted by the serpent's poison, they wept, overcome with compassion; but Ruru, stricken with grief, went away into the forest.
The Sūta said: While the brahmins sat there on all sides, Ruru went into the dense forest and wept aloud, overcome with great sorrow.
Struck down by grief, lamenting piteously and at length, he spoke these words in sorrow, thinking of his beloved Pramadvara:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"She, the slender-limbed one who multiplies my grief, lies upon the earth — what sorrow greater than this could there be for all her kinsmen?
If I have performed austerities, if I have duly honored my teachers — by that merit let my beloved come back to life.
As I have been self-restrained and steadfast in my vows from birth, so let the fiery Pramadvara rise up this very day."
A divine messenger said: "Ruru, what you speak in your grief is in vain — there is no life remaining for one whose life has departed, O righteous one.
This pitiable one, daughter of a gandharva and an apsara, has exhausted her lifespan. Therefore, dear son, do not in any way set your mind on grief.
Yet a means was ordained here long ago by the great-souled gods; if you wish to perform it, you shall recover this Pramadvara."
Ruru said: "What means did the gods ordain? Tell me truly, O sky-traveler. Having heard it I will perform it accordingly — you must save me."
The divine messenger said: "Give half of your remaining lifespan to the maiden, O son of Bhṛgu's line — then your wife Pramadvara will rise, O Ruru."
Ruru said: "I give half my lifespan to the maiden, O best of sky-travelers. Let my beloved, adorned with the ornaments of love's beauty, rise up."
The Sūta said: Then both the king of the gandharvas and the divine messenger, those most excellent ones, went to Dharmarāja and spoke these words:
"Let the auspicious Pramadvara, wife of Ruru, rise up in exchange for half of Ruru's lifespan — if you see fit, O Dharmarāja, even though she is dead."
Dharmarāja said: "O divine messenger, if you wish it, let Pramadvara, Ruru's wife, rise up endowed with half of Ruru's own lifespan."
The Sūta said: When this was spoken, then the maiden Pramadvara rose up, endowed with half of Ruru's lifespan, as if waking from sleep, that fair-complexioned one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This has been witnessed: for Ruru of supreme splendor, whose lifespan is greatly extended, let it be diminished by half for the sake of his wife" — so it was decreed.
Then on an auspicious day their two fathers joyfully performed the wedding, and those two who wished each other's good rejoiced together.
Having obtained his priceless wife who shone like lotus filaments, he of firm resolve made a vow to destroy all serpents.
He, filled with fierce rage, whenever he saw any serpent, would always seize a weapon and strike it down, however near it was.
One day the brahmin Ruru came to a great forest, and there he saw an aged dundubha serpent lying asleep.
Then the brahmin, filled with rage, raised his staff resembling the staff of death and struck at it; but the dundubha spoke:
"I have done you no wrong at all today, O ascetic. Why then do you attack me in this rage, filled with fury?"
Ruru said: "My wife, who is as dear to me as my own life, was bitten by a serpent; and because of that I have made a terrible vow regarding serpents:
"I will always slay whatever serpent I see." Therefore I intend to kill you — save yourself with your life if you can.
The dundubha said: "O brahmin, those serpents that bite men are different — the dundubhas merely bear the smell of snakes; you ought not to harm them.
Sharing the same calamities but with separate purposes, sharing the same sorrows but with separate joys — you who know dharma ought not to harm the dundubhas."
The Sūta said: Having heard the serpent's words, Ruru then did not kill it, startled and apprehensive, taking the dundubha for a rishi.
Then the blessed Ruru spoke to it as if to pacify it gently: "O serpent, tell me — who are you, come to this changed form?"
The dundubha said: "I was formerly a rishi named Sahasrapāt, O Ruru; and by the curse of a brahmin I have attained the state of a serpent."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Ruru said: "Why did the angry brahmin curse you, O best of serpents? And for how long will you bear this form?"
The dundubha said: "I had a friend in former times, a brahmin named Khagama, O dear one, of very sharp tongue, endowed with the power of austerity.
While we were playing in childhood, I fashioned a grass snake and, while he was absorbed in his agnihotra rite, I frightened him so that he fainted.
Regaining his senses, that one rich in austerity spoke to me, as if burning with rage, he of true speech and firm vows:
"Just as you made this snake — however powerless — to frighten me, so by my wrath shall you become a powerless serpent."
Knowing the power of his austerity, O one rich in austerity, with heart greatly distressed, I spoke to that forest-dweller:
"Purified in body, trembling, with joined palms, standing bowed low — O friend, this was done by me only for a joke, in jest.
"O brahmin, you must forgive me — let this curse be revoked." But he, seeing my heart greatly distressed, spoke to me:
Sighing hotly again and again, greatly agitated, that one rich in austerity said: "What I have spoken cannot be untrue — this will come to pass, somehow.
"But the words I shall now speak to you — hear them, O man of firm vows; and having heard, let these words abide in your heart, O one rich in austerity.
"There will be born a pure son of Pramati named Ruru; upon seeing him your release from the curse will come before long."
"You are that one known as Ruru, the pure son of Pramati. Now I shall recover my own form, and I will speak what is beneficial for you.
Non-violence is declared the highest dharma for all living beings; therefore a brahmin must never harm any living creature anywhere.
The supreme scripture declares, 'The brahmin is born here as the gentle one' — knowing the Vedas and their auxiliaries, dear one, he grants fearlessness to all beings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Non-violence, truthful speech, and forbearance — these are determined to be the supreme dharma of the brahmin, even above the preservation of the Vedas.
But the dharma of the kshatriya does not apply to you here — the bearing of the rod, fierce valor, and the protection of subjects.
That was a kshatriya's deed — hear from me, O Ruru, O righteous soul: the slaying of serpents long ago at Janamejaya's snake sacrifice.
And the deliverance of the terrified serpents at that snake sacrifice — by a brahmin endowed with the power of austerity and strength, master of the Vedas and their auxiliaries: Āstīka, foremost of twice-born men, O best of brahmins."
Ruru said: "How did the kshatriya Janamejaya harm the serpents? And why were the serpents harmed, dear one, O best of brahmins?"
"And why were the serpents saved by Āstīka? Tell me of him — I wish to hear all of it completely."
The rishi said: "You will hear, O Ruru, the entire great story of Āstīka from the brahmins who will recount it" — and having said this, he vanished.
The Sūta said: Ruru also ran through the entire forest in all directions seeking to see that rishi, then exhausted, fell to the ground.
Ruru regained his senses and came back; he reported all this to his father then, and when asked, his father recounted the entire story.
Śaunaka said: "For what reason did that tiger among kings, King Janamejaya, bring the serpents to their end with the snake sacrifice? Tell me of that.
"And why did Āstīka, best of twice-born men, foremost among those who recite prayers, rescue the serpents from that blazing sacrificial fire?"
Whose son was that king who performed the serpent sacrifice? And that foremost of the twice-born — whose son was he? Tell me this.
The Sūta said: The great legend called Āstīka, in which all this is proclaimed — O brahmin, best among speakers, hear it all from me without remainder.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śaunaka said: I wish to hear in full this delightful tale of Āstīka, that ancient brahmin of glorious renown.
The Sūta said: The elders who dwell in the Naimiṣa forest recount this as an ancient tale of sacred history, spoken by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
Formerly, urged on by the brahmins, my father Lomaharṣaṇa the Sūta, that wise disciple of Vyāsa, narrated this very tale.
Having heard it from him, I shall now tell this Āstīka legend to you exactly as it is, O Śaunaka who inquires of me.
The father of Āstīka was a lord equal to Prajāpati himself — a celibate student, restrained in food, ever devoted to fierce austerity.
Known as Jaratkāru, he was a great seer of upward-flowing seed, foremost among the Yāyāvaras who knew the law, firm in his vow.
Wandering once, he saw his own forefathers hanging in a great pit, their feet pointing upward and their faces downward.
Upon seeing them, Jaratkāru spoke to those forefathers: "Who are you who hang here in this pit, faces downward?"
Clinging to a clump of vīraṇa grass gnawed away on all sides by a hidden mouse that dwells perpetually in this pit.
The forefathers said: We are sages of the Yāyāvara lineage, firm in our vows. O brahmin, due to the extinction of our line we are sinking into the earth.
Our single descendant is known as Jaratkāru — the most ill-fated among the ill-fated; he has taken refuge only in asceticism.
That fool does not wish to take a wife or beget sons. Because of this extinction of lineage we hang here in the pit.
Bereft of that protector, we are like sinners without a refuge. Who are you, good sir, who grieves for us as though a kinsman?
We wish to know, O brahmin — who are you who stands here? And why do you take pity on us who are so pitiable?
Jaratkāru said: You are truly my forefathers, my fathers and their fathers before them. Tell me — what shall I do? I am Jaratkāru himself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The forefathers said: Strive diligently, dear son, for the continuation of our lineage — for your own sake, for our sake, and for the sake of dharma, O dear one.
For neither through the fruits of dharma, dear son, nor through austerities well accumulated do men attain here the state that those with sons attain.
Therefore, dear son, by our command, direct your effort toward taking a wife and continuing the line — this is our highest good.
Jaratkāru said: I had ever resolved never to take a wife; yet for your benefit I shall take one as a wife.
But I shall do so only on this condition and in accordance with the proper rite: only if I find one who is offered to me — I shall not do otherwise.
She who shall be my wife must bear the same name as I, must be freely given by her kinsmen; I shall accept that maiden as alms, according to the ordained rule.
For who would give a wife to one as poor as I? Yet I shall accept her as alms if someone offers her.
Thus for the purpose of taking a wife I shall strive, O forefathers, by this rule alone — I shall never act otherwise.
And a being shall be born of her for your deliverance. May my forefathers attain the eternal abode and rejoice.
The Sūta said: Thereupon that brahmin of firm vow roamed the earth in search of a wife for his dwelling, but found none.
Once, going into a forest and remembering the words of his forefathers, seeking a maiden as alms, he called out softly three times.
Vāsuki came forward and offered his sister to him. But he did not accept her, thinking she did not bear his name.
For the mind of that great-souled Jaratkāru was fixed on this: he would take only a bride who shared his name when she was offered.
Then the greatly wise Jaratkāru of mighty austerity spoke to him: "What is the name of this sister of yours? Tell me truly, O serpent."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vāsuki said: O Jaratkāru, this is Jaratkāru, my younger sister. She has been kept all along for your sake — accept her, best of the twice-born.
The Sūta said: For the serpents had been cursed of old by their mother, O best of those who know brahman — "At the sacrifice of Janamejaya, fire with the wind as its charioteer shall burn you."
For the pacification of that curse, the foremost of serpents gave his sister to that ascetic sage of excellent vow.
He accepted her according to the rite prescribed by tradition, and from her was born a son of that great-souled one, named Āstīka.
He was an ascetic and a great soul, versed in the Vedas and their limbs, equal-minded toward all beings, and a remover of the fears of both his father's and mother's kin.
Then, after a great span of time, the Pāṇḍava king, lord of men, performed the great sacrifice known as the serpent sacrifice — so the tradition declares.
While that sacrifice was in progress — designed as the destruction of the serpents — Āstīka of great renown released them from that curse.
He delivered the serpents who were his maternal uncles and other kinsmen; he also delivered his paternal ancestors through his lineage, austerities, various vows, and sacred study, O brahmin, and thus became free from debt.
He satisfied the gods with sacrifices and abundant fees, the seers with celibacy, and the forefathers with the continuation of the lineage.
Having removed the heavy burden from his forefathers, Jaratkāru of firm vow went to heaven together with his own ancestors.
Having obtained a son in Āstīka and having practiced the highest dharma, the sage Jaratkāru ascended to heaven after a very long time.
This Āstīka legend has been recounted by me exactly as it occurred. O tiger among Bhṛgus, tell me — what more shall be narrated?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śaunaka said: O Sauti, tell that tale again in detail. Our desire to hear the story of Āstīka, that wise and virtuous man, is very great.
You tell it sweetly, dear one, with smooth syllables and words; we are greatly pleased. Dear child, you speak just as your father did.
Your father was ever devoted to serving us and told this tale just as it should be told — tell it as he did.
The Sūta said: This life-bestowing Āstīka legend I now tell you exactly as I heard it from my father while he narrated it.
In ancient times, O brahmin, in the age of the gods, two daughters of Prajāpati lived — sisters endowed with wondrous, matchless beauty, sinless.
They were the wives of Kaśyapa — Kadrū and Vinatā. Their husband Kaśyapa, equal to Prajāpati, pleased, filled with the highest joy, granted a boon to those two lawful wives.
Hearing the supremely generous bestowal of boons from Kaśyapa, those two excellent women experienced incomparable delight born of joy.
Kadrū chose a thousand serpent sons of equal power; Vinatā chose two sons who would surpass Kadrū's sons in strength, vital force, radiance, and valor.
Her husband granted her the boon she desired — a son and a half as much again. "So be it," said Vinatā to Kaśyapa then.
Having obtained two sons surpassing in might, Vinatā was fulfilled; and Kadrū, having obtained a thousand sons of equal power —
"Bear the embryos with care" — so said that great ascetic; then Kaśyapa, with his two wives elated by the boons, entered the forest.
After a great length of time, Kadrū laid a hundred clusters of ten eggs; and Vinatā laid two eggs, O chief of brahmins.
Their delighted attendants placed the eggs in warm vessels and kept them there for five hundred years.
Then, when five hundred years had passed, Kadrū's sons emerged; but from Vinatā's two eggs no pair of offspring appeared.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then that austerity-practicing goddess, longing for a son and ashamed, broke open one egg; and there she saw a son.
His upper body was fully formed but the other half was not manifest. That son, filled with anger, cursed her — so the tradition says.
"Because you have done this to me, mother, driven by greed, leaving my body incomplete — therefore you shall become a slave."
"For five hundred years you shall serve her with whom you now rival; and this other son of yours, O mother, shall free you from servitude."
"If you do not, O mother, crack open his egg as you did mine, leaving him bodiless or crippled, that ascetic —"
"— then you must patiently await his time of birth, you who desire surpassing power, which comes only after five hundred years more."
Having thus cursed his mother, that son ascended into the sky; he is seen as Aruṇa, O brahmin, at the break of dawn each day.
And Garuḍa too, the destroyer of serpents, was born when his time had come; as soon as he was born he left Vinatā and soared into the sky.
He flew off to take for himself the food ordained for him by the Creator, O tiger among Bhṛgus, for he was hungry and longing to eat.
The Sūta said: At this very time, O you rich in austerity, those two sisters saw Uccaiḥśravas approaching from nearby.
Him all the hosts of gods joyously honored — born when the nectar was being churned, the peerless jewel among horses.
Of surpassing strength among horses, best of the swift, filled with beauty, undecaying, divine, marked with every auspicious sign.
Śaunaka said: How did the gods churn that nectar, and where? Tell me the place where that horse-king of great might and great radiance was born.
The Sūta said: Mount Meru, blazing and unshakeable, that matchless mass of splendor, outshining the sun's own radiance with its gold-gleaming peaks —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— adorned with golden ornaments, wondrous, attended by gods and gandharvas, immeasurable, unapproachable by those burdened with unrighteousness —
— roamed by terrible wild beasts, ablaze with divine herbs, that great mountain standing and filling the vault of heaven with its height —
— inaccessible even in thought to others, adorned with rivers and trees, resonant with flocks of many birds, exceedingly beautiful —
— Climbing its auspicious summit studded with many gems, vast and boundless, all the mighty gods —
— those dwellers in heaven, seated there, began to deliberate, assembled for the purpose of obtaining nectar, established in austerity and restraint.
While the gods were thus deliberating and consulting together on all sides, the divine Nārāyaṇa spoke these words to Brahmā:
"Let the ocean, the vessel of waters, be churned by gods together with the hosts of asuras; when the great ocean is churned, nectar shall arise from it."
"Cast all the herbs and all the jewels into it and churn the ocean, O gods — then you shall obtain the nectar from it."
The Sūta said: Then Mount Mandara, that foremost of mountains, adorned with peaks shaped like cloud-tops, wrapped in nets of creepers —
It resounded with many kinds of birds, and was filled with many fanged creatures; it was frequented by kinneras and apsarases and even by the gods.
It rose eleven thousand yojanas above the earth, and was planted just as deep — by the same number of thousands — below the ground.
All the hosts of gods were unable to uproot it; so they approached Viṣṇu where he sat, and together with Brahmā they spoke as follows.
"Let the two of you apply your highest wisdom to this matter; let effort be made to uproot Mandara for our benefit."
"So be it," said Viṣṇu together with Brahmā, O descendant of Bhṛgu. Then mighty Ananta, roused by Brahmā and urged also by Nārāyaṇa, arose to the task.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then great-armed Ananta, immensely powerful, forcibly uprooted that king of mountains, O Brahmin, together with its forests and all the creatures dwelling in them.
Then the gods, together with him, approached the ocean and said to it: "For the sake of the nectar of immortality, we shall churn your waters."
The lord of the waters then spoke: "Then let a share fall to me as well; for I shall endure the great churning pressure from the rotation of Mandara."
The gods and asuras also addressed Akūpāra, the king of tortoises: "You ought to serve as the support for this mountain."
The tortoise agreed, saying "So be it," and offered his back as its foundation; and Indra pressed down the summit of that mountain with a device to hold it firm.
Making Mandara the churning-rod and Vāsuki the rope, the gods — together with the daityas and dānavas — then began, O Brahmin, to churn the ocean, that treasure-house of waters, all intent upon the nectar of immortality.
The great asuras clung to one end of the serpent-king, while all the gods together took their position at the tail end.
The divine Lord Ananta stood where Nārāyaṇa stood; he repeatedly lifted the head of the great serpent and hurled it down again.
As the serpent Vāsuki was repeatedly pulled back and forth by the gods, smoke-laden winds with tongues of flame poured again and again from his mouth.
Those billowing masses of smoke became cloud-banks flashing with lightning, and they rained down upon the hosts of gods who were worn thin by exertion and scorching heat.
And showers of flowers falling from the rocky peak scattered garlands over the hosts of gods and asuras on all sides.
A tremendous roar arose there, like the sound of great thunder-clouds, as the ocean was churned with Mandara by the gods and asuras.
There, in the salt waters, hundreds of aquatic creatures of every kind, crushed by the great mountain, met their dissolution.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The mountain also brought about the destruction of various beings of Varuṇa's realm, of many kinds, dwelling in the depths of the underworld.
As the mountain spun around, great trees with birds perched on them crashed against one another and fell from the mountain's peaks.
Fire born from their friction blazed repeatedly with its tongues of flame and covered Mount Mandara, as lightning covers a dark cloud.
It burned elephants and lions fleeing from it, and all manner of creatures of every kind lost their lives.
Indra, the foremost of the immortals, then quenched that blazing fire on all sides with water drawn from rain-clouds.
Then many kinds of sap flowed into the ocean's waters — resins from the great trees and the juices of many medicinal plants.
Through those life-giving juices, through the milk of the ocean, and through the flowing of gold, the gods attained immortality.
Then the water of that ocean became like milk, mixed with the finest of juices; and from that milk ghee was produced.
Then the gods spoke to Brahmā, who sat as the boon-granter: "We are utterly exhausted, O Brahmin, and still the nectar has not appeared."
"Without the god Nārāyaṇa — the daityas, the great serpents, and we ourselves alike — and this churning of the ocean, long begun, has gone on without result."
Then Brahmā spoke a word to the divine Nārāyaṇa: "Bestow strength upon all these, O Viṣṇu; you are the refuge here."
Viṣṇu said: "I give strength to all who are engaged in this task. Let the vessel be agitated by all; let Mandara be made to revolve."
The Sūta said: Hearing the words of Nārāyaṇa, those powerful ones together churned the milk of the great ocean once more, vigorously.
Then the Moon, lord of a hundred thousand rays, arose from the ocean like a second sun — radiant and serene, with its cool beams blazing bright.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Next arose Śrī, clad in white garments, born from the ghee; then arose Surā, the goddess of wine; and likewise a white horse.
The divine Kaustubha gem arose as well, born of the amṛta, its rays blazing brilliantly; it was glorious, and came to rest upon the breast of Nārāyaṇa.
Śrī, Surā, Soma, and the horse swift as thought — all went where the gods went, taking the path of the sun.
Then the god Dhanvantari, possessed of a beautiful form, arose, bearing the white kamaṇḍalu vessel in which the nectar of immortality resided.
On seeing this utterly wondrous thing, a great clamour arose among the dānavas, all crying out: "It is mine! It is mine!"
Then the Lord Nārāyaṇa assumed the enchanting illusion of Mohinī, taking on a wondrous female form, and approached the dānavas.
Then all the dānavas and daityas, their minds deluded, their thoughts fixed entirely upon her, gave the nectar to that woman.
The Sūta said: Then the daityas and dānavas, taking up various coverings and weapons of every kind, rushed together against the gods.
Then the mighty god Viṣṇu, that powerful lord, together with Nara, took the nectar and carried it away from the lords of the dānavas.
Then all the hosts of gods, having received it from Viṣṇu, drank that nectar amid the tumultuous uproar and confusion.
Then, at the very moment the gods were drinking the coveted nectar, the dānava Rāhu, having assumed the guise of a god, drank some of it.
The moment the nectar reached the throat of that dānava, it was reported by the Moon and the Sun, who desired the welfare of the gods.
Then the Blessed Lord, with his cakra-weapon, the adorned discus, swiftly severed the head of the dānava as he was drinking the nectar.
That great head of the dānava, like a mountain peak, severed by the discus, fell to the earth and made it tremble.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From that time Rāhu, that disembodied head, formed an eternal enmity; to this very day he swallows the Moon and the Sun.
And the Blessed Lord Hari, abandoning that incomparable female form, shook the dānavas with many fearsome weapons.
Then a great and utterly terrible battle broke out near the salt ocean between the gods and the asuras.
Long sharp javelins fell in thousands; spears with very sharp points, and weapons of every kind fell upon them.
Then asuras, cleaved by the discus, vomiting much blood, struck down by swords, spears, and maces, fell to the ground.
And in that terrible battle, heads severed by broad-bladed weapons, covered in nets of heated gold, fell again and again.
Great asuras, their limbs smeared with blood, slain, lay like the red-ore peaks of mountains.
Cries of lamentation arose by the thousands in every direction as they cut each other down with weapons while the sun turned blood-red.
The noise of those striking one another in battle with iron clubs of tawny hue and with fists in close combat seemed to touch the sky.
"Cut! Pierce! Rush forward! Strike down! Charge!" — such terrifyingly fierce cries were heard on all sides.
While this dreadful and tumultuous battle raged, the divine pair Nara and Nārāyaṇa entered the fray.
There, beholding Nara's divine bow, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu also recalled to mind his discus, the destroyer of dānavas.
Then, the instant it was thought of, it came from the sky — the supremely radiant discus, scorcher of enemies, equal in brilliance to the sun, with its unblunted rim, the Sudarśana, fearsome, unconquerable, supreme.
When it arrived, blazing with the radiance of kindled fire and striking terror, the unfailing Acyuta, whose arms are like an elephant's trunk, released it — swift and fiercely fast, supremely brilliant, destroyer of enemy citadels.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Equal in brilliance to the fire of death, it flew back and again swiftly as it was hurled, rending the sons of Diti and Danu by the thousands, driven by the hand of that supreme being in battle.
Burning in one place, it licked like a flame; it violently cut down those hosts of asuras; sent spinning again and again through the sky and the earth, it drank blood in battle like a piśāca demon.
Then the asuras, undaunted in spirit and immensely powerful, with radiance like dispersing clouds, seized mountains and tormented the host of gods again and again, rising by the thousands into the sky.
Then from the sky there fell terror-inspiring great mountains with their trees, taking the form of many kinds of clouds, their topmost peaks crumbling away; they crashed swiftly against one another and roared.
Then the earth with all its forests shook violently, struck on all sides by the fall of great mountains, as the two sides roared fiercely at each other again and again on that great and fiercely raging battlefield.
Then Nara, with his mighty arrows tipped with fine gold, covered the sky's path and split the mountain peaks with feathered shafts, during that great and terrible battle with the host of asuras.
Then the great asuras, tormented by the gods and seeing the Sudarśana blazing with the radiance of kindled fire and enraged as it coursed through the sky, plunged into the earth and into the salt-water ocean.
Then, with victory won by the gods, Mandara, duly honoured, was returned to its own place; it resounded through the sky and the heavens on all sides; and thereafter the clouds went their way as before.
Then the gods, filled with supreme and complete joy, placed the nectar in safe keeping; and Indra, slayer of Bala, together with the immortals, gave over that treasure of nectar to the Crowned One to guard.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Sūta said: All this has been told to you — how the nectar was churned forth — and it is in this account that the glorious horse of incomparable power was born.
On seeing that horse, Kadrū then said to Vinatā: "What colour is Uccaiḥśravas, dear friend? Tell me without delay."
Vinatā said: "This king of horses is purely white. What do you think, O auspicious one? Tell me your view of his colour, and then let us make a wager on it."
Kadrū said: "I believe this horse has a black tail, O bright-toothed one. Come, let us wager together on servitude, O passionate one."
The Sūta said: Having thus made a compact with each other for servitude, the two went to their own homes, saying: "We shall look tomorrow."
Then Kadrū, wishing to play a trick, commanded her thousand sons to become hairs as black as collyrium and cling to the horse's tail.
"Enter the horse quickly so that I shall not become a slave." Those serpents did not comply with that command, and she cursed them.
"When the serpent sacrifice is being performed, fire shall consume you — at the sacrifice of Janamejaya, that wise royal sage, descendant of the Pāṇḍavas."
The Grandfather himself heard this curse, so exceedingly cruel as it was pronounced by Kadrū — heard it truly as if by fate.
Together with all the hosts of gods, he approved that pronouncement, seeing the great multitude of serpents and desiring the welfare of all living beings.
For these biting serpents are possessed of fierce and potent venom and are of great power; on account of their sharp-venom nature, and truly for the welfare of living beings, he bestowed the science of snake-charming upon the great-souled Kāśyapa.
Sūta said: Then, when the night had passed and dawn had broken with the sun rising, Kadrū and Vinatā, those two sisters, O sage of great austerities,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
both furious and deeply agitated, having made their wager with slavery as the stake, went together to see the horse Uccaiḥśravas up close.
There they beheld the ocean, that treasury of waters, teeming with timiṅgila fish and other great fish, and thronged with makaras.
It was filled with thousands upon thousands of creatures of many forms, fierce and ever unapproachable, swarming with tortoises and crocodiles.
It was the mine of all jewels, the abode of Varuṇa, the beautiful and supreme dwelling place of the nāgas, the lord of rivers.
It was the home of the fires of Pātāla, the prison of the asuras, terrifying to all beings — that ocean, the boundless reservoir of waters.
Auspicious and divine, the supreme source of nectar for the immortals, immeasurable and inconceivable, its waters were most holy and wondrous.
Terrible, with the fierce roar of its aquatic creatures, resounding with dreadful noise, its depths filled with swirling eddies, it struck terror into all beings.
Stirred by the wind that swings along the shore, agitated by turbulence and surging waves, with its billowing wave-hands it seemed to dance on every side.
Its towering waves surging with the waxing and waning of the moon made it unapproachable; it was the birthplace of Pāñcajanya, the incomparable mine of gems.
Its waters had been churned and muddied within when the blessed Govinda of boundless might, assuming the form of a great boar, had recovered the earth.
And the brahmarṣi Atri, performing austerities for a hundred years within it, had not touched its unfathomable bottom — imperishable Pātāla lay below.
There too was the repose of Padmanābha, Viṣṇu of boundless radiance, who at the dawn of each cosmic age sleeps the yogic slumber of deep spiritual absorption.
The water was the auspicious oblation-offering to the submarine fire blazing at the Vaḍavāmukha; the lord of rivers was fathomless in depth, vast in expanse, and beyond measure.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They beheld that great ocean, approached unceasingly by thousands upon thousands of mighty rivers as if each were vying with the others.
They saw that ocean, deep, filled with fierce timi fish and makaras, roaring with the terrible cries of its water creatures, vast and bright as the sky, fathomless — the great, boundless treasury of waters.
Thus beholding that ocean crowded with fish, makaras, and waves, deep and expansive and luminous as the sky, lit by the tongues of the submarine Pātāla-fire, the two of them at that moment hurried swiftly forward.
Sūta said: Having crossed over that ocean, Kadrū, swift as thought, descended with Vinatā near the horse in no time at all.
And having observed many black hairs attached to its tail, Kadrū pressed Vinatā, whose face had fallen, into servitude.
Then Vinatā, defeated by that wager, overcome with sorrow, assumed the condition of a slave.
In the meantime, when the proper time arrived, the mighty Garuḍa, of great radiance, burst open his shell and was born, without his mother.
Blazing like a heap of fire, fully kindled and utterly terrifying, that great-bodied bird grew in an instant and soared into the sky.
Seeing him, all creatures sought refuge in Agni, bowing down and addressing him as he sat there in his universal form.
"O Agni, do not grow any further! Surely you do not wish to burn us? That great blazing mass of yours is spreading on and on!"
Agni said: "It is not as you think, O slayers of asuras. This is Garuḍa, the mighty one — equal to me in his own radiance."
Sūta said: Thus addressed, the gods then went to Garuḍa and, together with the hosts of sages, approached him closely and praised him with words.
"You are a ṛṣi, you are supremely blessed, you are a god, lord of birds. You are the sovereign, blazing like the sun. You are our incomparable refuge."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"You are a wave of strength, noble, undaunted in spirit, full of prosperity, irresistible. You are austerity, you are all learning, O one of undimmed glory — all that is to come and all that has come to pass."
"You are the highest; this entire creation, moving and unmoving, shines through you as the sun illumines with its rays — eclipsing even the sun's own brilliance again and again. You are the Ender of all this, both the fixed and the unfixed."
"As the sun when enraged would burn all creatures, so you burn them, O one blazing like fire. You are terrifying, like the fire of dissolution arisen, destroying all, bringing about the end at the turning of the cosmic age."
"We have come seeking refuge in you, lord of birds, of great might, beyond darkness, who range the clouds — we approach Garuḍa, the sky-farer, the great-armed, the boon-granter, of unconquerable valor."
Thus praised by the gods together with the hosts of sages, Suparṇa then withdrew into himself his own blazing radiance.
Sūta said: Then that bird who travels at will, of great heroism and immense strength, came to his mother's side at the far shore of the great ocean.
There Vinatā, defeated in that wager, afflicted with the deepest sorrow, had assumed the state of a slave.
Then one day, summoning Vinatā who was bowed down in her son's presence, Kadrū addressed her with these words at an opportune moment:
"O fortunate Vinatā, carry me to the delightful abode of the nāgas, beautiful and lovely, situated in a secluded part of the ocean's bosom."
Then the mother of Suparṇa carried the mother of serpents, and Garuḍa too, prompted by his mother's word, carried the serpents.
As Vainateya, that bird, flew close around the sun, the serpents were enveloped by the sun's rays and fell unconscious. Seeing her sons in that condition, Kadrū then praised Śakra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Salutation to you, O lord of the lords of gods! Salutation to you, O slayer of Bala! Salutation to you, O slayer of Namuci! O thousand-eyed one, consort of Śacī, salutation to you!"
"Be a flood of water for the serpents scorched by the sun. You alone are our supreme protection, O best of the immortals."
"For you are capable of creating vast waters, O Purandara. You yourself are the cloud, you are the wind, you are Agni, you are the lightning fire in the sky."
"You are the thrower of dense clouds, and they call you the cloud itself once again. You are the thunderbolt, incomparable and dreadful; you are the thunder-voiced rain cloud Balāhaka."
"You alone are the creator of the worlds and the destroyer, unconquered. You are the light of all beings; you are Āditya, the blazing fire."
"You are a great, wondrous being. You are the king, you are the best of gods. You are Viṣṇu, you are the thousand-eyed, you are the god, you are the supreme refuge."
"You are all nectar, O god; you are Soma, supremely worshipped. You are the muhūrta, and the tithi; you are the lava, and the kṣaṇa."
"You are the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight, the kalā, kāṣṭhā, truṭi, years, seasons, months, nights, and days."
"You are the earth at her best with mountains and forests; you are the sky, luminous with the sun, free of darkness. You are the great ocean, filled with timi and timiṅgila fish, with great waves, many makaras, and a home for fish."
"You are great glory — so you are ever worshipped by the wise and by the great ṛṣis with joyful hearts. Praised, you drink the soma at sacrifices, and the havis offered with the vaṣaṭ call for the welfare of beings."
"You are ever worshipped here by the brāhmaṇas for the sake of fruit; you are sung of in the Vedic ancillaries, O flood of incomparable strength. For your sake the twice-born lords, devoted to sacrifice, master the Vedic ancillaries together with all the Vedas."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sūta said: Thus praised by Kadrū, the blessed Harivāhana covered the entire sky with masses of dark-blue clouds.
Those clouds, blazing with lightning, released abundant water and roared incessantly against one another in the sky as if competing.
The sky seemed to be packed solid with those most wondrous rain-clouds, which poured forth incomparable water ceaselessly with a tremendous roar.
The sky seemed to dance with the manifold surging waves of rain, and the firmament was filled with the resounding peal of thunder.
The nāgas were filled with the greatest joy when Vāsava rained down; and the earth too was flooded with water on every side.
Sūta said: Carried by Suparṇa, they quickly reached that place, which was encircled by the waters of the ocean and resounded with the cries of flocks of birds.
It was covered with rows of trees bearing varied fruits and flowers, enclosed by lovely mansions, and adorned with lotus pools as well.
It was embellished with lakes of clear water of variegated beauty, and fanned by holy breezes carrying divine fragrances.
It was beautified by sandal-wood trees that touched the sky with their fragrance, and which, shaken by the wind, were showering down rains of blossoms.
The showers of flowers and water seemed to be scattered over the nāgas assembled there; the place was heart-gladdening, holy, beloved of gandharvas and apsarases, resonant with the calls of many birds, lovely, and a source of delight for the sons of Kadrū.
Having reached that forest, the serpents sported there with joy, and they also addressed the mighty Suparṇa, that best of birds.
"Carry us to yet another island, most beautiful, with abundant water. For you, O sky-ranger, while flying, behold many lovely regions."
Reflecting on this, the bird then spoke to his mother Vinatā: "What is the reason, Mother, that I must do what the serpents say?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vinatā said: "I have become the slave of my ignoble sister, O best of birds — a false wager was contrived by the serpents through treachery."
Sūta said: When the reason had been told by his mother, the sky-traveler, pained by that sorrow, spoke these words to the serpents:
"By fetching what, or by knowing what, or by what act of valor here, may I be freed from slavery to you? Tell me truly, O tongue-flickering ones."
Hearing him, the serpents replied: "Bring us the amṛta by your power; then will your freedom from slavery come to pass, O sky-traveler."
Sūta said: Thus addressed by the serpents, Garuḍa then spoke to his mother: "I go to fetch the amṛta. I wish to know what I should eat on the way."
Vinatā said: "In a secluded part of the ocean's bosom is the supreme dwelling of the Niṣādas. After eating many thousands of them, bring back the amṛta."
"But you must never under any circumstance entertain the thought of killing a brāhmaṇa. A brāhmaṇa is not to be slain by any living being, for he is inviolable and without equal."
"When angered, a vipra becomes fire, the sun, poison, and a weapon. The vipra is the foremost among all creatures in receiving food, the best of the varṇas, a father, a teacher."
Garuḍa said: "Please tell me, Mother, since I ask — by what auspicious signs would I recognize a brāhmaṇa? You ought to explain this to me properly."
Vinatā said: "Son, whoever, once swallowed and lodged in your throat, burns like a live coal — like a swallowed hook — him you should know to be a bull among brāhmaṇas."
Sūta said: And Vinatā, from maternal love for her son, spoke these words to him — knowing his incomparable might — accompanied by a benediction.
"May the wind protect your wings, and the moon your back, my son. May fire protect your head, and the sun your entire being."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And I, my son, am ever devoted to your peace and well-being. Go by an unobstructed path, dear child, to the accomplishment of your purpose."
Then, having heard his mother's words, he spread his wings and soared into the sky; and the powerful one approached the Niṣādas, hungry as great Death itself at the end of time.
Driving those Niṣādas together then, he stirred up a great dust reaching to the sky, dried up the waters in the ocean's bosom, and shook the mountains standing nearby.
Then the king of birds opened his enormous mouth, blocking the path of the Niṣādas; and the Niṣādas rushed headlong toward the mouth of that devourer of serpents.
Into that gaping mouth of immense size they flew by the thousands, like birds flying into the sky, bewildered by the swirling dust-laden wind, like trees shaken by a great gale in the forest.
Then the bird, scorcher of enemies, swift and mighty, closed his mouth — slaying those who eat fish of many kinds — hungry, that lord of sky-travellers, at that moment.
Sūta said: A brahmin along with his wife had reached Garuḍa's throat. Garuḍa — blazing like a flaming coal — spoke to him as he flew through the sky.
"O best of twice-born, come out quickly from my open mouth. A brahmin is never to be slain by me, not even one who is always given to wicked deeds."
As Garuḍa spoke thus, the brahmin addressed him: "This Niṣādī woman is my wife — let her come out together with me."
Garuḍa said: "Take this Niṣādī woman too and fly out swiftly. Sustain yourself well — you have not yet been digested by my fierce energy."
Sūta said: Then that brahmin came out, accompanied by the Niṣādī woman. Having praised Garuḍa, he departed to his desired destination.
When that brahmin had departed with his wife, the king of birds spread his wings and soared into the sky with the speed of thought.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then he saw his father and, being questioned, told his father: "I have been sent by the serpents; I am resolved to fetch soma. I shall bring it this very day for the sake of freeing my mother from bondage."
"I was also instructed by my mother to eat Niṣādas. Yet I found no satisfaction even after devouring them by the thousands."
"Therefore, O blessed one, O lord, point out to me another food that I may eat and thereafter be capable of fetching the amṛta."
Kaśyapa said: "There was once a great sage named Vibhāvasu, exceedingly wrathful. He had a younger brother named Supratīka, great in his austerities."
"That great sage did not wish to hold wealth in common with his brother; Supratīka kept insisting on a partition, again and again."
"And his brother Vibhāvasu said to Supratīka: 'Many people desire to make a partition out of delusion, always. Once separated, they no longer regard one another, deluded by wealth.'"
"'Knowing those fools absorbed in self-interest, separated and each with his own wealth, enemies in the guise of friends then drive them further apart.'"
"'And others, knowing them to be divided, fall upon the gaps between them. The destruction of the divided is immeasurable and comes about swiftly.'"
"'Therefore the wise do not commend partition for those bound together under the teaching of a guru, who would come to be suspicious of one another.'"
"'Since you cannot be restrained and you desire to divide the wealth, therefore, O Supratīka, you shall become an elephant.'"
"Cursed thus, Supratīka then spoke to Vibhāvasu: 'You too shall become a tortoise that moves beneath the waters.'"
"Thus, through mutual curses, Supratīka and Vibhāvasu, their minds foolish on account of wealth, came to assume the forms of an elephant and a tortoise."
"Even though they had taken birth in animal wombs through the fault of their anger, they were devoted to mutual hatred, both proud of their extraordinary strength."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"These two with their great bodies, pursuing old enmity, dwell in that lake. One of them, the magnificent great elephant, now approaches."
"Hearing the trumpeting sound of the elephant, the tortoise, that great-bodied one who rests beneath the water, rises up, churning the entire lake."
"Seeing the tortoise, the elephant with its entwined trunk plunges into the water — mighty, with the force of its tusks, trunk, tail, and feet."
"As the elephant churns that lake filled with many fish, the tortoise too raises its head and comes forward mightily, eager for battle."
"The elephant stands six yojanas tall and is twice that in length; the tortoise is three yojanas in height and ten yojanas in circumference."
"These two, maddened for battle and each seeking victory over the other — make swift use of them and accomplish your desired goal."
Sūta said: Having heard his father's words, the sky-soarer of terrible speed seized the elephant with one talon and the tortoise with the other.
Then that great bird soared high into the sky and, reaching the sacred ford called Ālambatīrtha, he approached the trees of the gods.
Terrified, those divine trees with their golden branches trembled, struck by the wind of his wings, thinking, "Let him not break us."
Seeing those trees shaking their limbs — trees whose fruits fulfil all desires, with incomparably beautiful forms — the sky-ranger approached others.
He approached those great and radiant trees, their branches set with vaiḍūrya gems, bearing golden and silver fruits, surrounded by the waters of the ocean.
There, the Rohiṇa tree — exceedingly grown and very great — spoke to that best of birds as he came swooping with the speed of thought:
"This great branch of mine extends one hundred yojanas. Alight on this branch and devour these two — the elephant and the tortoise."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, swiftly swooping upon that tree frequented by thousands of birds, the best of birds — his body like a mountain — shook it with great speed and broke that branch, thickly covered with dense leaves.
Sūta said: The moment Garuḍa, so mighty, touched it with his feet, that branch of the tree snapped — and he caught hold of it as it broke.
Gazing and smiling at that broken great branch, he then saw the Vālakhilya sages hanging from it, head downward.
Out of fear of causing their destruction, the lord of birds swooped down, seized the branch in his beak out of concern for them, and flew gently, threading his way through the mountains.
Thus he flew over many regions, carrying the elephant and tortoise, out of compassion for the Vālakhilyas, yet found no place to set down.
Going to Gandhamādana, the foremost and imperishable of mountains, he there saw Kaśyapa, his father, standing in austerity.
His father too beheld that bird of divine form, endowed with splendour, heroism, and strength, swift as the mind and the wind.
