He resembled a mountain peak, like Brahmā's staff raised on high — inconceivable, unrecognisable in form, terrifying to all beings.
He bore within him a valour like magic, like a blazing fire raised aloft — not to be assailed, not to be conquered by gods, dānavas, or rākṣasas.
He was a cleaver of mountain peaks, a drainer of river waters, a terrible churner of the worlds, dreadful to behold as Death itself.
Seeing him arrive and knowing his intention, the blessed Kaśyapa then spoke these words:
"Son, do not act rashly; do not bring sudden pain upon yourself. May the Vālakhilyas who feed on rays of light and who are fiercely wrathful not burn you."
Then Kaśyapa, for the sake of his son, appeased those Vālakhilyas who had perfected their austerities, pointing to this reason:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"O wealth-of-austerity sages, Garuḍa's undertaking is for the benefit of all living beings. He desires to accomplish a great deed — you should grant him your permission."
Thus addressed by the blessed one, those sages agreed. Releasing the branch, those ascetics then made for the sacred Himavat mountain.
Then, when they had departed, the son of Vinatā — his face still occupied by the branch held in his beak — questioned his father Kaśyapa.
"O blessed one, where shall I release this tree branch? Let the blessed one tell me of a region free from brahmins."
Then Kaśyapa pointed out to him a mountain devoid of people, its ravines sealed by snow, inaccessible even to the mind of others.
Entering the vast hollow of that mountain with the speed of thought, Tārkṣya flew swiftly, bearing the branch along with the elephant and tortoise.
Not even a hundred large or small leather thongs could encircle that great branch of the tree which the bird had seized and carried away.
Then Garuḍa, best among fliers, covered a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas in no very great time.
Reaching that mountain in a mere moment, following his father's words, the sky-ranger released that great branch there with a resounding crash.
Struck by the wind of his wings, the king of mountains trembled; the trees, shaken all together, showered down a rain of flowers.
And the peaks of that mountain shattered on all sides — those peaks of jewels and gold, which adorned the great mountain.
Many of the trees, struck by that branch, shone with their golden blossoms like clouds lit by lightning.
Those trees, blazing with golden blossoms and mingled with the minerals of the mountain, shone there, reflecting the rays of the sun.
Then, alighting on the peak of that mountain, Garuḍa — best of birds — devoured both the elephant and the tortoise.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then he launched himself from the summit of the mountain peak with the speed of thought. Thereupon ill omens arose among the gods, portending fear.
Indra's beloved thunderbolt blazed with anguish, and a heavenly meteor with smoke and flame fell from the sky.
And so too the weapons of the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas in their entirety, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and whatever other hosts of gods — each one's weapon turned against the others.
Something unprecedented even in the war of gods and asuras then occurred: violent thundering winds blew, and meteors fell on every side.
Even the cloudless sky roared with tremendous sound, and the god who is the divine dispenser of rain rained down blood.
The garlands of the gods withered, their splendours grew dim; dreadful portent-clouds rained down much blood, and dust rose up to assail their crowns.
Then Śatakratu, greatly agitated with fear, seeing these dreadful omens together with the gods, spoke thus to Bṛhaspati:
"Why, O blessed one, have these terrible great omens arisen? And I see no enemy in battle who could challenge us."
Bṛhaspati said: "Through your transgression, O Devendra, and through your carelessness, O Śatakratu, a wondrous being has arisen through the austerities of the Vālakhilyas."
"The son of the sage Kaśyapa and of Vinatā, a flyer, powerful and capable of assuming any form, has arrived with intent to steal the soma."
"This bird, the foremost of the mighty, is capable of stealing the soma. I consider him capable of everything — he could even accomplish what is thought impossible."
Sūta said: Having heard these words, Śakra addressed the guardians of the amṛta: "A bird of great heroism and strength is here set on stealing the soma."
"I am alerting you so that he may not carry it off by force. Bṛhaspati has told me that his strength is matchless."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing these words, the gods were astonished and took up their effort; they stood surrounding the amṛta, and Indra the thunderbolt-wielder, Śatakratu, stood among them.
Those high-minded ones wore their most precious armour — golden and variegated, set with vaiḍūrya gems —
— and they raised up manifold weapons of terrible appearance, innumerable, sharp and keen of point and edge, by the thousands.
Everywhere blazing with sparks and flames, emitting smoke — discs, iron clubs, tridents, and battle-axes —
— and various sharp spears, and bright swords, in forms that matched their own bodies, and maces fierce to behold —
— armed with those radiant weapons, adorned with divine ornaments, those shining hosts of gods stood free from all impurity.
Those gods — of incomparable strength, heroism, and splendour — their minds set on guarding the amṛta, destroyers of the cities of the asuras, shone with bodies blazing like kindled fire.
Thus that excellent battle-array of the gods — crowded with hundreds of thousands of iron clubs, shining within the expanse of the sky as if it were the sun's own radiance — blazed forth in glory.
Śaunaka said: What was Mahendra's offence, and what was his blunder, O son of a sūta? And how was Garuḍa born through the austerities of the Vālakhilyas?
And how did the lord of birds become the son of the twice-born Kaśyapa? How did he become unassailable by all beings, and how did he become invincible?
And how did that sky-traveller move freely at will and possess strength at will? I wish to hear all this, if it is recorded in the Purāṇa.
The Sūta said: What you ask me about is indeed a subject treated in the Purāṇa. O twice-born, hear from me as I recount it all in brief.
When the progenitor Kaśyapa was performing a sacrifice desiring a son, the seers, the gods, and the Gandharvas all rendered him assistance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the fetching of firewood, Śakra was assigned by Kaśyapa, along with the Vālakhilya sages and whatever other hosts of divinities were present.
Śakra, the mighty lord, easily lifted a load of firewood equal in size to a mountain, commensurate with his own strength, and bore it forward without much effort.
Then on the path he saw the tiny sages, as small as a thumb-joint at the belly, all together carrying a single stalk of a palāśa leaf.
Those ascetic-wealthy ones, as though dissolved into their own limbs, without food, afflicted with fatigue, with feeble strength, were struggling in water flooded even in a cow's hoofprint.
Seized with pride and intoxicated by his own might, Purandara laughed at them all and quickly leaped over them with contempt, dishonoring them.
Then those sages, utterly seized by rage and deeply angered, undertook a great deed that would strike terror into Śakra.
Those brāhmaṇas of intense austerity poured oblations into the sacred fire according to rule, with mantras both high and low, for a particular purpose — hear what that was.
"Let there arise another Indra of all the gods — one possessed of strength at will and movement at will, one who strikes fear into the king of the gods" — so vowed those keepers of their vows.
"Let one who is a hundredfold superior to Indra in heroism and prowess, swift as thought, and formidable, now come into being through the fruit of our austerities" — thus they spoke.
Learning of this, the king of the gods, Śatakratu, greatly distressed, went for refuge to Kaśyapa of sharpened vow.
Having heard of the king of the gods' plight, the progenitor Kaśyapa approached the Vālakhilyas and inquired about the completion of their ritual act.
Those truth-speakers replied to him, "So be it." Then the progenitor Kaśyapa spoke these conciliatory words to them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This Indra has been appointed over the three worlds by Brahmā's command, and you too, O wealthy in austerities, have been striving for the sake of Indra."
"O best of beings, you ought not render Brahmā's word false; nor do I intend to make your resolve come to naught."
"Let this one become Indra of the winged beings, supremely powerful and courageous; and let your grace be shown to the king of the gods who now supplicates you."
Thus addressed by Kaśyapa, the Vālakhilyas, wealthy in austerities, replied after duly honoring that best of sages and progenitor.
"This undertaking of ours all together was for the sake of Indra, O Progenitor; and your desired undertaking is for the sake of offspring."
"So let this fruit-bearing act be accepted by you, and arrange things here as you see to be the greatest good."
At this very time, the goddess Vinatā — the auspicious, beautiful daughter of Dakṣa, that illustrious one who was desirous of sons —
— having performed austerities and being devoted to her vow, having bathed and purified herself in the puṃsavana rite, approached her husband. Then Kaśyapa spoke to her.
"This undertaking of yours, O goddess, shall bear the fruit you desired; you will give birth to two heroic sons, lords of the three worlds."
"Born through the austerities of the Vālakhilyas and from my own intention likewise, your two highly fortunate sons shall be worshipped throughout the worlds."
The venerable Mārīca then spoke to her again: "This embryo of great and auspicious potency must be carried with all care and without negligence."
"One of them, that heroic sky-ranger honoured throughout the worlds, possessed of strength at will, shall exercise the lordship of Indra over all winged creatures."
Then the progenitor, pleased, spoke to Śatakratu: "These two birds shall be your brothers and allies."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"No harm shall come to you from these two, O Purandara. Let your anxiety depart, O Śakra; you yourself shall remain Indra."
"And you must never again despise the knowers of Brahman, nor out of arrogance dishonor those whose words are venomous and who are provoked to fierce anger."
Thus addressed, Indra departed free of anxiety to heaven, and Vinatā too had her purpose accomplished and became joyful.
She gave birth to two sons — Aruṇa and Garuḍa. Of the two, Aruṇa was deformed and became the forerunner of the Sun.
Garuḍa was consecrated as Indra of the winged beings. O joy of the Bhṛgu line, hear now of this great deed of his.
The Sūta said: Then, O best of the twice-born, when that event had thus unfolded, Garutmān, the lord of birds, swiftly advanced against the gods.
Seeing him of such overwhelming strength, they trembled on all sides; and yet they struck one another even while wielding all their weapons.
There was present one of immeasurable spirit, blazing like lightning and fire, named Bhauvana, of very great heroism, the guardian of the Soma.
Wounded by that lord of birds with his wings, beak, and talons, he fought an incomparable battle for a moment and then was slain in combat.
The sky-traveller stirred up a great mass of dust with the wind of his wings, darkened the worlds so they were without light, and with it scattered the gods.
Enveloped in that dust, the gods fell into confusion; the guardians of the nectar, shrouded by the dust, could not see him.
Thus Garuḍa threw the abode of the three heavens into turmoil, and with blows of his wings and beak he tore the gods asunder.
Then the thousand-eyed god quickly urged on the Wind: "Disperse this rain of dust — that is your task, O Wind."
Then the mighty Wind swiftly blew away that dust. Once the darkness had cleared, the gods assailed the bird.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The powerful bird roared aloud with the sound of a great storm-cloud, terrifying all beings even while being assailed by the hosts of gods; and the lord of birds, of great heroism and slayer of enemy heroes, soared upward.
Soaring up and hovering above the gods in the midair, all the armoured gods showered him with weapons of every kind from below.
With axes, iron clubs, spears, and maces together with Vāsava, and also with blazing discuses with sharp edges resembling the sun in form.
Though struck on all sides by discharges of every kind of weapon and waging a most tumultuous battle, the lord of birds did not waver.
Roaring as if filling the sky, the valiant son of Vinatā flung the gods in every direction with his wings and chest.
Those gods, thus hurled away and tormented by Garuḍa, fled; wounded by his talons and beak, they bled profusely.
The Sādhyas along with the Gandharvas fled to the east; the Vasus fled to the south along with the Rudras, all driven away by the lord of birds.
The Ādityas fled to the western quarter, the Nāsatyas to the north, repeatedly glancing back and fighting against the one of great might.
With the hero Aśvakranda, with the bird Reṇuka, with the valiant Krathana, and with the sky-traveller Tapana —
— and with Ulūka and Śvasana, and with the bird Nimeṣa, and with Praruja and Praliha — with all these he waged battle.
With tips of his wings, talons, and beak the son of Vinatā tore them apart, infuriated like Śiva with his Pināka bow at the end of an age, possessed of great might.
Those beings of great heroism and great energy, lacerated in many ways by him, shone like dense storm clouds raining torrents of blood.
Having left all those beings deprived of their lives, the best of birds, advancing for the sake of the nectar, saw fire blazing on all sides.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It was enveloping the sky on all sides with its great flames, scorching like the fierce-rayed sun, terrible, fanned by the wind.
Then the swift and great-souled Garuḍa, having made ninety times ninety mouths, drank up rivers with those mouths and returned again with great speed.
That scorcher of enemies, the chariot of feathers, extinguished the blazing fire with those rivers. Then, wishing to enter and having quenched the fire, he assumed a different, small form.
The Sūta said: Becoming made of pure gold, blazing brilliantly with rays of light, the bird forcefully entered like a current of water rushing into the ocean.
He saw near the nectar a wheel rimmed with razor-sharp blades, whirling ceaselessly, of keen edge, made of iron.
Blazing with the radiance of fire and sun, terrible, a cutter-down of those who would steal the Soma — that device of most terrible form had been skillfully constructed by the gods.
The sky-traveller, perceiving the gaps in it, began to revolve; contracting his body in an instant, he darted through the spaces between the spokes.
Below the wheel, in that place, were two serpents of most fearsome kind — their tongues like lightning, their faces blazing, their eyes blazing — shining with the radiance of a blazing fire.
Those best of serpents, possessed of poison in their very gaze, of great heroism, perpetually enraged, and swift — he saw them stationed there for the very purpose of guarding the nectar.
Their eyes always inflamed, their gaze forever unwinking — whomever even one of the two looked upon would instantly be reduced to ashes.
Suparṇa swiftly blinded the eyes of the two with dust; his own form unseen, he then assailed them on all sides.
Mounting upon the bodies of the two, the sky-ranger, son of Vinatā, swiftly cut them down in the middle; then he rushed toward the Soma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That powerful and heroic son of Vinatā then tore out the nectar, and having shattered the device, he leaped upward with great speed.
Without drinking the nectar, the powerful bird, swiftly grasping it, departed without fatigue — that sky-traveller who was able to obscure the brilliance of the sun.
Then in the sky the son of Vinatā met Viṣṇu; Nārāyaṇa was pleased with him for that act of freedom from greed.
The imperishable god said to that sky-traveller, "I am a granter of boons." That sky-ranger chose: "May I always dwell above you."
And he spoke these words to Nārāyaṇa once more: "May I be free from old age and immortal even without the nectar."
Having received those two boons, Garuḍa said to Viṣṇu: "I also grant a boon to you; let the Blessed Lord choose as well."
Kṛṣṇa chose the mighty Garutmān as his mount; and the Blessed Lord made him his banner, saying to him: "You shall abide above me."
Chasing the bird, Indra struck him on the body with his vajra — that sky-ranger, that enemy of the gods, who was carrying away the nectar by force.
Thus struck by the vajra, Garuḍa, the best of fliers, spoke to Indra with a laugh and with gentle words:
"I shall honor the sage from whose bones the vajra was made; and I shall show honour to the vajra itself and to you as well, O Śatakratu."
"I now shed a single feather the end of which you shall never find; for the fall of the vajra has never caused me any pain at any time."
There all living beings, astonished, spoke at that time upon beholding that beautiful bird: 'Let this be Suparṇa.'
And seeing that marvel, Sahasrākṣa, the destroyer of cities, reflecting that this bird is a great being, addressed him.
'I wish to know the strength that is supreme and unsurpassed in you, and I desire an eternal friendship with you, O best of birds.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Garuḍa said: 'Let there be friendship between you and me, O god, as you wish, O Purandara. But know my strength to be great and truly unbearable.'
'Indeed, the virtuous do not commend self-praise of one's own strength, nor the recounting of one's own virtues by oneself, O Śatakratu.'
'But since you, O friend, treating me as a friend have asked me, I shall tell you; for that which is mixed with self-praise ought not to be spoken without reason.'
'This broad earth with its mountains and forests, and this ocean with its forests, and you yourself clinging here — all this with a single sinew of my wing, O Śakra —'
'— or all the worlds gathered together with their stationary and moving beings, I could carry without fatigue. Know this to be my great strength.'
The Sūta said: To that hero who had spoken thus, O Śaunaka, the diadem-wearer, best of the glorious, the lord Indra, benefactor of all beings, replied.
'Let this supreme and eternal friendship of mine be accepted now. You have no need of the Soma; give the Soma to me — for those from whom you would give it would trouble us.'
Garuḍa said: 'For a certain reason I am carrying this Soma. I will not give it to anyone whatsoever to take away.'
'But wherever I myself set it down, O Sahasrākṣa, then you swiftly take it away, O lord of the thirty gods.'
Śakra said: 'I am pleased by this speech you have spoken here, O born-of-an-egg. Whatever boon you desire from me, take it, O best of birds.'
The Sūta said: Thus addressed, he replied thus, remembering the sons of Kadrū, and also recalling the deception done regarding his mother's enslavement.
'I am master of all, and I shall fulfil your request as well. O Śakra, may the mighty serpents become my food.'
Having said 'So be it,' the slayer of demons then followed him, saying to him: 'I shall take the Soma once it is set down.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Suparṇa came swiftly to his mother's side, and then addressed all the serpents thus, with great joy.
'This amṛta I have brought I shall place on the kuśa grass for you. Having bathed and performed auspicious rites, then eat it, O serpents.'
'And this mother shall be a slave no longer; from this day let her be free to me. The word I gave to you has been fulfilled.'
Then the serpents went to bathe, having replied to him 'So be it.' And Śakra, snatching up the amṛta, returned again to the triple heaven.
Then the serpents, desiring the Soma, came to that spot — having bathed, performed their recitations, joyful, and having performed auspicious rites.
The serpents, knowing that it had been taken away and that it was a mere semblance, and that this was the place where the Soma had been, then licked the kuśa grass.
Thereupon, by that act, the tongues of the serpents became forked. And those blades of kuśa grass, from the touch of the amṛta, became sacred.
Then Suparṇa, supremely joyful, having sported with his mother in that forest — the devourer of serpents, greatly honoured by the birds, his glory unblemished — made Vinatā rejoice.
Whoever constantly hears this tale or recites it in an assembly of leading brāhmaṇas shall, without doubt, attain the triple heaven, gaining merit through the glorification of the great-souled lord of birds.
Śaunaka said: 'The cause of the curse on the serpents, and of the mother and her son, and of Vinatā, O son of a Sūta, you have narrated.'
'The granting of boons by the husband to Kadrū and Vinatā, and also the names of the two birds born of Vinatā, have been told by you.'
'But the names of the serpents you do not recite, O son of a Sūta. We wish to hear the principal names as well.'
The Sūta said: 'Because of the great number of names of the serpents, O wealth of asceticism, I shall not recite all of them. Hear from me only the principal ones.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śeṣa was born first, then Vāsuki; and Airāvata, Takṣaka, and Karkoṭaka and Dhanaṃjaya.
Kālīya and Maṇināga, and the serpent Apūraṇa, and also the serpent Piñjaraka, then Elāpatra and Vāmana.
The two serpents Nīla and Anīla, and also Kalmāṣa and Śabala, and Āryaka and Ādika, and also the serpent Śalapotaka.
Sumanomukha and Dadhimukha, and also Vimalapiṇḍaka; Āpta and also Koṭanaka, Śaṅkha and Vālaśikha as well.
Niṣṭhyūnaka, Hemaguha, Nahuṣa and Piṅgala, Bāhyakarṇa and Hastipada, and also Mudgarapiṇḍaka.
Kambala and Aśvatara, and also the serpent Kālīyaka, and the two serpents Vṛtta and Saṃvartaka, and two known as the Padmas.
The serpent Śaṅkhanaka, and also another named Sphaṇḍaka; the great serpent Kṣemaka and the serpent Piṇḍāraka as well.
Karavīra, Puṣpadaṃṣṭra, Eḷaka, Bilvapāṇḍuka, Mūṣakāda, Śaṅkhaśiras, Pūrṇadaṃṣṭra, and Haridraka.
Aparājita, Jyotika the serpent, and Śrīvaha; Kauravya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Puṣkara, and also Śalyaka.
Virajā, Subāhu, and the mighty Śālipiṇḍa, Hastibhadra, Pīṭharaka, Mukhara, and Koṇavāsana.
Kuñjara, Kurara, and also the serpent Prabhākara, Kumuda and Kumudākṣa, Tittiri and Halika, and both Karkara and Akarkara, and Kuṇḍodara and Mahodara.
These serpents have been named in order of prominence, O best of twice-born. Because of the great number of names, the others have not been recited.
The offspring of these, and the lineages of those offspring — regarding them I do not speak, O best of twice-born, deeming them to be without number.
Many thousands, millions, and tens of millions here — truly impossible to count — are the serpents, O wealth of asceticism.
Śaunaka said: 'Indeed the serpents were born, O dear one, mighty and unapproachable. But having come to know that curse, what did they do next?'
The Sūta said: Among them, the blessed Śeṣa of great renown, abandoning Kadrū, undertook vast austerities, living on air, with restrained vows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Reaching Gandhamādana, and Badarī, intent on asceticism; at Gokarṇa, in the forest of Puṣkara, and on the slopes of the Himālayas.
In those various holy tīrthas and sacred shrines, living in solitude, disciplined, constantly, with his senses conquered.
The Grandfather beheld him practising terrible austerities — the lord, his flesh, skin, and sinews withered, wearing matted locks and bark garments.
The Grandfather spoke to him, holding to truth, as he performed austerities: 'What is this you are doing, Śeṣa? Ensure the well-being of living creatures.'
'For with your fierce austerity you cause affliction to living creatures, O sinless one. Tell me your desire, O Śeṣa — that which has long been lodged in your heart.'
Śeṣa said: 'All my brothers from the same mother are of dull mind. I have no desire to live with them — may Your Honour consent to this.'
'They constantly envy one another like enemies; therefore I practise austerity, thinking: may I not see them.'
'They constantly do not endure Vinatā and her son, and our other brother Vainateya, O Grandfather.'
'They hate him exceedingly, and he too is of very great strength, by virtue of the boon from his father, the great-souled Kaśyapa.'
'Therefore I, having undertaken austerity, shall abandon this body — so that even after death there may be no association with them for me.'
Brahmā said: 'I know, O Śeṣa, the conduct of all your brothers. And from the fault of your mother there is indeed great danger for your brothers.'
'And a remedy has already been arranged here beforehand, O serpent. For all of your brothers, you ought not to grieve.'
'And choose a boon from me, O Śeṣa, whatever you desire. For I will grant you a boon today; my pleasure in you is supreme.'
'By good fortune your mind is fixed on dharma, O best of serpents. Therefore may your mind be firmly stable in dharma even more.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śeṣa said: 'This very thing is the boon I desire today, O Great-grandfather: may my mind delight in dharma, in tranquillity, and in austerity, O Lord.'
Brahmā said: 'I am pleased by this self-restraint and tranquillity of yours, O Śeṣa. But this task must be done by you, by my command, for the welfare of living beings.'
'This earth adorned with mountains and forests, with its oceans, with its towns and cities — O Śeṣa, support it properly as it trembles, so that it may be steady.'
Śeṣa said: 'As the god, the granter of boons, the lord of beings, the lord of the earth, the lord of the world commands, so shall I hold the earth steady. Place it upon my head, O Lord of beings.'
Brahmā said: 'Go beneath the earth, O best of serpents — she herself will give you an opening. By you holding this earth up, a great favour will be done for me, O Śeṣa.'
The Sūta said: Having said 'So be it,' he entered the opening. That lord of the earth, the foremost of the best of serpents, stands there, bearing on his head this goddess Earth, grasping her with her ocean-rim on all sides.
Brahmā said: 'You are Śeṣa, O best of serpents, the god of dharma. You alone bear this earth with your infinite coils encompassing it all — even as I do, even as Balabhit does.'
The Sūta said: Thus the serpent Ananta, powerful in might, dwells beneath the earth, holding the earth alone, the mighty one, by Brahmā's command.
And the blessed Grandfather, best of the immortals, then granted Suparṇa, the son of Vinatā, as a friend to Ananta.
The Sūta said: Having heard that curse from their mother, the best of serpents, Vāsuki, began to think: 'How may this curse not come to pass?'
Then he took counsel on all sides with his brothers led by Airāvata — those who were devoted to dharma.
Vāsuki said: 'This curse as declared you all know, O sinless ones. For the sake of release from that curse, having deliberated, let us strive.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'For all curses there is a counter-remedy; yet there may be no release for those who have been cursed by their own mother, O serpents.'
'Upon hearing that we were cursed in the presence of the Imperishable, the Immeasurable, and Truth itself, a trembling arises in my heart.'
'Surely this our complete destruction has been proclaimed. For that imperishable god did not restrain her as she cursed.'
'Therefore let us deliberate here on the welfare of the serpents, so that it may be for all of us; let not this time pass us by.'
'Even while deliberating we may perceive a means for deliverance — just as the gods once found the hidden fire that had entered a cave.'
'Such that that sacrifice may not take place, or such that it may be defeated — the sacrifice of Janamejaya that is the instrument of the serpents' destruction.'
The Sūta said: Saying 'So be it,' all those sons of Kadrū assembled together and made a compact there — skilled in the wisdom of counsel.
Some of the serpents there said: 'Let us become foremost brāhmaṇas and beg Janamejaya, saying: may your sacrifice not take place.'
But other serpents there, fancying themselves learned, said: 'All of us shall become his trusted ministers, well esteemed.'
He will ask us to determine the purpose in all matters; there we shall offer our counsel so that the sacrifice may be averted.
Knowing us, who are well esteemed, to be the best among the wise, that king will clearly ask us for the sake of the sacrifice — and we shall say: no.
Showing many terrible faults pertaining to the next world and to this one, with reasons and grounds, we shall argue that the sacrifice should not take place.
Or, whoever shall be the officiating priest at that rite — one who knows the ritual procedure of the serpent sacrifice and is devoted to serving the king's interest —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let some serpent go and bite him; he shall die. When that performer of the sacrifice is slain, the rite shall not proceed.
And whatever other priests versed in the serpent sacrifice shall serve as his officiants — we shall bite them all; thus the deed will be accomplished.
Then other serpents of righteous soul deliberated there: "This is foolishness on your part — the slaying of a brahmin is not a thing of merit."
"For calm in adversity, rooted properly in right conduct, is the highest good; but dominance of unrighteousness would destroy the entire world."
Other serpents then said: "Becoming clouds with lightning, we shall quench the blazing sacrificial fire with rain."
"Or let other excellent serpents go by night and swiftly steal the ladles and sacrificial vessels from the heedless attendants — thus the obstruction will be accomplished."
"Or let serpents at that sacrifice, in hundreds and thousands, bite all the people — thus terror will come about."
"Or let the serpents defile the prepared food with their own urine and excrement, destroying all the food."
Others said there: "Let us become his priests; we will obstruct the sacrifice — let fees be given." And having come under our sway, he will act as we desire.
Others said there: "Let us seize the king while he is sporting in the water, bring him home, and bind him — thus the rite shall not take place."
Other serpents who were doers of good deeds said there: "Let us quickly seize and bite him — thus the deed will be accomplished. When he is dead, the root of our misfortunes will be severed."
"This indeed is the final counsel agreed upon by all; or as you, O lord, may think best — let that be arranged quickly."
Having spoken thus, they all looked toward Vāsuki, the lord of serpents; and Vāsuki too, having reflected, spoke to those serpents.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This final counsel of yours is not what I consider should be done, O serpents; none of these plans of all the serpents pleases me."
"But what is to be arranged here for the benefit of all of you — I am greatly tormented by this, since both the merits and the defects rest with me."
The Sūta said: Having heard the words of all of them — the various proposals — and having heard the speech of Vāsuki, Elāpatra spoke thus.
"That sacrifice will not fail to take place; nor will that king be otherwise — Janamejaya the Pāṇḍava descendant, from whom comes our great fear."
"A man who is struck by fate, O king, must take shelter in fate alone — there is no other recourse in that matter."
"This fear of ours is thus from fate, O best of serpents; let us take shelter in fate alone in this matter — and hear my words."
"When the curse was being uttered, I heard those words at that time, seated in fear on our mother's lap, O best of serpents."
"O best among serpents, O lord of great splendor, the gods, afflicted with grief, approached the Grandfather, saying 'The fierce ones, the fierce ones!'"
The gods said: "Who indeed, having obtained beloved sons, would curse them thus, O Grandfather, except Kadrū of fierce nature — before you, O god of gods?"
"And you too uttered the words 'So be it' to her speech, O Grandfather — this we wish to understand: what is the reason why she was not restrained?"
Brahman said: "Many serpents are fierce, of terrible might, and overflowing with venom; wishing for the welfare of living beings, I did not restrain her at that time."
"Those that bite, the vile ones that walk in evil and overflow with venom — their destruction will come; but not those who walk in righteousness."
"And the reason for the deliverance of those serpents from that great fear — hear that now, when the time has come."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In the clan of the Yāyāvaras, a great wise sage shall arise, famed as Jaratkāru, of brilliant energy, with subdued senses."
"His son, born of Jaratkāru, of great austerity, named Āstīka, shall stop that sacrifice at that time; and there the serpents who shall be righteous will be released."
The gods said: "That chief of sages, O god, Jaratkāru of great austerity — upon whom shall that mighty one, valiant in power, beget his great-souled son?"
Brahman said: "Upon a maiden of the same name as himself, O gods — that best of twice-born, that mighty one, shall beget an offspring equal in valor."
Elāpatra said: "'So be it,' the gods said to that Grandfather; and having spoken thus, the gods departed, and so did that divine Grandfather."
"I thus foresee this, O Vāsuki: your sister who is known as Jaratkāru — give her to him."
"To the sage of holy vows who will come begging like a mendicant, give her for the pacification of the serpents' fear — this deliverance I heard of."
The Sūta said: O best of twice-born, having heard the words of Elāpatra, all the serpents, with rejoicing hearts, honored him saying "Well said, well said!"
From that time forward Vāsuki carefully guarded that maiden Jaratkāru, his sister; and he experienced the greatest joy.
Then no very great time seemed to pass before all the gods and asuras churned the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa.
There the serpent Vāsuki, best among the mighty, served as the rope; and having completed that labor, they approached the Grandfather.
The gods together with Vāsuki then said to the Grandfather: "O blessed one, this Vāsuki, afraid of the curse, is greatly tormented."
"You should remove this mental anguish arising from his mother's curse, O god — he who desires the welfare of his kinsmen."
"For this king of serpents has always been helpful and dear to us; show your grace, O lord of gods, and quench the fever of his mind."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Brahman said: "That which was declared to him long ago by the serpent Elāpatra — that very word was dispensed by my own mind, O immortals."
"Let this lord of serpents carry out that word which has come to its appointed time; the evil ones will perish, but not those who walk in righteousness."
"That twice-born Jaratkāru, devoted to fierce austerity, has been born; let this one give him his sister Jaratkāru at the proper time."
"What was spoken at that time by the serpent Elāpatra, O gods — that is for the benefit of the serpents; it is so and not otherwise."
The Sūta said: Hearing these words of the Grandfather, that lord of serpents then stationed many serpents, always engaged, to watch over Jaratkāru.
"When the mighty Jaratkāru wishes to choose a wife, come quickly and inform me — that will be for our good."
Śaunaka said: "O son of the Sūta, you have mentioned the name Jaratkāru — I wish to hear about that great-souled sage."
"For what reason is this name Jaratkāru renowned on earth? You should properly explain the derivation of the name Jaratkāru."
The Sūta said: "'Jarā' they call a terrible wasting away; 'kāru' denotes the body — he had such a body; and that wise one, little by little,
wore it away through fierce austerity — therefore he is called Jaratkāru, O brahmin; and likewise Vāsuki's sister."
Thus addressed, the righteous-souled Śaunaka laughed, and having acknowledged Ugraśravas, said "Well answered."
The Sūta said: Then, for a great length of time, that sage of sharpened vow, the wise one devoted to austerity, did not desire a wife.
That great-souled one, practicing upward retention of seed, absorbed in austerity, devoted to sacred study, free from fear and weariness, wandered over the whole earth; and he did not desire a wife even in his mind.
Then, at another time that arrived, there was a king renowned as Parīkṣit, the upholder of the Kaurava lineage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Just as the mighty-armed Pāṇḍu, the foremost archer on earth, was fond of hunting — so was his great-grandfather of old.
Piercing deer, boars, hyenas, buffaloes, and other various forest creatures, that lord of the earth wandered about.
Once, having wounded a deer with a straight-jointed arrow, he gave chase into the dense forest, bow in hand.
Just as the blessed Rudra, having wounded the sacrifice-deer in the sky, followed after it with bow in hand, searching here and there.
For a deer once wounded by him does not go away alive into the forest; but this was surely a portent of his going to heaven — the deer that was wounded and vanished on that king Parīkṣit.
Led far away by that deer, that lord of the earth, exhausted and suffering from thirst, came upon a sage in the forest.
He was seated in the cow-pasture, largely consuming the foam flowing from the mouths of calves drinking milk.
Running swiftly toward that sage of sharpened vow, the king, raising his bow and afflicted with hunger and fatigue, asked him.
"Ho there, O brahmin! I am the king Parīkṣit, son of Abhimanyu. A deer I wounded has gone missing — have you perhaps seen it?"
That sage, observing his vow of silence, said nothing at all to him; so the angry king placed a dead serpent on his shoulder with the tip of his bow.
Lifting it up with the tip of his bow, he looked at him, but spoke not a word to him — neither auspicious nor inauspicious.
That king, having cast off his anger, and distressed at seeing him in that condition, went to the city; the sage remained sitting just as he was.
He had a young son of sharp energy and great austerity, named Śṛṅgī, of great wrath, hard to appease, and of mighty vows.
He regularly attended upon the supreme lord Brahman, the divine one devoted to the welfare of all beings, with complete self-restraint; and having been given leave by that Brahman, he went home.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O best of twice-born, as he was coming, he was addressed in jest by a playful, laughing friend — the son of a sage named Kṛśa, who was extremely hot-tempered, wrathful, and like venom, the sage's son.
"Your father, though so energetic and such an ascetic, carries a corpse on his shoulder — do not be so proud, O Śṛṅgī."
"Do not speak any such words to the sons of sages — to the accomplished ones, the knowers of Brahman, the ascetics such as we are."
"Where is your self-importance now? Where are such words of yours, born of arrogance — you whose father you shall see carrying a corpse like that?"
The Sūta said: Thus addressed, that energetic Śṛṅgī, filled with anger, hearing that his teacher was carrying a dead thing, was consumed with fury.
Looking at that Kṛśa and suppressing a kind reply, he asked: "How is it that my father is today a carrier of a dead thing?"
Kṛśa said: "Dear friend, the king Parīkṣit, while ranging about on a hunt, today hung a dead serpent on your father's shoulder."
Śṛṅgī said: "What wrong did my father do to that evil-souled king? Tell me truthfully, O Kṛśa — and witness the power of my austerity."
Kṛśa said: That king Parīkṣit, son of Abhimanyu, having gone out hunting, chased a deer alone after wounding it with a feathered arrow.
Not finding the deer as he roamed that great forest, the king, upon seeing your father, questioned him — though he was one who did not speak.
Him standing there motionless as a post, the king — exhausted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue — questioned your father again and again about the lost deer.
But he, bound by his vow of silence, did not answer him at all; and the king, with the tip of his bow, placed a dead serpent upon his shoulder.
O Śṛṅgin, your father sits just so even now, steadfast in his vow; and that king has returned to his own city, Gajāhvaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Sūta said: Hearing this, the son of the sage stood as though he had struck the sky, his eyes red with rage, blazing as it were with wrath.
Seized by anger, that brilliant one then cursed the king, touching water and overpowered by the force and violence of his fury.
Śṛṅgin said: That sinful king who has thrown a dead serpent upon the shoulder of my aged father while he was in distress —
— that wicked one, Takṣaka the foremost of serpents, venomous-fanged, of fierce brilliance, urged on by the power of my words in great fury,
shall conduct him from this day to the abode of Yama within seven nights — this despiser of brahmins, this disgrace to the Kurus.
The Sūta said: Having thus cursed the king in his anger, Śṛṅgin went to his father, who sat in that grove still bearing the dead serpent.
Seeing his father with the dead serpent still upon his shoulder, Śṛṅgin was filled with grief and anger anew.
From grief he shed tears and spoke these words to his father: "Father, having heard of this insult inflicted upon you by that wicked one —
— by King Parīkṣit, I have in my fury cursed that king with the terrible curse he deserves, the lowest of the Kuru line.
On the seventh day, Takṣaka, the foremost of serpents, shall conduct that wretch to the dreadful abode of Vaivasvata.
His father addressed him, so filled with anger, and said: O brahmin, you have not done what is pleasing to me, my son; this is not the dharma of ascetics.
We dwell in the realm of that king; we are properly protected by him. Therefore I do not approve of his being harmed.
For such as we are, we must always forgive a king acting in any manner, my son — for dharma when destroyed destroys in return; of this there is no doubt.
If the king did not protect us, we would suffer greatly; we would not be able to practise dharma in peace and comfort, my son.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Being protected by kings who act according to the scriptures, we practise abundant dharma, and they too receive a rightful share of that dharma.
Parīkṣit in particular protects us even as his great-grandfather did; he protects his subjects as a king ought to protect them.
By him — wearied today, hungry and fatigued, an ascetic — this was done without knowing my vow. Of this there is no doubt.
Therefore this wrong act has been rashly committed by you out of childishness; for the king in no way deserves a curse from us, my son.
Śṛṅgin said: Whether this was rashness, father, or a wrong deed done, whether it pleases you or not — the word I have spoken is not false.
It shall not be otherwise, father — this I tell you. I do not speak falsehood even in jest; how much less when pronouncing a curse.
Śamīka said: I know you, my son, to be of fierce power and true speech; you have never spoken what is untrue — this too shall not prove false.
Nevertheless, a son, however grown, must always be instructed by his father, so that he may become endowed with virtues and attain great fame.
How much more so when you are but a child, though formed by asceticism, O lord. And indeed the anger of great souls who are powerful grows exceedingly.
So I see that you, O best upholder of dharma, must be spoken to, considering both your filial status and your youth, as well as this rashness of yours.
Therefore, be possessed of calmness, live subsisting on forest food, and abandon this anger — do not thus forsake dharma.
For anger destroys the dharma that ascetics have accumulated through suffering; and those bereft of dharma do not attain the desired goal.
Serenity alone is the cause of perfection for ascetics who possess forbearance; both this world and the next belong to those endowed with forbearance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore conduct yourself always with forbearance as your nature, with senses conquered; through forbearance you shall attain worlds next to that of Brahman.
But I, resorting to calmness, shall do what can be done today — I shall send a messenger to the king this very day.
"You have been cursed by my son, a child of immature understanding, O king, who was provoked to indignation upon witnessing this insult to me inflicted by you."
The Sūta said: Having given these instructions to his disciple, that great ascetic of good vows, moved by compassion, sent him to King Parīkṣit.
Having enjoined him to convey greetings and also to recount the entire matter, he sent the disciple named Gauramukha, a virtuous and composed man.
Quickly approaching the king, the enhancer of the Kuru line, and first being announced by the doorkeepers, he entered the royal palace.
After being duly honoured by the king, the brahmin Gauramukha, having rested, related everything in full to the king — the terrible message of Śamīka just as it was spoken — in the presence of the ministers.
"There lives in your realm, O king of kings, a sage named Śamīka — one of supreme righteous soul, self-restrained, calm, and of great austerity.
O tiger among men, O best of the Bhāratas, a serpent robbed of life was placed by you on his shoulder with the tip of your bow. He himself forgave your act, but his son could not endure it.
You have been cursed by him, O king, without his father's knowledge: Takṣaka shall be your death within seven nights.
'Protect yourself in this matter,' he said again and again; yet it cannot be made otherwise by anyone at all.
For he could not restrain his son overcome by anger; therefore I have been sent by him for your welfare, O king.
Hearing that terrible news, the king, delight of the Kurus, was tormented with remorse for having committed that wrong — the king of great penance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And hearing that the great sage had been observing a vow of silence, the king's heart was again burned with grief.
Recognising too the compassionate nature of Śamīka, he was tormented yet further for having committed that offence against the sage.
For the king did not grieve so much upon hearing of his impending death as he — who was like an immortal — lamented having committed that deed.
The king then sent Gauramukha back with the message: "May the revered one be gracious to me."
And as soon as Gauramukha had departed, the king, with an agitated mind, deliberated with his ministers.
Having decided, together with his ministers, and being expert in the essence of counsel, he had a palace built on a single pillar, well-guarded.
He stationed guards there, as well as physicians with medicines, and brahmins accomplished in mantras, on all sides.
Residing there, he conducted all affairs of state, learned in dharma, and guarded on all sides together with his ministers.
But on the seventh day arriving, O best of brahmins, the learned Kāśyapa came to treat that king.
For it had come to his hearing that today Takṣaka, foremost of serpents, would conduct that best of kings to the abode of Yama.
Thinking to himself: "I shall cure him after he is bitten by the lord of serpents — in that I shall find both profit and merit," he went forth.
But the king of serpents Takṣaka saw Kāśyapa going along the road with single-pointed mind, and assuming the form of a brahmin of advanced age,
the lord of serpents addressed Kāśyapa, foremost of sages: "Where does the venerable one hasten, and what task does he wish to accomplish?"
Kāśyapa said: Takṣaka, foremost of serpents, will today burn with his blazing power the king Parīkṣit, born of the Kuru lineage, the subduer of foes.
Him, bitten by that lord of serpents whose energy equals fire, that king of boundless might, the upholder of the Pāṇḍava lineage — I go, dear one, in haste to cure forthwith.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Takṣaka said: I am that Takṣaka, O brahmin; I shall burn that lord of the earth. Turn back — you are not able to cure one bitten by me.
Kāśyapa said: O serpent, it is my firm conviction that I shall cure that king after he has been bitten by you, relying on the power of my knowledge.
Takṣaka said: If you are able to cure one bitten by me here, then revive this tree that I have bitten, O Kāśyapa.
Display the utmost power of your mantras and exert yourself; I shall burn this banyan tree before your eyes, O foremost of brahmins.
Kāśyapa said: Bite, O king of serpents, whatever tree you have in mind; I shall revive it after you have bitten it, O serpent.
The Sūta said: Thus addressed by the great-souled Kāśyapa, that foremost of serpents, the lord of serpents, approached and bit a banyan tree.
That tree, bitten by him of great brilliance, immediately burst into flames on all sides, suffused with the venom of the poison-fanged serpent.
Having burned that tree, the serpent again addressed Kāśyapa: "Make the effort, O best of brahmins; revive this lord of the forest."
Then, the tree having been reduced to ash by the power of the king of serpents, Kāśyapa gathered all the ash and spoke these words:
"Behold the power of my knowledge upon this lord of the forest, O king of serpents; I shall revive it before your eyes, O serpent."
Then that blessed and learned Kāśyapa, best of brahmins, revived the tree that had been reduced to a heap of ash, by means of his knowledge.
He caused it first to sprout, then to bear two leaves, then to put forth foliage and branches, and then to become a full tree once again.
Seeing the tree restored to life by the great-souled Kāśyapa, Takṣaka said: "O brahmin, this is exceedingly wondrous in you.
O lord of brahmins, you who could neutralise the venom of one like me — what purpose do you seek to gain by going there, O treasury of austerity?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever fruit you desire to obtain from that best of kings, I myself will give you that, even if it be difficult to obtain.
For in the case of a king whose life is waning, overwhelmed by a brahmin's curse, even your best efforts may meet with uncertain success, O brahmin.
And then your fame, blazing and renowned throughout the three worlds, would vanish from here like a sunbeam robbed of its rays.
Kāśyapa said: I go there in desire of wealth — give me that, O serpent; then I shall return home, O best of serpents.
Takṣaka said: I will give you today more than whatever wealth you would seek from that king — turn back, O foremost of brahmins.
The Sūta said: Hearing the words of Takṣaka, that brilliant and wise Kāśyapa, best of brahmins, reflected deeply about the king.
That brilliant one endowed with divine knowledge, having understood that the king, the descendant of Pāṇḍu, had then exhausted his span of life, the sage Kāśyapa turned back — having obtained from Takṣaka as much wealth as he desired.
When that great-souled Kāśyapa had turned away at that moment, Takṣaka swiftly went to the city named after the serpents — Hāstinapura.
And as he went, Takṣaka heard that the lord of the earth was being carefully protected by means of charms, antidotes, and poison-neutralizing medicines.
He then reflected: "By what stratagem of illusion can I deceive this king? What means might there be?"
Then the serpent Takṣaka, taking fruits, leaves, and water, sent other snakes in the guise of ascetics to the king.
Takṣaka said: "Go to the king calmly, on the pretext of a mission, and have the king accept these — fruits, leaves, and water."
The Sūta said: Those snakes, instructed by Takṣaka, did exactly so — they presented to the king darbha grass, water, and fruits.
The mighty king of kings accepted all of it, and having attended to their business, he said to them: "You may go."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When those snakes in the disguise of ascetics had departed, the lord of men spoke to his ministers and friends.
"Let all of you eat these sweet fruits that the ascetics have brought — together with me."
Then the king along with his minister went to take the fruits. In the fruit taken by the king there appeared a tiny worm — small, dark-eyed, and copper-colored, O Śaunaka.
Taking it up, that foremost of kings said to his ministers: "The sun is setting; today I no longer have any fear of poison."
"Let that sage's words prove true — let this little worm bite me, becoming Takṣaka by name; in that way the prophecy shall be fulfilled."
And those ministers followed his lead, driven by fate. Having spoken thus, that king of kings placed the little worm on his neck, laughed aloud, and swiftly he who was near death lost consciousness.
Still laughing, he was coiled by Takṣaka in serpent form, who had emerged from that very fruit — the one that had been presented to the king.
The Sūta said: Seeing him thus encoiled by the serpent, all the ministers, their faces gone pale, wept, overwhelmed with grief.
Hearing that cry, those ministers fled in all directions, and they saw the wondrous serpent moving through the sky.
Overwhelmed with sorrow, they saw Takṣaka, that foremost of serpents, of lotus-like radiance, streaking across the sky as if parting it in two.
Then, as the serpent's venom set the palace ablaze and it burned, they abandoned it in fear and fled in all directions; and it fell like a tree struck by lightning.
When the king was slain by the power of Takṣaka, the pure brahmin who was the royal chaplain, and likewise all the ministers of that king, performed all the rites for the other world.
All the people of the city assembled and made his young son king — that hero of the Kurus whom they called the destroyer of enemies: Janamejaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Even as a child, that foremost of kings, noble-minded and pre-eminent among the bulls of the Kuru line, governed the kingdom together with those ministers and the royal priest, just as his valiant great-grandfather had done.
Then the ministers of that king, seeing him as the scorcher of enemies, approached the Kāśi king Suvarṇavarman and sued for Vapuṣṭamā on his behalf.
Then that king, having examined the match by dharmic standards, gave Vapuṣṭamā to that hero of the Kurus; and the hero, having obtained her, was filled with joy, and never again set his mind on any other woman.
The valiant one sported with a cheerful heart in lakes full of blooms and in forests; that best of kings disported himself just as Purūravas of old had done upon obtaining Urvaśī.
And Vapuṣṭamā too, having obtained that excellent and handsome lord of the earth as husband, delighted him with her love; that beauty of the inner quarters was his joy in all his hours of pleasure.
The Sūta said: At this very time, the sage Jaratkāru of great austerities, who had no fixed home, wandered over the entire earth, sleeping wherever evening found him.
Of great splendor, practising a severe vow of initiation impossible for the undisciplined, he wandered among sacred tirthas, bathing at each holy site.
Living on air alone, taking no food, the sage drying up day by day — he saw his ancestors hanging head-downward in a pit.
They were clinging to a clump of vīraṇa grass of which only a single stalk remained, and a rat that lived in the burrow below was slowly gnawing at that stalk.
Those without food, emaciated and wretched, hanging in the pit and longing for rescue — he approached those miserable ones, himself appearing wretched, and addressed them.
"Who are you, clinging to this clump of vīraṇa grass, now weak because its roots are being eaten by the rat that dwells in the burrow?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Even the one root of this vīraṇa clump that still remains here, this rat is slowly taking away with its sharp teeth."
"Because so little remains, even this will be severed before long; then you will fall head-downward into this very pit."
"Seeing you hanging head-downward and fallen into this dire calamity, grief has arisen in me. What good may I do for you?"
"Tell me without delay whether I can rescue you from this calamity with a quarter, or a third, or even half of my austerities."
"Or perhaps all of you may cross over this difficulty by means of the whole of my austerities — let it be arranged as you wish."
The ancestors said: You are a prosperous celibate student who desires to save us here; but, O foremost of brahmins, this cannot be removed by austerity alone.
"We have the fruit of our austerities, O son, O best among the eloquent; but, O brahmin, we are falling into an impure hell because our lineage is dying out."
"As we hang here, O son, understanding does not come to us — we do not recognize you, though your valor is renowned in the world."
"You are prosperous and greatly blessed; out of compassion you have come and grieve for us who are pitiable and deeply pained. Hear who we are, O brahmin."
"We are the sages called the Yāyāvaras, of sharp vows; we have fallen from the meritorious worlds into this place because our line is dying, O lord."
"Our meritorious austerities are being destroyed, for we have no thread of lineage. There is one thread left to us today, yet it is as good as gone."
"He who is the kinsman of the wretched in our family is himself unfortunate — known as Jaratkāru, versed in the Vedas and their auxiliaries, self-controlled, great-souled, of excellent vows, and of very great austerities."
"By his greed for austerity we have been brought to this calamity. He has no wife, no son, no kinsman whatsoever."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That is why we hang in this pit, our senses lost, like those without a protector. You, having seen our plight, should speak to him on our behalf so that we may have a guardian."
"'Your fathers hang wretched and head-downward in a pit — take a wife and beget offspring, O lord.' For you alone, O wealth of austerity, remain as the single thread of our lineage."
"This clump of vīraṇa grass to which you see us clinging, O brahmin — this was our family-stalk, the one that was to have enlarged our line."
"These roots of this plant that you see here, O brahmin — these are our lineage-threads, O son, consumed by time."
"And that root of it which you see half-gnawed away — to that we all cling; he too is the sole one, and he has taken to austerity."
"The rat you see, O brahmin — that is mighty Time itself; it slowly gnaws and wears away that one devoted to austerities — Jaratkāru, the witless, small-minded one, whose mind is consumed by his greed for austerity."
"For his austerity will not save us, O noble one — we whose roots are cut, who are utterly fallen, whose minds are struck by Time; behold us, destined for hell as though we were evildoers."
"When we have fallen here along with the forefathers before us, he too, cut off by Time, will then go to hell."
"Austerity, or sacrifice, or whatever other great purification there may be — none of it equals progeny: such is the opinion of the good, O son."
"Having seen this, O son, you should speak to the ascetic Jaratkāru; and what you have seen here must be told to him in full."
"So that he may take a wife and beget sons — in that manner, O brahmin, you must address him on our behalf, that we may have a guardian."
The Sūta said: Hearing this, Jaratkāru, overwhelmed with pain and sorrow, spoke to his own ancestors in a voice choked with tears out of grief.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I am that very Jaratkāru — the sinful son who is your offspring. Mete out your punishment to me, the ill-doer, the undisciplined one."
The ancestors said: O son, by good fortune you have arrived at this place by chance. But why, O brahmin, have you not taken a wife?
Jaratkāru said: This thought, O fathers, has always revolved in my heart: as an upward-semened celibate I would convey this body to the next world.
"But having seen you hanging thus like birds, O forefathers, my mind has been turned away from celibacy."
"I will do what you wish and take a wife — there is no doubt in this — if ever I shall find a maiden who shares my name."
"And she who is freely offered, as if in alms — I will accept her; but one whom I would have to maintain, her I will not take."
"If I can find such a match, I will enter householder life; otherwise I will not — this is my truth, O forefathers."
The Sūta said: Having thus spoken to his ancestors, the sage wandered the earth; yet he found no wife, O Śaunaka, for people said: "This one is too old."
When he had fallen into despondency, yet urged on by his ancestors as well, he went into a forest and cried out loudly in deep anguish.
"Whatever beings there are in this place — moving or unmoving, or those that are hidden — let them hear my words."
"My ancestors, though I abide in fierce austerity, urge me in their distress: 'Take a wife.' Desiring to do what is dear to them, I speak."
"I wander the entire earth seeking a maiden given as alms for the purpose of establishing a household; I am a poor man, of a sorrowful nature, set to this task by my ancestors."
"Whatever being has a maiden among those I have here proclaimed — let them give her to me as I roam in all directions."
"Let them give me that maiden who shares my name and who is offered as if in alms, and whom I will not have to maintain — give me that maiden."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the serpents who were attentive to Jaratkāru's affairs took that intelligence and reported it to Vāsuki.
Hearing their report, that lord of serpents took that maiden adorned with ornaments and went with her into the forest, to the vicinity of that sage.
There Vāsuki, the king of serpents, offered that maiden to that great-souled one as if in alms; but O brahmin, he did not accept her.
He thought her name was not the same as his; and with the question of maintenance unresolved, being one who stood in a state of liberation, he was of two minds about accepting.
Then he asked the name of the maiden, O joy of the Bhṛgu line, and he said to Vāsuki: "I will not maintain her."
The Sūta said: Then Vāsuki spoke these words to the sage Jaratkāru: "This maiden is your namesake — she is my sister, endowed with austerities."
"I will maintain your wife — accept her, O foremost of twice-born; and I will protect her with all my power, O treasure of austerity."
When the serpent had promised "I will maintain my sister," Jaratkāru then went to the dwelling of the serpent.
There, that foremost knower of mantras, great in austerity, of mighty vows, righteous-souled, took her hand according to the prescribed rites preceded by sacred formulas.
Then, taking his wife and praised by great sages, he went to the bright dwelling sanctioned by the lord of serpents.
There a bed was prepared, covered with splendid coverings; and there Jaratkāru dwelt together with his wife.
That best of men made a covenant with his wife there: "What is displeasing to me must never be done, nor ever spoken."
"For if you displease me, I shall abandon you and leave this house of yours. Take to heart this word I have now spoken."
Then the sister of the serpent lord, deeply agitated and filled with great sorrow, said to him: "So be it."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And that illustrious woman, ever wishing to please him, tended her difficult-tempered husband by every cautious and discreet means.
Then once, after her purificatory bath at the proper season, the sister of Vāsuki duly approached her husband, the great sage.
Then within her a child was conceived, blazing like fire, endowed with great ascetic power, brilliant as Vaiśvānara; and it grew like the moon in the bright fortnight.
Then after some days Jaratkāru of great austerity, resting his head in her lap, fell into deep sleep as though exhausted.
And while that foremost of brahmins slept, the sun moved toward its setting mountain at the close of the day, O brahmin; then Vāsuki's sister, that wise woman, became fearful of a lapse in religious duty and began to reflect.
"Would it be right for me to wake my husband, or not? He is righteous yet difficult-tempered — how can I not offend him?"
"Either the wrath of this righteous man, or else a lapse in his religious duty — a lapse in religious duty is certainly the graver of the two": thus she resolved in her mind.
"If I wake him, he will certainly be angry; but if the twilight prayer is missed, there will certainly be a breach of his religious duty."
Having thus resolved in her mind, that serpent-woman Jaratkāru, the sweet-spoken one, gently addressed the reclining sage of blazing austerity in these words.
"Arise, O greatly blessed one — the sun is setting. O lord, touch water and observe the twilight worship, you who are strict in your vows."
"This is the hour when the fire-sacrifice is kindled, both lovely and awesome; and now the twilight prayer begins in the western quarter, O master."
Thus addressed, the venerable Jaratkāru of great austerity, his lips quivering, spoke these words to his wife.
"This is an insult you have offered me, O serpent-woman. I will not stay with you any longer; I shall go the way I came."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For it is my firm conviction that while I sleep, the sun Vibhāvasu has no power to set at its proper time, O fair-thighed one."
"Nor would it please anyone who has been insulted to remain here — least of all one of righteous conduct such as I, of my disposition."
When Jaratkāru was thus addressed by her husband, Vāsuki's sister spoke with a trembling heart in that dwelling.
"It was not out of disrespect that I woke you; I did this so that there might be no breach of your religious duty, O brahmin."
Thus addressed by his wife, the great sage Jaratkāru of mighty austerity, seized by anger and resolved to abandon the serpent-woman, spoke.
"My word does not speak falsehood — I shall depart, O serpent-woman. For this was the covenant I made with you from the beginning."
"I have dwelt here in happiness, O auspicious one. Tell your brother, O timid one: 'That venerable one has departed from here.' And after I have gone, you too should not grieve."
Thus addressed, the blameless-limbed Jaratkāru, overwhelmed with worry and grief, replied to her husband Jaratkāru.
With a voice choked with tears, a face pale and dry, eyes brimming with tears, hands folded in supplication, that woman of fair limbs steadied herself with composure though her heart was trembling.
"O knower of dharma, you should not abandon me who am without fault, who stands firm in dharma, who is ever devoted to your welfare and happiness."
"And the purpose for which I was given to you, O best of twice-born ones — if I have not achieved that, what will Vāsuki say to wretched me?"
"The offspring longed for from you for the sake of my kinsmen who are oppressed by their mother's curse, O excellent one — that too has not yet come to be seen."
"Through the gaining of offspring from you, wellbeing would come to my kinsmen; let not this union with you be fruitless for me, O twice-born one."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Wishing the welfare of my kinsmen, O venerable one, I entreat you — having planted in me this child whose form is not yet manifest, O best of men, how can you, being a great soul, wish to abandon me who am without fault?"
Thus addressed, the sage Jaratkāru, wealth of austerity, spoke an apt and fitting word to his wife.
"This child exists within you, O fortunate one, comparable to Vaiśvānara — a seer of supreme righteousness, versed in the Vedas and all their branches."
Having spoken thus, that righteous-souled great sage Jaratkāru, firmly resolved, departed again for severe austerities.
The Sūta said: As soon as her husband had departed, Jaratkāru quickly came to her brother and told him the truth of what had happened, O wealth of austerity.
Then that foremost of serpents, having heard the deeply grievous news, spoke to his dejected sister, himself more dejected still.
"You know, dear one, what purpose was to be served and the reason you were given — whether a son would be born to you from him for the welfare of the serpents."
"That valiant one will surely rescue us from the serpent sacrifice — so did the grandfather formerly tell me, together with the gods."
"Is there indeed a child in you from that best of sages, O fortunate one? I do not want the act of marriage of that wise one to have been fruitless."
"Indeed it is not proper for me to question you on such a matter; but because the urgency of the task is paramount, I have thus pressed you."
"Knowing the difficult nature of your husband, that most austere one, I will not go after him — for he might curse me."
"Tell me, dear one, everything your husband did. Remove this terrible thorn that has long been lodged in my heart, O dear one."
Then Jaratkāru, thus addressed, replied with words comforting the afflicted Vāsuki, lord of serpents.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When I asked him for the sake of offspring, that great soul of mighty austerity said 'it exists,' pointing to my womb, and then he departed."
"Even in casual speech I do not recall him ever saying anything false — how then, O king, would he speak falsely in a matter of such consequence?"
"You must not grieve regarding the purpose, O serpent lord — your nephew will be born, blazing with the radiance of fire and sun."
"Having said this to me, O brother, my husband went to the forest of austerities; therefore let this great sorrow that lodges in your mind depart."
Having heard this, that lord of serpents Vāsuki accepted his sister's words with great joy, saying "So be it."
That foremost of serpents honored his sister born of the same womb with comforting words, gifts, and fitting reverence.
Then that child of mighty radiance, brilliant as the sun, grew in the womb — like the moon risen in the bright fortnight in the sky, O foremost of twice-born ones.
In due time, O brahmin, that sister of the serpent gave birth to a boy who resembled the embryo of a god, the remover of his father's and mother's fear.
And he grew up there in the dwelling of the serpent king; he mastered the Vedas along with their branches from the Bhārgava, the son of Cyavana.
Even as a boy he observed his vows, endowed with wisdom, courage, and virtue; and his name became known throughout the worlds as Āstīka.
Because his father departed for the forest saying 'it exists' even while he was still in the womb, therefore his name became celebrated as Āstīka.
While still a boy he moved about there, that one of boundless intellect, carefully guarded and protected in the house of the serpent king.
Growing up like the venerable lord of the gods, the trident-bearer, the bestower of gold, he filled all those serpents with joy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śaunaka said: What king Janamejaya then asked his ministers regarding his father's passing to heaven — tell me that again in full.
The Sūta said: Listen, O brahmin, to how the ministers, being questioned by the king, all narrated the death of Parīkṣit.
Janamejaya said: You gentlemen know how my father conducted himself and how that greatly renowned one met his death in due time.
"For having heard from you the full account of my father's life and conduct, I shall pursue what is good and never what is contrary to it."
The Sūta said: Then the ministers, questioned by that great-souled one, those learned men versed in all dharma, spoke their words to king Janamejaya.
"Your father was righteous-souled, great-souled, a protector of his subjects — hear how that great soul conducted himself here."
"That king, knowing dharma, protected the four social orders established in their own duties, ruling righteously — as though dharma incarnate."
"That glorious one of incomparable valor protected this noble earth; he had no enemies, nor did he hate anyone — equal to all beings, he was like Prajāpati himself."
"Brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, each established in their proper duties and contented in mind, O king, were well governed by that king."
"He cared for widows, the helpless, the wretched, and the disabled; that fair-looking one was like a second moon to all beings."
"His people were content and well-fed; that glorious king was true of speech and firm in valor; he was a student of the science of archery under Śāradvatī's son."
"Your father was dear to Govinda, O Janamejaya, and that greatly renowned one was dear to all the world."
"When the Kurus were all but extinct, he was born of Uttarā; through him, that mighty son of Saubhadra's line, Parīkṣit came to be."
"Skilled in royal dharma and statecraft, endowed with every virtue, that king had conquered his senses, was self-possessed, intelligent, and attended upon by elders."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Master of the six categories, of great intellect, supremely versed in policy and dharma — your father protected these subjects for sixty years, then met his fated end, which could not be turned aside, through a serpent."
"Then you, O best of men, rightfully obtained this kingdom that has come down through the Kuru lineage — you were born noble, a protector of all beings, even as a child."
Janamejaya said: In this family there never was a king who was not a benefactor and beloved of his subjects — as one sees by looking at the great conduct of our forefathers who were utterly devoted to right conduct.
"How did such a father of mine meet his death? Tell me truly; I wish to hear it in full."
The Sūta said: Thus urged by the king, all those ministers, devoted to the welfare of their lord, spoke the full account to the king.
"Your father, O king, was always fond of the hunt, like the greatly blessed Pāṇḍu — the foremost of bow-bearers in battle — entrusting all royal affairs entirely to us."
"Once, while roaming the forest, he pierced a deer with an arrow, and after wounding it, he swiftly pursued that deer into the dense jungle."
"Going on foot, sword belted at his side, quiver of arrows strapped on, your father could not find the deer that had vanished in the thicket."
"Exhausted, advanced in years, sixty years old and feeling the weight of age, and hungry, he spotted a sage close by in the great forest."
That king, best among kings, questioned the sage who was bound by a vow of silence; but the sage did not say anything to him, even though he was being asked.
Then the king, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, came immediately under the sway of anger toward that sage who stood like a post, observing his vow of silence, calm and quiet.
Indeed the king did not understand that the sage was observing a vow of silence; possessed by anger, your father insulted him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Lifting a dead serpent from the ground with the tip of his bow, he placed it on the shoulder of that pure-souled one, O best of the Bhāratas.
But that wise sage said nothing to him — neither good nor ill — he remained just as he was, neither angry, carrying the serpent on his shoulder.
The ministers said: Then that king, O best of kings, having placed the serpent on the shoulder of the sage — emaciated as he was from hunger — returned again to his own city.
But that sage had a son, born of a cow, of great fame, named Śṛṅgī, of great radiance, fierce in energy, and extremely wrathful.
The sage had gone to pay homage to Brahman; having paid his respects and been given leave, Śṛṅgī went there, and at that point he heard from a friend that his father had been insulted by your father in that manner.
That his father was carrying on his shoulder a dead serpent placed there by your father, O Janamejaya, O tiger among the Kurus — the father who had done no wrong.
A great ascetic, the foremost of sages, O king, one who had conquered the senses, pure, and engaged in wondrous action,
whose soul blazed with austerity, who was restrained in his own limbs, of auspicious conduct, of auspicious speech, perfectly steadfast and free from greed,
not petty, without envy, aged, abiding in the vow of silence, a refuge for all beings — such a one had been wronged by your father.
Having heard this, he cursed your father, filled with fury — the son of the sage, of great radiance, though a boy yet superior to elders.
Quickly touching water, he spoke these words in rage, blazing as it were with his fiery energy, directed against your father:
"He who placed a dead serpent on my innocent teacher — Takṣaka the serpent, in wrath, shall lay him low with his venom within seven nights from now. Wicked man, behold the power of my austerity!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus, he went to where his father was; and having seen his father, he reported to him that curse.
And that tiger among sages also sent a messenger to your father: "You have been cursed by my son — be on your guard, O lord of the earth; Takṣaka, O great king, will lay you low with his venom."
Hearing those terrible words, your father, O Janamejaya, was on his guard, terrified of Takṣaka, the foremost of serpents.
Then when the seventh day arrived, the brahmarṣi Kāśyapa wished to go to the king's presence.
Then Takṣaka, lord of serpents, saw Kāśyapa and spoke to him as he was hurrying on his way: "Where does your honour go in such haste, and what deed does he intend to perform?"
Kāśyapa said: There where the king, best of the Kurus, known as Parīkṣit, is to be burned by the serpent Takṣaka — that is where I am going, O twice-born one.
I go to him quickly to cure him at once of his affliction; one protected by me — the serpent shall not harm him.
Takṣaka said: Why do you wish to revive the one bitten by me? Tell me your desire — I will grant it to you today; go to your own home.
The ministers said: He replied to him that he was going there out of desire for wealth; and Takṣaka, honouring that great-souled one, addressed him with conciliatory words:
"Whatever wealth you desire from that king, take even more than that from me and turn back, O sinless one."
Thus addressed by the serpent, Kāśyapa, best among two-footed beings, having received from Takṣaka as much wealth as he desired, turned back.
After the brahmin departed, Takṣaka, approaching in disguise, that king — best of kings, your righteous father —
though he was on guard in his palace, burned him with the fire of his venom; then you, O tiger among men, were consecrated to victory.
All this, seen and heard by us in full, O best of kings, we have related to you in its entirety — this most terrible thing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having heard of this overthrow of the king, O best of rulers, and of this sage Uttaṅka as well, decide now what is to follow.
Janamejaya said: I wish to hear this — what was then the conversation between the lord of serpents and Kāśyapa in the lonely forest wilderness.
By whom was it seen and heard, and how did it reach your ears? Having heard it, I shall then resolve upon a course of action to destroy the serpents.
The ministers said: Listen, O king, as to how this was told to us before — the encounter on the road between the lord of twice-born ones and the lord of serpents.
On that tree, O lord of the earth, some man had previously climbed in search of firewood, to gather dry branches from the forest tree; the serpent and the twice-born one did not notice him sitting there in that tree.
He was reduced to ashes along with that very tree; but by the power of the twice-born one, O best of kings, he was restored to life together with the forest tree.
He went and reported to this city, O best of kings, all that had happened — the entire account of Takṣaka and the twice-born one.
This has been told to you, O king, exactly as it occurred and as we heard it; having heard it, O tiger among kings, do now as you desire.
The Sūta said: Having heard the words of the ministers, king Janamejaya was tormented with grief; afflicted with sorrow, he wrung his hands.
Repeatedly he exhaled long hot sighs; the lotus-eyed king shed tears continuously from both eyes; and the lord of the earth, overwhelmed with grief and sorrow, spoke:
"Having heard these words of yours regarding my father's passage to heaven, my resolve is firm — hear what it is from me.
I think that retribution must follow immediately against the wicked-souled Takṣaka, by whom my father was harmed.
