For had that wicked one, after fulfilling the words of the sage Śṛṅgin and burning the king, gone away — surely my father would be alive.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What would have been lost to him if that king had lived, by the grace of Kāśyapa and by the good counsel of the ministers?
But he, out of delusion, turned away Kāśyapa, the best of twice-born ones, who had come to revive the invincible king.
This is a great transgression by the wicked-souled Takṣaka — that he gave wealth to the brahmin so that the king might not be revived.
Doing what is dear to Uttaṅka, what is greatly dear to myself, and dear to all of you — I shall take vengeance for my father."
The Sūta said: Having spoken thus, that glorious king, approved by his ministers, O brahmin, then undertook the vow for the snake sacrifice — that tiger of the Bhāratas, king Pārikṣita Janamejaya.
Having summoned the household priest and the sacrificial priests, the lord of the earth, gifted in speech, uttered words that were purposeful and apt:
"That evil-minded Takṣaka who harmed my father — how I may retaliate against him: tell me that, gentlemen.
Is the method known to you by which I may bring Takṣaka, the serpent, together with his kinsmen, into the blazing fire?
Just as my father was formerly burned by him with the fire of venom, so too do I wish to burn that wicked serpent."
The priests said: There exists, O king, a great sacrifice ordained by the gods for your purpose; it is known as the Sarpasatra — the snake sacrifice — and is spoken of in the Purāṇas, O king.
"You and no other are the one to perform that sacrifice, O lord of men" — so the Purāṇic authorities declare; and that rite is within our knowledge."
The Sūta said: Thus addressed, that royal seer imagined the serpent Takṣaka already entered into the blazing mouth of the fire god, O good one.
Then the king, knower of sacred formulas, said to those brahmins: "I shall perform that sacrifice — let the materials be assembled for me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then those priests of his, O best of twice-born ones, measured out the ground according to scripture for the purpose of establishing the sacrificial site; all of them were knowers of sacred science, their minds reaching the highest wisdom.
It was endowed with supreme prosperity, delightful, thronged with multitudes of twice-born ones, abundantly rich in wealth and grain, well laid out by the officiating priests.
Having properly constructed the desired sacrificial ground according to rule, they then initiated the king for the attainment of the snake sacrifice.
And there had arisen previously at that snake sacrifice a great portent — a sign that an obstacle to the sacrifice would come.
When the sacrificial ground was being laid out, the master-builder, endowed with intelligence and learned in the science of architecture, spoke these words:
Thus spoke the master-builder, the versed narrator of Purāṇas at that time: "In the place and at the time when this measuring was initiated, owing to a brahmin being the cause, this sacrifice will not be completed."
Having heard this, the king said to the doorkeeper before the time of his initiation: "Let no one unknown to me enter here."
Then the work of the snake sacrifice began according to rule, and the officiating priests went about properly, each in his own assigned duty.
Having put on dark garments, their eyes reddened by smoke, they poured oblations with sacred formulas into the well-kindled fire.
Causing the minds of all serpents to tremble, they summoned all the snakes there into the mouth of fire.
Then the serpents fell into the blazing sacrificial fire, writhing pitifully, calling out to one another.
Some wriggling, others hissing, others coiling — they entered the fire of many colours head-first and tail-first repeatedly.
White ones, black ones, and blue ones — old and young alike — uttering terrible cries, they fell into the blazing fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In this way hundreds of thousands, millions, and tens of millions of serpents were helplessly destroyed, O best of twice-born ones.
Some were there like elephants with their trunks, others with limbs like elephant trunks, others like maddened elephants — all of great body and great strength.
Many of various sizes, of diverse colours, teeming with venom, terrible, like iron clubs, great serpents of great strength — all fell into the fire, tormented by the rod of their mother's words.
Śaunaka said: At that snake sacrifice of the wise king Janamejaya, descendant of the Pāṇḍavas, who were the officiating priests — the greatest of sages?
Who were the attending sages at that dreadful snake sacrifice — so exceedingly producing despair, in that great terror for the serpents?
You ought to relate everything in detail, dear one — for you are known as knowledgeable in the procedure of the snake sacrifice, O son of the Sūta.
The Sūta said: Come, I shall tell you here the names of the wise men who were the officiating priests and attending sages of that king at that time.
There the Hotā priest was the brahmin Caṇḍabhārgava, born in the lineage of Cyavana, renowned as the best among knowers of the Veda.
The Udgātā was the aged and learned brahmin Kautsāryajaimini; the Brahman priest was Śārṅgarava, and the Adhvaryu was Bodhapiṅgala.
Among the attending sages was Vyāsa, accompanied by his sons and disciples; Uddālaka; Śamaṭhaka; and Śvetaketu as the fifth.
Asita and Devala; Nārada and Parvata likewise; Ātreya; the twice-born Kuṇḍajaṭhara; and Kuṭighaṭa as well.
Vātsya; the aged Śrutaśravā, devoted to austerity and self-study; Kahoḍa; Devaśarmā; Maudgalya; and Śamasaubhara.
These and many other Brāhmaṇas of keen vows were the assembly-members at the snake-sacrifice of the son of Parīkṣit.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As the priests were offering oblations at that great rite, the snake-sacrifice, terrible serpents fell there, striking terror into all living creatures.
Streams of fat and marrow flowed from the serpents; and continuously, day and night, a tumultuous smell of burning rose from those that were being consumed.
The sound of those serpents falling and of those hovering in the sky was heard incessantly, as they were consumed with great intensity by the fire.
But Takṣaka, that lord of serpents, hearing that king Janamejaya had been consecrated, fled to the abode of Indra, the Destroyer of Pura.
Then, having told everything that had come to pass, that best of serpents, terror-stricken and conscious of his offence, sought refuge with Indra, the Destroyer of Pura.
Indra, greatly pleased, said to him: "O Takṣaka, O lord of serpents, you have nothing to fear here from that snake-sacrifice under any circumstances."
"The Grandsire was formerly propitiated by me on your behalf; therefore you have nothing to fear — let the fever of your mind depart."
Thus reassured by him, that best of serpents then dwelt in Śakra's mansion, joyful and at ease.
As serpents fell ceaselessly into the fire, Vāsuki, with his retinue much reduced, was greatly distressed and burned with anguish.
A terrible stupor seized Vāsuki, lord of serpents; his heart reeling, he spoke thus to his sister:
"My limbs burn, dear sister; the directions are unclear to me; I am as if sinking in confusion, and my mind seems to whirl."
"My vision spins exceedingly, and my heart seems to burst; today I shall fall helplessly into that blazing fire."
"That sacrifice of Parīkṣit's son is proceeding with intent to destroy us; clearly I too must go to the abode of the king of the dead."
"This is the moment for which you, my sister, were given in marriage to Jaratkāru long ago — protect us now together with all our kindred."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The Grandsire himself previously told me that Āstīka would indeed stop that sacrifice when it was proceeding with the best of serpents as its victim."
"Therefore, dear child, speak today to your own son, that youth revered by the elders, that foremost knower of the Vedas, for the liberation of me and my servants."
The Sūta said: Then Jaratkāru, the female serpent, summoning her own son, spoke these words at the bidding of Vāsuki, king of serpents:
"I was given to your father, my son, by my brother for a purpose; that moment has now arrived — do what is required of you accordingly."
Āstīka said: "For what purpose were you given to my father by my maternal uncle? Tell me the truth of it — having heard, I shall act accordingly."
The Sūta said: Then she, the sister of the king of serpents, Jaratkāru, composed and well-wishing toward her kindred, told him this:
"The mother of all the serpents without exception is known as Kadrū; by her, angered, were her sons cursed — hear the reason for that."
"Uccaiḥśravas, that king of horses — because you did not make him falsely mine in the wager made for Vinatā's sake, my sons, for the sake of enslaving her."
"'At Janamejaya's sacrifice, the fire whose charioteer is the wind shall burn you; meeting dissolution there, you shall go to the world of the dead.'"
"And the Grandsire of the world himself, seeing her who had thus cursed, spoke the words 'So be it' and approved of it."
"And Vāsuki, hearing that word of the Grandsire at the time the nectar was being churned, O dear one, sought the refuge of the gods."
"And all the gods, having attained the peerless nectar and their purpose fulfilled, with my brother at their head, approached Prajāpati."
"All the gods together propitiated the Grandsire along with king Vāsuki, that the curse might not take effect."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'This Vāsuki, king of serpents, is distressed on account of his kinsmen; let not this curse from his mother come to pass, O Lord.'"
"Brahmā said: 'A twice-born one born to Jaratkāru from the wife named Jaratkāru whom he shall obtain will deliver the serpents from the curse.'"
Jaratkāru said: "Hearing this speech, Vāsuki, lord of serpents, gave me, O one equal to the immortals, to your father, the great-souled one, even before the time came; therein you were born of me."
"This is that moment now arrived — you must rescue us from fear; you must rescue my brother as well from the fire."
"That act of mine would not be in vain — that I was given to your wise father for the sake of liberation. What do you think, my son?"
The Sūta said: Thus addressed, having said "So be it," Āstīka then spoke to his mother and, as if reviving Vāsuki, who was burning with sorrow:
"I will rescue you, O Vāsuki, O best of serpents, from that curse, O great being — this I tell you truly."
"Be of easy mind, O serpent — there is no fear for you. I shall strive in such a way that what is beneficial will come about. My speech has never spoken untruth even in play — how then otherwise?"
"Going to that best of kings, the consecrated Janamejaya, I shall today please him with words full of auspicious praise, O maternal uncle, in such a way that the king's sacrifice will be brought to a close, O noble one."
"O lord of serpents, O great-minded one, place all trust in me — your mind ought never to prove false in regard to me."
Vāsuki said: "Āstīka, I reel all around; my heart is bursting; I do not recognise the directions, crushed as I am by the rod of Brahmā's curse."
Āstīka said: "You must not grieve in any way, O best of serpents — I will destroy your fear that has arisen from the blazing fire."
"I will destroy the great and terrible rod of Brahmā's curse, equal in energy to the fire of dissolution — mother, you must not fear in any way."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Sūta said: Then, having removed the terrible anguish of mind from Vāsuki and bearing it upon his own limbs, he set forth with great haste.
That foremost of twice-born men, Āstīka, went to Janamejaya's sacrifice, endowed with all its qualities, for the liberation of the lords of serpents.
Going there, Āstīka beheld that excellent sacrificial ground surrounded by many assembly-members of a brilliance equal to the sun and fire.
Stopped there at the gate by the doorkeepers as he sought to enter, that best of twice-born men, that foremost among the twice-born, praised the sacrifice in order to gain admittance.
Āstīka said: "The sacrifice of Soma, the sacrifice of Varuṇa, the sacrifice of Prajāpati performed at Prayāga — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bhāratas, O son of Parīkṣit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"
"The sacrifice of Śakra is said to be one hundred in number; another equally counted is verily a hundred — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bhāratas, O son of Parīkṣit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"
"As was the sacrifice of Yama and of Harishmedha, as was the sacrifice of king Rantideva — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bhāratas, O son of Parīkṣit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"
"The sacrifice of Gaya, the sacrifice of king Śaśabindu, and the sacrifice of king Vaiśravaṇa — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bhāratas, O son of Parīkṣit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"
"The sacrifice of Nṛga and that of Ajamīḍha, as was the sacrifice of king Dāśarathi — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bhāratas, O son of Parīkṣit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"
"We have heard of the sacrifice in heaven of the son of the gods, the sacrifice of king Yudhiṣṭhira, the descendant of Ajamīḍha — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bhāratas, O son of Parīkṣit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The sacrifice of Kṛṣṇa, the son of Satyavatī, wherein he himself performed the rites — such is this sacrifice of yours, O foremost of the Bhāratas, O son of Parīkṣit. May there be welfare to us and to our dear ones!"
"For these ones here of a brilliance like the sun and fire are seated as at the rite of the Slayer of Vṛtra; no knowledge exists today to fully comprehend them — what is given to them can never in any way be lost."
"There is no equal to Dvaipāyana as a priest anywhere in the worlds — this is my firm conviction. For his disciples walk this earth as officiant priests, all skilled in their respective rites."
"Vibhāvasu, Citrabhānu, the great-souled one, bearer of golden seed, all-consumer, dark-pathed, with flame spiralling rightward, blazing — the god who is the eater of oblations desires this offering of yours."
"There is no other king found in this world of the living equal to you as a protector of subjects; I am always glad at heart by your steadfastness — you are either the king Dharmarāja or Yama himself."
"As Śakra, the thunderbolt-wielding Indra himself, is protector in this world, so are you here the protector of subjects; you are esteemed by us as the lord of men in this world — and there is none other than you who is master of this sacrifice."
"Equal to Khatvanga, Nābhāga, and Dilīpa, of prowess comparable to Yayāti and Māndhātā, of energy matching the brilliance of the Ādityas — you shine, O Suvarata, like Bhīṣma."
"Your composure is as firm as Vālmīki's; your anger is as restrained as Vasiṣṭha's; your lordship I deem equal to that of Indra; and your radiance shines like Nārāyaṇa's."
"As Yama you know the determination of dharma; as Kṛṣṇa you are endowed with every virtue; as Śrī is the abode of the Vasus, so are you the repository of sacrifices."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In strength you are equal to Dambhodbhava; like Rāma you are versed in weapons and missiles; in energy you are equal to Aurva and Trita; you are hard to look upon as the sun, or like Bhagīratha."
The Sūta said: Thus praised, all of them — the king, the assembly-members, the priests, and the bearer of oblations — were pleased. Seeing the contented gestures of all of them, king Janamejaya then spoke:
Janamejaya said: "This boy speaks like an elder; this is no boy — he is an elder in my estimation. I wish to grant him a boon — O Brāhmaṇas, assembled together, permit me this."
The assembly-members said: "Even a Brahmin boy is always worthy of honour from kings, whether unlearned or learned. He deserves all wishes from you properly today — and let Takṣaka come quickly to us."
The Sūta said: As the boon-granting king was about to speak, offering a boon to the twice-born youth, the Hotā then said with a heart not excessively joyful: "Choose a boon" — for Takṣaka had not yet come to the rite.
Janamejaya said: "May all of you strive with your utmost power that this rite of mine be completed and that Takṣaka comes quickly to us — for he is my enemy."
The officiating priests said: "As the scriptures tell us, and as the fire itself indicates — O king, Takṣaka is in the mansion of Indra, oppressed by fear."
The Sūta said: "Just as the great-souled Sūta Lohitākṣa, the Puranic bard, had known this beforehand and told the king when asked at that time — even as the Brāhmaṇas declare it, so is this the case, O lord of men."
"'Drawing on the Purāṇa, I tell you this: Indra gave him that boon, O king: "Dwell here in my presence, well protected — the fire shall not burn you."'"
Hearing this, the consecrated king, burning with ardour, sat urging the Hotā on at the time of the rite; the Hotā, alert, offered with mantras — and thereupon Indra himself came in person.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having mounted his celestial vehicle, the great and glorious one was praised by all the gods, accompanied also by Balāhaka spirits, by the Vidyādharas and by hosts of Apsaras.
That serpent, hidden in Indra's upper garment, could find no safety, agitated by fear; then the king, versed in spells, again spoke words in anger, desiring the end of Takṣaka:
"O Brāhmaṇas, if that serpent Takṣaka is in the mansion of Indra, then hurl him together with Indra himself into the fire."
The officiating priests said: "Takṣaka is indeed coming quickly under your power, O king; his great cry is heard, roaring terribly out of fear."
"Surely that serpent has been released by the thunder-bearer; fallen from Indra's embrace, his body loosened by the mantras, that lord of serpents comes whirling through the sky, having lost consciousness, breathing violent breaths."
"This rite of yours is proceeding according to rule, O lord of kings, O master. Now you should grant a boon to this foremost of twice-born men."
Janamejaya said: "O immeasurable one, fitting your youth and handsome form, I grant you a boon as is proper. Choose whatever rests in your heart as desired — I shall bestow it on you even if it be ungrantable."
The Sūta said: As the lord of serpents Takṣaka was on the verge of falling into the fire, seizing this interval, Āstīka then urged his request, saying: "This is the moment."
"If you grant me a boon, O Janamejaya, this is my choice: let this sacrifice of yours cease, and let no more serpents fall here."
The Sūta said: Thus addressed, the king, son of Parīkṣit, O Brahmin, was then not altogether of a rejoicing mind, and spoke these words to Āstīka:
Janamejaya said: Gold, silver, cows, and whatever else you may desire, O lord — all that I would give you as a boon, O brahmin; let my sacrifice not be turned back.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Āstīka said: Gold, silver, and cows — none of these do I choose from you, O king. Let this sacrifice of yours be stopped; may there be welfare for our mother's kin.
The Sūta said: Thus addressed by Āstīka, the king, son of Parīkṣit, then spoke again and again to Āstīka, saying, 'Choose among those who speak the best boon.'
He said: Choose another boon, good fortune to you, O best of the twice-born. But that son of the Bhṛgu line asked for no other boon.
Then all the learned members of the assembly who were versed in the Vedas together spoke to that king: Let the brahmin receive his boon.
Śaunaka said: Those serpents that fell into the fire in this snake sacrifice — I wish to hear the names of all of them, O son of the Sūta.
The Sūta said: Many thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions — they cannot be fully enumerated because of their great number, O best of Veda-knowers.
Yet as I remember them, hear from me the names of the chief serpents that were offered into the sacred fire, as I speak them.
Learn from me first, by way of eminence, those born in Vāsuki's lineage — dark, red, white, terrible, of great bodies, and fierce with venom.
Koṭika, Mānasa, Pūrṇa, Saha, Paila, Halīsaka, Picchila, Koṇapa, Cakra, Koṇavega, and Prakālana —
Hiraṇyavāha, Śaraṇa, Kakṣaka, and Kāladantaka — these serpents born of Vāsuki entered the sacrificial fire.
Those born in the lineage of Takṣaka I will now declare; hear them: Pucchaṇḍaka, Maṇḍalaka, Piṇḍabhettā, and Rabheṇaka —
Ucchikha, Surasā, Draṅga, Balaheḍa, Virohaṇa, Śilīśalakara, Mūka, Sukumāra, and Pravepana —
Mudgara, Śaśaromā, Sumanā, and Vegavāhana — these serpents born of Takṣaka entered the sacrificial fire.
Pārāvata, Pāriyātra, Pāṇḍara, Hariṇa, Kṛśa, Vihaṃga, Śarabha, Moda, Pramoda, and Saṃhatāṅgada —
These from the lineage of Airāvata entered the sacrificial fire. Now hear from me the serpents born in the lineage of Kauravya, O best of the twice-born.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Aiṇḍila, Kuṇḍala, Muṇḍa, Veṇiskandha, Kumāraka, Bāhuka, Śṛṅgavega, Dhūrtaka, and the pair Pāta and Pātara —
Hear in detail the serpents born in the lineage of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as I enumerate them, O brahmin — swift as the wind and fierce with venom.
Śaṅkukarṇa, Piṅgalaka, Kuṭhāramukha, Mecaka, Pūrṇāṅgada, Pūrṇamukha, Prahasa, Śakuni, and Hari —
Āmāhaṭha, Komaṭhaka, Śvasana, Mānava, Vaṭa, Bhairava, Muṇḍavedāṅga, Piśaṅga, and Udrapāraga —
Ṛṣabha, Vegavān, Piṇḍāraka, Mahāhanu, Raktāṅga, Sarvasāraṅga, Samṛddha, and the pair Pāṭa and Rākṣasa —
Varāhaka, Vāraṇaka, Sumitrā, Citravediha, Parāśara, Taruṇaka, Maṇiskandha, and Āruṇi —
Thus have I enumerated these fame-enhancing serpents, O brahmin — the chief ones principally; not all of them, given their great multitude.
The sons and grandsons of these, and the whole succession of their offspring who entered the blazing fire — they cannot be fully counted.
Those with seven heads, those with two heads, and others with five heads — terrible, bearing the venom of the fires of time — were offered by the hundreds of thousands.
Of vast body and great might, towering like mountain peaks, a yojana in length and breadth, or stretching two yojanas in extent —
Able to assume any form at will, moving wherever they wished, fierce with the venom of blazing fire — they were burned in that great sacrifice, crushed by the rod of Brahman's curse.
The Sūta said: We have heard of yet another most wonderful thing concerning Āstīka, when the king, son of Parīkṣit, was plying him with boons.
When the serpent slipped from Indra's hand and remained suspended in mid-air, King Janamejaya became deeply anxious.
Though the fire was burning fiercely and offerings were being made in the proper manner, Takṣaka, tormented by fear, did not fall into the fire.
Śaunaka said: Why, O Sūta, did the collection of mantras of those wise brahmins fail to work, so that Takṣaka did not then fall into the fire?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Sūta said: As that best of serpents slipped from Indra's hand and was losing consciousness, Āstīka raised his voice three times, calling out: Stop! Stop!
Then that serpent remained stationary in the sky, its heart trembling — just as a man might stand still when caught within a circle of cattle.
Then the king, strongly urged by the members of the assembly, spoke: Let it be so, as Āstīka has spoken, as he desires.
Let this rite be concluded; let the serpents be free from harm; let this Āstīka be pleased; and let the words of the Sūta prove true.
Then a cry of rejoicing arose; and when the boon was granted to Āstīka, it likewise came to rest — the sacrifice stopped.
That sacrifice of the king, the son of Pāṇḍu's line, the son of Parīkṣit — and King Janamejaya of the Bhārata race was pleased.
To the officiating priests and the assembled members of the council who had gathered there, he gave wealth in hundreds and thousands.
To Lohitākṣa the Sūta, and likewise to the architect, the mighty king gave a great gift — it was he who had foretold at the very start of the sacrifice that it would be stopped.
Saying, 'This brahmin was the omen,' he gave him abundant wealth; then he performed the concluding ablution in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
The king, his heart pleased, sent Āstīka — the wise one, pleased and fulfilled in his purpose — home with great honor.
And he said to him: You must come again; you shall be a member of my council at the great horse sacrifice.
Saying 'So be it,' Āstīka departed joyfully, having accomplished an incomparable purpose and having satisfied the king.
He went, supremely glad, approached his mother and his maternal uncle, embraced them, and reported to them everything that had transpired.
Hearing this, the serpents who had gathered there, freed from delusion and rejoicing, were filled with delight toward Āstīka; and they spoke to him: Choose whatever boon you desire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Again and again they all said to him on every side: What shall we do today that is dear to you, O wise one? We are pleased, and all of us have been saved; what desire shall we fulfill for you today, dear child?
Āstīka said: May those in the world — brahmins, ordinary men, and others too — who with pure hearts morning and evening recite this account of mine have no fear from you whatsoever.
The Sūta said: And addressed by them with pure hearts, their nephew was told: This is true; we who act thus with joy shall certainly fulfill every desire of yours, O nephew, being ever inclined to it.
May Āstīka, born of Jaratkāru from Jaratkārvā, of great renown, firm in his vow of truth, protect me from serpents.
Whoever remembers Asita, Ārtimanta, and Sunītha — whether by day or by night — shall have no fear of serpents.
The Sūta said: Having freed the serpents from the snake sacrifice, that best of twice-born, righteous in soul, went in time to his appointed end, blessed with sons and grandsons.
Thus has the tale of Āstīka been recounted to you by me faithfully; one who narrates it has no fear from serpents anywhere.
Having heard this most righteous tale of Āstīka — the meritorious story of the poet Āstīka, O brahmin, his glorious career from the very beginning —
Śaunaka said: The great tale has been told to me by you in full, O son of the Sūta, my dear — from the lineage of Bhṛgu onward; I am pleased with you for that.
And I shall question you further, O delight of the Sūta; tell me also again the story composed by Vyāsa.
During the intervals of that most difficult of rites — the snake sacrifice of those great souls — according to proper procedure, among the members of the council, O great poet —
Whatever wonderful stories arose and in what matters they were told truly — I wish to hear these from you, O Sūta, for you are indeed discerning.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Sūta said: During the intervals of the rite, the twice-born men told stories rooted in the Vedas; but Vyāsa always narrated the great tale, the Mahābhārata.
Śaunaka said: The tale of the Mahābhārata, that account glorifying the Pāṇḍavas — when Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana was questioned by Janamejaya —
He recited it in due form during those intervals of the rite; that sacred story I truly wish to hear in proper order.
Narrate it — that story born from the ocean of the great seer's mind, whose deeds are holy — O best among the righteous; I am never satiated, O son of the Sūta.
The Sūta said: Very well, I shall tell you that great and excellent story — the Mahābhārata as composed by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana — from the very beginning.
Enjoy it as I narrate it, O brahmin of supreme understanding; in recounting it, joy of mind arises within me here as well.
The Sūta said: Having heard that Janamejaya had consecrated himself for the snake sacrifice, the learned seer Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana then came to him.
The one whom Kālī — still a maiden — bore on the island in the Yamunā from Parāśara, son of Śakti, that grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas —
Who, even as soon as he was born, instantly grew in body by the power of his will, and mastered the Vedas with all their ancillary branches and histories — that one of great glory —
Whom no one could surpass in austerity, nor in the study of the Vedas, nor by vows, nor by fasting, nor by birth, nor by ardor —
Who divided the one Veda into four — he, the best of those who know the Vedas, knower of the far and near, a brahmin seer, a poet, firm in the vow of truth, and pure —
Who fathered Pāṇḍu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Vidura as well, extending the lineage of Śaṃtanu — he of holy fame and great glory —
He entered the sacrificial hall of Janamejaya the royal seer at that time, accompanied by disciples who had mastered the Vedas and all their branches.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There he saw King Janamejaya seated, surrounded by many members of the assembly — like Puraṃdara surrounded by the gods.
And also with consecrated kings from various countries, and with officiating priests equal to the gods, skilled in the spreading of the sacrificial ground.
Janamejaya the royal seer, best of the Bhāratas, seeing that seer arrive, rose swiftly with his retinue out of joy.
With the approval of the assembly members, the mighty king arranged a golden seat for him — just as Indra would for Bṛhaspati.
When he had taken his seat there — the bestower of boons, honored by the hosts of divine seers — the foremost of kings honored him with acts prescribed by scripture.
Water for washing the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, the guest offering, and a cow — all in due order — he presented to Kṛṣṇa, his grandfather, as was worthy of him.
Having received that honor from Janamejaya, the Pāṇḍava's descendant, and having given permission for the cow, Vyāsa was pleased at that time.
Having thus honored that great-grandfather with care, the king sat near him with a joyful heart and inquired after his welfare.
The blessed one in turn, seeing the king, communicated his well-being, was honored by all the assembly members, and honored the assembly members in return.
Then Janamejaya, after that best of twice-born had been duly honored by all the assembly members, thereafter addressed him with folded hands.
You have been a direct witness of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas; I wish to hear their deeds narrated by you, O brahmin.
How did the split arise between those whose deeds were beyond reproach? And how did that great war come to pass — the war that put an end to so many living beings?
Tell me all of this in full, concerning all those forefathers whose minds were possessed by fate, O Blessed One, for you are skilled in such telling.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing those words, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana then instructed his disciple Vaiśaṃpāyana, who was seated nearby.
Narrate to him in full how the split between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas came about in former times — everything that you have heard from me.
That bull among brahmins, having received the command of his guru, then narrated the entire ancient history.
To that king, to the members of the assembly, and to all the kshatriyas gathered there, he then told the story of the rift and the destruction of the kingdom of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas.
Vaiśaṃpāyana spoke: Having first bowed to my guru with mind, intellect, and concentrated thought, and having honoured all the brahmins and other learned persons present —
— I shall now set forth in full the teaching of Vyāsa, the great sage renowned throughout all the worlds, the wise one of immeasurable splendour.
O king, you are a worthy vessel to hear this Bhārata tale; the eagerness to speak on behalf of my guru urges me on with joy, as it were.
Hear, O king, how the rift between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas came about: the exile arising from the dice game over the kingdom, and all that followed.
And how the war came about — the war that laid waste to the earth — all of that I shall recount to you who ask, O bull of the Bhārata line.
When their father had died, those heroes returned from the forest to their own dwelling, and in no great time became learned in both the Veda and the bow.
Seeing the Pāṇḍavas endowed with beauty, valour, and vigour, approved of by the citizens, and bearing glory and renown, the Kurus could not endure them.
Then the cruel Duryodhana, together with Karṇa and Śakuni son of Subala, undertook various schemes to suppress and banish them.
That wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra then administered poison to Bhīma; but the hero Vṛkodara digested it along with his food.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, binding the sleeping Vṛkodara at Pramanakoți and hurling Bhīma into the waters of the Gaṅgā, he returned to the city.
When Kaunteya awoke, he snapped his bonds and arose, O great king — Bhīmasena, free of all distress.
He also had him bitten all over his body by venomous black serpents while he slept; yet that slayer of foes did not die.
In each and every one of those acts of harm, the great-minded Vidura was ever watchful in rescuing and countering them.
Just as Indra, dwelling in heaven, ever brings welfare to the living world, so too did Vidura ever bring welfare to the Pāṇḍavas.
But when, despite all manner of concealed and open stratagems, he could not kill those who were protected by fate and divine will —
— then, having taken counsel with his ministers headed by Vrisha and Duḥśāsana, and having obtained Dhṛtarāṣṭra's permission, he ordered the house of lac.
He had the Pāṇḍavas of boundless might housed there, and then, when they were off guard, he set fire to them with a conflagration.
But by Vidura's counsel a tunnel had been prepared beforehand; by this means he delivered them, and they, freed, fled in fear.
Then in the dreadful great forest, Bhīmasena of fearsome might, enraged, slew on the earth the rakshasa named Hiḍimba.
Then those heroes, scorchers of foes, having set out together for the city of Ekacakra, went there in the guise of brahmins, accompanied by their mother.
There, for the sake of a brahmin, they slew the mighty Baka, and then, in the company of brahmins, they departed for the city of the Pāñcālas.
There, having won Draupadī and resided for the full period of a year, those tamers of enemies returned to Hāstinapura, now known for who they were.
They were addressed by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra son of Śaṃtanu: "My dear sons, why should there be conflict between you and your brothers? We have thought of a dwelling for you at Khāṇḍavaprastha."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Therefore, setting aside your anger, go to Khāṇḍavaprastha to dwell there — a land endowed with populated territories and well-laid broad roads."
At the word of those two, they departed, taking all manner of gems and jewels, along with all their friends and well-wishers, for the city of Khāṇḍavaprastha.
There they dwelt, O king, for many years, bringing other kings under their dominion by the might of their arms.
Ever foremost in dharma, devoted to vows of truth, alert and diligent, forbearing, yet blazing with power against their enemies — such were they in those days.
The mighty Bhīmasena conquered the eastern quarter; the heroic Arjuna, the northern; and Nakula likewise conquered the western.
Sahadeva, slayer of enemy heroes, conquered the southern quarter; and together they brought the entire earth under their sway.
With five Pāṇḍavas resplendent as the sun, and with the sun itself blazing, the earth shone as if lit by six suns — the Pāṇḍavas of true valour.
Then, on account of a certain circumstance, King Yudhiṣṭhira the Dharmarāja sent his brother Dhanañjaya to the forest.
He dwelt in the forest for a full year and one month, and then at some point went to Hṛṣīkeśa at Dvāravatī.
There Bībhatsu obtained as wife the lotus-eyed Subhadrā, the younger sister of Vāsudeva, she of auspicious speech.
Subhadrā, delighted, was united with the Pāṇḍava Arjuna just as Śacī is with great Indra, or as Śrī is united with Kṛṣṇa.
And Bībhatsu, that Kaunteya, together with Vāsudeva, satisfied the fire — the carrier of oblations — in the Khāṇḍava forest, O best of kings.
For Pārtha, with Keśava as companion in his endeavours, bore no excessive burden — even as Viṣṇu is with his allies in the slaying of foes.
Agni also gave to Pārtha the supreme bow Gāṇḍīva, two inexhaustible quivers with arrows, and a chariot marked with the monkey-banner.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bībhatsu rescued there the great asura Maya, and he in turn fashioned a divine assembly hall filled with every kind of gem.
In that hall, the dull-witted and most evil-minded Duryodhana conceived his covetousness; and thereafter, with Śakuni son of Subala, he cheated Yudhiṣṭhira at dice.
He sent them to the forest for twelve years, and for the thirteenth year to live unrecognized within the kingdom — thus thirteen years in all.
Then in the fourteenth year, when they sought their rightful property, they did not obtain it, O great king, and so the war began.
Having then destroyed everything and slain King Duryodhana, the Pāṇḍavas recovered the kingdom, now emptied of most of its people.
Such was the ancient story of those whose deeds were beyond reproach: the rift, the destruction of the kingdom, and the victory — O best of conquerors.
Janamejaya spoke: You have narrated in summary, O best of brahmins, the entire Mahābhārata — the great story of the deeds of the Kurus.
But as you narrate this tale of wondrous import, O sinless one, an exceeding great curiosity has arisen in me to hear it at length.
You, sir, should narrate this again in full detail; for I am not satisfied, listening to the great deeds of the ancestors.
For the cause cannot have been trivial — those who know dharma, the Pāṇḍavas, killed men who were in principle inviolable, and yet they are praised by all people.
For what reason did those tigers among men, though capable and themselves without fault, endure the afflictions inflicted upon them by the wicked?
How was it that Vṛkodara, mighty of arm, with the strength of ten thousand elephants, could restrain his anger even while suffering great torment, O best of brahmins?
How was it that Draupadī the dark one, being tormented by the wicked, chaste as she was and possessed of terrible eyes, did not burn the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
How did the two Pārthas and the two sons of Mādrī, passing over the transgression at the dice game, follow that tiger among men even as he was being cheated by the wicked?
How was it that Yudhiṣṭhira, the foremost of those who uphold dharma, the son of Dharma himself, a knower of dharma, who deserved no such thing, could endure the utmost affliction?
And how did Dhanañjaya, the Pāṇḍava with Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer, single-handedly shooting arrows, send all those vast armies to the world of the fathers?
Tell me all of this as it truly occurred, O wealth of asceticism, and whatever those great chariot-warriors did on each occasion.
Vaiśaṃpāyana spoke: I shall now set forth in full the teaching of Vyāsa, the great sage of great soul worshipped throughout all the worlds, the one of immeasurable splendour.
For this collection of a hundred thousand verses of meritorious deeds has been expounded here by the son of Satyavatī, that one of boundless might.
The learned man who has this recited, and the person who hears it — they, having attained the abode of Brahman, shall reach a state equal to that of the gods.
This is equal to the Vedas, most sacred, most excellent; this Purāṇa is the foremost of all things worth hearing, and it is praised by the seers.
In this most meritorious history, artha, dharma, and ultimate wisdom are taught in their entirety.
One who, knowing this Veda of Kṛṣṇa, has it recited to those who are not petty-minded, who are given to charity, devoted to truth, and not unbelievers, shall attain the highest good.
Even the sin incurred by the killing of an embryo is undoubtedly shed — even a most hardened man, upon hearing this history.
This history named Jaya should be heard by one who desires victory; he shall conquer the entire earth and vanquish his enemies as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This is the best rite for obtaining a male child; this is a great rite of blessing; it should be heard many times by the queen and the crown prince alike.
This is a sacred treatise on wealth; this is the supreme treatise on dharma; this is declared to be the treatise on liberation, by Vyāsa of boundless intellect.
Some relate it even now; others will relate it hereafter; there are sons who are eager to serve, and attendants who do whatever is pleasing.
All the sin committed by body, by speech, and by mind — a person who always hears this swiftly sheds all of it.
Those who listen without envy to the great birth-narrative of the Bhāratas shall have no fear of disease — how then could they fear the world beyond?
This, which confers prosperity, renown, long life, heaven, and merit, was composed by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, who desired to bestow merit.
He composed it to spread the fame throughout the world of the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, and of the other kshatriyas of abundant wealth and splendour.
Just as the blessed ocean and the mountain Himavat are both renowned as treasuries of gems, so the Bhārata is called a treasury of gems.
The learned man who has this recited to brahmins here on the occasion of the parvan days — his sins shaken off, heaven won — he attains the state of Brahman.
And one who has even a single verse of this recited to brahmins at a shraddha ceremony — that shraddha of his shall remain inexhaustible, and shall fully reach his ancestors.
Whatever sin a person commits unknowingly in the course of a day — all of that dissolves simply upon hearing this narrative called the Mahābhārata.
The great birth of the Bhāratas is called the Mahābhārata; he who knows its etymology is freed from all sins.
Rising early each day for three years, the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana composed this excellent narrative, the Mahābhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever here concerns dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, O bull of the Bhāratas — that is found elsewhere too; but what is not here is nowhere else.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was a king named Rājoparicara, steadfast in dharma, a lord of the earth; though firm in his vows, he once set out for the hunt.
At Indra's instruction, Vasu, the joy of the Paurava line, that lord of the earth, took possession of the pleasant Cedi kingdom, worthy of acquisition.
To him who had laid aside his weapons and was dwelling in an hermitage delighting in austerity, the god himself — the wielder of the thunderbolt — came in person to that lord of the earth.
Reflecting that this king was worthy of Indra's station through his austerity, Indra gently turned him away from his penance in person.
Indra said: Let not dharma be confounded upon the earth, O lord of the earth — protect it; for dharma, when upheld, sustains the entire world.
Guard the dharma of the world, ever diligent and composed; yoked to dharma, you will thereby win blessed and eternal worlds.
Dwelling on earth while I dwell in heaven, become my friend and dear companion; inhabit that region which is the udder of the earth, O lord of men.
That land is rich in cattle, holy, stable, abounding in wealth and grain, easy to defend, pleasant, and endowed with the enjoyable gifts of the earth.
This region surpasses all others, richly furnished with riches and gems; the earth there is full of wealth — dwell among the Cedis, O lord of the Cedis.
The people of that realm are virtuous in character, easily contented, and righteous; there is no false speech even in casual talk, much less otherwise.
Men devoted to the welfare of their elders do not divide property from their fathers; they do not yoke lean cattle to the plough, and they do not allow the feeble to starve.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All the social orders always abide in their own dharma in the Cedi realm, O giver of honour; nothing that occurs in the three worlds is unknown to you.
A great divine crystal aerial chariot, fit for the enjoyment of the gods, moving through the sky — a flying vehicle given by me — shall attend upon you.
You alone among all mortals, mounted on the finest of aerial chariots, shall move on high like an embodied god.
I give you the Vaijayantī garland of unfading lotuses, which shall protect you unwounded by weapons in battle.
This very mark shall be yours, O lord of men — known as the Indra-garland, auspicious, matchless, and great.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The slayer of Vṛtra also gave him a bamboo staff, meant for bestowing desired gifts and protecting the righteous.
In honour of that staff of Indra, the lord of the earth had it planted in the ground once a year had passed.
From that time forward, even to this day, O king, the planting of the staff is performed by the best of kings just as he established it.
The next day too the staff is raised by kings, decked with boxes, fragrant unguents, garlands, and ornaments; wreathed with garlands and festoons it is duly honoured according to rule.
And the blessed Śaṃkara is worshipped here in a comic form, assumed by himself out of affection for the great-souled Vasu.
Seeing this auspicious worship, done by the gods and by Vasu the foremost of kings, the mighty Mahendra spoke with delight.
Those men and kings who shall worship my festival and celebrate it joyfully as the lord of the Cedis has done —
— for them, together with their kingdoms, there shall be prosperity and victory, and their realm shall be flourishing and joyful.
Thus was the great king Vasu honoured with affection by the great-souled Mahendra, the bounteous one, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those men who shall always celebrate Indra's festival — just as they are purified by great gift-bestowing sacrifices with gifts of land and the like, so also are they purified by the Indra-festival.
Thus duly honoured by the bounteous Indra, Vasu the lord of the Cedis governed the earth from Cedi with righteousness, and that lord of the earth celebrated the Indra-festival out of love for Indra.
He had five sons of great valour and boundless energy, and that emperor consecrated his sons over various kingdoms.
The renowned great warrior Bṛhadratha king of Magadha, Pratyagraha, Kuśāmba who is called Maṇivāhana, Macchilla, Yadu, and the warrior Aparājita —
These were the sons of that royal sage of abundant lustre, O king; those five Vāsava kings settled countries and cities with their own names and founded eternal separate dynasties.
Dwelling in the crystal aerial palace given by Indra, that great-souled king was attended upon by Gandharvas and Apsarases; thus his name became celebrated as Rājoparicara — the king who roams above.
The mountain Kolāhala, endowed with consciousness and overcome by desire, blocked the river Śuktimatī that flowed past his city.
Vasu struck that mountain Kolāhala with his foot; the river escaped through the cleft made by that blow.
The mountain had begotten a pair in that river; delighted at her release, the river presented them to the king.
The male child born there — that best of royal sages, Vasu the giver of wealth, made him a subduer-of-foes commander of the army; the king took the beloved girl, named Girikā, as his wife.
His wife Girikā, desiring a son, duly informed him that her fertile season had come; she had bathed, performed the puṃsavana rite, and was pure.
On that very day the ancestors spoke to him with affection — to that best of kings, the finest of the wise — saying: "Slay deer for us."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Not transgressing that command of the ancestors, the king went forth to hunt, yet, filled with desire, he kept thinking only of Girikā — she who was supremely beautiful, a very second Śrī made manifest.
As he roamed in that lovely forest his seed fell; the moment it fell the lord of the earth caught it on a leaf.
He caught it thinking: "My seed must not fall in vain; and the fertile season of my wife must not pass fruitless," so resolved the lord.
Having deliberated thus and pondered again and again, the best of kings, ascertaining that the seed must not be wasted —
— and reckoning the moment right for conveying the seed to his chief queen, he consecrated that seed with mantras; then, knowing the subtle truth of dharma and purpose, he discerned a swift hawk nearby and addressed it.
"For my sake, dear one, carry this seed swiftly to my home and deliver it to Girikā, for today is her fertile time."
Taking it, the hawk at once soared up swiftly and flew off at the greatest speed through the sky.
Another hawk, seeing that hawk coming, immediately rushed at it, suspecting that it carried meat.
The two then fought beak-to-beak in the sky; as they struggled the seed fell — and fell into the waters of the Yamunā.
There a celebrated celestial nymph named Adrikā, transformed into a fish by a brahmin's curse, was living in the Yamunā.
Adrikā, in the form of a fish, swiftly approached and swallowed that seed which had fallen from the hawk's talons — the seed of Vāsava's descendant.
Some time later, fishermen caught that fish; and when the tenth month had arrived, O best of the Bhāratas, they drew from her belly a human pair — one female, one male.
Thinking it a wonder, they reported to the king: "O king, these two human beings were born from the body of a fish."
Of the two, Rājoparicara took the male; he became the righteous king named Matsya, true to his word.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Apsarā was freed from her curse in an instant, as the blessed one had previously told her: "O fair one, after entering an animal womb and giving birth to two humans, you shall be released from the curse."
Then, after giving birth to those two and being cut open by the fisherman, she abandoned the fish form, regained her divine form, and that excellent Apsarā went on her way along the path of Siddhas, sages, and Cāraṇas.
The daughter, born of that fish and smelling of fish, endowed with beauty and character, adorned with all virtues — the king gave her to a fisherman saying: "Let her be yours."
She became known by the name Satyavatī; living with the fisherman-killer, she smelled of fish for some time, though she was sweet-smiled.
While she was ferrying her father's boat on the water in service to him, Parāśara, wandering on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, saw her.
Seeing her — supremely beautiful, desired even by the Siddhas, and lovely to behold — that wise and learned bull among sages desired her, that maiden of Vāsava's line, and resolved to act.
She said: "Look, revered sir — on both banks stand sages who can see us both; how could our union take place?"
Addressed thus by her, the blessed and mighty sage created a mist by which that entire region became as if enveloped in darkness.
Seeing the mist conjured by the great sage, the intelligent girl was amazed and spoke, abashed.
"Know me, revered sir, as a maiden ever under my father's authority; by union with you my maidenhood would be defiled, O sinless one."
"And with my maidenhood defiled, O best of twice-born, how shall I be able to go home? Nor can I bring myself to remain at home, O wise one. Considering all this, revered sir, do whatever is best thereafter."
To her who spoke thus, the delighted foremost of sages said: "After granting me my desire, you shall remain a maiden still."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Choose also a boon, timid one, whatever you desire, O beautiful lady; for my grace has never before been granted in vain, O sweet-smiled one."
Addressed thus, she chose as her boon a supreme fragrance of the body; and the blessed and mighty sage granted her the desire of her heart.
Then, having obtained her boon and delighted, adorned with the virtues of womanhood, she united with that sage of wondrous deeds.
From this her name Gandhavatī became celebrated on earth; people on earth could smell her fragrance from a yojana away.
Thus she became also widely known by the name Yojanagandha — "she whose fragrance reaches a yojana"; and the blessed Parāśara departed to his own abode.
Thus Satyavatī, overjoyed at obtaining that excellent boon, instantly conceived upon her union with Parāśara, and on an island in the Yamunā she gave birth; the mighty son of Parāśara was born.
He paid his respects to his mother, then set his mind on austerity; he said to her: "When you remember me, I shall appear to you in times of need."
Thus was Dvaipāyana born to Satyavatī from Parāśara; as that child was set down on an island (dvīpa) he became known as Dvaipāyana.
Knowing how dharma recedes step by step from age to age, and observing the lifespan and capacity of mortals age by age —
— wishing to confer benefit on Brahmā and on the brahmins, he divided the Vedas; and because of that dividing (vyāsa) he is remembered as Vyāsa.
He taught the Vedas — with the Mahābhārata as the fifth — to Sumanta, Jaimini, Paila, and his own son Śuka.
The mighty, greatest, boon-granting Vyāsa also taught Vaiśaṃpāyana; by them the saṃhitās of the Bhārata were published separately.
Likewise Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, of boundless splendour, was born from Gaṅgā through the power of the Vasus — of great valour and great renown.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The ancient sage who was impaled on a spike — though no thief — out of suspicion of theft: he became celebrated as Aṇīmāṇḍavya, of very great renown.
That great seer, summoning Dharma of old, said this: 'In my childhood I pierced a little bird with a reed-stalk.'
That sin I remember, O Dharma — no other evil do I remember. Why then has not my austerity, which is equal to a thousand, conquered it here?
Since the slaying of a brahmin is graver than the slaying of all other beings, therefore, on account of this sin, you shall be born in a shudra womb.
By that curse, Dharma himself was born in a shudra womb — learned, in the form of Vidura, a righteous body free from sin.
Sañjaya, resembling a sage, was born as a charioteer's son from Gavalgaṇa. And from the Sun, in the maiden daughter of Kuntī, was born Karṇa the great warrior, bearing congenital armor, his face radiant with earrings.
For the benefit of the worlds, Viṣṇu, revered by the world, the greatly glorious one, manifested himself from Vāsudeva through Devakī.
That god, without beginning or end, is the maker and lord of the universe — the unmanifest, imperishable Brahman, the primal cause, of the nature of that which is beyond qualities.
He is the imperishable Self, the supreme source of Nature, the Cosmic Person, the maker of the universe, the union with pure being, the eternal and imperishable.
Infinite, immovable, divine, the Swan, Nārāyaṇa the lord, the Sustainer, unaging, eternal — they call him the supreme and imperishable.
That all-pervading Person, the maker, the grandfather of all beings, was born among the Andhaka-Vṛṣṇis for the purpose of upholding righteousness.
Sātyaki and Kṛtavarmā, both of great valor, skilled in all weapons and expert in missiles, devoted followers of Nārāyaṇa, were born from Satyaka and Hṛdika respectively, both masters of arms.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The seed spilled from Bharadvaja developed in a vessel; from that severe-ascetic great seer's seed, Droṇa was born.
From Śaradvān of the Gautama line, a pair was born from a clump of reeds — the mother of Aśvatthāmā and Kṛpa the mighty. Aśvatthāmā was then born from Droṇa, the foremost among bearers of weapons.
Likewise Dhṛṣṭadyumna too, directly blazing like fire, was born from the sacred fire when a Vedic rite was being performed — the valiant hero, born with a bow, destined to destroy Droṇa.
Likewise from the sacrificial altar was born Kṛṣṇa (Draupadī) as well — radiant, auspicious, resplendent of form, bearing a most exquisite beauty.
Nagnajit, a pupil of Prahlāda, became Subala; his offspring, destroyers of dharma, were born due to the wrath of the gods.
The son of the king of Gāndhāra became Śakuni, the son of Subala; and the mother of Duryodhana — both were born, those two knowers of worldly affairs.
From Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana (Vyāsa) were born Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, and the mighty Pāṇḍu as well, in the field of Vicitravīrya.
From Pāṇḍu were born five sons equal to gods, each from different mothers of two wives; the eldest among them in virtue was Yudhiṣṭhira.
Yudhiṣṭhira was born from Dharma, Vṛkodara (Bhīma) from the wind god; from Indra was born the glorious Dhanañjaya (Arjuna), foremost among all bearers of weapons.
The twin pair, endowed with beauty, were born from the Aśvins — Nakula and Sahadeva, devoted to the service of their elders.
Likewise a hundred sons were born to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra — headed by Duryodhana, and Yuyutsu, and Karana (Vikarṇa) likewise.
Abhimanyu was born from Arjuna through Subhadrā — the nephew of Vāsudeva, the grandson of the great-souled Pāṇḍu.
From the five Pāṇḍavas through Kṛṣṇa (Draupadī) were born five princes, endowed with beauty and skilled in all weapons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Prativindhya from Yudhiṣṭhira, Sutasoma from Vṛkodara (Bhīma), Śrutakīrti from Arjuna, and Śatānīka the son of Nakula.
Likewise from Sahadeva came the valiant Śrutasena; and from Bhīma through Hiḍimba in the forest was born Ghaṭotkaca.
Śikhaṇḍin was born from Drupada — a girl who attained sonhood, whom the yaksha Sthuna made into a man out of desire to please.
In that conflict of the Kurus, hundreds of thousands of kings assembled, about to fight in battle.
Their names in their entirety cannot be reckoned — it is not possible to count them even in tens of thousands of years. But the chief ones have been named here, by whom this narrative is woven together.
Janamejaya said: O brahmin, those who have been named, and others who have not been fully named — I wish to hear about all of them properly, and about the other illustrious kings.
For what purpose were these great warriors, equal to gods, born here upon the earth — that, O greatly blessed one, you ought to explain to me fully.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: This is indeed a secret of the gods, O king — so we have heard. Yet I shall tell it to you, after bowing to the Self-born (Brahmā).
Having made the earth devoid of kshatriyas twenty-one times in the past, Jamadagni's son (Paraśurāma) practiced austerities on Mount Mahendra, the greatest of mountains.
Then, when the world had been made devoid of kshatriyas by the descendant of Bhṛgu, O king, the kshatriya women approached brahmin men seeking to conceive.
With them those brahmins of disciplined vows came together, O tiger among men, in the proper fertile season, not out of desire, nor out of season.
From those brahmins those kshatriya women conceived by the thousands; then they gave birth, O king, to kshatriyas honored for their valor — both boys and girls — for the replenishment of the kshatriya order.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus that kshatriya order, born from ascetic brahmins upon kshatriya women, prospered in righteousness, endowed with very long life; and all four social orders at that time were foremost in brahminic virtue.
They approached women only in the proper season, not out of desire, nor out of season; likewise the other creatures, even those of animal birth, would approach their mates in season then, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then those subjects grew in righteousness, living for hundreds of thousands of years, devoted to the vow of dharma, O protector of the earth; men were entirely free from mental anguish and physical disease.
Then the kshatriya order again ruled over this earth bounded by the ocean, traversed in its entirety with the gait of a great elephant, with its mountains, forests, and groves.
When the kshatriya order again governed this wealth-bearing earth by dharma, the social orders headed by the brahmins attained supreme joy.
The lords of men, having cast away the faults born of desire and anger, administered punishment to those deserving punishment in accordance with dharma, and thus protected their subjects.
While the kshatriya order was thus devoted to dharma, the thousand-eyed one of a hundred sacrifices (Indra) rained sweetly in the right place and season, nourishing the subjects.
In that age, O lord of men, no child died in infancy; nor did any male know a woman before reaching youth.
Thus, O bull of the Bhāratas, this earth bounded by the ocean was abundantly filled with long-lived subjects.
The kshatriyas performed great sacrifices with abundant fees; and the brahmins studied the Vedas along with their supplementary texts and the Upaniṣads.
The brahmins did not sell sacred knowledge in those days, O king; nor did they recite the Vedas in the proximity of those equal to shudras.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The vaishyas caused cultivation by means of oxen; they did not yoke a cow to the plough, nor did they keep thin-bodied animals alive for labor.
Men did not milk cows with suckling calves that were still drinking the froth-milk; nor did merchants sell goods with false weights in those days.
Men, O tiger among men, performed deeds imbued with righteousness, keeping dharma always in view, devoted to dharma.
All the social orders were absorbed in their own proper duties, O lord of men; thus in that age, O tiger among men, dharma did not diminish anywhere.
Cows gave birth in due season, and women likewise, O bull of the Bhāratas; trees bore flowers and fruits in their seasons.
Thus when the Kṛta age was proceeding properly in those days, O king, the entire earth was abundantly filled with many living beings.
Then, as the human world flourished, O bull of the Bhāratas, the asuras were born in the fields of kings, O foremost of men.
For the daityas, having been repeatedly defeated in battle by the Ādityas and deprived of their sovereignty, came to be born here upon the earth.
Desiring divinity here and endowed with proud minds, O lord, the asuras were born among human beings on earth, in this and that creature.
Among cattle, among horses, O king of kings, among donkeys, camels, and buffaloes, among carnivorous creatures, among elephants and deer as well —
— by those who had been born here and those still being born, O guardian of the earth, this earth could no longer bear herself by her own strength.
Then certain kings were born endowed with great strength — sons of Diti and of Danu, fallen from that higher world to this one.
Powerful and arrogant, bearing various forms, those crushers of foes roamed over this earth bounded by the ocean.
They oppressed brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas, and shudras alike; they oppressed all other creatures as well with their power.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Terrifying and slaying these various groups of beings, they wandered over the earth in all directions, O king, by the hundreds of thousands.
Assaulting great sages dwelling in their hermitages here and there, those enemies of brahmins, intoxicated with pride of valor and drunk with the intoxication of power —
— this earth, thus oppressed by those great asuras swollen with might and power, O protector of the earth, approached Brahmā.
For neither the wind, O king, nor the nagas, nor the mountains were able to bear this earth that had been forcibly overrun by the danavas.
Then the earth, O protector of the earth, weighed down by her burden and afflicted by fear, went for refuge to the god who is the grandfather of all beings.
She saw the god Brahmā, the imperishable maker of the worlds, surrounded by the greatly blessed gods, twice-born ones, and great seers.
Being praised by gandharvas and apsarases engaged in the work of eulogizing, filled with joy — she approached and paid reverence to him.
Then the earth, seeking refuge, presented her petition to him in the presence of all the world-guardians, O descendant of Bharata.
But the purpose of that earth's visit had already been known beforehand, O king, to the Self-born one of supreme nature, the one seated on the highest.
For how would the creator of the universe fail to know, O descendant of Bharata, the innermost thoughts of all worlds — of gods and asuras — without exception?
To her, O great king, spoke the lord of the earth, the all-pervading one, the source of all beings, the lord, the auspicious one, the Lord of Creatures (Brahmā).
For the purpose for which you have come into my presence, O holder of wealth, for that purpose I shall set all the celestial ones to work.
Having said this and dismissed the earth, O king, Brahmā the god, the creator of beings, himself gave instructions to all the wise ones.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He said: 'To remove the burden of this earth, be born separately, each in a portion, upon this very earth, for opposition against the asuras.'
Likewise, having assembled the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, the blessed one said this excellent word to them all: 'Be born as you please among human beings, each through your own portion.'
Then Indra and all the others, having heard the word of their divine preceptor — true, purposeful, and beneficial — accepted it then.
Then all of them, having resolved to go to the earth through their own portions, approached Nārāyaṇa the destroyer of foes at Vaikuṇṭha.
He who holds discus and mace in hand, clad in yellow, dark of radiance, lotus-naveled, destroyer of the foes of the gods, with broad and beautiful oblique eyes —
— to that Puruṣottama (Supreme Person), Indra, for the purification of the earth, said: 'Descend through a portion of yourself.' And Hari replied to him: 'So be it.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Indra, together with Nārāyaṇa, made an agreement to descend to earth from heaven, accompanied by the gods, each taking a partial incarnation.
And Śakra himself, having instructed all the heaven-dwellers, departed once again from the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
For the destruction of the enemies of the immortals and for the welfare of all the worlds, those heaven-dwellers descended in succession from heaven to this earth.
Then, O tiger among kings, those heaven-dwellers were born at will in the lineages of brahmarshis and in the royal families of earthly sages.
They slew danavas and rakshasas, gandharvas and nagas, and many other man-eating beings in great numbers.
But the danavas, rakshasas, gandharvas, and nagas — those mighty ones — could not slay them even in childhood, O best of the Bhāratas.
Janamejaya said: Of the assemblies of gods and danavas, of gandharvas and apsaras, of all humans, and also of yakshas and rakshasas —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I wish to hear truly, from the very beginning, the complete origin of all these, and of all living beings in their entirety — for you know all things.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Well then, I shall tell you — having bowed to the Self-born — the origin and dissolution of the worlds, beginning with the gods, completely and correctly.
The six great sages known as the mind-born sons of Brahmā are: Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Kaśyapa is the son of Marīci, and from Kaśyapa were born these offspring. The thirteen highly blessed daughters of Dakṣa gave birth to these creatures.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kāla, Anāyus, Siṃhikā, Muni, Krodha, Prava, Ariṣṭa, Vinatā, and Kapilā —
— and Kadrū, O tiger among men, these daughters of Dakṣa, O Bhārata: the offspring — sons and grandsons — of these ladies, endowed with might, is without end.
From Aditi were born the twelve Ādityas, lords of the worlds. I shall name them for you, O king, O Bhārata.
Dhata, Mitra, Aryamā, Śakra, Varuṇa, and Aṃśa; Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pusha, and Savitā the tenth —
— Tvaṣṭā the eleventh, and Viṣṇu is declared the twelfth. He, the last-born of all the Ādityas, surpasses them all in virtues.
Diti had but one son, remembered as Hiraṇyakaśipu. These five sons of that great-souled one were known by the following names:
Prahlāda was the eldest among them, then Saṃhrāda next; Anuhlada was the third, and after him came Śibi and Bāṣkala.
Prahlāda had three sons known everywhere, O Bhārata: Virocana, Kumbha, and Nikumbha, all renowned.
Virocana had one son, the mighty Bali; and Bali's famous son was the great asura named Bāṇa.
Danu had forty sons known everywhere, O Bhārata; the eldest among them was the king Vipracitti, of great renown.
Śambara, Namuci, the renowned Pulomā; Asiloma, Keśī, and the danava Durjaya —
— Ayaḥśirā, Ashvashira, and the mighty Ayahshanku; Gaganamurdha, the swift Ketumān —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— Svarbhānu, Aśva, Aśvapati, Vṛṣaparvā and Ajaka; Aśvagrīva, Sukshma, and the great asura Tuhunda —
— Isripa, Ekacakra, Virūpākṣa, Hara and Ahara; Nicandra, Nikumbha, Kupatha, and Kapatha —
— Śarabha, Śalabha, and also the pair Sūrya and Candramā: thus are the danavas of Danu's lineage enumerated. But those two — Sūrya and Candramā — are indeed remembered as belonging to the gods.
And these ten bull-like danavas, famous in their lineage, full of vitality and mighty in strength, are the sons of Danu, O great king.
Ekaksha, the heroic Mritapa, Pralamba and Naraka; Vātāpi, Shatrutapana, and the great asura Shatha —
— Gaviṣṭha, Danayu, and the danava Dirghajihva. Their sons and grandsons are remembered as innumerable, O Bhārata.
Siṃhikā bore the son Rāhu, the afflicting force of moon and sun; also Sucandra, the moon-slayer, and Chandravimardana.
The offspring — sons and grandsons — of this cruel-natured woman are without end; the host called Krodhavaśa, of cruel deeds and destroyer of enemies.
Anāyus had four bull-like asura sons: Vikshara, Bala, Vīra, and the great asura Vṛtra.
The renowned sons of Kāla, resembling Death itself in their striking power, are known on earth as mighty in valor among the danavas, afflicting their foes.
Vinaśana, Krodha, Hanta the other son of Krodha, and likewise Krodhashatru — these are renowned as the Kāleyas.
Śukra, son of the sage Bhṛgu, became the preceptor of the asuras. The four famous sons of Uśanas were officiant priests for the asuras.
Tvashtavara, Atri, and two others — performers of sacred rites — blazing in splendor equal to the sun, and powerful enough to illuminate Brahmā's world.
Thus has this origin of lineages been told to you — of the vigorous asuras and the gods — as I have heard it in the Purāṇa.
The offspring of these beings — qualities included — cannot be fully enumerated in its entirety, O lord of the earth; it is without end.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, and likewise Garuḍa and Aruṇa; Āruṇi and Vāruṇī — these are remembered as the sons of Vinatā.
Śeṣa, Ananta, Vāsuki, the serpent Takṣaka, Kurma, and Kulika — these mighty sons of Kadrū are the Kadruveyas.
Bhīmasena, Ugrasena, Suparṇa, and Varuṇa; Gopati, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Suryavarchas the seventh —
— Puravin, Arkaparna, and the renowned Prayuta; the celebrated Bhīma and Citraratha, known as all-knowing and self-controlled —
— and Shalishira, O king, Pradyumna the fourteenth, Kali the fifteenth, and Nārada the sixteenth — thus are these divine gandharvas, the Mauneyas, enumerated.
Now I shall name other beings, O Bhārata. Prava gave birth to: the blameless Anuvasham, Anunam, Aruṇa, Priya, Anūpa, Subhaga, and Bhasi.
Siddha, Purna, Barhi, the greatly renowned Purnasha, Brahmacārī, Ratiguṇa, and Suparṇa the seventh —
— Viśvāvasu, Bhānu, and Sucandra the tenth: thus are these divine gandharvas, the sons of Prava, enumerated.
This lineage of the apsaras, known for its auspicious qualities — the highly blessed goddess Prava bore it long ago, as received from the divine sages.
Alambusā, Miśrakeśī, Vidyutparṇa, Tulanagha, Aruṇā, Rakshita, Rambhā, and likewise Manoramā —
— Asita, Subāhu, Suvrata, Subhuja, Supriya, and Atibahu; and the renowned Hāhā, Hūhū, and Tumburu are remembered as the four foremost gandharvas.
Amrita, brahmanas, cows, gandharvas, and apsaras — these are celebrated in the Purāṇa as the offspring of Kapila.
Thus has the origin of all beings been told to you by me, counted out correctly, and likewise that of the gandharvas and apsaras.
Of serpents and of suparnas, of the Rudras and the Maruts, of cows and of brahmanas — of the glorious ones of meritorious deeds.
This account is life-prolonging, meritorious, and enriching; it is pleasant to hear, should always be listened to, and should be narrated with a heart free from envy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whoever recites this lineage of great souls with discipline in the presence of brahmanas and gods gains abundant progeny, prosperity, and renown, and after death an excellent destination.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The six great sages, known as the mind-born sons of Brahmā, are well known. The eleven supremely mind-born sons of Sthāṇu (Śiva) are also renowned.
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, the greatly renowned Nirṛti; Ajaikapat, Ahirbudhnya, and Pinākī the scorcher of foes —
— Dahana, Ishvara, Kapālī of great splendor, Sthāṇu, and the lord Bhava: these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu — these six are the mighty great-sage sons of Brahmā.
Aṅgiras had three sons renowned everywhere in the world: Bṛhaspati, Utathya, and Saṃvarta — all firm in their vows.
Atri had many sons, O lord of men — all knowers of the Vedas, perfected, tranquil-souled great sages, as is told.
Rākṣasas came from Pulastya, as did vanaras and kinnaras. From Pulaha came deer, lions, tigers, and kimpurushas.
Kratu's sons are equal to Kratu himself in power, companions of birds in flight, renowned throughout the three worlds, and wholly devoted to the vow of truth.
Dakṣa, the blessed sage, was born from the right thumb of Brahmā, O protector of the earth — the best of those who have sons.
From Brahmā's left thumb was born the wife of that great-souled one; and the sage himself fathered fifty daughters upon her.
All those daughters, faultless-limbed and lotus-eyed, the Prajāpati appointed as putrikas (daughters serving as sons), since he had no sons.
He gave ten to Dharma, twenty-seven to Soma (the moon), by divine rule, O king, and thirteen to Kaśyapa.
Learn from me the names of those wives of Dharma as I recite them: Kirti, Lakṣmī, Dhrti, Medha, Pushti, Śraddhā, and Kriya —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— Buddhi, Lajja, and Mati: these are the ten wives of Dharma. These are the gateways of Dharma appointed by the Self-born.
The twenty-seven wives of Soma are celebrated in the world; engaged in guiding time, wives of the moon, of pure vows, all connected to the nakshatras, established in the order of the world's journey.
The grandfather Muni is a god; his son is the Prajāpati (Dharma). That one had eight Vasus as sons — I shall speak of them in detail.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Aha, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa — these are remembered as the eight Vasus.
Dhara is the son of Dhūmra, and similarly Dhruva is a knower of Brahmā. Soma is the son of Manasvinī; from Shvasa came Shvasana (Anila, the wind).
Aha is the son of Rata; Hutāśana (fire) is the son of Śāṇḍilya. Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are remembered as the two sons of Prabhata.
The sons of Dhara are Dravina and Hutahavyavaha (carrier of oblations). The son of Dhruva is the blessed Kāla, who brings about the dissolution of the worlds.
Soma's son is Varcha, by whom the radiant are born. From Manohara were born Shishira, Prāṇa, and Ramana.
The sons of Aha are remembered as Jyoti, Shrama, Śānta, and Muni. The son of Agni (Anala) is the glorious Kumāra, who dwells in the shara-grass forest.
His sons are Shakha, Viśākha, and Naigameṣa born from his back. Because the Kṛttikās adopted him, he is remembered as Kārttikeya.
Śiva is the wife of Anila (the wind god); her son is Purojava. Avijnatagati is the other — these are the two sons of Anila.
Pratyūṣa's son is known as the sage named Devala. Devala also had two sons — patient and wise.
Bṛhaspati's sister, a noble woman, a celibate ascetic, accomplished in yoga, roams the entire world unattached — she is the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus.
The greatly blessed Viśvakarmā was born — the Prajāpati of crafts, the maker of thousands of works of art, the carpenter of the thirty gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is the maker of all ornaments, the foremost among artisans, who fashioned the celestial aerial chariots of the gods.
Men live by the craft of that great-souled one, and they worship the imperishable Viśvakarmā without ceasing.
Bursting through the right breast of Brahmā in human form, the blessed Dharma issued forth — he who brings happiness to all the worlds.
He has three excellent sons, delightful to all beings — Śama (Tranquility), Kāma (Desire), and Harṣa (Joy) — who by their radiance sustain the worlds.
Rati (Delight) is the wife of Kāma; Prāpti (Attainment) is the consort of Śama; and Nandī (Bliss) is the wife of Harṣa — in whom the worlds are established.
Kaśyapa is the son of Marīci; from Kaśyapa were born the gods and the asuras, O tiger among kings — he is indeed the progenitor of the worlds.
Tvāṣṭrī, the greatly blessed wife of Savitṛ, assuming the form of a mare, gave birth in the sky to both the Aśvins.
Aditi has exactly twelve sons, headed by Indra, O lord of men; the youngest of them is Viṣṇu, in whom the worlds are established.
These are the thirty-three gods. I shall now declare to you their lineages, their factions, their clans, and their groups.
Know the Bhārgavas as belonging to the other faction of the Rudras, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, the Vasus, and the Viśvedevas as well.
The mighty Garuḍa, son of Vinatā, and likewise Aruṇa, and the blessed Bṛhaspati — these are reckoned among the Ādityas.
Know the Guhyakas, all medicinal herbs, and animals as belonging to the Aśvins. O king, this host of gods has been proclaimed to you in order; a person who recites this list is freed from all sins.
The blessed Bhṛgu issued forth by splitting open the heart of Brahmā. The son of Bhṛgu is Kavi, the wise one; Śukra is the son of Kavi, and he became a planet (graha).

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Appointed by the Self-born (Brahmā) for the regulation of the life-journey of the three worlds, governing rain and drought, fear and safety, he courses through the universe.
He became the teacher of Yoga, of great intellect, the preceptor of the Daityas and also of the gods — supremely wise, observing celibacy and firm in his vows.
When that Bhārgava was appointed by the Lord for the welfare of the worlds, Bhṛgu sired another blameless son.
That son was Cyavana, blazing with ascetic power, righteous in soul and wise — he who fell from the womb in anger for the liberation of his mother, O Bhārata.
Āruṣī, the daughter of Manu, became the wife of that wise one (Cyavana). From her was born the greatly renowned Aurva, ripping through the thigh — endowed with mighty austerity, great radiance, and all virtues even as a child.
Ṛcīka was the son of Aurva; from him was born Jamadagni. The great-souled Jamadagni had four sons.
Rāma was the youngest of them, yet endowed with qualities not of the least — skilled in all weapons and missiles, the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, and master of himself.
Aurva had a hundred sons, headed by Jamadagni; from them arose thousands of descendants — this is the expansion of the Bhṛgu lineage.
Brahmā has two other sons by whose marks the world is governed — Dhātā and Vidhātā, who dwell together with Manu.
The auspicious goddess Lakṣmī, dwelling in the lotus, is the sister of those two. Her mind-born sons are the horses that move through the sky.
The eldest wife of Varuṇa, a goddess, was born from Śukra (Śukrā). Know her son to be Bala (Strength), and also Surā (Wine), the delight of the gods.
Among the creatures who hungered for food and who fell to devouring one another, Adharma (Unrighteousness) arose there — the destroyer of all beings.
His wife is Nirṛti; from her the Nairṛta Rākṣasas arise. She has three sons, ever given to wicked deeds: Bhaya (Fear), Mahābhaya (Great Fear), and Mṛtyu (Death), the ender of beings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The goddess Tāmrā gave birth to five daughters, renowned throughout the world: Kākī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Śukī.
Kākī gave birth to owls; Śyenī bore hawks; Bhāsī brought forth vultures and kites, O lord of the people.
