Dhṛtarāṣṭrī — that spirited one — gave birth to swans, royal swans, and chakravāka birds in full, blessings to you.
O knower of righteousness, Śukī — high-minded, endowed with auspicious qualities, honored by all marks of excellence — gave birth only to parrots.
Krodhavaśa also gave birth to nine daughters of her own: Mṛgī, Mṛgamandā, Hari, and Bhadramanā —
— and Mātaṅgī, Śārdūlī, Śvetā, Surabhī endowed with all auspicious marks, and the illustrious Surasā.
All deer are the offspring of Mṛgī, O son of the best of men. From Mṛgamandā came bears, sṛmaras (a deer species), and yaks.
From Bhadramanā was born the great serpent Airāvata as her son; Airāvata's son is the divine elephant Mahāgaja.
The offspring of Hari are the lions and the swift monkeys; the golāṅgūlas too — blessings to you — are called the children of Hari.
And Śārdūlī gave birth to lions, tigers, and leopards, O Bhārata — all of them, O greatly fortunate one, without doubt.
The offspring of Mātaṅgī are the mātaṅgas (elephants), O lord of men. And Śvetā gave birth to the swift directional elephant called Śveta.
Likewise, O king, Surabhī gave birth to two daughters — blessings to you — Rohiṇī and the illustrious Gandharvī. From Rohiṇī were born cattle, and from Gandharvī her sons were horses.
Surasā gave birth to nāgas, O king, and Kadrū brought forth serpents. Analā also gave birth to seven trees bearing round fruits. Śukī is the daughter of Analā, and Surasā is the daughter of Kadrū.
Śyenī, the wife of Aruṇa, gave birth to Saṃpāti and likewise Jaṭāyu — two mighty, powerful sons. And Vinatā's two famous sons are Garuḍa and Aruṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus has the origin of all these great beings been fully proclaimed by me, O lord of men, O best of the wise.
Having properly heard this, a person is purified of sin, attains omniscience, and finds the highest path.
Janamejaya said: O blessed one, I wish to hear truly about the births and deeds of all these great-souled beings — gods, dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and all other beings —
— how they were born among men, and their deeds, in proper order.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: O lord of men, I shall tell you in full about those heavenly beings and also the dānavas who were born among humans — them first.
He who was known as Vipracitti, the bull among dānavas — he was born among men as the famous Jarāsaṃdha, the bull among men.
He who, O king, is remembered as Hiraṇyakaśipu, son of Diti — he was born in the human world as Śiśupāla, the bull among men.
He who was famed as Saṃhrāda, the younger brother of Prahrāda — he was born as the renowned Śalya, the bull of the Bāhlīkas.
The radiant Anuhrāda, who was known as the lastborn, became famed as Dhṛṣṭaketu, a lord among men.
He who, O king, was celebrated as the Daitya named Śibi — he was widely known as Druma and was a king on earth.
He among them who was the excellent asura named Bāṣkala — he was known as Bhagadatta and was a lord among men.
Ayaḥśirā, Aśvaśirā, the valiant Ayaḥśaṅku, Gaganamūrdhā, and Vegavān as the fifth —
— these five valiant great asuras were born, O king, as great-souled ones among the Kekayas, the very best of royal bulls.
He who was otherwise known as the glorious Ketumān — he became known on earth as Amitaujā, a king.
He who was the glorious great asura known as Svarbhānu — he became known as Ugrasena, the fierce-actioned lord of men.
He who was the glorious great asura known as Aśva — he became the king named Aśoka, of mighty valor and prowess.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who was the younger brother of that one, O king, remembered as the Daitya Aśvapati — he became the king Hārdikya, the bull among men.
He who was the glorious great asura known as Vṛṣaparvan — he became known on earth as Dīrghaprajña, a king.
He who was the younger brother of Vṛṣaparvan, O king — Ajaka — became known on earth as Malla, a king.
He who was the powerful great asura known as Aśvagrīva — he became known on earth as Rocamāna, a king.
He who was celebrated, O king, as Sūkṣma, the wise and the famous — he became known on earth as Bṛhanta, a king.
He who was known as Tuhuṇḍa, the foremost among asuras — he became known as Senābindu, a lord of men.
He among those asuras named Isṛpā, who was supreme in strength — he became the king named Pāpajit on earth, renowned for his valor.
He who was known as the great asura Ekacakra — he became renowned on earth as Prativindhya.
The Daitya Virūpākṣa, a great asura of variegated warfare — he was known on earth as Citravarman and was a king.
He who was the heroic foremost of dānavas, Hara (or Arihara) — he was born as the bull among men known as Suvāstu.
Ahara, of great radiance, the destroyer of the enemy's side — he became the king renowned on earth as Bāhlika.
He who was the foremost asura known as Nicandra Candravaktra — the glorious Muñjakeśa was that king on earth.
Nikumbha, unvanquished in battle, of great intellect, was born on earth as the best of kings, remembered as Devādhipa.
He among those Daityas who was the great asura named Śarabha — he became the royal sage named Paurava here among men.
He who was the second among those asuras, named Śalabha — he became the lord of men known as Bāhlika Prahrāda.
Candra, the foremost of Diti's sons, comparable to the lord of stars, became the royal sage named Ṛṣika, the best of kings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who was known as Mṛtapā, the foremost of asuras — know that king as the lord of the western marshlands, O best of kings.
Gaviṣṭha, of great radiance, who was celebrated as a great asura — he became known on earth as Drumasena, a king.
He who was the glorious great asura known as Mayūra — he became renowned as Viśva and was a lord of the earth.
He who was the younger brother of that one, known as Suparṇa — he became known on earth as Kālakīrti, a king.
He among them who was celebrated as the pre-eminent asura Candrahanta — he became the royal sage named Śunaka, a lord of men.
He who was named the great asura Vināśana of the moon — he became the royal sage named Jānakī, a lord of men.
He who was called Dīrghajihva, the bull among dānavas, O descendant of the Kurus — he became known on earth as the Kāśirāja, lord of the earth.
The demon Siṃhī gave birth to that Graha who oppresses the moon and sun; he became known among men as King Krātha.
The foremost among the four sons of Anāyus was the powerful demon Vikṣara; that radiant one became King Vasumitra among men.
The second after Vikṣara, O lord of men, was a great demon who became king renowned as the lord of Pāṃsurāṣṭra.
He who was known as Balavīra, that foremost of demons, became the king called the lord of Pauṇḍramatsyaka among men.
He who was widely renowned as Vṛtra, that great demon, O king, became the royal sage known as Maṇimān, a lord of men.
The demon who was Vṛtra's younger brother, known as Krodhahantā, became the king on earth widely renowned as Daṇḍa.
He who was known as Krodhavardhana became the lord of men known as Daṇḍadhāra.
The sons of Kālakā — eight of them were born as lords of men, O tiger among kings, with valor equal to a tiger.
Among the Māgadhas, the illustrious Jayatsena was king; he was the foremost of those eight sons of Kālakā, that great demon.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The second among them, illustrious as Indra's steed, became the lord of men known as Aparājita, the unconquered.
The third, O great king, was a great demon of mighty arms who was born on earth as the lord of the Niṣādas, of fearsome valor.
He who is listed as the fourth among them became known on earth as Śreṇimān, the foremost of royal sages.
The fifth, who was the foremost great demon among them, became known here as Mahaujā, the scourge of foes.
The sixth, who was the wise great demon among them, became known on earth as Abhīru, the foremost of royal sages.
From that same group, the king Samudrasena was born, renowned across the sea-girdled earth, versed in the truth of righteousness and worldly gain.
Named Bṛhan, the eighth of those sons of Kālakā, O king, was a scorcher of foes, righteous in soul and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
The demonic host known as the Krodhavaśas, which I have enumerated for you, O king — from them were born heroes here on earth as lords of men.
Nandika, Karṇaveṣṭa, Siddhārtha, Kīṭaka, Suvīra, Subāhu, Mahāvīra, and Bāhlika —
Krodha, Vicitya, Surasā, the illustrious Nīla the earth-lord, Vīradhāman, and the one named Bhūmipāla, O descendant of Kuru —
Dantavaktra by name, Durjaya by name, Rukmī the tiger among kings, and King Janamejaya —
Āṣāḍha, Vāyuvega, Bhūritejas, Ekalavya, Sumitrā, Vāṭadhāna, and Gomukha —
The Kārūṣaka kings, Kṣemadhūrti, Śrutāyus, Uddhava, and Bṛhatsena as well —
Kṣemogratīrtha, Kuhara the lord of men among the Kaliṅgas, Matimān, and the one renowned as Īśvara, O lord of men —
From the Krodhavaśa host there thus arose on earth a multitude of kings, born in ancient times, O great king, of great fame and great strength.
He who was the chief lord of the Gandharvas, named Devaka, equal in splendor to the king of the gods, was born on earth as a lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Know, O descendant of Bharata, that Droṇa son of Bharadvāja, not born of a womb, arose from a portion of the divine sage Bṛhaspati of great renown.
He who was that Bṛhatkīrti of great radiance, the foremost knower of all weapons among archers, was born here among men, O tiger among kings.
Him whom those versed in the Vedas know as the supreme one in the science of archery and in the Veda, who performs deeds like Indra — that Droṇa, the enhancer of his lineage.
From the combined essence of Mahādeva and Antaka, from both desire and wrath, O descendant of Bharata, was born that hero, the scourge of foes.
Aśvatthāman of great valor, destroyer of the enemy host, that hero with eyes like lotus petals, was a lord of men upon the earth, O king.
The eight Vasus were born as sons of Śaṃtanu upon the Gaṅgā, both by the curse of Vasiṣṭha and by the command of Vāsava.
The youngest of them, Bhīṣma, the bestower of fearlessness upon the Kurus — wise, versed in the Veda, eloquent, and destroyer of the enemy host.
He who was the foremost among all knowers of wisdom, that greatly radiant one, fought with Rāma son of Jamadagni, the great-souled Bhārgava.
He who became the brahmarṣi known as Kṛpa upon the earth, O king — know him to have arisen from the host of the Rudras, of surpassing manhood.
He who was the great warrior King Śakuni in the world — know him, O king, to have arisen as the Dvāpara age incarnate, the crusher of foes.
Sātyaki, true to his word, the exalter of the Vṛṣṇi clan — that crusher of foes was born from a portion of the Marut gods.
Drupada too, the royal sage, arose from that same host and was born in this human world, O king, the foremost of all who bear weapons.
And know Kṛtavarmā, O king, that lord of people, to have been born as one beyond recompense, the very finest bull among kṣatriya sages.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Know the royal sage named Virāṭa, who terrorized the kingdoms of his rivals, to have been born from the host of the Maruts, a crusher of foes.
The son of Ariṣṭā widely known as Haṃsa — that chief of Gandharvas was born as an enhancer of the Kuru lineage.
Known as Dhṛtarāṣṭra, born also through Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the long-armed, greatly radiant lord of men who sees through wisdom — yet by reason of his mother's fault and the sage's wrath, he was born blind.
Know Vidura, born in this world as the most blessed and finest son among those who have sons, to be an incarnation of Atri, the foremost among the wise.
From a portion of Kali was born on earth King Duryodhana — of wicked mind, wicked intellect, the one who brought disgrace upon the Kurus.
He who was that embodiment of Kali, hated by the whole world, that lowest of men who caused the slaughter of all the earth — through whom the great enmity was kindled that brought destruction to all living beings.
All the brothers, sons of Pulastya's lineage, were born among men here — the hundred headed by Duḥśāsana, all of cruel deeds.
Durmukha, Duḥsaha, and the others who are not individually named — all those helpers of Duryodhana are sons of Pulastya's line, O bull among the Bhāratas.
Know King Yudhiṣṭhira to be a portion of Dharma, O king; Bhīmasena a portion of the Wind god; and Arjuna a portion of the king of gods.
Likewise Nakula and Sahadeva are portions of the twin Aśvins, peerless in beauty upon earth, captivating the hearts of all the worlds.
He who was known as Suvarcā, the mighty son of the Moon god — that Abhimanyu of great fame became the son of Arjuna.
Know Dhṛṣṭadyumna, that great warrior, to be a portion of Fire; and know Śikhaṇḍin, O king, who was both woman and man, to be a Rākṣasa.
The five sons of Draupadī who were born, O bull among the Bhāratas — know them, O king, to be members of the Viśvedeva host, O bull among the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Karṇa, that great warrior who was born with armor already upon him — know him to be the incomparable portion of the Sun god, the resplendent deity.
He who is known as Nārāyaṇa, the eternal god of gods — his portion among humans was the mighty Vāsudeva.
Baladeva of great strength was a portion of the serpent Śeṣa; know Pradyumna, O king, to be the mighty Sanatkumāra.
Thus many other portions of the celestials were born as enhancers of Vāsudeva's clan, O lord of men.
The host of Apsarases which I have enumerated for you, O king — a portion of them was born on earth also by the command of Vāsava.
Those sixteen thousand divine women, O lord of men, became in the human world the consorts of Nārāyaṇa.
A portion of Śrī was born for the purpose of desire upon the surface of the earth — a blameless maiden arising from the midst of the sacrificial altar in the family of Drupada.
Neither too short nor too tall, fragrant as the blue lotus, with long lotus-shaped eyes, lovely hips, and long dark hair —
Endowed with all auspicious marks, resembling a vaiḍūrya gem, she was in private the one who bewildered the minds of five lords among men.
The two goddesses Siddhi and Dhṛti were born as the mothers of the five — Kuntī and Mādrī; and Mati was born as the daughter of Subala.
Thus has been recounted for you, O king, the descent of portions of gods and demons, of Gandharvas and Apsarases, and of Rākṣasas.
The kings born on earth, intoxicated with battle, and the great-souled ones born in the vast clan of the Yadus —
This account of the descent of portions is auspicious, fame-giving, conducive to offspring, life-extending, and victory-bringing — it should be heard without envy.
A wise man who hears this account of the descent of portions of gods, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas, knowing their origin and dissolution, does not sink in times of distress.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Janamejaya said: I have heard from you, O brahmin, the full account of the descent of portions of gods, demons, and Rākṣasas, and likewise of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
But I wish to hear further from you, O learned one, the lineage of the Kurus from the very beginning, narrated in the presence of this assembly of brahmin sages.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The perpetuator of the Paurava lineage was the valorous king named Duḥṣanta, the protector of the four-cornered earth, O foremost of the Bhāratas.
That lord of men enjoyed a full quarter of the entire earth, and that conqueror in battle also held the ocean-girdled lands.
That crusher of foes enjoyed all the lands of the border peoples and forest dwellers, the lands extending to the jewel-bearing sea, inhabited by peoples of the four classes.
There was no one who caused the mixing of castes, no one who refused to till the land, no evildoer whatsoever while that king was ruling.
Pursuing lawful pleasures, men then attained both righteousness and wealth, O tiger among men, under that lord of the realm.
There was no fear of thieves, dear one, not the slightest fear of hunger, and no fear of disease either under that lord of the realm.
The castes delighted in their own duties, desireless in their divine observances; having taken refuge in that guardian of the earth, they were free from fear from any quarter.
Rain fell in its proper season, crops bore fruit abundantly, and the earth, the treasure-bearer, was rich with all gems at that time.
And he, of marvelous great valor, youthful and firm as the thunderbolt, could lift Mount Mandara with his two arms and carry it along with its forest of soma-pressing trees.
In archery, in mace combat, in fighting with sword and hilt, on elephant-back, and on horseback, he was fully accomplished.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In strength he was equal to Viṣṇu, in splendor like the sun, in imperturbability like the ocean, in forbearance like the earth.
That guardian of the earth, honored by all, his city and kingdom contented, dwelt among the people he knew well, with dispositions ever devoted to righteousness.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Once that long-armed one, possessed of abundant troops and vehicles, went into a dense forest, surrounded by hundreds of horses and elephants.
He went out surrounded by hundreds of warriors bearing swords and spears, holding maces and clubs in their hands, and carrying lances and javelins.
With the lion-roars of the warriors and the sounds of conch-shells and kettledrums, with the rumble of chariot-wheels and the trumpeting of great elephants,
Mixed with the neighing of horses and the sounds of war-cries and clapping of arms, a great tumultuous noise arose as the king set forth.
Women standing on the upper terraces of the finest palace beheld him, the hero who was the maker of his own glory, resplendent with the full majesty of a king.
The groups of women gazing upon that slayer of enemies, who was like Indra himself and was a great elephant against the elephants of his foes, bearing weapons in hand, were filled with wonder.
"This is that tiger among men, of wondrous valor in battle — having encountered the might of whose arms, the hosts of enemies survive no more."
Thus speaking, those women praised the lord of men with great affection and showered a rain of flowers upon his head.
Praised on all sides by foremost brahmins, he departed with great joy into the forest, eager to hunt deer.
The townspeople and country-folk followed him a great distance, then turned back when they had been dismissed by the king.
Then that lord of the earth, with a chariot swift as Garuḍa, filled the earth and the heavens alike with its thunderous noise.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As he traveled, that wise one beheld a forest resembling Nandana, strewn with bel, arka, and khadira trees, and crowded with kapittha and dhava trees.
It was uneven with mountain slopes and strewn with rocks, waterless and uninhabited by humans, extending for many leagues, filled with terrifying herds of deer and other creatures of the forest.
That tiger among men, Duḥṣanta, together with his retinue and his army and its mounts, roused that forest and slew various kinds of deer.
Duḥṣanta struck down many groups of tigers that came within arrow-range, piercing them through with his shafts.
That bull among men split those at a distance with arrows, while others that came near he cut down with his sword.
He slew certain black deer with his spear, that foremost of the mighty, skilled in the art of wielding the mace in circles, ranging about with boundless valor.
He ranged through the forest striking down the wild deer and birds with javelins, swords, maces, clubs, and short swords.
The great beasts abandoned the vast forest as it was beaten through by that king of wondrous valor and by his battle-loving warriors.
The herds of deer there, their leaders slain and their groups scattered, cried out here and there in their distress.
Reaching a dry river, emaciated from the hopelessness of finding water, their hearts exhausted from exertion, they fell senseless to the ground.
Overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, weary and fallen to the earth, some among them were devoured there by the hungry tiger-men.
Then some forest-dwellers, having kindled fire, properly chopped the flesh and ate it in the prescribed manner.
There some mighty elephants, maddened and wounded by weapons, drew in their trunks in fear and fled with great speed.
Voiding their dung and urine and streaming much blood, those great wild elephants there trampled many men to death.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That forest, thick with buffaloes, with its great animals slain, covered by the king as a cloud of force by its torrents of arrows, shone brilliantly.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having slain thousands of deer, that king with his great army entered yet another forest in pursuit of game.
Alone now, that one of supreme strength, afflicted by hunger and thirst, reached the end of the forest and came to a vast barren wasteland.
Having crossed even that, the king came to another great forest, endowed with the finest hermitages, delightful to the mind, charming to the eye, and touched by cool breezes.
Filled with flowering trees, exceedingly pleasant with lush grass, vast, and resonant with the sweet calls of birds —
Covered by trees with great spreading boughs offering cool shade, its vines swayed by bees, endowed with supreme beauty —
In that forest, not a single tree was without flowers, not one was without fruit, none had thorns, and none was without its covering of bees.
Resounding with birds, adorned most beautifully with flowers, with trees bearing blossoms of every season, exceedingly pleasant and delightful — that great archer entered this finest of forests.
There, the flower-laden trees loosened by the wind shed again and again a variegated rain of blossoms.
The trees touching the sky, resounding with birds of sweet voices, shone there in their garments of many-colored flowers.
On the tender shoots of those trees, bending under the weight of blossoms, the birds cried out softly together with the bees.
Beholding many a spot there adorned with heaps of flowers, enclosed by bowers of creepers, filling the heart with joy, that one of great splendor became filled with delight.
With trees whose branches intertwined with one another, laden with blossoms, resembling the banner-poles of great Indra, that forest shone magnificently.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A breeze, pleasantly cool and fragrant, carrying the pollen of flowers, moved through the forest as if approaching the trees out of a desire to play.
The king beheld this forest, endowed with such qualities, beautiful as the Mālinī riverbank, resembling a lofty banner.
And while he was gazing at that forest filled with joyful birds, he also saw a most charming and lovely hermitage.
It was filled with many kinds of trees, its sacred fires blazing brightly, surrounded by ascetics and Vālakhilya sages, attended by troops of holy men.
With many fire-shrines, its floor spread with flower offerings, and radiant with large, spacious enclosures, it shone brilliantly.
O king, on the banks of the holy Mālinī river with its pleasant waters, crowded with many flocks of birds, the hermitage-grove delightful — beholding there the gentle wild creatures, he was filled with joy.
That foremost of chariot-warriors, glorious, arrived at that hermitage, which resembled the world of the gods and was beautiful in every direction.
He saw the river intertwined with the hermitage, its waters holy, standing there like a mother to all living creatures.
Its sandbars graced with cakravāka birds, flowing with foam and flowers, the home of troops of Kiṃnaras, frequented by monkeys and bears —
Resounding with holy recitation, beautified by its sandbars, visited by maddened elephants, tigers, and great serpents —
Having seen the river thus joined to the hermitage, and the hermitage itself, that lord of the earth resolved then to enter it.
Adorned by the island-graced Mālinī with her lovely banks, the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, beautified like the Gaṅgā, resonant with intoxicated peacocks — he entered that great forest.
That lord of men, approaching what resembled the garden of Citra-ratha, endowed with manifold excellences and unsurpassed in splendor, then wished to see the great seer Kaṇva, the Kāśyapa, rich in austerities.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He stationed his army at the forest gate — chariots, horses crowded together, and masses of infantry — and spoke thus:
"I shall go to see the pure sage Kāśyapa, that storehouse of austerities. Remain here until I return."
Having entered that forest resembling Nandana, that lord of men, the king, shed his hunger and thirst and was filled with great rejoicing.
That lord of men, accompanied by his minister and chaplain, having set aside the marks of kingship, went to that excellent hermitage, wishing to see that undying mass of ascetic merit, the sage.
Beholding that hermitage resembling the world of Brahmā, resounding with the songs of bees, filled with many groups of brahmins,
That tiger among men heard the Ṛgvedic hymns being set in motion by foremost Ṛgvedins with their metrical progressions at the various rites being performed there.
The hermitage then shone with those of boundless spirit, well-disciplined, expert in the supplementary sciences of sacrifice, proceeding through their progressions in sequence.
Foremost among Atharva-Vedins, honored by assemblies of sacrificers, they chanted the Saṃhitā with its pada and krama recitations.
With other brahmins reciting with proper grammatical refinement, that glorious hermitage rang out, gleaming like the world of Brahmā.
With those expert in sacrificial rites, skilled in sequential recitation training, endowed with the knowledge of logical principles and true meanings, who had crossed to the far shore of the Vedas —
Skilled in the synthesis and combination of various textual statements, knowledgeable in special rites, devoted to the dharma of liberation —
Those who had attained mastery of establishing propositions, refuting objections, and knowing ultimate truths, together with foremost Lokāyata philosophers — with all of these it resounded on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Here and there he saw foremost brahmins, self-disciplined, firm in their vows, devoted to silent recitation and fire offerings — perfected sages. That destroyer of enemy heroes was filled with wonder.
Beholding the varied seats adorned with flowers, carefully arranged, that lord of the earth was struck with wonder.
Seeing the worship of the divine shrines performed by the brahmins, that best of kings imagined himself to be dwelling in the world of Brahmā.
He could not satisfy himself gazing at that excellent and auspicious hermitage protected by the austerities of the Kāśyapa, filled with troops of those rich in penance.
He, the destroyer of enemies, together with his minister and chaplain, entered the abode of the Kāśyapa, surrounded on all sides by sages of great vows and rich in austerities — a solitary, supremely charming, and auspicious place.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, going forward, that mighty-armed one, having dismissed his ministers, did not see in that hermitage the sage firm in his vows.
Not finding that sage and seeing the hermitage empty, he called out loudly, "Who is here?" as if making the forest ring with his voice.
Then, hearing that sound of his, a maiden came forth from that hermitage, beautiful as Śrī herself, wearing the garb of an ascetic.
She, dark-eyed, upon seeing king Duḥṣanta, at once said "Welcome to you" and honored him with due ceremony.
Having honored him with a seat and with water for the feet and the ritual offering, she inquired after the lord of men's health and well-being, O king.
Having honored him duly and inquired about his well-being, she said with a gentle smile: "What may be done for you?"
Then the king, having been duly honored, spoke to that sweet-spoken maiden with her flawless limbs:
"I have come to pay homage to the greatly blessed sage Kaṇva. Where has the venerable one gone, dear lady? Tell me, O lovely one."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śakuntalā said: My father the venerable one has gone from the hermitage to gather fruits. Wait a moment — you shall see him return here.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Not seeing the sage, spoken to thus by her, the king, beholding that woman of noble hips, radiant with beauty, and lovely of smile —
Shining with her beauty and with asceticism and self-discipline, endowed with form and youth — thus the lord of the earth spoke:
"Who are you, O lovely-hipped one? Whose are you? Why have you come to the forest, endowed with such beauty and qualities? Whence are you, O fair one?"
"By the mere sight of you, O auspicious one, my heart has been stolen away. I wish to know you — tell me, O lovely one."
Thus addressed by the king there in the hermitage, the maiden spoke these words with a smile, in syllables most sweet.
"O Duṣyanta, I am considered the daughter of the blessed Kanva — the ascetic, the steadfast, the knower of dharma, the illustrious one."
Duṣyanta said: "The blessed one is of supreme greatness, a practitioner of ūrdhvaretas, worshipped by the world — for even dharma might deviate from its course, but one of sharpened vow does not deviate."
"How have you, O fair-complexioned one, come to be his daughter? I have a great doubt in this matter; please resolve it for me here."
Śakuntalā said: "How this account came to me, and how it came to pass in former times — hear it truly, O king, how I am the daughter of the sage."
"A certain seer came here and prompted the account of my birth; the blessed one related it to him — hear it as it is, O lord of the earth."
"In former times, so it is said, Viśvāmitra was performing great austerities, and greatly afflicted Śakra, the lord of the hosts of gods."
"Fearing that this one, whose power blazed with asceticism, might dislodge him from his position, Purandara said this to Menakā:"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'O Menakā, you excel among the apsarases in divine qualities — do me a benefit, O auspicious one; hear what I shall tell you.'"
"'That Viśvāmitra, radiant as the sun, of great austerity, performing terrible penance — he makes my mind tremble.'"
"'O slender-waisted Menakā, this Viśvāmitra is your task — he of sharpened soul, most difficult to assail, engaged in fierce austerity.'"
"'So that he may not dislodge me from my position, go to him and entice him — create an obstacle to his austerity; do this best favor for me.'"
"'With beauty, youth, sweetness, gestures, smiles and speech — captivate him, O shapely one, and turn him away from his austerities.'"
Menakā said: "That blessed one is always of great splendor, great in austerity, and wrathful — for even the blessed lord himself knows this about him."
"You yourself tremble before his splendor, his austerity, and his wrath — that great-souled one — then how could I not tremble?"
"He who deprived the greatly blessed Vasiṣṭha of his beloved sons, and who, though born a kshatriya, became a brahmin by force of will —"
"— who, for purposes of purification, created a mighty river with many waters, which people know in the world as the most sacred Kauśikī —"
"— where, in a time of difficulty long ago, the righteous royal sage Mataṅga, gone to the condition of a hunter, supported this great-souled one's wife —"
"— where, in a time of famine in the past, the sage returned to his hermitage and the lord then gave the name 'Para' to the river —"
"— where he himself, with joyful mind, performed the sacrifice for Mataṅga, and out of fear of whom, O lord of heroes, you went to drink soma —"
"— who, in anger, created new lunar asterisms with richness of stars, surpassing the existing stellar lineages, the constellations beginning with Śravaṇa —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"These are the deeds of him before whom I greatly tremble — command me, O lord, so that when angered he does not burn me."
"He could burn the worlds with his splendor, shake the earth with his foot, compress mighty Meru, and quickly set it spinning."
"How could a young woman like me touch one such as he — endowed with austerity, blazing like fire, his senses fully mastered?"
"He whose face is the sacrificial fire, who blazes, whose eyes are the sun and moon and whose tongue is time itself, O best of gods — how could one like me touch him?"
"Yama and Soma and the great seers, the Sādhyas, the Viśvadevas, and all the Vālakhilyas — even these tremble before his power; why then should one like me not tremble?"
"Being thus commanded by you, O king of gods, how could I not go near the seer? But think of protection for me, O lord of the gods, so that I may act protected for your sake."
"Let the wind strip away my garment there while I am at play, O god; and let Manmatha be my helper there in that task, by your divine grace."
"And let a sweet-scented wind blow from the forest at that time, as I tempt the sage." Having said 'so be it' and having arranged all this, she then went to the hermitage of Kauśika.
Śakuntalā said: "Thus addressed by her, Śakra instructed the wind of eternal passage, and Menakā then departed at the appointed time along with the wind."
"Then that shapely, timid Menakā saw Viśvāmitra performing austerities in the hermitage, his sins burnt away by asceticism."
"Having saluted him, she then played before the sage, and the wind carried away her garment, white as the moon."
"She, the fair-complexioned one, rushed swiftly to the ground to grab that garment, seemingly smiling with shyness at the wind."
"That best of sages then saw Menakā, flustered, clutching her garment, her age and beauty beyond description, her form revealed."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Seeing the excellence of her beauty, that bull among brahmin seers then formed the intent to be with her, falling under the sway of desire."
"He invited her, and she, the blameless one, was willing; those two spent a very long time in the forest, delighting together according to their desire as though it were but a single day."
"That sage fathered Śakuntalā upon Menakā on the lovely slopes of the Himālayas, near the river Mālinī."
"Having delivered the child and abandoned the newborn along the Mālinī, Menakā, her task accomplished, then quickly went to Śakra's assembly."
"Seeing that newborn lying in the desolate forest teeming with lions and tigers, birds surrounded it on all sides."
"The flesh-eating, meat-craving predators of the forest did not harm this child — the birds guarded her there, that daughter of Menakā."
"I went there to touch the sacred waters, and I saw her lying in the desolate wilderness, surrounded by birds; I then brought her and appointed her as my daughter."
"He who made the body, he who gave life, and he whose food one eats — these three in turn are called fathers in the settled teaching of dharma."
"And because she was protected by birds in the desolate forest, I gave her the name 'Śakuntalā' then and there."
"Thus know her as my daughter, O gentle one — Śakuntalā — and the blameless Śakuntalā considers me her father."
"This he related when questioned by the great seer regarding my birth — thus know me as Kanva's daughter, O lord of men."
"Not knowing my true father, I consider Kanva my father — thus have I told you, O king, the account as I heard it occurred."
Duṣyanta said: "It is entirely clear that you are a princess, O auspicious one, speaking as you do — be my wife, O shapely one; tell me, what shall I do for you?"
"Gold garlands, garments, earrings, ornaments, beautiful shining cloth from many towns, splendid jewels and gems —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"— all this I shall bring you today, and golden ornaments and animal skins; let the entire kingdom be yours today — be my wife, O lovely one."
"Come to me, O timid one, O beautiful one, through the Gandharva form of marriage — for among marriages, the Gandharva is said to be the best, O you with thighs like plantain stems."
Śakuntalā said: "My father has gone from this hermitage to gather fruits, O king — wait a moment; he will give me to you."
Duṣyanta said: "I desire you, O shapely one, O blameless one who inclines toward me; know that I am here for your sake — my mind has gone to you."
"The self alone is one's own kinsman, the self alone is one's own path, the self alone is one's own refuge — you should give yourself in accordance with dharma."
"Eight forms of marriage in total are remembered as sanctioned by dharma: Brahmā, Daiva, Arsha, Prajapatya, and also Asura —"
"— Gandharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca as the eighth. Manu Svāyaṃbhuva proclaimed the dharmic rules for these in proper order."
"Know that the first four are commended for a brahmin; know that for a kshatriya six in order are righteous, O blameless one."
"The Rākṣasa form is also said to be valid for kings; the Asura is remembered for Vaiśyas and Śūdras. Of the five, three are righteous; two are remembered as unrighteous here."
"The Paiśāca and the Asura should never be performed under any circumstance; by this rule one should act — this is remembered as the path of dharma."
"The Gandharva and Rākṣasa forms are both righteous for a kshatriya — have no fear of them; whether separately or combined, they may be performed — there is no doubt in this."
"You who are desirous and I who am desirous — O fair-complexioned one, you deserve to become my wife through the Gandharva form of marriage."
Śakuntalā said: "If this is indeed the path of dharma, and if I am indeed master of my own giving — then hear my condition, O best of the Pauravas, O lord."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Promise me truly what I shall tell you in private: the son who is born of me shall be your heir after you."
"He shall be crown prince, O great king — tell me this truthfully; if it be so, O Duṣyanta, let there be union between you and me."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "'So be it,' the king replied to her without hesitation, 'and I shall also bring you to my own city, O bright-smiling one — as you deserve, O shapely one; I tell you this truly.'"
"Having said this, that royal sage took the hand of that blameless-gaited one according to the rite, and dwelt together with her."
"Having reassured her, he departed and said again and again: 'I shall send the four-division army for your sake; with it I shall bring you to my own home, O bright-smiling one.'"
"Having thus promised her, O Janamejaya, that king, lord of the earth, departed, pondering in his mind as he went toward Kaśyapa."
"'What will the blessed one endowed with austerity do upon hearing of this?' — thinking thus, he entered his own city."
"After some time had passed, Kanva too returned to the hermitage; but Śakuntalā, out of shame, did not go to meet her father."
"Then Kanva, of divine knowledge and great austerity, perceived the situation; the blessed one, pleased, spoke having seen all with his divine eye."
"'What you have done today, disregarding me, uniting with a man of royal lineage — that union is not a violation of dharma.'"
"'For the Gandharva form of marriage is called the best for a kshatriya — performed in private, without mantras, between two who desire each other.'"
"'Duṣyanta, the best of men, is righteous-souled and great-souled — you have gone to that highest of men as husband with devotion, O Śakuntalā.'"
"'A great-souled and mighty son shall be born to you in the world — one who shall enjoy this entire earth bounded by the ocean.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'And the wheel of that great-souled universal emperor shall roll forward unchecked, ever victorious.'"
"Then she washed his feet, and having set down the load and placed the fruits nearby, she spoke to the rested sage."
"'The one I have chosen as my husband is that Duṣyanta, the best of men — please bestow your grace upon him together with his ministers.'"
Kanva said: "I am indeed already pleased with him for your sake, O fair-complexioned one; receive from me the boon you desire on his account."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Then Śakuntalā, desiring the welfare of Duṣyanta, chose righteous conduct and steadiness in the kingdom for the Pauravas."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "After Duṣyanta had made his promise and departed, Śakuntalā, she of beautiful thighs, gave birth to a son of immeasurable might."
When three full years had passed, O Janamejaya, she bore Duḥṣanta's son, blazing with the splendour of a bright flame, endowed with beauty, noble bearing, and every virtue.
Kaṇva, foremost among the doers of righteous deeds, then caused the birth-rites and the other purificatory sacraments to be performed for that growing and wise child.
With white, peak-like teeth, the frame of a lion, the mark of the wheel on his palm, majestic in bearing, with a great head and immense strength, a boy godlike in radiance — he swiftly grew up there.
Even as a boy of only six, around the precinct of Kaṇva's hermitage, he would seize tigers, lions, boars, elephants, and buffaloes —
— binding them to trees on every side of the hermitage; the powerful boy would mount them, subdue them, and run about at play.
Then the inhabitants of Kaṇva's hermitage gave him his name: 'Let this boy be Sarvadamana — Tamer of All — for he tames everything.'
So the prince came to bear the name Sarvadamana, endowed with heroic prowess, brilliant energy, and might.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The sage, seeing the prince and his superhuman deeds, declared, 'The time has come for his installation as crown prince,' and so he told Śakuntalā.
Recognising that strength, Kaṇva addressed his disciples: 'Lead this Śakuntalā today, without delay, together with her son, from this hermitage to her husband — she who is honoured by every auspicious mark.'
For a woman's long sojourn among her kinsmen is not fitting; it destroys reputation, conduct, and righteousness. Therefore take her without further delay.
Saying 'So be it,' all of them, those of immeasurable energy, set out placing Śakuntalā together with her son at their head, bound for Hāstinapura.
Taking with her that lotus-eyed son, radiant as a child of the gods, the fair-complexioned Śakuntalā came forth from the forest that Duḥṣanta had known.
Having approached the king and been duly recognised, she was ushered into his presence together with that son of hers who shone with the lustre of the young sun.
Having paid him reverence according to due form, Śakuntalā spoke to him: 'O king, let this son whom you fathered be consecrated as crown prince.'
For this son, O king, was begotten by you upon me, and he is equal to the gods. Act towards him according to the compact you made, O best of men.
Recall, O greatly fortunate one, that compact which was earlier made by you at our meeting in the precinct of Kaṇva's hermitage.
Having heard that speech of hers, the king — though he remembered — declared, 'I do not remember. Whose woman are you, O wicked ascetic?'
'I recall no connection with you in respect of righteousness, pleasure, or worldly gain. Go, or stay, as you please — do whatever you wish.'
Thus addressed, that fair-hipped, proud-spirited woman stood as though shamed, almost insensible with grief, motionless as a post.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Her eyes red with fury and indignation, her lips quivering, she looked askance at the king as though burning him with her sideward glances.
Concealing her outward expression, stirred by wrath, she restrained at that moment the ascetic energy she had gathered through her austerities.
Having reflected for a moment, filled with grief and anger, and gazing steadily at her husband, she spoke these words in fury.
'Though you know, O great king, why do you speak thus — "I do not know" — as indifferently as some common, ordinary man?'
'Your own heart knows the truth and the untruth here; O auspicious one — you yourself are the witness. Do not demean yourself.'
'One who, being otherwise, passes himself off as otherwise — what sin has not been committed by that self-thief, that robber of his own soul?'
'You think yourself alone — you do not know the ancient sage dwelling in the heart, who is the knower of every sinful deed; yet it is before him that you commit this wrong.'
'He who has done evil thinks "no one knows me," yet the gods know him, and so does the inner Person who dwells within him.'
'The sun and the moon, wind and fire, sky, earth, water, the heart, Yama, day and night, and both twilights — and Dharma — all know a man's conduct.'
'Yama Vaivasvata exacts the penalty for the evil deeds of that man with whose conduct the witness of deeds, the knower of the field, dwelling in the heart, is displeased.'
'But of that wicked-souled man with whom this inner witness is not pleased, Yama exacts retribution for his evil deeds.'
'One who demeans himself and behaves contrary to his own nature — the gods do not bestow their grace upon him for whom even his own self is no authority.'
'Do not scorn me thus, thinking "she came of her own accord" — I, your faithful wife, I who deserve to be honoured, I who have come before you myself — you do not honour me.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Why do you look upon me like a common man in this assembly? I am not saying this in private — do you not hear me?'
'If you will not heed my plea, O Duḥṣanta, then this very day your head shall split into a hundred pieces.'
'Because a husband enters his wife and is born again from her, the ancient sages know the wifeness of a wife as jāyā — she from whom he is born anew.'
'The offspring that is born to a man comes from him — it delivers his lineage of deceased fathers and grandfathers who have gone before.'
'Because a son delivers his father from the hell called Put, the Self-existent One himself has called him putra — the deliverer.'
'She is a true wife who is capable in the home; she is a true wife who bears children; she is a true wife whose life is her husband; she is a true wife who is devoted to her husband.'
'A wife is half of a man; a wife is his best companion; a wife is the root of the three aims of life; a wife is the friend of him who is to die.'
'Those who have wives can perform rites; together with their wives they are true householders; those who have wives rejoice; those who have wives are endowed with prosperity.'
'In solitary moments wives become sweet-spoken companions; in the duties of righteousness they become fathers; to one in distress they become mothers.'
'Even in the wilderness a wife is the resting-place for the wayfaring man. He who has a wife is trustworthy; therefore a wife is the highest refuge.'
'Even the departed spirit wandering alone through difficult passages — a faithful wife ever follows her husband.'
'A wife who dies first waits for her husband after death; or if her husband dies first, the virtuous wife follows him afterwards.'
'For this reason, O king, the taking of a wife's hand in marriage is prescribed — for what a husband obtains in his wife belongs to him both in this world and in the next.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'The wise declare that a son is the self begotten by the self; therefore a man should regard his wife as the mother of his son, as he would regard his own mother.'
'A father, beholding the son born of his wife — like seeing his own face in a mirror — is gladdened, as if the meritorious man had attained heaven.'
'Men afflicted by the burnings of mental grief and by diseases find delight in their wives, as those tormented by the heat find relief in water.'
'Even in great anger a wise man should not speak harshly to women, seeing that pleasure, affection, and righteousness are all dependent upon them.'
'Women are the sacred, eternal field of one's own birth — what power would even the sages have to create offspring without a woman?'
'When a son, who has been running about covered in the dust of the earth, runs up and embraces his father's limbs — what greater joy can there be than that?'
'Why then do you disdain this very son who has come to you of himself, who longs for you, and who looks at you with expectant eyes?'
'Even ants carry their own eggs and do not break them — how then, knowing righteousness as you do, could you not support your own son?'
'The touch of garments, of women, or of water is not as pleasurable as the touch of a small child being embraced — the touch of one's own son.'
'A brahmin is the foremost among two-footed beings; the cow is the greatest among four-footed beings; a teacher is the best among elders; a son is the most excellent of all things that can be touched.'
'Let this comely son embrace you and touch you — there is no more pleasurable touch in the world than the touch of a son.'
'Three full years after I gave birth, O subduer of foes, O lord of kings — I bring you this prince who will put an end to your sorrows.'
'O Paurava, a voice from the sky once addressed me at his birth, saying he shall be the performer of a hundred horse-sacrifices.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Do not men, even when travelling to another village, having first inhaled the fragrance of their sons' heads and marked them with a name-sign out of affection, bid them farewell with blessings?'
'The twice-born recite this Vedic declaration at the birth-rite of sons — you too know it likewise:'
'"You are born from limb after limb, you spring forth from the heart; you are the self who bears the name of son — so live a hundred autumns."'
'My sustenance and my undying lineage depend upon you — therefore, live happily a hundred autumns, my dear child.'
'This second man born from a man — born from your limbs — behold your own self as if reflected in a spotless pool, O king; behold my son.'
'Just as the Āhavanīya fire is kindled from the Gārhapatya, so has this son been born from you — you being one, you are made twofold.'
'For it was you, pursuing game, drawn away by a deer, who found me, a maiden, in my father's hermitage while ranging in the hunt, O king.'
'Urvaśī, Pūrvacitti, Sahajanyā, Menakā, Viśvācī, and Ghṛtācī — these six are the foremost of the Apsarases.'
'Among them, Menakā by name, the foremost Apsaras sprung from Brahmā's creative power, descending from heaven to earth, bore me by Viśvāmitra.'
'That Apsaras Menakā gave birth to me on the slopes of the Himālaya, and having abandoned me there she departed — like a wicked woman casting aside another's child.'
'What inauspicious deed did I commit in a former birth, that I was abandoned by my kin in childhood and now again by you?'
'Abandoned by you I shall willingly go back to the hermitage — but you should not abandon this child, your own son born of yourself.'
Duḥṣanta spoke: 'I do not acknowledge a son born of you, O Śakuntalā. Women are untruthful in their speech — who would trust your words?'
'Your mother Menakā is a merciless harlot — she who cast you away on the slopes of the Himālaya like a discarded garland.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'And that merciless father of yours, Viśvāmitra — born of kṣatriya stock, greedy for brahminhood, entirely given over to lust.'
'Menakā is the best of Apsarases and your father is a great sage — the offspring of those two — yet why do you present yourself like a wanton woman?'
'Are you not ashamed to speak these unbelievable words, especially in my presence? Go away, O wicked ascetic woman.'
'Where stands the great sage, ever terrible, and where the Apsaras Menakā — and where do you stand, so pitiable, wearing the mere garb of an ascetic woman?'
'And this son of yours is huge, and even as a child immensely strong — how has he grown up in such a short time, like the trunk of a śāla tree?'
'Your origin is very low — you appear to me a wanton woman; for you were born of Menakā by random desire and lust.'
'All that you say, O ascetic woman, is unknown to me. I do not recognise you. Go wherever you please.'
Śakuntalā spoke: 'O king, you see the faults of others though they be but the size of a mustard seed, yet even when you behold your own faults, though they be the size of a bilva fruit, you do not see them.'
Menakā stands high among the thirty gods, and the thirty gods revere Menakā; my birth excels yours, Duḥṣanta, measured from your birth.
You roam upon the earth, O king, while I move through the sky — see the distance between us as that between Mount Meru and a mustard seed.
I visit the palaces of Mahendra, Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa — behold my power, O king.
What I am about to tell you, O sinless one, is a true saying — I speak it as an illustration, not out of hatred; having heard it, you should bear with it patiently.
As long as an ugly man does not see his own face in a mirror, he considers himself more handsome than others.
But when he looks into the mirror and sees his distorted face, he then knows himself truly — not the other person.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One who is supremely gifted in beauty does not belittle anything; but one who talks excessively with harsh words becomes a nuisance in this world.
A fool, hearing both good and bad words spoken by people, picks up only the bad words — like a pig that picks up filth.
But a wise man, hearing both good and bad words spoken by people, takes only the virtuous word — like a swan that separates milk from water.
Just as a good person feels anguish when he speaks ill of others, in the same way a wicked person feels delight when he slanders others.
Just as the righteous attain peace by respectfully saluting elders, so a fool attains a perverse contentment by reviling good people.
Fools who see no fault in themselves live happily while perceiving faults in others; wherever the virtuous are to be reproached by others, they call those others just such people.
There is nothing more laughable in this world than when a wicked man himself calls a virtuous man wicked.
From a man fallen from truth and righteousness, enraged, like a venomous serpent, even a non-believer shrinks away — how much more so a believer.
Whoever, having himself fathered a son in his own likeness, then disrespects him — the gods destroy his prosperity and he does not enjoy the higher worlds.
The forefathers declared a son to be the highest support of family and lineage, the foremost of all sacred duties — therefore one should never abandon a son.
Manu declared five kinds of sons: those born of one's own wife, those received as gifts, those purchased, those raised, those begotten on other women, and those adopted.
Sons bring righteousness and glory to men, they increase the joy of the heart, and — born as rafts of dharma — they rescue their fathers from hell.
Therefore you, O tiger among kings, lord of the earth, lion among rulers, should not abandon your son; protecting yourself, truth, and righteousness, you should not carry deceit in this world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A reservoir is better than a hundred wells; a sacrifice is better than a hundred reservoirs; a son is better than a hundred sacrifices; truth is better than a hundred sons.
If a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth are placed in a balance, truth alone surpasses a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Mastering all the Vedas and bathing in all the sacred fords — whether these equal speaking truth, O king, or do not equal it, truth is supreme.
There is no dharma higher than truth; there is nothing higher than truth; there is indeed nothing more terrible in this world than falsehood.
O king, truth is the supreme Brahman; truth is the highest covenant — do not abandon the covenant, O king; let truth be your companion.
If you are inclined to falsehood and do not believe in truth yourself, then I am leaving — there is no fellowship with one such as you.
Even without you, Duḥṣanta, my son will protect this four-bounded earth adorned with the king of mountains.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken these words, Śakuntalā departed. Then, while Duḥṣanta was surrounded by officiating priests, the chief priest, teachers, and ministers, a disembodied voice spoke to him from the sky.
The mother is only the bellows; the son belongs to the father from whom he is born. Maintain your son, Duḥṣanta; do not disrespect Śakuntalā.
The son of the seed-giver raises him from Yama's realm, O lord of men; and you are indeed the sustainer of this womb — Śakuntalā speaks the truth.
The wife bears a son — the self divided into two parts. Therefore, O king Duḥṣanta, maintain your son, the son of Śakuntalā.
This is disgrace — who would abandon a living son while himself alive? Maintain the great-souled Śākuntalā, your son Dauḥṣanti, O Paurava.
Because he is to be maintained by you, and also by our command, therefore let this son of yours be named Bharata — 'he who is to be maintained.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing the declaration of the heavenly beings, the Paurava king rejoiced and said this to the chief priest and ministers.
May you all hear the words of this divine messenger — I too recognize him myself as my own son in exactly this way.
If I had accepted him on her word alone, people would have had doubts, and in that way he would not have been certified as pure.
Having thus vindicated him through the divine messenger, O Bhārata, the king, filled with joy and delight, accepted his son.
He smelled the child's head and embraced him with affection; honored by brahmins and praised by bards, the king experienced the supreme joy born of a son's touch.
The king, who knew dharma, honored that wife according to righteousness, and then the king spoke these conciliatory words to her.
This union with you was made in secret, away from the world's gaze; therefore, O goddess, I deliberated thus in order to establish your purity.
The world might think, on account of you being a woman, that your union with me was improper, and so I accepted this son into the kingdom only after deliberation.
And what unpleasant words you, though beloved and devoted to me, spoke to me in great anger — all of that I forgive you, O large-eyed auspicious one.
Having spoken thus to her, the royal sage Duḥṣanta honored his beloved queen with garments and food and drink, O Bhārata.
Then King Duḥṣanta named his son born of Śakuntalā 'Bharata' and consecrated him as the crown prince.
The great-souled Bharata's glorious wheel of conquest began to roll — radiant, divine, unconquered, filling the worlds with its resounding might.
He conquered the rulers of the earth and made them submissive; he walked the path of the virtuous and attained unsurpassed glory.
That king became a sovereign emperor of the whole earth, blazing with majesty; he performed many sacrifices just as Śakra, the lord of the Maruts, does.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kaṇva caused him to perform a great horse-sacrifice with lavish fees, like Dakṣa; the illustrious one obtained the horse-sacrifice called Govitata, in which Bharata gave Kaṇva a thousand padmas of gold.
From Bharata came the glory of the Bhāratas, by which this family is called Bhārata; both earlier and later descendants became renowned as Bhāratas.
In the lineage of Bharata there were many foremost kings, equal to the gods in power, equal to Brahman in splendor.
Their names are beyond count in every respect, O Bhārata; of those most fortunate ones, equal to gods, devoted to truth and uprightness, I shall recite them to you in order of their eminence.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: In the lineage of Dakṣa the Progenitor, Manu Vaivasvata, Bharata, Kuru, Pūru, and Ajamīḍha —
— this lineage of the Yādavas and that of the Pauravas in full, and likewise of the Bhāratas — holy, conferring welfare, meritorious, glory-giving, life-prolonging — I shall recite to you, O sinless one.
All blazing with splendor equal to great sages, the ten sons of Pracetas are remembered as the primeval beings — those mighty ones who were burnt by the fire born of clouds.
From those ten was born Dakṣa, son of Pracetas; from Dakṣa, O tiger among men, these creatures came into being — he is indeed the grandfather of all the worlds.
Dakṣa, the sage son of Pracetas, uniting with Vīriṇī, fathered a thousand sons equal to himself, firm in their vows.
Nārada taught Dakṣa's thousand gathered sons the supreme knowledge of liberation, the unsurpassed wisdom of Sāṃkhya.
Then Dakṣa the Progenitor, wishing to multiply creation, appointed fifty daughters as his putrikās (daughters treated as sons), O Janamejaya.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, twenty-seven suited to the passage of time to Indu (the Moon).
Of the thirteen wives, the most excellent Dākṣāyaṇī — Kaśyapa, son of Marīci, begat upon her the Ādityas, endowed with might: Indra and the others, and also Vivasvat.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From Vivasvat was born the mighty Yama Vaivasvata; and from Yama too, O king, a son was born — Mārtāṇḍa.
From Mārtāṇḍa was born the wise and powerful Manu; from Manu this lineage of human beings became celebrated; from Manu were born the Mānavas — brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and the rest.
There, O king, brahminhood was united with the warrior order; those Mānavas who were brāhmaṇas studied the Veda together with its ancillary texts.
Vena, Dhṛṣṇu, Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Ikṣvāku, Karūṣa, Śaryāti, and also Ilā as the eighth —
— Pṛṣadhra as the ninth, devoted to the warrior's dharma, and Nābhāgāriṣṭa as the tenth — these are called Manu's mighty sons.
Fifty more sons of Manu were likewise born on earth; all of them perished through mutual strife — so we have heard.
The learned Purūravas was then born from Ilā — she was both his mother and his father, so we have heard.
The greatly glorious Purūravas, though human, consumed thirteen islands of the ocean, surrounded by non-human beings.
Purūravas, maddened by his own power, entered into conflict with brāhmaṇas and seized their jewels even as they cried out in protest.
Sanatkumāra, O king, came from the world of Brahman and then counseled him; but he did not accept that counsel.
Then that lord of men, overcome by greed, drunk on power, having lost all sense, was immediately cursed by the enraged great sages and perished.
For he, the sovereign, dwelling in the world of Gandharvas and accompanied by Urvaśī, properly brought the three fires appointed for the rite.
Six sons were born from Urvaśī: the wise Āyus, Amāvasu, Dṛḍhāyu, Vanāyu, Śrutāyu — sons of Urvaśī.
Nahuṣa, Vṛddhaśarman, Raji, Rambha, and Anenas — born of Svarbhānavī — these are declared to be the sons of Āyu.
Nahuṣa, son of Āyu, wise and true in valor, ruled a very great kingdom as lord of the earth by the law of righteousness.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nahuṣa protected the ancestors, gods, sages, brāhmaṇas, Gandharvas, serpents, Rākṣasas, the priestly order, the warrior order, and the merchant class.
Having slain hordes of robbers, the mighty Nahuṣa made sages pay tribute and yoked them to carry him on their backs like beasts of burden.
He caused himself to hold the position of Indra, having overpowered the dwellers of heaven by his radiance, austerity, valor, and might.
Nahuṣa fathered six sons on his beloved wife: Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, the fifth Uddhava, and a sixth.
Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, became emperor, true in his valor; he ruled the earth and performed various sacrifices.
Honoring the ancestors with supreme power and ever reverently worshiping the gods, the unconquered Yayāti bestowed his grace upon all creatures.
His sons, mighty archers endowed with every virtue, O great king, were born of Devayānī and also of Śarmiṣṭhā.
Yadu and Turvasu were born of Devayānī; and Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru were born of Śarmiṣṭhā.
He, the son of Nahuṣa, ruled his people righteously through endless years, O king, while enduring a terrible old age that was destroying his beauty.
Overwhelmed by old age, that king addressed his sons — Yadu, Pūru, Turvasu, Druhyu, and Anu — O Bhārata.
"I wish to roam in the pleasures of youth and to sport with young women as a young man — help me in this, my sons."
Then the elder son born of Devayānī, Yadu, said to him: "What is it that you need from us, and what use is our youth to you?"
Yayāti said to him: "Take my old age upon yourself; with your youth let me pursue the objects of pleasure."
"Through the curse of the sage Uśanas while I was performing long sacrificial sessions, I have been deprived of the fulfillment of desire, and I grieve because of it, my sons."
"Let one of you rule the kingdom with my body, while I, young in a fresh body, attain all pleasures."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Yadu and the others did not accept his old age. Then the youngest, Pūru, of true valor, spoke to him.
"O king, roam in the realm of youth with a new body; I, having taken on old age, will remain in the kingdom by your command."
Thus addressed, that royal sage, by the power of his ascetic vigor, transferred the old age then to his great-souled son.
Taking on the youth of the son of Pūru, the king entered into his prime; and bearing the age of Yayāti, Pūru governed the kingdom.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, the unconquered Yayāti, still unsatiated in his desires, spoke to his son Pūru.
"Through you I have obtained my inheritance; you are the son who carries on my lineage. The line of Pūru — by this name shall your fame go forth in the world."
Then that tiger among kings, having anointed Pūru to the kingdom, passed away to the law of time after a great span of years.
Janamejaya said: "Yayāti, our ancestor, who was the tenth from the Lord of Creatures — how did he obtain the daughter of Śukra, she who is supremely difficult to win?"
"I wish to hear this in detail, O best of twice-born men; and in due order tell me separately of those who carried on the line of Pūru."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Yayāti was a royal sage with the splendor equal to the king of gods. Both Śukra and Vṛṣaparvā chose him in affection in those ancient times."
"That I shall fully narrate to you as you ask, O Janamejaya — the union of Devayānī and of Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa."
A conflict for supremacy arose between the gods and the demons, throughout the three worlds with all their moving and unmoving beings.
Desiring victory, the gods chose the sage Āṅgirasa as their chaplain and sacrificial priest; the others chose Uśanas Kāvya. Those two brahmins were always in fierce rivalry with each other.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There, whichever demons were slain by the gods in battle, Kāvya revived them again by resort to the power of his knowledge; and rising again, they fought the gods once more.
But those gods whom the demons slew in the thick of battle, Bṛhaspati of great intellect could not revive.
For he did not know that knowledge — the life-restoring science — which the mighty Kāvya knew; and so the gods fell into the deepest despair.
Then the gods, anxious with fear of Uśanas Kāvya, approached Kaca, the eldest son of Bṛhaspati, and spoke to him.
"Favor those who favor you; render us the highest help. That knowledge which resides in the brahmin Śukra of boundless splendor — quickly bring it forth, and you shall share in our portion."
"That twice-born one can be found near Vṛṣaparvā; there he protects the demons and does not protect non-demons."
"You, in the freshness of your youth, are capable of pleasing that sage, and also Devayānī, the beloved daughter of that great soul."
"No one else exists who is capable of winning his favor — not through good conduct, courtesy, sweetness, right behavior, and self-restraint as you are. When Devayānī is pleased, you will surely obtain that knowledge."
Saying "So be it," Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, then set out — duly honored by the gods — toward the dwelling of Vṛṣaparvā.
Going swiftly, O king, sent forth by the gods, Kaca arrived at the city of the lord of demons, saw Śukra, and spoke these words.
"Let your honor accept me as a pupil — the grandson of the sage Āṅgiras, the direct son of Bṛhaspati, known by the name Kaca."
"I shall practice the highest celibate studentship under you, the supreme teacher; grant me your approval, O brahmin, for a thousand years."
Śukra said: "Kaca, be most welcome; I accept your words. I shall honor you who are worthy of honor, and may Bṛhaspati be honored through you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Kaca, saying 'so be it,' accepted the vow that was prescribed by Śukra Uśanas, the son of the poet, himself."
He accepted the prescribed duration of the vow as directed, attending upon his teacher and Devayānī, O Bhārata.
Ever intent on pleasing her, that young man, at the threshold of youth, delighted Devayānī with singing, dancing, and playing music.
Cultivating the company of Devayānī, the girl who had just come of age, he pleased her with flowers, fruits, and acts of service, O Bhārata.
And Devayānī too, that charming woman, singing along with him, attended upon that brahmin who practiced his vows and observances in private at that time.
Five hundred years passed thus while Kaca pursued his vow; then the demons, becoming aware of him, turned against Kaca.
Finding him alone in the forest tending the cows, in their rage and out of hatred for Bṛhaspati, and to protect the knowledge, they slew him; and having killed him, they ground him to sesame-sized pieces and fed him to wolves.
Then the cows returned to their fold without a cowherd. Seeing those cows come back from the forest without Kaca, Devayānī spoke these words at the right moment, O Bhārata.
"Your fire-sacrifice has not been offered, and the sun has set, my lord; the cows have come back without a cowherd — father, Kaca is nowhere to be seen."
"Clearly Kaca must have been slain or is dead, father; without him I cannot live — I tell you the truth."
Śukra said: "By uttering the word 'come here,' I shall revive the dead."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Employing the life-restoring knowledge, he called out to Kaca; summoned, Kaca appeared unharmed by virtue of that knowledge, and when questioned by the brahmin's daughter, he told her: 'I was slain.'"
Again, urged by Devayānī, the brahmin went to the forest at will to gather flowers; and the demons caught sight of him there.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the demons slew him a second time, burned him, reduced him to powder, and mixed him into the wine of the brahmin himself.
Again Devayānī spoke words to her father: "Kaca who went to gather flowers and run errands, father, is nowhere to be seen."
Śukra said: "Daughter, Bṛhaspati's son Kaca has gone the way of the dead. Though revived by the knowledge, he is slain again in this way — what can I do?"
"Do not grieve thus, do not weep, Devayānī; one such as you should not mourn a mortal. The gods, the Viśve-devas, and all the world bow before a transformation that has arrived."
Devayānī said: "He whose grandfather is the most venerable Āṅgiras, and whose father too is the ascetic-wealthy Bṛhaspati — how should I not grieve, how should I not weep for the son or even the grandson of such a sage?"
"He was a celibate student, rich in austerity, ever diligent and skilled in his duties. Father, I shall follow the path of Kaca — I will not eat; for dear to me is the handsome Kaca."
Śukra said: "Without doubt the demons hate me — these terrible ones who slay my blameless pupil and wish to make me a non-brahmin; they act toward me as demons have plotted. But there would be an end to this evil here; what person would the guilt of brahmin-slaughter not burn, even Indra himself?"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Urged by Devayānī, the great sage Kāvya called out to Bṛhaspati's son Kaca once more, with great intensity."
Summoned by the teacher's knowledge and speaking from fear of his guru, a faint voice arose from within the belly. He said to him: "Tell me, brahmin — by what path have you entered, and how do you remain in my belly?"
Kaca said: "By your grace, memory does not leave me; I remember everything — what happened and how. But it should not be that there is a waste of my austerity; and so I endure this terrible suffering."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I was given to you in wine by the demons, O Kāvya, after they slew, burned, and ground me to powder. How could the demonic magic ever prevail against the divine magic while you stand firm?"
Śukra said: "What shall I do that is pleasing to you today, my son? Kaca could live only at the cost of my death — for Kaca who is inside me, O Devayānī, could be seen only by splitting my belly."
Devayānī said: "Two griefs, like fire, would burn me: the destruction of Kaca and harm to you. In the destruction of Kaca there is no peace for me; yet if you are harmed I am unable to live."
Śukra said: "You are fully accomplished in form, O son of Bṛhaspati, since the devoted Devayānī cherishes you. Receive this life-restoring knowledge — for if you were not Kaca today, you would be Indra himself in that form."
"No one else living would return again from my belly — except a brahmin alone; therefore receive the knowledge."
"Becoming my son, sustain me who have sustained you; emerging from this body, my son, consider the righteous regard I have for you — and having received the knowledge from your teacher, be endowed with knowledge."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Having received the knowledge from his teacher, the handsome brahmin Kaca burst through the belly and came forth on the right side of the brahmin — like the moon on a full-moon night at the close of the bright fortnight."
And seeing that mass of brahmic splendor fallen, Kaca himself raised up the dead man. Having obtained that accomplished knowledge and having paid obeisance, Kaca then addressed him as teacher.
"Those who do not revere the teacher who is worthy of worship — the giver of the highest truth, the treasury of treasuries through four lineages — they go to sinful worlds without foundation."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Having brought about deception through the drinking of wine and the destruction of consciousness so terrible, and having seen Kaca who had been swallowed in wine by one who was deluded and who was also so handsome —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"— the great-souled one rose up in anger; Uśanas Kāvya himself, wishing to do what was good for brahmins and now deeply troubled about wine-drinking, spoke these words:"
"Whatever brahmin henceforth in this world, dull-witted, drinks wine out of delusion — he becomes one fallen from righteousness and also a slayer of brahmins; he shall be censured in this world and in the next."
"And this boundary of brahminical law that I have established throughout all the world — let the virtuous brahmins who hearken to their teachers, and let all the gods and all the worlds, hear it."
Having spoken thus, that great-souled one — the immeasurable treasury of all treasuries of austerity — summoned those demons whose minds were blinded by fate, and spoke these words to them.
"I declare to you — you demons are foolish. Kaca has succeeded and shall remain with me; having obtained the life-restoring knowledge of great import, he is equal in splendor to Brahman and has become Brahman-natured."
Having dwelt near his teacher for a thousand years, Kaca, given leave to depart, desired to go to the abode of the thirty gods.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "But as he, his vow completed and released by the teacher, set out toward the dwelling of the thirty gods, Devayānī said this to him."
"O grandson of the sage Āṅgiras, you shine by your conduct and birth, and also by knowledge, austerity, and self-restraint."
"Just as the sage Āṅgiras is revered and of great renown to my father, so too is Bṛhaspati to me — worthy of reverence and worship above all."
"Knowing this, understand what I say to you, O ascetic-wealthy one — understand how I have conducted myself toward you while you were engaged in your vow and observances."
"You, now returned with your knowledge, should favor me who am devoted to you; take my hand in the proper manner, with sacred mantras duly preceding."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kaca said: "Just as your venerable father is to be worshipped and revered by me, so too are you, O blameless-limbed one — even more deserving of my veneration."
You are dearer than life itself to the great-souled son of Bhṛgu; O noble one, you are by dharma always to be honoured by me as the daughter of my guru.
Just as Śukra, your father, is always my revered guru, so too are you, O Devayānī; therefore you ought not to speak to me in this way.
Devayānī said: You are indeed the son of a guru's son, but you are not my father's son; therefore you too are honourable and worthy of reverence to me, O best of twice-born.
When you were slain again and again by the asuras, O Kaca, recall for yourself the love I bore you from that time forward.
You know my supreme devotion in friendship and in love; you ought not, O knower of dharma, to abandon me who am devoted to you and guiltless.
Kaca said: You are pressing me into a duty in a matter where I cannot be employed, O you of beautiful vows; be gracious, O fair-browed one — to me you are more revered than even my guru, O auspicious one.
Where you dwelt, O wide-eyed one, O moon-faced one, there too did I dwell, O noble one — in the womb of Kāvya himself, O passionate one.
You are by dharma my sister; do not speak thus, O beautiful-faced one. I have dwelt at ease, O noble one; there is no anger in me.
I take my leave of you and shall go; wish me good fortune on my path. I am to be remembered without violating dharma. Rise ever with diligence and worship my guru.
Devayānī said: If you, having been urged, reject me for the sake of dharma and desire, then, O Kaca, this knowledge of yours shall not reach fulfilment.
Kaca said: I refuse because you are the guru's daughter, not because of any fault; and I have been released by my guru. Curse me thus if you wish.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I speak the ancient law of the seers, O Devayānī; as you have cursed me, I do not deserve this curse — it comes from passion, not from dharma.
Therefore the desire you have shall not be fulfilled thus; no son of a seer shall ever take your hand in marriage.
The knowledge shall not bear fruit for you — what you said of me shall be so likewise; but I shall teach another, and for him the knowledge shall bear fruit.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to Devayānī, Kaca, best of twice-born, quickly departed to the abode of the lord of the thirty gods.
Beholding him arrived, the gods with Indra at their head, rejoicing, honoured Bṛhaspati and then spoke these words to Kaca.
The most wonderful deed you have done for our benefit — your glory shall never perish; you shall be a sharer of our offerings.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Kaca had mastered his knowledge and returned, the gods, joyful in appearance, having studied that knowledge from Kaca, became fulfilled in their purpose, O bull of the Bhāratas.
All of them assembled together and then spoke to Śatakratu: "Now is the time for your valour; slay your enemies, O Purandara."
Thus addressed by the assembled thirty gods, Maghavan then said "So be it" and set forth; and he saw women in a forest.
Among the maidens who were playing in that forest resembling Caitraratha's garden, he, having become wind, mixed together all their garments.
Then those maidens, rising together from the water, seized those garments in many instances each as they came nearest to hand.
There Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, not knowing, took the mixed-up garment of Devayānī.
Then a quarrel arose between the two of them there, O king of kings, between Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā on account of it.
Devayānī said: Why do you take my garment, having become a pupil of mine, O demoness? It shall not go well with you, being devoid of proper conduct.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śarmiṣṭhā said: Your father praises and salutes my father again and again, whether seated or reclining, standing humbly and submissively.
You are the daughter of one who begs, praises, and receives; I am the daughter of one who is praised, who gives and does not receive.
Unarmed against one who is armed, empty against one who is full, you stir up trouble, O beggar-girl; you shall find a match to fight you back — I do not count you at all.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Śarmiṣṭhā threw Devayānī, who had grown haughty and was clinging to her garment, into a well, and then went home to her city.
