Thinking "She is dead," Śarmiṣṭhā of wicked resolve departed without looking back toward home, carried away by the force of her anger.
Then Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, came to that place, his horses exhausted, his steeds wearied, thirsting, seeking game.
He, the son of Nahuṣa, looking about at that waterless well, saw that maiden there, blazing like a flame of fire.
Having seen her, that best of kings, with most soothing and gracious words of comfort, questioned that maiden of divine complexion.
"Who are you, copper-nailed, dark-complexioned, with well-polished gem-set earrings? You meditate at great length and deeply — why do you sigh so distressed?"
"And how have you fallen into this well overgrown with creepers and grass? Whose daughter are you? Tell me everything, O slender-waisted one."
Devayānī said: I am the daughter of that Śukra who revives with his knowledge the demons slain by the gods; he surely does not know of me now.
This is my right hand, O king, with copper-hued nails on its fingers; take it and lift me up — you are deemed nobly-born in my estimation.
For I know you to be self-restrained, valiant, and illustrious; therefore you ought to raise me who have fallen from this well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Recognising her then as a brahmin woman, the son of Nahuṣa took her by the right hand and lifted her up out of that pit.
Having quickly raised her from that well, the lord of men Yayāti took his leave of that fair-hipped one and went to his own city.
Devayānī said: Go quickly, O Ghūrṇikā, and tell my father everything; for I shall not enter the city of Vṛṣaparvan now.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: She quickly went to the demon mansion, found Kāvya, and spoke these words to him, her mind agitated with alarm.
"I report to you, O greatly wise one, O greatly fortunate one, that Devayānī has been struck down in the forest by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan."
Having heard that his daughter had been struck down there by Śarmiṣṭhā, Kāvya went forth in haste, grieved, searching for his daughter in the forest.
Seeing his daughter Devayānī there in the forest, Kāvya embraced her with both arms and, sorrowing, spoke these words.
"All beings receive sorrow and happiness through their own faults; I think there must be some misdeed of yours for which this requital has come upon you."
Devayānī said: Whether there be a requital for me or not, hear me attentively — what was said to me by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan: and truly she said it — 'You are a singer of the demons.'
"Thus does Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, repeatedly speak sharp and harsh words to me, her eyes red with anger."
"You are the daughter of one who praises, who begs and receives; I am the daughter of one who is praised, who gives and does not receive."
"Thus does Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, speak to me again and again, her eyes flushed red with anger, filled with arrogance."
"If I am the daughter of one who praises and receives, then I shall placate Śarmiṣṭhā" — thus was spoken by a companion of mine to me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śukra said: You are not the daughter of one who praises, O noble one, nor of one who receives; you, O Devayānī, are the daughter of one who does not praise but is praised.
Vṛṣaparvan himself knows that, as does king Śakra and Nahuṣa's son; my power is the inconceivable, transcendent, lordly Brahman, beyond all duality.
Śukra said: The man who always endures the harsh words of others — know this, O Devayānī: by him all this world is conquered.
He who restrains surging anger like a horse — he is called a charioteer by the good, not he who merely hangs on the reins.
He who repels surging anger with non-anger — know this, O Devayānī: by him all this world is conquered.
He who repels surging anger here with patience, as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin — he is truly called a man.
He who restrains wrath, who endures harsh words, and who, though afflicted, does not afflict in return — he is truly a vessel worthy of prosperity.
One who sacrifices tirelessly every month for a hundred years, and one who is angered at nothing — of these two, the one without anger is the greater.
What enmity mindless boys and girls may stir up — a wise person ought not to follow that course; they do not know the distinction between strength and weakness.
Devayānī said: I know, father, even though I am young, the distinction between the paths of dharma here; I also know the difference in strength and weakness in the matter of non-anger and harsh speech.
For one who wishes to flourish ought not to tolerate the ungurly conduct of a disciple. Therefore dwelling among those of mixed conduct does not please me.
Those men who censure by conduct and by birth — a wise person seeking the highest good ought not to dwell among such evil-minded ones.
But those who recognise one's worth by conduct and by birth — among such virtuous ones one ought to dwell; that dwelling is said to be the highest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The ill-spoken, most terrible speech of the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan — I consider nothing harder to bear in all three worlds for one who, of lesser fortune, must attend upon the blazing prosperity of a rival.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Kāvya, best of the Bhṛgus, filled with anger, approached Vṛṣaparvan who was seated and spoke to him directly without deliberation.
"Unrighteous conduct does not bear fruit at once, O king, like a cow; but if one does not see it in one's own self, it ripens surely in one's sons or grandsons — evil, when swallowed, inevitably bears fruit, as if eaten by a pregnant woman in the womb."
"When you caused the brahmin Kaca, the grandson of Aṅgiras, to be slain then — he who was of blameless character, a knower of dharma, devoted to service, content in my house —"
"On account of the undeserved killing of him, and on account of the assault on my daughter too, hear this, O Vṛṣaparvan: I shall abandon you along with your kinsmen; I shall not be able to remain in your domain, O king, with you."
"Ah, do you regard me, O demon, as one who speaks falsely — that you neither restrain nor heed this fault of your own?"
Vṛṣaparvan said: I do not recognise unrighteousness or false speech in you, O Bhārgava; in you dwell both dharma and truth. May you be gracious to us.
"If you abandon us, O Bhārgava, and go hence, we shall enter the ocean; there is no other refuge for us."
Śukra said: Enter the ocean or flee to the four directions, O asuras; I am not able to bear anything displeasing to my daughter, for she is beloved by me.
"Let Devayānī be propitiated; my very life depends on her; I am the guardian of your welfare and security as Bṛhaspati is to Indra."
Vṛṣaparvan said: Whatever wealth of the lords of the asuras exists on earth, O Bhārgava, whether elephants, cattle, or horses — of all that you are the master over mine.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śukra said: Whatever treasure of the lords of the daityas there is, O great asura, I am its master; yet let Devayānī be propitiated if it pleases you.
Devayānī said: If you are the master of the king's wealth, O father, O Bhārgava, I do not acknowledge that for myself; let the king speak for himself.
Vṛṣaparvan said: Whatever desire you desire, O Devayānī, O pure-smiling one, that I shall bestow upon you even if it be hard to obtain.
Devayānī said: I desire Śarmiṣṭhā as my maidservant, together with a thousand maidens; let her attend upon me wherever my father shall give me away in marriage.
Vṛṣaparvan said: Rise, O attendant-woman, bring Śarmiṣṭhā quickly; and whatever desire Devayānī desires, let her fulfil it.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the nurse went there and spoke these words to Śarmiṣṭhā: "Arise, noble Śarmiṣṭhā, bring happiness to your kinsmen."
"The brahmin, urged on by Devayānī, is abandoning his pupils. Whatever desire she holds, that must be fulfilled by you today, O sinless one."
Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Whatever desire she holds, I will fulfill it today. But let not Śukra and Devayānī depart on my account."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, surrounded by a thousand maidens and carried in a palanquin, she swiftly departed from that foremost city by her father's command.
Śarmiṣṭhā said: "I, along with a thousand maidens, will be your servant and attendant. I will follow you wherever your father gives you in marriage."
Devayānī said: "You are the daughter of one who is praised and receives tribute, while I am the daughter of one who praises and renders tribute. How then can you become my servant?"
Śarmiṣṭhā said: "By whatever means one can bring happiness to afflicted kinsmen — for that reason I will follow you wherever your father gives you in marriage."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan had thus promised her state of servitude, Devayānī, O best of kings, spoke these words to her father:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I am entering the city, father; I am satisfied, O best of twice-born ones. Your wisdom is unfailing, and your power of learning is immense."
Thus addressed by his daughter, that best of twice-born men of great renown entered the city with joy, honored by all the demons.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, after a long time, O best of kings, the fair-complexioned Devayānī went out to that very forest for sport.
Together with that thousand servant-maids and with Śarmiṣṭhā, she reached that very place and wandered there at will, greatly delighted, accompanied by all those companions.
All of them were happily sporting, drinking honey-wine, eating various delicacies, and biting into fruits.
And once again King Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, arrived at that very spot by chance, seeking game, thirsting for water, and wearied by exertion.
He saw Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā and those women drinking and frolicking, adorned with divine ornaments.
And he saw the pure-smiling Devayānī seated among those women, incomparable in beauty, the finest of women, being waited upon by Śarmiṣṭhā with foot-massage and other services.
Yayāti said: "Each of you is attended by a thousand maidens. I ask you both your family lineages and names."
Devayānī said: "I will tell you — receive my words, O lord of men. Śukra is his name, the preceptor of the demons; know me as his daughter."
"And this one is my companion and servant, who goes wherever I go — Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, lord of the demons."
Yayāti said: "How can this maiden of fair complexion, the daughter of the lord of demons, be your companion and servant, O fair-browed one? I am greatly curious about this."
Devayānī said: "Everything follows the ordinance of fate, O tiger among men. Understanding this as decreed by fate, do not weave strange tales about it."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Your form and dress are like a king's, yet you speak with a brahmin's speech. What is your name, where do you come from, and whose son are you? Tell me."
Yayāti said: "Through brahmacharya the entire Veda has entered the path of my hearing. I am a king and a king's son, known by the name Yayāti."
Devayānī said: "For what purpose have you come to this place, O king — to gather lotus-flowers, or out of desire for game?"
Yayāti said: "I came seeking game and water, O noble lady. I have also been much engaged in duties — please grant me leave of that."
Devayānī said: "Along with two thousand maidens and with my servant Śarmiṣṭhā, I am dependent on you. Blessings on you — be my companion and husband."
Yayāti said: "Know me, O daughter of Uśanas, blessings on you — I am not worthy of you, O passionate one. For kings are not fit to be wedded by those of your father's lineage."
Devayānī said: "The brahmin is mingled with the kshatriya and the kshatriya is joined with the brahmin; a seer and a seer's son — O Nāhuṣa, therefore take me in marriage."
Yayāti said: "Though the four varṇas are born from one body, O finest of women, they have separate dharmas and separate purities, and among them the brahmin is supreme."
Devayānī said: "This rite of taking the hand, O Nāhuṣa, has not been observed by men before — you were the first to take my hand, therefore I choose you."
"How could any other man touch my hand — mine, a woman of spirit — after it has been taken by you, a seer's son, or rather by you who are yourself a seer?"
Yayāti said: "To a man who knows, a brahmin is more difficult to assail than an enraged venomous serpent or an all-consuming fire."
Devayānī said: "Why do you say a brahmin is more difficult to assail than a venomous serpent or an all-consuming fire, O bull among men?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yayāti said: "A venomous serpent kills one; one can be slain by a weapon — but an enraged brahmin destroys entire kingdoms and their cities."
"Therefore a brahmin is more difficult to assail, so I believe, O timid one — and for this reason, O noble lady, I will not marry you without your being given by your father."
Devayānī said: "Take me as given by my father, O king — for you have been chosen by me. There is no fear for one who accepts a woman given freely."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Devayānī quickly sent word to her father; and upon hearing it, the descendant of Bhṛgu presented the king before him.
Seeing Śukra arrived, Yayāti, lord of the earth, bowed to that brahmin, the descendant of Kavi, standing with folded hands in reverence.
Devayānī said: "This king, the son of Nahuṣa, took my hand in an inaccessible place, father. I bow to you — give me to him; I choose no other husband in the world."
Śukra said: "You have been chosen as husband by this daughter of mine whom I hold dear, O hero. Take her, given by me as your queen, O son of Nahuṣa."
Yayāti said: "Let no great transgression touch me here, O descendant of Bhṛgu — it is due to the sin born of mingling of varṇas that I appeal to you thus, O brahmin."
Śukra said: "I release you from the transgression — choose as you desire. Do not despair in this marriage; I remove the sin from you."
"Take the slender-waisted Devayānī as your wife according to dharma; together with her you will attain incomparable joy."
"And this maiden Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, should always be honored by you, O king — but never summon her to your bed."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, Yayāti circumambulated Śukra and departed for his own city with joy, having received leave from that great-souled one.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Yayāti reached his own city, resembling the city of great Indra, and entering the inner apartments, he installed Devayānī there.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With Devayānī's consent, he had a house built near the aśoka grove and installed there that daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of the asura line, attended by a thousand maidservants, was provided with garments, food, and drink, and treated with great honor.
Together with Devayānī, that king, son of Nahuṣa, sported for many years, greatly delighted like a god.
When the proper season came, Devayānī, that finest of women, conceived first and gave birth to a son.
When a thousand years had passed, Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, reaching the bloom of youth, saw that her season had come and reflected thus:
"The season has arrived, and yet I have no husband chosen for me. What has been gained? What must be done? What, if done, would be truly done?"
"Devayānī has borne a child, while I, having attained youth, am barren. As she chose her husband, so I too shall choose him."
"It is my firm resolve that the king must grant me the fruit of a son. Would that this righteous-souled one might come to me now in private."
Then, at that very time, the king came out by chance and encountered Śarmiṣṭhā standing near the aśoka grove.
Seeing him alone in a secluded spot, the lovely-smiling Śarmiṣṭhā went forward, made the anjali gesture, and spoke these words to the king:
"In the lineage of Soma, Indra, Viṣṇu, Yama, or Varuṇa — or in yours, O Nāhuṣa — who would be worthy to touch a woman?"
"For you, O king, have always known me by my beauty, lineage, and conduct. I, propitiating you, ask you — grant me the season's gift, O lord of men."
Yayāti said: "I know you as a maiden of the daitya race endowed with good conduct and without reproach; in your beauty I see not even a needle's point of fault."
"Yet Uśanas Kāvya told me when he entrusted Devayānī to me: 'This daughter of Vṛṣaparvan must never be summoned to your bed.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Words spoken in jest do not harm; nor do those spoken to women, O king, nor at the time of marriage, nor when life is at stake, nor when all one's wealth is being taken — these five kinds of untruth are said to be without sin."
"But one who speaks falsely when questioned as a witness, or one who is falsely accused — they say, O lord of men, that in a matter rightly and wholly agreed upon, falsehood does not harm the speaker of untruth."
Yayāti said: "A king is the measure of all beings; he would perish by speaking falsehood. Even in financial distress I am not inclined to act falsely."
Śarmiṣṭhā said: "These two are considered equal, O king: a husband and the husband of a companion. Marriage to both is called equal — you have been chosen as husband by my companion, so you are my husband too."
Yayāti said: "My vow is established that I must give to those who ask. You are asking me — speak your desire, what shall I do for you?"
Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Protect me from unrighteousness, O king, and establish dharma for me — having offspring from you, I could practice the highest dharma in the world."
"There are three who own no wealth, O king: the wife, the slave, and the son — whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong."
"I am a maidservant of Devayānī and subject to the descendant of Bhṛgu, and so am I also within your care, O king — therefore take me as one whom you must support."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the king recognized this as true and honored Śarmiṣṭhā, fulfilling dharma for her.
Having come together with Śarmiṣṭhā and satisfied their desires, they honored one another and departed each the way they had come.
From that union, the fair-browed, lovely-smiling Śarmiṣṭhā first conceived from that best of kings.
And in due time, O king, the lotus-eyed one gave birth to a son resembling the offspring of a god, with eyes like lotus petals.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that a son had been born, the pure-smiling Devayānī became distressed and began to reflect regarding Śarmiṣṭhā, O Bhārata.
And approaching Śarmiṣṭhā, Devayānī said: "What is this wrong that you have done, O fair-browed one, overcome by desire?"
Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Some sage of righteous soul, master of the Vedas, came as a guest. He who grants boons was asked by me for the desire in accordance with dharma."
"I do not act upon desire unjustly, O pure-smiling one. This offspring of mine is from that sage — this I tell you truly."
Devayānī said: "Very well, O timid one, if it is true — then let that brahmin be identified. I wish to know that twice-born man by his lineage, name, and family."
Śarmiṣṭhā said: "Blazing with energy and splendor like the sun — upon seeing him, I had no power to question him, O pure-smiling one."
Devayānī said: "If that is so, Śarmiṣṭhā, then I harbor no anger — if you have obtained offspring from a brahmin who is both the eldest and the best."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus spoken to one another and laughed together, the daughter of Bhṛgu returned home, accepting it as true.
King Yayāti begot two sons upon Devayānī — Yadu and Turvasu — who were like Indra and Viṣṇu themselves.
From that same royal sage, Śarmiṣṭhā the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan gave birth to three princes — Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru.
Then on a certain occasion, O king, the fair-smiling Devayānī went out into the great forest accompanied by Yayāti.
There she saw boys beautiful as gods playing at their ease, and astonished she said this:
"Whose are these children, O king, auspicious and resembling sons of gods? In radiance and form they seem to me like your own."
Having questioned the king thus, she then questioned the boys: "What are your names and lineage, little ones? Who is your brahmin father? Tell me truly — I wish to know him."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The boys pointed with their forefingers to that very best of kings, and they named Śarmiṣṭhā as their mother.
Having spoken so, they went together toward the king; but the king did not welcome them in Devayānī's presence. Then, weeping, the boys ran to Śarmiṣṭhā.
Seeing the boys' affection toward the king and understanding the truth of it, the noble lady spoke thus to Śarmiṣṭhā:
"Though you were under my authority, why have you done me this wrong? You have followed the ways of the asuras — do you not fear?"
Śarmiṣṭhā said: "What was said was that he was a sage — that is the truth, O lovely-smiling one. Acting rightly and in accordance with dharma, I do not fear you."
"When the king was chosen by you, he was then chosen by me as well — for a friend's husband is, by dharma, a husband, O beautiful one."
"You are my revered and honored elder — a brahmin woman, the most excellent. Yet even above you, the royal sage is most worthy of my veneration — do you not know that?"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing her words, Devayānī then said: "O king, I will not stay here any longer — you have done me wrong."
Seeing the dark-complexioned woman suddenly rise with tears in her eyes, setting out swiftly toward Kāvya's abode, the king was then distressed.
Agitated, the king followed behind her, trying to soothe her — but she, her eyes reddened with anger, did not turn back.
Without saying anything to the king, the lovely-eyed woman swiftly arrived at the presence of Kāvya Uśanas.
Seeing her father, she paid her respects and stood before him; and thereupon Yayāti also honored the Bhārgava sage.
Devayānī said: "Dharma has been defeated by adharma; a descent into wrong has begun. I have been transgressed against by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan."
"Three sons have been fathered upon her by this king Yayāti, while upon me, the ill-fortuned one, only two sons — this I tell you, father."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This king, renowned as a knower of dharma, O scion of Bhṛgu, has transgressed the bounds of propriety — this, O Kāvya, I tell you."
Śukra said: O great king, though you know righteousness, you performed an unrighteous act for the sake of pleasure. Therefore, old age — unconquerable — will afflict you before long.
Yayāti said: O blessed one, when the daughter of the lord of the asuras came to me seeking her season, I went to her with an undivided mind — what I did was in accordance with dharma.
O brahmin, the man who has been chosen and yet does not give himself to a woman seeking her season is declared by those who expound sacred learning to be guilty of the sin of killing an embryo.
And the man who, when privately solicited by a woman who desires him and who may lawfully be approached, does not go to her — the wise declare him guilty of embryo-slaying in matters of dharma.
Weighing these considerations, O scion of Bhṛgu, and trembling with fear of unrighteousness, I went to Śarmiṣṭhā.
Śukra said: Surely you should have consulted me — you are under my authority, O king. In matters of dharma, false conduct amounts to theft, O son of Nahuṣa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, was cursed by the enraged Uśanas; forthwith abandoning his former youth, he was instantly overtaken by old age.
Yayāti said: O scion of Bhṛgu, I am not yet sated with youth nor with Devayānī — show me your grace, O brahmin; let this old age not enter me.
Śukra said: I do not speak falsely in this — you have received old age, O lord of the earth. But this old age you may transfer to another, if you so wish.
Yayāti said: O brahmin, whichever son gives me his youth shall be heir to the kingdom, shall partake of merit, and shall also partake of glory — may you sanction this.
Śukra said: You will transfer the old age as you wish, O son of Nahuṣa — meditating on me with sincere heart you shall not incur sin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whichever son gives you his youth, he shall become king — long-lived, glorious, and blessed with many offspring as well.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having obtained old age and having returned to his own city, Yayāti spoke these words to his eldest and most excellent son Yadu:
"Old age, wrinkles, and white hairs have overtaken me, my son, by the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, and I am not yet satisfied with youth."
"You, Yadu, take up this affliction of old age; with your youth let me enjoy the pleasures of the senses."
"When a full thousand years have passed, I will give back your youth to you and resume my own affliction of old age."
Yadu said: "With white beard and white hair, wretched, loosened by old age, with wrinkles covering every limb, unsightly, feeble, emaciated —
"— incapable of action, scorned by the young and by dependents alike, such old age I do not desire."
Yayāti said: "Because you, born from my heart, do not give me your youth, your progeny, my son, shall not partake of kingship."
"Turvasu, take up this affliction of old age; with your youth I will indeed enjoy the pleasures of the senses, my son."
"When a full thousand years have passed, I will give back your youth and I myself will resume the affliction of old age."
Turvasu said: "I do not desire old age, father — it destroys the enjoyment of desires, it ends strength and beauty, it ruins intellect and vital breath."
Yayāti said: "Because you, born from my heart, do not give me your youth, your lineage, O Turvasu, shall come to complete extinction."
"Among those of mixed conduct and dharma, among those who act contrary to social order, among flesh-eaters and outcastes, you fool, shall you be a king."
"Among those addicted to their elders' wives, among those fallen into animal wombs, among the sinful who follow the ways of beasts, among the mlecchas, shall you hold sway."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus cursed Turvasu, Yayāti spoke these words to his own son Druhyu, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā:
"Druhyu, take up this old age that destroys complexion and form; give me your youth for a thousand years."
"When a full thousand years have passed, I will give back your youth and I myself will once again take up the affliction of old age."
Druhyu said: "An old man enjoys neither elephant, nor chariot, nor horse, nor woman — his speech too becomes broken. Therefore I do not desire that old age."
Yayāti said: "Because you, born from my heart, do not give me your youth, O Druhyu, your cherished desires shall nowhere be fulfilled."
"In a land where crossing is always only by raft and float, without a king, you and your descendants shall bear the name of Bhoja."
"Anu, take up this affliction of old age; for one thousand years let me enjoy with your youth."
Anu said: "An old man takes food like a child, at unseasonable times, like one impure; he does not offer into the sacred fire at the proper hour. That old age I do not desire."
Yayāti said: "Because you, born from my heart, do not give me your youth, the very fault of old age you have named — that you shall receive."
"And your offspring, O Anu, shall perish upon reaching youth; and you yourself shall likewise be devoted to neglecting the sacred fire."
"Pūru, you are my beloved son; you shall be the greatest. Old age, wrinkles, and white hair have overtaken me, my son, by the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, and I am not satisfied with youth."
"Pūru, take up this affliction of old age; for some time let me truly enjoy the pleasures of the senses with your youthful vigor."
"When a full thousand years have passed, I will give back your youth, and I myself will resume the affliction of old age."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, Pūru replied to his father straightforwardly: "As you have told me, O great king, so I will carry out your words."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I will take up from you the affliction of old age, O king. Take my youth and enjoy desires as you wish."
"Covered by old age, bearing your form of age, having given my youth to you, I will conduct myself as you have directed me."
Yayāti said: "Pūru, I am pleased with you, my child; and pleased, I give you this: your progeny in the kingdom shall be endowed with fulfillment of all desires."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, with the youth of the Paurava, Yayāti the son of Nahuṣa, delighted, that best of kings, pursued his beloved pleasures.
As he desired, with all his energy, in due season and according to his happiness, the lord of kings enjoyed pleasures unopposed to dharma, as was fitting for him.
He gratified the gods with sacrifices, and likewise the ancestors with śrāddha offerings; the needy with desired gifts and boons; and the best of the twice-born with desired goods.
He honored guests with food and drink, the commoners with protection, the śūdras with kindness, and suppressed bandits with firm restraint.
Delighting all his subjects properly with righteousness, Yayāti protected them like a second Indra himself.
That king, bold as a lion, youthful, roaming through the field of pleasures, pursued the highest happiness without transgressing dharma.
Having obtained auspicious pleasures, satisfied and yet wearied, the lord of men, that ruler of earth, recalled the time — the end of a thousand years.
Reckoning up the moments and the divisions of time, that knower of time, that valiant one, judged the period complete and spoke to his son Pūru:
"As I desired, with full energy, and in due season, O subduer of foes, pleasures have been enjoyed by me, my son, with your youth."
"Pūru, I am pleased with you — blessings upon you. Take back this your own youth, and take also this kingdom — for you are the son who has done me pleasure."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then King Yayāti the son of Nahuṣa resumed old age, and Pūru recovered his own youth once again.
When the king wished to consecrate Pūru, his youngest son, the four estates headed by the brahmins spoke these words:
"How, O lord, will you give the kingdom to Pūru, passing over the eldest, Yadu — the grandson of Śukra and son of Devayānī?"
"Yadu was born your eldest son; after him Turvasu; Śarmiṣṭhā's son Druhyu came next, then Anu, and only then Pūru."
"How can the youngest deserve the kingdom, passing over the elders? We set this before you — uphold dharma."
Yayāti said: "Let all the estates, headed by the brahmins, hear my words: as to the eldest, the kingdom is in no way to be given by me to him."
"My command was not followed by my eldest, Yadu; and he who acts contrary to his father is not considered a son by the righteous."
He who obeys the words of his mother and father, who is devoted and beneficial to them — he is a true son; and he who conducts himself toward his parents as a son should.
By Yadu I was disrespected, and likewise by Turvasu; by Druhyu and by Anu too, great contempt was shown toward me.
My word was fulfilled by Pūru, and I was honored by him especially; he is my youngest heir, he who bore my old age — and my desire was accomplished by Pūru, who proved himself a true son.
And a boon was granted by Śukra himself, the sage Uśanas Kavya: 'The son who obeys you shall be a king, lord of the earth.' Appealing to you on this ground, let Pūru be consecrated to the kingdom.
The subjects said: A son who is endowed with virtues and is always devoted to the welfare of his mother and father deserves all prosperity, O lord, even if he is the youngest.
Pūru deserves this kingdom; he is the son who has done what pleases you. By virtue of Śukra's boon, there is no reply that can be made against it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the satisfied townspeople and country folk, Nahuṣa's son at that time anointed his own son Pūru in the kingdom.
Having given the kingdom to Pūru and consecrated himself for forest-dwelling, the king departed from the city accompanied by brahmins and ascetics.
From Yadu were born the Yādavas; from Turvasu's sons came the Yavanas; from Druhyu's sons came the Bhojas; and from Anu came the tribes of the mlecchas.
From Pūru came the Paurava lineage, in which you were born, O king — he who was master enough to wield the kingdom for a thousand years.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus king Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, having joyfully consecrated his desired son to the kingdom, became a forest-dweller and a sage.
And having dwelt in the forest, taking refuge with brahmins, subsisting on fruits and roots, self-restrained and great-souled, he departed from here to heaven.
Having gone to the abode of the gods and dwelling there joyfully and happily, after no very great span of time he was cast down again by Śakra.
Falling, dislodged from heaven, before he could reach the surface of the earth, he stood suspended in mid-air — so I have heard.
And thence he again went to heaven — so goes the tradition — having met, it is said, in an assembly with king Vasumat, with the valiant Aṣṭaka, with Pratardana, and with Śibi.
Janamejaya said: By what deed did that lord of the earth once more attain heaven? I wish to hear all of this fully and truly, O brahmin, as related by you in the presence of the assembly of brahmin-sages.
For Yayāti, lord of the earth, was equal to the king of the gods; he was the increaser of the Kuru lineage, blazing with a splendor equal to the sun.
I wish to hear the conduct of that great-souled one of wide-spread fame and true renown — both in heaven and here on earth, in every regard.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Very well, I shall tell you the later story of Yayāti — meritorious both in heaven and here on earth, and destructive of all sins.
King Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, having joyfully consecrated his youngest son Pūru to the kingdom, then set forth to the forest.
Having placed his sons led by Yadu on the frontiers, the king, subsisting on fruits and roots, dwelt for a long time in the forest.
With sharpened self, having conquered anger, satisfying the ancestors and the gods, and offering oblations into the sacred fires according to rule, following the ordinances of the forest-dweller stage.
The mighty one honored guests with forest oblations, following the practice of gleaning fallen grain, eating only what remained after others were fed.
The king maintained this conduct for a full thousand years; for thirty autumns he subsisted on water alone, with restrained speech and mind.
Then he became a subsister on air alone for a year without slackening; and for a year the king performed austerities in the midst of the five fires.
And he stood on one foot for six months, subsisting on wind; then he of holy fame went to heaven, having pervaded both heaven and earth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: That foremost of kings, having gone to heaven, dwelling in the abode of the gods, was honored by the Tridaśa gods, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the Vasus.
Moving from the world of the gods to the world of Brahmā, that meritorious, self-controlled guardian of the earth dwelt there for a long time — so goes the tradition.
At some point that best of kings, Yayāti, came to Śakra; and at the end of their conversation, the lord of the earth was questioned by Śakra.
Śakra said: When Pūru, O king, bearing your old age in your form, roamed the earth, and when you gave the kingdom to him — what did you say to him? Tell me truly.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yayāti said: 'All this territory between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is yours; you are king in the middle of the earth — your brothers are rulers of the borderlands.'
'The one free from anger is superior to the wrathful; likewise the forbearing is superior to the unfor-bearing; humans are paramount over non-humans; and so the wise man is paramount over the ignorant.'
'When reviled, one should not revile in return — the patient man's anger alone burns up the reviler, and he himself gains merit.'
'One should not be wounding, nor speak cruelly; one should not seize upon another's weakness. The speech that causes another to tremble — one should not utter that harsh word that leads to evil worlds.'
'A man who is wounding, harsh of speech, piercing people with the thorns of his words — know him to be the most inauspicious of people, bearing destruction bound to his mouth.'
'One should be honored by the good from the front and protected by the good from behind; one should always forbear the excessive speech of the wicked; and conducting oneself nobly, one should adopt the conduct of the good.'
'Word-arrows fly forth from the mouth; struck by them, one grieves through nights and days. When they strike another's vital spots — a wise man should never discharge such words at others.'
'Indeed there is no means of winning over others in the three worlds like friendliness toward all beings, giving, and sweet speech.'
'Therefore one should always speak gently and never speak harshly anywhere; one should honor those worthy of honor; one should give and never beg.'
Indra said: Having completed all your duties, O king, you abandoned your home and went to the forest. This I ask you, O son of Nahuṣa — with whose austerity are you equal, O Yayāti?
Yayāti said: I see no one equal to myself in austerity — not among gods and men, not among gandharvas and great sages, O Vāsava.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Indra said: Because you held in contempt those equal to you and even superior to you, not knowing their power — therefore your worlds are now finite; your merit exhausted, you have fallen today, O king.
Yayāti said: If my worlds are exhausted, O Śakra, by having shown contempt for gods, sages, gandharvas, and men — then I wish, though bereft of the heavenly world, to fall among the good, O king of the gods.
Indra said: You have fallen in the presence of the good, O king; having fallen, you will regain your footing once more. Knowing this, O Yayāti, do not again despise those equal to you and those superior to you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, seeing Yayāti falling, having abandoned the blessed worlds cherished by the king of immortals, the foremost royal sage Aṣṭaka, guardian of the ordinances of right conduct, spoke to him.
'Who are you, youthful and equal in form to Vāsava, blazing with your own splendor like fire, falling from the sky out of the darkness of rising storm-clouds, like the sun, supreme among sky-travellers?'
'Seeing you falling from the path of the sun, your immeasurable radiance like fire and the sun, all of us, speculating what indeed is this that falls, are utterly bewildered.'
'And seeing you stationed in the path of the gods, with power equal to Śakra, the sun, and Viṣṇu, all of us have come forward today to meet you, desiring to know the truth of your fall.'
'We did not dare to question you first, and you do not ask us who we are. So we ask you of desirable form: whose son are you? And for what reason have you come?'
'But let fear depart from you; abandon grief and confusion quickly, O you of form equal to the lord of gods — for while you remain in the presence of the good, even Śakra, the slayer of Bala, is not able to harm you.'
'For the good are truly the foundation for those dislodged from happiness; the good are always like the king of immortals. Those lords of the moving and unmoving are gathered here; you stand firm among the good who are your equals.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Fire is lord in burning, earth is lord in sustaining, the sun is lord in illuminating — and one who has come to the good is lord.'
Yayāti said: I am Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, father of Pūru; through contempt for all beings I have been cast down from the worlds of gods, siddhas, and sages; having fallen away, I fall, my merit exhausted.
'I am older in age than all of you; therefore I do not offer salutation to you — for he who is elder by learning, austerity, or birth is worthy of worship among the twice-born.'
Aṣṭaka said: If you said that he who is elder in years is the elder, O king, then you should have saluted us in some manner — for he who is truly wise and elder in years is the one worthy of worship among the twice-born.
Yayāti said: They call sin the course contrary to right action; it dwells in one inclined toward evil worlds. The good do not go along with the wicked in this, like a self that speaks in accordance with what is agreeable to them.
'My wealth was immense and great; yet striving I could not retain it. He who, having reflected thus and fixed his mind on his own welfare, conducts himself accordingly — he truly knows how to live.'
'Many and various are the states of existence in the world of the living, governed by fate, with their efforts and powers lost. Encountering each such state, the wise man should not be distressed, thinking with steady mind: fate is supreme.'
'Whether a creature obtains happiness or suffering, it is under the control of fate, not by its own power. Therefore, holding fate to be supreme, one should neither burn with grief nor ever exult.'
'The wise man should not be tormented by sorrow nor exult in happiness; he should always conduct himself with equanimity, thinking fate to be supreme — he should neither burn with grief nor ever exult.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'I am never deluded by fear, O Aṣṭaka; there is no mental anguish in me whatsoever, thinking: as the Creator ordains my existence in the world, so certainly shall I be.'
'Creatures born from sweat, born from eggs, and those that sprout from the earth; reptiles, worms, fish in the waters; stones, grass, and wood — all at the exhaustion of their ordained span return to their own nature.'
'Understanding the impermanence of pleasure and pain, why should I, O Aṣṭaka, indulge in anguish? What shall I do, and having done what shall I not grieve? Therefore, vigilant, I abandon all anguish.'
Aṣṭaka said: What worlds, O foremost of earthly kings, were the chief ones you enjoyed, and for how long, and in what manner? Tell me all of this, O king, exactly as it was — for you speak of dharma like one who knows the field.
Yayāti said: I was here a universal sovereign of all the earth; then I won great worlds. I dwelt there for just a thousand years; then I advanced to a higher world.
Then in the delightful city of Puruhūta — with a thousand gates, extending a hundred yojanas — I dwelt for just a thousand years; then I advanced to a higher world.
Then having attained the divine, ageless world of Prajāpati, lord of worlds — difficult to reach — I dwelt there for just a thousand years; then I advanced to a higher world.
And in the dwelling of god after god, having won the worlds, I dwelt as I pleased, honored by all the Tridaśa gods, equal in power and splendor to the lords.
And thus I dwelt in Nandana, taking whatever form I desired, for a hundred times ten thousand years, roaming with the apsaras, smelling the sacred fragrances, beholding the flowering trees of beautiful form.
When I was stationed there, absorbed in the pleasures of the gods, after a very great time had passed, a messenger of the gods of terrible form cried out loudly three times in a prolonged voice: 'Fall!'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This is all that I know, O lion among kings; then I fell from Nandana, my merit exhausted. And I heard the voices of the gods in the sky, lamenting with compassion, O lord of men.
'Alas, how painful — Yayāti, whose merit is exhausted, he who wrought merit and had a holy name, is falling.' Then I, while falling, said to them: 'How might I fall among the good?'
By them was this sacrificial ground of yours pointed out to me; perceiving it, I came here swiftly, guided by the fragrance of the oblations of this sacrificial ground, following the trail of the smoke with confidence.
Aṣṭaka said: When you dwelt in Nandana taking whatever form you desired, for a hundred times ten thousand years — what was the reason, O foremost one of the Kṛta age, that abandoning that estate you descended to the earth?
Yayāti said: Just as here a kinsman, friend, or companion is abandoned by people when his wealth is exhausted — so there, when a person's merit is exhausted, the assemblies of gods together with their lords abandon him at once.
Aṣṭaka said: How does their merit become exhausted in that place? My mind is greatly bewildered on this point. What are their characteristics, and to whose abode do they go? Tell me that indeed — you are regarded by me as one who knows the field.
Yayāti said: They all fall into this earthly hell, O lord of men, lamenting. Exhausted, as food for herons, jackals, and vultures, they go in many directions to grow again.
'Therefore this corrupted and censurable action in the world is to be avoided by a man. All of this has been told to you, O king; say now what more I may tell you.'
Aṣṭaka said: When the birds peck at them — vultures, blue-necked herons, and insects — how do they come to be, how do they come into existence? I hear of no other hell than this earthly one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yayāti said: Rising upward from the body as karma expands, they clearly wander upon the earth; they fall into this earthly hell and do not look back for many, many years.
Sixty thousand years they fall through the sky, and then eighty more years besides; as they plummet headlong in their fall, terrible earthbound rākṣasas with sharp fangs torment them.
Aṣṭaka said: When those terrible earthbound rākṣasas with sharp fangs torment the falling sinners, how do they come into being, how do they come to exist — in what manner do they become embryonic beings?
Yayāti said: Blood, seed, and the essence of flowers and fruits — that which is emitted by the man follows along; that indeed enters the woman's menstrual blood, and becoming an embryo it arrives there.
They enter into trees and medicinal plants, into water, wind, earth, and the atmosphere, into all four-footed creatures and two-footed beings as well — in this manner do they become embryonic beings.
Aṣṭaka said: Does the embryo fashion a different body here, or does it go of its own will when entering this human womb? Explain this to me — I speak from doubt.
And how does the body with its form arise, and by what means does it gain awareness through eye and ear? Tell me all this truth when questioned — for we all regard you, dear one, as one who knows the field.
Yayāti said: The wind draws up the embryonic matrix; in the fertile season it is mingled with the essence of seed and flower. There, holding sway through the subtle elements, it gradually nourishes and develops the embryo here.
As it is born with its limbs fully formed, the human being is grounded in six modes of cognition; by means of the ears it perceives sound here, and sees all form through the eyes.
By the nose it smells fragrance, by the tongue it tastes flavour, by the skin it knows touch, and by the mind it knows inner states — so know, O Aṣṭaka, the accumulation of senses in the body of the great-souled living being.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Aṣṭaka said: When a man has died and is burned, or is buried, or is ground to dust — having passed into non-being and reached destruction, by what means does the self become conscious again hereafter?
Yayāti said: Having abandoned the vital breaths like one falling asleep, having groaned, having placed merit and demerit before it, it follows at the tip of the wind, O lion among kings, and having left the body it enters another womb.
Those who have done good go to an auspicious womb; those who have done evil go to an evil womb — the wicked become insects and moths. I have no desire to say more, O great one.
Four-footed creatures, two-footed beings, and six-legged insects — in this way do they become embryonic forms. All this has been told to you in full; what more do you ask, O lion among kings?
Aṣṭaka said: By doing what, dear one, does a mortal attain the highest worlds — by asceticism or by knowledge? Being asked, tell me all this truthfully, by what means one may reach the auspicious worlds in due order.
Yayāti said: Asceticism, charity, tranquillity of mind, self-restraint, modesty, uprightness, and compassion toward all beings — these always perish in a man when overcome by darkness through arrogance; so say the good.
He who studies and fancies himself a scholar yet destroys the reputation of others through his learning — his worlds come to an end, and that sacred knowledge bears no fruit for him.
Four acts that should bring fearlessness bring fear instead when performed with arrogance: the agnihotra performed with arrogance, silence practiced with arrogance, learning undertaken with arrogance, and the sacrifice offered with arrogance.
One should not take joy when honoured, nor grieve when dishonoured; the good honour the good in this world — the wicked never attain the insight of the virtuous.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Thus shall I give, thus shall I sacrifice, thus shall I study — this is my vow": in such attitude they speak of fearless deeds, yet these very things are to be avoided always when done from egotism.
Through that ancient refuge which the wise, devoted equally to honour and dishonour, come to know — attaining that supreme luminous form of the highest good, they reach perfect peace, both here and after death.
Aṣṭaka said: How does the householder, pursuing his duties, reach the gods? How does the mendicant? How does the teacher's pupil? And the forest-dweller established on the good path? Many things are now known about this.
Yayāti said: He who studies when called upon, who is diligent in the teacher's work without being prompted, who rises first and retires last, who is gentle, restrained, steadfast, and heedful, and devoted to personal study — such a brahmacharī attains success.
Having acquired wealth obtained by righteous means, one should sacrifice, give freely, and always feed guests; and one should not take what has not been given by others — this is the ancient secret teaching of the householder.
He who lives by his own exertion, who has turned away from sin, who gives to others without tormenting any being — such a sage, dwelling in the forest with regulated food and conduct, attains the highest success.
He who lives without a craft, perpetually without a home, with senses conquered, wholly freed from all bonds, who moves from one resting place to another, light and of few wants, wandering through lands alone — he is the true mendicant.
The night by which the worlds are won, by which desires are conquered and joys obtained — that very night the wise man, with a disciplined self, should strive to dwell in the forest.
Ten ancestors before him, ten relatives after, and himself as the twenty-first — the forest-dweller places them all in the realm of good deeds, releasing the constituent elements of his own body in the forest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Aṣṭaka said: How many kinds of sages are there, and how many kinds of silence are there? Tell us this — we wish to hear.
Yayāti said: He for whom the village lies behind while dwelling in the forest, or for whom the forest lies behind while dwelling in the village — that man may be called a sage, O lord of the people.
Aṣṭaka said: How is it that when one dwells in the forest the village comes to lie behind, and how is it that when dwelling in the village the forest comes to lie behind?
Yayāti said: He who would be a forest-dwelling sage should not make use of village things; in that way, even while dwelling in the forest, the village comes to lie behind him.
Without fire, without a fixed dwelling, moving without clan affiliations, the sage should desire clothing only to the extent of a loincloth for covering.
He should desire food only to the extent of sustaining the vital breaths — in that way, even while dwelling in the village, the forest comes to lie behind him.
But the sage who abandons desires, who has given up action, whose senses are conquered, and who abides in silence — he attains perfection in this world.
With teeth washed, nails trimmed, always bathed and adorned, dark in complexion yet established in pure deeds — who would not be worthy to worship such a one?
Emaciated by austerity, lean, with flesh, bone, and blood wasted away — when the sage becomes free from the pairs of opposites and abides in silence, then, having conquered this world, he conquers the world beyond.
When the sage seeks his food with his mouth alone like a cow, then whatever was his former world becomes fit for immortality.
Aṣṭaka said: Which of these two first attains oneness with the gods, as they both race, O king, like the sun and the moon?
Yayāti said: The mendicant who is without a fixed home, who is restrained amid householders given over to desire, who dwells in the very village — he of the two has gone ahead.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who has not attained a long life and yet has met with adversity should practise austerity; if he has done that and practises it, let him then proceed to other austerities beyond that.
What is cruel they call harmful; he who practises dharma with a mind set on what is not right — even he is without true self-mastery, O king; that uprightness is his concentration, that his nobility.
Aṣṭaka said: By whom were you sent as a messenger today, O king — young, garlanded, handsome, radiant? From where have you come, and in which direction are you? Or do you have a royal station?
Yayāti said: My merit exhausted, I have been scattered from the sky to enter this earthly hell; having spoken to you, I shall fall at once — the brahmins and the world-guardians urge me on.
My fall has been chosen in the presence of the good — they are all assembled here and endowed with virtue. This boon was obtained by me even from Indra — that I should fall upon the earth, O lord of men.
Aṣṭaka said: I ask you — do not fall in your fall; if there are worlds belonging to me here, whether stationed in the atmosphere or in the sky, take them — I regard you as one who knows the field of dharma.
Yayāti said: As many as the cows and horses distributed over the earth, along with the forest animals and mountains — that many worlds of yours are established in the sky. Know it thus, O lion among lords of men.
Aṣṭaka said: I give you those worlds of mine — do not fall in your fall; whatever worlds of mine exist in the sky, whether stationed in the atmosphere or established in the heavens, mount them quickly, O destroyer of enemies.
Yayāti said: One like me who is not a brahmin, even if learned in the Vedas, does not engage in receiving gifts, O foremost among kings; as what should constantly be given to the twice-born, so did I formerly give, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A non-brahmin should never live a wretched life depending on others; likewise a brahmin woman who is the wife of a hero — I am such a one; what good would it be if I were to do what was never done before, when seeking to know the truth?
Pratardana said: I ask you, O one of desirable form — I am Pratardana; if there are worlds belonging to me, whether stationed in the atmosphere or established in the sky, I offer them; I regard you as one who knows the field of dharma.
Yayāti said: Many worlds are yours, O lord of men; even individually they are seven times seven days each — dripping with honey, mixed with clarified butter, free from grief; those boundless worlds await you.
Pratardana said: I give you those worlds — do not fall in your fall; whatever worlds are mine, let them truly be yours; whether stationed in the atmosphere or established in the sky, mount them quickly, O one freed from delusion.
Yayāti said: One of equal splendour should not desire another's merits; being a king, O king, and meeting with adversity by the decree of fate, the wise man should not act cruelly — for a king should never do so.
Contemplating the path of righteousness and honour, a king should act with regard to dharma; one like me, who knows dharma in mind, knowing it, should not act so wretchedly as you describe.
I should do what is unprecedented, not done by others — what good is there in that when one is seeking to know the truth? As king Yayāti spoke thus, the most eminent of kings, Vasumanā, addressed him.
Vasumanā said: I ask you — I am Vasumanā, son of Rauśadaśva; if there is a world in the sky for me, O lord of men, whether spread through the atmosphere, O great-souled one, I offer it; I regard you as one who knows the field of dharma.
Yayāti said: What the atmosphere, the earth, the directions, and the radiant sun illuminates with its brilliance — that many worlds are established in the sky for you; those boundless worlds await you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vasumanā said: I give you those worlds — do not fall in your fall; whatever worlds are mine, let them truly be yours; buy them even for a blade of grass, O king — if the act of receiving a gift is truly corrupted for you.
Yayāti said: I do not recall having made a false sale; I would not doubtfully take something obtained in vain from a child, nor would I do what was never done by others — what good is there in that when seeking to know?
Vasumanā said: Accept those worlds, O king, given by me; if the purchase is not to your liking, I shall not take them back, O lord of men — let all those worlds truly be yours.
Śibi said: I ask you — I am Śibi, son of Uśīnara; if there are worlds for me here as well, dear one, whether in the atmosphere or established in the sky, I offer them — I regard you as one who knows the field of dharma.
Yayāti said: You, O wise one, have never slighted with word or even with heart those who sought your protection, O lord of men; therefore boundless worlds are established in the sky for you — vast, radiant as lightning, resonant with sound.
Śibi said: Accept those worlds, O king, given by me; if the purchase is not to your liking, I shall not take them back now having given them — go to those worlds which you worship, and dwell there.
Yayāti said: As you are equal in splendour to Indra, so too are your worlds boundless, O lord of men; yet I take no pleasure today in what has been given by another; therefore, O Śibi, I do not rejoice in the gift.
Aṣṭaka said: If you do not accept our worlds one by one, O king, then we shall all go to hell by giving them to you.
Yayāti said: Give what is worthy to one who is worthy — you who are good, by the virtue of truth and non-cruelty; but I do not dare to do what was never done by me before.
Aṣṭaka said: Whose are these five golden chariots that appear before us, standing high, gleaming, blazing like the flame of fire?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yayāti said: These five golden chariots will carry you — standing high, gleaming, blazing like the flame of fire.
Aṣṭaka said: Mount the chariot, O king, stride forth through the sky; we too will follow when the time comes.
Yayāti said: Now all must go together — we who have won heaven; this pure, unsullied path to the abode of the gods lies visible before us.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: They all mounted the chariots and set forth, those most excellent of kings, ascending to heaven with their radiance, filling both heaven and earth with their dharma.
Aṣṭaka said: I think I alone am going ahead — and Indra is my great-souled friend in every way; but why has this Śibi, son of Uśīnara, alone surpassed all others with full speed in his vehicle?
Yayāti said: This son of Uśīnara gave to the divine path all the wealth he possessed; therefore Śibi is indeed the best among us.
Charity, austerity, truth, dharma, modesty, fortune, forgiveness, O gentle one, and endurance — O king, these virtues of that matchless king, of Śibi of non-cruelty in mind, stand firm. And because he is of such conduct and restrained by modesty — therefore Śibi has indeed surpassed all in his chariot.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Aṣṭaka questioned his maternal grandfather once more out of curiosity, that one equal to Indra: "I ask you, O king, tell me truly — from where are you, whose son are you, and whose are you? What you have done, no other doer of that deed exists — no other kṣatriya or brahmin in the world besides you."
Yayāti said: I am Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa; I was here as the universal emperor, father of Pūru; I tell you this hidden matter as my own — I am your maternal grandfather, now revealed to you.
I conquered all this earth and, having bound it as a package, I gave it to the brahmins; I gave consecrated horses, single-hoofed and well-formed; then the gods became sharers in the merit.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I gave the earth to the brahmins — this entire full earth — along with cattle as tribute, gold, and the finest riches; therein were ten billion cows.
By my truth, both the sky and the earth-bearing goddess stand firm, and fire blazes among human beings; not one word spoken by me has been in vain — for the good honour truth, as do all the gods, the sages, and the worlds; it is the thought of my mind that the worthy are honoured by truth.
Whoever, without envy, recounts to the foremost of the twice-born all of us who have won heaven, exactly as it happened — he shall attain the same world as ours.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus that great-souled king Yayāti, the destroyer of foes, was ferried across by his own grandsons. Having abandoned the earth, he whose deeds were supremely noble ascended to heaven, his karmas pervading the whole world.
Janamejaya said: Venerable one, I wish to hear about the kings who continued the line of Pūru — what valor they possessed, what manner of men they were, how many there were, and what their prowess.
For in this lineage there has never at any time been a king who was lacking in good character, or lacking in valor, or without progeny.
O wealth of austerity, I wish to hear in detail the deeds of those kings whose conduct was celebrated and who were endowed with discernment.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Well then, I shall tell you what you ask of me — the heroic upholders of Pūru's lineage, whose splendor rivaled that of Indra.
Pravīra, Īśvara, and Raudrāśva — three great chariot-warriors — were born to Pūru by Pauṣṭī; of them, Pravīra continued the line.
From him was born Manasyu, valiant son of Śyenī, a lord and protector of the earth to its four horizons, with eyes like lotus petals.
Subhrū, Saṃhana, and Vāgmī — three sons of Sauvīrī — were born to Manasyu; all were brave great chariot-warriors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Raudrāśva's ten sons by an apsarā were great archers who performed sacrifices, born as brave men with abundant progeny and great learning; all were knowledgeable in every weapon, all were devoted to dharma.
They were Ṛcepu, Kakṣepu, the valiant Kṛkaṇepu, Sthaṇḍilepu, Vanepu, and Sthalepuṣa the great chariot-warrior.
Tejepu the powerful and wise, Satyepu of Indra-like valor, Dharmepu, Saṃnatepu — the tenth with the prowess of a god — these sons of Anādhṛṣṭi, dear one, all performed the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
After them king Matināra, learned son of Carcepu, was born; O king, Matināra's four sons were of boundless valor: the great Taṃsu, a warrior surpassing even chariot-fighters, and Druhyu of unrivaled brilliance.
Of them, Taṃsu of great valor, bearing the Paurava lineage onward, won blazing glory and conquered the earth.
The valiant Taṃsu fathered a son named Ilina, and he too conquered this entire earth — foremost among conquerors.
O king, Ilina then fathered five sons on Rathaṃtarī — sons comparable to the five elements — headed by Duḥṣanta.
They were Duḥṣanta, Śūra, Bhīma, Prapūrva, and Vasu; of them the eldest became king — Duḥṣanta, O Janamejaya.
From Duḥṣanta was born Bharata, the wise king son of Śakuntalā; from him the great glory of the Bharata lineage spread wide.
Bharata fathered nine sons on three wives, but the king did not rejoice in them, saying, "They do not resemble me."
Then Bharata, who had performed great sacrifices, obtained through Bharadvāja a son named Bhumanyu, O Bhārata.
Then, knowing himself to be blessed with a son, the delight of the Pauravas consecrated Bhumanyu as crown prince, O best of the Bhāratas.
Then for that great lord of the earth a son named Vitatha was born; thus Vitatha was the son of Bhumanyu.
Suhotra, Suhotā, Suhavi, and Suyaju — sons of Ṛcīka's daughter Puṣkariṇī — were born to Bhumanyu.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of them the eldest, Suhotra, obtained sovereignty over kings of the earth; he performed many sacrifices including the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha.
Suhotra enjoyed all the earth girdled by the ocean, full of elephants, cattle, and horses, and teeming with many treasures.
The earth seemed to sink under his enormous weight, overflowing with elephants, horses, and chariots, and exceedingly crowded with people.
While king Suhotra ruled his subjects according to dharma, the earth was marked with hundreds of thousands of sacrificial stakes and altars; teeming with flourishing people and grain, it shone together with the gods.
O Bhārata, Aikṣvākī bore to Suhotra, lord of the earth, three sons: Ajamīḍha, Sumīḍha, and Purumīḍha.
Ajamīḍha was the best of them; in him the lineage was established. He in turn fathered six sons on three wives, O Bhārata.
Dhūminī bore Ṛkṣa; Nīlī bore Duḥṣanta and Parameṣṭhin; Keśinī bore Jahnu and both called Janarūpiṇau.
Thus all the Pāñcālas are descendants of Duḥṣanta and Parameṣṭhin, O king, and the Kuśikas are descendants of Jahnu of boundless splendor.
Of the two Janarūpiṇas, the elder Ṛkṣa is called the lord of the people; from Ṛkṣa was born Saṃvaraṇa, O king, the one who continued your lineage.
When Saṃvaraṇa son of Ṛkṣa, O king, was ruling the earth, there came about a very great destruction of the people — so we have heard.
The kingdom then broke apart through various calamities — struck by famine, death, drought, and disease — and the armies of their enemies assailed the Bhāratas as well.
Shaking the very earth with his fourfold army, the Pāñcāla king came against him; having swiftly conquered the land, he defeated Saṃvaraṇa in battle with ten akṣauhiṇī armies.
Then king Saṃvaraṇa, together with his wives, ministers, sons, and friends, fled from there in great fear.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He then dwelt in a thicket on the bank of the great river Sindhu, at the edge of the river region near the mountains; the Bhāratas lived there for a long time, having taken refuge in that difficult terrain.
After they had lived there for a thousand years, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha came to the Bhāratas.
Going forth to meet him with great care and paying him homage, all the Bhāratas then brought him the guest-offering of arghya, and with due reverence reported everything to the resplendent sage.
Having stayed with them for eight years, the king himself then requested him: "Be our purohita — we strive for the kingdom." "So be it" — with this, Vasiṣṭha agreed and accepted the Bhāratas.
Then he consecrated the Paurava king to imperial sovereignty over all the kṣatriyas, as the foremost of all on earth — so we have heard.
He occupied that best of cities previously held by the Bhāratas, and made all kings of the earth his tribute-bearers once more.
Then, having regained the earth, that mighty descendant of Ajamīḍha performed many great sacrifices with lavish fees.
Then Tapatī, daughter of the Sun, bore to Saṃvaraṇa a son named Kuru; all the subjects chose him as their king, calling him "the knower of dharma."
By his name the Kurujāṅgala region on earth became celebrated; the great ascetic made Kurukṣetra sacred through his austerities.
We have heard that his sons were Aśvavanta, Abhiṣvanta, Citraratha the sage, and the renowned Janamejaya; a noble woman bore these five sons born of the army.
From Abhiṣvata came Parīkṣit; also born were the valiant Śabalāśva, Abhirāja, Virāja, and the mighty Śalmala.
Uccaiḥśravā, Bhadrakāra, and Jitāri the eighth — in the lineage of these men, their descendants became famous for virtues born of their deeds.
Janamejaya and six others, and likewise other mighty sons of Parīkṣit — seven in all — were all skilled in dharma and artha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They were named Kakṣasena, Ugrasena, the valiant Citrasena, Indrasena, Suṣeṇa, and Bhīmasena.
The mighty sons of Janamejaya, renowned on earth, were — Dhṛtarāṣṭra the firstborn, Pāṇḍu, and Bāhlika.
Also Niṣadha of great splendor, the strong Jāmbūnada, Kuṇḍodara, Padāti, and Vasāti the eighth — all were skilled in dharma and artha, all devoted to the welfare of living beings.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra then became king; his sons were Kuṇḍika, Hastī, Vitarka, Krātha, Kuṇḍala the fifth, Haviḥśravā, Indrābha, Sumanyu, and Aparājita.
O bull of the Bhāratas, three sons were born to Pratīpa: Devāpi, Śaṃtanu, and Bāhlika the great chariot-warrior.
Of them, Devāpi retired to the forest in pursuit of dharma; Śaṃtanu obtained the earth, and Bāhlika became a great chariot-warrior.
Many best of kings were born in Bharata's lineage, O king — great chariot-warriors of powerful nature, comparable to divine sages.
And likewise other great chariot-warriors comparable to gods were born in the lineage of Manu — those who augmented the Aila line.
Janamejaya said: O brahmin, I have heard from you the great origin of my ancestors, and I have now learned of the noble kings in this lineage.
But the pleasant narrative, being too brief in content, does not fully satisfy me — so please tell me again in greater detail.
This very divine story — the holy birth of those kings from Prajāpati down to Manu — whose heart would it not gladden?
Their fame, swelled by the greatness of good dharma and virtue, stands exalted, pervading all three worlds.
I am not sated hearing the tale of those endowed with virtue, splendor, valor, energy, strength, and zeal — a tale that tastes like nectar.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Listen, O king — hear fully what was properly heard by me from Dvaipāyana long ago, this auspicious account of the entire origin of your own lineage being now recounted.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From Dakṣa came Aditi; from Aditi came Vivasvat; from Vivasvat came Manu; from Manu came Ilā; from Ilā came Purūravas; from Purūravas came Āyu; from Āyu came Nahuṣa.
Yayāti had two wives: Devayānī, daughter of Uśanas, and Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvā. Here the genealogical succession continues.
Devayānī bore Yadu and Turvasu; Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvā, bore Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru.
Of these, the Yādavas descend from Yadu, and the Pauravas from Pūru.
Pūru's wife was named Kausalyā; to her was born his son Janamejaya, who performed three Aśvamedha sacrifices and then, after performing the Viśvajit sacrifice, entered the forest.
Janamejaya married Anantā, a Mādhavī princess; to her was born his son Prācinvān, who conquered the eastern direction as far as the sunrise — hence his name Prācinvān.
Prācinvān married a princess of the Aśmaka people; to her was born his son Saṃyāti.
Saṃyāti married a daughter of Dṛṣadvata named Varāṅgī; to her was born his son Ahaṃpāti.
Ahaṃpāti married a daughter of Kṛtavīrya named Bhānumatī; to her was born his son Sārvabhauma.
Sārvabhauma carried off by conquest a Kaikeyī princess named Sunandā; to her was born his son Jayatsena.
Jayatsena married a Vidarbhā princess named Suṣuvā; to her was born his son Arācīna.
Arācīna also married another Vidarbhā princess named Maryādā; to her was born his son Mahābhauma.
Mahābhauma married a princess of Prasenajiṭ named Suyajñā; to her was born his son Ayutanāyī, who performed ten thousand Puruṣamedha sacrifices — hence his name Ayutanāyī.
Ayutanāyī married a daughter of Pṛthuśravas named Bhāsā; to her was born his son Akrodhana.
Akrodhana married a Kaliṅga princess named Karaṇḍu; to her was born his son Devātithi.
Devātithi married a Videha princess named Maryādā; to her was born his son Ṛca.
Ṛca married an Aṅga princess named Sudevā; to her he fathered a son named Ṛkṣa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Ṛkṣa married a daughter of Takṣaka named Jvālā; to her he gave birth to a son named Matināra.
Matināra performed a twelve-year sacrificial session on the banks of the Sarasvatī.
When the sacrifice concluded, Sarasvatī herself approached and chose him as her husband; she bore him a son named Taṃsu.
Here a genealogical verse occurs.
Sarasvatī bore Taṃsu as a son to Matināra; Taṃsu in turn begot his own son Ilina upon Kālindī.
Ilina begot five sons on Rathaṃtarī, the eldest of whom was Duḥṣanta.
Duḥṣanta married Śakuntalā, the daughter of Viśvāmitra; she bore him Bharata. On this subject two verses are cited.
"The mother is but the vessel; the son belongs to his father — he who was begotten is himself the father's own. Acknowledge your son, Duḥṣanta; do not despise Śakuntalā."
"The seed-bearer raises his son up from the realm of Yama, O king; you are the maker of this child within the womb — Śakuntalā speaks the truth."
From that, his name Bharata is explained.
Bharata married Sunandā, called Sārvasenī, a princess of the Kāśī line; she bore him Bhumanyु.
Bhumanyु married Jayā, a princess of the Dāśārha line; she bore him Suhotra.
Suhotra married Suvarṇā, a princess of the Ikṣvāku line; she bore him Hastī, who founded this city of Hāstinapura — hence its name.
Hastī married Yaśodharā, a princess of the Trigarta line; she bore him Vikuṇṭhana.
Vikuṇṭhana married Sudevā, a princess of the Dāśārha line; she bore him Ajamīḍha.
Ajamīḍha had twenty-four hundred sons by Kaikeyī, Nāgā, Gāndhārī, Vimalā, and Ṛkṣā, each founding separate royal lines — and the chief line-founder among them was Saṃvaraṇa.
Saṃvaraṇa married Tapatī, the daughter of Vivasvat; she bore him Kuru.
Kuru married Śubhāṅgī, a princess of the Dāśārha line; she bore him Viḍūratha.
Viḍūratha married Saṃpriyā, a princess of Magadha; she bore him a son named Arugvān.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Arugvān married Amṛtā, a princess of Magadha; she bore him Parīkṣit.
Parīkṣit married Suyaśā, a princess of the Bāhuda line; she bore him Bhīmasena.
Bhīmasena married Sukumārī, a princess of Kekaya; she bore him Paryaśravā, who is known by the name Pratīpa.
Pratīpa married Sunandā, a princess of the Śibi clan; he fathered three sons upon her: Devāpi, Śaṃtanu, and Bāhlika.
Devāpi entered the forest while still a boy; Śaṃtanu became the king of the earth. A genealogical verse follows here.
"Whomsoever he touches with his two hands, the aged one gains ease and becomes young again — therefore they call him Śaṃtanu."
That is the explanation of his name Śaṃtanu.
Śaṃtanu married the Bhāgīrathī — Gaṅgā herself; she bore him Devavrata, who is known as Bhīṣma.
Bhīṣma, desiring to please his father, gave away in marriage Satyavatī — the woman known as Gandhakālī — as his father's bride.
She had already conceived before marriage a son by Parāśara — Dvaipāyana; and upon her Śaṃtanu also fathered two sons, Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya.
Of the two, Citrāṅgada was slain by a Gandharva before reaching manhood; Vicitravīrya then became king.
Vicitravīrya married the two daughters of the king of Kāśī — Ambikā and Ambālikā, born of Kausalyā.
But Vicitravīrya passed away without leaving any offspring.
Then Satyavatī reflected: "The line of Duḥṣanta's descendant is about to be extinguished."
She thought of the sage Dvaipāyana.
He stood before her at once and said: "What shall I do?"
She said to him: "Your brother Vicitravīrya has gone to heaven leaving no offspring — please beget children upon his wives."
Agreeing with the word "so be it," he fathered three sons: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura.
There, to king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, a hundred sons were born of Gāndhārī by the boon of Dvaipāyana.
Among Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, four were pre-eminent: Duryodhana, Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, and Citrasena.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Pāṇḍu had two wives — Kuntī and Mādrī — both jewels among women.
Now while Pāṇḍu was roaming on the hunt, he saw a sage engaged in intercourse with a doe; even as the sage was thus immersed, still unsatiated and not yet having tasted his desire's sweetness, Pāṇḍu struck him with an arrow.
Struck by the arrow, he spoke to Pāṇḍu: "You who call yourself a follower of dharma — because you, knowing better, have struck me down before I tasted the joy of love, you too shall meet this very fate: you shall pass away quickly, deprived of love's pleasure, in this very same condition."
Pāṇḍu, his color drained from his face, seeking to avoid the curse, did not approach his wives.
And he said: "Through my own rashness I have brought this upon myself; and I have heard that a man without offspring has no worlds hereafter."
He said to Kuntī: "Therefore you shall beget sons for my sake."
She then bore sons: Yudhiṣṭhira by Dharma, Bhīmasena by the Wind, and Arjuna by Indra.
Pāṇḍu said to Kuntī with a joyful countenance: "Your co-wife has no offspring — please arrange for a child to be born of her as well."
Kuntī agreed, saying "So be it."
Thereupon Nakula and Sahadeva were begotten upon Mādrī by the twin Aśvins.
Seeing Mādrī adorned and beautiful, Pāṇḍu was stirred with passion.
The very moment he touched her, he passed away.
There Mādrī ascended the funeral pyre where he lay.
She said to Kuntī: "The noble lady must raise the twins with unwavering care."
Then the five Pāṇḍavas, together with Kuntī, were brought to Hāstinapura by the forest ascetics and presented to Bhīṣma and Vidura.
There too an attempt was made to burn them in the lac-house, but it could not succeed owing to Vidura's counsel.
And having slain Hiḍimba along the way, they went to Ekacakrā.
There in Ekacakrā too, having slain the demon named Baka, they proceeded to the city of Pāñcāla.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From there they obtained Draupadī as their wife and returned safely to their own realm.
They also begot sons: Yudhiṣṭhira fathered Prativindhya, Vṛkodara fathered Sutasoma, Arjuna fathered Śrutakīrti, Nakula fathered Śatānīka, and Sahadeva fathered Śrutakarmā.
Yudhiṣṭhira also won at a svayaṃvara a maiden named Devikā, daughter of Govāsana of the Śibi clan, and fathered upon her a son named Yaudheya.
Bhīmasena also married Baladhārā, a princess of Kāśī, won by valor, and fathered upon her a son named Sarvaga.
Arjuna went to Dvāravatī and married Subhadrā, the sister of Vāsudeva; he fathered upon her a son named Abhimanyu.
Nakula married Kareṇuvatī, a princess of the Cedi, and fathered upon her a son named Niramitra.
Sahadeva also won at a svayaṃvara Vijayā, herself a Mādrī princess, and fathered upon her a son named Suhotra.
Bhīmasena had earlier also fathered upon the demoness Hiḍimbā a son named Ghaṭotkaca.
These then are the eleven sons of the Pāṇḍavas.
Abhimanyu married Uttarā, the daughter of Virāṭa; the child conceived in her womb was stillborn.
Pṛthā received that six-month foetus in her lap, at the command of the supreme Vāsudeva, saying: "I shall restore this one to life."
Having revived him, she declared: "Born when the family was brought to ruin, let this one be named Parīkṣit."
Parīkṣit married a princess named Mādravatī; she bore him Janamejaya.
From Janamejaya and Vapuṣṭamā were born two sons: Śatānīka and Śaṅku.
Śatānīka married a princess of Videha; she bore him a son named Aśvamedhadatta.
Thus the lineage of Pūru and of the Pāṇḍavas has been recounted; one who hears this line of Pūru is freed from all sins.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was a king who sprang from the Ikṣvāku line, lord of the earth, renowned as Mahābhiṣa — truthful in speech and true in valor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With a thousand aśvamedha sacrifices and a hundred vājapeya rites he pleased the lord of gods, Indra, and thereby that powerful king attained heaven.
On one occasion the gods assembled to attend upon Brahmā; among them were the royal sages, and king Mahābhiṣa was also present.
Then Gaṅgā, the foremost of rivers, came to approach the Grandfather; the wind blew aside her garment, white as moonlight.
Thereupon all the hosts of gods suddenly cast their eyes downward — but the royal sage Mahābhiṣa gazed upon the river without hesitation or shame.
Mahābhiṣa was censured by the venerable Brahmā, and was told: "You shall be born again among mortals, and then win back these worlds."
