That king, having reflected among all the ascetic kings, chose Pratīpa — a man of great splendor — as the father he wished to be born from.
The best of rivers, seeing that king Mahābhiṣa fall from his composure, turned her mind and heart upon him alone.
While going along the path she beheld the Vasus, those celestial gods, their forms wasted away and their vigour crushed by affliction.
Seeing them in such a state, the foremost of rivers asked: "Why have your forms thus perished? Are the dwellers of heaven well?"
The Vasus, the gods, replied to her: "O great river, we have been cursed by the great-souled Vasiṣṭha in a fit of rage for a trivial offence."
"For we all, heedless, once walked right past the foremost of sages, Vasiṣṭha, who was seated in twilight meditation in an unobtrusive spot."
"In his anger he cursed us to be born in a womb. What the knower of Brahman has spoken cannot be otherwise undone."
"Therefore you, becoming a mortal woman, bear us as sons upon the earth; for we cannot enter the inauspicious womb of ordinary mortal women."
Thus addressed, Gaṅgā said "so be it" to those Vasus and then asked: "Who among mortals will be the best of men to act as your father?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Vasus replied: "The righteous king named Śaṃtanu, son of Pratīpa, will exist in the mortal world; he shall be our father."
Gaṅgā said: "O gods of unblemished honour, my mind also agrees with what you have said. I will do what is pleasing to him, and this is your wish as well."
The Vasus said: "You should cast our newborn sons into the water, so that our release from the curse may come swiftly, O you who flow through the three worlds."
Gaṅgā said: "I will do this. Let there be provided for him a son; his union with me should not be fruitless, for he desires a son."
The Vasus said: "Each of us will contribute an eighth part of our own valour; with that valour your son — and his desired heir — will be born."
"That son of yours will never beget offspring among mortals; thus he will be without children of his own, though he will be mighty in valour."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus made this compact with Gaṅgā, the Vasus departed with joyful hearts, their purpose fulfilled exactly as they had intended.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then that king Pratīpa, devoted to the welfare of all beings, sat for many years on the bank of the Gaṅgā, engaged in prayer.
To him came Gaṅgā, endowed with beauty and virtues, like the goddess Śrī made manifest, rising from the water in a form most enchanting to behold.
She of divine form and noble spirit, her face radiant as the moon, seated herself on the right thigh of the royal sage as he sat in study, that thigh like the trunk of a śāla tree.
The sovereign Pratīpa then spoke to that noble-minded woman: "What may I do for you, fair one? What is it that you desire?"
The woman said: "O king, foremost of the Kurus, I desire you — accept me. For the rejection of women who offer themselves in love is condemned by the good."
Pratīpa replied: "O lady of excellent complexion, I would not out of desire go to another man's wife, nor to a woman of different caste, O fair one — know this as my sacred vow."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The woman said: "I am not unworthy, nor am I one to be avoided or rebuked at any time. Accept me, O king — a maiden, the finest of women, who offers herself to you."
Pratīpa replied: "What you urge upon me would overstep the bounds for me. Were I to act otherwise than I have vowed, the violation of dharma would be my ruin."
"You have come and seated yourself on my right thigh, O beautiful-limbed one. Know, O timid one, that this is the seat reserved for children and daughters-in-law."
"The left side is the place of a beloved wife, but you have not taken that seat. Therefore I shall not engage with you in desire, O beautiful-limbed one."
"Become my daughter-in-law, fair one — I choose you for the sake of my son; for you came and took your place on the side belonging to a daughter-in-law, O slender-thighed."
The woman said: "So be it then, O knower of dharma — I will be united with your son. Out of devotion to you I will honour the renowned lineage of the Bhāratas."
"Among all the rulers of the earth, you are the supreme refuge. Even in a hundred years I could not fully describe the virtues of this line — that peerless excellence which has proceeded from you all."
"Your son must not question my lineage, O lord, nor must he ever question whatever I may do — your son should never inquire into any of this."
"Dwelling thus with your son, I will bring him joy; and through virtuous, beloved sons your son will attain heaven."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having said "so be it," she vanished on the spot. The king, expecting the birth of a son, kept her words in his heart.
At this very time, O joy of the Kurus, the bull among kṣatriyas, Pratīpa, practised austerities together with his wife for the sake of a son.
To that aged pair was born a son — he was Mahābhiṣa; from Śānta was born Saṃtāna, and from him came Śaṃtanu.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Constantly remembering the imperishable worlds won by his own deeds in a former life, Śaṃtanu was ever a doer of righteous deeds, O best of Kurus.
Then Pratīpa instructed his son Śaṃtanu when he came of age: "Formerly a woman came to me, O Śaṃtanu, for your welfare."
"If that woman of lovely complexion — a divine woman full of beauty and desire, seeking a son — comes to you in private, O son, you must not ask her who she is or to whom she belongs."
"Whatever she may do that you think should not be done, you must not question her. By my command, honour her who offers herself to you" — so he instructed him.
Having thus instructed his son Śaṃtanu, and having consecrated him in his own kingdom, the king Pratīpa then entered the forest.
That wise king Śaṃtanu, renowned throughout the earth as a wielder of the bow, became fond of hunting and constantly ranged through the forests.
Slaying deer and buffaloes, that best of kings roamed alone along the Gaṅgā, that river frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas.
One day, O great king, he beheld a supremely beautiful woman, blazing in her form like the goddess Śrī herself standing before him.
She was flawless in every limb, with fine teeth, adorned with divine ornaments, wearing fine garments, standing alone, her radiance equal to the interior of a lotus.
Beholding her, the lord of men was filled with delight, his hair standing on end; marvelling at the perfection of her beauty, drinking her in with his eyes, he could not be satisfied.
And she too, having seen the king of great splendour as he wandered there, felt affection and tenderness stir within her, and the graceful one could not be satisfied.
Then the king spoke to her, addressing her with gentle, soothing words: "Are you a goddess, or a dānavī, a gandharvī, or an apsarā?"
"Or a yakṣī, or a nāgakanyā, or a mortal woman, O slender-waisted? Whoever you may be, O radiant as the womb of the gods, become my wife, O beautiful one."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing the king's words, soft, gentle, and sweet, that blameless one, remembering the compact of the Vasus, approached him with a smile.
And she spoke words that gladdened the king's heart: "I will become your queen, O ruler of the earth, obedient to your will."
"But whatever I may do, O king, whether it seems good or ill, I must not be restrained, nor must anything disagreeable be said to me regarding it."
"As long as things proceed thus between us, I will dwell with you, O king; but if I am restrained or spoken to disagreeably, I will assuredly leave you."
When the king said "so be it," O best of the Bhāratas, she experienced matchless joy upon obtaining that best of kings.
Having obtained her, the self-controlled Śaṃtanu enjoyed her as he desired, thinking "she is not to be questioned" — he said nothing at all to her.
The lord of the earth was fully pleased by her conduct and character, by her beauty, generosity, and virtues, and by her devoted attentiveness in private.
For she, the goddess Gaṅgā, the river flowing through the three paths, that woman of excellent complexion, had assumed a beautiful human form.
She had come and presented herself as a wife to Śaṃtanu, that lion among kings, equal in splendour to the king of the gods, whose desire had thus been brought to him by fortune.
She delighted the king with loving pleasures and clever arts, with charming coquetry and grace; and as she rejoiced, so did he.
The king, absorbed in love and captivated by the qualities of that most excellent of women, did not notice the many years, seasons, and months that passed.
Sporting with her as he wished, the lord of men fathered upon her eight sons, each of them radiant as the immortals.
Each son as he was born she would cast into the water, O Bhārata, saying "I am gratifying you" as she plunged him into the current of the Gaṅgā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This was not pleasing to king Śaṃtanu, yet the lord of the earth said nothing to her, fearing that she would leave him.
But when the eighth son was born, as she made as if to laugh, the king, tormented with grief, spoke to her, longing to keep a son for himself.
"Do not kill him! Who are you? Whose are you? Why do you harm your sons? O murderer of children, do not incur so great a sin — stop, O infamous one!"
The woman said: "O you who desire a son, best of those who have sons, I am not killing your son. But this agreement I made has now run its course, just as a garment wears out."
"I am Gaṅgā, daughter of Jahnu, attended upon by hosts of great sages. I have dwelt with you for the accomplishment of a divine purpose."
"These eight are the great and mighty Vasus, the gods; through the fault of Vasiṣṭha's curse they took on human birth."
"There is no father for them on earth other than you, nor is there any mortal woman like me who could serve as their mother."
"Therefore I took on human form for the purpose of bearing them. By fathering eight Vasus, imperishable worlds have been won by you."
"This was the compact of the gods, the Vasus, which was made known to me: 'You shall release each one as he is born from his human birth.'"
"Those Vasus have been released from the curse of the great-souled Āpava. Farewell to you — I will depart. Guard this son; he is a keeper of great vows."
"This stay with you was arranged in the presence of the Vasus as part of their plan. Know this son, born of me, as Gaṅgādatta — given by Gaṅgā."
Śaṃtanu said: "Who indeed is this one called Āpava? And what was the misdeeds of the Vasus, by whose curse they all came to take on a human body?"
"And what has been done by this boy, Gaṅgādatta, on account of whose deed he will remain dwelling among mortals?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Those Vasus who are lords of all the worlds — how did they come to be born among mortals? Tell me this, O daughter of Jahnu."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, Gaṅgā, the goddess, daughter of Jahnu, then spoke these words to the king, her husband, Śaṃtanu, that bull among men.
"The sage named Vasiṣṭha, who was obtained as a son by Varuṇa long ago, O best of the Bhāratas — that sage is also known by the name Āpava."
"His holy hermitage, filled with herds of deer and flocks of birds, lies on the flank of Meru, king of mountains, covered with flowers of every season."
"There that son of Varuṇa, best among doers of virtuous deeds, performed austerities in that forest, O best of the Bhāratas, which abounded in sweet roots, fruits, and water."
"The daughter of Dakṣa, known as Surabhī, exceedingly glorious — that goddess gave birth to a cow from Kaśyapa, O bull of the Bhāratas."
"For the benefit of the world that righteous-souled son of Varuṇa received that excellent wish-fulfilling cow, fit to be a sacrificial cow."
"That cow, dwelling in that forest of ascetics frequented by sages, wandered freely through the pleasant and sacred woodland, fearless."
"Then one day, O bull of the Bhāratas, all the Vasus, with Pṛthu at their head, came to that forest, which was frequented by gods and divine sages."
Those Vasus, together with their wives, roamed that forest in all directions and took delight in its charming mountains and woodland groves.
There, O hero rivalling Indra, the wife of one of those Vasus—a slender-waisted lady wandering in that forest—caught sight of the cow that was the wish-fulfilling gem of the sage Vasiṣṭha, supreme among all desire-yielding kine.
Filled with wonder at the cow's wealth of virtue and beauty, she pointed her out to her husband Dyaus, O bull-eyed one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The cow was deep-uddered, gave milk freely, had a fine tail and a beautiful face, was endowed with every good quality, and possessed a character utterly without equal.
The daughter of a Vasu, O lord of kings, O delight of the Pauravas, pointed out that cow, thus endowed with all these qualities, to her husband the Vasu Dyaus long ago.
Dyaus, upon seeing that cow, O king, mighty as the lord of elephants, spoke to his goddess-wife, describing the cow's beauty and virtues.
"This, O goddess, O dark-eyed one, O fair-hipped lady, is the supreme cow of Vāruṇī's son—that very sage whose this excellent forest is."
"Whoever among mortals drinks the sweet milk of this cow, O slender-waisted one, shall live for ten thousand years with unfading youth."
Hearing this, O best of kings, that slender-waisted, flawlessly-limbed goddess spoke to her blazingly radiant husband:
"In the world of mortals I have a friend, a princess—her name is Jinavati, adorned with beauty and the bloom of youth."
"She is the daughter of the royal sage Ushinarathe truthful and wise—and she is renowned throughout the mortal world for the wealth of her beauty."
"For her sake, O greatly fortunate one, O best of the immortals, O increaser of merit, quickly bring me this cow along with her calf—she is what I desire."
"So that my friend, drinking this cow's milk, may be the one among mortals who is free from old age and disease, O giver of honour."
"You, O greatly fortunate one, O blameless one, must do this favour for me, for there is nothing dearer to me than this—nothing at all."
Hearing these words of his goddess-wife and wishing to please her, Dyaus then stole that cow together with his brothers led by Prithva.
Impelled by that lotus-eyed goddess, Dyaus, O king, was unable to face the fierce austerities of that sage; he stole the cow then and there, and the fall that would follow was not foreseen.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Vasiṣṭha, son of Varuṇa, returned to his hermitage bearing fruits, but he did not see the cow with her calf anywhere in that excellent forest.
That sage, rich in austerities and of noble intellect, searched for her throughout that forest, yet searching he could not find the cow.
Knowing by his divine sight that she had been carried off by the Vasus, he immediately fell under the sway of anger and then cursed those Vasus.
"Since the Vasus have stolen my milch-cow with her fine tail, therefore all of them shall without doubt be born among mortals."
Thus did the venerable Āpava, best of sages, having come under the power of wrath, curse those Vasus, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Having cursed them, that greatly fortunate one turned his mind once again to his austerities. Thus, O king, did that sage of mighty power—that brahmarishi, rich in penance—curse all eight Vasus while filled with wrath against those gods.
Then, coming again to that hermitage of the great-souled sage, the Vasus—knowing they had been cursed—approached that rishi.
Though the Vasus sought to propitiate that sage, O bull of kings, they could not obtain grace from that best of rishis—from Āpava, O tiger among men, who was versed in all the ways of dharma.
And that righteous-souled sage said: "Seven of you—Dhara and the rest—will obtain release from the curse within a year."
"But this one—Dyaus—on whose account you were cursed by me, shall dwell for a long time in the world of mortals, reaping the fruit of his own deed."
"I do not wish to make false what I spoke to you in anger. Yet this high-minded one shall also beget no offspring among mortals."
"He shall be righteous-souled, versed in all the scriptures, devoted to what is dear and beneficial to his father, and he shall abstain from the enjoyment of women." Having spoken thus to all the Vasus, the venerable sage departed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thereupon all those Vasus came to me, O king, and begged a boon of me, and that boon I granted them: "As each of us is born, O Gaṅgā, cast us yourself into the water."
Thus, O best of kings, I duly did what was proper for the sake of releasing those who had been cursed—freeing them from the world of mortals.
This one alone, O best of kings, O Bhārata—Dyaus—shall dwell long in the world of mortals because of that sage's curse.
Having narrated all this, the goddess vanished from that very spot; and taking that prince with her, she departed as she wished.
That son of Śaṃtanu bore two names—Devavrata and Gangeyaand he surpassed even Śaṃtanu in virtues.
And Śaṃtanu, stricken with grief, then returned to his own city. I shall now recount the boundless virtues of Śaṃtanu.
And the great good fortune of that glorious Bhārata king—the resplendent history of whom is called the Mahābhārata.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: That wise Śaṃtanu—honoured by gods, kings, and sages—was celebrated in all worlds as righteous-souled and true of speech.
Self-restraint, generosity, forbearance, wisdom, modesty, steadfastness, and surpassing splendour—these were ever-present in the great-souled Śaṃtanu, bull among men.
So endowed with virtues, skilled in dharma and statecraft, that king was the protector of the Bharata lineage and of righteous people.
He had a conch-like neck, broad shoulders, and the gait of a lordly rutting elephant; he held firmly to the conviction that dharma stands supreme above desire and material gain.
All these qualities dwelt in the great-souled Śaṃtanu, O bull of the Bhāratas, and no other kshatriya was his equal in righteousness.
Because he abided in his own dharma and was the foremost of all who know dharma, the kings of the earth consecrated him as sovereign over kings.
Free from grief, fear, and affliction, waking from pleasant slumber, the kings of the earth rallied to him as protector of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the world was protected by kings with Śaṃtanu at their head, then by rule the order of all the varnas prevailed with brahminical excellence at the fore.
The brahmin order attended upon the kshatriyas; the vaishyas followed the kshatriyas dutifully; and the shudras, devoted to both brahmin and kshatriya, attended upon the vaishyas.
Dwelling in lovely Hāstinapura, the stronghold of the Kurus, he ruled the earth all the way to the ocean's edge.
Comparable to the king of gods, he was a knower of dharma, true of speech, upright of conduct, and endowed with supreme royal glory through the practice of giving, righteousness, and austerity.
Free from passion and hatred, he was pleasant to behold as the moon; in splendour he resembled the sun; in swiftness he equalled the wind; in wrath he was like Death himself; and in forbearance he was equal to the earth.
When Śaṃtanu was the guardian of the earth, O king, there was no wanton slaughter of cattle, boars, deer, or birds.
In a realm where dharma and brahminical order stood supreme, the humble-souled Śaṃtanu ruled all beings equally, free from desire and passion.
Rituals were then performed for the sake of gods, sages, and ancestors, and no living creature was slain contrary to dharma.
For the unhappy, the unprotected, and those dwelling in animal births—that king became the father of all beings.
While that best of Kuru lords, that sovereign of kings, reigned, speech was wedded to truth and the mind rested upon the dharma of giving.
For sixteen years, then eight, then four, then eight more—finding no pleasure in women—he roamed the forests.
Of such a form, such conduct, such behaviour, and such learning was his son by Gaṅgā—named Devavrata, also called Vasu.
Deeply versed in all weapons, both divine and earthly, he was a man of great strength, great fortitude, great valour, and a mighty chariot-warrior.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Once, having shot a deer and following the river, king Śaṃtanu saw the Bhāgīrathī—the Gaṅgā—low in her waters.
Seeing this, Śaṃtanu, bull among men, wondered: "Why does this best of rivers not flow today as she did of old?"
Then, searching for the cause, that high-minded one beheld a youth—handsome of form, tall, and beautiful to behold.
He was wielding divine weapons like the god Indra himself, standing there having covered the whole Gaṅgā with sharp arrows.
Seeing the river Gaṅgā thus covered with arrows nearby, the king was filled with astonishment, beholding an act surpassing human capacity.
Though Śaṃtanu had seen that son immediately at birth long ago, the wise king could not now recall enough to recognise him as his own child.
But that youth, seeing his father, cast a spell of bewilderment upon him with his magic, and having bewildered him, vanished from that very spot.
Having witnessed that wonder, king Śaṃtanu, suspecting this to be his son, called out to Gaṅgā: "Show him to me!"
Then Gaṅgā, wearing her most beautiful form, showed him that adorned youth, taking him by the right hand.
Though Śaṃtanu had seen her before, he did not recognise that faithful one, adorned with jewels and wearing spotless garments.
Gaṅgā said: "The eighth son whom you once begat upon me, O king—this is he, O tiger among men. Take him home with you."
"He has mastered the Vedas with all their ancillary texts under Vasiṣṭha himself; skilled in arms, an incomparable archer, he equals the king of gods in battle."
"He is ever honoured by both gods and demons, O Bhārata; whatever scripture Uśanas knows, this one knows it all and completely."
"Likewise, the son of Aṅgiras—Bṛhaspati, adored by gods and demons alike—whatever scripture he knows, all of that too is established fully in this mighty-armed, great-souled son of yours, with every supplement and sub-division."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The mighty sage Rāma Jāmadagnya, invincible by any foe—whatever weapon-lore he knows, that too is established in this son of yours."
"This great archer, skilled in the laws and aims of kingship, O king—this, my own son, a hero—I give to you; O hero, take him home."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus sent off by her, Śaṃtanu, taking his son who shone like the sun, set out toward his own city.
That scion of Pūru, arriving at his own city—rivalling the city of Indra, abundant in every desired object—considered himself fulfilled, and then installed his son as crown prince among the Pauravas.
The greatly renowned son of Śaṃtanu delighted the Pauravas, his father, and the kingdom by his conduct, O bull of the Bhāratas.
That king of boundless valour thus spent four years rejoicing together with his son.
Once, the king went to a forest near the river Yamunā, where he inhaled an indescribably excellent fragrance.
Seeking its source, he wandered in all directions and then saw a girl belonging to the fishermen's clan, beautiful as a goddess.
Having seen her, he asked that dark-eyed maiden: "Whose daughter are you? Who are you? And what do you intend to do, O timid one?"
She replied: "I am the daughter of a fisherman; by my father's command—the great-souled chief of the fishermen, blessings upon you—I ferry people across for the sake of dharma and livelihood."
Gazing upon her—endowed with beauty, sweetness, and fragrance, radiant as a goddess—king Śaṃtanu desired that daughter of the fisherman.
He went to her father and sought her hand, then questioned her father about his own purposes and conditions.
The fisher-king replied to that lord of the earth: "This fair-complexioned girl is mine to give in marriage the moment she is asked; but there is a certain wish in my heart — hear it, O lord of men."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"If you desire this girl as your lawful wife, O sinless one, you are known as a speaker of truth — therefore make a solemn compact with me in truth."
"Upon a pledge I will give you this maiden, O king; for no bridegroom equal to you shall ever come to me again."
Śaṃtanu said: "Having heard your condition, O fisher-man, I will consider whether I can grant it or not. What can be given I will give; what cannot be given I will never give under any circumstances."
The fisherman said: "Whatever son is born of her shall be consecrated king and lord of the earth after you — no other, O king."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Śaṃtanu did not wish to grant that boon to the fisherman, O Bhārata, even though he burned intensely with desire born of the body.
That great king, dwelling only in thought on the fisher's daughter, returned to Hāstinapura with his mind struck by grief.
Then one day his son Devavrata, approaching his father who was grieving and sunk in brooding thought, spoke these words to him.
"All the kings of the earth are subject to your welfare; for what reason then do you grieve here constantly, O sorrowful one? And why, as if lost in meditation, do you say nothing at all, O king?"
Thus addressed by his son, Śaṃtanu replied: "Without doubt I am indeed absorbed in brooding, just as you say."
"In this great lineage, you alone are our offspring, O Bhārata; and mortal men are impermanent — for this reason I grieve, my son."
"Should any misfortune befall you, O son of the Ganges, our lineage is extinct; you alone, without doubt, are worth a hundred sons."
"Nor am I willing to take a wife again without purpose; yet for the preservation of the lineage I desire it — may it go well with you. Those who speak of dharma call having only one son the same as being sonless."
"The agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, and all the yajñas together with their dakṣiṇās — all these do not equal a sixteenth part of the merit of having offspring."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"So it is likewise among men and among all creatures — this is the eternal triad of the ancients and of the best: that offspring is supreme. In this, O greatly wise one, I have no doubt."
"And you are a hero, ever proud, ever engaged with weapons, O Bhārata; your death, O sinless one, can come from nowhere other than a weapon."
"Thus I am fallen into doubt: should you be at peace, how will it be? I have told you in full, my dear son, the entire cause of my grief."
Then, having learned the entire cause in full, Devavrata of great intelligence departed, pondering it deeply.
He went quickly to seek the aged minister who was loyal to his father, and approaching him, inquired about the cause of his father's grief.
To that chief of the Kurus who asked him properly, the minister recounted in full the boon demanded, naming the maiden in question, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then Devavrata, accompanied by senior Kṣatriyas, went himself to the fisher-king and sought the maiden on behalf of his father.
The fisherman received him according to due rite and honored him, then spoke to him as he sat in the royal assembly, O Bhārata.
"You alone are a sufficient guardian for Śaṃtanu, O bull among men; you are the best son among those who have sons — what then shall I say to you?"
For who would not grieve upon passing up such a praiseworthy and desirable alliance — this very union — even Indra himself, the performer of a hundred sacrifices?
Moreover, this is the offspring of a noble one who is your equal in virtues — from whose seed the illustrious Satyavatī was born.
By him, dear child, your father has been repeatedly praised; he is worthy of marrying Satyavatī among all the kings, O Bhārata.
Even the divine sage Asita was once refused by me; that foremost of sages had ardently sought Satyavatī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But as her father I must speak a little, O bull of the Bhāratas: I see only one powerful flaw here — the matter of a rival stepmother.
For if you were the rival of anyone — be he a gandharva or an asura — he could never live happily when you are angered, O scorcher of foes.
This is the only flaw here; there is no other, O prince. Know this well — good fortune to you — in the matter of giving and receiving, O scorcher of foes.
Thus addressed, the son of Gaṅgā replied fittingly, in the hearing of the assembled kings, for his father's sake, O Bhārata.
"Accept this resolve of mine as true, O best among those who speak truth: neither one born nor yet to be born would dare to speak such words as these."
"I will do exactly as you say: whatever son is born of her shall be our king."
When he had said this, the fisherman chief spoke to him again, seeking to accomplish a difficult act regarding the kingship, O bull of the Bhāratas.
"You alone are the fitting lord of the immeasurably glorious Śaṃtanu, O righteous soul, and you are the master capable of giving away the maiden."
"But hear this word of mine and this matter too, O gentle one; I shall speak it in the manner of those who guard maidens, O subduer of foes."
"What you have pledged in the assembly of kings for the sake of Satyavatī, O you devoted to truth and righteousness, that is entirely fitting for you."
"It cannot be otherwise, O mighty-armed one; there is no doubt about that. But as for offspring that might be born of you — there our doubt is great."
Knowing that to be his concern, the one devoted to truth and righteousness then pledged anew, O king, wishing to do what was dear to his father.
Devavrata said: "O king of fishermen, O foremost of lords, hear this word of mine which I now speak for my father's sake in the hearing of these assembled kings."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The kingdom I have already renounced before, O lord of men; and now, for the sake of offspring as well, I make this firm resolve."
"From this day forward, O fisherman, I shall live in perpetual celibacy; even without a son, imperishable worlds in heaven shall be mine."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing these words, his body-hair standing erect with joy, the righteous fisherman replied to him: "I give her."
Then the apsaras in the sky, the gods, and the hosts of sages together rained down flowers and cried out: "This one is Bhīṣma — the Terrible One!"
Then, for his father's sake, he said to that illustrious woman: "Mount the chariot, mother; let us go to our own home."
Having said this, Bhīṣma helped that noble lady onto the chariot, came to Hāstinapura, and presented her to Śaṃtanu.
Kings both assembled together and separately praised that difficult deed of his, and cried out: "This one is Bhīṣma — the Terrible One!"
Seeing that difficult deed done by Bhīṣma, his father Śaṃtanu, well pleased, himself granted him the boon of death at will.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: After the marriage was concluded, King Śaṃtanu installed that maiden of surpassing beauty in his own home.
Then the wise son of Śaṃtanu was born of Satyavatī — the hero named Citrāṅgada, who surpassed all men in valour.
Then again the mighty lord begot upon Satyavatī another great archer, Prince Vicitravīrya.
While Vicitravīrya had not yet reached youth, O bull of the Bhāratas, the wise King Śaṃtanu submitted to the law of time and passed away.
With Śaṃtanu gone to heaven, Bhīṣma, abiding by Satyavatī's counsel, established the enemy-taming Citrāṅgada upon the throne.
But Citrāṅgada, through his valour, held all other kings in contempt; he considered no human being his equal.
As he was thus scorning gods, men, and asuras alike, a powerful Gandharva king bearing the same name came against him; and a mighty battle between them took place on the field of Kurukṣetra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Between those two powerful ones — the Gandharva chief and the chief of the Kurus — the battle raged for three years on the bank of the river Hiraṇvatī.
In that tumultuous clash, thick with a rain of weapons, the Gandharva, superior in magical power, slew the foremost of the Kurus.
Having slain Citrāṅgada, best of the Kurus, whose bow and arrows were varied and marvelous, the Gandharva then ascended to heaven.
When that tiger among kings, of great splendour, was slain, Bhīṣma son of Śaṃtanu performed the funeral rites, O king.
And the mighty-armed Bhīṣma then immediately consecrated the child Vicitravīrya, who had not yet come of age, to the Kuru kingship.
Vicitravīrya, abiding by Bhīṣma's counsel, then administered the realm that had been his father's and grandfather's, O great king.
That king, skilled in the science of dharma, honored Bhīṣma son of Śaṃtanu with righteous conduct, and Bhīṣma in turn protected him.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Citrāṅgada was slain, O sinless one, Bhīṣma, abiding by Satyavatī's counsel, administered that kingdom on behalf of his young brother.
Seeing that his brother, the best among the wise, had come of age, Bhīṣma resolved to arrange the marriage of Vicitravīrya.
Then Bhīṣma heard, O king, that three daughters of the king of Kāśī, equal in beauty to apsarases, were holding a svayaṃvara to choose their own husbands.
Then that best of chariot-warriors, clad in armour, set out with a single chariot, with his mother's permission, toward the city of Vārāṇasī.
There Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, saw the assembled kings who had gathered from all directions, and the maidens as well.
While the names of thousands of kings were being proclaimed, Bhīṣma himself, that mighty lord, then chose those maidens, O king.
And Bhīṣma, best of warriors, whose voice was like the roar of a rain-cloud, having placed those maidens on his chariot, addressed the assembled kings, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The gift of maidens after inviting worthy suitors, adorning the bride, and giving wealth according to one's means — this is ordained by the wise as one form of marriage."
"Others give a maiden in exchange for a pair of cattle, others for a stated price, others by force, and others by obtaining consent."
"Some take a maiden unawares, while others win her by mutual desire — that eighth form, O know well, is named among the sages."
"The svayaṃvara is praised and resorted to by Kṣatriyas; but those who speak of dharma declare that a bride seized by force after vanquishing opponents is the highest form of marriage for the warrior class."
"These maidens here I intend to carry away by force, O lords of the earth. Exert yourselves to the utmost, whether for victory or otherwise — I stand resolved for battle, O kings."
Having thus addressed the kings and the king of Kāśī, the valiant Kaurava placed all the maidens on his chariot, bade farewell to them all, and swiftly departed, the maidens in his possession.
Then all those kings sprang up in fury, slapping their own arms and biting their lips.
As they rushed forward hastily, removing their ornaments and putting on their armour, there was a great tumult.
There was a shower as of falling stars, O Janamejaya, of bright ornaments and coats of armour on all sides.
With their armour and ornaments gleaming swiftly in every direction, and with brows furrowed in anger and indignation and eyes red with rage, they stood thus.
Mounting their splendid chariots yoked by charioteers, drawn by excellent horses straining at the pole, those heroes equipped with every weapon followed the single Kaurava as he set forth, their weapons raised.
Then, O Bhārata, there arose a tumultuous and hair-raising battle between him alone and those many kings.
They simultaneously let fly ten thousand arrows at him, but Bhīṣma instantly cut down every one of them before they could reach him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all those kings, surrounding him on every side, poured upon him a shower of arrows as storm-clouds rain upon a mountain.
He intercepted that rain of shafts with his own arrows from every direction, and then pierced all those earth-lords, each with three arrows in return.
Even his enemies marvelled at his superhuman swiftness as a chariot-warrior and at his self-defence in battle.
Having utterly vanquished them in battle, that Bhārata — skilled in all weapons — departed with the maidens toward the Bhāratas.
Then, O king, the great chariot-warrior Śālva's king, immeasurable in spirit, attacked Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, from behind in battle.
Like a bull-elephant, foremost among the strong, who has come upon a cow in heat and strikes a rival bull from behind with his tusks.
"O woman-coveter, stand and fight! Stand and fight!" said that king, the great-armed king of Śālva, goaded on by indignation.
Then that tiger among men, Bhīṣma, crusher of enemy forces, stirred by those words, blazed with rage like a smokeless fire.
Abiding by the duty of a warrior, free from fear and agitation, that great chariot-warrior turned his chariot back toward Śālva.
Seeing him turn back, all those kings became mere spectators at the clash between Bhīṣma and Śālva.
Like two mighty bulls roaring and circling one another over a cow in heat, those two, possessed of great strength and valor, moved against each other.
Then Śālva's king, foremost among men, covered Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, with hundreds of thousands of swift arrows.
Seeing Bhīṣma thus assailed first by Śālva, those kings were astonished and exclaimed "Well done! Well done!"
Witnessing his swiftness in combat, all those lords of the earth, the kings, joyfully honored Śālva with words of praise.
Hearing then the words of the assembled warriors, the enraged Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu — conqueror of enemy cities — cried out, "Stand! Stand!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And in his fury he spoke to his charioteer: "Drive where that king stands, that I may today slay him as the king of birds slays a serpent."
Then the Kaurava duly invoked the Vāruṇa weapon, O lord of men, and with it he crushed the four horses of Śālva's king.
Warding off the weapons of Śālva's king with his own weapons, that Kaurava Bhīṣma, O tiger among kings, slew Śālva's charioteer, and with a single weapon further struck down his finest horses.
For the sake of the maidens, O best of men, Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, having vanquished him, then released that foremost of kings alive; and Śālva departed to his own city, O bull of the Bhāratas.
And those kings who had been present there, wishing to witness the svayamvara, likewise returned to their own kingdoms, O conqueror of enemy cities.
Having thus won those maidens, Bhīṣma, foremost among warriors, proceeded to Hāstinapura, where the Kaurava king resided.
In no long time, O lord of men, he traversed forests, rivers, and mountains adorned with manifold trees.
Uninjured himself, having destroyed his foes in battle — he whose valor was beyond measure — the son of the river Gaṅgā brought home the daughters of the king of Kāśi.
That righteous-souled one received them as daughters-in-law, as younger sisters, and as daughters, and escorted them to the Kurus.
All of them endowed with virtues, won by his valor — Bhīṣma, as a brother, gave them to his younger brother Vicitravīrya.
The righteous Bhīṣma, knowing the law of the virtuous, having accomplished that superhuman deed, set about arranging the marriage of his brother Vicitravīrya, having resolved the matter together with Satyavatī, self-possessed as he was.
As Bhīṣma was arranging the marriage, the eldest daughter of the king of Kāśi, that virtuous woman, then spoke these words:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The lord of Saubha has already been chosen by me in my heart as my husband, and he too had already chosen me — and this was also my father's wish."
"Śālva was to have been chosen by me at that svayamvara. Knowing this, O knower of dharma, do now what is right."
Thus addressed by that maiden in the assembly of brahmins, the heroic Bhīṣma fell into fitting reflection regarding what was to be done in this matter.
Having deliberated with brahmins who had crossed to the further shore of the Vedas, the knower of dharma then gave leave to the eldest, Ambā, daughter of the king of Kāśi.
Bhīṣma gave Ambikā and Ambalika as wives to his younger brother Vicitravīrya according to the rites prescribed by tradition.
Taking the hand of each of them, Vicitravīrya, the righteous-souled one, proud of his beauty and youth, became possessed by desire.
And they too were tall, dark, with blue curling hair, with reddish and prominent nails, and with full hips and breasts —
Certain that they had obtained a husband well-matched to themselves, both honored the auspicious Vicitravīrya.
And he, resembling the Aśvins in beauty, with the valor and spirit of the gods, became a captivator of the hearts of all women.
Sporting with those two for seven years, the young lord of the earth, Vicitravīrya, fell ill with consumption.
Despite the efforts of his friends and trusted physicians, that Kaurava went to Yama's abode like the sun setting.
Acting in accordance with Satyavatī's wishes, Bhīṣma, together with the officiating priests and all the foremost Kurus, duly performed all the funeral rites for King Vicitravīrya.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Satyavatī, sorrowful, pitiable, yearning for a son, having performed the funeral duties for her son together with her daughters-in-law, O Bhārata —
— that honored and greatly blessed woman, reflecting carefully on dharma, the paternal lineage, and the maternal lineage, spoke these words to the son of Gaṅgā:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In you rests the ancestral offering, the fame, and the continuity of Śaṃtanu, the ever-righteous Kaurava of great renown.
As ascent to heaven is assured upon doing virtuous deeds, as life is assured in truth, so dharma is assured in you.
You know the various duties of dharma both in summary and in detail, O knower of dharma; you know the diverse revealed scriptures and all the Vedas in their entirety.
I see in you steadfastness in dharma, adherence to family custom, and conduct in difficult situations like that of Śukra and Aṅgiras.
Therefore, O best of those who uphold dharma, I shall set you, greatly reassured, to a task; hear it and you ought to carry it out.
My son, your brother, the valiant one who was so dear to you, has gone to heaven even as a boy, without a son, O bull among men.
These two queens of your brother, O Bhārata — the fair daughters of the king of Kāśi, endowed with beauty and youth and longing for sons —
— you ought, O greatly blessed one, to beget offspring upon them at my command, for the perpetuation of our lineage; it is your duty to do so here.
Be consecrated in the kingdom, govern the Bhāratas, take wives according to dharma — do not let our ancestors sink down."
Thus addressed by his mother and by his friends, that scorcher of enemies, the righteous-souled one, gave in reply only a righteous answer:
"Without doubt, O mother, you have stated a highest duty; and you know well the supreme vow I took regarding offspring.
You know what happened in your presence for the sake of the bride-price, O Satyavatī; I swear to you the truth again:
I would renounce the three worlds, or a kingdom among the gods, or whatever else might surpass even these — but I would never in any way abandon truth.
The earth might abandon its smell, water might abandon its own taste, fire might abandon its form, wind might abandon its quality of touch —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The sun might cast off its radiance, the comet its heat, space might abandon sound, the moon might cast off its coolness —
The slayer of Vṛtra might abandon his valor, the king of dharma his righteousness — but I could never in any way be resolved to abandon truth."
Thus addressed by her son of immeasurable wealth and brilliance, mother Satyavatī then spoke again to Bhīṣma:
"I know your supreme steadfastness in truth, O you whose valor is your truth; if you wished, you could by your own power create three other worlds.
I know too that what you have spoken is truth, and you spoke it for my sake; but consider the dharma of emergencies — bear the ancestral burden.
Act, O scorcher of foes, in such a way that neither the family line nor dharma may come to ruin, and that your friends may rejoice."
As she lamented thus, pitiable and yearning for a son, speaking what deviated from dharma, Bhīṣma spoke once more to her:
"O queen, look to the laws of dharma — do not lead us all to ruin; departure from truth is not praised in the codes of dharma for a warrior.
I will declare to you, O queen, the eternal warrior dharma by which Śaṃtanu's lineage may endure imperishably on earth.
Having heard it, you should act upon it together with the wise men and the priest, who are skilled in the dharma of emergencies and in practical matters, having regard also for the ways of the world."
Bhīṣma said: O greatly blessed one, by Rāma son of Jamadagni, who could not endure his father's slaying and was consumed with wrath, the lord of the Haihayas was slain, and the thousand arms of Arjuna were hewn off.
And again, taking up his bow and releasing great weapons, conquering the earth with his chariot, he burned the warrior class not just once.
Thus, with various high and low weapons, the great-souled Bhārgava once made the earth devoid of warriors twenty-one times over.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thereupon, coming together from all directions, those warrior-women had children fathered upon them by self-controlled brahmins.
"The son belongs to him who took the hand" — this is established in the Vedas; with that dharma fixed in their minds, those women approached the brahmins; and in the world too this rebirth of the warrior class is seen to have been practiced.
Now, there was in ancient times a wise sage known by the name of Utathya, and his wife was named Mamata, held in the highest esteem.
But Utathya's younger brother, Bṛhaspati, the great-souled, the preceptor of the dwellers in the third heaven, approached Mamata with desire.
Mamata said to that brother-in-law, foremost among speakers: "I am pregnant by my elder brother-in-law; let it rest — do not proceed."
"And this child of mine, O greatly blessed Bṛhaspati, the son of Utathya, is even now in my womb reciting the Veda together with its six ancillaries here."
"Your seed too is never fruitless — you ought indeed to be so; therefore, given all this, you ought today to desist."
Though thus properly addressed by her, the great-souled Bṛhaspati could not restrain his own self, then so given over to desire.
Then he, consumed by desire, lay with her who did not desire it; and as he was releasing his seed, the child in the womb spoke to him.
O father, I speak as the younger: there is no room here for the two of us. You have infallible seed, and I arrived here first.
Thus addressed, Bṛhaspati flew into rage and cursed that one; the venerable seer, rebuking the child of Utathya still in the womb, pronounced his curse.
"Because at such a moment, while a thing desired by all beings was taking place, you have spoken such words, therefore you shall enter into prolonged darkness."
By reason of that curse the sage was born bearing the name Dīrghatamas — of the far-spreading glory of Bṛhaspati, equal to Bṛhaspati himself in brilliance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That illustrious one then begot sons beginning with Gautama, in order to continue the lineage and increase the family of the sage Utathya.
Those sons, Gautama and the rest, overcome by greed and delusion, placed him in a wooden box and cast him into the Gaṅgā.
"This one is blind and old and need not be supported by us" — having thought this, those cruel ones turned and went home.
Then, O king, the blind sage, floating downstream on that raft, drifted through very many lands.
Then a king named Bali, well versed in all duties, saw him as he was sinking, carried near by the current.
The righteous Bali, of true valour, rescued him; and recognizing who he was, that bull among men sought a boon from him — the blessing of sons.
"O greatly fortunate one, O bestower of honour, for the sake of continuing my line, please beget upon my wives sons who are skilled in dharma and artha."
Thus addressed, that splendid sage said "So be it" to him, and the king then sent his own wife Sudeṣṇā to him.
But the queen, deeming him blind and old, did not go herself; instead she sent her own handmaid to that aged one.
In her — a woman of śūdra birth — that self-controlled, righteous sage begot exactly eleven sons, beginning with Kakṣīvat.
Seeing those sons beginning with Kakṣīvat, all engaged in study, the valiant king said to the sage: "These are mine."
"No," said the great sage, declaring: "These are mine alone — Kakṣīvat and the rest were begotten by me upon a woman of śūdra birth."
"Your chief queen Sudeṣṇā, thinking me blind and old, disrespected me, and the foolish woman gave me a śūdra handmaid instead."
Then Bali propitiated that best of sages again, and sent his wife Sudeṣṇā to him once more.
Touching the queen with his limbs, Dīrghatamas then said to her: "A prince of great brilliance and truthful speech shall be born to you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There upon Sudeṣṇā was born the royal sage named Aṅga; and in this way other great bowmen — kṣatriyas — were born on earth through brāhmaṇas.
Born knowing the highest dharma, endowed with valour and great strength — having heard all this, O mother, do here as you wish.
Bhīṣma said: I shall speak once more of a means for the growth of the Bharata lineage and its continuity, O mother — listen as I tell it.
Let some virtuous brāhmaṇa be invited with wealth to beget offspring upon the wives who were Vicitravīrya's fields.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Satyavatī, her voice faltering, spoke these words to Bhīṣma with a slight smile tinged with embarrassment.
"What you say is true, O great-armed one, O Bhārata. Out of trust in you I shall tell you something for the sake of the family's continuity — a matter of such gravity that it cannot remain untold."
"You alone are dharma in our family, you are truth, you are the highest refuge — therefore hear my words and then act accordingly."
"O righteous-souled one, my righteous father had a ferry-boat; in my early youth I used to go there to that crossing."
"Then the foremost upholder of dharma, the supreme sage Parāśara, wise and intent on crossing the Yamunā river, came to the ferry."
"As I was ferrying him across the Yamunā, that best of sages, overcome with desire, approached me and spoke many sweet, coaxing words."
"Fearing his curse and fearing my father, O Bhārata, addressed with requests not easily refused, I did not dare to refuse him."
"He overpowered me, that child, and brought me under his sway by his ascetic power, shrouding the world in darkness right there on the boat, O Bhārata."
"There was once a great fishy smell about me that I found repulsive; removing that, the sage bestowed upon me this pleasing fragrance."
"The sage then said to me: once you have delivered my child, you shall remain a virgin on an island in this very river."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That great sage, the great yogin Pārāśarya, was my son born of a virgin — he has from of old been known as Dvaipāyana."
"He is the venerable sage who, by his austerity, divided the four Vedas and thereby attained the title of Vyāsa in the world, and the name Kṛṣṇa from his dark complexion."
"A speaker of truth, devoted to tranquillity, an ascetic whose sins are burned away — appointed by me and by you, O one of boundless splendour, he will beget auspicious offspring upon your brother's wives."
"For he told me there: 'Remember me when there is a task to be done.' I shall summon him to mind, O great-armed Bhīṣma, if you so wish."
"With your consent, O Bhīṣma, that mighty ascetic will most certainly beget sons upon the wives of Vicitravīrya."
Upon the mention of that great sage, Bhīṣma, joining his palms in reverence, spoke: "One who views the three — dharma, artha, and kāma —
"— artha and its consequences, dharma and its consequences, kāma and its consequences, as well as their opposites separately — and who, having pondered them rightly with his intellect, reaches a decision: that person is truly wise.
"This that you have proposed is both in accord with dharma and beneficial to our family; what you have declared as the highest good pleases me well."
Then, when Bhīṣma had given his consent, O joy of the Kurus, Kālī called the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana to mind.
That wise one, who was expounding the Vedas, perceived his mother's thought and appeared before her instantly and unannounced, O joy of the Kurus.
She then offered proper worship to her son, embraced him with both arms, sprinkled him with tears, and the daughter of the fisherman shed tears seeing that son after so long.
Sprinkling her with water and saluting her, the great sage Vyāsa — the elder-born son — addressed his grieving mother.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I have come to do whatever you intend. Command me, O you who know the true nature of dharma — I shall do what is dear to you."
Then the chief priest performed worship for that supreme sage, and he received it duly, with the proper rites and mantras.
With him seated, his mother enquired after his welfare; then Satyavatī, gazing at him, spoke the following words.
"Sons are born alike of both mother and father, O sage; as a father is their master, so too is a mother — of this there is no doubt."
"Ordained by the Creator, you are my first son; Vicitravīrya is my younger son — so too, O brahmarṣi."
"Just as Bhīṣma is Vicitravīrya's brother through the father, so are you through the mother — or consider it however you will, my son."
"This Śāntanava, maintaining his vow and of true valour, forms no resolve regarding offspring nor indeed regarding the governance of the kingdom."
"You, then, out of regard for your brother, for the continuity of the family, at the word and commission of this Bhīṣma, and at my bidding — O sinless one —
"— and out of compassion for all beings and for their protection, out of gentleness — what I tell you, you ought to hear and act upon."
"Your younger brother's wives — comparable to daughters of the gods, endowed with beauty and youth, and desirous of sons by dharma —
"— upon those two you are capable of begetting offspring, my son, fitting for this lineage, for its continuation and for its progeny."
Vyāsa said: You know dharma, O Satyavatī, both the higher and the lower, and how your mind, O knower of dharma, is set upon dharma.
"Therefore, appointed by you and keeping dharma as my purpose, I shall do what you desire — for this has been seen as the ancient practice."
"I shall give sons to your brother comparable to Mitra and Varuṇa — but let those queens observe the vow I prescribe here."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"They shall observe it properly for one year; then they will be purified. For no woman without the vow may approach me."
Satyavatī said: Arrange it so that the queen may conceive forthwith. In a kingless realm there is no rain, no deities.
"How can a kingless kingdom be sustained, O lord? Therefore plant the seed at once; Bhīṣma will nurture the child."
Vyāsa said: If a son is to be given by me swiftly, out of season, then let her endure my ugliness — that is the supreme vow required of her.
"If she can endure my smell, my form, my dress, and my body, then let Kausalyā conceive an excellent child this very day."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having said this in anticipation of the union, the sage vanished. Then she, the queen, approached her daughter-in-law in private and spoke words that were righteous, purposeful, and beneficial.
"O Kausalyā, understand what I tell you concerning the thread of dharma. The extinction of the Bhāratas has clearly come about through the waning of my fortune."
"Seeing me in anguish and the paternal lineage afflicted, Bhīṣma gave me counsel in this matter for the increase of dharma."
"That counsel depends on you, my daughter — know this. Raise up once more the Bharata lineage that has perished."
"Bear a son, O fair-hipped one, equal in splendour to the king of the gods; for he shall carry the heavy yoke of kingship for our family."
She somehow persuaded that righteous woman by appealing to dharma, and caused brāhmaṇas, divine sages, and guests to be fed.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then at the proper time Satyavatī, having settled her daughter-in-law — bathed at the end of her period — upon the bed, gently spoke these words.
"O Kausalyā, you have a brother-in-law; he will enter your chamber this night. Remain vigilant and await him — he will come at midnight."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing her mother-in-law's words, she lay upon the auspicious bed and thought of Bhīṣma and of the other bulls of the Kuru line.
Then the truth-speaking sage, appointed first to Ambikā, entered the bedchamber while the lamps were burning brightly.
Seeing his dark form, his reddish matted locks, his blazing eyes, and his tawny beard, the queen shut her eyes.
That night the daughter of the Kāśi king, wishing to please her mother-in-law yet seized by fear, could not bring herself to look at him.
When he had departed, the mother went to her son and asked: "My son, will a prince of good qualities be born to her?"
Hearing his mother's words, Vyāsa of supreme intelligence — knowing what transcends the senses, impelled by fate — spoke.
"He shall be born with the strength of ten thousand elephants, a man of learning, the best of royal sages, of great fortune, great valour, and great intelligence."
"He shall have a hundred sons, all of great strength — but owing to the failing of his mother, he himself will be blind."
Hearing those words of his, the mother then spoke to her son: 'A blind man is not a fitting king of the Kurus, O ascetic treasure.'
'You ought to give us another king — a protector of the kinsmen's lineage, an increaser of the ancestral line, a second king of the Kuru dynasty.'
He of great austerity promised 'So be it' and departed. And in time Kausalyā gave birth to that blind son.
But that blameless lady Satyavatī then instructed her daughter-in-law again and summoned the seer just as before.
Then the great seer approached her by the same method. He came to Ambālikā, and she, upon seeing the seer, turned pale as a corpse, crestfallen, O Bhārata.
Seeing her frightened, pale as a corpse, and despondent, O king, Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, spoke these words:
'Because you turned pale upon seeing my hideous form, therefore this son of yours shall be named Pāṇḍu — pale indeed.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'And that very name shall be his in this world, O fair-faced one.' Having spoken thus, the blessed best of sages departed.
Then Satyā, watching him depart, spoke to her son. He again reported to his mother the paleness of that child.
The mother begged him once more for yet another son. And the great seer replied to that mother, 'So be it.'
Then in due time that princess gave birth to the boy Pāṇḍu, endowed with auspicious marks and blazing with glory. From him were born the five Pāṇḍavas, mighty archers all.
Then at the fertile season she assigned the eldest daughter-in-law to him again. But that one, like the daughter of a god, reflecting on the seer’s appearance and smell, refused the queen's command out of fear.
Then the daughter of the king of Kāśī adorned a maidservant with her own ornaments, making her like an apsaras, and sent her to Kṛṣṇa (Vyāsa).
The maidservant went forward to meet the seer as he arrived, greeted him reverently, and, given leave, lay with him and attended him with great care.
The seer found satisfaction in pleasure with her; the great seer passed the night dwelling with her, who was joyful.
As he rose he said to her: 'You shall no longer be a slave. And this glorious child that has entered your womb, O auspicious one, shall be foremost among all the wise in the world, righteous in soul.'
He was born and was named Vidura — son of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, brother of both Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, of boundless intelligence.
Dharma himself, by the curse of that great-souled Māṇḍavya, was born in the form of Vidura — knowing the truth of meaning, free from desire and anger.
Having discharged his debt to Dharma, he (Vyāsa) came once more to his mother and informed her of the birth, then vanished there and then.
Thus, in the field of Vicitravīrya, even from Dvaipāyana were born those who shone like the offspring of gods, the increasers of the Kuru lineage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Janamejaya said: 'What deed did Dharma commit by which he incurred a curse? And by whose curse, O Brahmā-seer, was he born in a śūdra womb?'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: 'There was a certain brahmin renowned as Māṇḍavya — steadfast, knowing all dharma, abiding in truth and austerity.'
He of great austerity stood at the gate of his hermitage at the root of a tree, arms raised, a great yogī, observing the vow of silence.
After a long time, while he stood thus in austerity, some robbers carrying stolen goods arrived at that hermitage, pursued by many guards, O bull of the Bhāratas.
They hid the plunder in his dwelling, O best of Kurus, and, having hidden it, crouched in concealment there when the troops arrived in pursuit.
With the thieves thus hidden, the force of those guards quickly came there, and those trackers of thieves caught sight of that seer.
Then, O king, they questioned that treasure of austerity standing there: 'By which path did the robbers go, O best of twice-born? By that path, O brahmin, let us go with all speed.'
But that treasure of austerity, O king, though the guards were speaking thus, said not a word, neither good nor bad.
Then those royal servants, searching through that hermitage, found the thieves hidden there, along with the goods themselves.
Suspicion then arose among the guards against that sage; they bound him along with the thieves and reported everything to the king.
The king ordered him to be executed along with those thieves. And that one of great austerity, unrecognised, was impaled upon a spike by the executioners.
Then those guards, having raised that sage on the spike, went back to the king, taking those goods with them.
But that righteous soul, though impaled upon the spike, for a long time — without food, even — did not meet death, O brahmin-seer; he sustained his life-breath and drew other sages to him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Through the austerity being performed by that great-souled one on the tip of the spike, the sages were overwhelmed with extreme distress, O scorcher of foes.
They became birds at night and gathered round from every side, showing themselves as best they could, and questioned that best of twice-born: 'We wish to hear, O brahmin, what sin you have committed.'
Then that tiger among sages replied to those treasures of austerity: 'To what fault shall I trace it? For truly no other has wronged me.'
And the king, hearing of that seer, came out with his ministers and then sought to propitiate that best of sages mounted on the spike.
'Whatever wrong I did to you out of delusion and ignorance, O best of sages, I beg your forgiveness for that; you ought not be angry with me.'
Addressed thus by the king, the sage showed grace. When he had received grace, the king then had him brought down from the spike.
Having brought him down from the spike's tip, they tried to pull out the spike. Being unable to extract it fully, they cut it at the base.
That sage moved about with the spike still lodged inside him. By that austerity he conquered worlds difficult for others to attain. From then on he is known in the worlds as Aṇīmāṇḍavya — Spike-Māṇḍavya.
That brahmin, knowing the supreme truth, went to the abode of Dharma and, seeing Dharma seated there, reproached him, that powerful one.
'What evil deed was done by me unknowingly, whose fruit has been visited upon me in such a way? Tell me the truth quickly — see the power of my austerity.'
Dharma said: 'You once inserted straws into the tails of insects — the fruit of that deed has fallen upon you, O treasure of austerity.'
Aṇīmāṇḍavya said: 'For a trifling offence you have imposed a heavy punishment on me. Therefore, Dharma, you shall be born among men in a śūdra womb.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'I now establish this rule for the world regarding the arising of dharma's fruit: up to the fourteenth year of life there shall be no sin for those who do such things; beyond that it shall indeed be a transgression.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: 'It was by this offence, by the curse of that great-souled one, that Dharma was born in a śūdra womb in the form of Vidura.'
Skilled in dharma and artha, free from greed and anger, far-sighted, devoted to tranquillity, and ever engaged in the welfare of the Kurus.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: 'When those three princes were born, these three — Kuru-jāṅgala, the Kuru land, and Kuru-kṣetra — all flourished.'
The earth bore crops standing tall; the harvests were fruitful; the rain-cloud rained according to the seasons; the trees were laden with many flowers and fruits.
The beasts of burden were exhilarated; the deer and birds were joyful; the garlands were fragrant; the fruits were full of flavour.
The cities were filled with merchants and artisans; the brave, the learned, and the virtuous all lived happily.
There were no robbers, no people inclined to adharma; even in the outlying regions of the realm the Kṛta age prevailed.
The people, devoted to giving, righteous action, and dharma, intent on sacrifices and vows, bound to one another with affection, thrived in that time.
People were free from pride and anger, rid of greed; they flourished with one another; dharma reigned supreme.
That city shone, full like a great ocean, adorned with gateways, arches, and turrets like heaped clouds, crowded with hundreds of palaces, resembling the city of great Indra.
People sported joyfully along rivers, in groves, on the banks of ponds and pools, and in pleasant forests.
The southern Kurus then ranged about rivalling the northern Kurus and also the Siddhas, sages, and Cāraṇas. There was no wretch, and women were not widowed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In that lovely land many wells, parks, assembly halls, ponds, and brahmin dwellings were built by the Kurus, and everything was guarded on all sides according to the śāstra by Bhīṣma, O king.
That land was lovely, marked with hundreds of shrines and sacrificial posts, enlarged by the incorporation of neighbouring kingdoms; the wheel of dharma ordained by Bhīṣma turned in the realm.
As the rites for those great-souled princes were being performed, all the citizens and country-folk were in a state of perpetual festival.
In the houses of the leading Kurus and of the townspeople, O lord of men, the words 'Give! Eat!' were heard everywhere.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and the great-minded Vidura were all cared for from birth by Bhīṣma as though they were his own sons.
Consecrated with all rites, engaged in vows and Vedic study, skilled in exertion and exercise, they came to youth.
They became proficient in the science of archery, riding on horseback, fighting with the mace and sword-and-shield, likewise in the training of elephants, and in the science of statecraft.
In histories and purāṇas, in various branches of learning, O lord, knowing the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences — they applied themselves diligently in all.
Pāṇḍu was surpassingly valiant with the bow, excelling all men; Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the earth, was stronger than all others.
In all three worlds there was none equal to Vidura; ever fixed in dharma, O king, he had attained the highest in matters of dharma.
Seeing the line of Śaṃtanu, which had seemed lost, once more restored, this saying then spread through the world and all its kingdoms:
'Of lands for the sons of heroes, Kuru-jāṅgala; of daughters of Kāśī for knowledge of all dharma; of ancient cities, the Elephant-named city (Hāstinapura) — Bhīṣma has established all these.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not obtain the kingdom on account of his blindness; and Vidura because he was born of a servant woman; Pāṇḍu became lord of the earth.
Bhīṣma said: 'This family of ours, renowned and properly furnished with all virtues, holds sovereignty over the earth above all other kings of the earth.'
'Protected by kings of old, those great souls who knew dharma, never at any time has our family come to ruin here.'
'By me and by Satyavatī, and by the great-souled Kṛṣṇa (Vyāsa), it has been established once more in you, the threads of the lineage.'
'This family grows, my son, like the ocean. So it must be furthered by me and especially by you.'
'It is heard that a Yādava princess suitable for our family, and likewise the daughter of Subala and the daughter of the lord of Madra —'
'— are well-born, beautiful, and possessed of worthy guardians in every way; they are fitting for alliance with us, those bulls among kṣatriyas.'
'I think those women should be sought in marriage for the continuation of this family — O best of the wise, or else what do you think, Vidura?'
Vidura said: 'You are our father, you are our mother, you are our supreme teacher. Therefore deliberate yourself and do what is beneficial for this family.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then from brahmins he (Bhīṣma) heard of Gāndhārī, daughter of Subala — that she had propitiated the god who grants boons, Hara the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, and that the auspicious Gāndhārī had obtained a boon of a hundred sons.
Having truly heard this, Bhīṣma, the grandsire of the Kurus, thereupon dispatched a messenger to the king of Gāndhāra, O Bhārata.
There was hesitation on the part of Subala on account of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's blindness; but weighing carefully with his intellect the family, the fame, and the conduct of the Kurus, he gave Gāndhārī, that virtuous woman, to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Gāndhārī too had heard that Dhṛtarāṣṭra was blind and that she was being given to him by her father and mother, O Bhārata.
Then that auspicious woman, devoted to her vow of fidelity to her husband, resolved that she would not surpass her lord; she took a strip of cloth, folded it many times, and bound it over her own eyes, O king.
Then Śakuni, son of the king of Gāndhāra, came bringing his sister, endowed with great beauty, to the Kauravas.
That hero, having given his sister along with fitting gifts and apparel, returned to his own city, having been honored by Bhīṣma.
Gāndhārī too, that most excellent woman, through her conduct, deportment, and behavior, gave satisfaction to all the Kurus, O Bhārata.
Devoted to her vow of chastity, she propitiated them all by her conduct; and firm in her vow, she never praised even in speech any other man.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was a foremost of the Yadus named Śūra who was the father of Vāsudeva; he had a daughter named Pṛthā, unequaled in beauty on earth.
That mighty hero, having first made a solemn promise to his father's sister's son who was childless, gave to him the first-born of his own offspring.
He gave that first-born daughter, whom he had pledged as the foremost gift, to Kuntibhoja, his great-souled friend — given friend to friend.
She, appointed in her father's house to the service of gods and guests, attended with devotion a fierce and terrible Brahmin of intense austerity.
Him of deep resolve in righteousness, whom they know as Durvāsā — that fierce one of sharpened spirit — she pleased by every effort.
Considering the dharma applicable in times of difficulty, he gave her a mantra endowed with power to summon, and the sage spoke thus to her.
Whichever deity you invoke with this mantra, by that deity's favor a son shall be born to you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed by that Brahmin, that virtuous and glorious maiden, out of curiosity, then invoked the sun-god Arka.
She saw the sun, the illuminator of worlds, coming toward her; that woman of flawless limbs was filled with wonder upon beholding that great marvel.
Then the sun, whose work is to shine, placed his seed in her; she thereupon gave birth to a hero, the foremost of all who bear weapons — born already wearing his armor, splendid, divine in origin, and invested with radiance.
Bearing his natural armor and with his face lit by his earrings, was born the son Karṇa, renowned in all the worlds.
That most resplendent one, best among givers, restored her maidenhood to her, and having given thus, ascended to heaven.
Concealing that transgression out of fear of her kinsmen, Kuntī then cast that auspiciously marked infant into the water.
That abandoned child was then adopted as a son by the greatly renowned husband of Rādhā, a son of a suta, together with his wife.
Those two gave a name to that infant: "Since he was born along with wealth, let him be called Vasuṣeṇa."
Growing up and becoming powerful, he applied himself to all weapons; that mighty hero would stand in worship of the sun until the heat touched his back.
At the time when that hero of truthful pledge sat muttering prayers, there was nothing that this great-souled one would refuse to give to Brahmins.
Indra, the nourisher of all beings and of great splendor, taking the form of a Brahmin, approached him as a suppliant and begged for his earrings and his armor.
Karṇa, though pained, cut off from his own body his armor dripping with blood, and severing his earrings, gave them with joined palms.
Śakra, astonished, gave him the Śakti weapon and said: "Among gods, asuras, men, gandharvas, serpents, and rakshasas — at whomever you hurl this in anger, he shall be no more."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His former name had been known as Vasuṣeṇa; thereafter by that deed he became Vaikartana Karṇa — the cutter of his own flesh.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The daughter of Kuntibhoja, endowed with beauty, valor, and virtue, devoted to righteousness and of great vows, was presented by her father at a swayamvara.
She chose Pāṇḍu — lion-fanged, elephant-shouldered, bull-eyed, and of great might — from among thousands of kings.
That joy of the Kurus, of immeasurable good fortune, was united with her, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, as Maghavan was united with Paulomī.
By Devavrata's going also to the capital of the Madras, Mādrī, daughter of the lord of the Madras, renowned in the three worlds, was obtained.
She was celebrated among all kings and unequaled in beauty on earth; she was purchased for Pāṇḍu's sake with great wealth, and then Bhīṣma caused the marriage of the great-souled Pāṇḍu.
Seeing Pāṇḍu — lion-chested, elephant-shouldered, bull-eyed, high-minded, that tiger among men — people on earth were filled with wonder.
Then Pāṇḍu, having wed, endowed with strength and enthusiasm, desiring to conquer the earth, went against enemies on many fronts.
Going first against those who had given offence, the Daśārṇas were conquered in battle by Pāṇḍu, that lion among men, the bearer of the Kauravas' glory.
Then Pāṇḍu, taking an army bearing banners of many kinds, rich in elephants, horses, and chariots, and teeming with masses of foot-soldiers —
— the foe of all heroes, the adversary of all lords of the earth: Darva, the protector of the Magadha realm, was slain at Rājagṛha.
Then, after taking treasury, conveyances, and forces, Pāṇḍu marched to Mithilā and conquered the Videhas in battle.
Likewise among the Kāśis, the Suhmas, and the Puṇḍras, O bull of the Bhāratas, by the strength and valor of his own arms he brought glory to the Kurus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Coming against him — that tamer of foes blazing like a great fire with showers of arrows and flames of weapons, that Pāṇḍu-conflagration — kings were burned up.
Those kings, their forces shattered by Pāṇḍu and his forces, were brought into submission and assigned to the works of tribute.
By him all those kings of the earth were vanquished; they regarded him alone as the great hero, as the gods regard Purandara.
All those lords of the earth came to him with joined palms, bowing low, bearing wealth and various jewels.
Gems, pearls, and coral, gold and silver, choice cattle, choice horses, choice chariots, and elephants —
— and donkeys, camels, and buffaloes, and whatever sheep and goats there were — all this the king, the lord of Hāstinapura, accepted.
Taking all that, Pāṇḍu set out again with his army rejoicing, intending to gladden his own kingdom and the city of Hāstinapura.
The fame born of glory that had been lost to Śaṃtanu, that lion among kings, and to the wise Bharata, was raised up again by Pāṇḍu.
Those who had formerly seized the Kuru kingdoms and the wealth of the Kurus were made tribute-paying by Pāṇḍu, the lion of Hāstinapura.
So spoke the assembled kings and their ministers, their minds filled with satisfaction and joy, together with the townspeople and country folk.
All went forth to meet him on his arrival, led by Bhīṣma; those dwellers of Hāstinapura, going as if the road were not far, saw joyfully that the whole world was thronged with many kinds of people.
With jewels of high and low quality brought on various vehicles, with choice elephants, horses, and chariots, with cattle, camels, and sheep — the Kauravas together with Bhīṣma, coming upon it all, could see no end to it.
He, the increaser of Kausalyā's joy, paid reverence to his father's feet, and duly honored the townspeople and country folk as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma, meeting his son who had returned fulfilled in purpose after crushing enemy kingdoms, shed tears of joy.
To the great sounds of hundreds of musical instruments and kettledrums, gladdening the citizens on all sides, he entered Hāstinapura.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: With Dhṛtarāṣṭra's permission, he presented the wealth conquered by his own arms to Bhīṣma, to Satyavatī, and to his mother.
Pāṇḍu also sent that wealth to Vidura; and that righteous soul fully satisfied his friends with treasure.
Then Bhīṣma satisfied Satyavatī and the glorious Kausalyā with auspicious jewels won by Pāṇḍu, O Bhārata.
His mother Kausalyā rejoiced, embracing that bull among men of matchless splendor, even as Paulomī embraces the victorious Jayanta.
With the conquests of that hero, Dhṛtarāṣṭra performed a hundred horse-sacrifices — great rites with hundreds of thousands in sacrificial gifts.
Joined together with Kuntī and with Mādrī, O bull of the Bhāratas, Pāṇḍu, free from sloth, then became a wanderer of the forests.
Abandoning his palace dwelling and his fine beds, he became constantly given to forest life, ever devoted to the hunt.
Roaming the lovely southern slopes of the Himālayan mountain, he dwelt on mountain ridges and in forests of great shala trees.
Pāṇḍu shone in the forest dwelling together with Kuntī and Mādrī, like the splendid elephant of Purandara standing between two she-elephants.
The forest dwellers, seeing that Bhārata king roaming with his two wives, bearing arrows, sword, and bow, wearing varied armor, a hero and master of weapons supreme, thought him a god.
Men, ever diligent and urged on by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, brought constantly to the forest his desires and enjoyments.
Then the son of the Gaṅgā heard of a Pāraśava maiden, daughter of King Devaka, endowed with beauty and youth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then that bull among men, having wooed and brought her, caused the marriage of the great-minded Vidura.
And Vidura, the joy of the Kurus, begot upon her sons possessed of good breeding, equal to himself in qualities.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O Janamejaya, a hundred sons were born to Dhṛtarāṣṭra through Gāndhārī, and one more beyond the hundred through a Vaiśya woman.
To Pāṇḍu through Kuntī and through Mādrī were born five great warriors, obtained from the gods for the continuation of the family line.
Janamejaya said: How were a hundred sons born to Gāndhārī, O best of twice-born? And in how much time? And what was their highest lifespan?
How did that one son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra come to be through the Vaiśya woman? And how did Dhṛtarāṣṭra transgress against Gāndhārī his wife — a woman of righteous conduct equal to himself, living in devotion to him?
And how, from Pāṇḍu who had been cursed by that great soul, were born five sons, great warriors, from the gods?
Knowing all this as it happened, tell it in full, O wealth of austerity; I am not satisfied when my kinsmen are being told of.
