Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Gāndhārī satisfied Dvaipāyana when he came, worn out by hunger and fatigue; and Vyāsa gave her a boon.
She chose a hundred sons equal to her husband and herself; then in time she conceived through Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Gāndhārī, childless, bore that planted embryo for two full years; then sorrow overtook her.
Hearing that a son of Kuntī had been born, blazing in splendor like the morning sun, she reflected upon the steadfastness of her own womb.
Unknown to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with great effort and then faint with grief, Gāndhārī caused her own foetus — her very womb-child — to miscarry.
Then there issued forth a mass of flesh, hard as an iron ball, that had been carried in the womb for two full years; she set about expelling it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Dvaipāyana, having learned of this by his insight, came swiftly; that best of murmurers of mantras beheld the fleshy mass.
Then he said to the daughter of Subala: 'What is it you intend to do?' And she truthfully disclosed her own intention to that supreme seer.
'Having heard that Kuntī's eldest son was born, radiant as the sun, I caused this womb to be expelled by me out of extreme grief.'
'And indeed a hundred sons were granted to me by you before; yet this mass of flesh has been born — truly, as the gift of a hundred sons.'
Vyāsa said: 'So it shall be, O daughter of Subala — this can never be otherwise. I have never spoken falsely, not even in jest; how then could it be otherwise?'
'Let a hundred pots filled with clarified butter be prepared at once, and sprinkle this solid lump with cold water.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As that solid lump was being sprinkled, it split into a hundred portions at once — each being a separate embryo of the size of a thumb-joint.
One hundred and one in full number, O lord of the people — thus, O king, from that mass of flesh, each appeared in due order as time passed.
Then he placed those embryos each in its own pot, in well-guarded places, and thereafter arranged their protection.
And the blessed one also instructed the daughter of Subala: 'These pots are to be opened again only after this much time has elapsed.'
Having said this and having made all the arrangements, the blessed and wise Vyāsa departed for austerities to the Himālaya, that mountain of rocks.
Through this process, Duryodhana came to be born as the king among them; yet by birth reckoning, the elder king is Yudhiṣṭhira.
The very moment that son was born, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having summoned many Brāhmaṇas and also Bhīṣma and Vidura, spoke thus.
'Yudhiṣṭhira, the elder prince and increaser of our lineage, has attained the kingdom by his own merit — we have nothing to say against him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'But will this one, next after him, also become king? Tell me truly what shall certainly come to pass in this matter.'
At the end of these words, O Bhārata, in all directions terrifying flesh-eating creatures cried out, and jackals howled their ill omens.
Having observed those dreadful portents on every side, O king, the Brāhmaṇas spoke, as did the great-minded Vidura.
'Clearly this son of yours shall be the destroyer of the lineage. Peace lies in his abandonment; to keep him thriving is a great wrong.'
'Let your sons number one fewer than a hundred, O lord of the earth — secure the welfare of the world and of the lineage through that one act.'
'One should abandon one person for the sake of the family; abandon a family for the sake of a village; abandon a village for the sake of a kingdom; abandon the earth for the sake of the Self.'
Though thus advised by Vidura and by all those foremost twice-born, the king did not act accordingly, overcome as he was by affection for his son.
Then all one hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O king, were born within the space of a single month, and one daughter in addition to the hundred.
While Gāndhārī was afflicted by her ever-growing womb, a Vaiśyā woman it is said attended upon the mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
In that same year, O king, the greatly renowned and wise Yuyutsu — a Kāraṇa — was born from her by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O ruler of men.
Thus were born the hundred sons of the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra — all mighty warriors and heroes — and one daughter, Duḥśalā.
Janamejaya said: 'O master, recite in order the names and the seniority — eldest to youngest — of those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: 'Duryodhana, Yuyutsu, and also Duḥśāsana, O king; Duḥsaha, Duḥśalā, Jalasaṃdha, Sama, and Saha —
Vinda and Anuvinda, Durdharṣa, Subāhu, Duṣpradharṣaṇa, Durmarṣaṇa, Durmukha, Duṣkarṇa, and also Karṇa —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Viviṃśati, Vikarṇa, Jalasaṃdha, Sulocana, Citra and Upacitra, Citrākṣa, Ārucitra, and Śarāsana —
Durmada, Duṣpragāha, Vivityu, Vikaṭa, Sama, Ūrṇanābha, Sunābha, and likewise Nanda and Upanandaka —
Senāpati, Suṣeṇa, Kuṇḍodara, Mahodara, Citrabāṇa, Citravarmā, Suvarmā, and Durvimocana —
Ayobāhu, Mahābāhu, Citrāṅga, Citrakuṇḍala, Bhīmavega, Bhīmabala, Balākī, and Balavardhana —
Ugrāyudha, Bhīmakarman, Kanakāyu, Dṛḍhāyudha, Dṛḍhavarmā, Dṛḍhakṣatra, Somakīrti, and Anūdara —
Dṛḍhasaṃdha, Jarāsaṃdha, Satyasaṃdha, Sadaḥsuvāk, Ugraśravā, Aśvasena, Senānī, and Duṣparājaya —
Aparājita, Paṇḍitaka, Viśālākṣa, Durāvara, Dṛḍhahasta, Suhasta, and the pair Vātavega and Suvarcas —
Ādityaketu, Bahvāśī, Nāgadanta and Ugrayāyin, Kavacī, Niṣaṅgī, Pāśī, Daṇḍadhāra, and Dhanurgraha —
Ugra, Bhīmaratha, Vīra, Vīrabāhu, Alolupa, Abhaya, Raudrakarman, and likewise three others including Dṛḍharatha —
Anādhṛṣya, Kuṇḍabhedī, Virāvī, Dīrghalocana, Dīrghabāhu, Mahābāhu, Vyūḍhoru, and Kanakadhvaja —
Kuṇḍāśī and Virajā — and Duḥśalā as the one beyond the hundred. This is the full one hundred and one, O king, with one daughter named as well.'
'Know the order of birth by the sequence of names, O king. All were atiratha warriors, all heroes, all skilled in battle.
All were knowers of the Vedas and versed in the science of kingship; all excelled in the arts of association, adorned by learning and noble birth.
Wives befitting every one of them were secured, O lord of the earth, by Dhṛtarāṣṭra in due season, having considered carefully and according to proper rites.
At the proper time, O Bhārata, the king gave Duḥśalā to the king of Sindhu, Jayadratha, with the consent of the Subala line.'
Janamejaya said: 'The supernal and extraordinary origin of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — transcending the human even among humans — has been narrated by you, O best of those who know Brahman.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Their names too, spoken portion by portion, have been heard by me from you, O Brāhmaṇa. Now recite the birth of the Pāṇḍavas.'
'For all of them are great-souled, with the valour of the king of the gods; they themselves were declared by you to be divine portions descended in the chapter on the descent of the divine shares.'
'Therefore I wish to hear all about the origin of those whose deeds surpass the human. Recite it fully, O Vaiśaṃpāyana.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: King Pāṇḍu, in a great forest frequented by deer and serpents, came upon the leader of a deer herd at the time of its mating.
Then Pāṇḍu pierced both the doe and that stag with five swift, sharp arrows feathered with gold-tipped shafts.
And that one, O king, was in truth a great-spirited son of a seer, rich in austerity, a radiant being who had joined with his wife in the form of a deer.
While still locked together with that doe, uttering human speech, he fell to the ground in an instant and lamented, his senses distraught.
The deer said: 'Even men overcome by desire and anger, even those bereft of the limb of reason, even those addicted to sin — they shun acts of cruelty.
'Wisdom does not swallow fate, but fate swallows wisdom; wisdom does not comprehend those ends that have been overturned by fate.
'Born in the foremost lineage of those ever devoted to righteousness, O Bhārata — how has your mind been swayed, overpowered by desire and greed?'
Pāṇḍu said: 'The same conduct that applies to the slaying of enemies is held to apply to the slaying of deer for kings, O deer — you ought not, out of confusion, reproach me.'
'The slaying of deer without disguise and without deceit is indeed desired; that very conduct is the duty of kings — knowing this, why do you reproach me?'
'The sage Agastya, while seated at a sacrifice, went out to hunt; having consecrated all the forest-dwelling, divinity-dwelling deer in the great forest —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'— according to the dharma seen in scripture, how do you reproach us? Through the oblation-rite of Agastya, your very fat was indeed offered as an oblation.'
The deer said: 'Formerly arrows were not released aiming at enemies in the midst of this act — indeed it is the finding of their vulnerable moment that is especially praised as the time of slaying.
Pāṇḍu said: 'Whether heedless or heedful, whether exposed or concealed — kings slay powerfully, by stratagems and with sharp arrows. Why then do you reproach me, O deer?'
The deer said: 'I do not reproach you for slaying deer, O king, on my own account — but the act of mating should have been awaited by you here, out of non-cruelty.'
'At a time cherished and desired by all beings — what wise man would slay a deer engaged in mating in the forest? The dear fruit of the aims of man — that beloved thing you have made fruitless.'
'Born in the lineage of the Paurava kings and of those sages of effortless deeds, O Kauravya — this is not fitting for you.
'This deed is exceedingly cruel, condemned by all the world, non-conducive to heaven, destructive to fame, and most unrighteous, O Bhārata.
'A connoisseur of the pleasures of women, a knower of the true nature of the dharma and artha of the scriptures — you who are like a god should not perform such a deed that shuts the door to heaven.'
'By you, O best of kings, those humans who commit cruelty and evil conduct, who are devoid of the three aims of life, ought to be suppressed — not emulated.'
'What have you done, O best of men, in slaying me, innocent as I am — a sage subsisting on roots and fruits, wearing the form of a deer, O king, ever dwelling in the forests, wholly devoted to tranquillity?'
'Because you have injured me, therefore to you as well, without doubt — you who have acted cruelly toward both of us, who acted helplessly, deluded by desire — the end of life will come in this very same manner.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'For I am the sage Kiṃdama by name, without equal in austerity; being ashamed before humans, I was engaged in mating with my doe.'
'Having become a deer, I roam in the dense forest with other deer. Yet this shall not be a brahminicide for you, since you did not know you were slaying me who had taken the form of a deer, deluded thus by desire.'
'But you, O fool, shall reap a fruit exactly like this — when you, deluded by desire, are together with your beloved wife, you too in that very condition shall pass to the realm of the dead.'
'And the beloved one with whom you shall pass to the realm of Yama, king of the dead — that realm irresistible to all beings — she, out of devotion, O best of the wise, shall follow you there.'
'Just as I, in the midst of happiness, have been brought to grief by you — so grief shall come upon you when happiness has arrived.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, afflicted with the greatest pain, that deer was parted from life; and Pāṇḍu too was struck with grief in an instant.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The king, having stepped past that one who had passed away as though it were his own kinsman, together with his wife, afflicted with sorrow and grief, lamented in anguish.
Pāṇḍu said: 'Alas — even those born in noble lineages reach misfortune through their deeds, those who have not mastered the self, deluded by the snare of desire.
'My father, though born of one ever devoted to righteousness, even as a young man met his end — enslaved by desire, so we have heard.
'In the field of that desire-enslaved king, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana — the blessed one himself, restrained of speech — begot me directly.'
Now in his calamity this vile resolve has arisen in me — that of one abandoned by the gods through wickedness, a wicked-souled man cast off on the hunt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I resolve upon liberation alone, for bondage is a great affliction. I shall follow that imperishable good conduct of my father, and without any doubt I shall engage myself in the most intense austerities.
Therefore, alone, day by day, going from one forest tree to the next, begging alms as a shaven-headed sage, I shall wander over this earth.
Covered with dust, taking shelter in empty dwellings or making my abode at the roots of trees, having abandoned all that is dear and all that is not dear.
Neither grieving nor rejoicing, treating censure and self-praise as equal, without desire, without bowing to any, free from all pairs of opposites, possessing nothing.
Never mocking anyone, never knitting the brow at any time, ever serene of countenance, always devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Doing no harm to all four kinds of living beings, moving and stationary, always equal toward all that breathes as toward one's own offspring.
Begging alms only at one time of day, visiting two or five households, and when alms are not obtained, practicing fasts as well.
Little by little, eating only what is fit to eat, sometimes subsisting on what was obtained before, never exceeding proper measure, filling up seven bites whether gaining or not gaining.
If one hacks at one arm with an adze and anoints the other with sandalwood paste, harboring neither ill will nor good will toward either of those two persons.
Acting neither as one who desires to live nor as one who desires to die, neither welcoming nor hating death and life.
Passing beyond all the prospering actions that can be performed by a living being, remaining established in acts as slight as the blinking of an eye.
In all those states, having abandoned all activity of the senses, having wholly relinquished the sense of a dharmic self, with the impurities of the self fully cleansed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Liberated from all sins, having passed beyond all snares, not standing under anyone's sway, sharing the nature of the wind.
Wandering continually with this way of life, of such a character, I shall sustain the body, having entered upon the fearless path.
I will not delight in the path followed by a dog, fit only for the feeble and pitiable, perpetually straying from one's own duty, bereft of virility.
He who, whether honored or dishonored, approaches another livelihood with a miserable eye, driven by desire — he walks the path of dogs.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the king, afflicted with great grief, sighing deeply, looking at Kuntī and Mādrī, addressed them.
Kausalyā, Vidura the Kṣattṛ, the king together with his kinsmen, the venerable Satyavatī, Bhīṣma, and the royal priests —
And the great-souled Brāhmaṇas, drinkers of soma, of sharpened vows, and the elders of the Pauravas who dwell there under our protection — all of them are to be propitiated and told: Pāṇḍu has gone forth to the forest.
Having heard the words of their husband whose mind was resolved upon forest-dwelling, Kuntī and Mādrī both spoke words equal to his own.
O bull of the Bhāratas, there are also other ashramas that are possible; if we, your two lawful wives, perform great austerities together with you, you will assuredly be rewarded — even as regards heaven, there is no doubt.
Restraining the entire host of our senses, devoted to the world of our husband, having abandoned the pleasures of desire, we two shall practice abundant austerity.
O greatly wise one, O lord of men, if you abandon us two, this very day we two shall abandon life — of this there is no doubt.
Pāṇḍu said: If this resolve of yours two is in conformity with dharma, then I shall follow that imperishable way of conduct of my father.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having abandoned the practices and pleasures of village life, performing great austerity, wearing bark garments, eating fruits and roots, I shall wander in the great forest.
Offering oblations into the fire at both twilights, touching water at both twilights, lean, taking limited food, wearing rags and hides and matted locks.
Enduring cold, wind, and heat, accompanied by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, drying out this body with austerity that is hard to perform.
Inclined to solitude, reflecting, subsisting on cooked and uncooked food alike, satisfying the ancestors and gods with forest offerings, with words, and with water.
Never performing disagreeable acts even toward forest-dwelling persons and those who dwell in hermitages — how much less toward those who dwell in villages.
Thus desiring the fierce, yet fiercer rule prescribed by the forest treatises, I shall abide until this body is extinguished.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus spoken to those two wives of his, the king born of the Kaurava lineage then gave the crest-jewel, the neck-ornament, the armlets, the earrings, costly garments, and women's ornaments —
Having given all of these to the Brāhmaṇas, Pāṇḍu spoke again: Going to Nāgapura, it should be announced — Pāṇḍu has gone forth to the forest.
Having abandoned all wealth, desire, pleasure, and the supreme delight of the self, the bull of the Kurus set out with his wives.
Then his retinue and those attendants, hearing the various pitiful words of that lion of the Bhāratas, cried out in a terrible, anguished voice: "Alas! Alas!"
Shedding hot tears, abandoning that lord of the earth, they went swiftly to Nāgapura, carrying all of his message.
And having heard from them all that had happened in the great forest, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, foremost of men, grieved for Pāṇḍu alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The prince of the Kauravas, Pāṇḍu, subsisting on roots and fruits, then went together with his wives to the mountain Nagasabha.
Reaching the Caitraratha, passing beyond Varishena, crossing the Himavat, he journeyed on to the Gandhamādana.
Protected by the great spirits and by the Siddhas and supreme sages, the king then dwelt in level and uneven places alike.
O great king, having reached the lake Indradyumna and passed beyond Hamshakoota, he became an ascetic on the Śataśṛṅga.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Even there, engaged in the highest austerity, that mighty one became a beloved sight to the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Devoted to service, free from arrogance, self-controlled, his senses conquered, striving to reach heaven through his own prowess, O Bhārata.
To some he became a brother, to others a friend; and other sages protected him as if he were a son.
But after a long time, having attained stainless austerity, Pāṇḍu became like a Brahmarishi, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Desiring to cross to the far shore of heaven, he set forth with his wives from Śataśṛṅga, facing north; but the ascetics there spoke to him as they went up and ever further up the king of mountains, facing north.
We have seen many impassable regions of this mountain — the playgrounds of the gods and likewise of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The gardens of Kubera, level and uneven; the banks of great rivers; impassable places and mountain caverns.
There are regions of perpetual snow, devoid of trees, beasts, and birds; some places of great downpour; some that are impassable; some that are hard to reach.
No bird can cross those places, let alone other animals; only the wind passes through there, and the Siddhas and supreme sages.
On this king of mountains, how could these two royal ladies walking there not falter? O bull of the Bhāratas, you who do not deserve suffering — do not go.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Pāṇḍu said: O greatly fortunate ones, the gate to heaven is not declared open for one without offspring. Tormented by that, I who am without offspring — this I tell you.
Men are born on earth bound by four debts — the debts owed to ancestors, gods, sages, and men — by the hundreds of thousands.
But those who do not discharge these in due time — for them there are no higher worlds: this has been established by those who know dharma.
One satisfies the gods through sacrifices, sages through study and austerity, ancestors through sons and funeral rites, and men through kindness.
From the debt to sages, gods, and men I am free by dharma; but from the debt to the ancestors I am not free — and by that I am tormented, O you whose wealth is austerity.
When the body perishes, the ancestors perish with certainty — this is the settled truth. Therefore the best of men are born here for the purpose of offspring.
Just as I was created by that great soul in my father's field, so how indeed might offspring come to be in this field of mine?
The ascetics said: O man of dharma, O king, there is indeed auspicious, sinless offspring for you equal to the gods — this we know with divine sight.
O tiger among men, bring about here through action what is ordained by fate; a wise man, untroubled, obtains fruit without hardship.
When the fruit is thus seen, dear one, you should make the effort; having obtained offspring endowed with virtues, you will attain joy.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of the ascetics, Pāṇḍu became deeply anxious, knowing that his own capacity for begetting had been destroyed by the curse of the deer.
He spoke in private to Kuntī, his lawful wife of great renown, deliberating on the means for producing offspring in this difficult situation.
Offspring, O Kuntī, is indeed the foundation in the worlds, joined to dharma — thus the wise have known from the beginning as the eternal dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The sacrifice performed, the gift given, the austerity practiced, the vow duly observed — all of this is said here to bring no purification for the one without offspring.
Knowing this, O bright-smiling one, I see clearly, reflecting that I who am without offspring shall not attain the auspicious worlds.
My power of begetting has been destroyed by the curse of the deer, O timid one, for me of unrestrained self, a perpetrator of cruelty — destroyed as thoroughly as if it had been shattered.
In the view of dharma there are indeed six types of sons who are heirs of kinsmen, and six who are not heirs of kinsmen — hear them from me, O Pṛthā.
The self-born, the appointed, and the purchased son; the son of a remarried woman, the son born before marriage, and he who is born of a woman who goes freely.
The given, the bought, the adopted, and he who comes of his own accord; one carried in the womb at the time of marriage, one born from seed already deposited, and one maintained from a low womb.
In the absence of the prior and the most prior, understanding this, one should desire to obtain a son; inferior men seek a son from a superior man in adversity.
The good obtain the finest offspring that yields the fruit of dharma even from another's seed, O Pṛthā — so declared Manu Svāyaṃbhuva.
Therefore today I shall send you out, I myself being deficient in the power of begetting — know the offspring to be your own, O renowned one, from one equal to me or superior.
Hear also this story, O Kuntī, concerning Sharadandayani, that wife of a hero who was appointed by her elders for the birth of offspring.
Purified in her season and bathed, O Kuntī, at night at a crossroads, having chosen a perfected twice-born and offered oblations into the fire at the son-producing rite —
When that rite was concluded, she dwelt together with him; there she gave birth to three great warriors beginning with Durjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the same way, O auspicious one, by my command, go quickly to a Brahmin distinguished in austerity for the production of offspring.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: O great king, thus addressed, Kuntī spoke to Pāṇḍu, that bull of the Kurus, the brave lord of the earth, her husband.
O knower of dharma, O lotus-eyed one, you should not speak to me like this in any way — to me your lawful wife who delights in you.
Rather, O mighty-armed one, O hero, O Bhārata, you yourself shall beget on me offspring endowed with valor, in accordance with dharma.
I would go to heaven together with you, O tiger among men; come to me for the sake of offspring, O joy of the Kurus.
For I would not approach any other man even in thought apart from you; and who else is there in the world more excellent than you?
Now hear this ancient story rooted in dharma from me, O wide-eyed one, which I shall recount — a tale widely celebrated.
There was of old a king known as Vyuṣitāśva, supremely devoted to righteousness, the extender of the lineage of Pūru.
When that righteous and great-souled one was performing sacrifice, the gods together with Indra and the great sages came thither.
Indra became exhilarated with soma, and the twice-born with the sacrificial fees, at the great sacrifice of that royal sage Vyuṣitāśva.
Then Vyuṣitāśva, O king, shone beyond all mortals, surpassing all creatures as the sun surpasses them at the end of winter.
That best of kings, conquering and subduing the monarchs of the east, north, and the middle regions, brought the southern kings to submission.
At the great horse sacrifice, the valorous Vyuṣitāśva, that lord of kings, was possessed of the strength of ten elephants.
Even now those who know the ancient lore sing this verse about him: Vyuṣitāśva, having conquered this earth up to the shores of the sea, protected all the social orders as a father protects his own sons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Performing great sacrifices, he gave wealth to the brahmins; having collected unlimited riches, he conducted great rites, pressed many soma-libations, and spread out soma ceremonies.
He had a wife most highly esteemed, Kakshivati's daughter, named Bhadrā, O lord of men, unrivalled in beauty on earth.
They two loved each other passionately — so the tradition says; overcome with desire for her, he contracted consumption.
Before long he set like the sun, and when that lord of men was dead, his wife was overwhelmed with grief.
Childless, the deeply afflicted Bhadrā lamented piteously — so we have heard; know this, O lord of men.
O best knower of dharma, every woman deprived of a son who lives without her husband does not truly live — she lives in misery.
For a woman, death without her husband is better, O bull among Kṣatriyas; I wish to follow your path — be gracious and take me with you.
Bereft of you I cannot bear to live even a moment; show grace to me, O king, take me swiftly from here.
I shall follow behind you, O tiger among men, as you go on without turning back, through level and uneven paths alike.
Like a shadow that does not depart, O king, ever devoted to your will, I shall be, O tiger among men, always intent on your welfare and delight.
From this day forward, O king, terrible mental agonies that wither the heart will overwhelm me without you, O lotus-eyed one.
Surely in my misfortune, O king, unions with companions were severed in previous lives, or associations were broken.
And this sorrow born of separation from you has caught up with me now, O king — accumulated in former bodies by sinful deeds.
From this day forward, O king, I shall lie on a bed of kusha grass, filled with wretchedness, my whole aim set only upon seeing you again.
Show yourself to me, O tiger among men — to me who is wretched, helpless, miserable, and lamenting; be gracious, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While she thus lamented in many ways again and again and clasped that corpse, a disembodied voice is said to have spoken.
Rise, Bhadrā; go — I will grant you a boon here; I shall beget offspring upon you, O fair-smiling one.
On my own bed, O fair-limbed one, on the fourteenth or the eighth night after your purifying bath at the appointed season, lie down with me.
Thus addressed, that goddess devoted to her husband did exactly as was said; Bhadrā, desiring sons, did exactly as instructed.
That goddess bore sons by him — the corpse — O lord of men: three Śālvas and four sons of Madra, O best of the Bhāratas.
In the same way you too, O bull of the Bhāratas, are able by the power of austerity and spiritual discipline to beget sons in me by mental resolve alone.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by her, the king, that knower of dharma, spoke again to that goddess this most excellent speech in accordance with righteousness.
Exactly so did Vyuṣitāśva act in former times, O Kuntī, as you have described, O auspicious one — for he was like an immortal.
But now I shall speak of this dharma — hear it from me: the ancient usage seen by the great-souled knowers of dharma among the seers.
Women were unrestrained in former times, O fair-faced one, roaming freely as they pleased, independent, O lovely-eyed one.
When they went to other men from girlhood, apart from their husbands, O blessed one, there was no unrighteousness, O fair-limbed one — for that was the law in ancient times.
Even today creatures born in animal wombs follow that ancient law, free from desire and aversion; this dharma as seen by the ancients is still honored by the great seers.
Among the Northern Kurus even today that eternal dharma prevails, O Rambhorū, which confers freedom on women.
But in this world not long ago this boundary-rule was established, O pure-smiled one — hear from me at length by whom and for what reason.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There was a great seer named Uddālaka — so we have heard; his son, the sage who became known as Śvetaketu.
This boundary-rule was established by him among humans — so we have heard — out of anger, O lotus-eyed one; hear from me the reason for it.
Before Śvetaketu's very eyes, a brahmin took his mother by the hand in his father's presence and said, "Let us go."
The son of the seer then became angry and indignant when he saw his mother being led away thus as if by force.
Seeing him enraged, his father said to Śvetaketu: "Do not be angry, my son — this is the eternal law."
"For the women of all social orders are unrestrained on earth, my son; just as cattle are, so are people, each within their own social order."
But the seer's son Śvetaketu could not accept that law, and he established this boundary-rule for men and women on earth.
Among humans, O greatly blessed one, but not among other creatures — from that time this rule has been established, so we have heard.
From this day forward, for a woman who goes to another man abandoning her husband, the sin shall be equal to the slaying of an embryo — a painful transgression.
Likewise for a man who violates a woman who was chaste from girlhood and devoted to her husband, this same sin will apply on earth.
And for the wife who is directed by her husband for the purpose of offspring yet refuses to comply, this same sin will befall her as well.
Thus in ancient times this righteous boundary-rule was forcibly established, O timid one, by Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka.
And Madayantī, O Rambhorū, appointed for the production of offspring, went to the seer Vasiṣṭha by Saudāsa's direction — so we have heard.
From this she received a son named Aśmaka, that beautiful woman, the wife of Kalmāṣapāda, desiring to please her husband.
Our own birth is also known to you, O lotus-eyed one — that we were born of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana for the flourishing of the Kuru lineage, O timid one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Considering all these reasons, you ought to carry out this righteous request of mine, O blameless one.
"A husband should not be disobeyed by his wife in each fertile season, O princess devoted to your vow" — thus those who know dharma know this law.
In all other remaining times, a woman indeed is entitled to independence — good people describe this as the ancient dharma.
Whatever a husband commands his wife, O princess, whether righteous or even unrighteous, that must be carried out accordingly — so those who know dharma declare.
Especially one who is eager for sons yet is himself lacking in the power of procreation — as I am, O blameless-limbed one, longing to behold a son.
With palms reddened and resembling lotus petals, O auspicious one, this folded salutation is raised by me to your head to beg your grace.
By my direction, O beautiful-haired one, from a twice-born man excelling in austerity, you ought to beget sons endowed with virtues; for your sake, O broad-hipped one, I would reach the path of those who have sons.
Thus addressed, Kuntī then replied to Pāṇḍu, the conqueror of enemy cities — that fair-limbed woman devoted to her husband's welfare and delight.
"As a young girl in my father's house, appointed to the honor of guests, I attended there upon a fierce brahmin of sharp-edged vow."
"He whose resolve in dharma is hidden — him they know as Durvāsā; him I gratified with every effort, that one of disciplined soul."
"That blessed one declared to me a boon connected with invocation; he gave me a group of mantras and also spoke this to me."
"Whichever god you summon with this mantra, whether reluctantly or willingly, he will come under your control."
"So I was told at that time in my father's house by that brahmin, O Bhārata — that true word of his; now the time for it has come."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"With your permission, O king, I shall summon a god, O royal sage, with that mantra, so that we may have progeny, O lord."
"Tell me which god I shall summon, O best of knowers of truth; know me as standing ready in this matter, awaiting your permission."
Pāṇḍu said: This very day, O fair-limbed one, prepare yourself duly and summon Dharma, O auspicious one — for he is the meritorious one among the gods.
"Our son born of dharma will in no way be tainted by unrighteousness, O fair-limbed one; and this world will regard this as righteous."
"He will be righteous and the Kurus' heir — there is no doubt; even though begotten through delegation, his mind will not delight in unrighteousness."
"Therefore, placing dharma foremost, restrained and pure-smiled, worship Dharma with ritual service and invocation."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus directed by her husband, that beautiful woman assented saying "So be it"; saluting him and receiving his leave, she circumambulated him.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When a year had passed since Gāndhārī's pregnancy, O Janamejaya, Kuntī summoned the infallible Dharma for the sake of a child.
That goddess hastened and offered oblations to Dharma; she muttered the mantra given long ago by Durvāsā, according to prescribed rite.
Uniting with Dharma who bore the form of yogic power, that fair-limbed woman obtained a son — the foremost among all living beings.
In the auspicious lunar mansion presided over by Indra, in the eighth muhurta called Abhijit, when the sun was at midday, on a holy and honored lunar day —
— Kuntī at the proper time brought forth a son of abundant glory; and the moment that son was born, a disembodied voice spoke.
"This one will be the foremost among upholders of dharma — there is no doubt; known as Yudhiṣṭhira, the first-born son of Pāṇḍu."
He will become a celebrated king, renowned in all three worlds, endowed with fame, splendour, and righteous conduct.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having obtained that righteous son, Pāṇḍu spoke to her again: 'They say the warrior class is highest by strength; choose a son who is greatest in strength.'
Commanded thus by her husband, she invoked Vāyu, the wind-god; from him was born the mighty-armed Bhīma, of terrible valour.
When even that one of surpassing strength was born, a bodiless voice proclaimed: 'This one born is the greatest among all the strong,' O Bhārata.
This too was a great wonder at the very birth of Vṛkodara: having fallen from his mother's lap, he shattered a rock with his limbs.
Kuntī, startled by fear of a tiger, had suddenly leapt up and did not notice that Vṛkodara was sleeping in her own lap.
Then that boy, compact as a thunderbolt, fell upon the mountain rock, and as he fell the rock was shattered into a hundred pieces by his limbs; seeing that rock crushed, Pāṇḍu was astonished.
On the very day that Bhīma was born, O best of the Bhāratas, Duryodhana too was born there, O lord of the earth.
After Vṛkodara was born, Pāṇḍu reflected further: 'How might I have an excellent son who is the finest in the world?'
This world indeed rests on both fate and human effort; of these, fate is attained through prescribed rites joined with the proper time.
We have heard that Indra is the king and chief of the gods, of immeasurable strength and enterprise, endowed with heroism, of boundless splendour.
By satisfying him through austerity I shall obtain a son of great might; the son he grants me will be most excellent. By deed, thought, and word I shall therefore perform great penance.
Then Pāṇḍu of great splendour, having consulted with the great seers, enjoined on Kuntī, the scion of the Kauravas, the auspicious vow lasting a full year.
And the mighty-armed one himself stood on one foot and undertook fierce austerity with the highest concentration of mind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Desiring to propitiate that lord of the thirty gods, the righteous-souled one revolved together with the sun, O Bhārata.
After a long time, Vāsava spoke to him in reply: 'I shall grant you a son renowned in all three worlds.'
I shall give you a foremost son who will accomplish the purposes of gods, brahmins, and friends, and who will destroy all enemies.
Addressed thus by the great-souled Vāsava, the Kaurava king, righteous in soul, spoke to Kuntī, recalling the words of the king of gods.
One possessed of policy, great-souled, equal in splendour to the sun, difficult to assail, active in deeds, of truly wondrous appearance —
— such a son do you bear, O fair-hipped one, the very embodiment of kingly valour. The favour has been obtained from the lord of gods; invoke him, O bright-smiling one.
Thus addressed, the illustrious one invoked Śakra; Devendra came and begot Arjuna.
At the very moment the boy was born, a bodiless voice spoke, of deep and resonant sound, causing the sky to reverberate.
O Kuntī, equal to Kārtavīrya, of valour comparable to Śibi's, this one unconquerable like Śakra will spread your fame.
Just as Aditi's joy was increased by Viṣṇu, so Arjuna, equal to Viṣṇu, will increase your joy.
This one, having brought the Madras under his sway and the Kurus along with the Kekayas, and the Cedis, Kāśis, and Karūṣas, will adorn the glory of the Kuru line.
By the strength of this one's arms, the fire-god in the Khāṇḍava forest will attain the utmost satisfaction with the fat of all creatures.
Having conquered chieftains and rulers of the earth, this mighty hero, together with his brothers, will perform three great sacrifices.
O Kuntī, equal to Jamadagni's son, of valour comparable to Viṣṇu's, this one will be the foremost of the heroic and will remain undefeated.
Likewise this bull among men will acquire all divine weapons in their entirety, and will restore the prosperity that was lost to the brahmins.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The wind spoke this most wondrous speech in the sky at the birth of Kuntī's son, and Kuntī heard it.
Hearing that speech spoken aloud, the ascetics dwelling on mount Śataśṛṅga were filled with the utmost joy.
Likewise among the divine sages and the celestials together with Indra, and in the sky, there arose a tumultuous sound of kettledrums.
A great clamour arose, accompanied by showers of flowers; and the hosts of gods, having assembled, honoured Pārtha.
The sons of Kadrū, the sons of Vinatā, the Gandharvas and Apsaras, all the lords of creatures, and the seven great sages as well —
— Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, and Gautama; Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha; and the one who appeared when the sun was eclipsed — that very blessed Atri also came there.
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Prajāpati, and the Gandharvas and Apsaras likewise —
— wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with all ornaments, the Apsaras sang and danced before Bībhatsu; the glorious Tumburu together with the Gandharvas sang.
Bhīmasena, Ugrasena, Urnayu, Anagha, Gopati, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Suryavarcas as the seventh —
Yugapa, Trinapha, Kārṣṇi, Nandī, Citraratha as well, Shalisiras as the thirteenth, and Parjanya as the fourteenth —
Kali as the fifteenth here, and Nārada as the sixteenth; Sat, Brihad, Brihaka, and the greatly renowned Karāla —
Brahmacārī, Bahuguna, the famous Suparṇa, Viśvāvasu, Bhumanyu, and Sucandra as the tenth —
The famous Hāhā and Hūhū, endowed with sweetness of song — these divine Gandharvas all sang there for that bull among men.
Likewise the greatly blessed Apsaras, joyful and adorned with all ornaments, danced and sang, their eyes wide and lovely.
Anuna, Anavadya, Priyamukha, Gunavara, Adrika, Śacī, Miśrakeśī, and Alambusā —
Marīci, Shicuka, Vidyutparṇa, Tilottamā, Agnika, Lakshana, Kṣema, Devi, Rambhā, and Manoramā —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Asita, Subāhu, Supriya, Supavus, Puṇḍarīka, Sugandha, Suratha, and Pramathini —
Kamya and Sharadavati danced there in groups; Menakā, Sahajanya, Parnika, Puñjikasthalā —
Kratusthala, Ghṛtācī, Vishvaci, Purvacitti, the well-known Umloca, Pramloca — these ten, and Urvaśī as the eleventh — all these long-eyed ones sang.
Dhata, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Indra, Vivasvat, Pusha, Tvaṣṭā, and Savitā —
Parjanya and Viṣṇu — these Ādityas, blazing like fire, stood in the sky, magnifying the glory of the Pāṇḍava.
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, the greatly renowned Nirrita, Ajakapada, Ahirbudhnya, and Pinākī the scorcher of foes —
Dahana, Ishvara, Kapālī, O lord of people, Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhava — these Rudras stood there.
The two Aśvins, the eight Vasus, the mighty Maruts, the Viśvedevas, and the Sādhyas — all these were assembled and stationed there.
Karkoṭaka, Śeṣa, the serpent Vāsuki, Kacchapa, Apakunda, and the great serpent Takṣaka —
— endowed with splendour, of great wrath, of great strength, they came; these and many other Nāgas were stationed there.
Tarkhya, Ariṣṭanemi, Garuḍa of the dark banner, Aruṇa, and Āruṇi — the sons of Vinatā were stationed there.
Seeing that great wonder, the best of sages were astonished and thenceforth showed even greater regard toward the Pāṇḍavas.
But Pāṇḍu of great fame, out of desire for a son, urged the fair-limbed one again; Kuntī then spoke to him thus.
A fourth delivery is not sanctioned even in dire necessity, so they say; beyond that a woman becomes wanton, and at the fifth a harlot.
You who know this dharma, comprehensible to the intellect — how then do you speak to me, as if in heedlessness, urging me to transgress it for the sake of offspring?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the sons of Kuntī and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had been born, the daughter of the king of Madra spoke privately to Pāṇḍu.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O scorcher of foes, I feel no sorrow toward you even in your affliction; nor in the inferiority of one who deserves the best, O sinless one, while dwelling with you always.
O king, O delight of the Kurus, even hearing that a hundred sons have been born to Gāndhārī, my grief was not as great as this.
But this is my great sorrow — to be equal in status yet without a son. By good fortune, however, there is now offspring through Kuntī for my husband.
If the daughter of the Kuntiraja king would extend the lineage of offspring through me, it would be a favour to me and would also serve your welfare.
For I am inhibited by rivalry with a co-wife from speaking to Kuntī's daughter myself; but if you are pleased with me, urge her yourself.
Pāṇḍu said: O Mādrī, this very wish has always revolved in my heart too; but I did not venture to speak to you, weighing what is desirable and what is not.
But knowing this to be your wish, I shall endeavour henceforth; I believe that when spoken to by me she will certainly accept my words.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Pāṇḍu spoke these words to Kuntī again in private: 'Do what is dear to my lineage and to the world.'
For the sake of preventing the extinction of offerings to me and to my ancestors, and for my own sake, O auspicious one, do this highest good deed.
For the sake of renown also, perform this most difficult act — just as Indra, desiring glory, obtained his lordship through sacrifices.
Likewise, O beautiful one, brahmins who know the mantras, having performed most arduous austerity, approach their teachers for the sake of renown.
Likewise all the royal sages and the brahmins whose wealth is austerity have performed various difficult deeds, both high and low, for the sake of renown.
O blameless one, you — as if by a raft — ferry Mādrī across; by sharing offspring with her, attain the highest glory.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed, she said to Mādrī: 'Think of a deity just once; from that a fitting offspring will certainly be born to you, without doubt.'
Then Mādrī, having deliberated, went to the Aśvins in her mind; the two of them came and begot twin sons upon her.
Nakula and Sahadeva, unmatched in beauty in the world — at the birth of those twins too, a bodiless voice spoke.
These two, endowed with beauty, courage, and virtue, surpass all other men, blazing exceedingly with splendour and with the wealth of beauty.
The dwellers of Śataśṛṅga gave names to them with devotion, with ritual acts, and with blessings, O lord of peoples.
The eldest of Kuntī's sons they called Yudhiṣṭhira, the middle one Bhīmasena, and the third Arjuna.
The Brahmins, with joyful hearts, named the elder of Mādrī's sons Nakula and the other Sahadeva. Those best of Kurus were born year after year.
Then Pāṇḍu urged Kuntī again on Mādrī's behalf. Pṛthā said to him: 'O king, I was told this in private only once.'
'When spoken to once, she obtained a twin—by that I was deceived. I fear being surpassed by her; such is the way of women.'
'Foolish that I was, I did not know that invoking for a pair yields two sons. Therefore I should not be urged by you again—let this be my boon from you.'
Thus the five sons of Pāṇḍu, given by the gods and of great strength, were born—renowned and extenders of the Kuru lineage.
Endowed with auspicious marks, lovely to behold as the moon, proud as lions, great archers, striding with a lion's valor, lion-necked lords of men—they grew up with godlike might.
As they grew on that holy Himālayan mountain, they caused wonder among the great seers who gathered there.
And those five, together with a hundred, who all enlarged the Kuru race, grew in a short time like lotuses in water.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Pāṇḍu then rejoiced on the mountain in the great forest, beholding his five handsome sons, guarded by the strength of his own arms.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Once, in the sweet spring season when the forest was in full bloom and all creatures were bewildered with desire, the king wandered through the forest with his wife.
The forest was rich with palāśa, tilaka, mango, campaka, and pāribhadraka trees, and many other trees laden with fruits and flowers.
Adorned with various bodies of water and with lotus ponds, the forest captivated Pāṇḍu's gaze, and desire awakened in his heart.
As he roamed there with a joyful mind, carefree as an immortal, Mādrī alone followed him, wearing a beautiful garment.
Beholding her in the fullness of her youth, clad in thin garments, his desire blazed up like fire in a thicket.
Seeing her lotus-eyed and equal to himself in a secluded place, the king, overpowered by the force of desire, could not restrain that longing.
Then the king forcibly seized her in that solitary place, though the queen struggled and restrained him with all her strength.
His soul consumed by desire, he did not recall the curse as he came forcibly upon Mādrī in the act of union.
The Kaurava, fallen under the sway of Kāma to the end of his life, casting aside the fear born of the curse, came forcibly upon his beloved.
His intellect, enslaved to desire, was directly deluded by Fate itself; churned by the tumult of the senses, it vanished along with his consciousness.
Having united with his wife, O joy of the Kurus, the supremely virtuous Pāṇḍu met with the law of death.
Then Mādrī embraced the king, whose consciousness had departed, and cried out again and again in inconsolable grief.
Then Kuntī, together with her sons and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī, all came together to where the king lay thus.
Then Mādrī, distressed, spoke these words to Kuntī: 'Come here alone; let the children stay right there.'
Hearing those words, Kuntī stopped the children right there, and crying out 'I am undone!' she quickly came forward.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing Pāṇḍu and Mādrī lying on the ground, Kuntī's body was seized with grief, and she lamented in deep sorrow.
'O hero, always self-possessed, ever guarded by me—how did you transgress the curse knowingly, you who dwell in the forest?'
'O Mādrī, was it not your duty to protect the lord of men? How did you entice the king of men into a lonely place?'
'How could delight arise in one who was always afflicted, who had reached you alone in a secluded place, pondering that very curse?'
'You are fortunate, O princess of Bāhlika, more blessed than I; for you have seen the face of the king in his moment of joy.'
Mādrī said: 'Though I enticed him and though I restrained him repeatedly, he could not be stopped by me. Truly, he wished to fulfill his fate.'
Kuntī said: 'I am the elder lawful wife; the foremost reward of dharma is mine. What must be shall be—O Mādrī, do not turn me away.'
'I shall follow my husband who has passed into the realm of the dead. Rise, leave him to me, and protect these children.'
Mādrī said: 'I shall follow the husband who did not flee. I am not yet satisfied in my desires—let the elder consent to this.'
'This best of Bhāratas was exhausted coming to me in desire—how could I cut off his desire and leave him unsatisfied in Yama's abode?'
'Nor could I, O noble lady, treat your sons and mine without distinction; sin would touch me if I were to do so.'
'Therefore, O Kuntī, you must treat my two sons as your own; for this king who desired me has passed into the realm of the dead.'
'Along with the king's body, this body of mine too must be burned, well adorned. O noble one, do me this kindness.'
'And be vigilant and beneficent toward the children for my sake. I see nothing else that I need entrust to you.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, that glorious lawful wife, daughter of the Madra king, quickly mounted the funeral pyre beside the bull among men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: After performing the final purificatory rites for Pāṇḍu, the god-like great seers and ascetics assembled and took counsel.
'That great-souled one of great austerity, abandoning kingdom and realm, came to this place seeking refuge among ascetics to practice tapas.'
'King Pāṇḍu, having entrusted his newborn sons and his wives here to your care as a trust, has departed from this place to heaven.'
Taking leave of one another, those devoted to the welfare of all beings, placing Pāṇḍu's sons at their head, resolved to go to the city named for the elephant—Hāstinapura.
Those noble-minded perfected ones set their minds on the journey, intending to deliver the Pāṇḍavas to Bhīṣma and to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
At that very moment all the ascetics set out, taking with them Pāṇḍu's wives, his sons, and also his body.
She who had once been happy, always tender toward her children, though she had undertaken a long journey, felt it as brief.
In no great time that glorious one reached the Kuru countryside and arrived at the gate of the city of Vardhamāna.
Hearing of the arrival of thousands of wandering bards and sages at that time, the people of Nāgapura were filled with wonder.
As the sun rose a short while later, all the city's residents, placing dharma foremost, went out with their wives to see the ascetics.
Groups of women and groups of Kṣatriyas mounted on conveyances went out together with Brahmins, and the wives of Brahmins as well.
Likewise there was a great mingling of groups of Vaiśyas and Śūdras; no one acted with jealousy—they all came with minds turned to dharma.
So too Bhīṣma son of Śaṃtanu, and Somadatta, and Bāhlika, the royal sage who sees with the eyes of wisdom, and the charioteer's son Vidura himself.
And the goddess Satyavatī, and the glorious Kausalyā, and Gāndhārī surrounded by the royal women—all went out.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The heirs of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, led by Duryodhana, adorned with varied ornaments, went out numbering a hundred.
All the Kauravas, bowing their heads in salutation to all those groups of great seers, sat down near them together with their priests.
In the same way all the city folk and country people bowed their heads to the ground in reverence and sat down nearby.
Perceiving that multitude of people to be silent, as if mute, Bhīṣma then reported to the great seers the state of the kingdom and the realm.
Then the eldest among them, wearing matted locks and a deerskin, rose up, and discerning the mind of the great seers, that great seer spoke thus.
'He who was the Kaurava heir, the lord of men named Pāṇḍu, renouncing pleasures and enjoyments, departed from here to Śataśṛṅga.'
'While he abided in the vow of celibacy, by a divine cause, Yudhiṣṭhira, this son of his, was born directly from Dharma himself.'
'Likewise, to that great-souled king, Mātariśvan—the Wind—gave this son Bhīma by name, foremost of the strong and of great might.'
'This one of true valor was born to Kuntī from Indra, the lord of many; his glory will surpass all great archers.'
'And these two great archers, the best of Kurus and tigers among men, whom Mādrī bore from the Aśvins—they too stand here.'
'By the glorious Pāṇḍu who dwelt in the forest, ever constant in dharma, this ancestral lineage has been raised up once more.'
'As Pāṇḍu watched the birth, the growth, and the Vedic studies of his sons, his joy grew ever and always.'
'Abiding in the conduct of the good, having attained the gift of sons, Pāṇḍu departed from here to the world of the ancestors on the seventeenth day.'
'Learning that he had been placed on the funeral pyre and offered to Vaiśvānara, Mādrī entered the fire, abandoning her own life.'
'She has gone, devoted, to the world of her husband along with him. Let whatever rites are due for them both be performed forthwith.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Here are their two bodies, and here are their noble sons, scorchers of foes—let them be honored with the rites together with their mother.'
'And when the funeral rites are completed, let Pāṇḍu of great glory, the upholder of the Kuru house, who knows all dharma, receive the ancestral offering.'
Having spoken thus to all the Kurus, while the Kurus themselves watched, all the wandering bards together with the Guhyakas vanished in an instant.
Seeing that assembly of seers and perfected ones vanish right there like a city of the Gandharvas, they were overcome with supreme wonder.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: 'O Vidura, have all the funeral rites performed for Pāṇḍu in a manner befitting a king, for the lion among kings, and especially for Mādrī as well.'
'Distribute cattle, garments, jewels, and various wealth for Pāṇḍu and Mādrī—to whosoever wishes, as much as they desire.'
'Arrange also that Kuntī performs honor to Mādrī's rites; see that she is well-protected so that neither the wind nor the sun may look upon her.'
'Sinless Pāṇḍu is not to be mourned; that lord of men is praiseworthy—five heroic sons equal to sons of the gods have been born to him.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Vidura, having said 'so be it' to him, O Bhārata, together with Bhīṣma, performed the funerary consecration for Pāṇḍu in a most secluded spot.
Then from the city, blazing fires preceded by oblations of clarified butter were swiftly brought out by Pāṇḍu's royal priests.
Then they adorned the bier with seasonal fragrances and various choice garlands, covering it all over with cloth.
The ministers, kinsmen, and friends attended upon that bier thus adorned with garlands and with the most precious garments.
They bore that lion among men, well-covered, together with Mādrī, on the finest of vehicles, drawn by horses and supremely adorned.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They then honored him with a white royal parasol, with fans of chowrie, and with the sound of all manner of musical instruments.
Men, taking up gems by the hundreds, distributed there the post-mortem offerings of Pāṇḍu to all who desired them.
Then they brought white, bright, and large parasols for the sake of the Kaurava, as well as beautiful garments.
Sacrificial fires, blazing and well-adorned, tended by officiating priests clad in white, went before him while oblations were poured.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras by the thousands, weeping and burning with grief, followed the lord of men.
"This lord of men, our greatest protector, having abandoned us and cast us into perpetual sorrow, having left us without a guardian — where will he go?"
All the Pāṇḍavas, Bhīṣma, and Vidura, weeping aloud, came to a charming spot in the forest, on the even, auspicious bank of the Gaṅgā.
Those truth-speaking men then set down that palanquin bearing the lion among men, Pāṇḍu of untiring deeds, together with his wife.
Then they quickly sprinkled his body — which had been treated with all fragrances, anointed with pure kālīyaka paste and the like, and consecrated with the finest ritual bath — with water from golden vessels.
They anointed him with the finest white sandalwood paste, mixed with black aloe-wood and with tuṅgarasa.
Then they dressed him in pure white garments of local fabric; covered in robes, that bull among men — that tiger among men, accustomed to the most precious of beds — shone as though still alive.
Authorised by the officiating priests who had completed the funerary rites, they prepared the king — well-adorned and sprinkled with clarified butter — together with Mādrī.
They cremated them with fragrant sandalwood mixed with tuṅga and padmaka, and with many other various perfumes in great abundance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, seeing those two bodies, Kausalyā was overwhelmed with bewilderment and fell suddenly to the earth, crying "Ah! my son!"
Seeing her fallen and afflicted, all the people of the city and the countryside wept aloud, filled with compassion and devotion to the king.
All creatures, even those born in the animal kingdom, cried out together with the humans, as though wearied by the clamor of distress.
So too did Bhīṣma son of Śaṃtanu, the great-minded Vidura, and all the Kauravas weep, deeply overwhelmed with grief.
Then Bhīṣma, Vidura, the king along with his kinsmen, and all the women of the Kuru clan performed the water-libation rite for him.
O king, taking those Pāṇḍavas who had performed the water rites and were emaciated with grief, all the subjects surrounded them, themselves lamenting.
Just as the Pāṇḍavas lay down on the ground together with their kinsmen, so too did the citizens — brāhmaṇas and others — lie down in the same way, O king.
Together with the Pāṇḍavas, the city remained joyless, uneasy, downcast even to its children, and desolate for twelve nights.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Kṣattā (Vidura), the king, and Bhīṣma, together with their kinsmen, performed the śrāddha rite for Pāṇḍu, replete with the nectar of the ancestral offering.
They fed the Kurus and the foremost brāhmaṇas by the thousands, and gave floods of gems to the chief twice-born, as well as choice villages.
Then, after the purification rites were completed, the citizens took those Pāṇḍavas — the bulls of the Bhārata line — and returned to the city named after the elephant.
All the people of the city and countryside continually mourned that bull of the Bhārata line as though he were their own dead kinsman.
At the conclusion of the śrāddha, seeing the people so afflicted, bewildered, tormented by pain and grief, Vyāsa spoke to his mother.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The times of happiness have passed away; dreadful times have arrived. Day by day the days grow worse; the earth has lost its youth.
A terrible age is coming, filled with many deceits, overwhelmed with manifold faults, its righteous practices and customs vanished.
Go, take to renunciation, and dwell composed in the forest of austerity — you will not then behold the terrible destruction of this lineage with your own eyes."
She agreed with "So be it," then went in and spoke to her daughter-in-law: "O Ambikā, we have heard that on account of your son's misrule the Bhāratas along with their dependants — and even the grandchildren — will perish."
"Therefore, taking this afflicted Kausalyā who is tormented by grief for her son, we two will go to the forest — if you agree. May it be well with you."
When Ambikā said "So be it," Satyavatī of noble vows took leave of Bhīṣma and went to the forest together with her two daughters-in-law, O Bhārata.
Those divine women performed exceedingly severe austerities, O best of the Bhāratas, and then, O great king, casting off their bodies, attained the desired state.
The Pāṇḍavas then received the sacraments ordained in the Vedas and grew up enjoying their pleasures in their father's house.
Playing together with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in their father's house, the Pāṇḍavas proved superior in all childish games.
In speed, in hitting targets, in eating, and in rolling in the dust, Bhīmasena overpowered all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
With great delight that Pāṇḍava would seize them as they played, in the game of hide-and-seek, and holding them by their heads he would force them to fight.
Vṛkodara alone would crush all one hundred and one of those princes of great energy without very much difficulty.
That powerful one would seize them by the feet, beat them down by force, and drag them screaming along the ground until their knees, heads, and eyes were scraped raw.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While playing in the water he would clasp ten boys in his arms at once, remain submerged, and release them only when they were nearly dead.
Whenever they climbed a tree to gather fruit, Bhīma would shake the tree with a kick of his foot.
Struck by the force of the blow, the tree would whirl around, and the boys would quickly tumble down from it together with the fruit, falling loose.
In wrestling, in speed, or in any exercise, those princes who competed with Vṛkodara never once got the better of him.
Though Vṛkodara thus continually competed with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and kept them in a state of misery, it was entirely out of boyish spirit and not from any treacherous intent.
Then the mighty-spirited son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, knowing Bhīmasena's exceedingly renowned strength, revealed his wicked disposition.
In that one who had strayed from righteousness, surveying all manner of sins, a wicked mind arose out of delusion and greed for lordship.
"This Vṛkodara, son of Kuntī, the middle of the Pāṇḍu-sons, the foremost among the mighty — let him be slain by treachery."
"And then, having forcibly bound the younger and the eldest — Yudhiṣṭhira — in chains, I shall rule the earth."
Having thus resolved upon this wicked plan, Duryodhana from that time constantly watched for an opportunity against the great-souled Bhīma.
Then he had built large and variously adorned tents and pavilions of cloth and blankets for the purpose of water-sports, O Bhārata.
Reaching a certain spot of ground at Pramāṇakoṭi, at the end of their sports all of them, clad in clean garments and well-adorned, leisurely enjoyed food rich in every delight.
At the day's end, those heroes — the upholders of the Kuru line — were thoroughly fatigued from their revels and were pleased to take their rest in the very pavilions of sport.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the powerful Bhīma, that lord, exceedingly exhausted from his exertions, having carried those princes who had come for water-sports, climbed up that ground at Pramāṇakoṭi wishing to sleep there and fell fast asleep.
Finding a cool resting place, weary and befuddled with intoxication, that Pāṇḍava lay motionless, O king, and slept as though dead.
Then Duryodhana quietly bound Bhīma with bonds of creepers and hurled him — deep water and terrifying force notwithstanding — from the land into the river.
Then Bhīma, that foremost of strikers, the son of Kuntī, awoke, cut through all his bonds, and rose up out of the water.
Again, while he slept, Duryodhana had him bitten on every vital point of his body by enraged serpents with sharp fangs and terrible venom.
Yet the fangs of those venomous creatures, though driven into his vital spots, could not pierce his skin, because of the hardness of that broad-chested man's body.
But when Bhīma awoke he beat down all those serpents and with the back of his hand struck down Duryodhana's beloved charioteer.
Again Duryodhana introduced poison into Bhīmasena's food — fresh, potent kālakūṭa venom, collected and hair-raising in its power.
A vaiśya's son informed the Pārthas of it out of desire for their welfare; yet even having eaten that, Vṛkodara digested it without any adverse effect.
For that poison, however intensely sharp, produced no disorder in him; Bhīma, of terrible bodily constitution, digested even that.
Thus Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni son of Subala sought to kill the Pāṇḍavas by many stratagems.
And the Pāṇḍavas, those tamers of enemies, were fully aware of all that, yet made no show of it, abiding by Vidura's counsel.
Janamejaya said: O great brāhmaṇa, you should also tell the birth of Kṛpa — how was he born from a clump of reeds, and how did he obtain mastery of weapons?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: O great king, the great sage Gautama had a son named Śaradvān — born, it is said, together with arrows, O lord.
His mind did not incline to the study of the Vedas as it inclined toward the science of archery, O scorcher of foes.
Just as the speakers of Brahman master the Vedas through austerity, so he, endowed with austerity, mastered all weapons.
Through his supreme devotion to the science of archery and through his vast austerities, that Gautama greatly alarmed the king of the gods.
Then the lord of the gods sent a celestial maiden named Jālapadī, saying "Create an obstacle to his austerity," O Kaurava.
She approached the charming hermitage of Śaradvat and that young woman, finding Gautama with bow and arrows in hand, enticed him with desire.
Seeing that apsarā in the forest, clad in a single garment, of incomparable form in all the world, Gautama's eyes opened wide.
His bow and arrows fell from his hands to the ground, and seeing her a trembling arose in his body.
But that great sage, by reason of the excellence of his knowledge and in consequence of his austerity, stood firm with the utmost steadiness.
Yet, O king, the agitation that suddenly overcame him caused his seed to flow out, and he did not perceive it.
That sage, abandoning both that hermitage and the apsarā, departed; and his seed fell upon a clump of reeds.
Having fallen upon the clump of reeds it divided into two, O king, and from that was born a twin pair — the offspring of Gautama Śaradvat.
While king Śaṃtanu was out on a hunt, a certain soldier of his army happened to see that twin pair in the forest.
Seeing the bow with arrows and the black antelope skins, and judging the twins to be the offspring of a brāhmaṇa fully versed in the science of archery, he brought and showed the armed twin pair to the king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Taking that pair, the king, filled with compassion, came home saying, "These are my children."
Then he raised them and performed all their sacraments; and Gautama himself, returning at that time, became devoted to the science of archery.
"It is out of compassion (kṛpā) that I have raised these two children" — so saying, the king gave them that very name.
Gautama found those two who had been abandoned there through his ascetic power, and coming to the king, he then disclosed to him their lineage and all else.
He then fully disclosed to him the fourfold science of archery and all the various weapons with their secrets; and in no great time the king attained the highest rank of mastership.
Thereafter all those great warriors came to study the science of archery — the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the mighty Pāṇḍavas, the Vṛṣṇis, and other kings assembled from many regions.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Bhīṣma, desiring excellence for his grandsons and wishing them to be disciplined, inquired after teachers well-versed in archery and respected for their valour.
One of small intellect, or of no great good fortune, or not versed in the many weapons, or not equal to the gods — such a one could not train the mighty Kurus in the art of arms.
Now the great sage Bharadvāja, wandering long ago at the sacrificial fire-hall, beheld with his own eyes the apsarā Ghṛtācī bathing.
A gust of wind swept away her garment; thereupon his seed fell, and the sage received it in a vessel called droṇa.
In that vessel was born Droṇa, the son of that wise sage; and he studied the Vedas and all the Vedic ancillary sciences fully.
The glorious and mighty Bharadvāja, best of those who uphold dharma, taught the highly blessed Agniveśya the Āgneya weapon.
That sage, born of Agniṣṭut, O best of the Bhāratas, then in turn transmitted that great Āgneya weapon of Bharadvāja's line to Droṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There was a king named Pṛṣata who was a friend of Bharadvāja; his son was then born, named Drupada.
That son of Pṛṣata, bull among kṣatriyas, used to go regularly to the hermitage and played and studied there together with Droṇa.
Then, upon Pṛṣata's death, that long-armed man, Drupada, became king and lord of the Pāñcālas of the northern region.
The blessed Bharadvāja too ascended to heaven at that time; then Droṇa, of great renown, his mind directed by his father's wishes and longing for a son, found Kṛpī, daughter of Śaradvan, as his wife.
She who was ever devoted to the sacred fire, to dharma, and to self-restraint — Gautamī — gave birth to a son named Aśvatthāman.
The moment he was born he neighed just like the horse Uccaiḥśravas; hearing that, an invisible being standing in the sky spoke.
"The sound of this boy crying has spread in all directions like the neighing of a horse (aśva); therefore this child shall bear the name Aśvatthāman."
Bharadvāja's son was greatly delighted with that son; and the wise man, dwelling there, became profoundly versed in the science of archery.
He then heard, O king, that the great-souled Jāmadagnya, the scorcher of foes, was at that time distributing all his wealth to the brahmins.
As Rāma was setting out for the forest, Bharadvāja's son Droṇa addressed him: "Know that I, Droṇa, best of twice-born, have come desiring wealth."
Rāma said: Whatever gold and other wealth I possessed has all been given away to the brahmins, O ascetic.
Likewise this goddess Earth, bounded by the oceans, adorned with cities and towns in her entirety, has been given by me to Kaśyapa.
Only my body remains to me now, and my precious weapons and various arms. Choose — what shall I give you, Droṇa? Tell me quickly.
Droṇa said: You should give me all the weapons in their entirety, O Bhārgava, together with the means of recalling them and their applications and secrets, withholding nothing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Saying "So be it," the Bhārgava then gave him all the weapons along with their secret rites and the entire science of archery.
Having received all of this, that best of twice-born, now accomplished in the use of weapons, set out with great joy toward his dear friend Drupada.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Droṇa, the mighty son of Bharadvāja, approached Drupada and said to that son of Pṛṣata: "Know me as your friend, O king."
Drupada said: This reasoning of yours is ill-conceived, O brahmin, not well-founded — that you say to me boldly, "I am your friend," O twice-born.
With men of your condition — bereft of royal splendour and fallen from wealth — exalted kings never anywhere form friendships, O slow-witted one.
Even bonds of affection decay in time as all things decay; the friendship you and I had before was based on the equality of our circumstances.
Friendship that does not age is never to be seen anywhere in the world; desire destroys it and anger tears it asunder.
Do not come here clinging to that old friendship; seek a new one. The friendship between you and me, O best of twice-born, was grounded in our equal standing.
A poor man is not the friend of a wealthy one; the ignorant man is not the friend of the learned; a coward is not the friend of a hero. What is mere former friendship worth?
Friendship and marriage exist between those of equal wealth and equal lineage, not between the prosperous and the destitute.
One ignorant of the Vedas is not the friend of a Vedic scholar; a man without a chariot is not the friend of a chariot-warrior; one who is not a king is not the equal companion of a king. What is past friendship worth?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Drupada, the mighty Bharadvāja's son reflected for a moment, overwhelmed with anger.
Having resolved in his mind regarding Pāñcāla, that wise man went to the city of the foremost Kurus, the city named Nāgasāhvaya (Hāstinapura).

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the princes, having gone out together from Gajasāhvaya, were joyfully roaming about there, those heroes playing with a ball.
As they played, that ball fell into a well, and they could find no means to recover the ball.
Then Droṇa, seeing those princes at a loss, smiled gently and spoke to them out of his skill and confidence.
"Shame on kṣatriya strength! Shame on your claimed training in arms — born in the lineage of Bharata, yet you cannot retrieve a ball!"
"Here is a handful of reeds consecrated by me with a weapon-spell; observe the power of this which no other possesses."
"I shall pierce the ball with one reed, then that reed with another, and by joining them together I shall retrieve the ball — that is my method."
The princes watched this with eyes wide with amazement; and having seen the ball retrieved, they addressed the one who had pierced it.
"We bow to you, O brahmin! This skill is found in no other. Who are you? How shall we know you? And what shall we do for you?"
Droṇa said: Describe me to Bhīṣma by my appearance and my qualities; he alone, of great intelligence, will understand at once who I am.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Saying "So be it," they all went to their grandfather Bhīṣma and reported the brahmin's words along with that remarkable deed.
Bhīṣma, hearing the princes' account, recognized that it was Droṇa, reflecting: "He is indeed the fitting teacher."
Then Bhīṣma, best of weapon-bearers, having brought him and honoured him well himself, questioned him carefully about his purpose in coming; and Droṇa disclosed everything.
"O Acyuta, I formerly went to the great sage Agniveśya desiring to acquire weapons and wishing to master the science of archery."
"As a celibate student, with controlled mind, with matted hair, I dwelt there for many years with the desire to master the science of archery."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The mighty prince of the Pāñcālas, Yajñasena's son, also studied the same learning under the same teacher alongside me, striving and concentrated."
"He was my friend there, helpful and dear to me; delighting long in his company, O descendant of Kuru, we had been studying together from childhood indeed."
"That one, kind in deed and kind in word, approached me there and said to me, O Bhīṣma, words that increased my joy."
"'I am the dearest son to my great-souled father, O Droṇa; when that Pāñcāla king consecrates me in his kingdom —'"
"'— the kingdom shall be yours to enjoy, my friend; I swear it to you by truth: my pleasures, my wealth, and my happiness shall all be at your disposal.'"
"Thus assured, I set forth, having mastered the weapons, desirous of wealth; and hearing that he had been consecrated, I thought: 'My purpose is achieved.'"
"Full of joy, I came again to my dear friend who now held a kingdom, remembering our fellowship and those very words of his."
"Then, approaching Drupada and invoking our old friendship, I said to him, O lord, O tiger among men: 'Know me as your friend.'"
"But Drupada, though I had come to him as a friend and greeted him as one, seemed to dismiss me and laughingly said this:"
"'This thinking of yours is ill-formed, O brahmin, not well-founded — that you say to me boldly, "I am your friend," O twice-born.'"
"'Exalted kings never form friendships anywhere with men of your condition — bereft of royal splendour, fallen from wealth, O slow-witted one.'"
"'One ignorant of the Vedas is not the friend of a Vedic scholar; one without a chariot is not the friend of a chariot-warrior; a non-king is not the friend of a king. What is past friendship worth?'"
"Thus addressed by Drupada, overwhelmed with anger, I have come to the Kurus, O Bhīṣma, seeking worthy students endowed with noble qualities."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma accepted that teacher along with the sons of Pāṇḍu, bringing all his grandsons together with various precious gifts.
He gave them as pupils to Droṇa according to proper rites, O king; and that great archer accepted the Kauravas as his students.
Having accepted all of them, Droṇa spoke privately, alone, to those who had duly performed the rite of approaching a teacher, his heart at ease.
"There is a certain desired task that revolves in my heart; once you are accomplished in weapons, it must be rendered to me — speak truth about that, O sinless ones."
Hearing this, the descendants of Kuru fell silent, O lord of people; but Arjuna, the scorcher of foes, then pledged to do everything.
Then Droṇa smelled Arjuna's head again and again, embraced him with affection, and wept with joy.
Then mighty Droṇa proceeded to instruct the sons of Pāṇḍu in all the various weapons — both divine and human.
Other princes likewise came together, O bull of the Bhāratas, and approached that best of twice-born, Droṇa, for instruction in weapons — the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas and kings from many lands.
And the son of the sūta, Rādheya, also came to the teacher Droṇa at that time; but that son of a sūta, extremely intolerant, rivalling Pārtha, took shelter with Duryodhana and held the Pāṇḍavas in contempt.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: But Arjuna exerted the utmost effort in revering the teacher and applied himself supremely to the weapons; he became the beloved of Droṇa.
Droṇa summoned the one who prepared food and said to him privately: "You are never, under any circumstances, to serve food to Arjuna in the dark."
Then one day while Arjuna was eating, the wind blew and the burning lamp was extinguished by it.
Yet Arjuna went on eating his food; his glorious hand did not falter, always finding the food by force of habit. Recognizing this as the product of constant practice, the son of Pāṇḍu then practised archery by night.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Droṇa heard the twang of his bowstring in the night, O Bhārata; approaching him, he rose, embraced him, and spoke thus.
"I shall strive to make it so that no other archer in the world shall be your equal — this I tell you in truth."
Thereafter Droṇa further instructed Arjuna in the science of battle — on chariots, on elephants, on horses, and on foot.
Droṇa trained the Pāṇḍava in mace-fighting, in swordsmanship, and in the use of the javelin, lance, and spear, as well as in mixed forms of combat.
Witnessing his skill, kings and princes eager to acquire the science of archery came in their thousands.
Then, O great king, the son of the Niṣāda king Hiraṇyadhanus — Ekalavya — also came to Droṇa.
The dharma-knowing Droṇa did not accept him, thinking "he is a Niṣāda," and out of regard for the welfare of his own students in archery.
That scorcher of foes then clasped Droṇa's feet with bowed head, entered the forest, and fashioned a clay image of Droṇa.
Conducting himself toward that image as if toward his teacher, he applied himself with supreme discipline to the yoga of archery, following the strictest vows.
