Endowed with supreme faith and supreme concentrated effort, he attained the highest swiftness in the release, receipt, and nocking of arrows.
One day, with Droṇa's permission, all those crusher-of-enemies, the Kuru and Pāṇḍava princes, rode out in their chariots on a hunt.
O king, some servant happened to follow the Pāṇḍavas alone with the equipment, bringing with him a dog.
As they roamed there seeking their various quarries, the dog, wandering foolishly through the forest, strayed toward the Niṣāda youth.
The dog, catching sight of the Niṣāda in the forest — his limbs smeared with dark mud, wearing a dark deerskin — began barking and stood close by him.
Then, displaying his lightness of hand in archery, he simultaneously shot seven arrows into the barking dog's mouth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The dog, with its mouth filled with arrows, came back to the Pāṇḍavas; seeing it, the heroic Pāṇḍavas were filled with the greatest wonder.
Witnessing that supreme swiftness and the striking of a target by sound alone, they felt both ashamed and universally praised the feat.
Searching for him in the forest, O king, the Pāṇḍavas found that forest-dweller ceaselessly shooting arrows.
They did not recognise him, his appearance being so altered; then they asked him: "Who are you, and whose son?"
Ekalavya said: "O heroes, know me as the son of the Niṣāda king Hiraṇyadhanus, a disciple of Droṇa who has laboured in the science of archery."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having truly ascertained who he was, the Pāṇḍavas returned and reported everything that had happened — the whole wonderful occurrence — to Droṇa.
O king, the son of Kuntī, Arjuna, keeping Ekalavya in mind, privately approached Droṇa and said affectionately:
"Did you not embrace me alone and, with affection, declare: 'No disciple of mine shall surpass you'?"
"Then why does another disciple of yours exist who surpasses me and is mighty even by the world's reckoning — the son of the Niṣāda king?"
Having deliberated and resolved for a brief moment, Droṇa took Savyasācin with him and went toward the Niṣāda youth.
He saw Ekalavya — limbs smeared with mud, wearing matted hair and bark garments, bow in hand — ceaselessly shooting arrows.
Ekalavya, seeing Droṇa approaching near, went forward to meet him, clasped his feet, and touched the earth with his head.
Having honoured Droṇa duly, the son of the Niṣāda, declaring himself a disciple, stood before him with palms joined.
O king, Droṇa then said to Ekalavya: "If you are indeed my disciple, let my fee be paid at once."
Hearing this, Ekalavya replied with joy: "What shall I give, O venerable one? Let the teacher command me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For there is nothing I cannot give to my teacher" — and to him Droṇa said: "Let your right thumb be given to me."
Ekalavya, having heard that terrible word of Droṇa, honouring his own vow and ever devoted to truth —
— with the same cheerful face and the same undepressed heart, cut off without hesitation and gave Droṇa his own thumb.
After that, the Niṣāda youth drew the bow with his remaining fingers, but he was no longer as swift as before, O lord of men.
Thereupon Arjuna's heart was gladdened and his anxiety gone; and Droṇa was true to his word — no other surpassed Arjuna.
Among Droṇa's disciples at that time, Duryodhana and Bhīma especially excelled in mace-fighting among the Kurus.
Aśvatthāmā surpassed all others in secret and esoteric knowledge; the twin sons of Mādrī exceeded other men similarly; Yudhiṣṭhira was foremost among chariot fighters; but Dhanañjaya was supreme in all respects.
That Pāṇḍava became famous to the ends of the sea as the leader of chariot-leaders, excelling in intellect, discipline, strength, and ardour, and in all weapons.
Arjuna was distinguished in weapons and in affection for his teacher; though instruction in arms was equal for all, in grace and valour Arjuna alone among all the princes became an atiratha — a warrior beyond peers.
O lord of men, the evil-souled sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra could not tolerate Bhīmasena, dearer than life itself, nor the accomplished Dhanañjaya.
Wishing to test all of them, who had completed every branch of learning, in the knowledge of striking, O bull among men, Droṇa assembled them all.
He had craftsmen place an artificial bird made by artisans atop a tree, unknown to the princes, and set it as the target.
Droṇa said: "Quickly, all of you take your bows with haste; stand with arrows nocked, aiming at this bird."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The instant I give the word, let its head be struck off — I will engage you one by one; do so, my sons."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The best of the Āṅgirasa lineage then first addressed Yudhiṣṭhira: "O invincible one, nock your arrow and release it at the end of my word."
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, taking up his great bow first, stood aiming at the bird, spurred by his teacher's command.
After a moment, Droṇa spoke this word, O bull of the Bhāratas, to that joy of the Kurus standing with bow drawn:
"Do you see that bird perched at the treetop, O son of the best of men?" "I see it," Yudhiṣṭhira replied to his teacher.
After another moment Droṇa asked him again: "Do you see this tree, or me, or your brothers?"
The son of Kuntī replied to him: "I see this tree, and you, and my brothers, and the bird" — again and again.
Droṇa, as if displeased, told him to step aside, censuring him: "You are not capable of hitting this target."
Then the greatly renowned Droṇa, wishing to test them in the same order, questioned those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra headed by Duryodhana.
And the other disciples — beginning with Bhīma — and the kings from other lands; all of them said "we see all of that" and were rebuked.
Then Droṇa, smiling, addressed Dhanañjaya: "Now you are to strike this target — listen well."
"The instant my word falls, the arrow is to be released. Draw your bow, my son, and wait just a moment."
So addressed, Savyasācin stood with his bow bent in a circle, aiming at the target, urged on by his teacher's word.
After a moment Droṇa asked him in the same way: "Do you see that bird perched there, and the tree, and me?"
"I see the bird" — so Pārtha replied to Droṇa — "but I do not see the tree, nor you, O Bhārata."
Then Droṇa, with a gladdened heart, after a moment again addressed that invincible bull among the Pāṇḍava chariot warriors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"If you see the bird, tell me again." He replied: "I see the head of the bird — not its body."
Hearing Arjuna say this, Droṇa felt his body hair rise with joy and said to Pārtha: "Release!" — and he released without hesitation.
Then with a sharp razor-headed arrow, the Pāṇḍava swiftly cut off the head of that tree-perched bird and sent it falling.
When that deed was accomplished, Droṇa embraced Phalguna and considered Drupada as already defeated in battle along with his allies.
Some time after, the best of the Āṅgirasa line went with all his disciples to the Gaṅgā to bathe, O bull of the Bhāratas.
While Droṇa plunged into the water, a powerful aquatic creature — a crocodile — urged on by fate, seized him by the thigh.
Though capable of freeing himself, he urged all his disciples: "Kill the crocodile and free me!" — almost as if spurring them on as a test.
At the very instant of his word, Bībhatsu (Arjuna) struck the submerged crocodile with five sharp arrows in quick succession, while the others were bewildered and scattered this way and that.
Seeing him so capable in action, Droṇa judged that Pāṇḍava superior to all his other disciples and was filled with joy.
That crocodile, struck by Pārtha's arrows in many ways and cut to pieces, met its death, releasing the limb of the great-souled Droṇa.
Then the son of Bharadvāja said to that great-souled, mighty chariot warrior: "Receive this weapon, O mighty-armed one — the most excellent and supremely difficult to counter: named Brahmasira, complete with the method of its use and recall."
"You must never employ this against human beings under any circumstance — if unleashed upon one of little power, it would incinerate the world."
"This weapon, dear one, is called without equal in the worlds; keep it with the utmost care and with purity — hear this word of mine."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When some superhuman enemy oppresses you, O hero, you may use this weapon in battle to slay him then."
"So be it" — having agreed, Bībhatsu with joined palms accepted that supreme weapon; and his teacher said to him again: "There shall be no other man in the world equal to you as an archer."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having seen both the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the sons of Pāṇḍu fully trained in arms, O Bhārata, Droṇa spoke to king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men.
In the presence of Kṛpa, Somadatta, the wise Bāhlika, Gaṅgā's son Bhīṣma, Vyāsa, and Vidura —
— "O king, those princes have now fully acquired their learning, O best of Kurus; let them, with your permission, O king, display their training."
The great king then replied, his inner self filled with joy: "O son of Bharadvāja, a great deed has been accomplished by you, O best of twice-born."
"Whenever you think the time is right, and in whatever place and in whatever manner — command me yourself to make the arrangements accordingly."
"I am filled today with a longing, free from all despair, to see with my own eyes those sons of mine who have advanced through their mastery of arms — as others with eyes shall see them."
O Kṣattṛ, whatever the preceptor and teacher commands, carry it out accordingly; I think there will be no joy equal to this, O cherisher of dharma.
Then, taking leave of the king and accompanied by Vidura, the supremely wise son of Bharadvāja went outside and measured out a level ground, free of trees and shrubs, situated near a slope with access to water.
On that ground, on a lunar day when the asterism was auspicious and was duly worshipped, he performed the consecrating oblation; and a proclamation was also announced throughout the city for that purpose, O best of speakers.
On the tournament ground, craftsmen duly constructed a very spacious arena in accordance with the prescriptions of the treatises, well appointed and equipped with all weapons for the king and the ladies as well, O bull among men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The people of the countryside also had great platforms raised there, broad and lofty, as well as richly adorned palanquins.
When that day arrived, the king together with his ministers, placing Bhīṣma foremost and Kṛpa the best of teachers beside him,
proceeded to the divine viewing pavilion draped with nets of pearls, adorned with lapis lazuli gems, and fashioned from pure gold.
The illustrious Gāndhārī and Kuntī, O best of the victorious, together with all the royal ladies, their attendants and retinues, ascended the platforms with joy, like the divine women ascending Mount Meru.
The four social orders headed by brahmins and kshatriyas came quickly from the city, eager to witness the weapons-mastery of the princes.
With musical instruments sounding and the eager curiosity of the people, that assembly became agitated at that time like a great ocean.
Then, wearing white garments, with a white sacred thread, white hair, white beard, and anointed with white garlands and unguents,
that teacher entered the middle of the arena together with his son, like the sun with Mars entering a sky bereft of clouds.
He, the best among the mighty, performed the consecrating rites in the proper seasonal manner and had brahmins versed in sacred formulas recite auspicious hymns there.
Immediately after the proclamation of that auspicious day, warriors entered carrying various kinds of weapons and equipment.
Then the mighty bulls of the Bhārata line entered, their armor fastened, their girdles tied, their quivers strapped on, bows in hand.
Those princes of great valor, with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head, in order of seniority, performed feats of arms there that were most wondrous.
Some in the crowd bowed their heads in fear of being struck by arrows; others gazed boldly with astonishment.
They pierced various targets with arrows embellished with their names, shot with skillful dexterity in diverse ways, while being carried swiftly on horses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing that assembled force of princes there with bows and arrows in hand, arrayed like a city of the gandharvas, those onlookers were struck with wonder.
Hundreds of thousands of men suddenly burst out shouting there, their eyes wide with amazement, "Excellent! Excellent!" O Bhārata.
Having demonstrated their skills repeatedly with the bow, in chariot-driving, on the back of elephants, on the back of horses, and in close combat, those mighty ones,
then again taking sword and shield as combatants, moved through the prescribed sword-paths on all terrains as instructed.
In the use of sword and shield, the spectators there observed in all of them swiftness, elegance of form, beauty, steadiness, and firmness of grip.
Then those two ever-exuberant ones, Suyodhana and Vṛkodara, descended into the arena with maces in hand, like two mountains with a single peak.
Their girdles fastened, those two long-armed heroes, intent on displaying their manhood, roared like two musth elephants competing for a cow in heat.
Those two mighty ones with gleaming maces wheeled through circular maneuvers to the right and to the left, like two bulls of equal strength.
Vidura and the offspring of Pāṇḍu's wife reported all the activities of the princes, the one to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the other to Gāndhārī.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: With the king of the Kurus and Bhīma, the foremost of the mighty, both present in the arena, that crowd, whose affections were divided by partiality, became as if split in two.
Loud, swelling cries of men suddenly arose, shouting "Ah, hero, king of the Kurus!" and "Ah, Bhīma!"
Then the wise son of Bharadvāja, seeing the arena resembling a turbulent ocean, spoke to his beloved son Aśvatthāman:
"Restrain these two of great valor, both of whom are trained and ready; let there not be an uproar in the arena arising from Bhīma and Duryodhana."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then those two, with maces raised and of great momentum, were restrained by the teacher's son, like two oceans churned by the wind at the end of a cosmic age.
Then Droṇa, standing in the arena ground, silencing the orchestra whose sound was like that of a great thunder-cloud, spoke these words:
"Let that Pārtha be seen, who is dearer to me than my own son, the best of all who know the science of weapons, the son of Indra, equal to Indra's younger brother."
At the teacher's word, that youth, having duly performed the benedictory rites, with arm-guard and finger-guard fastened, quiver full, and bow in hand,
wearing his golden armor, Phalguna appeared like a rain-cloud with the sun, with Indra's rainbow, with lightning, and with the evening glow.
Then a great tumultuous uproar arose from the entire arena, and musical instruments with conch shells sounded on all sides.
"This is the glorious son of Kuntī, this is the middle of the Pāṇḍava brothers, this is the son of the great Indra, this is the protector of the Kurus!"
"This is the greatest among those learned in arms, this is the best of those who uphold dharma, and this too among those of good character is the supreme treasure-house of character and knowledge."
Hearing such unequalled words spoken by the spectators in this manner, Kuntī's chest became wet with tears mingled with perspiration.
At that great sound, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the best of men whose hearing was full of it, spoke to Vidura with a joyful heart:
"O Kṣattṛ, what is this very great sound like a churning ocean that has suddenly arisen in the arena, as if rending the vault of heaven?"
Vidura said: O great king, this is Pārtha Phalguna, the joy of Pāṇḍu, who has descended into the arena with his armor on — this is the source of that very great sound.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: I am fortunate, I am blessed, I am protected, O greatly wise one, by those three fires of the Pāṇḍavas sprung from the kindling sticks of Pṛthā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the arena had grown noisy and then somehow settled, Bībhatsu displayed his skill with weapons, surpassing even the teacher.
With the Āgneya weapon he created fire; with the Varuṇa weapon he created water; with the Vāyavya weapon he created wind; with the Parjanya weapon he created clouds.
With the Bhauma weapon he sank into the earth; with the Parvata weapon he conjured mountains; and with the weapon of invisibility he vanished from sight once more.
In one moment he was tall, in the next he was short; in one moment he was at the chariot shaft, in the next he stood in the middle of the chariot, and the next instant he alighted on the ground.
He who was dear to his teacher, endowed with perfect form, pierced with various arrows both the delicate and fine targets, and also the heavy ones.
Into the mouth of an iron boar as it revolved, he loosed five arrows in rapid succession without a pause, as if they were a single arrow.
Into a swinging leather ball suspended on a rope, that hero of great valor drove twenty-one arrows.
He who was skilled in weapons thus displayed such great and varied feats with sword, with bow, and with mace.
Then, O Bhārata, when those feats were mostly concluded and the noise of the assembly and the sound of the instruments had died down,
from the direction of the gate arose the sound of slapping arms, indicating great power and prowess, resembling the crash of a thunderbolt.
"Are the mountains splitting? Is the earth cracking open? Is the sky being filled with clouds heavy with rain?"
Such was the sudden thought of the arena, O lord of the earth, and at that moment all the spectators turned toward the gate.
Droṇa, surrounded by the five Pārtha brothers, shone like the moon in the solar constellation attended by five bright stars.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The mighty hundred brothers together with Aśvatthāman encircled the risen Duryodhana, slayer of foes.
He, standing there with mace in hand, surrounded by those brothers with weapons raised and arrayed around him, shone as Indra, the destroyer of cities, once surrounded by the host of gods at the time of the destruction of the demons.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Given way by men whose eyes were wide with astonishment, Karṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities, entered the vast arena.
Wearing the armor he was born with, his face radiant with his natural earrings, bow in hand, sword fastened at his side, he walked on foot like a moving mountain.
Born of a maiden's womb, of wide fame, broad-eyed son of Pṛthā, a ray of the sharp-rayed sun god — Karṇa, the destroyer of enemy hosts.
Equal in valor and heroic power to lion, bull, and lordly elephant, comparable in his qualities of blazing radiance, beauty, and brilliance to the sun, the moon, and fire.
Tall, with the complexion of a golden palm tree, with the build of a lion, a youth of innumerable virtues, auspicious and glorious, born of the self of the sun god.
That long-armed hero, having surveyed the entire arena all around, made his salutation to Droṇa and Kṛpa as though without much reverence.
All the assembled people became still and steady-eyed, overtaken by the excitement of "Who is this?" and full of curiosity.
That best of speakers spoke in a voice deep as a thunder-cloud — an unknown brother addressing his brother, as the sun speaks to Indra.
"O Pārtha, whatever remarkable feat you have performed, I shall surpass it before the eyes of all these men — do not be amazed at yourself."
Even before that speech of his was finished, O best of speakers, the crowd sprang up swiftly all around as if hurled by a catapult.
O tiger among men, delight then touched Duryodhana, while shame and anger entered Bībhatsu in an instant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Karṇa, who always loved battle, permitted by Droṇa, performed with great strength everything that Pārtha had done there.
Then Duryodhana, together with his brothers, O Bhārata, embraced Karṇa there with joy and spoke these words:
"Welcome to you, O long-armed one! By good fortune you have arrived, O giver of honor. Both I and the kingdom of the Kurus are yours to enjoy as you wish."
Karṇa said: All else has been accomplished for me; I choose your friendship. And I wish to fight a single combat with Pārtha, O Bhārata.
Duryodhana said: Enjoy pleasures together with me, be the delight of kinsmen, and place your foot on the heads of all ill-wishers, O subduer of foes.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Pārtha, feeling as though his self had been thrown down, addressed Karṇa who stood in the midst of the group of brothers like an immovable mountain.
"O Karṇa, the worlds that await those who come uninvited and speak uninvited — those worlds shall be yours, slain by me."
Karṇa said: This arena is open to all; what claim do you have here, O Phalguna? For those of royal blood who are supreme in valor, might follows righteousness.
What use are taunts that give comfort only to the weak? Speak with arrows, O Bhārata — I shall sever your head with arrows today in the presence of the teacher.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities, permitted by Droṇa, embraced by his brothers who urged him on in haste, advanced toward him for battle.
Then Karṇa, embraced by Duryodhana along with his brothers who were ready for battle, stood there holding his bow with arrows set.
Then the sky became covered with clouds accompanied by lightning and thunder, preceded by Indra's bow, with lines of cranes laughing in their wake.
Then the Sun god, out of affection, seeing his son Karṇa gazing at the arena, drove away the clouds that had drawn near.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Pāṇḍava then appeared hidden in cloud-shadow, while Karṇa, blazing in the light of the sun, was fully visible.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stationed themselves where Karṇa stood; Droṇa son of Bharadvāja, Kṛpa, and Bhīṣma went to where Arjuna stood.
The arena split into two sides; the women too were divided in heart. Kuntī, daughter of Kuntibhoja, understanding the situation, fell into a swoon.
Vidura, who knew all duties, comforted Kuntī who had thus fainted, by sprinkling her with water mixed with sandalwood.
Then, having recovered her senses, she saw both sons clad in armor, and though deeply distressed, she could not do anything.
When both had raised their great bows, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat spoke — he who was skilled in the conduct of duels and knew all duties.
"This is the younger son of Pṛthā, the Pāṇḍava, a Kaurava — he will fight a duel with you.
O mighty-armed one, do you likewise declare your mother, your father, and your lineage before these kings whose family you adorn — then, knowing who you are, Arjuna will decide whether to fight you or not."
The face of Karṇa, spoken to thus, drooped with shame and appeared like a lotus weighed down and dampened by raindrops.
Duryodhana said: "O teacher, scripture establishes three types of origin for kings: one born of noble lineage, one who is a hero, and one who leads armies.
If Phalguna does not wish to fight in battle with one who is not a king, then I shall consecrate this man as king over the realm of Aṅga."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, at that very moment, Karṇa the great chariot-warrior, endowed with glory and great strength, was consecrated as king of Aṅga by those who knew the sacred hymns, with golden pots adorned with flowers, upon a golden throne.
Honored with white umbrella and fly-whisks, and amid shouts of victory, that king Karṇa — the bull among men — then spoke to that Kaurava king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"What shall I give you in return for this gift of a kingdom? Tell me, O tiger among kings, and I shall do it." Suyodhana replied to him: "I desire your undying friendship."
Thus spoken to, Karṇa replied "So be it," and both, embracing each other with joy, attained the highest delight.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Adhiratha, the charioteer, with his upper garment slipping and trembling with perspiration, entered the arena, leaning on a staff, calling out as if summoning.
Seeing him, Karṇa, restrained by reverence for his father, laid down his bow, and with his head still wet from the consecration, bowed down at his feet.
Then, in great agitation, covering his feet with the hem of his garment, the charioteer called out with full feeling, "My son!"
And embracing his head, overcome with affection, he wetted again with his tears the head that was still moist from the Aṅga kingdom consecration.
Seeing this, the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena, having determined "this one is the son of a charioteer," then spoke these words, laughing as it were.
"You, O son of a charioteer, do not deserve to be slain in battle by Arjuna. Act in keeping with your lineage — quickly take up the goad instead."
"You are not fit to enjoy the kingdom of Aṅga, O vile man — like a dog standing near the sacred fire claiming the sacrificial cake at a ritual."
Thus addressed, Karṇa's lips quivered slightly; he sighed deeply and looked up at the Sun standing in the sky.
Then Duryodhana the mighty, in anger, sprang up from among that grove of brothers like an elephant maddened with rut.
He spoke to Bhīmasena of terrible deeds who stood there: "O Vṛkodara, it is not fitting for you to speak such words.
"Strength is the highest virtue among Kṣatriyas; one related to the warrior class must fight. The origins of heroes and of rivers are truly difficult to know.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Fire arose from water and pervades all moving and unmoving things; from the bones of Dadhīci the thunderbolt was made, the slayer of demons.
"The blessed god Guha is called the son of Fire, born of the Kṛttikās, son of Rudra, and son of the Gaṅgā — he who embodies all mysteries.
"Brahmins born of Kṣatriya women are also renowned; our teacher Droṇa was born from a pot; preceptor Kṛpa was born from a clump of reeds; and even the birth of your own family has been proclaimed by kings.
"How could a doe give birth to a tiger like him, blazing like the sun, adorned with divine earrings and armor, and marked by celestial signs?
"This lord of men deserves the kingship of the whole earth, not merely Aṅga's kingdom — by virtue of this arm-strength of his and by my authority as his ally."
"Or whoever among men does not approve of what I have done — let him mount his chariot or stand on foot and bend his bow."
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas!" arose throughout the arena, accompanied by shouts of "Bravo!" — and the sun went to its setting.
Then Duryodhana, O king, took Karṇa by the hand, and by the light of the torches they departed from that arena.
The Pāṇḍavas together with Droṇa and Kṛpa, O lord of men, and all along with Bhīṣma, departed each to his own quarters.
Some among the people departed crying "Arjuna!" some "Karṇa!" O Bhārata, and some "Duryodhana!" — so they went their ways.
And in Kuntī's heart, love concealed by affection grew, for she had recognized her son the king of Aṅga, indicated by his divine marks.
And for Duryodhana too, O king, upon obtaining Karṇa, the fear that had arisen on account of Arjuna quickly vanished.
And that hero, having demonstrated his mastery of weapons, addressed Suyodhana with high courtesy; and Yudhiṣṭhira too formed the opinion at that time: "There is no bowman on this earth equal to Karṇa."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having assembled all his students, Droṇa urged them all without exception to fetch his teacher's fee, O lord of the earth.
"Seize Drupada the king of Pāñcāla in the forefront of battle and bring him to me — that shall be your highest gift to me. May it go well with you."
Saying "So be it," all of them, those mighty strikers, swiftly mounted their chariots and went together with Droṇa to give the teacher his fee.
Then those bulls among men attacked the Pāñcālas, slaying them as they went, and crushed the city of the mighty Drupada.
Those bulls of the Bhārata clan seized Drupada son of Yajñasena at the forefront of battle and brought him along with his ministers to Droṇa.
His pride broken, his wealth taken, and now brought under subjection — Droṇa, reflecting on that old enmity in his mind, then spoke to Drupada.
"Your kingdom has been swiftly crushed and your city destroyed by me. Having fallen alive into the power of an enemy who was once your friend, what do you desire?"
Having said this and laughed at him, Droṇa considered and then spoke again: "Do not fear for your life, O king — we Brahmins are forgiving.
"The affection that grew between you and me, O bull among Kṣatriyas, was nurtured by those childhood games we played together in the hermitage.
"I would seek friendship with you once again, O bull among men. I give you a boon, O king — receive back half of your kingdom."
"Indeed, one who is not a king cannot be the friend of kings. That is why I have striven for a kingdom of your own, O Yajñasena.
"You are king on the southern bank of the Bhāgīrathī, and I am on the northern bank — know me as your friend, O Pāñcāla, if you are willing."
Drupada said: "This is not surprising, O Brahmin — among great souls of valor, such things occur. I am pleased with you and I desire an everlasting friendship with you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, Droṇa released him, O Bhārata, and honoring him with a glad heart, restored to him half the kingdom.
With a downcast heart, Drupada then settled in Makandi on the bank of the Gaṅgā, along with its dependent provinces, and in the great city of Kampilya, and over the southern Pāñcālas as far as the river Carmaṇvatī.
But remembering his enmity with Droṇa, Drupada did not rest, and he saw no way to defeat him by Kṣatriya force alone.
Knowing himself to be inferior in Brahminic power, that king resolved to seek the birth of a son — and Droṇa took possession of the territory of Ahicchatra.
Thus, O king, was the city of Ahicchatra along with its surrounding provinces conquered in battle by Arjuna and delivered to Droṇa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Duryodhana the evil-minded, observing Bhīmasena who was superior in physical strength and Dhanañjaya who had mastered every science, burned with envy.
Then Karṇa the son of Vikartana and Śakuni the son of Subala sought by many means to slay the Pāṇḍavas.
But the Pāṇḍavas, those crushers of foes, were fully aware of all of this; making no outward show of it, they abided by the counsel of Vidura.
The citizens, seeing the sons of Pāṇḍu full of virtues, would then gather and speak of them in the crossroads and assembly halls.
"Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, uses wisdom as his eyes because of his blindness — he could not obtain the kingdom before; how then should he become king now?
"And Bhīṣma son of Śaṃtanu, who is true to his word and bound by great vows, having renounced the kingdom long ago, will never take it up now.
"Let us therefore duly consecrate today the eldest Pāṇḍava, who is young in years yet old in conduct, truthful and compassionate."
"For he, knowing dharma, will honor and provide all manner of enjoyments to Bhīṣma son of Śaṃtanu, to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and to their sons alike."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Duryodhana the evil-minded, hearing those words of the citizens who were devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira, burned with anguish.
That wicked soul, burning with envy, could not endure those words; scorched by jealousy, he came to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then, finding his father alone and paying his respects, burning with the anguish of the citizens' affection for another, he afterwards spoke these words.
"Father, I have heard the inauspicious words of the chattering citizens — setting you aside and Bhīṣma too, they wish the Pāṇḍava as their lord."
"This is also Bhīṣma's view — he does not desire the kingdom; but the people of the city intend to inflict the greatest harm upon us."
"Pāṇḍu obtained the kingdom from his father and by his own virtues in former times; you too were given the kingdom but could not retain it due to the association of deficiencies."
"If this Pāṇḍava obtains the heritage of Pāṇḍu, then it will go surely to his son and to his son's son, so others will say."
"We, deprived of the royal lineage along with our sons, shall become despised by the world, O lord of the earth."
"So that we do not constantly fall into ruin and subsist on another's bounty, O king, make swift arrangements to prevent this."
"If only you had been firmly established in the kingdom from the start, O king, then we would have surely obtained the kingdom even if the people were unwilling."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard such words from his son, reflected for a moment and then spoke to Duryodhana.
"Pāṇḍu was ever devoted to righteousness and always acted for my good and benefit; he was so to all the kinsmen, and especially so to me."
I know nothing of his that he wishes done — food or anything else — without his informing me; firm in his vow, he always reports the kingdom to me.
His son is just as Pāṇḍu was — devoted to righteousness, virtuous, renowned throughout the world, and greatly honored by the citizens.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
How then can we forcibly wrest him from this kingdom inherited from his father and grandfather, especially when he has allies on his side?
The ministers appointed by Pāṇḍu are maintained, the army is continually maintained, and even their sons and grandsons are especially well maintained.
Those Paurava people who were honored in the past by Pāṇḍu, dear son — how would they not slay us along with our kinsmen for the sake of Yudhiṣṭhira?
Duryodhana said: All this has indeed been considered by me, father. Recognizing this weakness in myself, I have bound all the constituent elements of the state through gifts of wealth and honor.
They shall certainly become our allies first and foremost; the leading men of wealth together with the ministers are now on my side, O lord of the earth.
Therefore you, sire, should quickly send the Pāṇḍavas away by gentle means to the city of Vāraṇāvata.
When the kingdom is firmly established in me, O king, then Kuntī together with her sons shall return here, O Bhārata.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Duryodhana, this very thought revolves in my heart too, but because of the wickedness of such an intention I do not disclose it.
Neither Bhīṣma, nor Droṇa, nor Kṣattā, nor Gautama will ever approve of the sons of Kuntī being sent into exile.
For we and they are equal among the Kauravas, my son; these righteous and high-minded men would never desire unfairness.
How then would we not be condemned by the Kauravas and by these great-souled men, and likewise by the world, dear son?
Duryodhana said: Bhīṣma is always neutral; Droṇa's son stands on my side; wherever the son goes, so will Droṇa — there is no doubt in this.
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvan — wherever these three go, he will follow, and he will never abandon Droṇa and his sister's son.
Kṣattā is indeed bound to us by self-interest, and where the others stand is hidden; he alone is not capable of opposing us for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore, with confidence, send the sons of Pāṇḍu along with their mother into exile at Vāraṇāvata this very day — no fault will arise from this.
This terrible thing that robs one of sleep, like a dart lodged in the heart — this blazing fire of grief — extinguish it by this course of action.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Duryodhana, together with his younger brothers, gradually won over all those constituent elements of the state through gifts of wealth and honor.
Certain clever ministers deployed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra began to speak of the pleasant city of Vāraṇāvata.
"A great festival is taking place, the most delightful on earth, in the city of Vāraṇāvata, the city of the Lord of Beasts."
"It is a region filled with all precious gems, a place that delights the hearts of men." Thus, on the instruction of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, they spread such talk.
As the pleasant city of Vāraṇāvata was thus being spoken of, O king, there arose in the minds of the sons of Pāṇḍu a desire to go there.
When the king judged that their curiosity had been aroused, the son of Ambikā then addressed the Pāṇḍavas thus.
"These men of mine constantly speak again and again of the city of Vāraṇāvata as the most delightful in the world."
"If you think fit, dear sons, go with your retinues and attendants to enjoy the festival at Vāraṇāvata, like the gods at play."
"Bestow gems on the Brahmins and on singers of all kinds as you please, like radiant gods."
"Having sported there for some time and experienced the greatest joy, you shall return here to Hāstinapura, happy and well."
Perceiving the intention of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and also his own helplessness, Yudhiṣṭhira replied to him with the words "So be it."
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, quietly and with a heavy heart, spoke these words to the greatly wise Bhīṣma, the high-minded Vidura, Droṇa, Bāhlika, and the Kaurava Somadatta,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
to Kṛpa, to the son of the preceptor, and to the glorious Gāndhārī — Yudhiṣṭhira softly and sorrowfully spoke these words to them at that time.
"We shall dwell in the pleasant and populous city of Vāraṇāvata with our retinues, dear sir, by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
"With cheerful minds, all of you utter auspicious words; may evil not overpower us when we are strengthened by your blessings."
Thus addressed by the son of Pāṇḍu, all those Kauravas, with cheerful faces, turned toward the Pāṇḍavas.
"May you ever fare well upon the road, and may all beings everywhere bless you; may no ill whatsoever befall you from any quarter, O sons of Pāṇḍu."
Then the Pāṇḍavas, having been blessed with good omens and with the aim of regaining the kingdom, completed all their duties and departed for Vāraṇāvata.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the great-souled Pāṇḍavas had been thus addressed by the king, the wicked Duryodhana was overcome with great joy.
He took his minister Purocana aside in private, O bull of the Bhāratas, and grasping his right hand, spoke these words to him.
"This earth full of wealth is mine, Purocana; as it is mine, so it is yours — therefore you must guard it."
"For there is no other ally of mine more trustworthy than you, with whom I might deliberate and conspire as I can with you."
"Preserve secrecy, dear friend, and rid me of my enemies by a clever stratagem; do as I tell you."
"The Pāṇḍavas have been sent by Dhṛtarāṣṭra to Vāraṇāvata; they will enjoy the festival there by Dhṛtarāṣṭra's command."
"You yourself must go to Vāraṇāvata this very day by a swift chariot drawn by mules — see to it that you go."
"Having gone there, build near the armory a four-walled mansion, most well-enclosed, at great expense."
"Hemp, resin, and whatever other materials there are that are flammable — have all of them supplied there."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Mix clay with clarified butter, oil, and a generous quantity of lac, and have this mixture plastered on the walls."
"Hemp, bamboo, ghee, timber, and various implements — deposit all of these inside that dwelling all around."
"Do it in such a way that even if the Pāṇḍavas examine it, they will not suspect you, nor will other men think it a fire-trap."
"When the house has been built in this way, honor the Pāṇḍavas greatly and lodge them there — the sons of Pāṇḍu and Kuntī together with her companions."
"The finest seats, carriages, and beds must be provided for the Pāṇḍavas, so that my father may be pleased."
"Everything must be arranged so that they live with full confidence and delight in the city of Vāraṇāvata until the turning of the right moment."
"When you know that they are completely trusting, lying asleep without any fear, then you shall set fire to that dwelling from the door."
"Burnt thus in their own house, people will say 'they were burned,' or their kinsmen may say so whenever they speak on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas."
Promising "So be it" to the Kaurava, Purocana departed for the city of Vāraṇāvata with a mule-drawn chariot.
Having gone there swiftly, O king, standing firm in Duryodhana's resolve, Purocana did everything exactly as the prince had instructed.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The Pāṇḍavas, having yoked their chariots with excellent horses peerless in speed, as they were about to mount, sorrowfully clasped Bhīṣma's feet.
And those of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the great-souled Droṇa, and of all the other elders, and of Vidura and Kṛpa as well.
Thus the vow-observing Pāṇḍavas paid homage to all the elder Kurus, embraced those of equal station, and were saluted by the young.
Having asked leave of all the mothers and circumambulated them, and having taken leave of all the constituent elements of the kingdom as well, they departed for Vāraṇāvata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The greatly wise Vidura and the other bulls of the Kuru race, and the citizens as well, followed those tigers among men, worn thin with grief.
There, certain Brahmins spoke fearlessly at that time, grieving deeply for the sons of Pāṇḍu, O bull of the Bhāratas.
"The king looks upon things with partiality; Dhṛtarāṣṭra, his mind utterly shrouded in darkness, is very evil-minded and does not perceive righteousness."
"For the sinless Pāṇḍava would not sanction evil, nor would Bhīma the foremost among the strong, nor Dhanaṃjaya the son of Kuntī — how much less would the two greatly wise sons of Mādrī do so?"
"Dhṛtarāṣṭra cannot tolerate that kingdom obtained through their father; this is complete unrighteousness — why does this Bhīṣma approve of the sons of Kuntī, bulls of the Bhāratas, being sent into banishment unjustly?"
"For the son of Śaṃtanu was like a father to us in former times, as was the royal sage Vicitravīrya, and Pāṇḍu the joy of the Kurus."
"Now that that tiger among men has met his destined end, Dhṛtarāṣṭra cannot bear these young princes."
"Unwilling to bear this, let us all abandon our homes in this greatest of cities and go wherever Yudhiṣṭhira goes."
To those citizens speaking thus, distressed and worn with grief, the righteous king Yudhiṣṭhira spoke with the greatest affection, himself pained by their sorrow.
"What the lord of the earth has said, as our honored father and highest elder, that must be done by us without doubt — such is our vow."
"You are our friends — circumambulate us, bless us with your benedictions, and then return each to your own home."
"When the occasion arises in which you can be of service to us, then you shall do what is dear and beneficial to me."
They promised "So be it," circumambulated the Pāṇḍavas, blessed them with benedictions, and returned to the city.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the citizens had turned back, Vidura — who knows all righteousness, a wise man speaking to a wise man, one who knows the language of the learned, one who truly perceives the ends of right and wealth — spoke these words to the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas to enlighten him.
"Understanding this, one should act in such a way as to cross over the danger. A weapon sharp without being of iron is what cuts through the body; he who knows this — and who knows the counter-blow — enemies cannot strike him down."
"The burner of dry grass and the burner of cold — the creature that dwells in holes in the great thicket — he who guards himself thinking 'it shall not burn me' is the one who lives."
"One without eyes does not know the road; one without eyes does not find the directions; one without steadiness does not attain prosperity — understand this, you who have been awakened."
"A man receives from those not close to him a weapon not made of iron; gaining the shelter of a porcupine's burrow, he can escape the consuming fire."
"By travelling one learns the paths; by the stars one finds the directions; by subduing one's five senses oneself, one is not afflicted."
Having given this counsel, having walked with them a little way, having circumambulated the Pāṇḍavas, and having bade them farewell, Vidura returned home.
When Vidura and Bhīṣma and the citizens had turned back, Kuntī addressed Ajātaśatru and spoke these words.
The words that Vidura spoke, as though speaking without speaking in public — that you replied 'so be it' to him — we do not know what that was.
If it is possible for us to hear it, and if it contains nothing harmful, I wish to hear the entire conversation between you and him.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Vidura told me, "Beware of poison and of fire," and he also said, "Let no path remain unknown to you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He told me, "One who has conquered his senses will win the earth." I replied to Vidura, "All of this is understood."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Setting out on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight, on the day of Rohiṇī in the month of Phālguna, they arrived at Vāraṇāvata and beheld the citizens there.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all the subjects of the city of Vāraṇāvata, adorned with every auspicious article, according to scriptural injunction, with diligent care,
Hearing of the arrival of the sons of Pāṇḍu, came forth in thousands with various conveyances to meet those best of men, with utmost joy, the very moment they heard the news.
Those citizens of Vāraṇāvata, having approached the sons of Kuntī, all offered blessings of victory and stood surrounding them in attendance.
Surrounded by them, that tiger among men, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, shone like a god in appearance, like Vajrapāṇi amidst the immortals.
Honoured by the citizens, and having in turn honoured the citizens, those sinless ones entered Vāraṇāvata, which was adorned and crowded with people.
Having entered the city, those heroes quickly proceeded to the homes of the Brāhmaṇas, O protector of the earth, who were intent on their own duties,
and those best of men visited also the houses of the city's administrators and charioteers, and likewise the homes of Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Honoured by the citizens, those bulls among the Bhāratas, the Pāṇḍavas, thereafter went to their residence, with Purocana leading the way.
Purocana provided them with food and drink fit for consumption, good beds, and excellent seats.
There, honoured by him and furnished with very costly furnishings, attended upon by the men of the city, they dwelt.
But after they had dwelt there for ten nights, Purocana then pointed out to them a house called "Śiva" (auspicious) — though it was truly inauspicious.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There those tigers among men entered with their belongings, at Purocana's word, like the Guhyakas entering mount Kailāsa.
But examining that dwelling, Yudhiṣṭhira, versed in all righteousness, sniffing the scent of fat mixed with ghee and lac, said to Bhīmasena, "This is a fire-trap."
"Clearly this dwelling has been made as a fire-trap, O scorcher of foes — hemp and pine resin are plainly used in its construction, and all materials such as muñja-grass, reeds, and bamboo are thoroughly soaked in ghee."
"This was well constructed by trusted, skilled craftsmen versed in building — this wicked Purocana wishes to burn me when I am off-guard."
"It was this very danger that Vidura of great intellect foresaw, O Pārtha, and for that reason he warned me beforehand."
"We, having been warned by him, know this inauspicious house — well built by craftsmen who secretly follow Duryodhana's will."
Bhīma said: If you believe this dwelling to be a fire-trap as prepared, then it is well that we return to where we stayed before.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I think we should remain here, vigilant and showing no outward sign — like those who are lost seeking a safe and certain path from here.
"For if Purocana were to detect any sign from us, he would then act swiftly and burn us by force."
"This Purocana has no fear of public censure or of unrighteousness — for so does he behave, that dull-witted one, standing firm in Suyodhana's command."
"And even if we were burned here, would our grandfather Bhīṣma become angry? And why would he anger the Kauravas? He would be angry only out of righteousness, and so would the other bulls of the Kurus."
"But if we were to flee, fearing the fire, then Suyodhana, greedy for kingship, would have us all killed through his spies."
"One who stands secure in position would surely destroy those who have no footing; one with support would destroy those without allies; one with a great treasury would certainly destroy those with a depleted treasury, by his machinations."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Therefore we must deceive this wicked man and that wicked Suyodhana as well, and dwell in concealment, moving from place to place."
"We, adopting the habit of hunting, shall roam this earth, and thus the paths for our escape will become known to us."
"And let us this very day dig a well-concealed underground tunnel — breathing quietly there, the fire will not be able to consume us."
"While we live here, we must act diligently so that neither Purocana nor any citizen of the town suspects us."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: A certain friend of Vidura, a skilled digger, in a secluded spot, O king, spoke these words to the Pāṇḍavas:
"I am sent by Vidura; I am highly skilled as a digger. My task is to do what is dear to the Pāṇḍavas — what shall I do for you?"
"Vidura told me in secret, 'Secure the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas here with his full trust' — what shall I do for you?"
"On the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight, Purocana will set fire to the door of this dwelling of yours."
"The Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men, along with their mother, are to be burned alive — thus is the resolve of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, as I have heard, O Pārtha."
"Moreover, Vidura spoke something to you in the Mleccha tongue, O Pāṇḍava, and you replied 'so be it' — this is the reason for my trust."
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, firm in truth, said to him: "I recognise you, gentle one, as indeed a friend of Vidura."
"Pure, trustworthy, dear, and ever of firm devotion — there is no need of any further proof of recognition from the wise one."
"As he is to us, so are you to us — we make no distinction between you. We are yours as we are his. Protect us as the wise one would."
"It is my conviction that this shelter — a fire-trap — was arranged by Purocana for my destruction, at the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son."
"That wicked one, possessed of a treasury and with allies, the evil-minded, wicked-souled one — he harasses us constantly at all times."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"May you, with effort, deliver us from this fire — for if we are burned here, Suyodhana would have his wish fulfilled."
"This is an arsenal of that evil-souled one, built at the edge of the rampart, inescapable — this great construction."
"This is surely that inauspicious deed he intended to do — Vidura knew it beforehand, and for that reason he warned us."
"This is the very danger that Kṣattā foresaw before — while Purocana remains unaware of us, deliver us from it."
Having promised "so be it," the digger applied himself diligently and, excavating a trench, made a very large underground tunnel.
And he made in the middle of that dwelling a not-too-large opening fitted with a door, unknown to others and level with the ground, O Bhārata.
Out of fear of Purocana, he kept the opening covered; and that one of inauspicious mind (Purocana) dwelt always at the door of the house.
There they all dwelt, armed, through the nights, O king, and by day the sons of Pāṇḍu went hunting from forest to forest.
Appearing trusting though they trusted not, deceiving Purocana, appearing content though discontented, O king, they dwelt in the utmost misery.
And the men dwelling in the city did not come to know of them — except for the minister Vidura and that best of diggers.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Seeing them apparently cheerful, having dwelt there for a full year, and noting that they appeared quite at ease, Purocana felt joy.
When Purocana was thus rejoicing, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and knower of righteousness, then spoke to Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the twins:
"This wicked Purocana believes us to be fully at ease — this cruel-souled one has been deceived. I think the time for flight has come."
"Setting fire to the arsenal and burning Purocana as well, and leaving six living bodies here, let us flee undetected."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, under the pretext of charity, Kuntī gave a great feast to Brāhmaṇas by night, O king, and women came there.
They, having enjoyed themselves as they wished, having eaten and drunk, O Bhārata, departed in the night to their homes, taking leave of Mādhavī (Kuntī).
But a Niṣāda woman with five sons, seeking food, came to that feast by chance, driven by fate, together with her sons.
She, having drunk wine, was intoxicated, she and her sons overcome with intoxication, and together with all her sons, O king, she fell fast asleep in that very dwelling, bereft of consciousness, like one dead, O lord of men.
Then, when the wind was blowing fiercely, in the night, when the people had fallen asleep, O lord, Bhīma set fire to the place where Purocana slept.
Then a very great blaze and a loud crackling of the fire arose, and by that the crowd of people was awakened.
The citizens said: "That wicked one of perverted intellect, urged on by Duryodhana, had this house built and set on fire — for his own destruction."
"Alas, shame on Dhṛtarāṣṭra's intention — it is not at all proper — he who caused the innocent, young Pāṇḍavas to be burned by his minister."
"By good fortune, this evil-souled one of utterly perverted mind is now burned — he who would have burned these best of men, who were innocent and had trusted him completely."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus the citizens of Vāraṇāvata lamented, and surrounding that house, they stood on all sides through the night.
And the Pāṇḍavas too, O king, deeply distressed, together with their mother, came out through that tunnel and went away in secret, undetected.
But the Pāṇḍavas, those scorchers of enemies, on account of that lack of sleep and from exhaustion, were unable to move quickly along with their mother.
But Bhīmasena, O king of kings, of terrifying speed and prowess, went forward, taking all his brothers and their mother as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That mighty one placed his mother on his shoulder, held the twins in his lap, and grasped the two Pārthas — those brothers of immense strength — with his hands.
Swiftly snapping trees and splitting the earth with his feet, that radiant Vṛkodara, swift as the wind, advanced rapidly.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, when the night had passed, the entire populace of the city came there in haste, wishing to see the sons of Pāṇḍu.
While extinguishing the fire, those people then saw that house of lac burnt to ashes, and the minister Purocana burned as well.
"Surely this was arranged by the evil-acting Duryodhana for the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas" — thus did the people cry out.
"Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, without doubt, burned the heirs of Pāṇḍu with Dhṛtarāṣṭra's knowledge — for he (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) did not restrain him."
"Surely Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, does not follow righteousness, nor does Droṇa, nor Vidura, nor Kṛpa, nor the other Kauravas."
"We send word to that evil-souled Dhṛtarāṣṭra: your supreme desire is fulfilled — you have burned the Pāṇḍavas."
Then, as they cleared away the fire in search of the Pāṇḍavas, they saw the Niṣāda woman burned — she of five sons, who was innocent.
The tunnel which that very digger had made while clearing the house was filled in with earth and left unseen by those men.
Then the townspeople sent word to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that the Pāṇḍavas and the minister Purocana had been consumed by fire.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, hearing that most grievous news — the destruction of the sons of Pāṇḍu — lamented in deep sorrow.
"Today my brother King Pāṇḍu, so rare and dear, is truly dead — for those heroes have been burned together with their mother."
"Let men go at once to the city of Vāraṇāvata to render fitting honors to those heroes and to that daughter of the king of the Kuntīs."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let them also cause auspicious and great funeral mounds to be made, and let friends honor all those who have died there."
"In these circumstances, whatever beneficent rites I am able to have performed for the Pāṇḍavas and for Kuntī — let all of that be done with wealth."
Having spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Ambikā, surrounded by his kinsmen, then performed the water-offering for the sons of Pāṇḍu.
All the Kauravas wept aloud, wholly given over to grief; but Vidura grieved only a little, for he knew the higher truth.
The Pāṇḍavas, having escaped from the city of Vāraṇāvata, O king, swiftly journeyed on, keeping to the southern direction.
Discerning their path by the stars at night, facing southward and pressing hard, they entered a dense forest, O king.
Then the sons of Pāṇḍu, exhausted, tormented by thirst, and blinded by sleep, spoke again these words to the mighty Bhīmasena:
"What could be more wretched than this — that we wander in a dense forest, knowing not the directions and unable to walk?"
"And we do not know whether that wicked Purocana has been burned; how can we escape this fear while remaining unseen?"
"Take us up again as before and carry us, O Bhārata — for you alone among us are strong, like the ever-moving wind."
Thus addressed by the king of dharma, the immensely powerful Bhīmasena took up Kuntī and his brothers and departed swiftly.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As he strode swiftly, a wind arose driven by the speed of his thighs, O king, like the wind at the onset of the bright autumn season.
He crushed the flowering and fruit-bearing forest trees and snapped the wooden shrubs that stood along his path.
Thus breaking trees, he of measureless valor strode on; by his speed, something like a swoon came over the Pāṇḍus.
And again and again crossing wide rivers by the paddle of his arms, they reached a concealed path, driven by fear of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With great difficulty he carried on his back that one delicate and illustrious mother over the steep and uneven river banks.
Those bulls of the Bhāratas arrived at a region of the forest scarce in roots, fruits, and water, full of fierce birds and beasts, dreadful, toward evening.
The twilight was terrible; the beasts and birds were fearsome; all directions were dark; and unseasonable winds blew.
Those scions of the Kuru line, tormented by fatigue and thirst and overwhelmed by mounting sleep, could not walk on.
Then Bhīma, having entered that vast, desolate, dreadful forest, ran toward a great banyan tree with wide shade, lovely and inviting.
Having set them all down there, that bull of the Bhāratas said, "I will seek water here; rest yourselves, O lord."
"These cranes that move on water are crying sweetly — I believe there is certainly a great body of water here."
Permitted by his eldest brother with the word "go," O Bhārata, he went to the place where the water-birds were crying.
He drank water there and bathed, O bull of the Bhāratas, and then brought water back in his upper garment, O king.
Having returned swiftly from a distance of just a league toward his mother, wolf-bellied Bhīma saw his mother and brothers lying asleep on the bare ground and lamented, his soul overwhelmed with grief.
"Those who formerly at Vāraṇāvata did not reach sleep even on the most precious of beds — today they lie sleeping on the bare earth."
"She who is the sister of Vāsudeva, crusher of enemy hosts, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, Kuntī, honored for all auspicious marks —"
"— daughter-in-law of Vicitravīrya, wife of the great-souled Pāṇḍu, she who always slept in palaces, radiant as the inside of a lotus —"
"— most tender of women, fit for the most excellent of beds — behold her lying today here on the earth, where she does not belong."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"She who gave birth to these sons from Dharma, from Indra, and from Vāyu — this very one lies exhausted on the ground today, so undeserving of such a fate."
"What greater sorrow could I behold beyond this — I who today see these tigers among men lying asleep on the bare earth?"
"He who deserves kingship over all three worlds, that king who knows dharma — how does he lie exhausted on the ground like an ordinary man?"
"This one, dark as a blue raincloud, peerless among men on earth, lies on the ground like a common person — what could be more sorrowful than this?"
"These two, who in beauty of form are like the twin Aśvins among the gods — today these two lie sound asleep on the bare ground like ordinary folk."
"He whose kinsmen are not hostile, not besmirchers of the family — he lives happily in the world, like a solitary tree in a village."
"For a single tree in a village that is full of leaves and fruit becomes a shrine; without kinsmen to trouble it, it is revered and well honored."
"And those who have many kinsmen who are brave and grounded in dharma — they live happily in the world and remain free of affliction."
"Powerful, prosperous, rejoiced over by friends and kinsmen, they live leaning on one another, like trees that grow in the forest."
"But we have been exiled by the evil-souled Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with his son, and somehow escaped being burned by his command."
"Freed from that burning, we have taken refuge under this tree — having attained the utmost hardship, what direction shall we take?"
"I can see that a town is not very far from this forest. These ones must be guarded while they sleep — I myself shall keep watch."
"These ones will drink water later when they awaken, having conquered their fatigue." Having thus resolved, Bhīma kept vigil himself at that time.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While they lay sleeping there, a rākṣasa named Hiḍimba was perched in a śāla tree not far from that forest.
Cruel, a devourer of human flesh, of great valor and enormous strength, misshapen in form, tawny-eyed, fearsome, dreadful to behold, hungry for flesh, tormented by hunger — he happened to catch sight of them.
With fingers pointing upward he was scratching himself, shaking his matted, rough hair, yawning wide-mouthed, and looking at them again and again.
That vile devourer of human flesh, huge of body and great of strength, sniffing the smell of humans, said this to his sister:
"After a long time, food that is dear to my heart has come my way today. Fat drips down; my tongue goes around my mouth."
"My eight fangs, very sharp-tipped, so long unbearably eager to strike — I shall sink them into those sleek and juicy bodies."
"Seizing a human throat and severing the great artery, I shall drink the fresh, warm, frothy blood in abundance."
"Go, find out who these are that lie sleeping sheltered in the forest. The powerful smell of humans all but satisfies my nostrils."
"Slay all these humans and bring them to me. Those sleeping in our territory need have no fear from them; you need not fear them either."
"Having prepared the flesh of these humans to our liking, we two shall feast together. Quickly carry out my word."
Understanding her brother's command, the rākṣasī hastened to where the Pāṇḍavas were, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Going there, she saw the Pāṇḍavas along with Pṛthā lying asleep, and Bhīmasena, the unconquered one, keeping watch.
The moment the rākṣasī saw Bhīmasena, risen like the trunk of a śāla tree, she fell in love with him — peerless in beauty on earth.
"This one, dark-complexioned, long-armed, lion-shouldered, of great splendor, conch-necked, lotus-eyed — he would be a fitting husband for me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I shall never carry out my brother's word laden with cruelty, for the love of a husband is far more powerful than fraternal affection."
"My brother's satisfaction from their being slain would last but a moment, whereas if they are not slain I shall rejoice for endless years."
She, who could assume any form at will, took on the most beautiful human form and approached the long-armed Bhīmasena slowly, slowly.
Like a creeper vine seemingly bashful, adorned with divine ornaments, she smiled first and then spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"Where have you come from, and who are you, O bull among men? Who are these men sleeping here, godlike in form?"
"And who is this tall, dark, delicate woman of yours, O sinless one, who sleeps having entered this forest as at ease as if in her own home?"
"She does not know that this dense forest is haunted by rākṣasas; for there dwells here an evil-souled rākṣasa named Hiḍimba."
"It is by that rākṣasa, my brother of wicked disposition, who desires to eat your flesh, that I have been sent here, O one comparable to the immortals."
"But I, having set eyes on you, radiant as the embryo of a god, desire no other husband — this I tell you truly."
"Knowing this, O knower of dharma, act toward me as is proper; receive me who receive you, whose heart and body are smitten with love."
"I will protect you, O long-armed one, from that man-eating rākṣasa. We two shall dwell in mountain fastnesses — be my husband, O sinless one."
"For I am one who moves through the sky and can roam wherever I desire. Obtain unequaled delight here and there together with me."
Bhīma said: Who, even though powerful, would abandon today his mother, his eldest brother, these younger brothers — who could do so, O rākṣasī?
"For what man like me, overcome by desire, would surrender these sleeping brothers and his mother as food for a rākṣasa and then go away?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The rākṣasī said: I will do whatever pleases you. Awaken all of them — I will gladly deliver you all from that man-eating rākṣasa.
Bhīma said: I will not, out of fear of your evil-souled brother, awaken my brothers and my mother who are sleeping comfortably in the forest, O rākṣasī.
"For rākṣasas are not capable of enduring my valor, O timid one — nor are humans, nor gandharvas, nor yakṣas, O lovely-eyed one."
"Go or stay, O auspicious one — do whatever you wish; or send here that man-eating brother of yours, O slender one."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Knowing that she had been gone a long time, Hiḍimba, lord of rākṣasas, descended from that tree and came toward the Pāṇḍavas.
Red-eyed, long-armed, hair erect, of great strength, his body massive as a mass of storm-clouds, his face blazing with sharp fangs —
Seeing him rush toward them in so terrible a form, Hiḍimbā, trembling with fear, spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"This evil-souled man-eater is rushing toward us in a fury. Do as I tell you — together with your brothers.
I can go wherever I wish, hero, and I am endowed with the power of a rākṣasa. Climb onto my hips and I will carry you through the air.
Wake those who are sleeping soundly, and your mother too, O scorcher of foes. Taking all of you, I will fly through the sky."
Bhīma said: "Fear not, O broad-hipped one — while I stand here, this one is nothing. I will slay him before your very eyes, O slender-waisted lady.
This wretch of a rākṣasa has not the power, O timid one, to withstand my onset in battle — nor indeed could all the rākṣasas combined.
Look at these two well-rounded arms of mine, like the trunks of elephants; at these thighs, like iron clubs; and at this compact chest of mine.
Today you shall see my valor equal to Indra's, O beautiful one. Do not despise me, O broad-hipped lady, thinking me a mere mortal."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hiḍimbā said: "I do not despise you, O tiger among men — you are godlike in form. Yet the rākṣasa surpasses human beings even in the matter of footstep-speed."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Even as Bhīmasena was speaking thus, O Bhārata, the enraged man-eating rākṣasa heard those words.
Hiḍimba observed his sister's human form — her hair adorned with garland-strands and wreaths, her face like the full moon,
with beautiful brows, nose, eyes, and hair-ends, delicate nails and skin, decked in all ornaments, and clothed in the finest of garments.
Seeing her bearing that exceedingly beautiful human form and suspecting her of desire for a man, the man-eater flew into a rage.
The enraged rākṣasa, O best of the Kurus, rolling his great wide eyes at his sister, then spoke these words to her:
"Who is this fool who goes about obstructing me, eager as I am for my meal? Hiḍimbā, do you not fear my wrath? Are you so deluded?
Shame on you, wicked woman, lusting after a man, bringing dishonor upon me, and disgracing all our forebear chiefs among the rākṣasas!
Those very men whom you have taken under your protection, doing me this great disservice — I shall slay all of them this day, along with you."
Having said this, Hiḍimba with his blood-red eyes gnashed his teeth against his teeth and charged at Hiḍimbā to kill her.
Seeing him rushing forward, Bhīma, the foremost of warriors, that spirited hero, checked him with threats and cried: "Stand! Stand!"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Bhīmasena, seeing the rākṣasa enraged against his sister, said with something like a laugh:
"What do you want with those sleeping peacefully, Hiḍimba, whether woken or not? Come at me swiftly, O wicked-minded man-eater.
Strike at me alone — you ought not to slay a woman, especially one who has done you no harm, even if another has wronged you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This young woman is not of her own will desiring me here — she has been impelled by Kāma, who moves within the heart; she is your own sister, O wicked-minded disgrace of the rākṣasas.
Moreover, it was by your own command that she came here; having seen my form, this timid one desires me — she brings no disgrace upon the clan.
The fault was wrought by the bodiless one — while I stand here, you wicked-souled rākṣasa, you have no right to slay this woman.
Come and fight with me alone, one against one, O man-eater. Today I myself will conduct you to the abode of Yama.
Today let your head be crushed by my palm, O rākṣasa, split apart like a mighty elephant's foot crushing a skull.
Today let the flesh-eating vultures, hawks, and jackals joyfully drag your limbs along the earth, slain by me in battle.
In an instant today I shall make this forest free of its thorn — this forest that was forever befouled in the past by you devouring men.
Today, O sinner, your sister shall see you dragged along the ground by me, mountain-like, as a lion drags a great elephant.
With you slain by me, O disgrace of the rākṣasas, men who wander in forests will roam this forest free from all trouble."
Hiḍimba said: "What is the use of roaring and boasting in vain, O mortal? Accomplish this deed and then boast of it all — do not delay long."
"You think yourself strong and me lacking in valor — today, when you close with me, you shall know your own strength to be the lesser."
"I will not harm those sleeping there — let them sleep at their ease. It is you alone, O wicked-minded speaker of disagreeable words, that I slay today."
"After drinking your blood from your body, I will then slay them — and after that, this wretch who has done me harm."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having said this, the man-eater seized his arm and charged in fury at Bhīmasena, the subduer of foes.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As he charged swiftly, Bhīma of terrible prowess caught the arm that had been thrust at him with a kind of laugh.
Seizing him forcibly, Bhīma dragged the writhing rākṣasa eight bow-lengths from that spot, as a lion drags a small beast.
Then the rākṣasa, enraged, held fast by the Pāṇḍava, clasped Bhīmasena in his arms and let out a dreadful roar.
Again mighty Bhīma forcibly dragged him away, thinking: "Let there be no noise to wake my brothers who are sleeping soundly."
The two of them, coming at each other, dragged one another with all their might — the rākṣasa and Bhīmasena each displaying supreme valor.
They broke great trees and tore apart creepers, like two sixty-year-old elephants in rut, both fiercely enraged.
Roused by the great noise the two made, those bulls among men awoke along with their mother — and they saw Hiḍimbā standing before them.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Awakened and seeing Hiḍimbā's superhuman form, those tigers among men were filled with wonder, as was Pṛthā.
Then Kuntī, marveling at her beauty, spoke these sweet soothing words to her gently:
"Whose are you, O one radiant as the womb of the gods? Who are you, O lady of fine complexion? What is your purpose here, O beautiful-hipped one? And from where have you come?
Whether you are a deity of this forest or an Apsaras, tell me everything — and for what purpose do you stand here?"
Hiḍimbā said: "This great forest you see, dark as a rain-cloud — this is the dwelling place of the rākṣasa Hiḍimba, and of me as well.
Know me, O spirited lady, as the sister of that rākṣasa lord — sent by my brother, O noble one, who wished to kill you along with your sons.
Acting on the orders of that cruel-minded one, I came here and beheld your son, golden-complexioned and of great splendor.
Then I, wandering in the nature of all beings, was impelled by Manmatha who had entered your son — I came under his sway, O auspicious one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
So I chose your mighty son as my husband, and tried to carry him away — but I could not.
Knowing that I was delaying, that man-eater has himself come here to slay all your sons.
He has been forcibly crushed and dragged away from here by that wise great-souled one, your son, my beloved.
Behold those two of mighty speed roaring at each other — the man and the rākṣasa, both displaying valor in battle!"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The moment they heard her words, Yudhiṣṭhira, Arjuna, and valiant Nakula and Sahadeva leapt to their feet.
They saw the two locked together, dragging each other, each striving for victory, like two lions fierce in battle.
The two of them, clasping each other and dragging back and forth, raised a cloud of dust from the earth like the smoke of a forest fire.
Enveloped in the dust of the earth, resembling the pillars of the earth itself, the two blazed like two mountains wrapped in mist.
Watching Bhīma being hard pressed by the rākṣasa, Arjuna spoke these words with something of a laugh:
"Fear not, Bhīma, O great-armed one — we did not know you had met this fearsome form while we slept, wearied and worn out.
I am here to aid you, O son of Pṛthā — I will fight the rākṣasa. Nakula and Sahadeva shall guard our mother."
Bhīma said: "Stand aside and watch — no alarm is needed from you. This one, having come within the reach of my arms, shall never live again."
Arjuna said: "Why keep this sinful rākṣasa alive so long, Bhīma? We cannot linger here much longer, O subduer of foes.
Before long the east will redden; before long the twilight will begin; and at the dreadful hour, rākṣasas grow powerful.
Hurry, Bhīma — do not play games. Slay this fearsome demon before he works his magic; pour the essence of your arms into this."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus urged by Arjuna, Bhīma quickly lifted the dreadful rākṣasa's body and whirled it round more than a hundred times.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīma said: "Nourished on flesh in vain, grown up in vain, your mind wasted in vain — you deserve a futile death; today your futility will come to an end."
Arjuna said: "Or if you think this rākṣasa too heavy a burden in battle, I will help you — let him be slain quickly."
"Or I myself will slay him, O wolf-belly — you have done great deeds and are exhausted. Do take rest for a while."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing those words, the exceedingly wrathful Bhīmasena crushed the rākṣasa forcibly against the earth and killed him like a sacrificial animal.
As he was being killed by Bhīma, he let out a great loud cry that filled the entire forest, like a drum soaked in water.
That powerful son of Pāṇḍu, wrapping him with his arms, broke him at the waist — and that mighty hero delighted the Pāṇḍavas.
Seeing Hiḍimba slain, those swift heroes rejoiced and honored Bhīmasena, that tiger among men, that subduer of foes.
Having duly honored the great-souled Bhīma of terrible valor, Arjuna again spoke these words to that wolf-bellied one:
"I think a city is not far from this forest, lord. Let us go quickly — good fortune to you. Let Suyodhana not find us out."
Then all of them, those scorchers of foes, those tigers among men, said "So be it" and departed along with their mother — and Hiḍimbā the rākṣasī went with them.
Bhīma said: "Rākṣasas remember enmity and resort to bewildering illusion, Hiḍimbā — go you on the path trodden by your brother."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Even in your anger, O tiger among men, Bhīma, do not slay a woman — guard dharma, which is greater than protecting the body. Guard it, O Pāṇḍava."
You slew that mighty demon who came with murderous intent — what then can his sister do to us, even if she is enraged?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hiḍimbā then bowed before Kuntī with joined palms and spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"O noble lady, you know what suffering arises in women from the god of love — that very affliction, caused by Bhīmasena, has now come upon me, O auspicious one.
I have endured that supreme anguish while biding my time — and now that moment has arrived, which shall bring me happiness at last.
For I abandoned my friends, my own dharma, and my own people, and chose this tiger among men, your son, as my husband, O auspicious one.
Yet even though I spoke in this way, I was rejected by this man — and by you too, O illustrious one — regarding the act I sought.
Whether you consider me foolish or devoted and submissive, O greatly fortunate one, please unite me with your son as my husband.
Taking him — who is beautiful as a god — I shall go wherever I wish, and I shall return again; place your trust in me, O auspicious one.
For when summoned in thought, I shall always carry all of you away; I shall deliver these bull-like men from danger and through difficult passages.
I shall carry you all on my back, as swift as you could desire — grant me your grace, and let Bhīmasena take me as his wife."
By whatever means one may sustain one's life in crossing calamities, all of that must be done with care — for it is dharma that guides such action.
The highest knower of dharma is one who upholds dharma even in misfortune — for indeed, calamity itself is said to be the test of dharma for the righteous.
Virtue sustains life; virtue is what is called life-giving — whatever means one employs to practise dharma, no blame attaches to that.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "It is exactly as you have said, Hiḍimbā — there is no doubt in this. But you must abide by dharma as I shall prescribe, O slender-waisted one.
Having bathed and completed the daily rites, and with auspicious ornaments put on, you may enjoy Bhīmasena's company, O blessed one, before the sun sets.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
During the daytime roam with him as you wish, O swift as thought — but Bhīmasena must be brought back to us every night."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Agreeing to this with the words "so be it," the rakshasi Hiḍimbā thereupon took Bhīmasena and soared up into the sky.
On the lovely peaks of mountains, in the sanctuaries of the gods, in places always charming and resounding with the cries of deer and birds —
— assuming her most beautiful form, adorned with all ornaments, conversing with sweetest words, she delighted the son of Pāṇḍu.
Likewise on the steep slopes of forests adorned with flowering trees, at lovely lakes covered with lotuses and water-lilies,
on river islands and shore-lands, on sands gleaming like beryl, at forest streams with good fords, and at mountain rivers,
on shores of the ocean strewn with gems and gold, in beautiful harbor-towns, and in great forests of śāla trees,
in sacred groves of the gods and on mountain plateaus, in the abodes of the Guhyakas and in the hermitages of ascetics,
at the Mānasa lakes bearing fruits and flowers of every season — bearing her most beautiful form, she delighted the son of Pāṇḍu.
As she thus sported with Bhīma here and there, swift as thought, the rakshasi conceived and bore from Bhīmasena a mighty son.
He had misshapen eyes and a huge mouth; his ears were spike-like; he was terrifying to behold; his form was fearsome; his lips were copper-red; his teeth were sharp; and he was immensely powerful.
