He was a mighty archer, of great valor, great strength, mighty-armed, of great speed, of great body, possessed of great illusions, and a subduer of enemies.
Non-human yet born of a human, of terrible speed and great power — he surpassed other piśācas exceedingly, just as he surpassed ordinary humans.
Even as a child he attained youth — O lord of the people — and that mighty hero achieved supreme excellence in all weapons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For rakshasa women conceive and give birth at once; they can assume any form at will and take on many shapes.
Bowing in reverence, Vikaca — that greatest of archers — clasped the feet of both his father and his mother, and they gave him his name.
He addressed his mother as "Ghaṭabhāsotkaca," and from that name his own name became Ghaṭotkaca — so it is told.
Ghaṭotkaca was devoted to the Pāṇḍavas, and he became always dear to them, as if he were one of themselves.
Then Hiḍimbā spoke to him saying "the time of our living together is spent" — and having made her covenant, she returned to her own way.
"I shall come to you, O fathers, when the time of need arrives" — saying this, Ghaṭotkaca, foremost of rakshasas, took leave and departed toward the northern direction.
For he had been created by the great Indra, the lord of treasures, for the sake of the śakti weapon — to be the instrument of death for the irresistibly mighty Karṇa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those heroes, those great warriors, hastening onward, passed from forest to forest, slaying many herds of deer as they went, O king.
Passing through the lands of the Matsyas, Trigartas, Pāñcālas, and Kīcakas, they looked upon lovely forest regions and lakes.
All of them, those great souls, had matted their hair; they were clad in bark garments and deer-skins; along with Kuntī they bore the appearance of ascetics.
Sometimes those great warriors carried their mother in haste; sometimes they moved at their own pace — and so they journeyed on repeatedly.
Studying the Vedas of Brahmā, all the Vedic auxiliaries, and the science of statecraft, those knowers of dharma beheld their grandfather.
They bowed in reverence to that great soul, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, and then all of them, scorchers of foes, stood with joined palms, together with their mother.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vyāsa said: "O bulls of the Bhārata line, I had known this beforehand in my mind — how you were exiled through the unrighteous conduct of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Knowing that, I have come, wishing to do what is supremely good for you. No despondency should be felt here — all of this will lead to your happiness.
They are all equal to me, and you as well — there is no doubt of this. Kinsmen form attachments from helplessness and from childhood alike.
Therefore my affection for you is especially great at this time. I wish to do what is beneficial for you, out of that love — hear this from me.
Near here is a beautiful and wholesome city — dwell there in concealment, awaiting my return."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus comforted those sons of Pṛthā, the tamers of foes, the lord Vyāsa went to Ekacakrā and comforted Kuntī.
"Long live your sons, O daughter — this son of yours, Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, shall rule as king of dharma over all the kings of the earth.
Knowing dharma, self-controlled, he shall conquer the entire earth by dharma and enjoy it with the strength of Bhīmasena and Arjuna — of this there is no doubt.
Both your sons and the sons of Mādrī — all of them great warriors — shall then sport happily and with joyful minds in their own kingdom.
These tigers among men shall, having conquered this earth, perform great sacrifices — the Rājasūya, the Aśvamedha, and others — with abundant sacrificial fees.
Bestowing favour upon their circle of friends with wealth and happiness, your sons shall here enjoy the kingdom of their fathers and grandfathers."
Having spoken thus and settled them in the dwelling of a brahmin, the sage Dvaipāyana then spoke to the best of princes, Yudhiṣṭhira.
"Await me here — I shall come again. Knowing the right place and time, you shall attain the highest joy."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Answered with "so be it" by all of them with joined palms, O lord of men, the blessed sage Vyāsa, the lord, departed as he wished.
Janamejaya said: "After those mighty warriors, the sons of Kuntī, had gone to Ekacakrā, what did the Pāṇḍavas do next, O best of the twice-born?"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those mighty warriors, the sons of Kuntī, having gone to Ekacakrā, dwelt for no very long time in the dwelling of a brahmin.
They beheld the charming forests, various and beautiful, and royal districts too, and rivers and lakes.
They wandered begging for alms, all of them, O lord of the people, and by their own virtues became dear to the eyes of the townspeople.
Every evening they would present the alms they had gathered to Kuntī; and they would eat the portions she distributed, each separately.
Half of the food those heroes, those scorchers of foes, ate together with their mother; the other half of all the alms the mighty Bhīma ate alone.
Now while those great souls were dwelling there, O king, a very long time passed, O bull of the Bhārata line.
Then one day those bulls of the Bhārata line had gone out to beg for alms, and by chance Bhīmasena remained there with Pṛthā.
Then Kuntī heard a great and terrible sound of anguish rising loudly from within the brahmin's dwelling, O descendant of Bharata.
Hearing all of them weeping and lamenting, the queen, O king, could not bear it out of compassion and her naturally noble disposition.
With her heart churning as if with grief, the auspicious Pṛthā then spoke these words of compassion to Bhīma.
"We are dwelling in great happiness, my son, in this brahmin's house — unknown to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, honoured and free from anger.
I always think, my son, 'What can I do that is dear to this brahmin?' — just as those who dwell as guests should do to bring happiness to the household.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A man is as great as the good deed he does that does not perish — and as long as another might do something for him, he should do something more than that.
Now some definite sorrow has fallen upon this brahmin — if we were to help him in it, that would be a meritorious deed."
Bhīma said: "Let us find out what his sorrow is and from where it has arisen — once it is known, I shall resolve it, even if it should be exceedingly difficult."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the two of them were speaking thus, they again heard the sound of anguish from that brahmin along with his wife, O lord of the people.
Kuntī then quickly entered the inner apartments of that noble brahmin, like a cow hastening toward her tethered calf.
She then saw that brahmin there with his wife, his son, and his daughter — all of them with distorted faces.
The brahmin said: "Fie upon this life in the world — it is insubstantial as fire, purposeless, rooted in sorrow, dependent on others, and greatly burdened with the unpleasant.
In living there is supreme sorrow; in living there is supreme fever; for one who lives in the world, the coming of life's opposites is inevitable.
Even a single person cannot fully pursue dharma, artha, and kama all at once; and separation from these too is considered the greatest sorrow.
Some declare liberation to be the highest good, but that can never be attained; and in the acquisition of wealth, the whole of hell is incurred.
In desiring wealth there is supreme sorrow; in the actual gaining of wealth there is even more; and for one who has grown attached to riches, separation from them is the greatest sorrow of all.
For I see no means by which I might escape this calamity and flee safely together with my wife and child.
I have indeed striven before, as you well know, O Brahmin woman; yet you have not heeded my words about where we might go in safety.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'I was born here and grew up here, and my father too is here' — so you have said, O foolish one, even as I beseeched you again and again.
Your aged father has gone to heaven, and your mother has long since passed away; your former kinsmen too are gone — what delight then is there in dwelling here?
This ruin of our kin has now come upon you — you who longed for kinship yet would not hear my words — and it brings me the deepest grief.
Or rather, this is my own ruin; for I cannot abandon any of my kin of my own accord and live on in cruel indifference.
She who walks the path of dharma with me, who is self-restrained, who is ever like a mother to me, who was ordained by the gods as my companion and my highest refuge —
— she who was appointed by my mother and father to share always in the householder's life, whom I chose according to law and wed with sacred mantras —
— this noble and virtuous wife, the mother of my children, who has never done me wrong, who is ever devoted to me — I cannot abandon her to save my own life.
Still less could I abandon my daughter — a mere child, not yet come of age, in whom the marks of womanhood have not yet appeared.
She was entrusted to me as a sacred deposit by the great-souled Creator for her future husband's sake; and through her I hope to attain the worlds of my grandsons together with the ancestors. How can I bring myself to abandon this child whom I myself have brought into the world?
Some men hold that a father's love for his son is greater than for his daughter; yet in my view both are equal.
In her rest the worlds, my lineage, and perpetual happiness. How then can I bring myself to abandon this innocent child?
Even if I abandoned myself and passed under the power of the dead, those I left behind could clearly not survive here.
The abandonment of any one of these is cruel and condemned by the wise; and if I were to abandon myself, these too would perish without me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus fallen into this terrible strait, I am unable to cross over this calamity. Alas, what course shall I take today? To die together with all my kin would be better; life without them I cannot endure.
The Brahmin woman said: You must not grieve like an ordinary man. This is no time for lamentation; you who know the remedies have no occasion for despair.
All human beings must inevitably go to their death here; for what is unavoidable, grief serves no purpose.
Wife, son, and daughter — all are cherished for one's own sake. Cast off your anguish with clear understanding; I myself shall go there.
This indeed is the supreme and eternal duty of a woman in the world: that she act for her husband's welfare even at the cost of her own life.
Such a deed done there will bring you happiness even in this world, imperishable reward in the next, and glory in both worlds.
This is the highest dharma which I shall declare to you; your true purpose and your dharma are both abundantly manifest in this course.
The purpose for which a wife is desired has been fulfilled in me by you: a daughter and a son have been born, and I have been set free of debt by you.
You are capable of nourishing and protecting the two children; I, however, am not equally able to protect and nourish the two of them.
For me, bereft of you, all desires would be calamity: how could the two young children fare, and how indeed could I myself fare?
How, widowed and helpless, with infant children, without you, shall I sustain the two of us while remaining on the path trodden by the virtuous?
With arrogant and insolent men importuning this daughter of mine, men unworthy of alliance with you — how shall I be able to protect her?
Just as birds swoop upon flesh thrown to the ground, so all men importune a woman who is without a hero to protect her.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Shaken thus and importuned by wicked men, I shall not be able to remain on the path beloved of the righteous, O best of twice-born.
How can I bring myself to set this solitary, unformed girl of your lineage on the path of her fathers and grandfathers?
How shall I be able to instil in this child the virtues that are desired, she who is helpless and abandoned on all sides — as you, who perceive dharma, could have done?
Disregarding me and treating this orphaned girl of yours with contempt, unworthy men will importune her — as Śūdras importune the hearing of the Veda.
And if I were to refuse to give her away, one endowed with your virtues, those men would violently carry her off, as crows snatch the oblation from a sacrifice.
Watching your son, who seems unworthy even of me, and this daughter of yours as well fallen into the power of the unworthy —
— scorned by the world, not knowing what I myself am worth, at the hands of insolent men, O Brahmin, I shall surely die. There is no doubt of this.
Those two children of mine, bereft of me and of you, would perish without doubt — like two fish when their water dries up.
All three of us will surely perish in every way, bereft of you. Therefore you ought to abandon me.
This is the highest fulfilment for women: that the husband's welfare comes first and is the highest goal; but not, O Brahmin, to remain spinning in the domain of one's sons.
This son has been forsaken by me, and this daughter likewise; kinsmen too have been forsaken, and my very life — all for your sake.
Over sacrifices, austerities, observances, and various acts of giving, a woman's constant devotion to the welfare and happiness of her husband is far superior.
That which I am about to do is righteous and supremely approved; it is what is desired and beneficial — for you and for your lineage alike.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Even children dear to one, one's wealth, cherished friends — and even a wife — may be given up, according to the opinion of the good, to secure release by the law in times of calamity.
On one side the entire lineage, on the other a single self, O increaser of the family — the wise have firmly concluded that all the rest together are not equal to the self.
Therefore, act together with me in what must be done; save yourself by yourself. Give me leave, O noble one, and protect our two children.
Those who know dharma say in their determination of dharma that women must not be killed; and they call rakshasas knowers of dharma — so he should not kill me either.
The killing of a man is certain; the killing of a woman is uncertain. Therefore, O knower of dharma, you ought to send me instead.
I have enjoyed pleasant things and obtained what I desired; I have lived according to dharma; I have gained the cherished fruit of being born of you. I shall not grieve at death.
I am one who has borne a son, who is mature, and who has always sought your happiness. Considering all this, I now resolve upon this course.
Even when you have let me go, O noble one, you will take another wife; and thus your dharma will again be established.
Nor is it adharma for men to have many wives, O auspicious one; but for women the adharma is very great in transgressing against a prior husband.
Considering all this, and that self-destruction is condemned, save yourself through me; and save the lineage and these two children.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by her, the husband, O Bhārata, embraced her and, together with his wife, slowly shed tears, deeply afflicted with grief.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing those excessively sorrowful words of the two grief-stricken ones, the daughter, whose limbs were overwhelmed with intense grief, spoke to them both.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Why do you two, so deeply afflicted with grief, cry out like those who are helpless? Let something of mine be heard as well; and having heard it, do what is fit.
By dharma I am the one to be abandoned by the two of you — there is no doubt in this. Abandon me, she who is fit to be abandoned, and everything will be saved by me alone.
For this very reason offspring are desired — 'it will save me,' one thinks. Now that this occasion has arrived, use me as a raft to cross over.
Whether one saves from a danger here in this life or saves after death in the next — in every way a son saves; that is why the wise call him 'putra' (son, saviour).
Grandfathers also always long for their daughter's sons; I shall myself rescue them by protecting my father's life.
And this little brother of mine — if you, father, were to pass to yonder world, he would surely perish within no long time. There is no doubt of this.
For if father goes to heaven and my younger brother also perishes, the ancestral oblations would be cut off — and that would be displeasing to them.
Abandoned by my father, and likewise by my mother, and by my brother, there is no doubt that I, not accustomed to such, would die, having fallen into a grief worse than grief.
But if you are safely delivered, unharmed, then my mother, my young brother, the continuation of the lineage, and the ancestral oblations will all without doubt be established.
Oneself, one's son, a friend — that is a wife; a daughter is truly a burden, so they say. Therefore, free yourself from this burden and assign me to dharma.
Helpless, pitiable, a child, wandering wherever I may — I shall be wretched without you, father. Alas, how pitiable!
Or rather, I shall achieve the liberation of this family; I shall have attained the fruit of my existence by performing this most difficult deed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Or if you go there leaving me behind, O best of twice-born, I shall be afflicted — consider me as well in this.
Therefore, for our sake, for the sake of dharma, and for the sake of progeny, O virtuous one, protect yourself; and abandon me, who am fit to be abandoned.
In this matter which must inevitably be done, let not this moment pass you by. The water-oblation given by you will be of benefit to me.
What greater grief could there be than this — that we, with you gone to heaven, should run about begging food from others like dogs?
But if you are delivered safely, unharmed, from this affliction, with your kinsmen alive, I, dwelling in this world, shall be filled with happiness.
Hearing her lamentation of many kinds, the father, the mother, and the daughter herself all three wept aloud.
Then, hearing all of them weeping, the young son of the two of them, a mere boy with wide-open eyes, spoke softly in indistinct words.
Saying 'Do not weep, father; do not weep, mother; do not weep, sister,' he approached them one by one, seeming almost to smile.
Then he picked up a blade of grass and, joyful, spoke again: 'With this I shall slay that man-eating Rākṣasa!'
Even so, hearing those indistinct words of the child, great joy arose among them who were overcome with grief.
Recognizing that the moment had come, Kuntī approached them — as if reviving those at the point of death with nectar — and spoke these words.
Kuntī said: I wish to know the root cause of this grief in truth; and having known it, I would remove it, if it can indeed be removed.
The Brahmin said: What you say, O rich in austerity, is fitting for those who are good; yet this grief cannot be dispelled by a human being.
Near this city there lives a Rākṣasa named Baka, who is the lord of this countryside and of this town, and who is of great might.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nourished on human flesh, evil-minded, a devourer of men, this powerful one perpetually protects this countryside from other demons.
Attended by the power of that demon, both the city and the country are protected — because of him we have no fear from enemy armies or from spirits.
His appointed wage has been fixed: a cartload of rice, two buffaloes, and a single man — whoever carries that food goes to him.
Each family in turn delivers that food; the rotation comes around again only after many years, yet it costs men their lives — a burden impossible to bear.
And those men who have anywhere tried to liberate themselves from this — the demon has killed them together with their wives and children and devoured them.
The king dwelling in the Vetrakīya house has not adopted a policy here by which the lasting welfare of these people could be assured today.
We who live under the dominion of this weak man, constantly full of dread, sheltering under a bad king — we deserve precisely this fate.
To whom should brahmins speak, or those who wander as they please? These men of virtue are tamed by their own good qualities, like free-flying birds caught in a snare.
One should first find a king, then a wife, then wealth; and when those three are secured, one can then support one's kinsmen and children.
But I have acquired all three of these in the wrong order — and having now reached this calamity, we shall suffer greatly.
This turn — the destroyer of our family — has now come round to us; I must deliver as his wage one man along with the food.
I have no money anywhere to purchase a man, nor can I in any way give a friend; I see no way of escape from that demon.
Sunk thus deeply in this vast, uncrossable ocean of grief, I shall go today together with these relatives to the demon — and then that wretched creature will devour all of us together.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kuntī said: You must not give way to despair or to any fear on our account — a means of deliverance from that demon has been perceived here.
You have one young son, one ascetic daughter, and your wife — I do not favour the going of any of those three there.
I have five sons, O brahmin; one of them shall go on your behalf, carrying the food-offering for that wicked demon.
The brahmin said: I will not do this — not for my own life's sake, not under any circumstances — this severing of a brahmin guest from his life for my own benefit.
Not even among those of ignoble birth or unrighteous conduct is such a thing found — that one would sacrifice oneself or one's own child for the sake of a brahmin.
I hold it my duty to seek my own good; and whether it be the sin of killing a brahmin or the killing of myself, the death of myself is better for me.
The killing of a brahmin is the supreme sin, and there is no expiation for it; even if done without prior intent, my own death is better for me.
Yet I do not myself desire my own death, O auspicious one — when death is brought about by others, no sin whatsoever falls on me.
In the deliberate killing of a brahmin by me I see no expiation; it is both cruel and base.
To abandon one who has come to one's house, likewise one who has sought shelter, and to cause the death of one who is supplicating — these are considered the ultimate cruelty.
"One should never perform a censurable or cruel act" — so the great-souled men of former times, who knew the dharma of emergencies, have declared.
But my own destruction today, together with my wife, is better — I will not in any way consent to the killing of a brahmin.
Kuntī said: My own resolve too is firm, O brahmin — brahmins must be protected; nor would a son be unwanted by me even if I had a hundred sons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And that demon is not capable of destroying my son — my son is mighty, accomplished through sacred formulas, and full of blazing energy.
He will deliver all that food to the demon and will free himself — such is my firm conviction.
For demons — powerful, huge-bodied — have met that hero before and have been seen by him, and many have been slain by him.
But this must not be told to anyone at all, O brahmin — for those in pursuit of learning would, out of curiosity, interfere with my sons.
"That son of mine who has not been released by his guru should not employ that power" — such is the view of the righteous.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Pṛthā, that brahmin together with his wife, rejoicing, honoured her speech as equal to nectar.
Then Kuntī and the brahmin together addressed the son of the Wind: "Do it" — and he answered them: "So be it."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Bhīma had pledged "I shall do it," O descendant of Bharata, all the Pāṇḍavas then returned, having collected their alms.
Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Pāṇḍu, reading the situation from Bhīma's very bearing, sat apart alone and then questioned his mother.
"What deed does this Bhīma of terrible valour intend to do? Is this that he wishes to do here done with your consent?"
Kuntī said: At my own bidding this scorcher of foes will perform a great deed — for the sake of the brahmin and for the deliverance of the city.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What rash and reckless wrong has been done by you? Good men do not praise the abandonment of a son.
How can you wish to abandon your own son for the sake of another's? What you have done by giving up a son is contrary to the practice of the world.
Relying on whose arms we all sleep in comfort — it is by relying on them that we hope to win back the kingdom stolen by wicked men.
Thinking on whose valour — his, of boundless might — Duryodhana spends all his nights sleepless with grief, together with Śakuni.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By the valour of this hero we were freed from the house of lac; and from other wicked men too, and Purоcana was slain.
Relying on whose might we think it possible to gain this earth full of riches — after slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Resorting to what reasoning have you decided to abandon him? Has your mind perhaps been deranged by grief — have you lost your senses?
Kuntī said: Yudhiṣṭhira, you must have no anguish regarding Vṛkodara — nor has this resolve been made by me out of weakness of mind.
Here in the brahmin's house, my son, we have dwelt in comfort; this repayment to him has been carefully considered by me. Only so great a person is one in whom a good deed is not lost.
Having seen Bhīma's great heroism in the house of lac at that time, and also from the slaying of Hiḍimba — my trust in Vṛkodara is firm.
For the strength of Bhīma's arms is great — equal to ten thousand elephants — by which you, resembling great elephants yourselves, were carried out from Vāraṇāvata.
There is no other equal to Vṛkodara in strength — there has been none, nor shall there be — who could rise against even the greatest in battle, even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself.
Long ago, when he was just born, he fell from my lap onto a mountain — because of the heaviness of his body, the rock was shattered by his limbs.
Recalling that, O Pāṇḍava, with discernment — Bhīma's strength — and also the brahmin's need for repayment, I then formed this resolve.
This was not decided out of greed, nor out of ignorance, nor out of delusion — my effort for dharma has been undertaken with full deliberation.
Two purposes will both be accomplished, Yudhiṣṭhira: repayment for our lodging, and the practice of great dharma.
"A kṣatriya who ever renders assistance to a brahmin in his needs attains auspicious worlds" — thus have I heard.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A kṣatriya who brings about the liberation from death even of another kṣatriya alone wins great fame in this world and in the next.
And a kṣatriya who renders assistance even to a vaiśya in battle will assuredly delight the people in all the worlds.
And a king who saves a śūdra who has come seeking refuge — he gains birth here in a family that is prosperous and honoured by kings.
So the blessed Vyāsa, that wise man, declared this very clearly long ago, O joy of the Kuru line — therefore this is what I intend to do.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This is fitting, mother — what you have done with full deliberation, out of compassion for a brahmin in distress. Bhīma will certainly return after slaying the man-eater.
But the brahmin must be instructed and carefully persuaded in such a way that the townspeople do not come to know of this.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, when the night had passed, the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena took the food and went to the place where that man-eater dwelt.
And having reached the forest of that demon, the mighty Pāṇḍava called out to him by name, helping himself to the food.
Then that demon, hearing Bhīmasena's words, came in a great rage to where Bhīma stood.
Huge-bodied and of immense speed, seeming to cleave the earth, having drawn his brows into a three-peaked frown and biting his lip —
— seeing Bhīmasena eating the food, that demon, furious, opened wide his eyes and spoke these words:
"Who is this fool of corrupt mind who eats this food prepared for me, before my very eyes — who wishes to go to the abode of Yama?"
But Bhīmasena, hearing that, O Bhārata, as if laughing, paid no heed to that demon and ate on, turning his back to him.
Then, raising both his arms and uttering a terrible roar, that man-eater charged at Bhīmasena, intending to kill him.
Even then, utterly disregarding him and not looking at the demon, Vṛkodara, the Pāṇḍava, slayer of enemy heroes, simply went on eating the food.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Filled with wrath, the demon stood behind Kuntī's son and struck him on the back with both his palms.
Though struck hard on the back by that powerful being with his palms, Bhīma did not even glance at the demon — he simply went on eating.
Then, enraged still further, that mighty demon seized a tree and charged at Bhīma again, intending to strike him.
Then Bhīma, that bull among men, finished eating the food at his leisure, sipped water, and stood up in the field of battle, greatly pleased — that mighty-armed one.
The valiant Bhīma caught the tree hurled by the enraged demon with his left hand, as if laughing, O Bhārata.
Then that mighty one lifted up many more trees of various kinds and flung them at Bhīmasena — and the Pāṇḍava Bhīma flung them back at him.
That battle of trees — great, terrible in form, devastating to the forest — took place between Baka and the Pāṇḍava, O great king.
Then Baka, shouting his name aloud, rushed at the Pāṇḍava and seized mighty Bhīmasena with both his arms.
And Bhīmasena too, great-armed and mighty, threw his arms around that demon and, as he struggled with great force, dragged him away by sheer power.
Dragged by Bhīma and dragging the Pāṇḍava in turn, that man-eater was overcome by extreme exhaustion.
By their great force the earth trembled, and they pulverised the mighty trees standing around them.
But seeing that demon weakening, O bull of the Bhāratas, Vṛkodara pressed him down onto the ground with both his hands and struck him.
Then pressing down on its back with his knee, he forcibly seized the demon's neck with his right arm.
And with his left hand grasping the demon by the waist and garment, the Pāṇḍava bent that rakshasa double, while it roared terrifying cries.
Then blood poured from the mouth of that fearsome demon, O lord of men, as it was broken apart by Bhīma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Terrified by that sound, O king, the household of that demon rushed out of the house together with all its attendants.
The mighty Bhīma, foremost among warriors, pacified those who were frightened and bewildered, and made them agree to a covenant.
"Never again shall you harm human beings here at any time; for those who harm others shall meet swift death just like this," he declared.
Hearing those words, O Bhārata, those demons said "So be it" to him and accepted that covenant.
From that time forward, O Bhārata, only gentle demons appeared in that town, seen by the men who dwelt in the city.
Then Bhīma, taking up that man-eating demon whose life had departed, threw it down at the city gate and departed undetected.
Then that Bhīma, having slain the demon, went to that brahmin's dwelling and reported to the king everything that had happened, omitting nothing.
Then people came out of the city in the early morning and saw the demon lying slain on the ground, drenched in blood.
Others went to Ekacakrā and spread the news of that demon lying sprawled out, resembling a mountain peak, frightful to behold.
Then thousands of people from the city, O king, came there to see Baka — men, women, elders, and children alike.
Then all of them, amazed upon seeing that superhuman feat, worshipped the gods, every single one of them, O lord of men.
Then they began to reckon whose turn it was that day to supply food; and learning this, all of them came to that brahmin and asked him about it.
Questioned thus many times, and still protecting the Pāṇḍavas, that foremost of brahmins then spoke these words to all the townspeople.
"As I was ordered to provide food and was weeping together with my kinsmen, a certain brahmin of great power, perfected in sacred formulas, saw me."
"Having first asked me about my distress and the town's affliction, that best of brahmins consoled me and, smiling slightly, said:"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'I shall deliver this food to that evil-souled one myself; on my account there is no cause for fear,' said that heroic one."
"He took that food and went toward the forest of Baka — by him surely this deed has been done for the welfare of the world."
Then all those brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas, and shudras, filled with great wonder and joy, celebrated a festival in honor of the brahmins.
Then all the country folk came to the city to see that most wondrous event, while the sons of Pṛthā continued to dwell there.
Janamejaya said: After those tiger-like men had slain the demon Baka, O brahmin, what did the Pāṇḍavas do from that time onward?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: They continued to dwell there, O king, after slaying the demon Baka, studying the highest sacred texts in the brahmin's abode.
Then after a few days, a brahmin of sharpened vows came to that brahmin's house seeking lodging.
That learned foremost of brahmins, always devoted to the vow of hospitality to all guests, honored him properly and gave him lodging.
Then all those Pāṇḍavas, bulls among men, together with Kuntī, sat in attendance upon that brahmin as he was narrating stories.
He spoke of various lands, various sacred pilgrimage sites, various conduct and practices of kings, and various ancient cities.
At the end of his narratives there, O Janamejaya, that brahmin described the wondrous swayamvara of Yājñasenī among the Pāñcālas.
He described the birth of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the birth of Śikhaṇḍī, and the womb-less origin of Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) at Drupada's great sacrifice.
Having heard that most wondrous account of that great-souled man, those bulls among men asked him to tell the story in full detail.
"How was the wondrous birth of Drupada's son Dhṛṣṭadyumna from fire? And how was the wondrous birth of Kṛṣṇā from the midst of the sacrificial altar?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"How did Dhṛṣṭadyumna learn all weapons from the great archer Droṇa? And how were those two dear friends separated, and by whose doing?"
Thus prompted by those bulls among men, O king, that brahmin then narrated everything regarding the birth of Draupadī.
The brahmin said: Near the gateway to the Gaṅgā there lived a great sage of great austerities — Bharadvāja, supremely wise and ever firm in his vows.
He went to bathe in the Gaṅgā, and there the sage saw the apsara Ghṛtācī, who had arrived earlier and was bathing.
The wind carried away her garment on the river bank at that moment; seeing her with her clothing torn away, the sage was overcome with desire.
The mind of that celibate who had practiced chastity from boyhood became attached to her; overcome with rapture, his seed fell — and the sage Droṇa held it in a vessel.
From that, the boy Droṇa was born of that wise man; he studied the Vedas and all the Vedic auxiliaries in their entirety.
Now a king named Pṛṣata was a friend of Bharadvāja; and of him too there was born a son named Drupada at that time.
That son of Pṛṣata, bull among kshatriyas, would always go to the hermitage and together with Droṇa would sport and study.
After Pṛṣata passed away, Drupada became king; and Droṇa heard that Rāma was giving away all his wealth.
To Rāma who was departing to the forest, the son of Bharadvāja said: "Know me, O best of twice-born, as Droṇa, who has come seeking wealth."
Rāma said: Only my body alone remains to me now as my possession; choose either my weapons or my body, O brahmin — one or the other.
Droṇa said: You should give me all weapons, together with their means of withdrawal, and the method of application of each and every one of them.
The brahmin said: Saying "So be it," the son of Bhṛgu thereupon gave them to him; having received them, Droṇa then considered his purpose accomplished.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Overjoyed in heart, having received from Rāma the most excellent Brahmāstra, he became superior to all men.
Then the powerful son of Bharadvāja, tiger among men, approached Drupada and said: "Know me as your friend."
Drupada said: A non-vedic scholar cannot be the friend of a vedic scholar; a non-chariot-warrior cannot be the friend of a chariot-warrior; nor can a non-king be the friend of a king — what does this former friendship matter?
The brahmin said: Having decided in his mind, that wise man set out toward Pāñcāla and went to the city of the chief Kurus, called Nagasahvaya (Hāstinapura).
Bhīṣma, upon his arrival, gave the wise Droṇa his grandsons along with various riches, as pupils.
Then the learned Droṇa, having assembled all his pupils, spoke these words for the purpose of bringing grief to Drupada:
"Something in the way of a teacher's fee turns over in my heart; when you have mastered weapons, that should be given — tell me truly, O sinless ones."
And when all the Pāṇḍavas had mastered weapons and completed their training, Droṇa spoke these words again regarding the teacher's fee:
"Let the kingdom of Drupada, son of Pṛṣata, ruler of Chatravati, be swiftly seized and given to me."
Then the five sons of Pāṇḍu, having defeated Drupada in battle, brought him bound together with his ministers before Droṇa.
Droṇa said: "I desire friendship with you once again, O lord of men; for it is said that a non-king cannot deserve to be friend to a king."
"Therefore I have striven in your kingdom, O Yajñasena; you are king of the southern bank of the Bhāgīrathī, and I of the northern."
The brahmin said: That great insult never left the king's heart even for a moment; downcast in mind, he grew thin.
The brahmin said: King Drupada, burning with resentment, wandered through many brahmin hermitages seeking twice-born men accomplished in ritual action.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Desiring the birth of a son, his mind stricken with grief, he would always brood: "I have no excellent offspring."
In his despair he would curse even his born sons, saying "Shame on my kinsmen," and he was given over to sighing, desiring to requite Droṇa.
Reflecting on Droṇa's might, discipline, training, and conduct, and on his own kshatriya strength, that best of kings, O Bhārata, could find no way to requite him despite his efforts.
Wandering on the banks of the Kalmashin near the Gaṅgā, that lord of the earth came upon a holy brahmin hermitage.
There was no one who had not completed his studentship, no twice-born without a vow, and likewise none without high merit; and he saw two who were firm in their vows.
The son of Pṛṣata saw the two brahmin-sages Yāja and Upayāja, who were at rest, engaged in the study of the sacred collection, both belonging to the Kāśyapa lineage.
Those two best of sages, fit brahmins for conducting a rite of passage, he addressed with all manner of desirable things, tirelessly.
Perceiving the power and intelligence of both, he took the younger aside privately and approached Upayāja, who was firm in his vows, pleasing him with gifts.
Engaged in the service of his feet, speaking sweetly, giving him all his desires, he honored Upayāja duly and spoke to him:
"O brahmin, O Upayāja, by whatever rite a son might be born to me for the death of Droṇa — for that performed, I shall give you ten million cows."
"Or whatever else, O best of twice-born, may be deeply pleasing to your mind — all of that I shall give you; there is no doubt about this."
Thus addressed, the sage replied "Not I" — and Drupada, wishing to propitiate him, attended upon him again.
Then at the end of a year, that best of twice-born, Upayāja, spoke to Drupada, O king, at the right moment in a sweet voice:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"My elder brother, while wandering by a forest stream, picked up a fruit that had fallen to the ground whose purity was uncertain."
"I observed that improper action of my brother following him along, and I thought: he would never show discrimination in taking something impure."
"Seeing only the fruit, he did not notice the faults that attend it; one who does not discriminate purity — how could he do so in other matters?"
"He who, while studying the sacred texts and dwelling in his teacher's household, always eats the leftover alms-food of others, ever and again praising the merits of food and without shame —"
"I consider my brother to be one who seeks mere material fruit, by the eye of reasoning; go to him, O king — he will perform the sacrifice for you."
The king, though feeling a certain repugnance, reflected on this in his mind; having heard Upayāja's words, that king who knew all dharma duly honored the worthy sage Yāja and spoke to him:
"I shall give eighty thousand cows — perform the sacrifice for me, O lord; you ought to gladden me who am scorched by enmity toward Droṇa."
For he is the foremost among those who know the Brahman, and peerless in the Brahmā-weapon as well; it was for this reason that Droṇa defeated me in that conflict with my friend.
There is no warrior anywhere on earth who is his equal, no one who stands foremost — that wise Bhāradvāja, the chief preceptor of the Kauravas.
Droṇa's volleys of arrows strip away both life and body, and his bow — six cubits long — appears vast and without equal.
That great-souled great archer Bhāradvāja, with the force of a Brahmin, checks without doubt the force of the warrior class.
Stationed like Jāmadagnya, he is ordained for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas; his terrible power of arms is indeed irresistible by men on earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Pouring forth Brahmic energy like a fire fed with oblations, he consumes the warrior class in battle with the Brahman going before him; and when Brahmin and Kṣatriya power are ranged against each other, Brahmic energy prevails.
I, fallen short in the power of the warrior class and seeking Brahmic energy, have come to you — superior even to Droṇa and the most learned of those who know the Brahman.
I wish to obtain a son who will be Droṇa's death-in-battle, unconquerable in war — perform this rite for me, O Yāja; I will give you a hundred million cows.
Yāja agreed, saying 'so be it,' and prepared for the sacrifice on behalf of the patron; for the teacher's sake he also urged Upayāja, who was unwilling; and Yāja thus pledged himself for Droṇa's destruction.
Then the great ascetic Upayāja explained to that lord of men the sacrificial rite that would yield a son as its fruit.
"The son you desire — O king, one of great heroism, great energy and great strength — shall be just such a one as you wish."
With the intention of obtaining the slayer of Bharadvāja's son, king Drupada had all of that duly carried out for the success of the rite.
Then at the end of the oblation Yāja called out to the queen: "Come to me, O queen Pṛṣatī — a pair is ready awaiting you."
The queen said: "My face is anointed, O Brahmin, and I bear sacred fragrances upon me; I am detained on account of my desire for a son — wait for me, O Yāja, my dear."
Yāja said: "The oblation has been cooked by Yāja and consecrated by Upayāja — how can it fail to fulfil your wish? Come, O Brahmin lady, or stay as you will."
The narrator said: When Yāja had spoken thus, and the oblation had been poured and duly sanctified, a boy resembling a god arose from that fire.
Flame-colored, of terrible aspect, wearing a diadem and bearing the finest armor, sword in hand, arrow-equipped, bow in hand, he roared again and again.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He mounted a splendid chariot and set out in it; then the Pāñcālas shouted in delight, "Excellent! Excellent!"
"This prince, dispeller of fear, bringer of glory to the Pāñcālas, dispeller of the king's grief — he is born truly for the slaying of Droṇa!" — so said a great invisible being that moved through the sky at that time.
A maiden of Pāñcāla also arose from the midst of the sacrificial altar — lovely, beautiful of limb, slender-waisted, and delightful.
Dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals, curling dark hair, she bore a human form yet was visibly of celestial beauty.
From her wafted the fragrance of a blue lotus, perceptible from a league away; she bore supreme beauty for which there was no comparison on earth.
And as she of lovely hips was born, a bodiless voice spoke: "This Kṛṣṇā, foremost of all women, will bring about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas."
"This slender-waisted one will in time accomplish the work of the gods; on her account a great terror will arise among the Kṣatriyas."
Hearing this, all the Pāñcālas roared like a pride of lions; the earth could not bear those who were filled with such joy.
Seeing the two, Pṛṣatī — who had desired children — approached Yāja, saying: "Let these two know no other mother than me."
Yāja said "so be it" to her, wishing to please the king; and the twice-born, their hearts full of joy, gave names to the two.
"Because of his boldness and exceeding audacity, and because he arose from the sacred fire's brilliance, let this boy of Drupada be called Dhṛṣṭadyumna."
They called the girl Kṛṣṇā, for she was dark of complexion. Thus that twin pair was born at Drupada's great sacrifice.
Taking Dhṛṣṭadyumna of Pāñcāla into his own residence, the powerful Bhāradvāja trained him in the use of weapons.
The great-minded Droṇa, understanding that what is destined cannot be escaped, did this nonetheless — to preserve his own glory.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, the sons of Kuntī became as if pierced by lances, and those great warriors were all unsettled in mind.
Then Kuntī, seeing her sons distraught and out of their senses, spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira — she who ever speaks the truth.
"We have lodged here for a long time in the dwelling of the Brahmin, taking our pleasure in this delightful city and obtaining our alms, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
All the lovely forests and groves here have been seen again and again, O subduer of enemies.
Seen again and again, they no longer delight us as before; and alms too are not obtained as they were, O hero, O joy of the Kurus.
Let us go to Pāñcāla — if you think it good; we shall see things never seen before, my son, and it will be delightful.
The Pāñcālas are said to be prosperous, O you who wear down enemies, and that king Yajñasena too we have heard is devoted to Brahmins.
Long dwelling in one place is not good, and is not my view; let us go there to Pāñcāla — if you think so, my son."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Whatever you consider should be done is our highest good; as for my younger brothers, I know not whether they will go or not."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Kuntī spoke of the journey to Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the twins, and they too said "so be it" at that time.
Then, O king, Kuntī took leave of that Brahmin and set out together with her sons for the lovely city of the great-souled Drupada.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While those great-souled Pāṇḍavas were dwelling in disguise, Vyāsa the son of Satyavatī came to see them.
Seeing him arrive, those scorchers of enemies went forward to meet him, bowed down to him and greeted him, and then stood with hands joined in reverence.
Having given them all leave to be seated, the sage, pleased and honored by the sons of Pṛthā, spoke these words with affection.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Are you conducting yourselves according to dharma and the scriptures, O scorchers of enemies? Is your reverence toward the Brahmins who deserve reverence not diminishing?"
Having spoken words full of righteousness and purpose, and various other stories, that blessed sage then spoke again as follows.
"In a forest of asceticism there was once the daughter of a great-souled sage — slender-waisted, lovely-hipped, with beautiful brows, endowed with every virtue.
Yet through deeds done by herself she became ill-fated; that virtuous and beautiful maiden found no husband.
Unhappy, she then undertook to practice austerities for the sake of a husband, and with severe asceticism she propitiated Śaṃkara.
The blessed god, pleased with her, spoke to that ascetic woman: 'Choose a boon, fair one — good fortune to you; I am the giver of boons.'
Then she spoke to the Lord what was beneficial for her: 'I desire a husband endowed with every virtue' — she said this again and again.
Then the Lord, the best of speakers, replied to her: 'Five husbands shall be yours, O auspicious one' — so said Śaṃkara.
As she replied 'Give me one husband, O Śaṃkara,' he said to her once again these excellent words, O god:
'You have said to me five times \"give me a husband\"; when you have passed into another body, what I have said shall come to pass.'
'That maiden of divine appearance, born in Drupada's family — the blameless Kṛṣṇā Pārṣatī — is appointed as your wife.'
'Therefore enter the city of Pāñcāla, O men of great might; having obtained her you will be happy — there is no doubt.'
Having spoken thus, that most blessed grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas, the great ascetic, took leave of the sons of Pṛthā and Kuntī and departed.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those bulls among men, scorchers of enemies, set out with their mother placed in front, following level northward roads as directed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Traveling for a day and a night, those tigers among men, the sons of Pāṇḍu, reached the Somaśravāyaṇa ford on the Gaṅgā.
Lifting up a firebrand, the greatly famous Dhanaṃjaya went in front of them — to give light and for protection.
There, in the lovely waters of the Gaṅgā in a secluded spot, the jealous king of Gandharvas had come for water-sports, sporting with women.
He heard the sound of them approaching the river; possessed by that sound, that powerful one became extremely angry.
Seeing the Pāṇḍavas there together with their mother, those scorchers of enemies, he twanged his terrible bow and spoke these words.
"The terrible twilight that glows red at the coming of the early night — that moment, they say, is lacking eighty truṭas of the full period.
That time is ordained for the free movement of Yakṣas, Gandharvas and Rākṣasas; what remains besides is remembered here as the time for men to move at will.
Those foolish men who out of greed roam about at those hours — together with the Rākṣasas we seize and restrain those who transgress.
Those who know the Brahman censure all men who approach the water at night — even the powerful, even kings.
Stand far off — do not approach near to me! Why do you not recognize me who has come to the waters of the Bhāgīrathī?
Know me to be the Gandharva Aṅgāraparṇa, one who relies on his own strength; I am proud and jealous, and the beloved friend of Kubera.
This forest of mine is known as Aṅgāraparṇa — the beautiful one along the Gaṅgā and the Vākā — where I dwell.
Neither ghosts nor horned beasts, neither gods nor human beings approach this place — why then do you approach it?"
Arjuna said: "On the ocean, on the slopes of Himavat, or on this river, O wicked-minded one — whose domain is established for the night, the day, or the twilight?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
We are endowed with power and do not fear you even at an improper time; it is those who are powerless that honor you in a moment of danger.
"Of old this Gaṅgā issued forth from Himavat's golden peak, and flowing to the ocean's waters divides itself into seven streams.
And again, flowing pure as one stream through the sky, this Gaṅgā attains among the gods, O Gandharva, the form of the Alakanandā.
In the same way, for the ancestors she becomes the Vaitaraṇī, impassable by those of wicked deeds, O Gandharva — as Dvaipāyana has declared.
This unobstructed, auspicious divine river that leads to heaven — how do you wish to block it? This is not eternal dharma.
How should we not touch at will the sacred waters of the Bhāgīrathī, which cannot be stopped and is unobstructed — how can your words prevent us?"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that, Aṅgāraparṇa in fury bent his bow and discharged blazing arrows like venomous serpents.
Swiftly whirling the firebrand and raising his excellent shield, Dhanañjaya — the Pāṇḍava — deflected every single arrow of his.
Arjuna said: O gandharva, this terror of yours is not deployed against those who know the science of weapons; when directed at those who do know it, it dissolves like foam.
I regard all gandharvas as surpassing ordinary men, O gandharva; therefore I shall fight with a divine weapon, and not with illusion.
Long ago, O gandharva, Bṛhaspati — son of the guru of Śatakratu — bestowed this fire weapon upon Bharadvāja.
From Bharadvāja it passed to Agniveśa, and from Agniveśa to my guru; that foremost of brahmanas, Droṇa, gave it to me.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the Pāṇḍava, filled with wrath, released the blazing fire weapon at the gandharva, and it set his chariot ablaze.
That mighty gandharva was left without a chariot, utterly undone, bewildered by the brilliance of the weapon, and fell forward face downward.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhanañjaya seized him by his garlanded hair and dragged him — rendered senseless by the fall of the weapon — toward his brothers.
His wife, named Kumbhīnasī, seeking refuge and desiring to save her husband, threw herself before Yudhiṣṭhira as a suppliant.
The gandharva woman said: Save me, O great king, and release this husband of mine! I am a gandharva woman who has come to you for refuge — I am named Kumbhīnasī, O lord.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who indeed would slay an enemy who has been conquered in battle, stripped of glory, whose wife is his master, and who is no longer a warrior? O slayer of foes, release him.
Arjuna said: Take him back, O gandharva woman — go and do not grieve. The Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira grants you safety today.
The gandharva said: I have been defeated; I relinquish my former name Aṅgāraparṇa. Henceforth I shall not boast of my strength or my name in any gathering of people.
It is well indeed that I have gained this gain — that I, who wished to fight with gandharva illusion against one who wields divine weapons and is superior to me in age and valor.
My magnificent chariot has been burned by the fire of that weapon; I who was once Citraratha have now become Dagdharatha — the one with the burnt chariot — in name.
This knowledge was gathered by me through austerities long ago; today I shall present it to this great-souled one who has given me back my life.
He who reunites with life an enemy who was overpowered by force, defeated, and has come seeking refuge — does he not deserve every good fortune?
This knowledge is called Chakshushi — that which Manu gave to Soma; Soma gave it to Viśvāvasu, and Viśvāvasu gave it to me.
This guru-given knowledge, if it reaches a coward, is lost; I have described its origin — now hear from me its power.
Whatever one wishes to see with the eye in the three worlds, one can see it; and in whatever form one wishes to see it, one is able to behold it in that very form.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One who remains established in the vow for six months will obtain this knowledge; I myself will conduct this knowledge to you once the vow is observed.
By this knowledge, O king, we gandharvas are distinguished above men, yet we fall short of the gods, being moved by their power.
I shall give, O best of men, one hundred horses born of gandharvas each separately to your five brothers — a hundred for each.
These are the mounts of the gods and gandharvas, of divine fragrance, traveling at the speed of thought; though they may tire and tire again, their swiftness never diminishes.
Long ago, the thunderbolt of Mahendra, fashioned for the slaying of Vṛtra, was shattered tenfold and a hundredfold upon the head of Vṛtra.
Those portions were then distributed among the gods, and the share of the thunderbolt is worshipped in the world; whatever in the world serves as a means of power — that is said to be the body of the thunderbolt.
A brahmin is the thunderbolt in the hand; the kshatriya is said to be the thunderbolt of the chariot; the vaishyas are the thunderbolt of giving, and the youngest class the thunderbolt of action.
Horses are the thunderbolt of the kshatriya; horses are declared to be inviolable; a mare gives birth to the wheel of the chariot, and those considered chariot-drivers are among horses.
Of any color one desires, born as one desires, appearing at one's will — these horses born of gandharvas will fulfill your every wish.
Arjuna said: Whether given out of affection or when one's life was in danger — knowledge, wealth, or learning — I do not desire that, O gandharva.
The gandharva said: Fellowship indeed brings joy, as is seen in all assemblies; delighted by the gift of my life, I give you this knowledge.
From you I shall receive the supreme fire weapon in return, and likewise an enduring friendship, O Bībhatsu, O bull among the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Arjuna said: In exchange for the weapon I choose the horses from you; let our union be eternal, O friend. Tell me, O gandharva, what it is that would free you from fear.
Arjuna said: Tell me the reason, O gandharva — what was it by which we were assailed — we who were traveling, knowing the Vedas, virtuous, all of us, at night, O subduer of enemies?
The gandharva said: You were without fire, without offerings made into fire, and not accompanied by a brahmin in the lead — therefore you were assailed by me, O joy of the Pāṇḍavas.
Yakṣas, rakshasas, gandharvas, pisachas, serpents, and men — all these tell at length of the glory of your illustrious Kuru lineage.
And from Nārada and other divine sages I have heard, O hero, them recounting the virtues of your wise forebears.
And I myself have seen, as I wandered across this entire earth girdled by oceans, the power of your own lineage.
I recognize, O Arjuna, your teacher in the Veda and in archery — the illustrious Bharadvāja's son, renowned in the three worlds.
I know Dharma, Vāyu, and Śakra, likewise the Aśvins, and Pāṇḍu — these six, O tiger among Kurus, O Pārtha, these fathers, foremost among gods and men, who increased your lineage.
You brothers are of divine nature, great-souled, the foremost of all who bear weapons, heroic, all of you observing vows of noble conduct.
Yet knowing your sublime mind and intellect, O Pārtha, knowing you to be souls of disciplined spirit — I nevertheless committed this assault upon you here.
In the presence of women, O Kauravya, no man who relies upon the wealth of his arms ought to endure an insult to himself when he sees it.
And at night our strength increases even further; that is why wrath came upon me together with my wife, O son of Kuntī.
Yet I have been defeated by you here in battle, O enhancer of the lineage of Tapatī; learn from me by what means this glory is to be proclaimed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Brahmacharya — celibate discipline — is the supreme dharma, and that too is established in you; it is for this reason, O Pārtha, that I was conquered by you in this battle.
Whatever kshatriya, O scorcher of foes, is governed by desire and fights in battle at night — he cannot survive under any circumstances.
But a king who is even governed by desire, O descendant of Tapatī, can conquer all night-roaming beings in battle — provided he is guided by a purohita at the helm.
Therefore, O descendant of Tapatī, in whatever action men here seek their highest good, self-controlled purohitas should be engaged for that undertaking.
Those who are devoted to the Veda with its six limbs, who are pure, truthful in speech, righteous in soul, and disciplined in self — such men should be the purohitas of kings.
Victory is certain for a king, and heaven follows thereafter, whose chief priest is learned in dharma, eloquent, of noble character, and pure.
To gain what has not yet been gained, and to protect what has already been gained, a king should appoint a purohita endowed with virtuous qualities.
A king who wishes to obtain this entire earth, adorned by Meru as its crest jewel and girdled in all directions by ocean, should abide by the counsel of his purohita.
For no king, lacking brahmin support, can ever conquer the earth by valor alone or by noble birth alone — not anywhere.
Therefore understand this, O increaser of the Kuru lineage: a kingdom with brahmins at its head is alone capable of being sustained for a long time.
Arjuna said: The word 'Tapatya' that you have addressed to me here — I wish to understand the definitive meaning of 'Tapatya.'
Who is this Tapatī on account of whom we are called Tapatyas? We are the sons of Kuntī, O good one — I wish to know the truth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the gandharva caused Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, to hear a tale renowned throughout the three worlds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The gandharva said: Come then — I shall tell you this delightful tale in full and exactly as it happened, O Pārtha, O best of those who uphold dharma — a righteous tale.
The word by which I addressed you as 'Tapatya' — that I shall narrate to you now. Listen to me with an undivided mind.
He who pervades heaven with his seat and pervades the sky with his radiance — to him was born a daughter named Tapatī, matchless in form.
She was the daughter of Vivasvat, O son of Kuntī, the younger sister of Sāvitrī, O lord, renowned in the three worlds, and endowed with the heat of ascetic power.
She was not a goddess, nor an asuri, nor a yakshi, nor a rakshasi, nor an apsara, nor a gandharvi — no one possessed a form equal to hers.
Her limbs were well-proportioned and flawless; her eyes were dark and wide; she was virtuous in conduct, righteous, beautifully dressed, and resplendent.
Savitṛ found no one in the three worlds equal to her, O Bhārata — no one worthy to be her husband in beauty, character, lineage, and learning.
Seeing his daughter who had reached the bloom of youth, ready to be given in marriage, he found no peace as he pondered to whom to bestow her.
The son of Riksha and Artha, O son of Kuntī — Saṃvaraṇa, the bull among the Kurus, powerful king — always worshipped the Sun.
The king, ever steadfast, worshipped with offerings of water and garlands, with vows, fasts, and various austerities.
Devoted in service, free of arrogance, pure — the joy of the Paurava clan — he worshipped with devotion the radiant one rising with his rays.
Then the Sun regarded Saṃvaraṇa — grateful, learned in dharma, matchless in form on earth — as a worthy husband for Tapatī.
He then wished to give his daughter to that Saṃvaraṇa, O Kauravya — that foremost of kings, of illustrious lineage.
Just as the bright-rayed sun illumines the sky with his radiance, so did Saṃvaraṇa shine upon the earth with his own brilliance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Just as the knowers of Brahman worship the rising Āditya, so did the people — brahmins and lower orders alike — worship Saṃvaraṇa, O Pārtha.
That glorious king surpassed the moon in beauty and the sun in radiance — even in the eyes of enemies, not only of friends.
For a king of such qualities and such conduct, O Kauravya, the Sun himself resolved to give Tapatī.
Then one day that glorious king, of wide renown upon the earth, went hunting, O Pārtha, in the forest on a mountain — so it is said.
As he ranged in the hunt, his peerless horse — worn out by hunger, thirst, and fatigue — died on the mountain, O son of Kuntī.
His horse dead, the king wandered on the mountain on foot alone, O Pārtha, and he saw a maiden with wide eyes, matchless in the world.
He, the crusher of enemies, the tiger among kings, approaching that solitary maiden alone, stood still, gazing at her with unblinking eyes.
The king surmised her to be Śrī herself in form, then surmised again that she was like the radiance of the sun fallen to earth.
The mountain slope on which she stood, her eyes bright as a white blossom, glowed as though fashioned of gold — trees, shrubs, and all.
Beholding her, the king deemed her form surpassing that of every living creature; and he felt that his eyes had at last gained their true reward.
From the day of his birth the great king had seen many things, yet he reflected that he had never beheld any beauty comparable to hers.
His mind and eyes were bound by the cords woven from her virtues; he stirred not from that spot, and knew nothing of what passed around him.
"Surely," he thought, "the Creator churned the whole world — gods, asuras, and men alike — and brought forth this form of the wide-eyed one."
Thus did King Saṃvaraṇa reason to himself, marvelling at the treasure of her beauty, a maiden unequalled anywhere in the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That king of noble lineage, having gazed upon the auspicious maiden, fell into deep anxious thought, tormented by the arrows of desire.
Burning fiercely in the fire of Kāma, the bold king, though she was reticent, spoke to that renowned maiden.
"Who are you, O round-thighed one? Whose are you? For what purpose do you stand here? And how, O pure-smiling one, do you roam alone in this deserted forest?"
"You are blameless in every limb, adorned with every ornament; and yet you seem yourself to be the desired ornament of all these ornaments."
"I take you for neither a goddess nor an asura-woman, neither a yakṣī nor a rākṣasī, neither a serpent-princess of Bhogavatī, nor a gandharva-maiden, nor a mortal."
"Of all the beautiful women I have ever seen or heard of, I do not consider you the equal of any of them, O woman whose eyes are full and intoxicating."
Thus did the king address her; but she, in that solitary forest, did not reply a single word to the love-stricken man.
Then, as the king entreated her further, the large-eyed one vanished on that very spot, like a flash of lightning amid clouds.
Seeking her, the king wandered through that forest, eyes like lotus petals, roaming about like one who had lost his wits.
Not finding her, and having lamented greatly in that place, the foremost of the Kauravas stood motionless for a while, all movement ceased in him.
The Gandharva said: When she vanished from sight, the king, deluded by desire — he who was the feller of enemy hosts — fell to the ground.
When he had fallen upon the earth, that lovely-smiling, full and shapely-hipped woman revealed herself to the king once more.
Then the auspicious one spoke in a sweet voice to that king, founder of the Kuru line, whose mind was struck down by desire.
"Arise, arise! May fortune be yours! O subduer of foes, O tiger among kings, you ought not to yield to such delusion, lying exposed upon the earth."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed by her sweet voice, the king looked up and saw her — broad-hipped and fair — standing directly before him.
Then the lord of men, his soul consumed by the fire of Kāma, spoke to her of dark-tinged eyes in a voice uncertain and faltering.
"O dark-eyed one, O woman with full and bright eyes, favour me who am tormented by desire and who devotedly seeks you — for life is departing from me."
"For your sake, O wide-eyed one, O woman bright as the interior of a lotus, Kāma pierces me with his sharp arrows and does not abate."
"I am seized by the great serpent of desire and there is none to hear my cry, O fortunate one — O full-hipped, auspicious-faced woman, rescue me."
"My life depends entirely on you, O woman whose voice is like the song of a kiṃnara, whose every limb is beautiful and blameless, whose face resembles both the lotus and the moon."
"Without you, O timid one, I cannot sustain my life. Therefore, O wide-eyed woman, O graceful one, show compassion toward me."
"O dark-eyed one, you must not abandon me who am devoted to you. You have the power to save me with the bond of love, O passionate woman."
"Come, O timid one, beautiful woman, take me in the Gāndharva form of marriage — for of all marriage rites, O round-thighed one, the Gāndharva is said to be the highest."
Tapatī said: I am not mistress of my own person, O king — I am a maiden who has a father. If you truly love me, then go and ask my father.
"Just as you say your life has been seized by me, O lord of men, know too that at the very sight of you you have likewise taken away my life."
"Yet I am not free to dispose of my own body; therefore, O best of kings, I cannot draw near you — women are not independent."
"What maiden in all the worlds would not desire a king of celebrated lineage as her lord and husband, one who is kind and devoted to those who love him?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Therefore, in this situation, go and entreat my father, the sun-god Āditya, with prostrations, austerities, and observances."
"If he wishes to give me to you, O crusher of foes, then, O king, I shall forever be obedient to you."
"I am Tapatī by name, the younger sister of Sāvitrī, daughter of Savitṛ — of the sun who is the lamp of the world — O bull among kṣatriyas."
The Gandharva said: Having spoken thus, the blameless one swiftly rose upward; and the king fell once more upon the ground on that very spot.
The minister who had accompanied him found him in the great forest, fallen to the ground like the banner of Indra that has been cast down.
Seeing that great archer horseless and fallen to earth, the minister was as though set ablaze by fire.
He hastened to him with the agitation that love brings, and raised up the king who was dazed by desire.
Like a father lifting a fallen son from the ground, that minister — aged in wisdom, years, fame, and self-restraint — raised up the lord of earth.
Having raised the king, the minister's own anguish faded; and he spoke to him who had just risen, with auspicious, sweet words: "Fear not, O tiger among men; may good fortune be yours, O sinless one."
He surmised that the king — he who fells enemies in battle — had fallen to the ground overcome by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion.
He then sprinkled the king's head with very cool water fragrant as the white lotus, taking care not to disturb the royal crown.
When the powerful king had recovered his life-breath, he dismissed the entire army, retaining only that one minister.
By the king's command, the great army marched away; and the king sat down once more upon that mountain slope.
Then, on that excellent mountain, he became ritually pure, joined his palms in supplication, and stood upon the ground with arms raised, desiring to propitiate the sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And in his mind, King Saṃvaraṇa — the slayer of foes — turned also to Vasiṣṭha, the best of seers, his own household priest.
As the lord of the people remained thus in that solitary place through nights and days alike, the seer among brāhmaṇas came to him on the twelfth day.
That great and cultivated-souled seer, knowing by divine means that the king's heart had been taken by Tapatī, understood all.
That righteous-souled one then addressed the best of kings, who had been disciplining his self thus, desiring to accomplish his purpose.
While the lord of men watched, the blessed seer, radiant as the sun himself, ascended upward to behold the sun.
Standing before the thousand-rayed one with joined palms, Vasiṣṭha gladly made himself known, saying: "I am Vasiṣṭha."
Vivasvān, of great splendour, then said to the best of sages: "Welcome to you, O great seer — speak freely of whatever you wish."
Vasiṣṭha said: This daughter of yours named Tapatī, the younger sister of Sāvitrī — I ask you for her hand on behalf of Saṃvaraṇa, O Vibhāvasu.
"For that king Saṃvaraṇa is of great fame, learned in dharma and wealth, of noble mind — a fitting husband for your daughter, O one who roams the sky."
The Gandharva said: Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, Savitā the day-maker, resolved to give her, welcomed the seer and replied.
"Saṃvaraṇa is the best among kings; you are the best among sages, O muni; Tapatī is the best among women — what reason could there be for refusal?"
Then Tapana himself gave the blameless Tapatī — resplendent as fire — for Saṃvaraṇa's sake to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha; and the great seer accepted that maiden Tapatī.
Vasiṣṭha, having been sent off, came back again to the place where that bull of the Kurus of celebrated fame was waiting.
That king, who had been possessed by Kāma and whose inner self had dwelt entirely on her, seeing that goddess-daughter, the lovely-smiling Tapatī, coming with Vasiṣṭha, was filled with exceeding joy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the king's twelve nights of arduous vigil had been completed, the pure-souled, blessed seer Vasiṣṭha arrived.
Having propitiated through austerities the boon-granting god, the lord and master of the cattle of the sky, Saṃvaraṇa obtained his wife by the very power of Vasiṣṭha.
Then on that most excellent mountain, frequented by gods and gandharvas, that bull among men took Tapatī's hand according to the rites.
Permitted by Vasiṣṭha, that royal seer desired to dwell on that same mountain range in the company of his wife.
Thereupon the lord of earth gave command over the city, the realm, the transport, and the armies to that same minister.
Vasiṣṭha then took his leave of the king and departed; and the king too sported on that mountain, like one equal to an immortal.
For twelve years the king took his pleasure on that mountain, in its forests and waters, together with his wife alone.
During those twelve years, throughout that king's city and throughout all his realm, the thousand-eyed Indra sent no rain whatsoever.
That city then, with its people tormented by hunger, joyless, and reduced to the state of corpses, looked like the city of the king of the dead, crowded with ghosts.
Seeing the city in such a state, that same blessed seer — righteous-souled Vasiṣṭha — went to the best of kings.
He brought that tiger among kings back to his city — O king — together with Tapatī, after his having sojourned twelve years away.
Then, as that tiger among kings re-entered his city, the slayer of the enemies of the gods — Indra — caused rain to fall there as in former times.
Then that city, together with the whole kingdom, rejoiced with the greatest joy, enlivened by that foremost of kings, himself of enlivened soul.
Thereafter the lord of men performed sacrifice for twelve more years together with his wife Tapatī, just as Śakra the lord of the Maruts does.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Such was she — the greatly blessed Tapatī of ancient times, daughter of Vivasvat — O Pārtha; and it is from her that you are known as Tāpatya.
King Saṃvaraṇa begot upon Tapatī the ancestor Kuru, O best of those who blaze with splendour; from her descent you are called Tāpatya, O Arjuna.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of the gandharva, Arjuna, O bull of the Bhārata line, shone with the greatest delight, like the full moon.
And that great archer, best of the Kurus, deeply curious about the power of Vasiṣṭha's austerity, spoke to the gandharva.
"This name of the seer 'Vasiṣṭha' that you have uttered — I wish to hear the full account of it. Tell me truly."
O lord of the Gandharvas, who was this one who served as the family priest of our ancestors? Tell me of him — who indeed is this venerable sage?
The Gandharva said: He whose two feet were forever massaged by desire and anger — both of them conquered by his austerity, those two who are ever unconquerable even by the immortals —
who, though of noble spirit, did not bring about the destruction of the Kuśikas despite Viśvāmitra's offense, even while bearing the greatest wrath within —
who, though powerful and lordly and tormented by the calamity of his sons, did not choose the terrible deed of destroying Viśvāmitra —
who, even to bring back his dead sons from Yama's realm, did not transgress fate, just as the great ocean does not transgress its shore —
having obtained whom — that self-conquered, great-souled one — the Ikṣvāku kings, those guardians of the earth, won this world —
having obtained Vasiṣṭha, the best of household priests, the foremost of sages, those kings performed sacrifices, O joy of the Kurus —
for that brahmarshi presided over the sacrifices of all those foremost kings, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, just as Bṛhaspati does for the immortals —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
therefore a brahmin who is foremost in righteousness, who knows the dharma of the Vedas, who is sought-after and endowed with virtues — some such one should be carefully chosen as your priest.
For a man born as a kshatriya who desires to conquer the earth must first appoint a household priest, O Pārtha, for the increase of his kingdom.
A king who desires to conquer the earth must place a brahmin at the fore; therefore let some virtuous twice-born one be your household priest.
Arjuna said: What was the cause of the enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha as they dwelt in their holy hermitage? Tell us all of that fully.
The Gandharva said: This ancient tale of Vasiṣṭha is told throughout all the worlds, O Pārtha. Learn it fully from me.
In Kānyakubja there was a great king, O bull among Bhāratas, known in the world as Gādhi — devoted to truth and righteousness.
This righteous king's son, possessed of abundant forces and mounts, became known as Viśvāmitra, the crusher of foes.
He roamed the hunt with his ministers through dense forest, piercing deer and boars in the pleasant sandy tracts.
Worn thin by exertion, eager for game and overcome with thirst, he came, O foremost of men, toward the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Seeing him arrive, Vasiṣṭha the sage, foremost in good fortune, received Viśvāmitra, that foremost of men, with full honor.
With water for the feet, the guest-offering, water for sipping, and a warm welcome, O Bhārata, he received him likewise with forest oblations.
Then the wish-granting cow of great-souled Vasiṣṭha, told to yield all desires, duly milked them forth.
She milked herbs both domestic and wild, and milk itself, and the six tastes, and the nectar-like juice, the unsurpassed elixir of life.
Foods to be eaten, liquids to be drunk, various delicacies to be chewed, lickable things akin to ambrosia, and things to be sucked — all of these, O Arjuna.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Honored with all those desires fully provided, that lord of the earth together with his ministers and army was greatly pleased, that king.
With six elongated parts, fine flanks and thighs, three broad parts and five contracted ones, frog-like eyes, perfect form, and full udder — blameless —
with a handsome tail, spike-shaped ears, beautiful horns, and a lovely form, with well-nourished, elongated head and neck — gazing at her in wonder —
delighted by Nandini, Vasiṣṭha's milk-cow, Viśvāmitra, greatly pleased, spoke to the sage:
"Give me Nandini, O brahmin, in exchange for ten million cows, or else for my kingdom — enjoy my kingdom, O great sage."
Vasiṣṭha said: For the sake of the gods, guests, and ancestors, and for clarified butter offerings, this milk-cow Nandini is not to be given away by me, even for your kingdom, O sinless one.
Viśvāmitra said: I am a kshatriya; you are a brahmin whose means are austerity and Vedic study. Where does valor reside in brahmins, who are tranquil and self-controlled?
"Since you will not give me what I desire even for ten million cows, I will not abandon my own duty — I shall take your cow by force."
Vasiṣṭha said: You stand in power; you are a king; you are a kshatriya of mighty arm. Do quickly as you wish — do not deliberate.
The Gandharva said: Thus addressed, O Pārtha, Viśvāmitra then seized by force that cow Nandini, who resembled a swan or the moon.
Struck by whips and staffs, driven this way and that, lowing aloud, that auspicious Nandini of Vasiṣṭha —
turned back and stood facing him, O Pārtha, her face turned toward her lord; though beaten hard, she did not leave the hermitage.
Vasiṣṭha said: I hear your cry, dear one, as you call out again and again. You are being carried off by force, O Nandī — but I am a brahmin, and forbearance is my nature.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
