The Blessed Lord granted him one birth in the lineage; and since then, only one birth at a time has ever occurred in this family.
From all those earlier ancestors of mine, only boys were born; but this daughter of mine was born as the certain perpetuator of the lineage.
My conviction is that she is my son, O best of men; by the rule of the putrika she is designated thus, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Let this be the bride-price for her: a son born here shall be the founder of the lineage. On this condition accept her, O Pāṇḍava.
Having pledged "so be it" and having accepted that maiden, the son of Kuntī dwelt in that city for three winter seasons.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the bull of the Bhāratas proceeded to visit the most sacred shrines on the southern ocean, adorned by ascetics.
The ascetics there avoided five of those shrines — those which had previously been frequented by ascetics of old.
Agastya's shrine, Saubhadra, Pauloma — most purifying — Karandhama the clear, the one granting the fruit of the horse-sacrifice, and the great shrine of Bharadvāja that quells sin.
The Pāṇḍava noticed those shrines to be deserted, and seeing them shunned by the sages of righteous mind,
the descendant of Kuru then asked the ascetics with folded hands: "Why are these shrines avoided by those versed in sacred lore?"
The ascetics said: Five crocodiles dwell in these waters and drag down men rich in austerity; therefore these shrines are avoided, O descendant of Kuru.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing their words, the mighty-armed best of men — though restrained by the ascetics — went to see those shrines himself.
Then reaching Saubhadra, the foremost shrine of the great sage, the heroic scorcher of foes plunged in swiftly and bathed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then a great crocodile dwelling beneath the water seized in the depths that tiger among men, Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī.
The mighty-armed son of Kuntī, best among the strong, lifted that thrashing water-creature out of the water by sheer force.
As it was dragged out by the glorious Arjuna, the crocodile became a beautiful woman adorned with all ornaments, blazing with splendour, O king — divine in form and enchanting to behold.
Seeing that great marvel, Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī, was utterly delighted and spoke these words to that woman:
"Who are you, fair one? Where do you come from, you who were dwelling in the water? And why did you formerly commit this great sin?"
The woman said: I am an apsara, O mighty-armed one, who roams the divine forests; I am beloved of the Lord of wealth — Varga is my name, O great one.
I have four other companions, all beautiful and able to go wherever they wish; together with them I had journeyed to the abode of the World-guardians.
There we all beheld a brahmin firm in his vow, handsome, engaged in study, alone, wandering in solitude.
By his austerity, O king, that entire forest was covered with his radiance; like the sun, he illumined that whole region.
Seeing such austerity and a form so wondrous to behold, we descended to that place intending to obstruct his penances.
I, and Saurabheyī, Samici, Budbuda, and Lata — all together we approached that brahmin, O Bhārata.
Singing, laughing, and enticing that twice-born, he did not at all turn his mind toward us, O hero; the great-souled one did not waver, established in pure austerity.
That brahmin, angered, cursed us, O bull among warriors: 'You shall become crocodiles and roam the waters for a hundred years.'
Varga said: Then all of us, greatly distressed, O best of the Bhāratas, went for refuge to that unwavering brahmin rich in austerity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Intoxicated by beauty, youth, and the arrows of Kāma, we have done what was not fitting; please forgive us, O twice-born one.'
'This itself is punishment enough for us, O wealth of austerity, that we came here to tempt you, a man of sharpened soul.'
'Those who contemplate the law hold that women were created inviolable; therefore by the law, O knower of the law, you ought not to harm us.'
'A brahmin is called the friend of all beings, O knower of the law; may this saying of the wise prove true, O auspicious one.'
'The righteous protect those who come to them for refuge; we have come to you for refuge, therefore you ought to forgive us.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, that righteous brahmin, doer of auspicious deeds, radiant as the sun and moon combined, was gracious, O hero.
The brahmin said: A hundred, a thousand, the all — these words denote the inexhaustible; but "hundred" here is merely a measure and does not mean the inexhaustible.
When you, having become crocodiles, are seizing men in the water, and some best of men lifts one of you from the water to dry land —
then you shall all regain your own forms. Never before have I spoken an untruth, even in jest.
All those shrines from this time forward shall everywhere be known in the world as the Women's Shrines by name, and shall be holy and purifying for the wise.
Varga said: Then, having saluted that brahmin and circumambulated him, we departed from that region in great distress, pondering our fate.
"Where indeed and when shall we all meet that man who will restore us to our own forms once more?"
While we were pondering thus, O Bhārata, in a moment as it were, we caught sight of the greatly blessed divine sage Nārada.
All of us were delighted to see that divine sage of immeasurable brilliance; we saluted him, O Pārtha, and stood before him with anguished faces.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He asked us the root of our suffering; we told him everything; and having heard it and the entire occurrence, he spoke these words:
'On the southern shore of the ocean there are five sacred and delightful shrines — go there without delay.'
'There soon the tiger among men, the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya, pure of soul, will without doubt rescue you from your suffering.'
Hearing his words, all of us came here, O hero; and today that has come true — I have been freed by you, O sinless one.
These four other companions of mine still remain in the water; perform a good deed, O hero — free them all.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the foremost of Pāṇḍavas, lord of the people, undaunted in spirit, the valiant one, freed them all from that curse.
Rising from that water and regaining their own forms, those apsaras, O king, became visible again just as they had been before.
Having thus purified those shrines and taken leave of them, the lord went to the city of Manalura to see Citrāṅgada again.
Upon her he fathered a son, the king Babhruvāhana; having seen him, O king, the Pāṇḍava proceeded toward Gokarṇa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: He of immeasurable prowess visited in due order all the sacred shrines and holy places in the western coastal region.
Having visited all the shrines and holy places on the western ocean, he arrived at Prabhāsa.
The slayer of Madhu heard that Bībhatsu, the unconquered, had reached the Prabhāsa region and was travelling from shrine to shrine.
Then the Mādhava went unannounced to the son of Kuntī; and the two — Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava — beheld each other at Prabhāsa.
The two dear friends — those seers Nara and Nārāyaṇa — embraced one another and enquired after each other's welfare in the forest, and sat down together.
Then Vāsudeva asked Arjuna about that journey: "Why, O Pāṇḍava, do you travel through all these shrines?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Arjuna narrated everything as it had occurred; and hearing it, the lord of the Vṛṣṇi clan said "Even so it is."
After the two — Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava — had taken their pleasure at Prabhāsa as they wished, they went to the mountain Raivataka to spend the night.
At Kṛṣṇa's prior instruction, men had already adorned that mountain and brought food there.
Arjuna accepted everything, and the Pāṇḍava, having enjoyed it together with Vāsudeva, watched actors and dancers.
Having dismissed them all and honoured them, the Pāṇḍava of great radiance went to a well-appointed, divine bed.
He recounted to the Sātvata the sights of the shrines, the mountains, the rivers, and the forests, O Bhārata.
While still telling those tales, O Janamejaya, the son of Kuntī was carried away by sleep on that heaven-like bed.
Roused by sweet song and the sound of the vina, and by auspicious hymns of praise, O sinless one, he awoke.
Having performed his necessary duties and welcomed by the Vṛṣṇi lord, he set out for Dvārakā on a chariot with golden fittings.
Dvārakā was adorned, O Janamejaya, in honour of the son of Kuntī — even in the inner courtyards.
The people of Dvārakā, eager to see the son of Kuntī, rushed in hundreds of thousands to the king's highway.
At the viewing-galleries there were hundreds and thousands of women, and a great assembly of the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas gathered.
Honoured thus by all the sons of the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, saluting and being saluted by all, he was welcomed with joy.
Greeted with honour by princes on all sides, the hero embraced all those of equal age again and again.
In Kṛṣṇa's delightful palace, filled with jewels and rich food, he dwelt together with Kṛṣṇa, passing many nights there.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, after a few days, O king, a very great festival of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas took place on that Raivataka mountain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There the heroes of the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas gave gifts to brahmins by the thousands, in honour of that great mountain.
With palaces inlaid with gems all around that mountain, the region was made beautiful, O king, and with lamp-trees on every side.
Musicians played their instruments there; dancers danced; and singers sang their songs.
Adorned young princes of the Vṛṣṇis, of very great energy, moved about everywhere in carriages decorated with gold ornaments.
Citizens on foot and in vehicles great and small, accompanied by their wives and retinues, moved about in hundreds and thousands.
Then Balarāma, the wielder of the plough — intoxicated, accompanied by Revati, attended by Gandharvas — roamed there, O Bhārata.
Likewise the mighty king of the Vṛṣṇis, Ugrasena the illustrious, was being extolled by the Gandharvas, attended by a thousand women.
Rukmiṇī's son and Sāmba, both exhilarated and terrible in battle, wearing divine garlands and garments, sported there like two immortals.
Akrūra, Sāraṇa, Gada, Bhānu, Viḍūratha, Niśaṭha, Cārudeṣṇa, Pṛthu and Vipṛthu —
Satyaka, Sātyaki, and Bhangakara's companions, Hārdikya Kṛtavarman, and many others not named here —
all these, each accompanied by women and Gandharvas separately, adorned that festival on mount Raivataka at that time.
While that great and auspicious tumult was in progress, Vāsudeva and Pārtha wandered about together.
As the two strolled there, they beheld at that moment Vāsudeva's daughter Bhadra, fair and adorned, in the midst of her companions.
The moment Arjuna saw her, Kāma arose within him; and Kṛṣṇa noticed Pārtha thus with his mind fixed single-pointedly upon her.
Then the lotus-eyed one spoke, almost smiling, O Bhārata: "Why is the mind of this forest-dweller now stirred by desire?"
"This is my sister, O Pārtha, the full sister of Sāraṇa; if the thought abides in your mind, I shall speak to my father myself."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Arjuna said: She is the daughter of Vāsudeva and the sister of Vāsudeva; endowed with such beauty, whom would she not bewitch?
All good fortune would surely be mine if this lady of the Vṛṣṇi clan, your sister, were to become my principal queen.
But what means could there be of obtaining her — tell me, Janārdana; I will undertake everything, if it is achievable by a man.
Vāsudeva said: The svayamvara is the marriage form of Kṣatriyas, O bull among men; yet that too, O Pārtha, is uncertain because of the unpredictability of her own inclination.
Forcible abduction is also praised among Kṣatriyas for the purpose of marriage, among heroes — so those who know dharma declare.
Therefore, Arjuna, you yourself forcibly carry off my auspicious sister; for who can know what she intends in a svayamvara?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa, having resolved on the course of action, dispatched swift messengers, O king, at that time.
All of this was conveyed to Dharmarāja at Indraprastha, and that mighty-armed Pāṇḍava, having heard it, gave his consent.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O Janamejaya, once agreement was reached and Dhanañjaya had received permission, learning that the maiden had gone to mount Raivataka —
permitted by Vāsudeva, having announced the plan of action, and knowing Kṛṣṇa's intent, that bull of the Bhārata line set forth.
On a chariot with golden fittings, properly equipped, yoked with the horses Sainya and Sugrīva, and adorned with a net of small bells —
furnished with every weapon, thundering like a cloud in a forest, blazing bright as a burning fire, the slayer of enemies' joy —
fully armored, wearing his cuirass, sword at his side, wrist-guard and finger-guard fastened on — under the pretext of a hunt, simultaneously, O Bhārata.
Meanwhile Subhadrā, having worshipped the lord of mountains Raivataka together with all the deities, and having received the blessings of the Brāhmaṇas —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
having circumambulated the mountain clockwise, was proceeding toward Dvārakā; Kaunteya rushed upon her and forcibly lifted her onto the chariot.
Then that tiger among men, taking her of the pure smile, sped away on that sky-coursing chariot toward his own city.
Seeing Subhadrā being carried away, the soldiers all ran crying out in all directions toward the city of Dvārakā.
Coming together, they reached the assembly hall of Sudharma and reported to the hall-guardian everything of Pārtha's bold act.
Hearing their report, the hall-guardian then struck the great war drum, loud-sounding, adorned with gold.
Stirred by that sound, the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas then flung aside their food and drink and flocked to the assembly.
Then with golden frames, spread with costly coverings, inlaid with gems and coral, blazing with a fiery radiance —
the great warrior Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka heroes, tigers among men, occupied the hundreds of thrones like fires upon their altars.
When they were seated, like the assembly of gods, the hall-guardian and his attendants reported to them the deed of Jiṣṇu.
Hearing that, those Vṛṣṇi heroes, their eyes reddened at the corners with pride and wine, unable to endure it, rose up in arrogance against Pārtha.
"Yoke the chariots quickly!" and "Bring the lances!" and "Bring the great bows and the broad coats of mail!" —
some cried out to the charioteers "Yoke the chariots!" and some themselves led out the horses adorned with gold.
With chariots being brought, coats of mail and banners being borne out, and the war-cries of the warrior-heroes, there was a great tumult at that time.
Then Vanamali, intoxicated, resembling the peak of Mount Kailāsa, clad in blue, swelling with exhilaration, spoke these words:
"What are you doing, you imprudent ones? While Janārdana sits silent, you are in a rage without knowing his mind — these are empty roarings."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let this one of great wisdom first declare his own intention; whatever pleases him to do, that do you carry out without delay."
Then they, hearing that speech from Halaayudha — acceptable in its form — all fell silent, and said "Well said, well said."
Having heard the balanced words of wise Baladeva, all of them sat down again in the midst of the assembly.
Then Kamapala addressed Vāsudeva the scorcher of foes: "Why do you sit silent and merely watching, Janārdana?"
"Pārtha was honored by all of us out of regard for you, O Acyuta, and yet that evil-minded defiler of his lineage does not deserve such honor."
"For what man who considers himself born in a noble family would think it right to break the very vessel in which he has just eaten?"
"And who, desiring a connection and honoring one already formed, could act in so reckless a manner as to call himself a man of honor?"
"He, having insulted us and disregarded Keśava, has today forcibly carried off Subhadrā — it is his own death that he has seized."
"How can I endure the foot he has placed upon the very crown of my head, O Govinda — as a serpent endures the touch of a foot?"
"Today I alone will make the earth free of Kauravas; this transgression of Arjuna is not to be tolerated by me."
Him thus roaring like the thunder of a great drum of clouds, all the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas then followed at that time.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When all the Vṛṣṇis had spoken their words more than once, then Vāsudeva spoke words full of righteousness and purpose:
"Guḍākeśa has not offered any insult to this family; rather, a higher honor has been shown by him — of this there is no doubt."
"Pārtha does not regard you Sātvatas as greedy for gain; the Pāṇḍava also considers a svayamvara something not to be resisted, for him."
"Who would sanction the gift of a maiden as though she were cattle? And what man on earth would make a sale of his own offspring?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"It is my belief that Kaunteya saw these faults; it is for this reason that the Pāṇḍava carried off the maiden by force, and with dharma on his side."
"And this alliance is fitting, and Subhadrā is illustrious; and Pārtha himself is of such quality — it is for these reasons he has carried her off by force."
"Born in the lineage of Bharata and of the great-souled Śaṃtanu, the grandson of Kuntibhoja's daughter — who would not wish for Arjuna?"
"And I see no one who could defeat Pārtha by valor, even in all the worlds, O noble ones, including those of Indra and Rudra."
"And that chariot of mine, and those horses of mine, and Pārtha as a fighter swift with his weapons — who could be a match for him?"
"Pursue Dhanañjaya and turn him back with the highest conciliation — this is my paramount counsel, and you should follow it gladly."
"If Pārtha were to conquer you and depart by force to his own city, your glory would instantly be destroyed; but in conciliation there is no defeat."
Hearing that, they acted accordingly, O lord of the people; and Arjuna turned back, and there performed the marriage.
Kaunteya dwelt there for more than a year of nights, then the lord spent the remaining time at the Puṣkara tirthas; and when the full twelve years were completed, he entered Khāṇḍavaprastha.
Approaching the king with due humility and self-restraint, and having honored the Brāhmaṇas, Pārtha came to Draupadī.
Draupadī replied to that delighter of the Kurus with affection: "Go there, O Kaunteya, where that daughter of the Sātvata is; even a firmly tied knot loosens first at the old binding."
Dhanañjaya consoled Kṛṣṇā who was lamenting in many ways, and time and again besought her forgiveness.
And Pārtha, acting swiftly, dressed Subhadrā in red silk garments and sent her forward disguised in the form of a cowherdess.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Radiant beyond measure in that form, the illustrious one, wife of a hero and a beautiful woman, reaching the finest dwelling, Bhadra of wide copper-red eyes, that illustrious one, bowed to Pṛthā.
Then Bhadra, her face like the full moon, quickly approached and bowed to Draupadī, saying: "I am your servant."
And Kṛṣṇā, rising to meet her, embraced that sister of Mādhava, and spoke in delight: "May your husband be without a rival!" And Bhadra, equally gladdened, said: "So be it."
Then those great warrior Pāṇḍavas were gladdened in their hearts, and Kuntī was supremely delighted, O Janamejaya.
Hearing that Arjuna, best of the Pāṇḍavas, had arrived at his excellent city and had gone to Indraprastha —
Keśava of the pure soul came together with Rāma, accompanied by the great ministers and the heroic great warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
Encircled by his brothers and young princes and by warriors in their hundreds, the Śauri, that scorcher of foes, was guarded by a great army.
There too came the wise and greatly renowned lord of gifts, Akrūra, the commander of the Vṛṣṇi heroes, the subduer of enemies.
Anādhṛṣṭi of great splendor, and Uddhava of great fame — the very pupil of Bṛhaspati, of great intellect and great renown.
Satyaka and Sātyaki, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata, Pradyumna and Sāmba, and Niśaṭha and Śaṅku —
the valiant Cārudeṣṇa, Jhilli, and Vipṛthu, and the mighty-armed Sāraṇa, and Gada the foremost among the wise —
these and many others among the Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas, and Andhakas came to Khāṇḍavaprastha, bringing with them abundant wedding gifts.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, hearing that Mādhava had arrived, sent forth the twin brothers at that time to receive Kṛṣṇa with due honor.
Received and escorted by those two, that prosperous Vṛṣṇi host entered Khāṇḍavaprastha, which was brilliant with banners and standards.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The roads had been sprinkled and swept clean, adorned with heaps of flowers, and pervaded with the cool, sacred fragrance of sandalwood paste.
Fragrant aloe-wood was burning in every quarter; the streets were thronged with well-dressed crowds and graced by merchants on all sides.
The mighty-armed Keśava, best of men, accompanied by Rāma and surrounded by the great chiefs of the Vṛṣṇi, Andhaka, and Bhoja clans, entered the city.
Honored by the citizens and by thousands of Brahmins, he entered the king's palace, which was like the abode of Indra.
Yudhiṣṭhira met Rāma with due ceremony, and after smelling Keśava's head in affection, embraced him with both arms.
Kṛṣṇa honored him in return with great affection and humility, and duly paid his respects to Bhīma, that tiger among men.
The king of righteousness, Yudhiṣṭhira, received those foremost Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka warriors with due honor, each according to his rank and as they came forward.
Some he honored as elders, some as equals and companions; some he greeted with affection, and by others he was himself saluted.
Then the greatly renowned Vāsudeva gave, as the wedding gift — the share due from the bridegroom's kin — the finest wealth for Subhadrā's marriage portion.
Kṛṣṇa gave a thousand chariots with golden fittings, adorned with networks of bells, each drawn by four horses and driven by skilled charioteers, and also ten thousand cows.
The glorious Janārdana, with great joy, also gave a thousand milch cows from the Mathurā region, radiant in their auspicious splendor, and a thousand white mares with limbs bright as moonbeams, adorned with gold ornaments.
Likewise he gave five hundred groups of five each — tamed she-mules swift as the wind, with dark manes yet white in body.
Also a thousand fair-complexioned women skilled in bathing and anointing, well matched in age, beautifully dressed and radiant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The lotus-eyed one gave these women, each adorned with a hundred golden neck-ornaments, healthy and well-robed, expert in personal attendance.
Janārdana, scion of the Dāśārha line, gave ten man-loads of finest gold — both wrought and unwrought — blazing like fire.
Of elephants in triple rut, with ichor flowing from three places, resembling mountain peaks, never retreating in battle —
— well-caparisoned, adorned with sharp-sounding golden bells and gold garlands, each furnished with its mahout — a thousand such noble elephants did that lover of bold deeds bestow.
Rāma the plough-bearer, delighted and expressing his joy at the new alliance, gave Pārtha a gift to mark the taking of his feet — a token of reverential affection.
That great river of wealth and jewels, foaming with garments and blankets, filled with great elephants and mighty crocodiles, crowded with banners and water-weeds —
— that great river flowed into and filled the white sea of the Pāṇḍavas to overflowing, becoming a grief to their enemies.
Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira received all those gifts and duly honored the great Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka warriors.
Those great-souled ones — the best of Kurus, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas — assembled together and made merry, like virtuous men enjoying the abode of the immortals.
Here and there the Kurus and Vṛṣṇis reveled at grand drinking parties resounding with the clapping of excellent palms, each group as befitted the occasion and their own delight.
Thus, after those warriors of supreme valor had sported for many days and been duly honored by the Kurus, they departed once more for the city of Dvāravatī.
The great Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka warriors set out with Rāma at their head, carrying the bright jewels given to them by the best of the Kurus.
But Vāsudeva, O descendant of Bharata, remained right there in the beautiful city of Śakraprastha, great-souled, and roamed the banks of the Yamunā together with Pārtha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Subhadrā, the dear sister of Keśava, gave birth to a son, Abhimanyu, as radiant as Jayanta — just as Paulomī bore Jayanta to Indra.
Subhadrā brought forth the hero Abhimanyu, bull among men — long-armed, of great vitality, with eyes like a bull's, a crusher of foes.
Because he was fearless and full of wrath, and a trampler of enemies, they called that bull among men, son of Arjuna, Abhimanyu.
That supreme chariot-warrior was born from Dhanaṃjaya upon the Sātvata woman, like fire kindled from the womb of the śamī wood when it is churned at a sacrifice.
At his birth, the mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, gave ten thousand cows to the twice-born, and an equal number of gold coins.
From early childhood he became the beloved of Vāsudeva, and of all his fathers' hearts — as the moon is dear to all beings.
From his very birth, Kṛṣṇa performed all the auspicious rites for him, and the child grew like the moon in the bright fortnight.
That crusher of foes mastered from Arjuna — the knower of the Veda — the whole science of archery in its four sections and ten divisions, both divine and human.
In the theoretical knowledge of weapons, in graceful skill, and in all practical exercises as well, the mighty one surpassed even his teacher.
In both theory and practice he became almost Arjuna's equal, and Dhanaṃjaya rejoiced as he watched his son, Subhadrā's child.
Endowed with every bodily excellence, marked with every auspicious sign, irresistible, with the shoulders of a bull, and with gaping mouth like a serpent —
— with the pride of a lion, a mighty bowman, with the gait of a frenzied elephant, whose voice rumbled like a thundercloud or a drum, and whose face shone like the full moon —
— Arjuna beheld his son as equal to Kṛṣṇa in valor, prowess, form, and bearing, just as Maghavan (Indra) might behold such a one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the auspicious Pāñcālī too received from her five husbands five heroic, splendid sons, like five great mountains.
From Yudhiṣṭhira she bore Prativindhya; from Vṛkodara, Sutasoma; from Arjuna, Śrutakarmā; and from Nakula, Śatānīka.
And from Sahadeva she bore Śrutasena. These five great chariot-warriors did the Pāñcālī bring forth, as Aditi bore the Ādityas.
The Brahmins told Yudhiṣṭhira regarding that child: based on scripture, let his name be Prativindhya, for he is the equal of the Vindhya mountain in his knowledge of striking down enemies.
When a thousand soma oblations had been performed, she bore from Bhīmasena a mighty bowman as radiant as the sun and moon combined — and so he was called Sutasoma.
When the crowned one (Arjuna) had returned after accomplishing his celebrated great deeds, the news reached him: "A son is born to you" — and so that son was named Śrutakarmā.
Nakula, son of the Kurus, a delight of the Kuru line, who traced his lineage to the royal sage Śatānīka, gave his son the same name as that ancestor — one who would extend the family's glory.
Then Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) gave birth to a son by Sahadeva under the asterism presided over by the fire-god; hence they called him Śrutasena.
The sons of Draupadī, all renowned and devoted to one another's welfare, were born each a year apart, O king of kings.
Dhaumya performed for them in due order and in accordance with sacred rite the birth ceremonies, the tonsure, and the sacred thread investiture, O best of the Bhāratas.
Having completed their Vedic studies, those pure in conduct and observance then received from Arjuna all the science of archery — both divine and human.
Attended by sons comparable to divine offspring — broad-chested, of mighty strength — the Pāṇḍavas were filled with great joy, O tiger among kings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Dwelling at Indraprastha, they subdued other kings, acting under the command of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Śaṃtanu.
Resorting to the king of righteousness — whose marks and deeds were all auspicious — all people lived happily, as embodied souls dwell at ease in their own bodies.
That bull of the Bhāratas honored dharma, desire, and wealth equally, cherishing them as three kinsmen equal to himself, like a man who truly has kin.
With dharma, wealth, and desire equally apportioned among embodied beings upon the earth, the king shone like a fourth among them.
The Vedas found in him their supreme student; the great sacrifices found their performer; the social orders found their auspicious protector — so they all gained that lord of men.
Prosperity had its foundation in him; wisdom had its refuge; all of righteousness found a kinsman in him — so it was with that ruler of the earth.
The king, together with his four brothers, shone all the more brilliantly — like a great sacrifice spread wide, enhanced by the recitation of the Vedas.
Dhaumya and the other Brahmins — foremost, equal to Bṛhaspati — surrounded and attended him, as the immortals attend Prajāpati.
With supreme delight in the king of righteousness — pure as the full moon — the people's eyes and hearts rested on him with equal contentment.
But the people did not rejoice in him merely by fate or feeling; whatever was pleasing to the mind, that he accomplished by deed.
Indeed, from the lips of that wise Pārtha — sweet of speech — there arose nothing improper, nothing false, no untruth, and nothing disagreeable.
For that best of the Bhāratas, blazing with supreme energy, delighted in striving for the welfare of all the world as if it were his own welfare.
Thus all the Pāṇḍavas, joyful and free of grief, dwelt there, striking fear into the rulers of the earth with their own blazing energy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, after some days had passed, Bībhatsu (Arjuna) said to Kṛṣṇa: "The summer heat is upon us, Kṛṣṇa — let us go to the Yamunā."
"There, attended by our friends and companions, we shall sport awhile, O Madhusūdana, and return by evening — does this please you, O Janārdana?"
Vāsudeva said: O son of Kuntī's mother (i.e., Pārtha), this pleases me too — that we should sport at will in the water, attended by our friends and companions.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having taken leave of Dharmarāja and obtained his permission, O descendant of Bharata, Pārtha and Govinda then set out together, attended by their friends.
Reaching the pleasure grove — excellent, adorned with diverse trees, furnished with buildings high and low, like the dwelling of Indra —
— and well-stocked with savory foods both solid and liquid, rich and precious, and adorned with garlands of every variety, befitting the Vṛṣṇi hero and Pārtha —
— they entered it, filled as it was with jewels of every sort, high and low, auspicious; and all the people made merry as they pleased, O descendant of Bharata.
Some women of Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha's retinue played in the forest, some in the water, some in the pavilions — each in the place and manner that pleased them.
Draupadī and Subhadrā, elated with joy, distributed to those women costly garments and ornaments of great value.
Some women, overjoyed, danced; others cried out in delight; others laughed; and still others drank the finest liquor.
Some wept there with emotion, while others struck one another playfully; still others whispered secrets among themselves.
The sound of flutes, lutes, and mṛdaṅga drums — all of pleasing tone — filled that abundantly thriving grove on every side.
While this was taking place, the delight of the Kurus and the joy of the Dāśārhas moved apart to a certain nearby spot of great beauty.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having gone there, those two great souls — the two Kṛṣṇas, conquerors of enemy citadels — seated themselves, O king, upon splendid couches.
There Pārtha and Mādhava delighted themselves, recounting many past adventures and exploits and pleasures they had shared.
While the two sat there in joy, like the Aśvins in heaven, a brahmin then approached Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya.
He was like a great sala tree in stature, shining like refined gold, tawny-complexioned with a tawny beard, perfectly proportioned in height and breadth.
He resembled the rising sun, clad in dark garments, wearing matted locks, with a face like a lotus petal, tawny-hued, blazing as if with inner fire.
When that radiant best-of-twice-born approached, Arjuna and Vāsudeva quickly rose and stood to receive him.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: He spoke to Arjuna and to Vāsudeva of the Sātvata clan, those two heroes of the world standing near the Khāṇḍava forest.
"I am a brahmin who eats much; I always eat without limit. I beg of you, O Vārṣṇeya and Pārtha — grant me one single satisfaction."
Thus addressed, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava said to him: "With what food shall you be satisfied? We shall procure that food for you."
Thus questioned, the blessed one then spoke to both those heroes who had asked what food should be obtained:
"I do not hunger for ordinary food — know me as Fire! The food that befits me — that you two shall give me."
"Indra constantly protects this forest of Khāṇḍava. I cannot burn it while it is protected by that great-souled one."
"His friend the serpent Takṣaka dwells here always, and on his account Indra the wielder of the vajra guards this forest together with his retinue."
"Many beings are protected there along with him. Wishing to burn it, I am unable to do so because of Śakra's power."
"Seeing me ablaze, he pours down torrents of cloud-water, and thus I cannot burn the desired forest, though I wish to consume it."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"With you two as helpers — masters of weapons — I can burn the Khāṇḍava forest. This is the food I have chosen."
"For you two, skilled in the best weapons, shall properly ward off those streams of water and block the creatures from escaping in every direction."
When thus addressed, Bībhatsu (Arjuna) replied to Jātaveda (Fire), who desired to burn the Khāṇḍava forest against the will of Śatakratu (Indra):
"I possess many excellent weapons, both divine and otherwise, with which I could fight even many wielders of the thunderbolt."
"But I have no bow, O blessed one, equal to the strength of my arms — one that could endure my speed and exertion in battle."
"I also need many inexhaustible arrows, for I shoot swiftly; no chariot is capable of carrying as many arrows as I desire."
"I would also want divine white horses swift as the wind, and a chariot that thunders like a cloud and blazes like the sun."
"Likewise, there is no weapon equal to the valor of Kṛṣṇa — one with which Mādhava could slay nagas and pisachas in battle."
"O blessed one, you should indicate the means for the task's success — the means by which I could ward off Indra as he pours rain over the great forest."
"What is to be done through manly valor — that we two shall do, O Fire! But the capable instruments, O blessed one, you should provide."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the blessed one — Smoke-bannered Fire, the Oblation-eater — thought of Varuṇa, the guardian of the world, the sun-born god dwelling in the waters, the lord of the ocean, wishing to see him.
Knowing that thought, Varuṇa appeared before Fire. Smoke-bannered Fire, having duly honored the lord of the waters — the great lord, the fourth among the world-guardians — then spoke to him:
"That bow and those two quivers given to you by King Soma — hand them both over quickly, along with the chariot marked with a tawny emblem."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For Pārtha shall accomplish a very great task with the Gāṇḍīva, and Vāsudeva with the discus. Let them be given for my sake." And Varuṇa replied to Fire: "I shall give them."
Then he brought forth that wondrous bow of great power, enhancer of fame and glory, invincible against all weapons, destroyer of all weapons, the great measure of all arms, the crusher of enemy armies —
— worth a hundred thousand ordinary bows, increaser of kingdoms, beautiful with many-colored markings, smooth and without blemish —
— honored by gods, danavas, and gandharvas through endless ages. He gave that jewel of a bow, the Gāṇḍīva, and also two inexhaustible great quivers.
And also a chariot yoked to divine horses, bearing the banner of the chief of monkeys, fitted with silver horses of the Gandharva breed, garlanded with gold, white as autumn clouds, equal to mind and wind in speed —
— equipped with every fitting accessory, unconquerable by gods and danavas, blazing with light, of great thunder, pleasing to all beings.
That chariot had been fashioned by Prajāpati the lord of the world, the earthly creator, through his own austerities — its form as indescribable as the sun's.
Mounting that chariot, the powerful Soma had once conquered the danavas — it resembled a mountain or cloud and blazed with glory.
Adorning that finest of chariots was a flagstaff of gold equal to Indra's weapon, auspicious, very beautiful, unsurpassed.
Upon it a divine monkey, bearing the marks of a lion and tiger, stationed as if roaring, blazed gloriously at the summit.
On the banner too were various great beings whose roar causes the consciousness of enemy armies to vanish.
Arjuna circumambulated that finest chariot adorned with many banners, going around it clockwise, and bowed to the gods.
Armored, bearing sword, with his leather wrist-guard bound on, Pārtha mounted the chariot as a man of good deeds mounts a celestial car.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And taking up that divine best-of-bows, the Gāṇḍīva fashioned long ago by Brahmā, Arjuna was filled with joy.
After bowing to Fire, the valiant one then took it up with full strength and strung the bow with its bowstring.
When that bowstring was drawn by the mighty Pāṇḍava, those who heard the twang were afflicted in their hearts.
Having obtained the chariot, the bow, and the two inexhaustible great quivers, the son of Kuntī was ready and delighted to render assistance.
Then Fire gave to Kṛṣṇa the discus with the thunderbolt-navel — the beloved fiery weapon — and Kṛṣṇa too became ready.
And Fire said to him: "With this, O Madhusūdana, you shall conquer even superhuman foes in battle — there is no doubt."
"With this you shall always be superior to humans and even gods in battle, to rakshasas, pisachas, daityas, and nagas — no doubt, O slayer of foremost enemies."
"Hurled again and again in battle by you, O Mādhava, against your enemies, it shall kill without obstruction and return to your hand in combat."
And Varuṇa gave him a mace that thundered like lightning, terrible, destroyer of daityas — Hari's (Viṣṇu's) mace named Kaumodaki.
Then Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, delighted, equipped with weapons and fully armed, mounted on chariots with their banners, spoke to Fire:
"We are ready, O blessed one, to fight even all the gods and asuras together — how much more then against Indra alone who fights on behalf of the serpent!"
Arjuna said: "There is nothing in the three worlds that Janārdana the valiant Vārṣṇeya cannot conquer when releasing his discus and weapon in battle."
"Taking up the Gāṇḍīva bow and the two inexhaustible great quivers, I too am bold enough to conquer the worlds in battle, O Fire."
"Surround it on all sides with great blazing fire, O lord — blaze up this very day as you wish! We are ready to render assistance."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the descendant of Dāśārha and by Arjuna, the blessed one assumed his fiery form and began to burn the forest.
Surrounding it on all sides, the seven-tongued blazing fire then burned the Khāṇḍava in rage, presenting a sight like the end of an age.
Seizing and pervading that forest, O bull of the Bhāratas, roaring like thunder from clouds, he consumed all living beings.
As it burned, O Bhārata, the appearance of that forest blazed like the great-resplendent golden mountain Meru, king of peaks.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those two tigers among men, stationed on their chariots on both sides of the forest, caused great slaughter of the creatures in all directions.
Wherever creatures dwelling in the Khāṇḍava were seen fleeing, there those two heroes would rush to intercept them.
No gap was seen in their chariots because of their swift movement; those two supreme charioteers appeared as if whirling everywhere at once.
As the Khāṇḍava burned, thousands upon thousands of beings leaped up, uttering fearful cries in all ten directions.
Many had one part of their body burned; others were scorched all over; their eyes burst open; they fell apart and flew about, bereft of consciousness.
Some embraced their sons, others their fathers and mothers; unable to abandon them out of love, they perished together with them.
Others by the thousands leaped up with distorted appearances, reeling to and fro, and fell back into the fire again.
Creatures with wings, eyes, and feet burned, writhing on the ground, were seen here and there perishing.
In all the water pools as they were boiled away, O Bhārata, thousands of tortoises and fishes could be seen, their lives gone.
With their bodies blazing, the creatures in that forest appeared like fires with bodies, as their life-breath was extinguished.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those that flew up, Pārtha cut into pieces with his arrows and cast them laughing into the blazing path of Fire.
Pierced in every limb by arrows, uttering great cries, they leaped upward with speed and fell back into the fire.
The shriek of those forest-dwellers being struck by arrows and being burned was heard like the churning of the ocean.
From Fire blazing with joy, great flames shot into the sky, causing immense alarm among the denizens of heaven.
Then all the great-souled celestials went for refuge to the king of the gods, thousand-eyed Purandara (Indra).
The gods said: "Why are all these beings burned by the path of Fire? Has the destruction of the worlds come, O lord of immortals?"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, Vṛtra-slayer (Indra) personally surveyed the situation and then set out to liberate the Khāṇḍava, riding his horse Hari.
Covering the sky with a vast network of clouds of many forms, the wielder of the thunderbolt, lord of the gods, poured down rain.
Then thousand-eyed Indra, releasing streams as large as axles, hundreds of thousands of them, rained upon Fire and the Khāṇḍava.
But those streams, by the power of Jātaveda (Fire), dried up in mid-air before reaching him, not one of them reaching the fire.
Then Namuci-slayer (Indra), enraged, released abundant water and rained down again upon the intensely blazing fire.
The forest became terrible, with flames intertwined with streams, filled with smoke and lightning, resounding like thunder.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As Indra poured down water, the Pāṇḍava Bībhatsu (Arjuna) counter-warded it with a shower of arrows, displaying his supreme weapons.
With arrows on every side the Pāṇḍava also covered all of Khāṇḍava, driving that rain-shower away from the forest.
No creature whatsoever was able to escape from there, as the birds were covered by the shafts discharged by Savyasācin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Takṣaka, the mighty king of serpents, was not there; while that forest burned, he was then at Kurukṣetra.
But Aśvasena, Takṣaka's powerful son, was there; he strove intensely to free himself from the fire.
Pressed hard by the arrows of Kuntī's son, he could not escape; his mother, the serpent-born one, swallowed him and drew him free.
His head was swallowed first, then his tail was being swallowed; the serpent-woman, eager for her son, moved swiftly upward.
With a sharp, broad-bladed arrow the Pāṇḍava severed her head as she was flying away; the lord of the gods saw her.
The wielder of the thunderbolt, wishing to free him, bewildered the Pāṇḍava at that moment with a storm of wind and rain; and Aśvasena escaped.
Seeing that dreadful illusion and having been tricked by the serpent, he cut the birds flying in the air into two and three pieces, O Bhārata.
Bībhatsu in his fury cursed that crooked-moving one, and Pāvaka and Vāsudeva too, saying: "May he be without refuge."
Then Jiṣṇu, enraged, filling the sky with sharp arrows, fought against the thousand-eyed one, remembering that deception.
The king of gods, seeing Phalguna inflamed with wrath, released his own blazing weapon, which spread across the entire sky.
Then a wind arose with a great roar, churning all the oceans, standing in the sky and producing clouds that poured forth torrents of water in tumult.
To counter that, Arjuna too, expert in response, released the supreme wind-weapon, duly consecrated with its mantra.
By that weapon the vigor and power of Indra's thunderbolt-clouds were destroyed; those torrents of water dried up, and the lightnings vanished.
In an instant the sky became calm, free of dust and darkness, characterized by a pleasant cool breeze, with the sun's orb restored to its natural state.
And the fire, which assumes many forms, rejoicing at having no more obstruction, blazed up with incomparable flames, filling the world with its roaring sounds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing the forest fire protected by the two Kṛṣṇas, the Suparṇa birds and other winged creatures, filled with pride, rose up into the sky.
Garuḍas, with wings, beaks, and talons like thunderbolts, wishing to strike, swooped down from the sky upon Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava.
Likewise masses of serpents, with flaming mouths, moved near the Pāṇḍava, pouring forth terrible venom.
Pārtha cut down those infuriated sky-dwellers with his arrows as he saw them; helplessly they fell into the blazing fire for the dissolution of their bodies.
Then gods together with gandharvas, yakshas, rakshasas, and serpents rose up, releasing an incomparable roar, seeking battle.
With arms raised bearing iron pellets, discuses, stones, and muskets, their strength swooning with rage, they sought to kill Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha.
As they approached and released a rain of weapons, Bībhatsu smashed their heads with his sharp arrows.
And Kṛṣṇa, of great brilliance, the slayer of foes, made great carnage among the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas with his discus.
Then others, pierced by arrows and driven by the force of the discus, the greatly powerful ones stood arrested as if having reached a shore.
Then Śakra, the great lord of the thirty gods, furiously enraged, mounting his white elephant, charged at both of them.
Swiftly seizing the thunderbolt, the slayer of asuras released the weapon and said to the gods: "These two are slain."
Then seeing the great thunderbolt raised by the lord of gods, all the gods each took up their own weapons.
King Yama seized the staff of Death; the lord of wealth his litter; Varuṇa his noose; and Śiva too his discus.
The two Aśvins took up blazing medicinal herbs; Dhata seized his bow, and Jaya likewise his mace.
The mighty Tvaṣṭā in his rage seized a mountain; Amshu seized a spear; and the god Mṛtyu seized an axe.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Taking up a terrible iron club, Aryaman too roamed about; and Mitra, taking up a discus edged with razors, stood ready.
Pusha, and Bhaga enraged, and Savitā, O lord of men, with bows and swords taken up, charged at Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha.
The Rudras and the Vasus, and the mighty Maruts, the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas likewise, blazed with their own radiance.
These and many other gods, bearing various weapons, advanced against those two supreme beings, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha, seeking to slay them.
In that great battle, wondrous omens became visible, resembling those at the end of an age, for the destruction of beings, O Bhārata.
Even so, seeing Śakra furious together with the gods, the two Achyutas stood fearless in battle, those invincible ones, with bows strung.
And seeing those gods come, the two of them, enraged, repelled them one by one with arrows resembling thunderbolts.
The gods, their resolve broken again and again, were made to flee repeatedly; from fear they abandoned the battle and took refuge with Śakra alone.
Seeing the gods repelled by Mādhava and Arjuna, the sages stationed in heaven there were filled with wonder.
And Śakra too, perceiving again and again their valor in battle, was supremely pleased, and yet again he fought against those two.
Then the chastiser of Pāka released a tremendous shower of stones, wishing again to test the valor of Savyasācin; Arjuna, exceedingly wrathful, countered that shower with his arrows.
Seeing that shower being made futile, the king of gods of a hundred sacrifices then greatly increased that shower again.
The son of the chastiser of Pāka with swift arrows then caused that shower of stones to dissolve, bringing joy to his father.
Then Śakra, wishing to kill the son of Pāṇḍu, uprooted with his own hands a great peak from Mount Mandara, trees and all, and hurled it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Arjuna, with swift, straight-flying arrows with blazing tips, shattered the mountain peak into a thousand pieces.
The appearance of that crumbling mountain then shone like the sky breaking apart together with sun, moon, and planets.
By that great mountain falling down into the fire, the creatures dwelling in Khāṇḍava were again greatly slain there.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus terrified by the fall of the mountain, the inhabitants of Khāṇḍava — danavas, rakshasas, nagas, hyenas, tree-dwellers of the forest, elephants in rut, tigers, lions, and maned lions —
Deer and buffaloes, and birds by the hundreds, fled in agitation, and so too did other kinds of beings.
Looking upon that conflagration and upon the two Kṛṣṇas with weapons raised, they seemed as if terrified by the sound of the crashing omens.
Janārdana released his discus blazing with its own radiance; with it all those petty creatures together with danavas and night-wanderers were cut down by the hundreds and in an instant fell into the fire.
The rakshasas there, cloven by Kṛṣṇa's discus and mingled with fat and blood, were like rain-clouds at twilight.
The descendant of the Vṛṣṇis roamed there slaying pisachas, birds, nagas, and beasts by the thousands, like Death itself, O Bhārata.
That discus of Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of foes, thrown again and again, returned to his hand again and again after slaying many creatures.
And as he slew all those creatures, O Bhārata, his form became exceedingly fierce — he who is the soul of all beings — at that time.
Of all the assembled gods and danavas together, not one became a conqueror of Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava in battle.
When the gods were unable to rescue that forest from the power of those two, nor to extinguish it, then they turned away.
And Śatakratu, seeing the hosts of gods turned away, stood still, pleased, praising Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the gods had withdrawn, a disembodied voice, deep and resonant, addressed Śatakratu, looking upon him.
"Your friend Takṣaka, best of serpents, is not present; at the time of Khāṇḍava's burning he has gone to Kurukṣetra."
"Nor can these two who stand arrayed in this battle be conquered by you — Vāsudeva and Arjuna, O Śakra; hear this word of mine."
"These two are the gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa, renowned in heaven; you yourself know how great their valor and how great their prowess."
"These two, difficult to assail, unconquered in battle, cannot be vanquished; they are ancient and best among sages in all the worlds."
"These two are most worthy of worship by all — gods and asuras together with yakshas, rakshasas, gandharvas, narakas, kinnaras, and serpents."
"Therefore, O Vāsava, you should depart from here together with the gods; regard also the destruction of Khāṇḍava as the decree of fate."
Having heard that speech, the lord of immortals acknowledged it as true; relinquishing his anger and resentment, he then set out for heaven.
Seeing that great-souled one depart, the heavenly beings, O king, swiftly followed Śatakratu together.
Seeing the king of gods then departing with the gods, the two heroes Vāsudeva and Arjuna roared with the roar of lions.
The king of gods having gone, O king, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, overjoyed, then caused the forest fire to burn again without restraint.
Like the wind destroying clouds, Arjuna, having driven off the gods, cut down with showers of arrows the living creatures dwelling in Khāṇḍava.
No creature whatsoever was able to escape from there as it was cut apart by the arrows discharged by Savyasācin.
The creatures there, even the great ones, could not look upon Arjuna, whose shafts never miss, in battle — much less could they do battle.
With one arrow he pierced a hundred, and a hundred with a single shaft; lifeless they fell into the fire, as if struck down by Death himself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They found no shelter in embankments or in difficult terrain; even in the abodes of ancestors and gods distress arose.
Thousands upon thousands of creatures in their misery raised a great cry; elephants bellowed, and so too deer and birds; at that sound the fish dwelling in the Gaṅgā and the ocean trembled.
Indeed, no one was able even to look upon the mighty-armed Arjuna, nor upon the powerful Kṛṣṇa — much less to fight them.
Those who fled even along a single path, whoever escaped there — rakshasas, danavas, and nagas — Hari slew them with his discus.
Those great-bodied ones, their heads and bodies severed by the force of the discus, their lives gone, fell into the mouth of the blazing fire of golden seed.
Fanned by floods of flesh and blood and streams of fat, the fire blazing above in the sky appeared smokeless.
With blazing eyes, a blazing tongue, a blazing wide-open great mouth, blazing upright hair, and tawny eyes, he drank the marrow of living creatures.
Obtaining that nectar-feast made for him by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, the fire-god became joyful, satisfied, and attained supreme contentment.
Then Madhusūdana suddenly saw the asura named Maya fleeing in haste from the dwelling of Takṣaka.
The fire-god, wishing to burn him, with the wind as his charioteer, beseeched him, having taken on a bodily form with matted hair and roaring like a thundercloud; and Vāsudeva, wishing to kill him, stood with his discus raised.
Seeing the raised discus and the fire wishing to burn him, Maya cried out, "Run to Arjuna!" — thus, O Bhārata.
Hearing his frightened cry, Dhanañjaya replied to Maya, saying "Fear not" — Pārtha, as if granting him life, O Bhārata.
With Pārtha having granted him safety, the Dasharhaka did not wish to kill Maya, that brother of Namuci, and the fire did not burn him either.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While that forest burned, fire did not burn six beings: Aśvasena, Maya, and also the four Śārṅgakas.
Janamejaya said: Why did the fire not burn the Śārṅgakas when the forest was burning thus, O brahmin? Tell me this quickly.
For the reason for the non-burning of Aśvasena and the danava Maya has been told, O brahmin, but the reason for the Śārṅgakas has not been told.
This is indeed wondrous, O brahmin — the non-destruction of the Sharnagas. Recount it: how were they not destroyed in the conflagration of the fire?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: For what reason the fire did not burn the Śārṅgakas as it burned, I shall tell you everything just as it happened, O Bhārata.
Foremost among those who know dharma, an ascetic of sharp vows, a great seer learned in scripture, known as Mandapāla — such was he.
He followed the path of sages who preserve their seed upward, O king — devoted to sacred recitation, intent on dharma, an ascetic with conquered senses.
Having reached the far shore of austerity and abandoning his body, O Bhārata, he went to the world of the ancestors but did not obtain the expected fruit there.
Seeing those worlds to be fruitless even though won by austerity, he asked the celestials standing near the king of dharma.
Why are these worlds of mine, earned by austerity, closed to me? What have I not done such that this is the fruit of my deeds?
I shall do there whatever it is for which this fruit is blocked. Tell me, O celestials.
The gods said: Men are born indebted, O brahmin — hear by what they discharge it: through ritual acts, through celibate study, and through offspring — there is no doubt.
All of it is discharged by sacrifice, by austerity, and by sons. You are an ascetic and a sacrificer, but you have no offspring.
Therefore these worlds of yours are closed for want of progeny. Beget children; then you shall enjoy eternal worlds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"A son delivers the father from the hell named Put" — thus it is said, O sage. Therefore strive for the continuation of offspring, O best of twice-born.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing the words of those celestials, Mandapāla pondered: "Where can I quickly obtain abundant offspring?"
Reflecting thus, he approached the birds known for prolific reproduction; becoming a sharnaka bird himself, he came to Jaritā.
He begot four sons on her, versed in brahman. Abandoning them — those infant sons still within their eggs, along with their mother — the sage went off in that very forest to Lapitā.
After that great one had gone to Lapitā, O Bhārata, Jaritā, agitated by love for her children, pondered deeply.
Abandoned by him though undeserving of abandonment — those young seers still in their eggs in the forest — the distressed Jaritā did not forsake her little ones in Khāṇḍava, O king; she nurtured them as they were born, her heart overcome with love.
Then the sage Mandapāla, wandering in that forest with Lapitā, saw the fire coming to burn Khāṇḍava.
Understanding the fire's intention and knowing his infant sons were there, that brahmin sage, the seer Mandapāla, praised Jātaveda the mighty world-guardian with fear, entrusting his sons to him.
Mandapāla said: You are the mouth of all the gods, O fire; you are the carrier of oblations; you move secretly within all beings, O purifier.
The poets call you one; they also call you threefold. Having conceived you as eightfold, they ordained you as the vehicle of sacrifice.
The supreme seers declare this universe was created by you; for without you, O fire, the entire world could not exist for a moment.
Brahmins who bow to you attain the eternal destination won by their own deeds, together with their wives and children.
They call you, O fire, the cloud-givers suspended in the sky with lightning; the seasons that burn all beings issue forth from you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O Jātaveda, O greatly radiant one, this creation of the universe is yours alone; all being — both moving and unmoving — is decreed by your action alone.
The waters were ordained by you from the beginning; in you all this world rests; in you oblations to the gods and offerings to the ancestors are properly established.
O fire, you yourself are the flaming one; you are Dhata; you are Bṛhaspati; you are the twin Aśvins; you are Yama; you are Mitra; you are Soma; and you are the wind.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus praised by Mandapāla, the fire was pleased with that sage of boundless splendor, O king, and spoke to him with a gladdened heart: "What is your wish? What shall I do for you?"
Mandapāla, with joined palms, addressed the carrier of oblations: "While burning the Khāṇḍava forest, spare my sons."
Saying "So be it" and making that promise, the blessed fire-carrier blazed forth in Khāṇḍava at that time with the desire to burn.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the bright fire blazed, those Śārṅgakas were deeply grieved, tormented, and greatly distressed — they found no refuge.
Seeing her infant children, their ascetic mother Jaritā, scorched by grief, lamented, O lord of men.
"This fire, terrible and fearsome, burning the undergrowth, comes here, setting the world ablaze, the augmenter of my sorrow."
"These infants, slow of mind, without tail-feathers, lacking the use of their feet — our ancient refuge — torment me; and this fire comes licking the great trees, terrifying us."
"Because of their helplessness, my sons are not capable of fleeing; and I cannot flee elsewhere while carrying my children."
"Nor am I able to abandon them — my heart burns with pain. Which son shall I forsake? Taking which shall I go?"
"What would have been done being done — think, my little ones, how? Pondering your deliverance I find no way. Covering you with my body I shall die together with you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This lineage of Jaritāri is established by the eldest; Sarisrikva shall be born to increase the family of the ancestors."
"Stambamitra shall practice austerity; Droṇa shall be the supreme knower of brahman — saying thus, your father, pitiless one, departed long ago."
"Carrying which can one go? For whom would flight be best? What, if done, would the duty be done?" — distracted thus she thought.
She could not find by her own wit any deliverance for her sons from that fire. As she spoke thus, those Sharnagas then replied to their mother.
"Casting aside affection, O mother, fly to where the fire-carrier cannot reach. When we are gone you shall have other sons; but if you perish, O mother, there shall be no continuation of our lineage."
"Consider both sides — what would be best for our lineage. That is what ought to be done; this, O mother, should be your supreme moment of action."
"Do not make your affection for us the cause of the lineage's ruin. This deed of our father who desired the worlds shall not be in vain."
Jaritā said: Here in the earth near this tree is the burrow of a mouse. Enter it quickly — there is no fear of the fire for you here.
"Then I shall block the opening with dust, my little ones. Thus I think we may act against the blazing black-pathed fire."
"After the fire has passed I shall come back to scatter the mound of dust. Let this plan for your deliverance from the fire please you."
The Śārṅgakas said: The flesh-eating mouse would destroy us who are featherless and without tail-plumage. We cannot resort to this plan, seeing this danger before us.
"How might the fire not burn us? How might the mouse not devour us? How might our father not be in vain? How might our mother survive?"
"In the burrow destruction would come from the mouse; from the fire, for those who fly in the sky. Weighing both sides: burning is better than being devoured."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Death by being eaten by the mouse in the burrow would be shameful for us. More desirable than the shameful is the abandonment of the body in the fire."
Jaritā said: A hawk flew out from this very burrow and carried off that mouse, that small creature, gripping it with its talons. There will be no danger from it now.
The Śārṅgakas said: We do not know in the least that the mouse was carried off by a hawk. And there may be others here — from them too we face danger.
"The fire may or may not come — we have seen the wind turn it back. But death for us from the burrow's inhabitants would be certain, O mother."
"A doubtful death is better than a certain one, O mother. Go as is proper through the sky — you shall obtain splendid sons."
Jaritā said: I myself saw the hawk coming, moving near the burrow; that powerful one seized the mouse and carried it off from the burrow.
"That hawk as it flew I quickly followed behind, conferring blessings on it as it carried the mouse away from the burrow."
"O king of hawks, you who dash away carrying our enemy — may you become golden, foe-free, ascending the sky."
"When it is devoured by that hungry bird, then, having taken leave of him, I shall return home."
"Enter the burrow, my sons, with confidence — there is no danger for you. The mouse was carried off by the hawk while I watched — there is no doubt."
The Śārṅgakas said: We do not know, O mother, whether the mouse was carried off from here before. Without knowing for certain we cannot enter the burrow.
Jaritā said: I know that the mouse was carried off by the hawk. Therefore there is no danger — do as I say.
The Śārṅgakas said: You should not seek to rescue us by false comfort. In turbulent knowledge great fear is not subdued by mere reasoning.
"Nor have we done you any service, nor do you truly know who we are. You sustain us while we afflict you — what woman of virtue are you, and who are we to you?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"You are young and beautiful, capable of seeking a husband. Follow your own lord — you shall obtain splendid sons."
"We too, entering the fire, shall attain auspicious worlds. Or if the fire does not burn us, then come back to us again."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Addressed thus, the sharnaga hen, abandoning her sons in Khāṇḍava, quickly departed to a safe place, a refuge from the fire.
Then the fire-carrier blazed with sharp flames and came to where those Sharnagas were — the little sons of Mandapāla.
Those Sharnagas, seeing the blazing fire blazing with its own splendor, — Jaritāri then caused the fire to hear his voice.
Jaritāri said: A wise man stays vigilant before a time of peril arrives; having thus foreseen the time of peril, he does not suffer anguish at any moment when it comes.
But the witless one who does not perceive the peril before it arrives — when the time of peril comes, he is overwhelmed with distress and cannot comprehend anything at all.
Sārisṛkva said: You are steadfast and intelligent; and this is indeed a crisis for our very lives. Truly, a single brave and wise man becomes the support of many — there is no doubt of this.
Stambamitra said: It is indeed the eldest who becomes the protector; the eldest rescues from danger. But if the eldest does not understand, what can the younger ones do?
Droṇa said: He of golden seed comes swiftly blazing toward our destruction; the seven-tongued fire, lean and licking with his flames, is creeping close upon us.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by his brothers, Jaritāri praised Vibhāvasu, the fire, with joined palms. Hear how he did so, O king.
Jaritāri said: You are the very self of the wind; the wind is your body. You are the womb of all herbs and plants. O pure one, the waters too are your source; you are the womb of the waters.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Your flames, O greatly mighty one, rise upward and descend downward and spread out on every side — even as the rays of the sun.
Sārisṛkva said: Our mother has fled to our father; we do not know him. Our wings have not yet grown, O lotus-bannered one. There is no protector for us other than you, O Fire. Therefore do you alone guard us, O sole hero.
Whatever benign form you have, O Agni, and whatever are your seven weapons — with that protect us today, O praised one, for we seek your shelter.
You alone, O Jātavedas, are the one who blazes for austerity; no other scorcher is found among living beings, O divine one. Protect us who are sages and children. Pass beyond us, O carrier of oblations.
Stambamitra said: You alone are everything, O Agni; in you exists all this universe. You sustain all living beings; you uphold the entire world.
You are Agni the carrier of oblations; you yourself are also the supreme oblation. The wise ones worship you in many ways and also as a single unity.
Having created these three worlds, O carrier of oblations, when the time comes you blaze up and cook them again. You are the primal source of this entire universe; you, O Agni, again become its foundation.
You are the food consumed by all living beings; dwelling within them, O lord of the universe, you perpetually grow and digest it. In you everything is established.
Droṇa said: Becoming the sun with your rays, O Jātavedas, you draw up from the earth its waters and all the essences of what is born from the earth; then at the time of release, creating rain, you nourish all, O pure one.
From you, O pure one, these green-leafed plants are born anew; from you spring the lotus pools, the ocean, and the great sea.
This is indeed the abode and ultimate refuge of Varuṇa, O sharp-rayed one. Be our auspicious protector; do not destroy us today.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O tawny-eyed one, O red-throated one, O one whose path is black, O devourer of offerings — pass beyond us and release us, as one releases the dwellers of the ocean.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Droṇa of effortless deeds, Jātavedas, confident by virtue of Mandapāla's promise, spoke to Droṇa.
Fire said: You are truly the sage Droṇa; what you have spoken is the sacred word of Brahman itself. I shall do what you desire, and you need have no fear.
Indeed, you were presented to me beforehand by Mandapāla, who said: "Spare my little sons for my sake when burning the forest."
Both that word of his and what you have spoken here — both together weigh heavily with me. Tell me what I shall do for you. I am greatly pleased; good fortune to you, O brahmin, for your hymn, O lord.
Droṇa said: These cats, O pure one, ever torment us. Take them and their kin in your jaws, O carrier of oblations.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The fire did as asked; having granted leave to the śārṅga birds, he blazed up and burned the Khāṇḍava forest, O Janamejaya.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Mandapāla too, O descendant of Kuru, was thinking anxiously about his sons at that time; and though he had spoken to the fire himself, he was not without anguish.
Burning with worry for the sake of his sons, he said to Lapitā: "How are my little sons, who cannot yet fly, faring now?"
"With the oblation-carrier fire growing and the wind blowing swiftly, my children will be unable to escape."
"How will their wretched mother, unable to protect them, be seized with misery, seeing no means to save her sons?"
"How will she, burning with grief and crying out on all sides, run toward my children who are unable to flee or fly away?"
"How fares my son Jaritāri? How does Sārisṛkva fare? How does Stambamitra fare? How does Droṇa fare? And how does that wretched one fare?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As the sage Mandapāla lamented thus in the forest, Lapitā replied to him with words that seemed to carry a note of jealousy, O Bhārata.
Lapitā said: You have no real concern for your sons. You yourself said to those sages: "They are full of energy and might; they have no fear from the fire."
Moreover, they were entrusted by you to the fire, and in my very presence the great-souled fire promised accordingly.
A guardian of the worlds can never speak an untruth under any circumstances. And your sons are capable of speaking for themselves. Your mind, however, is not with them.
It is that rival of mine that you are thinking of and tormenting yourself about. Surely you have no affection for me as you once had for her.
For it is not proper for one who has wings to watch indifferently while one who loves him suffers, especially when he has the power to help.
Go to Jaritā herself, for whom you are tormenting yourself. I too shall wander alone, as one does in the case of a coward.
Mandapāla said: I do not move about in the world as you imagine. I wander on account of my children — and that situation is fraught with difficulty for me.
The dull-witted one who abandons what is present to cling to what is merely future — the world would hold him in contempt. Do as you wish.
For this blazing fire, licking up the great trees, generates in my heart an inauspicious and hateful anguish.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: After the fire had passed beyond that region, Jaritā, full of longing for her little ones, quickly rushed toward her children.
She found all of them safe and sound in the forest, freed from Jātavedas, and she saw her sons weeping piteously.
Finding their sight almost too wonderful to believe, she went to each of her crying sons one by one, again and again.
Then Mandapāla also came quickly, O Bhārata. But all his sons did not greet him with joy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Though he lamented to each of them one by one and to Jaritā again and again, they did not speak a single word to that sage — neither kind nor harsh.
Mandapāla said: Which is your eldest son? Which comes after him? Which son is the middle one? And which is your youngest?
Why do you not respond to me as I speak in distress? I made a pact with the fire-eater; and yet I find no peace here.
Jaritā said: What business do you have with the eldest son? Or with the one who comes after him? What business do you have with the middle one, or with the youngest, you wretched man?
You who abandoned me utterly and went away before — go back to that young Lapitā with her lovely smile.
Mandapāla said: For women there is nothing at all besides another man. Rivalry between co-wives is inescapable — it must be so in the world.
Even the virtuous and beautiful Arundhatī, renowned throughout all the worlds, suspected Vasiṣṭha, the greatest of sages.
She despised that utterly pure-hearted sage, ever devoted to her welfare and benefit, that hero dwelling among the seven sages.
Through that suspicion, her radiance became like smoky red; she can be barely seen, dim and without her former beauty — she is perceived now only as a pale mark.
I came here for the sake of offspring, and so you too are now forsaking the beloved and acting in the same way.
A man should never place total trust in a wife, for a wife who is a true mother of sons does not think of a husband's duty.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all his sons attended upon him properly, and he began to comfort his children, O king.
Mandapāla said: For the sake of protecting you I petitioned the fire, and the fire promised accordingly — "So be it" — even before this.
Knowing the word of the fire, your mother's knowledge of dharma, and your own supreme valor, I did not come here sooner.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You should not grieve over death, my dear children. Even the fire knows the sages and the sacred knowledge of Brahman; and you too understand this.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus comforted his sons and taking his wife with him, O Bhārata, Mandapāla departed from that place to another region.
The divine sharp-rayed fire also burned the blazing Khāṇḍava forest together with the two Kṛṣṇas, generating fearlessness for the world.
Drinking streams of fat and marrow flowing there, the purifying fire attained supreme satisfaction and revealed himself to Arjuna.
Then the lord of the gods, surrounded by the hosts of Maruts, descended from the sky and spoke these words to Pārtha and to Mādhava.
Indra said: You two have accomplished a feat difficult even for the immortals. Choose your boons — I am pleased; choose even those that are rare and beyond human reach.
Pārtha then chose from Śakra to receive all weapons in full; and Śakra set a proper time for granting them to him.
Indra said: When the divine Mahādeva shall be graciously disposed toward you, then I will grant you all the weapons of the Pāṇḍavas.
I myself will know that moment, O delight of the Kurus; and through great austerity I too shall grant those weapons to you.
All the weapons of Agni, all those of Vāyu as well, and all those that are mine — all of these you shall receive, O Dhanañjaya.
Vāsudeva also obtained eternal friendship with Pārtha; and the lord of gods, greatly pleased, granted him that boon at that time.
Having joyfully granted the boon to both of them, the lord of the Maruts, together with the gods, took leave of the fire and returned to the triple heaven.
The fire too, having burned that forest along with its animals and birds, rested for five days and one more, fully satisfied.
Having devoured the flesh and drunk the fat and blood, filled with supreme delight, he spoke to those two, O lord of the people.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Fire said: By the two of you, foremost among men, I have been satisfied to my full contentment. I grant you leave, O heroes; go wherever you desire.
Thus were those two — Arjuna and Vāsudeva — granted leave by the great-souled fire, as was the demon Maya.
Then all three of them, O bull of the Bhāratas, having circumambulated the fire, sat down together on the pleasant bank of the river.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Maya spoke to Pārtha in the presence of Vāsudeva, with joined palms, honouring him again and again with gentle words.
"By you I have been saved from this wrathful Kṛṣṇa and from Pāvaka who sought to burn me. O son of Kuntī, tell me — what shall I do for you?"
Arjuna said: "You have already done everything. Go in peace, O great asura. Be ever well-disposed toward me, and we too shall be well-disposed toward you."
Maya said: "This is fitting in you, O lord, O bull among men, just as you have said. Out of affection I still wish to do something for you, O Bhārata."
"For I am the Viśvakarmā of the dānavas, their great architect. I therefore wish to do something on your behalf, O Pāṇḍava."
Arjuna said: "You consider yourself delivered from mortal peril by me. Given this, I am unable to make you do anything for me."
"Nor do I wish your resolve to go in vain, O dānava. Let something be done for Kṛṣṇa in the same way as has been done for me."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus prompted by Maya, O bull of the Bhāratas, Vāsudeva reflected for a moment on what might be asked of him.
Kṛṣṇa then urged him: "Let a hall be built, O Daiteya, for the king Dharmarāja — such a one as you deem fitting here."
"Build such an assembly hall that no human, seeing it, would be able to replicate it, and all men in this mortal world would be amazed."
"Where we might behold divine designs arranged by you — both asura and human alike — build such a hall, O Maya."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Accepting those words with great delight, Maya then joyfully built the assembly hall for the Pāṇḍava, resembling a celestial palace.
Then Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha duly reported all of this to King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Dharmarāja, and presented Maya to him.
Yudhiṣṭhira then honoured Maya fittingly, and Maya, himself well honoured, accepted that honour with respect.
That Daiteya then recounted here and there the ancient deeds of the gods to the sons of Pāṇḍu, O lord of the people, O Bhārata.
Having rested for some time and deliberated, that Viśvakarmā set about building the assembly hall for the great-souled Pāṇḍavas.
In accordance with the wishes of the Pārthas and the great-souled Kṛṣṇa, on an auspicious day that greatly radiant one performed the auspicious rites with festive intent.
That mighty one satisfied thousands of the foremost twice-born with rice-milk porridge, and gave them also manifold wealth.
He measured out on all sides that hall — endowed with the qualities of all seasons, divine in form, enchanting to the mind — at ten thousand kiṣku in extent.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Janārdana, worthy of worship and duly worshipped, had dwelt in pleasant residence at Khāṇḍavaprastha together with the Pārthas, united in affection.
That broad-eyed one, longing to see his father, resolved to depart. He then took leave of Dharmarāja and of Pṛthā.
He who is worshipped by the world bowed his head to the feet of his father's sister; she smelled the top of his head and embraced Keśava.
Then the greatly glorious Kṛṣṇa saw his own sister. Approaching her, Hṛṣīkeśa went to her filled with affection and tears.
The blessed lord spoke to the auspicious Subhadrā, that sweet-spoken one, words that were meaningful, true, beneficial, brief, apt, and unsurpassed.
By her he was made to hear words conveying news of their kinsmen; she honoured him repeatedly and paid obeisance to him with bowed head.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having taken leave of that spirited lady and received her blessing, Janārdana the Vārṣṇeya then saw Kṛṣṇā and Dhaumya as well.
That best of men bowed to Dhaumya in the proper manner; and having comforted Draupadī and taken his leave, Janārdana
went, wise and mighty, to meet the brothers, accompanied by Pārtha. Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by the five brothers, shone like Śakra among the immortals.
