"Or perhaps, even Vāsudeva himself, acting out of desire to please, has followed Drupada's wishes — and in that case, how does this Mādhava deserve worship?"
"Do you consider Kṛṣṇa your teacher, O bull of the Kurus? But while Droṇa still lives, why have you worshipped this Vṛṣṇi scion?"
"Do you consider Kṛṣṇa your sacrificial priest, O joy of the Kurus? But while the brahmin Dvaipāyana still lives, how did you worship Kṛṣṇa?"
"Madhusūdana is neither a sacrificial priest, nor a teacher, nor a king — yet he has been worshipped, O best of Kurus. What other reason can there be but favoritism?"
"Or if this Madhusūdana is to be worshipped by you, then why, O descendant of Bharata, were the kings brought here — merely to be dishonored?"
"We all do not pay tribute to this great-souled son of Kuntī out of fear, nor out of greed, nor because we were appeased by him."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"We pay tribute to him who is devoted to dharma and who seeks to establish sovereign rule — yet he, this one, holds us in no regard."
"What other name can one give to this but dishonor — that in this royal assembly you have worshipped Kṛṣṇa with the arghya, one who has not attained the mark of kingship?"
"Without cause has the fame gone forth that Dharma's son is a righteous soul — for who would offer such fitting worship to one who has fallen from dharma, this one born in the Vṛṣṇi clan who formerly slew a king?"
"Today Yudhiṣṭhira's reputation for righteousness has been stripped away, and wretchedness has entered into him, through the presentation of the arghya to Kṛṣṇa."
"If the sons of Kuntī are afraid and wretched ascetics, surely even you should understand what worship Mādhava truly deserves."
"Or, O Janārdana — you who are unworthy — why did you accept this worship that was offered by these wretches?"
"And you, moreover, think highly of this worship that is not appropriate to yourself — like a dog licking up the drippings of an oblation in a deserted place."
"But this dishonor is not being directed at the lords of the earth — clearly, O Janārdana, it is you whom the Kauravas are deceiving."
"As meaningless as the marriage ceremony performed for an impotent man, or as showing forms to a blind man — so is the royal worship offered to you, O Madhusūdana, who are no king."
"I have now seen King Yudhiṣṭhira for what he is, and I have seen Bhīṣma for what he is, and this Vāsudeva has also been seen — all this is now exactly as it truly is."
Having spoken thus to them, Śiśupāla rose from his high seat and departed from that assembly, accompanied by the kings.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira hastened after Śiśupāla and spoke these sweet, conciliatory words to him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This is not proper, O lord of the earth, what you have said; it is the highest adharma, O king — this harshness that serves no purpose."
"For Bhīṣma son of Śaṃtanu would never be ignorant of the highest dharma, O earth-lord — do not think otherwise; do not slight him."
"Look at these many lords of the earth, far older than you — they accept the honor-offering given to Kṛṣṇa; in like manner you too ought to be patient."
"For Bhīṣma knows Kṛṣṇa in truth and deeply, O lord of the Cedi; you do not know him as the Kaurava elder knows him."
Bhīṣma said: "To him no conciliation is to be given; this one does not deserve to be appeased — the one who does not approve of the honor rendered to Kṛṣṇa, the eldest in the world."
"The kshatriya who, having conquered another kshatriya in battle — best of those who wage battle — sets him free after bringing him under control, becomes like a guru to him."
"And in this assembly of kings, I do not see a single lord of the earth who has not been conquered in battle by the might of the son of the Sātvata woman — Kṛṣṇa."
"For Acyuta — the imperishable one — is not only the most worthy of worship for us alone; Janārdana is worthy of worship in all three worlds."
"For by Kṛṣṇa in battle have many bull-like kshatriyas been conquered, and the entire world rests wholly in this scion of the Vṛṣṇis."
"Therefore, even in the presence of elders who are great, we worship Kṛṣṇa and no other. You have no right to speak thus — let not your mind dwell in such a disposition."
O king, I have attended upon many who are great in wisdom. Among those who spoke, I have heard from the assembled sages — those honored by the virtuous — the many and well-esteemed qualities of Śauri (Kṛṣṇa), the man of virtues.
And the deeds of this wise one since his very birth, being told repeatedly by men, have been heard by me again and again.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O king of Cedi, we do not honor Janārdana (Kṛṣṇa) merely out of desire, nor placing kinship first, nor for any personal advantage whatsoever.
We worship one who has been worshipped by the good. Understanding his fame, valor, and victory — which bring earthly well-being — we render him honor.
Not one person here, not even a mere boy, has been left unexamined by us. Surpassing all elders in qualities, Hari (Kṛṣṇa) is considered by us the most worthy of worship.
He is the greatest in wisdom among the twice-born, and superior in strength among the kshatriyas. Both these reasons for worship are established in Govinda (Kṛṣṇa) here.
Knowledge of the Vedas and their auxiliaries, and likewise immeasurable strength — in this world, who among men possesses these distinctions except Keśava (Kṛṣṇa)?
Generosity, skill, learning, valor, modesty, fame, supreme intelligence, humility, prosperity, steadfastness, contentment, and nourishment — all these are permanently fixed in Acyuta (Kṛṣṇa).
This one, endowed with all these qualities — teacher, father-figure, and guru; worthy of worship, already worshipped, and deserving of honor — all of you ought to acknowledge him.
Officiating priest, teacher, father-in-law, honored graduate, king, and beloved — all of these roles reside in Hṛṣīkeśa (Kṛṣṇa). Therefore Acyuta has been worshipped.
Kṛṣṇa alone is the origin and also the dissolution of the worlds. Indeed, for Kṛṣṇa's sake this entire universe has been offered up.
He is the unmanifest nature, the eternal agent, and beyond all beings. Therefore Acyuta is the most ancient and greatest of all.
Intellect, mind, the great principle (mahat), wind, fire, water, ether, and earth — whatever fourfold existence exists — all of it is established in Kṛṣṇa.
The sun, the moon, the constellations, the planets, the directions and sub-directions — all of it is established in Kṛṣṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But this foolish man Śiśupāla does not understand Kṛṣṇa — who is everywhere and at all times — and therefore speaks thus.
The wise man who truly examines the highest dharma would see things as they are according to dharma. But this king of Cedi does not see thus.
Among the aged and the young, or among the great-souled kings, who does not consider Kṛṣṇa worthy? And who would not worship him?
If Śiśupāla resolves that this worship was wrongly performed, then in accordance with justice, he ought to act accordingly in that wrongdoing.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the greatly renowned Bhīṣma then fell silent. Thereupon Sahadeva spoke a meaningful reply in that assembly.
"Keśava, the slayer of Keśī, who is of immeasurable valor — Kṛṣṇa who is being worshipped by me — whoever among you, O kings, cannot bear this —
"— upon the heads of all the mighty ones I have placed this foot. Let him who can properly respond to what I have said now speak his answer."
"And those kings here who are wise — let them acknowledge this one who is teacher, father-figure, and guru; worthy of worship, already worshipped, and deserving of honor."
Thereupon not one among them spoke — among those wise, virtuous, proud, and powerful kings — with the foot (of supremacy) thus displayed before them.
Then a rain of flowers fell upon Sahadeva's head, and invisible voices also cried out: "Well done! Well done!"
Nārada, the knower of all worlds, who speaks of past and future, the remover of all doubts, twirled his black deerskin toward Kṛṣṇa (in approval).
All those assembled there who had come when summoned — the factions led by Sunītha — appeared enraged and their faces pale with anger.
The kings there spoke out about the consecration of Yudhiṣṭhira and the honoring of Vāsudeva, with disgust and firm conviction of their own.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The appearance of those who were being restrained by their friends shone forth like lions roaring when dragged away from their prey.
Kṛṣṇa then understood that boundless ocean of kings — that inexhaustible ocean of rulers — which was forming a pact (for war), and he perceived the coming battle.
Having honored the one worthy of honor, especially the Brahmin and Kṣatriya orders, Sahadeva — the god among men — completed that rite.
When Kṛṣṇa had been thus honored, Sunītha — the crusher of enemies — with eyes reddened with anger, spoke to the assembled lords of men.
"I stand here as your commander. What do you think we should do now? Let us arm ourselves and stand in battle against the assembled Vṛṣṇis and Pāṇḍavas."
Having thus roused all those kings, the chief of the Cedis then consulted with the kings to disrupt the sacrifice.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, seeing that ocean of kings — resembling the actual ocean — agitated by fury, Yudhiṣṭhira said all this:
He (Yudhiṣṭhira), of great brilliance, like Indra the slayer of enemies, addressed Bhīṣma — the foremost of the wise, the aged grandfather of the Kurus — as Bṛhaspati (the divine teacher):
"That great ocean of kings has been stirred by fury. Tell me, O grandfather, what should be done here."
"So that there be no obstruction to the sacrifice, and so that well-being comes to the people — tell me everything such that this holds true in all respects, O grandfather."
When Yudhiṣṭhira, the dharma-knowing king of dharma, had spoken thus, the grandfather of the Kurus, Bhīṣma, then spoke these words:
"Fear not, O tiger among the Kurus. A dog cannot kill a lion. The auspicious and well-guided path — it was chosen by me here long before."
"For just as when a lion is asleep, dogs gathered there would bark at it all together, so too do these lords of the earth."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Standing before the sleeping lion of the Vṛṣṇis — like dogs barking furiously in the presence of a lion — so too do these stand, O dear one."
"For Acyuta, like a sleeping lion, does not yet rouse himself. By this, the man-lion (Narasimha), the chief of Cedis, emboldens them (Śiśupāla's followers) to act like lions."
"O best among kings, the dim-witted Śiśupāla desires, O dear one, to lead all these kings with his whole being to Yama's abode."
"Surely Adhokṣaja (Kṛṣṇa) desires to reclaim what is his — the splendor that resides in Śiśupāla — O Bhārata."
"The mind of the king of Cedi — and of all these lords of the earth — has become disordered. May it be well with you, O best of the wise, O son of Kuntī."
"For whenever this tiger among men (Kṛṣṇa) desires to take from someone, that person's mind becomes disordered — just as has happened with the lord of Cedi."
"Mādhava (Kṛṣṇa) is the origin and also the destruction of all fourfold beings in the three worlds, O Yudhiṣṭhira."
Having heard his words, the king, the lord of Cedi, then caused Bhīṣma to hear harsh-syllabled words, O Bhārata.
Śiśupāla said: "With your many intimidations, frightening all the kings — why do you not feel shame, old man and disgrace to your lineage?"
"It is fitting for you — one who dwells in the third nature (i.e., neither man nor woman) — to speak of matters contrary to dharma, for you are called the foremost among all the Kurus."
"As a boat is bound to a boat, or as one blind man follows another blind man — such indeed are the Kuravas, O Bhīṣma, with you as their leader."
"By you recounting to us his deeds — beginning with the killing of Pūtanā in particular — our minds have been further unsettled."
"How, O Bhīṣma, does your tongue not split into a hundred pieces as you, a fool full of arrogance, seek to praise Keśava?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Where younger men would employ censure, O Bhīṣma — this cowherd — you, being senior in wisdom, presume to praise him."
"If in childhood he (Kṛṣṇa) killed Śakuni (the demon) — what is remarkable in that? Or those two — the horse and the bull — O Bhīṣma, who were not skilled in warfare."
"If he knocked down with his foot the cart demon (Shakata) — a piece of wood devoid of consciousness — O Bhīṣma, what wonderful feat was accomplished there?"
"If he held aloft a mountain no bigger than an ant-hill for seven days — that Govardhana, O Bhīṣma — I do not consider that remarkable."
"'Much food was eaten by him while playing on the mountaintop' — those hearing this from you, O Bhīṣma, have been struck with great wonder (at what you say)."
"The powerful Kaṃsa, whose food he ate, O knower of dharma — that same Kaṃsa was killed by him — this too is no great wonder."
"This which I will tell you, O Bhīṣma, O ignorant one, O lowest of the Kuru clan — surely this has not been heard by you from the virtuous who speak."
"One should not raise weapons against women, cows, and Brahmins; nor against one whose food one has eaten; nor against one who has sought refuge."
"Thus do the good and virtuous righteous ones always instruct, O Bhīṣma. But in this world, all of that is seen to be false in you."
"You praise Keśava as though not knowing — as one greater in wisdom and age than me — O best of the Kurus. But being a cow-killer and a woman-killer, O Bhīṣma, how does he deserve praise?"
"If this one who is called lord of the universe, Janārdana, honors himself as the foremost of the wise on account of your words saying 'thus it is' — then surely all of that is false."
"A song does not teach the singer though he may sing much. Beings go to their true nature — as the sparrow and the hawk (each follow their kind)."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Surely this nature of yours is the lowest — there is no doubt in this. And even among the Pāṇḍavas, the nature is considered more wicked than this."
"You, whose most worthy of worship is Kṛṣṇa, and you who are their guide — you speak the words of dharma, yet you are ignorant of dharma, fallen from the path of the good."
"For who among the best of the wise, knowing himself to be righteous, would act as you have acted, O Bhīṣma, while claiming to regard dharma?"
"The maiden named Ambā who desired another — how was she abducted by you, O one who fancies himself wise, O knower of dharma? May it be well with you."
"The maiden whom you abducted, O Bhīṣma — your brother Vicitravīrya refused to take her, following the conduct of the virtuous."
"And the children begotten for another's wives while you, who fancy yourself wise, looked on — born on the path of virtuous conduct (by others for dynastic duty)."
"There is no dharma in you, O Bhīṣma. This celibacy you maintain is in vain — out of delusion or impotence, without doubt."
"I do not see any benefit in you, O knower of dharma, anywhere. For surely you have not attended upon those elders who have spoken of dharma in this way."
"Sacrifices performed, gifts given, study undertaken, and rituals with great fees — all of this is not worth a sixteenth part of (having) a child."
"Whatever is accomplished through many vows and fasts, O Bhīṣma — all of that for the childless man is certainly in vain."
"You, childless and old, because of your false teaching of dharma — like the hamsa (swan/goose), you too may now receive death at the hands of your kinsmen."
"For thus did other men, the knowers of wisdom in former times, speak — O Bhīṣma. That which I will now fully recount to you as you listen:"
"There was once, they say, an old hamsa (goose) living at the ocean's edge in former times — one who spoke of dharma but lived otherwise. He was instructing the birds."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'Practice dharma, not adharma' — so went his words, they say. The birds constantly heard him, O Bhīṣma, speaking of dharma."
"Then for the sake of dharma — so we have heard, O Bhīṣma — the egg-born birds that roam the ocean waters brought food for him (the hamsa)."
In that very vicinity, having laid their eggs everywhere, the birds roamed about joyfully in the waters of the sea, O Bhīṣma.
That wicked swan devoured the eggs of all those birds — vigilant in his own doings while they were careless and inattentive.
Then, as those eggs were steadily diminishing, another bird born of an egg — a wise and vigilant one — grew suspicious and one day happened to catch sight of him.
Then that bird, overcome with the deepest grief on behalf of all birds, reported the sinful deed of the swan to them after witnessing it.
Then those birds, assembling together and seeing it with their own eyes, killed that swan who had behaved so falsely, O foremost of the Kurus.
These kings of the earth too, O Bhīṣma, may slay you — who are of the same nature as that swan — just as those furious birds slew that egg-born creature.
Those who are versed in the ancient lore also sing a verse on this matter, O Bhīṣma — that verse I shall relate to you accurately, O Bhārata.
"When the inner self is invested in wrong, O winged one, you rage falsely; the eating of eggs is impure for you — your deed surpasses your words."
Śiśupāla said: That great and mighty king Jarāsandha is highly esteemed by me — one who refused to fight with this man in battle, saying "This one is a mere slave."
What Keśava did at the slaying of Jarāsandha, along with Bhīmasena and Arjuna — who considers that to have been a righteous act?
Kṛṣṇa, having entered by a back way in the guise of a Brāhmaṇa speaker, witnessed for himself the power of the wise Jarāsandha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who, knowing himself to be righteous and devoted to Brāhmaṇas, would not have offered the water of welcome first to that wicked-souled one.
Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, and Dhanañjaya were told by Jarāsandha, "Eat and be welcome" — yet Kṛṣṇa did what was improper, O Kauravya.
If he is truly the creator of the world, as you foolishly believe, then why does he not properly recognise himself as a Brāhmaṇa?
This is what amazes me — that these Pāṇḍavas, drawn away from the path of the righteous by you, still regard it as proper.
Or perhaps this is no wonder, O Bhārata — for you are their guide in all matters: you who are both of the nature of a woman and an old man.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing those harsh and rough-syllabled words of his, the glorious Bhīmasena, foremost among the strong, became exceedingly angry.
His eyes — naturally wide and expansive, resembling lotus petals — grew red once more, their corners flushed deep crimson with wrath.
All the assembled kings beheld on his forehead a triple-ridged frown — like the triple-peaked Trikūṭa mountain, or the Gaṅgā flowing in three streams.
They saw the face of him as he ground his teeth in rage — like the face of Time at the end of an age, as he would burn all beings.
But as he leapt up with fierce velocity, the mighty-armed Bhīṣma seized that high-spirited one, as a lord might restrain a great general.
Restrained by Bhīṣma with many varied words of counsel, O Bhārata, the wrath of that Bhīma subsided.
That subduer of enemies did not transgress the word of Bhīṣma — even when aroused, as the great ocean does not pass beyond the shoreline when the rains are over.
But Śiśupāla, O king of men, did not tremble even when Bhīmasena grew enraged — that hero stood firm in his own manliness.
As Bhīma leapt up again and again with furious speed, that subduer of foes paid him no regard at all — just as a lion pays no heed to a small animal.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Laughing, the glorious king of Cedi spoke these words upon seeing the exceedingly wrathful Bhīmasena, whose prowess is terrible.
"Release him, Bhīṣma — let the kings of the earth watch as he is consumed by the fire of my prowess, like a moth by a flame."
Then, having heard those words of the king of Cedi, the foremost of the Kurus — Bhīṣma, best among the wise — spoke thus to Bhīmasena.
Bhīṣma said: This one was born in the royal line of Cedi with three eyes and four arms, and he brayed and roared with a sound like that of a donkey.
By that, his mother and father, along with all the kinsmen, were terrified; and seeing that ill omen, the two of them resolved to abandon him.
Then a disembodied voice addressed the king with his wife, his ministers, and his priest — whose hearts were bewildered with anxiety.
"O king, this glorious and mighty son has been born to you — do not be afraid of us; without anxiety, protect this child."
"You are not this one's death, nor has his time come yet; his killer will slay him with a weapon, and that killer has already been born, O king."
Having heard those words uttered by the spirit, which then vanished from sight, the mother — burning with maternal love for her son — spoke.
"I bow with joined palms to that being who has spoken these words concerning my own son — let him speak again."
"I wish to hear who shall be the death of my son." Then that invisible spirit spoke these words once more.
"The one in whose lap this child is taken up — his two extra arms shall fall to the ground like two five-headed serpents."
"And this third eye on the child's forehead shall sink away; the one upon seeing whom that happens — he shall be the death of this child."
Having heard that he was three-eyed and four-armed, and that such a prophecy had been made, all the kings of the earth came to see him for themselves.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having duly honoured those who had arrived, the lord of the earth placed the child on the lap of each king one by one.
Thus the child was placed in the laps of thousands of kings one by one in order — but the prophesied sign did not occur.
Then the two Yādavas, Saṅkarṣaṇa and Janārdana, arrived at the city of Cedi to visit that Yādava woman — their father's sister.
Having duly saluted the elders in proper order and inquired after the welfare of those kings, Rāma and Keśava took their seats.
The two heroes having been honoured with exceeding affection, the queen herself then placed her son in the lap of Dāmodara.
The very moment the child was placed in his lap, both extra arms fell off, and that eye on the forehead sank and vanished.
Seeing that, she was distressed and frightened, and she begged a boon of Kṛṣṇa: "Grant me a boon, O Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one — I am overcome with fear."
"You are the refuge of the afflicted and the giver of fearlessness to the frightened." Janārdana said: "Do not be afraid, O father's sister."
"What boon shall I give, or what shall I do for you, O father's sister? Whether possible or impossible, I shall fulfil your words."
Thus addressed, she then said to Kṛṣṇa, the joy of the Yadus: "You must pardon the offences of Śiśupāla, O mighty one."
Kṛṣṇa said: A hundred offences of his I shall pardon, O father's sister — even of your son who deserves death. Do not let your mind dwell in grief.
Bhīṣma said: Thus this sinful king Śiśupāla, of utterly feeble understanding, challenges you, O hero — emboldened by the boon given by Govinda himself.
Bhīṣma said: This is not the king of Cedi's own intelligence by which he challenges the Imperishable One — surely this is none other than the will of Kṛṣṇa himself, the sustainer of the world.
For who among the kings of this earth could hurl insults at me — even Bhīmasena — whose soul is overcome by fate, as this disgrace to his lineage has done?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For this one is assuredly a part of Hari's own splendour, O mighty-armed one — and the wide-famed Hari, wishing to reclaim that portion, seeks it back.
It is by that power that this king of Cedi, O tiger among the Kurus, roars like a tiger — that one of utterly wicked understanding, giving no thought to any of us.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king of Cedi did not tolerate those words of Bhīṣma, and enraged, he spoke these further words in reply to Bhīṣma.
Śiśupāla said: May this power of Keśava — whose perpetual panegyrist you are, rising up like a bard — belong to our enemies, O Bhīṣma.
Your mind always delights in praising others, O Bhīṣma — if you must praise kings, then praise some other king and leave off Janārdana.
Praise the Darada, praise Bāhlika — this foremost of kings, at whose very birth the earth was split asunder.
Praise Karṇa, O Bhīṣma — the overlord of the Vaṅga and Aṅga regions, equal to the thousand-eyed Indra in might, the mighty stretcher of the great bow.
Rightly praise Droṇa and his son Aśvatthāmā — the father and son, both great warriors, both ever worthy of praise, O Bhīṣma, finest of twice-born men.
Either one of them, O Bhīṣma, if roused to anger, could reduce this entire earth — moving and unmoving — to nothing: such is my conviction.
I see no king equal to Droṇa in battle, nor to Aśvatthāmā either, O Bhīṣma — yet you have no desire to praise even these two.
Why do you not praise Śalya and the other lords of the earth, O Bhīṣma — if your mind is always inclined toward the giving of praise?
What can I do, O king — you who once recounted the words of the elders, the speakers of dharma, have surely not truly heard them.
Self-disparagement, self-praise, the defaming of others, and the flattering of others — these four kinds of conduct are not practised by the noble.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That you constantly praise this Keśava who is unworthy of such praise, through delusion and blind devotion — not a single person approves of this, O Bhīṣma.
How can you place the entire world in the person of this Bhoja — a mere herdsman, a wicked soul — out of sheer partiality?
Or perhaps this devotion of yours does not yield to reason, O Bhārata — as I have already described before, like the story of the bhulinga bird.
There is a bird called bhulinga on the far side of the Himālayas, O Bhīṣma — its words are always heard to be contrary to its own interest.
It constantly cries out, "Do not act rashly!" — yet itself acts with extreme rashness and does not even perceive it.
For that little-witted bird, O Bhīṣma, snatches away the morsel of flesh lodged between the teeth of a lion as it is eating.
It lives only because the lion permits it, O Bhīṣma — make no mistake about it. In the same way, O you who are ignorant of dharma, you always speak such words.
You live only because these lords of kings allow it, O Bhīṣma — make no mistake. For there is no one else like you who performs deeds so universally despised.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having heard those bitter words of the king of Cedi, Bhīṣma spoke these words while the king of Cedi listened, O king.
"Indeed it is said that I live at the pleasure of these lords of the earth — I who do not count these kings of men as worth more than blades of grass."
When Bhīṣma had spoken thus, the kings then became enraged; some among them rejoiced, while others reproached Bhīṣma.
Some of the great archers, having heard those words of Bhīṣma, said: "This Bhīṣma is sinful, arrogant, and old — he does not deserve to be forgiven."
"Let the evil-minded Bhīṣma be slain like a beast — it is proper that all the kings, massing together in fury, should kill him, or burn him in a fire of straw."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having heard those words of theirs, the grandfather of the Kurus — the wise Bhīṣma — then spoke to those very lords of the earth.
I see no end to what has already been said again and again; but hear all that I shall now say, O lords of the earth.
Let me be slain like a beast, or burned with fire of grass — I have placed this entire position at the head of you all.
Here stands Govinda, the infallible one, honored by us; let him who is eager to die challenge Mādhava.
Let him challenge Kṛṣṇa, the bearer of the Śārṅga bow and mace, in battle today — let the fallen one enter the body of this very god.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having heard Bhīṣma's words, the king of Cedi of great prowess, eager to fight, addressed Vāsudeva.
"I challenge you — go to battle with me, O Janārdana, until today I slay you together with all the Pāṇḍavas."
"The Pāṇḍavas too must certainly be slain by me along with you, O Kṛṣṇa, for by them — bypassing the kings — you, who are no king, have been honored."
"Those who, out of foolishness, honor you — a slave and no king — as if you were worthy of honor, O Kṛṣṇa, those wicked-minded ones deserve to be slain — this is my view." Having spoken thus, that tiger among kings stood roaring with indignation.
When this was said, Kṛṣṇa then spoke these words, gentle yet firm, before all the kings and the Pāṇḍavas assembled there.
"This son of Śiśupāla's mother is our ultimate enemy, O kings — cruel-natured toward the Sātvatas, and no friend to the innocent."
"This cruel-doer, though my cousin's son, burned Dvārakā when he learned that we had gone to Prāgjyotiṣapura, O lords of men."
"Formerly, this one slew and captured all the Bhoja princes who were sporting on Mount Raivataka and carried them to his own city."
"This one of wicked resolve stole the consecrated horse, guarded by its protectors and released for my father's Aśvamedha sacrifice, to obstruct that ritual."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And this one abducted from here the unwilling wife of the illustrious Babhru while he was in the Sauvīra country, acting out of delusion."
"This cruel-doer, disguised through illusion for the sake of Karūṣa, abducted the virtuous Bhadrā of Vaiśālī, the niece of my maternal uncle."
"For my father's sister's sake I have borne great sorrow; but by good fortune, the matter has now come to pass in the presence of all the kings."
"For you see yourselves today his extreme transgression against me; but hear now of those wrongs done against me in secret."
"This transgression of his — this arrogant one who deserves death — I shall not be able to forgive today before the entire assembly of kings."
"This fool had designs on Rukmiṇī though he was as good as dead; but the fool did not obtain her, just as a Śūdra cannot attain the hearing of the Vedas."
Thereupon all those lords of men together, having heard Vāsudeva's words of this and like nature, censured the king of Cedi.
Then the mighty Śiśupāla, having heard those words, laughed a loud, resonant laugh and, still laughing, spoke thus.
"O Kṛṣṇa, how do you feel no shame in proclaiming in assemblies — and especially among kings — that Rukmiṇī was formerly intended for me?"
"What self-respecting man would ever proclaim in good company that a woman was previously another's — who other than you, O Madhusūdana?"
"Forgive me if you wish, or do not forgive me, O Kṛṣṇa — whether in anger or in pleasure, what can I expect from you anyway?"
Even as he was speaking thus, the blessed Madhusūdana, the annihilator of enemies, in anger severed his head with the discus; the mighty-armed one fell like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Then the kings beheld a supreme radiance rising up from the body of the lord of Cedi, O great king, like the sun rising from the sky.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then that radiance paid homage to Kṛṣṇa of lotus-petal eyes, worshipped by the world, and entered into him, O lord of men.
All the rulers of the earth thought it a wonder when they saw that radiance enter the mighty-armed Puruṣottama.
When the Cedi king was slain by Kṛṣṇa, the sky rained without clouds, blazing thunderbolts fell, and the earth trembled.
Then some of the earth's rulers said nothing at all, gazing at Janārdana when the moment was past the reach of words.
Others, filled with indignation, pressed their hands together tight; still others, overcome with rage, bit their lips with their teeth.
But some lords of men praised the descendant of Vṛṣṇi in private; some were furious, while others remained neutral.
Rejoicing, the great sages came to Keśava praising him, as did the great-souled brāhmaṇas and the mighty kings.
Then the Pāṇḍava addressed his brothers: "With all honor, attend to the obsequies of this hero, son of Damaghoṣa — do not delay." And they indeed fulfilled their brother's command.
Then Pārtha, together with those lords of the earth, consecrated that king's son as the ruler over the Cedis.
Then that sacrifice of the Kuru king, complete in all its abundance, O king, blazed forth in its full splendor, bringing joy to the young.
Free from obstacles, auspiciously begun, abounding in wealth and grain, rich in food and many delicacies, it was well protected by Keśava.
And he brought to completion that great ritual, the Rājasūya; the mighty-armed Janārdana, the blessed Śauri, bearer of the Śārṅga bow, discus, and mace, guarded that sacrifice until its conclusion.
Then, having bathed after the avabhṛtha rite, the King of Dharma Yudhiṣṭhira was approached by the entire assembled Kṣatriya royalty, and he spoke thus.
"By fortune you thrive, O knower of dharma, O lord, having attained sovereignty; by this act, O king of kings, you have enhanced the glory of the Ajamīḍha line of Ājamīḍhas, and great dharma has been performed."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"We take our leave, O tiger among men, well honored with every wish fulfilled; we shall depart to our own kingdoms — please grant us permission."
Having heard the words of the kings, the King of Dharma Yudhiṣṭhira duly honored the sovereigns and then addressed all his brothers.
"All these kings came to us out of affection; these scorchers of foes, having taken leave of me, are now departing for their own kingdoms — accompany these best of kings to the borders of their territories. May it be well with you."
Understanding their brother's command, the Pāṇḍavas, followers of dharma, duly escorted each of those foremost kings one by one.
The mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna quickly accompanied Virāṭa; the great chariot-warrior Dhanaṃjaya accompanied the great-souled Yajñasena.
The immensely powerful Bhīmasena accompanied Bhīṣma and Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the great chariot-warrior Sahadeva accompanied the heroic Droṇa together with his son.
Nakula, O king, accompanied Subala together with his son; the sons of Draupadī along with Saubhadra accompanied the mountain kings.
Those bulls among Kṣatriyas similarly accompanied the other Kṣatriyas; thus well-honored, they all departed, as did the brāhmaṇas in every direction.
When all the royal lords had departed, O bull of the Bhārata line, the mighty Vāsudeva spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"I take my leave of you — I shall go to Dvārakā, O joy of the Kurus; by good fortune you have attained the Rājasūya, the foremost of sacrifices."
Thus addressed, the King of Dharma spoke to Madhusūdana: "By your grace, O Govinda, I have indeed attained the sacrifice."
"By your grace, the entire Kṣatriya royalty became obedient and, bringing the foremost tribute, presented itself before me alone."
"Without you, O hero, we shall in no way find joy here; yet you must certainly go to the city of Dvāravatī."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed, the righteous, widely-famed Hari, accompanied by Yudhiṣṭhira, approached Pṛthā and, filled with joy, spoke to her.
"Your sons, the nephews of your husband's brothers, have today attained sovereignty — their purposes fulfilled and rich in wealth; you, therefore, rejoice."
"With your permission, I am eager to depart to Dvārakā." Then Keśava duly honored Subhadrā and Draupadī.
Then, having come out of the inner apartments accompanied by Yudhiṣṭhira, having bathed and performed his prayers, and having received blessings from the brāhmaṇas,
Then Dāruka, O great king, having harnessed the well-equipped chariot that resembled a rain-cloud in color, presented it ready.
Seeing the chariot prepared, bearing the emblem of the great Tārkṣya, the high-minded Puṇḍarīkākṣa circumambulated it clockwise, mounted it, and then departed for the city of Dvāravatī.
The glorious King of Dharma Yudhiṣṭhira, accompanied by his brothers, followed on foot the mighty Vāsudeva.
Then Hari reined in his excellent chariot for a moment, and Puṇḍarīkākṣa addressed Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī.
"Ever vigilant and steadfast, protect your subjects, O lord of the people, as the rain-cloud protects living beings, as a great tree shelters birds; may your kinsmen live by your support as the immortals live by the thousand-eyed Indra."
Having thus made their mutual covenant, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava took leave of each other and departed each to his own home.
When Kṛṣṇa, the foremost of the Sātvatas, had departed for Dvāravatī, O king, king Duryodhana alone and also Śakuni, son of Subala — those two bulls among men — lingered in that divine assembly hall.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Dwelling in that assembly hall, O bull of the Bhārata line, Duryodhana leisurely surveyed the entire hall together with Śakuni.
In it the joy of the Kurus beheld divine wonders never seen before by him in the city called after the elephant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Once, in the middle of the hall, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that king of the earth, came upon a crystal floor, mistaking it for water.
The king, his mind confused, lifted up his garments; downcast and looking away, he wandered through that hall.
Then, mistaking for dry ground a pool of crystal water adorned with crystal lotus flowers, he fell into the water fully clothed.
Seeing him fallen in the water, the attendants laughed heartily, and by royal order presented him with fresh, fine garments.
Seeing him in such a state, the immensely powerful Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and both of the twins all laughed at that moment.
The proud one did not endure their mockery; guarding his composure, he did not look at them.
Then lifting his garment again as if trying to cross dry ground, he climbed out; and once more all those people laughed.
He also struck his forehead against a door that appeared to be open, thinking it was shut, and then drew back from the doorway.
Having thus suffered various humiliations there, O lord of the people, King Duryodhana was then dismissed by the Pāṇḍavas.
With a joyless heart, having witnessed that wondrous prosperity at the great Rājasūya sacrifice, he departed for the city named after the elephant.
As king Duryodhana went, scorched by the Pāṇḍavas' prosperity and sickened with brooding, a wicked thought arose in his mind.
Having seen the Pārthas cheerful and contented, the kings obedient to them, and the entire world well-disposed toward them down to the children, O bull of the Kuru line,
and having seen too the supreme greatness of the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, Duryodhana, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, became pale.
As he traveled on, his mind distracted, brooding only on that assembly hall and the incomparable glory of the wise King of Dharma,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son Duryodhana, his mind distracted, did not then address Śakuni, the son of Subala, though he spoke to him again and again.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing him thus scattered in mind, Śakuni spoke to him: "Duryodhana, what is the root of this — why do you walk sighing like one in grief?"
Duryodhana said: Having seen this entire earth brought under Yudhiṣṭhira's sway — won by the martial prowess of the great-souled Arjuna, the white-horsed hero —
and having witnessed that sacrifice of Pārtha conducted in such a manner — brilliant uncle, it was like Indra's sacrifice among the gods —
I am filled entirely with indignation, burning day and night — as a shallow pool dries up when the hot season of Śukra arrives.
See how Śiśupāla was struck down by the foremost of the Sātvatas — and not a single man there stood to follow him in support.
The kings, burning in the fire kindled by the Pāṇḍavas, forgave that offense. But who truly deserves to forgive such a thing?
That great deed was carried out so fittingly by Vāsudeva, and succeeded through the glory of the great-souled sons of Pāṇḍu.
And so kings bearing various treasures attend upon the son of Kuntī, paying tribute like merchants paying taxes to a king.
Having seen such blazing prosperity in the Pāṇḍava, I am seized by indignation and burn — I who am not suited to bear this.
I shall enter fire, or consume poison, or plunge into water — I cannot go on living.
What man of spirit in this world would tolerate it — watching his rivals prosper while he himself declines?
I am neither woman nor neuter, neither man nor eunuch — yet today I endure such prosperity come to others. What then am I?
Having witnessed such sovereignty over the earth, such wealth, and such a sacrifice as that — who like me would not be consumed by envy?
Alone and unable to seize that royal splendor, seeing no allies, I contemplate death.
I think fate alone is paramount; human effort is meaningless — having seen that resplendent prosperity thus acquired by the son of Kuntī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I made effort before for his destruction, O Saubala — yet he has surpassed all of that and grown, like a lotus in water.
Therefore I consider fate supreme and human effort pointless — the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra diminish while the sons of Pṛthā ever grow.
I, who have seen that prosperity and that assembly so magnificent, and the mockery by the guards — I am scorched as if by fire.
Therefore, uncle, give me leave — today I am deeply sorrowful and filled with indignation. Convey this to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Śakuni said: Duryodhana, you should not harbor indignation toward Yudhiṣṭhira — the Pāṇḍavas merely enjoy what is rightfully their own portion.
Those tiger-like men were attacked by you before through many schemes, yet they escaped — their portion of fate safeguarding them.
By them was won Draupadī as wife, and Drupada together with his sons as allies in gaining the earth, and the mighty Vāsudeva too.
And their paternal share of wealth, once obtained, has not been overpowered — it has grown through their own glory, O lord of earth. What cause for lament is there?
By Dhanañjaya was the Gāṇḍīva bow obtained, and the two inexhaustible quivers, and divine weapons — after propitiating the fire-god.
With that foremost of bows and by the strength of his own arms, kings of the earth were brought under his sway. What cause for lament is there?
Having rescued Maya the demon from being burned by fire, the ambidextrous Arjuna, scorcher of foes, had him build that assembly hall.
And by that Maya were summoned the Rākṣasas called Kimkaras — those terrible ones bear that assembly hall. What cause for lament is there?
As for what you said about having no allies, O king, O Bhārata — that is false. These brothers of yours are your allies, great warriors all.
Droṇa, your great archer, along with his wise son; and the son of a charioteer, Rādheya; and Gautama — all great warriors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And I together with my brothers, and the valiant son of Somadatta — united with all of these, go and conquer the entire earth.
Duryodhana said: Together with you, O king, and with these and other great warriors, I shall conquer them — if you give your approval.
When these are conquered, the earth will be mine, and all the kings of the earth, and that hall of immense wealth.
Śakuni said: Dhanañjaya, Vāsudeva, Bhīmasena, Yudhiṣṭhira, Nakula, Sahadeva, and Drupada together with his sons —
these cannot be conquered by force in battle even by the hosts of gods — great warriors, mighty archers, masters of weapons, mad with the lust for battle.
But I know the means by which Yudhiṣṭhira himself can be conquered, O king. Hear it and act upon it.
Duryodhana said: If they can be conquered without harm to friends and other noble ones, then tell me how, uncle.
Śakuni said: The son of Kuntī is fond of dice yet does not know how to play; and once challenged, the lord of kings will not be able to refuse.
I am skilled at gambling — there is none equal to me on earth or in the three worlds. Challenge that son of Kuntī to a game of dice.
I, skilled with dice, will without doubt win from him his kingdom and that blazing wealth, for your sake, O bull among men.
Present all of this to the king, Duryodhana. With your father's permission, I shall conquer him — of that there is no doubt.
Duryodhana said: You yourself convey this properly to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, foremost of the Kurus, O Saubala — I will not be able to declare it myself.
Vaishampyana said: Having witnessed that great Rājasūya sacrifice of king Yudhiṣṭhira, together with the son of Gāndhārī,
Śakuni of Subala's line, knowing before what would please Duryodhana, then approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who sat with the eye of wisdom —
Having heard Duryodhana's words, Śakuni went to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, and spoke to that greatly wise one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Duryodhana, O great king, is pale, wan, and emaciated, dejected and sunk in worry — know this, O bull of the Bhāratas."
"You do not examine properly this unbearable anguish that arises from his enemies. Why do you not perceive the sorrow of your eldest son?"
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "Duryodhana, my son, what is the root of your distress — you who are so deeply afflicted? If it is a matter I should hear, tell me, O joy of the Kurus."
"This Śakuni describes you as pale, wan, and emaciated, brooding — yet I myself cannot perceive the source of your grief."
"For great sovereignty has been entrusted entirely to you, my son. Your brothers and friends do nothing displeasing to you."
"You wear fine robes, you eat meat and fine food, thoroughbred horses carry you — why then are you wan and thin?"
"Couches of great worth, charming women, houses full of fine things, and pleasures as you wish —
all of this is bound to your word as if to that of the gods — no doubt of it. Why then, O unconquerable one, do you grieve like a helpless man, my son?"
Duryodhana said: "I eat and dress as an inferior man does, and I endure fierce indignation, tolerating the turn of time."
"He who, unable to endure, sees his own subjects overcome by others and seeks release from those afflictions by conquering the enemy — he truly is called a man."
"Contentment destroys prosperity, as does arrogance, O Bhārata; and both compassion and fear — he who is bound by these does not attain greatness."
"The food I eat gives me no comfort, having seen that blazing prosperity in Yudhiṣṭhira — in the son of Kuntī — the very sight of which drains my color."
"Watching my rivals prosper and myself decline, and seeing — though it be invisible — prosperity standing poised in the son of Kuntī as if raised aloft — therefore I am pale, dejected, wan, and thin."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Eighty-eight thousand learned householders who have completed their student-vows — each one attended by thirty slave-girls — are maintained by Yudhiṣṭhira."
"Another ten thousand daily eat the finest food from golden dishes in Yudhiṣṭhira's household."
"The Kāmbojas sent him priceless woolen blankets — those of banana-colored deer-brown, dark black, and red hues."
"By the hundreds and thousands roam chariots, women, cattle, and horses; and thirty hundreds of camel-mares go about as well."
"Kings brought diverse and abundant jewels of every kind to the son of Kuntī at this foremost of sacrifices, O lord of the earth."
"Nowhere have I seen nor heard of such an influx of wealth as at the sacrifice of that wise son of Pāṇḍu."
"Having seen that boundless flood of my enemy's wealth, O king, O lord, I find no peace, brooding on it ceaselessly."
"Brahmins and traders bearing cattle, in groups of hundreds, carrying tribute of three hundred million stood at the gate but were turned away."
"Taking up their water-pots made of pure gold, beautiful ones, and thus taking up their tribute, they then gained entry."
"Even honey that the celestial women do not ordinarily preserve for Indra — the ocean of Varuṇa's jars brought that in bronze vessels for him."
"A golden net worth a thousand gold pieces, adorned with many jewels — upon seeing all of that, it all felt to me like the burning of a fever."
"Taking their portion, they depart toward the eastern and southern oceans; and likewise taking their portion they go westward, O bull of the Bhāratas."
"But northward they do not go without winged birds to guide them, dear father. And there was something wondrous here — hear me as I tell it."
"When a full hundred thousand Brahmins had been served, a conch was installed there as a signal and it was blown unceasingly."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"From that conch sounding again and again, O Bhārata, I heard a supreme sound, and then my hairs stood on end."
"The court was thronged with many kings wishing to see it, and those kings, having brought all their jewels, O lord of men —"
"at the sacrifice of that wise son of Pāṇḍu, O great king, the rulers of the earth served the twice-born like merchants."
"That prosperity is not found in the king of the gods, nor in Yama, nor in Varuṇa, nor even in the lord of the Guhyakas — that prosperity which, O king, is in Yudhiṣṭhira."
"Having seen that supreme prosperity of the son of Pāṇḍu, I find no peace, my heart burning."
Śakuni said: "This supreme fortune you have seen in the Pāṇḍava — hear from me the means to win it, O you of true valor."
"I am expert in dice, O Bhārata — even famed across the earth — knowing the hearts of players, knowing the stakes, knowing the distinctions in gambling."
"The son of Kuntī loves dice yet does not know how to play. When summoned, he will clearly come. Invite him, saying: let us play."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Śakuni, King Duryodhana then spoke these words unhesitatingly to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"This one, O king, is skilled at dice and is eager to win the wealth of the son of Pāṇḍu by gambling — you ought to give your permission for this."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "Vidura is the counsellor of great wisdom, by whose guidance I abide. Having consulted with him, I shall determine what is to be done in this matter."
"For he, placing dharma foremost, far-sighted as he is, will declare what is supremely beneficial and what is proper for both sides, and will settle the matter definitively."
Duryodhana said: "If Vidura comes and dissuades you, then if you too desist, O king of kings, I shall surely die — there is no doubt of this."
"When I am dead, O king, be happy with Vidura — you will enjoy the whole earth; what use will you have of me?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that anguished and affectionate speech of his, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, yielding to Duryodhana's will, spoke to his servants.
"Let craftsmen quickly build for me a great and beautiful assembly hall with a thousand pillars and a hundred doors, pleasing to the mind and fair to behold."
"Then, having spread it with jewels and provided dice in every place, and when it is well finished and easily accessible, report to me gently."
Having thus resolved for the sake of pacifying Duryodhana, O great king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra then sent a messenger to Vidura.
For without consulting Vidura he could reach no firm resolution on anything; yet knowing the vices of gambling, he was drawn along by his love for his son.
Hearing this, the wise Vidura, seeing that the gateway of Kali had arrived and that destruction's mouth had opened, hastened to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Approaching that great-souled elder brother, brother to brother, and bowing his head at his feet, he spoke these words.
"I do not rejoice in this resolve of yours, O king, O lord. Act in such a way that there may be no quarrel among your sons on account of gambling."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "Vidura, no quarrel will come among my sons through their sons; the gods in heaven will surely grant us their grace — there is no doubt."
"Whether auspicious or inauspicious, beneficial or harmful, let this friendly gambling proceed — this is fate, without a doubt."
"With me present, and with Bhīṣma, that bull among Bhāratas, any mischief decreed by fate will not come to pass in any manner."
"Go, mounting a chariot with horses swift as the wind, and bring Yudhiṣṭhira from Khāṇḍavaprastha today itself."
"My resolve cannot be checked — I tell you this, Vidura. I hold fate alone to be supreme, by which this comes to pass."
Thus addressed, the wise Vidura, thinking "this must not be," went deeply grieved to the great-minded Bhīṣma, son of the river goddess.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Janamejaya said: "How did that gambling among the brothers come to be — that great calamity wherein my grandfathers the Pāṇḍavas met that disaster?"
"Who were the kings assembled there, O best of knowers of the Veda? Who approved of it and who tried to prevent it?"
"I wish to hear this told in detail by you, O twice-born one, for this is the root of the destruction of the earth, O best of twice-born men."
The Sūta said: Thus addressed by the king, the illustrious disciple of Vyāsa, the knower of all the Vedas, narrated everything as it had occurred.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Hear from me this story in detail, O best of Bhāratas — again, O great king, if your mind is inclined to hear it."
Having learned Vidura's opinion, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Ambikā, once again spoke these words to Duryodhana in private.
"Enough of gambling, O son of Gāndhārī — Vidura does not approve. For that one of great wisdom will not speak what is harmful to us."
"I hold whatever Vidura speaks to be supremely beneficial; let all of that be done, my son — I consider this to be your good."
"The divine sage Bṛhaspati, of noble mind, the teacher of Vāsava, taught the holy wisdom to the wise king of gods —"
"— all of that with its secrets does Vidura know, that great sage; and I too, my son, am ever abiding in his words."
"Indeed, the intelligent Vidura is considered the foremost among the Kurus, as Uddhava of great wisdom is honoured among the Vṛṣṇis, O prince."
"Therefore enough of gambling, my son — in gambling, division is clearly seen; in division, destruction of the kingdom follows. Avoid it, son."
"What is remembered as the highest duty of a father and mother toward their son — that position of your fathers and grandfathers you have already attained, dear child."
"You are learned, accomplished in the scriptures, cherished always at home, the eldest brother established in the kingdom — what beautiful thing do you lack?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"What food and clothing of the highest order, unattainable by ordinary men, that you have obtained, O mighty-armed — why then do you grieve, my son?"
"O mighty-armed, commanding the great and flourishing kingdom of your fathers and grandfathers constantly, you shine like the lord of gods in heaven."
"For you, O one of discerning wisdom, how has this most painful root of sorrow arisen? You ought to tell me that."
Duryodhana said: "'I eat, I am clothed' — a man who, seeing these things, feels no indignation is considered a base person."
"Shared prosperity does not delight me, O king of kings, O lord; and having seen the blazing glory of the son of Kuntī, I am pierced with anguish."
"That I remain steadfast after seeing all the earth subject to Yudhiṣṭhira's command — I tell you this out of grief: that is why I live."
"The Chaitrakikas, the Kukuras, the Karaskaras, the Lohajanghas — they shine there as though enchanted and subdued, at Yudhiṣṭhira's dwelling."
"Those who dwell along the Himālayas and the sea, all the treasuries of jewels, even the outcastes — all have been subdued and stand suppliant at Yudhiṣṭhira's dwelling."
"Thinking me the eldest and the most worthy, O lord of the people, I was honored by Yudhiṣṭhira and appointed to receive the jewels."
"Of the finest jewels being presented, those of the highest worth, no farther end could be seen — no other boundary either — O Bhārata."
"My hand was not equal to receiving all that wealth; as I grew tired, others took and accepted the wealth brought from distant lands."
"I saw a lotus pool built by Maya with the jewels of lake Bindu, its floor of crystal, full as if it were water, O Bhārata."
"As my garments were lifted up, that wolf-bellied one — Bhīma — laughed at me, confused and stripped of jewels by the exceptional prosperity of the enemy."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Had I been able to do so there, I would have felled that wolf-belly — for the mockery of an enemy burns me, O Bhārata."
"And again, mistaking a similar pool adorned with water-born flowers for solid ground, I fell into the water, O lord of men."
"There Kṛṣṇa laughed at me with a ringing sound, together with Pārtha; and Draupadī too, along with her women, tormenting my heart."
"And while I stood wet in the water, the servants, directed by the king, gave me different garments — and that too was most painful to me."
"Hear yet another humiliation I tell you, O lord of men: going out through what was no door but was shaped like a door, I struck the stone and was wounded again on my forehead."
"There the twin brothers, seeing me from afar, graceful as they were, both embraced me with their arms, sorrowful together, so they said."
"And Sahadeva, as if marveling, said to me there, 'Go this way, O king, this is the door' — saying it again and again."
"The names of the jewels that I saw there had never been heard by me before — and that too torments my mind."
Duryodhana said: "Hear what I saw at the Pāṇḍavas' court, O Bhārata — the finest wealth brought by kings from here and there."
"I cannot find firmness in myself having seen that wealth of the enemy — understand this from its fruits and from the ground reality, O Bhārata."
"The Kāmboja king gave wealth of the finest kind: garments of the Aila and Vaila and Varsha-damsha peoples adorned with gold, cloaks and skins of the highest quality."
"Three hundred horses of the Tittiri and Kalmasha breeds with parrot-like noses, and three hundred she-camels fattened on pilu, shami, and ingudi trees."
"Brahmin ascetics with cow-leather garments and servant-attendants of every kind, those greatly blessed ones, stood at the door waiting, bearing three kharva loads of tribute out of affection for the great-souled king of righteousness."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Having brought water-pots made of pure gold, auspicious ones, and having thus presented their tribute, they then gained entry."
"One hundred thousand maidservants from the Karpasika lands — dark, slender, long-haired, adorned with golden ornaments — along with Śūdras worthy of the finest brahmins, with wool-cloths and skins."
"The inhabitants of Bharukaccha, bearing their full tribute, brought, O great king, horses bred in the Gāndhāra country."
"Those men who live by grain sown by Indra's grace, at the mouths of rivers and in the island-forests of the ocean, and along the Sindhu —"
"— those Vairajas, the Paradasas and the Vaṅgas, together with gamesters, bringing varied tribute and diverse jewels —"
"— goats and sheep, cattle and gold, donkeys and camels, fruit-produced honey, and various woolen blankets, stood waiting at the door, held back."
"Bhagadatta, the heroic lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, the powerful overlord of the Mlecchas, the great warrior-king, came together with the Yavanas —"
"— bringing swift thoroughbred horses with the speed of wind, and bearing his full tribute, stood at the door, waiting."
"Bhagadatta of Prāgjyotiṣa, having given that vessel made of the finest iron-ore, and swords with handles of pure ivory, then departed."
"Two-eyed and three-eyed men, those with an eye in the forehead, assembled from various directions, those wearing turbans and those dwelling without fixed abode, the Bahukas and the man-eaters —"
"— and one-footed beings I saw there, waiting at the door, giving him much gold and silver as tribute."
"Horses of the color of the Indragopaka insect, of parrot-green color and swift as thought, others resembling Indra's rainbow, and some like twilight clouds —"
"— the one-footed beings took those many-colored forest horses of mind-like speed and gave him gold beyond all price."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The Cīnas, the Hunas, the Śakas, the Oḍras, dwellers in mountain fastnesses, the Vārṣṇeyas, the Harahūṇas, the dark ones, and those of the Himavat region —"
"— I cannot enumerate all those who came in their various forms, waiting at the door, giving him tribute of many kinds in countless numbers."
"They brought ten thousand black-necked, huge-bodied asses, capable of a hundred leagues, tame and celebrated in all directions."
"Woolen cloth and Rankava cloth, insect-produced silk and woven silk, rich in measure, color, and texture, produced in Bāhlika and China —"
"— beaten cloth and other fabrics of lotus-like appearance in thousands, smooth non-cotton cloth, soft sheep-wool cloth, and deer-skins —"
"— sharpened and long swords, lances, spears, and battle-axes, and also sharp axes produced in the western border lands —"
"— various juices and fragrances, and jewels by the thousands — bearing all this tribute in full, they stood waiting at the door."
The Śakas, Tukhāras, Kankas, Romashas, and Shringins — these peoples brought a counted ten-crore horses, both those that travel far and those fit for great journeys.
Bringing by crores and in great quantities gold measuring a padma, and bearing diverse tribute, they stood at the gate, held back from entry.
Seats of great worth, vehicles, and couches — decorated with gems and gold, and fashioned from elephant ivory —
Chariots of various forms adorned with pure gold, furnished with well-trained horses, and covered with tiger skins —
Variegated horse-cloths, jewels by the thousands, iron-tipped arrows, half-iron arrows, and weapons of every kind —
Having presented all this great wealth, the king who rules the eastern lands entered the sacrificial hall of the great-souled Pāṇḍava.
Duryodhana said: Hear me, O sinless one, as I describe the various gifts presented to him — the great accumulation of wealth given by kings for the purpose of the sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who dwell between Mount Meru and Mount Mandara along the river Shailoda, frequenting the pleasant shade of kichaka bamboos —
The Khaśas, the Ekashanas, the Ajyohas, the Pradaras, the Dirgha-Venavas, the Pashupas, the Kuṇindas, the Taṅgaṇas, and the Para-Taṅgaṇas —
Those kings brought in heaps the gold known as Pipilika — bestowed as a boon by ants — measured by the drona measure.
Dark yaks with marks, and white ones gleaming like the moon, and also the sweet honey born from Himālayan flowers — all this in abundance.
From the northern Kurus, garlands unwilted by water; and from Kailāsa in the north, medicinal herbs of very great potency.
Mountain peoples, having brought other tribute as well, stood bowing respectfully, waiting at the gate of the king who has no enemies — held back from entering.
The kings on the far side of the Himālayas, near the mountain of sunrise; those who dwell by the ocean of Varisena and around the Lohitya river; those who subsist on fruits and roots; and the Kirātas who are clad in skins —
Loads of sandalwood and aguru timber and Kaliyaka wood; and heaps of hides, jewels, gold, and fragrant substances —
Ten thousand Kirāta slave-women, O lord of the people, and bringing pleasant things from afar — deer and birds —
And gold piled up from the mountains, of great brilliance — having brought all this tribute they stood at the gate, held back from entering.
The Kayavyas, Daradas, Darvas, the valiant Vaiyamakas, the Audumbaras, the Durvibhagas, the Pāradas together with the Bāhlīkas —
The Kashmiris, Kundamanas, Purakas, Hamsakayanas, Śibis, Trigartas, Yaudheyas, the Rājanyas, Madras, and Kekayas —
The Ambaṣṭhas, Kaukuras, Tarkshyas, Vastrapas together with the Pahlavas, the Vasatayas, Saumeyas, together with the Kshudrakas and Mālavas —
The Shaundis, Kukuras, and Śakas, O lord of the people; the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Puṇḍras, the Shanavatyas, and the Gayas —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Well-born, organized in guilds, noble, weapons in hand — these Kṣatriyas brought wealth by the hundreds for him who has no enemies.
The Vaṅgas, the lords of Kaliṅga, the Tamraliptas together with the Pundrakas brought fine dukula cloth, silk, leaf-wool, and woolen garments as well.
There they were told by the doorkeepers, by royal command: 'When your tasks are accomplished and your tributes settled, then you will gain entry through the gate.'
Elephants with tusk-tips adorned in gold, draped in golden girths, lotus-colored, covered with housings, mountain-like in stature, perpetually in rut — surrounding the Kāmyaka lake —
Each giving a thousand elephants clad in armor, patient and of noble lineage, they then entered through the gate.
These and many other groups assembled here from all directions; and by other great-souled ones, too, jewels were brought here.
The Gandharva king named Citraratha, a follower of Vāsava (Indra), gave four hundred horses swift as the wind.
The Gandharva Tumburu, full of joy, gave a hundred horses wearing golden garlands, the color of mango leaves.
King Kṛti, O Kauravya, O lord of the people, gave very many hundreds of excellent elephants — the finest of their kind.
By Virāṭa the Matsya king, for the purpose of tribute, two thousand intoxicated elephants wearing golden garlands were offered.
Vasudāna, king of the Pāṃsurāṣṭras, gave twenty-six elephants and two thousand horses wearing golden garlands, O king.
Endowed with speed and strength, in prime of age, O lord of men — having taken all the tribute, he presented it to the Pāṇḍavas.
By Yajñasena (Drupada), fourteen thousand female slaves and ten thousand male slaves with their wives, O lord of the people —
Twenty-six chariots yoked with elephants, O great king, and his entire kingdom — all of this was offered to the sons of Pāṇḍu for the sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Lapis lazuli that is the essence of the ocean, pearls, conches, and by the hundreds — elephant cloths — the Siṃhalas (Ceylonese) duly brought there.
Dark women clad in jeweled garments with copper-tinged eyes — having received them, men stood there at the gate, held back from entering.
Out of affection, Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas — even those who had been subdued — brought gifts; Vaiśyas too, and Śūdras eager to serve, approached Yudhiṣṭhira out of love and deep respect.
All the Mlecchas, all the varnas — those born at the beginning, middle, and end of the social order — along with people of various births coming from various lands, the whole world seemed gathered in Yudhiṣṭhira's residence.
Seeing the many high and low tribute-bearers sent by kings — looking upon the grief of enemies — a wish to die arises in me today.
Now I shall tell you of the servants of the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata — those for whom Yudhiṣṭhira arranges both raw and cooked food.
Ten thousand elephant riders along with cavalry, a crore of chariots, and infantry in great numbers as well —
Food being measured out and prepared, being cooked, and also being distributed elsewhere — and the sound of auspicious recitations throughout —
I never saw any person of any varna in Yudhiṣṭhira's residence who had not eaten, who was not joyful, or who suffered from any scarcity.
Eighty-eight thousand householder graduates of sacred learning, each provided with thirty female servants — whom Yudhiṣṭhira maintains — greatly pleased and satisfied, they too pray for the destruction of his enemies.
Ten thousand more — ascetics who have elevated their vital energy — dine from golden vessels in Yudhiṣṭhira's residence.
All that was eaten or uneaten, done or undone — even the hunchbacked and the dwarfish — Yājñasenī (Draupadī), herself not yet eating, supervised all this, O lord of the people.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Two groups did not pay tribute to the son of Kuntī, O Bhārata: the Pāñcālas by virtue of the marriage alliance, and the Andhaka-Vṛṣṇis by reason of friendship.
Duryodhana said: Those noble kings who are true to their word, who observe great vows, who are fully learned, eloquent speakers, and who have bathed in the concluding rites of Vedantic study —
Patient, restrained by modesty, righteous in soul, of great renown — those anointed kings attend upon him.
Brought together by kings for the purpose of sacrificial fees, wild cows to be milked into bronze vessels — I saw many thousands of them here and there.
Having honored them, the kings themselves, with untroubled minds, brought there — O Bhārata — utensils of high and low quality for the consecration.
Bāhlika brought a chariot adorned with Jāmbūnada gold; Sudakṣiṇa yoked it with white Kambojan horses.
Sunītha, of great fame, brought for it an incomparable secondary car; the lord of the Cedis quickly himself raised the banner with his own hands.
The southern king provided the harness; the Magadha king provided garlands and a turban; Vasudāna, the mighty archer, provided the lord of elephants sixty years of age.
The Matsya king fastened the axle-pins; Ekalavya provided the sandals; the Avanti king provided water of many kinds for the consecration.
Cekitāna brought the quiver; the Kāśi king brought the bow; Śalya brought a sword with a golden hilt and a gold-adorned sheath.
Then Dhaumya and Vyāsa of very great austerity performed the consecration, placing Nārada in front, along with the sage Devala and Asita.
Joyfully, the great sages attended the consecration ceremony — along with Jāmadagnya (Paraśurāma) and other masters of the Vedas.
They approached the great-souled one, who bestowed lavish sacrificial fees, as the seven seers in heaven approach Mahendra, the king of gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sātyaki of true valor held the ceremonial umbrella over him; Dhanañjaya (Arjuna) held the fan; and the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena stood by.
The conch which Prajāpati in ancient times held back for Indra — that Varuṇa conch the ocean itself, as a jar of water, brought and presented to him.
Sprinkled with a thousand nishkas of gold, well-crafted by Viśvakarman — when he was consecrated with it by Kṛṣṇa, I fell into a swoon there.
They go from the eastern to the western ocean and even to the southern; but to the northern they do not go without birds, dear father.
There they blew conches by the hundreds for auspicious reasons; when those life-giving ones were fully sounded, my hair stood on end.
Even kings bowed and fell, diminished of their own splendor; Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Pāṇḍavas, Sātyaki, and Kṛṣṇa as the eighth stood firm.
Steadfast in spirit, endowed with heroism, taking delight in one another — seeing the unconscious kings and seeing me, they laughed.
Then the joyful Bībhatsu (Arjuna) gave five hundred bulls with gold-tipped horns to the foremost Brāhmaṇas, O Bhārata.
Not even Śambara's slayer (Indra) had such splendor, nor Yauvanashva (Māndhātā), nor Manu, nor king Pṛthu son of Vena, nor even Bhagīratha.
Just so the son of Kuntī, endowed with supreme prosperity beyond measure, having accomplished the Rājasūya — he shone like the lord Hariścandra.
Having seen this glory in the son of Pṛthā, equal to that of Hariścandra, O mighty one — how do you consider life to be better for me? Tell me, O Bhārata.
Like a yoke bound to a blind ox — things are inverted, O lord of men: the younger thrive while the elder decline, O Bhārata.
Having seen thus, I find no peace — though I search for it, O hero of the Kurus. Therefore I have come to such an emaciated state, and to pallor, and to sorrow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: You are the eldest, O son, the first-born of the eldest line — do not hate the Pāṇḍavas. A hater brings upon himself misery, just as death brings destruction.
Yudhiṣṭhira, who is not envious, who shares the same interests, who has the same friends — one who does not hate you, how could a person like you hate him, O bull of the Bhāratas?
Equal in lineage and valor — how, O king, O son, do you out of delusion covet your brother's prosperity? Be not thus; be calm here — that is the righteous course.
But if you desire that splendor of sacrifice, O bull of the Bhāratas, let your officiating priests perform for you the great sacrifice of the seven-stranded ritual.
Kings will bring for you too abundant wealth, and out of love and deep respect, jewels and ornaments as well.
Dear son, to covet another's property is to pursue what is useless. He who is content with his own, steadfast in his own duty — that one truly flourishes in happiness.
Non-interference in others' affairs, constant effort in one's own duties, and diligence in protecting what is one's own — these are the marks of true prosperity.
The man who is unshaken in adversity, ever capable and diligent, vigilant and self-controlled — he always beholds good fortune.
Give wealth in charitable rites, enjoy desired pleasures, sport with women free from fear — be at peace, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Duryodhana said: Though you know, you confuse me like a boat tethered to a ship. Why are you inattentive to your own interest — or do you perhaps hate me?
These sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are not yours to instruct — you always speak of what will happen and what serves your own purpose.
One who is led by another and who strays from the path while being called a leader — how could those following in his footsteps keep to the right road?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O king, though you are wise, a servant of elders, and master of your senses, you greatly confuse us who are engaged in our own affairs.
Bṛhaspati has said that the conduct of a king differs from the conduct of common people; therefore a king must always strive to think of his own interest.
O great king, the livelihood of a Kṣatriya is concentrated in victory — whether it be dharma or adharma, such is his proper conduct, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Desiring the blazing wealth of his enemies, a king should illuminate all directions like a charioteer with a whip, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Whatever stratagem binds the enemy, whether concealed or open — that is the true weapon of those who know weapons; a mere blade is not called a weapon.
Discontent is the root of prosperity; for that reason I desire it. He who strives for advancement, O king, is the supreme statesman.
One should not feel attachment to sovereignty or wealth; others take away what was formerly acquired — this, they say, is the law of kings.
Indra made a pact of non-hostility and then severed the head of Namuci — that, it is held, is his eternal policy toward enemies.
The earth swallows these two as a serpent swallows creatures in its burrow: the king who does not fight back, and the Brahmin who does not travel abroad.
O lord of the people, there is truly no enemy by birth; he with whom one shares a common livelihood — that person is the enemy, and no other.
He who out of delusion neglects a growing enemy faction — like a disease left to flourish — it will cut at his very root.
Even a small enemy with ever-growing might devours the nearby tree from the root, like a termite mound that springs from the base.
O Ajamīḍha, O Bhārata, may the fortune of your enemy not please you — this is the burden of statecraft borne on the heads of the strong-minded.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who desires increase of wealth as one desires growth from birth — he flourishes among his kinsmen; for valor is indeed swift increase.
Without obtaining the sovereignty of the Pāṇḍavas I shall have no peace of mind; I shall either win that prosperity or lie slain in battle.
Of what use to me today is a life such as this, O lord of the people? The Pāṇḍavas grow constantly while our growth remains stagnant.
Śakuni said: That very prosperity which you see in Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Pāṇḍu, and which burns you — I shall win it by gambling; let the other side be summoned.
Without going into danger and without fighting at the head of armies, I, expert in dice, shall conquer those ignorant of the game by casting the dice unharmed.
Know my stakes as bows, O Bhārata, and know the dice as my arrows; the mastery of dice is my bowstring and gambling is my chariot-armor.
Duryodhana said: This expert in dice is confident of winning the wealth from the sons of Pāṇḍu by gambling, O king — let this be pleasing to you, father.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: I abide by the counsel of my brother, the great-souled Vidura; conferring with him, I shall determine the right course of this matter.
Duryodhana said: Vidura, free from doubt and devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas, will frustrate your intention — he is not so devoted to my welfare, O Kaurava.
A man should not undertake his affairs depending on another's ability — the minds of two do not accord in matters of action, O joy of the Kurus.
The fool who avoids danger and merely protects himself, standing like a wet mat in the rains, simply perishes.
Neither diseases nor Yama waits for one to attain what is good; for as long as one is capable, one should pursue the good.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: In every way, my son, I do not approve of conflict with the mighty; enmity creates disorder — it is indeed an effortless weapon.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You regard what is harmful as beneficial, O prince — the binding of strife is exceedingly terrible; once set in motion by any means, it releases swords and arrows too.
Duryodhana said: The ancients established gambling as a recognized practice — in it there is no excess and no clash of arms; let Śakuni's proposal be pleasing today — quickly command that a hall be built here.
Gambling is for us an excellent gate to heaven, and it is likewise fitting for those who abide by it — thus make it equal on both sides; arrange a gambling match between us and the Pāṇḍavas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: What you have said does not please me; yet let what is dear to you be done, O lord of men — having undertaken this course you will repent afterward, for such a word is not righteous.
Vidura has already seen all this clearly with his wisdom and learning — yet this great fear, which destroys the seed of the Kṣatriyas, is coming upon us helplessly.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra, considering fate supreme and hard to overcome, loudly commanded his men in accordance with his son's words — the king stood firm, his mind bewildered by fate.
Let the workers quickly build for me a magnificent hall with a thousand pillars, decorated with gold and vaidurya gems, with a hundred doors, with spires of crystal over the arched gateways, a league in length and breadth accordingly.
Having heard this, the wise and skilled workers swiftly and without hesitation built it exactly as commanded; all manner of materials were brought to the hall, and thousands of craftsmen were engaged.
Then in a short time those workers reported joyfully to the king that the charming hall, filled with many gems, adorned with various designs, and furnished with golden seats of varied craftsmanship, had been completed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the wise king Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words to Vidura, the foremost of ministers: Go to prince Yudhiṣṭhira and quickly bring him here in my name.
Let this hall of mine, rich in gems and of varied design, furnished with most excellent couches and seats, be seen by him coming together with his brothers — and let a friendly gambling match take place here.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, knowing his son's intention and considering fate hard to overcome, did as commanded.
But Vidura, best of the wise, thus spoken to in an improper manner, did not welcome his brother's words, and spoke these words:
I do not welcome this errand, O king — do not do this; I fear the destruction of our clan. When sons are divided, strife for you would certainly follow — this is my apprehension arising from this gambling, O lord of men.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: No strife here shall distress me, O Kṣattā, if fate does not run contrary — for it is said that this entire world moves under the control of fate, in the power of what is destined, and is not independent.
Therefore, Vidura, go today and by my command quickly bring back the invincible Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, the king.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Vidura, compelled by force by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, set out with noble horses — swift, strong, and well-trained — toward the abode of the wise Pāṇḍavas.
Having swiftly traversed that road and reached the city of the king, the great-minded Vidura entered, honored by the twice-born.
