Reaching the royal palace, which resembled the mansion of Kubera, that righteous-souled one approached Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma.
The king of firm truth, the great-souled Ajātaśatru, received Vidura with due honor as was proper, and then inquired after Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his sons.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: It is evident that your mind is not joyful — have you come in good health, O Kṣattā? Are the sons of the aged king compliant and obedient to him? And are the subjects also submissive?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vidura said: The great-souled king is well and is with his sons; he dwells surrounded by kinsmen like Indra, O king — pleased with his dutiful sons, free from sorrow, self-content, and firm of spirit.
But the king of the Kurus, after first asking after your well-being and imperishable health, has said this to you: This hall, which rivals your own assembly hall in splendor — come and see it with your brothers, my son.
Coming together with your brothers, O Pārtha, let a friendly gambling match take place in it for enjoyment — we rejoice in your company, and all the Kauravas too have assembled.
The gamblers who have been arranged there by the great-souled King Dhṛtarāṣṭra — you shall see them seated; thus have I come, O king — be pleased with this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In gambling, O Kṣattā, there is strife for us — what thoughtful man would relish gambling? What do you yourself consider appropriate? We all abide by your word.
Vidura said: I know that gambling is the root of disaster, and I made every effort to prevent it; yet the king has sent me to your presence — having heard this, O learned one, do here what is for the good.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who are the other gamblers there who will be playing, besides the sons of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra? I ask you, Vidura — tell us about them, the ones with whom we would gamble, assembled in their hundreds.
Vidura said: Śakuni, king of Gāndhāra, O lord of the people — an expert gambler, skilled of hand and knowing the dice; Viviṃśati, king Citrasena, Satyavrata, Purumitra, and Jaya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Terrible and fearsome gamblers are assembled there — cheaters who play with deceit are present; yet it is said that this world is under the control of fate and what is destined — I shall not refuse to gamble with those gamesters today.
I do not wish to go for the gambling at King Dhṛtarāṣṭra's command, O wise one — yet the father is always dear to the son; so I shall do as you have told me, O Vidura.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I do not willingly wish to gamble with Śakuni; but if the bold one challenges me in the assembly hall, when challenged I never turn back — that is the eternal vow I have taken.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to Vidura, the king of dharma quickly gave all orders for the journey, and set out the next day with his retinue and attendants, together with the women headed by Draupadī.
Fate steals away wisdom and splendor like a sudden blow to the eye; and a man goes under the control of the creator, bound as if by cords.
Having spoken thus, king Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Pṛthā, the subduer of foes, departed together with Kṣattā, unable to disregard that summons.
The son of Pṛthā, the Pāṇḍava, slayer of enemy heroes, mounted the chariot given by Bāhlika and journeyed in disguise together with his brothers.
Blazing with royal splendor, he went forth preceded by Brahmins, summoned by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and by the appointed hour of fate.
Going to Hāstinapura, the righteous-souled Pāṇḍava proceeded to Dhṛtarāṣṭra's palace and met with Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The mighty one also met in due order with Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa.
The mighty-armed and valiant one also met with Somadatta, Duryodhana, Śalya, and the son of Subala.
And with the other kings who had gathered there before, as well as with Jayadratha, and with all the Kauravas in full.
Then the mighty-armed one, surrounded by all his brothers, entered the palace of the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
There he saw the queen Gāndhārī, devoted to her husband, surrounded by her daughters-in-law, ever like Rohiṇī surrounded by stars.
Paying homage to Gāndhārī and welcomed by her in return, he then saw the aged father, the lord whose eyes were wisdom itself.
By the king were sniffed on their heads — those four Pāṇḍavas, O king, the joys of the Kauravas, led by Bhīmasena.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then great joy arose among the Kauravas, O lord of the people, upon seeing those tiger-men among men, the Pāṇḍavas, beautiful to behold.
Having received permission, they entered their gem-filled quarters; and the women headed by Draupadī came and saw them as they arrived.
Seeing the supreme prosperity of Yājñasenī, blazing as it were, those daughters-in-law of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were not particularly pleased in their hearts.
Then those tiger-men among men, having gone and conversed with the women, performed their exercises and other duties as was their custom.
Then, having completed their daily rites, all anointed with divine sandalwood, their minds set on auspiciousness, they invoked blessings from the brahmins.
Having eaten delightful food, they then retired to their apartments; the sons of Kuru slept, serenaded by women singing.
That auspicious night passed for them as they reveled in pleasure; praised by bards, they rested, and in due time abandoned sleep.
Having spent that night in comfort, at dawn all completed their morning rites and entered the beautiful assembly hall, thronged with gamblers.
Śakuni said: O king, the hall is spread and ready; these men have appointed the time for play. Having cast the dice, let the moment of gambling be now, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Gambling through trickery is sinful; there is no warrior's valor in it, nor is there any firm statecraft, O king. Why then do you praise dicing?
They do not praise the honor of a gambler who wins through trickery. O Śakuni, do not defeat us by crooked means, like a cruel wretch.
Śakuni said: One who is versed in the science of trickery, who is tireless in the movements of dice, the great-minded gambler who knows the game — he endures all its procedures.
Such a master of dice will overcome our opponents; that is the moment for this, as you yourself say. O prince, let us gamble — have no fear; set your stake and do not delay.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Thus spoke the foremost of sages, the sage Asita Devala — that one who always moves through these gates of the world:
"This gambling with trickery among gamblers is sinful; but victory in battle by righteousness — that is the best and proper contest."
Warriors do not stoop to barbarous speech or deceit; straightforward and guileless combat — this is the vow of noble men.
To the best of our ability we strive to honor brahmins worthy of reverence and to learn from them — that is true wealth, O goddess of fortune. Do not defeat us further, O Śakuni.
I do not desire pleasures or wealth through deceit; even for a gambler, conduct without trickery is what is not honored — yet I will not adopt it.
Śakuni said: A learned man approaches an unlearned man, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and a wise man approaches a fool — people do not call that trickery.
If you consider me approaching you here to be trickery, then turn away from gambling, if you have any fear.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When summoned, I will not turn back — this is the vow I have undertaken; and fate is powerful, O king. I stand under the control of destiny.
In this assembly, with whom shall I gamble, and who else is there to counter-stake? Then let the gambling commence.
Duryodhana said: I shall be the provider of gems and wealth, O lord of men; and on my behalf this Śakuni, my maternal uncle, shall play.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For one person to gamble on behalf of another seems unfair to me. O learned one, accept this understanding — so let it proceed accordingly.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the gambling was about to begin, all those kings, placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at their head, then entered that assembly hall.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the great-minded Vidura followed, their hearts not entirely at ease, O Bhārata.
Those lion-necked, mighty-spirited ones took their places, each separately and in pairs, upon the many splendid and variegated lion-thrones.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That assembly hall shone beautifully, O king, with those kings assembled — like heaven resplendent with the greatly blessed gods gathered together.
All were knowers of the Vedas, all were heroes, all of brilliant form. Then, O great king, the gambling among friends commenced.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This gem, O king, born from the whirlpools of the ocean, excelling a necklace, splendid and adorned with the finest gold, is of great worth.
This, O king, is my stake — now what is your counter-stake? Let this be the order, my friend; I will win this wager.
Duryodhana said: I have gems and various riches too, and I have no greed for wealth. I will win this wager.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Śakuni, who knew the truth of dice, took those dice; and Śakuni spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won!"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Though I have been defeated by your dice-trick, O Śakuni, come — let us gamble, staking thousands.
These hundred jars each filled with a thousand niṣkas, a treasury of inexhaustible gold, refined gold in many forms — this, O king, is my wealth; with this I gamble against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, Śakuni said to that king: "Won!"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This tiger-chariot, worth a thousand, excellently fitted out, furnished with fine wheels, splendid, adorned with a network of bells —
— this royal chariot that brought us here, resounding like thunder, the best of victorious chariots, sacred, its roar like that of clouds and ocean —
— eight osprey-hued horses, acclaimed by the realm, draw it; not one of them can be said to touch the ground with its foot. This, O king, is my wealth; with this I gamble against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this, resolute and resorting to trickery, Śakuni said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won!"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have a thousand elephants, in rut, standing ready, O son of Subala — with golden girths, adorned with ornaments, bearing lotus-marks, garlanded with gold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Well-trained, fit to bear kings, able to endure all sounds in battle, with tusk-like teeth, of great body, each standing eight cubits tall.
All of them breakers of city-gates, those elephants resembling mountain-clouds — this, O king, is my wealth; with this I gamble against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: To that Pārtha speaking thus, the son of Subala, as if laughing, said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won!"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have a hundred thousand maidservants, young and auspicious, wearing conch-shell bracelets and armlets, adorned with gold necklaces, well-ornamented.
Wearing precious garlands and ornaments, clothed in fine garments, anointed with sandalwood, bearing gems and gold — all clad in fine silken robes.
These women skilled in dance and song perform services at my command for learned scholars, ministers, and kings. This, O king, is my wealth; with this I gamble against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this, resolute and resorting to trickery, Śakuni said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won!"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have that many thousands of male servants too — devoted and agreeable, always clothed in fine cloaks.
Wise, intelligent, skilled, young, wearing polished earrings, holding serving-vessels in hand, they feed guests day and night. This, O king, is my wealth; with this I gamble against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this, resolute and resorting to trickery, Śakuni said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won!"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have that many chariots too — fitted with golden equipment, bearing banners, furnished with trained horses and skilled chariot-fighters of varied combat.
Each of these receives wages of at most a thousand, whether in battle or not, paid monthly. This, O king, is my wealth; with this I gamble against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Pārtha had spoken thus, that evil-spirited one who had created enmity said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The horses, spotted like partridges, of Gandharva breed, garlanded with gold, which Citraratha, delighted, gave to the bearer of the Gāṇḍīva bow — this, O king, is my wealth; with this I gamble against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this, resolute and resorting to trickery, Śakuni said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won!"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have ten thousand chariots, carts, and horses, kept in readiness, surrounded by draft animals of various kinds.
Gathered by caste from each caste in their thousands, they stand drinking milk and eating rice of the finest grain.
Sixty thousand of them, all broad-chested — this, O king, is my wealth; with this I gamble against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this, resolute and resorting to trickery, Śakuni said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won!"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have four hundred treasure-chests encased in copper and iron, each containing five droṇas of unworked gold. This, O king, is my wealth; with this I gamble against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this, resolute and resorting to trickery, Śakuni said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won!"
Vidura said: O great king, understand and hear what I shall tell you — though it may not please you when heard, like medicine to a dying man.
When he was just born, that evil-minded Duryodhana, destroyer of the Bhārata line, howled like a jackal with a discordant cry — this same one is fated to be the instrument of death.
You keep a jackal dwelling in your house, yet you do not realize it under Duryodhana's form. Listen to my wise counsel.
A honey-seeker, having obtained honey, does not perceive the precipice; climbing upon it, he either sinks or meets his fall.
This Duryodhana, intoxicated with gambling as with honey, does not examine the precipice; he does not at all perceive the enmity he is creating with the great warriors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You know it, O great king — it is improper even among kings: the Andhakas, Yādavas, and Bhojas, gathered together, abandoned Kaṃsa.
And when he was slain by Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemies, at the bidding of all, then all your kinsmen rejoiced for a hundred years.
Let Savyasācī, commissioned by you, restrain Suyodhana; by restraining this wicked one, let the Kurus rejoice in happiness.
Would you exchange these Pāṇḍavas — peacocks — for a crow or a jackal, O king? Do not sink into an ocean of grief.
For the sake of the family one should abandon an individual; for the sake of the village, abandon the family; for the sake of the kingdom, abandon the village; for the sake of the self, abandon the earth.
"Omniscient, knowing all conditions, terrifying to all enemies" — thus spoke Uśanas Kāvya when Indra was to be abandoned for the great demons.
O king, a certain man who kept forest-roaming birds that voided gold in his house oppressed them out of greed.
Blinded by greed for gold, he destroyed what was perpetually to be enjoyed, O scorcher of foes — both future profit and present gain he destroyed at once.
Greedy for present gain, do not harm the Pāṇḍavas, O bull of the Bhāratas; deluded in spirit, you will repent afterward, like the man who killed the birds.
Gather the fruit as it arises from the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata — like a gardener in a garden, showing affection again and again.
Do not burn them down to the roots like a charcoal-maker burning trees; do not go with your sons, ministers, and army toward ruin.
For who could fight the Pārthas assembled together, O Bhārata? Not even Indra himself, O king, accompanied by the Maruts.
Vidura said: Gambling is the root of strife that follows — leading to great mutual division or to war. Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, who has set himself on this course, Duryodhana creates fierce enmity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The descendants of Prātīpa, the sons of Śaṃtanu, the sons of Bhīmasena, and those with Bāhlika — all shall encounter grave peril because of Duryodhana's offense.
Duryodhana, through sheer arrogance, pushes away the welfare of the kingdom; like a bull in rut he forcibly breaks off his own horn.
One who, O king, follows another's mind — a hero and a sage — overstepping his own sight, would board a ship steered by a child on the ocean, and in terrible disaster would drown.
Duryodhana gambles against the Pāṇḍava; you are pleased when he wins — yet from excessive jest arises violent conflict, from which destruction comes upon men.
Your dice-throw is ill-led and yields downward fruit; the counsel deep-seated in your heart is firm resolve. May the agreement with Yudhiṣṭhira prove fruitful; well-spoken is the conciliation of the enemy-tamer, the skilled archer Sudhanvan.
O king, you descendants of Pratīpa and of Śaṃtanu, hear this counsel-laden speech — do not let it pass you by. The blazing, terrible fire of Vaiśvānara has flared up; quench this rising flame without resort to battle.
When Yudhiṣṭhira, Ajātaśatru among the Pāṇḍavas, overwhelmed by intolerable provocation, can no longer restrain his wrath — and when Vṛkodara, Savyasācī, and the twin sons of Mādrī are unleashed — what refuge will there then be for you in that tumult?
O great king, you are master of all wealth; before this gambling began you could take in your mind as much as you desired. Even if you were to win great riches by defeating the Pāṇḍavas in dice, what good would that wealth be? Find your treasure in the sons of Pṛthā instead.
We know well the gambling of Subala's son; the mountain-born one understands the deceit of the dice. Let Śakuni return to the land from which he came — that fighter with illusion, that hill-man, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Duryodhana said: You boast only of the glory of others; ever concealed, you revile the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. We know you, Vidura, and to whom your heart belongs — you despise us as if we were children.
A man whose affections lie elsewhere is easily known, for he directs his censure and his praise accordingly. Your tongue, Vidura, betrays your heart and lays it bare; it declares plainly the mind's own opposition.
You have been raised in our lap like a serpent; like a cat you harm the very one who nourishes you. They say there is no greater sin than the betrayal of one's master — so why, O Kṣattā, do you not fear that sin?
We have conquered our enemies and obtained a great prize — do not, O Kṣattā, speak harsh words to us here. You rejoice in association with our foes and through bewilderment you turn again and again toward enmity with us.
A man who speaks what is intolerable creates enmity for himself; he hides his secrets while praising enemies. Does not the shame of the refuge you have taken weigh upon you? Today you speak here whatever you desire.
Do not insult us — we know the mind that is in you. Go and learn wisdom from the assembly of elders. Guard the reputation of this house, O Vidura, as it has been upheld — do not busy yourself in the affairs of others.
Do not insult us with "I am the one who acts", O Vidura; do not speak harsh words to us constantly here. I do not ask you, Vidura, for what is beneficial to me. Farewell, O Kṣattā — do not go on tormenting those who endure in patience.
There is one ordainer; there is no second ordainer. That ordainer directs a man even as he lies in the womb. Instructed by that one, I flow as water follows a downward slope — I carry forward exactly as I have been appointed.
He who shatters a mountain with his head and feeds a serpent — that same power alone governs the ordering of his actions.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One who imposes his counsel by force here becomes an enemy by that very act; but a wise man should overlook compliant, submissive conduct.
He who has kindled a blazing fire and does not run quickly toward it in time — even ashes he will not find remaining anywhere, O Bhārata.
One should not harbor in one's house an enemy, especially an ill-wishing person, O Kṣattā. Go wherever you wish, Vidura — for even a faithless woman, however well appeased, will in the end abandon her lord.
Vidura said: Those who abandon a man for so little — declare their friendship to be of short duration, O king. For the minds of kings are turbulent; they give gentle words and then strike with clubs.
You consider yourself not a child, O prince; and I too regard myself as no child, O you of very dull understanding. He who first establishes a man in friendship and afterwards defames him — that one is the true child.
A dull-witted man is not led toward the good — like a corrupt woman in the house of a learned brahmin. He will surely not please the bull of the Bhāratas — as a husband of sixty years cannot please a young maiden.
If you desire only pleasant words in all matters, both beneficial and harmful, then, O king, ask women and the dull and the lame and fools of that sort.
Indeed, O descendant of Pratīpa, a man who speaks only pleasant words is easily found in this world; but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet wholesome, and one who listens to such counsel, is rare.
But he who, resting on righteousness and setting aside alike what pleases and displeases his lord, speaks what is unpleasant yet salutary — by that one a king is truly assisted.
What the good must drink but the wicked will not — that which is bitter though not born of disease, sharp, burning, robbing one of glory, harsh, and ill-smelling — drink down your wrath, O great king, and be pacified.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I wish always for the glory and the wealth of Vicitravīrya's line, together with his sons. May it be so for you in whatever way it shall be; and my reverence too is yours. May the brahmins also grant well-being to me.
A wise man should not provoke those who carry venom in their fangs, or those who carry venom in their gaze. This is what I tell you now with care, O joy of the Kuru race.
Śakuni said: You have lost much wealth of the Pāṇḍavas, Yudhiṣṭhira. Declare what wealth remains, O son of Kuntī, if any you possess that is not yet lost.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: My wealth is beyond counting, as I myself know, O son of Subala. But why do you ask about wealth, O Śakuni?
Ten thousand, a million, a kharva, a padma, an arbuda, a shankha, a nikharva, and a samudra — let these be set as stake. This is my wealth, O king; with it I play against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, Śakuni, resolved and resorting to his deceit, said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: My cattle and horses, my countless cows and milch-animals, my sheep and goats, and whatever belongs to the peoples of all varnas this side of the Sindhu, O son of Subala — this is my wealth, O king; with it I play against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, Śakuni, resolved and resorting to his deceit, said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The city, the realm, the land, together with the wealth of those who are not brahmins, and all persons of non-brahmin birth — O king, this is the remaining wealth that is mine. With this, O king, I play against you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, Śakuni, resolved and resorting to his deceit, said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: These princes, O king, shine with their adornments — their earrings and gold necklaces and all their bodily ornaments. This is my wealth, O king; with it I play against you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, Śakuni, resolved and resorting to his deceit, said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Dark, young, with reddish eyes, lion-shouldered, great-armed — Nakula is my one stake, along with whatever wealth of mine belongs to him personally.
Śakuni said: Nakula is dear to you, O king, O prince Yudhiṣṭhira — he has now become our property. What now will you stake next?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Śakuni took those dice in hand; and said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This Sahadeva who instructs in dharma and has attained the name of wise man in this world — though he does not deserve to be staked — with that beloved prince I play against you, even though it is against my will.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, Śakuni, resolved and resorting to his deceit, said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won."
Śakuni said: These two sons of Mādrī, O king, are dear to you — both have been won by me. But I think the weightier stakes are Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You surely walk the path of unrighteousness, you who take no heed of right conduct — you who desire, O fool, to sow division among us who are of one mind.
Śakuni said: One who is intoxicated falls into a pit; one who is heedless stumbles into a post. You are the eldest, O king, the most venerable — my salutation to you, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Gamblers do not see those things in dream or waking, O Yudhiṣṭhira, of which they babble wildly while playing their dice — raving like the intoxicated.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: He who leads us in battle like a boat to the farther shore — that swift royal prince, conqueror of enemies — though he does not deserve to be staked, with that hero of the world, with Phalguna, I play against you, O Śakuni.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, Śakuni, resolved and resorting to his deceit, said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śakuni said: This bowman of the Pāṇḍavas — Savyasācī the Pāṇḍava — has been defeated by me. Now stake your beloved Bhīma, O king; stake whatever remains to be staked, O Pāṇḍava.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: He who is our leader, who leads us in battle like the Thunderbolt-bearer who is the sole foe of the demons — he of the sidelong glance, with joined eyebrows, great-souled, lion-shouldered, and ever beyond endurance of insult —
— he whose equal in strength no man exists, the foremost among mace-wielders here, the crusher of enemies — though he does not deserve to be staked, with that royal prince Bhīmasena I play against you, O king.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, Śakuni, resolved and resorting to his deceit, said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won."
Śakuni said: You have lost great wealth, and your brothers along with their elephants. Declare what wealth remains, O son of Kuntī, if any you possess that is not yet lost.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I am the foremost of all my brothers and equally their beloved. Now that my brothers are lost and our own calamity has fallen upon me, I stake myself.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, Śakuni, resolved and resorting to his deceit, said to Yudhiṣṭhira: "Won."
Śakuni said: This was the most sinful act you have done — staking yourself when you had already lost your brothers and while wealth still remained. O king, the staking of oneself is indeed sin.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the shrewd dice-player, by his casting, defeated separately, one by one, those world-heroes who stood as stakes in the game.
Śakuni said: There is indeed your beloved queen — one stake not yet lost. Stake Kṛṣṇā, the Pāñcālī princess; with her win yourself back.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: She is neither too short nor too tall, neither too dark nor too fair, with eyes tinged with passionate red — with her I play against you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Her eyes are like the petals of the autumnal lotus; her fragrance is that of the autumnal lotus; she is attended upon like the autumnal lotus; in beauty she is equal to Śrī herself.
And further she has compassion, beauty of form, and excellence of character — all the qualities for which a man could desire a woman.
She who retires last and wakes first, who knows everything done and undone, from the cowherds to the shepherds — that woman I stake.
Her face shines like a lotus even when lightly perspiring, and like jasmine. Her waist is slender as an altar, her hair long, her eyes copper-red, and her body not overly covered with hair.
With her, thus endowed, O king — with the Pāñcālī Draupadī, she of the beautiful slender waist and lovely limbs — I play the dice, O Subala's son.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the king of dharma spoke these words, O Bhārata, the voices of the elder assembly members burst forth with cries of "Shame! Shame!"
That assembly was convulsed, O king; conversations broke out among the kings, and sweat broke out upon Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others.
Vidura clasped his head and became as if bereft of his senses; he sat absorbed in thought, his face cast downward, sighing like a serpent.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, filled with delight, asked again and again: "What is won? What is won?" — he could not conceal the expression on his face.
Karṇa rejoiced exceedingly along with Duḥśāsana and the others; from the eyes of the remaining assembly members tears fell down.
But the son of Subala, without deliberating, exultant in victory, arrogant with elation, took up those dice once more with the cry: "Won!"
Duryodhana said: Come, O Kṣattā — bring Draupadī here, the beloved wife honoured by the Pāṇḍavas. Let her quickly come to sweep out the household; let there be joy for us together with our maidservants.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vidura said: What is about to happen is hard to conceive by one like you, O fool — you do not understand, bound as you are in the noose of fate, hanging over the precipice. Like a deer you are provoking tigers out of sheer childishness.
Deadly serpents, their poison sacs full, swollen with great venom, rest upon your head. Do not provoke them, O extremely foolish one — do not walk toward the realm of Yama.
Kṛṣṇā does not become a slave in this manner, O Bhārata — for it is my judgment that this queen was staked as a wager by a king who was no longer his own master.
This king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, bears fruit like a bamboo that destroys itself by its own fruiting. For dice lead to enmity and great terror; ripe as he is, this man does not understand — at the hour of his end.
One should not be sharp-tongued or speak cruelly; one should not raise oneself above another by belittling them. That stinging speech by which another is made to shudder — one should not speak that burning, sin-destining word.
Harsh and excessive words pour out from the mouth; struck by these, another grieves for days and nights. They do not fall upon the vital points of another — yet a wise man would not release such words upon others.
A goat once dug up a weapon for its own use; when the weapon failed, it cast aside the ground with its hooves — that ghastly cutter of its own throat. In like manner, do not dig up enmity with the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Dogs always bark at those who are praiseworthy — whether the forest-dweller, or the householder, or the ascetic, or the one replete with knowledge — they bark at them as evil.
You do not perceive the terrible, crooked gateway to hell, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Many of the Kurus will follow you down — together with Duḥśāsana — when this gambling-game reaches its outcome.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Gourds sink while stones float; boats are constantly bewildered upon the water — the foolish king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, does not listen to my words that are wholesome and true.
Surely the end of the Kurus is at hand — a terrible, all-consuming destruction. The wholesome words of wise friends go unheard; only greed grows.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Crying "Shame on Kṣattṛ!" and intoxicated with arrogance, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked toward the Pratikamin in the assembly and spoke to him in the midst of the great nobles.
"You, Pratikamin, go and fetch Draupadī. You need have no fear of the Pāṇḍavas. This Kṣattṛ is a coward who only argues; he has never truly wished for our welfare."
Thus commanded, that charioteer Pratikamin, hearing the king's word, went quickly and entered the lion's den as a dog might, and approached the queen of the Pāṇḍavas.
The Pratikamin said: "O Draupadī, Yudhiṣṭhira was maddened by the dice-game, and Duryodhana has won you. Therefore enter the house of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — I am taking you there to your duties, O daughter of Yajñasena."
Draupadī said: "How do you say such a thing, Pratikamin? What prince would wager his wife at dice? Is the king truly so foolish and maddened by the game, or was there no other stake he could find?"
The Pratikamin said: "When there was no other stake for him, then Yudhiṣṭhira the Pāṇḍava — the one who has no enemies — wagered. First he staked his brothers, then himself, and finally you, O princess."
Draupadī said: "Go, son of a charioteer — go to the gambler in the assembly and ask him this: O Bhārata, did you lose yourself first, or me? Having learned the answer, come back and then take me, O son of a charioteer."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Going to the assembly, he conveyed Draupadī's words: "Draupadī asks you — who is the master of whom did you lose first? Did you first lose yourself, or me?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Yudhiṣṭhira sat motionless, as if bereft of life. He gave the charioteer no reply — neither good nor ill.
Duryodhana said: "Let Kṛṣṇā the Pāñcālī come here herself and put her question here — let everyone hear her words and his answer."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: He who followed Duryodhana's will went to the royal quarters and, as if pained, the charioteer Pratikamin spoke to Draupadī.
"The men of the assembly summon you, O princess. I believe the destruction of the Kauravas is at hand — for no lesser deed preserves prosperity, that you must now enter the assembly, O princess."
Draupadī said: "Thus surely has the Creator ordained — that both the wise and the foolish are touched by touch alike. But there is one supreme dharma proclaimed in this world; if cherished, it will bring us peace."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Yudhiṣṭhira, hearing what Duryodhana intended, sent a messenger approved by Draupadī, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Clad in a single garment, her lower robe loose, weeping and in her monthly course, the Pāñcālī came to the assembly and stood before her father-in-law.
Then, looking at their faces, King Duryodhana, filled with joy, said to the charioteer: "Bring her here, Pratikamin — let the Kurus speak openly before her."
Then the charioteer, who followed his master's will but feared the wrath of the daughter of Drupada, setting aside his pride, turned to the assembly members again and said: "What shall I tell Kṛṣṇā?"
Duryodhana said: "Duḥśāsana, this charioteer's son of mine is faint-hearted, afraid of Vṛkodara. Yourself take the daughter of Yajñasena and bring her. What can her helpless enemies do to you?"
Then that prince arose, his eyes red with rage at his brother's words, entered the dwelling of the great warriors, and spoke thus to the princess Draupadī.
"Come, come, Pāñcālī, O Kṛṣṇā — you have been won! Look upon Duryodhana, O lotus-eyed one, cast off your shame and join the Kurus. You have been lawfully won; go to the assembly."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then she arose, deeply distressed, wiped her pale face with her hand, and in her affliction ran toward where the women were — the quarters of the aged king, bull of the Kurus.
Then Duḥśāsana rushed after her in fury, roaring at her, and seized the wife of the king of kings by her long, dark, wavy hair.
Those tresses which had been drenched with the sacred waters of the Rājasūya concluding bath, at that great ceremony purified by mantras — those were now seized by force by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who had overcome the valor of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having seized her, Duḥśāsana dragged Kṛṣṇā of the very dark tresses toward the assembly — dragging her who had protectors as though she had none, as the wind drags a plantain tree in distress.
As she was being dragged, her body bent, she said softly: "Today I am in my monthly course. I have but one garment, O dull-witted one; you should not take me to the assembly, O ignoble man."
Then, forcibly seizing her by her dark hair, he said to Kṛṣṇā: "Cry out for protection to Kṛṣṇa, to Jiṣṇu, to Hari, to Nara — I am taking you regardless."
"Whether you are in your monthly course, O Yājñasenī, whether you wear one garment or none — you have been won at dice; you are made a slave. Among the slave women you shall serve according to desire."
With her hair disheveled, her half-garment fallen, being shaken about by Duḥśāsana, burning with shame and indignation, Kṛṣṇā softly spoke these words.
"These men in the assembly are learned in scripture, all of them active and equal to Indra; all are elders, worthy of veneration as gurus. Before them I cannot bear to stand in this state."
"O doer of cruel deeds, you of ignoble conduct — do not strip me bare, do not drag me! Your royal enemies would not endure this — not even if all the gods with Indra were your allies."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The king who is the son of Dharma stands firm in righteousness. And dharma is subtle, discerned only by the wise. I do not wish to cause even an atom of fault to my husband, abandoning my own virtues even in word."
"But this is ignoble — that you drag me, in my monthly course, in the midst of Kuru heroes, and none here does me honor. Surely all these have followed your thinking."
"Shame! The dharma of the Bhāratas is truly lost, and so too the conduct of those who know the warrior code — for the Kurus all sit in the assembly and watch as the bounds of Kuru righteousness are transgressed."
"There is no firmness in Droṇa, nor in Bhīṣma, nor surely in that great-souled king either — for the foremost elders of the Kurus do not mark this terrible adharma."
As she spoke thus pitifully, the slender-waisted one glanced sideways and saw her husbands overcome with rage — the Pāṇḍavas with bodies consumed by anger — and inflamed them further with the glances of her eyes.
The pain caused by the loss of their kingdom, their wealth, and their finest jewels was not as great as the pain caused by Kṛṣṇā's sidelong glance charged with anguish and fury.
And Duḥśāsana, seeing Kṛṣṇā look piteously at those wretched husbands, shook her violently as if to render her unconscious, and said with a cruel laugh: "A slave woman!"
Karṇa was exceedingly delighted at that word and applauded it with a loud laugh. The king of Gāndhāra, son of Subala, likewise praised Duḥśāsana.
But all the other members of the assembly who were there — excepting those two and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — felt extreme sorrow upon seeing Kṛṣṇā being dragged about in the assembly.
Bhīṣma said: "O fortunate one, I am not able to answer your question properly on account of the subtlety of dharma. One who owns nothing cannot stake another's property — and women are subject to their husband's authority."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Yudhiṣṭhira would abandon the entire prosperous earth, but he would not abandon truth. And the Pāṇḍava has declared 'I am defeated' — therefore I cannot resolve this matter."
"Śakuni is unequalled among men at dice; invited by him, the son of Kuntī freely submitted to his desire. That great soul does not regard it as deception — therefore I cannot answer your question."
Draupadī said: "The king was summoned to the assembly by those skilled in trickery — by evil-souled, deceitful, ignoble gamblers — with no great effort on their part. How then is he said to have freely submitted his will?"
"He who is the foremost of the Kuru Pāṇḍavas — pure of heart, not perceiving the deceitful conduct — was overcome by all of them together, and it was only afterward that he accepted the terms of the gambling."
"These Kurus stand in the assembly — masters of sons and daughters-in-law alike. Let them all weigh my words as well. Answer my question truthfully, O kings."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As she spoke thus piteously and wept, repeatedly glancing at those husbands, Duḥśāsana spoke harsh, unpleasant, and bitter words to her.
Seeing her being dragged, in her monthly course, her upper garment slipping, trembling — and seeing Yudhiṣṭhira — Vṛkodara, his form the very image of extreme anguish, gave vent to his rage.
Bhīma said: "Gamblers keep women of ill repute in their homes, O Yudhiṣṭhira — they do not even wager those, and even for those women there is compassion."
"The tribute that the king of Kāśi brought, the other finest goods, and whatever jewels the other kings of the earth had offered —"
"— our vehicles, our wealth, our armor and weapons, our kingdom, our very selves and we ourselves — all were taken from us by the deceit of our enemies."
"And I felt no anger in all of that, for you are the master of all that is ours. But I consider this to be going too far — that Draupadī was staked."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This innocent girl, who did not deserve this fate, having come to the Pāṇḍavas, is now being tormented on your account by these petty, cruel, and deceit-loving Kauravas."
"This wrath is brought down upon you for her sake, O king. I will burn your arms to ashes — Sahadeva, bring fire!"
Arjuna said: "You have never before, O Bhīmasena, spoken such words. Surely the respect for dharma in you has been destroyed by these cruel enemies."
"Our enemies must not be made to rejoice. Practice only the highest dharma. One should not transgress the eldest brother who is righteous."
"The king, summoned by enemies, plays at dice keeping in mind the warrior's dharma, submitting to another's will — this is greatly glorious for us."
Bhīmasena said: "Had I known this was being done to me, O Dhanañjaya, I would have burned both his arms in a blazing fire, as if by force."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Seeing the Pāṇḍavas in such distress, and the Pāñcālī being tormented, Vikarṇa, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, spoke these words.
"Answer the words spoken by the daughter of Yajñasena, O kings. By not discerning the truth of her words, we will immediately fall into hell."
"Both Bhīṣma and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the two eldest of the Kurus, have said nothing after coming together here, nor has the great-minded Vidura."
"And the son of Bharadvaja, who is the preceptor of all, and Kṛpa — even these two foremost of the twice-born have not answered the question."
"But those other kings of the earth who have assembled here from all directions — setting aside desire and anger, let them speak according to their understanding."
"This word that auspicious Draupadī has repeatedly uttered — reflecting carefully, whose side is which? O kings, speak your reply."
Thus he repeatedly addressed all the members of the assembly, yet those kings of the earth said nothing to him — neither good nor ill.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having thus repeatedly addressed all the kings, Vikarṇa rubbed one palm against the other, and sighing, spoke these words.
"Speak, O kings, or speak not at all. What I consider to be just here, that I shall proclaim, O Kauravas."
"The foremost men declare four vices of kings: hunting, drinking, gambling, and excessive attachment to sensual pleasures."
"A man addicted to these lives having abandoned dharma, and the world does not regard an act done by one thus afflicted as valid."
"This son of Pāṇḍu, deeply caught in vice, summoned by gamblers, staked Draupadī as a wager."
"Moreover, she is the common wife of all the Pāṇḍavas, the irreproachable one. And the stake was made by this Pāṇḍava after he had already been won himself."
"And this Kṛṣṇā was named as a stake by Subala's son who desired to win. Considering all of this, I believe she has not been won."
Hearing this, a great roar arose from the members of the assembly — some praising Vikarṇa and condemning the son of Subala.
When that noise subsided, the son of Rādhā, nearly fainting with rage, lifted his beautiful arm and spoke these words.
"Many perversities are indeed visible in Vikarṇa. The fire born of the fire-sticks leads to the destruction of those very sticks — so too with him."
"All these have said nothing even when urged by Kṛṣṇā herself. I consider the daughter of Drupada to have been won by dharma — they too think so."
"But you, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are bursting with sheer childishness — speaking in the assembly like a child trying to sound like an elder."
"And you do not know dharma as it truly is, O lesser one to Duryodhana — you of very dull wit who proclaims the won Kṛṣṇā to be unwon."
"How can you consider Kṛṣṇā to be unwon, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, when the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas staked his entire self in the assembly?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And Draupadī is included within 'all that he possesses,' O bull of the Bhāratas. How then do you consider Kṛṣṇā, won by dharma, to be unwon?"
Draupadī has been named aloud and released by the Pāṇḍavas themselves — on what ground then do you hold that she is not conquered?
Or do you think that bringing her into this assembly in a single garment was an act of unrighteousness? Hear my further word on that point as well.
The gods have ordained that a woman shall have one husband, O delight of the Kurus; but this one is subject to many masters — she is therefore rightly judged a harlot.
In my opinion it is no wonder that she has been brought into the hall, nor that she is clad in a single garment, nor even that she should be stripped bare.
Whatever wealth belongs to them, and this woman herself, and the Pāṇḍavas — all that property has been lawfully won here by the son of Subala.
Duḥśāsana, this Vikarṇa is but a boy playing the wise man — bring in the garments of the Pāṇḍavas and of Draupadī too.
Hearing that, O Bhārata, all the Pāṇḍavas cast off their upper garments and sat down in the assembly.
Then Duḥśāsana, O king, seized Draupadī's garment by force in the middle of the assembly and began to strip it off.
As Draupadī's garment was being pulled away, O lord of the people, another robe of the same kind appeared, and then another, and yet another, in endless succession.
Then a loud and terrible cry of amazement arose there as all the assembled kings witnessed that most wondrous marvel in the world.
Then Bhīma, in the midst of the kings, with a great roar, his lips quivering with rage and grinding palm against palm, uttered a curse.
"Hear this my vow, all you Kṣatriyas who dwell in this world — a vow never spoken before by any man, nor shall another ever speak it:
If, having spoken thus, I do not carry it out, O lords of the earth, then may I not attain the path of all our forefathers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If in battle I do not split open the chest of this vile, low-born disgrace to the Bhāratas by force and drink his blood —
Hearing those words of his, which thrilled all the world with joy, the assembly gave him great honor while denouncing the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
When a heap of garments had accumulated in the middle of the assembly, Duḥśāsana at last, exhausted and ashamed, sat down.
Then a hair-raising cry of "Shame!" arose among the assembled god-like men as they looked upon the sons of Kuntī.
"The Kurus will not answer this question" — so the people there cried out, denouncing Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then Vidura, knower of all dharma, raised both arms high to silence the assembly and spoke these words:
Vidura said: "Draupadī has posed her question and is crying like one without a protector, yet you assembled members do not answer that question — dharma is being wounded here."
"For one in distress enters an assembly blazing like fire, and it is the duty of the assembled members to pacify that person with truth and with dharma.
"When a person in distress poses a question of dharma to the members of an assembly, those members, who have transcended the sway of desire and anger, should answer that question.
"The question has been answered by Vikarṇa to the best of his wisdom, O kings — let you too answer that question as your minds direct.
"For a man who, though seeing what is right, enters an assembly and does not answer a question, reaps one half of the fruit that accrues from falsehood.
"And he who, though seeing what is right, enters an assembly and gives a false answer — he obtains the entire fruit of untruth: this is certain.
"On this point they cite this ancient tale — the dialogue between Prahlāda and the sage of the Āṅgirasa line.
"There was a lord of the Daityas named Prahlāda; his son was Virocana. For the sake of a maiden Virocana challenged Sudhanvan, the descendant of Āṅgiras.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Each claiming 'I am the superior one, I am the superior one,' both of them, desiring the maiden, staked their very lives in a wager — so we have heard.
"A dispute over this question arose between them, and they both went to Prahlāda and asked him: 'Tell us truly — which of us two is the superior? Answer the question and do not lie.'
"Fearing to pronounce in the dispute, Prahlāda glanced sideways at Sudhanvan. Sudhanvan, enraged and blazing like the rod of Brahmā, spoke to him:
"'If you speak falsely, Prahlāda, or if you refuse to speak at all, the Thunderer will shatter your head into a hundred pieces with his vajra.'
"Thus threatened by Sudhanvan, the Daitya trembled like a leaf of the aśvattha tree and went to the mighty Kaśyapa to inquire further of him.
"Prahlāda said: 'You are the knower of dharma here — of the divine, the demonic, and the brahminical. O greatly wise one, hear this dilemma of dharma.'
"'Tell me, I ask you: what are the other worlds — the afterlife — of one who neither answers a question nor directs it falsely?'
"Kaśyapa said: 'One who knows and yet, out of desire, anger, or fear, does not answer a question, binds upon himself a thousand nooses of Varuṇa.
"'At the end of each full year one noose is released; therefore one who knows the truth must speak the truth plainly and directly.'
"Where dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly and the assembled members, who are themselves wounded by it, do not remove its thorn —
"— the chief man there carries off one half of the sin; one quarter falls upon those who committed the deed; one quarter falls upon the members of the assembly who do not condemn what deserves condemnation.
"But where the one deserving condemnation is duly condemned, the chief man is freed from sin and so are the members of the assembly — the guilt goes entirely to the doer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Those who, when asked about dharma, O Prahlāda, answer falsely — they destroy both the merit of their rituals and charitable works and seven generations of their ancestors and descendants alike.'
"The anguish of one whose wealth has been plundered, the anguish of one whose son has been slain, the anguish of one crushed by debt, and the anguish of one seized by the king —
"— the anguish of a woman bereft of her husband, the anguish of one separated from a caravan, the anguish of one whose marriage has been supplanted, and the anguish of one ruined by witnesses —
"— all these sorrows the lords of the thirty gods declare to be equal to one another; and all those sorrows does one incur who speaks falsely.
"Testimony comes from direct sight, from hearing, and from firm memory. Therefore a witness who speaks the truth suffers no loss in either dharma or worldly welfare.'
Vidura said: "Having heard Kaśyapa's words, Prahlāda said to his son: 'Sudhanvan is superior to you, and Āṅgiras is superior to me.'
"'Sudhanvan's mother too is superior to yours in terms of maternal lineage, Virocana — and this Sudhanvan is the master of your very life.'
Sudhanvan said: "Because you have set aside paternal affection and stood firm in dharma, I grant your son his life — may he live a hundred years."
Vidura said: "Having heard this supreme lesson of dharma, all of you members of the assembly — consider now what is the highest answer to Kṛṣṇā's question."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Having heard Vidura's words, the assembled kings said nothing at all; but Karṇa said to Duḥśāsana: 'Take this slave-woman Kṛṣṇā to the inner apartments.'
"Duḥśāsana dragged that afflicted woman — trembling, red with shame, calling out to the Pāṇḍavas — through the middle of the assembly.
Draupadī said: "The duty I should have performed first has not been done, nor the duty due afterward — I am in anguish, dragged by force by this one who has done such a deed."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I would offer my reverential salutation to these elders assembled here in the Kuru court — let the fault not be mine that this has not been done by me."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Shaken by that dragging and by her grief, the afflicted one — fallen down, undeserving of such treatment — lamented thus in the assembly."
Draupadī said: "I who was seen by the assembled kings at the svayaṃvara arena, and who had never been seen elsewhere — I have today been brought into this assembly."
"I whom neither the wind nor the sun had ever seen before in my own home — I am today being seen in the middle of this assembly, in the Kuru court."
"I whom the Pāṇḍavas formerly would not suffer to be touched even by the wind in my own home — those same Pāṇḍavas today endure this vile-souled man's touching me."
"These Kurus too endure it — I believe it is the turning of time — that their daughter-in-law and daughter is being afflicted, undeserving of such treatment."
"What could be more pitiable than this — that I, a chaste and virtuous woman, am today plunged into the middle of an assembly? Where now is the dharma of these kings?"
"We have heard that virtuous women are not to be brought into an assembly — that primordial and eternal dharma has perished among the Kauravas."
"How could I — wife of the Pāṇḍavas, true sister of Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, and a dear friend of Vāsudeva — come to be brought into this assembly of kings?"
"Declare me — this wife of Dharmarāja, born of equal class — a slave-woman or a free woman: whichever you declare, that I shall accept, O Kauravas."
"For this vile wretch, the destroyer of the Kauravas' glory, is tormenting me grievously — I cannot bear it much longer, O Kauravas."
"Whether you consider me won or not won, O kings — I desire to be answered accordingly, and whatever answer you give, that I shall accept, O Kauravas."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: "I have said before, O auspicious one, that the highest course of dharma cannot be pursued in this world even by wise and great-souled men."
"Yet as a powerful man sees dharma in the world, so that dharma, at the moment of dharma's testing, is declared by those who are his equals or superiors."
"I am not able to adjudicate your question with certainty — because of the subtlety and profundity of the matter, and because of the gravity of this situation."
"Surely the end of this family is not far off — for the Kurus are all given over entirely to greed and delusion."
"Those born in good families, O auspicious one, though assailed by misfortune, do not abandon the paths of dharma — just as you, our daughter-in-law, have steadfastly remained."
"And this conduct of yours is entirely fitting, O Pāñcālī — that even having fallen into this extremity, you look only to dharma."
"These elders — Droṇa and the others — who are knowers of dharma, stand here with bodies drained of life, bowed down as though their breath has already departed."
"In this question it is my view that Yudhiṣṭhira is the authority — it is for him himself to declare whether she was won or not won."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Seeing all of that, the assembled kings, fearful of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, did not speak a word — neither approval nor disapproval — while she wailed like a distressed osprey."
"Seeing those sons and grandsons of kings fallen silent, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra at that moment spoke these words with what seemed like a smile, addressing the daughter of the Pāñcāla king:"
"'Let this question rest with the noble-natured ones — with Bhīma, with Arjuna, with Sahadeva, and likewise with your husband Nakula, O Yājñasenī — let them speak the word that arises from you.'
"'Let them declare in this assembly of the noble that Yudhiṣṭhira has no mastery over you, O Pāñcālī — let them all make Dharmarāja speak falsehood on your account, and Pāñcālī, you shall be freed from the state of bondage.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'Or let the great-souled Dharmarāja, who stands in dharma, like unto Indra himself — let him declare it himself: is he your master or is he not? Speedily choose one answer from his own words.'
"'For all these Kaurava nobles of virtuous character who are gathered in this assembly, being themselves in the midst of suffering on your account, do not speak as they ought — eyeing your husbands of meager fortune.'"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Thereupon all the members of the Kuru king's assembly loudly praised those words; shouting and throwing their upper garments, a cry of 'Ah! Ah!' rose up there, and all the assembled kings were gladdened, honoring that most righteous one of the Kurus."
"And all those kings gazed at Yudhiṣṭhira with faces turned sidelong, thinking: 'What will the knower of dharma now say?'"
"'What will Bībhatsu say? What will Ajita, the unconquered Pāṇḍava in battle, say? What will Bhīmasena say, and the twins?' — so they thought, filled with intense curiosity."
When that noise had subsided, Bhīmasena spoke thus, raising his great round arm smeared with sandalwood paste.
If this Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, our elder, were not the master of this family, we would not endure this.
He is the lord of our virtuous austerities and even our very lives. If he considers himself conquered, then we are conquered.
He who, being subject to the law of mortals, has touched these tresses of the Pāñcālī lady, could not escape alive if he merely touched the earth with my foot.
Behold my two long, round arms like iron bars — even Indra of a hundred sacrifices, caught between them, could not escape.
But bound as I am by the bonds of dharma, I cannot find my way through this crisis, restrained also by respect and by Arjuna's restraint.
Released by the king of dharma, I would crush these sinful sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra like a lion crushing small deer with the flat of my sword.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Vidura all said to him: "Forgive — it is so — all this is possible in you."
Karṇa said: There are indeed three who are propertyless — a slave, a student, and a woman without independence. You, dear lady, are the property of a slave, the wife of a slave; you are low, the wealth of a slave, yourself a slave-woman.
Enter and serve us with your attendance; that is the remaining duty for you — go into the household. We are all your masters now, princess; the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are yours, not the Pārthas.
Choose another husband quickly, O beautiful one, from whom you will not obtain slavery through gambling. Indeed, a blameless woman's freedom among husbands is known in the Vedas — let that be always known to you as slavery now.
Nakula has been defeated, and Bhīmasena, Yudhiṣṭhira, Sahadeva, and Arjuna — enter as a slave-woman, Yājñasenī; your husbands are defeated, they are no more.
And what purpose does the Pārtha think he serves with his own valor and manhood here — he who staked this daughter of Drupada, the Pāñcālī princess, in the assembly's gambling?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that, Bhīmasena, deeply wrathful, sighed heavily, showing a tormented form; following the king, bound by the cords of dharma, he seemed to burn Karṇa with his eyes reddened by anger.
Bhīma said: I do not grow angry at the son of a charioteer, O king — this truth of slave-law has entered. For what could those who hate me do to restrain me today — if only you had not gambled with her, O lord of men.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of Rādheya (Karṇa), King Duryodhana then said this to Yudhiṣṭhira, who had fallen silent and was senseless:
"Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twin brothers are standing under your command, O king. Speak the answer to the question yourself — do you consider Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) to be unconquered?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having said this, he cast aside his own garment and, as if smiling, looked at the Pāñcālī woman, deluded by the intoxication of lordship.
His thigh, resembling the trunk of a banana tree, adorned with all auspicious marks, like the trunk of an elephant, with the weight and solidity of a thunderbolt —
— smiling scornfully at Rādheya and as if challenging Bhīma, he displayed his left thigh to the watching Draupadī.
Vṛkodara (Bhīma), seeing that, widened his eyes until they were bloodshot, and spoke in the midst of the kings, as if making the assembly hear:
"Let Vṛkodara not attain the same world as his fathers if I do not shatter this thigh of yours with my mace in the great battle!"
From all the apertures of that enraged man, flames of fire poured forth, like from the hollows of a burning tree.
Vidura said: See the great fear from Bhīmasena! Understand — it is like the noose of King Varuṇa. Surely this great calamity has arisen before us among the Bhāratas, driven by fate.
O sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, this gambling has gone too far. You who are quarreling over this woman in the assembly — great danger is seen for your welfare and security. The Kurus are taking evil counsel.
Know this dharma quickly, O Kurus! In this evil sight, the assembly would become corrupted. If the gambler had staked her first (before himself), he would have been the lord with an unconquered self.
Just as wealth won in a dream is unreal — I think the same of the winning of one who gambles without being his own master. Having heard the son of Gāndhārī's words, O Kurus, do not stray from this dharma.
Duryodhana said: I stand by Bhīma's words and likewise Arjuna's, and by those of the twins too. If they declare Yudhiṣṭhira to be his own master, then Yājñasenī, you shall be freed from slavery.
Arjuna said: The king was the master in our gambling — the great-souled Dharmarāja, son of Kuntī. But now this master, whose self has been defeated — of whom is he master? Know this, all you Kurus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O king, in King Dhṛtarāṣṭra's house, a jackal cried out loudly at the sacred fire; donkeys brayed in response to it, and fierce birds cried out all around.
That terrible sound was heard by Vidura, the knower of truth, and by Subala's daughter (Gāndhārī), and by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the learned Gautama — and they all cried out "Svasti! Svasti!" (May there be peace!) loudly.
Then Gāndhārī and the wise Vidura, observing that terrible omen, reported it to the king with distress; and then the king spoke these words:
"You are destroyed, Duryodhana, dull-witted one! You who address a woman in the assembly of the Kuru chiefs, O ill-mannered one — and especially Draupadī, the dharma-devoted wife."
Having said this, the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra, seeker of the welfare of his kinsmen, departed; then he spoke with conciliation to Kṛṣṇā the Pāñcālī woman, having considered the matter with his wisdom and true discernment.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Choose a boon from me, Pāñcālī — whatever you desire; for among my daughters-in-law you are foremost, devoted to dharma, a good woman.
Draupadī said: If you grant me a boon, O bull of the Bhāratas, I choose this: let the glorious Yudhiṣṭhira, follower of all dharma, be no slave.
So that children, not knowing him to be a noble soul, may not say of Prativindhya as he comes to them: 'This is the son of a slave.'
Having been a prince before, pampered as no other man anywhere — seeing himself become the son of a slave, he would surely perish, O Bhārata.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: A second boon I give you, dear lady — ask it of me; for my mind is pleased and you deserve more than one boon.
Draupadī said: As a second boon I choose Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya, both with their chariots and bows, and Nakula and Sahadeva.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Choose a third boon from me — you are not honored by just two; for among all my daughters-in-law you are the best, a walker of the path of dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Draupadī said: Greed destroys dharma, my lord; I do not venture to accept an undeserved boon — I am unworthy to take a third boon, O best of kings.
They say a Vaiśya woman merits one boon, a Kṣatriya woman two boons, a king three boons, O king of kings, and for a Brahmin, a hundred boons.
My husbands, having been made sinful, are now rescued; they will know all good things through meritorious deeds, O king.
Karṇa said: Among women honored for their beauty among men — we have never heard of such a deed as this by any of them.
While the Pārthas were seized by anger, and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were too, Draupadī — Kṛṣṇā — became the peace of the sons of Pāṇḍu here.
For the sons of Pāṇḍu sinking in waters without a raft, drowning in the fathomless deep, this Pāñcālī woman became the boat that took them to the other shore.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that, Bhīmasena, deeply wrathful in the midst of the Kurus, said with great anguish: "A woman is the resort of the sons of Pāṇḍu!"
"Three lights of a man," Devala indeed said: "offspring, deeds, and learning — from these the people are created."
"These three of a man are reborn from a body that has become impure, that has lost life, that is empty, abandoned by kinsmen."
"That light of ours has been struck down by the touching of our wives, Dhanañjaya — how indeed could there be offspring born of the defiled?"
Arjuna said: Whether addressed or unaddressed, cruel and base words — the highest men among the Bhāratas never babble such things back; the truly excellent men do so always.
The good, responding rightly and having gained certainty within themselves, remember only the good deeds done to them, never the enmities.
Bhīma said: Right here I will swiftly slay all these enemies gathered together — or, having gone out, cut them down root and all, O king of kings, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What is the use of arguing here? What is the use of suffering, O Bhārata? This very day I will slay them here — command us over this earth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having said this, Bhīmasena, surrounded by his younger brothers, looked repeatedly at his iron bar as a lion among deer.
Being soothed and fanned by Arjuna of untiring action, the mighty-armed hero, powerful in valor, sweated with the inner burning of his rage.
From all the apertures of that enraged man — from his ears and the rest, O lord of men — fire arose with smoke and sparks and flames.
His face, terrible to behold with its knitted brows, became like that of Death personified when the end of a cosmic age has arrived.
Yudhiṣṭhira, restraining that mighty-armed one with his own arm, said to him: "Do not do so" — and "Be still," O Bhārata.
Having restrained that mighty-armed one whose eyes were reddened with anger, he approached his elder Dhṛtarāṣṭra with folded hands.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O king, what shall we do for you? Command us — you are the lord. We always wish to remain under your command, O Bhārata.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: May good fortune be yours, Ajātaśatru — go unharmed, in peace. You are hereby dismissed with your wealth; rule your own kingdom.
But this teaching of mine, an old man, is to be understood: it is spoken with wisdom in full, beneficial, and supremely for your wellbeing.
You know the subtle course of dharmas, dear Yudhiṣṭhira; you are well-bred, greatly wise, an attendant of the elders.
Where there is wisdom, there is peace — seek calm, O Bhārata. A weapon does not move against what is not split; a weapon is brought down only against what is split (divided).
Those highest of men do not know enmities, do not see faults but only virtues, and do not arrive at opposition.
In a dispute, the basest of men speak harsh words, O Yudhiṣṭhira; the middling, when spoken to harshly, speak harsh words in return.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whether addressed or not addressed, the wise — the highest of men — never babble back hostile, harsh words; this is always so.
The good, responding rightly and having gained certainty within themselves, remember only the kind deeds done to them, never the enmities inflicted.
Such is the noble conduct you have shown in this assembly of the good — do not take Duryodhana's harshness to heart, dear son.
Regard also your mother Gāndhārī and me, longing for your virtues — your old, blind father who stands before you, O Bhārata.
This gambling was overlooked by me after observation, desiring to see the strength and weakness of friends and of my sons.
The Kurus need not be grieved over, O king, when you are their guide and Vidura, the wise counselor versed in all the shastras, is their minister.
In you resides dharma, in Arjuna valor, in Bhīmasena prowess; and faith and service to elders belong to the twin brothers, those foremost of men.
May good fortune be yours, Ajātaśatru — enter Khāṇḍavaprastha; let there be brotherhood among your brothers; let your mind be fixed on dharma.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the best of the Bhāratas, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, having made noble farewells to all, departed together with his brothers.
Mounting their cloud-like chariots together with Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī), they set out with joyful minds toward Indraprastha, the foremost of cities.
Janamejaya said: Knowing those Pāṇḍavas to have been dismissed along with their accumulated jewels and wealth, what was then the mind of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Knowing those Pāṇḍavas to have been dismissed by the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O king, Duḥśāsana quickly went to his brother.
Approaching Duryodhana along with his ministers, O bull of the Bhāratas, Duḥśāsana, tormented by grief, O foremost of the Bhāratas, spoke these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That which was gathered with such difficulty, the old man is now destroying; he is handing over our wealth to our enemies — understand this, O great warriors!"
Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala, proud in their enmity toward the Pāṇḍavas, came together in private counsel,
and hastening to the wise king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Vicitravīrya, they spoke these smooth words:
Duryodhana said: "Have you not heard, O king, what the wise Bṛhaspati, preceptor of the gods, declared when expounding statecraft to Indra?
Enemies must be destroyed by every means, O crusher of foes, before they do harm — before battle, before open force.
If the Pāṇḍavas, using their wealth, honor all the kings and then fight us, what will remain of us to escape their reach?
Who would be right to release enraged venomous serpents that have come ready to bite, after placing them around his neck and back?
The Pāṇḍavas, O father, armed and mounted on their chariots in anger, will annihilate us completely — for the enraged are like venomous serpents.
Arjuna departs fully armored, having uncovered his great quiver, taking up the Gāṇḍīva bow again and again, breathing heavily and looking around.
And Vṛkodara, raising his massive mace in haste, quickly yoked his chariot and departed — so we have heard.
Nakula took up his sword and his shield adorned with eight moons; and Sahadeva and the king too showed their intentions by their gestures.
All of them, mounting their chariots laden with many weapons, shaking the masses of vehicles, set out for the marshaling of the army.
Those who have been so wronged by us will never forgive — and who among them could forgive the humiliation of Draupadī?
Let us gamble again — good fortune to you — with the Pāṇḍavas for the stake of forest exile; in this way we shall be able to bring them under our power, O bull of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Either they, or we if defeated at dice, shall enter the great forest clad in the hides of deer.
And the thirteenth year they must spend unrecognized among people; if recognized, another twelve years in the forest.
So shall we or they dwell; let the game proceed thus — let the Pāṇḍavas throw the dice and play this second gambling match.
This is the most necessary action for us, O king, O bull of the Bhāratas; for Śakuni here knows the science and skill of dice.
We are firmly rooted in the kingdom, having gathered allies and honored a vast and formidable army of worth.
And if they fulfill their vow in the thirteenth year, we shall still defeat them, O king — let this please you, O scorcher of foes."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "Bring them back quickly, even though they have already set out on the road. Let them come back and let the Pāṇḍavas play this second game of dice."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Droṇa, Somadatta, the great warrior Bāhlika, Vidura, Droṇa's son, and the valiant son of Vaiśya —
Bhūriśravas, the son of Śaṃtanu, and the great warrior Vikarṇa — all of them said "No gambling!" and "Let there be peace!" in every way.
But Dhṛtarāṣṭra, devoted to his son, issued the summons to the Pāṇḍavas even against the will of all his well-wishers who could see what was truly beneficial.
Then Gāndhārī, wasted by grief, spoke righteously to the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, whose heart was swayed by love for his son:
"When Duryodhana was born, the great-minded Vidura declared: 'This one, the defiler of the family, should rightly be sent to the other world.'
For he cried out like a jackal the very moment he was born, O Bhārata — truly this is the end of this family; understand that, O Kurus.
O lord, do not follow the counsel of these foolish and ill-bred boys; do not yourself become the cause of this terrible destruction of the family.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Who would demolish a built dam? Who would blow upon a fire that is extinguished? Who, O Bhārata, would provoke the Pārthas who have been held in check by peace?
O Ajamīḍha, I remind you now as you yourself remember: scripture does not rule over the evil-minded — for their good or otherwise.
Surely the old should never have a childish mind, O king. Let your sons be guided by your eyes — let them not split apart and mock you.
May the understanding born of peace, righteousness, and another's wisdom prevail in you — not the contrary, destructive kind; for prosperity, firm yet gentle, passes on to sons and grandsons.
Then the great king replied to Gāndhārī who saw righteously: "Though my heart desires the good of the family, I am unable to restrain this.
Let it be as they wish. Let the Pāṇḍavas come back; let my sons play the second gambling match together with the Pāṇḍavas."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the messenger Pratikamin addressed Yudhiṣṭhira the Pārtha, who had already set out on the road, conveying the words of the wise king Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"The assembly hall is prepared, O king. After the dice have been cast, come, O Pāṇḍava — your father calls you to play, O Bhārata."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "By the command of the Creator, beings receive their good and evil — there is no escape from either; if I must play again —
— a summons to dice-play, and by the command of the elder — knowing even that it leads to ruin, I do not dare to transgress it."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Speaking thus, the Pāṇḍava turned back with his brothers; though knowing the deceit of Śakuni, the Pārtha went again to the gambling match.
Those great warriors, bulls of the Bhāratas, entered that assembly hall once again, distressing the hearts of their well-wishers.
They sat down as they pleased, pressed onward by fate, for the conduct of a second gambling match — and for the destruction of all the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śakuni said: "The old man has released the wealth that was already won — it remains honored. But now hear this one great stake from me, O bull of the Bhāratas:
We, defeated by you at dice, shall enter the great forest for twelve years, clad in the hides of the ruru deer —
and the thirteenth year we shall spend unrecognized among people; if recognized, another twelve years in the forest.
Or if you are conquered by us, you shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, together with Kṛṣṇā, clad in deerskins.
And when the thirteenth year has passed, the proper kingdom is to be reclaimed — by one side or the other.
With this as the agreed stake, come, Yudhiṣṭhira — throw the dice with us in this second gambling match, O Bhārata."
The spectators in the assembly said: "Alas, shame! His kinsmen do not warn him of this great danger; and the bulls of the Bhāratas themselves do not grasp with their own understanding what should be grasped by understanding."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing these many murmurs of the people, the lord of men — from a sense of honor and from adherence to dharma — the Pārtha went again to the gambling match.
Even knowing, the greatly intelligent one set the second game in motion, thinking: "Perhaps this will not be the destruction of the Kurus after all."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "How could a king like me, maintaining his own duty, turn back once summoned? I will play against you, O Śakuni."
Śakuni said: "Cattle and horses, many milk-cows beyond counting, goats and sheep, elephants, treasure, gold, and all male and female slaves —
this is our one single stake — forest exile for the Pāṇḍavas: either you or we, whichever is defeated, shall take refuge in the forest."
"With this resolve, let us play, O bull of the Bhāratas — with a single throw, for the stake of forest exile, O Bhārata."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The Pārtha accepted the stake; the son of Subala threw the dice. "Won!" — thus Śakuni declared to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Defeated, the Pārthas resolved themselves to forest exile and took up their deerskins as upper garments, one by one in order.
Seeing those subduer-of-foes clad in deerskins, their kingdom seized, setting out for forest exile, Duḥśāsana then spoke:
"The wheel of the great-souled king, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, has rolled forward; the sons of Pāṇḍu are defeated and have fallen into supreme misfortune.
Today the gods have departed by level paths, without obstacles; even those eldest in virtue, those elders — yet we are greater than our opponents.
The Pārthas have been cast into hell for a long and endless time; deprived of happiness and kingdom, they are ruined for eternal years.
Those who, intoxicated by strength, used to mock the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — those Pāṇḍavas, now defeated and their wealth seized, shall go to the forest.
"Let them remove their colorful armor and their resplendent divine garments; let them all now put on ruru-deer hides — as they agreed to the stake of Subala's son."
"Those who were always of the conviction that 'there are no men in the world like these' — those Pāṇḍavas will today know themselves in this reversal, like barren sesame plants bearing no fruit."
"For this is the fitting attire of such proud men, O Kaurava — may it not fall to us! Look at the Pāṇḍavas, those mighty ones, now like the uninitiated wearing deerskins."
"The greatly wise Somaka Yajñasena did an evil deed by giving the Pāñcālī maiden to the Pāṇḍavas; for the Pārthas, husbands of Yājñasenī, are no more — they are as eunuchs now."
"Having seen these fine garments exchanged for deerskins, your husbands in the forest destitute and without standing — what joy will you find, O Yājñasenī? Choose another husband here whom you desire."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"All the Kurus assembled here are patient, self-controlled, and richly endowed with wealth. Choose one among them as a husband — this reversal of fortune need not burn you."
"Like barren sesame plants bearing no fruit, like deer made of leather, like black barley — just so are all the Pāṇḍavas now."
"Why do you wait upon these fallen Pāṇḍavas? Service to barren sesame is wasted effort." Thus the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, cruel and harsh, made the Pārthas hear these words.
Hearing that, Bhīmasena, deeply furious, stepped forward suddenly, rebuked him loudly, seized him in his rage, and spoke these words — like a Himālayan lion to a jackal:
Bhīmasena said: "O cruel one, you speak what is fitting only for the wicked, for those who have accomplished nothing; it is by the dice-skill of Gāndhāra that you boast in the midst of kings.
Even as you pierce our vital points deeply here with word-arrows, so shall I remind you of it, cutting your vital points in battle.
And those who follow you, enslaved by desire and greed — those protectors along with their kin — I shall drive to the abode of Yama."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While Bhīma was speaking thus, clad in deerskins, overwhelmed with grief — bound to the path of dharma — Duḥśāsana danced around him in the midst of the Kurus, calling out "Cow! Cow!" utterly without shame.
