Bhīmasena said: "What is cruel, harsh, and vicious — that indeed you are capable of, O Duḥśāsana. Having gained wealth by fraud, who deserves to boast?
May the Pārtha Vṛkodara never attain the worlds of those who have done good deeds, if he does not drink your blood in battle after splitting open your chest."
"Having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle before the eyes of all the archers, I shall soon attain peace — this truth I declare to you."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As Bhīmasena moved with his lion-stride, king Duryodhana, that dull-witted one, joyfully mimicked Bhīmasena's gait with his own gait, as the Pāṇḍavas were leaving the assembly hall.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vṛkodara, turning back halfway, said to him: "This is not done with yet — I shall swiftly remind you of it after slaying you together with your kin, O fool."
Perceiving this insult upon himself, the mighty and proud Bhīma, suppressing his rage, spoke these words as he departed from the assembly of the Kauravas in the king's retinue.
I shall slay Duryodhana; Dhanañjaya shall slay Karṇa; and Sahadeva shall slay Śakuni, that dice-cheat of Gāndhāra.
And this further great vow I declare in the midst of the assembly — the gods shall make it true: there shall be war between us.
I shall kill this sinful Suyodhana with my mace in battle, and I shall plant my foot upon his head on the ground.
And the blood of this Duḥśāsana — this brave boaster of harsh words, this wicked soul — I shall drink like a lion.
Arjuna said: O Bhīma, what is resolved by words is not recognized as the resolve of the righteous. In fourteen years from now, we shall see what comes to pass.
The earth shall drink the blood of Duryodhana, Karṇa, the wicked Śakuni, and Duḥśāsana as the fourth.
The slanderer, the speaker of insults, the releaser of the wicked — at your command, O Bhīmasena, I shall slay Karṇa in battle.
Arjuna vows, for the sake of Bhīma's satisfaction, that he shall slay Karṇa and those who follow Karṇa in battle with his arrows.
And whatever other kings, deluded in their minds, shall fight against me — all of them I shall send to the abode of Yama with my sharp arrows.
The Himālaya may move from its place, the sun may lose its splendor, the moon may lose its coolness — but my truth shall never waver.
If Duryodhana does not restore the kingdom after fourteen years from now, this sworn truth shall come to pass — mark it well.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the son of Pṛthā had thus spoken, the glorious and valiant Sahadeva, son of Mādravatī, raising his mighty arm,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
eager to slay the son of Subala, spoke these words with eyes red with rage, hissing like a serpent:
O fool, O destroyer of the glory of Gāndhāra! Those dice you think so highly of — know that these are not dice but sharpened arrows that you have chosen in battle.
As Bhīma has already declared concerning you and your kinsmen, I shall perform that very deed. Do all that you need to do.
I shall swiftly slay you and your kinsmen in battle by my valor, if you stand firm in combat according to the dharma of the warrior class, O Saubala.
O lord of the people, having heard Sahadeva's words, Nakula — the most handsome among men — also spoke these words:
This daughter of Yajñasena — at this dice match those who stood in favor of Duryodhana, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, caused her to hear such harsh words.
Those ill-conducted sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who seek their own death and are driven by fate — I shall show them in full measure the abode of Vivasvat's son, Yama.
Following the command of the king of dharma, and walking the path of Draupadī, I shall before long make this earth free of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Thus those tiger-men, all long-armed, having made many vows, approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I take leave of the Bhāratas, and also of the aged grandfather Bhīṣma, of King Somadatta, and of the great king Bāhlika.
I take leave of Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the other kings, of Aśvatthāmā, of Vidura, of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and of all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Taking leave of Yuyutsu, Sañjaya, and likewise all the other members of the assembly, I depart. I shall see you all again upon my return.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Overcome with shame, they said nothing at all to Yudhiṣṭhira. Only in their minds did those righteous ones wish well to that wise king.
Vidura said: The noble Pṛthā, princess by birth, ought not to go to the forest. She is delicate, old, and always accustomed to ease and comfort.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This auspicious lady shall dwell here, well honored in my house. Know this, O sons of Pṛthā. May you all be free from disease.
Know this word of mine, O Yudhiṣṭhira, O bull among Bhāratas: no one who has been defeated by adharma is truly afflicted by defeat.
You are the knower of dharma; Dhanañjaya is the knower of battle; Bhīmasena is the slayer of enemies; Nakula is the gatherer of resources.
Sahadeva is the controller; Dhaumya is the foremost knower of Brahman; and Draupadī is skilled in dharma and artha, a woman who walks the path of dharma.
You are all dear to one another, and likewise speak kindly to one another; you are unbreakable by enemies and content. Who among men here would not envy you?
This, O Bhārata, is the all-auspicious resolution that you have — no enemy can withstand it, even one equal to Śakra himself. Be steadfast.
You were instructed long ago on the Himālayas by Meru-Sāvarṇi, and by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana in the city of Vāraṇāvata.
By Rāma on the peak of Bhṛgutuṅga, and by Shambhu on the banks of the Dṛṣadvatī — you have also heard the teachings of the great sage Asita concerning Mount Añjana.
Your priest Dhaumya is ever a beholder of Nārada's wisdom. Do not in adversity lose that understanding which the sages have honored.
O Pāṇḍava, you surpass Purūravas son of Ila in wisdom; you surpass other kings in power; and you surpass the sages in your devotion to dharma.
In Indra's sphere — steadfastness toward victory; in Yama's — restraint of wrath; in Kubera's — generosity; in Varuṇa's — self-control.
Self-giving and gentleness come from Soma; sustenance of life from the waters; forbearance from the earth; and full radiance from the orb of the sun.
Know that strength comes from Vāyu and that the self is born from the elements. May you all be free from affliction, may good be yours — I shall see you upon your return.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In crises of duty, purpose, and hardship, and in all affairs whatsoever, act rightly and in accordance with the time, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
You are bidden farewell here, O son of Kuntī. May you fare well, O Bhārata. We shall see you again when you return, your purpose accomplished and in safety.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, that Pāṇḍava of true valor said "So be it," and Yudhiṣṭhira, bowing to Bhīṣma and Droṇa, set forth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When he had set forth, Kṛṣṇā — Draupadī — deeply afflicted with grief, went to the glorious Pṛthā and took leave of her, as did the other women present there.
Having duly offered salutations and embraces as was befitting, she desired to depart; then a great wailing arose in the inner quarters of the Pāṇḍavas.
And Kuntī, deeply tormented, seeing Draupadī departing, spoke with voice faltering in grief, with great difficulty:
"Dear child, you must not grieve though this great calamity has befallen you. You know the dharma of women, and you are endowed with righteous conduct and behavior.
O pure-smiling one, I have no need to instruct you regarding your husbands. Both your lineages are adorned with the virtues of noble women.
Fortunate are these Kurus that they have not been consumed by you, O sinless one. Go along the auspicious path, sustained by my thoughts upon you.
For good women, faintheartedness does not arise when great things are at stake. Protected by the dharma of your elders, you shall quickly attain what is best.
And my son Sahadeva must be continually watched over while he dwells in the forest, so that when he encounters this adversity his noble mind does not sink."
Saying "So be it," that goddess, her eyes streaming with tears, wearing a single blood-stained garment, with hair unbound, departed.
Pṛthā followed after her as she went, crying out in grief. Then she saw all her sons stripped of their ornaments and fine garments,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
their bodies covered with deerskins and bark cloth, with faces slightly downcast in shame, surrounded by enemies rejoicing and lamented by their friends.
That most affectionate mother, approaching all her sons in that condition, embraced them and cried out in grief, lamenting again and again in many ways.
"How have you — adorned with righteous conduct, behavior, and steadfastness; not small-minded; firm in devotion; and always engaged in reverence to the gods —
come to meet with this calamity? What is this inversion of fate? By whose ill-thinking has this sin been born? I see it when I reflect with my understanding.
Surely this is the fault of my own fate, that I gave birth to you — you who are endowed with the highest virtues yet bear an exceeding portion of pain and suffering.
How shall you dwell in the difficult and harsh forests, stripped of your wealth — you who are not weak in valor, courage, strength, enterprise, and splendor — and yet made wretched?
If I had known that forest-exile was indeed certain for you, I would not have come to Hāstinapura from Shatashrunga after the death of Pāṇḍu.
I consider your father fortunate — endowed with austerity and wisdom — who, before reaching the grief over sons, made his longing for heaven a cherished goal.
And I consider blessed in every way Mādrī — the knower of dharma, the auspicious one — who today has attained that supreme state beyond the senses.
Cursed is this fondness for life that was instilled in me through love, wisdom, and circumstance — I who am a sharer in suffering."
Consoling Kuntī as she lamented thus, and bowing to her, the Pāṇḍavas, bereft of joy, set forth for the forest.
Vidura and the others, consoling the afflicted Kuntī with words of reason, led her into Vidura's house, themselves more grieved than she, moving slowly.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, his mind overwhelmed with sorrow, sent word to Vidura: "Come quickly."
Then Vidura went to Dhṛtarāṣṭra's dwelling. The agitated king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, questioned him.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: How does the son of Kuntī, King Yudhiṣṭhira the dharmaraja, go? And Bhīmasena, and the ambidextrous Arjuna, and those two sons of Mādrī?
And how does Dhaumya go? And the suffering Draupadī? O Vidura, I wish to hear all about the movements of their limbs and bearing.
Vidura said: The son of Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira, goes covering his face with his garment. And Bhīma the Pāṇḍava goes with his broad arms stretched wide.
Savyasācī, the ambidextrous Arjuna, follows the king scattering sand. The son of Mādrī, Sahadeva, goes with his face smeared.
Nakula, the most beautiful in the world, his entire body smeared with dust and his mind bewildered, follows the king.
Kṛṣṇā, with long eyes, beautiful, weeping, her face covered by her hair, follows the king.
Dhaumya, O lord of the people, goes along the roads chanting the Sāman hymns of Yama and of Rudra, holding kusa grass in his hand.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: The Pāṇḍavas go in various forms and bearing. Explain this to me, O Vidura — why do they go in this manner?
Vidura said: Even though deceived by your sons, even though his kingdom and wealth have been taken, the mind of the wise Dharmarāja never wavers from dharma.
That king, who is ever compassionate toward the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Bhārata, inflamed with anger at the treachery done to him, does not open his eyes —
"Lest I burn the people with my terrible gaze" — it is for this reason that the Pāṇḍava king covers his face and so departs.
And why Bhīma goes as he does — hear it from me as I describe it, O bull among Bhāratas: "There is none equal to me in the strength of my arms" —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
it is for this reason that Bhīma also goes with his broad arms stretched wide, displaying those arms — proud in the wealth of his arms, intending to perform deeds against his enemies befitting the treasure of those arms.
Pointing out the ranges of arrow-fall, Arjuna the son of Kuntī — the ambidextrous one — walked behind the king, scattering sand as he went.
"Just as this sand does not cling to him now, O Bhārata, so too shall he release showers of arrows unstoppably upon his enemies."
"Let no one recognize my face today" — so saying, O Bhārata, Sahadeva smeared his face and walked on in that manner.
"Let me not attract the minds of women along the road" — so thinking, O lord, Nakula covered his entire body with dust and walked on for that reason.
Draupadī, clad in a single garment, weeping, her hair unbound, in her monthly season, her wet garment stained with blood, spoke these words.
"For whose sake I have come to this state — in the fourteenth year from now, their wives shall be widowed, their sons slain, their dear kinsmen destroyed."
"Smeared with the blood of their kinsmen, their hair unbound, in their seasons, having performed such water-rites — thus shall the women enter Hāstinapura."
The steadfast priest Dhaumya, having strewn the kusha-grass in the direction of the southwest, walked ahead singing the Sama hymns addressed to Yama, O Bhārata.
"When the Bhāratas are slain in battle, the preceptors of the Kurus shall sing such Sama hymns then" — saying this, Dhaumya too walked on.
"Alas, alas, our protectors are leaving — behold this sight!" — thus the citizens, stricken with great grief, cried out on all sides.
Through such outward signs and gestures, conveying the resolve that lay within their minds, the noble sons of Kuntī departed to the forest.
As these foremost of men departed from Hāstinapura, lightning flashed in a cloudless sky and the earth trembled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Rāhu swallowed the sun outside of an eclipse, O lord of the people; and a meteor fell, circling the city counter-clockwise before crashing down.
Flesh-eating creatures — vultures, jackals, and crows — cried out ominously at the temples, shrines, and on the ramparts and turrets.
Such were these great evil omens as the Pāṇḍava went to the forest — portending, O king, the destruction of the Bhāratas through your ill counsel.
Nārada, standing in the midst of the assembly hall before the Kurus, surrounded by great sages, spoke these dreadful words.
"Fourteen years from now, the Kauravas shall be destroyed here — through the transgression of Duryodhana and by the might of Bhīma and Arjuna."
Having spoken thus, the greatest of divine sages, bearing the vast brahminical splendour, ascended to heaven and swiftly vanished.
Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala regarded Droṇa as their island of refuge and surrendered the kingdom to him.
Then Droṇa spoke to the wrathful Duryodhana, to Duḥśāsana, to Karṇa, and to all the Bhāratas.
"The twice-born declare the Pāṇḍavas, sons of gods, to be inviolable. I, for my part, while I live, protect those who have sought my shelter to the best of my power.
"The Dhārtarāṣṭras, together with the king, have gone over to my side with whole-souled devotion; I cannot in conscience abandon them — hence my conduct hereafter is rooted in fate.
"The sons of Pāṇḍu, defeated, are going to the forest in accordance with dharma; and for twelve years these Kauravas shall dwell in the forest.
"Having lived the life of chastity, driven by anger and indignation, the Pāṇḍavas will bring back their enmity — to my sorrow."
"Now, I had deprived Drupada of his kingdom in a quarrel over friendship; and in his fury, for the sake of a son to kill me, he performed a sacrifice, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Through the austerities of Yāja and Upayāja he obtained from the sacred fire Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and from the midst of the altar the fair-waisted Draupadī.
"He is flame-hued, bow-bearing, clad in armour, quiver-bearing, divine-born yet subject to mortal law — therefore fear of him entered me.
"The bull among men, the son of Pṛṣata, has indeed gone over to their side, his life-breath set free for this purpose; therefore shall I fight all the harder against your enemies."
"For it is well known in the world, and proclaimed far and wide, that he was born to slay me; surely this turn of time has come upon us through your doing.
"Act swiftly for your well-being — this has not been accomplished by what you have done so far. This happiness is but momentary, like the shade of a palm tree in winter.
"Perform great sacrifices, enjoy pleasures, give in charity — for fourteen years from now you shall suffer a great catastrophe.
"Duryodhana, having heard this, act as you see fit; employ conciliation towards the Pāṇḍavas if you think it right."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard Droṇa's words, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke thus: "The preceptor speaks rightly. Vidura, bring the Pāṇḍavas back."
"Or if they will not return, let the Pāṇḍavas go honoured — with weapons, chariots, and infantry, provided with all enjoyments, O son."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the sons of Pṛthā, defeated in that wicked game, had gone to the forest, anxiety seized Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O great king.
As Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the people, sat lost in thought, sighing, his mind distracted, Sañjaya spoke to him thus.
"Having obtained the earth full of wealth, O lord of the earth, and having banished the Pāṇḍavas from the kingdom, O king, why do you grieve?"
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "How should they not be grieved for, those with whom a great feud shall arise — with the Pāṇḍavas, mighty warriors eager for battle, who are like friends to great car-warriors?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sañjaya said: "This was well done by you, O king — a great enmity shall arise; the destruction of all the world along with its dependants shall come to pass."
"Though restrained by Bhīṣma, by Droṇa, and by Vidura — Draupadī, the beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas, the righteous one —
"— your son Duryodhana, foolish and shameless, sent the charioteer's son Pratikamin, saying 'Bring her here.'"
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "When the gods wish to bring ruin upon a man, they first remove his understanding; he then sees things in reverse."
"When the intellect has become turbid and destruction stands at hand, what looks like wise counsel but is its opposite does not depart from the heart."
"Harmful things arise in the form of beneficial, and beneficial things in the form of harmful, when a man's end is near — and he delights in that which harms him."
"Time does not cut off anyone's head by raising a stick; the power of Time is just this — the perception of things in reverse."
"This dreadful, turbulent, hair-raising act was committed by those who dragged Pāñcālī, the afflicted one, into the midst of the assembly hall —
"— she who was not born of a womb, who is beautiful, born in a noble lineage, brilliant, knowing all dharma, glorious — who could dishonour such a one?"
"Who would drag into the assembly hall a woman observing a woman's duty, of lovely form, stained with blood — except one made wicked by evil gambling?"
"Pāñcālī, clad in a single garment, gazed upon the Pāṇḍavas — those whose wealth was taken, whose minds were shattered, whose wives and prosperity were seized."
"Stripped of all their desires, reduced to the state of slaves, bound by the fetters of dharma, rendered incapable as if of all exertion."
"To Kṛṣṇā who was furious, indignant, and suffering in the Kuru assembly, Duryodhana and Karṇa spoke bitter words."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The earth itself might burn from the glance of her pitiable eyes — that any of my sons should survive today, Sañjaya!"
"All the women of the Bhāratas, gathered together with Gāndhārī, wailed terribly there upon seeing Kṛṣṇā brought into the assembly hall."
"The sacred fires were not invoked in the evening rite anywhere at all; the brahmins were enraged at the dragging of Draupadī."
"There was a terrible thunderous roar, and a great clap without cloud; dreadful meteors fell from the sky, and Rāhu swallowed the sun outside of eclipse — generating great terror among the people."
"Likewise in the chariot-halls fire appeared on its own; and the battle-standards of the Bhāratas shattered — portending their ruin."
"Jackals cried out terribly at Duryodhana's sacrificial fire; and at that moment donkeys brayed in response from every direction."
"Then Bhīṣma, O Sañjaya, departed together with Droṇa; as did Kṛpa, Somadatta, and the great car-warrior Bāhlika."
"Then I spoke there, urged on by Vidura: 'I grant a boon to Kṛṣṇā — whatever she desires, whatever she wishes for.'"
"Pāñcālī then chose the Pāṇḍavas of boundless might, with their chariots and their bows; and I too gave my assent to it."
"Then the greatly wise Vidura, knower of all dharma, spoke: 'O Bhāratas, you have reached the end of yourselves by the fact that Kṛṣṇā was brought into the assembly.'"
"'This daughter of the Pāñcāla king — this peerless goddess of fortune — Pāñcālī approaches these Pāṇḍavas as one sent by fate.'"
"'The sons of Pṛthā, being highly intolerant, will not forgive the wrong done to her — nor will the mighty-armed Vṛṣṇis, nor the greatly powerful Pāñcālas.'"
"'Protected by Vāsudeva, that one true to his pledges, Arjuna shall come, guarded by the Pāñcālas.'"
"'In their midst, Bhīmasena the great archer, of mighty strength, shall come brandishing his mace like the staff of Yama.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'Then, having heard the twang of Arjuna's Gāṇḍīva and felt the impact of Bhīma's mace, no king shall be able to withstand it.'"
"'In this matter, it has always seemed right to me that there be no conflict with the sons of Pṛthā; for I always consider the Pāṇḍavas more powerful than the Kurus.'"
"'For indeed the powerful king Jarāsandha, of great splendour, was slain in battle by Bhīma with his bare arms alone.'"
"'Therefore let there be peace between you and the Pāṇḍavas, O bull of the Bhāratas; let what is right for both sides be done without hesitation.'"
"Thus Vidura, son of Gavalgaṇa, spoke words encompassing both dharma and worldly good — and I did not accept them, being eager for the welfare of my son."
Janamejaya said: Thus were the Pārthas conquered at dice and provoked by the wicked sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with their ministers through treachery, O best of the twice-born.
Made to hear harsh words by those who were sowing the highest enmity, what did my great forebears, the scions of Kuru, do?
How did the Pārthas, whose splendour rivalled Indra's, suddenly fallen from their sovereignty and plunged into sorrow, pass their time in the forest?
Who followed those great-souled ones when they had met with supreme calamity? What was their food, what their conduct, and where did they dwell?
How did twelve years pass in the forest for those great-souled heroes, O best of brāhmaṇas, who slew their enemies?
And how did that princess, foremost of all women, devoted to her husbands, greatly blessed, ever truthful, she who deserved no suffering, come to endure that harsh forest exile?
Tell me all this in full detail, O wealth of asceticism; I wish to hear the deeds of those of vast wealth and splendour as narrated by you, O brāhmaṇa — my curiosity is very great.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus conquered at dice and provoked by the wicked sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with their ministers, the Pārthas departed from the city of the elephant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Issuing forth through the gate of the city called Vardhamāna, those weapon-bearing heroes set out facing northward, accompanied by Kṛṣṇā.
And fourteen servants, led by Indrasena, followed them on swift chariots, taking all the women along.
The townspeople, learning of their departure and oppressed by grief, repeatedly censuring Bhīṣma, Vidura, Droṇa, and Gautama, gathered together fearlessly and spoke to one another.
"Neither this entire clan nor we ourselves nor our homes have any worth where the sinful Duryodhana, guided by the son of Subala and by Karṇa and Duḥśāsana, seeks to rule this kingdom."
"Where this sinful man with his sinful allies desires to rule, there is no clan, no righteous conduct, no dharma, no wealth — whence then happiness?"
"Duryodhana hates his elders, has abandoned proper conduct and friends, is greedy for wealth, arrogant, base, and naturally without pity."
"This whole earth has no worth where Duryodhana is king. Let us all go well wherever the Pāṇḍavas go."
"They are compassionate, great-souled, conquerors of their senses and their enemies, modest, glorious, and devoted to the practice of dharma."
Having spoken thus, they followed after the Pāṇḍavas, and all gathered together, they addressed those sons of Kuntī and Mādrī with folded hands.
"Where will you go, may all be well with you, leaving us who share your sorrow? We too shall follow wherever you shall go."
"Having heard that you were defeated through unrighteousness by enemies devoid of mercy, we are all greatly distressed — you ought not to abandon us here."
"Devoted and attached friends, ever intent on your welfare and good — we would all be destroyed in a kingdom ruled by an evil king."
"And please listen, O bulls among men, as we describe the virtues and faults, how association with the good or evil shapes one's character."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"As fragrance perfumes cloth, water, sesame, and earth through the presence of flowers, so are qualities born of association."
"Association with fools is the source of the net of delusion; association with the good is the source of dharma day after day."
"Therefore one should seek the company of the wise, the aged, the virtuous, ascetics, the good, and those devoted to tranquillity."
"One should associate with those whose three things are pure — birth, knowledge, and conduct — for sitting with them is indeed more valuable than the scriptures themselves."
"Even without any effort of our own, by associating with those of virtuous nature, the good, we would gain merit here; and sin from attending upon the sinful."
"From the sight, touch, conversation, and laughter shared with the wicked, men's righteous conduct declines and they do not prosper."
"A man's intellect degrades by association with the lowly; it reaches a middling state with those of middling quality, and rises to excellence with the excellent."
"The qualities celebrated in the world, arising from dharma, desire, and wealth, born of worldly conduct and self, enjoined by the Vedas and approved by the learned —"
"— all those good qualities, both together and separately, are present in you. Desirous of the highest good, we wish to dwell among the virtuous."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: We are blessed that the people, led by the brāhmaṇas, moved by love and compassion, speak of virtues even in us who have none.
Therefore I, together with my brothers, make this request to you all: it must not be done otherwise — out of love and compassion for us.
My grandfather Bhīṣma, the king, Vidura, my mother, and the greater part of my dear ones remain in the city of Hāstinapura.
They, overwhelmed with grief and anguish, are to be carefully attended to and protected by all of you together for the sake of our welfare.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Turn back — you have come far enough, I adjure you by our reunion; my mind, filled with love, must be fixed upon my own people who are left as a trust.
This, indeed, is what lies highest in my heart among all my duties; by this good act both my satisfaction and honour will come about.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus dismissed by the king of dharma, those people, grieving, raised a terrible cry of anguish: "Alas, O king!"
Remembering the virtues of the son of Pṛthā, wracked with sorrow and utterly distressed, they unwillingly turned back after approaching the Pāṇḍavas.
When the townspeople had turned back, the Pāṇḍavas mounted their chariots and proceeded to the great banyan tree on the bank of the Jāhnavī called Pramāṇa.
The Pāṇḍavas reached that banyan tree with the remainder of the day; those heroes touched the pure water and spent that night there — afflicted by sorrow, they passed that night sustained by water alone.
Certain twice-born ones followed them there out of love — some with their sacred fires, some without, along with their circles of pupils and kinsmen; the king, surrounded by those speakers of Brahman, shone forth.
When their fires were kindled at an hour both delightful and awesome, conversation arose, led by the sound of Vedic recitation.
Those eminent brāhmaṇas, with voices sweet as swans, consoling the foremost king of the Kurus, passed the entire night.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When dawn came, brāhmaṇas who lived on alms stood in front of those whose deeds are untiring, as they were about to set out for the forest. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, addressed them.
"We are utterly stripped of everything — our kingdom taken, our fortune taken; we shall go to the forest in sorrow, to live on fruits, roots, and meat."
"The forest is full of dangers, with many serpents and crawling creatures, and I believe hardship there for you will certainly come to pass."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The affliction of brāhmaṇas would distress even the gods — how much more so me. Therefore, O brāhmaṇas, return from here as you please."
The brāhmaṇas said: Whatever path is yours, O king, we are ready to take it; you ought not to abandon us who are devoted to you and see the true dharma.
"Even the gods show compassion to the devoted — especially to brāhmaṇas who hold to right conduct."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: My devotion to brāhmaṇas too is always supreme, O twice-born ones; but this loss of resources to provide for attendants grieves me deeply.
"Those brothers of mine who might have gathered fruits, roots, and game for me — even they are bewildered by sorrows born of grief."
"I cannot bring myself to add hardships to these men already afflicted with sorrow — because of the outrage done to Draupadī and the theft of the kingdom."
The brāhmaṇas said: Let no anxiety about our sustenance lodge in your heart, O king; we ourselves shall bring forest provisions and follow along with you.
"Through meditation and chanting we shall bring about your well-being, and with agreeable stories we shall take delight together in the forest."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: There is no doubt that I would rejoice in the company of brāhmaṇas; yet because of my deficiency I see it as a kind of reproach to myself.
"How shall I look upon you all fetching your own food, suffering hardship in devotion to me, you who deserve no such hardship? Shame on the sinful sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra!"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the king, sorrowing, sat down upon the earth. Then a learned twice-born named Śaunaka, delighting in the knowledge of the self and skilled in Yoga and Sāṃkhya, spoke thus to the king.
Thousands of grounds for grief and hundreds of grounds for fear enter the fool day after day — not the wise man.
For the intelligent, men of your kind, do not cling to actions that are contrary to wisdom, fraught with many faults, and destructive of the highest good.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That eightfold intellect which is joined with what has been heard and remembered, and which they say destroys all that is inauspicious — that, O king, is established in you.
Men of your kind do not sink under difficulties of wealth, calamities, afflictions of kinsmen, or sufferings of body and mind.
And please listen as I recite the verses that the great-souled Janaka formerly sang, establishing the self in its proper station.
The world is tormented by two kinds of suffering — that arising from mind and that from body; hear this means of tranquillity concerning them both, in detail and in brief.
Bodily suffering arises from four causes: disease, contact with the unpleasant, fatigue, and separation from what is dear.
The calming of mental and bodily afflictions comes through two forms of action: swift remedying of the cause, and constant non-dwelling upon it in thought.
Therefore intelligent physicians first bring about relief of the mental suffering of men by means of pleasing narrations and the introduction of enjoyments.
For the body is tormented by mental suffering just as water in a pot is heated by a ball of hot iron.
Therefore one should calm the mental suffering with knowledge, as one quenches fire with water; when the mental suffering is pacified, the bodily suffering subsides.
The root of mental suffering is understood to be attachment; through attachment a being becomes ensnared and comes to encounter suffering.
Sorrows are rooted in attachment; fears too are born of attachment; grief and joy alike, and weariness — everything proceeds from attachment.
From attachment also arose passion of the senses and sensuality; both of these lead away from the good, and the former is considered the greater of the two.
As a fire in the hollow of a tree burns the entire tree down to its roots, so even a small fault of passion destroys one who aspires to dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A being who sees the fault in union but does not renounce at separation comes to dispassion — free of enmity, free of possessions.
Therefore one should, by means of knowledge, withdraw attachment from one's own side, from friends, from accumulation of wealth, and that which arises from one's own body.
In those foremost ones endowed with knowledge, learned in the scriptures, and of purified self, attachment does not cling — like water on a lotus leaf.
A man overwhelmed by passion is dragged along by desire; from that desire arises craving, and from that craving thirst spreads further.
Thirst indeed is the most sinful of all things, ever causing agitation in men, abounding in unrighteousness, terrible, and bound up with sin.
That which is hard to abandon for the foolish-minded, which does not decay even as the body decays, which is that life-ending disease — happiness comes to one who abandons that thirst.
That thirst, without beginning or end, lodged within the body of men, once arisen, destroys them — like fire born without a womb.
As firewood meets destruction by the fire that arises from itself, so the undisciplined self is destroyed by its innate greed.
The wealthy live in constant fear — from kings, from water, from fire, from thieves, from kinsmen — just as all living beings dwell in fear of death.
Just as flesh in the sky is devoured by birds, on land by beasts, in water by fish — so in every sphere is the wealthy man devoured.
For some men wealth itself becomes misfortune. One attached to wealth as the highest good never attains the highest good. Therefore all gains of wealth only deepen the delusion of the mind.
Meanness, arrogance, pride, fear, and anxiety — the wise know these miseries of embodied beings to be born of wealth.
There is suffering in earning wealth, suffering in guarding it and in its diminishment; suffering in its loss, suffering in its expenditure — and men even kill one another on account of wealth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Riches are painful to relinquish, and even when guarded bring no happiness; they are acquired with suffering — therefore one should not grieve at their loss.
The foolish pursue dissatisfaction; the wise attain contentment. Thirst has no end — contentment is the highest happiness.
Therefore the wise regard contentment itself as wealth in this world. Youth, beauty, life, accumulation of goods, lordship, and the company of loved ones — all are impermanent; the wise person should not covet these.
Therefore one should abandon hoarding — who could endure the distress born of it? For no one who accumulates is ever seen to be free from affliction.
Hence virtuous men praise freedom from desire for wealth. Indeed, it is better not to touch mire at all than to wash it off afterward.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, you should not hanker after possessions in this way. If you wish to act in accordance with dharma and desire liberation from the cycle of existence, act with that intent.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This desire for wealth in me is not for the sake of enjoying riches. O brahmin, I seek it only to maintain the brahmins — not out of greed.
How could one like me, living in the householder's stage of life, fail to provide for and protect those who follow him, O brahmin?
For the householder, sharing with all beings remains an obligation; likewise, food is to be given to those who come to eat.
Grass, ground, water, and as the fourth, kind and truthful speech — these things in the homes of the good are never exhausted at any time.
A bed should be given to the distressed, a seat to one standing and weary, water to the thirsty, and food to the hungry.
One should offer one's eyes, one's mind, and truthful speech; one should go forward to receive a guest, and offer homage in the proper manner.
The sacred fire, the draft ox, kinsmen, guests, relatives, sons, wife, and servants — if left unhonoured, they would burn a man as surely as fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One should not cook food for oneself alone, nor slaughter animals in vain, nor eat for oneself what one has not properly offered according to the rites.
One should cast food on the ground for dogs, for outcastes, and for birds — this is the Vaiśvadeva rite, prescribed to be performed morning and evening.
Therefore one should always eat only the remnants left by others, and partake of what is like nectar — remnants left by servants are vighasam, and remnants of sacrifice are amṛtam.
They say that one who lives in the householder's stage following this mode of conduct upholds the highest dharma. What, O brahmin, do you think of this?
Śaunaka said: Alas, how great is the hardship, and how inverted is this world — that by which the virtuous man is ashamed, by that very thing the wicked man is pleased.
The unwise man, overpowered by delusion and passion, enslaved to the objects of the senses, accumulates great quantities of food-remnants for the sake of belly and genitals.
Even a man who knows is carried away by his enticing senses, bewildered in understanding, like a charioteer dragged off by runaway, vicious horses.
When the six senses come together with their objects, then the mind — born of prior intention — manifests among them.
In one whose mind is urged toward the objects of the group of senses, restlessness arises and activity is born.
Then, pierced by desire — the power of intention — and by the sense objects, he falls into the fire of greed, just as a moth falls into flame out of craving for light.
Then, O lord of the people, deluded by pleasures and food, plunged into the mouth of great delusion, he no longer knows himself.
Thus he falls into saṃsāra, wandering through these various wombs, driven round and round like a wheel by ignorance, karma, and thirst.
He revolves through existences from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, being born again and again in water, on land, and in the sky.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This is the path of the unwise; now hear from me the path of the wise — those who delight in dharma and the highest good, who are devoted to liberation.
The Vedic injunction says both 'perform action' and 'renounce action' — therefore one should perform all these dharmic duties not out of pride or self-regard.
Sacrifice, study, giving, austerity, truthfulness, forbearance, restraint, and non-greed — this eightfold path is remembered as the way of dharma.
Of these, the first four belong to the path of the ancestors; whatever must be done should be performed as a duty, not out of pride.
The latter four constitute the path of the gods, always practised by the virtuous; one with a purified soul should follow this eightfold path.
Through right intention, right restraint of the senses, right observance of special vows, and right service to a teacher —
— through right discipline in food, right adherence to scriptural study, right renunciation of action, and right restraint of the mind — thus those who wish to conquer saṃsāra perform their actions.
Free from passion and aversion, they attain the sovereignty of the gods — the Rudras, the Sādhyas, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Aśvins — who, endowed with the power of yoga, uphold these living beings.
Likewise, O son of Kuntī, taking firm hold of supreme tranquility, seek perfection through austerity, and the perfection of yoga, O Bhārata.
The perfection born of father and mother has been attained by you, and that born of action too — now seek perfection through austerity, truly for the sake of maintaining the twice-born.
For the perfected ones, whatever they desire they accomplish through their grace. Therefore, taking recourse to austerity, fulfil the desire of your heart.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having been thus addressed by Śaunaka, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, approached the family priest Dhaumya and spoke these words in the midst of his brothers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
These brahmin masters of the Vedas are setting out to follow me wherever I go, and I am not capable of maintaining them, afflicted as I am with great suffering.
I cannot abandon them, and yet I have no power to give. Revered one, tell me what I ought to do in this matter.
Pondering for a moment and searching for the right course through dharma, Dhaumya — foremost among upholders of righteousness — spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira.
In primordial times, when all created beings were greatly tormented by hunger, the Sun, out of compassion for them, became like their own father.
Having gone to the northern course and drawn up the essence of light with his rays, the Sun returns on the southern course and pours it into the earth.
Then the Moon, lord of herbs, the earth having become the field, drawing up the celestial radiance and combining it with water, generates the herbs.
The Sun, resting in the earth and infused with the light of the Moon, gives birth to the herbs endowed with six tastes and purifying qualities — that is the food of living beings on earth.
Thus is food made of solar light the sustainer of life for all beings. He is the father of all beings — therefore take refuge in him.
For great-souled kings, purified by birth and action, uplift all their subjects by taking recourse to abundant austerity.
By Bhīmasena, by Kārtavīrya, by Vainya, and by Nahuṣa — all abiding in the absorption of austerity and yoga — were the subjects rescued from calamities.
Likewise, O righteous one, you too are purified by your deeds — taking recourse to austerity and dharma, sustain the twice-born, O Bhārata.
Thus addressed by Dhaumya with words befitting that time, the king of dharma, pure in soul, undertook supreme austerity.
Having worshipped the Sun with offerings of flowers and oblations, the dharma-souled one took his yoga posture, subsisting on air alone, with senses conquered, touching the waters of the Ganges, and stood firm in prāṇāyāma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Janamejaya said: How did that king Yudhiṣṭhira, the bull of the Kurus, propitiate the Sun of wondrous power for the sake of the brahmins?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Listen attentively, O king — become pure and composed, and for a moment be still, O lord of kings. I shall recount everything without remainder.
As recited by Dhaumya to the greatly noble son of Pṛthā — hear those holy one hundred and eight names, O greatly wise one.
Sūrya, Aryaman, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭā, Pūṣan, Arka, Savitā, Ravi, Gabhastimān, Aja, Kāla, Mṛtyu, Dhātā, Prabhākara —
Earth, Water, Fire, Sky, Wind, the Supreme Refuge, Soma, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Budha, and Aṅgāraka —
Indra, Vivasvān, Dīptāṃśu, Śuci, Śauri, Śanaiścara, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Skanda, Vaiśravaṇa, Yama —
The fire of lightning, the digestive fire, the fire of fuel, Lord of luminosities, Dharmadhvaja, Creator of the Vedas, Vedic limb, Bearer of the Vedas —
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali, Refuge of all immortals, the kaḷā, the kāṣṭhā, the muhūrtas, the fortnights, the months, and the seasons —
Maker of the year, the Aśvattha tree, the Wheel of Time, Vibhāvasu, the Eternal Person, the Yogi, the Manifest and Unmanifest, the Eternal —
Overseer of the worlds, Overseer of creatures, Viśvakarmā, Dispeller of darkness, Varuṇa, the Ocean, Ray of light, Cloud, Giver of life, Slayer of enemies —
Refuge of beings, Lord of beings, Worshipped by all beings, the Jewel, Gold, Origin of beings, Granter of desires, Facing all directions —
Victory, the Vast, Bestower of boons, Swift-moving, Sustainer of life-breath, Dhanvantari, Dhūmaketu, the Primordial God, Son of Aditi —
Twelve-natured, Lotus-eyed, Father, Mother, Grandsire, Gate of heaven, Gate of creatures, Gate of liberation, the Triple Heaven —
Maker of bodies, the Tranquil Soul, Soul of the universe, Facing all the world, Soul of moving and unmoving things, the Subtle Soul, endowed with a form of friendliness —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This indeed is the sacred set of one hundred and eight names of the great-souled Sun who is to be glorified, as proclaimed by the great-souled Indra.
Nārada received this from Indra, and Dhaumya received it next from Nārada; having received it from Dhaumya, Yudhiṣṭhira attained all his desires.
Attended upon by the hosts of gods and ancestral spirits and yakṣas, worshipped by asuras, night-wanderers, and siddhas, radiant as choice gold and blazing fire — hold the Sun also in your mind.
One who recites this at sunrise with a composed mind will gain sons, accumulate wealth and gems, always attain the memory of past births, and find supreme memory and intellect.
The person who glorifies this hymn of the best of gods, pure and clear-minded, with concentrated thought, shall be released from the ocean of the wildfire of grief, and shall attain all desires as wished for in the heart.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the Sun, well pleased, appeared before the son of Pāṇḍu, blazing with his own radiance, burning like a sacrificial fire.
"O king, you shall obtain everything you have desired. I shall grant you food for twelve years — five and seven."
"Fruits, roots, flesh, and vegetables — the fourfold food prepared in your kitchen shall be inexhaustible for you, and various wealth as well." Having said this, the Sun disappeared.
Having received the boon, the son of Kuntī, the knower of dharma, rose from the water, clasped the feet of Dhaumya, and the unwavering one embraced his brothers.
The lord met with Draupadī, and then, as all watched, the son of Pāṇḍu went and had the food in the kitchen prepared.
The fourfold food of the forest — prepared grain, fruits, roots, and greens — goes forth abundantly; the inexhaustible food keeps multiplying, and with it the lord feeds the twice-born.
When the brahmins have eaten, and the younger brothers have been fed as well, Yudhiṣṭhira eats afterwards the remnant known as vighasā; and when Yudhiṣṭhira has been fed, Draupadī, the daughter of Pṛṣata, eats whatever remains.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus, having received the boon from the Sun-god, the lord, himself blazing with the Sun's own radiance, bestowed upon the brahmins whatever desires and wishes of the heart they harboured.
With the family priest at their head, on the appointed lunar days, stellar conjunctions, and festival occasions, sacrificial rites were performed in accordance with prescribed injunctions and sacred formulas.
Then, having had auspicious benedictions performed by Dhaumya, the Pāṇḍavas, surrounded by hosts of twice-born, set out for the Kāmyaka forest.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: After the Pāṇḍavas had entered the forest, Ambikā's son, who sees with the eye of wisdom yet was burning with anguish, seated at ease, addressed Vidura — that soul of dharma, of unfathomable intellect — with these words.
Your wisdom is pure as that of Bhṛgu's line; you know dharma in its highest and most subtle form; you are esteemed as impartial among all the Kurus. Tell me, therefore, what is beneficial both for them and for me.
Given that matters have come to this pass, Vidura, what should be done now? How might the citizens still take our side? And may those Pāṇḍavas not uproot us utterly — yet I do not wish to see them destroyed either.
Vidura said: These three aims of life, O lord of men, are rooted in dharma; and kingship, they say, is likewise rooted in dharma. Therefore, O king, abiding in dharma with all your strength, protect all your sons — and the sons of Kuntī as well.
That very dharma was violated in the assembly-hall by wicked-souled men with Śakuni's son at their head: having invited the son of Kuntī to the dice-game, your son defeated him — that man of steadfast truth — by fraud.
For this wrong course of yours, O king, I see a remedy for what remains, whereby your son, O descendant of the Kurus, freed from his sins, may stand well-regarded in the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let the sons of Pāṇḍu receive back all that was once given away by you, O king. This is the highest dharma: that a king should be content with his own and should not covet what belongs to others.
This is the foremost of all duties before you: their satisfaction and the humbling of Śakuni. If such an outcome among your sons is still possible, then act upon this without delay, O king.
But if you do not act thus, O king, the destruction of the Kurus is certain; for when Bhīmasena or Arjuna is enraged, he will leave no remnant of the enemy's army on the field.
Among those whose warrior is the ambidextrous Savyasācī, master of arms; whose bow is the Gāṇḍīva, the essence of the world; and whose fighter is the mighty-armed Bhīma — what in this world is beyond their reach?
It was said by me even before, the moment your son was born — what was beneficial then: 'Abandon this child, who shall bring ruin to the family.' That, O king, you did not do. Now again beneficial counsel is given to you; if you do not act upon it, O king, you shall grieve hereafter.
If your son consents to this and is reconciled with the Pāṇḍavas in a single undivided kingdom, there will be no sorrow for you — joy will prevail. But if you do not restrain your son and his allies, then let another arise who, having curbed him, shall install the son of Pāṇḍu as sovereign.
Let Ajātaśatru, free from passion, rule this earth by dharma, O king; then, O king, all earthly rulers will immediately attend upon us like merchants seeking a patron.
Let Duryodhana, Śakuni, and the son of the charioteer approach the sons of Pāṇḍu with good will, O king; and let Duḥśāsana entreat Bhīmasena and the daughter of Drupada in the midst of the assembly-hall.
Pacify Yudhiṣṭhira yourself, and restore him to the kingdom with full honour. What more could I say when asked by you? Having done this, you will have accomplished everything, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: These words of yours, Vidura, spoken in the assembly-hall and spoken here in my presence — words beneficial to the Pāṇḍavas and harmful to my own — none of this enters my heart.
And how is it so resolutely decided now, this thing you advocate on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas? By this I now think you are no friend of mine. For how can I abandon my son for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas?
Doubtless the Pāṇḍavas too are sons to me; yet Duryodhana was born from my own body. Who, looking at the matter impartially, would say: 'Abandon your own body for the sake of another'?
You speak to me nothing but crooked counsel, Vidura; yet I still hold you in the highest regard. Go wherever you wish or stay — even a wicked woman, though well-soothed, will abandon her husband.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra abruptly rose and retreated into his inner apartments, O king. Then Vidura, still speaking — 'This is not right!' — ran swiftly to where the sons of Pṛthā were.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The Pāṇḍavas, bulls among the Bhāratas, set out from the bank of the Jāhnavī toward Kurukṣetra, intending to dwell in the forest, together with their followers.
After sojourning at the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī rivers and at the Yamunā, they journeyed continually through forest after forest toward the western direction.
Then, on the level sandy plains along the Sarasvatī bank, they came upon a forest called Kāmyaka, beloved of sages.
There those heroes dwelt in that forest teeming with deer and birds, waited upon by sages and comforted by them, O Bhārata.
Vidura too, burning with longing to see the Pāṇḍavas, then went with a single chariot to the prosperous Kāmyaka forest.
Having driven swiftly to that forest with fleet horses drawing his chariot, Vidura saw the King of Dharma seated in a secluded spot, together with Draupadī, his brothers, and the brahmins.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then that king of steadfast truth caught sight of Vidura approaching swiftly from afar, and said to his brother Bhīmasena: 'What will Kṣattā have to say to us when he arrives?'
'Perhaps he comes summoned at the word of Śakuni's son, bearing a challenge? Could that vile Śakuni be coming again to defeat us with weapons, or once more at the dice-board?'
'Summoned by someone, I cannot in any case withdraw from Bhīmasena's side; nor can I in any way set the Gāṇḍīva bow aside — for that would make our recovery of the kingdom doubtful.'
Then, rising up, all the sons of Pāṇḍu received Vidura with due respect, O king. Honoured by them, that descendant of Ajamīḍha in turn greeted the sons of Pāṇḍu as was fitting.
When Vidura had been set at ease, those bulls among men then asked him the reason for his coming; and he in turn told them in full detail how Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Ambikā, had behaved.
Vidura said: Dhṛtarāṣṭra took me aside in private, O Ajātaśatru, and having honoured me warmly, said: 'Given that things have come to this pass, and seeing them as equal to me, tell me what is beneficial for them and for me as well.'
I too spoke what was wholesome and beneficial for the Kurus and for Dhṛtarāṣṭra himself. But that wholesome counsel did not enter his heart; and therefore I do not see any other course as fitting.
The highest good was spoken by me to you, O sons of Pāṇḍu; yet Ambikā's son would not hear it from me. Just as a sick man has no relish for wholesome food, so that counsel, however beneficial, did not please him when it was uttered.
He is not led toward what is good, O Ajātaśatru — like a corrupt woman in a brahmin's household. My words found no favour with that bull among Bhāratas, just as a husband of sixty finds no favour with a young maiden.
The destruction of the Kurus is certain, O king; Dhṛtarāṣṭra does not pursue what is truly good. Just as water poured on a lotus leaf does not stay, so beneficial counsel, once spoken, does not remain in him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, angered, said to me: 'Go wherever you please, O Bhārata. I no longer desire your help in governing this earth or this city.'
So I, dismissed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O king, have hastened here to counsel you. Hold firm in all that I spoke in the assembly-hall; and now hear further what I shall say.
He who, though afflicted by harsh sufferings at the hands of enemies, practices forbearance and bides his time — nurturing himself like a small flame being fed to grow — that self-possessed man alone shall in the end enjoy the entire earth.
He whose resources are shared undivided with his allies — those allies will be sharers in his suffering as well. This is the means of retaining allies: through shared fortune. And in the gaining of allies, they say, lies the gaining of the earth.
Truth is supreme, O Pāṇḍava — truth without empty speech; and food shared equally and eaten together with allies; and let a king never overstep himself before them. A ruler who lives in this way shall prosper.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I shall act exactly as you counsel, bringing the highest understanding to bear, without carelessness. And whatever else is appropriate to time and place — that too you must tell me, and I shall carry it all out in full.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: But after Vidura had gone to the hermitage to the Pāṇḍavas, O king, the greatly wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra was tormented with anguish, O Bhārata.
Coming to the entrance of the assembly-hall, overcome with the grief of remembering Vidura, his senses overwhelmed, he fell down before the assembled kings.
Regaining consciousness, he rose from the earth, and the king addressed Saṃjaya, who was standing close by, with these words.
'My brother and my friend — verily a second Dharma made manifest — thinking of him now, my heart is riven asunder.
Bring back to me quickly that knower of dharma, my brother!' — saying this, the king lamented piteously.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Consumed by remorse, tormented by the remembrance of Vidura, out of love for his brother, O king, he spoke these words to Saṃjaya.
'Go, Saṃjaya, and find out whether my brother Vidura still lives, he who was driven away in anger by me, a sinner.
For that wise brother of mine, of boundless intellect, has never done me the slightest wrong, not even the most minute offense.
How has that supremely wise man received such injury from me? A wise man would not abandon his life for this. Go, Saṃjaya, bring him to me.'
Having heard the king's words and taken his leave, Saṃjaya said 'So be it' and ran swiftly to the Kāmyaka forest.
Reaching that forest without delay, where the Pāṇḍavas were, he then saw Yudhiṣṭhira clad in the hide of the ruru deer.
He was seated with Vidura and with thousands of brahmins, guarded by his brothers — like Indra of a hundred sacrifices attended by the gods.
Approaching Yudhiṣṭhira, Saṃjaya paid him homage; and he also rendered appropriate honour to Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins.
Questioned by the king about his well-being and seated comfortably, Saṃjaya told him the reason for his coming and spoke these words.
'King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Ambikā, remembers you, O Kṣattā. Go quickly to see him and revive the king's spirit.'
'Having taken leave of the best of men, the Pāṇḍavas, those joys of the Kuru line, you should go at the command of that lion among kings, O giver of honour.'
Thus addressed, the wise Vidura, who was affectionate to his own people, with Yudhiṣṭhira's consent, returned again to Gajāhvaya — the city named after the elephant.
The powerful Dhṛtarāṣṭra addressed that man of great wisdom: 'By good fortune you have arrived, O knower of dharma; by good fortune you remember me, O sinless one.'
'This night past and during the day, because of you, O bull of the Bhāratas, I lay awake and saw strange visions of my own body.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Taking Vidura upon his lap and smelling his head in welcome, he said: 'Let it be forgiven — all that was said to you by me in anger.'
Vidura said: It is already forgiven by me, O king; you are our supreme elder and guru. That is precisely why I have come back quickly, intent on seeing you.
For there are men, O tiger among men, whose hearts are rooted in dharma and who rush to the aid of the distressed, O king — in this there should be no deliberation.
The sons of Pāṇḍu are to me as your sons are to me; and it is with the thought 'they are suffering' that my mind has turned to them now.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus appeased each other in this way, those two brothers of great splendour — Vidura and Dhṛtarāṣṭra — experienced the greatest joy.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that Vidura had returned and been mollified by the king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son — that evil-minded king — was consumed with anguish.
Having summoned Śakuni, Karṇa, and Duḥśāsana, the king, entering the darkness born of folly, spoke these words.
'This Vidura, the trusted counsellor of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, has returned — the learned friend of the sons of Pāṇḍu, ever devoted to their welfare.
'Before Vidura can once again turn the king's mind in the direction of bringing back the Pāṇḍavas, deliberate quickly on what is beneficial for me.'
'If I should ever see the sons of Pṛthā arrive here again, I shall waste away once more — without hope, without support.
'I would take poison, hang myself, seize a weapon, or walk into fire — I cannot bring myself to see those prosperous ones again in this world.'
Śakuni said: 'Why do you entertain such childish thoughts, O king, O lord of men? They have gone after entering into an agreement — this will not come to pass as you fear.'
'All the Pāṇḍavas are bound to their word of truth, O bull of the Bhāratas; your father's command, dear one, they will never accept under any circumstances.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Or if they do accept it and return to the city, then, discarding the agreement, we shall have another round of the wager.'
Let us all remain neutral, acting in accordance with the king's wishes, carefully watching for many weaknesses in the Pāṇḍavas while keeping ourselves well concealed.
Duḥśāsana said: It is exactly so, O greatly wise one, just as you say, uncle. Indeed, whenever you speak, your counsel always pleases me.
Karṇa said: We all look upon whatever you desire, Duryodhana, as desirable. Indeed, O king, unanimity of purpose is evident among all of us.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Karṇa, King Duryodhana at that moment became not very joyful in mind and quickly turned away.
Then Karṇa, perceiving this, opened wide his bright eyes and in anger addressed both Duḥśāsana and the son of Subala together.
He spoke in utmost fury, rousing himself with his own resolve: "Ah, hear my opinion, O lords of men!"
"We all wish to do what is pleasing to the king, standing with joined hands as his servants, yet we are all unable to remain steadfastly in his service without lapses."
"But let us take up our weapons, mount our chariots, clad in armour, and go together to slay the Pāṇḍavas who roam in the forest."
"When all of them have been destroyed and have departed to an unknown destination, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and we alike shall live without dispute."
"While they are still impoverished, while they are still overwhelmed by grief, while they are still without allies — that is the time they can be overcome; such is my opinion."
Having heard that speech of his, they all applauded it again and again and replied to the son of a charioteer with "Very well! So be it!"
Having thus spoken, all of them, filled with rage, set out each in his own chariot, resolved in purpose as a band, to slay the Pāṇḍavas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Knowing them to be setting out, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana then came, that pure-souled one, perceiving them with his divine eye.
And stopping all of them, the Blessed One worshipped by the world went quickly and spoke to him who sat with wisdom as his eye.
Vyāsa said: O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, greatly wise one, hear my words. I shall speak to you of the highest good for all the Kauravas.
It does not please me, O mighty-armed one, that the Pāṇḍavas have gone to the forest, defeated by fraud by those who follow in Duryodhana's power.
Remembering their hardships, O Bhārata, when the thirteenth year is complete, they will release their venom in fury upon the Kauravas.
So why does this evil-souled son of yours, so utterly dull of wit, always enraged, seek to slay the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of the kingdom?
Let this fool be restrained properly; let your son find peace. Wishing to slay those dwelling in the forest, he will forfeit his own life.
As the wise Vidura says, as Bhīṣma says, as we say, as Kṛpa and Droṇa say — let what is proper be done accordingly.
For conflict with one's own kin is censured by good people, O greatly wise one; it is contrary to dharma and brings dishonour. Do not choose such a path, O king.
For whatever disregard he shows towards the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata — that indifference, O king, will touch upon a great calamity.
Or else let this dull-spirited son of yours go to the forest together with the Pāṇḍavas, O king, alone and without allies.
If then affection born of association should arise in your son towards the Pāṇḍavas, you would today have your purpose accomplished, O lord of men.
Or else whatever character arises from one's very birth — that, it is said, O great king, does not depart even with one's very life.
What indeed does Bhīṣma think, or Droṇa, or Vidura, or yourself? What is the proper course of action here, before the matter goes too far?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: O Blessed One, I too did not approve of praise for the dice-game. I believe that fate, overcoming my will, made me cause it, O sage.
Neither does Bhīṣma approve of it, nor Droṇa, nor Vidura, nor does Gāndhārī desire the dice-game. And yet it was set in motion out of delusion.
I am unable to abandon Duryodhana, that one devoid of wisdom, O Blessed One of disciplined vows, even though I know it — because of my love for my son.
Vyāsa said: O king, son of Vicitravīrya, what you say is true. I know firmly: there is nothing higher than a son, nothing higher than one's children.
Even Indra was awakened by the falling tears of Surabhī. With all other abundant blessings, there is nothing higher than one's own child.
On this matter I shall narrate to you a great and excellent tale — the conversation between Surabhī and Indra, O lord of men.
Surabhī, the mother of cows, having gone to heaven, wept there long ago, O king, O dear one, and Indra felt compassion for her.
Indra said: Why do you weep, O auspicious one? Is all well with the dwellers of heaven, or with humans, or with the cows? This must not be something small.
Surabhī said: No misfortune of yours is to be seen, O lord of the thirty gods. But I grieve for my son — for that reason I weep, O Kauśika.
"Look at this dreadful ploughman striking my weak little son with his goad, tormenting him with the plough."
"Seeing him thus utterly exhausted and being beaten, O king of the gods, O lord of Devas, I am seized by pity, and my heart trembles."
"One of them, endowed with strength, draws the yoke-load abundantly; the other, of little strength and vitality, lean and with veins standing out, with great difficulty draws that burden — him indeed I mourn, O Vāsava."
"Being beaten with the goad and pricked again and again, he is simply unable to bear that burden. See, O Vāsava!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Thus I, distressed by his suffering, deeply pained, cry out, shedding tears from my eyes, overcome with compassion."
Indra said: When thousands of your sons are suffering, O beautiful one, why is there compassion only here? Only one son suffers here.
Surabhī said: If a thousand sons are mine, they are equally mine in every respect. Yet, O Śakra, for a son who is poor and suffering, my compassion is greater.
Vyāsa said: Having heard that speech of Surabhī, Indra was greatly astonished, O Kauravya, and deemed one's own child as even more precious than life itself.
And the Blessed Pākaśāsana poured down copious water right there, creating an obstacle for the ploughman.
As Surabhī said, so let it be with you — let your compassion be greater for all your sons who are afflicted and poor, O king.
As Pāṇḍu is my son, so are you my child, and so is the greatly wise Vidura. I say this out of affection.
After a long time, your hundred and one sons, O king, are visible, while Pāṇḍu's are only five — and even those five are dull with deep suffering.
"How shall they live? How shall they prosper?" — thinking thus upon the distressed sons of Pṛthā, my heart burns with anguish.
If you desire the Kauravas to live here, O Parthiva, let your son Duryodhana make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: It is exactly so, O greatly wise sage, as you tell us. I myself know it, and so do all these lords of men.
What you consider proper — that which brings prosperity to the Kurus — that very thing Vidura also tells me, and Bhīṣma and Droṇa too, O sage.
If you would do me a favour, if you have compassion for the Kauravas — instruct my evil-souled son Duryodhana.
Vyāsa said: O king, this Blessed Sage Maitreya is coming here, having visited the Pāṇḍava brothers and now wishing to see us here.
This great sage will instruct your son Duryodhana duly and rightly for the peace of your family.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever this sage says, O lord of kings, that should be done without hesitation. For if the proper act is not done, he will curse your son in anger.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Vyāsa departed. Then Maitreya appeared, and the lord of men received him with honour together with his sons.
Having offered the arghya and all due rites, when the bull among sages had rested, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Ambikā, spoke to him with deference.
"Did you travel in comfort, O Blessed One, through the Kuru country? Are the five heroic Pāṇḍava brothers in good health?"
"Do those bulls among men intend to abide by the agreement? Will the brotherhood of the Kurus remain unbroken?"
Maitreya said: While proceeding on pilgrimage to sacred fords, I arrived in the Kuru country and by chance saw the Dharmarāja in the Kāmyaka forest.
Him — clad in matted locks and deer-skin, dwelling in the ascetic forest — groups of sages came to see, that great-souled one, O master.
There I heard, O great king, of the transgression of your sons and the great ruin that has befallen in the form of the dice-game.
Then I came to you out of concern for the Kauravas, for my affection and love for you has always been especially great, O master.
This is not fitting, O king, while you and Bhīṣma still live — that your sons should be at strife with one another, O lord of men.
You yourself are the central post, O king, for both restraint and support. Why do you ignore this terrible ruin as it rises?
By the conduct in the assembly-hall that was like that of bandits, O delight of the Kurus, you do not shine, O king, in the assembly of ascetics.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then turning towards King Duryodhana the impatient one, the Blessed Sage Maitreya spoke with gentle words.
"O Duryodhana of mighty arms, hear my words, O best among speakers, O greatly wise one — what I say that is for your welfare."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Do not act against the Pāṇḍavas, O king; do what is good for yourself, for the Pāṇḍavas, for the Kurus, and for the world, O bull among men."
"For they are all tigers among men, heroes who fight with great valour, all with the strength of ten thousand elephants, with bodies firm as the thunderbolt, resolute."
"All devoted to vows of truth, all honouring themselves as men, slayers of the enemies of the gods, of shape-shifting rakshasas — chief among them Hiḍimba, Baka, and the rakshasa Kirmīra."
"That one who, as those great-souled ones were departing from here one night, stood blocking their path, fierce in nature, immovable as a mountain —"
"— him Bhīma, glorious in battle, best of the strong, slew with the strike used to kill cattle, as a tiger slays a small deer."
"See, O king, how in the conquest of the directions, Jarāsandha — that mighty archer with the strength of ten thousand elephants — was felled by Bhīma in battle."
"Vāsudeva is their kinsman by marriage, and Pārṣata is their brother-in-law. What mortal man, subject to old age and death, could stand against them in battle?"
"Therefore let there be peace between you and the Pāṇḍavas, O bull of the Bhāratas. Do my bidding, O king; do not fall under the sway of death."
While Maitreya was speaking thus, O lord of men, he — Duryodhana — slapped his own thigh, which was shaped like the trunk of an elephant, with his hand.
Duryodhana, that dull-witted one, with a smile, scratched the ground with his foot and, saying nothing, stood with his face somewhat averted.
Seeing Duryodhana inattentive and scratching the earth, O king, anger entered into Maitreya.
He — Maitreya, that best of sages — having fallen under the power of anger, and being impelled by fate, set his mind upon cursing him.
Then Maitreya, his eyes reddened with anger, touched water and cursed that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that evil-minded one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Because you have disregarded me and refuse to heed these words, therefore receive at once the fruit of this arrogance."
"A great war shall arise born of enmity toward you, in which the mighty Bhīma shall shatter your thigh with blows of his mace."
When these words had been spoken, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra sought to appease the sage, saying, "Let it not be so."
Maitreya said: "If your son, O king, pursues peace by any means, then the curse shall not come to pass; but if he acts otherwise, it shall."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Embarrassed, the father of Duryodhana then asked Maitreya, "O king of sages, how was Kirmīra slain by Bhīma?"
Maitreya said: "I shall not tell it, for you bear jealousy, and your son does not heed my words. This Vidura will tell you everything once I have gone."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Maitreya departed by the way he had come; and Duryodhana, disturbed by the news of Kirmīra's slaying, went outside.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "O Kṣattā, I wish to hear of the slaying of Kirmīra — tell me how the encounter came about between Bhīmasena and that demon."
Vidura said: "Hear this deed of Bhīma, whose acts surpass human measure — I have heard it before in the accounts told of them again and again."
"From here, O king, the Pāṇḍavas departed after being defeated at dice, and within three days and nights they reached that forest called Kāmyaka."
"At midnight in the deep of night, O king, at the midpoint of that dreadful hour when man-eating demons of terrible deeds roam freely —"
"— that forest the ascetics and other forest-dwellers always avoided from afar, out of fear of the man-eaters, it is said."
"As they entered there, O Bhārata, a fearsome demon with blazing eyes appeared blocking their path, carrying a firebrand."
"He stood spreading his great arms wide and his terrible mouth agape, blocking the path along which the best of the Kurus were travelling."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"With lips and fangs gnashing, copper-red eyes, and hair blazing upright, he resembled a storm cloud charged with the rays of the sun and crackled with lightning."
"He unleashed demonic illusions and roared with a great tumultuous sound, releasing a vast rumble like a rain-laden cloud."
"Terrified by his roar, birds from every direction cried out and flew together in panic, those of the land joining those of the water."
"That forest, filled with fleeing deer, leopards, buffaloes and bears, seemed as though it were itself moving away at his roar."
"Struck by the great wind he raised, the reddish-leafed branches swayed, and creepers grown at a distance clasped the trees in embrace."
"At that same moment a most dreadful wind blew; covered by the dust it raised, the sky lost its stars and became dark."
"The great enemy, unrecognized by the five sons of Pāṇḍu, was like the incomparable surge of grief upon the five senses."
"Seeing the Pāṇḍavas from afar clad in black antelope skins, he blocked the entrance to that forest like the mountain Maināka."
"Approaching him, the terrified Kṛṣṇā of lotus eyes, having never seen such a creature before, closed her eyes in fright."
"With her hair still dishevelled and cast about by Duḥśāsana's hand, standing amidst the five mountains that were her husbands, she trembled like a river in flood."
"As she was near to fainting, the five Pāṇḍavas caught hold of her, just as the senses hold fast to the pleasure dwelling in objects."
"Then the valiant Dhaumya, duly deploying various demon-slaying mantras, dispelled before the eyes of the sons of Pāṇḍu that terrible demonic illusion that had arisen."
"His illusion dispelled, the exceedingly powerful creature appeared in his true form — eyes wide with rage, assuming a shape of terrible desire, wicked and resembling death itself."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Then the far-sighted King Yudhiṣṭhira addressed him: 'Who are you, and whose? What is your purpose here — tell us what must be done for you.'"
"Then that demon replied to Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira: 'I am the brother of Baka, known by the name Kirmīra.'"
"'I dwell in this desolate Kāmyaka forest at my ease, defeating men in battle and making them my daily food.'"
"'Who are you, arrived here as food for me? I shall defeat you all in combat and devour you without care.'"
"Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard the words of that wicked one, then declared his clan, name and all the rest, O Bhārata."
"'I am Yudhiṣṭhira the Pāṇḍava, the Dharma-king — if the name has reached your ears — together with all my brothers Bhīmasena, Arjuna and the rest.'"
"'Having had my kingdom taken away and resolved to live in the forest, I have entered this dreadful forest that is your domain.'"
"Kirmīra then said to him: 'By good fortune the gods have brought about for me today what I have long desired in my heart.'"
"'For the sake of killing Bhīmasena I have always roamed the whole earth with weapon raised, yet have never come upon him.'"
"'By good fortune he who killed my brother — long sought and now encountered — is here; for it was by him that my dear brother Baka was slain.'"
"'In the house of Vetrakiya, O king, disguised in the form of a Brahmin, relying on the power of trickery — for he has no real strength of his own.'"
"'And Hiḍimba, my dear friend who roamed these forests, was slain by this wicked one, and his sister was carried off by him long ago.'"
"'This fool has entered my deep forest at our hour of roaming, when midnight has arrived.'"
"'Today I shall repay that long-nurtured enmity, and I shall satisfy Baka with an abundance of his blood.'"
"'Today, having freed myself from the debt to my brother and my friend alike, I shall attain the highest peace by slaying this thorn in the flesh of demons.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'If Bhīmasena was formerly spared by Baka, today I shall devour him before your very eyes, Yudhiṣṭhira.'"
"'For having slain this mighty-souled Vṛkodara today and fully consumed him, I shall digest him as Agastya did the great demon.'"
"Thus addressed, the righteous and truth-pledged Yudhiṣṭhira, angered, retorted 'This shall not be' and threatened the demon."
"Then great-armed Bhīma, uprooting a tree swiftly, stripped it of leaves — a tree some ten fathoms tall that had been torn up."
"Likewise Vijaya Arjuna, in the space of a single moment, strung the Gāṇḍīva, weighty as the thunderbolt's impact."
"Waving Jiṣṇu aside, Bhīma rushed at that demon of dreadful aspect and called out the words 'Stand! Stand!' O Bhārata."
"Having spoken thus, the mighty Pāṇḍava charged at him in fury, pressing his girdle tight, cracking palm against palm, with lips bitten, wielding the tree as his weapon — so Bhīma rushed upon him with speed."
"Then he brought it crashing down upon his head with speed, like the thunderbolt of Maghavan, resembling the staff of Yama."
"But the demon appeared unshaken in that battle and hurled back a blazing firebrand like a flaming thunderbolt."
"But Bhīma, foremost among warriors, kicked away that hurled firebrand with his left foot; then the demon came at him again."
"And Kirmīra too, swiftly uprooting a tree, fought back against the Pāṇḍava in battle, like an enraged officer with his staff."
"That battle with trees became a destruction of the forest, like the fight of the brothers Vālī and Sugrīva of old, each striving for glory."
"Trees fell upon their heads and were broken in many pieces, just as lotus flowers and water-lilies are crushed between two rutting elephants."
"Many trees there were shredded like munja grass, and lay scattered like torn rags across that great forest."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That battle with trees lasted for a good while, O lord of the people, between the foremost of demons and the foremost of men."
"Then the enraged demon, lifting up a boulder, hurled it at Bhīma as he stood fighting; and Bhīmasena staggered."
"The demon rushed around the Pāṇḍava stunned by the boulder-blow, his arms flung wide like rays, like Svarbhānu circling the sun."
"They grappled with each other, each dragging at the other; both appeared as two bulls locked in combat."
"Between them arose a most tumultuous and fearsome struggle, like that of two proud tigers armed with claws and fangs."
