"Thus questioned by him, the grandsire, wise and knowing all conclusions, spoke to him in full as he inquired about this doubt.
"Prahlāda said: 'Fiery energy is not always better, nor is forbearance always better — know this, dear one: both of these, without doubt.
"'He who always forbears, dear one, incurs many faults: servants despise him, and indifferent persons likewise.
"'And all creatures never bow to him at any time; therefore perpetual forbearance, dear one, is condemned by the wise.
"'For servants, despising him, go on to great misconduct and the feeble-minded seek to take away his wealth.
"'Conveyances, garments, ornaments, beds and seats, food and drink, and all his equipment —
"'— his officials, mindless, would take as they please, and what has been prescribed to be given they would not give in accordance with the master's command.
"'And they would never honor him with the honors due to a master; for in this world contempt is even more condemned than death.
"'To such a forbearing man, dear one, even servants, sons, subordinates, and those who behave indifferently speak bitter words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'They even desire his wives after showing contempt for the forbearing man, and his wives, mindless, behave as they please.
"'And those who are always rising — if they deserve even a small punishment from the lord, the wicked ones transgress and do harm.
"'These and many others are the perpetual faults of those who are always forbearing. Now, O son of Vairocana, know the faults of those who are without forbearance.
"'Whether in the right place or the wrong, constantly overcome by passion, in anger he inflicts various punishments through his own fiery energy.
Enveloped in wrath, he falls into conflict even with his friends, and becomes an object of hatred both from the world and from his own kinsmen.
From contempt, that man gains loss of wealth, reproach, disrespect, grief, hatred, greed, and enemies.
A man who inflicts various punishments on people out of anger quickly falls from his sovereignty, his life, and his own kindred.
He who approaches both those who harm and those who help with sheer force — people shrink from him just as from a serpent that has entered the house.
How can prosperity come to one from whom the world recoils? For when people see any opening, they will surely act against him. Therefore one should neither always unleash fierceness, nor should one always be gentle.
He who is gentle at the right time and harsh at the right time truly attains happiness both in this world and in the next.
Now I shall speak to you at length of the times for forbearance — those occasions that must never be abandoned, as the wise have declared.
If one who has previously done a benefit commits an offense that is not too grave, his transgression should be forgiven in return for that earlier service.
The offenses of those who acted out of ignorance should be forgiven, for wisdom is not easily attained by every person in every situation.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But if those who commit a deliberate wrong then claim it arose from ignorance — those wicked and dishonest men should be punished even for a minor offense.
A single offense by any living being should be forgiven; but if he offends a second time, he deserves to be punished, even if the harm done is small.
If any offense was committed unknowingly, the wise say it should certainly be forgiven — but only after careful investigation.
Gentleness conquers the gentle; gentleness conquers even the harsh. There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by gentleness; thus gentleness is sharper than sharpness.
Having considered place and time and one's own strength and weakness, one should not act at the wrong place or time — place and time must be awaited. Likewise, an offender should be forgiven out of fear of the people's reaction.
These are the enumerated occasions for forbearance. In all other situations where people act contrary to these, it is said to be the time for the display of energy.
Draupadī said: That, I believe, is exactly the time for your energy, O king — with the Dhārtarāṣṭras who are ever greedy and ever harmful.
For there is no occasion for forbearance now toward the Kurus. The time for energy has arrived — you ought to release that energy.
The gentle man is despised; people recoil from the fierce man. He who knows how to use both at the right time — he is a true king of the earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Know this, O greatly wise one — anger is the destroyer of men, yet anger is also their sustainer. Both existence and non-existence are rooted in anger.
For the man who restrains anger, O lovely one, there is flourishing. But the man who can never endure anger, O auspicious one — for him anger becomes most terribly destructive.
The destruction of creatures in this world is seen to be rooted in anger. How then could one like me release that anger which destroys the world?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
An angry man commits sin; an angry man may even slay his elders; an angry man with harsh words insults even his superiors.
When enraged, a man never knows what ought to be said and what ought not to be said. For one who is angry, there is nothing that cannot be done and nothing that cannot be said.
Out of anger one may harm those who should not be harmed, and honor those who deserve to be slain. An angry man may even send himself to the abode of Yama.
Seeing these faults, anger has been conquered by the wise who desire the highest good here and the best in the next world.
How could one like me practice that anger which the steadfast have renounced? Bearing all this in mind, Draupadī, my anger does not grow.
He who does not return anger to one who is angry saves both himself and the other from great danger — he is the healer of both.
If a foolish and powerless man grows angry when afflicted, he ultimately destroys himself before those who are more powerful.
For one bereft of self who abandons himself, the worlds are lost. Therefore, Draupadī, it is prescribed that one who lacks power must restrain his anger.
Likewise, the learned and powerful man who does not become angry when afflicted — having destroyed his tormentor, he rejoices in the next world.
Therefore the wise say that a man — whether powerful or weak — must always be forbearing, even in adversity.
The virtuous here praise the conquest of anger, O Kṛṣṇā. It is the abiding view of the good and the righteous that victory forever belongs to the forbearing.
Truth is better than falsehood, and kindness better than cruelty. How then could one like me release that anger, so full of faults and abandoned by the virtuous — even for the slaying of Suyodhana?
Him whom the learned, far-sighted men call truly energetic — it is certain that anger does not dwell within him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who repels anger as it arises by means of wisdom — the learned who see the truth consider him to be truly energetic.
An angry man, O fair-hipped one, does not see his duty as it truly is; an angry man perceives neither duty nor the boundaries of proper conduct.
An angry man slays even those who should not be slain, and wounds even his elders with harsh words. Therefore, when energy is to be exercised, anger should be kept at a great distance.
Skill, intolerance of wrong, courage, and swiftness — these are the qualities of energy. They cannot straightforwardly be attained by one overwhelmed by anger.
Having abandoned anger, a man properly attains energy suited to the occasion, O greatly wise one. Energy wielded by the angry is very hard to bear.
But anger is constantly called energy by the unlearned — that is the quality of rajas, ordained for the destruction of people in the world.
Therefore a man who acts rightly should always abandon anger. It is certain that one who does not deviate from his own duty without anger is better.
If all the transgressions are those of the unintelligent and the witless, how, O blameless one, could there be a transgression by one such as I?
If there were no forbearing men among humans, patient as the earth, there would be no reconciliation among people — for quarrels are rooted in anger.
One who is abused would abuse in return; one who is struck by a senior would strike back. Thus the destruction of beings would spread, and unrighteousness would be proclaimed.
Every man who is reviled would revile in turn; one who is struck would strike back; one who is harmed would cause harm in return.
Fathers would slay sons and sons would slay fathers in return; wives would slay husbands and husbands would slay wives.
In a world thus inflamed with anger, O Kṛṣṇā, there would be no birth. For know, O fair-faced one, that birth is the very root of the continuity of creatures.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In such a state, all creatures would quickly perish, Draupadī. Therefore anger leads to the destruction and non-existence of creatures.
But because patient men, steadfast as the earth, are seen in the world, therefore the birth and existence of creatures continues.
A man must be forbearing in all adversities in this world, O beautiful one. For forbearance is proclaimed to be the very existence and birth of all beings.
He who, though reviled and struck and enraged, forbears against one stronger than himself, and who is always one who has conquered anger — that learned man is the highest of persons.
Even if a man is powerful, eternal worlds are his reward. But the wrathful man of little wisdom perishes both after death and here in this world.
On this very point they cite these verses, eternally belonging to the forbearing — sung by the great-souled Kāśyapa who himself possessed forbearance, O Kṛṣṇā.
Forbearance is dharma; forbearance is sacrifice; forbearance is the Vedas; forbearance is sacred learning. He who knows it thus is worthy of bearing all things.
Forbearance is Brahman; forbearance is truth; forbearance is what has been and what will be; forbearance is austerity; forbearance is purity; and by forbearance the world is upheld.
The forbearing surpass the worlds of those who know Brahman, and the worlds of the ascetics, and even those of the knowers of sacrifice.
Forbearance is the energy of the energetic; forbearance is Brahman for the ascetics; forbearance is truth for the truthful; forbearance is charity; forbearance is renown.
How could one like me abandon such forbearance, O Kṛṣṇā — forbearance in which Brahman, truth, sacrifices, and all the worlds are established? The worlds of sacrificers are enjoyed by sacrificers, and those other worlds likewise by the forbearing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A wise man must always be forbearing. For when one forbears all things, he attains to Brahman.
This world belongs to the forbearing, and the next world too belongs to the forbearing. Here they attain honor, and in the beyond they attain an auspicious course.
Those men whose anger is always slain by forbearance — they attain the highest worlds. Therefore forbearance is considered supreme.
Thus were sung by Kāśyapa these verses, eternally belonging to the forbearing. Having heard these verses on forbearance, be content, Draupadī — do not be angry.
The grandfather, the son of Śaṃtanu, will honor peace; the preceptor, Vidura the Kṣattā, will counsel peace; and Kṛpa and Saṃjaya will likewise counsel peace.
Somadatta, Yuyutsu, and the son of Droṇa likewise, and our grandfather Vyāsa — all speak of peace always.
Being constantly urged toward peace by these men, it is my belief that the king will return the kingdom — unless greed destroys him.
This dreadful time has come for the destruction of the Bhāratas — this I have always known with certainty, even from before, O passionate one.
Suyodhana does not find forbearance thus, thinking "he does not deserve it." But I think "I am worthy of it" — and therefore forbearance finds me.
This is the conduct of the self-possessed; this is the eternal dharma — forbearance and non-cruelty. I will practice this straightforwardly.
Draupadī said: Homage to Dhātar and Vidhātar, who have created delusion in you! For when your ancestral and patrimonial duty should have been upheld, your mind has turned otherwise.
A man does not attain prosperity here by dharma and non-cruelty, nor by forbearance, nor by straightforwardness, nor ever by compassion.
If this unbearable misfortune has come upon you, O Bhārata — misfortune that neither you nor these your mighty brothers deserve —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— for neither then nor now, O Bhārata, has there ever been anything dearer to you than dharma — even dearer than life itself —
— your kingdom is for the sake of dharma, and your very life is for the sake of dharma — the Brāhmaṇas, the elders, and the gods all know this —
— it is my belief that you would abandon Bhīmasena, Arjuna, the sons of Mādrī, and even me, but that you would not abandon dharma.
"Dharma, when protected, protects the king who guards dharma" — thus have I heard from the noble ones. But I believe dharma does not protect you.
For your mind, O tiger among men, is single-mindedly fixed on dharma forever; it follows you always like a man's own shadow.
You never despised your equals, much less those who were better than you. Having obtained the entire earth, your pride never grew.
With svāhā-offerings, svadhā-offerings, and acts of worship, O Pārtha, you perpetually honored the twice-born, the deities, and the ancestors.
The Brāhmaṇas were always gratified by you with all their desires, O Pārtha; the ascetics, those intent on liberation, and the householders too, O Bhārata.
You give iron vessels to the forest-dwellers; there is nothing in your house that cannot be given to Brāhmaṇas.
That which is offered at the close of the Vaiśvadeva rite morning and evening — having given that to guests and servants, O king, you live on what remains.
Sacrificial rites, animal offerings, optional and occasional ceremonies, domestic fire sacrifices, and the daily performance of sacrificial duties — all these continue.
Even here in this great wilderness, desolate and frequented by bandits, though you have left your kingdom and dwell in exile, your dharma does not decay.
The Aśvamedha, the Rājasūya, the Puṇḍarīka, and the Gosava — you have performed even these great sacrifices with abundant gifts of honor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O king, with a clouded mind at the calamitous dice defeat, you were vanquished — your kingdom, your wealth, your weapons, your brothers, and even me.
For one who is upright, gentle, generous, modest, and truthful — how did a mind born of addiction to dice come to descend upon you?
Extreme delusion overtakes me and my heart is seared within, witnessing this suffering of yours and such a calamity as this.
On this topic they cite this ancient tale: the world abides under the sway of the Lord, not under the power of one's own self.
The Creator alone indeed apportions pleasure and pain, the pleasant and the unpleasant, for all beings — the Lord who is supreme, who emits the seed from the beginning.
Just as a wooden puppet, O hero among men, when set in motion, moves its limb after limb, so too, O king, does He move these creatures.
Like the sky pervading all beings, O descendant of Bharata, the Lord here ordains both the auspicious and the evil.
Like a bird bound by a string, this creature is controlled and powerless; standing under the sway of the Lord, it is master neither of others nor of itself.
Like a gem threaded on a string, like a bull led by the nose-rope — it follows the Creator's command, for it is constituted of Him alone and wholly surrendered to Him.
This human being is not self-governed for any span of time, like a tree fallen from its bank into the midst of a current.
This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain; impelled by the Lord, it may go to heaven or even to hell.
Just as the tips of grass come under the sway of the mighty wind, so all beings come under the sway of the Creator, O descendant of Bharata.
Engaging beings in noble actions or again in sin, the Lord pervades and moves through all creatures — yet He is not perceived as such.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This body, known as the field, is merely the instrument of the Creator — through it the all-pervading Lord causes actions of auspicious and inauspicious fruit to be performed.
Behold this power of illusion fashioned by the Lord — He who slays beings by means of other beings, having deluded them with His own māyā.
Things are seen one way by the sages who behold the Veda, yet they turn out otherwise — like the gusts of the wind.
Men indeed think of those various things one way, yet the Lord makes and unmakes them in quite another way.
Just as wood may be split by wood, stone by stone, and iron by iron — all inert and insensate —
— so that blessed God, the Self-Existent, the great Progenitor, slays beings by means of other beings, assuming a disguise, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Joining and separating — this Lord who acts as He wills, the Blessed One, sports with beings as a child with toys.
The Creator does not behave toward creatures as a mother or father would, O king; He acts as if impelled by wrath, like any ordinary person.
Seeing the noble, the virtuous, the modest ground down in livelihood, while the ignoble are prosperous — I am overwhelmed, as it were, with anguish.
Seeing this calamity of yours and the prosperity of Suyodhana, I reproach the Creator, O Pārtha, who looks on unequally.
Having bestowed fortune on the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who transgresses the codes of the noble, who is cruel, greedy, and contemptuous of dharma — what fruit does the Creator enjoy?
If the deed follows its doer and does not go to another, then surely the Lord is stained by that sinful act.
Or if a sinful deed done does not return to its doer, then mere force is the only cause in this world — and I grieve for the powerless.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Yājñasenī, what you have spoken is eloquent, adorned with varied phrases, and smooth — we have heard it; yet you speak in the manner of an atheist.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I do not practice dharma in quest of its fruits, O princess; I give because it is to be given, I sacrifice because it is to be sacrificed.
Whether there be fruit in this or not — whatever a man living as a householder ought to do, O Kṛṣṇā, I do that to the best of my ability.
I practice dharma, O fair-hipped one, not for the sake of its fruit; not transgressing the scriptures, looking to the conduct of the virtuous — it is dharma alone, O Kṛṣṇā, to which my mind is held by its very nature.
He who wishes to milk dharma of its fruit does not attain the fruit of dharma; and he who, after practicing it, doubts it out of atheism, being of sinful mind — he too does not.
Do not excessively doubt dharma out of arrogance or pride; a man who excessively doubts dharma is destined for the state of beasts.
He of weak spirit for whom dharma or the teaching of the seers would be a matter of excessive doubt — he falls away from the undying, undecaying world, as a śūdra falls away from the Veda.
One who is a student of the Veda, devoted to dharma, born of an illustrious family — him should kings who walk in dharma employ among the elders.
He is more wicked than śūdras — especially more so than thieves — that dull-witted transgressor of scripture who excessively doubts dharma.
For you have seen with your own eyes the great ascetic, the seer Mārkaṇḍeya of immeasurable spirit, who has attained long life through dharma.
Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Maitreya, Nārada, Lomaśa, Śuka, and other accomplished seers of pure minds — all have attained perfection through dharma alone.
You see these very ones with your own eyes — endowed with divine yoga, capable of curse and benediction, weightier even than the gods.
These very ones, resplendent as immortals, whose understanding is grounded in direct scriptural knowledge, always declare dharma first as what must be done by me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore, O auspicious one, you should not revile the Creator or dharma itself with a mind clouded by passion, nor should you doubt them.
He who excessively doubts dharma finds no authority in anything else; puffed up with himself as his own authority, he is contemptuous of the good.
The fool thinks that only this — what is witnessed by the world and bound up with the pleasure of the senses — is all there is, and falls into delusion regarding what lies beyond.
There is no expiation for him who excessively doubts dharma; brooding, that wretch and sinner does not attain the higher worlds.
He who transgresses all authority, reviles the import of the Vedic scriptures, and follows desire and greed — that fool goes to hell.
But he who is always resolute in mind, who resorts to dharma alone without doubting, O auspicious one — he attains eternity in the world beyond.
He who transgresses the authority of the seers, does not protect the duties of dharma, and oversteps all scriptures — that fool finds no welfare across his births.
O Kṛṣṇā, do not excessively doubt the dharma practiced by the disciplined, the ancient teaching proclaimed by the all-knowing, all-seeing seers.
Dharma alone is the raft — there is no other — for those going to heaven, O Draupadī; it is the vessel, like a merchant's ship reaching the far shore of the ocean.
If dharma, when practiced by those who walk in dharma, were to bear no fruit, this blameless world would sink into groundless darkness.
Men would not attain liberation, they would live the life of beasts, they would be joined only with destruction, and they would attain nothing of value.
Austerity, celibacy, sacrifice, study, generosity, and uprightness — if all these were indeed fruitless —
— then neither those here nor those far beyond would practice dharma; this would be utter deceit if all these acts were fruitless.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The seers and the gods, the gandharvas, asuras, and rākṣasas — lords all — for what reason would they practice dharma with devotion?
Knowing the Creator here to be the giver of fruit in the certain highest good, they practice dharma, O Kṛṣṇā — for that is the eternal dharma.
And this dharma is indeed fruitful; dharma is not said to be fruitless — for the fruits of learning and likewise of austerities are visibly seen.
Know this to be so in your own case, O Kṛṣṇā, as it has been heard; you also know how the valiant Dhṛṣṭadyumna was born.
This much is sufficient illustration, O bright-smiling one — that there is fruit to actions; the wise man is satisfied even by a small example.
For the ignorant who lack understanding are never satisfied even by much; for them there is no solace born of dharma or of action after death.
The arising of the fruit of actions — both meritorious and sinful — their origin and their dissolution: these are the secret mysteries of the gods, O passionate one.
No one whatsoever knows these things — creatures are bewildered in this matter; these are to be kept hidden by the gods, for the deities have concealed their mysteries.
Slender-limbed, of good vows, their sins burned away by austerity, endowed with serene minds — such brāhmaṇas indeed behold these things.
Dharma should not be doubted because its fruit is not visible, nor should the gods be doubted; one should sacrifice with diligence and give without envy.
"There is fruit to actions" — thus runs this eternal dharma; Brahmā declared it to his sons, and the seer Kaśyapa knows it.
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇā, let your doubt vanish like mist; resolve that all this exists, and abandon the disposition of atheism.
Do not revile the Lord, the Creator of all beings; learn from Him, bow to Him — let such a disposition as this not be in you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By whose grace His devotee, though mortal, attains immortality — O Kṛṣṇā, do not speak ill in any way of that supreme divinity.
Draupadī said: I do not disrespect dharma, nor do I blame it in any way, O Pārtha; how should I disrespect the Lord, the Progenitor of creatures?
Know me to be speaking thus in grief, O descendant of Bharata; and I shall lament yet further — hear that from me with a peaceful mind.
Action must indeed be performed in this world by one who is born, O crusher of foes; for it is only the immobile that live without action — not other beings.
From the drinking of the mother's breast right up to the approach of death's bed, mobile creatures gain their livelihood through action, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Among mobile creatures, men in particular, O bull of the Bhāratas, desire to obtain livelihood through action — both here and after death.
All beings know exertion, O descendant of Bharata; they enjoy the visible fruit of actions, witnessed by the world.
I see creatures living by their own exertion — even the Creator and the Ordainer do so, like this heron standing in the water.
Perform your own duty; do not be despondent; be armored by action. For among a thousand men, he who knows what is to be done — whether he be or not — truly is.
And even for him there would be something to be done — in increase and in protection; for even the Himālaya decays when eaten away without replenishment.
All creatures would perish if they were not to perform action; and even if we see men performing action whose fruit is nil, they know no other way whatsoever to sustain life in this world.
He who in the world is wholly given to fate, and he who insists only on willful exertion — both of these are base; the intelligence that abides in action is to be praised.
For he who, relying on fate, sleeps in ease without any effort, sinks down in utter foolishness like an unbaked pot in water.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Likewise he who is governed by willfulness, though capable of action, sits doing nothing — he would not live long, like a weak man without a protector.
When any man whatsoever attains a result without apparent cause, they attribute it to willful effort; yet that effort truly belongs to no one in particular.
And whatever a man obtains that is called fate, O Pārtha, which comes by divine ordinance — that is certainly declared to be destiny.
Whatever fruit a man attains by his own action, directly seen with the eye — that is remembered as human effort.
Another, acting by natural disposition, obtains results without apparent cause — know that fruit to be the product of inherent nature, O best of men.
Thus what a man obtains through willful effort, fate, natural disposition, and action — all that fruit is the result of deeds done in a former life.
For the Creator himself, as the lord, through those very causes, ordains and distributes here below the fruit of former deeds for men.
Whatever good or evil this man does — know that to be ordained by the Creator, the arising of the fruit of former karma.
This body is the instrument for his deeds in each action; as the Creator impels it, so this man acts helplessly.
In each and every task the Great Lord is the director; all beings, O son of Kuntī, he causes to act even against their will.
Having resolved upon goals in the mind, a wise man thereafter attains them through action guided by his intellect — he himself is the cause therein.
The deeds of men cannot even be enumerated, O bull among men; the success of households and cities is indeed caused by human effort.
As oil lies in the sesame seed, milk in the cow, fire latent in the wood — a wise man should discern these through intelligence, and also the means for their extraction.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thereafter he proceeds to the means for its accomplishment; creatures here below subsist on that success born of their actions.
Work done by a skilled person is determined by the doer to be well done; that done by the unskilled is known to be deficient — one perceives this clearly through the distinction.
There would be no fruit of sacred rites and charitable works, no pupil, no teacher — if this man were without agency in matters accomplished by action.
Solely because of agency is a man praised when his action succeeds; likewise he is blamed when it fails — how then can action be destroyed here?
Some say everything arises from willful effort alone; others say from fate alone; some say from human endeavor — this is declared as threefold.
Others again hold that one should not act on this basis alone — everything unseen exists, and so do fate and willful effort; for from both willful effort and fate is seen the continuity of results.
Something from fate, something from willful effort, something from one's own action — a man obtains his fruit; there is no fourth cause, so declare the wise who know the truth.
Likewise the Creator who bestows desired and undesired fruits upon beings — if he did not exist, there would be no one wretched among beings.
Whatever purpose a man desires and acts to achieve — that would bear fruit in every case, if there were no prior deeds.
Those men who do not perceive success in results through these three doors, and likewise the arising of failure — they are as the common people are.
"Action indeed must be done" — this is Manu's firm conclusion; for one who is wholly indifferent to effort is completely overwhelmed.
For the one who acts here generally finds success, O Yudhiṣṭhira; but a lazy man never anywhere attains unqualified achievement of results.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When something proves impossible, the means of expiation is still to be observed; and when one has done what can be done, O king of kings, freedom from debt is thereby attained.
Ill-fortune enters that man who lies sleeping in idleness; the capable man, obtaining results without doubt, enjoys prosperity.
Wise men devoted to action, freed from doubt, choose the uncertain adverse outcome over the certain one; they never rest anywhere in absolute certainty.
For a definite misfortune prevails over us at this moment; yet if you were steadfastly engaged in action, there is no certainty it would remain so.
Or perhaps success itself would come, and great glory to you as well as to Vṛkodara, to Bībhatsu, and to the twin brothers.
The actions of others bear fruit; so too might ours again — one who has done the work understands in time what fruit it yields.
The farmer splits the earth with his plough alone and sows his seed, then sits silent — the rain-cloud is the cause therein.
If the rain should not favor this farmer, yet some other man acts — he may say, "All that was done has been done by me."
"If that proves fruitless for us, there is no fault in us anywhere" — having reflected thus, the wise man should not blame himself in that matter.
"Though I act, no achievement of purpose comes to me" — O Bhārata, despondency must not be indulged on this account; for action has only these two outcomes: either success or failure; inaction is otherwise.
For it is through the convergence of many factors that action succeeds; when a quality is absent the fruit is deficient or entirely absent; yet in non-commencement no fruit and no merit are seen at all, O Acyuta.
A wise man employs place, time, means, and auspicious observances for prosperity through his intelligence, according to his capacity and his strength.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That must be done with diligence; an instructor of valor — in the application of action, all is indeed valor.
Whoever a wise man, reflecting well, regards as superior in many virtues — by conciliation alone let him seek his aim from that one, and apply his action accordingly.
Or let him await that one's misfortune or destruction, O Yudhiṣṭhira — even an ocean or a mountain meets its end; what then of one subject to mortal law?
A man who is constantly devoted to effort, while looking for the openings of others, attains freedom from debt both toward others and toward himself.
Nor should a man ever despise himself; for one who has held himself in contempt will not find prosperity, O Bhārata.
Thus is success in the world constituted, O Bhārata; the varied movement of success has been described according to the divisions of time and circumstance.
My father formerly lodged a learned brahmin with him; that brahmin spoke this very teaching to my father, O bull of the Bhāratas.
He formerly had my brothers learn the statecraft taught by Bṛhaspati; I heard their discourse on this very topic at home at that time.
He spoke to me consolingly, O king, as I came eager for activity and sat in my father's lap attending respectfully, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of Yājñasenī, Bhīmasena, exceedingly impatient, sighing deeply, approached and spoke angrily to the king.
"Go forth on the righteous path of kingship, befitting good men — what is the use for us, bereft of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, in dwelling in the forest of austerity?
That kingdom was not taken from us by dharma, nor by honesty, nor by might; it was taken by Duryodhana resorting to the fraud of the dice.
As a jackal takes the prey of lions, as the weak takes the food of the strong, as a glutton seizes leftovers — so our kingdom has indeed been stolen.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Concealed by a pretense of dharma, having abandoned wealth — the source of dharma and pleasure — why, O king, do you torment yourself in these hardships?
Through compliance with your command, as we watched helplessly, our kingdom was stolen — though it was protected by the Gāṇḍīva-bowman and could not have been taken even by Indra.
Like bilva fruits taken from the crippled, like cows taken from the lame — our sovereignty has been stolen while we live, because of you.
Saying 'this is your wish' — we have accepted such a great calamity as this, O Bhārata, you who are devoted to dharma and pleasure.
We are causing our own allies to wither and giving joy to our enemies, restraining ourselves under your command, O bull of the Bhāratas.
That we did not at that very moment slay these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having taken up your command — that evil deed torments us.
Now look upon this life of wandering in the forest as your own — O king, this way of living unworthy of heroes, not pursued by those who stand in strength.
This way of life neither Kṛṣṇa nor Bībhatsu nor Abhimanyu nor Sṛñjaya approves — nor do I, nor do the two sons of Mādrī.
You are ever worn thin by vows, saying 'dharma, dharma' — have you, O king, through despondency fallen into the life of a eunuch?
Base men, unable to bring prosperity for themselves, resort to despondency — fruitless and destructive of everything — for their own pleasure.
Yet you are far-sighted and capable, perceiving manliness in yourself — yet being devoted to non-cruelty, O king, you do not recognize what is harmful.
These sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra consider us, though enduring and truly virtuous, to be simply incapable — that is the sorrow; death in battle would not be.
If, fighting there without crookedness and without retreat, total death would be better — we would gain the worlds hereafter.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Or else, slaying them ourselves, O bull of the Bhāratas, we would take back the entire earth — even so that is indeed the better course for us.
In every way this is what we must do — we who follow our own dharma, who desire vast glory, who wish to repay our enmity.
For those fighting in their own cause, when the nature of their duty is known and the kingdom has been seized by others — praise alone is fitting, not blame.
That dharma whose purpose is the wasting of friends and of oneself — that, O king, is called calamity, not dharma; that is false dharma.
A man perpetually devoted to dharma who yet abandons dharma when weakened by it — dharma and wealth leave him entirely, like a dead man's joys and sorrows.
He whose dharma bears nothing but suffering in the cause of dharma — he is no wise man; he does not know the meaning of dharma, as a blind man knows not the radiance of the sun.
He for whom wealth exists solely for wealth's own sake — he too is not wise about wealth; he is like a hired man guarding a forest: the forest is his in name only.
He who pursues wealth beyond measure and does not practice the other two — he is fit to be slain by all beings and is despised like a killer of a brahmin.
He who is always in pursuit of pleasure and does not practice the other two — his friends perish and he falls away from both dharma and wealth.
For him who is bereft of dharma and wealth, destruction at the end of pleasure is certain — like a fish delighting in water when the water runs dry.
Therefore the wise are never negligent in the constant pursuit of dharma and wealth; for the nature of pleasure is like the fire-drill of fire — the fire of desire springs from dharma and wealth.
Wealth is in every way rooted in dharma, and dharma in its turn depends on the support of wealth — know these two as each other's source, like the cloud and the ocean.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The delight that arises from the conjunction of the object of material sense with the senses — that is desire, a mental resolve; it has no body of its own.
The man who seeks wealth, O king, attains great dharma; the man who seeks pleasure attains wealth as well; but from pleasure alone nothing other than pleasure is obtained.
For desire does not accomplish any further desire — that is its only fruit; as from consuming a fruit one gets only ash from the wood — so says the wise man.
Just as a fowler kills these birds, O king, so does one who harms living beings — this is the very form of unrighteousness among those who do violence to creatures.
He who, out of desire and greed, does not perceive the operation of dharma — that evil-minded one is fit to be slain by all living beings, both in the next world and in this one.
Clearly, O king, you know the meaning of the acquisition of wealth; you know its nature and its many corruptions as well.
Its loss or destruction — whether by old age or death — is considered a misfortune; and that misfortune now abides with us.
The delight that arises from the objects of the five senses, the mind, and the heart — that, in my understanding, is desire (kāma), and it is the highest fruit of action.
Having thus separately observed dharma, artha, and kāma, a man should not be devoted solely to dharma, nor solely to artha, nor solely to kāma — he should always pursue all three.
One should practise dharma in the morning, wealth in the midday, and pleasure in the evening — this, day by day, is the rule laid down by the scriptures.
In youth one should practise pleasure first, wealth in the middle years, and dharma in old age — such, at each stage of life, is the rule prescribed by the scriptures.
The wise man, best among those who speak rightly about dharma, artha, and kāma, knowing the proper time, should apportion and pursue all three in their proper seasons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Liberation is the highest good for those who seek happiness, O king; or else, O joy of the Kurus, one should attain it by applying intelligence together with the proper means.
Therefore, O king, let this be done quickly, or let attainment be achieved; for the life of one trapped in affliction is like the life of a sick man — all suffering.
Dharma is known to you and you have ever practised it; your friends, who know you, praise and urge you to action.
Giving, sacrifice, honouring the good, preserving the Vedas, and uprightness — this is the highest dharma, O king, and it bears fruit both here and in the hereafter.
This cannot be practised by one devoid of wealth, O king; and all the other virtues too, O tiger among men, would be complete only if one has the means.
The world is rooted in dharma, O king; nothing is superior to dharma; and dharma, O king, can only be practised through great wealth.
Wealth cannot be acquired by begging, nor by cowardice, nor at any time by the mind of one who thinks only of dharma, O king.
For you, begging — by which a brahmin may prosper — is forbidden; strive therefore to acquire wealth through your own energy alone, O bull among men.
Begging is not prescribed for a kshatriya, nor is the livelihood of a vaishya or shudra; for a kshatriya especially, dharma lies in his own innate strength.
The wise and learned call only the noble path dharma; adopt the noble course — you should not remain at a lesser level.
Understand well, O lord of kings; you know the eternal laws of dharma. You were born to perform fierce deeds, before which people tremble.
The fruit arising from the protection of subjects is not blameworthy for you; this eternal dharma, O king, has been ordained for you by the Creator.
Therefore, O Pārtha, if you deviate from this you will become a laughingstock in the world; for deviation from one's own dharma is not praised among men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Make your heart that of a kshatriya; cast off this slackness of mind; relying on your valour, O son of Kuntī, bear the yoke like a draught-ox.
Never did any king conquer the earth, O king, by being devoted to dharma alone, nor did he achieve prosperity, nor recover royal fortune.
Indeed, by surrendering himself as prey to many petty and greedy minds, one obtains a kingdom through cunning, just as the porcupine obtains its food.
Even the asuras — elder-born and vastly prosperous in every way — were completely defeated by the gods through cunning strategy, O bull of the Pāṇḍavas.
Knowing thus that everything belongs to the strong, O lord of the earth, slay your enemies, O mighty-armed one, by resorting to consummate strategy.
There is no warrior in battle equal to Arjuna among bowmen, nor will there ever be; and no man is or will be my equal as a wielder of the mace.
Even a man of great strength wages war through courage of spirit, O king, not through mere size, not through enthusiasm alone — be grounded in spirit, O Pāṇḍava.
For courage of spirit is the root of all prosperity; what is otherwise is false; it does not endure, just as the shade of a tree in winter does not persist.
One who desires greater wealth must give up lesser wealth — by the analogy of the seed, O son of Kuntī; let there be no doubt in you on this point.
But where, by spending wealth, only equal wealth ��� and no increase — would be obtained, no transaction should be made there; that would be mere futile scratching like a donkey.
In the same way, O lord of men, a man who gives up a lesser dharma gains a greater dharma; he is surely to be considered wise.
The wise sow division among an enemy's allies; the enemy, deserted by his divided allies, is weakened and brought under control.
Even a very powerful man wages war through spirit, O king; not through exertion alone, nor through sacrificial offerings, does one bring all subjects under one's sway.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In every way, even a powerful enemy can be slain by weak ones acting in concert — just as a honey-bee is killed by a swarm of other bees.
Just as the sun, O king, both nourishes and consumes all subjects with its rays, so too be you like the sun.
This too is an ancient austerity, as we have heard, O king — the dutiful protection of the earth as our forefathers performed it.
It is said that the radiance might depart from the sun and Lakṣmī from the moon — thus the world concludes upon seeing your present distress.
Assemblies filled with talk — praise of you and reproach of the other — have gathered separately in various places, O king.
And this above all, O king: your elders and brahmins, assembled here, speak joyfully of your steadfastness to truth.
That you have spoken no falsehood — neither out of delusion, nor meanness, nor greed, nor fear, nor desire, nor for the sake of gain.
Whatever sin a king incurs in the course of conquering the earth — all of that he afterwards washes away through sacrifices with generous fees.
By giving villages and thousands of cows to brahmins, O king, one is freed from all sins — just as the moon is freed from darkness.
All the citizens and countryfolk — young and old together — for the most part praise you, O Yudhiṣṭhira, O joy of the Kurus.
As milk poured into a dog's skin, or the Veda lodged in a low-born man, as truth in a thief, as strength in a woman — so is kingship in Duryodhana.
This saying has long circulated in the world, O Bhārata; even women and children repeat it as though it were a sacred recitation.
Therefore let Your Honour mount the chariot equipped with all accessories and march forth swiftly — to achieve long-awaited prosperity.
Having the foremost brahmins recite auspicious verses this very day, set out for Hāstinapura, surrounded by your brothers who are firm-bowed and skilled in weapons — heroes like venomous serpents, like Indra the slayer of Vṛtra surrounded by the Maruts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Crushing your enemies with your splendour as Indra crushed the asuras, O son of Kuntī, O mighty one, reclaim your sovereignty from the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
No mortal can endure the touch of the arrows loosed from the Gāṇḍīva bow, feathered with vulture plumes and swift as venomous serpents.
There is no hero, no elephant, no fine horse, O Bhārata, that could withstand the force of my mace when I am enraged in battle.
With the Sṛñjayas, the Kekayas, and the bull of the Vṛṣṇis at our side, how could we not win back the kingdom in battle, O son of Kuntī?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Undoubtedly, O Bhārata, what you say is true; by piercing me with the darts of your words you wear me down. I do not reproach you for this contrary speech — for this calamity came upon us through my own transgression.
For I followed the dice, wishing to win back from Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son the kingdom with all its territory; but that rogue gambler — Subala's son, working for Suyodhana — played against me and defeated me.
That great illusionist Śakuni, the mountain prince, ever casting masses of dice in the assembly hall, defeated me — guileless as I was — by trickery; only then did I see the wrong of it, O Bhīmasena.
Had I truly seen Śakuni's dice for what they were — favouring desire, loaded and unloaded as he wished — my self-control might have been possible; but anger destroys a man's steadiness.
The self cannot be restrained by manhood, by pride, or by valour alone, dear one, when it is bound up in them. I do not blame your words, O Bhīmasena; I think that is how things were destined to be.
That son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, desiring kingship, plunged us into this calamity and brought us to servitude, O Bhīmasena — even Draupadī, who had been our refuge, was brought to that state.
You know it, and so does Dhanaṃjaya — when we had come to the assembly hall for the second game of dice, what Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son said to me, before the Bhāratas assembled, as a single stake.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Twelve years in the forest, O prince — as you know, O Ajātaśatru — and then a thirteenth year, moving unrecognised, concealed, with all your brothers in disguise."
"If the Bhāratas' spies learn of your living thus, dear one, you shall live equally many more years concealed; having decided that, agree to it, O Pārtha."
"If you pass this period undiscovered by spies, O king, having baffled my agents with cunning — I speak the truth here in the Kuru assembly — those five rivers, O Bhārata, shall be yours."
"And we, all brothers together, conquered by you — setting aside pleasures for the appointed time, we shall live thus" — so that king said before the Kurus. And I answered him: "So be it."
Then there was that wretched second gambling match; defeated in it, all of us were banished. And so we wander through lands and through difficult forests in this distressed condition.
And Suyodhana, desiring no peace, fell again under the sway of his anger and stirred up all the Kurus — and whoever else came under his influence.
Having made that agreement in the presence of the good — who would break it now for the sake of kingship? I think it worse than death for a noble man to rule the earth by transgressing dharma.
If you were going to do a heroic deed, you should have done it then — when in the gambling hall you reached for the iron bar, yearning to burn their arms, but were restrained by Phalguna. What wrong would there have been then, Bhīma?
Why did you not declare your manhood before the agreement was made? But now, having let the appointed moment pass, why do you speak to me so excessively at this late hour?
Even greater is my sorrow, O Bhīmasena — knowing in the dice hall the taste of poison itself — that I endured seeing Yājñasenī being dragged about. That is what was borne, O Bhīma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But what was declared before the midst of the Kuru heroes cannot be undone today, O foremost of the Bhāratas; wait for the time of happiness to arise — like the sower of seeds waiting for the ripening of fruits.
For when one who has been previously wronged through treachery, knowing that enmity has flowered and fruited, takes full revenge through manly valour — then a hero truly lives in the world of the living.
And he attains full sovereignty in the world; I believe his enemies bow before him, his friends adore him with deep devotion, and they live in his service as the gods live in the service of Indra.
Know my vow, which is true: I choose dharma over immortality and over life itself; kingdom, sons, glory, wealth — all this does not equal even a fraction of truth.
Bhīmasena said: Making a pact with Time — the destroyer, the swift-winged, the endless, the immeasurable, the current that sweeps all away —
— you, a mortal bound by Time, think you can see Time directly? O great king, like foam it arises, and like fruit it falls.
He whose lifespan diminishes even by a blink of the eye — like collyrium powder falling from a needle's tip — why should he wait?
Only one who had unlimited life, or who truly knew its measure, who could see all things directly — only such a one might wait for the right time.
While we wait, O king, Time — having consumed thirteen years of our lives — will bring us to death itself.
Death is ever lodged within the body of every embodied being; therefore, before death comes, let us strive for the kingdom itself.
He who does not undertake a reckoning, who is indistinct though a lord of the earth — he who does not pursue vengeance against enemies sinks down like a cow (mired in mud).
The man of feeble courage and effort who does not requite enmity — I consider his birth fruitless, born as one born ill.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Your arms are as golden, O king, and renown is gained by slaying the enemy in battle and then enjoying the wealth won by those arms.
If a man, O king, O tamer of foes, were to go to hell in an instant for slaying the one who wronged him, that hell would be equal to heaven for him.
For the burning anguish born of indignation is more blazing than fire; scorched by it, I sleep neither by night nor by day.
And this Arjuna, son of Pṛthā — Bībhatsu, supreme in drawing the bowstring — sits utterly tormented, like a lion confined to a den.
He who alone surpasses all bowmen in the world — this very man holds back his inner heat and ardour like a great elephant restrained.
Nakula and Sahadeva, and our aged mother who bore heroes — wishing only for what pleases you, they sit as if dumb and mute.
All your kinsmen along with the Sṛñjayas wish only what is dear to you; I alone am utterly scorched, as is the mother of Prativindhya.
Whatever I say is indeed for the good of all; all have fallen into calamity, and all are eager for war.
There can be no more wretched calamity than this, O king — that our kingdom is seized by base men of little strength and is being enjoyed by them.
Seized by pity through a flaw of character, out of tenderness, O scorcher of foes, you endure these sufferings, O king — no one else praises this.
You are compassionate and have the nature of a brahmin — how were you born into the kshatriya class? For in this womb they are mostly born with fierce minds.
You heard the duties of kings as Manu proclaimed them — cruel, combined with deceit, prescribed, and devoid of peace.
When action is called for, O tiger among men, why do you sit like a snake on a bench, though endowed with intellect, valour, learning, and noble birth?
With a single handful of grass you wish to cover the Himālaya mountain — such is what you wish when you want to conceal us, O son of Kuntī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A life of passing unrecognised, in disguise, for one so widely known on earth — it cannot be done by you, O Pārtha, any more than the sun can move hidden in the sky.
Like a great śāla tree in a marsh laden with branches, flowers, and leaves, like a white elephant — how can Jiṣṇu (Arjuna) pass about unknown?
And these two brothers who resemble lions, these young men who go together — Nakula and Sahadeva — how will they wander about unrecognised, O Pārtha?
Draupadī, the princess of sacred fame, the mother of heroes, widely renowned — how will Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) wander unrecognised, O Pārtha?
And the people have known me since boyhood, O king; I see a life of concealment as impossible as hiding Mount Meru.
Likewise, many kings and princes devoted to Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been driven out of their kingdoms by us.
Those who have been wronged and expelled will not be pacified; they and those who seek their favour must inevitably do harm to us.
They too would deploy many spies against us in secret, and having identified us, would report us — that would be a very great danger for us.
We have duly dwelt in the forest for thirteen months by measure — reckon those as equivalent to that many full years.
There is a substitute month, as the wise declare — just as pūtika plants (are used) in place of soma; let it be done accordingly.
Or again, O king, one is released from sin by a single act of gratifying feeding of an honest ox that carries a good burden.
Therefore, O king, let your resolve be fixed on the slaying of enemies; for a kshatriya there is no other duty than battle.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of Bhīmasena, Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, that tiger among men and scorcher of foes, sighed deeply and fell into thought.
Having reflected for a moment and determined what was to be done, he spoke these words to Bhīmasena without pause between syllables.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
So it is, O mighty-armed one — as you say, O descendant of Bharata; but attend to this other matter of mine too, O one skilled in speech.
Those greatly sinful deeds that are undertaken through mere recklessness, O Bhīmasena, O descendant of Bharata — they come to grief.
Purposes succeed when well-counselled, well-executed, well-done, and well-considered, O mighty-armed one; and when they are thus, fate too becomes favourable.
But you, puffed up by pride in your strength, out of sheer impulsiveness, think this action should be undertaken by yourself alone — hear my view on that.
Bhūriśravas, Śala, and the mighty Jalasandha, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and the valiant son of Droṇa —
— the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, difficult to assail, headed by Duryodhana, all of them trained in weapons and perpetually set on aggression —
— and the kings and rulers whom we previously afflicted, who have now taken the Kaurava side and have developed affection for it —
— devoted to Duryodhana's welfare, not so devoted to ours, O descendant of Bharata — with full treasuries and endowed with strength, they will strive to protect him.
All the army of the Kauravas, together with their sons, ministers, and soldiers, have been given shares proportionate to their rank and enjoyed pleasures in every way.
Those heroes have been especially honoured by Duryodhana; they will lay down their lives in battle — this is my firm conviction.
Even if the conduct of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and the great-souled Kṛpa were equal toward us and toward them, O mighty-armed one —
— they must inevitably repay the royal salt (i.e., the king's benefaction), this is my view; therefore they will give up their lives in battle, even those lives so hard to relinquish.
All know the divine weapons; all are devoted to righteousness; they are unconquerable — this is my understanding — even by the gods with Indra at their head.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And there among them is Karṇa, the great warrior, always exultant and full of wrath, master of all weapons, irresistible, clad in impenetrable armour.
Without conquering all these foremost of men in battle, it is impossible for you to slay Duryodhana singlehanded, without allies.
I cannot attain sleep, O Vṛkodara (Bhīma), when I reflect on the swiftness of the charioteer's son (Karṇa) which surpasses all bowmen.
Hearing this speech, Bhīmasena, extremely wrathful by nature, became disheartened and frightened, and said nothing at all.
While those two Pāṇḍavas were thus conversing together, the great yogin Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, arrived.
Having approached and been duly honoured by the Pāṇḍavas, he spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira, that best of speakers.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O mighty-armed one, I know what is in your heart and mind; it is because of this wisdom that I have come quickly, O bull among men.
The fear of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the son of Droṇa, O descendant of Bharata, O slayer of enemies — that which revolves in your heart —
— that I will destroy for you by a means prescribed by scriptural rule; having heard it, take courage and implement it through action.
Then the son of Parāśara (Vyāsa), skilled in speech, led Yudhiṣṭhira aside in private and spoke to him these words full of pertinent meaning.
The supreme time of your welfare has arrived, O best of the Bhāratas — the time when Arjuna, Dhanaṃjaya son of Pṛthā, will overcome the enemies in battle.
Receive this knowledge called Pratismṛti (the Recollection) which I now declare — it is as if success itself made incarnate; I speak it to you as a supplicant, and having obtained it, the mighty-armed Arjuna will accomplish his purpose.
For the sake of weapons let him approach Mahendra (Indra), Rudra, Varuṇa, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and the King of Dharma (Yama), O Pāṇḍava; for he is capable of seeing the gods through both austerity and valour.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This one (Arjuna) is a seer of great splendour, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa; he is ancient, eternal, divine — a portion of Viṣṇu, everlasting.
Having received the weapons from Indra, from Rudra, and from the guardians of the worlds, the mighty-armed one will accomplish a great deed.
And from this forest, O son of Kuntī, let another forest be sought out — whatever would be fitting for your residence, O lord of the earth.
For a prolonged stay in one place would not be pleasing, and it would cause disturbance to the peaceful ascetics living there.
There would also be the consumption of game and the depletion of plants and herbs; and you are supporting many brahmin scholars versed in the Vedas and their branches.
Having spoken thus, the blessed lord (Vyāsa), the knower of the truth of yoga, imparted to the pure supplicant the unsurpassed knowledge of yoga.
The wise Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, having imparted it to the King of Dharma and having taken leave of the son of Kuntī, vanished there and then.
But Yudhiṣṭhira, righteous in soul, that wise one, restrained in mind, retained that sacred knowledge, practising it repeatedly from time to time.
Gladdened by Vyāsa's words, he then departed from Dvaitavana forest and went to the forest named Kāmyaka on the bank of the Sarasvatī.
O great king, brahmin scholars versed in the syllables of learning, endowed with austerity, followed him, as the sages follow the lord of the gods.
Having reached Kāmyaka, those bulls of the Bharata line, great-souled, along with their ministers and followers, settled there again.
There they dwelt for some time, O king, those men of firm resolve, those heroes devoted to the science of archery, listening to the highest Veda.
Ranging the forest in daily hunting, seeking game with pure arrows, they made oblations to the ancestors, the gods, and the brahmins according to injunction.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, after some time had passed, King Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, recalling the sage's instruction, spoke these words.
In a secluded place, touching him with his hand, smiling gently, he addressed Arjuna, that bull of the Bhāratas, whose wisdom is well-known.
Having reflected for a moment on their forest exile, the dharma-king, tamer of foes, spoke these words to Dhanaṃjaya in private.
In Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the son of Droṇa, O descendant of Bharata — in these five today is established the four-footed science of archery.
The Brahmā, divine, and demoniac (classes of weapons), along with their application and remedy, and the deployment of all weapons — they know all this in its entirety.
All of them have been conciliated by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, given their portions, and satisfied; he behaves toward them as if they were his gurus.
And his conduct toward all warriors is ever excellent; honoured at the proper time, they will not fail to exert their full strength.
Today this entire earth follows under Duryodhana's sway; on you our refuge rests, on you the burden is placed — in that regard I see a task that the present time calls for, O tamer of foes.
From Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana (Vyāsa) I have received the secret wisdom, dear one; through that knowledge properly employed the whole world is illuminated — with that sacred wisdom, dear one, be united, with mind fully composed.
Wait upon the grace of the gods at the proper time; yoke yourself to fierce austerity, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Bearing your bow, clad in armour, carrying your sword, sage-like and possessed of essence, yielding the path to none, go northward, dear one — for in Indra all the divine weapons in their entirety dwell, O Dhanaṃjaya.
The gods, frightened of Vṛtra, then entrusted all their power to Indra; all of that collected in one place — you shall then obtain it all.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seek refuge with Śakra alone; he will bestow the weapons upon you. Be consecrated this very day and go to behold the god who shatters citadels, Purandara.
Having spoken thus, the lord Dharmarāja himself instructed him; the elder brother then gave leave to that hero, his brother, duly consecrated, with speech, body and mind fully restrained.
By the command of Dharmarāja, to behold the god Purandara, he took up the bow Gāṇḍīva and likewise the two inexhaustible great quivers.
Clad in armour, with arm-guard and finger-guard fastened on, the mighty-armed one offered oblations to the fire, honoured the brahmins with golden gifts, and had auspicious verses recited.
The mighty-armed one set forth, bow in hand, to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, breathing deeply and gazing upward.
Seeing that son of Kuntī there with bow raised, brahmins, siddhas, and invisible beings all spoke: "Swiftly attain, O son of Kuntī, whatever your mind desires."
As Arjuna moved away like a lion, his thighs like the trunk of a śāla tree, Kṛṣṇā, having captured the minds of all, spoke these words.
"Whatever Kuntī desired for you when you were born, O mighty-armed Dhanañjaya — may all of that be yours, O son of Kuntī, and even more as you yourself may wish."
"Let no one be born into our kṣatriya family — everlasting homage to the brahmins, whose livelihood does not depend on battle."
"Surely all your brothers, keeping vigil, will delight in tales of you, praising your heroic deeds again and again."
"O Pārtha, neither in pleasures nor in wealth nor in life itself will our satisfaction or our thoughts exist while you are long away."
"In you, O Pārtha, all our happiness and sorrow are concentrated — life and death itself, kingdom and lordship alike. You have taken leave of me, O son of Kuntī; go well, O Pāṇḍava."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Homage to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ! Go well and unharmed. May you be protected from aerial beings, O Bhārata, from earthly ones, from divine beings, and from whatever other adversaries there may be."
Then, having circumambulated his brothers and Dhaumya, the mighty-armed Pāṇḍava set forth, taking up his splendid bow.
All beings drew aside from his path as he went, for he was endowed with Indra's divine power and was mighty with valor and energy.
He, the great-souled one, reached the sacred mountain in a single day, moving with the speed of thought, united in yoga like the wind itself.
Crossing the Himālaya and Gandhamādana as well, he traversed those difficult mountain passes day and night without fatigue.
Reaching Indrakīla, Dhanañjaya then halted, for he heard a voice in the sky saying: "Stay here."
Then the left-handed archer saw at the foot of a tree an ascetic blazing with brahminical splendour — tawny-coloured, matted-haired and lean.
That great ascetic, seeing Arjuna standing there, said: "Who are you, dear one, who has arrived here bearing a bow, clad in armour, with arrows, arm-guard fastened on, following the dharma of a kṣatriya?"
"Here there is no use for weapons; this is the abode of the peaceful, of brahmins and ascetics who have subdued anger and joy."
"There is no purpose here for a bow, nor for battle at any time. Set down this bow, dear one — you have reached the highest path."
Thus the brahmin kept addressing that hero of boundless might repeatedly, just as he would address an ordinary man, yet he could not shake him from his composure, firm and resolute in his determination.
Then that twice-born one, pleased and as if smiling, said to him: "Choose a boon — good fortune to you! I am Śakra, O destroyer of enemies."
Thus addressed, Dhanañjaya, the hero and upholder of the Kuru lineage, bowed with joined palms and replied to the thousand-eyed one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This is indeed my cherished desire; grant me this boon: from you, O blessed one, I wish today to learn the whole science of weapons."
The great Indra replied to him, his heart pleased and as if smiling: "What need of weapons do you have now that you have arrived here, O Dhanañjaya? Choose desires and worlds — you have reached the highest state."
Thus addressed, Dhanañjaya replied to the thousand-eyed one: "Not worlds, nor desires once more, nor divinity — how much less pleasure!"
"Nor do I desire sovereignty over all the immortals, O lord of the thirty gods — for leaving those brothers of mine in the forest and failing to requite the enmity, I would bear infamy in all the worlds for eternal ages."
Thus addressed, the slayer of Vṛtra, worshipped by all the worlds, replied to the son of Pāṇḍu, soothing him with gentle speech.
"When you behold the lord of all beings, the three-eyed Śiva who bears the trident, then, dear one, I shall grant you all the divine weapons completely."
"Make effort to obtain a vision of the highest god; by the sight of him, O son of Kuntī, you will be perfected and will attain heaven."
Having spoken thus to Phalguna, Śakra then vanished from sight. And Arjuna too remained right there, absorbed in yoga.
Janamejaya said: "O blessed one, I wish to hear at length this account of Pārtha of tireless deeds — how he obtained the weapons."
"How did that tiger among men, the long-armed radiant Dhanañjaya, enter the forest void of humans without fear?"
"And what did he do while dwelling there, O best of knowers of Brahman? How were the blessed Sthāṇu and the king of the gods both pleased?"
"This I wish to hear through your grace, O best of twice-born ones, for you, the all-knowing, understand both divine and human matters."
"O greatly wise one, it is said that Arjuna, peerless in battle, the foremost of fighters and undefeated in combat, once fought an incomparable battle with Bhava — most wonderful and thrilling to hear."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Hearing of which, the hearts of even the heroic sons of Pṛthā trembled with a mingling of awe, elation and wonder."
"And whatever else Pārtha did — recount all of it in full. For I see not even the slightest reprehensible act in the deeds of that victorious hero. Tell me everything of that brave one's conduct."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "I shall narrate to you, dear one, this account of the great-souled one — divine, great and of incomparable wonder, O tiger of the Kurus."
"Hear attentively, O sinless one, the bodily contact and encounter between Pārtha and the three-eyed god of gods, that meeting in its proper order."
"By Yudhiṣṭhira's command that one of boundless valour went to behold Śakra, the lord of the gods, and also Śaṃkara, the god of gods."
"Taking up that divine bow and also his sword, Arjuna, that bull among men, mighty and great-armed, O Kauravya, set out toward the north, toward the peaks of the Himālaya, for the accomplishment of his purpose."
"The son of Indra, O king, steady of mind, the great warrior of all the worlds, filled with utmost urgency, firm in his resolve for austerity, entered alone into the terrible thorny forest."
"It was adorned with various flowers and fruits, frequented by various birds, filled with herds of various animals, and haunted by siddhas and cāraṇas."
"Then, when the son of Kuntī had set forth into that forest devoid of humans, the sound of conches and kettledrums arose in the sky."
"And a great shower of flowers fell upon the earth, while a vast web of clouds spread over and covered everything on all sides."
"Having crossed the difficult forest passes, near the great mountain, Arjuna dwelling on the slopes of the Himālaya shone with beauty."
"There he beheld trees in full bloom, sweetly ringing with birds, and rivers with many eddies resembling dark-blue lapis lazuli."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"They resounded with the songs of geese and karaṇḍava ducks, the calls of sārasa cranes, the cries of male cuckoos, and the clamour of krauñca birds and peacocks."
"Seeing in that place the charming forested regions, and the sacred, cool, clear waters, Arjuna, that supreme chariot-warrior, became delighted in heart."
"Arjuna, then delighting in that pleasant forest region, engaged in fierce austerity, blazing with fierce energy, great-souled."
"Wearing a robe of darbha grass, adorned with staff and deer-skin, eating only fruit once every three full nights, he passed the first month; and with doubly extended intervals he passed the second month."
"In the third month too, he ate only once a fortnight, subsisting on withered leaves that had fallen to the ground."
"When the fourth full month arrived, thereafter the mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu subsisted on air alone — arms raised high, unsupported, standing on the tips of his great toes."
"Through his constant contact with water, the matted locks of that great-souled one of boundless energy came to resemble lightning and the lotus clouds."
"Then all the great seers went to the divine bearer of the Pināka, the blue-throated one of great fortune, and prostrating themselves and propitiating him, they all reported that deed of Phalguna."
"This Pārtha of great energy has taken to the slopes of the Himālaya and stands fixed in fierce, unapproachable austerity, sending smoke into all the directions."
"O lord of the gods, none of us know what he intends; he is causing us all distress — please, let him be properly restrained."
Maheśvara said: "Go back quickly, joyful and without fatigue, the same way you came. I know the resolve that abides in his mind."
"He has no longing for heaven, nor for lordship, nor for long life. Whatever is desired by him in full — that I shall accomplish this very day."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Hearing the words of Śarva, those seers who speak the truth returned, their hearts rejoiced, each to their own hermitage."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "When all those great-souled ascetics had departed, the blessed Hara who bears the Pināka and removes all sins —
— assuming the guise of a Kirāta hunter, resembling a golden tree, blazing with his form like another Mount Meru —
— taking up a splendid bow and arrows like venomous serpents, descended with great blazing radiance, burning like fire consuming dry grass.
Accompanied by the goddess Umā, dressed in matching vow and garb, and attended by joyful beings wearing various costumes, the glorious one came thus.
Concealed in the guise of a Kirāta hunter, followed by thousands of women, that god then shone exceedingly, O king, O Bhārata.
In an instant that entire forest became silent; the sound of streams ceased, and even the birds fell quiet.
Approaching nearby, he saw a son of Diti named Mūka near the one of tireless deeds, Pārtha — a being of astonishing appearance.
Having assumed the form of a boar and seeming to stalk Arjuna for the kill, that supremely evil-souled one was then addressed by Phalguna.
Taking up the Gāṇḍīva bow and arrows like venomous serpents, stringing that best of bows and making it resound with the twang of its string —
"Because you seek to kill me, guiltless as I am who have come here — therefore I shall send you first to the abode of Yama."
Seeing Phalguna with bow firmly drawn, about to strike, Śaṃkara in the form of a Kirāta suddenly restrained him.
"This one dark as a rain-cloud was claimed by me first" — but disregarding that very word, Phalguna then struck.
And the Kirāta of great radiance simultaneously into that same single target released an arrow like a thunderbolt, like a flame of fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those two arrows released by both of them fell simultaneously on the vast, mountain-solid body of Mūka.
Like the crash of a thunderbolt, like Vajra striking a mountain, so was the collision of those two arrows then.
Pierced by many arrows like blazing-mouthed serpents, he died, having once more assumed a terrible rākṣasa form.
Then Jiṣṇu (Arjuna), slayer of enemies, saw a man of golden radiance, disguised in the garb of a Kirāta hunter and accompanied by women. The son of Kuntī, with a glad heart and as if laughing, addressed him.
"Who are you, wandering in this empty forest surrounded by a company of women? Do you feel no fear in this terrible forest, O man of golden radiance?"
"And why have you shot this deer that was my quarry? I had pursued it first — for this was a rakshasa that came here in disguise."
"Whether out of desire or out of contempt, you shall not escape me with your life. This is not the law of the hunt — what you have done to me today. Therefore I shall deprive you of your life, O dweller of the mountain."
Thus addressed by the son of Pāṇḍu, the Kirāta, as if laughing, spoke in a soft voice to Savyasācin, that Pāṇḍava.
"This was my target first — it was my quarry from the beginning, and it was by my blow alone that it was stripped of its life."
"You should not attribute your own faults to another, puffed up with your own strength. I am under a vow, O dull-witted one — you shall not escape from me alive."
"Stand firm! I shall release arrows like thunderbolts upon you. Strive with all your might — you too release your arrows."
Then those two, both enraged, roaring again and again at each other, cut at one another with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then Arjuna released a rain of arrows upon the Kirāta, and Śaṅkara (Śiva) received it with a serene and undisturbed mind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having received that rain of arrows for a moment, the wielder of the Pināka bow stood with his body utterly unhurt, immovable as a mountain.
Seeing that rain of arrows rendered utterly fruitless, Dhanañjaya was filled with the greatest wonder and said, "Well done! Well done!"
"Ah, this tender-limbed dweller of the Himālayan peaks receives iron arrows shot from the Gāṇḍīva bow without the slightest agitation!"
"Who can this be in person — a god, Rudra, a yaksha, or the lord of the gods? For on this best of mountains there is an assembly of the thirty gods."
"Truly, none other is capable of withstanding the force of my showers of arrows released by the thousands, except the god who holds the Pināka bow."
"Whether this be a god or a yaksha, someone stationed here other than Rudra — I shall send him to the abode of Yama with my sharp arrows."
Then Jiṣṇu, with a joyful heart, released by the hundreds iron arrows that could pierce vital spots, O king, like the sun sending forth its rays.
The blessed Lord, sustainer of the worlds, the trident-bearer, received all of them with a calm mind, like a mountain receiving a shower of stones.
In a moment Phalguna's arrows were exhausted; and then, seeing his supply of arrows depleted, he fell into fear.
Jiṣṇu then thought of the blessed fire-god Agni, who had formerly given him two inexhaustible quivers at the time of the Khāṇḍava forest fire.
"What shall I do with my bow now that my arrows are exhausted? And this man — whoever he is — swallows up all my arrows completely."
"I shall send him to the abode of Yama, the wielder of the rod, with the tip of my bow, as one would drive an elephant with the point of a goad."
The son of Kuntī, that slayer of enemy heroes, then fought with the tip of his bow — but that divine bow was swallowed up too by the mountain-dweller.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Arjuna, his bow having been swallowed, stood with sword in hand; desiring to bring the battle to an end, he charged at him with great speed.
The joy of the Kurus, striding forward with the strength of his arms, brought down his sharp sword upon the head of that one — even that sword, which does not stick even in mountains, shattered upon reaching his head.
Then Phalguna fought with trees and with rocks — but the great-bodied one received the trees and then the rocks without any harm.
Then Pārtha, of great strength, struck the blessed Lord who wore the Kirāta form — on the face of that one who was in the guise of a Kirāta, who was difficult to assail — with his fists, whose touch was like that of the thunderbolt, raising smoke upon impact.
Then the blessed Lord, in the guise of a Kirāta, tormented Phalguna with his own fists, which were dreadful and equal to the thunderbolt of Indra.
Then arose a loud and most terrible cracking sound from the fists of the Pāṇḍava and of the Kirāta as they fought.
For a good while there was that great battle, hair-raising and filled with blows of the arms, like the fight between Vṛtra and Vāsava (Indra).
Then mighty Jiṣṇu seized the Kirāta with his chest; and the Kirāta, in turn, forcefully struck the struggling Pāṇḍava.
From the crushing grip of their arms, and from the friction of their chests, fire with smoke and embers arose on their bodies.
Then Mahādeva, squeezing him with his limbs and utterly crushing him, overpowered him with his divine energy, in his fury bewildering his mind.
Then Phalguna, with his limbs crushed and his body compressed, appeared as if reduced to a lump, his body seized by the god of gods, O Bhārata.
He became unable to breathe, utterly held down by the great-souled one, and then fell down in a stupor — and thereupon Bhava (Śiva) was pleased.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Blessed One said: "Ho, ho, Phalguna! I am satisfied with your unmatched deed, with this valor of yours, and with your steadfastness. There is no kshatriya your equal."
"Equal today are your energy and valor and mine, O sinless one. I am pleased with you, O mighty-armed one — look upon me, O bull among men."
"I shall grant you the divine eye, O wide-eyed one. You are an ancient seer. You will conquer all your enemies in battle, even the celestials who dwell in heaven."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Phalguna there beheld the god, the great god, the mountain-dweller, the trident-bearer, of great radiance, together with the goddess.
He, Pārtha the conqueror of enemy cities, went down on both knees to the ground and bowing his head, sought to propitiate Hara.
Arjuna said: "O Kapardī (wearer of matted locks), lord of all beings, destroyer of Bhaga's eyes — O Blessed Lord, O Śaṅkara, please forgive my transgression."
"Longing for the sight of you, O Lord, I have come to this great mountain, this beloved and supreme abode of ascetics, O lord of the gods."
"I entreat you, O Blessed One, worshipped by all beings. May this offence of mine, committed out of reckless boldness toward Mahādeva, not count as a transgression."
