Seeing Cyavana and Sukanyā, who looked like two children of the gods, king Śaryāti rejoiced as if he had gained the entire earth.
Honored by that seer, the lord of the earth sat down with his wife and the great-minded one engaged in auspicious conversation.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the descendant of Bhṛgu, consoling him, O king, said: "I shall perform a sacrifice for you, O king — make ready the materials."
Then Śaryāti, lord of the earth, most greatly delighted, O great king, honored that word of Cyavana.
On an auspicious day fit for sacrifice, Śaryāti had an excellent sacrificial hall constructed, filled with every desired abundance.
There the descendant of Bhṛgu, Cyavana, officiated at the sacrifice for that king. And there were wonders there — hear them from me.
Cyavana then took the soma portion for the two divine Aśvins, but Indra tried to stop that cup being taken for them.
Indra said: "Both these Nāsatyas are not worthy of soma — such is my opinion. Being physicians to the sons of gods by their function, they are not entitled to it."
Cyavana said: "Do not despise those two great souls, superior in beauty and worth, O Maghavan, who made me ageless as if among the immortals."
"Apart from you and the other gods — how could they not deserve the soma feast? Know the Aśvins too as gods, O Indra, O destroyer of citadels."
Indra said: "They are healers, doers of tasks, who assume forms at will and roam the mortal world — how can they be worthy of soma here?"
Lomaśa said: When Vāsava kept repeating this same argument, the descendant of Bhṛgu, disregarding Śakra, took the cup.
Then the god who had slain Bala, seeing him about to take that excellent soma for the Aśvins, spoke these words:
"If you yourself take the soma for those two, I will hurl at you my thunderbolt, fearsome and unequalled in form."
Thus addressed, the descendant of Bhṛgu, smiling, looked at Indra and took, according to the proper rite, the excellent soma cup for the Aśvins.
Then the lord of Śacī hurled his fearsome thunderbolt at him, but the descendant of Bhṛgu paralyzed his arm as it was about to strike.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having paralyzed him, Cyavana, of surpassing splendor, poured oblations into the fire with mantras, intent on performing a rite and ready to harm the god.
Then from the power of that seer's austerities there arose from the rite a mighty being named Mada — a great asura of immense valor and vast body, whose form could not be described by gods or demons alike.
His mouth was terrifying and immense, with sharp-tipped teeth; one of his jaws rested on the earth and the other reached up to the sky.
His four long fangs each measured a hundred times a hundred leagues, while his other teeth were ten leagues each, shaped like ramparts and appearing like the tips of spears.
His two arms, like mountains, stretched ten thousand leagues each; his eyes resembled the sun and moon; his face was like that of Death himself.
He licked his mouth with a tongue flickering like lightning, his jaws gaping wide, his glance terrible, as if swallowing the entire world by force.
Enraged and about to devour him, he charged at the performer of a hundred sacrifices with his mighty and fearsome form, making all the worlds resound with his roar.
Lomaśa said: Seeing Mada of the dreadful mouth, coming to devour him with jaws agape like Death himself, the god of a hundred sacrifices —
— his arm already paralyzed with fear, repeatedly licking the corners of his mouth, the king of the gods then spoke to Cyavana, oppressed by fear:
"The Aśvins shall be worthy of soma from this day forward, O descendant of Bhṛgu. This word I speak to you truly, O brahmin."
"Let your undertaking not be in vain — this shall be the highest rule henceforth. I know, O seer among brahmins, that you will not act falsely."
"Just as the Aśvins have this day been made worthy of soma by you, O descendant of Bhṛgu, may your power shine even more brightly."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And may the fame of Sukanyā's father spread through the world — it is for this that I arranged this manifestation of your power. Therefore be gracious to me; let this be as you wish."
When Śakra had spoken thus to the great-souled Cyavana, his anger quickly departed and he released the destroyer of citadels.
And the mighty one divided Mada, O king, distributing him repeatedly — as previously created — among wine, women, dice, and the hunt.
Having thus dispersed Mada, and having satisfied Śakra with the soma, and having officiated at that king's sacrifice with the Aśvins included among the gods —
— having made his power known throughout all the worlds, that best of speakers then sported in the forest with the devoted Sukanyā.
This lake of his, O king, resounds with the chanting of twice-born men and shines with glory. Here you should satisfy the ancestors and the gods together with your brothers.
Having seen this, O lord of the earth, O Bhārata, and reaching the Saindhava forest with its sandy shallows, behold the streams. O great king, touch the water at all the lotus pools.
The Ārcīka mountain is indeed the abode of the wise, ever fruitful, ever flowing, the supreme station of the Maruts. These hundreds of sacred shrines here belong to the thirty gods, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
This is the sacred ford of the Moon, worshipped by seers — the Vaikhānasa sages and likewise the Vālakhilyas attend upon it.
The three sacred peaks and the three springs — circumambulate all of them and touch the waters as you wish.
Here, O son of Kuntī, O lord of men, Śaṃtanu, Śunaka, and both Nara and Nārāyaṇa have attained the eternal abode.
Here the gods who dwell eternally, and the ancestors, practised austerities on the Ārcīka mountain along with the great seers — worship them here, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Here the sages partook of the ritual rice-cakes, O lord of peoples. The Yamunā with its inexhaustible stream is here, and Kṛṣṇa is engaged in austerities in this place.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The twins, Bhīmasena, Kṛṣṇā — all of us will go there, O crusher of enemies, lean and deeply practised in austerities.
This is the sacred spring of Indra, O lord of men, where Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Varuṇa came in ancient times.
Here they dwelt, O king — forbearing and supremely righteous; this finest of mountains is auspicious for those of friendly and upright mind.
This is that Yamunā, O king, attended upon by hosts of royal sages, adorned with many sacrifices, O king — holy, dispelling the fear of sin.
Here king Māndhātā, the great archer, himself performed sacrifice; and Sahadeva, O son of Kuntī, and Somaka, the foremost of the generous, also did so.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Māndhātā, that tiger among kings, is renowned throughout the three worlds — how was he born, O great brahmin? That best of kings, the son of Yuvanāśva, of boundless splendor — how did he attain this supreme eminence?"
"The three worlds were subject to him like those of the great-souled Viṣṇu — I wish to hear the deeds of that wise one."
"And how did the name Māndhātā come to him who equals Śakra in splendor, and whose valor was unmatched? For you are skilled in narrating."
Lomaśa said: "Listen attentively, O king, to how the name Māndhātā of that great-souled king is sung throughout the worlds."
"Yuvanāśva, lord of the earth, sprung from the lineage of Ikṣvāku, O guardian of the earth, performed sacrifices with abundant gifts."
"Having performed a thousand horse sacrifices, that best of those who uphold dharma, and also other foremost and various sacrifices with ample gifts —"
"— yet that great-souled royal seer, firm in his vows, remained without a son; he entrusted the kingdom to his ministers and took to living in the forest."
"Uniting himself with his own self by the rule prescribed in scripture, his heart parched with thirst, he entered the hermitage of Bhṛgu."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That very night, O lord of kings, the great-souled son of Bhṛgu, the great seer, performed a rite for the sake of a son for Saudyumni."
"A great jar filled with water consecrated by mantras stood there, O lord of kings, having been prepared beforehand with concentrated intent — by drinking from it, the wife of him would give birth to a son equal to Śakra."
"Having placed that jar on the altar, the great seers fell asleep, wearied from their vigil through the night; and Saudyumni, passing them by —"
"— the king, parched of throat, sorely tormented by thirst, craving water, entered that hermitage exhausted and begged for water."
"As he, exhausted, cried out with his parched throat, no one then heard him — like the cry of a bird."
Then seeing that water-filled pot, the king rushed toward it swiftly, drank the water, and set it down.
Having drunk the cool water, that wise king — tormented by thirst — attained relief and became greatly content at that moment.
Then those seers, together with the lord of the gods, awoke and all of them saw that the pot was empty of water.
Assembled together they asked, "Whose deed is this?" Yuvanāśva, speaking truth, admitted, "It was I."
"This was not right," said the blessed Bhārgava to him then. "Those waters were stored for the purpose of a son, charged with the power of austerity."
"By me here was sacred power infused through terrible austerity, for the sake of your son, O royal sage of great strength and valor."
"One who would be mighty in strength and valor, endowed with the power of asceticism, who could by his prowess send even Indra to the abode of Yama."
"By this rite, O king, was this prepared by me — the drinking of the water by you, O king, was indeed an improper act done today."
"But now it is not possible for us to undo this otherwise — surely this was wrought by fate, that you acted in this way."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Those waters which you drank when thirsty, O great king, consecrated with sacred rites and mantras, charged with the power of my exalted austerity — from those waters you yourself shall beget a son of such prowess."
"We shall perform for you in that matter a most wondrous sacrificial rite, so that you, the valiant one, shall beget a son equal to Indra."
Then, when a full hundred years had elapsed, a son burst forth from the left side of that great-souled king, like a second sun.
The one of great radiance came forth, and death did not enter Yuvanāśva the lord of men — that seemed a marvel indeed.
Then Indra of great splendor came desiring to see him, and placed his index finger into the infant's mouth.
"This one shall suckle me" — thus declared the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the gods together with Indra gave the child the name Māndhātṛ.
That infant, having tasted the finger given by Indra, grew, O lord of the earth, thirteen kiṣkus in a single day.
The Vedas along with the Dhanurveda, and the divine weapons, approached him as master, O great king, coming to him in all ways merely by his thought.
The bow named Ājagava, the arrows sprung from horns, and an impenetrable armor — all these immediately came to attend upon him.
He was consecrated by bountiful Indra himself, O Bhārata, and by righteousness he conquered the three worlds with strides like Viṣṇu.
The unstoppable wheel of that great soul set in motion, and jewels of their own accord came to attend upon the royal sage.
This earth full of wealth was his, O lord of the earth, and by him were performed many and varied sacrifices with abundant ritual fees.
Having built altars and having attained abundant merit, that one of immeasurable radiance, O king, won a half-share of Indra's throne.
In a single day this steadfastly righteous wise one conquered, by mere command, the earth with all its jewel-bearing oceans and cities.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By his sacrificial fire-altars, O great king, of those rites with lavish gifts, the four-cornered earth was filled — there was nothing left uncovered.
By that great-souled one, they say, O great king, ten thousand lotus-thousands of cows were given to the brahmins.
By that great-souled one, during a twelve-year drought, rain was caused to fall for the growth of crops, before the very eyes of the thunderbolt-bearer.
By him the great lord of Gāndhāra, born of the Soma lineage, who roared like a great cloud, was overcome and slain with arrows.
The four kinds of subjects were conquered by him, O king, that great-souled one; by his self-austerity were the worlds also established in his splendor.
Here is that divine sacrificial ground, the site of that one radiant as the sun — behold it in the most sacred region, in the midst of Kurukṣetra.
All this has now been told to you — the great deeds of Māndhātṛ and his wondrous birth, O lord of the earth, which you asked me about.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what valor was that king Somaka, O best of speakers? I wish to hear in truth his deeds and his power.
Lomaśa said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, there was a righteous king named Somaka. He had a hundred wives of equal standing, O king.
That lord of the earth, though striving with great effort among them, could not obtain even a single son even over a great span of time.
Once, for that aged one striving with effort, a son named Jantu was born among that assembly of a hundred women.
All the mothers constantly surrounded that newborn and sat attending him, setting aside their pleasures, O lord of the people.
Then once an ant bit Jantu on the buttock, and the child, bitten, cried out, O king, in that pain.
Then all those mothers, deeply distressed, cried out together, surrounding Jantu, and there arose a tumultuous noise.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That distressed cry was suddenly heard by the lord of the earth, seated in the midst of his council of ministers along with his priests.
The king then sent someone asking "What is this?" and the chamberlain reported to him what had occurred regarding his son.
Rising in haste, Somaka the subduer of enemies entered the inner apartments together with his ministers and consoled his son.
Having consoled the son, the king departed from the inner apartments, O king, and sat down together with his officiating priests and ministers.
Somaka said: Shame on having only one son here! Sonlessness would be better. From the perpetual anxiety of all beings, having only one son is pure grief.
"This hundred of wives, O brahmin, was taken by me after careful selection, O lord, desiring sons, yet there is no offspring from them."
"Somehow one son, this Jantu, has been born to me despite my striving among all of them — what greater sorrow is there than this?"
"My age has passed together with my wives, O best of twice-born ones; the lives of all these women depend upon this one son of mine here."
"Is there any appropriate action, whether great or small, whether difficult or not, by which I might have a hundred sons?"
The priest said: There is indeed such an action by which you could have a hundred sons. If you are able to do it, then I shall tell you, Somaka.
Somaka said: Whether it is to be done or not to be done, if by it a hundred sons could be had — know that it is as good as done. Let the revered one tell me.
The priest said: Sacrifice with Jantu, O king, in a rite spread out by me. Then a glorious hundred sons will be yours before long.
When the omentum is being offered and the mothers smell the smoke, they will then bear sons of very great valor for you.
"And Jantu himself will again be born as your son in that very womb, and a golden mark will appear on his right side."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Somaka said: O brahmin, whatever must be done and in whatever manner — do it just so. Desiring sons, I shall do all that you say.
Lomaśa said: Then he caused Somaka to sacrifice with Jantu as the offering. But the mothers by force tried to pull away their son, overcome with compassion.
Crying out "Alas, we are slain!" filled with intense grief, the mothers pulled him back by the right hand, but the sacrificial priest too pulled by taking hold of the left hand.
Like distressed osprey-birds — having pulled away that son, he slew him according to the rite and offered his omentum into the fire.
When the omentum was being offered, the mothers smelled the aroma and swooned suddenly to the ground in anguish, O delight of the Kurus; and all those royal women then conceived.
Then, within ten months, O lord of the people, a full hundred sons were born among all those wives of Somaka, O Bhārata.
Jantu was born again as the eldest, in his own mother, O Bhārata. He was dear to all of them in a way that no other natural sons were.
And that golden mark was there on his right side. Among that hundred sons he was preeminent, endowed with virtues.
Then that teacher of Somaka departed to the highest world. And when time had passed, Somaka too departed to the beyond.
And then he saw him being tormented in a terrible hell. He asked him: "For what reason are you being cooked in hell, O twice-born one?"
That teacher, being tortured greatly by fire, said to him: "You were caused to sacrifice by me, O king — this is the fruit of that action."
Hearing this, that royal sage said to the king of dharma: "I shall enter here — let my officiating priest be freed. For my sake this blessed one is being burned in the fire of hell."
Dharma said: No one else ever experiences the fruit of the doer's act, O king. These rewards are seen as yours, O best of the generous.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Somaka said: I do not desire the meritorious worlds without this speaker of sacred wisdom. I wish to dwell with him in the abode of the gods.
"Or in hell, O king of dharma, I am indeed equal to him in this deed. Let the fruit of merit and demerit be equal for us both, O god."
Dharma said: If such is your desire, O king, then enjoy his fruit together with him for equal time; thereafter you shall attain a good destination along with him.
Lomaśa said: That lotus-eyed king did all this accordingly, and once again won his own auspicious worlds earned by his deeds — together with that brahmin teacher, he who was dear to his guru.
This is that holy hermitage, this one that shines before us. A patient man who dwells here for six nights attains a good passage.
In this place too, O king of kings, we shall dwell free from fever for six nights with controlled minds. Make yourself ready, O foremost of the Kurus.
Lomaśa said: In this place, O king, Prajāpati himself formerly performed a satra called Iṣṭīkṛta, lasting a thousand years.
And Ambarīṣa, son of Nābhāga, performed sacrifices along the Yamunā; through sacrifices and through austerity he attained the highest perfection.
This region of the Nāhuṣa sacrifices is the most sacred, O king — here he sacrificed and gave away ten padmas to those assembled at the rite.
Behold here this sacrificial ground of Yayāti, the universal sovereign, O son of Kuntī, the one of immeasurable energy who rivaled Indra.
Behold the earth covered over with fires of various forms, as if sinking, overwhelmed by the sacrificial acts of Yayāti.
Here is the śamī tree with a single leaf; that is the finest śaraka reed. Behold these lakes of Rāma; behold the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.
This, O lord of the earth, is the retreat of the son of Ṛcīka, the one of immeasurable energy, who wanders the earth through his yogic powers, at Raupyā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Here, O delight of the Kurus, hear from me the lineage recitation — what the piśācī adorned with mortars spoke.
"Having eaten curds at Yugaṃdhara and having dwelt at the place of Acyuta, and likewise having bathed at Bhūtilaya, you wish to dwell there with your sons."
"Having dwelt here one night, if you will stay a second — what happened during the day shall happen differently for you at night."
Here, O best of the Bhāratas, we shall spend the night today — for this, O son of Kuntī, is the gateway to Kurukṣetra, O Bhārata.
Here indeed, O king, King Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, performed sacrifices with many jewel-rich rites, at which even Indra was gladdened.
This is called Plakṣāvaraṇa, the sacred ford of the Yamunā; the wise declare this to be the gateway to the vault of heaven.
Here, O dear one, the great sages who have performed Sārasvata sacrifices, bearing the sacrificial post and the mortar, proceed to the final ablution bath.
Here indeed King Bharata released the consecrated horse — the dark-spotted steed — having won the earth by righteousness more than once.
Here too, O tiger among men, Marutta performed the highest sacrifice session, presided over by Saṃvarta, foremost among divine sages.
By touching the sacred waters here, O king of kings, one beholds all the worlds; and by duly touching them, O Bhārata, one is purified of all evil deeds.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There, having bathed along with his brothers and being praised by the great sages, the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas spoke these words to Lomaśa.
"I behold all the worlds by the power of austerity, O you whose valor is truth; standing here I see the foremost of Pāṇḍavas, the white-horsed Arjuna."
Lomaśa said: Even so, O mighty-armed one, the great sages see this; behold this holy Sarasvatī, adorned with Ekaśaraṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bathing here, O best of men, one becomes cleansed of sin; here the divine sages, the sages, O son of Kuntī, and the royal sages as well, have worshipped with Sārasvata sacrifices.
This is the altar of Prajāpati, extending five yojanas on all sides — this is the sacred field of Kuru the great soul, devoted to sacrifice.
Lomaśa said: Here, O Bhārata, mortals go to heaven by performing austerities; men desiring death, O king, come here by the thousands.
For such was the blessing pronounced long ago by Dakṣa when he sacrificed — those who die here are truly men who have conquered heaven.
This is the holy, divine Sarasvatī, the river of plentiful waters; and this, O lord of the people, is called Vinaśana, the disappearance of the Sarasvatī.
This is the gateway to the realm of the Niṣādas, out of hatred for whom the Sarasvatī entered the earth — for the river said, "May the Niṣādas not know me."
This is Camasodbheda, where the Sarasvatī becomes visible again, where the divine, holy rivers flowing to the sea converged upon her.
This is the great sacred ford of the Sindhu where Lopāmudrā, O subduer of foes, met and chose Agastya as her husband.
This is the sacred ford called Prabhāsa, O you who shine like the sun — the beloved holy shrine of Indra, pure and destroying sin.
Here is seen the excellent sacred ford named Viṣṇupada; and this is the lovely river Vipāśā, supremely purifying.
Here indeed the blessed sage Vasiṣṭha, overcome by grief for his son, bound himself and fell, but rose again unbound — hence the river Vipāśā, "the freed from bonds."
This is the entirely holy region of Kāśmīra, O subduer of foes, inhabited by great sages — behold it together with your brothers.
Here took place the dialogue of all the northern sages, and of Nahuṣa, and of Agni, and of Kāśyapa as well, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This, O great king, is the gateway that leads to Mānasa lake; the land in the middle of this mountain was established by the glorious Rāma.
This is the renowned Vāṭikaṣaṇḍa grove — of true valor — the gateway which one who has not surpassed the Videhas and the northerners does not approach.
This is the place called Ujjānaka, where the peaceful Yavakrī dwelt, and where the blessed sage Vasiṣṭha resided together with Arundhatī.
And this is the lake Kuśavān where the lotus blossoms; and here too is the hermitage where the wrathless Rukmiṇī was pacified.
The confluence of the Samādhī rivers you have heard of, O son of Pāṇḍu — you shall behold it, O great king, and also the great mountain Bhṛgutuṅga.
And the rivers Jalā and Upajalā near the Yamunā — it was here that Uśīnara, having sacrificed, surpassed even Vāsava in merit.
To test that king at his divine assembly, both Vāsava and Agni, O lord of the people, came to King Uśīnara, O Bhārata.
Desiring to examine the great-souled Uśīnara, those two boon-givers — Indra taking the form of a hawk and Agni the form of a pigeon — came to his sacrifice.
The pigeon, seeking refuge out of fear of the hawk, came to the king's thigh and pressed itself there, O king, tormented by fear and seeking shelter.
The hawk said: All rulers of the earth proclaim you alone to be righteous of soul, O king — why then do you wish to perform an act contrary to dharma?
The eating of this prey is ordained for me, O king, as I am tormented by hunger — do not deprive me of it; by clinging to one form of dharma you have abandoned dharma altogether.
The king said: This bird, terrified in form, seeking protection, frightened of you, O great twice-born, has come to me clinging to life.
For one who has thus come here seeking refuge — not granting protection to this pigeon would be the greatest adharma; what do you see in this, O hawk?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This pigeon, trembling and distressed, is seen to be seeking life by coming to me, O hawk — to abandon him is blameworthy.
The hawk said: All beings arise from food, O lord of the earth; through food they grow, and by it creatures live.
One may live for a long time even after relinquishing what is hard to abandon; but giving up food, one cannot sustain life for long.
Today, deprived of my prey, O lord of the people, my life-breath will leave this body and travel the path of no return.
If I die, O righteous one, my wife and children will perish; by protecting this pigeon you will destroy many lives.
A dharma that obstructs another dharma is no dharma — that is pseudo-dharma; but dharma that does not conflict with another dharma — that, O you of true valor, is true dharma.
When duties conflict, O lord of the earth, one should weigh what is greater and what is lesser, and practice whichever dharma causes no obstruction to others.
Having determined what is weightier and what is lighter in deciding between dharma and adharma, follow whichever is the greater, O king — thus make your determination of dharma.
The king said: You speak with much that is auspicious and good, O best of birds — are you Suparṇa, king of birds? You are certainly a knower of dharma, without doubt; for you speak much that is varied and full of dharma.
I perceive that there is nothing unknown to you; yet how do you consider it right to abandon one who is seeking refuge?
Your purpose in this undertaking is to obtain food, O bird, and that may be accomplished otherwise — and indeed greater food may be obtained by you.
A bull, or a boar, or a deer, or even a buffalo — let whichever you desire be prepared for you today, or whatever else you may wish for.
The hawk said: I do not eat boar, nor bull, nor various kinds of deer, O great king — what use is such food to me?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the prey ordained for me by fate, O bull among kṣatriyas — release it to me, O lord of the earth; give me this very pigeon.
Hawks eat pigeons — this is the eternal order of things; O king, knowing this path, do not climb a plantain trunk expecting fruit.
The king said: O hawk, O honored by flocks of birds, rule the prosperous kingdom of the Śibis, or take whatever you desire — I will give you everything, but not this bird, O hawk, who has come seeking refuge.
Whatever act would make you relinquish this one, tell me, O best of birds — I will do it; for I will not give up this little pigeon.
The hawk said: O Uśīnara, O lord of men, if you have such love for this pigeon — then cut flesh from your own body and weigh it against the pigeon in the balance.
When your flesh equals the pigeon's weight in the balance, O king, then give that to me — that will be my satisfaction.
The king said: I consider it a favor, O hawk, that you solicit me thus; therefore I will give you today my own flesh weighed in the balance.
Lomaśa said: Then the king, a supreme knower of dharma, cut flesh from his body and placed it on the scale against the pigeon, O son of Kuntī, O illustrious one.
But the pigeon, when weighed in the balance, outweighed the flesh; so King Uśīnara cut more flesh and added it again.
When no more flesh could be found equal in weight to the pigeon, then that one, his flesh cut away, climbed upon the scale himself.
The hawk said: I am Indra, O knower of dharma, and this pigeon is Agni, the carrier of oblations — we two came to your sacrificial arena wishing to examine you in dharma.
The flesh that has been cut from your limbs, O lord of the people — this your radiant fame will pervade all the worlds.
For as long as men in this world shall tell of you, O king, so long shall your fame and your worlds endure — eternal.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Lomaśa said: Behold, O son of Pāṇḍu, the abode of that great-souled king — see it together with me; it is holy and releases one from sin.
Here the gods and the eternal sages are ever seen, O king, by virtuous brāhmaṇas of great souls.
Lomaśa said: He who is celebrated on earth as a knower of sacred lore and of foremost intellect — Auddālaki Śvetaketu — behold his holy hermitage, O lord of men, adorned with ever-fruitful trees grown from the earth.
Here Śvetaketu directly beheld Sarasvatī in human bodily form; "I shall master sacred speech" — so saying to Sarasvatī, Śvetaketu addressed her.
At that time, the two foremost knowers of Brahman — maternal uncle and nephew — were present: Aṣṭāvakra the son of Kahoḍa, and Auddālaki Śvetaketu, O king.
Those two brāhmaṇas, uncle and nephew, entered the sacrificial arena of the king of Videha, that lord of the earth, and in debate subdued the immeasurable Bandin.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What was the power of that brāhmaṇa who thus subdued Bandin? How did Aṣṭāvakra come to be as he was? Tell me all of this truly, O Lomaśa.
Lomaśa said: There was one devoted disciple of Uddālaka, named Kahoḍa, O king, who served his teacher obediently and studied for a long time.
Yet the brāhmaṇa students surpassed him in learning; and knowing this slight, his teacher at once gave him both sacred knowledge and his own beautiful daughter Sujātā as wife.
A child like fire formed in her womb; while still in the womb that child then spoke to its father who was studying: "All night long you study — but, Father, this does not seem to me to be going rightly."
Reproached thus in the midst of his students, the great sage cursed that child in his womb in anger: "Because you speak while still in the belly, therefore you shall be crooked in eight places."
And so he was born crooked — the great sage renowned as Aṣṭāvakra, "crooked in eight places." His maternal uncle was Śvetaketu, who was equal to him in age.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Sujātā, then oppressed by the growing child in her womb and in need of wealth, took her husband aside in private, and having conciliated him, she said to him in his poverty.
"What shall I do without wealth, O great sage? This is my tenth month; you have not a single possession, O you who are to be a father — with which I might cross this difficulty."
Thus addressed by his wife, Kahoḍa went to Janaka for wealth; but there he was subdued by Bandin, skilled in debate, and the brāhmaṇa was drowned in the waters.
Then Uddālaka, hearing that he had been drowned in the water after being vanquished in debate by the sūta, said to Sujātā there and then: "This matter must be concealed from Aṣṭāvakra."
She guarded that secret exceedingly well; even after his birth, the brāhmaṇa [Aṣṭāvakra] did not come to know of it; and Aṣṭāvakra regarded Uddālaka as a father and Śvetaketu as a brother.
Then in the twelfth year, Śvetaketu pulled Aṣṭāvakra away by the hand as he sat weeping on his father's lap, and said to him: "This is not your father's lap."
The harsh words spoken by him then lodged in his heart as profound sorrow. Going home, weeping, he asked his mother: 'Where indeed is my father?'
Then Sujātā, overwhelmed with grief and afraid of the curse, revealed everything in full. Knowing the entire truth from his mother, that brahmin then addressed Śvetaketu.
'Let us go to the sacrifice of King Janaka — his sacrifice is said to be full of wonders. We shall listen to the debates among the brahmins there and partake of the finest food; we shall gain discernment, for the sound of the Veda there is auspicious and gentle.'
So those two — uncle and nephew — went to the opulent sacrifice of King Janaka. Aṣṭāvakra, encountering the king on the road and being turned away, spoke these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'The road belongs to the blind; the road belongs to the deaf; the road belongs to women; the road belongs to the burden-carrier. A king's road yields when a brahmin is present — when a brahmin is met, the road is the brahmin's alone.'
The king said: 'This road is granted to you by me today — go as you wish, freely. There is no purer light than fire, and even Indra himself perpetually bows to brahmins.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'We have come to witness the sacrifice, O lord. Our curiosity has grown very strong. Having arrived as guests, we desire entry — O doorkeeper, we await your command.'
'We two have come here to see the sacrifice of the son of Indradyumna, and we wish to speak with King Janaka and behold him. Not from anger nor from any great affliction — O doorkeeper, announce us in a moment.'
The doorkeeper said: 'We are the order-bearers of Bandin — hear the words I pronounce: no young brahmins enter here; only the aged and learned, the foremost among the twice-born, may enter.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'If entry here is granted to the aged, then it is fitting, O doorkeeper, that I enter — for we are old, observers of vows, and by the power of the Veda we are worthy of entry.'
'We are devoted to learning, have mastered our senses, and have reached perfection in the acquisition of knowledge. One should not be disrespected as a mere child — even fire, though young, burns when touched.'
The doorkeeper said: 'Set in motion Sarasvatī beloved of the Veda — the one syllable, multiform, radiant. Look at yourself, O child, body and soul. Why do you boast? Victory in debate is hard to win.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'Greatness is not known by bodily growth — just as the knot of the silk-cotton tree grows large yet is hollow. A short man of small body who bears fruit is truly great; one who bears no fruit has no true greatness.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The doorkeeper said: 'Children acquire wisdom here from the aged, and become old themselves with time. Knowledge cannot truly be won in a short span — why then do you, a child, speak as though you were an elder?'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'One does not become an elder merely because one's hair has turned grey. Even a child who truly knows — him the gods consider an elder.'
'Not by years, not by grey hair, not by wealth, not by kinsmen — the sages established dharma. He who has learned and taught the sacred texts — he is great among us.'
'I have come wishing to see Bandin in the royal assembly. Announce me, O doorkeeper, to the king who wears the lotus garland.'
'You shall see today, O doorkeeper, in debate grown intense among the wise — whether I shall rise high or fall low, or whether all remain silent today.'
The doorkeeper said: 'How shall you, ten years old, enter this sacrifice that is the domain of the learned and the humble? I will endeavour by proper means to arrange your entry — make the effort as is fitting.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'O king, O best of the Janaka line — you are worthy of reverence; all prosperity resides in you. You are the performer of sacrificial rites, as once was the sole king Yayāti before you.'
'Bandin the learned, having defeated in debate those who know the Vedas, without hesitation or second thought, causes all those broken ones — dispatched by your trusted men — to be drowned in the water. So we have heard.'
'Hearing that from the brahmins, I have come to engage in Brahmodya debate. Where is that Bandin? Once I meet him, I shall destroy him as the sun destroys the stars.'
The king said: 'You hope to defeat Bandin without knowing the power of his speech. Only one who has ascertained the strength of the opponent can speak thus — and he has been tested by brahmins skilled in debate.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'He has not been contested by ones like me. He speaks fearlessly, made bold as a lion. When he meets me he shall be struck down today, lying shattered on the road like a broken cart that weak-eyed oxen could not draw.'
The king said: 'He who knows the meaning of the Veda — the wheel with six hubs, twelve spokes, twenty-four segments, and three hundred and sixty-three spokes — he is the supreme sage.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'May that wheel of twenty-four segments, six hubs, twelve rims, three hundred and sixty-three spokes, ever-moving, protect you.'
The king said: 'In the union of two like mares, in the flight of the eagle among the celestials — who bears the embryo of those two, and what embryo did they bring forth?'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'May this never occur in your house, O king — not even in the houses of your enemies is it certain. Vāta, whose charioteer is wind, bears that embryo, and they brought it forth.'
The king said: 'What sleeps without blinking? What, once born, does not stir? Whose heart does not exist? What grows swiftly?'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'A fish sleeps without blinking; an egg, once born, does not stir; a stone has no heart; a river grows swiftly.'
The king said: 'I do not regard you as human — yours is the nature of a divine being. You are not a child; in my estimation you are an elder. There is none equal to you in the flow of speech. Therefore I grant you the door — and there is Bandin.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'O king, here where the assembly of Ugrasena has convened, where peerless kings have gathered — among these debaters there is no difference in the desire to know, like swans calling in a great lake.'
'You will not speak against me today, O you who pride yourself on excessive speech. Like the arrival of rivers, like the blazing brilliance of fire kindled — be firm here against me today, O Bandin.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bandin said: 'Do not rouse a sleeping tiger. Do not place your head where the venomous snake is flicking its tongue in rage — one who has stepped on it cannot escape unbitten. Understand this.'
'One who, puffed up with pride and however strong in frame, yet utterly feeble in true power, strikes against a mountain — only his own hand with its nails shatters; no wound at all is seen on the rock.'
'All kings stand like mere mountains before King Mithilā — made low, diminished, like calves before a draught-ox.'
Lomaśa said: 'Aṣṭāvakra, roaring in the assembly, filled with anger, addressed Bandin, O king: "To the word I have spoken, give me your reply — and I too shall give you the reply to your word."'
Bandin said: 'Fire is one, kindled in many forms; the sun is one, illuminating all this world; the hero, the destroyer, the king of gods, is one; Yama, the lord of the ancestors, is one alone.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'Indra and Agni, two companions, move together; two divine sages — Nārada and Parvata; two Aśvins; two wheels of a chariot; husband and wife — these two are ordained by the Creator.'
Bandin said: 'Progeny is produced three times through ritual action; three bearers carry the Vājapeya sacrifice; the Adhvaryus perform the three pressings; there are three worlds, and they speak of three lights.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'Fourfold is the abode of the brahmins; four bearers carry this sacrifice; four are the directions; four are the social orders; and the cow too is always called four-footed.'
Bandin said: 'Five are the sacred fires; the Paṅkti metre has five feet; five are the sacrifices; five the sense organs as seen in the Veda; and five are the five-crested ones — and the holy Pañcanada is famous in the world.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'Some say the sacrificial fee is sixfold at the fire installation; six are the seasons that make the wheel of time; six are the senses; six too are the Kṛttikā stars; and the six Sādyaskā rites are seen across all the Vedas.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bandin said: 'Seven are the domestic animals; seven the wild ones; seven metres carry the one sacrifice; seven are the seers; seven too are the forms of worship; and the seven-stringed lute is renowned.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'Eight Śāṇas make a Śatamāna; the eight-legged Śarabha slays the lion; we have heard eight Vasus among the gods; and the sacrificial post is appointed with eight corners in all sacrifices.'
Bandin said: 'The Sāmidhenī hymns for the ancestors are declared to be nine; nine too they call the Navayoga of emission; the Bṛhatī metre is prescribed as having nine syllables; and the Navayoga count proceeds for ever.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'Ten Daśās are counted for a man in the world; a thousand is said to be ten complete hundreds; pregnant women carry their burden for ten months; and there are the Daśeraka, the ten Dāśā, and the Daśārṇa.'
Bandin said: 'Eleven are the Ekādaśina sets of animals; eleven are the sacrificial posts here; eleven are the transformations of beings that breathe; and eleven Rudras are declared among the gods in heaven.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'A year is said to have twelve months; the Jagatī foot has exactly twelve syllables; the twelve-day rite is declared the natural sacrifice; and the brahmins here speak of twelve Ādityas.'
Bandin said: 'The thirteenth lunar day is declared most terrible and fierce; and the earth too has thirteen island-continents.'
Lomaśa said: 'Having spoken that much, Bandin fell silent — only half a verse. Aṣṭāvakra then spoke the other half: "Keśin traversed thirteen days; and those beginning with thirteen are called the Atichandas metres."'
Then a great roar arose, seeing Bandin the sūta's son fallen silent, head bowed, absorbed in thought — and Aṣṭāvakra still rising in triumph.
As that tumult prevailed at the opulent sacrifice of King Janaka, all the brahmins, with hands folded in reverence and hearts delighted, came forward to honour Aṣṭāvakra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'O brahmins — those who were defeated in debate by this man and reportedly drowned in the water — let this Bandin now receive those same laws today; seize him and plunge him into the water.'
Bandin said: 'I am the son of Varuṇa the king. There was a twelve-year satra sacrifice of his — contemporaneous in time with your sacrifice, O Janaka. For its purpose those foremost twice-born were sent there by me.'
'All of these have gone to witness Varuṇa's sacrifice and will come back here again. I honour the honourable Aṣṭāvakra — for whose sake I shall now go to meet his father.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'Those brahmins were plunged into the ocean's waters — defeated by speech, overwhelmed by intellect. Yet with that very intellect speech was then restored, just as the noble gather speech from speech.'
'Agni, Jātavedas, burning and releasing the homes of the virtuous with his radiance, did not scorch them even as their young children cried out piteously — thus do the noble gather speech from speech.'
'O Janaka, like a śleṣmātaka tree of diminished lustre — do you hear, or do praises merely intoxicate you? Like an elephant being goaded, you do not hear this my speech.'
Janaka said: 'I do hear your speech, divine in nature, superhuman — you are a divine form manifest. That you have conquered Bandin in debate — this your wish is granted; Bandin is released to you today.'
Aṣṭāvakra said: 'I have no use for this Bandin as long as he lives, O king. If his father is Varuṇa, then let him plunge him into the watery deep.'
Bandin said: 'I am the son of Varuṇa the king — I have no fear of being plunged into the water. In this very moment Aṣṭāvakra shall see his long-lost father Kahoḍa.'
Lomaśa said: 'Then those brahmins, honoured by the great-souled Varuṇa, all rose up in the presence of Janaka.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kahoḍa said: 'It is for this purpose that people desire sons, O Janaka — through his deeds, that which I was unable to do, my son has accomplished.'
'A powerful son is born of one who is weak, O Janaka; a learned son of one who is ignorant; and a knowledgeable son of one who does not know.'
Bandin said: 'May Death himself, with your sharpened axe, lop off the heads of your enemies in battle, O king. May all be well with you.'
'The great Ukthya is sung and the foremost Sāman; the Soma is duly pressed and drunk at this satra. With joy the gods themselves in person accepted their pure shares at the sacrifice of Janaka here.'
Lomaśa said: 'Then, O king, when all those brahmins of surpassing radiance had risen, with King Janaka's leave, Bandin entered the waters of the ocean.'
Aṣṭāvakra, having honoured his father and been duly honoured in return by those brahmins, came back to the foremost hermitage, having defeated Bandin, together with his maternal uncle.
'Here, O son of Kuntī, you shall dwell happily together with your brothers, accompanied by the brahmins and with joy. You shall perform other meritorious deeds — pure in action, devoted to one aim — along with me, O scion of Ajamīḍha.'
Lomaśa said: 'O king, this Madhuvilā — the Samaṅgā river — shines forth here. This is called the Kardamila, the site of Bharata's coronation bath.'
'It is said that the lord of Śacī, afflicted by the sin of killing Vṛtra, bathed here and was freed from all sins in the Samaṅgā.'
'This is the Vinaśana, in the flank of Mount Maināka, O bull among men — where Aditi once cooked that food for the sake of offspring.'
'Ascending this king of mountains, O bull among men, you shall drive away the ill-reputed, unspeakable inauspiciousness.'
'These are the Kanakahalā trees, O king, beloved of the seers. And here, O Yudhiṣṭhira, shines forth the great river Gaṅgā.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'The blessed Sanatkumāra attained the highest perfection here. O descendant of Ajamīḍha, plunge into this river and you shall be freed from all sins.'
'The holy lake called Apāṃhrada, the mountain Bhṛgutuṅga, and the silent Gaṅgā — O son of Kuntī, touch all these along with your ministers.'
'The charming hermitage of Sthūlaśiras shines forth here. O son of Kuntī, in this place abandon both pride and anger.'
'This is the glorious hermitage of Raibhya, shining forth, O son of Pāṇḍu — where the learned son of Bharadvāja, Yavakrīta, met his end.'
Yudhiṣṭhira said: 'How was the sage Bharadvāja of great power situated? And for what reason did Yavakrīta, son of the sage, perish?'
I wish to hear all this, just as it occurred, O Lomaśa — I greatly delight in hearing the deeds of those who are like the gods being recounted.
Lomaśa said: Bharadvāja and Raibhya were friends; those two dwelt here in the forest, greatly delighting in each other's company.
Raibhya had two sons, Arvāvasu and Parāvasu; and Yavakrī was the son of Bharadvāja, O Bhārata.
Raibhya was learned together with his sons, while the other was an ascetic; yet between those two there was incomparable affection from childhood onward, O Bhārata.
Yavakrī, seeing his father the ascetic dishonored, and seeing Raibhya honored along with his sons by the brahmins, O sinless one —
— that brilliant one burned with grief, overwhelmed by anger, and then performed terrible austerities to attain knowledge of the Vedas, O Pāṇḍava.
Torturing his body in a great blazing fire, that mighty ascetic generated intense anguish in Indra.
Then Indra approached Yavakrī, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and said: "For what reason have you undertaken this supreme austerity?"
Yavakrī said: "May the Vedas, unlearned by twice-borns, shine forth in me" — O you worshipped by the host of gods, for this I perform this supreme austerity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This undertaking of mine is for the purpose of sacred recitation, O Indra, lord of the slayer of Pāka; I wish to know all knowledge through austerity, O Kauśika."
"The Vedas can be attained through a teacher's mouth only after a great length of time, O lord; therefore this supreme effort has been undertaken by me."
Indra said: "This is a wrong path by which you wish to go, O brahmin-seer; what obstacle is there for you, O brahmin? Go and study from the mouth of a teacher."
Lomaśa said: Having spoken thus, Śakra departed; and Yavakrī, O Bhārata, once again made effort in austerity, O one of immeasurable valor.
Afflicting himself with terrible austerity, O king, that great ascetic greatly tormented the lord of the gods — so we have heard.
Then approaching that great sage performing such intense austerity, the god Balabhid once again tried to restrain him.
"The goal you have undertaken is unattainable; this is not a wise course for you — the Vedas will indeed shine forth in you and in your father."
Yavakrī said: "This desired goal of mine is not being accomplished thus, O king of gods; with great self-restraint I shall perform even more terrible austerity."
"I shall offer limb by limb into the blazing fire — know this, O Maghavan; if you do not grant all my desired wishes here, O king of gods."
Lomaśa said: Recognizing the resolve of that great-souled sage, the wise one reflected with his intellect on a means to restrain him.
Then Indra assumed the form of an ascetic brahmin many hundreds of years old, feeble and afflicted with consumption.
At the tirtha on the Bhāgīrathī customarily used by Yavakrī for his purification rituals, he began to build a bridge with handfuls of sand.
When that foremost of twice-borns paid no heed to his words, Śakra then began filling the Gaṅgā with sand.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He continuously cast handfuls of sand into the Bhāgīrathī and set about building the bridge, demonstrating this to Yavakrī.
Yavakrī saw him striving at this construction and laughing spoke these words, that bull among sages:
"What is going on here, O brahmin, and what is it you intend to do? This is an exceedingly great effort being made, and it is pointless."
Indra said: "I shall bind the Gaṅgā with a bridge so that the path may be easy; for the people suffer greatly when they cross repeatedly, my child."
Yavakrī said: "This mighty current cannot be bridged by you in any way; desist from the impossible and undertake a feasible task."
Indra said: "Just as this austerity undertaken by you to attain the Vedas is impossible, so likewise this burden has been undertaken by us."
Yavakrī said: "If you consider my undertaking equally pointless, O lord of the thirty gods, O Pākaśāsana —
"— then grant what may be possible for me, O lord of the host of gods, and give me other boons by which I may surpass all others."
Lomaśa said: To him Indra gave the boons that the great ascetic had declared: "The Vedas shall shine forth in you together with your father, as you desire."
"And whatever other wish you desire, Yavakrī, go to it." Having obtained his desire, he then approached his father and spoke.
Yavakrī said: "The Vedas shall indeed shine forth in both me and my father; and the boons obtained by me shall likewise be beyond all others."
Bharadvāja said: "Arrogance will come upon you, my child, having obtained the boons you desired; filled with that arrogance, the wretched one perishes quickly."
"On this point they cite these verses, declared by the gods: In ancient times, my son, there was a powerful sage named Baladhi."
"Distressed by grief for a son, he performed extremely difficult austerities, and he obtained this boon: that his son would be immortal."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"A boon was granted to him by the gods, yet not equal to the immortals: 'No mortal is immortal; your mortal son shall have a conditioned lifespan.'"
"Baladhi said: 'As these mountains stand forever, O best of gods, inexhaustible — let the mountains be the condition of my son's lifespan.'"
"Bharadvāja said: A son was then born to him, named Medhāvī, always wrathful; hearing this boon, he became arrogant and began to disrespect the sages."
"While acting wrongfully toward the sages and roaming this earth, he encountered the wise and mighty Dhanusha-ksha."
"Medhāvī insulted him; that powerful one cursed him: 'Become ashes!' But when so spoken to, he did not become ashes."
"But Dhanuṣākṣa, seeing Medhāvī unharmed, that powerful one shattered the conditioned support of his life with buffaloes."
"When the conditional support was destroyed, the child suddenly died; and taking up that dead son, his father then lamented."
"Seeing him lamenting in such pain, the sages spoke again with a verse taught in the Vedas — hear this from me."
"No mortal is ever able to transcend fate in any way; Dhanuṣākṣa shattered the mountains with his buffaloes."
"Thus, children who obtain boons and are filled with arrogance, however swift, perish quickly — may you not be so, my son."
"This Raibhya is greatly powerful and his sons are likewise; act diligently so that you do not approach him, my son."
"For when angered, he is capable of harming you in his wrath, my son — he is a physician, an ascetic, and a great irascible sage."
Yavakrī said: "I shall act accordingly; do not grieve in any way, father; for just as you are to be honored by me, so Raibhya is as a father to me."
Lomaśa said: Having spoken smoothly to his father, Yavakrī, fearless, went on wronging other sages and rejoiced with great delight.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Lomaśa said: Wandering about at that time, fearless Yavakrī went in the month of Mādhava toward the hermitage of Raibhya.
In that holy hermitage adorned with flowering trees, he saw Raibhya's daughter-in-law roaming about, like a kinnari, O Bhārata.
Yavakrī said to her, "Yield to me" — shameless, his mind stolen by desire, to her who was full of modesty.
She, knowing his character and fearing the curse from him and the fierce energy of Raibhya, saying "So be it," went with him.
Then, having led her to a secluded spot, he defiled her, O Bhārata; and then Raibhya came to his own hermitage, O subduer of enemies.
Seeing his daughter-in-law weeping, the distressed wife of Parāvasu, he comforted her with gentle words and inquired of her, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
That auspicious woman told him everything — what Yavakrī had said and what reply Yavakrī had received beforehand from her own self.
Even as Raibhya was hearing of Yavakrī's conduct, a mighty anger arose in his heart, burning as if with fire.
Then that ascetic, seized by fury and intensely enraged, plucked out one of his matted locks and offered it into the well-consecrated fire.
From that arose a woman matching the beauty of that daughter-in-law; and plucking another matted lock, he offered it into the fire again.
From that arose a demon with terrible eyes and a frightful appearance; those two then said to Raibhya, "What task shall we perform?"
The enraged sage said to them: "Let Yavakrī be slain." Those two said "So be it" and went with intent to kill Yavakrī.
Then the female demon sent by that great soul approached him and, having deluded him, stole his water-pot, O Bhārata.
With Yavakrī thus defiled and his water-pot taken away, then the demon with upraised spear rushed at him.
Seeing him rushing at him with spear in hand intent on killing, Yavakrī instantly rose up and fled toward a lake.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing the lake waterless, Yavakrī hurried on; he went to all the rivers, and those too had been dried up.
Being driven by the terrible demon with the spear in hand, in fear he suddenly rushed toward his father's sacred fire.
But as he was entering, he was forcibly seized by the blind shudra guardian at the gate, and he stood stopped there, O king.
The demon then struck with the spear Yavakrī who was seized by the shudra; his heart pierced, he fell.
Having killed Yavakrī, the demon came back to Raibhya; dismissed by Raibhya, he went away accompanied by that woman.
Lomaśa said: Bharadvāja, O son of Kuntī, having completed his daily recitation, took up his bundle of firewood and entered his own hermitage.
The sacred fires, which formerly all rose to greet him upon his arrival, did not attend upon him now that his son was slain.
Perceiving the disorder in the sacred fire-ritual, that great ascetic then spoke to the blind shudra sitting there as guardian of the household.
"Why do the fires not welcome my arrival, O shudra? And you too are not as before — is all well in this hermitage?"
"Has my son of little understanding gone to Raibhya? Tell me this quickly, for my mind is not at peace."
The shudra said: "Your son of dull understanding has surely gone to Raibhya — for indeed he lies slain by a powerful demon."
"As he was being driven by that demon with spear in hand toward the fire-chamber, at the gate he was restrained by me with my arms."
"Then he was killed here, for he was surely impure, thirsting for water, struck quickly by the demon with the upraised spear."
Lomaśa said: Bharadvāja, hearing those unwelcome words of the shudra, took up his son who had breathed his last and lamented in deep sorrow.
"Indeed you performed austerities for the sake of the brahmins — 'May the Vedas, unlearned by twice-borns, now shine forth' — so you said."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You who were thus of noble character toward the great-souled brahmins, blameless toward all beings, have now acquired harshness.
Though forbidden by me, dear son, from visiting the dwelling of Raibhya, you went anyway to that vile one who is like Death and the end-time Yama.
That one of great splendor, knowing he was my only son, an old man's sole child, was entirely given over to anger — a man of utterly wicked mind.
Having been overtaken by grief over a son through this deed of Raibhya's, I shall abandon, except for you, my son, these most dear breaths of life in this world.
Even as I, guilt-laden, shall abandon this body through grief for a son, so may the elder son of Raibhya quickly slay that blameless man.
Truly happy are those men who by their very birth have no son — never reaching the grief of a son, they wander about at ease.
But those whose minds are deeply distraught by grief caused by a son, who in their anguish curse their beloved friends — who indeed is more sinful than they?
My son has been seen as lifeless, and my beloved friend has been cursed by me — who else in the world could experience such a calamity a second time?
Having lamented thus in many ways, Bharadvāja cremated his son with a well-kindled fire, and thereafter entered the flames himself.
Lomaśa said: At this very time, the king Bṛhaddyumna, a man of great fortune and valor, the sacrificial patron of Raibhya, was performing a soma sacrifice.
By that wise Bṛhaddyumna, Raibhya's two sons, Arvāvasu and Parāvasu, were invited as assistants for the purpose of the sacrifice.
There, the two, having obtained their father's permission, O son of Kuntī, departed. In the hermitage, however, Raibhya remained, along with the wife of Parāvasu.
Then Parāvasu went home alone to look in on things, and in the forest he saw his father wrapped in a black antelope skin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the dead of night, blinded by sleep, with some darkness still remaining, he saw him moving through the dense forest and mistook his father for a deer.
Thinking him a deer, he then slew his father — not desiring to do so, only wishing to protect his own body.
He performed all the funeral rites for him, O Bhārata, and returning again to that sacrifice, he spoke these words to his brother.
"This deed you are in no way able to bear alone. I have slain father, mistaking him for a deer.
For our sake, duly observe the vow for brahmin-slaying; I am capable of performing this rite alone, O sage."
Arvāvasu said: "Let you carry out the sacrifice of the wise Bṛhaddyumna; I shall observe the penance for brahmin-slaying on your behalf, with my senses restrained."
Lomaśa said: Having passed beyond that sin of brahmin-slaying, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Arvāvasu the sage then returned again to the sacrifice.
Then Parāvasu, seeing his brother arrive, spoke these words to Bṛhaddyumna in the assembly:
"This brahmin-killer should not be allowed to enter and witness your sacrifice; even the mere sight of a brahmin-killer would afflict you, there is no doubt."
Being driven away by the servants, O king, Arvāvasu then said again and again, "This brahmin-slaying was not done by me!"
Though called brahmin-killer again and again by the servants, O Bhārata, he would not at all acknowledge the brahmin-slaying as done by himself: "This was done by my brother; by me it was only borne to protect him."
The gods were pleased by Arvāvasu's deed, O king; they exalted him and expelled Parāvasu.
Then the gods, with Agni at their head, granted him a boon; and he in turn chose the resurrection of his father and his own exoneration.
Also the blamelessness of his brother, and the forgetting of the killing by his father, and the resurrection of Bharadvāja and of Yavakrīta — both of them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all of them appeared, O Yudhiṣṭhira. Thereupon Yavakrīta addressed the gods, with Agni at their head:
"I have mastered the Veda and the vows have been observed by me — how then was Raibhya able to slay me, a student and ascetic, by such a method, O best among immortals?"
The gods said: "Do not do this, O Yavakrīta, as you speak, O sage! The Vedas were formerly studied by you easily, without a teacher.
But by this one — Arvāvasu — through great time and toil and by his own deeds, having pleased his teachers with difficulty, the highest Brahmā-knowledge was attained."
Lomaśa said: Having thus spoken to Yavakrīta, the gods with Agni at their head, having revived all of them, departed again to heaven.
"This is that holy hermitage, always filled with flowering and fruit-bearing trees. Having dwelt here, O tiger among kings, you shall be released from all sins."
Lomaśa said: You have passed beyond Uśīrabīja, the Maināka mountain, the White Mountain, O Bhārata, and Kālaśaila too, O king, O son of Kuntī.
Here the Gaṅgā shines in her sevenfold form, O bull of the Bhāratas — a pure and lovely place where fire is constantly kindled.
This indeed cannot ordinarily be seen even by a human being today — focus your minds with undivided attention, and you shall behold these sacred tīrthas.
We shall enter the White Mountain and also Mount Mandara, where the yakṣa Māṇicara dwells, and Kubera, the king of yakṣas.
Eighty-eight thousand gandharvas who move with speed, and kiṃpuruṣas, O king, and yakṣas four times their number —
— of many forms and bearing various weapons, they attend upon Maṇibhadra, the lord of yakṣas, O best among men.
Their prosperity is exceedingly great, and in movement they are equal to the wind — they could surely dislodge even the king of the gods from his position.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Protected by those mighty ones and guarded by the yātudhānas, these mountains are hard to approach, dear son; gather your highest concentration, O Pārtha.
There are also other rākṣasas, ministers of Kubera, both fierce and friendly — we shall encounter them, O son of Kuntī; be alert and ready for any advance.
Mount Kailāsa extends for six hundred yojanas, O king; it is vast, O Bhārata, and there the gods assemble.
Countless yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kiṃnaras, O son of Kuntī, as well as nāgas, suparṇas, and gandharvas — all approach the abode of Kubera.
Plunge among them today, O Pārtha, with asceticism and self-restraint, protected by me, O king, and by the strength of Bhīmasena.
May King Varuṇa and Yama the conqueror of battles, and the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, and the mountains grant you well-being.
"At the summit of Indra's golden Jāmbūnada mountain, I hear your voice, O goddess Gaṅgā — protect this auspicious one from these mountains. Be a shelter for this king, descendant of all the Ajamīḍhas, who is about to enter these peaks, O daughter of the mountain."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "This agitation of Lomaśa is unprecedented. All of you, guard Kṛṣṇā — be not careless! This region is considered by him to be extremely perilous. Therefore observe the highest purity here."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then he spoke to Bhīma of noble valor: "Guard Kṛṣṇā vigilantly, O Bhīmasena. When Arjuna is absent and not present, dear son, it is you alone who are devoted to Kṛṣṇā in times of hardship."
Then the great-souled king, gathering the twin sons of Yama to himself, smelling their heads and stroking their limbs, spoke to them with tears in his voice: "Do not be afraid; come, both of you, and be vigilant."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "The creatures that have vanished and the powerful rākṣasas — it is only by fire and by asceticism that one can pass through, O Vṛkodara.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Restrain hunger and thirst, O son of Kuntī, as befits your strength; then take recourse to strength and skill, O foremost of the Kurus.
You have heard the sage's words regarding Mount Kailāsa — consider carefully in your mind, O son of Kuntī, how Kṛṣṇā is to make the journey.
Or else, O splendid one, with Sahadeva, with Dhaumya, together with the cooks and the chief stewards and all the attendants —
— with chariots and horses, and those other brahmins who cannot endure hardship on the road — together with all of them, turn back, O Bhīma, O broad-eyed one.
Three of us shall go, eating lightly, with vows observed: I, and Nakula, and Lomaśa of great austerity.
Awaiting my return, dwell here at Gaṅgādvāra in a collected state of mind, guarding Draupadī, until I come back."
Bhīma said: "The princess, though afflicted by fatigue and overcome with suffering, O Bhārata, presses on nonetheless — that gracious one, eager to see the White-Horsed one.
And your own intense yearning grows as you do not see him — how much more so for Sahadeva, for me, and for Kṛṣṇā, O Bhārata?
Let the chariots turn back, willingly, and all the attendants, the cooks and the chief stewards — wherever you think best for us.
For I do not wish to leave you here at any time, in these mountains swarming with rākṣasas, in these difficult and treacherous places.
And this great-fortuned princess who keeps her vows — without you, O tiger among men, she would not venture to turn back.
Likewise this Sahadeva, ever devoted to you in vow, would never turn back — of this I am the knower of his mind.
Furthermore here, O great king, we are all filled with longing to see Savyasācī — therefore we shall go together.
If this mountain with its many ravines cannot be traversed by chariots, we shall go on foot — do not be disheartened, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I shall carry the Pāñcālī wherever she cannot manage — this is the resolve in my mind; do not be disheartened, O king.
And those two tender heroes, the twin joys of Mādrī — if they are unable, I shall carry both of them through the difficult passages."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Even as you speak thus, may your strength grow ever greater, O Bhīma — you who undertake to carry Draupadī on the vast road.
And blessings on you for the twin sons of Yama as well — such as this is found nowhere else. May your strength and your fame, your righteousness and your glory all increase.
You who undertake to lead both brothers together with Kṛṣṇā — may you feel no weariness, O great-armed one, and may no defeat be yours."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Kṛṣṇā, the lovely one, laughing gently, spoke these words: "I shall go — no distress need be felt on my account, O Bhārata."
Lomaśa said: "Mount Gandhamādana can only be reached through ascetic power; and through that ascetic power, O son of Kuntī, we shall all gird ourselves.
Nakula and Sahadeva, and Bhīmasena, O king, and I, and you, O son of Kuntī — we shall behold the White-Horsed one."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Conversing thus, they came joyfully to the great domain of Subāhu, O king, teeming with abundant elephants and horses.
Filled with Kirātas and Taṅgaṇas, thronged with hundreds of Kuṇindas, frequented by immortals on the Himālayas, and crowded with many wonders.
And Subāhu, the lord of the Kuṇindas, seeing them at the boundary of his territory, received them with honor and with affection.
There, honored by him and having dwelt comfortably, all of them set out toward the Himālaya mountain under a clear sun.
Handing over to them the servants headed by Indrasena, the chief stewards, the cooks, and all the retinue of Draupadī, O king —
— entrusting them to the king, the lord of the Kuṇindas, those great warriors, the joyful sons of the Kurus, of mighty valor, proceeded on foot.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All those Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇā, departed slowly from that region, overjoyed, longing to see Dhanañjaya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Bhīmasena, both twins, and Pāñcālī — hear me. There is truly no destruction of any living being; look upon us as wanderers in the forest.
Though you say to one another, 'We are weak and suffering,' yet we travel even toward what seems impossible, out of longing to see Dhanañjaya.
This burns my limbs like fire burns a heap of cotton — the fact that I do not see the hero Dhanañjaya near at hand.
The thirst to see him burns me, dwelling in the forest with my younger brothers; and the injury done to Yajñasena's daughter also burns me, O hero.
I do not see that Pārtha, elder brother of Nakula, of immeasurable might, that unconquerable wielder of the fierce bow — by that I am tormented, O Vṛkodara.
I roam the pleasant tīrthas, forests, and lakes together with you, yearning for the sight of him.
For five years I have not seen the hero Dhanañjaya, true to his word, the Bībhatsu — by that I am tormented, O Vṛkodara.
That dark-complexioned Guḍākeśa, who walks with the gait of a lion in his stride — the great-armed one I do not see; by that I am tormented, O Vṛkodara.
That master of weapons, skilled in battle, the equal of all bowmen — the foremost among men I do not see; by that I am tormented, O Vṛkodara.
Dhanañjaya, who moves among enemy hosts like Death when enraged, like a maddened elephant, lion-shouldered —
— who is not inferior to Śakra in valor or in wealth, that Pārtha elder brother of the twins, the white-horsed one of immeasurable prowess —
— seized by great sorrow that does not depart through any deed of mine, I do not see that unconquerable, fierce-bowed Phalguna.
He who is ever disposed to forbearance even when insulted by the most trivial; to one who has entered the path of righteousness he is a giver of peace and of fearlessness —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— but to one who acts crookedly and seeks to kill by deceit, he would be like deadly poison even to the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Even to an enemy who has come to him for refuge, that Bībhatsu is not cruel; he is glorious, a giver of safety, boundless in spirit and great in might.
He is the refuge of us all, the crusher of enemies in battle, the gatherer of every jewel, the bringer of happiness to all of us.
It was by his valor that I once possessed many divine jewels of many kinds, which Suyodhana has now obtained.
It was by the strength of his arms, O hero, that the hall of mine once stood, renowned throughout the three worlds, filled with every kind of gem, O Pāṇḍava.
Equal to Vāsudeva in valor, equal to Kārtavīrya in battle — unconquerable, never defeated in war — that Phalguna I do not see.
Born after Saṃkarṣaṇa of great valor and you, O Bhīma the unconquered, he is born equal in valor to Vāsudeva and is the slayer of foes.
In the strength of his arms and in power he is the equal of Purandara; in swiftness he equals the wind; in countenance the Moon; in wrath Death eternal.
All of us, eager to see that tiger among men, O hero, shall enter mount Gandhamādana, O great-armed one.
Where vast Badarī and the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa stand — that most excellent mountain, ever inhabited by yakṣas, we shall behold.
On foot we shall go to that lovely lake of Kubera, guarded by rākṣasas, performing great austerities as we travel.
That region cannot be reached by one who has not performed austerities, O Vṛkodara; nor by one who is cruel, or greedy, or not at peace, O Bhārata.
There we shall all go, seeking the footsteps of Bhīma and Arjuna, armed and with swords strapped on, together with the brāhmaṇas of great vows.
One who is undisciplined encounters flies, mosquitoes, gadflies, tigers, lions, and reptiles; one who is disciplined does not see them, O Pārtha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
We, with disciplined souls, eating sparingly, eager to see Dhanañjaya, shall enter mount Gandhamādana.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those heroes, with their bows strung and quivers full, arrows set, wrist-guards fastened, bearing swords, of immeasurable might —
— the foremost among all bowmen, taking with them the best among the twice-born, accompanied by Pāñcālī, O king, set out for Gandhamādana.
They beheld lakes and rivers and mountains and forests, trees with abundant shade, and on the mountain-summits regions ever bearing flowers and fruit, frequented by hosts of divine seers.
Placing themselves in themselves, subsisting on roots and fruits, those heroes roamed regions of varied terrain, difficult and perilous, beholding many diverse species of wild animals.
Those great-souled ones entered the mountain frequented by ṛṣis, siddhas, and immortals, beloved of gandharvas and apsarases, and haunted by kiṃnaras.
As the heroes were entering mount Gandhamādana, a fierce wind arose and a great rain fell, O lord of the people.
Then a great cloud of dust arose, laden with leaves, and covered the earth, the sky, and the heavens with darkness.
With the sky veiled by dust, nothing could be discerned; nor were they able to call out to one another.
They could not see one another, their eyes overcome by the darkness, dragged about by the wind laden with powdered stone, O Bhārata.
A great sound arose from trees broken by the wind and crashing heavily to the ground, and from other things of the earth.
"Is the sky falling to the earth? Are the mountains splitting apart?" — thus all of them thought, bewildered by the storm.
Feeling their way by hand along nearby trees, anthills, and uneven ground, fearful of the wind, they crouched and took shelter.
Then Bhīmasena of great might, lifting his bow, took hold of Kṛṣṇā and, meeting her, stood leaning against a tree.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Dharmarāja and Dhaumya took shelter in the great forest, while Sahadeva took shelter on the mountain, carrying the sacred fire-vessels.
Nakula, the other brāhmaṇas, and the great ascetic Lomaśa, trembling with fear, found trees here and there and crouched beneath them.
When the wind had weakened and the dust had settled, a heavy rain quickly came with great drops.
Then streams mixed with hailstones, covering everything on all sides, fell incessantly there, driven by the swift wind.
Then the waters rushing toward the ocean, scattered on all sides, appeared turbid and foaming, O lord of the people.
Carrying abundant water, covered with foam-rafts, roaring with great noise, they flowed in all directions, dragging away great trees.
When the rain ceased and the wind became calm, when the waters had flowed into the low places and the sun appeared —
— they all came out slowly and assembled together, O Bhārata; and the heroes set out again toward mount Gandhamādana.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, no sooner had the great-souled Pāṇḍavas set out on foot than Draupadī, unaccustomed to traveling thus, sat down.
Exhausted, overcome by grief, and by that wind and rain, and by reason of her delicacy, the glorious Pāñcālī fainted.
Overwhelmed by her swoon, the dark-eyed one clutched both her rounded, shapely thighs with her arms.
Clinging to both her thighs, which resembled elephant trunks, she suddenly fell to the ground, trembling like a plantain tree.
As she fell, the shapely one clinging like a vine, valiant Nakula ran to her and caught her.
Nakula said: O king, this dark-eyed daughter of the Pāñcāla king has fallen exhausted to the ground — look to her, O Bhārata.
She who is undeserving of suffering has met with the greatest grief; she who walks with gentle steps — reassure her, O great king, she who is worn down by fatigue.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: At his words the king, seized with great grief, and Bhīma and Sahadeva, all quickly ran to her.
Seeing her, pale-faced and thin, the son of Kuntī, righteous in soul, took her in his lap and lamented in distress.
How can she who was accustomed to well-spread couches in guarded palaces, who deserves comfort, the fair-complexioned one, now lie fallen on the bare ground?
How have her delicate feet and her lotus-bright face, which deserve all honor, become darkened today on my account?
What has been done by me, foolish and fond of gambling, bringing Kṛṣṇā along to roam this forest swarming with herds of deer?
"Pāñcālī will find happiness upon obtaining the Pāṇḍavas as husbands" — so thinking, her father king Drupada gave away this long-eyed one.
Without obtaining any of that, worn by toil and grief, she lies fallen on the ground because of my sinful deeds.
As the Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira lamented thus, Dhaumya and all the other foremost twice-born came there.
They comforted him and honored him with blessings; they also muttered protective spells against evil spirits and performed the rites.
As the great seers recited mantras for her well-being and the Pāṇḍavas again and again touched her with cool hands —
— and as she was attended by a cool breeze mixed with water, Pāñcālī found comfort and slowly, gradually, regained her senses.
Taking hold of that wretched Kṛṣṇā, they then let the suffering one, now restored to consciousness, rest on a deerskin spread on the ground.
The twins, with hands calloused from the bowstring, gently massaged her feet, rosy on their soles, adorned with auspicious marks.
The Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira also comforted her, and the foremost of the Kurus spoke these words to Bhīmasena.
"Many are the mountains, O Bhīma, uneven and hard to traverse with snow; how shall Kṛṣṇā wander through them, O great-armed one?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīmasena said: I myself shall carry you, O king, and the princess, and the twin bulls among men, O lord of kings — do not let your mind fall into despondency.
Or else Ghaṭotkaca, that winged one born of me, equal in strength to me, shall carry all of us at your command, O sinless one.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Permitted by the Dharmarāja, he called to mind his rākṣasa son; and Ghaṭotkaca, righteous in soul, the moment he was remembered by his father, appeared with folded hands and saluted the Pāṇḍavas.
And the great-armed one, of true valor, was greeted by them and saluted the brāhmaṇas; then he spoke to his father Bhīmasena.
"I have been remembered by you and have come quickly, eager to serve; command me, O great-armed one — I will do everything, without doubt." Hearing this, Bhīmasena embraced the rākṣasa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: He is learned in dharma, strong, and brave; he is at once a bull among rākṣasas; he is devoted to us and is a natural son — let him, O Bhīma, carry his mother.
By your strength, O Bhīma of exceedingly terrible prowess, I shall go unharmed together with Pāñcālī to Gandhamādana.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Understanding his brother's words, Bhīmasena, that tiger among men, instructed his son Ghaṭotkaca, the crusher of foes.
"O son of Hiḍimbā, your unconquered mother is utterly exhausted; and you, dear son, are able to move at will and are mighty — carry her, O winged one."
Having placed her on your shoulder, blessings be upon you — fly through the sky in our midst, but move gently so that you do not cause her pain.
Ghaṭotkaca said: Even alone I am capable of carrying the king of dharma, Dhaumya, the princess, and the twin brothers — how much more so now, when I have helpers with me.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Ghaṭotkaca then carried Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) upon his back; that hero moved among the Pāṇḍavas, while the other rakshasas carried the Pāṇḍavas themselves.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Lomaśa, of incomparable brilliance, traveled by the path of the siddhas, shining by his own inner power, like a second sun.
The rakshasas of fearsome valor took up all those brahmins as well and, by order of the lord of rakshasas, set forth.
Thus beholding the divinely beautiful forests and groves, they journeyed on toward the great Badarī.
