Borne by those swift-moving, mightily powerful rakshasas, the heroes traveled swiftly; the long road seemed as nothing.
They saw lands thronging with barbarian peoples, rich with mines of many jewels, and mountain foothills streaked with various minerals.
They saw regions crowded with hosts of vidyadharas, filled with apes and kinnaras, as well as kimpurushas and gandharvas on every side.
They saw lands laced with networks of rivers, filled with the calls of many birds, frequented by all manner of deer, and adorned with troops of monkeys.
Having passed through many lands and even the northern Kurus, they beheld the wondrous and extraordinary Kailāsa, the greatest of mountains.
Near that mountain they saw the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, adorned with divine trees ever laden with flowers and fruits.
They saw that jujube tree (badari), lovely with its rounded trunk, glossy, casting a dense unbroken shade, endowed with surpassing beauty.
It was covered with glossy, dense, soft, and auspicious leaves; its branches were wide and spreading, endowed with extraordinary radiance.
It was laden with divine fruits, heavily covered with sweet honey-dripping berries — that divine tree, always frequented by bands of great sages and by flocks of various birds perpetually joyful and enraptured.
In a place free of gnats and mosquitoes, abounding in roots and fruits and water, covered with blue-green grass, and visited by gods and gandharvas —
— in a region of ground naturally well-leveled and auspicious, where the air was cool and soft as dew, in a place clear of thorns —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— arriving at that place, the great-souled ones together with those foremost brahmins all descended gently from the shoulders of the rakshasas.
Then, O king, the Pāṇḍavas together with the foremost twice-born sages beheld that sacred hermitage, the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
It was free of darkness, holy, untouched by the rays of the sun, free from the afflictions of hunger, thirst, cold, and heat — a destroyer of grief.
It was thronged with hosts of great sages and endowed with the splendor of brahman; inaccessible, O great king, to men who have forsaken dharma.
It was divine, honored with offerings and ritual fire, its surfaces well-swept and anointed, radiant on all sides with offerings of divine flowers.
It was filled with spacious fire-halls and auspicious ritual vessels, adorned with large water-pots and wooden ladles; it was a refuge for all beings and resonant with the chanting of the Veda.
That divine hermitage, worthy of taking refuge in, a destroyer of weariness, endowed with beauty beyond description, resplendent with the practices of the gods.
It was filled with self-controlled ones who lived on fruits and roots, clad in bark-cloth and black deerskins, whose selves were refined by austerities equal to the sun and sacred fire —
— with great sages intent on liberation, ascetics whose senses were restrained, who had become Brahman, of great fortune, and who were expounders of brahman.
The wise Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, of great splendor, disciplined and pure, together with his brothers, went forward to meet those sages.
Endowed with divine knowledge, seeing that Yudhiṣṭhira had arrived, all the great sages came forward with great delight, uttering blessings upon him, devoted as they were to Vedic recitation.
Delighted, those sages who were like fire performed for him proper honor according to rite, and brought water, flowers, roots, and pure fruits.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, received with devotion the honor thus rendered to him by the great sages with love.
That hermitage resembling the abode of Śakra, fragrant with divine scents, lovely, equal to heaven in its holiness — the Pāṇḍava, full of joy, together with Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) —
— entered it, endowed with beauty, together with his brothers, O sinless one, and together with brahmins versed in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, accompanied by the unfailing one.
There that dharma-souled one saw the sacred seat of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, honored by gods and divine sages, adorned by the Bhāgīrathī.
Having reached that divine badari tree, dripping with honey and fruit, frequented by bands of great sages, the great-souled ones dwelt there together with the brahmins.
They beheld mount Maināka filled with many flocks of birds, and the golden-peaked mountain, and that auspicious lake Bindusaras.
They beheld the Bhāgīrathī with its excellent fords, its cool and pure waters, auspicious, with banks strewn with gems and coral, adorned with trees.
Beholding it, strewn with divine flowers and gladdening the mind, the great-souled Pāṇḍavas took their delight there.
There those foremost of men, those heroes, dwelling with the brahmins, repeatedly offered satisfaction to the gods and the ancestors.
Watching the various delightful pastimes of Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) there, those tiger-like men, the Pāṇḍavas, shining like immortals, rejoiced in that place.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There those tiger-like men, those heroes, observing the strictest purity and longing to see Dhanañjaya, the Pāṇḍavas dwelt for six nights, roaming and taking pleasure in that place.
In that most excellent and delightful forest, pleasing to all creatures, with trees in full bloom and bending under the weight of their fruits —
— adorned on every side by pleasing trees, crowded with flocks of male kokilas, with glossy dense leaves casting cool and lovely shade —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— and various lakes with clear waters gleaming on all sides with lotuses and blue water-lilies — beholding all these lovely forms, the Pāṇḍavas took their delight in that place.
There blew a breeze of holy fragrance and pleasant touch, gladdening all the Pāṇḍavas together with Kṛṣṇā and the foremost twice-born sages.
Then the wind blowing from the northeast carried by chance a divine lotus, brilliant as the sun, with a thousand petals.
The princess of Pāñcāla saw it — divinely fragrant, lovely, borne by the wind and fallen upon the ground, that pure water-born flower.
That auspicious one, having obtained that unrivaled saugandhika lotus, was exceedingly delighted, O king, and then spoke to Bhīmasena:
"Look, Bhīma, at this divine, exceedingly beautiful, unrivaled flower, perfect in fragrance and form — it is a delight to my heart."
"I shall give this to the king of dharma, O scorcher of foes; it is my wish to have more of these when we return to the Kāmyaka forest."
"If I am dear to you, O Pārtha, bring many of these flowers — I wish to take them back to the Kāmyaka hermitage."
Having spoken thus to Bhīmasena, the blameless princess of Pāñcāla took the flower and went to the king of dharma.
Understanding the intention of his queen, that bull among men, Bhīma of fearsome valor, desirous of pleasing his beloved —
— turned himself in the very direction of the wind from which that flower had come, intent on fetching it, and set off swiftly to get more flowers as well.
Taking up his bow with its golden back and arrows like venomous serpents, like a lion enraged, like an elephant in rut —
— seeking to please Draupadī, relying on the strength of his own arms, free from fear and confusion, the mighty one rushed up the mountain.
He who destroys enemies roamed over that mountain, beautiful, frequented by kinnaras, with its floor of dark rock covered with trees, creepers, and thickets.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The mountain was variegated with minerals, trees, animals, and birds of many colors, filled with every ornament, raised up like an arm of the earth.
On the peaks of Gandhamādana, lovely in every season, his eyes absorbed in the scenery, he reflected in his heart upon his purpose —
— with his ears, mind, and eyes riveted by the songs of male kokilas and the hum of bees, that one of boundless valor moved forward.
Inhaling the overpowering fragrance arising from the blossoms of every season, that one of great splendor moved freely through the forest like a maddened elephant.
His fatigue carried away by his father, his body hair thrilling with joy, touched by the cool breeze of Gandhamādana — the breeze that was his father's caress —
— that tamer of enemies churned through the forest — haunted by bands of yakshas, gandharvas, suras, and brahmarshis — in search of the flowers.
The mountain appeared smeared as if by fingers tracing uneven lines, its strata of brilliant minerals — golden, dark, and silver — creating varied streaks across its face.
The mountain seemed to dance with wings, with clouds clinging to its flanks; it seemed adorned with pearl necklaces, with cascades of water falling from its springs.
Its interior was filled with delightful river-groves and gorges with cascades; many peacocks danced within to the sound of the anklets of apsaras.
Its rocky surface was polished by the tusks of the elephants of the quarters; the waters flowing out of its streams made it appear as if its garment had slipped.
Bhīma was observed with curiosity by deer at ease, grazing on fresh shoots, moving about nearby, ignorant of fear.
Shaking many networks of creepers with the speed of his thighs, playing as he went, the glorious son of Kuntī, child of the Wind, moved on.
Intent on fulfilling the desire of his beloved, beautiful-eyed, tall, golden as a palm tree, with the build of a lion, youthful —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— with the stride of a maddened elephant, the speed of a maddened elephant, eyes red as a maddened elephant, and the unstoppability of a maddened elephant —
— he was observed by invisible yaksha and gandharva women who sat nearby, turning to look at him and making gestures of admiration.
As though displaying a freshly descended form of beauty, the Pāṇḍava roamed the delightful peaks of Gandhamādana.
Remembering the many and varied hardships inflicted by Duryodhana, he was intent on doing what was dear to Draupadī, who was dwelling in the forest.
He thought: "With Arjuna gone to heaven and myself gone in search of flowers, how will the noble Yudhiṣṭhira manage?"
"Out of affection, and out of distrust of the forest, that best of men Yudhiṣṭhira will surely not release Nakula and Sahadeva."
Thinking, "How shall I obtain the flowers quickly?" that tiger among men set off with the speed of the king of birds.
Making the earth tremble with his feet like a thunderclap upon a mountain, frightening herds of elephants, wolf-bellied Bhīma moved swift as the wind.
Crushing packs of lions and tigers, uprooting great trees and smashing them against his chest, the immensely strong and mighty one pressed on.
Tearing away creepers and vines with great force, the son of Pāṇḍu, roaring mightily like a thundercloud attended by lightning, strode upward to the summit of the mountain like an elephant.
At his terrible roar and the twang of his bow, O mighty one, herds of deer fled in terror on every side.
Then that mighty-armed one beheld on the slopes of Gandhamādana a most beautiful grove of plantain trees stretching for many leagues.
The immensely powerful Bhīma rushed toward it swiftly to disturb it, like a great rutting elephant breaking down trees of every kind.
Tearing up plantain trunks as tall as many palm trees, Bhīma, foremost among the mighty, hurled them in all directions with great force.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then many great creatures rushed at him — herds of deer and elephants, and water-buffalo that dwell near ponds.
Enraged lions and tigers also charged at Bhīmasena, their jaws gaping wide, terribly fierce, roaring most fearfully.
Then the son of the Wind-god, Bhīma, relying on the strength of his own arms and filled with fury, crushed elephant with elephant and overwhelmed lion with lion; the mighty Pāṇḍava struck down the others with blows of his open palms.
Slaughtered by Bhīma, the lions, tigers, and hyenas all fled in terror, voiding dung and urine as they ran.
Having brushed them aside, the glorious and immensely powerful son of Pāṇḍu quickly entered the forest, filling all the directions with his roar.
At that terrific sound, the roar of Bhīmasena, all the deer and birds within the depths of the forest trembled with fear.
Suddenly hearing that sound stirring the beasts and birds, water-birds with damp wings rose up in their thousands.
Watching those flocks of water-birds, that bull of the Bhārata race followed them and beheld a most lovely and very great lake.
Golden groves of plantains trembling in the gentle breeze seemed to be fanning the unruffled lake as they spread along its banks.
Descending swiftly into that lake covered with abundant lotuses and lilies, the powerful Bhīma, of boundless splendour, sported in it like an unrestrained great elephant; and having played there for a long time he climbed out.
Then, plunging swiftly into that forest full of trees, the Pāṇḍava blew his resonant conch with all his breath.
At the blast of his conch, the roar of Bhīmasena, and the fierce clap of his arms, the caves of the mountain seemed to bellow in response.
Hearing that tremendous sound, like the crash of a thunderbolt, the great roar released by lions sleeping in the mountain caves arose.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O Bhārata, the very great cry released by elephants terrified by the lion's roar filled the entire mountain.
Hearing that sound, a foremost monkey who had been sleeping — a great-bodied monkey by the name of Hanūmān — stretched and yawned awake.
Lying in the midst of the plantain grove, overcome by sleep, he yawned and lashed his enormous tail — raised aloft like Indra's banner — making a sound like Indra's thunderbolt.
The mountain re-echoed the thunderclap of his tail from all its cave-mouths on every side, like a cow bellowing its lowing.
That sound of his tail, like the trumpeting of a maddened elephant, subsided and wandered across the varied ridges of the mountain.
Bhīmasena, hearing that sound, his body hair bristling with excitement, ranged through the plantain forest seeking the source of the sound.
In the middle of the plantain grove, on a broad flat rock, that mighty-armed one beheld the lord of monkeys reclining.
He was as hard to look upon as a mass of lightning, tawny as a mass of lightning, like a mass of lightning in his form, and restless as a mass of lightning.
His thick short neck was nestled between his arms crossed in a svastika; because his body was mostly shoulders, his waist and hips seemed slender.
With his head somewhat bowed and his long hair bristling, and his tail held aloft like a banner, he shone magnificently.
His lips were red, his mouth with a copper-hued tongue, his ears red, his brows mobile; his face with its rounded fang-tips shone like the moon in full brilliance.
Adorned within his face by gleaming white teeth mixed with tufts of hair, he resembled a cluster of aśoka blossoms.
Resting amid golden plantain trees, blazing with great brilliance, glowing with his own body's light, he was like a flaming fire.
That foremost of monkeys, a hero of immense body and great strength, gazed without fear with his honey-tawny eyes.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Bhīma of fearful valor swiftly approached and let out a lion's roar to rouse the monkey.
At Bhīma's sound the deer and birds trembled; Hanūmān, the great being, barely opening his eyes, then looked at him with a contemptuous gaze from his honey-tawny eyes.
Addressing the son of Kuntī with a smile, the monkey said to the man: "For what reason have you roused me, who was sleeping peacefully, causing me pain?"
"Surely you who are learned should show compassion to all beings; we do not know dharma, we who are born in the animal womb.
"Human beings endowed with intelligence show compassion to living creatures — how then do the wise like yourself engage in cruel deeds, defiling body, speech, and mind, destroying dharma?"
"You do not know dharma; the elders have not been attended by you; out of smallness of mind you destroy the wild creatures of the forest."
"Tell me — who are you, and for what reason have you come to this forest shunned even by beings possessing human qualities, indeed shunned by all men?"
"Beyond this point this mountain is utterly impassable, O hero; without the movement of the perfected siddhas, there is no way forward here."
"Out of compassion and goodwill I warn you, O mighty one — you cannot go beyond this point; take comfort in that, O lord."
"Eat these roots and fruits fit for the immortals and turn back — if my words are worthy of acceptance."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of that wise lord of monkeys, the heroic Bhīmasena, crusher of enemies, then replied.
"Who are you, and for what reason have you taken the form of a monkey? A Kṣatriya, second only to a Brāhmaṇa in rank, asks you this."
"A Kaurava, born of the lunar dynasty, carried in the womb of Kuntī, a son of Pāṇḍu, son of the Wind-god, known as Bhīmasena — I am he."
Receiving Bhīmasena's words with a smile, Hanūmān, son of the Wind-god, spoke to that son of the Wind-god.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I am a monkey; I will not give you the way you desire. Go well, turn back — lest you suffer harm."
Bhīma said: "Whatever harm may come — that is my affair; I do not ask you about it, O monkey. Give way, stand aside from my path, lest you suffer harm."
Hanūmān said: "I have no strength to rise, for I am afflicted by illness. If you must go forward, then step over me and proceed."
Bhīma said: "The Paramātman, though without attributes, pervades and dwells within your body; I do not disrespect that which is to be known by knowledge and direct experience — therefore I will not step over you."
"Were I not to perceive through scripture the One who is the source of all beings, I would stride over you and this mountain, just as Hanūmān strode over the ocean."
Hanūmān said: "Who is this Hanūmān by whom the ocean was stridden over? I ask you, O best of the Kurus — tell me if you are able."
Bhīma said: "A brother of mine, praised for his virtues, endowed with wisdom, sattva, and strength, greatly celebrated in the Rāmāyaṇa — a hero, foremost among monkeys."
"For the sake of Rāma's wife, the ocean stretching a hundred yojanas was crossed in a single leap by that lord of leaping monkeys."
"He is my brother of great heroism; I am his equal in energy, and in strength and valor in battle I am capable of restraining you."
"Rise and give me the way, or witness my manly prowess today — if you do not obey my command I shall send you to the realm of Yama."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Recognizing him as intoxicated with strength and proud of his arm's prowess, Hanūmān laughed inwardly and spoke these words.
"Be appeased — I have no strength to rise, being oppressed by old age, O sinless one. Out of compassion for me, simply move this tail aside and proceed."
Then with a contemptuous smile, Bhīma grasped the tail with his left hand — yet he could not move the tail of the great monkey.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He tried again to lift it with both arms — raised like Indra's weapon — yet even the immensely powerful Bhīma could not raise it with both arms.
With eyebrows raised, eyes rolling, face contracted into a frown, and body drenched in sweat, Bhīma struggled — yet he utterly could not lift it.
Though he strained with effort, exhausted by his attempt to lift the tail, the glorious Bhīma stood beside the monkey with his head bowed in shame.
Then the son of Kuntī bowed down with joined palms and spoke: "Be gracious, O tiger among monkeys — may my harsh words be forgiven."
"Whether you are a siddha, a god, a gandharva, or a yakṣa — being asked, please tell me willingly who you are who bears the form of a monkey."
Hanūmān said: "O subduer of enemies, O joy of the Pāṇḍavas — since you have curiosity to know me fully, hear it all completely."
"I am the monkey named Hanūmān, born in the field of Kesarī by Vāyu, the life-breath of the world, O lotus-eyed one."
"Sugrīva son of the Sun and Vālin son of Indra — both kings of all monkeys, leaders of all monkey troops —
"— those greatly heroic ones attended me as well, O crusher of enemies. My friendship with Sugrīva was like that of wind and fire."
"Then, wronged by his brother for some other reason, Sugrīva lived for a long time on Ṛśyamūka together with me."
"Then the heroic and immensely powerful Rāma, son of Daśaratha — Viṣṇu in human form — wandered upon this earth."
"Seeking to fulfill his father's wish, accompanied by his wife and younger brother, bow in hand, foremost among archers, he took refuge in the Daṇḍaka forest."
"His wife was forcibly carried off from Janasthāna by Rāvaṇa, who had deceived the great-minded Rāghava by taking the form of a deer."
"With his wife abducted, that Rāghava, searching for his wife together with his brother, saw Sugrīva, the bull among monkeys, on a mountain peak."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Friendship was formed between that great-souled Rāghava and Sugrīva; having killed Vālin he restored Sugrīva to the kingdom, and sent out the monkey hosts in search of Sītā."
"Then, from among the directions in which we set out with tens of millions of monkeys, news of Sītā was made known by a vulture in our direction."
"Then I, for the accomplishment of the mission of Rāma whose deeds are effortless, leaped at once across the ocean stretching a hundred yojanas."
"That goddess was seen by me in Rāvaṇa's abode, and I returned again, having made my name known there."
"Then the heroic Rāma, having slain all those rākṣasas, recovered his wife who had been lost, as the Vedic tradition recovers what has been forgotten."
"Then, when Rāma was established in his kingdom, this hero was implored by me: 'O hero, O slayer of foes, as long as the tale of Rāma resounds in the worlds, may I live' — and he replied, 'So be it.'"
"Rāma caused his kingdom to be administered for ten thousand years and ten hundred years more, and then departed to heaven."
"Here the apsarases, dear one, and the gandharvas, O ever-sinless one, constantly delight me by singing the deeds of that hero."
"This path is impassable for mortals, O joy of the Kurus; therefore I have blocked your way along this road frequented by the gods, so that none may violate or curse it, O Bhārata."
This is the divine path of the gods; mortals do not travel here. The lake you have come for is quite near indeed.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the mighty-armed and valiant Bhīmasena, having bowed with joy and gladness of heart, spoke gently to Hanūmān, the lord of monkeys, calling him brother.
There is none more fortunate than I, for I have seen you, noble one. Your sight has bestowed on me a great blessing and deep satisfaction.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There is one favour I wish you to do for me now, noble one: that incomparable form you bore when you leaped across the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters — that form, O hero, I desire to behold.
In that way I shall be fully satisfied and shall truly believe your words. Thus addressed, that radiant monkey laughed and spoke.
That form cannot be seen by you, nor by anyone else; the condition of that time was different, and it does not obtain now.
Time was one thing in the Kṛta age, another in the Tretā, yet another in the Dvāpara; this present age is one of deterioration — I no longer have that form.
The earth, rivers, trees, mountains, siddhas, gods, and great sages all follow the course of time; the conditions of existence in each age vary accordingly, and strength, stature, and power diminish and arise in turn.
So enough — let it be; you cannot see that form, O ornament of the Kuru line. I conform to the age, for time is impossible to transgress.
Bhīma said: Describe to me the reckoning of the ages and the conduct in each age — the states of dharma, desire, and wealth, the stature, the strength, the rise and fall in each.
Hanūmān said: There is an age called Kṛta, dear one, in which eternal dharma prevails; in that supreme age, what is to be done is already done — no further effort is needed.
In it dharmas do not decline, nor do creatures diminish; and so, by virtue of its qualities, time has named it Kṛta.
In the Kṛta age, dear one, there were no gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, or serpents; and there was no buying and selling.
There were no Sama, Yajur, or Rig Vedic ritual classes, nor any human rite; dharma there was simply meditation on the fruit and renunciation alone.
In that confluence of ages there was no disease, no deterioration of the senses, no envy, no weeping, no arrogance, and no backbiting.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There was no strife, how could there be sloth, no hatred, no perversity, no fear, no sorrow, no jealousy, and no envy.
Then the supreme Brahman — that highest goal of yogins and the self of all beings — Nārāyaṇa was white (in that age).
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, bearing the marks of the Kṛta age, were in that age creatures fully devoted to their own duties.
With equal stages of life, equal conduct, equal knowledge and surpassing strength, the varnas, performing identical acts, attained to dharmas.
United in one Veda, performing rites of one mantra and one rule, though having separate dharmas they adhered to one Veda and followed one dharma.
Through action united with the four stages of life, in harmony with time, without attachment to the fruit of desire, they attained the highest state.
This dharma, marked by the Kṛta age's quality and united with self-yoga, was in the Kṛta age fourfold and eternal for the four varnas.
This is what is called the Kṛta age, free from the three qualities. Now learn about the Tretā age as well, in which the great soma sacrifice proceeds.
By one quarter dharma diminishes; Acyuta (Viṣṇu) takes on a reddish hue; and men, bent on truth, are devoted to ritual and dharma.
Then sacrifices come into being, and various dharmic rites; in the Tretā intentions and resolutions arise, and the fruits of ritual action and giving.
Devoted to austerity and giving, they do not swerve from dharma; people in the Tretā age abided in their own duty and were active in religious observance.
In the Dvāpara age too, dharma proceeds diminished by two quarters; Viṣṇu takes on a yellow hue, and the Veda is divided fourfold.
Then some know all four Vedas, others three, others two, others one; and yet others have no Vedic knowledge at all.
With the sacred texts thus divided, rites are conducted in many ways; people become passionate and oriented toward austerity and giving.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Because of the ignorance of the one Veda, many Vedas were made; and due to the decay of truth here, only a few remain established in truth.
For those who fall away from truth, many diseases arise, and desires and afflictions come, caused then by the gods.
Tormented greatly by these, men perform austerities; some, desiring enjoyment, others desiring heaven, spread out sacrifices.
Thus, having entered the Dvāpara, creatures decay through adharma; in the Kali age, O son of Kuntī, dharma stands on one quarter alone.
Having arrived at the dark age, Keśava becomes black; Vedic practices subside, and dharmic rites and sacrificial acts likewise.
Calamities, diseases, sloth, faults such as anger, afflictions, mental anguish, and physical ailments come to prevail.
As the ages revolve, dharma revolves again; as dharma revolves, the world revolves again.
When the world is exhausted, the forces that set the world in motion decay; dharmas created by the decay of ages distort their own aspirations.
This is what is called the Kali age, which before long comes into force; those who live long keep following this succession of ages.
And your curiosity about knowing me — what attachment should a wise man have to things of no ultimate purpose, O subduer of enemies?
All of what you asked me — the reckoning of the ages — has been told to you. Now fare you well, O mighty-armed one; go on your way.
Bhīma said: Without seeing your former form I shall not depart in any way. If you would favour me, reveal yourself by yourself.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Bhīma, the monkey smiled and displayed that form he had worn when leaping across the ocean.
Wishing to please his brother, he assumed a mighty body; his frame then grew exceedingly in length and breadth.
Of immeasurable radiance, covering a grove of plantain trees with that form, the monkey rose to the height of a mountain and stood there.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Rearing his immense body like a second mountain, with copper-red eyes, sharp fangs, and furrowed brows, the monkey swung his great tail and stood pervading all directions.
Beholding that vast form of his brother, Bhīma, the joy of the Kurus, was filled with wonder and thrilled again and again.
Seeing him blazing like the sun with his radiance, like a golden mountain, like the sky on fire, Bhīma closed his eyes.
And Hanūmān, smiling, spoke to Bhīmasena: "This much of my form are you able to behold here, O sinless one."
"I can grow still further, as much as my mind desires; and against enemies, Bhīma, my form grows exceedingly with vigour."
Beholding that wonderful, tremendously terrible frame of Hanūmān, like the Vindhya and Mandara mountains, the son of the wind was bewildered.
Then Bhīma, his body hair standing up in joy, replied to Hanūmān who stood before him, with folded hands, his spirit undaunted.
"The vast measure of your body has been seen, O lord; now, O greatly valiant one, withdraw yourself into yourself."
"For I cannot look at you, risen like the sun, immeasurable and unapproachable, like the mountain Maināka."
"And I have great wonder in my mind today, O hero, that with you at his side Rāma himself went against Rāvaṇa."
"You alone were capable of destroying that Laṅkā with all its warriors and vehicles, relying on your own arm's strength and vigour."
"For there is nothing unattainable for you, O son of the wind; Rāvaṇa with all his forces was not a match for you alone in battle."
Thus addressed by Bhīma, Hanūmān, the bull among monkeys, then replied with a voice gentle and deep.
"It is so, great-armed one, as you say, O Bhārata; Bhīmasena, that vile Rākṣasa was no match for me."
"But had I slain that thorn of the world, Rāvaṇa, the glory of Rāma would have been lost; therefore I refrained."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"By that hero, having slain the lord of Rākṣasas with all his forces, Sītā was brought back to his city and his glory was established in the world."
"So go now, O man of vast wisdom, devoted to your brother's welfare and happiness; may the path be free of ill and safe, protected by the wind."
"This is the path, O best of Kurus, to the Saugandhika forest; you will see the garden of Kubera guarded by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas."
"Do not by force gather the flowers yourself; the gods are to be especially honoured by a man."
"By offerings, oblations, salutations, and mantras, O bull of the Bhāratas, the gods in their grace act with devotion, O Bhārata."
"Do not act rashly, dear one; uphold your own dharma. Established in your own dharma, understand the highest dharma and approach it."
"Without knowing dharma, and without attending on the elders, dharma cannot truly be understood — not even by those equal to Bṛhaspati."
"Where adharma goes by the name of dharma and dharma is called adharma — that distinction must be discerned carefully, where the unintelligent are confused."
"Dharma is born of conduct; from dharma the Vedas arise; from the Vedas sacrifices are produced; by sacrifices the gods are established."
"The gods are sustained by sacrifices enjoined by Vedic conduct and rule; men are sustained by the policies declared by Bṛhaspati and Uśanas."
"By trade, mining, commerce, agriculture, and by the support of one's source of livelihood — by this economic activity and by these dharmas of the twice-born all is sustained."
"The three Vedas, economics, and statecraft — these are the three branches of knowledge for the wise; when properly applied together, the journey of the world is ordered."
"If these dharmic activities were absent, if the triple Veda were absent from the earth, and if statecraft were absent too, this world would be without limit or restraint."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Not following the dharma of livelihood, these people would perish; with these three dharmas well pursued, creatures truly flourish."
"For the twice-born, dharma is immortal; there is one dharma peculiar to each varna; sacrifice, study, and giving — these three are remembered as common to all."
"Both officiating at rites and teaching, as well as receiving gifts, are for Brāhmaṇas; protection is for Kṣatriyas; the dharma of Vaiśyas is nurturing."
"Service to the twice-born is said to be the dharma of Śūdras; likewise those who lack begging, fire-offerings, and vows — the duty of those who live at the guru's house."
"The Kṣatriya dharma here, O son of Kuntī, is the protection of dharma; take up your own dharma, with humility and controlled senses."
"Having taken counsel with the aged, the righteous, the wise, and those versed in scripture, one who is well established rules through the rod of chastisement; the self-indulgent is overwhelmed."
"When a king properly exercises both punishment and favour, then the boundaries of the world are well and truly established."
"Therefore, regarding territory, fortresses, and the strength of enemies and allies, one must always be alert through spies to one's position, growth, and decline."
A king has four instruments at his disposal: wise counsel, valor, the power to punish and reward, and skill in accomplishing the task at hand.
Affairs are to be accomplished through conciliation, gifts, division of enemies, punishment, and disregard — whether by brief or extended application of these means.
All statecraft and espionage are rooted in counsel, O bull of the Bhāratas. Success comes through well-deliberated policy; one should take counsel together with those who know these arts.
One should not share secrets with a woman, a fool, a greedy man, a child, or a frivolous person, nor with those who show signs of madness.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One should deliberate with the learned; have tasks executed by the capable; entrust the arrangements of policy to loyal men; and everywhere shun the foolish.
In matters of righteousness, employ the righteous; in matters of wealth, employ the wise; in matters concerning women, employ eunuchs; and in cruel tasks, employ the cruel.
The intelligence that discerns what must and must not be done — from one's own people and from the enemy — and the measure of the enemy's strength and weakness must be known in all affairs.
Toward those who conduct themselves well according to sound judgment, one should extend favor and acceptance; toward the ill-behaved and the lawless, one should apply restraint.
When a king rightly applies both restraint and reward, the boundaries of social order become well established for all people.
This, O Pārtha, is the stern and difficult dharma prescribed for you. Abiding in discipline, maintain it according to the divisions proper to your own duty.
Just as brahmins reach heaven through austerity, righteousness, self-restraint, and sacrifice, so vaishyas attain the good state through the dharma of giving, hospitality, and proper action.
So too the kshatriya attains heaven on earth through restraint and protection; wielding the rod of punishment rightly, free from desire and hatred, ungreedy and rid of anger, they reach the world of the righteous.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the monkey, drawing back in that vast body swollen by desire, embraced Bhīmasena once again with his arms.
As Bhīma was embraced by his brother, O Bhārata, his fatigue vanished at once and all auspicious signs attended him.
Then the monkey spoke again, his eyes brimming with tears, addressing Bhīma out of affection with a voice choked with weeping.
"Go, hero, to your own dwelling. Remember me when the time comes for stories; yet while I dwell here, O best of Kurus, you must not reveal my presence to anyone."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For the divine women of the gandharvas, released from the abode of Kubera, the lord of wealth, will come here at the right place and time, O great-armed one."
"My sight too has borne fruit, and I have been reminded of Rāma of the Raghu line. Having obtained the touch of a human body by meeting you, Bhīma, it has been worthwhile."
"So let this meeting of ours not be in vain for you, O hero, son of Kuntī. Placing our brotherhood foremost, ask a boon, O Bhārata."
"If those wretched sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are to be slain by me when I go to Hāstinapura, I shall do it now, as much as you wish."
"Or if that city must be crushed by me with a boulder, I shall do it today, as much as your desire requires, O great-armed one."
Bhīmasena, hearing those words of the great-souled one, replied to Hanūmān with his heart overflowing with joy.
"All has already been done by you for me, O bull among monkeys. May well-being be yours, O great-armed one. I ask your forgiveness — be gracious to me."
"All the Pāṇḍavas are protected, having you as our protector, O valiant one. By your very radiance we shall conquer all our enemies."
Thus addressed, Hanūmān spoke to Bhīmasena: "Out of brotherhood and affection I shall do what is dear to you."
"When you plunge into the enemy's army thick with arrows and javelins, O hero, and let forth your lion-roar, O great-armed one, then I shall amplify your cry with my own voice."
"Standing on Arjuna's banner, I shall release terrifying cries that will take the lives of your enemies." Saying this, he disappeared.
After that foremost of monkeys had departed, Bhīma too, the best among the strong, roamed widely over the Gandhamādana by the path he had come.
Recalling Hanūmān's form and his matchless splendor on earth, remembering the greatness and power of the son of Daśaratha, he went his way.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He then searched through those delightful forests and groves, eager to find the grove of saugandhika flowers.
He then saw forests rich with blooming lotuses, flowering woodlands, herds of rutting elephants mired in mud, and clouds gathered as if ready to pour rain, O Bhārata.
Seen on the path by deer with darting eyes accompanied by their does, chewing mouthfuls of young grass, the glorious one passed quickly on.
Bhīmasena, fearless through his valor, plunged into the mountain frequented by buffaloes, wild boars, and tigers.
He passed through the forest past trees with flower-laden branches, their tender copper-colored shoots soft, the trees swaying in the wind as if beseeching him.
On the path he passed lotus ponds with cupped blossoms like folded palms, attended by intoxicated bees, their forests and sacred fords beloved.
His mind and gaze riveted on the flowering mountain slopes, sustained by the words of Draupadī as his provisions, Bhīma went yet more swiftly.
Then, as the day turned and deer scattered through the forest, he beheld a vast river adorned with pure golden lotuses.
The river was filled with drunken karandava ducks, beautified by chakravaka birds, and seemed like a garland of pure lotuses fashioned for that mountain.
In that river the great-souled one beheld a vast grove of saugandhika lotuses, gladdening to behold, radiant as the morning sun.
Seeing it and thus having his heart's desire, the son of Pāṇḍu went in thought to his beloved, worn by the hardships of forest exile.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Going to that lovely lotus-lake guarded by rakshasas on the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, he saw it in a fair and auspicious grove.
Born near the dwelling of Kubera, fed by mountain torrents, most beautiful, broad-shaded, entwined with many trees and creepers.
Covered with green lotuses, divine, bearing golden water-lilies, purifying to the world, auspicious and wondrous to behold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There the son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava, beheld the water — cool, light, auspicious, pure, wholesome, and abundant, like the essence of nectar.
That lovely pond was filled with saugandhika lotuses, covered with blooms of purest gold, supremely fragrant.
With stalks of finest lapis lazuli, many-hued and heart-ravishing, disturbed by swans and karandava ducks that scattered spotless pollen.
It was the pleasure-ground of the great-souled king of yakshas, Kubera, and was most highly honored by gandharvas, apsarases, and gods.
It was frequented by divine sages, by yakshas, kimpurushas, rakshasas, and kinnaras, and was guarded by Vaiśravaṇa.
Beholding that lake, the son of Kuntī, Bhīmasena of great strength, was supremely delighted upon seeing that divine pond.
That lake was guarded by a hundred thousand rakshasas called the Krodhavaśa, by order of the king, armed and equipped with diverse weapons.
They, upon seeing the son of Kuntī clad in deerskins, wearing golden armlets, the hero Bhīma of terrible prowess —
— bearing weapons, his sword girt, the tamer of foes, approaching fearlessly in his desire to reach the lotuses — they cried out to one another.
"This tiger among men, bearing weapons and covered in deerskins, has come here with some intention — you ought to ask him what it is."
Then they all approached that great-armed Vṛkodara, radiant with energy, and asked: "Who are you? You should declare yourself."
"You appear to be wearing the garb of a sage, clothed in bark-cloth. Tell us, O greatly resplendent one, what purpose has brought you here."
Bhīma said: "I am Bhīmasena, a Pāṇḍava, next in rank after the son of Dharma; I have come to vast Badarī together with my brothers, O rakshasas."
"There the Pāñcālī princess saw an incomparable saugandhika lotus, clearly carried here by the wind; she desires many more of them."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I have come here to gather a bouquet of flowers for her sake — she of flawless limbs, my beloved, the lawfully wedded wife. Know this, O night-wanderers."
The rakshasas said: "This is the beloved pleasure-ground of Kubera, O bull among men. No mortal man subject to the law of death may sport here."
"Divine sages, yakshas, and gods, O Vṛkodara, drink and sport here after taking leave of the great yaksha lord; gandharvas and apsarases too sport here, O Pāṇḍava."
"Whoever, wrongly and without reverence for the lord of wealth, desires to sport here out of wicked conduct — that one shall surely perish without doubt."
"Disregarding him, you wish to take the lotuses from here by force — how then do you call yourself the brother of the king of righteousness?"
Bhīma said: "O rakshasas, I do not see the lord of wealth anywhere nearby; and even if I were to see the great king, I would not presume to beg from him."
"For kings do not beg — that is the eternal law. Nor do I wish to abandon the dharma of the kshatriya under any circumstances."
"Moreover, this lovely lotus-pond was born from a mountain stream; it has not reached the dwelling of the great-souled Kubera and thus does not belong to him exclusively."
"This belongs equally to all beings and to Vaiśravaṇa alike. When things stand thus in common, who has the right to beg from whom?"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to all the rakshasas, Bhīmasena plunged in. Then the mighty one was stopped by the rakshasas with words — "No! Not like this!" — threatening him angrily on all sides.
But that one of terrible prowess, treating those rakshasas with contempt, plunged forward; the great-souled one pressed in, and they all tried to stop him.
"Seize him! Bind him! Hack him down! Let us cook and eat Bhīmasena!" — crying out in rage, they swiftly pursued him, brandishing their weapons with rolling eyes.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, seizing his massive mace riveted with bands of gold, dreadful as the rod of Yama, he charged at them swiftly, crying out: "Stand! Stand your ground!"
They then hurled their weapons — darts, iron clubs and the rest — and charged him suddenly, those formidable rakshasas, the Krodhavaśa, consumed by wrath, fierce, surrounding Bhīma on all sides.
He who was born powerfully of Kuntī by the Wind, a hero, swift, slayer of enemies, ever devoted to truth and righteousness, unconquerable by foes in valor —
— that great-souled hero cut off their various approaches, shattered the weapons of the enemy, and slew them as they led their charge — more than a hundred — near the lotus-lake.
Seeing his valor and strength, his knowledge-power and the power of his arms alike, unable to withstand him together from all sides, their foremost warriors struck down, they suddenly turned back.
Being shattered right there, swiftly taking to the sky with their senses bewildered, the Krodhavaśa, broken and tormented by Bhīma, fled toward the peaks of Kailāsa.
Like Indra overcoming hosts of danavas and daityas, he stepped forth and conquered those troops of enemies in battle; plunging into that lotus-pond, his foes vanquished, he then gathered the lotus-blooms to his heart's content.
Then, drinking the nectar-like water, he became renewed in the highest vigor and energy; uprooting and gathering the saugandhika lotuses, supremely fragrant, he took them all.
Then those Krodhavaśa, driven back by Bhīma's might, gathered themselves and went to the lord of wealth; exceedingly distressed, they reported faithfully Bhīma's valor and strength in battle.
Hearing their words, the divine lord laughed and then addressed the rakshasas: "Let Bhīma take the water-born flowers as he pleases; I already know it is for Kṛṣṇā's sake."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, having taken leave of the lord of wealth, they went, their anger gone, to the best of the Kurus, and beheld Bhīma sporting alone in that lotus-lake as he pleased.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O bull of the Bhāratas, he gathered those many divine and most precious flowers, of many forms, pure and spotless.
Then a great and swift wind arose, harsh to the touch, driving gravel along the ground, urging on as if stirring up a battle.
A great and blazing meteor fell with a thunderous crash; the sun lost its radiance, its rays covered and enveloped in darkness.
There was a terrible clap of thunder while Bhīma was engaged in his mighty feat; the earth itself trembled, and a shower of dust fell.
The directions turned blood-red; beasts and birds cried out harshly; everything was enveloped in darkness so that nothing could be discerned.
Beholding that marvel, Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma and foremost among the eloquent, said: "Who is it that shall overcome us?"
"Be ready, O Pāṇḍavas, intoxicated with battle — fortune attend you! By what I see, our own prowess shall prove supreme."
Having spoken thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the dharma-king, looked around in all directions, but could not see Bhīma.
There the subduer of foes asked Draupadī and the twin brothers who stood nearby about his brother Bhīma, terrible in battle deeds.
"O Pāñcālī, has Bhīma not gone to do something? Or has that hero, fond of bold exploits, already performed some daring deed?"
"For these sudden ill omens, portending a great battle, have manifested on all sides showing terrible fear."
To him speaking thus, Kṛṣṇā — the wise one, his beloved, the beautiful-smiling queen eager to please her dear one — replied:
"O king, those Saugandhika lotuses which were brought by the wind — today I had them fetched for the delight of Bhīmasena.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And the hero was told by me: if you find many more of them, gather them all and return quickly."
"He, that mighty-armed Pāṇḍava, has surely gone from here in the north-eastward direction, O king, to fetch those flowers for my sake."
Addressed thus by her, the king then spoke to the twins: "Let us all go quickly in the direction Vṛkodara has gone."
"Let the rakshasas carry the brahmanas, weary and emaciated as they are; and you also, O Ghaṭotkaca, equal to the immortals, carry Kṛṣṇā."
"It is clear to my mind that Bhīma has gone deep and far from here; the time has grown long, and he is equal to the wind in speed."
"Swift, he is equal to Garuḍa's son in leaping on earth; he could spring up into the sky and descend again at will."
"Let us follow him — by your power, O night-rangers — before he commits any offense against the Siddhas and the Brahmā-speakers."
Saying "so be it," all of them, led by Hiḍimba's son, who knew the way to Kubera's lake, O bull of the Bhāratas —
— taking up the Pāṇḍavas and those many brahmanas, together with Lomaśa himself, set out with joyful hearts.
Going together, all of them saw there in the forest that charming lake adorned with fully blooming lotuses — most beautiful to behold.
And they saw that great-souled Bhīma standing on its bank, and also saw the yakshas with large eyes, slain.
He stood on the river-bank holding his mace aloft with both arms, like Death himself staff in hand at the time of universal dissolution.
Seeing him, the dharma-king embraced him again and again and said in gentle words: "O son of Kuntī, what is this that you have done?"
"This rashness, though it may bring you glory, is displeasing even to the gods. Do not do such a thing again, if you wish to please me."
Having admonished the son of Kuntī and receiving the lotus flowers, they — equal to the immortals — sported together in that very lake.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At this very time there appeared the mighty-bodied guardians of that garden, armed with rocks, coming forth.
Seeing the king of dharma, and the divine sage Lomaśa, and Nakula and Sahadeva, and the other brahmin-seers, all of them bowed with humility and prostrated, O Bhārata.
Appeased by the dharma-king, those night-wanderers became serene; and being known to Kubera, those bull-like men, the upholders of the Kuru line, stayed there for a while, sporting in delight.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, while those Pāṇḍavas were living there confidently — after those rakshasas and also the son of Bhīmasena had departed —
— left without Bhīmasena, a rakshasa one day seized them by chance — the dharma-king, the twins, and Kṛṣṇā.
Representing himself as a brahmin skilled in mantras and supremely learned in all weapons, he constantly attended upon the Pāṇḍavas daily.
He examined the quivers and bows of the Pārthas while seeking an opportunity, known by name as Jaṭāsura.
When the foe-subduing Bhīmasena had gone out for hunting, he assumed another form — terrible, monstrous, and enormous.
Seizing all the weapons and taking hold of Draupadī, that evil-souled one set off, having also captured three of the Pāṇḍavas.
But Sahadeva, the Pāṇḍava, managed to slip away with effort and cried out to Bhīmasena, that mighty one, in the direction he had gone.
While being carried off, the dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to him: "Your dharma declines, O fool — do you not see this at all?"
"Whatever beings there are among humans, and even those born in animal wombs — gandharvas, yakshas, rakshasas, birds, beasts — they all live dependent upon humans; and thus do you live dependent on them."
"For by the prosperity of this world, your world too prospers; when this world grieves, the gods also grieve; and when properly worshipped, they thrive on oblations and offerings."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"We are the guardians and protectors of the kingdom, O rakshasa; for an unprotected kingdom, how can there be prosperity? How can there be happiness?"
"A king who has committed no offense must never be disrespected by a rakshasa; and not even the smallest transgression exists on our part, O man-eater."
"One must never betray friends, nor those who have placed their trust; nor those whose food one has eaten, nor those who have given one shelter."
"You, who dwelt sheltered by us, were honored and lived in comfort; having eaten our food, how do you, O witless one, now seek to carry us off?"
"Such is your character — your growth is in vain, your intelligence in vain, your conduct in vain; you deserve a vain death, and this day you shall cease to exist in vain."
"But if you, corrupt in mind and devoid of all dharma, wish — give back our weapons and then win Draupadī by open combat."
"But if you do this deed without understanding, you will gain only unrighteousness and infamy in the world."
"By laying violent hands upon this woman today, O rakshasa — this human woman — it is poison you have drunk by the potful, having stirred it up yourself."
Then Yudhiṣṭhira became a burden upon him; the rakshasa, his spirit overwhelmed by the weight, could no longer move as swiftly as before.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira said to Draupadī and to Nakula: "Do not fear this foolish rakshasa — I have stolen away his power of movement."
"The mighty-armed son of the wind-god will not be far away; when this moment arrives, this rakshasa shall be no more."
Sahadeva, seeing that rakshasa of dulled mind, spoke these words to king Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī:
"O king, what deed is there higher for a kshatriya than this — that facing the enemy in battle he should either give up his life or conquer his foes?"
"Either this one shall destroy us or we shall destroy him in battle, O scorcher of foes, O mighty-armed one — for this is the right time and place, O king."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The time for kshatriya dharma has arrived, O man of true valor; whether conquering or being slain, we deserve to attain the highest state."
"If the sun were to set today with this rakshasa still alive, I would never again say 'I am a kshatriya,' O Bhārata."
"Ho there, rakshasa — stop! I am Sahadeva, the Pāṇḍava. Either slay me and then carry them off, or lie here slain this very day."
Even as he was speaking thus, Bhīmasena appeared by chance — mighty-armed, like Vāsava armed with the thunderbolt.
He saw his two brothers there, and the illustrious Draupadī, and Sahadeva on the ground hurling abuse at the rakshasa.
And he saw the foolish rakshasa, his mind stricken by fate, wandering here and there, checked and restrained by destiny.
The mighty Bhīma, seeing him carrying off his brothers and Draupadī, filled himself with wrath and spoke these words to the rakshasa:
"You were recognized by me earlier from your behavior while inspecting the weapons; but I placed no importance on you, and so you were not killed then — for you were disguised in brahmin form and did not say anything disagreeable to us."
"You who moved among the beloved ones, not doing anything harmful, a guest in brahmin form — how could I slay one who had committed no offense? Even one who knew you to be a rakshasa would go to hell for killing such a one."
"There is no slaying by time of one who is not yet ripe; but now surely you are fully ripe, since such a resolve has been given to you by time — marvelous in its workings — to carry off Kṛṣṇā."
"This hook has been swallowed by you, hung on the thread of time; like a fish in water with a pierced mouth — how will you escape from me today?"
"The destination to which you set out, where your mind already went beforehand — you will not reach it; you will go the way of Baka and Hiḍimba."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Addressed thus by Bhīma, the rakshasa, driven by fate, was frightened; releasing all of them, he presented himself for battle.
And with lips quivering from rage, he again spoke to Bhīma: "My directions are not confused, O sinner — the delay was only for your sake."
"All the rakshasas I have heard of who were slain by you in battle — for them today I shall perform the water libation using your blood."
Thus addressed, Bhīma then, licking the corners of his lips, as if smiling yet burning with rage, like Death and the destroyer at the end of time in person, desiring only the fury of his arms, rushed at the rakshasa.
The rakshasa too rushed at Bhīma who stood ready seeking battle, furious with rage, like Bali charging Indra the thunderbolt-bearer.
While the two of them were engaged in that most terrible wrestling match, the two sons of Mādrī, furious, both rushed forward as well.
Vṛkodara, son of Kuntī, laughing, restrained both of them, saying: "I am capable against this rakshasa — just watch."
"By myself, by my brothers, by dharma, by my good deeds, and by my sacrifices I swear, O king, I shall destroy this rakshasa."
Having spoken thus, those two heroes, competing with each other, grappled with their arms — both the rakshasa and Vṛkodara.
There was a fierce clash between the two — the furious Bhīma and the rakshasa — neither enduring the other, like gods and demons in battle.
The two of them, uprooting tree after tree, struck each other, roaring like two storm-clouds at the end of summer — those two mighty ones.
Those two best among the strong shattered great trees with their thighs, grappling with each other in fury, each seeking victory over the other.
That tree-battle brought destruction to the trees, just as the battle between the brothers Vālī and Sugrīva, those lions among monkeys, had done before.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Swinging trees again and again at each other for a while, they both struck blows, roaring repeatedly.
When in that place all the trees had been felled and piled in hundreds by those two, each intent on killing the other,
then, O Bhārata, they took up rocks and fought for a while, those two mighty ones like great mountains with thunderclouds.
With fierce, terrifying, massive boulders they struck each other like thunderbolts with great force, both filled with fury.
And having struck each other repeatedly, those two proud in strength then grappled with their arms and dragged each other like elephants.
They fell upon each other with terribly fierce fists, and a crackling sound arose from those two great-souled ones.
Then drawing back his fist like a five-headed serpent, Bhīma struck the neck of the Rākṣasa with great force.
Then, seeing that Rākṣasa wearied and utterly exhausted from the blows of Bhīmasena's arms, Bhīmasena pressed forward.
Then mighty-armed Bhīma, equal to an immortal, lifted him up forcibly with both arms and crushed him against the ground.
The Pāṇḍava crushed all his limbs and, striking him with his elbow, severed the head from the body.
Jaṭāsura's head, with lips bitten, eyes rolled back, like fruit fallen from its stalk, held by the force of Bhīmasena, fell drenched in blood, with teeth clenching the lips.
Having slain him, that great archer came to Yudhiṣṭhira, praised by those foremost brahmins, like Vāsava attended by the Maruts.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: With that Rākṣasa slain, King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, the lord, returned again to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa and made his abode there.
Gathering all his brothers together with Draupadī, he spoke these words in time, remembering his brother Arjuna:
"Four years have passed auspiciously for us dwelling in the forest, and Arjuna has accomplished his purpose — the fifth year is now approaching.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having reached Mount Śveta, best of peaks among mountains, there too his purpose was accomplished, and we longed to meet him again.
And that Pārtha of boundless splendour made an agreement with me: 'I will dwell five years seeking knowledge,' he said long ago.
We shall see the Gāṇḍīva-bowman, subduer of foes, who has obtained all weapons, returning from the world of the gods to this world."
Having spoken thus, the Pāṇḍava took leave of all the brahmins and explained to those ascetics the reason for his departure.
Those brahmins of fierce austerities, pleased, circumambulated Yudhiṣṭhira and blessed him with auspicious words and well-being.
"This hardship, O bull of the Bhāratas, O knower of dharma, will soon bear fruit in happiness; crossing through it by the law of warriors, you shall rule the earth."
The king, that scorcher of enemies, receiving those words of the ascetics, set out together with those brahmins and his brothers.
The glorious one, accompanied by Draupadī, followed by Rākṣasas headed by Ghaṭotkaca, son of Hidimbi, and protected by Lomaśa.
Somewhere he went on foot, somewhere he was carried by the Rākṣasas — that great-splendoured one of excellent vows, together with his brothers, here and there.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, reflecting on many hardships, journeyed northward toward the direction filled with lions, tigers, and elephants.
Gazing upon Kailāsa, Mount Maināka, the foothills of Gandhamādana, and Meru the rocky peak,
ever higher on the mountains, past many auspicious rivers, they reached the sacred plateau of the Himālayas on the seventeenth day.
The Pāṇḍavas, O king, saw Gandhamādana close at hand, on the sacred back of the Himālayas, covered with many trees and creepers.
Adorned with blooming great trees born from water-eddies, they saw the most sacred hermitage of Vṛṣaparvan.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Approaching that royal sage Vṛṣaparvan, righteous-souled, the Pāṇḍavas, subduers of foes, free from fatigue, paid reverence to him.
That royal sage welcomed the bulls of the Bhārata race as a father would his sons; honored, those subduers of enemies dwelt there for seven nights.
When the eighth day arrived, they took leave of that sage famed throughout the world, Vṛṣaparvan, and resolved to depart.
And presenting each of those brahmins one by one to Vṛṣaparvan, like treasured friends duly honoured, at the proper time,
then the Pāṇḍavas left behind their excellent garments and auspicious ornaments in that hermitage of Vṛṣaparvan.
That wise one, skilled in past and future, knower of all dharma, that knower of righteousness, instructed the bulls of the Bhārata race as a father would his sons.
Those great-souled heroes, given leave, journeyed northward together with Kṛṣṇā and great-souled brahmins; and Vṛṣaparvan, lord of the earth, followed them as they set out.
The great-splendoured Vṛṣaparvan commended the Pāṇḍavas to the brahmins, blessed the sons of Kuntī with benedictions, congratulated them, and after showing them the path, turned back.
Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, of true valour, set out on foot together with his brothers through forests filled with many herds of animals.
Dwelling on the mountain slopes amid many thickets of trees, the Pāṇḍavas entered Mount Śveta on the fourth day.
That mountain resembling a mass of great clouds, adorned with water, auspicious, beautiful with gems and gold, with its many soaring peaks.
They reached the path as described by Vṛṣaparvan and followed it to its destination, beholding diverse mountains.
Going ever higher on the mountain, those very many most impassable, utterly inaccessible caves they traversed with ease.
Dhaumya, Kṛṣṇā, the Pārthas, and the great sage Lomaśa all went together there; not one fell behind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That place resounded with animals and birds, teeming with many kinds of birds, frequented by troops of monkeys, and exceedingly beautiful.
Those of great might approached the great mountain Mālyavān, sacred, with its lotus lakes, its great forest full of ponds.
Then with hairs standing on end in delight they saw the mountain Gandhamādana, abode of the Kiṃpuruṣas, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Attended by Vidyādharas and Kinnaras, it was dense with elephants and lions and filled with rampaging sharabhas.
Adorned then with other deer that called in gentle tones, that forest of Gandhamādana resembled Nandana, the divine grove.
Joyful, the sons of Pāṇḍu, those heroes, entered step by step that forest, heart-gladdening and auspicious.
Those heroes together with Draupadī and those great-souled brahmins, listening to gladsome, sweet, intoxicating, auspicious, ear-delighting, melodious sounds uttered from the mouths of birds,
beholding trees laden with fruit of every season, blazing with blossoms of every season, and bowing down under their burden of fruit,
mangoes, blooming amrataka, coconuts, ebony trees, ajataka, jira trees, pomegranates, and citrons,
jackfruit, licucha, banana, date palms, mango-cane, pāravata trees, sweet-honey trees, and charming nipa trees,
bel trees, wood-apples, rose-apple trees, kashmari, jujube, plaksha, udumbara, banyan, peepal, and milky trees, marking-nut trees, emblic myrobalan, chebulic and belleric myrobalan,
inguda, oleander, and tinduka bearing large fruits — these and other diverse trees on the slopes of Gandhamādana,
those trees laden with sweet, nectar-like fruits, and likewise champaka, ashoka, ketaka, and bakula trees,
pumnaga, saptaparna, karnikara, saketaka, patala, charming kutaja, mandara, and indivara lotuses,
parijata, kovidara, and deodar trees, shala, palmyra, tamala, priyal, bakula, silk-cotton trees, flame of the forest, ashoka, simsapa, and tarala trees,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
frequented by cakora birds, shanapatra birds, bhringarajas, parrots, cuckoos, sparrows, harita birds, and chakravaka birds,
by chataka birds of pleasant ways and other varied birds cooing ear-delightingly sweet — they beheld those trees.
And beautiful lakes with clear water, covered on all sides with white water-lilies, lotuses, red and blue lotuses, water-lilies, and kamala lotuses.
Filled on all sides with kadamba ducks, chakravaka geese, kurara birds, water hens, karandava ducks, divers, swans, herons, and cormorants — these and other water-birds.
And those joyful birds, languid with the nectar-wine of lotus ponds, tinted red with pollen and filaments fallen from the hearts of lotuses,
they beheld those charming lotus-groves on the slopes of Gandhamādana, humming with sweet-voiced bees.
And likewise in the bower-pavilions of creepers adorned on all sides with clusters of lotuses, in company with their peahens, they saw peacocks greatly agitated by passion stirred by the roar of clouds like trumpets.
Having uttered sweet peacock-cries and sweet singing sounds, spreading their lovely tail-feathers with grace and languor — they saw those beautiful peacocks dancing in forest play.
They saw others sporting happily with their mates, dwelling in the thickets of creepers and in bracelets of clinging vines.
They also saw certain kinds of birds, preening in the tree-branches, their displays arranged with tail-feathers, as if wearing wonderful crowns, and they were seen in the hollows of trees, delighted.
And the sindhuvara plants, unbridled, like darts of the God of Love, scattered with golden flowers on the peaks of mountains,
the karnikara trees beautifully formed like exquisite ear-ornaments — they then saw kurabaka bushes in bloom in the forest rows, arousing eager desire as if they were love's own arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Similarly in the forest rows they saw tilaka trees, noble, as if arranged, blazing like the tilaka mark itself.
They saw likewise charming sahakara trees shaped like the shafts of the bodiless God of Love, resplendent with clusters of blossoms amid the hum of bees.
With flowers resembling gold and others resembling forest fire, and with crimson ones and blue-black ones and yet others resembling beryl,
and shala, tamala, patali, and bakula trees hanging together like garlands on the peaks of mountains —
Thus step by step those heroes, gazing all around at those slopes of Gandhamādana crowded with herds of elephants, filled with lions and tigers,
resounding with the cries of sharabhas, echoing with varied roars, rich with fruits and flowers of all seasons —
the rows of trees became yellow-gleaming and radiant in hue; here were no thorny trees, here none without flowers; the trees on the slopes of Gandhamādana had glossy leaves and fruits.
The Pārthas beheld on the mountain slopes lakes and rivers clear as crystal, visited by white-winged birds and royal swans, resounding with the cries of cranes.
Beautiful with lotuses and blue lilies, with pleasantly cool water, fragrant garlands, juicy fruits — exceedingly splendid were the blossoming trees on the mountain slopes.
These and many others were the forest-born trees there, and creepers of diverse shapes, laden with leaves, flowers, and fruits.
While Yudhiṣṭhira was gazing upon those trees on that best of mountains, he spoke these sweet-syllabled words to Bhīmasena.
"Behold, Bhīma, these auspicious regions on all sides — the playgrounds of the gods. We have attained a course beyond mortal reach and have truly accomplished our purpose, O Wolf-belly."
The finest trees, covered with blossoms and embraced by many creepers, shine on the slopes of Gandhamādana, O Pārtha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hear, O Bhīma, the resounding calls of peacocks sporting together with their hens, crying out on the mountain slopes.
Chakora partridges, red-legged partridges, intoxicated cuckoos, and mynahs — these birds cling to these blooming great trees.
Red, yellow, and ruddy — perched atop the trees, O Pārtha — many chakravaka birds gaze upon one another.
Cranes are seen everywhere among the green and reddish-hued meadows, and also at the mountain springs.
Sweet voices pleasing to all creatures are uttered by the king-bees, the chakravaka ducks, and the red-backed birds.
Four-tusked, lotus-hued elephants with their she-elephants are stirring this great lake that gleams like lapis lazuli.
Streams of water fall from many springs and from the mountain peaks, as tall as many palm trees in height.
Radiant as the sun, resembling thick autumnal clouds, the various silver-hued mineral ores adorn this great mountain, O Bhīma.
In some places the mineral veins are collyrium-dark, in others they resemble gold; in some places are deposits of orpiment, and in others of red arsenic.
There are realgar-veined caves resembling twilight clouds, and in some places ochre-red mineral deposits the color of red lac.
Resembling white and dark clouds, glowing like the morning sun — these manifold and brilliantly luminous minerals adorn the mountain.
Gandharvas with their beloved consorts, as described by Vṛṣaparvan, are seen on the mountain peaks together with the kinnaras, O Pārtha.
The sounds of songs, hand-clapping, and samans are heard in many ways here, O Bhīma, enchanting the hearts of all beings.
Behold the great Gaṅgā, the sacred and auspicious river of the gods, frequented by flocks of bar-headed geese, and attended by sages and kinnaras.
With its mineral streaks and streams, kinnaras, deer and birds, gandharvas and apsaras, and its enchanting groves —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— and with serpents of various forms and hundred-headed snakes all around, behold the king of mountains, O son of Kuntī, O subduer of foes.
Those heroes, joyful in heart, having attained the highest course, were not satiated with beholding the king of mountains, those scorchers of enemies.
Then they saw the hermitage of the royal sage Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, adorned with garlands and fruit-bearing trees.
Then they approached Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, that intense ascetic, lean and with prominent veins, who had traversed to the further shore of all dharmas.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Yudhiṣṭhira, approaching that one whose sins had been burned away by austerity, greeted him joyfully, bowing his head and pronouncing his name.
Then Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) and Bhīma and the glorious twins also came forward, bowing their heads to the royal sage, surrounding and standing near him.
Likewise Dhaumya, knower of dharma, the family priest of the Pāṇḍavas, approached that sage of sharpened vows in due and proper manner.
That wise sage, with his divine sight, recognized them as the sons of Pāṇḍu, the best of Kurus, and said to them: "Be seated."
After honoring the wise bull of the Kurus, the great ascetic inquired after his well-being as he sat with his brothers.
"Do you not incline toward falsehood? Do you conduct yourself in dharma? Does your conduct toward your mother and father not falter, O Pārtha?"
"Are all your elders, the aged, and the learned properly honored? Do you not incline toward sinful acts, O Pārtha?"
"Do you know, O best of Kurus, how to repay good deeds and to restrain evil deeds in due and proper measure, and do you not boast of it?"
"Do the virtuous rejoice, honored by you as they deserve? Even dwelling in the forests, do you follow dharma alone?"
"Is Dhaumya not distressed by your conduct, O Pārtha — by your charity, dharma, austerity, purity, uprightness, and forbearance?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Do you follow the conduct of your fathers and grandfathers, O Pārtha? Do you walk the path trodden by the royal sages, O son of Pāṇḍu?"
"It is said that the fathers dwelling in the world of the ancestors grieve and rejoice over each son or grandson born in their own respective lineage."
"'What shall we receive through his evil deeds?' they wonder, and 'What auspicious good shall we obtain through his meritorious deeds?'"
"Father, mother, fire, teacher, and the self as the fifth — whoever honors these, O Pārtha, has conquered both worlds."
"Sages who subsist on water and on air, floating through the sky, frequent this best of mountains at the junctions of the fortnights."
"Kinnaras who are devoted to their loves, faithful to one another, are seen standing on the mountain peaks, O king."
"Wearing dustless garments of silk, many hosts of gandharvas and apsaras are seen here, O Pārtha."
"Troops of vidyadharas, garlanded and fair to behold, and companies of great serpents, and garudas and nagas and the like —"
"— and above this mountain, at the junction of the fortnights, the sounds of kettledrums, small drums, conches, and mridangas are heard."
"All of this is to be heard from right here, O bulls of the Bhārata line — under no circumstances should you entertain any thought of going there."
"Nor is it possible to go beyond this point, O best of Bhāratas — that is the sport-realm of the gods, a course beyond mortal reach."
"All beings here hate a man who acts even slightly rashly, O Bhārata, and the rakshasas will beat him."
"Beyond the summit of this mountain, O Yudhiṣṭhira, lies the path of the highest perfected beings and the divine sages."
"One who proceeds rashly to that further realm, O Pārtha, O slayer of foes, is struck down by rakshasas with iron spears and other weapons."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Surrounded by apsaras and in full splendor, Vaiśravaṇa the lord who is carried by men is seen here at the junctions of the fortnights, my dear."
"All beings behold him seated on the peak, the lord of all rakshasas, like the sun risen in its splendor."
"This mountain summit is the garden of the gods, the danavas, the siddhas, and of Vaiśravaṇa himself, O best of the Bhāratas."
"While Tumburu waits upon the wealth-giver, the sounds of his song-samans are heard here on Gandhamādana at the junctions of the fortnights, my dear."
"Such marvelous things as these are witnessed here, my dear Yudhiṣṭhira, by all beings, many times at the junctions of the fortnights."
"Eating all manner of foods and flavorful fruits, dwell here, O best of Pāṇḍavas, until the sight of Arjuna."
"You must not be rash in any way having arrived here, my dear. Having dwelt here as long as you wish and sported as your faith dictates, you shall then, O best of weapon-bearers, protect the earth."
Janamejaya said: The great-souled sons of Pāṇḍu, all of divine valor — how long did they dwell on Mount Gandhamādana?
And what were the foods of those great-souled heroes of the world while they dwelt there? Tell me that, O best one.
Tell me in detail of Bhīmasena's feats — whatever the mighty-armed one did on that Himālayan mountain. Surely there was no further battle with the yakshas, O best of the twice-born?
Was there a meeting of theirs with Vaiśravaṇa? For the wealth-giver comes there, as Ārṣṭiṣeṇa had said.
This I wish to hear in detail, O storehouse of austerity — for there is no satiation in me as I listen to their deeds.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this counsel that was good for their own souls from that one of incomparable splendor, the bulls of the Bhārata line constantly followed his instructions in just that way.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Eating the foods of sages, flavorful fruits, and also the flesh of deer slain by pure arrows —
— and the pure and various honeys on the back of the Himālaya, the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls of the Bhārata line, thus dwelt there.
As they thus dwelt there, listening to the various discourses spoken by Lomaśa, the fifth year came upon them.
Having said "I shall come when the time of need arrives," Ghaṭotkaca departed beforehand together with all the rakshasas, O lord.
As those great-souled ones dwelt in the hermitage of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, many months passed as they beheld great wonders.
While the Pāṇḍavas sported and wandered about there in delight, joyful and greatly blessed sages and celestial bards —
— those of perfected souls and restrained vows came to behold the Pāṇḍavas, and the best of Bhāratas held divine conversations with each of them.
Then after a few days, a garuda suddenly seized a great and mighty serpent that dwelt in the deep lake.
The great mountain trembled and the great trees were crushed; all beings and the Pāṇḍavas beheld that wonder.
Then from the summit of that best of mountains, the wind bore toward the Pāṇḍavas all manner of garlands, fragrant and auspicious.
There the Pāṇḍavas, together with their friends, and the glorious Draupadī beheld divine flowers of five colors.
Then Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) spoke timely words to Bhīmasena, who sat at ease in a secluded mountain spot, that mighty-armed one.
"By the mighty wind with the velocity of Garuḍa's wings, flowers of five colors are being blown, O bull of the Bhāratas, before the eyes of all beings, toward the river Ashvaratha."
"In the Khāṇḍava forest, by your brother of true pledges, O lord of men, gandharvas, serpents, and rakshasas were repelled, and even Vāsava was checked; the terrible sorcerers were slain, and the Gāṇḍīva bow was obtained."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And your own splendor is very great, and your arm-strength is immense — unbearable and unapproachable, equal to the strength of Śatakratu (Indra)."
"Terrified by the force of your arm-strength, may all the rakshasas abandon the mountain and flee in the ten directions, O Bhīmasena."
"Then, free of fear and confusion, let your friends behold the summit of that best of mountains, adorned with beautiful garlands and auspicious."
"Thus is my heart fixed, O Bhīma — long have I wished to behold that mountain summit, resting on the strength of your arms."
Then that scorcher of foes, the mighty-armed one, could not tolerate being so urged by Draupadī, just as a good bull cannot tolerate a goad.
With the gait of a lion and a bull, glorious, noble, radiant as gold, high-spirited, strong, proud, self-respecting, and heroic — that son of Pāṇḍu —
— red-eyed, broad-shouldered, with the might of a rutting elephant, with lion-like fangs, with massive shoulders, rising like a young sala tree —
That great-souled one, beautiful in every limb, with a conch-like neck and mighty arms, took up his gold-backed bow, his sword, and his quivers.
Like a maned lion in its pride, like a bull elephant in rut, free from fear and confusion, that mighty one rushed toward the mountain.
All beings beheld him coming like the king of beasts, like a raging elephant, bearing arrows, sword, and bow.
Gladdening Draupadī's heart, that son of Pāṇḍu took up his mace, and free of fear and bewilderment, entered the king of mountains.
Lassitude, cowardice, distress, or envy — none of these ever afflict this son of Pārthā, this son of the Wind-god.
Reaching that single passage, terrible to behold, the mighty one climbed the peak towering with its many tall trees.
Delighting the Kiṃnaras, great Nāgas, sages, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas, that man of great strength reached the summit of the mountain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There the bull of the Bhāratas beheld the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, adorned with mansions of gold fashioned like crystal.
Born on the Gandhamādana, carrying every fragrance, a delightfully pleasant breeze blew there, gladdening all beings.
Wondrous trees of various colors and lustres, bearing variegated blossoms, inconceivable, of many kinds — supremely beautiful — stood there.
The bull of the Bhāratas beheld the auspicious dwelling of the lord of Rākṣasas, encircled by a net of gems and adorned with garlands of many hues.
Mace, sword, and bow in hand, having cast aside all regard for his life, mighty-armed Bhīmasena stood immovable as a mountain.
