Through the transgressions of kings, great dharma becomes confused, adharma increases, and likewise the subjects intermingle.
Dwarfs, hunchbacks, those with large heads, eunuchs, the blind, the deaf, and those with hanging ears are born — from the unrighteousness of kings the decline of subjects always follows.
This king Janaka sees all things through dharma, always favoring his subjects who are each devoted to their own dharma.
Both those who praise me and those who blame me — I satisfy all people through well-measured conduct.
Those who live by their own dharma and those kings who enjoy accordingly — those who are capable and diligent do not depend on anyone for their livelihood.
Constant giving of food according to one's ability, forbearance, steadfastness in dharma, honor given as befits each person, and compassion toward all beings — virtues of mortals rest nowhere in a person except through generosity.
One should shun false speech, should do what is pleasing without being asked, and should not abandon dharma out of desire, anger, or hatred.
One should not be excessively overjoyed at the pleasant nor burn in distress at the unpleasant; one should not be bewildered in financial difficulties, nor should one abandon dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If there is some other better course of action, one should not practice what is different from it. Whatever is auspicious — on that should one fix oneself.
One should not be wicked in return for wickedness; one should always be a good person. The wicked one who wishes to do evil is slain by his own self.
This is the conduct of the wicked, of sinners acting wickedly — those who think there is no dharma and who mock the pure. Those without faith in dharma perish — there is no doubt.
The wicked man is always puffed up like a great inflated water-skin; the speech of the foolish and arrogant is without substance. He reveals his inner self like the sun reveals its form by day.
A fool does not shine in the world by self-praise alone; even one who is without physical grace but has acquired learning shines forth.
Not speaking ill of anyone, not lauding oneself — no one who is endowed with virtues is seen to be prominently visible on the earth.
One who is tormented by wrongful action is freed from sin; resolving "I will not do this again," one is freed from the second offence.
By whatever action one is freed here from sin, O best of twice-born — thus, O brahmin, this teaching is seen throughout the dharma scriptures.
Sins formerly committed here in ignorance — one of virtuous character destroys them afterward. O brahmin, dharma drives away from men that which they do in sin and negligence here.
Having done wrong, a person should think "I am not that self" and should only desire to do good, being faithful and free from malice.
He who exposes the faults of the virtuous as one exposes the holes in a garment — if such a person, having done evil, turns toward the good, he is freed from all sins, as the moon is freed from great clouds.
Just as the sun rising dispels all darkness, so one who abides in virtue is freed from all sins.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Know that greed alone is the seat of all sins, O best of twice-born. The greedy and the poorly learned commit sin; those who follow unrighteousness under the guise of righteousness are like wells covered with grass.
For them, self-restraint and purifications are mere talk cloaked in dharma; everything may be found in them, yet the conduct of the righteous is exceedingly rare.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then that brahmin, most learned, asked the Dharma-Hunter: 'How may I know the conduct of the righteous, O best of men? Tell me truly, O hunter of great wisdom, exactly as it is.'
The hunter said: Sacrifice, charity, austerity, the Vedas, and truth, O best of twice-born — these five are always the purifications found in the conduct of the righteous.
Those who have subdued desire and anger, who have renounced pretense, greed, and dishonesty, who are satisfied with dharma alone — they are the righteous, honored by the righteous.
For those devoted to sacrifice and self-study there is no transgression; and observance of right conduct is indeed the second mark of the righteous.
Service to the teacher, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and charity — these four, O brahmin, are always present in the conduct of the righteous.
Fixing one's mind on righteous conduct and establishing oneself therein in every way, the satisfaction one obtains cannot be had by any other means.
The secret teaching of the Veda is truth; the secret teaching of truth is self-restraint; the secret teaching of restraint is renunciation — these are always present in the conduct of the righteous.
Those persons deluded in intellect who revile dharma travel the wrong path; even one who follows such people is harmed.
But those who are righteous, well-controlled, devoted to the knowledge of scripture and renunciation, who have mounted the path of dharma and are devoted to truth and righteousness —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— such persons endowed with righteous conduct restrain the highest intellect; established in the teaching of their preceptors, steadfast, they perceive dharma and its true purpose.
Abandon atheists, those who transgress boundaries, the cruel, and those fixed in sinful thought; taking refuge in wisdom, associate instead with the righteous.
Making fortitude your boat, cross the river of the five senses crowded with the demons of desire and greed, and traverse the difficult passages of existence.
Dharma accumulated gradually through the yoga of wisdom becomes great; attachment to righteous conduct in the virtuous is like whiteness in a garment.
Non-violence, truthful speech, and the highest good of all beings — non-violence is the supreme dharma, and it is established in truth; when one establishes oneself in truth, all one's activities proceed rightly.
Truth alone is most weighty when practiced in the conduct of the righteous; the conduct of the good is indeed dharma, and the good are known by their conduct.
Whatever is the nature of a creature, it experiences that very nature; the sinful soul, lacking self-mastery, incurs the faults of anger, desire, and the like.
Whatever undertaking is joined with justice is remembered as dharma; misconduct indeed is adharma — this is the teaching of the righteous.
Those who do not become angry, who do not envy, who are free from ego and jealousy, who are upright and endowed with tranquility — they possess the conduct of the righteous.
Those accomplished in the three Vedas, the pure, those of good character, the high-minded, those devoted to serving their teachers, the self-controlled — they too possess righteous conduct.
Of those of undepressed spirit who practice difficult austerities and are honored by their own deeds, even the harshness of their deeds completely disappears.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing that wondrous, ancient, eternal, and immovable good conduct as dharma through dharma, the wise attain heaven.
Those who are believers, free from pride, who honor the twice-born community, who are endowed with learning and good conduct — such righteous ones are bound for heaven.
The supreme dharma declared in the Vedas, the other in the law-treatises, and that practiced by the righteous — these are the threefold marks of dharma.
Mastery of the sciences, immersion in sacred fords, forbearance, truthfulness, straightforwardness, and purity — these are demonstrations of righteous conduct.
Those who are compassionate toward all beings, always devoted to non-violence, who never speak harshly — such good people are always dear to the twice-born.
Those who know the ripening of the accumulated fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds — they are the righteous, honored by the righteous.
Endowed with justice and virtue, desiring the good of all worlds, the pure good ones who have conquered heaven are established on the true path.
Those who give, who share equitably, who show grace to the wretched, who are compassionate toward all beings — they are the righteous, honored by the righteous.
Those worthy of universal honor, rich in learning, and also the ascetics who are ever given to charity — they attain pleasant worlds and prosperity here as well.
Even at cost of hardship to their spouse and dependents, the good who gather with the good give beyond their means.
Seeing the way of the world, dharma, and what is beneficial for the self, the good who live in this manner flourish for endless years.
Non-violence, truthful speech, gentleness, uprightness, absence of malice, freedom from excessive pride, modesty, forbearance, self-restraint, and tranquility —
— those who are wise and steadfast, compassionate toward all beings, free from desire and hatred — they are the good ones, honored by the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They declare only three steps to be the unsurpassed conduct of the good: do no harm to anyone, always give, and always speak the truth.
The good who are compassionate everywhere, who know compassion, who go along here fully contented on the righteous, supreme path — great-souled ones of righteous conduct whose dharma is firmly established.
Freedom from envy, forbearance, peace, contentment, pleasant speech, and the abandonment of desire and anger — these are the practice of righteous conduct.
Those endowed with learning through action, who tirelessly follow dharma, always practice the unsurpassed path of the good, which is righteous conduct.
Ascending the palace of wisdom and observing great masses of deluded people, and beholding the various activities of the world, O best of twice-born — the very sinful deeds among those are exceedingly meritorious, O best of the twice-born.
All this has been told to you, O brahmin, to the best of my wisdom and learning, placing foremost the virtues of righteous conduct, O bull among twice-born.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the Dharma-Hunter spoke to the brahmin, O Yudhiṣṭhira: 'That I indeed perform a terrible occupation — of this there is no doubt.'
'But fate is powerful, O brahmin; what was done in a former life is hard to overcome; this fault of action arises from sin committed in a former life. And in overcoming this fault, O brahmin, I am indeed striving.'
'What has been ordained by fate in a former life — a killer may become the mere occasion for it; we are indeed only the occasion for this action, O best of twice-born.'
'The flesh of those we slay and sell, O brahmin — dharma may arise even for them through its enjoyment and consumption, through the honoring of gods, guests, servants, and ancestors.'
'Herbs, plants, cattle, deer, and birds have become food and the like for the world — this too is heard in the Vedic teaching.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'By offering his own flesh, the forbearing king Śibi, son of Uśīnara, attained the very rare heaven, O best of twice-born.'
'In the royal kitchen of Rantideva in former times, O brahmin, two thousand animals were slaughtered daily.'
'Because Rantideva always gave food with meat, incomparable fame accrued to that king, O best of twice-born; at the four-monthly festivals animals were always slaughtered.'
'"The sacred fires too desire meat" — this also is heard in Vedic teaching. In sacrifices, O brahmin, animals are always slaughtered by twice-born; consecrated by mantras, those animals too are said to attain heaven.'
'If the sacred fires had never desired meat in former times, O brahmin, flesh would not have been food for anyone at all, O best of twice-born.'
'Even here the rule has been stated by sages regarding the eating of meat: one who always eats after offering to gods and ancestors, duly and with faith according to the rule, is not defiled by that eating.'
'"One becomes a non-meat-eater in this way" — this also is heard in Vedic teaching; a brahmin who approaches his wife only in the fertile season is a celibate student.'
'Having considered truth and untruth, a rule is stated here as well: in former times, human flesh was eaten by king Saudāsa who was overwhelmed by a curse. What do you think of that here, O brahmin?'
'Considering this my own duty, I do not abandon it, O best of twice-born; knowing it as what was determined in a former life, I live by this occupation.'
'For one who abandons his own duty, adharma is seen here; but one who is devoted to his own duty — that is dharma, this is the certainty.'
'The action ordained in a former life does not release the embodied being; this rule of the Creator has been seen in many ways in the determination of karma.'
'A wise person engaged in cruel occupation must consider: how may I perform auspicious deeds? How may I be freed from defeat? The determination of that terrible karma may arise in many ways.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'In charity, in truthful speech, in service to my teacher, and in honoring the twice-born — I am always devoted to dharma; from excessive speech and excessive pride I have withdrawn, O best of twice-born.'
'People think agriculture is good, yet great violence is considered inherent in it — those who plow with plows kill many creatures dwelling in the earth and many other living beings. What do you think of that here?'
'The grain seeds they speak of — rice and the rest, O best of twice-born — all these are living beings. What do you think of that here?'
'Humans attack and kill cattle too and eat them; and they also cut down trees and plants, O brahmin.'
'Many living beings are found in trees and fruits as well, and many also in water — what do you think of that here?'
'All this universe, O brahmin, is pervaded with living beings sustained by life; fish devour fish — what do you think of that here?'
'Beings live upon beings in many ways, O best of twice-born; living creatures eat one another — what do you think of that here?'
'While walking about, humans kill many living beings dwelling on the ground with their feet, O brahmin — what do you think of that here?'
'Even sitting and lying down they kill living beings in many ways, and so do those possessed of knowledge and science — what do you think of that here?'
'All this — sky and earth alike — is possessed by living beings; and out of ignorance they harm one another — what do you think of that here?'
'What was declared as non-violence by astonished men in former times — who, while living in this world, does not do harm, O best of twice-born? Considering much, there is truly no one in this world who is non-violent.'
'The ascetics devoted to non-violence, O best of twice-born, do commit harm; but through effort theirs becomes ever less.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Invisible persons born in good families, endowed with great virtues, after performing very terrible deeds, truly feel no shame.'
'Friends do not see other friends rightly, nor do enemies see enemies rightly; they do not rightly observe those who behave properly.'
'Kinsmen do not rejoice with kinsmen in prosperity; and the foolish who fancy themselves learned even revile their teachers.'
'Much in the world is seen to be inverted, O best of twice-born — unrighteousness mingled with righteousness — what do you think of that here?'
'Much of various kinds can be said about deeds in the realm of dharma and adharma; but one who is devoted to his own duty shall attain great fame.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The Dharma-Hunter then spoke skillfully once more, O Yudhiṣṭhira — that best among all upholders of dharma spoke thus to the foremost of brahmins:
'It has been said by elders that dharma has the Vedas as its authority; the course of dharma is subtle, with many branches and of unbounded scope.'
'In a life-threatening situation and at a wedding, an untruth may be spoken; and an untruth may become truth, and truth itself may become untruth.'
'What is supremely beneficial to beings — that is held to be truth; what produces the contrary is adharma. Observe the subtlety of dharma.'
Whatever inauspicious or auspicious action a man performs, O best of twice-born, he must inevitably reap that fruit — there is no doubt in this matter.
When he falls into adversity, the fool bitterly reviles the gods; he does not recognize that the faults in his own actions are to blame.
The deluded man, deceitful and fickle, O best of twice-born — when the reversal of pleasure and pain overtakes him, neither wisdom nor good conduct nor even manliness can save him.
If the fruit of a man's actions depended on no one else, then whatever desire he harbored he would attain that very desire exactly as he wished.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yet men who are self-restrained, capable, and intelligent are seen to be fruitless, cast aside despite all their efforts.
Another man, ever engaged in harming creatures and deceiving the world, lives here in comfort with ease.
Prosperity approaches one man who sits doing nothing; another who works tirelessly never attains what he seeks.
After worshipping the gods and performing austerities, miserly men greedy for sons see born from their wombs — carried ten months — children who disgrace the family.
Others are born into abundant wealth, grain, and enjoyments accumulated by their ancestors, having obtained those very auspicious blessings.
The diseases of human beings are indeed born of their actions — there is no doubt here. They are afflicted by mental anguish and bodily ailments just as small animals are hunted by hunters.
And yet those diseases are warded off by skillful physicians skilled in compounding medicines — just as animals are held at bay by hunters, O twice-born.
There are those who have the means to enjoy but, afflicted by digestive disorders, cannot eat — behold this, O best among upholders of dharma.
Others, possessed of great physical strength, struggle greatly, and only with difficulty do they obtain their food, O best of twice-born.
Thus this world, overwhelmed by delusion and sorrow, is again and again swept away like a current and carried off by something more powerful.
If sovereign mastery were truly within reach, none would die, none would grow old, all would fulfill every desire, and none would ever face what is unwished.
Everyone strives to rise higher and higher in the world and exerts himself according to his capacity — yet things do not turn out that way.
Many are seen who share the same birth-star and auspicious signs, yet great inequality of result is observed at the junctures of their actions.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
No one is master of seizing things by his own will alone, O brahmin, O best of good men — the fulfillment of ordinary actions is seen to depend on something else.
As this scriptural teaching holds, O brahmin: the self is indeed eternal, while the body in this world is impermanent for all living beings.
When the body is destroyed, the body perishes indeed; but the self migrates elsewhere, bound by the bonds of its accumulated karma.
The brahmin said: How is the self eternal, O best among upholders of dharma? I wish to know this truth — tell me, O best among those who speak truthfully.
The hunter said: There is no destruction of the self when the body dissolves; the fools who say 'it dies' speak falsely. The self departs, having passed through the body; the dissolution of the body is as nothing compared to the self.
For another does not eat the fruit of an action that has been done; the very doer himself experiences pleasure and pain. Whatever action has been done by him, he reaps that — there is no destruction of what has been done.
Those of sinful disposition may become meritorious, and best among men may become sinners — a man here is accompanied by his own actions, and is reborn shaped by them.
The brahmin said: How does conception in the womb occur? How do merit and demerit operate? How does one go to auspicious or inauspicious births, O good one?
The hunter said: This action connected with the planting of the embryo is observed here — I will explain it to you briefly and quickly, O best of twice-born.
Just as one who has accumulated provisions is born again, the doer of good is born in auspicious wombs, and the doer of evil in evil wombs.
By auspicious conduct one attains divinity; by mixed actions one becomes human; by deluding means one goes to lower births; and by sinful deeds one descends further.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Constantly assailed by the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, and cooked in the cycle of existence by the faults he himself has made, man wanders on.
Having passed through thousands of animal births and through hell itself, souls revolve in this cycle, bound by the bonds of karma.
The creature, suffering after death on account of its own various actions, obtains a low birth for the purpose of counteracting that suffering.
Then again it undertakes new and manifold actions, and is cooked anew by them — just as a sick man who eats harmful food suffers again.
Perpetually tormented yet calling itself free from pain and naming its state 'happiness,' and because its bondage never ceases even with the rise of new actions, it wanders through samsara like a wheel, experiencing many sufferings.
But if one has dissolved its bonds and is purified in its actions, it attains the worlds of the meritorious — having gone there, it grieves no more.
One who commits evil and lives evilly never reaches the end of sin; therefore one should strive to perform meritorious deeds and shun transgression.
One who is free from envy and grateful cultivates only the auspicious; such a man attains happiness, dharma, wealth, and heaven.
For the man of culture, self-controlled, disciplined, with mastered soul and wise — his sustenance is unobstructed, both in this world and the next.
One should live by the dharma of the good, conduct one's actions as the learned do, and seek one's livelihood without causing distress to the world, O twice-born.
For there are learned men, well-versed in scripture, who have attained wisdom; by living according to one's own dharma, action in the world remains without confusion.
The wise man delights in dharma and lives by dharma; with the wealth obtained through dharma, O best of twice-born, he waters its very root and perceives the virtues therein.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In this way he becomes righteous of soul and his mind grows serene; content among kindly people, he rejoices both here and hereafter.
Sound, touch, form, desired fragrances, and lordly power — all these he obtains; the wise know this to be the fruit of dharma, O good man.
Having obtained the fruit of dharma, he is not satisfied, O great twice-born; and in that dissatisfaction he takes up dispassion with the eye of knowledge.
The man whose eye is wisdom does not here conform to any fault; he becomes dispassionate as he wishes, yet does not abandon dharma.
Having seen the world to be of a perishing nature, he strives toward the renunciation of all things; then he strives toward liberation — not by indirect means but by the direct path.
Thus he takes up dispassion, abandons sinful action, becomes righteous, and attains supreme liberation.
Austerity is the highest good for a living being; its root is tranquility and self-restraint. By that one attains all the desires that the mind wishes for.
By the restraint of the senses, by truth, and by self-control, one attains the supreme state of Brahman, O best of twice-born.
The brahmin said: What are those that are called the senses, O you of firm vows? How is their restraint to be practiced, and what is the fruit of that restraint?
And how does one attain the fruit thereof, O best among upholders of dharma? I desire to know this dharma in truth, O you who are deeply righteous.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus addressed by the brahmin, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the dharma-hunter replied to the brahmin accordingly — hear that, O lord of men.
The hunter said: For the purpose of knowing, the mind of human beings first sets itself in motion; having obtained its object, it then indulges in desire and anger, O best of twice-born.
Then for that very purpose it strives and undertakes great action; it constantly pursues the habituation of desired forms and fragrances.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From that arises passion, and immediately after it hatred; from that arises greed, and immediately after it delusion.
Of one overwhelmed by greed and struck down by passion and hatred, the intellect does not arise toward dharma; he performs dharma only through pretense.
He practices dharma by pretense, he takes pleasure in wealth by pretense; when wealth is acquired through pretense, O best of twice-born, the intellect delights in that very thing and then desires to commit sin.
Even when restrained by friends and by learned men, O best of twice-born, he speaks a reply connected to scripture, invoking scripture to justify himself.
Adharma in three forms grows in him out of the fault of passion: he thinks sin, speaks sin, and commits sin.
For one who has turned toward adharma, good virtues perish; and those who are of like character come to enjoy his friendship — those who commit evil actions.
By this he obtains misery and is struck down in the hereafter — thus one becomes of sinful soul. Now hear from me the gaining of dharma.
But he who by wisdom foresees these very faults from the outset, who is skilled in pleasure and pain and frequents the company of the virtuous — through association with good beginnings, his intellect is born toward the ways of dharma.
The brahmin said: You speak dharma that is true and pleasant — there is no other speaker of it like you. Of divine splendor and exceeding greatness, you seem to me truly a sage.
The hunter said: Brahmins are indeed the most fortunate; they are the forefathers who partake first always. A wise man should with all his soul do what pleases them in the world.
What pleases them I will tell you, O best of twice-born — having paid homage to the brahmins, learn from me the knowledge born of Brahman.
This entire universe, wholly unconquerable in every respect, O brahmin, has the great elements as its soul; there is nothing higher than this.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The great elements are: space, wind, fire, water, and earth — and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities.
All of their qualities operate mutually on one another; each carries forward the qualities of the one preceding it — all in succession among the three modes of being.
The sixth is named consciousness — it is called the mind; the seventh is the intellect; and after that comes the ego-sense.
And the five senses, along with rajas, sattva, and tamas — this is the group of seventeen known by the name of the unmanifest.
Perfectly enveloped by all the objects of the senses here, both manifest and unmanifest, this is the twenty-fourth — the principle composed of both manifest and unmanifest. All this has been declared to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus addressed by the dharma-hunter, O Bhārata, that brahmin then spoke once more a discourse that increases the joy of the mind.
The brahmin said: O best among those who know dharma, those five great elements of which they speak — tell me properly the qualities of each of the five individually.
The hunter said: Earth, water, fire, wind, and space — all have qualities exceeding one another; I will tell you their qualities.
Earth has five qualities, O brahmin, and water has four; fire has three qualities, and space and wind each have two — or rather three between them.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth — these five qualities of earth are richest in qualities compared to all others.
Sound, touch, form, and taste — O best of twice-born, O brahmin, O you of excellent vows, these are proclaimed to be the qualities of water.
Sound, touch, and form — these three are the qualities of fire. In wind there are sound and touch; in space, sound alone.
These fifteen qualities, O brahmin, abide in the five elements — they are present in all beings, in whom the worlds are grounded. They do not transgress one another, and their conjunction brings well-being, O twice-born.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But when the moving and unmoving beings enter into a state of imbalance, then the embodied soul in the course of time mounts another body.
In succession they perish, and in succession they are born; here and there the elements composed of the five great ones are seen — by which this entire world, of moving and unmoving things, is enveloped.
Whatever is produced by the senses is known as the manifest; that which is beyond the grasp of the senses and is apprehended only through its marks is to be understood as the unmanifest.
These senses each grasp their respective objects — sound and the rest — and when the embodied being supports them here, he undergoes austerity.
He sees the Self spread through the world and the world within the Self; the knower of the near and far, though engaged, sees all beings.
For one who sees all beings in all conditions at all times, who has become Brahman, no association with the inauspicious can arise.
For one who has transcended the affliction rooted in knowledge and born of delusion, the world is seen by the light of the intellect on the path of what is to be known.
The wise Lord declared: the living being is without beginning or end, self-originated, eternally imperishable, incomparable, and formless — all this that you, O brahmin, ask me about has its root in austerity.
The senses are indeed everything — both heaven and hell; when restrained they lead to heaven, when let loose they lead to hell.
The entire discipline of yoga consists in the restraint of the senses; this is indeed the root of all austerity and likewise the root of all hell.
Through indulgence of the senses one falls into fault without doubt; by restraining those same senses, one thereafter attains perfection.
One who achieves mastery over the six ever-present senses within the self — that conqueror of the senses is not bound by sins, still less by misfortunes.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The body of a person is seen as a chariot; they say the Self is the driver and the senses are the horses — the skilled one, vigilant with well-trained and disciplined horses, travels comfortably like a wise charioteer.
The steadfast one who holds the reins of the six ever-present and turbulent senses within the self would be the supreme charioteer.
For senses let loose on their tracks like horses, one should exercise steadiness in charioteering; by steadiness one will certainly conquer them.
When the mind follows along with the roving senses, it carries away one's intellect as the wind carries away a boat upon the waters.
One who is resolute and studious in those six matters wherein people go astray from delusion when fruits arrive — that one obtains the fruit born of meditation.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Bhārata, when the Dharma-Hunter had thus spoken on subtle matters, that brahmin, with concentrated mind, asked once more about something subtle.
The brahmin said: Tell me accurately and in truth about the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas as they truly are, explaining them correctly to me as I ask here.
The hunter said: Come, I shall tell you what you ask of me — know the qualities of these separately as I speak.
Among these, tamas is characterized by delusion and rajas by agitation; sattva, because it is abundant in luminosity, is called the highest here.
Abounding in ignorance, bewildered, prone to sleep, unconscious, dim-sighted, overwhelmed by darkness, wrathful, and slothful — such is the tamasic person.
One who is verbose, scheming, attached, envious, inquisitive, O seer among brahmins, arrogant and proud — such is the rajasic person.
Abounding in luminosity, steadfast, without excessive curiosity, free from envy, not given to anger, wise and self-restrained — such a person is sattvic.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But when the sattvic person, being fully awakened, is troubled by worldly conduct and comes to understand what is to be understood, he turns away in disgust from worldly behavior.
For the form of dispassion arises first; the ego-sense becomes soft, and whatever straightforwardness there is becomes serene.
Thereafter all the pairs of opposites within him mutually subside; and no restraint whatsoever is needed for him anywhere.
For one born in the womb of a shudra who abides in good qualities, O brahmin, the state of a vaishya arises, and likewise the state of a kshatriya.
For one who lives in straightforwardness, brahminhood arises. All those qualities have been described — what more do you wish to hear?
The brahmin said: When the bodily fire meets the earthly element, how does it exist? And how does the wind function through the particular cavities of the body?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, this question raised by the brahmin — the hunter expounded it to that great-souled brahmin.
The hunter said: The fire, taking up residence in the head, protects the body; the vital breath, operating in both the head and the fire, stirs into action — all that has been, all that is, and all that shall be is established in the vital breath.
That very one is the best among beings — we worship the light of Brahman; that living being is the Self of all beings, the eternal Person; mind, intellect, ego-sense, and the objects of beings — he is all that.
Thus here he is everywhere sustained by the vital breath; behind it, the equalized breath, each taking up its own course.
At the base of the bladder and in the rectum, the fire takes up residence; the downward breath, carrying urine and feces, moves in rotation.
That one breath which operates in the three — in effort, action, and strength — those who know the inner self call it the udana breath.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The breath lodged in every joint throughout the body of human beings is designated the vyana breath.
The fire spread through the bodily elements, stirred by the wind, runs throughout, processing the essences, the elements, and the humors.
Through the confluence of the vital breaths, their joint action arises; the heat, which is to be known as the fire, digests the food of the embodied beings.
The prana and vyana breaths, concentrated between the apana and udana, together with them at their station, cause the fire to digest properly.
And its extent reaches to the anus, which is thus called the guda; from that arise the channels in all the vital breaths of the embodied.
The vital breath that carries the force of fire is repelled at the end of the rectum; coming upward again, it once more projects the fire upward.
The stomach of cooked food lies below the navel; above it stands the stomach of raw food; in the center of the navel, all the vital breaths are established.
All ten channels, flowing from the heart sideways, upward, and downward, carry the essences of food, impelled by the vital breaths.
This is the path of yogins by which they reach the Supreme — the steadfast ones who have mastered the posture of exhaustion place the Self in the crown of the head. Thus the prana and apana breaths are spread through all embodied beings.
Know that which has eleven modifications as its nature and is assembled from an accumulation of fractions — know it as the embodied one, eternally characterized by a self won through action.
The fire that is ever established in that one, placed as if in a cooking vessel — know that Self as eternally characterized by a self won through yoga.
The divine one who is established in that, like a drop of water on a lotus — know that knower of the field as eternally characterized by a self won through renunciation.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Know rajas, sattva, and tamas as belonging to the individual soul; know the individual soul as the quality of the self, and know the self as partaking of the Supreme Self.
They call the quality of the individual soul conscious; it acts and causes everything to act. Beyond that, the knowers of the field declare: the one who fashioned the seven worlds.
Thus the Self of beings does not manifest in all beings; yet it is seen by those who know knowledge, through a subtle, penetrating intellect.
Through the serenity of the mind one destroys both good and evil karma; with a serene self, established in the Self, one experiences happiness and eternity.
The mark of serenity is this: as a satisfied person sleeps pleasantly, or as a lamp kindled by a skilled hand burns in a windless place.
Constantly yoking the mind in the early and late watches of the night, eating lightly, with a purified soul, seeing the Self through the Self—
—he sees with the lamp of the mind, as with a lit lamp; having seen the Self as free from self, he is then liberated.
By all means, the restraint of greed and anger — this is considered the most purifying of sacrifices; austerity is indeed the crossing over.
Always protect austerity from anger, protect prosperity from envy, protect knowledge from honor and dishonor, and protect the self from heedlessness.
Non-cruelty is the supreme dharma; forgiveness is the supreme strength; self-knowledge is the supreme knowledge; the vow of truth is the supreme vow.
The utterance of truth is better; truth as knowledge brings welfare; that which is supremely beneficial to all beings — that is considered the highest truth.
One for whom all undertakings are always free from the bonds of desire, one for whom everything is offered in renunciation — that one is a true renunciant and truly wise.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That from which not even a guru could dislodge him through instruction — know that as union with Brahman, separation called union.
One should not harm any beings; one should conduct oneself in friendliness and equanimity; having obtained this life, one should not make enmity with anyone.
Possessionlessness, perfect contentment, freedom from craving, and steadiness — this alone is supreme knowledge; self-knowledge is ever the highest.
Abandoning acquisition, be disciplined in vow through the intellect; attain the sorrowless state, the immovable, both in the next world and in this.
One who desires to conquer what is unconquered must be a sage constant in austerity, self-restrained, with a controlled soul, unattached amid attachments.
Quality and the absence of quality, non-attachment, single-pointed action without interruption — this conduct of yours, O brahmin, they call the one step of happiness.
The person who renounces both sorrow and happiness attains Brahman utterly and proceeds through non-attachment.
All this, O best of twice-born, has been told to you in brief as I have heard it. Everything has been declared to you — what more do you wish to hear?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, when the entire teaching on the dharma of liberation had thus been spoken, the brahmin, with a heart firmly pleased, then addressed the Dharma-Hunter.
All of this proclaimed by you is endowed with right reasoning; nothing whatsoever in the matters of dharma here appears to be unknown to you.
The hunter said: See, O best of twice-born, the dharma that is manifest in me — the dharma by which I, O chief among brahmins, have attained this perfection.
Rise quickly, O revered one, and enter within the house — you, who know dharma, deserve to see my mother and father.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus addressed, he entered, and saw a mansion supremely adorned, charming, with four halls, and exceedingly beautiful to the heart.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It resembled the abode of the gods, was well-honored by divine beings, crowded with beds and seats, and filled with the finest fragrances.
There, dressed in white garments, his parents were honored, having been fed and utterly content, seated on excellent chairs — and the Dharma-Hunter, seeing them, prostrated his head at their feet.
The two elders said: Rise, rise, O knower of dharma — may dharma protect you; we are pleased; obtain long life through your purity. Son, you have always honored us well, with you as a true son.
You have no other deity — not even among the gods; through your diligence in serving the twice-born, you are endowed with self-restraint.
Your father's fathers and likewise their fathers too — they are always pleased with you, son, through your self-restraint and your reverence for us.
Your service in mind, action, and speech is never found wanting; nor is any other erroneous understanding seen in you at present.
As the two elders were well honored by Rāma the son of Jamadagni, so have you done everything — and even more than that, dear son.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the Dharma-Hunter introduced that brahmin to the two of them; and the two welcomed that brahmin and honored him with a proper greeting.
Having received that honor, the twice-born asked the two of them, along with their son and their servants: Is all well in your household? And are your two bodies always free from affliction here?
The two elders said: All is well in our home, O brahmin, and among our servants in every respect. And have you yourself arrived here without obstacle, O venerable one?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The brahmin replied to them both with the word "Indeed," filled with joy. And Dharma-the-hunter then spoke a meaningful word to that brahmin.
"Father and mother, O venerable one, are my highest deity. Whatever is to be done for the gods — that I do for these two."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Just as the thirty-three gods, all headed by Indra, are to be worshipped by all the worlds, so are these two elders to me."
"Just as brahmins bring offerings and perform rites for the gods, so I serve these two, tirelessly."
"These two — my father and my mother — are my supreme deity, O brahmin. I always please them with flowers, fruits, and jewels, O twice-born."
"These two indeed are the sacred fires for me that the wise speak of; they are the sacrifices, the four Vedas — they are everything to me, O twice-born."
"For their sake are my very life-breaths, my wife, my sons, my dear ones. Together with sons and wife I render them service constantly."
"I myself bathe them; I wash their feet as well; I personally give them their food, O best of twice-born."
"I speak pleasing words, avoiding whatever is disagreeable. Even what may be joined with unrighteousness, if it pleases them, I do for these two."
"Knowing dharma itself as my guru, I act, O best of twice-born. I always serve them tirelessly, O brahmin — this indeed is my service."
"There are exactly five gurus for a person who wishes to prosper, O brahmin: father, mother, fire, the self, and the teacher, O best of twice-born."
"One who conducts himself rightly toward these, O best of twice-born, shall have his sacred fires perpetually tended. This is the eternal dharma for one living the householder's life."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having presented both his parents — his two gurus — to the brahmin, that righteous-souled hunter again spoke to the brahmin.
"I have gained insight; behold the power of austerity. This is the very reason she told you: 'Go to Mithilā.'"
"By the devoted, self-restrained, truthful woman whose highest calling is service to her husband, it was said: 'The hunter dwelling in Mithilā will expound dharma to you.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The brahmin said: "Calling to mind the word of that faithful wife, truthful and abounding in noble character, O man of discipline — you are, O knower of dharma, one endowed with virtue in my judgment."
The hunter said: "What she told you then regarding me, O best of twice-born, O lord — that has been truly seen by her, that woman of single husband. There is no doubt."
"With the intention of doing you a favor, O brahmin, I have shown you this. And now hear my word, dear one — what I shall speak for your benefit, O twice-born."
"Your mother and father have been wronged by you, O best of twice-born. Without their leave you departed from the house, O blameless one — for the purpose of Veda recitation. That was not fitting of you."
"Those two aged and ascetic ones have gone blind from grief over you. Go and appease them — let not great dharma abandon you."
"You are an ascetic, a great soul, ever intent upon dharma — yet all of that is fruitless for you. Go quickly and propitiate those two."
"Have faith in my words, O brahmin — you must not do otherwise. Depart this very day, O sage among brahmins. I am telling you what is good for you."
The brahmin said: "All that you have said is true without doubt. I am pleased with you, O knower of dharma, O man of good conduct, endowed with virtue."
The hunter said: "You are indeed equal to a deity, you who are devoted to dharma — that ancient, eternal, divine dharma that is unattainable by those who have not refined their souls."
"Tirelessly and quickly perform the worship of your mother and father. Beyond this, I see no other dharma whatsoever."
The brahmin said: "By good fortune I came here; by good fortune I met with you. Such men as reveal dharma are rare in this world."
"Scarcely one among a thousand men, or perhaps none, truly knows dharma. I am satisfied by your truthfulness. May good come to you, O best of men."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"As I was falling into hell, I have been rescued by you. It was destined to be thus — that I would see you, O sinless one."
"Just as King Yayāti, fallen, was saved by his grandsons — good men — O tiger among men, so have I been saved here by you."
"I shall render service to my mother and father at your word. One who has not disciplined himself does not discern the determination of dharma and adharma."
"Eternal dharma is hard to know, yet here it dwells in a shudra birth. I do not regard you as a shudra — there must be a cause, some ripening of past karma, by which this shudra state has come to you."
"This I wish to understand truly, O great mind. Please tell me everything truthfully — you who are of disciplined soul."
The hunter said: "Brahmins are not to be transgressed, O best of twice-born. Hear all that transpired in my former birth, O sinless one."
"I was indeed a brahmin formerly, O son of the best twice-born — a student of the Vedas, well skilled, a master of the Vedic auxiliaries. By my own faults I have come to this condition, O brahmin."
"A certain king was my friend, devoted to the science of archery. Through association with him I became excellent in the bow, O twice-born."
"At that very time the king went out hunting, accompanied by his chief warriors and ministers, well attended. And there he slew very many deer near an ashrama."
"Then I too released a terrible arrow, O best of twice-born, and a sage was struck by that arrow with its joints bent back."
"Fallen to the ground, O brahmin, he cried out resonantly: 'I have done no wrong — by whom has this evil been done?'"
"Thinking it a deer, I had hastily approached and suddenly saw that sage — the seer pierced by the arrow with bent joints, that brahmin of fierce austerity, groaning upon the earth."
"My mind was deeply distressed at having done this unlawful act. 'This was done by me unknowingly,' I thought, and I said to him: 'You must forgive me, O brahmin.' Thus spoken to by me, the sage —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"— then spoke back a word to me, overcome with rage: 'You shall be a cruel hunter, born in a shudra womb,' O twice-born."
The hunter said: "Thus cursed by the sage at that time, O best among the twice-born, I sought to appease the sage with speech, skilled in words."
"'This unlawful act has been done by me today unknowingly, O sage. You must forgive all of it. Be gracious, O venerable one.'"
The sage said: "The curse cannot be otherwise — so it shall be, without doubt. Out of compassion I will bestow some grace upon you today."
"Though dwelling in a shudra birth, you shall be a knower of dharma, and you shall render service to your mother and father — of this there is no doubt."
"Through that service you shall attain great perfection. You shall remember your former birth, and you shall go to heaven as well. When the curse is exhausted and spent, you shall become a twice-born again."
The hunter said: "Thus was I cursed of old by that sage of fierce splendor, and such grace was bestowed upon me by him, O best among bipeds."
"And I drew out the arrow from him, O best of twice-born, and brought him to his ashrama. And he did not lose his life-breaths."
"All this has been told to you, as it came to pass for me long ago. And I am also to go to heaven soon, O best of twice-born."
The brahmin said: "Thus do men obtain sorrows and joys alike, O great-minded one. You should not be troubled. What is difficult has been accomplished — remembering your own previous birth, dear friend."
"The fault of karma produced by one's own past birth — endure it for a while, O learned one, and then you shall be a twice-born again. Even now I regard you as a brahmin; of this there is no doubt."
"A brahmin who engages in degrading acts, who is hypocritical and given largely to evil deeds, becomes equal to a shudra."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"But a shudra who is ever intent upon self-restraint, truth, and dharma — him I regard as a brahmin. For it is by conduct that one becomes twice-born."
"By the fault of karma one obtains a terrible and unequal condition. I regard your fault as already exhausted on all sides, O best of men."
"You should not be troubled. Those like you are undiscouraged, knowers of how the world conducts itself, ever devoted to dharma."
The hunter said: "Mental suffering is to be conquered by wisdom, bodily suffering by remedies. This is the power of knowledge — it should not be equated with the condition of fools."
"From conjunction with the unwanted and from separation from what is dear, men of little understanding are yoked to mental sorrows."
"Beings are joined together by the qualities of nature and separated by them as well — all of them. This is not a cause for grief for any single person alone."
"Seeing one connected with the unwanted, a person quickly turns away. And then they counteract it if they see a remedy. For one who laments, nothing is gained — he merely burns himself."
"Those men who abandon both sorrow and joy alike — they indeed prosper in happiness, those wise ones satisfied by knowledge."
"The deluded are devoted to discontent; the wise attain contentment. There is no end to discontent, but contentment is the highest happiness. Those who have traveled the path and see the highest goal do not grieve."
"One must not set the mind on dejection. Dejection is a supreme poison — it kills the unwise child, like an enraged serpent."
"One whom dejection overpowers when adversity presents itself — that man, diminished in his luster, has no human purpose left."
"The fruit of action necessarily performed is seen. For by coming to despondency one obtains nothing excellent."
"But if one sees a means for the removal of suffering, one should begin without lamenting, being disciplined and free from addiction."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Those who have gone beyond the intellect, contemplating the transience of beings, do not grieve — those of mature wisdom who see the highest goal."
"I do not grieve, O learned one; I stand awaiting my time. By these examples, O brahmin, I do not sink, O excellent one."
The brahmin said: "You are of mature wisdom, of great intelligence, and your understanding is vast. I do not grieve for you — you are satisfied by knowledge, O knower of dharma."
"I take my leave of you. May it be well with you. May dharma protect you. Vigilance must be maintained in dharma, O best among those who uphold it."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Indeed so," said the hunter to him, his hands folded in reverence. And then, having performed the circumambulation, that best of twice-born departed.
And that brahmin, having gone, rendered full service then to his two aged parents — mother and father — properly and with great discipline.
"All this has been told to you completely, O Yudhiṣṭhira. The dharma you asked about, dear one, O best among those who uphold dharma."
"The greatness of the devoted wife, and of the brahmin, O excellent one; the service of mother and father; and the dharma in the hunter — all have been proclaimed."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "This account of dharma is supremely wonderful and unsurpassed, O brahmin — told by you, O best among all who uphold dharma, O best of twice-born."
"By its sweetness of hearing, O learned one, it passed for me as but a moment. I am not yet satisfied, O venerable one, hearing this highest dharma."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this auspicious tale joined with dharma, the King of Dharma again questioned the ascetic sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "How did Agni go to the forest? And how did Aṅgiras in former times, when fire had disappeared, carry the oblation, himself having become a great sage-fire?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When fire is one alone, yet multiplicity of it is seen in its functions, O venerable one — all of this I wish to know."
"And how was Kumāra born? How did he become the son of Agni? How was he produced from Rudra, and in the Gaṅgā, and among the Kṛttikās?"
This I wish to hear from you, O joy of the Bhārgava line — filled with curiosity, I wish to know it exactly as it is, O great sage.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: On this point too they cite this ancient tale — how Hutavaha, enraged, went to the forest to perform austerities.
And how the blessed Agni himself became Aṅgiras, scorching with his own radiance and dispelling darkness.
Dwelling in the hermitage, the greatly blessed one surpassed Havyavāha; having become thus, he illumined the entire world.
And Hutabhuk, while performing austerities, was scorched by his heat; the radiant one, greatly afflicted, knew nothing at all.
Then the blessed Havyavāhana reflected: another fire has been set in motion by Brahmā for the worlds; my fire-nature is indeed lost, for this penance torments me.
Thinking "How can I become fire again?" he saw the great sage scorching the worlds like fire itself.
He approached slowly, afraid, and then Aṅgiras spoke to him: "Become fire once more without delay — you who sustain the worlds; you are known in the three worlds among those who dwell in the three stations."
"You, O Agni, were created first by Brahmā as the dispeller of darkness; return to your own station quickly, O destroyer of gloom."
Agni said: My fame is lost in the world; you have been born as Hutāśana; people will know only you as Pāvaka, not me.
"I abandon fire-hood; you become the first fire; I shall be the second, namely the Prājāpatya fire."
Aṅgiras said: "Do the meritorious work that leads creatures to heaven; be the fire that dispels darkness; and O god, O Agni, make me straightway your first son."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hearing the words of Aṅgiras, Jātavedas did accordingly, O king; and Bṛhaspati by name was the son of that Aṅgiras.
Knowing that firstborn son of fire, the Āṅgirasa, the gods approached and asked the reason there, O Bhārata.
Being questioned by the gods, he then stated the reason; and the gods accepted the word of Aṅgiras at that time.
Here I shall describe the many kinds of fires, greatly luminous, known by many deeds — their multiplicity among the brāhmaṇas in this world.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: He who was the third son of Brahmā, O ornament of the Kuru lineage — his wife was Apavā; hear from me his offspring as well.
Bṛhajjyotis, Bṛhatkīrti, Bṛhadbrahmā, Bṛhanmanās, Bṛhanmantra, Bṛhadbhāsa, and likewise, O king, Bṛhaspati.
Among all those creatures she was unrivalled in beauty — the goddess named Bhānumatī, the first daughter of Aṅgiras.
She in whom passion arose in all beings at that time — she is called Rāgā from passion; she is the second daughter of Aṅgiras.
She whom they call the daughter of Kapardī, "the seen and unseen" — she is Sinīvālī on account of her slenderness; she is the third daughter of Aṅgiras.
She who sees with radiant rays and is rich in oblations — Haviṣmatī; they call the sixth holy daughter of Aṅgiras Haviṣmatī.
In great sacrifices the Āṅgirasī, in brilliant rites the great-minded one — known as Mahāmatī, she is spoken of as the seventh daughter.
She the blessed one upon seeing whom people cry "kuhu kuhu" — her they call Ekānaṃśā; she is Kuhū, the daughter of Aṅgiras.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The illustrious lunar wife who became wife of Bṛhaspati — she bore six holy fires and one daughter as well.
That fire whose oblation of clarified butter is prescribed in the āhutis — that fire, son of Bṛhaspati, is named Śaṃyu, greatly radiant.
He at whose sacrifice in the Cāturmāsya rites the horse is the foremost victim — the single valiant fire blazing with many flames.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śaṃyu's wife was the incomparable Satyā, Satyā born of dharma; his son was Dīpta, the fire, and three virtuous daughters.
The fire who is honoured with the first share of clarified butter at the sacrifice — that fire's son is called Bharadvāja, the first.
At all the full-moon rites, with the ladle raised bearing the oblation of ghee — that fire named Bharata is the second son of Śaṃyu.
There are three other daughters of whom Bharata is the lord; but Bharata in turn has a son, and Bharatī as one daughter.
Bharata — of Bharata the fire; Pāvaka — of Prajāpati; and the great one, exceedingly harmful also — O best of the Bhāratas.
Bharadvāja's wife was Vīrā, and Vīra the giver of balls of rice; a brahmacārin, self-restrained, ever of vast vow — the twice-born speak of his worship with ghee as like that of Soma.
He who with the second oblation is yoked together with Soma — whose glory is that of a chariot, whose sound is that of a chariot — he is called Kumbharetā.
He begot Siddhi on Sarayū, enveloped Bhānu with his rays; he who always brings the Āgneya — he is spoken of in invocations.
He who never swerves from fame, brilliance, and splendour — that fire is named Niścyavana; he solely praises the earth.
Free of sin, released from impurities, pure and blazing with flames — the sinless Vipāpa fire, his son, is true in prescribed actions.
He who effects expiation for beings who are reviling — that fire is named Niṣkṛti; he beautifies those who attend on him.
He by whom people suffering pain here moan of their own accord — his son is named Svana, that Pāvaka who causes disease.
He who abides having seized the intellect of the entire world — those who know the self call him Viśvajit, Pāvaka by name.
He who is the inner fire and digests what has been eaten by embodied beings — at sacrifice he is named Viśvabhuṅ in all the worlds, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A brahmacārin, self-restrained, ever of vast vow — the brāhmaṇas worship this Pāvaka in the cooked-food sacrifices.
Renowned as Gopati by name, whose beloved was a river — in him all rites are performed by those who perform rites.
He who as the mare's-mouth fire drinks water, that most terrible one — going upward, he is named Ūrdhvabhāṅ, the wise one who dwells in the breath.
He in whose house the oblation is always given at the northern door — from that the clarified butter becomes well-offered; he is remembered as the supreme Sviṣṭakṛt.
He who is the wrathful Pāvaka among pacified beings — from wrath was born a juice, and then the daughter Manyatī; Svāhā, fierce and cruel, abides among all beings.
He to whom none in the triple heaven is equal in form — on account of incomparability the gods named this Pāvaka Kāma.
Holding wrath in exhilaration, bearing a bow and garland, standing on a chariot — he destroys enemies in battle; Amogha is the name of this Pāvaka.
Uktha by name, O greatly blessed one, praised by three uktha hymns — he begot Mahāvāca, that one with a willing horse whom they know.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Kāśyapa, Vāsiṣṭha, Prāṇa and Prāṇaputraka, Agni Āṅgirasa, and Cyavana Triṣuvarcaka —
— performed intense austerities for many years for the sake of a son: "May we obtain a son most righteous, equal to Brahmā in fame."
Meditated upon with the great utterances by those five at that time, there was born a being made of energy, radiant, of five colours, powerful.
His head was the kindled fire; his two arms likewise resembled the sun; his skin and eyes were golden-hued; his legs were dark, O Bhārata.
Of five colours, he was created by the austerities of those five persons; known in the Veda as Pāñcajanya, he is the creator of five lineages.
Having performed austerities for ten thousand years, that great ascetic begot a terrible Pāvaka, creating offspring for the ancestors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From his head Bṛhat and Rathaṃtara; from his mouth he swiftly brought forth two; from his navel Śiva; from his strength Indra; from his breath he created Vāyu and Agni.
From his arms the two Anudāttas and all the Viśve Bhūtas; having created these, he then created five sons of the ancestors.
The spy of Bṛhadūrja; the greater of Kāśyapa; Bhānu the heroic son of Aṅgiras; Saubhara the son of Varcas —
— and Anudātta of Prāṇa — these five born of lineages are explained; and he created other gods, the Yajñamuṣas, fifteen more.
Abhīma, Atibhīma, Bhīma, and Bhīmabalābala — these five gods called Yajñamuṣas he created through austerity.
Sumitrā, Mitravant, Mitrajña, Mitravardhan, and Mitradharman — these gods he created through austerity.
Surapravīra, Vīra, Sukeśa, Suvarcas, and the slayer of gods as well — these five he created through austerity.
These exist in three forms, five by five separately; stationed here they steal — these who are here steal from those who have gone to heaven by sacrifice.
They carry off what those have sacrificed and slay greatly on earth; out of rivalry with the bearers of oblations they slay and steal.
The taking of that oblation from the altar is set in motion by the skilled; those do not approach where fire is stationed.
The built fire, bearing the sacrifice on its two wings, repels them; calmed by mantras they do not steal what is sacrificial.
The son of Bṛhaduktha and Tapasya, who has taken refuge in the earth — when the agnihotra is offered, he is worshipped on earth by the good.
And the son of Rathaṃtara and Tapas is known as a fire; the adhvaryus know that his oblation goes to Mitravind; greatly pleased, the greatly famous one rejoiced together with his sons.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Endowed with great disciplines, the Pāvaka named Bharata — the fire named Puṣṭimati, when satisfied, bestows nourishment; this one sustains all creatures, hence he is called Bharata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That fire which is named Śiva, devoted to the worship of Śakti — he is the maker of good for all who are afflicted with sorrow, ever auspicious.
Seeing the fruit of austerity and great austerity greatly grown, wishing to surpass, the wise son was born — Puraṃdara.
And heat was born of the heated one; that fire is perceived among beings; and fire also — named Manu — established what belongs to Prajāpati.
The brāhmaṇas versed to the end of the Vedas call it the Śambhu fire; the twice-born call the blazing fire of great radiance the Āvasathya.
Agni truly begot through austerity five bearers of oblations here, makers of vigour, resplendent like gold, sons born of sacrifice.
When fire, O greatly blessed one, was exhausted and spent — Gavāṃpati — he begot the terrible asuras and mortals of various kinds.
And from Tapas he created the son Manu, and also Bhānu, Aṅgirā — the brāhmaṇas versed to the end of the Vedas call that one Bṛhadbhānu.
Bhānu's wife was Suprajā, and the Soma-born Bṛhadbhāsā — the two of them together begot six sons; hear the manner of their offspring.
He who grants a body to weak beings — that fire they call Balada; he is the first son of Bhānu.
He who becomes terrible wrath among pacified beings — that fire is named Manyumān; he is the second son of Bhānu.
He whose oblation here is declared at the new-moon and full-moon rites — that fire here is named Viṣṇu; and Dhṛtimān — he is Aṅgirā.
That fire whose oblation offered together with Indra is known as the āgrayaṇa — that fire is called Āgrayaṇa, and he too is a descendant of Bhānu.
That fire which, in the cāturmāsya rites, receives the regular oblations without interruption, accompanied by four sons — he too is a descendant of Bhānu.
Night herself bore a daughter, and both Agni and Soma likewise; she who had been Manu's wife gave birth to five purifying fires.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That fire who is worshipped with the choicest oblations in the cāturmāsya ceremonies, the glorious one who acts together with Parjanya — he is known as Vaiśvānara.
That fire who is celebrated as the lord of this entire world is named Viśvapati, the second son of Manu; through him the offered ghee becomes truly well-offered, and he is accordingly called Sviṣṭakṛt, the supreme maker of perfect sacrifice.
That maiden called Rohiṇī, daughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu, became his wife by his own action; that fire is also a Prajāpati.
That fire who, abiding in the vital breath, sustains the bodies of embodied beings — he is named Saṃnihita, the accomplisher of sound and form.
That deity who moves along both the bright and dark paths and sustains the fire of oblation — he is himself without blemish yet is the cause of impurities in others, and he abides in wrath.
That fire whom ascetics always proclaim as the great sage Kapila — he is named Kapila, the inaugurator of the Sāṃkhya yoga.
That fire by whom beings are constantly set in motion among the varied activities of this world — he is called Agraṇī, the foremost fire.
He created these and other well-known purifying fires on earth — fierce ones, meant as expiations for the defiled agnihotra.
If the fires should somehow come into contact with one another through the wind, an eight-potsherd iṣṭi offering must be performed for the fire called Śuci.
If the southern fire should become commingled with the other two, then an eight-potsherd iṣṭi offering must be performed for the fire called Vīta.
If the sacred fires kept in the household should be touched by a forest fire, an eight-potsherd iṣṭi offering must be performed for the fire called Śuci.
If a woman in her impure state should touch the agnihotra fire, an eight-potsherd iṣṭi offering must be performed for the fire called Dasyumant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If someone who was reported dead is heard to be alive, or if livestock perish, an eight-potsherd iṣṭi offering must be performed for the fire called Abhimata.
If a brahmin who is afflicted fails to offer into the fire for three nights, an eight-potsherd iṣṭi offering must be performed for the fire called Uttarāgni.
If the new-moon and full-moon observances remain established but are neglected, an eight-potsherd iṣṭi offering must be performed for the fire called Pathikṛt.
If the fire of the birthing chamber should touch the agnihotra fire, an eight-potsherd iṣṭi offering must be performed for the fire called Agnimant.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The joyful wife of Āpa and the most beloved wife of Saha — together with Bhūpati and Bhuvabhartā — gave birth to the supreme purifying fire.
Him whom they call the lord and purifier of all beings, the self and sustainer of the world — so he is proclaimed among twice-born men with their lineages.
He who is the lord of all great beings in this world — that blessed, supremely radiant purifying fire moves perpetually through all things.
The fire named Gṛhapati is perpetually worshipped in sacrificial rites; he it is who carries the oblations that are offered — the purifier of this world.
The glorious embryo of the waters, the wondrous son of Saha, Bhūpati, and Bhuvabhartā — he is called the lord of the great.
Burning the dead bodies of beings, Bharata became his fire; and in the agniṣṭoma rite, ordained as the foremost of sacrifices, he is the fire of Bharata.
Seeing one who was surely coming toward them, fire hid himself in the ocean out of fear; the gods could not find him though they searched in every direction.
But when fire saw Atharvan, he then spoke these words: "O hero, carry the oblations of the gods yourself — I am extremely weak. O Atharvan, go to the sweet-eyed one; do me this favour."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having sent Atharvan away, fire then departed to another region; but the fish reported his whereabouts. Angered, fire spoke to them.
"You shall become food for embodied beings in many ways and conditions!" — thus fire the oblation-carrier also spoke his words to Atharvan.
Though greatly entreated by him with the words of the gods, fire still refused to carry all the oblations and abandoned his body entirely.
Having cast off that body, he then entered the earth; and upon touching the ground he released the various minerals, one by one, in great profusion.
From his mouth came fragrant radiance and from his bones came the deva-dāru tree; from his phlegm came crystal, and from his bile came the emerald.
From his liver came black iron; through him three classes of creatures came into being; from his nails came layers of cloud, from his network of veins came coral, and from his body came many other diverse minerals, O king.
Having thus abandoned his body and remaining in supreme austerity, he was once again raised up from his penance by Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and the others.
Blazing intensely, his flame nourished and swelled by austerity, he saw the sages and from fear entered the great ocean once more.
When he had vanished, the world was seized with fear and took refuge in Atharvan; the divine sages then worshipped Atharvan himself.
Then Atharvan, perceiving fire within himself, created the worlds, and before the eyes of all beings he churned up the great ocean.
Thus fire, who had previously vanished, was called back by the blessed Atharvan, and henceforth he forever carries the oblations for all beings.
And so, wandering and roaming through many and various lands, he fathered the divine fire-altars — many wise ones as declared in the Vedas.
Excluding the Sindhu, five rivers — Devikā, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, Śatakumbhā, Śarayū, and the one called Gaṇḍa —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Carmaṇvatī, Mahī, Medhyā, Medhātithi, Tāmrāvatī, Vetravatī, those three rivers, and Kauśikī —
Tamasā, Narmadā, the river Godāvarī, Veṇṇā, Praveṇī, Bhīmā, and Medrathā, O Bhārata —
Bhāratī, Suprayogā, Kāverī, Murmurā, Kṛṣṇā, Kṛṣṇaveṇṇā, Kapilā, and Śoṇa — these rivers, which are proclaimed, are the mothers of the fire-altars.
The beloved wife of Adbhuta bore a son named Viḍūratha; and as many purifying fires as have been named, so many somas there are as well.
The mind-born offspring of Brahman were also born in the lineage of Atri; Atri, wishing to create sons, held them within himself, and the oblation-carrying fires draw them forth from the bodies of that brahmic power.
Thus have I recounted these great-souled fires to you — immeasurable in their origins, glorious, destroyers of darkness.
Know that the greatness of Adbhuta, as it is celebrated in the Vedas, is that of all of them together — for this oblation-carrier is truly the one fire.
This blessed one is to be known as one alone — the primeval Aṅgiras; he has issued forth in manifold forms from his body, just as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice does from its single rite.
Thus this supremely great lineage of fires has been recounted by me; purified by various sacred formulas, he carries the oblations for all embodied beings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The manifold lineage of fires has been recounted to you by me, O sinless one. Now hear, O Kauravya, the birth of the wise Kārttikeya.
I shall tell of the wondrous son of Adbhuta — of immeasurable might, born through the wives of the Seven Sages, devoted to brahmin virtues, and the increaser of glory.
In former times, gods and demons were constantly engaged in slaying one another; and in those battles the fearsome-formed dānavas always conquered the gods.
Seeing his forces repeatedly slaughtered by them, Puraṃdara fell into deep anxiety as to how he might find a leader for his own army.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That supremely mighty man who, seeing the divine army broken by the demons, would protect it by relying on his own valour — he is the one I must find."
Going to the Mānasa mountain and brooding deeply on this matter, he then heard a terrible cry of distress that had been let out by a woman.
"Let some man come running to me! Let him rescue me! Let him point out a husband for me, or let him become my husband himself!"
Puraṃdara said to her: "Do not be afraid; you have nothing to fear." Having spoken thus, he then saw Keśin standing before him.
Wearing a diadem, mace in hand, like a mountain rich with ores — he was holding the maiden by the arm. Then Vāsava spoke to him.
"Why do you, who do the deeds of the ignoble, seek to carry off this maiden? Know me to be the bearer of the thunderbolt — desist from tormenting her!"
Keśin said: "You, Śakra, should let her go — she has been desired by me. It would be wise for you, still living, to go back to your own city, O Pākaśāsana."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, Keśin hurled his mace intending to kill Indra; but Vāsava cut it in two in the middle with his thunderbolt as it came flying at him.
Then Keśin, enraged, hurled a mountain peak at him; but Śatakratu, watching it as it flew toward him, shattered that mountain crag with his thunderbolt, O king, and it fell to the ground.
But as it fell, Keśin was struck by that very crag; and sorely wounded, he abandoned the illustrious maiden and fled.
When that demon had departed, Vāsava said to the maiden: "Who are you? Whose are you? And what are you doing here, O fair-faced one?"
The maiden said: "I am the daughter of Prajāpati, known by the name Devasenā; my sister Daityasenā was previously abducted by Keśin."
"We two sisters came together with our companions to the Mānasa lake for pleasure, having taken leave of Prajāpati."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And the great demon Keśin always desires to carry off both of us; Daityasenā wishes him as a husband, but I do not, O Pākaśāsana."
"She has been carried off by him, O blessed one, while I have been freed by your strength. O Devendra, I desire the husband you shall appoint for me — one who is invincible."
Indra said: "You are the niece of my mother, the daughter of Dakṣa's daughter. But I wish you yourself to declare your own inherent power."
The maiden said: "I myself am without power, O mighty-armed one, but my husband shall be powerful; by the boon of my father he will come to be, and he will be bowed to by both gods and demons."
Indra said: "What manner of power, O goddess, will your husband possess? I wish to hear this from your own words, O blameless one."
The maiden said: "He is seen as the conqueror of gods, demons, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, nāgas, and rākṣasas, and of all the wicked — great in heroism and great in strength."
"He who shall conquer all beings together with you — he shall indeed be my husband, devoted to brahmin virtues and the increaser of glory."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hearing her words, Indra was troubled and brooded deeply: "There is no one who possesses the qualities this goddess speaks of."
Then he whose radiance rivals the sun's beheld the sun rising, and the glorious moon as well, entering the sun.
He saw the auspicious new-moon moment arriving, and the raudra muhūrta as well, and the battle between gods and demons at the rising mountain.
Śatakratu, the blessed one, beheld the eastern dawn filled with reddish clouds, and the ocean — Varuṇa's abode — flushed red with their reflection.
He saw the oblation offered with diverse sacred formulas by the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases, and fire himself, bearing the oblation, entering the sun.
He saw the twenty-fourth lunar phase approaching the sun, and likewise the moon — in the path of dharma, in the raudra aspect — having entered the sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beholding the perfect union of the moon and the sun, and seeing that fierce conjunction, Śakra fell into deep thought.
This fierce conjunction is great and charged with radiance — a wondrous meeting of Soma, Fire, and Sun. Whichever son Soma might beget from this, he shall become the husband of this goddess.
Agni, endowed with all these qualities, is himself a deity. If he should father a child, that son shall be the husband of this goddess.
Having thus reflected, the blessed Indra went then to the world of Brahmā. Taking Devasena with him, he bowed before the Grandfather and said: 'Be gracious — bestow on this goddess a valiant husband.'
Brahmā said: 'O slayer of demons, even as you have pondered this matter, so shall it be — a mighty womb shall bring forth a son of vast heroism.'
'He shall become the commander of your armies, O Indra of a hundred sacrifices, and he shall become the brave husband of this goddess.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hearing this, Indra bowed to Brahmā and departed with the maiden to the place where the divine sages dwelt — foremost among them Vasiṣṭha, the greatest among brahmin seers, all of mighty vows.
Thirsting for the soma those sages had earned through austerity at their sacrifice, the gods went there with Indra leading the way.
Having performed the rite as prescribed, into the well-kindled fire those great-souled sages poured oblations on behalf of all the dwellers in heaven.
Summoned, the wondrous fire-bearer emerged from the solar disc and came forth — the mighty lord, his speech restrained, as prescribed by rule — and approached the offering fire into which those twice-born had poured oblations with mantras.
There the fire-devourer received the various oblations, O best of the Bhāratas, and conveyed them to the heaven-dwellers on behalf of the sages.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As he came out, he also saw the wives of those great-souled sages seated in their own hermitages and bathing at their ease.
They were like golden altar-pedestals, pure as crescent moons, resembling the flames of the sacrificial fire, all of them wondrous as stars.
His mind fixed upon them, his senses became agitated; beholding the wives of those foremost brahmins, Fire fell under the sway of desire.
He reflected again: 'It is not right that I, agitated as I am, should desire the chaste wives of those great brahmins — women who do not desire me.'
'I cannot behold or touch them without cause — and so, entering the householder's fire, I gaze upon them again and again.'
As if touching them all with his golden-bright flames, watching them as he dwelt in the domestic fire, he rejoiced.
Having remained there for a very long time, Fire thus fell under the sway of desire, his mind cast upon those fair-limbed women whom he longed for.
With his heart scorched by desire, fully resolved to abandon his body if he could not obtain the brahmin wives, Agni went into the forest.
Svāhā, the daughter of Dakṣa, had long desired him. That passionate woman had sought an opening in the vigilant god's conduct, but found none, blameless as she was in her search.
When she learned truly that Fire had gone into the forest truly scorched by desire, that passionate woman began to ponder a plan.
'Taking on the forms of the seven sages' wives, I shall approach the love-stricken Fire — bewildering him with their likenesses — and desire him. If I do this, his pleasure will be mine, and my longing too shall be fulfilled.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Śiva, the wife of Aṅgiras, was endowed with virtue, beauty, and good qualities. Assuming her form first, the goddess approached the vicinity of Fire, O king, and that fair-limbed woman addressed him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'O Agni, I am tormented by love — you should desire me. If you do not do so, know that you shall see me dead.'
'I am Śiva, wife of Aṅgiras, O fire-devourer. I have come with my companions, having deliberated and made my resolve.'
Agni said: 'How do you know that I am afflicted with desire? And how do the others — all the beloved wives of the seven sages whom you have named — know this?'
Śiva said: 'You are ever dear to us, and we are ever in awe of you. Having read the signs of your heart, I have been sent to you.'
'I have come here for union. Fulfil your desire quickly — my mothers await me and I must return, O fire-devourer.'
