Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Agni united with Śiva, filled with joy and delight. And when they joined, the goddess received his seed in her hand with love.
She thought: 'Those who see this form of mine in the forest will falsely attribute blame to the brahmin women in connection with Fire.'
'Therefore, to guard against this, I shall take the form of a Garudi — and my departure from the forest will thus be easy.'
Having become a Suparṇa-bird, she flew out of the great forest and beheld the white mountain well-covered with reed-thickets.
It was guarded by wondrous serpents of seven heads with poison in their gaze, and filled with rakshasas, pishacas, and fierce troops of spirits, as well as female rakshasas and multitudes of beasts and birds.
She swiftly flew to the summit of that most inaccessible peak and, in haste, cast the seed into a golden vessel.
That goddess also took on the likenesses of the remaining wives of those great-souled seven sages and, in each form, desired Fire.
She was unable, however, to assume the divine form of Arundhatī — for by the power of Arundhatī's austerities and her devoted service to her husband, that form remained beyond Svāhā's reach.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Six times did that impassioned Svāhā cast Agni's seed into the golden vessel, O best of the Kurus, on the mountain's slope.
That spilled seed, gathered together and charged with brilliance, there generated a son. The sages honoured him as 'Skanna' — the spilled — and from that came his name Skanda.
The youth was born with six heads, twice the number of ears, twelve eyes arranged in order, twelve arms — and yet one neck and one body.
On the second day he became manifest; on the third day the child shone forth; on the fourth, with all his limbs and sub-limbs fully formed, Guha came into being.
Wrapped in a great crimson cloud together with lightning, he blazed in that vast red cloud like the rising sun.
He took up that great, hair-raising bow — the very bow set down by the Destroyer of the Three Cities — which cuts down the enemies of the gods.
Taking up that foremost of bows, the powerful one then roared, as if bewildering these three worlds with all their moving and unmoving beings.
Hearing his roar, which sounded like the thunder of great clouds, two great serpents leapt up — Citra and Airāvata.
Seeing them rushing at him, he who blazed like the rising sun seized those two with two of his hands, held his spear in another hand, and with yet another arm clasped the crimson-crested cock, son of Agni's lineage.
Gripping that great-bodied cock — best among the mighty — he roared fearfully and sported in his might.
With two arms the powerful one seized a great conch and blew it — a sound that struck terror into all beings, even the mighty.
With two arms he struck the sky repeatedly; at play, the great commander shone brilliantly — drinking in the three worlds with his faces, unfathomable in nature, blazing on the mountain peak like the sun at its rising.
Seated on the summit of that mountain, of wondrous valour, the immeasurable one surveyed the directions with his many faces; beholding the manifold aspects of existence, he roared once again.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing his roar, people fell down in many places; frightened and their minds agitated, they fled to him alone for refuge.
Those people of various kinds who then took refuge in that god — those too came to be called his attendants, mighty brahmins among them.
He, the mighty-armed, rose and comforted those people; then drawing his bow, he released arrows at the great white mountain.
With his arrows he split Mount Krauñca, the son of Himavān — and through that cleft, geese and vultures travel to Mount Meru.
The mountain, shattered, fell crying out in great anguish; when it fell, other mountains cried out in great fear.
Even hearing that cry of those in great distress, the best of the mighty was not troubled; unfathomable in soul, he raised his spear and roared.
Then that great spear, hurled by that great-souled one, swiftly split the dreadful peak of the white mountain.
Struck by it, the wretched white mountain, together with its immovable companions, leapt up, abandoning the earth in fear of that great soul.
Then the earth was shaken and crumbled on all sides; in her distress she approached Skanda and became strong and firm again.
The mountains too, bowing to him, returned to the earth. And from that time the world has celebrated the fifth bright day of Skanda's festivity.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The sages, seeing various great and terrible portents, were troubled and performed peace-rites for the welfare of the worlds.
The people who dwelt in the forest of Citraratha said: 'This great calamity has been brought upon us by Fire, who united with the six wives of the seven sages.'
Others said to the Garudi: 'This calamity was brought about by you' — for those who had seen the goddess moving in her form thought as much; but no one knew that the deed had been done by Svāhā.
The Suparṇa-bird, hearing those words, thought 'this child is mine.' She approached Skanda gently and said: 'I am your mother.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the seven sages, hearing that a son of great energy had been born, abandoned their six wives — all except the goddess Arundhatī.
The forest-dwellers said that the child was born of those six alone. And Svāhā told the seven sages: 'This is my son.' But O king, they said again and again: 'We know that this is not so.'
The great sage Viśvāmitra, having performed a rite on behalf of the seven sages, had followed Fire unseen from behind while he was scorched with desire — and through this he had come to know everything in full, exactly as it happened.
Viśvāmitra was the first to take refuge in the youth and composed a divine hymn of praise to Mahāsena.
The great sage also performed all the auspicious birth-rites and the thirteen Kaumara ceremonies, beginning with the birth-rite, for him.
He also established the greatness of the six-faced one, the worship of the cock, the worship with the spear and of the goddess, and likewise the worship of his attendants.
Viśvāmitra performed all this for the benefit of the worlds, and thus the sage Viśvāmitra became dear to Kumāra.
The great sage confirmed the shape-changing of Svāhā and declared to all the sages: 'The women are not guilty.' Having heard the truth from him, the sages accordingly abandoned their wives completely.
Then the gods, having heard of Skanda, spoke together to Vāsava: 'Skanda's power is unbearable — slay him, O Indra, quickly and without delay.'
'And if you do not slay him today, this one will become Indra — the mighty one will subjugate the three worlds and you along with us, O Śakra.'
He said to them, troubled: 'This child is of immense power — he could overpower and destroy even the creator of the worlds in battle.'
'Let all the mothers of the world go to Skanda today and destroy him with their power of will and might.' Saying 'so be it,' they went.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But seeing him beyond all opposition, their faces fell; thinking 'this one cannot be overcome,' they too took refuge in him alone.
And they said: 'You are our son; we sustain the world. Receive us all with joy — our breasts flow with milk, we are overcome with love.'
Mahāsena honoured them and granted their wishes; then the mighty one, mightiest of the strong, saw Fire coming toward him — his father.
Honoured by him, Fire, together with the host of mothers, encircled Mahāsena and stood firm, protecting him steadfastly.
Among all those mothers, the woman born of wrath — the wet-nurse — protected Skanda as a son, trident in hand.
The daughter of the crimson ocean — fierce, who feeds on blood — embraced Mahāsena and guarded him as a son.
Agni, having become Naigameya, the goat-faced one with many offspring, entertained the child dwelling on the mountain as if with playthings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The planets along with their sub-planets, the sages and the mothers, and also the blazing hosts of attendants with faces of fire—
These and many other dreadful dwellers of the three heavens, together with the bands of mothers, surrounded Mahāsena and stood around him.
Seeing victory as doubtful, the lord of the gods, eager for victory, mounted the shoulder of Airāvata and set out together with the divinities; Indra, desiring to slay Mahāsena, proceeded with all haste.
That fierce and swift divine army, radiant with great splendor, adorned with varied banners and armor, bearing many kinds of mounts and bows, clad in the finest garments, graced with beauty and ornaments—
The prince went forward to meet Śakra as he came eager to slay him, roaring on the way; and Śakra, of mighty strength, advanced swiftly, cheering the divine army, intent on slaying the son of Pāvaka.
Honored by the thirty gods and likewise by the great seers, Vāsava drew near to the presence of Kārttikeya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the lord of the gods let out a lion's roar together with the gods; and Guha, hearing that sound, roared back like the ocean.
By that great sound, resembling the surging of the sea, the divine army was thrown into confusion and reeled this way and that, senseless.
Seeing the gods approach with intent to slay him, the son of Pāvaka, enraged, discharged from his mouth great blazing flames of fire; those flames burnt the divine armies as they writhed upon the ground.
They, with heads and bodies ablaze, with weapons and mounts on fire, fell suddenly and shone like a multitude of brilliant stars.
Burning, those gods abandoned the wielder of the thunderbolt and sought the shelter of the son of Pāvaka; then they attained peace.
Abandoned by the gods, Śakra then hurled his thunderbolt at Skanda; that bolt, once hurled, quickly struck Skanda's right side and pierced the side of that great soul, O great king.
From the thunderbolt's blow upon Skanda there arose another being—a young man clad in golden armor, bearing a lance, adorned with divine earrings; because he was born from the splitting by the thunderbolt, he became known as Viśākha.
Seeing this other being born, blazing like the fire of universal dissolution, Indra, out of fear, then went with joined palms to seek refuge with Skanda.
Skanda granted him safety together with his army, O noble one; then the thirty gods, filled with joy, sounded their musical instruments.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hear of the dreadful attendants of Skanda, wondrous to behold—the boy-beings that were born there from the thunderbolt's blow upon Skanda, who are terrible and carry off newborn children and those still in the womb.
Also from the thunderbolt's blow were born great-powerful maidens and boy-beings, and those boys acknowledged Viśākha in the role of father.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That blessed one, having become goat-faced in battle to protect them, was then surrounded by all the bands of maidens and his own boy-children.
And with the mothers looking on, and Bhadraśākha displaying his skill, people on earth thereafter called Skanda the father of the Kumāras.
People who desire sons and those who already have sons always worship Rudra, Agni, Umā, and mighty Svāhā in the various sacred places.
Now those maidens whom Agni the oblation-eater had generated as Tapas approached Skanda and spoke to him, saying, "What shall we do?"
The mothers said: Let us become the highest mothers of all the worlds and, by your grace, be worshipped as well. Grant us this boon that is dear to us.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: He of noble mind said, "So be it," and declared, "You shall be of various kinds—both inauspicious and auspicious, again and again."
Then the band of mothers, having resolved to adopt Skanda as their son, approached him—Kākī and Halimā, and Rudra and Bṛhalī, and Āryā and Palālā and Mitra: these seven are the mothers of children.
Of these mothers there is a child endowed with prowess, named Śiśu, exceedingly terrible, born by Skanda's grace—the red-eyed, fearsome son.
This group of eight heroes, born of Skanda's band of mothers, together with the goat-faced one, is proclaimed a group of nine.
Know that the sixth, the goat-shaped face, belongs to Skanda himself; the innermost of the six heads, O king, is always worshipped by the band of mothers.
The chief among his six heads is here designated as the one with which he created the divine lance—this is called Bhadraśākha.
Thus all this multiform event occurred on the fifth day of the bright fortnight; and that great and terrible battle took place on the sixth, O lord of men.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Skanda was seen seated, wearing a golden armor and garland, with a golden crest and crown, golden-eyed, and of great radiance—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Clad in red garments, with sharp fangs, enchanting to behold, endowed with all auspicious marks, and deeply beloved even by the three worlds.
Then Śrī, of lotus form and herself embodied, chose of her own accord that boon-giving, heroic youth with polished earrings.
Graced by Śrī and of wide renown, that foremost prince, as he sat, was seen by all beings like the moon on a full-moon night.
The great-souled brahmins honored that mighty one, and the great seers then spoke these words to Skanda there:
"O golden-hued one, blessings be upon you—be the benefactor of the worlds! By you, born within six nights, all the worlds have been brought under sway.
And safety has been granted to them again by you alone, O best of gods; therefore let you be Indra, the giver of safety to the three worlds."
Skanda said: What does Indra do for all the worlds here, O those rich in austerity? How does the lord of the gods always protect the hosts of divinities?
The sages said: Indra bestows strength, energy, offspring, and happiness upon all beings; when pleased, the lord of the gods grants all boons likewise.
He destroys the wicked and sustains the righteous; the slayer of Bala guides all beings in their duties.
When the sun is absent he becomes the sun, and so too the moon when the moon is absent; fire and wind, earth and water—all these arise through his agency.
This is what Indra must do, for in Indra resides vast power; and you too, O hero, are supreme in strength—therefore become Indra for us.
Śakra said: Become Indra, O mighty-armed one—the bringer of happiness to all of us. Be consecrated this very day; you have attained the fitting form, O noble one.
Skanda said: You yourself govern the three worlds without confusion, devoted to victory; I am your servant, O Śakra—I do not desire lordship over Indra's realm.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śakra said: Your strength is wondrous, O hero; slay the enemies of the gods. The worlds will disrespect me, astonished by your might.
Even though I remain in the position of Indra, I have been shown powerless and defeated, O hero; and the diligent ones will strive to create a split between the two of us.
And when you are estranged from me, O lord, the world will split in two; when the worlds are divided in two and our rift is assured, conflict between beings will ensue, O mighty one.
There in battle you will defeat me at will, dear friend; therefore let you be Indra this very day—do not deliberate.
Skanda said: You alone are king—blessings to you—of the three worlds and of me as well; what command of yours, O Śakra, shall I carry out? Tell it to me.
Śakra said: If this word is truly spoken by you with full conviction, or if you wish to carry out my command, O Skanda, then listen.
Be consecrated as commander-in-chief of the gods, O mighty one; I shall be Indra by your word, O mighty one.
Skanda said: For the destruction of the Dānavas, for the accomplishment of the gods' purposes, for the protection of cattle and brahmins—consecrate me as commander-in-chief.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Consecrated by Maghavat together with all the hosts of gods, he shone there exceedingly, honored by the great seers.
His golden parasol, as it was held aloft, shone like the self-luminous halo of a well-kindled fire.
And his divine golden garland, fashioned by Viśvakarman, was fastened upon him by the glorious slayer of Tripura himself.
Coming there together with the Goddess, O scorcher of foes, O tiger among men, the blessed lord whose banner bears a bull worshipped him with great delight.
The twice-born call him son of Rudra and of Agni; and he became son of Rudra thereafter. The semen released by Rudra became the White Mountain, and the seed of Agni was received on that white peak by the Kṛttikās.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing him honored by Rudra, all the celestials then called him son of Rudra—Guha, the best among the virtuous.
For Rudra, having entered into Agni, this child was born; born there, Skanda then became the son of Rudra.
Born of the energy of Rudra, of Agni, of Svāhā, and of the six women, Skanda—best of the gods—thereafter became known as son of Rudra.
The son of Pāvaka, wearing two red spotless garments, blazes with a luminous body, glorious, like the sun amid red clouds.
The rooster given to him by Agni, adorned as his banner standard and raised aloft on his chariot, shines red like the fire of dissolution.
Then his innate bodily armor entered him; it always manifests for that divine one when he fights.
Power, armor, strength, energy, beauty, truth, inviolability, devotion to the brahmins, freedom from delusion, protection of devotees—
The destruction of enemies and the protection of the worlds—all these were born together with Skanda, O lord of men.
Thus consecrated by all the hosts of gods and splendidly adorned, he shone forth, radiant and pleased, like the sight of the full moon.
With beloved sounds of sacred recitation, with the noise of divine instruments, with songs of the divine Gandharvas, and with all the hosts of Apsarases—
With these and many other varied joyful and satisfied adorned beings, the son of Pāvaka was consecrated then, as if at play with the gods.
The celestials beheld Mahāsena consecrated, like the sun here that dispels darkness and rises.
Then all the divine armies, by the thousands, approached him from every direction, saying, "You are our lord."
Meeting them, the blessed one, surrounded by all the hosts of beings, and himself honored and praised, soothed them as well.
And Śatakratu, having consecrated Skanda as commander-in-chief, then remembered that divine army of women who had been liberated by him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thinking, "This one is surely ordained as her lord by Brahmā himself," he brought the beautifully adorned Devasenā.
And he said to Skanda: "This maiden, O best of gods, was appointed as your wife by the Self-born one before you were born.
Therefore take properly, according to ritual, accompanied by sacred formulas, the right hand of this goddess whose radiance is like a lotus—take it with your hand."
Thus instructed, he took her hand duly according to rule; and Bṛhaspati recited the ritual formulas and performed the fire oblations.
Thus the wise know Devasenā as the chief queen of Skanda—she whom the brahmins call the Sixth, Lakṣmī, hope, the bestower of happiness, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Sadvṛtti, and Aparājitā.
When Devasenā obtained Skanda as her eternal lord, then the goddess Lakṣmī herself, embodied, took refuge in him.
Because Skanda was graced by Śrī on the fifth, that fifth day is remembered as Śrī-pañcamī; because he attained his purpose on the sixth, the sixth is a great sacred day.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When Mahāsena, graced by Śrī, had been made commander of the divine army, the six goddesses who were wives of the Seven Sages then came to his presence.
Abandoned by their sages, those virtuous women of great vows came swiftly and cried out to the lord, the commander of the divine host.
"We, O son, have been abandoned by our husbands, equal to the gods, cast out from our sacred abodes without cause and in anger, dear child.
Someone proclaimed that you were born of us — having heard this falsehood, our husbands deserted us. Therefore you ought to protect us.
Through your grace, O lord, heaven will be imperishable for us. We desire you as our son — having done this much, be free of debt to us."
Skanda said: "You are indeed my mothers, O blameless ones, and I am your son. Whatever you desire shall come to pass for you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When this was spoken, Skanda then asked Śakra: "What task remains?" Addressed by Skanda with "Speak!", Vāsava then replied.
"Abhijit, the younger sister of Rohiṇī, competing with her and desiring precedence, has gone to the forest to practise austerities.
In this matter I am bewildered — blessings upon you; the constellation has fallen from the sky. Reflect now upon this critical time together with Brahmā, O Skanda.
The age ordained by Brahmā then began with Dhaniṣṭhā; previously it had begun with Rohiṇī — thus the count of the constellations was reckoned.
When this was said by Śakra, the Kṛttikās went up to heaven; that constellation, shaped like a cart, shines forth — it has Fire as its deity.
And Vinatā spoke to Skanda: "You are my son who offers me funerary cakes. I always wish to dwell with you, O son."
Skanda said: "So be it — homage to you. Out of a mother's affection, command me. Worshipped by your daughter-in-law, O goddess, you shall dwell here always."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the entire assembly of mothers spoke this word to Skanda: "We are the mothers of all the worlds, praised by the wise. We wish to be mothers to you — worship us."
Skanda said: "You are indeed my mothers, and I am the son of you all. Tell me what should be done by me, and what is desired by you."
The mothers said: "Those who were formerly ordained as the mothers of this world — that position should be ours, and not theirs.
We should be the ones worshipped by the world, not they, O bull among gods. Our progeny were taken away by them for your sake — give those children back to us."
Skanda said: "The progeny that were given cannot be reclaimed by you. What other progeny shall I grant you — tell me what you desire in your hearts."
The mothers said: "We wish to feed upon the progeny of those other mothers — grant us this. Also those lords who have separated themselves from them along with you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Skanda said: "I grant you progeny — but what you have said is harsh. Protect the children well — blessings upon you! Those who are duly honoured will be well."
The mothers said: "We shall protect the children as you wish, blessings to you, O Skanda. We desire to dwell long together with you, O lord."
Skanda said: "For as long as children are young, up to the age of sixteen years, afflict the progeny of humans with your various forms.
And I shall bestow upon you my terrible and imperishable supreme self. Together with that, you shall dwell in happiness, honoured by all."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then from the body of Skanda there sprang forth a great-armed being radiant as gold, mighty in strength, to feed upon the progeny of mortals.
He fell then to the ground, senseless and tormented by hunger; authorized by Skanda, he became a terrible-formed planetary spirit. The best of twice-born call that spirit Skanda-apasmāra.
Vinatā of terrifying form is known as the Śakuni-graha; they call Pūtanā a rākṣasī — one should know her as the Pūtanā-graha.
Terrible with a dreadful form, a hideous night-roamer, a piśācī of frightful shape — she is called Śīta-pūtanā; of fearsome appearance, she steals the wombs of human women.
They call Aditi the Revatī; the planetary spirit belonging to her is Raivata. That great terrible graha also afflicts young infants.
Diti, who is the mother of the daityas — they call her Mukha-maṇḍikā, exceedingly delighted by the flesh of infants, impossible to overcome.
And those youths and maidens who are said to have arisen from Skanda — they too are eaters of the womb, O Kauravya, all of them very great planetary spirits.
The husbands of those very maidens are proclaimed as well; acting unrecognized, those doers of terrible deeds seize children.
She who is known by the wise as Surabhī, the mother of cows, O king — Śakuni mounts her and feeds upon infants upon the earth alongside her.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
She who is called Saramā, the divine mother of dogs, O lord of the people — she too perpetually takes the wombs of human women.
And she who is the mother of trees, dwelling in the karañja tree — men who desire sons therefore worship her in the karañja.
These eighteen others among the grahas, lovers of flesh and honey, remain for twice five nights continually in the lying-in chamber.
When Kadrū, assuming a subtle form, enters a pregnant woman, she feeds upon that womb within; and the woman then gives birth to a serpent.
The mother of the Gandharvas seizes the womb and departs; that human woman is then seen upon the earth with her womb dissolved.
She who is the mother of the Apsarasas sits within after seizing the womb; the wise then call that pregnancy a seated or dormant one.
The daughter of the red ocean is remembered as the nurse of Skanda; known as Lohitāyanī, she is worshipped in the kadamba tree.
As Rudra is among men, so is Āryā among women. Āryā, the mother of the Kumāra, is separately propitiated for the fulfilment of desires.
Thus have I described these great planetary spirits of children. Up to the age of sixteen years they are inauspicious; thereafter they become auspicious.
The assemblies of mothers that have been described, and also the grahas who are persons — all of these are to be known always by embodied beings as the Skanda-grahas.
For their pacification, one should perform bathing, fumigation, and anointing; offering of bali and gifts; and in particular the worship of Skanda.
When all of these are thus worshipped and saluted with proper veneration, O king of kings, they bestow auspiciousness, long life, and vigour upon men.
Now I shall declare, after bowing to Maheśvara, those planetary spirits that afflict men beyond the age of sixteen years.
A man who sees the gods, whether waking or lying down, quickly falls into madness — him they know as seized by the Deva-graha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A man who sees the ancestors while sitting or lying down quickly becomes mad — he is to be known as seized by the Pitṛ-graha.
One who scorns the Siddhas, and whom those angered Siddhas curse, quickly goes mad — he is to be known as seized by the Siddha-graha.
One who smells odours and tastes of various kinds not present to others and quickly goes mad — he is to be known as seized by the Rākṣasa-graha.
When the divine Gandharvas touch a man on earth and he quickly goes mad — that planetary seizure is indeed the Gāndharva-graha.
When Yakṣas enter a man at a turn of time and he quickly goes mad — he is to be known as seized by the Yakṣa-graha.
When Piśācas continually mount a man in some place and he quickly goes mad — they know that planetary seizure as the Paiśāca-graha.
When by one's own faults the mind of an embodied being is disturbed and bewildered, and he quickly becomes mad — his remedy is prescribed by the scriptures.
When from weakness of spirit, fear, or the sight of terrible things a man quickly becomes mad — for him strength of character is the remedy.
Some are desirous of sport, another desires to eat, another is filled with desire — thus this planetary seizure is of three kinds.
These grahas afflict men for up to seventy years; beyond that age, for embodied beings, fever acts like a planetary seizure.
The grahas always shun a man whose senses are not scattered, who is self-controlled, pure, ever-vigilant, who believes in the scriptures, and who has faith.
Thus this account of the grahas as they afflict humans has been set forth. The grahas do not touch those men who are devoted to the god Maheśvara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When Skanda had thus done this favour for the mothers, Svāhā then spoke to him: "You are my own begotten son."
"I desire a gift of joy from you, most difficult to obtain." Skanda then asked her: "What kind of joy do you wish?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Svāhā said: "I am the beloved daughter of Dakṣa, named Svāhā, O mighty-armed one. From childhood I have been perpetually enamoured of Hutāśana, the god of fire.
But Pāvaka does not truly know me, though I long for him, O son. I wish to dwell always with Agni, O son."
Skanda said: "Whatever oblation — whether for the gods or for the ancestors — the twice-born, preceded by mantras, offer into fire, O goddess, shall always be offered with the utterance of the word 'Svāhā' as they prepare it.
From this day forward, the virtuous who walk the right path shall make this offering. Thus shall Agni always dwell with you, O beautiful one."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus addressed, Svāhā was satisfied, honoured by Skanda. Joined with Pāvaka, her husband, she in turn worshipped Skanda.
Then Brahmā, the lord of creatures, spoke to Mahāsena: "Go to Mahādeva, your father, the destroyer of Tripura.
By Rudra entering into Agni and entering into Svāhā along with Umā, for the benefit of all the worlds you were born, O unconquered one.
And the semen shed by the great-souled Rudra in Umā's womb fell upon the mountain and from it arose the pair called Miñjikā-miñjika.
What arose fell into the red lake as the residue of the semen; another part fell in the rays of the sun, another fell upon the earth, another adhered to trees — thus it fell in five ways.
These hosts of various forms are to be known by the wise as your terrible attendants — these flesh-eaters who form your retinue.
Saying "so be it," Mahāsena, of immeasurable spirit, worshipped Maheśvara, his father, with a son's deep affection.
Those five hosts should be worshipped with arka flowers by those who desire wealth; and for the removal of disease, one should perform their worship.
The couple Miñjikā-miñjika, born of Rudra, should always be reverently saluted here by one who wishes well for children.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The women-spirits who eat human flesh, called by the name Vṛddhikā, born in trees — those goddesses should be saluted by those who desire offspring.
Thus these innumerable hosts of piśācas have been recounted. Now hear from me the origin of the bell together with the banner, O king.
Two bells of Airāvata, known as the Vaijayantyau, were brought by the wise Śakra and given by him personally to Guha.
Of those, one bell belongs to Viśākha and the other to Skanda. The banner is Kārttikeya's, and the red one belongs to Viśākha.
The playthings that were given to him at that time by the gods — with those very things the mighty god Mahāsena delights himself.
Surrounded by hosts of piśācas and likewise by hosts of gods, blazing and encircled by glory, he shone upon the golden mountain.
With that hero upon it, the mountain with its beautiful forests was resplendent — as Mandara with its lovely caverns shines with the radiant sun.
With groves of blossoming Santānaka trees, with forests of Karavīra, with groves of Pārijāta, with forests of Japā and Aśoka —
With groves of kadamba trees and divine herds of deer, and with divine flocks of birds, the White Mountain shone with beauty.
There all the hosts of gods and all the great sages gathered, along with the sounds of kettledrums like thunderclouds, roaring like a churned ocean.
There the divine gandharvas danced, and the apsaras likewise; a great clamor was heard from the joyful beings assembled there.
Thus the entire world together with Indra, gathered on the White Mountain, gazed in delight upon Skanda and never wearied of beholding him.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the blessed son of Fire had been consecrated as commander of the army, the glorious Hara, the lord, set out joyfully for Bhadravaṭa together with Pārvatī, riding a chariot radiant as the sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A thousand lions were yoked to that best of chariots; propelled by time, it rose shining into the sky.
Those lions, as if drinking in the sky and terrifying all moving and unmoving creatures, traveled through the heavens roaring, with their beautiful manes flowing.
Standing in that chariot with Umā, the Lord of Beasts blazed forth like the sun accompanied by lightning within a cloud that bears Indra's rainbow.
Before him went the blessed lord of wealth, he who is borne by men, riding the lovely Puṣpaka chariot with his guhyaka attendants.
Mounting Airāvata, Śakra too followed behind with the gods, accompanying the granter of boons who bears the bull-banner.
Adorned with garlands, accompanied by jambhakas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, the mighty yakṣa Amogha proceeded, taking his position on the right flank.
To his right went the gods, the Maruts who fight in varied ways, proceeding together with the Vasus and joined with the Rudras.
Yama too went, accompanied by Death, surrounded on all sides by hundreds of dreadful diseases, himself of terrible form and appearance.
And behind Yama traveled Rudra's trident named Vijaya — dreadful, triple-peaked, sharp, and well adorned.
Behind it, Varuṇa, the blessed lord of waters, who wields the terrible noose, moved slowly, surrounded by diverse aquatic creatures.
Behind the trident Vijaya also traveled Rudra's battleaxe, surrounded by the finest weapons — clubs, pestles, pikes, and others.
After the battleaxe followed, O king, the great-effulgent umbrella of Rudra, and after it the water-pot, surrounded by hosts of great sages.
To his right the staff gleamed as it proceeded, clothed in splendor, accompanied by the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases, worshipped by the gods as well.
Behind all of these Rudra traveled, standing in his spotless chariot, gladdening all the inhabitants of the three heavens with his radiance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sages and gods, gandharvas and serpents, rivers and streams and trees, and likewise throngs of apsaras —
— the nakṣatras and planets, and the children of the gods, and women of various forms — all followed in the wake of Rudra, and the lovely women of beautiful shape showered rains of flowers.
Parjanya too followed, having paid homage to the Bearer of the Bow; Soma held the white umbrella above his head; Wind and Fire took up the fly-whisks and stood in attendance.
And Śakra, O king, went behind him, clothed in splendor, together with all the royal sages, praising him who bears the bull-banner.
Gaurī, Vidyā, Gāndhārī, Keśinī, she called Mitra — all of them followed behind Pārvatī together with Sāvitrī.
There all the hosts of sciences, whatever have been composed by the learned, whose word even the gods headed by Indra obey at the forefront of battle —
— that rākṣasa planet, taking up a banner, went ahead; he who is ever busy in the cremation ground, indeed a friend of Rudra — the king of yakṣas named Piṅgala, the joy-giver of the world.
Together with all these, the god traveled there at his ease, some going before and some behind — for his course of movement is not fixed.
Mortals here worship Rudra the divine through righteous deeds, calling him Śiva, calling him Īśa, calling him Rudra, calling him the Bow-bearer; with devotion of all kinds they worship the Great Lord.
Thus the divine army's commander, surrounded by the divine hosts, the son of the Kṛttikās who is devoted to the Brahman, followed the Lord of the Gods.
Then the Great God spoke a weighty word to Mahāsena: 'Guard the seventh atmospheric stratum without ever growing weary.'
Skanda said: I will guard the seventh atmospheric stratum, O lord. If there is any other task for me, O god, speak it without delay.
Rudra said: In matters of duty, O son, you must always look to me; for through seeing me and through devotion to me you will attain the highest good.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, the Great Lord embraced him and dismissed him. When Skanda was dismissed, there arose suddenly a great portent, O great king, which instantly threw all the gods into confusion.
The sky blazed up together with the nakṣatras; the world was utterly confounded; the earth quaked and cried out; the universe became filled with darkness, O lord.
Seeing that terrible sight, Śaṃkara became agitated, and so did the greatly blessed Umā and the gods together with the sages.
While they were thrown into confusion, there appeared a vast and terrible army resembling mountains and storm-clouds, bearing weapons of every kind.
That dreadful, innumerable host, roaring with manifold cries, rushed in battle upon the gods and upon the blessed Śaṃkara.
By them were hurled into the ranks countless showers of arrows, and mountains, and śataghnis, and javelins, and iron bars, and clubs.
Struck by those dreadful great weapons raining down, the divine army in an instant fled and was seen to have turned its face away.
The army of the gods, tormented by the dānavas, appeared to have turned away — its warrior-elephants and horses slain, its great chariot-warriors with weapons cut down.
Slaughtered by the asuras, it fell like a forest of great trees mostly burnt by fire.
The celestials, their heads severed from their bodies, fell down; being slaughtered in that great battle, they found no protector.
Then the god Puraṃdara, seeing that powerful army routed and afflicted by the dānavas, encouraged it, speaking thus:
'Abandon fear — blessings upon you! Take up your weapons, O heroes; set your minds on valor; let no distress come upon you.
Conquer these utterly wicked, terrible-to-behold dānavas; attack these great asuras — blessings upon you — together with me!'
Having heard Śakra's words, the celestials were reassured; they fought back against the dānavas, taking Śakra as their refuge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all the thirty gods and the mighty Maruts advanced with great speed, as did the Sādhyas together with the Vasus.
The weapons discharged by them in their fury into the ranks in that battle, and the arrows too, drank the copious blood flowing from the bodies of the daityas.
Those sharp arrows, piercing through the bodies of the daityas, were then seen flying forth like serpents out of mountains.
Those bodies of the daityas, pierced through by the arrows, fell to the ground, O king, on every side like clouds that have been cut apart.
Then that army of dānavas, terrified by all the hosts of gods in battle with various arrows, was made to turn its face away.
Then a great shout arose from all the joyful gods with weapons upraised, and all the various musical instruments sounded together in great numbers.
Thus the battle between the gods and the dānavas was utterly terrible, with flesh and blood for its mire, each side locked with the other.
Danger for the celestial world appeared suddenly, for the dreadful dānavas were slaying the celestials in such fashion.
Then arose the blaring of instruments and the great sounds of kettledrums on the side of the dānava lords, and their dreadful lion-roars.
Then from the terrible daitya forces there leapt forth a mighty dānava named Mahiṣa, seizing a great mountain.
Seeing him surrounded like the sun by clouds, O king, with the mountain raised aloft, the celestials fled in terror.
Then Mahiṣa rushed upon the gods and hurled that mountain; struck by that terrible-formed falling mountain, O king, ten thousand of the divine army fell to the ground.
Then Mahiṣa, together with those dānavas, terrifying the gods, charged swiftly in battle like a lion upon small deer.
Seeing Mahiṣa bearing down, the celestials together with Indra fled in fear from the battle, their weapons and banners shattered.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then that enraged Mahiṣa rushed swiftly toward Rudra's chariot, and rushing up he seized the pole of Rudra's chariot.
When the enraged Mahiṣa had swiftly reached Rudra's chariot, both earth and sky resounded mightily, and the great sages fell into a swoon.
The great-bodied daityas, resembling rain-clouds, roared aloud; and among them there was certainty: 'Victory is ours!'
Even in such a situation the blessed one did not slay Mahiṣa in battle, but rather he called to mind Skanda as the death of that evil-souled one.
Mahiṣa too, having seized Rudra's dreadful chariot, roared repeatedly, terrifying the gods and delighting the daityas.
Then, as that terrible danger for the gods arrived, Mahāsena came blazing with fury like the sun.
Clad in crimson garments, adorned with crimson garlands, crimson-faced, long-armed, wearing golden armor — the lord.
Mounted on a chariot resembling the sun, radiant as gold — seeing him, that daitya army suddenly fled from the battle.
And mighty Mahāsena, O lord of kings, released that blazing śakti-spear that was the destroyer of Mahiṣa.
Released, that śakti struck Mahiṣa's great head; when his head was split, Mahiṣa fell, his life departed.
That śakti, hurled once and hurled again, having slain enemies by the thousands, returned to Skanda's hand and was seen by gods and dānavas alike.
The remaining hosts of terrible daityas, mostly struck down by the wise Mahāsena's arrows — frightened and terrified — were slain by Skanda's attendants, who are hard to withstand, and devoured in hundreds of groups.
Devouring the dānavas and drinking their blood, those attendants in an instant made everything free of dānavas, exceedingly joyful.
As the sun conquers darkness, as fire conquers trees, as a bird conquers clouds, so Skanda the glorious conquered his enemies by his own valor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Worshipped by the thirty gods, having paid reverence to the Great Lord, the son of the Kṛttikās shone beautifully like the sun with its rays spread wide.
When Skanda, his enemy destroyed, went forward toward the Great Lord, Puraṃdara embraced Mahāsena and then spoke:
'O Skanda, he who received boons from Brahmā — the Mahiṣa before whom the gods became as grass, the best among conquerors — that thorn in the side of the gods, O long-armed one, has been subdued by you.
A hundred dānavas equal to Mahiṣa, enemies of the gods by whom we were previously tormented, have been slain by you in battle.
And other dānavas have been devoured by your followers in hundreds of groups. You are unconquerable in battle by your enemies, like the lord, the husband of Umā.
This, O god, shall be proclaimed as your first deed of glory; your fame in the three worlds shall be imperishable; and the gods shall be under your sway, O son of the gods.'
Having said thus 'O Mahāsena,' Śacīpati turned back together with the gods, having been permitted by the blessed Three-eyed Lord.
Rudra departed to Bhadravaṭa, and the heavenly dwellers withdrew; and Rudra said to the gods: 'Behold Skanda even as you behold me.'
He, the son of Fire, slaying the hosts of Dānavas and being worshipped by the great sages, conquered the entire three worlds in a single day.
Whoever reads this birth-story of Skanda with concentrated mind shall gain prosperity in this world and attain to the same realm as Skanda.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the Brāhmaṇas sat in attendance and the great-souled Pāṇḍavas were present, Draupadī and Satyabhāmā entered together at that time; delighting in laughter and deeply pleased, they sat there comfortably.
O king of kings, having met after a long time, those two sweet-spoken ones told each other varied tales of the Kurus' sorrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Satyabhāmā, the beloved queen of Kṛṣṇa, daughter of Satrājit, the slender-waisted one, privately said this to Yājñasenī:
'By what conduct, Draupadī, do you attend upon the Pāṇḍavas — those heroes equal to guardians of the worlds, young men held in highest esteem? How are they submissive to you and do not grow angry with you, O auspicious one?'
'For the Pāṇḍavas are ever obedient to you, O lovely one, and they all look to your face — tell me the truth of this.'
'Is it through vows, austerities, bathing, mantras, or medicines, or through the power of knowledge, the potency of roots, recitation, fire-offerings, or herbal charms?'
'Tell me, O Pāñcālī, that glorious and blessed knowledge by which Kṛṣṇa might forever remain submissive to me.'
Having spoken thus, Satyabhāmā fell silent; then the illustrious, devoted Draupadī, greatly blessed, replied to her.
'O Satyā, you ask me about the conduct of wicked women — how could I praise a path that is wrongly trodden?'
'Such a question or doubt does not become you, for you are endowed with wisdom and are the beloved queen of Kṛṣṇa.'
'The very moment a husband learns that his wife relies on spells and roots, he would recoil from her as from a serpent that has entered the house.'
'Where is peace for an anxious man, and where is happiness for a restless one? A husband can never be made submissive to a woman through sorcery.'
'Those who wish to kill administer poison through claims of roots, and also send most terrible diseases dispatched by enemies.'
'Powders mixed into what a man consumes with his tongue or applies to his skin kill quickly, without doubt.'
'By women have men been made bloated with dropsy, leprous, prematurely grey, impotent, dull-witted, blind, and deaf.'
'Those wicked women, followers of sin, afflict their husbands — but a woman should never under any circumstances do what is displeasing to her husband.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'But hear from me the true conduct I practise toward the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, O glorious Satyabhāmā.'
'Laying aside pride, desire, and anger always, I attend upon the Pāṇḍavas together with their wives, ever striving carefully.'
'Restraining affectation, placing myself within myself, I serve without arrogance, guarding my husbands' hearts.'
'I am wary of harsh speech, improper posture, unseemly looks, sitting wrongly, walking improperly, and even dwelling on gestures.
'I serve the Pārthas who are like the sun and fire, moon-like in their grace, great warriors whose fierce energy blinds the eyes.
'No other man — god, human, or gandharva, though young and well adorned, wealthy or handsome — is regarded by me.
'When my husband has not eaten, not bathed, not rested — I do not lie down, do not eat; the same applies always to the servants too.
'When my husband arrives home from field, forest, or village, I rise to welcome him with a seat and water.
'I keep vessels scoured, food clean, serve meals on time, am self-restrained, guard the grain, and keep the dwelling well swept.
'I do not speak disrespectfully, do not associate with wicked women, am ever agreeable, and never idle.
'Laughing without occasion, standing repeatedly at the door, lingering at the rubbish-heap, and loitering in the garden-court — these I avoid.
'I avoid excessive laughter, excessive anger, and all occasions of wrath; I am ever devoted, O Satyā, to the service of my husbands; being without a husband is in no way dear to me under any circumstances.
'When a husband travels away on some family business, I become one who observes vows, stripped of flowers and cosmetics.
'Whatever my husband does not drink, whatever he does not chew, whatever he does not eat — all that I also abstain from.
'Conducting myself in accordance with instruction, restrained, O lovely-limbed one, adorned and ever diligent, I am devoted to my husband's pleasure and welfare.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'The household duties taught to me long ago by my mother-in-law — almsgiving, offerings to spirits, ancestral rites, ritual pot-cooking at the fortnightly festivals, proper honouring of those worthy of honour, and whatever else I have learned —
'All these I follow day and night without fatigue, ever resorting with my whole being to the rules of propriety and restraint.
'I wait upon my husbands — gentle, virtuous, of truthful character, upholders of truth and duty — as upon angry venomous serpents.
'Reliance on one's husband is the eternal duty of women as I understand it; he is the god, he is the refuge, there is no other — who would do what displeases him?
'I do not outshine my husbands, do not eat to excess, do not over-adorn myself, nor do I speak ill of my mother-in-law — always I keep myself restrained.
'Through attentiveness, O auspicious one, through always rising to serve, and through service to the elders, my husbands are made submissive to me.
'I always attend in person on noble Kuntī, mother of heroes, speaker of truth, serving her alone with bathing, clothing, and food.
'I never outshine her in garments, ornaments, or food, nor do I speak ill of that Pṛthā who is equal to the earth.
'Eight thousand Brāhmaṇas used to eat daily in the residence of Yudhiṣṭhira, from golden vessels, in the foremost place.
'Eighty-eight thousand householder graduates, each attended by thirty maidservants, were maintained by Yudhiṣṭhira.
'Ten thousand other ascetics of upward-flowing seed had their well-prepared food carried to them in golden vessels.
'All those Brāhmaṇas, speakers of the Veda, I used to honour fittingly with drinks, clothing, and food, along with their land-grants.
'A hundred thousand maidservants of the great-souled son of Kuntī wore conch-shell bangles and armlets, gold neck-pieces, and were finely adorned.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'They wore garlands and ornaments of great value, were of golden complexion, anointed with sandal-paste, bearing gems and gold, skilled in dance and song.
'I knew the name, form, food, and clothing of all of them, and every task of theirs done or undone.
'A hundred thousand maidservants of the wise son of Kuntī, vessels in hand, fed guests day and night.
'A hundred thousand horses and a hundred thousand elephants formed the retinue of Yudhiṣṭhira, dweller of Indraprastha.
'Such was the household of the king who protected the earth; their number and arrangement I both directed and kept account of.
'Of all the inner chambers and of all the servants, down to the cowherds and shepherds, I knew everything done and undone.
'All the income and expenditure, all the revenue of the king — I alone knew it, O auspicious one, of the illustrious Pāṇḍavas.
'Having entrusted the entire household to me, those bulls among Bhāratas, all devoted to their duties, strove on, O fair-faced one.
'That burden, incumbent and unassailable by the wicked, I carry diligently day and night, abandoning all ease.
'The treasury of my righteous husbands, unassailable like Varuṇa's domain, full of riches like the ocean — I alone knew it.
'In serving the Kauravas, companions in hunger and thirst alike, in daylight and in dark, night and day are equal to me.
'I am the first to wake and the last to retire — this is always my practice, O Satyā; this is my winning of my husbands.
'This great winning of husbands I know how to accomplish — the conduct of wicked women I neither follow nor desire.
Having heard what Kṛṣṇā had spoken, filled with righteousness, Satyā then, honouring the righteous Pāñcālī, spoke thus:
'I am confounded, O Pāñcālī, O Yājñasenī — forgive me; for it is the habit of friends to speak with jesting freedom.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Draupadī said: 'Yet I shall tell you this path free of fault for winning your husband's heart — abiding upon it rightly, dear friend, you shall draw your husband away from other women.'
'There is no deity like a husband, O Satyā, in all the worlds among all the gods — from his favour all desires are gained, and when angered he can destroy.'
'Therefore children, varied enjoyments, wonderful beds and seats, garments, garlands, and fragrances, the world of heaven, and fame — all depend on him.
'Happiness is never obtained through pleasure alone in this world; a virtuous woman obtains joys through suffering — therefore worship Kṛṣṇa with wholehearted friendship, with love always, and with service in return.'
'With fine foods and choice garlands, with gracious attentions and various perfumes — once he knows "she loves me," he will embrace you alone with his whole being.'
'On hearing your husband's voice at the door, rise and stand in the middle of the house; having seen him enter, honour him quickly with a seat and water for his feet.'
'Even when a maidservant has been sent, rise and do everything yourself — let Kṛṣṇa know your disposition, O Satyā: "She serves me with her whole being."'
'What your husband says in your presence — even if not secret — must be guarded; should some rival wife report it back to Vāsudeva, that would cause estrangement.'
'Those who are dear, devoted, and beneficial to your husband, feed them by various means; from his enemies, partisans against him, and those harmful to him, separate yourself always, by stratagems and outright rejection.'
'Abandoning pride and heedlessness in the company of men, restrain your feelings, embracing silence; even the young princes Pradyumna and Sāmba must never be waited on by you in a secluded place.'
'Let your friendships be with women of noble birth, sinless, and virtuous; the violent, the drunkards, the gluttons, thieves, the wicked, and the fickle are to be avoided.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'This is glorious and conducive to blessed knowledge, celestial and destructive of enemies — adorned with choice garlands and ornaments, fragrant with holy perfumes, worship your husband.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having sat together in pleasant conversation with Mārkaṇḍeya and other sages and with the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, Janārdana —
— then Madhusūdana, having taken proper leave of them, wishing to mount his chariot, Keśava summoned Satyā.
Satyabhāmā then embraced the daughter of Drupada and spoke heartfelt words composed with sincere feeling:
'O Kṛṣṇā, let there be no longing in you, no anguish, no sleeplessness — you shall regain the earth won by husbands who are equal to the gods.'
'For women endowed with such virtue, bearing such auspicious marks, do not suffer long as you do now, O dark-eyed one.'
This earth, cleared of its thorns, shall surely be enjoyed by you together with your husbands — so have I heard it said, free of all doubt.
O daughter of Drupada, having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and avenged all enmities, you shall see the earth established in Yudhiṣṭhira's sovereignty.
Those Kuru women who, blinded by pride, mocked you as you went into exile — you shall soon see them stripped of all their schemes and purposes.
Know, O Kṛṣṇā, that all those who have done you wrong in your affliction are already on their way to the abode of Yama.
Your sons — Prativindhya, Sutasoma, and the mighty Vibhu, Śrutakarmā the son of Arjuna, Śatānīka the son of Nakula, and Śrutasena born of Sahadeva — all your children thrive.
All your heroic sons are well and trained in arms; like Abhimanyu, they are joyful and deeply content in Dvāravatī.
Subhadrā stands by them with complete devotion, just as you would; she cherishes them with wholehearted affection, her mind undivided, free of anxiety toward them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Pradyumna's mother also serves them with entire devotion, and Keśava himself distinguishes them with the favor of Bhānu and others of his kin.
My father-in-law constantly attends to their food and clothing; Rāma and all the Andhaka-Vṛṣṇi heroes honor them, and their affection for the boys equals that shown to Pradyumna himself, O fair one.
Having thus spoken these and other pleasing, heartfelt words that gladdened the mind, he turned his thoughts toward departing and toward his chariot, the chariot of Vāsudeva.
Kṛṣṇa's queen Satyabhāmā, that spirited woman, made a reverential circumambulation of Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) and then mounted the chariot of Śauri (Kṛṣṇa).
Then the best of the Yadus, scorcher of foes, smiled gently, consoled Draupadī once more, turned his swift horses around, and departed.
Janamejaya said: While those foremost of men lived in the forest, their bodies worn by cold, heat, wind, and sun, having reached that lake and that sacred woodland — what did the Pārthas do thereafter?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having reached that lake, the sons of Pāṇḍu took leave of their attendants, made arrangements for them, and then roamed through the lovely forests, mountains, and river regions.
As those great warriors dwelt in the forest, ancient sages who were versed in the Vedas and rich in austerities came to them; and those foremost of men honored those sages duly.
Then, on a certain occasion, a Brahmin skilled in narration came to the Kauravas (Pāṇḍavas) on earth; having met with them by chance, he went on and visited the king Vaicitravīrya (Dhṛtarāṣṭra).
Having been seated and duly honored, urged on by the aged king, that best of Kurus, he told the tale of those born of Dharma, the Wind, Indra, and the twin Aśvins.
He described them as thin, their limbs wasted by wind and sun, plunged into the jaws of severe suffering, and Kṛṣṇā too — she who has heroes as her lords yet looked helpless as one without a protector — beset by every manner of affliction.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, hearing that account, King Vaicitravīrya (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) was consumed with compassion; having heard that the sons and grandsons of kings were in the forest, plunged into a river of sorrow,
his inner soul struck down by wretchedness, overwhelmed by sighs and tears, he somehow regained composure and, reflecting that all of this had sprung from himself, he spoke these words about the Pārthas.
How is it that Dharmarāja, the truthful, the pure, the noble-natured, the eldest of my sons, he who has no enemy born against him — he who once slept on a palace couch — now lies on the bare ground?
He who was ever woken by throngs of Māgadha bards with constant hymns of praise, who is himself like Indra — now he is woken in the last watch of the night surely by flocks of birds, lying on the bare earth.
How does Vṛkodara, his limbs wasted by wind and sun, his body flooded with suppressed rage, he whose limbs deserve no such hardship, lie on the surface of the earth before the eyes of Kṛṣṇā?
And Arjuna — so tender, so high-minded — remaining under the authority of the king, Dharma's son, with all his limbs as if trembling with indignation, surely does not sleep through the night-watches from sheer impatience.
Seeing the twins and Kṛṣṇā, Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīma all deprived of happiness, he heaves deep sighs like a fierce-glowing serpent and surely does not sleep through the night-watches from impatience.
Likewise the twins, though worthy of every comfort, are unhappy; like immortals in heaven they are handsome and radiant, yet surely they lie awake, unable to find peace, restrained only by righteousness and truth.
Equal in strength even to the wind, and Bhīma the son of the Wind is mightier still; bound by the cord of righteousness, fierce in his blazing energy, he surely endures his wrath only with deep sighs.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He, tossing upon the ground, craving to slay my sons, restrained only by truth and righteousness, awaits the appointed time — he who surpasses all others in battle.
The harsh words that Duḥśāsana spoke when Ajātaśatru was conquered by deceit — those words have entered Vṛkodara's body and burn in his vital parts like a fire fed by fuel.
Dharma's son will not contemplate a sinful act, and Dhanaṃjaya follows his lead; but through the forest sojourn, Bhīma's wrath grows ever greater, like a fire fed by the wind.
That hero, torn apart by that wrath, presses one palm against the other and exhales fierce, scorching breath — as if burning these sons and grandsons of mine with it.
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva and Vṛkodara — both furious, both equal to the Ender at the time of final dissolution — showering arrows bright as thunderbolts, would leave no remnant of the enemy's army in battle.
Duryodhana, Śakuni, the charioteer's son, and the dull-witted Duḥśāsana — they see only the honey but not the precipice; they see neither Vṛkodara nor Dhanaṃjaya for what they are.
A man who performs an action, whether good or evil, waits as the doer for its fruit; he is joined to that fruit helplessly — how then can a man find escape from it?
Even in a well-tilled field with seed well-sown, even when the rain-god showers in the proper season — could there be no fruit? How then could success fail to follow? Save by the decree of fate alone — so I reflect.
The evil done by my sinful dice, by the righteous Pāṇḍava (Yudhiṣṭhira acting under compulsion), and by me in following the lead of my wicked son — such is the manner in which this time of destruction has come upon the Kurus.
Surely the wind blows even uninvited; surely a pregnant woman will bring forth her child; surely night perishes at the onset of day, and likewise day perishes at the onset of night — all is certain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Why then should some act while others do not? Why should men not give away wealth? Why should adversity come even after the right moment for success has been reached? How could such a thing be — and from where does it arise?
How should something not crack, not leak, not spill? — thus it must be guarded; left unguarded it would shatter into a hundred pieces. Surely what has been done does not perish from the world.
For Dhanaṃjaya has gone even from the forest to the world of Śakra — behold his valor! He has mastered the fourfold divine weapons and returned to this world once more.
For what mortal man, having gone bodily to heaven, would wish to return — save one who, looking upon the many Kurus struck down by time and hastening to their doom, cannot stay away?
And Arjuna the ambidextrous archer, and that bow the Gāṇḍīva which is the essence of the world, and his divine weapons — who could withstand the combined blazing energy of those three?
Hearing those words of the king, Duryodhana and Śakuni (Saubala) went to a private place and informed Karṇa of everything; and he too became displeased — that one of small understanding.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Karṇa, along with Śakuni (Saubala), spoke these words at the right moment to Duryodhana.
O Bhārata, having banished the heroic Pāṇḍavas by your own valor, enjoy this earth alone, as the slayer of Śambara (Indra) enjoys heaven.
The kings of the East, the South, the West, and the North — all have been made tribute-payers to you, O lord of men.
That Lakṣmī which once shone resplendently and cleaved to the Pāṇḍavas — that very Lakṣmī has now been won by you, O king, along with your brothers.
That blazing Śrī which we witnessed residing in Yudhiṣṭhira at Indraprastha — O king, we who were lately wasted by grief now see her here with us.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That very Śrī has been wrested by you, O mighty-armed one, from King Yudhiṣṭhira by the power of your intellect, and she is seen shining brilliantly here.
Likewise, O lord of kings, slayer of enemy heroes, all the kings are established under your command, saying, 'What are your orders?'
Today, O king, the entire earth is yours — she who is ocean-girt, adorned with mountains and forests, the divine one filled with villages, cities, and mines, replete with every kind of woodland tract and beautified with port towns.
Worshipped by Brahmins, O king, and honored by kings, through your own prowess you blaze among the gods in heaven like the sun with his rays.
As Yama is surrounded by the Rudras, and Vāsava by the Maruts, so you, O king, surrounded by the Kurus, shine like the lord of the constellations (the moon).
Those who never respected your commands, who were never afraid of you — we see those very ones now: the Pāṇḍavas, stripped of prosperity, dwelling in the forest.
For it is heard, O great king, that the Pāṇḍavas are dwelling near the lake in the Dvaitavana forest, together with Brahmins and forest-dwellers.
Therefore go, O great king, endowed with supreme prosperity, scorching the sons of Pāṇḍu with your splendor as the sun with his rays.
Established in your kingdom, yourself clothed in glory, look upon the sons of Pāṇḍu who have been cast out of the kingdom, stripped of prosperity, in want — while you have attained every wealth, O king.
Let the Pāṇḍavas behold you, O one endowed with great lineage, established in great station — even as they beheld Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, in his glory.
That prosperity which friends and foes alike behold blazing in a man — that, O lord of the people, becomes a true and effective prosperity.
He who, standing in ease, looks down upon enemies in misfortune — as one standing on a mountain looks down upon those on the earth — what pleasure is greater than that?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Not through the gain of sons, nor wealth, nor even a kingdom does a man find the delight, O tiger among kings, that he finds from seeing the downfall of his enemies.
And what joy would there not be for one who, his own aims accomplished, sees Dhanaṃjaya in the hermitage clad in bark and deerskin?
Your richly-dressed wives should look upon the unhappy Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) in her bark and deerskin garments; and she, bereft of wealth, should feel disgust anew and condemn both herself and her very life.
For that wretchedness which befits her is not what she felt in the midst of the assembly-hall — it is what she will feel upon seeing your richly adorned wives.
Having thus spoken to the king, Karṇa and Śakuni both fell silent, O Janamejaya, when their speech was done.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of Karṇa, King Duryodhana was at first gladdened, but then, despondent again, spoke these words.
What you say, Karṇa, is all that lies in my heart as well; but I shall not obtain permission to go where the Pāṇḍavas are.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the earth, laments those heroes and even now considers the Pāṇḍavas superior — grown greater through the discipline of austerity.
And if the king were to discover our intention — even thinking of the future — he would not grant permission.
For there is no other purpose in Dvaitavana than to taunt and torment those forest-dwelling enemies of mine.
For you know how Kṣattā (Vidura) spoke at the time of the dice-game, and what he said then to me, to you, and to Śakuni (Saubala).
Reflecting on those former words and on all the lamentation since, I cannot determine whether to go or not to go.
Yet my own joy would be immense if I could see Bhīma and Phalguna (Arjuna) afflicted in the forest, together with Kṛṣṇā.
Even if I were to gain the whole earth, I would not obtain such delight as I would from seeing the sons of Pāṇḍu in their garments of bark and deerskin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And what could be greater than that, O Karṇa, than that I should see Draupadī, the daughter of Drupada, clad in ochre robes in the forest?
If Dharmarāja and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava were to see me invested with supreme prosperity — my life would be worth living.
Yet I see no means by which we might go to that forest in such a way that the lord of the earth would give his leave as I departed.
Together with Śakuni (Saubala) and likewise with Duḥśāsana, find a clever means by which we may go to that forest.
And I myself, having resolved the matter — whether to go or not — shall go to the king's presence tomorrow morning.
When I am seated there together with Bhīṣma, that best of Kurus, whatever means you see to be fit — that you should declare, along with Saubala.
Having heard of Bhīṣma's and the king's intention to depart, I shall appease my grandfather and make my resolve.
Saying "so be it," they all went to their respective quarters. Then, when the night had passed, Karṇa approached the king.
Then Karṇa, laughing, said this to Duryodhana: "A means has been found — hear it, O lord of men."
"All the cattle-stations in the Dvaita forest await you, O lord of men. Under the pretext of a cattle-inspection tour, we shall go there — of this there is no doubt."
"For it is always customary to go on a cattle-inspection tour, O lord of men. Thus your father, O king, should rightly grant you permission."
While those two were thus discussing the resolution to go on the cattle-inspection tour, Śakuni, the king of Gāndhāra, replied, smiling as it were.
"This means of going there without impediment has been seen by me. The king will grant us permission and will indeed urge us on."
"All the cattle-stations in the Dvaita forest await you, O lord of men. Under the pretext of a cattle-inspection tour, we shall go there — of this there is no doubt."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, all of them laughing, they slapped each other's palms. Having resolved on that very plan, they went to see the foremost of the Kurus.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then they all came before Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Janamejaya. Having inquired of the king's well-being and having been inquired of by the king, O Bhārata.
Then a cowherd named Samanga, who had previously been appointed by them and whose cattle were nearby, reported to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Thereupon Rādheya and Śakuni, O lord of men, addressed Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the foremost of kings, the lord of men.
"In the pleasant regions, the cattle-stations are there now, O Kaurava. The time has come for the annual cattle-census, and also for branding the calves."
"And hunting is customary at this time, O king. You should give permission for your son Duryodhana to go."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "Hunting is fine, my dear, and so is the inspection of the cattle. But one should not go trusting the cowherds — that I remember."
"Those tigers among men are nearby there — so we have heard. Therefore I myself do not approve of your going there."
"For they have been defeated by deceit and made to suffer in the great forest, O Rādheya, yet they are devoted to austerity and are capable great warriors."
"Dharmarāja might not grow angry, but Bhīmasena is wrathful. The daughter of Yajñasena is pure blazing energy alone."
"And you too might give offense, filled as you are with pride and delusion. Then they, endowed with the power of austerity, would utterly burn you."
"Or else those heroes, armed and overwhelmed by wrath, banded together with swords drawn, would burn you with the brilliance of their weapons."
"Or if you were to attack them on account of your superior numbers, that would be supremely ignoble — and moreover I deem it impossible."
"For the mighty-armed Dhanañjaya dwelt in Indra's realm, acquired divine weapons, and then returned to the forest."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The entire earth was once conquered by Bībhatsu even before he had obtained his weapons — how much more will that great warrior now, armed with his weapons, not slay you?"
"Or if, having heard my words, you go there prepared and on guard, the anxiety of dwelling there and the troubles arising from overconfidence will certainly occur."
"Or if some soldiers were to do harm to Yudhiṣṭhira, that act done without proper judgment would bring a fault upon you."
"Therefore let trusted men go for the cattle-census. I do not approve of your going there yourself, O Bhārata."
Śakuni said: "The eldest Pāṇḍava knows dharma, and he pledged in the assembly that twelve years would be spent in exile, O Bhārata."
"And all those Pāṇḍavas are followers of dharma. Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, will not be angry with us."
"Our desire to go hunting has grown greatly, and we wish to conduct the cattle-census — not to see the Pāṇḍavas."
"No ignoble conduct will take place there. We shall not go to the place where they are encamped."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Śakuni, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, gave permission to Duryodhana along with his ministers — though not willingly.
Having received permission, the prince of Gāndhāra, together with Karṇa, set out — that foremost of the Bhāratas — surrounded by a great force.
Accompanied likewise by Duḥśāsana and by the gambler Subala's son, surrounded by other brothers as well, and by women in their thousands.
To see that mighty-armed one set out for the Dvaita lake and forest, all the townspeople followed him along with their wives.
Eight thousand chariots, thirty thousand elephants, foot soldiers by the many thousands, and nine thousand horses.
Wagons, market-traders, courtesans, merchants, bards, and hunters by the hundreds and thousands.
At the king's departure there arose a very great noise, like that of a mighty wind stirred up during the rainy season, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
King Duryodhana encamped at the distance of a gavyuta, and then, having set out with all his vehicles, proceeded to the Dvaita lake.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Duryodhana, dwelling here and there in the forest, went to the cattle-stations and established his camp there around them.
In a pleasant, well-known region, with water and trees, endowed with all good qualities, the men set up their encampment.
Likewise in proximity to it, many separate quarters were arranged — for Karṇa and for Śakuni, and for all the brothers as well.
He saw the cattle there by the hundreds and thousands, and the king noted all of them by their marks and brands.
He branded the calves as well, and noted those cows that had newly calved, and also the young calves and the cows he counted.
Having completed the census and noted the three-year-old cattle, surrounded by the cowherds, the joyful son of the Kuru dynasty sported about.
And all those townspeople and thousands of soldiers played at their pleasure in that forest, like the immortals.
Then cowherds who were skilled singers, expert in dance and music, attended on the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as did well-adorned young women.
That king, surrounded by groups of women, joyful, gave them wealth as was fitting, and various foods and drinks.
Then all of them together hunted on all sides — hyenas, buffaloes, deer, gayal-cattle, bears, and boars.
He pierced them with arrows, bound elephants in the great forest, and had deer captured in the pleasant regions.
Enjoying dairy products and pleasures, O Bhārata, and gazing upon the wonderfully lovely flowering forests.
Frequented by intoxicated bees and resonant with peacock cries, he proceeded in due order to the sacred Dvaita lake, endowed with supreme prosperity, like the thunderbolt-bearing Mahendra.
And it so happened that on that very day, O lord of men, Dharmaputra Yudhiṣṭhira, the king, the foremost of the Kurus, performed a royal-sage sacrifice according to divine rites, with forest products in the immediate manner.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That wise Kaurava, lord of men, having established his camp around that lake, was accompanied by Draupadī, his wife devoted to dharma.
Then Duryodhana, together with his brothers, commanded his servants: "Let the pleasure-pavilions be quickly prepared," O Bhārata.
Those obedient attendants, saying "so be it" to that Kaurava, wishing to set up the pleasure spots, went to the Dvaita lake.
As the advance guard of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son reached the Dvaita lake and sought to enter through the forest gate, the Gandharvas blocked their way.
For the king of the Gandharvas had come there earlier, O lord of men, O king, arriving from Kubera's abode, surrounded by his troops.
With troops of apsaras and the sons of the thirty gods, that pleasure-loving one had come for sport, and by him was that lake occupied.
Seeing it occupied by him, those royal attendants then went back, O king, to where King Duryodhana was.
But having heard their report, the Kaurava sent soldiers mad for battle, saying: "Drive them away!"
Hearing that command of the king, the leaders of his army went to the Dvaita lake and said this to the Gandharvas.
"A king named Duryodhana, the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, is coming here to sport. For that reason, move away."
Thus addressed, the Gandharvas, laughing, O lord of men, replied to those men with these very harsh words.
"Your king Suyodhana of dull intellect does not think clearly — he who gives us orders in this way as if we were his subjects, we who dwell in heaven."
"And you yourselves are dull-witted and wish to die — of this there is no doubt — you who speak to us thus at his command, you senseless ones."
"All of you go quickly to where that Kaurava king is, and that enemy — go right now to the encampment of Dharmarāja."
Thus addressed by the Gandharvas, the leaders of the king's army ran back to where the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the king, was.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all of them together came to Duryodhana and reported, O great king, what had been said to the Kaurava.
With his army blocked by the Gandharvas, the glorious son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, filled with indignation, addressed his troops, O Bhārata.
"Chastise these lawless ones who do what displeases me — even if Śatakratu himself were at play here with all the gods."
Hearing Duryodhana's words, the mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all of them, armed themselves, and the warriors by the thousands as well.
Then, overwhelming the Gandharvas, they forcibly entered that forest, filling the ten directions with a great lion's roar.
Then the Kuru soldiers were blocked by other Gandharvas. Being blocked by the Gandharvas, O lord of the earth, yet disregarding those Gandharvas, they entered that great forest.
When the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their king would not desist even by words, then all those sky-dwellers reported to Citrasena.
The lord of the Gandharvas, Citrasena, exceedingly wrathful, spoke to all of them regarding those Kauravas: "Chastise those ignoble ones!"
Authorized by Citrasena, O Bhārata, all the Gandharvas, weapons raised, charged at the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Seeing those Gandharvas swooping swiftly with weapons raised, all of them fled from the battle before the very eyes of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son.
Seeing all those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fleeing with their backs turned, the hero Vaikartana alone did not turn his back there.
But beholding the great army of the Gandharvas rushing forward, Rādheya checked them with a great shower of arrows.
With razor-headed shafts, keen arrows, broad-headed arrows, calf-tooth arrows, and iron-shafted ones, the son of a charioteer struck down the Gandharvas by the hundreds, owing to his swiftness.
That great chariot-warrior, striking down the heads of the Gandharvas, in a single moment shattered the entire army of Citrasena.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yet those Gandharvas, though being slaughtered by the wise son of a charioteer, came on again in hundreds and thousands.
In an instant the earth seemed transformed into Gandharva-land, covered by the troops of Citrasena rushing forward with tremendous speed.
Then King Duryodhana, Śakuni the son of Subala, Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, and the other sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra struck down that enemy force with their chariots thundering like Garuḍa.
They fought again, placing Karṇa at the fore, and with a great roar of chariots and the swift movement of horses, seeking to protect the son of Vikartana, they checked the Gandharvas.
Then all the Gandharvas clashed together with the Kauravas, and a tremendous, hair-raising battle commenced.
Then the Gandharvas, tormented by arrows, began to give way, and the Kauravas shouted aloud seeing the Gandharvas pressed hard.
Seeing his Gandharvas thrown into panic, Citrasena, exceedingly wrathful, leapt from his seat in fury, intent on their destruction.
Then Citrasena, a master of wondrous stratagems, deployed his weapon of illusion and fought; by his magical power the Kauravas were bewildered.
For at that time, O Bhārata, each single warrior of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's army found himself surrounded by ten Gandharvas fighting against him.
Crushed by that great force, they fled in fear from the battlefield to where King Yudhiṣṭhira stood.
While the armies of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra broke and fled on all sides, O king, Karṇa the son of Vikartana stood firm as an immovable mountain.
Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala continued to fight the Gandharvas in battle, though grievously wounded.
Then all the Gandharvas in hundreds and thousands, united in their desire to kill him, rushed upon Karṇa in battle.
Those mighty warriors, seeking to slay the charioteer's son, surrounded him on all sides with swords, broad-bladed spears, lances, and maces.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some severed his yoke, others struck down his banner; some cut his shaft, some felled his horses, and others brought down his charioteer.
Others shattered his parasol, his chariot-casing, and the curved railing, and those many thousands of Gandharvas smashed his chariot to pieces.
