Jayadratha said: "Enough of a morning meal — all due honor has been rendered to me; come, mount my chariot, and enjoy happiness alone."
"The Pārthas have lost their glory, fallen from their kingdom, pitiable, broken in spirit, dwelling in the forest — you ought not to bind yourself to them."
"Wise women do not attach themselves to a husband bereft of fortune; one should attach oneself to a husband who is active and prospering — one should not dwell where prosperity has dried up."
"Deprived of fortune and of their kingdom, destroyed for years without end — enough of this trouble of devotion to the sons of Pāṇḍu."
"Become my wife, O fair-hipped one; abandon these men and enjoy happiness. Come with me and obtain all the lands of the Sindhu and the Sauvīras."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the king of Sindhu with words that made the heart tremble, Kṛṣṇā moved away from that spot with furrowed brows.
Scorning his words and rebuking him, the slender-waisted Kṛṣṇā said to the king of Sindhu, "Do not do this — be ashamed!"
She, the blameless one, longing for the arrival of her husbands, tried to dissuade him further by joining her words of rebuke with words of persuasion.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: With a lovely face flushed with anger and passion, with eyes reddened and brows knit high and low, turning her face fully toward the lord of the Sauvīra realm, the daughter of Drupada then spoke again.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Reviling those illustrious great warriors, sharp as venom, equal to Mahendra, devoted to their own duties, who stand firm even among hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas — how, O fool, are you not ashamed?"
"Dogs speak so even of praiseworthy men — whether a forest-dweller, a householder, or an ascetic fully accomplished in learning. They bark without praising anything good, O king of the Sauvīras."
"I think there is no one among such an assembly of kṣatriyas who could today seize your falling hand as you tumble toward the mouth of hell and pull you back."
"You, who aspire to conquer Dharmarāja, are like one who tries to drive away with a stick a maddened elephant, mountain-like, roaming the Himālayan slopes from its herd."
"You pluck the eyelashes from the mouth of a mighty sleeping lion — and then you flee on foot. When you see Bhīmasena in his wrath, what will become of you?"
"You strike with your toe-tip a terrible, fully-grown, mighty lion born in mountain caves while it sleeps — you who would dare to approach the fierce and enraged Jiṣṇu."
"You recklessly tread upon the tails of two sharp-fanged, dark cobras with keen venom — you who would fight with the two younger-born among the Pāṇḍavas, those best of men."
"Just as the bamboo, the plantain, and the reed bear fruit only for their own destruction and not for their flourishing, so you will seize me who am protected by them — and it will bring about your end, like the womb of a she-crab."
Jayadratha said: "I know it, Kṛṣṇā, I know well what manner of men are these sons of the god-king. Yet we cannot be frightened today by you with this boasting and threatening."
"We, O Kṛṣṇā, are all born in seventeen illustrious clans. We consider the sons of Pāṇḍu, O Draupadī, inferior to us in six virtues and more."
"So quickly mount an elephant or a chariot — we cannot be stopped by words alone. Or beg piteously and seek once more the grace of the king of the Sauvīras."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Draupadī said: "Though mighty, shall I appear weak here? Shall I, who am known for my valor, beg piteously of the king of the Sauvīras? Am I so regarded by the king of the Sauvīras?"
"She in whose steps Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna — allies seated together on one chariot — would follow: even Indra could not carry her away; how then any mere mortal, let alone this wretch?"
"When Kirīṭī, the slayer of enemy heroes, standing in his chariot and crushing the hearts of foes, enters your army to find me — like fire burning through dry grass in summer heat —"
"— all the Vṛṣṇi heroes who follow Janārdana, the great bowmen and the Kekaya warriors too — all these princes of mine would joyfully follow his track."
"The terrible arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow, loosed from the bowstring with the roar of thunder, of exceeding swiftness, strike Dhanañjaya's hand and roar with a sound most dreadful."
"The mighty torrents of arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, swift as swarms of locusts — when the Gāṇḍīva-bearer, blowing his conch and sounding his palm-guard, repeatedly pours those arrows upon your chest, what then will become of your spirit?"
"Seeing Bhīma rushing at you with mace in hand, the two sons of Mādrī flying at you from all directions, spewing the venom of their indignant rage — you will suffer long torment, O wretch."
"And just as I would never transgress in any way my most worthy husbands — not even in my mind — by that truth I shall today see you subdued and dragged away by the Pārthas."
"I shall not flee in confusion though dragged away by you, O cruel one. For I have come together with the foremost heroes of the Kuru line and have returned to the Kāmyaka forest."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The wide-eyed one glanced at them as they reached out to seize her, rebuking them; frightened, she cried out "Touch me not! Touch me not!" and called loudly to Dhaumya, the family priest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Jayadratha seized her by the hem of her upper garment; she wrenched herself away — and that sinful one, his body jerked by her, fell like a tree with its roots cut through.
Yet seized with great force, the royal daughter Kṛṣṇā heaved repeated sighs; dragged along, she was made to mount the chariot — though not before she bowed at the feet of Dhaumya.
Dhaumya said: "She cannot be taken by you without first conquering those great warriors. Reflect on the ancient duty of the kṣatriya order, Jayadratha."
"Having committed this base act, you will without doubt reap a sinful fruit when you encounter those heroic Pāṇḍavas led by Dharmarāja."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Dhaumya then followed that illustrious royal princess as she was being carried away, walking in the midst of the foot-soldiers.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the Pārthas, having ranged in all directions — those foremost bowmen on earth — slaying deer, boars, and buffaloes while roaming separately, came together again.
Then, in that great forest thronging with deer and snakes and echoing with the cries of birds, Yudhiṣṭhira addressed those brothers, having heard the voices of the deer calling out.
"Turning toward the direction lit by the sun, the deer and birds speak harshly, foretelling a terrible ordeal — a great battle with enemies, or an insult suffered."
"Turn back quickly — enough of hunting for us. My mind is pained and burning; anger has overwhelmed my reason, and the lord of life is stirred and churned within my body."
"The Kāmyaka forest appears to me like a lake whose serpents have been carried off by Garuḍa, like a kingdom stripped of its king and bereft of prosperity, like a jar whose liquor has been drunk by drunkards."
Then those heroic men, borne by great swift horses of the Sindhu breed, swift as a gust of wind, harnessed to large and fine chariots, turned their faces toward the hermitage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then a jackal, clamorous with no small noise, approached the left flank of those who were returning and howled. Having reflected on this, the king spoke to Bhīma and Dhanañjaya.
"As this low-born jackal howls, approaching our left flank — it is quite clear that sinful men have committed a violent assault upon us, overpowering us, the Kurus."
Thus speaking, as they entered the forest — having hunted in that great wilderness — they then saw, weeping, the young nurse-maid and attendant of their beloved wife.
Indrasena, hastening toward her, leaped from the chariot and ran to her; O lord of men, he spoke to that nurse-maid these words, greatly distressed at that moment.
"Why do you weep, fallen on the ground? Why does your face wither with a wretched hue? Surely Draupadī, the royal princess, of blameless form and very wide eyes, who equals the very bodies of the foremost Kurus — has she not been violated by those sinful and most cruel men?"
"Even if the goddess has entered the earth, or gone to heaven, or plunged into the ocean — the Pārthas will follow her track; for Dharmarāja burns with grief."
"For who, among such enemies of foes, enduring hardship, unconquered — who would wish to steal one who is dearer to them than their own lives? That hero who is devoted to them is my husband Nakula, the swordsman of light and wondrous hand, and great wise Sahadeva, without equal."
"Whose body will those dreadful sharp and foremost arrows pierce today before entering the earth? Do not grieve regarding her, O timid one — know that Kṛṣṇā will return today. The Pārthas will come with the daughter of Yajña after slaying all their enemies to the last man."
Then the nurse-maid, wiping her lovely face, said to the charioteer Indrasena: "Kṛṣṇā has been carried off by Jayadratha, who violently overpowered and dishonored those five men equal to Indra."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The tracks are fresh and clear; even the broken trees have not yet wilted. Turn around and follow quickly — the royal princess has not gone far at all."
"All of you, O Indra-like ones, don your great and fine armor; take up your mighty bows and arrows and quickly follow the track."
"For before long she — bewildered by threat and force, her mind in confusion, her face withering — may give her body to one who does not deserve it, like a ladle full of choice ghee poured into ashes."
"Before the offering is poured as if into a fire of husks; before the garland is cast away as if in a cremation ground; before the soma, moving through the ritual, is lapped up by a dog while the assembly is deluded — go now! Before the jackal wallows in the lotus lake, having hunted in the great forest."
"Let no evildoer touch the beautiful, fine-nosed, fine-eyed, moon-bright, serene face of your beloved — as a dog would devour the sacrificial cake. Follow these tracks quickly; let not the moment swiftly pass you by."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Good woman, be silent and restrain your speech — do not say harsh things in our presence. Kings and princes drunk on power meet with their undoing."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having said just that much, they went forth swiftly, following those very tracks, again and again hissing like serpents and plucking the bowstrings of their great bows.
Then they saw the dust of that army, whirled up and driven by the hooves of horses, and Dhaumya in the midst of the foot-soldiers, crying out, "Bhīma! Rush forward!"
Consoling the deeply distressed Dhaumya with the words "May you go in peace" — those princes then rushed at that army with speed, like hawks when prey is in sight.
The wrath of those men of valor equal to great Indra blazed up, inflamed by the insult to the daughter of Yajña, and at the sight of Jayadratha and their beloved standing on his chariot.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vṛkodara, Dhanañjaya, the twin brothers, and the king — all those great wielders of bows — cried out at the king of Sindhu; and then the directions became bewildered for the enemies.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, in the forest, a most dreadful uproar arose among those kṣatriyas filled with rage upon seeing Bhīmasena and Arjuna.
Seeing the banner-tops of those foremost Kurus, the evil-souled King Jayadratha himself — his power now broken — said to the daughter of Yajña, Bhānumatī, standing on his chariot:
"These five great chariots are approaching; I believe these are your husbands, O Kṛṣṇā. You who know them — tell us, O beautiful-haired one, who stands highest on each chariot among the Pāṇḍavas."
Draupadī said: "What use to you, O fool, is knowing those great wielders of bows, having committed this most heinous and life-destroying act? These heroes, my husbands, have come together — not one of you shall remain alive in this battle."
"Yet it is my duty to tell everything when asked, even to one doomed to die — that is the dharma for me. I have no anguish nor any fear of you, now that I see Dharmarāja together with his younger brothers."
"He on whose banner-top the two sweet and well-matched drums, Nanda and Upananda, resound — this one who is expert in determining what is right in duty and purpose — him men always follow when they have matters of importance."
"He who is pure gold-bright in complexion, with a fierce nose, slender build, and long eyes — he whom they call the foremost of all the Kurus: that is Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, my husband."
"Even for an enemy who comes seeking refuge would this righteous hero give his life. Approach him quickly, O fool, for your own welfare — hands folded, weapons laid aside."
"And him you see standing on his chariot — long-armed, tall as a great śāla tree, biting his lip, his brows knit in a frown — that is Vṛkodara, my husband."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Thoroughbred, strong, well-trained horses of great power carry this hero along. His deeds are superhuman — the name Bhīma has spread across the earth on his account."
"Those who have wronged him do not survive here; nor does he ever forget an enmity. He brings about the end of a feud — but he does not become excessively calm afterward."
"Gentle, generous, steadfast, illustrious, master of his senses, devoted to his elders — this heroic man, both brother and pupil of Yudhiṣṭhira: that is Dhanañjaya, my husband."
"He who would not abandon dharma out of desire, or fear, or greed — and would do no cruelty: he, the son of Kuntī, is of blazing splendor equal to Vaiśvānara fire, capable of enduring enemies, and a destroyer of foes."
"He who is expert in determining all matters of duty and purpose, the remover of fear for those afflicted by fear, the wise one — whose form they call the finest on earth, whom all the Pāṇḍavas guard closely —"
"— who is dearer to them than their own lives and who is wholly devoted to them: that hero is Nakula, my husband. And he who is a sword-fighter of light and wondrous hand, the great and wise Sahadeva, without equal —"
"— whose deeds you will witness today, O dull-witted one, as if Śatakratu himself were fighting in the armies of the daityas: a hero, skilled in arms, intelligent, wise, and beloved of King Dharmasuta —"
"— he who is of splendor equal to the moon and sun, the youngest-born of the Pāṇḍavas and dearly loved, whose equal in intelligence no man is to be found, and who is likewise a speaker and expert in determining truth among the good —"
"— that hero, ever wrathful and spirited, wise and prudent: that is Sahadeva, my husband. He would give up his life, enter the fire — but he would never speak what is contrary to dharma. Always high-minded, devoted to the duty of the warrior, the most beloved of Kuntī's sons among men."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"You will see this army of yours — all its warriors slain — tossed and churned by the sons of Pāṇḍu, like a treasure-laden ship crumbling at the ocean's edge on the back of a sea-monster."
"Thus have the sons of Pāṇḍu been described to you — whom you, in your delusion, dared to dishonor. If you escape from them with your body unharmed, you will be born again — you will have gained a second life."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then those five Pārthas, equal to five Indras, bypassing the terrified foot-soldiers with their folded hands, in their rage overwhelmed and enveloped the chariot-host from all sides in a darkness of arrow-rain.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: "Stand firm! Strike quickly! Charge in all directions!" — thus the king of Sindhu urged on those princes.
Then a most dreadful uproar arose in the battle at that time, among the soldiers, upon seeing Bhīma, Arjuna, the twin brothers, and Yudhiṣṭhira together.
Despondency arose among the Śibis, Sindhus, and Trigartans when they saw those tiger-like men — fierce in strength like tigers indeed.
Bhīma seized his mace — all of sharpened iron, adorned with golden designs, tall and splendid — and charged at the Sindhava king, driven as if by Death itself.
Meanwhile, Koṭikāśya wheeled around and attacked, surrounding Vṛkodara with a great array of chariots.
Though showered by javelins, lances, and iron arrows hurled by the arms of heroes, Bhīma did not tremble.
In the vanguard of the Sindhava army, Bhīma slew with his mace an elephant along with its rider, and fourteen foot-soldiers as well.
Pārtha, eager to protect the Sauvīra, slew five hundred mountain heroes and great chariot-warriors at the forefront of that army.
The king himself slew a hundred of the foremost, most valiant, hard-striking Suvīras in that battle in the space of a mere blink.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nakula was seen there, leaping down from his chariot with sword in hand, repeatedly scattering the heads of the foot-guards like seeds sown broadcast.
Sahadeva, advancing with his chariot against elephant-fighters, brought them down with iron arrows as peacocks are knocked from trees.
Then a Trigarta warrior, bow in hand, descended from his great chariot and with his mace slew four horses of that king.
When that warrior came close on foot, the righteous king, son of Kuntī, pierced him in the chest with a crescent-headed arrow.
His heart split open, that hero vomited blood from his mouth and fell forward facing Pārtha, like a tree uprooted at its base.
The righteous king, his horses slain, leapt from his chariot along with Indrasena and took refuge on Sahadeva's great chariot.
Kṣemaṃkara and Mahāmukha, targeting Nakula, both rained showers of sharp arrows on him from either side.
Those two, pouring down arrows like monsoon clouds, were each slain with a single decisive shot by Mādrī's son.
Then Suratha, king of the Trigartans, expert in elephant warfare, charged from the chariot's pole and caused his chariot to crash by means of an elephant.
Nakula, fearless, leapt from that chariot with shield and sword in hand, took up a commanding position, and stood immovable as a mountain.
Suratha then furiously urged that great elephant — its trunk raised — toward Nakula for the kill.
As that elephant came close upon him, Nakula severed its trunk at the root with his sword — the trunk complete with its tusk.
That elephant, adorned with anklet ornaments, let out a great roar and fell headlong to the ground, crushing its riders beneath it.
Having accomplished that great feat, the heroic son of Mādrī, that great chariot-warrior, found safety by reaching Bhīmasena's chariot.
In the battle, as king Koṭikāśya bore down, Bhīma severed with a razor-headed arrow the head of that king's charioteer as he urged the horses on.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The king did not realize his charioteer had been slain by that mighty-armed one; his horses, driverless, bolted in all directions across the battlefield.
Bhīma, the foremost striker, the Pāṇḍava, advanced and slew that king — turned away and driverless — with a palm-strengthened javelin.
Dhanaṃjaya cut off, with sharp broad-headed arrows, both the bows and the heads of all twelve of the Sauvīra warriors.
That superb chariot-warrior slew in battle the Śibis, the foremost of the Ikṣvākus, the Trigartans, and the Sindhavans as they came within range of his arrows.
Many were laid low by Savyasācī — elephants with their banners still flying, great chariot-warriors with their standards still raised.
Headless trunks and detached heads lay strewn across the whole field of battle, covering the earth.
Dogs, vultures, herons, crows, kites, jackals, and ravens feasted insatiably there on the flesh and blood of the slain heroes.
With those heroes slain, Jayadratha the king of Sindhu, terror-stricken, released Kṛṣṇā and devoted himself entirely to flight.
That lowest of men, intent on saving his own life, set Draupadī down amid that chaotic army and fled toward the forest.
Yudhiṣṭhira the righteous king, seeing Draupadī with Dhaumya at her side, had the heroic son of Mādrī place her upon a chariot.
Then, with Jayadratha gone, Vṛkodara struck that fleeing army again and again, targeting them with iron arrows.
But Savyasācī, seeing Jayadratha fleeing, restrained Bhīma who was slaughtering the Sindhava soldiers.
Arjuna said: The one through whose offense this intolerable suffering has come upon us — I do not see that Jayadratha anywhere on this battlefield.
Seek him out — blessings be on you. What purpose is served by felling these soldiers? How do you regard this fruitless work?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the wise Guḍākeśa, the eloquent Bhīmasena glanced toward Yudhiṣṭhira and spoke these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The enemies' champions are slain; they have largely scattered in all directions. Taking Draupadī with you, O king, let Your Majesty turn back from here.
Together with the twin brothers and with the great-souled Dhaumya, return to the hermitage, O king of kings, and console Draupadī.
That foolish Sindhava king shall not escape me with his life — even if he shelters in the depths of Pātāla and Indra himself acts as his charioteer.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That Sindhava must not be slain, O mighty-armed one, even wicked though he is — remember Duḥśalā and the glorious Gāndhārī.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that, Draupadī — distraught, furious, yet modest and wise — spoke to Bhīma, addressing both her husbands Bhīma and Arjuna.
If you truly wish to do what is dear to me, then that vile wretch must be killed — that outcast of the Sindhava line, that wicked, evil-minded stain upon his family.
One who abducts another's wife, who without any quarrel robs an enemy of his kingdom — such a man does not deserve to live even if he begs for mercy in battle.
Addressed thus, those two tiger-like men went to where the Sindhava had fled; the king meanwhile turned back, taking Kṛṣṇā with him along with the family priest.
Entering the hermitage, he found it — its rush-mat seats overturned and scattered — thronged with brāhmaṇas headed by Mārkaṇḍeya.
The greatly wise king, surrounded by his brothers and with his wife beside him, rejoined those assembled brāhmaṇas who were lamenting over Draupadī.
They rejoiced to see the king returned once more, having defeated the Sindhus and Sauvīras and having recovered Draupadī.
The king, surrounded by them, sat down right there; and the spirited Kṛṣṇā entered the hermitage together with the twin brothers.
Bhīma and Arjuna, hearing that the enemy had gone only a kośa away, themselves goaded their horses and charged after him at full speed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Herein Arjuna performed a feat most wonderful: he slew the horses of the Sindhava who had gone but a single kośa away.
Endowed with divine weapons, unagitated even in moments of crisis, he accomplished that difficult feat with arrows charged with sacred weapon-spells.
Then both heroes, Bhīma and Dhanaṃjaya, charged toward the Sindhava — his horses slain, alone, frightened, his mind in turmoil.
The Sindhava, deeply distressed to see his horses slain and beholding the feats of valor that Dhanaṃjaya was performing, mustered his resolve for flight and ran toward the forest.
Watching the Sindhava stride away in flight, the mighty-armed Phalguna gave chase and called out these words.
With this much valor you dared seize a woman by force? Turn back, O prince — flight does not befit you. How can you flee abandoning your followers in the midst of the enemy?
Thus addressed by Pārtha, the Sindhava did not turn back. "Stand! Stand!" — with that cry the mighty Bhīma suddenly charged at him, while the compassionate Pārtha called out to him: "Do not kill him!"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Jayadratha, seeing both brothers with weapons raised, ran swiftly — composed on the surface but deeply distressed, eager for his life.
Bhīmasena, mighty and furious beyond measure, leapt from his chariot, gave chase, and seized him by the hair.
Lifting him up in rage, he dashed the king to the ground, seized him by the throat, and beat him repeatedly.
As the king revived and tried again to leap up, the mighty-armed Bhīma kicked him in the head as he was wailing.
Bhīma drove his knee into him and struck him with his elbow; overwhelmed by the force of those blows, the king fell into unconsciousness.
Then Phalguna restrained the enraged Bhīmasena, saying: "O Kaurava, remember what the king said — spare him for Duḥśalā's sake."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīmasena said: This one of wicked conduct does not deserve to live at my hands — this lowest of men who tormented Draupadī, who was entirely undeserving of such treatment.
What can I do, since the king is always merciful, and you too with your childish reasoning forever hinder us?
Having spoken thus, Vṛkodara shaved five locks of hair from the king's head with a crescent-headed arrow, while he lay speechless.
Having thus dishonored the king, Vṛkodara then said to him: "If you wish to live, you fool, listen to the terms I am about to state."
"You must declare 'I am a slave' in all assemblies and gatherings. If you do this, I shall grant you your life — this is the rule of the battle-won."
"So be it" — with these words the barely-breathing king Jayadratha spoke to Bhīma, that tiger among men, who shone magnificently in battle.
Then the Pārtha Vṛkodara bound the writhing, senseless, dust-covered king and placed him upon his chariot.
Then Bhīma, mounting that chariot and following Pārtha, drove to the center of the hermitage and approached Yudhiṣṭhira.
Bhīma then displayed Jayadratha in that wretched condition; the king laughed on seeing him and said: "Let him be released."
Bhīma also told the king: "Let it be reported to Draupadī — this evil-minded one has entered the state of a slave to the Pāṇḍavas."
Then the eldest brother spoke to him with affectionate words: "Release this man of base conduct — if we are of any authority to you."
Draupadī too, glancing at Yudhiṣṭhira, told Bhīma: "Let this slave be freed — you have already given him five tufts of hair by the king's grace."
Freed, that trembling king came forward, paid his respects to Yudhiṣṭhira, and then bowed before all the sages assembled there.
The merciful king Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, then spoke to him — seeing Jayadratha in that state, caught by Savyasācī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"You are no slave — go, you are freed. Never do this again anywhere. Shame on you, you wretch, lusting after women, low-born with base associates. Who else but you, lowest of men, would have done such a deed?"
Knowing that the doer of this evil had lost his spirit — the best of the Bhāratas, that lord among kings, looked upon him and felt compassion.
"May your understanding grow in righteousness and may you not set your mind on unrighteousness. Go in peace, Jayadratha, with your horses, chariot, and foot-soldiers."
Thus addressed, O Bhārata, the king went away in shame, silent, his face slightly downcast, grieved, toward the Gate of the Ganges.
Going for refuge to the god Virūpākṣa, the lord of Umā, he performed intense austerities; and Vṛṣadhvaja (Śiva) was pleased with him.
The three-eyed god himself, well pleased, received his oblation and granted him a boon; hear what he chose.
"May I conquer in battle all five Pāṇḍavas along with their chariots" — so the king said to the god; but the god replied, "No."
"You will be able to check them in battle — those who are unconquerable and unslayable — all except the mighty-armed Arjuna, who is difficult to approach even by the gods."
"He whom they call the unvanquished god who bears conch, discus, and mace — that foremost among weapon-masters, Kṛṣṇa, protects him."
Thus addressed, the king returned to his own abode, while the Pāṇḍavas continued to dwell in the Kāmyaka forest.
Janamejaya said: After Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) had been abducted and the greatest distress had been suffered, what did those tiger-men, the Pāṇḍavas, do thereafter?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus freed Kṛṣṇā and thoroughly defeated Jayadratha, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira sat in the company of the hosts of sages.
In the midst of those great sages who were listening and lamenting with him, the son of Pāṇḍu spoke these words to Mārkaṇḍeya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I believe that Time is mighty, and so is Fate ordained by providence — and the inevitable destiny of beings which none can transgress.
"For how could such a calamity touch our wife, who knows and practises dharma, who is pure — like theft touching what is false?
"For Draupadī has never done any sinful act or blameworthy deed anywhere; on the contrary, she has always observed great dharma toward the brāhmaṇas.
"Yet the dull-witted king Jayadratha abducted her by force; for that abduction he received the shaving of his head, and along with his allies he was fully defeated in battle.
"She has been recovered by us after slaughtering that Saindhava army, yet this abduction of our wife was something we never anticipated.
"Painful is this forest life, and our livelihood through hunting; painful is the killing of animals by those who dwell in the forest among other forest dwellers; and painful is this banishment from our kinsmen through the machinations of the wicked.
"Surely there must be some man more unfortunate than I — have you, venerable one, ever seen or heard of such a one?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O bull of the Bhāratas, Rāma suffered incomparable sorrow — his wife Jānakī was carried off by a mighty demon.
From his hermitage, the lord of rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa, taking to the sky and resorting to magic, swiftly killed the vulture Jaṭāyus and carried her away.
Rāma recovered her, relying on the forces of Sugrīva, building a bridge across the ocean and burning Laṅkā with his sharp arrows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In what lineage was Rāma born? What was his prowess, what his valour? Whose son was Rāvaṇa? And what was the enmity between them?
All this, O venerable one, you should narrate to me properly; I wish to hear the story of Rāma of untiring deeds.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: There was a great king named Aja, born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku; his son was Daśaratha, ever devoted to sacred study and pure of conduct.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He had four sons skilled in dharma and statecraft: Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and the mighty Bharata.
Kausalyā was Rāma's mother; Kaikeyī was Bharata's; the two scorchers of foes, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, were sons of Sumitrā.
Janaka was king of Videha; Sītā was his daughter, O lord — whom Tvaṣṭṛ himself fashioned as the beloved queen of Rāma.
Thus the birth of Rāma and of Sītā has been related to you; now I shall also explain the birth of Rāvaṇa, O lord of men.
Rāvaṇa's grandfather was no less than the god Prajāpati, the Self-existent, lord and creator of all the worlds, of great austerity.
Pulastya by name was his beloved mind-born son; Pulastya had a son named Vaiśravaṇa, born of a cow, who became a lord.
He abandoned his father and attended upon his grandfather; in anger at this, his father, O king, created another self from himself.
That one was born as the twice-born Viśravā, made from half of himself, wrathful, as a countermeasure against Vaiśravaṇa.
But the grandfather, pleased in heart, granted Vaiśravaṇa immortality, lordship of wealth, and the rank of world-guardian.
And also friendship with Īśāna (Śiva), a son named Nalakūbara, and the city of Laṅkā, filled with hosts of rākṣasas, as his capital.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The sage who had been born as a half-body from Pulastya's wrath — that wrathful one named Viśravā — he looked upon Vaiśravaṇa.
The lord of rākṣasas, Kubera, recognized his father as wrathful, O king, and ever strove to propitiate him.
That king of kings, Naravāhana (Kubera), dwelling in Laṅkā, gave three rākṣasī women to his father as attendants.
Those women, skilled in song and dance, then strove to please that great-souled sage, O tiger of the Bhāratas.
Puṣpotkaṭā and Rākā and Mālinī — O lord of men, O king — those slender-waisted ones, eager for the best, vied with one another.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Pleased with them, that blessed great-souled one granted boons to each of them — sons comparable to world-guardians, as each desired.
In Puṣpotkaṭā were born two sons who became lords of rākṣasas — Kumbhakarṇa and Daśagrīva — matchless in strength on earth.
Mālinī gave birth to one son, Vibhīṣaṇa; in Rākā were born twins — Khara and Śūrpaṇakhā.
Vibhīṣaṇa surpassed all others in beauty; he became greatly blessed, a guardian of dharma, devoted to righteous acts.
Daśagrīva was the eldest of all, the foremost among rākṣasas, of great energy, great heroism, great strength and valour.
Kumbhakarṇa surpassed all others in physical strength at that time; he was a master of illusion, keen in battle, fierce, and a night-wanderer.
Khara was valiant with the bow, a hater of brāhmaṇas, a flesh-eater; and Śūrpaṇakhā too was fierce, one who creates obstacles for the virtuous.
All of them were learned in the Vedas, all were heroes, all observed excellent vows; devoted to their father, they lived on Mount Gandhamādana.
Then there they saw Vaiśravaṇa, the bearer of human conveyance (Kubera), seated together with their father, endowed with supreme prosperity.
Rivalry having arisen in them, they resolved upon asceticism and pleased Brahmā with fierce austerities.
Daśagrīva stood on one foot for a thousand years, subsisting on air, practising the five-fire penance, perfectly concentrated.
Kumbhakarṇa lay face-downward, disciplined in food and vows; Vibhīṣaṇa subsisted on a single fallen leaf.
Devoted to fasting, wise, ever intent on recitation of mantras, that noble-minded one maintained that same intense austerity throughout the entire period.
Khara and Śūrpaṇakhā, with joyful hearts, attended upon and guarded the others as they performed their austerities.
When a thousand years were complete, the irresistible ten-headed one cut off his head and offered it in fire; by this the lord of the universe was pleased.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Brahmā himself went there, stopped them from their austerities, and enticed each of them separately with the granting of boons.
Brahmā said: I am pleased with you; desist, dear sons, and choose boons — whatever is desired, save one thing: immortality — let that be so.
"All those heads of yours that were offered in the fire with great desire — even so, all of them shall exist on your body as you wish."
"And your body shall bear no deformity; you will be able to assume any form at will, and you will be victorious over your enemies in battle — of this there is no doubt."
Rāvaṇa said: From gandharvas, gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, serpents, kiṃnaras, and spirits — may I never suffer defeat.
Brahmā said: From all those you have mentioned, there shall be no fear for you — except from a human. Be well; so has it been ordained by me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thus addressed, Daśagrīva became satisfied at that time; for that evil-minded man-eater despised human beings.
Then the great-grandfather spoke similarly to Kumbhakarṇa; but his mind being seized by delusion, he chose great sleep.
Saying "So shall it be," he then spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa: "Choose a boon, my son" — repeatedly saying "I am pleased with you."
Vibhīṣaṇa said: Even when fallen into the greatest adversity, may my mind never turn to adharma; and O blessed one, may the Brahmāstra manifest to me though untaught.
Brahmā said: Because, though born in the rākṣasa womb, O scorcher of foes, your mind takes no pleasure in adharma — I grant you immortality.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having obtained the boon, O lord of men, Daśagrīva the rākṣasa expelled the lord of wealth from Laṅkā after defeating him in battle.
The blessed Kubera abandoned Laṅkā and retired to Gandhamādana, accompanied by gandharvas and yakṣas along with rākṣasas and kiṃpuruṣas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Rāvaṇa seized and carried off his aerial chariot Puṣpaka; Vaiśravaṇa cursed him: "This shall no longer carry you."
"This shall carry him who kills you in battle; having dishonoured your elder and me, you shall swiftly cease to be."
But Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous in soul, ever mindful of the dharma of the virtuous, followed Kubera, O great king, endowed with supreme prosperity.
Pleased with him, that blessed lord of wealth, the wise brother, gave his brother the commandership of both the yakṣa and rākṣasa armies.
The rākṣasas, man-eaters, and the mighty piśācas — all assembled and consecrated Daśānana as king.
Daśagrīva, excelling in power over daityas and gods alike, moving through the sky and assuming any form at will, seized and carried off their treasures.
Because he made the worlds cry out in terror, Daśagrīva is therefore called Rāvaṇa; powerful as he willed, he instilled fear in the gods.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the brahmarṣis, the siddhas, and the divine royal sages, placing Agni (the fire-carrier) before them, sought refuge with Brahmā.
Agni said: That son of Viśravā, Daśagrīva the mighty, has been made unkillable in times past by the blessed one's boon.
The mighty one oppresses all creatures with his outrages; therefore, O blessed one, protect us — for no other protector exists.
Brahmā said: O Fire, he cannot be conquered in battle by gods or asuras; yet what needs to be done for his destruction has been arranged all around.
"For this very purpose, the four-armed Viṣṇu, the foremost among those who strike, has descended at my command; he shall accomplish this deed."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: The Grandfather then spoke this word in the presence of all those assembled, together with all the hosts of gods: "Be born on the earth."
"Beget valiant sons as helpers of Viṣṇu, everywhere among the she-bears and female monkeys — sons endowed with strength and the power to assume any form."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, by their respective portions and allotments, the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas all descended to the earth and filled it with delight straightway.
In their presence the boon-granting god commanded a gandharva woman named Dundubhī, for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose.
Hearing the word of the Grandfather, the gandharva woman Dundubhī then became Mantharā, a hunchback, in the human world.
And Indra and all those foremost gods begat sons upon the noblest she-monkeys and she-bears; those sons all followed in their fathers' footsteps in both glory and strength.
They were breakers of mountain peaks, armed with śāla-trees, palm-trees, and rocks; all of them had frames hard as the thunderbolt, and all possessed power like a rushing torrent.
All were endowed with valor and prowess at will, all were skilled in battle; their vital breath equaled ten thousand elephants, their speed equaled the wind. Some among these forest-dwellers could live wherever they wished.
Having arranged all this thus, the blessed lord, sustainer of the worlds, instructed Mantharā concerning every task that had to be done and in what manner.
She, swift as thought, heeded his word and acted accordingly, going here and there, devoted to kindling enmity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The birth of Rāma and the others has been told severally by the blessed one; O brahmin, I wish to hear the reason for the departure — please tell it.
How were the two heroic brothers, sons of Daśaratha — Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa — sent to the forest, O brahmin, and the glorious Maithilī as well?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: King Daśaratha, having sons born to him, became joyful — devoted to rites, intent on dharma, ever honoring elders.
In time those sons of his grew up, mighty in energy, masters of the Vedas with their secret teachings and of the science of archery.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When they had completed their celibate studentship and taken wives, O king, then Daśaratha was joyful and content.
The eldest among them was Rāma; the wise one delighted the people by his captivating nature and gladdened his father's heart.
Then that wise king, considering himself advanced in years, took counsel with his ministers and with the priests who knew dharma.
Regarding the consecration of Rāma as crown prince, O Bhārata, all those foremost counselors deemed the time had come.
Red-eyed, great-armed, walking like a maddened elephant, long-armed, broad-chested, with dark curling locks —
— blazing with splendor, heroic, in strength not inferior to Indra, a master of all the dharmas, equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect —
— whose subjects were all devoted to him, who was expert in all branches of knowledge, who had mastered his senses, and whose very appearance charmed even enemies —
— a restrainer of the wicked, protector of the righteous, steadfast, unconquerable, a victor who was never defeated —
— this son who increased the joy of Kausalyā — King Daśaratha, beholding him, was filled with the greatest delight, O delight of the Kurus.
And that great-souled, mighty one, reflecting on Rāma's virtues, addressed his pleased purohita with the words: "May it go well with you."
"Tonight, O brahmin, the auspicious conjunction of the Puṣya asterism will come; let the requisite materials be gathered, and let Rāma be invited here."
Hearing that word of the king, Mantharā then went to Kaikeyī and at the right moment spoke these words.
"Today, O Kaikeyī, the king has made known your great misfortune; a fierce venomous serpent, enraged, bites you, O wretched one."
"Fortunate indeed is Kausalyā whose son will be consecrated — what fortune is there for you, whose son will not inherit the kingdom?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
She, understanding that speech, adorned with all her ornaments, bearing a most excellent form like an altar-post slender at the waist —
— approached her husband in private, smiling as it were, bright-smiled, expressing affection as it were, and spoke sweet words.
"O king of true vows, you once granted me one boon of my desire — fulfill it now, O king, and release yourself from the debt."
The king said: "Well then, I grant you the boon — take whatever you wish. Today, who should be executed — let him be executed; who should be released — let him be released."
"Today I give wealth to whom it should be given, or let it be taken from whom it should be taken; anything of mine other than brahmin property that exists here."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: She, knowing his word and recognizing her own power over the lord of men, embraced him and then spoke thus to him.
"Whatever has been prepared for Rāma's consecration — let Bharata receive that; let the Rāghava go to the forest."
The king, hearing those words so unwelcome and dreadful in consequence, tormented by grief, O foremost of the Bhāratas, said not a single word.
Then Rāma, the mighty one, understanding his father thus addressed, set out for the forest — the righteous-souled one saying: "Let the king be true to his word."
The glorious bowman Lakṣmaṇa followed him then, as did his wife Sītā — may it go well with you — the Vaidehī, daughter of Janaka.
Then, when Rāma had gone to the forest, King Daśaratha at that time was united with the law of the body — that which comes in the course of time — and died.
Knowing that Rāma had gone and the king had likewise gone, Queen Kaikeyī had Bharata brought and spoke to him.
"Daśaratha has gone to heaven; Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa are in the forest — take the vast, secure, thorn-free kingdom."
The righteous-souled one said to her: "Alas, how cruel a deed you have done — having killed your husband and destroyed this family out of greed for wealth!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Having cast dishonor upon my head, you destroyer of the family — be content, O my mother" — saying thus, he wept.
And having cleansed his conduct in the presence of all the subjects, he followed after his brother Rāma, eager to bring him back.
Grieving deeply, he had Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and Kaikeyī sent ahead in carriages, and he himself went together with Śatrughna.
Together with Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva and thousands of other brahmins and the citizens and country folk, longing to bring Rāma back.
He saw Rāma stationed at Citrakūṭa together with Lakṣmaṇa — an ornament among ascetics, bearing his bow.
Dismissed by Rāma who was acting on his father's word, he administered the kingdom from Nandigrāma, placing Rāma's sandals at the fore.
But Rāma, fearing another visit of the citizens and country folk, entered the great forest toward the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Having honored Śarabhaṅga, he took refuge in the Daṇḍaka forest and then dwelt near the lovely river Godāvarī.
While Rāma was dwelling there, a great enmity arose with Khara, the inhabitant of Janasthāna — owing to what Śūrpaṇakhā had done.
For the protection of the ascetics, the Rāghava who cherished dharma slew fourteen thousand rākṣasas on the earth.
Having slain Dūṣaṇa and Khara too — those two of immense might — the wise Rāghava once again made the forest of dharma safe.
When those rākṣasas were slain, Śūrpaṇakhā then, with her nose and lips cut off, went to Laṅkā, her brother's dwelling.
Then the rākṣasī, swooning with grief, approached Rāvaṇa and fell at her brother's feet, her face smeared with dried blood.
Seeing her thus disfigured, Rāvaṇa was overcome by rage; he sprang from his seat in fury, grinding his teeth together.
Having dismissed his own ministers, he spoke to her in private: "By whom have you been made thus, dear one, having shown contempt for me without a thought?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Who seizes a sharp spear and touches it with every limb? Who places fire upon his head and sleeps in contentment, unsuspecting?"
"Who touches with his foot the most terrible venomous serpent here? And who touches the maned lion by its fangs and stands there?"
As he spoke thus, flames of fire issued from his orifices, as sparks issue at night from the hollows of a burning tree.
His sister told him all of it — Rāma's prowess and the defeat of the rākṣasas together with Khara and Dūṣaṇa.
Having resolved on his course of action and consoled his sister, the king set off, having first made the necessary arrangements in the city.
Crossing beyond Trikūṭa and also Mount Kāla, he saw the great ocean, deep in its waters, abode of the makara sea-monsters.
Crossing beyond it, the ten-faced one approached Gokarṇa, the beloved and undisturbed abode of the great-souled Śūlapāṇi.
There the ten-faced one approached Mārīca, his former minister, who had formerly taken to asceticism out of fear of Rāma alone.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Mārīca then, startled at seeing Rāvaṇa arrive, honored him with hospitality — with fruits, roots, and the like.
When he was seated and rested, that rākṣasa sat beside him and spoke respectful words — one skilled in speech addressing one versed in speech.
"Your complexion is not its natural self — is all well in your city? Do all your subjects still serve you as before?"
"And what is the purpose of your coming here, O lord of rākṣasas? Know that it is already done, even if it should be most difficult to accomplish."
Rāvaṇa told him all of Rāma's deeds; and Mārīca, having heard, spoke briefly to Rāvaṇa thus.
"Enough of confronting Rāma — I know his valor well. Who indeed can bear the speed of that great-souled one's arrows?"
"That bull among men is indeed the very cause of my renunciation. This is the mouth of destruction for you — by what wicked soul has it been told to you?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Rāvaṇa, full of anger, spoke to him with harsh reproof: "Death will certainly be yours if you do not carry out my command."
Mārīca reflected: "When death inevitably comes, a better death is preferable — I shall do what is his intention."
Then Mārīca replied to that lord of rākṣasas: "What assistance of mine is needed by you? I will do it, even helplessly."
The ten-necked one said to him: "Go and entice Sītā — become a deer with jeweled horns, with a body variegated with gems."
"Sītā will certainly, upon seeing you, urge Rāma on; and when the Kākutstha has gone forth, Sītā will be in my power."
"I will carry her away, and then that evil-minded one will cease to be, due to separation from his wife. Render me this assistance."
Thus addressed, Mārīca performed his water-rite, and then, deeply grieved, followed after Rāvaṇa who went ahead.
Then, having gone to the hermitage of Rāma of untiring deeds, the two of them did all that which had been previously planned.
Rāvaṇa became a wandering mendicant — shaven-headed, carrying a water pot and triple staff; and Mārīca, having become a deer, the two approached that place.
Mārīca, wearing the deer's form, displayed himself to the Vaidehī; she, impelled by fate, urged Rāma for the sake of it.
Rāma, wishing to please her, quickly took up his bow, stationed Lakṣmaṇa to guard her, and went off in pursuit of the deer.
Bearing his bow, quiver fastened, sword at his side, leather wrist-guard on his fingers, Rāma chased the deer — as Rudra pursues the celestial deer among the stars.
The demon, going unseen, lured Rāma's gaze onward; it repeatedly vanished and reappeared, drawing him far along a great distance — and then Rāma understood what it was.
Recognizing it as a night-roaming demon, the quick-witted son of Raghu fitted an unerring arrow to his bow and slew the creature that had taken the form of a deer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Struck by Rāma's arrow, the demon then cried out in Rāma's own voice, screaming in a tone of anguish: "Ah, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa!"
The daughter of Videha heard that pitiful cry and rushed toward the sound; but Lakṣmaṇa spoke to her.
"Fear not, timid one — who could overpower Rāma? Within a moment you shall see him return, O bright-smiling one."
Though he spoke thus, she burst into tears and harboured suspicion of her brother-in-law — she was overcome by the nature of women, she whose ornament was her pure character.
The chaste and devoted wife began to speak harshly to him: "Fool, the time you are craving in your heart has not come."
"I would take a weapon and kill myself, or leap from a mountain peak, or enter a blazing fire —
— rather than, abandoning Rāma my husband, ever submit to you, a base creature — as a tigress would not stoop to a jackal."
Hearing such words, Lakṣmaṇa — who loved Rāma and was of righteous conduct — covered his ears and set out in the direction Rāma had gone; the bowman followed in Rāma's very footsteps.
At that very moment the demon Rāvaṇa appeared — inauspicious though wearing an auspicious disguise, like fire concealed under ashes — dressed as an ascetic mendicant, intent on carrying off the blameless woman.
The daughter of Janaka, knowing the duties of dharma, perceived him arriving and received him with an offering of fruits, roots, and other forest food.
Scorning all of that, the foremost of demons resumed his true form and set about winning Vaidehī over with soft words.
"Sītā, I am the celebrated king of the demons, Rāvaṇa by name; my city, Laṅkā by name, lies beautiful on the far shore of the great ocean."
"There among the finest women you shall shine at my side. Become my wife, O lovely-hipped one; abandon the ascetic Rāghava."
Having heard these and similar words, Sītā, daughter of Janaka, covered her ears and spoke in reply: "It shall not be so."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let the sky with all its stars fall; let the earth shatter into fragments; let fire turn cold — I will not abandon the son of Raghu."
"How could a female elephant, having served the great tusker — its ichor streaming, lotus-decked, ranging the forest — stoop to touch a boar?"
"How could any woman, having drunk the madhvīka wine and sweet spring honey, ever desire the crude sour gruel — so I hold in my heart."
Having spoken thus to him, she turned and re-entered the hermitage; Rāvaṇa rushed after the fair-hipped woman and blocked her way.
Having terrified her senseless with a harsh voice, he seized her by the hair and then ascended into the sky.
Then the vulture Jaṭāyu, who ranged the mountain heights, saw the wretched woman being carried off weeping, "Rāma! Rāma!"
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Jaṭāyu, son of Aruṇa, was a dear friend of Daśaratha — the great and mighty king of vultures, whose full brother was Saṃpāti.
He saw Sītā, his friend's daughter-in-law, clasped in Rāvaṇa's arms; filled with rage, the bird flew at Rāvaṇa, lord of the demons.
The vulture cried out to him: "Release her, release the Maithilī! Night-wanderer, while I yet live how will you carry her away? You shall not escape me alive if you do not let this woman go."
Having spoken thus to the lord of demons, he tore into him fiercely with his talons; again and again rent by blows of wings and beak, Rāvaṇa poured forth rivers of blood like a mountain streaming waterfalls.
Being mauled by the vulture who sought the good of Rāma's beloved, Rāvaṇa drew his sword and cut off both wings of the bird.
Having struck down the king of vultures — who now resembled a peak of a severed cloud — the demon took Sītā in his arms and soared upward into the sky.
Wherever Vaidehī caught sight of a hermitage settlement, a lake, or a river, she dropped one of her ornaments there.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
She saw five great monkeys on a mountain slope; there the spirited woman cast down her large and splendid garment.
Borne aloft by the wind, it fell among those five monkey lords — brilliant yellow amid them like lightning flashing between clouds.
While Vaidehī was thus being abducted, the wise Rāma, having slain the great deer, turned back and came upon his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing his brother coming, he reproved him: "How have you abandoned Vaidehī in a forest frequented by demons and come here?"
Thinking over the demon's luring him away in the form of a deer, and now his brother's arrival, he burned with anguish.
Even as he reproached him, Rāma hurried back to the hermitage. He said: "Lakṣmaṇa, I cannot see whether Vaidehī still lives."
Lakṣmaṇa related to him all of Sītā's words — the unworthy last speech that Vaidehī had spoken.
With his heart burning, Rāma rushed to the hermitage; there he saw the vulture lying slain, huge as a mountain.
Suspecting a demon, the scion of Kākutstha drew his powerful bow and charged at it, together with Lakṣmaṇa.
The radiant bird spoke to both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa as they stood together: "I am the king of vultures; blessings on you — I was a friend of Daśaratha."
Hearing those words, both drew back their fine bows and said: "Who are you, who speaks our father by name?"
Then they saw him with both wings severed; and the vulture told them how he had been struck down by Rāvaṇa on Sītā's behalf.
Rāghava asked the vulture: "In which direction did Rāvaṇa go?" The vulture indicated it by nodding his head — and then he died.
Understanding from his gesture that the direction was south, the scion of Kākutstha performed the funeral rites, honouring him as a friend of his father.
Then, seeing the hermitage site — cushions and water-pots scattered, the sacred jars overturned, deserted, prowled by packs of jackals —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— both overwhelmed with grief and anguish, tormented by Vaidehī's abduction, the two scorchers of foes entered the Daṇḍaka forest heading southward.
In that great forest, Rāma together with the son of Sumitrā saw herds of deer fleeing in all directions and heard a dreadful roar of creatures swelling like a forest fire.
And shortly they saw Kabandha — dreadful to behold — resembling a cloud-mountain, massive as a śāla trunk, with enormous arms, wide eyes set in his chest, a vast belly, and an enormous mouth.
Then, O Bhārata, that demon seized Lakṣmaṇa in his hand at random; Saumitri was instantly seized with despair.
Looking toward Rāma as he was being dragged — his face turned that way — he said despondently to Rāma: "See the plight I am in."
"The abduction of Vaidehī, and now this calamity of mine — your loss of the kingdom, and the death of our father as well —
"— I shall not see you arrived in Kosala together with Vaidehī, established in the ancestral kingdom of your fathers."
"Fortunate are those who will see the noble one's face after his coronation — like the moon glimmering through rifts in a cloud — adorned with kuśa grass, aja, and śamī branches."
Thus in many ways did the wise Lakṣmaṇa lament; and Kākutstha, who kept composure even in crises, spoke to him.
"Do not despair, tiger among men — while I stand here, this creature is nothing. Cut off his right arm; I have already severed the left."
Even as he spoke these words, Rāma's exceedingly sharp sword sliced off the arm — cut clean as a stalk of sesame.
Then the mighty Saumitri too, glancing at his brother Rāghava standing firm, hewed off the demon's right arm with his sword.
Lakṣmaṇa struck that demon hard in the flank again, and then the immense Kabandha fell lifeless to the ground.
From his body there emerged a being of divine appearance, who was seen rising to the sky and blazing there like the sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The eloquent Rāma asked him: "Who are you? Tell me, I ask. By what cause does this wonderful marvel appear before me?"
The gandharva revealed to him: "O king, I am Viśvāvasu; through a curse of Brahmā I fell into a birth haunted by demons."
"Sītā has been abducted by the king Rāvaṇa, who dwells in Laṅkā. Seek out Sugrīva — he will render you aid."
"Here is the Pampā lake — its waters auspicious, full of geese and karaṇḍava ducks — a lovely tarn close to the mountain Ṛśyamūka."
"Sugrīva dwells here with four ministers — the brother of Vālin, the golden-garlanded king of the monkeys."
"This much is within my power to tell you: you will see Jānakī. The abode of Rāvaṇa is certainly known to the king of monkeys."
Having spoken thus, that divine being of great radiance disappeared; and both those heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, were filled with wonder.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, not far off, Rāma — his heart aching over Sītā's abduction — came to Pampā, a pond full of abundant lotuses and blue water-lilies.
Fanned by a cool and gentle breeze fragrant as nectar, he wandered through that forest, going in his mind to his beloved.
That lord among kings lamented there, calling his beloved to mind, scorched by the arrows of love; and Saumitri then spoke to him.
"Such a state of feeling does not befit you, O giver of honour — no more than illness befits a self-possessed man of mature virtue."
"You have obtained tidings of Vaidehī and of Rāvaṇa; pursue that now through manly effort and through reason."
"Let us approach Sugrīva, that foremost of monkeys dwelling on the mountain. Take heart — in me you have a disciple, a servant, and an ally."
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa with many such words, that son of Raghu regained his composure and became single-minded in the task at hand.
Having drunk from the waters of Pampā and poured libations to their ancestors, both hero brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, set forth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Approaching Ṛśyamūka — the mountain rich in roots and fruits — the two heroes saw five monkeys on the mountain's summit.
Sugrīva dispatched to them his minister, the monkey Hanūmān — steady as the Himālaya and possessed of great wisdom.
After first conversing with him, the two went to Sugrīva; and then, O king, Rāma formed a bond of friendship with the king of monkeys.
When his need was made known, the monkeys showed him that garment which Sītā, as she was being carried away, had cast down upon them.
Having received that proof, Rāma himself consecrated Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, to sovereignty over all the monkeys of the earth.
The scion of Kākutstha pledged to slay Vālin in battle, O king, and Sugrīva in turn pledged to bring back the daughter of Videha.
Having spoken thus and made their compact, placing mutual trust in one another, they all approached Kiṣkindhā and stood there eager for battle.
Sugrīva, reaching Kiṣkindhā, roared with a sound like a thunder-cloud. Vālin did not tolerate that, but Tārā tried to restrain him.
"As Sugrīva roars like this, this mighty monkey must have come with a powerful protector—you should not go out."
Then Vālin, lord of monkeys, he who wears a golden garland, eloquent of speech, spoke to Tārā, whose face was like the lord of stars.
"You who understand the cries of all creatures, consider carefully with your wisdom: by whose support has this one who resembles my brother come here?"
Having reflected for a moment, Tārā, radiant as the lord of stars, spoke wisely to her husband: "Hear everything, O lord of monkeys."
"Rāma, son of Daśaratha, great-souled and a master of the bow, whose wife has been carried off, has entered into an alliance with Sugrīva as an equal."
"His brother too, the mighty-armed and unconquered son of Sumitrā, the wise Lakṣmaṇa, stands ready to accomplish their purpose."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Mainda and Dvivida, Hanūmān son of the Wind, Jāmbavān king of bears—all of Sugrīva's ministers stand with him."
"All these great souls, wise and mighty, relying on the valour of Rāma, are more than enough to bring about your destruction."
The lord of monkeys dismissed her well-meaning words and, filled with jealousy, suspected her heart of being set upon Sugrīva.
Having spoken harshly to Tārā, he went out from the mouth of the cave and addressed Sugrīva, who stood near mount Mālyavat.
"Fool, you have been defeated by me more than once, and spared because you clung to life—I let you go knowing you were a kinsman. What haste is this to die again?"
Thus addressed, Sugrīva, slayer of foes, replied to his brother with reasoned words fitting the moment, as though prompting Rāma.
"O king, my wife has been taken by you and my kingdom stripped away—know then that I have come, for what worth is a life so diminished?"
Having spoken at length in this manner, the two of them then fell upon one another in battle—Vālin and Sugrīva, armed with sala-trees, palm-trees, and rocks.
Both struck each other, both fell to the ground, both leapt up again wonderfully, and both struck with their fists.
Both drenched in blood, both lacerated by nails and teeth, those two heroes shone at that moment like two flowering kimsuka trees.
No distinction between the two could be discerned in battle at that time; so Hanūmān placed a garland around Sugrīva's neck as a mark.
The hero then shone with the garland hanging about his neck like the great and splendid mount Malaya garlanded by a wreath of clouds.
Seeing Sugrīva thus marked, Rāma of the great bow drew back his supreme bow and took aim at Vālin as at a target.
The twang of his bow resounded then like a great mechanical contrivance; and Vālin, struck to the heart by the arrow, was terrified.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His vital points pierced and struck, vomiting blood from his mouth, he saw Rāma standing nearby together with the son of Sumitrā.
Having censured the scion of Kākutstha, he fell senseless to the earth; and Tārā saw him lying on the ground like the lord of stars fallen from heaven.
With Vālin slain, Sugrīva returned to Kiṣkindhā and to Tārā, whose face was like the moon, whose lord had fallen.
Wise Rāma then dwelt for four months on the auspicious slopes of mount Mālyavat, attended upon by Sugrīva.
Rāvaṇa too, going to the city of Laṅkā, impelled by the force of desire, lodged Sītā in a palace like Nandana, near the Aśoka grove, which resembled the hermitage of an ascetic.
Slender from constant remembrance of her husband, clad in an ascetic's garb, given to fasting and austerity, that wide-eyed one dwelt there in miserable abode, living on fruits and roots.
The lord of rakshasas posted rakshasis there to guard her, wielding lances, swords, spears, axes, clubs, and firebrands.
Two-eyed, three-eyed, forehead-eyed, long-tongued, tongueless, three-breasted, one-footed, Trijaṭā, and one-eyed—
these and others besides, with blazing eyes and hair as thick as an elephant's trunk, surrounded Sītā day and night without rest.
Those she-demons, terrible in voice, fearsome, speaking harsh and grating syllables, constantly menaced that long-eyed one.
"Let us eat her, tear her apart, divide her into pieces—she who dares to dishonour our master and yet lives!"
As they threatened her thus, frightening her again and again, she, overcome by grief for her husband, heaved a sigh and spoke to them.
"Noble ladies, eat me quickly—I have no desire for life without that lotus-eyed one with dark, curling hair."
"Even so, I, without food and freed from any love of life, will wither my limbs like a serpent coiled around a palm tree."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I will never approach any man other than the son of Raghu—know this as truth; do with me whatever comes next."
Hearing those words of hers, those harsh-voiced rakshasis went to report everything from the beginning to the lord of rakshasas.
When all of them had gone, a rakshasi named Trijaṭā, learned in righteousness and speaking kind words, consoled the daughter of Videha.
"Sītā, I will tell you something—place your trust in me, my friend; let your fear depart, O fair-thighed one; hear these words of mine."
"There is a wise and aged foremost rakshasa named Avindhya, a well-wisher of Rāma; he spoke to me on your behalf."
"'Tell Sītā in my words, after comforting and reassuring her: your husband Rāma is well, mighty, and accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa.'"
"The illustrious son of Raghu has made alliance with the king of monkeys, whose splendour rivals Indra, and is fully exerting himself on your behalf."
"Let there be no fear in you, timid one, from Rāvaṇa who is condemned by the world—for you are protected by the curse of Nalakūbara, O blameless one."
"For this wicked one was formerly cursed when he touched the young woman Rambhā; the one of uncontrolled senses is incapable of approaching a woman against her will."
"Your husband, wise and guarded by Sugrīva, will come swiftly with the son of Sumitrā and will free you from this torment."
"For I have seen in dreams most terrible and ill-omened signs portending the destruction of this evil-minded one, destroyer of the family of Pulastya."
"For this night-wanderer is cruel, of corrupt soul, of base deeds, and by his very nature and moral wickedness increases the fear of all beings."
"He who vies with all the gods, his mind struck by Time—I have truly seen in my dream the omens of his destruction."
"The ten-faced one, anointed with oil, hair dishevelled, sinking into mud, riding again and again in a chariot drawn by asses, as though dancing."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Kumbhakarṇa and the others too—naked, hair fallen loose, anointed with red garlands and unguents—are dragged toward the southern quarter."
"Vibhīṣaṇa alone, bearing a white parasol, wearing a white turban, adorned with white garlands, mounted a white mountain."
"And his four ministers, adorned with white garlands and white unguents, mounted the white mountain—they will be freed from this great peril."
"The earth with its oceans will be encompassed by Rāma's weapon, and your husband will fill the entire world with his fame."
"And I saw Lakṣmaṇa too, seated on a heap of bones, eating honey-rice pudding and gazing in all directions."
"And you I saw more than once, weeping, your limbs wet with blood, guarded by a tiger, going toward the northern quarter."
"You will attain joy, O daughter of Videha, quickly reunited with your husband; Sītā, you will be with the son of Raghu and his brother before long."
Hearing Trijaṭā's words thus, she of the doe-eyed gaze, that young woman, became filled with hope of reunion with her husband.
Meanwhile the fearsome and utterly dreadful she-demons returned and saw her seated with Trijaṭā, just as before.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, that devoted wife afflicted by grief for her husband, wretched, wearing soiled garments, adorned only with the remnant of her jewels, weeping—
—being attended by rakshasis, seated on a flat rock, Rāvaṇa, tormented by the arrows of desire, saw her and drew near.
He who is unvanquished in battle by gods, danavas, gandharvas, yakshas, and kimpurushas went to the Aśoka grove, bewildered by Kandarpa the god of love.
Wearing divine garments, resplendent, with polished gem-set earrings and a crown of varied garlands, he was like spring embodied.
Though adorned with care, he was like a wish-fulfilling tree—yet even so adorned, he was fearsome like a funeral tree at a cremation ground.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That night-wanderer, approaching near to her of slender waist, appeared beside her like Saturn the slow-moving planet approaching Rohiṇī.
Addressing that beautiful-hipped one, struck by the flower-bannered god's arrow, he spoke thus to the young woman, frightened as the constellation Rohiṇī beset.
"Sītā, this much has been enough—sufficient favour shown to your husband. Be gracious, O slender one; let your adornment be attended to."
"Accept me, O splendid one; wearing ornaments and garments of great worth, be the foremost of all my women, O beautiful one."
"I have daughters of gods, and the wives of royal sages; I have daughters of danavas and women of the daityas as well."
"Fourteen crores of pisachas stand at my command; twice that many man-eating rakshasas of terrible deeds."
"Beyond that, three times as many yakshas who carry out my commands—only a few have taken shelter with my brother Kubera, lord of wealth."
"Gandharvas and apsaras, O auspicious one, O fair-thighed one, always attend upon me when I drink, even as they do my brother."
"I am the son of the brahmin sage Viśravas himself; my fame is renowned as the fifth among the guardians of the worlds."
"Divine foods to eat and drink of all varieties are mine just as they are Indra's, O passionate one."
"Let the evil karma of forest-dwelling be exhausted for you; be my wife, O beautiful-hipped one, even as Mandodarī is."
Thus addressed by him, the daughter of Videha, her face beautiful, turned away and placing a blade of grass between herself and him, spoke to that night-wanderer.
That young woman of exquisitely beautiful thighs, inauspicious in his sight, her two breasts struck together while she continuously rained tears from her eyes—the daughter of Videha, who holds her husband as her god, spoke this word to that wretch.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"O lord of rakshasas, such words as these have been heard by me—unfortunate that I am—from you speaking not once but many times; and they are filled with degradation."
"Therefore, O one fond of the auspicious, may good come to you—turn back your mind; I am another man's wife, unattainable, and ever devoted to my husband."
A human wife is not suitable for you, nor is she your wretched possession. Having violated a helpless woman against her will, what pleasure will you gain?
Your father is a brahmin equal to Prajāpati, born of Brahmā himself — and you, who are compared to a guardian of the worlds, how is it that you do not uphold dharma?
Citing your brother — the king of kings, the friend of Maheśvara, lord and master of wealth — how is it that you feel no shame here?
Having spoken thus, Sītā wept, her breasts trembling and her slender neck quivering, as she covered her face with the edge of her garment.
As that passionate woman wept, her long, neatly bound braid — dark, lustrous, and black — was seen resting on her head like a serpent.
Having heard those harsh words spoken by Sītā, Rāvaṇa, evil-minded though he had been rejected, spoke once more.
"Let the god whose banner bears the sea-monster torment my limbs, O Sītā — I will not approach you, fair-hipped and lovely-smiling one, when you are unwilling."
"What indeed can I do, when even now you keep pining for Rāma — that human who is fit only to be food for us?"
Having said this to the blameless-limbed Sītā, that lord of the host of rākṣasas vanished on the spot and departed in his desired direction.
The princess of Videha, emaciated by grief, surrounded by rākṣasī women and attended upon by Trijaṭā, remained there at that very place.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Rāghava, together with Saumitri, under Sugrīva's protection, dwelling on the summit of Mount Mālyavat, beheld the clear sky.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He, the destroyer of enemies, seeing in the clear sky the spotless moon — its hare-mark distinct — attended by planets, asterisms, and stars,
was suddenly roused from sleep by the cool wind as it carried the fragrance of kumuda, utpala, and lotus flowers, while he stood on the mountain.
At daybreak, filled with sorrow, his mind on the righteous path, recalling Sītā imprisoned in the rākṣasa's dwelling, he addressed the heroic Lakṣmaṇa.
"Go, Lakṣmaṇa, and learn of the lord of monkeys in Kiṣkindhā — that ingrate, clever only in his own interests, intoxicated with the pleasures of the senses."
"That lowest of his line, that fool whom I installed on the throne — all the monkeys with their tufted tails and the bears follow him as their lord."
"O scion of the Raghu line, O mighty-armed one — it was for his sake that Vālin was slain by me alongside you in the forest of Kiṣkindhā."
"I consider him an ungrateful wretch, the vilest of monkeys on earth — that fool, in such a state as he is, does not even acknowledge me today, Lakṣmaṇa."
"I think he does not know the fulfilment of his sworn agreement; with his limited intellect, he surely disregards me, who rendered him such service."
"If he still lies inactive, given over to sensual pleasure, you must send him the way of Vālin — the path that all beings must travel."
"Or if that bull among monkeys is still willing to serve our cause, then bring him here, O Kākutstha — make haste and do not delay."
Thus addressed by his elder brother, Lakṣmaṇa — devoted to the welfare of his guru's words — set forth, taking up his splendid bow strung with a straight bowstring, and reaching the gate of Kiṣkindhā entered it unchallenged.
Perceiving him to be angry, the monkey king Sugrīva, lord of the leaping hosts, went forward to meet him; that self-composed lord of monkeys, together with his wife, received him with joyful honor befitting Lakṣmaṇa's worth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saumitri, who feared nothing, conveyed Rāma's words to him; having heard it all completely, Sugrīva bowed with joined palms.
Sugrīva, lord of monkeys, O king of kings, together with his retinue and wives, pleased, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa, that elephant among men.
"I am not evil-minded, Lakṣmaṇa, nor ungrateful, nor merciless — hear what effort I have made in the search for Sītā."
"All the trained monkeys have been dispatched in every direction by me, and for all of them the time for return was set at one month."
"By them this earth, with its forests, mountains, and cities, girdled by the ocean, with its villages, towns, and mines — all of it was to be searched, O hero."
"That month is due to be completed in five more nights — then, together with Rāma, you will hear exceedingly good tidings."
Thus addressed by that wise lord of monkeys, Lakṣmaṇa — noble-souled and undejected — set aside his anger and honored Sugrīva in return.
Then Sugrīva, approaching Rāma who was stationed on the summit of Mālyavat, reported to him the progress of that undertaking.
Thus those monkey chiefs came back in thousands, having searched three directions — but not those who had gone south.
They reported to Rāma that the earth girdled by the ocean had been searched, but that neither Vaidehī nor Rāvaṇa had been seen.
But as for the bulls among monkeys who had gone toward the southern quarter, Kākutstha, though tormented, held on to his life placing his hope in them.
When nearly two months had elapsed, those leaping ones then hastily approached Sugrīva and spoke these words.
"That great and flourishing Madhu-forest which was guarded by Vālin and then by you, O best of leaping ones — the son of the wind god is now enjoying it."
"Vālin's son Aṅgada and the other bulls among monkeys whom you, O king, dispatched to search the southern quarter —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing that affectionate request of theirs, he concluded that their mission was accomplished — for such is indeed the conduct of servants who have fulfilled their purpose.
That wise bull among monkeys reported it to Rāma, and Rāma too by inference concluded that the Maithilī princess had indeed been seen.
Those leaping ones, with Hanūmān at their head, having rested, came to that lord of monkeys in the presence of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing Hanūmān's gait and the color of his face, Rāma became all the more convinced, O Bhārata, that Sītā had been found.
Those monkeys, with Hanūmān foremost, their hearts full, bowed down in due form before Rāma, Sugrīva, and Lakṣmaṇa.
Taking up his arrow-fitted bow, Rāma spoke to them as they arrived: "Will you restore me to life? Have you accomplished your purpose?"
"Shall I once again rule the kingdom in Ayodhyā, having slain my enemies in battle and recovered the daughter of Janaka?"
"Without freeing Vaidehī and without slaying my foes in battle, robbed of my wife and cast aside, I have no will to live."
To Rāma who had spoken thus, the son of the wind god replied: "I bring you glad tidings, Rāma — I have seen that Jānakī."
"Having searched the southern quarter with its mountains, forests, and mines, we grew weary as time passed and came upon a great cave."
"We entered it — extending for many leagues, dark, thickly forested, impenetrable, teeming with insects."
"After traveling a very great distance, we then saw the light of the sun and right there in the midst of it a divine dwelling."
"It was said to have been the abode of the Daitya Maya, O Rāghava; there an ascetic woman named Prabhāvatī performed her austerities."
"Having eaten the food and various drinks given by her, we regained our strength and then went along the path she had shown us."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Emerging from that place, we saw near the salt-watered sea the Sahya and Malaya ranges and the great mountain Dardura."
"Then, having climbed Malaya and gazing at Varuṇa's ocean, we sat dejected, distressed, despondent, wholly bereft of hope for life."
"Contemplating the great ocean stretching hundreds of leagues in width, the home of timinakra fish and other great sea creatures, we were exceedingly sorrowful."
"Having resolved to fast unto death, we sat there; then, at the end of our talk, the subject of the vulture Jaṭāyu came up."
"Then we saw a bird — terrible in form, terrifying, like another Vainateya — its shape resembling a mountain peak."
"He had intended to eat us, but then he came up and spoke: 'Ho, who is this who speaks of my brother Jaṭāyu?'"
"'I am Saṃpāti by name, the elder brother of Jaṭāyu, lord of birds; the two of us, competing with each other, had soared to the assembly of the Sun.'"
"'Then my wings were burned, but Jaṭāyu's wings were not; at that time, that beloved brother of mine, king of vultures, whom I had not seen for long — and I, my wings utterly scorched, fell onto this great mountain.'"
"As he spoke thus, we reported to him that his brother had been slain; we also briefly informed him of your misfortune."
"Then Saṃpāti, O king, O subduer of foes, having heard that most grievous news, his heart overwhelmed, questioned us further."
"'Who is this Rāma? What has become of Sītā? And how was Jaṭāyu slain? O best of leaping ones, I wish to hear all of this.'"
"I then described to him at length the entire story of your calamity and also the reason for our resolve to fast unto death."
"That king of birds then raised us up with these words: 'Rāvaṇa is known to me, and so is his great city of Laṅkā.'"
"'Vaidehī will be found on the far side of the ocean, in the cave of Mount Trikūṭa — of this I have no doubt.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Hearing his words, we arose quickly and took counsel together about crossing the ocean, O scorcher of foes."
"When no one else resolved to cross the ocean, I then, entering into my father's spirit, leaped across the great sea — a hundred leagues in width — slaying a water-rākṣasī."
"There Sītā was seen by me, a chaste woman in Rāvaṇa's inner apartments — devoted to fasting and austerity, longing to see her husband, her hair matted, her body smeared with grime, emaciated, wretched, an ascetic."
"Having identified that Sītā by various signs, I approached her as she was alone in a secluded spot and addressed that noble lady."
