"'Sītā, I am a monkey, the son of Mārutha, Rāma's messenger — I have come here through the sky, eager to see you.'"
"'The two princes, brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, are well, and are under the protection of Sugrīva, lord of all the tree-dwelling monkeys.'"
"'Rāma enquires after your well-being, Sītā, together with Saumitri; and Sugrīva, in friendship, likewise enquires after your welfare.'"
"'Your husband will come swiftly with all the monkeys; trust me, O queen — I am a monkey, not a rākṣasa.'"
"After reflecting for a moment, Sītā spoke to me: 'I know you to be Hanūmān by the words of Avindhya.'"
"'For Avindhya, O mighty-armed one, is a rākṣasa respected by the elders; by him Sugrīva was described as attended by ministers such as you.'"
"Saying 'You may go,' Sītā gave me this jewel — the one with which the blameless Vaidehī has borne this time of trial."
"For the sake of proof, Jānakī also told this tale: the blade of grass hurled at the crow on the great mountain Citrakūṭa by you, O tiger among men, as a token of recognition."
"Having made him hear it himself, and then having burned that city, I have returned" — so spoke he; and Rāma honored that bearer of glad tidings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, right there where Rāma was seated among them, the foremost of monkeys came together at that time, acting on Sugrīva's command.
Attended by a thousand crores of swift monkeys, the glorious Suṣeṇa — father-in-law of Vālin — approached Rāma.
And the two mighty monkey-lords Gaja and Gavaya, each surrounded by a hundred crore warriors, were seen separately from one another.
O great king, the fearsome Golāṅgūla and Gavākṣa were seen leading sixty thousand crore troops.
The celebrated Gandhamādana, dweller of the Gandhamādana mountain, gathered a thousand crore fierce monkeys.
A monkey named Panasa, wise and of immense strength, led ten, twelve, and thirty-five crore troops.
The illustrious Dadhimukha, an aged monkey yet full of valor, led a vast army of monkeys possessed of terrible energy.
Jāmbavān was seen with a hundred thousand crore of bears — dark ones with face-markings, doers of terrible deeds.
These and many other leaders of monkey troops, innumerable, O great king, came together for the sake of Rāma.
A tumultuous sound was heard everywhere of those rushing about — roaring like lions, radiant as shirisha blossoms.
Some were like mountain peaks, some resembled great buffaloes, some shone like autumnal clouds, some had complexions red as powdered vermillion.
Monkeys leaping up, falling down, and bounding forward, while others raised clouds of dust, came together from all directions.
That vast multitude of monkeys, resembling the full ocean, made camp there at that time by Sugrīva's command.
Then, when all the monkey chiefs had assembled on every side, on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable asterism, at a well-honored muhurta,
the illustrious Rāghava set forth with Sugrīva, leading that arrayed army as if to turn the worlds upside down.
Hanūmān, son of the Wind-god, led the van of the army, while Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, fearless of all, guarded the rear.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The two Rāghavas, with leather finger-guards strapped on, shone there surrounded by the great monkey chiefs, like the moon and sun surrounded by planets.
That monkey army, armed with sala trees, palm trees, and rocks, shone brilliantly like a vast field of rice at sunrise.
That great army, protected by Nala, Nīla, Aṅgada, Krātha, Mainda, and Dvivida, marched forth for the accomplishment of Rāghava's purpose.
Halting duly at duly auspicious places abounding in roots and fruits, rich in honey and meat, with water and pleasant surroundings,
staying without disturbance on mountain slopes as well, that monkey army at last reached the salt sea, the ocean.
That army, like a second ocean, with its many banners, upon reaching the seashore forest, made camp there.
Then the illustrious son of Daśaratha spoke to Sugrīva in the midst of the monkey chiefs, saying these timely words:
"What plan do you all consider best for crossing the ocean? This army is great, and the ocean is difficult to cross."
Some monkeys who thought themselves clever spoke up there saying that some monkeys were capable of leaping across the ocean, but not all.
Some proposed boats, others various kinds of rafts. Rāma pacified them all and replied, "No" —
"Not all the monkeys are capable of crossing this sea, a hundred yojanas wide, O heroes. That is not the final plan for you."
"There are not enough ships to ferry this whole army, and how could one like us bring harm to merchants? That is not acceptable."
"Our army is spread wide, and the enemy would strike at gaps. Crossing by rafts or boats does not please me here."
"I shall address this ocean through means — I will lie in fast, and it will then reveal itself to me."
"If it will not show me a way, I shall then burn it up with my irresistible great weapons, blazing more fiercely than fire and wind."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, sipped water and ritually lay down on a bed of kusa grass facing the ocean.
Then the ocean, lord of rivers and streams, the god surrounded by hosts of aquatic creatures, appeared to Rāghava in a dream.
Addressing him sweetly as "Son of Kausalyā," and surrounded by hundreds of treasure-mines, the ocean spoke thus:
"Tell me, what assistance shall I render you here, O bull among men?" And Rāma replied, "I am of the Ikṣvāku lineage; you are my kinsman."
"I desire a path granted for my army, O lord of rivers and streams, by which I may go and slay the ten-headed one, Rāvaṇa, disgrace of the Pulastyas."
"If you do not grant the path I thus beseech, I shall dry you up with arrows charged with divine weapon-spells."
Hearing Rāma speak thus, the abode of Varuṇa, greatly distressed, stood with folded hands and spoke these words:
"I do not wish to oppose you; I am not an obstacle to you. Hear this word, O Rāma, and having heard it, act accordingly."
"If I give your army a path by command, others too will command me thus by the force of their bows."
"There is, however, a monkey named Nala here, regarded as a craftsman, the mighty son of the divine Tvaṣṭṛ, Viśvakarman."
"Whatever wood, grass, or rock he casts upon me, I shall bear all of it — it will become a bridge for you."
When that one had spoken and disappeared, Rāma said to Nala: "Build a bridge across the ocean — you are capable of it in my judgment."
By that means, the descendant of Kākutstha had the bridge built — ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long.
Known as "Nala's bridge," it is still renowned on earth even today, mountain-like, maintained under Rāma's command.
Then righteous Vibhīṣaṇa, brother of the king of the rakshasas, came to him there with four ministers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The magnanimous Rāma received him with a welcome. But Sugrīva was suspicious, thinking he might be a spy.
When Rāghava was truly satisfied by Vibhīṣaṇa's conduct, behavior, and deportment, he then honored him.
He anointed Vibhīṣaṇa as king over all the realm of the rakshasas, and made him a counselor-companion and friend of Lakṣmaṇa.
And on Vibhīṣaṇa's advice, he crossed the great ocean with his army by that bridge — in just one month, O lord of men.
Then, having gone and reached Laṅkā, he had the many great gardens of Laṅkā broken and destroyed by the monkeys.
There were two rakshasa ministers of Rāvaṇa, Śuka and Sāraṇa, who had taken monkey form as spies — Vibhīṣaṇa caught them.
When those two night-rangers had reverted to their rakshasa forms and shown themselves, Rāma thereafter released them after showing the army.
Having settled the army in the grove, that heroic one then sent the wise monkey Aṅgada as an emissary to Rāvaṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having settled the army in that forest abounding in food, water, roots, and fruits, the descendant of Kākutstha duly kept guard.
And Rāvaṇa made the prescribed arrangements in Laṅkā as ordained by the scriptures. By its very nature Laṅkā was hard to assail, with sturdy ramparts and gateways.
There were seven moats, fathomless in water, swarming with fish and crocodiles, difficult to overcome, studded with stakes of khadira wood.
The battlements were formidable with their machines and projecting cornices, with sharp-edged stones, fighters with pots of venomous serpents, and dust mixed with poisonous resin.
They were furnished with pestles, firebrands, nārācas, tomaras, swords, axes, sataghnīs, and clubs smeared with pitch.
At every city gate there were stationary and mobile guard-posts, with abundant infantry, elephants, and horses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Aṅgada approached the gateway of Laṅkā, made himself known to the king of the rakshasas, and entered fearlessly.
Of immense strength, in the midst of many crores of rakshasas, he shone like the sun surrounded by rows of clouds.
Approaching Rāvaṇa, son of Paulastya, surrounded by his ministers, and announcing Rāma's message, the eloquent one began to speak.
"O king, Rāghava, lord of Kosala, of great renown, says this timely message to you — receive it and act upon it:
'When they encounter a king of uncontrolled self who revels in wrongdoing, lands and cities possessed by that wrongdoing perish.'
'You alone have wronged me by forcibly abducting Sītā — yet this will bring about the killing of others who have not wronged me.'
'The forest-dwellers and sages who were harmed by you, seized by arrogance and pride of strength, and the gods too who were dishonored —'
'— and the royal sages who were slain, and the weeping women who were carried off — this fruit of that wrongdoing of yours has now arrived.'
'I shall slay you along with your ministers. Fight — be a man! Behold the power of my bow, O night-ranger, though I am but human.'
'Let Jānakī Sītā be released. You shall never escape from me. I shall make this world free of rakshasas with my sharpened arrows.'
Hearing those harsh words of the messenger as he spoke thus, king Rāvaṇa, overcome with rage, did not endure them.
Then four night-rangers, skilled in reading their master's signs, seized him at four limbs, as birds would seize a tiger.
Aṅgada, taking those night-rangers as they clung to his limbs, leapt into the sky and landed on the roof of the palace.
As he flew up with great speed, those night-rangers fell to the ground with crushed hearts, tormented by his blows.
Freed from that palace roof, he leapt again, cleared the city of Laṅkā entirely, and landed near his own army.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, having gone to the lord of Kosala and reported everything, that glorious Aṅgada rested, honored by Rāghava.
Then the delight of the Raghu line, with the full assault of the wind-swift monkeys, broke through the rampart of Laṅkā.
And Lakṣmaṇa, placing Vibhīṣaṇa and the lord of bears at the front, crushed the southern city gate, which was hard to assail.
Then a hundred thousand crore of battle-skilled monkeys with reddish-brown limbs like elephant trunks attacked Laṅkā.
With monkeys leaping up, falling down, and swooping, the sun could not be seen at that time — its radiance destroyed by the dust.
With monkeys resembling rice-blossoms, shining like shirisha flowers, like the young sun, and fair as autumn reeds —
— the rakshasas, O king, along with their women and elders, marveled to see the rampart turned tawny on all sides.
They shattered the jewelled pillars and the turret-tops of the ramparts, and hurled away the war-engines, their mechanisms broken and crushed by the force.
The mighty ones seized the śataghnis — fitted with wheels and loaded with spiked stones — and flung them by the strength of their arms into the midst of Laṅkā.
Whatever bands of night-roamers stood upon the battlements then fled in hundreds, driven away by the onslaught of the monkeys.
Then, at the king's command, the shape-shifting rākṣasas poured out in hundreds of thousands, wearing hideous forms.
Raining down showers of weapons and routing the forest-dwellers, they cleared the ramparts and stood forth in supreme valor.
By those night-wanderers resembling heaps of black gram — terrible to behold — the battlements were once again cleared of monkeys.
Many foremost monkeys fell with their bodies pierced by spears; and there too the night-roamers fell with pillars and gate-arches shattered upon them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A hair-grappling battle raged between the rākṣasas and the monkeys, the warriors tearing at each other with claws and teeth.
Groaning on both sides, those monkeys and rākṣasas, slain and fallen to the ground, did not release their grip on one another even then.
Rāma for his part rained volleys of arrows like a thunder-cloud; reaching Laṅkā, those arrows slew the night-wanderers.
And Saumitri too, with iron arrows, his bow firm and his weariness conquered, selecting his marks one after another, felled the rākṣasas stationed in the fortress.
Then, by Rāghava's command, the armies withdrew, having wrought destruction in Laṅkā, the objective gained and victory assured.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, as those soldiers were retiring to camp, some of Rāvaṇa's followers — troops of piśācas and lesser rākṣasas — fell upon them.
Among them were Parvana, Pūtanā, Jambha, Khara, Krodhavaśa, Hari, Prarujas, Āruja, Praghasas, and others of that ilk.
Then, as those evil-souled ones swooped down while remaining invisible, Vibhīṣaṇa, who knew the secret of slaying those concealed, worked their destruction.
Made visible, O king, they were slain on all sides by the powerful monkeys who struck from afar, and fell lifeless to the earth.
Then Rāvaṇa, unable to endure this, sallied forth with his full force, arraying the formation known as the Cauśanasa, and drove against all the monkeys.
But Rāghava, marching out to meet the ten-faced one who had drawn up his army, adopted the Bārhaspatya disposition and counter-arrayed against the demon.
Coming together there, Rāvaṇa fought with Rāma; and Lakṣmaṇa likewise fought with Indrajit.
Sugrīva fought with Virūpākṣa; Nikharvaṭa with Tāra; and Nala there with Tuṇḍa, and Paṭuśa with Panasa.
Whoever deemed another his match engaged him: each at the hour of battle took his stand relying on the strength of his own arms.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That encounter grew fierce, multiplying terror in the timid, raising the hair on end, dreadful as the ancient war of gods and demons.
Rāvaṇa assailed Rāma with showers of śaktis, spears, and swords of sharp iron; and Rāghava likewise assailed Rāvaṇa.
So too did Lakṣmaṇa strike the alert Indrajit with arrows that pierced vital points; and Indrajit in turn struck Saumitri with many shafts.
Vibhīṣaṇa fought with Prahasta, and Prahasta with Vibhīṣaṇa, each drenching the other with sharp arrows feathered with bird-plumes, unwavering in the fight.
The clash of those mighty wielders of great weapons was such that all three worlds, with all their moving and unmoving creatures, trembled.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Prahasta, rough in battle, suddenly charged at Vibhīṣaṇa and struck him with his mace, roaring aloud.
Though struck by that mace of terrible force, the wise and mighty-armed Vibhīṣaṇa did not waver — firm as the Himālaya itself.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, seizing his great missile adorned with a hundred bells, charged it with a mighty spell and hurled it straight at Prahasta's head.
Struck by it as it fell with the roar of a thunderbolt, the rākṣasa was seen with his head torn away, like a tree shattered by the wind.
Seeing Prahasta, that night-roamer, slain in battle, Dhūmrākṣa charged with great speed against the monkeys.
Seeing his army rushing forward, fearful to behold like a storm-cloud, the foremost monkeys were suddenly panic-stricken in the battle.
Then, seeing those foremost monkeys suddenly seized with fear, Hanūmān — tiger among monkeys — issued forth and stood firm before them.
Seeing the son of the Wind standing steady in the fight, O king, the monkeys rallied with great swiftness on every side.
Then a great tumultuous clamor arose, thrilling the hair on end, as the armies of Rāma and Rāvaṇa charged against each other.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As that dreadful battle raged, turning the ground to a mire of blood, Dhūmrākṣa routed the monkey host with his arrows.
Hanūmān, son of the Wind, that slayer of enemies, swiftly intercepted that great minister among rākṣasas as he charged forward.
A dreadful battle ensued between those two heroes — monkey and rākṣasa — each striving to conquer the other in combat, like Indra and Prahlāda of old.
The rākṣasa struck the monkey with maces and iron clubs; and the monkey struck the demon with trees — branches and boughs and all.
Then the wise Hanūmān, son of the Wind, slew the massive-bodied Dhūmrākṣa along with his horses, chariot, and charioteer.
Then, seeing that foremost rākṣasa Dhūmrākṣa slain, the monkeys, their confidence restored, closed in and struck down the enemy soldiers.
Slaughtered by those powerful, victorious monkeys, the rākṣasas, their resolve broken, fled in terror toward Laṅkā.
Those night-wanderers, routed and reduced to the remnant that survived, rushed into the city and reported all that had happened to King Rāvaṇa.
Hearing from them that Prahasta had been slain in battle, and Dhūmrākṣa the great bowman along with his army, by those foremost of monkeys —
— Rāvaṇa breathed a long sigh, sprang from his excellent throne, and said: "The time for Kumbhakarṇa's work has come."
Having said so, he had Kumbhakarṇa — who lay plunged in deepest slumber — roused by various instruments of enormously loud sound.
Having with great effort awakened him — with no trace of distress upon himself — the lord of rākṣasas waited until he sat composed and alert and free of sleep; then Daśagrīva spoke to the mighty Kumbhakarṇa:
"You are fortunate, Kumbhakarṇa, that your sleep is such — for you know nothing of this dreadful time of great peril.
This Rāma, crossing the ocean with a bridge and with his monkeys, holds us all in contempt and is working great carnage here.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I carried off his wife, Sītā by name, the daughter of Janaka; and to rescue her he has come, having built a bridge across the great ocean.
By him, Prahasta and many other great kinsmen of ours have been slain. There is no one but you to kill him, O afflicitor of enemies.
So gird yourself and march out today, O best of the mighty, and slay all the enemies — Rāma and the rest — in battle, O subduer of foes.
The two younger brothers of Dūṣaṇa — Vajravega and Pramāthin — will follow you with great strength at your side."
Having spoken thus, the lord of rākṣasas instructed the swift Kumbhakarṇa in what must be done, and likewise Vajravega and Pramāthin.
Saying "So be it" to Rāvaṇa, those two warriors — the younger brothers of Dūṣaṇa — placing Kumbhakarṇa at their head, quickly marched out of the city.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Kumbhakarṇa, having issued forth from the city with his followers, beheld that monkey army standing before him with the bearing of victors.
The monkeys quickly rushed up to him, surrounding him on all sides; some struck him with many great tree-trunks, others raked him with their claws — casting aside all fear.
Those monkeys, fighting in many ways by many modes of warfare, struck the dreadful lord of rākṣasas with every manner of weapon.
As he was being struck he laughed and began to devour the monkeys — Panasa, Gavākṣa, and the monkey Vajrabāhu among them.
Seeing the devastating deeds of Kumbhakarṇa the demon, Tāra and the other monkey chiefs cried out in terror.
Seeing Tāra crying out and the other monkey chieftains in distress, Sugrīva charged at Kumbhakarṇa without fear.
Then that great-souled foremost of monkeys charged swiftly and struck Kumbhakarṇa on the head with a śāla tree, with great force.
Though the great-souled, swift Sugrīva split the śāla tree upon Kumbhakarṇa's head, the monkey did not succeed in paining him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Kumbhakarṇa, roused by the touch of the śāla tree, roared with laughter, seized Sugrīva in both arms, and carried him off by force.
Seeing Sugrīva being carried off by the demon Kumbhakarṇa, the heroic Saumitri — the joy of his friends — rushed forward.
Charging in, Lakṣmaṇa — slayer of enemy heroes — dispatched a great arrow with golden fletching at Kumbhakarṇa with tremendous force.
That shaft, piercing through his armor and his body, passed on and split the earth, drenched in blood.
His heart thus pierced, Kumbhakarṇa the great bowman released the king of monkeys, and — taking up a massive boulder for a weapon — charged at Saumitri, raising the great rock aloft.
As he charged swiftly, Lakṣmaṇa severed his two upraised arms with two razor-headed shafts of keen edge; he became four-armed.
All those arms of his too, still grasping their boulder-weapons, Saumitri severed with razor-arrows, displaying swiftness of hand in archery.
Though he grew even more immense and many-footed and many-headed and many-armed, Saumitri burned him — mountain-piled as he was — with the Brahmāstra.
That mighty warrior, struck by the divine weapon, fell in battle — scorched as if by a mighty thunderbolt, like a flowering tree blasted down.
Seeing the swift Kumbhakarṇa — terrible as Vṛtra — lifeless and fallen to the ground, the rākṣasas fled in fear.
Seeing those warriors fleeing thus, the two younger brothers of Dūṣaṇa rallied the troops and then, blazing with fury, charged at Saumitri.
Saumitri received those two — Vajravega and Pramāthin — as they charged in fury, meeting them both with arrows, roaring aloud.
Then a very tumultuous battle ensued, thrilling the hair on end, O Pārtha, between the two brothers of Dūṣaṇa and the wise Lakṣmaṇa.
He drenched those two rākṣasas with a great rain of arrows; and those two fierce warriors, furious, drenched him in return — both of them together.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For a moment the dreadful combat between Vajravega and Pramāthin on one side and the mighty-armed Saumitri on the other continued thus.
Then Hanūmān, son of the Wind, seizing a mountain peak, charged and took the life of the demon Vajravega.
And Nīla the monkey, of great strength, charging with a huge rock, crushed Pramāthin — the younger brother of Dūṣaṇa.
Then the battle broke out again, bitter and fierce, as the armies of Rāma and Rāvaṇa charged at one another.
The forest-dwellers slew the demons by the hundreds, and the demons slew the forest-dwellers in turn; yet in that place it was the demons who were chiefly slain, and not the monkeys.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, upon hearing that Kumbhakarṇa together with his followers had been slain in battle, and also the great archer Prahasta, and the exceedingly fierce Dhūmrākṣa,
Rāvaṇa addressed his valiant son Indrajit: "O slayer of enemies, kill Rāma, and Sugrīva together with Lakṣmaṇa."
"For it is by you, O good son, that blazing glory has been won for me — by conquering in battle the bearer of the thunderbolt, the thousand-eyed lord of Śacī."
"Whether hidden or visible, with your divine arrows whose boons have been granted, slay our enemies, O destroyer of foes, O best among those who bear weapons for my sake."
"Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sugrīva are not capable of enduring the touch of your arrows, O sinless one — how much less, then, their followers?"
"The vengeance for Khara that was left unaccomplished by Prahasta and Kumbhakarṇa in battle — go and accomplish that, O mighty-armed one."
"Today, having slain the enemies together with their forces by your sharp arrows, delight me, my son, as you once did by binding Vāsava himself."
Thus addressed, Indrajit replied "So be it," and clad in armour, mounting his chariot, he quickly set out toward the battlefield, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There that foremost of rakshasas, having announced his name clearly, challenged Lakṣmaṇa of auspicious marks to combat.
Lakṣmaṇa too rushed at him, grasping his arrow-strung bow, terrifying him with the slap of his palm, as a lion intimidates a lesser beast.
Between those two, eager for victory, both versed in divine weapons, a mighty and fierce battle arose, each striving to outdo the other.
When Rāvaṇa's son could not gain the upper hand over him with arrows, that best of the mighty redoubled his effort.
Then he assailed him with javelins of great speed; but Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, cut them down with sharp arrows. Severed by the keen arrows, they fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then the glorious Aṅgada, son of Vālī, swift as the wind, snatched up a tree and rushing forward struck him on the head.
Unshaken, the valiant Indrajit wished to strike him on the chest with a spear; but Lakṣmaṇa cut that spear of his to pieces.
The son of Rāvaṇa then struck that hero Aṅgada, the foremost of monkeys, who had come close, with his mace on the left flank.
That powerful son of Vālī, the slayer of enemies, paying no heed to the blow, hurled in fury at Indrajit the trunk of a shala tree.
That tree, hurled in wrath by Aṅgada to destroy Indrajit, O Pārtha, smashed Indrajit's chariot together with its horses and charioteer.
Then, leaping down from the chariot whose horses had been slain, his charioteer killed, that son of Rāvaṇa vanished on that very spot through his power of illusion, O king.
Knowing that the demon possessed of many illusions had become invisible, Rāma came to that place and stood guard over his army.
Then, aiming at Rāma with his boon-given arrows, he pierced him all over his limbs, and likewise the great warrior Lakṣmaṇa.
Both heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, fought against that Rāvaṇa's son who was hidden by illusion and invisible, shooting arrows at him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He, in fury, released arrows upon every limb of those two lion-men, again and again, by the hundreds and thousands.
Seeking him who was invisible yet ceaselessly releasing arrows, the monkeys entered the sky grasping great boulders.
And those two as well as all the monkeys — the invisible demon pierced with arrows; that hero, the son of Rāvaṇa, veiled by illusion, struck them violently.
Those two heroic brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, covered with arrows, fell from the sky to the earth like the sun and moon fallen from heaven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Seeing those two brothers of boundless might both fallen, the son of Rāvaṇa then again bound them with his boon-given arrows.
Those two tiger-men, bound in battle by Indrajit in a net of arrows, lay there shining like two birds in a cage.
Seeing those two fallen on the ground, covered with hundreds of arrows, Sugrīva stood there surrounding them together with the monkeys.
The lord of monkeys stood there with Suṣeṇa, Mainda, Dvivida, Kumuda, Aṅgada, Hanūmān, Nīla, Tāra, and Nala.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, who had accomplished his task, came to that place and awakened those two heroes; they were revived by the weapon of wisdom.
Sugrīva also rendered them both free of arrows in an instant, using the great herb Viśalyā, applied with divine incantations.
Those two best of men, having regained consciousness and freed of arrows, rose up; both great warriors were in an instant free of fatigue and exhaustion.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, O Pārtha, seeing Rāma the joy of the Ikṣvāku line free of fever, spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
"This water has been brought: by order of the king of kings, a Guhyaka has come from Mount Śveta to your presence, O subduer of enemies."
"This water, O scorcher of foes, the great king Kubera offers to you, so that you may behold beings that are hidden from sight."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"One whose eyes are touched by this will see beings that are hidden; and so too will anyone to whom you give it."
Saying "So be it," Rāma received that water with due honour and purified his eyes with it; and the great-souled Lakṣmaṇa did likewise.
Sugrīva and Jāmbavān, Hanūmān, Aṅgada, Mainda, Dvivida, Nīla — all the foremost among the monkeys did the same.
And it came to pass just as Vibhīṣaṇa had said: in an instant, O Yudhiṣṭhira, their eyes became capable of perceiving the supersensible.
But Indrajit, having accomplished his deed, reported his exploit to his father and then came back swiftly toward the sacrificial ground.
Lakṣmaṇa, acting on Vibhīṣaṇa's counsel, rushed forward against him as he came charging in fury once more with desire for battle.
Lakṣmaṇa, fully alert, in great fury, wishing to slay him before he could perform his daily rites, struck with arrows that one who bore the air of a conqueror.
A battle arose between those two, each striving to conquer the other, exceedingly marvellous and wonderful, like the combat of Śakra and Prahlāda.
Indrajit pierced the son of Sumitrā with sharp arrows that struck the vital points; and the son of Sumitrā pierced the son of Rāvaṇa with arrows that burned like fire.
Maddened with rage from the touch of the son of Sumitrā's arrows, the son of Rāvaṇa released eight shafts at Lakṣmaṇa, each comparable to a venomous serpent.
How that hero, the son of Sumitrā, drew out his vital breaths with three feathered arrows whose touch was like fire — hear me as I tell it.
With one arrow he severed the bow-bearing arm from his body; with a second he sent to the ground the arm along with its iron-shafted arrows.
With a third arrow, broad-bladed and blazing, he severed the handsome head with its bright-gleaming earrings and well-shaped nose.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having slain that headless trunk with its arms and shoulders cut off — terrible to behold — that best of the mighty then slew the charioteer too with his weapons.
The horses then drove the chariot into Laṅkā; and Rāvaṇa saw that chariot bereft of his son.
Seeing his son slain, Rāvaṇa, his eyes bewildered with terror, overwhelmed by grief and delusion, rose up with intent to kill the daughter of Videha.
That evil-souled one seized his sword and rushed swiftly upon her who dwelt in the Aśoka grove, longing to behold Rāma.
Seeing that wicked resolve of the evil-minded one, Avindhya appeased his fury — hear by what reasoning.
"Established in your blazing great sovereignty, you ought not to slay a woman. She is as good as already slain — she is a woman and imprisoned in your house."
"It is my view that she should not be killed by destroying her body. Kill her husband instead; when he is slain, she will be slain."
"For none equals you in valour, not even the hundred-sacrificed Indra himself — it was you who more than once drove the gods together with Indra to terror in battle."
With such diverse arguments Avindhya then pacified the enraged Rāvaṇa, and Rāvaṇa took those words to heart.
Having made up his mind to march out, that night-roamer laid aside his sword and commanded: "Let my chariot be made ready."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, furious at the fall of his beloved son, marched out riding a chariot adorned with gold and jewels.
Surrounded by terrible rakshasas bearing various weapons in their hands, he charged toward Rāma, crushing the leaders of the monkey troops.
Mainda, Nīla, Nala, Aṅgada, Hanūmān, and Jāmbavān, together with their forces, surrounded him as he charged in fury.
Those leaders of bear and monkey troops shattered Rāvaṇa's army with trees, as Rāvaṇa watched.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, seeing his own army being slaughtered by the foes, Rāvaṇa the lord of rakshasas, master of illusion, deployed his illusion.
Hundreds and thousands of rakshasas issued forth from his body and became visible, holding arrows, spears, and javelins in their hands.
Rāma slew all those rakshasas with his divine weapon; but then the lord of rakshasas deployed yet another illusion.
Assuming the forms of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, O Bhārata, the ten-faced one charged toward both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Then those night-wanderers, assailing Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with those forms, advanced upon them, O king, with bows drawn high.
Seeing that illusion of the lord of rakshasas, Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, the delight of the Ikṣvākus, unperturbed, spoke these bold words to Rāma:
"Slay these evil rakshasas who have assumed your likeness!" And Rāma slew those and others who had taken on his likeness.
Then Mātali, charioteer of Indra, came up to Rāma on the battlefield in a chariot yoked with tawny horses and blazing like the sun.
Mātali said: "This is the victorious, best of chariots of Indra, yoked with tawny horses. With this noble chariot, O Kākutstha, O tiger of men, Indra slew the Daityas and Dānavas by the hundreds in battle."
"Therefore, O tiger of men, mount this chariot brought by me — the same one — and swiftly slay Rāvaṇa; do not delay."
Thus addressed, the Rāghava doubted the truth of Mātali's words — thinking: "This may be the demon's illusion" — and Vibhīṣaṇa said to him:
"This is not the illusion of the evil-souled Rāvaṇa, O tiger of men. Therefore mount this chariot of Indra quickly, O greatly resplendent one."
Then the Kākutstha, greatly delighted, saying "So be it" to Vibhīṣaṇa, swiftly charged upon the ten-necked Rāvaṇa with that chariot, filled with fury.
As Rāvaṇa was charged upon, cries of "Alas! Alas!" arose from all beings; lion-roars with kettle-drums resounded in the sky, and divine sounds rang out.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That night-wanderer hurled at Rāma a most terrible trident, comparable to Indra's thunderbolt, like the rod of Brahmā raised aloft.
Rāma cut that trident in mid-flight with his keen arrows; seeing that feat so hard to accomplish, fear entered Rāvaṇa.
Then the ten-headed one, enraged, quickly hurled against Rāma sharp arrows by the thousands and ten-thousands, and weapons of every kind.
He also launched iron clubs, spears, pestles, battle-axes, lances of every shape, hundred-slayers, and razor-edged missiles.
Beholding that terrible sorcery of the ten-necked demon, all the monkeys fled in terror in every direction.
Then Kākutstha took from his quiver that supreme arrow — well-feathered, fair-nocked, gold-flighted — and charged it with the Brahmā-weapon.
Seeing that best of arrows consecrated by Rāma with the Brahmā-weapon, the gods and Gandharvas headed by Indra rejoiced.
Then the gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras understood that only a little of the demon's life remained, seeing the enemy discharge the Brahmā-weapon.
Then Rāma released that arrow of matchless energy — dreadful, the very end of Rāvaṇa — like Brahmā's staff raised on high.
Struck by it, that foremost of demons blazed up together with his chariot, horses, and charioteer, wrapped in a great fire and engulfed in flames.
Then the thirty gods, together with Gandharvas and Cāraṇas, were filled with joy upon seeing Rāvaṇa slain by Rāma of effortless deeds.
The five great elements abandoned the illustrious Rāvaṇa, for by the power of the Brahmā-weapon he was cast out from all the worlds.
His bodily constituents — flesh and blood alike — were utterly consumed by the Brahmā-weapon; not even ashes were to be seen.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having slain that base enemy of the gods, the lord of the Rākṣasas Rāvaṇa, Rāma became filled with delight together with his friends and with Saumitri.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, with the ten-headed one slain, the gods led by the sages honored that mighty-armed hero with blessings of victory.
All the divinities praised lotus-eyed Rāma; the Gandharvas and dwellers in the celestial realm rained flowers upon him and glorified him with hymns.
Having honored Rāma as was fitting, they returned the way they had come; the sky, O Acyuta, looked like a great festival.
Then Rāma of great fame, conqueror of enemy cities, having slain the ten-headed one, gave Laṅkā as a gift to Vibhīṣaṇa.
Then Avindhya, a wise old minister, leading Sītā — who had been placed under Vibhīṣaṇa's escort — came forward.
And he spoke to the great-souled Kākutstha, who stood humbled: 'Great soul, receive the Lady Jānakī, she who is of virtuous conduct.'
Hearing those words from him and descending from his excellent chariot, the scion of the Ikṣvāku line beheld Sītā whose face was veiled in tears.
He saw her — lovely in every limb yet wasted by grief as she sat in her palanquin, her whole body smeared with grime, her hair matted, clad in dark garments.
Rāma, troubled by suspicion of her having been touched, spoke to Vaidehī: 'Go, Vaidehī, you are free; what needed to be done has been done by me.'
'So that you, auspicious one, having me as your husband, should not grow old in a demon's dwelling — for that reason this night-ranger has been slain by me.'
'For how could one like me, knowing the settled rule of dharma, accept even for a moment a woman who has passed into another man's hands?'
'Whether you have kept good conduct or not, O Maithilī, I cannot bring myself to take you back for enjoyment — like an oblation licked by a dog.'
Then that young goddess, having suddenly heard those cruel words, fell to the ground in anguish, like a plantain tree cut down.
For the flush of joy that had risen to her face vanished in an instant, like breath from a mirror.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all those monkeys, hearing Rāma's speech, stood motionless as if bereft of life, along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Then the god of pure soul, the four-faced Grandsire, creator of the world, revealed himself to Rāghava in his celestial vehicle.
Indra and Agni and Vāyu, Yama and Varuṇa, the blessed lord of the Yakṣas, and the seven pure sages as well —
— and King Daśaratha too, his form radiant with divine splendor, in a magnificent celestial vehicle yoked with swans and blazing with light —
Then all that sky, filled with gods and Gandharvas, shone beautifully, dotted with stars, like the autumn firmament.
Then Vaidehī, the auspicious and glorious one, rising up in the midst of them, spoke these words to broad-chested Rāma:
'O prince, I bear you no anger, for I know well the way of men toward women. But hear these words of mine.
'Mātariśvan, who ever moves within all living beings, let him release my life-breath if I have committed any sin.
'Fire, water, sky, earth, and wind — let them all release my life-breath if I have committed any sin.'
Then from the sky arose a voice resounding in all directions, holy and filling those great-souled monkeys with joy.
Vāyu said: 'Ho, Rāghava! I am indeed Vāyu, who ever moves without ceasing. Maithilī is sinless, O king; be united with your wife.'
Agni said: 'I dwell within the bodies of all beings, O joy of the Raghus. Not even in the subtlest degree has Maithilī transgressed, O Kākutstha.'
Varuṇa said: 'The vital fluids that pervade the bodies of all beings spring from me, O Rāghava. I declare to you: let Maithilī be received back.'
Brahmā said: 'Son, this is no wonder in you who uphold the dharma of a royal sage, O virtuous one who walks the path of right conduct. Hear these words of mine.
'This enemy of the gods, Gandharvas, Bhogins, Yakṣas, Dānavas, and great sages has been laid low by you, O hero.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'He had formerly become unkillable by all beings through my grace, and for some reason this sinful one was overlooked for a time.
'Sītā was abducted by that evil-souled one so as to bring about his own death, and I arranged her protection through the curse of Nalakūbara.
'For it was declared of old that if he were to violate any woman against her will, his body would assuredly split into a hundred pieces.
'You must harbor no doubt here; receive her back, O greatly resplendent one. A great service to the gods has been done by you, O one equal to the immortals.'
Daśaratha said: 'I am pleased, dear child; may good come to you. I am your father Daśaratha. I grant you permission — rule the kingdom, O best of men.'
Rāma said: 'I pay homage to you, O king of kings. If you are indeed my father, then by your command I shall go to the beautiful city of Ayodhyā.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: His father spoke to him again, greatly delighted, O lord of men: 'Go to Ayodhyā and rule it, O Rāma of red-cornered eyes.'
Then, having bowed to the gods and been celebrated by his friends, he was reunited with his wife, even as Mahendra with Paulomī.
Then the scorcher of foes granted a boon to Avindhya, and he appointed the Rākṣasī Trijaṭā, who had been sought for her virtuous service, to tend Sītā.
Then Brahmā, surrounded by the gods headed by Indra, spoke to him: 'O son of Kausalyā, what boons do you desire? I grant them to you today.'
Rāma chose steadfastness in dharma, invincibility against enemies, and the revival of the monkeys who had been slain by the Rākṣasas.
Then, O great king, when Brahmā had spoken those words 'so be it,' the monkeys rose up, their consciousness restored.
The greatly blessed Sītā too granted a boon to Hanūmān: 'Your life, my son, shall be equal to the fame of Rāma.'
'And divine pleasures, granted by my favor, shall always be present for you, O Hanūmān' — so she spoke, O monkey-eyed one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, as those men of effortless deeds looked on, all the gods headed by Indra vanished from sight.
But Mātali, charioteer of Indra, seeing Rāma reunited with Jānakī, was filled with the greatest joy and spoke these words in the midst of the friends:
'The suffering of gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, humans, Asuras, and Bhogins has been removed by you, O true hero of real valor.'
'The worlds — gods, Asuras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and serpents — shall sing of you for as long as the earth endures.'
Having thus spoken and taken leave of Rāma, best of weapon-bearers, and having duly honored him, Mātali departed in that chariot blazing like the sun.
Then Rāma, placing Sītā at his side, together with Saumitri and all the monkeys headed by Sugrīva,
having arranged the protection of Laṅkā with Vibhīṣaṇa at the fore, crossed again over the sea — the abode of sea-monsters — by that same bridge.
Accompanied by his chief ministers as was fitting, the self-controlled one traveled in the Puṣpaka celestial vehicle, that sky-farer blazing with splendor, that goes wherever one wishes.
Then at the shore of the ocean, at the very place where that king had rested before, the righteous-souled one halted together with all the monkeys.
Then, in due time, Rāghava summoned them, honored them, satisfied them thoroughly with jewels, and dismissed them.
When the monkey-lords and the bear-tailed bears had departed, Rāma together with Sugrīva returned once more to Kiṣkindhā.
Accompanied by Vibhīṣaṇa and together with Sugrīva, he showed Vaidehī the forests from the Puṣpaka celestial vehicle.
Having arrived at Kiṣkindhā, Rāma, best of warriors, consecrated Aṅgada — who had distinguished himself in battle — as crown prince.
Then Rāma, together with those same companions and with Saumitri, set out toward his own city by the same way they had come.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having approached the city of Ayodhyā, the lord of the realm then dispatched Hanūmān as a messenger to Bharata.
Having read all of Bharata's signals and reported the glad tidings to him, when the son of Vāyu returned, Rāma went to Nandigrāma.
There he saw Bharata, his body smeared with grime, clad in bark garments, seated upon a seat with the sandals placed before him.
Having met with Bharata and with Śatrughna, O bull among Bhāratas, the valiant Rāghava rejoiced together with Saumitri.
Likewise Bharata and Śatrughna, reunited with their elder, were filled with great joy at the sight of Vaidehī.
Bharata, suffused with supreme delight, restored to the returning hero that kingdom which had been held as a trust for him and had been properly honored.
Then Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva together consecrated that hero on an auspicious day under a Vaiṣṇava asterism.
Once consecrated, he gave leave to Sugrīva, best of monkeys, together with his companions, and to Vibhīṣaṇa of the line of Pulastya, to return to their homes.
Having honored them with various gems, and both filled with love and joy, having made all proper arrangements, he dismissed them with a sorrowful heart.
And that Puṣpaka celestial vehicle — having reverently honored it, that son of Raghu, that Rāghava, joyfully returned it to Vaiśravaṇa himself.
Then, accompanied by divine sages along the river Gomatī, he performed ten unimpeded Aśvamedha sacrifices of the Jārūthya type.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O mighty-armed one, thus did Rāma of boundless splendor in former times endure that most severe affliction born of forest-exile.
Do not grieve, O tiger among men; you are a warrior, O scorcher of foes. You travel a path supported by the strength of your arms, a path of blazing resolution.
Not even the slightest fault is visible in you. Upon this path, even gods and demons together with Indra would despair.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vṛtra was slain in battle by the Maruts and Indra the thunderbolt-wielder; so too was the invincible Namuci and the demoness Dīrghajihvā.
All purposes are fully achieved when one has allies. What indeed could be unconquered in battle for one whose brother is Dhanaṃjaya?
And here is Bhīma, best among the mighty, of terrifying valor; and the two young great archers, the twins sons of Mādrī. With such allies, O scorcher of foes, why do you grieve?
These men who could conquer even the army of Indra together with the Maruts — with these great bowmen as allies, gods in form, you too shall vanquish all your enemies in battle, O bull of the Bhārata line.
Furthermore, consider this: Draupadī was carried off by the wicked, powerful, and pride-maddened Jayadratha of Sindhu, yet these great-souled ones brought her back.
Kṛṣṇā Draupadī was recovered after that most difficult feat was accomplished, and King Jayadratha himself was conquered and brought under control.
By Rāma, fighting virtually alone, Vaidehī was recovered after slaying in battle the ten-headed demon Rāvaṇa of terrifying valor.
His allies were monkeys, bears, and the Kālamukhas — beings of a different species entirely. Reflect on this with your mind, O king.
Therefore, O tiger among the Kurus, do not grieve, O bull of the Bhārata line. Great-souled men like you do not grieve, O scorcher of foes.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus consoled by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya, the king, casting off his sorrow, undepressed in spirit, spoke again as follows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I do not grieve for myself, O great sage, nor for these brothers, nor even for the loss of the kingdom, as much as I grieve for this daughter of Drupada.
Tormented by wicked men at the dice game, we were yet saved by Kṛṣṇā; and now she has again been forcibly carried off from the forest by Jayadratha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Has any woman ever been seen or heard of — any woman with a parting, devoted to her husband, of great good fortune — who is the equal of this daughter of Drupada?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hear, O king Yudhiṣṭhira, of the great good fortune of nobly born women — all of this as it was attained by Sāvitrī, the princess.
There was among the Madras a righteous king, supremely virtuous, devoted to Brahmins, a refuge for all, true to his word, and master of his senses.
A performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, skillful, beloved of the townspeople and the countryside — that king was named Aśvapati, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Endowed with forbearance, yet childless, truthful in speech, master of his senses — as his years advanced he was seized by sorrow.
For the purpose of begetting offspring he undertook a severe austerity: eating only a measured portion at the proper time, practicing celibacy, subduing his senses.
Offering a hundred thousand oblations to Sāvitrī, O best of kings, he subsisted every sixth mealtime on scanty food.
By this practice he continued for exactly eighteen years; when the eighteenth year was completed, Sāvitrī was pleased and, O king, appeared to that monarch in her own form.
Rising from the sacrificial fire, filled with great joy, the boon-giver spoke these words to that king.
"By your pure celibacy, self-restraint, and discipline, and by your whole-hearted devotion to me, I am pleased with you, O king."
"Choose a boon, O Aśvapati, king of the Madras, whatever you desire. And you must never be negligent in matters of righteousness under any circumstances."
Aśvapati said: "This undertaking was begun by me out of desire for offspring, with longing for righteousness. May I have many sons, O goddess, who will uphold our lineage."
"If you are pleased with me, O goddess, this is the boon I choose. The twice-born tell me that progeny is the highest righteousness."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sāvitrī said: "O king, knowing already this intention of yours, the Grandfather was already addressed on your behalf beforehand, for the sake of sons."
"And by his grace, as ordained by the Self-Born, a radiant daughter will come to you on earth very soon, O gentle one."
"You should say nothing further about this under any circumstance. I am pleased with the Grandfather's decree — this is what I tell you."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having agreed with "So be it" to Sāvitrī's words, the king beseeched her again: "May it be so quickly."
When Sāvitrī disappeared, the king returned to his own home; he dwelt in his own kingdom with joy, ruling his subjects by righteousness.
Then, as some time passed, that king, firm in his vows, begot a child upon his eldest queen, a righteous woman.
That embryo in the Mālavī princess grew, O bull of the Bhārata line, like the lord of stars in the bright fortnight of the sky.
When the time came she gave birth to a lotus-eyed daughter; and the king joyfully performed the rites for her.
She was given as a gift by a pleased Sāvitrī, born of oblations offered to Sāvitrī — so the Brahmins and her father gave her the name Sāvitrī.
That princess grew like the goddess Śrī incarnate; and in time that maiden reached the bloom of youth.
Seeing her with slender waist and broad hips, like a golden image, people thought: "Surely this must be a celestial maiden descended here."
Yet no one sought her in marriage — she whose eyes were like lotus petals and who blazed with radiance — for they were repelled by her splendor.
Then, having fasted and bathed her head, having approached the divinities and offered into the fire according to rite, she had Brahmins recite on the holy day.
Then, taking the remaining flowers as blessed offerings from those great-souled ones, she went before her father like the goddess Śrī in human form.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
She paid homage to her father's feet, first presented the remaining offerings, stood with joined palms, that noble-hipped woman, at the king's side.
Seeing his own daughter, goddess-like in form, arrived at the bloom of youth yet unsought by suitors, the king was grieved.
The king said: "Daughter, your time for being given in marriage has come, yet no one seeks me. Yourself seek out a husband equal to you in virtues."
"Whatever man you desire, tell him to me; I shall reflect and bestow you. Choose as you wish."
"For I have heard this recited by twice-born men from the textbook of righteousness — and you too, O auspicious one, hear my words as I speak them."
"A father who does not bestow her is blameworthy; a husband who does not love her is blameworthy; a son who does not protect his mother after the husband's death is blameworthy."
"Having heard these words of mine, hasten to seek a husband; act in such a way that the gods will not have cause to blame me."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having thus spoken to his daughter, the king also instructed the elder counselors and urged the escort party: "Let them go."
She paid homage to her father's feet and, proud-spirited yet seemingly abashed, having received her father's command, departed without hesitation.
She mounted a golden chariot and, surrounded by elder counselors, she visited the delightful forest-hermitages of the royal sages.
Paying homage at the feet of the revered elders there, she visited all the forests in order, my son.
Thus, distributing wealth at all the sacred fords, the princess went from place to place among the chief twice-born.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then the king, lord of the Madras, was met by Nārada and sat together with him in the midst of the assembly hall in conversation, O Bhārata.
Then, having visited all the sacred fords and the hermitages as well, Sāvitrī returned to her father's house together with the counselors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The auspicious one, seeing her father seated with Nārada, bowed her head and paid homage at the feet of both.
Nārada said: "Where had this daughter of yours gone, O king, and from where has she now returned? Why do you not bestow this young woman on a husband?"
Aśvapati said: "It is for this very purpose that she was sent out, and she has just now returned. Hear, O divine sage, about the husband she has chosen."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Urged by her father with "Speak fully about it," the auspicious Sāvitrī, receiving his word as if it were a divine command, spoke thus.
"There was among the Śālvas a righteous Kṣatriya, lord of the earth, known as Dyumatsena; he later became blind."
"When he lost his sight, his kingdom was seized while his son was still young — a wise king — by a former enemy who exploited this vulnerability."
"He went to the forest together with his wife, who still cared for him like a child; entering the great forest, he practiced austerities of great vows."
"His son, born in the city but grown up in the hermitage, Satyavān — fitting to be my husband — I have chosen in my heart."
Nārada said: "Ah, what a great wrong has been done unknowingly by Sāvitrī, O king — that she has chosen this virtuous Satyavān!"
"His father speaks truth, his mother speaks truth — therefore the Brahmins gave him this name: Satyavān, 'the truthful one.'"
"As a child he loved horses; he used to make clay horses and drew horses in pictures — so he is also called Citrāśva, 'the one of painted horses.'"
The king said: "Is he then radiant, wise, that son of a king? Is Satyavān, who delights his father, also patient and valiant?"
Nārada said: "He is radiant as Vivasvān, equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect, valiant as great Indra, and endowed with patience like the earth."
Aśvapati said: "Is Satyavān, the prince, also a giver, devoted to Brahmins, handsome, noble-spirited, or of pleasant appearance?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nārada said: "In giving, according to his ability, he equals Rantideva of Saṅkṛti's line; devoted to Brahmins and truthful in speech like Śibi of Uśīnara's line."
"Noble as Yayāti, of pleasant appearance like the Moon — in beauty, Dyumatsena's powerful son is unsurpassed, a match for the Aśvins."
"He is self-restrained, gentle, and brave; truthful and master of his senses; friendly and free from envy; modest and steadfast."
"In him there is ever directness, and his steadfastness is unwavering. In brief, this is what is said of him by those venerable in austerity and those venerable in character."
Aśvapati said: "You describe him to me as endowed with all virtues, O blessed one. Tell me also of his faults, if there are any here."
Nārada said: "He has one flaw and no other: Satyavān, from this very day, will exhaust his lifespan and lay down his body within a year."
The king said: "Come, Sāvitrī, go and choose another, O lovely one. His one great flaw overshadows and overcomes all his virtues."
"As the blessed Nārada, honored by the gods, has told me: within a year that short-lived one will lay down his body."
Sāvitrī said: "A lot falls but once; a daughter is given but once; and one says 'I give' but once — these three things happen only once, each only once."
Whether long-lived or short-lived, whether endowed with virtues or lacking them — a husband once chosen by me, I shall not choose a second time.
A resolve formed first in the mind is then declared in speech, and afterward carried out in deed; the mind is therefore my authority.
Nārada said: The understanding of Sāvitrī, your daughter, O best of men, is firm; she cannot by any means be turned away from this dharma.
The qualities that Satyavān possesses are not found in any other man. Therefore the giving away of your daughter pleases me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The king said: What has been spoken by the blessed one is true and beyond deliberation; I shall do exactly this, for you, O blessed one, are my guru.
Nārada said: May the giving of your daughter Sāvitrī be free of obstacles. We shall accomplish it. May good befall all of you.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, Nārada soared into the sky and departed to heaven. The king too made all the wedding preparations for his daughter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, reflecting on that very matter of giving away his daughter, the king assembled all the requisite goods for the wedding.
Then, having summoned all the elder twice-born, the officiating priests, and the family chaplain, he set out with his daughter on an auspicious day.
Arriving at the sacred forest, the king proceeded on foot together with the brahmins and approached the hermitage of Dyumatsena, that royal sage.
There they saw the greatly fortunate blind king sitting on a cushion of kuśa grass, leaning against a śāla tree.
That king paid homage to the royal sage as was fitting and, restraining his speech carefully, introduced himself.
That knower of dharma offered him the arghya, a seat, and a cow, and then the king asked the other king: "What is the purpose of your coming?"
He disclosed to him his entire intention and the entire course of action to be done, directing it all toward Satyavān.
Aśvapati said: O royal sage, this lovely daughter of mine is named Sāvitrī. O knower of dharma, receive her from me according to proper rite as a daughter-in-law.
Dyumatsena said: We have been deprived of our kingdom and have taken to forest life; we practice dharma with discipline as ascetics. How shall your daughter, who is undeserving of such hardship, endure this toil in the hermitage?
Aśvapati said: When my daughter and I both understand that joy and sorrow are of the nature of coming and going, such words do not befit one like me. I have come to you with firm resolve, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You ought not to destroy my hope out of friendship and affection; you should not refuse one who has come to you from all sides with love.
We are indeed well-matched for this union — you for me and I for you. Accept my daughter as a daughter-in-law, as a wife for Satyavān.
Dyumatsena said: This alliance with you was desired by me even before, but I was deprived of my kingdom, and so I held back from it.
But let that desire of mine, which was longed for even before, be fulfilled this very day; for you are a guest I have desired.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, having assembled all the brahmins dwelling in the hermitage, the two kings had the marriage performed according to rite.
After giving his daughter and a suitable dowry of possessions, Aśvapati returned to his own home filled with the highest joy.
Satyavān too rejoiced upon obtaining that wife endowed with every virtue, and she rejoiced upon obtaining him as the husband she had desired in her heart.
After her father departed, she put aside all her ornaments and took up only the bark garments and the ochre-colored cloth.
By her service, her virtues, her modesty and self-restraint, and by fulfilling every desire, she won the satisfaction of all.
She pleased her mother-in-law with all the attentions to her body and with clothing and such things, and her father-in-law with the performance of divine rites and with restraint of speech.
Likewise, she completely pleased her husband with pleasant speech, with skillfulness, with tranquility, and with attendance upon him in private.
Thus, O Bhārata, some time passed for those virtuous people as they dwelt in that hermitage engaged in their ascetic practices.
But for Sāvitrī, whether lying down or standing, day and night, that speech spoken by Nārada ever remained in her mind.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, after much time had elapsed, there arrived, O king, that moment when Satyavān was to die.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And as Sāvitrī counted each passing day, that word spoken by Nārada rested perpetually in her heart.
Reflecting that death was to come on the fourth day, the beautiful woman undertook a three-night vow and stood still both day and night.
Hearing of his daughter-in-law's painful vow, the king rose, afflicted with sorrow, and spoke words to Sāvitrī to comfort her.
This undertaking you have begun is exceedingly severe, O princess; standing for three full days and nights is supremely difficult.
Sāvitrī said: You should not be distressed, father. I shall complete the vow; this is done by firm resolve, and resolve is the cause.
Dyumatsena said: I am in no way able to tell you to break the vow; one such as I should say only the proper word: "Complete it."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, the noble-minded Dyumatsena fell silent, and Sāvitrī as she stood appeared like a wooden post.
On the eve of her husband's death, O bull of the Bhāratas, that night passed for Sāvitrī as she stood, afflicted with grief.
"Today is that day" — having offered oblations into the blazing fire, when the sun had risen a yoke's height, and having performed the morning rites,
she then saluted in due order all the elder twice-born, her mother-in-law, and her father-in-law, and stood with folded hands, composed.
All the ascetics dwelling in the ascetic forest then spoke auspicious blessings of non-widowhood for Sāvitrī's sake.
"So be it" — Sāvitrī, wholly intent on meditative absorption, accepted all those words of the ascetics with her mind.
Awaiting that time and that moment, the princess thought on the words of Nārada just as he had spoken them, deeply distressed.
Then her mother-in-law and father-in-law, O foremost of the Bhāratas, spoke these words with affection to the princess who stood apart.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The parents-in-law said: This vow, as it was prescribed, has been properly completed by you. The time for eating has arrived; do now what comes next.
Sāvitrī said: I shall eat after the sun has set, when my wish has been fulfilled. This is the resolve in my heart and the pledge I have made.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: While Sāvitrī was thus speaking about food, Satyavān took his axe upon his shoulder and set out for the forest.
But Sāvitrī said to her husband: "You should not go alone. I shall go with you; I cannot bear to be separated from you."
Satyavān said: You have not gone to the forest before, and the path is difficult, O beautiful one; weakened as you are by vow and fast, how will you walk on foot?
Sāvitrī said: I feel no fatigue from the fast, nor any weariness. I have resolved to go; you should not prevent me.
Satyavān said: If you are resolved on going, I shall do what pleases you; but first take leave of my elders, so that no fault may touch me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: She who had taken the great vow approached and spoke to her mother-in-law and father-in-law: "My husband is going to the great forest for fruits."
"I desire to be permitted by the noble lady and by my father-in-law to go out with him; separation from him is not bearable for me."
"Your son is going out for the sake of the sacred fire and the guru; he cannot be stopped. He might be stopped if he were going to the forest otherwise."
"For nearly a year I have not gone outside the hermitage; I have a great longing to see the forest in bloom."
Dyumatsena said: Ever since Sāvitrī was given to me as a daughter-in-law by her father, I do not recall that she has ever made an improper request.
Let this daughter-in-law then obtain the wish she desires. But care must be taken, my daughter, on the path alongside Satyavān.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Permitted by both, the illustrious Sāvitrī went forth with her husband, appearing to smile while her heart was torn with anguish.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The wide-eyed woman beheld the varied and delightful forests all around, resounding with the calls of peacocks.
The holy-flowing rivers and the blossoming trees — Satyavān kept saying to Sāvitrī in sweet words: "Look at this!"
The blameless woman, watching her husband in all his moods, already regarded him as dead, recalling in that moment the sage's words.
Yet following her husband, she walked with gentle gait, as if her heart were split in two, all the while watching for that moment.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then that valiant man, with his wife as his companion, gathered fruits and filled his basket, and afterward split firewood.
As he split the wood, sweat broke out upon him, and from the exertion he felt a pain arise in his head.
Approaching his dear wife, he said, tormented by fatigue: "From this exertion of mine a pain has arisen in my head."
"And all my limbs and my heart seem to burn, O Sāvitrī, O you of measured speech; I perceive that I am unwell."
"I perceive that my head is pierced as if by spears; I wish to sleep, O auspicious one — I have no strength to stand."
Then Sāvitrī approached, embraced her husband, placed his head in her lap, and sat down upon the ground.
Then that ascetic woman, reflecting on Nārada's words, reckoned that moment, that instant, that hour, and that day together.
And within a moment she saw a man clad in yellow garments, with a bound diadem, magnificent in form, with radiance equal to the sun's.
Dark-complexioned and fair, with red eyes, a noose in his hand, inspiring dread, he stood at Satyavān's side, gazing intently at him.
Seeing him, she quickly rose, gently laid her husband's head down, stood with folded hands, and spoke, distressed, her heart trembling.
"I recognize you as a divine being, for this form is superhuman. Tell me of your own will, O god — who are you, and what do you intend to do?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yama said: "You are a devoted wife, Sāvitrī, and likewise endowed with ascetic power; therefore I address you directly. Know me, O auspicious one — I am Yama."
"This Satyavān, your husband, the son of a king, has exhausted his lifespan; I shall bind him and lead him away — know this to be my intention."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, the blessed lord of the fathers began to explain fully his entire intention for her sake, wishing to please her.
"For this man is endowed with righteousness, handsome, an ocean of virtues; he is not fit to be led away by my messengers — therefore I have come myself."
Then Yama forcibly drew from the body of Satyavān the thumb-sized person bound with a noose, come under his sway.
Then that body, its life-breath extracted, its breath gone, its lustre lost, motionless — became a pitiable sight to behold.
Yama, having thus bound him, departed facing southward; and Sāvitrī too, tormented by grief, followed Yama himself — she who was perfected in vows and observances, the greatly blessed devoted wife.
Yama said: Turn back, go, Sāvitrī; perform the post-mortem rites for him. Your debt to your husband has been paid; you have gone as far as one may go.
Sāvitrī said: Where my husband is led, or where he himself goes, I too must go there — this is the eternal law.
Through austerity, devoted service to the teacher, love for my husband, and through vows, and by your own grace, my path is not obstructed.
The wise who perceive the truth of things declare that seven steps together make a friendship; honouring that friendship, I shall say something — listen to it.
Those of various natures wander in the forest, enduring dharma, dwelling, and hardship; the wise declare dharma through understanding; therefore the good say dharma is paramount.
By the dharma of the one, by the conviction of the good, all of us enter that path; let no one desire a second or a third; therefore the good say dharma is paramount.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yama said: Turn back — I am pleased by this speech of yours, composed of excellent syllables, letters, and logic; choose a boon here, excepting this one's life; I grant you any boon, blameless one.
Sāvitrī said: My father-in-law, fallen from his own kingdom and dwelling in the forest, his eyes destroyed, lives in the hermitage; may he by your grace regain his sight, becoming a powerful king, blazing like fire and sun.
Yama said: I grant you all of this boon, blameless one; it shall be as you have said. I perceive what seems like weariness in your path; turn back, go — let there be no fatigue for you.
Sāvitrī said: How can there be weariness for me near my husband? For where my husband is, that is my certain course; wherever you will lead my lord, there is my path. O lord of the gods, hear yet another word from me.
A single meeting with the good is supremely desired; beyond that, it is called true friendship; association with a virtuous person is never fruitless; therefore one should dwell in the company of the good.
Yama said: You have spoken to me words pleasing to the mind, increasing the wisdom of the wise, conducive to welfare — again excepting the life of this Satyavān; choose a second boon, passionate lady.
Sāvitrī said: The kingdom of my wise father-in-law was stolen of old; may that king regain his own realm, and may my venerable father-in-law never abandon his own dharma — this second boon I ask of you.
Yama said: He shall soon regain his own kingdom; the king shall not be separated from his own dharma — this wish is granted by me, O daughter of a king; turn back, go, let there be no fatigue for you.
Sāvitrī said: These creatures are restrained by you through law; having restrained them you lead them, not from desire — thus your lordship as Yama, O god, is renowned; hear also this word spoken by me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Non-malice toward all beings in deed, thought, and speech, along with benevolence and giving — this is the eternal dharma of the good.
Such indeed is this world — human beings are delicate in their power; yet even the good show compassion toward enemies when they are in distress.
Yama said: As water is to one who thirsts, so has this speech been uttered by you; again excepting the life of this Satyavān, choose here whatever boon you wish, auspicious one.
Sāvitrī said: My father, the lord of the earth, is without offspring; may there be a hundred sons born of my father himself, continuing the lineage of his family — this third boon I ask of you.
Yama said: A hundred sons of your father, continuing the lineage, of great splendour — may they be yours, auspicious one; this wish is granted, O daughter of a king; turn back — you have come a long way.
Sāvitrī said: This is not far for me when near my husband; for my mind races even farther ahead; thus even as you walk, listen once more to the words I am ready to speak.
You are the glorious son of Vivasvat; therefore the wise call you Vaivasvata; the creatures are won over by your peace and dharma — hence, O lord, you hold here the kingship of dharma.
Even in oneself there is not as much trust as there is in the good; therefore everyone especially desires affection from the good.
From the goodwill of all beings, trust is born; therefore people especially place their trust in the good.
Yama said: The words you have uttered, O slender-waisted, auspicious one — such have not been heard by me from any other; by these I am pleased; excepting this one's life, choose a fourth boon and go.
Sāvitrī said: May there be born sons of my own body from Satyavān, a hundred sons bearing strength and valour, upholding both our families here — this fourth boon I ask of you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yama said: A hundred sons bearing strength and valour shall be born to your delight, gentle one; let there be no weariness for you, O daughter of a king; turn back — you have come a long way.
Sāvitrī said: The conduct in dharma of the good is always eternal; the good neither sink nor tremble; association with the good is never fruitless; the good do not follow fear from the good.
For the good guide the sun by truth; the good uphold the earth through austerity; the good are the course of the past and the future, O king; among the good, the good do not sink.
Knowing this conduct to be eternal, honoured by the noble, the good, acting for the sake of others, do not look for any return.
Grace bestowed upon the virtuous is never wasted; neither wealth nor honour is lost; because this is certain and constant among the good — therefore the good become protectors.
Yama said: The more you speak words combined with dharma, pleasing to the mind, well-formed and full of great meaning, the more my supreme devotion grows toward you; choose an incomparable boon, O lady of firm vows.
Sāvitrī said: Your release from meritorious action does not happen without being granted, O giver of honour, as in the other boons; I choose this boon: let this Satyavān live — for without my husband I am as if dead.
I do not desire happiness bereft of my husband; I do not desire heaven bereft of my husband; I do not desire prosperity bereft of my husband; I do not resolve to live as one without a husband.
The grant of the boon — my having a hundred sons — was given by you yourself, yet my husband is being taken away; I choose the boon: let this Satyavān live; thus your own word will be true.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having said "So be it" and releasing those bonds, Yama Vaivasvata, the king of dharma, his soul filled with joy, spoke these words to Sāvitrī:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This husband of yours, auspicious one, delighter of your family, has been released by me; free from disease, he will lead you and his purposes shall be fulfilled."
"He shall attain a lifespan of four hundred years together with you; having performed sacrifices with dharma, he shall gain renown in the world."
"Satyavān shall beget on you a hundred sons; all of them shall be kings, warriors, with sons and grandsons, renowned and bearing your name — they shall be eternal here."
"And a hundred sons shall be born to your father by your mother, of the Mālava lineage — Mālavas by name, eternal, with sons and grandsons; they shall be your brothers, warriors equal to the thirty gods."
Having thus granted the boons to her, the glorious king of dharma, turning Sāvitrī back, went to his own abode.
And Sāvitrī too, when Yama had departed and she had recovered her husband, went to where the lifeless body of her husband lay.
Seeing her husband on the ground, she approached and embraced him, and placing his head in her lap, she sat down on the earth.
And Satyavān, having regained consciousness, spoke to Sāvitrī; gazing at her again and again with affection, as if returned from a journey.
Satyavān said: "Alas, I have slept very long — why was I not awakened? And where is that dark man who was dragging me away?"
Sāvitrī said: "Alas, you have slept very long on my lap, O bull among men; that blessed god who restrains the creatures, Yama, has gone."
"You are rested, O greatly fortunate one, and free from sleep, O son of a king; if you are able, rise up and behold the deep night."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then, having regained his senses, he rose as if from a pleasant sleep; gazing at all the directions and the edges of the forest, Satyavān spoke:
"I went out to gather fruits with you, O slender-waisted one; then, while splitting wood, a pain arose in my head."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Scorched by the burning heat in my head, unable to stand for long, I fell asleep in your lap — all this I remember, auspicious one."
"And while being embraced by you, my mind was carried away by sleep; then I saw terrible darkness and a man of great radiance."
"If you know what that was, tell me, O slender-waisted one — whether it was a dream I saw, or whether it was real indeed."
Then Sāvitrī said to him: "The night is deepening; tomorrow, O son of a king, I shall tell you everything exactly as it occurred."
"Rise up, rise up — may good come to you; see your parents, O one of pure vows; this night is deep and the day-maker has departed."
"These night-wanderers roam about, joyful and uttering fierce cries; the sounds of leaves and of animals roaming in the forest are heard."
"These jackals, with their terrible cries, taking up the south-western direction, howl fiercely, shaking my heart."
Satyavān said: "The forest appears terrifying, wrapped in dense darkness; you will not be able to discern the path, and you will not be able to go."
Sāvitrī said: "In this forest that was burned today, a dry tree stands blazing; fanned by the wind, fire is visible here and there."
"Then, having brought fire here, I shall kindle it on all sides; there is wood here — cast off the anguish of your heart."
"If you are not able to go, I observe that you are in pain; and you will not know the path in the forest covered by darkness."
"Tomorrow at dawn, when the forest is visible, we shall go with your consent; let us stay here this night, if it pleases you, O sinless one."
Satyavān said: "The pain in my head has subsided; I perceive my limbs to be well; I wish to meet my mother and father — and this meeting is born of your grace."
"Never before have I gone to the hermitage at an improper time; my mother stops me whenever the evening has not yet come."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Even when I go out during the day, both my venerable parents are distressed; my father searches for me together with the hermitage-dwellers."
"By my mother and father, greatly afflicted, I have often been reproached in the past: 'You have come back late.'"
"What is their condition today on my account, I think; when I am unseen by them, great sorrow will befall them."
"They used to speak to me before as well, not tearful in the night, greatly afflicted, the two elders, many times full of affection:"
"'Without you we cannot live even for a moment, my son; as long as you shall live, my son, for that long our life is certain.'"
"'You are the staff of two old blind people; in you the lineage is established; in you rest our funeral offerings, our renown, and our continuity.'"
"My mother is old, my father is old, and I am their staff; not seeing me this night, what condition will those two come to?"
"And I am angry at sleep, on account of which my father and my innocent mother have come to uncertainty because of me."
"And I myself have come to uncertainty, fallen into terrible danger; for without my mother and father I do not resolve to live."
"Clearly my father, whose sight is wisdom, with an agitated mind, at this very hour questions each hermitage-dweller one by one."
"I do not grieve for myself as much as I grieve for my father, O auspicious one, and for my mother who has followed her husband and is utterly frail."
"For on my account the two of them shall today reach the greatest anguish; as long as they live I live after them — they are to be supported by me; thinking 'I must do what is dear to them,' I too live."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having spoken thus, that righteous-souled one, devoted to his elders and dear to them, raised his arms and, tormented by grief, wept aloud.
Then, seeing her husband thus emaciated by grief, Sāvitrī the dharma-walking one, wiping the tears from his eyes, spoke:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"If austerity has been practiced by me, if gifts have been given, if oblations have been offered — may this night be auspicious for my mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband."
"I do not recall having ever spoken an untruth even in casual matters; by that truth, may both my parents-in-law be sustained today."
Satyavān said: I long to see my parents — go at once, Sāvitrī, do not delay. If I were to see any affliction of my mother or father, I could not live, O fair-limbed one; I swear this on my own soul by truth.
If your mind is set on dharma, and if you wish me to live, and if you desire to do what pleases me, then go now — leave at once for the hermitage nearby.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then Sāvitrī rose, bound up her hair, and that devoted woman raised her husband, clasping him firmly with both arms.
Satyavān rose, wiped his limbs with his hand, surveyed all the directions, and then fixed his gaze upon the firewood bundle.
Then Sāvitrī said to him: You shall carry the fruits tomorrow; for your welfare and support I will carry the axe for you now.
