We shall not abandon that undertaking in which you engage us. Let your lordship arrange everything; we shall swiftly conquer the enemies.
When Bhīmasena had spoken thus, the brahmins pronounced supreme blessings, took their leave of the Bhāratas, and each departed to his own home.
All the foremost knowers of the Vedas, the ascetics and sages, having pronounced blessings duly and wishing to see them again, departed.
Then those five wise Pāṇḍava heroes, together with Dhaumya and taking Kṛṣṇa along, rose and departed, O Bhārata.
Having traveled only a krosa from that region due to a certain sign, those tigers among men, on the morrow, made themselves ready for the life of concealment.
All were separately versed in the treatises, all were skilled in counsel, all knew the proper times for alliance and war — they sat together in council.
Janamejaya said: How did my great-grandfathers dwell unrecognised in the city of Virāṭa, tormented by fear of Duryodhana?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus received boons from Dharma, that best upholder of righteousness among righteous men went to the hermitage and recounted everything to the brāhmaṇas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having told all of that to the brāhmaṇas, Yudhiṣṭhira returned the fire-sticks together with the kindling-wood to that brāhmaṇa.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma and great-souled one, having assembled all his younger brothers together, spoke thus, O Bhārata.
These twelve years we have dwelt in exile from the kingdom; now the thirteenth has arrived, the most difficult and hard to endure.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, O Arjuna, please choose well a place of residence from here, where all of us may dwell entirely unrecognised by our enemies.
Arjuna said: By the very boon of Dharma himself, O lord of men, O bull of the Bhāratas, we shall move about unrecognised among people.
Yet I shall name certain kingdoms that are pleasant and well-concealed as places to reside; please choose whichever one of them appeals to you.
There are pleasant countries rich in food surrounding the Kurus: the Pāñcālas, the Cedis, the Matsyas, the Śūrasenas, the Paṭaccaras, the Daśārṇas, the Navarāṣṭra, the Mallas, the Śālvas, and the Yugaṃdharas.
Which of these, O king, O lord of kings, does it please you to reside in? We shall dwell wherever you choose for this one year.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: It is exactly so, O mighty-armed one; as that blessed lord, the master of all beings, has spoken, so it shall be, and not otherwise.
Yet for the purpose of our dwelling we must necessarily deliberate together, all of us, and find a place that is pleasant, auspicious, comfortable, and free from all danger.
Virāṭa, king of the Matsyas, is powerful, and he would protect the Pāṇḍavas; he is virtuous in conduct, generous, advanced in age, and of very great wealth.
In the city of Virāṭa, dear one, we shall spend this one year performing service for him, O Bhārata.
And whatever tasks each of us is able to perform for him—let each one, O sons of Kuru's line, declare that task.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Arjuna said: O king of men, O virtuous one, what work will you perform in the kingdom of King Virāṭa? In what occupation will you find pleasure?
You are gentle, generous, modest, righteous, and one whose prowess is proven in truth—yet you are afflicted, O king, O Pāṇḍava; what will you do?
You are not accustomed to any hardship in the manner that common people are; having encountered this terrible calamity, how will you endure it?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Listen, O sons of Kuru's line, to what work I shall indeed perform upon reaching Virāṭa, that bull among men and king.
I shall become a dice-companion in the assembly of that great-souled king, presenting myself as a brāhmaṇa named Kaṅka, skilled at dice and fond of gambling.
I shall fashion beautiful dice of beryl, gold, and ivory, together with fruit-seeds and bright resins—black-spotted and red-spotted ones to delight the mind.
'I was formerly the dearest friend of Yudhiṣṭhira, equal to his very life'—so shall I tell the king, if he should question me.
Thus I have told you how I shall conduct myself. O Vṛkodara, in what occupation will you find pleasure in Virāṭa's kingdom?
Bhīma said: Presenting myself as a head cook named Ballava, I shall attend King Virāṭa—this is my intention.
I shall prepare broths for him; I am skilled in the kitchen, and in the side-dishes those well-trained cooks have made before—I shall surpass even them, generating his delight.
I shall also bring in great stores of firewood, and seeing that prodigious labour the king will be pleased.
Should powerful elephants or mighty bulls need to be restrained, O king, I shall restrain those as well.
And whatever wrestlers may engage in bouts at festivals, I shall defeat them, increasing his delight.
Yet I shall not slay those fighters in any manner whatsoever; I shall fell them in such a way that they suffer no mortal harm.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'I was a pastry-cook, a meat-cutter, a broth-maker, and a wrestler for Yudhiṣṭhira'—so shall I say to those who question me.
Guarding myself by my own self, O lord of the people, I shall move about—this I pledge, and this is how I shall conduct myself.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: He whom the god Fire once approached in the form of a brāhmaṇa, desiring to burn the Khāṇḍava forest, seeking the best of men together with the son of Dāśārha—
That immensely strong, long-armed, unconquered son of Kuru's line—what task will that Dhanaṃjaya, son of Kuntī, now perform?
He who, having approached that forest, gratified the god of fire, having conquered Indra single-handedly with his chariot and slain serpents and rākṣasas—that Arjuna, foremost among warriors, what will he do?
The sun is the foremost among those that blaze with heat; the brāhmaṇa is the best among two-footed beings; the venomous serpent is the best among snakes; and fire is the best among the radiant ones.
The thunderbolt is the best of weapons; the bull with a hump is the best of cattle; the ocean is the greatest among lakes and reservoirs; Parjanya is the best among those that rain.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra is the best among serpents; Airāvata is foremost among elephants; a son exceeds all that is dear; and a wife is the best among friends.
Just as these are pre-eminent each in their own kind, O Vṛkodara, so too that young man Guḍākeśa is the foremost among all who wield the bow.
This Bībhatsu, wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, drawn by white horses, inferior to none save Indra and Vāsudeva—O Bhārata, what will he do?
Having dwelt for five years in the abode of the thousand-eyed Indra and having obtained divine weapons, gleaming with the form of a god—
He whom I regard as the twelfth Rudra and the thirteenth Āditya, whose two arms are equal and long, the skin hardened by bowstring-slaps, and whose right and left arms bear the calluses of a cowherd's yoke—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As the Himālayas among mountains, as the ocean among rivers, as Śakra among the thirty gods, as fire the bearer of oblations among the Vasus—
As the tiger among deer, as Garuḍa foremost among birds in flight—so Arjuna, the best of those who arm themselves for battle—what will he do?
Arjuna said: I shall make a declaration that I am a eunuch, O lord of the earth; for my two great bowstring-marks are difficult to conceal, O king.
Adorning my ears with earrings blazing like fire, braiding my hair into a plait, O king, I shall go by the name of Bṛhannaḍā.
Reciting the repertoire of stories, again and again adopting the nature of a woman, I shall delight the lord of the earth and the other people within the inner apartments.
Song, varied and wonderful dance, and diverse instrumental music—these I shall teach, O king, to the women in the palace of Virāṭa.
Speaking of the conventions of common folk and of many accomplished deeds, O son of Kuntī, I shall conceal my true self from myself through this artifice.
'I have lived in Yudhiṣṭhira's household as an attendant of Draupadī'—so shall I say when questioned by the king, O Bhārata.
By this means, disguised with an assumed identity as Nala was, I shall dwell happily in the palace of Virāṭa, O lord of kings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What will you do there, dear Nakula, going about? You are tender, brave, handsome to behold, and accustomed to comfort.
Nakula said: I shall become the horse-keeper of King Virāṭa; by name I shall be called Granthika—this work is very dear to me.
I am skilled in horse-training and equally in the treatment of horses; horses are always dear to me, O king of Kurus, just as they are to you.
To those people in the city of Virāṭa who address me, I shall speak in the following manner, and thus I shall conduct myself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Sahadeva, how will you conduct yourself in his presence? And what will you do, dear one, moving about in disguise?
Sahadeva said: I shall become the cattle-enumerator of Virāṭa, lord of the earth; a herd-protector and a milker as well, skilled in the counting of cattle.
Known by the name Tantipāla—let this be known to you; I shall move about with skill. Let the fever of your mind depart.
For I was constantly engaged by you in the care of cattle in former times; there my skilled work was learned and understood, O lord of the people.
The marks, the behaviour, and whatever is auspicious about cattle—all of that is well known to me, and much else besides, O lord of the earth.
I also know bulls of distinguished marks, O king, whose urine, when smelled, causes even a barren cow to conceive.
I shall conduct myself in this way, for my delight always lies here, and no enemy shall recognise me. May this please you, O lord of the earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: But this dear wife of ours, more precious to us than our very lives—she must be protected like a mother and honoured like an elder sister.
By what work will Kṛṣṇā Draupadī move about? For she does not know any task in the way that ordinary women do.
She is delicate, still young, a princess of great renown, devoted to her husband, supremely blessed—how indeed will she go about?
Garlands, perfumes, ornaments, and various garments—these alone she is acquainted with, for from birth she has been a highborn lady.
Draupadī said: There exist in the world, O Bhārata, independent female attendants who are unprotected—it is the settled conviction of people that no other women go about in that way.
Presenting myself as a sairandhrī skilled in hairdressing, I shall move about protecting myself—since you ask me about it.
I shall present myself in service to Sudeṣṇā, the illustrious royal wife; she will protect me when I have arrived—let not such sorrow be yours.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You speak auspiciously, O Kṛṣṇā, as one born of a noble lineage would speak. You know no sin; well done, you who stand firm in the vow of a virtuous wife.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The tasks you have each declared, those you shall carry out; and mine also, agreeable as they are to my intellect, are firmly determined.
Let this our family priest guard the sacred fires, together with the cooks and provisioners, in the abode of Drupada.
And let these men, headed by Indrasena, taking only the chariots, proceed quickly to Dvāravatī—this is the thinking that prevails in my mind.
And all these women who are attendants of Draupadī—let them go to the Pāñcālas, together with the cooks and provisioners.
And all should say: 'The Pāṇḍavas are nowhere to be found; indeed they all departed from the Dvaita forest after abandoning us.'
Dhaumya said: Even to those who know the truth, dear friends should speak with affection; therefore I too shall speak just the reason for it—hear me.
Come, O princes, I shall tell you how one who moves about in a royal household in service shall not come to harm.
Truly, O scions of Kuru, those who know the hardship of royal dwellings, who deserve great honour yet go unhonoured, who are unrecognised—they must endure it for the full year.
One should obtain access through the appointed gate and should not trust in kings; one should seek out only that seat where no enemy will assail him.
He should not mount the king's conveyance, nor his couch, nor his seat, nor his elephant, nor his chariot, thinking 'I am esteemed'—thus he may dwell in a royal household.
And wherever those of corrupt conduct might suspect him when he is seated, he should never sit there—thus he may dwell in a royal household.
One should never instruct a king who has not asked; rather, one should wait upon him in silence, showing reverence at the proper time.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For kings take offense at those who speak falsely, and they likewise hold in contempt a minister who utters falsehoods.
A wise man should never in any way cultivate friendship with the wives of kings, nor with those who dwell in the inner apartments, nor with those who are hostile or unfavorable to him.
One should perform even the smallest duties with the king's knowledge; a king whose servant acts thus suffers no harm anywhere.
One should serve him with care, as one would serve fire or a god; for one who serves him with deceit will undoubtedly harm him.
Whatever the master enjoins, one should carry out accordingly; one should shun negligence, contempt, and anger.
In all matters where one is capable, one should represent what is both beneficial and pleasing; indeed, one should speak what is beneficial to him even above what is merely pleasing.
One should be agreeable to him in all matters and conversations, and should not describe to him anything that is displeasing or harmful.
A wise man should not serve with the thought 'I am not dear to him'; rather, being vigilant and attentive, he should do what is beneficial and pleasing.
One should not pursue what is undesired by him, should not dwell with those who are hostile to him, should not waver from one's proper station — such a one may dwell in a royal household.
A wise man should sit at the right or left side; the position behind is ordained for armed guards, and sitting directly in front is always strictly forbidden — it is a seat of great importance.
One should not whisper anything at all during an audience, however important it may be; for even this is the foremost seat of offense for the poor.
One should not reveal among men what the king has spoken falsely, and one should not mention the person whom kings resent.
One should not be arrogant thinking 'I am a hero' or 'I am wise'; by doing only what is pleasing to the king, one becomes dear to him and enjoys his favor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having obtained power that was hard to obtain, and having won the king's favor, one should remain vigilant in what is dear and beneficial to the king.
Whose anger is a great calamity and whose favor yields great fruit — who, deemed wise, would even in his mind desire ill toward such a one?
One should never twist the lips, nor interrupt speech; one should always sneeze, pass wind, and spit quietly.
Even when amusing things occur in his presence, one should not be excessively delighted, nor should one laugh like a madman.
One should not comport oneself with excessive gravity, for that way one becomes heavy; rather, a gentle smile born of graciousness should be shown.
One who does not rejoice at gain, who does not feel pain when dishonored, and who is always unconfused — such a one may dwell in a royal household.
A minister who, having become wise, always attends upon the king or a prince, long enjoys prosperity.
A minister who is favored and also restrained with cause, and who does not bind the king with obligations, gains favor once more.
A discerning dependant who speaks of virtues both in the king's presence and in his absence, and whoever dwells in the king's domain — such a one thrives.
A minister who demands enjoyment from the king by force will not long keep his position and will come to danger of his life.
Seeing always what is best for himself, one should not converse with the king about something superior, and one should never surpass the king in any domain where he is competent.
One who is unfading, strong, brave, always present like a shadow, truthful, gentle, and self-controlled — such a one may dwell in a royal household.
One who, when another is being sent, steps forward first saying 'What shall I do?' — such a one may dwell in a royal household.
One who, when commanded, does not make excuses whether in heat or cold, by night or by day — such a one may dwell in a royal household.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One who, when away from home, does not dwell in memory of loved ones, and who seeks happiness even through hardship — such a one may dwell in a royal household.
One should not dress alike with the king, should not laugh too loudly in his presence, and should not make counsel widely known — thus one becomes dear to the king.
One who is appointed to a task should not touch any wealth; for one who steals property gains either imprisonment or death.
Whatever conveyance, garment, or ornament the king gives, along with anything else — one should always wear that alone; thus one becomes more beloved.
Dear ones, for this one year, behave thus and desire to prosper; then, having reached your own domain, you will move about as you please.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: We have been instructed; good fortune to you. No one could say these things save our mother Kuntī and the great-minded Vidura.
Whatever must now be done immediately, please do it — for our deliverance from this sorrow, for our departure, and for victory.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the king, Dhaumya, the foremost of twice-born men, duly performed all that is prescribed for a departure.
He kindled their fires and made offerings with mantras for the increase of prosperity and abundance, and for the conquest of the earth.
Having circumambulated the fire and honored the brahmins who were rich in austerity, with Yājñasenī (Draupadī) at their head, the six of them then set out.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those heroes, with their swords buckled on, their quivers of arrows strapped in place, and their leather finger-guards bound, went along the Kālindī river.
Then those archers proceeded on foot along the southern bank, dwelling in mountain fastnesses and forest strongholds.
Those mighty archers, great bowmen, piercing various kinds of deer, passed with Dasharna to the north of them and Pāñcāla to the south.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Pāṇḍavas passed between Yakrilloma and Śūrasena, speaking as hunters, and entered the territory of Matsya from the forest.
Then, having reached the inhabited country, Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) said to the king: 'Look — plowed fields are visible on every side, and various kinds of fields can be seen.'
'Clearly the capital of Virāṭa must be far away. Let us spend the night here — my fatigue is great.'
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Dhanañjaya, O Bhārata, take up Pāñcālī and carry her; we shall dwell in the capital, freed at last from forest life.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Arjuna quickly took Draupadī and, like a lordly elephant, having reached the vicinity of the city, Arjuna set her down.
Having reached the capital, the son of Kuntī (Yudhiṣṭhira) said to Arjuna: 'Where shall we deposit our weapons and then enter the city?'
'If we enter the city armed, dear one, we will without doubt cause alarm among its people.'
'Then we would have to enter the forest again for twelve years, for if even one of us is recognized, that is what we vowed.'
Arjuna said: O lord of men, here on this eminence stands a great and dense shami tree with massive branches, hard to climb, near a cremation ground.
'And there is no one at all to be found here, O king, for it has grown in a pathless forest frequented by deer and serpents.'
'Let us hang our weapons on this tree and go toward the city; thus we shall move about here as we please, O Bhārata.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to the righteous-souled king Yudhiṣṭhira, he proceeded to deposit the weapons, O bull of the Bhāratas.
With which bow the son of Kuru's joy, alone on his chariot, had conquered gods, men, and serpents, and had subdued other flourishing kingdoms —
— that noble, greatly resounding Gāṇḍīva, which strikes fear into enemies and destroys multitudes of foes, the son of Pṛthā (Arjuna) now unstrung.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The bowstring of that bow with which the hero, scorcher of foes, had protected Kurukṣetra — its inexhaustible string — Yudhiṣṭhira unloosed.
With which bow the mighty Bhīmasena had conquered the Pāñcālas in battle, and alone had repelled many enemies in the conquest of the directions —
— hearing the twang of which, enemies fled in battle, like the crack of a splitting mountain or the burst of a thunderbolt —
— with which the blameless one had seized the king of Sindhu — the bowstring of that bow Bhīmasena now removed.
With which bow the Pāṇḍava had conquered the western quarter, the string of that bow the heroic Sankrandana (Arjuna) drew off in battle.
With which bow the lord, skilled in southern ways, had conquered the southern quarter — the hero Sahadeva now unstrung that weapon.
They deposited together with their bows their golden, long swords, their quivers of great worth, their scabbards, and their razor-edged arrows.
Nakula, climbing the tree, himself deposited the bows in those forks which he judged to be firm and solid.
And where he saw it had rained across the years he bound them there very tightly with strong cords.
The Pāṇḍavas also bound there the body of one dead, so that men would stay away from this shami tree even from a distance, smelling the foul stench and thinking 'a corpse is tied here.'
Those who said 'This is a mother aged a hundred and eighty years — it is not so' would declare: 'This is the family custom practiced by our ancestors too — hanging them upon this tree.'
Telling their stories down to the cowherd boys and shepherd lads, the Pārthas, scorchers of foes, destroyers of enemies, came near to the city.
Jaya, Jayanta, Vijaya, Jayatsena, Jayadbala — these were the secret names that Yudhiṣṭhira assigned to them.
Then, true to their vows, they entered the great city, intending to live unrecognized in the kingdom through the thirteenth year.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Yudhiṣṭhira approached Virāṭa first, the king seated in his assembly hall, having donned lapis-blue golden dice and holding them under his arm wrapped in cloth.
The lord of men — of great renown, increaser of the Kaurava line, of great majesty, honored by the king of men, unapproachable as a sharp-venomed serpent — approached the glorious lord of the realm.
That great bull among men appeared youthful in form, and radiant as an immortal; covered with brilliant rays like the sun, and mighty as fire concealed beneath ash.
Seeing the Pāṇḍava approach like the moon covered by clouds, the king of Virāṭa asked his ministers, brahmins, and charioteers, as well as the commoners and all who were seated in the assembly: 'Who is this who has come first, and who is this one who now surveys the hall?'
'He will not be a mere brahmin — he is the best of men; in my mind I think he must be a lord of the earth. He has no slave, no chariot, no earrings — yet he shines near us like Indra.'
'His bodily marks point to this — in my mind it is as if he were a consecrated king. He approaches me free of distress, like a rutting elephant going to a lotus pond.'
While he was thus reflecting, that bull among men, Yudhiṣṭhira, approached Virāṭa and said: 'Let the emperor know that a brahmin who has lost all his wealth, seeking a livelihood, has come here.'
'Here I wish to dwell near you, blameless one, moving freely as I please, O lord.' The king, filled with joy, immediately replied: 'Welcome! Accept my hospitality.'
'I address you gladly, my friend — from whose king's territory have you come here? Tell me truly your clan and name, and what skill or craft you possess.'
Yudhiṣṭhira said: 'I was formerly a friend of Yudhiṣṭhira; I am a brahmin of the Vyaghrapada lineage. I am skilled at throwing dice and gambling. I am known, O Virāṭa, by the name Kaṅka.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Virāṭa said: 'Come then, I grant you whatever boon you desire; command the Matsyas — I am at your disposal. My gamblers who are dear to me have always pleased me; and you, O equal of the gods, are worthy of a kingdom.'
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The highest outcome of a contest has been obtained, O lord of the people; nothing whatsoever is lacking, O Matsya. No one whom I have defeated retains the winnings — let this be my boon, by your grace.
Virāṭa said: I would strike down even one who should not be struck, should he act against your wish; likewise I would banish Brahmins from the realm. Let the assembled people of the land hear this: as I am master of the kingdom, so too is Kaṅka.
You shall be my companion and friend of equal standing; you shall have abundant garments, drink, and food. You may move freely both within and without at all times, and I have made the door open for you.
Those who might speak ill of you, though worn down by want — you need only mention them to me and I will provide them everything, there is no doubt. No fear exists for you in my presence.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus obtained the boon and the fellowship of King Virāṭa, that bull among men, that hero, lived there highly honored and happy; and no one at all came to know his true conduct.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then another came, blazing with the splendor of mighty strength, striding with the gait and grace of a lion — he held in his hand a ladle, a stirring rod, and a dark-bladed sword unsheathed and unblemished.
In the guise of a cook, yet blazing with supreme radiance like the sun illumining this world, clad in dark garments and firm as the king of mountains, he came and stood before the king of the Matsyas.
The king, beholding him as he approached and wishing to honor him, then spoke to the assembled people of the land: "This one with shoulders raised like a lion's is exceedingly handsome — who is this bull among men, this youth?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This is a man I have never seen before, like the sun. Pondering, I cannot fathom his fortune; and pondering likewise his disposition, I cannot to this day arrive at the truth about this bull among men."
Then the Pāṇḍava, approaching Virāṭa with a seemingly humble appearance yet great in spirit, said: "I am a cook, O king of men, Ballava by name — accept me as a master preparer of dishes."
Virāṭa said: "I do not believe in your being a cook, O giver of honor; for you appear like Indra of a thousand eyes in splendor, in form, and in valor. You shine here as second to none among men, my friend."
Bhīma said: "O king of men, I am your cook and servant. I know the art of soups and dishes perfectly — those same dishes that were once tasted with pleasure, O king, by King Yudhiṣṭhira in every respect."
"None is found equal to me in strength; I am ever fond of wrestling, O king, and I have contended with elephants and lions alike. I shall always do what is pleasing to you, O blameless one."
Virāṭa said: "Very well, I grant you the boon of the kitchen; work there as you wish, for you speak skillfully. Yet I do not think that work suits you at all — you deserve the earth girdled by the sea."
"As your desire is, so it shall be done — be foremost for me in the kitchen. And the men who were formerly my appointed ones there — be you, by my decree, their master."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus Bhīma, installed in the kitchen, became the firm favorite of King Virāṭa. He dwelt there, O king, and no ordinary person, nor any attendant there, came to know him.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then she, the dark-eyed one, gathering up her tresses whose tips were curled and which were beyond reproach, concealed them along her right side, those soft locks.
And donning a single great dark and very soiled garment, and taking on the disguise of a sairandhri (a skilled female attendant), Kṛṣṇā moved about as one in distress.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Men and women ran toward her as she moved about; and seeing her, they questioned her: "Who are you, and what do you wish to do?"
She said to them: "O lord of kings, I have come as a sairandhri; I wish to do service for whoever will take me in."
Because of her beauty, her bearing, and her sweet speech, they did not believe that she was a maidservant come merely for food.
But Kaikeyī, the greatly honored wife of Virāṭa, looking out from the palace, caught sight of the daughter of Drupada.
She, having observed her of such beauty, unprotected and clad in but a single garment, called to her and said: "Blessed one, who are you and what do you wish to do?"
She said to her: "O queen, I have come as a sairandhri; I wish to serve whoever will take me in."
Sudeṣṇā said: "Those who are as you describe yourself — maidservants — are not of such beauty, O lovely one; many send out maidservants and manservants of that kind."
"Your ankles are hidden, your thighs compact, three things about you are deep, six are elevated, five are red in their redness, and you speak with the sweet broken voice of a swan."
"You have beautiful hair, well-formed breasts, a dark complexion, full hips and bosom, and you are endowed with every quality — like a Kashmiri mare in her excellence."
"Your eyes are bright with lovely lashes, your lips like the bimba fruit, your waist slender, your neck like a conch shell, your veins hidden, and your face like the full moon."
"Tell me truly, blessed one — you are by no means a maidservant. Are you a yakshi, or a goddess, a gandharvi, or an apsara?"
"Are you Alambusā, Mishrakesha, Puṇḍarīkā, or Mālinī? Are you Indrāṇī, Vāruṇī, or a goddess of Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhata, or Prajāpati? Those goddesses are renowned among the gods — which of them are you, auspicious one?"
Draupadī said: "I am not a goddess, nor a gandharvi, nor an asuri, nor a rakshasi — I am indeed a sairandhri, a free attendant. This is the truth I tell you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I know how to dress hair; I grind fragrant unguents well; and I shall weave garlands of varied flowers of the most beautiful kind."
"I served Satyabhāmā, the beloved chief queen of Kṛṣṇa, and also Kṛṣṇā, the wife of the Pāṇḍavas, the one beauty among the Kurus."
"I move thus from place to place, receiving beautiful garments wherever I can obtain them, and wherever I receive them, there I dwell in happiness."
"Mālinī is the very name the goddess herself gave me. It is thus that I, O goddess Sudeṣṇā, have come to your dwelling."
Sudeṣṇā said: "I would shelter you on my very head — there is no doubt of that — were it not that the king here might pursue you with his entire heart."
"Look at the women of the royal household here in my chambers — they gaze fixedly at you. What man would you not bewitch?"
"Look at the trees standing here in my dwelling — even they seem to bow toward you. What man would you not enchant?"
"King Virāṭa, seeing your superhuman form, O fair-hipped one, would abandon me, O woman of lovely limbs, and pursue you with his whole mind."
"Whatever man you, O flawless-limbed one with long eyes, were to gaze upon with longing — he would fall under the power of desire."
"And whatever man were constantly to behold you, O one of lovely smile, of such entirely flawless limbs — he too would fall under the sway of the god of love."
"As a female crab bears in her womb her own death, so I regard your dwelling here to be of that nature, O bright-smiled one."
Draupadī said: "I cannot be obtained by Virāṭa, nor by any other, in any manner. My husbands are five Gandharvas who are young, O lovely one."
"They are sons of a certain great-souled king of the Gandharvas; they protect me always — and so those who behave harshly toward me suffer for it, and so indeed do I."
"The one who would not give me his leavings, nor bow to wash my feet — my Gandharva husbands are pleased with such a dwelling for me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Whatever man might lust after me as he would after any ordinary woman — that very night he would enter another body (i.e., meet his death)."
"Nor can I be led astray by anyone, O beautiful one, for those Gandharvas are fierce in nature and are far more powerful than I."
Sudeṣṇā said: "I shall shelter you on such terms as you yourself desire, O Nandini; you shall never be made to touch feet, nor shall you ever in any way touch leavings."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus Kṛṣṇā was kindly reassured by the wife of Virāṭa; and no one else there, O Janamejaya, came to know her true identity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Sahadeva too, donning the best disguise of a cowherd and adopting their manner of speech, then approached Virāṭa.
Beholding him approaching and radiant, that bull among men, the king drew near and questioned the delight of the Kurus.
"Whose are you, and from where do you come, and what do you wish to do, my friend? I have not seen you before — tell me truly, O bull among men."
He, the scorcher of enemies, having reached the king, then spoke with a voice resonant as the great roar of thunderclouds: "I am a Vaiśya; Ariṣṭanemi is my name; I was the cattle-counter of the foremost Kurus."
"I wish to dwell with you, O best among the Vaishas; for I do not know where those lions among kings, the Pārthas, are. It is not possible to live by any other work, and no other king pleases me besides you."
Virāṭa said: "Whether you are a Brahmin or a Kṣatriya, you are endowed with the form of a lord who rules the earth girdled by the sea. Tell me truly, O crusher of enemies — the work of a Vaiśya does not suit you at all."
"From whose king's realm have you come here? And what skill have you cultivated? How will you dwell among us always? Tell me also what your wages should be here."
Sahadeva said: "The eldest of the five sons of Pāṇḍu is King Yudhiṣṭhira. His cattle herds numbered eight hundred thousand, in groups of hundreds upon hundreds."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Others numbered ten thousand, and yet others twice as many. I was the cattle-counter of those herds — Tantipāla is the name by which I am known."
"What has been, what is, and what will be, and whatever tally exists anywhere — there is nothing unknown to me within ten leagues in every direction."
"My qualities were well known to that great-souled one, and King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Kuru king, was pleased with me."
"By this means and that, all known to me, cattle swiftly multiply; no disease whatsoever afflicts them here. These skills reside in me."
"I know also the bulls of auspicious marks, O king — those whose urine, when smelled, can cause even a barren cow to give birth."
Virāṭa said: "A hundred thousand head of cattle gathered together — of each class and variety, their qualities ascertained — I give to you along with their herdsmen. Let my cattle here be under your care."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus that lord of men, unknown to the king, O lord of the people, dwelt there in comfort. And no others either came to know him in any way; and the king gave him maintenance as he desired.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then another appeared — a great man in the full splendor of his form, wearing women's ornaments, with earrings fastened at his ears on the rampart-top, and wearing long beautiful conch-shell bangles and bracelets.
He shook out many long tresses upon his head; great-armed, he moved with the gait of a rut elephant, making the earth tremble with his step; and he came up to Virāṭa near the hall of assembly.
The king, beholding him as he came upon the floor of the assembly hall — concealed beneath the appearance of a satra performer, yet a crusher of enemies, blazing with supreme radiance — saw the son of great Indra with the gait of a lord among elephants.
He questioned all those who moved near him: "From where does this one come? I have not heard of him before." The men did not tell him — they did not know. Then the king, full of wonder, spoke these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This man is endowed with every quality, charming to the mind, dark and young, like a lordly elephant in his herd. He has put off his conch-shell bangles and bracelets, undone his braid and fastened on earrings —"
"— wearing a crest and fine hair in another fashion. Become an archer, put on armor, take up arrows too; mount a chariot and ride about. Be equal to my sons or equal to me!"
"For I am old and desire relief from burdens — swiftly protect all the Matsyas! Those of eunuch form are never of this kind, it seems to my mind."
Arjuna said: "I sing, I dance, and I play instruments; I am skilled in dancing, I am expert in singing. Assign me yourself to Uttara — I will be the dancing-teacher of the princess, O king of men."
"But this form of mine — what would proclaiming it accomplish? It would only greatly increase grief. Know me, O king of men, as Bṛhannaḍā — as a son or daughter bereft of both father and mother."
Virāṭa said: "Very well, Bṛhannaḍā, I grant you the boon — teach my daughter and those like her to dance. Yet I do not think this work befits you; you deserve the earth girdled by the sea."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The king of the Matsyas, having observed Bṛhannaḍā's skills in the arts, in dancing, and likewise in instrumental music, and having ascertained the certainty of his eunuchhood, then dismissed him to the women's quarter of the princesses.
And the lordly Dhanañjaya instructed the daughter of Virāṭa in singing and playing instruments, as well as her companions and attendants; and that Pāṇḍava became dear to them all.
Thus Dhanañjaya, self-controlled, dwelt there under his disguise, doing what was pleasing to those women; and the people there — whether those who moved outside or those within — did not come to know him for what he was.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then another Pāṇḍava, a lord, appeared as King Virāṭa was inspecting his horses. The common people saw him approach like the solar orb freed from cloud.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He indeed gazed at the horses here and there; and the king of the Matsyas saw him gazing. Then the slayer of enemies spoke to his attendants: "From where does this man come, shining like an immortal?"
"This one gazes at my horses most intently — he must certainly be a skilled knower of horses, an expert. Let him be brought swiftly near me; for this hero shines just as an immortal would."
Approaching the king, the slayer of enemies said: 'Victory to you, O lord of the earth, and may all blessings be yours. Yoked to horses, O king, I am always skilled; I shall be your expert groom.'
Virāṭa said: 'I give you carriages, wealth, and a dwelling — you are worthy to be my horse-keeper. But where are you from? Whose are you? How did you come here? Tell me fully the skill that you possess.'
Nakula said: 'Among the five sons of Pāṇḍu, the eldest king is Yudhiṣṭhira. By him I was formerly appointed over horses, O afflicator of enemies.'
'I know the nature of horses and their training in every respect, the handling of vicious ones, and the complete treatment of their ailments.'
'No mount would ever be timid under me; I have no unruly mares — much less stallions. The people call me Granthika, and so too does that Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira.'
Virāṭa said: 'Whatever horse-conveyances I possess, let all of them be under your authority from this day forward. And whatever horse-trainers and charioteers I have, let them be under your command.'
'If this pleases you, O god-like one, tell me whatever wealth you desire. The work of a groom seems unworthy of you — you shine like a king in my estimation.'
'Indeed, your appearance equals that of Yudhiṣṭhira himself in my sight, O fair one. But how is it that the blameless Pāṇḍava, separated from his servants, dwells in the forest and finds his pleasure there?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus that youth, who resembled the foremost of Gandharvas, was honored by the delighted king Virāṭa. And no others knew him in the least as he moved about among them, charming and agreeable.
Thus the Pāṇḍavas, those lords whose vision never fails and whose vows are unfailing, dwelt in the land of Matsya, passing their time of incognito with composed minds — they who are lords whose realm extends to the rim of the ocean — in great suffering.
Janamejaya said: 'When the Pāṇḍavas of great valor were dwelling thus in the city of Matsya, O brahmin, what did they do after that?'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: 'Hear what those descendants of Kuru, concealed in that place, did while dwelling there and pleasing the king.'
Yudhiṣṭhira became the beloved companion of the assembly members in the hall, and likewise a favorite of Virāṭa and his son, O lord of the people.
For that Pāṇḍava, knowing the secrets of dice, entertained them at gambling as he pleased, like a puppeteer controlling brahmins on strings.
And the king of righteousness, that tiger among men, secretly winning Virāṭa's wealth, would distribute it fittingly among his brothers.
Bhīmasena too, with the various eatables and meats lavishly provided by Matsya, would sell them and give the proceeds to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Arjuna too, obtaining worn-out garments from the women's quarters, would sell them and distribute the proceeds to all the Pāṇḍavas.
Sahadeva too, that Pāṇḍava, adopting the guise of a cowherd, would provide curds, milk, and ghee to the Pāṇḍavas.
Nakula too, obtaining wealth for his work with the horses when that lord of men was pleased, would give it to the Pāṇḍavas.
And Kṛṣṇā too — that noble lady in her suffering — would look upon all those brothers and move about as before, unrecognized.
Thus those great warriors, providing for each other in this way, and yet beholding Kṛṣṇā in that condition, dwelt there in concealment, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, in the fourth month, there arose a grand festival of Brahmā among the Matsyas — prosperous and well-regarded by the people.
There, wrestlers gathered from all directions, O king, by the thousands — of great bodies and great strength, like the Kalakhanja demons.
Swelling with valor, overflowing with strength, honored by the king, with shoulders, waists, and necks like lions — proud and high-minded men who had repeatedly won glory in the arena before the king.
Among them one was pre-eminent and challenged all the wrestlers. As he strutted about the arena, none would stand up to him.
When all the wrestlers were disheartened and their spirits broken, the king of Matsya had that wrestler fight against his cook.
Then Bhīma, though urged with difficulty, made up his mind — for in public he could not refuse the lord of men.
Then that tiger among men, moving with the relaxed gait of a lion, entered the great arena, filling Virāṭa with delight.
The son of Kuntī tied his sash and thereupon gladdened the crowd. Then Bhīma challenged that wrestler who was like Vṛtra himself.
Both were of tremendous enthusiasm and both of fierce valor — like two great bull elephants of sixty years in rut.
Bhīma, slayer of enemies, tearing the wrestler away with his arms, dragged him — roaring and shrieking — like a tiger with an elephant.
The mighty-armed and valorous one, lifting him up, whirled him around. Then both the wrestlers and the Matsyas were struck with the greatest amazement.
Having whirled him a hundredfold, with the wrestler's life gone and his senses extinguished, the mighty-armed Vṛkodara ground him into the earth.
When that wrestler Jimuta, world-renowned, was slain, Virāṭa was filled with the utmost joy along with his kinsmen.
Overflowing with joy, the high-minded king gave great wealth to Ballava in the great arena, as generously as Kubera himself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In this way, slaying very many wrestlers and men of great strength, he brought the highest delight to the king of Matsya.
When no man equal to him could be found there, he then fought with tigers and lions and elephants as well.
Again, having entered the women's quarters, Vṛkodara would fight among the women at Virāṭa's command against maddened lions of great strength.
And Bībhatsu too, that Pāṇḍava, satisfied Virāṭa and all the women of the inner quarters with song and beautiful dancing.
With well-trained and swift horses gathered from various places, Nakula gratified the king, O best of kings.
Pleased upon seeing the well-trained cattle belonging to Sahadeva, the king gave him much wealth as his due reward, O mighty one.
Thus those bulls among men lived there in concealment, performing services for Virāṭa the king in those days.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the sons of Pṛthā, those great warriors, were dwelling thus in concealment in the city of Matsya, ten months passed by.
Yājñasenī, serving Sudeṣṇā, O lord of the people, dwelt there in great suffering — she who deserved to be served, O Janamejaya.
As she moved about in that manner in Sudeṣṇā's household, the commander of Virāṭa's army beheld the Pāñcālī, she of lotus-like face.
Seeing her as she moved about, radiant as one born of divine seed, like a goddess herself, Kīcaka desired her, pierced by the arrows of Kāma.
Scorched by the fire of desire, the commander approached Sudeṣṇā and, as if smiling, spoke these words:
'This beautiful one was never seen by me before in the abode of King Virāṭa. With her beauty she maddens me utterly — this lady, born fragrant like wine.'
'Who is this one with the form of a goddess, captivating to the heart, O fair one? Tell me — who is she and where is she from, this lovely woman? She churns my mind and brings me under her sway. I know no other remedy for this today.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Ah, this handmaid of yours is beautiful — she of fresh, youthful beauty appears before me. Indeed she performs work unworthy of her form. Let her command me and all that I possess.'
'Let her adorn my great house — rich in elephants, horses, and chariots, possessed of great wealth, full of prosperity, with abundant drink and food, charming, decorated with golden ornaments.'
Then Kīcaka, having taken leave of Sudeṣṇā, approached the daughter of the king of men and spoke then to Kṛṣṇā with words of enticement — like a jackal in the forest approaching the daughter of the lion.
'This beauty of yours, and your youth — both are rendered purposeless and barren today, O passionate one. Like a supreme garland that goes unworn, you do not shine, O beautiful one, though you are truly lovely.'
'I will abandon my former wives — let them become your maidservants, O fair-smiling one. And I myself, O beautiful woman, shall stand like a slave before you; I shall always be under your command, O lovely-faced one.'
Draupadī said: 'O son of a charioteer, you court me here as one not to be courted — a Sairandhrī woman of lower standing, a contemptible hairdresser.'
'I am another's wife — may it be well with you; this is not fitting for you at this time. The wives of living beings are dear to them — reflect on dharma.'
'Your mind should never in any way turn toward another's wife. The renunciation of improper deeds — that is the vow of good men.'
'For a man of sinful soul who wrongly lusts and has entered into delusion will gain terrible infamy and will incur very great fear.'
'Do not be elated, O son of a charioteer — today you will lose your life, coveting me who am difficult to attain, guarded by heroes.'
'And I cannot be taken by you. My husbands are Gandharvas — they will kill you when angered. Stop, it is enough — do not bring about your own destruction.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Just as a foolish boy, standing on a bank, mindlessly wishes to cross to the far bank though he cannot — so you, a man who cannot accomplish what you desire, wish to do what is beyond you.'
'Whether you enter the earth, or fly upward, or run to the far shore of the ocean — even so you shall not escape them. For my husbands are mighty sons of gods.'
'Like some afflicted man who rushes toward the night of doom — why do you importune me so stubbornly today, O Kīcaka? Do you think of me like a child lying in its mother's lap who wants to grasp the moon?'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Rejected by the princess-born, Kīcaka, overwhelmed by unbridled and terrible desire, spoke to Sudeṣṇā:
'Let it be arranged that I may meet with the Sairandhrī by some means, O Kaikeyī. Seek to obtain her for me, Sudeṣṇā — otherwise I shall give up my life.'
Hearing his lamentations again and again, the wise queen, chief consort of Virāṭa, felt compassion for him.
Keeping her own interest in mind and reflecting upon his interest as well, and also upon Kṛṣṇā's distress, Sudeṣṇā spoke to the charioteer's son:
'You prepare wine and food on the occasion of the festival day. I will send her to you there — the wine-fetcher — into your presence.'
'There, when she has been sent and is alone without restraint, you may coax her as you please — if, when coaxed, she is willing to sport with you.'
Kīcaka then, going home at his sister's word, had wine fetched — of royal quality, well-filtered and refined.
And he had much roast meat and many kinds of game, great and small, prepared by skilled cooks — splendid food and drink.
When this had been done and Kīcaka had sent word to the queen, Sudeṣṇā dispatched the Sairandhrī to Kīcaka's dwelling.
Sudeṣṇā said: 'Rise and go, Sairandhrī, to Kīcaka's dwelling. Bring wine, dear one — thirst torments me.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Draupadī said: 'I should not go to his dwelling, O princess. You yourself know, O queen, how shameless he is.'
'And I, O blameless-limbed one, O passionate lady, shall not become one who acts out of lust in your house, unfaithful to my husbands.'
'And you yourself know, O goddess, what agreement was made when I first entered your house, O passionate one.'
'And Kīcaka — foolish and arrogant with the pride of Kāma — he will dishonor me upon seeing me. I will not go there, O lovely one.'
'You have many other attendants obedient to your command, O princess — send another. May it be well with you, for he will dishonor me.'
Sudeṣṇā said: 'He will never harm you when you are sent by me from here.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: With these words she placed in her hands a bronze vessel with a golden lid. She, full of suspicion, weeping, having taken refuge in fate, set forth as the wine-fetcher to Kīcaka's dwelling.
Draupadī said: "As I know no other man but the Pāṇḍavas, by that truth I have been protected — do not bring me under Kīcaka's power."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: That frail woman stood before the Sun for a moment; then the Sun understood everything regarding that slender-waisted one.
Then the Sun, becoming invisible, assigned a Rākṣasa to guard her, and that being did not abandon the blameless woman in any circumstance thereafter.
Seeing Kṛṣṇā approach trembling like a doe, the charioteer's son rose up joyfully, like a ferryman who has found a boat to cross the river.
Kīcaka said: "Welcome, O beautiful-haired one! The night has passed well for me. You, my mistress, have arrived — grant me my desire."
"Let them bring golden garlands, conch-shell ornaments, earrings and bracelets, and garments of silk and deerskin."
"There is a bright bed prepared for your sake — come there with me and drink the sweet spring wine."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Draupadī said: "The princess sent me to fetch wine for you — quickly bring the drink for me, she said, I am thirsty — thus she spoke."
Kīcaka said: "Others will carry the princess's wine, dear lady."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Saying this, the charioteer's son seized her by the right hand; she, though grasped, shook him off and hurled Kīcaka to the ground, then fled to the assembly hall for refuge, where King Yudhiṣṭhira sat.
Kīcaka chased after her and seized her by the side of her hair; then, even before the watching king, he threw her down and kicked her with his foot.
Then that Rākṣasa who had been assigned to her by the Sun at that moment hurled Kīcaka away with the speed of wind, O Bhārata.
Struck by the power of the Rākṣasa, he fell to the ground, spinning and motionless, like a tree torn up by the roots.
Bhīmasena and Yudhiṣṭhira, seated there, both saw it, unable to endure Kīcaka's assault on Kṛṣṇā with his foot.
The great-souled Bhīma, yearning to kill that wicked Kīcaka, then ground his teeth against his teeth in fury.
Then the king of righteousness pressed down Bhīma's thumb with his own thumb, O king, fearing that Bhīma might reveal himself.
Reaching the door of the assembly hall, she, the beautiful-hipped one, wept and addressed the Matsya king, glancing at those dejected husbands.
Guarding her composure and the vow in accordance with dharma, the daughter of Drupada stood as if burning, with fierce blazing eyes.
Draupadī said: "Those men whose enemy dares not sleep touching the ground with his feet — the charioteer's son has kicked me, their self-respecting wife, with his foot."
"Those who give but never beg, who are devoted to Brahmins and speak only truth — the charioteer's son has kicked me, their self-respecting wife."
"Those from whom the rumble of kettledrums and the twang of bowstrings is heard unceasingly — the charioteer's son has kicked me, their self-respecting wife."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Those who are glorious, self-restrained, mighty, and proud — the charioteer's son has kicked me, their self-respecting wife."
"Those who, bound by the cord of dharma, could destroy the entire world — the charioteer's son has kicked me, their self-respecting wife."
"Those great warriors who become refuge for the refuge-seeking, who roam the world in disguise — where are they today?"
"How can those mighty men of boundless valour endure, like eunuchs, watching their beloved chaste wife being beaten by the charioteer's son?"
"Where is their indignation, their heroism, and their splendour, that they do not protect their wife being beaten by that wicked soul?"
"What can I do here, when Virāṭa, who corrupts dharma, looks on and endures my being beaten though I am innocent?"
"O king, you do nothing befitting a king regarding Kīcaka — your conduct is like that of brigands; it does not befit a royal assembly."
"Kīcaka is not standing by his own dharma, nor is the Matsya king in any way; even the assembly members are ignorant of dharma, those who attend upon this man."
"I do not reproach you openly in this public assembly, O king Virāṭa; I am not fit to kill him here in your presence, O Matsya — yet let the assembly members witness Kīcaka's transgression."
Virāṭa said: "I did not witness the quarrel between the two of you in person; without knowing the truth of the matter, how could it be well for me to intervene?"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the assembly members, understanding the situation, honoured Kṛṣṇā further, saying "Well done, well done," and condemned Kīcaka.
The assembly members said: "He whose wife this woman is — beautiful in every limb, with wide lotus-like eyes — would have gained the greatest treasure; he need never grieve."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the assembly members thus honoured and gazed upon Kṛṣṇā, sweat broke out on Yudhiṣṭhira's brow from suppressed rage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the Kaurava spoke to the princess, his dear wife: "Go, Sairandhrī, do not stay here — return to Sudeṣṇā's quarters."
"Wives of heroes suffer hardship in serving their husbands; those who suffer thus through devoted service win the world of their husbands in the end."
"I believe your husbands, the Gandharvas brilliant as the sun, do not see this as the right moment for anger — that is why they do not rush forward for you."
"You do not understand the right moment, Sairandhrī; you rush about like an actress and create disturbance for the Matsyas gambling in the royal assembly. Go, Sairandhrī — the Gandharvas will do what is pleasing to you."
Draupadī said: "I, a righteous woman acting in their interest, am exceedingly worthy of compassion — I am to be beaten here in their cause, when their eldest is addicted to dicing."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇā ran to Sudeṣṇā's quarters, the beautiful-hipped one, her hair dishevelled, her eyes red with passion and grief.
Her face, now that she had ceased weeping, shone like the disc of the moon freed from a streak of cloud in the sky.
Sudeṣṇā said: "Who has struck you, O lovely-limbed one? Why do you weep, beautiful woman? Whose offence brings you no happiness today, dear one? Who has wronged you?"
Draupadī said: "Kīcaka struck me there when I had gone to fetch wine for you — in the assembly hall, before the watching king, just as if I were alone."
Sudeṣṇā said: "I shall have Kīcaka killed, if you think it right — he who, maddened by desire, pursues you who are so hard to obtain."
Draupadī said: "Others will indeed kill him — those against whom he commits his offences. I believe he will most certainly go to the next world even this very day."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Struck by the charioteer's son, the princess blazed with fury; desiring the death of the army's commander, that passionate woman, the daughter of Drupada, then went to her own dwelling.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kṛṣṇā, the slender-waisted one, having duly performed her purification, washed her limbs and garments with water.
Weeping, she pondered the resolution of this suffering: "What shall I do? Where shall I go? How should I proceed?"
Having thus reflected, her mind went to Bhīma: "There is no one but Bhīma who can today do what is dear to my heart."
Then, rising at night and abandoning her own bed, Kṛṣṇā ran off seeking her protector — she who had a protector, chaste, overwhelmed by great mental anguish, that woman of resolute mind.
Reaching the kitchen and finding Bhīmasena, that bright-smiling Pāñcālī stood before him like a white three-year-old cow born in the forest, like a cow in heat before a great elephant.
Like a creeper clinging to a great flowering sāla tree on the Gomatī's bank, she embraced him with both arms and awakened him, the blameless one, like a lioness rousing a sleeping lion in a difficult forest.
With speech sweet as a vīṇā perfectly tuned to the gāndhāra note, that blameless Pāñcālī addressed Bhīmasena.
"Rise, rise! Why do you sleep like a dead man, Bhīmasena? A sinful man who is not dead cannot live on after laying hands upon a wife."
"While that most wicked army commander, my enemy, who has committed such a deed, still lives today — how can you indulge in sleep?"
Awakened by the princess, he sprang up abandoning his bed, like a cloud in appearance, and sat up on his couch with its cushioned covering.
Then the Kaurava spoke to the princess, his dear wife: "For what purpose have you come to me hastily like this?"
"Your complexion does not appear natural — you look thin and pale. Tell me everything fully so that I may know it all."
"Whether it is happiness or suffering, whether hateful or dear — tell me everything accurately; having heard, I will know what further is to be done."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I alone, Kṛṣṇā, am your trusted one in all matters; I too shall rescue you from dangers again and again."
"Speak quickly whatever you wish to say, whatever your purpose — then go back to sleep before anyone else becomes aware of it."
Draupadī said: "How should she not grieve, whose husband is Yudhiṣṭhira — knowing all her sufferings, why do you even ask me?"
"That the attendant brought me then with the taunt of 'slave-woman,' into the midst of the assembly — that burns me, O Bhārata."
"Who else called a king's daughter, like me, could live on after enduring such intense suffering — except Draupadī, O lord?"
"And who else could endure to bear the second molestation by the wicked Sindhava while dwelling in forest exile?"
"Touched by Kīcaka's foot in the presence of the Matsya king and before that scoundrel's eyes — who like me could live on?"
"Thus afflicted by so many kinds of suffering, O Bhārata, you do not truly know me, O son of Kuntī — what is the fruit of life for me?"
"This one, O Bhārata, O tiger among men — the army commander of King Virāṭa named Kīcaka, the king's brother-in-law, of utterly wicked mind —"
"That evil-souled one, while I dwell in the royal palace in the guise of a Sairandhrī, constantly tells me: 'Become my wife.'"
"Being thus solicited by him who deserves death, O slayer of foes, my heart splits like a fruit ripe with time."
"And blame your eldest brother, that wicked gambler at dice — through whose action I have obtained this endless suffering."
"Who indeed, having abandoned his kingdom and all his possessions along with his own person, would gamble as if in voluntary renunciation — except that wicked dice-player?"
"If he had gambled morning and evening with a thousand niṣkas and with whatever other substantial wealth, even for many years —"
"Gold, silver, garments, vehicles with their teams, goats and sheep, and herds of horses and mules — none of these would ever have been exhausted."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Yet this same man, stripped of his royal splendour through gambling, sits silent like a fool, pondering his own deeds."
"He whom ten thousand lotus-marked elephants, garlanded in gold, used to follow as he went — that same man now lives by gambling."
"Likewise hundreds of thousands of men of boundless splendour used to attend the great king Yudhiṣṭhira at Indraprastha."
"A hundred thousand maidservants, with vessels in hand, used to feed guests day and night in his kitchen."
"This foremost of givers, who gave away thousands of niṣkas, is now overwhelmed by the great calamity born of gambling."
"Many bards and panegyrists, possessed of melodious voices, wearing polished jewelled earrings, used to attend upon him morning and evening."
He in whose assembly a thousand sages constantly sat as members — men endowed with austerity and learning, attended upon by every wish they desired —
— that Yudhiṣṭhira, out of compassion, always supported cheerfully all the blind, the aged, the destitute, and all those in distress throughout his kingdoms —
— that same Yudhiṣṭhira has fallen to ruin; he who used to gamble in the king's assembly is now a servant of the Matsya king, called Kaṅka.
He at whose court, when he dwelt at Indraprastha, all kings used to bring tribute — that very one now seeks wages from others.
Kings and rulers of the earth were once subject to his will; that same king, now robbed of his will, lives today under the power of others.
He who scorched the entire earth with his splendour like the sun with its rays — that same Yudhiṣṭhira is now a dice-player in the court of king Virāṭa.
Him whom kings waited upon together with sages in his assembly — behold that Pāṇḍava now waiting upon another, O Pāṇḍava!
Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira, the great-minded, the righteous-souled, undeserving of this fate, reduced to seeking refuge for the sake of bare life — whose heart would not grieve?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whom the entire earth, O hero, waited upon in assembly — behold that Bhārata now waiting upon another, O Bhārata!
Thus tormented by so many griefs, helpless as one without a protector, standing in the midst of an ocean of sorrow — why, O Bhīma, do you not see me?
Draupadī said: This great sorrow which I am about to tell you, O Bhārata — you must not blame me for it; it is out of pain that I speak of it.
When you fight within the house with tigers, buffaloes, and lions, while Kaikeyī's woman watches — at such times a faintness comes over me.
And the Kaikeyī woman, rising from her watching, would say to those women, seeing me, flawless of form, as though overcome by faintness —
"Out of affection born of long cohabitation, I think, this sweet-smiling woman grieves for this cook being fought with by mighty warriors."
"The sairandhrī is of lovely form, and the cook Ballava exceedingly handsome; the hearts of women are hard to know — in my view they are well matched."
"The sairandhrī, ever tender-hearted from pleasant intimacy, and these two are residents of this royal household for the same length of time."
Speaking such words, she would constantly needle me; and seeing me grow angry, she would suspect me of feelings for you.
When she spoke thus, a great sorrow would come over me; sunk in grief for Yudhiṣṭhira, I have no will left to live.
He who in a single chariot conquered gods, men, and serpents alike — that one is now a young dancing-master for the daughters of king Virāṭa.
He whose immeasurable soul once satisfied Agni in the Khāṇḍava forest — that Pārtha is now confined within the inner apartments like fire hidden in a well.
He from whom the enemies ever feared — that bull among men — Dhanañjaya now sits in a guise scorned by the world.
At the sound of whose bowstring the enemies trembled — women now cheerfully attend upon him at the sound of song.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
On whose head shone a diadem blazing like the sun — that same Dhanañjaya today has his hair plaited and braided like a woman's.
He in whom all divine weapons reside, that great-souled one, the repository of all sciences — he now wears earrings.
Whom thousands of kings of unequalled glory dared not challenge in battle, as the great ocean does not transgress its shore —
— that same one is now a young dancing-master for the daughters of king Virāṭa, living in disguise as a servant of the maidens.
At the sound of whose chariot the earth trembled together with its mountains and forests, O Bhīma, along with all that is stationary and that moves —
At whose birth, O greatly fortunate one, Kuntī's sorrow vanished — that younger brother of yours, O Bhīmasena, now causes me grief.
Seeing him adorned with ornaments, with earrings of wrought gold, coming with shell-like wrists — my heart sinks.
Seeing that terrible archer Arjuna, his hair twisted into a braid, surrounded by maidens — O Bhīma, my heart sinks.
When I see him, divine in form, surrounded by maidens — like a rut-maddened elephant encircled by she-elephants —
— Pārtha, the master of wealth, standing in attendance upon Matsya Virāṭa amid the sound of instruments — at such times the directions vanish from my sight.
Surely the noble lady (Kuntī) does not know of the hardship that has befallen Dhanañjaya, the Kaurava who never made an enemy, now sunk by evil gambling.
And seeing Sahadeva the younger, the lord of warriors, coming disguised in cowherds' dress among the cattle, I have become pale as the Pāṇḍu plant, O Bhārata.
Thinking again and again on Sahadeva's deeds, I cannot find, O mighty-armed, any misdeed of Sahadeva by reason of which a man of such true valour should suffer this kind of sorrow.
I burn with pain, O foremost of Bhāratas, seeing your dear brother, resembling a mighty bull among cattle, set to work among cattle by Matsya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When I see him full of spirit, dressed in red, walking at the head of the cowherds, saluting Virāṭa — then fever seizes me.
The noble lady (Kuntī) always praised the heroic Sahadeva to me: "He is of great lineage, of excellent conduct, and of good character."
"He who is restrained by modesty, sweet-spoken, righteous, and dear to me — that one is to be protected by you in the forests, O Yājñasenī, even through the nights."
Seeing Sahadeva, the best of warriors, engaged among the cattle, sleeping at night on a calf's skin — can I go on living, O Pāṇḍava?
He who is always endowed with three excellences — beauty, skill in weapons, and intelligence — is now a groom of horses for Virāṭa. Behold the reversal of time!
Crowds gather to watch him as he tames the horses of the great king with garlands and bonds, training them swiftly.
I saw that glorious one, brilliant and noble, standing in attendance upon the Matsya Virāṭa and presenting the horses to him.
Do you think me happy, O Pārtha, O scorcher of foes? — I am thus overwhelmed by hundreds of sorrows on account of Yudhiṣṭhira.
Beyond these, O Bhārata, other distinct sorrows also beset me, O son of Kuntī — hear them too, I shall tell you.
While you all are alive, manifold sorrows are desiccating my body. What greater sorrow than this can there be?
Draupadī said: I, moving about in the royal palace in the guise of a sairandhrī, am a cleaning-maid of Sudeṣṇā — because of that gambling cheat.
Behold my dire degradation, O scorcher of foes — I, a king's daughter, sit waiting upon time; all sorrow, it is said, has its season.
For mortals, it is said, the attainment of goals, and victory and defeat alike, are all impermanent — keeping this in mind, I wait for my husbands' rise again.
Whatever is the cause of a man's victory is also the cause of his defeat — keeping this truth in mind, I wait with patience.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Men who give are themselves asked in return; those who kill are slain in return; those who bring others down are brought down by others in turn — so have I heard.
Fate has no burden too great and fate cannot be transcended — so too says the scripture; keeping faith in fate still more, I wait.
Water that has stood before returns to the same place again — desiring the turn of the cycle, I wait again for the rise.
When by fate even well-directed effort comes to ruin, then — so the wise know — one must still strive when fate's moment arrives.
The purpose behind these words I have spoken — ask me, or else I shall tell you unsolicited, for I am one in distress.
The chief queen of the sons of Pāṇḍu, the daughter of Drupada — having reached this condition, who other than I would still wish to live?
Surpassing all the Kurus, even the Pāñcālas, O Bhārata, and the sons of Pāṇḍu — such affliction has come upon me, O subduer of foes.
With brothers, fathers-in-law, and many sons — a woman thus richly provided — what other woman could be so afflicted, O slayer of enemy heroes?
Surely I must have offended fate in my childhood — by whose displeasure I have come to this ill fate, O bull of the Bhāratas.
See also, O Pāṇḍava, the situation of my complexion — the space for colour that was not there in my extremest grief then.
You alone know, O Bhīma, what happiness was mine before, O Pārtha — that same I, having fallen into servitude, can find no peace, helpless as I am.
I do not think this is fate's doing — that Pārtha Dhanañjaya, the mighty-armed wielder of the terrible bow, sits quiet as a fire that has gone out.
The course of living beings cannot be known by men, O Pārtha — this downfall of yours I consider not to have been anticipated.
You who are equal to Indra always used to look to my face for guidance — that best of virtuous women am I, now looking up at the faces of women lesser than myself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Behold my condition, O Pāṇḍava, how undeserved it is — even while you all live, behold the reversal of time.
She to whom the earth bounded by the ocean was obedient — today I, frightened, am obedient to Sudeṣṇā.
She before whom attendants used to walk and behind whom they used to follow — that same I today walk before and behind Sudeṣṇā. Know this as my unbearable sorrow, O son of Kuntī.
I who never ground the unguents for my own body — except for Kuntī, bless you — today grind sandalwood paste. Behold, O son of Kuntī, my hands — not as they were before for you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Saying this, she showed him both her hands, bound with calluses.
Draupadī said: I who never feared Kuntī nor any of you — today I stand frightened before Virāṭa as a servant-girl.
What will the queen say to me — is the paste well prepared or not? For the Matsya king, they say, takes pleasure only in sandalwood ground by no other hand.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: That passionate woman Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī), while recounting her sorrows to Bhīmasena, wept softly, gazing up at Bhīmasena.
She, with a voice choked by tears, sighing again and again, thus spoke, striking at the heart of Bhīmasena.
No small offence must I have committed against the gods in a former life, O Bhīma — unhappy that I am, I live on when I ought to die, O Pāṇḍava.
Then Vṛkodara (Bhīma), the slayer of enemy heroes, brought to his face her two hands, swollen and bound with calluses, and wept, while she trembled.
Taking those hands in his, the son of Kuntī, the mighty one, releasing his tears, spoke these words, overwhelmed by the deepest grief.
Bhīmasena said: Shame on the strength of my arms and on Phalguna's Gāṇḍīva — that your hands, once flushed with beauty, have now become callused on both!
I would have wrought great slaughter in Virāṭa's assembly, but Dharmarāja restrained me there with a sideways glance — understanding his intention, I have held back, O passionate one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the expulsion of the Kurus from their kingdom, and the slaying — of Suyodhana, of Karṇa, of Śakuni the son of Subala,
and of the sinful Duḥśāsana — that I have not taken his head burns in my heart like a dart planted there, O lovely one. Do not abandon righteousness, O fair-hipped one; abandon your anger, O great-minded one.
If King Yudhiṣṭhira were to hear this reproach of yours, O auspicious one, he would entirely abandon his life.
Or if Dhanaṃjaya, O lovely-hipped one, or the twins were to pass to another world, I could not continue living, O slender-waisted one.
Sukanyā, daughter of Śāryāta, a proud and beautiful woman, followed the sage Cyavana of the Bhṛgu lineage into the forest, where he sat in meditation, having become an anthill.
And if you have heard of Nāḍāyanī and Indrasenā, radiant in beauty — she followed her aged husband, who had lived for a thousand years.
And if you have heard of Vaidehī, daughter of Janaka — Sītā followed her husband Rāma who dwelt in the great forest.
Though seized and oppressed by a demon, Rāma's beloved queen, O lovely-hipped one, followed Rāma alone even in her affliction.
So too Lopāmudrā, O timid one, though endowed with youth and beauty, followed Agastya, abandoning all superhuman pleasures.
Just as these women, praised for their beauty and devotion to their husbands, are celebrated, so too are you, O auspicious one, endowed with all virtues.
Bear this long period patiently — it amounts to only a month and a half more; when the thirteenth year is complete, you shall be queen of the king again.
Draupadī said: It is out of distress, O Bhīma, that I have shed these tears, being unable to bear my sufferings — I do not reproach the king.
O Bhīmasena of great might, now that the period of concealment has passed and the time for action is at hand, be ready to act without delay.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Here, O Bhīma, the princess Kaikeyī always torments me out of fear that I might surpass her in beauty — the king constantly worries about how to keep her satisfied.
And knowing her feelings, this Kīcaka, wicked-souled and himself of crooked vision, always importunes me.
Angry at him, O Bhīma, yet restraining my anger again and again, I spoke to that one blinded by desire: 'Protect yourself, Kīcaka.'
'I am the wife of the Gandharvas, the beloved queen of five of them — those fierce, bold warriors will slay you.'
Thus addressed, that wicked-souled Kīcaka replied: 'I do not fear the Gandharvas, O Sairandhrī of bright smile.'
'Even a hundred or a thousand Gandharvas assembled in battle I would slay — O timid one, grant me even one moment of your company.'
When he spoke thus, I again told that charioteer's son consumed by desire: 'You are no match for those glorious Gandharvas.'
'I am always established in righteousness, endowed with noble lineage and virtue — I do not wish anyone to be slain, and that is why you still live, Kīcaka.'
Thus addressed, that wicked-souled one laughed loudly then — he did not remain on the path of righteousness, nor did he desire to follow dharma.
Evil-souled, evil-minded, enslaved to lust and passion, rude and wicked — though rejected again and again, he would torment me at every encounter, and so I would rather abandon my life.
Therefore, if you strive in dharma, great dharma will not perish for those who keep their vow — but if you do not protect your wife, she will no longer be yours.
When a wife is protected, progeny is protected; when progeny is protected, the self is protected.
I have heard from Brahmins who expound the duties of the castes that the dharma of a Kṣatriya is always nothing other than the destruction of enemies.
In the sight of the king of dharma and before your very eyes, O mighty Bhīmasena, Kīcaka struck me with his foot.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It was you who rescued me from that terrible demon Jaṭāsura; and likewise you conquered Jayadratha together with your brothers.
Slay this wretch too, O Bhārata, this Kīcaka who insults me, relying on the king's favor, and who causes me grief.
Smash him who is thus maddened by lust — smash him like a pot against a stone — for he is the cause of many calamities for me, O Bhārata.
If the sun rises tomorrow and he still lives, I will mix poison and drink it — I will not fall under Kīcaka's power; death before you, O Bhīmasena, is better for me.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇā wept, leaning against Bhīma's chest; and Bhīma, embracing her and offering great consolation, turned his mind to Kīcaka, licking the corners of his lips.
Bhīmasena said: I shall do exactly as you say, O fortunate one, O timid lady — today I will slay Kīcaka along with all his kinsmen.
At the early part of this night, O Yājñasenī of bright smile, shaking off your sorrow and grief, arrange a meeting with him.
There is the dance hall built by the king of Matsya — during the day young women dance there, at night they go to their homes.
There is a bed there, O timid one, firm-framed and well set — there I will show him his forefathers who have gone before to the realm of the dead.
Arrange matters, O auspicious one, so that no one sees you making this assignation with him, and so that I may be close at hand.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to each other and shedding tears, the two of them, filled with grief, bore that terribly harsh remainder of the night in their hearts.
When that night had passed, Kīcaka rose at dawn and going directly to the royal household, spoke these words to Draupadī.
'In the assembly hall, before the king's eyes, I kicked you down, and yet you found no protection even when you appealed to one mightier than I.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'For it is only by name that this one is called king of the Matsyas — I myself am truly the king of the Matsyas, the commander of the army.'
'Come willingly to me, O timid one — I shall become your slave; I will give you a hundred gold coins this very day, O lovely-hipped one.'
'And I would give you a hundred maidservants, and male servants beyond that, and a chariot yoked with mules — O timid one, let there be a union between us.'
Draupadī said: Agree to one condition of mine today, Kīcaka — let no friend or brother of yours know that you have met with me.
For I am afraid of the glorious Gandharvas finding out; promise me this, and then I shall be yours to command.
Kīcaka said: I will do exactly as you say, O lovely-hipped one; I shall go alone, O blessed one, to your empty dwelling.
For the sake of union with you, O round-thighed one, I am maddened by desire — so that the Gandharvas of solar splendor will not discover you.
Draupadī said: That dance hall which was built by the king of Matsya — during the day young women dance there, at night they go to their homes.
Go there in the darkness — the Gandharvas do not know of it; the fault will be avoided there, without doubt.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While Kṛṣṇā was speaking these words and Kīcaka was responding, O king, half a day passed — it seemed equal to an entire month.
Then Kīcaka went home, overwhelmed with joy — the fool did not perceive that what appeared to him as the Sairandhrī was in fact Death itself.
Engrossed especially in perfumes, ornaments, and garlands, he hastily adorned himself, blinded by desire.
While he was doing this, time seemed very long to him, as he thought over and over of that long-eyed woman.
His splendor appeared even greater than usual — like a lamp's wick about to flare up at the moment of extinction, the splendor of one about to lose all splendor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
