With his mind made up about the meeting, Kīcaka, blinded by desire, did not notice the day passing as he brooded on the assignation.
Then Draupadī, the auspicious one of Kuru lineage, went to the kitchen and approached her husband Bhīma closely.
With her beautiful hair ends, she spoke to him: 'I have arranged a meeting with Kīcaka in the dance hall, as you instructed me, O scorcher of foes.'
'That Kīcaka will come alone to the empty dance hall at night, O mighty-armed one — slay that Kīcaka.'
'That son of a charioteer, Kīcaka, arrogant with pride — go to the dance hall, O son of Kuntī, and render him lifeless, O Pāṇḍava.'
'And that son of a charioteer out of arrogance insults the Gandharvas — uproot him, O best of warriors, as an elephant uproots a reed.'
'Wipe away the tears of me who am overcome with grief, O Bhārata — do what is good for yourself, and uphold the honor of our family.'
Bhīmasena said: Welcome, O lovely-hipped one, is the glad news you bring me — I desire no helper at all for this task, O woman of excellent complexion.
The joy you have told me of — this meeting with Kīcaka — is the same joy I felt when I slew Hiḍimba, O woman of excellent complexion.
Placing truth, my brothers, and dharma before me, I tell you truly: I will slay Kīcaka as the lord of the gods slew Vṛtra.
Whether in a hidden place or in the open, I will crush Kīcaka — and if anyone should discover it, I will certainly slay the Matsyas as well.
Then, having slain Duryodhana, I will reclaim the earth — let Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, serve under the Matsya king as long as he likes.
Draupadī said: Act so that you do not abandon your pledge of truth on my account, O mighty one — staying concealed, O hero, bring Kīcaka down in that way.
Bhīmasena said: I will do exactly as you say, O timid one — unseen by him, this very night in the darkness, O blameless one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As an elephant tramples a bilva fruit, I will crush the head of that wicked-souled Kīcaka who desires what cannot be obtained.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Bhīma went first and sat concealed in the night — like a lion invisible to its prey, he waited for Kīcaka.
And Kīcaka, having adorned himself to his heart's desire, approached that time and place at the dance hall with the hope of union with Pāñcālī.
Thinking of the assignation, he entered that dwelling; and entering, he found that great hall enveloped in darkness.
Then that evil-minded one encountered Bhīma of incomparable might, who had arrived first and was sitting there alone in a corner.
The charioteer's son touched the one lying on the bed — and that one was Death itself, blazing with fury born of the insult to Kṛṣṇā.
And approaching him, Kīcaka, blinded by desire, his mind and soul churned by excitement, said with a smile:
'I have provided you with wealth of many kinds and without limit — with all of that in mind for you, I have hastened here.'
'Women who stay at home always praise me without cause — I am well-dressed and handsome, and there is no man like you,' — meaning himself.
Bhīmasena said: How fortunate that you are so handsome, how fortunate that you praise yourself — but such a touch as you are about to receive from me you have never felt before.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Bhīma of terrible prowess, son of Kuntī, leapt up and laughing at that lowest of men, Bhīma seized him by the hair adorned with garlands and sweet-smelling.
Seized by the hair by that force, Kīcaka — the best among the strong — swiftly pulled away from the hair-grip and grasped the Pāṇḍava by the arms.
A wrestling match ensued between those two lions among men in their fury, like two mighty elephants fighting in spring over a cow in heat.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Though slightly slipping and stepping unsteadily out of rage, the powerful Kīcaka struck Bhīma down to the ground with his knees.
Though knocked to the ground by the mighty Kīcaka, Bhīma leapt up again with speed, like a serpent struck by a rod.
Drunk on their own strength and rival pride, that pair—the charioteer's son and the Pāṇḍava—grappled and dragged each other at midnight in the deserted darkness.
That finest of halls trembled again and again, and the two mighty men, blazing with fury, roared at each other.
Though struck on the chest by Bhīma's open palms, the mighty Kīcaka, burning with rage, did not give a single step of ground.
But after bearing for a moment that assault—hard to endure on earth—the charioteer, tormented by Bhīma's power, at last began to falter.
Perceiving him flagging, the great-powered Bhīmasena swiftly seized him against his chest and churned him until he lost his senses.
Possessed by fury, Vṛkodara—best among the victorious—exhaled a hot breath and seized him violently by the hair.
Gripping Kīcaka, the mighty Bhīma let out a great roar, like a tiger that craves flesh having seized a great quarry.
His feet, his hands, his head, his neck—all of them Bhīma thrust entirely into his body, as Śiva the bearer of the Pināka bow does to a beast.
Having reduced him—all his limbs crushed—to a mere lump of flesh, the mighty Bhīmasena showed him to Kṛṣṇā.
And the blazing son of Pāṇḍu said to Draupadī: 'Come and see, Pāñcālī, what has been made of this lustful one.'
Having thus slain Kīcaka and letting his rage subside, he took leave of Kṛṣṇā Draupadī and quickly returned to the royal kitchen.
And Draupadī, best among women, having seen Kīcaka slain, was filled with joy, her anguish gone, and she spoke to the guards of the hall.
'This Kīcaka lies slain—by my gandharva husbands—he who was maddened by lust for another man's wife. Come together and see.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing her words, the guards of the dance hall came rushing together at once, carrying torches by the thousands.
Going to that chamber, they saw Kīcaka flung down—lifeless, drenched in blood upon the ground.
"Where is his neck? Where his feet? Where his hands? Where his head?"—thus they examined him, slain by the gandharva.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: At that time all his kinsmen gathered there; surrounding Kīcaka on all sides, they wept at the sight of him.
Their hair standing on end, all of them terrified, they beheld Kīcaka with every limb crushed inward, like a tortoise dragged out onto dry land.
Pounded by Bhīmasena as Indra pounds a demon, they resolved to perform his last rites and began carrying him outside.
Then those assembled charioteer-sons caught sight of Kṛṣṇā not far away—her limbs flawless—standing there clinging to a pillar.
When the charioteer-sons had assembled, the leader of the Upakīcakas spoke to them: 'Let this unchaste woman be killed at once—she for whose sake Kīcaka was slain.'
'Or rather, she should not be killed here—let her be burned together with her lover. Even in death, what is dear to the charioteer's son must be done in every way.'
Then they went to Virāṭa and said: 'Kīcaka was slain on account of this woman; she should be burned with him today—please grant your permission.'
Considering the valor of the charioteer-clan, O lord of the people, the king gave his consent that the Sairandhrī be burned together with the charioteer's son.
Approaching the trembling, lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇā as she was fainting, the Kīcakas there seized her violently.
They lifted her up, bound the slender-waisted woman, and all of them set out, carrying her toward the cremation ground.
As she was being dragged away, O king, by the charioteer-sons, blameless Kṛṣṇā—a true wife longing for her protector—cried out aloud.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Draupadī cried: 'Jaya, Jayanta, Vijaya, Jayatsena, Jayadbala—let them hear my words: the charioteer-sons are taking me away!'
'Those whose bowstring-twang sounds in great battle like the crash of a thunderbolt—the fierce, dreadful roar of those swift ones—'
'—and the mighty chariot-thunder of those glorious gandharvas—let them hear my words: the charioteer-sons are taking me away!'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing those pitiful, lamenting words of Kṛṣṇā, Bhīma leapt from his bed without a moment's hesitation.
Bhīmasena said: 'I hear the words you have spoken, Sairandhrī. Therefore, timid one, you need have no fear from the charioteer-sons.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having said this, the mighty-armed one stretched himself with the desire to kill; then, adjusting his disguise and wrapping it around, he leapt out through a side passage and issued forth.
Bhīmasena swiftly tore a tree from the rampart wall and set off toward the cremation ground, where the Kīcakas had gone.
Grasping that tree—ten fathoms long, with its trunk and branches intact—the mighty one charged at the charioteers like Yama with his staff.
From the force of his thighs as he ran, the nyagrodha, aśvattha, and kiṃśuka trees fell to the ground and lay there in heaps.
Seeing the gandharva arrive like a lion blazing with fury, the charioteers were terrified on all sides, trembling with dread and despair.
Seeing that gandharva approaching like Death himself, the Upakīcakas—who had been about to burn their eldest brother—said to one another, trembling with fear and despair:
'A mighty gandharva comes in rage, raising up a tree! Release the Sairandhrī at once—great danger has come upon us!'
Seeing the tree whirled by Bhīmasena, they released Draupadī on the spot and fled toward the city.
Watching them flee as Indra watches fleeing demons, Bhīma dispatched one hundred and five of them to the abode of Yama.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, O lord of the people, he set her free and comforted Kṛṣṇā; the invincible Vṛkodara, the mighty-armed one, spoke there to the Pāñcālī Draupadī, whose face was filled with tears and who was wretched.
'Thus, timid one, are those slain who torment you though you are innocent. Go to the city, Kṛṣṇā—you have nothing to fear. I shall go back by a different way to Virāṭa's kitchen.'
And those one hundred and five lay slain there, O Bhārata, like a great forest felled, its trees scattered about.
Thus, O king, those one hundred and five Kīcakas were slain, along with the general who was killed before—making a total of six hundred charioteers.
Seeing that great wonder, the men and women who had gathered fell into the utmost amazement and said not a single word, O Bhārata.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those who had seen the charioteers slain went and reported to the king: 'O king, more than a hundred charioteer-sons have been killed by the gandharvas.'
'As the great summit of a mountain shattered by the thunderbolt might be seen scattered about, so lay the charioteers on the earth.'
'The Sairandhrī has been released and is coming back to your house again. O king, your entire city will be thrown into doubt and danger.'
'For the Sairandhrī is of such a beauty, and the gandharvas are of such great power, and the subject of desire between men is without doubt agreeable for union.'
'Therefore, O king, such a policy must be devised that your city does not quickly come to ruin through keeping the Sairandhrī here.'
Hearing their words, Virāṭa, lord of the army, said: 'Let the final rites of these charioteers be performed.'
'Let all the Kīcakas be burned quickly together in a single well-kindled fire, with jewels and fragrances of every kind.'
The king, seized with fear, also said to his queen Sudeṣṇā: 'When the Sairandhrī arrives, tell her this on my behalf:'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'"Go, Sairandhrī, be well—go wherever you wish, dear girl. The king, O fine-hipped one, fears defeat at the hands of the gandharvas."'
'I do not dare to speak to her myself—she who is protected by gandharvas. But women are without fault in speaking to her, and so I charge you to tell her.'
Then Kṛṣṇā, freed from fear, the charioteer-sons driven off, having been rescued by Bhīmasena, made her way toward the city.
Like a young doe frightened by a tiger, the high-minded one washed her limbs and garments with water.
Seeing her, O king, men fled in all ten directions, terrified of the gandharvas; some shut their eyes tight.
Then, O king, the Pāñcālī saw Bhīmasena standing at the kitchen door—like a mighty elephant in rut.
Marveling at him, she approached slowly and said with a gesture: 'Homage to the king of the gandharvas, by whom I have been freed.'
Bhīmasena said: 'Those men who move about here as her obedient servants—having heard her word, they move about free of debt.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then she saw in the dance hall Dhanaṃjaya—the great-armed one—teaching the dance to the daughters of king Virāṭa.
Then the girls, coming out of the dance hall together with Arjuna, saw Kṛṣṇā approaching—afflicted but blameless.
The girls said: 'By good fortune, Sairandhrī, you are freed! By good fortune you have come back! By good fortune the charioteers who tormented you though innocent are slain!'
Bṛhannaḍā said: 'How were you freed, Sairandhrī? And how were those sinners killed? I wish to hear everything from you, exactly as it happened.'
The Sairandhrī said: 'What business do you have today with the Sairandhrī, Bṛhannaḍā? You who always dwell in comfort, dear one, in the girls' quarters?'
'You do not suffer the pain that the Sairandhrī endures, and yet you question me in my grief as if laughing.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bṛhannaḍā said: 'Even Bṛhannaḍā, dear lady, suffers the most extreme grief—born into an in-between existence, young woman—yet you do not understand her.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Draupadī, unflinching, entered that royal palace together with the girls, and came before Sudeṣṇā.
The princess said to her the words of Virāṭa: 'Sairandhrī, go quickly wherever you wish to go.'
'The king, be assured, fears defeat at the hands of the gandharvas, and you too are young, O fine-browed one, unmatched in beauty upon the earth.'
The Sairandhrī said: 'Let the king grant me merely thirteen days, dear lady; the gandharvas will have accomplished their purpose, without doubt.'
'Then they will take me away and do what is pleasing; and the king will certainly be joined with prosperity together with his kinsmen.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: O lord of the people, at the slaying of Kīcaka together with his younger brothers, the common people reflected on that great calamity and were filled with wonder.
Throughout that city and countryside, talk spread on every side: 'By his valor Kīcaka was the king's favorite and a man of great spirit—'
'—he was a striker of men, an ill-minded violator of others' wives; that evil-souled, wicked man has been slain by the gandharvas, as was fitting.'
Thus people in every region spoke, O great king, destroyer of enemy armies, of Kīcaka who had been so hard to assail.
Now those spies sent out by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having searched through many villages, kingdoms, and cities—
Having made arrangements as instructed and having shown themselves in their respective regions, having completed their deliberations, they then turned back toward Nāgapura.
There, having seen the Kaurava king, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, assembled together with Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, and with the great-souled Bhīṣma,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
gathered with his brothers and with the Trigarta great chariot warriors, they addressed Duryodhana who was seated in the midst of the assembly, saying this:
"O lord of men, we have always made the greatest effort in searching for the Pāṇḍavas in that great forest,
which is desolate and filled with deer, covered with many kinds of trees and creepers, thick with spreading vines, and overgrown with all manner of shrubs.
Yet we do not know by which route the Pārthas, those of firm valor, may have gone — searching here and there in every direction for their footprints.
On lofty mountain peaks, in various kingdoms, in thickly populated regions, in villages, and in cities —
O lord of men, we have searched repeatedly and still we do not find the Pāṇḍavas. They have vanished utterly. May it be well with you, O bull among men.
O best of chariot warriors, O lord of men, for a time we followed in the tracks of chariots and the paths of charioteers while searching their routes.
Having searched as was proper and having come to know the truth of the matter, the charioteers arrived at Dvāravatī without the Pārthas, O scorcher of foes.
The Pāṇḍavas were not there, O king, nor was Kṛṣṇā the devoted wife. They have disappeared altogether. We bow to you, O bull of the Bhāratas.
We do not know the movement of those great-souled Pāṇḍavas, nor their dwelling, nor their doings, nor the deeds done by them. Instruct us, O lord of men, O lord of people, as to what we should do hereafter.
What more shall we do in the search for the Pāṇḍavas? Hear also this pleasing, auspicious, and agreeable speech from us.
O king, Kīcaka, the great charioteer, the commander of King Matsya's forces — he by whose great power the Trigartas were brought low —
that wicked-souled one has been slain and lies fallen, O Bhārata, O Acyuta, killed at night by invisible Gandharvas together with his brothers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having heard this delightful news of the enemy's defeat, O Kauravya, consider yourself accomplished and decide what should be done next."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Duryodhana, having heard their words, became absorbed in his own thoughts for a long while and then replied to those assembled in the hall:
"It is indeed very difficult to know in the end where affairs will lead. Therefore let all of you reflect carefully on where the Pāṇḍavas might have gone.
In this thirteenth year, the greater part of the time of their life of incognito has already passed; only a little time remains at the end.
If the Pāṇḍavas, devoted as they are to their vow of truth, pass through what remains of this year, their term of exile would be completed.
Like mighty elephants in musth, all of them resembling venomous serpents, they will surely become fierce and terrible toward the Kauravas, filled with rage.
But if they are discovered before the time is up while still wearing their disguise, having subdued their anger, they would then have to enter the forest once more for the same duration.
Therefore, quickly seek to find out how our kingdom may remain permanently ours, undisputed, untroubled, free of rivals, and enduring."
Then Karṇa spoke: "O Bhārata, let others who are more clever, capable, discreet, and efficient go quickly.
Let them travel through the prosperous and populous provinces in disguise, in gatherings there and elsewhere, among ascetics and wandering mendicants.
In pleasure grounds, at various sacred fords, and at different sources of wealth, they are to be identified by those men through well-trained inference and deduction.
By various means, by men fully intent on the task, expert in their knowledge, subtle and concealed, the Pāṇḍavas living in disguise are to be searched for with great skill.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In forest thickets along rivers, at sacred fords, in villages and cities, in pleasant hermitages, on mountains, and in caves —
Then Duḥśāsana, the one born next after the eldest, addressed his elder brother who was inclined to sinful thoughts, saying:
"All that Karṇa has said — let us look into it. Let all the spies search as directed here and there. These and many other more numerous agents should go from region to region according to procedure.
Yet their movement, their dwelling, and their activities are not to be detected; or perhaps, in hiding, they have gone to the far shore of the wave-tossed ocean.
Or perhaps those who fancy themselves heroes have been devoured by tigers in the great forest, or having met with some calamity, they have perished for all time.
Therefore, O joy of the Kurus, O lord of men, with an undisturbed mind, do whatever work you consider appropriate with whatever energy you have."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Droṇa, the greatly valiant one who sees the true meaning of things, spoke: "Such men do not perish, nor do they come to defeat.
They are brave, learned in all knowledge, wise, masters of their senses, knowing dharma, grateful, and devoted to the king of dharma.
They follow the eldest who is the knower of the true nature of statecraft, dharma, and wealth, who is as steady as a father, established in righteousness, firm in truth, and who reverences the eldest.
O king, brothers devoted to the great-souled brother — to the one who has no enemies, who is full of modesty — and he in turn devoted to his brothers:
why should the wise Pārtha not bring about the welfare of those great-souled ones who are thus disciplined and discreet?
Therefore with effort they await the arrival of their proper time. I see by my understanding that they surely cannot come to ruin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And whatever needs to be done now, without delay — let it be done quickly after due deliberation, and let their place of dwelling also be thought over carefully.
The sons of Pāṇḍu, steadfast in all matters, blameless, endowed with austerity — those heroes are indeed difficult to track in their proper form.
Pārtha is pure-souled, virtuous, truthful, wise, and pure; he is an immeasurable mass of brilliance that could captivate even the eyes of others.
Therefore, having understood this, let action be taken; and let us search further through learned Brahmins, accomplished spies, and others who have knowledge of such matters."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, the grandfather of the Bhāratas, learned, knowing time and place, knowing truth, and versed in all dharma,
when the teacher's speech had ended, taking up that speech and joining it to his own for the sake of their welfare, he spoke this address to the Bhāratas:
Bhīṣma there spoke a speech anchored in Yudhiṣṭhira, the knower of dharma, resting on dharma, ever rare among the wicked, always beloved of the good — a speech honored by the virtuous.
"Just as this Brahmin Droṇa, who knows the true nature of all things, has said: the Pāṇḍavas, endowed with all auspicious marks, do not deserve destruction.
They are furnished with learning and good conduct, endowed with virtuous vows, immersed in the teaching of their elders, and devoted to their vow of truth.
Knowing the proper time, observing their pure vows, upholding the burden of the righteous — they do not deserve to sink in despair.
Protected both by dharma and by their own valor, the Pāṇḍavas cannot come to ruin — this is how my thinking stands.
I shall direct my understanding toward the matter of the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata; yet the policy of one who is truly wise cannot be traced by others.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But what I am able to say here, having thought carefully about those Pāṇḍavas — I will speak through understanding, not through hostility. Hear that.
And what is to be said should be said well — there should be no injustice at all — for one who abides by the teaching of elders, O dear one, and whose nature is truth.
Surely the steadfast man who wishes to speak in the midst of the virtuous must speak in every way according to his understanding, out of desire for dharma.
In this matter I do not think as these others do: in whatever city or province King Yudhiṣṭhira resides —
the people there will not be envious, nor jealous, nor given to excessive speech, nor spiteful; they will each follow their own dharma.
The chanting of the Vedas will increase greatly, as will complete oblations; and sacrifices will be many, with abundant gifts.
And there the rain-cloud will always shower in due season, without doubt; the earth will be rich with crops and free from calamities.
The grains will be full of sap, the fruits rich in virtue, the garlands fragrant, and the speech auspicious.
The wind will be pleasant to the touch, and the sight will be without obstruction; fear will not enter there where King Yudhiṣṭhira dwells.
Cows will be plentiful there, neither lean nor hard to milk; milk, curds, and clarified butter will be full of taste and wholesome.
The drinks will be virtuous and the foods full of flavor — these things will exist in whatever region King Yudhiṣṭhira dwells.
Tastes, textures, fragrances, sounds — all endowed with virtue — and all sights will be pleasant, wherever King Yudhiṣṭhira is.
Endowed each with their own proper qualities, in this thirteenth year, these things will exist in the region that shelters the Pāṇḍavas, dear one.
The people there will be affectionate, satisfied, pure, and steadfast, loving in the worship of gods and guests, and kindly toward all beings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Generous in giving, greatly enthusiastic, forever devoted to dharma, hating what is inauspicious, seeking what is auspicious, always sacrificing, observing auspicious vows — such will the people be wherever King Yudhiṣṭhira dwells.
Having abandoned falsehood in speech, dear one, auspicious, propitious, and fortunate, seeking auspicious ends, thinking auspicious thoughts — wherever King Yudhiṣṭhira is, the people there will always observe vows pleasing to their desires.
That dharma-souled one is thus invisible even to the twice-born in that form, dear one; how much less can the Pārtha be fully recognized by ordinary people?
In whom reside truth, steadiness, generosity, supreme peace, unfailing patience, modesty, prosperity, fame, the highest brilliance, non-cruelty, and straightforwardness —
therefore the concealed dwelling of that wise one, like a sacrifice hidden in disguise, or his supreme course — I do not venture to speak of it otherwise.
Having considered all this, whatever you think is for the good — do that quickly, O Kauravya, if you trust what I say."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvan, spoke thus: "Fitting and appropriate is what the elder has said regarding the Pāṇḍavas.
Gracious, accompanied by dharma and artha, true, and well-reasoned — what Bhīṣma has said there is appropriate. Now hear my speech on this matter as well.
Let the movements of those Pāṇḍavas through the sacred fords, and their dwelling, be considered carefully; and let whatever policy is now beneficial be determined.
O dear one, even an ordinary enemy is not to be despised by one who desires to prosper — how much less the Pāṇḍavas, dear one, who are skilled in all weapons in battle?
Therefore, now that the great-souled Pāṇḍavas have entered their concealment, hidden and disguised, and the time of reckoning is approaching —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
one's own strength in one's own kingdom and in enemy kingdoms is to be known; and when the time of the Pāṇḍavas' rise is reached — there is no doubt about it.
When their term is ended, the Pārthas, those great-souled, supremely powerful, and greatly energetic Pāṇḍavas of surpassing brilliance, will be roused to action.
Therefore let military strength, treasury, and statecraft all be arranged so that when the time of reckoning arrives, we may properly come to terms with them.
Dear one, I think all of this is so — understand your own strength, fixed as it is in relation to all your allies, the powerful and the weak alike."
Having assessed the forces as high, middling, or low, O Bhārata, and knowing who is pleased and who is not, let us then make peace with our enemies accordingly.
Through conciliation, through sowing discord, through gifts, through chastisement, through tribute — bring the powerful to submission by righteous means, and bend the weak by force.
Having appeased your allies and encouraged the army with reassurance, you, grown strong with treasury and forces, will properly achieve success.
You will have to fight against powerful enemies who are arrayed before you — whether others or the Pāṇḍavas themselves — even if they are reduced in their own forces and vehicles.
Having resolved upon all this and applying your effort according to your own duty, O lord of men, you will long enjoy happiness at the right moment.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Suśarmā, king of the Trigartas, lord of chariot-hosts, hurriedly spoke these timely words with great urgency.
"I have been wronged again and again — first by the Matsyas together with the Sālveyas, and time and again by Kīcaka, the commander of Matsya's forces.
Harassed together with my kinsmen by one mighty through force, O lord" — thus saying, he glanced at Karṇa and then addressed Duryodhana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"My kingdom has been oppressed time and again by the king of Matsya with might, and Kīcaka was his mighty commander-in-chief in former times.
That cruel, wrathful, evil-souled one, renowned throughout the earth for his valor, that wicked and brutal man was slain there by the Gandharvas.
And with him slain, O king, Virāṭa will be stripped of his pride and support, and will be without courage — so is my conviction.
An expedition there is what I have in mind, if it pleases you, O sinless one, and all the Kauravas, and the great-souled Karṇa.
This I consider a task that is both urgent and beneficial — let us swiftly march upon his kingdom, so abundant in grain.
Let us carry off his many and various gems and riches, or we shall plunder his villages and territories in division.
Or else we shall seize many thousands of fine cattle of various kinds, pressing upon his city by force.
Uniting with the Kauravas and the Trigartas, O lord of the people, let us all together swiftly drive away his cattle, well-assembled in force.
Or having made a treaty with him, let us restrain his manhood; or having slaughtered his entire army, let us bring him under our dominion.
Having brought him under rightful subjection, we shall dwell in ease, and your strength will increase beyond all doubt."
Hearing these words of his, Karṇa said to the king: "What Suśarmā has spoken is well-said — timely and beneficial to us.
Therefore let us set out quickly, having marshaled the army and arrayed the divisions as you see fit, O sinless one.
This wise elder of the Kurus, our grandsire Bhīṣma, and the preceptor Droṇa, and Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat —
— as all of them think fit, so let the expedition be arranged; and having deliberated quickly, let us march to achieve the king's purpose.
And what business do we have with the Pāṇḍavas, diminished in wealth, strength, and valor? They are either utterly lost, or else they have reached the realm of Yama."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let us go, O king, without anxiety, into the territory of Virāṭa; we shall take his cattle and various other riches."
Then king Duryodhana, accepting that word of Karṇa, son of Vikartana, himself gave the command swiftly.
"Duḥśāsana, ever devoted to my command, consult with the elders immediately and then quickly marshal the army.
We shall march to the designated place together with all the Kauravas; and let the great warrior Suśarmā proceed to the assigned territory.
The king, together with the Trigartas and with his full complement of forces and vehicles, well-guarded, shall go first into Matsya's territory.
We shall follow in the rear a day later, marching in a solid body into the well-prosperous territory of the king of Matsya.
Going quickly toward Virāṭa's city, let them swiftly fall upon the herdsmen there and seize great wealth.
Hundreds of thousands of cattle, fine and of good quality — these too we shall seize, dividing our army in two.
And so, going in the assigned direction of the fire — the southwest — that lord of earth Suśarmā seized the cattle on the seventh day of the fortnight of heat.
The next day, O king, all the Kauravas assembled together and on the eighth day seized those herds of cattle by the thousands.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O great king, for those great-souled Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable splendor who had entered there in disguise —
— the agreed period had fully elapsed while they dwelt in that best of cities, performing the services of that lord of earth, Virāṭa.
Then, O Bhārata, at the close of that thirteenth year, the great cattle-wealth was seized by force by Suśarmā.
Then with great speed a herdsman came to the city; and having leapt down from his chariot, his earrings swinging, he approached the king of Matsya.
He saw the king surrounded by brave warriors wearing earrings and armlets, and together with noble ministers and the bull-like Pāṇḍavas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Approaching Virāṭa, that great king seated in the assembly hall, increaser of the kingdom, he spoke with a bow.
"Defeating us in battle and humiliating us along with our kinsmen, the Trigartas are driving away hundreds of thousands of cattle. O lord of men, pursue them — let not your livestock be lost!"
Hearing that, the lord of the Matsyas marshaled his army — crowded with chariots, elephants, and horses, swarming with infantry and banners.
Kings and princes here put on their armor — radiant and variegated, finely crafted — each according to his own portion.
Śatānīka, the beloved brother of Virāṭa, brought armor reinforced with iron lightning-bolts and trimmed with heated gold.
Madirāśva, younger than Śatānīka, brought armor crafted entirely of excellent iron, covered with auspicious plates and very strong.
The king of the Matsyas himself brought his armor — blazing like a hundred suns, with a hundred swirling designs, a hundred spots, a hundred eyes, practically impenetrable.
Sūryadatta brought armor whose raised surfaces bore a hundred fragrant lotuses, with a golden back, gleaming like the sun.
Śaṅkha, the eldest heroic son of Virāṭa, brought armor that was firm, reinforced with iron, white, and set with a hundred eyes.
And the great warriors, god-like in form and fierce in attack, bound on their own armor by the hundreds as they prepared for battle.
The great chariot-warriors yoked their horses, each with golden harnesses, separately to fine, bright, and great chariots.
The great standard of Matsya, resembling the sun and moon, was then raised high on his divine, golden chariot.
Then other brave Kṣatriyas fastened various kinds of gold-adorned banners each to his own chariot.
Then king Matsya said to the youngest, Śatānīka: "Kaṅka, Ballava, Gopāla, and the valiant Dāmagrantha — it is my intention that they should fight; of this there is no doubt."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let chariots with banners and flags be given to these as well; let varied armor — both firm and flexible — be fastened on their bodies, and let weapons be given to them."
"Men of heroic build and resembling the trunks of elephant-lords — surely such men would never fail to fight. So runs my thinking."
Hearing the king's words and with his mind urgent, Śatānīka, O king, assigned chariots to the sons of Pṛthā — to Sahadeva, and to the king Yudhiṣṭhira, and to Bhīma, and to Nakula.
Then the chariot-drivers, filled with joy and with devotion to the king foremost in their hearts, quickly yoked those chariots designated by the lord of men.
The varied armor, firm and flexible, which Virāṭa had issued for those tireless warriors — having fastened it on their bodies, those scorchers of foes were clad in armor.
Swift, disguised in form, all skilled in battle, the four heroic Pāṇḍava brothers, bulls among Kurus, of true valor, followed behind Virāṭa together.
Fearsome elephants in rut, with ichor flowing from their temples, dripping like rain-clouds, with fine tusks, sixty years old —
— mounted by trained and battle-skilled elephant-drivers, followed the king from behind, moving like mountains.
Eight thousand chariots, ten hundred elephants, and sixty thousand horses of the Matsyas, ready, obedient, joyful, and following, sallied forth.
That army of Virāṭa shone brilliantly, O bull of the Bhāratas, O great king, as it marched forth to retrieve the track of the cattle.
That foremost army of Virāṭa set out and shone with splendor, crowded with men bearing firm weapons, thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having sallied forth from the city, the brave, array-formed, fierce Matsyas came upon the Trigartas as the sun was declining.
Those Trigartas and Matsyas, enraged, frenzied for battle, roaring at one another, greedy for cattle, mighty in strength —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— and fearsome elephants in rut, goaded with iron darts and elephant-hooks, mounted by village leaders skilled as elephant-drivers —
— their encounter was terrible, tumultuous, hair-raising, equal to the battle of gods and Asuras, O king, as the sun slanted down.
Earthen dust arose and nothing could be discerned; birds fell to the ground, obscured by the dust of the armies.
The sun was hidden by the crossing arrows; the sky shone as if filled with fireflies.
The gold-backed bows of the bowmen intertwined as the world's heroes fell — shooting left and right.
Chariots clashed with chariots, foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers, cavalry with cavalry, and great elephants with great elephants.
With swords, battle-axes, lances, javelins, and iron darts, enraged in the battle, O king, they slew one another.
Slaying one another in battle, those heroes with club-like arms, furiously engaged, were unable to make the heroes turn their backs.
A severed head was seen, with trimmed upper lip, fine nose, dressed hair, and adorned with earrings, covered with dust.
In that great slaughter of Kṣatriyas, limbs were seen, cut to pieces by arrows, resembling the trunks of Śala trees.
The earth was strewn there with arms like serpents' coils, anointed with sandalwood paste, and with heads bearing earrings.
The earthen dust was quelled by the spreading blood; a terrible, boundless faintness pervaded the field and raged without restraint.
Śatānīka, having slain a hundred, and Viśālākṣa, having slain four hundred, both great warriors, plunged into the vast Trigarta army and grappled in fierce combat, hair gripping hair, nails tearing nails.
Seeing those two plunge into the Trigartas' chariot host, Sūryadatta and Madirāśva followed behind them.
Virāṭa in that battle, having destroyed five hundred chariots and having slain here five hundred horses and five great warriors —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Ranging across many paths as a chieftain among chariot-warriors, he encountered Suśarman of the Trigartasthe one with the golden chariot—in battle.
Those two great-souled and mighty warriors fought there, roaring at each other like two bulls in a cattle-pen.
Then those two chariot-warriors, circling each other on their chariots from all sides, swiftly released arrows like rain-laden clouds pouring streams of water.
Extremely enraged at each other, impatient and skilled in weapons, bearing sword, spear, and mace, they ranged about, piercing each other with sharp arrows.
Then the king pierced Suśarman with ten arrows, and with five and five more he pierced his four horses.
Likewise Suśarman, frenzied in battle and a supreme master of weapons, pierced the king of Matsya with fifty sharp arrows.
Then the armies of both the Matsya king and Suśarman, enveloped in the dust of dusk, could no longer distinguish one another.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: O Bhārata, with the world flooded by darkness and dust, the arrayed armies of combatants halted for a moment.
Then the moon rose, dispelling the darkness, making the night bright and bringing joy to the Kṣatriyas in battle.
Then, as light returned, the terrible battle resumed; even so, they could no longer properly observe one another.
Then Suśarman of Trigarta, together with his younger brother, charged at the king of Matsya from all sides with a multitude of chariots.
Then those two brothers, bulls among Kṣatriyas, leaped down from their chariots and, maces in hand, full of fury, charged toward the horses.
Likewise their forces, enraged, charged at one another with maces, swords, axes, and lances with sharp points and well-whetted edges.
But Suśarman, the lord of Trigarta, having crushed and forcibly overcome all the forces of Matsya with his own forces, charged at the mighty Virāṭa of Matsya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having slain separately the draft-horses and both rear-guard charioteers, those two seized the king of Matsya alive, his chariot rendered useless.
Suśarman, having seized him and placed him on his own chariot like a weeping bride, sped away with swift horses.
When the mighty Virāṭa was thus captured and left without a chariot, the Matsyas fled in fear, greatly tormented by the Trigartasas.
While they were being routed in terror, Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, addressed the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, the subduer of foes.
The king of Matsya has been seized by Suśarman of Trigarta—free him, O mighty-armed one; let him not fall under the power of our enemies.
We have all dwelt in comfort, honored with every wish fulfilled; O Bhīmasena, you must repay that hospitality now.
Bhīmasena said: By your command, O king, I shall rescue him. Behold my great deed as I fight against the enemies.
Relying on the strength of my own arms, stand aside with your brothers, O king; withdrawing to one side, witness my prowess today.
This great tree with its sturdy trunk stands like a mace; uprooting it, I shall rout the enemies.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As that one, like a maddened elephant, was eyeing the forest lord, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to his heroic brother.
Do not act rashly, O Bhīma; let this forest tree remain. O Bhārata, lest people, seeing you perform superhuman deeds with a tree, recognize you as Bhīma.
Take up some other, more human weapon instead—a bow, a lance, a sword, or an axe.
Whatever human weapon, O Bhīma, would go unnoticed by others—take up that weapon and quickly free the lord of the earth.
And the two mighty twins shall be your wheel-guards; they will array themselves in battle, dear one, seeking to protect the king of Matsya.
Then all of them together urged their horses forward, invoking divine weapons and full of fury toward the Trigartasas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing the Pāṇḍavas with their chariots turned back toward them, that great army of Virāṭa, supremely enraged, fought in a most wondrous manner.
There Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, slew a thousand; Bhīma dispatched seven hundred warriors to the next world; Nakula too sent seven hundred with his arrows.
The glorious Sahadeva, that bull among men, commanded by Yudhiṣṭhira, slew three hundred heroes, breaking through that great army of the Trigartasas, O bull among men.
Then king Yudhiṣṭhira, that great chariot-warrior, swiftly charging at Suśarman, struck him hard with arrows.
Suśarman too, greatly enraged, swiftly pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with nine arrows and his four horses with four each.
Then, O king, Vṛkodara, son of Kuntī, swift in action, charging at Suśarman, slaughtered his horses.
And having slain his two rear-guards with supreme arrows, enraged, he then dragged his charioteer down from the chariot-platform.
And the wheel-guard, the renowned hero called Śoṇāśva, seeing the Trigarta in single-chariot combat, then fled in fear.
Then Virāṭa, having leaped down from Suśarman's chariot, grabbed his mace and struck him with it; that powerful man moved about mace in hand like a young man, though aged.
But Bhīma, dreadful in appearance and earring-adorned, leaped from his chariot and seized the king of Trigarta as a lion seizes a small animal.
When that great chariot-warrior of the Trigartasas was seized and left without his chariot, the entire Trigarta army broke and fled, stricken with terror.
Then the mighty sons of Pāṇḍu, having recovered all the cattle, having subdued Suśarman, and having seized all his wealth,
endowed with the strength of their own arms, restrained by modesty, steadfast in their vows, passed that night happily in the midst of the battlefield.
Then Virāṭa honored those great chariot-warriors, the sons of Kuntī, of superhuman valor, with wealth and esteem.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Virāṭa said: Whatever jewels are mine are equally yours; use them all as you desire and as pleases you.
I shall give you adorned maidens and various riches, and whatever else your hearts desire, O destroyers of foes.
By your valor I am today freed and stand here in safety; therefore, all of you are indeed lords over the Matsyas.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: All the descendants of the Kurus, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, with joined palms, each replied to Matsya who had spoken thus.
We receive your words with joy, O lord of the people, and we are satisfied by this alone—that you are today freed from your enemies.
Then with a joyful heart, the king of Matsya, the mighty-armed Virāṭa, best of kings, once again said to Yudhiṣṭhira: Come, I shall consecrate you—be our king of Matsya.
And whatever your heart desires, O destroyer of foes, all of that I shall give you; you are worthy of our everything.
Jewels, cattle, gold, gems and pearls—O descendant of Vyāghrapāda, O lord of brāhmaṇas, to you all homage in every way.
For because of you I today see both my kingdom and myself; and the one from whom the conflict arose—that enemy too has been brought under control.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira once again addressed Matsya: I joyfully accept your words; you speak pleasingly, O Matsya.
Be ever dedicated to non-cruelty and always be very happy. Let swift messengers go to your city, O king, to announce the glad tidings to your friends and proclaim your victory.
Then, at those words, king Matsya instructed the messengers: Go to the city and announce my victory in battle.
Let the princes come adorned from my city, and all the musical instruments, and the courtesans well-adorned.
Those messengers, having traveled through the entire night and toward sunrise, proclaimed the victory near the city of Virāṭa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the Matsya king had gone toward the Trigartasas to recover his cattle, Duryodhana with his ministers then marched against Virāṭa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa the supreme weapon-master, Drauṇi and the son of Subala, and the lord Duḥśāsana—
Viviṃśati, Vikarṇa, the valiant Citrasena, Durmukha, Duḥsaha—and whatever other great chariot-warriors there were.
These, having come against the Matsyas, the subjects of king Virāṭa, swiftly scattered the settlements and with force carried off the cattle.
The Kurus were driving sixty thousand cows, surrounding them on all sides with a great multitude of chariots.
In the settlements of the cowherds, as they were being slaughtered by those great chariot-warriors, a tremendous uproar arose in the terrifying encounter.
The superintendent of cattle, terrified, quickly mounted a chariot and went directly to the city, crying out piteously in distress.
Having entered the city, he went then to the king's palace; quickly alighting from the chariot, he entered to deliver the news.
Seeing Bhūmiṃjaya, the proud son of Matsya, he reported to him all the plundering of the kingdom's cattle.
The Kurus are driving away sixty thousand cows—arise to conquer that wealth of cattle, the prosperity of the kingdom.
O prince, wishing your welfare, please go out yourself quickly; the Matsya king, lord of the earth, has appointed you here as guardian in his absence.
That lord of men praises you in the assembly, saying: 'My son is suited to me, a hero, and the upholder of our lineage.'
'A fighter skilled in archery and ever heroic is my son'—let the words of that lord of men prove true.
Turn back the Kurus after defeating them and recover the cattle, O best among the wealthy; burn their armies with the fierce blazing of your arrows.
With gold-feathered, well-jointed arrows loosed from the bow, pierce the enemies' armies like a bull-elephant leading a herd.
Play the bow-vīṇā, whose strings are the bowstring, whose pillow is the arrow-notch, whose shaft is the handle, which resounds greatly and is adorned with arrows, in the midst of the enemies.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let white horses, resplendent as silver, be yoked to your chariot, and let the golden lion-banner be raised on high for you, O lord.
Let your gold-feathered arrows with bright tips, released by your skillful hand—arrows that cut short the lives of kings—cover even the sun.
Having conquered all the Kurus in battle as Vajrapāṇi conquered the demons, having won great glory, enter this city again.
You are the supreme refuge of the kingdom, son of the Matsya lord; let all the subjects of the realm today find their recourse through you.
Thus addressed in the midst of women, that one, boasting in the inner chambers, spoke this fearless-seeming word in response.
Uttara said: Today I would follow the tracks of the cattle, firm-bowed as I am, if only I had a charioteer who is skilled with horses.
But I cannot find the man who would be my driver; look quickly for a charioteer suitable for me as I am about to set out.
Twenty-eight nights ago, or at most a month, there was that great battle in which my charioteer was slain.
If only I could find another man skilled in driving horses, I would go today with all speed, my great banner raised high.
Plunging into their army, crowded with elephants, horses and chariots, I would defeat the Kurus — stripped of valour by my weapons — and bring back the cattle.
Duryodhana, the son of Śaṃtanu, Karṇa the son of Vikartana, Kṛpa, Droṇa together with his son — all these great archers assembled —
— I would terrify them in battle as the bearer of the thunderbolt terrifies the demons, and in this very hour bring the cattle back again.
The Kurus seized their opportunity when the land was empty of defenders and march off taking the cattle-wealth. What could I do, since I was not there?
Let those assembled Kurus witness my valor today — as if to say, 'Can this be Pārtha Arjuna himself who harasses us?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As he kept repeating these words again and again among the women, the Pāñcālī princess could not bear to hear Bībhatsu's name spoken thus.
Then that distressed woman came forward from among the ladies and, as if shyly, spoke these words to him softly.
"That youth of mighty elephant-like splendor, handsome and delightful to behold, known by the name Bṛhannaḍā — he was the charioteer of Pārtha.
He was also second to none in archery, a pupil of that great soul. I saw him before, O hero, when I was moving among the Pāṇḍavas.
When the fire burned that great forest of Khāṇḍava, it was he who controlled the excellent horses for Arjuna at that time.
With that charioteer, Pārtha conquered all creatures on every side at Khāṇḍavaprastha — for there is no driver like him.
This beautiful-hipped princess, your younger sister — he will do whatever she says, O hero; of this there is no doubt.
If he were to serve as charioteer, then without any doubt you would conquer all the Kurus, recover the cattle and certainly return home."
Thus addressed by the Sairandhrī, he spoke to his sister: "Go, O blameless-limbed one, and bring Bṛhannaḍā to me."
Sent by her brother, she went quickly to the dance-hall where that mighty-armed Pāṇḍava dwelt, living in disguise.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Seeing that wide-eyed princess, his companion addressed his companion with a laugh: "Where have you come from, O princess?"
The princess approached that bull among men and, cultivating intimacy, spoke these words in the midst of the women companions:
"The cattle of the kingdom are being driven off by the Kurus, O Bṛhannaḍā. My brother, the bowman, is going to set out to defeat them.
Not long ago his charioteer was killed in battle, and there is no driver equal to him who could now serve as his charioteer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For him who is thus seeking a charioteer, O Bṛhannaḍā, the Sairandhrī spoke of your skill in horse-lore.
Do serve well as charioteer for my brother, O Bṛhannaḍā — for the Kurus are already driving our cattle far away.
If today, being urged out of affection, you will not do this thing I ask, I shall abandon my life."
Thus addressed by that beautiful-hipped companion, the scorcher of foes went to the presence of the prince of immeasurable might.
She of wide eyes followed behind him as he walked quickly, like a young elephant-cow following behind a great maddened elephant.
Seeing him from a distance, the prince spoke to him: "With you as charioteer, Pārtha satisfied the fire in the Khāṇḍava forest.
Dhanaṃjaya, son of Kuntī, conquered the entire earth. The Sairandhrī has told me of you — for she knows the Pāṇḍavas.
So take hold of my horses, O Bṛhannaḍā — for me as I am about to fight the Kurus in order to recover the cattle-wealth."
"You were indeed formerly the beloved charioteer of Arjuna; with your help as ally, that bull of the Pāṇḍavas conquered the earth.
Thus addressed, Bṛhannaḍā replied to the prince: "What power have I to serve as charioteer at the head of battle?
Singing, or dancing, or playing various instruments — that I will do; blessings on you — but where would chariot-driving come from in me?"
Uttara said: "Be a singer or a dancer again later, O Bṛhannaḍā — for now, quickly mount my chariot and take hold of the excellent horses."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There the Pāṇḍava, knowing everything, performed many playful acts right in front of Uttarā, O subduer of foes.
He tossed a piece of armor up into the air and then buckled it onto his body; the wide-eyed maidens there, seeing him, laughed aloud.
Seeing him fumbling, Uttara himself then bound on Bṛhannaḍā the most excellent and precious armor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He himself also wore the finest armor, brilliant as rays of light, and raising the lion-banner, prepared himself for the role of charioteer.
Taking up the most precious bows and many beautiful arrows, the hero set out with Bṛhannaḍā as charioteer.
Then Uttarā and the maiden companions said to her: "O Bṛhannaḍā, bring us beautiful garments —
— fine and variegated and of many kinds, for the sake of our dolls, after defeating in battle the Kurus headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa."
Then to those maidens speaking together, the son of Pāṇḍu replied with a laugh — Pārtha, whose voice resounded like the drum of a thunder-cloud:
"If this Uttara defeats the great warriors in battle, then I shall bring back divine and beautiful garments for you."
Having said this, Bībhatsu the hero then urged on the horses toward the Kurus, who displayed many banners and pennants.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having departed from the royal capital, Vairāṭi the earth-conqueror said to his charioteer: "Drive on to where the Kurus have gone."
"Having swiftly defeated the assembled Kurus who seek victory, and having quickly recovered their cattle, I shall return to my own city."
Then the son of Pāṇḍu urged on the excellent horses. Those steeds, urged on by the lion among men, swift as the wind, seemed to scratch at the sky as they sped forward, wearing their golden garlands.
Having gone not too great a distance, the son of Matsya and Dhanaṃjaya — both destroyers of enemies — surveyed the great host of the powerful Kurus. Going toward the cremation ground, they then came upon the Kurus.
That great army of theirs blazed forth with the roar of the ocean, seeming to spread across the sky like a forest dense with trees.
The dust raised by that army spreading out was seen — touching the sky, destroying the sight of all beings, O best of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing that great army crowded with elephants, horses and chariots, guarded by Karṇa, Duryodhana, Kṛpa and the son of Śaṃtanu,
— and by Droṇa together with his son, that great archer of keen intellect — with hair standing on end and shaken by fear, Vairāṭi spoke to Pārtha:
"I do not dare to fight with the Kurus — look at how my hair stands on end! Full of many heroes and utterly terrible, difficult to approach even for the gods, I cannot face the endless Kuru army in battle."
"I have no confidence in entering the Bhārata army with its terrible bows, crowded with chariots, elephants and horses, swarming with foot-soldiers and banners — for merely at the sight of the foe in battle, my own self seems to tremble.
Where Droṇa and Bhīṣma are, Kṛpa, Karṇa and Viviṃśati, Aśvatthāmā and Vikarṇa, Somadatta and Bāhlika —
— and also the heroic Duryodhana, that king foremost among chariot-warriors — all of them glorious great archers, all skilled in warfare —
— merely beholding these Kurus arrayed in battle-formation, ready to strike, my hair has bristled and faintness has come upon me.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: In the very presence of the left-handed archer, this foolish one — through his own stupidity — laments before the knowledgeable one who has ventured what he has not ventured.
"My father has gone against the Trigarta king, leaving me behind in an empty city with all the army taken — I have no soldiers here.
I alone, a mere boy, untrained in effort, cannot face so many skilled warriors in battle. Turn back, O Bṛhannaḍā!"
Arjuna said: "You appear wretched with fear, increasing the joy of your enemies — and yet the foes have not yet done any deed on the battlefield.
And you yourself told me, 'Drive me against the Kauravas.' I shall take you to that very place where all these banners are flying.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Into the midst of those flesh-greedy, violent Kurus — fighters of the earth — I shall take you, O mighty-armed one.
Having thus promised valor to the women and boasted of it among men, having marched out — why will you not fight?
If you return home without having won back those cattle, O hero, men and women gathered together will mock you.
I too was here praised by the Sairandhrī for the task of charioteering — I cannot go back to the city without having won the cattle.
Given the Sairandhrī's praise and your own words to me, how could I not fight all the Kurus? Be steady!"
Uttara said: "Let the Kurus take away the greater part of the Matsya people's wealth if they wish, and let women and men mock me too, O Bṛhannaḍā —
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having said this, the dull-witted one, wearing his earrings, leaped down from the chariot in terror and ran away, abandoning his pride and casting aside his arrow-laden bow.
Bṛhannaḍā said: "Flight has never been remembered by the ancients as the duty of a Kṣatriya. Death in battle is better for you — not the flight of a coward."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus spoken, the son of Kuntī — Dhanaṃjaya — leaped down from that excellent chariot and chased after the fleeing prince, shaking his long braid and wearing his crimson garments.
As he ran with his braid flying, certain soldiers who did not recognize Arjuna laughed, seeing him in such a form.
Seeing him running swiftly, the Kurus said: "Who is this one concealed by his disguise, like fire hidden under ashes?
Something about him is like a man, and something about him is like a woman; yet he bears a resemblance to Arjuna even while wearing an eunuch's guise.
That very same head and neck, those two arms like iron bars, the same heroic bearing — this one is none other than Dhanaṃjaya.
As Indra, lord of the gods, is among the immortals — so is Dhanaṃjaya among men. Who else in the world but Dhanaṃjaya would come against us alone?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Only one son of Virāṭa, left alone in the empty city — he has indeed marched out, but out of boyish rashness, not out of manly valor.
Surely Uttara has made Pārtha Arjuna — who was living in disguise — his charioteer and marched out of the city.
It seems to me that he, frightened upon seeing our banners, is fleeing, and Dhanaṃjaya is surely running to catch him as he runs away."
Thus all the Kurus reflected separately, each to themselves, and they could not decide anything definite about Uttara, seeing that Pāṇḍava likewise in his disguise, O Bhārata.
But Dhanaṃjaya, pursuing Uttara as he ran headlong, went swiftly a hundred steps and seized him by the hair.
Seized by Arjuna, the son of Virāṭa lamented piteously then, weeping much and pitifully.
"I will give you a hundred niṣkas of pure refined gold, and eight great-lustred beryl gems set in gold.
A chariot fitted with gold staffs and harnessed with fine horses, and ten maddened elephants — release me, O Bṛhannaḍā!"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Laughing at these and such words of the senseless, lamenting one, the tiger among men brought the chariot near.
Then Pārtha spoke to him who was overcome with fear and had lost his wits: "If you dare not fight the enemies, O tormentor of foes, come and hold the horses for me while I engage the enemies in battle."
"Advance toward that army of chariots, protected by the strength of my arms — that terrible, most formidable force guarded by great warriors and mighty chariot-fighters."
"Fear not, O foremost of princes! You are a kṣatriya, O scorcher of foes. I shall fight the Kurus and recover your cattle."
"Enter this chariot army that is unassailable and hard to approach; be the charioteer, O best of men, while I fight with the Kurus."
Speaking thus, the invincible Bībhatsu, O bull of the Bhārata line, for a moment comforted that prince Uttara, the son of Virāṭa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Pārtha, the foremost of warriors, mounted him — unwilling and oppressed with fear and struggling — onto the chariot.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Seeing that bull among men, clad in eunuch's garb, standing on the chariot with Uttara now mounted, heading toward the śamī tree —
— the foremost chariot warriors of the Kurus, led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, were all struck with terror at the fear inspired by Dhanaṃjaya.
Observing them dispirited and beholding also the portentous omens, the preceptor Bhāradvāja, foremost of weapon-bearers, addressed them.
"Harsh winds blow restlessly with rough, harsh sounds; the sky is covered with darkness of an ashen hue.
Clouds of grim colour appear with wondrous appearance; and various weapons are issuing out of their sheaths by themselves.
Terrible jackals howl in the blazing quarter; horses shed tears and standards tremble though there is no wind.
Given the many signs and forms seen here, let all of you stand alert — battle seems to be at hand.
Guard yourselves; array the army in battle-formation; be ready for slaughter; and protect the cattle as well.
This great bowman, the best of all weapon-bearers, who has come in the disguise of a eunuch — he is Pārtha; there is no doubt in this.
This very Pārtha, valiant Savyasācī, the scorcher of foes — he would not turn back from battle even against all the hosts of the Maruts.
Afflicted in the forest, trained by Vāsava himself, this hero — overcome by righteous wrath — will fight. Of this there is no doubt.
I see no opponent worthy of him here, O Kauravas. Even Mahādeva, it is heard, was pleased with Pārtha in battle.
Karṇa said: "You always boast to us of Phalguna's virtues; yet Arjuna is not a full part equal to me or to Duryodhana."
Duryodhana said: "If this is indeed Pārtha, O son of Rādhā, my purpose would be accomplished — our kinsmen would have to spend another twelve years in exile."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Or if this is merely some other man dressed as a eunuch, I shall strike him down to the ground with my well-sharpened arrows."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that scorcher of foes, spoke those words, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa applauded that sentiment of valor.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Approaching that śamī tree, Pārtha addressed the son of Virāṭa — that delicate youth of noble birth, not greatly skilled in battle.
"As I have commanded you, quickly bring down the bows from this tree, Uttara — for these own bows of yours cannot bear my strength."
"They could not bear the heavy weight, nor endure an elephant's crushing force, nor the sweeping pull of my arms as I conquer the enemies here."
"Therefore, O Bhūmiṃjaya, climb this leafy śamī tree — for in it the bows of the sons of Pāṇḍu are deposited."
"The standards, arrows and divine armour of those heroes — of Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Bībhatsu, and the twin sons of Mādrī — are all there."
"Here too is this Gāṇḍīva, Pārtha's bow of great power, equal in worth to a hundred thousand bows — the increaser of the kingdom."
"Exceedingly capable of enduring great exertion, great as the king of grasses, supreme among all weapons, the afflicting cause of enemies."
"Adorned with gold, divine, smooth, long, without blemish, fully capable of bearing great weight, terrible yet beautiful to behold — and all the others are equally powerful and sturdy."
Uttara said: "We have heard that a corpse is bound in this tree. How then can I, being a prince, touch it with my hand?"
"It is not proper for me, born of kṣatriya lineage, a great prince, knower of mantras and sacrifices and of virtuous character, to touch such a thing."
"Having touched a corpse, impure as a corpse-carrier, how could you then deal with me as with a pure person, O Bṛhannaḍā?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bṛhannaḍā said: "You will remain fit for dealings with others and pure indeed, O lord of kings. Fear not these bows — there is no corpse here."
"How could I make you, the heir and son born in the lineage of the king of the Matsyas, a man of noble spirit, do a censurable act, O son of a king?"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Pārtha, the earring-adorned son of Virāṭa leapt from the chariot and unwillingly climbed the śamī tree.
Standing on the chariot, Dhanaṃjaya instructed him and quickly undid the coverings of those weapons.
Loosening all their fastenings on every side likewise, he saw the Gāṇḍīva there together with four other bows.
As those bows bright as the sun were being loosened, their divine radiance blazed forth like the rising of planets.
Beholding their forms stretching out like serpents uncoiling, his hair stood erect and in an instant he became stricken with fear.
Having touched those radiant and great bows, the son of Virāṭa spoke these words to Arjuna, O king.
Uttara said: "On which a hundred drops of refined gold have been set, and thousands of golden fittings — whose is this excellent bow?"
"On whose back golden elephants shine, armour-clad, with fine sides and easy to grip — whose is this excellent bow?"
"On whose back sixty indragopaka insects of pure refined gold are arranged and gleam — whose is this excellent bow?"
"On which three golden suns blaze, armour-clad, blazing with splendour — whose is this excellent bow?"
"On which golden locusts variegated in refined gold are set, and which is adorned with gold and gems — whose is this excellent bow?"
"And whose are these thousands of iron arrows with quill-like flights, tipped all around with refined silver, in a golden quiver?"
"Whose are these broad, thick arrows with vulture feathers, sharpened on stone, turmeric-coloured, well-tipped, yellow, and wholly iron?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Whose is this dark-inlaid quiver bearing the mark of five tigers, mixed with boar-ear feathered arrows, holding ten shafts?"
"Whose are these broad, long, entirely iron arrows — seven hundred nārāca shafts that drink blood standing ready?"
"Whose are these arrows — their forward halves beautifully feathered like parrot wings, their rear halves yellow iron with golden nocks, sharpened on stone?"
"Whose is this long arrow, smooth-backed and sharp-pointed, placed in a tiger-skin sheath, with a large handle adorned in gold?"
"Whose is this sword with a fine blade, in a decorated sheath, a great arrow hung with small bells, with a divine golden hilt, completely unblemished?"
"Whose is this spotless sword placed in a cow-hide sheath, with a golden hilt, irresistible — the sword of Naiṣadha, capable of bearing great weight?"
"Whose arrow in a five-nailed sheath has a golden form, endowed with perfect measure and appearance, yellow and resembling the sky?"
"Whose is this heavy, yellow, polished, entirely unblemished sword — a nistriṃśa blade in a golden sheath, well-heated and blazing like fire?"
"Tell me truthfully as I ask you, O Bṛhannaḍā — great wonder has arisen in me upon seeing all these magnificent things."
Bṛhannaḍā said: "What you first asked me about — the destroyer of enemy armies — this is Gāṇḍīva, Pārtha's bow, renowned throughout the worlds."
"This supreme weapon of all arms, adorned with refined gold — this is Arjuna's Gāṇḍīva, the paramount weapon."
"That which is equal in worth to a hundred thousand bows, the increaser of the kingdom — with this Pārtha withstands both gods and men in battle."
"Honoured by gods, dānavas and gandharvas through eternal ages — Brahmā first held this bow for a thousand years."
"After him, Prajāpati held it; then three hundred and five hundred years; and Śakra held it for eighty-five years."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"King Soma held it for five hundred years; likewise Varuṇa for a hundred; and Pārtha the white-horsed one has held it for sixty-five years."
"Of great power, great, divine — this supreme bow, honoured among gods and mortals, bears its paramount form."
"The bow with fine sides and a gold grip — that is Bhīmasena's, with which Pārtha the scorcher of foes conquered the entire eastern quarter."
"And this one, beautifully formed and adorned with indragopaka insects — this is the excellent bow of King Yudhiṣṭhira, O son of Virāṭa."
"On which golden suns shine brilliantly, blazing with splendour — this is Nakula's weapon."
"On which golden locusts variegated in refined gold are set — this is the bow of the son of Mādrī, Sahadeva."
"And these thousands of razor-like arrows with quill feathers — these are Arjuna's arrows in the land of Virāṭa, equal in venom to serpents."
"These, blazing in battle with their splendour, swift in flight, are the hero's inexhaustible arrows that scatter enemies in combat."
"And these broad, long arrows that resemble a half-disk of the moon — these are Bhīma's sharp arrows that bring destruction to enemies."
"These turmeric-coloured ones with golden nocks, sharpened on stone — this is Nakula's quiver bearing the mark of five tigers."
"With which that wise son of Mādrī conquered the entire western quarter in battle — this quiver was his."
"And these arrows shaped like the sun, entirely iron, variegated and furnished with ritual markings — these belong to the wise Sahadeva."
"And these sharp, yellow, broad, long-shafted great arrows with golden nocks and three nodes — these, O prince, are the king's great arrows."
"And this long arrow, smooth-backed and sharp-pointed, capable of bearing great weight and firm — this is Arjuna's in battle."
The great tiger-skin-scabbarded sword belonging to Bhīmasena — divine, capable of bearing heavy weight — is a source of terror to his enemies.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This straight-bladed sword with a beautiful variegated scabbard and a golden hilt, unsurpassed in excellence, belongs to the Kaurava Dharmarāja, the wise one.
This straight-bladed sword stored in a scabbard adorned with five-nailed designs and bright embellishments — heavy-bearing and firm — belongs to Nakula.
Know that this spotless sword sheathed in a cowhide scabbard, capable of bearing all weight and firm, belongs to Sahadeva.
Uttara said: These weapons of the great-souled Pārthas, wrought with gold and variously fashioned, shine beautifully — belonging to swift-acting warriors.
Where indeed are Arjuna the son of Pṛthā, or the Kaurava Yudhiṣṭhira, and Nakula and Sahadeva and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava?
All of them — great souls, destroyers of all enemies — having lost their kingdom at dice, are never heard of anymore.
And where is Draupadī the Pāñcālī, celebrated as a jewel among women? When the dark one's husbands were defeated at dice, she followed them into the forest.
Arjuna said: I am Arjuna, son of Pṛthā. Yudhiṣṭhira is the keeper of the assembly hall. Bhīmasena is Ballava, your father's cook.
Nakula is the horse-keeper, and Sahadeva works among the cattle. Know Draupadī to be the Sairandhrī on whose account Kīcaka was slain.
Uttara said: If you were to recite for me the ten names of the son of Pṛthā that I have heard before, then I would believe everything you say.
Arjuna said: Come then, I shall tell you my ten names: Arjuna, Phalguna, Jiṣṇu, Kirīṭī, Śvetavāhana, Bībhatsu, Vijaya, Kṛṣṇa, Savyasācin, and Dhanañjaya.
Uttara said: Why are you called Vijaya? Why are you called Śvetavāhana? Why Kirīṭī? And how are you Savyasācin?
And why are you Arjuna, Phalguna, Jiṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Bībhatsu, and Dhanañjaya? Tell me truly. I have heard only the names of that hero, but not the reasons for them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Arjuna said: Having conquered all the realms and seized their wealth alone, I stand at the center of that treasure — therefore they call me Dhanañjaya, the winner of wealth.
Because when I advance into battle against those arrogant in war, I do not turn back without conquering — therefore they know me as Vijaya, the victorious.
White horses clad in golden armor are yoked to my chariot when I fight in battle — therefore I am Śvetavāhana, the one with white steeds.
I was born by day on the slopes of the Himālayas under the two Phālgunī asterisms — northern and southern — therefore they know me as Phalguna.
Long ago Śakra gave me, while I was fighting the lords of the Dānavas, a diadem radiant as the sun placed on my head — therefore they call me Kirīṭī, the diademed one.
I would never perform a loathsome deed in any manner while fighting — therefore among gods and men they know me as Bībhatsu, the one who shuns the abhorrent.
Both my hands are right-handed in the drawing of the Gāṇḍīva bow — therefore among gods and men they call me Savyasācin, the ambidextrous.
In the earth bounded by its four limits, my hue is rare and unblemished, and I perform pure deeds — therefore they know me as Arjuna, the bright one.
I am hard to approach, difficult to assail, a tamer of foes, the chastiser of Pāka — therefore among gods and men I am renowned by the name Jiṣṇu, the triumphant.
My father gave me Kṛṣṇa as my tenth name out of affection for the child, me, who was dark yet spotless and virtuous.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the son of Virāṭa approached the son of Pṛthā and greeted him respectfully, saying: "My name is Bhuminjaya, and I am also called Uttara."
"By good fortune do I behold you, O Pārtha! Welcome, O Dhanañjaya, red-eyed and mighty-armed, like the hood of a lord of serpents! Whatever I said to you in ignorance, please forgive me for that."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Because of the wondrous and difficult deeds you have performed in the past, my fear has passed away and my affection for you is the greatest."
Uttara said: Having mounted your great chariot, O hero, with me as charioteer, against which army will you advance? Tell me, and I shall go there as you direct.
Arjuna said: I am pleased, O tiger among men! There is no fear for you. I shall drive away all your enemies in battle, O you who are skilled in combat.
Be at ease, O great-minded one! Watch me fighting with the enemies in this clash, performing a great and terrifying feat.
Quickly fasten all these quivers to my chariot, and bring that straight-bladed sword adorned with pure gold — I shall indeed fight the Kurus and win back your cattle.
With wings spread by intent, its archways formed by mighty arms, thronged with triple-staffed quivers and crowded with many banners —
— with the twanging of the bowstring done in wrath, the rumble of the wheel-rims like a kettledrum, this chariot beneath you shall be, for you, a city protected by me.
This chariot, commanded in battle by me, the bearer of the Gāṇḍīva bow, is unconquerable by enemy armies, O son of Virāṭa! Let your fear depart.
Uttara said: I do not fear them; I know you to be steadfast in battle, equal in combat even to Keśava himself, or indeed to Indra in person.
Yet pondering this very thing I become utterly confused — being of poor understanding, I cannot in any way reach a conclusion.
For one whose body is that of a hero and who is endowed with appropriate marks of distinction — how has this state of being a eunuch come about through the ripening of deeds?
I think you to be the trident-bearing god himself, or perhaps the king of the Gandharvas, moving about in the disguise of a eunuch — or even Śatakratu, the god of a hundred sacrifices.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Arjuna said: By the command of my eldest brother I have observed this vow for a year, practicing celibacy — this is the truth I tell you.
I am not a eunuch, O mighty-armed one — I am bound by dharma, subject to another's will. Know me to have completed my vow and to have passed through it, O son of a king.
Uttara said: Today I receive the greatest favor, because my inference was not in vain — for those of eunuch appearance are surely not supreme men of this kind.
I shall be your ally in battle and could fight even against the immortals! My timidity has vanished. Tell me — what shall I do?
I shall hold the reins of your horses, breaker of enemy chariots — for I am trained in chariot-driving through proper instruction, O bull among men.
As Dāruka is to Vāsudeva, as Mātali is to Śakra, so know me to be trained in chariotship, O foremost of men.
The horse yoked on the right shaft, resembling Sugrīva in quality, is one whose hoof-prints on the ground cannot be seen as he gallops.
This splendid horse, best of draft animals, who draws the left shaft — I consider it equal in speed to Meghapuṣpa.
This splendid horse clad in golden armor who draws the left flank-position — I consider it mightier in speed than the whole army's left flank.
This one who draws your right flank with body arched and neck raised — even compared to Balāhaka he is reckoned mightier in speed and valor.
This chariot is worthy of carrying you, the bowman, into battle; and you, having mounted this chariot, are worthy to fight — in my opinion.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then that valiant one removed the bracelets from his arms and, amid a wondrous kettledrum roll, slapped his two auspicious palms.
Having bound up his curly dark hair with a white cloth, he swiftly strung the Gāṇḍīva bow and bent it with force.
As that bow was being drawn, a great sound arose — like a great mountain being struck by another mountain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The earth shook with thunderclaps; the wind blew mightily in all directions; the sky was filled with wheeling birds, and the great trees trembled.
The Kurus recognized that sound — like the cracking of a thunderbolt — as Arjuna drawing the foremost of bows with his arms upon the chariot.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having made Uttara his charioteer, having circumambulated the shami tree clockwise, and having taken up all the weapons, Dhanañjaya then set forth.
The great chariot-warrior removed the lion banner from that chariot, placed it at the root of the shami tree, and then departed with Uttara as his charioteer.
Having attached to the chariot the divine magical device fashioned by Viśvakarman — the golden banner bearing a lion's tail and marked with a monkey —
— he mentally meditated on and invoked the grace of Pāvaka (Fire); and Pāvaka, knowing what had been thought, impelled supernatural beings onto the banner.
Mounting the chariot adorned with banners and variously decorated limbs, with quivers attached, the great chariot-warrior Bībhatsu, son of Kuntī, the White-horsed one —
— with sword girt on, clad in armor, and bow taken up in hand, he then marched northward, he who bears the banner of the foremost of monkeys.
The mighty crusher of enemies blew his great resonant conch with full strength — a sound that made the hair of his foes stand on end.
Then those swift draft horses fell to their knees upon the ground, and Uttara too, terror-stricken, sank down onto the chariot floor.
The son of Kuntī steadied the horses and raised them up with the reins; then Arjuna embraced Uttara and reassured him.
"Do not be afraid, O foremost of princes! You are a Kṣatriya, a scorcher of foes. How is it, O tiger among men, that you despond in the midst of enemies?"
"You have heard the sounds of conches and the full-toned sounds of war-drums, and the roaring of elephants standing in battle array —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"— how is it that you, that very man, are now terrified by this conch-sound and appear dejected and frightened like an ordinary person?"
Uttara said: I have indeed heard the sounds of conches and the full-toned sounds of war-drums, and the cries of elephants standing in battle formations —
