— but never before have I heard a conch-sound like this; nor have I ever seen a banner such as this before; nor anywhere have I ever heard the twang of a bow like this.
By the sound of this conch, by the twang of this bow, and by the rumbling of this chariot, my mind is utterly bewildered.
All the directions are turbulent and my heart seems to tremble; all directions appear concealed to me by that banner; and by the sound of the Gāṇḍīva my ears are deafened.
Arjuna said: Standing the chariot in a secluded spot, press down firmly with your feet and hold the reins tight — I shall blow the conch again.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: At the sound of that conch, the rumble of the chariot wheel-rims, and the roar of the Gāṇḍīva, the earth trembled.
Droṇa said: The way this chariot resounds, the way this conch is blown, the way the earth trembles — this can be none other than Savyasācin.
Our weapons do not shine; the horses do not grow spirited; and the fires do not blaze even when kindled — this is not auspicious.
All our animals cry ominously facing the sun; crows settle on the banners — that is not auspicious; and birds circle us inauspiciously on the left, presaging great danger.
This jackal is howling and running through the middle of the army; it has come forth of itself without being struck and portends great danger; I observe that the hair on your bodies stands erect.
Your army is already defeated and no one wishes to fight; most of the warriors are pale-faced and bewildered. Let us drive away the cattle and stand here in battle array, ready to strike.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Duryodhana spoke in the battle to Bhīṣma, and to Droṇa the tiger among chariot-warriors, and to Kṛpa the great chariot-warrior.
"This matter has been spoken of by me and by Karṇa to the preceptor many times, and I shall say it again — for I am not satisfied merely speaking of it."
"The defeated ones must dwell — those defeated ones — for twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year unrecognized among people; this indeed was the stake agreed upon by us."
Their term of exile has not yet expired — the thirteenth year of incognito dwelling is still in progress — and yet Arjuna (Bībhatsu) has now come and engaged us in battle.
If Bībhatsu has come before the term of exile has ended, the Pāṇḍavas will have to dwell in the forest for twelve more years.
Either through greed they have miscalculated, or delusion has overtaken them; whether their reckoning falls short or exceeds the term, Bhīṣma is best able to determine this.
When matters are disputed there is always doubt, for an affair considered one way turns out another way altogether.
Among those who were pursuing Uttara and eager to fight the Matsya army, if Bībhatsu has come, who among them would turn his back in flight?
We came here to fight the Matsyas on behalf of the Trigarta kings; the Matsyas had done many wrongs to them and spoken ill of us.
To them when they came to us in fear we gave our pledge: first they were to seize the vast cattle wealth of the Matsyas.
It was arranged with them that on the seventh day in the afternoon they would act, and on the eighth day we would advance at sunrise.
Either they do not see the cattle, or they have been defeated; or they may have been deceived and joined forces with the Matsya king against us.
Or perhaps Matsya, accompanied by his countrymen and together with his entire army, has come against us for battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Among them some mighty champion has come forward to conquer us, or it may be Matsya himself who has come in person.
If it is the king of the Matsyas who has come, or if it is Bībhatsu who has come, we must all fight — this is the agreement we made.
Then why do these foremost charioteers stand idle in their cars — Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Vikarṇa, and Drauṇi?
All these great warriors are confused in mind at this moment. There is no better course than battle — let that resolve be fixed in each man's heart.
Once our cattle wealth has been seized, who — even if opposed by the god wielding the thunderbolt or by Yama himself in battle — would go back to Hāstinapura?
Of those struck down by arrows and routed into the dense forest, which foot soldier could survive? There would be doubt even for the cavalry. Let the teacher be placed in the rear guard, and let our strategy be arranged accordingly.
He knows the counsel of the Pāṇḍavas, and so he appears to intimidate us; I observe that his special affection is for Arjuna.
And indeed, upon seeing Bībhatsu approach he sings his praises. Let strategy be devised so that the army does not break and flee.
Like an army without a guide, lost in a vast forest in summer, fallen into the enemy's power — let strategy be devised so that the army does not go astray.
What praise should there be merely upon hearing the neighing of horses from the enemy? Horses neigh at all times, whether standing still or moving.
The winds always blow, Indra always sends rain, and the roar of thunder is heard repeatedly — these are no omens.
What business does Arjuna have here, and why is he being praised? It can only be out of desire, or hatred, or sheer anger toward us.
Teachers are compassionate and wise, and they foresee danger; in this great peril that has come upon us, they should on no account be consulted.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In splendid palaces, in learned assemblies, and in pleasant lodgings, those who hold diverse learned conversations — scholars shine there.
Performing many wondrous feats before gatherings of people, and in the graceful drawing of the bow — scholars shine in those arenas.
In discerning the gaps in others' arguments, in understanding human conduct, and in detecting faults in the preparation of food — scholars shine in those matters.
Placing the scholars in the rear, and taking those who praise the enemy's virtues out of the equation, let strategy be arranged such that the foe may be slain.
Let the cattle be secured and held; let the army form its battle array without delay; and let guards be posted where we shall fight the enemy.
Karṇa said: I see that all of the men of this long-lived one are frightened and terrified; they are all disinclined to fight and altogether unsettled.
Whether it is the king of the Matsyas who has come or Bībhatsu who has come, I shall hold them back as the shore holds back the shark-filled ocean.
The arrows I release from my bow, with their joints bent, will not turn back once loosed, just as serpents do not turn back when they glide forward.
Let the arrows released by my skilled hand — gold-feathered and with very sharp tips — cover Arjuna as locusts cover a tree.
Let the sound of the palms striking the bowstring as it drives the fletched arrows hard resound like two kettledrums being beaten.
Bībhatsu, fully composed and trained for thirteen years, has also developed a fondness for battle — he will strike at me with relish.
Let the son of Kuntī, being a worthy vessel just as a virtuous brahmin is, receive the torrents of arrows loosed by me in their thousands.
This great archer is renowned in all three worlds; yet I too, O best of the Kurus, am in no way inferior to Arjuna.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let the sky today be seen covered on all sides by golden arrows fletched with vulture feathers, as though filled with fireflies.
Today I shall discharge the undying debt I promised in words long ago to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, by slaying Arjuna in battle.
Let the severed nocks of arrows, shattered between them, be seen drifting about in the sky like locusts.
I shall afflict Arjuna — whose touch is like Indra's thunderbolt and whose blazing energy equals that of great Indra — as one drives an elephant with firebrands.
That blazing Pāṇḍava fire — hard to assail, fueled by sword, spear, and arrow, burning brightly and scorching enemies — I shall extinguish.
I, a great cloud with the speed of horses for its forewind, the mass of chariots for its thunder, and showers of arrows for its rain, shall quench the Pāṇḍava fire.
Let the arrows released from my bow, like venomous serpents, glide toward Arjuna as serpents converge on an anthill.
Relying on the weapon-lore I received from Rāma Jāmadagnya, that best of sages, and on my own valour, I could fight even Indra himself.
The monkey perched at the top of his banner, struck down by my broad-headed arrow, shall fall to the earth this very day, shrieking terrible cries.
The wail of the spirit-beings dwelling in the enemy's banner, scattered in all directions as I assail them, shall rise up to heaven.
Today I shall uproot from its very root the thorn that has long been lodged in Duryodhana's heart, by casting Bībhatsu down from his chariot.
Let the Kauravas today behold Arjuna, his horses slain, his chariot wrecked, desperate in his manhood, heaving breath like a great serpent.
Let the Kauravas go freely and take whatever wealth they wish, or let them stand in their chariots and watch my battle unfold.
Kṛpa said: O son of Rādhā, your mind is always crueller than needful in battle. You do not understand the nature of affairs, nor do you consider their consequences.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There are many paths of statecraft, deliberated upon by reliance on the scriptures; among them, those who know antiquity declare battle to be the most wicked.
Battle suited to the right place and the right time grants victory; that very same battle, if untimely, does not bear fruit here. Valour exercised in the right place and the right time is ordained for prosperity.
An interval should be arranged in harmony with the flow of affairs; the wise do not undertake the burden of the chariot-maker — that is, they do not take on what exceeds their capacity.
After careful thought, a direct clash with Arjuna is not advisable for us: alone he defended the Kurus, alone he satisfied the fire god.
Alone he maintained brahmacharya for five years; alone he abducted Subhadrā and challenged Kṛṣṇa to single combat from his chariot; and in this very forest he rescued Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) who had been carried away.
Alone he learned the divine weapons from Indra for five years; and alone, having conquered the army of Yama (the disciplined host), he brought glory to the Kurus.
Alone, that subduer of foes, he swiftly defeated in battle the Gandharva king Citrasena and his well-nigh unconquerable army.
Likewise the Nivātakavacas and the Kālakhañja demons — invincible even by the gods — were felled in battle by him alone.
O Karṇa, what exactly have you accomplished here alone in the past, comparable to how those kings were each individually brought under subjection by him?
Even Indra himself is not fit to fight Arjuna in battle; whoever boasts that he will fight him — medicine is what that person needs.
You desire, without reflection, to pluck the fang of an enraged venomous serpent with your index finger while its right hood is raised.
Or else you wish, wandering alone in the forest, to mount a maddened elephant without a goad and ride it into the city.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Or you wish, anointed with ghee and wearing bark garments, to wade through a blazing fire fed with ghee, marrow, and fat.
What kind of manliness is it for someone to bind himself hand and foot, tie a great boulder around his neck, and then try to swim across the ocean with his arms?
O Karṇa, whoever — unskilled in arms, very weak — wishes to fight Arjuna, who is skilled in arms and mighty: such a man is one of feeble wit.
We have kept this lion pinned down for thirteen years; now that the lion is freed from its noose, it will leave none of us alive.
We rashly assailed Arjuna sitting apart — like fire concealed in a well — and out of ignorance we have come to face the greatest terror.
Let us fight Arjuna together as he comes, drunk with battle-fury; let the soldiers stand armed and arrayed in formation, ready to strike.
Droṇa, Duryodhana, Bhīṣma, you yourself, Drauṇi, and the rest of us — we shall all fight Arjuna together. O Karṇa, do not act rashly alone.
We six charioteers shall be able to face and fight the resolute Arjuna, raised like Vajra-wielding Indra — if we stand united.
Let the troops be arranged in battle formations; as supreme archers, alert and ready, we shall fight Arjuna in battle as the demons once fought Indra.
Aśvatthāman said: The cattle have not yet been won, nor has the border been crossed, nor has Hāstinapura been reached — and yet you boast, O Karṇa.
Men who have won very many battles, gained great wealth, and conquered enemy territory — they do not boast of their manliness at all.
Fire burns without speaking; the sun shines in silence; the earth bears all the worlds with their moving and unmoving beings in silence.
The duties of the four social orders have been prescribed by the wise — duties by which wealth is to be acquired, and which, when performed, do not taint the doer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A brahmin, having studied the Vedas, should officiate at sacrifices for others and sacrifice for himself. A kṣatriya, relying on the bow, should sacrifice but not officiate for others. A vaiśya, having acquired goods, should arrange for the sacred rites of the brahmin class.
Those of great fortune who live according to the scriptures and have attained their place in this world — the noble ones honour their teachers, even those teachers who may be flawed.
What kṣatriya who has won a kingdom by gambling deserves to feel satisfied by it — satisfied in such a cruel manner as a common, base person would?
And when wealth is obtained in such a way, what discerning man would boast of it — obtained by fraud and deception, like a trapper who lives by snaring?
In which chariot duel did you conquer Dhanañjaya, or Nakula and Sahadeva, whose wealth you claim to have seized?
In what battle was Yudhiṣṭhira defeated, and Bhīma, the best among the strong? In what battle did you formerly conquer Indraprastha?
And in what battle was Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) conquered by you — she who, O wicked one, was dragged into the assembly hall clad in a single garment while in her monthly period?
You cut down their great root, like one seeking the heartwood of a sandalwood tree. You made them perform such deeds, O hero — what did Vidura say at that time?
We observe the capacity for peace in human beings according to their strength, and also in other creatures, even down to insects and ants.
The Pāṇḍava should not forgive that torment inflicted on Draupadī. Dhanaṃjaya has appeared for the ruin of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
And you, having made yourself out to be wise, wish to speak such words here. Jiṣṇu, the ender of enmities, will leave none of us remaining.
This son of Kuntī, Dhanaṃjaya, would not refrain from fighting here out of fear — not of gods, not of gandharvas, not of asuras, not of rākṣasas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whoever he, enraged, shall charge at in battle, he will strike them down with the speed of Garuḍa striking a tree, and return.
Who would not honor that Pārtha, who surpasses you in valor, who is equal to the king of the immortals in archery, who is equal to Vāsudeva in battle?
The divine should be fought with the divine, the human with the human, weapon with weapon. What man is equal to Arjuna?
Those who know dharma understand that a disciple is next after a son. For this reason too, the Pāṇḍava is dear to Droṇa.
As you played at dice, as you took Indraprastha, as you dragged Kṛṣṇā into the assembly hall — in that same manner, fight the Pāṇḍava now.
Here is your wise maternal uncle, skilled in the dharma of the warrior, that Gāndhāran Śakuni who is the deity of crooked gambling — let him fight here.
The Gāṇḍīva does not cast dice; no Dvāpara throw is made with it. The Gāṇḍīva casts flaming, sharp, keen arrows.
For the vulture-feathered, keen-edged arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva do not pause in the spaces between — they can even split mountains.
Antaka, Śamana (Yama), Death itself, and the submarine fire — these might leave some remnant somewhere. But not the enraged Dhanaṃjaya.
Let the teacher fight if he wishes; I will not fight Dhanaṃjaya. The Matsya king is the one we should fight, if he comes to reclaim the cattle.
Bhīṣma said: Droṇa indeed sees rightly; Kṛpa also sees rightly. But Karṇa wishes to fight in accordance with warrior dharma, as is proper.
A teacher should not be reproached by one who is wise. One should fight after considering place and time — this is my view.
When one's five enemies are equal to the sun in striking power, how would a wise man not be confounded in the face of their rising might?
All people are confounded in their own self-interest, even those who know dharma. Therefore, O king, I tell you this — hear my word if it pleases you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What Karṇa said to us was meant to kindle our martial spirit. Let Aśvatthāman (the teacher's son) forgive it — a great task is at hand.
This is not the time for internal discord, now that the son of Kuntī stands before us. You must forgive all of it, as must the teacher and Kṛpa.
Your mastery of arms is like the radiance in the sun, like the mark on the moon — it can never be taken away. Thus are both brāhmaṇic virtue and the brahma-weapon firmly established in you.
The four Vedas are found in one place, and kṣatriya skill in another. We have never heard of both of these together combined in any single person.
Except in the Bhārata teacher (Droṇa) together with his son — this is my view. The brahma-weapon and the Vedas both — this is seen nowhere else.
Let the teacher's son forgive. This is not the time for division among ourselves. Let us all fight united against the son of Pākaśāsana (Indra) who has come.
Among the calamities of an army that have been enumerated by the wise, internal dissension is foremost — it is considered the most evil by men of learning.
Aśvatthāman said: Let the teacher himself forgive; let peace be made here. For when one's own guru is being reproached, that conduct was driven by anger.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Duryodhana begged forgiveness from Droṇa, O Bhārata, along with Karṇa, Bhīṣma, and the great-souled Kṛpa.
Droṇa said: I am indeed pleased by that very first word which Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, spoke. Let that be the course followed here.
Just as an elephant touches soldiers when Duryodhana is careless — whether through rashness or delusion — let the policy be devised accordingly.
As the forest exile has not yet been completed, Dhanaṃjaya should not have revealed himself here. Whether seeking wealth or not, he ought not to be forgiven by us today.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let policy be devised in such a way that he cannot engage with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in any manner, and also so that he cannot be defeated.
Such a word was also spoken before by Duryodhana himself. Remembering that, O son of Gaṅgā (Bhīṣma), you should speak as is fitting.
Bhīṣma said: Dear child, the fractions of time are joined together — moments, days, fortnights, months, lunar asterisms, and planets too.
Seasons are joined together, and years as well. Thus, by the divisions of time, the wheel of time turns.
By the excess of time and the displacement of the celestial bodies, two extra months arise every fifth year.
Of those, there are five extra months and twelve extra nights in thirteen years — such is my reckoning.
All of what has been fully accomplished by them as has been heard — knowing this for certain, Bībhatsu (Arjuna) has now come.
All of them are great souls; all are skilled in dharma and artha. When Yudhiṣṭhira is their king, how could they transgress against dharma?
The sons of Kuntī are without greed, and they have accomplished what is hard to accomplish. Nor would they desire the kingdom alone without the proper means.
Indeed, those joys of the Kuru line wanted to act with their heroic power right then, but bound by the bonds of dharma, they did not stray from their warrior's vow.
That which would be called falsehood, and that which would lead to dishonor — the Pārthas would choose death rather than untruth under any circumstances.
But when the proper time has come, those bulls among men would not abandon what is to be obtained. The Pāṇḍavas are of such valor that even what is guarded by the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) they would seize.
Let us fight in battle against the best of all weapon-bearers. Therefore let that which is auspicious and practiced by the good in this world be quickly arranged — lest our purpose pass to our enemies.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For I never see, O Kaurava, any certainty of absolute success in battle, O king of kings — and Dhanaṃjaya has arrived.
When battle is engaged, gain or loss, victory or defeat — one of these must come to pass. This has been seen without doubt.
Therefore, O king of kings, let a course of action related to battle, or one in keeping with dharma, be quickly decided upon — for Dhanaṃjaya has arrived.
Duryodhana said: I will not give the kingdom to the Pāṇḍavas, O grandfather. But let whatever pertains to battle be quickly arranged.
Bhīṣma said: If it pleases you, hear my own counsel in this matter. Quickly take one quarter of the army and go toward the city; then let another quarter take the cattle and go.
We, however, with the remaining half of the army, shall fight the Pāṇḍava, or the Matsya king if he comes again, or even Śatakratu (Indra) himself.
Let the teacher (Droṇa) stand in the center; let Aśvatthāman stand to the left; let the wise Kṛpa, son of Śaradvan, guard the right flank.
Let Karṇa, the charioteer's son, stand fully armored at the front. I shall stand at the rear, guarding the entire army.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: With the armies thus arrayed by the great chariot-warriors of the Kuru line, Arjuna quickly advanced, making the battlefield resound with the thunder of his chariot.
They saw the top of his banner and heard the sound of his chariot, and the great twanging sound of the Gāṇḍīva being vigorously drawn.
Then, having observed all of this and seeing the great chariot-warrior, the bearer of the Gāṇḍīva, arrive, Droṇa spoke.
There, from afar, the tip of Pārtha's banner shines; this is the roar of the cloud-like sound, and there the monkey on his standard screams.
There he stands on his chariot, the best of chariots, the one praised by the best of chariot-warriors; he draws the finest of bows, the Gāṇḍīva, which sounds like a thunderbolt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
These two arrows together have come to rest at my feet; and two others have already passed beyond, the shafts grazing my ears.
Having completed his forest exile and accomplished superhuman deeds, Pārtha now pays his respects and inquires after my welfare — through these arrows near my ears.
Arjuna said: Within arrow-range of the army, rein in the horses, O charioteer, so that I may observe in this army — where is that wretch of the Kuru lineage?
Disregarding all the others, once I have seen that arrogant one, I will descend upon his head — and then all these others will be defeated.
There stands Droṇa, and right after him Drauṇi (Aśvatthāman); Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, and Karṇa — all great bowmen — stand arrayed.
I do not see the king (Duryodhana) here. He goes along with the cattle, taking the southern road — I suspect he is intent on saving his life.
Leaving this chariot-army, go to where Suyodhana (Duryodhana) is. O son of Virāṭa, there is no battle without a stake. Having conquered him, I shall return with the cattle.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the son of Virāṭa carefully reined in the horses and gathered the reins, then urged the steeds toward where those bulls of the Kuru line stood, in the direction where Duryodhana was.
When the white-horsed one (Arjuna) had departed, leaving the chariot-army behind, Droṇa, having understood his intention, spoke.
Bībhatsu (Arjuna) does not wish to stop without reaching the king. We shall seize him from the rear as he speeds swiftly forward.
For no one could fight this enraged one alone in battle, other than the thousand-eyed god (Indra) or Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī.
What use to us are the cattle, or even abundant wealth? Duryodhana is already sinking in the water of Pārtha, like a boat that went under long ago.
Going just so, Bībhatsu announced his own name, and then quickly covered that army with arrows, like locusts descending on a field.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those warriors, being covered by the showers of arrows impelled by Pārtha, saw not a single patch of uncovered earth or sky, so dense were the feathered shafts.
Their minds were fixed neither on fighting nor on fleeing. In their hearts they could only marvel at the swiftness of Pārtha.
Then he blew his conch, making the hair of his enemies stand on end, and drawing his finest bow, he roused the spirits dwelling on his banner.
By the sound of his conch and the rumble of his chariot-wheels, and by those supernatural beings residing on his banner,
The cattle, tossing their tails upward and lowing on all sides, turned back and set out in the southern direction.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having swiftly routed the enemy army and having won back those cattle, Arjuna, the foremost bearer of the bow, set out toward Duryodhana — seeking once more to do what was pleasing in battle.
When the cattle had swiftly departed, and thinking the diademed one (Arjuna) to have accomplished his task, the heroes of the Kuru line suddenly rushed toward him as he advanced toward Duryodhana.
Seeing those many armies closely arrayed, bristling with numerous banners, the slayer of enemies addressed the son of Virāṭa and then spoke.
Lead me quickly by this way to those white horses yoked with golden reins; apply every effort with full speed — bring me close to that pride of chariot-lions.
That wicked son of a charioteer who desires to fight me — bring me to him, O prince, as elephant meets elephant; his arrogance born of shelter under Duryodhana shall be met.
With those great horses swift as wind, girt with golden girths, the son of Virāṭa, scattering the array of the enemy charioteers, then bore the Pāṇḍava into the midst of battle.
Against him as he charged, Citrasena with barbed shafts, Saṃgrāmajit, Śatrusaha, and Jaya — great chariot-warriors desiring to protect Karṇa — rode out against that descendant of Bharata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then he, foremost of men, blazing with his bow, scorching with the velocity of his arrows, his wrath burnt up the swarms of Kuru bulls' chariots as fire burns a forest.
While that tumultuous battle raged, Vikarṇa — a great Kuru hero — in his chariot, pouring a rain of piercing shafts, approached Pārtha, that foremost of chariot-fighters, the younger brother of the mighty Bhīma.
Then Arjuna, seizing Vikarṇa's bow — studded with fine gold and fitted with a firm string — brought it down, and smashed his banner; with his banner cut down, Vikarṇa too fled swiftly.
Him who was afflicting the masses of enemies and performing superhuman feats — Śatruṃtapa, unable to endure his anger, assailed Pārtha with a tortoise-nail arrow.
Pierced by that king who was a foremost chariot-fighter, Arjuna, plunging deeper into the Kuru host, quickly struck Śatruṃtapa with five arrows and then killed his charioteer with ten.
Then he, pierced by that bull of the Bhāratas with an arrow that penetrated his body-armor, fell lifeless upon the field, like a great elephant toppling from a mountain peak uprooted by the wind.
Those bulls among chariot-warriors, those heroes, broken in battle by that still greater hero, trembled as great forests shaken by the force of the wind in the season of storms.
Slain by Pārtha, those foremost of men lay sleeping on the earth — young, finely dressed, generous with wealth, equal in valor to Indra, defeated in battle by Indra's son — clad in armor of gold and dark iron, like great elephants of the Himālayan slopes.
Thus slaying enemies in battle, the Gāṇḍīva-bowman, foremost of men, ranged the field in all directions and intermediate quarters, like fire burning a forest at the end of summer.
As the great gale in spring, driving through the sky, strips trees of their scattered leaves, so the Diademed One, scattering his foes, ranged the battlefield as a supreme chariot-warrior on his car.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having slain the horses of him who drove red horses, the wearer of the diadem — that undaunted soul — with a single arrow cut off the head of Saṃgrāmajit, the brother of the son of Vikartana.
When his brother was slain, the son of the charioteer — Vaikartana — gathered his valor; like the lord of elephants lifting his tusks, he charged at that great bull like a tiger.
Vaikartana swiftly struck the Pāṇḍava with twelve winged shafts, pierced his limbs and all his horses, and struck the son of Virāṭa with arrows.
He, like the lord of elephants struck by another elephant, drew sharp bhalla arrows from his quiver, drew his bow to the full extent of his ear, and pierced the son of the charioteer with arrows.
Then, with arrows loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, bright as thunderbolts, that crusher of foes pierced his arms, thighs, head, forehead, throat, and all the parts of his chariot as he stood in battle.
Driven back by the shafts loosed by Pārtha, like a swift elephant vanquished by another elephant, scorched by the arrows of the Pāṇḍava, Vaikartana abandoned the foremost of the battle and departed.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the son of Rādhā had retreated, the warriors led by Duryodhana attacked the Pāṇḍava with their respective divisions with showers of arrows.
Recognizing which of those many divisions of his army advancing in array with arrows was to be confronted, the son of Virāṭa spoke these words.
"I, as charioteer, have mounted this splendid chariot, O Jiṣṇu — tell me, which division will you go to? I shall go wherever you direct me."
Arjuna said: "Do you see that one, O Uttara, with red eyes, auspicious, wearing a tiger skin, standing in his chariot under a dark blue banner — bring me to him."
"That is the chariot-force of Kṛpa — bring me to that very one. I shall demonstrate to this firm-bowed man my swift mastery of weapons."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"He on whose banner a beautiful water-pot of gold is displayed — that teacher is Droṇa himself, best among all who bear arms."
"With a glad mind, O hero, circumambulate him to the right — here and without obstruction; this is the eternal rule of righteousness."
"If Droṇa strikes my body first, then I will strike him in return — and he will not be angry at that."
"Not far from him, the one whose bow is visible at the top of his banner — that is the teacher's son, Aśvatthāmā, a great chariot-warrior."
"He is always to be honored by me, and by all who bear arms. Having reached his chariot, you must turn back again and again without engaging him."
"He who stands there in the chariot array, clad in golden armor, at the head of the third division of the army, in the battle formation —"
"He on whose banner-top an elephant is displayed, set upon a golden standard — that resplendent son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is King Suyodhana."
"Turn the chariot to face him, O hero who shatters enemy chariots — bring me to him; this one destroys brilliance and is maddened in battle."
"He is considered the foremost in swift archery among Droṇa's disciples. I shall demonstrate to him my vast swiftness with arrows."
"He whose beautiful serpent-girth stands atop his banner — that is Vaikartana Karṇa, known to you already."
"Approaching the chariot of this wicked son of Rādhā, you must be vigilant in battle — he always contends with me as a rival."
"He who stands in his chariot, mighty, bearing arm-guards, with a great bow, under a banner that is blue adorned with five stars —"
"He whose finest banner on his chariot is adorned with stars and the sun, and above whose head stands that white, spotless parasol —"
"He who stands at the forefront of that great chariot lineage with its many banners and pennants, like the sun at the head of the Balāhaka clouds —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"He whose golden armor shines like the moon and sun, whose helmet is of pure gold — he fills my heart with something like awe."
"This is Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, grandsire of us all — though bound by the royal fortune and following in obedience to Duryodhana."
"He is to be approached last, lest he become an obstacle to me. While I fight with these others, hold my horses steady and attentive."
Then the son of Virāṭa, unperturbed, drove the Left-handed Archer to where Kṛpa stood, O King, ready to do battle with Dhanaṃjaya.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The armies of the Kurus, terrible with their bows, could be seen creeping forward like clouds driven by gentle winds at the end of the hot season.
Nearby, horses stood mounted by fighters, and terrible-looking elephants were urged on with lances and goads.
Then Śakra, mounting Sudarśana together with hosts of gods, arrived there, O King, with the Viśvas, the Aśvins, and the troops of Maruts.
That sky, thronged with gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and great serpents, and freed from clouds, shone like the heavens adorned with planets.
And the power of those divine weapons as they were employed against humans, and that terrible great battle at the encounter between Bhīṣma and Arjuna —
— where a hundred times a hundred thousand golden pillars, and others made of jewels and precious stones, supported a palace —
— there the celestial sky-going palace of the king of gods, adorned with all manner of gems, going wherever its master willed, shone beautifully in the air.
There stood the thirty-three gods together with Vāsava, gandharvas, rākṣasas, serpents, and the ancestors along with great sages.
And likewise King Vasumanas, Balākṣa, Supratardana, Aṣṭaka, Śibi, Yayāti, Nahuṣa, and Gaya —
— Manu, Kṣupa, Raghu, Bhānu, Kṛśāśva, Sagara, and Śala — all were to be seen, radiant, in the palace of the king of gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The celestial vehicles of Agni, Īśa, Soma, Varuṇa, Prajāpati, of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, of Kubera, and of Yama —
— and of Alambusa, Ugrasena, and the gandharva Tumburu — each in its proper place and according to its allotted station, the celestial cars shone resplendent.
All the hosts of gods, the siddhas, and the greatest sages had come to witness the battle between Arjuna and the Kurus.
There the pure fragrance of divine garlands spread in all directions, as the scent of blooming forests spreads at the onset of spring.
Of the gods as they stood there, their red and non-red parasols, garments, garlands, and fans were all to be seen.
The earthly dust subsided, all was pervaded by rays of light, and the wind, carrying divine fragrances, attended upon the warriors.
The sky shone brilliantly, adorned with wonderful forms — illuminated by the many jewels of the various brilliant celestial cars, of every kind and pattern, brought there by the greatest of the gods, some flying, others stationed still.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: At that juncture, the great-souled Kṛpa — of great might and valor, best of those who bear arms — arrived, that great chariot-warrior, desirous of battle, to fight against Arjuna.
Those two chariots, bright as the sun, of those two mighty warriors poised to fight, shone brilliantly where they stood like two autumn clouds.
Pārtha too, drawing the Gāṇḍīva — that supreme weapon renowned throughout the world — loosed many iron shafts that pierced to the vital points.
Those iron arrows, feeders on blood, before they even arrived — Kṛpa cut them with his sharp shafts, by the hundreds and thousands.
Then Pārtha, enraged, displaying varied trajectories and covering all directions and intermediate quarters with arrows, that great chariot-warrior —
— making the sky as if of one uniform shade on all sides, that measureless-souled lord Pārtha covered Kṛpa with hundreds of arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Struck with those sharp arrows like flames of fire and angered, Kṛpa swiftly struck that great-souled Pārtha — of matchless energy — with a thousand arrows in return, and then roared in the battle.
Then the hero Arjuna, with haste, shot from the Gāṇḍīva arrows tipped with gold, with smooth joints, four supreme shafts — piercing each of his four horses with one each.
Those horses, pierced by sharp arrows like blazing serpents, all leaped up at once, and Kṛpa was dislodged from his position.
But seeing Gautama Kṛpa dislodged from his position, the joy of the Kurus — that slayer of enemy heroes — did not strike him, respecting his dignity.
But Gautama Kṛpa, having regained his footing, swiftly pierced the Left-handed Archer with ten arrows feathered with heron-plumes.
Then Pārtha cut his bow with a single sharp bhalla arrow, and then again wrested the bow from his hand.
Then with sharp arrows that pierced to the vital spots, Pārtha struck his armor — yet Pārtha did not wound his body itself.
As his armor fell away from him, his body shone forth, like the body of a serpent at the fitting moment as it sloughs its skin.
When his bow was cut by Pārtha, Gautama Kṛpa took up another and strung it — and that seemed wondrous indeed.
The son of Kuntī cut that one too with a smooth-jointed shaft; and thus many other bows as well the Pāṇḍava, slayer of enemy heroes, cut with skilled hands — those of Śaradvatī's son one after another.
Then, his bow cut away, the valiant one took up a lance and hurled it at the son of Pāṇḍu, blazing like a thunderbolt.
That lance as it came — adorned with gold, soaring through the sky, bright as a great meteor — Arjuna cut with ten arrows; falling in ten pieces, it was cut to the ground by the wise Pārtha.
Then, in the middle of the yoke, with bhalla arrows, Kṛpa — his bow now restored — swiftly pierced Pārtha with ten sharp shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Pārtha, of great splendor, enraged in battle, released thirteen arrows sharpened on stone, blazing with the fire of their energy.
With one arrow he severed Kṛpa's yoke, with four arrows he struck down his four horses, and with a sixth shaft he cut off the charioteer's head from his body.
With three arrows the mighty one cut the triple bamboo shaft of the chariot, with two he severed the axles, and with a twelfth broad-headed arrow he cut down Kṛpa's banner.
Then Phalguna, equal to Indra, as if smiling, struck Kṛpa in the chest with a thirteenth shaft that blazed like a thunderbolt.
His bow severed, his chariot shattered, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, Kṛpa leaped down swiftly, mace in hand, and hurled that mace.
But that heavy, well-adorned mace hurled by Kṛpa was deflected by Arjuna's arrows and returned along its own path.
Then warriors seeking to protect the wrathful Sharadvata's son (Kṛpa) poured showers of arrows upon Pārtha from all sides in the battle.
Then Virāṭa's son (Uttara), wheeling his horses to the left and executing a twin circular maneuver, countered those warriors.
Then those bull-like men, of great swiftness, took up the chariotless Kṛpa and bore him away from Kuntī's son Dhanañjaya.
Arjuna said: Where that golden altar rises, resembling a blazing flame of fire, adorned with banners on its golden post — drive me there, my friend, toward Droṇa's army, blessings upon you.
His red horses shine forth — large, finely gaited, glossy as polished coral, copper-faced, lovely to behold — yoked to the finest chariot, skilled in every art of warfare.
Long-armed, of great splendor, possessed of strength and form, renowned in all the worlds — Bhāradvāja's son (Droṇa) blazes with might.
In wisdom he is equal to Uśanas (Śukra), in statecraft equal to Bṛhaspati; he has mastered all four Vedas and likewise the vow of brahmacharya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All the divine weapons together with their withdrawal formulas, O friend, and the entire science of archery in its completeness are ever established in him.
Forbearance, self-restraint, truthfulness, non-cruelty, and uprightness — these and many other virtues reside in that best of twice-born men.
I wish to fight with that greatly fortunate one in battle. Therefore, O Uttara, quickly drive me to the preceptor — urge the horses forward.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Addressed thus by Arjuna, Virāṭa's son (Uttara) urged those gold-adorned horses toward the chariot of Bhāradvāja's son (Droṇa).
Droṇa advanced to meet that best of chariot warriors, the Pāṇḍava, as he came on with speed — Droṇa meeting Pārtha as one maddened elephant meets another.
Then he (Droṇa) blew his conch, which resounded like a hundred kettledrums; the entire army was agitated like a sea churned by the wind.
Then men in battle marveled to see those noble red horses mingled with the swift, swan-white ones on the battlefield.
Seeing those two chariots, filled with valor, at the front of the battle — the teacher and the pupil, both unconquered, both accomplished in all learning, both resolute of mind —
— seeing Droṇa and Pārtha, both of great might, thus engaged with each other, the great army of the Bhāratas trembled again and again.
And Pārtha, filled with joy, as if smiling, that heroic great chariot warrior, drew alongside Droṇa's chariot with his own.
Having paid obeisance, the mighty-armed son of Kuntī, slayer of enemy heroes, spoke these soothing and gentle words:
"We have dwelt in the forest, wishing to repay what was done to us. You ought not be angry with us, O you who are ever unconquerable in battle."
"But I shall strike only after you have struck first, O sinless one — such is the thought in my mind. May the revered one (preceptor) therefore act accordingly."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Droṇa shot more than twenty arrows at him; but before they reached him, Pārtha cut them all down with practiced hand.
Then the valiant Droṇa showered a thousand arrows upon Pārtha's chariot, quickly displaying his mastery of weaponry.
Thus the battle unfolded between Bhāradvāja's son (Droṇa) and the diademed one (Arjuna), both releasing blazing-tipped arrows equally in the contest.
Both renowned for their deeds, both equal to the wind in speed, both versed in celestial weapons, both of supreme splendor — as they hurled their nets of arrows, they bewildered even the kings.
Then all the warriors assembled there marveled, honoring them with cries of "Excellent! Excellent!" as they released their arrows with such swiftness.
"Who else but Phalguna is worthy to fight Droṇa in battle? This is the fierce dharma of the warrior class — that he fights even against his own preceptor" — so spoke the men standing at the front of the battle.
And those two heroes, both enraged, both great chariot warriors drawing close to each other, both undefeated, covered each other with masses of arrows.
Then Bhāradvāja's son, enraged, drawing his immense bow with its golden back — a bow hard to approach — fought back against Phalguna.
With nets of arrows, whetted on stone and blazing with light, launched toward Arjuna's chariot, he covered even the radiance of the sun.
And that great chariot warrior, the mighty-armed one, pierced Pārtha with swift, sharp arrows, as a cloud pierces a mountain with rain.
Likewise the Pāṇḍava, taking up his divine Gāṇḍīva bow — that supreme instrument of bearing the burden of battle, the enemy's destroyer, swift as the wind — boldly released many varied arrows fashioned with golden decorations.
Destroying Bhāradvāja's son's showers of arrows with shafts quickly loosed from his bow, the valiant one performed what seemed like a wonder.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhanañjaya, Pārtha, moving in his chariot — a splendid sight to behold — simultaneously displayed all his weapons in every direction.
He made the sky like a single shadow with arrows on all sides; Droṇa was not visible at that moment, covered as if by a mist.
His form at that moment, enveloped by those finest of arrows blazing all around, was like a mountain blazing with fire on all sides.
But seeing his own chariot covered by Pārtha's arrows in battle, Droṇa drew his wondrous bow, whose sound was like the rumbling of thunder clouds,
— terrible as a wheel of fire — drawing that supreme weapon to its fullest, that glorious one in battle, Droṇa, shattered those arrows; and then there arose a great sound like that of bamboos burning.
With arrows whose nocks were made of refined gold, issuing from that excellent and decorated bow, the immeasurable-souled one covered the directions and the brilliance of the sun.
Then those gold-nocked arrows with their smooth joints, flying through the sky, were seen in great numbers by the people — filling the heavens.
The arrows issuing from Droṇa's bow, clinging together nock to nock, appeared in the sky as a single long, continuous arrow.
Thus those two heroes, releasing great arrows adorned with gold, made the sky as if covered with meteors.
And their arrows, feathered with heron and peacock plumes, shone like lines of swans moving through the autumn sky.
A fierce, terrible battle arose there between those two great souls, Droṇa and the Pāṇḍava, like the battle between Vṛtra and Vāsava (Indra).
And like two elephants approaching each other and striking with the tips of their tusks, they struck each other with arrows released at full draw.
Those two heroes, both enraged and resplendent in battle, fought each other, invoking their divine weapons in sequence.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Arjuna, the foremost among the victorious, warded off with sharp arrows those stone-whetted shafts released by the chief of preceptors.
Displaying himself, Indra's son (Arjuna), fierce and of fierce valor, swiftly covered the sky with many arrows.
Droṇa, the chief of preceptors, the best of weapon-bearers, sported with Arjuna in battle — even as Arjuna, that tiger among men of blazing splendor, sought to slay him — playing with arrows of smooth-jointed shafts.
Against Bhāradvāja's son releasing divine weapons in the great battle, Phalguna countered weapon with weapon and fought him equally.
The collision of those two lions among men, both enraged, both intolerant of each other, was like the clash of gods and demons.
The Pāṇḍava absorbed with his own weapon, again and again, the Aindra (Indra's), the Vāyavya (wind-god's), and the Āgneya (fire-god's) weapons as Droṇa released them one after another.
Thus those two heroes, those great bowmen, releasing sharp arrows, made the sky like a single shadow with their showers of shafts.
Then, as Arjuna's arrows were released and fell upon living bodies, there was heard the sound of those shafts — like thunderbolts falling upon mountains.
Then, O lord of the people, elephants, chariots, and horsemen, drenched in blood, were seen like blossoming kimshuka trees.
And with arms still bearing their armlets, with great chariot warriors fallen, with golden and variegated armor and with banners brought down —
— and with warriors slain there, tormented by Pārtha's arrows, the army was thrown into turmoil at the clash of Droṇa and Arjuna.
But those two heroes, brandishing their bows — those instruments for bearing the burden of battle — covered each other with arrows, enduring the shafts of war.
Then there arose a sound in the sky from those praising Droṇa: "Droṇa has accomplished a feat hard to perform — that he fought against Arjuna."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That agitator of all, of great valor, firm of fist, hard to approach, the conqueror of gods, demons, and serpents, that great chariot warrior —"
And seeing Pārtha's ceaseless skill, swiftness, and ability to shoot at distant targets in battle, Droṇa too was filled with wonder.
Then, O bull of the Bhāratas, the intolerant Pārtha, taking up his divine Gāṇḍīva bow, drew it with both arms in battle.
His rain of arrows, like an extending swarm of locusts — even the wind could not pass through the gaps between those shafts.
No interval whatsoever was seen in Pārtha at that moment, whether he was nocking arrows ceaselessly, releasing them, or taking them up again.
And so, while that terrible battle of swift weapons proceeded, Pārtha released yet more arrows — faster than fast.
Then hundreds of thousands of arrows with smooth joints descended upon Droṇa's chariot simultaneously from close range.
As Droṇa was being showered by the arrows of the Gāṇḍīva-bearer, O bull of the Bhāratas, a great cry of "Ah! Ah!" rose from the troops.
Maghavan (Indra) honored the Pāṇḍava's swift weaponry, and so did the gandharvas, the apsaras, and all who had assembled there.
Then Aśvatthāmā, the son of the preceptor, commander of a chariot division, suddenly checked the Pāṇḍava with a great multitude of chariots.
Yet Aśvatthāmā in his heart honored the feat of the great-souled Pārtha, even as he aroused in himself great anger.
He, overcome by rage, charged at Pārtha in battle, showering thousands of arrows like a rain-laden thundercloud.
But the mighty-armed Pārtha, turning his horses toward where Droṇa's son (Aśvatthāmā) was, gave Droṇa an interval to withdraw.
And Droṇa, having gained that interval, quickly departed with his swift horses — that hero, his armor and banner cut down, himself struck by the finest arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Pārtha received him (Aśvatthāmā) — rising like a gust of wind, pouring arrows like a cloud — with a great net of arrows.
Their great clash, both of them hurling nets of arrows, was like the meeting of gods and demons — like the clash of Vṛtra and Vāsava.
The sun did not shine at that moment, nor did the wind blow, as the sky was made dense with arrows and became shadow all around.
A tremendous crackling sound arose from the two warriors as they struck each other, like the sound of bamboos burning in fire, O conqueror of enemy cities.
Arjuna made all the horses of his opponent nearly lifeless with his arrows; that king, O lord, could not discern any direction, so bewildered was he.
Then Droṇa's son, of great might, spying a tiny opening as Pārtha moved about, severed his bowstring with a razor-headed arrow. The gods praised that deed of his, seeing it to be superhuman.
Then Droṇa's son, having shattered eight of that bull among men's bows, once again struck Pārtha in the chest with heron-feathered shafts.
Then Pārtha the long-armed, laughing aloud, strung Gāṇḍīva with a new bowstring with vigor.
Then Pārtha, drawing back a crescent-shaped arrow, closed in upon him, like a maddened bull elephant advancing upon another maddened leader of a herd.
Then a great battle commenced between those two heroes, unique in the world, in the midst of the fighting, hair-raising and extraordinary.
All the Kurus watched those two great-souled heroes in combat with amazement, like two leaders of elephant herds come together.
Those two heroic bulls among men struck each other with arrows resembling venomous serpents, blazing like fiery serpents.
The great-souled son of Pāṇḍu had two divine quivers that never emptied; thus Pārtha, the hero, stood firm in battle like an immovable mountain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The arrows of Aśvatthāmā, who was shooting swiftly in battle, went into rapid exhaustion; by this it became clear that Arjuna was superior to him.
Then Karṇa, drawing his great bow with exceeding fury, released it downward; thereupon arose a great cry of lamentation.
Pārtha turned his eyes toward where the bow was being drawn; he saw Rādhā's son there, and his anger flared beyond measure.
Seized by rage, that bull of the Kurus stared fixedly at Karṇa with both eyes wide open, desiring to slay him.
While Pārtha had turned away like this, O king, swift men brought thousands of arrows to Droṇa's son.
And Dhanañjaya the long-armed, the slayer of foes, leaving Droṇa's son, suddenly rushed straight at Karṇa.
Rushing at him, Kuntī's son, his eyes red with anger, desiring single combat on chariots, spoke these words:
Arjuna said: O Karṇa, what you boasted loudly in the midst of the assembly hall in words — that there is no one equal to me in battle — that moment has now arrived.
You spoke harsh words, abandoning righteousness entirely; yet I consider what you now intend to do to be very difficult indeed.
What you declared before without having met me in any way — do that today, O son of Rādhā, in the midst of the Kurus, against me.
You witnessed the princess of Pāñcāla being tormented by those evil-souled men in the assembly hall; now reap the fruit of that, and that alone.
What I endured before, bound by the bonds of dharma — behold my victory born of that anger now, O son of Rādhā, in this battle.
Come, O Karṇa, engage in combat with me; let all the Kurus together with their armies be spectators.
Karṇa said: What you say in words, O Pārtha, accomplish in deeds; for it is well-known in the world that action surpasses speech.
What you endured before — I take it that it was endured out of weakness, O Pārtha, having now witnessed your inferior valor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If you endured before bound by the cords of dharma, even so you think yourself unbound, though you are bound in the same way.
If indeed the forest dwelling was observed by you as stipulated, then you who know the purpose of dharma are distressed and wish to break the covenant.
Even if Indra himself were to fight on your behalf, O Pārtha, still no distress whatsoever would befall me as I display my valor.
This desire of yours, O son of Kuntī, has arrived soon enough; you will fight with me today — behold my strength.
Arjuna said: Just now you retreated from my battle, and by that you live, O son of Rādhā; but your younger brother has been slain.
Having caused your brother to be slain and having abandoned the forefront of battle, what other man among the good, placed in your position, would speak thus?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Speaking thus to Karṇa, the invincible Bībhatsu advanced, releasing arrows that pierced through bodily armor.
Karṇa received those arrows, resembling flames of fire, with a great shower of arrows, like a rain cloud pouring rain.
Terrifying nets of arrows flew out in all directions; he pierced the horses, and separately struck both his arms and the arm-guard of his hand.
He, unable to endure it, severed the strap of Karṇa's quiver with a sharp-tipped arrow of bent joints.
Then Karṇa, taking arrows from another quiver, pierced the son of Pāṇḍu in the hand; his grip was shattered.
Then Pārtha the long-armed cut Karṇa's bow; he hurled a spear at Pārtha, and Pārtha shattered it with arrows.
Then many of Rādhā's son's foot-soldiers rushed forward; those he dispatched to the abode of Yama with shafts released from Gāṇḍīva.
Then Bībhatsu struck Karṇa's horses with sharp arrows, effective for heavy work, drawn to the ear; they fell slain upon the earth.
Then with another blazing arrow, the mighty-armed and valiant son of Kuntī pierced Karṇa in the chest with a sharp shaft.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That arrow, piercing through his armor, struck his body; then he was overcome by darkness and knew nothing at all.
He, in deep pain, abandoned the battle and went away northward; then Arjuna cried out in triumph, and so did the great warrior Uttara.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having conquered the son of Vikartana, Pārtha said to the son of Virāṭa: Drive me to the army where the golden palm-tree standard stands.
Here the son of Śaṃtanu, Bhīṣma, our grandsire, godlike in appearance, stands wishing to fight with me; I will even take his bowstring in battle.
Behold me today releasing wonderful divine weapons, like lightning coming from a storm cloud in the sky.
The Kurus will see my gold-backed Gāṇḍīva — and all the assembled enemies will wonder: with which hand, right or left, does he shoot?
I will cause a river to flow, with blood for water, with chariots for its eddies, with elephants for its crocodiles, impassable, flowing toward the other world.
I will cut down the forest of the Kurus — dense with hands, feet, heads, backs, and arms as its branches — with broad-headed arrows of bent joints.
As I alone as an archer conquer the Kaurava army, a hundred paths will open, as fire moves through a forest; you will see only the army struck as if by a discus.
Stand unperturbed on the chariot on level and uneven ground; I will split the mountain that stands filling the sky with my arrow-bearing shafts.
I, at Indra's command, once slew in battle the Paulomas and the Kālakhañjas by the hundreds and thousands.
From Indra I obtained the firm grip, from Brahmā the skilled handwork, the deep, tumultuous, and wonderful release — the art of the Lord of Creatures.
I, beyond the ocean, destroyed the golden city, conquering sixty thousand fierce bowmen in chariots.
The forest of the Kurus — with standards for trees, foot soldiers for grass, and filled with hosts of chariot-lions — I will set ablaze with the fire of my weapons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I alone will sweep them from their chariot-nests with bent-jointed arrows, as the Wielder of the Thunderbolt swept away the demons.
From Rudra I obtained the Raudra weapon, from Varuṇa the Vāruṇa weapon, from Agni the Āgneya weapon, from the wind-god the Vāyavya weapon, and from Indra the thunderbolt and other weapons.
I will uproot the terrible forest of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, guarded by human lions; let your fear depart, O son of Virāṭa.
Thus reassured by the ambidextrous one, the son of Virāṭa plunged into the formidable chariot-army of the wise Bhīṣma.
The doer of cruel deeds, composedly, opposed Dhanañjaya the long-armed as he came, wishing to conquer enemies in battle.
Those of varied garlands and ornaments, skilled in knowledge, and resolute of mind came against him of the terrible bow, having strung their bowstrings upon their arms.
Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, Duhhsaha, and Viviṃśati came and surrounded the terrible-bowed Bībhatsu.
But Duḥśāsana the hero, with one broad-headed arrow pierced Uttara the son of Virāṭa, and with a second pierced Arjuna in the chest.
Turning toward him, Jiṣṇu cut that broad-edged bow with a vulture-feathered shaft adorned with gold.
Then he pierced him in the chest with five more arrows from behind; he departed, abandoning the battle, tormented by Pārtha's arrows.
Vikarṇa, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, pierced Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, with sharp, straight-flying, vulture-feathered arrows.
Then the son of Kuntī quickly struck him too on the forehead with a bent-jointed arrow; struck, he fell from his chariot.
Then Duhsaha together with Viviṃśati rushed at Pārtha and covered him with sharp arrows, seeking to protect his brother in battle.
Dhanañjaya, undisturbed, piercing both of them simultaneously with two sharp vulture-feathered arrows, slew their horses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those two sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, their horses slain and their bodies pierced, were carried away on other chariots, followed by their foot soldiers.
The invincible Bībhatsu, the son of Kuntī, wearing the diadem and garlands, mighty and having attained his aim, swooped upon all directions.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all the great warriors of the Kauravas, coming together, joined forces and vigilantly fought back against Arjuna, O Bhārata.
He of immeasurable spirit covered those great warriors on all sides with nets of arrows, like mist covering mountains.
With roaring great elephants and neighing horses, and with the sounds of kettledrums and conches, that noise became tumultuous.
Piercing through the bodies of men and horses and through iron armors, Pārtha's nets of arrows flew out by the thousands.
Swiftly releasing arrows, the son of Pāṇḍu shone in battle like the autumn sun at midday, blazing with rays.
Terrified chariot-warriors then tumbled from their chariots, horsemen from the backs of their horses, and foot soldiers fell upon the ground.
A great sound arose from the armors of the great souls being struck by arrows — armors of copper, silver, and iron.
The entire battlefield was covered with the bodies of those who had lost consciousness — elephants, horses, riders, and others whose lives had been taken by sharp arrows.
The earth was strewn with men who had fallen from their chariot platforms; Dhanañjaya with bow in hand seemed to dance in the battle.
Hearing the twang of Gāṇḍīva, like the crash of a thunderbolt, all living beings, terrified, fled from that great battle.
Heads adorned with earrings and turbans, garlanded with gold, could be seen fallen at the forefront of battle.
The earth shone covered with limbs torn apart by arrows, and with arms still clutching bows, adorned with bracelets and other ornaments.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O bull of the Bhārata line, as heads were being felled by sharp arrows, it was as though a rain of stones fell from the sky.
Having thus revealed his terrible form, with the valor of Rudra himself, Pārtha the son of Pāṇḍu — who had been constrained and wandering for thirteen years — now unleashed the dreadful fire of his wrath upon the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Seeing him burn the army and beholding his valor, all the warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son became intent on making peace, while their king looked on.
Having terrified that army and routed the great chariot-warriors, Arjuna, the foremost among the victorious, wheeled about, O Bhārata.
He set in motion a dreadful river with waves of torrential blood, choked with bones serving as its moss, fashioned by Time at the end of an age.
Pārtha created a great and dreadful river flowing northward with blood — its rafts were arrows and bows, its mud was flesh and gore, its great islands were mighty chariot-warriors, and it resounded with the sound of conches and drums.
As he picked up arrows, nocked them, and released them, and as he drew the Gāṇḍīva bow, no interval whatsoever could be perceived in his actions.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Duryodhana, Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, Viviṃśati, Droṇa together with his son, and Kṛpa — an outstanding chariot-warrior in battle —
— came forward again in great fury, with the desire to slay Dhanañjaya, twanging their powerful and sturdy bows.
O great king, the one with the monkey banner advanced to meet them all together in his chariot, whose scattered pennants blazed like the sun.
Then Kṛpa, Karṇa, and Droṇa — the foremost among chariot-warriors — surrounded Dhanañjaya, that man of immense valor, with great celestial weapons.
Releasing volleys of arrows accurately, like monsoon clouds in the rainy season, they rained down showers of arrows upon the diademed warrior as he advanced.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Taking their stand nearby in battle, they diligently filled him quickly with many arrows that caused the hair to stand on end.
As he was covered on all sides by those divine weapons, not even two finger-breadths of his body remained uncovered.
Then Bībhatsu, that great chariot-warrior, smiled and invoked upon the Gāṇḍīva the divine Aindra weapon, blazing like the sun.
Like the sun with its rays, the mighty diademed son of Kuntī, blazing in battle, covered over all the Kurus.
Just as lightning flashes in a storm-cloud, or fire blazes on a rocky mountain, so the Gāṇḍīva appeared like Indra's own weapon stretched wide.
Just as lightning blazes in the sky when the rain-cloud pours down, so the flying Gāṇḍīva covered all ten directions.
All the chariot-warriors everywhere became terrified; becoming intent on peace, they could not collect their own thoughts. All those warriors turned their faces away from battle, their spirits broken.
Thus, O bull of the Bhārata line, all the armies were broken and fled in every direction, without hope for their own lives.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu — irresistible and of great prowess — charged at Dhanañjaya while the warriors were being slaughtered.
Taking up his finest bow adorned with gold, and taking sharp-tipped arrows capable of piercing the vital points and causing destruction —
— that tiger among men, with a white umbrella held above his head, shone like a mountain at sunrise.
Blowing his conch and filling the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with joy, the son of the Gaṅgā circled to the right and checked Bībhatsu.
Beholding him coming thus, the son of Kuntī, slayer of enemy heroes, received him with joyful spirit, like a mountain receiving a rain-bearing cloud.
Then valiant Bhīṣma shot eight arrows of great speed into Pārtha's banner — arrows hissing like serpents.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those feathered and blazing arrows, reaching the banner of the son of Pāṇḍu, struck the monkey and those other beings dwelling at the top of the standard.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu swiftly cut Bhīṣma's umbrella with a great broad-bladed arrow, and it fell to the ground.
The son of Kuntī, swift in action, also struck his banner hard with arrows, and likewise both his horses, his chariot-drivers, and both rear-guard warriors.
The tumultuous and hair-raising battle between Bhīṣma and Pārtha was like that of Bali and Vāsava (Indra).
In the battle between Bhīṣma and the Pāṇḍava, broad-headed arrows meeting broad-headed arrows glittered in the sky like fireflies in the rainy season.
O king, the Gāṇḍīva of Pārtha as he released arrows, shooting to the left and right, appeared like a spinning wheel of fire.
He covered Bhīṣma with hundreds of sharp arrows, like a rain-cloud covering a mountain with streams of water.
Bhīṣma dispersed that rising shower of arrows, like a wave tossed up by the sea, with his own shafts and checked Arjuna.
Then those nets of arrows, cut apart piece by piece in battle, fell scattered toward Phalguna's chariot.
Then the rising shower of gold-fletched arrows from the Pāṇḍava's chariot — coming swiftly like a swarm of locusts — Bhīṣma in turn dispersed with hundreds of sharp arrows.
Then all the Kurus cried out "Bravo! Bravo!" saying that Bhīṣma had done a difficult thing in fighting Arjuna.
The Pāṇḍava is powerful, young, skilled, and swift in action — who else is capable of withstanding Pārtha's speed in battle?
— except Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, or Kṛṣṇa the son of Devakī, or the foremost of teachers, Bhāradvāja's son of great strength.
Those two bulls among men, of great power, countering weapons with weapons as if at play, bewildered the eyes of all creatures.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those two great-souled ones moved about in battle employing the weapons of Prajāpati, Indra, the terrible Āgneya weapon, those of Kubera, Varuṇa, Yama, and the wind-god.
Then all beings were astonished, seeing the two in combat, and cried out "Well done, Pārtha, mighty-armed! Well done, Bhīṣma!"
"This great deployment of celestial weapons that is seen in the battle between Bhīṣma and Pārtha is not fitting for mortals."
Thus the weapon-battle of those two who knew all weapons continued. Then Jiṣṇu (Arjuna), wheeling about, cut Bhīṣma's bow adorned with gold, with a broad-bladed arrow.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, mighty-armed Bhīṣma of great strength took up another bow in battle, strung it, and in anger quickly released very many arrows at Dhanañjaya.
Arjuna too, of very great energy, hurled many varied and sharp arrows at Bhīṣma, and Bhīṣma likewise hurled arrows at the Pāṇḍava.
O king, as those two great-souled masters of celestial weapons released arrows ceaselessly, no difference between them could be perceived.
Then the diademed son of Kuntī, that supreme chariot-warrior, covered the ten directions with arrows, and likewise the brave son of Śaṃtanu.
O king, the Pāṇḍava surpassed Bhīṣma exceedingly, and Bhīṣma surpassed the Pāṇḍava exceedingly — in that battle it was a wonder to the world.
O king, the heroic chariot-guards of Bhīṣma, slain by the Pāṇḍava, lay all around the chariot of the son of Kuntī.
Then the feathered arrows of the white-horsed warrior, loosed from the Gāṇḍīva and desiring to make an end of enemies, came forward, tightly bound at the nock.
Leaping forth from his chariot, gleaming and clothed in gold, they appeared in the sky like lines of swans.
As he released that wondrous and deeply potent divine weapon, all the gods together with Vāsava (Indra) who stood in the sky looked on.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing that marvelous and wondrous feat, the illustrious gandharva Citrasena, supremely pleased, reported it to the king of the gods.
"See these enemy-destroyers going as if linked together — this is the wondrous form of Jiṣṇu's divine weapon as it blazes forth."
"Mortals would not believe this — indeed it does not exist among them. This wondrous conjunction of ancient great weapons is beyond them."
Like the sun blazing in the sky at midday, the armies could not look directly at the Pāṇḍava.
Both were celebrated for their deeds, both were skilled in battle, both performed equal feats, both were unapproachable in combat.
Thus addressed, O Bhārata, the king of the gods honored the encounter of Pārtha and Bhīṣma with a divine shower of flowers.
Then Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, having taken aim and found an opening, planted a shaft in the left side of Savyasācin (Arjuna) as he was shooting.
Then Bībhatsu, smiling, cut the bow of Bhīṣma of immeasurable energy with a broad-bladed, vulture-feathered arrow.
Then Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī, pierced him in the chest with ten arrows as he strove and pressed forward.
Tormented, the mighty-armed son of the Gaṅgā — irresistible in battle — stood gripping the chariot-pole for a long time as if in pain.
The charioteer, recalling his instructions and protecting the great warrior, drove him away while he was insensible.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Bhīṣma had abandoned the head of battle and fled, the great-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra raised his standard and, roaring, came himself to grapple with Arjuna.
He pierced Dhanañjaya — wielder of the mighty bow, of lofty valor, ranging among the throng of enemies — right in the middle of the forehead with a broad-bladed arrow drawn fully to the ear.
Struck by that well-aimed arrow of refined gold, O king, the doer of noble deeds shone like a single-knotted, beautiful single-peaked mountain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then from him, pierced by the arrow, warm blood flowed freely — that garland of gold-colored flowers upon him shone resplendent with its varied hues.
Struck by that arrow, the swift and undaunted warrior, his anger aroused by Duryodhana, took up arrows like poison and fire and pierced the king.
And Duryodhana of fierce energy struck him, and Pārtha the sole hero struck Duryodhana — those two foremost heroes of the Ajamīḍha clan struck each other equally in battle.
Then Vikarṇa, with a great elephant in rut resembling a moving mountain, along with four chariots protecting the elephant's flanks, charged at Jiṣṇu, the son of Kuntī.
Dhanañjaya pierced that lord of elephants charging swiftly right between the frontal lobes with a swift, firm iron arrow drawn fully to the ear.
That vulture-feathered arrow released by Pārtha entered the elephant all the way to the nock, tearing through that creature radiant as a great mountain — like a thunderbolt sent by Indra into a peak.
That king of elephants, scorched by the arrow, his limbs trembling and his inner spirit tormented, sinking down, fell to the earth like the peak of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
When the finest of tusked elephants fell to the earth, Vikarṇa in fear instantly descended and, quickly going eight hundred paces, mounted the chariot of Viviṃśati.
Having slain the elephant with that arrow — that arrow like a thunderbolt, like the best of mountains, like a rain-cloud — with that same kind of arrow Pārtha then pierced Duryodhana in the chest.
Then, with both the elephant and the king struck down, and Vikarṇa along with his foot-guards routed, those foremost warriors, driven away by the shafts loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, suddenly fled.
Seeing the elephant felled by the arrow and learning that all his warriors were fleeing, that foremost hero of the Kurus turned his chariot and fled from the battle to where Pārtha was not.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing that fearsome Duryodhana fleeing swiftly, the quiver-bearing Kirīṭī, eager to fight and enduring of enemies, roared a challenge at him — who had been pierced by an arrow and was vomiting blood.
Arjuna said: Abandoning your vast fame and glory, why do you flee, turning away from battle? Why do your war-drums not sound properly now as they did when you went to fight?
I act on Yudhiṣṭhira's command; I am Pārtha, the third, and I stand firm in battle. For his sake, turn your face and fight — remember the conduct of a king, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Your name in this world — 'Duryodhana,' given to you before — is rendered vain; for there is no quality of Duryodhana in you now, as you flee abandoning the battle.
I see no protector of yours, neither in front nor behind you, O Duryodhana. Come, O foremost of the Kurus, protect your dear life from the Pāṇḍava through battle today.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Being thus summoned by him in battle, that great-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was turned back by his words as by a goad — like a maddened elephant turned by a goad.
Unable to endure being struck by those words of the great chariot-warrior, that swift hero, who surpassed all chariot-warriors, wheeled around in his chariot — like a serpent touched by the sole of a foot.
Seeing him turn back, Karṇa, though his body was pierced by arrows, steadied himself and turned back; that hero among men, wearing a garland of gold, came to Duryodhana's right flank to face Pārtha in battle.
Then Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, turning back and urging his gold-girthed horses, with his bow strung, the mighty-armed one guarded Duryodhana on the western flank from the sons of Pṛthā.
Droṇa, Kṛpa, Viviṃśati, and Duḥśāsana — all of them quickly turned back, with their bows bent and arrows ready, and swiftly came to the front for the sake of Duryodhana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing those armies turning back, resembling the fullness of flood-tide, Pārtha Dhanañjaya swiftly rushed toward them — as a swan flies toward an approaching cloud.
They surrounded Pārtha from all sides, taking up their divine weapons, and advancing, showered him with arrows on every side — as clouds drench a mountain with torrents of water.
Then the wielder of Gāṇḍīva, bearing down the weapons of those foremost Kuru heroes with counter-weapons, the enemy-subduing son of Indra revealed another weapon — the irresistible Sammohana (bewildering) weapon.
Then, turning in all the cardinal and intermediate directions, he of great strength, with well-edged, sharp, well-feathered arrows and by the roar of the Gāṇḍīva, caused terror to the minds of those warriors.
Then, taking up his great conch of magnificent sound, the slayer of enemies Pārtha blew it mightily with his arms, and the sound filled all the cardinal and intermediate directions, the sky and the earth.
Those foremost Kuru heroes, bewildered by the blast of the conch blown by Pārtha, all let go of their formidable bows and became intent on peace at that moment.
While the enemies were thus rendered unconscious, Pārtha, remembering the words of Uttara, said to the son of Virāṭa: 'Drive out from among them, while the Kurus are still insensible.'
Fetch the two pure white garments of the teacher and of Śāradvata's son, the bright yellow garment of Karṇa, and likewise the dark blue garments of Droṇa's son and the king, O hero among men.
I think Bhīṣma has his senses — he knows how to counter my weapons. Keep his horses on the left side; that is how one must pass those who have not lost their senses.
Then the great-souled son of Virāṭa, releasing the reins, leapt down from the chariot, collected the garments of those great chariot-warriors, and quickly remounted his own chariot.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the son of Virāṭa guided the four excellent gold-girthed horses; the white steeds, bearing Arjuna, passed through the army of the banner-bearers and out from the midst of the battle.
As that foremost of men was thus moving away, the swift Bhīṣma struck him with arrows; and he in turn, having struck down Bhīṣma's horses, pierced him in the side with ten swift arrows.
Then Arjuna, having set aside Bhīṣma in the battle and pierced his charioteer, with his bow intact, stood free from amid the multitude of chariots — as the thousand-rayed sun stands after rending Rāhu.
Having regained consciousness, that foremost of Kuru heroes, seeing Pārtha standing alone in the field, freed from the battle, equal to great Indra, that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke quickly.
He said: 'How has this one escaped from you? Capture him so he cannot get away!' To him Śaṃtanu's son laughed and said: 'Where has your intelligence gone? Where your valor?'
You yourself stood at peace, breathing again, having let go of your arrows and your marvelous bow. But Bībhatsu is not capable of cruelty — his mind is not set on wickedness.
He would not abandon his own dharma even for the sake of the three worlds — that is why not all have been slain in this battle. Go quickly back to the Kuru lands, O foremost of Kurus; let Pārtha return, having won back the cattle.
Hearing those words of the grandfather, which were truly for his own good, Duryodhana, the king, excessively wrathful and having lost the chance to win in battle, heaved a deep sigh and fell silent.
Seeing that beneficial speech of Bhīṣma, and the ever-growing fire of Dhanañjaya, all those who were protecting Duryodhana set their minds on retreating.
Seeing those foremost Kuru heroes setting out, Pārtha Dhanañjaya, with a gladdened mind, followed them for a moment, addressing them, and there that great-souled one honored his elders.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Honoring with bowed head the aged grandfather Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, the teacher Droṇa, and paying salutation with varied arrows to Droṇa's son, Kṛpa, and all his elders —
— Pārtha cut off with an arrow the crown of Duryodhana, adorned with the finest jewels; and having taken leave of those heroes and venerable ones alike, and filling the worlds with the roar of the Gāṇḍīva —
— that hero, suddenly blowing his Devadatta conch and splitting the hearts of his foes, having overpowered all enemies with his banner, shining with his net of gold —
— seeing the Kurus depart, the diademed Kirīṭī, overjoyed, said to the son of Matsya there: 'Turn the horses around — your cattle have been won. The enemies have gone. Go to your city rejoicing.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having conquered the Kurus in battle, he whose eyes were like a bull's gathered together the great wealth of Virāṭa.
And when the forces of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son had all gone away, broken and dispersed in every direction, many of the Kuru soldiers emerged from the dense forest.
With minds terrified by fear they came from here and there; they appeared with unbound hair, standing with folded hands.
Exhausted by hunger and thirst, bewildered, in a foreign land and out of their senses, they bowed and said in confusion: 'O Pārtha, what shall we do for you?'
Arjuna said: 'Go in safety, good fortune be with you — you need not fear at all. I do not wish to slay the distressed. I greatly reassure you.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing his words of assurance, the assembled warriors gladdened him with blessings of long life, fame, and glory.
Then the Kurus, turned back and utterly routed, came under his sway; approaching the road, Phalguna spoke this word.
He said: 'O prince, O mighty-armed hero, review all the herds of cattle that have been rounded up together along with the cowherds.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then in the afternoon we shall go toward the city of Virāṭa, after resting the horses, giving them water, and refreshing them.'
'Let the cowherds whom you send go quickly to the city to announce the good news and proclaim your victory.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Uttara, acting swiftly, commanded messengers accordingly, saying: 'Go and, by Arjuna's word, announce my victory.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Virāṭa, the commander of the army, having also won back the wealth, entered the city rejoicing, together with the four Pāṇḍavas.
Having defeated the Trigartas in battle and recovered the cattle alone, the great king shone resplendent, accompanied by the sons of Pṛthā, enveloped in glory.
