When that hero, who increased the joy of his friends, was seated upon his throne, all his ministers along with the brahmins attended upon him.
Honored and congratulated along with his army, the king of Matsya then dismissed the twice-born brahmins and the ministers.
Then that king of the Matsyas, Virāṭa, the commander of the army, eagerly inquired about Uttara, saying: 'Where has he gone?'
The women, maidens, and those who moved within the inner apartments joyfully told him at home that the cattle-wealth had been taken away by the Kurus.
The conqueror of the earth had gone out alone, determined to win them back, with exceeding boldness, with Bṛhannaḍā as his companion.
Six great chariot-warriors had come to oppose him: Droṇa, Śaṃtanu's son Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, Karṇa, Duryodhana, and Droṇa's son.
King Virāṭa, greatly distressed upon hearing that his son had gone with but one chariot, with Bṛhannaḍā as charioteer, he who increases victory in battle, then spoke to all the chief ministers.
The Kurus in particular, and whatever other lords of the earth, will certainly never stand idle upon hearing that the Trigartas have been defeated.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore let my warriors go, surrounded by a great force — those who were not wounded by the Trigartas — for the purpose of protecting Uttara.
He quickly dispatched horses, elephants, chariots, and hosts of infantry — heroic warriors furnished with varied weapons and ornaments — for the sake of his son.
Thus that king of the Matsyas, Virāṭa, the lord of an akshauhini, commanded that fourfold army to march out swiftly.
He said: 'Find the prince quickly — whether he lives or not. A eunuch went as his charioteer; I think he cannot be alive.'
The Dharma-king laughed and said to Virāṭa, afflicted and distressed by the Kurus: 'O lord of men, if Bṛhannaḍā is the charioteer, your enemies will not carry off those cattle today.'
'Your son is fully capable of conquering in battle all the kings together with the Kurus, and likewise the gods, demons, yakshas, and nagas — guided well by that charioteer.'
Then those swift-moving messengers sent by Uttara reached the city of Virāṭa and announced the victory.
The minister then reported to the king the supreme victory, the defeat of the Kurus, and Uttara's return.
'All the cattle have been fully won back, the Kurus have been defeated, and Uttara is safe along with his charioteer, O scorcher of enemies.'
Kaṅka said: 'By good fortune your cattle have been won back and the Kurus defeated. By good fortune your son is heard to be alive, O bull among kings.'
'I do not consider it a wonder that your son conquered the Kurus — certain indeed is the victory of one whose charioteer is Bṛhannaḍā.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Virāṭa, his body hair thrilling with delight upon hearing the victory of that prince of boundless energy, rewarded those messengers with garments and urged his ministers on.
'Let my royal roads be decorated with banners; let the gods be worshipped everywhere with floral offerings.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Let the princes, chief warriors, and courtesans, all well adorned, and all the musical instruments go forth to meet my son.'
'Let the drummer quickly mount a maddened elephant and proclaim my victory at every crossroads.'
'And let Uttara, accompanied by many maidens, adorned in fine dress and ornaments, go forth to meet Bṛhannaḍā.'
Hearing the king's command, all with auspicious articles in hand, together with kettledrums, musical instruments, conches, and auspicious women beautifully attired in the finest garments —
— and likewise bards along with panegyrists, players of the nandi drum, players of the paṇava and other instruments, went forth from the city of mighty Virāṭa to meet the son of boundless valor.
Having dispatched the army and the maidens and courtesans, all well adorned, the highly wise king of Matsya, overjoyed, said: 'Fetch the dice, Sairandhrī; let gambling begin, Kaṅka.'
Seeing him speak thus, the Pāṇḍava replied: 'We have heard it said that a gambler elated with joy should not gamble.'
'I am not willing to gamble with you today when you are filled with joy; but I wish to do what is pleasing to you — let it proceed if you think it right.'
Virāṭa said: 'Women, cattle, gold, and whatever other wealth there may be — nothing of mine is to be withheld by you; you may gamble without restraint.'
Kaṅka said: 'What use is gambling to you, O lord of kings, O granter of honor? Gambling has many faults; therefore one should avoid it.'
'Have you heard of, or perhaps seen, the Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira? He, his great and flourishing kingdom, and his brothers equal to the thirty gods —'
'— all were lost in gambling. Therefore I do not favor gambling. Or if you think otherwise, O king, let us gamble if it pleases you.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the game of dice was in progress, Matsya said to the Pāṇḍava: 'See — such Kurus as these have been defeated in battle by my son.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Dharmaputra Yudhiṣṭhira said to the king of Matsya: 'He whose charioteer is Bṛhannaḍā — how could he not be victorious?'
At these words king Matsya grew angry and said to the Pāṇḍava: 'You equate a eunuch with my son and praise him — you wretch of a brahmin!'
'You do not know what should and should not be said; surely you hold me in contempt. Why would he not conquer them all — Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the rest?'
'Out of friendship I forgive this offence of yours, brahmin — but such a thing must not be spoken again by you, if you wish to live.'
Yudhiṣṭhira said: 'Where Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Drauṇi, Karṇa the son of Vikartana, Kṛpa, Duryodhana, and other great warriors stand together, O king —'
'— even Indra of a hundred sacrifices, surrounded by the hosts of Maruts, could scarcely face them in array. Who else but Bṛhannaḍā could oppose them when united?'
Virāṭa said: 'You have been restrained many times, yet you do not check your tongue. If there were no one to restrain, no one would observe dharma.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king, inflamed with rage, struck Yudhiṣṭhira hard on the face with a dice, chiding him in anger: 'Not so!'
Struck with great force, blood flowed from his nose; before it could reach the ground, the son of Pṛthā caught it in his cupped hands.
The righteous-souled one glanced at Draupadī standing nearby; she, who always followed her husband's thoughts, understood his intention.
The blameless one filled a golden bronze vessel and received in it the blood that had flowed from the Pāṇḍava, letting not a drop fall.
Meanwhile Uttara, showered with sweet fragrant garlands and flowers of many kinds, came joyfully at his ease into the city.
Honoured by the citizens, by women, and by country folk, he reached the gate of the palace and presented himself before his father.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then a door-keeper entered and reported to Virāṭa: 'Your son Uttara stands at the gate, accompanied by Bṛhannaḍā.'
Then the delighted king of Matsya said to his chamberlain: 'Let both of them be brought in at once — I am eager to see them.'
But the Kuru king — Yudhiṣṭhira — whispered softly to the chamberlain: 'Let Uttara enter alone; Bṛhannaḍā is not to be admitted.'
'For this mighty-armed one has taken this firm vow: whoever makes a wound on his body or causes blood to appear — except on the field of battle — shall not live, without doubt.'
'Seeing me with blood on my face, he would not endure it in his fierce anger — he would slay Virāṭa here along with his ministers, troops, and vehicles.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king's eldest son, Pṛthivīṃjaya, entered; having saluted his father's feet, he noticed Dharmarāja.
He saw him seated apart on the ground, spattered with blood, his mind deeply concentrated, innocent of any offence, attended by the Sairandhrī.
Then Uttara hastily questioned his father: 'By whom has this man been struck, O king? Who has committed this evil deed?'
Virāṭa said: 'This crooked one was struck by me, and he deserved even more than that — one who praises a eunuch when a hero like you is being praised.'
Uttara said: 'You have done what should not be done, O king — appease him at once. Let the terrible poison of a brahmin's curse not burn you up, roots and all.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing his son's words, Virāṭa, that enlarger of his kingdom, sought forgiveness from the son of Kuntī — as one would seek to placate a fire covered with ashes.
The Pāṇḍava replied to the king who was seeking forgiveness: 'I have long since forgiven it, O king; there is no anger in me.'
'For if this blood from my nose had fallen on the ground, you, great king, together with your whole kingdom, would surely have been destroyed — there is no doubt.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'I do not blame you, O king. But one who strikes an innocent man will quickly meet a terrible fate, great king.'
Once the blood had been dealt with, Bṛhannaḍā entered, saluted Virāṭa, and attended upon Kaṅka as well.
Having reconciled with the Kauravya, Matsya then praised Uttara — who had come back from battle — within the hearing of Savyasācin.
'Through you I have an heir, O joy and glory of the Kaikeyīs. A son equal to you has not existed before me nor shall exist hereafter.'
'He who strides a thousand paces and never errs — how was your encounter with that Karṇa, my child?'
'He who has no equal in all the world of men, who is as unshakeable as the ocean and as unbearable as the fire of destruction — how was your encounter with that Bhīṣma, my child?'
'He who is the preceptor of the Vṛṣṇi heroes and of the Pāṇḍavas, the teacher of all the kṣatriyas, the foremost of all who bear weapons — how was your encounter with that Droṇa, my child?'
'The son of the preceptor who is the hero famed above all bearers of weapons, known as Aśvatthāmā — how was your encounter with him?'
'He at whose sight in battle men quail like merchants who have lost their wealth — how was your encounter with that Kṛpa, my child?'
'The royal prince who could pierce a mountain with his mighty arrows — how was your encounter with that Duryodhana, my child?'
Uttara said: 'It was not I who won back the cattle, nor I who defeated the enemy. All that was accomplished by a certain son of a god.'
'For when I was frightened and fleeing, that son of a god stopped me; the young man, resembling Indra the thunderbolt-holder, stood in the rear of the chariot.'
'By him were the cattle won back; by him were those Kurus defeated. That deed belongs to that hero — it was not done by me, father.'
'That mighty one turned back with his arrows Śāradvatī's son Kṛpa, Droṇa, Droṇa's son, the son of a sūta, and Bhīṣma.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'And in battle he rebuked Duryodhana, the mighty prince, who was broken like a bull-elephant driven from the herd, trembling with fear.'
'"I see no refuge for you in Hāstinapura; strive with all effort to save your life, son of the Kurus."'
'"You will not escape by fleeing, O king; set your mind on battle — conquer and you shall enjoy the earth, or fall and you shall attain heaven."'
'Then that tiger among men turned back, releasing arrows like thunderbolts, the king surrounded by his ministers, panting in his chariot like an elephant.'
'There my hair stood on end and my thighs became rigid, O worthy one, as he shattered that army — dark as a mass of thunder-clouds — with his arrows.'
'Repelling the force of chariots, that lion-built youth laughed at those Kurus, O king, and the powerful one stripped them of their garments.'
'By that single hero, six warriors in their chariots were surrounded — like deer grazing in the forest surrounded by a maddened tiger.'
Virāṭa said: 'Where is that mighty-armed hero, the son of a god, of great renown, who won back my wealth seized by the Kurus in battle?'
'I wish to see and honour that mighty one by whose — that divine son's — power both you and my cattle were protected.'
Uttara said: 'That glorious son of a god has vanished from sight, father; but I think he will reappear tomorrow or the day after.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Even as this account was being given, Virāṭa did not recognise the Pāṇḍava — Pārtha Arjuna — who was dwelling there concealed by his guise.
Then Pārtha, having obtained the permission of the great-souled Virāṭa, himself gave those garments to Virāṭa's daughter.
And Uttarā, the spirited princess, accepted those garments — precious and of many kinds and delicate — and was pleased.
Then the son of Kuntī privately counselled with Uttara about everything that needed to be done — the entire course of action — regarding king Yudhiṣṭhira.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And so the bull among men, bull among Bhāratas, duly arranged all of that, joyful, together with the son of Matsya.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: On the third day thereafter, the five Pāṇḍava brothers, bathed, clad in white garments, having fulfilled the vow that was theirs to keep —
— with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head, adorned with all their ornaments, like great bull-elephants in full array, those great warriors shining resplendent —
— entered the assembly hall of Virāṭa and there sat down upon the seats of rulers — all of them blazing like fire, like sacred fires upon their hearths.
While they were seated there, Virāṭa, the lord of the earth, came to the assembly hall to attend to all the affairs of state.
Seeing the glorious Pāṇḍavas blazing like fires, Matsya said to Kaṅka — who sat there in godlike bearing, attended by them like the lord of the thirty gods attended by the Marut hosts:
'You are said to be merely a dice-player whom I made a floor-scrubber of the assembly; why then do you sit adorned upon a royal seat?'
Hearing that mocking remark of Virāṭa, Arjuna, smiling, spoke these words, O king:
'Even Indra's seat, O king, is deserved by this man — devoted to brahmins, learned, generous, practised in sacrifice, firm in his vows.'
'This is the bull of the Kurus, Kuntī's son Yudhiṣṭhira; his fame stands in the world like the radiance of the risen sun.'
'The rays of his glory course through all directions, just as the rays of the sun's radiance course when it has risen.'
'Ten thousand swift elephants followed behind him, O king, for as long as he dwelt among the Kurus.'
'Thirty thousand chariots wreathed in gold, furnished with excellent horses, always followed behind him.'
'Eight hundred bards, wearing finely polished jewelled earrings, used to sing his praises together with the Māgadha singers, as sages praise Indra.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'The Kurus waited upon him constantly as upon a master; all kings as well, O king, attended him as the immortals attend the lord of wealth.'
'This one exacted tribute from all the rulers of the earth at that time — even those who yielded of their own will and those who did not — as a lord exacts tribute from vaiśyas, great king.'
'Eighty-eight thousand great-souled snātakas lived by the patronage of this king, who was steadfast in his vows of good conduct.'
'This one protected the aged, the helpless, the maimed, and the lame among men as if they were his own children, and governed his subjects by dharma, O overlord.'
'This king is disciplined in dharma, in self-restraint, and even in anger; of great grace, devoted to brahmins, and ever truthful.'
'Suyodhana with his followers, along with Karṇa and the son of Subala — that mighty one — is scorched by his brilliance and majesty.'
'His virtues cannot be fully enumerated, O lord of men; this Pāṇḍava is ever devoted to dharma and ever free from cruelty.'
'Endowed with such qualities, this great king, this Pāṇḍava, this bull among kings, this lord of the earth — how is he unworthy of a royal seat?'
Virāṭa said: 'If this is king Yudhiṣṭhira, the Kauravya, son of Kuntī — then which of these is his brother Arjuna, and which is the mighty Bhīma?'
'Where is Nakula, where Sahadeva, where the illustrious Draupadī? When the Pārthas were defeated at dice, they were nowhere to be found.'
Arjuna said: 'He who served as your cook and was called Ballava, O lord of men — that is Bhīma, the mighty-armed one, of terrible speed and valour.'
This one, overcome by rage, slew [them] on the Gandhamādana mountain and brought back divine saugandhika flowers for Kṛṣṇā's sake.
This one is indeed the slayer of the wicked Kīcakas — and it was he who killed tigers, bears, and boars in your women's quarter.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who was your horse-keeper is this Nakula, the scorcher of foes; and Sahadeva was the cattle-counter — both sons of Mādrī, both great warriors on the chariot.
Adorned in ornaments of beauty, handsome, renowned, capable of handling thousands of diverse chariots — these two are bulls among men.
This lotus-petal-eyed one, slender-waisted, lovely-smiling — she is Draupadī the sairandhrī, O king, on whose account the Kīcakas were slain.
I am Arjuna, O great king — I have now clearly come to your ears. I am Pārtha, younger than Bhīma and elder than the two Yamas' sons.
We have lived happily, O great king, in your abode, dwelling unrecognized like creatures dwelling in a womb.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Arjuna had thus described those five Pāṇḍava heroes, the son of Virāṭa then recounted Arjuna's own feats of valor.
This one moved among the enemy's chariot-hosts like a lion among deer, striking down their foremost warriors one after another.
By him a great elephant was pierced and slain with a single arrow; Hiraṇyakakṣya fell to the ground in battle, felled by his tusks.
By him the cattle were recovered and the Kurus were defeated in battle; the blast of his conch made my ears go deaf.
Hearing those words of his, the powerful king of the Matsyas, his heart inclined toward Yudhiṣṭhira, replied to Uttara thus:
I think it is the proper time to propitiate the Pāṇḍava, and I am willing to give Uttarā to Pārtha — if that is agreeable to you.
Uttara said: They are worthy of honor, of worship, of reverence — and it is my view that the time is right. Let the greatly fortunate Pāṇḍavas, who deserve all worship, be duly honored.
Virāṭa said: I too fell into the enemy's power in battle and was rescued by Bhīmasena; and the cattle were likewise recovered.
Whatever victory was ours in battle came through the might of their arms; therefore let all of us together with our ministers propitiate Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī — good fortune to you — along with his brothers, that bull among the Pāṇḍavas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever was said to that lord of men by us who did not recognize him, this virtuous-souled Pāṇḍava ought to forgive it all.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Virāṭa, supremely pleased, met with the king and made a pact with him, and the great-souled one surrendered to him his entire kingdom along with its treasury, army, and city.
Then the powerful king of the Matsyas, placing Dhanaṃjaya at the fore, addressed all the Pāṇḍavas saying, 'Fortune! Fortune!'
Smelling their heads and embracing them again and again — Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, and the two sons of Mādrī —
Virāṭa, lord of the army, could not be sated with the sight of them; rejoicing greatly, he then spoke to king Yudhiṣṭhira:
'By good fortune you have all returned safe from the forest! By good fortune the hardship imposed by those wicked ones — the incognito year — has been completed!'
'Let the sons of Kuntī accept without hesitation this kingdom of ours and whatever other wealth there may be — let them take it all.'
'Let the left-handed Dhanaṃjaya accept Uttarā; this best of men is the fitting husband for her.'
Thus addressed, the king of dharma glanced at Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya; and Arjuna, so regarded by his brother, spoke these words to Matsya:
'I accept your daughter as a daughter-in-law, O king; the alliance between us two is fitting — the best of the Matsyas and the best of the Bhāratas.'
Virāṭa said: Why, O foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, do you not wish to take my daughter, offered by me, as your own wife here?
Arjuna said: I lived in the inner apartments always beholding your daughter, in private and in public, while she trusted me as a father.
I was dear and highly regarded as a dancing-master skilled in song; your daughter always regarded me as a teacher.
O king, O lord, I dwelt a year together with her, a young woman of age; great suspicion would arise — rightly — in you and in the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore I ask this of you regarding your daughter, O lord of the earth: I am pure, my senses are conquered, self-restrained; her purity has been maintained by me.
Whether as daughter-in-law or as daughter, whether for a son or for myself — I see no doubt in this; by that arrangement her purity shall be established.
I am afraid of impure attachment, O scorcher of foes, and of improper conduct; therefore, O king, I accept your daughter Uttarā as a daughter-in-law.
The nephew of Vāsudeva, like a divine child incarnate, beloved of the discus-wielder — though still a boy he is already versed in the science of weapons —
Abhimanyu of the great arms, my son, O lord of the people — he is indeed the fitting son-in-law for you and the proper husband for your daughter.
Virāṭa said: This befits you, O best of the Kurus, O Dhanaṃjaya son of Kuntī — you who are thus ever steadfast in dharma and whose wisdom has arisen, O Pāṇḍava.
Whatever you think should be done, O Pārtha, let it be done forthwith; all my desires are fulfilled, since Arjuna is my kinsman by marriage.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As the king of kings spoke thus, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Kuntī then gave his approval to the union between the Matsya and the Pārtha at the appointed time.
Then, O Bhārata, the son of Kuntī and Virāṭa, lord of the earth, sent messages to all their friends and to Vāsudeva.
Then, when the thirteenth year had passed, the five Pāṇḍavas assembled altogether at Upaplavya, in Virāṭa's territory.
While residing there, Bībhatsu the Pāṇḍava brought Janārdana and the Dāśārhas from the Ānartas, and Abhimanyu as well.
The king of Kāśī and Śaibya, both devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira, came along with two akṣauhiṇī armies, O lord of the earth.
The splendid and mighty Yajñasena came with one akṣauhiṇī; the heroic sons of Draupadī came, and the unvanquished Śikhaṇḍī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The irresistible Dhṛṣṭadyumna, foremost of all who bear weapons, came; and all the commanders of the combined akṣauhiṇī forces — sacrificers who give lavish dakṣiṇā, all skilled in weapons and arms, all heroes ready to lay down their lives.
Seeing them arrived, Matsya, best of those who uphold dharma, was filled with joy at having given his daughter to Abhimanyu.
Then, as kings arrived from here and there, Vāsudeva wearing the forest-garland came there, and Halāyudha, and Kṛtavarmā the son of Hārdika, and Yuyudhāna Sātyaki.
Anādhṛṣṭi and Akrūra, Sāmba and Niśaṭha likewise — those scorchers of foes came bringing Abhimanyu along with his mother.
Indrasena and the others too came together in those well-equipped chariots — all who had dwelt apart for the full year.
Ten thousand elephants, ten million horses, a full arbuda of chariots, and a nikh arva of infantry —
Many Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas and Bhojas of supreme vigor followed Vāsudeva, the tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, of great splendor.
Kṛṣṇa gave bridal gifts to the great-souled Pāṇḍavas — women, jewels, and garments separately in great abundance; then the wedding between the Matsya princess and the Pārtha proceeded according to proper rite.
Then conches, kettle-drums, trumpets, and large drums resounded in the dwelling of Matsya as his alliance with the Pārthas was being celebrated.
They slaughtered various deer and hundreds of sacrificially pure animals; copious drinks of surā and maireya liquor were brought forth.
Singers skilled in narrative, actors, and bards approached praising them; sūtas together with māgadhas attended upon them with eulogies.
Placing Sudeṣṇā at their head, the finest women of the Matsyas came — beautiful in every limb, their gem-earrings gleaming bright.
Those women, endowed with fine complexion, beautiful, well-adorned — yet Kṛṣṇā surpassed them all in beauty, fame, and glory.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Surrounding the adorned princess Uttarā — like the daughter of great Indra — they placed her at the fore and attended upon her.
The son of Kuntī, Dhanaṃjaya, then accepted her — the flawless-limbed daughter of Virāṭa — on behalf of his son, Saubhadra.
Standing there in the form of great Indra, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Kuntī formally received her as a daughter-in-law.
And having received her, placing Janārdana at the fore, Pārtha caused the wedding of the great-souled Saubhadra to be performed.
To him he gave seven thousand swift-as-wind horses and two hundred foremost elephants and much wealth besides.
When the wedding was accomplished, then Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma gave to the brahmins the wealth that Acyuta had brought.
Thousands of cows, jewels, garments of every kind, choice ornaments, vehicles, and couches —
That city of the Matsya king, resembling a great festival, thronged with happy and well-fed people, shone brilliantly, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having performed the marriage, the Kuru heroes — their own side gladdened on account of Abhimanyu — rested for four dawns and then, refreshed, proceeded to the hall of Virāṭa.
That hall of the lord of the Matsyas was splendid — adorned with the finest gems and precious stones, furnished with seats, garlanded, and fragrant. Into it entered those foremost of noble kings.
Then the two foremost lords of men, Virāṭa and Drupada, took their seats in front; and the elder, held in honour among the lords of earth, the Grandsire, took his seat alongside Rāma and Janārdana.
Near the king of the Pāñcālas sat the hero of the Śini clan together with the son of Rohiṇī; and very close to the king of the Matsyas sat Janārdana himself and Yudhiṣṭhira.
All the sons of king Drupada, Bhīma and Arjuna, the two sons of Mādravatī, and Pradyumna and Sāmba — both heroes in battle — and the son of Virāṭa together with Abhimanyu.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the young princes, the sons of Draupadī — all heroes equal to their fathers in valour, form, and strength — took their seats upon the excellent seats embellished with gold.
As those great car-warriors sat there, resplendent in their garments and ornaments, that royal and prosperous hall shone like the sky adorned with bright planets.
Then those foremost of men, having engaged in various assembled conversations, stood silent for a moment in thought, those kings gazing upon Kṛṣṇa.
And having reached the end of conversation, stirred together by the Mādhava for the sake of the Pāṇḍava cause, those lion-like kings assembled and heard words of great import and great consequence.
Kṛṣṇa said: It is known to all of you how Yudhiṣṭhira was defeated at dice by the son of Subala through trickery, and how his kingdom was taken away, and how the compact was made for a further period of exile.
Though capable of conquering the earth by force, and steadfast in truth, those foremost of the Bhāratas, the sons of Pāṇḍu, fulfilled that severe vow — thirteen years in exile.
And this thirteenth year, most difficult to endure — spent unrecognized in your midst, enduring unbearable hardships — how it was passed is known to all of you.
Things being so, reflect on what would be beneficial to the son of Dharma as king, and to Duryodhana as well — what is righteous, proper, and honour-winning for the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas.
Even the sovereignty of the gods, if tainted by unrighteousness, the king of righteousness would not desire; but lordship over the earth, if coupled with righteousness and right purpose, he would wish to possess even in the smallest village.
The ancestral kingdom is known to all kings — how it was wrested away by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through deceitful means; and yet through all this, great and unbearable hardship has been endured.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nor has Pārtha been defeated in battle by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through their own prowess; and yet the king, together with his friends, wishes for nothing but their well-being.
What the sons of Pāṇḍu themselves won by conquest, subjugating the lords of the earth and bringing it all together — that is what these foremost of men, the sons of Kuntī and the sons of Mādravatī, now seek.
But these heroes, though foe-conquering, were set upon by those wicked and violent men using various stratagems, seeking to kill them and seize the kingdom — all of which is fully known to you.
Considering the deep greed of those men, and the righteous nature of Yudhiṣṭhira, and also the kinship between them — deliberate, both together and separately, and form your judgment.
These men, ever devoted to truth, have fulfilled the compact as agreed; yet if treated otherwise by those others, they could destroy the assembled sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Hearing of the wrong done by them, the friends of the king would surround them; they would press upon those men with battle; and being attacked by them in war, they would slay them in return.
Yet lest the opinion among you be that these men are insufficient for victory over them — let all together, united with their friends, strive for the destruction of those opponents.
The intention of Duryodhana is not truly known — what will he do? And when the intent of the other side is unknown, what course is most to be undertaken in your judgment?
Therefore let there go from here a man of righteous character, pure, well-born, and vigilant — a capable envoy to seek peace with them and the granting of half the kingdom to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Hearing the words of Janārdana — righteous, purposeful, sweet, and impartial — his elder brother then took up the reply, honouring those words highly, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Baladeva said: You have heard the words of the elder brother of Gada — how they are righteous and purposeful, and beneficial alike to Ajātaśatru and equally to king Duryodhana.
For the heroes, the sons of Kuntī, strive after giving up half the kingdom on his account; and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, by granting half, would rejoice greatly in happiness together with us.
For having obtained the kingdom, those foremost of men — if the other side conducts themselves rightly — would assuredly find peace and enter into happiness; and their peace is the welfare of the subjects.
To learn also the mind of Duryodhana, and to speak the words of Yudhiṣṭhira — it would please me if someone were to go there for the sake of peace between the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas.
He should address Bhīṣma, that hero of the Kurus, and the great-souled son of Vicitravīrya, and Droṇa with his son, and Vidura and Kṛpa, and the king of Gāndhāra together with the charioteer's son.
And all the other sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who are foremost in strength and foremost in scriptural learning, who are established in their own respective duties — heroes among men, mature in learning and age.
When all these are assembled together, and the elders of the city are gathered, let the envoy speak words accompanied with humble salutation, such as would serve the interest of the son of Kuntī.
And in all circumstances it was not through deceit on their part but by force that Yudhiṣṭhira's interest was seized — the kingdom was taken by trickery when Yudhiṣṭhira was captivated by the pleasure of the game.
Though restrained by all the Kuru heroes and friends, this descendant of Ajamīḍha, being himself ignorant of the game, challenged the skilled dice-player son of the Gāndhāra king to play.
There were thousands of other skilled dice-players whom Yudhiṣṭhira could have endured and beaten; but setting them aside, he challenged Śakuni alone, and by him was defeated at dice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He played in return, with the dice always turning away from him in ill luck, and being overcome by force in his eagerness — in that matter, no fault belongs to Śakuni.
Therefore let the envoy speak humbly and with much conciliation to the son of Vicitravīrya; for thus is the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra capable of being induced by that man to act in his own proper interest.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Even as the hero of the Madhu clan spoke thus, the hero of the Śini clan suddenly sprang up, and censuring that speech, took up these words with indignation.
Sātyaki said: As a man's inner self is, so he speaks. As your inner self is shaped, so shaped are your words.
Surely there are brave men and there are cowardly men as well; both these firm tendencies are seen to exist among men.
In one and the same family are born both a eunuch and a great chariot-warrior, just as a tree may have branches bearing fruit and branches without fruit.
I do not blame you for speaking such words, O bearer of the plough-banner; but those who listen to your words — them I blame, O Mādhava.
How can one who speaks even slightly of the faults of the king of righteousness dare to utter such words in the midst of this assembly without fear?
Skilled dice-players challenged that great soul, who was not knowledgeable in dice and whose trust was exploited — where is the righteousness in such a victory over him?
If they had come to the home of the son of Kuntī playing with his brothers and conquered him there — that would have been a victory by dharma for them.
But having summoned the king who is ever devoted to the Kṣatriya duty and defeated him by trickery — what good fortune can there be for them beyond that?
How should he bow down who, having made the supreme wager, has now been freed from forest exile and has attained the ancestral station?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Even if Yudhiṣṭhira were to covet the wealth of others, even then he would not deserve to beg from his enemies to this extreme degree.
And how can those who are righteous and not desirous of seizing the kingdom say that the sons of Kuntī, having completed their exile, are recognized and known?
Though conciliated by Bhīṣma and the great-souled Droṇa, they do not resolve to give the sons of Pāṇḍu their ancestral property.
But I, conciliating them with sharp arrows, shall by force in battle make them fall at the feet of that great-souled son of Kuntī.
If they do not resolve to bow down before the wise one, they shall go along with their ministers to the abode of Yama.
For they are not capable of withstanding the fury of the wrathful and battle-eager Yuyudhāna, just as mountains cannot withstand the velocity of the thunderbolt.
Who indeed can endure in battle the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, or the wielder of the discus weapon? And who can endure me, and who can endure Bhīma, who is difficult to approach?
And the twin brothers, wielders of firm bows, of great splendour, comparable to the god of death — what man wishing to live would approach them, or Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata?
These five Pāṇḍavas, and the five sons of Draupadī who enhance her glory, equal in measure to the sons of Pāṇḍu, equal in valour, drunk with battle-ardour —
— and the great archer Saubhadra, difficult to bear even for the immortals, and Gada, Pradyumna, and Sāmba, comparable to the thunderbolt of Death, unassailable —
— we, having slain in battle the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with Śakuni and Karṇa, shall consecrate the Pāṇḍava king.
There is no unrighteousness whatsoever in slaying enemies who are aggressors; it is unrighteous and dishonourable to beg from enemies.
Fulfil diligently whatever desire lies in his heart; let the Pāṇḍava obtain the kingdom that was surrendered by Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Today let Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Pāṇḍu obtain the kingdom, or let all of them be slain in battle and sleep upon the surface of the earth.
Drupada said: So it shall be, O mighty-armed one — there is no doubt. For Duryodhana will not give up the kingdom through gentle persuasion.
And Dhṛtarāṣṭra, fond of his son, will follow him; and Bhīṣma and Droṇa out of weakness; and the son of Rādhā and the son of Subala out of folly.
Baladeva's speech, in my judgment, is not appropriate; for this is indeed what should be done first by a man who desires sound policy.
Gentle words, however, should by no means be spoken to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; for in my view that evil-minded one is not to be won over by mildness.
One might show gentleness to a donkey and employ sharpness toward cattle; but whoever would speak mild words to Duryodhana of wicked mind —
— the wicked man would think the gentle speech springs from weakness; the fool would consider the matter won when met with mildness.
This therefore we shall do, and let effort be made here: let us send word to our allies and let them mobilise forces for us.
To Śalya, and to Dhṛṣṭaketu, and to Jayatsena, and to all the Kekayas — let swift messengers go.
For Duryodhana will surely send word everywhere; and those who have been previously approached tend to side with the one who solicited them first.
Therefore make haste to solicit the lords of men before he does; it is my firm conviction that a great task is to be accomplished.
Let word be sent swiftly to Śalya and the kings who follow him, and to king Bhagadatta who dwells by the eastern sea.
To Amitojas and to the fierce Ugra, and to Hārdikya and Āhuka, and to the far-sighted Malla and to Rocamāna, O lord.
Let Bṛhanta and king Senābindu be brought, and Papajit and Prativindhya, and Chitravarma and Suvastuka.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bāhlika and Munjakesa, and the lord of the Cedis, and Suparshva and Subāhu, and Pourava the great chariot-warrior.
The kings of the Śakas, the Pahlavas, and the Daradas; the Kāmbojas, the Rishikas, and those of the western riverine regions.
And Jayatsena and the king of Kāśi, and likewise the kings of the five rivers, and the irresistible son of Krātha, and the mountain kings.
And Jānakī and Suśarmā and Maṇimān and Pautimatsyaka, and the lord of the Pamsurashra, and the valiant Dhṛṣṭaketu.
And Audra and Daṇḍadhāra, and the valiant Brhatsena, and Aparajita and the Niṣāda king, and Śreṇimān and Vasuman.
And Bṛhadbala and Mahaujas, and Bahu and Parapuramjaya, and king Samudrasena together with his valiant son.
Adāri and Nadīja and the king Karṇaveṣṭa, and Samartha and Suvīra and Mārjāra and likewise Kanyaka —
and Mahāvīra and Kadrū, and Nikara, Tumula, Krātha, and Nīla and Vīradharman and the valiant Bhūmipāla —
Durjaya and Dantavaktra and Rukmī and Janamejaya, Āṣāḍha and Vāyuvega and the king Pūrvapālī —
Bhūritejā and Devaka and the son of Ekalavya, the kings of Kārūṣa and the valiant Kṣemadhūrti —
Udbhava and Kṣemaka and king Vāṭadhāna, and Śrutāyu and Dṛḍhāyu and the valiant son of Śalva —
and Kumāra, lord of the Kaliṅgas, who is maddened in battle — let swift messengers be sent to all of these; this indeed is my desire.
And let my own priest, this brahmin, be swiftly sent, O king, to Dhṛtarāṣṭra; let the message be entrusted to him.
Let him know how Duryodhana is to be addressed, and how the son of Śaṃtanu the king, and how Dhṛtarāṣṭra is to be addressed, and Droṇa the foremost of the wise.
Vāsudeva said: This counsel is fitting, O foremost bearer of the Somakas' yoke — it will bring about the success of the mighty Pāṇḍava king.
And this is the proper first course of action for us who seek the right policy; for a man who acts otherwise in such matters would be utterly foolish.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yet our kinship and bond is equal with both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, who both conduct themselves as they please.
We were all brought here for the sake of the wedding, even as you were, O king; when the marriage is done, we shall return home joyfully.
You are the eldest among kings in age and in learning; we are all here as your disciples — of this there is no doubt.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra too holds you in constant high regard; and you are the friend of both the preceptors, of Droṇa and of Kṛpa.
Therefore let you now send forth the word that will serve the Pāṇḍavas' cause; all of us are certain that whatever you send forth, so it shall be.
If the bull of the Kurus should make peace through righteous means, then the great destruction of Kurus and Pāṇḍavas as brothers will not come to pass.
But if the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, filled with pride and delusion, should refuse, then after sending to the others, you may summon us in turn.
Then that dull-witted Duryodhana, foolish together with his ministers and kinsmen, will meet his end when the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow is enraged.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Virāṭa, lord of the earth, having duly honoured the Vārṣṇeya, sent him homeward together with his retinue and kinsmen.
When Kṛṣṇa had departed for Dvārakā, Yudhiṣṭhira and his brothers, along with king Virāṭa lord of the earth, made all preparations for war.
Then Virāṭa together with his kinsmen, and king Drupada lord of the earth, sent messengers to all the rulers of the land.
At the word of the lion-like Kurus and of the Matsyas and Pāñcālas, those mighty lords of the earth came together, filled with joy.
Hearing of the gathering of the sons of Pāṇḍu, a great host assembled; and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra likewise assembled kings to his side.
O king, the entire earth became filled with turmoil on account of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, as the lords of the earth set out on their march.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The armies of those heroes came from every direction, shaking, as it were, this very earth, goddess adorned with mountains and forests.
Then the king of Pāñcāla, with Yudhiṣṭhira's approval, sent his own priest — venerable in wisdom and years — to the Kurus.
Drupada said: Among living beings, those that breathe are the highest; among those that breathe, the highest are those who live by intellect; among the intelligent, men are highest; and among men, the twice-born are supreme.
Among the twice-born, those learned in the Vedas are better; and among Vedic scholars, those of perfected understanding are best. You, good sir, are the foremost among those of perfected understanding — so it is my judgment.
You are distinguished by lineage, by age, and by sacred learning; and in wisdom you are not inferior to Śukra and Aṅgiras themselves.
You also know fully how the Kaurava has conducted himself, and how the Pāṇḍava, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Kuntī, has conducted himself.
With Dhṛtarāṣṭra's knowledge the Pāṇḍavas were deceived by their enemies; and even though entreated by Vidura, he only follows his son.
For Śakuni, himself expert at dice, deliberately challenged the son of Kuntī — who was ignorant of dice but stood firm in the warrior's code, a man of purity.
Having cheated Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma in that manner, they will never of their own will restore the kingdom under any circumstances.
But you, speaking righteous words to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, will certainly turn the minds of his warriors.
And Vidura will further your message and will sow discord among Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa.
And when the counsellors are divided and the warriors turned away, it will be hard work for them to reunite those forces.
In that interval the sons of Pṛthā, with undivided attention and ease, will accomplish their military tasks and the gathering of resources.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And while their own ranks are divided and you delay, they will not be able to carry out their military preparations with the same effect — of this there is no doubt.
This is the chief purpose to be gained here; and through the combined effect, Dhṛtarāṣṭra may even act on your righteous counsel.
Therefore let you, devoted to righteousness, deal righteously with those compassionate ones, recounting to them the sufferings of the Pāṇḍavas.
Speaking of the family duty as observed by the ancestors to those elders, you will divide their minds — of this I have no doubt.
And you have no reason to fear them: you are a brahmin, learned in the Vedas, skilled in the office of envoy, and an elder besides.
Therefore let you depart swiftly to the Kauravas under the auspicious lunar asterism Puṣya and in a victorious moment, for the accomplishment of the Kauteya's purpose.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus instructed by the great-souled Drupada, the priest, a man of excellent conduct, set out for the city called the Abode of the Serpent.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Kṛṣṇa the Mādhava had departed for Dvāravatī along with Baladeva and all the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas and hundreds of Bhojas as well —
the king, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, had his spies and secret agents bring him full intelligence of all that the Pāṇḍavas were doing.
Having heard that the Mādhava had departed with fine horses matchless as the wind, Duryodhana went with a not-too-large force to the city of Dvārakā.
On that very same day, Dhanaṃjaya the son of Kuntī, the delight of the Pāṇḍus, swiftly went to the beautiful city of Ānarta.
Those two tiger-like men, both delights of the Kurus, went to Dvārakā and found Kṛṣṇa asleep; and they drew near as he lay resting.
Then, while Govinda lay sleeping, Suyodhana entered and sat down on a splendid seat at Kṛṣṇa's head.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the diademed one, that high-minded hero, entered after him and stood humbly at Kṛṣṇa's feet, hands joined in reverence.
When the Vārṣṇeya awoke, he saw the diademed Arjuna before him; having welcomed them both fittingly and honoured them as they deserved, the Slayer of Madhu asked the reason for their coming.
Then Duryodhana, speaking as if with a laugh, said to Kṛṣṇa: In this conflict, O noble one, it is fitting that you render assistance to me.
For your friendship with me and with Arjuna is equal, and likewise our kinship with you is equal on both sides, O Mādhava.
And I have come to you first this day, O Slayer of Madhu; the good honour the one who comes first, favouring those who arrive before others.
And you are today the most honoured among the righteous in the world, O Janārdana, always held in high esteem — uphold then the conduct of the good.
Kṛṣṇa said: That you came first, of this I have no doubt; but it was Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya whom I saw first upon waking, O king.
On account of your having come first, and likewise on account of his having been seen first, I shall render assistance to both of you, Suyodhana.
But tradition holds that the younger should be offered first choice; therefore it is Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya who deserves to be offered first selection.
A great host of ten crores of cowherds equal to me in bodily strength, known by the name of Nārāyaṇas — all of them battle-fighters —
let those warriors, formidable in battle, be the soldiers of one party; while on the other side stands I alone, not fighting in the battle, my weapons laid aside.
O Pārtha, whichever of these two alternatives seems more pleasing to your heart, choose that first; for by right you are to be offered the first choice.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, Dhanaṃjaya the son of Kuntī chose Keśava — the one who would not fight in the battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O Bhārata, obtaining a thousand thousands of warriors and knowing that Kṛṣṇa was thereby taken away from him, Duryodhana reached the highest joy.
Then king Duryodhana, taking all that army, went thereafter to Rauhiṇeya of tremendous might and fearsome strength.
He laid before him the full reason for his coming, and then the Śauri, the descendant of Śūra, replied to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with these words.
O tiger among men, all that I said formerly at the wedding ceremony of Virāṭa's daughter — all of it ought to be known to you.
Though the Hṛṣīkeśa was restrained and addressed on your behalf, O delight of the Kurus, by me saying again and again 'our kinship is equal,' O king —
yet Keśava did not accept those words when spoken; and I do not presume to stand apart from Kṛṣṇa even for a moment.
I shall not be the ally of the Pārthas, nor indeed of Duryodhana — this is my firm resolve, having weighed Vāsudeva's decision.
You are born in the Bhārata lineage, honoured by all kings; go, fight in accordance with the warrior's dharma, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Thus addressed, Duryodhana then embraced the wielder of the plough; and knowing that Kṛṣṇa had been secured away from the battle, he reckoned the victory already won.
The king, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, then approached Kṛtavarman, and Kṛtavarman gave him at that time a full akṣauhiṇī division of the army.
Escorted by that formidable combined army, the delight of the Kurus returned joyfully, gladdening the hearts of his friends.
When Duryodhana had gone, Kṛṣṇa then spoke to the diademed Arjuna: I who shall not fight in the battle — on what reasoning have you chosen me?
Arjuna said: You are capable of slaying all of them — of this there is no doubt; and I too am capable of slaying them alone, O highest of men.
But you are celebrated in the world, and that glory will go to you; and I too am a seeker of fame — therefore you have been chosen by me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And it has always been my heart's desire that you should act as my charioteer — that long-cherished wish, O noble one, it is fitting that you fulfil.
Vāsudeva said: This is fitting, O Pārtha, that you would vie with me in this way; I shall be your charioteer — let your desire be fulfilled.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus gladdened, Pārtha, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa and escorted by the foremost of the Dāśārhas, then returned to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the messengers, Śalya, surrounded by a great army, advanced toward the Pāṇḍavas, O king, together with his sons, those great warriors.
His encampment extended for about one and a half yojanas, for that bull among men commanded so large an army.
The warriors wore varied armor and bore varied banners and bows; all were adorned with varied ornaments and rode in varied chariots and vehicles.
Heroes clad in the dress and ornaments of their own countries, in hundreds of thousands, became the leaders of his army — those bulls among kshatriyas.
As if distressing all creatures and making the earth tremble, he slowly rested his army and marched toward where the Pāṇḍava was.
Then Duryodhana, hearing that the great warrior with his great army was approaching, ran out and honoured him in person, O Bhārata.
Duryodhana caused to be built for his honour rest-houses adorned with jewels and well decorated, in pleasant spots along the way.
Reaching those rest-houses, honoured by Duryodhana's ministers in each locality as befitted him — like a god — he came at last to another hall that shone like a divine abode.
There, surrounded by auspicious pleasures beyond human measure, he thought himself superior to all and held even Indra the destroyer of cities in contempt.
Delighted, that bull among kshatriyas then asked his attendants: 'Who are the men of Yudhiṣṭhira who built these halls? Let the builders be brought here; they deserve gifts from me, I think.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There Duryodhana, who had kept himself hidden, revealed himself to his maternal uncle. On seeing him, the king of Madra understood the effort he had made, and embracing him with affection, said: 'Excellent! Choose any boon you wish.'
Duryodhana said: Be true to your word, O auspicious one, and grant me this boon: you should become the commander-in-chief of all my armies.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Śalya replied 'Done!' and said, 'What else shall I do?' And the son of Gāndhārī replied again and again, 'It is done, it is done!'
Having thus taken leave of Śalya, he returned to his own city. Śalya went to the sons of Kuntī to inform them of this event.
Going to Upaplavya and entering the encampment, Śalya saw all the Pāṇḍavas assembled there.
Meeting with the sons of Pāṇḍu, the mighty-armed Śalya received water for his feet, the honour-gift, and the cow, all according to proper rite.
Then the king of Madra, that destroyer of foes, filled with the greatest affection, first exchanged words of welcome and embraced Yudhiṣṭhira.
Likewise he greeted the joyful Bhīma and Arjuna, and both of his sister's sons, the twins. Then, seated on a seat, Śalya spoke to the son of Pṛthā.
Are you well, O tiger among kings, O joy of the Kurus? By good fortune you are freed from your forest exile, O foremost among the victorious!
A very difficult thing has been accomplished, O king — dwelling in the uninhabited forest together with your brothers and with this Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī), O lord of kings.
The terrible year of incognito living was also endured with difficulty. Where indeed is happiness for one bereft of his kingdom? Only suffering, O Bhārata.
From this great sorrow caused by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, you shall attain happiness, O king, having slain your enemies, O scorcher of foes.
The truth of the world is known to you, O great king, O lord of men; therefore, my dear, nothing caused by greed is found in you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the king told him of his encounter with Duryodhana — all the hospitable service he had received and the granting of the boon, O Bhārata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Well done, O king! What you, O hero, promised by word to Duryodhana was done with a rejoicing heart. Yet one thing I wish to be done, may it go well with you, O lord of the earth.
You, O great king, are the equal of Vāsudeva in battle. When the single combat between Karṇa and Arjuna takes place, O foremost of kings, you should act as charioteer for Karṇa — there is no doubt about this.
In that situation Arjuna is to be protected, O king, if you wish what is dear to me. And you must also undermine the spirit of the son of the charioteer, bringing victory to our side. Though this is improper, you should do it, O uncle.
Śalya said: Hear me, O Pāṇḍava, may it go well with you! You speak of me as one who will crush the spirit of that wicked-souled son of the charioteer in battle.
I shall certainly be his charioteer in battle. For he always considers me the equal of Vāsudeva.
To him, when he desires to fight in battle, I shall certainly speak discouraging and harmful words, O tiger of the Kurus.
So that he will become robbed of his pride and robbed of his spirit, O Pāṇḍava, and easily slain — this I tell you truly.
I shall do this exactly as you have told me, my dear. And whatever else I am able to do, I shall do what is pleasing to you.
The suffering that was inflicted on you at the dice game together with Kṛṣṇā, and the harsh words spoken by the son of the charioteer —
The affliction from Jaṭāsura, and from Kīcaka — all that was obtained by Draupadī, O greatly resplendent one, just as Damayantī suffered misfortune —
All this suffering, O hero, shall bear fruit as happiness. You must not be angry about this, for fate is more powerful.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For great souls encounter sufferings, O Yudhiṣṭhira; even by the gods have sufferings been encountered, O lord of the earth.
It is heard, O king, that Indra, together with his wife, that great soul, the king of the gods, experienced great suffering, O Bhārata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How did Indra, together with his wife, that great soul, O king of kings, come to experience extreme and terrible suffering? I wish to know this.
Śalya said: Hear, O king, this ancient history of former times — how Indra together with his wife came to experience suffering, O Bhārata.
Tvaṣṭṛ was a lord of creatures (Prajāpati), the foremost of the gods, of great austerity. He created a son named Triśiras (Three-headed) out of enmity toward Indra.
He, Viśvarūpa of great brilliance, coveted the station of Indra, with his three terrible faces blazing like the sun, fire, and lightning.
With one mouth he studied the Vedas; with another he drank Sura (liquor); and with the third he gazed upon all the directions as if drinking them in.
This ascetic was gentle and self-controlled, devoted to duty and austerity; he performed great and severe austerities that were very hard to undertake, O subduer of foes.
Seeing the power of his asceticism and the might of one of immeasurable brilliance, Śakra fell into anxiety, thinking: 'May this one not become Indra.'
'How can he be made to attach himself to pleasures and not perform great austerity? As Triśiras grows, he might devour all three worlds.'
Thinking in many ways, that wise one, O bull of the Bhāratas, commanded the apsaras (celestial nymphs) to go and tempt the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
'So that Triśiras may be deeply attached to the pleasures of desire, quickly do this, go forth, seduce him — do not delay!'
'Adorned in amorous dress, O fair-hipped ones, equipped with enchanting ways, seduce him — may it go well with you! Dispel my fear.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'For I perceive that I am not at ease within myself, O lovely women. Quickly destroy this great and terrible fear, O you gentle ones.'
The apsaras said: We shall make such effort to seduce him, O Śakra, that you will no longer feel fear from him, O destroyer of Bala.
That treasure of austerity who sits as if burning everything with his eyes — to seduce him, O god, we go together; we shall strive to bring him under control and to remove your fear.
Śalya said: Permitted by Indra, they went to the presence of Triśiras. There those lovely women tried to seduce him with various moods, displaying their dancing and likewise the grace of their limbs.
They roamed about delightfully, yet they did not reach him — the great ascetic, having subdued his senses, was like a full ocean (unagitated).
Having made their utmost effort, they returned to Śakra; and all of them, with palms joined, spoke then to the king of the gods.
He is not capable of being moved from his steadfastness, O lord — he is very difficult to assail. Whatever is your purpose, O greatly fortunate one, let that be done next.
Śakra, that great-minded one, honoured the apsaras and dismissed them, and then began to contemplate a means of slaying that great soul.
That hero, the powerful king of the gods, deliberating in silence, the wise one with mind made up, decided on the slaying of Triśiras.
'I shall hurl my thunderbolt at him today; he will quickly cease to be. An enemy grown powerful must not be ignored, even by the strong, even if he be weak.'
Having determined this with the reasoning of scripture and having firmly made up his mind to slay, Śakra, enraged, then hurled the thunderbolt — resembling fire, of terrible form, inspiring fear — at Triśiras.
He fell, slain, struck hard by that thunderbolt, like the peak of a mountain shattered to the surface of the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But seeing him struck by the thunderbolt and lying motionless like a mountain, the lord of the gods found no comfort, being scorched by his brilliance; even slain, he blazed with radiance and appeared as if still alive.
There the lord of Śacī (Indra, Pākaśāsana) saw a carpenter at work nearby and hastily said to him: 'Quickly cut off his heads! Do my bidding.'
The carpenter said: This axe is very large — it will not succeed (in cutting through his great trunk). And I am not able to perform a deed censured by the good.
Indra said: Do not be afraid; quickly do my bidding. By my favour your tool shall become equal to the thunderbolt.
The carpenter said: Whom should I know you to be — you who would have me do this terrible deed today? I wish to hear this truly; tell me in truth.
Indra said: I am Indra, the king of the gods, O carpenter — let this be known to you. Do exactly as I have told you, O carpenter; do not deliberate.
The carpenter said: Are you not ashamed of this cruel deed, O Śakra? Having slain this son of a rishi, do you not fear the sin of brahmin-slaughter?
Indra said: Afterwards I shall undertake the very difficult dharmic practices for purification. This enemy was of great power; he has been struck down by my thunderbolt.
Even now I am troubled, O carpenter, and I fear him. Quickly cut off his heads; I shall bestow a favour upon you.
Men will give you the heads of animals as your share in sacrifices — this is your favour, O carpenter. Quickly do what pleases me.
Śalya said: Having heard that speech of the great Indra, the carpenter then cut off the heads of Triśiras with his axe.
When those heads were severed, from Triśiras as he lay came forth partridges, francolin-partridges (tittira), and sparrows (kalavinka) on all sides.
From the mouth with which he had studied the Vedas and also drunk Soma, kapiñjala birds quickly flew forth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From the mouth with which he had gazed upon all directions as if drinking them in, O king, tittira birds flew forth from his mouth, O Pāṇḍava.
And from the mouth of Triśiras that had drunk liquor, kalaviṅka (sparrow) birds flew forth, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then, with those heads cut off, Maghavan (Indra) was free from fever and went joyfully to the three heavens; the carpenter too went to his own home.
Tvaṣṭṛ the Prajāpati, hearing that his son had been slain by Śakra, with eyes reddened by rage, spoke these words:
'Because you have slain my son — ever performing austerity, patient, self-controlled, with conquered senses, blameless —
Therefore I shall create Vṛtra for the purpose of slaying Śakra! Let the worlds behold my might and the great power of my austerity — and let that wicked-minded, evil-hearted lord of the gods behold it too!'
Then that ascetic of very great renown, enraged, sipped water for purification and offered oblations into the fire. He created the terrible Vṛtra and said: 'O enemy of Indra, grow mighty through the power of my austerity!'
He grew, propping up the sky, blazing like the sun and fire together. Rising like the sun of doom, he said: 'What shall I do?' And when told 'Kill Indra,' he set off for the highest heaven.
Then a fierce and terrible battle broke out between Vṛtra and Vāsava — both enraged — that continued without pause, O best of the Kurus.
Then the mighty Vṛtra seized the lord of gods, the hundred-sacrificed Śakra; opening wide, Vṛtra swallowed him in rage.
When Śakra had been swallowed by Vṛtra, the gods were seized with panic; those great beings then emitted the yawning power that would destroy Vṛtra.
As Vṛtra yawned and his mouth gaped open, the slayer of Bala contracted his own limbs and slipped out. From that time onward, the yawn has dwelt among living creatures in the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All the gods rejoiced on seeing Śakra come out. Then the terrible battle between Vṛtra and Vāsava began again, both furious, lasting a long while, O bull of the Bhāratas.
When Vṛtra, empowered by the strength of Tvaṣṭṛ's austerities, grew mightier in battle, the wise Śakra then turned back.
When he retreated, the gods fell into deep despair. Coming together with Śakra, bewildered by the power of Tvaṣṭṛ, they all took counsel with the sages, O Bhārata.
Deliberating on what must be done, O king, and bewildered by fear, they all went in their minds to the imperishable great-souled Viṣṇu; they all gathered on the peak of Mandara, all desiring the slaying of Vṛtra.
Indra said: 'O gods, this entire imperishable world has been pervaded by Vṛtra. There is nothing comparable that could serve to oppose him.'
'Formerly I was capable; now I am not. How then can I secure your welfare? My view is that he is extremely difficult to overcome.'
'He is radiant, great-souled, and of boundless might in battle; he could devour all three worlds together with gods, asuras, and men.'
'Therefore, O dwellers of heaven, hear this resolution of mine: let us go to the abode of Viṣṇu, meet with that great-souled one, and through counsel with him discover the means of slaying that evil being.'
Śalya said: When Maghavat had spoken thus, the gods along with the hosts of sages went to Viṣṇu, the mighty god who is refuge for the refugeless.
Tormented by fear of Vṛtra, they all addressed Viṣṇu, lord of gods: 'O lord, you have traversed the three worlds with your three strides.
'O Viṣṇu, you brought back the nectar of immortality, the daityas were slain in battle, and having bound the great daitya Bali, Śakra was made lord of the gods.
'You are the lord of all worlds; by you all this is pervaded. You, O god, are the great god, revered by all the worlds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Be the refuge of the gods together with Indra, O best of immortals, O slayer of asuras. This entire world is pervaded by Vṛtra.'
Viṣṇu said: 'I must certainly do what is supremely beneficial for you. Therefore I shall declare the means by which that one shall cease to exist.'
'Go — sages and gandharvas — to where that bearer of the universal form dwells; employ conciliation toward him, and thereby you shall overcome him.'
'O gods, I shall be Śakra's refuge through my own power. Becoming invisible, I shall enter the thunderbolt, that foremost of weapons, which he shall hurl.'
'Go, O best of gods, together with the sages and gandharvas; without delay, make peace between Vṛtra and Śakra.'
Śalya said: Thus addressed by the god, the sages and the thirty gods went together, placing Śakra in the lead.
Drawing near, all of them, mighty in splendour, beheld that one blazing with radiance and scorching the ten directions —
— as though swallowing the three worlds, like the sun and the moon. The gods, along with Śakra, saw Vṛtra there.
Then the sages approached Vṛtra and spoke pleasing words: 'O unconquerable one, this entire world is pervaded by your splendour.
'Yet you have not been able to conquer Vāsava, who is of vast might; and a very great time has passed here while the two of you have fought.
'All living creatures are tormented — gods, asuras, and men alike. O Vṛtra, let friendship be established between you and Śakra forever. You shall obtain happiness and the eternal worlds of Śakra.'
Having heard the words of the sages, that extremely powerful Vṛtra, the asura, bowed his head to them all and then spoke:
'You are all of great fortune, and the gandharvas as well in every respect. All that you say has been heard by me. Now hear me also, O sinless ones.
'How can there ever be peace between me and Śakra? How, O gods, can friendship come to pass between two such forces of power?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The sages said: 'Fellowship with the good is to be sought even once; whatever is to be thereafter will be as it must be. One should not overstep fellowship with good men. Therefore fellowship with the good is always to be sought.'
'Fellowship with the good is firm and ever enduring; the wise man speaks truth in difficult situations of meaning. Fellowship with a good person is of great significance. Therefore a wise man should not seek to harm the virtuous.'
'Indra is honoured by the virtuous and is the abode of great souls; he is a speaker of truth, undepressed, a knower of righteousness, and ever resolute.'
'Let there be with him — with Śakra — an everlasting peace. Come to this trust; let your mind not be otherwise disposed.'
Śalya said: Hearing the words of the great sages, the one of great splendour addressed them: 'Certainly, O blessed ones, the ascetics are to be honoured by me.
'O gods, let all that I say be done here; and I shall do all that the foremost of twice-born have said to me.'
'Not by that which is dry, not by that which is wet, not by stone, not by wood, not by weapon, not by the thunderbolt, not by day, and not by night —
'— under these conditions may I be slain by Śakra together with the gods, O foremost of brahmins. Such a peace with Śakra pleases me forever.'
'So be it,' the sages said to him, O bull of the Bhāratas. With peace thus established, Vṛtra became joyful.
But Śakra, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, was ever vigilant and filled with resentment, constantly thinking of means for killing Vṛtra, perpetually anxious and watching for an opening.
Once he saw that great asura at the ocean's edge at the time of twilight, that moment both beautiful and dreadful.
Then the blessed god reflected on the boon of the great-souled one: 'This is the fearful twilight — neither night nor day. And Vṛtra, this enemy who plunders everything, must certainly be killed by me.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'If I do not slay Vṛtra today, having deceived this great asura of enormous strength and massive body, no good will come to me.'
Even as Śakra was thus deliberating and calling Viṣṇu to mind, he then saw in the ocean a mountain-like mass of foam.
'This is neither dry nor wet, nor is it a weapon as such. I shall hurl this at Vṛtra — in an instant he shall perish.'
Then along with the thunderbolt he swiftly hurled that foam at Vṛtra; and Viṣṇu, having entered that foam, destroyed Vṛtra.
With Vṛtra slain, the directions became free of darkness, an auspicious wind blew, and all creatures rejoiced.
Then the gods together with gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and serpents, and the sages too, praised great Indra with various hymns.
Saluted by all beings, soothing all beings, his enemy slain and his heart overjoyed, Vāsava, together with the gods, honoured Viṣṇu, the foremost of the three worlds — Vāsava, who knows righteousness.
Then, after mighty Vṛtra, the terror of the gods, was slain, Śakra became overwhelmed by falsehood and utterly despondent — beset also by the guilt of the three-headed one, and by brahminicide from before.
Taking refuge at the edge of the worlds, bereft of consciousness and sense, the lord of gods could not be found, overwhelmed by his own sins; hidden away, he dwelt in the waters like a snake coiling within.
Then, with the lord of gods gone and tormented by the dread of brahminicide, the earth appeared devastated — treeless, its forests withered, rivers with broken courses, and lakes without water.
There was also a tumult among living beings caused by drought; the gods were greatly frightened, as were all the great sages.
The entire world, kingless, was overcome by calamities; and the gods became afraid, wondering: 'Who will be our king?'
In heaven, the divine sages too were bereft of their king of gods, and none among the gods turned their mind toward kingship.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śalya said: Then all the sages and the gods, lords of the thirty, spoke: 'Let this glorious Nahuṣa be consecrated to the kingship of the gods.' They all went and said to him: 'Be our king, O lord of earth.'
Nahuṣa addressed those gods and the hosts of sages together with the ancestors, O king, seeking what was beneficial for himself:
'I am weak; I have not the strength to protect you. A king is born from strength, and strength ever resides in Śakra.'
All the gods, with the sages at their head, spoke to him again: 'Endowed with the power of our austerities, rule the kingdom in heaven.'
'Without doubt a terrible mutual fear prevails among us. Be consecrated, O lord of kings; be king in heaven.'
'You shall absorb the energy of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, sages, rākṣasas, ancestors, gandharvas, and beings that fall within range of your sight — and thus you shall become powerful.'
'Always placing righteousness foremost, be lord over all worlds. Protect the brahmin sages and the gods in heaven.'
Having obtained that most rare boon and attained the kingship of heaven, having been virtuous of soul continually, he now became enslaved to desire.
In all the divine gardens and in the groves of Nandana, on Kailāsa and the slope of the Himālayas, on Mandara, Śvetaparvata, Sahya, Mahendra, Malaya, in the oceans and in the rivers —
— surrounded by apsarases and encircled by divine maidens, Nahuṣa, now king of the gods, sported in many ways.
He listened to various divine tales delightful to the ear, to all manner of musical instruments, and to singing with sweet voices.
Viśvāvasu and Nārada, the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, and the six seasons in bodily form attended upon the lord of gods; a fragrant, charming, cool and pleasant wind blew.
While the great-souled Nahuṣa was thus sporting, there came into his sight the beloved queen of Śakra, the goddess.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing her, the corrupt-souled one said to all those in his assembly: 'Why does the divine queen of Indra not attend upon me?'
'I am Indra of the gods, and likewise lord of the worlds; let Śacī come to my dwelling swiftly today.'
Hearing this, the goddess, dejected in heart, said to Bṛhaspati: 'Protect me from Nahuṣa, O brahmin; I have come to you for refuge.'
'You address me, O brahmin, as one endowed with all auspicious marks, the beloved of the king of gods, partaker of supreme bliss,
'as one joined to a living husband, a devoted wife true to one husband. You have spoken words to me before — make those words true now.'
'Never before have you spoken anything false, O blessed lord. Therefore let what you have said to me come true, O best of twice-born.'
Then Bṛhaspati said to Indrāṇī, bewildered by fear: 'What I have said to you, O goddess, will certainly come true.
'You will see the king of gods, Indra, coming here soon. You need have no fear of Nahuṣa — this I truly tell you. I shall reunite you with Śakra before long.'
Then Nahuṣa heard that Indrāṇī had taken refuge with Bṛhaspati, son of Aṅgiras, and that king became enraged.
Śalya said: Knowing Nahuṣa to be enraged, the gods, with the sages at their head, addressed Nahuṣa, king of the gods, terrible in aspect:
'O king of gods, O lord of the world, abandon your anger. When you are enraged, the world is frightened — asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and great serpents alike.'
Abandon this anger, O virtuous one — those of your stature do not grow wrathful. She is the wife of another, that divine lady. Be appeased, O lord of the gods.
Turn your mind away from sin, from the violation of another man's wife. You are the king of the gods — may it be well with you. Rule your subjects by righteousness.
Addressed thus, he did not heed those words, for he was deluded by desire. Then the lord of the gods spoke thus to the gods, with regard to Indra:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Ahalyā, the illustrious wife of a sage, was violated of old by Indra while her husband still lived — why did you not restrain him then?
Many cruel and unrighteous deeds, many deceits, were committed by Indra in former times — why did you not restrain him then?
Let the goddess come to attend upon me — this is the highest good for her. And for you, O gods, there shall always be welfare if it is so.
The gods said: We shall bring Indrāṇī to you as you desire, O lord of heaven. Abandon this anger, O hero. Be pleased, O lord of the gods.
Śalya said: Having spoken thus, the gods, together with the seers, O Bhārata, went to Bṛhaspati to speak to Indrāṇī those inauspicious words.
We know that Indrāṇī has come to you for refuge, into your home, and that you have granted her freedom from fear, O best of the twice-born, O foremost of divine seers.
The gods, together with the gandharvas and the seers, O greatly resplendent one, entreat you — let Indrāṇī be given over to Nahuṣa.
Nahuṣa surpasses Indra and is the great-resplendent king of the gods — let this woman of beautiful hips and fair complexion choose him as her husband.
When this was said, that divine lady, weeping with a cry, shed her tears and spoke these piteous words to Bṛhaspati:
I do not desire Nahuṣa as my husband — I will wait upon that lord, my husband. I have come to you for refuge, O Brahman; save me from this great fear.
Bṛhaspati said: I would never abandon one who has sought refuge — this is my firm resolve, O Indrāṇī. You who know dharma and are devoted to dharma — I shall not forsake you, O blameless one.
I have no wish to do what ought not be done, especially being a brahmin who is learned in dharma, who is devoted to truth, and who knows the teaching of righteousness.
I shall not do this. Depart, O best of gods. And in this matter, hear what was sung of old by Brahmā:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His seed does not sprout at the time of sowing; the rain does not fall for him at the time of rain — one who surrenders a frightened refugee to the enemy finds no refuge himself when he desires protection.
He obtains his food in vain, devoid of wisdom; he falls from the heavenly realm, his efforts lost — one who surrenders a frightened refugee: the gods do not accept his oblations.
His offspring perish untimely; his ancestors always make him homeless — one who surrenders a frightened refugee: the gods together with Indra hurl the thunderbolt upon him.
Knowing this to be so, I shall not give away this Śacī, this Indrāṇī renowned in the world, the beloved queen of Śakra.
Whatever would be for her welfare and whatever would be for my welfare — let that be done, O best of gods. I shall not give up Śacī.
Śalya said: Then the gods spoke to him, the foremost among the sages of the Aṅgiras line: "How then may right policy be achieved? Deliberate upon it, O Bṛhaspati."
Bṛhaspati said: Let the auspicious lady request of Nahuṣa a little interval of time — this is indeed for the good of Indrāṇī, and likewise it shall be for our good as well.
Time is the creator of many obstacles; time will lead time onward. Nahuṣa, though arrogant and powerful by reason of the boon he received, will be brought down by time.
Śalya said: When he had spoken thus, the pleased gods addressed him: "O Brahman, what you have said is excellent and for the welfare of all the dwellers in heaven. O best of the twice-born, it is just so — and let this goddess too be persuaded."
Then all the gods, with Fire at their head, spoke to Indrāṇī calmly, desiring the welfare of the worlds:
By you this entire world, both the moving and the unmoving, is upheld. You are faithful to one husband and truthful — go now towards Nahuṣa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nahuṣa, who lusts for you, O goddess, will swiftly be destroyed, and Śakra shall regain his sovereignty over the gods.
Having thus resolved upon this plan for the accomplishment of the purpose, Indrāṇī, overcome with shame, went toward Nahuṣa of terrible aspect.
Seeing her, endowed with youth and beauty, Nahuṣa of wicked soul, his mind overwhelmed by desire, was greatly thrilled.
Śalya said: Then, looking at her, Nahuṣa the king of gods spoke to her: "I am Indra of all three worlds, O bright-smiling one. Accept me, O lady of beautiful hips and fair complexion, as your husband."
Addressed thus by Nahuṣa, the devoted wife, agitated with fear, trembled like a plantain tree in the wind.
Reverencing Brahmā with joined palms raised to her head, she then spoke to Nahuṣa, that king of gods of terrible aspect:
"I desire to obtain a little time from you, O lord of the gods. For it is not known whether Śakra has met some end, or where he has gone."
"Having ascertained this truth, if he is indeed not to be found, O lord, then I shall attend upon you — this I tell you truly." Addressed thus by Indrāṇī, Nahuṣa became pleased.
Nahuṣa said: So be it, O lady of beautiful hips, as you have spoken to me. And having ascertained the matter, remember that your coming to me is an obligation of truth.
Śalya said: Dismissed by Nahuṣa, that auspicious and ascetic woman departed and went to the dwelling of Bṛhaspati.
Hearing her words, the gods with Fire at their head deliberated with single-minded purpose for the sake of Śakra, O best of kings.
Meeting with Viṣṇu, the god of gods, the all-pervading one, those skilled in speech spoke to him in great distress:
"Śakra, the lord of the host of gods, is indeed overwhelmed by the sin of brahmin-slaughter. You are our refuge, O lord of gods, the firstborn, the master of the universe, who has assumed the state of Viṣṇu for the protection of all beings."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"By your valor Vṛtra was slain, and Vāsava is now beset by the guilt of brahmin-slaughter. O foremost among the hosts of gods, prescribe his liberation."
Hearing those words of the gods, Viṣṇu said: "Let Śakra worship me alone — I shall purify the wielder of the thunderbolt."
"Having worshipped me with the meritorious horse-sacrifice, the chastiser of Pāka shall once again attain the lordship over the gods, free from all fear."
"And Nahuṣa of wicked mind shall come to ruin through his own deeds. Bear with this state for a little while, O gods — remain vigilant without delay."
Hearing that auspicious, true, and nectar-like speech of Viṣṇu, all the hosts of gods, together with their teachers and with the seers, approached the place where Śakra, afflicted with fear, was hiding.
