There a most grand horse-sacrifice of the great-souled Mahendra was performed for the purpose of purification — the destroyer of the sin of brahmin-slaughter, O king.
Distributing the guilt of brahmin-slaughter among trees, rivers, mountains, the earth, and women, O Yudhiṣṭhira —
— distributing it among all beings and releasing it, the lord of the gods became free of fever, purified of sin; Vāsava became himself again.
Seeing Nahuṣa, immovable in his position and by reason of the boon he had received, the slayer of Bala beheld him as one who diminishes the splendor of all beings and who is difficult to overcome.
Then the heroic lord of Śacī vanished once more, became invisible to all beings, and wandered about awaiting the right time.
When Śakra had thus disappeared, Śacī, filled with grief, lamented in great distress, crying out: "Ah, Śakra!"
"If I have given gifts, if I have offered oblations, if I have pleased my elders, if it is true that I have been faithful to one husband alone, if there is any truth in me —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— I shall worship this sacred, divine Night-goddess who moves during the northward course of the sun. May my heart's desire be fulfilled."
With ritual purity she worshipped the Night-goddess there, and through the power of her vow of devotion to her husband and through truth, she summoned the goddess Upaśruti.
"Show me the place where that king of gods abides" — thus the goddess called upon Upaśruti: "Let truth be revealed through truth."
Śalya said: Then Upaśruti, taking a beautiful form, appeared before that virtuous lady. Seeing the goddess arrived, endowed with youth and beauty —
— Indrāṇī, greatly delighted, honored her and then asked: "I wish to know who you are. Tell me, O fair-faced one."
Upaśruti said: I am Upaśruti, O goddess, come to your presence. I have obtained the vision of you and am gratified by your truthfulness.
"You are devoted to your husband and disciplined in restraint and vows. I shall show you Śakra, the god who slew Vṛtra. Follow quickly — may it be well with you; you shall see the foremost of the gods."
Śalya said: Then Indrāṇī followed behind that goddess as she set forth, crossing the divine forests and many mountains; crossing the Himavān, she reached the northern slopes.
Reaching the ocean, extending for many leagues, she came to a great island covered with diverse trees and creeping plants.
There she beheld a divine lake, surrounded by many kinds of birds, a hundred leagues wide and equally long — beautiful.
There, O Bhārata, thousands of divine lotuses of five colors bloomed in full blossom, humming with bees that sang around them.
Piercing the stalk of a lotus, she entered together with her guide; and there, hidden within the filament of the lotus, she beheld the hundred-sacrificed Śatakratu.
Seeing the lord dwelling there in a most minute form, the goddess too assumed a minute form, as did Upaśruti.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Indrāṇī praised Indra with accounts of his renowned former deeds. Being thus praised, the god Puraṃdara then spoke to Śacī:
"For what purpose have you come here, and how did you find me?" Then she proceeded to tell him all the deeds of Nahuṣa:
"Having obtained the lordship over the three worlds, filled with the intoxication of valor, that wicked-souled one, seized by arrogance, spoke to me, O Śatakratu: 'Attend upon me,' the cruel one said, and he set a time-limit upon me."
"If you do not rescue me, O mighty one, he will bring me under his power. Tormented by this, I have come to you, O Śakra. Slay Nahuṣa, that fierce, long-armed one whose resolve is evil."
"Reveal yourself, O slayer of the daityas and dānavas. Regain your splendor, O mighty one. Rule over the kingdom of the gods once more."
Śalya said: Addressed thus by Śacī, that blessed one replied again: "This is not the time for valor — Nahuṣa is the more powerful."
"And he has been strengthened by the seers through oblations to the gods and to the ancestors, O passionate one. Here I shall devise a strategy, O goddess — you must carry it out."
"This must be kept secret by you and disclosed nowhere, O auspicious one. Go and speak to Nahuṣa in private, O slender-waisted one."
"Tell him: 'Come to me drawn by a divine vehicle borne by seers, O lord of the universe — then, pleased, I shall come under your power.'"
Addressed thus by the king of gods, that wife of lotus eyes said, "So be it," and went toward Nahuṣa.
Nahuṣa then, seeing her, spoke in surprise: "Welcome to you, O lady of beautiful hips. What may I do for you, O bright-smiling one?"
"Accept me who am devoted to you, O auspicious lady. What do you desire, O wise one? Whatever needs to be done for you, O fair-waisted one, I shall do it."
"And you need have no shame before me, O beautiful-hipped one. Trust me. I swear by truth, O goddess, I shall do your bidding."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Indrāṇī said: I am awaiting the time you have set for me, O lord of the universe. After that, you shall indeed be my husband, O lord of the gods.
"And the desire I hold in my heart — hear it, O king of gods. I shall tell it to you: if you, O king, will do what is dear to me, this word spoken with affection — then I shall become subject to your will."
Indra has swift horses, elephants, and chariots as his conveyances. But I desire for you, O lord of the gods, a vehicle unprecedented here — one that belongs neither to Viṣṇu, nor to Rudra, nor to the asuras, nor to the rākṣasas.
Let the assembled sages carry you, O great king, O mighty lord, all together in a palanquin, O king — this is what pleases me.
You should not be considered equal to the asuras or the gods — you ought to surpass them all. Draw upon the splendor of all by the mere sight of your valor. No powerful being would dare to stand before you.
Śalya said: Thus addressed, Nahuṣa was filled with great delight at that time. He too spoke these words to that blameless queen of the lord of the gods.
This unprecedented vehicle you have described, O fair-complexioned one, has deeply pleased me, O goddess. I am under your command, O beautiful-faced one.
Indeed, one who makes sages serve as his bearers is no man of meager valor. I am an ascetic, powerful, the lord of the past, the future, and the present.
Were I to be angered, the world would cease to exist — in me all things are established. Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, serpents, and rākṣasas alike.
When I am enraged, all the worlds together are not sufficient to withstand me, O bright-smiling one. Whomever I behold with my eyes, I steal away their radiance.
Therefore I shall carry out your word, O goddess — of this there is no doubt. The seven sages and all the brahmarṣis shall bear me. Behold our greatness and our prosperity, O fair-complexioned one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus and dismissed that lovely-faced goddess, he yoked to the celestial vehicle the sages who were devoted to their vows.
Disregarding the brāhmaṇas, drunk with power and intoxicated by the pride of the boon, acting as he willed, that wicked-souled one made those sages carry him.
Dismissed by Nahuṣa, she said to Bṛhaspati: The term Nahuṣa set for me here is nearly exhausted. Seek out Śakra quickly — have mercy on me, your devoted one.
The venerable Bṛhaspati said to her: Very well. You need not fear Nahuṣa, O goddess, evil-minded though he is.
This vilest of men shall not endure long — he has already fallen. Ignorant of righteousness, he is as good as slain by having made the great sages serve as his bearers, O auspicious one.
I shall perform a sacred rite for the destruction of this evil-minded one, and I shall find Śakra. Do not be afraid — may all be well with you.
Then the immensely radiant Bṛhaspati, kindling the fire according to ritual injunction, offered the highest oblation for the purpose of recovering the lord of the gods.
From that fire the venerable god Agni, the oblation-eater, himself assumed a wondrous female form and suddenly vanished.
Searching through the cardinal directions and intermediate quarters, the mountains and forests, the earth and the atmosphere, moving faster than thought, he returned to Bṛhaspati in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Agni said: O Bṛhaspati, I cannot find the king of the gods anywhere. Waters are all that remain — and I am not able to enter the waters at all. There is no path for me there, O brahmin. What else shall I do for you?
Śalya said: The preceptor of the gods said to him: Enter the waters, O greatly resplendent one.
Agni said: I am not capable of entering the waters — my extinction would come about therein. I have taken refuge in you. May all be well with you, O greatly resplendent one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Fire arose from the waters, the warrior class arose from the brahmin, iron arose from stone — their all-pervading splendor is quenched in their own original sources.
Bṛhaspati said: You, O Agni, are the mouth of all the gods; you are the carrier of oblations. You dwell hidden within all beings and move about as their witness.
The wise call you one, and again they call you threefold. Were you to abandon it, this world would instantly perish, O consumer of oblations.
The learned, having paid homage to you, attain the eternal path won by their own deeds, together with their wives and sons.
You alone, O Agni, are the carrier of oblations; you alone are the highest oblation. It is you alone that men worship with sacrificial sessions and with rites at the supreme sacrifice.
Having created these three worlds, O carrier of oblations, at the appointed time you cook them once more, being kindled. You are the origin of this entire universe, O Agni, and you become its resting place once again.
They call you, O Agni, the giver of rain, and lightning too is nothing but you. It is from you that the seasons emerge and go forth to consume all beings.
All the waters are deposited in you; in you rests this entire universe. There is nothing whatsoever unknown to you in the three worlds, O purifier.
Every being seeks out its own source — enter the waters without any apprehension. I shall strengthen you with the eternal brahminical mantras.
Śalya said: Thus praised, the venerable Agni, carrier of oblations, the supremely wise one, spoke these excellent words to Bṛhaspati with gladness: I shall show you Śakra — this I tell you truly.
Fire then entered the waters — oceans, lakes, and ponds alike — and, concealed, came to that lake where the hundred-sacrificer lay hidden.
Then, searching through the lotus plants there, O bull of the Bhāratas, Agni perceived the lord of the gods standing concealed within the lotus stalks.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Coming back swiftly, he reported to Bṛhaspati that the lord was abiding within the lotus filaments, his body reduced to the size of an atom.
Going there, accompanied by divine sages and gandharvas, Bṛhaspati then praised the god who had slain Bala with ancient hymns of praise.
The great asura Namuci the terrible was slain by you, O Śakra, and likewise Śambara and Bala too — both of dreadful might.
Grow in strength, O performer of a hundred sacrifices; annihilate all your enemies. Rise up, O wielder of the thunderbolt, and behold the assembled divine sages who have come.
O great Indra, the worlds were saved by you when you slew the dānavas, O mighty one. Employing the foam of waters, strengthened by the power of Viṣṇu, you formerly slew Vṛtra, O king of the gods, O lord of the universe.
You are the most excellent and the most praiseworthy among all beings. There exists no creature here equal to you. By you are all beings upheld, O Śakra; you have established the greatness of the gods.
Protect the gods and those who dwell in their worlds, O great Indra; regain your strength. Thus praised in this manner, he grew in power slowly but surely.
Resuming his own form, he became endowed with full strength. And the god addressed his teacher Bṛhaspati who stood before him.
What task remains for you all? The great asura, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, has been slain — Vṛtra of the immense body, who had sought to swallow the worlds.
Bṛhaspati said: The human king Nahuṣa, by virtue of the radiance of groups of divine sages, has attained sovereignty over the gods and is tormenting us all greatly.
Indra said: How did Nahuṣa attain the kingship of the gods, which is so difficult to obtain? By what asceticism, or with what power? What kind of valor does he possess, O Bṛhaspati?
Bṛhaspati said: The frightened gods longed for Śakra. That great position of Indra having been abandoned by you, then all the gods, the ancestors, the atharvan sages, and the assemblies of gandharvas came together.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And going there, O Śakra, they said to Nahuṣa: Be our king, the protector of the universe. Nahuṣa said to them: I am not capable. Nourish me with your asceticism and your splendor.
Thus addressed and strengthened by the gods, Nahuṣa of terrible might became king. And having attained sovereignty over the three worlds, that wicked-souled one made the ascetics serve as his bearers and traverses the realms.
He steals splendor and his gaze is poison — he is utterly dreadful. You must never behold Nahuṣa at any time. All the gods, terrified of Nahuṣa, move about in disguised forms, not revealing themselves to him.
Śalya said: While the foremost of the descendants of Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, was speaking thus, the world-guardian Kubera, and ancient Yama the son of Vivasvat, the god Soma, and Varuṇa came there.
They, having come together, said to the great Indra: By good fortune Vṛtra the son of Tvaṣṭṛ has been slain. By good fortune we behold you well and unharmed, and your enemy destroyed, O Śakra.
Śakra addressed them all in due order and, urging them on, said: Nahuṣa of dreadful form has become king of the gods — let your assistance be given to me in this matter.
They replied: Nahuṣa is of dreadful form and his gaze is poisonous — we fear him, O god. But if you, O king, were to defeat Nahuṣa, then we deserve a share, O Śakra.
Indra said: So be it — let the lord Varuṇa be the lord of the waters; let Yama and Kubera this day receive the great consecration together with him. Let us conquer our enemy Nahuṣa of the terrible gaze.
Then Agni too said to Śakra: Grant me a share and I shall render you assistance. Śakra said to him: There shall be your share also, O Agni — in the great sacrifice, one share shall belong jointly to Indra and Agni.
Having deliberated thus, the venerable great Indra, the chastiser of Pāka, appointed Kubera as the lord of all yakṣas and lord of all wealth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Śakra, the bestower of boons, duly honoring them, granted Vaivasvata lordship over the ancestors and Varuṇa lordship over the waters.
Śalya said: Now, while the wise king of the gods was contemplating a means for the destruction of Nahuṣa together with those world-guardians, the venerable ascetic Agastya appeared there.
He, after honoring the lord of the gods, said: By good fortune you are prospering — through the destruction of Viśvarūpa and by the slaying of the asura Vṛtra.
By good fortune Nahuṣa too has fallen from the kingship of the gods, O destroyer of citadels. By good fortune I see you, your enemies slain, O slayer of Bala.
Indra said: Welcome to you, O great sage. I am gratified by the sight of you. Please accept from me water for your feet, water for rinsing the mouth, a cow, and the guest-offering.
Śalya said: When that foremost of sages, that bull among brāhmaṇas, had been honored and was seated, the lord of the gods, filled with joy, asked him:
This I wish to hear recounted, O venerable one, O foremost of the twice-born: how Nahuṣa, of wicked resolve, fell from heaven.
Agastya said: Hear, O Śakra, these glad tidings — how the wicked-souled king, the ill-conducting Nahuṣa, intoxicated with power, fell from heaven.
The greatly fortunate divine sages and the spotless brahmarṣis, weary from carrying that evil-doing Nahuṣa, asked him a question in doubt, O god — O foremost among conquerors.
The brāhmaṇas who recite these mantras at the sprinkling of cows — are these authoritative for you or not, O Vāsava? Nahuṣa, his mind clouded by darkness, said to them: No, they are not.
The sages said: You are engaged in unrighteousness; you do not accept what is righteous. This is authoritative for us — it was declared of old by the great sages.
Agastya said: Then while he was disputing with the sages, O Vāsava, he, oppressed by unrighteousness, struck me on the head with his foot.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By that act he became bereft of splendor and stripped of fortune, O husband of Śacī. Then I spoke to him as he stood trembling and seized with fear:
Because you have corrupted what is sacred, which was established of old and practiced by the brahmarṣis — and because you have touched me on the head with your foot —
And because you, O fool, have made sages equivalent to brahmin priests, those who are difficult to assail, serve as your bearers — by this you are cast from heaven, your splendor extinguished.
Fall, O sinner, utterly fallen, your merit exhausted, to the surface of the earth. For ten thousand years you shall roam in the form of a great serpent, and when that time is fulfilled, you shall regain heaven.
Thus did that wicked-souled one fall from the kingship of the gods, O subduer of enemies. By good fortune we flourish, O Śakra — the thorn in the brāhmaṇas' side has been destroyed.
Return to heaven, O husband of Śacī; protect the worlds — your senses mastered, your enemies conquered, praised by the great sages.
Śalya said: Then the gods were greatly delighted, surrounded by hosts of great sages, as were the ancestors, the yakṣas, the serpents, and the rākṣasas as well.
The gandharvas and the daughters of the gods, all the hosts of apsarases, the lakes, the rivers, the mountains, and the oceans, O lord of the people —
All came forward and said: By good fortune you flourish, O slayer of enemies. The sinful Nahuṣa has been slain — by good fortune, through the wise Agastya. By good fortune the evil-behaving one has been made a serpent on the earth.
Śalya said: Then Śakra, being praised by hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, mounted Airāvata, that king among elephants, endowed with auspicious marks.
And Agni of great radiance, and the great sage Bṛhaspati, and Yama and Varuṇa, and Kubera the lord of wealth —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śakra the slayer of Vṛtra, that mighty lord, surrounded by all the gods, and accompanied by gandharvas and apsarases, traversed the three worlds.
He, the king of the gods, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, the sovereign of the gods, being reunited with Mahendrāṇī, filled with the highest joy, governed his realm.
Then the blessed Aṅgiras appeared there and worshipped the lord of the gods with the mantras of the Atharvaveda.
Then the blessed Indra was greatly pleased and granted a boon to that Atharvāṅgiras.
"In this Veda shall arise the name Atharvāṅgirasa — for this is the illustration — and you shall receive a share of the sacrifice."
Having thus honoured Atharvāṅgiras, O great king, the lord of the gods, performer of a hundred sacrifices, then dismissed him.
Having honoured all the thirty gods and likewise the sages rich in austerity, O king, Indra, greatly rejoiced, protected the people with righteousness.
In this way Indra too had come to suffer, dwelling incognito together with his wife, desiring the slaying of his enemies.
You should not harbour anger that you have suffered in the great forest, O lord of kings, together with Draupadī and your noble brothers.
Even so shall you too, O lord of kings, O descendant of Bharata, regain your kingdom, just as Śakra gained it after slaying Vṛtra, O joy of the Kurus.
And the wicked Nahuṣa, hater of Brahmins, evil-minded one, was struck by Agastya's curse and perished for endless years.
Likewise your wicked enemies, O slayer of foes, Karṇa, Duryodhana and the rest, shall swiftly come to ruin.
Then, O hero, O lord, you shall enjoy this earth bounded by the ocean, together with your brothers and with Draupadī.
This narrative of Śakra's victory, equal in authority to the Veda, should be heard by a king who desires victory when his armies are arrayed for battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore I proclaim to you victory, O best of the victorious — the great souls grow when they are praised, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
This destruction of the great warrior-lords, O Yudhiṣṭhira, shall come through Duryodhana's transgression and through the might of Bhīma and Arjuna.
Whoever steadfastly recites this tale of Indra's victory shall be cleansed of sin, shall have conquered heaven, and shall rejoice both here and in the hereafter.
He shall know no fear born of enemies, nor shall he be without sons; he shall meet with no calamity whatsoever, shall gain long life, shall attain victory everywhere, and shall never suffer defeat.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus consoled by Śalya, O bull among Bhāratas, the king — foremost of those who uphold righteousness — honoured Śalya according to proper rite.
Having heard Śalya's words, the mighty-armed son of Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira, replied to the king of the Madras with these words.
"You will without doubt act as charioteer to Karṇa. In that role you must diminish Karṇa's spirit through praise of me."
Śalya said: I shall do exactly as you tell me. And whatever else I am able to do for you, that too I shall do.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having taken leave of the sons of Kuntī, Śalya the lord of the Madras, the glorious subduer of foes, departed with his army to Duryodhana.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Yuyudhāna the hero, the great chariot-warrior of the Sātvatas, came to Yudhiṣṭhira with a great four-division army.
His warriors of great valour, gathered from many lands, bearing many kinds of weapons — those heroes adorned his army.
With battle-axes and slings, with lances, javelins, and clubs, with pikes, spears, axes, and darts, and with gleaming swords —
— with swords, bows, and sheaths, and with arrows of various kinds, oil-polished and gleaming, that army shone resplendently.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That army, radiant as a cloud and adorned with those weapons, had the appearance of a storm-cloud blazing with lightning.
For that one akṣauhiṇī force entered the army of Yudhiṣṭhira and disappeared within it, O king, as a small river disappears into the ocean.
Likewise the powerful bull of the Cedis, Dhṛṣṭaketu, took up one akṣauhiṇī and came to the immeasurably valiant Pāṇḍavas.
And Jayatsena the Māgadha, son of Jarāsaṃdha and of great strength, came to the king of righteousness with a single akṣauhiṇī of troops.
Likewise the Pāṇḍya king, O lord of kings, surrounded by many kinds of warriors dwelling along the seashore, came to Yudhiṣṭhira.
His army at that massing of forces was most splendid to behold, O king — finely adorned and powerful.
Drupada too had an army adorned with valiant men gathered from many lands and with his sons, the great chariot-warriors.
Likewise Virāṭa, king of the Matsyas and lord of his forces, together with mountain-dwelling kings, went to the Pāṇḍavas.
From here and there the great forces converged upon the noble sons of Pāṇḍu — exactly seven akṣauhiṇīs crowded with varied banners, eager to fight the Kurus, gladdened the Pāṇḍavas.
Likewise, augmenting the joy of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the earth-lord Bhagadatta gave a force of one akṣauhiṇī.
His irresistible army, covered by Chinese and Kirāta warriors as if with gold, shone like a forest of karṇikāra trees.
Likewise the valiant Bhūriśravas and Śalya, O joy of the Kurus, came to Duryodhana each with a separate akṣauhiṇī.
And Kṛtavarmā the son of Hṛdika, together with the forces of the Bhojas and Andhakas, came to Duryodhana with a single akṣauhiṇī of troops.
His army, adorned by those tiger-like warriors wearing garlands of forest flowers, shone like a forest filled with frolicsome rutting elephants.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Others headed by Jayadratha, earth-lords dwelling in Sindhu and Sauvīra, came as if shaking the mountains.
The vast akṣauhiṇī army of those kings shone brilliantly then, tossed by the wind, like clouds of many forms.
And Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja, together with Yavanas and Śakas, came to the Kaurava chief with one akṣauhiṇī, O lord of peoples.
The gathering of his army appeared like a swarm of locusts; and having reached the Kaurava chief, it disappeared within that host.
Likewise Nīla, the earth-lord dwelling in Māhiṣmatī, with his dark-weaponed warriors of great valour, inhabitants of the southern road —
— and the two earth-lords of the Avantis, well surrounded by great forces, those two came to Suyodhana with separate akṣauhiṇīs.
And the five Kekaya kings, those tiger-like men and full brothers, gladdening the Kaurava chief, rushed forward with one akṣauhiṇī.
From here and there, three other armies of all those great earth-lords assembled, O bull among Bhāratas.
Thus eleven complete armies of Duryodhana, eager to fight the sons of Kuntī, were crowded with varied banners.
There was no room at that time in Hāstinapura, O king, even for the foremost leaders of the kings along with their armies, O Bhārata.
Then the Pañcanada region, the whole of the Kuru forest-land, the Rohitaka wilderness, and the desert tract alone —
— Ahicchatra, Kālakūṭa, the Gaṅgā bank, O Bhārata, Vāraṇā, Vāṭadhāna, and the Yamunā mountain —
— this vast region, rich in wealth and grain, became thoroughly crowded with the armies of the Kaurava host.
There the priest who had been sent by the king of Pāñcāla to the Kauravas saw that army thus arrayed.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having reached the Kaurava court, Drupada's priest was duly honoured by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, by Bhīṣma, and by Vidura.
Having first spoken all the words of courtesy and having enquired about their welfare, he spoke his message in the midst of all the army commanders.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The eternal law of kings is known to all of you; yet for the sake of establishing the argument I shall speak even though it is already known.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu are both renowned sons of the same father; the ancestral wealth belongs equally to both of them — there is no doubt in this.
If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have received the paternal wealth, how is it that the sons of Pāṇḍu have not received the paternal wealth?
As matters stand, it is known to you from before how the ancestral wealth was withheld and not received, concealed by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Though they tried repeatedly with means even that threatened their very lives, those who survived were unable to be led to Yama's abode.
And the kingdom, which had been enlarged again by their own strength by those great souls, was treacherously seized by the petty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with Śakuni.
And that deed too was sanctioned and set up by this man — and they were made to dwell in the great forest for thirteen years.
After those heroes were tormented together with their wife in the assembly hall, very grievous and varied hardships were then suffered by them in the forest.
Likewise in the city of Virāṭa, as though they had entered a different womb, extreme suffering was endured by those noble ones — as if by sinners.
Yet those bulls among the Kurus, having put all those earlier offences behind them, desire nothing but peace together with the Kurus.
Knowing both the conduct of these men and the conduct of Duryodhana, well-wishers here ought to bring Dhṛtarāṣṭra around.
For those heroes, the Pāṇḍavas, do not enter into conflict with the Kurus — they desire what is their own without the destruction of the world.
And whatever reason the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra may have for conflict — that reason should not be heeded, for the Pāṇḍavas are the stronger side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For seven akṣauhiṇīs have gathered under the son of Dharma, eager to fight the Kurus, and await his command.
Other tiger-like men equal to a thousand akṣauhiṇīs — Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, and the twin brothers of immense power —
— these eleven armies have assembled on one side, and on the other side stands the mighty-armed Dhanaṃjaya, he of many forms.
As Arjuna the diademed surpasses all armies, so too does the mighty-armed Vāsudeva of great splendour.
Knowing the vastness of the armies, the valour of the diademed one, and the wisdom of Kṛṣṇa — what man would choose to fight?
Let your honours give what ought to be given, in accordance with righteousness and in accordance with the agreement — let not this moment pass you by."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard his words, the one great in wisdom and of great splendour — Bhīṣma — having duly honoured him at the fitting moment, then spoke.
"By good fortune all the Pāṇḍavas are well together with their kinsmen; by good fortune they have allies; by good fortune they are devoted to righteousness.
By good fortune those brothers, the joy of the Kurus, desire peace; by good fortune they are not minded for war, together with Dāmodara.
All that you have said is true — there is no doubt. Yet your speech is overly sharp, I think, on account of your Brahmin nature.
Without doubt those Pāṇḍavas were made to suffer, in the forest and here; and without doubt they have rightfully earned all their father's wealth.
Arjuna the diademed son of Pāṇḍu is strong, skilled in weapons, and of great might — who indeed could withstand Dhanaṃjaya in battle?"
Even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself would not be capable — what then of other bowmen? He is capable of facing even the three worlds, in my judgment.
While Bhīṣma was speaking those words, Karṇa, filled with anger, boldly contradicted him; glancing at Duryodhana, he spoke these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There is nothing in this world, O brahmin, that is not known to any creature. What purpose is served by repeating the same thing again and again?
For Duryodhana's sake, Śakuni defeated him at dice in former times; and Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Pāṇḍu, went to the forest under the terms of the agreement.
Without honoring that agreement, the king desires the paternal kingdom, relying on the strength of the Matsyas and the Pāñcālas.
Out of fear, O wise one, Duryodhana would not yield even a step; yet by the law of righteousness he might give the whole earth even to an enemy.
If they desire again the ancestral kingdom, let them fulfill the appointed time as promised, dwelling in the forest.
Then let them live under Duryodhana's protection, free from all fear. This unrighteous counsel they pursue out of sheer folly.
But if the Pāṇḍavas abandon righteousness and desire war, they will remember my words when they encounter these best of the Kurus.
Bhīṣma said: O son of Rādhā, what use are your words? You ought to remember that deed — when Pārtha alone conquered six warriors in battle.
If we do not do as this brahmin has said, we shall surely be slain by him in battle and shall swallow dust.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having honored and appeased Bhīṣma, and having rebuked the son of Rādhā, spoke these words.
Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, has spoken what is beneficial for us, beneficial for the Pāṇḍavas as well, and beneficial for the whole world.
Having reflected, I shall send Sañjaya to the sons of Pṛthā. Let your honor now depart to the Pāṇḍavas without delay.
Having honored him thus, the descendant of the Kurus sent him off to the Pāṇḍavas; and summoning Sañjaya into the midst of the assembly, he spoke these words.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: They say the sons of Pāṇḍu have arrived at Upaplavya, O Sañjaya. Go there, learn of their state, and pay honor to Ajātaśatru. By good fortune, O sinless one, you have reached the town.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Tell them all, O Sañjaya, that they are well. After dwelling in hardship unworthy of them, peace between them and us is close at hand — for those noble benefactors who have been wronged.
I have never, O Sañjaya, at any time observed any wrongful conduct on the part of the Pāṇḍavas. Having won all their prosperity by their own valor, the Pāṇḍavas yielded it all to me.
Searching always, I find no fault in them, however small, for which I could blame the sons of Pṛthā. They always act in accordance with righteousness and the proper ends of life; though fond of pleasure, they never pursue their desires unrestrained.
Overcoming heat and cold, hunger and thirst, sleep and drowsiness, anger and elation, and heedlessness — through steadfastness and wisdom, the sons of Pṛthā strive for righteousness and proper purpose.
They give up wealth in due season for their friends; their friendship does not wither through mere long dwelling together. The sons of Pṛthā bestow honor and benefit according to what is fitting. Among the descendants of Ajamīḍha, there is none who hates them.
Except from the evil, crooked, dull-witted Duryodhana and the yet more petty Karṇa — these wretched beings who are fond of base pleasures — these great-souled ones generate their splendor.
Duryodhana, thriving in comfort with energetic might, regards that as a meritorious act — and the childish one thinks the portion belonging to the Pāṇḍavas can be seized while they still live.
He who has Arjuna, Keśava, Vṛkodara, Sātyaki, Ajātaśatru, the two sons of Mādrī, and all the Sṛñjayas in his train — it is good to offer unto him before a war.
For Savyasācin alone, standing in his chariot with the Gāṇḍīva bow, can drive back the whole earth; and likewise Keśava Viṣṇu is irresistible — the great-souled lord of the three worlds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What mortal could stand before him who is worthy of adoration among all the gods — he who scatters showers of arrows with the roar of rain clouds, swift as flocks of birds in flight?
With his single chariot and the Gāṇḍīva bow, he conquered even the northern quarter and the Northern Kurus; Savyasācin carried off their wealth and made their followers bring tribute.
And it was Savyasācin with his Gāṇḍīva who conquered even the gods together with Indra at Khāṇḍava, and Phalguna offered up the fire to Jātaveda, thereby increasing the glory and honor of the Pāṇḍavas.
Among mace-bearers today there is none equal to Bhīma; nor is there his equal in mounting an elephant. In the chariot they say none is inferior to Arjuna, and in the strength of his arms he has the power of ten thousand elephants.
Well-trained, a confirmed enemy, and valiant, when enraged he could swiftly burn up the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Ever intolerant and powerful, he cannot be defeated in battle even by Vāsava himself in person.
Keen-minded, powerful, swift of hand, well-trained by Phalguna — the two brothers, sons of Mādrī, tearing apart troops of warriors like two hawks rending flocks of birds, would let none of the Kurus escape.
Moving in their midst, the valiant Dhṛṣṭadyumna is here the sole chief of the Pāṇḍavas, together with the counselors, the foremost of the Somakas, his very life surrendered for the Pāṇḍavas' victory.
Virāṭa, king of the Śālveyas, having achieved his purpose by dwelling with them and being of mature age, is said, along with his sons, to be always devoted to the cause of the Pāṇḍavas and to Yudhiṣṭhira — so I have heard.
Five powerful brothers, great bowmen, are kept excluded from the Kekayas and desire the Kekaya kingdom; longing for battle, they dwell with the sons of Pṛthā.
And all the warriors, the lords of the earth, have been assembled and have committed themselves to the cause of the Pāṇḍavas. I hear of the heroes devoted with affection, united in love, attached to Dharmarāja.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Warriors from the mountain retreats and the residents of inaccessible places, high-born and pure throughout the world, and also barbarians powerful with various weapons, have assembled and committed themselves to the Pāṇḍavas' cause.
The Pāṇḍya king too, of boundless energy, equal to Indra, accompanied by many great warriors in battle, that great-souled one has come for the Pāṇḍavas' cause — foremost hero of the world, his valor and splendor unrivaled.
He who, I hear, has received weapons from Droṇa, Arjuna, Vāsudeva, Kṛpa, and Bhīṣma — him they call the only one equal to the son of Kṛṣṇa. That Sātyaki has committed himself to the Pāṇḍavas' cause.
And the Cedis and the Karūṣas, together with earth-lords of every valor, have taken their side; in their midst shines the lord of the Cedis, blazing with glory like the sun in splendor.
Thinking himself unstoppable in battle, the foremost of all who draw the bowstring on earth, Śiśupāla mustered all his kingly energy — yet Kṛṣṇa violently slew him and crushed him with his might.
Increasing the glory and honor of the Yādavas, he slew Śiśupāla in battle in former times; all the kings of the earth, headed by the lord of Karusha, used to increase his honor.
Regarding Keśava there as irresistible, the other kings, abandoning the lord of the Cedis, fled from Kṛṣṇa with his Sugrīva-yoked chariot, like small animals on seeing a lion.
He who came swiftly against him in opposition, hoping to challenge Vāsudeva in a single-chariot duel — that one lay slain by Kṛṣṇa, his life gone, uprooted by Kṛṣṇa like a Karṇikāra tree by the wind.
When they reported to me the prowess of Keśava for the sake of those Pāṇḍavas, O Sañjaya, reflecting on the deeds of Viṣṇu — O son of Gavalgaṇa, I find no peace.
No enemy could ever withstand those at whose head stands that lion of the Vṛṣṇis. My heart trembles with fear at hearing of the two Kṛṣṇas riding together in one chariot.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Unless my dull-witted and perverse son goes to battle against those two — unless they burn up the Kurus as Indra and Viṣṇu burned the Daitya host — for in my opinion Dhanañjaya is equal to Śakra and the eternal hero of the Vṛṣṇis is Viṣṇu himself.
The valiant son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava Ajātaśatru, who delights in righteousness and is restrained by modesty — that high-minded one, deceived by Duryodhana, unless he in anger burns up the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
For I do not fear Arjuna, Vāsudeva, Bhīma, or the twin sons of Mādrī so much, O charioteer, as I am always more afraid of the wrath of the king blazing with anger.
Endowed with austerity and celibacy aplenty, whatever mental resolve he forms would be accomplished. Knowing his wrath in battle, O Sañjaya, I am greatly afraid today — and rightly so.
So go quickly, dispatched by chariot; passing by the army of the Pāñcāla king, inquire after the welfare of Ajātaśatru, and speak lovingly to him again and again.
And meeting Janārdana as well, O dear one — the greatest among the mighty, the noble one — inquire after his welfare in my name, saying: Dhṛtarāṣṭra desires peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
The son of Kuntī would do nothing contrary to Vāsudeva's word, O charioteer; Kṛṣṇa is dear to them and regarded as their very self, and he is ever engaged in their affairs, being wise.
Having assembled the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas, inquire after the welfare of Janārdana, Yuyudhāna, and Virāṭa in my name; and likewise of all the five sons of Draupadī.
Whatever you deem timely there, on behalf of our opponents, and whatever is beneficial for the Bhāratas — all that speak out, O Sañjaya, in the assembly of kings, so that no one may faint and that there be no war.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sañjaya went to Upaplavya to see the Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable might.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And having reached the righteous-souled King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of the charioteer first prostrated himself and then addressed him.
Gavalgaṇa's son Sañjaya, the charioteer's grandson, addressed Ajātaśatru with confidence: 'By good fortune, O king, I see you in good health, with your allies, resembling great Indra himself.'
'The aged king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Ambikā, that wise one, inquires after your welfare. Is Bhīma, foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, in good health? And Dhanañjaya? And the two sons of Mādrī?'
'Is Kṛṣṇā Draupadī, the royal princess, that one firm in her vow, wife of heroes, together with her sons, that high-minded lady, well? And wherever you desire, O Bhārata, do you obtain your cherished wishes? May you be blessed.'
Yudhiṣṭhira said: 'O son of Gavalgaṇa, O Sañjaya, welcome to you. I greet you with a glad heart, O charioteer. I declare that I am well; and together with my brothers I am in good health, O wise one.'
'After a long time, O charioteer, hearing this welfare of the king, the aged Kuru, I consider it as if I have seen the lord of men in person — for in seeing you, O Sañjaya, I am joined with gladness.'
'Our grandfather, that aged, high-minded one, supremely wise, endowed with all righteousness — is that descendant of the Kurus, Bhīṣma, in good health, O dear one? And does his conduct remain as before?'
'Is King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Vicitravīrya, together with his sons, in good health, that great-souled one? Is the great king Bāhlika, son of Pratīpa, in good health, that learned one, O son of a charioteer?'
'Is Somadatta in good health, O dear one? And Bhūriśravas, Śalya the firm in his vows, Droṇa with his son, and Kṛpa the brahmin — are these great bowmen also free from illness?'
'Supremely wise, versed in all the sciences, the foremost of bowmen on this earth — do these receive the honor they deserve, O dear one? And are these bowmen also free from illness?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'All the young bowmen on earth envy the Kurus, O Sañjaya — in whose kingdom dwells Droṇa's son, that handsome great bowman of noble character.'
'Is the son of a vaishya woman, that most wise royal son Yuyutsu, in good health, O dear one? Is Karṇa, the minister, in good health, O dear one — whose Suyodhana is the dull and obedient tool?'
'The aged women, the mothers of the Bhāratas, the ladies of the kitchen, the wives of servants, O charioteer — the daughters-in-law, the sons, the nephews, the sisters, and the daughters' sons — are all of these also well?'
'Does the king conduct himself toward the brahmins duly, as formerly, O dear one? Does the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fail to withhold the shares belonging to me for the twice-born ones, O Sañjaya?'
'Does King Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with his sons overlook the transgressions of brahmins? Does he not, as one looking after his road, overlook such deficient conduct toward them?'
'This is the supreme light in the living world, the pure brightness ordained by the Creator for the subjects. If those dull ones do not restrain their greed, the complete ruin of the Kauravas is at hand.'
'Does King Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with his sons desire proper conduct in the ranks of his ministers? Do those who appear as friends but are secret enemies not seek to live by sowing division, sharing one set of allies?'
'Do the Kurus all not speak evil of the Pāṇḍavas, O dear one? And on seeing the assembled hosts of the enemy, do they remember Pārtha, the leader in battle?'
'Do they recall those arrows loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, straight-flying, thundering like storm clouds, shot from the arm's end of the bowstring by the quivering bowman, O dear one?'
'For I have not seen or heard of anyone on earth equal to Arjuna or greater — he whose sixty-one sharp-edged arrows, well-feathered and well-regarded, are released with perfect hand-speed.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'The valiant Bhīmasena, mace in hand, making hosts of enemies tremble in battle, roaming like a maddened elephant among reeds — do they remember him?'
'Sahadeva, son of Mādrī, who conquered the assembled Kaliṅgas at Dantakura, shooting with his left hand and his right alike — that one of great strength, do they remember him?'
'This Nakula, when dispatched by me and rising up — even as you watched, O son of Gavalgaṇa, O Sañjaya — brought the western quarter under my sway. That son of Mādrī, do they remember him?'
'The victory that occurred in the Dvaita forest, over those who came on the ill-advised cattle-raid — where those foolish ones, fallen into the enemy's power, were freed by Bhīmasena and Arjuna the victorious.'
'I protected Arjuna from behind, while the two sons of Mādrī and Bhīmasena formed the guard; and the bearer of the Gāṇḍīva, driving off the enemy's hosts, returned safe. Do they remember that?'
Surely by good deeds alone it cannot be done here, Sañjaya — to fully overcome them; for with all our might we are unable to defeat the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Sañjaya said: As you deserve, O Pāṇḍava, even so it is; you ask after the Kurus, O best of Kurus, and after their people. May those wise ones of whom you ask, O Pārtha, be free from affliction, O dear one.
Among the Dhārtarāṣṭras there are indeed virtuous elders; there are also sinners among them — know this, O Pāṇḍava. The Dhārtarāṣṭra would give even to an enemy; how then would he withhold gifts from brahmins?
What he does toward you is not righteous; to act with hostility toward those who have not harmed him is not good. Dhṛtarāṣṭra with his son has betrayed friends — he who is wicked despises you who are virtuous in conduct.
He neither approves nor is he at peace, and he is deeply tormented; inwardly the old man grieves, O Ajātaśatru. For he hears from assembled brahmins that treachery toward a friend is the gravest of all sins.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They remember you, O king of men, on the battlefield; and in war they remember Jiṣṇu, the leader of warriors. When the roar of kettledrums and conches rises high, they remember Bhīmasena with his mace in hand.
They also remember the two sons of Mādrī in the midst of the battle, ranging in all directions, incessantly showering arrows upon the army — two great warriors, impossible to shake in combat.
I do not think, O king, that the future of a man can be known in advance — what will come to pass. If you, O Pāṇḍava, endowed with all righteousness, have come to this severe and painful suffering —
You alone should set all this right and even more, O Ajātaśatru, through your wisdom. For the sons of Pāṇḍu, all equal to Indra, would never abandon dharma for the sake of desire or wealth.
You alone, O Ajātaśatru, through your wisdom should bring about peace, whereby the Dhārtarāṣṭras, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Sṛñjayans, and whatever other kings are assembled, may all find happiness.
What Dhṛtarāṣṭra, your father's brother, spoke to me at night, O Ajātaśatru — together with his ministers and his sons, O king — hear now that speech of his.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayans are assembled, along with Janārdana, Yuyudhāna, and Virāṭa. Speak, O son of Gavalgaṇa, O son of a charioteer, that word instructed to you by Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Sañjaya said: I address Ajātaśatru and Vṛkodara, Dhanañjaya and the two sons of Mādravatī, Vāsudeva the Śauri, Yuyudhāna, Cekitāna, and Virāṭa —
And the aged lord of the Pāñcālas, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, and the daughter of Yajñasena — let all of you hear this word of mine, which I shall speak desiring the welfare of the Kurus.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, welcoming peace, swiftly yoked my chariot on behalf of the king together with his brothers, sons, and kinsmen. Let this be pleasing — let there be peace for the Pāṇḍavas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You sons of Pṛthā are endowed with all virtues; by your lineage, your gentleness, and your straightforwardness, you are born into a noble family — compassionate, generous, restrained by modesty, and firm in resolve.
An ignoble act does not befit you, O Bhīmasena; for your nature is such that even a blemish in you would stand out like a drop of collyrium on a white garment.
Where total annihilation of all is seen, where sin arises and hell is ever present — who, knowing this, would ever commit that act where defeat is the same as victory?
Blessed indeed are those who have done their duty to kinsmen; your sons, friends, and relatives who would give up a life of reproach — from that would surely come the prosperity of the Kurus.
If you sons of Pṛthā were to govern the Kurus, leading all and subduing enemies, that life of yours would be equal to death — for to live by slaying kinsmen is not good.
For who could endure to conquer you together with Keśava, protected by the arms of the son of Pṛṣata, with Sātyaki by your side — even having the gods as allies with Indra at their head?
Or who could endure in battle to withstand the Kurus protected by Droṇa and Bhīṣma, and by Aśvatthāmā, Śalya, Kṛpa and others, O king — guarded by the son of Rādhā, together with the kings of earth?
The army of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son is great; who indeed is capable of destroying it without himself being diminished? I myself see no lasting good in either victory or defeat.
For how could the sons of Pṛthā, like the baseborn from a low family, do deeds bereft of righteousness? I, having propitiated and bowed to Vāsudeva and the aged lord of the Pāñcālas —
With folded hands I take refuge with you all — how may there be welfare for the Kurus and the Sṛñjayans? For neither Vāsudeva nor Dhanañjaya would ever fail to act upon any word of yours.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When his very life is being asked first, what else remains? Knowing this, I speak for the sake of settlement. This is the view of the king, with Bhīṣma foremost among his counselors — that peace is the highest good for you here.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What word of mine do you hear, Sañjaya, as seeking war, that you fear battle? Non-war is indeed, dear one, greater than war; who, having obtained that, would ever fight, O charioteer?
If, O Sañjaya, every intention a man wished for in his mind were to succeed without effort, then he would do no work — this is known to me. There is much that is far easier than war.
What man, truly knowing, would ever choose war? Who, unless cursed by fate, would embrace battle? The sons of Pṛthā act for the sake of happiness, and for what is not opposed to dharma and beneficial to the world.
One who, hoping for happiness arising from action, yet truly knows that action by arduous means is suffering — one who desires happiness and wishes to overcome suffering, yet follows the pull of the senses' pleasure, torments his own body through the craving of desire, and impelled by that craving, only brings suffering upon himself.
Just as the power of fire blazing with its kindled splendor increases ever more, so too, with the gaining of wealth and desire, one is never satisfied — like a fire fed with ghee. Behold this vast accumulation of enjoyments belonging to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with us.
The unrighteous man does not become a master of pleasures; the unrighteous man does not hear the sound of song; the unrighteous man does not enjoy garlands and perfumes, nor does the unrighteous one enjoy ointments.
The unrighteous man does not dwell in fine garments; then how could he drive us away from the Kurus? Right here, having shaken us off, this very desire torments the heart within the body.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The king, himself in an uneven position, seeks evenness from others — that is not good. Just as one observes one's own conduct, so should one regard the conduct of others too.
Just as one who, having set a fire near deep, dense thickets of dry grass in the hot season, would grieve as the old fire spreads under the wind — so too the one seeking safety laments when winter passes.
Having attained sovereignty, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra now laments — for what reason, O Sañjaya? He clings to a son of wicked intellect, devoted to crookedness, dull, foolish, and without counsel.
Though unworthy, Suyodhana disregarded the words of the most trustworthy Vidura; and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, doting on his son, though perceiving rightly, yet enters into unrighteousness.
The intelligent one, devoted to the welfare of the Kurus, the learned, eloquent, and virtuous Vidura — King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O charioteer, forgot him in the affairs of the Kurus out of love for his son.
Of one who destroys honor, who is self-seeking and envious, violent and transgressing wealth and dharma, foul-spoken, enslaved to anger, whose soul is given over to desire, whose heart is wicked, and who is always calculating —
Of such a son — ungovernable, inauspicious, long-resentful, a betrayer of friends, O Sañjaya, of sinful mind — King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, though clearly seeing, abandoned dharma and righteous desire out of love.
Even then, O Sañjaya, it was evident to me when I was in prosperity: unless the Kurus met with ruin. Vidura, speaking words of wisdom, found no appreciation from Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
When they followed the counsel of Vidura, hardship did not come upon the Kurus; so long as they followed his wisdom, so long did the prosperity of their kingdom flourish.
Know from me today, O son of Gavalgaṇa, the counselors of the greedy Dhārtarāṣṭra — Duḥśāsana, Śakuni, and the son of a charioteer — behold his delusion!

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I, examining carefully, cannot see how there may be welfare for the Kurus and the Sṛñjayans, when Dhṛtarāṣṭra has taken sovereignty over others and banished Vidura of far-seeing wisdom.
Indeed Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his son hope for undisputed sovereignty over the entire earth; from him no trace of peace is to be found. He thinks the matter that belongs to me is already close at hand and in his grasp.
What Karṇa thinks he can sustain in battle, when Arjuna has taken up his weapon — great battles were fought in the past; why was Karṇa not their refuge even then?
Karṇa knows, and Suyodhana knows, Droṇa knows, and the grandfather knows, and the other Kurus who are there — that there is no other bowman equal to Arjuna.
All these Kurus know, and so do the other kings assembled there, that Duryodhana has been acting in transgression, and that without Phalguna the subduer of foes, there would be none.
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra thinks that by reason of his wealth it is possible to seize the possessions of the Pāṇḍavas — with the diademed one, whose weapon is as tall as a palm tree, going to the battlefield and knowing that ground.
The Dhārtarāṣṭras survive only because they have not yet heard the twang of the Gāṇḍīva in battle; and if the onset of the enraged Bhīmasena has not come — Suyodhana thinks his purpose already accomplished.
Even Indra would not dare to seize this sovereignty of ours, dear one, as long as Bhīmasena lives, as long as Dhanañjaya, Nakula, O charioteer, and likewise that hero Sahadeva of mine live.
If the aged king together with his son were to adopt this resolve, O charioteer — then the Dhārtarāṣṭras would not perish, O Sañjaya, burned by the wrath of the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
You know the suffering that has been inflicted upon us; honoring you, O Sañjaya, I would endure it. And what the Kauravas did to us in the past — the treatment we received from the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — that too I could bear.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Even now let all that continue as it is there; I shall pursue peace as you say. Let Indraprastha be my kingdom alone — let Suyodhana, foremost of the Bhāratas, grant that much.
Sañjaya said: Your conduct, O Pāṇḍava, is ever fixed in dharma; it is heard of and seen in the world, O Pārtha. Life is a great torrent and also impermanent — perceive this, O Pāṇḍava; do not bring yourself to ruin.
If the Kurus do not grant you a share except through war, O Ajātaśatru, I think it better to live by begging in the kingdom of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis than to rule through war.
Life in the human world is brief, a great torrent, constantly painful, and unstable; and it is further unworthy of the dignity of your age. Therefore, O Pāṇḍava, do not set evil in motion.
Desires indeed bind a man — they are the very root of obstruction to dharma, O king of men. A man of firm resolve who first crushes them wins blameless praise in the world.
The craving for wealth is the binding fetter here, O Pārtha; dharma itself is obstructed when one pursues that craving. But the one who chooses dharma is wise; the one greedy for pleasure falls away, following the pull of wealth.
Having made dharma the foremost of all actions, dear one, the man of great splendor shines like the sun; but through the abandonment of dharma, a man of sinful mind sinks even having gained this entire earth.
The Vedas studied, the vow of brahmacharya observed, sacrifices performed, gifts given to brahmins — one who considers the highest state supreme and again gives up the self from pleasures for many years —
One who excessively indulges in pleasure and what is dear, and does not practice the discipline of yoga — when his wealth is exhausted, diminished in happiness, he lies in endless suffering, driven by the impulse of desire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus, once more attached to the pursuit of wealth, one who abandons dharma and propagates unrighteousness — the foolish one, lacking faith in the next world, after leaving the body suffers in the realm of the dead, the dull one.
There is no destruction of deeds in the hereafter, whether of merit or of sin. The merit and sin of the doer go ahead of him; afterward the doer himself follows them.
Food offered to brahmins in the proper manner, purified by faith, endowed with fragrance and flavor, at funerary rites with the finest fees — such deeds as these are celebrated to your credit.
Here in this field, O Pārtha, is the action to be done; truly nothing remains to be done after death. What you have done — and the duty for the next world — is great merit praised by the righteous.
He abandons death, old age, and fear, hunger and thirst, and the unpleasantnesses of the mind — nothing remains to be done there, except for the satisfaction of the senses.
Such is the fruit of action, O king of men; with what is dear to the heart in its proper measure — do not, O Pāṇḍava, give up both worlds for a long time for the sake of what is born of anger or of joy.
The praise that comes at the end of righteous deeds — truth, restraint, straightforwardness, compassion; the ashvamedha and the rajasuya duly performed — do not again go toward the end of sinful deeds.
If you sons of Pṛthā are to commit this sinful act for a long time in the manner it seems, then dwell for years in the forests, O Pāṇḍavas — a painful dwelling for the sake of dharma.
Before going into exile, having arrayed the force that was then under your own command — always the Pāñcālas as your allies, Janārdana and the heroic Yuyudhāna —
Matsya the king of the golden chariot with his sons, Virāṭa with his warrior sons, and the kings who were previously conquered by you — all of them would take refuge in you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With great allies, blazing with power, standing in strength, placed at the fore by Vāsudeva and Arjuna, you would have struck down the best of your enemies in the midst of the arena and crushed the pride of the Dhārtarāṣṭra.
Why did you strengthen the power of the enemy? Why did you exhaust your own allies? Why did you spend years dwelling in the forests? Now, O Pāṇḍava, you wish to fight at an unfavorable time.
Either the unwise man fighting, O Pāṇḍava, or the one ignorant of adharma, strays from the path of prosperity; or even the wise man, though perceiving dharma, may through anger also stray from prosperity.
Your mind, O Pārtha, does not dwell on unrighteousness; and you have not committed sinful deeds out of anger. What then is that reason for whose sake you wish to commit this act that goes against wisdom?
Anger — not born of disease, yet bitter as a headache, a thief of glory, productive of sinful fruits — which the righteous drink but the wicked do not drink — drink it, O great king, and be at peace.
Who would desire that which is followed by sin? Forgiveness is indeed greater for you than enjoyments. Where Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu would be slain, where Droṇa with his son would be slain —
Kṛpa, Śalya, the son of Somadatta, Vikarṇa, Vivinshatí, Karṇa and Duryodhana — having slain these, what sort of happiness could there be? Tell me what joy you would find, O Pārtha.
Even having gained this entire earth bounded by the ocean, you would not escape old age and death, O king, nor the pleasant and the unpleasant, pleasure and pain. Knowing this, do not make war.
If it is for the sake of the ministers' desire that you intend to do a deed so arranged, then withdraw after handing over your own to them — do not today, I tell you, stray from the path that leads to the divine.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Without doubt, Saṃjaya, what you have said is true — dharma is the highest of all deeds. But having known me, Saṃjaya, you censure me; whether I practise dharma or adharma, you reproach me.
In a situation where adharma, wearing the guise of dharma, appears entirely as dharma in adharma's form, and where dharma, bearing the form of dharma, the wise perceive it clearly with their discernment —
Thus, in adversity, these two — dharma and adharma — who are eternally present in conduct, share the same outward mark. The first mark of whichever one is present is the standard; understand that, Saṃjaya, as the dharma of adversity.
When one's normal mode of living has been disrupted, the destitute man should seek to accomplish the deed by which he can restore it; yet both the man who, despite being in his normal state, acts in adversity's mode, and the man already destitute who persists in it — both are blameworthy, O Saṃjaya.
For brāhmaṇas who desire the preservation of their duties, the Creator has prescribed expiation; but in adversity one should censure those who engage in forbidden acts and stand in wrong conduct, O Saṃjaya.
For the purpose of imparting true understanding to the wise, conduct among the good is always prescribed; but as for those who are not brāhmaṇas and not learned — from them one should consider total severance to be the right course.
For that very purpose our fathers of old, and the grandfathers, and those others yet further back who sought wisdom and performed their deeds — I believe that in the end there is nothing, nothing, nothing for them.
Whatever wealth exists in this world, whatever belongs to the thirty gods in the realm beyond — the world of Prajāpati, the triple heaven, the realm of Brahman — none of that do I desire, O Saṃjaya, if it must come through adharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kṛṣṇa is master of dharma, skilled, versed in statecraft, devoted to brāhmaṇas, and wise; he governs kings of many kinds and great might, the Rājanya chiefs who enjoy royal fare.
If I, by renouncing, would be blameless, or if by fighting I would abandon my own dharma — let the greatly renowned Keśava declare that; Vāsudeva, who desires the welfare of both sides.
The Śaineyas, Caitrakās, Andhakas, Vārṣṇeya-Bhojas, Kaukuras, and Sṛñjayas — abiding by Vāsudeva's counsel, they curb their enemies and delight their friends.
The Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, Ugrasena and the others, all led by Kṛṣṇa and equal to Indra himself — the Yādavas, high-minded, of true valour, immensely powerful, and wealthy in pleasures.
Babhru of the Kāśī line has attained the highest prosperity, having obtained Kṛṣṇa, the lord, as his brother — Vāsudeva rains down desires upon him, as a cloud at the end of summer rains upon all creatures.
Such indeed is Keśava, dear one — moreover, we know him as one who discerns with certainty the right course of action; Kṛṣṇa is dear to us and the most righteous of all. I do not transgress the word of Keśava.
Vāsudeva said: O Saṃjaya, I desire the imperishable prosperity of the Pāṇḍavas and their welfare; and I always wish for the flourishing of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O sūta, who has many sons.
My desire, O Saṃjaya, is always just this — I would say nothing other than 'let there be peace' to them; and I hear that this is also dear to the king. I consider this to be equally proper for the Pāṇḍavas.
But the peace shown here is certainly very hard to achieve, O Saṃjaya — the Pāṇḍava has demonstrated it. Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his sons are greedy for what belongs to them; why then should their quarrel not intensify here?
You, O Saṃjaya, roaming here in search of the truth of dharma, know it from me and from Yudhiṣṭhira both. Then why do you speak of the proper disruption, according to an earlier settled principle, of a Pāṇḍava who is energetic, who fulfils his own duty as declared, and who maintains his household?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While this ordinance holds as it should, the opinions of the brāhmaṇas are many and varied: some declare fulfilment in the hereafter through action; some others, abandoning action, declare fulfilment through knowledge. A learned man who does not partake of food and drink cannot be satisfied — that is what is established and known among the brāhmaṇas here.
The branches of learning that accomplish action in this world — their fruit is attainable, not that of the others. In this matter, action has a visible fruit here: just as one afflicted by thirst is appeased after drinking water.
This ordinance is prescribed through action alone; action abides within it, O Saṃjaya. Whoever in that context deems something other than action to be good — that weak person's chatter is in vain.
It is through action that the gods shine in the world beyond; it is through action alone that the wind blows here below; apportioning night and day through action itself, the sun rises without cease, ever untiring.
The moon, untiring, traverses the months, the fortnights, and the conjunctions of the lunar mansions; the fire, untiring and blazing, burns and performs its action for all creatures.
Untiring, the goddess Earth bears this great burden by her strength; untiring, the rivers swiftly carry their waters, satisfying all living beings.
Untiring, the one of abundant splendour sends down rain, filling the atmosphere and heaven with its sound; untiring, Indra, the slayer of Bala, practised brahmacharya, desiring pre-eminence among the gods.
Having forsaken ease and the mind's pleasures, Śakra attained supremacy through that action; guarding truth and dharma vigilantly, practising self-restraint, forbearance, equanimity, and affection — cultivating all these, Maghavan won the chief sovereignty of the gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bṛhaspati practised brahmacharya with composure, his mind sharpened, in the proper manner; having forsaken ease and controlled his senses, he thereby attained honour among the gods.
The lunar mansions shine in that realm through action; the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and the All-gods too; King Yama, Vaiśravaṇa Kubera; the bright Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Apsarases — and sages who practise brahmacharya, the knowledge of the Vedas, and rites shine in that realm as well.
Knowing this dharma of all the worlds — of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas — why is it that you, O Saṃjaya, being knowledgeable among those who know, still exert yourself on behalf of the Kauravas?
Know that he is perpetually joined to the sacred recitations, as also to the Aśvamedha and Rājasūya; he is joined likewise to the bow, to armour, to wrist-guards, and further to the weapons of the chariot.
If the Pārthas should find a means of dealing with the Kauravas without slaying them — by restraining Bhīmasena in noble conduct — then a meritorious protection of dharma would be accomplished for them.
But if, while engaged in their ancestral duty and fulfilling their own task to the best of their ability, they should meet death by the decree of fate — that death too would be praiseworthy for them.
Or do you think that the entire principle of dharma for kings rests in battle, or alternatively that the principle of dharma rests in non-battle? That is just how I understand this speech of yours.
Having considered the primary division of the four varṇas, O Saṃjaya, and having heard your own duty, then consider the Pāṇḍavas' own duty — praise it or censure it, as your mind inclines.
A brāhmaṇa should study, then perform sacrifice, give gifts, and go to the foremost of holy tīrthas; he should teach others, officiate at the sacrifices of those fit to sacrifice, or receive lawful gifts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Similarly, a kṣatriya, having protected his subjects with dharma and vigilance, and having given gifts, performed sacrifices, studied all the Vedas, and taken a wife — doing meritorious deeds, he should dwell in his household.
A vaiśya, after studying, should diligently accumulate wealth through agriculture, cattle-herding, and trade, and protect it without negligence; doing what is pleasing to brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas, devoted to dharma, performing meritorious deeds, he should dwell in his household.
Service and reverence to brāhmaṇas — a śūdra should not study; sacrifice is prohibited for him; he should always rise early for the welfare of others and be untiring — this is remembered as the ancient dharma of the śūdra.
A king, guarding these carefully and vigilantly, engaging all the varṇas in their own dharmas, free from self-seeking desire, impartial towards his subjects, should not indulge unrighteous desires.
If one wiser than that, endowed with full knowledge of all dharmas, were to be found, he should discipline the offender, knowing him fully; but if he would not do so out of covetousness — that is not good in such a person.
When a cruel man, defying ordinance and seizing power, covets another's land — from that arises this war among kings. Armour, weapon, and bow were created there for that purpose; this deed was set in motion by Indra for the slaying of brigands — armour, weapon, and bow.
Where a thief steals wealth unseen, or where he takes it by force in the open — both of these are blameworthy, O Saṃjaya. What distinction do you make, then, regarding Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son who, driven by greed and following anger's sway, takes this as dharma?
The Pāṇḍavas' portion is established; others have seized it from us without cause. In our situation, even death in battle is praiseworthy — the ancestral domain is superior to another's kingdom. Declare these ancient dharmas of the Kauravas, O Saṃjaya, in the midst of the court.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those foolish and slow-witted men who have come under the sway of death and have been assembled by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — this deed again is even more sinful. Look at what the Kurus have done in the midst of the assembly.
The beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas, Draupadī, renowned and endowed with noble character and conduct — the Kauravas, with Bhīṣma at their head, stood by and ignored her when she was being constrained and violated by one driven by lust, weeping.
If the assembled Kauravas, with their young men and elders, had then restrained him, Dhṛtarāṣṭra would have done what is dear to me, and it would have been a deed accomplished for his sons.
Duḥśāsana dragged Kṛṣṇā in an outrageous manner into the midst of the assembly, even before her fathers-in-law; brought there, she spoke piteously, seeing no other protector than Vidura.
All who were there in that assembly, out of dependence on the king, were unable to speak in reply; only Vidura, speaking the righteous cause and understanding dharma, answered back to the man of little wisdom.
Without having spoken thus for dharma in that assembly, you now wish to instruct the Pāṇḍava. But Kṛṣṇā performed this pure and extraordinarily difficult deed — entering that assembly and from that ordeal rescuing the Pāṇḍavas, and herself as well, as a ship rescues from the ocean's flood.
Where the son of the sūta spoke in the assembly, to Kṛṣṇā standing there near her fathers-in-law: 'O Yājñasenī, you have no refuge; go now to the house of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Your husbands are defeated — they no longer exist as husbands. O beautiful one, choose yourself another husband.'
That which was deeply lodged in Bībhatsu's heart — bone-splitting, vital-point-piercing, terrifying — the sharp-flamed arrow of words, shot from Karṇa's mouth, fixed itself in Phalguna's heart.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As she stood wearing deer-hide garments, Duḥśāsana spoke harsh words: 'All of these are ruined, seedless like impotent sesame — they have gone to ruin, they will go to hell for a long time.'
The king of Gāndhāra, Śakuni, by trickery, said this at the time of the dicing to the Pārthas: 'Nakula is defeated — what do you have left? Stake Yājñasenī Kṛṣṇā in the game.'
You know all this, O Saṃjaya — this speech that was unspeakable in a game of dice, spoken just so. As for me, I myself intend to go there and to resolve this ruined matter.
If I can bring about peace for the Kauravas without sacrificing the Pāṇḍavas' cause, then my conduct would be meritorious and of great benefit, and the Kauravas would be freed from the noose of death.
Would the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra attend to the eloquent speech I would speak — delighting in dharma, purposeful, and non-violent — and would the Kauravas honour me when I arrived in their presence?
Otherwise, know that the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — sprinkled with arrows by the chariot-warrior Phalguna and by Bhīma, armoured for battle — are fools being consumed by their own deed.
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra speaks fierce words to the Pāṇḍavas who were defeated; but Bhīmasena, mace in hand, vigilant, will in due time remind Duryodhana of those words.
Suyodhana is a great tree made of wrath; its trunk is Karṇa, Śakuni its branches; Duḥśāsana is the flower and fruit in full abundance; the root is King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that man of no wisdom.
Yudhiṣṭhira is a great tree made of dharma; its trunk is Arjuna, Bhīmasena its branches; the two sons of Mādrī are the flower and fruit in full abundance; but the root is I, and brahman, and the brāhmaṇas.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with his sons is the forest; the Pāṇḍavas, O Saṃjaya, are the tigers in that forest. Do not cut down the forest that contains its tigers; do not destroy the tigers away from the forest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Without a forest, the tiger is slain; without tigers, the forest is cut down. Therefore the tiger should protect the forest, and the forest should shelter the tiger.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are of the nature of creepers; the Pāṇḍavas, O Saṃjaya, are the great Śala trees. A creeper does not grow without clinging to a great tree.
The Pārthas are prepared to serve; those tamers of enemies are also prepared to fight. Whatever Dhṛtarāṣṭra should do — let that lord of men do it.
The great-souled Pāṇḍavas, who walk in dharma, stand committed to peace; they are warriors in full strength — knowing this, O wise one, do not report it other than as it truly is.
Saṃjaya said: I take my leave of you, O god among men, O Pāṇḍava; I am going — may all be well with you. I hope I have not spoken any harsh or injurious word through my tongue's attachment to my mind.
Having taken leave of Janārdana, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, the two sons of Mādrī, Sātyaki, and Cekitāna — I depart. May all be auspicious and pleasant for you. Look upon me with a gentle eye, O kings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Go with our leave, Saṃjaya — go in well-being. You have never done anything displeasing to us. We know you, as you know us, and we all know you — pure in soul, standing in the middle, established in the assembly.
You are a trusted envoy, O Saṃjaya, and very dear to us; you speak auspiciously, are virtuous, and endowed with insight. You, O Saṃjaya, are never confused in your understanding, and you do not grow angry even when truth is spoken to you.
You never speak words that pierce to the vital point and are harsh; nor hollow flattery, nor bitter reproach. I know your speech, O sūta, to be this: delighting in dharma, purposeful, and non-violent.
You are the one most dear to us as envoy; Vidura would be the second who might come here. For you were seen often among us in former times; you are a friend equal to Dhanañjaya's own self.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
On your way from here, O Saṃjaya, go quickly and attend upon those brāhmaṇas who are worthy of it — those of pure vigour, endowed with right conduct, born in noble families, and possessed of all dharmas.
Brāhmaṇas devoted to Vedic recitation, those who live by alms, and the ascetics who dwell permanently in the forests — the elders among these should be saluted with my words; and to the rest enquire about their welfare.
The purohita of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the ācāryas, and the officiating priests who serve him — together with them, dear one, meet as is fitting and with all due propriety, O sūta.
The beloved teacher who did not abandon, who was obedient — desiring the Vedas, he practised brahmacharya; he who restored the science of weapons in its fourfold completeness — may Droṇa, when he is pleased, be saluted as is proper.
He who has mastered learning, is endowed with right conduct, who has restored the science of weapons in its fourfold completeness — the swift one who is like the son of a Gandharva: do enquire after Aśvatthāman's welfare.
Going to the dwelling of Śāradvatī's son, the great chariot-warrior, foremost among those who know the science of weapons — repeatedly proclaiming my name, O Saṃjaya, touch with your hand the feet of Kṛpa.
In whom reside valour, compassion, ascetic power, wisdom, noble character, truth in learning and being, and steadfastness — clasping the feet of Bhīṣma, the best of the Kurus, announce me to him there.
He whose eye is wisdom, the guide of the Kurus, widely learned, devoted to the service of elders, and sagacious — having paid your respects to that venerable king, tell him, O Saṃjaya, that I am in good health.
The eldest son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is dull-witted, foolish, treacherous, and wicked in conduct, O Sañjaya — yet it is he by whom the whole earth is ruled. Ask after the welfare of Suyodhana, dear friend.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His younger brother is equally dull, of the same disposition, O Sañjaya — yet he is ever a great archer, the most valiant among the Kurus. Ask after the welfare of Duḥśāsana, dear friend.
Vrindara — the wise, never confused in matters of policy, of great intelligence, endowed with all virtues — he never approves of war at any time. Ask after the welfare of the son of the Vaiśya, dear friend.
He who is unrivaled at dicing and gambling, of concealed stratagems, skilled at playing with dice, he who is unconquerable in the battle of dice — that Citrasena should be asked of his welfare, dear friend.
He whose constant desire has ever been that there be no other way for the Bhāratas than peace — that bull of the Bāhlīkas, noble-minded, may he greet me with affection as he did before.
Endowed with many excellent virtues, possessed of wisdom and never harsh, he who always bears anger out of affection — that Somadatta is worthy of reverence in my estimation.
Somadatta's son is the most worthy among the Kurus — he is our brother, O Sañjaya, and also my friend, a great bowman, the foremost of chariot-warriors. Ask after his welfare together with his ministers.
And whatever other young foremost Kurus there are — sons, grandsons, and brothers of ours — whichever of them you approach in turn, each shall be greeted with my words asking of his health.
The kings who have been assembled by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra for battle against the Pāṇḍavas — the Vasatas, the Salvakas, the Kekayas, the Ambaṣṭhas, and the foremost of the Trigartas —
— the heroes from the east and the north, from the south, and from the west and the mountains — all who are not cruel, who are endowed with good character and conduct — ask after the welfare of all of them, dear friend.
The elephant-riders, the chariot-warriors, the cavalry, the infantry, and the great assemblies of noble men — having announced that I am well, inquire of the health of all of them in full.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Likewise the ministers of the king who are skilled in statecraft, the door-keepers, those who lead the army, those who are diligently reckoning income and expenditure, and those who deliberate on great affairs —
Śakuni, the king of the Gāndhāras, the mountain-dweller, who is unrivaled at gambling and cheating at dice, who feeds the pride of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that one of crooked intellect — ask of his welfare, dear friend.
