Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: All these warriors of great valor whom you have enumerated — even if all of them were gathered together on one side, Bhīma alone would stand on the other.
My fear of Bhīmasena arises ever greater, Sañjaya — of that enraged, implacable warrior, as of a tiger before a great roebuck.
I lie awake through all the nights, breathing long hot sighs, afraid of Vṛkodara, dear Sañjaya, as a weak animal is afraid before a lion.
For in this army I see no one equal in might to that mighty-armed one whose splendor rivals Indra's — no one who could withstand him in battle.
That son of Kuntī, that Pāṇḍava, is implacable and relentless in enmity — he does not laugh without cause, he seems frenzied, he glances sidelong, and his voice is thunderous.
Of tremendous speed, tremendous energy, mighty-armed, of immense strength — he will bring an end through battle to my foolish sons.
Vṛkodara, bearing the mace seized in the grip of his thighs, stands like Death with rod in hand as the bull among the Kurus in battle.
In my mind I see that terrible mace of his — made of iron and steel, adorned with gold — raised like the staff of Brahmā.
As a powerful lion roams among herds of deer, so will Bhīma range through my armies.
Of all my sons he alone is of fierce valor — a great eater, contrary and always impetuous even in childhood.
My heart trembles when I recall how even in childhood Duryodhana and the others, fighting against him, were crushed like creatures by an elephant.
My sons have always been tormented by his prowess. He alone — Bhīma of terrible valor — has been the cause of the breach between us.
I seem to see Bhīma before me in battle, swallowing whole the armies of men, elephants, and horses, maddened with rage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Tell me, Sañjaya, of that hero Bhīmasena the implacable — equal to Droṇa and Arjuna in weaponry, equal to the wind in speed.
I count it a great gain that that slayer of enemies, that high-spirited one, did not kill all my sons right then and there.
He by whose might the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas of great strength were slain — how shall any human withstand his onslaught in battle?
He never remained under my control even as a child, Sañjaya — how much less now, when he has been wronged and tormented by my wicked sons?
Hard and cruel by nature, he would sooner break than bend; with his sidelong glance and knitted brows — how could Vṛkodara ever be pacified?
Broad-shouldered, matchless in strength, fair-complexioned, towering like a palm tree — Bhīmasena by measure exceeds Arjuna by a span.
In speed he surpasses horses; in strength he surpasses elephants; the middle Pāṇḍava of muted speech, with the eyes of a bee, is immensely powerful.
Thus did I hear from the mouth of Vyāsa himself in former times of this Pāṇḍava as a child — his form and his valor described truly and accurately.
With his iron rod, Bhīma — the foremost of strikers — when enraged will destroy in battle chariots, elephants, horses, and men.
Implacable, ever-wrathful, fierce, of terrible valor — he who previously acted against me and was dishonored, dear Sañjaya.
His mace of iron and steel — massive, well-jointed, gold-adorned, a slayer of hundreds, resounding with a hundred peals — how shall my sons be able to withstand it?
Like a boundless, unfathomable ocean swift as arrows — Bhīmasena is a fortress impossible to breach, dear Sañjaya, yet the fools wish to cross him.
The young fools who fancy themselves wise do not listen even as I cry out; seeing only the honey, they do not perceive the precipice ahead.
Those who engage in battle with this Wind in human form are surely urged on by fate — like great deer goaded toward a lion.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His iron-and-steel mace — four cubits long, six-edged, of immeasurable power, whose touch brings agony — how shall my sons endure its blow, dear Sañjaya?
As he whirls his mace and splits the heads of elephants, licking the corners of his mouth, tears flowing again and again —
— charging headlong in aimed attacks, uttering terrible roars, lunging against maddened elephants, roaring back at them —
— plunging into the chariot lanes and striking down warriors one by one — could my people escape even from blazing fire such as his?
That mighty-armed one, clearing a path, routing my army, dancing as it were with mace in hand, will show them the end of an age.
Like a rut-maddened elephant breaking flowering trees, Vṛkodara will plunge into the army of my sons in battle.
That tiger among men will strip the chariots of their warriors and banners and shatter their wheels, and he will tear down chariot-fighters and cavalry alike.
As the Ganges' current sweeps down the many diverse trees growing on the marshy banks, so will he plunge into the vast army of my sons, Sañjaya.
Surely my sons, my servants, and the kings allied with us will all come under his sway, crushed by the might of Bhīmasena, Sañjaya.
He it was who, entering the inner apartments of the palace in former times with Vāsudeva as his ally, brought down Jarāsandha, that king of mighty valor.
The entire earth had been subjugated and oppressed by the wise and powerful king of Magadha, Jarāsandha.
The Kurus through Bhīṣma's might, and the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis through policy — they alone did not come under his sway; only fate protected them.
Yet he was slain by the son of Pāṇḍu — that hero relying only on the strength of his arms, fighting without weapons. What greater feat can there be?
Like venom accumulated over a long time in a venomous serpent, he will release his power in battle upon my sons, Sañjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As the great Indra, best of gods, slays demons with his thunderbolt, so will Bhīmasena with mace in hand destroy my sons.
I seem to see Vṛkodara rushing forward — irresistible, unstoppable, of fierce speed and valor, his eyes blazing copper-red.
Even without a weapon, even without a bow, even dismounted from his chariot, even without armor — fighting with bare arms alone — what man could stand before him?
Bhīṣma, Droṇa the brahmin, and Kṛpa son of Śaradvat — they know that wise one's valor just as I, who know valor, know it.
Yet knowing the code of noble warriors and not wishing to flee from battle, these bulls among men will take their stand at the forefront of my armies.
Fate is mightier than all and specifically mightier than any man — it is because I see that victory is theirs, yet cannot restrain my sons.
Those great bowmen, taking the ancient path of Indra, will give up their lives in the tumult of battle, protecting their kingly honor.
Just as they are my own people, dear Sañjaya, so equally are the Pāṇḍavas — all are Bhīṣma's grandsons and disciples of Droṇa and Kṛpa.
Whatever gifts or honors were bestowed on them from our side, Sañjaya — those three elders out of their nobleness will repay that debt.
For one who takes up arms and seeks to uphold the duty of a warrior, death on the battlefield is said to be the highest good — so say even the brahmins.
I grieve for all of them — those who fight against the Pāṇḍavas. This very danger that Vidura foretold and cried out against from the beginning has now arrived.
Yet I do not believe that knowledge avails to ward off suffering, Sañjaya — for in the face of overwhelming power, even knowledge itself becomes destructive.
Even the sages, though liberated, observing the course of the world, are happy in happiness and pained by pain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What then of me, who am attached in a thousand ways to sons, to the kingdom and wives, to grandchildren and to kinsmen?
In this great uncertainty, what is the most fitting course for me? For when I reflect, I see nothing but the destruction of the Kurus.
The great calamity of the Kurus appears to have begun with the dicing — this evil was done out of greed by one foolishly craving sovereignty.
I believe this is the regular law of Time, which moves to its inexorable end — like the rim fixed to the wheel, there is no fleeing from it.
What is to be done? How should I act? Where shall I go, Sañjaya? These foolish Kurus perish, fallen into the power of Time.
Helpless, when the hundred sons are slain, I will hear the wailing of the women — and then how shall death not touch me?
As a blazing fire in the summer heat, fanned by the wind, burns through dry grass — just so will that Pāṇḍava with mace in hand, together with Arjuna, be the slayer of my people.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Of that warrior whose words, we have heard, have never proved false — even the three worlds together could stand as his opponent, if Dhanañjaya were his champion.
Even reflecting on it without ceasing, I cannot find any warrior who could face in battle with his chariot the one who wields the Gāṇḍīva bow.
As he shoots barbed arrows and reeds and heart-piercing shafts, no equal can be found to face in battle the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva.
Even if those two heroes among men, Droṇa and Karṇa, were to face him — there might be doubt in the world about the outcome due to their greatness, yet victory is not mine.
Karṇa is tender-hearted and negligent; the Teacher is aged and venerable; but the son of Pṛthā is capable, powerful, of the firm bow, and one who has conquered fatigue — the battle will be utterly tumultuous and yet he would remain unvanquished on all sides.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All are skilled in weapons, all are heroes, all have earned great renown — they would sooner give up the lordship of all the immortals than surrender victory. Only in the death of one of them or of Phalguna would there come peace.
Yet Arjuna has no conqueror, and no slayer of him exists; his wrath — how could it be pacified, that wrath which has risen up against fools?
Others too know the weapons — they are sometimes defeated, sometimes victorious — but of Phalguna alone is absolute and undivided victory spoken.
He summoned the thirty-three gods and satisfied the fire at Khāṇḍava; he conquered all the gods — I know of no defeat of his.
He whose charioteer is Hṛṣīkeśa, equal in character and conduct in battle — his victory is certain, dear Sañjaya, as is the victory of Indra himself.
The two Kṛṣṇas straining together on one chariot, and the Gāṇḍīva bow with its string drawn — we have heard that three blazing splendors are united in one.
We have no such bow, no such warrior, and no such charioteer — and this the fools who follow Duryodhana do not know.
A blazing thunderbolt falling on the head would leave something behind, Sañjaya — but the arrows shot by the Diademed one would leave nothing at all.
I seem to see Phalguna shooting, striking, tearing heads from bodies with showers of arrows.
I seem to see a blazing fire of arrows lit everywhere by the Gāṇḍīva, burning the army of my sons on the battlefield.
I seem to see that great Bhārata army, terrified by the thunder of Savyasācin's chariot, trembling and overwhelmed with fear.
As a fire blazing and ranging everywhere with its great flames, fanned by the wind, burns through dry grass — so will he burn my people.
When the Diademed one, standing firm as a relentless aggressor in battle, vomits forth his showers of sharp arrows — like Death the all-destroyer as fashioned by the Creator — he will be utterly unstoppable.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For when I repeatedly hear of those many diverse deeds in the dwelling place of the Kurus, and of their destruction on all sides and at the front of battle — then surely this annihilation comes upon the Bharatas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Just as all the Pāṇḍavas are valiant and desirous of victory, so too their allies, having abandoned concern for their own lives, are firmly committed to their triumph.
You yourself have described to me the valiant enemies — the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, the Matsyas, the Māgadhas, and the lords of the Vatsa country.
And that mighty one who, desiring to bring under his sway these worlds together with Indra, is the foremost of the universe — Kṛṣṇa — is devoted to the victory of the Pāṇḍavas.
Sātyaki, the grandson of Śini, quickly mastered the entire science of arms from Arjuna; he stands firm in battle, scattering arrows like seeds being sown.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna of the Pāñcālas, cruel in his deeds and a great warrior, will wreak havoc upon my forces in battle — he is a supreme master of weapons.
From the wrath of Yudhiṣṭhira, from the valor of Arjuna, from the twin sons of Yama, and from Bhīmasena — fear arises in me, my son.
A superhuman net spread in the midst — these lords of men will destroy my army. That is why I cry out, O Sañjaya.
Handsome, high-minded, radiant with prosperity, resplendent with brahmic lustre, wise, endowed with good judgment and understanding, righteous in soul — such is the son of Pāṇḍu.
Well endowed with friends and ministers, rich in those who wield and deploy resources, attended by brothers, fathers-in-law, and sons — all great warriors.
That tiger among men, the son of Pāṇḍu, is possessed of steadfastness and modesty, free from cruelty, generous, possessed of a sense of shame, and true in his valor.
Learned, self-disciplined, devoted to serving elders, master of his senses — him, endowed with all virtues, blazing like a kindled fire,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
scorching like the sun — what fool would fly into him like a moth into the Pāṇḍava fire, unstoppable, with a dull mind wishing for death?
Slender, tall, crested, that king, radiant as pure gold, will put an end to my dull-witted sons in battle.
I deem it right not to fight with them. Know this, O Kurus — in battle the destruction of the entire family will be certain.
This is the highest peace for me, by which my mind is calmed. If peace without war is what you desire, then let us strive for reconciliation.
But Yudhiṣṭhira would not disregard us even as we implore — for he abhors unrighteousness and has me particularly as the cause of it.
Sañjaya said: It is exactly as you say, O great king, O descendant of Bharata — the destruction of the warrior class through the Gāṇḍīva bow is clearly visible in battle.
But this I do not understand about you, steadfast as you always are — that you, who know the true nature of things, have come under the sway of your son regarding the left-handed archer.
This is not the time, O great king, for you who have always been the offender — for it was you yourself who first wronged the sons of Pṛthā, O bull among Bhāratas.
A father is the best friend, and one who is properly focused in his inner self — his beneficial counsel should be followed. One who causes harm is not called a guardian.
"This is won, this is gained" — hearing these words while the Pāṇḍavas were defeated, at the time of the dice-game, O great king, you smiled like a child.
You overlooked the harsh words spoken to the sons of Pṛthā in former times, thinking "we are winning the entire kingdom," without seeing the abyss ahead.
O great king, your Kurus with the Jangala region held the ancestral kingdom; then by means of heroes they won and occupied the entire earth.
The earth won by the arm-strength of the Pārthas was presented to you, and yet you think "I did this" — O best of kings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Your sons who had been seized by the king of the Gandharvas and were sinking in waters without a raft — the son of Pṛthā brought them back again, O best of kings.
And you smiled like a child when the Pāṇḍavas were cheated at dice and went into the forest again and again, O king.
Of Arjuna raining down many sharp torrents of arrows — even oceans would dry up, let alone those born of flesh.
Phalguna is the foremost among archers, the Gāṇḍīva the best of bows; Keśava is the foremost among all beings, and the Sudarśana the best of discs.
The glowing monkey is the best of banners among the bannered. Bearing all these on his chariot with white horses in battle, O king, he will destroy us like a revolving wheel of time raised on high.
Today the entire earth belongs to him, O king, O bull among Bhāratas — the king who has Bhīma and Arjuna as his warriors. He is the best of kings.
Likewise, seeing your army nearly slain by Bhīma and sinking, the Kauravas led by Duryodhana will come to ruin.
Struck with fear of Bhīma, your sons, O great king, and the kings who follow them will not obtain victory, O lord.
The Matsyas do not honor you today, nor do the Pāñcālas together with the Kekayas; the Śālvas and the Śūrasenas all disrespect you — for all these, knowing his valor, have gone over to the wise son of Pṛthā.
Those who do not deserve death yet act wrongfully through unrighteous deeds must be restrained by every means along with their followers — such an evil person is your son, O great king. You should not grieve over this.
What was said by me and by the wise Vidura at the time of the dice-game — this lamentation of yours concerning the Pāṇḍavas, O descendant of Bharata, all of this is futile, like the cry of one who is powerless, O lord of kings.
Duryodhana said: You must not be afraid, O great king, and you should not grieve for us. We are capable of defeating the enemies in battle, O king, O lord.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the sons of Pṛthā were exiled to the forest, Madhusūdana came with a great wheel of forces capable of crushing enemy kingdoms.
The Kekayas, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, and many other kings followed the sons of Pṛthā as their adherents.
And those great warriors came from near Indraprastha, and having assembled, they censured you along with the Kurus.
They, with Kṛṣṇa at their head, having gathered together, attended upon Yudhiṣṭhira as he sat clad in deer-skins, O descendant of Bharata.
The lords of men spoke of the necessity of recovering the kingdom, desiring to utterly destroy you along with your kinsmen.
Hearing this, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa were then addressed by me, O king, as I was frightened by fear of the destruction of kinsmen, O bull among Bhāratas.
"The Pāṇḍavas will not abide by the agreement" — such is my conviction. For Vāsudeva desires the complete destruction of us all.
"Excepting Vidura, all of you deserve death at the hands of that great soul; and Dhṛtarāṣṭra who knows dharma is not to be killed — he is the best of Kurus."
"And having utterly destroyed all of us, O father, Janārdana wishes to establish the sole kingship of the Kurus in Yudhiṣṭhira."
In that case, what is appropriate for us now — prostration, flight, or abandoning our lives and fighting back against the enemies?
"In fighting back, our defeat would be certain, for all the kings are under the sway of Yudhiṣṭhira."
"We have a disaffected kingdom, our allies are angry with us, we are condemned by all the kings and by our own people on all sides."
"But in prostration there is disgrace for kinsmen for all time." Yet I grieve only for my father, the lord of the people whose wisdom is his eyes — he has fallen into sorrow and endless affliction on my account.
For the obstruction of the enemies was carried out by your sons, and this was done for my sake — this was known to you before, O best of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those mighty warriors, the Pāṇḍavas, will retaliate the enmity against King Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with his ministers by destroying the family.
Then Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa spoke, O descendant of Bharata, perceiving that I was afflicted by great anxiety with my senses distressed.
"If the enemies attack us, you must not be afraid, O scorcher of foes. The enemies are incapable of defeating us in battle, O lord of the people."
"Each of us individually is capable of conquering all the kings. Let them come — we will destroy their pride with our sharp arrows."
"In former times, all the kings were conquered by Bhīṣma alone, enraged at his father's death, with a single chariot, O descendant of Bharata."
"That best of Kurus, enraged, slew very many of them; then they took refuge with this Devavrata out of fear."
"This Bhīṣma, supremely capable, together with us in battle, will conquer the enemies. Therefore let your fear depart, O bull among Bhāratas." This was indeed the firm conviction of those of immeasurable energy at that time.
"Formerly the whole earth was under the sway of the enemies; but now these men are not capable of defeating us in battle. For the Pāṇḍavas today have their wings clipped and are devoid of valor."
"The earth stands under our control, O bull among Bhāratas; and the kings, united in purpose in pleasure and pain, have been brought over by me."
"Even into fire they would enter, or into the ocean, O scorcher of foes — all those kings for my sake. Know this, O best of Kurus."
"And here they laugh at you as if you were a madman — you who are distressed, lamenting in many ways, frightened, while the enemies boast."
"For each one of these kings considers himself individually capable against the Pāṇḍavas. Let the fear that has come upon you depart."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Even Vāsava could not slay my entire assembled army — this army of inexhaustible form — nor even Brahmā the self-born."
"Yudhiṣṭhira, having abandoned the city, begs for five villages — he is afraid of my army and of my power, O lord."
"Whatever capability you attribute to the son of Kuntī, Vṛkodara — that is false. You do not know my full power, O descendant of Bharata."
"For there is no one on earth equal to me in mace-fighting; there was no one in the past who surpassed me, and there will be no one in the future."
"I am disciplined, accustomed to hardship, and one who has crossed to the far shore of knowledge. Therefore I have no fear anywhere — neither from Bhīma nor from any others."
"There is no one equal to Duryodhana in the mace — this is the firm conviction of Saṃkarṣaṇa. Good for you that I attended upon him at that time."
"Equal to Saṃkarṣaṇa in battle, superior in strength on earth — Bhīma could never endure my mace-blow in combat."
"A single blow that I would deliver to Bhīma in anger, O king — that alone would swiftly send him to the terrible realm of the son of Vivasvat."
"And I wish to see Vṛkodara with mace in hand, O king — this has long been sought after and is ever the desire of my heart."
"For slain by my mace in battle, that son of Pṛthā, Vṛkodara, with his limbs shattered, will fall to the earth bereft of life."
"Even the Himālaya mountain, struck by my mace-blow once, would be shattered by me into a hundred thousand fragments."
"He too knows this, and so do Vāsudeva and Arjuna — the firm conviction is that there is none equal to Duryodhana in the mace."
"Therefore let that fear of Vṛkodara depart from you in the great battle — I will remove him. Do not be downcast, O king."
"When he is swiftly slain by me, many chariot-warriors equal and superior in form will assail Arjuna, O bull among Bhāratas."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, Bhūriśravas, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, Śalya, and Jayadratha the king of the Sindhu —"
"each one of these individually is capable of slaying the Pāṇḍavas, O descendant of Bharata; and together they will send them all to the abode of Yama in an instant."
"That the entire army of kings is incapable of completely defeating Arjuna alone, the winner of wealth — there is no reason for that to be so."
"By Bhīṣma's torrents of arrows — hundreds and thousands of them — and by Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛpa as well, the son of Pṛthā will go to the realm of Yama."
For the grandsire Bhīṣma, son of Gaṅgā, born of Śaṃtanu, O Bhārata, was born equal to a brahmarishi and even the gods find him hard to overcome. His pleased father told him: "You shall not die against your will."
And Droṇa was born of the brahmarishi Bharadvāja, from the vessel called Droni. From Droṇa in turn was born Aśvatthāman, O great king, who is supreme in knowledge of weapons.
And Kṛpa, foremost among teachers, was born from the great sage Gautama, having sprung from a clump of reeds. He is glorious, and in my judgment he is invincible.
These three — father, mother, and maternal uncle — were not born of a womb, O great king. Aśvatthāman too is a hero, and he stands on my side.
All of these, O great king, are great chariot-warriors equal to the gods; in battle they would cause even Indra distress, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Karṇa I consider equal to Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Kṛpa. And Paraśurāma sanctioned him saying, "You are my equal," O Bhārata.
Karṇa had two beautiful, auspicious, natural earrings. He, the scorcher of foes, was asked by great Indra for them on behalf of Śacī, O great king, and was given instead an infallible, supremely terrible spear.
How could Dhanañjaya survive once that spear is employed against him? Victory is certain for me, O king, like a fruit already placed in hand; and the complete defeat of the enemy on this earth is manifest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In a single day Bhīṣma slays ten thousand warriors, O Bhārata. And Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, and Kṛpa are equal to him in their prowess as great bowmen.
And bands of sworn warriors among the kshatriyas, O scorcher of foes, have taken the oath: "Either Arjuna or we" — so shall Dhanañjaya meet them.
The kings consider these warriors sufficient for the slaying of Savyasācin. O lord, why then, O king, do you suddenly feel distress?
If Bhīmasena is slain, who else among the enemy would fight? Tell me that, O Bhārata, if you know it, O scorcher of foes.
Your five brothers, then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and Sātyaki — these seven warriors of the enemy, O king, constitute their supreme strength.
On our side the distinguished ones are Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa and others; Aśvatthāman, Karṇa son of the charioteer, Somadatta, and Bāhlika.
The lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, Śalya, the king of Avanti, Jayadratha, Duḥśāsana, Durmukha, and Duhsaha, O lord of men.
Śrutāyus, Citrasena, Purumitra, Vivingsati, Śala, both Bhūriśravas, and Vikarṇa — your own son.
I have assembled eleven akshauhinis, O king, while the enemy has only seven — how then could I be defeated?
Bṛhaspati has said that a force three times weaker may still be fought. My army, O king, is three times greater than the enemy's.
I see many deficiencies in the enemy, O Bhārata, and I see many virtues and abundant merits on my own side, O lord of men.
Having assessed all this — my supreme strength, O Bhārata, and the weakness of the Pāṇḍavas — you ought not to fall into delusion.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, he who was the conqueror of enemy cities, wishing to know what was timely and understanding the moment, questioned Sañjaya further.
Duryodhana said: Having obtained seven akshauhinis together with allied kings, O Sañjaya, what does Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, who is eager for battle, intend?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sañjaya said: Yudhiṣṭhira is exceedingly joyful, O king, and eager for war. Both Bhīmasena and Arjuna, and even the twins, feel no fear.
Arjuna, son of Kuntī, illuminating all directions, yoked his divine chariot, and Bībhatsu, wishing to recite his mantras, did so.
We saw him arrayed, shining like a lightning-lit cloud. After meditating upon his mantras, filled with joy, he spoke thus.
"See this as a good omen — we shall be victorious, O Sañjaya." Whatever Bībhatsu said to me, I find it to be true as well.
Duryodhana said: You praise and glorify those sons of Pṛthā who were defeated at dice. Tell me about the horses on Arjuna's chariot, and about his banner.
Sañjaya said: Viśvakarmā, the son of Bhuvana, together with Indra, O lord of men, fashioned many wondrous forms, as did Tvaṣṭṛ together with Dhata, O lord.
On that banner they placed forms through divine illusion — forms of great value, celestial, both large and small.
That banner blocked all directions to a distance of a yojana, horizontally and upward; yet it would not catch on trees even when surrounded by them — such was the illusion arranged by the son of Bhuvana.
Just as Indra's rainbow shines in the sky — not one color, and we cannot tell what it is — so too the banner fashioned by the son of Bhuvana: its form appears in many shapes.
Just as smoke from fire rises filling the sky, bearing luminous hues in its fiery body, so too the banner fashioned by the son of Bhuvana — it would be no burden and would cause no obstruction.
White horses swift as the wind, noble and divine, given by Citraratha, were yoked to it. Whenever they fell they were replaced — such was the boon granted beforehand.
Similarly, the king's horses, ivory-colored and large, yoked to the chariot, shine forth, equal to him in valor. Bhīmasena's steeds, resembling spotted deer, were equal in speed to the wind in battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dapple-bodied horses with partridge-speckled backs, given joyfully by his brother Phalguna, superior to his heroic brother's own horses, were joyfully yoked and carried Sahadeva.
Nakula, son of Mādrī, of the Ajamīḍha lineage, was carried by tawny horses, foremost of steeds, given by great Indra — powerful as the wind in speed — carrying the hero like Indra slayer of Vṛtra.
Horses equal to these in age, valor, and speed — unmatched, noble steeds, large and god-given — carry the young princes, Abhimanyu and the sons of Draupadī.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Whom did you see there, O Sañjaya, who had come as allies to fight the army of my son on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas?
Sañjaya said: I saw the foremost of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, Kṛṣṇa, who had arrived; and there also Cekitāna and Yuyudhāna the Sātyaki.
These two great chariot-warriors, each with separate akshauhinis, had joined the Pāṇḍavas. Both are renowned and consider themselves great men.
Then the Pāñcāla king with an akshauhini, surrounded by his ten sons with Satyajit at their head, with Dhṛṣṭadyumna as their leader.
Drupada, enhancing his glory, protected by Śikhaṇḍī, advanced, at that time overwhelming the body of all the armies.
Virāṭa together with his two sons Śaṅkha and Uttara, and with heroes led by Suryadatta, with Madirāśva at their head.
That guardian of the earth, together with his brothers and sons, surrounded by a full akshauhini of soldiers, had joined Pārtha's side.
Jarasandhi of Magadha and Dhṛṣṭaketu king of the Cedis had arrived separately, each surrounded by separate akshauhinis.
The five brothers of Kekaya, all bearing crimson banners, surrounded by an akshauhini, had joined the Pāṇḍavas.
These and so many others I saw assembled there, who will fight the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who knows the human battle-array, the divine, the gandharva, and the demonic — that great-minded Dhṛṣṭadyumna stands at the head of their army.
Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, O king, has been assigned as the portion of Śikhaṇḍī. Virāṭa with the Matsyas, who are fierce fighters, shall follow in that battle.
The powerful lord of the Madras was assigned as the portion of the eldest son of Pāṇḍu. But some of them said there: "The two of them seem unequal to us."
Duryodhana with his hundred sons, along with his hundred brothers, and the eastern and southern kings — these were assigned as the portion of Bhīmasena.
As Arjuna's appointed portion: Karṇa the son of the charioteer, Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and Jayadratha the king of Sindhu.
And whoever on earth considers himself a hero and is difficult to overcome — all of them Arjuna, son of Pṛthā, has assigned as his own portion.
The five brothers, princes of Kekaya, great bowmen, have designated the Kekayas as their own portion and will fight them in battle.
Their assigned portion also includes the Mālavas and the Śālva-Kekayas, and the two chief leaders of the Trigartas who are known as the sworn warriors.
All the sons of Duryodhana, and likewise those of Duḥśāsana, and also king Bṛhadbala — these were assigned as the portion of Abhimanyu, son of Subhadrā.
The sons of Draupadī, great bowmen bearing banners adorned with gold, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, will march against Droṇa, O Bhārata.
Cekitāna desires to fight Somadatta in single-chariot combat. And Yuyudhāna desires to fight the Bhoja, Kṛtavarman.
Sahadeva, son of Mādrī, a hero who makes enemies cry out in battle, assigned as his own portion your brother-in-law, the son of Subala.
Ulūka the son of the gambler, and the tribes of the Sārasvata region — Nakula, son of Mādravatī, assigned these as his portion.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever other kings, O king, shall march forth in battle to face them — the sons of Pāṇḍu have by challenge assigned those as well.
Thus their armies have been divided into portions. Whatever needs to be done regarding you and your sons, let it be done without delay.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: All my sons are fools, addicted to crooked gambling — those whose battle with the mighty Bhīma will come at the forefront of the fight.
All the kings, all those rulers of earth, already sprinkled by the law of Time, will enter the fire of the Gāṇḍīva bow like moths entering a flame.
I believe the army will be scattered by those great-souled ones who have been made into enemies. Who will follow it in battle once it has been shattered by the Pāṇḍavas in war?
For they are all atirathas — great warriors, heroes, glorious, blazing with energy — equal in brilliance to the sun and fire, conquerors in battle.
Whose leader is Yudhiṣṭhira and whose protector is the slayer of Madhu, and whose warriors are the two heroic Pāṇḍavas Savyasācin and Vṛkodara.
Nakula and Sahadeva, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna son of Pṛṣata, and Sātyaki, and Drupada, and the son of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
And Uttamaujas the Pāñcāla, and the unconquerable Yudhāmanyu, and Śikhaṇḍī, and Kṣatradeva, and Uttara son of Virāṭa.
The Kāśis and the Cedis, all the Matsyas and all the Sṛñjayas, and Babhru son of Virāṭa, and the Pāñcālas and the Prabhadrakas.
From whom not even Indra could wrest this earth against their will — those heroes, steadfast in battle, who could cleave even mountains.
Against all these, endowed with virtues, blazing with superhuman energy, my wicked son, while I cry out, desires to fight, O Sañjaya.
Duryodhana said: Both sides are of the same birth, and both move on the same earth. Why then do you consider victory to rest on the side of the Pāṇḍavas alone?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The grandsire and Droṇa, and Kṛpa, and the unconquerable Karṇa, and Jayadratha, Somadatta, and Aśvatthāman —
— wise-minded great bowmen whom even Indra together with the immortals is unable to conquer in battle — how then can the Pāṇḍavas, O father?
And all this earth has been created for my sake, O father, to crush those noble, resolute, heroic, fire-like Pāṇḍavas.
The Pāṇḍavas are not capable of looking upon my forces. I am fully prepared to fight the sons of Pāṇḍu together with their sons in battle.
All the kings who desire to do what pleases me, O Bhārata, will bind them as with a thread, like black deer.
Attacked by my great forces of chariots and by my nets of arrows, the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas will be overwhelmed.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: My son raves like a madman, O Sañjaya. For he is not capable of conquering Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira in battle.
For Bhīṣma always knows the might of those illustrious Pāṇḍavas together with their sons — great-souled ones who are versed in righteousness.
It is for this reason that I have never approved of war with those great-souled ones. But, Sañjaya, tell me again of their doings.
Who is it that keeps inflaming those vigorous Pāṇḍavas — those blazing great bowmen — as one feeds fire with oblations?
Sañjaya said: It is Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O Bhārata, who constantly inflames them, saying, "Fight! Do not fear battle, O best of Bhāratas!"
Whatever kings are there, assembled under the banner of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, will come together in battle — in the tumultuous sea of armour.
All of them gathered there in battle — enraged, along with their allies — I alone shall swallow, as a fish-eating reptile swallows fish in the water.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, Droṇa's son, Śalya, and Suyodhana — all of these I shall check, as the shore restrains the ocean that is home to sea-monsters.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As he spoke thus, the righteous king Yudhiṣṭhira addressed him: "Upon your courage and valour, all the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas are fully resting — rescue us in battle."
"I know you, O mighty-armed one, as one firmly established in the warrior's duty, capable alone and sufficient against the Kauravas who desire battle. Whatever you shall ordain will be our good, O scorcher of foes."
"The hero who stands in the forefront, showing his manliness when the routed are fleeing from battle and the broken are seeking refuge — a wise man would purchase such a man with a thousand. That indeed is the mark of nobility."
"Such are you — a hero, a warrior, and one of conquering valour, O bull among men. You are undoubtedly the protector of those afflicted by fear in battles."
While the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, was speaking thus, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, freed from all fear, spoke these words to me.
"O charioteer, go and tell all those warriors of Duryodhana in every province — the Kurus together with the Bāhlīkas, and the descendants of Pratīpa, and the son of Śaradvān."
"And likewise the son of a charioteer (Karṇa), and Droṇa together with his son, and Jayadratha, and Duḥśāsana, and Vikarṇa, and the king Duryodhana."
"Go quickly and tell Bhīṣma too: approach Yudhiṣṭhira with good faith only. Let not Arjuna, guarded by the gods, slay you. Quickly supplicate that Pāṇḍava, the hero of the world."
"For there is no warrior on this earth such as the ambidextrous Pāṇḍava (Arjuna) — the most knowledgeable of weapons."
"For the divine chariot of the Gāṇḍīva-wielder was furnished by the gods — he cannot be conquered by any mortal. Do not set your heart on battle."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: That Pāṇḍava (Arjuna) has the martial fire of a warrior and has been a celibate student from his very boyhood. Only the foolish — who lament like me — would go to battle against him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Turn back from war, O Duryodhana, O best of the Bhāratas. War is not to be praised in any and every circumstance, O subduer of foes."
"Half of the earth is enough for you and your ministers to live upon. Give to the sons of Pāṇḍu what is rightfully theirs, O subduer of foes."
"All the Kurus consider it to be in accord with righteousness that you should seek peace with the great-souled sons of Pāṇḍu."
"Come, my son, and look at your own army. Your forces have been wasting away from the very moment of your birth, but you do not perceive it out of delusion."
"For I do not desire war, nor does Bāhlika desire it, nor Bhīṣma, nor Droṇa, nor Aśvatthāman, nor Sañjaya."
"Neither Somadatta, nor Śalya, nor Kṛpa desires war, nor do Satyavrata, Purumitra, Jaya, and Bhūriśravas."
"Those very men upon whom the Kurus would rely when pressed hard by their enemies — those men do not welcome war. Let that, my son, please you as well."
"You do not act of your own will — it is Karṇa who makes you act, and the wicked-souled Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni the son of Subala."
Duryodhana said: I place no burden — neither on you, nor on Droṇa, nor on Aśvatthāman, nor on Sañjaya, nor on Vikarṇa, nor on the Kāmboja king, nor on Kṛpa, nor on Bāhlika.
"Nor on Satyavrata, nor on Purumitra, nor again on Bhūriśravas, nor on any others of your party do I lay a burden — and yet I give challenge."
"I and Karṇa, O father, having spread the sacrificial battle and made Yudhiṣṭhira the sacrificial victim, are consecrated for it, O bull of the Bhāratas."
"The chariot is the sacrificial altar; the sword is the ladle; the mace is the large spoon; the armour is the assembly hall; the four-priest rite is my chariot-team; my arrows are the sacrificial grass; glory is the oblation."
"By this self-sacrifice, O king, having worshipped Yama (son of Vivasvat) in battle, the two of us shall return in victory, having slain our enemies, clothed in glory."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I, Karṇa, and my brother Duḥśāsana — the three of us will slay the Pāṇḍavas in battle, O father."
"For either I, having slain the Pāṇḍavas, will rule this earth, or the sons of Pāṇḍu, having slain me, will enjoy this earth."
"I have renounced life, O king, and wealth and kingdom, O lord of the earth. I shall never, ever dwell together with the Pāṇḍavas, O Acyuta."
"Even as much land as a sharp needle's tip could pierce — that much, O venerable one, is not to be relinquished by us to the Pāṇḍavas."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: I grieve for all of you, my son — Duryodhana has been abandoned by me, and those who will slowly follow him as he walks to the abode of Yama.
"As tigers — the foremost of those who strike — slay the finest among herds of deer, so the Pāṇḍavas, assembled together in battle, will slay the best of your men one by one."
"It seems to me as something running against the current — that the wife of Bhārata (Draupadī), her hair parted, was flung down, terrified, and dishonoured by the long-armed one (Duḥśāsana)."
"Mādhava (Kṛṣṇa) will go on replenishing the already full strength of Pārtha's forces, and Sātyaki, the descendant of Śini, will stand in battle, scattering arrows like seeds."
"Bhīmasena will be at the front of those fighting at the van of the army — all will take shelter in him as a rampart that fears nothing."
"When you shall see elephants felled by Bhīma — their tusks shattered, like mountains in collapse, their foreheads split and streaming with blood —"
"— beholding them in battle, fallen like mountains, and in dread of the onslaught of Bhīma, you will remember my words."
"When you behold your army burnt down by Bhīmasena — its chariots and elephants destroyed, looking like a fire's path — you will remember my words."
"Great danger is coming upon you. If you do not make peace with the Pāṇḍavas, then slain by Bhīmasena's mace, you will attain peace (only in death)."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When you see the Kuru forces cut down and fallen in battle like a great forest felled, then you will remember my words."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus much and addressed all those kings, the king again questioned Sañjaya, O great king.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Tell me what those two great-souled ones, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya, said to each other — O greatly wise one, I am eager to hear your words.
Sañjaya said: Listen, O king, to how I saw Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya, and what those two heroes said to each other — that I shall tell you, O Bhārata.
"Keeping my eyes fixed on the tips of my toes, with reverence and hands joined in salutation, I entered the inner chamber, O king, to deliver the message to those two lords of men."
"Neither Abhimanyu nor the twins (Nakula and Sahadeva) approach that place where the two Kṛṣṇas (Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna) were, and where the beautiful Draupadī and Satyabhāmā were."
"Both had drunk madhu and asava liquors; both were smeared with sandalwood paste; both wore garlands, excellent garments, and were adorned with divine ornaments."
"There was a great golden seat, variegated with many kinds of gems and spread with diverse coverings, where those two subdurers of foes were seated."
"I noticed that Keśava's feet rested in Arjuna's lap, and those of the great-souled Arjuna were in (the laps of) Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) and Satyā (Satyabhāmā)."
"Pārtha then pointed me to a golden footstool; I touched it with my hand and sat down on the ground."
"I then saw, drawn away from the footstool, the two auspicious feet of Pārtha, with upward-rising lines on their soles — bearing auspicious marks."
"Upon seeing those two dark, large, youthful (feet) — rising like the trunks of sala trees, placed together on one seat — great fear came over me."
"These two are equal to Indra and Viṣṇu — the dull-minded do not perceive this, owing to their dependence on Droṇa and Bhīṣma and the boastfulness of Karṇa."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"These two are under whose command — in the mind of that man (Yudhiṣṭhira), the resolve of the righteous king will succeed. This conviction came to me then."
"Honoured with food and drink, covered (with hospitality), having received proper courtesies, I joined my palms above my head and prompted those two with (my) message."
"With one hand, accustomed to bow and arrows, bowing to the auspicious foot (of Kṛṣṇa), Pārtha prompted Keśava (to speak)."
"Rising like Indra's banner, adorned with all ornaments, Kṛṣṇa — whose valour is comparable to Indra's — being seated (again), addressed me."
"He, the foremost of speakers, (spoke) a speech that was pleasing, capable of expression, terrifying to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, gentle at first, and utterly formidable."
"That speech of one worthy to speak — properly syllabled and enunciated, pleasing in purport at first, but in the end withering to the heart — I heard."
Vāsudeva said: Sañjaya, speak these words to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra — in the presence of the chief of the Kurus, and also in the presence of Droṇa who is listening.
"Worship with great sacrifices; give fees to the Brāhmaṇas; take joy in your sons and wives — great danger has come upon you."
"Bestow wealth upon deserving recipients; beget sons born of desire; show affection to those who are dear to you — for the king hastens toward victory."
"This debt has grown large and does not depart from my heart — that Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī) cried out to me, 'O Govinda!' while I dwelt far away."
"The enmity you have is with the ambidextrous Arjuna, whose bow is the Gāṇḍīva — blazing with energy and invincible — and who has me as his second."
"Who, unless he is already claimed by Death — or even Indra himself in person — wishes to challenge Pārtha who has me as his second?"
"Whoever would conquer Arjuna in battle could lift the earth with his arms, could burn these creatures in his wrath, could hurl the gods down from the three heavens."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Among gods, demons, men, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and serpents — I do not see one who could approach the Pāṇḍava in battle, who could oppose him in combat."
"What was heard of at the city of Virāṭa — that great and wonderful feat of one against many — that is sufficient proof."
"When by a single son of Pāṇḍu, in the city of Virāṭa, the (Kuru forces) were routed and fled in all directions — that is sufficient proof."
"Strength, valour, energy, swiftness, lightness of hand, undepressedness, and steadiness — these are found in the Pārthas (Pāṇḍavas) and nowhere else."
Sañjaya said: Thus spoke Hṛṣīkeśa (Kṛṣṇa), exhilarating Pārtha with his words, thundering like Indra (Pākaśāsana) raining in the proper season in the sky.
Having heard Keśava's words, Arjuna — the diademed one (Kirīṭī), the white-horsed — spoke that great speech which causes the hair to stand on end.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard Sañjaya's words, the lord of men whose eyes are wisdom (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) then began to weigh those words according to their merits and defects.
And having calculated subtly the merits and defects, that discerning one — wishing for victory and thinking truly according to his understanding — with regard to his sons,
Having ascertained the strength and weakness of each truly and accurately, that wise lord of men then began to reckon (their) power.
Having weighed the Pāṇḍavas by the power and energy belonging to both gods and men, and the Kurus as having lesser power, he then spoke to Duryodhana.
O Duryodhana, this anxiety of mine never ceases; I believe this to be truly self-evident, not merely inferred.
All beings cherish supreme love for their own offspring, and they do whatever is pleasing and beneficial to them according to their ability.
In the same way, we observe that those who receive help from benefactors generally wish greatly to repay them with something highly pleasing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Agni, remembering what was done for him in the Khāṇḍava forest, may become an ally of Arjuna in this most dreadful clash between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
And the celestial beings, led by Dharma himself, who have become greatly devoted to the Pāṇḍavas, will come in many ways when summoned.
My conviction is that the gods, wishing to protect them, will rise up in fury equal to the thunderbolt, out of fear of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and others.
The sons of Pāṇḍu, those tigers among men, mighty and masters of weaponry, aided by the gods, cannot be withstood even by glance of a mortal.
He whose divine bow Gāṇḍīva is unapproachable, that supreme weapon; and whose two divine inexhaustible quivers full of arrows, gifts of Varuṇa, are vast treasuries of shafts—
Whose divine banner bears the monkey and moves swift as smoke, unimpeded; whose chariot has no equal in splendor in the four-cornered earth—
The rumble of whose chariot is heard by men like the roar of great clouds, and whose sound, comparable to a great thunderbolt, is terrifying to his enemies—
Him whom the entire world judges to possess superhuman valor, whom the kings know in battle as one who can conquer even the gods—
Who appears as if tossing five hundred arrows in an instant, releasing them in the mere twinkling of an eye and sending them flying far—
Of whom Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Droṇa's son Aśvatthāmā, the king of Madra Śalya, and all neutral men have spoken—
That subduer of enemies, Pārtha, tiger among chariot warriors, standing ready for battle, cannot be defeated by kings even with superhuman effort.
That son of Pāṇḍu, who launches five hundred arrows in a single burst, is equal in the strength of his arms to Kārtavīrya himself.
In this great and terrible conflict, I see that great bowman Arjuna, protected by Mahendra and Upendra, striking down enemies as it were.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus reflecting upon all of this day and night, O Bhārata, I am sleepless and joyless, consumed by thoughts of peace for the Kurus.
A very great rise and fall of the Kurus is at hand; and for this conflict there is no end other than peace.
Peace with the Pāṇḍavas always pleases me, my son, not conflict; for I always believe the Pāṇḍavas to be more powerful than the Kurus.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard his father's words, Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, exceedingly wrathful, harboring immense anger, spoke again thus:
O best of kings, let that fear of yours depart — that fear in which you think the Pāṇḍavas would be aided by the gods and thus impossible to overcome.
O Bhārata, the gods attained their divine status by freedom from desire and hatred, by abstaining from treachery and greed, and by equanimity in their dispositions.
Thus Dvaipāyana Vyāsa, and Nārada the great ascetic, and Rāma the son of Jamadagni once told us this teaching.
The gods never act as humans do — out of desire, greed, compassion, or hatred, O bull of the Bhāratas.
For if Agni, Vāyu, Dharma, Indra, and the two Aśvins were to act out of passionate attachment, the Pāṇḍavas would not have suffered as they did.
Therefore you should never worry about this, O Bhārata; for these gods are always evenhanded in their regard for all things.
But if divine authority were seen in the gods to stem from desire, hatred, or greed, it would never hold sway.
Agni, the knower of all things born, whom I have always energized with my mantras, ever blazes with the desire to burn all the worlds, encircling them on all sides.
Whatever supreme energy the celestial beings possess — know, O Bhārata, that I have an energy beyond theirs, incomparable and surpassing.
O king, when the earth is splitting apart and the peaks of mountains are crumbling, I stabilize them through my incantations, even as the world watches.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever terrifying, immense sound arises for the destruction of moving and non-moving, conscious and unconscious beings—
—showers of stones and violent winds I always calm here, even as the world beholds it, out of compassion for all creatures.
Chariots and foot soldiers march over waters that I have made solid; I alone set in motion the course of both the gods and the asuras.
In whatever regions I march with akshauhini armies for some purpose, water flows wherever I desire.
In my domain, O king, there are no terrors such as serpents; fearsome creatures do not harm those who sleep under my protection.
O king, the rain clouds shower abundantly for those dwelling in my realm; all the people are virtuous; and there are no calamities in my domain.
The two Aśvins, Vāyu, Agni, the Maruts along with the slayer of Vṛtra, and Dharma himself do not venture to protect those I hate.
For had they been capable of protecting those I hate by their power, the Pāṇḍavas would not have suffered for thirteen years.
Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the asuras, nor the rakshasas are capable of saving one whom I hate — I tell you this truly.
Whatever I continually contemplate — whether auspicious or inauspicious — that has never failed for me regarding both friends and enemies alike.
Whatever I declare saying 'this shall come to pass,' O scorcher of foes, that has never turned out otherwise — they know me as one who speaks truth.
This greatness of mine, witnessed by the world and renowned in all directions, has been spoken for your reassurance, O king, not out of boastfulness.
For I, O king, have never before been one to boast; indeed, it is improper conduct for one to praise oneself.
You shall hear of the Pāṇḍavas and the Matsyas and the Pāñcālas together with the Kekayas, and Sātyaki and Vāsudeva, conquered by me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Just as rivers perish entirely upon reaching the ocean, so too shall they perish completely, together with their kinsmen, when they encounter me.
Supreme intelligence, supreme energy, supreme heroic strength are in me; supreme knowledge and supreme discipline are mine, surpassing those of the Pāṇḍavas.
Whatever the grandsire Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Śala know in the science of weapons — all of that resides in me.
Having spoken thus, O Bhārata, O subduer of enemies, he who sought battle questioned Sañjaya again, wishing to know what tasks needed to be done at the right moment.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: But as that son of Vicitravīrya was thus eagerly inquiring about the Pāṇḍavas, Karṇa, disregarding him, spoke to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, gladdening the assembly of the Kauravas.
The divine weapon known as Brahmā's city, which I obtained from Rāma by making a false claim — knowing this, he told me even then: 'At your time of death it will fail you.'
Though I bowed humbly in my great transgression, the great seer and teacher cursed me — that great sage of blazing splendor who is capable of burning even the earth along with the ocean.
Yet his mind was appeased by my devoted service and my own heroic exertion; thus that weapon still remains available to me in some measure — therefore I am capable, and this is my responsibility.
Having obtained that grace of the sage even for an instant, I shall slay the Pāñcālas, the Karūṣas, the Matsyas, and the Pāṇḍavas together with their sons and grandsons, and I shall attain worlds conquered by the sword.
Let the grandsire stand near you, and Droṇa and all the foremost kings — advancing with force in proper array, I shall slay the Pāṇḍavas; this is my burden.
Bhīṣma spoke to him who was boasting thus: 'Why do you boast, O Karṇa, whose intellect is seized by fate? Do you not know, Karṇa, that when the chief warrior is slain in battle, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra would be slain too?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What Dhanañjaya, with Kṛṣṇa as his second, accomplished in burning the Khāṇḍava forest — upon merely hearing of that deed, you together with your kinsmen might have been able to restrain yourself.
And that power weapon which the great-souled lord Mahendra, king of the thirty gods, gave you — you shall see it reduced to ashes, fallen and shattered, struck by Keśava's discus.
And that serpent-headed arrow of yours which shines and is always honored with the finest garlands and kept with great care — struck by the Pāṇḍava's shafts, it shall go to destruction along with you, O Karṇa.
O Karṇa, Vāsudeva protects Kirīṭī — the slayer of Bāṇa and Bhaumasura — he who is the slayer of enemies greater than even ones such as you in the thick of battle.
Karṇa said: Without doubt, the lord of the Vṛṣṇis is as described — and even more, that great-souled one. But as for the harsh words the grandsire has spoken to me — let the grandsire hear the fruit of those words.
I lay down my weapons — never shall the grandsire see me in battle, nor in the assembly hall; but when you are at peace, all the kings on earth shall witness my power.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, that great bowman left the assembly hall and went to his own dwelling. Then Bhīṣma, O king, laughing, spoke to Duryodhana alone in the midst of the Kauravas.
'The son of the charioteer is said to be true to his vow — then why can he not bear that burden? Counter his battle-array, cleave open skulls, and behold the destruction of the world from Bhīmasena!'
'When the Avantis, Kaliṅgas, Jayadratha, Vedadhvaja, and Bāhlika stand firm, I shall always slay thousands upon tens of thousands of the enemy's warriors.'
'From the very moment that the son of Vikartana, that basest of men, falsely claiming brahminhood, obtained that weapon from the blessed and blameless Rāma — from that very moment his dharma and his austerities were destroyed.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, after Bhīṣma had spoken to the king and Karṇa had laid down his weapons and departed, Duryodhana, the dim-witted son of Vicitravīrya's son, spoke to the son of Śaṃtanu.
Duryodhana said: Among all men who are equal and of the same birth, how can you believe that victory belongs exclusively to those Pāṇḍavas?
We are all of the same lineage, all born of human wombs — O grandsire, how do you foresee victory for the sons of Pāṇḍu?
I do not undertake this enterprise relying on you, nor on Droṇa, nor on Kṛpa, nor on Bāhlika, nor on any other foremost kings.
I, Karṇa the son of Vikartana, and my brother Duḥśāsana — we three shall slay the five Pāṇḍavas in battle with sharp arrows.
After that, O king, with great sacrifices of various kinds and immense gifts, I shall gratify the brahmanas with cows, horses, and wealth.
Vidura said: O dear one, we have heard that a certain fowler of old spread a snare on the ground for the purpose of catching birds.
In that snare two birds of equal strength were caught simultaneously; picking up that snare, both of those sky-goers flew away.
Seeing those two having taken to the sky, the fowler then chased after them persistently, following wherever they went.
Then a certain sage who had completed his daily rites and was dwelling in his hermitage saw that hunter running thus after the birds he desired.
O Kauravya, the sage then questioned that earth-dweller who was swiftly pursuing those two who moved through the sky, with this verse:
'This strikes me as a remarkable wonder, O hunter — you are pursuing on foot two birds that fly and soar through the air!'
The fowler said: 'Both of these birds together are carrying off my single snare; wherever they quarrel with each other, there they shall fall into my power.'
Vidura said: Those two birds, having come to quarrel, bound together by the snare of death, grappling with each other in their utter foolishness, fell to the ground.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, as those two fought furiously, led by the noose of death, the hunter approached undetected and seized them both.
Likewise, those kinsmen who fall into mutual strife over wealth come under the power of their enemies, just as the two birds did through their quarrel.
Eating together, conversing together, asking after one another, and meeting together — these are the duties of kinsmen; never is strife among them proper.
In that age when all men of good will serve and honour their elders, they become invincible, like a forest protected by a lion.
Those who, having obtained wealth, sit dejected and despondent, hand over their prosperity to their enemies, O bull of the Bhārata line.
Kinsmen separated from each other smoulder like firebrands of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; united, they blaze brightly, O bull of the Bhāratas.
I will now tell you something else that I myself witnessed on a mountain. Hear it too, O Kauravya, and act for your own good accordingly.
We were travelling together with Kirātas and with Brahmins equal to the gods — those skilled in the lore of the Jambhaka and Vatika sciences — towards the northern mountain.
The whole of Gandhamādana mountain was densely forested, its masses of herbs glowing with light, and it was frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
There we all saw honey, pale and free of bees, stored in a jar-sized deposit, lodged in a difficult desert ravine.
It was guarded by venomous serpents and was exceedingly dear to Kubera; a mortal man who tasted it would attain immortality.
"The sightless gain sight; the old become young again" — so declared those Brahmins who were adepts in the Jambhaka science.
Then the Kirātas, O king, beholding it and coveting it, perished in that treacherous mountain cave infested with serpents.
In just the same way, your son desires to possess the whole earth alone; blinded by delusion, he sees the honey but does not see the precipice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Duryodhana is eager to fight Savyasācin in battle, yet I do not see in him such splendour or valour as would match that.
That hero who conquered the entire earth single-handedly from his chariot stands waiting, bearing your gaze with patience, O king.
Drupada, the king of the Matsyas, and the enraged Dhanañjaya — like fires fanned by the wind, they would leave no remnant on the battlefield.
Take king Yudhiṣṭhira to your heart, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra; for when two such warriors fight, victory cannot be certain for either side.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Duryodhana, understand what I am about to say to you, my son. You think a wrong path is the right road, like a traveller who has lost his way.
You presume to measure the splendour of the five sons of Pāṇḍu as if measuring the five great elements — those souls of surpassing greatness.
As for Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, who is established in the highest Dharma here — you are not capable of knowing him without perceiving his ultimate station.
And Bhīmasena, the son of Kuntī, who has no equal in strength — you reckon him, the ender of battles, as a tree might reckon a great storm.
The wielder of Gāṇḍīva's bow, foremost among all bearers of weapons, like Mount Meru among mountains — what wise man would fight him in battle?
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna of the Pāñcālas — like Indra hurling his thunderbolt, loosing arrows into the midst of enemies, whom today would he not strike down?
And Sātyaki too, fierce and invincible, honoured among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍava line, will shatter your army.
And that Kṛṣṇa of the lotus eyes who surpasses the three worlds in glory — what wise man would fight him?
On one side are his wives, his kinsmen, and his relations, and this whole earth itself; on the other side stands Dhanañjaya alone — and he values them equally.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vāsudeva too is fierce and self-controlled; wherever the Pāṇḍava stands, that force is unbearable even for the earth — for Keśava is there.
Abide, my son, by the counsel of the virtuous and of friends who speak for your benefit. Endure with patience your grandsire Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu.
And heed me as I counsel you for the good of the Kurus. Listen also to Droṇa, Kṛpa, Vikarṇa, and the great king Bāhlika.
These men you should regard just as you regard me, O Bhārata; for all of them are versed in Dharma and bear equal affection for you.
What happened in the city of Virāṭa, when your army, panic-stricken, abandoned the cattle and scattered before Arjuna and his brothers —
— and what extraordinary and wondrous things are heard to have occurred in that city, wrought by one against many — that example alone should suffice you.
If Arjuna alone accomplished all that, what more need be said when all of them act together? Acknowledge your brothers and provide for them according to their due.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to Suyodhana, the greatly wise and illustrious Dhṛtarāṣṭra turned again to question Sañjaya.
"Tell me, Sañjaya, what remained after Vāsudeva had spoken — what Arjuna said to you; I am greatly eager to hear it."
Sañjaya said: Having heard the words of Vāsudeva, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī — fierce and unyielding — spoke in due course while Vāsudeva listened.
"Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Sañjaya, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the great king Bāhlika —
— Aśvatthāmā, Somadatta, Śakuni the son of Subala, Duḥśāsana, Śala, Purumitra, and Viviṃśati —
— Vikarṇa, Citrasena, King Jayadratha, Vinda and Anuvinda from the Avantis, and Durmukha of the Kuru line —
— the Sindhu king, Duhsaha, Bhūriśravas, King Bhagadatta, and the king Jalanandha —
— and whatever other kings have assembled there to fight for the good of the Kauravas, ready to die in the fire of the Pāṇḍavas when it blazes up, gathered there by Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, O charioteer —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— all these assembled men are to be greeted with proper courtesy and salutation on my behalf; say this, Sañjaya, in the midst of that assembly: to Suyodhana, the foremost of evil-doers —
— that wrathful, evil-minded prince, that wicked and utterly greedy son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — let him together with his counsellors hear this entire message of mine, O Sañjaya.
Having thus established his charge to me, Dhanañjaya then turned to look at Vāsudeva and spoke this further word, purposeful and righteous — Pṛthā's son, the wise one, his wide eyes red at their corners.
"As you have heard the collected words of that great-souled hero Madhupravira spoken, so too shall my words be delivered by you, to all the assembled kings, everywhere."
"As no sacrificial oblation is performed amid the smoke of arrow-fire and the din of chariot-wheels, with the bow as ladle and the power of weapons as the oblation — so, having come together, strive with care and reverence before that great battle begins."
"If you will not yield to the slayer of foes the share of Yudhiṣṭhira that is rightfully desired, then with sharp arrows I shall send your horses, foot-soldiers, and elephants to the inauspicious realm of the ancestors."
Then, having taken leave of four-armed Hari and bowing to Dhanañjaya, I swiftly departed and came here with speed, O you of divine radiance, to bring this momentous message to your presence.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, did not welcome that speech and all fell silent, the assembled kings rose from their seats.
O great king, when all the kings of the earth had risen and departed and they were alone, the king proceeded to question Sañjaya.
Led by submission to his son's will, yet hoping for their victory, he sought to know the resolve of both sides — his own and the Pāṇḍavas'.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Son of Gavalgaṇa, tell us what is substance and what is dross — whatever exists in our own army — for you know everything about the Pāṇḍavas with precision. What is greater on their side, what is lesser on ours?
You are the one who knows the essence of both sides and sees all; you are skilled in Dharma and wealth, knowing the certain truth. Thus questioned by me, O Sañjaya, tell all — which of those who would fight will not survive this?
Sañjaya said: I would never tell you anything in private, O king, for envy would overpower you. Bring your father, firm in his vows, and Queen Gāndhārī, O descendant of Ajamīḍha.
Those two would curb your envy, O lord of men; both are knowers of Dharma, both skilled and sure in judgment. In their presence I would tell you in full the entire counsel of Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having understood the mind of Sañjaya and of his own son, the greatly wise Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana came forward and spoke.
"Sañjaya, to Dhṛtarāṣṭra who asks you, declare everything as far as he inquires; declare everything you truly know about the matter, exactly as it stands — the truth regarding Vāsudeva and Arjuna."
Sañjaya said: Arjuna and Vāsudeva — two supreme archers, supremely honoured, arisen beyond desire, balanced toward the welfare of all beings —
— dwelling in the space between heaven and earth as is befitting to those great souls, Vāsudeva's wheel turns there by his maya, O lord.
Having known the strength and weakness of the force that is adverse to the Pāṇḍavas yet highly esteemed among the Pāṇḍavas themselves, hear it from me in brief.
Naraka, Śambara, Kaṃsa, and the Cedi king — all of terrible aspect — Mādhava, Janārdana, conquered them as if in sport.
The earth, the sky, and the heavens — the Uttama Puruṣa, that supremely distinguished soul, the self-controlled one, brings them all under his own will by mind alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Since you keep asking again and again, O king, in order to know the strength and weakness of the Pāṇḍava force, hear it from me as I speak.
On one side the whole universe; on the other Janārdana — Janārdana surpasses the entire universe in essence.
Janārdana could reduce this universe to ash by mind alone; but the entire universe is not capable of reducing Janārdana to ash.
Where truth is, where Dharma is, where modesty and uprightness are — there Govinda abides. Where Kṛṣṇa is, there is victory.
The Uttama Puruṣa, the soul of all beings, Janārdana, stirs earth, sky, and heaven as if in sport.
Making the Pāṇḍavas his sacrificial session and bewitching the world, as it were, he desires to burn your sons — those fools devoted to unrighteousness.
Keśava, the Bhagavān, turns the wheel of time, the wheel of the world, and the wheel of the ages without ceasing by means of his own yoga.
Of time, of death, and of all that moves and stands still, the Bhagavān alone is the lord — this is the truth I declare to you.
Even though Hari, the great Yogin, is lord of the entire universe, he undertakes actions to perform them as if he were a weak labourer.
By that means Keśava bewilders the worlds through his yoga of maya; but those mortals who surrender to him alone are not deluded.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: How is it that you know Mādhava as the great lord of all worlds, while I do not know him so? Tell me this, Sañjaya.
Sañjaya said: Knowledge, O king — you do not have it; my knowledge is not diminished. One devoid of knowledge, overwhelmed by darkness, does not recognise Keśava.
By knowledge, dear one, I know Madhusūdana as he who pervades the three ages — the uncreated maker, the god who is the origin and dissolution of all beings.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Son of Gavalgaṇa, what devotion is it that you have constantly toward Janārdana, by which you know Madhusūdana as pervading the three ages?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sañjaya said: I do not resort to illusion — may it go well with you; I do not practise unrighteous conduct in vain. With a purified heart, through devotion and through scripture, I know Janārdana.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Duryodhana, surrender to Hṛṣīkeśa, to Janārdana. Our trusted Sañjaya has spoken — dear son, seek refuge in Keśava.
Duryodhana said: If the Bhagavān, the son of Devakī, will destroy the world while proclaiming his friendship for Arjuna, I will not go to Keśava today.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Downward goes this son of yours and Gāndhārī — this man of utterly wicked mind, envious, evil-souled, arrogant, and a transgressor of the counsel of his betters.
Gāndhārī said: O you who crave dominion, O wicked-souled one, O transgressor of the elders' commands — foolish one, having abandoned your father and me for the sake of a life built on power,
increasing the joy of the ill-willed and multiplying my grief — slain by Bhīmasena, you will then remember your father's words.
Vyāsa said: You are dear to Kṛṣṇa, O king Dhṛtarāṣṭra — hear me. Sañjaya, whose envoy he is, will engage you in what is beneficial.
This one knows Hṛṣīkeśa in both his ancient and his present aspect; by listening to him with single-pointed devotion, one is freed from a great fear.
O son of Vicitravīrya, men enveloped by anger, elation, and delusion, bound by snares of many kinds, who are not content with their own wealth —
those blinded by desire come again and again under the sway of Yama, led by their own deeds like the blind leading the blind.
This is the one path by which the wise travel; having seen it, the great soul transcends death and is not ensnared there.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Come, Sañjaya, tell me the path free from all fear, by treading which I may reach Hṛṣīkeśa and attain the highest peace.
Sañjaya said: One who has not disciplined the self can never know Janārdana, who has disciplined his self. Yet the means for the self lies nowhere else but in the restraint of the senses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The renunciation of desire when the senses are aroused, vigilance, and non-injury — these are, without doubt, the source of true knowledge.
Strive diligently, O king, in the restraint of the senses and without sloth; let your intellect not waver — rein it in from wherever it strays.
The Brāhmaṇas declare this to be certain knowledge — the steady holding of the senses in check. This is indeed the knowledge and the path by which the wise proceed.
Keśava cannot be attained, O king, by men whose senses remain unconquered. He who is self-controlled, having approached through scripture and yoga, becomes serene in the truth.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Tell me further, Sañjaya, of Puṇḍarīkākṣa as I ask — knowing the meaning of his names and deeds, may I attain the Supreme Person.
Sañjaya said: I have heard the auspicious etymological explanation of that god's names, to the extent that I know it — for Keśava is indeed immeasurable.
Because he dwells in all beings, because of his divinity as Vasu, and because of his divine origin — he is known as Vāsudeva. Because of his righteousness he is called Vṛṣṇi.
Know that Mādhava is so called because of his silence, meditation, and yoga, O Bhārata; and Madhusūdana, the slayer of Madhu, is so called because he dissolves into all principles of reality.
The syllable 'kri' denotes existence, and 'na' denotes bliss; by the union of these two meanings Kṛṣṇa eternally becomes Kṛṣṇa.
The lotus is the supreme abode, eternal, indestructible, and imperishable; because of that nature he is Puṇḍarīkākṣa. Because he strikes terror into demons he is called Janārdana.
Because sattva does not depart from him and nothing is diminished from sattva — because of his sattva nature he is called Sātvata, and because of his bull-like excellence he is called Vrishabhekshana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Because he is not born from a mother he is unborn, and therefore called Anikajit the conqueror of armies. Because he is self-luminous among the gods and because of his self-restraint they know him as Dāmodara.
Because of his joy, happiness, and lordship in bliss he attains the status of Hṛṣīkeśa, lord of the senses. Because with his arms he holds up heaven and earth he is remembered as Mahābāhu, the mighty-armed.
Because he never diminishes downward he is called Adhokṣaja. Because he is the refuge of men he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa; and because he pervades and is the abode of all, he is the Puruṣottama, the Supreme Person.
Because he is the source and dissolution of all that is unreal and real, and because he is ever the knower of all — all things declare him to be everything.
Kṛṣṇa is established in truth, and truth is established in him; Govinda is truth derived from truth — therefore by name he is also called Satya, the True.
Viṣṇu is so called from his striding; Jiṣṇu from his conquering; Ananta from his eternality; and Govinda from his knowledge of the cows.
He makes the unreal appear as real and thereby deludes creatures. Such is the nature of the Lord, eternally established in dharma — the mighty-armed Acyuta, the imperishable one, will indeed come together with the sages for the sake of non-cruelty.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: I envy those with sight, O Sañjaya, who will see Vāsudeva nearby, blazing with a transcendent form, illuminating all the quarters and directions.
— proclaiming speech that is for the Bharatas, worthy of reverence, auspicious for the Sṛñjayas, capable of being grasped by those who desire to know, beyond reproach, and of a form imperceptible to those whose lives are spent.
— rising as the sole hero of the Sātvata clan, the guide and bull of the Yādavas, the slayer and agitator of enemies, and the one who robs the glory of those who hate him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the assembled Kurus will see that great-souled one, the slayer of enemies, the most excellent, speaking words of compassionate form — the best of the Vṛṣṇis — while he bewilders my own people.
— the most ancient of sages, the wise one, the ocean of speech, the vessel of ascetics, Ariṣṭanemi, Garuḍa, Suparṇa, the lord of creatures, and the abode of the world.
I take refuge in the ancient Person of a thousand heads, without beginning, middle, or end, of infinite fame, the supporter of Śukra, the unborn progenitor, the highest refuge beyond all others.
I take refuge in him, the maker and progenitor of the three worlds, the foremost among gods, demons, Nāgas, Rākṣasas, kings, and the learned — the younger brother of Indra.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Sañjaya had departed, King Yudhiṣṭhira the Dharmarāja addressed Janārdana, the bull of the Dāśārha clan, the best of all the Sātvatas.
This is the time, Janārdana, that has come for my friends; and I see no one other than you who can rescue us from calamities.
Relying on you, O Mādhava, and free from fear, we seek to reclaim our portion from the Dhārtarāṣṭra who is intoxicated by delusion, together with his ministers.
Just as you protect the Vṛṣṇis in all calamities, O conqueror of enemies, so must the Pāṇḍavas be protected by you — protect us from this great danger.
The Lord said: Here I am, O mighty-armed one — speak what you wish to say. I shall do everything that you tell me, O Bhārata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have heard the intentions of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with his son — for Sañjaya told me everything in full, O Kṛṣṇa.
That is the mind of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — his inner self stands revealed. A messenger who reports as told must not speak otherwise; to do so would make him liable to death.
Without giving back the kingdom, he seeks peace with us — a greedy man, acting with a sinful mind, acting unequally with regard to his own self.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
We dwelt in the forest for twelve years and by stealth for one year more — all under the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra was to abide by that agreement with us, O lord — we did not violate the terms, O Kṛṣṇa; indeed our Brāhmaṇas know this.
The old king Dhṛtarāṣṭra does not regard his own duty; or if he sees it, out of greed for his son he follows the command of that foolish one.
Standing by the judgment of Suyodhana, the king conducts himself falsely toward us, O Janārdana — a greedy man, acting as though it were pleasing to himself.
What could be more painful than this — that I cannot provide for my mother, for my father, or for my friends, O Janārdana?
With the Kāśi, the Cedi, the Pāñcāla, and the Matsya as allies, and with you as our lord, O Madhusūdana, I have sought only five villages.
Kushastala, Vrukasthala, Asandi, Vāraṇāvata, and O Govinda, whatever the fifth place among these may be.
Let five be given to us, my dear — whether villages or towns — in which we may dwell together, so that the Bharatas may not perish.
Yet even those the wicked-souled Dhārtarāṣṭra will not consent to, considering himself the sole lord. What could be more painful than this?
In one well-born, grown old, yet covetous of another's wealth — greed destroys wisdom; and wisdom, once destroyed, slays shame.
Shame, once slain, oppresses dharma; dharma, once slain, destroys prosperity; prosperity, once destroyed, slays the man; and the destruction of a man is his destitution.
From the destitute man, kinsmen, friends, and priests depart, O dear one — as birds depart from a tree that has neither flowers nor fruit.
