"Along with his allies, ministers, brothers, and followers — if I am able to bring him back onto the right path once more."
Then the Kṣattā brought Duryodhana back into the assembly against his will, surrounded by his brothers and the kings.
Then King Dhṛtarāṣṭra addressed Duryodhana, who was surrounded by Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and the assembled kings.
"O cruel one, O most sinful one, aided by helpers in vile deeds — you conspire with your wicked allies to perpetrate a wicked act."
"An impossible and inglorious deed, condemned even by good men — only such a fool as you, a disgrace to the family, would resolve upon it."
"You, together with your wicked allies, desire to restrain this lotus-eyed one who is unconquerable and unapproachable."
"You, O dull one, crave to overpower him whom even the gods with Vāsava are unable to constrain by force — as a child might reach for the moon."
"You do not recognize Keśava, whom gods, men, gandharvas, asuras, and serpents together are unable to withstand in battle."
"Wind cannot be grasped in the hand; the moon cannot be touched by the hand; the earth cannot be held upon the head; and Keśava cannot be seized by force."
When Dhṛtarāṣṭra had spoken thus, the Kṣattā Vidura also spoke, looking at Duryodhana, the impatient son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"At the gate of Saubha, the king of monkeys named Dvivida covered Keśava with a mighty shower of rocks —
"— desiring to capture him, striving with every effort to seize Mādhava, he could not grasp him there. Yet you seek to seize him by force."
"At Nirmocana, six thousand great asuras, having bound him with nooses, could not capture him. Yet you seek to seize him by force."
"When Śauri had gone to Prāgjyotiṣa, Naraka together with his danavas could not seize him there. Yet you seek to seize him by force."
"For by this one, even as a child, Pūtanā was slain; and Govardhana was lifted up for the sake of the cows, O bull of the Bhāratas."
"Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka, the mighty Cāṇūra, the king of horses — all were slain, as was Kaṃsa who acted wickedly."
"Jarāsandha, Vakra, the valiant Śiśupāla, and Bāṇa were slain in battle, and many kings were destroyed."
"King Varuṇa was vanquished, and Fire was overcome by this one of immeasurable might; even Indra, the lord of Śacī, was conquered when this one carried off the Pārijāta tree."
"Lying on the cosmic ocean, he slew those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha; and taking another birth, he slew Hayagrīva likewise."
"This one acts but is not acted upon; he is the cause behind human effort. Whatever Śauri desires, that he accomplishes without exertion."
"You do not recognize Govinda, of terrible valor, the Immovable, that mass of splendor who cannot be conquered — angry like a venomous serpent."
"Attacking the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, the tireless in action, you and your ministers shall cease to exist, like a moth rushing into fire."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Vidura had spoken thus, the valiant Keśava, the slayer of hosts of enemies, addressed Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"Through your delusion you think me alone and isolated, O Suyodhana, and with your corrupt mind you desire to seize and humiliate me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Right here are all the Pāṇḍavas, and likewise the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis; here too are the Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus, together with the great sages."
Having spoken thus, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes, laughed aloud; and from the body of that great-souled Śauri as he smiled, divine beings of the size of a thumb, shaped like lightning, emitted flames of fire.
Brahmā appeared on his forehead; Rudra appeared on his chest; the Guardians of the Worlds took their places on his arms; and Fire emerged from his mouth.
The Ādityas, the Sādhyas, the Vasus, the Aśvins, the Maruts with Indra, the Viśvadevas — all these appeared; and there also appeared the forms of yakshas, gandharvas, and rakshasas.
From his two arms there appeared Saṃkarṣaṇa and Dhanañjaya: on his right was Arjuna with his bow, and on his left was Rāma bearing the plough.
Bhīma and Yudhiṣṭhira and the two sons of Mādrī appeared behind him; and the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis headed by Pradyumna appeared there as well.
Before Kṛṣṇa appeared his great weapons upraised: the conch, the discus, the mace, the spear, the Śārṅga bow, the plough, and the Nandaka sword.
And all his weapons were seen upraised, blazing on Kṛṣṇa's many arms in every direction.
From his two eyes and his nose and his two ears on all sides there burst forth terrible, smoke-bearing flames of fire; and from his very pores there blazed rays like those of the sun.
Beholding that terrible form of the great-souled Keśava, the kings with terrified minds closed their eyes.
Except for Droṇa, Bhīṣma, the great-minded Vidura, the illustrious Sañjaya, and the sages rich in austerities — to all of these the blessed Janārdana granted divine sight.
Beholding that great wonder of Mādhava in the hall of the assembly, divine kettledrums sounded and a shower of flowers fell.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The whole earth trembled and the ocean was agitated; the kings were filled with utmost wonder, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then that tiger among men, that subduer of enemies, withdrew his own divine, wondrous, brilliant, and glorious form.
Then, taking Sātyaki and Hārdikya by the hand, and being permitted to depart by those sages, the Madhusūdana went forth.
Then those sages, Nārada and the others, vanished from sight and departed; and amidst that tumult, a wondrous thing came to pass.
Beholding him setting out, the Kauravas together with the assembled kings followed that tiger among men, as gods follow the hundred-sacrificed Indra.
Giving no thought to all that assemblage of kings, the immeasurable-souled Śauri then went forth like a fire with its smoke.
Then with a bright, great chariot adorned with bells, decorated with nets of gold, swift and thundering like a cloud —
— well-equipped and bright, covered with tiger-skins for its canopy, yoked with Sainya and Sugrīva — there appeared Dāruka the charioteer.
Likewise, mounting his chariot, the great chariot-warrior Kṛtavarman, the hero honored by the Vṛṣṇis, the son of Hṛdika, also appeared.
As Śauri, the subduer of enemies, stood ready at his chariot about to depart, the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke to him once more.
"O Janārdana, you see this much power in my sons directly before you — nothing is hidden from you, O afflicterof enemies."
"Knowing me to be one who desires peace for the Kurus and is striving for it, O Keśava, you should not harbor excessive suspicion of me."
"I have no wicked intention toward the Pāṇḍavas, O Keśava; you already know the words with which I addressed Suyodhana."
"All the Kurus know, as do the assembled kings and lords of earth, that I have been striving for peace with every effort, O Mādhava."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the mighty-armed one spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra the lord of men, to Droṇa, the grandsire Bhīṣma, the Kṣattā, Bāhlika, and Kṛpa:
"What has transpired in this assembly of the Kurus is evident to you all — how this dull one, ill-mannered, has repeatedly risen up in anger."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the earth, declaring himself powerless, takes leave of all of you — I shall go to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having bidden farewell to Śauri as he set out, mounted on his chariot — that bull among men — the great archers, the heroic bulls of the Bhārata line, followed after him.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Vidura, and then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bāhlika, Aśvatthāmā, Vikarṇa, and the great chariot-warrior Yuyutsu.
Then, on a splendid great chariot adorned with small bells, while the Kurus watched, he departed to visit Pṛthā, his father's sister.
Vaishampаyana said: Entering her house and touching her feet in reverence, he told her in brief all that had transpired in the Kuru assembly.
Vāsudeva said: Many kinds of words worthy of acceptance, with sound reasons, were spoken both by the sages and by me — yet he did not take them to heart.
All of this has been ripened by Time and follows the will of Duryodhana. I take leave of you now — I shall swiftly set out toward the Pāṇḍavas.
What shall I say to those sons of Pāṇḍu on your behalf? Tell me, O greatly wise one — I am eager to hear your words.
Kuntī said: Say to the king Yudhiṣṭhira, whose soul is dharma, O Keśava: "Your dharma diminishes ever more — do not act in vain, my son."
Like that of a dull and ignorant student of scripture, O king, your intellect, dulled by mere recitation, sees only one aspect of dharma.
Contemplate dharma in its entirety — as the Self-born One created it: the Kṣatriya was created chest-first, to live by the strength of his arms, for fierce action and for the constant protection of his subjects.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hear also this one illustration which I have heard from the elders: Vaiśravaṇa, pleased of old, offered this very earth to the royal sage Mucukunda — yet he did not accept it.
"I desire to enjoy a kingdom won by the strength of my own arms" — at this, Vaiśravaṇa was delighted and filled with wonder.
Then King Mucukunda duly governed the earth, won by the strength of his arms, steadfastly devoted to the dharma of the Kṣatriya.
Of whatever dharma the subjects practice here, well protected by the king, the king, O Bhārata, obtains a fourth share of that merit.
If the king practices dharma, he qualifies for divinity; if he practices adharma, he goes straight to hell.
The science of punishment, wielded according to its own dharma, holds the four social orders in check; properly applied by the master, it restrains them from adharma as well.
When the king acts fully and properly according to the science of punishment, then the best of ages, known as the Kṛta Yuga, comes into being.
Whether Time is the cause of the king, or the king is the cause of Time — let there be no doubt in your mind: the king is the cause of Time.
The king is the creator of the Kṛta Yuga and of the Tretā; the king is the cause of the Dvāpara and also of the fourth age.
By being the cause of the Kṛta, the king enjoys heaven permanently; by being the cause of the Tretā, the king does not enjoy heaven permanently; from bringing about the Dvāpara, he enjoys it in proportion to his share.
Thereafter the evildoer dwells in hell for eternal years; for the world is touched by the king's fault, and he in turn is touched by the world's.
Attend to the royal dharmas befitting your fathers and grandfathers — for the position in which you wish to remain is not the conduct of a royal sage.
A king who is joined to feebleness and established in compassion obtains no fruit whatsoever that arises from the protection of his subjects.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For neither Pāṇḍu, nor I, nor your grandfather ever previously employed that wisdom by which you now conduct yourself.
Sacrifice, giving, austerity, valor, and the continuance of progeny, as well as magnanimity, strength, and vigor — these I always wished for you.
The deities among men always offer the svaha and svadha oblations; when properly worshipped, the auspicious ones bestow long life, wealth, and sons.
The ancestors and the gods ever hope for from their sons: giving, study of scripture, sacrifice, and the protection of subjects.
Whether this is dharma or adharma, you were born into it from birth itself; you are skilled, born in a noble family, yet afflicted by want of proper livelihood, my son.
When wanderers of the earth, hungry, find a lord of giving who is a hero, and go away satisfied — what dharma is higher than that?
By giving he wins some, by strength he wins others, by gentle truth yet others — the righteous man, having obtained a kingdom here, should receive tribute from all sides.
A Brahmin should go about begging alms; a Kṣatriya should protect; a Vaiśya should earn wealth; a Śūdra should serve all of them.
Begging is forbidden to you; agriculture does not suit you either; you are a Kṣatriya — one who protects from harm, who lives by the strength of his arms.
O mighty-armed one, retrieve again your paternal inheritance that has been submerged — by conciliation, by giving, by creating dissension, by force, or by statecraft.
What could be more painful than this — that I, bereft of kinsmen, having borne you, O joy of enemies, now look on while you depend on another's food?
Fight according to royal dharma; do not drown your ancestors; do not go, you and your younger brothers, your merit exhausted, to a sinful destiny.
Kuntī said: In this connection, O scorcher of foes, they also cite this ancient tale — the dialogue between Vidurā and her son.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In this matter she speaks of what is truly better and more beneficial, as she deserves — the glorious, indignant Vibhavari, born of a noble family.
Vidurā — blessed, far-sighted, devoted to Kṣatriya dharma — was renowned in royal assemblies, her words heard with attention, a woman of great learning.
The truthful woman named Vidurā indeed rebuked her own son — defeated by the king of Sindhu, lying down with a dejected mind, joyless, ignorant of dharma, a source of delight to his enemies.
You were born neither of me nor of your father — from where indeed have you come? You are without spirit, a side-branch sort of man, a coward's tool.
If you are without hope of good fortune for as long as you live, then bear the yoke; do not demean yourself, do not support yourself on so little — set your mind on full well-being, do not be afraid; brace yourself.
Rise up, O coward — do not lie like this, defeated, gladdening all your enemies, without honor, causing grief to your kinsmen.
A small stream is easily filled; a mouse's cupped paws are easily filled; a coward is easily satisfied — he is content with very little.
Either wrench out the fang of your enemy and go swiftly to death, or, even when your life hangs in the balance, show valor.
Either watch like a hawk for an opening in your enemy as you move about — calling out or in silence, or unsuspected in the sky above.
Why do you lie like this, like a ghost or one struck by the thunderbolt? Rise up, O coward — do not lie like this, defeated.
Do not fall into wretchedness; be known by your own deeds. Do not remain in the middle ranks, nor in the lowest — do not be slack; stand vigorous and strong.
Blaze forth even for a moment, like a firebrand of tinduka wood — do not smolder flameless like a fire of chaff, clinging to life like a crow's wish. To blaze for a moment is better than to smolder with smoke for a long time.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In no man's house should a woman born of a king, gentle as a she-ass, live; having performed the human duty and entered battle to the highest degree, one becomes free from the debt of dharma and does not reproach oneself.
Whether they obtain it or not, the wise do not grieve; they undertake action without pause and do not treasure their lives like wealth.
Either manifest your valor or go to that certain path — with dharma placed before you, my son; for what reason do you live?
Your sacrificial merit and the merit of public works are destroyed, O coward; your entire fame is slain and the root of your enjoyment cut off — for what reason then do you live?
An enemy who is sinking should be seized by the thigh; one who is about to fall should be grabbed; even one whose roots are entirely severed should not despair in any way — he should lift up the yoke with effort, recalling the acts of a thoroughbred horse.
Cultivate courage and self-respect; know your own manliness; raise up your family that has submerged — for it is because of you that it has sunk.
He whose conduct men do not extol as great and wonderful, who merely adds to his heap — he is neither a woman nor yet a man.
He whose fame is not spread abroad in giving, in austerity, in valor, or in learning or the gaining of wealth — he is nothing but his mother's excrement.
He who surpasses other people by learning, by austerity, by prosperity, by valor, or by action — he truly is a man.
But you ought not to seek out the wretched, beggarly mode of life — cruel, inglorious, painful, fit only for cowards.
That wretched man whom enemies would welcome — weak, universally despised by the world, in mean food and clothing —
— pitiable, inspiring only the cry "Alas, the wretch!", of little life and little worth — obtaining such a kinsman, no kinsman prospers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
We ourselves shall perish from want — exiled from our kingdom, deprived of all the pleasures of desire, fallen from our station, possessing nothing.
I bore you, Sañjaya, as a source of reproach among the good, a destroyer of the family line, a discord — and now your name is spoken only in shame.
Without indignation, without enthusiasm, without valor, a delight to enemies — may no woman with a parting in her hair ever give birth to such a son.
Do not merely smolder — blaze forth with full intensity; advance and slay your foes; burn on the heads of your enemies even for a moment or an instant.
A man is a man to precisely this extent: that he is full of indignation and does not endure wrong; one who endures but is without indignation is neither a woman nor yet a man.
Contentment indeed destroys prosperity, and so does excessive compassion; both the fear of exertion and inertia — the inactive man does not obtain greatness.
Free yourself from these sinful evils of baseness by your own will; make your heart like iron and seek again what is your own.
Because he endures and bears the citadel of the body, he is called a purusha — a man; they say his name is meaningless, like a woman's, who lives thus in this world.
Even the leavings of a hero of vigorous spirit who walks with the stride of a lion — even one who has gone to the fate decreed — his subjects rejoice in those leavings.
He who, abandoning his own personal pleasure and ease, seeks prosperity — he quickly brings joy to his ministers.
The son said: What is the whole earth worth to you who have lost sight of me? What need have you of ornaments, of pleasures, or of life itself?
The mother said: May those who are enemies today obtain the worlds of those who are enemies; but may the worlds of those who honor themselves, the worlds of friends, come to us.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Do not follow the way of life of those abandoned by their servants, who live on another's food — wretched, without spirit.
May Brahmins and friends live following after you, my son — as living beings follow the rain-cloud, as the gods follow the hundred-sacrificed Indra.
The man whom all creatures live by, O Sañjaya — approaching him as they would a ripe tree — his life is full of meaning.
The hero by whose valorous deeds his kinsmen prosper in happiness — as the thirty gods thrive by Śakra's might — well indeed is his life lived here.
The man who lives and prospers relying on the strength of his own arms — he obtains fame in this world and an auspicious passage in the next.
Vidurā said: And yet in this condition you wish to abandon manliness — it seems you will shortly take the path trodden by the low.
For a Kṣatriya who does not display his energy to the full extent of his power through valorous action, yet clings to life — him they know as nothing but a thief.
Words full of meaning, well-reasoned and rich in virtue — they do not reach you, just as medicine fails to reach one who is dying.
Indeed, many people are content with the king of the Sindhus; foolishly, out of weakness, they sit awaiting a flood of misfortune.
After gathering supporters and resolving your course step by step, others will cease to find fault, seeing your manliness.
Having allied with them, roam the mountain fastnesses; awaiting the enemy's moment of adversity, for he is not immortal and undying.
You bear the name Sañjaya — 'he who conquers completely' — yet I do not see that quality in you. Live up to your name, my son; do not let it be an empty name.
A brahmin of keen sight and great wisdom spoke thus of you when you were a child: 'This one, having passed through great hardship, will rise again to prosperity.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Remembering his words, I hope for your victory. That is why, my dear, I speak to you now and will speak to you again and again.
He in whose accomplishment of goals others are enriched — for him who follows statecraft's path, success in his aims is assured.
Whether prosperity or adversity came to those before us, my Sañjaya — knowing this, be battle-minded; do not retreat.
Śambara declared there is no more wretched condition than that in which no food is seen — not today, not tomorrow morning.
He said this surpasses even the grief of losing husband and son; what is called poverty is indeed death by instalments.
I was born in a great lineage, passed from one fine pool to another like water; a mistress of all auspiciousness, supremely honoured by my husband.
Adorned once with costly garlands and jewels, dressed in fine, bright garments — now the circle of friends who knew me thus sees me utterly fallen.
When you see both me and your wife reduced to extreme weakness, then life will hold no worth for you, Sañjaya.
Seeing slaves, labourers, servants, teachers, officiants, and priests abandon us for want of livelihood — what good is life to you then?
If I cannot see you doing here today what is praiseworthy and glorious, as in former times, what peace can there be for my heart?
If I were forced to say 'no' to brahmins, my heart would shatter — for neither I nor my husband has ever said 'no' to a brahmin.
We were ones others took refuge in, not those who sheltered under another's roof. I — who must now live depending on strangers — will give up life itself.
Be a far shore for us who have no shore; be a raft for us who have no boat; make a place where there is none; bring us back to life from the dead.
All your enemies are endurable — if you do not wish to go on living; but if you adopt this cowardly way of life instead —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— with your spirit crushed and your courage slain, then abandon this sinful existence: by slaying even a single enemy, a hero attains great renown.
By slaying Vṛtra alone, Indra became the great Indra; he obtained the Mahendra asterism and became the lord of all the worlds.
Whether by proclaiming his name on the battlefield, or by challenging armoured foes, or by routing the van of an army, or by slaying a great warrior —
— the very moment a hero wins great glory through noble combat, his enemies are filled with dread and bow before him.
Cowards, unable to help themselves, heap every desired wealth upon a skilled and valiant hero who has abandoned all care for his own life in battle.
Even when the kingdom is utterly lost or life itself is in doubt, noble men make sure the deceiving enemy does not escape — they leave him no remainder.
Regarding a kingdom — equal to the gateway of heaven, or equal to nectar — as something blocked on a single narrow path, move against your enemies like a blazing torch.
Slay your enemies in battle, O king; uphold your own duty. Never let a prosperous enemy see you pitifully wretched.
Even though wretched myself, I would not wish to see you surrounded by our own people weeping and your enemies exulting, standing there in misery.
Dwell with the girls of Sauvīra; pursue your aims with pride as in former times; do not, while dwelling there, fall under the sway of the Saindhava maidens.
A young man endowed with beauty, learning, and noble birth — one of your calibre who is famous and widely renowned — if such a one behaves dishonourably, then I deem it death for a bull of burden to flinch from the yoke it should bear.
If I were to see you speaking pleasant words to another's man and following at his heels, what peace could there ever be for my heart?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Never has one born in this lineage walked behind another. You, my dear, have no right to live as a lesser yoke-bearer under someone else.
For I know the eternal heart of the kṣatriya, as proclaimed by the forefathers and by those before them, and by those who came still later.
Whatever kṣatriya is born in this world and knows the duty of his class — whether out of fear or in quest of a livelihood — he should bow down to no one here.
He must rise up and not bow; for rising up is itself manliness. Even if he breaks at the wrong moment, let him not bow to anyone here.
Like a rutting elephant, let him move about with a most exalted spirit; let him bow always to brahmins and to righteousness alone, Sañjaya.
Restraining the other social orders, striking down all wrongdoers — whether with allies or without — let him be thus for as long as he lives.
The son said: You have fashioned your heart as though of black iron, O Mother — pitiless, wise in enmity, and filled with wrath.
Ah, such is the conduct of the kṣatriya — that you would speak such words to me, your only son, as though to a stranger!
What good is all the earth to you if you cannot see me? What use are ornaments to you? What use are pleasures, or life itself?
The mother said: All undertakings of the wise, my dear, are for the sake of righteousness and gain. Keeping exactly those aims in view, Sañjaya, I have urged you on.
This is the foremost moment, full of judicious opportunity, that has arrived. If, when this moment has come, you do not take up the task, you — a man of unproven worth — will act very cruelly.
If I did not speak to you when you are touched by disgrace, Sañjaya, they would call that the affection of a she-ass — helplessness disguised as love, without reason.
Abandon the path condemned by the good and frequented by fools. There is a great ignorance, and the people who have taken refuge in it are many.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If you were to have right conduct, you would be dear to me by that alone — by conduct endowed with righteousness, wealth, and virtue; not by any other means; conduct joined with divine and human qualities and practised by the good.
He who takes pleasure in sons and grandsons who are thus ill-disciplined and without the impulse to rise — for him, the fruit of offspring is barren.
Those lowest of men who neither do what ought to be done, nor do what is blamed for being done, find no happiness — neither here nor in the hereafter.
The kṣatriya is created for battle and for victory, Sañjaya; for fierce deeds and forever for the protection of subjects. Whether he conquers or is slain, he attains to the world of Indra.
Not even in the sacred abode of Śakra in heaven does there exist such happiness as a kṣatriya enjoys when he brings his enemies under his power.
For a high-minded man burning with wrath, deceived repeatedly here, with the desire to conquer his enemies —
— either by abandoning himself entirely, or by laying his enemies low — by any means other than these, where can peace come to him?
A wise man in this world wills only a little that is unpleasant; he whose pleasure in the world is small — for him, certainly, the unpleasant too is small.
Without the pleasant, a man never obtains what is beautiful; and he who avoids action certainly moves toward non-existence, as the Gaṅgā goes to the ocean.
The son said: This reasoning should not be spoken by you, Mother — especially not to a son. See only compassion here; be here like one dumb and dull.
The mother said: This delights me all the more — that you perceive the urging this way and urge me with it; it is precisely this that I urge upon you most strongly.
Then I shall honour you — after you have slain all the Saindhava forces. I see complete and certain victory coming to you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The son said: Without a treasury, without allies — how indeed can victory be mine? Knowing this harsh condition within myself, my attachment to the kingdom has left me, as a sinner is cut off from heaven.
If you, O ripened in wisdom, see some means out of a situation like this, tell me it fully, for I am asking; I will do all of it exactly according to your instruction.
The mother said: One who is the soul of his son should not be underestimated on account of earlier failures. Things that did not exist come into being; and things that exist perish.
Nor should affairs be undertaken by the very young through impatience alone. In the fruit of all actions, my dear, there is always impermanence.
Those who know that things are impermanent — they sometimes fail to prosper, and they sometimes prosper. But those who never act — they never prosper at all.
In the absence of effort, there is only one possibility — the non-occurrence of the fruit of action. With effort, there are two possibilities — the fruit may or may not come.
He who has understood beforehand the impermanence of all things will drive forward prosperity and success even in adverse circumstances, O son of a king.
One must rise up, keep vigil, and apply oneself to acts of prosperity — keeping the mind always fixed on 'it shall be so' without faltering, placing auspicious rites foremost, and acting together with brahmins and men of power.
For the wise king, prosperity comes swiftly, my boy; Lakṣmī advances toward him as the sun advances toward the eastern quarter.
Many examples, means, and encouragements have been shown to you; your true form has been made visible to you. I see it — perform your manliness; you are fit to gather here the human goal you have in mind.
The wrathful, the greedy, the exhausted, the overlooked, the dishonoured, and the rivals — whoever they may be — regard them with a fitting eye and hold them fast.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By this method you will split apart great hosts, just as the wind, rising with mighty force, scatters the rain clouds.
Be the first to give them gifts; be one who rises early and speaks pleasant words. They will make you dear to them and will surely place you at their fore.
The very moment an enemy knows his rival has cast aside all care for his life, he recoils from him — just as from a serpent that has entered the house.
If, knowing him to be bold and aggressive, the enemy does not bring him under control, he will wear him down with reproaches — and in the end that will come to pass.
Having gained a foothold through wearing the enemy down, wealth will grow; for it is the wealthy man whom friends seek out and lean upon.
When a man stumbles in his affairs, my dear, even kinsmen abandon him; and in that same state, they both take shelter with him and despise him — such is the way of things.
He who, having made an enemy into an ally, places trust in him — it is precisely from this that the recovery of the kingdom is to be expected.
The mother said: A king should never show fear in any adversity whatsoever. And even if he is shattered, he should not conduct himself like one who is shattered.
For seeing a king shattered, everything shatters in turn; the kingdom, the army, and the ministers each take their minds elsewhere.
Some go over to the enemies; others simply desert; and yet others — those who were humiliated before — now seek to do him harm in turn.
Only those who are his truest friends gather around him — powerless themselves, wishing him well, like cows bound to their calves; they grieve for him in his grief, as kinsmen mourn for the departed.
Even those who were previously honoured by you, even those regarded as your friends — who now covet the kingdom of a king who has fallen into misfortune — do not let your friends see you shattered; do not let them abandon you as one broken.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Wishing to test your power, your manliness, and your intellect, I was encouraging you with words of comfort, as a strong man encourages the weak.
If you recognise this truth, if what I say is right, then make your spirit resolute and rise for victory, O Sañjaya.
There is a great accumulation of treasure that you do not know of; I know it, and no one else does — I shall make it available to you.
You have many hundreds of friends, O Sañjaya, companions in joy and sorrow, heroes worthy of a hundred, who never turn back in battle.
Such are the allies that befit a man who desires greatness — counsellors who crush enemies and who need only a small effort to be roused.
The son said: Whose darkness of mind would not be dispelled upon hearing such words — words whose syllables and meaning are so wonderfully varied — even if his understanding were small?
This burden must be borne upon the water; I must now move swiftly down the slope — for you, who see things as they truly are, shall be my guide.
Indeed, eager to hear word after word from you, replying with a word here and a word there, I fell silent again and again.
Like one not satiated by nectar obtained with difficulty from a kinsman, I rise now to the subduing of enemies and to victory.
Kuntī said: Urged on and spurred like a noble horse by the arrows of her words, he did everything just as she had instructed.
A counsellor should recite this formidable and excellent exhortation — which augments heroic energy — to a king who is sinking, oppressed by enemies.
This is the history called Jaya and it should be heard by one who desires conquest; upon hearing it he swiftly conquers the earth and crushes his enemies.
This is both a rite for the generation of a male child and a generator of heroes; if a pregnant woman hears it repeatedly she will certainly give birth to a hero.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Heroic in learning, heroic in austerity, heroic in self-restraint, an ascetic blazing with the glory of Brahman, honoured with praise by the righteous —
Radiant, endowed with strength, of great fortune, a great chariot-warrior, bold yet unapproachable, a victor never defeated —
A restrainer of the wicked, a protector of the righteous — it is for this purpose that a kṣatriya woman gives birth to a hero of true valour.
Kuntī said: Tell Arjuna, O Keśava, that at the time of his birth, when I was sitting in my lying-in chamber surrounded by women in the hermitage —
— a divine, beautiful, enchanting voice arose in the sky: 'O Kuntī, this son of yours shall be equal to the Thousand-Eyed One.
He shall conquer in battle all the Kurus assembled together, and together with Bhīmasena as his second, he will overturn the world.
Your son shall conquer the earth and his fame shall touch the sky; slaying the Kurus in the great battle, he will have Vāsudeva as his ally.
He shall recover the paternal inheritance that has been lost, and together with his brothers, in his splendour, he will perform three great sacrifices.'
O Acyuta, I know that Bībhatsu, the left-handed archer, that man of true pledges, is mighty and difficult to assail — may it be so, O Dāśārha, as the voice declared.
If dharma exists, O Vārṣṇeya, truth shall be fulfilled; and you too, O Kṛṣṇa, shall bring all of it to accomplishment.
I do not begrudge what the voice declared; homage to the great dharma — it is dharma that sustains all living beings.
Tell Dhanañjaya and the ever-ready Vṛkodara that the time has come for that purpose for which a kṣatriya woman gives birth — for bulls among men do not falter when they encounter enmity.
You have always known Bhīma's disposition — that chastiser of enemies will not rest until he brings the enemies to their final end.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O Mādhava, please speak to the auspicious, illustrious Kṛṣṇā — the daughter-in-law of the great-souled Pāṇḍu, who is versed in all the distinctions of dharma.
This is fitting, O greatly fortunate one born in a noble lineage, O illustrious one — that you have conducted yourself rightly toward all my sons.
And say to the two sons of Mādrī, who are both devoted to the kṣatriya dharma: 'Choose the enjoyments won by valour, even at the cost of life itself.'
For the riches obtained through valour by one who lives according to the kṣatriya dharma always delight the heart of a man, O best of men.
And as for Pāñcālī — she who enhances all dharma — while you all looked on she was spoken to with harsh words; who could bear that?
The seizure of the kingdom does not grieve me, nor does defeat at dice, nor the exile of my sons — none of these is the cause of my suffering.
But that she — tall and dark — weeping in the assembly, heard those harsh words at that time — that, I consider, is a greater sorrow to me.
Though devoted to a woman's duty, beautiful of form, always engaged in the kṣatriya dharma, Kṛṣṇā could find no protector then — she who has protectors and is a virtuous wife.
Tell him — O mighty-armed one, tell Arjuna, that tiger among men, the foremost of all who bear weapons — to follow the path of Draupadī.
For you know them well — Bhīma and Arjuna, like death and the Ender when enraged; they could bring even the gods to their final end.
This was the insult to those two — that Kṛṣṇā was dragged into the assembly, and that Duḥśāsana spoke harsh words to Bhīma while the Kuru heroes looked on — remind them of that again.
Ask the Pāṇḍavas of their welfare, along with their sons and with Kṛṣṇā; and tell them I am well, O Janārdana. More than all else, travel a safe road and protect my sons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Kṛṣṇa paid his respects to her and circumambulated her, and the mighty-armed one departed from there with the gait of a lion at play.
Then he took leave of Bhīṣma and the other foremost Kurus, and having taken Karṇa up onto his chariot, he departed together with Sātyaki.
When the Dāśārha departed, the Kurus gathered together and spoke among themselves about the great and most wondrous marvel that was Keśava.
The whole earth, bound in the noose of death, was bewildered; and because of Duryodhana's foolishness they said: 'This cannot be.'
Then the best of men went forth from the city and conversed for a long time with Karṇa.
Having taken leave of the son of Rādhā, that joy of all the Yādavas then urged his horses forward with great and swift speed.
Urged on by Dāruka, those horses of great speed went as if drinking the sky, swift as thought and wind.
Swiftly crossing that road like swift-moving hawks, they brought the bearer of the Śārṅga bow to Upaplavya before the sun had risen high.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard Kuntī's words, the two great chariot-warriors Bhīṣma and Droṇa spoke this speech to Duryodhana, who transgresses all authority.
You have heard, O tiger among men, the weighty, composed, righteous, and incomparable words that Kuntī spoke in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
The sons of Kuntī will do what is approved by Vāsudeva; they will never rest, O Kaurava, unless they receive the kingdom.
The Pārthas were oppressed by you, bound in the noose of dharma at that time, and Draupadī too — and all of that was endured from you by them.
For having Arjuna who is accomplished in weapons, and Bhīma who is practised in effort, and the Gāṇḍīva bow and two quivers, and the chariot and the standard, and Vāsudeva as ally — Yudhiṣṭhira will no longer endure it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It is before your eyes, O mighty-armed one, how the wise Pārtha formerly conquered us all in battle at the city of Virāṭa.
The Dānavas of terrible deeds — the Nivātakavacas — he burned in battle, drawing the fearful Raudra weapon and incinerating them with the fire of his missiles.
And these men headed by Karṇa, and you yourself — armoured and mounted on your chariot — were all released by him during the cattle-raid excursion. That example alone is sufficient.
Make peace, O foremost of the Bhāratas, with the Pāṇḍava brothers, and let us protect this whole earth which has entered the jaws of death.
The eldest brother is righteous in conduct, affectionate, gentle of speech, and pure; go to him, that tiger among men, and remove the sin from here.
If you are seen by the Pāṇḍava with your bow laid aside, your brow unclouded and serene, O splendid one, then peace will have been made for our lineage.
Approach him accompanied by your ministers, embrace the son of the king, and honour the king as you did before, O subduer of foes.
May Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, the elder brother of Bhīma, receive you as you offer homage, clasping you with both arms out of friendship.
May Bhīma — with the shoulders and thighs of a lion, with arms long, round, and mighty — the foremost among those who strike, embrace you with both arms.
And then may Pārtha Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī, lion-necked and thick-haired, with eyes like lotus petals, pay homage to you.
And may those two sons of the Aśvins, tigers among men, matchless in beauty upon the earth, rise to honour you with affection, as they would a teacher.
May the kings headed by the Dāśārha shed tears of joy; meet with your brothers, O king, and abandon your pride.
Then rule the entire earth together with those brothers; having embraced one another in joy, may the kings go forth to one another.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Enough of war, O king of kings; hear the counsel of your well-wishers — in battle the certain destruction of kṣatriyas is clearly foretold.
Adverse celestial omens, dreadful beasts and birds, and various portents foreboding the destruction of kṣatriyas are being seen, O hero.
Especially here among us are signs pointing to destruction; your army shall be slain by blazing meteors.
The draft animals are joyless, weeping as it were, O lord of the people; vultures attend your forces from all sides.
The city and the royal palace are no longer as they once were; jackals with inauspicious cries hover about the flaming directions.
Do what your father, your mother, and we your well-wishers say; on you depend both peace and exertion, O mighty-armed one.
If you do not act on the counsel of your well-wishers, O crusher of enemies, you will burn with anguish when you see your army struck down by Pārtha's arrows.
And hearing the mighty roar of Bhīma bellowing with fiery vigour in battle, and the twang of the Gāṇḍīva — then you will remember my words, if these words of mine prove to have gone against the grain for you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, he sat dejected, his gaze averted, his face downcast, knitting his brows together, and spoke not a word.
Seeing him thus dejected, those two bulls among men glanced at each other nearby and once again spoke their reply.
Bhīṣma said: We shall fight against Pārtha — who is eager to learn, free from envy, devoted to the Brahman, and true to his pledges; what could be more painful than this?
Droṇa said: O king, the high esteem and reverence I have for Dhanañjaya — the bearer of the monkey-banner — exceeds even what I have for my own son Aśvatthāman.
If I must fight against Dhanañjaya, who is dearer to me than my own son, while following the kṣatriya dharma — shame upon the kṣatriya's way of life!

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There is no other archer in the world equal to him; by my grace, that Bībhatsu surpasses all other bearers of the bow.
One who betrays friends, who is malicious, an unbeliever, crooked, and deceitful — he receives no honour among the good, like a fool who arrives at a sacrifice uninvited.
Even when restrained from evil, the evil-souled man desires evil; even when urged toward evil, the pure-souled man desires good.
For these faults, O best of the Bhāratas, though seemingly friendly while being indulged, lead only to harm.
You have been counselled by the elder of the Kurus, by me, by Vidura, and by Vāsudeva, yet you do not take the path of your own welfare.
Thinking only 'I have strength,' you rashly seek to cross, as if in the hot season one would brave the current of the Ganges filled with crocodiles and sharks.
You now imagine yourself adorned like one wearing a garland — yet through greed you would seize the royal glory of Yudhiṣṭhira as if it were a garland already discarded.
Who, even while established in a kingdom, could outlive the son of Pṛthā accompanied by Draupadī, surrounded by his armed brothers — even when they dwell in the forest?
The dharma-king shone resplendent after obtaining the abode of Ailavila — he at whose command all kings stood ready as servants.
Having reached Kubera's dwelling, having gained those treasures, and having overrun that prosperous realm — it is thus that the Pāṇḍavas now desire the kingdom.
Gifts have been given, oblations poured, scriptures studied, and Brāhmaṇas satisfied with wealth — know that for the two of us our lifespan has been well spent and our purpose fulfilled.
But you, having abandoned a prosperous kingdom, friends, and wealth, by making war against the Pāṇḍavas will bring upon yourself a great calamity.
Draupadī, that truth-speaking goddess of fierce ascetic vows, prays for his victory — you will not conquer the son of Pāṇḍu.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whose counsellor is Janārdana, and whose brother is Dhanañjaya, the foremost among all bearers of weapons — how will you conquer the son of Pāṇḍu?
Whose allies are firm-souled Brāhmaṇas who have mastered their senses — that hero of fierce austerities — how will you conquer that son of Pāṇḍu?
I shall speak again what must be done by one who desires prosperity — by a friend when his friends are sinking in the ocean of calamity.
Enough of war with those heroes — make peace, for the welfare of the Kurus; do not bring upon yourself, your sons, your ministers, and your army, utter ruin.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Sañjaya, surrounded by princes and ministers, having taken Karṇa up onto his chariot, how did Madhusūdana depart?
What did the slayer of enemy heroes say to Rādheya while on the chariot? What words of conciliation did Govinda employ upon the son of the charioteer?
Whatever Kṛṣṇa, whose voice is like the roar of rushing clouds, spoke in due time to Karṇa — whether gentle or sharp — tell me all of it, Sañjaya.
Sañjaya said: In due order, words that were smooth and gentle, affectionate, grounded in dharma, truthful, and beneficial —
— words that would capture the heart — these the immeasurable-souled Madhusūdana spoke to Rādheya; hear them from me, O Bhārata.
Vāsudeva said: O Rādheya, you have attended upon Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas, and questioned them on the true meaning with discipline and without envy.
You alone, O Karṇa, know the eternal teachings of the Vedas; you alone are deeply versed in the subtle points of the dharma-shastras.
The son born of a maiden before marriage, the son born along with the bride, and the son born of a maiden — the knowers of scripture declare the husband who marries the mother to be the father of such a child.
You are such a one, O Karṇa — you are by dharma the son of Pāṇḍu; by the authority of the dharma-shastras, come, and you shall be king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
On your father's side the Pārthas are your kin, and on your mother's side the Vṛṣṇis — acknowledge these two lineages, O bull among men.
Come with me from here today, dear one, so the Pāṇḍavas may acknowledge you as the son of Kuntī, the eldest-born before Yudhiṣṭhira.
The five Pāṇḍava brothers shall clasp your feet, as shall the five sons of Draupadī and the unvanquished son of Subhadrā.
The kings and princes assembled on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas shall clasp your feet, and all the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis as well.
Golden jars, silver ones, and earthen ones, along with herbs, all manner of seeds, all jewels, and plants —
— let royal ladies and royal princesses bring them for your consecration; and Draupadī too shall come to you in due time as the sixth.
Let the twice-born versed in the four Vedas consecrate you today, seated on a tiger skin as the Pāṇḍavas' chief priest officiates.
Likewise the five Pāṇḍava brothers, those bulls among men, the five sons of Draupadī, the Pāñcālas, and the Cedis as well —
— and I myself shall consecrate you as king and lord of the earth; let Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, be your crown-prince.
Taking the white fan, the righteous one of firm vows, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Kuntī, shall mount the chariot following behind you.
The mighty Bhīmasena, son of Kuntī, shall hold the great white parasol over you once you are consecrated, O son of Kuntī.
Arjuna shall drive the chariot yoked with white horses, resounding with hundreds of bells and adorned with tiger-skins.
Abhimanyu shall always be close by your side, as will Nakula, Sahadeva, and the five sons of Draupadī.
The Pāñcālas shall follow you, as shall the great warrior Śikhaṇḍin; I too shall follow you, as will all the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis — the Dāśārhas and Dashernas shall form your retinue, O lord of the people.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Enjoy the kingdom, O mighty-armed one, together with your Pāṇḍava brothers, accompanied by japa, fire-offerings, and auspicious rites of every kind.
Let the Draviḍas along with the Kuntalas march before you, as well as the Andhras, the Talacharas, the Chuchupas, and the Venupas.
Let the sutas and magadhas praise you today with many eulogies; let the Pāṇḍavas proclaim the victory of Vasuṣeṇa.
You, surrounded by the sons of Pṛthā as the moon is by the stars — rule the kingdom, O son of Kuntī, and bring joy to Kuntī.
Let your friends rejoice and your enemies be shaken; and today let there be true brotherhood between you and the Pāṇḍava brothers.
Karṇa said: Without doubt, O Keśava, you have spoken to me out of friendship, affection, and fellowship, O Vārṣṇeya, and indeed out of a desire for my welfare.
I know all of this and acknowledge it — I am by dharma the son of Pāṇḍu, by the authority of the dharma-shastras, just as you, O Kṛṣṇa, believe.
A maiden conceived me through Bhāskara, O Janārdana; and by the word of Āditya himself, having borne me, she abandoned me at birth.
Such am I, O Kṛṣṇa — I am by dharma the son of Pāṇḍu; but I was cast off by Kuntī in a manner that was not right or good.
The charioteer Adhiratha, having found me, brought me to his home and out of affection gave me to Rādhā, O Madhusūdana.
And out of love for me Rādhā's milk flowed at once; she accepted my urine and excrement, O Mādhava.
How could one such as I, a knower of dharma, ever neglect to perform the funeral oblations for her — one who is ever devoted to hearing the dharma-shastras?
The charioteer Adhiratha likewise acknowledges me as his son, and I always acknowledge him as my father with heartfelt love.
For he performed for me the birth-rites and all the sacraments from the beginning, O Mādhava, according to the rites prescribed by scripture, with the joy of a father, O Janārdana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He had twice-born priests give me the name Vasuṣeṇa; and when I came of age, it was he who arranged my marriages, O Keśava.
By those wives sons and grandsons have been born to me, O Janārdana; in them, O Kṛṣṇa, my heart has become bound by the ties of love.
Not for the sake of the whole earth, not for heaps of gold, neither from joy nor from fear, O Govinda, do I venture to speak falsehood.
In the house of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Kṛṣṇa, under the shelter of Duryodhana, I have enjoyed uncontested royal power for thirteen years.
I have performed many sacrifices together with the sutas, and betrothal-feasts and weddings have been celebrated by me together with the sutas more than once.
And it is relying on me, O Kṛṣṇa, that Duryodhana, O Vārṣṇeya, has taken up arms and entered into conflict with the Pāṇḍavas.
Therefore it is against me, who comes forward to face him in single chariot combat, O Acyuta, that Savyasācī has chosen to stand in opposition, with utmost eagerness.
For fear of death, bondage, or out of fear, or out of greed, O Janārdana, I am not able to speak falsely against the wise son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
For if I were not to go today to the single chariot duel with Savyasācī, O Hṛṣīkeśa, it would bring infamy upon both myself and the son of Pṛthā.
Without doubt you speak for my good, O Madhusūdana, and the Pāṇḍavas would do whatever you say, being wholly under your sway — there is no doubt of that.
You should ensure the secrecy of this counsel, O Puruṣottama; that I consider to be the beneficial course here, O delight of all the Yādavas.
If the king, that righteous one of firm vows, were to know me as the first-born son of Kuntī, he would not accept the kingdom.
And even if I obtained that great and prosperous kingdom, O Madhusūdana, O crusher of enemies, I would give it all over to Duryodhana alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let Yudhiṣṭhira, that ever-righteous soul, be the eternal king — whose guide is Hṛṣīkeśa and whose warrior is Dhanañjaya.
The earth and the kingdom belong to him whose great warrior is Bhīma, and who has Nakula, Sahadeva, and the sons of Draupadī, O Mādhava.
Uttamaujas, Yudhāmanyu, the Somaka of true dharma, Caidya, Cekitāna, and the unvanquished Śikhaṇḍī —
— those of Indragopaka hue, the Kekaya brothers as well, and Kuntibhoja the great warrior, of the colour of Indra's rainbow —
— the maternal uncle of Bhīmasena, and the great warrior Senajit, Śaṅkha the son of Virāṭa, and you yourself, O Janārdana, his treasure —
This is a great mustering of the kshatriya order you have assembled, O Kṛṣṇa; this blazing and celebrated kingdom has been won and is renowned among all kings.
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's weapon-sacrifice shall take place, O Vārṣṇeya; you shall be the knower of this sacrifice, O Janārdana; and you, O Kṛṣṇa, shall perform the role of the Adhvaryu priest in this rite.
Bībhatsu, girt for battle and bearing the monkey-banner, shall be the hotar-priest; the Gāṇḍīva shall be the sacrificial ladle, valor the clarified butter.
The Aindra, the Pāśupata, the Brahmā, and the Sthūṇākarṇa weapons, O Mādhava — these shall be the mantras deployed there by Savyasācī.
Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadrā — who follows his father or surpasses him in valor — shall properly perform the role of the Gravastotrin chanter there.
Bhīma of immense strength shall again be the Udgatar singer there, the Prostota — that tiger among men who roars and destroys armies of elephants in battle.
And that ever-righteous king Yudhiṣṭhira himself, engaged in prayer and fire-offerings, shall perform the office of the Brahmin priest there.
The sounds of conches, the roll of drums, and the kettledrums, O Madhusūdana, and the exalted lion-roars — these shall be the Subrahmania chants of this sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nakula and Sahadeva, the glorious sons of Mādrī, those two of great valor, shall duly perform the Shamitra rite there.
Let the sacrificial posts be prepared for this sacrifice, O Govinda, O Janārdana — the speckled-shafted, pure chariot-javelins.
Karṇa-arrows, reed shafts, iron arrows, and Vatsadanta-tipped bolts, lances, Soma-vessels, straining-cloths, and bows — let these be the implements of this sacrifice.
The swords here are the sacrificial ladles, the oblation-cakes are the severed heads, O Kṛṣṇa, and blood shall be the clarified butter-offering in this sacrifice.
The firewood and enclosing sticks are the spears and bright maces, and the priests at the session are the disciples of Droṇa and of Kṛpa, son of Śaradvān.
The arrows shot by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, and those launched by great warriors and urged on by Droṇa and Aśvatthāmā, are the sacrificial straw-bundles here.
Sātyaki shall perform the assistant's rite here; the consecrated sacrificer is the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and his great army serves as the sacrificial wife.
The mighty Ghaṭotkaca shall perform the slaughtering rite here, O great-armed one, when the sacrifice is extended into the all-night ceremony.
The sacrificial fee of this sacrifice is the valiant Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O Kṛṣṇa — he who was born from fire when the Vedic ritual was performed.
Whatever harsh words I spoke to the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of pleasing the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — O Kṛṣṇa, I am now burned by that deed.
When you shall see me slain, O Kṛṣṇa, by Savyasācin, then shall the re-piling of the altar fire of this sacrifice take place.
When the Pāṇḍava drinks the blood of Duḥśāsana, roaring as he roars aloud — then shall the soma-pressing day of this sacrifice arrive.
When the two sons of Pāñcāla shall lay low both Droṇa and Bhīṣma, that shall be the concluding rite of this sacrifice, O Janārdana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the mighty Bhīmasena shall slay Duryodhana, then the sacrifice of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall be complete, O Mādhava.
The daughters-in-law and granddaughters-in-law of Dhṛtarāṣṭra assembled together, their lords slain, their sons slain, their protectors slain, O Keśava —
— weeping together with Gāndhārī amid jackals, vultures, and ospreys: that shall be the concluding bath of this sacrifice, O Janārdana.
Kṣatriyas advanced in learning and advanced in age should not be caused to die in vain on your account, O bull among kshatriyas, O Madhusūdana.
Let the full circle of the kshatriya order find death by the sword at Kurukṣetra, the holiest of all three worlds, O Keśava.
Therefore, O lotus-eyed one, O Vārṣṇeya, arrange what you desire, so that the entire kshatriya class may attain heaven.
As long as the mountains and rivers shall stand, O Janārdana, so long shall this fame-born, eternal renown endure.
Brahmins shall tell of the great Bhārata battle at their assemblies, O Vārṣṇeya — that battle which upholds the glory of the kshatriyas.
Bring the son of Kuntī to battle against me, O Keśava, always keeping your counsels concealed, O scorcher of foes.
Sañjaya said: Having heard the words of Karṇa, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes, then spoke this speech laughing, beginning with a smile.
Does not the gaining of a kingdom burn you, O Karṇa? The earth that has been offered to you, you do not wish to rule.
The victory of the Pāṇḍavas is certain — of this there is no doubt whatsoever here; the victory-banner of the Pāṇḍava is seen raised aloft, with the fierce monkey-king upon it.
A divine illusion has been arranged by the lord of the worlds; it is raised up, blazing like Indra's banner; divine beings, terrifying and fearsome, are seen there as well.
It does not catch on mountains or forest trees; extending a yojana upward and across, the glorious banner of Dhanañjaya is raised up, O Karṇa, blazing like fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When in battle you shall see the white-horsed one with Kṛṣṇa as charioteer, wielding the Aindra weapon and both the fire and wind weapons —
— and hear the twanging of the Gāṇḍīva bow like the crash of a thunderbolt, then there shall be neither the Tretā age nor the Kṛta nor the Dvāpara.
When in battle you shall see Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, engaged in muttered prayer and fire-offerings, protecting his great army —
— irresistible like the sun, scorching the enemy host, then there shall be neither the Tretā age nor the Kṛta nor the Dvāpara.
When in battle you shall see the mighty Bhīmasena drinking the blood of Duḥśāsana and dancing in the fight —
— like a rogue elephant, a slayer of rival elephants, then there shall be neither the Tretā age nor the Kṛta nor the Dvāpara.
When in battle you shall see the two great chariot-warriors, sons of Mādrī, shaking the army of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra like two elephants —
— plunging into the thick of weapons, smashing the chariots of enemy heroes, then there shall be neither the Tretā age nor the Kṛta nor the Dvāpara.
When in battle you shall see Droṇa, Śāntanava Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, King Suyodhana, and Jayadratha the Sindhu king —
— rushing swiftly into combat, held at bay by Savyasācin, then there shall be neither the Tretā age nor the Kṛta nor the Dvāpara.
Go from here, O Karṇa, and tell Droṇa, Śāntanava, and Kṛpa: 'This mild month is at hand, well-supplied with barley, food, and fuel.'
'The forests of ripened herbs are full, there is fruit, few insects; the water is free of mud and full of flavor; the weather is neither too hot nor too cold — it is pleasant.'
'From the seventh day, the new moon will come — let battle be joined then; they say that day is under the lordship of Indra.'
'Also tell the king and all those who have come ready for war: whatever you have wished for, I shall accomplish all of it for you.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kings and princes who follow Duryodhana's command, attaining death by the sword, shall reach the highest state.
Sañjaya said: Having heard that beneficial and auspicious speech of Keśava, Karṇa, honoring Kṛṣṇa the slayer of Madhu, said: 'Knowing me as you do, O great-armed one, why do you wish to bewilder me?'
'This destruction of the whole earth that has now come upon us — the occasions for it were Śakuni, myself, Duḥśāsana, and King Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.'
'Without doubt, O Kṛṣṇa, this great battle is at hand between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus — terrible, a mire of blood.'
'Kings and princes who follow Duryodhana's command, consumed by the fire of weapons in battle, shall reach the abode of Yama.'
'For many dreadful dreams are seen, O Madhusūdana, and dreadful omens, and fearful portents too.'
'Various hair-raising signs seem to proclaim defeat for the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and victory for Yudhiṣṭhira, O Vārṣṇeya.'
'For the fierce planet of great brilliance, Saturn, afflicts the constellation of Prajāpati, oppressing living beings exceedingly.'
'And Mars, having turned retrograde in Jyeshtha, O Madhusūdana, moves toward Anuradha, as though appeasing Mitra.'
'Surely a great terror has come upon the Kurus, O Kṛṣṇa; for particularly, O Vārṣṇeya, a planet afflicts the star Citra.'
'The mark of the moon has shifted; Rāhu will approach the sun; and from the sky these meteors fall with thunderclaps and tremors.'
'Elephants groan and horses shed tears; they do not take joy even in water and barley, O Mādhava.'
'When these omens appear, they say that a dreadful peril is at hand, O great-armed one — a destruction of living beings.'
'Even with little eaten, abundant excrement is seen here from horses, from elephants, and from men, O Keśava.'
'In all the armies of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Madhusūdana — the wise declare that to be a sign of defeat.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'The mounts of the Pāṇḍavas are described as joyful, O Kṛṣṇa, and deer circle them clockwise — that is the sign of victory for them.'
'All the deer circle counter-clockwise around the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Keśava, and there are disembodied voices as well — that is the sign of defeat.'
'Peacocks, flower-birds, geese, sarus cranes, chataka birds, and flocks of jivanjivaka birds follow the Pāṇḍavas.'
'Vultures, crows, herons, hawks, rakshasas, jackals, and swarms of flies follow the Kauravas.'
'In the armies of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the war-drums make no sound; but the kettledrums of the Pāṇḍavas sound unbeaten on their own.'
'Wells bellow like bulls in the armies of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — that is the sign of defeat.'
'A rain of flesh and blood has been rained down by heaven, O Mādhava, and a celestial city of the Gandharvas has appeared near the sun — complete with ramparts, moat, altar-mound, and beautiful gateways.'
'A dark halo stands there encircling the sun; at the morning and evening twilight it portends great terror. A lone she-jackal howls terribly — that is the sign of defeat.'
'Black-necked birds, hanging in a frightful manner, fly toward the twilight — that is the sign of defeat.'
'He first comes to hate brahmins and then his teachers, O Madhusūdana, and also servants who are devoted to him — that is the sign of defeat.'
'The eastern quarter has the color of blood, the southern has the color of weapons, and the western, O Madhusūdana, resembles an unripe vessel.'
'And all the quarters blaze for the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Mādhava; these portent-signs proclaim great terror.'
'At the end of a dream, I saw Yudhiṣṭhira ascending a thousand-pillared palace together with his brothers, O Acyuta.'
'All of them are seen wearing white turbans, dressed in white garments; and I observe white seats for all of them.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'And you too, O Kṛṣṇa, were seen by me at the end of a dream encircling the earth, covered in blood, with entrails, O Janārdana.'
'Yudhiṣṭhira of boundless valor, having climbed a heap of bones, joyfully ate rice cooked in clarified butter from a golden vessel.'
'Yudhiṣṭhira was seen by me devouring the earth — clearly he shall enjoy this earth given to him by you.'
'Bhīma of fierce deeds, Vṛkodara, having climbed a high mountain, club in hand, tiger among men, looks over this earth as if surveying it.'
'He will very clearly annihilate all of us in the great battle. I know this, O Hṛṣīkeśa: where dharma is, there is victory.'
'That Dhanañjaya, the Gāṇḍīva-wielder, mounted on a white elephant, blazing with supreme glory together with you, O Hṛṣīkeśa —'
'— you shall all slay the kings led by Duryodhana in battle, O Kṛṣṇa. Of this I have no doubt.'
'Nakula and Sahadeva and the great chariot-warrior Sātyaki, their armlets and neck-guards gleaming, clad in white garlands and white garments —'
'— these three tigers among men, great ministers, sheltered by white parasols and white garments, were mounted on the finest human vehicle.'
'And three are seen wearing white turbans in the armies of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Janārdana — know them, O Keśava.'
'Aśvatthāmā, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarmā the Sātvata — and all the kings are seen wearing red turbans, O Mādhava.'
'Bhīṣma and Droṇa were seen by me mounted on a camel-drawn vehicle, O Janārdana, together with me and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O great-armed, O resplendent one.'
'We were going toward the quarter governed by Agastya, O Janārdana — in no long time we shall reach the abode of Yama.'
I and the other kings and all the circle of warriors shall enter the fire of Gāṇḍīva — of this I have no doubt.
Kṛṣṇa said: The earth must surely be facing destruction today, for my words, O Karṇa, do not reach your heart.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When destruction is at hand for all creatures, O dear one, what looks like wise counsel does not depart from the hearts of men — it is wrongdoing disguised as policy.
Karṇa said: May we see you again, O Kṛṣṇa, having survived this great battle, O mighty-armed one, having crossed through the destruction and ruin of heroes.
Or else, O Kṛṣṇa, our reunion shall surely be in heaven — there we shall meet again, together with you, O sinless one.
Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus to Mādhava and embraced him tightly, Karṇa, dismissed by Keśava, descended from the floor of the chariot.
Then, mounting his own chariot adorned with gold, Rādheya returned with us, his heart despondent.
Then Keśava drove away swiftly, together with Sātyaki, repeatedly calling out to his charioteer, "Go, go!"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Kṛṣṇa had departed from the Kurus to the Pāṇḍavas with his mission of conciliation unfulfilled, Vidura approached Pṛthā and spoke to her gently, as if grieving.
O you whose sons are living, you know my disposition, always devoted to your welfare — yet Suyodhana does not accept my words, though I cry out repeatedly.
That king is supported by the Cedis, Pāñcālas, and Kekayas, by Bhīma and Arjuna, by Kṛṣṇa, Yuyudhāna, and the Yamas as well.
Even while encamped at Upaplavya, Yudhiṣṭhira — powerful as he is — desires only righteousness out of affection for his kinsmen, like a weak man.
But this king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, though old in years, does not calm himself — intoxicated solely by pride in his son, he walks the path of unrighteousness.
Through the evil counsel of Jayadratha, Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni's son, mutual strife is being fanned.
The kingdom has indeed been seized by unrighteous means from those who are most righteous — this very unrighteousness, with all its consequences, shall return upon those who took it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Who would not burn with indignation when righteousness is forcibly wrested away by the Kurus? With Keśava gone without conciliation, the Pāṇḍavas shall make ready for war.
Then the Kurus will meet with ruin and the slaughter of their heroes. Thinking of this, I find no sleep by day or by night.
Kuntī, hearing those words spoken with genuine purpose, unwilling to accept what she did not desire, afflicted with grief, reflected deeply in her mind.
Shame on wealth, for the sake of which this great destruction among kinsmen will occur — for in this war the defeat of these friends shall surely come to pass.
If the Pāṇḍavas, the Cedis, the Pāñcālas, and the Yādavas, assembled together, fight against the Bharatas, what sorrow could be greater than this?
I see only certain calamity in this war, and defeat in this war as well. Death is better than poverty, for victory is no victory when it comes through the slaughter of kinsmen.
Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu, the preceptor who is lord of warriors, and Karṇa — all fighting for the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son — increase my fear.
Surely teacher Droṇa, who has no desire for personal gain, would never willingly fight against his pupils — and how could the grandsire Bhīṣma not feel affection for the Pāṇḍavas?
But this one alone — evil, holding perverse views, always following delusion, the wicked man who serves the evil-minded Dhārtarāṣṭra — constantly hates the Pāṇḍavas.
Karṇa is particularly insistent on great calamity, and he is especially powerful; he always opposes the Pāṇḍavas — this burns me now.
But today I hope to appease Karṇa's mind toward the Pāṇḍavas, by approaching him and showing him the truth of the matter.
When I had pleased the revered Durvāsas, he gave me a boon — a divine invocation connected with the gods, while I was living in my father's house.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I was then in the inner quarters of king Kuntibhoja's palace, my heart aching, thinking in many ways.
I kept thinking again and again about the strength and weakness of the mantras, about the power of a brahmin's word, and about the weaknesses of a woman and a child.
Protected then by a trusted nurse, surrounded by my circle of companions, guarding against transgression, and preserving my father's honor.
Thinking "How may I do what is right? How may I be without guilt?" and having bowed to that brahmin,
Out of curiosity upon receiving it, and acting foolishly out of childishness, I, a chaste girl, then invoked the god Sūrya.
He who was born of me before wedlock and has been treated as a son — why would he not heed words that are wholesome and beneficial to his brothers?
Having thus resolved upon this as the highest and most certain course of action, Kuntī set out on her errand and went to the Bhāgīrathī river.
On the bank of the Gaṅgā, Pṛthā then heard the sound of her own son's recitation — that compassionate and truth-devoted man.
That ascetic woman stood behind him, who faced east with upraised arms, waiting for the end of his silent recitation so she could accomplish her purpose.
She stood on the northern robe of Karṇa, scorched by the sun, the wife of a Kaurava and daughter of the Vṛṣṇis, withering like a garland of lotuses.
Having recited until his back too was scorched by the sun, that disciplined man turned around; seeing Kuntī, the great-spirited and honorable Karṇa, best among upholders of righteousness, approached and greeted her with joined palms as propriety required.
Karṇa said: I am Karṇa, son of Rādhā, son of Adhiratha — I salute you. What brings you here, noble lady? Tell me, what may I do for you?
Kuntī said: You are a son of Kuntī, not of Rādhā; Adhiratha is not your father. You were not born in a sūta family, O Karṇa — know this from my words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You were born of me before my marriage, carried in my womb as my firstborn, in the house of Kuntibhoja — you are a son of Pṛthā, dear child.
This god who performs brilliant deeds, the sun, who illumines all — he begot you in me, O Karṇa, best among bearers of weapons.
Born wearing earrings, with armor fastened on, conceived of a god, and endowed with splendor, you, O invincible one, were born of me, my son, in my father's house.
That you, failing to recognize your brothers, serve the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra out of delusion — that is not fitting for you, my son, especially not for you.
This is the fruit of righteousness for men when righteousness is their aim, O son — that his fathers are pleased, and his mother who shares the same vision.
Seize back from the Dhārtarāṣṭras the royal glory of Yudhiṣṭhira, which was earned by Arjuna and taken by wicked men out of greed, and enjoy it.
Today let the Kurus behold the union of Karṇa and Arjuna; witnessing that brotherhood, let the wicked ones bow their heads.
If Karṇa and Arjuna were as Rāma and Janārdana together, what in the world would be unachievable for you two with united hearts?
O Karṇa, you will surely shine, surrounded by five brothers, as Brahmā is surrounded by the Vedas together with the five Vedāṅgas.
Endowed with the finest qualities, the eldest among the most excellent kinsmen — let the epithet "son of a charioteer" not be spoken; you are a son of Pṛthā, O valiant one.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Karṇa heard words issuing from the sun — irresistible, affectionate, urging him as a father would, sent by Bhāskara.
Pṛthā speaks the truth, O Karṇa — heed your mother's words. It shall be for your good, O tiger among men, if you act accordingly in everything.
Although thus addressed by his mother and by the sun himself, his father, the resolve of Karṇa, steadfast in truth, did not waver even then.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Karṇa said: I do not disbelieve the words you, O kṣatriya lady, have spoken to me — this your commission may be the gate of righteousness for me.
The great transgression you committed against me — by that act you have cast me out, and it destroyed my fame and reputation.
I was born a kṣatriya yet did not attain the rites proper to a kṣatriya — because of you. What worse harm could an enemy do to me?
Not showing compassion for me at the time of the rites, you left me then in a state deprived of proper sacraments — and now today you urge me.
You did not act toward me before as a mother concerned with my welfare — and now you counsel me, seeking only your own benefit.
Who would not tremble before Dhanaṃjaya, who is united with Kṛṣṇa? Who would not know me today as afraid, if I went over to the assembly of the Pārthas?
Unknown as a brother before, revealed only at the time of war — if I now go to the Pāṇḍavas, what will the kṣatriyas say of me?
I have been given every pleasure and been constantly and greatly honored by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — how can I render their efforts fruitless?
Those who have incurred the enmity of others on my account, who always attend upon me and ever bow to me as the Vasus bow to Indra —
Those who believe themselves able, through my life's effort, to withstand their enemies — how today could I shatter their heart's desire?
Those who wish to cross the impassable battle with me as their boat, who desire the other shore of the shoreless sea — how could I abandon them?
For this is the time that has come for those who live in dependence on Dhārtarāṣṭra — I must discharge my debt there, without sparing my life.
Those who, having been well maintained and their purposes fulfilled, act treacherously when the time of need arrives, disregarding what was done for them — they are wicked and unstable.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For those sinful men who are guilty of betraying their king and who steal the master's bread — neither this world nor the next exists.
I shall fight for the sake of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra against your sons, employing all my strength and power — truly I do not speak falsely to you.
Protecting compassion and the conduct befitting an honorable man, even though your proposal would benefit me, I shall not follow your words today.
Yet your undertaking shall not be in vain with respect to me — in battle I shall not slay your sons who are worthy of being slain and who can be defeated: Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, and the twins — save only for Arjuna.
My combat with Arjuna in the army of Yudhiṣṭhira will be even — for by slaying Arjuna in battle the goal shall be achieved by me, and I shall also be united with glory even if slain by Savyasācin.
Your five sons, O glorious lady, shall never perish — whether without Arjuna but with Karṇa alive, or with Arjuna but with me slain.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing Karṇa's words, Kuntī trembled with grief; she embraced her son Karṇa, who remained unshaken in his steadfastness, and spoke.
"So it must be — through this the Kurus shall meet their destruction. As you speak, O Karṇa, fate is the more powerful."
"The safety you have granted to my four sons, O vanquisher of foes — pledge that promise, the release from battle."
"Be well, be safe," said Pṛthā to Karṇa; Karṇa responded to her with affection, and then the two departed separately.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having come from Hāstinapura to Upaplavya, the subduer of enemies, Keśava, told the Pāṇḍavas everything that had occurred.
Having conversed for a long time and deliberated again and again, Śauri went to his own quarters to rest.
Having dismissed all the kings headed by Virāṭa, the five Pāṇḍava brothers, when the sun had set,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
having performed the twilight prayer and meditating, their minds fixed on that same matter, brought Kṛṣṇa of the Dāśārha clan once more and deliberated in counsel again.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Having gone to the elephant city, O Lotus-eyed one, what did you say to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the assembly? Please tell us all of it.
Vāsudeva said: Having gone to the elephant city, I spoke to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the assembly words that were truthful, beneficial, and good — yet that wicked-minded one does not accept them.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When that one had gone astray, O Hṛṣīkeśa, what did the elder of the Kurus, the grandsire, say? And what did the preceptor, the mighty-armed son of Bhāradvāja, say to the impatient Duryodhana?
And what did our younger father Vidura, the foremost among upholders of righteousness, afflicted with grief over his son, say to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
And what did all the kings assembled in that hall say truthfully? Tell us all of this, O Janārdana.
For you have spoken everything to the two foremost of the Kurus — to that dull-witted one overwhelmed by desire and greed, who fancies himself wise.
That unpleasant news does not rest easy in my heart, O Keśava. I wish to hear their words, O Govinda, O lord.
And do act, dear one, so that the critical moment does not arrive. You are our refuge, O Kṛṣṇa; you are our master; you are our guide.
Vāsudeva said: Listen, O king, to how King Suyodhana was addressed in the midst of the Kurus in the assembly. Hear it from me, O lord of kings.
When my words were spoken, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra laughed. Then Bhīṣma, greatly enraged, spoke these words:
"Duryodhana, understand what I say to you for the sake of your lineage. Having heard it, O tiger among kings, do what is beneficial for your own clan.
My father, dear boy, was King Śaṃtanu, renowned throughout the world. I was his sole son, the foremost among those who have sons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A thought arose in his mind: how might a second son come to be? For the wise declare that one with only one son is as good as sonless.
And lest the line become extinct, and lest his fame cease to spread — understanding his wish, I brought Kālī as his mother.
Having made a terrible vow for my father's sake and for the sake of the lineage — remaining celibate and kingless, as is well known to you — I have lived here faithfully, keeping that vow.
From her was born the mighty-armed, glorious uplifter of the Kuru lineage — Vicitravīrya, righteous of soul, the younger king, my brother.
When my father had ascended to heaven, I installed King Vicitravīrya in his own kingdom, myself serving as a subordinate, walking humbly below.
I brought suitable wives for him, O lord of kings, having conquered an assembly of kings — this too you have heard many times.
Then I met Rāma in single combat on the battlefield. For being driven out by the inhabitants of that city through fear of Rāma, and being overly attached to his wives, Vicitravīrya contracted consumption.
When the lord of the gods did not rain upon the kingless realm, the subjects, tormented by hunger and fear, came rushing to me alone.
