The subjects said: All the people are perishing. Become our king for our welfare. Drive away our afflictions. Good fortune to you, O increaser of Śaṃtanu's lineage.
All those subjects are afflicted by greatly terrible diseases and are nearly spent. O son of the Gaṅgā, you must protect them.
Drive away the diseases, O hero, and protect the subjects righteously. While you are alive, let not the kingdom come to ruin.
Bhīṣma said: Even as the subjects were lamenting, my mind was not shaken — protecting my vow, and remembering likewise my good conduct.
Then the citizens, O great king, and my auspicious mother Kālī, the servants, the chaplain, the teachers, and the greatly learned Brahmins, all deeply grieved, spoke to me repeatedly: 'Become king.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'The kingdom protected by Pratīpa will perish now that it has come to you. For our welfare, become king, O great-minded one.'
Thus addressed, I folded my hands, deeply grieved and distressed. Out of reverence for my father, I declared my vow to them repeatedly — that I was celibate and without kingship, for the sake of the lineage.
Then, with folded hands, I appeased my mother, saying: 'No, mother — I, born of Śaṃtanu and bearing up the Kaurava lineage, would never make my vow false' — thus, O king, again and again.
'And especially for your sake — do not yoke me to this burden. I am your servant and your slave, O mother who loves your son.'
Having thus appeased my mother and the people, I then besought the great sage Vyāsa regarding wives for my brothers.
Together with my mother, O great king, having propitiated that sage, I begged him for offspring. He granted the grace, and he then fathered three sons, O best of the Bhāratas.
Because he was blind and lacking faculties, your father was not king. Rather, the great-souled Pāṇḍu became king, renowned throughout the world.
He was the king, and his sons — your cousins — are the heirs to their father's inheritance. Do not quarrel, dear boy; let half the kingdom be given to them.
While I still live, what man should rule the kingdom here? Do not disregard my words. I always desire peace for you all.
There is no distinction for me between you and them, O king, my son. This is the view of your father, of Gāndhārī, and of Vidura.
If the words of elders are to be heeded, do not be suspicious of my counsel. You will not destroy everything — yourself and the earth alike."
Vāsudeva said: After Bhīṣma had spoken, Droṇa then addressed Duryodhana in the midst of the kings — he who was capable of speech spoke words of good counsel:
"Just as Prātīpa's son Śaṃtanu arose for the sake of his lineage, so too Devavrata Bhīṣma stood firm for the sake of the lineage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Pāṇḍu, the lord of men, true to his word, master of his senses, the king of the Kurus, righteous in soul, of noble vows, and composed of mind —
— that increaser of the Kuru lineage gave the kingdom to the elder Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the wise one, and likewise acknowledged the younger Vidura.
Then, O king, having installed that unfailing one upon the lion-throne, the Kaurava prince departed to the forest together with his two wives, O sinless one.
And Vidura, that tiger among men, stood humbly in a low place attending like a servant, waving the yak-tail fan.
Then all the subjects, dear boy, followed Dhṛtarāṣṭra as their lord of men, duly, just as they had followed Pāṇḍu, the ruler of men.
Having handed the kingdom over to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Vidura, Pāṇḍu, the conqueror of enemy cities, ranged over the entire earth.
In building up the treasury, in giving gifts, in overseeing the servants, and in maintaining everything — Vidura, true to his word, took charge.
Bhīṣma, of great splendor and conqueror of enemy cities, superintended the matters of peace and war and attended to the affairs of the king.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra of great might sat upon the lion-throne, constantly attended upon by the great-souled Vidura.
Being born in that lineage, how do you resolve to divide it? Unite with your brothers and enjoy your pleasures together, O lord of the people.
I say this not out of pity, nor for any material reason whatsoever. I eat what is given by Bhīṣma, not by you, O best of kings.
I shall not seek from you any means of livelihood, O lord of the people. Where Bhīṣma is, there is Droṇa. Do what Bhīṣma has said.
Let half the kingdom be given to the sons of Pāṇḍu, O scourge of enemies. My preceptorship is equal to both you and them at all times, dear boy.
As Aśvatthāmā is to me, so too is the white-horsed Arjuna to me. What need is there for much talk? Where there is dharma, there is victory."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the immeasurably splendid Droṇa had thus spoken, O great king, Vidura, true to his word and knower of dharma, turning and looking at his father's face, then spoke these words:
"Devavrata, hear these words I speak: the Kaurava lineage had been all but lost, and you raised it up again.
Yet you disregard my lamentation's words. Who is this Duryodhana, this defiler of the clan, in this lineage?
You follow the will of one overwhelmed by greed, ignoble and ungrateful, whose mind is destroyed by greed — one who transgresses the counsel of his father who sees dharma and artha.
These Kurus are perishing through what Duryodhana has done. O great king, act so that they do not perish.
Having made me and Dhṛtarāṣṭra as mere paintings at the outset, O greatly radiant one, do not destroy us. As Prajāpati, having created beings, withdraws them, so too would you.
Do not be indifferent, O mighty-armed one, seeing the destruction of the lineage. Or if your mind is now lost, with ruin at hand, then go to the forest together with me and with Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Or else, having bound up that wicked-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra of treacherous intellect, let this kingdom now be well protected by the Pāṇḍavas.
Be gracious, O tiger among kings. Great destruction is foreseen — of the Pāṇḍavas, the Kurus, and kings of immeasurable splendor."
Having spoken thus, Vidura fell silent, his mind despondent, brooding, and sighing again and again.
Then the daughter of King Subala, fearful of the destruction of the lineage and speaking in accordance with dharma and artha, addressed in anger her wicked-minded and cruel son Duryodhana in the presence of the kings:
"Let all the kings who have entered this royal assembly, and the brahmin seers and other members of the assembly, hear — I shall speak of the transgression of this sinful one along with his ministers and entourage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The kingdom of the Kurus is to be enjoyed in proper succession — this is our lineage's custom handed down in order. You of wicked mind and extremely cruel deeds are unjustly destroying the Kurus' kingdom.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra the wise stands in the kingdom; his younger brother Vidura is far-sighted. Passing over these two, how do you today out of delusion seek kingship, Duryodhana?
Both the king and Vidura, those of great majesty, would be subservient while Bhīṣma stands. Yet that great-souled best of men, the river-born, desires no kingdom through his knowledge of dharma.
This kingdom of Pāṇḍu is inviolable; his sons alone are the lords of it today, none others. That entire kingdom belongs to the Pāṇḍavas, the ancestral inheritance passing to sons and grandsons.
Whatever the great-souled foremost of the Kurus, Devavrata, true to his word and wise, has said — all of that is to be accepted by us, laying aside other dharma, while upholding our own dharma.
And whatever the king Vidura would say with the permission of that great-vowed one — that too should be done, appointed by friends, placing dharma foremost, for a very long time.
Let Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, rule this kingdom of the Kurus which has come to him by right — urged on by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and honored also by the son of Śaṃtanu."
Vāsudeva said: When Gāndhārī had spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, addressed Duryodhana with these words in the midst of the kings, O lord of the people:
"Duryodhana, understand what I shall say to you, dear son. Do accordingly — good fortune to you — if you have reverence for your father.
Soma the Prajāpati was the primordial increaser of the Kuru lineage. From Soma in the sixth generation was born Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.
He had five sons, the best of royal sages. Among them, the mighty-souled Yadu became the eldest and the lord.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And then there was Pūru, the younger, who is the increaser of our lineage, born of Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
And Yadu, O best of the Bhāratas, was the son of Devayānī, the grandson of Śukra Kāvya of immeasurable splendor, dear boy.
He, the founder of the Yādava lineage, was mighty and esteemed for his valor. But filled with pride and of very dull wit, he disrespected the warrior class.
Deluded by pride in his strength, he did not abide by his father's instruction. He also disrespected his father and his brothers — that undefeated one.
Yadu alone became the mighty one on the earth bounded by the four horizons. Having subjugated the kings, he dwelt in the city named after the elephant.
His father Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, in extreme fury cursed that son, O Gāndhāra king, and removed him from the kingdom.
And those brothers who followed him in his arrogant pride — Yayāti, enraged, cursed those sons as well.
Then that best of kings installed his younger son Pūru, who was obedient and compliant, upon the throne.
Thus even a proud elder son does not obtain the kingdom, while younger sons obtain it through service to the elders.
Similarly, my father's grandfather Pratīpa, the earth-protector, knower of all dharma, was renowned in all three worlds.
Of that lion among kings, ruling his kingdom righteously, three illustrious sons were born, equal to the gods in glory.
Devāpi was the eldest, Bāhlika came next, and the third, O father, was the steadfast Śaṃtanu, my grandfather.
But Devāpi, though of great splendor and best of kings, had a skin disease; he was righteous, truthful, and devoted to serving his father.
Devāpi was honored by the people of the city and countryside, respected by the virtuous, and dear to the hearts of all — young and old alike.
He was wise, true to his word, devoted to the welfare of all beings, and lived by the teachings of his father and the brahmaṇas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He was dear as a brother to Bāhlika and to the great-souled Śaṃtanu, and there was supreme fraternal harmony among those noble souls united together.
Then in the course of time, the aged king, that best of rulers, had the materials for the consecration prepared according to scripture, and had all the auspicious rites performed as well — he who was sovereign over all.
But the brahmaṇas and elders, together with the people of city and countryside, all prevented the consecration of Devāpi.
Hearing that the consecration was barred, the king's throat choked with tears, and he grieved deeply for his son.
Although so generous, so learned in dharma, so true to his vow, and so dear to the people, he was disqualified by the blemish of a skin disease.
"The gods do not favor a king with a bodily defect" — on this ground the foremost of twice-born men barred that best of kings.
Then that king, his soul deeply troubled and grief-stricken for his son, died; and seeing him dead, Devāpi took refuge in the forest.
Bāhlika, abandoning the kingdom, settled in his mother's family, renouncing his father's brothers, and attained a prosperous city.
With Bāhlika's permission, O king, the world-renowned Śaṃtanu ruled the kingdom as king after his father's death.
In the same way, O Bhārata, I — the elder — was removed from the kingdom by the wise Pāṇḍu on the ground that I am defective in a limb.
Pāṇḍu, though younger, obtained the kingdom as king. Now with his sons destroyed, this kingdom belongs here; I am unfit for kingship — how then, O subduer of foes, can you desire this kingdom?
Yudhiṣṭhira is a noble prince of great soul; this kingdom has come to him by rightful succession. He is the lord of this Kaurava people, and a ruler of great majesty.
He is true to his vow, ever vigilant, steadfast in his duty, virtuous toward his kin, beloved of the people, compassionate to friends, master of his senses, and protector of the good.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Forbearance, patience, self-control, uprightness, adherence to the vow of truth, learning, heedfulness, compassion for all beings, and the power of command — all the virtues of a king are united in Yudhiṣṭhira.
You are no true prince, you follow ignoble conduct, you are greedy, you harbor wicked thoughts toward your own kin — how can you, so ill-behaved, seize this kingdom that belongs by succession to another?
Free yourself from delusion and give up half the kingdom — with its cavalry and all its furnishings. Then the remainder of your life, together with your brother's, may still be secured, O lord of men.
Vāsudeva said: Though Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Vidura, Gāndhārī, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke thus, the foolish one did not come to his senses.
He shook off their words, rose up in anger, his eyes red with rage; and the kings, reckless of their lives, ran after him.
And that evil-minded king commanded those rulers again and again: "March to Kurukṣetra — today is the auspicious Puṣya asterism!"
Then those lords of the earth marched out with their armies, making Bhīṣma their commander, rejoicing, driven on by fate.
Eleven akṣauhiṇī armies of the kings assembled; at their head Bhīṣma, bearing the palm-tree banner, shone resplendent. Do now, O lord of the earth, whatever is fitting and proper here.
O Bhārata, the words spoken by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Vidura, Gāndhārī, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra in my presence — all that transpired in the Kuru assembly, O king, I have now told you.
Conciliation was first employed by me, O king, as I desired brotherly harmony — for the preservation of the unity of the Kuru lineage and the prosperity of the people.
Then division too was my instrument when conciliation was not accepted — along with the recounting of deeds that combined the divine and the human.
When Suyodhana did not honor speech beginning with conciliation, then I, having summoned all the kings together, drove them apart.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And I demonstrated marvellous, terrifying, dreadful, superhuman deeds, O Bhārata, O lord.
And after threatening those kings and making Suyodhana seem as nothing as straw, and frightening Rādheya and Śakuni again and again —
— proclaiming again and again the inferiority and censure of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and dividing all the kings through speech and counsel repeatedly —
— I then again spoke of conciliation combined with the gift, for the unity of the Kuru lineage and also for the sake of what needed to be done.
"Let all the Pāṇḍavas abide by the words of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bhīṣma, and Vidura, setting aside pride, and living humbly subordinate."
"Let them yield up the kingdom and become powerless, as the river-born king Bhīṣma and Vidura have declared — let it be so."
"Let all the kingdom be yours — but give up five villages; for your father's sons must certainly be provided for, O best of kings."
But spoken to thus, the evil-souled one did not relent at all. I see the fourth expedient — force — as the only recourse against those sinful ones; there is no other way.
And the lords of men have marched out to Kurukṣetra for their destruction. All that occurred in the Kuru assembly I have now recounted to you.
They will not give you the kingdom without war, O Pāṇḍava. All of them are causes of destruction, with death standing ready before them.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of Janārdana, the righteous king Yudhiṣṭhira, whose soul was in dharma, spoke to his brothers in the presence of Keśava.
"You have all heard what transpired in the assembly of the Kuru council, and every word that Keśava spoke has been well taken in."
"Therefore, O best of men, carry out for me the division of the army. These seven akṣauhiṇī forces have assembled here for victory."
"The seven commanders of these forces are well known — hear them: Drupada and Virāṭa, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin,"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Sātyaki, Cekitāna, and the mighty Bhīmasena — these are the army's leading heroes, all ready to lay down their lives."
"All are versed in the Vedas and valiant, all of pure and observed vows, all endowed with modesty and wisdom, all skilled in battle, expert in archery, and fighters with every weapon."
"But who shall be the one leader over all seven armies, skilled in their distribution — one who in battle could withstand Bhīṣma, who is like a blazing fire of arrows?"
"You, Sahadeva, speak up here, O delight of the Kurus, tiger among men — tell us your opinion: who is fit to be our commander?"
Sahadeva said: He is allied with us, shares in our grief, is mighty, a lord of the earth, a knower of dharma — relying on him we seek to recover our own portion.
The Matsya king Virāṭa, strong, skilled in arms, intoxicated with battle-fury — he will be able to withstand Bhīṣma and those great chariot-warriors in combat.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Sahadeva had spoken thus, Nakula, the eloquent in speech, immediately took up the matter after him with these words.
"By age, by learning in the scriptures, by steadfastness, by lineage and noble birth, he is endowed with modesty, graced with high family, possessed of glory, expert in all the sacred sciences —"
"— he has learned weaponcraft from Bharadvāja's son, he is indomitable and true to his pledge, and he perpetually rivals Droṇa and the mighty Bhīṣma —"
"— praiseworthy as the foremost commander before the assembly of kings, surrounded by sons and grandsons like a tree with a hundred branches —"
"— that hero and lord of the earth, together with his wife, performed fierce austerities out of fury for the destruction of Droṇa, and he shines in every assembly —"
"— he who always provides for us like a father, that bull among kings — let our father-in-law Drupada lead the army at the vanguard."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"He, I believe, could withstand both Droṇa and Bhīṣma as they advance in battle — for he is a king who knows divine weapons and is a friend and disciple of the descendant of Āṅgiras."
When the two sons of Mādrī had spoken their views, the son of Vāsava, equal to Vāsava himself, the left-handed archer Arjuna, spoke up.
"He who was born a divine person through the power of austerity and the satisfaction of the sages, blazing in color and of great strength —"
"— bearing a bow, clad in armor, wielding a sword, mounting his chariot in full battle-gear, drawn by the finest divine horses, risen up from the sacrificial fire-pit —"
"— roaring like a great storm-cloud with the thunder of his chariot, that valiant hero with a lion's build and a lion's mighty stride —"
"— lion-chested, long-armed, with a lion's breast and great strength, roaring like a lion, with a lion's shoulders, of great radiance —"
"— with beautiful brows, beautiful teeth, a beautiful jaw, beautiful arms, a beautiful face, not lean, a beautiful clavicle, wide beautiful eyes, beautiful feet, and standing beautifully —"
"— impenetrable to all weapons, like a rutting elephant in his force, born for the destruction of Droṇa, truthful in speech, master of his senses —"
"— I believe Dhṛṣṭadyumna could withstand Bhīṣma's arrows, which are like the touch of the thunderbolt and lightning, like fire-mouthed serpents —"
"— equal to Yama's messengers in speed and descent, like fire in their fury, borne up even by Rāma in battle, dreadful as the crushing stroke of the thunderbolt —"
"I see no man who could withstand the great-vowed Bhīṣma other than Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O king — such is my considered opinion."
"Quick of hand, varied in his fighting — he is my choice for commander, his armor impenetrable, glorious, like a great elephant leading the herd."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīma said: Śikhaṇḍin, son of Drupada, was born for the purpose of killing — so declare the Siddhas and the sages assembled together, O king of kings.
In the midst of battles, when he deploys his divine weapon, men will behold his form as they behold the great-souled Rāma himself.
I see no one in battles, O king, who could pierce Śikhaṇḍin with a weapon in combat, when he stands armored upon his chariot.
None other could withstand Bhīṣma of the great vow in single chariot combat, O king, save the hero Śikhaṇḍin — he is my choice for commander.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O father, the soul of dharma Keśava knows the essence and the non-essence, the strength and weakness, of all the world — past and future alike.
Whoever Kṛṣṇa of the Dāśārha clan names — whether skilled in arms or not, whether old or young — let that one be our commander of the army.
He is the root of our victory, O father, and of our defeat as well. In him lie our lives and our kingdom, our being and non-being, our joy and sorrow.
He is the creator and the ordainer; success is established here. Whom Kṛṣṇa of the Dāśārha clan has named — he is fit to be our commander. Let the best among speakers speak; the night is passing.
Then, having installed as commander one who follows Kṛṣṇa's will, when the remainder of the night has passed, we shall march to the battlefield — our weapons consecrated and auspicious rites performed with joy.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of the wise Dharma-king, the lotus-eyed one, glancing toward Dhanañjaya, spoke.
These leaders of your army whom you have named, O great king — they are heroes, mighty warriors. All of them are capable of crushing your enemies.
In great battle, these men could strike fear even in Indra himself — what then of the greedy, evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I too, O mighty-armed slayer of foes, made great effort for your sake — hoping there might be peace, O Bhārata. The debt of dharma has been paid; those who wish to speak cannot reproach us.
That childish, unwise Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son considers himself accomplished. The afflicted one considers himself strong — a fool's self-delusion.
Let the army be marshalled well — for in my judgment those foes are to be subdued by slaughter. The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will not be able to stand firm when they behold Dhanañjaya.
And furious Bhīmasena, and the twins who are like Yama himself, and Yuyudhāna as his second, and the wrathful Dhṛṣṭadyumna —
Abhimanyu, the sons of Draupadī, Virāṭa and Drupada as well, and the other lords of akshauhini divisions — kings of firm valor —
Our army, full of essence and irresistible, impregnable — without doubt it will slay the Dhṛtarāṣṭra forces in battle.
When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, the foremost of men rejoiced greatly; and from those whose hearts were delighted a great roar arose.
"To arms!" — and the armies rushed forward in haste. The cries of horses and elephants, the clatter of wheel-rims from every direction, the tumultuous blast of conches and kettledrums arose on all sides.
As the Pāṇḍavas set forth with their armies in every direction, the host appeared like the Gaṅgā in flood — full and irresistible.
In the vanguard marched Bhīmasena and the armored sons of Mādrī, Subhadrā's son and the sons of Draupadī, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, and the Prabhadrakas and Pāñcālas — all with Bhīmasena at their head.
Then a sound arose like the ocean at high tide; the clamor of the joyful marching host seemed to touch the sky.
Joyful and armored, those warriors, destroyers of enemy ranks, marched; and in their midst went the king, Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The wagon-shops and market stalls, all manner of conveyances and draft animals, the treasury, siege-engines and weapons, as well as physicians and healers —
Whatever weak or feeble auxiliary force there was, however lean and infirm — the king gathered all of it, together with the attendants and camp-followers, and marched on.
But at Upaplavya, the Pāñcālī Draupadī, the truth-speaker, remained behind with the other women, surrounded by her maidservants and male servants.
Having made arrangements for the base camp with stationary and mobile guard detachments, the sons of Pāṇḍu marched forth with a great cantonment-army.
Bestowing cows and gold, surrounded by brahmins who chanted their praises, they marched, O king, in chariots adorned with jewels.
The Kekayas, Dhṛṣṭaketu, the son of the king of Kāśi named Abhibhū, Śreṇimān, Vasudāna, and the unvanquished Śikhaṇḍī —
Joyful and content, clad in armor, armed and adorned, all of them followed the king, surrounding Yudhiṣṭhira.
In the rear guard were Virāṭa, Yajñasena the Somaka, Sudharma, Kuntibhoja, and the sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Four times ten thousand chariots, horses five times as many, infantry ten times that number, and sixty thousand cavalry.
Anādhṛṣṭi, Cekitāna, the king of the Cedis, and Sātyaki — all of them marched surrounding Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya.
Having reached Kurukṣetra, the Pāṇḍavas appeared with their armies arrayed and ready to strike, roaring like bulls.
Those slayers of foes, having entered Kurukṣetra, blew their conches; and likewise Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya both blew their conches.
Hearing the blast of the Pāñcajanya conch, like the crack of a thunderbolt, all the armies thrilled with joy on every side.
The lion-roars of those swift warriors, mingled with the sound of conches and kettledrums, made the earth, the sky, and the oceans resound in echo.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then king Yudhiṣṭhira encamped his army in a level, pleasant region, rich in barley, fodder, and fuel.
Avoiding cremation grounds and temples of the gods, the hermitages of great sages, sacred fords, and holy sites —
— in a pleasant, lightly saline tract, auspicious and holy, the lord of the earth, Yudhiṣṭhira son of Kuntī, had the camp laid out.
Then, rising again, at ease and with rested mounts, he marched forward, surrounded by kings in their hundreds of thousands.
Routing hundreds of outpost detachments of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's soldiers, Keśava together with Pārtha ranged about on all sides.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, son of Pṛṣata, and the noble chariot-warrior Sātyaki — the valiant Yuyudhāna — measured out and marked the camp.
Having reached the sacred river Hiraṇvatī in Kurukṣetra — blessed with good fords, with pure water, free of gravel and mire —
— there, O Bhārata, Keśava had a moat dug for protection, and, having stationed guards, he settled the army in that place.
Whatever the arrangement of the camp had been for the great-souled Pāṇḍavas — Keśava had the camps of all the kings laid out in the same manner.
Abundantly supplied with water and firewood, made even more difficult to assail, stocked with food and provisions — by the hundreds and thousands —
— the splendid camps of the kings were pitched there, each separately from the others, like celestial palaces set down upon the earth, O lord of kings.
There were skilled craftsmen by the hundreds, paid their wages, furnished with all implements, and physicians highly expert in their art.
Heaps like mountains were amassed — of bowstrings, bows, armor, and weapons, and likewise of honey, clarified butter, medicinal juices, and powders.
Plentiful water, good fodder, chaff and charcoal — king Yudhiṣṭhira caused all of this to be gathered in camp after camp.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Great siege-engines, iron arrows, javelins, lances, battle-axes, bows, armor and the rest — all of these were close to the hearts of the men in that hour.
Elephants harnessed in mail-armor, covered with iron-plate barding, were seen there — mountain-like, each capable of fighting hundreds and thousands of foes.
Learning that the Pāṇḍavas were encamped there, O Bhārata, their allies came streaming in as appointed, with their forces and vehicles.
Those kings who had observed celibacy, drunken the soma, and performed sacrifices with lavish gifts came together for the victory of the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Janamejaya said: Yudhiṣṭhira approaching with his army, eager for battle, encamped at Kurukṣetra, protected by Vāsudeva —
— accompanied by Virāṭa and Drupada with their sons, surrounded by the Kekayas and the Vṛṣṇis, and by hundreds of kings —
— guarded by great chariot-warriors like Mahendra guarded by the Ādityas — hearing of this, what course of action did king Duryodhana adopt?
This I wish to hear in full detail, O ascetic sage — what transpired in that tumult and commotion on the Kuru plain.
For in battle the Pāṇḍavas, Vāsudeva, and likewise Virāṭa and Drupada could torment even the army of the gods when they are assembled.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna of the Pāñcālas, and Śikhaṇḍī the great chariot-warrior, and the valiant Yuyudhāna — unapproachable even by the gods.
All of this I wish to hear in full, O ascetic sage — whatever the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas did and how they each conducted themselves.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the Dāśārha hero had departed, king Duryodhana then spoke this to Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni:
"Adhokṣaja has gone to the Pārthas with the mission unaccomplished. Filled with anger at them, he will certainly incite them — there is no doubt."
"For conflict with me is dear to Vāsudeva's Pāṇḍavas; both Bhīmasena and Arjuna stand in agreement with the Dāśārha's counsel."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Even Ajātaśatru today follows the will of Bhīma and Arjuna; and he was previously deceived by me along with all my brothers."
"Virāṭa and Drupada too have been made enemies of mine, and they are the leaders of that army, followers of Vāsudeva's will."
"This war that is coming will be tumultuous, hair-raising. Therefore, without delay, have all war preparations made."
"Let camps be established at Kurukṣetra, O lords of the earth — with ample space, and made difficult for enemies to attack."
"Close to water and firewood, by the hundreds and thousands; with supply lines that cannot be cut; piled with heaps of gems; filled with all manner of weapons; adorned with banners and pennants."
"And let level roads be made for them outside the city. Let the departure be announced today: 'tomorrow at dawn' — delay no longer."
They pledged "So be it," and at the next dawn the great-souled warriors did as commanded, their faces joyful — though it was for the destruction of the kings of earth.
Then all those kings, hearing the royal command, rose from their magnificent seats, burning with impatience.
They stroked their arms — like iron bolts, blazing with golden armlets, adorned with sandalwood and aloe —
— tightening their turbans with lotus-like hands, arranging inner and outer garments and all their ornaments —
— the finest chariot-warriors prepared their chariots; those expert in horses prepared their horses; those trained in the lore of elephants prepared their elephants.
Then they readied their variegated armor of gold in great quantity, and all manner of weapons — making everything ready on every side.
And foot-soldiers, men bearing all kinds of weapons, attached to their bodies gold-inlaid arms in manifold ways.
Like a great festival, the city of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son was thronged with delighted men, joyfully astir, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A whirlpool of the waters of human multitudes, filled with chariots, elephants, and horses as fish — resounding with conches and kettledrums — heaped with treasuries of gems —
— its waves the variegated ornaments and armor, its foam the gleaming weapons, its mountains the rows of palaces, its great lake the streets and markets —
— stirred by the rising moon of warriors, the great ocean that was the Kuru king's realm appeared then, O king, like the ocean at the rising of the moon.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Recalling the words of Vāsudeva, Yudhiṣṭhira again questioned the Vṛṣṇi hero — how that foolish one had spoken thus:
"Now that this time has come upon us, what is proper for us, O Acyuta? And how, conducting ourselves rightly, shall we not swerve from our own dharma?"
"You know the minds of Duryodhana, Karṇa, Śakuni the son of Subala, O Vāsudeva — and of me with my brothers as well."
"The words of Vidura you have heard, and of both Bhīṣma as well; and the wisdom of Kuntī in its entirety has been heard by you, O one of vast intelligence."
Setting all of this aside, and having pondered again and again, O mighty-armed one, tell us without hesitation what is fitting for us.
Having heard these words of the Dharma King, which were filled with righteousness and purpose, Kṛṣṇa, whose voice resounds like the thunder of clouds and drums, spoke.
I have spoken words that were beneficial, full of righteousness and purpose — but they do not take hold in that Kaurava whose mind is bent on wickedness.
That fool of wicked intellect heeds not the counsel of Bhīṣma, nor of Vidura, nor of me — he transgresses all of it entirely.
He desires neither righteousness nor glory; that wicked soul, relying on Karṇa, believes he has already conquered all.
Suyodhana even ordered my arrest, yet that wicked transgressor of all order did not obtain his desire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Neither Bhīṣma nor Droṇa uttered a fitting word on that occasion; all follow him except Vidura, O Acyuta.
Śakuni, the son of Subala, and also Karṇa and Duḥśāsana — those fools spoke unseemly words against you, O impatient one, to a fool.
And what use was what I said? Whatever the Kauravas spoke, in brief — that wicked soul does not conduct himself fittingly toward you.
Among all the kings and among all these soldiers of yours, whatever is sinful and whatever is not wholesome — all of that is established in him.
Nor do we at all desire peace with the Kauravas through excessive concession — after that, war is the only recourse.
Having heard these words of Vāsudeva, all the kings, O Bhārata, looked silently at the face of the king, saying nothing.
Yudhiṣṭhira, perceiving the intent of the kings, ordered the march together with Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins.
Then the Pāṇḍava's army broke into a great tumult of joyful cries, and when the march was ordered, the soldiers rejoiced exceedingly.
The Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing the slaughter of those who should not be slain, groaned and spoke thus to Bhīmasena and Vijaya:
That great calamity for whose sake the forest exile was endured, and the suffering I have borne — that very calamity now comes upon us despite all our efforts.
The goal for which we have exerted ourselves has failed us in our endeavour; yet without our effort, this great calamity would have returned to us all the same.
How indeed shall we wage battle with those who should not be slain? How shall victory be ours after killing our elders and venerable ones?
Hearing this from the Dharma King, Savyasācī, the scorcher of foes, caused him to hear again what Vāsudeva had said.
The son of Devakī has spoken, and O king, you have heard in full the counsels of Kuntī and of Vidura.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
My firm conviction is that neither of those two would counsel unrighteousness; nor, O son of Kuntī, is it proper to turn back without fighting.
Hearing those words of Savyasācī, Vāsudeva too smiled and spoke to Pārtha, saying: "It is even so."
Then those Pāṇḍavas, O great king, resolved upon war, dwelt that night in comfort together with their soldiers.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the night had passed, King Duryodhana then arrayed those armies — eleven in all, O Bhārata.
Among foot-soldiers, elephants, chariots, and horses — the excellent, the middling, and the inferior — the king of the earth assigned each to all these divisions.
Equipped with drag-ropes and quivers, with chariot bodies and lances, with sword-sheaths and javelins, with arrow-pouches and bludgeons —
With standards and banners, with bows and javelins, with variegated ropes, with nooses and protective armour —
With hair-grasping flings, with oil, molasses, and sand, all furnished with pots of venomous serpents, and with resin-sap and dust —
All equipped with bells and shields, with axes and wood-cutters, covered with tiger skins and clad in leopard hides —
With bandages and horns, with pikes and various weapons, with axes and mattocks, with oil, linen, and ghee —
The ranks were splendid, the men well-formed, blazing like fires — those armoured heroes, practiced and skilled in weapons.
Of noble birth, versed in the breeding of horses, installed as charioteers — with protective charms bound on, with girths fastened, with standards and banners secured.
All the chariots were drawn by four horses, all were fully armed with weapons, all had spirited mounts, and all were equipped with a hundred bows.
One man managed the two draft horses, two others served as rear-guard charioteers, and those two were the finest among chariot warriors — and the chariot warrior himself was likewise an expert in horses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There were thousands of chariots, garlanded with gold all around, like well-guarded cities difficult for enemies to assail.
Just as the chariots, so too the elephants — with girths fastened and richly adorned — had seven men each, like gem-bearing mountains.
Of these seven, two bore elephant-hooks, two bore the finest bows, two bore excellent swords, O king, and one bore a lance and a banner.
That force of the Kaurava, O king, was filled with thousands of maddened elephants bearing armour, weapons, and housings.
There were tens of thousands of horses, adorned with variegated armour and ornaments, bearing banners, and accompanied by cavalry.
Easily handled and well-contented, with golden trappings and equipment — those many hundreds of thousands stood under the command of the cavalry.
There also were foot-soldiers of various forms and kinds, wearing armour of many types and bearing weapons, garlanded with gold.
To each chariot belonged ten elephants; to each elephant, ten horses; and ten men served as foot-guards around each horse on all sides.
Fifty elephants were allotted to each chariot; a hundred horses to each elephant; and seven men to each horse, skilled in mending and binding wounds.
A sena consists of five hundred elephants and the same number of chariots; ten senas make a pritana, and ten pritanas make a vahini.
Vahini, pritana, sena, dhvajini, sadini, camu — these are the synonymous terms for an akshauhini, also called varuthi. In this manner the armies were arrayed by the wise Kaurava.
Eleven akshauhinis in all, and also seven — the strength of the Pāṇḍavas was seven akshauhinis, while the strength of the Kauravas was eleven akshauhinis.
A patti consists of fifty-five men; three such senamukhas make a gulma, as it is named.
Ten gulmas made a gana; and ganas numbering ten thousand were the fighters ready for battle in Duryodhana's armies.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There, the mighty-armed King Duryodhana, having carefully considered brave and wise men, then appointed generals.
He gathered the leading commanders of the separate akshauhinis — the finest of men — and consecrated those kings with due rite.
Kṛpa, Droṇa, Śalya, the great chariot-warrior Saindhava, Sudakṣiṇa of Kāmboja, and Kṛtavarman —
The son of Droṇa, and Karṇa, and Bhūriśravas, and Śakuni the son of Subala, and the great chariot-warrior Bāhlika —
Day after day, and at every watch, O Bhārata, he arranged various signals among them, and confirmed them in his own presence again and again.
Thus all of them were disciplined, and those soldiers who followed in their footsteps, O king, were desirous of pleasing the king.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with folded hands, along with all the kings of the earth, addressed Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu with these words:
Without a commander of the army, even the greatest force, when it meets battle, falls apart like an anthill.
The minds of two commanders are never alike at any time, and the valour of leaders by its very nature rivals itself.
It is heard, O greatly wise one, that against the Haihayas of immeasurable might, all the Brāhmaṇas advanced, bearing aloft banners of sacred kusha-grass.
After them followed the Vaiśyas and also the Śūdras, O Grandsire — on one side the three varnas together, and on the other the bulls among Kṣatriyas alone.
The three varnas were routed in battle again and again, while the Kṣatriyas alone, though a numerous force on one side, kept winning.
Then those best of twice-born ones questioned the Kṣatriyas themselves, and those who knew dharma declared to them the truth of the matter, O Grandsire.
We follow a single man of great intelligence in battle, but you are all separately following the dictates of your own individual minds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then those Brāhmaṇas appointed a single twice-born general, skilled in statecraft and brave, and thereafter they defeated the Kṣatriyas.
Thus, those who appoint as general a man skilled, brave, devoted to the good, and free from sin — they conquer their enemies in battle.
You are equal to Uśanas, and you are always a well-wisher of mine; immovable, established in dharma — be our general.
As the sun is to the rays of light, as the moon to the creeping plants, as Kubera to the yakshas, as Vāsava to the Maruts —
As Mount Meru is to mountains, as Suparṇa to birds, as Kumāra to beings, as Havyavat to the Vasus —
Protected by you, we shall be as the dwellers of heaven protected by Śakra — truly unassailable even by the thirty gods.
May you march ahead of us as Pavaki leads the gods; we shall follow you as the sons of Surabhī follow the bull.
Bhīṣma said: O mighty-armed one, it is even as you say, O Bhārata; just as you are to me, so too are the Pāṇḍavas to me.
And yet, O lord of men, I must speak what is good for them; but I shall fight for your cause, as that agreement was made.
But I see no warrior on earth who is my equal, save only that tiger among men, the son of Kuntī, Dhanañjaya.
That mighty-armed one knows all the divine weapons in their entirety; yet the Pāṇḍava would never fight me openly in battle.
He and I together could in a single moment, by the sheer force of our weapons, empty this world of men — gods, asuras, and rakshasas included.
But the sons of Pāṇḍu are not to be annihilated by me, O lord of men; therefore I shall always slay ten thousand warriors each day through my skill.
Thus I shall bring about the destruction of their forces, O delight of the Kurus — unless they slay me first when battle is joined.
But I shall be your general, O king, upon another condition of my own choosing — you ought to hear it from me now.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Either Karṇa shall fight first, or I shall, O lord of the earth — for the son of a charioteer constantly and excessively rivals me in battle.
Karṇa said: I shall not fight in any manner, O king, while the son of the Gaṅgā lives; but when Bhīṣma is slain, I shall fight with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with due rite and lavish gifts, installed Bhīṣma as general; and he, thus consecrated, shone resplendent.
Then, by royal command, men without distraction beat kettledrums and conch-shells and kettle-drums by the hundreds.
Diverse lion-roars arose and the cries of beasts of burden, and from a cloudless sky there fell a rain of blood and mud.
Thunderbolts, earthquakes, and the screaming of elephants arose and struck terror into the hearts of all warriors.
Bodiless voices were heard, and meteors fell from the sky; jackals that foretell evil cried out loudly with blazing voices again and again.
When the king consecrated Bhīṣma, son of the Ganges, as commander of the army, O king, these terrible omens manifested by the hundreds.
Then, having made Bhīṣma, the crusher of enemy forces, commander, and having caused the foremost brahmins to recite blessings and having given them golden coins and cattle in abundance,
swelling with benedictions of victory, Duryodhana marched out surrounded by soldiers, with his brothers and with Bhīṣma at the fore, and went with a great army to Kurukṣetra.
Having circumambulated Kurukṣetra together with Karṇa, the Kaurava king had his camp measured out on level ground.
In a region pleasant and not too saline, rich in barley and fodder, the camp shone just like Hāstinapura itself.
Janamejaya said: When the great-souled Bhīṣma, son of the river, foremost among weapon-bearers, grandfather of the Bharatas and banner of all kings of the earth,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom, equal to the earth in forbearance, like the ocean in depth, and firm as the Himālayas,
like Prajāpati in generosity, like the sun in splendor, and like great Indra in destroying enemies with showers of arrows—
when king Yudhiṣṭhira heard that he had been consecrated for a long time to the sacrifice of battle, dreadful and hair-raising—
what did the mighty-armed one, skilled in all dharma, say? And what did Bhīmasena, Arjuna, or Kṛṣṇa do in response?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Yudhiṣṭhira, the great-minded one skilled in the duties of adversity and polity, gathered all his brothers and Vāsudeva of the Sātvata clan, and, foremost among speakers, said these words with gentle reassurance:
"Patrol the armies, stand ready, clad in armor. The battle with your grandfather will come first. Therefore look upon the seven leaders of my forces."
Vāsudeva said: "As befits you to speak at this time that has arrived, so too this meaningful speech has been uttered by you, O bull of the Bhāratas."
"It pleases me, O mighty-armed one. Let what follows be done: let seven commanders be consecrated for your army."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, summoning Drupada and Virāṭa and the bull of the Śinis, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the Pāñcāla prince, and the king Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Śikhaṇḍī the Pāñcāla, and Sahadeva the Magadha king,
these seven great archers, heroes who delighted in battle—Yudhiṣṭhira consecrated them as army commanders according to rite.
And as commander-in-chief over all he appointed Dhṛṣṭadyumna—he who was born from the blazing fire for the very purpose of slaying Droṇa.
But over all of them assembled, those great-souled ones, he made Guḍākeśa Dhanañjaya the lord of commanders.
And as guide and charioteer of Arjuna's horses stood the glorious and greatly wise Janārdana, younger brother of Saṅkarṣaṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing the battle imminent, the great calamity close at hand, Halāyudha entered the dwelling of the Pāṇḍava king.
He came accompanied by Akrūra and others, by Gada, Sāmba, Ulmuka and the rest, by the sons of Rukmiṇī and Āhuka, and with Cārudeṣṇa at the fore.
Escorted by the chief Vṛṣṇis who came like mighty tigers, the great-armed one was protected as Vāsava is by the Maruts.
Clad in dark silk garments, resembling a peak of mount Kailāsa, moving with the leisurely gait of a lion, glorious, with eyes reddened at the corners by wine—
seeing him, the king of dharma and the greatly radiant Keśava rose, and so did the son of Pṛthā the terrible-actioned Vṛkodara.
The Gāṇḍīva-bowman and whatever other kings were there—all of them approached and honored Halāyudha.
Then the Pāṇḍava king touched his hand with his own hand, and all the others with Vāsudeva at their head saluted him.
Halāyudha, the subduer of foes, paid homage to the elders Virāṭa and Drupada, and then sat down together with Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, when the kings had sat down on all sides, Rauhiṇeya gazed upon Vāsudeva and spoke:
"There will be a great and terrible slaughter of men—this I regard as fated and certain; it cannot be averted.
My wish is that I might see you, along with your dear ones, emerge safe from this battle, healthy and with bodies unharmed.
The assembled royal Kṣatriya clan is ripened by Time without doubt; a great crushing is coming, a mire of flesh and blood.
Again and again in private I urged Vāsudeva: 'Madhusūdana, maintain equal conduct toward your kinsmen on both sides.'
"'The Pāṇḍavas are as much ours as is king Duryodhana; show him too the proper honor'—this I urged again and again.
But Madhusūdana did not heed that counsel of mine; he was wholly committed with all his being, with eyes fixed on Dhanañjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Victory of the Pāṇḍavas is certain—this is my firm conviction; for such indeed is the absorption of Vāsudeva, O Bhārata.
And I cannot bear to witness the world without Kṛṣṇa; therefore I shall follow what Keśava intends to do.
For both are my heroic pupils, skilled in mace-fighting; my affection is equal for Bhīma and for king Duryodhana.
Therefore I shall go to visit the sacred fords along the Sarasvatī; I cannot bear to stand by as the Kauravas perish."
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Rāma, with the permission of the Pāṇḍavas, departed on his pilgrimage to the sacred fords, taking leave of Madhusūdana.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: At that very time, the son of the great-souled Bhīṣmaka, king of the golden-fleeced, who was himself a friend of Indra—
the son of that lord of abundance, the exceedingly glorious Bhoja, lord of the southern regions—known in all directions as Rukmī—
he who was the pupil of the lion among Kiṃpuruṣas who dwells on Gandhamādana, and had mastered the complete four-footed science of archery,
the mighty-armed one who obtained the bow Mahendra, equal in splendor to the Gāṇḍīva, and the divine inexhaustible Śārṅga which is on a par with it—
these three are the only divine bows that traverse the heavens: the Vāruṇa bow called Gāṇḍīva, the Mahendra called Vijaya,
and Śārṅga, they say, the Vaiṣṇava bow, divine and made of pure radiance—which Kṛṣṇa bore, striking terror into enemy armies.
The son of Pāka's slayer received the Gāṇḍīva from the fire in the Khāṇḍava forest; the greatly splendid Rukmī obtained Vijaya from a tree.
Having severed the bonds of Mura, having slain Mura by force, having conquered Naraka the earth-born, and having recovered the jeweled earrings,
Hṛṣīkeśa recovered sixteen thousand women and various jewels and the supreme bow Śārṅga.
But Rukmī, having obtained the bow Vijaya whose sound was like a thundercloud, came to the Pāṇḍavas as though threatening the whole world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This hero, proud of the strength of his own arms, had in the past not forgiven the abduction of Rukmiṇī by the wise Vāsudeva.
Having made the vow "I shall not return without slaying Keśava," he then pursued the Vṛṣṇi hero, foremost among all weapon-bearers.
With a great four-fold army, far-reaching, equipped with varied weapons and armor, swollen like the flooding Gaṅgā,
he encountered the Vṛṣṇi hero, lord and master of yogas, was utterly defeated and humiliated, O king, and returned to Kundina.
Right there where he had been defeated in battle by Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, he built a fine city named Bhojakaṭa.
With that great army rich in elephants and horses, that city became renowned on earth by the name Bhojakaṭa, O king.
That Bhoja king, of great valor, surrounded by a great army comprising a full akshauhini division, came to the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, clad in armor, bearing sword and arrows and bow and palm-shield, riding his chariot, with a banner the color of the sun, he entered the great host.
Known to the Pāṇḍavas, and desiring to please Vāsudeva, king Yudhiṣṭhira went out to meet him and honored him.
Duly honored and well-received by the sons of Pāṇḍu, he honored them all in return; then, rested, along with his soldiers, he spoke in the midst of the heroes to Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī:
"I stand ready as your ally in battle. If you are afraid, O Pāṇḍava, I shall render you in combat an assistance that your enemies cannot withstand."
"For there is no man in this world equal to me in valor; slaying your enemies in battle, I shall give them to you, O Phalguna."
Addressed thus, in the presence of the king of dharma and Keśava, and with all the lords of the earth and everyone else listening,
the wise son of Kuntī glanced at Vāsudeva and at the Pāṇḍava king of dharma, and spoke laughing in a tone of friendly warmth:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Hero, when I was fighting the exceedingly mighty Gandharvas during the cattle-raid expedition, who was my ally, who was my friend then?
Likewise in that terrifying encounter in the Khāṇḍava forest, filled with gods and demons—who was my ally when I fought then?
In battle against the Nivātakavacas and the Kālakeya demons—who was my ally when I fought there?
Likewise in Virāṭa's city, when I fought many Kurus in battle—who was my ally then, dear friend?
Taking shelter in battle upon Rudra, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, Yama, Varuṇa, Pāvaka, Kṛpa, Droṇa, and Mādhava—
bearing the divine Gāṇḍīva bow, made of pure radiance and firm, furnished with inexhaustible arrows, and augmented by celestial weapons—
born in the lineage of the Kauravas, and above all as the son of Pāṇḍu, pointing to Droṇa as my teacher, I am the pupil who has Vāsudeva as ally.
How could one such as I speak the inglorious words 'I am afraid'—even were the thunderbolt-wielding Indra himself my enemy, O tiger among men?
I am not afraid, O mighty-armed one, nor do I have any need of an ally. Go wherever you wish, however you see fit, or remain elsewhere."
Then Rukmī turned back with his ocean-like army and went to Duryodhana in the same manner, O bull of the Bhāratas.
And having approached him likewise, he said the same things to that king, and was equally rejected by him who thought himself a hero.
Two thus withdrew from that war, O great king: Rauhiṇeya the Vṛṣṇi hero, and Rukmī the lord of the earth.
With Rāma departed on his pilgrimage to sacred fords, and the son of Bhīṣmaka likewise withdrawn, the Pāṇḍavas sat down once again to take counsel.
That assembly of the king of dharma, crowded with lords of the earth, shone resplendent — like the sky bright with stars and the moon, O Bhārata.
Janamejaya said: When the armies had thus been arrayed on the field of Kurukṣetra, O bull among twice-born, what did the Kurus do, impelled by time?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When those armies had thus been arrayed, O bull of the Bhāratas, the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words to Sañjaya.
"Come, Sañjaya — tell me everything without remainder: whatever has occurred at the camp among the armies of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas."
"I consider destiny supreme and human effort fruitless — for even though I know the evils of war and its ruinous consequences,"
"Yet I cannot restrain my son, whose judgment is warped and who plays at wicked dice, nor can I act for my own welfare."
"Indeed, O Sūta, a discernment of faults arises in me, but when it encounters Duryodhana, it turns back again."
"Things being so, O Sañjaya, whatever is destined shall come to pass. The duty of a warrior, it is said, is revered as the laying down of the body in battle."
Sañjaya said: "This inquiry of yours is appropriate, O great king, as befits you. Yet you ought not to fix this blame on Duryodhana alone. Hear me fully as I speak, O lord of the earth."
"A man who incurs misfortune through his own misconduct ought not to lay that sin upon destiny or upon time."
"O great king, a man who practices everything blameworthy among men, who commits what all the world condemns, deserves destruction by all the world."
"O foremost of men, the Pāṇḍavas endured insults, waiting on you, deceived with their ministers through the crooked dice-play."
"Hear from me in full what slaughter has occurred in battle — of horses, of elephants, and of kings of immeasurable splendor."
"Be steadfast, O great king, and having heard of the rise and fall of all the world as it truly occurred in this great war, do not become despondent."
"For a person is not truly the author of good or evil actions; a person is not free — he is driven like a wooden puppet."
"Some are directed by the Lord, some by chance, and others by the actions of former lives — this threefold force pulls men apart."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sañjaya said: When the great-souled Pāṇḍavas had encamped on the Hiraṇvatī, O great king, Duryodhana — together with Karṇa, O Bhārata —
— and with Śakuni the son of Subala, O king of kings, and with Duḥśāsana — having summoned Ulūka aside, O king, spoke thus:
"Go, Ulūka, son of Śakuni — go to the Pāṇḍavas together with the Somakas, and speak my words in the hearing of Vāsudeva."
"This war, terrible to all the world, which has been pondered over many years by the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus alike, has now arrived."
"That great boast which Sañjaya spoke in the midst of the Kurus, O son of Kuntī — the time for it has come. Let everything be done as you have pledged."
"Remember the wrath, O Pāṇḍava — the seizure of the kingdom, the forest exile, and the humiliation of Draupadī — and be a man!"
"That for which a warrior woman bears a son in her womb has now arrived. Showing your strength, valor, heroism, and supreme skill with weapons in battle, make expiation for your wrath."
"Whose heart would not burst — one who has been tormented, impoverished, who has lived long in hardship, and who has been stripped of sovereignty?"
"Of a hero born in a noble house, whose kingdom was seized by one greedy for another's wealth — whose anger would not be kindled?"
"Let that great speech which was spoken be now demonstrated by deeds; the virtuous know that one who boasts but does not act is a base person."
"Two outcomes attend a warrior in battle: to remain under the power of enemies, or to recover the kingdom. Therefore, show your manhood!"
"Either defeat us and rule this earth, or be slain by us and go to the world of heroes."
"Remember the banishment from the kingdom, the suffering, the forest exile, O Pāṇḍava, and the humiliation of Kṛṣṇā — and be a man!"
"As unpleasant words were spoken and you went into exile again and again — show your indignation now, for indignation itself is manhood."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let your wrath, strength, valor, mastery of knowledge, and lightness of hand with weapons be seen here in the battle, O Pārtha — be a man!"
"And to that glutton Bhīmasena, O Ulūka — that dullard, that ignorant braggart — repeat my words more than once:"
"'What was sworn in the assembly hall by one who was powerless, O wolf-belly — let the blood of Duḥśāsana be drunk, if it can be done!'"
"The supply of iron is ready, Kurukṣetra is free of mud, your horses are well-fed, your warriors are paid — tomorrow fight together with Keśava!"
Sañjaya said: Having reached the camp of the Pāṇḍavas, Ulūka, son of Śakuni, was brought before Yudhiṣṭhira by the Pāṇḍava princes and addressed him.
"Knowing the protocols of envoys and the words I speak as instructed, you should not grow angry upon hearing Duryodhana's commission."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Ulūka, you have no cause for fear — speak without anxiety what is the view of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that greedy man of short-sighted vision."
Sañjaya said: Then, in the midst of the brilliant great-souled Pāṇḍavas, and of all the Sṛñjayas, and of the illustrious Kṛṣṇa —
— in the presence of Drupada with his sons, and of Virāṭa, and in the midst of all those lords of the earth, Ulūka spoke the following words:
"Thus spoke the great-minded king, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, while the Kuru heroes listened. Understand this, O lord of men:"
"'You were defeated at dice, and Kṛṣṇā was dragged into the assembly hall. A man who considers himself a man ought to be able to feel indignation.'"
"'You were exiled from your home for twelve full years in the forest, and lived as servants in Virāṭa's court for one year.'"
"'Remember the wrath, the seizure of the kingdom, the forest exile, O Pāṇḍava, and the humiliation of Draupadī — and be a man!'"
"'What was sworn by the powerless Bhīmasena, O Pāṇḍava — let the blood of Duḥśāsana be drunk, if it can be done!'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'The supply of iron is ready, Kurukṣetra is free of mud, the road is even, the warriors are paid — tomorrow fight together with Keśava!'"
"'Why do you boast without having encountered Bhīṣma in battle — like a fool wishing to climb Mount Gandhamādana?'"
"'Without defeating Droṇa, the foremost of warriors, equal in battle to the lord of Śacī, how do you desire the kingdom here, O Pārtha?'"
"'The teacher who is supreme in the brahma-bow, who knows the distinction between the two Vedas, who bears the army unshaken and steadfast in battle, the unfailing one —'"
"'That you wish in delusion to conquer Droṇa in battle, O Pārtha — that is false. For we have never heard of Mount Meru being shaken by the wind.'"
"'The wind might carry off Mount Meru, or the sky might fall upon the earth, or the age might be reversed — if what you say about me were true.'"
"'Who, wishing to live, having once received the weapons of those two foe-crushers — be it elephant, horse, or man — would return safely home again?'"
"'How could one who is targeted by those two and who has come into contact with their terrible weapons escape alive from battle, even touching the earth with his feet?'"
"'Are you like a frog dwelling in a well, that you do not perceive this royal army assembled — invincible, brilliant as the army of the gods, protected by lords of men like the sky by the thirty gods?'"
"'— With the easterners, the westerners, the southerners, the northerners, the Kāmbojas, the Śakas, the Khaśas, the Śālvas, the Matsyas, the people of the Kuru midlands, the Mlecchas, the Pulindas, the Draviḍas, the Andhras, and the Kanchis —'"
"'— the vast flood of diverse peoples swelling in battle, unstoppable as the current of the Gaṅgā — and me standing in the midst of a force strong as elephants — do you wish to fight me, O dullard of little intelligence?'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus to king Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, Ulūka turned and again addressed Arjuna, the victorious one:
"Fight without boasting — why do you boast so much, Arjuna? Success in this comes in due course; it is not achieved by boasting."
"If deeds in the world were accomplished by boasting, O Dhanañjaya, then every person in want could boast greatly and have all their aims fulfilled."
"I know you have Vāsudeva as your ally; I know your bow Gāṇḍīva is as tall as a palm tree; I know all this — that there is no warrior like you — and yet knowing this, I take your kingdom."
"Yet one does not attain great success merely by the law of due course; for the Creator brings beings under his control through the mind alone."
"For thirteen years I enjoyed the kingdom while you lamented; I shall rule it again after slaying you along with your kinsmen."
"Where was your Gāṇḍīva then when you were staked and lost as a slave? Where was the strength of Bhīmasena then, O Phalguna?"
"From Bhīmasena with his mace and from Pārtha with his Gāṇḍīva — there was no deliverance for you at that time without the blameless Kṛṣṇā."
"That noble lady rescued you when you had fallen into slavery, you who were caught in inhuman conditions and reduced to servitude."
"What I called you — sesame seeds without kernel — that was the very truth; for Pārtha kept his braided hair tied up in the city of Virāṭa at that time."
"And Bhīmasena, O son of Kuntī, exhausted in the work of a cook in Virāṭa's great kitchen — that too speaks to my manhood."
"In this very way have warriors always punished a warrior — in rank, in girdle, and in braid — who flees in battle."
"Not out of fear of Vāsudeva, nor of you, O Phalguna, will I surrender the kingdom — fight together with Keśava!"
"Illusions, conjuror's tricks, sorcery, or terrifying spectacles — these counter-roarings carry no weight against me when I stand weapons in hand in battle."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"A thousand Vāsudevas or hundreds of Phalgunas — upon encountering me, whose arrows never miss, they will flee in all ten directions."
"Go meet Bhīṣma in battle — smash a mountain with your head! — cross this great unfathomable ocean of warriors with your own two arms!"
"— whose heights are Śāradvata, teeming with Viviṃśati as its fish, whose swells are Bṛhadbala, whose sea-monsters are Saumadatti —"
"— whose floods are Duḥśāsana, whose fish are Śala and Śalya, whose crocodiles are Suṣeṇa and Citrāyudha, whose mountain is Jayadratha, whose depths are Purumitra, whose eddies are Durmarṣaṇa, whose cataracts are Śakuni —"
"— the inexhaustible, ever-swelling torrent of weapons — when you plunge into it and emerge with mind exhausted and all kinsmen slain, then your mind will know torment."
"Then, O Pārtha, may your mind turn back from ruling the earth, as the impure are turned back from the third heaven — for to govern a kingdom is as impossible for you as reaching heaven is for one who has not practiced austerities."
Sañjaya said: Ulūka again spoke to Arjuna the words as he had been told, stinging him with verbal darts like one goading an angry venomous serpent.
Hearing those words, the Pāṇḍavas were greatly enraged — already deeply angered as they had been, now further provoked by Ulūka, son of Śakuni.
They could not remain seated; they flung their arms out and looked at one another like enraged venomous serpents.
Bhīmasena, with head bent down, looked up at Keśava with eyes reddened at the corners, hissing like a venomous serpent.
Seeing the son of the Wind-god distressed and deeply stricken by wrath, the descendant of Dāśārha, smiling slightly, replied to Ulūka, son of Śakuni.
Go quickly, O son of a gambler, and say to Suyodhana: your message has been heard, your purpose understood; let it be as you wish.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And tell Suyodhana this further word of mine: tomorrow you shall see what a man looks like — be a man if you can, O foolish-minded one.
You think, O fool, that Janārdana will not fight because he has been engaged by the Pārthas as a charioteer — and so you do not fear.
Even at the last moment it could happen that I, in my wrath, would burn all the kings as fire burns grass.
But at the command of Yudhiṣṭhira and of the great-souled Phalguna, I shall serve as charioteer to him who fights and who knows the self.
Whether you soar through the three worlds or burrow into the earth, at dawn you shall see Arjuna's chariot right before you, wherever you may be.
And as for what you regard as Bhīmasena's empty roar — let it be firmly fixed in your mind that Duḥśāsana's blood shall be drunk.
Pārtha does not even deign to look at you, nor does King Yudhiṣṭhira, nor Bhīmasena, nor the twins — you who speak so contrarily.
Sañjaya said: Upon hearing those words of Duryodhana, the bull of the Bhāratas gazed at the son of the gambler with eyes that had turned deep crimson.
He, the great-glorious Guḍākeśa, glancing toward Keśava, stretched out his mighty arm and addressed the son of the gambler.
One who, relying on his own valor, challenges his foes fearlessly and to the full measure of his power — he is truly called a man.
But one who, relying on others' valor, challenges his foes — that mere kinsman of a kṣatriya, powerless on his own, is the lowest of men in the world.
You are such a one — you count others' valor as your own, a coward and a fool yourself, yet you wish to revile those greater than you.
You who have consecrated that elder — the wise counselor of all kings, master of his senses, of great intellect — to death, and then boast about it.
Your intention is known to us, O evil-minded defiler of your lineage — that the Pāṇḍavas will not kill Gāṅgeya out of compassion.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The one whose valor you lean on while you boast, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — I shall slay Bhīṣma first, in the sight of all archers.
Go back, O son of the gambler, join the Bharatas and tell Suyodhana, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, what Arjuna Savyasācī has said: at the end of this night the clash shall begin.
What he, of undaunted spirit and true to his vows, declared in the midst of the Kurus to their joy — that he would slay the armies of the Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Śalva — that burden now falls to me.
Were I to slay even Droṇa, you would not fear the Pāṇḍavas at all — so runs his thought: that your kingdom would then be securely won, and the Pāṇḍavas reduced to ruin.
But you, filled with arrogance, do not perceive the calamity that is unfolding upon yourself — therefore I shall be the one to slay, before your eyes in the midst of battle, that elder of the Kurus first.
At sunrise, having marshaled my forces and waited — with banner and chariot — guard the true-vowed one; for I shall, before your eyes, bring Bhīṣma down from his chariot with my arrows.
Tomorrow, when day breaks, Suyodhana shall learn the worth of all this boasting when he sees his grandfather tormented by the net of my arrows.
And as for what was said in the assembly hall by that short-sighted man — your brother Duḥśāsana — to the wrathful Bhīmasena,
O Suyodhana, that ignorant of dharma, that perpetual enemy, that evil-minded doer of cruelty — that oath taken truly shall be fulfilled ere long; of that I assure you.
For pride, arrogance, and wrathful harshness, for cruelty, insolence, and self-conceit —
— for ruthlessness and sharpness of tongue, for hatred of dharma, for transgression into unrighteousness, for speaking too harshly, and for disrespecting elders —
— and for your crooked ways and all your wrongdoing, you shall soon see the bitter fruit, O Suyodhana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With me enraged and Vāsudeva beside me, O lord of men, on what grounds do you, fool, hold any hope of life or kingdom?
When Bhīṣma is laid low, and Droṇa likewise, and the son of the charioteer is slain, you shall be left without hope of life, kingdom, or sons.
Seeing your brothers slain and your sons too, O Suyodhana, when Bhīmasena strikes you down, you shall remember all your misdeeds.
Keśava will not make a second vow; I speak the truth to you — all of this shall indeed come to pass as truly said.
Thus addressed, O king, the son of the gambler took those words to heart, and, having received leave to depart, returned the same way he had come.
Turning back from the Pāṇḍavas, the son of the gambler went to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and reported everything exactly as it had been said, in the assembly of the Kurus.
Having heard the words of Keśava and Arjuna, that bull of the Bhāratas addressed Duḥśāsana, Karṇa, and Śakuni.
He commanded the kings and their forces and the allied contingents that the entire army should stand ready and equipped before sunrise.
Then messengers dispatched by Karṇa went out in great haste — some in chariots, others on camels and mules, others on fine swift horses.
Under Karṇa's orders they swiftly circled the entire army, commanding all the kings: be in battle-readiness before sunrise.
Sañjaya said: Having heard Ulūka's words, Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, set his army in motion with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at its head.
Comprising infantry, elephants, chariots, and masses of cavalry — a fourfold force, terrible and immovable as the earth itself.
Protected by Bhīmasena and the other great chariot-warriors including Arjuna, that formidable army under Dhṛṣṭadyumna's control was steady as the ocean's depth.
At the head of that army marched the great archer Dhṛṣṭadyumna of Pāñcāla, maddened for battle, eager to seize Droṇa, leading the divisions forward.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
According to the strength and keenness of each, he assigned the chariot-warriors: Arjuna against the son of the charioteer, Bhīma against Duryodhana.
Nakula he assigned against Aśvatthāman, Śaibya against Kṛtavarman, and Yuyudhāna of the Vṛṣṇis against the king of Sindhu.
Śikhaṇḍin he appointed in the vanguard against Bhīṣma; Sahadeva against Śakuni; and Cekitāna against Śala.
Dhṛṣṭaketu he set against Śalya; Uttamaujā against Gautama; and the five sons of Draupadī he assigned against the five Trigarta chiefs.
Saubhadra he set against Vṛṣasena, and appointed other kings against the remaining foes — for Abhimanyu was deemed more capable in battle than even Arjuna himself.
Having distributed those warriors both individually and collectively in this way, that great archer of flame-like complexion assigned to himself the share that was Droṇa.
Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, that great archer, supreme commander of the army, wise and resolute for battle, arrayed the formation in proper order.
He deployed the divisions of the Pāṇḍavas as they had been directed, and stood alert in the field of battle for the victory of the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When Phalguna had vowed to slay Bhīṣma, O Sañjaya, what did my dull-witted sons — Duryodhana and the rest — do?
I see the son of Gaṅgā, that father-like elder, as already slain in battle by Pārtha, firm of bow, with Vāsudeva as his ally.
And that man of boundless wisdom, Bhīṣma, best of those who strike — what did he say upon hearing Pārtha's declaration?
And having assumed the generalship of the Kaurava forces, how did that bearer of the yoke, Gāṅgeya of great intellect and prowess, conduct himself?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Sañjaya reported all of that to him exactly as it had been spoken by Bhīṣma, the elder of the Kurus, of immeasurable splendor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sañjaya said: Having received the generalship, Bhīṣma son of Śaṃtanu addressed Duryodhana with these words, as if to gladden him, O king.
Having saluted the young prince, the spear-bearing commander of the vanguard: I shall without doubt be your general today.
I am versed in the duties of commanding an army, in the various battle-formations, and in directing the work both of those in service and those not in service.
In marches and movements, in battle, and in consolidating gains — I know these deeply, O great king, as Bṛhaspati himself knows them.
Even the great formations of divine, Gandharva, and human type — with those I shall bewilder the Pāṇḍavas; let your fever of anxiety depart.
I shall fight with full commitment, protecting your army in accordance with the teachings of the treatises, O king; let your mental anguish pass.
Duryodhana said: I have no fear, O Gāṅgeya, O mighty-armed one, even from all the gods and demons together — this I tell you truly.
How much less when you, the irresistible, are installed as commander, and Droṇa, the tiger among men, who delights in battle, stands ready beside you.
With both of you, foremost of men, standing firm, my victory is not difficult, O best of Kurus — even the sovereignty of the gods would be certain.
I wish to hear a full accounting of the chariot-warriors — of the enemy's side and of ours, and likewise of the great chariot-warriors, O Kaurava.
For the grandsire is expert in the reckoning of enemy and allied forces alike; I wish to hear it together with all these lords of the earth.
Bhīṣma said: O lord of Gāndhāra, O king of kings, hear the count of the chariot-warriors in your own force — those who are chariot-warriors and those who are great chariot-warriors, O guardian of the earth.
Many thousands, ten-thousands, and ten-millions of chariots are in your army — but hear from me the account of the principal ones.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You yourself are foremost, a noble chariot-warrior, together with all your brothers — the hundred brothers beginning with Duḥśāsana.
All of them are trained in weapons, skilled in cutting and piercing, expert on chariot-platform and elephant-back, in mace-fighting, and in sword-and-shield.
They are controllers and attackers, trained in weapons and able to bear their loads; in archery they are disciples of Droṇa and of Kṛpa son of Śaradvat.
These high-spirited sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, their offenses done by the sons of Pāṇḍu weighing upon them, shall slay in battle the battle-maddened Pāñcālas.
Then I, O best of Bhāratas, your supreme commander, shall destroy your enemies, reducing the Pāṇḍavas to naught — though it is not for me to extol my own qualities; you know me well.
Kṛtavarman of the Bhojas, a great chariot-warrior, the foremost of those who strike — he shall without doubt accomplish your objectives in battle.
Irresistible to those who know weapons, a far-shooter, firm of arms — he shall slay your enemies as great Indra slays the demons.
Śalya, the great archer, king of the Madras — I count him a great chariot-warrior; he is one who rivals Vāsudeva himself in battle after battle.
Forsaking his own nephews, Śalya that best of chariot-warriors shall fight on your side in battle against Kṛṣṇa, the bearer of discus and mace.
With onslaughts like the waves of the ocean, inundating his enemies as it were — Bhūriśravas, skilled in weapons, is also your devoted friend and ally.
Saumadatti, the great archer, commander of commanders of chariot divisions, shall bring about a very great diminishing of the strength of your foes.
The king of Sindhu, O great king, I count as double the worth of a chariot-warrior — he shall fight in battle, O king, with valor, best of chariot-warriors that he is.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having been humiliated in the past during the abduction of Draupadī by the Pāṇḍavas, he, the slayer of enemy heroes, shall fight remembering that humiliation.
For he it was, O king, who once undertook a fearsome austerity and won a boon most difficult to obtain — to fight the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
That tiger among chariot-warriors, remembering that enmity in battle, will fight the Pāṇḍavas, my son, casting aside his own life that is so hard to cast away.
Bhīṣma said: Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja I reckon a chariot-warrior of single measure; desiring the fulfillment of your cause, he will fight the foe in battle.
The valor of this lion among chariot-warriors, spent in your cause, O best of kings, the Kurus shall behold in the fray as though it were Indra's own.
His ranks of chariots, O great king, manned by the Kāmbojas who strike with fierce and sudden speed, stretch on like a swarm of locusts.
Nīla, dweller in Māhiṣmatī, clad in dark-blue armor, will work with his chariot ranks a great slaughter of your enemies.
Having made enmity of old with Sahadeva, that prince will fight unceasingly in your cause, O king, O best of the Kurus.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, united, are foremost among chariot-warriors, accomplished in battle, my son, firm in might and valor.
These two tigers among men will consume the enemy host with mace and javelin, sword and iron shaft, and with lances hurled from their arms.
Eager for battle, sporting in the fray like two herd-leaders, they will range through the midst of the host, O great king, like Death itself.
The five Trigarta brothers I count exalted among chariot-warriors, who made their enmity with Pārtha then, in the city of Virāṭa.
Like sea-monsters, O lord of kings, churning the Gaṅgā with her high-tossing waves, they will throw the army of the Pārthas into turmoil in the fight.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
These five are chariot-warriors, O lord of kings, with Satyaratha at their head; they will fight in battle, remembering what was done of old.
They remember the wrong done by the son of Pāṇḍu, the younger brother of Bhīmasena, who, conquering the quarters with his white-horsed car, O king, O Bhārata —
— closing in, these bearers of the warrior's burden will slay the great chariot-warriors of the Pārthas, the choicest of the mighty archers among the kṣatriyas.
Your son Lakṣmaṇa, and likewise the son of Duḥśāsana — both these tigers among men never turn back in battle.
Young and tender, both these princes are swift and spirited, skilled in the particulars of war and leaders in every kind of it.
These two chariot-warriors, O tiger among them, I reckon foremost; devoted to the kṣatriya's duty, those heroes will accomplish a mighty deed.
Daṇḍadhāra, O great king, is a chariot-warrior of single measure, a bull among men; reaching the battlefield, guarded by his own troops, he will fight.
And King Bṛhadbala of Kosala, foremost among chariot-warriors, I count a true chariot-warrior, my son, firm in onset and valor.
He will fight in the battle, rousing his own army to joy, a great archer wielding fearsome weapons, intent on the welfare of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son.
Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat, O king, is a leader among the leaders of chariot-bands; surrendering his own dear life, he will consume your foes.
He who was born from a clump of reeds, son of the great sage Gautama, the teacher Śaradvat — unconquerable like Kārttikeya.
