He will range through the manifold host arrayed with diverse weapons and bows, my son, like fire in the battle, crushing it as he goes.
Bhīṣma said: Śakuni, your maternal uncle, O ruler of men, is a chariot-warrior of single measure; clinging to his enmity with the Pāṇḍavas, he will fight — of this there is no doubt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His soldiers are hard to assail, irresistible in battle, armed for the most part with strange weapons, in swiftness equal to the speed of the wind.
The son of Droṇa, a great archer above all bowmen, fights with cunning craft in battle, sure of aim, a mighty chariot-warrior.
For his arrows, O great king, like those of the wielder of Gāṇḍīva, loosed from the bow, fly forth in unbroken streams.
This hero, foremost among chariot-warriors, I cannot fully reckon; this man of great renown could, if he wished, burn down the three worlds.
His wrath and fiery splendor were gathered through the austerity of the hermitage-dweller, and that noble-minded one was favored by Droṇa with celestial weapons.
Yet one great fault he has, on whose account, O bull of the Bhāratas, I count him neither a chariot-warrior nor a great chariot-warrior, O best of kings.
Life is exceedingly dear to him; this brāhmaṇa ever longs to live. Yet none is his equal in either of the two armies.
With a single chariot he could slay even the army of the gods, and that mighty-framed one could split mountains with the thunder of his palms.
A hero of countless qualities, a striker of terrible splendor, irresistible like Yama staff in hand, he will range the field like Death itself.
In wrath like the fire at the world's end, lion-necked, of mighty mind — this man, O Bhārata, will bring the back of the war to its close.
But his father, of great splendor, though aged is finer than the young; that he will do a mighty deed in battle, of this I have no doubt.
Fanned by the wind of his weapons' speed, kindled by the host as by dry grass for fuel, he will burn up the armies of Pāṇḍu's son, fixed upon victory.
That bull among men, leader of the bands of chariot-leaders, the son of Bharadvāja, will do a fierce deed for your benefit.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The teacher and aged preceptor of all the consecrated kings, he could bring the Sṛñjayas to their end — yet Dhanaṃjaya is dear to him.
Never would this great archer slay Pārtha, the tireless doer, remembering his own blazing teaching and how it was conquered by Pārtha's virtues.
This hero ever praises the abundance of Pārtha's virtues; the son of Bharadvāja looks upon him as more than a son.
With a single chariot the mighty one could slay the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas, even were they joined as one in battle, with his celestial weapons.
Paurava, that tiger among kings, O king, your great chariot-warrior, I count a true chariot-warrior, O hero — a breaker of the cars of enemy heroes.
United with his own troops, scorching the enemy host, he will consume the Pāñcālas as fire whose path is black devours dry grass.
Satyavrata, foremost of chariot-warriors, a prince and a great chariot-warrior, will range through the enemy's host, O king, like Death itself.
His warriors, O lord of kings, in armor and arms of many colors, will range through the battle, striking down your enemies.
Vṛṣasena, foremost of your chariot-warriors, son of Karṇa and a great chariot-warrior, best of the mighty, will burn up the forces of your foes.
Jalasaṃdha of great splendor, O king, your foremost chariot-warrior, the Māgadha, slayer of enemy heroes, will yield up his life in battle.
He will fight in the battle, skilled upon the shoulders of an elephant, or by chariot — that mighty-armed one, wasting away the enemy host.
This chariot-warrior, O great king, I count a bull among men; in your cause he will lay down his life, together with his troops, in the great battle.
He fights with valor and with cunning craft in the fray, and free of fear, O king, he will do battle with your enemies.
Bāhlika too is a great chariot-warrior and one who never turns back in battle; in the fight, O king, I count him a hero, the equal of Yama, son of the Sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For once he has reached the battle he would in no way turn back, O king, any more than the ever-moving wind, until he has struck down his foes in the fray.
Your commander Satyavat, O great king, a great chariot-warrior, of wondrous deeds in battle, is a chariot-warrior who breaks the cars of his enemies.
Beholding battle, there is in him no faltering whatever; smiling, he advances upon the foes who stand in his chariot's path.
Valiant against his enemies, this best of men will do, in the crush of battle, a very great deed worthy of the noble, in your cause.
Alāyudha, lord of the rākṣasas, cruel in deed and of great might, will slay your foes, O king, remembering the enmity of old.
He, foremost chariot-warrior of all the rākṣasa hosts, a master of illusion and firm in his hatred, will range through the battle.
Bhagadatta, lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, a valorous and mighty hero, foremost among wielders of the elephant-goad and skilled also upon the chariot —
With him the wielder of Gāṇḍīva once did battle for very many days, O king, both of them greedy for victory.
Then, O Gāndhāra, honoring the chastiser of Pāka as his friend, he made a compact with that great-souled son of Pāṇḍu.
He will fight in the battle, skilled upon the shoulders of his elephant, that king mounted as Vāsava mounted upon Airāvata among the gods.
Bhīṣma said: Acala and Vṛṣaka, two brothers united, are chariot-warriors of yours hard to assail; they will shatter your enemies.
Mighty tigers among men, firm in their wrath, strikers in battle, chiefs of the Gāndhāras, young, handsome, and of great strength.
Your ever-beloved friend, hardened to war, who incites you, O king, to the quarrel with the Pāṇḍavas —
— harsh, boastful, base, your Karṇa Vaikartana, your counselor, leader, and kinsman, proud and exceedingly puffed up.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is neither a full chariot-warrior nor a great chariot-warrior, O king; parted from the armor born with him, witless, and parted too from his two celestial earrings, he is ever soft of heart.
By the curse of Rāma, by the word of a brāhmaṇa, and by the loss of his accoutrements, I therefore count him but half a chariot-warrior; once he meets Phalguna, he will not escape again alive.
Saṃjaya said: Then the mighty-armed Droṇa, best of weapon-bearers, spoke: "It is just as you have said; there is not a word of falsehood in it."
"In battle after battle he is seen overproud and turning away from the fight; soft-hearted and heedless is Karṇa, and therefore I too count him but half a chariot-warrior."
Hearing this, the son of Rādhā, his eyes wide with anger, O lord of kings, spoke to Bhīṣma, goading him with words as with a whip.
"Grandsire, you cut me at your pleasure with arrows of speech, though I am guiltless, ever out of hatred, at every step thus; yet I bear it all, every bit of it, for Duryodhana's sake."
"But you deem me unfit, as though I were a coward; in my eyes it is you who are but half a chariot-warrior — of that there is no doubt."
"I speak no falsehood before all the world, O son of Gaṅgā: you are forever the enemy of the Kurus, and the king does not perceive it."
"For who indeed, among kings equal and lofty in deed, would wreak such a slaying of another's spirit, eager to sow division before the battle, as you, under the guise of naming our qualities, seek to do us wrong?"
"Not by years, not by gray hairs, not by wealth, nor by kinsmen can the rank of a great chariot-warrior of the kṣatriya be reckoned, O Kaurava."
"The kṣatriya is held to rank by strength, the twice-born by their counsel, the vaiśyas are reckoned by their wealth, but the śūdras by seniority of age."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"At your own whim and by your own arbitrary grasp you make out chariot-warriors and great chariot-warriors thus, swayed by desire and hatred, out of delusion."
"O mighty-armed Duryodhana, let it be well and rightly considered; let this Bhīṣma of evil disposition be cast off, who works your harm."
"For an army once divided, O king, becomes hard to reunite — even one of hereditary loyalty, O tiger among men; how much more one raised from sundry sources?"
A division has arisen among these warriors on the eve of battle, O Bhārata, and our ardor is being plainly and grievously sapped.
What does Bhīṣma, dull of wit, know of the reckoning of chariot-warriors? I myself will hold back the host of the Pāṇḍavas.
Coming upon me, whose arrows never miss, the Pāṇḍavas with their Pāñcālas will scatter to the ten directions as bulls flee before a tiger.
What has the clash of battle, or counsels well spoken, to do with Bhīṣma, his vigor spent, feeble in spirit, befuddled by age?
For he is forever contending with the whole world, and in his vain conceit he esteems no other man at all.
"The aged are indeed to be heeded"—so the scriptures teach; yet not the overaged, for such are reckoned children once more.
I alone shall slay the Pāṇḍavas, of this there is no doubt; yet in a well-fought battle, O tiger among kings, the glory will fall to Bhīṣma.
You have made this Bhīṣma your commander, O lord of men; the honor will go to the commander, never in any way to the fighters.
While the son of Gaṅgā lives, O king, I will by no means fight; but once Bhīṣma is slain, I shall do battle against all the great chariot-warriors.
Bhīṣma said: This burden of mine that I take up is mighty, vast as the sea—the war of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, brooded upon for years on end.
Now that the hour has come, scorching and hair-raising, I must work no discord among us—and it is for that you live, O son of a sūta.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For old as I am, were I to put forth my strength this day, I could in battle cut short both your appetite for war and your very life, O son of a sūta.
When Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, loosed his great weapons against me, not a tremor touched me—and what then will you do to me?
The good, to be sure, do not praise this vaunting of one's own might; yet, stung as I am, I will speak to you, base wretch, blot upon your line.
At the bride-choice of the king of Kāśi, with but a single chariot I overcame the whole assembled warrior nobility and carried off the maidens by main force.
Thousands of such men, and of finer ones besides, were swept aside by me alone, together with their armies, upon the field of battle.
With you for their man of strife a great calamity has come upon the Kurus, for their destruction. Make your effort; prove yourself a man.
Fight Pārtha in battle, with whom you so vie—and I shall watch you come away unscathed from that combat, O most evil-minded one.
Saṃjaya said: Then the high-minded king, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, spoke to him: Have regard for me, son of Gaṅgā, for a great task is upon us.
Let this above all be considered first—what is my highest good; for both of you, my lords, shall do great deeds for me.
And further I wish to hear of the foremost chariot-warriors among the foe, and who among them are atirathas, and likewise the leaders of chariot-bands.
I wish to hear the strength and weakness of my enemies, O Kaurava; for when night has brightened into dawn this war will begin.
Bhīṣma said: These chariot-warriors of yours have been numbered, O king, and likewise the atirathas; and now, O monarch, hear of the half-chariot warriors of the Pāṇḍavas.
If today you are eager, O king, to know the strength of the Pāṇḍavas—their tally of chariot-warriors, O mighty-armed one, together with these lords of the earth—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The king himself, that noble chariot-warrior, the son of Pāṇḍu, the joy of Kuntī—he will range through the battle like fire, my child, of this there is no doubt.
As for Bhīmasena, O lord of kings, he is reckoned a chariot-warrior eightfold over—proud, with the strength of ten thousand elephants; in his fierce energy he is no mere mortal.
The two sons of Mādrī are both chariot-warriors, bulls among men, in beauty like the Aśvins and endowed with like splendor.
Standing at the forefront of the host, remembering the wrongs done them, they will rage abroad like Rudra—of this I have no doubt.
All of them are great-souled, towering like śāla trunks, and in stature they exceed other men by a span's measure.
Lion-framed are all the sons of Pāṇḍu, of mighty strength; all have kept the vow of chastity and all are men of surpassing austerity.
Modest, tigers among men, fierce in strength like tigers; in speed, in the striking blow, and in the press of battle every one of them is more than human; all of them, O bull of the Bhāratas, have subdued the kings of the earth in their conquest of the quarters.
And no men can ever match them in handling their weapons, maces, and arrows, O Kaurava—neither in stringing the bow, nor in lifting the heavy mace, nor in drawing the shaft to the head.
In speed, in striking the mark, in eating, in flinging up the dust of sport—even as boys they outdid you all.
Falling upon your army like tigers raging in strength, they will lay it waste in battle—let there be no encounter with them!
Each one of them, in battle, could slay all the lords of the earth—as you yourself saw, O king of kings, at the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Remembering the torment of Draupadī and the harsh words at the dicing, they will move through the battle like Death itself.
Red-eyed, with hair drawn into a knot, and having Nārāyaṇa for his ally—in neither army, O hero, is there a chariot-warrior like that one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For never of old, neither among gods nor Dānavas nor serpents, nor among Rākṣasas nor Yakṣas—still less among men—
have I heard of any chariot, past or yet to come, O great king, so equipped as that of the wise Pārtha.
Vāsudeva for his charioteer, and Dhanaṃjaya himself for the warrior; the Gāṇḍīva for his divine bow, and those horses swift as the wind;
the impenetrable, divine armor, and the two inexhaustible great quivers; and the whole arsenal of weapons—those of Mahendra, of Rudra, and of Kubera;
those of Yama and of Varuṇa, and maces dreadful to behold, and the chief weapons headed by the thunderbolt, missiles of every kind.
Thousands of Dānavas, dwellers in the City of Gold, were slain by that single chariot in battle—what chariot-warrior is the equal of him?
In his fury this mighty-armed one, strong and true in valor, would slay your army even while he guards his own.
I, or else the teacher, might go forth against this Dhanaṃjaya; there is no third in either army, O king of kings, who could advance upon him as he pours down his torrents of arrows.
Like a storm-cloud at summer's end driven on by a great wind—so is the son of Kuntī when arrayed for war, with Vāsudeva for his ally; he is young and skilled, while we two are worn with age.
Saṃjaya said: Hearing this from Bhīṣma, the kings then felt their spirits sink, their stout arms ringed with golden armlets and smeared with sandal-paste.
Their minds in turmoil, they recalled the prowess of the sons of Pāṇḍu of old, as though they beheld it before their very eyes.
Bhīṣma said: The sons of Draupadī, O great king, are all five great chariot-warriors; and Uttara, the son of Virāṭa, I count a mighty chariot-warrior.
Abhimanyu, O great king, is a chief among the leaders of chariot-bands; in battle he may prove the equal of Pārtha or of Vāsudeva.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Quick with his weapons, fighting with brilliant variety, spirited and firm in valor, he will show his prowess, remembering the wrongs done to his father.
Sātyaki of the Mādhava line, a hero, a chief among the leaders of chariot-bands—he, foremost of the Vṛṣṇi champions, is unforgiving and has conquered all fear.
Uttamaujas too, O king, I count a mighty chariot-warrior; and Yudhāmanyu the valiant, a noble chariot-warrior, a bull among men.
These have many thousands of chariots, elephants, and horses; they will fight, casting away their lives out of love for the sons of Kuntī.
Together with the Pāṇḍavas, O king of kings, they will range through your armies, O Bhārata, like fire fanned by the wind, challenging one another.
Unconquerable in battle though aged, both Virāṭa and Drupada—great chariot-warriors of mighty valor—I count as bulls among men.
Old in years though they are, devoted to the warrior's duty, they will strive to the utmost of their power, holding to the path that heroes tread.
By their kinship, O king of kings, and through their lineage of valor and strength, these two great archers of noble conduct are both bound fast in the cords of affection.
When a sufficient cause arises, O bull among men, all men of mighty arms become either heroes or cowards.
These two, made one in purpose with Pārtha and steadfast in devotion, will labor to the utmost of their power, O lord of men, casting away their very lives.
Each at the head of an akṣauhiṇī, terrible in the fray, these two—guarding the bond of kinship—will do a great deed.
Heroes renowned in the world, great archers who have renounced all care for their lives, O Bhārata, guarding the trust placed in them, they will do a great deed.
Bhīṣma said: The son of the king of the Pāñcālas, O king, the conqueror of hostile cities, Śikhaṇḍin—him I count a foremost chariot-warrior on Pārtha's side, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He will fight in the battle, undoing what was settled of old, spreading his great fame abroad through your armies, O Bhārata.
Many are his hosts, the Pāñcālas and the Prabhadrakas; and with that array of chariots he will do a great deed.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna, commander of all their forces, O Bhārata, I count an atiratha, O king—the pupil of Droṇa, a great chariot-warrior.
He will fight in the battle, cutting down the foe in combat, like the blessed Lord of the Pināka in his wrath at the dissolution of an age.
Of his army of chariots, those who delight in war say that, for its multitude, it is like the ocean, as in the battle-array of the gods.
But Kṣatradharman, O king of kings, I count a half-chariot warrior, O monarch—the son of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who by reason of his youth is not yet greatly seasoned.
The son of Śiśupāla, the heroic king of the Cedis, a great chariot-warrior and mighty archer—Dhṛṣṭaketu, a kinsman of the Pāṇḍava;
this valiant lord of the Cedis, together with his son, O Bhārata, a great chariot-warrior, will do a great and hard-wrought deed.
Devoted to the warrior's duty, a conqueror of hostile cities, I count Kṣatradeva, O king of kings, a foremost chariot-warrior among the Pāṇḍavas; and Jayanta, and Amitaujas, and Satyajit the great chariot-warrior.
Great chariot-warriors and great-souled, all the foremost of the Pāñcālas—they will fight in battle, my child, like elephants in fury.
Aja and Bhoja, both valiant, great chariot-warriors among the Pāṇḍavas, will strive to the utmost of their power in aid of the Pāṇḍavas—swift with their weapons, fighting with brilliant variety, skilled and firm in valor.
The five Kekaya brothers, O king of kings, frenzied for battle—all of them noble chariot-warriors, all with crimson banners.
The king of Kāśi, and Sukumāra, and Nīla, and that other king, and Sūryadatta, and Śaṅkha, and one named Madirāśva—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
all these are noble chariot-warriors, all bearing the marks of battle, all masters of every weapon, all great-souled—so I judge them.
Vārdhakṣemi, O great king, I count a mighty chariot-warrior; and king Citrāyudha I count a foremost chariot-warrior, for he is a splendor in battle and is devoted to the Diademed One.
Cekitāna and Satyadhṛti, two great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas—these two, tigers among men and noble chariot-warriors, so I judge them.
And Vyāghradatta, O king of kings, and Candrasena, O Bhārata—both I count noble chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, beyond doubt.
And Senābindu, O lord of kings, called by name Krodhahantā, the slayer of wrath, who is the equal of Vāsudeva and of Bhīmasena, that overpowering one—he will fight here valiantly in battle against your soldiers.
Even as Your Honour reckons me, and Droṇa, and Kṛpa, so too must that one, glorious in battle, be reckoned the foremost of chariot-warriors.
The king of Kāśi, swiftest of all in his weaponry, praiseworthy, an excellent chariot-warrior, the conqueror of his enemies' cities—him I reckon a chariot-warrior of single measure.
And this one, valiant in war, must be reckoned a chariot-warrior of eightfold measure—Satyajit, glorious in battle, the young son of Drupada.
He has attained the rank of an atiratha, a super-warrior, reckoned the equal of Dhṛṣṭadyumna; desiring glory for the Pāṇḍavas, he will perform a supreme deed.
And this other great chariot-warrior, devoted and brave, is the king of the Pāṇḍyas, mighty in valour, a bearer of the Pāṇḍavas' burden.
Dṛḍhadhanvan, the great archer, a foremost chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas, is Śreṇimat, O best of the Kurus; and there is the king Vasudāna—both of these I reckon super-warriors, O scorcher of foes.
Bhīṣma said: Rocamāna, O great king, a great chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas, will fight in battle like an immortal against the enemy's hosts, O descendant of Bharata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Purujit Kuntibhoja, the great archer of mighty strength, the maternal uncle of Bhīmasena—him too I reckon a super-warrior.
This hero, a great archer, accomplished and skilful, a versatile fighter and powerful—him I reckon a bull among chariot-warriors.
For he will fight valiantly, as Maghavat does against the Dānavas; and his warriors are all renowned and well-versed in war.
For his nephews' sake that hero, the king, devoted to what is dear and good for the Pāṇḍavas, will perform a very great deed in the encounter.
The son of Bhīmasena, O great king, the son of Hiḍimbā, lord of the rākṣasas, master of many illusions, a leader of leaders of chariot-bands—him I reckon highly.
He will fight in battle with illusions, my son, loving the fray, and so too the brave rākṣasas, his obedient companions.
These and many others, lords of various lands, have assembled for the Pāṇḍava's cause, with Vāsudeva at their head.
These, O king, are the principal chariot-warriors and super-warriors of the great-souled Pāṇḍava, and those reckoned half-warriors as well.
They will lead in battle Yudhiṣṭhira's dreadful army, O king, guarded by the hero Kirīṭin as by the great Indra himself.
Against these, O hero, who advance upon you seeking victory, I shall fight in battle, longing either for victory or for death in the fray.
And Pārtha and Vāsudeva, wielders of the discus and the Gāṇḍīva, those most excellent of men, I shall meet as the sun and moon meeting at twilight.
And those noble chariot-warriors, the soldiers of Pāṇḍu's son—those too, together with their hosts, I shall face at the forefront of battle.
These chariot-warriors and super-warriors I have named to you according to their rank, O king; and likewise certain half-warriors among them, O lord of the Kurus.
Arjuna and Vāsudeva and whatever other kings are there—all of them I shall hold off, so long as I have sight, O descendant of Bharata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the Pāñcāla Śikhaṇḍin, O mighty-armed one, I shall not slay, even when I see him with arrow raised and fighting back against me in battle.
The world knows this, that I, wishing to do what pleased my father, renounced the kingdom that had come to me and held fast to the vow of celibacy.
I consecrated Citrāṅgada to the kingship of the Kurus, and I consecrated the child Vicitravīrya to the office of crown prince.
Having proclaimed my devotion to my vow before all the kings on earth, I would never slay a woman, nor by any means one who was once a woman.
For that Śikhaṇḍin was once a woman, O king, if you have heard it: having first been a maiden, he was born a man; with him I shall not fight, O descendant of Bharata.
But all the other kings I shall slay, O bull of the Bhāratas, whomever I meet in battle—save the sons of Kuntī, O king.
Duryodhana said: For what reason, O best of the Bhāratas, would you not slay Śikhaṇḍin, even seeing him in battle with arrow raised and bent on assault?
Having said before, O mighty-armed one, 'I shall slay the Pāṇḍavas together with the Somakas,' O son of Gaṅgā—tell me of this, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: Hear, Duryodhana, together with these lords of the earth, the tale of why I would not slay Śikhaṇḍin even when I see him in battle.
The great king, my father Śaṃtanu, bull of the Bhāratas, righteous in soul, reached his appointed end in due time, O bull among men.
Then I, O best of the Bhāratas, keeping my vow, consecrated my brother Citrāṅgada to the great kingship.
And when he met his death, abiding by Satyavatī's wish, I consecrated Vicitravīrya as king according to the rites.
Though consecrated by me, O lord of kings, and though my younger, rightly so, the righteous Vicitravīrya still looked to me for guidance.
Wishing then to bring about his marriage, my son, I set my mind on it, thinking, 'from a family worthy of him.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then I heard, O mighty-armed one, that three maidens at a self-choice ceremony, all of matchless beauty, daughters of the king of Kāśi—Ambā, and Ambikā, and Ambālikā the third.
And the kings of the earth were summoned, O bull of the Bhāratas. Ambā was the eldest of them, Ambikā the middle one, and Ambālikā, O lord of kings, was the youngest of those royal maidens.
I, going to the city of the king of Kāśi with but a single chariot, saw those three maidens, O mighty-armed one, well adorned, and the kings, the assembled princes, O lord of the earth.
Then, challenging all those kings who stood ready for battle, I made those maidens mount my chariot, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Knowing that they were to be won by valour as their price, having set them upon my chariot, I addressed all the princes gathered there, again and again: 'Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, carries off the maidens!'
'Strive, all of you, with utmost might to wrest them free, O princes; for by force I carry them off, even as you look on, O rulers of men!'
Then those guardians of the earth sprang up with weapons raised, crying in fury 'To arms! To arms!' and urged on their charioteers.
Those kings rushed forth with weapons raised—in chariots resembling clouds, the elephant-fighters upon elephants, and others upon horses bred for the saddle.
Then those kings, every one of them, O lord of peoples, surrounded me on all sides with a great host of chariots.
Them I held off with a mighty rain of arrows, and I vanquished all those kings, as the king of the gods vanquishes the Dānavas.
Of those who rushed upon me, their bright banners adorned with gold, I cast each one to the earth with a single arrow apiece.
And their horses and their elephants and their charioteers I felled in the fray with blazing arrows, laughing the while, O bull among men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing that deftness of mine, they turned back and were broken; and then, having conquered those rulers of the earth, I came to Hāstinapura.
Then those maidens, O descendant of Bharata, won for my brother's sake, and that deed too, O mighty-armed one, I reported to Satyavatī.
Bhīṣma said: Then, O best of the Bhāratas, approaching my mother, the mother of a hero, the daughter of the fisherman, and clasping her feet, I spoke these words.
'These daughters of the king of Kāśi, won at the price of valour, I have gained for Vicitravīrya's sake, having vanquished the kings.'
Then, O king, smelling my head and with tears brimming in her eyes, Satyavatī said, rejoicing: 'By good fortune, my son, you have triumphed!'
But when, with Satyavatī's consent, the wedding was at hand, the eldest daughter of the king of Kāśi, abashed, spoke these words.
'Bhīṣma, you are a knower of dharma, well-versed in all the scriptures; having heard my words, which are righteous, you ought to act on them here.'
'The lord of Śālva was once chosen by me in my heart as my groom, and by him too I was chosen before, in secret, unknown to my father.'
'How, O king, having studied the scriptures, would you keep me in your house, Bhīṣma, when my heart longs for another—you, of all men, being a Kaurava?'
'Having weighed this and resolved it in your mind, O bull of the Bhāratas, whatever is fitting for you, that, mighty-armed one, you ought to undertake here.'
'Plainly the king of Śālva awaits me, O lord of peoples. Show mercy to me, O mighty-armed one, best of the upholders of dharma; for you, O hero, are known throughout the earth as true to your vows—so have we heard.'
Bhīṣma said: Then, having taken leave of Kālī Satyavatī, and of the ministers and the brāhmaṇas and likewise the house-priests, I gave leave to the eldest maiden, Ambā, O ruler of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Given leave, that maiden went to the city of the lord of Śālva, guarded by aged brāhmaṇas and attended by her nurse; and having crossed that road, she came before the king.
Coming before that king, Śālva, she spoke these words: 'I have come, O mighty-armed one, seeking you, O greatly radiant one.'
The lord of Śālva said to her, with something like a smile, O lord of peoples: 'I do not desire you for my wife, O fair-complexioned one, since you have already belonged to another.'
'Go, gentle lady, back there into the presence of the descendant of Bharata; I do not want you, who were seized by force by Bhīṣma.'
'For you, having been won by Bhīṣma, were then led away content—he laid hands on you in that great battle, having vanquished the lords of the earth; I do not desire you for my wife, O fair-complexioned one, since you have belonged to another before.'
'How should a king such as I take into his house a woman who has belonged to another—one of discerning knowledge, who lays down the law of conduct for others? Go where you will, gentle lady; let not this time of yours slip past you.'
Ambā said to him, O king, tormented by the arrows of the bodiless one, Kāma: 'Speak not thus, O guardian of the earth; this is by no means so.'
'I was not led away content by Bhīṣma, O harrower of foes; I was carried off by force, weeping, when he had put the lords of the earth to flight.'
'Take me to yourself, O lord of Śālva—a devoted girl, innocent; for the abandonment of those devoted to one is not praised in the codes of dharma.'
'I, having taken my leave of the son of Gaṅgā, who never turns back in battle, and being granted leave by him, have come to your house alone.'
'That mighty-armed Bhīṣma does not desire me, O lord of peoples; Bhīṣma's whole undertaking was for his brother's sake—so I have heard.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'My two sisters who were carried off, Ambikā and Ambālikā, O king—the son of Gaṅgā gave them to his younger brother Vicitravīrya.'
'As, O lord of Śālva, I think of no other man at all but you, O tiger among men—so do I touch my own head in oath.'
'Not having belonged to another, O lord of kings, have I come before you. I speak the truth, Śālva—by that truth I touch my own self in oath.'
'Take me to yourself, O wide-eyed one—a maiden come of her own accord, who has belonged to no other, O lord of kings, longing for your favour.'
But Śālva cast off that daughter of the king of Kāśi as she spoke thus, O best of the Bhāratas, as a serpent casts off its worn-out skin.
Though entreated thus by her with words of many kinds, O sinless one, the lord of Śālva put no faith in the maiden, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then that eldest daughter of the king of Kāśi, possessed by anguish, spoke with tearful eyes, in a voice broken by weeping.
'Forsaken by you, I shall go wherever I may, O lord of peoples; wherever that be, may the good be my refuges, even as I have spoken the truth.'
But as she was speaking thus, the cruel king of Śālva then cast her off utterly, O Kaurava, as she lamented piteously.
"Go, go!" Śālva said to her again and again. "I fear Bhīṣma, fair-hipped one, and you are Bhīṣma's prize."
Thus addressed by Śālva, that man of short sight, she went forth from the city, wretched, weeping like an osprey.
Bhīṣma said: As she went out from the city, O Bhārata, she thought: "On this earth there is no maiden more wretchedly placed than I. Bereft of my kinsmen, I am spurned by Śālva as well."
"Nor can I go back to the city named for the elephant, for I was released by Bhīṣma on Śālva's account."
"Whom then shall I blame—myself, or the unassailable Bhīṣma, or my foolish father, who arranged for me a self-choice of husband?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This is a fault of my own making, that long ago, when the deadly battle was joined, I did not leap from Bhīṣma's chariot for Śālva's sake. This is the fruit ripened of that, that I have come to ruin like a fool."
"A curse on Bhīṣma, and a curse on my dull-witted, foolish father, by whom I was flung forth like a woman for sale, with valor as the bride-price."
"A curse on me, a curse on King Śālva, and a curse on the Creator too, by whose ill-conduct I have come to this utmost calamity."
"In every way a mortal reaps his own allotted portions; yet the fountainhead of this misfortune of mine is Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu."
"I now see that vengeance must be wrought upon Bhīṣma, whether by austerity or by war—for I deem him the cause of my sorrow. Yet what king would dare to conquer Bhīṣma in battle?"
Having thus resolved, she went forth from the city to the hermitage of holy-natured, great-souled ascetics; and there she passed the night, surrounded by the ascetics.
And she told them all that had befallen her, O mighty-armed Bhārata, fully and in detail—she of the bright smile told of her seizure, her release, and her dismissal by Śālva.
Now there was there a great Brāhmaṇa of firm vows, Śaikhāvatya, grown old in austerity, a master of the forest-lore.
To her in her distress that sage Śaikhāvatya, of great austerity, spoke—to the virtuous, sighing girl wholly given over to grief and sorrow:
"Things being so, good lady, what can be done by ascetics—by the blessed great-souled ones who dwell in the hermitage and are ever devoted to austerity?"
And she said to him, O king: "Let a favor be granted me. I wish to go forth as a recluse here; I shall practice austerity hard to perform."
"Surely these evil deeds were done by me, deluded, in former bodies; this is the certain fruit of them."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I cannot bear to go back to my own people, O ascetics—rejected, joyless, and spurned by Śālva."
"I wish to be taught the ascetic life here by you, O sinless ones who are like gods. Let your compassion rest upon me."
He comforted the maiden with examples and with reasons drawn from scripture, soothed her, and together with the other Brāhmaṇas pledged to undertake her cause.
Bhīṣma said: Then all those ascetics, righteous men, became intent upon the matter, pondering concerning that maiden, "What is to be done?"
Some of the ascetics said, "Let her be taken to her father's house"; some of the foremost of the twice-born set their minds on rebuking us.
Some thought that they should go to the lord of Śālva and constrain him; others resolved against it, since she had been rejected by him.
"Things being so, good lady, what can be done by us, the wise?" And then all those ascetics of firm vows spoke again:
"Enough of renunciation here, good lady; hear our wholesome counsel. Go from here—blessings on you—to your own father's dwelling."
"Your father the king will see to whatever comes next. There you shall dwell in happiness, fair one, possessed of every comfort. No other refuge would be fitting for you, good lady, as your father is."
"A husband or a father is a woman's refuge, fair-complexioned one: when her fortunes are even, the husband is her refuge; but in adversity, the father is her refuge."
"The renunciant life is full of hardship, especially for a delicate woman—and by nature for a king's daughter, and for a maiden such as you, O proud lady."
"Good lady, fair one, many dangers exist for one dwelling in a hermitage; these would not be so in your father's house."
Then the Brāhmaṇas spoke this word to her, the ascetic woman: "Seeing you here alone in this deserted, dense forest, great kings will woo you; therefore do not set your mind on this."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Ambā said: "I cannot return to the city of Kāśi, to my father's house. I would become an object of contempt to my kinsmen—there is no doubt of it."
"In a different way I dwelt in my childhood in my father's house, O ascetics. I shall not go—blessings on you—to where my father is. I wish to perform austerity, guarded by ascetics."
"So that in the next world too there may not be for me this same great ruin and misfortune, O best of Brāhmaṇas—therefore shall I practice austerity."
Bhīṣma said: While those Brāhmaṇas were thus pondering this way and that, the royal sage Hotravāhana, an ascetic, came to that forest.
Then all those ascetics honored that king with the rites of hospitality—with welcome and the rest, with a seat and with water.
When he was seated and rested and listening, the forest-dwellers once again took up their talk concerning the maiden.
Hearing that story of Ambā and of the king of Kāśi, O Bhārata, he—the father of her mother—rose up trembling, and taking the maiden upon his lap, he comforted her, O lord.
He asked her in full about the origin of her misfortune from the beginning, and she related to him in detail all that had happened.
Then that royal sage was filled with grief and sorrow, and that one of great austerity resolved in his mind upon the deed to be done.
And trembling, in deep sorrow, he said to the afflicted maiden: "Do not go to your father's house, good lady; for I am your mother's father."
"I shall cut away your sorrow; depend upon me, little daughter. Enough has your mind, my child, been thus withered with grief."
"Go at my word to Rāma, son of Jamadagni, the ascetic. Rāma will take away your great grief and sorrow; he will slay Bhīṣma in battle if he will not heed his word."
"Go to that best of the Bhārgavas, whose splendor equals the fire of doom. That one of great austerity will set you again upon an even path."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, shedding tears aloud again and again, she spoke to her mother's father, Hotravāhana:
"Having bowed my head, I shall go at your command. But can I now even behold that noble one, renowned throughout the world?"
"And how shall that Bhārgava destroy my keen sorrow? This I wish to hear, and then indeed I shall go there."
Hotravāhana said: "You shall see Rāma, son of Jamadagni, my child, in the great forest, engaged in fierce austerity—true to his word, of mighty strength."
"On Mahendra, the best of mountains, sages versed in the Vedas ever attend upon Rāma, and Gandharvas and Apsarases too."
"Go there—blessings on you—and speak to him this word of mine, having first bowed your head to him, grown old in austerity, of firm vows."
"And tell him further, good lady, whatever purpose you have in mind; when I am named, Rāma will do all of it for you."
"Rāma is my friend, my child, bound to me in affection, and my well-wisher—the heroic son of Jamadagni, the foremost of all who bear weapons."
While the king Hotravāhana was thus speaking to the maiden, Akṛtavraṇa appeared, the dear companion of Rāma.
Then all those sages rose up by the thousands, and that aged king Hotravāhana, of the Sṛñjayas, as well.
Then, having greeted one another in due form, those forest-dwellers, O best of the Bhāratas, sat down together, surrounding him.
Then they told one tale after another, delightful, lovely and sublime, O great king, full of love and joy and gladness.
Then, at the end of the talk, the great-souled royal sage Hotravāhana asked Akṛtavraṇa about Rāma, foremost of the great sages:
"Where now, O mighty-armed Akṛtavraṇa, is the valiant son of Jamadagni? Can he be seen—he, the best of those who know the Vedas?"
Akṛtavraṇa said: "Rāma is ever speaking of you yourself, my lord—'the Sṛñjaya is my dear friend, a royal sage,' so he says, O king."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"It is my thought that Rāma will be here tomorrow at dawn; you shall see him coming here, eager for the sight of you."
"And this maiden, O royal sage—for what purpose has she come to the forest? Whose is she, and what is she to you? I wish to know."
Hotravāhana said: "This is my daughter's daughter, my lord—the fair daughter of the king of Kāśi. The eldest, she stood at the self-choice along with her sisters, O sinless one."
"This eldest daughter of the lord of Kāśi is known as Ambā; the other two, the younger, are Ambikā and Ambālikā, O you whose wealth is austerity."
"The kingly warrior-host of the kings had gathered then in the city of Kāśi; on account of the maidens, O Brahmā-sage, there was a great festival there."
"Then, it is said, the mighty Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, of great splendor, scattered the kings and carried off those three maidens."
"Having conquered the rulers of the earth, Bhīṣma of pure soul came then to the city named for the elephant together with the maidens, O Bhārata."
"Having then made them known to Satyavatī, the lord forthwith commanded that they be married to his brother Vicitravīrya."
"Then, seeing the marriage preparations, this maiden, the one who had been won, spoke there to the son of Gaṅgā in the midst of the counselors, O bull among the twice-born:"
"'O hero, the lord of Śālva has been chosen by me in my heart as my husband; you ought not, O knower of dharma, to give me away when my heart is set on another.'"
"Having heard that word, Bhīṣma, after taking counsel with the ministers and reaching a decision, released her, abiding by the judgment of Satyavatī."
"Permitted then by Bhīṣma, this maiden, glad at heart, went to Śālva, lord of Saubha, O Brāhmaṇa, and in due time spoke these words:"
"'I have been released by Bhīṣma; grant me my rightful place. You, O bull among kings, were earlier chosen by me in my heart.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"But Śālva refused her too, suspicious of her conduct. So she has come to the penance-grove, devoted utterly to the ascetic life."
"And I recognized her by the recital of her lineage. As for the source of this sorrow, she holds Bhīṣma alone to be its cause here."
Ambā said: "Reverend one, it is even so, just as the king says—Hotravāhana the Sṛñjaya, the begetter of my mother's body."
"For I cannot bear to return to my own city, O you whose wealth is austerity—both from fear of dishonor and from shame, O great sage."
"But whatever the reverend Rāma shall bid me, O best of the twice-born, that is the deed most fit for me to do—such, reverend sir, is my resolve."
Akṛtavraṇa said: "This is a twofold sorrow, good lady; for which of the two do you wish redress to be wrought, O frail one? Tell me that, my child."
"If, good lady, the lord of Saubha is to be constrained in your judgment, the great-souled Rāma will constrain him for your welfare."
"But if you wish to see that Bhīṣma, son of the river, conquered in battle by the wise Rāma, the Bhārgava would do that too."
"Having heard the word of the Sṛñjaya and your own, O bright-smiling one, let what is next to be done in this matter be considered this very day."
Ambā said: I was carried off by Bhīṣma, holy one, who did not know my heart; for Bhīṣma does not know, O brāhmaṇa, that my mind was set upon Śālva.
Weighing this in your mind, let your honour himself reach the decision rightly, and let the remedy be made accordingly.
Whether against Bhīṣma, that tiger of the Kurus, or else against King Śālva, or indeed against them both, O brāhmaṇa—do what is fitting.
For I have laid before you the root of my sorrow just as it is; in this matter, holy one, you ought to provide a remedy by sound reason.
Akṛtavraṇa said: This is fitting, gentle and lovely lady, that you should speak thus in regard to what is right; now hear these words of mine.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If the son of the River had not borne you off to the City named for the Elephant, then Śālva, O timid one, urged on by Rāma, would have received you with bowed head.
Because you were won by him, gentle lady, because you were carried off, O passionate one, therefore is King Śālva in doubt concerning you, slender-waisted one.
Bhīṣma too is proud of his manhood and exults in his victories; therefore it is fitting that you have redress exacted from Bhīṣma.
Ambā said: In my heart too, O brāhmaṇa, this great longing ever stirs—that I might have Bhīṣma slain in battle, this and nothing else, always.
Whether Bhīṣma or King Śālva—whomever you find at fault—chastise that one, O mighty-armed one, on whose account I am so deeply afflicted.
Bhīṣma said: As they were thus conversing, that day passed away, and the night too, O best of the Bhāratas, with its breezes pleasantly cool and warm.
Then Rāma appeared, blazing as it were with his splendour, surrounded by his disciples, O king—the sage wearing matted locks and garments of bark.
Bow in hand, undaunted in spirit, bearing a sword and an axe, stainless, O tiger among kings, he approached the Sṛñjaya king.
Then the ascetics, seeing him, and that king of great austerity, all stood with palms joined together—and so too that suffering maiden.
Calmly they honoured the descendant of Bhṛgu with the honey-offering; and, duly worshipped, he sat down together with them.
Then the two of them recounted to each other the things of bygone days—both that royal sage of the Sṛñjayas and the son of Jamadagni, O Bhārata.
Then, when the talk was done, the royal sage at the right moment spoke to Rāma, that mighty best of the Bhṛgus, in sweet and meaningful words.
Rāma, this is my daughter's daughter, the child of the king of Kāśi, O lord; hear her cause just as it truly stands, O you skilled in counsel.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let her tell it fully," Rāma answered him; and then she approached Rāma, who blazed like fire itself.
And that fair maiden, saluting Rāma's feet with her head and touching them with hands like lotus petals, stood before him.
Stricken with grief, her eyes troubled with tears, she wept, and sought refuge with the son of Bhṛgu, the giver of refuge.
Rāma said: As you are to this Sṛñjaya king, so are you to me, O daughter of a king. Tell me the sorrow of your heart; I shall do your bidding.
Ambā said: Holy one of mighty vows, this day I have come to you for refuge; lift me out of the dreadful ocean whose mire is sorrow, O lord.
Bhīṣma said: Beholding her beauty, her tender youth, and her exceeding delicacy, Rāma fell to brooding thought.
"What will she say?" Thus the best of the Bhṛgus pondered; long did Rāma meditate, overwhelmed with compassion.
"Tell it," Rāma said to her again; and she of the bright smile recounted everything just as it truly was to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Hearing then the words of the king's daughter, the son of Jamadagni, having settled the certain conclusion of the matter, said to her of the fair hips:
I shall send word to Bhīṣma, best of the Kurus, O passionate lady; that ruler of men, on hearing me, will carry out my righteous command.
But if the son of Jāhnavī will not do as I bid, then in battle, gentle lady, I shall burn him up, ministers and all, with the fire of my weapons.
Or else, O king's daughter, if your mind turns away from that, then I shall instead set the heroic lord of Śālva to this task.
Ambā said: I was let go by Bhīṣma, O son of Bhṛgu, as soon as he heard that my heart had long before been resolved upon King Śālva.
Going to the lord of Saubha, I spoke words hard to utter; but he would not receive me back, mistrustful of my conduct.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Weighing all this with your own judgement, O son of Bhṛgu, you ought to consider what course of action is here the fitting one.
The root of this calamity of mine is Bhīṣma of the mighty vow, by whom I was then seized up by force and brought under his power.
Slay Bhīṣma, O mighty-armed one, on whose account such sorrow has befallen me; for his sake, O tiger of the Bhṛgus, I wander on in utmost misery.
For he is greedy, and proud, and exultant in victory, O descendant of Bhṛgu; therefore it is fitting that you exact redress upon him, O sinless one.
This was the resolve that arose in my heart, O lord, when I was being carried off by the Bhārata: that I would have him of the mighty vow slain.
Therefore fulfil this longing of mine this day, O sinless Rāma; slay Bhīṣma, mighty-armed one, as Purandara slew Vṛtra.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed with "Slay Bhīṣma," O lord, Rāma then spoke to the weeping maiden, who urged him again and again:
O daughter of Kāśi, willingly I take up no weapon, lovely lady, save for the sake of the knowers of the Veda. What else can I do for you?
By my word both Bhīṣma and Śālva, O queenly one, shall become obedient to my will, O flawless-limbed one; that I shall do—grieve not.
But by no means whatever shall I take up a weapon, O passionate lady, except at the bidding of the brāhmaṇas; this is the vow I have made.
Ambā said: My sorrow must by all means be taken away by your honour; and since it is Bhīṣma who has begotten it for me, slay him, O lord, without delay.
Rāma said: Speak once more, maiden of Kāśi: Bhīṣma, though himself worthy to be revered, will at my word take hold of both your feet with his head.
Ambā said: Slay Bhīṣma in battle, Rāma, if you wish to do me a kindness; and if that was promised, you ought here to make it come true.
Bhīṣma said: As the two of them, Rāma and Ambā, were thus conversing, O king, Akṛtavraṇa spoke these words to the son of Jamadagni:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O mighty-armed one, you ought not to abandon a maiden who has come to you for refuge; slay Bhīṣma in battle, Rāma, as one slays a roaring demon.
If Bhīṣma, summoned by you to battle, Rāma, O great sage, should say "I am vanquished," or should do your bidding,
then this maiden's cause would be accomplished, O son of Bhṛgu, and your word, O hero, would be made true and fulfilled, O lord.
And this too was the vow you once made, Rāma, O great sage, when, having conquered all the kṣatriyas, you gave your pledge before the brāhmaṇas:
"If in battle a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or even a śūdra shall prove a hater of the brāhmaṇas, him will I slay"—so you swore, O descendant of Bhṛgu.
"Of those who come to me for refuge, frightened and longing to live, I shall never be able, so long as I live, to forsake any."
"And whoever shall vanquish in battle the whole kṣatriya host assembled, him too, that arrogant one, will I slay"—so you swore, O descendant of Bhṛgu.
Now Bhīṣma, the upholder of the Kuru line, is just such a conqueror, Rāma; meet him and fight with him in combat, O son of Bhṛgu.
Rāma said: I remember the vow I made of old, O best of sages, and I shall act accordingly—yet so that the end may first be gained by conciliation.
This is a great matter, O brāhmaṇa, that dwells in the heart of the maiden of Kāśi; I shall go there myself, taking the maiden, to where he is.
If Bhīṣma, who glories in battle, will not do as I say, then I shall slay that overweening one; such is my settled resolve.
For the arrows loosed by me do not cling fast in the bodies of living beings—as is known to you from of old, in my battles with the kṣatriyas.
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, Rāma then, together with those expounders of the Veda, resolved upon setting forth, and the great-souled one rose up.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then those ascetics, having passed that night there, having offered into the fire and murmured their prayers, set out with the desire to have me slain.
Then Rāma, together with those bulls among brāhmaṇas, came to Kurukṣetra, O great king, along with the maiden, O Bhārata.
Then they all encamped, having taken up their station along the Sarasvatī—those great-souled ascetics, with the best of the Bhṛgus at their head.
Bhīṣma said: Then, on the third day, taking his stand upon level ground, he of the mighty vow sent word to me, O king: "I have arrived."
Hearing that the mighty one had come to the border of the realm, I went swiftly forth to meet him with joy—that lord who was a treasury of splendour.
Putting a cow before me, O king of kings, surrounded by brāhmaṇas, by priests of the sacrifice godlike in their nature, and likewise by household chaplains.
Seeing me come to him, the valiant son of Jamadagni accepted that worship and spoke these words:
Bhīṣma, with what intent was this daughter of the king of Kāśi brought here by you against her will, and then again sent away?
For by you she has been made to fall from the winning of righteousness, in its higher and lower forms; and who indeed could now take her, whom you have laid hands upon?
For she has been rejected by Śālva, saying "she was carried off by you," O Bhārata; therefore, at my command, take her back, O Bhārata.
Let this king's daughter, O tiger among men, attain her own proper estate; it is not fitting that this slight should be put upon her by you, a king, O sinless one.
Then, looking upon him whose mind was ill at ease, I said: I shall in no way give her again to my brother, O brāhmaṇa.
"I belong to Śālva," she declared to me here long ago, O descendant of Bhṛgu; and granted leave by me, she went off toward the city of Saubha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Neither out of fear, nor out of pity, nor out of greed, nor from desire of gain shall I abandon the kṣatriya's law; such is the vow I have laid upon myself.
Then Rāma, his eyes troubled with wrath, said to me: If you will not do as these words of mine require, O bull of the Kurus,
"I shall slay you this very day, ministers and all"—so again and again, in his fury, Rāma spoke, his eyes troubled with wrath.
With pleasing words I again and again entreated that subduer of foes, that tiger of the Bhṛgus; yet he would not be appeased.
Bowing my head once more to that best of brāhmaṇas, I said: What is the reason for which you wish to fight with me here?
The fourfold science of missile and weapon was taught to me, when I was a boy, by you yourself, O mighty-armed one; I am your pupil, O descendant of Bhṛgu.
Then Rāma, his eyes red with anger, said to me: You know me to be your teacher, Bhīṣma, and yet you will not take back this daughter of the king of Kāśi to please me, O Kaurava, O lord of the earth?
For in no other way is there peace for you, O joy of the Kurus; take her, mighty-armed one, and preserve your own line. For she, made to fall by you, can win no husband.
To Rāma, conqueror of hostile cities, as he spoke thus, I replied: "This shall not come to pass, O brahmin-sage; why do you trouble yourself?"
Looking upon your ancient standing as my teacher, O son of Jamadagni, I seek your favor, O blessed one; for she was renounced by me long ago.
For who, knowing the grievous faults that ruin women, would ever house a woman whose heart belongs to another, one who dwells like a serpent within his home?
Not even out of fear of Vāsava would I abandon my duty, O greatly radiant one. Be gracious, or else do without delay whatever you intend.
And this verse too, O pure-souled and mighty lord, is heard in the ancient lore, sung by the great-minded, great-souled Marutta:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Even a teacher who is arrogant, who knows not right action from wrong, who has strayed onto a crooked path—him it is proper to chastise."
You, deemed my teacher, I have honored exceedingly out of affection; yet you know not the conduct befitting a teacher—therefore I shall fight with you.
I would not slay a teacher in battle, and least of all a brahmin, and most of all one grown great in austerity—thus have I borne with you.
But when a brahmin, like a kinsman of the warrior caste, is seen with arrow drawn, whoever in wrath should slay him in battle as he fights and does not flee—upon him no guilt of brahmin-slaughter falls: such is the settled rule in the sacred laws.
I am a kṣatriya, abiding in the duty of kṣatriyas, O you whose wealth is penance. The man who deals with another just as that other deals with him incurs no unrighteousness and attains what is best.
He who is competent in matters of gain or of duty, who knows place and time, even when fallen into doubt and adversity, fares better than one who acts without due reflection.
Since in this doubtful matter you proceed according to your own notion of justice, therefore I shall join battle with you, Rāma, in this great fight. Behold the might of my arms and my more-than-human valor.
Even with things come to this pass, O delight of the Bhṛgus, I shall do what lies in my power. On Kurukṣetra I shall fight with you, O brahmin; in single combat, Rāma, as you wish—make ready, O great sage.
There, Rāma, slain by me and bristling with a hundred shafts, purified by weapons in that great battle, you shall win the worlds you have conquered.
So go now, turn back toward Kurukṣetra, O lover of battle. There I shall come to you for combat, O mighty-armed one whose wealth is penance.
And in that very place where once, Rāma, you performed the purifying rite for your father, there too, having slain you, I shall perform the purifying rite, O Bhārgava.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Go there, Rāma, in haste, O you maddened for battle; I shall strip away your old pride, you who are a brahmin but in name.
And as for your repeated boast in assemblies, Rāma—'By me alone were the kṣatriyas of the world subdued'—hear now my answer to that.
In those days there was born no Bhīṣma, nor any kṣatriya of my measure, who could have destroyed your battle-pride and your desire.
But now that Bhīṣma is born, O mighty-armed one, conqueror of hostile cities—I shall undo your pride in battle, Rāma, of that there is no doubt.
Bhīṣma said: Then Rāma, as if laughing, said to me, O Bhārata: "By good fortune, Bhīṣma, you wish to do battle with me in the field."
"Here I go, O Kaurava, to Kurukṣetra together with you; I shall make good my word. Come there, O scorcher of foes."
"There may your mother Jāhnavī behold you slain by me, Bhīṣma, bristling with a hundred shafts, made food for vultures, herons, and crows."
"Gazing piteously upon you slain by me, let the goddess, attended by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, weep this day, O prince."
"Undeserving of such grief is that blessed river, daughter of Bhagīratha, who bore you—a fool, sick with the lust for war."
"Come, go with me, Bhīṣma; let the battle take place this very day. Take up all your gear—chariot and the rest—O Kaurava, bull of the Bhāratas."
To Rāma, conqueror of hostile cities, as he spoke thus, I bowed my head, O king, and said, "So be it."
Having said this, Rāma set off for Kurukṣetra eager to fight; and I, entering the city, made it known to Satyavatī.
Then, the rites of blessing performed and welcomed by my mother, having had the twice-born pronounce the auspicious day and the benediction, O greatly radiant one—
—mounting a gleaming silver chariot drawn by white horses, well equipped, sturdily framed, draped about with tiger-skins,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
furnished with great weapons and provided with every appurtenance, O king—that chariot, with a hero of noble birth, learned in the science of horses,
yoked with a well-bred charioteer many times proven in action—I, mailed in white armor that lent splendor to my frame,
taking up a white bow, set forth, O best of the Bhāratas, with a white parasol held above my head,
fanned with white yak-tail whisks, O lord of men, clad in white, turbaned in white, adorned with ornaments all of white,
hymned with blessings of victory, I went forth from the City named for the Elephant and came to Kurukṣetra, the field of battle, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Urged on by that charioteer toward the great fight, those horses, swift as thought and wind, bore me swiftly onward, O king.
Having reached Kurukṣetra, both I and the valorous Rāma at once advanced against each other for combat, O king.
Then I took my stand within sight of Rāma, that supreme ascetic, and taking up my finest conch, I blew upon it a mighty blast.
Then, O king, the twice-born and the ascetics dwelling in the forest, and the gods with their hosts of seers, looked on at that wondrous combat.
Then again and again heavenly garlands appeared, and heavenly music sounded, and gathered banks of cloud.
Then all those ascetics, the followers of the Bhārgava, became onlookers, ringing about the field of battle.
Then the goddess, my mother, who seeks the welfare of all beings, appearing in her own form, said to me, O king: "What is this you intend to do?"
"I shall go to the son of Jamadagni and entreat him, O upholder of the Kurus, again and again: 'Do not fight with Bhīṣma, who is your pupil.'"
"Do not, do not, my son, persist thus in fighting in battle with a brahmin, the son of Jamadagni"—so she reproached me.
"Is not Rāma known to you, my son—the slayer of kṣatriyas, whose valor equals Hara's—that you wish to do battle with him?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, saluting the goddess with joined palms, I told her all, O best of the Bhāratas—everything that had befallen at the bride-choosing,
and how Rāma had earlier been entreated by me, O king of kings, and what the long-standing desire of the daughter of the king of Kāśi had been.
Then my mother, the great river-goddess, went up to Rāma and for my sake sought to appease that seer, the Bhārgava, saying, "Do not fight with Bhīṣma, who is your pupil."
But he said to her as she pleaded, "Turn Bhīṣma back instead, for he will not do my will"—and so I came up against him.
Saṃjaya said: Then Gaṅgā, out of love for her son, approached Bhīṣma once more; but he, his eyes troubled with wrath, would not heed her word.
Then the righteous one, foremost of the Bhṛgus, great in austerity, came into view, and that best of the twice-born once again summoned him to battle.
Bhīṣma said: As he stood ready in the field, I answered him, smiling, as it were: "Standing on the ground, I cannot bring myself to fight you while I am mounted upon a chariot."
"Mount a chariot, O hero, and gird on armor, O mighty-armed Rāma, if you wish to do battle with me in the field."
Then Rāma said to me, smiling on the field of battle: "The earth is my chariot, Bhīṣma; the Vedas are my horses, like fine steeds."
"The Wind is my charioteer, and the mothers of the Vedas are my armor; well sheathed in these, I shall fight in the field, O delight of the Kurus."
Speaking thus, O Gāndhāra, Rāma of unfailing valor enveloped me on every side with a vast multitude of arrows.
Then I beheld the son of Jamadagni stationed upon a heavenly chariot, bearing every weapon, splendid, of a wondrous aspect beyond compare,
fashioned by thought, holy, spacious as a city, yoked with heavenly steeds, fully arrayed and adorned with gold,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and with a banner, O mighty-armed one, marked by the emblem of the moon. A bowman, his quiver bound on, his lizard-skin guard and finger-guards fastened—
and there Akṛtavraṇa, the friend of the Bhārgava, knower of the Vedas and exceedingly dear to him, served as charioteer for the warrior eager to fight.
As he summoned me to battle, the Bhārgava seemed to gladden my heart, crying out again and again, "Come on, advance!"
That Rāma—like the rising sun, unassailable, of mighty strength, the ender of the kṣatriyas—I, alone, advanced upon, alone.
Then, at a distance of three arrow-falls, I reined in my horses, and descending and laying aside my bow, I went on foot toward that best of seers,
approaching Rāma, that best of the twice-born, to do him honor; and saluting him in due form, I spoke these noble words:
"I shall fight with you in battle, Rāma—with one greater and superior, a teacher of righteous conduct. Wish me victory, O lord."
Rāma said: "Even so it is, O best of the Kurus; thus should one act who desires prosperity. For this is the duty, O mighty-armed one, of those who fight with their superiors."
"I would have cursed you had you not come thus, O lord of the people. Fight on, then, in the field, intent and steadfast, O Kaurava."
"Yet I do not wish you victory, for I am here to conquer you. Go, fight by the rule of righteousness; I am pleased with your conduct."
Bhīṣma said: Then, bowing to him, I quickly mounted my chariot and once more blew upon my gold-adorned conch in the field.
Then battle was joined between me and him, O Bhārata, for very many days, O king, each seeking to vanquish the other.
In that combat he struck me first with shafts fledged with heron-feathers—nine hundred and sixty arrows blazing like fire.
By them my four horses and my charioteer too were checked, O lord of the people; yet I stood firm in the fray, clad in mail.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And bowing to the gods and to the brahmins, O Bhārata, I answered him, smiling, as it were, as he stood ready in the field:
"Your teacherhood has been honored by me, even though you have overstepped all bounds; yet hear from me further, O brahmin, what is fitting in the gathering of righteousness."
"The Vedas that dwell within your body, your great brahmin-hood, and the mighty austerity you have practiced—at these I do not strike."
"I strike at the warrior's office, which you, Rāma, have assumed; for a brahmin passes into the state of a kṣatriya by the lifting of weapons."
"Behold the prowess of my bow, behold the strength of my arms. Lo, hero, I split your bow in two, arrow and all."
I let fly at him a sharp broad-headed shaft, O bull of the Bhāratas; by it the tip of his bow was severed and fell to the ground.
And nine hundred arrows, straight-jointed and fledged with heron-feathers, I sent flying at the chariot of the son of Jamadagni.
Lodged then in his body and stirred by the wind, those arrows quivered, dripping blood, like serpents.
His every limb drenched in blood, streaming gore from his wounds, Rāma shone then, O king, like Mount Meru pouring forth its mineral ores.
Like an aśoka tree at winter's end adorned with clusters of red blossoms, Rāma shone then, O king, in places resembling a kiṃśuka in flower.
Then, taking up another bow, Rāma, filled with wrath, rained down upon me arrows keenly sharpened and fletched with gold.
Reaching me, those fearsome shafts, piercing my vital parts in many places, made me tremble — of mighty speed, like serpents, fire, and poison.
Then I, steadying myself once more in the battle, in my wrath covered Rāma with arrows by the hundred.
Sorely afflicted by those sharp arrows, blazing like fire and the sun and like venomous snakes, Rāma seemed to grow faint of mind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, overcome with pity, reproaching myself within myself, I cried, 'Shame, shame upon this battle and upon the warrior's calling!' O bull of the Bhāratas.
And again and again I said, O king, swept away by the surge of grief: 'Alas, what an evil deed I have done through this warrior's office!'
'My teacher, a brāhmaṇa, a man of righteous soul, is thus tormented by my arrows!' — and so I struck no longer at the son of Jamadagni, O Bhārata.
Then, having scorched the earth, the thousand-rayed Pūṣan, the sun, went down to his setting as the day waned, and with that the fighting ceased.
Bhīṣma said: Then, O lord of peoples, my charioteer, esteemed for his skill, drew out the arrowheads from himself, from the horses, and from me.
When dawn broke and the sun had risen, with the horses bathed, rested, watered, and unwearied, the battle began again.
Seeing me come swiftly on, armored and standing in my chariot, the valiant Rāma made his own car fully ready for the fray.
Then I, seeing Rāma advancing, eager for combat, set aside my excellent bow and at once stepped down from my chariot.
Having saluted him, I mounted my car again, O Bhārata, and, eager to fight and free of fear, took my stand before the son of Jamadagni.
Then he covered me with a great downpour of arrows, and I in turn covered him, as he rained his shafts, with a downpour of my own.
But the son of Jamadagni, full of wrath, once more sent winged shafts against me, O king, like serpents with blazing mouths.
Those I cut down with sharp broad-headed arrows, by hundreds and by thousands, O king, cleaving them in the air again and again.
Then the valiant son of Jamadagni loosed celestial weapons against me, and these I warded off.
With weapon meeting weapon, O mighty-armed one, as he sought to gain the upper hand, a great roar arose in the heavens on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then I employed the wind-weapon against the son of Jamadagni, but Rāma struck it back with the weapon of the Guhyakas, O Bhārata.
Then I, with proper incantation, sent forth the fire-weapon, but the mighty Rāma turned mine aside with the weapon of Varuṇa.
Thus I warded off Rāma's celestial weapons, and Rāma too — blazing, knower of divine arms, subduer of foes — warded off mine.
Then, turning me to his left, O king, that foremost of brāhmaṇas, the mighty son of Jamadagni, in his fury pierced me in the chest.
Then I, O best of the Bhāratas, sank down upon my noble car, and the charioteer, seeing me overcome with faintness and sorely afflicted by Rāma's arrow, swiftly bore me away a krośa's distance, O best of the Bhāratas.
Then, seeing me borne off, grievously wounded and senseless, Rāma's followers — Akṛtavraṇa foremost among them, and the maiden of Kāśī — all rejoiced and raised a shout, O Bhārata.
Then, when I had regained my senses, I knew my situation and said to the charioteer: 'Drive on, charioteer, to where Rāma is; I am ready, my pain has passed.'
Then the charioteer bore me on with steeds most splendid, as if dancing in their stride, O Kaurava, and equal to the wind in their swiftness.
Then, reaching Rāma, O Kaurava, in great agitation I covered that agitated foe with a net of arrows, longing for victory.
But as those straight-flying arrows came on, Rāma swiftly cut each single one with three arrows of his own in that battle.
Then all those well-sharpened arrows of mine were shattered, cleft in two by Rāma's shafts, by the hundred in that great battle.
Then again I loosed at the son of Jamadagni, at Rāma, a blazing, bright shaft equal to Death itself, seeking to slay him.
Struck hard by it and brought under the power of that arrow's stroke, Rāma suddenly swooned and fell to the ground.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, when Rāma had sunk to the earth, all the world cried out in dismay, and the whole creation grew troubled, O Bhārata, as if at the falling of the sun.
Then, deeply alarmed, all those ascetics rich in penance, together with the maiden of Kāśī, rushed at once toward the delight of the Bhṛgus.
Embracing him, they gently revived him then with hands cooled by water and with blessings for his victory, O Kaurava.
Then Rāma, still reeling, rose and spoke to me, fitting an arrow to his bow: 'Stand fast, Bhīṣma — you are as good as slain!'
Loosed, it fell swiftly upon my left side in that great battle, by which I was sorely shaken, reeling like a tree about to topple.
Then, having slain my horses in that great battle with his swift-weapon, O king, he confidently covered me with arrows fletched with feathers.
Then I too loosed in battle the swift-weapon that none could withstand, O mighty-armed one; and the arrows, Rāma's and mine alike, swiftly met and held the space between us, veiling the whole sky on every side.
The sun could not shine through, veiled by that web of arrows; and the wind, caught in that space between, roared as though pent in by clouds.
Then from the churning of the wind, from the rays of the sun, from the scorching heat, and from their own nature, the arrows kindled into fire.
Those arrows, set ablaze by the fire risen from themselves, then all fell to the earth, O king, reduced to ashes.
Then by hundreds of thousands, by millions and tens of millions, by ten-thousands, by hundred-billions and thousand-billions, O Kaurava, Rāma in his wrath swiftly rained his arrows down upon me.
Then I too, with arrows like venomous serpents, cut those down in battle, O king, and brought them to earth like so many snakes.
Thus did that battle go, O best of the Bhāratas; and when the hour of twilight had passed, my teacher withdrew.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: When I had joined battle with Rāma once more, the next day there was again a fight most terrible and tumultuous, O best of the Bhāratas.
Then the hero, knower of celestial weapons, that righteous and mighty lord, deployed divine arms in great number, day after day.
Those weapons I scattered with counter-weapons, weapon against weapon, O Bhārata, in that tumultuous battle, having set aside this life so hard to give up.
When his weapons had been struck down again and again by mine, the Bhārgava of mighty splendor grew wrathful, having himself cast away all care for life in that combat.
Then the great-souled son of Jamadagni, his weapons blocked, hurled a spear of fearsome form, blazing like a meteor loosed by Time, its point aflame, wrapping the worlds in its glare.
Then, as it came on, blazing like the sun at the world's end, I cut it with flaming arrows into three pieces and brought it down to earth; whereupon a wind blew, fragrant and holy.
When it was cut down, Rāma, ablaze with anger, hurled twelve more fearsome spears; their form, O Bhārata, could not be told, so dazzling were they and so swift.
Indeed I was bewildered to behold them, from every quarter, like great meteors of fire, of varied form, blazing with fierce splendor, like the twelve suns at the world's dissolution.
Then, spreading out a net made of arrows, sighting them and piercing them with that net of shafts, O king, I loosed twelve arrows in the battle, and so beat down those spears of fearsome form.
Then the great-souled son of Jamadagni flung yet other fearsome spears with golden shafts, richly wrought and bound with bands of gold, blazing each like a great meteor.
Those fierce spears too I warded off with my shield and struck down in battle with my sword, O lord of men; and with celestial arrows I rained upon the son of Jamadagni's divine horses and his charioteer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing his gold-wrought spears, like serpents new-sloughed of their skins, cut to pieces, the great-souled crusher of the Haihaya lord, seized by wrath, brought forth a celestial weapon.
Then ranks of blazing arrows came on, fierce as swarms of locusts, and densely covered my body, my horses, my charioteer, and my whole chariot.
My chariot was thickly studded with arrows on every side, and so too the horses and the charioteer, O king; the yoke, the pole, and likewise the wheels, and the axle as well, were cut by the arrows and broke.
Then, when that downpour of arrows had passed, I rained back a flood of shafts upon my teacher; and he, that mass of brahminic power, wounded by my missiles, poured ceaselessly much blood from his body.
As Rāma was sorely tormented by my web of arrows, so was I most grievously and deeply wounded; then the battle ceased in the late afternoon, as the sun sought the mountain of its setting.
Bhīṣma said: Then at dawn, O lord of kings, when the sun had risen clear, the battle between the Bhārgava and me began once more.
Then, standing in his wheeling chariot, Rāma, best of warriors, rained showers of arrows upon me, as Śakra rains upon a mountain.
Struck by that downpour of arrows, my charioteer, who was my friend, fell to the floor of the chariot, casting my heart into grief.
Then that charioteer of mine, overcome by deep and great faintness, fell to the ground from the blows of the arrows and swooned away.
Then the charioteer, sorely afflicted by Rāma's arrows, gave up his life within a moment, O lord of kings; and fear entered into me then.
Then, when my charioteer had been slain, O king, as I, distracted in mind, was loosing my arrows, Rāma sent against me shafts that were equal to Death.
Then, while I was distraught at the loss of my charioteer and in disarray, the Bhārgava, drawing his powerful bow, struck me hard with an arrow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It fell, O king, between my collarbones — that blood-drinking shaft — and along with me, O lord of kings, it went down to the surface of the earth.
Believing me slain, then, O bull of the Bhāratas, Rāma roared aloud like a thundercloud and rejoiced again and again.
And when I had fallen thus, O king, Rāma, filled with joy, raised a great shout together with those his followers.
But the Kauravas who were there, standing at my side, and the people who had come, eager to behold that battle, fell into utmost anguish when I was struck down.
Then, fallen, O lion among kings, I beheld eight brāhmaṇas, radiant as the sun and fire; they stood surrounding me on every side and, in the midst of the battlefield, upheld me with their own arms.
Guarded by those brāhmaṇas, I touched not the ground but remained held aloft in the air by those brāhmaṇas as by kinsmen, as if sleeping in mid-air, sprinkled with drops of water.
Then those brāhmaṇas, O king, holding me up, all said together, 'Fear not,' and again and again, 'May it be well with you.'
Then, refreshed by their words, I rose up at once and saw my mother, the best of rivers, standing in my chariot.
And my horses had been held in check by her, the great river, in the midst of the battle, O lord of the Kurus; and I, having honored my mother's feet and likewise Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, mounted my chariot.
She had guarded my chariot, my horses, and all my gear; and I, with palms joined in reverence, then took my leave of her again.
Then I myself, taking up the reins of those wind-swift horses, fought on against the son of Jamadagni as the day waned, O Bhārata.
Then, O best of the Bhāratas, in that battle I loosed against Rāma a swift and mighty arrow that would cleave his heart.
Then Rāma, sorely afflicted by the arrow's force, sank to the earth upon his knees, let his bow fall, and passed into a swoon.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And when Rāma, giver of many thousand gifts, had fallen, the rain-clouds veiled the sky, pouring down blood in abundance.
Meteors fell by the hundred, with thunderclaps and tremors, and Svarbhānu suddenly swallowed up the blazing sun.
Harsh winds blew, the earth itself shook, and vultures, baḍa-birds, and herons wheeled down, filled with glee.
In a quarter of the sky that blazed, a jackal howled grimly again and again, and kettledrums, untouched by any hand, resounded with a deafening din.
Such was the dreadful array of portents, O most excellent of the Bhāratas, when the great-souled Rāma, well-nigh senseless, had sunk to the ground.
Then the sun, its orb of rays grown dim and sunk deep within heaped clouds of dust, went down to its setting; night drew on with its pleasant, cooling breeze, and so we two withdrew from battle.
Thus, O king, the withdrawal came about; and again at clear dawn the fearsome combat resumed, day after day for twenty days, and likewise for three days more.
Bhīṣma said: Then in the night, O lord of kings, bowing my head, I paid homage in full to the brāhmaṇas, to the ancestors, and to the gods.
And to the beings that roam by night and to the Night herself, O lord of peoples; then, reaching my couch in solitude, I pondered within my mind.
This grievous combat of mine with the son of Jamadagni has gone on now for very many days, and it bears the gravest peril.
And I am unable in the forefront of the fray to conquer Rāma of mighty valor, that brāhmaṇa son of Jamadagni, vast in strength.
If the resplendent son of Jamadagni can be vanquished by me, let the gracious gods reveal it to me this night.
Then in the night, O lord of kings, wounded by arrows, I fell asleep upon my right side, as the hour of dawn drew near.
Then by those very foremost of brāhmaṇas, by whom I had been raised when I fell from my chariot and upheld, I was comforted with the words, "Fear not."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those same ones, O great king, came to me in a dream-vision, surrounded me, and spoke this word—mark it well, O scion of the Kurus.
"Arise, fear not, O son of Gaṅgā; there is no danger whatsoever for you. We guard you, O tiger among men, for you are to us as our own body."
