"Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, shall in no way conquer you in battle; it is you who shall vanquish Rāma in the fray, O bull of the Bhāratas."
"This well-beloved weapon you shall recognize anew, for it was known to you as well in your former bearing of a body."
"It is the weapon of Prajāpati, fashioned by Viśvakarman, called Prasvāpa, the Inducer of Sleep, O Bhārata; not even Rāma knows it, nor any man anywhere upon the earth."
"Call it to mind, O mighty-armed one, and fix it firmly to your bow; nor shall Rāma meet his end by that weapon, O ruler of men."
"Nor shall you ever incur any sin thereby, O giver of honor; the son of Jamadagni, oppressed by the force of your shaft, shall but fall asleep."
"Then, having vanquished him, you yourself shall raise him up again in the fray, O Bhīṣma, by the cherished weapon of Awakening."
"Do thus, O Kaurava, mounting your chariot at dawn; whether a man lie sleeping or dead, we deem the two to be alike."
"And Rāma must never die, O king; therefore let this Prasvāpa, which has now arisen to you, be put to use."
Having so spoken, O king, those most excellent of the twice-born vanished, all eight of them alike in form, all of radiant aspect.
Bhīṣma said: Then, when the night had passed, I awoke, O Bhārata; and recalling that dream, I was filled with the highest joy.
Then the battle began between him and me, O Bhārata—tumultuous, marvelous, and making the hair of all beings stand on end.
Then the Bhārgava rained upon me a downpour made of arrows, and I warded it off with a net of shafts, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then that great ascetic, wrought to the height of fury, with the same wrath as the day before, hurled a spear at me.
Its touch was like the thunderbolt of Indra, its splendor like the rod of Yama, blazing like fire in the fight and licking out flames on every side.
Then, O tiger of the Bhāratas, like a blazing meteor coursing through the sky, that spear struck me swiftly upon the region of the shoulder, O Bhārata.
Then my blood flowed dreadfully, like the red-ochre ore from a mountainside, O mighty-armed one, where Rāma had wounded me, O you whose eyes are red as blood.
Then I, filled with vehement wrath, sent against the son of Jamadagni an arrow that resembled death itself and was like the venom of a serpent.
Struck thereby upon the forehead, that heroic and most excellent of the twice-born shone, O great king, like a mountain crowned with a peak.
In fury he rounded upon me, and drawing back with might a dreadful arrow, the destroyer of foes, like Time the all-ending, he fitted it to his bow.
That fierce shaft fell upon my breast, hissing like a serpent; and then, O king, I sank to the earth, drenched in blood.
But regaining my senses once more, I hurled at the wise son of Jamadagni a gleaming spear, blazing like the thunderbolt.
It fell upon the shoulder of that foremost of the twice-born; he grew faint, O king, and a trembling came over him.
Then his friend, the brāhmaṇa Akṛtavraṇa, great in austerity, embraced him and comforted him in many ways with gracious words.
Then Rāma, recovered and filled with wrath and indignation, that hero of mighty vows, brought forth the supreme Brāhma weapon.
Then, to counter it, the same most excellent Brāhma weapon, loosed by me, blazed forth, showing as it were the end of an age.
Between those two Brahmā weapons there came a clash in mid-course, before either could reach Rāma or me, O most excellent of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then in the sky there appeared nothing but a sheer blaze of fire, and all beings fell into anguish, O lord of peoples.
The seers, together with the gandharvas and the gods, O Bhārata, fell into the utmost torment, oppressed by the fiery splendor of those weapons.
Then the earth, with its mountains, forests, and trees, trembled, and the scorched creatures fell into the deepest despair.
The firmament blazed, O king, and the ten quarters were wreathed in smoke; nor could the beings that course the heavens hold their place in the sky.
Then, while the world with its gods, asuras, and rākṣasas cried out in dismay, I, thinking, "This is the moment," resolved to employ the weapon, O Bhārata.
The cherished Prasvāpa weapon, by the word of those expounders of the Veda; and that weapon, when I called it to mind, shone forth within my thought.
Bhīṣma said: Then a great clamor of "Halā! Halā!" arose in the heavens, O king: "Bhīṣma, loose not the Prasvāpa!"—so it cried, O delight of the Kurus.
Yet I was fixing that weapon upon the descendant of Bhṛgu; and as I was setting the Prasvāpa, Nārada spoke these words to me.
"Behold, O Kaurava, the hosts of the gods stand yonder in the sky; they restrain you this day—do not employ the Prasvāpa."
"Rāma is an ascetic, devoted to the brāhmaṇas, himself a brāhmaṇa, and your preceptor; do him no dishonor in any way, O Kaurava."
Then I beheld those eight expounders of the Veda standing in the heavens; smiling upon me, O lord of kings, they gently spoke this word.
"As Nārada bids you, O best of the Bhāratas, so do; for this is the highest good of the worlds, O bull of the Bhāratas."
Then, withdrawing that sleep-bringing weapon in the fray, I kindled forth the Brahmā weapon in that battle, according to the rite.
Then Rāma, O prince, was enraged; seeing that weapon withdrawn, he suddenly let fall these words: "I, dull of wit, am conquered by Bhīṣma!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the son of Jamadagni saw his father, and his father's father, and yet another beyond him; they stood encircling him and spoke to him then with words of comfort.
"Never again, dear child, commit such a rash deed in any way—to enter into combat with Bhīṣma, and a kṣatriya at that."
"For battle is the duty of a kṣatriya, O delight of the Bhṛgus; but the study of scripture and the practice of vows are the supreme wealth of brāhmaṇas."
"For some particular cause this most fierce bearing of arms was once enjoined upon you by us, and that task you have indeed accomplished."
"Dear child, enough of this; your clash in combat with Bhīṣma is sufficient, O mighty-armed one—withdraw now from the battle here."
"Enough is this bearing of the bow by you—blessings upon you; lay it aside, O unassailable one, and devote yourself to austerity, O Bhārgava."
"This Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, has been restrained by all the gods, who urged him, 'Withdraw from this battle.'"
"'Do not fight with Rāma, your preceptor,' they said again and again, 'for Rāma ought not in justice to be vanquished by you in battle, O scion of the Kurus; show honor, O son of Gaṅgā, to the brāhmaṇa upon the field of war.'"
"And we are your elders; therefore we restrain you. Bhīṣma is one among the Vasus; by good fortune you yet live, O little son."
"This son of Gaṅgā, the son of Śaṃtanu, is a Vasu of great renown; how could he be vanquished by you in battle, O Rāma? Withdraw, then."
"Arjuna, the best of the Pāṇḍavas, the mighty son of Purandara—he is Nara, the heroic Prajāpati, the ancient god, the everlasting one."
"Renowned through the three worlds as Savyasācin, valiant—he has been ordained by the Self-existent as the death of Bhīṣma when his time shall come."
Thus addressed by his forefathers, Rāma spoke this to them: "I will not turn back in battle—such is the vow I have laid upon myself."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Never before have I turned back in the forefront of battle. Let the son of the river-goddess be turned from the fight if you will, O grandsires; but I shall in no way withdraw from this combat."
Then those sages, O king, with Ṛcīka at their head, together with Nārada, drew near and spoke this word.
"Withdraw from the battle, dear child; show honor to these most excellent of the twice-born." But I said "No" to them, out of regard for the duty of a kṣatriya.
"This is my vow before the world: never in any way will I turn my back upon battle and withdraw, to be struck with arrows from behind."
"Not out of greed, not out of meanness, not out of fear, nor for any gain's sake would I forsake the eternal law—such is my settled resolve."
Then all those sages, with Nārada at their head, O king, and Bhāgīrathī, my mother, came into the midst of the battlefield.
Still I stood, my arrow taken up, bow in hand, my resolve as firm as ever, ready to fight in the fray; then they, gathering together once more, spoke to Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, upon the field of battle.
"The hearts of brāhmaṇas are soft as fresh butter; be at peace, O Bhārgava. Rāma, Rāma, withdraw from this battle, O best of the twice-born; for Bhīṣma is not to be slain by you, nor you by Bhīṣma, O Bhārgava."
Speaking thus, all those forefathers barred the field of battle and made the descendant of Bhṛgu lay down his weapon.
Then once more I beheld those eight expounders of the Veda, blazing like eight planets newly risen.
With affection they spoke this word to me as I stood in the battle: 'Approach Rāma, O mighty-armed one; honor your teacher and act for the welfare of the worlds.'
Seeing that Rāma had been turned back by the words of his well-wishers, I too, acting for the welfare of the worlds, took up that counsel.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, sorely wounded, I came up to Rāma and saluted him; and Rāma, that great ascetic, smiling upon me with affection, said:
'There is no warrior walking the earth equal to you in all this world. Go now, Bhīṣma; in this battle I have been greatly pleased by you.'
And in my very presence the descendant of Bhṛgu summoned that maiden and, in the midst of those ascetics, spoke to her in a sorrowful voice:
Rāma said: It is plain before the eyes of all the worlds, O fair lady, how with my utmost might I have performed great feats of prowess.
Yet even displaying my supreme weapons I am wholly unable in battle to gain the upper hand over Bhīṣma, the best of those who bear arms.
This is my utmost power, this my utmost strength. Go where you will, gentle one; what else can I do for you?
Turn to Bhīṣma himself for refuge; no other recourse is left to you. For I have been vanquished by Bhīṣma as he loosed his mighty weapons.
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, the high-souled Rāma sighed and fell silent; then the maiden addressed the delight of the Bhṛgus:
'O blessed one, it is even so as your lordship has said: this Bhīṣma of noble mind is unconquerable in battle, even by the gods.'
'You have done my work to the full measure of your power and zeal, withholding in the fight neither your valor nor your manifold weapons.'
'Yet in the end he cannot be overcome in battle; and never again, by any means, will I go to this Bhīṣma.'
'But I shall go there, O treasury of austerity, whence I may myself fell Bhīṣma in battle, O foremost of the Bhṛgus.'
Having spoken thus, the maiden departed, her eyes troubled with wrath, her resolve fixed upon austerity, brooding on my death.
Then the best of the Bhṛgus, Rāma, together with those sages, took his leave of me and returned to Mahendra as he had come, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, mounting my chariot and praised by the twice-born, I entered the city and reported to my mother Satyavatī all that had passed, O great king; and she rejoiced over me.
And I appointed wise men to the task of watching the maiden's doings; day by day they, set diligently upon my good and welfare, reported to me her goings, her words, and her acts.
From the very moment that maiden went to the forest, bent upon austerity, I became troubled and downcast, as though my senses had fled.
For no warrior could conquer me in battle by valor, my son, save one knowing the Veda, made keen by austerity and firm in his vow.
And this too, O king, I disclosed out of fear to Nārada and to Vyāsa, that the deed might be averted; and both of them said to me:
'You must not grieve, Bhīṣma, on account of the daughter of Kāśi. Who could venture by human effort to turn back fate?'
But that maiden, O great king, entering the circle of hermitages and taking her stand on the bank of the Yamunā, practiced superhuman austerity.
Without food, gaunt, withered, her hair matted, caked with dirt, that ascetic for six months lived on air alone, motionless as a post.
Reaching the bank of the Yamunā, the fair lady passed yet another full year standing in the water, taking no food at all.
And, fierce in her wrath, she passed yet another year upon a single withered leaf, poised upon the tips of her toes.
Thus for twelve years she scorched heaven and earth; and though her kinsmen sought to turn her back, she could by no means be dissuaded.
Then she went to the land of the Vatsas, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, to the hermitage of the high-souled ascetics of holy conduct.
There, in those holy regions, the daughter of Kāśi, her limbs bathed in the sacred waters, wandered day and night, roaming at her own will.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At the hermitage of Nanda, O great king, and then at the fair hermitage of Ulūka, and at the hermitage of Cyavana, and at the abode of Brahmā;
at Prayāga, the sacrificial ground of the gods, and in the forests of the gods, and in Bhogavatī, O king, and likewise at the hermitage of Kauśika;
at the hermitage of Māṇḍavya, O king, and at the hermitage of Dilīpa, and at the pool of Rāma, O Kaurava, and at the hermitage of Paila and Gārgya—
in all these holy fords, O lord of peoples, did the daughter of Kāśi then bathe her limbs, undertaking the fiercest austerity.
My mother, O scion of Kuru, rising up from the water, said to her: 'Why do you torment yourself, gentle one? Tell me the truth of this.'
Then she, the blameless one, with hands folded in reverence, answered her, O king: 'Bhīṣma was not conquered by Rāma in battle, O fair-eyed one.'
'What other could venture to conquer that lord of earth with arrow raised? Therefore I shall practice the most terrible austerity for the destruction of Bhīṣma.'
'I wander the earth, O goddess, that I may slay that king; let the fruit of this vow be mine in another body.'
Then the river that goes to the ocean said: 'You walk a crooked path, fair lady. This desire, O flawless of limb, you cannot attain, O weak one.'
'If, O daughter of Kāśi, you keep this vow for the destruction of Bhīṣma, and if while keeping the vow you shall give up your body, then you shall become a river, O fair one—crooked, watered only in the rains;'
'hard to ford and trackless, flowing in the rains but dry the eight months, full of fearsome crocodiles, dreadful, a terror to all creatures.'
Having spoken thus to the daughter of Kāśi, O king, my illustrious mother, the fair lady, turned back as if smiling.
Sometimes in the eighth month, sometimes in the tenth, that maiden of fair complexion would again not so much as taste water.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That daughter of the lord of Kāśi, O Kaurava, in her craving for holy fords, kept rushing here and there over the land of the Vatsas, again and again falling and running on.
And in the land of the Vatsas that river became renowned as Ambā, O Bhārata—watered in the rains, teeming with crocodiles, hard to ford, and winding.
By that austerity the maiden was born again from half of herself: she became both a river among the Vatsas, O king, and yet remained a maiden as well.
Bhīṣma said: Then all those ascetics, seeing her fixed in her resolve upon austerity, sought to turn her back, my son, and asked: 'What is your purpose?'
Then the maiden answered those seers grown old in austerity: 'I have been spurned by Bhīṣma, cast out from the estate of a wife.'
'My vow is for his slaying, not for any heavenly world, O treasuries of austerity. When I have slain Bhīṣma I shall find peace—such is my resolve.'
'On whose account I have entered upon this everlasting abode of sorrow, bereft of the world of a husband, neither woman nor man am I here.'
'Without slaying the son of Gaṅgā in battle I shall not turn back, O treasuries of austerity. This is the resolve in my heart, the very end for which this effort is undertaken.'
'Wearied utterly of womanhood, resolved upon manhood, I would requite myself upon Bhīṣma; I am not to be turned aside'—so she said again.
To that fair lady the god who bears the trident, the consort of Umā, showed himself in his own form, in the midst of those great seers.
Offered a boon, she chose my defeat; and the god answered that resolute woman: 'You shall slay him.'
Then once again the maiden spoke to Rudra: 'How, O god, can victory in battle be mine, a woman? And by my womanly nature my mind is wholly stilled, O consort of Umā.'
'The defeat of Bhīṣma has been promised by you, O lord of beings; so act, O bull-bannered one, that it may come true—that I, meeting Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu in battle, may slay him.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
To that maiden Mahādeva, the bull-bannered, replied: 'My word, gentle one, speaks no untruth; it shall come true.'
'You shall slay Bhīṣma in battle and shall obtain manhood; and when you have passed into another body you shall remember all of this.'
'Born in the line of Drupada, you shall become a great chariot-warrior; swift with weapons, skilled in varied modes of fighting, you shall become highly honored.'
'Even as I have said, O blessed one, all this shall come to pass: in time, after some passing of the years, you shall become a man.'
Having spoken thus, the mighty-splendored, matted-haired, bull-bannered god vanished then and there before the very eyes of the brāhmaṇas.
Then, in the sight of those great seers, the blameless maiden of fair complexion gathered firewood from that forest;
and when she had built a great pyre and set fire to it, the flames blazing up, O great king, with a mind inflamed by wrath,
crying 'For the slaying of Bhīṣma!' the eldest daughter of Kāśi entered the fire, O king, beside the river Yamunā.
Duryodhana said: How, O son of Gaṅgā, did Śikhaṇḍin, having first been a maiden, become a man, O best in battle? Tell me that, grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: The wife of that lord of earth Drupada, O king of kings, his beloved chief queen, was childless, O lord of peoples.
At that very time the lord of earth Drupada, for the sake of offspring, O great king, propitiated Śaṃkara.
Resolved upon my destruction, he undertook terrible austerity and obtained from Mahādeva a daughter, though he had prayed, 'Let a son be mine.'
'O blessed one, I desire a son, to requite myself upon Bhīṣma'—thus he spoke, and the god of gods replied: 'A woman-and-man shall be yours.'
'Turn back, O ruler of earth; this shall never be otherwise.' And he, going to the city, said this to his wife:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'A great effort was made by me, O queen, through austerity, for the sake of a son; and I have been told by Śambhu, "Having been a maiden, it shall become a man."'
'Though entreated again and again, Śiva said only, "It is so destined"; for it shall be no otherwise—what must be will be even thus.'
Then that resolute woman, the wife of King Drupada, having purified herself, in her season approached Drupada.
In due time she conceived by the son of Pṛṣata, through the natural means ordained by rule, O ruler of earth, as Nārada told me.
Then the lotus-eyed queen bore that child; and King Drupada, the mighty-armed, O delight of the Kurus, out of love for the child tended his dear wife with all comfort.
Then to that sonless king Drupada, lord of earth, was born a daughter of surpassing beauty, O ruler of men.
But the illustrious wife of that sonless king Drupada gave it out, O king of kings: 'A son has been born to me.'
Then King Drupada, O ruler of men, had all the rites proper to a son performed for her, concealed as she was, as if for a son.
And the chief queen of Drupada guarded the secret with all care, declaring 'It is a son'; for none in the city knew the truth save the son of Pṛṣata.
For, trusting in the word of the god of wondrous splendor, he concealed that daughter, and declared, 'It is a man.'
The king had all the birth-rites duly performed as for a male child, complete with their proper ordinances; and they knew her as Śikhaṇḍin.
I alone came to know the truth—through my spies, through the words of Nārada, through the speech of the gods, and through the austerities of Ambā.
Bhīṣma said: Drupada took the greatest pains over all that concerned his own child; and so, O lord of kings, that child attained excellence in writing and the other arts, and in the crafts, and in archery became a pupil of Droṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The fair-complexioned mother of that child, O great king, then urged the king to seek a wife for the maiden as though for a son.
Then the son of Pṛṣata, seeing that the maiden had reached her youth and knowing her to be a woman, fell into anxiety together with his wife.
Drupada said: This maiden of mine, who increases my sorrow, has come to her youth; and I have kept her concealed in obedience to the word of the trident-bearer.
That word, O great queen, can in no way prove false; for why should the maker of the three worlds make it untrue?
His wife said: If it please you, O king, I will speak; hear my words. Hearing them now, O son of Pṛṣata, you may set about your own affair.
Let a wife be duly taken for this child, O king; my settled conviction is that the word of the god will come true.
Bhīṣma said: Then the husband and wife, having made their decision in that matter, sought as bride the daughter of the lord of the Daśārṇas.
Then King Drupada, that lion among kings, having reviewed all the kings by their lineage, sought as a wife for Śikhaṇḍin the daughter of the Dāśārṇaka king.
The king known as Hiraṇyavarman, that Dāśārṇaka, that protector of the earth, gave his daughter to that Śikhaṇḍin.
And that king Hiraṇyavarman was a great lord of the earth among the Daśārṇas—unassailable, master of a mighty army, lofty of mind.
When the marriage had been made, O best of kings, that maiden came to her youth, and the maiden Śikhaṇḍinī likewise.
Śikhaṇḍin, now wedded, returned again to Kāmpilya; and for some time that maiden did not learn that the other was a woman.
But the daughter of Hiraṇyavarman, having found out that Śikhaṇḍinī was a woman, in shame reported to her nurses and her companions that the daughter of the Pāñcāla king, that Śikhaṇḍinī, was indeed a maiden.
Then, O tiger among kings, those Daśārṇa nurses fell into the deepest distress out of grief, and sent word.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the messengers reported the whole deceit, just as it had happened, to the lord of the Daśārṇas; and that king flew into a rage.
Śikhaṇḍin too, O great king, lived in the royal household after the manner of a man, full of joy, in no way relishing womanhood.
Then after a few days, O bull of the Bhāratas, hearing this, King Hiraṇyavarman, O lord of kings, was driven to anguish by his fury.
Then the Dāśārṇaka king, filled with fierce wrath, dispatched a messenger to the dwelling of Drupada.
Then the messenger of Kāñcanavarman, coming to Drupada, drew him aside alone and spoke in secret these words.
The Daśārṇa king, O sovereign, sends you these words, enraged at the affront, deceived by you, O blameless one:
You hold me in contempt, O king—surely your counsel has been evil—in that out of folly you asked of me my daughter for the sake of your own daughter.
Receive now the fruit of that deceit, O fool. Stand firm—I shall root you out, together with your kinsmen and your ministers.
Bhīṣma said: When Drupada was thus addressed by the messenger, O king, his speech failed him, as though he were a thief caught in the act.
He made a strenuous effort, sending word through kinsmen with soothing assurances and through messengers of honeyed speech, declaring, "This is not so."
But that king, having once more learned the truth—that the child of the Pāñcāla was a maiden—set out in haste.
Then he sent word to his allies of measureless might of the deceit practised upon his daughter, on the testimony of the nurses.
Then that best of kings, mustering his forces, resolved to march against Drupada, O Bhārata.
Then King Hiraṇyavarman, O lord of kings, took counsel with his allies concerning the Pāñcāla sovereign.
There this was resolved among those high-souled kings: "If, O king, it prove true that Śikhaṇḍinī is a maiden, we shall bind the Pāñcāla king and bring him to our homes;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and having set up another king, another lord of men, among the Pāñcālas, we shall put to death King Drupada together with Śikhaṇḍin."
Then that lord again instructed a messenger, an envoy, and dispatched him to the son of Pṛṣata: "I shall slay you—stand firm!"
And that lord of men, timid by nature and conscious of guilt, King Drupada, ruler of the earth, was seized with sharp dread.
Having dismissed the Daśārṇa messenger, Drupada, worn with grief, came to his wife in private and the king spoke these words.
Possessed by great fear and stricken to the heart with sorrow, the Pāñcāla king said to the beloved mother of Śikhaṇḍin:
"My kinsman of mighty strength, King Hiraṇyavarman, will march against me in his wrath, dragging his host along.
What shall I now do, bewildered, concerning this maiden? Śikhaṇḍin, said to be your son, is suspected to be a maiden.
Having ascertained this as the truth, with his allies and his host of followers, deeming himself deceived, he wishes, it seems, to uproot me.
What in this is true, O fair-hipped one, and what is false? Tell me, O lovely one. Having heard your word, O auspicious one, I shall act accordingly.
For I am fallen into doubt, and this Śikhaṇḍinī is but a child; and you too, O queen, fair of hue, have come into great straits.
Tell me then the truth, as I ask, for our deliverance from all this, so that I may take measures in this matter, O fair-hipped, bright-smiling one; and do not fear for Śikhaṇḍin—I shall surely make provision there.
By my own deed, O lovely one, I have been deceived as to the office of a son; and the Dāśārṇaka king too, that lord of the earth, has been deceived by me. So tell me, O blessed one, and I shall do in this what is best.
Though the king knew the truth, he urged it openly so as to make it plain to the other; and the queen replied to the lord of the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Then the mother of Śikhaṇḍin, O ruler of men, O mighty-armed one, declared the truth to her husband—that Śikhaṇḍinī was a maiden:
"Being without a son, O king, and through fear of my co-wives, I declared this maiden Śikhaṇḍinī, when she was born, to be a male.
And you, O best of men, approved this of me out of love; the rites of a son were performed for the maiden, O bull among kings, and a wife was taken for her by you, O king—the daughter of the lord of the Daśārṇas.
And it was you who said before, considering the meaning of the god's word, 'Having been a maiden, she shall become a man'—and so this was let be.
Hearing this, Drupada Yajñasena, O king, laid the whole truth before his counsellors versed in deliberation, and took counsel as to whatever was fitting for the protection of his people.
And having weighed the kinship-bond with that Dāśārṇaka king, O lord of men—since he had himself wrought the deceit as it had happened—intent upon his counsel, he came to a resolve.
In that time of peril, O Bhārata, the king secured on every side his city—naturally well guarded and fully arrayed for defence, O lord of kings.
And the king, together with his wife, fell into the deepest distress over the strife with the lord of the Daśārṇas, O bull of the Bhāratas.
"How may there be no great quarrel between me and my kinsman?"—thus reflecting in his mind, he then worshipped the gods.
Seeing him then, O king, devoted to the gods and engaged in worship, the queen, his wife, spoke these words.
"Reverence for the gods is ever true and esteemed by the good; and it may avail us, who have fallen into an ocean of grief, if we worship them earnestly.
Let all the gods be honoured with abundant gifts, and let the sacred fires too be fed with oblations, for the turning back of the Daśārṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And ponder in your mind, O lord, his turning back without battle; by the grace of the gods all this shall come to pass.
And what has been deliberated by your ministers together with you, O wide-eyed one, for the saving of this city, O king, that too carry out accordingly.
For the divine, joined with human effort, succeeds full well, O king; but from the mutual opposition of the two there is no success at all."
"Therefore, having made arrangements in the city together with your counsellors, worship the gods to your heart's content, O lord of peoples."
Seeing the two thus conversing, given over wholly to grief, the maiden Śikhaṇḍinī, high-minded, was as if overcome with shame.
Then she thought, "It is on my account that these two are grieving"; and thereupon she set her mind upon ending her life.
Having thus made her resolve, utterly given over to grief, she left the palace and went to a dense, deserted forest,
guarded, O king, by a yakṣa rich in power, Sthūṇākarṇa; and for very dread of him men shun that forest.
There stood the dwelling of Sthūṇa, plastered with lime and clay, rich with the smoke of parched grain and frankincense, with high ramparts and gateway-arches.
Entering it, Śikhaṇḍin, the child of Drupada, O king, took no food for many days and wasted away her body.
The yakṣa Sthūṇa, gracious of eye, showed himself to her: "For what purpose is this endeavour of yours? I shall accomplish it—tell me, do not delay."
"It cannot be done," she said to the yakṣa again and again; and the guhyaka answered her, "I shall do it."
"I am a follower of the lord of wealth and a bestower of boons, O daughter of a king; even what may not be given, I shall give. Speak what you wish to ask."
Then Śikhaṇḍin laid the whole matter, entire, before that chief of yakṣas, Sthūṇākarṇa, O Bhārata:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"My father is in peril, O yakṣa; before long he will perish, for the lord of the Daśārṇas in his wrath will march against him—
a king of great might and great vigour, clad in golden armour. Therefore save me, O yakṣa, and my father and my mother.
For you have promised to take away my sorrow. Let me become a man, O yakṣa, blameless, by your grace.
Only until that king draws near my city—until then, O great yakṣa, O guhyaka, show me your favour."
Bhīṣma said: Hearing the words of Śikhaṇḍin, O bull of the Bhāratas, that yakṣa, pressed by fate, reflected in his mind and spoke—for it was destined to be, and to my own sorrow, O Kaurava:
"Gentle one, I shall do your will, but mark my condition. For a certain space of time I shall give you this my own manhood; but you must return at the appointed time. This I tell you truly.
I am a lord whose will is fulfilled, a sky-ranger who can take any form at pleasure. By my grace save your city and all your kinsmen entire.
I shall bear your womanhood, O daughter of a king. Promise me truly, and I shall do you this kindness."
Śikhaṇḍin said: "I shall give back to you this manhood again, O blessed one; for a certain space of time bear my womanhood, O night-ranger.
When the Dāśārṇa king Hemavarman has gone back again, I shall become a maiden once more, and you shall become a man.
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, the two of them, O king, made a pact there—that they would do no harm to one another—and then they exchanged their forms.
The yakṣa Sthūṇa took on the female sign, O lord of men, and Śikhaṇḍin received that blazing form of the yakṣa.
Then Śikhaṇḍin of the Pāñcālas, having attained manhood, O king, entered the city rejoicing, came to his father, and recounted to Drupada all that had befallen, just as it had happened.
When Drupada heard this from him, he conceived the greatest joy, and together with his wife he then called to mind the words of Maheśvara.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then he sent word to the lord of the Daśārṇas, O king: "This son of mine is a man—let your honour believe me in this."
Thereupon the Dāśārṇa king came at once against Drupada, the king of the Pāñcālas, filled with grief and indignation.
Then, having reached Kāmpilya, the lord of the Daśārṇas, with due honour, dispatched as his envoy the foremost of those learned in the Veda.
"Say in my name, O envoy, to that Pāñcāla, the basest of kings: 'Since you, O evil-minded one, chose a maiden for the sake of my daughter, this very day you shall see the fruit of that arrogance—of this there is no doubt.'"
Thus addressed by him, O best of kings, that brāhmaṇa envoy, urged on by the Dāśārṇa king, set out for the city.
Then the chaplain came upon Drupada within the city, and the Pāñcāla king, O lord of kings, offered him a cow and the welcome-water, well honoured, together with Śikhaṇḍin.
He did not welcome that homage, but spoke these words, the very words that had been uttered by that heroic king Kāñcanavarman:
"Since I, O man of base conduct, have been deceived by you in the matter of my daughter, reap now the fruit of that sin you have wrought, O evil-minded one!"
"Give me battle, O king, this day at the front of the fray; at once I shall uproot you, together with your counsellors, your sons, and your kinsmen."
That speech, fraught with reproach, the king was made to hear, in the midst of his counsellors, from the chaplain who was envoy of the Daśārṇa lord.
Then Drupada, O best of the Bhāratas, bowing in conciliation, said: "As for the speech your honour, O brāhmaṇa, has spoken to me at the bidding of my kinsman, an envoy of mine shall himself bear the answer in reply to it."
Then Drupada too sent forth to the great-souled Hiraṇyavarman an envoy, a brāhmaṇa who had reached the far shore of the Veda.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having come into the presence of the king, the lord of the Daśārṇas, he then delivered, O king, the message that had been spoken by Drupada:
"Let an inquiry be made openly: my son is indeed a youth. This has been falsely said by someone; it is not to be believed."
Then that king, having heard Drupada's words, fell to pondering, and sent forth young women of the highest rank, of surpassing beauty, to learn whether Śikhaṇḍin was woman or man.
Those women, being sent, learned the truth of the matter, and gladly reported it all to the king—that Śikhaṇḍin, O lord of the Kurus, was a man, a mighty soul—to the Dāśārṇa king.
Then that king, having made the inquiry, was pleased, and meeting with his kinsman, he stayed there in joy and took up his lodging.
And to Śikhaṇḍin the lord of men, gladdened, gave wealth—elephants and horses and cattle, and many hundreds of female servants—and, having been honoured, he turned back his daughter and departed.
When the Dāśārṇa king Hemavarman, his rancour soothed and his heart pleased, had gone back, Śikhaṇḍin was a figure of delight.
Now after some time Kubera, borne by men, while making his circuit through the worlds, came to the dwelling of Sthūṇa.
Poised above that house, the guardian of riches looked down, and beheld the dwelling of the yakṣa Sthūṇa, finely adorned and bright with strands of garlands,
honoured with parched grain and perfumes and canopies, made fragrant with incense, decked with standards and banners, and with offerings of food, drink, and flesh laid out in oblation.
Seeing his abode thus adorned on every side, the lord of the yakṣas then spoke to those yakṣas, his attendants:
"Well adorned is this dwelling of Sthūṇa, O you of boundless valour. Yet why does that dull-witted one not approach me today?"
"Since that exceedingly dull-spirited one, though he knows I am here, does not approach me, it is my judgement that a great punishment must be meted out to him."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The yakṣas said: O king, a daughter, Śikhaṇḍinī, was born to King Drupada; and for some reason he gave to her the mark of manhood,
and took in exchange the mark of women; turned female, he stays within the house. For that reason, ashamed and bearing a woman's form, he does not approach.
For this reason, O king, does Sthūṇa not look upon you today. Having heard it, do as is fitting; let your chariot stay here a while.
Bhīṣma said: "Let Sthūṇa be brought," the lord of the yakṣas then said. "I will lay punishment upon him," he declared again and again.
Summoned, he came before the lord of the yakṣas, O lord of the earth; bearing a woman's form, O great king, he stood overcome with shame.
In great wrath the giver of wealth cursed him, O joy of the Kurus: "Even so let the womanhood of this sinful one remain, O guhyakas!"
Then the great-souled lord of the yakṣas spoke: "Since, scorning the yakṣas here, you gave your mark to Śikhaṇḍin, O evil-minded one, and took the mark of woman, O doer of sin,
since this unheard-of thing has been done by you, O most foolish one, therefore from this day onward you shall be a woman, and he a man."
Then the yakṣas sought to appease Vaiśravaṇa for Sthūṇa's sake, saying again and again: "Set a limit to the curse."
Then the great-souled lord of the yakṣas, my son, replied to all his attendant bands of yakṣas, wishing to set an end to the curse:
"When Śikhaṇḍin has been slain in battle, the yakṣa Sthūṇa shall regain his own form," said the high-minded one. "Let him be free of distress."
Having spoken thus, the blessed god, honoured by yakṣas and rākṣasas, departed together with all those who move in the span between two blinkings of the eye.
But Sthūṇa, having received the curse, dwelt on there in that place; and at the appointed time Śikhaṇḍin came to him, that wanderer of the night.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Drawing near, he spoke these words: "I have come, O blessed one." Then Sthūṇa said to him, again and again, "I am pleased."
Seeing the prince Śikhaṇḍin come in good faith, he told Śikhaṇḍin all that had befallen, just as it had happened.
The yakṣa said: I have been cursed by Vaiśravaṇa on your account, O son of a king. Go now, and roam the worlds at your will and your ease.
This, I deem, was ordained of old, and could not be overpassed—your coming, and likewise the visit of Paulastya.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by the yakṣa Sthūṇa, O Bhārata, Śikhaṇḍin returned to the city filled with great joy.
With perfumes and garlands of many kinds, and with rich gifts, he honoured the twice-born and the gods, the sanctuaries, and the crossroad shrines.
And Drupada the Pāñcāla, together with his son Śikhaṇḍin whose purpose was now fulfilled, and with his kinsmen, attained the highest joy.
And he gave over Śikhaṇḍin as a pupil to Droṇa, O bull of the Kurus—that son, O great king, who had once been a woman.
That prince Śikhaṇḍin received the fourfold science of archery, together with you all, and so did Dhṛṣṭadyumna, son of Pṛṣata.
But to me, my son, all this was duly reported by my spies, who, in the guise of dullards, the blind, and the deaf, had been set by me upon Drupada.
Thus, O great king, this son of Drupada, woman-and-man, came into being—Śikhaṇḍin, O best of the Kauravas, the foremost of warriors on the car.
The eldest daughter of the lord of Kāśi, renowned by the name of Ambā, was born in the line of Drupada as Śikhaṇḍin, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Even for a moment I would not look upon him, bow in hand and come forward eager to fight; nor would I strike him.
This vow of mine has ever been famed throughout the earth: that upon a woman, or upon one who was once a woman, one who bears a woman's name or a woman's form,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I would never loose my arrows, O joy of the Kurus. For this reason I will not slay Śikhaṇḍin.
I know the truth of Śikhaṇḍin's birth, my son; therefore I will not slay him in battle, even when he comes against me with weapon raised.
If Bhīṣma should slay a woman, he would as surely slay his own self. Therefore I will not slay him, even seeing him stand before me in the fray.
Saṃjaya said: Having heard this, King Duryodhana of the Kuru line then pondered for a moment, and deemed it fitting in Bhīṣma.
Saṃjaya said: When the night had brightened into dawn, your son once again, in the midst of all the host, questioned the grandsire:
"O son of Gaṅgā, this supreme army of the Pāṇḍava, abounding in men and elephants and horses, thronged with great chariot-warriors,
guarded by mighty bowmen of great strength, Bhīma and Arjuna and the rest, peers of the world-guardians, with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at their head—
unassailable, irresistible, surging like the swollen ocean, an ocean of an army not to be shaken even by the gods in great battle—
in what time, O son of Gaṅgā of great splendour, would you destroy it? Or the preceptor, that mighty bowman, or Kṛpa of exceeding strength,
or Karṇa who exults in battle, or Drauṇi, the best of the twice-born? For you are all versed in the divine weapons, and all in my host."
"This I wish to know, for a great curiosity dwells ever in my heart, O mighty-armed one; it behoves you to tell it to me."
Bhīṣma said: This befits you, O best of the Kurus, O lord of the earth—if you ask of the strength and weakness of your foes and of your own.
Hear, O king, what my utmost power in battle would be, and the might of my weapons in the fray, and the strength of my two arms, O mighty-armed one.
The honest foe is to be fought by open battle, the wielder of illusion by battle of illusion—such is the settled rule of dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I would slay, O mighty-armed one, the army of the Pāṇḍavas day by day, setting myself a forenoon's portion each day.
Ten thousand warriors, O greatly resplendent one, set as my portion, and one thousand chariot-fighters besides—this is the share I reckon mine.
By this measure, armed and ever ready, I would destroy that great army in the span of such a time, O Bhārata.
But if, standing in the battle, I should loose the great weapons that slay by hundreds of thousands, I would make an end within a month, O Bhārata.
Saṃjaya said: Having heard those words of Bhīṣma, King Duryodhana then, O lord of kings, put his question to Droṇa, the best of the Āṅgirasas:
"O preceptor, in what time would you slay the soldiers of the son of Pāṇḍu?" To him Droṇa, as though with a smile, made answer:
"I am old, O best of the Kurus, slow now in breath and action; yet with the fire of my weapons I would burn up the army of the Pāṇḍavas,
in a month, even as Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu has said—such is my judgement. This is my utmost power, this my utmost strength."
Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat said: "In two months only." But Drauṇi pledged the destruction of the host in ten nights; and Karṇa, the knower of the great weapons, pledged it in five.
Hearing those words of the sūta's son, the son of her who flows to the sea laughed aloud a ringing laugh, and spoke these words.
"Only because you have never yet met Pārtha in battle—bearing arrow, sword, and bow, joined with Vāsudeva, charging forward upon his chariot, that unfaltering one—
do you presume so, O Rādheya. For that reason you may go on boasting like this as much as you please."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, the son of Kuntī, O best of the Bhāratas, summoned all his brothers aside in private and spoke these words.
"The spies of mine who move among the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son bring me this report, now that the night has passed:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Duryodhana, it is said, asked the son of the river, the man of mighty vows: 'In what span of time, O lord, could you slay the army of the Pāṇḍavas?'
'In a month,' he was told; and the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra heard from Droṇa too that he would do it in just that span of time.
Gautama named twice that time, so we have heard; but Droṇa's son, knower of the great weapons, vowed to do it in ten nights.
And Karṇa, knower of celestial weapons, being asked in the assembly of the Kurus, vowed to destroy the army in five days."
"Therefore I too wish to hear your word, Arjuna: in how great a span of time could you annihilate the foes in battle?"
Thus addressed by the king, Dhanaṃjaya, the thick-haired one, looked toward Vāsudeva and answered with these words.
"All these are great souls, accomplished in arms, varied in their fighting; without doubt, O great king, they could indeed slay your host.
Let the anguish of your mind depart; I speak to you in accordance with truth. With a single chariot, having Vāsudeva for my comrade, I could slay them—
yes, the three worlds together with their gods, with all that is moving and unmoving, all that has been, that is, and that shall be—and in the blink of an eye, such is my conviction.
That terrible and mighty weapon which the Lord of Beasts granted me in our single combat, when he wore the mountaineer's form—that very weapon abides in me.
That which the Lord of Beasts wields at the end of an age, O tiger among men, when he gathers in all beings—that very weapon abides in me.
That neither the son of Gaṅgā knows, nor Droṇa, nor Gautama, nor Droṇa's son, O king—and how then the son of the sūta?
But it is not right in battle to slay common men with celestial weapons; by fair fighting alone shall we conquer the foe.
And these tigers among men, your allies, O king, are all of them knowers of celestial weapons, all of them rejoicers in battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All these unconquered ones, bathed in the final ablution of the Veda's culmination, could destroy in battle even the army of the gods, O Pāṇḍava.
Śikhaṇḍin and Yuyudhāna, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the grandson of Pṛṣata, Bhīmasena and the twins both, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas—
and Virāṭa and Drupada both, equal in battle to Bhīṣma and Droṇa; and you yourself are able even to wipe out the three worlds.
The man upon whom you cast your gaze in anger, O you whose splendor equals Vāsava's, that man would swiftly cease to be—this is plain, and so I know you, O Kaurava."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, when the cloudless dawn had broken, the kings, urged on by Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son Duryodhana, set forth against the Pāṇḍavas.
All of them purified by bathing, garlanded, clad in white raiment, weapons taken up, standards raised, the blessing pronounced, the fires offered into;
all knowers of the Veda, all heroes, all of upright observances, all doers of the rites, and all bearing the marks of battle;
the mighty ones, seeking through battle to win the higher worlds, all of single-pointed mind, and full of faith in what lies beyond.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, the Kekayas together with the Bāhlīkas—all these set forth with the son of Bharadvāja at their head.
Aśvatthāman, the son of Śaṃtanu, then Jayadratha of the Sindhus, and the warriors who came from the south, from the west, and from the mountains—
Śakuni the king of Gāndhāra, and those from the east and the north on every side, the Śakas, the Kirātas, the Yavanas, the Śibis, and then the Vasātis—
all these great chariot-warriors, joined each with his own troops, surrounding the great chariot-hero, marched forth in the second division of the host.
Kṛtavarman with his troops, and the mighty Trigartas, and King Duryodhana surrounded by his brothers;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śala, Bhūriśravas, Śalya, and then Bṛhadbala of Kosala—these moved in the rear, with the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra at their head.
Having advanced along a level road, those great chariot-warriors, ready to give battle, took their stand armored in the western half of Kurukṣetra.
Duryodhana then had a camp made, O Bhārata, adorned to be like a second Hāstinapura.
Not even skilled city-dwelling men, O lord of kings, could tell the difference between the city and the camp.
Such strongholds, too, for the kings, the Kaurava lord of the earth had built by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Leaving clear a circle of five yojanas for the field of battle, the army's encampments, O king, filled it in their hundreds of companies.
There those guardians of the earth, according to their zeal and according to their strength, swiftly entered camps well stocked with goods, by the thousands.
For those great-souled ones, together with their armies and their attendants, King Duryodhana ordained provisions of food and drink beyond compare.
For the elephants, the horses, and the men, and those who lived by their crafts, and the others who had come along there—the bards, the heralds, and the panegyrists—
the merchants, the courtesans, the harlots, and the people who came merely to watch—all these the Kaurava king looked after duly.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: In just the same way the king, the son of Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma, urged on the heroes led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O Bhārata.
He appointed Dhṛṣṭaketu—leader of the Cedis, the Kāśis, and the Karūṣas, firm in valor, slayer of foes—as commander of the host.
Virāṭa and Drupada, and Yuyudhāna and Śikhaṇḍin, and the two great archers of Pāñcāla, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas—
those heroes of brilliant armor, wearing burnished earrings, blazing like fires fed with ghee upon their altars—those great archers shone like flaming planets.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then that bull among men, that guardian of the earth, having honored the army each according to his due, commanded those troops to march.
Abhimanyu and Bṛhanta, and the sons of Draupadī all together, these led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the joy of Pāṇḍu sent forward.
Bhīma and Yuyudhāna and the Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya—these Yudhiṣṭhira dispatched as the second wing of the army.
Of the warriors there loading the baggage, moving about and rushing to and fro, gladdened, the clamor seemed to touch the very heavens.
Then the lord of the earth himself, accompanied by Virāṭa and Drupada and the other guardians of the earth, marched in the rear.
That army, moving with its dreadful bows, with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at its head, appeared like the Gaṅgā in full flood, calm yet ever flowing on.
Then once more the wise one redeployed his divisions, baffling thereby the draining away of the wits of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons.
The sons of Draupadī, those great archers, and Abhimanyu, and Nakula and Sahadeva, and all the Prabhadrakas, the Pāṇḍava arrayed—
and ten thousand horses, and two thousand elephants, and ten thousand foot-soldiers, and five hundred chariots likewise.
And the unassailable Bhīmasena he assigned to the first force; in the center, Virāṭa, and Jayatsena the Māgadha;
and the two great chariot-warriors of Pāñcāla, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, valorous, great-souled, bearing mace and bow—and then in the center followed Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya.
The men grew fiercely impassioned, their blows made ready; their banners, twenty thousand strong, were manned by heroes.
Five thousand elephants, and chariot-lines on every side, and the heroic foot-soldiers bearing bow, sword, and mace, followed by the thousands behind and by the thousands in front.
Where in that ocean of force Yudhiṣṭhira himself was stationed, there for the most part those guardians of the earth took up their places.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There were thousands of elephants and tens of thousands of horses, and thousands of chariots and of foot-soldiers, O Bhārata, relying upon which he went to do battle with Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then others, by the hundreds behind, men by the thousands and tens of thousands, roaring as they went, marched on—their divisions numbering in the thousands.
There thousands of kettledrums and tens of thousands of conches were sounded by the men in their thousands and tens of thousands, exultant.
Janamejaya said: How did they wage war, those heroes — the Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Somakas — and the high-fortuned kings gathered from many lands?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: How those heroes — the Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Somakas — waged war upon Kurukṣetra, that field of austerities, hear it now, O lord of the earth.
Descending upon Kurukṣetra, the Pāṇḍavas together with the Somakas, mighty in strength and eager for victory, advanced against the Kauravas.
All of them accomplished in Vedic study, all rejoicing in battle, they hoped for victory in the war, or else for death facing the foe in combat.
Having advanced against the unassailable army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, they encamped with their troops on the western side, their faces turned eastward.
Outside Samantapañcaka, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Kuntī had encampments by the thousands raised according to due rule.
The whole earth seemed emptied, with only the young and the aged left behind; it was bereft of horses and of men, stripped of chariots and elephants.
As far as the sun shines upon the circle of Jambūdvīpa, over all that expanse was the host assembled, O best of kings.
Gathered in one place, men of every class, they overspread a circle many leagues across, covering regions, rivers, mountains, and forests.
To all of them, O bull among men, King Yudhiṣṭhira appointed, for them and their mounts, food and provisions of the finest kind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Yudhiṣṭhira devised for them watchwords of various kinds: 'He who gives this sign is to be known as one of the Pāṇḍavas.'
The Kaurava prince assigned to all of them tokens of recognition, signs, and emblems, now that the hour of battle had arrived.
Beholding the crests of the Pārthas' banners, the high-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with all the rulers of the earth, drew up his ranks against the Pāṇḍavas.
With a white parasol held above his head, surrounded by his brothers in the midst of a thousand elephants —
beholding Duryodhana so arrayed, all the Pāṇḍava warriors, exultant, blew their great conches and beat their war-drums by the thousands.
Then the Pāṇḍavas, looking upon their own exultant army, grew glad of heart, and so too did the valiant Vāsudeva.
Then, gladdening their warriors, Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya, those two tigers among men, standing upon their chariot, blew their divine conches.
Hearing the blast of both the Pāñcajanya and the Devadatta, the warriors together with their mounts let flow their dung and urine.
As other beasts tremble at hearing the roar of a lion, even so was Dhṛtarāṣṭra's host stricken with fear in that hour.
A cloud of earthly dust arose, so that nothing could be discerned; and the sun was hidden, veiled by the dust raised by the army.
And there the cloud rained down a shower of flesh and blood, drenching all the ranks — a portent strange to behold.
Then a low wind arose, driving gravel before it, buffeting those ranks and scattering that dust about.
Both armies then, O king, exceedingly eager for battle, stood arrayed upon Kurukṣetra like two storm-tossed oceans.
And the meeting of those two armies was a wondrous thing, like the clash of two oceans when the end of an age is come.
The whole earth was emptied, with only the young and the aged left behind, by reason of that vast host gathered together by the Kauravas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Somakas made a covenant, and they established the rules of warfare, O bull of the Bhāratas.
'When our war has ceased, let there be goodwill between us once more, as before and as is fitting, and let there be no further treachery.'
'When the fighting between us is waged with words, the answering also shall be only with words; one who has withdrawn from the midst of the host is on no account to be slain.'
'A chariot-warrior is to be fought by a chariot-warrior, one mounted on an elephant by an elephant, a horseman by a horseman, and a foot-soldier only by a foot-soldier, O Bhārata.'
'According to fitness, prowess, ardor, and age, one shall strike only after first giving challenge — never one who trusts unguarded, never one who is in distress.'
'One engaged with another, one off his guard, one turned away, one whose weapons are spent, one without armor — none of these is on any account to be slain.'
'Not against charioteers, not against draft-animals, not against those who carry weapons to the warriors, nor against those who sound the drums and conches, shall a blow ever be struck.'
Having made this covenant, the Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Somakas fell into utter wonder as they gazed upon one another.
And having taken up their stations, those great-souled bulls among men became, with all their troops, of joyful aspect and of good cheer.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, observing the twilights of dawn and dusk, the holy sage, foremost of all the knowers of the Vedas, Vyāsa the son of Satyavatī —
the holy grandsire of the Bhāratas, who saw with his own eyes what should come to pass in the dreadful war, knower of past, present, and future —
to King Vaicitravīrya, grieving, afflicted, brooding then upon the folly of his sons, he spoke this in secret.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vyāsa said: O king, your sons and the other rulers of the earth have run out their allotted time; meeting one another in battle, they will slay each other.
As they, whose time is spent, go to their ruin, O Bhārata, understand the turning of time, and do not set your mind to grief.
Yet if you wish to behold this battle, O lord of the people, then look — I grant you sight; witness this war.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: I have no wish to look upon the slaughter of my kinsmen, O best of brahmin sages; yet by your power may I hear this war in its entirety.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When he wished not to see the battle but desired to hear of it, the lord and bestower of boons granted a boon to Saṃjaya.
Vyāsa said: This Saṃjaya of yours, O king, shall tell you of this war; nothing in the battle shall be hidden from his sight.
Endowed with a divine eye, O king, this Saṃjaya will recount the war to you, and he shall become all-knowing.
Whether open or secret, whether by night or by day, even what is conceived in the mind — all of it Saṃjaya will know.
Weapons shall not pierce him, nor shall weariness afflict him; this son of Gavalgaṇa shall come forth alive from this war.
And I shall spread abroad the fame of these Kurus, O bull of the Bhāratas, and of all the Pāṇḍavas; grieve not.
This was ordained of old; here you have no cause to grieve, nor can it be held back: where there is righteousness, there is victory.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the holy great-grandsire of the Kurus addressed the mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra once again.
In this war, O great king, there shall be a vast destruction, even as I now mark these omens that portend terror.
Hawks and vultures, crows and herons, gathered together with the armies, swoop down at the forest's edge and form their flocks.
And the birds, rejoicing, foresee a most terrible battle; the flesh-eaters shall devour the flesh of elephants and horses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Shrieking 'khaṭā, khaṭā' in dread, harbingers of fear, the cranes pass through the midst of the sky toward the southern quarter.
At both twilights, of dawn and of dusk, I behold without fail, O Bhārata, the sun at its rising and its setting ringed about with headless trunks.
Bordered with white and red, dark-necked, and charged with lightning, three-colored bars of cloud screen the sun at twilight.
A day and a night I have beheld in which sun, moon, and stars all blazed alike, with no distinction between day and dark: this shall be for destruction.
On the full-moon night of Kārttika the moon was unseen, robbed of its radiance, the color of fire against a sky of one same hue.
Heroes shall sleep slain, kings covering the earth, sovereigns and princes, brave men whose arms are like iron bars.
In the sky, by night, I mark without ceasing the fierce clamor of a boar and a cat warring together.
The images of the gods, too, tremble and laugh, vomit blood from their mouths, sweat, and fall down.
War-drums sound though none has struck them, O lord of the people, and the great chariots of the warriors roll forth though none has yoked them.
Cuckoos and woodpeckers, blue jays and vultures, parrots, cranes, and peacocks utter dreadful cries.
At the reddening of dawn there appear by the hundreds swarms of locusts, as it were warriors bearing weapons and ornaments, armored and mounted upon horses' backs.
Both twilights blaze forth, attended by a burning of the quarters of the sky; and there fell a rain of blood and a rain of bones, O Bhārata.
And she who is renowned throughout the three worlds, esteemed by the virtuous, Arundhatī — even by her has Vasiṣṭha been set behind.
Yonder stands Śanaiścara, O king, afflicting Rohiṇī; the mark upon the moon is turned awry: a great terror shall come to pass.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And from a cloudless sky a most dreadful thundering is heard without cease, and from the weeping draft-animals teardrops fall.
Vyāsa said: Asses are born of cows, and sons take pleasure with their mothers; the trees in the forest put forth flower and fruit out of their season.
Princesses heavy with child bring forth monstrous things — flesh-eating creatures and birds, jackals and beasts of other kinds.
Ill-omened beasts are born, three-horned, four-eyed, five-footed, with two organs, two heads, two tails, and fanged.
They are born with gaping mouths, uttering inauspicious cries — three-footed, crested, eagle-like, four-fanged, and horned.
And likewise are seen other women, even those of the reciters of the Veda, bringing forth eagles and peacocks within your city.
A mare gives birth to a calf, O lord of the earth, and a bitch to a jackal; partridges, mynahs, and parrots cry out words of ill omen.
Some women bring forth four or five daughters at a birth, and these, the very moment they are born, dance and sing and laugh.
The little ones of common folk, still at the breast, dance and sing aloud within the houses of thieves, foretelling a great terror.
Others, driven by fate, scrawl figures of armed men; and infants, cudgels in hand, rush at one another, and, eager to fight, fashion mock cities and lay siege to them.
Lotuses, blue lilies, and water-lilies spring up upon the trees; fierce winds blow from every side, and the dust never settles.
Again and again the earth quakes, and Rāhu has seized the sun; and a white planet, passing beyond Citrā, stands fixed.
Most especially does it foretell the undoing of the Kurus, this comet of dreadful aspect, that has mounted Puṣya and there stands still.
A great planet shall work fearful ill upon both armies: Aṅgāraka stands retrograde in Maghā, and Bṛhaspati in Śravaṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Encroaching upon the lunar mansion Bhāgya, Śukra is afflicted by the son of Sūrya; having mounted into the eastern Proṣṭhapada, O lord of peoples, and then circled round into the northern, he stands waiting in conjunction.
A dark planet, blazing, wreathed in smoke and fire, has encroached upon the brilliant mansion of Indra, Jyeṣṭhā, and there it stands.
The Pole Star, blazing dreadfully, turns from right to left; and a harsh planet has taken its station between Citrā and Svāti.
Moving in retrograde and counter-retrograde course, bright as fire upon Śravaṇa, the Red-bodied one (Mars) has overspread the constellation of Brahmā and there abides.
The earth, mantled with every kind of grain and garlanded with fruit, brings forth barley with five heads and rice with a hundred heads.
The cows, foremost of all the world, upon whom this whole creation depends — they, giving milk to their calves, ooze blood instead.
Swords, fiercely ablaze, leap forth from their scabbards; plainly the weapons foresee the battle now at hand.
The radiance of the weapons and of the waters is as the color of fire; there shall be a great destruction of armor and of banners.
Toward the quarters of the sky, beasts and birds with flaming mouths cry out, foretelling calamity and announcing a great terror.
A bird with but one wing, one eye, and one foot, ranging the sky by night, cries out fiercely in its rage, spewing forth blood again and again.
Two planets, copper-red of crest and seeming to blaze, stand there, having veiled over the splendor of the noble Seven Seers.
And both planets, abiding for a full year and both ablaze — Bṛhaspati and Śanaiścara (Jupiter and Saturn) — stand close beside the two stars of Viśākhā.
In Kṛttikā, the first of mansions, a fierce planet, blazing and stealing away forms with its glare, stands like a smoking comet.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Through all three of the earlier mansions, O lord of peoples, Budha (Mercury) repeatedly speeds, engendering exceedingly great fear.
A fourteenth-day moon, a fifteenth-day moon, and once even a sixteenth I have known; but this new moon falling on a thirteenth day I have never known before.
Both moon and sun eclipsed within a single month, on the thirteenth day and out of their proper season — these two seizures shall bring the peoples to ruin.
All the quarters are wrapped in dust, with showers of grit on every side; and dreadful portent-clouds rain down blood in the night.
Again, on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, at midnight, there came a fierce and most terrible rain of flesh, whereat the rākṣasas glutted themselves unsated.
The rivers flowed backward against their stream, their waters turned to blood; the wells, foaming over, bellow like bulls; and meteors fall amid thunderclaps, mingled with dry lightning-bolts.
And this very day, when the night had passed, at sunrise the sun was struck on every side by four great blazing meteors.
And the great seers, as they paid worship to the Sun, declared therein: the earth shall drink the blood of thousands of kings.
From Kailāsa and Mandara, and from the mountain Himavat as well, peaks crash down by the thousand with a mighty roar.
In the quaking of the earth the great elemental beings make each of the four oceans, severally, heave up their shores, churning them again and again.
Fierce winds blow, uprooting trees and dragging gravel along; and the sacred shrine-trees topple down in villages and in cities.
The fire, when offered into by the brāhmaṇas, blazes up yellow, red, and blue, its flame veering leftward, smelling of corpses, thick with smoke and harsh of sound; and touch, smell, and taste are all turned awry, O lord of the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The banners of the kings smoke and quiver again and again, and shed showers of live coals; and so too do the kettledrums and the war-drums.
Upon the tops of palace-spires and at the city gates fierce vultures wheel and settle, taking up a circling course to the left.
And the birds cry out shrilly, again and again, "Cooked! cooked!" and roost upon the banner-tips, portending the destruction of the rulers of the earth.
Brooding and shaking out their tails, trembling all over, the horses and the elephants, piteous, weep by the thousand.
Having heard all this, let your lordship resolve upon what the hour demands, so that this world may not go to utter ruin, O Bhārata.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard these words of his father, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke thus: This, I think, was ordained long ago; it shall come to pass, there is no doubt.
If kṣatriyas are slain in battle according to the law of kṣatriyas, then, attaining the world of heroes, they shall win nothing but bliss.
These tigers among men, having yielded up their lives in the great battle, shall win renown here and, in the world beyond, great happiness for a long age.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by his son Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the sage, lord of poets, O best of kings, knowing the truth of things, sank into deep meditation.
Then once more the great ascetic, the proclaimer of Time, spoke these words: Without doubt, O lord of kings, it is Time that draws the world together to its end.
And again Time brings forth the worlds; nothing here is everlasting — neither of your kinsmen, nor of the Kurus, nor of your allies and friends.
Point out the righteous path, for you are able to hold them back; men call the slaughter of one's own kin a base thing — do not do what is hateful to me.
This is Time, born in the shape of your son, O lord of peoples. In the Veda no slaughter is honored; this is in no wise a good.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who would slay his own kindred slays the law of his line and his very own body. By the power of Time you are about to stray from the path, though, while it is yet possible, you might keep to the road.
For the destruction of this house, and likewise of the rulers of the earth, this calamity has come in the guise of kingship — let it be cast off, this bringer of misery.
By another your wisdom has been undone; show your sons the path of dharma. What use to you, O unassailable one, is a kingdom by which you have come to sin?
Guarding your honor, your dharma, and your renown, you shall win heaven. Let the Pāṇḍavas have the kingdom, and let the Kauravas come to peace.
As the foremost of brāhmaṇas spoke thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Ambikā, skilled in speech, broke in upon his words and went again into the way of discourse.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Even as your lordship knows, so do I know; being and non-being are known to me as they truly are. Yet in its own concerns, dear sir, the world is bewildered — and know me too to be of one nature with the world.
I beseech you of matchless might: you are our refuge and our steadfast guide. But these of mine are not in my power, O great seer; you ought not to burden me here with the guilt.
For you are dharma itself, and purity, honor, renown, constancy, and memory; and you are the venerable grandsire of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas alike.
Vyāsa said: O king, son of Vicitravīrya, whatever stirs within your mind, speak it freely as you will; I shall cut away your doubt.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Those signs which appear in battle for them that shall be victorious — all of these, O blessed one, I wish to hear of truly.
Vyāsa said: When the fire is clear of radiance, its beams rising upward, its flame whirling to the right and free of smoke, and holy fragrances waft from the oblations — this, they say, is the very mark of coming victory.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Where conches and drums, deep-voiced and loud-sounding, resound, and the sun and the moon shine with rays unsullied — this, they say, is the very mark of coming victory.
Auspicious are the cries of crows behind those who have set out and those about to go, O king: those behind urge them onward, while those in front would hold them back.
Where birds of fair-sounding voice — royal swans, parrots, herons, and woodpeckers — wheel to the right in the battle, there the brāhmaṇas declare victory is certain.
They whose host is radiant and hard to look upon for its splendor — with ornaments, armor, and standards, and with the golden-hued, serene faces of its men — they conquer their foes.
Where the voices and the spirit of the warriors are glad, O Bhārata, and their garlands do not wither, they overcome their enemies in battle.
A favorable wind from the south, for one who has entered or is about to enter the field, accomplishes his purpose when at his back, but thwarts it when in his face.
They for whom sound, form, taste, touch, and smell show themselves auspicious, and whose warriors are ever glad — for them victory is sure.
The winds blow in their favor, and so the clouds and the birds, and the storm-clouds float along behind them, and so too do the rainbows.
These, O lord of peoples, are the marks of them that are winning; for them that are about to die they are reversed, O ruler of men.
Whether the army be small or great, this is held for certain: the gladness of the host of warriors is, by itself, called a mark of victory.
A single man, broken in spirit, breaks even a very great army; and after that one broken man even the bravest warriors give way in turn.
And a great host once shattered is most hard to check, like the mighty rush of waters, like a herd of deer struck with panic.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the clash of battle a great host, once broken, can in no way be set in order again; at the mere word "broken!" even the bravest warriors are broken, and at the sight of men frightened and routed the terror swells the more.
A great host suddenly shattered, O king, and driven scattering to the quarters by the foe, cannot be made to stand fast, not even by brave men.
Having gathered a great army of the four arms, let the wise king, ever vigilant, strive by means of good policy first of all.
Victory by stratagem they call the best, by sowing discord the middling; lowest is that victory which is won by battle, O lord of peoples. The pitched clash is a great evil, and therefore it is called the maimed kind of conquest.
Brave men who know one another well, full of spirit, resolute and steadfast — even fifty such churn up a mighty host; or even five, six, or seven, who will not turn back, win the day.
Garuḍa, son of Vinatā, does not esteem a great multitude, O Bhārata, even on beholding a vast gathering of fine-feathered birds.
Victory does not come by the mere multitude of an army, O Bhārata; victory, indeed, is a thing uncertain, and fate is here the final refuge; for even those who win in battle suffer their own losses.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vyāsa departed; and Dhṛtarāṣṭra too, having heard it, sank into meditation.
Having brooded for the space of a moment, and sighing again and again, he questioned Saṃjaya of disciplined soul, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Saṃjaya, these rulers of the earth, heroes who delight in battle, strike one another down with weapons high and low.
The kings, having flung away their very lives for the earth's sake, do not cease from the slaughter, swelling the realm of Yama.
Coveting earthly sovereignty, they cannot endure one another. The earth, I think, must hold many a virtue; tell me of it, Saṃjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Many thousands, many myriads, hundreds of millions, and tens of millions of the world's heroes are gathered together in Kurujāṅgala.
And the measure of the lands and of the cities from which these have come together, Saṃjaya, I wish to hear of truly.
You are endowed with the lamp of divine understanding and with the eye of knowledge, by the grace of that brāhmaṇa-seer Vyāsa of measureless splendor.
Saṃjaya said: As far as my understanding reaches, O greatly wise one, I shall tell you of the earth's qualities; look on them with the eye of the scriptures. Homage to you, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Beings here are of two kinds: the moving and the unmoving. Of the moving, the womb is threefold — those born of eggs, of sweat, and of the womb-membrane.
Of all moving beings, O king, the womb-born are the foremost; and of the womb-born, the highest are humankind and the beasts that there are.
Bearing manifold forms, of these there are fourteen divisions: seven that dwell in the wilderness and seven of them that dwell in villages.
Lions, tigers, and boars, buffaloes and elephants, and bears, and monkeys too—these seven, O king, are reckoned the creatures of the wild.
The cow, the goat, man, the ram, the horse, the mule, and the ass—these seven are declared by the good to be the domestic animals.
These, O king, are the fourteen animals, tame and wild, named in the Vedas, O guardian of the earth, upon which the sacrifices are established.
Among the domestic kinds man is foremost, and the lion among the dwellers of the wild; yet of all beings alike the living is by one upon another.
The immovable beings are said to be those that spring from the soil, and of them there are five kinds: trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing vines, the pithless-barked plants, and the grasses.
These come to nineteen, lacking one; with the five great elements they are reckoned twenty-four—the Gāyatrī, honored by the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who truly knows this holy Gāyatrī, endowed with every quality, O best of the Bhāratas, does not perish from the worlds.
For upon the earth is everything born, and upon the earth does everything perish; the earth is the foundation of beings, the earth indeed is their last resort.
His who holds the earth is the whole world, all that moves and stands still; greedy for it, kings slay one another.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: The names of the rivers and of the mountains, Saṃjaya, and of the peoples too, and of others that dwell upon the earth—
and the measure of the earth as well, O knower of measures, in its entirety—relate it all to me fully, Saṃjaya, and the forests too.
Saṃjaya said: These five great elements, O great king, in sum, the wise declare to be equal, by which all things in the world subsist.
Earth, water, and wind, fire, and ether as well—each surpassing the next in qualities; and among them earth is chief.
Sound, and touch, and form, and taste, and odor for the fifth—these are declared the qualities of earth by the seers who know the truth.
Four qualities are in water, O king—odor is not found therein; sound, and touch, and form; then fire has three qualities; sound and touch belong to wind; and in ether sound alone.
These five qualities, O king, abide in the five great elements throughout all the worlds, upon which the worlds are established.
They do not encroach upon one another when balance prevails; but when they fall into disproportion among themselves, then the embodied rise up clothed in bodies—not otherwise.
In due succession they perish, and in due succession are born—all of them beyond measure; such is their lordly form.
Here and there are seen the constituents born of the five elements; of these men by reasoning set forth the measures.
Those states that are beyond thought one should not establish by reasoning; and that which lies beyond the primal natures is the mark of the unthinkable.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I shall declare to you the continent Sudarśana, O delight of the Kurus; circular it is, O great king, that continent, shaped like a wheel.
Covered over with river-waters and with mountains like clouds, with cities of varied form and with pleasant peopled lands,
with trees laden with flower and fruit, abounding in wealth and grain, and girt about on every side by the salt sea.
And as a man might behold his own face in a mirror, so does the continent Sudarśana appear in the orb of the moon.
In two of its parts is the holy fig tree, and in two parts the great hare, with the sowing of all healing herbs swelling it on every side; and beyond that the waters are to be known—this is told in brief.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: The continent has been told in brief; now tell its extent, Saṃjaya. As far as this expanse of earth appears within the figure marked by the hare, declare its measure, and then you shall speak of the fig tree.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the king, Saṃjaya spoke these words: Stretching eastward, O great king, are these six jeweled mountains, plunging on both sides into the eastern and the western seas.
Himavān and Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha the foremost of mountains, and Nīla made of lapis, and Śveta with the gleam of silver, and the mountain named Śṛṅgavān, bound about with every metal.
These mountains, O king, are frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas; the span between them is many thousands of yojanas.
There are the holy peopled lands, those regions, O Bhārata; in them dwell living creatures of every kind and all manner of births.
This here is the region Bhārata; beyond it is Haimavata; and beyond Hemakūṭa they declare the region Harivarṣa.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha stretches eastward, O great king, the mountain named Mālyavān.
Beyond Mālyavān is the mountain Gandhamādana, and circular between the two stands Meru, the golden mountain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With the radiance of the morning sun, like fire without smoke, it descends, it is said, sixteen thousand yojanas below.
And high it rises eighty-four thousand yojanas, O lord of the earth, standing above, within, and athwart, embracing the worlds.
At its sides these four continents are set, O lord: Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla, and Jambūdvīpa, O Bhārata, and the Northern Kurus, the refuge of those who have earned merit.
There the bird Sumukha, the son of Suparṇa it is said, fell to pondering when he beheld the crows turned golden:
"Since Meru makes no distinction among birds—the highest, the middling, and the lowest—therefore I shall forsake it."
Around it the sun, the lord of lights, ceaselessly circles, and the moon with its constellations, and the wind, keeping it ever on their right.
