That mountain, O great king, is endowed with heavenly flowers and fruits, encompassed all about with fair mansions wrought of jāmbūnada gold.
There the hosts of gods, O king, the Gandharvas, Asuras, and Rākṣasas, together with throngs of Apsarases, sport upon that mountain everlastingly.
There Brahmā and Rudra and Śakra, the lord of the gods, assemble and worship with manifold sacrifices of abundant gifts.
Tumburu and Nārada, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū, those foremost of immortals, draw near and praise them with hymns, O lord.
The seven great-souled seers, and Kaśyapa the lord of creatures, go there—good fortune be yours—ever at each holy juncture of the moon.
Upon its very summit dwells Uśanas, son of Kavi, with the Daityas, O lord of the earth; his are these jewels, his these jeweled mountains.
From him the lord Kubera enjoys a fourth part, and of that he gives a fraction of the wealth to men.
On its northern side is a heavenly grove of karṇikāra trees, blossoming in every season, auspicious and lovely, springing up amid a lattice of rocks.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There Paśupati himself, surrounded by his heavenly attendant spirits, the lord, the source of beings, sports with Umā at his side.
He wears a garland of karṇikāra flowers hanging down to his feet, alight with his three eyes as with three risen suns.
Him the Siddhas of fierce austerity, firm in their vows and speaking truth, behold; for by the ill-conducted Maheśvara cannot be seen.
From the summit of that mountain, O lord of men, a stream like milk, broad enough to be spanned by thirty arm-lengths, with a voice like a terrible thunderbolt,
holy, frequented by the holiest, the fair Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī falls with unceasing rush into the fair lake of the moon; and by her was made that holy lake, vast as the ocean.
Her, unbearable even to the mountains, Maheśvara of old bore upon his head for a hundred thousand years.
On the western side of Meru is Ketumāla, O lord of the earth, and there too the great Jambū grove, like the garden Nandana.
The span of life there is ten thousand years, O Bhārata, and the men are golden-hued, and the women like Apsarases.
Free from sickness, freed from grief, ever glad of heart are the men born there, with the gleam of refined gold.
On the peaks of Gandhamādana, Kubera with the Rākṣasas, surrounded by throngs of Apsarases, rejoices, the lord of the Guhyakas.
At the farther foothills of Gandhamādana, the outlying tracts beyond, the utmost span of life is eleven thousand years.
There the men are dark, O king, full of vigor and mighty in strength, and the women all are hued like lotus-petals, fair to look upon.
Beyond Nīla is Śveta, and beyond Śveta the Hairaṇyaka land; the region named Airāvata is beyond that, past Śṛṅgavān.
Bow-shaped, O great king, are the two regions, southern and northern; and Ilāvṛta is the middle one—so there are five regions in all.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Each farther region beyond these surpasses in excellences: in length of life and health, in righteousness, in pleasure, and in wealth,
endowed are the beings in those regions, O Bhārata. Thus, O great king, is this earth heaped about with mountains.
And Hemakūṭa, vast indeed, is the mountain named Kailāsa, where King Vaiśravaṇa rejoices together with the Guhyakas.
To the north of Kailāsa, near the mountain Maināka, stands the great heavenly mountain Hiraṇyaśṛṅga, made of jewels.
At its side is the great, heavenly, fair lake of golden sands, the lovely lake named Bindusaras, where King Bhagīratha, beholding the Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī, dwelt for many years.
There are sacrificial posts of jewels and altars too of gold; and having sacrificed there, the thousand-eyed one of great renown attained perfection.
There the eternal lord of beings, of keen splendor, having created all the worlds, is worshipped, surrounded by the assembled spirits—Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Manu, and Sthāṇu for the fifth.
There the goddess of the threefold path first took her stand; descending from the world of Brahmā, she divides into seven streams:
Vasvokasārā, Nalinī, and Pāvanā, and Sarasvatī, and Jambūnadī, and Sītā, and Gaṅgā, and Sindhu for the seventh.
Unthinkable, of heavenly resolve—such is the ordinance of the Lord—where they perform the sacrificial session at the close of a thousand ages.
And here and there Sarasvatī becomes now seen, now unseen; these are the seven heavenly Gaṅgās, famed throughout the three worlds.
On Himavān dwell the Rākṣasas, on Hemakūṭa the Guhyakas, serpents and Nāgas on Niṣadha, and on Gokarṇa those rich in austerity.
The Śveta mountain is called the home of gods and Asuras; the Gandharvas on the Niṣadha mountain, the brahmā-seers on Nīla, O king; and Śṛṅgavān, O great king, is the haunt of the fathers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus, O great king, these are the seven regions, portion by portion, wherein the beings have settled, both the moving and the fixed.
Their prosperity, manifold, is seen to be both divine and human, impossible to reckon up, yet to be believed by one who would prosper.
As for this heavenly hare-shape about which you ask me, O king—at the hare's sides are two regions, both south and north, and its two ears are Nāgadvīpa and Kaśyapadvīpa.
Its head is copper-hued, O king—the splendid Malaya mountain; this is seen as the second part of the continent, set in the form of a hare.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Now describe to me, Saṃjaya, the northern and the eastern side of Meru, in full, O great of mind, and the mountain Mālyavān.
Saṃjaya said: To the south of Nīla and on the northern side of Meru, O king, are the holy Northern Kurus, frequented by the Siddhas.
There the trees bear honeyed fruit and are ever laden with blossom and fruit; their flowers are sweetly fragrant and their fruits are full of juice.
Some trees there yield the fruit of every desire, O lord of men; and others there, O ruler of men, are the trees called the milk-bearers.
These ever pour forth milk endowed with the six flavors and like to nectar; and within their fruits are brought forth garments and ornaments as well.
The whole earth there is made of jewels, with fine golden sand; everywhere it is pleasant to the touch and free of mire, O lord of men.
All the men born there have fallen from the world of the gods, endowed with equal beauty and equal virtues, in fair times and foul alike.
They are born as couples, and the women are like the apsarases; and they drink the milk of those milk-bearing trees, milk that is like nectar.
Each couple, being born together, grows up as equals, alike in beauty and virtue and likewise alike in garb; and each is devoted to the other, even as the cakravāka pair, O mighty one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Free of sickness and bereft of sorrow, their minds ever joyful, they live, O great king, for ten thousand years and ten hundred years besides, and they never forsake one another.
There are birds named bhāruṇḍas, sharp-beaked and of great strength; these carry off the dead and cast them into mountain caverns.
The Northern Kurus, O king, have thus been described to you in brief; now I shall tell of the eastern flank of Meru in due order.
Its eastern domain is Bhadrāśva, O lord of peoples, where lies the forest of Bhadraśāla and the great tree called Kālāmra.
And the Kālāmra, O great king, is fair and ever laden with blossom and fruit, a tree a yojana in height, frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas.
The men there are fair, possessed of splendor and great strength; and the women are of the hue of the white lotus, lovely and pleasing to behold.
Bright as the moon, moon-hued, their faces like the full moon, their limbs cool as the moon, skilled in dance and song.
Their lifespan there is ten thousand years, O bull of the Bhāratas; nourished on the juice of the Kālāmra, they remain forever in their youth.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha stands the great and everlasting Jambū tree named Sudarśana.
Yielding the fruit of every desire, holy, frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas; from its name the eternal Jambūdvīpa is so called.
A thousand and a hundred yojanas, O bull of the Bhāratas, is the height of that king of trees, touching the heavens, O lord of men.
A thousand cubits, and fifteen hundred more, is the girth of that tree, whose fruits are of varied juices.
Falling upon the earth, those fruits make a mighty sound, and they release, O king, a juice that resembles silver.
The fruit-juice of that Jambū, becoming a river, O lord of men, circles Meru in reverence and flows on to the Northern Kurus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The people there drink that juice with delight forever, O lord of men; and when that fruit-juice is drunk, old age does not afflict them.
There is the gold called Jāmbūnada, the adornment of the gods; and the men born there are of the hue of the youthful sun.
Likewise upon the peak of Mālyavān there blazes the bearer of oblations, the fire of time named Saṃvartaka, O bull of the Bhāratas.
And on the eastern peak of Mālyavān lies the eastern boundary-rock; Mālyavān stands fifty thousand yojanas in extent.
The men born there shine like fine silver; all have fallen from the world of Brahmā, and all are expounders of the sacred word.
Performing austerities, they become men of upward-flowing seed; and for the protection of all beings they enter into the sun.
Sixty thousand of them, and sixty hundred besides, go before Aruṇa, surrounding the maker of day.
For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years besides, scorched by the heat of the sun, they enter at last the orb of the moon.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: The names of the regions and of the mountains, O Saṃjaya, tell me truly, and who dwell upon the mountains.
Saṃjaya said: To the south of Śveta and to the north of Nīla is the region named Ramaṇaka, and there men are born.
Endowed with pure lineage, all most fair to look upon, and given over to delight, are the men born there.
For ten thousand years and fifteen hundred years besides they live, O great king, their minds ever joyful.
To the south of Śṛṅgavān and to the north of Śveta is the region named Hairaṇvata, where flows the river Hairaṇvatī.
Followers of the yakṣas, O great king, wealthy and fair to behold, of great strength they ever are there, O king, with joyful minds.
Eleven thousand years, O lord of men, is the measure of their life, and fifteen hundred years besides they live.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The peaks of Śṛṅgavān are three, O lord of men: one there is made of jewels, and one is wondrously of gold.
And one is made of every gem, adorned with mansions; there dwells forever the self-luminous goddess Śāṇḍilī.
To the north of Śṛṅgavān, at the shore of the sea, O lord of men, is the region named Airāvata, beyond that very Śṛṅgavān.
There the sun does not scorch, nor do those men grow old; and the moon with its constellations is veiled, as though become a single radiance.
Lustrous as the lotus, lotus-hued, their eyes like lotus-petals, and fragrant as lotus-leaves are the men born there.
Unmoving, sweet of fragrance, taking no food, masters of their senses, all are fallen from the world of the gods and free of passion, O king.
Thirteen thousand years, O lord of men, is the measure of life that those men live, O best of the Bhāratas.
And to the north of the ocean of milk the lord Hari, Vaikuṇṭha, dwells upon a chariot wrought of gold.
That vehicle is eight-wheeled, yoked with elemental beings, swift as thought, fire-hued, of great speed, adorned with Jāmbūnada gold.
He is the lord of all beings and the all-pervading, O bull of the Bhāratas; he is contraction and expansion, the doer and the cause of doing.
Earth, water, and space, wind and fire, O king—he is the sacrifice of all beings, and the devourer of oblations is his mouth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Saṃjaya, the great-minded king Dhṛtarāṣṭra fell to brooding upon his sons, O lord of men.
Having pondered, O great king, he spoke again these words: Without doubt, O son of a sūta, Time draws in the world and creates all anew; nothing here abides forever.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the all-knowing, the sustainer of all beings—him the gods call Vaikuṇṭha, and the Vedas call that lord Viṣṇu.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: This land of Bhārata, where this host has gathered in its frenzy, where this son of mine, Duryodhana, is greedy beyond all measure—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Where the sons of Pāṇḍu too are covetous, and where my mind clings fast—of this tell me the truth, for you are skilled, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: The Pāṇḍavas are not covetous of it—hear my words, O king; covetous of it are Duryodhana and also Śakuni, the son of Subala.
And other kṣatriyas besides, lords of many lands, who are covetous of the land of Bhārata and cannot endure one another.
Here I shall describe to you, O Bhārata, the land of Bhārata, dear to the god Indra and to Manu, son of Vivasvat,
and to Pṛthu, son of Vena, O king, and to the great-souled Ikṣvāku, to Yayāti and Ambarīṣa, to Māndhātṛ and Nahuṣa,
and likewise to Mucukunda, to Śibi son of Uśīnara, to Ṛṣabha and to Ila, and to the king Nṛga as well,
and to others, O great king, mighty kṣatriyas all—to every one of them, O king of kings, was the land of Bhārata dear, O Bhārata.
That land I shall declare to you as I have heard it, O subduer of foes; hear me as I speak, O king, what you ask of me.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimān, and Ṛkṣavān too, Vindhya and Pāriyātra—these seven are the principal mountains.
Near these, O king, are mountains by the thousand, well-known, massive, vast, with peaks of many hues.
And others beyond these, unknown, small, and inhabited by lowly folk; āryas and mlecchas, O Kaurava, and men mingled with both, O mighty one.
They drink of many rivers: the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Sarasvatī, the Godāvarī and the Narmadā, and the great river Bāhudā,
the Śatadru and the Candrabhāgā, and the great river Yamunā, the Dṛṣadvatī and the Vipāśā, the Vipāpā and the Sthūlavālukā,
the river Vetravatī, and the stream Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Irāvatī and the Vitastā, the Payoṣṇī and the Devikā too,
the Vedasmṛti, the Vetasinī, the Tridivā and the Iṣkumālinī, the Karīṣiṇī, the Citravahā, and the stream Citrasenā,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the Gomatī and the Dhūtapāpā, and the great river Vandanā, the Kauśikī, the Tridivā, the Kṛtyā, the Vicitrā, and the Lohatāriṇī,
the Rathasthā and the Śatakumbhā, and the Sarayū, O lord of men, the Carmaṇvatī, the Vetravatī, the Hastisomā, and the Diś as well,
the Śatāvarī and the Payoṣṇī, and beyond them the Bhaimarathī, the Kāverī and the Culukā, and the Vāpī and the Śatabalā too,
the Nicīrā and the Mahitā, and the Suprayogā, O ruler of men, the Pavitrā, the Kuṇḍalā, the Sindhu, the Vājinī, the Puramālinī,
the Pūrvābhirāmā and the Vīrā, the Bhīmā and the Oghavatī as well, the Palāśinī, the Pāpaharā, the Mahendra, and the Pippalāvatī,
the Pāriṣeṇā and the Asiknī, the Saralā and the Bhāramardinī, the Puruhī, the Pravarā, the Menā, the Moghā, and the Ghṛtavatī too,
the Dhūmatī and the Atikṛṣṇā, the Sūcī and the Chāvī, O Kaurava, the Sadānīrā and the Adhṛṣyā, and the great river Kuśadhārā,
the Śaśikāntā and the Śivā, and the Vīravatī as well, the Vāstu, the Suvāstu, the Gaurī, the Kampanā, and the Hiraṇvatī,
the Hiraṇvatī, the Citravatī, and the stream Citrasenā, the Rathacitrā, the Jyotirathā, the Viśvāmitra, and the Kapiñjalā,
the Upendrā and the Bahulā, the Kucarā, the Ambuvāhinī, the Vainandī, the Piñjalā, the Veṇṇā, and the great river Tuṅgaveṇā,
the Vidiśā and the Kṛṣṇaveṇṇā, and the Tāmrā and the Kapilā too, the Śalu, the Suvāmā, the Vedāśvā, and the great stream Harisrāvā,
the Śīghrā and the Picchilā, and the stream Bhāradvājī, the stream Kauśikī, the Śoṇā, the Bāhudā, and then the Candanā,
the Durgā and the Antaḥśilā, the Brahmamedhyā, the Bṛhadvatī, the Carakṣā and the Mahirohī, and likewise the Jambunadī too,
the Sunasā, the Tamasā, the Dāsī, the Trasā, another, the Vārāṇasī, the Loloddhṛtakarā, and the great river Pūrṇāśā.
The Mānavī and the Vṛṣabhā too, great rivers, O lord of men, the ever-wholesome Nirāmayā, the Vṛtyā, the Mandagā, and the slow-flowing Mandavāhinī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Brāhmaṇī and the great Gaurī, and the Durgā too, O Bhārata, the Citropalā, the Citrabarhā, the Mañju, and the Makaravāhinī.
The Mandākinī, the Vaitaraṇī, and the Kokā, a great river, the Śuktimatī, the Araṇyā, the Puṣpaveṇī, and the Utpalāvatī.
The Lohityā and the Karatoyā, and likewise the Vṛṣabhaṅginī, the Kumārī, the Ṛṣikulyā, and the Brahmakulyā too, O Bhārata.
The most holy Sarasvatīs and all the Gaṅgās, O honored one — all of them mothers of the world, and all of them of mighty power.
And rivers beyond reckoning besides, by the hundreds and the thousands. Thus, O king, have these streams been recounted, as memory serves.
Now learn from me, as I declare them, the peoples that come next. There are the Kurus and Pāñcālas, the Śālvas, the Mādreyas, and the Jāṅgalas.
The Śūrasenas and the Kaliṅgas, the Bodhas and the Maukas as well, the Matsyas, the Sukuṭyas, the Saubalyas, the Kuntalas, the Kāśis, and the Kosalas.
The Cedis, the Vatsas, and the Karūṣas, the Bhojas, the Sindhus, and the Pulindakas, the Uttamaujas, the Daśārṇas, and the Mekalas together with the Utkalas.
The Pāñcālas and the Kauśijas, the Ekapṛṣṭhas, the Yugaṃdharas, the Saudhas, the Madras, and the Bhujiṅgas, the Kāśis and the Aparakāśis.
The Jaṭharas and the Kukkuśas, and the Sudāśārṇas too, O Bhārata, the Kuntīs and the Avantis, and the Aparakuntis as well.
The Govindas, the Mandakas, the Ṣaṇḍas, the Vidarbhas, the Anūpavāsikas, the Aśmakas, the Pāṃsurāṣṭras, the Goparāṣṭras, and the Panītakas.
The Ādirāṣṭras and the Sukuṭṭas, and the Balirāṣṭra entire, the Vānarāsyas, the Pravāhas, the Vakras, the Vakrabhayas, and the Śakas.
The Videhas and the Māgadhas, the Suhmas and the Vijayas likewise, the Aṅgas, the Vaṅgas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Yakṛllomans as well.
The Mallas, the Sudeṣṇas, the Prāhūtas, and the Māhiṣas and Kārṣikas, the Vāhīkas, the Vāṭadhānas, the Ābhīras, and the Kālatoyakas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Aparāndhras and the Śūdras, the Pahlavas and the Carmakhaṇḍikas, the Aṭavīśabaras too, and the dwellers of the desert lands, O honored one.
The Upāvṛts, the Anupāvṛts, the Surāṣṭras, and the Kekayas likewise, the Kuṭṭas, the Aparāntas, the Dvaidheyas, the Kākṣas, and the Sāmudraniṣkuṭas.
And the Andhras in great number, O king, and the Antargiris likewise, the Bahirgiris, the Aṅgas, the Maladas, the Māgadhas, and the Mānavarjakas.
The Mahyuttaras, the Prāvṛṣeyas, and the Bhārgavas, O lord of men, the Puṇḍras, the Bhārgas, the Kirātas, the Sudoṣṇas, and the Pramudas likewise.
The Śakas, the Niṣādas, the Niṣadhas, and likewise the Ānartas and the Nairṛtas, the Dugūlas, the Pratimatsyas, the Kuśalas, and the Kunaṭas as well.
The Tīragrāhas, the Taratoyas, the Rājikas, the hosts of the Rasyakas, the Tilakas, the Pārasīkas, the Madhumantas, and the Prakutsakas.
The Kāśmīras, the Sindhus and Sauvīras, the Gāndhāras, and the Darśakas likewise, the Abhīsāras, the Kulūtas, the Śaivalas, and the Bāhlīkas as well.
The Darvīkas with the Kacas, the Darvas, the Vāṭadhānas, the Amarathas, the Uragas, the Bahuvādyas too, O Kaurava, the Sudāmans, and the Sumallikas.
The Vadhras and the Karīṣakas too, and the Kulindas of the foothills likewise, the Vanāyus, the Daśāpārśvas, the Romans, and the Kuśabindus.
The Kacchas and the Gopālakacchas, the Lāṅgalas, the Paravallakas, the Kirātas, the Barbaras, the Siddhas, the Videhas, and the Tāmraliṅgakas.
The Oṣṭras, the Puṇḍras, the Sairandhras as well, and the mountain peoples, O honored one. Now the other peoples, those of the south, O bull of the Bhāratas:
The Draviḍas, the Keralas, the Prācyas, the Bhūṣikas, the forest-dwellers, the Unnatyakas, the Māhiṣakas, the Vikalpas, and the Mūṣakas likewise.
The Karṇikas and the Kuntikas, the Saudbhidas, the Nalakālakas, the Kaukuṭṭakas as well, the Colas, the Koṅkaṇas, and the Mālavāṇakas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Samaṅgas and the Kopanas, the Kukuras, the Aṅgadas, O honored one, the Dhvajinīs, the Utsavasaṃketas, the Trigartas, and the Sarvasenas.
The Tryaṅgas, the Kekarakas, the Proṣṭhas, and the Parasaṃcarakas likewise, and the Vindhya tribes as well, the Pulindas together with the Kalkalas.
The Mālakas and the Mallakas, and the Aparavartakas as well, the Kulindas and the Kulakas, the Karaṇṭhas, and the Kurakas likewise.
The Mūṣakas and the Stanabālas, the Satiyas, the Pattipañjakas, the Ādidāyas, the Sirālas, the Stūbakas, and the Stanapas as well.
The Hṛṣīvidarbhas, the Kāntīkas, the Taṅgaṇas, the Parataṅgaṇas, and others, the barbarian peoples of the north, O best of the Bhāratas:
The Yavanas together with the Kāmbojas, savage barbarian tribes, the Kṣaddruhas, the Kuntalas, and the Hūṇas together with the Paratakas.
And likewise the Maradhas and the Cīnas, and the Daśamālikas as well, settlements of kṣatriyas, and families of vaiśyas and śūdras.
The Śūdras and Ābhīras, then the Daradas, the Kāśmīras together with their herds, the Khaśikas and the Tukhāras, the Pallavas, and the dwellers of the mountain caverns.
The Ātreyas with the Bharadvājas, and likewise the Stanayoṣikas, the Aupakas and the Kaliṅgas, and the tribes of the Kirātas.
The Tāmaras and the Haṃsamārgas, and likewise the Karabhañjakas. These lands have I named, O lord, only by way of brief mention.
And rightly tended, the earth yields, in measure of its quality and strength, the great fruit of the threefold aim of life, like a cow that gives milk, a cow that grants every wish.
For her the kings are greedy, brave men skilled in dharma and gain; coveting her richness, those swift and strong ones lay down their very lives in battle.
The earth is, beyond question, the refuge of the bodies of gods and men; and for her men prey upon one another, as dogs snatch at a piece of meat.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kings, O best of the Bhāratas, long to enjoy the earth that bears all wealth; yet here no man's desires are ever satisfied.
Therefore, O king, the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas strive to seize the earth — by conciliation, by gift, by sowing discord, and by force.
Tended aright, the earth becomes father, mother, and son, sky and heaven to all living beings, O bull among men, looking upon them with a flawless eye.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Of this land of Bhārata, and of Haimavata as well, O sūta, tell me the measure of the span of life, and its fruit, both fair and foul.
What is to come, what has passed, and what now is, O Saṃjaya — tell me of these at length, and of Harivarṣa as well.
Saṃjaya said: In the land of Bhārata there are four ages, O bull of the Bhāratas: the Kṛta, the Tretā, the Dvāpara, and the Puṣya, O increaser of the Kurus.
First comes the age called Kṛta, then the Tretā age, O lord; thereafter, with the shortening of the Dvāpara, the Puṣya sets in.
Four thousand years, O best of the Kurus, is the reckoned span of life in the Kṛta age, O best of kings.
Three thousand in the Tretā, O ruler of men, two thousand in the Dvāpara; but now it stands at a mere hundred.
In this Puṣya age there is no fixed measure of life at all, O bull of the Bhāratas: here some die yet in the womb, and some die as soon as they are born.
In the Kṛta age, O king, men were born of great strength, great courage, and endowed with every excellence of progeny — sages rich in the wealth of austerity.
Of great zeal, great-souled, righteous, and truthful in speech — so were men born in the Kṛta age, O king, wealthy and fair to look upon.
Long-lived, of great valor, foremost among bowmen in battle — so are the kṣatriyas born in the Tretā: heroes and universal emperors.
In the Dvāpara, O great king, men of all the orders are born, of great zeal and great might, yet bent upon the slaughter of one another.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Endowed with but little luster, prone to wrath, greedy and given to falsehood — such are the men born in the Puṣya age, O Bhārata.
Envy, pride, and wrath, deceit and spite as well, passion and greed — these arise among mortals in the Puṣya age, O Bhārata.
In this Dvāpara, O king, there is a dwindling, O ruler of men. Higher in excellence is Haimavata, and Harivarṣa higher still beyond that.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: You have duly described to me the Jambū continent, O Saṃjaya. Now tell me of its breadth and its extent, truly and exactly.
And the measure of the ocean, O you of flawless sight; tell me too of the Śāka continent and the Kuśa continent, O Saṃjaya.
And truly of the Śālmala, and of the Krauñca continent as well; tell me all, O son of Gavalgaṇa, of Rāhu and of the Moon and the Sun.
Saṃjaya said: O king, many indeed are the continents by which this world is spread out; but I shall declare to you the seven, and the Moon and Sun and planets as well.
Eighteen thousand yojanas, O lord of peoples, and six hundred full besides — such is the breadth of the Jambū mountain region.
The breadth of the Salt Ocean is reckoned twice as great, strewn with diverse peoples and bright with gems and coral.
Adorned with mountains gleaming with manifold minerals, thronged by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, the ocean lies girdling all around.
I shall now describe the Śāka continent duly, O king. Hear me as I speak of it in proper order, O delight of the Kurus.
By the measure of the Jambū continent it is twice as great in breadth, O ruler of men, O great king; and so too is the Sea of Milk in due proportion, O best of the Bhāratas, by which it is encircled all about.
There the lands are holy, and there no man dies; how then could there be famine? For its people are endowed with patience and luster.
This, O bull of the Bhāratas, is a brief account of the Śāka continent, duly given, O great king. What else do you wish to hear?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: You have duly given me a brief account of the Śāka continent, O Saṃjaya, O greatly blessed one. Now tell me of it in full and exactly.
Saṃjaya said: There too, O king, are seven mountains adorned with gems, and rivers that are mines of jewels — hear from me their names. All there is supremely rich in excellence and holy, O lord of men.
Frequented by gods, sages, and Gandharvas, the supreme one is called Meru; and stretching to the east, O great king, is the mountain named Malaya, from which the clouds arise and spread forth on every side.
Beyond that, O Kaurava, is the great mountain Jaladhāra, where Vāsava ever draws up the choicest waters, whence rain springs forth in the season of rains, O lord of men.
Lofty is the mountain Raivataka, where the constellation Revatī is ever fixed in the sky — so was it ordained by the Grandsire.
And to the north, O king of kings, is the great mountain named Śyāma, from which the people have come to be dark of hue, O lord of the realms.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: A great doubt is mine this day at what you have said, O Saṃjaya. How, O son of the sūta, have the people there come to be dark of hue?
Saṃjaya said: In all the continents alike, O greatly wise one, O delight of the Kurus, there are two colors, fair and dark; and between the two, O king, lie all the other hues.
From what the darkness has arisen I shall tell you, O Bhārata: the blessed Kṛṣṇa abides there, and by his radiance the people have taken on a dusky hue.
Beyond that, O lord of the Kurus, is the mighty mountain Durgaśaila of great glory, the Kesarin clothed in fragrant blooms, from which the wind blows forth.
The breadth of these in yojanas is twice as great, region by region; and the lands within them, O Kaurava, have been declared by the wise.
Mahāmeru, Mahākāśa, Jalada, and Kumudottara, O king; and beyond Jaladhāra is the one remembered as Sukumāra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For Raivata there is Kaumāra, for Śyāma there is Maṇīcaka, for Kesara there is Modākī, and beyond that the great Mahāpuruṣa.
Encircling it, O Kaurava, in its length and breadth, it is famed in proportion to Jambūdvīpa; and in its midst stands a great tree.
It is named Śāka, O great king, standing at the center of that island. There the lands are holy, and there Śaṃkara is worshipped.
There go the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and the gods; and righteous are the people there, O king, the four classes exceedingly so, O Bhārata.
The classes are devoted each to its own duty, and no thief is seen there; long-lived are they, O great king, free from old age and death.
The people there flourish like rivers flowing to the sea in the rains; the streams there are of holy water, and the Gaṅgā runs in many courses.
Sukumārī and Kumārī, Sītā and Kāverakā, the Mahānadī too, O Kaurava, and the river Maṇijalā, and Ikṣuvardhanikā as well, O best of the Bhāratas.
From there flow forth holy-watered rivers, O upholder of the Kuru line, hundreds upon thousands of them, wherever Vāsava sends his rain.
Their names and likewise their number cannot be reckoned in full, for they are holy, those finest of rivers.
There are four holy lands, esteemed by the world: the Magas and the Maśakas, the Mānasas and the Mandagas.
The Magas are mostly brāhmaṇas, devoted to their own duty, O king; among the Maśakas dwell kṣatriyas, righteous and granting every desire.
Among the Mānasas, O great king, are vaiśyas who live by their work, endowed with every wish, valiant, resolute in dharma and wealth; and in Mandaga ever dwell śūdras, men of righteous conduct.
There is no king there, O lord of kings, no rod of punishment nor those who wield it; by their own dharma alone they guard one another's righteousness.
This much only can be told of that island, and this much only is to be heard concerning the mighty Śākadvīpa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Of the islands to the north, O Kaurava, a tale is heard; as I have heard it, O great king, hear it now from me as I tell it.
Here is a sea whose waters are clarified butter, another whose waters are curds and whey, an ocean of wine, and yet another, a sea of warm water.
Each is double the last, O ruler of men, all the islands; and on every side, O great king, they are girded round by mountains.
In the middle island stands a great mountain, white, of realgar; and to the west a dark mountain, resembling Nārāyaṇa, O king.
There Keśava himself guards the divine jewels, and, attending upon Prajāpati, ordains the welfare of the creatures.
In Kuśadvīpa a clump of kuśa-grass, at the center of the land, is held in worship; and the śalmali tree on the island Śālmalika, O king.
In Krauñcadvīpa the great mountain Krauñca, a mine heaped with jewels, is worshipped ever, O great king, by all four classes.
There is the great mountain Gomanda, O king, rich in every mineral, where the glorious lotus-eyed Lord dwells forever, ever praised by those who seek release, the lord Nārāyaṇa Hari.
In Kuśadvīpa, O lord of kings, is a mountain studded with coral, named Sudhāman, hard to assail; and a second, the golden mountain.
Named Dyutimat, O Kaurava; third, the mountain Kumuda; fourth, the one named Puṣpavat; and fifth, Kuśeśaya.
Sixth is the one named Harigiri; these six are the foremost of mountains, and the span between them, region by region, is double each preceding.
The first region is Audbhida, the second Veṇumaṇḍala, the third indeed Rathākāra, and the fourth is remembered as Pālana.
Dhṛtimat is the fifth region, Prabhākara the sixth, and Kāpila the seventh region; these are the seven clusters of regions.
In these the gods, the gandharvas, and the people, O lord of the earth, roam and take their delight, and no one there dies.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In them there are no robbers, nor any of barbarian birth, O king; all the folk are fair of hue and delicate, O Pārtha.
Concerning the remaining regions I shall speak, O lord of men, as I have heard it, O great king; hear it with an untroubled mind.
In Krauñcadvīpa, O great king, is the great mountain named Krauñca; beyond Krauñca is Vāmanaka, and beyond Vāmana, Andhakāraka.
Beyond Andhakāra, O king, is Maināka, foremost of mountains; and beyond Maināka, O king, the lofty mountain Govinda.
And beyond Govinda, O king, is a mountain named Nibiḍa; the span of each is double the last, O increaser of your line.
I shall tell you the countries there; hear me as I declare them. The country of Krauñca is Kuśala, that of Vāmana is Manonuga.
Beyond Manonuga is the country Uṣṇa, O upholder of the Kuru line; beyond Uṣṇa is Prāvaraka, and beyond Prāvara, Andhakāraka.
Beyond the country of Andhakāraka is remembered the country of Muni; and beyond the country of Muni is named Dundubhisvana.
Thronged with Siddhas and Cāraṇas, its people mostly fair of hue, O lord of men; these countries, O great king, are frequented by gods and gandharvas.
In Puṣkara is a mountain named Puṣkara, rich in gems and jewels; there the god Prajāpati himself dwells forever.
Upon him all the gods, with the great seers, ever wait in attendance, honoring him with words that gladden the heart, O lord of men.
From Jambūdvīpa proceed jewels of many kinds, indeed, to all those islands, for the people, O joy of the Kurus.
Through the brāhmaṇas' chastity, their truth, and their self-restraint, in measure of health and length of life it is double and ever doubling thereafter.
There is but one community, O king, in all these islands, O Bhārata, the lands of which I have spoken, where a single dharma is seen.
The Lord himself, Prajāpati, raising the rod of rule, O great king, stands ever guarding these islands.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is king, he is the auspicious one, O king; he is father, he is grandfather; he shelters, O best of men, the people, both the dull and the wise.
And here, O Kaurava, the people partake of food that comes to them of itself, already prepared, O great king, ever there.
Beyond that is seen a region of the world named Samā, four-cornered, O great king, with a circuit of thirty-three.
There stand, O Kaurava, four elephants of the quarters, esteemed by the world, O best of the Bhāratas, Vāmana, Airāvata, and the rest, and Supratīka too, O king, his cheeks and face streaming with rut.
Its measure I cannot venture to reckon here, for it is forever beyond counting, across, above, and below alike.
There indeed the winds blow from all the quarters, unobstructed, O great king, and those elephants take them in.
With their trunks, like lotuses, broad and of mighty splendor, they then slowly, yet swiftly again, release the winds without end.
Released by the breathing elephants of the quarters, the winds come hither, O great king, and thereby the creatures live on.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: A vast expanse indeed have you recounted to excess, O Saṃjaya; you have shown the disposition of the islands. Now tell me what is beyond, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: The islands have been told, O great king; now hear of the planets truly from me: Svarbhānu, O best of the Kauravas, how great he is in his might.
Round in shape, O great king, the planet Svarbhānu is said to be; its diameter is full twelve thousand yojanas.
In girth six and thirty thousand, and in breadth, O sinless one, the learned and the masters of the old lore declare it six thousand.
The moon, O king, is remembered as eleven thousand in diameter, O best of the Kurus, and thirty-three thousand in circuit, fifty-nine thousand in breadth, the great cool-rayed one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The sun is ten thousand—eight thousand and two more, O joy of the Kurus—in diameter; and thence, O king, its circuit is a full thirty thousand.
Fifty-eight thousand, O king, in breadth, O sinless one, that most exalted soaring one of light is said to be; such is the measure of the sun declared here, O Bhārata.
That Rāhu, by reason of his greatness, eclipses these two in their season, the moon and the sun, O great king; this is the account told in brief.
Thus, O great king, to you who asked, all has been told according to the truth, with the eye of the scriptures; therefore attain to peace.
This world, with its goings-forth, I have told as I have seen it; therefore take comfort, O Kaurava, concerning your son Duryodhana.
Having heard this Section of the Earth, O best of the Bhāratas, pleasing to the mind, the prince becomes glorious, his purpose fulfilled, esteemed by the good; and his life, strength, valor, and splendor increase.
Whoever, O ruler of the earth, hears this on a parva-day, firm in his vows, his fathers are gladdened, and so too his forefathers.
But this region of Bhārata, wherein we dwell, holy from of old, now unfolds; all of it you have now heard.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the wise Saṃjaya, son of Gavalgaṇa, having come from the battle, an eyewitness of all, knower of past, present, and to come,
approaching in haste, grieving, declared to the brooding Dhṛtarāṣṭra that Bhīṣma, the foremost among the Bhāratas, had been slain.
"I am Saṃjaya, O great king; homage to you, O bull of the Bhāratas. Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, the grandsire of the Bhāratas, is slain.
The crest of all warriors, the abode of all who bear the bow, that grandsire of the Kurus lies today upon a bed of arrows.
He upon whose valor relying your son made bold to play at dice—he, Bhīṣma, lies slain, O king, in the fray by Śikhaṇḍin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who, in a great battle at the city of Kāśi, vanquished all the rulers of the earth gathered together, with a single chariot, that mighty car-warrior—
he, born of the Vasus, who fought Rāma the son of Jamadagni in combat and was not slain by the son of Jamadagni, is today slain by Śikhaṇḍin.
Like great Indra in prowess, like Himavat in steadfastness, like the ocean in depth, in forbearance the equal of the earth—
his fangs his arrows, his mouth the bow, his tongue the sword, unassailable, that man-lion, your father, has today been struck down by the Pāñcāla prince.
The great host of the Pāṇḍavas, beholding him rise up in the battle, trembled, stricken with fear, as a herd of cattle at the sight of a lion.
For ten nights, guarding your army, that destroyer of hosts, having wrought a deed most hard to do, went down like the setting sun.
He who, unshakable as Śakra, raining arrows by the thousand, slew in battle a hundred million of the warriors in ten days—
he lies groaning upon the ground like a tree felled by the wind, through your evil counsel, O king, though he deserved no such fate, O Bhārata."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: How was Bhīṣma, the bull of the Kurus, slain by Śikhaṇḍin? How did he fall from his chariot, my father, the peer of Vāsava?
And how fared my sons, bereft of Bhīṣma, O Saṃjaya—of him so mighty, godlike, who for his elders' sake kept the vow of chastity?
When that great-souled one was slain — the mighty archer, vast in strength, the great chariot-warrior, the tiger among men — what then, tell me, was the temper of their minds?
A boundless anguish enters me, since you tell me he is slain — the bull of the Kurus, the unshakable hero, that bull among men.
Who followed after him as he advanced, and who went before him? Who held their ground, who turned back, and who pressed onward, Saṃjaya?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What heroes followed close behind that tiger among chariot-warriors, the unfaltering one, the bull among kṣatriyas, as he plunged headlong into the host of chariots?
He who, like the sun dispelling darkness, that slayer of foes scattered the enemy host — like one of a thousand rays — and struck terror into his adversaries, performing in battle a deed hard to do, at the command of the Kauravas.
As he was devouring whole armies, who hemmed him in close at hand — that accomplished and unassailable warrior, advancing straight upon them? How did the Pāṇḍavas hold back the son of Śaṃtanu in the fight?
He who hewed down the armies, swift, his fangs of arrows, his mouth gaping wide as a bow, terrible, his tongue a sword, unapproachable —
He who surpassed all other tigers among men, modest and unconquered — how did the son of Kuntī bring down that one who had never been vanquished in battle?
With his fierce bow and fierce shafts, standing upon his peerless chariot, harvesting the heads of his foes with whetted arrows —
He whom the great host of the Pāṇḍavas, beholding him rise up in the fray unassailable like the fire of doom, encircled again and again —
For ten nights that destroyer of armies harrowed my host, and then, like the sun, he set, having wrought a deed most hard to do.
He who, like Śakra, loosed an unfailing rain made of arrows, and in ten days slew a hundred million of the warriors in battle —
He now lies groaning upon the earth like a tree shattered by the wind — that descendant of Bharata, who deserved no such fate, brought low by my evil counsel.
How was the army of the Pāṇḍavas able, beholding the son of Śaṃtanu there, to strike at Bhīṣma of terrible prowess?
How did the sons of Pāṇḍu wage war against Bhīṣma, and how did Bhīṣma fail to conquer while Droṇa yet lived, Saṃjaya?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With Kṛpa close at hand there, and the son of Bharadvāja as well, how did Bhīṣma, the best of those who strike, come to his death?
And how was that supreme chariot-warrior Bhīṣma — hard for even the gods to withstand — slain in battle by the Pāñcāla, Śikhaṇḍin?
He who in battle ever rivaled the mighty son of Jamadagni, unvanquished by that son of Jamadagni, his valor the equal of Śakra's —
Tell me, Saṃjaya, of that hero Bhīṣma, slain in the fight, worthy of the strength of the greatest chariot-warriors — he without whom we know no refuge.
Which of my mighty archers did not abandon that unfaltering one, Saṃjaya? Which heroes, charged by Duryodhana, encircled him to guard him?
When all the Pāṇḍavas, with Śikhaṇḍin at their head, advanced upon Bhīṣma, did the Kurus not, in their fear, abandon that unfaltering one, Saṃjaya?
With the twang of his bowstring for thunder, his arrows for a dappling of raindrops, the great roar of his bow for its mighty voice — towering like a vast storm-cloud —
As he rained down upon the sons of Kuntī with the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas, that hero smiting the enemy chariots like the wielder of the thunderbolt smiting the Dānavas —
A dreadful ocean of arrows and missiles, with shafts for its sea-monsters, unapproachable, its waves the bows, inexhaustible, in battle without an isle and without a raft, its whirlpools the maces and swords, its crocodiles the horses, its waters thronged with elephants —
He who swiftly drowned horses, elephants, foot-soldiers, and chariots in throngs upon the field, that carrier-off of the enemy's heroes —
That scorcher of foes, blazing with wrath and with splendor — what heroes encircled him as a shore holds back the home of sea-monsters?
When Bhīṣma, that slayer of foes, did his deed in battle for Duryodhana's sake, Saṃjaya — who were they that stood before him then?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Who guarded the right wheel of Bhīṣma of measureless splendor? What heroes, steadfast in their vows, held off the foe from behind?
Who took their station in front, guarding Bhīṣma close at hand? What heroes guarded the left wheel of the hero as he fought?
Stationed at the left wheel, who slew the Sṛñjayas, Saṃjaya? Who, gathered at the forefront of the ranks, guarded that unassailable one?
Who pressed forward at his flanks, following a path hard to tread? Amid the throng, who did battle against the heroes of the foe, Saṃjaya?
If he was guarded by heroes, and they in turn were sheltered by him, how did the armies of those hard to conquer not swiftly prevail in the fight?
As though against the lord of all worlds, the supreme Prajāpati — how were the Pāṇḍavas even able to strike at him, Saṃjaya?
The island upon which the Kurus relied as they fought their foes — that tiger among men, Bhīṣma, now sunk beneath the waters, you tell me is fallen, Saṃjaya.
In whose valor my son, mighty in strength, set his trust and reckoned the Pāṇḍavas as nothing — how was he slain by the foe?
He who long ago, frenzied for war, was sought as an ally by the gods with Indra at their head when they smote the Dānavas — my father, great in his vow —
At whose birth Śaṃtanu, in that son of mighty valor, blessing to the world and his father's pride, cast off sorrow, grief, and despair —
That refuge of wisdom, knower of it, devoted to the true law, pure, versed in the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliaries — how do you tell me he is slain?
Endowed with the discipline of every weapon, self-controlled, serene, high-minded — hearing that the son of Śaṃtanu is slain, I deem the rest of my army slain as well.
Unrighteousness has grown stronger than righteousness — such is my judgment — where the Pāṇḍavas, having slain their aged elder, still desire the kingdom.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Long ago Rāma, son of Jamadagni, knower of every weapon, unsurpassed, took up arms in the cause of Ambā and in the battle was vanquished by Bhīṣma.
That Bhīṣma, whose deeds were the equal of Indra's, the crest of all bowmen — you tell me he is slain. What grief can be greater than this?
He by whom hosts of kṣatriyas were again and again overcome in battle, and Rāma, son of Jamadagni, too — that slayer of the enemy's heroes —
Surely, then, in splendor, valor, and strength, Śikhaṇḍin the son of Drupada was greater than that mighty descendant of Bhṛgu, frenzied for war.
He who slew that hero — valiant, accomplished in war, skilled in every science, master of the supreme weapons, that bull of the Bhāratas —
What heroes followed that slayer of foes into the assembly of the enemy? Tell me how it came to pass — the battle of Bhīṣma with the Pāṇḍavas.
My son's army is like a woman whose hero is slain, Saṃjaya; that host of mine is like a herd of cattle scattered in panic, without a herdsman.
He whose manhood in the great battle surpassed that of all the world — when he was struck down, what then was the temper of your minds?
What strength is there in us even to live this day, Saṃjaya, having caused the death of that father of mighty valor, righteous before all the world?
Like men seeking the farther shore who see their boat foundering in fathomless water, my sons, I think, grieve sorely now that Bhīṣma is slain.
Surely my heart is made of the very substance of mountains, exceedingly hard, that, hearing the tiger among men, Bhīṣma, is slain, it does not burst asunder.
In whom — that bull of the Bhāratas, unassailable — weaponry, wisdom, and statecraft were beyond all measure: how was he slain in battle?
Not by weapon, not by valor, not by austerity nor by wisdom, not by steadfastness, nor again by renunciation — by none of these is any creature delivered from death.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Surely Time is of mighty power, not to be overpassed by all the worlds, since you tell me that the son of Śaṃtanu, Bhīṣma, is slain, Saṃjaya.
Consumed by grief for my sons, brooding on this great sorrow — once I had hoped for protection from Bhīṣma, the joy of Śaṃtanu.
When Duryodhana saw the son of Śaṃtanu fallen to the earth like the sun, Saṃjaya — what did he do then?
Pondering with my mind, Saṃjaya, over my own and over the foe, I see nothing whatever remaining among the kings ranged against us.
Cruel is this duty of the kṣatriya, set forth by the seers, wherein the Pāṇḍavas, having slain the son of Śaṃtanu, still desire the kingdom.
Or it is we who desire the kingdom, having caused the grandsire's death; standing fast in the kṣatriya's duty, the sons of Pṛthā commit no wrong, my sons.
This is what a noble man must do in dire calamities, Saṃjaya: to strive valiantly with all his power — and in him that valor was firmly set.
As he was destroying the armies, modest and unconquered — how, dear one, did the sons of Pāṇḍu bring down the son of Śaṃtanu?
How were the armies arrayed, how did the great-souled ones do battle, and how was Bhīṣma, my father, slain by the foe, Saṃjaya?
And Duryodhana, and Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala, and the cheat Duḥśāsana — when Bhīṣma was slain, what did they say?
That assembly strewn with the bodies of men, elephants, and horses, with arrows, spears, maces, swords, and javelins for its dice, dreadful to behold —
The foolish gamblers entered that hall of battle, hard to enter — in that fearful game played for life itself, which bulls among men cast the dice?
Who won there and who were defeated, their stakes lost, struck down — besides Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
There is no peace for me here; hearing that Devavrata, my father of terrible deeds, has been slain in battle, sorrow has entered into me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The great anguish rooted in my heart, brought on by my sons — you inflame it as one pouring clarified butter inflames a fire, Saṃjaya.
Beholding Bhīṣma slain — who had taken up that great burden, renowned throughout all the worlds — my sons, I think, now grieve.
I shall hear all those sorrows wrought by Duryodhana; therefore tell me everything that came to pass there, Saṃjaya.
In the battle of the lords of the earth, whatever sprang from the folly of that dullard, whether ill-counselled or well-counselled — tell me that, Saṃjaya.
What was done there by Bhīṣma in the battle as he sought victory — full of splendor, accomplished in arms — tell me that too, leaving nothing out.
How that battle of the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas came to be — in what sequence, at what time, what happened and in what manner — tell it all.
Saṃjaya said: This question is worthy of you, great king, as befits you; yet you ought not to lay this blame upon Duryodhana.
The man who through his own ill conduct meets with misfortune ought not to lay the guilt of that sin upon another.
Great king, the man who commits among men every blameworthy deed deserves to be slain by all the world, doing as he does what is condemned.
Insult was endured by the Pāṇḍavas, deep in cunning, out of deference to you, together with their counsellors; and long indeed did they bear it patiently in the forest.
What I have seen with my own eyes of the horses, the elephants, and the heroes of measureless might, and what I have seen by the power of yoga —
Hear it, protector of the earth, and set not your mind on grief; this was surely ordained of old to come to pass thus, lord of men.
Having made obeisance to your father, the wise son of Parāśara, by whose grace I have obtained the divine and unsurpassed knowledge —
And by his grace, O king, I have gained sight that transcends the senses, hearing across great distances, knowledge of others' thoughts, and awareness of things past and yet to come.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Knowledge of births that have arisen out of due course, the power to move ever through the sky, and immunity from weapons in battle — all this from the boon of that great-souled one.
Hear from me, then, in full this wondrous tale, most marvelous and hair-raising — how the great war of the Bhāratas came to pass.
When those armies had been drawn up in array according to rule, Duryodhana, O great king, then spoke to Duḥśāsana.
"Duḥśāsana, let the chariots that guard Bhīṣma be yoked at once, and urge on all the divisions with all speed.
This clash of the Pāṇḍavas with their hosts and of the Kurus, brooded upon through many long years, has at last come upon me.
I deem no task in battle more urgent than the guarding of Bhīṣma; for, well protected, he will slay the Pārthas, the Somakas, and the Sṛñjayas with them.
And he of pure heart has said, 'I will not slay Śikhaṇḍin; for it is told that he was once a woman, and so he must be spared by me in battle.'
Therefore Bhīṣma must be guarded with especial care — such is my judgment; let all my men stand ready, bent on the slaying of Śikhaṇḍin.
Let the warriors of the East and the West, of the South and of the Northern road, skilled in every weapon and missile, guard the grandsire.
For unguarded, even a wolf may slay a lion of mighty strength; let us not have our lion slain by Śikhaṇḍin as though by a mere jackal.
Yudhāmanyu guards Phalguna's left wheel and Uttamaujas his right — these two are Phalguna's protectors, and Phalguna himself protects Śikhaṇḍin.
So act, Duḥśāsana, that Śikhaṇḍin — guarded by Pārtha and shunned by Bhīṣma — may not be able to slay the son of Gaṅgā."
Then, when the night had passed into dawn, a great clamor arose from the kings crying out, "Yoke them! Yoke them!"
With the blare of conches and kettledrums, with lion-roars, O Bhārata, with the neighing of horses and the rumble of chariot wheels,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
with the trumpeting of elephants and the roaring of warriors, with shouts and the slapping of arms and battle cries — a tumult rose up on every side.
At sunrise, O great king, the whole vast host of the Kuru and Pāṇḍava armies arose, fully arrayed without exception — the forces of your sons, O lord of kings, and of the Pāṇḍavas alike.
There the elephants and chariots, adorned with gold, were seen gleaming like clouds shot through with lightning.
The masses of chariots looked like cities beyond number; and there your father shone exceedingly, like the full moon.
With bows, spears, and swords, with maces, lances, and javelins, with gleaming weapons of war, the warriors stood firm each in his own division.
Elephants, chariots, foot soldiers, and horses, O lord of peoples, stood ranged like an outspread net, in their hundreds and their thousands.
Banners of many fashions were seen raised aloft, radiant by the thousand, both of one's own side and of the foe.
Golden, their staffs bright with gems, blazing like fires, the flaming banners of the kings shone forth by the thousand.
Bright as the banners of great Indra raised in great Indra's halls; and among them those armored heroes, longing for battle, were beheld.
With weapons raised, splendid, their hand-guards bound, their quivers slung, those bull-eyed lords of men shone forth at the head of their hosts.
Śakuni the son of Subala, Śalya, the Sindhu king Jayadratha, Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja,
Śrutāyudha the Kaliṅga, the king Jayatsena, Bṛhadbala of Kosala, and Kṛtavarman of the Sātvatas —
these ten tigers among men, heroes with arms like iron bars, commanders of full divisions, performers of sacrifices with abundant gifts,
these and many other kings and princes, wise in statecraft and of great might, followed in Duryodhana's command.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Armored, they were seen each stationed in his own division, all wearing black antelope skins and bearing banners, girt with garlands of muñja grass —
consecrated, as it were, for Duryodhana's cause and dedicated to the world of Brahmā; ten flourishing divisions stood drawn up and ready.
The eleventh, the great host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, the mighty Kaurava army, stood before all the troops, with the son of Śaṃtanu at its head.
White-turbaned, with white horses and white armor, unshaken, we beheld Bhīṣma, O great king, like the risen moon.
The Kurus and Pāṇḍavas saw Bhīṣma, his banner a golden palm, standing in his silver chariot like the keen-rayed sun amid a white cloud.
Beholding Bhīṣma at the head of the host, the Pāṇḍavas trembled, and the mighty bowmen of the Sṛñjayas with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at their head.
As small beasts shrink before a great lion yawning wide, so all those led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna shuddered again and again.
These eleven divisions of yours, O Bhārata, were graced with splendor, while the Pāṇḍavas' seven were guarded by mighty men.
The two hosts looked like two oceans met together at the end of an age — their whirlpools maddened, teeming with great sea-monsters.
Never before, O king, had we seen or heard of such a gathering of assembled armies as this.
Saṃjaya said: Even as the blessed Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, had foretold, so did all the lords of earth come together, gathered as one.
On that day the moon stood in the mansion of Maghā, and the seven great planets, blazing, came together in the sky.
At its rising the sun seemed cleft in two, and the radiant orb, risen in the heavens, blazed again with a flaming crest.
And toward the blazing quarter jackals and crows cried out, hungering for the bodies, eaters of flesh and blood.
Day after day the aged Kuru grandsire and the son of Bharadvāja, rising at dawn with controlled minds, would say of the Pārthas —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let there be victory to the sons of Pāṇḍu" — thus those two tamers of foes spoke, yet fought for your cause, as the compact had been made.
Your father Devavrata, knowing all the niceties of dharma, gathered the kings together and spoke these words:
"O warriors, here is the great gate to heaven, flung open for you; pass through it to dwell in the world of Śakra and of Brahmā.
This is the eternal path trodden by your forefathers and those before them; honor yourselves in battle with minds undismayed.
For Nābhāga and Yayāti, Māndhātṛ, Nahuṣa, and Nṛga, made perfect by deeds such as these, attained the highest abode.
It is unrighteousness for a warrior to meet death by sickness in his home; but to fall in battle is his eternal dharma."
Thus addressed by Bhīṣma, O bull of the Bhāratas, the kings marched forth, gracing their own divisions with their splendid chariots.
But that Karṇa, son of the Sun, with his counselors and kinsmen, was made by Bhīṣma to lay down his weapons in the battle, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then your sons and the kings on your side, now without Karṇa, marched forth, making the ten quarters resound with their lion-roars.
With white parasols and pennons, with banners, elephants, and horses, with chariots and foot soldiers, those divisions shone in splendor.
With the sound of drums and tabors and the din of war-drums, and with the rumble of chariot wheels, the earth was set atremble.
With golden armlets and bracelets and with their bows, the great chariot-warriors were seen gleaming like moving mountains.
Bhīṣma, the lord of the Kuru host, bearing as his standard a great palm-tree with five stars, stood there like the spotless sun.
Those mighty bowmen, the kings of your side, O bull of the Bhāratas, moved according to the command of the son of Śaṃtanu, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the Śaibya king Govāsana, with all his royal allies, advanced upon a kingly, pennoned lordly elephant; lotus-hued, he stood at the very front of all the divisions.
Aśvatthāman marched out, intent, his banner bearing a lion's tail; and Śrutāyu, Citrasena, Purumitra, and Viviṃśati,
Śalya, Bhūriśravas, and Vikarṇa the great chariot-warrior — these seven mighty bowmen, led by Droṇa's son, with their chariots of splendid hue, formed Bhīṣma's vanguard.
Their banners too, lofty and wrought of gold, gracing those splendid chariots, were seen shining bright.
A golden altar adorned with a water-pot, together with a bow, was the standard of Droṇa, foremost of teachers.
Drawing along a host of many hundreds of thousands, Duryodhana's great standard was an elephant fashioned of jewels.
Before him stood, in their chariots, Paurava and the Kaliṅga king, Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja, Kṣemadhanvan, and Sumitrā.
And the king of Magadha marched forth in a costly chariot, his standard a bull, as though drawing the army's van after him.
Guarded by the lord of the Aṅgas and by the great-souled Kṛpa, the host of the easterners looked like a mass of autumn clouds.
Standing at the head of his division, the illustrious Jayadratha shone with his foremost standard, a silver boar.
A hundred thousand chariots obeyed his command, eight thousand elephants, and sixty thousand horsemen.
That vanguard of the army, guarded by the lord of the Sindhus, O king — a great force with chariots, elephants, and horses past counting — shone in splendor.
With sixty thousand chariots and ten thousand elephants, the lord of all the Kaliṅgas marched forth, together with Ketumat.
His great elephants, like mountains, shone forth, adorned with engines, lances, and quivers, and with pennons.
The Kaliṅga king shone with his foremost standard of a tree, with his white parasol, his golden ornament, and his yak-tail fan.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Ketumat too, mounted in battle upon an elephant with a wondrously fine goad, O king, was like the sun set within a cloud.
Blazing with splendor, mounted upon a noble elephant, King Bhagadatta marched forth like the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Riding upon the shoulders of elephants, the equals of Bhagadatta, Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti followed in Ketumat's train.
That formation, rich in chariot-troops, with elephant-bodies and a noble head, with cavalry for wings, descended fierce and struck out, facing every way.
It was ordered, O king, by Droṇa and by the royal son of Śaṃtanu, and likewise by the teacher's son, by Bāhlika, and by Kṛpa.
Saṃjaya said: Then in a moment, O great king, a tumultuous, heart-shaking din was heard from the warriors eager to fight.
With the blare of conches and kettledrums, with the trumpeting of elephants, and with the rumble of chariot wheels, the earth itself seemed to split apart.
From the neighing of the horses and the roaring of the warriors there, in an instant the sky and all the quarters were filled with the din.
O unassailable king, the armies of your sons and of the Pāṇḍavas alike trembled as they came together against one another.
There the elephants and the chariots, adorned with gold, were seen gleaming like clouds shot through with lightning.
The banners of your men, O lord of men, fashioned in manifold shapes and ringed with golden armlets, shone like blazing fires.
Among your own and among the foe alike, O Bhārata, the great standards of Indra appeared, gleaming white as in the halls of mighty Indra himself.
Girt in golden corselets bright as fire and the sun, the heroes appeared like blazing planets.
With raised and gleaming weapons, leather-guards bound to their hands, bearing pennons, bull-eyed and mighty archers, they shone at the front of the host.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As guardians of Bhīṣma's rear, O lord of men, stood your sons—Duḥśāsana, Durviṣaha, Durmukha, and Duḥsaha as well,
Viviṃśati, Citrasena, and Vikarṇa the great chariot-warrior, Satyavrata, Purumitra, Jaya, Bhūriśravas, and Śala.
Twenty thousand chariots followed in their train—the Abhīṣāhas, the Śūrasenas, the Śibis, and the Vasātis,
the Śālvas, the Matsyas, the Ambaṣṭhas, the Trigartas and the Kekayas, the Sauvīras, the Kitavas, and the men of the East, the West, the North, and the Mālavas.
These twelve peoples, all heroes ready to lay down their lives, guarded the grandsire with a great array of chariots.
A division of ten thousand swift elephants, led by the king of Magadha, followed behind that array of chariots.
As wheel-guards for the chariots and foot-guards for the tuskers, there were in the midst of the host six myriads of hundreds.
In front marched the foot-soldiers, bearing bows, shields, and swords—many hundreds of thousands, fighting with claw-spears and javelins.
Eleven akṣauhiṇīs of your son, O Bhārata, were seen, great king, like the Gaṅgā within the bounds of the Yamunā.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Beholding the eleven akṣauhiṇīs arrayed, how did Yudhiṣṭhira the Pāṇḍava draw up his counter-array with so small a force?
He who knows the human battle-array and the divine, the gandharva and the demonic—how did that son of Kuntī, the Pāṇḍava, array his forces against Bhīṣma?
Saṃjaya said: Beholding the divisions of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son drawn up in array, the righteous-souled Pāṇḍava, the king of justice, spoke thus to Dhanaṃjaya:
By the word of the great seer Bṛhaspati, my dear, they teach this: let a small force fight close-massed, but let a large one spread out at will.
For the few against the many the array should be needle-pointed; and our army is far smaller than the enemy's.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Heeding this word of the great seer, draw up the array, O Pāṇḍava." Hearing this from the king of justice, Phalguna replied:
"This array I shall set in order for you, O king—an array most hard to conquer, the unshakable one called Vajra, ordained by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
He who, like a rising wind, is unbearable to the foe in battle—Bhīma, best of strikers—shall fight in our van.
Crushing the splendor of the enemy's hosts, that best of men, skilled in the arts of war, shall go before us as our foremost leader.
At the sight of whom all the kings led by Duryodhana will turn back in panic, as small beasts before a lion.
Him we shall all take as our fearless rampart—Bhīma, best of strikers—as the immortals take refuge in the wielder of the thunderbolt.
For there is no man in the world who could bear even to look upon Vṛkodara enraged, that bull among men of most terrible deeds.
Bhīmasena, bearing his firm mace forged with the strength of the thunderbolt, ranging on with mighty speed, could dry up even the ocean."
"The Kekayas, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the valiant Cekitāna—these stand by with their counselors as your onlookers, O lord of men,
as heirs against Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons," said Bībhatsu. And as Pārtha spoke thus, O honored one, all the troops honored him then in the battle with words of approval.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Dhanaṃjaya did so; and having swiftly arrayed those forces, Phalguna then advanced.
Beholding the Kurus set in motion, the great host of the Pāṇḍavas appeared like the Gaṅgā in flood—still yet flowing on.
Their foremost were Bhīmasena and Dhṛṣṭadyumna son of Pṛṣata, Nakula and Sahadeva, and the valiant Dhṛṣṭaketu.
Then, marshaling them, the king too, encircled by an akṣauhiṇī, together with his brothers and sons, guarded the rear behind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As wheel-guards of Bhīma stood the two sons of Mādrī of great luster, while the swift sons of Draupadī together with Subhadrā's son guarded his rear.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna of Pāñcāla, that great chariot-warrior, was their protector, joined by the heroes of the host, the foremost charioteers, the Prabhadrakas.
Behind him came Śikhaṇḍin, guarded by Arjuna and bent upon the destruction of Bhīṣma, advancing on, O bull of the Bhāratas.
As Arjuna's rear-guard rode Yuyudhāna, the great chariot-warrior, and his wheel-guards were the two Pāñcālas, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas.
The king Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, stood in the central division, with huge rutting elephants that moved like moving mountains.
And the high-minded Yajñasena of Pāñcāla, with an akṣauhiṇī, valorous in the Pāṇḍavas' cause, followed Virāṭa from behind.
Their great banners, bright as sun and moon, adorned with finest gold and bearing diverse emblems, O king, stood upon the chariots.
Then, moving up from behind, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the great chariot-warrior, together with his brothers and sons, guarded Yudhiṣṭhira.
Surpassing the manifold banners upon the chariots of your men and of the foe, Arjuna's single standard, the great ape, stood high above all.
In front marched the foot-soldiers, bearing swords, spears, and lances—many hundreds of thousands, the protectors of Bhīmasena.
Ten thousand elephants, their cheeks and faces flowing with rut, gleaming in nets of gold, blazed like mountains.
Like raining clouds, wet with rut and fragrant as lotuses, they followed the king from behind like moving mountains.
Bhīmasena, brandishing his fearsome mace that resembled an iron bar, the high-minded and unassailable one, drew on that mighty host.
Him, hard to look upon as the burning, ray-wreathed sun, the warriors on every side could not bear to gaze upon at close quarters.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This was the array named Vajra, hard to break, facing every way—terrible, its banners flashing like lightning over the bow, guarded by the wielder of Gāṇḍīva.
Having arrayed it against your host, the Pāṇḍavas stood firm—an array unconquerable in the world of men, guarded by the Pāṇḍavas.
As the armies stood at the twilight hour, toward the rising of the sun a wind blew, scattering droplets, thundering though no cloud was there.
Fierce winds blew from every side, sweeping up grit low along the ground, and the dust that was raised veiled the world in darkness.
A great meteor fell, facing eastward, O bull of the Bhāratas, and striking the rising sun, it burst asunder with a mighty roar.
Then, as the armies were being made ready, O bull of the Bhāratas, the sun rose dim, and with a great noise the earth shook and split asunder with a roar, O best of the Bhāratas.
Many thunderclaps broke out in all the quarters, O king, and a thick dust arose so that nothing at all could be discerned.
With the sudden tossing by the wind of the banners, hung with networks of little bells and wreathed in gold, and with their jangling,
those great pennoned standards, splendid as the sun, set everything ringing with their clang, as in groves of fan-palms.
Thus those tigers among men, the Pāṇḍavas, exulting in battle, stood arrayed against your son's host.
The very marrow of the warriors seemed to melt away, O bull of the Bhāratas, at the sight of Bhīmasena stationed in front, mace in hand.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: At sunrise, Saṃjaya, which were the first, eager to fight and seeming to rejoice—my men led by Bhīṣma upon the field, or the Pāṇḍavas led by Bhīma at that hour?
To whose rear were moon, sun, and wind? At whose army did the beasts of prey howl? Whose young men's faces were serene? Tell me all this truly, as it was.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Both armies advanced as if matched, O lord of men; both arrays wore an exultant aspect; both were splendid, gleaming like rows of forest, and both were filled with elephants, chariots, and horses.
Both armies were vast and fearsome in form, O Bhārata, and both alike unbearable; both were marshaled for the winning of heaven, and both were guarded by good and noble men.
The Kurus, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, stood facing westward; the Pārthas, ready to fight, faced east. The host of the Kauravas was like the army of the lord of the Daityas, and the host of the Pāṇḍavas like the army of the lord of the gods.
A clear wind was at the back of the Pāṇḍavas; at the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra the beasts of prey howled. The pungent rut-scent of the lordly elephants your son's elephants could not endure.
Duryodhana, mounted on a lotus-hued elephant, girt with golden girths, of noble strength and flowing with rut, stood in the midst of the Kurus, extolled by bards and panegyrists.
His white parasol shone with the radiance of the moon, and a golden wreath gleamed upon his head; on every side Śakuni, king of Gāndhāra, guarded him with his hillmen and Gāndhāras.
At the head of the whole army stood the aged Bhīṣma, with white parasol, white bow, and conch, white-turbaned, with a pale banner and white horses, gleaming like a mountain of white.
His army comprised all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, one portion of the Bāhlīkas and Śala, the Ambaṣṭha warriors and the Kṣatriyas dwelling by the Sindhu, and the valiant Sauvīras and men of the Five Rivers.
With his blood-red horses and golden chariot, the great-souled, mighty-armed Droṇa of undaunted spirit—the teacher, renowned among all kings—stood guarding the host from the rear like Indra.
In the midst of the whole army stood the son of Vṛddhakṣatra, with Bhūriśravas, Purumitra, and Jaya; and the Śālvas, Matsyas, and all the Kekaya brothers stood ready to fight with their elephant-divisions.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The great-souled son of Śaradvat, the mighty archer of Gautama's line, skilled in varied modes of war, held the northern flank and guarded the host from the north with Śakas, Kirātas, Yavanas, and Pahlavas.
With the great chariot-warriors of the Andhakas, Vṛṣṇis, and Bhojas, with the Saurāṣṭrakas and Nairṛtas, weapons in hand, Kṛtavarman of mighty strength, well-guarded, protected your force from the south.
A myriad chariots of the saṃśaptakas, sworn either to die or to conquer Arjuna, were sent forth; and wherever Arjuna was, there, O king, those weapon-skilled and valiant Trigartas advanced.
A hundred thousand elephants and more were yours, O Bhārata; for every elephant a hundred chariots, and for every chariot a hundred horses,
for every horse ten bowmen, and for every bowman ten shield-bearers: thus were the divisions arrayed by Bhīṣma for you, O Bhārata.
Day after day as it came, Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu and foremost of leaders, set up the array—now human, now divine, now gandharva, now demonic.
Vast with its flood of great chariot-warriors, like the sea at the turn of the moon, the array of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, set up by Bhīṣma, faced westward in the battle.
Boundless in form was your banner-host, O lord of men, and fearsome—yet not so the Pāṇḍavas'. Still, theirs I deem the mighty and unassailable one, whose leaders are Keśava and Arjuna.
Saṃjaya said: Beholding the vast army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons drawn up for battle, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, was overcome with dejection.
Seeing the impenetrable battle-array marshalled by Bhīṣma, and perceiving it to be as if unbreakable, the son of Pāṇḍu, downcast, spoke to Arjuna.
O Dhanaṃjaya, mighty-armed one, how shall we be able to fight in battle against the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose champion is the grandsire himself?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This array, unshakable and impenetrable, has been formed by Bhīṣma, scourge of foes, of abundant splendour, according to the method ordained in the science of war.
We, with our troops, are plunged into doubt, O scourge of foes. How shall there be escape for us from this mighty array?
Then Arjuna, slayer of foes, looking upon the army of yours, O king, addressed the dejected son of Pṛthā, Yudhiṣṭhira.
By that means whereby the few overcome even the many heroes, men superior in wisdom and endowed with virtues—understand it, O lord of the people.
I shall declare to you that cause, O king, since you bear no malice. The sage Nārada knows it, and so do Bhīṣma and Droṇa, O son of Pāṇḍu.
Resting upon this very truth, the Grandsire, long ago, in the war between the gods and the demons, spoke to the dwellers of heaven led by mighty Indra.
Those who seek to conquer do not win victory so much by strength and prowess as by truth and compassion, by righteousness and by exertion.
Casting off unrighteousness, greed, and delusion, and taking your stand upon exertion, fight without arrogance; for where there is righteousness, there is victory.
Know this, O king: certain is our victory in battle. For as Nārada has told me, where Kṛṣṇa is, there is victory.
Victory is an attribute inherent in Kṛṣṇa; it follows close behind Mādhava. And conquest is his besides, while humility is yet another of his virtues.
Govinda, of boundless splendour, is untroubled amid hosts of enemies; he is the most ancient Person. Where Kṛṣṇa is, there is victory.
For of old, becoming Hari, the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha, whose shafts are never blunted, thundering forth amid gods and demons, he asked: 'Who shall be victorious?'
By those who said, 'Following Kṛṣṇa may we conquer,' victory was won; for by his grace the three worlds were gained by Śakra and the other gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For you, O Bhārata, whose victory the all-consuming lord of the gods himself desires, I see no cause whatever for distress.
Saṃjaya said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira urged on his own army, drawing up its divisions to counter those of Bhīṣma, O bull of the Bhāratas.
The Pāṇḍavas, those upholders of the Kuru line, arrayed their divisions as appointed, longing for the supreme heaven to be won through noble battle.
In the centre, Śikhaṇḍin's division was guarded by Savyasācin, and that of Dhṛṣṭadyumna was protected by Bhīma himself.
The right wing, O king, was guarded by Yuyudhāna, the glorious foremost of the Sātvatas, like Śakra wielding the bow.
Yudhiṣṭhira mounted his chariot, like the very car of great Indra, furnished with all its equipment, bright with gold and gems, its harness and trappings of gold, taking his place in the midst of the host of elephants.
Held high above him, his snow-white parasol with ribs of ivory shone exceedingly fair, and the great sages, circling that lord of men reverently, attended him with hymns of praise.
The household priests, aged great sages versed in sacred lore, pronouncing the doom of the foe, performed on every side the rites of benediction with muttered prayers, with sacred verses, and with healing herbs.
Then that high-souled foremost of the Kurus, bestowing upon the brāhmaṇas garments and cattle, fruits and flowers and pieces of gold, went forth like Śakra among the immortals.
Bright as a thousand suns, hung with a hundred little bells, adorned with the most precious river-born gold, the chariot of Arjuna, garlanded with flame like fire itself, blazed forth, drawn by white steeds and shod with goodly wheels.
Mounted upon it, ape-bannered, the reins held by Keśava, with Gāṇḍīva and shafts in hand, stood the bowman whose equal on earth there is not, nor shall ever be at any time.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
About to overthrow the army of your son, he wore a form most terrible—he who, fair-armed and weaponless, could with his bare arms reduce men, horses, and elephants to ashes in battle.
That Bhīmasena, Vṛkodara, together with the twins, was the guardian of the heroes' chariot-host; beholding him sporting like a maddened bull or a lion, peerless in the world and the equal of great Indra—
—gazing upon Vṛkodara, unassailable, at the army's van, proud as a king of elephants, your warriors trembled, their spirits broken with fear, like camels mired in mud.
Then Janārdana spoke to the prince standing in the midst of the army, the unassailable, the best of the Bhāratas, Guḍākeśa.
Vāsudeva said: This guardian, blazing in his strength, who eyes our army like a lion—this is Bhīṣma, the banner of the Kuru race, by whom thirty horse-sacrifices were performed.
These divisions hide the mighty one as clouds conceal the hot-rayed sun. Having destroyed these, O foremost of men, then seek your battle with the bull of the Bhāratas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: On which side, Saṃjaya, did the warriors at the front fight gladly? Who there were high of heart, and who were dispirited and bewildered?
Who struck first there in that heart-shaking battle—my men or the Pāṇḍavas? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
In whose gathered army arose the fragrance of perfumes and garlands, and the auspicious words of the warriors as they roared aloud?
Saṃjaya said: In both armies there the warriors rejoiced with gladness, and on both sides arose the scents of garlands, incense, and drink.
As the close-massed, arrayed divisions, surging and swelling, crept forward, O bull of the Bhāratas, the clash between them grew immense.
Tumultuous was the din of the instruments, mingled with conches and kettledrums, with the trumpeting of elephants and the exultant shouts of the troops.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: On the field of righteousness, on Kurukṣetra, gathered together and eager to fight, what did my men and the Pāṇḍavas do, O Saṃjaya?
Saṃjaya said: But King Duryodhana, beholding the Pāṇḍava army drawn up in array, then approached his teacher and spoke these words.
Behold, O teacher, this mighty host of the sons of Pāṇḍu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.
Here are heroes, mighty archers, equal in battle to Bhīma and Arjuna: Yuyudhāna and Virāṭa, and Drupada the great chariot-warrior;
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the valiant king of Kāśi; Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, a bull among men;
Yudhāmanyu the bold, and the valiant Uttamaujas; the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī—all of them great chariot-warriors.
But of our own who are the most distinguished, mark them, O best of the twice-born: the leaders of my army; for your knowledge I name them to you.
Your honoured self, and Bhīṣma, and Karṇa, and Kṛpa, ever victorious in battle; Aśvatthāman and Vikarṇa, and likewise the son of Somadatta;
and many other heroes besides, who have laid down their lives for my sake, armed with manifold weapons, all skilled in war.
Boundless is this force of ours, guarded by Bhīṣma, whereas the force of theirs, guarded by Bhīma, is limited.
Therefore, stationed each in his proper place at all the points of access, let all of you, every one, guard Bhīṣma above all.
Then, kindling his joy, the aged Kuru grandsire, the glorious one, roaring loud like a lion, blew his conch.
