Thereupon conches and kettledrums, tabors and drums and horns were sounded all at once, and the noise of it was tumultuous.
Then, standing in their great chariot yoked with white steeds, Mādhava and the son of Pāṇḍu blew their divine conches.
Hṛṣīkeśa blew Pāñcajanya, Dhanaṃjaya blew Devadatta, and Vṛkodara of dreadful deeds blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka.
The king of Kāśi, that supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍin the great chariot-warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa, and the unvanquished Sātyaki;
Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, on every side, O lord of the earth, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā—each blew his several conch.
That tumultuous din, making sky and earth resound, rent the hearts of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons.
Then, beholding Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons drawn up in their ranks, as the clash of weapons was about to begin, the ape-bannered son of Pāṇḍu raised his bow
and then spoke this word to Hṛṣīkeśa, O lord of the earth: 'Set my chariot, O Acyuta, between the two armies,
that I may look upon these who stand here eager for battle, and see with whom I must do combat in this enterprise of war.
I would behold those who are gathered here ready to fight, seeking to do service in war to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.'
Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, having stationed that finest of chariots between the two armies
before Bhīṣma and Droṇa and all the lords of the earth, said: 'O Pārtha, behold these Kurus gathered together.'
There the son of Pṛthā saw standing fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and comrades too;
fathers-in-law and well-wishers as well, in both the armies. Beholding all these kinsmen arrayed there, the son of Kuntī
was filled with deep compassion, and in dejection spoke this: 'Seeing these my own people, O Kṛṣṇa, drawn up and longing to fight,
my limbs give way and my mouth grows parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.
Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand, and my very skin is aflame; I cannot stand firm, and my mind seems to reel.
And I behold omens of evil import, O Keśava; nor do I foresee any good in slaying my own kinsmen in battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I crave not victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingship, nor pleasures. What is kingship to us, O Govinda, what enjoyments, or even life itself?
Those for whose sake we desire kingship, enjoyments, and pleasures—these very ones stand here in battle, having renounced their lives and their wealth:
teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and kinsmen besides.
These I would not wish to slay, O slayer of Madhu, even though they slay me—no, not for the sovereignty of the three worlds, how much less for the earth!
By killing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, what joy could be ours, O Janārdana? Only sin would cling to us were we to slay these, though they be aggressors.
Therefore we ought not to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with their kin; for having killed our own people, how could we be happy, O Mādhava?
Even though these, their minds overcome by greed, see no fault in the ruin of the family, no crime in treachery to friends,
how should we not know to turn back from this sin, O Janārdana, we who clearly see the fault in the ruin of the family?
In the ruin of the family, the eternal laws of the family perish; and when the law has perished, lawlessness overwhelms the whole family.
From the prevalence of lawlessness, O Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family are corrupted; and when the women are corrupted, O scion of Vṛṣṇi, there arises confusion of castes.
Such confusion leads only to hell, both for the destroyers of the family and for the family itself; for their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice and water.
By these misdeeds of the destroyers of the family, which bring about the confusion of castes, the eternal laws of caste and the eternal laws of the family are uprooted.
And for those men whose family laws have been destroyed, O Janārdana, a dwelling in hell is ordained — so we have heard handed down.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Alas! We are resolved to commit a great sin, in that, out of greed for the pleasures of kingship, we stand ready to slay our own kin.
If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be the more blessed end for me.
Having spoken thus on the field of battle, Arjuna sank down upon the seat of the chariot, casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
Saṃjaya said: To him thus overcome by pity, his troubled eyes brimming with tears, despondent, the Slayer of Madhu spoke these words.
The Blessed Lord said: Whence has this faintheartedness come upon you in this hour of peril, O Arjuna — a thing unworthy of the noble, barring the way to heaven, bringing dishonor?
Yield not to unmanliness, O Pārtha; it does not become you. Cast off this base weakness of heart and arise, scorcher of foes!
Arjuna said: How, O Slayer of Madhu, shall I fight back with arrows in battle against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are worthy of my worship, O Slayer of foes?
For it were better in this world to eat even the bread of beggary than to slay these noble-souled elders. If I slew my elders, though they covet gain, I should taste, here and now, only delights smeared with blood.
Nor do we know which is the better for us — that we should conquer them, or that they should conquer us. Those whom if we slew we should not wish to live — the very sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — stand arrayed against us.
My very nature undone by the taint of pitiable weakness, my mind bewildered as to what is right, I ask you: tell me with certainty what is the better course. I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you.
For I do not see what could dispel this grief that withers my senses, even were I to win on earth an unrivaled and prosperous kingdom, or even lordship over the gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes, said to Govinda, "I shall not fight," and fell silent.
To him, O descendant of Bharata, as he sat despondent between the two armies, Hṛṣīkeśa spoke these words, as if with a smile.
The Blessed Lord said: You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living.
Never was there a time when I was not, nor you, nor these lords of men; nor shall any of us ever cease to be hereafter.
As the embodied soul passes, within this body, through childhood, youth, and old age, so does it pass to another body. The steadfast are not bewildered by this.
The contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and are impermanent; endure them, O descendant of Bharata.
The man whom these do not disturb, O bull among men — the steadfast one, alike in pain and pleasure — he is fit for immortality.
Of the unreal there is no being; of the real there is no ceasing to be. The truth of both has been perceived by the seers of reality.
Know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded. None can bring about the destruction of this imperishable one.
These bodies of the eternal embodied soul are said to come to an end, while it is indestructible and immeasurable. Therefore fight, O descendant of Bharata.
He who thinks this one to be a slayer, and he who thinks it slain — neither of them understands. It neither slays nor is slain.
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come to be, it shall not again cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
He who knows this one to be indestructible, eternal, unborn, and undiminishing — how, O Pārtha, can such a man cause anyone to be slain, or slay anyone?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As a man casts off worn-out garments and takes on others that are new, so the embodied soul casts off worn-out bodies and enters into others that are new.
Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, waters do not wet it, nor does the wind wither it.
It cannot be cut, it cannot be burned, it cannot be wetted, nor can it be dried. Eternal, all-pervading, fixed, unmoving, it is everlasting.
It is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchanging. Therefore, knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve.
And even if you should think it to be ever born and ever dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve for it.
For of one that is born, death is certain; and of one that is dead, birth is certain. Therefore, over a thing that cannot be averted, you ought not to grieve.
Beings are unmanifest in their beginnings, manifest in their middle states, and unmanifest again at their end, O descendant of Bharata. What occasion, then, for lament?
One beholds it as a marvel; another likewise speaks of it as a marvel; and another hears of it as a marvel; yet even having heard, no one truly knows it.
This embodied soul, dwelling in the body of every being, is eternally inviolable, O descendant of Bharata. Therefore you ought not to grieve for any creature.
And looking to your own dharma, you ought not to waver; for there is no greater good for a warrior than a righteous battle.
Happy are the warriors, O Pārtha, to whom comes unsought such a battle, an open gate to heaven.
But if you will not wage this righteous war, then, forsaking your own dharma and your honor, you shall incur sin.
People, too, will tell of your undying disgrace; and for one held in honor, dishonor is worse than death.
The great warriors will think that you withdrew from the battle out of fear; and you who were once highly esteemed by them will fall into contempt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And your enemies will speak many unspeakable words, scorning your prowess. What could be more painful than that?
Either slain, you shall attain heaven, or victorious, you shall enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved upon battle.
Holding pleasure and pain alike, gain and loss, victory and defeat, gird yourself then for battle; thus you shall incur no sin.
This wisdom has been declared to you according to Sāṃkhya; now hear it as it pertains to yoga, by which understanding, O Pārtha, once joined with it, you shall cast off the bondage of action.
In this path no effort is ever lost, and no obstacle arises; even a little of this dharma saves one from great fear.
Here the resolute understanding is one and single, O joy of the Kurus; but the thoughts of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.
The flowery speech that the unwise utter, O Pārtha — those who delight in the letter of the Veda, declaring that there is nothing more —
full of desire, intent on heaven, promising rebirth as the fruit of works, thronged with manifold rites directed toward enjoyment and power —
in those attached to enjoyment and power, whose minds are carried away by that speech, the resolute understanding fixed in contemplation is not established.
The Vedas have the three guṇas for their province; be free of the three guṇas, O Arjuna. Be free of the pairs of opposites, ever poised in purity, indifferent to acquisition and possession, master of yourself.
As much use as there is in a well when water floods on every side, so much is there in all the Vedas for the brāhmaṇa who truly knows.
Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.
Established in yoga, perform your actions, abandoning attachment, O Dhanaṃjaya, alike in success and in failure; for this evenness of mind is called yoga.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For action is far inferior to the yoga of understanding, O Dhanaṃjaya. Seek refuge in understanding; pitiable are those who act for the sake of fruits.
He who is joined to understanding casts off, here in this life, both good deeds and evil deeds. Therefore devote yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in action.
For the wise, joined to understanding, abandoning the fruit born of action, are freed from the bondage of birth and reach the state beyond all ill.
When your understanding crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, then you shall grow indifferent to all that has been heard and all that is yet to be heard.
When your understanding, bewildered by scripture, shall stand unmoving and unwavering, fixed in contemplation, then you shall attain to yoga.
Arjuna said: What is the description of the man of steadfast wisdom, who abides in contemplation, O Keśava? How does the man of steady mind speak, how does he sit, how does he walk?
The Blessed Lord said: When a man casts off all the desires that come into his mind, O Pārtha, content in the Self by the Self alone, then is he called a man of steadfast wisdom.
He whose mind is untroubled amid sorrows, who has no craving for pleasures, and from whom longing, fear, and anger have departed — he is called a sage of steady mind.
He who is without attachment on every side, who, meeting with whatever is good or evil, neither rejoices nor recoils — his wisdom stands firm.
And when, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs from every side, he withdraws his senses from the objects of sense, his wisdom stands firm.
The objects of sense turn away from the embodied one who abstains from them, yet the relish for them remains; but even that relish departs once he has beheld the Supreme.
For even in the man of discernment who strives, O son of Kuntī, the turbulent senses carry away the mind by force.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having restrained all these, let him sit, steadfast in yoga, intent on Me; for he whose senses are mastered — his wisdom stands firm.
In the man who dwells in thought upon the objects of sense, attachment to them is born; from attachment springs desire, and from desire arises anger.
From anger comes delusion, from delusion the wandering of memory; from the loss of memory comes the ruin of understanding, and from the ruin of understanding he perishes.
But the man of disciplined self, moving among the objects of sense with senses freed from longing and aversion and brought under his own control, attains to serenity.
In that serenity there arises for him the cessation of all his sorrows; for in the man of serene mind the understanding soon becomes firmly established.
There is no understanding for the undisciplined, nor for the undisciplined any power of contemplation; and for him without contemplation there is no peace — and for the peaceless, whence happiness?
For when the mind yields to the roving senses, it carries away his wisdom, as the wind carries away a ship upon the waters.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, he whose senses are wholly restrained from the objects of sense — his wisdom stands firm.
In that which is night for all beings, the man of self-restraint is awake; and that in which all beings are awake is night for the sage who sees.
As the waters enter the ocean, which, ever filling, abides unmoved, so he into whom all desires enter attains peace — not he who lusts after desires.
The man who, abandoning all desires, moves about free from longing, without the sense of "mine" and without egoism — he attains to peace.
This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; attaining it, none is deluded. Abiding in it even at the hour of death, one reaches the nirvāṇa of Brahman.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Arjuna said: If you hold understanding to be better than action, O Janārdana, then why do you urge me to this terrible deed, O Keśava?
With words that seem confused, you bewilder, as it were, my understanding. Tell me, therefore, with certainty, the one path by which I may attain the higher good.
The Blessed Lord said: In this world a twofold path was taught of old by me, O blameless one — that of knowledge for the followers of Sāṃkhya, and that of action for those devoted to yoga.
Not by abstaining from actions does a man attain freedom from action, nor by renunciation alone does he reach perfection.
For no one ever, even for a moment, remains without performing action; everyone is driven to act, helplessly, by the qualities born of material nature.
He who, restraining the organs of action, sits dwelling in his mind upon the objects of sense — that deluded soul is called a hypocrite.
But he who, restraining the senses with the mind, O Arjuna, undertakes through the organs of action the yoga of action, unattached — he excels.
Perform your appointed action, for action is better than inaction; even the maintenance of your body could not be accomplished without action.
Save for action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action; therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.
Having of old created mankind together with sacrifice, the Lord of Creatures said: By this shall you bring forth offspring; let this be the cow that yields all your desires.
By this nourish the gods, and let the gods nourish you; nourishing one another, you shall attain the highest good.
For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will grant you the enjoyments you desire; but he who enjoys their gifts without offering anything in return to them is verily a thief.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The good, who eat the remnants of sacrifice, are freed from all sins; but the wicked, who cook only for their own sake, partake of evil.
From food creatures come into being; from rain food is produced; from sacrifice arises rain; and sacrifice is born of action.
Know that action springs from Brahman, and Brahman springs from the Imperishable; therefore the all-pervading Brahman is ever established in sacrifice.
He who in this world does not keep turning the wheel thus set in motion lives in vain, O Pārtha — a man of sinful life, delighting in the senses.
But the man whose delight is in the Self alone, who is content in the Self, and satisfied within the Self — for him there exists no duty to be done.
For him there is no purpose whatever in what is done, nor any in what is left undone; nor has he any need to depend upon any being among all creatures.
Therefore, ever unattached, perform the action that ought to be done; for performing action without attachment, a man attains the Supreme.
For by action alone did Janaka and others attain perfection; and with regard to the welfare of the world too, you ought to act.
Whatever a great man does, that very thing other people do; whatever standard he sets, the world follows it.
For me, O Pārtha, there is nothing whatever to be done in the three worlds, nothing unattained that need be attained; yet I remain engaged in action.
For if I did not remain ever tirelessly engaged in action, men would follow my path in every way, O Pārtha.
These worlds would fall to ruin if I did not perform action; I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these creatures.
As the ignorant act, attached to action, O Bhārata, so should the wise man act, but unattached, desiring the welfare of the world.
Let him not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant who are attached to action; the wise man, himself disciplined, should engage in all actions and so encourage them to do likewise.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Actions are in every way performed by the qualities of material nature; but he whose soul is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer."
But he who knows the truth, O mighty-armed, about the divisions of the qualities and of action, recognizing that it is the qualities that act upon the qualities, does not become attached.
Those deluded by the qualities of material nature become attached to the actions of those qualities; but let not the man of complete knowledge unsettle those dull ones of incomplete knowledge.
Surrendering all actions to me, with your mind fixed on the Supreme Self, and becoming free from longing and from the sense of "mine," fight, your fever gone.
Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine, full of faith and free from cavil, they too are released from the bondage of actions.
But those who, cavilling at it, do not follow this teaching of mine — know them to be deluded in all knowledge, mindless, and lost.
Even the man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature; beings follow their nature — what can restraint accomplish?
In the object of each sense, attraction and aversion are seated; let none come under their sway, for they are his two waylayers.
Better is one's own duty, though imperfectly done, than the duty of another well performed; better is death in one's own duty — the duty of another is fraught with danger.
Arjuna said: But impelled by what does a man commit sin, O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if driven by force?
The Blessed Lord said: It is desire, it is wrath, born of the quality of passion, all-devouring and most sinful — know this to be the enemy here.
As fire is obscured by smoke, and a mirror by dust, as an embryo is enveloped by the womb's membrane, so is this enveloped by that.
Knowledge is enveloped by this constant enemy of the wise, O son of Kuntī — in the form of desire, an insatiable fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its seat; through these it deludes the embodied one, veiling his knowledge.
Therefore, O bull among the Bhāratas, first restraining the senses, cast off this sinful thing, the destroyer of knowledge and discrimination.
The senses, they say, are great; greater than the senses is the mind; greater than the mind is the intellect; but greater than the intellect is He.
Thus knowing Him who is beyond the intellect, and steadying the self by the Self, slay, O mighty-armed, the enemy in the form of desire, hard to overcome.
The Blessed Lord said: This imperishable yoga I declared to Vivasvat; Vivasvat told it to Manu; and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.
Thus received in succession, the royal sages knew it; but through the long lapse of time that yoga was lost here, O scorcher of foes.
That very same ancient yoga has today been declared by me to you, for you are my devotee and my friend; and this is the supreme secret.
Arjuna said: Later was your birth, earlier the birth of Vivasvat; how then am I to understand this — that you declared it in the beginning?
The Blessed Lord said: Many are the births that have passed for me and for you, O Arjuna; all of them I know, but you do not know them, O scorcher of foes.
Though I am unborn and of imperishable Self, though I am the Lord of all beings, yet, governing my own material nature, I come into being through my own power of illusion.
For whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata, and a rising up of unrighteousness, then I send forth myself.
For the protection of the good, for the destruction of the wicked, and for the firm establishment of righteousness, I come into being age after age.
He who thus knows in truth my divine birth and action, on leaving the body is not born again, but comes to me, O Arjuna.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Freed from passion, fear, and wrath, absorbed in me and taking refuge in me, many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have come to my state of being.
In whatever way men approach me, in that same way do I favor them; in every way, O Pārtha, men follow my path.
Desiring the fruition of their actions, men here worship the gods; for swiftly in the world of men comes the success born of action.
The fourfold order was created by me according to the divisions of quality and action; though I am its author, know me to be the non-doer, the changeless.
Actions do not taint me, nor have I any longing for the fruit of action; he who knows me thus is not bound by actions.
Knowing this, the ancient seekers of liberation also performed action; therefore do you too perform action, as it was done by those of old in former times.
What is action, what is inaction? — even the wise are bewildered here. I shall declare to you that action, knowing which you shall be freed from evil.
For the nature of action must be understood, and the nature of wrong action must be understood, and the nature of inaction too must be understood; profound is the course of action.
He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among men; he is disciplined, a doer of all action.
He whose every undertaking is free from the prompting of desire, whose actions are burned up in the fire of knowledge — him the wise call a sage.
Having abandoned attachment to the fruit of action, ever content, depending on nothing, even when fully engaged in action he does nothing at all.
Free from longing, his mind and self restrained, having relinquished all possessions, performing action with the body alone, he incurs no sin.
Content with what comes unsought, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, even-minded in success and in failure — though he acts, he is not bound.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, who acts for the sake of sacrifice — his whole action dissolves away.
Brahman is the offering, Brahman the oblation, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman; Brahman alone is to be reached by him who meditates upon Brahman in his action.
Some yogins perform sacrifice to the gods alone, while others offer the sacrifice itself as oblation into the fire of Brahman.
Some offer the senses, hearing and the rest, into the fires of restraint; others offer sound and the other objects of sense into the fires of the senses.
And others offer all the activities of the senses and the activities of the vital breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.
Some make sacrifice with material things, some with austerity, some with yoga; and others, ascetics of strict vows, sacrifice with study of scripture and with knowledge.
Some offer the outgoing breath into the incoming breath, and likewise the incoming into the outgoing, restraining the courses of inhalation and exhalation, intent upon the control of breath.
Others, with regulated diet, offer the vital breaths into the vital breaths; all these indeed are knowers of sacrifice, their impurities consumed by sacrifice.
Those who feed on the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman; this world is not for him who offers no sacrifice — how then the other, O best of the Kurus?
Thus manifold sacrifices are spread out before the face of Brahman; know them all to be born of action, and knowing this, you shall be liberated.
Better than the sacrifice of material things is the sacrifice of knowledge, O scorcher of foes; all action in its entirety, O Pārtha, culminates in knowledge.
Know that by humble reverence, by inquiry, and by service; the wise, the seers of truth, will instruct you in that knowledge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Knowing which you shall not again fall into such delusion, O son of Pāṇḍu, and through which you shall see all beings, without exception, within yourself and then in me.
Even if you were the most sinful of all sinners, by the raft of knowledge alone you shall cross over all wickedness.
As a kindled fire reduces firewood to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes.
For there exists here no purifier equal to knowledge; he who is himself perfected in yoga finds it in time within his own self.
The man of faith, devoted to it and master of his senses, attains knowledge; and having attained knowledge, he quickly reaches the supreme peace.
The ignorant one, devoid of faith, whose very self is doubt, comes to ruin; for the doubting soul there is neither this world nor the world beyond, nor any happiness.
The one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubt has been severed by knowledge, who is possessed of the self—such a one, O Dhanaṃjaya, actions do not bind.
Therefore, having cut away with the sword of knowledge this doubt born of ignorance that dwells in your heart, take your stand in yoga, and rise up, O Bhārata!
Arjuna said: You praise the renunciation of actions, O Kṛṣṇa, and again you praise yoga. Tell me with full certainty which one of these two is the better.
The Blessed Lord said: Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the highest good; yet of the two, the yoga of action is more excellent than the renunciation of action.
He is to be known as the perpetual renouncer who neither hates nor craves; for the one free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed, is easily released from bondage.
It is children, not the wise, who speak of Sāṃkhya and yoga as distinct; one who is rightly established in even one of them gains the fruit of both.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached by the yogins as well; he who sees Sāṃkhya and yoga as one, he truly sees.
But renunciation, O mighty-armed, is hard to attain without yoga; the sage yoked in yoga reaches Brahman before long.
Yoked in yoga, of purified self, his self mastered and his senses conquered, his self become the self of all beings—though he acts, he is not stained.
"I do nothing at all"—so should the yoked one, the knower of truth, think, even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing,
speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and closing his eyes—holding fast to the truth that it is the senses alone that move among the objects of the senses.
He who acts, surrendering his actions to Brahman and abandoning attachment, is untouched by evil, as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
With the body, the mind, the intellect, and the senses alone, the yogins perform action, abandoning attachment, for the purification of the self.
The yoked one, having abandoned the fruit of action, attains lasting peace; the unyoked one, driven by desire and attached to the fruit, is bound.
Renouncing all actions with the mind, the master of himself, the embodied one rests happily in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing to act.
The Lord creates for the world neither agency nor actions, nor the union of action with its fruit; it is inherent nature that takes its course.
The all-pervading one takes on no one's evil deed, nor indeed any good deed; knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and by this creatures are deluded.
But for those whose ignorance of the self has been destroyed by knowledge, their knowledge, like the sun, illumines that Supreme.
With their understanding fixed on That, their self in That, established in That, holding That as their supreme goal, they go to that from which there is no return, their stains shaken off by knowledge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In a brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant, and in a dog, and even in one who eats the flesh of dogs, the wise see the same.
Even here the round of birth is conquered by those whose mind is established in equanimity; for Brahman is flawless and the same in all, and therefore they abide in Brahman.
He would not rejoice on gaining what is pleasant, nor shudder on gaining what is unpleasant—steady of understanding, undeluded, the knower of Brahman, established in Brahman.
With his self unattached to outward contacts, he finds the happiness that lies within the self; with his self yoked in union with Brahman, he enjoys imperishable happiness.
For the enjoyments born of contact are wombs of pain alone; they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī, and the wise man does not delight in them.
He who is able, here in this very life, before he is freed from the body, to withstand the surge born of desire and anger—he is yoked, he is the happy man.
He whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, whose light too is within—that yogin, having become Brahman, attains the extinction that is Brahman.
The seers whose stains are worn away attain the extinction that is Brahman—their dualities cut away, their selves controlled, rejoicing in the welfare of all beings.
For the ascetics freed from desire and anger, their minds controlled, who have come to know the self, the extinction that is Brahman is present on every side.
Shutting out external contacts, fixing the gaze between the brows, making even the inward and outward breaths that move within the nostrils,
the sage whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained, intent on liberation, from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed—he is forever truly free.
Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all the worlds, the friend of all beings, one attains peace.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Blessed Lord said: He who performs the work that ought to be done without depending on its fruit—he is both a renouncer and a yogin, not the one who is without sacred fire and without rites.
That which they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava; for no one becomes a yogin who has not renounced his selfish purposes.
For the sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same one who has ascended to yoga, serenity is said to be the means.
For when one clings neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, having renounced all selfish intentions, then he is said to have ascended to yoga.
Let a man lift up the self by the self, and not let the self sink down; for the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
For him who has conquered the self by the self, the self is the friend of the self; but for one without self-mastery, the self alone abides in enmity, like a foe.
For one of conquered self, who is tranquil, the supreme Self stays steadfast amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and likewise in honor and dishonor.
He whose self is content with knowledge and discernment, who stands unmoved on the summit, whose senses are conquered, to whom a clod, a stone, and gold are alike—such a yogin is called yoked.
He whose understanding is the same toward well-wisher, friend, and foe, toward the indifferent, the neutral, the hateful, and the kinsman, and toward the good and the wicked alike—he is the most excellent.
Let the yogin ever yoke himself, abiding in a secret place, alone, his mind and self controlled, free of expectation and free of possessions.
Setting up for himself in a clean place a firm seat, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass,
there, making the mind one-pointed, with the activity of thought and senses restrained, seated upon his seat, let him practice yoga for the purification of the self.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Holding body, head, and neck erect, motionless and steady, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking about in any direction,
his self tranquil, his fear gone, firm in the vow of chastity, restraining the mind, with his thought on Me, let him sit yoked, holding Me as the supreme.
Thus ever yoking the self, the yogin of disciplined mind attains the peace that culminates in extinction and abides in Me.
Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, nor for one given to too much sleep, nor again for one who keeps awake, O Arjuna.
For one moderate in eating and recreation, moderate in his efforts at work, moderate in sleeping and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
When the disciplined mind comes to rest in the self alone, free of longing for all desires, then one is said to be yoked.
As a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker—that is the likeness remembered of the yogin of controlled mind, practicing the yoga of the self.
When the mind comes to rest, stilled by the practice of yoga, and when, beholding the self by the self, one is content within the self;
when one knows that boundless happiness which is grasped by the intellect and lies beyond the senses, and, established there, this man no longer wavers from the truth;
having gained which, he thinks no other gain greater than it, and, established in which, he is not shaken even by heavy sorrow—
let him know that disjunction from union with pain to be what is named yoga. That yoga is to be practiced with resolve and with an unwearied mind.
Abandoning without remainder all desires born of selfish intention, and restraining the whole host of the senses on every side by the mind alone,
little by little let him come to rest, by an intellect held firm in steadfastness; fixing the mind upon the self, let him not think of anything at all.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whenever and wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders away, from there let him rein it in and bring it under the sway of the self alone.
For supreme happiness comes to this yogin whose mind is tranquil, whose passion is stilled, who has become Brahman and is free of stain.
Thus ever yoking the self, the yogin freed from stain easily enjoys the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman.
His self yoked in yoga, seeing the same everywhere, he beholds the self abiding in all beings and all beings in the self.
He who sees Me everywhere and sees all things in Me—for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me.
The yogin who, established in oneness, worships Me as abiding in all beings—in whatever way he lives, that yogin lives in Me.
He who, by the likeness of himself, sees the same everywhere, O Arjuna, whether it be pleasure or pain—that yogin is held to be the highest.
Arjuna said: This yoga that you have declared to consist of equanimity, O slayer of Madhu—of it I do not see any stable foundation, because of the restlessness of the mind.
For the mind is restless, O Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate; I think the restraining of it as hard to achieve as that of the wind.
The Blessed Lord said: Without doubt, O mighty-armed, the mind is hard to restrain and unsteady; yet by practice, O son of Kuntī, and by dispassion it is held in check.
By one whose self is unrestrained, yoga is hard to attain—such is My judgment; but by one whose self is mastered and who strives, it can be attained by the proper means.
Arjuna said: One who does not strive, though endowed with faith, his mind fallen away from yoga, having failed to reach perfection in yoga—what path, O Kṛṣṇa, does he go to?
Does he not, fallen from both, perish like a scattered cloud, O mighty-armed, without foundation and bewildered upon the path of Brahman?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This doubt of mine, O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to cut away without remainder; for no other than you can be found to dispel this doubt.
The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha, neither here nor in the world beyond is there any ruin for him; for no one who does good, my dear, comes to a sorry end.
Having attained the worlds of those who do meritorious deeds, and having dwelt there for endless years, the one fallen from yoga is born again in the house of the pure and the prosperous.
Or else he comes to be born in the family of wise yogins; for such a birth as this is the more difficult to win in this world.
There he regains that union with the understanding gained in his former body, and from there he strives onward once more toward perfection, O joy of the Kurus.
For by that very practice of his former life he is carried onward, even against his will; and merely seeking to know yoga, he passes beyond the Brahman of the word.
But the yogin who strives with effort, his stains thoroughly purified, perfected through many births, then attains the supreme goal.
The yogin is greater than the ascetics, and held to be greater even than the men of knowledge, and the yogin is greater than the men of works; therefore become a yogin, O Arjuna.
And of all yogins, he who worships Me full of faith, his inmost self gone forth to Me—him I hold to be the most deeply yoked.
The Blessed Lord said: With your mind attached to Me, O Pārtha, practicing yoga and taking refuge in Me, hear how you shall know Me wholly and without doubt.
I shall declare to you in full this knowledge together with its realization, knowing which nothing further remains here to be known.
Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and attain it, scarcely one knows Me in truth.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego-sense — thus is My nature divided eightfold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This is My lower nature; but know, O mighty-armed one, My other and higher nature, which has become the living soul, by which this world is sustained.
Understand that all beings have their womb in these two natures. I am the origin of the whole universe, and likewise its dissolution.
There is nothing whatever higher than Me, O Dhanaṃjaya. Upon Me all this is strung, like rows of pearls upon a thread.
I am the savor in the waters, O son of Kuntī; I am the radiance in the moon and the sun; the sacred syllable Oṃ in all the Vedas, sound in the ether, and manhood in men.
I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the brilliance in fire; I am the life in all beings, and the austerity in ascetics.
Know Me, O Pārtha, as the eternal seed of all beings. I am the intelligence of the intelligent, the splendor of the splendid.
I am the strength of the strong, freed from desire and passion; and in beings I am desire that is not opposed to dharma, O bull of the Bhāratas.
And whatever states of being there are — of sattva, of rajas, or of tamas — know that they proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.
Deluded by these three states composed of the guṇas, all this world fails to recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
For this divine māyā of Mine, composed of the guṇas, is hard to overcome; but those who take refuge in Me alone cross beyond this māyā.
The evildoers, the deluded, the basest of men do not take refuge in Me; their knowledge carried off by māyā, they cleave to the demonic nature.
Four kinds of virtuous men worship Me, O Arjuna: the afflicted, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of gain, and the one who knows, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Of these, the knower, ever steadfast and devoted to the One, excels; for to the knower I am exceedingly dear, and he is dear to Me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Noble indeed are all of these, but the knower I hold to be My very Self; for, his soul made steadfast, he is established in Me alone as the supreme goal.
At the end of many births, the man of knowledge takes refuge in Me, realizing, 'Vāsudeva is all.' Such a great soul is very hard to find.
Those whose knowledge is carried off by this or that desire resort to other deities, observing this or that rite, constrained by their own nature.
Whatever form any devotee desires to worship with faith, that same unwavering faith I bestow upon him.
Endowed with that faith, he seeks to propitiate that form, and from it he obtains his desires — desires ordained by Me alone.
But the fruit gained by these men of little understanding is perishable. The worshippers of the gods go to the gods; My devotees come to Me.
The unintelligent think of Me, the unmanifest, as having come into manifestation, not knowing My higher nature, imperishable and supreme.
I am not revealed to all, veiled as I am by My yoga-māyā. This deluded world does not recognize Me, the unborn and imperishable.
I know the beings that are past, that are present, and that are yet to come, O Arjuna; but Me no one knows.
By the delusion of the pairs of opposites, sprung from desire and aversion, O Bhārata, all beings fall into bewilderment at their birth, O scorcher of foes.
But those men of virtuous deeds in whom sin has come to an end — they, freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites, worship Me, firm in their vows.
Those who take refuge in Me and strive for release from old age and death — they come to know that Brahman in its fullness, the supreme Self, and action in its entirety.
Those who know Me together with the Adhibhūta, the Adhidaiva, and the Adhiyajña — they, their minds made steadfast, know Me even at the hour of departure.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Arjuna said: What is that Brahman? What is the Adhyātma, the supreme Self? What is action, O best of beings? What is declared to be the Adhibhūta, and what is called the Adhidaiva?
Who and how is the Adhiyajña here in this body, O slayer of Madhu? And how, at the hour of departure, are You to be known by those of disciplined self?
The Blessed Lord said: The imperishable, the supreme, is Brahman; one's own essential nature is called the Adhyātma; and the creative force that brings about the origin of the states of beings is named action (karman).
The Adhibhūta is the perishable existence; the Puruṣa is the Adhidaiva; and the Adhiyajña am I Myself, here within this body, O best of the embodied.
And whoever, at the hour of his end, departs leaving the body while remembering Me alone, attains to My being; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever state of being one remembers when at the last he gives up the body, to that very state he goes, O son of Kuntī, ever shaped by the thought of it.
Therefore at all times remember Me, and fight. With mind and intellect fixed on Me, you shall surely come to Me alone.
With a mind made steadfast by the yoga of practice, not straying to anything else, meditating upon Him, one attains the supreme, the divine Puruṣa, O Pārtha.
He who meditates upon the Seer, the ancient, the ruler, subtler than the subtlest, the sustainer of all, whose form is beyond thought, sun-hued, beyond the darkness —
at the hour of departure, with unwavering mind, endowed with devotion and with the power of yoga, fixing the breath rightly between the brows — he attains that supreme, divine Puruṣa.
That which the knowers of the Veda call the imperishable, which the passion-free ascetics enter, desiring which men practice the discipline of brahmacarya — that state I shall declare to you in brief.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Controlling all the gates of the body, confining the mind within the heart, fixing one's own breath in the head, established in the steadfastness of yoga,
uttering the single syllable Oṃ, which is Brahman, and remembering Me — he who thus departs, giving up the body, goes to the supreme goal.
To him whose mind dwells on no other, who remembers Me constantly and without ceasing — to that ever-steadfast yogin, O Pārtha, I am easy to attain.
Having come to Me, the great souls who have reached the highest perfection do not return to rebirth, that impermanent abode of sorrow.
All the worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return, O Arjuna; but having come to Me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth.
Those who know that a day of Brahmā lasts a thousand ages, and that his night too ends only after a thousand ages — they are the men who know day and night.
At the coming of the day, all manifestations spring forth from the unmanifest; at the coming of the night they dissolve back into that same source called the unmanifest.
This same multitude of beings, coming into existence again and again, dissolves helplessly at the coming of the night, O Pārtha, and comes forth again at the coming of the day.
But higher than that unmanifest is another, an eternal Unmanifest, which, when all beings perish, does not itself perish.
That Unmanifest is called the Imperishable; they declare it the supreme goal, attaining which men do not return. That is My supreme abode.
That supreme Puruṣa, O Pārtha, within whom all beings dwell and by whom all this is pervaded, is to be attained by undivided devotion.
Now I shall tell you, O bull of the Bhāratas, of the time at which yogins, having departed, go to return no more, and of that at which they go to return again.
Fire, light, the day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the sun's northern course — departing then, men who know Brahman go to Brahman.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Smoke, the night, likewise the dark fortnight, the six months of the sun's southern course — departing then, the yogin attains the lunar light and returns.
These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are held to be eternal. By the one a man goes never to return; by the other he returns again.
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin is ever deluded. Therefore at all times be steadfast in yoga, O Arjuna.
Whatever fruit of merit is laid down for the Vedas, for sacrifices, for austerities, and for gifts — the yogin, knowing all this, transcends it all and attains the supreme, primal abode.
The Blessed Lord said: To you, who do not cavil, I shall now declare this most secret knowledge together with its realization, knowing which you shall be freed from evil.
This is the king of sciences, the king of secrets, the supreme purifier, directly intelligible, in accord with dharma, easy to practice, and imperishable.
Men without faith in this dharma, O scorcher of foes, fail to attain Me and return upon the path of death and the round of rebirth.
By Me, in My unmanifest form, all this universe is pervaded. All beings abide in Me, but I do not abide in them.
And yet the beings do not abide in Me — behold My sovereign yoga! Sustaining all beings, yet not dwelling in them, My Self is the source of beings.
As the mighty wind, ranging everywhere, abides forever in the ether, so understand that all beings abide in Me.
All beings, O son of Kuntī, return into My nature at the end of a kalpa; at the beginning of the next kalpa I send them forth again.
Resting upon My own nature, I send forth again and again this whole multitude of beings, helpless under the sway of that nature.
Nor do these actions bind Me, O Dhanaṃjaya, for I remain seated as one indifferent, unattached to those actions.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Under My oversight, nature brings forth all that moves and does not move; by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves.
The deluded despise Me, dwelling as I do in a human form, not knowing My higher nature as the great Lord of all beings.
Vain in their hopes, vain in their deeds, vain in their knowledge, and bereft of discernment, they cleave to a deluding nature, demonic and fiendish.
But the great souls, O Pārtha, who have taken refuge in the divine nature, worship Me with minds undistracted, knowing Me as the imperishable source of all beings.
Ever glorifying Me, striving, firm in their vows, and bowing before Me with devotion, ever steadfast they worship Me.
Others too, sacrificing through the sacrifice of knowledge, worship Me — as the One, as the manifold, as variously present, facing in every direction.
I am the rite, I am the sacrifice, I am the offering to the ancestors, I am the healing herb, I am the sacred chant, I am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation.
I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, the grandsire; I am the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable Oṃ, and the Ṛk, the Sāman, and the Yajus as well.
I am the goal, the upholder, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend; the origin, the dissolution, the foundation, the resting-place, and the imperishable seed.
I give heat; I withhold the rain and send it forth. I am immortality and also death; I am being and non-being, O Arjuna.
The knowers of the three Vedas, the soma-drinkers, purified of sin, worshipping Me with sacrifices, pray for passage to heaven; reaching the holy world of Indra, lord of the gods, they enjoy in heaven the divine pleasures of the gods.
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, when their merit is exhausted they enter the world of mortals. Thus, following the dharma of the three Vedas and craving objects of desire, they obtain only the coming and the going.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But to those men who, thinking on no other, worship Me — to them, ever steadfast, I bring attainment of what they lack and preservation of what they have.
Even those devotees of other gods who sacrifice endowed with faith — they too sacrifice to Me alone, O son of Kuntī, though not according to the prescribed rite.
For I am the enjoyer and the lord of all sacrifices; but men do not truly know me, and therefore they fall away.
Those vowed to the gods go to the gods; those vowed to the ancestors go to the ancestors; the worshippers of spirits go to the spirits; but those who sacrifice to me come to me.
Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—that offering, presented with devotion by the pure of heart, I accept and partake of.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you perform—do that, O son of Kuntī, as an offering to me.
Thus you shall be freed from the bonds of action that bear fruits good and ill; with your self yoked to the discipline of renunciation, liberated, you shall come to me.
I am the same toward all beings; to me none is hateful and none is dear. But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I too am in them.
Even if a man of the most evil conduct worships me with undivided devotion, he is to be reckoned righteous, for he has rightly resolved.
Swiftly he becomes righteous of soul and attains lasting peace. Know this for certain, O son of Kuntī: my devotee never perishes.
For taking refuge in me, O Pārtha, even those of sinful birth—women, vaiśyas, and śūdras alike—they too attain the supreme goal.
How much more, then, the holy brāhmaṇas and devout royal sages! Having come into this impermanent and joyless world, worship me.
Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow down to me; having thus yoked your self with me as your highest goal, you shall come to me alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Blessed Lord said: Once more, O mighty-armed, hear my supreme word, which I shall speak to you, who delight in me, out of desire for your good.
Neither the hosts of gods nor the great sages know my origin, for I am in every way the source of the gods and the great sages.
Whoever knows me as unborn and without beginning, the great lord of the worlds, he, undeluded among mortals, is freed from all sins.
Understanding, knowledge, freedom from delusion, patience, truth, self-restraint, tranquility, pleasure, pain, being, non-being, fear, and fearlessness—
non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy—these manifold states of beings arise from me alone.
The seven great sages of old, and likewise the four Manus, sharing in my nature, were born of my mind; from them came these creatures of the world.
Whoever truly knows this manifest power and the yoga of mine is united with me through unshakable yoga; of this there is no doubt.
I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds. Knowing this, the wise, endowed with feeling, worship me.
With their thoughts fixed on me, their lives surrendered to me, enlightening one another and ever speaking of me, they are content and they rejoice.
To those who are ever steadfast and worship me with love, I grant that yoga of understanding by which they come to me.
Out of compassion for them alone, dwelling within their being, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
Arjuna said: You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier; the eternal, divine Spirit, the primal god, unborn and all-pervading.
So all the seers proclaim you—the divine sage Nārada, and Asita Devala, and Vyāsa; and you yourself declare it to me.
All that you tell me I hold to be true, O Keśava; for neither the gods nor the dānavas know your manifestation, O Blessed One.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You alone know yourself by yourself, O supreme Spirit, source of beings, lord of beings, god of gods, master of the world.
You alone are fit to declare in full your divine self-manifestations, by which manifest powers you stand pervading these worlds.
How may I know you, O master of yoga, by meditating on you constantly? In what various forms, O Blessed One, are you to be contemplated by me?
Tell me again in detail of your yoga and your manifest power, O Janārdana; for as I listen there is no satiety in me for this nectar.
The Blessed Lord said: Come, I shall declare to you my divine self-manifestations—but only the chief of them, O best of the Kurus, for there is no end to my extent.
I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings; I am the beginning, the middle, and the very end of all beings.
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among lights, the radiant sun; among the Maruts I am Marīci; among the lunar mansions I am the moon.
Among the Vedas I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods I am Vāsava; among the senses I am the mind; in beings I am consciousness.
Among the Rudras I am Śaṃkara; among the yakṣas and rākṣasas, the lord of wealth; among the Vasus I am fire; among the peaks I am Meru.
Among priests know me to be their chief, Bṛhaspati, O Pārtha; among commanders of armies I am Skanda; among waters I am the ocean.
Among the great sages I am Bhṛgu; among utterances I am the single syllable Oṃ; among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of muttered prayer; among the immovable, the Himālaya.
Among all trees I am the aśvattha; among the divine sages, Nārada; among the gandharvas, Citraratha; among the perfected ones, the sage Kapila.
Among horses know me to be Uccaiḥśravas, born of the nectar; among lordly elephants, Airāvata; and among men, the king.
Among weapons I am the thunderbolt; among cows I am Kāmadhuk, the wish-granting cow; I am Kandarpa, the begetter; among serpents I am Vāsuki.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Among the nāgas I am Ananta; among the dwellers in the waters I am Varuṇa; among the ancestors I am Aryaman; among those who govern I am Yama.
Among the daityas I am Prahlāda; among reckoners I am Time; among beasts I am the king of beasts, the lion; and among birds I am Vainateya, Garuḍa.
Among purifiers I am the wind; among bearers of weapons I am Rāma; among fishes I am the makara; among flowing rivers I am the Jāhnavī, the Gaṅgā.
Of creations I am the beginning, the end, and the middle as well, O Arjuna; among sciences I am the science of the supreme Self; among those who debate, I am their reasoned argument.
Among letters I am the letter A; among compounds I am the copulative dvandva. I alone am imperishable Time; I am the Sustainer facing in every direction.
I am all-seizing Death, and the origin of things yet to be; and among feminine powers I am fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, constancy, and patience.
Among the Sāman hymns I am the Bṛhatsāman; among meters I am the Gāyatrī; among months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; among seasons I am the flower-bearing spring.
Among the deceitful I am the gambling of dice; I am the splendor of the splendid; I am victory, I am resolve; I am the goodness of the good.
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanaṃjaya; among sages I am Vyāsa; among seers I am Uśanā the poet.
Among those who chastise I am the rod; among those who seek victory I am statecraft; among secret things I am silence; and I am the wisdom of the wise.
And whatever is the seed of all beings, that too am I, O Arjuna; there is no being, moving or unmoving, that could exist apart from me.
There is no end to my divine manifestations, O scorcher of foes; what I have declared of the extent of my power is but by way of illustration.
Whatever being possesses power, beauty, or might, know that each has sprung from a fragment of my splendor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But what need have you, O Arjuna, to know all this in detail? With a single fragment of myself I stand supporting this entire world.
Arjuna said: By the supreme and secret word concerning the Self, which out of grace toward me you have spoken, this delusion of mine has been dispelled.
For the arising and the passing away of beings I have heard from you in full, O lotus-eyed one, and your imperishable majesty as well.
Even as you have declared yourself to be, O supreme Lord, so it is. Yet I long to behold your sovereign form, O supreme Spirit.
If you think it possible for me to behold it, O Lord, then, O master of yoga, show me your imperishable Self.
The Blessed Lord said: Behold my forms, O Pārtha, by the hundreds and by the thousands—manifold and divine, of many colors and many shapes.
Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts; behold, O descendant of Bharata, many marvels never seen before.
Here, gathered together in one place within my body, behold now the whole world, with all that moves and is unmoving, O Guḍākeśa, and whatever else you wish to see.
But you cannot behold me with this eye of your own; I give you a divine eye—behold my sovereign yoga.
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus, O king, Hari, the great lord of yoga, then revealed to Pārtha his supreme sovereign form—
with many mouths and eyes, with many wondrous aspects, with many divine ornaments, with many divine weapons raised on high;
wearing divine garlands and raiment, anointed with divine fragrances—the all-marvelous god, infinite, facing in every direction.
If the light of a thousand suns were to blaze forth all at once in the sky, that might resemble the splendor of that great-souled one.
There, gathered together in one place yet divided in manifold ways, the son of Pāṇḍu then beheld the whole world within the body of the god of gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Dhanaṃjaya, seized with wonder and his hair standing on end, bowing his head to the god with joined palms, spoke:
Arjuna said: I behold within your body, O god, the gods and all the assembled hosts of beings—Brahmā the lord seated upon his lotus throne, and all the seers and the divine serpents.
With many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes I behold you, infinite of form on every side. I see in you no end, no middle, nor any beginning, O lord of all, O form of all.
Crowned with a diadem, bearing mace and discus, a mass of radiance blazing on every side—I behold you, hard to gaze upon all around, with the brilliance of blazing fire and sun, immeasurable.
You are the supreme Imperishable, the one to be known; you are the highest resting-place of this universe; you are the changeless guardian of the eternal dharma; you are the everlasting Spirit, so I deem you.
Without beginning, middle, or end, of infinite power, with countless arms, the moon and sun your eyes—I behold you, your mouth a blazing sacrificial fire, scorching this universe with your own splendor.
This space between heaven and earth, and all the quarters, are pervaded by you alone. Seeing this wondrous and terrible form of yours, the three worlds tremble in anguish, O great-souled one.
Yonder hosts of gods enter into you; some, afraid, with joined palms extol you. Crying "Hail!" the throngs of great sages and perfected ones praise you with abundant hymns of praise.
The Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the drinkers of vapor, the hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras, and siddhas—all gaze upon you, and all are amazed.
Beholding your mighty form of many mouths and eyes, O mighty-armed, of many arms, thighs, and feet, of many bellies, terrible with many fangs, the worlds tremble in anguish, and so do I.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Touching the sky, ablaze, of many hues, with gaping mouths and vast blazing eyes—seeing you thus, my inmost self trembles, and I find neither steadiness nor peace, O Viṣṇu.
Seeing your mouths, terrible with fangs and resembling the fire of universal dissolution, I know not the quarters of the sky, and I find no refuge. Be gracious, O lord of gods, O dwelling-place of the world.
And yonder, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all of them, together with the hosts of kings—Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of the charioteer too—along with our own foremost warriors as well,
hastening, they enter your mouths, terrible with fangs and dreadful; some are seen clinging between your teeth, their heads ground to powder.
As the many torrents of the rivers race straight toward the sea, so do these heroes of the world of men enter your blazing mouths.
As moths in headlong speed plunge into a blazing fire to their destruction, so too do these peoples plunge into your mouths in headlong speed, to their destruction.
Devouring on every side, you lick up all the worlds with your flaming mouths; filling the whole universe with radiance, your terrible splendors scorch it, O Viṣṇu.
Tell me who you are, you of terrible form. Homage to you, O best of gods; be gracious. I long to know you, the Primal One, for I do not comprehend your working.
The Blessed Lord said: I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of the worlds, set in motion here to annihilate the worlds. Even without you, all these warriors arrayed in the opposing ranks shall cease to be.
Therefore rise up and win glory; conquer your foes and enjoy a flourishing kingdom. By me alone are these already slain; be you merely the instrument, O Savyasācin.
Droṇa and Bhīṣma and Jayadratha, and Karṇa, and the other warrior-heroes as well — slay them, already slain by me. Do not falter. Fight! You shall conquer your rivals in battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Hearing this speech of Keśava, the Diademed One, trembling, his palms joined, made obeisance, and bowing low spoke once more to Kṛṣṇa in a faltering voice, sore afraid.
Arjuna said: Rightly, O Hṛṣīkeśa, does the world rejoice and take delight in your glory; the rākṣasas flee in terror to every quarter, and all the hosts of the siddhas bow before you.
And why should they not bow to you, O great-souled one, greater even than Brahmā, the first creator? O infinite Lord of gods, abode of the universe, you are the Imperishable, the existent, the non-existent, and what lies beyond both.
You are the primal God, the ancient Spirit; you are the supreme resting-place of this universe. You are the knower and the known, the highest abode; by you the universe is pervaded, O you of infinite form.
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, the moon, Prajāpati, and the great-grandsire. Homage, homage to you a thousandfold, and again and yet again, homage, homage to you!
Homage to you from before and from behind; homage to you on every side, O All. Of infinite valor and boundless might, you encompass all things, and therefore you are all.
Whatever I said rashly, thinking you but a friend — 'Hey Kṛṣṇa! Hey Yādava! Hey friend!' — in ignorance of this your majesty, through heedlessness or through affection,
and however, for jest's sake, I slighted you at play, in bed, while seated, or at meals, whether alone or before others, O Acyuta — for that I beg your pardon, O immeasurable one.
You are the father of the world, of all that moves and is still; you are its object of worship, its venerable teacher. There is none equal to you — how then could there be another greater? — in the three worlds, O you of incomparable power.
Therefore, bowing down and prostrating my body, I implore your grace, O Lord, worthy of praise. As a father bears with a son, a friend with a friend, a lover with his beloved, so should you bear with me, O God.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I am thrilled to have seen what was never seen before, yet my mind is shaken with fear. Show me, O God, that other form of yours; be gracious, O Lord of gods, abode of the universe.
I long to see you just as before, crowned with the diadem, bearing the mace and the discus in your hand. Take on once more that four-armed form, O thousand-armed one, O you whose body is the universe.
The Blessed Lord said: By my grace, O Arjuna, and through my own power, this supreme form of mine has been shown to you — full of light, universal, infinite, primal — which none but you has ever beheld.
Not by study of the Vedas and sacrifices, not by gifts, not by rites, not by fierce austerities, can I be seen in this form in the world of men by any other than you, O foremost of the Kurus.
Let there be no fear in you, no bewilderment, at beholding this dread form of mine. Free from fear, glad of heart, behold once more this very form of mine.
Saṃjaya said: Having thus spoken to Arjuna, Vāsudeva revealed again his own form, and the great-souled one, becoming once more gentle of aspect, comforted him in his terror.
Arjuna said: Beholding this gentle human form of yours, O Janārdana, I am now composed, my mind restored, returned to my natural state.
The Blessed Lord said: This form of mine that you have seen is very hard to behold; even the gods forever long for the sight of this form.
Not by the Vedas, not by austerity, not by almsgiving, nor by sacrifice, can I be seen in such a form as you have seen me.
But by undivided devotion, O Arjuna, can I in this form be known and truly seen and entered into, O scorcher of foes.
He who does my work, who holds me supreme, who is devoted to me, freed from attachment, without enmity toward any being — he comes to me, O Pāṇḍava.
Arjuna said: Those devotees who, ever steadfast, thus worship you, and those who worship the Imperishable, the Unmanifest — which of these are the better versed in yoga?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Blessed Lord said: Those who fix their minds on me and, ever steadfast, worship me, endowed with supreme faith — these I deem the most perfect in yoga.
But those who worship the Imperishable, the indefinable, the Unmanifest, the all-pervading and unthinkable, the changeless, the immovable, the eternal,
restraining the whole host of the senses, even-minded toward all, rejoicing in the welfare of all beings — they too attain me.
Greater is the toil of those whose minds are fixed upon the Unmanifest; for the goal of the Unmanifest is hard for the embodied to reach.
But those who, renouncing all their actions in me and holding me supreme, worship me, meditating on me with undivided yoga —
of these, whose thought is set on me, I become ere long the deliverer from the ocean of death-bound transmigration, O Pārtha.
Fix your mind on me alone, let your understanding rest in me; thereafter you shall dwell in me alone — of this there is no doubt.
But if you cannot fix your thought steadily upon me, then seek to reach me through the yoga of repeated practice, O Dhanaṃjaya.
If you are unable even in practice, be intent on works done for my sake; doing your deeds for my sake, you shall attain perfection.
And if you are unable to do even this, then, taking refuge in union with me, renounce the fruit of all action, with the self subdued.
For knowledge is better than practice, and meditation surpasses knowledge, and the renunciation of the fruit of action is better than meditation; from renunciation peace follows at once.
He who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of 'mine' and from egoism, the same in pain and pleasure, forbearing,
ever content, the yogin, self-controlled, of firm resolve, his mind and understanding offered up to me — such a devotee of mine is dear to me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He from whom the world does not shrink, and who does not shrink from the world, who is freed from elation, impatience, fear, and agitation — he too is dear to me.
Free from expectation, pure, capable, indifferent, untroubled, renouncing every undertaking — such a devotee of mine is dear to me.
He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced both the fair and the foul, and is full of devotion — he is dear to me.
The same to foe and to friend, the same in honor and dishonor, the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, freed from attachment,
alike in blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, with no fixed abode, steadfast in mind, full of devotion — that man is dear to me.
But those who honor this nectar of dharma as it has been declared, full of faith, holding me supreme — those devotees are exceedingly dear to me.
The Blessed Lord said: This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field; and him who knows it, those who know such things call the knower of the field.
Know me too as the knower of the field in all fields, O Bhārata. The knowledge of the field and its knower — that I hold to be true knowledge.
What that field is, and of what nature, and with what modifications, and whence it arises; and who he is, and what his powers — hear this from me in brief.
It has been sung in many ways by the seers, severally in the diverse Vedic hymns, and also in the words of the aphorisms on Brahman, reasoned and well-determined.
The great elements, egoism, the intellect, and the Unmanifest; the eleven senses, and the five objects of the senses;
desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness, steadfastness — this, in brief, is the field declared together with its modifications.
Humility, freedom from pretense, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness, service to one's teacher, purity, steadiness, self-restraint;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
dispassion toward the objects of sense, and absence of egoism; insight into the evil of birth, death, old age, sickness, and pain;
non-attachment, freedom from clinging to son, wife, home, and the rest; and constant evenness of mind amid the befalling of the desired and the undesired;
unswerving devotion to me through undivided yoga, resort to solitary places, and distaste for the throng of people;
constancy in the knowledge of the Self, and insight into the goal of the knowledge of truth — this is declared to be knowledge; and ignorance is whatever differs from this.
I shall now declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains immortality: the supreme Brahman, without beginning, of which it is said neither that it is existent nor non-existent.
With hands and feet on every side, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side, with ears on every side, it stands enveloping all things in the world.
Shining through the functions of all the senses, yet devoid of all the senses; unattached, yet the support of all; free from the strands of nature, yet their enjoyer.
Without and within all beings, unmoving yet moving; by reason of its subtlety it is unknowable, and it is far off and yet near.
Undivided, yet abiding as though divided among beings; that which is to be known is the sustainer of beings, their devourer, and their creator.
It is the light even of lights, said to be beyond all darkness; it is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the goal of knowledge, seated in the heart of all.
Thus the field, and likewise knowledge, and that which is to be known, have been told in brief. My devotee, understanding this, attains to my being.
Know that both Nature and the Spirit are without beginning; and know that the modifications and the strands of nature arise from Nature.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the production of effect and cause and agency, Nature is said to be the cause; the Spirit is said to be the cause in the experiencing of pleasures and pains.
For the Spirit, seated in Nature, experiences the strands born of Nature; attachment to the strands is the cause of its births in good and evil wombs.
The witness, the consenter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the Great Lord, and also called the Supreme Self — such is the supreme Spirit within this body.
He who thus knows the Spirit and Nature together with its strands, in whatever state he may live, is not born again.
By meditation some behold the Self in the self by the self; others by the yoga of knowledge, and yet others by the yoga of action.
But others, not knowing thus, worship having heard it from others; they too, devoted to what they have heard, cross beyond death.
Whatever being comes into existence, whether unmoving or moving, know that it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field, O bull of the Bhāratas.
He who sees the Supreme Lord abiding alike in all beings, the imperishable amid the perishing — he truly sees.
For seeing the Lord present alike everywhere, he does not destroy the Self by the self, and thereby he attains the supreme goal.
He who sees that actions are in every way performed by Nature alone, and the Self as the non-doer — he truly sees.
When he perceives the separate existence of beings as resting in the One, and their expansion from that alone, then he attains to Brahman.
Being beginningless and free from the strands of nature, this imperishable Supreme Self, though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, neither acts nor is tainted.
As the all-pervading ether, by reason of its subtlety, is never tainted, so the Self, abiding everywhere in the body, is never tainted.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As the single sun illumines this whole world, so does the Field-knower illumine the entire Field, O Bhārata.
Those who thus discern, with the eye of knowledge, the difference between the Field and the Field-knower, and the release of beings from material nature—they attain the Supreme.
The Blessed Lord said: Once more I shall declare the supreme knowledge, the highest of all knowings, by knowing which all the sages have passed from here to the highest perfection.
Having taken refuge in this knowledge and come to share in My own nature, they are not born again even at a new creation, nor are they disturbed at the dissolution.
My womb is the great Brahman; in it I cast the seed. From that, O Bhārata, comes the birth of all beings.
Whatever forms take birth in all the wombs, O son of Kuntī, the great Brahman is their womb, and I am the seed-giving father.
Goodness, passion, and darkness—these are the qualities born of material nature, O mighty-armed; they bind the imperishable embodied one within the body.
Of these, goodness, being pure, is luminous and free from ill; it binds, O sinless one, through attachment to happiness and through attachment to knowledge.
Know passion to be of the nature of craving, arising from thirst and attachment; it binds the embodied one, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action.
But darkness, know, is born of ignorance and deludes all embodied beings; it binds, O Bhārata, through heedlessness, sloth, and sleep.
Goodness binds one to happiness, O Bhārata, and passion to action; but darkness, veiling knowledge, binds one to heedlessness.
Goodness prevails by overpowering passion and darkness, O Bhārata; and passion overpowers goodness and darkness, while darkness overpowers goodness and passion.
When through all the gates of this body the light of knowledge arises, then one should know that goodness has grown strong.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Greed, activity, the undertaking of works, restlessness, and longing—these arise when passion has grown strong, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Darkness, inertia, heedlessness, and delusion—these arise when darkness has grown strong, O joy of the Kurus.
When the embodied one meets dissolution while goodness is strong, he then attains the spotless worlds of those who know the highest.
Meeting dissolution in passion, one is born among those attached to action; and dissolving in darkness, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
They say the fruit of good action is of the nature of goodness, pure; but the fruit of passion is suffering, and the fruit of darkness is ignorance.
From goodness arises knowledge, and from passion greed; from darkness arise heedlessness, delusion, and ignorance.
Those established in goodness go upward; the passionate remain in the middle; and those who dwell in the workings of the lowest quality, the darkened, go downward.
When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities, and knows that which is beyond the qualities, he attains to My being.
Transcending these three qualities that spring from the body, the embodied one, freed from birth, death, old age, and sorrow, attains immortality.
Arjuna said: By what marks is one known who has transcended these three qualities, O Lord? What is his conduct, and how does he pass beyond these three qualities?
The Blessed Lord said: He who hates not illumination, activity, or delusion when they arise, O Pāṇḍava, nor longs for them when they cease;
who, seated as though indifferent, is not disturbed by the qualities; who, thinking only "the qualities are at work," stands firm and does not waver;
