who is alike in sorrow and joy, self-poised, regarding clod, stone, and gold as equal; who is steadfast, the same toward the dear and the unwelcome, the same in blame and in praise of himself;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward the side of friend and of foe, renouncing all undertakings—he is said to have transcended the qualities.
And he who serves Me with unswerving devotion in yoga—he, transcending these qualities, is fit to become Brahman.
For I am the ground of Brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss.
The Blessed Lord said: They speak of an imperishable aśvattha tree, with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the hymns; he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas.
Its branches stretch below and above, nourished by the qualities, with sense-objects as their twigs; and below, its roots reach onward, binding to action in the world of men.
Its form is not perceived here as it truly is—it has no end, no beginning, no foundation. Having cut down this aśvattha with its firmly grown roots, by the strong axe of detachment,
then that goal is to be sought, gaining which one returns no more: "I take refuge in that primal Person from whom the ancient streaming-forth has flowed."
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever devoted to the supreme Self, with desires stilled, released from the dualities known as pleasure and pain—the undeluded go to that imperishable goal.
Neither sun nor moon nor fire illumines that, gaining which they return no more—that is My supreme abode.
An eternal portion of My very Self, become a living soul in the world of the living, draws to itself the senses, with mind as the sixth, that abide in material nature.
When the lord of the body takes on a body, and again when he departs from it, he takes these along and moves on, as the wind bears scents from their source.
Presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste, and smell, and over the mind as well, this one enjoys the objects of the senses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whether departing, abiding, or enjoying, accompanied by the qualities, the deluded do not perceive him; but those with the eye of knowledge perceive him.
The yogins, striving, behold him established in the self; but the unrefined of soul, the mindless, though they strive, do not behold him.
The radiance that resides in the sun and illumines the whole world, and that which is in the moon and in fire—know that radiance to be Mine.
Entering the earth, I sustain all beings by My energy; and becoming the sap-filled Soma, I nourish all the plants.
Becoming the fire Vaiśvānara, I dwell in the bodies of living creatures and, joined with the in-breath and out-breath, I digest the four kinds of food.
And I am seated in the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. By all the Vedas I alone am to be known; I am the author of Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas.
There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable is all beings; the unchanging is called the imperishable.
But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the highest Self, who, entering the three worlds, sustains them—the imperishable Lord.
Since I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, therefore in the world and in the Veda I am renowned as the Supreme Person.
He who, undeluded, knows Me thus as the Supreme Person—he, knowing all, worships Me with his whole being, O Bhārata.
Thus this most secret teaching has been declared by Me, O sinless one. Awakening to this, a man becomes wise and has accomplished all there is to do, O Bhārata.
The Blessed Lord said: Fearlessness, purity of heart, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness;
non-violence, truth, freedom from anger, renunciation, peace, freedom from slander, compassion toward beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, freedom from malice, and freedom from overweening pride—these belong, O Bhārata, to one born to the divine endowment.
Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance—these belong, O Pārtha, to one born to the demonic endowment.
The divine endowment is held to lead to liberation, the demonic to bondage. Grieve not, O Pāṇḍava; you are born to the divine endowment.
There are two orders of created beings in this world, the divine and the demonic. The divine has been described at length; now hear from Me, O Pārtha, of the demonic.
Demonic men know neither action nor abstention from action; in them there is found neither purity nor good conduct nor truth.
They say the world is without truth, without foundation, without a Lord, brought into being by no orderly mutual cause—what else but born of desire?
Holding fast to this view, ruined in soul and feeble in understanding, they rise up as enemies of the world, doers of fierce deeds, bent on its destruction.
Clinging to insatiable desire, filled with hypocrisy, conceit, and pride, having seized through delusion upon false notions, they act with impure resolves.
Beset by measureless cares that end only with death, devoted to the enjoyment of desires as the highest aim, convinced that this is all there is;
bound by a hundred cords of hope, given over to desire and anger, they strive to amass wealth by unjust means for the sake of sensual enjoyment.
"This I have gained today; this longing of my heart I shall attain; this is mine, and this wealth too shall be mine hereafter."
"That foe I have slain, and others too I shall slay. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, mighty, and happy."
"I am rich and high-born; who else is equal to me? I shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice"—thus deluded by ignorance,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
bewildered by many thoughts, enmeshed in the net of delusion, addicted to the enjoyment of desires, they fall into a foul hell.
Self-conceited, unbending, filled with the pride and intoxication of wealth, they perform sacrifices that are sacrifices in name only, with hypocrisy and without due rite.
Given over to egotism, force, arrogance, desire, and anger, these spiteful men hate Me, who dwell within their own bodies and the bodies of others.
These haters, cruel and vile among men, the most degraded, I hurl ceaselessly, those evil ones, into demonic wombs amid the rounds of rebirth.
Fallen into demonic wombs, deluded birth after birth, never reaching Me, O son of Kuntī, they thence go to the lowest course.
Threefold is this gate of hell, the ruin of the self—desire, anger, and greed; therefore one should abandon these three.
Released from these three gates of darkness, O son of Kuntī, a man works for the good of his soul and thence goes to the supreme course.
He who, casting aside the ordinance of scripture, acts under the impulse of desire attains neither perfection nor happiness nor the supreme course.
Therefore let scripture be your authority in determining what is to be done and what is not; knowing what is declared by the ordinance of scripture, you should act here in this world.
Arjuna said: Those who, casting aside the ordinance of scripture, yet sacrifice filled with faith—what is their standing, O Kṛṣṇa? Is it goodness, passion, or darkness?
The Blessed Lord said: The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature—of goodness, of passion, and of darkness. Hear of it.
The faith of each is in accord with his nature, O Bhārata. Man is made of his faith; as his faith is, so is he.
Those of goodness worship the gods; those of passion worship the yakṣas and rākṣasas; and the others, men of darkness, worship the departed and the hordes of spirits.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those men who practice grim austerity not ordained by scripture, joined to hypocrisy and egotism, driven by the force of desire and passion,
torturing, in their senselessness, the host of elements within the body, and Me too who dwell within the body—know them to be of demonic resolve.
The food, too, that is dear to each is of three kinds, and so are sacrifice, austerity, and giving. Hear now of their distinction.
Foods that promote length of life, vitality, strength, health, ease, and delight, that are savory, smooth, substantial, and gladdening to the heart — such are dear to those of sāttvika nature.
Foods that are bitter, sour, salty, exceedingly hot, pungent, harsh, and burning are sought by the man of rajas; they bring pain, sorrow, and disease.
Food that is stale, drained of its savor, putrid, kept overnight, the leavings of others, and unfit for offering — such is dear to the man of tamas.
That sacrifice which is offered according to the ordinance by those who crave no fruit, the mind being settled in the thought 'this is to be sacrificed and nothing more' — that sacrifice is sāttvika.
But that sacrifice which is offered with an eye to its fruit, and likewise for the sake of display — know that sacrifice, O best of the Bhāratas, to be rājasa.
A sacrifice devoid of ordinance, with no food distributed, lacking the sacred verses, without priestly gifts, and destitute of faith — that they declare to be tāmasa.
Reverence shown to the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, uprightness, continence, and non-injury — this is called austerity of the body.
Speech that causes no agitation, that is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, together with the constant practice of sacred recitation — this is called austerity of speech.
Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, and purity of disposition — this is called austerity of the mind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This threefold austerity, practiced with the highest faith by disciplined men who crave no fruit, is declared to be sāttvika.
That austerity which is performed for the sake of respect, honor, and reverence, and out of ostentation, is here declared rājasa — unsteady and impermanent.
That austerity which is performed through a deluded notion, with self-torture, or for the purpose of ruining another, is declared to be tāmasa.
That gift which is given with the thought 'it ought to be given,' to one who can make no return, in a fit place and time and to a worthy recipient — that gift is held to be sāttvika.
But that gift which is given for the sake of a return, or with an eye to its fruit, or grudgingly — that gift is held to be rājasa.
That gift which is given in the wrong place and time and to unworthy persons, without due respect and with contempt, is declared to be tāmasa.
'Oṃ Tat Sat' — this is held to be the threefold designation of Brahman; by it of old were ordained the brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices.
Therefore, with the utterance of 'Oṃ,' the acts of sacrifice, gift, and austerity prescribed by ordinance ever proceed among those who expound Brahman.
With the word 'Tat,' and without aiming at any fruit, the various acts of sacrifice and austerity and the acts of giving are performed by those who seek release (mokṣa).
In the sense of 'reality' and of 'goodness' the word 'Sat' is employed; and likewise, O Pārtha, the word 'Sat' is applied to an auspicious deed.
Steadfastness in sacrifice, in austerity, and in giving is called 'Sat'; and an action done for the sake of That is likewise designated 'Sat.'
Whatever is offered, given, or undertaken as austerity, and whatever is done without faith, is called 'Asat,' O Pārtha; it avails nothing hereafter, nor here.
Arjuna said: I wish to know, O mighty-armed one, the truth of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and likewise, distinctly, of relinquishment (tyāga), O Hṛṣīkeśa, O slayer of Keśin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Blessed Lord said: The seers understand by renunciation the laying aside of acts done from desire; the discerning declare the relinquishment of the fruit of all actions to be relinquishment.
Some thoughtful men declare that action is to be relinquished as a thing of evil; others, that acts of sacrifice, gift, and austerity are not to be relinquished.
Hear my conclusion on this matter of relinquishment, O best of the Bhāratas; for relinquishment, O tiger among men, is declared to be of three kinds.
Acts of sacrifice, gift, and austerity are not to be relinquished; they must indeed be performed. Sacrifice, gift, and austerity are purifiers of the thoughtful.
Yet even these actions are to be performed having abandoned attachment and their fruits — this, O Pārtha, is my settled and supreme conviction.
But the renunciation of a prescribed action is not fitting; its abandonment through delusion is declared to be tāmasa.
He who relinquishes an action merely because it is painful, from fear of bodily affliction, makes a rājasa relinquishment, and gains none of the fruit of relinquishment.
When a prescribed action is performed simply because it ought to be done, O Arjuna, having abandoned attachment and the fruit as well — that relinquishment is held to be sāttvika.
He does not loathe disagreeable work, nor cling to agreeable work — the relinquisher, suffused with sattva, wise, and his doubts cut away.
For it is not possible for an embodied being to relinquish actions entirely; but he who relinquishes the fruit of action is called a relinquisher.
The fruit of action is of three kinds — unwished, wished, and mixed — and it accrues after death to those who have not relinquished, but never to the renouncers.
Learn from me, O mighty-armed one, these five causes, declared in the Sāṃkhya doctrine that brings actions to their end, for the accomplishment of all works.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The seat of action, likewise the agent, and the instruments of various kinds, the manifold and distinct exertions, and divine providence as the fifth among them.
Whatever action a man undertakes with body, speech, or mind, be it right or wrong, these five are its causes.
This being so, he who, through an untrained understanding, looks upon the self alone as the agent — that man of perverse mind does not truly see.
He whose disposition is free of the sense of 'I,' whose understanding is not stained — even though he slay these worlds, he slays not, nor is he bound.
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower — this is the threefold impulse to action; the instrument, the act, and the agent — this is the threefold sum of action.
Knowledge, action, and the agent are each declared to be of three kinds according to the distinction of the guṇas; hear of these too, duly, in the enumeration of the qualities.
That knowledge by which one beholds in all beings a single, imperishable Being, undivided amid the divided — know that knowledge to be sāttvika.
But that knowledge which, by reason of separateness, perceives in all beings manifold existences of distinct kinds — know that knowledge to be rājasa.
But that which clings to a single effect as though it were the whole, without reason, having no grasp of the real, and trifling — that is declared to be tāmasa.
An action that is prescribed, free of attachment, done without passion or aversion by one who seeks no fruit — that is called sāttvika.
But that action which is performed by one seeking to gratify desire, or again with the sense of 'I,' and with great toil — that is declared to be rājasa.
That action which is undertaken through delusion, with no regard for its consequence, for loss, for injury, or for one's own capacity — that is called tāmasa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Free from attachment, not speaking of himself, endowed with steadfastness and zeal, unmoved in success and failure — such an agent is called sāttvika.
Passionate, eager for the fruit of action, greedy, of a violent nature, impure, swayed by joy and grief — such an agent is declared to be rājasa.
Undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, slothful, despondent, and procrastinating — such an agent is called tāmasa.
Hear now, O Dhanaṃjaya, the threefold distinction of understanding and of steadfastness according to the guṇas, set forth fully and severally.
That understanding which knows action and abstention, what is to be done and what is not, fear and fearlessness, bondage and release — that, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
That understanding by which one discerns wrongly right and wrong, and what is to be done and what is not — that understanding, O Pārtha, is rājasa.
That understanding which, enveloped in darkness, deems wrong to be right and sees all things reversed — that, O Pārtha, is tāmasa.
That steadfastness by which, through unwavering yoga, one holds fast the workings of the mind, the breaths, and the senses — that, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
But that steadfastness by which, O Arjuna, one clings to duty, pleasure, and wealth, craving their fruit with attachment — that, O Pārtha, is rājasa.
That steadfastness by which a dull-witted man does not let go of sleep, fear, grief, despondency, and conceit — that, O Pārtha, is tāmasa.
Now hear from me, O bull of the Bhāratas, of the threefold happiness — that in which one delights through practice and comes to the end of sorrow.
That which at first is like poison but in its ripening is like nectar — that happiness, born of the serenity of one's own understanding of the self, is declared sāttvika.
That which, born of the contact of the senses with their objects, is at first like nectar but in its ripening is like poison — that happiness is held to be rājasa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That happiness which both at first and in its sequel deludes the self, arising from sleep, sloth, and heedlessness — that is declared to be tāmasa.
There is no being on earth, nor again in heaven among the gods, that could be free from these three guṇas born of Prakṛti.
The duties of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas, and of śūdras too, O scorcher of foes, are apportioned according to the guṇas that spring from their own nature.
Calm, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness, knowledge, discernment, and faith in what is — these are the duties of the brāhmaṇa, born of his own nature.
Heroism, majesty, steadfastness, skill, and not fleeing in battle, generosity, and a lordly bearing — these are the duties of the kṣatriya, born of his own nature.
Tillage, the tending of cattle, and trade are the duties of the vaiśya, born of his own nature; and the śūdra's duty, born of his nature too, consists of service.
Devoted each to his own duty, a man attains perfection. Hear now how one intent on his own work finds that perfection.
That One from whom the activity of all beings springs, by whom all this is pervaded — worshiping Him through his own work, a man finds perfection.
Better one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Performing the work ordained by one's own nature, a man incurs no guilt.
One should not abandon, O son of Kuntī, the work to which one is born, even though it be flawed; for all undertakings are veiled by flaw, as fire by smoke.
He whose understanding is unattached everywhere, who has mastered himself and from whom longing has departed, attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of actionlessness.
Learn from me in brief, O son of Kuntī, how, having attained perfection, one reaches Brahman — that which is the highest consummation of knowledge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Endowed with a purified understanding, restraining the self with steadfastness, abandoning the objects of sense beginning with sound, and casting away passion and aversion;
frequenting solitude, eating but little, with speech, body, and mind controlled, ever devoted to the yoga of meditation, taking refuge in dispassion;
having let go of egoism, force, arrogance, desire, anger, and possession, free from the sense of 'mine' and at peace — he becomes fit for oneness with Brahman.
Become Brahman, serene in self, he neither grieves nor craves; alike toward all beings, he gains supreme devotion to Me.
Through devotion he comes to know Me — how great I am and who I am in truth; then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me forthwith.
Though ever performing all actions, taking refuge in Me, he attains by My grace the eternal, imperishable abode.
Renouncing in thought all actions unto Me, intent on Me, having recourse to the yoga of understanding, be ever fixed in thought upon Me.
With your thought on Me, by My grace you shall cross over all difficulties; but if from egoism you will not heed, you shall perish.
If, clinging to egoism, you think 'I will not fight,' vain is this resolve of yours; your own nature will compel you.
Bound, O son of Kuntī, by your own deeds born of your innate nature, that very thing which in delusion you wish not to do, you shall do even against your will.
The Lord, O Arjuna, dwells in the heart-region of all beings, whirling all beings round by his māyā as though they were mounted upon a machine.
To him alone go for refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata; by his grace you shall attain the supreme peace and the eternal abode.
Thus has the knowledge, more secret than all that is secret, been declared to you by me. Ponder it fully, and then act as you will.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hear again my supreme word, the most secret of all. Because you are dearly beloved by me, I shall now declare to you what is for your good.
Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow down to me. To me alone you shall come; truly I promise you this, for you are dear to me.
Abandoning all duties, come to me alone for refuge. I shall liberate you from all sins; grieve not.
This is never to be told by you to one who practices no austerity, nor to one without devotion, nor to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who scoffs at me.
Whoever shall declare this supreme secret among my devotees, rendering the highest devotion to me, shall come to me alone, without doubt.
And among men there shall be none who renders me more cherished service than he, nor shall there be another on earth dearer to me than he.
And whoever shall study this sacred dialogue of ours, by him I shall be worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge: such is my conviction.
And the man who, full of faith and free from spite, should merely listen to it—he too, set free, shall attain the blessed worlds of those whose deeds are meritorious.
Has this been heard by you, O Pārtha, with a mind fixed upon one point? Has the delusion born of ignorance been destroyed in you, O Dhanaṃjaya?
Arjuna said: My delusion is destroyed, and through your grace, O Acyuta, I have regained my memory. I stand firm, my doubts dispelled; I will do your word.
Saṃjaya said: Thus did I hear this marvelous dialogue, making the hair stand on end, between Vāsudeva and the great-souled Pārtha.
By the grace of Vyāsa I have heard this supreme secret, this yoga, from Kṛṣṇa, the lord of yoga, declaring it in person and with his own voice.
O king, recalling again and again this wondrous and holy dialogue of Keśava and Arjuna, I thrill with joy time after time.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And recalling again and again that exceedingly marvelous form of Hari, great is my wonder, O king, and I rejoice over and over.
Wherever there is Kṛṣṇa, the lord of yoga, wherever there is Pārtha the bowman, there are fortune, victory, prosperity, and steadfast righteousness: such is my conviction.
Saṃjaya said: Then, beholding Dhanaṃjaya bearing his arrows and the Gāṇḍīva bow, the great chariot-warriors once again let loose a mighty roar.
The Pāṇḍavas and the Somakas, and those who followed them, gladdened heroes, blew their conches, born of the sea.
Then kettledrums and tabors, krakaca-trumpets and cow-horns were all struck at once, and a tremendous din arose.
Then the gods together with the gandharvas and the ancestors, O lord of men, and the hosts of siddhas and cāraṇas, gathered there eager to behold the spectacle.
And the highly blessed sages, placing Śatakratu at their head, assembled there together to witness that great slaughter.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, beholding those two armies, vast as the ocean, roused and arrayed for battle and surging again and again, O king—
the hero loosed his armor, laid aside his excellent weapon, swiftly descended from his chariot, and on foot, with hands joined in reverence—
gazing toward his grandsire, Yudhiṣṭhira the king of righteousness, with words restrained, set forth, facing eastward, toward the host of the foe.
Beholding him setting forth, Dhanaṃjaya the son of Kuntī swiftly stepped down from his chariot and, together with his brothers, followed him.
And the lord Vāsudeva walked behind him, and the foremost kings too, full of eagerness, went after him.
Arjuna said: What have you resolved, O king, that leaving us behind you set out on foot, facing eastward toward the army of the enemy?
Bhīmasena said: Where will you go, O king of kings, with armor and weapons cast aside, while the enemy's hosts stand mailed, and forsaking your brothers, O lord of the earth?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nakula said: When you, my eldest brother, go forth in this manner, O Bhārata, fear torments my heart. Tell me, whither do you mean to go?
Sahadeva said: While this dreadful press of battle is upon us and the fight is to be joined, where will you go, advancing thus toward the foe, O king?
Saṃjaya said: Though thus addressed by his brothers, O delight of the Kurus, Yudhiṣṭhira, his speech restrained, said nothing at all, but went straight on.
To them the greatly wise and high-minded Vāsudeva spoke, as though smiling: His purpose I have understood.
This king, having sought the leave of Bhīṣma and Droṇa, of Gautama and of Śalya, indeed of all his elders, will then do battle with his foes.
For it is heard that in the ancient ordinance whoever does battle without seeking the leave of his elders is plainly held in ill regard by those who are greater than he.
But he who, having sought their leave according to the scriptures, fights with those greater than himself—his is certain victory in war: such is my conviction.
As Kṛṣṇa spoke thus, in the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son there arose a great cry of dismay, while others among them fell silent.
Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira from afar, the soldiers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son spoke to one another: This man is a disgrace to his line, undone.
Plainly, as if afraid, this king Yudhiṣṭhira approaches Bhīṣma, drawing near with his brothers, a suppliant begging for refuge.
With Dhanaṃjaya for protector, and Vṛkodara the Pāṇḍava, and Nakula and Sahadeva—how is it that the son of Pāṇḍu comes forward in fear?
Surely he was not born in a kṣatriya line renowned upon the earth, weak of spirit as he is, whose heart is thus stricken with terror in the fray.
Then all those kṣatriyas fell to praising the Kauravas and, become glad and joyful at heart, each waved his garments aloft.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all the warriors there reviled Yudhiṣṭhira, O lord of the people, together with his brothers and with Keśava.
Then that Kaurava host, having cried shame upon Yudhiṣṭhira, fell silent again all at once, O lord of the people.
What will this king say? What will Bhīṣma answer? What will Bhīma, who glories in battle, say? And what will Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna say?—thus they wondered.
What does he intend to say? A very great uncertainty then arose in both armies, O king, on account of Yudhiṣṭhira.
Plunging into the enemy's host, thronged with arrows and spears, he swiftly approached Bhīṣma, encircled by his brothers.
Then, clasping his feet with both hands, the Pāṇḍava king addressed Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, who stood ready for battle.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I take my leave of you, O unassailable one; I shall fight against you, dear father. Grant me your leave, dear father, and bestow upon me your blessings.
Bhīṣma said: Had you not come to me thus before the battle, O lord of the earth, I should have cursed you, great king, unto your defeat, O Bhārata.
I am pleased, my son; fight, and win victory, O Pāṇḍava. Whatever else you desire, that too may you obtain in the battle.
And let a boon be chosen, O Pārtha; what do you wish from us? When matters stand thus, O great king, defeat shall not be yours.
A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is no one's slave: this is the truth, O great king. By their wealth I am bound to the Kauravas.
Therefore I speak to you, O delight of the Kurus, words as of a eunuch: I have been bought with wealth, O Kaurava. What do you desire other than battle?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Counsel me, O greatly wise one, ever seeking my good; fight for the Kaurava's sake. This is forever the boon I ask of you.
Bhīṣma said: O king, what help can I render you in this, O delight of the Kurus? Fight I shall, willingly, for another's sake; tell me what you wish to say.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How may I conquer you, unvanquished, in the fray? Counsel me in this for my good, if you see what is best.
Bhīṣma said: I see no man, O son of Kuntī, who could vanquish me as I fight in the battle—not even Śatakratu himself in person.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Then, grandsire, I ask you—homage be to you—tell me yourself the means by which you may be overcome by foes in battle.
Bhīṣma said: I see no enemy, my child, who could conquer me in battle; the hour of my death has not yet come. Come to me again.
Saṃjaya said: Then Yudhiṣṭhira, O delight of the Kurus, received Bhīṣma's words with bowed head and once more saluted him.
Then the mighty-armed one set forth again toward the teacher's chariot, in full view of all the armies, passing through their midst together with his brothers.
Having saluted Droṇa and made the rightward circumambulation about him, he spoke to that unassailable one a word that sought his own highest good.
I take my leave of you, O venerable one; I shall fight, freed of all guilt, and may I conquer all my foes when granted your leave, O brāhmaṇa.
Droṇa said: Had you not come to me, resolved upon battle, I should have cursed you wholly, great king, unto your utter defeat.
Therefore, Yudhiṣṭhira, I am content, and honored by you, O sinless one. I grant you leave: fight, and win the victory.
And I shall fulfill your desire; tell me what you long for. When matters stand thus, O great king, what do you wish other than battle?
A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is no one's slave: this is the truth, O great king. By their wealth I am bound to the Kauravas.
Therefore I speak to you words as of a eunuch: what do you wish other than battle? I shall fight for the Kaurava's sake, yet your victory is to be wished for by me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Wish me victory, O brāhmaṇa, and counsel me for my good; fight for the Kaurava's sake. This is the boon I have chosen.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Droṇa said: Certain is your victory, O king, you whose counselor is Hari. And I assure you: in battle you shall conquer your foes.
Where there is righteousness, there is Kṛṣṇa; where there is Kṛṣṇa, there is victory. Fight, go forth, O son of Kuntī; ask of me—what shall I tell you?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I ask you, O best of the twice-born; hear what I wish to say. How may I conquer you, unvanquished, in the fray?
Droṇa said: There is no victory for you so long as I fight in battle. Strive swiftly, O king, together with your brothers, for my slaying.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Alas! Then tell me, O mighty-armed one, the means of your own destruction. Bowing low, O teacher, I ask you this—homage be to you.
Droṇa said: I see no enemy, my child, who could slay me as I stand in battle, fighting in full fury and pouring forth floods and torrents of arrows—
save when, O king, I have resolved to fast unto death, have laid down my weapons and grown senseless to the world—then among warriors one might slay me in battle. This truth I tell you.
And I shall cast away my weapons in the battle on hearing some most grievous tidings from a man whose word is to be trusted: this truth I tell you.
Saṃjaya said: Having heard these words of the wise son of Bhāradvāja, O great king, and having taken leave of that teacher, he went toward the son of Śaradvat.
Saluting Kṛpa and walking around him in reverence, that king, skilled in speech, spoke this word to the most unassailable of men.
I ask your leave, O teacher; I shall fight, freed of all blame. With your sanction, O sinless one, may I conquer all my foes.
Kṛpa said: Had you not come to me, resolved upon the battle, I would have cursed you, O great king, to utter ruin in every way.
A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is no man's slave. That is the truth, O great king: I am bound by wealth to the Kauravas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For their sake I must fight—such is my resolve, O great king. Therefore I speak to you like one unmanned: what do you wish, other than battle?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Then come, I shall ask you, O teacher; hear my words.
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus, the king grew troubled and, his senses faltering, said nothing more. But the descendant of Gotama, perceiving what he meant to ask, answered him: I cannot be slain, O lord of earth; fight, and win the victory.
Pleased by your coming, O ruler of men, I shall ever rise up and pray for your victory. This truth I tell you.
Having heard these words of the descendant of Gotama, O great king, and having taken leave of Kṛpa, the king went on toward the lord of the Madras.
Then, saluting Śalya and walking around him in reverence, the king spoke to that unassailable one a word that sought his own highest good.
I ask your leave, O teacher; I shall fight, freed of all blame. With your sanction, O great king, may I conquer my foes.
Śalya said: Had you not come to me, resolved upon the battle, I would have cursed you, O great king, to defeat in the field.
I am pleased, and I am honored; let what you desire be yours. I grant you leave: fight, and win the victory.
Speak further, O hero: what do you need, what shall I give you? Things being as they are, O great king, what do you wish, other than battle?
A man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is no man's slave. That is the truth, O great king: I am bound by wealth to the Kauravas.
I shall fulfill your desire as you wish it, O sister's son. Therefore I speak to you like one unmanned: what do you wish, other than battle?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Counsel me always toward my highest good, O great king. Fight, if you must, for the enemy's sake—this is the boon I choose.
Śalya said: Tell me what help I may render you here, O best of kings. I shall fight, if I must, for the enemy's sake, for I have been bought by the Kauravas with wealth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That very promise you made me during the preparations is my boon, in truth: in battle you must break the fire and spirit of the charioteer's son.
Śalya said: This desire of yours shall be fulfilled as you wish it, O son of Kuntī. Go, fight without fear; I pledge you your victory.
Saṃjaya said: Then the son of Kuntī, having taken leave of his maternal uncle, the lord of the Madrakas, went forth from the great host, surrounded by his brothers.
But Vāsudeva approached the son of Rādhā upon the field, and then the elder brother of Gada spoke to him thus, for the Pāṇḍavas' sake:
I have heard, Karṇa, that out of enmity toward Bhīṣma you will not fight. Choose our side, O son of Rādhā, so long as Bhīṣma is not slain.
And when Bhīṣma is slain, O son of Rādhā, you may return again to the battle to aid the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, if you deem it fair and fitting.
Karṇa said: I shall do nothing displeasing to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Keśava. Know that I have laid down my very life as one who seeks Duryodhana's good.
Saṃjaya said: Hearing that word, Kṛṣṇa turned back, O descendant of Bharata, and rejoined the Pāṇḍavas, with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head.
Then in the midst of the host the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas proclaimed aloud: Whoever chooses us, him I in turn choose, for the sake of his aid.
Then, looking upon them, Yuyutsu, his heart gladdened, said this to the King of Righteousness, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Kuntī:
I shall fight, before his very eyes, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the battle, for your cause, O great king, if you will choose me, O sinless one.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Come, come! We shall all fight your foolish brothers. Yuyutsu, both Vāsudeva and we say so with one accord.
I choose you, O mighty-armed one; fight for my sake. In you alone are seen the funeral offering and the continuing line of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Cleave to us, O prince of splendor, who cleave to you. The evil-minded, overbearing son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall not endure.
Saṃjaya said: Then Yuyutsu of the Kuru race, forsaking your sons, went over to the army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, sounding the war-drum as he went.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, greatly rejoicing along with his younger brothers, once more took up his radiant armor, bright with gold.
All those bulls among men mounted again their several chariots, and then they once more arrayed their battle-formation as it had been before.
They sounded their war-drums and kettledrums by the hundreds, and those bulls among men raised lion-roars of many kinds.
Beholding the Pāṇḍavas, those tigers among men, standing upon their chariots, the kings led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna all rejoiced again with gladness.
Seeing the dignity of the sons of Pāṇḍu, who honored those worthy of honor, the rulers of earth there praised them exceedingly.
And the kings spoke of the friendship and the compassion of those great souls, timely as it was, and of their supreme tenderness toward their kinsmen.
"Well done, well done!" rang out on every side—holy words of praise from men of renown, gladdening the mind and the heart.
The barbarians and the noble Āryas who there saw and heard of that conduct of the sons of Pāṇḍu wept then, their voices choked with feeling.
Then those high-spirited men, full of joy, beat their great war-drums and kettledrums by the hundreds, and blew their conches white as cow's milk.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the armies were thus arrayed, both mine and the others', who struck the first blow there—the Kurus or the Pāṇḍavas?
Saṃjaya said: Together with his brothers, O king, your son Duryodhana, placing Bhīṣma at the head, advanced with his army.
Likewise all the Pāṇḍavas, with Bhīmasena at their head, eager for battle with Bhīṣma, advanced with gladdened hearts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Roars and shrill clamoring cries, krakaca trumpets and cow-horn pipes, kettledrums, tabors, and drums, the neighing of horses and the trumpeting of elephants—
—rose from both armies, O king. Then they charged at us, and we roared back in answer; and at that there arose a vast tumult.
At that great upheaval, in the clash of the Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the mighty hosts trembled at the blasts of conches and drums, like forests shaken by the wind.
As the armies, thronged with kings and elephants, horses and chariots, advanced in that inauspicious hour, there arose a tumultuous roar of the hosts, like that of oceans churned by the gale.
As that tumultuous, hair-raising din arose, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena bellowed like a bull.
The blare of conches and drums, the trumpeting of elephants, and the lion-roars of the troops—all these the roar of Bhīmasena overwhelmed.
Over the neighing of horses in their thousands throughout the ranks, the cry of Bhīmasena rose above every other sound.
Hearing that roar of his, loud as a thundercloud and ringing like Indra's bolt, your soldiers were stricken with terror.
And all the beasts of burden voided their dung and urine at that hero's cry, as lesser creatures do at the roar of a lion.
Showing himself in dreadful form, roaring like a great storm-cloud, terrifying your sons, he bore down upon your army.
As that great archer came on, his own brothers surrounded him, covering him with showers of arrows as clouds veil the sun.
There were Duryodhana your son, and Durmukha, Duḥsaha, Śala, Duḥśāsana the mighty car-warrior, and Durmarṣaṇa too, O king,
Viviṃśati, Citrasena, and Vikarṇa the great car-warrior, Purumitra, Jaya, Bhoja, and the valiant son of Somadatta.
Brandishing their great bows like storm-clouds flashing lightning, and taking up iron shafts like vipers darting forth from their holes,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Against them the sons of Draupadī, and the son of Subhadrā that great car-warrior, and Nakula and Sahadeva, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the grandson of Pṛṣata,
advanced against the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, harrowing them with sharp arrows as thunderbolts of great force shatter the peaks of mountains.
In that first onset, amid the dreadful twang of bowstrings against bracers, not one of yours nor of the foe turned his face from the fight.
I beheld the deftness of Droṇa's pupils, O bull of the Bhāratas—marksmen who struck their targets unfailingly, loosing their arrows in dense streams, O king.
The din of the twanging bows did not cease, and blazing arrows shot forth like meteors falling from the vault of heaven.
But all the other rulers of earth, like mere spectators, O descendant of Bharata, looked on at that dreadful yet wondrous clash of kinsmen.
Then those great car-warriors, their fury kindled, each having wronged the other, strove against one another in rivalry, O king.
The hosts of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, shone exceedingly upon the field, like a painting wrought upon a canvas.
Then all those kings, with bows grasped firm, fell upon the foe together with their troops, at your son's command.
And the kings, by their thousands, commanded by Yudhiṣṭhira, rushed roaring upon your son's host.
Fierce was that meeting of the troops of both armies; and the sun was hidden away, the host shrouded in dust.
Among those who fought, those who broke and fled, and those who rallied again, no distinction could be made there between one's own men and the foe.
And as that tumultuous, terrible battle raged, your father shone forth surpassing all the hosts.
Saṃjaya said: In the forenoon of that fearful day, O lord of peoples, there began a most dreadful battle, the hewing-asunder of the bodies of kings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, longing for victory in the fray, there rose a roar like that of lions, making heaven and earth resound.
There were shrill clamoring cries mingled with the clap of palms and the blare of conches, and the lion-roars of heroes bellowing back at one another arose.
There was the twang of bowstrings struck by the leather guards, O bull of the Bhāratas, the tread of foot-soldiers, and the loud neighing of horses,
the fall of goads and elephant-hooks, the clash of weapons, and the ringing of the bells of elephants as they charged against one another.
As that tumultuous, hair-raising din arose, the rumble of chariots became like the thunder of a rain-cloud.
Setting their minds upon cruelty and casting their lives utterly aside, they all, with banners raised on high, bore down upon the Pāṇḍavas.
The son of Śaṃtanu himself, O king, charged upon Dhanaṃjaya in the battle, gripping his dreadful bow that was like the rod of Death.
Arjuna too, the radiant one, seizing his bow Gāṇḍīva renowned throughout the world, rushed against the son of Gaṅgā at the head of the battle.
Those two tigers among the Kurus each sought to slay the other; yet the mighty son of Gaṅgā, though he pierced Pārtha in the fight, could not make him waver, and likewise, O king, the son of Pāṇḍu could not make Bhīṣma waver in the battle.
And Sātyaki, the great archer, advanced upon Kṛtavarman; between those two there arose a tumultuous, hair-raising combat.
Sātyaki assailed Kṛtavarman and Kṛtavarman Sātyaki, the two of them mangling each other with terrible arrows.
Their every limb studded with arrows, those two mighty warriors shone like a pair of kiṃśuka trees in springtime, dappled and bright with blossoms in flower.
Abhimanyu, the great archer, gave battle to Bṛhadbala; thereupon, O lord of peoples, the king of Kosala cut down in the fight the banner of Subhadrā's son and felled his charioteer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the son of Subhadrā, enraged at the slaying of his charioteer, pierced Bṛhadbala, O great king, with nine arrows.
Then with two more broad-headed shafts, golden-hued, that crusher of foes cut the banner with one and the rein-driver with the other; and the two of them, enraged, O king, mangled each other with sharp arrows.
Proud, insolent in battle, a great car-warrior who had earned his enmity—such was your son Duryodhana, whom Bhīmasena now engaged.
Those two tigers among men, foremost of the Kurus, mighty in strength, rained upon each other showers of arrows on the field of battle.
Beholding those two great-souled and accomplished warriors, masters of the wondrous arts of combat, amazement seized all beings, O descendant of Bharata.
Duḥśāsana, advancing against the great car-warrior Nakula, struck him with many whetted arrows that pierced to the vitals.
The son of Mādrī, as if laughing, cut apart with sharp arrows his standard and his bow together with its shaft, O descendant of Bharata; and then he tormented him with twenty-five small darts.
But your son, hard to assail, in that great battle cut with his arrows the yoke-pole of Nakula's car and brought down his banner as well.
Durmukha, advancing against the mighty Sahadeva, pierced him with a shower of arrows as he strove in the great battle.
Then the hero Sahadeva, in that great battle, with an exceedingly sharp arrow brought down Durmukha's charioteer.
Closing upon each other in the fight, those two, frenzied for combat and bent on stroke and counter-stroke, terrified one another with terrible arrows.
King Yudhiṣṭhira himself advanced against the king of the Madras; and the lord of the Madras cut his bow in two, O venerable one.
Casting aside that severed bow, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Kuntī took up another, swifter and stronger.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the king, enraged, covered the lord of the Madras with smooth-jointed arrows and cried, "Stand! Stand!"
Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna rushed upon Droṇa, O descendant of Bharata; but Droṇa, greatly enraged, cut into three pieces in the fight his stout bow—the very life-taker—as he strove with it.
And he loosed in the battle a most dreadful arrow, like a second rod of Death, which sank deep into his body.
Then taking up another bow and fourteen arrows, the son of Drupada pierced Droṇa in return in that engagement; and the two of them, greatly enraged, waged a most furious combat against each other.
In the fight Śaṅkha, the impetuous, advanced against the impetuous son of Somadatta, O great king, crying, "Stand! Stand!"
The hero pierced his right arm in the fight; and the son of Somadatta in turn struck Śaṅkha in the region of the collarbone.
Between those two, proud and swift in battle, O lord of peoples, there arose a combat of terrible form, like that between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
Against Bāhlika, enraged in the fight, the immeasurable-souled Dhṛṣṭaketu, that great car-warrior, fierce of aspect, charged, O lord of peoples.
Then Bāhlika, O king, assailed the indignant Dhṛṣṭaketu with many arrows and let forth a lion's roar.
But the king of the Cedis, greatly enraged, swiftly pierced Bāhlika in the fight with nine arrows, as a rutting elephant assails another in rut.
There in the fight those two, enraged and roaring again and again, came together in fury like Mars and Mercury.
Against the rākṣasa Alambuṣa, cruel in his deeds, the cruel-deeded Ghaṭotkaca advanced in battle, as Śakra against Bala.
Then Ghaṭotkaca, greatly enraged, rent that mighty rākṣasa with ninety sharp arrows, O descendant of Bharata.
But Alambuṣa in the fight again and again held off the mighty son of Bhīmasena with smooth-jointed arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Wounded by arrows, those two then shone in the engagement like the mighty Bala and Śakra in the war of gods and demons.
The mighty Śikhaṇḍin in the fight advanced against the son of Droṇa, O king; thereupon Aśvatthāman, enraged, struck Śikhaṇḍin as he stood firm.
Piercing him grievously with a keen iron shaft, he made him quake; yet Śikhaṇḍin too, O king, then smote the son of Droṇa.
With a fine, sharp, well-whetted arrow he struck him; and the two of them then smote each other in the fray with manifold arrows.
Against the valiant Bhagadatta in the fight, Virāṭa the commander of hosts advanced in haste, O king; and thereupon a battle arose between them.
Virāṭa, struck by Bhagadatta with a shower of arrows, greatly enraged, rained upon him in return, as a cloud pours its rain upon a mountain.
Then Bhagadatta swiftly covered Virāṭa, lord of the earth, in the fight, as a cloud covers the risen sun.
Against Bṛhatkṣatra the Kaikeya, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat advanced; and Kṛpa covered him with a shower of arrows, O descendant of Bharata.
The Kekaya, enraged, overwhelmed the son of Gautama with a downpour of arrows; and the two, having slain each other's horses and cut apart each other's bows—
Bereft of their cars, the indignant pair came together for combat with swords; and between them there arose a battle of terrible form, most fierce.
Then King Drupada, full of gladness, advanced against the gladsome Jayadratha, lord of the Sindhus, O scorcher of foes.
Then the king of the Sindhus struck Drupada in the fight with three arrows, and Drupada pierced him in return.
Between them there arose a battle of terrible form, most fierce, delighting the beholders, like that between Venus and Mars.
Your son Vikarṇa advanced with swift horses against the mighty Sutasoma; and thereupon a battle arose.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vikarṇa, though he pierced Sutasoma with arrows, could not make him waver; and neither could Sutasoma make Vikarṇa waver—and that was a wondrous thing.
Against Suśarman, that tiger among men, the great car-warrior Cekitāna, valorous and greatly enraged, charged for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
But Suśarman, O great king, held off the great car-warrior Cekitāna in the engagement with a vast shower of arrows.
Cekitāna too, in fury, covered Suśarman in that great battle with arrows, as a great cloud covers a mountain.
Śakuni, the valorous, charged against the valiant Prativindhya, O lord of kings, as a rutting elephant against another in rut.
But the son of Yudhiṣṭhira, greatly enraged, rent the son of Subala in the fight with sharp arrows, as Maghavat rends a dānava.
And Śakuni, the highly sagacious, rent Prativindhya, who was piercing him in return in the battle, with smooth-jointed arrows.
Against Sudakṣiṇa, O lord of kings, the valiant great car-warrior of the Kāmbojas, Śrutakarman charged in the engagement.
But Sudakṣiṇa in the fight, though he pierced the great car-warrior son of Sahadeva, could not make him waver, any more than the mountain Maināka.
Then Śrutakarman, enraged, assailed the great car-warrior of the Kāmbojas with many arrows, rending him, as it were, on every side.
Then Irāvān, greatly enraged and on his guard, advanced in the fight against the indignant Śrutāyus, who was yet more on his guard.
The son of Arjuna, that great car-warrior, having slain his horses in the fight, roared a mighty roar that filled the host.
But Śrutāyus, greatly enraged, slew the horses of Phalguna's son in the fight with the head of his mace; and thereupon a battle arose.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti closed in battle with the great car-warrior Kuntibhoja, that hero, together with his host and his sons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There we beheld a wondrous feat of valor by the men of Avanti, in that, standing firm, they fought against a mighty host.
Anuvinda struck Kuntibhoja with his mace; and Kuntibhoja then swiftly overwhelmed him with volleys of arrows.
And the son of Kuntibhoja, too, pierced Vinda with arrows, and Vinda pierced him in return—and that was a wondrous thing.
The five Kekaya brothers, with their hosts, gave battle to five Gāndhāras with their hosts, O venerable one.
And your son Vīrabāhu gave battle to Uttara, son of Virāṭa, that best of car-warriors, and pierced him with sharp arrows; and Uttara too pierced that steadfast warrior with sharp arrows.
The king of the Cedis in the fight rushed upon Ulūka, O king; and Ulūka too assailed him with sharp, feathered arrows.
Between them there arose a combat of terrible form, O lord of peoples; greatly enraged and unvanquished, they rent each other.
Thus in thousands of single combats of car-warriors, elephants, horsemen, and foot-soldiers, your forces and theirs grew confounded in the fight.
For a moment that battle was fair to behold; but thereafter, O king, as in a frenzy, nothing whatever could be discerned.
Elephant met elephant in the fight, and car-warrior met car-warrior, horse closed with horse, and foot-soldier with foot-soldier.
Then a most unbearable and tumultuous battle came about there, as the heroes in the fight closed upon one another.
There the divine seers, the siddhas, and the cāraṇas, gathered together, gazed upon that terrible battle, like the war of gods and demons.
Then thousands of elephants and of chariots, floods of horses and floods of men, O venerable one, came together in confusion.
Here and there were seen car-warriors, elephants, and foot-soldiers, and horsemen too, O tiger among men, fighting again and again.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: O king, hundreds of thousands fought there, here and there, then and again, beyond all bounds; of this I shall tell you, O descendant of Bharata.
There son knew not father, nor father his own begotten son, nor brother brother, nor uncle his sister's son.
Nor sister's son his uncle, nor friend his friend; as if possessed, the Pāṇḍavas fought together with the Kurus.
Some of those tigers among men hurled themselves with their chariots upon the array of cars, and yoke shattered against yoke, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Chariot-poles clashed with chariot-poles and chariot-shafts with chariot-shafts; some warriors, their cars locked fast against locked cars, each strained to slay the other.
Some chariots, once they had collided with chariots, could not stir at all; and the great-bodied elephants in rut, charging together, crashed elephant upon elephant.
In their fury the war-elephants gored one another again and again with their tusks, and the foe's elephants, bearing lances and banners, tore into them.
O great king, when the swift and mighty elephants rushed upon them and struck them with their tusks, the wounded beasts shrieked there in utter agony.
Trained well in their lessons and goaded by spike and hook, the rut-maddened elephants advanced face to face against other rut-maddened elephants.
Some of the great elephants, locked in struggle even with those in rut, let loose a cry like the curlew's and fled this way and that.
Well-handled elephants, the ichor flowing from their cheeks and trunks, those noble war-beasts pierced through by sword, lance, and iron shaft—
their vital parts shattered, they screamed and fell down lifeless, while some, bellowing dreadful roars, stampeded toward every quarter.
The foot-guards of the elephants, broad-chested smiters, armed with swords and bows and gleaming battle-axes,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
with maces and pestles, with slings and lances, with iron bludgeons and with bright, keen-edged blades—
these were seen, O great king, running here and there in fierce excitement, weapons raised, each eager to kill the other.
And the gleaming swords, drenched in the blood of men, shone forth as the heroes charged upon one another.
From the swords flung down and swept about by the arms of heroes there arose a tumultuous din as they fell upon the vital parts of the foe.
Of those crushed by mace and pestle, of those cleft by fine swords, of those split apart by elephants' tusks and trampled under elephants—
of those throngs of men crying out to one another here and there, terrible voices were heard, O Bhārata, like the voices of the departed dead.
And horsemen, on horses decked with chowries and crests, swift as wild geese, rushed against one another.
The great javelins they hurled, adorned with gold, swift and bright and keen, flew on like serpents.
Some horsemen, leaping upon the great chariots with their swiftest steeds, took off the heads of the heroic charioteers.
And many horsemen who came within his arrow-range a chariot-warrior, drawing near, struck down with broad-headed, smooth-jointed shafts.
Elephants like mountains and clouds, frenzied and decked in gold, dashed the horses aside and crushed them under their feet.
Their frontal globes split open and their flanks laid bare, some elephants, struck down by javelins, screamed in utmost anguish.
Some noble elephants, seizing the horses together with their riders and dashing them up, hurled them violently there amid the dreadful press of battle.
The elephants, tossing up horses with their riders upon the points of their tusks, ranged about, trampling whole hosts of chariots together with their banners.
Out of their masculine fury and their rutting frenzy, some of the great elephants there slew the horses and their riders with their trunks and their feet.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some elephants, seizing with their trunks the chariots together with their horses and dragging them off, ranged toward every quarter, answering to every command.
Swift, bright, and keen, the arrows flew on like serpents, piercing through the bodies of men and horses and through their iron armor.
Bright spears, launched by the arms of heroes, fell here and there, O lord of the peoples, dreadful as great meteors.
With shields bound in panther-hide and tiger-skin, with bare and gleaming swords, the warriors smote down their foes in battle.
Charging in, full of wrath and gashed open along one flank, displaying their prowess, they rushed together with sword, shield, and battle-axe.
Some were torn open by spears and some hewn apart by battle-axes; some were crushed by elephants and others trampled down by horses.
Cut down by chariot-rims and hewn by sharpened arrows, the men cried out, O king, here and there, calling upon their kinsmen—
some upon their sons, some upon their fathers, some upon their brothers along with their kindred, upon uncles and nephews, and even upon their foes in the fray.
Very many, O Bhārata, their entrails strewn forth and their thighs broken, their fine arms severed and their flanks ripped open, were seen wailing, parched with thirst, still longing for life.
Some, overcome by thirst and weak of strength, O lord of the peoples, fallen upon the ground in battle, begged only for water.
Drenched in streams of blood and racked with pain, O Bhārata, they bitterly reproached themselves and your assembled sons.
Other valiant warriors, having made enmity with one another, would neither cast away their weapons nor cry out, O honored sir, but, exulting, threatened one another here and there.
Biting through their own lips with their teeth in their wrath, with faces drawn into knotted frowns, they glared at one another.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Others, sorely afflicted, tormented by their wounds and pierced by arrows, men of firm courage and great strength, fell utterly silent.
Other heroes, their chariots lost, seeking out another's car in the fray, fell and were crushed by the noble elephants, and they shone, O great king, like kiṃśuka trees in flower.
Many a fearful clamor arose throughout the ranks as that most terrible slaughter of the foremost heroes went on.
In that battle father slew son and son slew father; the sister's son slew the uncle, and the uncle slew the sister's son.
Friend slew friend, O king, and kinsman slew kinsman; thus did the Kurus there do battle with the Pāṇḍavas.
As that terror unfolded in that boundless, mighty war, the host of the Pārthas, coming up against Bhīṣma, trembled.
With his banner of five stars, a palmyra wrought in silver and raised high upon his great chariot, O bull of the Bhāratas, the mighty-armed Bhīṣma then shone, O king, like the moon above Meru.
Saṃjaya said: When the greater part of the forenoon had passed on that dread day, as the immense and terrible slaughter of the foremost heroes went on,
Durmukha and Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, Śalya, and Viviṃśati, urged on by your son, came up and guarded Bhīṣma.
Guarded by these five mighty car-warriors, O bull of the Bhāratas, the great chariot-hero plunged into the ranks of the Pāṇḍavas.
Among the Cedis, the Kāśis, the Karūṣas, and the Pāñcālas, O Bhārata, Bhīṣma's palmyra banner was seen ranging about in many directions.
And then Bhīṣma struck off heads, and arms together with their weapons, with swift, broad-headed, smooth-jointed shafts.
As Bhīṣma seemed to dance along the paths of his chariot, O bull of the Bhāratas, some of the elephants, struck in their vital parts, raised cries of agony.
Then Abhimanyu, in towering wrath, mounting his chariot yoked with excellent tawny steeds, drove straight toward Bhīṣma's car.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With his banner of the karṇikāra blossom, bright with gold, he rained his shafts upon Bhīṣma and upon those foremost of car-warriors.
Striking the banner of him whose ensign was the palmyra with a keen, feathered shaft, that hero did battle with Bhīṣma and with his followers.
Having pierced Kṛtavarman with one iron shaft and Śalya with five, he struck the great-grandsire with nine keen-pointed arrows.
With a single arrow, loosed from a fully drawn bow and well aimed, he pierced the gold-adorned banner.
And with a broad-headed, smooth-jointed shaft that cleaves through every guard, he struck the head of Durmukha's charioteer from his body.
With a keen-pointed broad-headed shaft he cut apart the gold-adorned bow of Kṛpa, and assailed those warriors with sharp-mouthed arrows.
In utmost fury that great car-warrior smote them, seeming to dance; and beholding his deftness, even the gods were delighted.
By the unerring aim of the son of Kṛṣṇa's sister, all the car-warriors led by Bhīṣma deemed him a man of valor, Dhanaṃjaya himself made manifest.
His bow, kept ever in the path of deftness, glowing like a firebrand, ranged about all the quarters, loud-voiced like the Gāṇḍīva.
Coming up against him, Bhīṣma, slayer of hostile heroes, swiftly pierced the son of Arjuna in battle with nine fast-flying arrows.
And with three broad-headed shafts he cut down the banner of that one of surpassing might, and that man of steadfast vows struck his charioteer with three arrows.
In like manner Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and Śalya, O honored sir, though they pierced the son of Kṛṣṇa's sister, could not make him waver, like the mountain Maināka.
Surrounded by those great car-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's side, that hero, the son of Kṛṣṇa's sister, poured showers of arrows upon the five chariot-fighters.
Then, warding off their great missiles with showers of arrows, the mighty son of Kṛṣṇa's sister roared aloud, loosing his shafts against Bhīṣma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There, O king, the exceeding strength of his arms was made plain as he strove in battle and harried Bhīṣma with his arrows.
Against that very valiant one Bhīṣma too sent forth his shafts; but he cut to pieces in battle those arrows loosed from Bhīṣma's bow.
Then that hero of unfailing aim cut down Bhīṣma's banner in battle with nine arrows, and thereupon the people shouted aloud.
That silver palmyra of mighty stem, adorned with gold, cut down by the shafts of Subhadrā's son, fell to the earth, O Bhārata.
Seeing the banner fallen by the arrows of Subhadrā's son, O bull of the Bhāratas, Bhīma roared in delight, gladdening the heart of Subhadrā's son.
Then Bhīṣma, of fearful aspect and great strength, brought forth in that moment many mighty and celestial missiles.
Then the great-grandsire of immeasurable spirit overwhelmed the son of Subhadrā with a hundred thousand smooth-jointed arrows.
Then ten great bowmen, mighty car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, sped forward upon their chariots to protect the son of Subhadrā.
Virāṭa with his son, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the grandson of Pṛṣata, and Bhīma, and the Kekayas, and Sātyaki, O lord of the peoples—
As these swept down in haste, Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu, in battle, struck the Pāñcāla prince with three arrows and Sātyaki with sharp ones.
And with a single keen, razor-edged, feathered shaft, loosed from a fully drawn bow, he cut down the banner of Bhīmasena.
The golden banner of Bhīmasena, bearing a lion, O best of men, struck down by Bhīṣma, fell from his chariot.
Bhīmasena, having pierced Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu with three arrows in battle, struck Kṛpa with one and Kṛtavarman with eight.
And Uttara, the son of Virāṭa, mounted upon an elephant whose trunk was raised on high, rushed against the king, the lord of the Madras.
As that royal elephant came rushing down in haste, the charioteer Śalya checked its matchless onset in the battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Enraged, that lordly elephant of Uttara—huge and well-trained—set its foot upon the yoke and crushed all four of Śalya's horses.
Standing in his car whose horses were slain, the lord of the Madras hurled an iron spear, like a serpent, that would be the death of Uttara.
His armor pierced through by it, entering a vast darkness, he fell from the elephant's shoulder, his goad and lance slipping from his grasp.
Then Śalya, taking up his sword and leaping down from his splendid chariot, advanced boldly and severed the great trunk of the lordly elephant.
Its vital parts torn by showers of shafts, its trunk cut off, that elephant gave a terrible cry of agony, then fell and died.
Having performed this feat, the king of the Madras, that mighty car-warrior, swiftly mounted the gleaming chariot of Kṛtavarman.
Seeing his noble brother Uttara slain, and seeing Śalya stationed there together with Kṛtavarman, Virāṭa's son Śaṅkha blazed up with wrath like fire fed with oblations.
Twanging his great bow adorned with gold, the mighty one rushed forward, eager to slay Śalya, the lord of the Madras.
Surrounded on every side by a great host of chariots, pouring forth a rain of arrows, he advanced toward Śalya's car.
Seeing him bearing down with the might of a rutting elephant, seven of your warriors' chariots hemmed him in on all sides, seeking to rescue the king of the Madras, who had passed between the very fangs of death.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīṣma, roaring like a thundercloud, seized a bow tall as a palm tree and charged upon Śaṅkha in the fray.
Beholding that mighty archer of vast strength rise up, the Pāṇḍava army trembled like a ship struck by the force of the wind.
Then Arjuna swiftly placed himself in front of Śaṅkha, thinking, "This man must be guarded today from Bhīṣma," and so the battle was joined.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A great cry of dismay arose among the warriors fighting in the field; "Splendor has met splendor," they said, and were filled with wonder.
Then Śalya, mace in hand, descending from his great chariot, slew the four steeds of Śaṅkha, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Quickly taking up his sword, Śaṅkha fled from the car whose horses were slain, and reaching the chariot of Bībhatsu he found safety there.
Then from Bhīṣma's chariot the winged shafts flew swiftly forth, and by them the sky and the earth were everywhere overspread.
The Pāñcālas, the Matsyas, the Kekayas, and the Prabhadrakas—Bhīṣma, the foremost of strikers, laid them low with his arrows.
Quickly leaving the Pāṇḍava Savyasācin on the field, he rushed against the Pāñcāla Drupada, who was surrounded by his army; and upon that dear kinsman, O king, he poured down a multitude of shafts.
Like forests scorched by fire at winter's end, the troops of Drupada appeared, burnt up by his arrows; and Bhīṣma stood in the battle like a smokeless flame.
As none can gaze upon the midday sun blazing with its splendor, so the warriors of the Pāṇḍava could not look upon Bhīṣma.
The Pāṇḍavas, oppressed by fear, looked about them on every side, but found no protector, like cattle tormented by the cold.
As the army, struck down and scattered, dispirited and crushed, gave way, a great cry of distress arose among the troops of the Pāṇḍus, O Bhārata.
Then Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, his bow ever drawn into a circle, loosed flaming-tipped shafts like venomous serpents.
Making all the quarters a single path with his arrows, that man of firm vows slew the chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, singling out each one by name, O Bhārata.
Then, as the armies broke and were churned to pieces on every side, and as the maker of day reached his setting, nothing whatever could be discerned.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And seeing Bhīṣma raging on in that great battle, the sons of Pṛthā sounded the recall of their troops, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Saṃjaya said: When the first day's withdrawal of the armies had been made, O bull of the Bhāratas—Bhīṣma furious in the fight and Duryodhana exultant—
the Dharma-king, going swiftly to Janārdana, together with all his brothers and all the lords of men,
filled with the deepest grief, brooding upon defeat, spoke thus to the scion of the Vṛṣṇis, O king, having beheld Bhīṣma's prowess:
"Kṛṣṇa, behold the great archer Bhīṣma of terrible might, burning up my army with his shafts as fire burns dry grass in summer.
How shall we even be able to look upon this great soul, who licks up my army as fire licks at the oblation?
For at the sight of this tiger among men, this mighty bowman of vast strength, my army has scattered in flight, smitten by his arrows.
Yama in his wrath might be conquered in battle, and the wielder of the thunderbolt, and Varuṇa bearing his noose, and Kubera with his mace—
but Bhīṣma of vast splendor and mighty strength cannot be conquered. So matters standing, I am sunk in the fathomless waters of Bhīṣma, without a raft.
Through the weakness of my own judgment, Keśava, I have come up against Bhīṣma; I shall go to the forest, Govinda—better for me to live there.
I cannot give over these guardians of the earth to Bhīṣma, to their death; Bhīṣma, knower of great weapons, will surely destroy my army, Kṛṣṇa.
As moths rushing into a blazing fire go only to their destruction, so do the men of my army.
For the sake of a kingdom I, though valiant, have been brought to ruin, scion of the Vṛṣṇis; and my heroic brothers are worn thin, tormented by arrows.
For my sake, out of brotherly love, they have been cast out from kingdom and from ease. I now hold life itself a precious thing, for life today is hard to keep.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With what remains of my life I shall practice harsh austerities; I will not have these friends of mine slain in battle, Keśava.
Mighty Bhīṣma ceaselessly destroys my chariot-warriors by the many thousands, the foremost of strikers, with his celestial weapons.
What can I do that my purpose may be accomplished? Tell me, Mādhava, without delay. I see Savyasācin standing in the battle as though indifferent.
Bhīma alone, the mighty-armed, fights with utmost strength, remembering the warrior's duty, by sheer might of arm alone.
With his hero-slaying mace, that great-spirited one, to the utmost of his vigor, performs deeds hard to do among elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers.
Yet even he is not able, sir, to bring the enemy host to destruction by fair fighting alone, that hero, not in a hundred years.
This friend of yours alone knows the weapons, yet even he disregards us, while we are consumed by Bhīṣma and by the great-souled Droṇa.
The celestial weapons of Bhīṣma and of the great-souled Droṇa, loosed again and again, will burn up all the warriors.
Kṛṣṇa, Bhīṣma, fierce in his fury, joined with all the kings, will surely make an end of us—such is his prowess.
Therefore, O lord of yoga, look out for some great archer, some mighty car-warrior, who might quell Bhīṣma in the fight as a raincloud quells a forest fire.
By your grace, Govinda, the Pāṇḍavas, their foes slain, having regained their own kingdom, will rejoice together with their kinsmen."
Having spoken thus, the great-spirited son of Pṛthā sat sunk in thought, long turned inward, his mind overwhelmed by grief.
Knowing the Pāṇḍava stricken with grief, his mind broken by sorrow, Govinda then spoke, gladdening all the Pāṇḍavas:
"Grieve not, foremost of the Bhāratas; you ought not to grieve, you whose brothers are heroes, archers above all the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And I am here to do you good, O king, and Sātyaki the great car-warrior, and the aged Virāṭa and Drupada, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna son of Pṛṣata.
And likewise all the kings with their forces, O best of kings, devoted to you, await your favor, O lord of peoples.
This son of Pṛṣata, Dhṛṣṭadyumna of mighty strength, ever wishing your good and devoted to your welfare, has been made the commander of your host; and Śikhaṇḍin too, O mighty-armed one, is to be the death of Bhīṣma.
Hearing this, the king then spoke to Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the great car-warrior, in that assembly, while Vāsudeva listened:
"Dhṛṣṭadyumna, mark well what I shall say to you, sir; this word of mine, once spoken, must not be transgressed.
You are my commander-in-chief, approved by Vāsudeva; as Kārttikeya was of old the eternal leader of the gods, so are you the general of the Pāṇḍus, O bull among men.
Therefore, O tiger among men, advance boldly and slay the Kauravas; and I will follow after you, and Bhīma, and Kṛṣṇa, sir,
and the two sons of Mādrī together, and the sons of Draupadī clad in armor, and those other foremost guardians of the earth, O bull among men."
Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, rousing the spirits of all, said: "I, O Pārtha, was ordained of old by Śambhu to be the ender of Droṇa.
Bhīṣma in battle, and Droṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, Jayadratha—all of them, arrogant in war, I shall this day meet in combat, O king."
Then a shout went up from the great archers, the Pāṇḍavas mad for battle, when that lord of kings, the son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of foes, rose up.
Then the son of Pṛthā said to the son of Pṛṣata, the commander of the host: "There is a formation called the Krauñca-aruṇa, the crusher of all foes—
the one which Bṛhaspati then declared to Indra in the war of gods and demons. Array it duly, the destroyer of the enemy's ranks; let the kings, together with the Kurus, behold what was never seen before."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed by the god among men, as Viṣṇu was by the bearer of the thunderbolt, at daybreak he placed Dhanaṃjaya at the head of all the forces.
His banner, ranging the path of the sun, wondrous and ravishing to behold, had been fashioned by Viśvakarman at the command of Puruhūta.
Adorned with pennants of the hue of Indra's bow, moving through the sky like a thing of the air, resembling a city of the Gandharvas, it seemed to dance, sir, as the chariot wheeled through its courses.
With that jewel-bright banner and with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, the son of Pṛthā shone supremely furnished, like the Self-Existent with the sun.
King Drupada, surrounded by a great army, formed the head; and Kuntibhoja and the Caidya stood at the eyes, O lord of men.
The Dāśārṇakas and the Prayāgas, together with the bands of the Dāśerakas, the dwellers of the watered lowlands, and the Kirātas, formed the neck, O bull of the Bhāratas.
And with the Paṭaccaras and the Huṇḍas, O king, and the Pauravakas, and together with the Niṣādas, Yudhiṣṭhira held the back.
The two wings were Bhīmasena and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, the sons of Draupadī and Abhimanyu, and Sātyaki the great car-warrior.
The Piśācas and the Daradas, the Puṇḍras together with the Kuṇḍīviṣas, the Maḍakas and the Laḍakas, the Taṅgaṇas and the Parataṅgaṇas—
the Bāhlīkas and the Tittiras, the Colas and the Pāṇḍyas, O Bhārata—these peoples, O king, took their station on the right wing.
The Agniveṣyas, the Jagattuṇḍas, and the Paladāśas, O Bhārata, the Śabaras and the Tumbupas, and the Vatsas together with the Nākulas—and Nakula and Sahadeva took their station on the left flank.
The two wings held ten thousand chariots, and the head a hundred thousand; the back numbered a hundred million and twenty thousand besides; and at the neck were a hundred thousand and seventy thousand more.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At the wings, their tips, the outer wings, and the wings' ends, the elephants moved hemmed in on every side, O king, like mountains on the march.
Virāṭa, together with the Kekayas, guarded the rear, as did the king of Kāśi and Śaibya, with thirty thousand chariots.
Having marshalled this great battle-array, O Bhārata, the Pāṇḍavas, armoured and longing for the sunrise, stood ready for battle.
Sun-coloured, spotless, and vast, their white parasols shone resplendent upon the elephants and the chariots.
Saṃjaya said: Then, beholding the great Krauñca formation—impenetrable and most terrible—drawn up by Pārtha of immeasurable splendour, your son,
approaching the preceptor, O venerable one, and Kṛpa and Śalya, and the son of Somadatta and Vikarṇa, and Aśvatthāman as well,
and Duḥśāsana and his other brothers, all of them, O Bhārata, and the many other heroes who had assembled for battle,
your son, gladdening them, spoke these timely words: "All of you wield manifold weapons and are versed in arms and missiles.
Each one of you, all great chariot-warriors, is alone able to slay the sons of Pāṇḍu with their host in battle—how much more so when united!
Unlimited is this our force, guarded by Bhīṣma, while limited is this force of theirs, O best of kings.
Let the Saṃsthānas and the Śūrasenas, the Veṇikas and the Kukuras, the Ārevakas and the Trigartas, the Madrakas and the Yavanas,
together with Śatruṃjaya and with Duḥśāsana, and with the heroic Vikarṇa, and with Nanda and Upananda,
joined with Citrasena and with the Pāṇibhadrakas, set their armies before them and guard Bhīṣma above all."
Then Droṇa and Bhīṣma and your son, O venerable one, drew up a great formation to repel the Pāṇḍavas.
Bhīṣma, surrounded on every side by a mighty host, advanced, leading on the great army like the king of the gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Behind him followed the mighty archer, the valorous son of Bhāradvāja, with the Kuntalas and the Daśārṇas and the Māgadhas, O lord of peoples,
with the Vidarbhas and the Mekalas and the Karṇaprāvaraṇas as well, together with the whole army, behind Bhīṣma resplendent in battle.
The Gāndhāras, the Sindhus and Sauvīras, the Śibis, and then the Vasātis—and Śakuni with his own troops—guarded the son of Bhāradvāja.
Then King Duryodhana, together with all his brothers, with the Aśvātakas and the Vikarṇas, and likewise with the Śarmilas and the Kosalas,
and with the Daradas and the Cūcupas, and likewise the Kṣudrakas and the Mālavas, joyfully guarded the host of Subala's son.
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, and Bhagadatta, O venerable one, and Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, guarded the left flank.
The son of Somadatta and Suśarman, and Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja, and Śatāyus and Śrutāyus, took their place on the right flank.
Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman of the Sātvata line, with a great army stationed themselves at the rear of the host.
The guardians of its rear were kings from various lands—Ketumat and Vasudāna, and Abhibhū the son of the king of Kāśi.
Then all your warriors, rejoicing for battle, O Bhārata, filled with gladness blew their conches and let loose their lion-roars.
Hearing the lion-roar of those joyful men, the aged grandsire of the Kurus, the valorous one, roared aloud in answer and blew his conch.
Then conches and kettledrums and tabors of many kinds, and war-drums, were sounded by the foe, and the din became tumultuous.
Then, stationed upon a great chariot yoked with white horses, the two blew their excellent conches, adorned with gold and gems—
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanaṃjaya the Devadatta, and Vṛkodara of terrible deeds blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew the Anantavijaya, while Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughoṣa and the Maṇipuṣpaka.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
