The king of Kāśi and Śaibya, and Śikhaṇḍin the great chariot-warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa, and Sātyaki of great renown,
and the Pāñcāla prince the mighty archer, and the five sons of Draupadī—all blew their great conches and sounded their lion-roars.
That mighty din, raised there by those heroes, tumultuous, made both sky and earth resound.
Thus, O great king, the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, exultant, came together once more for battle, tormenting one another.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the armies were thus drawn up, my own and the others, how did those foremost of warriors begin their onslaught?
Saṃjaya said: When the armies stood evenly arrayed, accoutred and bright with banners, beholding the host like a shoreless ocean,
in their midst stood King Duryodhana, your son, and said to all your warriors: "Fight, you who are armoured!"
Hardening their hearts to cruelty, casting away their lives, they all advanced upon the Pāṇḍavas with banners upraised.
Then there arose a tumultuous, hair-raising battle between your men and the foe, with chariots and elephants entangled together.
Arrows loosed by the chariot-warriors, gold-feathered and keen-edged, with unblunted points, fell upon the elephants and the horses.
As the battle thus raged, the mighty-armed Bhīṣma of terrible prowess, armoured, raised his bow and charged forward.
Upon the son of Subhadrā and upon Bhīmasena, upon Śini's grandson the great chariot-warrior, upon Kekaya and Virāṭa, and upon Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata—
upon these heroes among men, and upon the Cedis and Matsyas all around, the aged grandsire of the Kurus rained showers of arrows.
The great formation shook in that meeting of heroes, and there was a vast confusion among all the armies.
With their banners and elephants cast down, their finest steeds slain, and their ranks of chariots scattered, so the Pāṇḍavas became.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Arjuna, the tiger among men, seeing Bhīṣma the great chariot-warrior, said in wrath to the Vṛṣṇi hero: "Drive to where the grandsire is.
This Bhīṣma, sorely enraged, O Vṛṣṇi hero, will surely destroy my host, intent upon Duryodhana's good.
This Droṇa, and Kṛpa, Śalya, and Vikarṇa, O Janārdana, and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra united, with Duryodhana at their head,
will slaughter the Pāñcālas, guarded by that firm-bowed one. Therefore I shall go against Bhīṣma for the sake of the army, O Janārdana."
To him Vāsudeva said: "Be on your guard, Dhanaṃjaya. I am bringing you, O hero, against the grandsire's chariot."
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Śūra brought that world-famed chariot up against Bhīṣma's chariot, O lord of men.
With its many fluttering pennons, with horses the colour of cranes, with its great and most terrible roaring ape-banner upraised, with the mighty thunder of his chariot bright as the sun,
the Pāṇḍava, smiting the Kaurava host and the Śūrasenas, came on swiftly, loosing arrows—he who dispels the grief of friends.
As he rushed on with violence like a rutting elephant, terrifying the heroes in battle and felling them with his shafts,
Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu, guarded by the Saindhava chiefs and by the Easterners, Sauvīras, and Kekayas, suddenly came forth to meet Arjuna.
For what chariot-warrior, other than the Kuru grandsire, or Droṇa, or the son of the Sun, was fit to encounter the wielder of Gāṇḍīva?
Then Bhīṣma, O great king, the grandsire of the Kauravas, covered Arjuna with seventy-seven iron arrows.
Droṇa pierced him with twenty-five, Kṛpa with fifty arrows, Duryodhana with sixty-four, and Śalya with nine arrows,
and the lord of the Sindhus with nine, and Śakuni too with five, and Vikarṇa with ten broad-headed shafts, O king, pierced the Pāṇḍava.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Pierced on every side by those whetted arrows, the mighty archer of great arms did not waver, like a mountain being split.
That tiger among men, in turn, pierced Bhīṣma with twenty-five arrows and Kṛpa with nine, Droṇa with sixty and Vikarṇa with three arrows,
and the son of Ṛtāyana with three shafts and the king with five did the diademed one of immeasurable spirit strike back, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Sātyaki and Virāṭa, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, and the sons of Draupadī, and Abhimanyu, surrounded Dhanaṃjaya.
Then the Pāñcāla prince, joined with the Somakas, rained arrows upon Droṇa the mighty archer, who was intent on the welfare of the son of Gaṅgā.
But Bhīṣma, foremost of chariot-warriors, swiftly pierced the Pāṇḍava with eighty whetted arrows, and at that your men cried out in joy.
Hearing the clamour of those exultant men, the valorous lion among chariot-warriors, himself exultant, then plunged into their midst.
Reaching the midst of those lions among chariot-warriors, Dhanaṃjaya sported with his bow, O king, making targets of those great chariot-warriors.
Then King Duryodhana, the lord of men, seeing his own army hard pressed by Pārtha in the fray, said to Bhīṣma:
"This mighty son of Pāṇḍu, dear sire, joined with Kṛṣṇa, cuts away the very root of our whole striving army, even while you, the son of Gaṅgā, and Droṇa, foremost of chariot-warriors, yet live.
For on your account even this Karṇa, the great chariot-warrior, has laid down his weapons and does not fight Pārtha in battle, though ever desiring my welfare.
Act, then, O son of Gaṅgā, so that Phalguna may be slain." Thus addressed, O king, your sire Devavrata said, "Shame upon the warrior's code!"—and drove against Pārtha's chariot.
Beholding the two white-horsed warriors locked in combat, O king, the kings raised loud lion-roars and conch-blasts, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The son of Droṇa, and Duryodhana, and Vikarṇa your son, surrounding Bhīṣma in the battle, stood ready to fight, O venerable one.
In the same way all the Pāṇḍavas, surrounding Dhanaṃjaya, stood ready for the great battle; and then the fight began.
The son of Gaṅgā struck Pārtha in the battle with nine arrows, and Arjuna struck him back with ten that pierced the vitals.
Then, with a thousand well-aimed arrows, Arjuna the Pāṇḍava, glorious in battle, hemmed in all the quarters around Bhīṣma.
But that net of arrows, O Kaurava, Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu warded off in turn with his own net of arrows against Pārtha.
Both supremely exultant, both rejoicing in the battle, they fought as equals, each seeking to answer stroke with stroke.
The nets of arrows loosed from Bhīṣma's bow were seen breaking apart in masses, shattered by Arjuna's shafts.
And likewise the nets of arrows loosed by Arjuna, struck piecemeal by the son of Gaṅgā's shafts, fell down upon the earth.
Arjuna struck Bhīṣma with twenty-five sharp arrows, and Bhīṣma too, in the battle, pierced Pārtha with thirty arrows.
Piercing each other's horses and both their banners, the two mighty subduers of foes, those great-strengthed warriors, sported also with each other's chariot-poles and chariot-wheels.
Then, O great king, the wrathful Bhīṣma, foremost of those who strike, smote Vāsudeva with three arrows in the breast.
Pierced by the shafts loosed from Bhīṣma's bow, the slayer of Madhu shone in the battle, O king, like a kiṃśuka tree in full flower.
Then Arjuna, exceedingly enraged at seeing Mādhava wounded, pierced Gāṅgeya's charioteer in the encounter with three arrows.
Though both those heroes strove for each other's destruction, they could not, in that battle, gain any opening upon one another.
Through the skill and deftness of their charioteers they displayed in manifold ways their wondrous wheeling courses, advancing and retreating again.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Watching for an opening to strike, those two great car-warriors, O king, kept their stations again and again upon the intervening paths.
Both of them raised the blast of their conches mingled with lion-roars, and likewise those two great car-warriors made the twang of their bows resound.
By the blast of their conches and the din of their chariot-wheels the earth was suddenly rent, and it quaked and roared.
None, O bull of the Bhāratas, could perceive any opening in either of them; both were mighty and brave in battle, and equal to one another.
By his ensign alone could the Kauravas there recognize Bhīṣma, and likewise the sons of Pāṇḍu knew Pārtha by his ensign alone.
Beholding such prowess in those two best of men, O king, all beings were struck with wonder in that battle, O Bhārata.
None could see a weak point in either of them in the fight, O Bhārata, even as in a man steadfast in righteousness none can find any fault anywhere.
Both of them became invisible behind their net of arrows, and both again quickly became visible in the battle.
There the gods together with the Gandharvas and the Cāraṇas, along with the seers, spoke to one another, beholding the prowess of those two.
These two great car-warriors, when roused in battle, cannot be vanquished in any wise, not even by all the worlds together with their gods, Asuras, and Gandharvas.
This battle, a marvel in the worlds, is exceedingly wondrous; battles such as this shall never come to pass in any way again.
Nor can Bhīṣma be conquered in the fight by the wise Pārtha, while bow in hand and stationed on his car he showers his shafts in battle.
And likewise the son of Pāṇḍu, that bowman hard to assail even by the gods in battle, Bhīṣma cannot venture to vanquish in the fray.
Such words, laden with praise of Gāṅgeya and Arjuna in their combat, were heard rising up here and there, O lord of peoples.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then thy warriors and those of the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata, smote one another in the battle amid the prowess of those two.
With keen-edged swords and bright battle-axes, with arrows and with many other weapons of various kinds, the heroes of both armies cut one another down in the fight.
While that dreadful and most cruel battle was thus raging, O king, there came about a great encounter between Droṇa and the Pāñcāla prince.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: How did the great bowman Droṇa and the Pāñcāla son of Pṛṣata, both intent, come together in battle? Recount that to me, Saṃjaya.
I deem destiny supreme, even above manly effort, Saṃjaya, since Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu could not overcome the son of Pāṇḍu in the fight.
For Bhīṣma, enraged in battle, could slay the worlds with all that moves and moves not; how then could he not, by his own might, overcome the son of Pāṇḍu in the fight, Saṃjaya?
Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, with a steady mind, of this most dreadful battle. The son of Pāṇḍu cannot be vanquished even by the gods led by Vāsava.
Droṇa fought against Dhṛṣṭadyumna with sharp arrows, and with a broad-headed shaft struck down his charioteer from the chariot-box.
Then in his wrath, O venerable one, he afflicted the four steeds of Dhṛṣṭadyumna with four excellent shafts.
Thereupon the hero Dhṛṣṭadyumna, laughing, pierced Droṇa with ninety sharp arrows, and cried out, 'Stand! Stand!'
Then once more the immeasurable and valorous son of Bhāradvāja covered with his shafts the wrathful Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
And he took up a dreadful arrow for the slaying of Pṛṣata's son, of touch like Śakra's thunderbolt, like a second rod of Death.
A great cry of dismay arose from all the host, O Bhārata, when they saw that shaft fitted to the string by the son of Bhāradvāja in the encounter.
Therein we beheld a wondrous feat of manliness in Dhṛṣṭadyumna, that the hero alone in battle stood firm as an unmoving mountain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And that blazing, dreadful arrow speeding toward him, his own death, he cut asunder, and let loose a shower of arrows upon the son of Bhāradvāja.
Then all the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas raised a shout, beholding that most difficult feat accomplished by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Then that valiant one, longing for Droṇa's death, hurled a swift lance adorned with gold and lapis.
That gold-decked lance rushing suddenly upon him, the son of Bhāradvāja, as if laughing, cut into three pieces in the battle.
Seeing his lance struck down, the valorous Dhṛṣṭadyumna poured showers of arrows upon Droṇa, O lord of men.
Then the illustrious Droṇa, warding off that shower of arrows, cut asunder in the middle the bow of Drupada's son.
His bow being severed, that mighty and illustrious one hurled at Droṇa in the battle a heavy mace made of mountain-stuff.
That mace, loosed with force, sped on, eager to slay Droṇa; therein we beheld a wondrous feat of prowess in the son of Bhāradvāja.
By his deftness he turned aside that gold-adorned mace, and having turned it aside, he sent forth arrows upon Pṛṣata's son.
Well-sharpened broad-headed shafts, dyed yellow, gold-feathered, and whetted on stone — they pierced his armor and drank his blood in the fight.
Then the high-souled Dhṛṣṭadyumna, taking up another bow and pressing forward against Droṇa in the fight, pierced him with five arrows.
Then those two bulls among men, smeared with blood, shone forth, O king, like two kiṃśuka trees in flower in the springtime.
Then, full of indignation, O king, and pressing forward at the head of the host, Droṇa again cut asunder the bow of Drupada's son.
Then the immeasurable one overwhelmed him, his bow severed, with smooth-jointed arrows, as a cloud drenches a mountain with rain.
And with a broad-headed shaft he struck down his charioteer from the chariot-box, and then his four steeds with four sharp arrows —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
these he felled in the battle, and he uttered a lion-roar; then with another broad-headed shaft he cut the bow from his hand.
His bow severed, his car gone, his steeds slain, his charioteer killed, he descended mace in hand, making known his great manhood.
That mace, too, Droṇa swiftly struck down with his shafts, O Bhārata, before he had even descended from the car; that seemed a wonder.
Then that strong, fair-armed hero, seizing a broad shield marked with a hundred moons and gleaming bright, and a broad celestial sword,
rushed forward with speed, longing to slay Droṇa, as a lion seeking prey rushes upon a rutting elephant in the forest.
Therein we beheld a wondrous feat of manliness in the son of Bhāradvāja — his deftness, his mastery of weapons, and the strength of his arms, O Bhārata —
in that he held off Pṛṣata's son with a shower of arrows, so that, mighty though he was, he could not advance in the battle.
There we beheld the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna standing firm, warding off the floods of arrows with his shield, like one of practiced hand.
Then the mighty-armed and strong Bhīma suddenly rushed up, rendering aid in the battle to the high-souled son of Pṛṣata.
He pierced Droṇa, O king, with seven sharp arrows, and then quickly mounted Pṛṣata's son upon another car.
Then King Duryodhana urged on the Kaliṅga, attended by a great host, for the protection of the son of Bhāradvāja.
Then that great host of the Kaliṅgas, O lord of men, advanced swiftly upon Bhīma at thy son's command.
And Droṇa too, that foremost of car-warriors, leaving the Pāñcāla prince, gave battle to the aged Virāṭa and Drupada, who had joined together; and Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the battle went forth to the King of Righteousness.
Then there arose a tumultuous, hair-raising battle between the Kaliṅgas and the high-souled Bhīma, world-destroying, of dreadful form, and terrifying.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Being thus commanded, how did the Kaliṅga, that leader of hosts, fight in battle, together with his army, against the mighty Bhīmasena of wondrous deeds —
that hero ranging with his mace like Death himself with rod in hand? How did the Kaliṅga, with his army, give him battle in the encounter?
Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed by thy son, O king of kings, that mighty one, guarded by a great host, set forth against Bhīma's car.
That great host of the Kaliṅgas rushing suddenly on, thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, its mighty weapons raised —
Bhīmasena assailed that army of the Kaliṅgas, O Bhārata, and Ketumat the Niṣāda prince advancing with the Cedis.
Then Śrutāyus, sorely enraged, together with King Ketumat, encountered Bhīma in the battle, while the Cedi ranks were arrayed.
With many thousands of cars, the lord of the Kaliṅgas, and Ketumat with ten thousand elephants and with the Niṣādas, beset Bhīmasena, O king, on every side in the battle.
And the Cedis, Matsyas, and Karūṣas, with Bhīmasena at their head, suddenly advanced upon the Niṣādas together with their kings.
Then there arose a battle of dreadful form and terrifying, the warriors in their lust to slay one another no longer knowing their own.
Then dreadful was Bhīma's sudden battle with the foe, O great king, like that of Indra with the great host of the Daityas.
From that army warring in the encounter, O Bhārata, there arose a mighty roar like that of the thundering sea.
The warriors then, cutting one another down, O lord of peoples, made the whole earth strewn over and red as the blood of a hare.
In their eagerness to slay, the warriors knew neither their own nor the foe; the heroes, hard to vanquish in battle, struck down even their own and their own kin.
A very great slaughter there was of the few against the many — of the Cedis against the Kaliṅgas and the Niṣādas, O lord of peoples.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having put forth their manly might to the utmost, the strong Cedis abandoned Bhīmasena and turned back.
Though beset by all the Kaliṅgas when the Cedis had withdrawn, the son of Pāṇḍu, relying on the strength of his own arms, did not turn back.
The mighty Bhīmasena stirred not from his place upon the car, and overwhelmed the host of the Kaliṅgas with his keen arrows.
But the Kaliṅga king, a mighty archer, and his son, a great car-warrior renowned as Śakradeva, struck at the Pāṇḍava with their arrows.
Then mighty-armed Bhīma, shaking his gleaming bow, gave battle to the Kaliṅgas, relying on the strength of his own arms.
But Śakradeva, loosing many shafts in the fray, slew Bhīmasena's horses with his arrows, and rained down showers of arrows like a cloud at the end of the hot season.
But Bhīmasena of great might, standing upon his car whose horses were slain, hurled at Śakradeva a mace made wholly of refined iron.
Struck down by it, O king, the son of the Kaliṅga king fell from his car, together with his banner and his charioteer, to the surface of the earth.
Seeing his own son slain, the lord of the Kaliṅgas hemmed in Bhīma on every side with many thousands of cars.
Then mighty-armed Bhīma, casting aside his heavy great mace, drew forth his sword, eager to perform a terrible deed.
And he took up, O king, O bull among men, a peerless shield of bull's hide, adorned with stars and half-moons wrought of gold.
Then the Kaliṅga king, enraged, stroked his bowstring, and taking up one dreadful arrow like the venom of a serpent, the lord of men sent it forth at Bhīmasena, longing to slay him.
That sharp arrow speeding swiftly upon him, Bhīmasena cut in two, O king, with his broad sword, and shouted aloud in his joy, striking terror into the host.
Then the Kaliṅga king, enraged, swiftly hurled at Bhīmasena in the encounter fourteen lances whetted upon stone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Before they reached him, while they were still in the air, the mighty-armed Pāṇḍava cut them apart at once, O king, unflustered, with his excellent sword.
Having shorn through those fourteen lances in the battle, Bhīma, that bull among men, fixed his gaze upon Bhānumat and rushed at him.
But Bhānumat then, covering Bhīma with a shower of arrows, raised a mighty roar, making the vault of heaven resound.
Bhīma did not endure that lion's roar in the great battle, and so he too bellowed forth a loud cry with a mighty voice.
Terrified by that sound, the army of the Kaliṅgas, O bull of the Bhāratas, no longer reckoned Bhīma in the fight to be a man.
Then Bhīma, O great king, having roared a vast cry, sword in hand, leapt swiftly and, by its two tusks, seized that finest of elephants.
Then he mounted upon the middle of that king of elephants, O sire, and with his broad sword cut Bhānumat asunder through the middle.
Having slain the prince fighting close beside him, that subduer of foes brought down his sword upon the elephant's shoulder, which could bear a heavy load.
With its shoulder cleft, that lord of the elephant herd, crying out, fell, like a crag-crested mountain washed away by the rush of a river.
Then, O Bhārata, the descendant of Bharata, leaping down from that elephant, sword in hand, undaunted in spirit, stood mailed upon the ground.
He ranged along many paths, fearless, felling elephants, and appeared on every side like a whirling wheel of fire.
Overpowering them, smiting down troops of horses, elephants, ranks of cars, and bands of foot-soldiers, drenched in blood, Bhīma ranged like a hawk through the battle, terrible amid the host of his foes.
Swift as he was, he severed the bodies and the heads of those elephant-warriors in the encounter with his keen-edged sword.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A single foot-soldier, enraged, swelling the terror of his foes, he bewildered them then, like Yama, the ender, at the time of doom.
And those bewildered men, roaring, rushed upon him in the battle, as he ranged with utmost speed, sword in hand, through the great fray.
Cutting through the car-poles and yokes of the car-warriors in the battle, that mighty crusher of foes slew the car-warriors as well.
Bhīmasena, ranging along very many paths, was seen everywhere; the Pāṇḍava displayed the wheeling, the upward whirling, the brandishing, the leaping, the springing forth, the gliding, the onset and the upward thrust.
Some, cleft by the point of the sword of the high-souled Pāṇḍava, cried out, their vitals pierced, and fell down lifeless.
And some elephants, their tusk-tips and trunks lopped off, their frontal lobes shattered, riderless, smote their own ranks, O Bhārata, and fell upon the earth, bellowing great cries.
And severed lances and bows and the heads of elephant-drivers, gay-colored housings and girths gleaming with gold,
and neck-ornaments and spears, banners and barbed darts, quivers and engines and many-hued bows,
and bright fire-pots, and goads together with elephant-hooks, and bells of many kinds, O king, and gold-cored sword-hilts, falling and fallen, together with their riders — all these we saw.
With elephants slain, their limb-guards and trunks shorn away, the earth in that place was strewn over with the fallen, as though with mountains.
Having thus crushed those great elephants, that bull among men trampled the horses and struck down the finest of the horsemen, O Bhārata; and dreadful was that battle between him and them, O Bhārata.
And bits and harness-straps and whips gleaming with gold, and housings and javelins and costly swords,
and corselets and shields and gaily-colored saddle-cloths, scattered here and there, were seen in that great battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With manifold horse-trappings and with bright weapons he made the earth bestrewn, as though with many-colored flowers.
Leaping upon and seizing certain car-warriors, the mighty Pāṇḍava struck them down with his sword, banners and all.
As that glorious one again and again sprang up in all directions, and ran, and ranged along wondrous paths, the people in the battle marveled.
Some he slew with his foot; others he seized and dashed to the ground; others he cut down with his sword; and yet others he terrified with his roar.
Others again he felled to the ground by the force of his thighs; and some, merely beholding him, in their terror passed into death.
Thus that numerous army of the swift Kaliṅgas, having ringed Bhīṣma about in the battle, rushed upon Bhīmasena.
Then, O bull of the Bhāratas, fixing his gaze upon Śrutāyus at the head of the Kaliṅga host, Bhīmasena advanced against him.
Seeing him coming on, the Kaliṅga king of immeasurable spirit pierced Bhīmasena in the breast with nine arrows.
Struck by the Kaliṅga's arrows, like an elephant tormented by the goad, Bhīmasena blazed up with wrath, as fire blazes with fuel.
Then Aśoka, bringing up a car adorned with gold, the charioteer furnished Bhīma with that car.
Swiftly mounting that car, the son of Kuntī, slayer of foes, rushed upon the Kaliṅga king, crying, 'Stand! Stand!'
Then mighty Śrutāyus, enraged, sent forth sharp arrows at Bhīma, displaying the lightness of his hand.
Sorely struck by nine sharp arrows loosed from that excellent bow by the Kaliṅga king, O king, the glorious Bhīma grew exceedingly wrathful, like a serpent beaten with a staff.
And enraged, that best of the mighty, the son of Pṛthā, Bhīma, drawing his bow with force, slew the Kaliṅga king with seven iron shafts.
And with two razor-edged arrows he dispatched to the abode of Yama the two mighty wheel-guards of the Kaliṅga king, Satyadeva and Satya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then again, Bhīma of immeasurable spirit, with three sharp iron arrows, sent Ketumat in the battle to the abode of Yama.
Then the Kaliṅgas, enraged, the warriors hemmed in the impatient Bhīmasena with many thousands of troops.
Then with spears and maces and swords, with lances and javelins and battle-axes, the Kaliṅgas, O king, overwhelmed Bhīmasena.
Warding off that terrible shower of arrows that had risen against him, the mighty Bhīma, taking up his mace and swiftly leaping forth, led seven hundred heroes to the abode of Yama.
And once more that crusher of foes sent two thousand Kaliṅgas to the world of death; and that was as though a marvel.
Thus again and again the hero shattered those ranks of the Kaliṅgas in the battle, with his gaze upon Bhīṣma of the great vow.
And the elephants, their riders slain by the high-souled Pāṇḍava, scattered through the ranks like clouds driven by the wind, trampling their own troops and bellowing, sore wounded by arrows.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, that strong one, blew his conch and made the hearts of all the Kaliṅga soldiery tremble.
And a stupor seized upon the Kaliṅgas, O scorcher of foes, and their soldiers and their mounts trembled in every part.
By Bhīma in the battle, O king, ranging on every side like a lordly elephant along many paths, running here and there, again and again springing up, a bewilderment was wrought among them.
And the host, panic-stricken with fear of Bhīmasena, quivered, churned and broken open, like a great lake stirred by a crocodile.
When the heroes had been terrified by Bhīma of wondrous deeds, some rallying back and some fleeing away in companies,
while all the Kaliṅga warriors were thus, the commander of the Pāṇḍava host, the son of Pṛṣata, said to his own ranks, 'Fight!'
Hearing the words of their commander, the troops led by Śikhaṇḍin advanced toward Bhīma with their smiting bands of cars.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the Pāṇḍava, the King of Righteousness, supported them all from behind with a great cloud-colored division of elephants.
Having thus urged on all his own ranks, the son of Pṛṣata took up the guarding of Bhīmasena's rear, as befits a good man.
For in the world there was none other for the king of the Pāñcālas, save Bhīma and Sātyaki, dearer than his own life's breath.
The son of Pṛṣata, slayer of hostile heroes, beheld that slayer of foes, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, ranging among the Kaliṅgas.
He roared again and again, O king, and was filled with joy, that scorcher of foes; and in the battle he blew his conch and gave forth a lion's roar.
And Bhīmasena, beholding upon the gold-adorned car of him whose horses were dove-gray the banner of the kovidāra tree, took heart again.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna of immeasurable spirit, seeing Bhīmasena beset by the Kaliṅgas, advanced in the battle to his rescue.
Sātyaki, seeing from afar those two, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Vṛkodara, the high-minded heroes giving battle to the Kaliṅgas in the fray,
the grandson of Śini, that best of victors, having sped thither swiftly, that bull among men, took up the guarding of the rear of the son of Pṛthā and the son of Pṛṣata.
There, working havoc, his bow taken up, abiding in a terrible mood, he slew his foes in the battle.
And there Bhīma set flowing a river, sprung from the Kaliṅgas, miry with flesh and blood, streaming with gore.
Between the host of the Kaliṅgas and that of the Pāṇḍavas, the mighty Bhīmasena crossed over that river most hard to cross.
Seeing Bhīmasena thus, O king, your men cried out, 'This is Death himself, in the form of Bhīma, doing battle with the Kaliṅgas!'
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, hearing that uproar in the battle, made haste against Bhīma, his ranks arrayed on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At him rushed Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata, charging upon Bhīṣma's chariot adorned with gold.
Surrounding on every side the impetuous son of Gaṅgā in the fray, they all swiftly struck Bhīṣma, each with three terrible arrows.
Your father Devavrata pierced them all in return—those great bowmen straining at their utmost—with three straight-flying shafts apiece.
Then, holding off those mighty car-warriors with a thousand arrows, he slew with his shafts Bhīma's steeds caparisoned in golden trappings.
Standing in his chariot whose horses were slain, the valorous Bhīmasena hurled a lance with force against the chariot of the son of Gaṅgā.
That lance, before ever it reached him, your father Devavrata cut into three in the battle, and it fell shattered to the earth.
Then, seizing a heavy mace of tempered iron, the mighty Bhīmasena leaped swiftly down from his chariot, O bull among men.
And Sātyaki too, at once, wishing to please Bhīma, brought down with his shafts the charioteer of the aged Kuru.
But Bhīṣma, foremost of car-warriors, when his charioteer was slain, was carried off from the field of battle by those horses that ran like the wind.
Then, O king, when he of the great vows had been borne away, Bhīmasena blazed up like a fire grown high as it consumes dry brushwood.
Having slain all the Kaliṅgas, he stood in the midst of the host, and none of your warriors dared confront him, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, foremost of car-warriors, taking the illustrious one up into his own chariot, bore him away in the sight of all the armies.
Honored by the Pāñcālas and the Matsyas, O bull of the Bhāratas, having embraced Dhṛṣṭadyumna, he then came to Sātyaki.
Then Sātyaki of true valor, the tiger of the Yadus, gladdening him, spoke to Bhīmasena while Dhṛṣṭadyumna looked on:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By good fortune the king of the Kaliṅgas, and the prince Ketumān, and Śakradeva the Kaliṅga, and the Kaliṅgas themselves are slain in the fight.
By the strength and valor of your own arm, the great battle-array of the Kaliṅgas, thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, has been crushed by you alone.
Having spoken thus, the long-armed grandson of Śini, the tamer of foes, springing from chariot to chariot, embraced the son of Pāṇḍu.
Then, mounting his own chariot once more, that great car-warrior, enraged, slew your men, lending strength to Bhīma's force.
Saṃjaya said: When the greater part of the afternoon of that day had passed, O Bhārata, amid the great destruction of chariots, elephants, horses, foot-soldiers, and cavalry,
the prince of Pāñcāla engaged with these three great car-warriors—the son of Droṇa, Śalya, and the high-souled Kṛpa.
That mighty heir of the Pāñcālas struck down the world-famed steeds of the son of Droṇa with ten sharp, swift-flying arrows.
Then the son of Droṇa, his horses slain, quickly mounted Śalya's chariot and rained arrows upon the heir of the Pāñcālas.
Seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna locked in combat with the son of Droṇa, O Bhārata, the son of Subhadrā rushed up at once, scattering whetted shafts.
He pierced Śalya with twenty-five arrows, Kṛpa with nine, and Aśvatthāman with eight, O bull among men.
Then the son of Droṇa swiftly pierced the son of Arjuna with a feathered shaft, Śalya with twelve, and Kṛpa with three whetted arrows.
And Lakṣmaṇa, your grandson, advanced exultantly against your grandson who stood there, and thereupon a battle ensued.
Then Duryodhana's son, full of wrath, pierced the son of Subhadrā with nine arrows in the fight, O king, and it seemed a marvel.
But Abhimanyu, enraged, O bull of the Bhāratas, quick of hand, pierced his cousin with fifty arrows, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Lakṣmaṇa with a feathered shaft cut his bow at the grip, O great king, and at that the people raised a great shout.
Casting aside that severed bow, the son of Subhadrā, slayer of hostile heroes, took up another splendid bow of swifter force.
Those two bulls among men, eager in that battle, each seeking to repay the other blow for blow, struck one another with sharp, keen arrows.
Then King Duryodhana, lord of men, seeing his son, that great car-warrior, hard pressed by your grandson, went thither.
When your son had turned to the fight, all the lords of men hemmed in the son of Arjuna on every side with their array of chariots.
Surrounded by those heroes, hard to conquer in battle, that hero, whose prowess equaled Kṛṣṇa's, was not shaken at all, O king.
Then Dhanaṃjaya, seeing the son of Subhadrā locked in combat there, rushed forward in fury, longing to rescue his own son.
Then the kings, with their chariots, elephants, and horses, led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, advanced together against Savyasācin.
The dust of the earth, suddenly thrown up by elephants, horses, chariots, and cavalry, rose dense to the path of the sun and was seen on high.
Those thousands of elephants and hundreds of kings, coming within the range of his arrows, could in no way press forward.
All creatures wailed, the quarters grew dark, and a fierce, dreadful calamity of the Kurus was plainly seen.
Neither the sky, nor the quarters, nor the earth, nor the sun could be made out, O best of the Bhāratas, for the masses of arrows loosed by the diademed one.
Some leaders of chariot-bands were seen with their banners and elephants brought low, their steeds slain, the warriors sorely stricken, their chariots scattered in flight.
Other car-warriors, deprived of their chariots, were seen here and there running on every side, still bearing their weapons, with armlets upon their arms.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Riders abandoning their horses, and mahouts their tusked beasts, fled in every direction out of fear of Arjuna, O king.
Lords of men, struck by Arjuna, were seen fallen and falling from their chariots, their elephants, and their horses.
Arms raised on high, grasping maces and swords, O lord of the people, holding lances and quivers, arrows and bows,
and goads and standards—these of the warriors Arjuna hewed off here and there with his fierce arrows, wearing then a dreadful form.
Of massive iron clubs and of war-hammers, my lord, of lances and slings and swords in the battle,
of sharp battle-axes and javelins, O Bhārata, and of shattered mail-coats and cuirasses upon the ground,
of banners and shields and fans on every side, of parasols with golden staves and yak-tail whisks, O Bhārata,
and of goads and whips and harness-straps, my lord—heaps of these were seen strewn there upon the field of battle.
There was not a single man of your army, O Bhārata, who could in any wise advance against the heroic Arjuna in battle.
For whoever advanced against Pārtha in the fight, O lord of the people, he was sent to the other world by his sharp shafts.
As your warriors fled in every direction, Arjuna and Vāsudeva blew their excellent conches.
Seeing that host broken, your father Devavrata spoke in the battle to the hero, the son of Bhāradvāja, as if with a smile:
This heroic son of Pāṇḍu, joined with Kṛṣṇa, the mighty one, deals with the armies just as Dhanaṃjaya would.
For he can in no way be conquered today in battle, since the form he wears appears like Yama the all-ending Death.
Nor can this great host be turned back: behold, this army flees, each man only watching the other run.
And the sun is now reaching the best of mountains, where it sets, as if withdrawing utterly the forms of all the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I think the hour for withdrawal has come, O bull among men; our warriors, weary and afraid, will not fight at all.
Having spoken thus to Droṇa, the best of teachers, Bhīṣma, that great car-warrior, then ordered the withdrawal of your forces.
Then came the withdrawal of the armies, both yours and theirs, O Bhārata, as the sun went down and the hour of twilight set in.
Saṃjaya said: When the night had brightened into dawn, Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu then gave orders for the marshalling of the troops, O Bhārata.
And the son of Śaṃtanu then formed the great battle-array of the Garuḍa, Bhīṣma, the grandsire of the Kurus, longing for the victory of your sons.
At Garuḍa's beak was your father Devavrata himself; as its two eyes were the son of Bhāradvāja and Kṛtavarman of the Sātvatas.
Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa, the two illustrious ones, stood at the head, joined by the Trigartas, the Matsyas, the Kekayas, and the Vāṭadhānas.
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, and Bhagadatta, my lord, the Madrakas, the Sindhu-Sauvīras, and the men of the Five Rivers,
together with Jayadratha, were stationed at the neck; at the back was King Duryodhana, surrounded by his brothers and his followers.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and the Kāmboja chief with the Śakas, formed the tail, O great king, and the Śūrasenas as well in their entirety.
The Māgadhas and the Kaliṅgas, with the hosts of the Dāśerakas, taking up the right wing of the array, stood there clad in armor.
The Kānanas and the Vikuñjas, the Muktas, and the Puṇḍrāviṣas, together with Bṛhadbala, took up the left wing.
Seeing that host marshalled, Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, together with Dhṛṣṭadyumna, drew up his counter-array in the battle, opposing that most terrible formation with an array in the shape of a crescent moon.
Holding the right horn, Bhīmasena shone resplendent, surrounded by kings of many lands furnished with floods of diverse weapons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Next to him came Virāṭa and Drupada, the great car-warrior; and immediately after them stood Nīla with his blue-armored troops.
Next after Nīla stood Dhṛṣṭaketu, the great car-warrior, encompassed by the Cedis, the Kāśis, the Karūṣas, and the Pauravas.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, with the Pāñcālas and the Prabhadrakas, stood in the center of the great host, ready for battle, O Bhārata.
Likewise the King of Righteousness, encompassed by his division of elephants; and then, O king, Sātyaki and the five sons of Draupadī.
Then Abhimanyu close at hand, and Irāvat beyond him, and then the son of Bhīmasena, O king, and the Kekaya princes, those great car-warriors.
Then the best of two-footed beings took the left flank, the guardian of all the world, whose own guardian was Janārdana.
Thus did the Pāṇḍavas draw up this great counter-array, for the destruction of your sons and of those who had joined their side.
Then the battle began, with chariots and elephants entangled together, as your men and the foe struck down one another.
Floods of horses and floods of chariots, O lord of peoples, were seen rushing together here and there, striking one another down.
From the streaming masses of chariots, racing onward and striking down each its own foe, there arose a tumultuous din mingled with the booming of war-drums.
In that exceedingly tumultuous clash, O Bhārata, as the heroic men slew one another—yours and theirs alike—the uproar touched the very heavens.
Saṃjaya said: Then, when the armies were arrayed—both yours and the others'—Dhanaṃjaya, that surpassing chariot-warrior, smote your host of chariots, O Bhārata, felling the leaders of chariot-bands with his arrows in the battle.
Slaughtered by Pārtha as though by Time itself at the dissolution of an age, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, straining hard in the fight, battled back against the Pāṇḍavas, seeking blazing glory and making death their only retreat.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With single-minded resolve they shattered the Pāṇḍava host again and again, O king, and were themselves shattered in turn in the combat.
With the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas now fleeing, now broken, now wheeling about to charge again, nothing whatever could be made out.
A dust rose up from the earth that veiled the sun, and there none could in any way distinguish the quarters or the intermediate quarters of the sky.
By guesswork, by watchwords, and by names and lineages the fighting was carried on then, here and there, O lord of peoples.
There the battle-array of the Kauravas could in no way be broken, guarded as it was by the wise Bhāradvāja, true to his word.
In like manner the great array of the Pāṇḍavas, guarded by Savyasācin and well protected by Bhīma, could not be pierced.
Sallying forth from the front of the host, the men fought there, O king, the chariots and elephants of both armies locked together in the fray.
In that great battle horsemen were brought down by horsemen with bright-pointed lances and with javelins in the fight.
Closing with a chariot-warrior, a chariot-warrior felled him with gold-adorned arrows in that exceedingly terrible battle.
Elephant-riders, locked in combat, brought down elephant-riders in companies—yours and theirs alike—with iron shafts, arrows, and lances.
Bands of foot-soldiers in the fray, exhilarated and bearing mutual wrongs, struck down foot-soldiers with slings and battle-axes.
In the encounter a foot-soldier felled a chariot-warrior, and a chariot-warrior too a foot-soldier, with sharpened weapons, on both sides alike.
Elephant-riders then brought down horsemen, and horsemen those mounted on elephants; and this seemed a marvel.
By foremost elephant-riders foot-soldiers were seen struck down here and there, and by those foot-soldiers in turn the elephant-warriors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bands of foot-soldiers being felled by horsemen, and bands of cavalry by foot-soldiers, were seen by the hundreds and by the thousands.
With banners cast down there, with bows and lances, with javelins and maces, with iron clubs and tremor-shafts,
with spears and gleaming variegated coats of mail, with barbed darts and goads, with bright swords, and with gold-feathered arrows,
with horse-cloths and elephant-housings and costly blankets, the earth shone, O best of the Bhāratas, as though figured all over with wreaths and garlands.
With the fallen bodies of men and horses, and with elephants, in that great battle the earth became impassable, miry with flesh and blood.
The dust of the earth, drenched with the blood of battle, settled, and all the quarters became clear, O lord of men.
Headless trunks beyond counting rose up on every side, become as it were portents foretelling the destruction of the world, O Bhārata.
As that most fearsome and dreadful battle was raging, chariot-warriors were seen racing about on every side.
Then Droṇa and Bhīṣma, and Jayadratha lord of the Sindhus, Purumitra and Vikarṇa, and Śakuni son of Subala—
these, unassailable in battle and lion-like in prowess, shattered the ranks of the Pāṇḍavas again and again.
In like manner Bhīmasena too, and the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, Sātyaki and Cekitāna, and the sons of Draupadī, O Bhārata,
drove your men and your sons, together with all the kings, in flight upon the field, as the thirty gods rout the dānavas.
Thus those bulls among warriors, slaying one another in the fight, drenched with blood and dreadful of aspect, shone like dānavas.
Having vanquished their foes, the heroic high officers of both armies were seen like planets in the vault of heaven.
Then your son Duryodhana, with a thousand chariots, advanced upon the Pāṇḍavas in battle and upon the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In like manner all the Pāṇḍavas, with a mighty host, advanced to meet the valiant, foe-subduing Droṇa and Bhīṣma in the battle.
The Diademed One, enraged, advanced against the most capable of kings, while the son of Arjuna and Sātyaki advanced against the host of Subala's son.
Then once more there arose a hair-raising combat between your men and the foe, each striving for victory in the fight.
Saṃjaya said: Then those kings, enraged at the sight of Phalguna in the battle, surrounded him on every side with many thousands of chariots.
And having penned him in, O Bhārata, within a ring of chariots, they hemmed him about on every side with many thousands of arrows.
Bright sharp spears, maces and iron bludgeons, javelins and battle-axes, mallets and pestles too—enraged, they hurled them all in the battle against the chariot of Phalguna.
That downpour of weapons, sweeping on like a swarm of locusts, Pārtha checked on every side with his gold-adorned arrows.
Beholding there that more-than-human dexterity of Bībhatsu, the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, the piśācas, serpents, and rākṣasas honored Phalguna, O lord of kings, crying 'Well done! Well done!'
And the valiant Gāndhāras, together with the sons of Subala, with a great host beset Sātyaki and Abhimanyu in the battle.
There the enraged followers of Subala's son, in their wrath, cut the splendid chariot of the Vārṣṇeya to bits in the fight with weapons of every kind.
But Sātyaki, scorcher of foes, abandoning his chariot amid that great peril, swiftly mounted the chariot of Abhimanyu.
The two of them, joined upon a single chariot, swiftly shattered the host of Subala's son with sharp, smooth-jointed arrows.
Droṇa and Bhīṣma, straining hard in the battle, laid waste the host of the King of Righteousness with keen, heron-feathered arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the royal son of Dharma and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī, before the eyes of all the troops, charged the array of Droṇa.
There ensued a vast, tumultuous, hair-raising battle, as dreadful as was of old the war between the gods and the asuras.
As Bhīmasena and Ghaṭotkaca were performing mighty deeds, Duryodhana then came up and beset them both.
There we beheld the marvelous prowess of Hiḍimbā's son, in that he fought in the battle surpassing even his father, O Bhārata.
But Bhīmasena, greatly enraged, smote the unforgiving Duryodhana in the breast with a shaft, the Pāṇḍava as it were laughing the while.
Then King Duryodhana, stunned by that grievous blow, sank down upon the floor of his chariot and fell into a swoon.
Then his charioteer, perceiving him senseless, in haste bore him away from the battle, O king; and thereupon the army broke apart.
Then Bhīma, smiting with keen arrows that Kaurava host as it fled on every side, pursued it from behind.
And the son of Pṛṣata, foremost of chariot-warriors, and the Pāṇḍava son of Dharma, while Droṇa looked on and the son of Gaṅgā looked on, struck down the host with keen shafts that scatter the ranks of the foe.
That host of your son, fleeing in the battle, the great chariot-warriors Bhīṣma and Droṇa were not able to stay.
For though held back by Bhīṣma and by Droṇa, O lord of peoples, that host kept fleeing on, even as Droṇa and Bhīṣma looked on.
Then, as thousands of chariots fled this way and that, the son of Subhadrā and the bull of the Śini line, mounted upon a single chariot, hewed down the host of Subala's son on every side in the battle.
Those two then, the scion of the Śinis and the bull of the Kurus, shone forth like the moon and the sun met together in the sky on the night of the new moon.
Then Arjuna, enraged, rained upon your host, O lord of peoples, a shower of arrows, as a rain-cloud pours down its streams.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Slaughtered by Pārtha's arrows in the battle, the Kaurava host then fled, trembling with despair and terror.
Beholding them in flight, the great chariot-warriors Bhīṣma and Droṇa, wrought up and seeking Duryodhana's welfare, sought to stay them.
Then King Duryodhana, having recovered his senses, O lord of peoples, turned back that host which was fleeing on every side.
Wherever any man caught sight of your son, O Bhārata, there the great chariot-warriors among the warriors turned back.
Seeing those turn back, the other men too then took their stand—some out of rivalry with one another, O king, and others out of shame.
As they returned, their onrush was such, O lord of peoples, as is the swelling of the ocean at the rising of the moon.
Then King Suyodhana, seeing them rallied, went in haste to Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, and spoke these words.
Grandsire, mark what I shall say to you, O Bhārata. I deem it unbecoming, O Kaurava, while you yet live—
and while Droṇa, foremost of those skilled in arms, lives with his son and his friends, and Kṛpa the mighty archer—that this army of ours should flee.
The Pāṇḍavas are in no way a match for you, O king, nor in battle for Droṇa, nor for Droṇa's son, nor for Kṛpa.
Surely the sons of Pāṇḍu are objects of your favor, O grandsire, since you suffer, O hero, this army to be slaughtered.
You should have told me, O king, even before the encounter: 'I will not fight the Pāṇḍavas in battle, nor the son of Pṛṣata, nor Sātyaki.'
Hearing such a word from you, from the preceptor, and from Kṛpa, I should then and there, together with Karṇa, have pondered what was to be done.
If I am not to be forsaken by you two here in the battle, then fight, O bulls among men, with prowess befitting you.
Hearing these words, Bhīṣma, laughing again and again, his eyes rolling with anger, spoke to your son.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Many a time, O king, have I spoken to you the truthful and salutary word: the Pāṇḍavas are unconquerable in battle, even by the gods together with Vāsava.
Yet what I, an old man, am able to do this day, O best of kings, I shall do to the utmost of my power. Behold it now with your kinsmen.
This day, before the eyes of all, I shall hold back all the sons of Pāṇḍu, with their troops and their kinsmen, while the whole world looks on.
When Bhīṣma had thus spoken, O lord of men, your sons, filled with joy, blew their conches and beat their drums loudly.
And the Pāṇḍavas too, O king, on hearing that mighty din, blew their conches and sounded their kettledrums and tabours.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When Bhīṣma had taken his vow in that most terrible battle, having been provoked to wrath—especially by my grieving son—
what then did Bhīṣma do among the Pāṇḍavas, O Saṃjaya, and what did the Pāñcālas do against the grandsire? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: When the greater part of the forenoon of that day had passed, O Bhārata, and the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, having gained the advantage, were exultant,
your father Devavrata, knower of all the finer points of duty, advanced with swift horses against the host of the Pāṇḍavas, guarded by a great army and by your sons on every side.
Then there began a tumultuous, hair-raising battle between us and the Pāṇḍavas, born of your folly, O Bhārata.
From the twanging of bows and the clapping of bowstring-guards there arose a mighty sound there, as of mountains splitting apart.
"Stand! I am standing! Strike this man! Turn back! Hold firm! I am at my post! Smite away!"—such cries were heard on every side.
Upon the golden coats of mail, the diadems, and the banners there arose a clatter, like that of rocks falling upon mountains.
Heads cut off and ornamented arms, fallen by the hundreds and by the thousands, writhed upon the ground when they reached it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some of those foremost of men, though their heads had been struck off, stood yet with bows raised and weapons grasped firm.
A river of swift current began to flow, bearing blood, dreadful with the limbs of elephants for its rocks, its mire of flesh and gore.
Springing then from the bodies of fine horses, men, and elephants, it flowed toward the ocean of the other world, gladdening vultures and jackals.
Never was such a battle seen or heard of, O king, as that of your sons and of the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata.
No path remained there for chariots, so covered was it with warriors struck down in the fight and with fallen dark elephants, like mountain peaks.
With scattered, gleaming mail, with banners and parasols, O sire, that field of battle shone like the vault of heaven in autumn.
Some, pierced through by arrows and dragging their wounds in their last agony, yet fearless and mailed, rushed upon the foe in battle.
"Father! Brother! Friend! Kinsman! Comrade! My uncle! Do not abandon me!"—so cried others who had fallen in the fight.
"Charge! Come on! Do not flee! Why are you afraid? Where are you going? I stand here in the battle—fear not!"—thus others cried aloud.
There Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, his bow ever bent into a circle, loosed arrows blazing at the tips, like venomous serpents.
Making all the quarters one solid mass of arrows, that firm-vowed one slew the chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, marking out one after another, O Bhārata.
Dancing, as it were, upon his chariot-platform and displaying the swiftness of his hands, he appeared here and there, O king, like a whirling firebrand.
That single hero in battle the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas beheld, by reason of his swiftness, as if he were many hundreds of thousands.
They reckoned Bhīṣma there to have multiplied himself by magic; for having seen him in the east, men beheld him in the west.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beholding him in the north, they saw him again in the south, O lord; thus did that hero, the son of Gaṅgā, show himself in the battle.
None among the Pāṇḍavas was able even to look upon him; they saw only the many shafts loosed from Bhīṣma's bow.
Beholding him working his feats in battle and destroying their host—your father ranging there in superhuman form—the heroes in that fight wailed aloud in many ways and grievously.
Like locusts, the kings fell, driven on by fate, by the thousands into the wrathful fire that was Bhīṣma, to their own destruction.
For no shaft of Bhīṣma's was ever in vain in that combat; piercing keenly, by reason of the multitude of bodies of men, elephants, and horses, none missed its mark.
With a single well-loosed feathered arrow he would pierce an elephant's mail and armour, as a thunderbolt cleaves the loftiest mountain.
Two and even three elephant-riders, packed close together and armoured though they were, your father slew with a single keen iron shaft.
Whoever came against Bhīṣma, that tiger among men, in the fight, was seen by me but for a moment, and then beheld struck down upon the earth.
Thus that great army of the Dharma-king, slaughtered by Bhīṣma of matchless valour, was shattered into a thousand pieces.
That mighty host, scorched by the rain of arrows, was scattered before the very eyes of Vāsudeva and of the great-souled Pārtha.
Though they strove, those heroes, tormented by Bhīṣma's arrows, could not check the great chariot-warriors who were fleeing.
Slaughtered by him whose valour equalled great Indra's, the mighty host broke, O great king, and not even two fled together.
With its men, elephants, and horses pierced through, its banners and chariot-poles fallen, the army of Pāṇḍu's sons grew senseless and broke into cries of woe.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There, compelled by the force of fate, father slew son and son slew father, and friend struck down his dear friend amid the wailing.
Others among the soldiers of Pāṇḍu's son were seen casting off their armour and fleeing with hair dishevelled, O Bhārata.
Like a herd of cattle in panic, its chariot-leaders thrown into confusion, the army of Pāṇḍu's son was then seen, raised in cries of anguish.
Seeing that army breaking apart, the son of Devakī, reining in the splendid chariot, spoke to Pārtha, the Bībhatsu:
"The hour has come, O Pārtha, that you have longed for. Strike at him, O tiger among men, unless you are bewildered by delusion!
What you declared of old, O hero, in the assembly of kings—that you would slay all the warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa,
with their followers—all who would do battle with me—that make true now, O son of Kuntī, that word of yours, O scorcher of foes!"
"O Bībhatsu, behold your own army breaking on every side, and all the lords of earth in Yudhiṣṭhira's host taking to flight.
For seeing Bhīṣma in battle, like Death with jaws agape, they perish in their terror, as little beasts before a lion."
Thus addressed, Dhanaṃjaya answered Vāsudeva: "Plunging into this ocean of troops, drive the horses to where Bhīṣma is."
Then Mādhava urged on the silver-hued steeds toward where Bhīṣma's chariot stood, O king, hard to gaze upon as the radiant sun.
Then that great host of Yudhiṣṭhira rallied once more, seeing the mighty-armed Pārtha rising up against Bhīṣma in the battle.
Then Bhīṣma, foremost of the Kurus, roaring again and again like a lion, swiftly covered the chariot of Dhanaṃjaya with showers of arrows.
In a moment that chariot of his, with its horses and its driver, veiled by the great rain of shafts, was no longer to be seen.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Vāsudeva, unflinching, holding firm with steadfast resolve, urged on those horses, sorely wounded by Bhīṣma's arrows.
Then Pārtha, taking up his celestial bow that roared like a thundercloud, cut Bhīṣma's bow with three arrows and brought it down.
His bow thus severed, the Kaurava—your father—in the mere span between two blinks strung yet another great bow.
Then with both arms he drew that bow that thundered like a cloud; but Arjuna, wrathful, cut that bow of his too.
The son of Śaṃtanu applauded that swiftness of his: "Well done, mighty-armed Pārtha! Well done, O delight of Pāṇḍu!
In you alone, Dhanaṃjaya, does this great feat befit. I am exceedingly pleased, my son—do battle with me!"
Thus praising Pārtha, the hero took up another great bow and loosed his shafts in battle against Pārtha's chariot.
Vāsudeva displayed the highest skill in the driving of the steeds; rendering his shafts vain, he wheeled deftly in circling courses.
Even so, Bhīṣma pierced both Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya hard with whetted arrows in every limb, O sire.
Those two tigers among men, gashed by Bhīṣma's shafts, shone like two bellowing bulls scored and marked by each other's horns.
And once again, greatly enraged and furious in the fight, Bhīṣma with smooth-jointed arrows shut off all the quarters around the two Kṛṣṇas.
Wrathful, he made the Vārṣṇeya tremble with keen shafts, while Bhīṣma, smiling again and again, laughed aloud the while.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the mighty-armed, beholding in battle the prowess of Bhīṣma, and marking the gentleness of Pārtha's fighting,
and seeing Bhīṣma pouring forth showers of arrows ceaselessly in the fight, blazing like the sun as he reached the midst between the two armies,
striking down the best and bravest of the soldiers of Pāṇḍu's son, working as it were the end of an age upon Yudhiṣṭhira's host—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the blessed Keśava, slayer of hostile heroes, no longer able to bear it, that one of measureless soul, thought: "Yudhiṣṭhira's army is as good as no more.
For in a single day Bhīṣma could destroy in battle the gods and dānavas—how much more the sons of Pāṇḍu, with their forces and their followers!
The great army of the high-souled Pāṇḍava is fleeing; and these Kauravas, seeing the Somakas swiftly broken, rush forward in the fight exultant, gladdening the grandsire.
I myself will slay Bhīṣma this day for the Pāṇḍavas' sake, girt in mail; this burden of the great-souled Pāṇḍavas I shall lift away."
Arjuna too, struck by the keen arrows in the combat, knew not what he should do in the fight, out of reverence for Bhīṣma.
As he was thinking thus, the grandsire, enraged, once more let fly his arrows against Pārtha's chariot.
By the very multitude of those arrows all the quarters were utterly veiled; neither sky nor quarters nor earth could be seen, nor the garland-rayed sun; tumultuous winds laden with smoke arose, and all the quarters were thrown into turmoil.
Droṇa and Vikarṇa, and Jayadratha, Bhūriśravas, Kṛtavarman, and Kṛpa, King Śrutāyus and the lord of the Ambaṣṭhas, and Vinda and Anuvinda, and Sudakṣiṇa,
and all the men of the East and the hosts of the Sauvīras, the Vasātis, and the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas—obedient to the command of King Śaṃtanu's son—hastened against the Diademed One.
The grandson of Śini beheld the Diademed One being hemmed in by floods and nets of horse, foot, and chariots, by many hundreds of thousands, and by leaders of elephant-herds.
Then, seeing Arjuna and Vāsudeva, those foremost of weapon-bearers, beset on every side by foot, elephants, horse, and chariots, the hero of the Śinis swiftly advanced.
That mighty bowman, the hero of the Śinis, rushing suddenly upon those hosts, came to Arjuna's aid, as Viṣṇu once aided the slayer of Vṛtra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beholding the army of Yudhiṣṭhira, its masses of elephants, horses, chariots, and banners shattered, all its warriors terrified by Bhīṣma, fleeing away, the hero of the Śinis spoke:
"Whither do you go, O kṣatriyas? This is no righteous course; it was proclaimed by the ancients before all good men. Do not forsake your vow, O heroes; uphold your own warrior's duty!"
When the younger brother of Vāsava beheld those foremost of kings fleeing on every side, and marked the slackness of Pārtha's fighting, and saw Bhīṣma rising up in the battle,
then that great-souled lord of all the Dāśārhas, no longer brooking it, looked upon the Kurus rushing on from every quarter and, in praise, spoke to the illustrious grandson of Śini:
"Let those who flee flee on, O hero of Śini's line; and those who yet stand firm, O Sātvata, let them go too. Behold Bhīṣma flung down from his car by me this day, and Droṇa with his hosts brought low in the battle."
"Not one warrior of that host of the Kauravas, O Sātvata, shall escape me in my wrath upon the field this day. Therefore, taking up my terrible discus, I shall take the life of him of the mighty vow."
"Having slain Bhīṣma with his hosts in the battle, and Droṇa too, that foremost of warriors, O grandson of Śini, I shall do a pleasing thing for Dhanaṃjaya, and for the king, and for Bhīma, and for the twin sons of the Aśvins."
"Having slain all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and those foremost of kings who hold to their side, I shall this day, rejoicing, establish King Ajātaśatru in his kingdom."
Then the son of Vāsudeva, leaping down from the chariot and loosing his steeds, raised in his arm the fair-naved discus, bright as the sun, of might equal to the thunderbolt, its edge keen as a razor.
Making the earth tremble with his steps, the great-souled Kṛṣṇa rushed with fury upon Bhīṣma, swollen with pride in the fray, as a lion bent on slaying springs upon a lordly elephant blind with rut.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He, the destroyer, the younger brother of mighty Indra, in his wrath bore down upon Bhīṣma amid the host; his trailing yellow-bordered garment streaming, he blazed like a cloud in the sky wreathed about with lightning's flash.
And the Sudarśana of that descendant of Śūra shone forth—that lotus-discus whose stalk was his strong and mighty arm; like the primeval lotus of the hue of the young sun, it shone, born from the navel of Nārāyaṇa.
That lotus, opened by the rising sun of Kṛṣṇa's wrath, its petals fair-formed with edges sharp as razors, grown upon the broad lake of his very body, shone forth, with the arm of Nārāyaṇa for its stalk.
Seeing the younger brother of mighty Indra wrathful, discus in hand and roaring aloud, all beings cried out in dread, thinking, "This is the doom of the Kurus."
That Vāsudeva, discus grasped in hand, as though about to dissolve the world of the living, springing forward, the teacher of the worlds shone like the fire of Time that would consume all creatures.
Beholding that god, the best of two-footed beings, rushing on with discus seized in hand, the son of Śaṃtanu, bow and arrow in hand, standing in his chariot, without dismay addressed him:
"Come, come, O Lord of the gods, dwelling-place of the worlds! Homage be to thee, O wielder of Śārṅga and the discus! By force cast me down, O Lord of the worlds, from this noblest of cars, O refuge of all beings, here in the battle."
"Slain by thee this day, O Kṛṣṇa, mine shall be blessedness here and in the world beyond. By thy onset, O lord of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, I am honored, O hero, throughout the three worlds."
Then Pārtha too, leaping in haste from his chariot and running after that hero of the Yadus, seized Hari—him of stout, long, full-hanging arms—by the arms, himself broad-armed and powerful.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Though held back, that primeval god, the great yogin, sorely wrathful indeed, Viṣṇu, with violence dragged Jiṣṇu along with him, as a great wind drags a lone tree.
But Pārtha, planting his feet with might, the diademed and garlanded one, by force held back him who was swiftly rushing toward Bhīṣma—at the tenth step, O king, and that only with difficulty.
And when Kṛṣṇa stood still, Arjuna, garlanded with a wreath of wrought gold, bowed low and, well pleased, said: "Draw back thy wrath. Thou, O Keśava, art the refuge of the Pāṇḍavas."
"The deed shall not be left undone according to my vow—I swear it by my sons and by my brothers, O Keśava. I shall make an end of the Kurus, urged on by thee, O younger brother of Indra."
Then Janārdana, his mind made glad to hear that vow and pledge, abiding by the wish of the best of the Kauravas, mounted the chariot once more, his discus still in hand.
Taking up the reins again and seizing his conch, that slayer of foes, the descendant of Śūra, made the quarters resound with the blast of Pāñcajanya.
With necklace, armlets, and earrings tossed awry, his curved lashes and eyes besprent with dust, his teeth gleaming bright, the conch grasped in his hand—seeing him, the heroes of the Kurus cried aloud.
Then the din of tabors, kettledrums, and war-drums, the rumble of chariot-wheels and the boom of great drums, and fierce lion-roars arose throughout all the hosts of the Kurus.
The twang of Pārtha's Gāṇḍīva, like rolling thunder, went forth to the sky and to all the quarters; and the bright, clear shafts loosed from the Pāṇḍava's bow flew to every region.
Against him the lord of the Kauravas, with his force, together with Bhīṣma and Bhūriśravas, advanced, arrow uplifted in hand, like fire eager to consume dry grass.
Then Bhūriśravas hurled at Arjuna seven golden-feathered broad-arrows, Duryodhana a fierce-speeding javelin, Śalya a mace, and the son of Śaṃtanu a spear.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With seven shafts he warded off the seven choice arrows loosed by Bhūriśravas, and with a keen razor-edged shaft he cut down that javelin sped from Duryodhana's arm.
Then the hero, with two shafts, cut asunder the bright spear, gleaming like lightning, hurled by the son of Śaṃtanu, and the mace flung from the arm of the lord of the Madras.
Then, drawing back mightily with both arms his wondrous, immeasurable Gāṇḍīva bow, he brought forth, duly and according to rite, the terrible weapon of mighty Indra, marvelous, into the sky.
With that supreme weapon the great-souled bearer of the mighty bow, the diademed and garlanded one, held back all the hosts with floods and nets of arrows bright as the hue of flame.
The arrows loosed from Pārtha's bow, having cleft chariots, banner-tops, bows, and arms, pierced into the bodies of the foe—of lordly men, lordly elephants, and horses.
Then Pārtha, the diademed and garlanded one, covering the quarters and the intermediate quarters with keen, well-edged shafts, with the sound of the Gāṇḍīva made their hearts to quail.
As that most dreadful tumult was unleashed, the blare of conches, the boom of drums, and the fierce war-cries were swallowed up and silenced by the twang of the Gāṇḍīva.
Then, recognizing that sound of the Gāṇḍīva, the warrior-heroes led by King Virāṭa, and the king of the Pāñcālas, the valiant Drupada, came to that place, undaunted in spirit.
But all thy hosts, wherever rose the roar born of the Gāṇḍīva, there and thither only gave way; not one came up against him in opposition.
In that most terrible clash of kings, foremost warriors were slain together with their cars and charioteers, and elephants, scorched by the fall of iron shafts, bearing great banners and bright golden girths,
their strength spent, fell suddenly to the ground, their armor and bodies rent by the diademed one, struck hard by Pārtha's feathered shafts of fierce velocity, by keen broad-arrows with sharpened points.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Their frames cut through, their base-pegs shattered, the great banners at the forefront of the armies, and the bands of foot-soldiers and the chariots in the battle, and the horses and elephants—all by Dhanaṃjaya,
struck by arrows, their strength swiftly fled, their limbs grown rigid, fell upon the earth, their armor and bodies riven, O king, by that supreme weapon of Indra in the great battle.
Then by the diademed one, with floods of keen shafts, a most dreadful river was set flowing there upon the field of battle—its waters the blood streaming from the weapon-gashed bodies of men, its foam the bodies of men.
With a violent current, broad in its flow, it streamed forth in a shape of terrible roaring, its course dammed by the corpses of slain elephants and horses, its mire of flesh laden with the entrails and marrow of men.
Thronged by hosts of demons and goblins, its grassy banks strewn with skulls and tangled hair, bearing along thousands of heaped corpses, churning with a tumult of waves of shattered armor of every kind,
its gravel the cut bones of men, horses, and elephants, with the abyss of destruction for its depths, fearful to behold—that river, beset by rows of herons, by vultures and ospreys, by packs of carrion-eaters and hyenas,
its banks crowded, they beheld on every side—cruel, with the semblance of the great Vaitaraṇī, set flowing by the volleys of Arjuna's arrows, streaming with fat, marrow, and blood, most terrible.
Those Cedis, Pāñcālas, Karūṣas, and Matsyas, and all the sons of Pṛthā together, roared aloud, scattering in terror the army of the host-commanders, as a lion the gathered herds of deer; and those two, filled with surpassing joy, sounded forth—the bearer of the Gāṇḍīva and Janārdana.
Then, seeing the sun with its web of rays withdrawn, and gazing up at that Aindra weapon spread wide and most dreadful, unbearable, like the end of an age, their limbs sorely gashed by weapons,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the Kurus, with Bhīṣma, and with Droṇa, Duryodhana, and Bāhlika, made their retreat, seeing the night drawing on, edged with the reddish streaks of the fading sun.
And Dhanaṃjaya too, having won glory and renown in the world and vanquished his foes, his task accomplished, went at nightfall to the camp together with the kings and his brothers. Then arose a tumultuous and most dreadful clamor among the Kurus at the onset of night.
"In the battle Arjuna has slain ten thousand chariots, and seven hundred elephants have been killed; and all the Easterners and the bands of Sauvīras, and the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas, have been struck down. A great deed has been done by Dhanaṃjaya, such as none other could do."
"Śrutāyus, the king and lord of the Ambaṣṭhas, and likewise Durmarṣaṇa and Citrasena, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the Saindhava and Bāhlika, Bhūriśravas, Śalya and Śala, O king—all of them, with Bhīṣma, were vanquished by the might of his own arm, by the diademed one, that great warrior of the world."
Speaking thus, all thy troops, O Bhārata, went to their tents; and with thousands of well-kindled torches and with shining lamps, the army of the Kurus, all its warriors terrified by the diademed one, made its encampment.
Saṃjaya said: When the night had passed, O Bhārata, the great-souled Bhīṣma, his wrath kindled against the foe, marched at the forefront of the Bhārata armies toward his adversaries, surrounded by the whole of his force.
Him Droṇa, Duryodhana, and Bāhlika, and likewise Durmarṣaṇa and Citrasena, and the exceedingly mighty Jayadratha, and other kings besides, followed on every side with their floods of troops.
Encircled by those great and mighty warriors, glorious and valorous, O king, by those foremost of monarchs, O best of kings, he shone like the Wielder of the Thunderbolt amid the gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At the forefront of that host, fixed aloft and tossing in the wind, the great banners—deep red, yellow, black, and white of hue—set upon the shoulders of mighty elephants, blazed forth.
That host, with the kingly son of Śaṃtanu, with its great warriors, elephants, and horses, shone like a sky filled with new-gathered clouds at the coming of the rains, charged with lightning and thunder.
Then the most fierce army of the Kurus, guarded by the son of Śaṃtanu, set forth facing the battle, marching against Arjuna with sudden onrush, like the terrible flood of a great river.
That array—its hidden strength made of beasts of many kinds, its wings the masses of elephants, horses, foot-soldiers, and chariots, like a vast cloud—the great-souled one whose banner bore the monkey-king beheld from afar.
That bull among men, the hero, the great-souled one, went forth at the head of his army in his bannered, white-horsed, fenced chariot, set upon the slaughter of all his youthful foes.
Beholding in the battle that monkey-bannered car, well-equipped, with fine seat and pole, made ready and driven by the bull of the Yadus, thy Kauravas, together with thy sons, sank into despair upon the field.
Drawn onward, guarded by the diademed one with weapon uplifted, that great warrior of the world—thy men beheld that royal array, thronged with four times four thousand war-elephants.
Even as on the former day the array had been formed by the King of Righteousness, the delight of the Kurus, so, each coming to his appointed place, did the foremost of the Cedis stand together with the foremost of the Pāñcālas.
Then thousands of kettledrums, struck with mighty force, resounded in the battle, and the blare of conches and the boom of war-drums, with lion-roars, rose throughout all the hosts.
Then the loud-twanging bows, with their arrows, stretched taut by the heroes, in an instant swallowed up the din of kettledrums and tabors, and the great blare of the conches too.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beholding the sky veiled with the sound of conches, the web of earthen dust swiftly raised aloft, its radiance spread out like a vast canopy, the heroes suddenly rushed upon one another.
Car-warrior, struck by car-warrior, fell with his charioteer, with his horses, his chariot, and his banner; elephant, struck by elephant, fell; and foot-soldier, struck by foot-soldier, fell.
Wheeling and charging, troops of noble steeds, wondrous to behold, gashed by arrows and smitten by lances and swords, fell upon other troops of noble steeds.
Shields adorned with clusters of golden stars, flung by the heroes and cleft asunder by battle-axes and lances and swords, fell upon the earth.
Some car-warriors, crushed with their charioteers by elephants with their tusks—those mighty trunk-hands—fell down; and bull-elephants too, struck by arrows from the foremost of car-warriors, sank upon the ground.
Hearing the wail of anguish of the young horsemen and foot-soldiers, beaten down by the tusks and bodies of the beasts, hurled and laid low by the rushing flood of elephants, men sank to the earth.
As elephants, horses, and chariots reeled in confusion, and a great terror was loosed among the young horsemen and foot-soldiers, Bhīṣma beheld him of the monkey-king banner being hemmed about by the great car-warriors.
Against that diademed one—whose path blazed with great weapons, arrows, and thunderbolts—the son of Śaṃtanu, his palm-tree banner raised five palm-trees high, borne on by the spirited speed of his noble steeds, rushed forward.
And likewise against the son of Indra, the peer of Śakra himself, there rushed those led by Droṇa—Kṛpa and Śalya and Viviṃśati, Duryodhana and the son of Somadatta, O king.
Then, coming forth from the van of the chariot-host, the hero Abhimanyu, son of Arjuna, knower of all weapons, clad in armor wrought with gold, advanced with speed against them all.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having struck down the great weapons of those great car-warriors, the son of Kṛṣṇa's sister, untiring in his deeds, shone wreathed in flames fed by mighty incantations, like the lord Agni present at the sacrifice.
Then Bhīṣma, swiftly making a river whose waters were blood and whose foam was the slaughter of the foe, passed beyond the son of Subhadrā and, undaunted in spirit, advanced upon the great car-warrior Pārtha.
Then the diademed and garlanded one, laughing, with the great roar of the Gāṇḍīva, wondrous to behold, with a net of broad-headed shafts destroyed that net of mighty weapons.
Upon that Bhīṣma, the highest of all bearers of the bow, the great-souled one of the monkey-king banner, untiring in his deeds, swiftly rained down floods and nets of arrows and bright broad-shafts.
Such was that single combat between the two best of true men, fought without faintheartedness, terrible with the thunder of their bows: the whole world, and the Kurus and Sṛñjayas, beheld that duel of chariots waged by Bhīṣma and Dhanaṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Droṇa's son, Bhūriśravas, Śalya, and Citrasena, and the son of Saṃyamana too, O honored one, together gave battle to the son of Subhadrā.
The people watched him, alone and locked in fight with those five tigers among men of surpassing valor, as one might watch a lion's cub set upon by elephants.
In eluding aim, in heroism, in prowess, in mastery of weapons, and in nimbleness of hand, not one of them proved a match for the son of Kṛṣṇa's sister.
Beholding his son, that tamer of foes, displaying such prowess in the fight, Pārtha, intent in battle, then raised aloud a lion's roar.
Seeing your grandson harrying that host, O lord of peoples, your warriors, O king of kings, surrounded him on every side.
Undismayed, the bane of his enemies' spirit, the son of Subhadrā advanced to meet the bannered army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, with fiery energy and with strength.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As he fought his foes in battle, his great bow, kept ever in the path of swift movement and bright as the sun, was seen by all.
Piercing Droṇa's son with a single shaft and Śalya with five, with eight more he struck down the banner of Saṃyamana's son.
That mighty, gold-shafted spear, like a serpent, hurled at him by the son of Somadatta, he struck aside with a sharp winged arrow.
Warding off the hundreds of dreadful arrows that Śalya loosed, the heir of Arjuna slew his horses in the battle.
Bhūriśravas and Śalya, Droṇa's son, the son of Saṃyamana, and Śala—though furious, they could make no headway against the strength of the arm of Kṛṣṇa's nephew.
Then, O king of kings, the Trigartas and the Madras together with the Kekayas, five-and-thirty thousand strong, urged on by your son—
foremost masters of the science of archery, unconquerable by foes in battle—closed in around the Diademed One, who, with his son, sought to destroy them.
Those two bulls among charioteers, father and son, hemmed in there, the Pāñcāla commander, conqueror of foes, beheld, O king.
Encircled by many thousands of floods of elephants and chariots, encircled too by horsemen and footmen by the hundred thousand,
twanging his bow in wrath and urging on his host, that scorcher of foes advanced against that division of the Madrakas and the Kekayas.
Guarded by that glorious warrior of the steadfast bow, the division, with its chariots, elephants, and horses arrayed and eager for the fray, shone resplendent.
That Pāñcāla, O delight of the Kurus, struck the son of Śaradvat, who was advancing at the front toward Arjuna, with three arrows in the region of the collarbone.
Then, slaying the Madrakas with shafts by tens upon tens, exulting and alone, he slew with a broad-headed arrow the horse of Kṛtavarman.
And Damana, heir of the great-souled Paurava, that scorcher of foes slew with a broad-pointed iron shaft.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the son of Saṃyamana pierced the Pāñcāla, frenzied in battle, with thirty arrows, and his charioteer with ten.
