Having slain in battle his foes endowed with great strength—and a tumultuous bewilderment then fell upon the Kurus.
Karṇa and Duryodhana too sighed again and again; and when Bhīṣma, the chief upholder of the Kauravas, had thus fallen, all became a cry of woe, and everything passed beyond restraint.
And seeing Bhīṣma fallen, your son Duḥśāsana, taking on the utmost speed, rushed toward the division of Droṇa.
Sent forth by his brother, that hero, mailed and amid his own host, that tiger among men advanced, urging on his troops.
Beholding him approach, the Kurus gathered round Duḥśāsana, O great king, wondering, "What will he have to say?"
Then the Kaurava announced to Droṇa that Bhīṣma had been slain; and Droṇa, hearing those unwelcome tidings, fell at once from his chariot.
Then, regaining his senses, the valiant son of Bharadvāja held back his own divisions at that moment, O honored one.
Seeing the Kurus withdraw, the Pāṇḍavas too, through messengers mounted on swift horses, caused their own troops to retire from the field.
When the armies had everywhere withdrawn in succession, all the kings, their armor laid aside, went to Bhīṣma.
Then, ceasing from battle, the warriors in their hundreds of thousands stood attending upon that great-souled one, as the immortals attend Prajāpati.
Approaching Bhīṣma, that bull of the Bhāratas, as he lay there, the Pāṇḍavas together with the Kurus paid him homage and took their places around him.
Then to the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus, who stood bowing before him, the righteous Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, spoke.
"Welcome to you, illustrious ones; welcome to you, great chariot-warriors. I rejoice at the sight of you, who are like the immortals."
Having greeted them thus, with his head hanging down he said: "My head hangs too low; let a pillow be given to me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the kings brought choice pillows, thin and soft; but the grandsire would not have them.
And that tiger among men said to those kings, as if smiling: "These, O princes, are not fitting for a hero's bed."
Then, looking upon that best of men, the Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya, the long-armed great chariot-warrior of all the worlds, he addressed him.
"O Dhanaṃjaya, mighty-armed, this head of mine hangs down; let such a pillow be given as you here deem fitting."
Setting aside his great bow and saluting the grandsire, with his two eyes brimming with tears he spoke these words.
"Command me, O best of the Kurus, foremost of all wielders of weapons. I am your servant, O unassailable one; what shall be done, grandsire?"
The son of Śaṃtanu said to him: "My head hangs down, my son. O best of the Kurus, Phalguna, fetch me a pillow; quickly, O hero, give me one befitting this bed of mine."
"For you, O Pārtha, mighty-armed, are the foremost of all bowmen, knower of the kṣatriya's law, endowed with the virtues of wisdom and resolve."
Phalguna, saying "So be it," swift and forward in resolve, took up the Gāṇḍīva and, with sacred utterance, his keen-jointed arrows.
Having sought the leave of that great-souled, peerless one among the Bhāratas, with three sharp, swift-flying arrows he upheld his head.
When his intent was understood by Savyasācin, the righteous one, Bhīṣma, that best of the Bhāratas, knower of the truths of dharma and artha, was well pleased.
With the pillow thus given, he praised Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, the best of fighters, the increaser of his friends' delight.
"O Pāṇḍava, you have provided what befits one who lies thus. Had you acted otherwise, I would have cursed you in my wrath."
"This is so, O mighty-armed one, established firmly in the laws: thus must a kṣatriya sleep in battle, lying upon a bed of arrows."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus to Bībhatsu, he addressed these words to all those kings and princes who stood gathered with the Pāṇḍava.
"I shall lie upon this bed until the sun turns back in its course. Those kings who shall then survive will indeed behold me."
"When the sun, the day-maker, blazing and scorching the worlds with his chariot of supreme splendor, shall pass to the quarter ruled by Vaiśravaṇa, then shall I release my life-breaths, dear though my friends be to me."
"Let a trench be dug here, O kings, around my dwelling-place; thus pierced by a hundred arrows, I shall worship Vivasvat. Desist from battle, O princes, and cast off your enmities."
Then physicians came near, skilled in the drawing-out of arrows, furnished with all their instruments, expert and well-trained.
Seeing them, the son of Jāhnavī then spoke these words: "Let the physicians be honored, given their due, and dismissed."
"In this pass there is now no need of physicians for me, for I have attained the supreme goal, lauded by the kṣatriya's law."
"This is not the way, O guardians of the earth, for me who lie upon a bed of arrows; with these very arrows, O kings, I must be burned at the end."
Hearing those words of his, your son Duryodhana dismissed the physicians, having honored them as they deserved.
Then the lords of diverse realms were filled with wonder, beholding the supreme steadfastness in dharma of Bhīṣma of boundless splendor.
Then, having given a pillow to your father, O lord of men, all the Pāṇḍavas together and the Kuru great chariot-warriors—
—approaching that great-souled one as he lay upon his auspicious bed, saluted Bhīṣma and circled him with reverence.
Having set guards about Bhīṣma on every side, all those heroes, deep in thought and sorely grieved, went toward their own camps at evening to take their rest, drenched in blood.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And to the Pāṇḍava great chariot-warriors, encamped and rejoicing, gladdened by the fall of Bhīṣma, the Yādava drew near at the fit time and spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
"By good fortune you triumph, O Kaurava; by good fortune Bhīṣma is laid low—he, the great chariot-warrior, true to his word, unslayable by mortals."
"Or rather, O Pārtha, he who was master of all weapons and missiles, even by the gods could not be slain—but, encountering you whose very glance destroys, he was consumed by your terrible eye."
Thus addressed, the King of Righteousness replied to Janārdana: "Through your grace comes victory, through your wrath comes defeat. For you, O Kṛṣṇa, are our refuge, the giver of fearlessness to your devotees."
"No wonder is victory for those whose protector in battle you ever are, O Keśava, ever devoted to their good. Having gained you in every way, that there should be no wonder—such is my conviction."
Thus addressed, Janārdana replied, smiling: "This speech befits none but you, O best of kings."
Saṃjaya said: When the night had passed, O great king, all the princes—the Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—went forth to the grandsire.
That hero, best of the Kurus, as he lay upon his hero's bed, the kṣatriyas saluted and attended upon, that bull among kṣatriyas.
Maidens with sandal-powder and parched grain and garlands on every side, women, children, and the aged, and onlookers of the common folk, drew near the son of Śaṃtanu as living beings draw near the dispeller of darkness.
Musicians, courtesans, and likewise actors and dancers danced and sang before the aged grandsire of the Kurus.
Ceasing from their battles, loosing off their armor, and laying down their weapons, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas together—
—sat attending upon the unassailable Devavrata, that subduer of foes, affectionate toward one another as before, each according to his age.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That assembly of the Bhāratas, thronged with a hundred princes and graced by Bhīṣma, shone resplendent like the orb of the sun blazing in the sky.
And that gathering of kings waiting upon the grandsire shone forth like the gods waiting upon the lord of gods, the Grandsire of all.
But Bhīṣma, O bull of the Bhāratas, mastering his pain through fortitude, sore-tormented by the arrows, spoke with a mind not over-glad.
"My body is scorched by the arrows, and I swoon with the burning of their wounds; I long for water"—thus he spoke to those kings.
Then those kṣatriyas, O king, brought from all around foods of every kind and jars of cool water.
Seeing what was brought, Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, said: "It is not possible for me now, my son, to take any human enjoyments."
"For I, removed from men and come to a bed of arrows, remain awaiting the turning-back of the moon and the sun."
Having spoken thus to all the princes in a feeble voice, the son of Śaṃtanu addressed the mighty-armed Dhanaṃjaya, O Bhārata.
Then the mighty-armed one, approaching and saluting the grandsire, stood with joined palms, bowing, and said: "What shall I do?"
Seeing that Pāṇḍava, O king, standing before him with salutation, the righteous Bhīṣma, well pleased, addressed Dhanaṃjaya.
"This body of mine burns; I am pierced through and through by great arrows; my vital points are aflame, and my mouth runs dry."
"To cool my body, give me water, O Arjuna; for you, great archer, are able to bring forth water in the proper way."
Arjuna, saying "So be it," the valiant one, mounted his chariot and, drawing the Gāṇḍīva mightily to the string, twanged the bow.
At the sound of his bowstring and palm-guard, like the crashing of a thunderbolt, all beings, hearing it, trembled, and so did all the kings.
Then that best of charioteers, having circled in his chariot that best of the Bhāratas, foremost of all wielders of weapons, as he lay there—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
—and fixing a blazing arrow, consecrating it with sacred utterance, the illustrious Pārtha joined it to the Parjanya weapon and, before the eyes of all the world, pierced the earth at Bhīṣma's right side.
Thereupon there sprang up a pure and blessed jet of water, cool and like ambrosia, of divine fragrance and savor.
Then Pārtha, of divine deeds and prowess, refreshed with that cool jet of water Bhīṣma, the bull of the Kurus.
At that deed of Pārtha, who wrought wonders like Śakra himself, the lords of the earth then fell into the utmost amazement.
Beholding that superhuman and marvelous deed of Bībhatsu, the Kurus shook all over, like cattle tormented by cold.
In their wonder the kings waved their upper garments on every side, and with the blare of conches and kettledrums a tumult arose all around.
And the son of Śaṃtanu, his thirst quenched, O king, spoke to Bībhatsu in the presence of all the princely heroes, as if honoring him.
"This is no marvel in you, O mighty-armed delight of the Kurus; by Nārada you were declared to be an ancient seer of boundless luster."
"With Vāsudeva as your ally, you shall accomplish a mighty deed that even Indra, lord of the gods, together with the gods, surely could not dare."
"Those who know such things know you, O Pārtha, to be the destroyer of all the kṣatriya race; alone among bowmen, you are the foremost of men upon the earth."
"Among the creatures of the world men are the best; of birds Garuḍa is supreme; of waters the ocean is best; of four-footed beasts the cow is highest."
"The sun is best of the radiant ones, Himavat the highest of mountains, the brāhmaṇa the best of castes—and you are the best of bowmen."
"The counsel given by Vidura was not heeded by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, nor that of Droṇa and Rāma and Janārdana, urged again and again, and spoken too by Saṃjaya."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For Duryodhana, his mind deranged and well-nigh senseless, took no joy in my words; transgressor of the scriptures, struck down by Bhīma's might, he shall lie slain for ages to come."
Then, hearing those words, the lord of the Kurus, Duryodhana, became dejected in heart; and the son of Śaṃtanu, looking upon him, said: "Hear me, O king, and let your anger pass."
"You have seen, Duryodhana, how by the wise Pārtha this jet of cool water, fragrant as ambrosia, was brought forth; of such a deed there is none other in this world who can be the doer."
"The weapons of Agni, of Varuṇa, of Soma, of Vāyu, and then of Viṣṇu, of Indra, of Paśupati, of Brahmā, of Parameṣṭhin and Prajāpati, of Dhātṛ, of Tvaṣṭṛ, and of Savitṛ—all the divine missiles—"
"In all the world of men, Dhanaṃjaya alone knows them, or Kṛṣṇa the son of Devakī—no other knows them at all. The Pāṇḍavas, my son, cannot in any wise be conquered in battle."
Superhuman are these deeds of that great-souled one; with him, the resolute, the valiant, who shines in combat and is accomplished in war, O king — let a peace be made with him, my son.
While mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa is still amenable in the assembly of the Kurus, even now, my son, let a peace be made with the valiant Pārtha.
While Arjuna has not yet destroyed what remains of your army with his straight-jointed arrows, even now, my son, let a peace be made with him.
While your own brothers, the survivors of the slaughter, and many kings still stand in the battle, O king, even now let a peace be concluded.
While Yudhiṣṭhira, his eyes blazing with wrath, has not yet burned up your army, even now, my son, let a peace be made with him.
While Nakula and Sahadeva, and Bhīmasena the son of Pāṇḍu, have not yet destroyed your army utterly, O great king, even now, my son, let brotherhood with the Pāṇḍavas find favor with you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let this war end with me, my son; be reconciled with the Pāṇḍavas. May the words I have spoken to you find favor with you, O blameless one. This I judge to be for the welfare of yourself and of your lineage.
Cast off your wrath and make peace with the Pārthas; enough is the slaughter that Phalguna has wrought. With the passing of Bhīṣma let there be friendship between you; reunion is good, O king — be gracious.
Let half the kingdom be given to the Pāṇḍavas; let the King of Righteousness rule from Indraprastha. Do not become a betrayer of friends, the basest of kings, lest you win an evil fame, O lord of the Kauravas.
With my end let there be peace for the peoples; let the kings come together in gladness. Let father go to son, and nephew to uncle, and brother to brother, O king.
But if, sunk in delusion and folly, you do not heed these timely words of mine, then with the end of Bhīṣma all of you shall meet your end — this true word do I declare, O Bhārata.
Having out of affection made the Bhārata hear these words in the midst of the kings, the son of the river fell silent, his vitals seared by the darts, mastering himself and holding back his pain.
Saṃjaya said: Then, when Bhīṣma the delight of Śaṃtanu had fallen silent, O great king, all those kings went back again to their own dwellings.
But when Rādheya, the bull among men, heard that Bhīṣma had been struck down, seized with a touch of fear he came swiftly to him.
He beheld the great-souled one lying then upon his bed of arrows, like the god Kārttikeya, the lord, lying upon the couch of his birth.
That hero lay with his eyes closed; and the Bull, his throat choked with tears, of great splendor, drew near and fell down at his feet.
"I am Rādheya, O best of the Kurus, ever before your eyes, hated by you utterly though I had done no wrong" — thus he spoke to him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing this, the aged Kuru, forcing open his closed eyes, gazed up slowly and with affection spoke these words.
Seeing the place was secluded, and having sent away the guards, the son of Gaṅgā embraced him with one arm, as a father embraces a son.
"Come, come to me, you who set yourself against me, contending with me. Had you not come to me, surely it would not have been well for you.
You are the son of Kuntī, not the son of Rādhā — this I know from Nārada, and from Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, and from Keśava too; of this there is no doubt.
I bear you no hatred, my son — I speak the truth to you; it was only to curb your fierce energy that I uttered harsh words.
You hate the Pāṇḍavas without cause — such was my thought; and for that reason I goaded you again and again with rough speech, O son of the Sun.
I know your prowess in battle, hard for foes to bear, and your reverence for the brahmins, your heroism, and your supreme excellence in giving.
There is none among men your equal, O peer of the immortals; yet, fearing a division of the family, I always spoke to you harshly.
In archery and missile-craft, in bearing strain, in swiftness, and in the might of your weapons, you are the equal of Phalguna and of the great-souled Kṛṣṇa.
O Karṇa, going to the royal city, you alone, bearing your bow, crushed kings in battle for the sake of that king of the Kurus.
And likewise the mighty king Jarāsaṃdha, hard to assail and proud of his warring, proved no match for you in combat.
Devoted to the brahmins and truthful in speech, in splendor like a second sun, sprung from a god, unconquered in battle — on earth you surpass all men.
Gone now is the wrath I once nursed against you. Fate cannot be overcome by human effort.
The heroic Pāṇḍavas are your own brothers, born of the same womb, O slayer of foes. Join with them, mighty-armed one, if you would do what pleases me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let this enmity be ended with me, O son of the Sun; let all the kings on earth this day be free of affliction."
Karṇa said: I know all this, O greatly wise one; there is no doubt of it. As you say, O unassailable one, I am the son of Kuntī and not born of a charioteer.
Yet I was cast off by Kuntī and raised by a charioteer; and having enjoyed Duryodhana's bounty, I cannot now prove false to it.
My wealth, my body, and my noble fame — all of it I have surrendered for Duryodhana's sake, O giver of abundant gifts; and, taking my stand with Suyodhana, I have ever provoked the Pāṇḍavas.
That which is destined to be cannot be turned aside; who could venture to reverse fate by human effort?
The omens foretelling the destruction of the earth, O grandsire, have been perceived by you and declared in the assembly.
The Pāṇḍavas and Vāsudeva are known to me in every way as unconquerable by other men; yet even against them we will dare to strive.
Give me your leave, my father, in this war, ever with a glad heart; with your leave, O hero, it is my resolve to fight.
Whatever harsh or perverse word I spoke amiss, out of anger or recklessness, whatever offense I have done — you ought to forgive it.
Bhīṣma said: If this most dreadful enmity cannot be cast off, then I give you leave, O Karṇa — fight, in your longing for heaven.
Free of wrath, free of agitation, do the king's work, according to your strength and your zeal, abiding by the conduct of the good.
I give you my leave; attain what you desire. You shall surely win the worlds conquered by the duty of the warrior — of this there is no doubt.
Fight without pride, relying on your strength and prowess; for there is no higher duty known for a warrior than righteous battle.
Long and again long have I striven for peace, yet I have not been able to make it; for where there is righteousness, there is victory.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: When the son of Gaṅgā had thus spoken, Rādheya saluted him and won his grace, then mounted his chariot and set out toward your son.
Janamejaya said: When he had heard that Devavrata—peerless in courage, vigor, strength, valor, and prowess—had been slain by Śikhaṇḍin the Pāñcāla,
what then did King Dhṛtarāṣṭra do, his mind distraught with grief, O sage among brahmins, when that valiant father of his had fallen?
For his son, O reverend one, sought the kingdom by overcoming the great-bowed Pāṇḍavas with chariot-warriors led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa.
Now that he was slain, O reverend one—he who was the banner of all bowmen—tell me what the Kaurava did, O best of the twice-born.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing that his father was slain, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, found no peace—that Kaurava, given over wholly to anxiety and grief.
As the king brooded ceaselessly upon that sorrow, the pure-souled son of Gavalgaṇa came once more before him.
When Saṃjaya had come by night from the camp to the city named for the elephant, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Ambikā, questioned him, O great king.
Hearing of Bhīṣma's death, his heart utterly without joy, yet longing for the victory of his sons, he lamented as one stricken.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When they had overcome the great-souled Bhīṣma of terrible prowess, what then did the Kurus do, my son, urged on by fate?
When that hero—unassailable, of mighty energy—was struck down, what did the Kurus do, sunk in an ocean of grief?
That great army of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas, once roused, could strike fierce terror even into the three worlds, O Saṃjaya.
When Devavrata, that bull of the Kurus, was slain, tell me what the kings then did, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, with single mind the words I speak—what your sons did when Devavrata had fallen in the fray.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When Bhīṣma of truthful prowess was slain, O king, both your men and the Pāṇḍavas fell to brooding, each side apart.
Amazed and yet exultant, beholding the law of the warrior, and reproaching their own calling, they bowed down before that great soul.
They made ready a bed for Bhīṣma of measureless splendor, O tiger among men, with a pillow too, fashioned of arrows with bent-down joints.
Having set a guard about Bhīṣma, and spoken each with the other, and taken leave of the son of Gaṅgā, and walked round him in reverence,
their eyes red with wrath, the warriors, gazing upon one another, marched forth again to battle, driven on by fate.
Then to the blare of trumpets and the great booming of war-drums, the divisions of your host and of the foe alike went forth.
As the day turned, O lord of kings, with the son of Jāhnavī fallen, they yielded to fury, their minds undone by fate.
Heedless of the wholesome counsel of the great-souled son of Gaṅgā, the foremost of the Bhāratas marched out, taking up their weapons on every side.
Through your folly and that of your sons, and through the slaying of the son of Śaṃtanu, the Kauravas, together with all their kings, were made over to death.
Like sheep and goats without a herdsman in a forest thronged with beasts of prey, their hearts deeply troubled, were they, bereft of Devavrata.
When the foremost of the Bhāratas had fallen, the Kuru host became like a sky with its stars departed, like the firmament without wind.
like the earth with its harvest withered, like speech left unrefined, like the army of the Asuras of old when Bali was overthrown.
like a fair-hipped woman widowed, like a river with its waters dried, like a spotted doe whose herd-leader is slain, hemmed in by wolves in the wood,
like a great mountain-cavern, once unassailable, with its lion slain—such, O best of the Bhāratas, was the host of Bhārata when the son of Jāhnavī had fallen.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It was like a ship battered and broken by winds from every quarter on the great sea, sorely afflicted by the mighty Pāṇḍava heroes who had found their mark.
That army then was sorely shaken, its horses, chariots, and elephants in disarray, most of its men downcast; pitiful it appeared to behold.
Within it the kings and soldiers of every kind were filled with dread, sinking as if into the nether world, bereft of Devavrata; and so the Kurus called Karṇa to mind, for he was the equal of Devavrata.
To him, the foremost of all who bear arms, shining like a welcome guest, like a kinsman to one fallen into peril—to him their thoughts turned.
"Karṇa! Karṇa!" the kings cried out there, O Bhārata—the son of Rādhā, our well-wisher, the charioteer's son who would lay down his very body for us.
For he of great renown, Karṇa, had not fought for those ten days, he and his counselors and kinsmen; "Summon him without delay!"
For Bhīṣma, before the eyes of all the warriors, when the chariot-warriors endowed with strength and valor were being reckoned, had counted the mighty-armed Karṇa—that bull among men, though twofold in might—as but half a chariot-warrior.
—he who in the reckoning of chariot-warriors and great chariot-warriors stood foremost, esteemed of heroes, who would dare to do battle even with the lords of the fathers, of wealth, of waters, and of the gods.
And it was through that very anger, O king, that Karṇa had said to the son of Gaṅgā: "While you live, O Kaurava, I will not fight at all.
But when by you the Pāṇḍavas have been slain in the great battle, I shall take leave of Duryodhana and go to the forest, O Kaurava.
Or if Bhīṣma is slain by the Pāṇḍavas, and you have gone to heaven, then I alone, with a single chariot, will slay all those whom you account chariot-warriors."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus, O great king, the illustrious Karṇa fought not for ten days, by the consent of your son.
Bhīṣma, valiant in battle, O king, of prowess beyond all counting, slew countless warriors of the Pāṇḍava host in the field.
But when that hero, true to his word and of mighty energy, was slain, your sons called Karṇa to mind, as men longing to cross the water think of a raft.
Your men and your sons, together with all the kings, cried out "Alas, Karṇa!" and said, "This is the hour."
To Karṇa—sanctioned in arms by the son of Jamadagni, of manhood not to be withstood—our thoughts went out, as to a kinsman in times of dire need.
For he was able in battle, O king, to save us from great peril, as Govinda ever saved the thirty gods from exceeding great peril.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As Saṃjaya thus praised Karṇa again and again as the best in battle, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, hissing like a venomous serpent, spoke these words:
"When your thoughts then went out to Karṇa, son of the sun, did you indeed see the son of Rādhā, the charioteer's son who would yield up his body?
Did he, of truthful prowess, not prove false to it in battle—to those bewildered, stricken, and afraid, who looked to him for deliverance?
Did that best of bowmen fill in battle the breach that had been laid open among the Kauravas when Bhīṣma was slain?
Did he fill that gap, striking dread into the foe, and make fruitful at last the hope of victory of my sons?"
Saṃjaya said: When the son of Adhiratha learned that Bhīṣma was slain—the host of the Kurus like a shattered ship upon a bottomless deep—that charioteer's son, like a brother in their calamity, set out to bear your son's army across to safety.
And Karṇa, hearing that the lord of men, the unfailing son of Śaṃtanu, that great chariot-warrior, had been struck down, came swiftly forth, that scourge of foes, the bull and foremost among bowmen.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When Bhīṣma, best of chariot-warriors, was slain by the foe, he hastened to the Kurus, who were sinking like a ship in the sea—as a father to his sons—to bear your son's army across to safety.
Karṇa said: In whom dwelt steadfastness, wisdom, valor, and energy, self-mastery, truth, and all a hero's virtues, divine weapons, humility, modesty, and gracious speech—all unfailing in Bhīṣma;
in him, the ever-slayer of those who hate the brahmins, the ever-grateful, in whom virtue was eternal as the mark upon the moon—if he, the slayer of enemy heroes, is now stilled, then I deem all our warriors already slain.
Nothing here is ever found to be fixed, by reason of the impermanence that cleaves to all deeds in this world. Who, when the great-vowed one is slain, could at sunrise today, free of doubt, count on any thing's enduring?
Now that the lord of the earth—sprung of the splendor of the Vasus, born of the might of the Vasus—has gone to the Vasus themselves, mourn now your wealth, your sons, the earth, the Kurus, and this whole host.
Saṃjaya said: When the boon-granting son of Śaṃtanu, of great splendor and mighty energy, the foremost in the world, was struck down, and the Bhāratas were vanquished, Karṇa, downcast, sighed long and let his tears fall.
And hearing these words of the son of Rādhā, your sons too, O king, and your soldiers, cried out aloud to one another in their anguish, and let fall their tears with sound from their eyes.
But as the great battle was joined once more, and the kings plunged into the warring hosts, that bull among all great chariot-warriors then spoke heartening words to those bulls among chariot-warriors:
Karṇa said: In a world impermanent, forever hastening on, I see plainly today how unstable it is. While you yourselves stood here, how was the bull of the Kurus, like a very mountain, cast down in battle?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With the great chariot-warrior, the son of Śaṃtanu, struck down—as though the sun had sunk to the earth—the kings can no more withstand Dhanaṃjaya than trees can withstand the wind that carries mountains away.
This army of the Kurus, its chief now slain, stricken in look, its spirit broken by the foe, left masterless this day—must be guarded by me in battle as that great soul once guarded it.
Such a burden is laid upon me; and I see how impermanent this world is—he, drunk with battle, struck down in battle. How then should I let battle make me afraid?
As for me, ranging the field and speeding those bulls of the Kurus to the house of Yama with my straight-flying shafts, I shall win the highest glory in the world—or else, struck down by the foe, lie slain in battle.
Yudhiṣṭhira, firm and versed in the very truth of dharma; Vṛkodara, whose valor equals a hundred elephants; and Arjuna, son of the foremost of the gods—because of them, that host is not easily conquered even by the immortals.
Where in battle stand the twins, the equals of Yama in strength, and where stands the son of Devakī with Sātyaki—no coward who comes against that host but turns back, again and again, as if from the very jaws of death.
Towering austerity is met only by austerity, and strength too by strength, so the wise hold; and my mind is fixed, unshaken as a mountain, upon repelling the foe and upon guarding my own.
And though I well know their might, I shall go forth this very day, O charioteer, and conquer them. Betrayal of a friend is not to be borne by me: he who stands by you when the army is broken—he is the true friend.
This noble deed worthy of a true man I shall do: laying down my life, I shall follow after Bhīṣma. I shall slay all the throngs of the foe in battle, or, slain by them, shall go to the world of heroes.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the women and children wail and weep aloud, and the manhood of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is brought low, then there is something I must do—this I know, O charioteer; and so I shall vanquish the foes of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son.
Guarding the Kurus, seeking to slay the sons of Pāṇḍu, casting away my life in this battle of dread aspect, having struck down all the throngs of the foe in the field, I shall give the kingdom to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Let my wondrous armor be bound on—golden, gleaming bright with gems and jewels—and my helmet too, radiant as the sun, my bow, and my arrows like venomous serpents.
Let them fit on sixteen quivers, and bring forth divine bows as well, and swords and spears and heavy maces, and a conch bright with the sheen of Jāmbūnada gold.
This golden elephant-girth that brings victory, and my victorious banner with the hue of the blue lotus—wipe them clean with soft cloths and bring them to me, and bind upon it a bright garland with its netting.
My finest horses, gleaming like pale clouds, well-fed, bathed, and washed with waters hallowed by sacred chants, decked with vessels of refined gold and swift of foot—bring them quickly, O charioteer's son.
And my excellent chariot, bound about with a net of gold, bright with jewels that shine like moon and sun, furnished with the gear that battle requires and yoked with its steeds—wheel it swiftly round to me.
And the splendid swift bows, and the finest bowstrings of firm make, and the great quivers full of arrows—lay these all together, and the guards for the limbs as well.
And let them quickly bring all that befits the march, the maidens, and the golden hero's-cup brimming full; and having brought a garland and bound it upon my body, let them straightway sound the drums for victory.
Drive on swiftly, O charioteer, to where the Diademed one is, and Vṛkodara, the son of Dharma, and the twins. Either I shall slay them, joining battle in the field, or, struck down by the foe, I shall go the way of Bhīṣma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That host in which stand King Yudhiṣṭhira, steadfast in truth, and Bhīmasena and Arjuna, and Vāsudeva, Sātyaki, and the Sṛñjayas—that host, I deem, is unconquerable by the kings of earth.
Even if Death himself, who carries off all, should guard that crowned one—Kirīṭin—ever-watchful in the fray, even then I shall slay him when we close in battle, or else I shall go to Yama by the road Bhīṣma has taken.
Yet I will surely go into the midst of those heroes—this I declare as it is. But those who betray their friends, whose loyalty is feeble, those evil-souled men—they are no comrades of mine.
Saṃjaya said: Mounting his splendid, sturdy, well-equipped chariot—its pole adorned, wrought with gold, fair to see, crowned with a banner and yoked to the finest horses swift as the wind—he set forth to victory.
Honored by the Kurus, that great-souled bull among charioteers, drawn by pale steeds, the fierce-bowed warrior, went forth then to the battleground, to where the bull of the Bhāratas had met his end.
In a chariot great and armored, with its banner, gleaming with gold and pearls and gems and diamonds, yoked to noble horses and thundering like a cloud, Karṇa rode—measureless in might, like the sun itself.
Bright as the fire-eater, in his fire-bright, fair chariot the radiant bowman stood—Adhiratha's son, that mighty car-warrior, shining as he stood, like the king of the gods himself stationed in his celestial car.
Saṃjaya said: That great-souled one of boundless might lay upon his bed of arrows, like the ocean drained dry by a vast gathering of winds.
That great archer, felled by Savyasācin with celestial weapons—and with him the hope of victory of your sons, their shelter and their armor, all shattered.
He who had been like an island in a shoreless deep to men longing for footing in the fathomless waters—now flooded over by a torrent of arrows as by the current of the Yamunā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Like the great Maināka mountain, unbearable, cast down upon the earth; like the sun fallen from the sky, lying upon the ground.
Unthinkable, like the defeat of Śatakratu by Vṛtra in olden days—the felling of Bhīṣma in battle, a thing to daze the whole army.
The crest of all the armies, the very emblem of all bowmen, pierced through by Dhanaṃjaya's shafts—your father, the man of the great vow.
When Adhiratha's son beheld that hero lying upon the bed of heroes, that bull among men, Bhīṣma, peerless among the Bhāratas—
—he stepped down from his chariot, stricken, his voice broken with tears, and saluting him, his palms joined in reverence, spoke in homage.
"I am Karṇa—blessings be upon you! Speak to me today, O Bhārata; look upon me with a kind and gracious word, and with your eyes."
"Surely no one in this world reaps the fruit of his good deeds, when you—aged, devoted to dharma—lie here upon the bare earth."
"In raising up a treasury, in counsel, in battle-arrays and in the wielding of weapons, I see no other protector for the Kurus, O best of the Kurus."
"You, endowed with a clear and stainless mind, who could carry the Kurus across their peril—now you leave the warriors without a vessel and depart to the world of the fathers."
"From this day on, enraged like tigers wreaking slaughter among deer, the Pāṇḍavas, O best of the Bhāratas, will work the ruin of the Kurus."
"Today the Kurus, who know the prowess of Savyasācin, will tremble at the roar of the Gāṇḍīva, as the asuras tremble before the wielder of the thunderbolt."
"Today the sound of the shafts loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, like thunderbolts, will strike terror in battle into the Kurus and the other kings as well."
"As a kindled fire with mighty flames burns up the trees, O hero, so will Kirīṭin's arrows consume the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Wherever the wind and fire advance together through the forest, there those two mighty lords burn whatever they will."
"As is the kindled fire, such is Pārtha—of that there is no doubt; and as is the wind, O tiger among men, such is Kṛṣṇa—of that no doubt at all."
"Hearing the blare of the Pāñcajanya and the twang of the Gāṇḍīva, all the armies will be seized with terror, O Bhārata."
"And at the onrush of the ape-bannered chariot of the foe-grinding warrior, none of the kings save you, O hero, will be able to endure its thunder."
"For what king but you is fit to fight Arjuna in battle—he whose deeds the wise proclaim to be divine?"
"More than human was his combat with the three-eyed god, and from him too the wise one won a boon unattainable by men of unperfected souls."
"Today, unable to brook that war-loving son of Pāṇḍu—a venomous serpent, sight-destroying, most dread—and instructed by you, I shall go forth to meet him, setting before me either his death or my own victory."
Saṃjaya said: Hearing him lament thus, the aged grandsire of the Kurus, his heart well pleased, spoke words fitting to the place and the hour.
"As the ocean is to the rivers, as the sun is to the lights of heaven, as the good are to truth, as fertile soil is to the seeds—"
"—as the rain-cloud is to living things, so be a stay to your friends. May your kinsmen live under you, as the immortals live under the thousand-eyed one."
"By the strength and valor of your own arm, seeking the good of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, O Karṇa, you went to Rājapura and there slew the Kāmbojas."
"The kings dwelling at Girivraja, with Nagnajit at their head, and the Ambaṣṭhas, the Videhas, and the Gāndhāras—all were conquered by you."
"The Kirātas, dwelling in the fastnesses of the Himavat, hardened in war, you, Karṇa, made subject to Duryodhana in days gone by."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And in battle here and there, seeking Duryodhana's welfare, many heroes were vanquished by you, O Karṇa of mighty energy."
"As Duryodhana is, my son, with his kinsmen, clan, and relations, so be you too a refuge for all the Kauravas."
"With a blessing I bid you farewell: go, do battle with the foes, lead the Kurus in the fray, and set victory in Duryodhana's hands."
"You are as a grandson to us, even as Duryodhana is; and by dharma we are all yours, just as we are his."
"The fellowship of the good, O best of men, the wise declare to be in this world more excellent than the bond of marriage or of blood—the union of the worthy with the worthy."
"True to your pledge, then, resolved that 'this host is mine,' guard the army of the Kurus, even as Duryodhana would."
Having heard these words, and having bowed at his feet, Vaikartana Karṇa swiftly went toward the field of battle.
Surveying the vast, matchless station of those throngs of men, he marshaled that army, its breast arrayed with weapons, into fuller strength.
Seeing the great archer Karṇa take his stand for battle, the Kurus honored him with roars and the slapping of arms, with lion-shouts, and with the manifold twanging of bows.
Saṃjaya said: Beholding that tiger among men, Karṇa, stationed and ready in his chariot, Duryodhana, O king, rejoiced and spoke these words.
"This army, guarded by you, is now exceedingly well-led, I think. Yet let it be considered well what course is fit and beneficial."
Karṇa said: "Tell it yourself, O tiger among men, for you, O king, are the wisest; as the master of an affair sees what must be done, no other does so."
"We are all eager to hear your word, O lord of men; for you would utter nothing unjust—such is my conviction."
Duryodhana said: "Bhīṣma was leader of our host, well endowed in years and valor and learning, and in all a warrior's qualities besides."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"By that most glorious one, O Karṇa, who slew the hosts of my foes, by that great-souled man's good warfare, we were protected for ten days."
"Now that he has done the hard task and ascended to heaven, whom do you deem fit to be leader of the host in his stead?"
"Without a leader an army cannot stand even a moment in battle, O best in war, any more than a rudderless ship upon the water."
"As a ship without a helmsman, or a chariot without a charioteer, would drift whither it would, so would a host be without its commander."
"Therefore, looking upon all my great-souled men, do you mark out one fit to be commander, next after Śaṃtanu's son."
"For whomever you name as leader of the host in the fight, him shall we all together set up, good sir."
Karṇa said: "All these great-souled men, these best of men, are worthy of the command—herein no debate is needed."
"Endowed with noble birth, hardihood, and skill, with strength, prowess, and judgment, grateful, full of modesty, never turning back in battle—"
"—yet they cannot all be made leaders at once. One alone must be chosen here, in whom the special virtues reside."
"They vie with one another; if you honor one of them, the rest, downcast, will plainly refuse to fight, O Bhārata."
"But this one—the teacher of all the warriors, the venerable preceptor—is fit to be made commander: Droṇa, foremost of those who bear arms."
"For while the unassailable Droṇa stands—best of the knowers of Brahman, with the insight of Śukra and Aṅgiras—who other than he could be commander?"
"And there is not, among all your kings, a single warrior, O Bhārata, who would not follow Droṇa as he advances into the thick of battle."
"He is the best of leaders of hosts, the best of those who bear arms, the best of the wise as well—and he is your preceptor, O king."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Therefore, Duryodhana, make the preceptor commander at once, as the immortals, longing to conquer the asuras in battle, made Kārttikeya their own."
Saṃjaya said: Having heard Karṇa's words, King Duryodhana then spoke these words to Droṇa, who stood in the midst of the army.
"By eminence of caste, by birth of family, by learning, by years, by wisdom, by valor, by skill, by invincibility, by knowledge of affairs, by statecraft, by victory—"
"—and by austerity and by gratitude, you who are aged and endowed with every virtue: among kings there is no other protector your equal."
"So may you guard us all, as Vāsava guards the gods. With you as our guide we long to conquer the foe, O best of the twice-born."
"As the Skull-bearer among the Rudras, as the Fire among the Vasus, as Kubera among the Yakṣas, as Vāsava among the Maruts—"
"—as Vasiṣṭha among the brāhmaṇas, as the sun among the radiant powers, as Dharma among the fathers, as the lord of waters among the Ādityas—"
"—as the moon among the stars, as Uśanas among the sons of Diti—so, best of the leaders of hosts, be you our commander."
"Let the eleven akṣauhiṇīs be subject to you, O sinless one; with them array against the foe and slay them, as Indra slew the dānavas."
"Let you go before us, as the son of Fire goes before the gods; and we shall follow you into battle as bullocks follow the bull."
"Fierce-bowed, a great archer, twanging your celestial bow—seeing you at our head, not even Arjuna will withstand us."
"Surely I shall conquer Yudhiṣṭhira in battle, with his followers and his kinsmen, O tiger among men, if you are our commander."
When Droṇa had been so addressed, the kings cried out "Victory!" and with a great lion-roar they gladdened your son.
And the soldiers, filled with joy, acclaimed that best of the twice-born, setting Duryodhana at their head and praying for great glory.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Droṇa said: "I know the Veda with its six branches, and the science of statecraft taught by Manu, and the archery of the three-eyed god, and weapons of many kinds."
"And those virtues which you, longing for victory, have named in me—seeking to make them true, I shall do battle with the Pāṇḍavas."
Saṃjaya said: Granted leave thus, your son then made Droṇa commander of the host, O king, with the rite ordained by precept.
Then the kings, led by Duryodhana, consecrated Droṇa to the supreme command, even as the gods of old, led by Śakra, had consecrated Skanda.
Then, with the sound of musical instruments mingling with the mighty cries of the men, great joy arose when Droṇa was made commander of the host.
Then with the proclamation of the auspicious day and the chant of benediction, with the praises and the songs of the bards, the heralds, and the panegyrists,
and with the victory-cries of the foremost brāhmaṇas and the dances of fair women, they honored Droṇa according to rite, and deemed the Pāṇḍavas already vanquished.
Saṃjaya said: Having attained the supreme command, the son of Bharadvāja, that mighty car-warrior, eager for battle, marshaled the troops in array and advanced together with your sons.
The lord of the Sindhus, the king of the Kaliṅgas, and Vikarṇa your son took their stand upon the right flank, clad in armor.
As their outer wing, Śakuni advanced with his choice horsemen, together with the men of Gāndhāra, warriors armed with bright lances.
Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, Citrasena, and Viviṃśati, led by Duḥśāsana and on the alert, guarded the left flank.
As their outer wing, the Kāmbojas, with Sudakṣiṇa at their head, advanced on swift-flying horses, along with the Śakas and the Yavanas.
The Madras, the Trigartas, the Ambaṣṭhas, the dwellers of the west and the north, the Śibis and the Śūrasenas, the Śūdras together with the Maladas,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the Sauvīras, the Kitavas, the easterners and the southerners, every one of them, placing your son at their head, marched behind the son of the charioteer.
Gladdening all the troops and lending strength to the strong, Karṇa the son of Vikartana advanced at the forefront of all the bowmen.
His great banner, blazing and huge of body, bearing the device of an elephant's girth and gladdening his own divisions, shone with a splendor equal to the sun's.
Beholding Karṇa, not one reckoned the calamity of Bhīṣma's fall; and all the kings, together with the Kurus, became free of grief.
And many of the warriors, gathered together and rejoicing, spoke thus among themselves: 'When once they behold Karṇa in the fray, the Pāṇḍavas will not stand their ground in battle.'
'For Karṇa is able in combat to vanquish the gods themselves, with Vāsava at their head—how much more the sons of Pāṇḍu, whose valor and might are now diminished in war.'
'The sons of Pṛthā were shielded in battle by the mighty-armed Bhīṣma; but Karṇa with his sharp shafts will destroy them, beyond all doubt.'
Speaking thus to one another, joyful of countenance, O lord of peoples, honoring and praising the son of Rādhā, they marched forth.
Ours was the wagon-array, formed by Droṇa; but the array of the high-souled foe was the heron, O king—formed in delight by the King of Righteousness, O descendant of Bharata.
At the front of their array stood those two bulls among men, Viṣvaksena and Dhanaṃjaya, raising aloft the ape-bannered standard.
The standard of Pārtha of measureless splendor—the summit of all the hosts, the ensign of all the bowmen—ranged along the very path of the sun.
It set ablaze that army of the high-souled Pāṇḍava, as the blazing sun at the dissolution of an age sets the whole earth aflame.
Among archers Arjuna is supreme, among bows the Gāṇḍīva is foremost, among beings Vāsudeva, and among discuses the Sudarśana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bearing these four splendors, the white-horsed chariot stood before the foe like the uplifted wheel of Time.
Thus these two great-souled ones both stood at the vanguard of their armies: Karṇa the front of your host, and Dhanaṃjaya that of the foe.
Then, both kindled to fury and each seeking the other's death, Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava gazed upon one another in the field of battle.
Then, as the mighty car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, suddenly advanced, the earth trembled with a terrible inner roar.
Then a fierce dust, raised up by the wind and tumultuous, like a heap of silken cloth, veiled the sky together with the sun.
From a cloudless heaven there rained down flesh and bones and blood; and vultures, hawks, herons, kites, and crows by the thousand then wheeled circling above the host, O king.
Jackals howled dreadful, fear-bringing cries, and again and again circled your army from the left, hungering to devour the flesh and thirsting for the blood.
And there fell a blazing meteor, flaming, attended by thunderclaps and tremors, veiling the whole field of battle on every side with its tail of fire.
And a great halo, attended by lightning and thunder, appeared about the sun, O king, as the lord of the host advanced.
These and many other most dreadful portents arose, foretelling in the war the destruction of the heroes' lives.
Then began the battle of the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, each seeking the other's death, making the world resound with its din.
Greatly enraged at one another, the Pāṇḍavas with the Kauravas, those smiters greedy for victory, struck back with whetted shafts.
That mighty bowman of great splendor rushed with speed upon the great army of the Pāṇḍavas, scattering hundreds of sharpened arrows.
Seeing Droṇa thus risen against them, the Pāṇḍavas together with the Sṛñjayas received him then, O king, each in his turn, with showers of arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Shaken and rent asunder by Droṇa, the great host with the Pāñcālas was scattered like banks of cloud before the wind.
Wielding in that combat many celestial weapons, Droṇa in but a moment sorely oppressed the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas.
Slaughtered by Droṇa as the Dānavas by Vāsava, the Pāñcālas, with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at their head, trembled.
Then the hero, the son of Yajñasena, that mighty car-warrior, skilled in celestial weapons, broke Droṇa's division asunder in many places with a shower of shafts.
With his showers of shafts that powerful one warded off, part by part, the showers of Droṇa's arrows, and then slew the army of the Kurus as well.
Then Droṇa, the mighty-armed, having rallied and steadied his own division in the fray, rushed upon the son of Pṛṣata.
He loosed a vast shower of arrows against the son of Pṛṣata, as Maghavan in sudden wrath against the Dānavas.
Made to tremble by Droṇa's arrows, the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas broke and fled again and again, like lesser beasts before a lion.
Then the mighty Droṇa wheeled about through the army of the Pāṇḍavas like a whirling firebrand, O king, and that seemed a wondrous thing.
Mounted upon his peerless chariot—like a city moving through the air, fashioned by the lore of scripture, its pennon fluttering in the shifting wind, thundering, its horses prancing, its standard pure as crystal, a scorcher of foes—he annihilated the army of his enemies.
Saṃjaya said: Beholding Droṇa thus smiting their horses, charioteers, chariots, and elephants, the Pāṇḍavas were stricken with dread and could not hem him in.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira said to Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Dhanaṃjaya: 'Let the pitcher-born one be checked by men set on guard upon every side.'
Thereupon Arjuna and the son of Pṛṣata with his followers, and then all the mighty car-warriors, hemmed in that advancing foe.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Kekayas and Bhīmasena, the son of Subhadrā, and Ghaṭotkaca, Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins, the Matsyas, and the sons of Drupada,
the sons of Draupadī full of joy, Dhṛṣṭaketu with Sātyaki, the wrathful Cekitāna, and Yuyutsu the mighty car-warrior,
and whatever other princes, O king, were followers of the Pāṇḍava, wrought deeds in great number worthy of their lineage and their valor.
Seeing his army being thus hemmed in by the Pāṇḍavas in the battle, the son of Bharadvāja, rolling his eyes in wrath, looked upon them.
Yielding to fierce anger upon his chariot, that one furious in battle scattered the army of the Pāṇḍavas as the ever-moving wind scatters the clouds.
Charging chariots, horses, men, and elephants this way and that, Droṇa ranged about as one frenzied, and, though aged, was as a youth.
His red steeds, swift as the wind, of noble breed, their bodies smeared with blood, O king, unswerving, bore a surpassing splendor.
Beholding that man of steadfast vow rushing upon them, wrathful as the Ender himself, the warriors of the Pāṇḍava fled in every direction.
From them—some fleeing, some turning back again, some gazing on, and some standing fast—there arose a most terrible din.
Begetting joy in the brave and swelling the fear of the timid, it filled on every side the gulf between heaven and earth.
Then once again Droṇa, proclaiming his name aloud in the battle, made himself terrible, scattering hundreds of shafts upon the foe.
Thus did the mighty Droṇa slay those divisions of the wise Pāṇḍava like Time itself—an old man, yet as a youth.
And the fierce mighty car-warrior, lopping off heads and arms still bedecked with ornaments, leaving the chariot-seats empty, raised a great shout.
At his shout of joy and the rush of his arrows, O lord, the warriors trembled in the battle like cattle tormented by the cold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From the roar of Droṇa's chariot, the lashing of his bowstring, and the twang of his bow, a great sound arose in the sky.
Then his arrows, issuing forth in their thousands, filling all the quarters, fell upon elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers.
Upon that Droṇa, mighty in the speed of his bow, his weapons blazing like kindled fire, the Pāñcālas with the Pāṇḍavas closed in.
Them, with their chariots, elephants, and horses, Droṇa sent to the abode of Yama, and in no long while made the earth a mire of blood.
As he plied his supreme weapons and ceaselessly loosed his shafts, a net of arrows woven by Droṇa was seen across the quarters of the sky.
Ranging over the foot-soldiers, the chariots and horses, and the elephants on every side, his banner was seen like lightning amid the clouds.
Having crushed with his shafts the five chief warriors of the Kekayas and the king of the Pāñcālas, Droṇa, that undaunted fighter, bow and arrow in hand, advanced upon Yudhiṣṭhira's division.
At him Bhīmasena and Dhanaṃjaya, the grandson of Śini, the son of Drupada, the son of Śaibyā, the lord of Kāśi, and Śibi, exulting and roaring aloud, hurled torrents of arrows.
Then the feathered shafts loosed from Droṇa's bow, their golden, many-hued nocks bright, piercing the bodies of their elephants, horses, and men, passed into the earth, their plumes drenched with blood.
That earth, strewn over with hosts of fallen warriors and chariots, with shattered arrows and elephants and horses, became as the sky overspread on every side with the clouds of doom.
The leaders of the hosts of Sātyaki, Bhīma, and Arjuna; Śaibya and Abhimanyu, together with the king of Kāśi; and other heroes besides—Droṇa, desiring the welfare of your sons, crushed them in the fight.
Having wrought these deeds and others in the battle, O lord of the Kurus, the high-souled Droṇa, scorching the worlds as the sun of doom, departed hence to heaven, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus the hero of the golden chariot, having slain the warriors of the Pāṇḍavas in the battle by the hundred thousand, was struck down by the son of Pṛṣata.
Having slain more than a full akṣauhiṇī of heroes who never turned back, that steadfast one thereafter attained the supreme goal.
By the Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas—malign and cruel of deed—was the hero of the golden chariot slain, O king, after he had wrought a most arduous deed.
Then a cry of all beings arose in the sky, and likewise of the armies, O king, when the preceptor was slain in the battle.
Making heaven, earth, the sky, the quarters, the waters, and the intermediate regions resound, a great cry went up from all beings: "Alas! Shame!"
The gods, the ancestral fathers, and those who had been his kinsmen of old looked down and beheld Bhāradvāja, that mighty warrior, lying slain.
The Pāṇḍavas, having won the victory, raised lion-roars, and at that mighty roar the whole earth trembled.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: While Droṇa was doing what in battle did the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas slay him — him so skilled in weapons, foremost among all who bear arms?
Did his chariot break apart, or did his bow shatter as he shot, or did Droṇa grow heedless, that he thus met his death?
How, my son, did the son of Pṛṣata strike down one whom foes could not assail, who scattered showers of gold-feathered arrows in their thousands —
that swift-handed best of brahmins, the accomplished one, the dazzling fighter, who struck from afar, the self-controlled, the master of warfare with divine weapons?
By cruel fate the Pāñcāla prince slew that unfaltering, supreme warrior, who was performing terrible deeds and striving with all his might in the battle.
Surely destiny is mightier than human valor — this is my conviction — since the hero Droṇa was slain by the great-souled son of Pṛṣata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In that hero the fourfold science of weapons was firmly established; yet you tell me that Droṇa, the supreme teacher of archery, is slain.
Hearing that he of the golden chariot is slain — he whose car was draped with tiger-skins and adorned with gold — I cannot today drive away my grief.
Surely no one dies of another's sorrow, Saṃjaya, since I, having heard that Droṇa is slain, still live and do not die.
Surely my heart is made of iron, exceedingly hard, that it does not burst into a hundred pieces on hearing that Droṇa is slain.
He whom brahmins and princes seeking excellence waited upon in the sacred Veda, in archery, and in divine weapons — how was he struck down by death?
Like the drying-up of the ocean, like the toppling of Meru, like the falling of the sun — I cannot bear the felling of Droṇa.
He was the curber of the arrogant and the protector of the righteous, that scorcher of foes who would lay down even his life for the sake of the helpless.
He in whose prowess lay the hope of victory for my dull-witted sons, the equal of Bṛhaspati and Uśanas in wisdom — how was he slain?
And those tall red horses of the Sindhu breed, garlanded with gold, swift as the wind, yoked to his chariot, unshaken by every clamor of battle —
strong, loud-neighing, well-trained Sindhu steeds, drawing smoothly, steadfast in the thick of the fray — were they perhaps thrown into confusion?
They could endure in battle the trumpeting of elephants, the blare of conches and kettledrums, the twang of bowstrings, the showers of arrows, and the clash of weapons —
those horses that bore Bhāradvāja's chariot, eager to conquer the foe, masters of their own breath, mastering all pain, swift and urged to speed.
Yoked to the golden chariot, set in motion by that hero among men — how, my son, did they fail to break through the host of the Pāṇḍavas?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Mounted upon his excellent chariot adorned with gold, what did the heroic, war-shouting Bhāradvāja do in the battle?
He upon whose learning all the bowmen of the world depend — that strong Droṇa, true to his vows, what did he do in the fight?
He who was foremost among bowmen as Śakra is in heaven, that mighty one — what warriors in their chariots dared advance against him of terrible deeds in battle?
Surely, on seeing him of the golden chariot wielding divine weapons and thinning their inexhaustible army, the Pāṇḍavas would flee?
Or did the King of Righteousness, together with his younger brothers and with the Pāñcāla prince at their head, with his whole army surround Droṇa on every side?
Surely Pārtha held off the other chariot-warriors with his straight-flying shafts, and then the son of Pṛṣata, doer of an evil deed, fell upon Droṇa.
For I can see no other capable of slaying that valiant one except the fierce Dhṛṣṭadyumna, guarded as he was by the Diademed Arjuna.
Then that base-born Pāñcāla, surrounded on all sides by those heroes — by the Kekayas, the Cedis, the Karūṣas, the Matsyas, and other kings —
slew the teacher, who had been thrown into confusion as a serpent is by ants, while he was engaged in a deed hard to perform — such is my belief.
He who, having studied the four Vedas together with the legends as a fifth, stood as the refuge of brahmins as the ocean is of streams — how did that aged brahmin meet his death by the sword?
Impatient by nature, he yet bore patiently, though ever harassed by me. The son of Kuntī, who deserved no such treatment, has reaped the fruit of that conduct.
He on whose accomplishment all the bowmen in the world depend for their livelihood — that virtuous one, true to his word, how was he slain by men greedy for glory?
He who was foremost as Śakra is in heaven, of great courage and great strength — how was he slain by the sons of Pṛthā, as a great whale is slain by little fishes?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Swift-handed and strong, with a stout bow, a crusher of foes, into whose range no one desiring to live could come and yet live —
whom, while he lived, two sounds never left: the chant of the Veda for those who sought sacred lore, and the twang of the bowstring for those who bear arms.
I cannot bear that Droṇa is slain — he of the prowess of a lion or an elephant. How, Saṃjaya, did this unassailable one, of unconquerable fame and might, fall?
Who guarded the right wheel of that great soul, and who the left, and who stood before the hero as he fought in the encounter?
And what heroes there, casting away their bodies, went forth to meet death head-on, what warriors showed the highest resolve in Droṇa's battle?
This is what a noble man must do in dire calamities, Saṃjaya — to strive with all his power; and that was firmly established in him.
My mind grows faint, my son; let the narration pause awhile. When I have regained my senses, I shall question you again, Saṃjaya.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus questioned the sūta's son, sorely afflicted with grief of heart and despairing of his sons' victory, Dhṛtarāṣṭra fell to the ground.
As he lay fallen and senseless, the attendants sprinkled him with exceedingly cool, fragrant water and fanned him.
Aware that he had fallen, the women of the Bhāratas gathered round the great king on every side and touched him with their hands.
Slowly raising the king from the surface of the earth, those lovely women, their throats choked with tears, brought him to his seat.
Having reached his seat, the king, overwhelmed by a swoon, remained motionless, while he was fanned on every side.
Slowly regaining consciousness, the trembling lord of the earth questioned the sūta, son of Gavalgaṇa, once more, point by point.
When Ajātaśatru advanced, dispelling the darkness with his radiance like the rising sun, who held him back from Droṇa?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Like a rutting elephant, thus enraged and swift, his mind fixed on the foe, blazing, slaying the elephants that opposed him — unconquerable by rival herd-leaders as in the rivalry for a cow-elephant —
surpassing the other warriors in battle, that hero, best of men, the mighty-armed, who alone, steadfast and true to his oath, could burn up Duryodhana's whole host with the mere glare of his terrible eyes —
him whose gaze could destroy, bent upon victory, guarded by the best of bowmen, self-controlled and honored throughout the world — what heroes hemmed him in?
What men of mine there closed in upon that unassailable king, the best of bowmen, the unfaltering, that tiger among men, the son of Kuntī?
He who, charging swiftly, fell upon Droṇa — what heroes surrounded that Bhīmasena as he came on?
When Bībhatsu advanced, his chariot dark as a rain-cloud, of supreme valor, hurling tumultuous thunderbolts like Parjanya —
he of the monkey-bannered standard rained down showers of arrows as Maghavan rains the rains, choking the sky with shafts and making all the quarters crash with the din of his palm-guards and wheel-rims —
terrible, his bow flashing like lightning, his chariot-squadrons a thundercloud, thundering with the roar of his chariot-rims, made fearsome by the rush of arrows —
his fury surpassing the storm-clouds, moving swift as thought, a downpour of arrows that pierced the vitals, tumultuous, with blood for its waters —
flooding the whole earth and strewing it with the slain, fierce, resounding with the clash of maces, roused up by Duryodhana's doing —
when the wise Vijaya in that battle, wielding the Gāṇḍīva, bathed the field with vulture-feathered shafts honed on stone — what then was the temper of your minds?
Did not your army perish at the sound of the Gāṇḍīva, when Arjuna, raising that fearful roar, bore down upon you in fury?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Did not Dhanaṃjaya drive you back from Droṇa with his shafts, scattering you with a forest-felling wind of arrows as the gale scatters clouds? What man is able to withstand the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva in battle?
When the armies trembled and fear laid hold of the heroes, who there did not abandon Droṇa, and what mean-spirited men fled away in terror?
Or who there, casting away their bodies, went forth to meet death head-on against Dhanaṃjaya, the conqueror even of more-than-human foes in battle?
My men cannot endure the onset of him whose horses are white, nor the roar of the Gāṇḍīva, like the rumble of the rain-clouds of the monsoon.
That chariot whose driver is Viṣvaksena and whose warrior is Dhanaṃjaya is, I think, impossible to conquer even by gods and demons together.
Delicate, young, heroic, and fair to behold is that son of Pāṇḍu, intelligent, skilled, wise, of true valor in battle —
when the wise Nakula advanced, raising a vast war-cry and dismaying all the Kauravas, what heroes hemmed him in?
When Sahadeva, enraged like a venomous serpent, came on, wreaking havoc among the foes — that hard-to-conquer one, a victor in battle —
as he advanced toward Droṇa — that man of noble vows, whose arrows never miss, modest and unconquered — what heroes hemmed him in?
He who, having crushed the great host of the Sauvīra king, carried off his cherished and desirable queen, lovely in every limb —
truth, firmness, valor, and perfect continence — all these dwell forever in this Yuyudhāna, this bull among men.
Strong, true in deed, undaunted, unconquered, equal to Vāsudeva in battle and second only to Vāsudeva —
that hero ready in Dhanaṃjaya's service, skilled in a teacher's office, equal to Pārtha in weapons — who held him back from Droṇa?
The foremost hero of the Vṛṣṇis, valiant among all bowmen, the equal of Rāma in weapons, in fame, and in prowess —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
truth, firmness, self-restraint, valor, and continence unsurpassed — all these are present in that Sātvata, as the three worlds are present in Keśava.
That great archer, endowed with such qualities, hard to ward off even by the gods — what heroes closed in and hemmed him round?
The foremost hero among the Pāñcālas, beloved for his noble birth, ever doing the highest deeds, of supreme energy in battle —
devoted to Dhanaṃjaya's welfare and the foremost cause of my ruin, the equal of Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, Āditya, great Indra, and Varuṇa —
renowned as a mighty chariot-warrior, rising up against Droṇa in battle and ready to lay down his life in the tumult — what heroes hemmed him in?
Who held off from Droṇa that Dhṛṣṭaketu as he came on—he who, alone, broke away from the Cedis and gave his allegiance to the Pāṇḍavas?
That brave Ketumat who slew the prince Sudarśana at the gateway of the western mountains—who kept him back from Droṇa?
That tiger among men, once a woman, who knows men's merits and faults—Śikhaṇḍin, son of Yajñasena, unflinching in heart upon the field—
the appointed cause of the death in battle of high-souled Devavrata—as he advanced straight upon Droṇa, what heroes hemmed him in?
That hero in whom all virtues surpass even those of Dhanaṃjaya, in whom dwell forever the celestial weapons, truth, and continence—
the equal of Vāsudeva in valor, the equal of Dhanaṃjaya in strength, like the sun in splendor, like Bṛhaspati in wisdom—
the high-souled Abhimanyu, like the Ender with gaping jaws—as he advanced straight upon Droṇa, what heroes hemmed him in?
When the youthful son of Subhadrā, glowing like the dawn, slayer of enemy heroes, charged upon Droṇa—how then stood your hearts?
When the sons of Draupadī, those tigers among men, rushed upon Droṇa in battle like rivers upon the sea, what heroes turned them back?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those boys who for twelve years forsook all play and, keeping the highest vow, dwelt with Bhīṣma for the sake of mastering arms—
Kṣatraṃjaya, Kṣatradeva, and proud Kṣatradharman, heroic sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna—who kept them back from Droṇa?
That mighty archer Cekitāna, whom the Vṛṣṇis reckoned in battle worth more than a hundred men—who kept him back from Droṇa?
Anādhṛṣṭi, son of Vṛddhakṣema, undaunted in soul, who carried off the maiden of the Kaliṅgas by force of arms—who kept him back from Droṇa?
The five Kaikeya brothers, righteous men of truthful valor, of the hue of the cochineal insect, with crimson armor, weapons, and banners—
those heroes, sons of their mother's sister, who sought victory for the Pāṇḍavas—as they came on to slay Droṇa, what heroes hemmed them in?
That lord of warriors whom the kings, battling against him at Vāraṇāvata in fury for six months, bent on his death, could not conquer—
that tiger among men, foremost of bowmen, brave, true to his word, of mighty strength—who held back the eager Yuyutsu from Droṇa?
He who in battle at Vārāṇasī struck down with a broad-headed shaft from his chariot the great chariot-warrior, the son of the king of Kāśi, as he lusted after the women—
that mighty archer Dhṛṣṭadyumna, keeper of the counsels of the Pārthas, bound to Duryodhana's ruin and born for the slaying of Droṇa—
as he burned the warriors in battle and tore them apart on every side, advancing straight upon Droṇa, what heroes hemmed him in?
Kṣatradeva, son of Śikhaṇḍin, most skilled in arms, reared as it were in Drupada's lap—who kept him back from Droṇa?
That great chariot-warrior, slayer of the foremost foes, who with his vast line of chariots wrapped this whole earth as in a hide—
who performed ten horse-sacrifices with abundant food and drink and ample gifts, unhindered and complete, while guarding his people like his own sons—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
at whose sacrifice the cattle drinking down their fee drank the whole stream of the Gaṅgā—so many cows did that hero, the son of Uśīnara, bestow—
"No men of old, nor any to come, have wrought this deed"—so cried the gods aloud when that hard task was done.
"Among the still and the moving in the three worlds we see no second to him—neither born before, nor to be born, nor living now."
"None other than Śaibya, son of Uśīnara, can bear such a yoke"—whose course the men who dwell in the world shall never attain.
His grandson Śaibya, as he came on—who held him back, advancing straight upon Droṇa like the Ender with gaping jaws?
As the chariot-host of Virāṭa, the Matsya king and slayer of foes, sought to reach Droṇa in battle, what heroes hemmed them in?
That dread rākṣasa, a master of illusion, of mighty strength and prowess, born in a single day of Vṛkodara, from whom comes my great fear—
the mighty-armed Ghaṭotkaca, longing for the victory of the Pārthas, a thorn in the side of my sons—who kept him back from Droṇa?
These and many others, Saṃjaya, who in their cause would lay down their lives in battle—what could remain unconquered for such men in war?
And those whose refuge is that tiger among men, the bearer of the Śārṅga bow, who seeks the good of the Pārthas—how can there be defeat for them?
He is the supreme teacher of the worlds, the eternal lord of the worlds, Nārāyaṇa, the protector in battle, divine, of divine essence, the Lord—
whose divine deeds the wise recount; these I shall proclaim with devotion, for the steadying of my own soul.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Hear the divine deeds of Vāsudeva, Saṃjaya—deeds that Govinda performed as no other man anywhere ever has.
While yet a child growing up in the herdsmen's clan, the high-souled one made the might of his arms renowned throughout the three worlds, Saṃjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He slew the king of horses that dwelt in the forest by the Yamunā, a steed equal in strength to Uccaiḥśravas and matching the wind in swiftness.
In his boyhood, with his bare arms, he slew that dānava of dreadful deeds, who had taken the form of a bull and risen up like death itself against the cattle.
The lotus-eyed one slew Pralamba, Naraka, Jambha, the great asura Pīṭha, and Muru, who was like a mountain.
So too Kaṃsa of great splendor, protected by Jarāsaṃdha, was struck down in battle by Kṛṣṇa's prowess alone, together with his followers.
The valiant Sunāman, lord of a full akṣauhiṇī, a leader among the Bhojas and the mighty brother of Kaṃsa—
that swift king of the Śūrasenas was consumed in battle, army and all, by Kṛṣṇa the slayer of foes, with Baladeva at his side.
The brahmin-sage named Durvāsas, of utmost wrath, was propitiated by him together with his wife, and bestowed boons upon him.
So too the lotus-eyed hero, at her self-choosing, vanquished the lords of the earth and bore away the daughter of the king of Gāndhāra.
The kings, unable to endure it, were yoked like thoroughbred horses to his wedding chariot and made to bear the wounds of his goad.
Janārdana, by a stratagem, had the mighty-armed Jarāsaṃdha, lord in his own right of a whole akṣauhiṇī, slain by another's hand.
And the mighty one then slew like a sacrificial beast the valiant king of the Cedis, that commander of the kings' host, when he disputed the offering of homage.
Mādhava, charging in, cast down Saubha—that secure city of the daityas, guarded by Śālva and hard to assail—into the belly of the sea.
He conquered in battle the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, and Kaliṅgas, the Māgadhas, the men of Kāśi and Kosala, the Vatsas, Gargas, and Karūṣas, and the Puṇḍras as well.
The Āvantyas and the southern peoples, the mountain-dwellers and the Dāśerakas, the Kāśmīrakas, the Aurasakas, and the Piśācas with the Mandaras—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the Kāmbojas and Vāṭadhānas, the Colas and Pāṇḍyas, Saṃjaya, the Trigartas, the Mālavas, and the Daradas so hard to conquer—
the lotus-eyed one vanquished too the bands gathered from every quarter, those of the Aśvas and Śakas, and the Yavanas together with their followers.
Of old, entering the abode of sea-monsters, hemmed about by water-creatures, he conquered Varuṇa in battle within the waters.
Having slain in battle Pañcajana, who dwelt in the depths of the netherworld, Hṛṣīkeśa won the divine conch Pāñcajanya.
At Khāṇḍava, together with Pārtha, the mighty one gratified the Eater of Oblations and obtained the irresistible fiery weapon, the discus.
Mounting the son of Vinatā and striking terror into Amarāvatī, the hero carried off the pārijāta tree from the abode of great Indra.
And Śakra bore that patiently, knowing his prowess; nor have we heard of any king here who was not conquered by Kṛṣṇa.
And that great marvel which the lotus-eyed one wrought in my assembly hall, Saṃjaya—what other man here is capable of it?
And when in devotion I took refuge in him, I beheld Kṛṣṇa as the Lord; all that is well known to me, and came to me as though before my very eyes.
No end can be reached, Saṃjaya, of the deeds of Hṛṣīkeśa, who is endowed with valor and again with wisdom.
So too Gada and Sāmba, Pradyumna and Viḍūratha, Āgāvaha and Aniruddha, Cārudeṣṇa and Sāraṇa,
Ulmuka and Niśaṭha, Jhallī and the valiant Babhru, Pṛthu and Vipṛthu, Śamīka and Arimejaya—
these mighty Vṛṣṇi heroes, hard-striking warriors, might somehow take their stand with the Pāṇḍava army and abide in the battle.
Summoned by the Vṛṣṇi hero, the high-souled Keśava—then all would be cast into doubt: such is my conviction.
And the hero Rāma, strong as ten thousand elephants, like the peak of Kailāsa, garlanded with wildflowers and bearing the plough, is there where Janārdana is.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And he whom the twice-born call Vāsudeva, the father of all—he too, Saṃjaya, may well fight for the cause of the Pāṇḍavas.
When Keśava arms himself, my son, for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, then there will be no one among the opposing ranks to stand against him.
Were all the Kurus to conquer all the Pāṇḍavas, the Vārṣṇeya would surely take up his supreme weapon for their sake.
Then that tiger among men, the mighty-armed one, having slain in battle all the lords of men and the Kauravas, would give the earth to Kuntī.
The chariot whose driver is Hṛṣīkeśa and whose warrior is Dhanaṃjaya—what chariot in the field could be its match?
By no means whatsoever do I see victory for the Kurus; therefore tell me all, just as the battle came to pass.
Arjuna is the very soul of Keśava, and Kṛṣṇa too is the soul of the Diademed one; in Arjuna victory dwells forever, and in Kṛṣṇa undying renown.
For preeminently and beyond all measure do the virtues abound in Keśava; yet out of delusion Duryodhana does not know Kṛṣṇa, the Mādhava, here in this world.
Deluded by the working of fate, with the noose of death set before him, he knows neither Kṛṣṇa of the Dāśārha line nor Arjuna the Pāṇḍava.
Those two high-souled primeval gods, Nara and Nārāyaṇa both, one in soul yet become twofold, are seen by men upon the earth.
Those two glorious and irresistible ones could, if they wished, destroy this army by a mere thought; but being in human form, they do not wish it.
The slaying of Bhīṣma, my son, and of the high-souled Droṇa is like the overturning of an age, like the bewildering of the worlds.
For not by continence, nor by the study of the Vedas, nor by rites, nor by weapons is any man freed from death.
Hearing that Bhīṣma and Droṇa are slain—those two heroes honored by the world, masters of arms, unconquerable in the fury of battle—why should I go on living, Saṃjaya?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That sovereign splendour which we once begrudged when it passed long ago to Yudhiṣṭhira—today, with the slaying of Bhīṣma and Droṇa, we acknowledge it as his.
And so, through my doing, this destruction of the Kurus has come to pass; for when the ripe are to be slain, O charioteer, even blades of grass become as thunderbolts.
Yudhiṣṭhira has gained in this world a sovereignty that has no rival—he by whose wrath those two great archers, Bhīṣma and Droṇa, have been struck down.
By its very nature righteousness has prevailed over men, not unrighteousness; yet cruel Time, bent on the ruin of all, overrides every law.
For the aims that thoughtful men devise in one way, my son, turn out quite otherwise; this, I hold, is the work of fate.
Therefore, since a thing unavoidable, a calamity most grievous, beyond crossing and beyond comprehension, has befallen us, tell me how it truly came about.
Saṃjaya said: Come then, I shall describe it all to you, for I saw it with my own eyes—how Droṇa fell, brought low by the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas.
Having attained the command of the army, Bhāradvāja, that mighty car-warrior, in the midst of all the host spoke these words to your son.
"In that next after the bull of the Kurus, the son of the river Gaṅgā, you have today honoured me, O king, with the office of commander,
receive a reward worthy of that deed, O prince. I will grant your wish: choose now whatever boon you desire."
Then Duryodhana, having taken counsel with Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and the rest, spoke thus to the unassailable teacher, the foremost of the victorious:
"If you grant me a boon, then seize Yudhiṣṭhira alive—take that best of car-warriors captive and bring him here before me."
Then the teacher of the Kurus, hearing your son's words, gladdening the whole army, spoke these words:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Blessed is King Kuntī's son, whose capture you desire; for it is not his death, O unconquerable one, that you ask of me as a boon today.
And why, O tiger among men, do you not crave his slaying? You surely do not wish this deed of me, Duryodhana.
Or is it that the son of Dharma has no hater anywhere, that you wish him alive and so preserve the lineage within yourself?
Or rather, O best of the Bhāratas, having conquered the Pāṇḍavas in battle and restored to them their share of the kingdom, do you wish to make brotherhood with them?
