Blessed is King Kuntī's son, and well earned is that wise man's name—Ajātaśatru, 'he whose enemy is not born'—proven true, since even you bear him such affection."
But when Droṇa had spoken thus, O Bhārata, from your son there suddenly broke forth that disposition which forever moves within him.
A man's true bent cannot be hidden, not even by those equal to Bṛhaspati; and so your son, O king, in his eagerness, spoke these words:
"In the slaying of Kuntī's son in battle, O teacher, lies no victory for me; for were Yudhiṣṭhira killed, the son of Pṛthā would surely slay us all.
Nor can they all be killed in war, not even by the immortals; and whichever of them might be left would leave none of us remaining.
But once he whose vows are true is brought here and defeated again at dice, the sons of Kuntī, devoted to him, will go once more into the forest.
Such, plainly, would be my victory, and it would last a long while. Therefore I do not in any way wish the death of the Dharma-king."
Knowing his crooked intent, Droṇa, who understood the true nature of things, having reflected, granted him that boon—but with a reservation, wise as he was.
Droṇa said: "If Arjuna does not guard Yudhiṣṭhira in the battle, O hero, then count the eldest Pāṇḍava as already brought into your power.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the son of Pṛthā cannot be withstood in battle, not even by the gods and demons together with Indra; and so, my son, I will not provoke that contest.
Beyond doubt he is my pupil, and in the wielding of weapons he had me first as his teacher; yet he is young, crowned with fame, and wholly single-minded in his course.
He has gained many weapons from Indra and from Rudra, and he is full of indignation against you, O king; for that reason I will not rouse him.
Let him be drawn away from the battle by whatever means is possible; and once the son of Pṛthā is removed, the Dharma-king is as good as conquered by you.
If you reckon his capture to be victory, O bull among men, then by this expedient his capture will surely come to pass.
I will seize the king, devoted to truth and righteousness, and bring him into your power this very day, O king—of that there is no doubt,
if only he will stand before me in the fray for even a moment, once that tiger among men, Kuntī's son Dhanaṃjaya, has been led away.
But in Phalguna's very presence, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Pṛthā cannot be taken in battle, not even by the gods and demons together with Indra."
Saṃjaya said: But when Droṇa had pledged the king's capture with that reservation, your sons, foolish as they were, deemed him already taken.
Your son knew that Droṇa was partial toward the Pāṇḍavas; and therefore, to make the pledge seem firm, that counsel was spread far and wide.
Then by Duryodhana too that capture of the Pāṇḍava was proclaimed aloud throughout all the stations of the army, O crusher of foes.
Saṃjaya said: Then those soldiers, hearing of that capture of Yudhiṣṭhira, raised lion-roars together with the clamour of arrows and conch-shells.
But all that had taken place—Bhāradvāja's design—was swiftly learned in full by the Dharma-king, O Bhārata, through trusted men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, having summoned all his brothers and the troops on every side, the Dharma-king spoke these words to Dhanaṃjaya:
"You have heard, O tiger among men, what Droṇa intends to do today; let such a course be devised that it may not come true.
For Droṇa has made his pledge with a reservation, O scourge of foes, and that reservation he has fixed upon you, whose every arrow strikes home.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, fight today close at my side, so that Duryodhana may not gain this wish from Droṇa."
Arjuna said: "As the slaying of the teacher is by no means a thing I would do, so neither, O king, is your abandonment anything I would intend.
Even so, O Pāṇḍava, I would sooner give up my life in battle—I will not turn against the teacher, nor will I ever forsake you in any way.
That wish which Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son cherishes—to seize you in battle, O king—he shall in no way attain so long as I live in this world of the living.
Sooner might the sky fall with its stars, sooner might the earth break into fragments, than Droṇa take you captive while I yet live—of this be certain.
Even if the wielder of the thunderbolt himself should aid him in the fight, or the gods together with the demons, he shall not reach you in the battle.
While I live, O lord of kings, you ought to feel no fear of Droṇa, foremost of all who bear weapons, nor of any other wielder of arms.
I do not recall an untrue word from my lips, I do not recall a defeat, nor do I recall ever having promised a thing and left it undone."
Saṃjaya said: Then conches and kettledrums and tabors, together with war-drums, sounded out, O great king, in the encampment of the Pāṇḍavas.
And a lion-roar arose from the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, and the sound of bowstrings slapped from the palm, touching the heavens, most terrible.
Hearing that blare of the conch of the great-souled Pāṇḍava, in your own ranks too the instruments were struck up in answer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the marshalled hosts, both yours and theirs, O Bhārata, advanced slowly toward one another, ready to do battle in the field.
Then there broke out a tumultuous, hair-raising battle between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus, and between Droṇa and the Pāñcāla prince.
Striving with all their effort to shatter Droṇa's array, the Sṛñjayas could not prevail, O king, for it was guarded by Droṇa himself.
Likewise the noble, hard-striking car-warriors of your son could not break the Pāṇḍava army, guarded as it was by the Diademed One.
Both those armies stood motionless, each warding off the other, like two fair-flowering forest-tracts asleep together in the night.
Then the warrior of the golden car, O king, blazing like the very sun with his guard-railed chariot, dashed forth and ranged through the midst of the host.
Him, raised aloft and alone upon his chariot, swift in action in the fray, the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas in their terror reckoned to be many.
The dreadful arrows loosed by him ranged in every direction, terrifying, O great king, the army of the Pāṇḍava.
As the noonday sun, ringed about with its hundred rays, appears when it reaches the meridian, so too did Droṇa appear.
And no one among the Pāṇḍavas, good sir, could so much as look upon him in his battle-fury, as the demons could not gaze upon great Indra.
Then Bhāradvāja, the majestic one, having bewildered the army, swiftly scattered Dhṛṣṭadyumna's force with his whetted arrows.
Blocking the quarters on every side and covering the very sky with his straight-flying shafts, wherever the son of Pṛṣata was, there did he crush the Pāṇḍava host.
Saṃjaya said: Then, raising a great tumult in the Pāṇḍava ranks, Droṇa ranged among the Pāṇḍavas, burning them as a fire burns dry brushwood.
Seeing the warrior of the golden car consuming their armies, like fire itself risen up in the battle, the Sṛñjayas trembled.

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
Its chariot-wheels were its turtles, its maces its crocodiles, and it teemed with arrows for its little fishes; it was haunted by dreadful packs of herons, vultures, and jackals.
O best of kings, it bore by hundreds to the realm of the fathers the living beings whom mighty Droṇa had slain in battle with his arrows.
Choked with hundreds of corpses, its weeds and grass the hair of the dead, such a river did he set flowing, O king—a river that swelled the terror of the fearful.
As he triumphed thus, O Bhārata, those very armies, with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head, charged upon Droṇa from every side.
Your warriors, their bows held firm, received those onrushing heroes from every quarter, and the encounter made the hair stand on end.
Śakuni of a hundred wiles rushed against Sahadeva and pierced him with whetted arrows, together with his charioteer, his banner, and his car.
The son of Mādrī, not greatly angered, cut down his uncle's banner, bow, charioteer, and horses with his shafts, and pierced him with sixty arrows.
But the son of Subala, seizing his mace, leapt down from his splendid chariot, and with that mace, O king, he struck Sahadeva's charioteer from his car.
Then those two mighty warriors, O king, both bereft of their chariots, maces in hand, sported in the battle like two peaked mountains.
Droṇa pierced the king of the Pāñcālas with ten swift arrows; and being himself struck by many in return, he pierced that king with more than a hundred.
Bhīmasena pierced Viviṃśati with twenty whetted arrows, yet the hero could not make him waver, and that seemed a wonder.
But Viviṃśati at once made Bhīma horseless, bannerless, and bowless, O great king; and thereupon the troops applauded him.
The hero could not brook this triumph of his foe in the fray; and so with his mace he struck down all the well-trained horses of his enemy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the hero Śalya, smiling, pierced with his arrows Nakula, his own beloved sister's son, as if caressing him, yet provoking him.
But the valorous Nakula, having brought down his horses, his parasol, his banner, his charioteer, and his bow, blew his conch upon the field.
Dhṛṣṭaketu, having cut down the many arrows loosed by Kṛpa, pierced Kṛpa with seventy shafts and with three struck away his emblem.
Kṛpa overwhelmed him with a great rain of arrows, and the brahmin, checking him in battle, fought on against Dhṛṣṭaketu.
Sātyaki, piercing Kṛtavarman in the breast with an iron shaft, smiling as it were, pierced him again with seventy other arrows.
The Bhoja chief, piercing him with seventy-seven whetted arrows, could no more shake the grandson of Śini than a swift wind shakes a mountain.
The commander Dhṛṣṭadyumna swiftly struck Suśarman in his vital parts, and Suśarman in turn struck him with a lance upon the collarbone.
And Virāṭa, together with the mighty Matsyas, held back Vaikartana in the fight, and that seemed a marvel.
Terrible there was the prowess of the charioteer's son, in that he held back that whole army with his smooth-jointed arrows.
And King Drupada himself closed with Bhagadatta; their combat, O great king, was as a wondrous spectacle, and those two masters of weaponry wrought a thing that struck terror into all creatures.
In the battle, O king, the valiant Bhūriśravas covered the great warrior, the son of Yajñasena, with a vast flood of arrows.
But Śikhaṇḍin then, enraged, O lord of peoples, made the son of Somadatta tremble with ninety arrows, O Bhārata.
The two rākṣasas of dreadful deeds, the son of Hiḍimbā and Alambusa, both seeking each other's death, waged a most wondrous battle.
Proud conjurers of a hundred illusions, by their illusions each vanished from the other, and the two ranged about, working great amazement.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Cekitāna fought most fearsomely with Anuvinda, as in the war of gods and demons the mighty Bala and Śakra once fought.
Lakṣmaṇa made a fierce clash with Kṣatradeva, as Viṣṇu of old, O king, did with Hiraṇyākṣa in battle.
Then with horses urged to full speed and a chariot fitly equipped, the Paurava, O king, rushed roaring upon the son of Subhadrā.
And the mighty Abhimanyu, that tamer of foes, eager for battle, swiftly advanced and waged a great fight with him.
The Paurava then showered the son of Subhadrā with masses of arrows, but Arjuna's son brought down his banner, his parasol, and his bow to the earth.
And the son of Subhadrā, piercing the Paurava with seven other swift shafts, struck his horses and his charioteer with five more arrows.
Then, gladdening his own army and roaring again and again like a lion, the son of Arjuna swiftly took up an arrow that would make an end of the Paurava.
But the son of Hṛdika, with two arrows, cut asunder his bow with its fitted shaft; and the son of Subhadrā, slayer of hostile heroes, casting aside the severed bow, drew his bright sword and took up his shield.
With that shield set with many stars, like one of practiced hand, he ranged the sword-paths with whirling blade, displaying his own valor.
Now whirled, now whirled aloft, now shaken, now upraised again—the shield and the sword, O king, were seen as though there were no difference between them.
Leaping suddenly with a roar onto the pole of the Paurava's chariot, he mounted the Paurava's car and seized him by the locks of his hair.
With his foot he struck down the charioteer and with his sword felled the banner; then he flung the Paurava down as Garuḍa, churning the ocean, seizes a great serpent.
All the kings beheld him, his hair clutched fast and senseless, being borne down like a bull brought down by a lion.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing the Paurava fallen into the power of Arjuna's son, dragged helplessly like a masterless thing, Jayadratha could not endure it.
Taking up a sword and a shield decked with great peacock plumes and meshed with a hundred little bells, he leapt down from his chariot with a roar.
Then, beholding the lord of the Sindhus, the son of Kṛṣṇa let go the Paurava and sprang swiftly from the chariot, and swooped down like a hawk.
The javelins, pikes, and swords hurled at him by his foes the son of Kṛṣṇa cut apart with his sword and warded off with his shield.
Having displayed to the armies the might of his own arms, the strong one then raised aloft his great sword and his shield once more,
and the hero advanced straight upon the heir of Vṛddhakṣatra, his father's bitterest foe, as a tiger upon an elephant.
Closing upon each other, their swords for teeth and claws, the two struck joyfully, like a tiger and a lion.
In the clashings, the onslaughts, and the descents of sword and shield, none could see any opening in those two lions among men.
The flinging down, the clang of swords, the spying of an opening between the weapons, and the strokes outward and inward—all seemed as one, without distinction.
Ranging the outer and the inner along the supreme paths of swordcraft, the two great-souled ones appeared like winged mountains.
Then, as the illustrious son of Subhadrā was sweeping his sword across, Jayadratha smote upon the edge of his shield's rim.
Caught in the gold-bordered rim of that gleaming shield, the great sword, wrenched by the strength of the king of the Sindhus, snapped asunder.
Knowing his sword broken, he leapt back six paces, and in the twinkling of an eye was seen mounted again upon his own chariot.
As the son of Kṛṣṇa, withdrawn from that single combat, stood mounted on his splendid chariot, all the kings together hemmed him in on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the mighty heir of Arjuna, raising on high his shield and his sword, roared aloud, his eyes upon Jayadratha.
Leaving the king of the Sindhus, the son of Subhadrā, slayer of hostile heroes, scorched that army as the sun scorches the world.
At him Śalya hurled in the fight a dreadful spear, all of iron and adorned with gold, blazing like a tongue of fire.
Leaping up, the son of Kṛṣṇa caught it as Garuḍa, son of Vinatā, catches a falling serpent-prince, and he sheathed his sword.
Seeing the deftness and the courage of him of boundless splendor, all the kings together then raised a lion's roar.
Then that very spear, its haft wrought with cat's-eye gems, the son of Subhadrā, slayer of hostile heroes, loosed back at Śalya by the strength of his arm.
Reaching his chariot like a serpent loosed from its slough, it struck down Śalya's charioteer and hurled him from the car.
Then Virāṭa and Drupada, Dhṛṣṭaketu, Yudhiṣṭhira, Sātyaki, the Kekayas, Bhīma, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, the twins, and the sons of Draupadī cried out, "Well done! Well done!"
Manifold twangings of bows and abundant lion-roars arose, gladdening the son of Subhadrā who never fled; but your sons could not endure that mark of triumph in their foe.
Then all of them at once, O great king, showered him with whetted arrows from every side, as rain-clouds drench a mountain.
And seeking to do them a pleasure, and stung by the defeat of his charioteer, the son of Ārtāyana, slayer of foes, advanced in wrath upon the son of Subhadrā.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Hearing of the many wondrous single combats you have told of, Saṃjaya, I envy those who have eyes to see.
As a marvel in all the worlds will men tell of this war of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, like the war of gods and demons.
For I have no surfeit in hearing of this surpassing battle; therefore tell me of the combat of the son of Ārtāyana and the son of Subhadrā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Seeing his charioteer struck down, Śalya, raising aloft a wholly iron mace and roaring in wrath, leapt from his splendid chariot.
At him—blazing like the fire of doom, like Death with staff in hand—Bhīma rushed swiftly, gripping his great mace.
The son of Subhadrā too, seizing a mighty mace like the thunderbolt, cried, "Come on, come on!" to Śalya, but with effort Bhīma held him back.
Having checked the son of Subhadrā, the valorous Bhīmasena, advancing upon Śalya in the fray, stood firm as an unshaken mountain.
And likewise the king of the Madras, beholding the mighty Bhīma, advanced swiftly straight upon him, as a tiger upon an elephant.
Then the blare of trumpets and the sound of conches by the thousand, lion-roars, and the great booming of kettledrums arose together.
And among the hundreds of onlookers, Pāṇḍavas and Kurus alike of equal mind, there arose the cry, "Well done! Well done!"
For among all the kings, O Bhārata, none save the lord of the Madras could endure the onset of Bhīmasena in battle.
And likewise, who else in the world but Vṛkodara could endure in battle the mace-onset of the great-souled lord of the Madras?
Bound about with bands of fine gold, the great mace of Bhīma was a delight to all who saw it, and brandished thus it blazed forth.
And in like manner, as it ranged the paths and circling sweeps in turn, the mace of Śalya, resembling a great flash of lightning, shone resplendent.
Bellowing like two bulls, the pair ranged in circling sweeps—Śalya and Vṛkodara both, their maces lowered like horns turned for the charge.
In the wheeling, circling courses and in the play of their maces, the combat of those two lions among men was beyond all distinction.
Struck by Bhīmasena, Śalya's great mace, blazing with flame and terrible to behold, was shattered into mace-dust.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In like manner Bhīmasena's mace, smitten by his foe, gleamed like a tree thronged with fireflies in the early dusk of the rainy season.
The mace hurled in battle by the king of the Madras, O Bhārata, kindling the sky, scattered fire in abundance.
So too the mace sped by Bhīmasena against his foe scorched that host like a great meteor falling.
And those two surpassing maces, meeting each other, hissing like serpent-maidens, gave forth fire.
Like two great tigers with their claws, like two great elephants with their tusks, those two ranged about, closing upon each other with their maces.
Then, struck by the heads of the maces and in a moment drenched with blood, those two great-souled warriors appeared like a pair of kiṃśuka trees in flower.
In every quarter was heard the clash and crash of the mace-blows of those two lions among men, like to the thunderbolt of Indra.
Struck on left and right by the king of the Madras' mace, Bhīma did not waver then, like a mountain being riven yet unmoved.
So too, battered by the onsets of Bhīma's mace, the mighty lord of the Madras stood firm by his steadfastness, like a mountain smitten by thunderbolts.
Rushing on with great speed, their huge maces raised aloft, again, taking the intervening paths, they wheeled about in circles.
Then, springing forward eight paces and clashing together like two elephants, of a sudden they smote each other with their iron staves.
And by their mutual onslaught and by their maces sorely battered, the two heroes fell at once to the earth like two banners of Indra.
Then to Śalya, reeling and gasping again and again, Kṛtavarman the great chariot-warrior swiftly came.
And seeing him, O great king, crushed by the mace, writhing like a serpent and overwhelmed by a swoon,
then, lifting the lord of the Madras together with his mace onto his chariot, Kṛtavarman the great chariot-warrior swiftly bore him away from the battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The hero, reeling as though drunken, rose again within the twinkling of an eye; and mighty-armed Bhīma too was seen, mace in hand.
Then, seeing the lord of the Madras turned away in flight, your sons, with their elephants, chariots, foot, and horse, trembled, O venerable one.
Your men, harried by the victory-flushed Pāṇḍavas, took in fear to the quarters of the sky like clouds driven before the wind.
Having vanquished the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas shone resplendent in the battle, O king, blazing and full of glory.
Loudly they raised their lion-roars and, in their joy, blew their conches and sounded kettledrums and tabors along with the war-drums.
Saṃjaya said: Beholding that vast host of yours broken in flight, valiant Vṛṣasena alone withstood the Pāṇḍavas in battle by the cunning of his weapons.
The arrows loosed by Vṛṣasena toward the ten quarters ranged abroad, O venerable one, piercing through men, horses, chariots, and elephants.
His blazing great shafts issued forth by the thousand, O mighty-armed one, like the rays of the sun in the season of summer.
Tormented by him, O great king, chariot-warriors and horsemen alike fell suddenly upon the earth like trees uprooted by the wind.
Floods of horses, floods of chariots, and floods of elephants on every side he brought down in battle, O king, by hundreds and by thousands.
Seeing him thus ranging fearless through the battle, all the kings together hemmed him in on every side.
But Śatānīka, son of Nakula, advanced against Vṛṣasena and pierced him with ten iron shafts that cut to the vitals.
Karṇa's son sundered his bow and felled his banner; and the sons of Draupadī, seeking to protect that brother of theirs, advanced together.
With showers of arrows they made Karṇa's son straightway invisible; whereupon the chariot-warriors, with Droṇa's son at their head, ran roaring against them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Swiftly veiling the great chariot-warriors, the sons of Draupadī, with arrows of many kinds, O great king, as rain-clouds veil the mountains.
The Pāṇḍavas, eager for their sons, received them in haste—the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, the Matsyas, and the Sṛñjayas, weapons upraised.
Dreadful, tumultuous, and hair-raising was that battle between your men and the sons of Pāṇḍu, as of the gods with the dānavas.
Thus, with utmost fury, the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas fought, glaring upon one another, each having wronged the other.
In their wrath the forms of those of measureless might were seen, like the bodies of the noblest of winged serpents joined in combat in the sky.
With Bhīma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Droṇa, Droṇa's son, the son of Pṛṣata, and Sātyaki, that field of battle shone as with risen suns of doom.
Then was waged a tumultuous battle of mighty ones smiting one another, as of the strong gods with the dānavas.
Then the host of Yudhiṣṭhira, roaring like an upheaved ocean, smote down your army, whose great chariot-warriors had taken to flight.
Seeing that host broken and sorely afflicted by the foe, Droṇa cried out, "Enough of your flight, O heroes!"
Then he of the red steeds, enraged, like a four-tusked elephant, entered the host of the Pāṇḍavas and rushed upon Yudhiṣṭhira.
Yudhiṣṭhira pierced him with sharp shafts feathered with heron-plumes; but Droṇa, sundering his bow, swiftly bore down upon him.
But the prince Kumāra, guardian of the chariot-wheel and bringer of glory to the Pāñcālas, stayed the advancing Droṇa as the shore stays the lord of rivers.
Seeing Droṇa, that bull among the twice-born, held back by Kumāra, there arose a lion-roar from those who cried, "Well done! Well done!"
Then Kumāra, in that great fray, in his wrath pierced Droṇa in the breast with a shaft, roaring again and again like a lion.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the mighty Droṇa, deft of hand and unwearied, having checked Kumāra in the battle with many thousands of arrows,
that best of the twice-born crushed Kumāra—the hero, faithful to noble vows, schooled in the lore of weapons, the guardian of the wheel.
Reaching the midst of the army and ranging through all the quarters, Bhāradvāja, that bull among chariot-warriors, became the protector of your host.
Piercing Śikhaṇḍin with twelve shafts, Uttamaujas with twenty, Nakula with five, and Sahadeva with seven,
Yudhiṣṭhira with twelve, the sons of Draupadī with three apiece, Sātyaki with five, and the Matsya king with ten arrows—
he threw the foremost warriors into confusion in the battle, charging upon them; and he pressed forward, seeking to seize Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
Then, O king, Yugaṃdhara held back Bhāradvāja, that great chariot-warrior in his wrath, as a shore holds back the wind-tossed ocean.
But he, piercing Yudhiṣṭhira with arrows of well-bent joints, with a broad-headed shaft swept Yugaṃdhara from the platform of his chariot.
Then Virāṭa and Drupada, the Kekayas, Sātyaki, Śibi, Vyāghradatta the Pāñcāla, and the valiant Siṃhasena,
these and many others, seeking to protect Yudhiṣṭhira, barred his path, pouring forth many arrows.
And Vyāghradatta the Pāñcāla pierced Droṇa with fifty sharp arrows, O king; whereat the people raised a great shout.
And Siṃhasena, swiftly piercing Droṇa, that great chariot-warrior, laughed aloud of a sudden in his joy, seeking to daunt that man of steadfast vows.
Then, his eyes wide with rage, drawing back the bowstring and making a great clap with his palm, Droṇa bore down upon him.
Then the mighty one, closing in, with two broad-headed shafts struck off from their bodies the heads of Siṃhasena and of Vyāghradatta, earrings and all.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having crushed those great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas with showers of arrows, he stood close by Yudhiṣṭhira like Death the ender.
Then there arose a great clamor, O king, in the host of Yudhiṣṭhira—"The king is taken!"—from the warriors, as the steadfast-vowed one drew near.
Beholding Droṇa's prowess, the soldiers there said, "Today shall the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra surely have his desire; surely he will come to us in the battle of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
While your men were thus talking together, the great chariot-warrior, the son of Kuntī, came on at speed, making all resound with the thunder of his car.
On the field of slaughter he made a river whose waters were blood and whose eddies were chariots, strewn with heaps of heroes' bones, sweeping away the corpses on its banks;
and crossing in haste that river, whose great foam was the floods of arrows and which teemed with javelins for fishes, the Pāṇḍava put the Kurus to flight.
Then the Diademed one suddenly fell upon Droṇa's host, veiling it with a vast net of arrows as though to bewilder it.
As he swiftly loosed his shafts and ceaselessly fitted them anew, no one could mark any interval in the work of the glorious son of Kuntī.
Neither the quarters, nor the mid-air, nor the heavens, nor the earth could be seen, O great king; all was become, as it were, one mass of arrows.
Nothing whatsoever could then be seen there in the battle, O king, so great a darkness of arrows had the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva made.
And as the sun reached its setting and all was wrapped in dust, neither foe nor friend nor anything at all could then be known.
Then Droṇa, Duryodhana, and the rest drew off their forces; and the Pāṇḍava, perceiving the foe sorely affrighted and with no heart for fighting,
Bībhatsu gently withdrew his own troops; whereupon the Pāṇḍus, the Sṛñjayas, and the Pāñcālas, rejoicing, extolled Pārtha with pleasing words, as the seers extol the sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus, having conquered the foe, Dhanaṃjaya, glad of heart and with Keśava beside him, made his way to his own camp behind all the host.
On his car bright with sapphire, agate, gold, and silver, and with choice diamonds, coral, and crystal, the son of Pāṇḍu shone like the moon in a sky aglitter with stars.
Saṃjaya said: Those two armies, having gone to their camps, settled down, O lord of peoples, each in its portion, in due order, and by its companies throughout.
Having drawn off the troops, Droṇa, exceedingly downcast, looked upon Duryodhana and spoke these words in shame.
"This I told you before: while Dhanaṃjaya holds his ground, Yudhiṣṭhira cannot be seized in battle, not even by the gods.
So, though you strove, it was thwarted by Pārtha in the battle. Do not too greatly doubt my word: unconquerable are Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava.
But if by some device he of the white steeds be drawn away, then, O king, Yudhiṣṭhira shall this day come into your power.
Let someone challenge him in the fight and draw him off to another quarter; for the son of Kuntī will in no wise return without having vanquished him."
In that undefended interval, O king, I shall break through the host and seize the Dharma-king, even before the very eyes of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
And if, bereft of Arjuna, he does not abandon the battle when he beholds me bearing down upon him, know him then as already taken.
Thus, O king, in a single rush I shall this very day bring Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, together with his retinue, into your power—of this there is no doubt.
If the Pāṇḍava stands his ground in battle even for a moment—but should he flee from the field, that would be better still than victory.
Having heard the words of Droṇa, the lord of the Trigartas then, O king, together with his brothers, spoke these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
We have ever been wronged, O king, by the wielder of Gāṇḍīva, who, O bull of the Bhāratas, has done us injury though we were guiltless.
Remembering those manifold humiliations, we, burning in the fire of wrath, can find no sleep through all our nights.
Now he, mighty in celestial weapons, has come within the range of our sight; we shall accomplish all that we have long desired in our hearts.
What would be pleasing to you and bring glory to us—this we shall do: we shall slay him, having drawn him away beyond the field of battle.
This day let the earth be without Arjuna, or else without the Trigartas; truly we swear it to you, and this shall not prove false.
So having spoken, O Bhārata, Satyaratha and Satyadharman, and Satyavarman and Satyeṣu, and Satyakarman likewise,
the five brothers together, with ten thousand chariots, turned aside, O great king, having taken their oath upon the battle.
The Mālavas and the Tuṇḍikeras with thirty thousand chariots, and Suśarman, that tiger among men, the Trigarta lord of Prasthala,
together with the Mācellakas, the Lalitthas, and the Madrakas, with ten thousand chariots, took the oath together with his brothers.
And from sundry realms yet another ten thousand chariots of chosen warriors had risen up and come forward to swear the oath.
Then, taking up the kindled fire and making oblation each one severally, they donned garments of kuśa-grass and bright-patterned coats of mail.
Their armor bound on, anointed with clarified butter, clad in kuśa-grass, girt with bowstring-belts—those heroes whose sacrificial fees ran to hundreds of thousands—
performers of sacrifice, blessed with sons, worthy of the worlds, their duties fulfilled, ready to lay down their bodies, about to yoke their very selves to glory and to victory,
having attained the heavenly worlds through chastity, sacred learning, and rites whose fees were duly bestowed, eager to go thither swiftly through fair-fought battle,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
having gratified the brāhmaṇas and bestowed upon them gold pieces each in turn, and cattle and garments, they spoke once more to one another,
and having kindled the black-pathed Fire and approached it, they then, in that flame, took their battle-vow, firm in resolve, and made their pledge.
In the hearing of all beings they made their utterances aloud, and binding themselves to the slaying of Dhanaṃjaya, they took their solemn oath.
"Those worlds which belong to liars, and those that belong to the slayers of brāhmaṇas, the worlds of the drinker of strong drink and of him who lusts after his teacher's wife,
the worlds of him who steals a brāhmaṇa's wealth and of him who plunders the king's grant, of him who forsakes one come for refuge and slays a suppliant,
the worlds of house-burners and of cattle-slayers, the worlds of the wicked and of those who hate the brāhmaṇas,
and of those who out of folly shun their wives in the season fit for offspring, and of those who betray a fellowship pledged over the funeral rites, and of those who destroy their own souls—
and the worlds of those who steal what was entrusted to them, of those who let their sacred learning perish, of those who fight in anger, and of those who follow base men,
and the worlds of unbelievers, and of those who abandon the fire-rites and forsake their forefathers—those worlds may we attain, and those of evildoers besides,
if we should turn back from the battle without having slain Dhanaṃjaya, or if, pressed hard by him, we should out of fear show him our backs.
But if in the fray we accomplish that deed so hard to do in this world, then beyond doubt we shall attain the cherished worlds of those who have done meritorious deeds."
Having spoken thus, O king, those heroes advanced into the battle, summoning Arjuna toward the quarter beloved of the forefathers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Challenged by those tigers among men, Pārtha, conqueror of hostile cities, spoke these words to the Dharma-king without delay.
"Once challenged, I shall not turn back—such is the vow I have taken; and these sworn warriors, O king, summon me again and again.
And here Suśarman, together with his brothers, calls me to battle; you ought to give me leave to go for the slaying of him and his band."
"This challenge I cannot endure, O bull among men. Truly I declare to you: hold the foe as already slain in battle."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have heard, my dear son, what Droṇa intends to do; so act that his purpose shall come to nothing.
For Droṇa is strong and valiant, skilled in arms and untiring, and he has pledged this capture of me, O great chariot-warrior.
Arjuna said: This Satyajit, O king, shall be your guardian in battle today; so long as the Pāñcāla stands his ground, the preceptor shall not gain his desire.
But should that tiger among men Satyajit be slain in battle, O lord, then you must on no account stand your ground, even with all your forces gathered together.
Saṃjaya said: Then Phalguna, given leave by the king, was embraced and looked upon with love in many ways, and was sped on with benedictions.
Then the mighty Pārtha, leaving him, advanced against the Trigartas, as a famished lion against a herd of deer to still his hunger.
Then, Arjuna being gone, Duryodhana's army, filled with the highest joy and fiercely intent on the seizing of the Dharma-king,
then the two armies came together against each other with might, like the Gaṅgā and the Sarayū rushing in the rains, their waters swollen and turbulent.
Saṃjaya said: Then the sworn warriors, O king, arrayed upon level ground, drew up their host of chariots in the formation called the half-moon, filled with gladness.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beholding the Diademed One advancing, those tigers among men, O sire, raised a great shout in their exultation.
That clamor filled all the intermediate quarters, the main quarters, and the sky; and because the whole world was so filled, there arose no echo of it there.
Perceiving them so exceedingly elated, Dhanaṃjaya, smiling somewhat, spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa.
"Behold these, O son of Devakī, these Trigarta brothers, doomed to die this day in battle, thus rejoicing when they ought rather to weep.
Or rather, this is indeed a time of joy for the Trigartas, beyond doubt, for they shall attain those most excellent worlds so hard for base men to win."
Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, the mighty-armed Arjuna then closed in battle upon the arrayed host of the Trigartas.
Phalguna, taking up Devadatta, his conch adorned with gold, blew it with great force, filling all the quarters with its sound.
Terrified by that blast, the army of the sworn warriors stood motionless in the fray, as though wrought of iron-hard stone.
Their steeds, with eyes rolled back, ears and necks rigid, and legs braced stiff, let flow their urine and their blood.
But recovering their senses and steadying their force, they hurled all at once their heron-feathered arrows against the son of Pāṇḍu.
Those fifteen thousand shafts Arjuna, swift in valor, cut down with his own fleet arrows before ever they reached him.
Then again they struck back at Arjuna with ten sharp arrows apiece; and Pārtha in turn pierced each of them with three.
Then each one severally, O king, pierced Pārtha with five shafts, and he, the valiant one, pierced them back with two apiece.
Then yet again, enraged, they covered over Arjuna together with Keśava with their keen shafts, as a pond is filled with showers of rain.
Then thousands of arrows came falling upon Arjuna, like swarms of bees in a forest among groves of flowering trees.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Subāhu with thirty firm arrows of adamantine temper struck the Ambidextrous One deep upon the diadem.
With those gold-nocked, straight-flying shafts lodged in his diadem, the Diademed One, crowned as with a wreath of gold, shone like an uplifted sacrificial post.
With a broad-headed arrow the Pāṇḍava cut away the leather hand-guard of Subāhu in the fight, and then again overwhelmed him with showers of shafts.
Then Suśarman with ten arrows, and Suratha, Sudharman, Sudhanus, and Subāhu likewise, beset the Diademed One.
But he whose banner bore the foremost of monkeys pierced them all back, each with his arrows, and with broad-headed shafts cut down their golden standards.
Having cut asunder the bow of Sudhanus, he slew his horses with his shafts, and then struck off from the trunk his head together with its helmet.
When that hero had fallen, his followers, stricken with terror, fled in their fear to where Duryodhana's army stood.
Then the son of Vāsava, sorely enraged, smote that great host with unbroken nets of arrows, as the sun dispels the darkness with its beams.
Then, when that force was broken and scattered on every side, and the Ambidextrous One was wrathful, fear entered into the Trigartas.
Slaughtered by Pārtha with his smooth-jointed shafts, they swooned away here and there, frightened like herds of deer.
Then the king of the Trigartas, enraged, spoke to those great chariot-warriors: "Enough of your flight, O heroes; you ought not to give way to fear.
Having sworn dreadful oaths before the eyes of the whole army, what will you, foremost of men, say when you go to Duryodhana's host?
How shall we all together not become a mockery in the world by such a deed in battle? Turn back, each according to his strength!"
Thus addressed, O king, those heroes shouted again and again and blew their conches, heartening one another.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the bands of sworn warriors turned again to the fight, and the Nārāyaṇa cowherds too, making death itself their place of return.
Saṃjaya said: But seeing the bands of sworn warriors turn back once more to the battle, Arjuna spoke to the great-souled Vāsudeva.
"Urge on the horses, O Hṛṣīkeśa, against the bands of sworn warriors; these men will not quit the battle while they live—such is my judgment.
Behold the dread strength of my weapons, of my two arms and of my bow; this day, in my wrath, I shall lay them low as Rudra lays low the beasts."
Then Kṛṣṇa, smiling and greeting him with an auspicious word, drove the chariot, unassailable, wherever Arjuna wished it to go.
That chariot, borne along in the battle then, shone exceeding bright, drawn by its pale horses like a celestial car borne through the sky.
Then it wheeled in circles, advancing and returning, O king, as did the chariot of Śakra of old in the war between the gods and the asuras.
Then the Nārāyaṇa troops, enraged and bearing weapons of every kind, blanketing him with showers of arrows, surrounded Dhanaṃjaya on all sides.
And in a moment, O bull of the Bhāratas, they made Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, together with Kṛṣṇa, invisible in the battle.
But Phalguna, enraged in the fray, his prowess redoubled, stroked the Gāṇḍīva and swiftly took it up in the combat.
Knitting his brow upon his face, the very mark of wrath, the Pāṇḍava filled with breath the great conch Devadatta.
Then Arjuna loosed the weapon of Tvaṣṭṛ, slayer of hosts of foes, and at once thousands of forms appeared, each one distinct.
Deluded by those counterfeit likenesses of him, of manifold shapes, they took one another for Arjuna and slew their very own selves.
"Here is Arjuna! Here is Govinda! Here are the Yādava and the Pāṇḍava!"—so crying, bewildered, they slew one another in the battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Deluded by the supreme weapon, they wrought one another's destruction; the warriors gleamed upon the field like kiṃśuka trees in flower.
Then that weapon, reducing to ashes the thousands of arrows loosed by them, conducted those heroes to the abode of Yama.
Then Bībhatsu, laughing, tormented with his arrows the Lalitthas and the Mālavas, the Mācellakas, the Trigartas, and the Yaudheyas.
Those Kṣatriyas, slaughtered by the hero and driven on by fate, poured upon Pārtha showers of arrows of every kind.
Then neither Arjuna nor the chariot nor Keśava could there be seen, shrouded by that dreadful rain of arrows.
Then, believing they had found their mark, they shouted to one another in joy, "The two Kṛṣṇas are slain!"—and shook out their garments.
The warriors by the thousand sounded kettledrums, tabors, and conches, and there, O venerable one, they raised fierce roars like the roaring of lions.
Then Kṛṣṇa broke into sweat, and weary he said to Arjuna: "Where are you, Pārtha? I do not see you—do you yet live, O slayer of foes?"
Reading that mortal feeling in him, the Pāṇḍava, who knew all hearts, swept away with the weapon of Vāyu the rain of arrows they had loosed.
Then the lord Vāyu bore off the hosts of the Saṃśaptakas, with their horses, elephants, chariots, and weapons, as if they were heaps of dry leaves.
Borne aloft by the wind, O king, they made a strange spectacle, O venerable one, like birds flying up from the trees in their season.
Having thus thrown them into confusion, Dhanaṃjaya in haste slew with his whetted arrows hundreds and thousands of them.
With broad-headed shafts he struck off heads and arms still grasping their weapons, and with his arrows he felled to the earth thighs like the trunks of elephants.
Dhanaṃjaya made his foes broken-backed and legless, their brains, eyes, and fingers shorn away, robbed of their various limbs and members.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Shattering with his arrows the chariots, duly fashioned and resembling the cities of the Gandharvas, he left them stripped of horses, chariots, and elephants.
Here and there shone the throngs of chariots with banners cut away, like groves of headless palms—some here, some there, in this place and in that.
Elephants with their upper weapons, with banners, goads, and arms, fell like wooded mountains struck by the thunderbolt of Śakra.
Horses with chowries, head-ornaments, and armor, their entrails, eyes, and breath slipping from them, fell to the ground with their riders, struck down by Pārtha's arrows.
Their swords and daggers flung aside, their armor, lances, and spears hewn through, the foot-soldiers with sundered mail lay slain in pitiful array.
With the slain and the dying, with those falling and those fallen, with those reeling about and those groaning aloud, the battlefield grew terrible to behold.
The great cloud of dust that had risen was laid to rest by the showers of blood, and the earth, thronged with hundreds of headless trunks, became impassable.
That course of Bībhatsu in the battle, fierce and ghastly, shone like the sporting-ground of Rudra slaughtering his creatures at the end of an age.
Slaughtered by Pārtha, their horses, chariots, and elephants thrown into disorder, they, dwindling away yet still facing him, became the guests of Śakra.
That ground, O best of the Bhāratas, strewn all over with those slain great chariot-warriors turned into corpses, presented a fearful sight on every side.
Meanwhile, while Savyasācin was thus occupied, Droṇa, his ranks arrayed in battle order, rushed upon Yudhiṣṭhira.
Swiftly the warriors with their ordered ranks received him, seeking to shield Yudhiṣṭhira; and then there arose a great tumult.
Saṃjaya said: When the great chariot-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, had passed that night, and had spoken much, O king, to King Suyodhana,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
having arranged the engagement of Pārtha with the bands of the Saṃśaptakas, and when Pārtha had withdrawn from the field toward the slaying of the Saṃśaptakas,
then Droṇa, his army arrayed for battle, advanced, O best of the Bhāratas, against the great host of the Pāṇḍavas, seeking to seize the King of Righteousness.
Beholding then the Garuḍa-array fashioned by the son of Bharadvāja, Yudhiṣṭhira drew up his counter-formation in the shape of a half-circle.
The mouth of the Garuḍa was the great chariot-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja; its head was King Duryodhana with his brothers and followers.
Its two eyes were Kṛtavarman and the descendant of Gotama, the best of bowmen, together with Bhūtavarman, Kṣemaśarman, and the valiant Karakarṣa.
The Kaliṅgas, the Siṃhalas, the Easterners, the valiant Ābhīras, the Dāśerakas, the Śakas, the Yavanas, the Kāmbojas, and those who were the Haṃsapadas,
and the Śūrasenas, the Daradas, the Madras, and the Kekayas stood at the neck, a flood of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers in their hundreds of thousands.
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, Somadatta, and Bāhlika, heroes encompassed by an akṣauhiṇī, took their stand upon the right wing.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja, taking their position on the left wing, stood with the son of Droṇa at their head.
At the back were the Kaliṅgas, the Ambaṣṭhas, the Māgadhas, the Pauṇḍras and Madrakas, the Gāndhāras led by Śakuni, the mountaineers, and the Vasātis.
At the tail stood Karṇa, son of Vikartana, with his sons, kinsmen, and friends, attended by a mighty host that bristled with banners of every kind.
Jayadratha, Bhīmaratha, Sāṃyātrika, Sabhā, Jaya, Bhūmiṃjaya, Vṛṣakrātha, and the mighty Naiṣadha,
surrounded by a great force and having the world of Brahmā as their goal, stood above the array, O king, those men skilled in war.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The array marshalled by Droṇa, with its foot-soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants, looked like the ocean lashed by the wind and surging into motion.
From its wings and outer wings the eager combatants poured forth, like clouds charged with lightning and thunder from every quarter in the hot season.
In its midst the king of Prāgjyotiṣa, mounted upon an elephant duly caparisoned, shone, O king, like the radiant sun at its rising.
The king, borne beneath a white parasol hung with wreaths and garlands, was like the full moon on the night of the full, in conjunction with the Kṛttikā stars.
That elephant, dark as a heap of black collyrium and blind with rut, gleamed like a great mountain rained upon by mighty clouds.
Attended by sundry heroic kings of the mountains, adorned with weapons of every kind, he was like Śakra amid the hosts of the gods.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, beholding that more-than-human array, unconquerable by foes in battle, spoke these words to the son of Pṛṣata:
"O lord, master of horses gray as the dove, let such a plan be devised that I do not this day fall into the power of the Brāhmaṇa."
Dhṛṣṭadyumna said: "You shall not fall into the power of Droṇa, however he may strive, O true to your vows; this day I shall hold off Droṇa together with his followers.
While I live, O descendant of Kuru, you ought not to be troubled; for Droṇa is by no means able to vanquish me in battle."
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus and scattering arrows, the mighty son of Drupada, his horses gray as the dove, himself rushed against Droṇa.
Seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna planted before him, of unwelcome aspect, Droṇa in an instant became as one whose heart was not greatly cheered.
But beholding him, your son Durmukha, scourge of foes, wishing to do Droṇa a service, held off Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
That tumultuous clash between the heroic son of Pṛṣata and Durmukha, O Bhārata, seemed to be a contest of equals.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The son of Pṛṣata, swiftly veiling Durmukha with a net of arrows, beat back the son of Bharadvāja with a great flood of shafts.
Seeing Droṇa held at bay, your son, sorely strained, bewildered the son of Pṛṣata with showers of arrows of every device.
While those two chiefs, the Pāñcāla and the Kuru, were locked together in the fray, Droṇa with his arrows scattered Yudhiṣṭhira's army in many directions.
As clouds are torn asunder on every side by the wind, so were Pārtha's forces torn apart, here and there.
For a moment that battle was fair to behold; then, O king, it raged on as if frenzied, beyond all bounds.
Neither one's own men nor the foe, O king, could any longer be told apart; that battle was waged by guesswork and by watchwords.
From their crest-jewels, their golden chains, their ornaments, their swords and shields, beams shone forth with the splendor of the sun.
The aspect of the chariots, elephants, and horses, with their banners scattered abroad, appeared in the battle like a sky dappled with cranes and clouds.
Men slew men, and fierce horses slew horses; charioteers slew charioteers, and elephants slew great elephants.
Between elephants whose banners were upraised and other mighty elephants there arose in a moment a tumultuous and terrible combat.
From those beasts, their bodies locked together as they dragged at one another, fire mixed with smoke sprang up from the grinding clash of their tusks.
With their banners scattered and fire kindled from their tusks, they became, as they reached toward the sky, like clouds charged with lightning.
With the elephants—bleeding, trumpeting, and falling—the earth was strewn over, as the autumn sky is strewn with clouds.
From those elephants, smitten by the showers of arrows and lances, there arose a roar like the roar of clouds at the dissolution of the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some of the great elephants, struck by lances and by arrows, trembled in terror; others took to flight at the very din of every creature.
And some elephants there, gored by the tusks of other elephants, raised a dreadful cry of anguish, like storm-clouds at a portent.
And the elephants that were being driven backward by mighty elephants, urged on again by the keen goads, churned forward and returned to the charge.
The elephant-drivers, smitten by the arrows and lances of other drivers, let fall their weapons and goads and went down from the elephants to the ground.
And the elephants, bereft of their men and trumpeting on every side, rushed together and crashed into one another like sundered clouds.
Bearing away the slain and held fast by the finest weapons, the great elephants scattered to every quarter, some wandering off alone as though solitary beasts.
Struck and struck again by lances, spears, and battle-axes, the elephants fell with cries of anguish there amid the slaughter.
As their mountain-like bodies came crashing down on every side, the earth, struck all at once, both trembled and resounded.
With elephants brought low on every side, their riders and banners with them, the ground shone as if strewn with scattered mountains.
The mahouts upon the elephants, their hearts pierced through in battle, were felled by the chariot-warriors' broad-headed shafts, their goads and lances flung about.
Other elephants, smitten by iron arrows, trumpeting like cranes, fled crashing through the ten directions, trampling enemy and friend alike.
Covered with the heaped bodies of hosts of elephants, horses, and chariots, the earth, O king, became a mire of flesh and blood.
Crushed and tossed aloft by the elephants' tusk-tips, the great chariot-warriors, with their cars whole or with wheels torn away, lay strewn upon the field.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Chariots bereft of their warriors, horses bereft of their men, and elephants whose riders were slain fled to every quarter, tormented by arrows.
There a father slew his son and a son his father; so tumultuous was the battle that nothing whatever could be discerned.
Men sank to their ankles in the mire of blood, hemmed in as great trees encircled by blazing forest fires.
Garments and armor, parasols and banners, all drenched with blood, appeared crimson to the eye.
Multitudes of horses, of chariots, and of men, struck down, were rolled over and over again and ground in many ways by the chariot-wheels.
That ocean of armies shone forth, its great surge the throng of elephants, its waterweed the lifeless men, its turbulent whirlpools the masses of chariots.
Plunging into it with their mounts for great ships, the warriors who craved the wealth of victory, though sinking down, gave way to no bewilderment.
Among the warriors rained upon by showers of arrows, their tokens of valor not yet won, not one who bore the marks of wounds could keep his own composure.
As that battle, terrible of aspect and dreadful, raged on, Droṇa, having confounded the foe, rushed upon Yudhiṣṭhira.
Saṃjaya said: Then Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing Droṇa drawn near, received him fearlessly with a great shower of arrows.
Then a tumultuous din arose within Yudhiṣṭhira's host, as when a great lion seeks to seize the leader of a herd of elephants.
Seeing Droṇa bent on reaching Yudhiṣṭhira, the hero Satyajit, of truthful valor, then rushed upon the teacher.
Then the teacher and the Pāñcāla fought one another, throwing that army into turmoil like Indra and the son of Virocana of old.
Then the teacher swiftly pierced Satyajit with ten keen, vital-rending shafts, cutting away his bow with its arrow set.
Taking up another bow more swiftly still, the valiant warrior at once struck Droṇa with twenty heron-feathered arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing Droṇa as if devoured by Satyajit in the fight, the Pāñcāla Vṛka harried Droṇa with hundreds of keen arrows.
Beholding the great chariot-warrior Droṇa overwhelmed in the fight, the Pāṇḍavas raised a shout, O king, and waved their garments aloft.
And the mighty Vṛka, in utmost wrath, pierced Droṇa between the breasts with sixty shafts, O king; and that seemed a marvel.
But the great chariot-warrior Droṇa, that mighty force, overspread by the shower of arrows, gathered his speed, his eyes rolling with wrath.
Then Droṇa cut away the bows of both Satyajit and Vṛka, and with six arrows Droṇa slew Vṛka together with his charioteer and horses.
Then Satyajit, taking up another swifter bow, pierced Droṇa with his horses, charioteer, and banner, with shafts.
Droṇa could not brook this harrying by the Pāñcāla in the fray; so for his destruction he loosed his arrows in haste.
His horses, his banner, the grip of his bow, and both his flanking charioteers—all these Droṇa then overwhelmed with showers of arrows by the thousand.
Though his bows were cut to pieces again and again, the Pāñcāla, supreme master of weapons, kept battling him whose horses were red.
Marking Satyajit risen up so in the great battle, Droṇa with a crescent-headed shaft severed the head of that noble man.
When that mighty bull among the chariot-warriors of the Pāñcālas was slain, Yudhiṣṭhira, in dread of Droṇa, withdrew on his swift horses.
The Pāñcālas, Kekayas, Matsyas, Cedis, Karūṣas, and Kosalas, looking to Yudhiṣṭhira, joyfully rushed upon Droṇa.
Then the teacher, slayer of throngs of foes, eager to reach Yudhiṣṭhira, scattered those battalions as the wind scatters a heap of cotton.
As Droṇa burned through those battalions again and again, Śatānīka, younger brother of the Matsya king, advanced against him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With six arrows bright as the sun's rays and burnished by the smith, he pierced Droṇa together with his charioteer and horses, and roared aloud.
As he roared, Droṇa with a razor-headed shaft swiftly struck his head, with its earrings, from his body; and thereupon the Matsyas fled.
Having vanquished the Matsyas, the son of Bharadvāja conquered the Cedis, the Karūṣas, the Kekayas, the Pāñcālas, the Sṛñjayas, and the Pāṇḍus, again and again.
Seeing him of the golden chariot, wrathful, consuming the battalions like a raging fire a forest, the Sṛñjayas trembled.
As that swift-handed one drew his peerless bow and struck down his foes, the twang of his bowstring was heard in all the quarters.
Elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers, chariot-warriors and elephant-riders—the dreadful arrows loosed by that deft hand crushed them all.
Like a thundering rain-cloud mingled with wind at winter's end, he rained down what seemed a hail of stones, striking terror into the foe.
That mighty hero, the great archer, giver of safety to his friends, ranged over all the quarters as though convulsing the host.
Like lightning amid the clouds, we beheld in every quarter the gold-adorned bow of Droṇa of boundless splendor.
And Droṇa wrought great havoc in the Pāṇḍava host, as Viṣṇu, honored by gods and demons alike, once did among the throngs of the Daityas.
That hero, truthful in speech, wise, mighty, of true valor, and of great majesty—at the end of time, dreadful and terrifying to the timid—
a river whose waves were coats of mail and whose whirlpools were banners, sweeping away the banks of mortal men, with elephants and horses for its great crocodiles, swords for its fish, hard to cross,
with the bones of heroes for its gravel, dreadful, with kettledrums and tabors for its turtles, with shields and armor for its rafts, terrible, with hair for its waterweed and water-grass,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
running with floods of arrows, its currents bows, thronged with arms for serpents, the dread stream that the battlefield bore along, the river of the Kurus and Sṛñjayas, with men's heads for stones, spears for fish, and maces for its boats,
with turbans for its foam and raiment, with spilled entrails for its crawling reptiles, fierce, bearing away heroes, terrible, its mire of flesh and blood,
with elephants for its alligators and banners for its trees, drowning the warriors, cruel, with heaped bodies for its rafts and cavalrymen for its crocodiles, impassable—such a river, flowing to the realm of Death, did Droṇa set coursing there.
It rang with the cries of flesh-eating throngs, swarmed with packs of dogs and jackals, and was haunted on every side by the most dreadful devourers of carrion.
As that lordly chariot-warrior, like Death itself, burned through their battalions, the sons of Kuntī at their head rushed upon Droṇa from every side.
But your kings and princes, their weapons raised, surrounded those heroic great archers on every side.
Then Droṇa, true to his word, like an elephant in rut, broke through the chariot-ranks and brought down Dṛḍhasena.
Then, falling upon king Kṣema as he struck fearlessly, he pierced him with nine arrows; and Kṣema, slain, dropped from his chariot.
Reaching the midst of the armies and ranging through all the quarters, he became the protector of others, while he himself could in no way be brought to bay.
With twelve arrows he struck Śikhaṇḍin, with twenty Uttamaujas, and with a broad-headed shaft he sent Vasudāna to the abode of Yama.
With eighty arrows he pierced Kṣatravarman, with twenty-six Sudakṣiṇa, and with a broad-headed shaft he struck Kṣatradeva from the seat of his chariot.
Having pierced Yudhāmanyu with sixty-four arrows and Sātyaki with thirty, he of the golden chariot swiftly rushed upon Yudhiṣṭhira.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, best of kings, withdrew at once on his swift horses; and Kitava the Pāñcāla advanced against Droṇa.
Droṇa struck him down together with his bow, his horses, and his driver; and slain, he fell to the ground from his chariot, like a star from the sky.
When that prince, the glory of the Pāñcālas, was slain, a great tumult arose: "Slay Droṇa! Slay Droṇa!"
The mighty Droṇa threw into disorder those furiously enraged Pāñcālas, Matsyas, Kekayas, Sṛñjayas, and Pāṇḍavas.
Sātyaki and Cekitāna, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, Vārdhakṣemi, Citrasena, Senābindu, and Suvarcas—
these and many others besides, lords of various realms, all of them Droṇa vanquished in battle, surrounded by the Kurus.
And your men, O great king, having won victory in that mighty battle, slew the Pāṇḍava forces as they fled in all directions.
Slain by the great-souled Droṇa as the Dānavas were once slain by Indra, the Pāñcālas, Kekayas, and Matsyas trembled, O Bhārata.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the Pāṇḍavas and all the Pāñcālas were broken by the son of Bharadvāja in that great battle, did any other turn back to face him,
having set his mind in battle upon the noble resolve that brings the warrior fame—shunned by cowards, embraced by bulls among men?
For that man, O charioteer, is a hero who turns back when others are routed. Alas, was there not a single man who stood firm at the sight of Droṇa,
who, like a yawning tiger, like an elephant in rut, laying down his very life in battle, stood armed and skilled in varied modes of warfare,
the great archer, that tiger among men, who multiplied the woes of his foes, grateful, devoted to truth, seeker of Duryodhana's good?
Seeing the son of Bharadvāja, that hero, thus standing firm in the front of battle, which heroes turned back to meet him? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Seeing them shaken in the fray and driven off by Droṇa's arrows—the Pāñcālas, Pāṇḍavas, Matsyas, Sṛñjayas, Cedis, and Kekayas—
borne away by the life-stealing flood of arrows loosed from Droṇa's bow, like rafts swept off by the great current of a river,
the Kauravas, with lions' roars and the din of many instruments, with chariots, elephants, men, and horses, surrounded them on every side.
Beholding them, king Duryodhana, standing in the midst of his host and surrounded by his kinsmen, in high delight and as if laughing, spoke to Karṇa.
Behold, Rādheya, the Pāñcālas driven back by Droṇa's arrows, terrified by that mighty bowman as wild deer are terrified by a lion.
Never again, I think, will these men long for battle, broken as they are by Droṇa as great trees are broken by the wind.
Tormented by the gold-feathered shafts of that great-souled one, they flee by no single road, reeling this way and that.
Hemmed in by the Kauravas and by the great-souled Droṇa, these others have huddled into a ring, like elephants ringed about by fire.
Beset as if by swarming bees by Droṇa's whetted arrows, bent wholly on flight, they cling close to one another.
There stands Bhīma, fierce in his wrath, cut off from the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas, ringed about by my warriors, and yet, Karṇa, he seems to threaten me still.
Plainly that fool sees the whole world made of Droṇa today; surely now the Pāṇḍava has given up hope of life and of his kingdom.
Karṇa said: Never, while he lives, will that mighty-armed one quit the fight, nor, O tiger among men, will he leave off these his lion-roars.
Nor, I think, will the Pāṇḍavas be broken in battle, for they are brave and strong, masters of weapons, and frenzied for the fray.
Remembering the poison, the fire, the gambling, and all their torments, and their exile in the forest, the Pāṇḍavas will not abandon the battle — so I judge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Wronged as he has been, the mighty-armed Vṛkodara of measureless strength — that son of Kuntī — will slay our finest, the best of our great chariot-warriors.
With sword, with bow, with spear, with horses, elephants, men, and chariots, and with his iron mace, he will slay them in troop after troop.
And these chariot-warriors follow him, led by Sātyaki — the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, the Matsyas, and above all the Pāṇḍavas themselves.
Brave they are, and strong, and valiant — great chariot-warriors — and above all spurred on by the wrathful Bhīma.
From every side, those bulls among the Kurus close in upon Droṇa, seeking to shield Vṛkodara, as banks of cloud close round the sun.
Gathered into one single path, these men might press hard upon the steadfast keeper of vows, were he left unguarded — as moths bent on their own death press upon a lamp; for beyond doubt they are masters of weapons and fit to hold him off.
Too heavy a burden, I think, has been laid upon the son of Bharadvāja; let us go swiftly to where Droṇa has taken his stand, lest, as crows would a great serpent, they slay the steadfast keeper of vows.
Saṃjaya said: Hearing the words of Rādheya, King Duryodhana then, together with his brothers, O king, set forth toward Droṇa's chariot.
There arose a mighty uproar from the Pāṇḍavas, who had turned back with their splendid horses of many hues, all eager to kill Droṇa alone.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Tell me, Saṃjaya, the chariot-ensigns of every one of them — those who, with Bhīma at their head, in their fury bore down upon Droṇa.
Saṃjaya said: Seeing Vṛkodara striving on with horses the color of the antelope, the brave Śaineya, his steeds silver-white, then turned to join him.
Bearing Nakula swiftly on, the comely Kāmboja horses, decked in trappings green as parrots' wings, rushed upon your men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And dark horses like thunderclouds, terrible in their speed and swift as the wind, bore Sahadeva, that tiger among men, his weapon raised on high.
With horses caparisoned in finest gold and matching the wind in speed, all the armies advanced about Yudhiṣṭhira.
Next to the king came the Pāñcāla king Drupada, beneath a parasol wrought of gold, guarded all about by his own men.
Drawn by handsome bay steeds, inured to every din of war, that mighty bowman, fearless and unmoved, advanced amid the kings.
Behind him followed Virāṭa with his brave great chariot-warriors; and the Kekayas, and Śikhaṇḍin, and Dhṛṣṭaketu likewise, each ringed by his own troops, followed the king of the Matsyas.
Excellent horses the color of trumpet-flowers, bearing on the foe-slaying king of the Matsyas, shone resplendent.
Swift horses turmeric-yellow in hue, garlanded with gold, bore in haste the son of King Virāṭa.
Borne by horses red as the cochineal insect came the five Kekaya brothers, gleaming like gold, every one of them under a crimson banner.
Those heroes, garlanded in gold, all skilled in war and clad in armor, appeared like raining storm-clouds.
Well-broken horses, copper-red and the color of unbaked clay, yoked to his car, bore the Pāñcāla Śikhaṇḍin of boundless might.
Twelve thousand were the great chariot-warriors of the Pāñcālas, and of these six thousand followed Śikhaṇḍin.
And the son of Śiśupāla, that lion among men, O sire, was borne along by dappled, fawn-colored horses that seemed to sport as they ran.
And Dhṛṣṭaketu, that bull among the Cedis, swollen with surpassing might and hard to conquer, advanced with dappled Kāmboja steeds.
And the delicate Bṛhatkṣatra of the Kaikeyas was borne swiftly on by excellent Saindhava horses the color of straw-smoke.
Bāhlika-bred horses, jasmine-eyed and lotus-hued, finely adorned, bore the brave Kṣatradeva, son of Śikhaṇḍin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Excellent horses the color of the curlew bore into battle the youthful Sukumāra, that great chariot-warrior, son of Abhibhū the king of Kāśi.
White horses with black manes, swift as thought and obedient to the charioteer's command, bore the prince Prativindhya, O king.
Sutasoma, the son whom Pārtha had begged of Dhaumya, was borne in the battle by steeds the color of the bean-flower.
Bright as a thousand moons they shone; and because he was born in that city of the Kurus called Udayendu, amid the rite of pressing the Soma, therefore he became known as Sutasoma.
Horses like the blossoms of the sāla tree, radiant as the young rising sun, bore the praiseworthy Śatānīka, son of Nakula.
Horses with the sheen of a peacock's neck, harnessed with traces of gold, bore Śrutakarman, son of Draupadī, that tiger among men.
Excellent horses the color of the blue jay's wing bore Śrutakīrti, that treasure of renown, son of Draupadī, the peer of Pārtha in battle.
Tawny horses bore into the fray the boy Abhimanyu, of whom men said that in combat he was half again the worth of Kṛṣṇa and of Pārtha.
And Yuyutsu, who alone of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons had taken refuge with the Pāṇḍavas, was borne into battle by tall, great-bodied steeds.
Spirited horses, finely adorned and the color of straw-stalks, bore the swift Vārdhakṣemi in that most tumultuous battle.
White-footed horses, their breastplates leaved with gold, obedient to the charioteer's command, bore the young Saucitti into battle.
Horses smooth as silk, their backs strewn with gold, garlanded in gold and gentle of temper, bore Śreṇimat.
Spirited horses of golden hue, finely adorned and wearing golden garlands, the finest of steeds, bore the praiseworthy king of Kāśi.
Ruddy horses bore on the advancing Satyadhṛti, a master to the very end of weapons, of the science of the bow, and of the Vedic lore of Brahman.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Horses dove-gray in color bore Dhṛṣṭadyumna, that commander of the Pāñcāla host, who had marked out Droṇa as his appointed share.
Him there followed Satyadhṛti, and Saucitti frenzied for the fight, and Śreṇimat, and Vasudāna, and the son of the king of Kāśi, O lord.
Drawn by swift, gold-garlanded steeds of the finest Kāmboja breed, they struck terror into the enemy host, peers of Yama and of Vaiśravaṇa.
And the Prabhadraka Pāñcālas, six thousand strong with weapons raised, their chariots and banners bright with gold, came on with the finest horses of many hues.
Their bows full-drawn, shaking the foe with showers of arrows, vowed to a common death, they followed Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Excellent horses the tawny color of silk, hung with garlands of choice gold, bore the unwearied-hearted Cekitāna.
Mounted on excellent, well-trained horses the color of Indra's bow, came Purujit Kuntibhoja, the maternal uncle of Savyasācin.
Horses the color of the sky, as though spangled with stars, bore King Rocamāna into the battle.
Excellent dappled horses with white feet, draped in netting of gold, bore Sahadeva, the son of Jarāsaṃdha.
Excellent dappled horses the color of the lotus-stalk, swift as hawks in speed, bore Sudāman.
Horses red as the hare, marked with pale streaks rising along their flanks, bore the Pāñcāla Siṃhasena, son of Gopati.
And he who was renowned among the Pāñcālas as Janamejaya, that tiger among men, had excellent horses the color of mustard-blossoms.
Swift, tall horses the color of beans, garlanded with gold, curd-white along the back and moon-faced, bore the Pāñcāla onward at speed.
And the brave and goodly horses, hued like reed-stalks and gleaming like the lotus-filament, bore Daṇḍadhāra.
Steeds wearing garlands of gold, their bellies ruddy as the cakravāka bird's, bore Sukṣatra, son of the lord of Kosala.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dappled horses, tall and stately, well-broken and decked with garlands of pure gold, bore in battle Satyadhṛti, son of Kṣema.
Banner, armor, horses, and bow all of one single hue and all white, Śukla turned and came on, white himself.
Sea-bred horses, white as the hare-marked moon, bore Candradeva, son of Samudrasena, fierce in his splendor as Rudra.
Horses the color of the blue lotus, adorned with refined gold and bright with garlands, bore into battle Citraratha of the Śaibyas.
Excellent horses the color of the pea-flower, streaked with white and red, bore Rathasena, frenzied for the fight.
And the king whom men called braver than all other men, that slayer of the Paṭaccaras, was borne by parrot-green horses.
Excellent horses the color of kiṃśuka-blossoms bore Citrāyudha — bright of garland, bright of armor, weapon, and banner.
Banner, armor, bow, and chariot-steeds all of one single hue and all blue, Nīla came on, blue himself.
With car-guards, banners, and bows of varied form bright with gems, with motley horse-pennons and standards, Citra came on, dappled himself.
Excellent horses the color of the lotus-leaf bore the golden-hued son of Rocamāna.
And warlike, well-formed horses, bred along the Śaradaṇḍā and the Anudaṇḍā, white-flanked and gleaming like hens' eggs, bore Daṇḍaketu.
Horses gleaming like the blossoms of the āṭarūṣaka bore fourteen myriads of the foremost chariot-warriors who followed the Pāṇḍyas.
Horses of varied hue, their faces of strange and varied form, bore the hero Ghaṭotkaca, whose banner bore the device of a chariot-wheel.
Gold-colored, the finest of steeds bore Yudhiṣṭhira, knower of dharma, best of kings, as he stood amid his host; and on every side, behind him, came the Prabhadrakas with their noble horses of high and low celestial hues.
Vigilant and arrayed with Bhīmasena, their golden banners aloft, they appeared, O lord of kings, like the dwellers of heaven with Indra at their head.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛṣṭadyumna outshone all those gathered warriors; yet over all the armies, the son of Bharadvāja shone more brilliantly still.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: These chariot-warriors, with Vṛkodara at their head, who wheeled back into the fray, could shake even the host of the gods in battle.
A man, it seems, is yoked fast to his fate; and within that fate alone are all his manifold ends seen to lie.
For a long span Yudhiṣṭhira dwelt exiled in the forest, his hair matted, clad in deerskin, and wandered unknown to the world.
That very man has now marshalled a mighty army for battle. What was this, if not the working of destiny, that has befallen my son?
Surely a man is born already bound to his lot, and is dragged along by it, not as he himself would wish.
Having fallen into the calamity of the dice, Yudhiṣṭhira was sorely afflicted; yet again, by his appointed fortune, he has gained allies.
Half the Kekayas have fallen to me, and the Kāśis, the Kosalas, the Cedis, and besides them the Vaṅgas have leaned upon me alone.
"Mine is the greater part of the earth, dear sire, not so the son of Pṛthā's" — thus, O sūta, did foolish Duryodhana speak to me then.
In the midst of that gathered host Droṇa was well guarded, yet he has been slain in the field by the son of Pṛṣata. What was this, if not the work of fate?
How did death come upon Droṇa — the mighty-armed, ever rejoicing in battle, master of every weapon — there in the very midst of kings?
Overtaken by anguish, I have sunk into utter bewilderment; hearing that both Bhīṣma and Droṇa are slain, I have no heart to live.
All that Vidura, seeing me greedy for my sons' sake, foretold to me, dear sire — all that, O sūta, has now come to pass for Duryodhana along with me.
Yet it would be the height of cruelty if, forsaking Duryodhana, I should seek to preserve my remaining sons; only hardship, and not death, would follow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the man who forsakes righteousness and becomes devoted to gain falls away from this world too, and sinks into baseness.
And now too, Saṃjaya, of this kingdom whose spirit is broken, I see no remnant left, its very hump crushed in.
How can anything remain when the two draught-bulls have passed away — those two forbearing bulls among men, upon whom we forever lived?
Tell me plainly how the battle unfolded: who fought, who drew back, and which base men fled in fear.
And tell me of Dhanaṃjaya, all that the bull among chariot-warriors did; for from him is our greatest fear, and from that foeman-cousin above all.
And when the Pāṇḍavas had wheeled about, Saṃjaya, how did the dreadful clash of what remained of my army come to be, and which of my heroes held off which foes there?
Saṃjaya said: A great terror seized us when the Pāṇḍavas had wheeled about, beholding Droṇa overspread by them as the sun by storm-clouds.
The fierce dust they raised wrapped your host in darkness, and when the line of sight was lost we believed Droṇa already slain.
But seeing those heroes, great archers bent on a cruel deed, Duryodhana swiftly urged on his own troops.
"To the utmost of your strength, your zeal, and your mettle, O kings, hold back as best you can the army of the Pāṇḍavas!"
Then your son Durmarṣaṇa, seeing Bhīma from afar, advanced upon him, scattering arrows, longing to preserve Droṇa's life.
Enraged, he covered Bhīma with shafts, like Death himself in battle; and Bhīma struck back at him with arrows, and a great tumult arose.
Those wise and valiant strikers, commanded by their lord, set aside all fear of death and stood firm against their foes in the fight.
Kṛtavarman, O lord of peoples, beset the grandson of Śini as he came on — that hero, ornament of the assembly, eager to reach Droṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The grandson of Śini, enraged, held off the enraged Kṛtavarman with showers of shafts, and Kṛtavarman held off the grandson of Śini, as one rutting elephant another.
The Saindhava, fierce of bow and a great archer, with effort held back from Droṇa the onrushing Kṣatradharman, that wielder of arrow-floods.
Kṣatradharman, having shorn away the banner and bow of the lord of the Sindhus, struck him in wrath with many iron shafts in all his vital parts.
Then, taking up another bow, the Saindhava, deft of hand, pierced Kṣatradharman in the field with shafts wholly of iron.
Subāhu, with effort, held off from Droṇa his own brother — the great chariot-warrior Yuyutsu, that hero who strove for the Pāṇḍavas' cause.
As Subāhu, mace-like of arm, loosed his arrows, Yuyutsu severed both his arms, bow and shaft and all, with two whetted, gold-bright razor-shafts.
The king of the Madras held back King Yudhiṣṭhira, best of the Pāṇḍavas, the righteous-souled, as a shore holds back the heaving sea.
The King of Righteousness covered him with many vital-piercing shafts, and the lord of the Madras, having pierced him with sixty-four arrows, roared aloud.
As the Madra king roared, the best of the Pāṇḍavas struck off his banner together with his bow by two razor-shafts, and at that the people raised a shout.
Even so King Bāhlika, with his own host, held off with his shafts King Drupada, who came charging on with his host.
Terrible grew the battle of those two aged kings with their armies, like that of two great herd-leading elephants, both in rut.
The two Avanti princes, Vinda and Anuvinda, with their troops, fell upon Virāṭa the Matsya king and his host, as of old Indra and Agni fell upon Bali.
A churning, confused fight arose, like that of gods and demons, between the Matsyas and the Kekayas, with horse and chariot and elephant unafraid.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhūtakarman, lord of the assembly, held back from Droṇa the son of Nakula, Śatānīka, as he came on loosing nets of arrows.
Then the heir of Nakula, with three keenly whetted broad-headed shafts, made Bhūtakarman armless and headless in the fray.
Viviṃśati held back the valiant Sutasoma, that hero, as he rushed on with floods of arrows, his face set toward Droṇa.
But Sutasoma, in great wrath, having pierced his own uncle Viviṃśati with straight-flying shafts, did not turn back, armoured as he was.
Then Bhīmaratha, with six swift, whetted iron shafts, sent Śālva, together with his horses and driver, to the abode of Yama.
Śrutakarman, who came on with peacock-hued horses, was held back, O great king, by the son of Citrasena, your grandson.
Those two unassailable grandsons of yours, each seeking the other's death, waged a surpassing combat for the sake of their fathers' cause.
Seeing Prativindhya standing before him in the field, the son of Droṇa, doing honour to his father, held him back with his arrows.
