In wrath Prativindhya pierced him back with whetted shafts — him whose ensign bore the lion's tail, who stood there for his father's sake.
As one scattering seed in the sowing-season, O bull among men, the son of Droṇa covered the son of Draupadī with showers of shafts.
He who was held the most valiant, O king, in both armies — that slayer of the Paṭaccaras — Lakṣmaṇa held back.
He, having severed Lakṣmaṇa's bow and his ensign, O Bhārata, loosing nets of arrows upon Lakṣmaṇa, shone forth exceedingly.
Vikarṇa, deeply wise, a youth himself, beset the young Śikhaṇḍin, son of Yajñasena, as he came on into the battle.
Then the son of Yajñasena enveloped him in a net of arrows; but your mighty son, shaking off that net of shafts, shone forth.
Aṅgada, turning to face the hero Uttamaujas in battle as he advanced toward Droṇa, held him back with calf-tooth shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That tumultuous clash of those two lions among men heightened the delight of all the soldiers, and of the two themselves as well.
And the mighty Durmukha, a great archer, held back the hero Purujit Kuntibhoja as he advanced toward Droṇa.
He struck Durmukha with an iron shaft between the brows, and that face of his shone like a lotus upon its stalk.
And Karṇa held back with showers of shafts the five Kekaya brothers, their banners crimson, as they advanced toward Droṇa.
And they, in great wrath, covered him with masses of shafts, and he in turn overspread them again and again with nets of arrows.
Neither Karṇa nor those five could be seen, so wrapped were they in arrows — horses, drivers, banners, and chariots all studded with one another's shafts.
Your sons Durjaya, Jaya, and Vijaya — those three heroes — held off in turn the three: Nīla, the Kāśi prince, and Jaya.
Terrible grew that battle, heightening the delight of those who watched, as of lions, tigers, and hyenas with elephants, buffaloes, and bulls.
The two brothers Kṣemadhūrti and Bṛhanta hewed at the Sātvata in the fight with sharp shafts as he advanced toward Droṇa.
The combat of those two and of him became wondrous indeed, like that of a lion with two lordly elephants in rut in the forest.
And the king of the Cedis, loosing his shafts in wrath, held off from Droṇa the king of the Ambaṣṭhas, who alone rejoiced in battle.
The Ambaṣṭha pierced him through with a bone-cleaving dart, and he, letting go bow and arrow, fell from his chariot to the ground.
Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat, no mean warrior, with small arrows held off from Droṇa the wrathful-seeming Vārdhakṣemi of the Vṛṣṇis.
Those who watched Kṛpa and the Vṛṣṇi fighting, brilliant in combat, became so engrossed in the battle that they marked no other doings.
The son of Somadatta beset King Maṇimat, the unwearied, as he came on, thus increasing Droṇa's glory.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He, swiftly cutting away the son of Somadatta's bow and banner, then cast down his pennon, his driver, and his parasol from the chariot.
Then the foe-slayer whose ensign was the sacrificial post, leaping swiftly from his chariot, cut him to pieces — horses, driver, banner, and car — with his excellent sword.
And mounting his own chariot, taking up another bow, himself reining his horses, O king, he shattered the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
With pestles, mallets, discs, slings, and battle-axes, with dust and wind and fire and water, with ashes, clods, grass, and trees —
breaking, crushing, shattering, slaying, scattering, and hurling, terrifying the host, Ghaṭotkaca came on, eager to reach Droṇa.
But the rākṣasa Alambusa, in wrath, fell upon that rākṣasa with weapons of every kind and every variety of war-craft.
The battle of those two foremost chiefs of the rākṣasas became such as once befell of old between Śambara and the king of the gods.
Thus there were hundreds of single combats of chariots, elephants, and horsemen — and of foot-soldiers too — a mêlée, blessings upon you, between your men and theirs.
Never before had such a battle been seen, nor even heard of, as the one that broke out among those who were caught up in the doubt of whether Droṇa lived or was no more.
"This is terrible, this is wondrous, this is fierce!"—so men cried, O lord, and there many a combat was seen, drawn out and beyond counting.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When those warriors had thus turned back and advanced again in their several divisions, how did the swift sons of Pṛthā and my own men do battle?
And what did Arjuna do against the host of the Saṃśaptakas, and what, Saṃjaya, did the Saṃśaptakas do against the son of Pṛthā?
Saṃjaya said: When they had thus turned back and advanced again in their several divisions, your son himself rushed upon Bhīma with a corps of elephants.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Bhīma, challenged by the king himself—as elephant meets elephant, as bull meets bull—charged that corps of elephants in turn.
That son of Pṛthā, skilled in war and endowed with the strength of his arms, shattered the corps of elephants in but a moment, O venerable one.
Those elephants, huge as hills, oozing rut on every side, were turned back by Bhīmasena's iron shafts and stripped of their frenzy.
As the wind scatters the masses of cloud on every side, so did the son of the Wind scatter those formations.
Loosing his arrows among those elephants, Bhīma shone like the risen sun casting its rays over all the worlds.
Pierced by Bhīma's arrows in their hundreds, those elephants shone like the varied clouds in the sky shot through by the rays of the sun.
As the son of the Wind wrought such havoc among the elephants, Duryodhana in fury drew near and struck him back with sharpened arrows.
Then in an instant Bhīma, his eyes red as blood and bent on the king's destruction, pierced that lord of earth with keen feathered shafts.
His every limb studded with arrows, Duryodhana in wrath pierced the Pāṇḍava in return, smiting Bhīmasena with iron shafts bright as the sun's rays, and smiling the while.
With two broad-headed shafts the Pāṇḍava swiftly cut away the jewelled elephant, gleaming with gems, that stood upon his banner, and his bow as well.
Seeing Duryodhana hard pressed by Bhīma, O venerable one, the king of the Aṅgas, mounted upon an elephant, came on, eager to throw Bhīma into confusion.
As that elephant, with a trumpeting like the roar of a raincloud, came rushing on, Bhīmasena struck it hard between its frontal lobes with an iron shaft.
Piercing through its body, the shaft sank into the earth, and the elephant fell like a mountain struck by the thunderbolt.
And as that barbarian, his elephant toppling, was himself about to fall, swift-handed Vṛkodara severed his head with a broad-headed shaft.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When that hero had fallen, that host broke and fled, its horses, elephants, and chariots in panic, trampling down its own foot-soldiers.
And while all those formations were fleeing on every side, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa then charged Bhīma upon his elephant.
That foremost of elephants—the very one on which Maghavan had conquered the Daityas and Dānavas—now rushed of a sudden upon Bhīma.
With its ears, its feet, and its coiled trunk, eyes rolling and enraged, it seemed as if it would burn the Pāṇḍava to ash.
Then there arose a mighty cry from the whole army: "Alas, alas! Bhīma is slain by the elephant!"—so it ran, O venerable one.
Alarmed by that cry, O king, the host of the Pāṇḍavas rushed of a sudden to where Vṛkodara stood.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, believing Vṛkodara slain, together with the Pāñcālas hemmed in Bhagadatta on every side.
Surrounding him on all sides with their chariots, those foremost of chariot-warriors showered him with sharp arrows by the hundred and by the thousand.
Warding off those shafts with his goad, the lord of the mountain land scattered the Pāṇḍus and Pāñcālas with his elephant.
A marvel we beheld in that battle, O lord of peoples—such was the feat of the aged Bhagadatta with his elephant.
Then the king of the Daśārṇas charged the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa with his elephant—a rutting beast, swift-moving, advancing aslant.
A battle arose between those two elephants of terrible form, as of old between two winged mountains clad with trees.
The elephant of the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, closing in and then wheeling about, pierced the elephant of the lord of the Daśārṇas in the flank and brought it down.
Then with seven lances bright as the sun's rays, Bhagadatta struck down that foe upon his elephant, shaken now from his seat.
But Yudhiṣṭhira, drawing near to King Bhagadatta, encircled him on every side with a great corps of chariots.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Mounted on his elephant and ringed about on all sides by chariot-warriors, he shone like a blazing fire set amid the forest upon a mountain.
That elephant wheeled within the close-knit ring of fierce-bowed chariot-warriors as they poured down their showers of arrows.
Then the king of Prāgjyotiṣa, gathering up that bull among elephants, sent it of a sudden against the chariot of Yuyudhāna.
Seizing the chariot of the grandson of Śini, the great elephant hurled it away with force; but Yuyudhāna leaped clear.
His charioteer, raising up the great Saindhava horses, reached Sātyaki, and leaping aboard once more, stood firm with him in the chariot again.
That elephant, having found its opening, swiftly broke forth from the ring of chariots and then flung down all the kings about it.
Terrified by that swift-moving beast, those bulls among men, those hundreds of kings, deemed that one elephant in the battle to be a hundred.
The Pāṇḍavas were driven before Bhagadatta upon his elephant, as the Dānavas before the king of the gods mounted on Airāvata.
As the Pāñcālas fled hither and thither before him, a tremendous din arose, made by elephants and horses.
As the Pāṇḍus were driven before Bhagadatta in the battle, Bhīma in fury charged the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa once again.
As Bhīma charged, the elephant drenched his horses with water flung from its trunk and frighted them, and so they bore the son of Pṛthā away.
Then the son of Ruciparvan, like unto Death and standing upon his chariot, charged the elephant swiftly, drenching it with a shower of arrows.
Then with a smooth-jointed arrow the lord of the mountain Suparvan sent Ruciraparvan to the abode of the son of the Sun, Yama.
When that hero had fallen, the son of Subhadrā, the sons of Draupadī, Cekitāna, Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Yuyutsu fell upon the elephant and harried it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They drenched it with streams of arrows, as raincloud's drench with downpours, roaring terrible cries and bent upon its slaughter.
Then, urged on by the skilled driver with heel and goad and thumb, the elephant, trunk outstretched, ears and eyes rigid, charged swiftly forward.
Treading down the horses of Yuyutsu with its feet, it crushed his charioteer; but your son, in confusion, sprang onto the chariot of Subhadrā's son.
That king, mounted on his elephant and loosing his shafts among his foes, shone like the sun casting his rays across the worlds.
Arjuna's son pierced him with twelve arrows, Yuyutsu with ten, and the sons of Draupadī and Dhṛṣṭaketu each with three.
That elephant, studded with the arrows driven home by his foes' striving, shone like a great cloud shot through by the rays of the sun.
Driven by the skill and effort of its master, though tormented by the foes' arrows, that elephant flung down those enemies to left and right.
As a herdsman with his staff drives the herds of beasts together in the forest, so did Bhagadatta hem in that army again and again.
Swift as the clamor of crows fallen upon by a hawk was the clamor of the Pāṇḍavas as they fled in utter rout.
That king of elephants, struck by the foremost of goads, was like a winged mountain of old, O king; and it sowed deep terror among the foes, as the storm-tossed ocean among bands of merchants.
Then a most fearful din, raised by elephants, chariots, horses, and kings fleeing in terror, filled the earth, the air, the heavens, and all the quarters and their bounds, O lord, in that battle.
With that foremost of elephants, the king plunged deep into the host of his foes, as of old Virocana into the well-guarded army of the gods in battle, defended though it was by the wise ones.
The friend of fire, the wind, blew strongly, and the dust shrouded the sky and again and again the soldiers; and men deemed that one elephant to be a whole troop of elephants charging swiftly on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Since you ask me of the deeds of the son of Pṛthā in the battle, hear now, O great king, what Pārtha did in the fray.
Seeing the dust risen up and hearing the trumpeting of the elephant as his men were broken by Bhagadatta, the son of Kuntī spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"By the way the king of Prāgjyotiṣa has pressed swiftly forward with his elephant, O slayer of Madhu, this surely is the sound of that beast."
"In battle he is not inferior to Indra, and skilled in elephant-craft; first upon the earth, or second—such is my judgment of him."
"And that finest of elephants, never matched by any rival elephant in war, unshaken by every sound in battle, proven in its deeds and tireless—"
"—able to endure the fall of weapons and the touch of fire, O sinless one, that beast alone will plainly destroy the Pāṇḍava host this very day."
"And save we two there is no other able to withstand it; therefore make haste and drive to where the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa is."
"Proud through his friendship with Śakra, through the strength of his elephants, and through his years—him will I send this day, a welcome guest, to the slayer of Bala."
Then at the word of Savyasācin, Kṛṣṇa drove on to where the Pāṇḍava army was being rent apart by Bhagadatta.
As he set forth, the Saṃśaptakas, those great chariot-warriors, fourteen thousand strong, came up behind, calling him to combat.
Ten thousand of them were Trigartas, O lord of men, and four thousand were those who followed Vāsudeva.
Seeing his army being rent apart by Bhagadatta, O venerable one, and being challenged by the Saṃśaptakas, Arjuna's heart was torn in two.
Pondering which course would prove the more profitable—"Shall I turn back from here, or shall I go on to Yudhiṣṭhira?"—
weighing this in his mind, O foremost of the Kurus, Arjuna's stronger resolve settled firm upon the slaying of the Saṃśaptakas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whose banner bore the foremost of apes turned suddenly back, the son of Vāsava, alone, to slay thousands of chariots in the fray.
For such was the design of both Duryodhana and Karṇa, contrived as a means to Arjuna's slaying; by it they had wrought this division.
But the Pāṇḍava turned that very division back upon them, and with his single chariot he made the design of those foremost of chariot-warriors come to nothing.
Then, O king, the great chariot-warriors among the Saṃśaptakas loosed hundreds of thousands of smooth-jointed arrows upon Arjuna.
Then, O king, neither Pārtha the son of Kuntī, nor Kṛṣṇa Janārdana, nor the horses, nor the chariot could be seen, so thickly were they covered with arrows.
When Janārdana himself had fallen into a daze and was bathed in sweat, then Pārtha slew the most of them with the weapon of the thunderbolt.
By the hundreds their hands were severed, still gripping arrows, bowstrings, hand-guards and bows; standards, horses, charioteers, and warriors fell to the earth.
Like trees, like mountain peaks, like rain-clouds in form, the well-caparisoned elephants, their riders slain, fell to the ground, struck down by Pārtha's shafts.
Their saddle-cloths and reins flung apart, their trappings cut, their lives gone, the horses fell with their riders, mangled by Pārtha's arrows.
Sundered by the Diademed One's broad-headed shafts, the arms of men fell to earth still holding spears, shields, swords, nails, maces, and battle-axes.
O lord, heads like the rising sun, like lotuses, like the moon in their beauty, severed by Arjuna's arrows, came to rest upon the earth.
When the wrathful Phalguna struck down his foes, the host blazed with his ornamented, life-devouring, many-marked feathered shafts.
As Dhanaṃjaya churned the army like an elephant churning a lotus-pond, the hosts of spirits honored him, crying "Well done! Well done!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing that deed of Pārtha's, worthy of Vāsava himself, Mādhava fell into the utmost wonder and, clapping his hand, paid him homage.
Then, having slain most of the Saṃśaptakas who had stood their ground, Pārtha urged Kṛṣṇa on, saying, "Drive toward Bhagadatta."
Saṃjaya said: As Pārtha wished to set out, Kṛṣṇa then urged on his white steeds, swift as thought and decked in gold, toward Droṇa's array.
As that best of the Kurus set forth to save his own folk, who were sorely pressed by Droṇa, Suśarman, eager for battle, followed at his back together with his brothers.
Then he of the white horses, the unvanquished victor, said to Kṛṣṇa: "O Acyuta, here is Suśarman, with his brothers, challenging me."
"And in the north there our host is being rent asunder, O slayer of foes; today these Saṃśaptakas have made my mind divided in two."
"Shall I slay the Saṃśaptakas, or shall I guard my own who are afflicted by the foe? You know my thought in this — which course would be the right one?"
Thus addressed, the Dāśārha turned the chariot back to where the lord of the Trigartas was summoning the son of Pāṇḍu.
Then Arjuna, having pierced Suśarman with seven swift arrows, cut down his standard and his bow with two razor-edged shafts.
And the brother of the Trigarta lord, together with his horses and his charioteer, Pārtha swiftly dispatched to Yama's abode with six iron shafts.
Then Suśarman hurled at Arjuna an iron lance resembling a serpent, and at Vāsudeva a javelin.
Arjuna cut the lance apart with three arrows and the javelin with three, and having stunned Suśarman with a volley of shafts, he turned away.
O king, as he advanced like Vāsava, pouring forth a flooding rain of arrows, not one fierce warrior of your host could stay him.
Then Dhanaṃjaya pressed forward, slaying the great car-warriors of the Kurus with his arrows, as a fire consumes dry brushwood.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The irresistible onslaught of that wise son of Kuntī they could no more endure than living creatures can endure the touch of fire.
Enveloping the ranks with a downpour of arrows, the son of Pāṇḍu, O king, swept on toward the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa with the swoop of Suparṇa.
That bow which the victorious Jiṣṇu now drew — a bringer of safety in battle to the fleeing Bhāratas, and a multiplier of the tears of foes —
that very bow, O king, did Arjuna bend for the destruction of the warrior class, all on account of your son, that gambler at the wicked dice.
Thus shaken by Pārtha, your army was rent asunder, great king, like a boat that has struck against a mountain.
Then ten thousand bowmen turned back, heroes resolved in their wrath upon either victory or defeat in the fight.
His heart free of fear, that car-warrior — who in the law of dire need surpassed all others — Pārtha, who could bear every burden, took upon himself a heavy load in the battle.
As a rutting elephant of sixty years in its fury would trample a thicket of reeds, so did Pārtha, straining at his utmost, trample your host.
When that army had been thus crushed, King Bhagadatta on that elephant rushed all at once upon Dhanaṃjaya.
That tiger among men received him fearlessly with his chariot, and tumultuous was the clash between the car and the elephant.
Each equipped according to the rules of warfare — the one with his chariot, the other with his elephant — the two heroes, Bhagadatta and Dhanaṃjaya, ranged about in the battle.
Then, from his elephant huge as a thundercloud, Bhagadatta, overpowering like Indra, rained a flood of arrows upon Dhanaṃjaya.
But the valiant son of Vāsava cut apart with his own rain of arrows that shower of Bhagadatta's shafts even before it could reach him.
Then the king of Prāgjyotiṣa, having warded off that downpour of arrows, struck the mighty-armed Pārtha and Kṛṣṇa with his shafts, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, having covered them both with a vast net of arrows, he goaded that elephant on to slay Acyuta and Pārtha.
Seeing that elephant bearing down upon them like wrathful Death itself, Janārdana swiftly wheeled the chariot to keep it on the left.
Though the great elephant had now wheeled close, Dhanaṃjaya, mindful of righteousness, did not wish to consign it and its rider to death.
But that elephant, O lord, crushing other elephants, chariots, and horses, dispatched them to the realm of death; thereupon Dhanaṃjaya grew wrathful.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Thus angered, what did the son of Pāṇḍu do to Bhagadatta, or the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa to Pārtha? Tell me that exactly as it befell.
Saṃjaya said: When both the Dāśārha and the son of Pāṇḍu were locked in struggle with the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, all creatures believed them brought near to death.
For indeed, O lord, Bhagadatta poured down unceasing showers of arrows from his elephant's shoulders upon the two Kṛṣṇas as they stood upon the chariot.
Then with shafts of black iron, gold-feathered and whetted on stone, loosed from a fully drawn bow, he pierced the son of Devakī.
Sharp as the touch of fire, those arrows, driven by Bhagadatta, pierced through the son of Devakī and then sank into the ground.
Pārtha cut his bow, struck down his quiver, and fought King Bhagadatta as though toying with him.
He hurled fourteen sharp javelins, bright as the rays of the sun; and Savyasācin cut each of them into three.
Then the son of the Chastiser of Pāka tore away the elephant's armor with a net of arrows, so that it shone like a cloudless king of mountains.
Then the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa hurled at Vāsudeva an iron lance with a golden shaft, and Arjuna cut it in two.
Then, having cut down the king's parasol and standard with his arrows, Arjuna swiftly pierced the lord of the mountains with ten shafts, smiling the while.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Deeply pierced by Arjuna's well-feathered shafts winged with heron-plumes, Bhagadatta then, full of wrath against the great-souled son of Pāṇḍu,
hurled javelins at the head of him whose steeds were white, and roared aloud; and by them Arjuna's diadem was knocked askew in the battle.
Setting his displaced diadem aright, Phalguna said to the king, "Take now a good last look at the world."
Thus addressed, he in great wrath took up his shining bow and rained arrows upon the son of Pāṇḍu together with Govinda.
Pārtha cut his bow, shattered his quivers, and in haste smote him in all his vital parts with seventy-two arrows.
Though so pierced, undismayed, he summoned forth the Vaiṣṇava weapon and, having charged his elephant-goad with mantras, in fury flung it at the breast of the son of Pāṇḍu.
That all-destroying weapon loosed by Bhagadatta, Keśava received upon his own breast, shielding Pārtha.
Upon Keśava's breast that weapon became a garland of victory; then Arjuna, troubled in mind, said to Keśava:
"I am the driver of the horses, taking no part in the fight — so you said, O Janārdana; yet, lotus-eyed one, you do not keep your own vow."
"Were I in distress, or unable to ward it off, then such a deed would fall to you; but it ought not to be done while I stand firm."
"With my arrows and my bow I am able to conquer these worlds with their gods, demons, and men — and this too is known to you."
Then Vāsudeva answered Arjuna with words full of meaning: "Hear this secret, O sinless Pārtha, even as it came to pass of old."
"In four forms am I forever exerted for the protection of the worlds; dividing myself here, I take up the welfare of the worlds."
"One of my forms, abiding on earth, performs austerities; another beholds the world doing its deeds, good and evil."
"Another, dwelling in the world of men, performs action; and a fourth lies asleep in a slumber of a thousand years."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That form of mine which rises at the close of the thousand years bestows at that time the choicest boons upon those worthy of boons."
"Knowing that time was come, the Earth then begged of me a boon for the sake of Naraka — hear what it was."
"'Let my son be unslayable by gods and demons alike, endowed with the Vaiṣṇava weapon — this you ought to grant me.'"
"Hearing that prayer for a boon, I then, of old, gave to the son of the Earth that unfailing Vaiṣṇava weapon."
"And I declared: 'Let this weapon be unfailing and able to bear all; for the protection of Naraka, none shall be able to slay him.'"
"'Guarded by this weapon, your son, the crusher of hostile hosts, shall be unassailable in all the worlds for all time.'"
"Saying 'So be it,' the noble-minded goddess departed, her wish fulfilled; and so Naraka, the tormentor of foes, became unassailable."
"From him this weapon of mine has come down to the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, O Pārtha; in the worlds, even with Indra and Rudra, none is beyond its slaying, O lord."
"For your sake I have made it null, disarming it of its supreme power; now, Pārtha, slay that great demon."
"Slay the foe, hard to vanquish in battle, Bhagadatta, the hater of the gods, even as I formerly slew Naraka for the good of all."
Thus addressed by the great-souled Keśava, Pārtha then suddenly covered Bhagadatta over with his sharp arrows.
Then the mighty-armed Pārtha, unflurried and high of heart, struck the elephant between its two frontal globes with an iron shaft.
Reaching that elephant, the arrow, like a thunderbolt striking a mountain, sank in up to its feathers, as a serpent enters an anthill.
And that great elephant, bracing its limbs, sank to the earth upon its tusks, and crying out in a voice of anguish, gave up its life.
Then with a straight-jointed arrow shaped like the half-moon's disc, the son of Pāṇḍu pierced the heart of King Bhagadatta.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
King Bhagadatta, his heart pierced through by the Diademed One, let fall his bow and his arrows even as the life went out of him.
From his head the fine elephant-goad slipped loose and fell, as a petal falls from a lotus when the stalk is struck.
Garlanded in gold, he fell from the mountain-like elephant with its gilded trappings, like a karṇikāra tree in full blossom snapped by the rushing wind from the summit of a hill.
Having slain in battle that lord of men, valorous as Indra and Indra's own friend, the son of Indra then broke the rest of your warriors who longed for victory, as a mighty wind shatters the trees.
Saṃjaya said: Having slain the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa, the ever-dear friend of Indra and a man of measureless might, Pārtha circled him reverently to the right.
Then the two sons of the king of Gāndhāra, conquerors of hostile cities, the brothers Vṛṣaka and Acala, came upon Arjuna in the fray.
The two heroic bowmen, closing upon Arjuna from before and from behind, pierced him sorely with swift, sharp, fast-flying shafts.
With his keen arrows Pārtha shredded to bits the horses, the charioteer, the bow, the parasol, the car, and the banner of Vṛṣaka, son of Subala.
Then with floods of arrows and weapons of many kinds Arjuna once more threw into confusion the Gāndhāras led by the son of Subala.
Then in his wrath Dhanaṃjaya sped five hundred heroic Gāndhāras, their weapons upraised, with his shafts to the realm of Death.
Quickly leaping down from his car whose horses were slain, the mighty-armed one mounted his brother's chariot and took up another bow.
The two brothers Vṛṣaka and Acala, mounted now on a single car, pierced Bībhatsu again and again with a rain of arrows.
Your two great-souled brothers-in-law, the kings Vṛṣaka and Acala, smote Pārtha grievously, as the hosts of Vṛtra once smote Indra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The two Gāndhāras, sure of their aim, struck the Pāṇḍava once more, as the months of summer and the rains drench the world with heat and water.
Those tigers among men, the kings Vṛṣaka and Acala, standing upon the car with bodies close pressed together, O king, Arjuna slew with a single arrow.
Lion-like, red-eyed, mighty-armed, those two heroes—born of one mother and alike in every mark—fell lifeless from the car.
The bodies of those two, beloved of their kinsmen, went from the car to the earth, having sent their holy fame abroad to the ten directions, where it stood fast.
Seeing their uncles, who never fled, slain in the fight, your sons, O lord of peoples, shed tears in plenty.
Seeing his brothers slain, Śakuni, skilled in a hundred sorceries, then wove an illusion to bewilder the two Kṛṣṇas.
Cudgels, iron balls, stones, and śataghnīs together with javelins; maces, iron bars, swords, spears, hammers, and battle-axes—
lances, double-edged blades, and clawed weapons, pestles and broad-axes, razors and razor-edged tubular darts, calf-tooth shafts and three-jointed missiles,
discs, barbed arrows, and pikes, and weapons of every kind, fell upon Arjuna from all the quarters and the points between.
Asses, camels, and buffaloes, lions, tigers, and antelopes and hawks, bears, wolves, and vultures, apes, and creeping serpents,
and demons of many kinds, ravenous and enraged, rushed against Arjuna, together with birds of every sort.
Then the valiant son of Kuntī, Dhanaṃjaya, knower of celestial weapons, loosing nets of arrows, struck them all down at once.
Smitten by the hero with his choicest, sturdy shafts, they shrieked with mighty cries and perished, slain on every side.
Then a darkness arose before Arjuna's car, and out of that darkness cruel voices reviled Pārtha.
That darkness Arjuna slew with the great weapon of light; and when it was destroyed, terrible floods of water appeared.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
To destroy that water Arjuna then employed the weapon of the Sun, and by it the flood was for the most part dried away.
Thus the manifold illusions wrought again and again by the son of Subala, Arjuna, laughing, swiftly destroyed by the power of his weapons.
When his illusions were thus undone, Śakuni, struck by Arjuna's shafts and seized with terror, fled away on his swift horses like a common man.
Then Arjuna, displaying among his foes the supremacy of his skill in weapons, rained down a flood of arrows upon the host of the Kauravas.
That army of your son, smitten by Pārtha, split in two, O great king, like the Gaṅgā when she meets a mountain.
Some of the great car-warriors there made their way to Droṇa, and some, O king, sore pressed by the Diademed One, to Duryodhana.
After that we could not see that host, veiled as it was in darkness; but the twang of the Gāṇḍīva I heard upon the right.
The blare of conches and kettledrums and the sound of the instruments—the twang of the Gāṇḍīva overtopped them all and touched the heavens.
Then again on the right was the battle of those who fight in wondrous fashion; well fought was Arjuna's contest, but I followed after Droṇa.
The hosts of your sons, of many kinds, O Bhārata, Arjuna scattered, as in due season the wind scatters the clouds in the sky.
As he came on like Vāsava, pouring down great floods of arrows, that mighty bowman, that tiger among men—none could stay him.
Your men, smitten by Pārtha and grievously distressed, many of them in their flight hither and thither slew their own comrades.
The arrows loosed by Arjuna, heron-feathered and rending the body, fell like locusts, covering the ten directions.
Piercing through horse and car-warrior, elephant and foot-soldier alike, O sire, they entered the earth like serpents entering an anthill.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Not a second arrow did he loose against elephant, horse, or man; each, struck by a single shaft, fell down bereft of life.
With slain men and horses everywhere, and elephants struck down beneath the rain of arrows, the field of battle, loud with the cries of dogs and jackals and crows, became a strange and dreadful sight.
The father forsook the son, the friend his dearest friend, and the son likewise forsook his father, tormented by the arrows; bent now only upon saving themselves, men harried by Pārtha abandoned even their mounts.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When those hosts were broken by the son of Pāṇḍu, O Saṃjaya, what was the temper of your minds as you wavered and took to flight?
Hard is it to rally hosts once shattered, when men can see no place to make their stand; tell me of that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Even so, O lord of peoples, seeking your son's good, those heroes, guarding their fame throughout the worlds, followed after Droṇa.
With weapons upraised, and Yudhiṣṭhira drawing near, in that fearful hour they wrought the deeds of noble men, like those who fear to break their word.
They sought to find an opening upon Bhīmasena of measureless might, and upon the valiant Sātyaki, and upon Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O lord.
"Droṇa! Droṇa!" the fierce Pāñcālas urged one another on; "Not Droṇa!" your sons cried, rousing all the Kurus.
"Droṇa! Droṇa!" cried the one side, "Not Droṇa!" the other; between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas a gambling-match for Droṇa was being played.
Whatever band of Pāñcāla cars Droṇa fell upon, there at once the Pāñcāla prince Dhṛṣṭadyumna was set against him.
As the appointed ranks were thrown into confusion in that terrible battle, hero closed with hero, and the cowards went against the foe.
There the Pāṇḍavas stood unshaken by their enemies, and they shook the hostile hosts, remembering their own afflictions.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yielding to wrath, full of self-respect and driven by their courage, they turned back ready to give up their lives, striving to slay Droṇa in that great battle.
It was like the clash of iron, like the crash of stones, as those men of boundless splendour gambled with their very lives in the tumultuous fight.
Not even the aged could recall a battle of such a kind, O great king, ever before seen or ever before heard.
The earth seemed to tremble in that destruction of heroes, weighed down and oppressed by the great flood of armies surging upon her.
From the reeling flood of warriors a roar arose, of the wrathful Ajātaśatru and of your son, as though it filled and stilled the very sky.
As Droṇa ranged through the battle, the hosts of the Pāṇḍavas, met by him in their thousands, were broken by his keen arrows.
As they were being crushed by Droṇa of wondrous deeds, the commander himself drew near and beset Droṇa on every side.
Wondrous then was the combat of Droṇa and the Pāñcāla prince; to it, I think, no comparison could be found.
Then Nīla, bright as fire, burned the Kuru army, his arrows for sparks and his bow for flame, like a fire consuming dry grass.
As he burned the hosts, the valorous son of Droṇa, speaking first and very smoothly, smiling, addressed him:
"Nīla, what use are the many warriors you have burned with your flaming shafts? Fight with me alone; in your wrath, strike at me with your swift arrows."
Him, who had the hue of a cluster of lotuses, whose eyes were like lotus-petals, whose face shone like a full-blown lotus, Nīla pierced with his shafts.
Sorely pierced by him, the son of Droṇa straightway, with three sharp broad-headed shafts, cut down his enemy's bow and banner and parasol.
Leaping down from his car, Nīla, bearing fine shield and sword, sought to take the head from the body of the son of Droṇa, swift as a bird.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As his sword was upraised, the son of Droṇa, smiling as it were, O sinless one, struck off with a broad-headed shaft that fair-nosed head with its earrings from the body.
His face bright as the full moon, his eyes like lotus-petals, tall and of the hue of a lotus's inner bloom, he fell slain to the earth.
Then the Pāṇḍava army was sorely shaken and thrown into confusion, when Nīla of blazing splendour was slain by the teacher's son.
And all the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas thought to themselves, O sire: "How shall the son of Vāsava deliver us from our foes?"
Meanwhile, on the right of the army, the mighty one was making havoc of what remained of the Saṃśaptakas and of the Nārāyaṇa host.
Saṃjaya said: But Vṛkodara could not endure this check to the host; he pierced Bāhlika with sixty shafts and Karṇa with ten.
At him Droṇa, with keen iron arrows of sharp edge, seeking to end his life, swiftly struck at his vital parts.
Karṇa with twelve arrows, Aśvatthāman with seven, and King Duryodhana with six then covered him over.
Bhīmasena too, of great might, pierced them all in return: Droṇa with fifty arrows, Karṇa with ten,
Duryodhana with twelve, and the son of Droṇa with eight swift shafts; raising a tumultuous roar, he bore down upon them in the fight.
As he, ready to give up his life, was bringing it level with death itself, Ajātaśatru urged on his warriors, crying, "Save Bhīma!"
Then those warriors of boundless might—Yuyudhāna and the rest, together with the two sons of Mādrī—drew near to Bhīmasena.
United and roused to fury, those bulls among men joined forces, eager to break through Droṇa's host, which was guarded by the foremost of great archers.
On rushed those car-warriors of mighty valour, Bhīma at their head; and Droṇa too, the best of chariot-fighters, received them undismayed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Casting all fear of death aside, your warriors advanced upon those Pāṇḍava heroes—mighty, surpassing car-warriors, splendid in battle.
Horseman struck down horseman, and likewise car-warrior smote car-warrior; there was a clashing of lances and swords, and the battle raged with battle-axes.
A close and bitter sword-fight broke out, fierce in its issue; and through the colliding masses of elephants the combat grew exceedingly terrible.
One man fell headlong from an elephant, another from a horse, and another, pierced through by an arrow, dropped from his chariot, O lord.
And there, in the crush, an elephant trod upon the breast of another man who had fallen, his armour stripped away, and crushed his head to pieces.
Other elephants slew other men who had fallen, and driving their tusks into the earth, ripped open many a car-warrior.
Elephants by the hundred roamed about, their tusks clotted and dripping with men's entrails, trampling men by the hundred.
The elephants ground down fallen men, horses, chariots, and elephants, clad in armour of bronze and iron, as though they were thick reeds.
Proud lords of men, ripened now by Time, lay down in anguish upon their beds—those couches haunted by vultures' wings.
There a father slew his son and drove his chariot over him, and a son in his bewilderment slew his father—all bounds were overthrown.
An axle was shattered, a banner cut down, a parasol flung to the earth; and a horse, dragging half a severed yoke, bolted away.
An arm fell, still grasping its sword; a severed head dropped with its earrings; and a mighty elephant, seizing a chariot, dashed it to splinters upon the ground.
An elephant, struck by a car-warrior's iron shaft, fell down lifeless; and a horse with its rider, smitten hard by an elephant, fell as well.
A great and most terrible battle raged on, with no bounds left: "Alas, father! Alas, my son! Friend, where are you? Stand! Whither do you flee?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Strike! Strike! Slay this one!"—with laughter and shouts and roaring, such varied cries were heard ringing forth.
The blood of man, of horse, and of elephant ran together and mingled; the dust of the earth was laid, and faintness came over the timid.
There was tearing of hair and a savage fight with fists, and combat with nails and teeth among warriors who, weaponless, sought weapons where there were none.
There one hero's upraised arm was severed, sword and all; and another's likewise, holding bow and arrow and goad together.
Here one man shouted at another, while another turned his back and fled; and one struck the head from the body of another who had come within his reach.
One charged toward a sound, while another fled hard away from a sound; one slew his own men, and another the foe, with whetted arrows.
There an elephant like a mountain-peak, struck down by an iron shaft, fell upon the earth like a riverbank crumbling in the hot season.
Likewise an elephant, like a streaming mountain, crushed a car-warrior, and pinned him to the ground beneath its foot, together with his horses and his charioteer.
At the sight of those many warriors, skilled in arms and bathed in blood, smiting on, a stupor seized the timid and faint of heart.
All became confusion; nothing could be discerned; and when the army was blotted out by dust, every bound was overthrown.
Then the commander, crying swiftly "Now is the hour!", urged on the Pāṇḍavas, ever eager though they already were.
Obeying his command, the glorious Pāṇḍava warriors swept down upon Droṇa's chariot, slaying as they came, like wild geese descending upon a lake.
"Seize them! Charge them! Cut them down without fear!"—such was the tumultuous din that rose about the chariot of the indomitable one.
Then Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, Droṇa's son, the king, Jayadratha, the two Avanti princes Vinda and Anuvinda, and Śalya held them back.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the Pāñcālas, with the Pāṇḍavas—fired by the duty of the noble, irresistible, hard to assail—though sore wounded by arrows, would not abandon their assault on Droṇa.
Then Droṇa, transported with fury, loosing arrows by the hundred, wrought a great slaughter among the Cedis, the Pāñcālas, and the Pāṇḍavas.
The din of his bowstring and palm-guard, O lord, was heard in every quarter, like the crash of a thunderbolt, terrifying many of the Pāṇḍavas.
In that interval the mighty Jiṣṇu, having slain the Saṃśaptakas, hastened to the place where Droṇa was crushing the Pāṇḍavas.
Having crossed that great lake whose whirlpools were floods of arrows and whose waters were blood, and having slain the Saṃśaptakas, Phalguna came into view.
We beheld the emblem of that glorious one, splendid as the sun—his ape-bannered standard blazing with radiance.
Having dried up that ocean of the Saṃśaptakas with the beams of his weapons, that Pāṇḍava—a sun of the world's ending—scorched the Kurus as well.
Arjuna consumed all the Kurus with the blaze of his weapons, as the fire of doom, risen at the end of the age, consumes all beings.
Smitten by him with floods of arrows in their thousands, the warriors on elephants, horses, and chariots, their weapons dropping from their hands and tormented by his shafts, sank to the earth.
Some raised cries of anguish, others shrieked aloud, and some, struck down by Pārtha's arrows, fell lifeless.
Mindful of a warrior's vow, Arjuna did not slay those among them who fled, or who had fallen, or who turned their backs.
Their chariots, horses, and elephants shattered, the Kurus, mostly turned to flight, cried out "Karṇa! Karṇa!" and "Alas! Alas!"
Hearing that cry of the men who sought refuge, the son of Adhiratha answered, "Fear not!", and advanced to meet Arjuna face to face.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That best of Bhārata car-warriors, the delight of all the Bhāratas, foremost of those who knew weapons, brought forth the fiery Āgneya weapon.
Against him, blazing with floods of arrows and wielding a flaming bow, Dhanaṃjaya scattered those streams of shafts with a net of his own; and warding off weapon with weapon, he roared aloud as he loosed his arrows.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Bhīma and the great car-warrior Sātyaki closed upon Karṇa and pierced him, each with three straight-flying shafts.
But the son of Rādhā, warding off Arjuna's weapon with showers of arrows, cut asunder the bows of those three with three keen shafts.
Their weapons cut away, those heroes—like serpents drained of venom—snatched up the lances of their chariots and roared aloud like lions.
Hurled with great force from the tips of their arms, those mighty lances, blazing and serpent-like, sped toward the son of Adhiratha.
Cutting them down, each with three sharp straight-flying arrows, the mighty Karṇa roared and loosed his shafts at Pārtha.
And Arjuna too, having pierced the son of Rādhā with seven swift shafts, slew Karṇa's younger brother with three whetted arrows.
Then, having slain Śatruṃjaya with six straight shafts, Pārtha straightway swept the head of Vipāṭa from his chariot with a broad-headed arrow.
Before the very eyes of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, and in the presence of the charioteer's son, the Diademed One alone slew three brothers.
Then Bhīma, springing from his own chariot like the son of Vinatā, slew fifteen of Karṇa's followers with his excellent sword.
Mounting his chariot again and taking up another bow, he pierced Karṇa with ten arrows, and his charioteer and horses with five.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna too, taking up an excellent sword and a gleaming shield, slew Candravarman and Bṛhatkṣatra of the Paurava line.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then mounting his chariot and taking up another bow, the Pāñcāla prince pierced Karṇa with seventy-three arrows, roaring in the battle.
The grandson of Śini too, taking up another bow that shone like Indra's rainbow, pierced the charioteer's son with sixty-four shafts and roared like a lion.
With two well-aimed broad-headed shafts he cut Karṇa's bow asunder, and again drove three arrows into Karṇa's arms and breast.
Then Duryodhana and Droṇa, and King Jayadratha as well, drew up the son of Rādhā, who was sinking, from the ocean that was Sātyaki.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Bhīma, Subhadrā's son and Arjuna himself, Nakula and Sahadeva, guarded Sātyaki in the battle.
Thus did this most fearful battle rage on, for the destruction of all the bowmen—of your men and of the foe alike—who flung their very lives away.
With footmen, chariots, elephants, and horses—elephants, horses, chariots, and footmen; car-warriors with elephants, footmen, and horses; chariots and footmen with chariots and elephants—
horse locked with horse, elephant with elephant, car-warrior with car-warrior, and footman with footman, all were seen grappling together.
So tangled and terrible was that battle, a joy to the eaters of flesh, swelling the realm of Yama with those great and fearless warriors.
Then by men, chariots, horses, and elephants were slain, again and again, elephants and chariots, horses and footmen; elephants by elephants, chariots with raised weapons by car-warriors, horses by horses, and footmen by bands of footmen.
By chariots fell elephants, by lordly elephants the great horses, by horses men, and by mighty car-warriors the steeds—their tongues, teeth, and eyes torn out, their armour and ornaments crushed, they met their end upon the earth.
So too were they slain by the foe with many devices and excellent weapons, and sank to the earth, dreadful to behold—mangled, beaten down by the feet of horses and elephants, and crushed in their distress by chariot-wheels and rims and hooves.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While that terrible destruction of men went on, to the delight of beasts and birds and demons, those mighty warriors, enraged, ranged about with all their force, slaughtering one another.
Then, when both armies were sorely shattered and drenched in floods of blood, gazing upon one another, and the sun had slowly settled upon the western mountain, both withdrew to their camps, O Bhārata.
Saṃjaya said: When we had first been broken by Phalguna of boundless might, and Droṇa's purpose had come to nothing and Yudhiṣṭhira had been kept safe,
all your men, their armour shattered, vanquished in the fight, covered with dust and sorely troubled, stood gazing about them in all ten directions.
Then, having drawn back with the consent of Bharadvāja's son, they were dejected, while the foe had gained their aim, and they were bitterly mocked in the battle.
And as all beings extolled the boundless virtues of Phalguna, and the loving friendship of Keśava toward Arjuna was praised aloud, your men became as though accursed, and sank into a brooding silence.
Then, at the hour of dawn, Duryodhana spoke to Droṇa—out of affection, out of wounded pride, and out of grief at the growing power of the foe—heavy at heart, and skilled in speech he spoke in his fury, while all who stood there listened:
"Surely we belong to the side you would see slain, O best of those who know the sacred lore; for today you did not seize Yudhiṣṭhira, though he came within your reach.
Had you but wished it, no foe once come within your sight in battle could have escaped you, were you minded to seize him—though guarded by the Pāṇḍavas with the very gods themselves.
Having granted me a boon in your favour, you afterward turned against it. The noble never in any way break the hopes of one who is devoted to them."
Then, thus addressed and displeased, the son of Bharadvāja answered the king: "You ought not to think otherwise of me, who strive for your welfare.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The worlds entire — with their gods, asuras, and gandharvas, with yakṣas, serpents, and rākṣasas — are not equal to conquering in battle the host guarded by the Diademed One.
Where Govinda, maker of the universe, stands, and where Arjuna, the bane of armies, stands — whose strength could prevail there, save that of the three-eyed Lord himself?
Yet truly I tell you this day, and it shall in no way prove otherwise: this very day I shall bring down the foremost hero among them, a mighty car-warrior.
And I shall array such a battle-formation as not even the thirty gods could pierce; only, O king, by some device let Arjuna be drawn away.
For in battle there is nothing unknown to him, nothing beyond his power; from this source and that he has gathered to himself all knowledge in its strength.
When Droṇa had spoken thus, the bands of the Saṃśaptakas once again summoned Arjuna to battle, away toward the southern quarter.
There a battle arose between Arjuna and the foe — such a battle as no other was ever heard of or seen anywhere.
Then, O king, the formation arrayed by Droṇa shone forth, hard to look upon, like the sun blazing at midday as it moves through the heavens.
And at the word of his eldest uncle, O descendant of Bharata, Abhimanyu broke that wheel-formation in battle — hard though it was to pierce — in many places.
Having wrought that deed hard to accomplish and slain heroes by the thousand, locked in combat with six warriors, he fell into the power of Duḥśāsana's son.
We were filled with utmost joy, while the Pāṇḍavas were wasted with grief; and when the son of Subhadrā was slain, O king, they withdrew from the field.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Hearing that the son of that lion among men — a boy who had not yet reached his youth, O Saṃjaya — was slain in battle, my heart is torn asunder.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Harsh indeed is this law of the warrior, ordained by the framers of duty, wherein heroes greedy for kingship let fall their weapons upon a child.
A boy reared in utmost ease, ranging the field unafraid — how did many trained in arms strike him down? Tell me, son of Gavalgaṇa, how it came to pass.
As the son of Subhadrā, of measureless might, sought to break the array of chariots and sported in the battle — tell me of that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: That which you ask of me, O lord of kings — the felling of the son of Subhadrā — that I shall tell you in full; listen, O king, with a steady mind, how the prince sported as he sought to break the host.
Such was the terror of your men as the terror of forest-dwellers in a wood thick with thickets, grass, and trees, when the wildfire closes about them on every side.
Saṃjaya said: Most fierce in their deeds in battle, their toil made manifest by their feats, the five Pāṇḍavas, with Kṛṣṇa among them, are hard to assail even by the gods.
In courage, in deeds, in lineage, in wisdom, in nature, in fame, and in fortune, never has there been, nor will there be, a man equal in virtues to Kṛṣṇa.
Devoted to truth and duty, a giver, endowed with such virtues as reverence for the brāhmaṇas, King Yudhiṣṭhira has, they say, ever attained heaven itself.
The Ender at the close of an age, O king, the valiant son of Jamadagni, and Bhīmasena standing in battle — these three, men say, are alike.
For the bearer of the Gāṇḍīva, sure to fulfil his vows in deed, in battle — for the son of Pṛthā I can find no fitting likeness upon this earth.
Boundless tenderness toward his elders, modesty, discipline, self-restraint, beauty beyond compare, and valour — these six are fixed firm in Nakula.
In learning, gravity, sweetness, courage, vigour, and prowess, the hero Sahadeva is, they say, the equal of the two Aśvin gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All the abundant virtues that are in Kṛṣṇa, and all the virtues that are in the Pāṇḍavas — those gathered hoards of virtues, they say, are seen united in Abhimanyu alone.
In the steadfastness of Yudhiṣṭhira, in the conduct of Kṛṣṇa, and in the deeds of Bhīmasena of terrible feats, he was their match.
In the beauty, the prowess, and the learning of Dhanaṃjaya, and in the modesty of Sahadeva and of Nakula, he was their equal.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Of Abhimanyu, the unconquered son of Subhadrā, O sūta, I wish to hear in full — how was he slain upon the field of battle?
Saṃjaya said: The wheel-formation, great king, was devised by the preceptor, and within it were stationed kings, every one the peer of Śakra.
There was then a gathering of all the princes, all bound by a common compact, all with banners wrought of gold.
All clad in crimson raiment, all in crimson ornaments, all with crimson pennons, and all garlanded with gold.
Of these firm-bowed warriors there were ten thousand, who set at their head your grandson, the fair-to-look-upon Lakṣmaṇa.
Sharing one another's sorrows, sharing one another's daring, vying each with each, and each devoted to the welfare of the rest.
Encircled by the great car-warriors Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Kṛpa, the king — like the lord of the gods, radiant, shaded by a white umbrella, fanned by the sweep of yak-tail whisks — was as the rising sun.
At the front of that army, with Droṇa stationed as its commander, the lord of the Sindhus took his stand, glorious and unmoving as Mount Meru.
At the side of the lord of the Sindhus, led by Aśvatthāman, stood your sons, great king — thirty of them, like unto the gods.
The king of Gāndhāra, the gambler, Śalya, and Bhūriśravas — these mighty car-warriors shone forth at the flank of the lord of the Sindhus.
Saṃjaya said: Against that host, unassailable and guarded by the son of Bharadvāja, the Pārthas advanced, with Bhīmasena at their head.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sātyaki and Cekitāna, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the grandson of Pṛṣata, and the valiant Kuntibhoja, and Drupada the great car-warrior;
the son of Arjuna, and Kṣatradharman, and the valiant Bṛhatkṣatra, the lord of the Cedis, and Dhṛṣṭaketu, the two sons of Mādrī, and Ghaṭotkaca;
the valorous Yudhāmanyu, and the unvanquished Śikhaṇḍin, and the unyielding Uttamaujas, and Virāṭa the great car-warrior;
the sons of Draupadī in their fury, and the valiant son of Śiśupāla, and the mighty Kekayas, and the Sṛñjayas in their thousands;
these and others with their bands, masters of arms and frenzied for war, rushed of a sudden upon the son of Bharadvāja, eager to do battle.
But the valiant son of Bharadvāja, all unshaken, held back all those gathered foes with a vast flood of arrows.
As great floods of water reaching a mountain hard to breach, as seas reaching the shore, they could not press past Droṇa.
Tormented, O king, by the shafts loosed from Droṇa's bow, the Pāṇḍavas could not stand before the face of the son of Bharadvāja.
We beheld then the marvellous strength of Droṇa's arms, in that the Pāñcālas together with the Sṛñjayas could not press past him.
Seeing Droṇa advancing in his wrath, Yudhiṣṭhira pondered in many ways how Droṇa might be held back.
Judging that Droṇa could be withstood by no other, Yudhiṣṭhira laid that heavy, unbearable burden upon the son of Subhadrā.
To Abhimanyu — no whit inferior to Vāsudeva, of measureless might like Phalguna, slayer of enemy heroes — he spoke these words:
So act, dear child, that Arjuna may not return and reproach us; for we know not by any means how to break the wheel-formation.
You, or Arjuna, or Kṛṣṇa, or Pradyumna alone could break this wheel-formation, mighty-armed one; a fifth there is none.
O Abhimanyu, dear child, you ought to grant the boon we beg — for the sake of your fathers and your uncles and all the host alike.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For Dhanaṃjaya, dear child, would return from the war and reproach us; so quickly take up your weapons and shatter Droṇa's array.
Abhimanyu said: Droṇa's foremost array, firm and unwavering in battle, I shall plunge into and shall break, longing for my fathers' victory.
For the art of breaking through a battle-array was taught me by my father; but to issue forth again, should some peril arise, that I am unable to do.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Break the array, best of warriors, and open a gateway for us; we shall follow after you, dear child, by whatever path you go.
Holding you, dear child, the equal of Dhanaṃjaya in war, we shall follow close behind you in the fray, guarding you, facing every side.
Bhīma said: I shall follow you, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and Sātyaki, the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, the Matsyas, and all the Prabhadrakas.
The formation once broken by you, here and there, again and again, we shall shatter it utterly, striking down the best of their warriors one upon another.
Abhimanyu said: I shall enter this unassailable array of Droṇa as a moth, all enraged, enters the blazing fire.
This day I shall do that deed which serves the good of both my lineages, and which shall bring joy to my uncle and to my father.
This day shall all beings behold the armies of the foe driven on in their multitudes in battle by a single child — by me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: As you speak thus, son of Subhadrā, may your strength increase — you who dare to break Droṇa's array, so very hard to break;
guarded by tigers among men, great archers and smiters, like the Sādhyas, the Rudras, and the Maruts, with the prowess of the Vasus, of Agni, and of the Ādityas.
Saṃjaya said: Hearing those words of his, he urged on his driver: "Sumitrā, drive the horses swiftly into battle, toward Droṇa's array!"
Saṃjaya said: But the son of Subhadrā, having heard the word of the wise Dharma-king, urged on his driver toward Droṇa's array, O descendant of Bharata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the charioteer, thus urged on with "Go, go!", answered then, O king, and spoke these words to Abhimanyu:
Too heavy a burden, O long-lived one, have the Pāṇḍavas laid upon you; weigh well with your mind what is fitting, and only then ought you to fight.
For the preceptor Droṇa is accomplished, well-practised in the highest weapons, while you have been reared in utmost ease — though you too are skilled in war.
Then Abhimanyu, laughing, spoke these words to the charioteer: "O charioteer, who indeed is this Droṇa, or the whole warrior caste besides?
I would do battle at the forefront of the fray with Śakra himself, mounted upon Airāvata, together with all the host of gods; this day no awe of the warrior caste is in me. This army of the foe is not worth to me a sixteenth part.
Having for my uncle Viṣṇu, conqueror of all, and for my father Arjuna in battle, O son of a sūta, no fear shall ever come upon me.
Then Abhimanyu, making nothing of the charioteer's speech, said to him only, "Go, and tarry not — toward Droṇa's array!"
Then the sūta, his heart not over-glad, urged on his three-year-old steeds, decked in trappings of gold.
Those horses, sent on by Sumitrā toward Droṇa's array, rushed upon Droṇa, O king, with great speed and force.
Beholding him come on thus, all the Kauravas, led by Droṇa, advanced against him, and the Pāṇḍavas followed after him.
His banner raised high with a peerless karṇikāra blossom, clad in golden mail, the son of Arjuna — finer even than Arjuna — fell with eagerness for battle upon the great car-warriors led by Droṇa, as a lion's cub upon elephants.
Halting at twenty paces, intent, they joined the clash of arms; for a moment it was like the whirlpool of the Gaṅgā, like that of the ocean.
As the heroes fought, striking one another down, a tumultuous and most terrible battle arose, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As that most terrifying battle raged on, the son of Arjuna, before Droṇa's very eyes, broke through the formation and entered it.
As that mighty one entered and struck down the foe in the enemy's midst, throngs of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, weapons upraised, closed in around him.
With the din of varied instruments, with whoops and shouts and roars, with snarls and lion-cries and cries of "Stand! Stand!",
with dreadful clamoring uproar—"Do not flee! Stand! Come to me! That one is mine, I am here!"—crying out again and again,
with the trumpeting of elephants, the jingling of ornaments, with laughter, and the clatter of hooves and wheel-rims, making the earth resound, they rushed upon the son of Arjuna.
As they fell upon him, the hero—swift of weapon and knowing the vital points—slew their bands first quickly, then surely, with shafts that pierced the vitals.
Though they were thus being slain by his sharp arrows of many kinds, they hurled themselves upon him in the fray like moths into a flame.
Then with their bodies and the limbs of their bodies he swiftly strewed the ground, as one strews the altar with kuśa grass at a sacrifice.
Their arms bound with iguana-hide and finger-guards, bearing arrows, shields, and bows, with swords, leather, goads, and reins, with lances and battle-axes,
with iron-tipped barbed javelins, with spears, lances, and tridents, with slings and clubs, with darts and excellent quivering pikes,
with goads and great conches, with barbed spears, with grappling-hooks, with mallets and slingstones, with nooses, bludgeons, and stones—
the rounded arms of your men, adorned with armlets and bracelets and anointed with fragrant unguents, the son of Arjuna severed by the thousand.
With those quivering, blood-drenched arms, O great king, the field shone as if with five-headed serpents cut asunder by Garuḍa, good sir.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With heads of fair noses, faces, and flowing hair, unblemished, with lovely earrings, with lips bitten in rage, streaming much blood,
with lovely garlands, crowns, and diadems, gleaming with gems and jewels, shaped like stalkless lotuses, with the radiance of sun and moon,
with many sweet-spoken heads of the foe, which had spoken kindly and well in their time and were of holy fragrance, the son of Phalguna covered the earth.
Chariots shaped like the cities of the gandharvas, fashioned according to rule—their shafts shattered, their triple-poles broken, their staves and yokes scattered,
their axles, poles, and pins gone, their rims gone, their drivers gone, their wheels, gear, and seats undone, their fittings broken as well,
their equipment hewn away, their warriors slain by the thousand—shattering them to fragments with his arrows, he was seen in every direction.
And again the elephants and their riders, the banners, goads, and standards, the quivers, the armor, the girths, the neck-ropes, the blankets,
the bells, the trunks, the tusk-tips, the foot-guards, and the attendants of the enemy—all these he cut down with his keen-edged, sharp-pointed arrows.
Steeds from Vanāyu, from the mountains, from Kāmboja, Āraṭṭa, and Bāhlika—of steady tails, ears, and eyes, swift and well-trained to bear,
well-mounted by trained warriors who fought with darts, lances, and javelins—their chowries and trappings undone, their plumes scattered about,
with tongues and eyes thrust out, with entrails, livers, and hearts spilling forth, their riders slain, their harness broken, a feast for the flesh-eating throngs,
their armor and mail cut away, drenched in dung and urine and blood—felling these fine horses of your men, he shone resplendent.
Alone, unfathomable as Viṣṇu, having wrought before this a deed hard to do, he so churned up the three branches of your great host; and he struck down the floods of your foot-soldiers as well, O descendant of Bharata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing that army thus grievously battered by Subhadrā's son alone with his sharp arrows, as the asuras' host was once smitten by Skanda,
your men and your sons, gazing about them in all ten directions, their mouths gone dry, their eyes darting, sweating, their hair on end,
bent on fleeing, drained of all heart for the conquest of the foe, calling out to one another by clan and name, longing for their lives,
abandoning their slain sons and fathers, their friends, kinsmen, and relations, they took flight, urging on their horses and elephants.
Saṃjaya said: Seeing that host shattered by the son of Subhadrā of boundless might, Duryodhana, sorely enraged, advanced himself against the son of Subhadrā.
Then, seeing the king turn toward Subhadrā's son in the fray, Droṇa said to the warriors, "Shield the lord of men!
Before mighty Abhimanyu slays the mark of our gaze—rush upon him! Do not fear! Swiftly guard the Kaurava!"
Then those grateful, mighty comrades, flushed with victory yet harried by fear, surrounded your son to shield him from the hero.
Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, Kṛtavarman, and the son of Subala, Bṛhadbala, the king of the Madras, Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala,
the Paurava and Vṛṣasena—loosing sharp arrows, they overwhelmed the son of Subhadrā with a great rain of shafts.
Having bewildered him, they then bore Duryodhana off to safety; but the son of Arjuna could not brook it, as a lion cannot brook a morsel snatched from its jaws.
With a great flood of arrows the son of Subhadrā turned those great chariot-warriors back, horses and drivers and all, and then let loose a lion's roar.
Hearing his cry, like that of a lion craving its prey, the chariot-warriors led by Droṇa, greatly incensed, could not endure it once again.
Penning him in with their array of chariots, good sir, they loosed nets of arrows of many kinds upon him in massed volleys.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Your grandson cut these apart in mid-air with his sharp arrows, and pierced those warriors in return—and that was a marvel to behold.
Then, provoked by him with arrows like venomous serpents, they surrounded the unflinching son of Subhadrā, bent on his death.
That ocean-host of yours, surging like the sea, Abhimanyu alone held back, as the shore holds back the abode of sea-monsters.
Among the heroes fighting and striking one another—Abhimanyu and the foe alike—not one turned his face away.
While that dreadful, terrifying battle raged on, Duḥsaha pierced Abhimanyu with nine arrows.
Duḥśāsana struck him with twelve, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat with three, and Droṇa with seventeen arrows like venomous serpents.
Viviṃśati with twenty, Kṛtavarman with seven, Bṛhadbala likewise with eight, and Aśvatthāman with seven,
Bhūriśravas with three arrows, the lord of the Madras with six swift shafts, Śakuni with two, and king Duryodhana with three.
But he pierced each of them in return with three straight-flying shafts, as if dancing, O great king, bow in hand, that splendid warrior.
Then Abhimanyu, enraged and sorely pressed by your sons, displayed the mighty power of his training and his own native strength.
With horses swift as Garuḍa or the wind, tamed and obedient to their driver's word, he hastened to attack the heir of Aśmaka, pierced him with ten arrows, and cried, "Stand!"
With ten arrows Abhimanyu, smiling, brought down to earth his driver, his horses, his banner, his arms, his bow, and his head.
Then, when that hero, the lord of Aśmaka, was slain by the son of Subhadrā, the whole host wavered and gave itself over to flight.
Then Karṇa, Kṛpa, Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, the king of Gāndhāra, Śala, Śalya, Bhūriśravas, Krātha, Somadatta, Viviṃśati,
Vṛṣasena and Suṣeṇa, Kuṇḍabhedin, Pratardana, Vṛndāraka, Lalittha, Prabāhu, Dīrghalocana, and Duryodhana, all in fury, overwhelmed him with showers of arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Greatly enraged by those mighty archers, Abhimanyu took up against Karṇa a straight-flying arrow that pierces the bodies of foes.
That swift shaft, cleaving his armor and piercing his body, entered the earth, O king, like a serpent entering an anthill.
Stricken by that mighty blow and reeling as if dazed, Karṇa swayed upon the field like a mountain in an earthquake.
Then with other keen arrows the mighty one, in his wrath, slew the three—Suṣeṇa, Dīrghalocana, and Kuṇḍabhedin—with three shafts.
Karṇa let fly at him twenty-five iron shafts, Aśvatthāman twenty, and Kṛtavarman seven.
His every limb tormented by arrows, the son of Indra's son, in his wrath, was seen ranging through the host like Death with noose in hand.
And with a rain of arrows he overwhelmed Śalya, who stood close by, that mighty-armed one crying aloud and striking terror into your armies.
Then, pierced by that master of weapons with straight shafts that cleave the vitals, Śalya, O king, sank down upon the floor of his chariot and swooned away.
Seeing him so pierced by the glorious son of Subhadrā, the whole host took to flight before the very eyes of the son of Bharadvāja.
Beholding that mighty-armed one encompassed by his gold-feathered arrows, your men too fled, like deer harried by a lion.
And he, honored for his glory in battle by the throngs of ancestors, gods, cāraṇas, siddhas, and yakṣas, and by the hosts of beings upon the earth, blazed forth like fire fed with clarified butter.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: As that mighty archer, the son of Arjuna, churned them so with his straight shafts, which of my men all overwhelmed him?
Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, the great sport of the youth in battle, as he sought to break through the chariot-array guarded by the son of Bharadvāja.
Seeing the lord of the Madras struck down by the son of Subhadrā with swift shafts in the fray, Śalya's younger brother, enraged, advanced upon him, scattering arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Piercing the son of Arjuna, horses and driver and all, with ten arrows, he cried out in a great voice, "Stand! Stand!"
His head and neck, hands and feet, his bow, his horses, his parasol, his banner, his driver, the triple-pole, the pegs and gear,
the wheels, the yoke-shaft, the quivers, and the under-pole—with his arrows, and the pennon, the two wheel-guards, and all the fittings, the son of Arjuna shattered with such swiftness that none could mark how he did it.
He fell to the earth undone, his ornaments and garments scattered, like a great sacred tree snapped by the wind—broken by that one of boundless splendor; and his followers, terror-struck, fled in every direction.
Seeing that deed of the son of Arjuna, all beings on every side cried out with a great shout, "Well done! Well done!", O descendant of Bharata.
Now that Śalya's brother was struck down, his soldiers in great numbers, proclaiming aloud to the son of Arjuna the names of their clans and dwelling-places,
advanced in fury, weapons of every kind in hand, some with chariots, horses, and elephants, others on foot, swollen with strength.
With the great twang of bowstrings and the clatter of hooves and wheel-rims, with snarls, whoops, and shouts, with lion-roars and bellowings,
others with the twang of bowstring and finger-guard, roaring at the son of Arjuna and crying, "You shall not escape us alive while we yet live!"
Seeing them speak thus, the son of Subhadrā, as if smiling, pierced with his feathered shafts each man, one after another, who had first struck at him.
Meaning to display his weapons, both wondrous and swift, the heroic son of Arjuna fought on in the battle, gently at first.
Whatever weapon the son of Kārṣṇi had received from Vāsudeva and from Dhanaṃjaya, that he displayed, showing himself in no way inferior to the two Kṛṣṇas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Shooting far, bearing the heavy burden, and pressing on again and again, nocking and loosing his arrows, he appeared without a single break in his motion.
Only the circle of his bow, quivering, was seen in every quarter, like the blazing disk of the sun as it destroys the darkness.
The twang of his bowstring was heard, and the terrible clap of his palm-guard, like the roar of a storm-cloud loosing its great thunderbolts in season.
Modest yet unforgiving, the son of Subhadrā, proud and fair to look upon, fought on, wishing even to do honor to the heroic archers.
Having been gentle, O great king, he turned terrible, like the blessed sun grown fierce in autumn after the rains have passed.
Wrathful, he loosed by the hundred his great and wondrous arrows, gold-feathered and whetted on stone, as the sun pours forth its rays.
With razor-edged shafts and calf-tooth points, with broad-headed and barbed arrows, with iron bolts and half-iron bolts, with crescent heads and finger-broad heads, the illustrious one fought;
he overwhelmed the chariot host before the very eyes of Bhāradvāja, and that army, sore pressed by his arrows, turned its face away.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: My mind is torn in two, Saṃjaya, between shame and delight, that the son of Subhadrā held back the army of my son.
Tell me again in full detail, son of Gavalgaṇa, all the sport of that young prince, like Skanda's against the Asuras.
Saṃjaya said: Then I shall recount to you that most fearful struggle, and the tumultuous battle as it raged between the one and the many.
Abhimanyu, his ardor kindled, standing upon his chariot, dismayed all your warriors—those eager chariot-fighters and subduers of foes.
Droṇa, Karṇa, Kṛpa, Śalya, the son of Droṇa, the Bhoja, Bṛhadbala, Duryodhana, the son of Somadatta, and mighty Śakuni—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the many kings and sons of kings, and the manifold armies—ranging among them all like a whirling firebrand, he assailed them with his arrows.
Slaying his foes, the son of Subhadrā, master of supreme weapons, glorious and full of splendor, showed himself in every quarter, O Bhārata.
Seeing that exploit of the son of Subhadrā of measureless might, your armies trembled again and again.
Then the deeply wise and valiant Bhāradvāja, his eyes wide with delight, swiftly addressed Kṛpa and said:
As though striking at the vital parts of your son, O honored one, when he beheld Abhimanyu, that master of battle, in the fray—
"There goes the young son of Subhadrā, at the head of the Pārthas, gladdening all his friends and King Yudhiṣṭhira,
and Nakula and Sahadeva and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, and his other kinsmen and relations, the neutrals and the well-wishers alike.
In battle I think no other bowman is his equal; should he wish it, he could slay this whole army—yet for some reason he does not so wish."
Hearing these words of Droṇa, spoken with affection, your son grew wrathful against the son of Arjuna, and looking at Droṇa he seemed to smile.
Then Duryodhana spoke to Karṇa, to Bāhlika, to Kṛpa, to Duḥśāsana, to the king of the Madras, and to those other great chariot-warriors:
"The preceptor of all the anointed kings, deepest knower of the Veda, has no wish here to strike down this deluded son of Arjuna.
For in battle not even Death himself, were he the assailant, could escape him—how much less any other mortal? I tell you the truth.
Out of regard for his pupil, he shields the son of Arjuna; for to the righteous, sons and pupils are dear alike, and so too is this their child.
Guarded by Droṇa, he fancies his own prowess; that vain fool, puffed up with self-conceit—crush him without delay!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed by the king, they rushed upon the son of the Sātvatī woman, furious and bent on killing him, before the very eyes of Bhāradvāja.
But Duḥśāsana, that tiger among the Kurus, having heard Duryodhana's words, then said this to Duryodhana:
"I shall slay him, great king—I tell you so. Before the watching eyes of the sons of Pāṇḍu and the Pāñcālas, this day I shall devour the son of Subhadrā as Rāhu devours the sun."
And shouting aloud, he spoke again these words to the king of the Kurus: "When the two over-proud Kṛṣṇas hear that the son of Subhadrā has been devoured by me, they will pass from the world of the living to the world of the dead—of this there is no doubt."
"And once those two are clearly dead, the sons sprung from Pāṇḍu's field, together with their company of friends, will in a single day yield up their lives out of despair."
"Therefore, when this enemy is slain, all your foes are slain. Bless me, O king, and think on my welfare; here I go to kill your enemy!"
Having spoken thus and roaring, O king, your son Duḥśāsana rushed in fury upon the son of Subhadrā and overwhelmed him with showers of arrows.
As your son came on in his wrath, Abhimanyu, that subduer of foes, met him with twenty-six keen arrows.
And Duḥśāsana, enraged like an elephant in rut, gave battle to the son of Subhadrā, and Abhimanyu fought him in turn upon the field.
Wheeling their chariots leftward and rightward in wondrous circling patterns, the two, skilled in the art of chariot-craft, fought on.
Then the men raised a mighty din of small drums and tabors and kettledrums, of cymbals and great war-drums and trumpets and rattles, mingled with a roar like that of the briny ocean.
Saṃjaya said: His limbs torn by arrows, wise Abhimanyu, smiling, then spoke to Duḥśāsana, who stood before him as his foe:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"By good fortune I behold, come into battle, my arrogant enemy—cruel, having cast off all righteousness, given over to reviling.
For in the assembly hall, while King Dhṛtarāṣṭra listened, you, drunk with triumph, provoked the Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira with harsh words, and Bhīma too, prating much that was unseemly.
For the seizing of another's wealth, for unappeased wrath, for greed, for the ruin of wisdom, for grievous treachery,
and for the robbing of the kingdom of my fierce-bowed forefathers—this has now overtaken you, born of the wrath of those great-souled men.
Reap this very moment the fierce fruit of your unrighteousness, O evil-minded one! Today I shall chastise you with my arrows before the eyes of the whole army.
Today in this battle I shall free myself of the debt I owe to that wrath—to the indignant Kṛṣṇā and to the longing of my father.
Today, O Kaurava, I shall discharge in battle my debt to Bhīma. You shall not escape me alive unless you flee the fight."
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed slayer of hostile heroes nocked an arrow to end Duḥśāsana, gleaming like the fire and wind of doomsday.
Swiftly reaching his breast, it pierced him through at the collarbone; and then once more he met him with twenty-five arrows.
Deeply pierced and racked with pain, Duḥśāsana sank down upon the floor of his chariot, O great king, and a great swoon came over him.
His charioteer in haste bore the senseless Duḥśāsana, sore pressed by the arrows of the son of Subhadrā, out of the thick of the battle.
The Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Draupadī, and Virāṭa, the Pāñcālas and the Kekayas, beholding this, then raised a lion's roar.
And the warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, filled with joy, sounded forth on every side all their instruments of many kinds.
They watched and smiled at the feat of the son of Subhadrā, seeing their utter and insolent foe defeated.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The sons of Draupadī, those great chariot-warriors, bore upon the tips of their standards the images of Dharma, the Wind-god, Śakra, and the two Aśvins.
Sātyaki and Cekitāna, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, the Kekayas and Dhṛṣṭaketu, the Matsyas, the Pāñcālas, and the Sṛñjayas,
and the Pāṇḍavas, filled with gladness and led by Yudhiṣṭhira, advanced together, eager to break the host of Droṇa.
Then there arose a mighty battle between your men and their foes, between heroes who longed for victory and would never turn back.
Duryodhana, O great king, said this to the son of Rādhā: "Look at the hero Duḥśāsana, fallen into Abhimanyu's power!
And the Pāṇḍavas come rushing on, roused to rescue him, while the son of Subhadrā, blazing like the sun, strikes down his foes in battle."
Then Karṇa, enraged and acting for your son's good, rained keen arrows upon the unassailable Abhimanyu.
