And on the field of battle that hero, with scorn, pierced with his keen, supreme shafts the followers of the son of Subhadrā.
But Abhimanyu, high-souled, eager to reach Droṇa, swiftly pierced the son of Rādhā with seventy-three stone-whetted arrows, O king.
None then could hold him back from Droṇa in the battle as he shattered the foremost chariot-warriors, like the Thunderbolt-bearer scattering the Asuras.
Then Karṇa, proudest of all bowmen and longing for victory, pierced the son of Subhadrā a hundredfold, displaying his supreme weapons.
With those weapons the valiant pupil of Rāma, foremost of those who know the weapons, harried in battle Abhimanyu, whom foes could not withstand.
Yet though thus harried by the son of Rādhā with showers of weapons, the son of Subhadrā, like a god in the battle, did not falter.
Then, with keen, stone-whetted, smooth-jointed broad-headed arrows, the son of Arjuna cut the bows of the heroes and tormented Karṇa; and severing his standard and his bow, he cast them to the ground.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, seeing Karṇa brought to grief, Karṇa's younger brother rushed swiftly upon the son of Subhadrā, raising his stout bow.
Then the Pārthas and the men who followed them shouted aloud, and sounded their instruments, and gave praise to the son of Subhadrā.
Saṃjaya said: Roaring aloud, bow in hand, drawing the string again and again, he swiftly closed the gap between the chariots of those two great-souled warriors.
Smiling, as it were, he swiftly pierced the unassailable Abhimanyu with ten arrows, together with his parasol, standard, charioteer, and horses.
Seeing the son of Kārṣṇi—who wrought superhuman deeds worthy of his father and forefathers—now wounded by arrows, your men rejoiced.
But Abhimanyu, drawing his bow with a smile, struck off that man's head with a single feathered shaft, and he fell from his chariot to the earth.
Seeing his brother slain—like a karṇikāra blossom torn by the wind and shaken from the mountain—Karṇa, O king, was struck with grief.
Having turned Karṇa away with his heron-feathered arrows, the son of Subhadrā at once rushed upon the other great archers as well.
Then the illustrious Abhimanyu broke through that wide-spread net of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, like an angry fish tearing through a snare.
And Karṇa, tormented by Abhimanyu's many arrows, withdrew upon his swift horses; thereupon the host was broken open.
With the sky covered over by Abhimanyu's arrows, as though by locusts or by torrents of rain, O king, nothing could be discerned at all.
And as your warriors were being cut down by his sharp arrows, none, O king, save the lord of the Sindhus, stood his ground.
Then Subhadrā's son, that bull among men, blew his conch and swiftly fell upon the army of the Bhāratas, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Like fire let loose in dry brush, consuming his foes with sudden force, Arjuna's son ranged through the midst of the Bhārata host.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Tormenting chariots, elephants, horses, and men with his whetted shafts, he plunged in and made the earth thick with throngs of headless trunks.
Cut down by the matchless arrows sprung from Subhadrā's son's bow, men fled in their longing for life, striking even their own comrades who faced them.
Those dreadful broad-headed shafts, sharp and terrible in their work, slew chariots, elephants, and horses, and swiftly buried themselves in the earth.
In that battle there could be seen severed arms, still gripping weapons, still wearing finger-guards, swords, and armlets, adorned with golden ornaments.
Arrows and bows and swords, bodies and heads—wearing earrings and garlands—lay upon the ground by the thousands.
With wheel-frames and floor-boards, with poles, shafts, and seat-rails, with shattered axles and broken wheels, with chariots smashed in many ways, with spears, bows, and weapons, and with great fallen banners—
with slain warriors, horses, and elephants, O lord of peoples, in a moment the earth became all but impassable and most fearsome to behold.
From the princes being slaughtered, crying out to one another, there arose a mighty din that swelled the terror of the timid; and that sound, O best of the Bhāratas, made all the quarters resound.
Subhadrā's son charged the army, striking down horses, chariots, and elephants; he ranged through all the quarters and the intermediate quarters, crushing the foe.
We could not then make him out, veiled by the army's dust as he took the lives of elephants, horses, and men, O Bhārata.
In a moment we saw him again, O great king, like the noonday sun—Abhimanyu, scorching the hosts of his enemies.
Equal to Vāsava in battle, the son of Vāsava's son's son, Abhimanyu, O great king, shone resplendent in the midst of the army.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: A boy, reared in utter ease, proud with irresistible strength, skilled in battle, a hero, a scion of a noble house, ready to lay down his life—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
as he plunged into the ranks with his fine three-year-old steeds, did any chariot-warrior from Yudhiṣṭhira's army follow after him?
Saṃjaya said: Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Śikhaṇḍin, Sātyaki, the twins, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, Drupada with the Kekayas, the furious Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the Matsyas followed after him into the battle.
In their eagerness to protect him those smiters charged, their ranks arrayed; and seeing those heroes rushing on, your men turned their faces away.
Then, seeing the great host of your son turned away, your splendid son-in-law charged forward, resolved to hold the line.
The king Jayadratha, son of the lord of the Sindhus, O great king, held back the sons of Pṛthā together with their army as they pressed on, hungry to reach their son.
Of dreadful bow, a great archer, the son of Vṛddhakṣatra invoked a divine weapon and checked them, as one checks elephants charging down a slope.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: A burden too great, I think, was laid upon the lord of the Sindhus, Saṃjaya, in that alone he held back the wrathful Pāṇḍavas longing to reach their son.
Most wondrous, I deem, are the strength and valor in the lord of the Sindhus. Tell me then of that great soul's prowess and his foremost deed.
What did the king of the Sindhus give, or offer in oblation, or sacrifice, or what austerity did he duly perform, that alone he could hold back the wrathful sons of Pṛthā?
Saṃjaya said: When, at the carrying off of Draupadī, that king was vanquished by Bhīmasena, then out of wounded pride, seeking a boon, he performed exceedingly severe austerity.
Drawing back his senses from their dear objects, enduring hunger, thirst, and heat, grown lean, his veins standing forth, he worshipped the god Śarva, reciting the eternal sacred word.
The Lord, compassionate to his devotees, then took pity on him; and at the end of a dream Hara said to the son of the lord of the Sindhus: 'Choose a boon, I am pleased, Jayadratha—what do you desire?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
So addressed by Śarva, Jayadratha, king of the Sindhus, bowing low before Rudra with joined palms, his soul composed, replied:
'May I, alone in battle, hold back the sons of Pāṇḍu, of terrible valor and might, all of them together'—so he prayed, O Bhārata.
So addressed, the lord of the gods then said to Jayadratha: 'I grant you the boon, gentle one—save only Pṛthā's son Dhanaṃjaya.
In battle you shall hold back the four sons of Pāṇḍu.' Saying 'So be it' to the lord of the gods, the king awoke.
By that granting of the boon and by the power of his divine weapon, he alone held back the host of the Pāṇḍavas.
At the twang of his bowstring and the slap of his palm, fear entered the warriors of the foe, while in your army there arose the highest joy.
And seeing the whole burden laid upon the lord of the Sindhus, the warriors, raising a shout, charged, O king, against Yudhiṣṭhira's host.
Saṃjaya said: As to the valor of the king of the Sindhus about which you ask me, O king of kings—hear it; I shall tell it all, how he fought the Pāṇḍavas.
Him the great Sindhu horses bore on, obedient to the charioteer, well-trained and high-mettled, prancing, swift as the wind.
His chariot, fashioned according to rule and shaped like a Gandharva's city, was adorned by a banner bearing a great silver boar.
With white parasol and pennants and with whisk and fan, he shone forth in those marks of royalty like the lord of the stars in the sky.
Adorned with pearls, diamonds, gems, and gold, his iron fender shone like the firmament strewn with stars.
Twanging his great bow and scattering many showers of shafts, he filled up that gap which the son of Arjuna had torn open.
He pierced Sātyaki with three arrows, Vṛkodara with eight, Dhṛṣṭadyumna with sixty, and Virāṭa with ten shafts;
Drupada with five keen ones, and Śikhaṇḍin with ten, the Kekayas with twenty-five, and the sons of Draupadī with three apiece;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and Yudhiṣṭhira with seventy; then he drove off the rest with a vast web of arrows—a thing that seemed a marvel.
Then, taking aim at his bow with a sharp, gold-bright broad-headed shaft, the mighty King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Dharma-born, laughing, cut it in two.
In but the twinkling of an eye he took up another bow and pierced him with ten shafts, O Pārtha, and the others, each with three.
Marking that lightness of hand, Bhīma with three broad-headed shafts swiftly brought down to the ground his bow, his banner, and his parasol.
The strong one, taking up another bow and stringing it, shattered Bhīma's banner, bow, and horses, O honored one.
His horses slain and his bow cut through, Bhīma leapt down from his splendid car and sprang onto Sātyaki's chariot, like a lion onto a mountain peak.
Then your men, exulting, cried out 'Well done! Well done!' beholding that supreme and scarcely credible feat of the king of the Sindhus.
That he alone, by the splendor of his weapons, held back the wrathful Pāṇḍavas—at that deed of his all beings did him homage.
The path opened for the Pāṇḍavas by the elephants—with their riders and weapons—earlier slain by Subhadrā's son, was now barred by the lord of the Sindhus.
Though those heroes strove—the Matsyas, the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, and the Pāṇḍavas—they came against the lord of the Sindhus only one by one.
Whatever foe of yours strove to break through Droṇa's array, that one the lord of the Sindhus, by virtue of the god's boon, turned back.
Saṃjaya said: When the sons of Pāṇḍu, hungry for victory, had been checked by the lord of the Sindhus, a most terrible battle arose between your men and the foe.
Having entered that unassailable army, the son of Arjuna, true to his vow and full of splendor, churned it up as a sea-monster churns the ocean.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As that tamer of foes, Subhadrā's son, thus churned the host with his rain of arrows, the foremost of the Kurus, each in his rank, advanced upon him.
A fearsome and unbroken clash came to pass between them and him, as those of measureless might poured forth their showers of arrows.
Hemmed in by that throng of chariots, by those foes, Arjuna's son slew Vṛṣasena's charioteer and cut through his bow.
The strong one pierced his horses with straight-flying shafts, and by those steeds, now bolting like the wind, Vṛṣasena was carried off from the field.
In that interval Abhimanyu's charioteer drove his chariot forward; then the throngs of car-warriors, delighted, cried out 'Well done! Well done!'
As he came on from afar, wrathful as a lion, crushing his foes with arrows, the prince of the Vasātis met him and swiftly charged.
He showered Abhimanyu with sixty gold-feathered shafts and said: 'While I live, you shall not escape from me alive in battle.'
Him, clad in iron mail, Subhadrā's son pierced in the heart with a swift-falling arrow, and he fell lifeless to the earth.
Seeing the Vasāti slain, the bulls among warriors, enraged, then surrounded your grandson, O king, eager to kill him.
Twanging their bows of many shapes and many kinds, they fought a dreadful battle, the foes against Subhadrā's son.
Their arrows together with their bows, and their bodies and heads—wearing earrings and garlands—the wrathful son of Phalguna cut asunder.
Severed arms could be seen, still holding swords, finger-guards, spiked maces, and axes, adorned with golden ornaments.
With garlands, ornaments, and garments, with fallen great banners, with cuirasses, shields, necklaces, diadems, parasols, and whisks—
with wheel-frames and floor-boards, with poles, shafts, and seat-rails, with shattered axles and broken wheels, with yokes smashed in many ways—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
with under-poles and pennants, with charioteers and steeds, with broken chariots and slain elephants, the earth was strewn.
Covered with slain warriors, heroes, lords of many lands, all hungry for victory, the earth became a fearsome thing.
As wrathful Abhimanyu ranged through all the quarters and the intermediate quarters in battle, his form vanished from sight.
Whatever golden armor and ornaments were his, and the gold of his bow and arrows—that alone could we see.
None then could gaze upon him with his eyes, as he took the warriors' lives with his shafts, standing in their midst like the sun.
Saṃjaya said: Taking the lives of heroes, the son of Arjuna became like the Ender of all beings, like Time itself come to seize their breath.
Valiant as Śakra, the mighty son of Śakra's son—Abhimanyu—shone surpassingly as he tossed that army into confusion.
Having plunged in, O king of kings, like Death to the lords of warriors, he took the life of Satyaśravas, as a tiger takes a fierce deer.
When Satyaśravas had been struck down, the great car-warriors in haste, seizing their broad weapons, rushed upon Abhimanyu.
'I first! I first!'—so vying with one another, the bulls among warriors came on together, bent on slaying Arjuna's son.
The ranks of warriors that came charging on he swallowed up as a great fish in the ocean falls upon and devours the little fish.
Whoever among the unflinching drew near to him never returned again, as rivers that have entered the sea do not flow back.
As though seized by a great sea-monster, tormented by terror of the wind's force, that army trembled and broke apart like a ship foundering on the ocean.
Then a mighty warrior named Rukmaratha, son of the lord of the Madras, himself unshaken, reassured the frightened host and spoke these words:
"Enough of your fear, O heroes! While I stand here he is nothing. I shall take him alive — of that there is no doubt."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus, the valorous one rushed upon the son of Subhadrā, borne along by a splendid, well-fitted chariot.
He pierced Abhimanyu in the chest with three arrows and roared aloud, struck him with three on the right arm and three sharp shafts on the left.
But the son of Phalguna, severing his bow, swiftly brought down to the earth both his arms, left and right, and his head with its fair eyes and brows.
Seeing Rukmaratha — Śalya's proud son who had sought to take him captive — broken thus by the glorious son of Subhadrā,
those princes, O king, battle-frenzied and hard-striking, comrades of Śalya's son, their banners wrought of gold,
those great chariot-warriors, drawing bows tall as palm-trees, hemmed in the son of Arjuna on every side with a downpour of arrows.
Seeing that lone hero, the unconquered son of Subhadrā, amid the fray, beset by valiant youths trained in skill and full of fury,
shrouded by their swarms of arrows, Duryodhana grew glad, for he reckoned that the youth had already gone to the abode of Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
With gold-feathered arrows of many marks, three by three, those king's sons in the twinkling of an eye made the son of Arjuna vanish from sight.
And his chariot, O sire, with its charioteer, horses, and banner, we saw so thickly covered with shafts that it was like a porcupine bristling with quills.
Deeply pierced and enraged, like an elephant goaded with hooks, he drew forth the Gāndharva weapon and called up the magic of chariot-craft.
With that weapon, which Arjuna had won through austerities from the Gandharvas led by Tumburu, he bewildered his foes.
That single warrior, O king, appeared a hundredfold, a thousandfold, swiftly displaying his weapons in the battle like a whirling brand of fire.
Having confounded them, O king, with his chariot-evolutions and the illusions of his weapons, that scorcher of foes pierced the bodies of the lords of the earth a hundredfold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The life-breaths of those creatures, sped forth in battle by his sharp arrows, O king, attained the world beyond, while their bodies went down to the earth.
Their bows, horses, drivers, banners, and arms with their armlets, and their heads as well — all these the son of Phalguna sheared off with sharp broad-headed shafts.
As a mango grove in its fifth year of fruiting is shattered, so a hundred princes fell slain by the son of Subhadrā.
Seeing them — tender-bodied, bred to ease, yet like enraged venomous serpents — struck down by one man alone, Duryodhana was seized with fear.
Seeing chariot-warriors, elephants, horses, and footmen crushed alike, Duryodhana, unable to endure it, swiftly bore down upon him.
For but a moment the combat between the two ran its full course; then your son, tormented by a hundred arrows, turned his face from the fight.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: As you tell me, O charioteer, of the tumultuous, dreadful battle of that one against the many, and of the high-souled youth's victory —
the prowess of the son of Subhadrā seems a marvel hard to believe; yet nothing is too wondrous for those whose refuge is righteousness.
When Duryodhana had turned away and a hundred princes lay slain, what counsel did my men take against the son of Subhadrā?
Saṃjaya said: With mouths gone dry, eyes darting, sweating and with hair standing on end, eager only to flee, with no heart left to vanquish the foe,
abandoning their slain brothers, fathers, sons, friends, kinsmen, and relations one after another, they fled together, urging on their horses and elephants.
Seeing them thus routed, Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, Bṛhadbala, Kṛpa, Duryodhana, Karṇa, Kṛtavarman, and the son of Subala —
these too, in great wrath, charged upon the unconquered son of Subhadrā; yet they also, O king, were for the most part turned back by your grandson.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But one — Lakṣmaṇa, reared in ease, fearless from youth and pride, skilled in arrows, full of fierce splendor — advanced upon the son of Arjuna.
Close behind him his father, doting on his son, turned back to the fight, and behind Duryodhana the other great chariot-warriors turned back as well.
They drenched him with arrows as clouds drench a mountain with rain; yet he alone scattered them as the wind scatters clouds in all directions.
But your grandson, the unassailable Lakṣmaṇa, fair to look upon, that hero standing near his father with bow upraised,
reared in utmost comfort, like a son of Kubera, lord of riches — him the son of Kṛṣṇa's sister met in battle as one rutting elephant meets another.
Closing with Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Subhadrā, slayer of hostile heroes, was struck on the arms and chest with keen, sharp-pointed arrows.
Then the mighty-armed one, enraged like a serpent struck with a staff — your grandson, O great king — spoke to your grandson:
"Look well upon this world, for you shall go to the next. Before the eyes of your kinsmen I send you to the abode of Yama."
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, slayer of hostile heroes, drew forth a broad-headed shaft that gleamed like a serpent freshly sloughed of its skin.
Loosed from his arm, it struck off Lakṣmaṇa's lovely head — fair-nosed, fair-browed, well-tressed, still wearing its earrings; and seeing Lakṣmaṇa slain, the people cried out, "Alas! Alas!"
Then Duryodhana, enraged at the fall of his dear son, that bull among warriors, cried out to the kṣatriyas, "Slay him!"
Then Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, Bṛhadbala, and Kṛtavarman the son of Hṛdika — these six chariot-warriors closed in around him.
Piercing them with sharp arrows and turning them back, the son of Arjuna in his fury fell with speed upon the great host of the Saindhava.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Kaliṅgas, the Niṣādas, and the valiant son of Krātha, mailed and ranged with their elephant-host, barred his path; and the fighting that followed, O lord of peoples, became unbroken and exceedingly fierce.
Then the son of Arjuna scattered that elephant-host in its insolence as the ever-moving wind scatters the rain-clouds by the hundred across the sky.
Then Krātha covered the son of Arjuna with showers of arrows; and the other chariot-warriors led by Droṇa, having rallied, brandishing their mightiest weapons, rushed once more upon the son of Subhadrā.
Warding them off with his arrows, the son of Arjuna then in his eagerness to slay tormented the son of Krātha with a measureless flood of shafts.
His two arms with their bow, arrows, and armlets, his head with its diadem, his parasol, his banner, his driver, and his horses — all these he brought down.
When that one — endowed with noble birth, character, learning, strength, renown, and mastery of weapons — was slain, the warriors for the most part turned away from the fight.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the young, unconquered son of Subhadrā had thus entered in, acting worthily of his lineage, never fleeing in battle,
yoked to strong, well-bred three-year-old horses, soaring as if through the sky — what heroes withstood him?
Saṃjaya said: No sooner had Abhimanyu, the delight of the Pāṇḍus, entered in than with his sharp arrows he turned back all your kings.
But Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa together with Bṛhadbala, and Kṛtavarman the son of Hṛdika — these six chariot-warriors encircled him.
But seeing the burden laid too heavily upon the Saindhava, your army, O great king, charged upon Yudhiṣṭhira.
The other great chariot-warriors, drawing bows tall as palm-trees, rained streams of arrows upon the heroic son of Subhadrā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But all those mighty archers, accomplished in every branch of knowledge, the son of Subhadrā, slayer of hostile heroes, held in check with his arrows in the field.
He pierced Droṇa with fifty shafts, Bṛhadbala with twenty, Kṛtavarman with eighty, and Kṛpa with sixty arrows.
With ten arrows, gold-feathered and of great speed, drawn back to the ear, the son of Arjuna struck Aśvatthāman.
And the son of Phalguna, amid the enemy, struck Karṇa upon the ear with a sharp, yellow-tipped barbed arrow, a supreme shaft.
Having felled Kṛpa's horses and both his flanking charioteers, he struck him in return with ten arrows between the breasts.
Then the mighty one slew the hero Vṛndāraka, enhancer of the Kurus' fame, before the very eyes of your valiant sons.
The son of Droṇa let fly twenty-five small arrows at him as he, fearless, broke down the foremost of his foes one after another.
But the son of Arjuna, O sire, swiftly struck Aśvatthāman in return with sharp arrows, before the eyes of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
With sixty arrows, keen-edged, well-sharpened, and fierce, the son of Droṇa pierced him, yet could not make him tremble — like Mount Maināka.
But he of great splendor and strength struck the son of Droṇa, his assailant, in return with seventy-three gold-feathered, straight-flying shafts.
Upon him Droṇa, doting on his son, let fall a hundred arrows, and Aśvatthāman eight more, seeking to shield his father in the fray.
Karṇa loosed twenty-two broad-headed shafts, Kṛtavarman fourteen, Bṛhadbala fifty, and Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat ten.
But the son of Subhadrā, tormented on every side by their sharp arrows, struck back at them all, ten arrows for each.
The lord of the Kosalas struck him in the chest with a barbed arrow; but he brought down to the earth that king's horses, banner, bow, and charioteer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the king of the Kosalas, deprived of his chariot, taking up sword and shield, sought to strike the earringed head from the body of the son of Phalguna.
But he pierced through the heart with an arrow the prince Bṛhadbala, lord of the Kosalas, and with heart cleft asunder that king fell.
And he broke, O king, ten thousand great-souled warriors who bore swords and bows and hurled malign cries against him.
Having thus slain Bṛhadbala, the son of Subhadrā ranged through the battle, holding off your mighty archers and warriors with streams of arrows.
Saṃjaya said: Once more the son of Phalguna struck Karṇa upon the ear with a barbed arrow, and pierced him with fifty shafts, rousing him to great wrath.
The son of Rādhā struck him back with as many again; and with his every limb thickly studded with them, he shone resplendent, O descendant of Bharata.
In his rage he also made Karṇa stream with gushing blood; and Karṇa too, that hero, dappled with arrows and bathed in gore, shone forth.
Both those high-souled warriors, their limbs spangled with arrows and drenched in blood, appeared like two kiṃśuka trees in full flower.
Then the son of Subhadrā slew six valiant attendants of Karṇa, brilliant fighters, together with their horses, drivers, banners, and chariots.
Then, unflustered, he struck the other mighty archers in return, ten arrows for each — and that seemed a marvel indeed.
Then, slaying with six straight-flying arrows the youthful son of the Māgadha king, Aśvaketu, he brought him down together with his horses and his charioteer.
Then with a razor-edged shaft he hewed down the Bhoja of Mārtikāvata, whose banner bore an elephant, and roared aloud as he loosed his arrows.
Then the son of Duḥśāsana pierced his four horses with four shafts, struck his charioteer with one, and the son of Arjuna with ten.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the son of Kṛṣṇā's lord, having pierced the son of Duḥśāsana with seven swift arrows, his eyes red with fury, spoke aloud these words:
"Your father has fled the battle and gone away like a coward; by good fortune you too know how to fight—yet today you shall not escape."
Having spoken these words, he loosed at him an iron shaft burnished by the smith; but the son of Droṇa cut it apart with three arrows.
The son of Arjuna, having cut down his banner, struck Śalya with three shafts; and Śalya struck him in turn with nine vulture-feathered arrows.
The son of Arjuna cut down his banner and both his flanking charioteers, and pierced him with six iron shafts, so that he withdrew to another chariot.
Having slain these five—Śatruṃjaya, Candraketu, Meghavega, Suvarcas, and Sūryabhāsa—he pierced the son of Subala.
Subala's son, having pierced him with three shafts, then said to Duryodhana: "Let us all crush him together, before he destroys us one by one."
Then Karṇa Vaikartana, the bull among men, said to Droṇa: "Before he crushes us all, tell us quickly the means of his slaying."
Then Droṇa, the mighty archer, answered them all: "Does any one of you perceive a single flaw in this youth?
"Behold today the swiftness of this lion among men, this scion of Pāṇḍu, who ranges in every direction even as his father does.
"Along the courses of his chariot only the circle of his bow is seen, as he nocks his shafts and looses them with speed.
"Though he wrenches at my very life-breath and bewilders me with his shafts, this son of Subhadrā, slayer of enemy heroes, gladdens me all the more.
"This son of Subhadrā delights me beyond measure as he ranges through the battle—he whose flaw the furious great car-warriors cannot find.
"As he shoots his great arrows light-handed in every direction, I can see no difference in battle between him and the wielder of Gāṇḍīva."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Karṇa, tormented by the arrows of Arjuna's son, said again to Droṇa: "I hold my ground only because I must, though I am sorely pressed by Abhimanyu.
"The arrows of this fiery youth, most terrible, dreadful, blazing like fire, today waste away my very heart."
To this the preceptor said softly to Karṇa, as if with a smile: "His armor cannot be pierced, and the youth is swift in valor.
"The wearing of armor was taught by me to his father, and this conqueror of hostile cities knows it surely in its entirety.
"Yet his bow can be cut, and his bowstring too, with well-aimed arrows—and likewise his reins, his horses, and both his flanking charioteers.
"Do this, O mighty archer, son of Rādhā, if it can be done; then, having turned him away, strike him afterward.
"While he holds his bow, not even the gods and demons together could vanquish him; so, if you wish, make him chariotless and bowless."
Hearing the preceptor's word, Karṇa Vaikartana made haste, and with his shafts cut the bow of the light-handed archer as he shot.
The Bhoja slew his horses, Gautama his flanking charioteer, while the rest, his bow now severed, overwhelmed him with showers of arrows.
Hastening in the hour of haste, six great car-warriors, pitiless, overwhelmed with showers of arrows that one boy, now chariotless.
His bow cut, his chariot gone, yet upholding his own warrior's duty, the illustrious one, bearing sword and shield, leaped up into the sky.
With the gliding maneuvers called kaiśika and the rest, with lightness and with strength, the son of Arjuna ranged the heavens, much like the king of birds.
"He is falling upon me, sword in hand!"—thus with upturned gaze the mighty archers, watching for an opening in the fight, pierced him.
Droṇa cut off, at the hilt, his sword with its jewel-studded pommel, and the son of Rādhā shattered with his sharp arrows that excellent shield.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bereft of sword and shield, his limbs full of arrows, he came down again from the sky to the earth, and lifting up a chariot-wheel, in his wrath he rushed upon Droṇa.
His limbs shining bright with the dust of the wheel, his wheel-bearing arm raised high, Abhimanyu, that night-born son of Subhadrā, blazed in the battle, imitating the very likeness of Vāsudeva.
His face dyed a single hue by the streaming blood, his brow knit and crooked with frowning, roaring like a great lion—the lord Abhimanyu of measureless strength shone resplendent in battle, set amid the foremost of kings.
Saṃjaya said: That peerless car-warrior, the joy of Viṣṇu's sister, adorned with the weapon of Viṣṇu, shone in the battle like a second Janārdana.
The lords of earth beheld his form—the ends of his hair tossed by the wind, his fine weapon raised against his foes—a form hard to look upon even for the gods.
Sorely alarmed, they cut that wheel apart in many pieces; then the great car-warrior, the son of Kṛṣṇa's sister, seized a great mace.
Stripped by those foes of bow, chariot, and sword, and made wheelless as well, Abhimanyu, mace in hand, rushed upon Aśvatthāman.
Seeing that uplifted mace blazing like a thunderbolt, that bull among men sprang from the floor of his chariot, taking three strides away.
Having slain with his mace that one's horses and both his flanking charioteers, the son of Subhadrā, his body bristling with arrows, appeared like a porcupine.
Then he crushed Kālakeya, the heir of Subala, and slew his followers, seventy and seven Gāndhāras.
Again he slew ten chariot-warriors of the Brahmavasātīyas, and having destroyed seven chariots of the Kekayas and ten elephants, he crushed with his mace the chariot of Duḥśāsana's son together with its horses.
Then the son of Duḥśāsana, enraged, O lord, raised his mace and rushed at the son of Subhadrā, crying, "Stand! Stand!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those two heroes, their maces upraised, each longing to slay the other—cousins both—fell upon one another like Tryambaka and the Ender of old.
Smiting each other with the heads of their maces, those two scorchers of foes fell to the ground in the midst of the battle, like two banners of Indra cast down.
Then the son of Duḥśāsana, that enhancer of the Kurus' fame, rose up first, and struck the son of Subhadrā upon the head with his mace as he was rising.
Stunned by the great force of the mace and by his own exertion, the son of Subhadrā, slayer of enemy heroes, fell senseless to the earth. Thus, O king, was he slain—one against many in the battle.
Having shaken the whole host as an elephant churns a lotus-pond, the slain hero shone even in death, like a wild elephant brought down by hunters.
As that hero lay thus fallen, your warriors surrounded him, as men gather round a fire grown calm at winter's end after it has burned the forest.
He was like the wind grown still after crushing the crowns of trees, like the sun gone to its setting after scorching the host of the Bhāratas;
like the moon overtaken by eclipse, like an ocean run dry—he whose face was as the full moon, whose eyes were framed by curling side-locks.
Beholding him fallen to the earth, your great car-warriors, filled with the highest joy, again and again roared aloud like lions.
Supreme was the gladness of your men, O lord of peoples; but from the eyes of the other heroes the tears came falling down.
The beings in the sky cried out in lamentation, O lord of peoples, beholding the hero fallen, like the moon dropped from the firmament.
"By six great car-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's side, led by Droṇa and Karṇa, this one alone has been slain and now lies dead—this we do not hold to be righteous."
When that hero was slain, the earth shone richly forth, even as the heavens, garlanded with their throng of stars, shine with the full moon.

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
For in the battle the son of Arjuna, having first slain many princes who were like venomous serpents in the fight, followed after them in death at last.
Having slain ten thousand warriors and the great car-warrior of Kosala, the son of Kṛṣṇa's sister, equal to Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, has surely gone to the abode of Śakra.
Having destroyed chariots, horses, men, and elephants by the thousand, unsated still of battle, he is not to be mourned, for he wrought deeds of merit.
"But we, having slain the foremost of them, and ourselves tormented by their arrows, drew near to our camp at evening, drenched in blood."
"Gazing upon the battlefield, we and the foe alike withdrew slowly, O great king, overcome with weariness and bereft of our senses."
Then there came on, inauspicious and loud with the howling of jackals, the wondrous juncture of night and day, as the sun, like a chaplet of lotuses, lingered low and drew near the mountain of its setting.
Stealing away the brightness of fine swords, spears, lances, chariot-guards, shields, and ornaments, and seeming to draw heaven and earth together as one, the sun went to embrace the fire, his beloved form.
With many elephants resembling the peaks of great cloud-mountains, struck down as if by the thunderbolt—their pennons, goads, armor, and drivers with them—lying fallen, the earth seemed to groan, so heaped was she.
With great chariots shattered to pieces—their lords slain, their footmen and gear ground to dust, their horses and drivers killed, their flags and standards gone—the earth shone, O ruler of men, like cities laid waste by the foe.
With throngs of chariots and horses slain with their riders, their trappings and ornaments of every kind flung about, their tongues, teeth, entrails, and eyes torn out, the earth shone with an aspect dreadful and deformed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Men whose armor and ornaments were flung aside, whose fine weapons lay scattered, whose elephants, horses, chariots, and attendants had perished—men ever wonted to costly beds and coverlets—lay slain upon the ground, as though forlorn and masterless.
Exceedingly glad were the dogs, jackals, and crows, the herons and great birds, the wolves and hyenas, the carrion fowl that drink blood, the hosts of rākṣasas, and the fearsome bands of piśācas upon that battlefield.
Tearing through the skin they drank the fat and the blood, and likewise devoured the marrow and the flesh; they ripped away the entrails, laughing and singing as they dragged off the corpses, many at a time.
It bore along masses of bodies, its water was blood, chariots were its rafts, hemmed in by elephants like crags; men's heads were its stones, flesh its mire, and it was garlanded with scattered weapons of every kind.
Set flowing then by the foremost warriors, a river dreadful and uncrossable as the Vaitaraṇī coursed mightily through the midst of the battlefield, terrifying, carrying along the living and the dead.
There the hideous, manifold, most frightful bands of piśācas drank and feasted, rejoicing greatly, terrible to all that breathe, sharing their feast alike with dogs, jackals, and birds.
That battlefield, grim to behold at the onset of night, resembling the realm of the lord of the dead, thronged with risen ghosts and heaps of headless trunks—gazing upon it, the men slowly withdrew.
Then the people beheld Abhimanyu, that great chariot-warrior equal to Śakra, cast down in battle, his precious ornaments fallen away and shattered—like a sacrificial fire in the assembly from which the oblation has been borne off.
Saṃjaya said: When that hero, the son of Subhadrā, leader of chariot-bands, had been slain, all the warriors loosened their chariot-armor and laid down their bows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They sat down, encircling King Yudhiṣṭhira, brooding upon that one grief alone, their minds fixed upon the son of Subhadrā.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, sore stricken with grief, lamented, now that the hero Abhimanyu, his brother's son, that great chariot-warrior, was slain:
Wishing to do me a kindness, he broke through the impenetrable host of Droṇa and entered the battle-array, like a lion into the midst of a herd of cattle.
Before him the brave great archers who faced him in the hostile ranks, accomplished in arms and mad for war, were broken and turned back.
By his arrows Duḥśāsana, our bitterest foe, though he stood to face him in battle, was swiftly stunned and driven to flight.
Having crossed the unfordable great ocean that was Droṇa's host, that hero, the son of Kṛṣṇā, reached Duḥśāsana's son and then went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
How shall I look upon Arjuna, son of Kuntī, now that the son of Subhadrā is slain? Or upon the illustrious Subhadrā, who shall not see her beloved son?
What senseless, incoherent, unfitting words shall we two speak in answer to them both, to Hṛṣīkeśa and to Dhanaṃjaya?
It is I alone who, wishing to please Subhadrā and Keśava and Arjuna, longing for victory, have wrought this grievous wrong.
The greedy man perceives not the faults of his act; from delusion greed arises. Coveting the honey, I did not see this precipice before me.
He who should have been set first at the feast, in carriages, on couches, and in adornments—him, a mere boy, we set foremost in battle.
How could a boy, so young, unskilled in the ways of war, win safety in that perilous press, like a fine horse in a treacherous defile?
Surely we too shall lie down upon the earth beside him, scorched by the pitying glance of Bībhatsu, ablaze with wrath.
Free of greed, wise, modest, forbearing, handsome, strong, well-formed, honoring others, heroic, beloved, devoted to truth—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whose mighty deeds even the gods extol—that valiant one slew the Nivātakavacas and the Kālakeyas.
By him the foes of great Indra who dwelt in Hiraṇyapura, the Paulomas with their hosts, were slain in the mere twinkling of an eye.
That mighty one who grants safety even to strangers who seek it of him—his own son we have not been able to save this day from peril.
A most dreadful fear has come upon the great host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son; Pārtha, enraged at the slaying of his son, will wither the Kauravas away.
Mean himself and mean of allies, Duryodhana, beholding in his anguish the ruin of his own faction, will surely grieve and give up his life.
No victory gladdens me, nor kingdom, nor immortality, nor a place in the world of the gods—seeing him struck down, this matchless one in valor and manhood, the son of the son of the foremost of the gods.
Saṃjaya said: When that day had ended in dread destruction of living things, when the sun had set and the glorious hour of twilight had come,
and the armies had departed to their rest, O bull of the Bhāratas—having slain the bands of the Saṃśaptakas with celestial weapons, the warrior with the ape upon his banner,
Jiṣṇu, mounting that victorious chariot, set out for his own camp; and as he went, with choking voice he spoke to Govinda:
Why is my heart so troubled, Keśava, why does my speech falter, why do ill-boding tremors seize me and my limbs grow faint, O Acyuta?
An evil foreboding clings fast and will not depart from my heart; the fierce portents that show upon the earth and in every quarter affright me.
Of many kinds they appear, and all forebode calamity. May it yet be well with the king, with his counselors, and with my elders!
Vāsudeva said: Surely it shall be well with your brother and his counselors. Grieve not; yet some other misfortune there will be.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Then, having performed their twilight worship, the two heroes, in their grief for heroes, went on mounted in the chariot, recounting what had befallen in the battle.
Then Vāsudeva and Arjuna, having wrought a most arduous deed, reached their own camp, now bereft of joy and bereft of splendor.
Marking the camp's downcast aspect, Bībhatsu, slayer of hostile heroes, his heart now ill at ease, said to Kṛṣṇa:
Today the auspicious instruments raise no joyful sound, Janārdana; no conches mingled with the boom of kettledrums and tabors, nor lutes, are played today with the beat of cymbals and time-keeping clappers.
Nor do the bards in my ranks sing or recite the auspicious, lovely songs full of praise.
And the warriors too, seeing me, turn away with downcast faces, and having done their tasks as before, do not greet me.
May it yet be well today with my brothers, Mādhava; for my mind cannot be eased, seeing my own people in such distress.
May all be whole, O bestower of honor, with the king of the Pāñcālas and with Virāṭa, and with all my warriors, O Acyuta.
And the son of Subhadrā does not, glad among his brothers as is his wont, come forth smiling to meet me today as I return from battle.
Conversing thus, the two entered their own camp, and beheld the Pāṇḍavas, sorely troubled and stricken out of their senses.
Seeing his brothers and his sons, and not seeing the son of Subhadrā, he of the ape-banner, downcast, spoke these words:
The hue of your faces, all of you, is seen to be joyless; I do not see Abhimanyu, nor do you greet me.
I have heard that Droṇa arrayed the wheel-formation, and that among you there was none to break it in battle save the son of Subhadrā.
But the way out of that array had not been taught to him by me. Surely you did not send the boy into the enemy's host?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having broken the foes' array again and again in battle, that great archer, the son of Subhadrā, slayer of hostile heroes—surely he does not lie slain?
Red-eyed, mighty-armed, like a lion born among the mountains, like Upendra himself—tell me, how was he slain on the field?
That tender great archer, the son of the son of Vāsava, ever dear to me—tell me, how was he slain on the field?
That hero, beloved of the Vārṣṇeya woman, ever cherished by me, ever dear to his mother—who, driven by fate, has slain him?
In valor, in fame, in greatness of soul the equal of the lion of the Vṛṣṇis, the high-souled Keśava—how was he slain on the field?
Ever dear to Subhadrā, to Draupadī, and to Keśava—if I do not see my son, I shall go to the abode of Yama.
With soft, curling hair, a youth with the eyes of a young fawn, striding like a maddened elephant, sprung up like a young śāla tree—
Speaking with a smile, self-controlled, ever obedient to his elders' word, even in boyhood doing no boyish deeds, sweet of speech and without envy—
Of great resolve, mighty-armed, with long lotus-petal eyes, compassionate to those devoted to him, self-restrained, and following nothing base—
Grateful, endowed with knowledge, skilled in arms, never turning back, ever delighting in battle, increaser of his foes' woe—
Devoted to the welfare of his own, eager for his fathers' victory, never the first to strike, unflustered in battle—if I do not see my son, I shall go to the abode of Yama.
His fair brow, his fair hair, his lovely eyebrows, eyes, and lips—if I see not that face, what peace can there be for my heart?
His voice, sweet as the sound of strings, lovely, melodious as the male cuckoo's note—if I hear not that voice, what peace can there be for my heart?
That beauty without compare, hard to find even among the gods—if I see not the hero's beauty this day, what peace can there be for my heart?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Skilled in courteous salutation, devoted to the word of his elders—if I do not see him this day, what peace can there be for my heart?
That tender hero, ever fit for the most precious couch—he, surely the best of those who have protectors, now lies upon the bare earth like one forlorn.
He whom of old the loveliest women attended as he lay—him today, his limbs flung wide, the inauspicious she-jackals attend.
He whom of old, when he slept, the bards, heralds, and panegyrists awakened—him today, surely, the beasts of prey awaken with their hideous cries.
That fair face of his, accustomed to the shade of the parasol, the dust of battle will surely cover this day with grime.
Alas, my little son! How, by the working of time, are you torn by force from me—luckless, and never sated with the sight of my son!
Surely the city of restraint, the ever-lovely goal of the virtuous, lit by your own radiance, shines this day exceedingly because of you.
Surely Vaivasvata and Varuṇa, fond of guests, and Śatakratu and the lord of wealth honor you, the fearless one, now that you have come to them.
Having lamented thus in many ways, like a merchant whose ship is wrecked, overwhelmed by great grief, he questioned Yudhiṣṭhira:
Tell me, O son of Pāṇḍu, did that bull among men, having wrought havoc among the foes, go to heaven facing them, fighting in the battle?
Surely, fighting against many straining bulls among men, helpless and craving a helper, he thought of me, of that I am certain.
Tormented by arrows, the boy crying out, 'Father, come quickly to my aid!'—thus lamenting, I think, he was slain by many cruel men.
Yet, born of me, the sister's son of Mādhava too, sprung from Subhadrā—he is not one to speak so.
Surely my heart is made of the very stuff of adamant, so hard that it does not burst, though I see not that long-armed, red-eyed one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
How could those cruel men loose their vital-piercing arrows upon a boy, a great archer, the sister's son of Vāsudeva, my own son?
He who, never downcast in spirit, would ever come forth to greet me with joy as I drew near from slaying the foe—why does he not look upon me today?
Surely he lies fallen upon the earth, drenched in blood, gracing the ground with his limbs, like the sun cast down.
When she hears that he has been slain in battle, Subhadrā, stricken with grief, will surely perish. Not seeing Abhimanyu, what will she say to me? And Draupadī too, anguished with sorrow—what shall I say to them both?
Surely my heart is made of the hardness of the thunderbolt, that it does not shatter into a thousand pieces when I behold the young bride weeping, wasted away with grief.
I heard the lion's roar of the exultant sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Yuyutsu too was heard by Kṛṣṇa, reproaching their warriors.
"Unable to face Bībhatsu, you great chariot-warriors who slew a mere boy—why do you roar, you who know nothing of dharma? Let your strength be shown against Pārtha himself!"
"Having wrought this outrage against Keśava and Arjuna in battle, why do you roar like lions in delight, when an hour of grief is upon you?"
"Swiftly the fruit of your evil deed will come upon you. A grievous unrighteousness has been done—how should it stay fruitless for long?"
Thus speaking against them, the high-minded son of the vaiśya woman cast aside his weapon and departed, filled with wrath and sorrow.
"Why, Kṛṣṇa, was this told to me in the field? Else I would have burned them all then—those cruel great chariot-warriors."
Restraining him as he was overwhelmed by anguish for his son, Vāsudeva—Kṛṣṇa—said "Not so!" to him who was filled with bitter grief.
"This is the path of all heroes who never turn back—above all of kṣatriyas, whose livelihood is war."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This is the destiny ordained by those who know the law for heroes who fight and never retreat, O best of those who attain their goal."
"Death in battle is certain for heroes who never turn back. Abhimanyu has gone to the worlds of those who have done meritorious deeds—of this there is no doubt."
"And this is the very wish of all heroes, O bull of the Bhāratas: 'May we meet death face to face in battle,' O giver of honor."
"And he, having slain mighty heroes and princes in the field, has attained the death longed for by heroes, fronting it in battle."
"Grieve not, O tiger among men. This is the eternal law made by the righteous men of old: that the kṣatriyas should perish in battle."
"All these your brothers are downcast, O best of the Bhāratas, while you are overwhelmed by grief—and so are the kings, your friends."
"Comfort them with gentle words, O giver of honor. You know what is to be known; you ought not to give way to grief."
Thus consoled by Kṛṣṇa of wondrous deeds, Pārtha then spoke to all his brothers, who were choked with sobs.
That long-armed, broad-shouldered one, with eyes like long lotus-petals, said: "How Abhimanyu fell—just so I wish to hear it."
"You shall behold my son's foes slain by me in battle, together with their elephants, chariots, and horses, and all their kinsmen."
"How, with all of you accomplished in arms and weapons in hand, could the son of Subhadrā meet his death—he who could withstand even the wielder of the thunderbolt?"
"Had I known that the Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas were thus unable to protect my son, he would have been guarded by me."
"And how, while you stood in your chariots loosing showers of arrows, was Abhimanyu brought to his death, you being set at naught by the foe?"
"Alas, there is no manhood in you, nor any valor, since Abhimanyu was struck down in the battle before your very eyes."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Nay, I should blame myself, that knowing you so feeble, so timid and untrained in toil, I yet went forth and left you."
"Or were your armor, weapons, and arms worn only for ornament, and your speeches only to be uttered in assemblies—since you did not guard my son?"
Having spoken these words, Bībhatsu stood there, the bearer of the bow and sword, and no one could bear to look upon him.
He was like Death enraged, sighing again and again, scorched by grief for his son, his face filled with tears.
His friends could neither speak to Arjuna nor even look upon him—none save Vāsudeva and the eldest son of Pāṇḍu.
Those two, devoted to Arjuna's welfare in all conditions and dear to his heart—they alone, through his high regard and love, were fit to address him.
Then to him, his mind sorely tormented by grief for his son, the lotus-eyed one in his wrath, the king spoke these words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When you had gone, O mighty-armed one, against the host of the Saṃśaptakas, the teacher made a fierce effort to take me captive.
We held Droṇa back on every side as he marshaled his battle-array, arraying our own host of chariots against him as he strove in the fight.
Though held off by the chariot-warriors who guarded me, he swiftly smote even us, harrying us with his whetted shafts.
So hard pressed by Droṇa, we could not even gaze upon Droṇa's array in the battle—how then could we break it?
Then all of us said to your son, the son of Subhadrā, peerless in valor: "Dear child, break the array, O lord!"
Thus urged by us, that valorous one, like a noble steed, set himself to bear even that unbearable burden.
Endowed with your instruction in arms and with his own prowess, the boy entered that host as Suparṇa plunges into the sea.
We followed that hero, the son of the Sātvata princess, into the fray, eager to enter by the very breach through which he had pierced the host.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the king of the Sindhus, the base Jayadratha, dear child, by a boon granted of Rudra held us all back.
Then Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, Bṛhadbala, and Kṛtavarman—six chariot-warriors—surrounded the son of Subhadrā.
Hemmed in by all those great chariot-warriors, the boy, striving to the utmost of his strength, was deprived of his chariot by their many hands.
Then the son of Duḥśāsana, when he had thus been swiftly stripped of his chariot and brought to utter peril, dispatched him to his appointed end.
But he had slain thousands of riders on elephants, horses, and chariots, a full hundred foremost princes, and many unnamed heroes,
and having sent King Bṛhadbala to heaven in the fight—then that one of supremely righteous soul met his appointed end.
This is all that has befallen us, swelling our grief; and so that tiger among men has attained the world of heaven.
Saṃjaya said: Then Arjuna, hearing the words spoken by the Dharma-king, sighed "Alas, my son!" and, stricken, fell to the ground.
With downcast faces all of them clasped Dhanaṃjaya, and, wretched, gazed upon one another with unblinking eyes.
Then the son of Vāsava, regaining his senses, swooning with rage, trembling as if in a fever and sighing again and again,
wringing hand in hand, breathing hard, his eyes streaming with tears, glaring about him like a madman, spoke these words:
"Truly I vow to you: tomorrow I shall be the slayer of Jayadratha—unless, frightened by fear of death, he abandons the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
and unless he seeks refuge with us, or with Kṛṣṇa the supreme being, or with you, O great king—tomorrow I shall be the slayer of Jayadratha!
That doer of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's pleasure, who has forgotten his friendship toward me, the wicked one who was the cause of the boy's death—tomorrow I shall be the slayer of Jayadratha!

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And whoever shall fight against me while guarding him in the battle—even the heroes Droṇa and Kṛpa—those I shall cover over with my arrows.
"If I do not accomplish this thus in the battle, O bulls among men, may I not attain the worlds of the righteous, honored by heroes—
those worlds that are for slayers of mothers, for killers of fathers, for those who violate the teacher's wife, and for slanderers,
and for those who revile the good, and for backbiters, and for those who steal what is left in trust, and for betrayers of confidence;
the worlds of those who revile a woman they have once enjoyed, of speakers of evil, of slayers of brahmins, and of killers of cattle as well;
the worlds of those who eat in vain milk-pudding or barley-food, vegetables, or rice-and-sesame, wheat-cakes, baked sweets, or meat—into those very worlds may I go this day, if I do not slay Jayadratha.
"Those worlds to which a man goes who scorns a diligent student of the Veda, a steadfast and best of brahmins, the aged, the good, and his teachers—
the destiny one earns by touching a brahmin, a cow, or the fire with one's foot, the destiny of those who cast phlegm, ordure, or urine into the waters—to that dreadful destiny may I go, if I do not slay Jayadratha.
"The destiny of one who bathes naked, of one whose guest departs unfed, the destiny of takers of bribes, of liars, and of deceivers, the destiny of those who give themselves false airs and of those who bear false witness—
the destiny of the mean who, watched by their servants and dependents, their sons and wives, eat dainty food without sharing—to that dreadful destiny may I go, if I do not slay Jayadratha.
"He who, cruel of soul, forsakes a good man who has taken refuge with him and is devoted to his word, fails to support him, and reviles his benefactor;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
he who gives no funeral offering to a worthy neighbor, and gives it instead to the unworthy, and the husband of a śūdra woman—
the drunkard, the breaker of bounds, the ingrate, the reviler of his brother—their destiny may I swiftly come to, if I do not slay Jayadratha.
"And the others fallen from dharma whom I have not named here, and those whom I have named—may I swiftly attain their destiny, if, when this night has passed, I do not slay Jayadratha tomorrow.
"And hear this further vow of mine besides: if the sun should go down while this wicked one is yet unslain, here on this very spot I shall enter the blazing fire.
"Asuras, gods, or men, birds or serpents, the fathers or the night-roamers, the brahmā-seers or the divine seers, all that moves and all that moves not, and whatever is beyond even that—none of these is able to guard that foe of mine from me.
"Though he enter the uttermost depths of the netherworld, or the sky, or the city of the gods, or the city of Diti—even there, at daybreak, with hundreds of arrows, falling fiercely upon him, I shall strike off my foe's head."
Having spoken thus, he drew the Gāṇḍīva to left and right; and surpassing his very voice, the twang of the bow touched the heavens.
When Arjuna had taken his vow, Janārdana, sorely wrathful, blew his conch Pāñcajanya, and Dhanaṃjaya his Devadatta.
That Pāñcajanya, its sound bursting forth from its well-filled belly through the breath of Acyuta's mouth, set the whole world trembling—with its netherworlds, its sky, and the guardians of the quarters—as at the ending of an age.
Then the sounds of instruments arose on every side, and the lion-roars of the Pāṇḍavas, when the great-souled one had taken his vow.
Saṃjaya said: But hearing that mighty uproar of the Pāṇḍavas who were grieving for the boy, and informed of it there by his spies, Jayadratha rose up,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
his heart bewildered with grief, sorely smitten by sorrow, like one sinking in a fathomless, vast ocean of woe.
The lord of the Sindhus went, pondering much, to the assembly of the kings, and there in the presence of those god-like rulers he made his lament.
Fearful of Abhimanyu's father, abashed, he spoke these words: "That one who was begotten, they say, in Pāṇḍu's field by Śakra in his desire—
"that evil-minded one means, they say, to lead me alone to the abode of Yama. Therefore, fare you well—I shall go to my own home, in my longing to live.
"Or, if you are strong enough to save me, O bulls among kṣatriyas, then, heroes, grant me—whom Pārtha has marked for death—your protection."
Droṇa, Duryodhana, and Kṛpa, Karṇa, the lord of the Madras, and Bāhlika, Duḥśāsana and the rest are able to rescue even one beset by Death himself.
How much more, then, when it is a single Phalguna who seeks to slay me — could you not protect me, you lords of the earth, all together?
Hearing the exultation of the Pāṇḍavas, great is my fear, O kings; my limbs grow faint, as though I were a man about to die.
Surely my slaying has been vowed by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, for the Pāṇḍavas, even in a time of grief, shout aloud in their joy.
Neither gods nor gandharvas, nor asuras, serpents, or rākṣasas, dare to make it otherwise — how then could kings of men?
Therefore grant me leave, and may it be well with you, O bulls among men; I shall pass out of sight, where the Pāṇḍavas will not see me.
As he lamented thus, his mind distraught with fear, King Duryodhana, weighing the gravity of his own purpose, spoke to him.
You must not fear, O tiger among men; for who, O bull among men, would assail you in battle as you stand amid the kṣatriya heroes?
I myself, and Karṇa the son of Vikartana, Citrasena, Viviṃśati, Bhūriśravas, Śala, Śalya, and the unassailable Vṛṣasena;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Purumitra, Jaya, the Bhoja, and Sudakṣiṇa of the Kāmbojas, the mighty-armed Satyavrata, Vikarṇa, Durmukha, and Saha;
Duḥśāsana and Subāhu, and the Kaliṅga too, weapons upraised, Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, Droṇa, Droṇa's son, and the son of Subala —
and you yourself the best of chariot-warriors, a hero of boundless splendor — how then, O lord of the Sindhus, do you look in fear upon the Pāṇḍavas?
Eleven akṣauhiṇīs of mine, intent upon your protection, shall stand in battle — fear not, O lord of the Sindhus, let your terror depart.
Reassured thus, O king, by your son, the lord of the Sindhus, together with Duryodhana, went by night to Droṇa.
Having paid homage to Droṇa, O lord of peoples, and seating himself near him in reverence, he then asked this:
In taking aim, in striking from afar, in swiftness of hand, in piercing firmly — let the blessed one tell me the difference between myself and Phalguna.
I wish to know in truth, O teacher, the difference in skill between Arjuna and myself; declare it to me, O lord, exactly as it is.
Droṇa said: The instruction you received was the same, my child, as Arjuna's; yet through diligent practice and through being inured to hardship, Arjuna is therefore superior to you.
But you must feel no terror in battle on Pārtha's account in any way; for I shall be your protector from danger, my child — of this there is no doubt.
For against one guarded by my arm not even the immortals can prevail; and I shall array that battle-formation which Pārtha will not break through.
Therefore fight, and fear not; uphold your own duty, and follow the path of your fathers and forefathers, O ruler of men.
Having studied the Vedas as ordained, having duly fed the sacred fires, and having worshiped with many sacrifices, you need have no fear of death's terror.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having attained great good fortune, hard for feeble mortals to win, you shall reach the celestial, unsurpassed worlds, earned by the valor of your arms.
The Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, the Vṛṣṇis and other men, and I too together with my son — let it be considered that all are impermanent.
Each in his turn, all of us, struck down by mighty Time, shall pass to the other world, attended each by his own deeds.
Those worlds which ascetics attain by practicing austerity — those same worlds the heroic kṣatriyas attain who cleave to the warrior's duty.
Saṃjaya said: Reassured thus, O king, by the son of Bharadvāja, the lord of the Sindhus drove away his fear of Pārtha and set his mind upon battle.
Saṃjaya said: When Pārtha had vowed the slaying of the king of the Sindhus, then the mighty-armed Vāsudeva addressed Dhanaṃjaya.
Without learning the mind of your brothers, you have pledged with your word, 'Tomorrow I will slay the lord of the Sindhus' — a most reckless thing you have done.
Without taking counsel with me, this excessive burden has been taken up; how shall we not become a laughingstock to all the world?
Spies I had posted in the camp of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son — these, coming swiftly, now report to us the tidings.
When you had vowed the slaying of the king of the Sindhus, then a mighty lion-roar, mingled with instruments, was heard by them here.
Terrified by that sound, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with the Saindhava took their stand, judging, 'This lion-roar is not without cause.'
A vast clash of sound arose among the Kauravas, O mighty-armed one — of elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers — and the terrible din of chariots.
'Having heard of Abhimanyu's slaying, surely Dhanaṃjaya in his anguish will sally forth this very night in wrath' — so judging, they stood ready.
By them, as they made ready, this truthful vow of yours, the truthful one, for the slaying of the king of the Sindhus was heard, O lotus-eyed one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then dejected, all of them, trembling like little deer, were Suyodhana's counselors, and King Jayadratha as well.
Then rising up with his counselors, downcast, the lord of the Sauvīras and the Sindhus, sorely grieved, came to his own tent.
In the hour of counsel, having deliberated upon all the measures that might serve his welfare, he spoke these words to Suyodhana in the assembly of kings:
'Branding me the slayer of his son, Dhanaṃjaya will march against me tomorrow; for in the midst of the army he has vowed my death.'
'That vow of Savyasācin, neither gods nor gandharvas, nor asuras, serpents, or rākṣasas dare to make otherwise.'
'Therefore guard me in the battle, lest Dhanaṃjaya, setting his foot upon your heads, attain his mark; let provision for this be made.'
'But if no protection is granted me in the fray, O delight of the Kurus, then give me leave, O king — I shall return to my home.'
Addressed thus, Suyodhana, his head bowed and his spirit cast down, hearing that you had pronounced this dread oath, fell to brooding.
Looking upon him so distressed, the king, the lord of the Sindhus, then spoke these words, gentle, mindful of his own welfare, and full of longing for aid:
'I see among you no bowman of such prowess as could ward off Arjuna's weapon with his own weapon in the great battle.'
'When he has Vāsudeva for his ally and brandishes the Gāṇḍīva bow, who could stand before Arjuna — even Śatakratu himself in person?'
'Even Maheśvara, it is told, was fought of old by Pārtha — the lord of mighty radiance, by one on foot, upon the Himālaya mountain.'
'Thousands of dānavas, dwellers in the City of Gold, he slew with a single chariot, urged on by the king of the gods.'
'Joined with the wise Vāsudeva, the son of Kuntī could destroy the three worlds together with their gods — such is my conviction.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'So I desire either to be given leave, or to be protected by the great-souled hero Droṇa together with his son — if you think it good.'
By the king himself the teacher was earnestly implored, O Arjuna; and so the arrangement was made, and the chariots, it is said, were made ready.
Karṇa, Bhūriśravas, Droṇa's son, the unconquerable Vṛṣasena, and Kṛpa, and the king of the Madras — these six were his vanguard.
A half-formation shaped as a cart and a lotus was devised by Droṇa; and stationed at the heart of the lotus, within the needle's eye, the king of the Sindhus, Jayadratha, would stand, guarded by warriors mad for battle.
In bow, in weapon, in valor, in life-breath, and in steadfast chest, these six chariot-warriors are deemed most irresistible, O Pārtha; and without conquering them and their hosts, Jayadratha cannot be reached.
Consider one by one the valor of those six; for those tigers among men, united, cannot easily be conquered.
And I shall further devise a policy for my own welfare, together with counselors skilled in deliberation and with friends, for the achievement of the end.
Arjuna said: The six chariot-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son whom you reckon superior in strength — their valor, I judge, is not equal to even half of mine.
The weapon of every one of these, O slayer of Madhu, you shall see shattered by my own weapon, as I seek the slaying of Jayadratha.
Before the very eyes of Droṇa and his host, lamenting though they be, I shall bring down the head of the king of the Sindhus upon the earth.
If the Sādhyas and the Rudras, the Vasus together with the Aśvins, and the Maruts with Indra, the Viśvedevas, and the asuras as well;
the fathers together with the gandharvas, the great birds, the oceans and the mountains, the heaven, the firmament, and this earth, and the quarters with their guardian lords;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the creatures of village and forest, things that stand fast and things that move — if all these become protectors of the king of the Sindhus, O slayer of Madhu —
even then you shall see him slain tomorrow by my shafts in battle; by truth I swear it to you, Kṛṣṇa, and so I lay my hand upon my weapon.
And that great bowman who guards that wicked, evil-minded one — against him, against Droṇa first, I shall advance, O Keśava.
Upon him Suyodhana has staked this game; therefore, breaking through the very front of his host, I shall press on toward the Saindhava.
You shall see tomorrow the great bowmen, with my keen-edged iron shafts, cleft asunder by me in battle, like the peaks of a mountain by thunderbolts.
From the bodies of men, elephants, and horses, falling and fallen, riven by sharp arrows, the blood shall stream forth.
The arrows sped from the Gāṇḍīva, swift as the mind and the wind, shall by the thousand leave men, elephants, and horses bereft of life.
The dread weapons that I have received from Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, Rudra, and Indra — those men shall behold in battle.
And with the brāhma weapon you shall see the weapons of all the protectors of the Saindhava struck down by me in the fight.
With the heads of kings shorn off by the rush of my arrows, you shall see the earth strewn over by me tomorrow in battle, O Keśava.
I shall sate the flesh-eaters, I shall put my foes to flight, I shall gladden my friends, and I shall lay low the Saindhava.
A doer of many wrongs, of evil kinship, sprung from a sinful land — slain by me, the king of the Sindhus shall set his own kin to mourning.
Eaters of every milk-rich food, evil in conduct, the Sindhus together with their king, driven by my arrows on the field of battle, shall perish.
At dawn I shall so act, Kṛṣṇa, that Suyodhana shall reckon no other bowman in the world to be my equal in battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Gāṇḍīva is a celestial bow, and I am the warrior, O bull among men, and you are my charioteer, Hṛṣīkeśa — what then could remain unconquered by me?
As surely as there is the mark upon the moon, and as surely as there is water in the sea, so surely know this vow of mine to be true, O Janārdana.
Slight not my weapons, slight not my firm bow, slight not the strength of my arms, slight not Dhanaṃjaya.
As surely as, having gone into battle, I am not vanquished but conquer — by that truth know Jayadratha already slain in the fray.
Truth dwells assured in the Brāhmaṇa, humility assured in the good, prosperity assured in the able, and victory assured in Nārāyaṇa.
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Arjuna, the son of Vāsava, roaring aloud, charged his own self by his own resolve and addressed the lord Keśava.
"When night has brightened into dawn, let my chariot be made ready. So must you act, Kṛṣṇa, for a great deed is now undertaken."
Saṃjaya said: Through that night Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya, stricken with grief and sorrow, hissing like serpents, found no sleep at all.
Knowing Nara and Nārāyaṇa to be enraged, the gods together with Vāsava grew troubled and pondered: "What now is to come of this?"
Harsh and savage winds blew, foreboding terror, and across the face of the sun there was seen a headless trunk and an iron bar.
Dry thunderbolts fell with crashing peals and lightning, and the earth trembled with its mountains, woods, and forests.
The oceans, abodes of sea-monsters, were churned into uproar, great king, and the rivers that flow to the sea began to run backward against their current.
Chariots, horses, men, and elephants were turned upside down, for the delight of the flesh-eaters and the swelling of Yama's realm.
The draught-animals let fall their dung and urine and wept aloud; and beholding all these dreadful, hair-raising portents—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
—all your troops were filled with dismay, O bull of the Bhāratas, hearing the fierce vow of the mighty Savyasācin.
Then the mighty-armed son of the Chastiser of Pāka said to Kṛṣṇa: "Console your sister Subhadrā, and her daughter-in-law with her."
"Set the daughter-in-law and her mother-in-law, the blameless ones, free of grief, Mādhava; with gentle, true, and fitting words console them, O lord."
Then Vāsudeva, sore at heart, went to Arjuna's dwelling and consoled his grieving sister, stricken with sorrow for her son.
"Grieve not for the boy, daughter of the Vṛṣṇis, you and your daughter-in-law; for all living beings, O timid one, this is the end appointed by Time."
"For a hero born in a noble line, and most of all a Kṣatriya, such a death is befitting; grieve not for your son."
"By good fortune the heroic great warrior, equal in valor to his father, has by the law of the Kṣatriyas attained the goal that heroes long for."
"Having conquered foes in great numbers and sent them to their death, he has gone to the imperishable worlds of the doers of good, that yield every desire."
"That goal which the good seek through austerity, through chastity, through sacred learning and through wisdom—that goal your son has attained."
"You are the mother of a hero, the wife of a hero, kinswoman to heroic fathers-in-law; grieve not for your son, good lady, for he has gone to the highest goal."
"And that base Saindhava, the slayer of a boy, shall reap the fruit of his insolence, he together with his band of friends and kinsmen."
"When the night has passed, O fair-hipped one, that doer of evil deeds shall not escape Pārtha, even though he enter Amarāvatī itself."
"Tomorrow you shall hear that the head of that Saindhava has been struck off in battle, cast beyond Samantapañcaka. Be free of grief; weep not."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Holding the law of the Kṣatriya foremost, the hero has gone to the goal of the good—the goal which we too may attain, and others who live by the sword."
"Broad-chested, mighty-armed, never turning back, humbler of the foremost foes—your son, O fair-hipped one, has gone to heaven. Cast off your fever of grief."
"Taking after his father and his mother's line, the valiant one, having slain enemies by the thousand, the heroic great warrior was himself slain."
"Console your daughter-in-law, O lady; grieve not so deeply, O Kṣatriya woman. Tomorrow, hearing tidings most welcome and great, you shall be free of grief, O joyful one."
"What Pārtha has vowed shall be so and not otherwise; for what your brother resolves to do can never come to nothing."
"Even if men and serpents, demons, night-rovers, and birds, gods and antigods, should rush to the side of the king of Sindhu in battle, he shall be no more, nor they with him, when morning comes."
Saṃjaya said: Having heard these words of the great-souled Keśava, Subhadrā, stricken with grief for her son and sorely afflicted, lamented aloud.
"Alas, my son! How is it that, going into battle, you who were equal to your father in valor have met your end, dear child, son of luckless me?"
"How is it that your face, dark as the blue lotus, with fine teeth and lovely eyes, is now seen, my darling, veiled in the dust of battle?"
"Surely they now look upon you, the hero fallen, who never turned back—fair of head, neck, arms, and shoulders, broad-chested, lean of belly—"
"—every limb beautifully formed, fair-eyed, strewn with weapon-wounds; surely the creatures gaze upon you as upon the risen moon."
"You whose couch was once spread with coverlets to be envied—how do you lie today upon the bare ground, flung down, you who were used to comfort?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The hero, mighty-armed, once waited upon by the loveliest of women—how is it that he, fallen in battle, is today waited upon by jackals?"
"He who was once praised by joyful bards, heralds, and minstrels is today attended by dreadful, howling packs of flesh-eaters."
"With the Pāṇḍavas for your protectors, O mighty one, and the heroes of the Vṛṣṇis and the heroes of the Pāñcālas—by whom were you slain, as though you had no protector at all?"
"Never sated with the sight of you, my blameless son, I, ill-fated, shall surely go today to the realm of Yama."
"Wide-eyed, fair-haired at the temples, sweet of speech and fragrant—when, my son, shall I look again upon your unwounded face?"
"A curse upon the strength of Bhīmasena, a curse upon Pārtha among the bowmen, a curse upon the prowess of the Vṛṣṇi heroes, and a curse upon the might of the Pāñcālas!"
"A curse upon the Kekayas, the Cedis, the Matsyas, and the Sṛñjayas, who knew not that you, the hero, had gone into the fray and been struck down."
"Today, not seeing Abhimanyu, with eyes troubled by grief, I behold the earth as if empty, its splendor put out."
"Sister's son of Vāsudeva, son of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva—how shall I look upon you, the hero, robbed of your chariot and brought down by others?"
"Alas, hero, seen and then lost, you are to me like wealth in a dream! Ah, how fleeting is human life, unsteady as a bubble on the water!"
"This your young wife, overwhelmed with grief for you—how shall I sustain her, like a cow bereft of her calf?"
"Ah, you have set forth out of season, my little son, forsaking me—who longed so to see you—at the very time of harvest."
"Surely the course of Fate is hard to fathom even for the wise, since you, with Keśava for your protector, were slain in battle as though protectorless."
"That goal which belongs to performers of sacrifice, to the charitable, to the Brāhmaṇas of perfected souls, to those who have kept the vow of chastity and have bathed at holy fords—"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"—to the grateful, the generous, those devoted to the service of their elders, and those who give the thousandfold sacrificial fee—that goal may you attain."
"That goal which belongs to heroes fighting on and never turning back, who slay their foes and are themselves slain in battle—to that goal go."
"That goal which is the givers' of a thousand cows and of the offerings of sacrifice, that blessed goal of those who bestow a cherished dwelling—"
"—that goal which sages of strict vows reach through chastity, and which faithful wives of a single husband reach—to that goal go, my little son."
"That everlasting goal which comes to kings by their good conduct, and to those of the four life-stages, purified and well-guarded by their meritorious deeds—"
"—that goal of those who pity the wretched, who ever share what they have, and who have turned away from slander—to that goal go, my little son."
"That goal of those true to their vows, of righteous nature, devoted to the service of their elders, who never turn a guest away in vain—to that goal go, my little son."
"That goal of the high-minded who go to their own wives only in the proper season and never resort to the wives of others—to that goal go, my little son."
"That goal of those, free from envy, who approach all beings with gentleness, who wound no one and are forbearing—that goal may you attain."
"That goal of those who abstain from wine and flesh, who have renounced pride, hypocrisy, and falsehood, and the tormenting of others—to that goal go, my little son."
"That goal which the good attain—the modest, the masters of all the scriptures, content in knowledge, with senses subdued—to that goal go, my little son."
As Subhadrā lamented thus, forlorn and wasted with grief, the Pāñcāla princess, together with Virāṭa's daughter, then came to her side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having wept their fill and lamented in deep distress, those women, like ones gone mad, fell senseless to the ground, O king.
But Kṛṣṇa, himself sorely grieved, tended to her in her sorrow, sprinkling water upon her and reviving her, speaking now this, now that, kindly word.
To his sister—well-nigh senseless, weeping, fallen prostrate and trembling—the lotus-eyed one spoke these words:
"Subhadrā, grieve not for your son; with the Pāñcāla princess console Uttarā. Abhimanyu, that bull among Kṣatriyas, has gone to the renowned goal."
"And whatever other men there are in our line, O fair-faced one—may they all attain the goal of the glorious Abhimanyu."
"May we, and our friends as well, perform such a deed as your son, the lone great warrior, has wrought this day."
Having thus consoled his sister, and Draupadī and Uttarā as well, the mighty-armed subduer of foes returned to Pārtha's side.
Then the lord Kṛṣṇa, taking leave of the kings and the kinsmen, entered the inner apartments, O king, while the others went each to his own quarters.
Saṃjaya said: Then the lotus-eyed lord entered Arjuna's peerless dwelling, and having touched water, spread upon an auspiciously marked patch of cleared ground a fair bed of darbha grasses that gleamed like beryl.
