With sharp shafts fledged with heron feathers, O honored one, Arjuna swiftly brought down the horses of that struggling foe; and Pārtha, having sheared his bow apart with other arrows, pressed onward.
But the Ambaṣṭha chief, seizing his mace, his eyes clouded with wrath, fell upon Pārtha in battle and upon Keśava, that great chariot-warrior.
Then that hero, laughing aloud, O Bhārata, raised his mace and, blocking the chariot, smote Keśava with it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing Keśava struck by the mace, Arjuna, slayer of hostile heroes, blazed into utter fury against the Ambaṣṭha chief, O Bhārata.
Then with golden-shafted arrows he covered that best of chariot-warriors, mace and all, even as a cloud veils the risen sun in battle.
Then with still other arrows Pārtha smashed to powder the mace of that great-souled warrior; and the deed seemed a marvel.
Then, seeing that mace fallen, he caught up another mighty mace and struck again and again at Arjuna and Vāsudeva.
With two razor-edged arrows Arjuna severed both his upraised arms—shaped like Indra's banner—that still held the mace, and with a third feathered shaft his head.
Slain, he fell, O king, making the earth resound, like Indra's banner-pole let go when the fastenings of its mechanism are loosed.
Plunged deep within the chariot-ranks and ringed by hundreds of elephants and horses, Pārtha then appeared like the sun shrouded by clouds.
Saṃjaya said: Then, when the son of Kuntī had broken through Droṇa's division and the well-nigh impassable division of the Bhojas, bent on slaying the king of the Sindhus,
and when, O king, Sudakṣiṇa, heir of the Kāmboja, had been slain, and the valiant Śrutāyudha laid low by Savyasācin,
with the troops fleeing apart and shattered on every side, your son, seeing his own host broken, went up to Droṇa.
Hastening up on a single chariot, he came to Droṇa and said: "That tiger among men has passed through, after crushing this great army of ours."
"Consider now with your wisdom what must next be done to thwart Arjuna in this dreadful slaughter of men."
"Contrive it so that Jayadratha, that tiger among men, be not slain—blessings upon you—for you are our highest refuge."
"Yonder Dhanaṃjaya-fire, driven by the wind of his wrath, burns the dry brush of my army, like a blaze risen amid the thicket."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For now that the son of Kuntī has burst through the army and passed beyond, O scorcher of foes, the guardians of Jayadratha have fallen into the gravest doubt."
"Firm had been the conviction of the lords of men, O best of the knowers of Brahman, that Dhanaṃjaya could never while living pass beyond Droṇa."
"Yet that Pārtha has passed through before your very eyes, O resplendent one; all this host I now reckon stricken—it is no longer an army of mine."
"I know you, O greatly blessed one, to be devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas; and so I am bewildered, O Brahman, when I ponder what is to be done."
"To the best of my power, O Brahman, I provide for your every want and please you as I am able; yet this you do not heed."
"Though we are ever devoted to you, O you of measureless prowess, you do not wish us well; you forever favor the Pāṇḍavas, who delight in our undoing."
"Living off us, you yet take pleasure in what harms us; I had not understood you to be like a razor smeared with honey."
"Had you not granted me a boon for the curbing of the Pāṇḍavas, I would never have stopped the lord of the Sindhus when he was going home."
"But I, in my folly, hoping for protection from you, reassured the lord of the Sindhus, and so, deluded, have delivered him over to death."
"A man caught between the fangs of Yama might yet escape; but Jayadratha, fallen into Arjuna's power, will never escape from the battle."
"So act, O you of the red steeds, that the Saindhava be saved; and be not angered at the laments of one in anguish—save the Saindhava."
Droṇa said: I take no offense at your words; to me you are as Aśvatthāman. But I shall tell you the truth—accept it, O lord of peoples.
Kṛṣṇa is a peerless charioteer, and his fine horses are swift; making but a small opening, Dhanaṃjaya passes through in an instant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Do you not see the floods of Kirīṭin's arrows, loosed as he speeds swiftly on, falling fully a krośa behind his chariot?
And I, weighed down with years, am no longer fit for swift pursuit today; moreover, this force of the Pārthas stands here at the army's front.
And Yudhiṣṭhira is to be seized by me before the eyes of all the bowmen—thus have I vowed amid the kṣatriyas, O mighty-armed one.
Left behind by Dhanaṃjaya, he now stands before me; therefore I will not abandon the front of the array to go after Phalguna.
Go yourself, with comrades at your side, and fight that single foe, your equal in birth and in deeds; have no fear—you are the lord of this world.
You are a king, brave, accomplished, and skilled, and have stirred up enmity with the Pāṇḍavas; go yourself, O hero, swiftly to where Dhanaṃjaya has gone.
Duryodhana said: When Dhanaṃjaya, the best of all who bear arms, has passed even beyond you, how, O teacher, am I able to hold him off?
Puraṃdara, the thunderbolt-wielder himself, might be conquered in battle, but Arjuna, conqueror of hostile cities, cannot be conquered in war.
He by whose blaze of weapons the Bhoja, the son of Hṛdika, and you yourself—a peer of the gods—were vanquished, and Śrutāyus struck down;
by whom Sudakṣiṇa was slain, and King Śrutāyudha, and Śrutāyus and Acyutāyus, and the mlecchas slain in their hundreds—
how shall I fight against that unassailable Pāṇḍava in battle, who consumes so many of his foes? Tell me this, O master of weapons.
If you deem battle with him fitting for me today, then direct me; I am at your bidding, your servant—guard my honor.
Droṇa said: You speak truly, O Kaurava—Dhanaṃjaya is hard to assail. Yet I shall so contrive it that you will be able to withstand him.
Let all the bowmen in the world behold today a marvel: the son of Kuntī held fast in combat with you, while Vāsudeva looks on.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Behold, O king, I bind upon you a golden corselet, so fashioned that neither arrows nor missiles shall prevail against you in battle.
Though the gods with the asuras, with the yakṣas, serpents, and rākṣasas, and the three worlds together with men should war against you, you have nothing to fear.
Neither Kṛṣṇa, nor the son of Kuntī, nor any other bearer of arms in battle shall be able to lodge his shafts in this corselet of yours.
So, donning this corselet, go yourself in haste this day against the wrathful Arjuna in battle, and he shall not withstand you.
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus, Droṇa, in haste, touched water and bound on that most wondrous, gleaming corselet, murmuring the sacred formula in due form.
In that vast battle, for your son's victory, that foremost knower of Brahman, wishing to astonish the world with his lore, did so.
Droṇa said: May Brahmā grant you well-being, and the twice-born grant you well-being; and from those that are foremost among creeping things, well-being to you, O Bhārata.
May Yayāti and Nahuṣa, Dhundhumāra and Bhagīratha, and all the royal sages in every way work your well-being.
Well-being be yours from the one-footed and from the many-footed alike, and well-being from the footless ones, ever, in the great battle.
May Svāhā, Svadhā, and Śacī ever work your well-being; may Lakṣmī and Arundhatī make for your well-being, O sinless one.
May Asita and Devala, Viśvāmitra and Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa work your well-being, O king.
May Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, the Lord of the world, and the quarters with their guardians grant you well-being this day, and six-faced Kārttikeya as well.
May the blessed Vivasvān work your well-being in every way, and the four elephants of the quarters, the earth, the sky, the firmament, and the planets.
And he who from below forever upholds the earth, O king—that Śeṣa, foremost of serpents—may he grant you well-being.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O prince of Gāndhāra, of old the noblest of the gods, advancing in battle, were vanquished by the daitya Vṛtra, their bodies torn open in their thousands.
All the dwellers of heaven then, robbed of their splendor and strength, with Indra at their head, took refuge in Brahmā, in terror of Vṛtra, that great asura.
The gods said: To the gods crushed by Vṛtra, O noblest of deities, be a refuge, O best of the gods; save us from this great peril.
Droṇa said: Then to Viṣṇu, who stood at his side, and to Śakra and the other foremost gods—those noblest deities, downcast—Brahmā spoke this true word.
"The gods, with Indra and the twice-born, are ever to be protected by me. Most hard to withstand is the energy of Tvaṣṭṛ, by which Vṛtra was fashioned."
"By Tvaṣṭṛ of old, after he had practiced austerity for a hundred times ten thousand years and gained the leave of Maheśvara, was Vṛtra fashioned, O gods."
"That mighty foe can be slain only by His grace; yet the blessed Hara cannot be beheld without going to Śaṃkara's abode."
"Having beheld Him, you shall slay the foe; go quickly to Mandara, where dwells the source of all austerities, the destroyer of Dakṣa's sacrifice, the bearer of the Pināka, lord of all beings, who struck down Bhaga's eye."
The gods, going together with Brahmā to Mandara, beheld a mass of radiance bright as ten million suns.
He said: "Welcome, O gods; tell me what I am to do. The sight of me is never in vain; let your desire be fulfilled thereby."
Thus addressed, all those dwellers of heaven answered Him: "Our splendor has been carried off by Vṛtra; be the refuge of the dwellers of heaven."
"Behold our bodies, O god, battered to pieces by his blows; we have come to you for refuge—be our recourse, O Maheśvara."
Maheśvara said: I know, O gods, how this conjured being, of vast might and terrible, sprung from the energy of Tvaṣṭṛ, is hard for the unperfected of soul to ward off.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But surely I must render aid to all the dwellers of heaven. Take, O Śakra, this gleaming corselet born of my own body, and bind it on, O lord of the gods, with this mind-born formula.
Droṇa said: Having spoken thus, the boon-giver bestowed that armor together with its sacred spell; and guarded by that armor he went forth against the host of Vṛtra.
Though floods of weapons of every kind were hurled down upon it in the great battle, the seam of that armor's binding could not be sundered.
Then the lord of the gods himself slew Vṛtra in battle, and that armor with its spell-wrought binding he gave to Aṅgiras.
Aṅgiras imparted it to his son Bṛhaspati, knower of the spell; and Bṛhaspati in turn declared it to the wise Agniveśya.
Agniveśya bestowed it upon me, and with it, O best of kings, I now bind on your armor with the spell, this day, for the guarding of your body.
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus to your son, Droṇa of mighty splendor, that bull among teachers, softly addressed him with these further words.
With the thread of Brahman I bind on your cuirass, O king, even as Hiraṇyagarbha bound it on Viṣṇu of old in battle.
And as in the war over Tārakā the celestial cuirass of Śakra was bound on by Brahmā, so do I bind on yours.
Having bound on his cuirass with the spell according to rite, the brāhmaṇa sent forth the king to the great combat.
Thus arrayed for war by the great-souled teacher, that mighty-armed one set out, attended by a thousand chariots of the smiting Trigartas,
and by a thousand rut-maddened, valor-flush elephants, by a myriad of horses, and by other great car-warriors as well.
Surrounded thus, the mighty-armed one advanced toward Arjuna's chariot amid the din of many instruments, even as the son of Virocana once marched forth.
Then arose a mighty clamor from your armies, O Bhārata, as they beheld the Kaurava host setting forth, fathomless as the ocean.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: When the Pārtha and the Vārṣṇeya had entered the field, O great king, and when Duryodhana, that bull among men, had set out behind them,
the Pāṇḍavas together with the Somakas rushed upon Droṇa with great speed and a mighty roar, and then the battle was joined.
That battle between the Pāñcālas and the Kurus before the array grew terrible, tumultuous, hair-raising, and wondrous to behold.
O king, never had we seen, nor ever heard of, such a battle as raged when the sun stood at midheaven, O lord of peoples.
The Pārthas, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, their ranks marshaled and ready to strike, all together overwhelmed Droṇa's host with showers of arrows.
We, placing Droṇa at our head, that best of all who bear arms, rained shafts upon the Pārthas led by the son of Pṛṣata.
Like two great clouds risen up with mingling winds at winter's end, the two hosts shone resplendent at the van, gleaming and adorned with chariots.
Meeting, the two great armies wrought a surpassing onrush, like the rivers Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the rains, swollen with turbulent waters.
With manifold weapons for its forward gale, thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, its lightning the maces, terrible and vast, rose the great storm-cloud of battle.
Driven up by the wind that was the son of Bharadvāja, bearing a thousand torrents of arrows, that most terrible cloud rained down upon the surging fire of the Pāṇḍava host.
As a dread great wind blowing at the close of the hot season churns the sea, so did that best of brāhmaṇas throw the ranks of the Pāṇḍavas into turmoil.
They too, with every effort, charged straight at Droṇa, like mighty floods of water seeking to breach a great dam.
But Droṇa held them back, as a mountain holds back the floodwaters—the wrathful Pāṇḍavas in battle, and the Pāñcālas with the Kekayas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then other kings as well, wheeling about on every side—mighty and heroic in battle—turned to check the Pāñcālas.
Then in the battle that tiger among men, the son of Pṛṣata, together with the Pāṇḍavas, struck again and again at Droṇa, seeking to breach the enemy's host.
Even as Droṇa rained showers of arrows upon the son of Pṛṣata, so did Dhṛṣṭadyumna rain showers of arrows in return.
With swords for its forward gale, thronged with spears, darts, and lances, the bowstring its lightning and the twang of bows its thunder, rose the storm-cloud that was Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
He loosed torrents of arrows like a hail of stones in every direction, and striking down floods of chariots, horses, and the best of warriors, he covered the host.
Whatever band of Pāṇḍava chariots Droṇa assailed with his shafts, from that very place the son of Pṛṣata drew Droṇa off with his arrows.
But while Droṇa strove thus in the fight, O Bhārata, his army, on encountering Dhṛṣṭadyumna, was split into three.
Some turned toward the Bhoja, others toward Jalasaṃdha, while still others, smitten by the Pāṇḍavas, fled straight to Droṇa.
And whatever ranks Droṇa, that best of car-warriors, mustered together, those Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the great car-warrior, scattered apart.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, broken into three, were slain by the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas, like cattle without a herdsman in the forest set upon by many beasts of prey.
"Time itself is devouring the warriors, bewildered by Dhṛṣṭadyumna in that tumultuous battle"—so did men believe.
As the realm of a wicked king is harried by famine, sickness, and thieves, so was your host beset and driven into ruin by the Pāṇḍavas.
As the sun's rays broke and flashed upon the weapons and the cuirasses, the eyes of the soldiers were dazzled and struck blind by that glare and by the dust.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When his armies, split in three, were being slaughtered by the Pāṇḍavas, Droṇa, unable to bear it, then scattered the Pāñcālas with his shafts.
As he crushed those ranks and struck them down with his arrows, the form of Droṇa became like the blazing fire of doomsday.
Chariot and elephant and horse, and the foot-soldiers too, O lord of peoples—each one the great car-warrior pierced through with a single arrow in the fray.
Among the armies of the Pāṇḍavas there was not one, O Bhārata, who could withstand in battle the keen arrows loosed from Droṇa's bow.
Scorched by the sun and seared by Droṇa's shafts, the host of the son of Pṛṣata reeled and wandered here and there, O Bhārata.
And so too your force, harried by the son of Pṛṣata, blazed up on every side, like a dry forest set ablaze by fire.
As the armies were cut down by the shafts of Droṇa and of the son of Pṛṣata, the soldiers, abandoning all thought of their lives, fought on with the utmost of their strength.
Among your men and the foe alike as they fought, O bull of the Bhāratas, there was not one, great king, who forsook the battle out of fear.
Bhīmasena, the son of Kuntī, his own brothers hemmed in—Viviṃśati, Citrasena, and Vikarṇa the great car-warrior,
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, and the valiant Kṣemadhūrti—these three came as followers of those three sons of yours.
The splendid king of the Bāhlīkas, nobly born and a great car-warrior, with his army and his counselors, held back the sons of Draupadī.
Govāsana, the Śaibya king, with no fewer than a thousand warriors, held back the valiant son of Abhibhū, the king of Kāśi.
Ajātaśatru, the son of Kuntī, blazing like fire—him, the king, did Śalya, lord of the Madras, hold in check.
But the unforbearing Duḥśāsana, having set his own division in array, advanced in wrath against Sātyaki, that hero and best of car-warriors, in the fight.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I myself, with my own division, clad in fastened mail, with four hundred mighty archers, held Cekitāna in check.
And Śakuni with his division held back the son of Mādrī, with seven hundred Gāndhārakas armed with bows, darts, arrows, and swords.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti assailed Virāṭa of the Matsyas; those two great archers, ready to lay down their lives, rose up in battle for their friend's sake.
Śikhaṇḍin, the son of Yajñasena, unconquered and pressing forward to bar the way—him the valiant did Bāhlika, fully arrayed, hold in check.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna the Pāñcāla, together with the fierce Prabhadrakas—him, raging in form, the king of Avanti with the Sauvīras held back.
The heroic Ghaṭotkaca, that rākṣasa and cruel fighter, advancing in wrath upon the field—Alāyudha swiftly rushed against him.
Alambusa, that lord of rākṣasas, raging in form—Kuntibhoja, the great car-warrior, joined by a mighty host, held in check.
The lord of the Sindhus stood at the rear of the whole army, O Bhārata, guarded by supreme archers, by Kṛpa and the other car-warriors.
Two mightiest guardians of his wheels had the lord of the Sindhus: the son of Droṇa on his right, O king, and the son of the sūta on his left.
And as guardians of his rear there were, led by the son of Somadatta, Kṛpa and Vṛṣasena, Śala and the unconquerable Śalya.
Wise in policy, mighty archers, all skilled in war—having thus arranged the protection of the lord of the Sindhus, they did battle then.
Saṃjaya said: O king, hear of the wondrous battle as I recount it—how the combat of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas came to pass.
Coming upon the son of Bharadvāja stationed at the front of the array, the Pārthas fought him in battle, seeking to breach Droṇa's division.
Guarding their own array, the soldiers of Droṇa likewise fought the Pārthas in battle, longing for great renown.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti struck Virāṭa with ten arrows, those two well-roused and seeking the welfare of your sons.
And Virāṭa, O great king, sallying forth in valor, gave battle to those two valiant ones stationed in the fray, together with their followers.
Their battle grew terrible, its waters running with blood, like the strife of a lion with two rut-streaming chief elephants in the forest.
Bāhlika, furious in the fight, the mighty son of Yajñasena struck with sharp, dreadful, barbless shafts that cleave the vitals and the bone.
And Bāhlika, sorely enraged, smote the son of Yajñasena hard with nine gold-shafted, stone-whetted arrows with bent knots.
That battle grew terrible, thick with arrows and spears, breeding terror in the timid and swelling the joy of the brave.
By the arrows loosed from those two, the sky and the quarters there were all so covered over that nothing whatever could be discerned.
Govāsana the Śaibya, with his host, gave battle to the great car-warrior, the son of Kāśi, as one elephant fights against another.
The king of the Bāhlīkas, enraged, fighting the great car-warriors who were the sons of Draupadī in the battle, shone like the mind contending with the five senses.
And they fought him fiercely with floods of arrows on every side, even as the objects of sense forever assail the body, O best of the embodied.
Sātyaki of the Vṛṣṇis your son Duḥśāsana struck in the fight with nine sharp arrows with bent knots.
Sorely pierced by that strong, mighty archer and bowman, Sātyaki of true valor swiftly sank into a faint for a while.
But the Vārṣṇeya, recovering himself, swiftly pierced your son, that great car-warrior, with ten heron-feathered arrows.
Each having pierced the other deeply, each gashed by the other's shafts, the two of them shone in the battle, O king, like two kiṃśuka trees in full bloom.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Alambusa, enraged and tormented by Kuntibhoja's arrows, gleamed with surpassing splendor, like a kiṃśuka rich with blossoms.
Then that demon, having pierced Kuntibhoja with many iron shafts, roared a fearsome roar at the head of your army.
Then all beings beheld those two heroes contending against each other in the battle, as once they beheld Śakra and Jambha of old.
And the two sons of Mādrī, furious in the fray, O Bhārata, tormented with their arrows the impetuous Śakuni, who had wrought enmity against them.
From that source, O great king, arose this destruction of men—begotten in full measure by you, and swollen yet greater by Karṇa.
And the fire of wrath was fanned to flame by your son—that fire which, O king, rose up to consume this whole earth.
Turned to flight by the arrows of the two sons of Pāṇḍu, Śakuni could no longer find any feat of valor to perform in the fight.
And seeing him put to flight, the two great warriors, the sons of Mādrī, rained their arrows upon him again, as two clouds upon a great mountain.
Struck down by many smooth-jointed arrows, the son of Subala sped away on his swift horses toward Droṇa's division.
Ghaṭotkaca likewise advanced upon the valiant rākṣasa Alāyudha, impetuous in battle, taking up a moderate speed.
The combat between those two, O great king, took on a marvelous aspect, like that which long ago passed in the fray between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
Then king Yudhiṣṭhira, having pierced the king of the Madras in battle with fifty arrows, pierced him again with seven.
Then there arose between those two a most wondrous combat, O lord of men, like the great battle of old between Śambara and the king of the gods.
Viviṃśati, Citrasena, and your son Vikarṇa, surrounded by a great host, gave battle to Bhīmasena.
Saṃjaya said: When that hair-raising battle was thus joined, the Pāṇḍavas fell upon the Kauravas, who had divided themselves into three.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The mighty-armed Bhīmasena held back Jalasaṃdha, while Yudhiṣṭhira with his host checked Kṛtavarman in the battle.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O great king, rushed in the fray upon Droṇa, who, pouring forth showers of arrows, shone like the radiant sun.
Then a battle arose between all those eager bowmen, the Kurus and the Somakas, each enraged against the other.
While that fearful carnage was thus going forward, the armies, paired off in single combats, fought on fearlessly.
Mighty Droṇa, contending with the mighty son of Pāñcāla, hurled torrents of shafts; it was a thing of wonder to behold.
Droṇa and the Pāñcāla strewed the heads of men in multitudes all around, like beds of white lotuses laid waste on every side.
Scattered all about among the ranks lay the garments, ornaments, and weapons of the heroes, their banners, armor, and arms.
With bodies adorned in bright gold and drenched in blood, they appeared like masses of clouds clinging together, lit with lightning.
The great warriors, drawing bows as tall as palm trees, felled elephants, horses, and men in the battle with their winged shafts.
Swords and shields, bows, heads, and coats of mail were scattered abroad in the onslaught of those great-souled heroes.
Countless headless trunks, risen upright on every side, were seen, O great king, in that utmost tumult.
Vultures, herons, kites, hawks, crows, and jackals, and many other flesh-eating creatures, were seen there, O honored one.
They devoured the flesh and drank the blood, and tore away the hair and marrow in many ways, O king.
They dragged about the corpses, and the severed limbs, and the heads of multitudes of men, horses, and elephants, hither and thither.
The skilled archers, consecrated by the vows of battle and bearing their arrows, fought fiercely then, longing for victory in the fray.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Your warriors plied many kinds of sword-strokes in the battle, with double-edged swords, lances, javelins, pikes, darts, and tridents.
Others, with maces and iron bars, and some even weaponless with bare arms, smote one another in their fury, those men come to the arena of war.
Car-warriors closed with car-warriors, horsemen with horsemen, mighty elephants with mighty elephants, and foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers.
Others, as if drunk and frenzied, like minstrels upon the stage, shouted aloud at one another and slew one another in the battle.
As that lawless battle was being waged, O lord of the people, Dhṛṣṭadyumna mingled his own horses with the horses of Droṇa.
Those horses, swift as the wind, shone splendidly thus commingled; dove-colored and blood-red, the steeds in that encounter gleamed, O king, like clouds shot through with lightning.
And the hero Dhṛṣṭadyumna, seeing Droṇa come close at hand, cast aside his bow and took up sword and shield, O Bhārata.
The son of Pṛṣata, slayer of hostile heroes, resolved to perform a difficult feat, and stepping across the chariot-pole, he mounted into Droṇa's car.
He stood in the midst of the yoke and upon the lashings of the yoke, and struck at the flanks of the horses; the armies applauded that deed.
As he ranged about with his sword, treading upon the red horses, Droṇa could find no opening against him; it was a thing of wonder.
As the swoop of a hawk greedy for flesh in the woods, so was his onset as he sought to slay Droṇa.
Then Droṇa shattered with a hundred shafts the hundred-mooned shield of Drupada's son, and his sword with ten arrows.
And the mighty one slew his horses with sixty-four arrows, and with two broad-headed shafts struck down his banner and his parasol and both his flank-charioteers.
Then in haste he loosed at him another arrow, a bringer of death, drawn back full to the ear, as the wielder of the thunderbolt hurls his bolt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sātyaki cut that arrow apart with fourteen arrows, and so released Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who had been seized by the foremost of preceptors.
As a deer seized by a lion, so was the Pāñcāla seized by that lion among men, Droṇa; and the bull of Śini's line, that lion among men, set him free, O honored one.
Seeing Sātyaki the protector of the Pāñcāla in that great battle, Droṇa swiftly assailed him with twenty-six arrows.
Then the grandson of Śini struck back at Droṇa, who was as if devouring the Sṛñjayas, piercing him in the breast with twenty-six sharp arrows.
Then, when the Sātvata had thus assailed Droṇa, all the Pāñcāla car-warriors, eager for victory, swiftly delivered Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that arrow had been cut down and Dhṛṣṭadyumna had been set free by that foremost hero of the Vṛṣṇis, by Yuyudhāna, O Saṃjaya—
—what did that great archer Droṇa, the tiger among men, foremost of all bearers of arms, filled with indignation, do against the grandson of Śini in the fight?
Saṃjaya said: Rushing forward, his venom of wrath upraised, his bow a gaping mouth, his teeth the keen-edged arrows, his fangs the whetted iron shafts—
—his eyes red with fury and resentment, hissing like a great serpent, with his red horses of great speed, rejoicing among heroic men—
—as though leaping up to the sky, as though striding over all things, he sped upon Yuyudhāna, hurling gold-feathered arrows.
With its great downpour of falling arrows, with the rumble of chariots for its thundercloud, scattered abroad by the drawing of bows, lit with the lightning of its many iron shafts—
—bearing spears, swords, and bolts, risen up in the rush of his wrath, that irresistible cloud of Droṇa, driven on by the wind of his horses.
Seeing him bearing down thus, the heroic grandson of Śini, conqueror of hostile cities, mad with the lust of battle, said to his charioteer, laughing aloud:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This cruel brahmin, who keeps not to his own appointed duty, the refuge of king Dhārtarāṣṭra, the bringer of sorrow and fear—
"—drive swiftly forth with hastening horses, joyfully, to meet this preceptor of the princes, who ever deems himself a hero."
Then the excellent horses of the Mādhava, silver-bright and swift as the wind, advanced quickly to face Droṇa.
Then there came a dreadful, unbroken darkness, veiled by a net of arrows, that seemed unassailable to all other heroes.
Then, between Droṇa and the Sātvata, those two lions among men skilled in swift weaponry, no gap could be seen in the showers of their arrows.
From the clashing together of the arrows there arose a sound, born of the striking of their streams, that was heard like the roar of thunderbolts loosed by Śakra.
The aspect of the arrows pierced deeply by the iron shafts shone forth, O Bhārata, like that of serpents bitten by venomous snakes.
The dreadful clamor of their bowstrings and palm-guards was heard unceasingly, as of mountain-peaks struck again and again by the thunderbolt.
The chariots of both, O king, their horses and their charioteers, covered with gold-feathered arrows, then shone forth in wondrous forms.
Most terrible, O lord of the people, was the falling together of those bright, straight iron shafts, that gleamed like venomous serpents loosed from their sloughs.
The parasols of both were struck down, and likewise both their banners fell; both had their limbs bathed in blood, and both were eager for victory.
With their limbs streaming blood, like two elephants in rut, they pierced each other with arrows that bring life to its end.
The roars, the shouts, the clamor, and the sound of conches and drums fell silent, O great king; no one spoke a word.
The hosts fell still, the warriors ceased from fighting, and the people, filled with wonder, gazed upon the single combat of those two.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Car-warriors, elephant-drivers, horsemen, and foot-soldiers, encircling those two bulls among chariot-fighters, looked on with unwavering eyes.
The divisions of elephants stood still, and so the divisions of horse, and the chariot-columns too stood ranged in their array.
With banners bright with pearl and coral and adorned with gems and gold, with brilliant ornaments and golden coats of mail,
with victory-pennons and flags, with caparisons and body-cloths, with bright and whetted weapons, and with the tail-fans of the horses,
and with frontlets of gold and silver upon the brows of the elephants, and the wreaths upon their temple-bosses and the bands about their tusks, O Bhārata—
—they appeared, with their cranes and fireflies, with their rainbows and lightnings, like the gathering nets of clouds in the season of heat.
Both our men and the followers of Yudhiṣṭhira stood and watched that combat of Yuyudhāna and of the great-souled Droṇa.
The gods, with Brahmā and Śakra at their head, borne aloft in the foremost of celestial cars, and the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, the Vidyādharas and the great serpents,
At the wondrous, weapon-shattering passes—advances, recoils, and feints of every kind—shown by those two lions among men, the onlookers were filled with amazement.
Displaying the deftness of their hands in the wielding of weapons, those two mighty warriors, Droṇa and Sātyaki, pierced each other with their shafts.
Then, O lord of great splendour, the Dāśārha swiftly cut apart Droṇa's arrows in the fray with his own well-feathered shafts, and severed his bow as well.
In the mere blink of an eye Bhāradvāja strung another bow, but that too Sātyaki swiftly cut to pieces.
Then in haste Droṇa stood once more with bow in hand; yet each time he strung it, Sātyaki cut it asunder again with his keen shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, O king of kings, beholding in the combat the more-than-human feat of Yuyudhāna, Droṇa pondered thus in his heart:
"Such mastery of weapons as is found in this best of the Sātvatas was found only in Rāma, in Kārtavīrya, in Dhanaṃjaya, and in Bhīṣma, that tiger among men."
And Droṇa, that best of the twice-born, honoured his valour in his heart, beholding a deftness like Vāsava's own.
That foremost of those skilled in arms was well pleased, and so too were the gods together with Vāsava; yet for all their swiftness they could not discern the lightness of his hand.
The gods, O lord of peoples, and the Gandharvas, and the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, marked well that feat of Yuyudhāna and of Droṇa alike.
Then, taking up another bow, Droṇa, the crusher of warriors, that foremost of those who know weapons, did battle with his missiles, O Bhārata.
Sātyaki, beating back his missiles by the magic of his own weaponry, struck him with keen arrows—and that was a thing of wonder.
Beholding that more-than-human feat of his, unmatched by any other in the battle and joined with practised skill, your own men, who knew such skill, gave him their praise.
Whatever missile Droṇa hurled, that very missile Sātyaki hurled in turn; yet the preceptor, scorcher of foes, fought on undismayed.
Then, O great king, wrathful, that master who had reached the far shore of the science of archery raised a celestial weapon to slay Yuyudhāna.
Marking that terrible foe-destroying Āgneya weapon, that mighty archer raised in answer the celestial Vāruṇa weapon.
A great cry of dismay went up at the sight of the two wielders of celestial arms, and the very creatures that move through the sky ceased to range the heavens.
Those two weapons, of Varuṇa and of Agni, loosed by the pair upon their arrows, did not yet clash together—and meanwhile the sun began to decline.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, and Nakula and Sahadeva, closed round Sātyaki to guard him.
And led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa together with the Kekayas, the Matsyas, and the host of the Śālveyas, came straight upon Droṇa.
Setting Duḥśāsana at their head, the king's sons by the thousand hastened to the aid of Droṇa, who was hemmed in by his foes.
Then, O king, a battle was joined between your bowmen and theirs, while the world was shrouded in dust and overspread with a netting of arrows.
All became confusion; nothing could be made out at all; and with the host smothered in dust the fighting raged on past all bounds.
Saṃjaya said: As the sun wheeled on, the soldiers there, blinded by the sun's rays and bestrewn with dust, grew faint and slack.
For those who stood firm, who fought on, who turned back again, who broke and fled, and who conquered, that day passed slowly away.
While the armies were thus locked together, greedy for victory, Arjuna and Vāsudeva pressed on straight toward the Saindhava.
With his keen shafts the son of Kuntī cleared there a path wide enough for a chariot, along which Janārdana drove.
Wherever the chariot of the great-souled Pāṇḍava went, O lord of peoples, there your armies were torn asunder.
And the valiant Dāśārha displayed his mastery of the chariot, tracing wheeling courses high and low and midway.
Those shafts, marked with his name, yellow, like the fire of doom, bound with sinew, well-jointed, broad, and far-flying—
shafts made of reed and of iron, well-drawn, of many-fashioned heads—drank, along with the birds of the air, the blood of living creatures in the fray.
The arrows that Arjuna, standing upon his car, loosed when foes were a krośa off—by the time his chariot had crossed that krośa, were striking down those very enemies.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With horses swift as Tārkṣya and the wind, well-trained to draw, Hṛṣīkeśa drove onward, filling the whole world with wonder.
Not so swiftly, O lord of peoples, moves the chariot of the Sun, nor of Indra, nor of Rudra, nor even of Vaiśravaṇa,
nor, O king, has the chariot of any other ever gone in battle as went the car of Arjuna, swift as the speeding of thought.
Plunging into the battle, O king, Keśava, slayer of hostile heroes, swiftly urged the steeds into the midst of the host, O Bhārata.
Then, having reached the midst of that flood of chariots, those noble horses, beset by hunger, thirst, and weariness, drew the car only with great labour.
Wounded by many weapons of the war-drunk foe, again and again they wheeled through their wondrous circling courses.
By the thousand they passed over the slain—horses and elephants and chariots together with their men—heaped up like hills.
At this juncture, O king, the two heroic brothers of Avanti, with their armies, fell upon the Pāṇḍava, whose horses were now wearied.
Filled with eager joy, the two pierced Arjuna with sixty-four arrows, Janārdana with seventy, and the horses with a hundred.
Those two, O great king, Arjuna in his wrath struck in the battle with nine smooth-jointed shafts, vital-piercing arrows loosed by one who knew the vital spots.
Then the two, enraged, covered Bībhatsu together with Keśava beneath a flood of arrows, and roared aloud their lion's roar.
But he of the white steeds swiftly, with two broad-headed shafts, cut apart their gleaming bows in the fight, and their standards bright with gold.
Then, O king, taking up other bows in the combat, the two, fiercely enraged, tormented the Pāṇḍava with their arrows.
But the son of Pāṇḍu, exceedingly wrathful, with two arrows swiftly cut their bows apart once again—Dhanaṃjaya did.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then with other golden-shafted, stone-whetted arrows he swiftly slew their horses and the footmen with them, and the flanking charioteers of both.
And with a razor-edged shaft he severed the elder's head from his body; slain, he fell to the earth like a tree shattered by the wind.
Seeing Vinda slain, the mighty and valorous Anuvinda left his horseless chariot and took up his mace.
Remembering his brother's slaughter, that foremost of mace-wielders, that great chariot-warrior, rushed forward in the battle, mace in hand, as though dancing.
Anuvinda in his wrath struck the slayer of Madhu upon the brow with his mace, yet shook him no more than one might shake Mount Maināka.
With six arrows Arjuna shore off his neck, his feet, his arms, and his head; thus dismembered, he fell like a heap of mountain crags.
Then, O king, seeing those two slain, their followers rushed forward in fury, showering arrows by the hundred.
Swiftly slaying them with his shafts, O bull of the Bhāratas, Arjuna shone forth like a fire that has burnt up a forest at winter's end.
Passing through the army of those two and emerging from it with hard labour, Dhanaṃjaya shone like the risen sun breaking through the clouds.
Beholding him, the Kurus were stricken with fear, then took heart again, O bull of the Bhāratas, and rained their shafts on Pārtha from every side.
Marking that he was wearied, and knowing the Saindhava still far off, they hemmed him in on all sides with a mighty lion's roar.
Seeing them in their high fury, that bull among men, Arjuna, smiling, spoke softly these words to the Dāśārha:
"The horses are wounded by arrows and spent, and the Saindhava is still far off. What course seems best to you to be taken next?
Tell me truly, Kṛṣṇa, for you are ever the wisest of all; with you as their guide the Pāṇḍavas shall surely conquer their foes in battle here.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As for what I must do next, hear it from me: unyoke the horses and ease them, and draw the arrows from their flesh, O Mādhava."
Thus addressed by Pārtha, Keśava answered him: "This too is my own mind, O Pārtha, even as you have spoken."
Arjuna said: "I will hold off all the armies, Keśava; and you, meanwhile, do here in due order what next must be done."
Saṃjaya said: Then, descending undismayed from the floor of his chariot, Dhanaṃjaya took up the Gāṇḍīva bow and stood unshaken as a mountain.
The warriors, longing for victory, rushed shouting upon him, judging this their opening, since Dhanaṃjaya now stood upon the ground.
With a great array of chariots they encircled him alone, drawing their bows and loosing their arrows.
In their wrath they displayed there their many wondrous weapons, veiling Pārtha with arrows as the clouds veil the sun.
With great force the warriors, lordly upon their cars, rushed upon that bull among warriors, that lion among chariot-fighters, as rutting elephants rush upon a lion.
Then was seen the mighty strength of Pārtha's two arms, in that, enraged, he held off the numerous armies from every side.
Warding off the weapons of his foes with his own weapons on every hand, the mighty one swiftly enveloped them all with his many shafts.
There in the middle air, O lord of peoples, from the friction of the densely massed arrows there arose a great blazing fire.
There on every side, with mighty bowmen panting and bathed in blood, with horses and elephants gashed and screaming and harrowing their foes—
and with furious heroic foes, craving victory in the fray, gathered many in one place and enraged—there arose as it were a scorching heat.
Its waves were arrows, its whirlpools banners, its crocodiles elephants—hard to cross; thick with footmen for its fish, resounding with the blare of conches and kettledrums—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
numberless and shoreless, its dust a fearful murk; covered over with turbans for its tortoises, garlanded with foam of fluttering pennons—
that unfathomable ocean of chariots, strewn with the bodies of elephants for its rocks—Pārtha, become its very shore, held back with his feathered shafts.
Then in the battle the mighty-armed Janārdana, unperturbed, spoke these words to Arjuna, his beloved, that best of men:
"There is no well here for the horses upon the battlefield, Arjuna; they crave water to drink, yet not for bathing."
Saying calmly, "Here it is," Arjuna smote the earth with a weapon and made a fair lake for the watering of the horses.
With a lattice of arrows, with pillars of arrows, with a wondrous roof of arrows, Pārtha fashioned a chamber of arrows, like Tvaṣṭṛ the worker of marvellous deeds.
Then Govinda laughed and cried, "Well done! Well done!" when Pārtha had fashioned that house of arrows there in the midst of the great battle.
Saṃjaya said: When that water had been brought forth by the great-souled son of Kuntī, when the enemy host had been held off and the house of arrows wrought,
Vāsudeva of great splendour swiftly dismounted from the chariot and unyoked the horses, pierced as they were by heron-feathered shafts.
Beholding that thing never seen before, a mighty lion-roar arose on every side from the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas and from the soldiers.
Yet those bulls among men could not hold back the son of Kuntī as he fought on foot — and that was as if a marvel.
Though floods of chariots came rushing on, thick with elephants and horses, Pārtha was not dismayed — and this surpassed all other men.
Those kings loosed floods of arrows against the Pāṇḍava, yet the righteous son of Vāsava, slayer of hostile heroes, did not falter.
Those nets of arrows, those maces and javelins that came upon him, the valiant Pārtha swallowed up as the ocean swallows the rivers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With the great speed of his weapons and the strength of his arms, Pārtha swallowed up the finest shafts of all those lords of kings.
That prowess of both Pārtha and Vāsudeva, O great king, the Kauravas extolled as utterly wondrous.
What greater marvel has ever been in the world, or shall ever be, than that Pārtha and Govinda should unyoke their horses in the very midst of battle?
Those two best of men struck vast fear into us and displayed their fierce energy, wholly unconcerned at the very front of the fray.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, smiling, as though amid women, O Bhārata, when Arjuna had made that inner chamber of arrows on the field,
The lotus-eyed one, untroubled, led those horses round, before the very eyes of all your hosts, O lord of peoples.
Their fatigue and faintness, their trembling, their retching, their wounds — all of it Kṛṣṇa drove away, skilled as he was in the handling of horses.
Drawing out the barbs with his hands and rubbing down those horses, he turned them about in due order and gave them the water to drink.
Then, well pleased, he yoked them once more to that finest of chariots — watered, washed, fed, and freed of weariness.
Then Śauri of great splendour, foremost of all who bear arms, mounted that excellent chariot together with Arjuna and swiftly drove on.
Seeing the chariot of that best of warriors yoked with horses now watered, the foremost of the Kuru host grew downcast once again.
Hissing, O king, like serpents whose fangs are broken, they each cried out, "Shame, oh shame! Pārtha and Kṛṣṇa have slipped away!"
Before the eyes of all the warriors, those two mailed in armour, with a single chariot, made our might contemptible, as though it were a child's plaything.
While we cried out and strove against them, those two scorchers of foes, untouched, displayed their valour and passed on through all the kings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing the two pressing on again, other soldiers then cried, "Make haste, all you Kurus, to slay Kṛṣṇa and the Diademed One!"
"For the Dāśārha, having yoked the chariot before the eyes of all the bowmen, drives on toward Jayadratha, making mock of us in battle!"
There some of the kings spoke among themselves, O king, beholding in that battle that great marvel never seen before:
"All these hosts, and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra too, are come to ruin; through Duryodhana's offence the whole warrior race and the entire earth,
"have come to dissolution, and yet the king does not perceive it." Thus did the warriors there speak, and others too, O Bhārata.
"Whatever rites are due for the king of the Sindhus, now gone to Yama's abode, let Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son perform — he of vain vision, ignorant of the means."
Then the Pāṇḍava drove faster still toward the Saindhava, as the fierce-rayed sun was sinking, with horses now glad and watered.
The warriors could not hold back that mighty-armed one, foremost of all who bear arms, as he drove on like Death enraged.
Then the Pāṇḍava, tormentor of foes, having scattered the host, churned it up for the Saindhava's sake as a lion churns a herd of deer.
Plunging into the ranks, the Dāśārha swiftly urged on the crane-coloured horses and made Pāñcajanya resound.
The arrows loosed in front by the son of Kuntī fell behind him, so swiftly — faster than fast — did those wind-swift horses bear him on.
Beholding that terrible ape-bannered chariot, its pennon tossing in the wind, rumbling like a thundercloud, the chariot-warriors fell into despair.
And as the sun was thickly veiled on every side by dust, the warriors, sore beset by arrows, could not even look upon the two Kṛṣṇas in the fight.
Then the kings, enraged, encircled Dhanaṃjaya, and many other warriors as well, as he sought the slaying of Jayadratha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While the barbs were being drawn out, Duryodhana came hastening against Pārtha, that steadfast bull among men, in the great battle.
Saṃjaya said: The very marrow of your men seemed to melt with fear, O king, when they saw Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya break clean through.
Yet all the great-souled ones, stung to wrath, full of shame, urged on by their own courage, stood firm and went forth again to meet Dhanaṃjaya.
Those who went against the Pāṇḍava in the fight, filled with wrath and indignation — even now they do not turn back, as rivers do not turn back from the sea.
But the base ones turned away, as unbelievers turn from the Vedas, and, partaking of hell, they came into sin.
Those two bulls among men, having passed beyond the chariot-array and broken free, appeared like two suns escaped from the maw of Rāhu.
As two fishes that have rent a great net are freed of their distress, so did the two Kṛṣṇas appear, having torn through that net of the army.
Set free from the press of weapons, from Droṇa's array so hard to pierce, those two great-souled ones appeared like two risen suns of the Doom-time.
Released from the crush of missiles, freed from the throng of weapons, those two great-souled ones appeared, dealers of distress to their foes.
Freed from a touch like fire, as two fishes from the jaws of a crocodile, the two convulsed the host as a pair of sea-monsters convulse the ocean.
Your men and your sons, while those two were still within Droṇa's array, resolved in their minds: "These two shall not pass beyond Droṇa."
But when they saw those two of great splendour break past Droṇa's array, O great king, they no longer hoped for the life of the king of the Sindhus.
A strong hope had been your sons', O king: "From Droṇa and the son of Hṛdika the two Kṛṣṇas shall not escape," O lord.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Making that hope fruitless, those two scorchers of foes crossed beyond Droṇa's array, O great king, and the Bhoja array so hard to pass.
Then, seeing the two pass through like blazing fires, they grew hopeless and no longer looked for the life of the king of the Sindhus.
And the two — Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya, fearless and striking fear into others — spoke together such words as these concerning the slaying of Jayadratha:
"Yonder Saindhava, set in the midst by six great car-warriors, sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, has come within range of our sight; he shall not escape us."
"Even though Śakra with the hosts of gods should guard him in the battle, even so we shall slay him" — thus spoke the two Kṛṣṇas.
As the two mighty-armed Kṛṣṇas spoke thus to each other, gazing upon the king of the Sindhus, your sons overheard them.
Like two thirsting elephants who, having crossed a desert waste, drink water and are refreshed and pass on, so stood those two subduers of foes.
Like men who have crossed mountains thronged with tigers, lions, and elephants, the two mighty-armed ones appeared, as though gone beyond death and old age.
"Such indeed is the look upon the faces of these two," so thought your men, and seeing them broken free, they cried out on every side.
From Droṇa, shaped like a venomous serpent, like a blazing fire, and from the other kings, the two shone forth radiant as twin suns.
Those two subduers of foes, freed from Droṇa's array that was like an ocean, appeared filled with joy, as men who have crossed over the sea.
Freed from the vast floods of weapons guarded by Droṇa and the son of Hṛdika, the two appeared resplendent in the fight, the equals of Indra and Agni.
Their blood welling forth, the two Kṛṣṇas, studded with the sharp shafts of Bhāradvāja, shone like two mountains decked with karṇikāra blossoms.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Released from the lake whose crocodile was Droṇa, beset with the venomous serpents of its spears, with iron arrows for its fierce sea-monsters, with the foremost warriors for its waters —
— with the twang of bowstrings and the slap of palms for its roar, with maces and swords for its lightning: from that cloud of Droṇa's weapons the two broke free, like sun and moon from the dark.
As though they had crossed by their own arms the brimming rivers that run to the sea, the Sindhu sixth among them, swollen at summer's end and teeming with great monsters —
— so did all beings deem the two Kṛṣṇas, those great archers renowned throughout the worlds for their glory, in their wonder at the might of Droṇa's weapons.
Gazing with longing to slay upon Jayadratha, who stood close by, the two waited like tigers eager to take a ruru-deer at the watering place.
"Such indeed is the look upon the faces of these two," thought your warriors, O great king, and they counted Jayadratha already slain.
Red-eyed and mighty-armed, intent upon their purpose, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, gazing upon the king of the Sindhus, roared again and again in their gladness.
From Śauri with the reins in his hands and from Pārtha bearing his bow there came a radiance as of the sun and fire.
Joy alone was theirs, freed now from Droṇa's array, as they saw the Saindhava close at hand, as two hawks behold their prey.
Beholding the Saindhava as though within their very reach, the two, enraged, swooped down at once and swiftly, like two hawks upon their prey.
But seeing Hṛṣīkeśa and Dhanaṃjaya break through, your son strode forth in valour to guard the king of the Sindhus.
His armour fastened on by Droṇa, King Duryodhana, knowing well the management of horses, then drove into the battle with a single chariot, O lord.
Passing the great archers Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha, your son then went forth to confront the lotus-eyed one face to face, O ruler of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then throughout all the hosts the instruments sounded out joyfully when your son had passed beyond Dhanaṃjaya.
And lion-roars arose, mingled with the blare of conches and drums, as they saw Duryodhana standing there before the two Kṛṣṇas.
And those who were the guardians of the king of the Sindhus, like flames of fire, rejoiced in the battle to behold your son, O lord.
But seeing Duryodhana come forth with his followers, Kṛṣṇa spoke to Arjuna, O king, these words befitting the hour:
Vāsudeva said: Behold this Suyodhana come forth before us, Dhanaṃjaya; fallen into peril, I deem him — there is no chariot-warrior the equal of his.
A great archer whose shafts fly far, accomplished in arms, drunk with the lust of battle, firm in his weapons and a wily fighter — such is the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Reared amid boundless ease and honored by the great car-warriors, ever adept, O Pārtha, he forever hates the Pāṇḍavas.
With him, O sinless one, I judge that the hour of battle has come for you; here the dicing of you both has arrived again — for victory, or else for the other end.
Here, O Pārtha, loose the venom of your wrath, long stored up; this great car-warrior is the very root of the Pāṇḍavas' miseries.
He has come within your reach — behold the fruit of your own striving. How else should a king bent on the kingdom come to do battle with you?
By good fortune he has now come within the range of your arrows; act so, O Dhanaṃjaya, that he may yield up his life.
Deluded by the intoxication of sovereignty, he has never known sorrow, nor does he know your valor in battle, O bull among men.
For the three worlds, O Pārtha, with their gods, demons, and men, cannot prevail to conquer you in battle — how much less Suyodhana alone?
By good fortune he has come near your chariot, O Pārtha; slay him, mighty-armed one, as Puraṃdara slew Vṛtra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For he has ever striven for your ruin, O sinless one, and by trickery he cheated the King of Righteousness at the dice.
Many a cruel deed has this man of evil mind wrought, O giver of honor, against you who are blameless, and that without ceasing.
That ignoble, ever-base man, who follows only his own willful desire — bend your mind to noble battle, O Pārtha, and slay him without hesitation.
Holding in your heart, O son of Pāṇḍu, the theft of the kingdom by fraud, the dwelling in the forest, and the abuse of Kṛṣṇā, put forth your might.
By good fortune he moves within the range of your arrows; by good fortune he strives at the forefront to thwart your purpose.
By good fortune he knows at last that he must fight with you in battle; by good fortune, O Pārtha, all your cherished desires are now fulfilled.
Therefore slay in battle, O Pārtha, this son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the disgrace of his line, as of old Jambha was slain by Indra in the war of gods and demons.
With him slain by you, let this host, left without a lord, break apart; this is the final bath that ends the feud — cut away the root of these evil-souled men.
Saṃjaya said: "So be it," answered Pārtha; "this is the very deed for me. Heeding nothing else, drive on to where Suyodhana stands.
By whom our kingdom was so long enjoyed unopposed — let me press forward in the fray and strike off his head in battle.
Would that I might reach, O Mādhava, the day of reckoning for the undeserved torment of Kṛṣṇā, for the seizing of her hair.
Speaking thus, the two Kṛṣṇas, exultant, urged on their splendid white steeds in the battle, eager to come at that lord of men.
When your son had come near the two, O bull of the Bhāratas, he showed no fear, though a great peril had come upon him, O venerable one.
For this all the warriors there honored him: that he went out without hesitation to meet Arjuna and Hṛṣīkeśa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then from all your host, O lord of peoples, there rose a great roar there, beholding the king in the battle.
While that dreadful clamor of men went up, your son, making light of the danger, held back his foe.
But the son of Kuntī, checked by your bowman son, flew into still greater fury; and that scorcher of foes flamed up against him.
Seeing the two, Duryodhana and Dhanaṃjaya, thus enraged against each other, the kings of terrible aspect gazed upon them from every side.
But beholding Pārtha enraged, and Vāsudeva too, O venerable one, your son, as though smiling, eager for the fight, called them out.
Then the joyful Dāśārha and the son of Pāṇḍu, Dhanaṃjaya, raised a great war-cry and blew their finest conch-shells.
Seeing the two so full of gladness, the Kauravas on every side grew hopeless of your son's life.
And the Kurus all fell into deepest grief, and deemed your son already cast as an oblation into the mouth of Vaiśvānara.
Beholding thus the joyful Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, those warriors, stricken with fear, cried out, "The king is slain, the king is slain!"
But Duryodhana, hearing the clamor of the host, said: "Let your fear depart; I shall send the two Kṛṣṇas to death."
Having so spoken to all his soldiers, that lord of men, looking for victory, addressed Pārtha and in his fury uttered these words:
"O Pārtha, whatever weapon you have learned, divine or human, show it on me at once — if indeed you were begotten of Pāṇḍu.
Whatever strength and valor are yours, and Keśava's as well, exert it on me at once — let us see your manhood.
Out of our sight, men tell of deeds you are said to have done, deeds meant to win your master's favor — show those very deeds here."
Saṃjaya said: Having so spoken to Arjuna, the king pierced him in return with three arrows that pierced the vitals, and with four swift shafts struck his four horses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And he pierced Vāsudeva with ten arrows between the breasts, and cutting his goad with a broad-headed shaft, cast it to the ground.
Him Pārtha, unflurried, swiftly pierced with fourteen stone-whetted shafts of gaily feathered shanks; but they glanced off from his armor.
Seeing them fall fruitless, he loosed again fourteen more sharp arrows; and these too glanced off from his armor.
Seeing those twenty-eight shafts that he had shot fall in vain, Kṛṣṇa, slayer of hostile heroes, spoke these words to Arjuna:
"A thing never seen before I now behold — your arrows creep away like stones. The feathered shafts you send, O Pārtha, accomplish nothing.
Is the life of the Gāṇḍīva still the same, O bull of the Bhāratas? Is your grip as of old, and the strength of your two arms?
If this be not the last hour decreed by fate, come today for you and for this foe — then tell me, who ask you.
Great is my wonder, O Pārtha, to see these arrows of yours fall vainly in battle against Duryodhana's chariot.
Your arrows, terrible as the thunderbolt and the lightning, cleavers of an enemy's body, accomplish nothing — what mockery is this today, O Pārtha?"
Arjuna said: This device, O Kṛṣṇa, was set by Droṇa upon the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; this fitting of armor is the last of the lore of weapons.
In this armor, O Kṛṣṇa, even the three worlds lie hidden and warded; Droṇa alone knows this art, and I from that best of men.
This armor cannot be pierced by arrows in any wise, O Govinda — no, not by the thunderbolt itself in the hand of Maghavat in battle.
Knowing all this, O Kṛṣṇa, why do you seek to bewilder me? Whatever has passed in the three worlds, and whatever now comes to pass, O Keśava,
and whatever shall be — all of it is known to you; nor does any other know it as you do, O slayer of Madhu.
This Duryodhana, O Kṛṣṇa, wearing this armor wrought by Droṇa, stands fearless in the battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the rite that must here accompany it he does not know, O Mādhava; like a woman he wears this well-fitted armor in vain.
Behold the might of my arms and of my bow, O Janārdana; I shall overcome the Kaurava, guarded by his armor though he be.
This shining armor the Lord of the gods once gave to Aṅgiras; and again the lord of the gods gave to me that armor together with its mystic rite.
Though this armor of his be divine, or fashioned by Brahmā himself, it shall not save that fool today, smitten by my arrows.
Saṃjaya said: Having so spoken, Arjuna, charging his arrows with sacred spells, drew them back; but as he drew those shafts set at the middle of the bow, the son of Droṇa cut them apart with his weapon that destroys all weapons.
Seeing those arrows cut down from afar by that knower of the sacred word, the white-steeded warrior, amazed, made it known to Keśava:
"This weapon I cannot loose a second time, O Janārdana, for the weapon would then turn and slay me; yet behold today my strength."
Then Duryodhana, O king, pierced the two Kṛṣṇas in battle with nine smooth-jointed arrows like venomous serpents, and again rained his shafts upon Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava in the fray.
At that great rain of arrows your men rejoiced, and raised the din of instruments and roars like lions.
Then Pārtha, enraged in battle, licking the corners of his mouth, looked but could find no limb of his that was not guarded by the armor.
Then with sharp arrows, well loosed and like Death himself, he made his horses lifeless, and both his flank-charioteers as well.
The valiant one cut his gaily-wrought bow and his hand-guard, and the Ambidextrous Archer set about to splinter his chariot to pieces.
And Duryodhana, now bereft of his chariot, Arjuna then pierced in both palms of his hands with two keen arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing him fallen into so dire a strait, tormented by Dhanaṃjaya's shafts, the foremost bowmen rushed up, eager to rescue him.
With chariots by the many thousands, with elephants and horses arrayed, and with raging floods of foot-soldiers, they hemmed in Dhanaṃjaya.
Then neither Arjuna nor Govinda, nor even their chariot, could be seen, so enveloped were they by the great rain of weapons and the throngs of men.
Then Arjuna, by the might of his weapons, smote that host; there, maimed by the hundred, fell the chariots and the elephants.
Slain and being slain, they yet hemmed in that noblest of chariots; halted in its course, it stood there, ringed about for a krośa on every side.
Then the hero of the Vṛṣṇis swiftly said to Arjuna: "Twang your bow with all your might, and I shall blow my conch."
Then, twanging the Gāṇḍīva mightily, Arjuna smote his foes with a great rain of arrows and with the clap of his bowstring on his palm.
And Keśava blew the Pāñcajanya loud and shrill, the edges of his eyelashes clogged with dust, his face streaming heavily with sweat.
At the blast of that conch and the twang of that bow, the men, both the spiritless and the stout-hearted, fell then to the earth.
Freed of them, the chariot shone like a cloud driven on by the wind; thereupon the guardians of Jayadratha, with their followers, were thrown into turmoil.
But the guardians of the lord of the Sindhus, seeing Pārtha suddenly upon them, raised cries of many kinds, making the earth tremble.
Those great-souled warriors sent forth fierce twangings of arrows mingled with the blare of conches, and roars like lions as well.
Hearing that terrible din arisen from your men, Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya then blew their conches.
By that mighty blast this earth was filled, with its mountains, its sea-girt isles, and its nether realms, O lord of peoples.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That sound, O best of the Bhāratas, spreading through all the ten directions, echoed back upon the very hosts of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
Beholding Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya there, your car-warriors, the great chariot-fighters, were seized with the utmost fury and hastened forward.
Then your warriors, seeing the two illustrious Kṛṣṇas clad in their armor, rushed against them in wrath, and that was a wondrous thing to behold.
Saṃjaya said: But your men, the moment they caught sight of the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas and Kurus, pressed forward eager to slay them; and even so did Vijaya, eager to slay his foes.
With their great chariots gleaming with gold and clothed in tiger-skins, resounding as they rolled, they lit up all the directions as though with blazing fires.
With their bows gold-backed and hard to gaze upon, O lord of the earth, twanging forth incomparable notes like enraged serpents,
Bhūriśravas, Śala, Karṇa, Vṛṣasena, Jayadratha, Kṛpa, the king of the Madras, and the son of Droṇa, foremost of car-warriors —
those eight great chariot-warriors, seeming as if to drink up the sky with their steeds, made the ten directions resplendent with their tiger-skin coverings adorned with golden orbs.
Armored and furious, with their chariots rumbling like masses of clouds, they covered all the directions, and Pārtha as well, with their sharp shafts.
The spirited horses of the Kulūta breed, dappled and swift, bearing those great car-warriors, shone forth then, lighting up the ten directions.
With steeds of noble lineage and great speed, sprung from many lands — mountain-bred, river-born, and of the Sindhu country, the finest of horses —
the foremost of the Kuru warriors, O king, longing to protect your son, swiftly assailed the chariot of Dhanaṃjaya from every side.
Those best of men, taking up their great conches, blew them, filling heaven, O king, and the earth with its seas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In like manner Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya, the foremost of all beings, blew their two conches, the best of all conches on earth — the son of Kuntī his Devadatta, and Keśava his Pāñcajanya.
The sound of Devadatta, sent forth by Dhanaṃjaya, filled the earth, the firmament, and all the directions.
So too the Pāñcajanya, sounded by Vāsudeva, surpassing all other sounds, filled heaven and earth.
While that terrible tumult of clamor raged on, striking terror into the timid and swelling the joy of the brave,
while kettledrums, jharjharas, tabors, and tom-toms were beaten, O lord of kings, sounding forth in countless number,
those renowned as mighty car-warriors, the well-wishers of Duryodhana, unable to brook that sound, the wrathful and supreme bowmen, kings of many lands, guardians of their own troops,
those heroes, the great chariot-warriors, in their indignation blew their great conches, resolved to answer the deed of Keśava and Arjuna.
That army of yours, stirred by the blasts of the conches, with its chariots, elephants, and horses thrown into agitation, seemed, O lord, as though disquieted.
The sky, as it were, set ringing by the heroes with the blare of conches, became greatly troubled, as though resounding with thunderclaps.
That mighty sound, O king, made all the directions resound and terrified that army, gathering like the doom of the world's end.
Then Duryodhana and those eight kings, the great car-warriors, surrounded the son of Pāṇḍu for the protection of Jayadratha.
Then the son of Droṇa struck Vāsudeva with seventy-three arrows, and Arjuna with three broad-headed shafts, his banner and his horses with five.
Arjuna, exceedingly enraged because Janārdana had been struck, smote him in turn with six hundred arrows.
Piercing Karṇa with twelve arrows and Vṛṣasena with three, the valiant one cut asunder, at the grip, the bow of Śalya together with its arrow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Taking up another bow, Śalya pierced the son of Pāṇḍu; and Bhūriśravas struck him with three arrows, gold-feathered and whetted on stone.
Karṇa with thirty-two, Vṛṣasena with five, Jayadratha with seventy-three, Kṛpa with ten arrows, and the king of the Madras with ten — all pierced Phalguna in the battle.
Then the son of Droṇa covered Pārtha with sixty arrows, Vāsudeva with seventy, and Pārtha again with five.
But that tiger among men, of the white steeds and with Kṛṣṇa for his charioteer, laughing, pierced them all in return, displaying the swiftness of his hand.
Piercing Karṇa with twelve and Vṛṣasena with three arrows, he cut off Śalya's bow at the place of the grip in the fight.
Piercing the son of Somadatta with three arrows and Śalya with ten sharp shafts shaped like tongues of flame, he struck the son of Droṇa with eight.
He smote Gautama with twenty-five, the ruler of the Sindhus with a hundred, and the son of Droṇa again with seventy arrows.
But Bhūriśravas, greatly enraged, cut off the goad of Hari and struck Arjuna with seventy-three arrows.
Then he of the white steeds, wrathful, swiftly checked those foes with hundreds of sharp arrows, as a mighty wind scatters the clouds.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Of the banners of many shapes, gleaming with surpassing splendor, both of the sons of Pṛthā and of my own men — tell me of those, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Hear of the banners of many shapes belonging to those high-souled ones; learn from me their forms, their colors, and their names.
Upon the chariots of those who rode therein, O lord of kings, divers banners were seen, blazing like fires.
Golden they were, with golden crests, adorned with golden wreaths, like the golden peaks of the great golden mountain.
Those banners of theirs, wrapped about on every side with pennants of varied and brilliant hues, shone forth, encompassed all around.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And those pennants, stirred by the wind, were seen dancing, like graceful courtesans amid the dancing-ground.
The pennants, glowing with the hues of Indra's bow, O bull of the Bhāratas, fluttering, lent beauty to those great car-warriors.
With its lion's tail and fierce mouth, the banner bearing the sign of the ape — Dhanaṃjaya's, terrible to behold — we beheld in the battle.
That foremost of apes, O king, adorned with pennants — the banner of the wielder of Gāṇḍīva — struck terror into that army.
In like manner, O Bhārata, we beheld the lion's-tail crest atop the banner of Droṇa's son, radiant as the rising sun.
Golden, tossed by the wind, splendid as the banner of Śakra, gladdening the lords of the Kurus, the emblem of Droṇa's son was raised on high.
And again, a golden elephant-girth was upon the banner of the son of Adhiratha, which in the battle, O great king, seemed to fill the very sky.
Decked with pennants and golden wreaths, the banner of Karṇa in the fight seemed to dance upon the chariot-platform, stirred by the wind.
And the preceptor of the Pāṇḍus, the illustrious Brāhmaṇa Gautama, Kṛpa, bore a bull most finely wrought.
With that bull, O king, the great car-warrior shone, even as the chariot of the destroyer of Tripura is resplendent with its bull.
Vṛṣasena's peacock, golden and set with gems and jewels, stood as if about to cry out, lending beauty even to the van of the host.
With that peacock the chariot of that high-souled one shone, O lord of kings, even as Skanda's is resplendent with its glittering peacock.
Atop the banner of Śalya, king of the Madras, we beheld a golden plough-furrow, peerless and fair, like a tongue of flame.
That furrow shone, set upon his chariot, O sire, as a furrow sprung up with every kind of seed, encompassed with splendor.
The boar of the king of the Sindhus, of silver, gleamed atop his banner, bright as the unreddened sun and wrought with a net of gold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With that silver standard Jayadratha shone forth, even as Pūṣan of old shone in the war of the gods and the asuras.
Again, the banner of the son of Somadatta — that wise one devoted to sacrifice — bore a sacrificial post that shone like the sun, and upon it the moon could be seen.
That golden sacrificial post of the son of Somadatta was resplendent, O king, like the post raised aloft at the Rājasūya, the foremost of sacrifices.
And Śala's standard, O great king, was a great silver elephant, adorned with peacocks whose limbs were variegated with gold.
That standard lent beauty to your army, O bull of the Bhāratas, even as the great white elephant graces the host of the king of the gods.
The king's banner was an elephant fashioned of gems, sheathed in gold, ringing with a hundred little bells, shining upon his splendid and excellent chariot.
Your son shone forth exceedingly, O king, O lord of peoples, with that mighty banner in the battle — that bull among the Kurus.
These nine supreme banners, raised aloft in your host, lit up the army, resembling the suns of the world's end.
But the tenth was Arjuna's — that one mighty ape alone — by which Arjuna blazed forth like the Himālaya wrapped in fire.
Then those great car-warriors, scorchers of foes, swiftly took up their bows — variegated, bright, and very great — for the sake of opposing Arjuna.
And so too Pārtha, the destroyer of foes, of divine deeds, drew his Gāṇḍīva, O king — all owing to your evil counsel.
For through your fault many men, summoned from every quarter, were slain in the battle, together with their horses, their chariots, and their elephants.
There arose a fierce exchange of blows among them, as they roared at one another — those led by Duryodhana and that bull among the sons of Pāṇḍu.
There the son of Kuntī, with Kṛṣṇa for his charioteer, wrought a supreme marvel, in that, alone, he closed fearlessly with many.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The mighty-armed one shone as he wielded the Gāṇḍīva bow, eager to vanquish those tigers among men and to slay Jayadratha.
There Arjuna, O great king, the tormentor of foes, with arrows loosed by the thousand, made your warriors invisible.
Then those tigers among men too, all the great car-warriors, made Pārtha invisible in the battle with floods of arrows from every side.
When Arjuna, that bull among the Kurus, was thus enveloped by those lions among men, a mighty uproar arose from that army.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When Arjuna had reached the ruler of the Sindhus, what did the Pāñcālas, hemmed in by the son of Bharadvāja together with the Kurus, do, Saṃjaya?
Saṃjaya said: In the afternoon, O great king, amid the hair-raising combat, a gambling-match was waged between the Pāñcālas and the Kurus over Droṇa.
For the Pāñcālas, eager to slay Droṇa, with hearts elated, poured down showers of arrows, roaring, O sire.
Then a most tumultuous and wondrous battle was waged between them, between the Pāñcālas and the Kurus, terrible and like the war of the gods and the asuras.
All the Pāñcālas, together with the sons of Pāṇḍu, reaching the chariot of Droṇa and seeking to pierce that division, displayed their great weapons.
The car-warriors, mounted upon their chariots, advanced right up to the chariot of Droṇa, making it tremble, pressing on at a moderate speed.
Against him advanced Bṛhatkṣatra, the great chariot-warrior of the Kekayas, sowing whetted arrows that resembled the thunderbolt of mighty Indra.
But the illustrious Kṣemadhūrti swiftly rose to meet him, loosing whetted arrows by the hundred and by the thousand.
And Dhṛṣṭaketu, the bull of the Cedis, risen up in surpassing strength, rushed in haste upon Droṇa as great Indra upon Śambara.
As he bore down all at once, like Death with gaping jaws, the mighty archer Vīradhanvan hastened forth to confront him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, O great king, the valiant Droṇa held back Yudhiṣṭhira, who stood firm with his host, eager for victory.
Your valiant son Vikarṇa, O lord, went forth against Nakula, skilled and prowess-filled in battle, as he came on.
And as Sahadeva likewise advanced, Durmukha, the harrier of foes, overwhelmed him with many thousands of swift-flying shafts.
Vyāghradatta held off Sātyaki, that tiger among men, with keen and sharpened arrows, shaking him again and again.
Saumadatti held back the sons of Draupadī, those tigers among men, foremost of chariot-warriors, who in their fury loosed their finest shafts.
And the great chariot-warrior Ārṣyaśṛṅgi, dreadful and fearsome in form, withstood the wrathful Bhīmasena as he came on.
A battle arose between the two of them on the field, that man and that rākṣasa, O king, even such as once took place between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira struck Droṇa with ninety smooth-jointed arrows in all his vital parts, O best of the Bhāratas, O Bhārata.
Droṇa, enraged by the illustrious son of Kuntī, struck him in turn between the breasts with twenty-five shafts, O best of the Bhāratas.
And once more Droṇa covered him over with a score of arrows, together with his horses, charioteer, and banner, before the eyes of all the bowmen.
But the righteous son of Pāṇḍu warded off those arrows loosed by Droṇa with a shower of his own, displaying the swiftness of his hand.
Then Droṇa the bowman, exceedingly wroth, suddenly cut asunder in the fray the bow of that high-souled king of righteousness.
And as his bow was severed, the great chariot-warrior in haste covered him over on every side with many thousands of arrows.
Seeing the king made invisible by the shafts of Bharadvāja's son, all beings thought Yudhiṣṭhira already slain.
Some thought him thus turned away in flight: "The king is carried off," O lord of kings, "by the illustrious brāhmaṇa."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The king of righteousness, Yudhiṣṭhira, fallen into the utmost extremity, cast aside that bow cut down by Bharadvāja's son in the fray and took up another, a celestial bow, burden-crushing and swifter still.
Then the hero cut to pieces in the battle all those arrows loosed by Droṇa by the thousand, and it was as a marvel to behold.
And having cut those shafts apart, the king, his eyes red with wrath, seized in the battle a spear that could rend even mountains, gold-shafted, most terrible, hung with eight bells, and dread to behold.
And raising it aloft in his joy, the mighty one roared with a great roar, as if terrifying all beings with that cry, O Bhārata.
Seeing the spear uplifted by the king of righteousness in the fray, all beings cried out at once, "Hail to Droṇa! May it be well with Droṇa!"
Loosed from the king's arm, like a serpent that has cast its slough, blazing across the sky and the quarters and the intermediate quarters, it drew near to Droṇa like a flaming-mouthed she-snake.
Seeing it bearing down upon him all at once, O lord of peoples, Droṇa, the best of those versed in weapons, brought forth the brāhma weapon.
That weapon reduced to ashes the spear of dreadful aspect and sped swiftly toward the chariot of the illustrious son of Pāṇḍu.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, exceedingly wise, quelled that uplifted weapon of Droṇa with the brahma weapon itself, O Bhārata.
And he pierced Droṇa in the fight with five smooth-jointed shafts, and with a sharp razor-headed arrow cut asunder his great bow.
Casting aside that severed bow, Droṇa, the crusher of kṣatriyas, suddenly hurled a mace at the son of Dharma, O worthy one.
Seeing that mace bearing down on him all at once, Yudhiṣṭhira, scorcher of foes, in his wrath seized a mace of his own and hurled it.
Those two maces, suddenly loosed, met each other and, striking out fire from their collision, came together upon the ground.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
