Then Droṇa, exceedingly enraged, O worthy one, slew the horses of the king of righteousness with four keen and sharpened, choicest shafts.
With a single arrow he cut his bow, and with one he severed his banner that rose like Indra's standard, and with three he tormented the son of Pāṇḍu.
Leaping down swiftly from his chariot with its slain horses, King Yudhiṣṭhira stood with arms upraised, weaponless, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Beholding him bereft of his chariot and weaponless besides, Droṇa threw the foes and all their armies into confusion, O lord.
Loosing volleys of sharp arrows, swift of hand and firm of vow, he rushed upon the king as a fierce lion upon a deer.
Seeing him thus assailed by Droṇa, the slayer of foes, a sudden cry of "Alas! Alas!" arose all at once among the Pāṇḍavas.
"The king is carried off, the king is carried off by Bharadvāja's son!" O worthy one, such was the mighty clamor that rose on every side from the army of the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, swiftly mounting Sahadeva's chariot, withdrew with its fleet horses.
Saṃjaya said: As Bṛhatkṣatra the Kekaya, firm in valor, came on, Kṣemadhūrti, O great king, pierced him in the breast with arrows.
But King Bṛhatkṣatra, eager in the fight to breach Droṇa's array, swiftly struck him with ninety smooth-jointed shafts.
But Kṣemadhūrti, greatly enraged, cut asunder the bow of the high-souled Kekaya with a sharp, yellow-burnished broad-headed arrow.
And as his bow was severed, he swiftly pierced in the heart with a smooth-jointed shaft that foremost of all the bowmen.
Then taking up another bow, Bṛhatkṣatra, as if with a smile, stripped the great chariot-warrior Kṣemadhūrti of his horses, charioteer, and banner.
Then with another sharp, yellow-burnished broad-headed arrow he severed from the king's body his head with its blazing earrings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That head of his, suddenly severed, with its curling locks and its diadem, falling to the earth, shone like a star fallen from the sky.
Having slain him in battle, the great chariot-warrior Bṛhatkṣatra, exultant, fell suddenly upon your host for the sake of the sons of Pṛthā.
And as Dhṛṣṭaketu came on, the valiant mighty archer Vīradhanvan held him back for Droṇa's sake, O Bhārata.
Closing with each other, those two swift warriors, their teeth as arrows, struck one another with many thousands of shafts.
Those two tigers among men fought with each other like two leader-elephants of the herd, fierce with rut, in a great forest.
Like two enraged tigers met within a mountain cavern, those two mighty heroes fought, each seeking to slay the other.
That battle was tumultuous and worth the beholding, O lord of peoples, a marvelous and wondrous sight for the throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Then Vīradhanvan, enraged, cut Dhṛṣṭaketu's bow in two with a broad-headed arrow, as if with a laugh, O Bhārata.
Casting aside that severed bow, the great chariot-warrior, king of the Cedis, seized a broad spear, gold-shafted and wrought of iron.
Drawing back that mighty spear with both arms, O Bhārata, he hurled it all at once, with full effort, against the chariot of Vīradhanvan.
Struck hard by that hero-slaying spear, his heart pierced through, he swiftly fell from his chariot to the earth.
When that hero, the great chariot-warrior of the Trigartas, was slain, your force was broken on every side by the Pāṇḍavas, O lord.
Then Durmukha cast sixty arrows at Sahadeva and roared a great roar, threatening the son of Pāṇḍu in the fray.
Then the son of Mādrī, enraged, pierced the oncoming Durmukha with ten arrows, brother piercing brother, as if with a laugh.
Seeing the mighty Sahadeva impetuous in battle, Durmukha smote him with nine arrows, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the mighty Sahadeva, having cut down Durmukha's banner with a broad-headed arrow, slew his four steeds with four whetted shafts.
And with another sharp, yellow-burnished broad-headed arrow he severed from the charioteer's body his head with its blazing earrings.
And with a sharp razor-headed arrow Sahadeva cut asunder in the fight the great bow of the Kaurava and pierced him with five shafts.
Then Durmukha, dejected, abandoning his chariot with its slain horses, mounted the chariot of Niramitra, O king, O Bhārata.
Then Sahadeva, the slayer of hostile heroes, in his wrath struck down Niramitra in the great battle, in the midst of the host, with a broad-headed arrow.
Niramitra, lord of men, son of the king of the Trigartas, fell from the floor of his chariot, troubling your host as he fell.
Having slain him, the mighty-armed Sahadeva shone forth as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, when he had slain the mighty Khara.
A great cry of dismay arose among the Trigartas, O lord of men, when they saw the mighty prince Niramitra slain.
Nakula, O king, overcame your son Vikarṇa of the large eyes in battle within a moment, and it was as a marvel.
But Vyāghradatta made Sātyaki, together with his horses, charioteer, and banner, invisible amid the host with smooth-jointed arrows.
Warding off those arrows, the hero, the grandson of Śini, with the skill of a master hand, brought down Vyāghradatta with his shafts, together with his horses, charioteer, and banner.
When that prince, the son of the king of Magadha, was slain, O lord, the men of Magadha, straining on every side, rushed upon Yuyudhāna.
Hurling by the thousand arrows and lances, slings and javelins, maces and pestles as well,
those heroes did battle in the fray with the Sātvata, mad for combat; but the mighty Sātyaki, himself mad for combat, vanquished them all without great trouble, as if with a laugh, O bull among men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing the men of Magadha, those who survived the slaughter, fleeing on every side, your force, tormented by the arrows of Yuyudhāna, was broken, O lord.
Having destroyed your host in the fight, the illustrious chief of the Mādhavas shone forth, brandishing his excellent bow.
The force being broken, O king, by the high-souled Sātvata, terrified by the long-armed hero, did not turn back to the battle.
Then Droṇa, exceedingly enraged, his eyes suddenly rolling, himself rushed upon Sātyaki of the truthful deeds.
Saṃjaya said: The illustrious Saumadatti, having pierced each of the mighty-archer sons of Draupadī with five arrows, pierced them again with seven.
Sorely pressed by that fierce warrior all at once, O lord, they were so dazed that they could not tell what was to be done in the fray.
But Śatānīka, Nakula's son, that scorcher of foes, having pierced Saumadatti, that bull among men, with two arrows, roared aloud in delight.
And the others too, steadfast in the battle, swiftly pierced the wrathful Saumadatti, each with three straight-flying shafts.
Against them, O great king, that warrior of high renown hurled five arrows, striking each one of them in the heart with a single shaft.
Then the five brothers, pierced by the shafts of that great-souled one, surrounded the hero with their chariots and pierced him sorely with their arrows.
But the son of Arjuna, filled with wrath, dispatched his horses to the abode of Yama with four whetted shafts.
The son of Bhīmasena, having cut the bow of the great-souled Saumadatti, roared a mighty roar and pierced him with sharpened arrows.
The son of Yudhiṣṭhira, cutting down his banner, brought it to the ground, while Nakula's son swept the charioteer from the chariot-box.
But the high-minded son of Sahadeva, perceiving him turned aside by his brothers, severed his head, O king, with a razor-headed shaft.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That head, adorned with refined gold, fell to the earth, lighting up that quarter of the battlefield, radiant as the rising sun.
Seeing the head of the great-souled Saumadatti falling, your warriors, O king, took fright and fled in many directions.
But Alambusa, full of wrath, fought in battle with the mighty Bhīmasena, as the son of Rāvaṇa fought with Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing those two, the man and the rākṣasa, locked together in combat, wonder and delight then arose in all beings.
Then Bhīma, laughing, O king, pierced the son of Ṛśyaśṛṅga, that wrathful lord of rākṣasas, with nine whetted shafts.
That rākṣasa, pierced in the fight, raised a terrifying roar and rushed upon Bhīma, together with those who followed in his train.
Having pierced Bhīma with five smooth-jointed arrows, that subduer of foes swiftly slew thirty chariots of Bhīma's followers, and again, after slaying four hundred, he pierced Bhīma with a feathered shaft.
Then the mighty Bhīma, deeply pierced by the rākṣasa, sank down upon the floor of his chariot, overwhelmed by a swoon.
Regaining his senses, the son of the Wind-god, beside himself with rage, drew his dreadful bow, that supreme weapon of heavy work, and tormented Alambusa on every side with keen arrows.
Pierced by many shafts, that rākṣasa, dark as a heap of black collyrium, shone all over, O king, like a kiṃśuka tree in full blossom.
As he was being struck in the fight by the arrows loosed from Bhīma's bow, he remembered the slaying of his brother by the great-souled son of Pāṇḍu.
Then, assuming a fearsome form, he addressed Bhīmasena: "Stand now in the battle, O son of Pṛthā, and behold this day my prowess."
"There was one named Baka, O fool, a mighty chief among rākṣasas; out of my sight that deed was done, when my brother was slain by you."
Having spoken thus, then, vanishing from sight, he covered Bhīma utterly with a mighty downpour of arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Bhīma in the battle, O king, when the rākṣasa had become invisible, filled the sky with his smooth-jointed shafts.
Struck by Bhīma, that vile one, in the twinkling of an eye, now mounting his chariot, now reaching the earth, and now suddenly springing into the sky.
He took on many forms, high and low, and uttered on every side voices loud and faint.
By him the elephants of the Pāṇḍava army were crushed in the fight, and many horses too, O king, and foot-soldiers as well; and the chariot-warriors, struck by his arrows, fell from their chariots.
With blood for its water, chariots for its whirlpools, thronged with elephants for its crocodiles, parasols for its swans, mire for its silt, and crowded with severed arms for its snakes—
—he set flowing a river teeming with hosts of rākṣasas, bearing along in many places, O king, the Cedis, the Pāñcālas, and the Sṛñjayas.
As he ranged thus fearlessly through the battle, O king, the Pāṇḍavas, deeply troubled, beheld his prowess.
But among your troops great delight arose, and there rose a fierce and mighty din of instruments that made the hair stand on end.
Hearing that dreadful clamor of your host, the son of Pāṇḍu could not brook it, even as an elephant cannot brook the clapping of hands.
Then, his eyes red with wrath and scorching like a blazing fire, he fitted the weapon of Tvaṣṭṛ, himself like Tvaṣṭṛ in person, O sire.
Then thousands of arrows appeared on every side, and by those arrows a great rout of your army was wrought.
That weapon, loosed by Bhīmasena in the encounter, after destroying the great magic of the rākṣasa, tormented the rākṣasa himself.
That rākṣasa, struck in many ways by Bhīmasena, abandoning Bhīma in the encounter, ran toward the division of Droṇa.
When that lord of rākṣasas had been vanquished by the great-souled one, O king, the Pāṇḍavas made all the quarters resound with their lion-roars.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And, filled with joy, they honored the mighty son of the Wind-god, as the hosts of the Maruts honored Śakra when he had vanquished Prahlāda in battle.
Saṃjaya said: As Alambusa ranged thus fearlessly through the battle, the son of Hiḍimbā advanced swiftly upon him and pierced him with sharpened arrows.
Terrible was the combat of those two lions among rākṣasas, as they wrought their manifold illusions, like that of Śakra and Śambara.
Alambusa, exceedingly wrathful, struck Ghaṭotkaca; but Ghaṭotkaca, having pierced Alambusa between the breasts with twenty iron shafts, roared again and again like a lion.
In the same way Alambusa, O king, piercing again and again the son of Hiḍimbā, that warrior maddened with battle, roared in delight, filling the sky on every side.
Thus those two mighty lords of rākṣasas, exceedingly enraged, fought each other without distinction by means of their illusions.
Sending forth a hundred illusions, proud, bewildering each other, well skilled in the warfare of illusion, they fought a battle of illusion.
Whatever illusion Ghaṭotkaca displayed in the fight, O king, that very illusion Alambusa, O monarch, destroyed by illusion in turn.
Seeing Alambusa, that lord of rākṣasas, fighting thus and skilled in the warfare of illusion, the Pāṇḍavas grew wroth.
Greatly enraged, those foremost warriors, Bhīmasena and the rest, O king, rushed upon him in their wrath from every side with their chariots.
Hemming him in with the array of their chariots, O sire, they showered him from all sides with arrows, as men beset an elephant with firebrands.
Having warded off the force of their weapons by the magic of his own weapons, he broke free from that ring of chariots like an elephant escaping a forest fire.
Twanging his dreadful bow, whose sound was like the thunderbolt of Indra, he pierced the son of the Wind-god with twenty-five shafts, the son of Bhīmasena with five, Yudhiṣṭhira with three, and Sahadeva with seven.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And having pierced Nakula with seventy-three shafts and the sons of Drupada each with five, O sire, he uttered a dreadful roar.
Bhīmasena pierced that rākṣasa in return with nine shafts, Sahadeva with five, Yudhiṣṭhira with a hundred, Nakula with sixty-four, and the sons of Draupadī each with three.
The son of Hiḍimbā, having pierced that rākṣasa in the fight with fifty arrows, pierced him again with seventy, and the mighty one roared aloud.
That mighty bowman, deeply pierced on all sides by those great chariot-warriors, pierced them all in return, each with five shafts.
That rākṣasa, the son of Hiḍimbā, O best of the Bhāratas, enraged in turn against the enraged rākṣasa in the fight, pierced him with seven arrows.
That mighty lord of rākṣasas, deeply pierced by the strong one, swiftly loosed arrows feathered with gold and whetted on stone.
Those smooth-jointed arrows then entered the rākṣasa as fierce and mighty serpents in their fury enter a mountain.
Then those Pāṇḍavas, O king, troubled, dispatched sharpened arrows from all sides, and so did Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Hiḍimbā.
As he was being struck in the battle by the Pāṇḍavas flushed with victory, he seized that rākṣasa—like the scorched peak of a mountain, like a riven heap of black collyrium—
—and lifting him up with both arms and whirling him round again and again, he swiftly dashed him upon the earth, as one dashes a full pitcher against a rock.
Endowed with strength and dexterity, and endowed with prowess as well, the son of Bhīmasena, wrathful in the fight, struck terror into all the troops.
With all his limbs shattered and the ornaments of his bones ground to powder, that rākṣasa Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa was slain by the hero Ghaṭotkaca.
Then the sons of Pṛthā, joyful at heart when that night-ranger was slain, raised lion-roars and waved their garments.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And your troops, O bull of the Bhāratas, seeing that mighty lord of rākṣasas, Alambusa of fearsome form, slain like a mountain crumbled to ruin, raised a cry of woe.
And the people beheld that rākṣasa, filled with wonder, fallen by chance to the earth like the planet Mars.
And Ghaṭotkaca, having slain that rākṣasa, foremost among the mighty, let forth a powerful roar, as Vāsava did when he had slain Bala.
Honored by his fathers and kinsmen for that hard deed accomplished, Ghaṭotkaca then, having slain his foe, rejoiced indeed, having taken Alambusa as one gathers a ripe āḍambusa fruit.
Then a great clamor arose, mingled with conch-blasts and the din of arrows of every kind; and hearing it the Kauravas roared in answer, and that sound thereupon touched the very world with its might.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: How did Yuyudhāna withstand the son of Bharadvāja in the battle? Tell me truly, Saṃjaya, for great is my curiosity.
Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king of great wisdom, of the hair-raising battle of Droṇa with the Pāṇḍavas, led on by Yuyudhāna.
Seeing his force being struck down by Yuyudhāna, O sire, Droṇa himself rushed upon Sātyaki of unfailing prowess.
As that great chariot-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, came swiftly on, Sātyaki met him with twenty-five small arrows.
Droṇa too, valiant in the fight and intent, swiftly pierced Yuyudhāna with five gold-feathered arrows whetted on stone.
Those shafts, feeders on the flesh of foes, having pierced his stout armor, entered the earth, O king, hissing like serpents.
The long-armed warrior, enraged like an elephant goaded by the hook, pierced Droṇa with fifty iron shafts resembling fire.
The son of Bharadvāja, swiftly pierced in the battle by Yuyudhāna, pierced in return the striving Sātyaki with many arrows.
Then that mighty bowman of great strength, enraged once more, oppressed the Sātvata with a hundred smooth-jointed shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sātyaki, being struck down in the battle by the son of Bharadvāja, could find nothing whatever that should be done, O lord of peoples.
And Yuyudhāna, O king, grew downcast of countenance, seeing the son of Bharadvāja in the battle loosing his sharpened arrows.
Beholding him thus, O lord of peoples, your sons and your soldiers, their hearts filled with joy, roared again and again like lions.
Hearing that terrible roar, and that Mādhava was being hard pressed, Yudhiṣṭhira, O king, addressed all his armies, O descendant of Bharata.
Yonder the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, the hero Sātyaki, doer of true deeds, is being devoured in battle by a hero as the sun is devoured by Rāhu. Charge, hasten to where Sātyaki is fighting!
And the lord of men spoke thus to Dhṛṣṭadyumna of the Pāñcālas: "Charge swiftly upon Droṇa! Why do you stand idle, O son of Pṛṣata? Do you not see the terrible peril that has come upon us from Droṇa?"
That mighty bowman Droṇa toys with Yuyudhāna in the battle as a child toys with a bird bound by a string.
Let all the chariot-warriors, with Bhīmasena at their head, joined with you and resolute, go there toward Yuyudhāna's chariot.
I myself, with my troops, shall follow behind you. Deliver Sātyaki today, who has passed between the very fangs of Yama.
Having spoken thus, the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, then charged upon Droṇa in battle with all his army for Yuyudhāna's sake.
Then there arose a mighty uproar—blessings upon you!—from the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas on every side, all eager to do battle with Droṇa alone.
Those tigers among men, closing in, rained down upon the great chariot-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, sharp arrows fledged with the feathers of heron and peacock.
But Droṇa, smiling, received those heroes himself, as one receives guests arrived, with water and a seat.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They were gratified by the arrows of that bowman, the son of Bharadvāja, O king, as guests are gratified on reaching a hospitable house.
And none of them could so much as look upon the son of Bharadvāja, O lord, who was like the thousand-rayed sun arrived at midday.
And Droṇa, foremost of weapon-bearers, scorched all those mighty bowmen with showers of arrows, as the sun scorches with its rays.
Slain in the battle, O king, the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas alike found no deliverer, like elephants sunk in the mire.
And Droṇa's great arrows were seen darting forth, blazing on every side like the rays of the sun.
In that fight twenty-five Pāñcālas were slain by Droṇa, men renowned as great chariot-warriors and esteemed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Throughout all the armies of the Pāṇḍus and of the Pāñcālas alike, they beheld the valiant Droṇa striking down their best warriors one after another.
Having slain a hundred of the Kekayas and driven them off on every side, Droṇa stood, O great king, like Death with gaping jaws.
The mighty-armed Droṇa vanquished the Pāñcālas, the Sṛñjayas, the Matsyas, the Kekayas, and the Pāṇḍavas too, by the hundreds and by the thousands.
From them, as they were slain by Droṇa's arrows, arose a clamor like that of forest-dwellers being burned in the woods by the fire.
Thereupon the gods, the Gandharvas, and the ancestors said, O king: "Yonder the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas flee with their troops."
As Droṇa thus struck down the Somakas in the fray, some would not advance against him at all, and others did not even pierce him.
As that fearful slaughter of the foremost heroes was thus proceeding, Pārtha of a sudden heard the blast of the Pāñcajanya.
Filled with breath by Vāsudeva, the king of conches sounded loud, while the heroes who guarded the Saindhava fought on, and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra roared against the chariot of the victorious one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And as the twang of the Gāṇḍīva died away utterly on every side, the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, smitten with dismay, fell to brooding.
"Surely it is not well with Pārtha, the way the king of conches blares, and the way the Kauravas roar exultantly again and again."
Having pondered thus, with his inmost soul in turmoil, Ajātaśatru, the son of Kuntī, spoke to the Sātvata.
In a voice choked with tears, faltering again and again, looking to what must next be done, he addressed the grandson of Śini, that bull of Śini's line.
"That eternal duty which the good of old beheld, O grandson of Śini—the service a friend renders in the hour of crisis—the time for it has now come.
Reflecting upon all the warriors, O bull of Śini's line, I can recognize none a dearer friend than you, O Sātyaki.
For he who is ever loving of heart, and who is ever devoted—it is my conviction that such a one is to be appointed to a task in a time of crisis.
As Keśava is ever the refuge of the Pāṇḍavas, so too are you, O Vārṣṇeya, equal to Kṛṣṇa in prowess.
Therefore I shall lay this burden upon you; it is for you to bear it. And my wish you ought never to render vain.
So do you, O bull among men, render aid in this peril to my brother Arjuna in the battle—your friend and your teacher as well.
For you are vowed to truth, a hero, a giver of fearlessness to friends; you are renowned in the world, O hero, by your deeds as a man of true word.
For he who, fighting for a friend's sake, O grandson of Śini, lays down his body, and he who gives the whole earth to the twice-born—the two are equal.
And we have heard of many kings who went to heaven, having given this whole earth to the Brāhmaṇas according to the ordinance.
So I too beseech you, O righteous one, with joined palms: the reward shall be equal to the gift of the earth, or even greater, O mighty one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kṛṣṇa alone has ever been a giver of fearlessness to friends, ready to lay down his life in battle—and you, O Sātyaki, are the second such.
For a valiant hero who seeks glory in battle, only a brave man can be a fit companion—not some other, common fellow.
And in such a crushing onslaught as is now under way, O Mādhava, there is no protector of the victorious one in battle other than you.
For the son of Pāṇḍu, praising your deeds a hundredfold and kindling joy in me, recounted them again and again:
"Swift of hand with weapons, fighting in dazzling fashion, nimble in valor, wise, knowing every weapon, a hero—he is never bewildered in battle.
Broad of shoulder, broad of chest, mighty-armed, wielder of a great bow, of great strength and great might, that great-souled one is a great chariot-warrior.
My pupil and my friend as well—I am dear to him and he is dear to me. Yuyudhāna, my ally, will crush the Kauravas.
And, O lord of kings, were Keśava to arm himself for our sake, or Rāma, or Aniruddha, or Pradyumna the great chariot-warrior,
or Gada, or Sāraṇa, or Sāmba together with the Vṛṣṇis, to lend their aid, O great king, at the forefront of the great battle—
even then I would appoint to that aid the grandson of Śini, that tiger among men of true valor; for I have no other equal to him."
Thus, dear one, in the Dvaita forest, Dhanaṃjaya spoke to me, recounting your true qualities in your absence, in the assembly of the noble.
You ought not, O Vārṣṇeya, to render vain such a resolve of his—of Dhanaṃjaya, and of myself and Bhīma, both of us.
And when, journeying on pilgrimage to the holy fords, I went toward Dvārakā, there too I beheld your devotion toward Arjuna.
Such friendship as you show us, dwelling at Upaplavya, I have marked in none other, O grandson of Śini.
Therefore, for the sake of your noble birth and your devotion, for friendship's sake and the sake of your tutelage, for affection and valor and high lineage, O Mādhava,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and for the sake of truth, O mighty-armed one, and out of compassion as well—it is for you, O great bowman, to do a deed befitting all this.
For Duryodhana has swiftly gone forth, armed, with Droṇa; and the great chariot-warriors of the Kauravas had set out before him.
And a very great roar is heard against the victorious one. Therefore, O grandson of Śini, O Mādhava, it is for you to go there with all speed.
Bhīmasena and I myself, made ready with our troops, will hold off Droṇa, should he move against you.
Behold, O grandson of Śini, the armies fleeing in the battle, and the mighty din in the fray, and the host of the Bhāratas being torn asunder—
the force of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, dear one, scattered by Savyasācin as the sea is by the rush of a great wind at the turning of the moon.
With chariots dashing about in all directions, and with men and with horses, this army, wrapped in the dust it has raised, whirls round and round.
Phalguna, the slayer of enemy heroes, is hemmed in by the men of Sindhu and Sauvīra, warriors fighting with claw-like spears and javelins, valiant and ever honored.
Without first turning back this host, Jayadratha cannot be slain; for all these have laid down their lives for the Saindhava's sake.
Behold this army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, a forest of arrows, spears, and banners, thronged with horses and elephants, exceedingly hard to assail.
Hear the thunder of the kettledrums, and the abundant blasts of conches, and the lion-roars, and likewise the rumble of chariot-wheels.
Hear too the noise of the elephants, and of the foot-soldiers by the thousands, and hear the horsemen as they charge, making the earth tremble.
In front is the Saindhava's host, and at the rear the host of Droṇa; by its very numbers, O tiger among men, it could press hard even upon the lord of the gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sunk within that boundless host, he might lay down his very life; and were he slain in that battle, how could one like me go on living? In every way, alas, my life has come to a most grievous pass.
Dark of hue, youthful, with thick locks, fair to look upon—the son of Pāṇḍu, swift of hand and dazzling in fight, has plunged, dear one, into the host of the Bhāratas.
At sunrise the mighty-armed one went forth, and now the day is wearing away; whether he lives or not, O Vārṣṇeya, I do not know. And that army of the Kurus is vast, like the very ocean.
And Bībhatsu, the mighty-armed, has plunged alone, dear one, into the host of the Bhāratas, unassailable even by the gods, in that great battle.
And today my mind cannot rest at all upon the battle; Droṇa too, fierce in the fray, presses hard upon my force—before your very eyes, O mighty-armed one, you see how that twice-born one ranges.
And you are skilled in tasks that crowd upon you all at once; it is for you, O Mādhava, to do the great thing, joined with swiftness.
Of all my purposes, this has ever been the purpose I hold supreme: that the rescue of Arjuna must be accomplished in the battle.
I do not grieve for the Dāśārha, the protector of the world, its lord; for he, dear one, is able in battle to conquer even the three worlds when they stand together.
This I tell you in truth, O tiger among men—how much the more, then, this army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, which is so very weak.
But Arjuna himself, O Vārṣṇeya, pressed hard by many in the fight, might yield up his life in the battle—and therefore I am seized with dismay.
Go you upon his track, as those like you ought to go, urged on by one like me at such a time on behalf of such a one as he.
Of the foremost heroes of the Vṛṣṇis, two only are reckoned supreme chariot-warriors in battle: the mighty-armed Pradyumna, and you, O renowned Sātvata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In weapons you are the equal of Nārāyaṇa, in strength the equal of Saṃkarṣaṇa, and in heroism, O tiger among men, you are indeed the equal of Dhanaṃjaya.
Passing over Bhīṣma and Droṇa, the good in the world today proclaim you, O tiger among men, the most skilled in all warfare.
In this world there is nothing Sātyaki cannot achieve, O Mādhava; therefore do that which I am about to ask of you, O mighty-armed one.
The world's high regard rests upon both you and Pārtha alike; it must not be otherwise, O mighty-armed one—you must make it good here and now.
Forsaking your own dear life, range across the battlefield like a hero; for the Dāśārhas, O Śaineya, do not guard their lives in war.
To refuse to fight, to falter, to flee from the field—this is the path of cowards and base men; it is not the way the Dāśārhas walk.
Arjuna, righteous of soul, is your teacher, dear child, O bull of the Śinis, and Vāsudeva too is the teacher both of you and of the wise Pārtha.
Knowing these two grounds, I have spoken to you thus; do not scorn my word, for I am the teacher even of your teacher.
This is the will of Vāsudeva, and mine, and Arjuna's as well; what I have told you is the truth. Go now to where Dhanaṃjaya is.
Heeding this word of mine, O you of true valor, break into this army of the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, dear child.
And having entered as is fitting, and closed with the great chariot-warriors, show forth in battle the deeds worthy of yourself, O Sātvata.
Saṃjaya said: That speech—affectionate and heartfelt, sweet of syllable, timely and finely turned, and spoken with his own native grace—
having heard that speech of the King of Righteousness, Sātyaki, the bull of the Śinis, O best of the Bhāratas, answered Yudhiṣṭhira thus.
I have heard all of this speech of yours as you uttered it, O unshaken one—just and finely framed, and glorious in its purpose for Phalguna's sake.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At such a moment as this, O lord of kings, having regarded one esteemed like me, it is right that you should speak to me even as to Pārtha himself.
For Dhanaṃjaya's sake my own life is in no wise to be guarded; and once dispatched by you, what would I not do in the great battle?
At your command I would do battle with the three worlds, gods, asuras, and men together, O lord of men—how much more, then, with this feeble host?
This day I shall give battle on every side to Suyodhana's army, and I shall conquer it in the field, O king; this I tell you for truth.
Safe and well I shall reach Dhanaṃjaya, safe and well, and once Jayadratha is slain, O king, I shall return again to your side.
Yet of necessity I must make all of this known to you, O ruler of men—the word of Vāsudeva and of the wise Phalguna.
For I was firmly bound by Arjuna, again and again, in the midst of the whole army, while Vāsudeva listened.
"This day, O Mādhava, watch over the king vigilantly, holding firm to your noble resolve in the fighting, until I slay Jayadratha."
"Having entrusted the king to you, O mighty-armed one, or to the great chariot-warrior Pradyumna, I would go untroubled against Jayadratha."
"For you know Droṇa to be impetuous in battle and held the foremost of all, and you have ever heard, O Mādhava, of Droṇa's vow."
"The son of Bharadvāja longs to capture the King of Righteousness, and Droṇa is indeed able in battle to seize Yudhiṣṭhira."
"Having thus committed the King of Righteousness, that best of men, into your charge, I shall set out this day to slay the lord of the Sindhus."
"Having slain Jayadratha I shall surely return, O Mādhava—lest Droṇa should seize the King of Righteousness by force in the field."
"For if that best of men were captured by the son of Bharadvāja, O Mādhava, the slaying of the Saindhava would avail nothing, and so my joy would turn to grief."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In such a case, O best of men—should the truth-speaking Pāṇḍava be taken—it is clear that we should have to go once more into the forest."
"And so my victory would plainly come to nothing, if Droṇa, wrathful in battle, should seize Yudhiṣṭhira."
"Therefore this day, O mighty-armed Mādhava, for my sake, and for victory, and for honor, guard the king in the battle."
You, my lord, have been laid upon me as a sacred trust by Savyasācin, who ever foresees danger to you from the son of Bharadvāja.
And he too, O mighty-armed lord, ever sees in the fray no other fit to oppose the wise son of Bharadvāja in combat, save the son of Rukmiṇī—or else myself.
And so I cannot bring myself to set aside that honor and the teacher's charge, nor to abandon you, O lord of the earth.
For the teacher, by the swiftness of his hand and clad in armor none can pierce, would, once he found you in battle, toy with you as a child toys with a bird.
If the son of Kṛṣṇa, bow in hand and bearing the sea-monster banner, were here, to him I would commit you, and he would guard you even as Arjuna would.
See to your own protection: who shall be your guardian once I am gone—one who could withstand Droṇa in battle—while I go to the Pāṇḍava?
And let there be no fear in you this day, O king, on Arjuna's account; never does that mighty-armed one falter once he has taken up his burden.
The warriors of the Sauvīras, and the men of Sindhu and of Pūru, the northerners and the southerners, and whatever other great chariot-warriors there are—
and those eminent chariot-warriors renowned with Karṇa at their head, O king—all these are not worth a sixteenth part of the wrathful Arjuna.
Though the whole earth should rise up in arms, with gods, asuras, and men, with the hosts of the rākṣasas, O king, with kiṃnaras and great serpents,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
all that moves together with all that stands still—none of it is a match for Pārtha in combat. Knowing this, O great king, let your fear for Dhanaṃjaya depart.
Where the two heroes, those mighty archers, the two Kṛṣṇas of true valor, are present, there no mischance to the undertaking can ever come to be.
Call to mind your brother's destiny, his mastery of weapons, his discipline, his unrelenting wrath in war, his gratitude, and his compassion.
And when I have departed, gone forth toward Arjuna, bear in mind too, O king, Droṇa's wondrous skill with weapons in the fray.
For the teacher, O king, hungers keenly to take you captive, guarding his own vow and resolved to make it good, O Bhārata.
See this day to your own protection: who shall be your guardian once I am gone, O Pārtha—one in whom I might trust as I set out toward Phalguna?
For never, O great king, shall I go anywhere in this great battle without first entrusting you to safe keeping, O Kaurava; this I tell you for truth.
Having weighed this many times with your mind, O best of the wise, and discerned with judgment the highest good, then, O king, command me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: It is even so, O mighty-armed Mādhava, as you say; yet my heart is not at ease concerning him of the white horses, O worthy one.
I shall make the utmost effort for my own protection; go, then, with my leave, to where Dhanaṃjaya has gone.
My own safety in battle and your going toward Arjuna—having weighed these two with reason, I judge your going there the better course.
So make ready then for the journey to where Dhanaṃjaya has gone; the mighty Bhīma will see to my protection.
The son of Pṛṣata with his brothers, and the mighty kings, and the sons of Draupadī will guard me, dear child—of that there is no doubt.
The five Kekaya brothers, and the rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, Virāṭa and Drupada, and Śikhaṇḍin the great chariot-warrior—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and the mighty Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Kuntibhoja, O worthy one, Nakula and Sahadeva, and the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas—all these, intent and ready, will guard me, dear child, without doubt.
Droṇa, together with his army, and Kṛtavarman as well, will not be able to reach me in the fray, nor shall they overpower me.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna, scorcher of foes, will boldly hold off the wrathful Droṇa in battle, as the shore holds back the abode of sea-monsters.
Wherever in the battle the son of Pṛṣata, slayer of enemy heroes, takes his stand, there Droṇa's mighty host can in no way advance.
He sprang from the sacrificial fire for the destruction of Droṇa—armored, bearing arrows, sword, and bow, and adorned with splendid ornaments.
Go with confidence, O Śaineya; have no anxiety on my account. Dhṛṣṭadyumna, wrathful in battle, will hold Droṇa at bay.
Saṃjaya said: Having heard that speech of the King of Righteousness, the bull of the Śinis, fearing both peril from Pārtha and the charge of abandoning the king,
and guarding himself above all from the world's reproach—lest, as he went toward Phalguna, men should say of him, "He is afraid"—
having thus resolved the matter in many ways, that Sātyaki, drunk with the lust for battle, spoke this word to the King of Righteousness, O bull among men.
If you deem your protection assured, may it be well with you, O lord of peoples; I shall follow after Bībhatsu and carry out your bidding.
For in the three worlds there is none dearer to me than the Pāṇḍava, O king; this I tell you for truth.
I shall go upon his track at your command, O giver of honor; for your sake there is nothing whatsoever I would leave undone.
For just as my teacher's word stands high with me, O best of two-footed beings, so your word too stands even higher with me.
For the two brothers, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, abide in your love; and know me too, O bull among kings, to stand within the love of those two.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Taking your command upon my head, for the Pāṇḍava's sake, O lord, I shall break through this army that none can break and go forth, O best of men.
Even now, in my wrath, I enter Droṇa's host as a great fish enters the ocean; there I shall go, where that king Jayadratha is, O king.
where, sheltered behind the army, he stands in dread of the Pāṇḍava, guarded by the foremost of great chariot-warriors—Droṇa's son, Karṇa, Kṛpa, and the rest.
I reckon that road from here to be three yojanas, O lord of peoples—to where Pārtha stands bent upon the slaying of Jayadratha.
Though he has gone three yojanas away, I shall follow his footsteps, O king, with a steadfast inner resolve, until the lord of the Sindhus is slain.
What man, unbidden by his teacher, would do battle? But once bidden by you, O king, what man like me would not fight? I know well that ground whither I shall go, O lord.
That ocean of an army—dense with shields, spears, maces, javelins, swords, bucklers, lances, and pikes, thronged with arrows and the finest weapons—I shall set churning.
That host of elephants, a thousand strong, which you behold yonder—those mighty beasts are of the lineage called Añjanaka.
Mounted by many barbarians, battle-hardened and fierce in the strike, those elephants are like clouds, O king, raining down like rain-clouds in their rut.
Never would these turn back once urged on by their riders; save by death alone, O king, there is no defeating them.
And those chariot-warriors whom you see on every side, O king—these are the princes called the Rukmarathas, great chariot-warriors all.
Skilled in chariots, in weapons, and in elephants, O lord of peoples, masters who have reached the far shore of the science of archery, and adept in fist-fighting,
expert in the special arts of mace-combat and skilled likewise in close grappling, practiced in the wielding of the sword and in the clash of blade and shield.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They are heroes, masters of their craft, and they vie with one another; ever, O king, do they long to conquer their fellow men in battle.
Subdued by Karṇa, O king, they are devoted followers of Duḥśāsana; even Vāsudeva praises these noble chariot-warriors.
Always eager to please, they stand under Karṇa's command; it was at his word, O king, that they turned back from him whose steeds are white.
Unwounded and unwearied, with sturdy armor and bows, they wait now on my account, surely by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son.
Crushing these in battle for your pleasure, O Kaurava, I shall afterward set out upon the track of Savyasācin.
And those others you behold, O king—seven hundred elephants sheathed in armor, mounted by Kirātas—
these the king of the Kirātas, taken captive by Savyasācin, gave as servants, well adorned, desiring to keep his own life.
Formerly, O king, these were your steadfast servants; today they are eager to fight against you. Behold the turning of time!
Their mahouts are these Kirātas, frenzied for battle, skilled in the lore of elephants, and all of them sprung from fire.
All these were vanquished in battle by Savyasācin; today, arrayed against me, they follow the will of Duryodhana.
Having shattered these battle-maddened Kirātas with my arrows, O king, I shall follow the Pāṇḍava, intent on the slaying of the Saindhava.
And those mighty elephants born of the line of Añjana—rugged yet well trained, their cheeks and trunks streaming with rut—
all richly adorned with armor of pure gold, unerring of aim in battle, O king, the equals of Airāvaṇa in war—
these, from the northern mountain, are ridden by fierce marauders, rugged and matchless warriors clad in coats of black iron.
Among them are some of cattle-born stock and some of monkey-born stock, and others of manifold origin, and some of human origin as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Smoke-colored, this host of the wicked rises up—of Mlecchas, doers of evil, dwellers in the fastnesses of Himavat.
Having gained this whole circle of elephants, Duryodhana, driven by his doom, holds in contempt Kṛpa, the son of Somadatta, Droṇa best of chariot-warriors,
the king of the Sindhus, and Karṇa too, and disdains the Pāṇḍavas, and reckons his own purpose already accomplished.
And all these, once come within range of my iron shafts, shall not escape, O son of Kuntī, even were they swift as thought.
Ever favored by him who lives upon the valor of others, they shall go to their destruction, beaten down by the floods of my arrows.
And those chariot-warriors you see, O king, with banners of gold—these are the Kāmbojas called Durvāraṇa, if you have heard of them.
Heroes, masters of their craft, accomplished in the science of the bow, tightly knit together, each seeking the welfare of the others.
Whole armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, roused to fury, O Bhārata, stand ready on my account, guarded round by the Kuru heroes.
Vigilant, O great king, they have ranged themselves against me; yet I shall consume them as fire consumes blades of grass.
Therefore, O king, let the chariot-fitters set in proper order upon my car all the quivers and all the equipment.
In this battle indeed weapons of many kinds must be taken up; as the teachers have prescribed, the chariot must be fivefold furnished.
For I shall meet the Kāmbojas, enraged and like venomous serpents, masters of many missiles, warriors of manifold weapons.
And I shall meet the Kirātas, smiters like poison, ever cherished by the king and seeking Duryodhana's good.
And I shall meet the Śakas too, in prowess the equals of Śakra, like fire itself, unassailable, blazing as kindled flames.
And with many other warriors of every kind, like Death itself and hard to withstand, I shall close in battle, O king—with hosts of them, frenzied for war.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore let my chief horses, rested and of auspicious marks, watered and given drink, be yoked again to my chariot.
For him the king had set upon the chariot all the quivers and all the equipment and weapons of many kinds.
Then the men, unyoking on every side the four fine steeds, gave them a savory draught to drink, a brew that quickened their spirit.
The four horses, watered and turned out, bathed, fed with grain, well adorned, their thorns and burrs removed, garlanded with gold,
these, ready and gleaming gold of hue, well broken, swift of foot, glad of heart and unflustered—they yoked to the chariot duly made ready,
a chariot crowned with a great lion-standard maned in gold, hung about with golden ensigns inlaid with gems and coral, and adorned with banners bright as pale clouds,
a chariot with a parasol raised on a golden staff and arrayed with many weapons—to it they yoked them duly, decked in golden trappings.
Dāruka's younger brother, his charioteer and dear friend, announced the yoked chariot, as Mātali does to Vāsava.
Then, bathed and made pure, the rites of good omen performed, Sātyaki, best of the glorious, caused golden coins to be given to a thousand graduate Brahmins, and was enfolded in their blessings.
Then, worthy of the honey-offering, having drunk the mead of Kailāvata, the red-eyed one shone there, his eyes swimming with its potency.
Touching the hero's bowl, filled with great gladness, his splendor redoubled, blazing like fire, the best of chariot-warriors took up upon his lap his bow with its arrows,
the rites of blessing done for him by the Brahmins—armored, well adorned, greeted with parched grain, fragrances, and garlands, and by maidens.
Having saluted the feet of Yudhiṣṭhira with joined palms, and kissed by him upon the head, he mounted his great chariot.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then those Saindhava steeds, glad and well nourished, swift as the wind and unconquerable, drew that conqueror along, prancing as they went.
Then Sātyaki, his every limb flooded with joy, said to Bhīma: "Do you, Bhīma, guard the king; that is the foremost of your duties.
I shall break through and enter this host now ripened for doom; both for the time to come and for the present, the guarding of the king is the greater good."
"You know my valor, and I yours, O scourge of foes; therefore, Bhīma, turn back, if you wish me well."
So addressed, he said to Sātyaki: "Go you to the accomplishing of your task; I shall keep guard over the king, O best of men."
Thus addressed, that Mādhava replied to Bhīmasena: "Go, go swiftly, O Pārtha; sure is my victory this day.
For you, loving and devoted, stand today obedient to me, and the omens speak of good fortune to me, O Bhīma.
When the wicked Saindhava is slain by the great-souled Pāṇḍava, I shall embrace the king, that soul of righteousness—of this there is no doubt."
Having said this much to Bhīma and taken his leave of him, the great-spirited one surveyed your army as a tiger surveys the herds of deer.
Seeing him about to enter, O lord of men, your army was bewildered yet more and trembled exceedingly.
Then Sātyaki advanced at once against your host, longing to behold Arjuna, O king, at the command of the Dharma King.
Saṃjaya said: When Yuyudhāna had advanced against your army in his eagerness for battle, the Dharma King, O great king, encircled by his own troops, set forth behind Yuyudhāna, seeking to reach Droṇa's chariot.
Then the son of the Pāñcāla king, frenzied in battle, and the prince Vasudāna cried aloud within the Pāṇḍava host:
"Come on, strike, run swiftly hither and yon, so that Sātyaki, frenzied for battle, may pass through with ease.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For many great chariot-warriors will strive for his defeat." So saying, they fell with fury upon your host.
We, seeking to overcome them, rushed against them there; then a mighty din arose about Yuyudhāna's chariot.
The great army of your son, shaken by the Sātvata, O great king, was rent asunder a hundredfold.
As it was being torn apart, the grandson of Śini, that great chariot-warrior, crushed seven heroic, mighty archers in the forefront of the host.
Terrified, ground down and swept away by the long-armed one, those heroes abandoned the field of battle, seeing him more than human.
With chariots whose axles were broken and whose frames were shattered, O sire, with wheels crushed and split, and banners cast down,
with chariot-poles, pennants, golden helmets, and arms smeared with sandal and braced with armlets, O lord of the people,
and with the thighs of men, like the trunks of elephants, like the coils of serpents, was the earth strewn over, O best of men.
With the fallen faces of bull-eyed men, faces like the moon and adorned with lovely earrings, the earth shone, O Bhārata.
And with elephants hewn in many pieces, lying like mountains, the ground gleamed exceedingly, as though strewn with shattered hills.
With harness of bright gold, decked with nets of pearl, and with bright-figured breast-plates, the horses gleamed—lifeless now, fallen to the earth, swept down by the long-armed one.
Having slain your troops of many kinds, the Sātvata pierced deep into your host, and put your army to violent flight.
Then Sātyaki sought to go by that very road by which Dhanaṃjaya had passed; but he was checked by Droṇa.
Coming upon the son of Bharadvāja, Yuyudhāna, O sire, though enraged, advanced no farther—as the sea does not pass its shore.
Having stayed in battle Yuyudhāna, that great chariot-warrior, Droṇa pierced him with five sharp, vital-rending arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Sātyaki in the fight pierced Droṇa, O king, with seven shafts of golden notch, whetted on stone, fledged with heron and peacock feathers.
With six arrows Droṇa struck him, together with his horses and his driver; but Yuyudhāna, that great chariot-warrior, would not brook this from Droṇa.
Then, with a lion's roar, Sātyaki pierced Droṇa with ten arrows, and with six others, and with eight again.
Yuyudhāna pierced Droṇa once more with ten arrows, and his charioteer with one, and his four horses with four, and with a single shaft he pierced his banner in the fight, O sire.
Him, with his horses and driver, his chariot and banner, Droṇa swiftly covered with his fleet arrows, as with swarms of locusts.
And in the same way Yuyudhāna too, unflinching, covered Droṇa with many fleet arrows; then Droṇa spoke:
"Your teacher has left the battle and gone, like a coward; for he forsook me while I fought, and turned aside, keeping me on his right.
You shall not escape me with your life today while I do battle, O Mādhava—unless you too forsake me in the fight and flee in haste, as your teacher did."
Sātyaki said: At the command of the Dharma-king I am following the track of Dhanaṃjaya. Fare you well, O brāhmaṇa—let no time of mine be lost.
Saṃjaya said: Having said only this much, O king, the grandson of Śini avoided the preceptor and swiftly drove on, and he spoke thus to his charioteer:
Droṇa will make every effort to bar my way. Drive on with care in the battle, O charioteer, and hear besides this further word of mine.
There is seen the army of the Āvantyas, of great splendour; and next to it that mighty host of the southerners.
And next to that is this great force of the Bāhlīkas; and close beside the Bāhlīkas, joined with them, is also the mighty host of Karṇa.
These armies, though distinct one from another, O charioteer, lean each upon the other and will not abandon the field of battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Reaching the gap between them, urge on the horses gladly; holding a middling pace, carry me through there, O charioteer.
There where the Bāhlīkas are seen, raising their varied weapons, and the many southerners with the Sūta's son at their head—
and that division which is seen thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, and beset with foot-soldiers risen from many lands—
Having said this much to his driver, and shunning the brāhmaṇa, he passed on to where stood the fierce and exceeding mighty force of Karṇa.
Wrathful, Droṇa pursued him, scattering many shafts—Yuyudhāna the mighty-armed, who advanced and would not turn back.
Having struck Karṇa's great host with his sharp arrows, that Sātyaki entered the boundless Bhārata army.
When Yuyudhāna had entered and the soldiers had fled, the unforbearing Kṛtavarman moved to hem Sātyaki in on every side.
As he rushed upon him, the valiant Sātyaki struck him with six shafts and swiftly smote his four horses with four arrows.
Then again, with sixteen swift, smooth-jointed arrows, Sātyaki pierced Kṛtavarman in the centre of the chest.
Tormented by the Sātvata with many shafts of keen point, O great king, Kṛtavarman could not endure it.
Fitting a calf-tooth arrow, like a fire that flies aslant, and drawing it back to his ear, O king, he pierced Sātyaki in the breast.
That arrow, feathered to its butt, having cleft the armour that guarded his body and his body too, entered the earth, drenched with blood.
Then Kṛtavarman, master of the highest weapons, with many arrows cut asunder Sātyaki's bow, O king, together with its arrow and its string.
And in fury, O king, he pierced Sātyaki of true valour in the centre of the chest with ten keen shafts in that battle.
Then, his bow being shattered, Sātyaki, foremost of the mighty, struck Kṛtavarman's right arm with a spear.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the hero Sātyaki, taking up another very stout bow, quickly loosed his shafts by hundreds and by thousands.
That Sātyaki covered Kṛtavarman together with his chariot on every side, and screened the son of Hṛdika utterly in the battle.
Then with a broad-headed shaft he severed the head of his charioteer; slain, the driver of the son of Hṛdika fell from that great car, and, the driver being slain, the horses bolted wildly.
But the Bhoja chief, unflustered, himself reined in the horses and stood, arrows and bow in hand—and the armies honoured him for it.
Having recovered breath for a moment, he urged on his good horses; free of fear, he carried great terror into the foes. Sātyaki passed on from him, while Kṛtavarman rushed upon Bhīma.
Yuyudhāna too, O lord of kings, having issued forth from Droṇa's division, sped swiftly and at once toward the great host of the Kāmbojas.
Though there hemmed in by many heroic great car-warriors, Sātyaki of true valour did not waver then, O king.
And Droṇa, having marshalled his division and laid the burden of it upon the Bhoja, pursued Yuyudhāna in battle with intent to fight, full of care.
As he thus pursued, following at Yuyudhāna's back, the mightiest warriors in the Pāṇḍava army, greatly enraged, held him off.
But the Pāñcālas, with Bhīmasena at their head, having closed with the son of Hṛdika—foremost car among cars—lost their ardour; for though they showed their prowess, they were held back, O king, by the hero Kṛtavarman.
All of them, striving on yet somewhat bereft of their senses, their mounts grown weary, he warded off on every side with floods of arrows.
Checked by the Bhoja, those heroes who longed to break through the Bhoja division stood their ground in battle like noblemen, seeking great renown.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: An army so manifold, so excellently arrayed, so marshalled in due order, and so vast, O Saṃjaya—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
ever honoured by us and ever well-disposed toward us, mature, of most wondrous aspect, and steadfast in valour in the van—
neither too old nor too young, neither lean nor over-stout, nimble and long of wind, sturdy of limb and free of sickness—
furnished with donned armour, equipped with manifold weapons, and perfected in the many arts of wielding arms—
skilled in mounting and in leaping down, in charging and in vaulting across, in striking truly, in advancing and in withdrawing—
tested again and again upon elephants, horses, and chariots, and, once duly tested, provided with its wages—
in my army there was none who came uninvited, none unpaid—not through mere fellowship, nor flattery, nor by reason of kinship.
manned by high-born and honourable folk, contented and well-nourished, unarrogant, shown honour and good service, glorious and high of spirit—
and guarded, my son, by other chief counsellors—many of them, doers of foremost deeds, like the guardians of the worlds, those best of men—
protected by many kings who sought to do us pleasure, who had come to us of their own desire with their forces and their followers—
full like the great ocean filled on every side by rivers, encompassed by chariots and horses that, though wingless, were like winged birds—
a fearsome sea whose inexhaustible waters were its warriors, whose surging waves were its mounts, teeming as with fishes with slings, swords, maces, lances, arrows, and javelins—
thronged with banners and ornaments, heaped with bands of jewels, and stirred to trembling, as by the speed of the wind, by its onrushing mounts—
with Droṇa for its deep abyss, Kṛtavarman for its great whirlpool, Jalasaṃdha for its mighty shark, and roused high by Karṇa as by the moon's rising—
when the bull of the Pāṇḍavas had gone, cleaving through that ocean of my host by his swiftness, O Saṃjaya, and Yuyudhāna too, with but a single chariot—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
once Savyasācin had entered, and the high-souled Sātvata car-warrior, I see no remnant of my army there, O Saṃjaya.
Seeing those two impetuous and fearless warriors break clean through, and beholding the king of the Sindhus within the range of Gāṇḍīva's arrows—
what task did the Kurus then set themselves, driven on by fate? And how did they bear themselves in that dread and narrow pass of time?
For I think the Kauravas are seized, my son, gripped close by death; for their prowess in battle no longer shows itself today as it once did.
Unhurt, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava have penetrated into that battle, and there is no one here to bar them, O Saṃjaya.
And many warriors were maintained, great car-warriors taken on only after testing, with fitting pay—and others with kindly words.
In my army, my son, there is none kept on without cause; for the wages of a retainer are earned by service that befits them.
And there was not, O Saṃjaya, a single warrior in my army maintained on scant gifts, my son, nor any man hired with paltry goods.
For they were honoured to my utmost means with gifts, with respect, and with seats of rank—by me, and by my sons, my son, and by my kinsmen and their relations alike.
Yet these very men, when they met them in battle, were vanquished by Savyasācin and overwhelmed by the grandson of Śini. What is this but the work of destiny?
He who is guarded in battle, O Saṃjaya, and those who are his guardians—one common road lies before the guarded and his guards alike.
Seeing Arjuna stationed in battle before the Saindhava, what course did my son, sorely bewildered, resolve upon?
And seeing Sātyaki entering the battle fearlessly, what task fit for the hour did Duryodhana then deem to be his?
Seeing those two best of car-warriors, surpassing all in arms, enter the army, what firmness in the fight did my people muster?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beholding Kṛṣṇa the Dāśārha set there for Arjuna's sake, and the bull of the Śinis as well, I think my poor sons are grieving.
Seeing the army broken through by the Sātvata and by Arjuna, and the Kurus in flight, I think my poor sons are grieving.
Seeing the car-warriors scattered, void of zeal to conquer the foe and bent all their zeal upon flight, I think my poor sons are grieving.
Beholding the chariot-platforms emptied by the Sātvata and by Arjuna, and the warriors slain, I think my poor sons are grieving.
Seeing heroes there by the thousand, stripped of horses, elephants, and chariots, running distraught about the field, I think my poor sons are grieving.
Seeing the horses left riderless and the men left chariotless there by Sātyaki and Pārtha, I think my poor sons are grieving.
Seeing the bands of foot-soldiers running every which way in the battle, all of them despairing of victory, I think my poor sons are grieving.
Seeing those two unconquered heroes break clean through Droṇa's division in an instant, I think my poor sons are grieving.
I am sorely bewildered, my son, to hear that Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya, together with the Sātvata, those unfaltering ones, have entered my army.
When that foremost car-warrior of the Śinis had entered the host and broken through the Bhoja division, how then fared the Kauravas?
And when the Pāṇḍavas were held in check by Droṇa in the battle, how did the fighting go there? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya.
For Droṇa is strong, a hero, accomplished in arms, and firm in valour; how did the Pāñcālas fight against that great archer in the battle?
They had sworn a bitter feud with Droṇa and sought the Dharma-king's victory; and the great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja, had likewise sworn enmity against them.
And whatever Arjuna did toward the slaying of the king of the Sindhus, tell me all of that, O Saṃjaya, for you are skilled in the telling.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: This calamity has arisen from your own offence, O bull of the Bhāratas; having met with it, O hero, you ought not to grieve like a common man.
Knowing your want of virtue, your partiality toward your sons, your double-mindedness in matters of duty, your spite against the Pāṇḍavas, and your many wails of distress, O best of rulers of men—
Vāsudeva, the lord who knows the truth of all the worlds, the teacher of all the worlds, thereupon brought about this great war of the Kurus.
From your own offence has this exceedingly vast destruction come upon you; for no good deed of yours is seen at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end, O Bhārata—the defeat has its root in you alone.
Therefore now, holding yourself steady and grasping the world's appointed end, hear how the battle was waged—terrible, like the war of gods and demons.
When the Śaineya of true valor had entered your army, the sons of Pṛthā with Bhīmasena at their head advanced against your host.
As they came on suddenly, wrathful in aspect and with their followers, Kṛtavarman the great chariot-warrior alone held back the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
As the shore holds back the surging ocean of waters, so in the fray did the son of Hṛdika hold back the Pāṇḍava army.
There they deemed it a marvel, the prowess of the son of Hṛdika, that the sons of Pṛthā united could not overpass him in the battle.
Then Bhīma, having pierced Kṛtavarman with three iron shafts, the mighty-armed one blew his conch, gladdening all the Pāṇḍavas.
Sahadeva with twenty, the King of Righteousness with five, and Nakula too with a hundred shafts pierced the son of Hṛdika.
The sons of Draupadī with seventy-three, Ghaṭotkaca with seven, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna with three afflicted Kṛtavarman; Virāṭa and Drupada, and the son of Yājñasenī, each with five.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Śikhaṇḍin too, having pierced the son of Hṛdika with five swift arrows, struck him again with twenty shafts, as though laughing.
Then, O King, Kṛtavarman, piercing each one of those great chariot-warriors all about with five shafts apiece, struck Bhīma with seven; and, intent, he cast his bow and his banner from the chariot down to the earth.
Then upon him whose bow was severed, the great chariot-warrior in haste and wrath struck him on the chest with seventy sharpened shafts.
Deeply wounded by the son of Hṛdika's finest shafts, the mighty one, standing in the midst of his chariot, swayed like a mountain in an earthquake.
Seeing Bhīmasena thus, those led by the King of Righteousness, loosing terrible shafts, afflicted Kṛtavarman.
Having thus penned him in with a wall of chariots, O honored one, they joyfully pierced him with shafts to protect the son of the Wind-god in the fray.
Then, having regained his senses, Bhīmasena of mighty strength seized in battle a golden-shafted iron spear and swiftly hurled it from his chariot at the chariot of Kṛtavarman.
Released from Bhīma's arm, like a serpent that has cast its slough, dreadful, it blazed up all about Kṛtavarman.
As it fell suddenly upon him, gleaming like the fire at the end of an age, the son of Hṛdika then cut it in two with a pair of shafts.
Severed, the gold-adorned spear fell to the earth, lighting up the quarters, O King, like a great meteor fallen from the sky; and seeing the spear struck down, Bhīma grew exceedingly wrathful.
Then, taking up another bow, swift and of mighty twang, Bhīmasena, wrathful in the battle, beset the son of Hṛdika.
Then Bhīma of terrible strength struck him with five arrows between the breasts, O King—and all by your ill counsel.
The Bhoja, every limb wounded by Bhīmasena, O honored one, shone upon the field of battle like a red aśoka tree in full bloom.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then in wrath, as though laughing, he struck Bhīmasena hard with three arrows in the fight, and shot back at all of them.
The mighty archer struck those striving great chariot-warriors with three shafts each, and they in turn pierced him back with seven shafts apiece.
Then the great chariot-warrior, wrathful, with a razor-tipped shaft cut Śikhaṇḍin's bow in the battle, as though laughing, O Bhārata.
Then Śikhaṇḍin, wrathful at his bow being cut, quickly seized in the battle a sword and a gleaming hundred-mooned shield.
Whirling his great gold-adorned shield, he sent that sword flying toward the chariot of Kṛtavarman.
That great sword, having cut his bow together with the arrow upon it in the fray, fell to the earth, O King, like a star fallen from the heavens.
At that very moment the great chariot-warriors, hastening, pierced Kṛtavarman deeply with shafts in the battle.
Then, casting aside that great shattered bow and taking up another, the son of Hṛdika, slayer of enemy heroes, O best of the Bhāratas,
pierced the Pāṇḍavas in the fight with three straight-flying shafts each, and pierced Śikhaṇḍin with three and then with five.
But Śikhaṇḍin of great renown, taking up another bow, held back the son of Hṛdika with swift tortoise-nailed shafts.
Then, wrathful in the battle, O King, the son sprung from Hṛdika rushed swiftly upon the son of Yājñasenī, that great chariot-warrior,
upon him who in battle was the cause of high-souled Bhīṣma's death, O King—the hero displaying his strength like a tiger against an elephant.
Those two, like the elephants of the quarters, blazing like flames, those two tamers of foes, closed upon each other with masses of arrows.
Shaking their splendid bows, nocking their shafts, and loosing them by the hundred like two suns sending forth their rays,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
scorching each other with sharp shafts, those two great chariot-warriors, those heroes like the end of an age, shone like two suns.
But Kṛtavarman, fiercely piercing the son of Yājñasenī, that great chariot-warrior, with seventy-three arrows, struck him again with seven.
Deeply wounded and distressed, he sank down upon the floor of his chariot, letting fall his bow with its arrow, overwhelmed by a swoon.
Seeing him sunk down in his chariot, your men, O bull of the Bhāratas, honored the son of Hṛdika and waved their garments aloft.
Knowing Śikhaṇḍin thus tormented by the son of Hṛdika's shafts, his charioteer in haste bore the great chariot-warrior away from the battle.
But seeing Śikhaṇḍin laid low upon the floor of his chariot, the sons of Pṛthā swiftly hemmed in Kṛtavarman with their chariots in the battle.
There Kṛtavarman the great chariot-warrior wrought a surpassing marvel, in that alone in battle he held back the sons of Pṛthā with their followers.
Having vanquished the sons of Pṛthā, Kṛtavarman the great chariot-warrior overcame the Cedis, the Pāñcālas, and the Sṛñjayas too, and the mighty Kekayas.
The Pāṇḍavas, being struck down in battle by the son of Hṛdika, running this way and that, could find no firmness in the fray.
Having vanquished the sons of Pāṇḍu in the fight, those led by Bhīmasena, the son of Hṛdika stood in the battle like a smokeless fire.
Those great chariot-warriors, driven off in the battle by the son of Hṛdika and afflicted by his showers of arrows, were turned to flight.
Saṃjaya said: Hear with single mind, O King, that which you ask of me, when that host was being driven off by the high-souled son of Hṛdika.
And while your men rejoiced and the Pāṇḍavas were bowed down with shame, he who had been an island to them as they sought a foothold in fathomless depths—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
hearing the terrible roar of your men in the great battle, the Śaineya in haste, O King, advanced upon Kṛtavarman.
But Kṛtavarman, son of Hṛdika, in great wrath covered the Śaineya with sharpened shafts; thereat Sātyaki grew wrathful.
Then the Śaineya sent a well-sharpened broad-headed shaft at Kṛtavarman in the battle, and four other arrows besides.
They slew his horses; with a broad-headed shaft he severed his bow, and he pierced the rear-guard and the charioteer too with sharpened shafts.
Then, having made him chariotless, Sātyaki of true valor afflicted his army with smooth-jointed shafts.
Then that host, tormented by the Śaineya's shafts, broke apart; and Sātyaki of true valor pressed swiftly onward.
Hear, O King, what that valiant one did among your troops, when, O great King, he had passed beyond the great ocean that was Droṇa's host.
And the hero, gladdened at having vanquished Kṛtavarman in the battle, said calmly and without flurry to his charioteer, "Go on slowly."
But beholding that army of yours, thronged with chariots, horses, and elephants and filled with foot-soldiers, he spoke again to his charioteer:
"That vast elephant-division, dark like a cloud, to the left of Droṇa's host, whose front is the warrior of the golden chariot—
these many, O charioteer, are hard to ward off in battle—commanded by Duryodhana, having given up their lives for my sake, princes and mighty archers, all of them warriors of daring valor.
The noble chariot-warriors of the Trigartas, with banners wrought of gold, those heroes stand drawn up facing me alone, ready to fight.
Bring me there quickly; urge on the horses, O charioteer—I shall fight with the Trigartas before the very eyes of the son of Bharadvāja."
Then the charioteer, abiding by the Sātvata's wish, advanced slowly with the chariot sun-hued, gleaming, and bannered.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Obedient to the charioteer, prancing, the excellent horses bore him, swift as the wind in battle, gleaming like jasmine, the moon, and silver.
As that chariot rushed on with its conch-hued excellent horses, the heroes then hemmed it in on every side with an elephant-division, scattering various sharp, swift-piercing shafts.
The Sātvata too with whetted arrows assailed the elephant-division, as a great cloud assails the mountains with rain at the end of the hot season.
Struck by arrows whose touch was like the thunderbolt and lightning, sped by the strength of Śini's line, the elephants fled, abandoning the battle.
Their tusks broken, bleeding, the bony swellings of their heads burst open, ears, mouths, and trunks torn, bereft of drivers and banners,
their armor and bells shattered, their great standards cut down, their riders slain and their housings fallen, they fled, O King, in all directions.
Bellowing manifold cries, with a din like that of clouds, they were torn open by the Sātvata with iron shafts and calf-tooth arrows.
When that elephant-division was put to flight, Jalasaṃdha the great chariot-warrior, intent, brought his elephant toward the silver-horsed chariot.
The hero, gold-hued of hand, with armlets of refined gold, pure, wearing earrings, a crown, and a conch-armlet, smeared with red sandal,
bearing on his head a blazing garland wrought of refined gold, bearing on his breast a golden ornament and a gleaming neck-chain,
and brandishing a bow wrought with gold upon the elephant's head, shone, O great King, like a rain-cloud charged with lightning.
As the Magadha king's noble elephant rushed suddenly on, Sātyaki held it back as the shore holds the surging sea.
Seeing his elephant held back by the Śaineya's finest shafts, Jalasaṃdha of mighty strength grew wrathful in the battle, O King.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the wrathful mighty archer Jalasaṃdha pierced the grandson of Śini upon the broad chest with shafts that bear a heavy work.
Then with another broad-headed shaft, yellow and sharpened, he cut asunder the bow of the Vṛṣṇi hero as he was shooting.
At Sātyaki, whose bow was severed, as though laughing, O Bhārata, the Magadha hero shot, striking him with five sharpened shafts.
Though pierced by many arrows from Jalasaṃdha, the valiant, mighty-armed one did not waver—and that was as it were a marvel.
Heeding the arrows not at all, the mighty one, without much flurry, took up another bow and said, "Stand, stand!"
Having spoken thus, the grandson of Śini pierced Jalasaṃdha full in his broad chest with sixty arrows, driving them home with force, as though laughing the while.
And with a yellow razor-edged shaft he cut through Jalasaṃdha's great bow at the grip, and struck him with three more arrows.
But Jalasaṃdha, casting aside that bow with its arrow, swiftly hurled a lance at Sātyaki, O honoured one.
Having pierced through the left arm of the Mādhava in that great battle, the dreadful weapon plunged into the earth, hissing like a mighty serpent.
Though his left arm was pierced through, Sātyaki of true valour smote Jalasaṃdha with thirty sharp shafts.
Then mighty Jalasaṃdha, seizing a sword and a great bull's-hide shield adorned with a hundred moons, and whirling that sword, flung it at the Sātvata.
That sword, having cut through the bow of the grandson of Śini, fell to the earth, and lying upon the ground it gleamed like a whirling circle of firebrand.
Then, taking up another bow that could tear through any body, like the trunk of a śāla tree, twanging like Indra's thunderbolt, the wrathful one drew it and pierced Jalasaṃdha with an arrow.
Then with two razor-shafts the foremost of the Mādhavas, as though laughing, cut off both of Jalasaṃdha's arms, still bearing their ornaments and armlets.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those two arms, like iron bludgeons, fell from that finest of elephants, dropping from him who bore them earthward, like a pair of five-hooded serpents.
Then with a third razor-shaft Sātyaki severed his head, fine of tooth and jaw, with comely earrings and a lifted nose.
That headless, armless trunk, terrible to behold, drenched Jalasaṃdha's elephant with its blood.
Having slain Jalasaṃdha in the fray, the Sātvata in haste struck down the Niṣāda prince too from the elephant's shoulders, O lord of peoples.
Jalasaṃdha's elephant, its limbs bathed in blood, bore upon it the splendid seat hanging askew and clinging fast to its back.
Tormented by the Sātvata's arrows, the great elephant, trampling its own ranks and uttering a dreadful cry of anguish, fled away.
A great cry of woe arose among your troops, O honoured one, when they saw Jalasaṃdha slain by that bull of the Vṛṣṇis.
Your warriors, turning their faces away, fled on every side, eager now for flight and without heart to vanquish the foe.
At that moment, O king, Droṇa, foremost of those who bear arms, advanced with swift horses upon Yuyudhāna, the great chariot-warrior.
Seeing the grandson of Śini thus raging, the bulls of the Kurus, wrathful, together with Droṇa hemmed Sātyaki in on all sides.
Then there broke out a battle between the Kurus and the Sātvata, and between Droṇa and him in that fray, O king — dreadful, like the war of gods and demons.
Saṃjaya said: All those striking warriors, straining to the utmost and showering volleys of arrows, fought Yuyudhāna in haste, O great king.
Droṇa struck him with seventy-seven sharp arrows, Durmarṣaṇa with twelve, and Duḥsaha with ten shafts.
And Vikarṇa pierced him with thirty sharp heron-feathered arrows in the left flank, and in the space between his breasts.
Durmukha struck the grandson of Śini with ten arrows, Duḥśāsana with eight, and Citrasena with two, O honoured one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Duryodhana with a great rain of arrows beset the Mādhava in the battle, O king, as did other heroic great chariot-warriors.
Though pierced on every side by your sons, those great chariot-warriors, the grandson of Śini struck back at each of them severally with straight-flying shafts.
He struck the son of Bharadvāja with three arrows, Duḥsaha with nine, Vikarṇa with twenty-five, and Citrasena with seven.
He struck Durmarṣaṇa with twelve, Viviṃśati with four, Satyavrata with nine, and Vijaya with ten arrows.
Then, brandishing his gold-banded bow, the great chariot-warrior Sātyaki swiftly advanced upon your son, that great chariot-warrior.
He smote with deep-driven arrows that king of all the world, that best of all who bear weapons; then there arose a battle between the two.
Loosing sharp arrows and fitting fresh shafts to string, those two great chariot-warriors made each other invisible in the battle.
Sātyaki, pierced deep by the king of the Kurus, shone resplendent, the blood flowing freely from him like sap from a sandal tree.
And your son, pierced through by the floods of the Sātvata's arrows, gleamed like a tall sacrificial post crowned with a golden wreath.
But the Mādhava in that fray, O king, swiftly cut through the bow of the Kuru king, that bowman, with a razor-shaft, as though laughing; and then, his bow severed, he covered him with many arrows.
Pierced by the arrows of that swift-acting foe, the king could not endure in battle this mark of his enemy's triumph.
Then, taking up another bow, gold-backed and hard to withstand, he swiftly pierced Sātyaki with a hundred shafts.
Sorely pierced by your mighty son, that bowman, and overcome with fury, he beset your son in turn.
Seeing the king hard pressed, your sons, those great chariot-warriors, at once covered the Sātvata with a rain of arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Covered by your many sons, those great chariot-warriors, he pierced each of them with five arrows and then struck them again with seven.
And swiftly he pierced Duryodhana with eight fleet shafts, and laughing, he cut through his bow that struck terror in foes.
With his arrows he brought down the jewelled serpent-banner, and slaying the four horses with four sharp shafts, the illustrious one struck down the charioteer with a razor-shaft.
And at that same moment, exulting, he overwhelmed the Kuru king, that great chariot-warrior, with many arrows that pierce the vital parts.
Struck down in the fray by the finest arrows of the grandson of Śini, your son Duryodhana suddenly fled, O king, and leapt up into the chariot of Citrasena the bowman.
The whole world cried out in dismay to see the king in that battle being devoured by Sātyaki, as the moon in the sky is devoured by Rāhu.
Hearing that great clamour, Kṛtavarman, the great chariot-warrior, rushed at once to the place where the lordly Mādhava stood.
Brandishing his excellent bow, urging on his horses, and fiercely chiding his charioteer, he cried in haste, "On, on!"
Beholding him bearing down like Death with gaping jaws, Yuyudhāna, O great king, spoke thus to his driver:
"Kṛtavarman, armed with arrows, comes swiftly upon us in his chariot. Drive forward to meet him, this foremost of all bowmen."
Then, with horses urged to full speed and his chariot duly arrayed, he closed in battle with the Bhoja, the very measure of all archers.
Then those two tigers among men, blazing in utmost wrath like two fires, came together like two swift and furious tigers.
Kṛtavarman assailed the grandson of Śini with twenty-six sharp, keen shafts, and his charioteer with seven.
And with four excellent arrows he struck the four noble horses of the Sātvata, those well-trained steeds of the Sindhu breed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He of the golden banner, the golden armlets, and the golden mail, twanging his great gold-backed bow, poured forth gold-feathered arrows.
Then the grandson of Śini, intent and eager to behold Dhanaṃjaya, swiftly sped eighty shafts at Kṛtavarman.
