Sorely pierced by his mighty foe, that scorcher of foes, unassailable though he was, trembled as a mountain trembles in an earthquake.
With sixty-three sharp arrows Sātyaki swiftly pierced Kṛtavarman's four horses, and his charioteer with seven.
Fitting a gold-feathered shaft to his bow, Sātyaki loosed it, blazing with great flame like an enraged serpent.
That arrow, like the rod of Yama, entered Kṛtavarman, and piercing through his shining armour wrought of gold, it plunged fierce into the earth, drenched with blood.
Bleeding in the fray and tormented by the Sātvata's arrows, he reeled, and letting fall his bow, sank down upon his splendid chariot.
That bull among men, lion-toothed and of measureless valour, tormented by Sātyaki's arrows, fell to his knees upon the floor of his chariot.
Having checked Kṛtavarman — peer of the thousand-armed Arjuna, unshakable as the ocean — Sātyaki then passed onward.
Strewn with swords, spears, and bows, thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots, made to flow with rivers of dread blood by hundreds of bulls among the warriors —
— through the midst of that host the bull of the Śinis broke, before the eyes of all the troops, cleaving the army as the slayer of Vṛtra cleaves the demon array.
And the son of Hṛdika, having recovered himself and taken up another great bow, stood his ground there, mighty as he was, holding back the Pāṇḍavas in the fight.
Saṃjaya said: As the troops were being driven hither and thither by the grandson of Śini, the son of Bharadvāja overwhelmed him with great showers of arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Tumultuous grew that combat between Droṇa and the Sātvata, before the eyes of all the troops, like the strife of Bali and Vāsava.
Then Droṇa pierced the grandson of Śini in the forehead with three bright all-iron arrows shaped like venomous snakes.
With those straight-flying arrows fixed in his forehead, Yuyudhāna shone, O great king, like a three-peaked mountain.
Then the son of Bharadvāja, watching for his opening, sped at him still more arrows that rang like Indra's thunderbolt in the fray.
Those arrows loosed from Droṇa's bow as they came flying, the Dāśārha, that master of supreme weapons, cut down two by two with well-feathered shafts.
Beholding that nimbleness of his, O lord of peoples, Droṇa laughed and suddenly pierced the bull of the Śinis with twenty arrows.
Again he assailed him with fifty arrows and then with a hundred, surpassing Yuyudhāna's nimbleness with his own swiftness of hand.
As angry great serpents dart up from an anthill, so, O king, did the body-cleaving shafts dart up from Droṇa's chariot.
And in like manner the arrows loosed by Yuyudhāna in their hundreds and thousands, those blood-drinking shafts, rained down upon Droṇa's chariot.
Between the swiftness of hand of that foremost of brāhmaṇas and of the Sātvata, O honoured one, we could mark no difference: those two bulls among men were equal.
Then Sātyaki, sorely wroth, smote Droṇa with nine smooth-jointed arrows, and his banner with sharp shafts, and his charioteer with a full hundred, while the son of Bharadvāja looked on.
Seeing Yuyudhāna's swiftness of hand, Droṇa, the great chariot-warrior, pierced Sātyaki with seventy arrows, his horses with three apiece, and with a single shaft struck the banner standing on the Mādhava's chariot.
Then with another gold-feathered, broad-headed winged shaft he cut through, in the battle, the bow of the high-souled Mādhava.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Sātyaki, that great chariot-warrior, wroth, cast aside his bow, seized a mighty mace, and hurled it at the son of Bharadvāja.
That iron mace bound about with cloth, as it came hurtling on, Droṇa warded off with many arrows of manifold forms.
Then Sātyaki, whose valor was unfailing, took up another bow and pierced the hero, the son of Bharadvāja, with many shafts whetted on stone.
Having wounded Droṇa in the battle, he let loose a lion's roar; but Droṇa, foremost of all who bear arms, would not endure it.
Then, taking up a spear of iron with a golden shaft, he hurled it with force toward the chariot of the Mādhava.
But that spear, like unto Death, failing to reach the grandson of Śini, cleaved through the chariot and, fierce and dreadful in its sound, plunged into the earth.
Then, O king, the grandson of Śini pierced Droṇa with a winged shaft, striking his right arm and afflicting him sorely, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Droṇa too, O king, in the battle severed the great bow of the Mādhava with a crescent-headed arrow, and struck down his charioteer with a chariot-lance.
His charioteer, smitten by the chariot-lance, swooned away; sinking down into the floor of the car, he sat there senseless for a while.
Then Sātyaki, O king, performed there a more than human feat, for he both fought against Droṇa and himself took up the reins.
Then the great car-warrior Yuyudhāna, his face glad with joy, O lord of peoples, pierced the brāhmaṇa in the battle with a hundred shafts.
Droṇa sent against him five arrows, O Bhārata; piercing his armor, they drank his blood in the fray.
Sorely pierced by those dreadful shafts, Sātyaki grew exceedingly wrathful, and the hero loosed his arrows against the golden-charioted one.
Then, having felled Droṇa's driver to the ground with a single arrow, with his shafts he drove off the horses of that high-souled one, now bereft of their charioteer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That chariot, careering through the battle, traced circles by the thousand, O king, shining like the radiant sun.
"Charge! Seize Droṇa's horses! Run!" — thus did all the princes, together with their kings, cry out.
Setting Sātyaki aside in haste, O king, those great car-warriors all at once rushed forward to wherever Droṇa was.
Seeing them all in flight, tormented by the arrows of the Sātvata, your army, broken once more, fell again into confusion.
Having gone again to the gate of the battle-array, Droṇa took his stand there, carried thither by those horses that ran like the wind, sorely afflicted by the shafts of the Vṛṣṇi.
Beholding his array shattered by the Pāṇḍavas and the Pāñcālas, the valiant one made no further effort against the grandson of Śini, but turned to the guarding of the array itself.
Driving back the Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas, Droṇa, like a fire consuming all, stood there blazing with the fire of his wrath, like the sun of doom risen high.
Saṃjaya said: That foremost of men, the hero of Śini's line, having vanquished Droṇa and likewise your warriors led by the son of Hṛdika, laughed and spoke these words to his charioteer, O chief among the bulls of the Kurus.
"We are but the instrument here, O charioteer; the foes have been consumed by Keśava and Phalguna. Here we but slay the already slain — through that bull among men, sprung from the very self of the lord of the gods."
Having spoken thus, that bull of Śini's line, the foremost bowman, the slayer of foes, the mighty one, scattering his shafts on every side at once in that great battle, swooped down as a hawk upon its prey.
As he advanced, borne by horses of the hue of the moon and the conch, plunging into the host, that foremost of men, that chief of warriors, equal to the rays of the sun, they could not on any side hold him back.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Him of irresistible prowess and undaunted spirit, hard to withstand, O Bhārata, all those companies found unbearable — equal in might to the thousand-eyed one, like the sun in the sky when the clouds have passed.
But Sudarśana, that best of kings, filled with wrath, a wondrously skilled fighter, a great bowman clad in golden mail, by main force checked the onrushing Sātyaki.
Then there arose between the two, O Bhārata, a most terrible encounter, which both your warriors and the Somakas applauded, even as the hosts of the immortals praised the combat of Vṛtra and Indra.
With keen shafts by the hundred Sudarśana pierced the chief of the Sātvatas in the battle; but that bull of Śini's line cut those arrows asunder with his own shafts before ever they reached him.
In like manner, the arrows that Sātyaki, the peer of Śakra, hurled at Sudarśana, Sudarśana, mounted on his excellent car, split into two and into three with his choicest shafts.
Beholding his arrows then struck down by the force of Sātyaki's shafts, Sudarśana, of fierce energy, as though about to consume him in his wrath, loosed arrows bright as burnished gold.
Again, with three arrows like unto fire, drawn back to the ear, keen and well-feathered, he pierced him; breaking through his body-armor, they entered Sātyaki's flesh.
Then likewise the king's son, fixing other blazing arrows to the string, struck by main force, with four shafts, those four horses bright as silver.
Thus smitten by him, the swift grandson of Śini, whose valor was equal to Indra's, swiftly slew Sudarśana's horses with his keen volleys of arrows and sounded a roar.
Then, having cut off the head of his charioteer with a broad-headed shaft like the thunderbolt of Indra, the hero of Śini's line by main force severed the head of Sudarśana himself with a razor-edged arrow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That radiant face, decked with earrings and bright as the full moon, he struck from the body, even as of old the wielder of the thunderbolt by force struck off the head of the exceedingly mighty Bala in battle, O king.
Having slain in battle that son and grandson of kings, the swift bull of the Yadus, that high-souled one, filled with the highest joy, shone forth, O king, like the king of the gods.
Then, holding back your host with floods of arrows, that hero among men set forth toward Arjuna, riding on a chariot yoked with goodly steeds, as if to fill the worlds with wonder as he went.
That supreme and marvelous deed of his the assembled foremost warriors honored — that he consumed with his shafts the foes who came within the range of his arrows, even as the fire-god devours all.
Saṃjaya said: Then that wise and high-souled Sātyaki, the bull of the Vṛṣṇis, having slain Sudarśana in the battle, spoke thus to his charioteer:
"Choked with chariots, horses, and elephants, garlanded with waves of arrows and spears, with swords for its fishes and maces for its sea-monsters, loud with the din of the weapons of heroes;
life-stealing and terrible, resounding with the clamor of war-instruments, painful to the touch of warriors, unassailable to those who longed to conquer it —
we have crossed, dear friend, that hard-to-cross great ocean which is Droṇa's army, beset in battle by the force of Jalasandha as if by man-eating demons.
The remnant of the host beyond this I deem but a paltry rivulet, fordable and shallow of water; urge on the horses, untroubled.
Now that I have vanquished in battle the irresistible Droṇa together with his followers, I count Savyasācin as good as reached by my hand.
Having overcome the son of Hṛdika, that best of warriors, I count Dhanaṃjaya as reached; for no fear arises in me at the sight of these manifold hosts, which are to me like dry grass and reeds before a blazing fire in summer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Behold the ground traversed by the diademed chief of the Pāṇḍavas, made rough with the fallen masses of foot-soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants.
I deem him near at hand — him of the white steeds, whose charioteer is Kṛṣṇa; for there, lo, is heard the sound of Gāṇḍīva of boundless might.
By such omens as appear to me, before the sun has set Arjuna shall slay the ruler of the Sindhus.
Soothing the horses gently, drive on with care against the enemy's host, to where these warriors clad in armor stand, led by Suyodhana —
the mailed Kāmbojas of cruel deeds, frenzied for battle, bearers of arrows and bows, and the Yavanas, hard smiters,
the Śakas, Kirātas, Daradas, Barbaras, and the men of Tāmralipta, and many other barbarians, weapons of every kind in hand — all stand facing me, eager for the fight.
Once I have slain these in battle, with their chariots, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers, know this dread and most terrible stronghold to be already crossed.
The charioteer said: No agitation is in me, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis, O thou of unfailing valor, even were the wrathful son of Jamadagni to stand before us;
or Droṇa, the best of car-warriors, or Kṛpa, or even the lord of the Madras — still no agitation would there be, leaning upon thee, O mighty-armed one.
Very many hast thou vanquished in battle, O slayer of foes, and never before has any agitation come upon me at any time — how much less now, O hero, on meeting this mere cow's-hoofprint of a fight?
O long-lived one, by which way shall I bring thee to Dhanaṃjaya? Against whom art thou wrathful, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis? For whom has death drawn near? Whose minds are eager today to go to the city of Yama?
Who, beholding thee in battle ranging in thy prowess, like Yama the ender at the time of doom, endowed with valor, shall flee in the fray? Of whom does king Vaivasvata think today, O mighty-armed one?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sātyaki said: These shaven-headed ones I shall slay, as Vāsava slew the Dānavas; I shall fulfill my vow. Bear me straight against the Kāmbojas; having wrought their slaughter today, swiftly shall I go to the Pāṇḍava.
Today shall the Kauravas with Suyodhana behold my valor, O charioteer, when the host of the shaven-headed ones, and all the armies, are slain again and again.
Today, hearing the manifold outcry of the Kaurava host as it is rent asunder in the battle, Suyodhana shall be consumed with grief.
Today, in the battle, I shall display the path of mastery taught me by my teacher — the high-souled chief of the Pāṇḍavas, him of the white steeds.
Today, beholding the foremost warriors slain by my shafts in their thousands, king Duryodhana shall fall into remorse.
Today the Kauravas shall behold my bow, as I let fly my choicest arrows with swift hand, like a wheel of blazing firebrands.
Beholding the slaughter of the soldiers, their limbs studded with my shafts and streaming much blood, Suyodhana shall be consumed with grief.
Today, as I strike down the best of the best in my form of wrath, that Suyodhana shall deem this world to hold a second Arjuna.
Today, beholding kings by the thousand slain by me in the battle, king Duryodhana shall be consumed with grief in that great encounter.
Today, slaying kings by the thousand, I shall show forth among the kings my love and my devotion to the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.
Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed, the charioteer then urged on sharply the well-trained, smoothly-bearing steeds, white as the moon.
Those excellent horses, swift as thought and wind, as if drinking up the sky, bore Yuyudhāna swiftly to the Yavanas.
Coming upon Sātyaki, who never turned back in battle, many of them, light of hand, covered him with showers of arrows.
But their arrows and their weapons Sātyaki cut down with swift, smooth-jointed shafts, O king, and those arrows of theirs did not reach him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With keen, straight-flying shafts, gold-nocked and winged with vulture-feathers, the fierce one struck off the heads of the Yavanas, and their arms as well.
Cleaving on every side their armor of wrought iron and of bronze, and likewise their bodies, his arrows passed on into the surface of the earth.
Those barbarians, smitten by the hero Sātyaki in the battle, fell there by the hundred, lifeless, upon the bosom of the earth.
With shafts loosed from a fully-drawn bow, falling unbroken and close-clustered, he pierced the Yavanas five, six, seven, and eight at a time.
With the thousands of the Kāmbojas and of the Śakas, O lord of peoples, of the Śabaras, the Kirātas, and the Barbaras as well,
the grandson of Śini made the earth there impassable to look upon, a mire of flesh and blood, as he wasted away your host.
With the helmeted heads of the marauders, their locks shorn off, the earth was strewn here and there, as if with plumeless birds.
Covered all over with those headless trunks, every limb sprinkled with blood, that battlefield shone like the sky overspread with coppery clouds.
Slain by his well-jointed, straight-flying shafts, whose touch was as the thunderbolt and the lightning, they, together with their horses and chariots, lay covering the earth.
Few left remaining, broken, their lives barely clinging, bereft of sense — thus, O great king, were the mailed warriors vanquished in battle by Yuyudhāna.
Goading their horses with heels and whips, the warriors took to their swiftest pace and fled in terror in every direction.
Having routed the Kāmboja host, hard to vanquish in battle, O Bhārata, and the army of the Yavanas and the great force of the Śakas,
that tiger among men, Sātyaki of true valour, having joyfully conquered your troops, urged his charioteer, saying, 'Drive on!'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As he rode on, the guardian of Arjuna's rear, O lord of peoples, the Cāraṇas beheld him with delight, and even your own warriors paid him honour.
Saṃjaya said: Having conquered the Yavanas and the Kāmbojas, Yuyudhāna, that foremost of chariot-warriors, then advanced toward Arjuna through the midst of your army.
That tiger among men, sharp-fanged and gleaming in his many-coloured armour, terrified your army as a tiger sniffing out deer strikes fear into them.
Coursing along the paths in his chariot, he whirled his bow with great force—a bow gold-backed, mighty in might, studded with golden crescents.
With golden armlets and golden helm, encased in golden mail, that hero of the splendid golden banner shone like a peak of Meru.
His drawn bow bent into a circle in the fray, radiant with beams of brilliant lustre, that sun among men blazed forth like the autumn sun newly risen.
Striding with shoulders like a bull's, bull-eyed, that bull among men shone amid your troops as a bull amid the cattle.
Resembling a rutting elephant, moving with the gait of a rutting elephant, standing like a must elephant with temples streaming in the midst of his herd—your men, like tigers bent on the kill, rushed upon him in battle.
He had passed through Droṇa's division and the Bhoja division, hard to cross, and had crossed the ocean-like array and the host of the Kāmbojas as one fords a flood-swollen sea.
As he won free of that sea of soldiers, with Hārdikya for its sea-monster, and crossed it, your chariot-warriors in great wrath encircled Sātyaki.
Duryodhana, Citrasena, Duḥśāsana and Viviṃśati, Śakuni and Duḥsaha, the youth Durmarṣaṇa, and Krātha—
and many other heroes, weapon-bearing and unassailable, gave chase, enraged, to Sātyaki as he rode ahead of them.
Then there arose a mighty din from your army, O sire, like that of the sea whipped to fury by the wind on the day of the full moon.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beholding them all rushing upon him, that bull of Śini's line said to his charioteer, smiling, as it were, 'Drive on, but slowly.'
'See how the host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son comes surging on, straight and swift against me, with its elephants, horse, chariots, and foot.'
'It makes all the quarters resound with the rumble of its chariots, O charioteer, and makes the earth and the sky tremble, and the very seas besides.'
'This ocean of armies, my friend, I shall stem in the great battle, as the shore stems the swollen waters on the night of the full moon.'
'Behold my prowess in the great fray, O charioteer, like that of Indra; see, I scatter the armies of the foe with my whetted shafts.'
'Behold foot, horse, chariots, and elephants slain in battle by my shafts, bright as fire, robbed of their lives by the thousand.'
As Sātyaki of measureless might spoke thus, your soldiers, eager for the fight, swiftly closed upon him, crying, 'Strike! Charge! Stand fast! Look there, look there!'
As those heroes shouted thus, Sātyaki with his keen shafts slew three hundred of their horses and four hundred of their elephants.
That tumultuous clash between him and those bowmen, like the war of gods and demons, set in motion a great slaughter of men.
The grandson of Śini received the army of your son, dense as a mass of clouds, O sire, with shafts that were like venomous serpents.
Though veiled over in the battle by nets of arrows, that valiant one, unflustered, O great king, slew many of your warriors.
A very great marvel did I behold there, O lord of kings: not one shaft of Sātyaki's, O lord, fell in vain.
Thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, churning with waves of foot-soldiers, that vast ocean of an army, reaching the shore that was the scion of Śini, came to a halt.
With its men, elephants, and horses thrown into confusion, it wheeled about again and again; that army, smitten on every side by his arrows, milled hither and thither like cattle tormented by the cold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Footman, chariot, elephant, horseman, and horse alike—not one did I see there unpierced by the shafts of Yuyudhāna.
Not such havoc, O king, did Phalguna work there as the destruction Sātyaki wrought among the divisions; the grandson of Śini fought surpassing even Arjuna, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then King Duryodhana pierced the charioteer of the Sātvata with three keen shafts, and with four more his four horses.
Having struck Sātyaki with three shafts, he pierced him again with eight, while Duḥśāsana pierced that bull of Śini's line with sixteen.
Śakuni with twenty-five, Citrasena with five, and Duḥsaha with fifteen pierced Sātyaki in the breast.
That tiger of the Vṛṣṇis, smiling though thus smitten with arrows, pierced every one of them, O great king, with three shafts apiece.
Having pierced his foes deeply with those exceedingly sharp arrows, the scion of Śini ranged through the battle like a hawk, swift and nimble in his movements.
Having cut Saubala's bow and severed his leather hand-guard, he struck Duryodhana with three arrows between the breasts.
That bull of Śini's line pierced Citrasena with a hundred shafts, Duḥsaha with ten, and Duḥśāsana with twenty.
Then your brother-in-law, taking up another bow, O lord of peoples, pierced Sātyaki with eight shafts and again with five.
And Duḥśāsana with ten, Duḥsaha with three shafts, and Durmukha with twelve, O king, pierced Sātyaki.
Duryodhana, O Bhārata, having pierced the Mādhava with seventy-three shafts, then struck his charioteer with three keen arrows.
All those heroes together, those mighty car-warriors straining their utmost, Sātyaki pierced again, each with five arrows.
Then that foremost of chariot-warriors swiftly struck the charioteer of your son with a broad-headed shaft, and the slain man fell to the ground.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When that charioteer was struck down, the chariot of your son, O lord, was carried off from the field by those horses that ran like the wind.
Then your sons, O king, and the soldiers, O lord of peoples, beholding the king's chariot borne away, fled by the hundreds.
Seeing that army in flight, O Bhārata, Sātyaki overwhelmed it with sharp arrows, gold-feathered and whetted on stone.
Having routed all your troops on every side, Sātyaki went on, O king, toward the chariot of him whose steeds were white.
As he took up his arrows, guarded his charioteer, and delivered his own self from peril, your warriors paid him honour.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the scion of Śini, having crushed that great army, was going on toward Arjuna, what did my shameless sons do then, O Saṃjaya?
And how, in such a battle, could there be any firmness left in those doomed men, when they had seen the scion of Śini bear himself like Savyasācin himself?
What will they say of their warriorhood, vanquished there in the midst of the host? And how did Sātyaki of great renown pass them by in the battle?
And how, while my sons yet lived, did the scion of Śini press on there in the fight, O Saṃjaya? Tell me that truly.
Most wondrous is this that I hear from you, my son—the battle of one man against many foes, all of them mighty car-warriors.
I deem it an ill omen turned against my luckless sons, that they should be cut down in battle by the high-souled Sātvata.
For my whole army is not a match for that one man, O Saṃjaya—for Yuyudhāna in his wrath; let all the Pāṇḍavas stand aside!
Having vanquished in battle Droṇa, the skilled, the unconquerable in war, he slays my sons as a lion slays a herd of beasts.
By Kṛtavarman and the many other heroes, striving hard in the fray, Yuyudhāna, that bull among men, could not be slain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Not such a fight did Phalguna wage there as the fight that the grandson of Śini, of great renown, has waged.
Saṃjaya said: This is the fruit of your ill counsel, O king, and of Duryodhana's deeds. Listen attentively to what I shall tell you, O Bhārata.
They turned back once more, binding themselves to one another as sworn warriors, setting their hearts firmly upon battle, at the command of your son.
Three thousand horsemen, with Duryodhana at their head—Śakas, Kāmbojas, Bāhlīkas, Yavanas, and Pāradas as well—
Kuṇindas, Taṅgaṇas, Ambaṣṭhas, and the Paiśācas together with the Mandaras—rushed upon the scion of Śini as locusts rush upon a flame.
And the harnessed chariots of the highlanders who fight with stones, five hundred heroes strong, O king, charged upon the scion of Śini.
Then with a thousand chariots and a hundred mighty car-warriors, with a thousand elephants and two thousand horses,
those great car-warriors, loosing showers of arrows of every kind, rushed upon the scion of Śini, together with footmen past counting.
Urging them all on with the cry 'Slay him!', O Bhārata, Duḥśāsana, O great king, hemmed Sātyaki round about.
There we beheld the great and wondrous feat of the scion of Śini—that he alone fought, unflinching, against so many.
He slew the chariot-division and that force of elephants, and all the horsemen, and the barbarians too, every one of them.
There, with wheels crushed and the finest weapons shattered, with axles broken in many places, and shafts, poles, and chariot-frames,
with splintered chariot-poles and banners struck down, with coats of mail and yak-tail whisks, the earth lay all bestrewn.
With garlands, ornaments, garments, and chariot-trappings, O sire, the earth was covered over there, as the sky is covered with planets, O Bhārata.
And lordly elephants, mountain-like in form, lay fallen—born of the line of Añjana and of Vāmana, O Bhārata, born of the line of Supratīka and of the line of Mahāpadma as well,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and of the line of Airāvaṇa, and of yet other lines as well—those choicest of tuskers, O king, lay there slain in great numbers.
Horses of the finest breed—from Vanāyu, from the hill-country, from Kāmboja, Āraṭṭa, and Bāhlika—Sātyaki slew there, O king.
And footmen sprung from many lands and of many races the scion of Śini slew there by the hundreds and by the thousands.
As they were being driven before him, Duḥśāsana said to the barbarians, 'Turn back, you who know no law! Fight on! What good is your fleeing?'
And looking upon them all, your son Duḥśāsana spurred on the highland heroes who fought with stones.
'You are skilled in battle with stones; this Sātyaki knows it not. He knows not stone-warfare—slay him, this man so eager for the fight!'
'Just so, none of the Kurus are versed in battle with stones. Charge on, fear not! Sātyaki shall not overtake you.'
Then the mountain-dwellers, taking up boulders as large as young elephants, stood facing Yuyudhāna, longing for death.
Others too, hurling missiles and seeking the death of the Sātvata, urged on by your son, hemmed him in from every side.
As they rushed upon him, eager to wage war with stones, Sātyaki took aim and let fly thirty arrows.
That tumultuous rain of stones, loosed by the mountaineers, the bull of Śini's line shattered with iron shafts like serpents.
By the splinters of stone, blazing like swarms of fireflies, the troops for the most part were struck down, crying out in dismay, O honored one.
Then five hundred warriors, their great stones raised aloft, their arms severed, O king, fell to the surface of the earth.
He slew many thousands of those stone-fighting warriors who stood their ground and struggled on; and that seemed a marvel.
Then once more, on every side, a rain of stones was cast by the goat-faced ones, by the Ayohastas, the spear-wielders, the Daradas, and the throngs of Khaśas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As the Ambaṣṭhas and the Kuṇindas hurled them again and again, the mighty Sātyaki, watching keenly, pierced each in turn with iron arrows.
As the boulders were split in mid-air by his sharp arrows, at that din, O king, the elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers fled.
Covered over with stone-dust, both men and birds were unable to hold their ground, as though stung by bees.
The elephants that survived the slaughter, streaming blood, their temple-bosses split open, turned away from the path of Yuyudhāna's chariot.
Then there arose from your army, tormented by the Mādhava, a din terrible as the roar of the ocean, O honored one.
Hearing that tumultuous din, Droṇa said to his charioteer: "Yonder, O charioteer, is the wrathful great warrior of the Sātvatas in battle.
Rending the host in many places, he ranges over the field like Death itself. Where that tumultuous din is heard, there, O charioteer, drive the chariot.
Surely Yuyudhāna has clashed with the stone-fighters, for all our chariot-warriors are being borne away by their bolting horses.
Stripped of weapons and armor, shattered, they fall here and there, and the drivers cannot rein in their horses amid the tumult."
As the wise son of Bharadvāja spoke thus, O king, the charioteer then answered Droṇa, foremost of weapon-bearers:
"O long-lived one, the Kaurava host is fleeing on every side. Behold the warriors broken in battle, running this way and that.
And these heroic Pāñcālas, united with the Pāṇḍavas, seeking to slay you yourself, are rushing forward from all sides.
Determine here what the moment demands, O tamer of foes—whether to stand fast or to advance; for Sātyaki has gone far afield."
Even as the son of Bharadvāja was speaking thus, O honored one, the scion of Śini came into view, striking down chariots of every kind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Your men, being slaughtered in battle by Yuyudhāna, abandoned Yuyudhāna's chariot and fled toward Droṇa's division.
And those chariots with which Duḥśāsana had earlier turned to the fight—all of them, terrified, ran toward Droṇa's chariot.
Saṃjaya said: Seeing Duḥśāsana's chariot drawn up close at hand, the son of Bharadvāja then spoke these words to Duḥśāsana:
"Duḥśāsana, why have all these chariots fled away? Is it well with the king? Does the lord of the Sindhus yet live?
You are here a king's son, a king's brother, a great chariot-warrior who has attained the rank of crown prince. Why then do you flee from the battle?
Having yourself stirred up this great enmity with the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, how is it that on meeting Sātyaki alone you are afraid in battle?
Long ago, while you grasped the dice in the gaming hall, you did not know that these arrows would come to be, cruel as venomous serpents.
The speaking of harsh words to the Pāṇḍavas in particular, and the affliction of Draupadī—of these you alone were the root, long ago.
Where now is your pride and your arrogance? Where, O hero, is that roaring of yours? Having enraged the Pārthas, who are like venomous serpents, where will you go?
Pitiable is this army of the Bhāratas, and pitiable is King Suyodhana, whose hard-hearted brother you are—you who are bent on flight.
Surely, O hero, this host being torn apart and stricken with fear ought to have been guarded by you, relying on the might of your own arms; yet you this day, forsaking the battle in your terror, gladden the foe.
When you, the leader of the host, have fled, O slayer of foes, who else will stand his ground in battle, the fearful taking refuge in one already afraid?
Today, fighting against the Sātvata alone, O blameless one, your mind turns to flight from the battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When you behold in battle the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, and Bhīmasena, O Kaurava, and the twins, then what will you do?
Not equal to Phalguna's arrows in battle, whose splendor is like the sun and fire, are these shafts of Sātyaki from which you flee in terror.
If indeed your mind is set on flight, then let the earth be given over to the King of Righteousness, and so make peace.
While Phalguna's iron shafts, like serpents loosed from their slough, have not yet entered your body, make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
While the high-souled Pārthas, having slain your hundred brothers in battle, have not yet seized the earth, make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
While King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Dharma, is not yet wrathful, nor Kṛṣṇa who glories in battle, make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
While mighty-armed Bhīma, plunging into the great host, has not yet crushed your own brothers, make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
Long ago your brother Suyodhana was told by Bhīṣma: 'The Pāṇḍavas are unconquerable in war, O gentle one; make your peace with the Pāṇḍavas.' Yet that dull-witted brother of yours, Suyodhana, did not do so.
Now, summoning steadfastness in battle, fight on with effort against the Pāṇḍavas. Go swiftly by chariot to where Sātyaki stands.
This host, bereft of you, will scatter, O Bhārata. For your own sake, give battle in the field to Sātyaki of true valor."
Thus addressed, your son answered not a word, but, treating what he had heard as though unheard, set out toward where Sātyaki was.
Joined with a great host of unyielding Mlecchas, and reaching the field, he strove and gave battle to Yuyudhāna.
Droṇa too, foremost of chariot-warriors, in great wrath rushed upon the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, holding to a measured speed.
And entering the array of the Pāñcālas in battle, Droṇa put their warriors to flight by hundreds and by thousands.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Droṇa, O great king, proclaiming his name aloud in the battle, wrought a great slaughter among the Pāṇḍavas, Pāñcālas, and Matsyas.
As the son of Bharadvāja was conquering the divisions on every side, the radiant Vīraketu, son of the Pāñcāla king, advanced against him.
He pierced Droṇa with five arrows of well-smoothed joints, struck his standard with one, and his charioteer with seven.
There, O great king, I beheld a marvel in the battle: that Droṇa did not at once move against the impetuous Pāñcāla prince in the fight.
Seeing Droṇa held in check in the battle, O honored one, the Pāñcālas, desiring the victory of Dharma's son, surrounded him on every side, O king.
With arrows like fire, with costly lances, and with weapons of every kind, O king, they overwhelmed Droṇa alone.
Droṇa struck down those swarms of arrows on every side, O king, as the wind sweeping the sky scatters great rain-clouds.
Then the slayer of enemy heroes fitted to his bow a most dreadful arrow, like the sun and fire, aimed at Vīraketu's chariot.
That arrow, O king, piercing the Pāñcāla prince, the delight of his line, swiftly entered the earth, wet with blood and blazing as it went.
Then the Pāñcāla prince, the delight of his line, fell swiftly from his chariot, like a great campaka tree from a mountain peak, beaten down by the wind.
When that mighty-armed prince, a great archer, was slain, the Pāñcālas in haste surrounded Droṇa on every side.
Citraketu and Sudhanvan, and Citravarman, O Bhārata, and Citraratha as well, racked by grief at their brother's ruin,
rushed together upon the son of Bharadvāja, eager to fight, loosing showers of arrows like rain-clouds at the close of the hot season.
Assailed in many ways by those princely great chariot-warriors, he, enraged in battle, stripped those youths of their horses, charioteers, and cars.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And with other keen-edged broad arrows, the illustrious one struck down their heads, as though plucking flowers.
Slain, those splendid warriors fell from their chariots to the earth, O king, as the Daiteyas and Dānavas fell of old in the war of the gods and demons.
Having slain them in battle, O king, the valiant son of Bharadvāja whirled his unassailable, gold-backed bow.
Seeing the godlike Pāñcāla great chariot-warriors slain, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, exceedingly wrathful, letting tears fall from his eyes, advanced in his fury toward Droṇa's chariot in the battle.
Then of a sudden a cry of "Alas! Alas!" arose, O king, when men saw Droṇa hemmed in by the arrows of the Pāñcāla prince in the battle.
Though covered over in many ways by the high-souled grandson of Pṛṣata, Droṇa did not waver, but fought on, even smiling.
Then the Pāñcāla prince, O great king, beside himself with rage, struck Droṇa upon the chest in his wrath with ninety arrows of bent joints.
Deeply wounded by that strong warrior, the illustrious son of Bharadvāja sank down upon the floor of his chariot and fell into a swoon.
Seeing him brought to such a pass, the valiant, heroic Dhṛṣṭadyumna swiftly cast aside his bow and seized his sword.
Leaping down from his chariot, that great warrior in haste swiftly mounted the chariot of the son of Bharadvāja, O honored one, his eyes red with wrath, longing to sever the head from his body.
Then the mighty Droṇa, recovering, took up his bow and, with span-long arrows ever fit for close fighting, O king, gave battle in the field to the great chariot-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Those arrows called span-long, made for fighting at close quarters and well known to Droṇa, O king, beat Dhṛṣṭadyumna back.
Assailed by those many shafts, that mighty and valiant one, his onset broken, leaped swiftly down from the chariot.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Mounting his own chariot, the hero, the great warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna, took up his mighty bow and pierced Droṇa in the battle.
That marvelous combat between the two the hosts of beings hailed with praise, and the kṣatriyas too, O great king, and whatever other soldiers were there.
"Droṇa, now joined in combat with Dhṛṣṭadyumna, will surely fall into the power of our king"—so the Pāñcālas cried aloud.
But Droṇa, swift in battle, struck off the head of Dhṛṣṭadyumna's charioteer, as one knocks a ripe fruit from a tree; and thereupon the horses of that high-souled one bolted away, O king.
As they fled in rout, Droṇa, valorous everywhere upon the field, drove off the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas in the battle.
Having vanquished the Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas, the majestic son of Bharadvāja, that subduer of foes, took his stand once more within his own array and stood unshaken; nor did the Pāṇḍavas dare to conquer him in battle, O lord.
Saṃjaya said: Then, O king, Duḥśāsana rushed upon Śaineya, scattering arrows by the thousand like a rain-laden thundercloud.
Though he pierced Sātyaki with sixty arrows and then with sixteen more, he could not make him waver, who stood firm in the fight like Maināka, the mountain.
But that hero covered Duḥśāsana thickly with his shafts, as a spider, with its web, enmeshes a gnat that has blundered into it.
Seeing Duḥśāsana so studded with a hundred arrows, the king urged on the Trigartas against the chariot of Yuyudhāna.
Those doers of cruel deeds drew near to Yuyudhāna—three thousand chariot-warriors of the Trigartas, skilled in battle.
They surrounded him with a vast host of chariots, having steadied their resolve for the fight, bound to one another as sworn confederates unto death.
As they strove in the fight and loosed their showers of arrows, he crushed five hundred of their foremost warriors in the front of the array.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Swiftly slain by the shafts of the chief of the Śinis, they fell like great trees shattered by the force of a mighty gale.
With chariots broken in many parts, with banners, O lord of peoples, and with horses adorned in gold all fallen there, the earth was strewn.
With those mangled by Śaineya's arrows and drenched in floods of blood, the field shone, O great king, as though with kiṃśuka trees in full flower.
Slaughtered in battle by Yuyudhāna, your men found no deliverer, like elephants sunk fast in the mire.
Then they all turned back toward Droṇa's chariot, as great serpents flee to their holes in dread of the king of birds.
Having slain five hundred warriors with arrows like venomous serpents, that hero advanced slowly toward the chariot of Dhanaṃjaya.
As that best of men went forward, your son Duḥśāsana swiftly pierced him with nine arrows of smooth-jointed shafts.
But that mighty bowman pierced him in turn with five whetted arrows, gold-feathered, fledged with vulture-plumes, and flying straight.
And Duḥśāsana, as if laughing, O great king, O Bhārata, having struck Sātyaki with three arrows, pierced him again with five.
But Śaineya, having struck your son with five swift arrows and severed his bow in the fight, went on toward Arjuna, leaving him astonished.
Then Duḥśāsana, enraged, hurled at the departing hero of the Vṛṣṇis an all-steel javelin, eager to slay him.
But that dreadful javelin of your son Sātyaki cut into a hundred pieces, O king, with whetted heron-feathered shafts.
Then your son, O lord of men, taking up another bow and piercing Sātyaki with ten arrows, roared aloud like a lion.
But Sātyaki, enraged in battle, having bewildered your son, smote him upon the breast with arrows shaped like tongues of fire, and pierced him again with eight all-iron, keen-pointed shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Duḥśāsana then pierced Sātyaki in turn with twenty arrows; and the Sātvata too, O great king, struck him upon the breast with three smooth-jointed shafts of mighty speed.
Then that great chariot-warrior, sorely enraged, slew his steeds with sharp arrows, and his charioteer too with smooth-jointed shafts.
With one broad-headed shaft that master of the highest weapons cut his bow, with five his hand-guard, with two more his banner and his chariot-lance, and with keen arrows both his flanking charioteers as well.
His bow cut, his chariot wrecked, his horses and charioteer slain, he was borne away upon his own chariot by the commander of the Trigarta host.
Though Śaineya rushed upon him, for a moment, O Bhārata, that mighty-armed one did not slay him, remembering the words of Bhīmasena.
For Bhīmasena had vowed, O Bhārata, in the midst of the assembly, the slaying of all your sons in battle.
And so, having conquered Duḥśāsana in the fight, O lord, Sātyaki went swiftly, O king, in the direction whither Dhanaṃjaya had gone.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Were there in that army of mine no great chariot-warriors at all, who neither slew nor even checked Sātyaki as he went on his way?
For alone he wrought his deeds in the battle, that hero of true valor, equal in might to Śakra, as great Indra among the Dānavas.
Or was that path empty by which Sātyaki passed—he, a bull among men, crushing alone the teeming armies?
And how did Śaineya, one against many, pass out from the midst of those great-souled warriors as they fought? Tell me this, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: O king, the muster of your armies—with chariots, elephants, horse, and foot—grew tumultuous, like the ending of an age.
Among the daily-gathered hosts of your army, O giver of honor, there was, I think, no muster in the world to equal it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There the gods, and the cāraṇas assembled together, were saying: 'Surely the hosts upon this earth shall have their ending here.'
And never was there such an array, O lord of peoples, as the one Droṇa had ordered at the slaying-quest of Jayadratha.
Like the roar of oceans lashed by a furious gale was the din in the battle of those floods of troops as they rushed upon one another.
Of the assembled kings, O best of men, there were many—in your host and in the Pāṇḍavas'—thousands and hundreds.
Of those furious champions, steadfast in their deeds in battle, there arose a vast and turbulent uproar that made the hair stand on end.
Then Bhīmasena cried aloud, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O sire, and Nakula and Sahadeva and the Pāṇḍava, the king of righteousness.
'Come on! Strike! Range about with all your might! For the two heroes, the Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava, have entered the host of the foe.'
'So contrive it swiftly that those two may pass with ease toward the slaying of Jayadratha'—thus he urged on the armies; 'were they to fail, the Kurus would gain their end, and we be conquered.'
'Therefore do you, joined together and swift, churn up at once that ocean of troops, even as the high-rushing winds churn the sea.'
Urged on by Bhīmasena, O king, and by the prince of Pāñcāla, they smote the Kauravas in the fray, casting away their own dear lives.
Desiring death in battle, those men of surpassing splendor, for the sake of heaven and for their friends' cause, did not guard their lives with their weapons.
Even so your men, O king, longing for great renown and fixing their minds upon the noble resolve in battle, drew up only for the fight.
And while that turbulent and dreadful battle was raging, Sātyaki, having cut down all the troops, went on toward Arjuna.
There the gleams of the armor, made dazzling by the rays of the sun, smote the eyes of the soldiers in the battle on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While the Pāṇḍavas were thus striving, Duryodhana, fearless, O great king, plunged into that vast host.
That tumultuous clash between them and him, O Bhārata, became a great undoing of all the armies.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: With the armies in such a plight, and himself fallen into hardship, did not Duryodhana, O sūta, wage the battle from the front rather than turn his back?
This clash of one against the many in that great battle, and a king at that, seems to me a grievously unequal thing.
He who was reared in the height of comfort, lord of fortune and of the world—encountering many alone, did he not turn his face away?
Saṃjaya said: O king, O Bhārata, hear of the wondrous combat of your son, one against the many—a marvel, as I relate it.
By Duryodhana, of a sudden, the Pāṇḍava host in battle was thrown into confusion on every side, as a lotus-pool is churned up by an elephant.
Seeing the army thus made by your son, O Kaurava, the Pāñcālas, with Bhīmasena at their head, rushed upon him.
He pierced Bhīmasena with ten arrows, the two sons of Mādrī with three apiece, Virāṭa and Drupada with six, and Śikhaṇḍin with a hundred.
And piercing Dhṛṣṭadyumna with twenty arrows, the son of Dharma with seven, the Kekayas with ten, and the sons of Draupadī with three apiece,
with fierce arrows in the battle he hewed down hundreds of other warriors and their chariots with their elephants, enraged like Death amid living beings.
Whether nocking or loosing, he could not be seen, his bow bent into a circle, as he smote the foe by his training and the power of his weapons.
As he smote the foe, the eldest Pāṇḍava with two broad-headed shafts cut his great gold-backed bow into three pieces, O sire.
And he pierced him with many keen arrows well aimed; but striking his mail at once they broke and sank into the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the rejoicing Pārthas gathered round Yudhiṣṭhira, as at the slaying of Vṛtra the gods, with the great seers, in their joy gathered round Śakra.
Then King Duryodhana, taking up a stout bow and crying 'Stand! Stand!' to the king, advanced upon the Pāṇḍava.
As your son, that great chariot-warrior, spoke thus, O king, the Pāñcālas, rejoicing and greedy for victory, went forth to meet him.
These Droṇa held in check, seeking to win the Pāṇḍava in the fight, as a mountain holds the water-laden clouds driven up by a raging wind.
There, O king, was a great combat that swelled vastly, like the playground of Rudra, a destruction of all embodied beings.
Saṃjaya said: In the afternoon, O great king, the combat broke out anew, loud as a thundercloud, between Droṇa and the Somakas.
Mounting his chariot drawn by red steeds, that hero among men, composed, rushed in the battle upon the Pāṇḍavas at a moderate speed.
Devoted to your welfare and weal, that mighty bowman of great strength, born from the noblest of pitchers, with whetted arrows of variegated feathers—
singling out, as it were, the choicest among the warriors, O Bhārata—the majestic son of Bharadvāja, O king, sported in the battle.
Against him came Bṛhatkṣatra, the great chariot-warrior of the Kekayas, eldest of five heroic brothers, hardened in battle.
Loosing keen arrows and thickly covering the preceptor, as a great cloud loosing rain upon Gandhamādana.
At him Droṇa, O great king, in fury sent seventeen gold-feathered shafts whetted upon stone.
But those dread shafts loosed from Droṇa's bow, like venomous serpents, he cut each one with ten arrows in the fight, as though delighting in it.
Seeing that deftness of his, the best of the twice-born, smiling, sent eight smooth-jointed arrows.
Seeing those arrows sped from Droṇa's bow swiftly descending, he warded them off with just as many sharp and stout arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, O great king, there came wonder upon your army, beholding that most arduous feat performed by Bṛhatkṣatra.
Then, O great king, Droṇa of mighty austerities, singling out the Kekaya prince, brought forth in battle the divine Brāhma weapon.
That weapon, O king, the unshaken Kaikeya of mighty arms warded off in the fray, countering it with the very Brahmā weapon as it was launched.
Having beaten back that weapon of the son of Bharadvāja in the encounter, he pierced the brāhmaṇa with sixty stone-whetted shafts feathered with gold.
Droṇa, foremost among men, answered him with an iron arrow, which, cleaving his armour, sank into the surface of the earth.
As a black serpent set loose enters an anthill, O best of kings, so did that arrow, having pierced the Kaikeya in the fight, enter the earth.
Sorely pierced, O great king, by Droṇa the master of weapons, and seized with a mighty wrath, he rolled his fair eyes.
He pierced Droṇa with seventy stone-whetted shafts feathered with gold, and struck his charioteer with a broad-headed arrow upon the arms and breast.
But Droṇa, pierced in many places by Bṛhatkṣatra, O noble one, let fly sharp arrows toward the Kekaya's chariot.
Having thrown Bṛhatkṣatra, that great car-warrior, into confusion, Droṇa loosed a keen arrow toward the Kekaya, O descendant of Bharata.
Deeply pierced by it at once between the breasts, O great king, that tiger among men, his heart cleft asunder, fell from his chariot.
When Bṛhatkṣatra, the great car-warrior of the Kekayas, was slain, O king, the son of Śiśupāla, greatly enraged, spoke thus to his driver:
"Charioteer, drive to where this mailed Droṇa stands, slaughtering all the Kekayas and the host of the Pāñcālas."
Hearing those words of his, the charioteer bore that foremost of car-warriors toward Droṇa with swift Kāmboja steeds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Dhṛṣṭaketu, the bull among the Cedis, of surpassing might, fell suddenly upon Droṇa as a moth falls upon the flame.
He pierced Droṇa, with his horses, car, and standard, with sixty arrows, and again with other keen shafts, as one prodding a sleeping tiger.
Droṇa, with a sharp razor-headed arrow, cut asunder in the middle the bow of that mighty king as he strove in the encounter.
Then the son of Śiśupāla, that great car-warrior, taking up another bow, pierced Droṇa again with sharp and sturdy arrows.
Droṇa of mighty strength, having slain his horses and his charioteer, then assailed him with twenty-five arrows.
Deprived of his car and bereft of his bow, the king of the Cedis too, enraged in the fray, hurled his mace toward the chariot of the son of Bharadvāja.
That mace, rushing down in sudden onset—of terrible form and fearsome, heavy, made of iron and adorned with gold—the son of Bharadvāja brought to the ground with many thousands of arrows.
That mace, struck down by the son of Bharadvāja, fell to the earth, decked with red garlands and cloth, like a star falling from the floor of heaven.
Seeing his mace struck down, the wrathful Dhṛṣṭaketu swiftly let fly a lance and a gold-gleaming spear.
But Droṇa, deft of hand and of mighty strength, cleaving the lance with three arrows in that great battle, sundered the spear at once.
Then the glorious son of Bharadvāja, bent on his death, sent against him in battle a sharp arrow to slay him.
That arrow, cleaving the armour and the heart of him of measureless might, entered the earth as a wild goose enters a lotus-pool.
As a hungry blue jay, O king, devours a moth, so did the heroic Droṇa devour Dhṛṣṭaketu in that great battle.
When the king of the Cedis was slain, his son, a master of the highest weapons, overcome by wrath, took his stand in his father's portion of the field.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Him too Droṇa, smiling, sent with his arrows to the abode of Yama, as a mighty tiger in the great forest carries off a fawn.
As the warriors of the Pāṇḍava side were being thus destroyed, O descendant of Bharata, the heroic son of Jarāsaṃdha himself rushed against Droṇa.
And he, O great king, veiling Droṇa with sharp arrows, swiftly made him unseen, as a rain-cloud veils the sun.
Beholding that lightness of hand, Droṇa, the crusher of warriors, swiftly loosed his arrows by the hundred and the thousand.
Having covered him over in battle, Droṇa then slew the son of Jarāsaṃdha, that foremost of car-warriors standing in his car, before the eyes of all the bowmen.
Whoever closed with Droṇa, him Droṇa, like the Ender himself, took away, as the Ender at the appointed hour takes away all living beings.
Then Droṇa, the mighty archer, proclaiming his name aloud in the battle, bewildered the warriors of the Pāṇḍava side with many thousands of arrows.
Then the arrows that bore Droṇa's mark, gold-feathered and stone-whetted, struck down men, elephants, and horses on every side in the battle.
Slaughtered by Droṇa as the great asuras by Śakra, the Pāñcālas trembled like cattle tormented by the cold.
Then a terrible wailing arose among the Pāṇḍavas as their troops were being slain by Droṇa, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Bewildered by the arrow-shower of the son of Bharadvāja in the fight, the great car-warriors of the Pāñcālas were as if seized by a cramp in the thighs.
And the Cedis, O great king, and the Sṛñjayas and the Somakas, eager and exultant, rushed upon the son of Bharadvāja with longing for battle.
"Slay Droṇa, slay Droṇa!" crying thus, those tigers among men advanced upon Droṇa, striving with all their might, seeking in battle to send that one of great splendour to the abode of Yama.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But those striving heroes the son of Bharadvāja sent on to Yama with his shafts, the chiefs of the Cedis above all.
As those chiefs of the Cedis were being destroyed, O descendant of Bharata, the Pāñcālas, sorely pressed by Droṇa's arrows, trembled.
Seeing such deeds of Droṇa, O noble one, they cried out to Bhīmasena and toward the chariot of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
"Surely this brāhmaṇa has performed some mighty penance, hard to perform, that he so prevails in battle and consumes the bulls among the warriors."
"War is the duty of the warrior, but austerity the highest calling of the brāhmaṇa; an ascetic accomplished in learning could burn up a foe with a mere glance."
Into Droṇa's weapon, whose touch is like fire, many bulls among the warriors have entered, O descendant of Bharata, and there, beyond crossing and terrible, have been consumed.
"Each according to his strength, his zeal, his courage—Droṇa of great splendour, confounding all beings, slays our forces."
Hearing those words of theirs, Kṣatradharman, taking his stand, cut off with a crescent-headed arrow Droṇa's bow together with the shaft set upon it.
Grown the more furious thereat, Droṇa, the crusher of warriors, took up another bow, shining and of swifter force.
Fitting to it a keen arrow, burden-destroying, bright and firm, the mighty preceptor drew it to the ear and let it fly.
That arrow, having slain Kṣatradharman, passed on into the surface of the earth; and he, his heart cleft, fell from his car upon the ground.
Then, when the son of Dhṛṣṭadyumna was slain, the armies trembled; and the great car-warrior Cekitāna closed upon Droṇa.
He pierced Droṇa with ten arrows between the breasts, his charioteer with four, and his four horses with four.
The preceptor pierced his right arm with sixteen arrows, his standard with sixteen, and his driver with seven.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When his charioteer was slain, those horses, enwrapped in the arrows of the son of Bharadvāja, bolted in the battle, dragging the car away, O noble one.
Seeing Cekitāna's car bolting with its charioteer slain, a great fear came over the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas alike.
Routing on every side those gathered heroes in the battle—the Cedis, the Pāñcālas, and the Sṛñjayas—Droṇa shone forth in great splendour, O noble one.
Grey to the ears and dark of hue, past eighty years of age, the aged Droṇa ranged through the battle like a youth of sixteen.
And his foes, O great king, deemed Droṇa, the slayer of foes, ranging fearlessly, to be Indra himself with the thunderbolt in his hand.
Then, O great king, the wise Drupada spoke, O monarch: "This greedy man slays the warriors as a tiger slays small game."
"The wicked, evil-minded Duryodhana shall come to grievous realms—he through whose greed the bulls among the warriors are slain in battle."
"By the hundred they lie upon the earth, cut down like bulls, their limbs bathed in blood, made food for dogs and jackals."
Having spoken thus, O great king, Drupada, lord of an army, placing the sons of Pṛthā at the front, swiftly rushed upon Droṇa in battle.
Saṃjaya said: As the battle-arrays of the Pāṇḍavas were thrown into turmoil here and there, the sons of Pṛthā, the Pāñcālas, and the Somakas pursued the foe far afield.
While that fierce battle, hair-raising, raged on in the dire destruction of the world, as at the ending of an age, O descendant of Bharata—
—while Droṇa pressed valiantly in the fight, roaring again and again, and the Pāñcālas dwindled and the Pāṇḍavas were being slain—
Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of righteousness, saw no refuge anywhere, and pondered, O lord of kings: "How shall this end?"
Looking then in every direction with a longing to behold Savyasācin, Yudhiṣṭhira saw neither the son of Pṛthā nor the descendant of Madhu.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Not seeing that tiger among men marked by the standard of the bull among monkeys, and not hearing the twang of the Gāṇḍīva, his senses were stricken with distress.
Nor seeing Sātyaki either, that foremost car-warrior of the Vṛṣṇis, the king of righteousness Yudhiṣṭhira, his whole frame overcome with anxiety, found then no peace, beholding not those two bulls among men.
From fear of the world's reproach, the greatly renowned king of righteousness, of mighty arms, fell to musing concerning the chariot of the grandson of Śini.
"By me has the grandson of Śini, the true Sātyaki, giver of fearlessness to his friends, been sent upon the track of Phalguna in the battle."
"What was once a single care has now become twofold for me this day: for I must look both to Sātyaki and to the Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya."
"Having sent Sātyaki to follow upon the track of the Pāṇḍava, whom now shall I send in the battle to follow upon the track of the Sātvata as well?"
"If with all effort I make search for my brother, yet seek not after Yuyudhāna, the world will censure me."
"'In searching for his brother, Yudhiṣṭhira the king of righteousness has forsaken the Vṛṣṇi Sātyaki of true valour'—so will they say."
"From fear of the world's blame, I shall therefore send the son of Pṛthā, Vṛkodara, upon the track of the high-souled descendant of Madhu."
"For even as is my love for Arjuna, the slayer of foes, so too is it for that Vṛṣṇi hero, the Sātvata, fierce and unrelenting in battle."
"To an overwhelming burden have I appointed the joy of Śini's line; and he, mighty in strength, out of regard for his friends and out of reverence, has entered the Bhārata host as a sea-monster plunges into the ocean."
"For yonder is heard the clamour of warriors who turn not back, locked in mutual combat with the wise hero of the Vṛṣṇis."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having weighed the matter many times over and judged it most fitting to the hour, it seems best to me that Bhīmasena the bowman, the son of Pāṇḍu, should go to that very place where the two great car-warriors have gone.
There is nothing on earth that Bhīma cannot endure; relying on the strength of his own arms, he is able with ease to hold at bay in battle all the bowmen of the earth, however resolute they stand.
Leaning upon the might of that great-souled one's arms, we all returned from our dwelling in the forest, and in our battles we were never overcome.
If Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava goes from here toward the Sātvata, then in the fight the Sātvata and Phalguna will both have a protector at hand.
To be sure, the Sātvata and Phalguna need not be grieved over in battle, for they are guarded by Vāsudeva himself, and are themselves masters of every weapon.
Yet I must surely do something to dispel my own grief; therefore I shall appoint Bhīma to follow upon the Sātvata's track. By this I think the measure on behalf of Sātyaki will be fulfilled.
Having resolved thus in his mind, O king, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma said to his charioteer, "Drive me toward Bhīma."
Hearing the word of the Dharma-king, the charioteer skilled with horses brought the gold-adorned car near to Bhīma.
Having reached Bhīmasena, and calling to mind what the hour demanded, the king sank into despondency even as he gave him many commands.
"He who, alone upon his car, conquered the gods together with the Gandharvas and the Daityas — of him, your younger brother Bhīmasena, I see no sign."
Then Bhīmasena said to the Dharma-king, who had come to him in such a state, "Never have I seen nor heard such despondency in you."
"In days past, when we were torn by sorrows, it was you who were our refuge. Rise up, rise up, lord of kings; command me — what shall I do for you?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"There is nothing impossible for me, nor anything I will not do, O giver of honor. Give the order, best of the Kurus, and do not set your mind upon grief."
To him the king, his eyes brimming with tears, hissing like a black serpent, his face withered, spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"As the blast of the conch Pāñcajanya is heard, blown by the glorious Vāsudeva in his fury, surely your brother Dhanaṃjaya lies slain this day."
"He being struck down, Janārdana himself surely fights on now — he, by whose valor, mighty in spirit, the Pāṇḍavas live."
"To whom in times of peril we resort as the immortals resort to the thousand-eyed one — that hero, seeking the ruler of the Sindhus, followed after the Bhārata host."
"Of his going, Bhīma, we know; of his return we have no word — that dark, youthful one, Guḍākeśa, fair to look upon, mighty-armed,"
"broad-chested, great-shouldered, with the stride of a rutting elephant, eyes like the cakora bird, copper-hued of eye, swelling the woes of his foes."
"This, then — blessings upon you, crusher of foes — is the ground of my grief: for Arjuna's sake, O mighty-armed one, and on the Sātvata's account."
"It grows as fire kindled with oblation grows, blazing up again and again. Of him I see no sign, and so I am overcome with despondency."
"Know too that tiger among men, the Sātvata, the great car-warrior: he followed afterward upon the track of that great car-warrior, your younger brother. Not seeing that mighty-armed one, I am sunk in despondency."
"Therefore Kṛṣṇa, skilled in war, surely now fights on in battle — he by whose valor, mighty in might, the Pāṇḍavas live."
"Go you there, son of Kuntī, where Dhanaṃjaya has gone, and Sātyaki of great valor — if you hold my word fit to be obeyed, O knower of dharma, for I am your eldest brother."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"You need not be so concerned for Arjuna as you must be for Sātyaki, O Pārtha, who, wishing to do me a kindness, set out along Savyasācin's path — hard to traverse, terrible, impassable to the unschooled in soul."
Bhīmasena said: "The car that of old bore Brahmā, Īśāna, Indra, and Varuṇa — mounted upon that, the two Kṛṣṇas have gone; for them there is no fear."
"Yet bearing your command upon my head, here I go — grieve not. Having met those tigers among men, I shall send you tidings."
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus much, the mighty one set forth, entrusting Yudhiṣṭhira again and again to Dhṛṣṭadyumna and to his friends; and Bhīmasena of great strength said this to Dhṛṣṭadyumna:
"You know, mighty-armed one, how Droṇa the great car-warrior bends every means toward the capture of the Dharma-king."
"No duty in my going, O son of Pṛṣata, weighs upon me as does the guarding of the king; for that is our most pressing task."
"Thus has Pārtha bidden me, and I cannot gainsay it; I shall go there where the Saindhava, doomed to die, has taken his stand. By the word of the Dharma-king one must stand without misgiving."
"So this day, intent in battle, guard Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira; for this is, of all our charges, the highest task in the fray."
To him, O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna said to Vṛkodara, "Go, mighty-armed one, as you desire, untroubled in heart, O Pārtha."
"Not until in battle he has slain Dhṛṣṭadyumna will Droṇa ever in the encounter lay hold of the Dharma-king."
Then the Pāṇḍava, committing the king to Dhṛṣṭadyumna and saluting his elder, his guide, set forth to where Phalguna was.
The son of Kuntī, O Bhārata, was embraced by the Dharma-king, kissed upon the head, and given fair blessings to hear.
Bhīmasena, the mighty-armed, mailed, with bright earrings, with armlets, with cuirass, with arrows — the foremost of car-warriors —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
his armor of black iron, figured with gold and richly wrought, shone like a lightning-laced rain-cloud clinging to a mountain.
Well-wrapped in cloths of yellow, red, black, and white, and with his throat-guard, he gleamed like a cloud spanned by Indra's bow.
When Bhīmasena had set forth eager for battle against your army, again, O lord of peoples, there rose the terrible blast of the Pāñcajanya.
Hearing that terrible roar, vast and terrifying to the three worlds, the mighty-armed son of Dharma again spoke to Bhīma:
"This king of conches, the water-born, blown hard by the Vṛṣṇi hero, makes earth and the mid-air resound."
"Surely, some great calamity having befallen Savyasācin, the bearer of discus and mace fights now against all the Kurus."
"Surely the noble Kuntī, and Draupadī, and Subhadrā behold this day, together with their kinsfolk, the showing of a great evil."
"So, Bhīma, set with haste, go where Dhanaṃjaya is; for all the quarters and their sub-quarters seem to swim before me, O Pārtha, out of longing to see Dhanaṃjaya, and on the Sātvata's account."
"Go, go," he said again to Bhīmasena. Urged on hard by his brother, that brother who did his brother's pleasure, Bhīma struck the war-drum and blew the conch again and again,
and roaring his lion's roar, drawing the bowstring again and again, showing forth his terrible self, he rushed suddenly upon the foe.
Him the swift, well-broken, prancing best of horses bore on, harnessed by Viśoka, fleet as mind and wind.
Shattering and crushing, drawing the bowstring with his hand, Pārtha, dragging it down and drawing it back, churned up the vanguard of the host.
As he went on, that mighty-armed one, the Pāñcālas together with the Somakas, heroes, followed behind him as the immortals follow Maghavan.
Him, O great king, your sons born of one womb hemmed in with their troops — Duḥśalā and Citrasena and Kuṇḍabhedī and Viviṃśati,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Durmukha and Duḥsaha, and Vikarṇa, and Śala too, Vinda and Anuvinda, Sumukha, Dīrghabāhu, Sudarśana,
Vṛndāraka and Suhasta, Suṣeṇa, Dīrghalocana, Abhaya and Raudrakarman, Suvarman and Durvimocana —
these foremost of car-warriors, with their varied troops and their followers, girt for battle, the heroes, rushed upon Bhīmasena.
Beholding them, the son of Kuntī, valiant Bhīmasena, turned upon them with speed, as a lion upon lesser beasts.
There those heroes displayed great celestial weapons, holding off Bhīma with their arrows as clouds hold off the risen sun.
Passing them by with speed, he rushed upon Droṇa's division, and the elephant-host before him he overwhelmed with showers of arrows.
In but a little while the son of the Wind, sweeping his swift shafts in every direction, scattered that elephant-host.
As beasts in the forest are frightened by the roar of the śarabha, all those elephants fled, bellowing dreadful cries.
And again, passing on with speed, he rushed upon Droṇa's division; the preceptor held him back as the shore holds back the swollen sea.
He struck him on the forehead with an iron shaft, smiling as it were; and the Pāṇḍava shone there like the sun with rays upraised.
And the preceptor, supposing that Bhīma would do him honor as Phalguna would, said to Vṛkodara:
"Bhīmasena, you cannot pierce into the enemy's host without first conquering me in battle, O mighty one, here amid the foes."
"If that younger brother of yours, and Kṛṣṇa, entered with my leave, yet this array, sir, cannot be entered here by you."
Then Bhīma, fearless, hearing that word of the teacher, wrathful, his eyes red as copper, hissing with breath, spoke to Droṇa:
"Not by your leave, O wretch of a brahmin, did Arjuna enter the field of war; for he, unassailable, could pierce even the host of Śakra."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"By him, doing you the highest honor, you have indeed been honored; but I am no Arjuna full of compassion, Droṇa — I am Bhīmasena, your enemy."
"You are our father, our teacher, our kinsman, and we are your sons — so we all hold you, and stand before you bowed."
"But this day the contrary of that is seen in you as you speak to us. If you hold yourself our enemy, then so be it here; behold, I, Bhīma, do unto you the deed befitting a foe."
Then whirling his mace like Death wielding the rod of Time, Bhīma hurled it at Droṇa, O king; and he leaped down from his car.
Then it crushed Droṇa's vehicle together with horses, driver, and banner, and ground down many warriors, as the wind grinds trees by its force.
Then again your sons surrounded that best of cars; and Droṇa, foremost of strikers, mounting another car —
Then, O great king, the wrathful and valiant Bhīmasena overwhelmed the chariot-host before him with showers of arrows.
Being struck down in the battle, your sons, the great car-warriors, fought against Bhīma of terrible strength in the fight, seeking victory.
Then Duḥśāsana, enraged, hurled a chariot-lance, all of steel and keen, eager to slay the son of Pāṇḍu.
That great lance flying upon him, sped by your son, Bhīma cleft in two; and that seemed a wondrous thing.
Then, enraged, with other whetted arrows the mighty one slew with three shafts the three — Kuṇḍabhedī, Suṣeṇa, and Dīrghanetra.
Then he slew again Vṛndāraka, the hero, the increaser of the Kurus' fame, one of your valiant sons as they fought.
Abhaya and Raudrakarman, and Durvimocana too — these three sons of yours Bhīma slew again with three shafts.
Being slain, O great king, by that stronger one, your sons hemmed in on every side Bhīma, the foremost of strikers.
Vinda and Anuvinda together, and your son Suvarman as well — the son of Kuntī, as though smiling, dispatched them all with his arrows to the abode of Yama.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, O bull of the Bhāratas, he swiftly pierced your heroic son Sudarśana in the battle, and that one fell and died.
In but a little while the son of Pāṇḍu, scattering them with his swift shafts in every direction, shattered that division of chariots.
Then, O lord of peoples, like deer at the thunder of his chariot's roar, your sons, slaughtered in the battle and afflicted with dread of Bhīmasena, all fled away together with their chariots.
But the son of Kuntī, pursuing the great host of your sons, O king, pierced the Kauravas on every side in the battle.
Being slaughtered by Bhīmasena, O great king, your men abandoned Bhīma in the fight and fled, urging on their finest horses.
Having vanquished them in the battle, the mighty Bhīmasena, son of Pāṇḍu, let loose a lion's roar and clapped his arms in challenge.
And making a great resounding clap of his palms, the mighty Bhīma, leaving the chariot-warriors behind, charged upon Droṇa's division.
Saṃjaya said: As he emerged from that division of chariots like the sun from darkness, the preceptor, seeking to hold him back, overwhelmed him with showers of arrows.
As though drinking up those floods of shafts loosed from the foremost bow of Droṇa, he advanced against his brothers, bewildering the host with his cunning.
Putting forth their utmost speed in the fray, those mighty archers, urged on by your sons, surrounded him on every side.
Thus hemmed in, Bhīma, as though laughing, O Bhārata, raised against them that terrible mace and, roaring like a lion, hurled it among them with force, and the mighty one crushed them.
Like the thunderbolt hurled by Indra with a steadfast aim, O king, filling the earth as it were with its mighty din, blazing with splendor and terrible, it struck terror into your sons.
Seeing that mace of tremendous speed descending, wreathed in splendor, your men all fled, uttering frightful cries.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And marking that unbearable sound of it, O sir, the men there, the chariot-warriors, fell down then from their chariots.
Having put his foes to flight in the battle, the unassailable son of Kuntī, swift as Suparṇa the king of birds, passed beyond the host.
As Bhīmasena, that leader among the leaders of chariot-troops, was thus working havoc, the son of Bharadvāja, O great king, advanced against him.
But Droṇa, having checked Bhīma in the battle with waves of arrows, suddenly raised a shout, striking dread into the Pāṇḍavas.
That fight between Droṇa and the great-souled Bhīma, O great king, was vast and terrible, like the war of gods and demons.
When the warriors were being slain in the battle by hundreds and by thousands by the keen shafts loosed from Droṇa's bow,
then the son of Pāṇḍu, leaping down from his chariot and gathering his speed, closing his eyes, O king, advanced on foot against Droṇa.
Just as a bull receives the rain at his ease, so Bhīma, that tiger among men, took upon himself the shower of arrows.
Though thus assailed in the battle, the mighty one, O sir, seized Droṇa's chariot by the shaft-pole with his hand and flung it away.
But Droṇa, hurled aside by Bhīma in the fight, O king, swiftly mounted another chariot and made his way to the gateway of the battle-array.
In that instant Bhīmasena's charioteer swiftly urged on his horses, O Kaurava, and that was a wondrous thing to behold.
Then, having mounted his own chariot, the mighty Bhīmasena charged with speed against the host of your son.
Crushing the warriors in the fray like a raging wind that crushes trees, he went on, cleaving the army like a river's current rending its banks.
Reaching the Bhoja division, guarded by the son of Hṛdika, Bhīmasena, having broken it utterly, O king, pressed onward.
Terrifying the troops with the clap of his palms, O sir, he overcame all the armies as a tiger overcomes bulls.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Passing beyond the Bhoja division and the host of the Kāmbojas, and likewise many other bands of barbarians skilled in warfare,
and beholding Sātyaki too, that bull among men, fighting, the son of Kuntī, intent in his chariot, then sped onward swiftly.
Bhīmasena, O great king, the son of Pāṇḍu, longing to behold Dhanaṃjaya, passed beyond your warriors in the battle.
That valiant one beheld Arjuna there, that bull among men, fighting and striving valiantly for the slaying of the lord of the Sindhus.
Seeing Arjuna there, he then sent forth mighty roars, and the son of Pṛthā heard that great shout of his as he roared.
Then the son of Pṛthā, uttering a great shout, and Mādhava as well, advanced, O great king, both roaring like bulls.
Vāsudeva and Arjuna, hearing the roar of that impetuous one, cried out again and again, longing to behold Vṛkodara.
Hearing the roar of Bhīmasena and of Phalguna the archer, the son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, rejoiced, O great king.
The king became free of sorrow on hearing that mighty roar, and the lord hoped for Dhanaṃjaya's victory in the battle.
As Bhīmasena thus roared, fierce in the fray, the mighty-armed son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, smiled,
and that best of the upholders of righteousness, reflecting, spoke within his heart: 'You have given the signal, Bhīma, and so have fulfilled your elder's word.'
'There is no victory in war for those whose enemy you are, O son of Pāṇḍu. By good fortune, Dhanaṃjaya the ambidextrous archer yet lives in the battle.'
'By good fortune the hero Sātyaki, of true valor, is safe; by good fortune I hear Vāsudeva and Dhanaṃjaya roaring.'
'He by whom, after vanquishing Śakra in battle, the bearer of oblations was gratified — that slayer of foes in the fight, Phalguna, by good fortune lives.'
'He upon the strength of whose arms we all depend for our lives — that destroyer of enemy hosts, Phalguna, by good fortune lives.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'He by whom, a single chariot-warrior, the Nivātakavacas, hard for even the gods to conquer, were overcome — by good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives.'
'He who vanquished all the Kauravas gathered together for the seizing of the cattle at the city of the Matsyas — by good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives.'
'He who slew fourteen thousand Kālakeyas in the great battle by the might of his arms — by good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives.'
'He who, on account of Duryodhana's plight, vanquished by the power of his weapons the mighty king of the Gandharvas — by good fortune that son of Pṛthā lives.'
'The mighty one crowned with the diadem, with white steeds and Kṛṣṇa for charioteer, ever dear to me — by good fortune Phalguna lives.'
'He who, burning with grief for his son and resolved to accomplish a hard deed, seeking the slaying of Jayadratha, took an oath — will that Dhanaṃjaya, I wonder, slay the lord of the Sindhus in battle?'
'Shall I, I wonder, meet Arjuna before the sun has set — Arjuna with his vow fulfilled, guarded by Vāsudeva?'
'Shall the king of the Sindhus, who delights in Duryodhana's welfare, struck down by Phalguna, gladden our foes — or not?'
'Will King Duryodhana, on seeing the lord of the Sindhus laid low in battle by Phalguna, make peace with us?'
'On seeing his brothers slain by Bhīmasena in the fight, will the foolish Duryodhana make peace with us?'
'And on seeing many other warriors cast down upon the earth, will the foolish Duryodhana feel remorse?'
'Shall our enmity be appeased through Bhīṣma alone, and will Suyodhana make a treaty for the protection of those who remain?'
As he pondered thus in many ways, O king, overcome with compassion, the terrible battle raged on.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: As the mighty Bhīmasena thus roared with a din like the thunder of clouds, what heroes surrounded him?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For I do not see anyone, Saṃjaya, in the three worlds who could stand before the enraged Bhīmasena in battle.
As he lifts his mace in the great fray like Death himself, I do not see, my child, who could stand his ground on the field of battle.
He who would smash a chariot with a chariot and an elephant with an elephant — who could withstand him in battle, even Śatakratu in person?
When the enraged Bhīmasena sought to slay my sons, who, devoted to Duryodhana's good, stood up before him?
When the wildfire that is Bhīmasena was about to burn up my sons like grass and reeds at the front of the battle, what heroes stood in his way?
Seeing my sons driven off by Bhīma in the fight, as all creatures are by Time, who surrounded Bhīma?
When the blazing fire of Bhīma sought to consume my sons, what brave men turned to face him? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: As that great chariot-warrior Bhīmasena thus roared, the mighty Karṇa too rushed upon him with a tumultuous shout.
