Drawing his powerful bow to its utmost, the impatient and mighty Karṇa, eager for the fight, made ready to display his strength.
At the meeting of Karṇa and Bhīma, the limbs of the chariot-warriors and the horsemen alike trembled, as they heard the clap of the two heroes' palms.
Hearing the terrible roar of Bhīmasena on the field of battle, the foremost of warriors fancied that sky and earth had become one.
At another terrible roar of the great-souled son of Pāṇḍu, the bows of all the warriors in the battle fell to the ground.
All the beasts of burden, terrified, let flow their dung and urine, O great king, and lost their senses.
Many dreadful portents appeared, O king, at that tumultuous encounter of Bhīma and Karṇa.
Then Karṇa wounded Bhīma with a score of arrows, and swiftly pierced his charioteer with five swift shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Bhīmasena, laughing, the mighty one quick of hand, repaid Karṇa in the fight with sixty-four arrows.
Karṇa, the great archer, hurled four arrows at him; but Bhīma, before they reached him, cut them to many pieces with his smooth-jointed shafts, O king, displaying the deftness of his hand.
Karṇa covered him over with multitudes of arrows again and again, and the son of Pāṇḍu was thus enveloped by Karṇa on every side.
The great chariot-warrior cut Karṇa's bow at the grip, and pierced him with many smooth-jointed shafts.
Then the son of the charioteer, taking up another bow and stringing it, that great chariot-warrior of terrible deeds, pierced Bhīma in the battle.
At this Bhīma, exceedingly enraged and impelled with force, then drove three smooth-jointed shafts deep into the breast of the charioteer's son.
With those arrows lodged in the midst of his chest, Karṇa then shone forth, O bull of the Bhāratas, like a lofty three-peaked mountain.
And the blood streamed from him, pierced as he was by those mightiest of shafts, as streaks of red ochre run down from a mountain that oozes its mineral ores.
Shaken a little, Karṇa, sorely afflicted by that well-aimed blow, set arrow to bow and pierced Bhīma, O sire, and loosed his shafts again by the hundreds and the thousands.
Overwhelmed all at once by Karṇa, that firm-bowed archer, the son of Pāṇḍu, smiling, swiftly cut through his bowstring.
With a broad-headed shaft he dispatched his charioteer to the abode of Yama, and in the battle that great car-warrior made his four horses lifeless.
Then from that chariot whose horses were slain Karṇa leapt down, O lord of peoples, and the great car-warrior mounted the chariot of Vṛṣasena.
Having vanquished Karṇa in battle, the valiant Bhīmasena roared a mighty roar like the thunder of a storm-cloud.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing that roar of his, Yudhiṣṭhira was filled with joy, deeming Karṇa vanquished by Bhīmasena, O Bhārata.
On every side the host of Pāṇḍu then raised the blare of conches; and hearing the clamour of the enemy's army your men too sent up their cries. Pārtha twanged the Gāṇḍīva, and Kṛṣṇa sounded his conch Pāñcajanya.
Drowning out that din, the roar of Bhīma as he bellowed was heard, O great king, throughout all the armies, O Bhārata.
Then those two tamers of foes contended each apart with their weapons: Rādheya gently at first, and the son of Pāṇḍu with full force.
Saṃjaya said: When that host was thrown into confusion, with Arjuna gone toward the Saindhava, and the Sātvata and Bhīmasena as well, your son hastened up to Droṇa upon his single chariot, pondering the many things that must be done.
That chariot of your son, urged with the utmost speed, swift as thought and as the wind, rushed straight upon Droṇa.
And your son, his eyes red with agitation, said to him: "Arjuna and Bhīmasena and the unvanquished Sātyaki—
these great car-warriors, having overcome our vast armies, those grinders of foes, have reached the neighbourhood of the king of the Sindhus; and there too they all contend, every one of them unvanquished.
If indeed Pārtha, that great car-warrior, has passed you by in battle, how is it that you have been passed by Sātyaki and Bhīma as well, O bestower of honour?
It is held a marvel in this world, like the drying up of the ocean, that you, O foremost of brāhmaṇas, should be overcome by the Sātvata and by Arjuna.
And by Bhīmasena likewise—so all the world keeps saying in wonder: how was Droṇa, that master of the whole science of archery, conquered in battle?
Surely it is my own ruin in this war—luckless that I am—when three car-warriors have passed beyond you, O tiger among men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Things having come to this pass, tell me what you would say. What is gone is gone; consider now what remains, O bestower of honour.
Whatever must be done at once for the king of the Sindhus, now that the moment has come—let your honour speak it quickly, and let it be well arranged."
Droṇa said: Much, O great king, is the work to be pondered there; hear my mind upon it. Three great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas have broken through; as great is the danger behind them as before them.
That side I deem the weightier where Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya are; for the Bhārata host is now hemmed in both before and behind.
In this case I judge the task to be the guarding of the Saindhava; he, my son, is most to be protected by us, terrified as he is of the wrathful Dhanaṃjaya.
For the heroes Yuyudhāna and Vṛkodara have gone against the Saindhava; now is come upon us that very gambling-match which sprang from Śakuni's cunning.
In the assembly-hall there was neither true victory nor defeat; but here, my son, as we throw our stakes today, victory and defeat are at hand.
Those dread dice that Śakuni cast in the Kuru assembly—reckoning them mere dice—they were in truth unconquerable arrows.
Where your many Kurus stand arrayed, my son, know the army for the gaming-board and the arrows for the dice, O lord of peoples.
And the Saindhava is the stake, O king; herein lies the issue of this game; for upon the Saindhava the great gambling with the foe is now joined.
Here, O great king, all of us, laying down our very lives, must duly make the protection of the Saindhava in the fight; for there, my son, as we cast our stakes, victory and defeat are certain to fall.
Where your mighty archers stand intent, guarding the Saindhava—go there yourself with all speed, and protect those very protectors.
But I myself shall remain right here, and I will send others, and will hold off the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍus and the Sṛñjayas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Duryodhana set forth at once at the teacher's command, rousing himself for the fierce deed, with his train of followers behind him.
But the two Pāñcālas, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, guards of Arjuna's wheels, having come round the army by an outer path, made their way to Savyasācin.
For those two, O great king, had earlier been held off by Kṛtavarman when Arjuna, O king, had entered your host in his eagerness to fight.
With those two the mighty Bhārata Duryodhana joined a surpassing combat—swift against the swift, the brothers and he.
Both of them, bows uplifted, rushed upon him—those two renowned as great car-warriors, foremost of kṣatriyas in battle.
Yudhāmanyu, blazing with wrath, in haste loosed thirty steel shafts into your son's breast.
Duryodhana too, O lord of kings, slew the four horses of Uttamaujas the Pāñcāla and both his flanking charioteers.
Uttamaujas, his horses slain and his driver slain in the fight, made haste and mounted the chariot of his brother Yudhāmanyu.
Having gained his brother's chariot, he struck Duryodhana's horses with many shafts; slain, they fell to the ground.
His horses fallen, Yudhāmanyu with a choice shaft swiftly cut Duryodhana's bow and his quiver in the battle.
Leaping down from that chariot whose horses and driver were slain, your son, the great car-warrior, took up his mace and rushed at the two Pāñcālas.
Beholding him bearing down upon them in fury—that conqueror of hostile cities—Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas sprang down from their chariot's seat.
Then, mace in hand, he shattered with his mace that splendid car bright with gold, horses, driver, banner and all, in the fray.
Having destroyed it, your son—his own horses slain and his driver slain—that scorcher of foes swiftly mounted the chariot of the king of the Madras.
And the two princes, foremost of the Pāñcālas and mighty in strength, mounting another chariot, went on toward Dhanaṃjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Those two mighty ones, Karṇa and Bhīma, locked in combat near Arjuna's chariot—what manner of battle did it become?
For Karṇa had earlier been vanquished by Bhīmasena in the fight; how did Rādheya, that great car-warrior, come once more against Bhīma?
Or how did Bhīma go forth in battle to meet the son of the sūta, that man renowned as a great car-warrior, the foremost chariot-fighter on earth?
Passing over Bhīṣma and Droṇa, the son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, took no fear from any other save Karṇa the bowman.
Out of fear he never sleeps, ever brooding on that great car-warrior; how then did Bhīma fight that son of the sūta in battle?
How did Bhīma do battle with Karṇa—reverent of brāhmaṇas, endowed with valour, never turning back in fights, the best of warriors?
Those two heroes who came together near Arjuna's chariot—how indeed did they fight, the son of the sūta and Vṛkodara?
Brotherhood had been shown to him before, and that son of the sūta is compassionate too; how did he fight with Bhīma, remembering Kuntī's words?
Or how did the hero Bhīma, recalling the enmity wrought of old, do battle with the son of the sūta, with Karṇa, in the fight?
And ever, O sūta, does my son Duryodhana cherish the hope, "Karṇa will conquer the assembled Pāṇḍavas in the war."
He on whom rests the hope of victory of my dull-witted son in the war—how did he do battle with Bhīmasena of terrible deeds?
He, leaning upon whom my sons, the great car-warriors, made this feud—how, my son, did Bhīma fight that son of the sūta?
Recalling the many insults that had sprung from the son of the sūta, how did Bhīma do battle with the sūta's offspring?
He who, valiant, conquered the whole earth with a single chariot—how did Bhīma fight that son of the sūta in battle?
He who was born together with his earrings and his armour—how did Bhīma fight that son of the sūta in the encounter?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
How the battle between those two went, and which of the two was victorious—tell me that truly, for you are skilled in such telling, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: But Bhīmasena, leaving aside Rādheya, that best of car-warriors, sought to go to where the heroes Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya stood.
As he set off, Rādheya rushed after him and rained upon him heron-feathered shafts, O great king, as a cloud rains upon a mountain.
His face, with its smile, like a blooming lotus, the mighty son of Adhiratha then hailed Bhīma in challenge as he went on through the battle.
Bhīmasena could not brook that challenge from Karṇa in the fight; wheeling round in a half-circle, he engaged the son of the sūta in battle.
With straight-flying arrows of mighty iron he rained upon him in that single combat—upon that mailed and resolute one, the best of all who bear arms.
Wishing to make an end of the quarrel, eager to slay Karṇa, the mighty one wore him down, longing, once he had killed him, to slay all the rest.
Against him that scorcher of foes, the wrathful, impatient son of Pāṇḍu, loosed fierce showers of arrows of every kind, O sire.
Those arrow-showers of his, who moved with the gait of a rutting elephant, the son of the sūta of mighty fame swallowed up by his magic art of weapons.
Thus, O great king, that great archer Karṇa, well honoured by his learning as is fitting, moved through the battle like a master.
As Bhīmasena fought with vehemence, Rādheya, as if smiling, the impatient one, bore down upon that Vṛkodara.
That smile of Karṇa in the encounter the son of Kuntī could not endure, while the heroes fought and looked on from every side.
As Karṇa drew near, the mighty Bhīmasena, in wrath, pierced him in the breast with calf-tooth shafts, as one goads a great elephant with the hook.
And the bright-armoured charioteer of the son of the sūta he pierced with thrice seven keen, fair-feathered, well-loosed shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The hero Karṇa pierced Bhīma's horses, swift as the wind and covered with nets of gold, with five arrows and five more apiece.
Then a net wrought of arrows, fashioned by Karṇa against Bhīmasena's chariot, appeared, O king, in half the wink of an eye.
There the son of Pāṇḍu, with his chariot, his banner and his driver, was wholly covered over, O great king, by the shafts sped from Karṇa's bow.
Karṇa with sixty-four shafts shattered Bhīma's stout armour, and in his wrath smote him in the side with iron arrows that pierced the vitals.
Then, heedless of those swift shafts sped from Karṇa's bow, Vṛkodara, unshaken, closed in upon the son of the sūta.
Bearing the arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow, O great king—shafts like venomous serpents—Bhīma felt no flinch of distress in the battle.
Then with thirty-two whetted, keen-pointed broad-headed arrows the valorous Bhīmasena pierced Karṇa in the fight.
With no effort at all Karṇa overwhelmed with his shafts the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, who sought the death of the Saindhava.
Rādheya fought Bhīma in the battle gently at first, while Bhīma, recalling their old enmity, fought him in wrath.
Bhīmasena, intolerant of insult, would not endure the slight; that conqueror of foes swiftly let loose a rain of arrows upon him.
Those arrows sped by Bhīmasena in the fray, O king, fearsome and falling on every side, screamed like birds in flight.
Gold-feathered, O great king, sped from Bhīmasena's bow, they rushed upon Rādheya as wolves upon a lesser beast.
But Karṇa, foremost of chariot-warriors, covered on every side, O king, loosed in turn his own fierce showers of arrows in the fight.
Those shafts of his, like thunderbolts, splendid in battle, Vṛkodara cut down with many broad-headed arrows before they reached him.
And again, O Bhārata, Karṇa Vaikartana covered the great chariot-warrior Bhīmasena with a rain of arrows in the fight.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There, O Bhārata, we beheld Bhīma in the battle, his body bristling with arrows like a porcupine with its quills.
Gold-feathered, stone-whetted shafts sped from Karṇa's bow the hero bore in battle, as the sun bears its own rays.
His every limb drenched with blood, Bhīmasena shone like a palāśa tree in the forest with its blossoms bright as gold.
But Bhīma, O great king, that mighty archer, did not endure this deed of Karṇa's in the battle, and in his wrath he rolled his eyes.
He struck Karṇa with twenty-five iron shafts—as one strikes a white mountain—shafts whose barbs lay hidden and whose touch was venomous.
Then Bhīma, valiant as a god, pierced the son of the charioteer once more, with six and then with eight shafts in his vital points in that great battle.
Then the valorous Bhīmasena, full of fury, swiftly cut to pieces Karṇa's bow and all its fittings.
In haste he slew his four horses and his charioteer with arrows, and with iron shafts bright as the sun's rays he pierced Karṇa in the breast.
All those shafts, having pierced Karṇa through, sank into the earth, O sir, as the rays of the sun pass through and beyond a cloud, O king.
Reduced to great helplessness, his bow severed and tormented by arrows, that proud man, full of manhood as he was, withdrew to another chariot.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: He in whom my sons forever placed their hope of victory, Saṃjaya—seeing him turned away from the battle, what then did Duryodhana say, and what, my son, did Karṇa do next in the fight?
Saṃjaya said: Beholding Bhīmasena in the battle blazing like fire, Karṇa mounted another chariot duly equipped and rushed again upon the Pāṇḍava, like the ocean lashed by the wind.
Seeing the son of Adhiratha enraged, O lord of peoples, your sons reckoned Bhīmasena as already offered into the mouth of the son of Vivasvat.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Making a great twang of his bow and a terrible slap of his palm, Rādheya bore down upon Bhīmasena's chariot.
Then once more, O king, there arose a great and most dreadful clash between the son of the charioteer and Bhīma, O lord of peoples.
For those two mighty-armed warriors, enraged and each seeking the other's death, gazed upon one another as though they would burn each other with their eyes.
Their eyes red with wrath, both enraged and breathing hard, those great chariot-warriors, those tamers of foes, closing on each other in the fight, hewed at one another.
Furious as two tigers, swift as two hawks, raging as two śarabhas, they fought with one another.
Then Bhīma, that tamer of foes, recalled the torments suffered at the dice-game and in the forest too, and the misery endured in the city of Virāṭa.
And the seizing of their kingdoms, rich in jewels, by your sons, and the unending torments inflicted by you together with your son—
How you sought to burn Kuntī, guiltless, together with her sons, and the abuse of Kṛṣṇā in the midst of the assembly by those wicked men—
"Seek another husband; your husbands are no more; the Pārthas are all fallen into hell, like seeds of sesame without kernel."
What the Kurus said then before your eyes, O Kaurava, when your sons desired to use Kṛṣṇā as a bondwoman to be enjoyed—
And the harsh words Karṇa spoke against them as they set forth into exile, clothed in black antelope-skins, there in the assembly, in your presence—
And how, counting the Pārthas as so much straw, your son had exulted—he, secure himself, over them in their distress, his wits gone in his fury—
Brooding on these sorrows from his childhood on, that slayer of foes, the righteous Vṛkodara, grew weary of his very life.
Then, drawing his great gold-backed and unassailable bow, that tiger of the Bhāratas, careless of his own life, rushed upon Karṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With nets of arrows, gleaming and stone-whetted, Bhīma cloaked Karṇa's chariot and veiled the very radiance of the sun.
Then the son of Adhiratha, laughing, swiftly hurling his keen shafts, scattered Bhīmasena's nets of arrows with his own feathered ones.
The great chariot-warrior, mighty-armed and mighty in strength, the son of Adhiratha, pierced Bhīma with nine swift and whetted arrows.
Like an elephant goaded with hooks, held back by those winged shafts, Vṛkodara, undismayed, charged at the son of the charioteer.
As that bull of the Pāṇḍavas rushed on swift and impetuous, Karṇa advanced to meet him in combat, as one rutting elephant meets another.
Then, his conch blown and a hundred kettledrums resounding, the host was stirred with joy, like the ocean upheaved.
Seeing that host upheaved, with its chariots, elephants, horses, and foot, Bhīma closed with Karṇa and covered him with arrows.
Karṇa, his horses the color of the antelope, mingled them in battle with the swan-white steeds of the Pāṇḍava as he covered him with shafts.
Seeing the antelope-hued horses mingled with the white ones, swift as the wind, the host of your sons broke into cries of dismay.
Those horses, swift as the wind, mingled together, shone in their multitude, white and dark, O great king, like clouds in the sky.
Beholding Karṇa and Vṛkodara enraged, their eyes copper-red with wrath, the great chariot-warriors of your side trembled in terror.
The battlefield of those two was terrible as the realm of Yama, hard to look upon, O best of the Bhāratas, like the city of the king of the dead.
Watching that wondrous spectacle as if it were a festival, the great chariot-warriors could not clearly discern victory for either in the warding off of the other.
They watched the clash of those two, their great weapons drawn close, a clash born of your ill counsel, O king, yours and your son's, O lord of peoples.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those two slayers of foes, covering one another with keen arrows, made the sky veiled with nets of shafts by their showers of arrows.
Those two great chariot-warriors, each striving to slay the other with sharp arrows, were a most beautiful sight, like two rain-laden clouds pouring down.
Loosing arrows wrought with gold, those two tamers of foes made the sky blaze as if with falling meteors of fire, O lord.
Loosed by the two, the shafts fledged with heron and peacock feathers shone in their rows, like flights of exultant cranes in the autumn sky.
Seeing Bhīma, that tamer of foes, locked in combat with the son of the charioteer, Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya thought the burden upon Bhīma too great.
There, struck hard by the arrows loosed by the son of Adhiratha and by Bhīma, horses, men, and elephants fell beyond even the range of the shafts.
By the many falling and fallen, lifeless beyond number, a great slaughter was wrought, O great king, among the people of your sons.
In an instant the earth was covered over with the lifeless bodies of men, horses, and elephants, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Most wondrous I deem the prowess of Bhīmasena, in that he made Karṇa, deft and swift in battle, give fight to him.
That Karṇa, who in battle could hold off even the thirty gods arrayed for war and bearing every weapon, together with yakṣas, asuras, and men—
How could he not overcome the Pāṇḍava in the fight, who shone as if with glory in the battle? Tell me that, my son Saṃjaya.
And how did the battle between those two unfold once more, that desperate gamble for life? On this, I think, hangs victory or defeat.
Having Karṇa in the battle, O charioteer, my son Suyodhana dares to hope he can conquer the Pārthas, together with Govinda and the Sātvatas.
But hearing that Karṇa was vanquished, and not once only, by Bhīmasena of dreadful deeds in the battle, a daze well-nigh overcomes me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Undone I deem the Kauravas through the misrule of my son; for Karṇa will not vanquish the Pārthas, those mighty archers, O Saṃjaya.
In all the battles Karṇa has waged with the sons of Pāṇḍu, everywhere the Pāṇḍavas have defeated Karṇa on the field of war.
Unconquerable are the Pāṇḍavas, my son, even by the gods with Vāsava among them; yet my dull-witted son Duryodhana does not perceive it.
Having seized the wealth of Pārtha as one might seize the wealth of the lord of riches, my foolish son, like a man greedy for honey, does not see the fall before him.
Skilled in fraud, having stolen by fraud the kingdom of those great-souled ones, and reckoning them already conquered, he holds the Pāṇḍavas in contempt.
And by me too, overborne by love for my son and undisciplined in soul, were the great-souled sons of Pāṇḍu, steadfast in dharma, wronged.
Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira, ever desiring peace and far-sighted, was spurned by my sons, who reckoned him powerless.
Taking all those manifold sorrows and outrages to heart, the mighty-armed Bhīma fought the son of the charioteer.
Therefore tell me, Saṃjaya, how Karṇa and Bhīma, those two foremost in war, fought in the battle, each seeking the other's death.
Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, how the combat unfolded between Karṇa and Bhīma, each seeking the other's death, like two elephants in the forest.
O king, Vaikartana, enraged, advancing in valor upon Bhīma the tamer of foes—enraged and valiant in turn—pierced him with thirty arrows.
With swift, bright-pointed arrows adorned with gold, Vaikartana struck Bhīma, O best of the Bhāratas.
As he loosed his shafts, Bhīma cut his bow with three whetted arrows, and with a broad-headed shaft struck his driver down from the chariot-seat to the ground.
Then Vaikartana, that bull among men, longing for Bhīmasena's death, laid hold of a spear with a shaft bright with gold and lapis.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Grasping that great spear, like a second spear of Death, the mighty Rādheya raised it, took his aim, and hurled it at Bhīmasena, as though to make an end of his life.
Having hurled the spear as Puraṃdara hurls the thunderbolt, the mighty son of the sūta, Rādheya, roared a tremendous roar; and hearing that roar your sons were filled with joy.
That spear loosed from Karṇa's arm, blazing like the sun and like fire, Bhīma cut to pieces in mid-air with seven swift arrows.
Having shattered that spear, which resembled a serpent freed from its slough, Bhīma then, O venerable one, as though seeking out the very life-breath of the son of the sūta,
in his fury sent forth in battle nine arrows fledged with peacock plumes, gold-shafted, whetted upon stone, like to the rod of Yama.
Karṇa too, taking up another bow, gold-backed and hard to withstand, and drawing it, that mighty-splendored one let fly nine shafts.
Those the son of Pāṇḍu cut apart with nine smooth-jointed shafts; and having severed the nine great arrows loosed by Vasuṣeṇa, O great king, Bhīma roared as a lion roars.
The two mighty ones, bellowing like bulls over a cow in heat, roared exceedingly at one another like two tigers.
Each longing to strike the other, each watching for the other's opening, they glared at one another like two great bulls in the cattle-pens.
Closing like two great elephants goring each other with the tips of their tusks, they smote one another with arrows loosed from bows drawn to the full.
Scorching each other, O great king, with showers of arrows, they glared at one another, their eyes wide open in wrath.
Laughing at one another and taunting each other again and again, sounding their conches the while, they fought together.
Once more Bhīma cut his bow asunder at the grip, O venerable one, and with his arrows sent his conch-white horses to the abode of Yama.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing Karṇa thus brought to straits, King Duryodhana, trembling as it were with rage, then gave command to Durjaya:
"Go, Durjaya, before the Pāṇḍava devours Rādheya; swiftly slay this hornless one and lend your strength to Karṇa."
Thus addressed, your son answered "So be it," and rushed upon Bhīmasena, who was engaged elsewhere, scattering arrows as he came.
He afflicted Bhīma with nine arrows, his horses with eight, his driver with six, his standard with three, and Bhīma again with seven.
Bhīmasena too, greatly enraged, with his swift shafts pierced Durjaya in his vitals and, horses and charioteer with him, sent him to the dwelling of Yama.
As your richly adorned son lay crushed upon the earth, writhing like a serpent, Karṇa, weeping and stricken with grief, made a reverent circuit about him.
But Bhīma, having stripped his bitter foe of his chariot, smiling, covered him over with masses of arrows as a śataghnī is studded with spikes.
Yet even so the mighty car-warrior Karṇa, that scorcher of foes, though pierced through by the shafts, did not abandon the wrathful-visaged Bhīma in the fight.
Saṃjaya said: Karṇa, thus deprived of his chariot and again vanquished by Bhīma, mounting another car, straightway pierced the Pāṇḍava.
Closing like two great elephants goring each other with the tips of their tusks, they smote one another with arrows loosed from bows drawn to the full.
Then Karṇa afflicted Bhīma sorely with multitudes of arrows, roared a mighty roar, and again pierced him in the chest.
Bhīma pierced him back with ten straight-flying arrows, and pierced him again with twenty smooth-jointed shafts.
But Karṇa, O king, having pierced Bhīma with nine arrows between the breasts, pierced his standard with a single keen shaft.
Then the son of Pṛthā pierced him in return with sixty-three shafts, as a great elephant is goaded with hooks, or a horse with whips.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sorely pierced, O great king, by the illustrious Pāṇḍava, that hero, licking the corners of his mouth, his eyes red with wrath,
then, O great king, loosed at Bhīmasena an arrow that could rend any body, as Indra hurls the thunderbolt against the Daityas.
That gaily-feathered shaft, loosed from the sūta's son's bow, having pierced the son of Pṛthā in battle, passed on and split the ground.
Without hesitation Bhīma hurled at the sūta's son a heavy mace, wholly of iron, four cubits long, banded with gold and six-edged.
With that mace the wrathful Bhārata slew the goodly, well-trained steeds of the son of Adhiratha, as Indra slew the Asuras with the thunderbolt.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, O bull of the Bhāratas, with two razor-edged arrows cut down the standard of Adhiratha's son and struck down his charioteer.
Forsaking the car whose horses and driver were slain and whose standard had fallen, Karṇa, twanging his bow, stood there, O Bhārata, downcast in heart.
There we beheld a wondrous feat of Rādheya's prowess: bereft of his chariot, that best of car-warriors yet held his enemy at bay.
Seeing the son of Adhiratha, that foremost of car-warriors, deprived of his car in the battle, Duryodhana then, O king, spoke to Durmukha:
"This Rādheya, O Durmukha, has been stripped of his chariot by Bhīma; furnish that best of men, that mighty car-warrior, with a car."
Hearing Duryodhana's word, O Bhārata, Durmukha hastened to Karṇa and held Bhīma off with arrows.
Beholding Durmukha in the fray hastening to the side of the sūta's son, the son of Vāyu rejoiced, licking the corners of his mouth.
Then, O great king, having warded off Karṇa with his arrows, the Pāṇḍava swiftly drove his car toward Durmukha.
In that instant, O great king, with nine well-feathered, smooth-jointed shafts Bhīma sent Durmukha to the abode of Yama.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, Durmukha being slain, the son of Adhiratha mounted that very car and shone, O king, like the radiant sun.
Seeing Durmukha lying with his vitals pierced and bathed in blood, Karṇa, his eyes filled with tears, for a moment did not advance.
Passing by the lifeless one and making a reverent circuit about him, the hero Karṇa, sighing long and hot, could do nothing at all.
In that opening, O king, Bhīmasena loosed at the sūta's son fourteen iron arrows fledged with vulture-feathers.
Those gold-shafted, exceedingly powerful arrows, splendidly wrought with gold, O great king, having pierced his armor, lit up the ten directions,
and, feeding upon blood, drank the blood of the sūta's son, O lord of men, like enraged serpents urged on by Death.
Gliding upon the earth, those shafts shone forth as, half-entered into their holes, great serpents furiously dart.
Rādheya pierced him in return, without hesitation, with fourteen exceedingly fierce iron arrows adorned with gold.
Those terrible winged shafts, having pierced through Bhīmasena's left arm, entered the earth as birds plunge into the Krauñca mountain.
Those iron arrows, entering the earth, shone like the blazing rays of the day-maker as he goes to his setting.
Bhīma, pierced in battle by those vital-rending iron arrows, streamed forth blood in abundance as a mountain pours down water.
That Bhīma, stretched to his utmost, pierced the sūta's son with three winged shafts swift as Suparṇa, and his charioteer with seven.
Reeling, O great king, and sore afflicted by Bhīma's might, the illustrious Karṇa abandoned the battle and fled away with his swift horses.
But Bhīmasena, twanging his gold-decked bow, that mighty car-warrior stood in the battle blazing like the fire that devours offerings.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Fate, I deem, is supreme; fie upon human effort, that comes to naught, since the son of Adhiratha, straining his utmost, could not overcome the Pāṇḍava in battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Karṇa is able to conquer the sons of Pṛthā together with Govinda in battle, and I see no warrior in the world equal to Karṇa" — thus did I hear Duryodhana prate again and again.
"For Karṇa is mighty, a hero, firm of bow, conqueror of fatigue" — thus the foolish Duryodhana spoke to me of old, O sūta.
"With Vasuṣeṇa for my ally, not even the gods are a match for me in war, O king — how much less the sons of Pāṇḍu, drained of strength and bereft of sense."
Now, seeing Karṇa there vanquished, like a serpent drained of its venom, withdrawn from the fight — what, pray, did Duryodhana say?
Alas, in his bewilderment he sent Durmukha alone, unskilled in warfare, into the battle, as a moth is sent into the fire.
Aśvatthāman, the king of the Madras, Kṛpa, and Karṇa, even joined together, are surely unable to stand before Bhīma, O Saṃjaya.
They too, knowing his most terrible strength, like that of ten thousand elephants, and the cruel resolve of that one whose splendor is the Wind's,
why, knowing his might, his fury, and his valor, would they provoke in battle that one of cruel deeds, who is like Yama, Time, and the Ender?
Yet Karṇa alone, the mighty-armed son of the sūta, relying on the strength of his own arms, made light of Bhīmasena and fought him in battle.
He who vanquished Karṇa in battle as Puraṃdara vanquished the Asura — that son of Pāṇḍu can be conquered by none in the fight.
Bhīma, who, crushing Droṇa, alone penetrated my host in search of Dhanaṃjaya — who that wished to live would withstand him?
For who, O Saṃjaya, would dare to stand before Bhīma, as a Dānava before great Indra with his thunderbolt upraised?
A man might come even to the city of the king of the dead and return, but having come upon Bhīmasena he would never return.
Like moths into the fire those dull-witted ones plunged, who in their bewilderment rushed against the wrathful Bhīmasena.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That oath which Bhīma swore in the assembly, touching the slaughter of my sons, the fierce and furious one, in the hearing of the Kurus then —
surely remembering that, and seeing Karṇa vanquished, Duḥśāsana with his brother drew back from Bhīma out of fear.
And he of evil mind, O Saṃjaya, who said again and again in the council, "Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and I shall conquer the Pāṇḍavas in battle" —
he, surely, seeing Karṇa stripped of his car and vanquished by Bhīma, and recalling his rejection of Kṛṣṇa, grieves bitterly, O Saṃjaya.
Seeing his mailed brothers slain in battle by Bhīmasena, my little son, surely, grieves exceedingly for his own transgression.
For who that wished to live would advance against the Pāṇḍava Bhīma, of terrible weapons, enraged, standing there like Death made manifest?
A man set in the midst of the mare-mouthed fire beneath the sea might yet escape, but one who has come within Bhīma's reach cannot escape — such is my conviction.
Neither the Pāṇḍavas, nor the Pāñcālas, nor Keśava and Sātyaki, when roused in battle, know how to guard their lives.
Saṃjaya said: That you grieve, O Kaurava, now that the slaughter of folk is upon us — you yourself are the root of this world's destruction, there is no doubt.
Having yourself stirred up this great enmity, and abiding by the word of your sons, though counseled you would not take the counsel, as a dying man refuses wholesome medicine.
Having yourself drunk down, O great king, the Kālakūṭa poison so hard to digest, now reap its fruit in full, O best of men.
As for your reviling of the warriors who fought with all their strength, I shall now describe to you how the battle truly unfolded.
When they saw Karṇa worsted by Bhīmasena, your five sons, born of the same mother and mighty archers, could not endure it, O honored one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Durmarṣaṇa, Duḥsaha, Durmada, Durdhara, and Jaya, splendid in their armor, rushed against that son of Pāṇḍu to oppose him.
Surrounding the mighty-armed Vṛkodara on every side, they veiled the quarters with arrows, as though with swarms of locusts.
As those princes, fair as the gods, came swiftly on, Bhīmasena received them in battle as though with a laugh.
But seeing your sons drawn close to Bhīmasena, Rādheya advanced against the mighty Bhīmasena.
Loosing shafts with golden nocks, whetted on stone, O king, he came on; and Bhīma rushed at him at once, though held back by your sons.
Then the Kurus, encircling Karṇa on all sides, covered Bhīmasena with arrows of smooth-jointed shafts.
With twenty-five arrows, O king, Bhīma of the fearsome bow sent those bull-like men, together with their horses and charioteers, to the abode of Yama.
Lifeless, they fell from their chariots together with their charioteers, like great flowering trees laden with bright blossoms, broken by the wind.
There we beheld the wondrous valor of Bhīmasena, who, while warding off the son of Adhiratha with his arrows, yet slew your sons.
Though held off on every side by Bhīma's sharp arrows, the son of the sūta, O great king, kept his gaze fixed upon Bhīmasena.
And Bhīmasena, in his fury, his eyes red with wrath, drawing his vast bow taut, gazed again and again upon Karṇa.
Saṃjaya said: When valiant Karṇa saw your sons fallen, he was seized with a great wrath and grew weary of his own life.
The son of Adhiratha then deemed himself an offender, as it were; and in his anger he rushed upon Bhīmasena in haste.
Rādheya, having pierced Bhīma with five shafts as though with a smile, struck him again with seventy arrows golden-nocked and whetted on stone.
But Vṛkodara, son of Pṛthā, would not brook that mockery, and pierced Rādheya in turn with a hundred smooth-jointed shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And again, having pierced him with five swift, keen arrows, he cut asunder the bow of the sūta's son with a broad-headed shaft, O honored one.
Then Karṇa, taking up another bow, O Bhārata, sore at heart, covered Bhīmasena on every side with his arrows.
But Bhīma, having slain his horses and struck down his charioteer, laughed a great laugh, the deed repaid once more.
And that bull among men cut his bow apart with arrows; it fell, O great king, gold-backed and loud-resounding.
Then Karṇa, that mighty car-warrior, descended from his chariot, and seizing a mace, hurled it at Bhīmasena in the fray.
Seeing that mace come hurtling suddenly upon him, Vṛkodara warded it off with his arrows, O king, in the sight of the whole army.
Then the valiant son of Pāṇḍu, eager to slay the sūta's son, sent forth in haste thousands of arrows.
Warding off those shafts with his own arrows in that great battle, Karṇa with his darts struck down the armor of Bhīmasena.
Then he pierced him with twenty-five small arrows; and to all beings who beheld it, that seemed a wondrous thing.
Then Bhīma, O great king, in his wrath sent against the sūta's son in battle nine smooth-jointed shafts, O honored one.
Piercing his armor and his right arm, those keen shafts entered the earth like serpents entering an anthill.
But seeing Rādheya standing on foot in the battle, sore beset by Bhīmasena, King Duryodhana said: 'Make haste, all of you, intent and ready, to bring a chariot to Rādheya.'
Then your sons, O king, hearing their brother's word, swiftly advanced against the son of Pāṇḍu in battle, loosing keen arrows.
Citra, Upacitra, Citrākṣa, Cārucitra, Śarāsana, Citrāyudha, and Citravarman—warriors of wondrous skill in battle.
As they came on swiftly, Bhīma, that mighty car-warrior, O king, struck them down in the fray together with their horses, charioteers, and standards; slain, they fell to the earth like trees felled by the wind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing your sons, those mighty car-warriors, slain, O king, Karṇa, his face full of tears, fell into a swoon of grief.
Mounting another chariot duly equipped, the valiant one again advanced in haste against the son of Pāṇḍu in battle.
Piercing each other with arrows golden-nocked and whetted on stone, the two shone, O great king, like a pair of kiṃśuka trees in flower.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu, in his wrath, with thirty-six sharp broad-headed shafts of fierce point, shattered the armor of the sūta's son.
Their limbs as if smeared with red sandal, deeply wounded by arrows and bathed in blood, the two shone like twin suns of the world's end newly risen.
With their bodies drenched in blood, their armor riven by arrows, the two, stripped of mail, shone like serpents that had cast their slough.
Like two tigers tearing each other with their fangs, those tamers of foes, those tigers among men, brandishing arrows for fangs, rent one another.
Locked together like two elephants, they shone in the midst of the field, striking each other with keen shafts, in prowess like rutting elephants.
Covering each other in battle with nets of arrows, and making all the quarters resound with their chariots, the two ranged about.
With their chariots, O great king, in wheeling rounds and like maneuvers, those two high-souled ones shone like Vṛtra and the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Drawing his bow with arms adorned with bracelets, Bhīma shone in the battle like a thunderhead lit with lightning.
Thundering with the roar of his bow, that great rain-cloud of arrow-showers, the dread cloud that was Bhīma, O great king, advanced upon the mountain that was Karṇa.
Then with a thousand arrows loosed from his bow, O Bhārata, the son of Pāṇḍu covered Karṇa as a cloud covers a mountain with its rains.
There your sons beheld the valor of Bhīmasena, who covered Karṇa with shafts fair-nocked and fledged with heron's feathers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Gladdening the son of Pṛthā in battle, and the glorious Keśava, and Sātyaki and the two guardians of the wheels, Bhīma fought against Karṇa.
The prowess of his arms, the valor and the steadfastness of that self-possessed hero—your sons, O great king, beheld it all in the son of Pāṇḍu.
Saṃjaya said: When Rādheya heard the twang of Bhīmasena's bowstring and the slap of his palm, he brooked it no more, as a rutting elephant brooks not the trumpeting of a rival.
Withdrawing for a moment from the range of Bhīma's arrows, the son of Adhiratha beheld your sons fallen from their chariots.
Slain by Bhīmasena, they lay there; downcast and grieved, sighing long and hot, he again advanced upon the son of Pāṇḍu.
His eyes red as copper with wrath, hissing like a great serpent, Karṇa, loosing his arrows, blazed like the radiant sun shedding its beams.
As if by the spreading webs of the sun's rays, O bull of the Bhāratas, Vṛkodara was overspread by the arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow.
The bright arrows fledged with peacock-feathers, loosed from Karṇa's bow, entered the son of Pṛthā from every side, as birds settle upon a tree to roost.
The golden-nocked arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow, flying hither and thither, shone like wild geese ranged in rows.
Springing forth, as it seemed, from his bow, his banner, and the gear of his car, from his parasol, from the shaft-end of the pole, and from the yoke, the arrows of Adhiratha's son were seen, O king.
Filling the sky, the son of Adhiratha let fly his arrows of great speed, sky-coursing and feather-fledged, bright and wrought with gold.
As he bore down like Death himself strained for the kill, Vṛkodara, with his own life held cheap and burning with wrath, pierced him with nine arrows.
Seeing the unbearable onslaught of Karṇa and those great floods of arrows, the valiant son of Pāṇḍu was not in the least dismayed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, scattering the nets of arrows of Adhiratha's son, the son of Pāṇḍu pierced Karṇa with twenty more keen shafts.
Even as the son of Pṛthā had been covered with arrows by the sūta's son, so too did the son of Pāṇḍu cover Karṇa in the battle.
Beholding the valor of Bhīmasena in battle, O Bhārata, your own people and the celestial bards rejoiced and applauded with delight.
Bhūriśravas, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, the king of the Madras, Jayadratha, Uttamaujas, Yudhāmanyu, Sātyaki, Keśava, and Arjuna—
these ten foremost mighty car-warriors among the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, O king, crying 'Well done! Well done!' raised forthwith a mighty lion's roar.
While that tumultuous, hair-raising clamor arose, O king, Duryodhana hastily addressed your sons.
To the kings and the princes, and his own brothers especially: 'Go to Karṇa—good fortune to you—seeking to deliver him from Vṛkodara.'
'Before the arrows loosed from Bhīma's bow strike down Rādheya, exert yourselves, O great archers, to guard the sūta's son.'
At Duryodhana's command, seven of his brothers, O honored one, rushed furiously upon Bhīmasena and surrounded him.
Closing in upon the son of Kuntī, they enveloped him with showers of arrows, as rain-clouds in the wet season enwrap a mountain with their torrents.
Those seven mighty car-warriors in their wrath beset Bhīmasena, O king, as the seven planets beset the moon at the time of the dissolution of beings.
Then the son of Kuntī, the son of Pāṇḍu, gripping his bow tightly in his firm left fist, O king—that well-wrought bow—
and judging them but men like himself, fitted seven arrows like the sun's own beams, and the mighty one, drawing them taut, loosed them upon those foes.
As if casting forth the very life-breaths from the bodies of your sons, Bhīmasena, O great king, remembered the old enmity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those arrows hurled by Bhīmasena, O Bhārata, golden-nocked and whetted on stone, having pierced the Bhāratas, sprang up into the sky.
Having rent open their hearts, those gold-adorned arrows shone, O great king, like sky-coursing eagles.
Their feathered tips smeared with blood, those seven gold-wrought shafts, O lord of kings, sprang up again, having drunk the blood of your sons.
Their vital parts pierced by the arrows, they fell from their chariots to the earth, like great trees grown on mountain ridges, broken by an elephant.
Śatruṃjaya, Śatrusaha, Citra, Citrāyudha, Dṛḍha, Citrasena, and Vikarṇa—these seven were laid low.
Having slain them, the mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu, before the very eyes of Rādheya, sent forth a terrible roar like a lion's.
That roar of the hero, O Bhārata, seemed to proclaim to the King of Righteousness that battle and his own great victory.
Hearing that mighty roar of Bhīmasena the bowman, the Dharmarāja was filled with the highest joy in the battle.
Then, O great king, the delighted Pārtha answered Bhīmasena's roar on every side with the loud blare of musical instruments.
And when Vṛkodara had given the signal, filled with great gladness he advanced in the battle against Droṇa, the foremost of weapon-bearers.
Seeing thirty-one of your sons, great car-warriors all, slain, O great king, Duryodhana remembered those words of Vidura the steward.
"Now has come to pass that beneficial word of the steward,"—so reflecting, that king found no answer to make.
What your evil-minded son had spoken at the time of the dice-game, and the harsh words that Karṇa had spoken to Kṛṣṇā in the assembly—
in the presence of the sons of Pāṇḍu, and of yourself, O lord of peoples, and of all the Kauravas, and in the very presence of the preceptor—
"The Pāṇḍavas are utterly ruined, O Kṛṣṇā; they have gone to everlasting hell. Choose yourself another husband"—the fruit of that has now arrived.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When, having brought Draupadī into the assembly, they spoke harsh words to her, your sons enraged the Pāṇḍavas of terrible bows.
Loosing that fire of wrath which had abided in him thirteen years, Bhīmasena, O Kaurava, is bringing your sons to their end.
Lamenting much, the steward could find no peace with you, O best of the Bhāratas, you together with your sons; now reap the ripening of that fruit. Vikarṇa is slain, O lord of kings, and valiant Citrasena too.
The foremost among your sons, and other of your sons, great car-warriors—whomever Bhīma saw come within range of his eye, those sons of yours, O mighty-armed one, he slew in haste.
On your account I have beheld the host consumed as if by fire, by the arrows loosed in their thousands by the Pāṇḍava and by the Bull Karṇa.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Great was the misgovernance, O charioteer, mine above all herein; that has now come home, I think, O Saṃjaya, to me who grieve.
"What is gone is gone"—this was fixed in my mind; now what is to be done here, what shall I do, O Saṃjaya?
But how this destruction of heroes, born of my own misrule, came to pass—tell me that; I have grown steady, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Karṇa and Bhīma, O great king, putting forth their valour in the great battle, rained down showers of arrows like two rain-laden clouds.
Arrows marked with Bhīma's name, golden-feathered and whetted on stone, reaching Karṇa entered him as though cleaving his very life.
Even so was Bhīma covered in the fight, by hundreds and by thousands, with the shafts loosed from Karṇa, like venomous serpents.
From the arrows of those two falling on every side, O great king, there arose among your armies a tumult like that of the ocean.
By the arrows loosed from Bhīma's bow, O subduer of foes, your army was slaughtered in the midst of the host—dreadful shafts, the likeness of snakes of deadly poison.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Strewn with fallen elephants, O king, and with horses and men together, the earth appeared as if littered with trees uprooted by the wind.
Being slain in the battle by the arrows loosed from Bhīma's bow, your warriors fled, crying out, "What is this?"
Then that army of the Sindhus, the Sauvīras, and the Kauravas was scattered and driven off by the swift arrows of Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava.
Sore wounded with arrows for the most part, their horses, men, and mounts slain, they abandoned Karṇa and Bhīma and fled in every direction.
"Surely for Pārtha's sake the dwellers of heaven bewilder us, in that our host is being slain by the arrows that spring from Karṇa and Bhīma."
Speaking thus, your warriors, oppressed by fear, withdrew beyond arrow-range and stood there, eager only to watch the fight.
Then there flowed, in that great battle, a river of dreadful aspect, which especially heightened the terror of the timorous.
It rose from the streaming blood of elephants, horses, and men, and was thronged with lifeless men, elephants, and steeds.
With the trappings of elephants, horses, and cars, with their axle-poles and banners, and with chariots cast aside, their wheels, axles, and shafts broken—
with bows adorned with gold and of exceeding worth, with golden-feathered shafts, and with iron arrows by the thousand—
loosed by Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava like serpents set free, with masses of darts and lances, with swords and battle-axes—
and with maces, clubs, and spiked spears wrought with gold, with thunderbolt-darts of many shapes, with spears and bludgeons, and with gleaming hundred-slayers, the earth shone bright, O Bhārata.
With golden armlets and bracelets, with earrings and shining gems, with coats of mail and with hand-guards, with necklaces and ornaments of gold, O Bhārata—
with garments and parasols torn asunder, with yak-tail whisks and fans, with the cleft bodies of elephants, horses, and men, with weapons and the trappings of chariots—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
with these manifold objects of every kind, fallen and flung about here and there, the earth shone like the firmament with its planets.
Beholding the unimaginable, wondrous, and more-than-human deeds of those two, amazement seized the Cāraṇas and the Siddhas.
As fire aided by the wind sweeps through dry brushwood, so was the course in battle of the son of Adhiratha, having Bhīma for his match; terrible was that course, casting down banners and cars and slaying horses, men, and elephants.
As a thicket of reeds is crushed by two elephants joined in combat, so was that great army brought low in the battle, O Bhārata; and supreme was the havoc wrought by Karṇa and Bhīma in the fight.
Saṃjaya said: Then Karṇa, O great king, having pierced Bhīma with three shafts, loosed showers of arrows, brilliant and manifold.
Though smitten by the son of the charioteer, O great king, the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena did not waver, like a mountain being riven.
Then Bhīmasena, O lord of kings, pierced Karṇa in the ear with a barbed, whetted, yellow-hued, feathered shaft in the fight.
He struck the great earring of refined gold from Karṇa's ear to the ground, O great king, like a blazing light falling from the sky.
Then with another broad-headed arrow the mighty Bhīma, as if smiling, struck the charioteer's son hard between the breasts.
Then again, in haste, Bhīma sped at him in the battle ten iron arrows of great swiftness, O Bhārata, like the rod of Yama.
Reaching the forehead of the charioteer's son, O sire, those arrows, driven by him, entered it as serpents enter an ant-hill.
With those arrows fixed in his forehead the charioteer's son shone forth, as he had of old when wearing a garland wrought of blue lotuses.
Then Karṇa, enraged in the fight, sore pressed by the strong bowman, mighty in speed, put forth his swiftness to slay Bhīmasena.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At him Karṇa, O king, impatient, strong, and wrathful, sped a hundred arrows feathered with vulture-plumes, O Bhārata.
Then the Pāṇḍava loosed fierce showers of arrows; heeding him not in the battle, he gave no thought to his prowess.
Then Karṇa, O great king, that scorcher of foes, in his wrath struck the wrathful-looking Pāṇḍava upon the breast with whetted shafts.
Like two storm-clouds they rained upon each other in the battle, terrifying one another with the cracking sounds of their bow-strings.
With manifold nets of arrows they covered each other in the fray, both wrathful in the battle, each seeking to repay deed with deed.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, having cut the bow of the high-souled Rādheya with a razor-tipped arrow, pierced Karṇa with a feathered shaft.
Casting aside that severed bow, the high-minded son of the charioteer took up another, swift-striking and able to bear a heavy strain.
And seeing the destruction of the host of the Kurus, the Sauvīras, and the Saindhavas, and the earth covered with fallen armour, banners, and weapons—
and beholding on every side the lifeless bodies of elephants, horses, and men, the form of the charioteer's son grew blazing with fury.
Twanging his great bow adorned with gold, Rādheya gazed upon Bhīma, O king, with a terrible eye.
Then the wrathful son of the charioteer, hurling his shafts, shone forth radiant like the autumn sun risen to the meridian.
Like the form of the sun blossoming with its rays, O king, was the dreadful form of the son of Adhiratha, ablaze with hundreds of arrows.
As he took up his swift shafts with both hands, set them to the string, drew them back, and loosed them, none in the battle could mark the interval.
As he discharged his shafts to the left and to the right, the weapon of Karṇa, O great king, dreadful as a wheel of fire, seemed drawn into a circle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Golden-feathered and well-whetted, the arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow veiled, O great king, the quarters and the splendour of the sun.
Then in the sky was seen, in manifold array, a flight of gold-feathered arrows with smooth-bending joints, loosed from his bow.
Issuing from the bow of the son of Adhiratha, the shafts, ranged in lines, shone forth, O king, like cranes in the heavens.
Vulture-feathered, stone-whetted, adorned with gold, of great swiftness and blazing points—such arrows did the son of Adhiratha loose.
Hurled by the force of the bow and decked with gold, those arrows poured ceaselessly upon the chariot of Pārtha's son Bhīma.
Gem-wrought, they shone in the sky by the thousand—the arrows sped by Karṇa, like swarms of locusts.
Loosed from the bow of the son of Adhiratha, the falling shafts seemed, as they sped forth, to be a single long and towering arrow.
As a rain-cloud veils a mountain with its torrents, so did the wrathful Karṇa cover Bhīma with showers of arrows.
There, O Bhārata, your sons together with the Kurus beheld the strength, the valour, the prowess, and the resolve of Bhīma.
Heedless of that risen shower of arrows, swollen like the surging sea, the wrathful Bhīma rushed upon Karṇa.
The great gold-backed bow of Bhīma, O lord of peoples, drawn into a circle by his pull, seemed a second rainbow of Indra; from it the arrows came forth as if filling the firmament.
By the gold-feathered, smooth-jointed shafts of Bhīma there was wrought in the sky a garland that shone as if of gold.
Then the nets of arrows clinging in the sky, struck piece by piece by the feathered shafts of Bhīmasena, were scattered asunder.
By the floods of arrow-nets of both Karṇa and Bhīmasena, touching like sparks of fire and flying straight in the battle, the sky was wholly covered with flights of gold-feathered shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Covering Bhīma with arrows of many kinds, the charioteer's son pressed upon him, making light of the prowess of that high-souled one.
As those two there loosed their nets of arrows, O sire, they seemed to become like winds, clashing one against the other.
At him Karṇa, in his wrath, sped sharp arrows burnished by the smith and wrought with gold, longing to slay him.
Those Bhīma cut down in mid-air with his shafts, each into three, and outdoing the charioteer's son he cried, "Stand and fight!"
Once more the mighty Pāṇḍava, brooking no insult and ablaze with wrath, let loose his fierce torrents of arrows, like a fire bent on consuming all.
But Karṇa, the charioteer's son, fearlessly received all those weapons of the warring son of Pāṇḍu, neutralizing them by the wizardry of his own missiles.
With his smooth-jointed shafts Karṇa Vaikartana cut apart Bhīma's quivers, his bowstring, and the reins and traces of his horses.
Then, having slain his horses, with three arrows he pierced his charioteer, who leapt down and fled swiftly to the chariot of Yuyudhāna.
As though smiling, the wrathful Rādheya, radiant as the fire of doom, severed Bhīma's banner and brought down his pennons.
Bereft of his bow, O great king, Bhīma seized the lance kept in his car, and whirling it in his fury, hurled it at Karṇa's chariot.
But the son of Adhiratha, straining hard, with ten arrows cut to pieces that gold-adorned lance as it came on, blazing like a great meteor.
Cleft into ten pieces by the shafts of Karṇa, it fell, O king — shafts loosed by that charioteer's son, fighter of wondrous skill, in the cause of his friend.
Then the son of Kuntī took up his shield and his gold-mounted sword, seeking now one of two ends — death or victory; but Karṇa, as if laughing, shattered them both in an instant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Stripped of his shield, O great king, his chariot gone, swooning with rage, Bhīma whirled his sword and flung it in haste at Karṇa's car.
That keen-edged blade, having cut through the charioteer's son's bow and its string, fell to the earth like a serpent dropping from the sky.
Then, laughing, the son of Adhiratha, enraged, took up in the battle another bow — slayer of foes, firm-stringed, and swifter still.
Then mighty Bhīmasena, true in valor and roused to wrath, sprang up into the sky, troubling the heart of Karṇa.
Seeing this feat of him who sought victory in the fray, Rādheya, biding his moment, foiled Bhīmasena.
Not finding him — for Bhīma, his senses shaken, had crouched hidden upon a chariot floor — Karṇa came up to his banner and stood there upon the ground.
For this all the Kurus and the celestial bards honored Bhīma — that from his car he had sought to slay Karṇa, as Tārkṣya seizes a serpent.
His bow shorn away and his chariot lost, yet keeping to the duty of his order, Bhīma set his own car at his back and stood firm, still ready to fight.
Having broken his resolve, Rādheya then bore down upon the Pāṇḍava, furious, as he stood there in the battle, ready for combat.
The two mighty warriors met in that great arena, contending, roaring like two thunderclouds in the heavens at the close of the hot season.
Fierce was the encounter of those two wrathful lions among men, neither brooking the other in the fray, like that of a god and a demon.
His weapons spent and hard pressed by Karṇa, the son of Kuntī, seeing elephants slain by Arjuna lying fallen like mountains, and being weaponless, entered in among them to bar the path of Karṇa's chariot.
Reaching the herd of elephants and entering that rampart against chariots, the Pāṇḍava, desiring to keep his life, did not press his attack upon Rādheya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, seeking a foothold, the son of Pṛthā, conqueror of hostile cities, heaved up an elephant slain by Dhanaṃjaya's shafts and stood his ground.
Karṇa with his arrows blasted that elephant of his to pieces; then the Pāṇḍava, roaring, flung the elephant's limbs at Karṇa.
Chariot-wheels, horses, draught-beasts — whatever he saw upon the ground, that the enraged Pāṇḍava caught up and hurled at Karṇa.
All this, as fast as it was flung, Karṇa cut apart with his sharp shafts; yet, weaponless though Bhīma was, Karṇa did not slay him, remembering the word he had given to Kuntī.
Rushing upon him, Karṇa touched him with the tip of his bow, and Rādheya, as if smiling, spoke thus to Bhīmasena:
"Again and again, you beardless dolt, you slave of your belly, you who have learned no weapon-craft — do not fight, you child, you coward in battle!"
"Where there is food of many kinds, things to chew and things to drink, O Pāṇḍava — there, foolish one, you belong; never anywhere in battle."
"Become an ascetic, Bhīma, and live on fruits, O most witless one; go to the forest, son of Kuntī — you are no master of warfare."
"You are fit for feeding on fruits and roots and for entertaining guests; I do not think you fit for the wielding of weapons, Vṛkodara."
"With flowers, roots, and fruits for your fare, amid vows and observances, you suit the forest, Bhīma — you are no master of warfare."
"What has war to do with the life of a sage? Go to the forest, Vṛkodara; you are not made for battle, my friend — take your delight in dwelling in the woods."
"Chivvying cooks and servants and slaves in the house, you are fit to thrash them in your rage for the sake of a meal, Vṛkodara."
And whatever galling things had passed in their boyhood, O lord of peoples, those old harsh deeds too he made him hear over and over.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then again, as Bhīma cowered there, the Bull of men touched him with his bow, and laughing, addressed him once more:
"If you must fight, fall upon someone else; you should not fight with such as me. Those who battle men of my kind meet with this and worse."
"Or go to where the two Kṛṣṇas are — they will guard you in the fight; or go home, son of Kuntī. What have you, child, to do with war?"
Having thus stripped him of his chariot, Karṇa, O king, vaunted over him in the very presence of the Lion of the Vṛṣṇis and of the great-souled son of Pṛthā.
Then, O king, the hero whose banner bore the monkey, urged on by Keśava, sent stone-whetted arrows against the charioteer's son.
Then the gold-decked shafts loosed from the arm of Pṛthā's son, sprung from Gāṇḍīva, fell upon Karṇa as swans descend on the Krauñca mountain.
With arrows shot from Gāṇḍīva, taut like outstretched serpents, Dhanaṃjaya drove the charioteer's son back from Bhīmasena.
His bow shorn by Bhīma and himself struck by Dhanaṃjaya's shafts, Karṇa swiftly withdrew from Bhīma upon his great chariot.
And Bhīma too, that bull among men, mounting a horse of Sātyaki's, followed in the battle his brother, the Pāṇḍava Savyasācin.
Then, taking aim at Karṇa, Dhanaṃjaya in haste, his eyes red with wrath, sent forth an iron shaft as Death sends out the destroyer.
Like Garutmān in the sky stooping upon the foremost of serpents, that iron shaft, sped from Gāṇḍīva, flew swiftly down upon Karṇa.
That iron shaft Droṇa's son cut in mid-air with a feathered arrow, the great chariot-warrior seeking to deliver Karṇa from the peril of Dhanaṃjaya.
Then the wrathful Arjuna pierced Droṇa's son with sixty-four stone-honed arrows, O great king, crying, "Do not flee — stand fast!"
But Droṇa's son, sore beset by Dhanaṃjaya's shafts, swiftly plunged into the host thronged with rutting elephants and crowded with chariots.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then with the roar of Gāṇḍīva the mighty son of Kuntī overwhelmed the twanging din of the gold-backed bows that sang upon the field.
Dhanaṃjaya, as Droṇa's son thus fled, pursued him from behind for no great distance, terrifying the host with his arrows.
Rending with his iron shafts the bodies of men, elephants, and horses, Arjuna scattered the host with arrows fledged in the plumes of heron and peacock.
That host, O best of the Bhāratas, with its horses, elephants, and men, the son of Pṛthā — offspring of the Chastiser of Pāka — straining hard, smote down utterly.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Day after day my blazing glory falls away, Saṃjaya; many of my warriors are slain. I deem this the turning of Time.
Dhanaṃjaya in his fury has entered my host — a host guarded by Droṇa and Karṇa, one that not even the gods could penetrate —
his prowess swelled by those two of mighty valor, joined with Kṛṣṇa and Bhīma and with the Bull of the Śinis.
From that hour grief burns me like a fire within my heart, for I see the lords of earth, the Saindhava among them, already in its grip.
Having done so grievous a wrong to the Diademed one, how can the king of the Sindhus, once come within his sight, escape with his life?
By reasoning I see, Saṃjaya, that the Saindhava is no more. Tell me, then, as I ask, how that battle came to pass.
And tell of him who, having shaken and churned that great army again and again, entered it alone in his wrath, as an elephant breaks into a lotus-pool.
Tell me truly of the battle of that Vṛṣṇi hero, of what he did for Dhanaṃjaya's sake — for in this you are skilled, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Seeing Bhīma, that foremost of men, thus harried by Vaikartana and now moving away amid the heroes, O king, the hero of the Śinis followed after him in his chariot.
Roaring like the Wielder of the thunderbolt at the end of the heats, blazing like the sun at the close of the rains, he smote his foes with his firm bow, making your son's army tremble.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As that hero among men ranged the field, borne by horses bright as silver, all your chariot-warriors, O Bhārata, could not turn back that foremost of the Mādhavas.
But Alambusa, that best of kings, filled with indignation, fighting without retreat, bow in hand and clad in golden mail, rushed upon Sātyaki, the foremost of the Mādhavas, and stayed him.
Such an encounter arose between them, Bhārata, as had never been before; the warriors, both yours and the foes', all stood merely gazing at the two, splendid in battle.
Alambusa, that best of kings, with main force pierced him with ten shafts; but the Bull of the Śinis cut down those shafts with his own arrows even before they reached him.
Again, with three keen, well-feathered arrows like fire, drawn to the ear, he pierced him; rending his armor, they sank into Sātyaki's body.
Tearing his body with those blazing arrows, swift as fire and wind, with yet others Sātyaki forcibly struck down his four horses, bright as silver, with four shafts.
Thus struck by him, the swift grandson of Śini, in might like the Wielder of the discus, slew Alambusa's horses with four arrows of surpassing speed.
Then, with a broad-headed shaft like the fire of doom, he struck off the head of his charioteer, and severed from the trunk that radiant face, earringed and bright as the full moon.
Having slain in battle that son and grandson of a king, the crushing Bull of the Madhus then, O king, the hero turned back your troops and followed after Arjuna alone.
Seeing that best of the Vṛṣṇis come on, wheeling thus amid the foe and smiting the Kuru forces with his arrows, again and again, as the wind scatters masses of cloud —
his Sindhu-bred steeds, well broken, bright as cow's milk, jasmine, the moon, and snow, decked with nets of gold, those noble horses bore him wherever the lion among men desired.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then your sons together, and other warriors of yours, rushed upon him in haste, O scion of Ajamīḍha, putting at their head, O Bhārata, your son Duḥśāsana, foremost of fighters.
Hemming in the son of Śini on every side in the battle, those who could withstand whole armies smote him; but that hero, the foremost of the Sātvatas, held them off with a net of arrows.
Swiftly driving them off with feathered shafts like fire, the slayer of foes, the grandson of Śini, raising his bow, struck down even the horses of Duḥśāsana, O scion of Ajamīḍha.
Saṃjaya said: As the mighty-armed one rose up against the chariot of Duḥśāsana, swift in the hour that called for swiftness and seeking Dhanaṃjaya's welfare —
the great archers of the Trigartas, with banners wrought of gold, surrounded the Ānarta hero who had plunged into the ocean of their host.
Then, hemming him in on all sides with their array of chariots, those wrathful, peerless bowmen overwhelmed him with showers of arrows.
Sātyaki, whose valour was unfailing, alone vanquished those princes who strove against him in the great battle—fifty foes laid low by his single hand.
He had reached the midst of the Bhārata host, loud with the clapping of palms, thronged with swords and spears and maces, like waters that offer no raft for crossing.
There in the fray we beheld the wondrous course of Śaineya: glimpsing him in the western quarter, by his swiftness we saw him next in the east.
North, south, east, and west he ranged, the hero moving as though he danced, as if he were a hundred chariots at once.
Beholding the feats of him who moved with the stride of a lion's prowess, the Trigartas turned back, anguished for their own kinsmen.
Then other warriors among the Śūrasenas checked him in the battle, restraining him with showers of arrows as goads restrain a maddened elephant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sātyaki, of inconceivable strength and valour, held those straining warriors off but a moment, and then did battle with the Kaliṅgas.
Having passed beyond that host of the Kaliṅgas, hard to traverse, the mighty-armed one drew near to Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya.
As a swimmer wearied in the water gains the shore at last, so Yuyudhāna, seeing that tiger among men, took heart again.
Beholding him approach, Keśava said to Arjuna: "Yonder comes Śaineya, O Pārtha, your follower in the field."
"This is your disciple and your friend, whose prowess never fails; counting all those warriors as so much straw, that bull among men has conquered them."
"Having wrought dread havoc among the Kaurava warriors, Sātyaki—dearer to you than your own breath, O Kirīṭin—now draws near."
"Having brought low Droṇa, the Bhoja, and Kṛtavarman with his arrows, Sātyaki comes toward Phalguna."
"Seeking the welfare of the Dharma-king, having slain warrior after chosen warrior—a hero and a master of arms—Sātyaki comes toward Phalguna."
"Having done a deed most hard to do in the midst of the host, the mighty one, longing to see you, comes toward the Pāṇḍava—Sātyaki draws near."
"Having fought with a single chariot against many great car-warriors, foremost the Preceptor among them, this Sātyaki, O Pārtha, comes onward."
"Relying on the strength of his own arms, having torn through the army, sent forth by the son of Dharma, this Sātyaki comes toward you, O Pārtha."
"He to whom no warrior among the Kauravas is in any wise an equal—he, O Kaunteya, comes onward: Sātyaki of unfailing valour."
"Loosed from the Kuru host like a lion from the midst of a herd of cattle, having slain whole armies, this Sātyaki comes toward you, O Pārtha."
"Having strewn the earth with the lotus-like faces of thousands of kings, O Pārtha, Sātyaki comes swiftly on."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Having conquered Duryodhana together with his brothers in the battle, and slain Jalasaṃdha, Sātyaki comes swiftly on."
"Having made a river that runs in floods of blood, miry with gore, and cast down the Kauravas like so much grass, Sātyaki comes onward."
Then the son of Kuntī, far from glad, spoke these words to Keśava: "It pleases me not, O mighty-armed one, that Sātyaki comes toward me."
"For I do not know the tidings of the Dharma-king, O Keśava—whether, bereft of the Sātvata, he yet lives or no."
"By him, O mighty-armed one, that king ought to have been guarded; how then, O Kṛṣṇa, has this my follower forsaken him?"
"The king is left exposed to Droṇa, the Saindhava is not yet struck down, and this Bhūriśravas advances against Śaineya in the field."
"Now this is a burden heavier than the Saindhava laid upon me: I must learn how the king fares, and I must protect Sātyaki."
"And Jayadratha must be slain, and the sun is sinking low; and this mighty-armed one is now wearied and short of breath."
"Spent are his horses, O Mādhava, and his driver too; but Bhūriśravas is not weary, and he has comrades at his side, O Keśava."
"Might it now go well with him in this encounter? May Sātyaki of unfailing valour, that bull of Śini's line of mighty energy, not founder in a cow's hoofprint after crossing the very ocean!"
"May Sātyaki come through unharmed in his meeting with Bhūriśravas, that foremost of the Kauravas, a master of arms and a great soul."
"I count this a transgression on the part of the Dharma-king, O Keśava, who, casting aside his fear of the Preceptor, sends Sātyaki forth."
"Droṇa forever yearns to seize the Dharma-king, as a hawk on the wing yearns for its prey. Is the king, I wonder, yet safe?"
Saṃjaya said: Beholding that Sātvata, frenzied for battle, rushing on, Bhūriśravas, O king, in his wrath charged against him at once.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The mighty-armed Kaurava spoke to that bull of Śini's line: "By good fortune you have come this day within the range of my sight!"
"The desire long cherished I shall fulfil this day in combat; you shall not escape me alive unless you abandon the fight."
"Slaying you this day in battle—you who ever account yourself a hero, O Dāśārha—I shall gladden Suyodhana, king of the Kurus."
"This day, scorched by my shafts and fallen to the earth, you shall the two heroes Keśava and Arjuna behold together in the field."
"This day the king, the son of Dharma, by whom you were sent into this fray, hearing that you have been slain by me, shall at once be filled with shame."
"This day shall Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya know my prowess, when you lie struck down upon the earth, drenched in blood."
"This meeting with you, long desired, is come to me this day, as of old in the war of gods and demons the encounter of Śakra with Bali."
"This day I shall give you most dreadful battle, O Sātvata; then shall you know in truth my valour, my strength, and my manhood."
"This day, slain by me in battle, you shall fare to the city of Yama, as in the fray Rāvaṇa's son was slain by Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāma."
"This day, O Mādhava, when you are slain, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha and the Dharma-king, robbed of all heart, shall doubtless abandon the battle."
"This day, O Mādhava, having taken vengeance upon you with whetted shafts, I shall gladden the women of those whom you slew in the field."
"Come within the range of my sight, O Mādhava, you shall not escape, even as a little deer that has come within a lion's reach."
But Yuyudhāna, O king, answered him as though laughing: "O scion of Kuru, no terror dwells in me amid combat."
"He alone could slay me in battle who first could leave me weaponless; and he who would slay me in combat must strive through unending years to do it."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"What use this much idle talk? Set to the deed itself! Your thunder is as barren as that of an autumn cloud."
"Hearing this thundering of yours, O hero, laughter rises in me. Let the battle long desired in this world be ours this day, O Kaurava!"
"My mind hastens eagerly, sir, now that you long for battle. I shall not turn back this day, O basest of men, until I have slain you."
Then those two bulls among men, gashing one another with words, athirst to kill and wrought to utmost fury, fell upon each other in the fray.
Those two tigers among men, fierce and rivalrous, met in the battle like two enraged elephants frenzied with rut, contending for a she-elephant.
Bhūriśravas and Sātyaki, those tamers of foes, rained dreadful showers of arrows upon each other like two storm-clouds.
The son of Somadatta, O best of the Bhāratas, veiling Śaineya with swift-flying shafts and athirst to slay him, pierced him with whetted arrows.
Having pierced Sātyaki with ten shafts, the son of Somadatta then let fly yet more keen arrows, eager to slay that bull of Śini's line.
Those sharp arrows of his, O lord of peoples, Sātyaki devoured in mid-air by the magic of his weapons, O mighty one, before ever they reached him.
Each of those two heroes of noblest birth, who brought glory upon the Kuru and the Vṛṣṇi lines, rained showers of arrows upon the other.
As two tigers with their claws, as two great elephants with their tusks, so did they rend each other with chariot-spears and with arrows.
Piercing each other's limbs and pouring forth their blood, they held one another at bay, gamblers staking life itself in the play.
Thus those two of supreme deeds, who brought glory upon the Kuru and the Vṛṣṇi lines, fought one against the other like two leaders of elephant herds.
In no long time, with the world of Brahmā set before them, each striving to win the supreme abode, they smote upon one another.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sātyaki and the son of Somadatta rained shafts upon each other as though in joy, while the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked on.
The hosts gazed there upon those two lords of warriors as they fought, like two herd-bull elephants battling for the sake of a she-elephant.
Having slain each other's horses and cut apart each other's bows, the two, bereft of their chariots, closed for sword-combat in that great battle.
Taking up their broad and gleaming shields of bull's hide, bright with figures, and drawing their swords from the scabbard, the two ranged about the field.
Moving along varied tracks and through their circling figures one by one, those crushers of foes in their wrath struck again and again at each other.
Swords in hand, in figured mail, adorned with golden necklets and armlets, those two who exulted in war, O king, dragged each other to and fro in the battle.
For a while, O lord of kings, having hauled each other about before the gaze of all the hosts, the two heroes drew breath again.
Having hewn apart with their swords the bright broad shields that warded off the shafts, those two tigers among men set themselves to wrestling with bare arms.
Broad-chested and long-armed, both skilled in the wrestler's art, they grappled with their arms as though with bars of iron.
Their blows of arm, their grips and counter-grips, sprung from skill and strength, were a delight to all the warriors there.
As those two best of men contended in the field, O king, there arose a fearful, mighty din, as of mountains of adamant.
Like two elephants with the points of their tusks, like two great bulls with their horns, those high-souled bulls of the Kuru and Sātvata lines did battle.
As the Sātvata fought on, his weapons now spent, Vāsudeva spoke then to Arjuna: "Behold him fighting without his chariot in the fray—the banner of all who bear the bow!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"He entered the Bhārata host at your back, O Pāṇḍava, and was set upon by all the Bhāratas of mighty valour, O scion of Bharata."
"Worn out, that best of warriors has come upon Bhūriśravas, who advances athirst for battle. This is no even match, O Arjuna."
Then Bhūriśravas in his wrath, O king, lifting up Sātyaki, who was frenzied for the fight, dashed him down as a maddened elephant dashes down another in rut.
Even as those two foremost of warriors, Keśava and Arjuna, stationed wrathful upon their chariot, looked on at the battle, O king—
—then mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa spoke again to Arjuna: "See, that tiger of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas has fallen into the power of Somadatta's son!"
"Worn out and brought to the ground, after performing a deed most hard to do, is your own pupil, the brave Sātyaki. Protect him, Arjuna!"
"Let him not fall into the power of this lover of sacrifices, O best slayer of foes. For your own sake, O tiger among men, let it be done at once, O mighty one!"
Then Dhanaṃjaya, his mind exultant, said to Vāsudeva: "Look at that bull of the Kurus sporting with the foremost hero of the Vṛṣṇis—as a furious great elephant in the forest sports with the leader of a lion-pride."
