A great cry of dismay went up from the armies, O bull of the Bhāratas, when the mighty-armed one, lifting Sātyaki up, struck him down to the ground.
Dragging the foremost of the Sātvatas like a lion hauling an elephant, the best of the Kurus, lavish in his sacrificial gifts, shone resplendent in the battle.
Then, drawing his sword from its sheath in the fray, Bhūriśravas seized Sātyaki by the hair and struck him on the chest with his foot.
Seeing the Sātvata thus being dragged about in the battle, O king, Vāsudeva spoke once more to Arjuna:
"Behold this tiger of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas fallen into the power of Somadatta's son—your own pupil, O mighty-armed one, second to none but you in archery!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Untrue is the show of valor, O Pārtha, when in this battle Bhūriśravas gets the better of Sātyaki of the Vṛṣṇis, whose own prowess is true."
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, the mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu honored Bhūriśravas in his heart for his conduct in the battle:
"Dragging the foremost of the Sātvatas about, as if in sport in the battle, this enhancer of the Kurus' glory delights me all the more."
"For he does not slay Sātyaki, the foremost of the Vṛṣṇi heroes; like a lion dragging a great elephant in the forest, so does he haul him about."
Thus having honored the Kaurava in his heart, O king, the mighty-armed Pārtha, Arjuna, replied to Vāsudeva:
"Since my gaze is fixed upon the lord of the Sindhus, I do not see him clearly, O Mādhava. Yet this hard deed I will do, for the Yādava's sake."
So saying, and carrying out the word of Vāsudeva, the son of Pāṇḍu with a feathered shaft severed the sword-wielding arm of that lover of sacrifices.
Saṃjaya said: That noble arm, still gripping the sword and bright with its fair armlet, fell to the ground, bringing the keenest grief to the world of the living.
That arm, raised to strike but cut off by the unseen Kirīṭin, fell swiftly to the earth like a five-headed serpent.
Seeing himself thus thwarted by Pārtha, the Kaurava released Sātyaki and in his wrath rebuked the son of Pāṇḍu:
"A cruel deed, alas, O son of Kuntī, you have done, in that you cut off my arm while I was looking elsewhere, my mind engaged with another."
"What will you say to King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma? 'Bhūriśravas was slain by me in battle while doing what?'"
"Was this the weapon taught you in person by great-souled Indra, O Pārtha, or by Rudra, or by Droṇa, or by Kṛpa?"
"Are you not indeed known throughout the world as one who knows his own duty, surpassing others? How then have you struck in battle a man not fighting against you?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Men of wisdom do not strike one who is heedless, one who is afraid, one whose chariot is gone, one who begs for mercy, or one caught in distress."
"This base conduct, practiced only by ignoble men—how have you, O Pārtha, performed so unworthy a deed?"
"For they say a noble deed is easy for a noble man, O Dhanaṃjaya; but an ignoble deed done by a noble man is the hardest thing on earth."
"In whatever company a man moves, O Pārtha, and in whatever circumstances he lives, he soon takes on its character—and this is seen now in you."
"How is it that you, born of a royal line, and a Kaurava above all, of fair conduct and faithful to your vows, have strayed from the duty of a warrior?"
"This utterly mean act, done by you for the Vṛṣṇi's sake, was surely the counsel of Vāsudeva—it does not befit you."
"For who that was not the friend of Kṛṣṇa would inflict such a calamity upon a man engaged in fighting with another?"
"The Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas are outcastes given to vile dealings, despised by their very nature—how, O Pārtha, have you made them your standard?"
Having said this, the mighty-armed and far-famed hero of the sacrificial-post banner abandoned Yuyudhāna and sat down upon the battlefield to fast unto death.
Spreading out arrows with his left hand, that man of holy marks, desiring to go to the world of Brahmā, then offered his life-breaths as an oblation into the breaths themselves.
Fixing his eyes upon the sun and his serene mind upon the waters, meditating on the great mystic doctrine and joined in yoga, he became a sage.
Then throughout all the host the men reproached Kṛṣṇa and Dhanaṃjaya, and they praised that bull among men.
Though thus reviled, the two Kṛṣṇas said nothing unkind in reply; and though thus praised, the bearer of the sacrificial-post banner felt no elation.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O king, Dhanaṃjaya, unable in his heart to bear those words of your sons and of Bhūriśravas as they spoke,
yet with a mind free of anger, as if reminding them, O Bhārata, the son of Pāṇḍu, Phalguna, spoke, almost with a tone of reproach:
"All the kings know this great vow of mine: that none of my own people may be slain by another, if he comes within the range of my arrows."
"O bearer of the sacrificial-post banner, reflect, and you ought not to censure me; for it is not right to blame another without first understanding the law."
"That in battle I cut off the arm of you who, weapon in hand, were bent on slaying the Vṛṣṇi hero—that is no conduct to be condemned."
"As for the slaying of Abhimanyu—a mere boy, his weapons laid down, his chariot lost, his armor gone—what righteous man, dear sir, would commend it?"
Thus addressed by Pārtha, Bhūriśravas touched the ground with his head, and with his left hand he flung aside his own severed right arm.
Having heard these words of Pārtha, the splendid bearer of the sacrificial-post banner, O great king, fell silent, his face bowed down.
Arjuna said: "The love I bear to the King of Righteousness, and to Bhīma, best of speakers, and to Nakula and Sahadeva—that same love I bear to you, O elder brother of Śala."
"With my leave, and that of great-souled Kṛṣṇa, go now to the worlds of those who have done holy deeds, even as Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, once did."
Saṃjaya said: Then the grandson of Śini, released by Somadatta's son, rose up and, taking up his sword, sought to cut off the head of that great-souled one.
Sātyaki sought to slay that sinless elder brother of Śala—the lavish giver of sacrificial gifts—who, while heedless, had already been struck down by the son of Pāṇḍu.
As all the troops cried out, Sātyaki, reviled by them and sick at heart, advanced upon him as he sat with his arm hewn off, like an elephant whose trunk has been severed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Though restrained by Kṛṣṇa, by great-souled Pārtha, by Bhīma, by the two wheel-guards, by Aśvatthāman and by Kṛpa,
and by Karṇa, by Vṛṣasena and by the lord of the Sindhus as well, and amid the outcry of all the troops, he slew that man of disciplined vows.
As that Kaurava lord, his arm cut off by Pārtha, sat fasting unto death on the battlefield, Sātyaki struck off his head with his sword.
The troops did not applaud Sātyaki for that deed—that he had slain this glory of the Kurus who had already been struck down before by Arjuna.
There the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and men alike, beholding Bhūriśravas—the equal of the thousand-eyed Indra—slain in battle as he sat fasting,
the gods honored him, amazed at his deeds; and his own soldiers spoke many words taking his part.
"It is no fault of the Vṛṣṇi, for what was destined had to be so. Therefore you should bear him no grudge—wrath only brings grief to men."
"This hero was fated to be slain, and on that there should be no debate; for the Ordainer himself had appointed Sātyaki to be his death in battle."
Sātyaki said: "You who tell me, 'He must not be slain, he must not be slain,' with your talk of righteousness—most unrighteous men, you have wrapped yourselves in a mere cloak of righteousness!"
"When the boy, Subhadrā's son, stripped of his weapons, was slain by you in battle—where then had your righteousness gone?"
"This vow I once made, upon some taunt or other: that whoever should crush me in battle and, while I yet lived, strike me with his foot in fury—that enemy should be slain by me, even were he bound by the vows of a sage."
"You, who have eyes, deem me dead though I was struggling to strike back and still had my arm—such is the shallowness of your judgment! The retaliation I have wrought upon him was fitting, O bulls of the Kurus."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That Pārtha, out of love for me and to keep his own vow, cut off this man's sword-bearing arm—by that very act I have been cheated of my due."
"What is to be must be, and fate, as it were, drives men to act. He has been slain in this fray—what unrighteous deed is there in that?"
"And moreover this verse was sung of old by Vālmīki upon the earth: 'Whatever brings harm to one's enemies, that very thing must be done.'"
Saṃjaya said: When this had been spoken, O great king, all the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas said nothing, but honored Bhūriśravas in their hearts.
For of him—purified by sacred chants at his great rites, glorious, the giver of countless thousands, now like a sage gone to the forest—of his slaying not one there approved.
The head of that bounteous, brave one, dark-blue-haired and dove-red of eye, lay severed like the head of a sacrificial horse set down to the north of the oblation-cart.
Purified by that splendor smitten down by the sword, he cast off his noble body in the great battle, and that bounteous one, worthy of the highest boons, rose upward, filling heaven and earth with his surpassing righteousness.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Unconquered by Droṇa, by Rādheya, by Vikarṇa and Kṛtavarman, that hero, having pledged himself to Yudhiṣṭhira, had crossed the ocean of the army.
How was it that he, unchecked in battle, came to be seized by the Kaurava Bhūriśravas and hurled by force to the ground?
Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, the origin of the grandson of Śini in days of old, and that of Bhūriśravas as well, wherein lies your doubt, O lord of men.
From Atri was born Soma; of Soma, Budha is recorded; and Budha had one son, Purūravas, splendid as the great Indra.
Of Purūravas came Āyus; of Āyus, Nahuṣa is recorded; and of Nahuṣa, Yayāti, a royal sage held equal to the gods.
Of Yayāti by Devayānī, Yadu was born, the eldest son; and in the lineage of Yadu there arose one famed as Devamīḍha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His son was the Yādava Śūra, honored throughout the three worlds; and of Śūra came his son, the foremost of men, the far-famed Vāsudeva.
Unsurpassed in archery, a brave man equal to Kārtavīrya in battle—and of like prowess, in that very line, was born King Śini.
Now at that very time, O king, at the self-choice ceremony of the daughter of great-souled Devaka, where all the warrior caste had assembled,
there indeed Śini, vanquishing all the kings, won the lady Devakī for Vāsudeva's sake and set her upon his chariot.
Seeing that Devakī standing on Śini's chariot, O king, the bull among men, the mighty Somadatta, could not endure it.
A combat arose between the two, O king, wondrous and astonishing, lasting half a day—a wrestling match of two mighty men, like that of Śakra and Prahrāda.
By Śini, Somadatta was overpowered and flung to the ground; and seizing him by the hair and raising his sword, Śini struck him with his foot.
In the midst of thousands of kings looking on from every side, out of pity he was released by him with the words, "Live!"
Reduced to that condition by him, Somadatta then, O honored one, gave himself up to indignation and set about propitiating Mahādeva.
Pleased with him, Mahādeva, the Lord, granter of boons among boons, offered him a choice; and that king chose his boon.
"I desire a son, O Blessed One, who shall slay the son of Śini, and in the midst of thousands of kings shall strike him down with his foot in battle."
Hearing those words of Somadatta, O king, the god said, "So be it," and there vanished.
By that granting of the boon he obtained Bhūriśravas of abundant sacrificial gifts; and in battle the son of Somadatta did indeed lay low the son of Śini.
This have I told you, O king, concerning that whereof you ask me; the Sātvatas cannot be conquered in battle, O bull among men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Many among them are sure of their aim in combat and fight with wondrous skill; unbewildered, they are conquerors of gods, dānavas, and gandharvas; bent upon victory won by their own valor, they are not subject to any other's possession.
Nothing equal to the Vṛṣṇis is seen here, O lord—nothing that has been, that is, or that shall be, in strength, O bull of the Bhāratas.
They never slight a kinsman, and delight in the rule of their elders; neither gods, asuras, nor gandharvas, neither yakṣas, serpents, nor rākṣasas can vanquish the Vṛṣṇi heroes in war—still less men.
Toward the wealth of brahmins, of teachers, and of kinsmen they do no harm; and they are protectors of these, should any one of them fall into distress.
Wealthy yet not arrogant, devoted to brahmins, speakers of truth, they do not slight the powerful, and they raise up the wretched.
Ever devoted to the gods, self-controlled, generous, and free from boasting—therefore the wheel of the Vṛṣṇi heroes' dominion is never broken.
One might bear Mount Meru, or swim across the abode of sea-monsters, but he could not, having met the Vṛṣṇi heroes, come to their end, O king.
All this have I declared to you, wherein your doubt lay, O mighty one; O king of the Kurus, best of men, great indeed is your misconduct.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that Kaurava Bhūriśravas had been slain in such a plight, tell me, Saṃjaya, how the battle raged on once more.
Saṃjaya said: When Bhūriśravas had passed on to the other world, O Bhārata, the mighty-armed Arjuna urged Vāsudeva onward.
"Drive the horses hard, Kṛṣṇa, to where King Jayadratha is; the maker of day hastens, O mighty-armed one, to its setting."
"For this great deed I have undertaken, O tiger among men; and this man is being guarded by the great chariot-warriors of the Kuru host."
"So drive the horses, Kṛṣṇa, that the sun shall not set, that my word may prove true, that I may slay Jayadratha."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, knower of horses, urged the silver-hued steeds onward toward the chariot of Jayadratha.
As he sped on, his shafts never failing, with arrows that flew as if leaping upward, the chief warriors of the host hastened to close round him, O great king.
Duryodhana and Karṇa and Vṛṣasena, the king of the Madras, Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa, and the lord of the Sindhus himself.
Drawing near, Bībhatsu beheld the lord of the Sindhus stationed at the front, and gazed upon him with eyes blazing with wrath, as if to burn him up.
Then King Duryodhana, seeing Arjuna advancing toward Jayadratha's chariot, swiftly said to the son of Rādhā:
"This, O Vaikartana, is the hour of battle; show forth your own strength, great soul. So act, Karṇa, that Jayadratha be not slain by Arjuna in the fight."
"Little of the day remains, O hero among men; strike down the foe now with floods of arrows. Once the day's end is reached, O foremost of men, our victory, Karṇa, shall surely be assured."
"If the lord of the Sindhus be but guarded until the setting of the sun, the son of Kuntī, his vow proved false, shall enter the fire."
"And on an earth bereft of Arjuna, O giver of honor, his brothers with their followers would not bear to live even for a moment."
"And with the sons of Pāṇḍu destroyed, we shall enjoy this earth, Karṇa, with its mountains, woods, and forests, its thorns plucked out."
"Smitten by fate and turned awry, O giver of honor, Pārtha, not knowing the doable from the undoable, made his vow in battle."
"Surely it was for his own destruction that the diademed son of Pāṇḍu made this vow, Karṇa, touching the slaying of Jayadratha."
"How, while you live, O unassailable son of Rādhā, shall Phalguna slay the Saindhava king before the sun has set?"
"Jayadratha, guarded at the battle's front by the king of the Madras and by the great-souled Kṛpa—how shall Dhanaṃjaya slay him?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And how, urged on by fate, shall Bībhatsu reach the lord of the Sindhus, who is guarded by Droṇa's son, by me, and by Duḥśāsana?"
"Many heroes are fighting, and the sun hangs low; I think, O giver of honor, that Pārtha shall not reach Jayadratha at all."
"Therefore, Karṇa, do you, together with me and with the other heroic great car-warriors, putting forth supreme effort, fight against Pārtha in the combat."
Thus addressed by your son, O honored one, the son of Rādhā spoke these words in answer to Duryodhana, the foremost of the Kurus:
"Sorely harassed in the fray, time and again, by the bowman Bhīmasena—that hero of unerring aim—with his nets of arrows,
"yet, resolved that I must stand, I stand even now in the battle, O giver of honor; though scorched by the shafts of war, no limb of mine so much as stirs."
"I shall fight, O king, in battle with all my utmost might, so that that chief of the Pāṇḍavas shall not slay the lord of the Sindhus."
"For while I fight and loose my whetted shafts, the hero Savyasācin Dhanaṃjaya shall not reach the lord of the Sindhus."
"Whatever ought to be done by one of power, who ever works for your good, that I shall do, O Kaurava; but victory rests with fate."
"Today I shall fight Arjuna, relying on my own manhood, for your sake, O tiger among men; but victory rests with fate."
"Today, O best of the Kurus, let all beings behold the dreadful, hair-raising battle of us two, of mine and Pārtha's."
While Karṇa and the Kaurava thus conversed in the field, Arjuna with his whetted shafts smote your host.
With keen-pointed arrows he severed in battle the arms of the unflinching heroes—arms like iron bars, like the trunks of elephants.
And the mighty-armed one clove with whetted shafts their heads, the trunks of elephants, the necks of horses, and the axles of chariots on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With razor-edged shafts Bībhatsu cleft, each into two and into three, the blood-drenched horsemen who gripped their lances and pikes.
And the foremost of horses and elephants fell by thousands, with banners, parasols, bows, yak-tail fans, and heads.
Burning your host like a fire blazing up through dry brushwood, in but a little while Pārtha made the earth flooded over with blood.
Having made the greater part of your army's warriors slain, the mighty, unassailable hero of true valor bore down upon the lord of the Sindhus.
Bībhatsu, guarded by Bhīmasena and by the Sātvata, shone forth, O best of the Bhāratas, like a blazing fire.
Beholding Phalguna so stationed, your great bowmen, esteemed for their valor, bulls among men, could not endure it.
Duryodhana and Karṇa and Vṛṣasena, the king of the Madras, Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa, and the lord of the Sindhus himself—
these, enraged, for the Saindhava's sake hemmed in the diademed one, who danced along the chariot-paths to the twang of his bowstring and the slap of his palm-guard.
All skilled in war, fearless, they closed round Pārtha, the master of combat, as round Death with gaping jaws.
Keeping the lord of the Sindhus behind them, seeking to slay Arjuna and Acyuta, they longed for the sun's setting as the day-maker turned red.
With arms like the coils of serpents they drew their bows and loosed by hundreds at Phalguna shafts that gleamed like the rays of the sun.
But the diademed one, frenzied in battle, cleaving each of those loosed and flying shafts into two, three, and eight, pierced his foes in turn in the fray.
Then the son of Śāradvatī, whose banner bore the lion's tail, showing forth his own might, O king, withstood Arjuna.
Having pierced Pārtha with ten shafts and Vāsudeva with seven, he held his ground upon the chariot-paths, guarding the lord of the Sindhus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all the foremost of the Kuru great car-warriors hemmed him in on every side with a vast array of chariots.
Twanging their bows and loosing their shafts, they guarded the lord of the Sindhus round about, by the command of your son.
There was seen the strength of the heroic Pārtha's arms, the inexhaustibility of his arrows, and the might of his bow Gāṇḍīva.
Warding off with his weapons the weapons of Droṇa's son and of the son of Śaradvat, he assailed every one of them, each with nine shafts.
Him Droṇa's son struck with twenty-five shafts, and Vṛṣasena with seven, Duryodhana with twenty, and Karṇa and Śalya each with three.
Roaring at him and piercing him again and again, and shaking their bows, they hemmed him in on every side.
Those great car-warriors, longing for the sun's setting, swiftly drew their ring of chariots close-locked on every side.
Bellowing at him and shaking their bows, they drenched him with dreadful shafts as the clouds drench a mountain with their waters.
There, O king, those heroes with arms like iron bars displayed their mighty celestial weapons upon the limbs of Dhanaṃjaya.
Having made the greater part of your army's warriors slain, the mighty, unassailable hero of true valor bore down upon the lord of the Sindhus.
Him Karṇa withstood in the combat, O king, with his swift arrows, before the very eyes of Bhīmasena and of the Sātvata, O Bhārata.
Him in turn the mighty-armed Pārtha pierced with ten shafts on the field of battle—the son of the charioteer—while all the host looked on.
And the Sātvata pierced Karṇa with three shafts, O honored one, and Bhīmasena with three, and Pārtha again with seven.
Karṇa, the great car-warrior, pierced them each in return with sixty shafts; and so, O king, there arose that battle of Karṇa against many.
There we beheld a marvel in the son of the charioteer, O honored one—that, wrathful and alone in the fray, he held three chariot-warriors at bay.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the mighty-armed Phalguna struck Karṇa Vaikartana in the battle, with a full hundred shafts, upon all his vital parts.
His every limb bathed in blood, the valorous son of the charioteer, that hero, pierced Phalguna in return with fifty shafts; and seeing his deftness, Arjuna could not endure it in the fight.
Then Pārtha, severing his bow, pierced him between the breasts; the hero Dhanaṃjaya did so in haste, with nine shafts.
And to slay him in battle Dhanaṃjaya, swift in the hour that called for swiftness, hurled an arrow blazing like the sun.
But Droṇa's son, with a sharp crescent-headed shaft, cleft that arrow as it rushed upon him with speed, and so severed it fell to the earth.
Then the mighty son of the charioteer, Karṇa, the slayer of foes, took up another bow and, eager to repay blow with blow, covered Phalguna with arrows by the many thousands.
Those two great car-warriors, lions among men, bellowing like bulls, with their straight-flying shafts made the sky one mass of arrow-streams; veiled from sight by the floods of arrows, each struck at the other.
"I am Pārtha—stand and face me!" "I am Karṇa—stand, Phalguna!" Thus challenging each other, they pierced one another with the barbs of their words.
The two heroes fought in battle with skill, with swiftness, and with grace, and amid the gathering of all the warriors they were a sight worth beholding.
Praised in the fray by the throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, O great king, they fought on, each seeking the other's death.
Then, O king, Duryodhana addressed your men: "Guard Rādheya with all your effort! The bull-like Karṇa has told me, 'I shall not turn back from the battle until I have slain Arjuna.'"
Meanwhile, O king, seeing Karṇa's prowess, Arjuna with arrows drawn to the ear sent Karṇa's four steeds to the realm of death with four excellent shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With a broad-headed arrow he swept Karṇa's charioteer from the seat of the car, and covered him with shafts before the eyes of your son.
Overwhelmed in the fight, his horses slain and his driver slain, bewildered by the net of arrows, Karṇa could not tell what should be done.
Seeing him thus deprived of his car, O great king, Aśvatthāman took him up onto his own chariot, and once more did battle with Arjuna.
The king of the Madras pierced the son of Kuntī with thirty arrows, while Śāradvata struck Vāsudeva with twenty and smote Dhanaṃjaya with twelve bee-like shafts.
And the king of the Sindhus with four, and Vṛṣasena with seven, each in turn, O great king, pierced Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha.
In like manner Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, pierced them in return—the son of Droṇa with sixty-four shafts and the king of the Madras with a hundred.
Having pierced the lord of the Sindhus with ten broad-headed arrows, Vṛṣasena with three shafts, and Śāradvata with twenty, Pārtha gave a great roar.
Wishing to thwart the vow of Savyasācin, your warriors together rushed swiftly upon Dhanaṃjaya.
Then Arjuna brought forth the weapon that cuts on every side, terrifying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; yet the Kurus advanced against the son of Pāṇḍu and, upon their costly chariots, poured down showers of arrows.
Then, O Bhārata, when that terrible, bewildering tumult arose, the diademed prince, far from being dazed, loosed his arrows undismayed.
Seeking to win back the kingdom, Savyasācin, remembering the sufferings he had borne for twelve years at the hands of the Kurus, that great soul, with countless arrows loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, covered every quarter of the sky.
The firmament seemed ablaze with falling meteors, and birds in multitudes alighted upon the corpses, as the diademed hero in his wrath slew his foes with his tawny-stringed bow, the Ājagava.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The diademed one, of great renown, conqueror of armies, with his mighty bow struck down with his shafts the foremost Kuru heroes—those mounted on the choicest horses and at the head of the great elephants.
And the kings, dreadful to behold, seizing heavy maces, iron bludgeons, swords and spears and great weapons, all at once rushed upon Pārtha in the fray.
But that hero, the mighty bowman, made those onrushing foes—with their chariots, horses, and elephants, and their bands of footmen—bereft of all their weapons and of their lives, swelling the realm of Yama.
Saṃjaya said: Pārtha, the splendid Dhanaṃjaya, ranged across the battlefield, displaying in all directions at once his wondrous weapons, a sight worth beholding.
As none can gaze upon the sun blazing in the sky at noon, so could no creature look full upon the Pāṇḍava.
The flights of arrows streaming from the Gāṇḍīva of that great soul we beheld in the battle like rows of wild geese across the sky.
Having warded off on every side the weapons of those heroes with his own weapons, he revealed his terrible self, fixed firmly upon his fierce work.
Bewildering those foremost car-warriors, as it were, with his iron shafts, Arjuna pressed past them all, O king, in his longing to slay Jayadratha.
Loosing his arrows in every direction, his dark-hued charioteer beside him, the splendid Dhanaṃjaya ranged swiftly across the field, a sight worth beholding.
The flights of arrows of that great-souled hero, as though wheeling through the air, were seen poised aloft by the hundreds and the thousands.
The mighty bowman drawing forth his shafts, the Pāṇḍava fitting them to the string, and the son of Kuntī loosing them—of these we could discern nothing then.
Having thrown into confusion all the quarters and all the car-warriors in the fray, O king, the son of Kuntī bore down upon Jayadratha and pierced him with sixty-four smooth-jointed arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the lord of the Sindhus, thus pierced by the arrows of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, did not endure it, raging like an elephant goaded by the hook.
He of the boar-banner swiftly loosed in battle at Savyasācin keen shafts—vulture-feathered, straight-flying, like venomous serpents, burnished by the smith.
With three iron shafts he pierced the Gāṇḍīva, Arjuna with six, the horses with eight, and the banner with a single feathered arrow.
Arjuna, scattering the sharp shafts sent by the Saindhava, at one stroke with two arrows severed from the body the head of the Saindhava's charioteer and his ornamented banner.
Its staff cut through, that great boar of the Sindhu king's banner, shattered and struck by the arrow, fell like a tongue of flame.
At that very moment, as the sun was swiftly setting, Janārdana in haste spoke to the Pāṇḍava:
"Dhanaṃjaya, cut off the head of the wicked Saindhava! The day-maker is about to descend behind the foremost of mountains. Hear, too, my word concerning the slaying of Jayadratha."
"Vṛddhakṣatra, the father of the Saindhava, is renowned throughout the world. After a long age he obtained the Saindhava as his son."
"And to that king, the foe-slaying Jayadratha, a disembodied voice, deep as the thunder of clouds, then spoke:"
"'This son of yours, O lord, shall be among mortals worthy of both your lineages in his virtues—in family, in conduct, in self-restraint, and the rest—foremost of Kṣatriyas in the world, ever honored by the brave.'"
"'Yet as this bowman fights his enemies in battle, an angered foe, unmarked upon the earth, shall cut off his head.'"
"Hearing this, O tamer of foes, the Sindhu king pondered long, and, tormented by love for his son, said this to all his kinsmen:"
"'Whoever, while my son fights in battle bearing his mighty burden, shall cast his head upon the earth—that man's head too shall burst into a hundred pieces; of this there is no doubt.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Having spoken thus and set Jayadratha upon the throne, Vṛddhakṣatra went to the forest and gave himself to the practice of austerity."
"That radiant one, O you of the monkey-banner, is even now practicing terrible, hard-won austerity, just outside this field of Samantapañcaka."
"Therefore, O slayer of foes, when in this great battle you have cut off Jayadratha's head with a divine weapon of terrible and wondrous power—"
"—cast it, O younger brother of the Wind-god's son, still wearing its earrings, swiftly into the lap of Vṛddhakṣatra, O Bhārata, the head of the lord of the Sindhus."
"But if you let his head fall upon the ground, then your own head too shall burst into a hundred pieces; of this there is no doubt."
"And contrive it, O best of the Kurus, that this king, the lord of the earth, may not know of it—having recourse to the divine weapon."
"For there is nothing impossible or undoable for you in any of the three worlds entire, O delight of Vāsava."
Hearing these words, Arjuna, licking the corners of his mouth, took up an arrow whose touch was like Indra's thunderbolt, hallowed with divine spells—
—a shaft able to bear every burden, ever honored with perfumes and garlands; this Arjuna swiftly let fly, bent upon the slaying of the Saindhava.
That arrow, loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, swift as a hawk, bore off the head of the Saindhava as a hawk carries off a bird from the treetop.
And Dhanaṃjaya bore that head still higher with his arrows, to the dismay of his enemies and the joy of his friends.
Bearing it aloft on a cluster of arrows at that hour, the Pāṇḍava then carried that head beyond Samantapañcaka.
At that very moment, O revered one, the radiant king Vṛddhakṣatra, your kinsman by marriage, was performing his twilight worship.
As he sat at worship, Arjuna let fall into his lap the head of the Sindhu king, black-haired and still wearing its earrings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That head with its fair earrings fell into the lap of King Vṛddhakṣatra unnoticed, O tamer of foes.
Then, as the wise Vṛddhakṣatra, his muttered prayers completed, rose up, that head suddenly slipped to the surface of the earth.
And then, when his son's head had fallen to the ground from that king's lap, his own head too, O tamer of foes, burst into a hundred pieces.
Then all beings were struck with the utmost wonder, and Vāsudeva praised Bībhatsu, that mighty car-warrior.
Then, beholding Jayadratha, the king of the Sindhus, slain, much water fell in grief from the eyes of your sons.
Bhīmasena too, as though signaling to the Pāṇḍava in the fray, filled heaven and earth with a great lion's roar.
Hearing that mighty roar, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, judged that the Saindhava had been slain by the great-souled Phalguna.
Then, gladdening his own warriors with the clamor of instruments, he advanced into the battle against the son of Bharadvāja, eager to fight.
Then, O king, as the sun was setting, a hair-raising battle broke out between Droṇa and the Somakas.
Those great car-warriors, O king, seeking with all their might to slay the son of Bharadvāja now that the Saindhava was slain, fought on.
And the Pāṇḍavas, having won the victory and slain the Saindhava, then, frenzied with triumph, did battle with Droṇa on every side.
Arjuna too, O great king, having slain the king of the Sindhus, did battle in the fray with your warriors, those foremost of car-warriors.
Having fulfilled his earlier vow, the diademed hero scattered them on every side, as the king of the gods scatters the foes of the gods, and as the risen dispeller of darkness dispels the shadows.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that hero, the Saindhava, had been slain by Savyasācin, tell me, Saṃjaya, what my men then did.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Seeing the Saindhava slain in battle by Pārtha, O revered one, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, was then overcome with wrath.
With a great shower of arrows he covered the Pāṇḍava, and Droṇa's son too, mounting his chariot, charged upon Pārtha, upon Phalguna.
Those two foremost of car-warriors, from their two chariots, both on either side, rained sharp arrows upon him, the best of car-warriors.
Thus assailed by those two mighty showers of arrows, that strong-armed one, the best of car-warriors, fell into the deepest distress.
Unwilling to slay in battle his teacher's kinsman and the son of his teacher, Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, there displayed his mastery of the craft.
Warding off with his weapons the weapons of both Droṇa's son and the son of Śaradvat, he loosed at the two of them slow-flying arrows, having no wish to kill them.
Though the shafts, urged on toward victory, did not strike them too grievously, by their sheer multitude the two warriors were brought to the utmost anguish.
Then, O king, the son of Śaradvat, tormented by the arrows of Kuntī's son, sank down upon the floor of his chariot and fell into a swoon.
Perceiving his master reeling and stricken by arrows, and thinking him slain, the charioteer bore him away from the field.
When Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat, had collapsed in the battle, O great king, Aśvatthāman too withdrew from the Pāṇḍava to another part of the field.
Beholding the son of Śaradvat swooning, racked by arrows, the great archer Pārtha, there upon his chariot, lamented piteously.
Beholding this, the deeply wise Vidura had spoken to the king when wicked Suyodhana, destroyer of the lineage, was but newly born:
'Let this defiler of the line be sent rightly to the other world; for from him will arise a great terror for the chiefs of the Kurus.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That word of the truth-speaker has now come to pass, for on his account I see Kṛpa today laid out upon a bed of arrows.
Fie upon the warrior's code, fie upon strength and manly valor! For who like me would do violence to a brāhmaṇa, his own teacher?
My teacher, son of a seer, the beloved friend of Droṇa — here he lies upon his chariot, oppressed by my arrows.
Though I wished it not, sorely afflicted by my shafts he sank upon his chariot; it is as though he wrings the very life from me.
For I, myself worn by arrows yet observant of the tenfold duty, have driven back with many shafts this man of splendor, lovely to behold.
His falling grieves me more even than the slaying of a son. See, Kṛṣṇa, how piteously he has sunk, undone, upon his own chariot.
Those bulls among men who, having received learning from their teachers, render to them here the objects of their desire — they attain to godhood.
But those basest of men who, having taken learning from their elders, then slay those very ones — such evil-doers go to hell.
Surely, then, this deed I have done today leads to hell — bringing low my teacher Kṛpa upon his chariot with a rain of arrows.
For when of old he was imparting the weapon to me, Kṛpa told me: 'In no wise, O Kaurava, is a blow ever to be struck against one's teacher.'
That word of my good and great-souled teacher I have not heeded — raining shafts upon that very man in battle.
Homage to that most worthy Gautama, who never flees the fight! Fie upon me, O Vārṣṇeya, who strike a blow against him!
While Savyasācin was thus lamenting over him, the son of Rādhā, beholding the lord of the Sindhus slain, rushed forward.
Seeing the son of Rādhā advancing, the great chariot-warrior Pārtha, smiling, spoke this word to the son of Devakī:
'There goes the son of Adhiratha toward Sātyaki's chariot; surely he cannot bear that Bhūriśravas was slain in the fray.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Wherever he goes, drive the horses thither, Janārdana, lest that bull Karṇa send Sātyaki down the road that Somadatta's son has trodden.'
Thus addressed by Savyasācin, the mighty-armed Keśava of great splendor replied with this word, fitting to the hour:
'Alone, O Pāṇḍava, this mighty-armed bull of the Sātvatas is a match enough for Karṇa — how much more so when joined by the two sons of Draupadī!'
'And the time is not yet fit, Pārtha, for your clash with Karṇa; for Indra's weapon stands by him, blazing like a great meteor, kept and honored, O slayer of foes, that he may loose it upon you.'
'Therefore let Karṇa go yonder against the Sātvata, come what may; I shall know, O Kaurava, the appointed hour of that evil-souled one.'
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: That encounter of the Vārṣṇeya with the hero Karṇa, after Bhūriśravas was slain and the lord of the Sindhus brought down —
And Sātyaki, his car undone, what chariot did he mount? And who were the two Pāñcāla guards of his wheels? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Come then, I shall describe to you all that befell in the great battle; listen calmly, and hear of your own misconduct.
For long before, O lord, this was in Kṛṣṇa's mind: that the hero Sātyaki was to be vanquished by Karṇa, whose banner bears the sacrificial post.
For Janārdana, O king, knows past and future; therefore, summoning his charioteer Dāruka, that mighty one gave command: 'Let my chariot be yoked betimes.'
For neither gods nor gandharvas, nor yakṣas, serpents, or rākṣasas, nor any men whatsoever, are there to vanquish the two Kṛṣṇas.
The gods, with the Grandsire at their head, and the siddhas, know this. Hear now of the matchless might of those two, and how that battle went.
Seeing Sātyaki bereft of his car and Karṇa with weapon upraised, Mādhava blew a mighty blast upon his ox-strong conch.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dāruka, knowing the command and hearing the conch's note, brought up for him the chariot whose ensign of Garuḍa was raised on high.
With Keśava's leave, the grandson of Śini mounted that chariot driven by Dāruka, radiant as fire and the sun.
It was drawn by the steeds Sainya, Sugrīva, Meghapuṣpa, and Balāhaka — coursers that go where they will, towering, of great speed, adorned with trappings of gold.
Mounting that well-yoked chariot, like a celestial car, he rushed upon the son of Rādhā, sowing many arrows as he came.
Then too the two wheel-guards, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, leaving Dhanaṃjaya's chariot, advanced against the son of Rādhā.
The son of Rādhā too, O great king, loosing a downpour of arrows, in high fury charged the steadfast grandson of Śini in the fight.
No such battle, of gods or gandharvas, of asuras, serpents, or rākṣasas, was ever heard of, whether on earth or in heaven.
That host, with its chariots, horses, men, and elephants, stood still, O great king, its senses bewildered at beholding the feats of those two.
And all gazed upon that superhuman combat of those two foremost of men, O king, and upon the charioteering of Dāruka.
They marveled at the son of Kaśyapa as he stood at his post, with his goings forth and returnings, his wheelings and his turnings about.
And the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas in the vault of heaven were most intent to behold the battle of Karṇa and the grandson of Śini.
For their friends' sake the two strove on, rivals fierce and mettlesome in the fray — Karṇa, like an immortal, and Yuyudhāna, the son of Sātyaka.
Each upon the other, O great king, they rained their showers of arrows; and Karṇa battered the grandson of Śini with floods of shafts.
Unable to brook the slaying of the Kaurava and of Jalasaṃdha, Karṇa, filled with grief, hissed like a great serpent.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That tamer of foes, enraged, as if consuming the grandson of Śini with his very gaze, charged him again and again with vehemence in the fray.
But beholding him in his wrath, Sātyaki pierced him back with a mighty downpour of arrows, as one elephant withstands another.
Those two tigers among men, closing like swift and tireless tigers, hewed at each other in the battle, peerless in prowess.
Then the grandson of Śini, that tamer of foes, pierced Karṇa in every limb, again and again, with shafts all wrought of iron.
With a broad-headed arrow he swept his charioteer from the chariot-box, and with whetted shafts he slew his four white steeds.
Cleaving his banner a hundredfold with a hundred arrows, that bull among men left Karṇa without a car, before the very eyes of your son.
Then your bulls among men were dismayed, O king — Vṛṣasena, the son of Karṇa, and Śalya, the lord of the Madras,
and the son of Droṇa — they surrounded the grandson of Śini on every side; thereupon all became a tumult, and nothing could be discerned.
When the heroic son of the sūta had thus been left carless by Sātyaki, a cry of dismay arose, O king, throughout all the armies.
And Karṇa too, reeling, O king, tormented by the Sātvata's arrows, mounted Duryodhana's chariot, breathing hard.
Honoring the friendship he had borne your son from boyhood, and keeping the vow he had made when granted the kingdom,
even with Karṇa thus carless, the self-controlled Sātyaki did not slay your heroic sons, O king, with Duḥśāsana at their head.
Guarding too the vow Bhīmasena had once made of old, he made them carless and reeling, yet did not part them from their lives.
For the slaying of your sons had been pledged by Bhīmasena, and at the second dicing the slaying of Karṇa had been vowed by Pārtha.
Though they made every effort then to slay him, those foremost chariot-warriors with Karṇa at their head were unable to slay that Sātyaki.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The son of Droṇa, and Kṛtavarman, and likewise other great chariot-warriors — bulls among the kṣatriyas by the hundred — were vanquished with a single bow by one who sought the other world and the favor of the King of Righteousness.
Sātyaki, scourge of his foes, was equal in valor to the two Kṛṣṇas; in the world there is Kṛṣṇa, or Pārtha the bowman, or the grandson of Śini, that tiger among men — a fourth such is not to be found.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Mounting the unconquerable chariot of Vāsudeva, the youthful Sātyaki, the peer of Vāsudeva, left Karṇa without a car —
the car driven by Dāruka — proud of the strength of his own arms. Did Sātyaki then mount yet another chariot of his own?
This I wish to hear, for you are skilled in the telling; I deem him irresistible — tell me of it, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, how the wise younger brother of Dāruka swiftly made ready for him another chariot, fashioned with every proper appointment —
bound with bands of iron and of gold, fitted with its pole, studded with a thousand stars, bearing a banner and pennon marked with a lion.
It was yoked with horses swift as the wind, caparisoned with golden trappings, white and bright as the moon, hardy, and heedless of every clamor.
With foremost steeds in armor of variegated gold, O lord of peoples — a chariot loud with the ringing of clustered bells, flashing with lances and javelins —
furnished with all the gear of war, abounding in many weapons — such a chariot, deep-voiced as a thundercloud, he made ready.
Mounting it, the grandson of Śini fell upon your host; and Dāruka, as he pleased, went off to the side of Keśava.
For Karṇa too, O great king, they brought up a chariot — drawn by goodly steeds, swifter still, white as the conch and as cow's milk, clad in armor of variegated gold,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
furnished with girths of gold and with a banner, decked with well-wrought gear and pennon, a peerless car with a good driver, abounding in many weapons.
This they brought up, and mounting it Karṇa too charged upon his foes. All this have I told you, even as you asked of me.
Now learn further of the ruin born of your own misrule: one-and-thirty of your sons have been struck down by Bhīmasena,
with Durmukha, that ever-skillful and wondrous fighter, at their head; and heroes by the hundred have been slain by the Sātvata and by Arjuna.
Setting Bhīṣma and Bhagadatta at the forefront, good sir — thus, O king, has this destruction come to pass, all through your evil counsel.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the heroes on their side and on mine had thus fared, Saṃjaya, what then did Bhīma do? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Bhīmasena, his chariot broken and stung by the barbed words of Karṇa, fell into the grip of fury and spoke this word to Phalguna.
Again and again he taunted me — 'Beardless oaf, fool, glutton, untrained in arms, do not fight, you child, you coward of the battlefield!' —
thus did Karṇa speak to me before your very eyes, Dhanaṃjaya. He who speaks so to me deserves death at my hands, and by him have I been so addressed, O Bhārata.
This vow, O mighty-armed one, I have taken together with you; as this is my charge, son of Kuntī, so is it yours — of this there is no doubt.
For his slaying, O best of men, remember this word of mine; so act, Dhanaṃjaya, that it be made true.
Hearing that word of Bhīma's, Arjuna of measureless valour drew a little closer in the battle and spoke to Karṇa.
Karṇa, O Karṇa, vain in your seeing, charioteer's son who praises only himself, mind set on unrighteousness — hear from me now what I shall tell you.
Twofold is the fortune of heroes in war: victory and defeat. And both are uncertain, Rādheya — even for Vāsava when he fights.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When you were near death at Yuyudhāna's hands, your chariot wrecked, you were spared and let go; and only by chance did you make Bhīmasena chariotless.
But this was unrighteous, Rādheya, that you spoke so to Bhīma — one who knows the law of war, who fights and does not flee, who fulfils to the utmost of his power a hero's work in the fray.
Before the eyes of all the armies, of Keśava and of me, you were made chariotless by Bhīmasena many a time in battle, yet the son of Pāṇḍu never spoke one harsh word to you.
But because you made Vṛkodara hear much that was cruel, and because Subhadrā's son was slain by you all in unfair fashion —
for that arrogance reap now its instant fruit. You cut his bowstring to your own undoing, O evil-minded one.
Therefore you, fool, are to be slain by me, together with your servants, your forces, and your steeds. Do all that you must do — a great terror has come upon you.
I shall slay your Vṛṣasena before your watching eyes in the fight; and whatever other kings shall come at me through delusion of mind, them too shall I slay, all of them — by truth I lay hand upon my weapon.
And when dull Duryodhana sees you — fool of unripe wit, overweening — struck down in battle, he shall grieve bitterly.
When Arjuna had vowed the slaying of Karṇa's son, a great and tumultuous clamour rose then among the chariot-warriors.
While that confused and dreadful battle was raging, the thousand-rayed sun, its beams grown faint, drew near the mountain of setting.
Then, O king, Hṛṣīkeśa embraced Bībhatsu, who stood at the battle's head, his vow fulfilled, and spoke thus to him.
By good fortune, Jiṣṇu, your great vow has been accomplished by you; and by good fortune the wicked Vṛddhakṣatra is slain together with his son.
Even an army of gods, Bhārata, on meeting Dhṛtarāṣṭra's host would sink in the battle, Jiṣṇu — of this there can be no doubt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Though I ponder it, I see nowhere in the worlds, O tiger among men, any man but you who could do battle with this force.
Many guardians of the earth of great might, equal to you or greater, gathered for Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son's sake; yet, meeting you wrathful in battle, mailed though they were, they could not stand their ground.
Your prowess and your strength are like those of Rudra, Śakra, and Yama. No one could perform in battle such a feat as you alone have done this day, O scorcher of foes.
Even so, when the evil-souled Karṇa is slain with all his kin, I shall exalt you the more — conqueror of your enemies, slayer of your foes.
To him Arjuna replied: By your grace, Mādhava, this vow has been carried through by me — a vow hard to cross even for the gods.
No wonder is victory for those whose lord you are, Mādhava. By your grace Yudhiṣṭhira shall gain the whole earth.
Yours alone is the burden, Vārṣṇeya, yours alone the victory, O lord. We are yours to raise up and yours to command, slayer of Madhu.
Addressed thus, Kṛṣṇa, smiling, gently driving the horses on, showed to Pārtha that vast and cruel field of battle.
The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: Craving victory in war and far-famed glory, the heroes and the kings lie upon the earth, slain by your shafts.
Their weapons and ornaments scattered, their horses, chariots, and elephants undone, their armour cleft and shattered, they have come to utter ruin.
The living and the lifeless alike, endowed with surpassing radiance — these lords of men, though life has fled, seem still as though alive.
Behold the earth filled with their gold-feathered arrows, their many sharp weapons, their mounts and their armaments.
With cuirasses, with shields, with necklaces, with heads still bearing their earrings, with turbans, diadems, garlands, crest-jewels, and garments —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
with necklets and armlets and bright gold ornaments, and with other gleaming jewels of every kind, the earth shines, O Bhārata.
With yak-tail whisks, with gay fans, with banners, with horses, chariots, and elephants, with coverlets of many sorts, and with the fly-whisks of the horses —
with richly patterned elephant-housings and with costly chariot-guards — behold the earth strewn over, as though robed in figured cloth.
Behold others fallen from their elephants — those caparisoned beasts — together with the elephants themselves, like lions tumbled from mountain peaks struck down by the thunderbolt.
Behold yet others sewn to the ground along with their horses, and the throngs of footmen and riders awash in floods of blood.
Saṃjaya said: Thus showing the field of battle to the Diademed One, Kṛṣṇa, joined by his own and filled with joy, sounded the conch Pāñcajanya.
Saṃjaya said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, leaping down from his chariot, O Bhārata, embraced the two Kṛṣṇas, overflowing with tears of joy.
Wiping his bright face, radiant as a white lotus, he spoke to Vāsudeva and to the Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya.
By good fortune I behold you both, great chariot-warriors, your burden in battle crossed; and by good fortune the wicked lord of Sindhu, basest of men, is slain.
By good fortune, Kṛṣṇa, my great gladness has been brought to pass; and by good fortune the hosts of foes are plunged into an ocean of grief.
For those whose lord you are, the teacher of all the worlds, nothing in the three worlds is hard to achieve, O slayer of Madhu.
By your grace, Govinda, we shall vanquish our foes, even as of old, by your grace, the Chastiser of Pāka overcame the Dānavas.
Conquest of the earth, or even conquest of the three worlds, is assured, Vārṣṇeya, for those with whom you are pleased, Mādhava.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For them there is no sin, nor defeat in battle, whose lord is you, the lord of the lord of the thirty gods, with whom you are pleased, Mādhava.
By your grace, Hṛṣīkeśa, glorious Śakra, lord of the hosts of gods, won the conquest of the three worlds at the head of battle.
And by your grace, O lord of the thirty gods, the thirty themselves attained immortality, Kṛṣṇa, and enjoy imperishable worlds.
By a prowess sprung from your grace, O slayer of foes, Śakra attained lordship over the gods, having slain the Daityas by the thousands.
By your grace, Hṛṣīkeśa, the world of moving and unmoving things abides each in its own course, O hero, and engages in muttered prayer and oblation.
In the beginning all this was one ocean, wholly wrapped in darkness; by your grace the world attained to light, O best of men.
They who have taken refuge in Hṛṣīkeśa — creator of all the worlds, the supreme Self, the unfallen — are never at any time deluded.
They who are devoted to you, Hṛṣīkeśa — the god without beginning or end, the maker of the worlds, the imperishable — cross over all hardships.
To him who takes refuge in the supreme Person, the ancient One, that which is highest among all things primeval, the highest prosperity is ordained.
He who chanted forth the four Vedas, and he who is hymned within the Vedas — taking refuge in that great-souled one, a man attains a prosperity beyond all others.
He who is Dhanaṃjaya's friend and Dhanaṃjaya's good — taking refuge in that guardian of Dhanaṃjaya, a man thrives in happiness.
Thus addressed, those two great-souled ones, Keśava and the Pāṇḍava both, then spoke gladly to the king, the lord of the earth.
By the fire of your wrath the wicked King Jayadratha has been consumed; and the surging, vast host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son in battle —
is being slain, is slain already, and shall perish utterly, O Bhārata; for these Kauravas are struck down by your anger, slayer of foes.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For having angered you, a hero who slays with a mere glance, ill-minded Suyodhana, together with his friends and kinsmen, shall yield up his life in the fray.
Struck down before by your wrath, Bhīṣma the grandsire of the Kurus, hard to conquer even by the gods, lies upon his bed of arrows.
Hard to win is victory in battle for those, O slayer of foes; truly they pass into the power of death with whom you are wrathful, Pāṇḍava.
Kingdom, life, beloved sons, and pleasures of every kind — soon do these perish for those with whom you are wrathful, O giver of honour.
I deem the Kauravas already destroyed, with their sons, their cattle, and their kin, now that you, ever devoted to the duty of kings, are wrathful, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then mighty-armed Bhīma and the great chariot-warrior Sātyaki, having saluted their elder and superior, those two great bowmen stood gashed and torn by arrows, encircled by the Pāñcālas.
Beholding those two heroes glad before him, standing with hands folded in reverence, the son of Kuntī rejoiced over them both, Bhīma and Sātyaki.
By good fortune I behold you, heroes, delivered from the ocean of armies — from the unassailable Droṇa-crocodile, from the lair of the sea-monster Hārdikya; and by good fortune all the kings of the earth are vanquished in the fight.
By good fortune I behold you both victorious in the battle; and by good fortune Droṇa is overcome in the fray, and the mighty Hārdikya as well.
By good fortune I behold you, blameless ones, crossed safely over the ocean of armies — heroes glorious in battle, never fleeing the fight; and by good fortune I behold you both, who are dear to me as my own breath.
Having spoken thus, the Pāṇḍava king embraced Yuyudhāna and Vṛkodara, those tigers among men, and for very joy let fall his tears.
Then, O lord of peoples, the whole army of the Pāṇḍavas was filled with delight, and beholding their victory set its mind upon the battle still to come.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: When the lord of Sindhu was slain, O king, your son Suyodhana, his face wet with tears, wretched and bereft of hope of conquering his foes, thought that there was no warrior on earth equal to Arjuna.
Neither Droṇa, nor Rādheya, nor Aśvatthāman, nor Kṛpa was able to stand before him in his wrath — so he thought, good sir.
For Pārtha, having vanquished in battle all my great chariot-warriors, slew the lord of Sindhu in the fight, and none could turn him back.
In every way this great host of the Kauravas is already as good as slain; for it has no protector — not even Purandara himself in person.
He upon whom we leaned to raise our arms for battle — that Karṇa has been vanquished in the fight, and Jayadratha too is slain.
That Karṇa who hurled harsh words at the Pāṇḍavas in the midst of the assembly hall has been worsted in battle, and the lord of the Sindhus laid low as well.
That Karṇa, leaning on whose prowess I held the unfallen one who came seeking peace to be no more than a blade of grass — that very Karṇa has been beaten in the fight.
Thus crushed in spirit, O king, your son — he who has wronged the whole world — drew near to look upon Droṇa, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then he recounted the whole of it: the great slaughter of the Kurus, the foes carrying off the victory, and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra going under.
Duryodhana said: Behold, O teacher, the havoc wrought among the consecrated kings — though we set in the forefront the hero Bhīṣma, my grandsire.
Having struck him down, this Śikhaṇḍin, greedy and swollen with pride, together with all the Pāñcālas presses upon the van of our army.
And another, unassailable — your own pupil, the ambidextrous archer — after destroying seven full armies, has slain King Jayadratha.
How shall I ever discharge my debt to friends who longed for my victory and served my cause, now that they have gone to the abode of Yama?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those lords of the earth who sought to win the earth for my sake — they have forsaken dominion over the earth and now lie sleeping upon it.
I, a coward, having brought about such ruin of my friends — not by a thousand horse-sacrifices could I dare to redeem myself.
For me — the greedy, the sinful, the transgressor of righteousness — they strove and sought to conquer, and so have come to the dwelling of Vaivasvata.
How is it that the earth could not open a cleft to swallow me — fallen in conduct, betrayer of my own friends — there in the assembly of kings?
I could not save my grandsire, his limbs drenched in blood, lying in the midst of the kings — Bhīṣma struck down upon the field of battle.
When that unassailable conqueror of the world beyond meets me — ignoble man, betrayer of friends, doer of unrighteousness — what will he say to me?
Behold the mighty archer Jalasaṃdha, slain by Sātyaki — a hero who rose up for my sake and gave his life, a great chariot-warrior.
Seeing the Kāmboja struck down, and Alambusa too, and many other friends besides — what use to me now is the wish to live?
The heroes who, never turning their backs, exerted themselves and fell for my sake, striving with all their might to conquer my enemies —
to them, O scorcher of foes, I shall this day discharge my debt as best I can: I shall offer them the water of libation along the Yamunā.
Truly I vow it to you, O foremost of all who bear arms — I swear it by my sacrifices and pious works, by my valor, and by my sons —
having slain in battle all those Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas, I shall win peace — or else I shall go to share their world in the fight.
For now my allies, ill requited, no longer desire to aid me; they reckon the sons of Pāṇḍu worthier than us, O mighty-armed one.
Death itself has been ordained in battle by him whose vows are truth; yet you show indifference toward Dhanaṃjaya, because he is so apt a pupil.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And so all who wished to make me victorious have been struck down; in Karṇa alone do I now see one who still seeks my triumph.
The dull-witted man who, not truly knowing his friend, yet employs him in a friend's behalf — his purpose comes to nothing.
Such has been this enterprise of mine, contrived out of folly by those who only call themselves friends — by their crooked dealings, here and there, against a greedy and sinful man.
Slain is Jayadratha, and the valiant son of Somadatta, and the Abhīṣāhas, the Śūrasenas, the Śibis, and the Vasātis.
This very day I too shall go where those bulls among men have gone — slain for my sake in battle as they fought against the diademed one.
For I have no use for life bereft of those bulls among men. Let the teacher of the sons of Pāṇḍu grant me his leave to go.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the king of the Sindhus had been slain in battle by the ambidextrous archer, dear son, and Bhūriśravas likewise, what then was the temper of your minds?
And Droṇa, thus addressed by Duryodhana in the assembly of the Kurus — what did he say in reply to that? Tell me this, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: A great clamor of dismay arose among your troops, O Bhārata, when they beheld the lord of the Sindhus slain and Bhūriśravas as well.
They all scorned the whole of your son's counsel — that counsel by which warriors among the kṣatriyas had been slain by the hundred.
But Droṇa, hearing those words of your son, grew downcast in spirit; and after pondering a moment, sorely afflicted, he spoke.
O Duryodhana, why do you thus pierce me with the shafts of your words, when I have ever told you the ambidextrous archer is unconquerable in battle?
By this alone, O Kaurava, you might have understood Arjuna in war — that Śikhaṇḍin slew Bhīṣma while guarded by the diademed one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When I saw one whom neither gods nor men could slay struck down in battle, even then I knew: this host of ours shall be no more.
When that hero is slain whom we held the bravest of men in all three worlds, what remnant do we still cling to?
Those dice which father Śakuni cast in the assembly of the Kurus — they were no dice but whetted arrows, tormentors of the foe.
Those very shafts, dear son, now slay us, driven on toward our undoing — the shafts of which Vidura warned you then, though you would not understand.
You would not heed those words of the great-souled, steadfast Vidura, though he cried them out for your welfare — auspicious counsel spoken for your good.
And now this dreadful thing is come to pass, this great slaughter — through your scorning of that counsel, Duryodhana, for your sake.
And in that you had Kṛṣṇā dragged before the assembly while we looked on — she undeserving of it, nobly born, a follower of every sacred duty —
of that unrighteousness, O son of Gāndhārī, you have now received the fruit; and were it not so, you would meet a sin still greater in the world beyond.
And in that you conquered the Pāṇḍavas at dice by foul play and drove them then into the forest, clad in the skins of black antelopes —
toward these men, who walk ever in righteousness as though they were my own sons — what man in the world, save me who am called a brāhmaṇa, would deal so treacherously?
This wrath of the Pāṇḍavas was brought down by you together with Śakuni, with Dhṛtarāṣṭra's assent, in the assembly of the Kurus.
Joined to it was Duḥśāsana, and Karṇa nourished it the more; and you, disregarding the steward's words, fed it again and again.
When all of you, overpowering Abhimanyu, hemmed him round while rallying about the king of the Sindhus — how then was that king slain in your very midst?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
How, while you and Karṇa and Kṛpa and Śalya yet lived, and Aśvatthāman too, O Kaurava, did the lord of the Sindhus go to his death?
When all those kings of yours waited upon his fierce splendor to save the lord of the Sindhus — how was he slain in your very midst?
On me above all, O Duryodhana, and on you, that lord of earth set his hope of deliverance from Arjuna.
And now, since he found no rescue from Phalguna, I see no way at all to save my own life.
I see myself, as it were, sinking into the guilt that is Dhṛṣṭadyumna, so long as I have not slain the Pāñcālas together with that Śikhaṇḍin.
Why then do you pierce me with the shafts of your words while I burn with grief, O Bhārata, when you yourself were powerless to save the king of the Sindhus?
You did not see, in battle, the golden banner of Bhīṣma, the tireless-handed one whose word was truth — how then do you still hope for victory?
Where, in the midst of mighty chariot-warriors, the lord of the Sindhus was slain, and Bhūriśravas too — what remnant do you suppose is left there?
If the unassailable Kṛpa yet lives, O king — he who has not gone the road of the lord of the Sindhus — him I honor.
And in that I saw Bhīṣma slain before the very eyes of your younger brother Duḥśāsana, O Kaurava — Bhīṣma, who wrought deeds so hard to do, well-nigh unslayable in battle even by the gods with Vāsava at their head —
this I now think, O king: that the earth is no longer yours. For here, O Bhārata, the hosts of the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas, joined together, are charging upon me this day, honored sir.
Not until I have slain all the Pāñcālas will I loose my armor; in battle, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, I shall do the deed that serves your good.
O king, say to my son Aśvatthāman in the fray: the Somakas must not be spared by one who would guard his own life.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And keep faith with the counsel your father gave you: stand firm in mercy, in self-restraint, in truth, and in uprightness.
Skilled in duty, gain, and pleasure, never letting duty or gain suffer harm, holding duty foremost — so should you perform your tasks, again and again.
The brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with eye and mind, and served according to one's power; nothing should be done to displease them, for they are like tongues of fire.
But now I plunge into the hostile ranks, O slayer of foes, for a great battle, O king — wounded as I am by the barb of your words.
And you, Duryodhana, hold the army together if you can; for even by night the Kurus and Sṛñjayas, roused to fury, will fight on.
So saying, Droṇa went forth against the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas, stealing away the splendor of the warriors as the sun steals the light of the stars.
Saṃjaya said: Then King Duryodhana, so goaded by Droṇa, fell into the grip of indignation and set his mind on battle alone.
And then your son Duryodhana said to Karṇa: Behold — the battle-array drawn up by the teacher, hard for the very gods to break, has been broken by the diademed son of Pāṇḍu with Kṛṣṇa for his ally.
While you exerted yourself, and the great-souled Droṇa too, and the foremost of warriors looked on, the lord of the Sindhus was struck down.
Behold, O son of Rādhā, the kings, the foremost upon earth in war, slain by Pārtha alone, as lesser beasts are slain by a lion.
Though I strove in the battle, O slayer of foes, my army has been brought to a scant remnant by the son of Śakra.
For how, if Droṇa had not willed it, could Phalguna in battle have broken that array so hard to break, however he might have striven in the fray?
For Phalguna is ever dear to the great-souled teacher; and so, O crusher of foes, he granted him passage without a fight.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Droṇa, scorcher of foes, having granted safety to the lord of the Sindhus in the fight, yet opened the gate for the diademed one — behold how poorly I am served.
Had I but given leave at the outset for the king of the Sindhus to go home, there would have been no slaughter of men in the battle.
Jayadratha, longing for life, was setting out toward home, having won safety from Droṇa in the fight — and I, ignoble, held him back.
This day my brothers, Citrasena and the rest, are spent in battle, having come up against Bhīmasena before our wicked-hearted eyes.
Karṇa said: Do not reproach the teacher; that brāhmaṇa fights with all his might. I deem the Pāṇḍavas unconquerable in the fray, even by Droṇa who knows every weapon.
For even so, passing him by, the white-horsed one broke through. The course of things is ordained by fate; I think there is nowhere any altering it.
Then, O Suyodhana, while we fought with the utmost of our power, the lord of the Sindhus was slain, O king; in this, destiny is reckoned the highest cause.
Though we strove our utmost together with you on the field of battle, destiny undid our manly valor and set us behind, for all our ceaseless striving with both cunning and prowess.
Whatever deed a man assailed by destiny may anywhere perform, that deed, once done, is undone again for him by destiny.
What is to be done by a man who is resolute and true, that he must do without misgiving; but success rests upon destiny.
By trickery the sons of Pṛthā were cheated, O Bhārata, and by poisoned draughts, and they were nearly burned in the house of lac, and they were vanquished at dice.
By recourse to statecraft they were sent away to the forest; yet whatever was thus contrived by effort was cast down by destiny.
Fight on, taking up your effort, and make death your only turning-back; as you strive and as they strive, destiny will go its own appointed way.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
No deliberate good deed of theirs is anywhere to be seen, nor any wicked deed of yours, O hero, devoid of judgment, O upholder of the Kurus.
Destiny is the measure of every deed, good or otherwise; for destiny, whose work cannot be turned aside, keeps watch even over those who sleep.
Many were your armies and many likewise your warriors—not so those of the sons of Pāṇḍu; and yet the battle went thus.
By those few you many strikers have been brought to ruin; I think this is the work of destiny, by which manly valor has been brought to naught.
Saṃjaya said: While they were conversing thus at length on this and that, O lord of men, the battalions of the Pāṇḍavas appeared before them in the fray.
Then began the battle, chariots and elephants locked together, between your men and their foes, O king, through your own ill counsel.
Saṃjaya said: That host of yours, O lord of men, with its surging flood of elephants and horses, rushed upon the army of the Pāṇḍavas and gave it battle on every side.
The Pāñcālas and the Kurus, fighting one another, were as men consecrated for the great realm of Yama, for the world beyond.
Heroes closing with heroes pierced one another swiftly in the fight with arrows, lances, and spears, and led each other to the abode of Yama.
Between car-warriors and car-warriors a great and terrible battle, streaming with blood, broke out as they struck one another down.
And the elephants, O great king, closing upon one another, enraged and frenzied with rut, gored each other with their tusks.
Horsemen pierced horsemen with darts, spears, and battle-axes in the tumultuous fight, each seeking great renown.
And the foot-soldiers, O mighty-armed one, by the hundreds, weapons in hand, harried one another, O king, ever intent upon valor.
By the names of their lineages and their families, O venerable one, heard upon the field, we knew the Pāñcālas apart from the Kurus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the fray the warriors, ranging about without fear, sent one another to the world beyond with arrows, spears, and battle-axes.
By the arrows loosed in their thousands, O king, the ten quarters of the sky, even after the sun had set, no longer shone as before.
While the Pāṇḍava warriors were thus fighting on, Duryodhana, undaunted, O great king, plunged into that host.
Sorely stricken with grief at the slaying of the lord of the Sindhus, and resolving that he too must die, he entered the army of the foe.
Making the air resound with the rumble of his chariot and seeming to shake the earth, your son advanced against the host of the Pāṇḍavas.
That tumultuous clash between him and them, O Bhārata, became a great wreaking of destruction upon all the troops.
As the noonday sun blazing with its rays, so blazed your son in their midst with his waves of arrows.
The Pāṇḍavas could not even look upon that descendant of Bharata in the fight; their spirit roused only to flight, they had lost all heart for victory over the foe.
The Pāñcālas, slaughtered by the great-souled one, ran about in flight; and harried swiftly by the gold-feathered, keen-pointed arrows of your son the bowman, the Pāṇḍava soldiers fell.
Not such a feat in battle did your men perform as the king, your son, performed, O lord of peoples.
By your son that Pāṇḍava army was churned in the battle, like a lotus-pool with its blooming lilies trampled on every side by an elephant.
Like a lotus-pond robbed of its splendor when its waters fail and the wind and sun assail it, so became the Pāṇḍava army through the fiery might of your son.
Seeing the Pāṇḍava army stricken by your son, O Bhārata, the Pāñcālas, with Bhīmasena at their head, rushed upon him.
He pierced Bhīmasena with ten arrows, the two sons of Mādrī with three each, Virāṭa and Drupada with six, and Śikhaṇḍin with a hundred.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna with seventy, the son of Dharma with seven, and the Kekayas and the Cedis with many whetted arrows.
Having pierced the Sātvata with five, the sons of Draupadī with three each, and Ghaṭotkaca in the battle, he roared like a lion.
And other warriors by the hundreds, with their elephants, horses, and chariots, he cut down in the fight with cruel arrows, like wrathful Death cutting down living beings.
As he was striking down those foes, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas cut his great gold-backed bow into three with two broad-headed shafts, O venerable one.
And he pierced him with ten well-aimed, sharpened arrows; but all of these, after piercing his vital parts, broke and fell to the ground.
Then the gladdened warriors gathered round Yudhiṣṭhira, as the gods gathered round Puraṃdara for the slaying of Vṛtra.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira loosed at your son in the fray an arrow most hard to ward off, O venerable one; and grievously pierced by it, your son sank down upon his splendid chariot.
Then from the Pāñcāla troops there rose a great loud clamor on every side, O lord of kings, as they rejoiced, crying, 'The king is slain!'
And a fierce din of the twang of arrows was heard there, O venerable one; then Droṇa swiftly appeared upon that field.
And Duryodhana, heartened, taking up his stout bow, advanced upon King Yudhiṣṭhira the Pāṇḍava, crying, 'Stand, stand!'
The Pāñcālas, eager for the king, swiftly went out against him; but Droṇa received them, seeking to save the best of the Kurus, as the ray-shedding sun beats back clouds driven up by a fierce gale.
Then, O king, there was a great battle, swelling ever larger, between your men and their foes, all met together in their lust for combat.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the self-controlled preceptor, in his wrath, entered among the Pāṇḍavas, having justly rebuked my son Duryodhana for transgressing his counsel—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
how did the Pāṇḍavas surround Droṇa, that mighty archer, the hero, as he ranged and stood firm in the battle he had entered?
Who guarded the right wheel of the great-souled preceptor, and who guarded the left, as he slew his foes in the fight?
Dancing along the chariot-paths, that foremost of all who bear arms, wrathful like a comet, how did he come to meet his death?
Saṃjaya said: In the late afternoon, having slain the lord of the Sindhus, the son of Pṛthā, joining the king, and Sātyaki, that great archer—the two rushed upon Droṇa himself.
Likewise Yudhiṣṭhira swiftly, and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, each engaged with his own division, rushed upon Droṇa himself.
So too the wise Nakula and the unconquerable Sahadeva, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śatānīka, and Virāṭa with the Kekayas, the Matsyas and the Śālveya troops—all went against Droṇa in the fight.
And King Drupada too, guarded all about by the Pāñcālas, the father of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O king, advanced upon Droṇa himself.
The sons of Draupadī, those mighty archers, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, together with their troops, advanced upon Droṇa of great splendor.
And the Prabhadraka Pāñcālas, six thousand strikers strong, advanced upon Droṇa, with Śikhaṇḍin set at their head.
So too the other tigers among men, the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, banded together and turned upon Droṇa, that bull among the twice-born.
When those heroes had gone forth to battle, O bull of the Bhāratas, there came on a dreadful night, deepening the terror of the timid.
For the warriors it was a baleful, terrible night, O king, bound for the abode of Death, making an end of the lives of elephants, horses, and men.
In that dreadful night the jackals, howling on every side with flaming gobbets in their mouths, gave warning of a terrible peril.
And owls too appeared, foretelling vast terror, most dire of all in the host of the Kauravas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then among the armies, O lord of kings, there arose a great din, with the mighty sound of kettledrums and the boom of tabors,
and with the trumpeting of elephants and the neighing of horses and the clatter of falling hooves, a tumult arose on every side.
Then in the twilight there broke out a most dreadful battle, O great king, between Droṇa and the Sṛñjayas on every hand.
When the world was wrapped in darkness, nothing whatever could be discerned, with the dust raised up on every side by the host.
The blood of man and horse and elephant ran mingled together; we could no longer see the dust of the earth, shrouded as it was by the gore.
As of a thicket of bamboo burning by night upon a mountain, so arose a fearful crackling sound from the weapons that fell.
Neither one's own men nor the foe could be told apart, O king, in that enveloping darkness; at the onset of night the whole field became as if maddened.
The dust of the earth, O lord of kings, was laid by the blood; but with the golden mail and ornaments the darkness was lit up.
Then that Bhārata host, adorned with gems and gold, was like the star-strewn sky by night, O bull of the Bhāratas.
It rang with the cries of jackals and ravens, it was thronged with spears and banners, terrible with dreadful howls, resounding with roars and shouts.
Then there arose a great tumultuous uproar that made the hair stand on end, filling all the quarters, like the crash of mighty Indra's thunderbolt.
At midnight, O great king, that Bhārata army was seen lit up with armlets, earrings, golden necklaces, and weapons.
There the elephants and the chariots, decked with gold, appeared in the night like clouds shot through with lightning.
Swords, spears, maces, arrows, clubs, darts, and lances, as they fell in showers, were seen flashing like flames of fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With Duryodhana for its forewind, with chariots and elephants for its thunderheads, thundering with the blare of instruments, hung about with bows for lightning and with banners,
with Droṇa and the Pāṇḍavas for its rain-clouds, with swords, spears, and maces for its thunderbolts, with showers of arrows and missiles for its wind, fraught utterly with cold and heat—
that army—dreadful, astounding, fierce, life-severing, with no raft to cross it, most terrible—those who longed to fight entered in.
At that dreadful onset of night, resounding with a great uproar, that bred terror in the timid and swelled the joy of the brave—
As the dreadful night-battle raged on, terrible beyond measure, the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas, united and enraged, rushed upon Droṇa.
Whoever, O king, came to oppose that great-souled one face to face, all of these he turned away routed, and some of them he dispatched to the realm of Yama.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that unassailable one of boundless might had plunged among the Sṛñjayas, impatient and roused to fury, what then was your resolve?
When that one of immeasurable spirit, having rebuked my son Duryodhana for transgressing the rules, had broken into the foe, how did Pārtha respond?
After the heroic ruler of the Saindhavas had been slain, and Bhūriśravas too, how did that one of great splendor, unconquered, advance against the Pāñcālas?
When that scorcher of foes, hard to assail, had broken in, what did Duryodhana think the fitting deed for the hour to be?
Which heroes followed that boon-granting warrior, best of the twice-born? Which heroes went behind that valiant one as he fought? Which fought before him as he struck down his enemies in battle?
