None could descry him, shrouded by the Varuṇa weapon, by reason of Arjuna's swiftness and of the splendor that enveloped him.
Bhīma, with horses, charioteer, and car, shrouded by the weapon of Droṇa's son, garlanded in flame and scarcely to be looked upon, was like fire cast into fire.
As at the close of night, O king, the stars sink toward the western mountain, so did the arrows converge upon the chariot of Bhīmasena.
For Bhīma, and his chariot, his horses, and his charioteer, O sire, enveloped by Droṇa's son, seemed sunk within the very fire.
As the fire, having burned at the appointed time the whole world with all that moves and moves not, passes into the mouth of the Almighty, so did that weapon enwrap Bhīma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As fire might enter the sun, or the sun enter fire, so that splendor entered in, and nothing whatever could be discerned.
Seeing that weapon poured forth upon Bhīma's chariot, and the son of Droṇa rising up without a rival in the battle,
all the hosts of the Pāṇḍavas, weapons laid aside and senses fled, with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head—those mighty chariot-warriors turned their faces away.
Then Arjuna and Vāsudeva, those two heroes of great splendor, leaping in haste from their chariot, ran toward Bhīma.
Then those two mighty ones plunged into the splendor of Droṇa's son, born of the weapon's power, and entered it by their magic art.
They had laid aside their weapons, and so the fire born of the weapon could not burn them—both by the working of the Varuṇa weapon and by the might of the two Kṛṣṇas.
Then Nara and Nārāyaṇa, to quell the Nārāyaṇa weapon, forcibly dragged forth Bhīma and all his weapons.
Even as he was being dragged away, the son of Kuntī, that mighty car-warrior, kept roaring on; and the dreadful, scarce-conquerable weapon of Droṇa's son kept growing.
Vāsudeva said to him: "What is this, son of Pāṇḍu? Why, O son of Kuntī, though restrained, do you not turn back from battle?
Were these sons of the Kurus to be conquered by fighting, we too would fight here, and so would these bulls among men.
But all your own people have dismounted from their chariots; therefore you too, O son of Kuntī, withdraw at once from your car."
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa brought him down from the chariot to the ground, hissing like a serpent, his eyes red with wrath.
When he had been dragged from the chariot and his weapon laid upon the ground, then that Nārāyaṇa weapon, scorcher of foes, grew still.
When that unbearable splendor was thus quelled by the prescribed device, all the quarters and the intermediate quarters became clear.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Auspicious breezes blew, the beasts and birds grew calm, and the vehicles and the warriors were filled with cheer, O lord of men.
And when that terrible splendor was withdrawn, O Bhārata, the wise Bhīma shone forth like the sun risen at the close of night.
There stood the remnant of the Pāṇḍavas' host that the slaughter had spared, rejoicing at the ceasing of the weapon, eager to slay your son.
When that army had rallied and the weapon had been thus countered, Duryodhana, O great king, spoke to the son of Droṇa.
"Aśvatthāman, loose this weapon again, and swiftly; for the Pāñcālas have rallied once more, hungry for victory."
Aśvatthāman, thus addressed by your son, O sire, sighing most piteously, said this to the king.
"This weapon does not return, O king; it cannot be employed a second time. He who would call it back, it slays him who wields it—of this there is no doubt.
And this Vāsudeva has applied the counter to the weapon; otherwise the slaughter of the foe in battle had been ordained, O lord of men.
Defeat or death—death is the better, not so this victory; for these foes, vanquished, are as good as dead, having cast away their weapons."
Duryodhana said: "Son of the preceptor, if this weapon may not be loosed twice, then with other weapons let the slayers of the teacher be slain, O best of those who know the arts of war.
For in you the celestial weapons abide as they do in the Three-eyed God; should you wish it in your wrath, not even Purandara could escape you."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that weapon had been countered, and Droṇa slain by guile, and the son of Droṇa thus addressed by Duryodhana, what did he do next?
And seeing the Pārthas arrayed for battle in the fray, freed from the Nārāyaṇa weapon, ranging at the head of the host—
Saṃjaya said: He whose banner bore the lion's tail, knowing the slaying of his father, full of wrath, casting off all fear, rushed upon the son of Pṛṣata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And rushing on, that bull among men pierced that bull among men with twenty small arrows and with five more, in a great fury.
Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O king, pierced the son of Droṇa—blazing like fire—with sixty-three feathered shafts, O king.
And he pierced his charioteer with twenty gold-feathered, stone-whetted shafts, and his four horses with four sharp arrows.
Piercing and piercing again, the son of Droṇa roared, as though making the earth tremble, as though seizing the life-breaths of all the world in that great battle.
But the mighty son of Pṛṣata, O king, accomplished in arms and tireless in toil, rushed straight at the son of Droṇa, having made death itself the boundary of his turning back.
Then the prince of the Pāñcālas, that immeasurable spirit, the best of chariot-warriors, loosed a rain of arrows upon the head of Droṇa's son.
Enraged in the battle, the son of Droṇa veiled him with feathered shafts and pierced him with ten, remembering the slaying of his father.
With two well-drawn razor-headed arrows the son of Droṇa cut down the standard and the bow of the Pāñcāla king, and with others he tormented him sorely.
In that great battle the son of Droṇa stripped him of horses, charioteer, and car, and in his wrath he overspread all his followers with arrows.
Then the army of the Pāñcālas broke and fled, O lord of peoples, bewildered in aspect, anguished, and mangled by the rain of arrows.
Seeing the warriors turning away and Dhṛṣṭadyumna hard pressed, the grandson of Śini swiftly urged the fight on toward the chariot of Droṇa's son.
With eight whetted arrows he afflicted Aśvatthāman, and striking that unforgiving warrior again with twenty of varied form, he pierced likewise the charioteer with four and the four horses each with one.
Deeply pierced by those many-marked shafts of Yuyudhāna, the unforgiving mighty bowman, the son of Droṇa, laughed and spoke these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Grandson of Śini, I know your loyalty toward the slayer of my teacher; yet you shall not rescue him from me, who is in my grasp—nor yourself either."
So speaking, the son of Droṇa loosed at the Sātvata a peerless, well-jointed arrow bright as a sunbeam, as Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra.
That shaft, sped by him, pierced through both the warrior and his armor, and cleaving the earth it entered her, hissing like a serpent entering its hole.
His armor shattered, the hero, like an elephant stung by the goad, let fall his bow with its arrow, streaming from many wounds.
Sinking and drenched in blood, he sank down upon the floor of his car, and was swiftly borne by his charioteer to another chariot, away from the son of Droṇa.
Then with another well-feathered, smooth-jointed arrow that scorcher of foes struck Dhṛṣṭadyumna between the brows.
Already deeply pierced before and grievously afflicted thereafter, the Pāñcāla prince sank down in the battle and leaned upon his standard.
Upon him—like a rutting elephant tormented by a lion, O king—five heroic chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍava side charged at speed.
The Diademed One, Bhīmasena, Vṛddhakṣatra the Paurava, the crown-prince of the Cedis, and Sudarśana the Mālava struck him together from every side, each with five arrows.
With twenty serpent-venom-like arrows, and with five more, the son of Droṇa cut down all at once those twenty-five shafts.
With seven sharpened arrows the son of Droṇa tormented the Paurava, the Mālava with three, Pārtha with one, and Vṛkodara with six.
Then all those great chariot-warriors, O king, pierced the son of Droṇa, together and severally, with arrows gold-feathered and whetted on stone.
The crown-prince pierced the son of Droṇa with twenty feathered shafts, Pārtha again with eight, and all the rest each with three.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the son of Droṇa struck Arjuna with six arrows, Vāsudeva with ten, Bhīma with five, the crown-prince with four; and having cut the prince's bow and standard with two, the son of Droṇa, piercing Pārtha again with a shower of arrows, roared a terrible lion's roar.
As the son of Droṇa shot his well-whetted, sharp-edged shafts behind and before, the earth, the air, the heavens, the quarters and the intermediate quarters were covered with arrows of dreadful form.
That warrior of fierce splendor, of valor equal to Indra's, with three arrows at once severed the two arms—shining like Indra's banner—and the head of Sudarśana as he sat in his own car.
Slaying the Paurava with a chariot-lance, and cutting his car to bits with arrows, he severed his two arms anointed with fine sandal, and with a broad-headed shaft lifted his head from his trunk.
Laughing, with swift arrows like blazing fire he pierced the young crown-prince, beloved of the Cedis, dark as a wreath of blue lotuses, and gave him over to death together with his horses and charioteer.
Having slain them in battle, the heroic son of Droṇa, that unvanquished lord of warriors, blew his great conch in his joy.
Then all the Pāñcālas, and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava, in terror abandoned the chariot of Dhṛṣṭadyumna and fled in every direction.
As they broke, the son of Droṇa, scattering arrows upon their backs, bore down with speed upon the host of the Pāṇḍavas like Death himself.
As they were slaughtered in the battle by Droṇa's son, those warriors, O king, in their terror saw the son of Droṇa in all the quarters.
Saṃjaya said: Seeing that army broken, Dhanaṃjaya the son of Kuntī, that immeasurable spirit, held it back, longing to slay the son of Droṇa.
Yet those soldiers, O king, would not stand fast there, though Govinda and Arjuna strove with all their effort to rally them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Bībhatsu alone, with the remnants of the Somakas, the Matsyas, and others, marshalled his ranks and turned back against the Kauravas.
Then Savyasācin, swiftly outstripping him whose banner bore the lion's tail, spoke to the mighty bowman Aśvatthāman.
"Whatever is your power, your valor, your knowledge and your manhood, whatever your love for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and your hatred of us, and whatever splendor still is yours—show me all of it now, to the utmost."
"That very son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of Droṇa, will break your pride—he who is like the fire of doom, the ender of foes in battle. Come, then, against the Pāñcāla, and against me too, with Keśava beside me."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: The teacher's son is worthy of honor and mighty too, Saṃjaya; he bears love toward Dhanaṃjaya, and dear is he in turn to the son of Vāsava.
Never before has such harsh speech come from Bībhatsu; why, then, did the son of Kuntī speak so roughly to his friend?
Saṃjaya said: When the crown-prince had been slain, and Vṛddhakṣatra the Paurava, and Sudarśana the Mālava, perfect in the rites of bow and arrow—
—and when Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Sātyaki, and Bhīma had been overcome, and Yudhiṣṭhira had been struck to the quick by his words—
—and when a rift had opened within them, and remembering his grief, O lord, an unprecedented wrath was born of sorrow in Bībhatsu.
Therefore he spoke to the son of Droṇa words undeserved, unseemly, and unkind—to the honorable son of his teacher he spoke harshly, as a base man might.
Thus addressed, O king, that foremost of mighty bowmen, hissing with wrath at Pārtha's harsh speech and at words that struck every vital part, the son of Droṇa grew enraged—against Pārtha, and against Kṛṣṇa above all.
Standing intent upon his car, the valiant one touched water in purification and took up the fiery weapon, hard to withstand even by the gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Aiming at the hosts of his foes, both seen and unseen, the teacher's son, that slayer of enemy heroes, charged a blazing arrow with mantras—like smokeless fire—and, filled with wrath on every side, hurled it forth.
Then a tumultuous rain of arrows arose in the sky; chill winds blew, and the sun gave no more heat.
The Dānavas too cried out frightfully in all the quarters, and raining down blood, they roared amid the rain-clouded sky.
Birds, beasts, and cattle, and even the sages of holy vows, though most self-restrained in spirit, could find no peace.
All the great elements were thrown into disorder, the maker of day was overturned, and the three worlds were scorched, stricken as if seized by a burning fever.
Scorched by the heat of the arrows, the serpents that dwell beneath the earth rose up hissing, eager to discharge their dreadful venom.
And the creatures of the waters, scorched, O descendant of Bharata, found no relief, for the very pools that held them were burning.
Upon the quarters and the sky, the intermediate quarters and the earth, showers of arrows great and small fell down with the speed of Garuḍa and the wind.
By those arrows of Droṇa's son, sped with the force of the thunderbolt, the foes were burned and fell like trees consumed by fire.
Great elephants, blazing, fell upon the earth on every side, bellowing fearful cries that rumbled like rain-clouds.
Other great elephants there, ablaze, fled away, and yet others trembled, like beasts ringed about by a forest fire in a dreadful wood.
Like the crowns of trees seared by a forest blaze, O honored one, the troops of horses and the masses of chariots appeared, O lord; and floods of chariots fell here and there by the thousands.
That army the lord Agni burned in the battle, O descendant of Bharata, as the all-dissolving fire consumes every being at the end of an age.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But seeing the Pāṇḍava host burning in that great battle, your men, O king, rejoiced and let forth lion-roars.
Then your men, O descendant of Bharata, exulting and wearing the look of victory, joyfully struck up a thousand instruments of many kinds at once.
As the world was wrapped in darkness, an entire akṣauhiṇī, O king, and Savyasācin the Pāṇḍava, could no longer be seen in that great battle.
Never had we seen or even heard, O king, of such a weapon as the unforgiving son of Droṇa let loose.
But Arjuna, O great king, raised up the Brāhma weapon, ordained by the Lotus-born to counter every other weapon.
Then within a moment that darkness was stilled; a cool wind blew, and the quarters grew clear.
There we beheld a marvel: an entire akṣauhiṇī slain, its forms past recognition, burned utterly by the magic of that weapon.
Then the two heroes, the mighty bowmen Keśava and Arjuna, delivered unscathed, appeared together like the dispellers of darkness in the sky.
With its pennants, standard, and horses, with its axle-pole and its excellent weapons, that delivered chariot shone forth, a terror to your men.
Then in an instant a glad uproar arose from the rejoicing Pāṇḍavas, mingled with the blare of conches and drums.
"The two are slain"—such had been the thought of both the armies, until they saw Keśava and Arjuna come on swiftly, delivered and unharmed.
Unhurt and joyful, the two blew their finest of conches; and seeing the sons of Pṛthā so glad, your men were thrown into distress.
Seeing those two great-souled ones delivered, the son of Droṇa, sorely grieved, pondered for a moment, "What is this, then?" O honored one.
Having pondered, O lord of kings, given over to brooding and grief, sighing long and hot, he then grew downcast in heart.
Then the son of Droṇa laid down his bow and leapt in haste from his car, and crying, "Shame, shame! all this is in vain," he fled from the battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, by the dwelling of Sarasvatī, he beheld Veda-Vyāsa, stainless, with the sheen of a glistening rain-cloud—Vyāsa himself he saw.
Seeing him standing before him, O upholder of the Kuru line, the son of Droṇa, his throat choked, saluted him and spoke most piteously.
"O sir, O sir, is it illusion, or mere chance? I know not what this may be. How has this weapon of mine come to nothing? And what was my transgression?"
"Is this the world turned upside down, or the undoing of the worlds, that these two Kṛṣṇas yet live? For Time, indeed, is hard to overpass."
"Not Asuras, gods, or Gandharvas, not Piśācas, not Rākṣasas, not serpents, Yakṣas, or birds, nor men in any wise—"
"—are able to make otherwise this weapon launched by me. Yet here it has slain only a single arrayed akṣauhiṇī, blazing as it went."
"By what cause did it not slay these two, Keśava and Arjuna, who share the nature of mortals? Declare this to me, O blessed one, asked by me, even as it truly is."
Vyāsa said: This is a mighty matter on which, in wonder, you question me. I shall declare it all to you; compose your mind and listen.
He who is named Nārāyaṇa, born before even the most ancient ones, was born for a purpose as the son of Dharma, the maker of all the world.
He undertook a fierce penance, stationed upon Mount Maināka, his arms raised aloft, of vast splendor, resembling fire and the sun.
For sixty thousand years, and as many hundreds besides, the lotus-eyed one, feeding only on air, wasted away his own body.
Then, having performed yet another austerity, and twice again another great one, he filled the gulf between heaven and earth with his splendor.
When by that penance, my son, he had become one with Brahman, he then beheld the Lord of all, the source of the universe, the master of the whole world —

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
Then the lotus-eyed one, full of devotion, having paid homage to Rudra, the slayer of Andhaka in an instant, began to praise that god of the strange-set eyes:
"From you, O most excellent, sprang the makers of beings, the elder gods who today guard the world, who of old, entering this earth, protected your ancient creation, O God.
Gods and demons, Nāgas, Rākṣasas and Piśācas, men, Suparṇas, and Gandharvas and Yakṣas, and all the manifold hosts of beings — we know them all alike sprung from you. The work of Indra and of Yama, of Varuṇa and of the Lord of Wealth, of Mitra and of Tvaṣṭṛ, and of Soma, is yours.
Form and light, sound, ether and wind, touch, the tasted, water, scent, the earth, desire, Brahmā, the Veda, and the Brāhmaṇas — all this, the unmoving and the moving, has sprung from you.
As drops issue forth from the waters into separateness, and at dissolution return again into oneness with them, so the wise one, knowing both the origin and the passing of beings, leaves them behind and attains union there with you.
The two birds, mind-born, wrapped in divine concealment; the pippala tree whose branches turn downward; the seven herdsmen, and the ten others who sustain the body's city — these were created by you, and beyond them all are you. What was, what shall be, and what is to come, unassailable — all the worlds here have sprung from you.
Cherish me, your devotee who cherishes you; harm me not by anything unfriendly. He who knows you as his very self, in undivided being, thus attains the radiant Brahman.
I have praised you, longing for your favor, seeking you out together with your bull, O best of gods. Grant me the boons I cherish, hard though they are to win; and, thus extolled, turn me not away."
To him, the worthy chief of gods, the blue-throated wielder of the Pināka, whose nature is beyond thought, praised by sages, he granted boons:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The blue-throated one said: By my grace, O Nārāyaṇa, among men and in the wombs of gods and Gandharvas, you shall be of immeasurable strength of soul.
Neither gods nor demons nor great serpents shall prevail against you, nor Piśācas, nor Gandharvas, nor men, nor Rākṣasas,
nor Suparṇas, nor Nāgas, nor any of the misbegotten creatures of the world; not even a god shall ever vanquish you in battle.
Not by weapon, not by the thunderbolt, not by fire, nor by wind, not by the wet nor by the dry, not by the moving nor by the unmoving,
shall anyone, by my grace, ever do you injury in any way; and should you go to battle, you shall be greater even than I.
Vyāsa said: Know that these boons were thus won of old by the heroic one. This same god walks abroad by his māyā, bewildering the world.
Born of that same one's austerity was the great sage named Nara, the equal of this god; know that one to be ever Arjuna.
These two sages, most exalted among the elder gods, are born age after age to order the course of the worlds.
And likewise, O wise and great-minded one, from the whole of that great work and austerity were you born, fierce in splendor and in wrath, a very form of Rudra.
You, godlike and wise, knowing the world to be pervaded by Bhava, drew yourself inward through self-restraints, longing to win his favor.
Fashioning a fair and fresh image of the Great Person in the manner of Ūrva, you worshipped him, O giver of honor, with prayers, oblations, and offerings.
That elder god, so worshipped by you, was well pleased, and granted you, O wise one, the abundant boons that dwelt within your heart.
The birth, the deeds, the austerity, and the discipline of those two and of you are alike abundant; by those two the god is worshipped in the liṅga, and by you in the image, age after age.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whoever, knowing Bhava to be of all forms, worships the Lord in the liṅga, in him are everlasting union of the self and union prescribed by scripture.
Thus the gods and the Siddhas and the supreme sages, by sacrificing, seek the highest and everlasting station in the world.
This very Keśava is both a devotee of Rudra and sprung from Rudra; Kṛṣṇa indeed is the one to be worshipped, and he is the eternal one to be honored with sacrifices.
To him who, knowing Bhava as the source of all beings, worships the Lord in the liṅga, the bull-bannered god shows surpassing favor.
Saṃjaya said: Hearing that speech of his, the son of Droṇa, the mighty car-warrior, made obeisance to Rudra and held Keśava in high honor.
His hair bristling with joy, his soul subdued, having bowed to the great sage, he turned toward the army and ordered the withdrawal.
Then there was a withdrawal of the Pāṇḍavas, O lord of peoples, and of the stricken Kauravas, now that Droṇa had fallen in the fight.
Having waged war for five days and destroyed many a host, Droṇa, the Brāhmaṇa who had crossed to the far shore of the Vedas, went to the world of Brahmā, O king.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When that surpassing car-warrior Droṇa had been slain there, O Saṃjaya, what did my men and the Pāṇḍavas do thereafter?
Saṃjaya said: When that surpassing car-warrior Droṇa had been slain by the son of Pṛṣata, and the Kauravas were broken, Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī,
having beheld a very great marvel that brought him victory, questioned Vyāsa, who had come by chance, O bull of the Bhāratas:
"As I slew my foes in battle with floods of gleaming arrows, I marked before me a Person moving on, with the radiance of fire,
holding aloft a blazing trident; and in whatever quarter he advanced, in that quarter my foes fell shattered, O great sage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His feet touched not the ground, nor did he ever cast his trident; yet from that trident, by his splendor, thousands of tridents shot forth.
All the foes broken by him the people deem broken by me; the armies consumed by him I do but burn over again from behind.
Tell me this, O blessed one: who is that supreme Person, the great trident-bearer, dark of hue, in splendor like the sun?"
Vyāsa said: It was the first of the Lords of Creatures, the Person of fiery splendor, the all-pervading, the very abode of being, earth and atmosphere, the god, the Lord and master of all the worlds —
the Ruler, the boon-giver, Śaṃkara, whom you have seen, O Pārtha. Go for refuge to that god, the origin of all, the Lord of the world —
Mahādeva, the great of soul, the Ruler, the matted-haired, the auspicious Śiva, the three-eyed, the mighty-armed Rudra, crested, clad in rags, the giver to his devotees of boons granted in his grace.
The divine attendants of that pervading Lord are of forms manifold and various — dwarfish, matted-haired, shaven, short of neck, huge of belly,
and others vast of body, of great vigor, great of ear, with distorted faces and feet, O Pārtha, and with monstrous garbs.
Worshipped by such as these, that Mahādeva, the Great Lord, that splendid Śiva, my son, moves of his grace before you, O Pārtha, in that dreadful, hair-raising battle.
That army, guarded by Droṇa, Karṇa, and Kṛpa, mighty bowmen and smiters — who then, O Pārtha, could even in thought assail it, save the gods and the great bowman of many forms, the Great Lord?
None dares to stand his ground when that one stands before him; for no being is found equal to him in all the three worlds.
In battle, at the very scent of him when he is enraged, his foes, swooning and all but slain, tremble and fall.
Doing him homage, the gods abide in heaven, and so do other men in the world, and those mortals who have conquered heaven.

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
the vast-bellied, the great-bodied, clad in a panther's skin, the Lord of the world, the boon-giver, the shaven, the friend of holiness, dear to the Brāhmaṇas;
the trident-handed, the boon-giver, the Lord who bears sword and shield, the wielder of the Pināka, the one of the broken axe, the Lord and Master of the worlds — to that god, the refuge of all, clad in rags, I go for shelter.
Homage to that Lord of the gods, whose friend is Vaiśravaṇa; to the well-clad, ever homage, to the one of holy vows, the bearer of the goodly bow;
to the god with the sacrificial ladle in hand, the one of the gladdening bow, the bowman, the one in the bow's interval, the bow itself, the master of archery, the archer.
Homage to the god of dreadful weapons, and to the best of the gods; homage be to him of manifold forms, and homage to him who wields many bows.
Homage forever to Sthāṇu, the firm of vows, the bearer of the goodly bow; homage to the slayer of Tripura, and homage indeed to him who struck down Bhaga.
Homage to the lord of the forest trees, to the lord of men; homage forever to the lord of the waters, and homage to the lord of sacrifices.
Homage to the destroyer of Pūṣan's teeth, to the three-eyed boon-giver, to the blue-throated, the tawny, the golden-haired indeed.
And the divine deeds of the wise Mahādeva — these I shall recount to you, as far as my understanding reaches and as I have heard them.
When he is angered, neither gods nor demons in the world, neither Gandharvas nor Rākṣasas, prosper in happiness — not even those who have hidden themselves in a cave.
Enraged, Bhava, the fearless, then pierced the sacrifice, and loosing an arrow from his bow he roared aloud with a great cry.
Then the gods found no shelter, much less peace, when the sacrifice scattered all at once and Maheśvara was wroth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At that sound of the bowstring and the palm striking it, all the worlds were thrown into turmoil, O Pārtha, and gods and demons alike, overmastered, fell down.
All the waters were stirred up, the earth trembled, the mountains were shattered, and the quarters of the sky and the Nāgas were stupefied.
And the worlds, blinded by darkness and shrouded over, gave no light, for he had stricken away, along with the Sun, the radiance of all the luminaries.
And the seers, terror-stricken, cried out, and likewise performed rites of appeasement, desiring the welfare of all beings and of themselves.
Śaṃkara, as if laughing, rushed upon Pūṣan and dashed out the teeth of the god as he was eating the sacrificial cake.
Then the gods went forth, trembling and bowing low to him; and once more he fitted to the string his blazing, sharpened arrow aimed at the gods.
And out of fear the gods then assigned to Rudra a distinguished share in the sacrifice, O king, and took refuge with him.
And by that very excess of his wrath the sacrifice was then restored; the gods grew watchful of him, and watchful they remain toward him even to this day.
The mighty Asuras had three great cities in the sky: one of iron, one of silver, and another, the greatest, of gold.
The iron city was Tārakākṣa's, the silver Kamalākṣa's, and the supreme golden one belonged to Vidyunmālin.
Maghavan was unable to break those cities even with all his weapons; then all the immortals, sorely afflicted, went to Rudra for refuge.
All the gods, with Vāsava at their head, spoke to that great one: 'Rudra, beasts shall become the offering in all sacred rites; lay low these Asuras, O lord of the worlds.'
Thus addressed, he said 'So be it,' and out of desire for the gods' welfare he stood motionless as a post for a thousand full years.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When at last the three cities came together in the firmament, he pierced them with that three-jointed, three-barbed shaft.
And the Dānavas of those cities could not so much as look upon that arrow, joined with the fire of doom and conjoined with Viṣṇu and Soma.
Making himself a child with five tufts of hair seated in her lap, Umā, wishing to test the gods, asked them, 'Who is this?'
The Lord paralyzed the thunderbolt-bearing arm of the angered Śakra — he, this very god, the blessed one, sovereign of all the worlds.
Yet the gods, together with the Prajāpatis, all failed to recognize him, the lord of the worlds, whose radiance was like the newly risen sun.
Then Brahmā, drawing near and beholding that Maheśvara, knew 'This is the highest,' and the Grandfather paid him homage.
Thereupon those gods propitiated Umā and Rudra, and the arm of the thunderbolt-wielder became once more as it had been by nature.
The Lord, with his consort, the bull-bannered, best of the Thirty among gods, the destroyer of Dakṣa's sacrifice, was gracious to them.
He indeed is Rudra, and he is Śiva; he is Agni, he is Śarva, he the all-knowing; he is both Indra and Vāyu, he the Aśvins, and he the lightnings.
He is Bhava, and he is Parjanya; he is Mahādeva, and he the sinless; he is the moon, he is Īśāna, he is the Sun, and he is Varuṇa.
He is Time, he is the Ender, he is Death; he is Yama, and the nights and days; the months, the fortnights, the seasons, the twilights, and the year — that is he.
He is both Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, the soul of all, the doer of every work; and he, the formless, bears the form of all the deities.
Praised by all the gods, the god is one and yet manifold — a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and so a hundred-thousandfold.
Such is that Mahādeva, and yet more is the blessed unborn one; for not all the virtues of the Lord can be told by me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those seized by every malign planet and beset with every sin — them, well pleased, he sets free, the refuge of those who come to him for refuge.
Long life, health, lordship, wealth, and abundant desires he grants to men; and he too snatches them away again.
His sovereignty is proclaimed over the gods, Indra and the rest; and it is he who ordains in the world the good and the ill of men.
Because of his lordship over all desires he is again called the Lord; and he is Maheśvara, the great lord of beings, the lord of the mighty ones.
With many forms in many ways he pervades the whole universe; and that mouth of this god abides within the ocean.
And this god dwells perpetually in the cremation grounds; there men worship him, the Lord, by the name 'Abode of Heroes.'
His forms are blazing and terrible and many; those which men make and speak of in the world are his.
His names in the worlds are many, and here they are fittingly derived, according to his greatness, his pervading power, and his deeds.
And in the Veda the supreme Śatarudrīya is handed down concerning him, and by the name 'Endless Rudra' the worship of the great-souled one is performed.
That god is lord of all desires, the heavenly and the human alike; he is the all-pervading, he the sovereign god who fills the whole great universe.
The Brāhmaṇas and the sages call him the eldest of beings; for he is the first of the gods, and from his mouth the fire arose.
Because in every way he protects the creatures and again takes his delight in them, and because he is their overlord, he is therefore called Paśupati.
Because by his perpetual chastity his liṅga stands erect, and because the worlds magnify him, he is remembered as Maheśvara.
The seers and the gods, and likewise the Gandharvas and Apsarases, worship his liṅga, and it too stands upraised.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When that liṅga is worshipped, Maheśvara rejoices; Śaṃkara becomes happy and pleased and well delighted.
Because his form is manifold, abiding in past, future, and present, both unmoving and moving, he is therefore remembered as Bahurūpa, of many forms.
He sits blazing as the one-eyed, or else made all of eyes on every side; and because in wrath he entered into the worlds, he is therefore remembered as Śarva.
Because his form is smoke-grey he is called Dhūrjaṭi; and because all the gods abide in him, he is therefore remembered as Viśvarūpa.
And because the lord of the worlds embraces the three goddesses — heaven, the waters, and the earth — he is therefore remembered as Tryambaka.
Because he ever furthers all ends in all undertakings, desiring the welfare of men, he is therefore remembered as Śiva, the auspicious.
Thousand-eyed, or ten-thousand-eyed, or made all of eyes on every side, and because he protects this whole great universe, he is therefore remembered as Mahādeva.
Because, standing upright, he burns, and because he abides at the source of the life-breaths, and because his liṅga ever stands fixed, he is therefore remembered as Sthāṇu, the pillar.
Dwelling unevenly in bodies, yet equal in all living beings here, he is the Vāyu coursing unevenly within the bodies as the in-breath and the out-breath.
Whoever worships his image, or duly honors his liṅga — he who ever worships the liṅga attains great prosperity.
From the thighs upward, half his auspicious body is of fire and half of the moon; one half of himself is said to be Agni, and again the other half is Soma.
Toward the gods his auspicious body is fiery, vast, and blazing; among men this radiant body of his is called the dreadful fire.
With that body of his which is auspicious he practices chastity; but with that more terrible form of his the Lord devours all things.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Because he burns all utterly, because he is sharp, fierce, and full of scorching might, and because he is the devourer of flesh, blood, and marrow, he is therefore called Rudra.
This god is Mahādeva, he whom you, O Pārtha, beheld before you in battle, smiting down your foes — the bearer of the Pināka.
It is this blessed god who goes before you in battle — he by whom your weapons were given, and by which you slew the Dānavas.
The Śatarudriya of the god of gods — bestowing fortune, fame, and long life, holy, and named in the Vedas — has now been expounded to you, O Pārtha.
It accomplishes all ends, it is holy, it destroys all defilements, it stills all sins, and it takes away all sorrow and fear.
The man who ever hears this fourfold hymn of praise conquers all his enemies and is exalted in the world of Rudra.
This auspicious, divine, warlike deed of the great-souled one — reciting the Śatarudrīya and hearing it, ever diligent —
the man who among mortals is ever devoted to the god Viśveśvara obtains the boons of his desire when Tryambaka is well pleased.
Go, fight, O son of Kuntī; there is no defeat for you, for at your side, as counselor and protector, stands Janārdana.
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus to Arjuna on the field of battle, the son of Parāśara then departed, O best of the Bhāratas, scourge of foes, by the way he had come.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O king, when Droṇa had been slain, the kings led by Duryodhana, their minds sorely troubled, came to Droṇa's son.
Grieving for Droṇa, their vigour struck down by despair, stricken with sorrow they gathered round the son of Śāradvatī's daughter.
Having for a while consoled one another with reasons drawn from the scriptures, when night came on those guardians of the earth withdrew to their own quarters.
Above all the son of the charioteer, and King Suyodhana, and Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni could find no sleep.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Even within their dwellings, O Kaurava, those lords of the earth found no ease; brooding on the dire ruin, they could not sleep at all.
Gathered together that night in Duryodhana's abode, out of their fierce and burning hatred for the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
recalling how they had dragged Kṛṣṇā, tormented by the dice-game, into the assembly hall, they were filled with remorse, their minds sorely distressed.
And brooding on those afflictions of the sons of Pṛthā that the dice-game had wrought, O king, they passed the night in misery, and it seemed to them as long as a hundred years.
Then in the clear dawn, abiding under the rule of fate, they all performed their necessary rites with the observances ordained by scripture.
Having done their needful tasks and taken heart again, O Bhārata, they gave the order to array the troops and marched out for battle.
Having made Karṇa their commander, performing the auspicious rites of consecration, having the foremost of the twice-born pronounce blessings over them with bowls of curds, clarified butter, and unbroken grains,
honoured with gold coins, with cattle, with gold, and with garments of great worth, and exalted with benedictions of victory by bards, minstrels, and panegyrists,
likewise the Pāṇḍavas, O king, having completed all their daily observances, marched out from their camp, O king, resolved upon battle.
Then there broke out a tumultuous, hair-raising battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, each side seeking the slaughter of the other.
For two days the battle of those two armies, the Kuru and the Pāṇḍava hosts, raged on while Karṇa was commander, O king, a wondrous sight to behold.
Then, when the Bull among men had wrought a very great destruction of the foe in battle, he was struck down by Phalguna before the very eyes of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Saṃjaya, going to the city named after the elephant, related the whole of it to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, all that had come to pass in the land of the Kurus.
Janamejaya said: When the aged king, the son of Ambikā, heard that the son of the river-goddess and Droṇa had been slain in battle by their foes, and was plunged into the deepest anguish—
when he heard that Karṇa too, who sought Duryodhana's welfare, was slain, how, O best of the twice-born, did he in his grief sustain his life?
That king reposed his sons' hope of victory in Karṇa; when he was slain, how did the Kaurava keep his life within him?
Hard to die indeed, I think, is it for men, even those who dwell in misery, since on hearing that Karṇa was slain the king did not yet give up his life.
So too the aged son of Śaṃtanu, O brahmin, and Bāhlika as well, and Droṇa, and Somadatta, and Bhūriśravas—
and likewise his other friends, and his sons and grandsons struck down—that on hearing of these he did not let his life go, that, O twice-born one, I deem a thing hard to do.
Tell me all this in full, O you whose wealth is austerity; for I am not sated, hearing the great deeds of the men of old.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Karṇa was slain, O great king, the son of Gavalgaṇa, downcast, set out that night for the city of the elephant with horses swift as the wind.
Reaching Hāstinapura, his mind sorely troubled, he went to the dwelling of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, now bereft of its kinsmen.
Beholding the king, his vigour struck down by despair, with joined palms he made his obeisance, and touched the king's feet with his head.
And having honoured Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the earth, as was due, and crying, "Alas, what calamity!", he then took up his speech.
"I am Saṃjaya, O lord of the earth. I trust your Majesty fares well. Having come to this disaster through your own fault, are you not today utterly bewildered?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Recalling the wholesome counsels spoken by Vidura, Droṇa, the son of Gaṅgā, and Keśava, counsels you did not heed—do you not now feel anguish?
Recalling the wholesome words spoken by Rāma, Nārada, and Kaṇva in the assembly hall, words you did not heed—do you not now feel anguish?
Recalling your friends, devoted to your good and led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, slain in battle by the foe—do you not now feel anguish?"
To the charioteer's son who spoke thus with joined palms, the king, drawing a long, deep sigh, stricken with grief, said this:
"Now that the heroic son of Gaṅgā, who wielded divine weapons, has been slain, O Saṃjaya, and Droṇa too, that supreme bowman, my mind is sorely afflicted.
He who, born of the Vasus and full of splendour, day after day slew ten thousand mailed warriors on their chariots—
that he was slain by Yajñasena's son Śikhaṇḍin, shielded by the Pāṇḍavas—at this my mind is sorely afflicted.
He to whom, the high-souled one, the descendant of Bhṛgu gave the supreme weapon, he who in boyhood was instructed in the science of the bow by Rāma himself—
by whose grace the sons of Kuntī, those mighty princes, and other lords of the earth as well, attained the rank of great chariot-warriors—
hearing that this Droṇa, true to his word, that great bowman, was slain in battle by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, my mind is sorely afflicted.
He whose equal in the science of arms was not to be found among men in all the three worlds—when they heard that this Droṇa was slain, what did my men do?
When the host of the saṃśaptakas was sent, by the valour of the high-souled Pāṇḍava Dhanaṃjaya, to the abode of Yama,
and when the Nārāyaṇa weapon of the wise son of Droṇa had been undone, and the surviving ranks of the army stood, what did my men do?
I think them put to flight, sunk in an ocean of grief when Droṇa was slain, drifting like men whose ship has foundered upon the sea.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of Duryodhana, of Karṇa, of the Bhoja Kṛtavarman, of Śalya the king of the Madras, and of Droṇa's son, and of Kṛpa—
and of my surviving sons, and likewise of the others, O Saṃjaya—when their ranks were scattered, what hue was upon their faces?
Tell me, O son of Gavalgaṇa, all this just as it came to pass in battle, truly and in full, of both the Pāṇḍavas and my own men."
Saṃjaya said: What the Pāṇḍavas did to the Kauravas, O honoured one—hearing it, do not give way to anguish; over what is destined the mind is not afflicted.
Since whatever outcome is to befall a man, whether it shall come to pass or not, no wise man is troubled by its coming or its failing to come.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: No anguish whatever is in me as I listen, Saṃjaya; this, I think, was ordained long ago. Tell it as you will.
Saṃjaya said: When Droṇa the great bowman was slain, your sons, those mighty chariot-warriors, grew downcast of face, dejected, and bereft of spirit.
With faces bowed down, those bearers of weapons, every one of them, O lord of peoples, not even looking at one another, stricken with grief, spoke not among themselves.
Seeing them in their stricken aspect, your troops, O Bhārata, gazed only upward, oftentimes panicked with grief.
And their weapons, O lord of kings, all of them stained with blood, slipped from their fingertips at the sight of Droṇa struck down.
Those weapons, still bound to them yet unwelcome, hanging loose, O Bhārata, appeared, O great king, like the stars in the sky.
Seeing his own army thus stricken and motionless, standing as though its very life had gone out of it, O great king, King Duryodhana spoke:
"Relying upon the strength of your arms, I challenged the Pāṇḍavas to battle, and this war was set in motion.
Now that Droṇa is slain, this host seems sunk in dejection; yet warriors who fight in battle are struck down on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whether victory or death befall the man who fights in battle—what marvel is there in that? Fight on, then, facing every quarter!
And behold the high-souled Karṇa, son of the Sun, that great bowman of mighty strength, ranging through the battle with his divine weapons!
He, from dread of whom in battle Kuntī's son Dhanaṃjaya ever turns back in vexation, as a small beast from a lion—
he by whom Bhīmasena, mighty in strength, with the vigour of ten thousand elephants, was brought to such a plight by mere human combat—
he by whom that hero Ghaṭotkaca, knower of divine weapons and master of illusions, was slain in battle with the unfailing spear, even as he roared a fearsome roar—
the inexhaustible might of the arms of that wise hero, true to his word and unconquerable in valour, you shall behold this day in battle.
The prowess of both these high-souled ones, of Droṇa's son and of the son of Rādhā, you shall also behold amid the hosts of the Pāṇḍavas and the Pāñcālas.
And you yourselves, all of you—heroes, wise, nobly born, of good conduct, and skilled in arms—shall this day behold one another's deeds."
When this had been said, O great king, Karṇa, son of the Sun, the mighty prince, raising aloud a lion's roar, gave battle with all his great strength.
Before the eyes of all the Sṛñjayas, the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, and the Videhas, he wrought a great slaughter.
From his bow there poured forth showers of arrows by the hundred, joined point to feathered shaft like ranks of bees.
Having harried the Pāñcālas and the swift Pāṇḍavas, and having slain warriors by the thousand, he was at last struck down by Arjuna.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When he had heard this, O great king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra the son of Ambikā, seeing no end to his grief and believing Suyodhana slain, fell distraught upon the ground like an elephant bereft of consciousness.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When that best of kings, distraught, had fallen upon the ground, there arose a great cry of anguish from the women, O best of the Bhāratas.
That sound filled the whole earth on every side; the women of the Bharatas were plunged in a vast and terrible ocean of sorrow.
And drawing near to the king, O bull of the Bhāratas, Gāndhārī fell senseless to the ground, and so did all the women of the inner apartments.
Then Saṃjaya, O king, comforted those stricken women, who were swooning again and again and shedding the water born of their eyes.
Though comforted, those women trembled again and again, shaken on every side like plantain trees buffeted by the wind.
And Vidura too then comforted the king, that lord whose only sight was wisdom, sprinkling the Kaurava with water.
Slowly regaining his senses, and beholding those women, O king, the king stood silent like one out of his mind, O lord of peoples.
Then, having brooded a long while and sighing again and again, he reproached his own sons and held the Pāṇḍavas in high regard.
Having condemned his own judgement and that of Śakuni the son of Subala, and having pondered for a very long while, trembling again and again,
and having steadied his mind once more, the king, now possessed of fortitude, questioned again the charioteer Saṃjaya, the son of Gavalgaṇa.
The words you have spoken, Saṃjaya, I have heard; but tell me, charioteer—surely Duryodhana has not gone to the abode of Yama? Speak truly, Saṃjaya, and tell over again this same account.
Thus addressed, Janamejaya, the charioteer answered the king: Slain is Vaikartana, O king, together with his sons, the mighty warriors, and with his brothers, the great archers, the sons of charioteers who gave up their bodies in battle.
And Duḥśāsana was slain by the glorious son of Pāṇḍu, and in his wrath Bhīmasena drank his blood upon the field of battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this, O great king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, his mind distracted with grief, spoke to Saṃjaya the charioteer.
My son, my soul is overwhelmed by my own ill counsel; hearing that Vaikartana is slain, grief cuts me to the quick.
Among the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas, supreme masters of weapons longing to cross to the further shore of sorrow—who now live, and who are dead?
Saṃjaya said: Slain, O king, is the son of Śaṃtanu, the unassailable and majestic one, after he had slain a host of the Pāṇḍava warriors in the space of ten days.
Then Droṇa, the great archer, hard to overcome in battle, having slain the chariot-ranks of the Pāñcālas, was afterward struck down—he of the golden car.
And Karṇa, son of Vikartana, having slain half of the army that remained after the slaughter wrought by Bhīṣma and the great-souled Droṇa, was himself slain.
Viviṃśati, O great king, the mighty prince, having slain the Ānarta warriors by hundreds, was himself slain in battle.
Then your son Vikarṇa, mindful of the kṣatriya's vow, the hero whose mount and weapons were spent, stood facing the foe.
He was struck down by Bhīmasena, who remembered the many dreadful torments wrought by Duryodhana, and his own oath as well.
Vinda and Anuvinda, the two princes of Avanti, mighty in strength, having performed a deed no easy thing to do, went to the abode of the son of Vivasvat.
That hero under whose sway ten realms, the kingdom of Sindhu chief among them, abode, and who stood firm in your command—
that Jayadratha of great valor, having vanquished eleven divisions of troops with his sharpened arrows, was slain by Arjuna, O king.
So too the swift son of Duryodhana, frenzied for battle, abiding by his father's command, was struck down by the son of Subhadrā.
So too the heroic son of Duḥśāsana, strong of arm and fierce in battle, was sent valorously to the seat of Yama by the son of Draupadī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The lord of the Kirātas who dwell along the sea-marshes, righteous of soul, the dear and highly esteemed friend of the king of the gods—
that king Bhagadatta, ever devoted to the kṣatriya's law, was sent valorously to the seat of Yama by Dhanaṃjaya.
So too the heir of the Kurus, the son of Somadatta, of great renown, the hero Bhūriśravas, was slain in battle by Sātyaki, O king.
And Śrutāyu of the Ambaṣṭhas, a bowman among kṣatriyas, ranging fearlessly through the fray, was slain by Savyasācin.
Your son Duḥśāsana, ever skilled in arms in battle and frenzied for the fight, was struck down by Bhīmasena, O great king.
That Sudakṣiṇa, O king, whose elephant host was many thousands strong and wondrous, was slain in the encounter by Savyasācin.
The lord of the Kosalas, having slain his foes by the hundreds, was sent valorously to the seat of Yama by the son of Subhadrā.
Your son Citrasena, a great chariot-warrior, having fought many a bout with Bhīmasena, was struck down by Bhīmasena himself.
The heroic son of the king of the Madras, who heightened the terror of his foes, the resplendent bearer of sword and shield, was struck down by the son of Subhadrā.
Vṛṣasena, of great splendor, swift with his weapons and firm of resolve, the equal of Karṇa in battle, before the very eyes of Karṇa—
recalling the slaying of Abhimanyu and his own vow as well, Dhanaṃjaya sent him valorously to the seat of Yama.
That lord of earth Śrutāyu, ever bound in unceasing enmity with the Pāṇḍavas, having proclaimed his feud, was struck down by Pārtha.
And the valiant son of Śalya, Rukmaratha, your nephew on the mother's side, O honored one, was slain in battle by Sahadeva, O king.
The aged king Bhagīratha and Bṛhatkṣatra of the Kekayas, two valiant ones of surpassing might, striving in their prowess, were slain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The son of Bhagadatta, O king, sagacious and mighty in strength, was struck down by Nakula, who ranged through the battle like a hawk.
Your grandsire too, Bāhlika, together with the Bāhlīkas, was sent valorously to the seat of Yama by Bhīmasena.
So too Jayatsena, son of Jarāsaṃdha, of great strength, the Māgadha, was slain in battle by the great-souled son of Subhadrā.
Your sons Durmukha and Duḥsaha, the great chariot-warrior, O king, who held themselves heroes, were both slain by Bhīmasena with his mace.
Durmarṣaṇa, Durviṣaha, and Durjaya the great chariot-warrior, having performed a deed no easy thing to do, went to the abode of the son of Vivasvat.
Your counselor Vṛṣavarman, the charioteer of supreme valor, was sent valorously to the seat of Yama by Bhīmasena.
The king Nāgāyutabala, mighty with the strength of ten thousand elephants, together with his troop, was slain by the son of Pāṇḍu, Savyasācin.
The Vasātis, O great king, two thousand fighting men, and the valiant Śūrasenas, were all struck down in battle.
The mailed Abhīṣāhas, smiting and frenzied with battle-fury, and the noble car-warriors among the Śibis, together with the Kaliṅgas, were slain.
The bands reared ever among the cow-herds, supremely skilled in war, the troops many thousands strong, and the hosts of the saṃśaptakas—all these, having come against Pārtha, went to the abode of the son of Vivasvat.
Your two brothers-in-law, O great king, the kings Vṛṣaka and Acala, who strove valiantly for your sake, were slain by Savyasācin.
The king of the Śālvas, a great archer fierce in deed both in name and in act, O great king, was struck down by Bhīmasena.
Oghavat and Bṛhanta together, O great king, striving in battle for their ally's sake, went to the abode of the son of Vivasvat.
So too the foremost of car-warriors, Kṣemadhūrti, O lord of peoples, was slain with the mace by Bhīmasena in the fray, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
So too the king Jalasaṃdha, a great archer of mighty strength, having wrought a vast slaughter, was slain by Sātyaki in battle.
Alāyudha, lord of the rākṣasas, who rode a car drawn by asses, was sent valorously to the seat of Yama by Ghaṭotkaca.
The sons of Rādhā and the charioteers' sons, and his brothers the great car-warriors, and the Kekayas as well, were all slain by Savyasācin.
The Mālavas and the Madrakas, the Draviḍas of fierce prowess, the Yaudheyas and the Lalitthas, the Kṣudrakas and the Uśīnaras—
the Māvellakas, the Tuṇḍikeras, the Sāvitrīputras and the Kāñcalas, the men of the East and the North, of the West and of the South, O honored one—
the throngs of footmen were slain, and tens of thousands of horses, and the ranks of chariots were destroyed, and the noble elephants slain.
Heroes with their banners, their weapons, their armor, raiment, and ornaments, prepared over a long span of time and reared each in his own line—
these were slain in battle, O king, by Pārtha of untiring deeds, and others of measureless strength who sought one another's destruction.
These and many other kings with their hosts were slain by the thousands in battle, O king, as you ask of me; thus came about this destruction at the meeting of Karṇa and Arjuna.
As Vṛtra was slain by great Indra, as Rāvaṇa by Rāma, as Muru was cast down and slain in battle by Kṛṣṇa, and as Kārtavīrya was slain by Rāma of the Bhṛgu line—
so the hero with his kinsmen and friends, frenzied for the fight in battle, having waged a great and terrible war renowned through the three worlds—
even so Karṇa, the best of smiters, frenzied for the fight, was slain in single chariot-combat by Arjuna, together with his counselors and kinsmen, O king.
The hope of victory of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and the very source of the feud, that have the Pāṇḍavas now passed beyond, O king—that which long ago you would not perceive.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Though told of it, O great king, by kinsmen who wished you well, this calamity of great ruin has now overtaken you.
Wishing well to your sons who craved a kingdom, O king, you wrought what was as if to their harm; the fruit of those deeds has now come upon you.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: You have told me, my son, of my own men slain in battle by the Pāṇḍavas; now tell me, Saṃjaya, of the Pāṇḍavas' men slain by mine.
Saṃjaya said: The Kuntīs, valiant in battle, of great courage and great strength, with their followers and counselors, were struck down in battle by Bhīṣma.
Satyajit, the equal in battle of the diademed one in valor and in strength, was slain in the fray by the true-vowed Droṇa.
So too the aged kings Virāṭa and Drupada, together with their sons, striving for their ally's sake, were slain in battle by Droṇa.
He who, though but a boy in battle, was reckoned the equal of Savyasācin, of Keśava, and of Baladeva, unassailable and overpowering—
that very Abhimanyu, skilled in war, having wrought a great slaughter, was surrounded by six foremost mighty chariot-warriors who could not withstand Bībhatsu, and was struck down.
That hero, made carless yet steadfast in the kṣatriya's law, the son of Subhadrā, was slain in battle by the son of Duḥśāsana, O great king.
Bṛhanta, the great archer skilled in arms and frenzied for the fight, was sent valorously to the seat of Yama by Duḥśāsana.
Maṇimat and Daṇḍadhāra, two kings frenzied for the fight, striving for their ally's sake, were struck down by Droṇa.
Aṃśumat, the Bhoja king, a great chariot-warrior, together with his army, was sent valorously to the seat of Yama by the son of Bharadvāja.
Citrāyudha and Citrayodhin, having both wrought a great slaughter, were slain in battle by Karṇa, who struck them valorously by a wondrous course of arms.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Kekaya prince, the equal of Vṛkodara in battle and steadfast in the fray, was struck down valorously by his own brother, a Kekaya—brother by brother.
Janamejaya, the mace-fighter of the mountain-folk, full of majesty, was struck down by your son Durmukha, O great king.
The two Rocamānas, tigers among men, shining like two planets, were sent at once to heaven by Droṇa's arrows, O king.
And kings who fought back valiantly, O lord of peoples, having performed a deed no easy thing to do, went to the abode of the son of Vivasvat.
Purujit Kuntibhoja, the maternal uncle of Savyasācin, was sent by Droṇa's shafts to the worlds won by battle.
Abhibhū, the king of Kāśi, surrounded by many men of Kāśi, was made to lay down his body in the fight by the son of Vasudāna.
Yudhāmanyu of measureless might and the valiant Uttamaujas, having slain heroes by the hundreds, were slain by the foe in battle.
Kṣatradharman the Pāñcāla and Kṣatravarman, O honored one, those two supreme archers, were sent to the seat of Yama by Droṇa.
The son of Śikhaṇḍin, Kṣatradeva, a lord of warriors, was slain in battle by Lakṣmaṇa, your grandson, O king, O descendant of Bharata.
Sucitra and Citradharman, father and son, both mighty chariot-warriors of great valor, while they ranged across the field were slain in battle by Droṇa.
Vārdhakṣemi, O great king, after wreaking havoc in the fray, was struck down, O great king, by the Kaurava Bāhlika.
Dhṛṣṭaketu, O great king, foremost chariot-warrior of the Cedis, having done a deed hard to accomplish, went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
So too Satyadhṛti, my son, having wrought slaughter in the fray and shown his prowess for the Pāṇḍavas' cause, was sent to the dwelling of Yama.
And the son of Śiśupāla, Suketu, O lord of the earth, having slain his foes in the clash, was himself slain in battle by Droṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Likewise the hero Satyadhṛti, the valiant Madirāśva, and the bold Sūryadatta were laid low by the arrows of Droṇa.
And Śreṇimat, O great king, valorous as he fought, having performed a deed hard to do, went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
In the same way the Māgadha, bold in battle, slayer of enemy heroes, valorous as he fought, was slain, O king, by Bhīṣma.
And Vasudāna, wreaking great carnage in the conflict, was sent by the prowess of the son of Bharadvāja to the dwelling of Yama.
These and many other great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas were slain by Droṇa through his valor — this is what you ask of me.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Now that the foremost heroes of this my army are slain, O best of speakers, tell me, O Sūta, of those unslain — whoever among them still lives.
Now that those you have named are slain, even those whom you reckon unslain — they too, I deem, are as good as won over by heaven.
Saṃjaya said: He in whom the great weapons were vested — wondrous, gleaming, of four kinds, and divine, O king — bestowed upon him by Droṇa, best of heroic brahmins;
that great chariot-warrior, skilled and swift of hand, firm in his weapons, firm in grip, firm in his arrows — the valiant, impetuous son of Droṇa stands ready, eager to fight for your sake.
That dweller of Ānarta, the son of Hṛdika, a great chariot-warrior, foremost among the Sātvatas — Kṛtavarman the Bhoja himself, master of weapons — stands ready, eager to fight for your sake.
The son of Śaradvat, the Gautama too, O king, mighty in strength, a fighter with many varied weapons, taking up his wondrous bow, great and able to bear the strain, stands ready and willing to fight.
The son of Ṛtāyana, unshakable in battle, leader of the host, first among your men — having spared those his nephews, the sons of Pāṇḍu, the impetuous one, wishing to make true his pledged word.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having vowed before Ajātaśatru in the clash to quell the splendor of the Sūta's son, the unassailable Śalya, of valor equal to Śakra's, stands ready, eager to fight for your sake.
With horses of high breed, those of Sindhu and the mountains, and the river-born ones of Kāmboja, Vanāyu, and Bāhlika, the king of Gāndhāra, joined with his own host, stands ready, eager to fight for your sake.
And your son too, O foremost of the Kurus, mounting a chariot blazing like fire and sun, Kurumitra stands ready, O lord of men, like the sun shining in a cloudless sky.
Duryodhana, amid his host of elephants, of mighty valor, together with the foremost warriors of the army, on his chariot adorned with gold, stands ready in the battle, eager to fight.
That foremost of men, amid the kings, shone forth in his bright golden mail, lotus-hued, like a fire with little smoke, radiant as the sun gleaming between the clouds.
So too Suṣeṇa, sword and shield in hand, your son, and the hero Satyasena, both stand together with Citrasena, glad of heart, eager to fight in the battle.
The Bharata princes who shun all that is shameful — Citrāyudha, Śrutakarman, and Jaya, and Śala, and Satyavrata and Duḥśalā — stand ready, mighty and eager to fight.
The lord of the Kaitavyas, proud in his valor, a slayer of foes in battle after battle, that prince, with foot and horse, marching with his elephants and chariots, stands ready, eager to fight for your sake.
The hero Śrutāyus and Śrutāyudha, Citrāṅgada and that hero Citravarman — those foremost of men in the army stand ready, smiters all, proud and true to their pledges.
The son of Karṇa, the high-souled Satyasena, stands ready in battle, eager to fight; and two other worthy sons of Karṇa, deft of hand, O lord of men, stand ready, leaning upon a mighty host hard for the faint-hearted to break, willing to fight for your sake.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With these and other chief warriors, foremost in arms, of boundless might, the king of the Kurus stands amid his host of elephants, like great Indra, bent on victory.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: You have told me truly of those who yet live and of the others as well; thus I clearly perceive how things will come to pass, by reckoning the course of events.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Even as he spoke thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, hearing that his own army was shattered, its heroes slain, with but a remnant left, fell into a swoon, his senses overwhelmed by grief.
Swooning, he said: Hold a moment, Saṃjaya; my mind is distraught, my son, hearing of so great a sorrow. And then the lord of the earth lost his senses.
Janamejaya said: Hearing that Karṇa was slain in the battle and that his sons did not flee, what did the king, somewhat recovered, then say, O best of the twice-born?
He who had won the utmost grief, the great sorrow born of his sons' ruin — what he said at that hour, tell me that, for I ask of you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing of Karṇa's death — incredible, marvelous, bewildering to all beings, and terrible as the overturning of Meru;
like an unaccountable bewilderment of mind in the wise descendant of Bhṛgu, like a defeat of Indra of fearsome deeds at the hands of his foes;
like the fall of the radiant sun from heaven to the earth, like the unthinkable drying up of the ocean of inexhaustible waters;
like the marvelous total destruction of earth, sky, and the guardians of the quarters, like the fruitlessness of both deeds, the meritorious and the sinful alike.
Pondering it shrewdly in his mind, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the people, reflecting upon Karṇa's death, thought: "This cannot be."
"Yet, since this is the very nature of living things, such destruction may indeed be" — and his heart was consumed by the fire of grief, as though fanned into flame.

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
He whom the king of Magadha, having won, by conciliation, honor, gifts, and esteem, hemmed in all the warrior princes of the earth, save the Kauravas and the Yādavas.
Hearing that Karṇa was slain in single combat by Savyasācin, I am plunged in an ocean of grief, like one without a raft upon the sea.
If I am not destroyed by such sorrows, Saṃjaya, I deem my heart harder than the thunderbolt and impossible to break.
Hearing of this defeat of kinsmen, relations, and friends, what other man in the world but me, O Sūta, would not give up his life?
I would choose poison, or fire, or a plunge from a mountain's peak; for I shall not be able to bear these grievous sorrows, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: For your splendor, your lineage, your fame, your austerity, and your learning, the good this day reckon you the equal of Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa.
In learning you are the peer of a great sage; you have fulfilled your purpose, O king. Compose yourself; do not set your mind upon despair.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: I deem fate supreme; a curse upon manly effort, which is in vain — for there Karṇa, the equal of Rāma, was slain in battle.
That great chariot-warrior, having slain Yudhiṣṭhira's host and the chariot-squadrons of the Pāñcālas, scorching all the quarters with his rain of arrows —
having bewildered the Pārthas in battle as the thunderbolt-handed one bewilders the Asuras — how is it that he, slain, lies low like a tree shattered by the wind?
I see no end to my grief, as a drowning man sees none to the ocean. My sharp anguish grows, and a longing to die is born in me.
Hearing of Karṇa's death and of Phalguna's victory, I hold the slaying of Karṇa beyond belief, Saṃjaya.
Surely my heart is made of the essence of adamant, and most firm, since, hearing that Karṇa, the tiger among men, is slain, it does not burst asunder.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Surely a very long life was ordained for me by the gods of old, since, hearing that Karṇa is slain, I yet live on here in deep sorrow.
A curse upon this life of mine today, bereft of friends, Saṃjaya. This day, Saṃjaya, fallen into this contemptible state, I shall pass my days in misery, pitiable to all, dull of wit.
I who once was honored by all the world — how, O Sūta, despised, shall I be able to live on again? From sorrow to deeper sorrow I have come, into calamity, Saṃjaya.
Therefore, after the slaying of Bhīṣma and of the high-souled Droṇa, now that the Sūta's son too is slain in battle, I see no remnant left.
For he was the great further shore for my sons, Saṃjaya — that hero, slain in battle while loosing many arrows.
What use is life to me without that bull among men? That surpassing chariot-warrior must have fallen from his car, tormented by arrows,
like a mountain's peak riven by the fall of the thunderbolt; surely he lies upon the earth, adorning it, drenched in blood, like an elephant struck down by a rutting elephant.
He who was the strength of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and from whom came the Pāṇḍavas' fear — that Karṇa, the standard by which bowmen are measured, was slain by Arjuna.
For that hero, the great archer, who gave my sons their freedom from fear — that hero now lies slain, as Bala was slain by Śakra.
Duryodhana's design has proved like the journeying of a cripple, like the desire of a pauper, like the water-droplets craved by one athirst.
The deed is purposed one way, yet it comes to pass in another. Ah, how mighty is fate, and how impossible to overstep is time!
Fleeing piteously, his spirit broken, his manhood failing — has my son Duḥśāsana not been slain, O Sūta?
Did he not act basely in the fray, my son? Was that hero not slain — slain not as warriors are slain in honor?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira's word, ever "Let there be no war" — that the deluded Duryodhana would not accept, as a fool will not take wholesome medicine.
When Bhīṣma, that most high-souled one, lying upon his bed of arrows, asked for water, Pārtha pierced the surface of the earth.
Seeing that stream of water sent forth by the Pāṇḍava, the mighty-armed one said, my child: "Make peace with the Pāṇḍavas."
"For from reconciliation peace would come; let this raging war be ended. In brotherhood enjoy the earth together with the sons of Pāṇḍu."
Surely my son now grieves, having not heeded his words; for now there has come to pass this very utterance of that far-sighted one.
But I, my counsellors slain and my sons slain, O Saṃjaya, have through the dice-game fallen into misery, like a bird with its wings clipped.
For just as little boys, O Saṃjaya, seizing a bird and clipping its two wings, set it loose in their delight, sporting at play—
and with its wings cut off no flight is possible for it—so too am I now reduced, like a bird with its wings clipped.
Wasted away, stripped of every aim, without kinsmen, bereft of my relations—to what quarter shall I turn, wretched and fallen into the power of my foes?
He, the lord who for Duryodhana's increase had conquered the earth, has been vanquished by the Pāṇḍavas—heroes, mighty, abounding in valour.
When that great archer Karṇa was slain in battle by the Diademed one, which heroes still stood their ground? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya.
Was he not abandoned and alone when the Pāṇḍavas struck him down in battle? You told me before, brave one, how the heroes were laid low.
Bhīṣma, who would not fight back, Śikhaṇḍin felled in battle with his finest shafts—him, the best of all who bear weapons.
So too Droṇa—that great archer who had laid down all his weapons in the fight and was rapt in yoga, pierced with many arrows—was slain by Draupadī's son, by Dhṛṣṭadyumna with upraised sword, O Saṃjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By stealth were these two slain, and above all by trickery—so I have heard, that Bhīṣma and Droṇa were brought down.
For Bhīṣma and Droṇa, were they fighting by fair means, not even the Wielder of the Thunderbolt himself could slay them in battle—this truth I declare to you.
But Karṇa, hurling his many celestial weapons—how did death touch in battle that hero who was the equal of Indra?
He to whom, in exchange for his earrings, Purandara gave that celestial spear, gleaming like lightning and adorned with gold, the slayer of foes—
he whose celestial serpent-mouthed shaft, gold-adorned and feathered, the destroyer of foes, lay resting amid the sandalwood—
he who, scorning such heroes and great chariot-warriors as Bhīṣma and Droṇa, learned from the son of Jamadagni the most terrible Brāhma weapon—
he, the mighty-armed, who when he saw Droṇa and the rest turned away and tormented by arrows, shattered with his shafts the bow of Subhadrā's son—
he who, having made my brother's foe Bhīmasena chariotless—him whose strength was that of ten thousand elephants, swift as the wind and unfaltering—laughed at him in mockery—
he who, having vanquished Sahadeva with his straight-jointed arrows and left him chariotless, out of compassion and his knowledge of the right did not slay him—
he who, having scattered a thousand illusions, struck down with Śakra's spear that lord of the Rākṣasas, the battle-frenzied Ghaṭotkaca—
all these days Dhanaṃjaya, afraid of him in battle, that hero, never came to single combat—how then was he slain in the fight?
If his chariot was not stuck fast, if his bow did not shatter, if his weapons did not fail him—how then was he slain by the foe?
Who indeed was able in battle to conquer Karṇa, that tiger among men—shaking his great bow, loosing his dreadful shafts and celestial weapons in the fray, swift as a tiger in its rush?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Surely his bow was cut through, or his chariot sank into the earth, or his weapons failed—since you tell me he is slain; for I can see no other cause of his destruction.
"I will not wash my feet until I have slain Arjuna"—such was the most terrible vow of that great-souled one.
He of whom Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Righteousness, that bull among men, was ever afraid in the forest, and for thirteen years could find no sleep—
he upon whose valour—the valour of that mighty, great-souled one—my son relied when he dragged by force into the assembly the wife of the Pāṇḍavas—
and there too, in the midst of the assembly, before the very eyes of the Pāṇḍavas, called Pāñcālī "a slave's wife" in the gathering of the Kurus—
he who, reckoning nothing of the fierce touch of shafts loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, said "Kṛṣṇā, you have now no husband," and gazed upon the sons of Pṛthā—
he who, relying on the strength of his own arms, had no fear of the sons of Pṛthā, even for a moment, O Saṃjaya—not though their sons and Janārdana stood with them—
his slaying I cannot believe possible even by the gods with Vāsava himself rushing against him—how much less, my child, by the Pāṇḍavas.
For when the son of Adhiratha touched his bowstring and took up his leather guard, no man living was fit to stand before him.
Sooner might the earth be bereft of the radiant beams of moon and sun than that lord of men, who never fled the field, should be slain in battle.
If that dull-witted fool, with his brother Duḥśāsana for ally, took pleasure in rejecting the counsel of Vāsudeva—
surely now, beholding bull-shouldered Karṇa struck down and Duḥśāsana slain, my poor son must grieve—so I think.
Hearing that Vaikartana was slain in single combat by the Ambidextrous one, and seeing the Pāṇḍavas victorious, what then did Duryodhana say?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing that Durmarṣaṇa was slain, and Vṛṣasena too in the fight, and seeing his host broken and cut down by the great chariot-warriors—
and seeing his kings turned away, bent only on flight, his chariot-warriors scattered in rout—my poor son, I think, must grieve.
Unteachable through pride, childish of mind, unforgiving—seeing his host's spirit broken, what then did Duryodhana say?
Seeing his brother slain in the fight by Bhīmasena, who drank his blood—what then did Duryodhana say?
"Karṇa shall slay Arjuna in battle"—so he declared in the assembly together with the king of Gāndhāra; now that Karṇa is slain, what did he say?
Śakuni, the son of Subala, who once played the dice in glee and cheated the Pāṇḍavas—what, my child, did he say when Karṇa was slain?
Kṛtavarman, that great archer, the mighty chariot-warrior of the Sātvatas, the son of Hṛdika—seeing Karṇa utterly slain, what did he say?
He at whose instruction Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas wait, longing to master the science of the bow—the wise son of Droṇa—
that youthful one, endowed with beauty, fair to look upon, of great renown—Aśvatthāman, when Karṇa was slain, what did he say, O Saṃjaya?
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, who had attained mastery in the science of the bow and knew the highest truths—what, my child, did he say when Karṇa was slain?
Śalya, the king of the Madras, that great archer, the ornament of assemblies—surely all that was ordained by him, the manner in which Karṇa was brought down.
And whatever kings of the earth had come to do battle—seeing Vaikartana slain, what did they say, O Saṃjaya?
When the hero Karṇa was slain—that tiger among chariot-warriors, that bull among men—what, O Saṃjaya, became of the front ranks of your several armies?
How came Śalya, the king of the Madras, the best of chariot-warriors, to be appointed to the charioteering of Vaikartana? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Who guarded the right wheel of the Sūta's son in the fight, who the left wheel, and who guarded the hero from behind?
Which heroes stood by Karṇa, and which base ones fled in fear? And how, while you were all assembled together, was the great chariot-warrior Karṇa slain?
And how did the heroic Pāṇḍavas come on against that great chariot-warrior as he poured forth showers of arrows, like a cloud loosing streams of rain?
And how did that celestial serpent-mouthed shaft, the choicest of great arrows, then come to naught? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya.
Of this my host, its eminence now plucked away, O Saṃjaya, I can see no remnant left, its very crest crushed.
Those two heroes, those great archers, those best of the Kurus—Bhīṣma and Droṇa—slain in my cause: hearing it, what worth has life for me?
And I cannot bear that Rādheya is slain, the ornament of battle, the strength of whose two arms was equal to a hundred hundred elephants.
And what befell the Kauravas, the heroes among men, in their battle with the foe after Droṇa was slain—tell me that, O Saṃjaya.
And how Karṇa joined battle with the sons of Kuntī, and how that slayer of foes was stilled in the fight—let that be told.
Saṃjaya said: When the great archer Droṇa had been slain on that day, O descendant of Bharata, and when the great chariot-warrior, Droṇa's son, had been made vain in his resolve—
as the host of the Kauravas streamed away in flight, O great king, the son of Pṛthā drew up his own army in array and stood firm together with his brothers.
Knowing him to stand his ground, O bull of the Bhāratas, and seeing his own force in flight, your son by his manly might held it back.
Having steadied his own ranks and taken his stand upon the strength of his arms, he fought for a long while with the Pāṇḍavas, O descendant of Bharata—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
with foes who had found their mark, exultant, long striving against him; and then, as the hour of twilight came on, he ordered the withdrawal.
Having drawn back their forces and entered their own camp, the Kurus then took counsel together for their own welfare.
Seated upon priceless couches spread with coverings beyond compare, upon excellent seats, they were like the immortals upon their pleasant beds.
Then King Duryodhana, addressing those great archers with words most winning and gentle, spoke what the moment called for:
"You best of the wise, declare your counsel, all of you, without delay—what task, things being thus, would best serve our purpose, O kings."
When the lord of men had thus spoken, those lions among men, eager for the fight, then made gestures of many kinds, seated upon their lion-thrones.
Marking the bearing of those who longed to offer up their lives in battle, and gazing upon the face of the king, whose splendour was like the rising sun, the Preceptor's son, wise and skilled in speech, took up the word:
"Zeal, application, skill, and good policy—these means of achieving an end have been named by the learned; yet all of them rest upon fate."
"Those foremost heroes of the world among us, the godlike great chariot-warriors, prudent, disciplined, skilled, and devoted—they have been slain."
"Yet we must not despair of victory; by sound policy in all our undertakings even fate may be turned to favour."
"So let us make Karṇa, the foremost of men, endowed with every host of virtues, our commander, and crush the foe."
Then Duryodhana, delighted to hear that pleasing speech—charged with the grace of affection, true, salutary, and auspicious to himself—
having steadied his mind and leaning upon the strength of his arms, Duryodhana, O great king, said this to Rādheya:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Karṇa, I know your valour and your supreme love for me; yet even so, mighty-armed one, I shall speak to you a word for your good."
