"Having heard it, do then as you will, brave one, whatever pleases you; for you are ever the wisest of all, and my supreme refuge."
Bhīṣma and Droṇa, those peerless warriors, my two commanders, are slain. Let your good self be my commander, richer in might than both of them.
Those two mighty archers were aged, and both bore tenderness toward Dhanaṃjaya; yet, O Rādheya, those heroes were honored by me at your word.
Mindful of his grandsire's bond, dear one, Bhīṣma spared the sons of Pāṇḍu in the great battle for ten whole days.
And when his weapons were laid down, the grandsire Bhīṣma was slain in the great battle by Phalguna, who put Śikhaṇḍin to the fore.
When that illustrious one fell and lay upon a bed of arrows, then, O tiger among men, at your word Droṇa became the foremost.
He too spared the sons of Pṛthā in this combat, for they had been his pupils; and that aged one was swiftly slain by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Now that those two chief warriors are slain, O man of measureless valor, however I ponder it, I see no other fighter in battle who is your equal.
You alone are able to win us the victory, of this there is no doubt; before, in the midst, and after, all of this has been known to you indeed.
You, then, like a yoke-bearing steed, are worthy to bear the burden in battle; consecrate yourself by your own hand to the office of commander.
As Skanda is the imperishable lord and commander of the gods, so let your good self sustain this army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son for me; strike down all the hosts of foes, as great Indra struck the Dānavas.
When they learn that you, the great car-warrior, stand firm in battle, the Pāṇḍavas with the Pāñcālas will flee as the Dānavas fled at the sight of Viṣṇu; therefore, O tiger among men, lead forth the mighty host.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When you stand fast, the Pāṇḍavas, together with their counselors and with the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas, will be robbed of their senses.
For as the risen Sun, blazing with his own splendor, drives away the thick darkness, so do you drive away our foes.
Karṇa said: This was spoken by me before, O son of Gāndhārī, in your presence: I shall conquer the Pāṇḍavas, O king, with their sons and with Janārdana.
I shall be your commander, herein there is no doubt; be steadfast, O great king, and know the Pāṇḍavas already vanquished.
Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed, the mighty-spirited king Duryodhana then rose up together with the kings, like Indra of the hundred sacrifices amid the gods, to honor Karṇa with the command, as the immortals honored Skanda.
Then swiftly, with rite ordained by scripture, the kings led by Duryodhana, O king, desiring victory, consecrated him with golden jars and with earthen ones over which the sacred mantras had been pronounced,
and with water-filled horns of leopards and rhinoceroses and great bulls, and with others made of gems and pearls, and with fragrant herbs of holy scent.
He was seated upon a throne of fig-wood draped with linen, consecrated by the rite seen in the scriptures and with the requisites well assembled.
"Conquer the sons of Pṛthā, with Govinda and their followers, in the great battle!" Thus, O bull of the Bhāratas, the bards and the twice-born addressed him.
"Strike down the sons of Pṛthā with the Pāñcālas, O Rādheya, for our victory, as the ever-rising Sun strikes the darkness with his fierce rays!"
"For they, with Keśava, are no more a match for the arrows loosed by you than the ungrateful are for the gaze of the blazing rays of the Sun."
"For the sons of Pṛthā with the Pāñcālas can no more stand before you, weapon in hand in battle, than the Dānavas before great Indra."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Consecrated, Rādheya of boundless radiance overflowed in his splendor of form, like a second maker of the day.
Having consecrated Rādheya to the command, your son, driven on by fate, then deemed his purpose accomplished.
And Karṇa too, O king, that subduer of foes, having gained the command, ordered the army to make ready against the rising of the Sun.
Surrounded by your sons, Karṇa shone there, O Bhārata, as Skanda shone amid the gods in the war against Tāraka.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When Karṇa Vaikartana had gained the command and was thus addressed by the king himself with tender words, as to a brother,
having ordered the army to make ready when the Sun had risen, what did that man of great wisdom do? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Learning Karṇa's purpose, O bull of the Bhāratas, your son ordered the array to be made ready, heralded by auspicious music.
In the great hours before dawn, O honored one, there arose all at once in your son's host a mighty din: "To arms! To arms!"
As the elephants were being harnessed and the guarded chariots made ready, as the foot-soldiers and the horses were being armed, O lord of peoples,
and as the warriors hurried, shouting to one another, there rose then a tumultuous uproar, vast and reaching the sky.
Then with a white banner, with horses of the hue of the morning sun, with a gold-backed bow, with the elephant-girth ensign,
with a quiver full of arrows, with an arm-band, guarded all round, bearing the hundred-slayer engines, bells, javelins, lances, and pikes,
furnished with a bow, with the radiance of the spotless sun, upon his tall-bannered chariot, the son of the charioteer appeared.
He was blowing his conch, dear one, adorned with a net of gold, and brandishing his great bow decked with gold.
Seeing Karṇa, the great archer, the foremost of car-warriors, standing on his chariot like the rising Sun dispelling the darkness a thousandfold—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
none of the Kauravas there, O honored one, then took to heart the calamity of Bhīṣma, nor of Droṇa, nor of the others, O tiger among men.
Then, urging on the warriors with the blast of his conch, O honored one, Karṇa led forth the host of the Kauravas.
Having arrayed his troops in the crocodile-formation, the great archer Karṇa, scorcher of foes, then advanced against the Pāṇḍavas, longing for victory.
At the snout of the crocodile Karṇa took his stand, O king; at its two eyes were the brave Śakuni and Ulūka, the great car-warrior.
At the head was the son of Droṇa; at the neck were all your full brothers; in the center stood King Duryodhana, encircled by a mighty force.
At the left foot, O lord of kings, stood Kṛtavarman, joined with the Nārāyaṇa hosts, the cowherds, hard to vanquish in war.
At the right foot, O king, was Gautama of true valor, surrounded by the Trigartas, great archers, and by the men of the south.
At the left hindfoot stood Śalya, together with a great army raised from the land of the Madras.
At the right, O great king, was Suṣeṇa, true to his pledge, encircled by thousands of chariots and by hundreds of tusked elephants.
At the tail stood the two great heroes, the royal brothers, Citrasena and Citra, encircled by a mighty army.
Then, when Karṇa, the best of warriors, had set forth, O lord of kings, the King of Righteousness looked upon Dhanaṃjaya and said this:
"Behold, O Pārtha, the great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son in the battle, arrayed by Karṇa, O hero, and guarded by heroic car-warriors."
"Robbed of its bravest, this great host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, with but its dregs remaining, O mighty-armed one, I deem no better than straw."
"One great archer alone stands firm here, the son of the charioteer, the best of car-warriors, who is unconquerable by the three worlds, moving and unmoving, with their gods, demons, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and great serpents."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Slaying him today, O mighty-armed Phalguna, victory shall be yours, and the thorn of twelve years' standing shall be plucked from me; knowing this, O mighty-armed one, array the troops as you wish."
Hearing his brother's words, the white-horsed son of Pāṇḍu countered that host with a half-moon formation.
On the left flank, O king, Bhīmasena took his stand, and on the right the great archer Dhṛṣṭadyumna of mighty strength.
In the very center of the array stood the son of Pāṇḍu with Kṛṣṇa for his charioteer; behind him were Nakula and Sahadeva and the King of Righteousness.
The two Pāñcālas, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, his wheel-guards, did not forsake Arjuna in battle, themselves protected by the Diademed One.
The remaining heroic kings, mailed, took their places in the array, each according to his rank, his ardor, and his strength, O Bhārata.
Having thus arrayed that great formation, O Bhārata, the Pāṇḍavas and your own great archers set their minds upon battle alone.
Seeing your host arrayed for battle by the son of the charioteer, your son, with his kinsmen, deemed the Pāṇḍavas already slain.
And likewise, seeing the Pāṇḍava army arrayed, Yudhiṣṭhira deemed the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with Karṇa, already slain, O lord of men.
Then the conches and kettledrums, the tabors, drums, and cow-horns were all at once sounded together, resounding on every side.
In both armies, O king, the great-voiced instruments rang out, and the lion-roar of the heroes greedy for victory arose.
The neighing of horses, the trumpeting of elephants, and the fierce rumble of chariot-wheels arose, O lord of men.
No one took to heart the calamity of Droṇa, O bull of the Bhāratas, on seeing the great archer Karṇa, mailed, at the front of the array.
Both armies, of great might, with men and elephants exultant, eager to fight, stood ready, O king, to slay one another at once.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There, intent and inflamed with wrath, having beheld each other take their stand in the midst of the hosts, Karṇa and the son of Pāṇḍu shone forth, O lord of kings.
As the two armies seemed to dance, they came together against each other; and from their wings and from the wings beyond the wings the eager combatants sallied forth.
Then began the battle of men, elephants, and horses, and of car-warriors, O great king, smiting one another fiercely.
Saṃjaya said: Those two armies, vast, with horses, men, and elephants exultant, closing upon each other, fell to blows, like the hosts of gods and demons.
Then elephants, chariots, horses, and foot-soldiers in the great battle dealt one another a supreme onslaught that made an end of body and of sin.
With the severed heads of lions among men—heads matching in loveliness, luster, and fragrance the full moon, the sun, and the lotus—the lions among men strewed the earth.
With crescent-headed shafts, with broad arrows, with razor-tipped darts, with swords and spears, and with battle-axes, they cut off the heads of those who fought.
By the long, outstretched arms of warriors with long, outstretched arms, the long arms of others were made to fall, their fists, weapons, and arm-bands severed.
The earth then gleamed with those quivering arms, their fingers and palms blood-red, like fierce five-hooded serpents struck down by Garuḍa.
From horses, chariots, and elephants the heroes, slain by their foes, fell as the dwellers in heaven fall from their celestial cars when their merit is spent.
Crushed by heavy maces, by iron bludgeons and by pestles, the heroes fell by the hundreds, struck down by braver heroes in the battle.
Chariots were destroyed by chariots, frenzied elephants by frenzied elephants, and horsemen by horsemen, in that utmost tumult.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Chariots slain by noble chariots and by elephants, and horsemen by foot-soldiers, and foot-soldiers by horsemen, lay outstretched, slain in the fight.
Chariots, horses, and foot-soldiers were slain by elephants, and elephants and foot-soldiers by chariots; chariots, foot-soldiers, and elephants by horses, and horses, chariots, and elephants by men.
A great slaughter of chariots, horses, elephants, and men was wrought by men, horses, elephants, and chariots—by hands and feet, by weapons, and by chariots alike.
As that host was being cut down and slain by the brave, the sons of Pṛthā, with Vṛkodara at their head, advanced upon us.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, the sons of Draupadī, the Prabhadrakas, Sātyaki and Cekitāna, together with the Draviḍa soldiers—
and the Pāṇḍyas, the Auḍras, and the Keralas, paid with great wealth—broad-chested, long-armed, tall, and fair to look upon—
crowned with garlands, their teeth reddened, valorous as rutting elephants, clad in robes of many dyes and powdered with fragrant scents,
with swords girded on and nooses in hand, able to ward off charging elephants, sworn to a common death, O king, standing in the ranks shoulder to shoulder—
bearing quivers and bows in hand, long-haired and loving battle—the Āndhra footmen of Sātyaki, dreadful in form and prowess.
Then yet other warriors—the Cedis, the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas, the Karūṣas, the Kosalas, the Kāśis, and the Māgadhas—rushed forth.
Their chariots and elephants and choicest footmen, exultant with cries of every kind, danced and laughed for joy.
Surrounded by the foremost of mighty elephant-drivers, Vṛkodara, mounted at the head of his elephant, drove into the midst of that great host of thine.
That foremost of elephants, most terrible and duly caparisoned, shone like the lofty mansion of the eastern mount when the risen sun stands upon it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Its splendid iron armor, adorned with the choicest gems, gleamed with a radiance equal to the autumn sky aglow with stars.
With lance and javelin in hand, fair-crowned and well-adorned, ranging like the noonday sun, he scorched his foes with his splendor.
Beholding that elephant from afar, Kṣemadhūrti, himself mounted on an elephant, charged exultantly upon the still more exultant one, calling him to combat.
A battle arose between those two elephants of dreadful aspect, like that between two great mountains, tree-clad, met by chance.
Their elephants locked together, those two heroes, piercing each other again and again with lances bright as the rays of the sun, roared mightily.
Drawing their elephants apart, they wheeled in circling courses, and taking up their bows, they smote each other.
With shouts and the slapping of arms and the twang of arrows on every side, gladdening the warriors, the two raised lion-roars.
Both skilled and mighty, they fought upon their two elephants—their trunks upraised, their banners tossed by the wind.
Having cut each other's bows, the two roared, raining spears and lances upon one another as the rain-clouds pour down water.
Then Kṣemadhūrti, roaring, pierced Bhīma forcefully between the breasts with a lance, and with six others besides.
Bhīmasena, his body blazing with wrath, the lances clinging to his limbs, shone like the sun, the seven-horsed, amid the clouds.
Then Bhīma, with effort, hurled at his foe a lance of straight flight, wrought wholly of iron and bright as the sun.
Then the lord of the Kulūtas, drawing his bow, cut down that lance with ten arrows and pierced the Pāṇḍava with a spear.
Then, taking up a bow that thundered like a great storm-cloud, the furious Pāṇḍava tormented the foe's elephant with his arrows.
That elephant, afflicted by the flood of arrows from Bhīmasena in the fight and held in check, could not stand its ground, like a cloud scattered by the wind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The royal elephant rushed upon the elephant of Bhīmasena, as one wind-driven cloud rushes upon another stirred by a mighty gale.
Wheeling back his own elephant with effort, Kṣemadhūrti pierced with arrows the charging Bhīmasena together with his elephant.
Then that bull among men, with a well-aimed razor-headed shaft, cut his foe's bow and tormented the enemy's elephant.
Then Kṣemadhūrti struck Bhīma hard with a barbed shaft and smote his elephant with iron arrows in all its vital parts.
Before his elephant could fall, Bhīmasena leaped down and, standing upon the ground, crushed the foe's elephant with his mace.
As Kṣemadhūrti leaped down from that shattered elephant and came on with uplifted sword, Vṛkodara struck him with his mace.
Slain, his sword still in hand and his life gone, he fell beside his own elephant, like a lion struck by the thunderbolt beside a mountain riven by the same.
Beholding slain the glorious king of the Kulūtas, thy army, O bull of the Bhāratas, fled away in distress.
Saṃjaya said: Then Karṇa, the great archer, that hero, smote the host of the Pāṇḍavas in battle with his straight-jointed shafts.
Even so, O king, the Pāṇḍavas, those great car-warriors, enraged, slaughtered the army of thy son before the very face of Karṇa.
Karṇa, O king, the mighty-armed, slew the Pāṇḍava host with iron shafts bright as the sun's rays, polished smooth by the smith.
There, O Bhārata, the elephants struck by Karṇa's iron shafts trumpeted and sank down and grew faint and reeled through the ten directions.
As that host was being slain by the son of the charioteer, O venerable one, Nakula swiftly charged upon the Sūtaputra in the great battle.
Bhīmasena withstood the son of Droṇa, who was performing deeds hard to achieve, and Sātyaki withstood the Kaikeya brothers Vinda and Anuvinda.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
King Citrasena met the advancing Śrutakarman, and Citra, with his bow of brilliant device and standard, met Prativindhya.
Duryodhana met King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, while Dhanaṃjaya, enraged, rushed upon the bands of the saṃśaptakas.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna met Kṛpa, and in that destruction of the foremost of heroes Śikhaṇḍin closed with the steadfast Kṛtavarman.
Śrutakīrti met Śalya, and the valiant Sahadeva, son of Mādrī, met thy son Duḥśāsana, O great king.
The two Kekaya brothers covered Sātyaki in battle with a gleaming shower of arrows, and Sātyaki in turn covered the two Kekayas, O Bhārata.
Those two brothers struck that hero hard in the breast, as two elephants strike a rival elephant with their tusks in a great battle.
Their armor riven by arrows, those two brothers in the fight pierced Sātyaki, true in deed, with their shafts, O king.
But Sātyaki, O great king, laughing, covered those two on every side with a shower of arrows and held them in check, O Bhārata.
Held back then by the showers of arrows from the grandson of Śini, the two swiftly covered the chariot of the Śaineya with their shafts.
But the grandson of Śūra, having cut their two bright bows in that great battle, then covered them both with sharp and unbearable arrows.
Then, taking up two other polished bows and great arrows, the two ranged lightly and skillfully, raining their shafts upon Sātyaki.
The great arrows loosed by the two, feathered with heron and peacock plumes and adorned with gold, flew on, lighting up all the quarters.
A darkness of arrows arose between them in that great battle, O king, and those great car-warriors cut one another's bows.
Then the Sātvata, O great king, enraged and frenzied for battle, took up another bow and strung it, and in the fight, with a keen razor-headed shaft, struck off the head of Anuvinda.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That great head, weighed down by its ear-rings, fell to the earth like the head of Śambara slain in a great battle, and, withering all the Kekayas, it swiftly passed to the ground.
Beholding that hero slain, his brother, the great car-warrior, strung another bow and withstood the grandson of Śini.
Piercing Sātyaki with a spear and with gold-feathered, stone-whetted shafts, he roared a mighty roar and cried, "Stand, stand!"
That great car-warrior of the Kekayas, enraged again, tormented Sātyaki in the arms and breast with arrows shaped like tongues of fire.
His every limb wounded by the arrows, the Sātvata, skilled in courage, shone in the battle, O king, like a kiṃśuka tree in full leaf.
Sātyaki, pierced in battle by the high-souled Kekaya, pierced the Kekaya in turn with twenty-five shafts, as though laughing.
Taking up their shields decked with a hundred moons, those two strong-armed warriors, bearing excellent swords, shone in the great arena like the mighty Jambha and Śakra in the war of gods and demons.
Then those two, wheeling in circling courses in the great battle, swiftly smote each other with their swords in the fray.
Then the Sātvata cleft the Kekaya's shield in two, and the prince likewise cleft the shield of Sātyaki.
Having cleft the shield set about with hundreds of stars, the Kaikeya ranged in circling courses, advancing and retreating.
As he ranged in the great arena bearing his excellent sword, the grandson of Śini, in haste, cut him down with a back-handed stroke.
The Kekaya, with his armor, O king, cleft in two in that great battle—that mighty archer fell like a mountain smitten by the thunderbolt.
Having slain him in battle, the heroic Śaineya, that best of car-warriors, that scorcher of foes, swiftly mounted the chariot of Yudhāmanyu.
Then, mounting another chariot duly equipped, Sātyaki once more scattered the great host of the Kekayas with his arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That great host of the Kekayas, being slain in the battle, abandoned that hostile chariot and fled through the ten directions.
Saṃjaya said: Śrutakarman, O great king, enraged, struck King Citrasena in battle with fifty arrows.
But King Abhisāra, striking Śrutakarman with nine sharp arrows, pierced his charioteer with five.
Then Śrutakarman, enraged, tormented Citrasena at the head of the army, striking him in a vital spot with a keen iron shaft.
Meanwhile the illustrious Śrutakīrti covered that guardian of the earth with ninety feathered shafts.
Then, regaining his senses, Citrasena, the great car-warrior, cut his bow with a broad-headed shaft and pierced him with seven arrows.
Taking up another bow, swift and gold-adorned, he made Citrasena yet more many-hued with his waves of arrows.
Decked with arrows, O king, that youth, wearing a bright garland, shone like a youth well-adorned in the midst of an assembly.
Then, enraged, he pierced Śrutakarman between the breasts with an iron shaft in the battle and cried, "Stand, stand!"
Śrutakarman too, tormented in the battle by the iron shaft, poured forth abundant blood like a mountain streaming with red ochre.
Then, his limbs smeared with blood and his hue made ruddy by it, he shone in the battle, O king, like a kiṃśuka tree in full flower.
Then Śrutakarman, O king, charged upon by his foes, warded off the enemy and cut his bow in two.
Then, O best of the Bhāratas, when his bow had been cut away, the illustrious Śrutakarman pierced him with three hundred iron-shafted arrows.
Then with another broad-headed shaft, exceedingly sharp, the swift warrior swept off the head of that great-souled one, helmet and all.
That mighty head of Citravarman fell upon the earth, as the moon, fallen by some chance from heaven, might drop to the ground.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing their king slain and Abhisāra fallen too, O honored one, the soldiers of Citrasena rushed forward with fury.
Then that wrathful mighty bowman scattered the host with his arrows; as the lord of the dead in his fury drives all creatures before him at the hour of doom, so Śrutakarman, swiftly routing them with his shafts, shone resplendent.
Then Prativindhya, having pierced Citra with five swift arrows, struck his charioteer with three, and his banner thereafter with a single shaft.
Citra in turn tormented him in the arms and breast with nine broad-headed shafts, gold-feathered, whetted on stone, and winged with the plumes of heron and peacock.
Prativindhya, O Bhārata, cut his bow asunder with arrows, and then smote him fiercely with five sharpened shafts.
Then, O great king, he hurled at your son a lance with a golden shaft, hard to withstand, terrible as a tongue of flame.
As that lance came rushing down like a meteor from the sky, Prativindhya, as if smiling, cut it in twain upon the field.
Cleft by Prativindhya's keen arrows, it fell to earth, like a thunderbolt at the end of an age that strikes terror into all beings.
Seeing his lance struck down, Citra seized a great mace, adorned with a network of gold, and flung it at Prativindhya.
In that great battle it slew his horses and his charioteer, and crushing the chariot with its force, sank into the earth.
At that very moment, O Bhārata, leaping down from his chariot, he hurled at Citra a lance bedecked with bells of gold.
As it flew toward him, the high-souled Citra caught it, O king, and hurled that same lance back at Prativindhya, O Bhārata.
Reaching the hero Prativindhya in battle, that lance of great brilliance pierced his right arm and fell to the ground; and where it fell it lit up that place like a thunderbolt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, O king, Prativindhya in his wrath sent forth a gold-decked iron dart, desiring the death of Citra.
Piercing the bright armor that guarded him, and his very heart as well, it passed swiftly into the earth, like a great serpent gliding into its hole.
Smitten by that dart, he fell then, O king, stretching out his two broad arms, thick and round as iron bludgeons.
Seeing Citra slain, your warriors, the ornaments of battle, rushed with fury upon Prativindhya from every side.
Loosing arrows of many kinds and bell-hung śataghnīs, they covered him over as banks of cloud cover the sun.
But the mighty-armed one swept them aside with his web of arrows in the fray, and routed your host as the wielder of the thunderbolt routs the army of the Asuras.
Slaughtered in the battle by the Pāṇḍavas, O king, your men were scattered all at once like clouds driven before the wind.
When that army had fled and was being slain on every side, the son of Droṇa, alone, swiftly bore down upon the mighty Bhīmasena.
Then there arose of a sudden a fearful encounter between the two, such as was the clash of Vṛtra and Vāsava in the war of the gods and the Asuras.
Saṃjaya said: Then, O king, the son of Droṇa pierced Bhīmasena with a winged shaft, moving with utmost speed and displaying the lightness of his hand with weapons.
Then again he struck him with ninety sharpened arrows, marking all his vital points—knowing the vitals well, and nimble of hand.
Bhīmasena, thickly studded by the son of Droṇa with keen arrows, shone in the battle, O king, like the radiant sun crowned with its beams.
Then with a thousand well-aimed arrows the son of Pāṇḍu veiled the son of Droṇa, and let loose a lion's roar.
Then the son of Droṇa, warding off arrows with arrows in the fight, struck the son of Pāṇḍu upon the brow with an iron shaft, O king, as if in mockery.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The son of Pāṇḍu bore that arrow lodged in his forehead, O king, as a proud rhinoceros of the forest bears its horn.
Then the valiant Bhīma, as the son of Droṇa pressed on in battle, pierced him in the brow with three iron shafts, as if to amaze him.
With those arrows fixed upon his forehead the Brāhmaṇa shone forth, like some lofty three-peaked mountain drenched in the rains.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu tormented the son of Droṇa with hundreds of arrows, yet shook him not, as the wind cannot shake a mountain.
In like manner the son of Droṇa, exultant, could not shake the son of Pāṇḍu in the fight with hundreds of keen arrows, as a flood cannot shake a mountain.
Those two great car-warriors, veiling each other with terrible arrows, both heroes skilled in the maneuvers of the chariot, shone resplendent, fierce in the joy of battle.
Both blazing like two suns that work the world's destruction, they scorched each other with their finest shafts as suns scorch with their own rays.
In that great battle they strove, each to answer the other's stroke with a stroke; fearlessly the two contended, blow for matching blow.
Like two tigers the two mighty car-warriors ranged the field, their arrows for fangs, unassailable, their bows agape like jaws, terrible to behold.
The two became invisible, hidden on every side by their webs of arrows, like the moon and the sun veiled by masses of cloud in the sky.
And in a moment those subduers of foes shone forth again upon that field, like the moon and the sun in the heavens freed from the masses of cloud.
Then the son of Droṇa wheeled to the left around Vṛkodara there, drenching him with hundreds of fierce arrows as rain-streams drench a mountain.
But Bhīma could not brook that mark of his foe's mastery, and the son of Pāṇḍu, O king, wheeled in answer about him likewise to the left.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Through the divisions of their circling courses, in their advances and returns, a tumultuous combat arose between the two upon that great field.
Coursing through their various movements—the circle and the steady stand—they smote each other with arrows loosed from bows drawn to the full.
The two great car-warriors each strove to slay the other, and each sought in the encounter to strip the other of his chariot.
Then the son of Droṇa, that mighty car-warrior, brought forth his great celestial weapons; and in the battle the son of Pāṇḍu beat them back with weapons of his own.
Then, O great king, a fearful battle of celestial weapons raged on, terrible as the war of the planets at the destruction of all created beings.
Those arrows, hurled by the two, clashed together, O Bhārata, lighting up all the quarters and that army round about.
The sky grew terrible, overspread by the throngs of arrows, as though strewn with falling meteors at the destruction of created beings, O king.
From the clash of arrows a fire was born there, O Bhārata, scattering sparks and blazing with flame, and it scorched both the contending hosts.
Then the Siddhas, O great king, hovering above, spoke these words: "This battle surpasses all battles whatsoever; greater is it than all the rest.
All other battles are not worth a sixteenth part of this; no such combat has ever been, nor shall ever be again.
Ah, how endowed with knowledge are these two, and how fierce in valor! Ah, the dreadful strength of Bhīma, and the weapon-skill of both!
Ah, the very pith of prowess, ah, the perfect mastery of these two! There they stand in the battle, like Yama the Ender at the close of time.
Like two Rudras come to being, like two suns, or like the twin Aśvins—so are these tigers among men, terrible of form upon the field."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Such words of the Siddhas were heard then again and again, and a lion's roar arose from the assembled dwellers of heaven, beholding the wondrous and unimaginable deeds of the two in that fray.
Those two heroes in the battle, O king, each having wronged the other, glared upon each other, rolling their eyes in wrath.
Their eyes red with anger, their lips quivering in anger, in their anger grinding their teeth and biting their lips,
the two great car-warriors veiled each other with a downpour of arrows, raining floods of shafts upon the field, gleaming with the lightning of their weapons.
Those two great car-warriors, having pierced each other's banner and charioteer, and having pierced each other's horses, wounded one another.
Then in their wrath, O great king, in that great battle, both seized arrows and swiftly hurled them, each seeking the other's death.
Those two arrows, O great king, gleaming at the head of the host, swift as the thunderbolt and hard to bear, met and struck home.
By the force of their rushing and grievously smitten by those two shafts, the two great heroes then sank down, each upon the floor of his own chariot.
Then the charioteer, knowing the son of Droṇa to be senseless, bore him away from the battle, O king, while all the warriors looked on.
In like manner, O king, the charioteer bore away from the fight upon his car that scorcher of foes, the son of Pāṇḍu, who reeled again and again.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Tell me how the battle of Arjuna went against the Saṃśaptakas, and how it fared for the others of my side against the Pāṇḍavas.
Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king, as I relate the battle as it befell—the combat of our heroes against their foes, a combat that purges away the body's sins.
The son of Pṛthā, that slayer of foes, plunging into the host of the Saṃśaptakas which was like an ocean, churned it up as a great wind churns the sea.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Striking off with keen broad-headed shafts the heads of the heroes—faces bright as the full moon, with fair eyes, brows, and teeth—Dhanaṃjaya swiftly strewed the earth with them, as with lotuses bereft of their stalks.
The arms of his foes—shapely, long, and full, anointed with sandal and aloe, bearing weapons, clad in armor, like five-hooded serpents—Arjuna severed with his razor-edged shafts in the battle.
Yoke-horses and the foremost team-horses, charioteers, banners, bows, arrows, hands and forearms—again and again the son of Pāṇḍu cut them away with his broad-headed shafts.
Elephants, horses, and chariots with their riders, Arjuna in the battle, O king, sent with arrows by the many thousands to the abode of Yama.
Advancing upon that great hero, bellowing like bulls enraged for the sake of a cow, they rushed at him with roars; and as he smote them, they struck back at him with their arrows, as bulls gore with their horns.
That battle of his with them made the hair stand on end, like the war of the Daityas with the wielder of the thunderbolt for the conquest of the three worlds.
Warding off the weapons of his foes on every side with weapons of his own, Arjuna swiftly pierced their very lives with a multitude of shafts, and roared aloud.
With their triple bamboo poles, wheels, and axles severed, their warriors, horses, and charioteers slain, their weapons and quivers shattered, their banners struck down,
their traces and reins cut through, robbed of their poles and shafts, their seats and yokes broken apart, the array of their weapons hewn down—those chariots he shattered into fragments, as the wind tears great clouds asunder.
Filling all with wonder, a sight worth beholding and a terror to his foes, Arjuna wrought a deed equal to that of a thousand great car-warriors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The hosts of Siddhas, divine sages, and Cāraṇas sang his praises; the kettledrums of the gods resounded, showers of flowers fell upon the heads of Keśava and Arjuna, and a bodiless voice spoke.
These two heroes, Keśava and Arjuna, who forever bear the loveliness of the moon, the blaze of the sun, the force of the wind, and the splendour of fire.
Unconquerable as Brahmā and Īśāna, the two heroes stood upon a single chariot — the foremost of all beings, the two heroes who are Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Beholding and hearing of this great wonder, O Bhārata, Aśvatthāman, fully girded, rushed upon the two Kṛṣṇas in battle.
Then, as the son of Pāṇḍu was loosing arrows like Yama, Time, and the Ender, the son of Droṇa hailed him with arrow-laden hand, and laughing spoke.
"If, O hero, you reckon me come to you as a guest deserving of welcome, then with all your soul grant me this day the hospitality of battle."
Thus challenged by the teacher's son with desire for combat, Arjuna held himself in high honour, and said this to Janārdana:
"The Saṃśaptakas too are mine to slay, and the son of Droṇa now summons me. O mighty-armed one, instruct me which of these is to be met first."
So addressed, Kṛṣṇa bore Pārtha into the presence of Droṇa's son — as the Wind bears Indra summoned by victorious rite into the sacrifice.
Addressing him with single mind, Keśava said to Droṇa's son: "Aśvatthāman, stand firm, strike swiftly, and endure!"
"This is the hour for dependants to repay the bread of their lord. Subtle is the dispute of brāhmaṇas; gross are the victory and defeat of the kṣatriya."
"Since out of folly you cannot brook the divine welcome Pārtha would do you, then, desiring to win it, stand firm this day and fight the son of Pāṇḍu."
So addressed by Vāsudeva, the best of the twice-born said "So be it," and pierced Keśava with sixty iron shafts and Arjuna with three.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At this Arjuna, sorely enraged, severed his bow with three broad-headed arrows; whereupon Droṇa's son took up another, still more terrible, bow.
Stringing it in the blink of an eye, he pierced Arjuna and Keśava — Vāsudeva with three arrows and the son of Pāṇḍu with a thousand.
Then, straining himself, Droṇa's son loosed arrows by the thousand, by the million, by the hundred million, and in the battle held Arjuna in check.
From his quiver, his bow, his bowstring, his fingers, O honoured one, from his arms, his two hands, his breast, his face, his nostrils, his eyes,
from his two ears, his head, his limbs, even from the very pores of his skin, and from his chariot and banner, the arrows of that reciter of the Veda streamed forth.
Having pierced Keśava and the son of Pāṇḍu with a vast net of arrows, Droṇa's son roared in delight with a voice like a mass of great thunderclouds.
Hearing him roar, the son of Pāṇḍu said to Acyuta: "Behold, Mādhava, the malice of Droṇa's son toward me."
"Having shut us within a house of arrows, he thinks us slain; this resolve of his I shall undo by skill and by strength."
Cutting each of the arrows loosed by Aśvatthāman into three and three, the best of the Bhāratas scattered them as the wind scatters mist.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu once more pierced the Saṃśaptakas — with their horses, drivers, chariots, and elephants, their banners and bands of foot — with fierce arrows.
Whoever there beheld any form, in whatever wise, each thought that form, and his own self, all covered over with arrows.
Sped from the Gāṇḍīva, those winged shafts of many shapes struck down elephants and men standing a full krośa away in the battle.
Severed by broad-headed arrows, the trunks of the rut-streaming elephants fell, like full-grown autumn trees felled by axes.
And thereafter those elephants fell like mountains, together with their riders, even as ranges of hills shattered by the thunderbolt of the Thunderer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The chariots, fashioned by rule and like to the cities of the Gandharvas, drawn by horses trained to swiftness and well-guided, mounted by warriors mad for battle —
these Dhanaṃjaya rained his foes with arrows, hewing them to splinters, and slew the bedecked horsemen and the foot-soldiers.
Dhanaṃjaya, the sun of the world's ending, dried up the great, unfordable ocean of the Saṃśaptakas with the fierce rays of his arrows.
Then again, with swift, sun-bright iron shafts of mighty force, he hastened to cleave the great mountain that was Droṇa's son, as the Thunderer cleaves a hill.
The teacher's son, enraged and eager to fight, sought with swift arrows to strike him together with his horses and driver, but could not, for Pārtha cut the shafts down in mid-air.
Then Aśvatthāman, exceedingly enraged, loosed whole sheaves of arrows upon the worthy Arjuna — as one offers a house to a guest.
Then, leaving the Saṃśaptakas, the son of Pāṇḍu fell upon Droṇa's son — as a giver leaves an unworthy man to attend a worthy suppliant.
Then there arose a combat between those two, splendid as Śukra and Aṅgiras — like Venus and the planet of Aṅgiras around a star in the sky.
Scorching each other with the blazing rays of their arrows, they stood, striking terror into the worlds, like two planets straying from their courses.
Then Arjuna pierced him sorely between the brows with an iron shaft; and Droṇa's son shone thereby like the sun with rays flung upward.
Then the two Kṛṣṇas, sorely afflicted by Aśvatthāman with hundreds of arrows, stood with their masses of beams entangled, like two suns at the world's ending.
Then Arjuna, guarded by Vāsudeva, loosed the weapon that strikes on every side, and smote the son of Droṇa with shafts like the thunderbolt, like fire, like the rod of Yama.
He of surpassing fire and most fearsome deeds pierced Keśava and Arjuna in their vital parts with well-loosed arrows of utmost speed, by which even Death, if struck, would tremble.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Warding off the arrows of the straining Droṇa's son with twice as many fair-feathered shafts, Arjuna enveloped that lone hero with his horses, driver, and banner, and then turned upon the Saṃśaptaka host.
Their bows, their arrows, their quivers, their bowstrings, their hands, their arms, the weapons held in their hands, their parasols, their banners, their horses, their garments, their garlands, and their ornaments —
their shields, their armour, their cherished hopes, all that was dear to them, and their very heads — Pārtha clove asunder with the arrows he loosed at his foes, who stood without turning their faces away.
The well-equipped chariots, horses, and elephants, mounted by manful heroes who strove with effort, struck down by the hosts of arrows Pārtha sped, fell together with those best of men.
Faces fair as lotuses, as the sun, as the full moon, splendid with diadems, garlands, and crowns — smitten by broad-heads, crescent-arrows, and razor-shafts, the heads of men fell ceaselessly to the earth.
Then with elephants like the elephant of the lord of the gods, swelling with the pride and wrath of the foes of the gods, the heroes of the Kaliṅgas, Vaṅgas, Aṅgas, and Niṣādas, seeking to slay him, charged upon the son of Pāṇḍu.
The armour, the vital parts, the trunks, and the drivers of those elephants Pārtha rent apart; and their banners and pennons then fell down like the peaks of a mountain struck by the thunderbolt.
When these were broken, the Diademed one covered the teacher's son with arrows the hue of the new-risen sun — as the wind veils the toiling sun with great nets of cloud.
Then, beating off Arjuna's arrows with his own, Droṇa's son covered Arjuna and Vāsudeva with shafts as the moon and sun are veiled in the sky, and roared like a raincloud at the end of the hot season.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sorely pressed by him and by your warriors, whose weapons were yet unbroken, Arjuna made at once a darkness of arrows and pierced them all with fair-feathered shafts.
Neither taking up, nor nocking, nor loosing his arrows could Savyasācin be seen in the battle; men saw only the slain elephants, horses, foot-soldiers, and chariots, their bodies sewn through with shafts.
Nocking ten choice iron shafts in haste, Droṇa's son loosed them as though they were but one; and of these, five well-sped shafts struck Arjuna and five pierced Acyuta.
Struck by these, those two foremost of all men, streaming blood, like Kubera and Indra, seemed overcome by one whose lore was complete; and others wondered, "Are these two slain?"
Then the lord of the Dāśārhas said to Arjuna: "Why are you heedless? Slay this warrior! Neglected, he will work mischief, and grow grievous as a malady left untreated."
Saying "So be it" to Acyuta, and now alert, he hewed at Droṇa's son with arrows in earnest; and cutting the reins, he struck the horses, which bore him far away from the battle.
Wheeling about, that wise one, best of the line of Aṅgiras, desired no further combat with Pārtha; for, reflecting, he knew that victory was assured to the Vṛṣṇi hero and to Dhanaṃjaya.
When Aśvatthāman of hostile frame had been borne off from the battle by his horses — as a disease is driven from the body by spells, herbs, treatment, and gifts —
Keśava and Arjuna advanced together to face the Saṃśaptakas, upon their chariot, its banner tossed by the wind, thundering like a flood.
Saṃjaya said: Then to the north, in the army of the Pāṇḍavas, an uproar arose from chariots, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers being slaughtered by Daṇḍadhāra.
Turning the chariot back, Keśava, even as he urged on the horses swift as Garuḍa and the wind, said to Arjuna:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The lord of Magadha too has pressed forward upon his crushing elephant, in no way inferior to Bhagadatta in skill and in strength."
"When you have slain him, you shall slay the Saṃśaptakas again." And at the end of his words he brought Pārtha into the presence of Daṇḍadhāra.
That chief of the Māgadhas, his goad in hand, irresistible among adversaries as a comet among the planets, that dreadful one churned the enemy's host as a flaming comet would scourge the whole earth.
Mounted upon his well-caparisoned elephant — like a Dānava-elephant, roaring like a great cloud, a crusher of foes — he slew chariots, horses, and herds of elephants by the thousand, and elephants too, with his arrows.
Bearing down upon the chariots with their horses and drivers, in haste he ground the chariots beneath the elephant's feet; and mounted on the elephant he slew other elephants with its legs, its feet, and its trunk, like the wheel of Time.
And men decked in armour of black iron, with their horses, together with the foot-soldiers, he cast down and crushed with his furious, noble tusker, as one tramples thick reeds with a crackling sound.
Then Arjuna, amid the twang of bowstring, the slap of the leather guard, and the rim's roar, amid the din of drums, kettledrums, and many conches, and the clamour of men, horses, and elephants by the thousand, swept down upon that noble elephant on his peerless chariot.
Then Daṇḍadhāra smote Arjuna with twelve choice arrows, Janārdana with sixteen, and the horses with three apiece; and thereupon he roared and laughed again and again.
Then Pārtha with his broad-headed arrows cut away his bowstring, his arrows, and his bow, and his bedecked banner too, and again the drivers along with the foot-guards; and at this the lord of Girivraja flew into a rage.
Then, seeking to throw Arjuna into utter confusion with his elephant, its temples burst with rut, dense as a thundercloud and swift as the wind, he smote Janārdana and Dhanaṃjaya with lances.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the son of Pāṇḍu, with three razor-shafts, severed at one stroke his two arms, like elephant trunks, and his head, with its face like the full moon; and thereafter he smote the elephant with hundreds of arrows.
That elephant, clad in golden mail, shone with Pārtha's arrows tipped with refined gold, and so blazed as at night a mountain blazes, its herbs and trees set alight by a forest fire.
Tormented with pain, trumpeting with a voice like a thundercloud, staggering, reeling, stumbling, stricken, in flight, broken, that elephant fell together with its driver, as a mountain falls crushed by the descent of the thunderbolt.
When his brother had been slain in battle, Daṇḍa came on upon an elephant white as snow, garlanded with gold, and like the peak of the snowy mountain, seeking to slay Dhanaṃjaya, the younger brother of Indra.
Striking Janārdana with three lances bright as the sun's rays and Arjuna with five, he roared as he tormented them; then the son of Pāṇḍu hewed off his two arms.
Cleanly cut off by razor-arrows, the two arms, still grasping their lances, their armlets fallen, smeared with sandal-paste, falling together from the elephant, gleamed like two great serpents tumbling from a mountain crag.
Then the head of Daṇḍa, struck off by the Diademed one with a crescent-arrow, fell from the elephant to the earth; and that blood-red head, as it fell, gleamed like the sun sinking from his setting-place toward the western quarter.
Then Pārtha pierced the elephant, like the peak of a white mountain, with choice arrows bright as the sun's rays; and it fell trumpeting, as a peak of the snowy mountain falls when struck by the thunderbolt.
Then other noble elephants like to that one, seeking in the fray to conquer Savyasācin, were made by him even as those two elephants had been; and thereupon the foe's vast host was shattered.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Elephants, chariots, horses, and men in throngs, slaying one another, fell in the battle, stumbling against one another and struck down; and calling out their several clan-names, they were sorely slain.
Then his own soldiers, gathering about Arjuna as the hosts of the gods about Purandara, said: "He of whom we went in dread, as creatures dread death — that foe, O hero, by good fortune you have slain!"
Had you not rescued these folk from their terror, hard-pressed as they were by such mighty foes, the joy of our enemies would have been as great as our own joy now is, when you have slain these foes of ours here.
Hearing such words and yet more spoken by his comrades, Arjuna, glad at heart, honored those people as was fitting, and then, the slayer of the host of the Saṃśaptakas, set forth once more.
Saṃjaya said: Returning once again, the victorious one slew many of the Saṃśaptakas, moving with crooked turns and counter-turns like the planet Aṅgāraka.
Struck by Pārtha's arrows, O king, men, horses, chariots, and elephants reeled, wheeled about, cried out, fell, and wilted, good sir.
The Pāṇḍava cut down draft-beasts, sturdier draft-beasts, drivers, and chariots, and likewise hands, the weapons in those hands, arms too, and heads,
with broad-headed shafts, razor-arrows, crescent-points, and calf-tooth barbs—the heads of the hostile warriors who fought against him in battle.
As bulls eager to fight over a cow rush upon a rival bull, so the heroes fell upon Arjuna by hundreds and by thousands.
The battle between them and him was such as to make the hair stand on end, like that of the Daityas with the wielder of the thunderbolt in the conquest of the three worlds.
A warrior of fierce weapons pierced him with three arrows, like venomous biting serpents; thereupon Arjuna struck that man's head from his body.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Enraged, they rained down on Arjuna from every side with weapons of every kind, as clouds driven by the Maruts pour upon the Himavat in the hot season.
Warding off the enemies' weapons on all sides with his own weapons, Arjuna, with well-aimed shafts, slew all those many foes together.
With their triple bamboo poles, shafts, and supports severed, their flank-guards and drivers slain, their reins, traces, and axles cut, their draw-bars and yokes broken, and all their gear shattered—such did Arjuna swiftly make the chariots with his arrows.
Those priceless chariots, shattered there in their numbers, gleamed like the mansions of the wealthy ruined by fire, wind, and flood.
Elephants, their vital parts pierced through by arrows like thunderbolt and lightning, fell as mountain-top dwellings fall before bolt, gale, and fire.
Many horses with their riders fell, struck down by Arjuna, their tongues and entrails hanging out, spent upon the earth, drenched in blood, ghastly to behold.
Men, horses, and elephants, sewn through by Savyasācin's iron shafts, wheeled about, stumbled, fell, cried out, and wilted, good sir.
With fine arrows whetted on stone, like thunderbolt, lightning, and venom, Pārtha struck them down as great Indra struck the Dānavas.
Heroes in costly armor and ornaments, with garments and weapons of every kind, with their chariots and banners, lie slain by Pārtha.
Vanquished, men of pious deeds, of distinguished birth and learning, they have gone with their bodies to the earth, and by their mighty deeds to heaven.
Then your heroes rushed upon Arjuna's chariot—lords of various realms, with their troops, their wrath kindled.
Borne by chariot-horses, and the foot-soldiers too, bent on killing, they ran at him, swiftly hurling weapons of every kind.
That great downpour of weapons, hurled by those great storm-cloud warriors, the wind that was Arjuna swiftly scattered with his sharp arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That shoreless flood of mighty weapons—with its horses, foot, elephants, and chariots—Pārtha sought all at once to cross by the causeway of his missiles and shafts.
Then Vāsudeva said to Pārtha: "Why do you toy with them, O sinless one? Crush these Saṃśaptakas and then make haste to the slaying of Karṇa."
Saying "So be it," Arjuna at once assailed the Saṃśaptakas who yet remained, and with his weapon slew them by force, as Indra slew the Daityas.
Some saw Arjuna in the fray drawing his arrows or fitting them to the string; by others he was seen only as he loosed the shafts, so swift was he.
Crying "A marvel!" Govinda urged on the horses; white as a goose's wing, they entered the enemy host as geese enter a lake.
Then Govinda, gazing over that field of battle while the slaughter of men went on, spoke to Savyasācin:
"O Pārtha, here rages the dread destruction of the Bharatas, the great ruin of the kings of the earth, brought about for Duryodhana's sake."
"Behold, O Bhārata, the gold-backed bows of the great archers cast aside, and the bundles of arrows and the quivers as well."
"And the arrows with golden nocks and bent joints, and the oil-washed iron shafts, like serpents that have shed their skins."
"Swords with ivory hilts adorned with gold, lances scattered about, and bows bright and decked with gold."
"Coats of mail flung off, gold-backed, O Bhārata, and lances wrought with gold, and javelins adorned with gold."
"And great maces bound with bands of pure gold, and pikes of gold, and spiked clubs adorned with gold."
"Battle-axes with shafts bright with gold flung about, and iron-pointed goads fallen, and heavy pestles."
"Behold the gaily-wrought hundred-slayers, and the huge iron bludgeons, and the discuses cast away, and the many hammers on the field."
"Grasping weapons of every kind, those swift warriors, greedy for victory, though their life is fled, seem still as though alive."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Behold the warriors by thousands—their limbs crushed by maces, their heads broken by pestles, trampled by elephants, horses, and chariots."
"By arrows, spears, swords, and lances, by sabres, pikes, javelins, claw-weapons, and clubs, men, elephants, and horses—"
"—with bodies hewn in many ways, awash in floods of blood, their breath gone, the battlefields are covered, O slayer of foes."
"With arms smeared with sandal paste, bearing armlets and fair ornaments, with guards on them and bracelets, the earth shines, O Bhārata."
"With finger-guarded hands and forearms flung about, all bedecked, and with the severed thighs of those swift warriors, like elephants' trunks."
"With the severed heads of those bull-eyed men, bound with choice crest-jewels and wearing earrings, the earth is resplendent."
"With headless trunks smeared with blood, their limbs and necks lopped off, the earth shines, O best of the Bhāratas, as if with fires whose flames have died."
"Behold the chariots of many sorts, broken, fair with their golden bells, and the horses too, in many places drenched with blood."
"And the great conch-shells of the warriors, and the white whisks scattered about, and the elephants with their tongues lolling out, lying like mountains."
"And the slain elephant-fighters bright with their banners, and the housings of the elephants, with their well-fitted cloths and woolen rugs."
"And the gay rugs of varied figures torn apart, and the bells broken in many ways, ground to bits by the falling elephants."
"And the goads with handles of beryl gems fallen to the ground, and the gold-wrought whips bound to the banner-tops of the riders."
"And the horse-cloths and coverings, varied and gem-bright, wrought of gold and made of antelope-wool, fallen upon the ground."
"The crest-jewels of the kings, the bright golden garlands, the parasols flung aside, and the yak-tail whisks and fans."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Behold the earth, miry with blood, strewn with the faces of heroes—faces bright as moon and stars, with lovely earrings and trimmed beards, exceedingly adorned."
"And behold the men still living, moaning on every side, tended by many who have laid down their weapons, O lord of peoples."
"There, with kinsmen gathered round, weeping again and again, having covered over other warriors who have departed, the swift ones, greedy for victory and full of wrath, go forth again to battle."
"Others, proud men, run hither and thither there, begged for water by their fallen kinsmen, the heroes."
"And some who went for water, O Arjuna, lie breathless, many of them; and those heroes who came back, at the very sight of them, lost their senses."
"At the sight of water they rush forward, crying out to one another; behold, O Bhārata, some dead from drinking the water, and others still drinking."
"Others, O lover of kinsmen, forsaking their dear ones and their kin, were seen passing away here and there in that great battle."
"Behold yet others, O best of men, biting their lips, gazing all about with faces knit in scowling brows."
"This deed in the great battle befits you alone, O Arjuna, or the king of the gods in heaven—what you have wrought in this fight."
Thus Kṛṣṇa, showing that field of battle to the Diademed One as he drove on, heard a great clamor from Duryodhana's army.
The blare of conches and kettledrums mingled with tabors and drums, the din of chariots, horses, and elephants, and the dreadful clash of weapons.
Entering that host with his wind-swift horses, Kṛṣṇa halted, beholding your army hard pressed by Pāṇḍya.
For he, the foremost of bowmen, with arrows of every kind slew the throngs of his enemies in battle, robbing them of life like Death himself.
That best of strikers, piercing with sharp arrows the bodies of elephants, horses, and men, made them depart from their flesh, bereft of life.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Cutting apart with his shafts the various weapons hurled by the foremost of his foes, Pāṇḍya slew those enemies as Śakra slew the Asuras.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: This great hero, renowned in the world, you named before, but his deeds in battle you have not recounted, O Saṃjaya.
Tell me now in full the valor of that great hero—his skill, his might, his prowess, his measure, and his pride.
Saṃjaya said: Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, Arjuna, and Janārdana—those masters of their craft whom you deem foremost with the bow in battle—
—by him a parity with Karṇa and Bhīṣma was shown in himself, nor would he own himself inferior to Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
That Pāṇḍya, best of kings, foremost of all bearers of arms, slew Karṇa's host like Death scorned and roused to fury.
That force, with its surging chariots and horses, its choice foot-soldiers and elephants, beset by Pāṇḍya, whirled about like a potter's wheel.
His foes, their horses, drivers, banners, and chariots gone, their weapons flung from their hands, Pāṇḍya scattered with well-aimed shafts as the wind scatters clouds.
Elephants with their trunks struck off, their pennons, banners, and weapons gone, together with their foot-guards, that slayer of foes slew as the foe-slayer slew his enemies with the thunderbolt.
Horsemen with their lances, javelins, and quivers, and their horses too, the Pulindas, Khaśas, Bāhlīkas, the Niṣādas, and the Taṅgaṇas,
the southerners and the Bhojas, cruel and hardened in war—stripping them of weapons and armor with his arrows, Pāṇḍya robbed them of life.
Seeing Pāṇḍya, undaunted, smiting the fourfold host with his arrows in the fray, the son of Droṇa, more undaunted still, advanced upon him.
Addressing him sweetly, dancing forward as if without fear, that best of strikers spoke, smiling first, as he summoned him:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"O king, lotus-petal-eyed, master of the finest weapons and mounts, you whose frame seems forged of the thunderbolt, foremost in strength and manhood,"
"twanging your great bow with both long arms, your weapon clasped fast in your fists, you shine exceedingly like a great rain-cloud."
As you rain upon your foes torrents of arrows of tremendous force, I see no champion in this battle fit to stand against you save myself.
Single-handed you crush chariots, elephants, foot-soldiers, and horsemen in their multitudes, as a fearless lion of terrible strength crushes herds of deer in the forest.
With the mighty roar of your chariot you make heaven and earth resound, as the sun at the rains' end, drinking up the grain-fields, floods all things with his rays.
Drawing keen shafts from your quiver, like venomous serpents, do battle with me alone, as the Andhaka demon fought with the three-eyed Rudra.
Thus addressed, the king of the Malaya banner answered, "So be it," and crying "Strike!" he pierced the son of Droṇa with a barbed arrow.
Then Droṇa's son, foremost of the teacher's line, smiling, struck the Pāṇḍya king with vital-piercing, terrible arrows that resembled tongues of flame.
Then Aśvatthāman loosed nine more sharp iron shafts, fledged with heron feathers and endowed with the tenfold speed of flight.
Of these the Pāṇḍya cut five apart with five whetted arrows; the remaining four struck his horses, and they were swiftly bereft of life.
Then, having cut those arrows of Droṇa's son with whetted shafts, the Pāṇḍya, splendid as the sun, severed the drawn bowstring.
Restringing his unstrung bow, Droṇa's son, the slayer of foes, sent forth thousands of arrows at the Pāṇḍya, choking the sky and all the quarters with shafts.
Then the Pāṇḍya, that bull among men, though he knew the arrows of the great-souled Droṇi to be inexhaustible, cut down all those that were hurled at him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having with effort cut those arrows that Droṇi sped at him, the foe then drove off his two wheel-guards with whetted shafts.
Then, seeing the deftness of his foe, Droṇa's son bent his bow into a circle and let fly his arrows in a downpour, as the younger brother of Pūṣan pours down rain.
That store of weapons which eight wagons, each drawn by eight oxen, bore away — all that, O honoured one, Droṇi hurled in an eighth part of a day.
Whoever looked upon him there — wrathful as Death itself, like the destroyer at the end of time — most of them fell senseless.
As the rain-cloud at summer's end drenches with its showers the earth with its mountains and trees, so the teacher's son drenched that army with a downpour of arrows.
That well-nigh unbearable rain of arrows loosed by the cloud that was Droṇi, the Pāṇḍya, a very wind, swiftly checked with the weapon of Vāyu, and roared aloud.
As he roared, Droṇi cut down his standard, adorned with sandal and aloe and rising like the Malaya mountain, and slew his four horses.
Slaying his charioteer with a single arrow, with a crescent-headed shaft he cut his bow, loud as a great thundercloud, and shattered his chariot to fragments fine as sesame.
Having warded off weapon with weapon and cut all the foe's arms apart, Droṇi, though his enemy was now in his power, did not slay him, in his longing for the fight.
A noble, well-caparisoned elephant, its driver slain, was sent in haste against him; armoured and mighty, the great lord of Malaya mounted it, as a lion roaring climbs a mountain peak.
Goading the elephant, the lord of the mountain-king, roaring, swiftly hurled at the teacher's son a lance bright as the sun's rays, with all the force, fury, and supreme effort of his weapon's release.
That lance, adorned with strings of gems, fine diamonds and gold, with silk, garlands and pearls, he drove home, crying again and again in his joy, "You are slain!" — and it pierced the splendid ornament on Droṇi's body.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That ornament, gleaming like the sun, moon, planets and fire, fell shattered to powder by the violent blow, as a great forest on a mountain peak, smitten by mighty Indra's bolt, falls to the ground.
Then he blazed up with surpassing fury, like a serpent-king trodden underfoot, and fitted to his bow fourteen arrows like the rod of Death, makers of an end to foes.
With five he struck off the elephant's feet and trunk, with three the king's arms and head, and with six he slew the six great car-warriors who followed the Pāṇḍya king, splendid as the six seasons.
The king's two arms, long and rounded, anointed with choice sandal, decked with gold, pearls, gems and diamonds, fell to the earth and writhed there like serpents struck down by Garuḍa.
And his head, its face bright as the full moon, with long eyes coppery in wrath and a high-bridged nose, falling earthward with its earrings, shone like the moon set between the two Viśākhā stars.
Then your son the king, approaching the teacher's son — perfect in his learning, his deed accomplished — surrounded by his friends, honoured him exceedingly with joy, as the lord of the immortals honoured Viṣṇu when Bali was conquered.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When the Pāṇḍya was slain, Saṃjaya, what did Arjuna do in the battle, and when the foe had been driven off by Karṇa, that lone champion?
Perfect in learning, mighty, disciplined, a hero is that son of Pāṇḍu, granted favour over all beings by the great-souled Śaṃkara.
Grievous and keen is the fear that comes from Dhanaṃjaya, slayer of foes. Tell me, Saṃjaya, what Pārtha did there.
Saṃjaya said: When the Pāṇḍya was slain, Kṛṣṇa hastily spoke salutary words to Arjuna: "Behold the overproud king, and the Pāṇḍavas in retreat.
By Aśvatthāman's resolve and by Karṇa the Sṛñjayas have been slain, and great is the slaughter wrought among horses, men, and elephants" — thus the unassailable Vāsudeva spoke to the diademed one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having heard this and seen the terrible, great peril to his brothers, the son of Pāṇḍu said, "Hṛṣīkeśa, drive the horses on, swiftly!"
Then Hṛṣīkeśa set forth with that chariot none could withstand, and once more a fearful encounter arose there.
Then again, O best of kings, a battle broke out between Karṇa and the Pāṇḍavas, swelling the realm of Yama.
Bows, arrows, iron clubs, swords, lances, spears, maces, slings, javelins, daggers, and battle-axes —
maces, darts, swords, spears, slings, and great goads — seizing these, the warriors swiftly fell upon one another, each longing to overcome the rest.
Making heaven, the quarters, the intermediate points, and the sky resound with the noise of arrows, bowstrings and palm-guards, and the earth with the rumble of chariot-wheels, they rushed upon their foes.
Thrilled by that mighty din, the heroes joined battle with heroes, fiercely terrible, each eager to fight the quarrel through to its end.
The sound of bowstrings, palm-guards and bows, the trumpeting of elephants, and the cries of the stricken as they fell — a tremendous uproar arose.
Hearing the manifold whistling of arrows and the roaring of the brave, O Bhārata, men trembled exceedingly, struck others down, and themselves grew faint.
As they roared and loosed a rain of weapons, Karṇa, the son of Adhiratha, crushed many of them with his battle-shafts.
Fifteen chariots of the Pāñcāla heroes, with their horses, drivers, and standards, Karṇa with his arrows sent to the abode of Yama.
The foremost warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, of great valour and swift weapons, veiling the sky, surrounded Karṇa in the battle on every side.
Then Karṇa, churning the enemy host with showers of arrows, plunged into it as a lord of the herd plunges into a lotus-pond filled with birds.
Springing into the midst of the foe, the son of Rādhā, shaking his peerless bow, with sharpened arrows struck off heads and made them fall.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Cutting through shields and armour, as if extinguishing the lives of embodied beings, they could not endure the touch of a second of his winged shafts.
With arrows sped from his bow that shattered armour, body, and life, and with the bowstring and palm-guards, he slew them as a charioteer drives his horses with the whip.
He brought the Pāṇḍus, Sṛñjayas, and Pāñcālas within range of his arrows, and Karṇa crushed them with vehemence, as a lion crushes herds of deer.
Then, O honoured one, the sons of the Pāñcālas and the sons of Draupadī, the twins, and Yuyudhāna together rushed upon Karṇa.
Striving with all their might, the Kuru, Pāṇḍava, and Sṛñjaya warriors, casting away their dear lives in battle, closed with one another.
Well-girt, mailed, adorned with helmets, the great car-warriors — some with maces, some with clubs, and others with iron bars —
rushed fiercely upon each other, like gods with raised rods, roaring, challenging, and bounding about, O honoured one.
Then they slew one another and fell, smitten in the fray, vomiting blood from their limbs, their brains and eyes dashed out in battle.
With faces full of teeth, blood-smeared and red as pomegranates, propped upright by the weapons within them, these slain men yet stood as though alive.
And still others fell upon one another with spears, swords, lances, slings, claw-weapons, darts, and javelins,
and others, in their wrath, hacked, cut, pierced, hurled, mangled, slew, and tore one another asunder.
Slain by one another, lifeless and drenched in gore, they fell, oozing their own bright blood like sandal trees that bleed their sap.
Chariots were destroyed by chariots, elephants by elephants, men by foremost of men, and horses by horses fell in their thousands.
Standards, heads, parasols, elephants' trunks, and the arms of men, severed by razor-shafts, broad-heads, and crescent-blades, let fall their weapons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Men, elephants, chariots, and horses were crushed in the battle; the brave were slain by horsemen, and the tuskers had their trunks cut off.
Standards with their banners fell like crumbling mountains; and foot-soldiers, swarming up, brought down both elephants and chariots.
Smitten, being struck down, and fallen on every side, horsemen swiftly closed and were slain by foot-soldiers, and bands of foot-soldiers, killed by horsemen, lay slain upon the field.
Like crushed lotuses and withered garlands, O most wise one, were the faces and the limbs of the slain.
The once exceedingly beautiful forms of elephants, horses, and men, O king, like soaked garments, became most grievous to look upon.
Saṃjaya said: Then the elephant-riders, urged on by your son, wrathful and seeking to slay Dhṛṣṭadyumna, rushed with their elephants upon the son of Pṛṣata.
The eastern and southern champions skilled in elephant-warfare — the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Puṇḍras, Māgadhas, and Tāmraliptakas,
the Mekalas, Kośalas, Madras, Daśārṇas, and Niṣadhas, skilled in elephant-battle, together with the Kaliṅgas, O Bhārata —
all of these, like rain-laden clouds, drenched in the battle the mountain that was the Pāñcāla prince with arrows, lances, and iron shafts.
Eager to crush those elephants, sorely goaded by heels, toes, and hooks, the son of Pṛṣata drenched them with arrows and iron shafts.
Each one of those mountain-like elephants he pierced with ten, with six, or with eight arrows hurled at them, O Bhārata, even as he was being veiled by the elephants like the sun by clouds.
The Pāṇḍus and Pāñcālas, roaring, their weapons whetted, surrounded those elephants, raining upon them with the twang of bowstrings and the cry of arrows.
Nakula and Sahadeva, the sons of Draupadī, the Prabhadrakas, Sātyaki, Śikhaṇḍin, and the valiant Cekitāna —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
those elephants, sped on by the barbarians, seizing men, horses, and chariots with their trunks, in their great fury crushed them underfoot.
They gored with the points of their tusks, snatched up and flung men about, and others, terrible to behold, rushed on with bodies impaled upon their tusks.
But the elephant of the Vaṅga that stood at the forefront, Sātyaki, piercing it in a vital spot with an iron shaft of terrible speed, brought down.
As that warrior, his elephant felled, was springing down from it, Sātyaki pierced his breast with an iron shaft, and he fell to the earth.
As the Puṇḍra's elephant, like a moving mountain, came rushing on, Sahadeva with effort struck it down with three iron shafts.
Having stripped that elephant of its banner, its driver, its armour, its standard, and its very life, Sahadeva once more bore down upon the king of Aṅga.
But Nakula, holding Sahadeva back, himself afflicted the Aṅga, striking the king with three iron shafts like the rods of Yama, and the elephant with a hundred.
The Aṅga hurled at Nakula eight hundred javelins bright as the rays of the sun, but he cut each one into three pieces.
Then with a crescent-headed arrow the Pāṇḍava severed his head, and the slain barbarian fell to the ground together with his tusked beast.
When the preceptor's son, skilled in the lore of elephants, had been slain, the enraged elephant-drivers of the Aṅgas rushed upon Nakula with their beasts.
With fluttering banners on their foreheads, with golden girths and body-coverings, they came on swiftly, eager to crush him, like blazing mountains in motion.
The Mekalas, Utkalas, and Kaliṅgas, the Niṣādas and the men of Tāmraliptaka, bent on slaughter, loosed showers of arrows and javelins.
Seeing Nakula overspread by them as the sun is veiled by clouds, the Pāṇḍavas, Pāñcālas, and Somakas, much enraged, rushed forward all around him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then there arose a battle between the car-warriors and the elephants, both pouring forth showers of arrows and javelins by the thousand.
The frontal globes of the elephants burst asunder, and their various vital parts, and the tusks of the deeply pierced beasts, and their ornaments, were shattered by the iron shafts.
With sixty-four keenly sharpened arrows Sahadeva quickly slew eight of those great elephants, and they fell together with their riders.
Drawing his excellent bow with effort, Nakula, O delight of the Kurus, smote the elephants with straight-flying iron shafts.
Then the descendant of Śini and the Pāñcāla prince, the sons of Draupadī, the Prabhadrakas, and Śikhaṇḍin drenched the great elephants with showers of arrows.
Those mountainlike elephants of the foe, struck by the arrow-showers of the Pāṇḍava warriors who were like rain-clouds, fell as mountains fall beneath downpours of thunderbolts.
Having thus slain your elephants, those bulls among men of the Pāṇḍava side looked upon your army, swiftly scattering like a river whose banks have been breached.
Beholding that host, the warriors of the son of Pāṇḍu threw it into confusion, and then once again rushed straight at Karṇa.
Then, O great king, Duḥśāsana the brother advanced against his brother Sahadeva, who in his fury was consuming your host.
Seeing those two meet in mighty combat, the lords of men there raised lionlike roars and waved their garments aloft.
Then, O Bhārata, the mighty son of Pāṇḍu was struck upon the chest with three arrows by your wrathful bowman son.
Thereupon, O king, Sahadeva pierced your son with an iron shaft, then struck him with seventy more and his charioteer with three apiece.
Then, O king, Duḥśāsana, having cut his bow asunder in that great fray, afflicted Sahadeva with seventy-three shafts upon his arms and chest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the wrathful Sahadeva, best of warriors and full of splendour, seized a sword in that great battle and whirled it at your son.
That great blade, having cut through his bow together with its fitted arrows, then fell to the earth like a serpent dropping from the sky.
Then the valiant Sahadeva took up another bow and let fly at Duḥśāsana a death-dealing arrow.
As that shaft came flying on, gleaming like the rod of Yama, the Kaurava cut it in two with his keen-edged sword.
As that sword came suddenly hurtling on, Sahadeva, as if smiling, struck it down in the battle with his sharp arrows.
Then, O Bhārata, your son in that great battle quickly let fall sixty-four arrows upon Sahadeva's car.
Those many arrows speeding upon him in the fight, O king, Sahadeva cut to pieces, each one with five shafts.
Having warded off the great arrows sent by your son, the son of Mādrī then gathered very many shafts and aimed them at him.
Then in his fury, O great king, the valiant Sahadeva fitted a dreadful shaft like Death, Time, and the Ender, and drawing his bow mightily, loosed it at your son.
Piercing him with speed and rending his great armour, the shaft entered the earth, O king, as a serpent enters an anthill; and thereupon, O king, your son, that mighty car-warrior, swooned away.
Seeing him senseless, his charioteer, sorely afraid, swiftly bore the car away as it was being raked by sharp arrows.
Having vanquished him in battle, the son of Pāṇḍu, O descendant of Pāṇḍu's line, joyfully crushed Duryodhana's force on every side.
As a man in anger tramples an anthill of ants, O king, so was that Kaurava army crushed by him, O Bhārata.
Then, O king, Karṇa the son of the sun checked Nakula, who in his fury was rending the host asunder in the battle.
And Nakula, smiling, then said this to Karṇa: "After long, alas, the gods have looked upon me with kindly eyes,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
since you, O wretch, have come within the range of my sight in battle. For you are the root of all our calamities, of the enmity and the strife.
Through your fault the Kurus have been wasted, falling upon one another. Slaying you this day in battle, I shall have achieved my purpose and be freed of fever."
Thus addressed, the son of the charioteer answered Nakula in words befitting a prince and, above all, a bowman:
"Strike in battle, O boy, that we may see your manhood. Having done some deed in the fight, O hero, then are you fit to boast.
Without speaking, my son, do the brave fight to the utmost of their power. So fight with me with all your might; this day I shall humble your pride."
Having said this, the charioteer's son swiftly smote the son of Pāṇḍu, and pierced him in the battle with seventy-three arrows.
Then Nakula, thus pierced by the charioteer's son, O Bhārata, struck the charioteer's son in turn with eighty shafts like venomous serpents.
Karṇa, that foremost of archers, cut his bow asunder and afflicted the Pāṇḍava with thirty stone-whetted, golden-feathered arrows.
Piercing his armour, they drank his blood in the battle, as venomous serpents, having broken through the earth, drink water.
Then, taking up another bow, gold-backed and hard to withstand, he pierced Karṇa with twenty arrows and his charioteer with three.
Then in his wrath, O great king, Nakula, slayer of hostile heroes, cut off Karṇa's bow with an exceedingly sharp razor-headed shaft.
Then, while his bow was severed, the hero, laughing, smote that mighty car-warrior renowned in all the worlds with three hundred shafts.
Seeing Karṇa thus sorely pressed by the son of Pāṇḍu, O sire, the car-warriors, together with the gods, were filled with the utmost amazement.
Then Karṇa, the son of the sun, taking up another bow, afflicted Nakula with five arrows in the region of the collarbone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With those arrows fixed upon his breast, the son of Mādrī shone resplendent, like the sun shedding its light upon the world with its own rays.
Then Nakula, having pierced Karṇa with seven iron shafts, once more cut off the tip of his bow, O sire.
Taking up another bow of swifter force in the battle, Karṇa then with his arrows blocked the quarters on every side around Nakula.
Being suddenly overspread by the arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow, that great car-warrior swiftly cut those arrows asunder with arrows of his own.
Then a net wrought of arrows was seen stretched across the sky, as the heavens appear when filled with swarms of darting fireflies.
By the hundreds of arrows loosed by the two, the sky was then covered over, and it was as thronged as when swarms of locusts fill it.
Those arrows wrought of gold, falling again and again in ordered rows, gleamed like ranks of wild geese flying in lines.
When the sky was veiled in the net of arrows and the sun was hidden, only with difficulty could any creature move about, O lord of peoples.
With the path obstructed all around by masses of arrows, the two illustrious warriors shone like two newly risen morning suns.
The Somakas, being slain by the arrows loosed from Karṇa's bow, shrank away, O king of kings, tormented by pain and afflicted by the shafts.
Likewise your host, being slain by Nakula's arrows, scattered to the quarters, O king, as clouds are driven apart by the wind.
Both armies, being smitten by those two with great celestial arrows, withdrew beyond the reach of the shafts and then stood by as mere onlookers.
When the host had been driven back by the arrows of Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava, those two high-souled warriors pierced each other with showers of shafts.
Displaying their celestial weapons at the head of the battle and suddenly veiling each other, each sought the other's death.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The arrows loosed by Nakula, feathered with heron and peacock plumes, having shrouded Karṇa, then took their stand as though foes encircling him.
