Your son and the valiant king of the Madras received those onrushing warriors, the two of them standing firm like the mountains of the eastern and western horizons confronting a host of great storm-clouds.
Śalya, glorying in battle, rained showers of arrows upon Yudhiṣṭhira, that tamer of foes, even as Maghavan pours down the rain.
In like manner the high-souled king of the Kurus too, taking up his splendid bow, displayed the manifold lessons taught him by Droṇa.
He poured forth showers of arrows, wondrously, swiftly, and well; and as he ranged across the field of battle none could mark an opening in his guard.
With their various shafts the two of them wounded each other, like two valiant tigers in combat, each greedy for the flesh of its prey.
Bhīma closed with your son, that drunkard of battle; and the prince of the Pāñcālas, and Sātyaki, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī received from every side the heroes led by Śakuni.
Then once again, O king, fierce grew the battle between your men and the foe, both eager for victory—the fruit of your evil counsels.
Duryodhana, taking deliberate aim, with a smooth-jointed arrow cut down in the fight Bhīma's banner adorned with gold.
Fair to behold, with its great net of little bells, the splendid lion that was Bhīmasena's emblem fell roaring to the ground.
And again the king severed with a sharp-edged razor-shaft his brilliant bow, which was thick as the trunk of a lordly elephant.
His bow thus cut, the fiery Bhīma, advancing with a car-borne lance, pierced your son in the breast, and Duryodhana sank down upon the floor of his chariot.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While your son lay swooning, Vṛkodara then with a razor-headed shaft struck the head of his driver from his body.
Their charioteer slain, his horses, O Bhārata, bearing the car away, fled in all directions, O king, and a cry of dismay arose.
To his rescue rushed the mighty car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman, all bent on saving your son.
As that host was thrown into confusion, his foot-soldiers fled in terror; but the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, twanging his bow, struck them down with his shafts.
And Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with wrath, charged upon the lord of the Madras, himself urging on his horses, ivory-white and swift as thought.
There we beheld a marvel in Kuntī's son Yudhiṣṭhira: he who before had been gentle and self-controlled had now grown terrible.
With eyes wide open and trembling with fury, the son of Kuntī cut down warriors by hundreds of thousands with his whetted shafts.
Whatever host advanced to meet him, that host the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas brought down with his arrows, O king, as great mountains are shattered by thunderbolts.
Felling many car-warriors with their horses, drivers, banners, and cars, the mighty one sported there alone, like the wind scattering the clouds.
Horses with their riders, and foot-soldiers by the thousand, he crushed in the battle, as Rudra in his wrath crushes the beasts.
Having swept the field empty on every side with his showers of arrows, he charged upon the lord of the Madras and cried, "Stand, Śalya!"
Beholding this exploit of him whose deeds were dreadful in battle, all your men were seized with terror; but Śalya advanced to meet him.
Then the two of them, swollen with fury, blew their conches born of the waters, and, challenging and defying one another, closed in combat.
Śalya overwhelmed Yudhiṣṭhira with a shower of arrows, and the son of Kuntī in turn overwhelmed the king of the Madras with showers of arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, O king, the two heroes, the king of the Madras and Yudhiṣṭhira, were seen in the fight bristling with heron-feathered shafts, their blood gushing forth.
The two high-souled warriors shone like a flowering śalmali and a kiṃśuka tree in the forest, ablaze with splendor, frenzied in their battle for life itself.
Beholding them, none of all the armies could foretell which of the two would win: "Once he has slain the lord of the Madras, Pārtha shall this day enjoy the earth;
"or else Śalya, having slain the Pāṇḍava, shall bestow the earth on Duryodhana"—thus, O Bhārata, no certainty came to the warriors there.
Yet for Yudhiṣṭhira, as he fought, every omen turned auspicious.
Then Śalya swiftly loosed a hundred arrows at Yudhiṣṭhira, and with a sharp-pointed shaft he cut his bow asunder.
Taking up another bow, Yudhiṣṭhira pierced Śalya with three hundred arrows and severed his bow with a razor-shaft.
Then with smooth-jointed shafts he slew Śalya's four horses, and with two sharp-pointed ones the two drivers who guarded his flanks.
Then, as Śalya stood before him, with a blazing, golden, whetted broad-headed shaft he struck down his banner; and thereupon, O tamer of foes, that host of Duryodhana was broken.
Then the son of Droṇa rushed to the lord of the Madras, brought thus to such a pass, and lifting him into his own chariot bore him swiftly away.
Having gone but a little way, while Yudhiṣṭhira roared aloud, the lord of the Madras halted and mounted another chariot,
a gleaming car duly equipped, that rumbled like a great rain-cloud, furnished with all its gear in readiness—a thing to make the foe's hair stand on end.
Saṃjaya said: Then, taking up another bow, mightier and swifter still, the lord of the Madras pierced Yudhiṣṭhira and roared like a lion.
Then that bull among warriors, immeasurable of soul, rained down a shower of arrows upon the kṣatriyas, like Parjanya pouring forth the rain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Piercing Sātyaki with ten shafts, Bhīmasena with three, and Sahadeva with three, he then pressed hard upon Yudhiṣṭhira.
That foremost of car-warriors slew sundry other mighty bowmen together with their horses, chariots, and elephants—elephants with their riders, horses with their cavalrymen, and chariots together with their warriors.
He severed arms still grasping their weapons, and banners as well, and made the earth thickly strewn with warriors as an altar is strewn with kuśa grass.
As he slaughtered the hostile hosts like Death the all-ender himself, the Pāṇḍavas, Pāñcālas, and Somakas, exceedingly enraged, surrounded him on every side.
Bhīmasena, and the grandson of Śini, and the two sons of Mādrī, foremost of men, came upon him as he closed with their king of dreadful might; and, calling upon one another, they hemmed him in.
Then those heroes, having reached that king, the lord of the Madras, best of fighters, and having hemmed him about in the battle, those manly warriors struck him with feathered shafts of terrible speed.
Guarded by Bhīmasena, by the two sons of Mādrī, and by Mādhava, the son of Dharma struck the lord of the Madras between the breasts with feathered shafts of terrible speed.
Then in the battle the throngs of your car-warriors, the foremost among them, seeing the lord of the Madras sore beset with arrows, surrounded him on all sides, with Duryodhana's consent.
Then swiftly the king of the Madra folk pierced Yudhiṣṭhira in the fight with seven shafts; and the high-souled Pārtha in turn pierced him with nine arrows, O king, amid that tumult.
With arrows drawn back to the ear, oil-washed and well-aimed, the two great car-warriors—the lord of the Madras and Yudhiṣṭhira—then veiled each other from sight in the battle.
Then swiftly those two great car-warriors, those best of kings, mighty in strength and unassailable by their foes, watching for each other's opening, pierced one another sorely with their shafts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As those two high-souled heroes, the Madra warrior and the son of Pāṇḍu, rained masses of arrows upon each other, the great twang of their bowstrings against their wrist-guards rang out like the crash of great Indra's thunderbolt.
The two ranged the field, bright as tiger-cubs greedy for flesh in the great forest, and like two tusked lordly elephants they gashed each other, their pride born of the combat.
Then the high-souled lord of the Madras, overpowering Yudhiṣṭhira of terrible might, pierced that hero with great force in the heart, with a shaft bright as the sun and as fire.
Then, sorely wounded, the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira too, O king, struck the lord of the Madras with a well-aimed shaft, and that bull of the Kurus took joy thereat.
Then, after a moment, that lord of kings, recovering his senses, his eyes red with wrath, his might like that of the thousand-eyed one, swiftly struck Pārtha with a hundred shafts.
Then the high-souled son of Dharma in haste and wrath, with nine shafts piercing Śalya's breast and his golden mail, smote him again with six other arrows.
Then the lord of the Madras, full of joy, drawing his bow, let fly his shafts, and with two razor-headed arrows cut the bow of the king, that bull among the Kurus.
Then in the battle the high-souled king, taking up another bow, yet more terrible, pierced Śalya on every side with whetted shafts, as great Indra pierced Namuci with his sharp-pointed bolts.
Then the high-souled Śalya, with nine shafts, having cut through the stout golden corslets of both Bhīma and king Yudhiṣṭhira, tore open their arms.
Then with another razor-shaft, blazing with the sun's splendor, he shattered the king's bow; and Kṛpa with six arrows slew the king's charioteer, who fell forward upon his face.
And the lord of the Madras with four arrows slew the horses of Yudhiṣṭhira; and having slain them, that high-souled one wrought havoc among the warriors of king Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the king was thus served, the high-souled Bhīmasena swiftly cut the bow of the lord of the Madras with a fast-flying shaft and pierced that king sorely with two arrows.
Then with another shaft he struck the head of his driver from his body, from the midst of his armor; and the sorely enraged Bhīmasena swiftly slew his four horses as well.
As that foremost of all bowmen ranged the battle alone with great swiftness, Bhīma covered him with a hundred arrows, and so too did Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī.
Seeing Śalya dazed by those shafts, Bhīma with his arrows cut through his armor; and his corslet thus rent by Bhīmasena, the lord of the Madras seized a shield set with a thousand stars.
And taking up a sword, the high-souled one leapt down from his chariot and rushed upon the son of Kuntī; having cut the chariot-pole of Nakula, that one of dreadful might bore down upon Yudhiṣṭhira.
And as that king sprang forward, wrathful, swooping like Death the all-ender, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the sons of Draupadī, Śikhaṇḍin, and the grandson of Śini suddenly surrounded him.
Then the high-souled Bhīma cut his peerless shield to pieces with ten shafts, and with broad-headed arrows severed his sword at the hilt, roaring with joy in the midst of your host.
Beholding that deed of Bhīma, the foremost throngs of the Pāṇḍavas' car-warriors, rejoicing, raised a mighty shout, laughing aloud, and blew their conches white as the moon.
At that terrible din your army was sore afflicted and joyless, overcome with sweat, its limbs drenched in blood, half-senseless and downcast.
That king of the Madras, suddenly hemmed in by the chief Pāṇḍava warriors led by Bhīma, sped swiftly straight toward Yudhiṣṭhira, as a lion makes for its prey.
And Yudhiṣṭhira, beholding the lord of the Madras, his horses and driver slain, blazing with wrath like a kindled fire, swiftly rushed upon that foe with all his might.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Calling swiftly to mind the words of Govinda, he set his heart upon the slaying of Śalya; and Yudhiṣṭhira, standing in his chariot whose horses and driver were slain, longed for his spear.
And, marking that deed of the high-souled Śalya, and remembering the portion of doom that yet remained for him, the self-controlled king bent his mind upon Śalya's slaying, even as Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Indra, had bidden him.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira seized a spear, golden of sheen, its shaft set with gems and gold; and opening wide his blazing eyes, with mind enraged he gazed upon the lord of the Madras.
Gazed upon, O king of men, by that pure-souled monarch whose sins were purged away, that the king of the Madras was not reduced to ashes—this seems to me a marvel, O king.
Then that high-souled and foremost of the Kurus hurled with great force and swiftness at the lord of the Madras the blazing spear, its splendid fierce shaft alight with gems and coral.
As it sped down blazing, hurled with mighty strength, scattering sparks, all the assembled Kurus gazed upon it as upon a great meteor at the ending of an age.
That spear, like the Night of Doom with her noose in hand, like the dread nurse of Yama, terrible of aspect, unfailing, the very likeness of Brahmā's rod, Yudhiṣṭhira, intent, let fly in the battle.
That spear, worshipped with diligence by the sons of Pāṇḍu with perfumes and garlands, with the choicest seats, drink, and food, blazed like the fire of universal dissolution, terrible as a destroying spell of the Atharvan and Aṅgiras seers.
That spear had been forged by Tvaṣṭṛ for Īśāna's sake, a devourer of the lives and bodies of foes, with power to slay by force the beings that dwell in earth, in the sky, in the waters, and elsewhere.
It was hung with bells and banners, set with gems and adamant, gleaming with cat's-eye, its shaft of refined gold; fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ with effort and due rite, it was unfailing, the bringer of death to the haters of Brahman.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Charged with momentum by force and effort, hallowed with terrible mantras, he then loosed it along that surpassing course for the slaying of the lord of the Madras.
"You are slain!" the King of Righteousness roared aloud, as Rudra lets fly the death-dealing shaft against Death himself, stretching forth his firm, fair-handed arm, all but dancing in his wrath.
That spear, hurled by Yudhiṣṭhira with all his might, its force not to be turned aside, Śalya roared out to receive, as fire roars to welcome a stream of butter rightly poured in oblation.
Cleaving his vital parts and his broad bright chest, and likewise his armor, it sank in as water sinks unhindered into the earth, consuming the king's wide-spread glory.
With the blood that streamed from his nose, eyes, ears, and mouth, and that welled forth from the wound, his limbs were drenched—like the great mountain Krauñca smitten by Skanda.
His armor cleft asunder by the joy of the Kurus, the great-souled one, who matched the mount of mighty Indra, flung wide his arms and fell from his chariot to the earth, like the peak of a mountain struck by the thunderbolt.
Stretching out his arms, the king of the Madras, facing the King of Righteousness, then fell to the ground like an upraised banner of Indra.
With every limb thus rent and bathed in blood, that bull among men seemed as if the earth herself had risen up in love to meet him.
Like a lover sinking upon the breast of his cherished beloved, having long enjoyed the bountiful earth as a man enjoys his dear and lovely wife, that lord, embracing her with all his limbs, seemed as one fallen asleep.
Slain in righteous battle by the righteous-souled son of Dharma, he was like a fire well-fed with rightful oblation, grown calm at the close of the sacrifice.
Though his heart was riven by the spear, his weapons and banner cast away, and though the lord of the Madras lay stilled in death, splendor would not forsake him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, taking up his bow bright as Indra's rainbow, scattered his foes in the fight as the king of birds scatters serpents, in an instant destroying with his keen broad-headed shafts the bodies and the lives of his enemies.
Then your soldiers, enveloped by the floods of the Pārtha's arrows, their eyes shut fast, sorely afflicted, wasting one another grievously, cast off their mail, their bodies stripped of weapons, of armor, and of life.
Then, when Śalya had fallen, the young brother of the Madra king, a charioteer the equal of his brother in every quality, rushed upon the Pāṇḍava.
And that best of men, frenzied with battle, eager to avenge his slain brother, swiftly pierced him with many iron shafts.
The King of Righteousness, moving as if in haste, pierced him with six swift arrows and, with two razor-edged shafts, cut apart his bow and his banner too.
Then, with a blazing, firm, and whetted broad-headed shaft, he struck off the head of that warrior who stood there before him.
That head, still wearing its earrings, was seen to fall from the chariot, like a dweller in heaven plummeting down upon the exhaustion of his merit.
Seeing his headless body, fallen from the chariot, its limbs drenched with blood, the army broke and fled.
When that brother of the Madra king, clad in many-hued armor, was slain, the Kurus, raising cries of woe, scattered in flight.
Seeing Śalya's younger brother slain, your men, ready to lay down their lives, covered thickly with dust, trembled exceedingly in their dread of the Pāṇḍavas.
Upon those Kauravas thus broken and terrified, O bull of the Bhāratas, Sātyaki, grandson of Śini, advanced, showering them with arrows.
As that mighty bowman came on, irresistible and hard to withstand, Hārdikya, O king, swiftly and without fear received him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those two great-souled and unconquered scions of the Vṛṣṇis came together, Hārdikya and Sātyaki, like two lions maddened with rut.
With arrows of spotless luster they veiled each other, bright as the sun's own beams, each rivaling the day-maker in radiance.
The shafts of those two Vṛṣṇi lions, sped by the force of their bowstrings' course, we beheld in the sky moving swift as flights of birds.
Hārdikya pierced Sātyaki with ten arrows and his horses with three, and with a single keen-jointed shaft cut asunder his bow.
Casting aside that fine bow now severed, the bull of the Śinis swiftly took up another weapon, mightier still in force.
Taking up that excellent bow, the foremost of all archers struck Hārdikya in return, full upon the breast, with ten arrows.
Then, cutting apart his chariot, yoke, and pole with well-aimed broad-headed shafts, he swiftly slew his horses and both his flanking charioteers.
With the king of the Madras slain, O king, and Kṛtavarman robbed of his chariot, the whole host of Duryodhana once again turned its back in flight.
The enemy did not perceive it, the field being shrouded by the army's dust; yet that force, the greater part of it slain, had then turned away in retreat.
Then in a moment they saw the dust that had risen from the earth laid to rest by the manifold streams of blood, O bull among men.
Then Duryodhana, seeing his own force shattered close at hand, alone held back all the Pārthas as they swiftly bore down upon him.
Seeing the Pāṇḍavas with their chariots, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna son of Pṛṣata, and the unassailable man of Ānarta, he overwhelmed them with whetted arrows.
The foe did not close with him, as mortals shun Death come near; and Hārdikya too, mounting another chariot, returned to the fight.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, that great chariot-warrior, in haste slew Kṛtavarman's horses with four feathered shafts, and pierced Gautama too with six keen broad-headed arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Aśvatthāman bore Hārdikya away from Yudhiṣṭhira upon his own chariot, since the king had killed his horses and left him without a car.
Then the son of Śaradvat struck Yudhiṣṭhira in return with eight arrows, and pierced his horses with eight keen shafts.
Thus it was, O great king, that this remnant of the battle came to pass, through your evil counsel, O Bhārata, yours and your son's together.
When that foremost of mighty bowmen had been laid low in the midst of battle by the bull of the Kurus, the Pārthas, gathered together and filled with utmost joy, blew their conches at the sight of Śalya slain.
And they praised Yudhiṣṭhira in the fray as of old the gods praised Indra at the slaying of Vṛtra, and they raised the sounds of instruments of every kind, making the earth resound on every side.
Saṃjaya said: When Śalya had been slain, O king, the followers of the Madra king, seven hundred heroic chariot-warriors, sallied forth from the great host.
But Duryodhana, mounted upon an elephant like a mountain, the parasol held above him and the yak-tail whisks fanning him, restrained the Madras, crying, "You must not go! You must not go!"
Though held back again and again by Duryodhana, those heroes, longing to slay Yudhiṣṭhira, plunged into the host of the Pāṇḍavas.
Those heroes, O great king, their minds resolved upon battle, raising a mighty twang of bowstrings, fought all together against the Pāṇḍavas.
But hearing that Śalya was slain and that the son of Dharma was hard pressed by the great chariot-warriors of the Madras, who were intent upon their king's pleasure—
—the Pārtha then came on, drawing his bow Gāṇḍīva, that great chariot-warrior filling all the quarters with the thunder of his car.
Then Arjuna and Bhīma, and the two sons of Mādrī, the Pāṇḍavas, and Sātyaki, that tiger among men, and the sons of Draupadī, every one—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
—Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, and the Pāñcālas together with the Somakas, seeking to protect Yudhiṣṭhira, ringed him about on every side.
Those bulls among men, surrounded on all sides by the Pāṇḍavas, set that army churning as sea-monsters churn the ocean.
Like the great river Gaṅgā lashed into turmoil by a head-on gale, the banner-host of the Pāṇḍavas was once again, O king, thrown into uproar.
Storming into that great army, the great chariot-warriors who held their lives as nothing made your men quake as mighty winds shake the trees.
Many cried out there, "Where is that king Yudhiṣṭhira? Nor are any of his heroic brothers to be seen here at all."
"The mighty warriors of the Pāñcālas, and Śikhaṇḍin that great chariot-fighter, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and the grandson of Śini, and the sons of Draupadī, all of them—"
As they spoke thus, the heroic sons of Draupadī, great chariot-warriors, and Yuyudhāna, smote those followers of the Madra king.
Some with their wheels crushed, some with their tall banners cut down, your men were seen in the battle, slain by the foe.
Beholding the Pāṇḍavas in the battle, your warriors, O king, though restrained by your son, rushed forth with violence on every side, O Bhārata.
Duryodhana sought to restrain those heroes, soothing them with gentle words, yet not one of those great chariot-warriors there obeyed his command.
Then the son of the Gāndhāra king, Śakuni, skilled in speech, spoke these words to Duryodhana, O great king:
"Why is the force of the Madras being cut down before our very eyes? This is not fitting, O Bhārata, while you stand fast in the battle.
"That we should fight in concert—such a compact was made; then why, O king, do you suffer the foe to go on slaying?"
Duryodhana said: "Restrained by me before, these men would not heed my word; for all these who have been slain plunged headlong into the host of the Pāṇḍavas."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śakuni said: "Heroes in their wrath heed not their lord's command in battle. Enough of being angered at them; this is no time to stand aloof.
"Let us all here join together, with our horse and chariots and elephants, and go to rescue those mighty bowmen, the followers of the Madra king.
"Let us guard one another with great effort, O king." So, all taking thought together, they set out to where the soldiers were.
Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed, the king, encircled by a great host, advanced, making the earth tremble with his lion's roar.
"Strike! Pierce! Seize! Smite! Cut them down!"—such was the tumultuous cry of your army, O Bhārata.
But the Pāṇḍavas, seeing in the battle the followers of the Madra king joined together, advanced upon them, taking up a central formation.
In a moment, O lord of peoples, those heroes, the followers of the Madra king, were seen slain in the battle, hand to hand.
Then, as we pressed forward, the swift foe, their enemies slain, exultant and gathered together, raised shouts of triumph.
Then headless trunks were seen rising up on every side, and a great meteor fell straight through the disk of the sun.
With chariots shattered, with their yokes and axles broken, with great warriors slain, and with horses fallen, the earth was covered over.
Borne along by horses swift as the wind, by steeds still fastened to their yokes, warriors were seen there, O great king, upon that field of battle.
In the battle some horses dragged chariots with broken wheels; some, bearing off half a car, wandered to the ten quarters; and here and there were seen steeds still tangled in their harness.
And chariot-warriors were seen falling, O best of men, like Siddhas cast down from heaven at the exhaustion of their merits.
And when the heroes, the followers of the Madra king, had been slain, and the Pārthas, those great chariot-warriors, saw us bearing down upon them as well—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
—those smiters, greedy for victory, advanced with violence, raising the din of their arrows mingled with the blare of conches.
But falling upon us once more, those striking warriors, sure of their aim, brandished their bows and raised great lion-roars.
Then, beholding the great host of the king of the Madras struck down, and seeing the valiant king of the Madras laid low in battle, the whole army of Duryodhana once again turned its face away.
Cut down, O great king, by the Pāṇḍavas flushed with victory, terrified and bewildered, it scattered to all directions, driven in panic by those firm-bowed warriors.
Saṃjaya said: When the unassailable king of the Madras, that great chariot-warrior, was felled in battle, your men and your sons for the most part turned their backs.
With that great-souled hero slain, they were like merchants whose ship has broken apart upon a bottomless, boatless, shoreless sea, longing for the farther bank.
When the king of the Madras fell, O great king, terrified and torn by arrows, defenseless and longing for a protector, they were like deer harried by a lion.
Like bulls with broken horns, like elephants with shattered tusks, at midday we withdrew, vanquished by the son of Dharma.
When Śalya was slain, O king, not one of your warriors had the mind either to rally the ranks or to display valor.
O Bhārata, the grief and the fear that came upon your warriors when Bhīṣma and Droṇa and the son of the sūta were slain, O lord of peoples — that fear and that sorrow now returned upon us even more greatly.
Despairing now of victory, with Śalya the great chariot-warrior slain, their champions dead, scattered and gashed by sharp arrows — when the king of the Madras fell, O king, your warriors fled in fear.
Some mounting horses, some elephants, some chariots, those great warriors, and the foot-soldiers too, swift of foot, fled in fear.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And two thousand war-elephants, mountainous and battle-ready, fled together when Śalya fell, goaded by the hook and the thumb.
O best of the Bharatas, your men fled from the battlefield in every direction, and even as they ran they were seen gasping, tormented by arrows.
Seeing them broken, fleeing, their spirit gone, defeated, the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, eager for victory, rushed upon them.
And there arose a fearsome din — the twang and whistle of arrows, abundant lion-roars, and the blare of the conches of the heroes.
Seeing the Kaurava army fear-stricken and fleeing in all directions, the Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, spoke to one another.
Today King Yudhiṣṭhira, steadfast in truth, has conquered his foes; today Duryodhana is stripped of his blazing royal splendor.
Today, hearing that his son is slain, may King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, fall senseless to the ground and reap the fruit of his sin.
Today let him know the son of Kuntī to be the equal of all bowmen; today that evil-minded doer of wrong shall reproach himself; today let him remember the true and salutary words once spoken by Vidura.
From this day, reduced to a servant and waiting upon the sons of Pṛthā, let the king know the sorrow that has befallen the joys of Pāṇḍu's sons.
Today let that lord of the earth know the greatness of Kṛṣṇa; today let him know the dread thunder of Arjuna's bow in battle.
Today he shall know in battle the full power of his weapons and the strength of his arms — the terrible might of the great-souled Bhīma.
When Duryodhana is slain in battle — as the demon Maya was slain by Śakra — that deed which Bhīmasena wrought in the killing of Duḥśāsana, no other in the world but Bhīma of mighty strength could have done.
Today let them know the valor of the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, hearing that the king of the Madras — hard to withstand even for the gods — has been slain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Today he shall know in battle the two mighty sons of Mādrī, when the valiant son of Subala is slain and the Gāndhāras are slaughtered to the last.
How could victory not be theirs, whose warriors are Dhanaṃjaya, Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the grandson of Pṛṣata?
The five sons of Draupadī, the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī, Śikhaṇḍin the great archer, and King Yudhiṣṭhira himself —
and whose protector is Kṛṣṇa Janārdana, the lord of the worlds — how could victory not be theirs, whose refuge is righteousness?
Bhīṣma and Droṇa and Karṇa, and the king of the Madras too, and other heroic kings besides, by the hundreds and the thousands —
who else but Pṛthā's son Yudhiṣṭhira could vanquish them in battle, he whose protector is Hṛṣīkeśa, the everlasting treasury of righteousness and fame?
Speaking thus and filled with great joy, the Sṛñjayas, O king, pursued your broken men from behind.
The valiant Dhanaṃjaya bore down upon the chariot-host, while the two sons of Mādrī and Sātyaki the great chariot-warrior fell upon Śakuni.
Beholding them all fleeing, tormented by fear of Bhīmasena, Duryodhana then spoke to his charioteer, smiling as it were.
"The son of Pṛthā shall not pass beyond me while I stand bow in hand. Drive my horses to the rear of all the troops."
"With me fighting at the rear, Dhanaṃjaya the son of Kuntī shall no more dare to pass beyond me than the great ocean dares overstep its shore."
"Behold, O charioteer, the great army overrun by the Pāṇḍavas; look upon the dust of the host raised up on every side."
"Hear the many lion-roars, dreadful and terrifying. Therefore go slowly, O charioteer, and guard the rear."
"With me standing firm in battle and the Pāṇḍavas held in check, my host will swiftly rally and return in full force."
Hearing those words of your son, worthy of a foremost hero, the charioteer gently urged on the horses adorned with gold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bereft of elephants, horses, and chariots, having forsaken all care for their lives, twenty-one thousand foot-soldiers stood ready for battle.
Sprung from many lands, clad in garments of many hues, those warriors took their stand, seeking great glory.
As they rushed upon one another there, exultant, a mighty clash arose, dreadful of form and terrifying.
Then, O king, men of many lands held back Bhīmasena and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the grandson of Pṛṣata with a fourfold force.
But other foot-soldiers bore down upon Bhīma alone in battle — roaring and slapping their arms, exultant, eager to attain the world of heroes.
Falling upon Bhīmasena, furious and maddened with the lust of battle, the followers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son roared aloud and spoke of nothing else; surrounding Bhīma in the fray, they struck at him from every side.
Though assailed in battle, hemmed in by the throng of foot-soldiers, he did not stir from his chariot-seat, like Maināka the mountain.
Enraged, O great king, they set themselves to seize that great chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas, and held off the other warriors.
Bhīma grew wrathful in battle at those who beset him; quickly descending from his chariot, he took his stand on foot.
Grasping his great mace plated with gold, he slew your warriors like Death with his staff in hand.
Mighty Bhīma, with his mace, crushed those twenty-one thousand foot-soldiers, bereft of chariots, horses, and elephants.
Having destroyed that host of men, Bhīma of true valor, placing Dhṛṣṭadyumna before him, soon came again into view.
The slain foot-soldiers lay upon the ground, drenched in blood, like karṇikāra trees in full bloom broken down by the wind.
Wearing garlands of varied flowers and earrings of varied kinds, of varied birth and gathered from varied lands, they lay there slain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That great host of foot-soldiers, covered with banners and standards, cut down, appeared there dreadful of aspect and terrifying.
Then, with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head, the great chariot-warriors of the whole army charged against your great-souled son Duryodhana.
But all of them, seeing your great archers turned away in flight, did not press upon your son, as the shore does not encroach upon the abode of sea-monsters.
We beheld that marvel — the manhood of your son — that the sons of Pṛthā united could not overpass him, one though he was.
Duryodhana then spoke to his own army — sorely wounded, fled not far off, and bent upon flight —
"I see no place on earth or among the mountains where the Pāṇḍavas would not slay you once you fled there. What use is flight to you?"
"Small is their force, and the two Kṛṣṇas are sorely wounded. If we all stand firm here, our victory is assured."
"But if you flee, scattered and guilty of wrong, the Pāṇḍavas will follow and slay you. Better for us to stand firm in battle."
"Hear me, all you Kṣatriyas, as many as are gathered here: since Death ever slays alike the brave and the coward, what fool of a man who calls himself a Kṣatriya would not fight?"
"It is better for us to stand before the wrathful Bhīmasena. Death in battle is a blessing for those who fight by the law of the Kṣatriya: victorious, one wins happiness here; slain, one wins a great reward hereafter."
"There is no path to heaven better than the law of battle, O Kauravas. Slain in war, a man soon attains the worlds he has won."
Hearing his words and honoring them, the kings once more, with bows drawn to slay, turned upon the Pāṇḍavas.
As those striking warriors swiftly fell upon them in arrayed ranks, the striking sons of Pṛthā, greedy for victory, then went forth to meet them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The valiant Dhanaṃjaya advanced into the fray upon his chariot, drawing wide the bow Gāṇḍīva, renowned throughout the three worlds.
And the two sons of Mādrī and the mighty Sātyaki, exultant, swiftly fell upon Śakuni, there where your host stood.
Saṃjaya said: When the flood of the host had turned back, Śālva, lord of the throngs of Mlecchas, in great fury advanced upon the very great army of the Pāṇḍavas.
Mounted upon a mighty elephant in rut, like a mountain, proud, resembling Airāvata, a crusher of throngs of foes —
that elephant sprung of a great and noble breed, ever honored by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, well caparisoned by those skilled in the rules of the science, and always ridden into battle, O king —
Mounted upon it, that foremost of kings shone like the sun risen at the dawning. Upon that excellent elephant, O king, he advanced against the sons of Pāṇḍu on every side, and tore through them with sharp, dreadful arrows that were like the thunderbolt of great Indra.
As he loosed his arrows in that great battle, O king, and led warriors to Yama, neither friend nor foe could find a chink in him — as of old the Daityas could find none in the wielder of the thunderbolt.
The Pāṇḍavas, the Somakas, and the Sṛñjayas saw that single elephant on every side, ranging as though it were a thousand, like the elephant of great Indra close at hand.
The army of the foe, driven in rout, appeared on every side as if encircled; in their great fear it stood no longer firm in battle, but trampled one upon another.
Then that great Pāṇḍava host, suddenly broken by that lord of men, fled at once to the four quarters, unable to withstand the onset of that lord of elephants.
And seeing it broken by that swift charge, all your foremost warriors in the battle there honored that lord of men, and blew their conches white as the moon.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, hearing the shout of the Kauravas let loose in joy together with the blare of conches, the commander of the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas, the son of Pāñcāla, could not endure it for wrath.
Then that great-souled one, hastening for victory, went forth to meet that elephant, as Jambha of old, in his clash with Śakra, met Airāvaṇa, lord of elephants, the mount of Indra.
Seeing the king of the Pāñcālas suddenly rushing upon him in battle, that lion among kings swiftly sent forth that elephant, O king, to slay the son of Drupada.
As that elephant came rushing suddenly upon him, he pierced it with arrows bright as the sun—three foremost iron shafts, keen, blazing, burnished by the smith, and terrible in their speed.
Then the great-souled one loosed five more sharpened iron shafts into the beast's frontal lobes; and that foremost of elephants, sorely struck by them in battle, wheeled about and fled away in haste.
But Śālva, seizing that lord of elephants as it was suddenly driven back and put to flight, with goad and hook urged it swiftly forward, directing it against the chariot of the Pāñcāla king.
Seeing the elephant suddenly bearing down on him, the hero Dhṛṣṭadyumna swiftly seized his mace and leapt down at once from his own chariot, his limbs trembling with fear, and set foot upon the ground.
That mighty elephant crushed in an instant the chariot adorned with gold, together with its horses and driver, and lifting it up with its trunk dashed it down upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing the son of the Pāñcāla king thus hard-pressed by that foremost of elephants, Bhīma, Śikhaṇḍin, and the grandson of Śini rushed upon it at once with great speed.
Checking with their arrows the onrushing charge of the elephant that bore down upon them, those chariot-warriors held the beast in their grip; and so beset and stayed by them in battle, it staggered.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the king rained down his shafts on every side, as the sun pours forth its web of rays; and the hosts of chariots, smitten by those swift arrows, fled away in all directions.
Beholding that feat of Śālva, O king, all the Pāñcālas, Matsyas, and Sṛñjayas—foremost of men—filling the battle with cries of dismay, hemmed in the elephant on every side.
But the valiant king of the Pāñcālas, slayer of foes, swiftly grasping a mace like the peak of a mountain, O descendant of Bharata, pursued the elephant with speed, the hero unshaken and unafraid.
Then the swift son of the Pāñcāla king, whirling his mace, struck mightily that elephant which was like a mountain bearing the earth, dark as a rain-cloud, and streaming with rut.
Its frontal lobes shattered, the elephant, vast as a mountain, suddenly bellowed and, vomiting a great gush of blood from its mouth, fell to earth like a peak shaken loose by an earthquake.
As that lordly elephant was being brought down, and your son's host raised its cry of dismay, the hero of Śini's line struck off, with a keen broad-headed shaft, the head of King Śālva.
His head struck off in battle by the Sātvata, he fell to the ground together with the lordly elephant, like a great mountain-peak shattered and hurled down by the thunderbolt sped by the lord of the gods.
Saṃjaya said: When that valiant Śālva, the ornament of the assembly of battle, was slain, your host broke apart in headlong flight, as a great tree is shattered by the wind.
Seeing that host put to rout, the great chariot-warrior Kṛtavarman, valiant and of mighty strength, held back the army of the foe in battle.
Then those warriors turned back, beholding the Sātvata standing firm in the fray like a mountain, O king, though showered over with arrows in the fight.
Then the battle was joined afresh between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, O great king—the Kurus who had turned back, having made death itself the price of their return.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Wondrous there was the battle of the Sātvata with the foe, in that he alone held back the invincible army of the Pāṇḍavas.
When that hard deed was done by him, the lion-roar of those exultant comrades, fond friends each of the other, rose vast enough to touch the heavens.
The Pāñcālas, terrified by that sound, O bull of the Bhāratas, the mighty-armed Sātyaki, grandson of Śini, came up in support of.
Closing with the mighty king Kṣemadhūrti, he sent him with seven keen arrows to the abode of Yama.
As that mighty-armed bull of Śini's line came on, scattering sharp arrows, the sagacious son of Hṛdika fell upon him with speed.
Those two bowmen, foremost of chariot-warriors, roaring like lions and bearing the choicest of weapons, rushed each upon the other.
The Pāṇḍavas with the Pāñcālas, and the other warriors, those best of kings, became spectators of those two lions among men.
With iron shafts and calf-toothed arrows the two great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas struck at each other, like two rutting elephants in their joy of battle.
Ranging through manifold courses of fight, the son of Hṛdika and the bull of Śini's line again and again hid each other from view beneath a rain of arrows.
We saw the shafts of those two lions of the Vṛṣṇis, driven up by the force and might of their bows, speeding swift as locusts through the sky.
Closing with that lone hero of true deeds, the son of Hṛdika pierced his four horses with four keen arrows.
Then that long-armed hero, enraged like an elephant stung by the goad, pierced Kṛtavarman with eight excellent shafts.
Then Kṛtavarman, with arrows whetted on stone and loosed from a fully drawn bow, struck Sātyaki with three and with one severed his bow.
Casting aside that excellent bow now cut asunder, the bull of Śini's line, the grandson of Śini, swiftly took up another bow with an arrow already fitted.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Taking up that excellent bow, the best of all bowmen, of mighty valor, mighty wisdom, and mighty strength, strung it.
Unable to brook the cutting of his bow by Kṛtavarman, that surpassing chariot-warrior, in his wrath, swiftly bore down upon Kṛtavarman.
Then with ten well-sharpened arrows the bull of Śini's line slew the driver, the horses, and the banner of Kṛtavarman.
Then, O king, the great bowman Kṛtavarman, that mighty chariot-warrior, beheld his chariot wrought with gold, its horses and driver slain.
Seized by great wrath, O sire, he raised a lance and hurled it with the force of his arm, eager to slay the bull of Śini's line.
But the Sātvata in battle, splitting that lance with keen arrows, brought it down shattered to pieces, as though to confound the Mādhava; and then with another broad-headed shaft he struck him upon the breast.
His horses slain and his charioteer slain in battle by Yuyudhāna, accomplished in arms, Kṛtavarman sank down upon the earth.
When that hero was unhorsed by Sātyaki in their single chariot-duel, a very great fear came upon all the host.
And exceeding great was the despondency that came upon your son when Kṛtavarman, his driver slain and his horses slain, was robbed of his chariot.
Marking that tamer of foes with his horses slain and his driver slain, Kṛpa rushed forward, O king, eager to slay the bull of Śini's line.
Lifting him up into the seat of his chariot, before the eyes of all the bowmen, the mighty-armed one swiftly bore him away even from the field of battle.
When the grandson of Śini held the field, O king, and Kṛtavarman was bereft of his chariot, the whole host of Duryodhana once more turned its face away in flight.
The foe did not perceive it, the host being veiled in dust; and your men fled away, O king, save only King Duryodhana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Duryodhana, beholding his own host broken close at hand, dashed forward swiftly with speed and alone held back them all.
In wrath he checked all the Pāṇḍavas, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna son of Pṛṣata, and Śikhaṇḍin, and the sons of Draupadī, and the bands of the Pāñcālas,
and the Kekayas and the Somakas and the Pāñcālas too, O sire; unflinching and unassailable, he held them back with keen weapons.
Your mighty son stood intent in the fray, blazing forth like the great fire of the sacrifice, hallowed by sacred chants.
The foe could not stand against him in battle, as mortals cannot stand against death; and meanwhile the son of Hṛdika, mounting another chariot, came up once more.
Saṃjaya said: Your son, O great king, foremost of chariot-warriors, standing in his car, shone irresistible in battle like the glowing Rudra.
By his thousands of arrows the earth was covered over, and he drenched the foe with shafts as rain-streams drench the mountains.
There was no man among the Pāṇḍavas in that great battle, nor horse, nor elephant, nor chariot, that was left unwounded by his arrows.
Whatever warrior I beheld in the fight, O lord of peoples, that one was found covered over with arrows by your son, O descendant of Bharata.
As an army appears veiled in the dust raised by its own host, so did the host appear shrouded by the arrows of that great-souled one.
We saw the earth become all arrows, O lord of the earth, made so by Duryodhana, that bowman of nimble hand.
Among those thousands of warriors, your own and the foe's alike, Duryodhana alone was a man indeed—such is my judgment.
There we beheld the wondrous prowess of your son, in that the sons of Pṛthā, all united, could not overcome him single-handed, O descendant of Bharata.
He pierced Yudhiṣṭhira in battle with a hundred shafts, O bull of the Bhāratas, and Bhīmasena with seventy, and Sahadeva with seven,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and Nakula with sixty-four, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna with five, and the sons of Draupadī with seven, and Sātyaki with three; and with a broad-headed shaft he cut asunder the bow of Sahadeva, O sire.
Casting aside that broken bow, the valiant son of Mādrī took up another great bow and rushed upon the king; then in the fight he pierced Duryodhana with ten arrows.
And then the hero Nakula, that great bowman, pierced the king with nine arrows of dreadful form, and raised a shout.
Sātyaki too struck the king with a smooth-jointed shaft, and the sons of Draupadī with seventy-three, and the king of righteousness with seven, and Bhīmasena tormented the king with eighty arrows.
Though showered on every side with masses of arrows by those great-souled ones, he did not waver, O great king, while all the host looked on.
The deftness, the dexterity, and the valor of that great-souled one—all beings, all men, beheld them surpassing all.
But the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O lord of kings, having gone but a little way, and seeing not their king, turned back, clad once more in their mail.
As they came rushing on, a terrible tumult arose, like that of the troubled ocean by night in the season of rains.
Rejoining the unconquered king in battle, those great bowmen advanced to meet the Pāṇḍavas, who came on with weapons raised to slay.
The son of Droṇa held back Bhīmasena, enraged in battle; and then, O great king, by the arrows loosed on every side, neither the heroes nor the quarters nor the intermediate points could be discerned in the fray.
Those two, both grim in their deeds, both hard to bear, O descendant of Bharata, fought in dreadful fashion, each seeking to repay blow with blow, terrifying the whole world, the skin of their forearms torn by the lashing of their bowstrings.
But the hero Śakuni in battle pressed Yudhiṣṭhira hard; and the mighty lord, the son of Subala, having slain his four horses, raised a roar that made all the hosts tremble.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In that interval the valiant Sahadeva bore away the unconquered king, the hero, from the battle upon his own chariot.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, king of righteousness, mounting another chariot, pierced Śakuni with nine shafts and again with five, and that foremost of all bowmen sent forth a mighty roar.
Wondrous was that battle, and dreadful of form, O sire, delighting the hearts of the onlookers, and graced by the presence of the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
But Ulūka, of measureless spirit, rushed upon the great bowman Nakula, that frenzied warrior, with showers of arrows on every side.
And in like manner the valiant Nakula, in battle, hemmed in the son of Subala on every side with a great shower of arrows.
Those two heroes there in battle, scions of noble houses and mighty chariot-warriors, were seen fighting on, each having wronged the other.
And so too Kṛtavarman, fighting the grandson of Śini, that scorcher of foes, shone resplendent, O king, like Śakra contending with Bala in battle.
Duryodhana, having cut the bow of Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the fight, then pierced him, his bow severed, with keen arrows.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna too, taking up a supreme weapon in the battle, gave fight to the king before the eyes of all the bowmen.
Great was the combat between those two in the fray, O bull of the Bhāratas, like the clash of two rut-maddened lordly elephants with temples streaming.
But the descendant of Gautama, enraged in the battle, that hero pierced the mighty sons of Draupadī with many keen-jointed shafts.
His battle with them was like that of an embodied soul with its senses—terrible in aspect, irresistible, and utterly without bounds.
They harried him as the senses harry a foolish man, while he, roused to fury, fought them back in the encounter.
Thus wondrous, O Bhārata, was his battle with them, surging up again and again, O lord, like a man's strife with his senses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Foot soldiers locked with foot soldiers, tuskers with tuskers, horses with horses, and chariot warriors with chariot warriors; and once more, O lord of peoples, the tumult grew terrible in aspect.
"This is wondrous, this is terrible, this is fierce!"—thus, O lord, were the combats, O great king, dreadful and many.
Those tamers of foes, closing upon one another in the fray, pierced and slew as they met in the great encounter.
A fierce dust, raised by their weapons, was seen, O king, whirled up by the gusting wind and by the galloping horsemen.
Stirred up by the chariot wheels and by the breathing of the elephants, the dust, tawny as a cloud at twilight, rose to the path of the sun.
When the sun was shrouded by that dust and robbed of its brightness, the earth was overspread, and so too those heroes, the mighty chariot-warriors.
In but a moment all around grew free of dust, O best of the Bhāratas, for upon the earth, drenched with the blood of heroes, that fierce and dreadful-looking dust then was laid.
Then, O great king, I beheld the single combats, O Bhārata, ranged by foremost and by eldest, at that most dreadful noontide; and there, O lord of kings, the blazing gleams of the armor were seen.
A roaring tumult arose in the battle from the falling shafts, like that of a great bamboo forest burning on every side.
Saṃjaya said: As that battle, terrible in aspect and fearsome, went on, the army of your son was there broken by the Pāṇḍavas.
But your son, checking with great effort those mighty chariot-warriors, set them to fight the host of the Pāṇḍavas.
Suddenly the warriors who sought your son's welfare turned back to the fight, and when they had thus turned, the battle grew most dreadful.
Of your men and of the foe it was like the war of gods and demons; neither among the enemy nor in your host was there a single one who turned his back.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They fought one another by guesswork and by signals, and great was the slaughter among them as they battled each against each.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with mighty wrath, longing to conquer in the fray the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with their king—
having pierced the son of Śaradvat with three gold-feathered, stone-whetted shafts, with four he struck down the goodly horses of Kṛtavarman.
But Aśvatthāman bore away the illustrious son of Hṛdika; then the son of Śaradvat struck Yudhiṣṭhira back with eight shafts.
Then King Duryodhana sent forth in the battle seven hundred chariots to where that king, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma, stood.
Those chariots, manned by their warriors and swift as mind and wind, rushed in the fray against the chariot of Kuntī's son.
On every side, O great king, surrounding Yudhiṣṭhira, they made him invisible with their arrows, as clouds make the sun.
The chariot-warriors led by Śikhaṇḍin, greatly enraged, brooked it not, and with chariots yoked to swiftest steeds and hung about with nets of little bells they came to guard Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
Then there arose a fierce combat between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus, its waters of blood, swelling the realm of Yama.
Having slain the seven hundred chariots of the assailant Kurus, the Pāṇḍavas together with the Pāñcālas once again held the foe at bay.
There was a great battle of your son with the Pāṇḍavas, the like of which we had never seen, nor ever heard tell.
As that boundless battle raged on every side, while warriors of your side and of the other were being slain—
while the warriors shouted, and the finest conches were blown, and lion-roars were raised on high, and the bowmen thundered—
as the battle swelled beyond measure, while vital points were being pierced, and warriors greedy for victory ran to and fro, O sir—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
when destruction had arisen on every side upon the earth, the spring of grief, and the partings were stripped from the hair of many noble women—
as that boundless and most dreadful battle went on, then portents most dreadful appeared, foreboding ruin, and the earth, with its mountains and forests, shook, sounding aloud.
Meteors with trails and firebrands, O king, shattering on every side, fell from the sky to the earth, striking the orb of the sun.
Winds blew from every quarter, raining gravel low to the ground; the elephants shed tears, and a violent trembling seized them.
Heedless of these terrible and most dreadful portents, the warriors, having taken counsel together, stood unshaken for battle once more, on the fair and holy field of Kurukṣetra, eager to attain heaven.
Then Śakuni, son of the king of Gāndhāra, said: "Fight you in front, while I strike the Pāṇḍavas from behind."
Then, as we set forth, the impetuous warriors of the Madras, exultant, raised a cry of triumph, and so did the others.
But coming again upon us, those unassailable ones, sure of their aim, shaking their bows, overwhelmed us with showers of arrows.
Then, seeing there the army of the Madra king slain by the foe, the host of Duryodhana once more turned its back.
But the mighty king of Gāndhāra then spoke again these words: "Turn back, you who know not righteousness! Fight! What good is flight to you?"
A division of ten thousand horse, O bull of the Bhāratas, belonged to the king of Gāndhāra, fighting with gleaming lances.
Charging with that force amid the carnage of men, they struck the Pāṇḍava host from behind with whetted shafts.
Driven on all sides like a cloud by the wind, the very great army of the Pāṇḍavas was broken, O great king.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing his own army broken close at hand, unflustered, urged on the mighty Sahadeva:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Yonder son of Subala, in his mail, pressing upon our rear, is slaughtering the army. Behold him, O Pāṇḍava, that evil-minded one!
Go you and the sons of Draupadī, and slay Śakuni the son of Subala; I, with the Pāñcālas, shall guard the chariot division, O sinless one.
Let all the elephants and the horses go with you, and three thousand foot soldiers; slay Śakuni the son of Subala."
Then seven hundred elephants, mounted by bow-bearing men, and five thousand horse, and the valiant Sahadeva,
and three thousand foot soldiers, and the sons of Draupadī—all of them in the battle rushed upon Śakuni, frenzied for combat.
But the son of Subala, O king, pressing past the Pāṇḍavas, the glorious one, greedy for victory, struck the army from behind.
But the impetuous horsemen of the swift Pāṇḍavas, in fury, passing those chariots, entered the host of Subala's son.
Those heroic horsemen there, taking their stand amid the elephants, overwhelmed with showers of arrows the great host of Subala's son.
That great battle, with maces and lances upraised, the resort of no coward, broke out, O king, through your evil counsel.
The twang of bowstrings ceased; the chariot-warriors became mere onlookers, for no difference could be seen between one's own and the foe.
The Kurus and Pāṇḍavas beheld the lances loosed by heroes' arms, O bull of the Bhāratas, fall like a shower of shooting stars.
With bright pikes flying here and there, O lord of peoples, the sky, overspread, shone exceedingly.
The aspect of the falling lances, O king, was on every side like that of locusts in the sky, O best of the Bhāratas.
Their every limb sprinkled with blood, their riders flung off, the horses fell down by hundreds and by thousands.
Crushed against one another as they met, some were seen unwounded yet vomiting blood from their mouths.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then there fell a terrible darkness as the army was shrouded in dust; I saw those tamers of foes withdrawing from that place—the horses, O king, and the men, when all was wrapped in dust.
Others, fallen upon the earth, vomiting much blood, locked hair to hair, the men could not so much as stir.
Dragging one another from the backs of their horses, the mighty men, closing like wrestlers, slew each other; and many here, their lives fled, were dragged along by the horses.
Many others, who had longed for victory, fallen upon the earth, were seen here and there—men who had thought themselves heroes.
With men blood-bespattered, their arms hewn off, their hair torn away, the earth was seen strewn by hundreds and by thousands.
There it was not possible for any horse to go far, for the floor of the earth was covered with slain horses and their riders.
With their armor drenched in blood, their weapons seized and upraised, with diverse and dreadful arms, seeking each other's death, drawn close together in the fray, their soldiery for the most part slain—
having fought thus for a while, the son of Subala, O lord of peoples—Śakuni—then withdrew with six thousand horse that remained.
In like manner the Pāṇḍava force, bathed in blood, withdrew with six thousand horse that remained, their mounts spent.
But the horsemen of the Pāṇḍavas, blood-bespattered, drawn close together in the fray, for the most part with lives cast aside, said:
"Here one cannot fight with chariots, how much less with great elephants! Let chariots go against chariots, and elephants against elephants.
Śakuni has gone back and taken his stand within his own division; King Subala's son will not come again to battle."
Then the sons of Draupadī and those rut-maddened great elephants went to where the Pāñcāla Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the mighty chariot-warrior, was.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sahadeva too, O scion of Kuru, when the cloud of dust had risen, went alone to where King Yudhiṣṭhira was.
Then, when they had gone, Śakuni the son of Subala, enraged, once more struck the host of Dhṛṣṭadyumna upon its flank.
Then once again a tumultuous battle broke forth, with lives cast aside, between your men and the foe, each seeking the other's death.
For they glared at one another in that meeting of heroes, and the warriors fell, O king, by hundreds and by thousands.
As heads were severed by swords in that destruction of the world, there arose a great noise, like that of palmyra fruits falling.
From bodies sundered and falling to the earth, and from arms still grasping their weapons, and from thighs, O lord of peoples, there arose a great rattling, crackling sound that made the hair stand on end.
Striking down brothers, sons, and even friends with their sharpened weapons, the warriors fell upon one another like birds contending over a scrap of flesh.
Enraged against each other, closing in man to man, crying "I first! I first!" they slew by the thousand.
With their riders flung from the saddle and lifeless, the horses too fell in heaps by the hundred and by the thousand.
From the swift-coursing horses, twitching and crushed, and from the armored men groaning aloud, O lord of peoples,
there arose a tumultuous din of lances, swords, and javelins, as they pierced one another's vital points—O king, the fruit of your evil counsel.
Overcome by exhaustion, frenzied, their mounts worn out, parched with thirst, and torn by sharpened weapons, your men yet pressed on into battle.
Maddened by the smell of blood, many here lost their senses and struck down foe and kinsman alike, whoever came next within reach.
And many warriors, greedy for victory, their lives gone out, fell to the earth, O king, enveloped in showers of arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
On that day of riotous feasting for wolves, vultures, and jackals, a fearful destruction of the host came to pass before your son's very eyes.
The ground, O lord of peoples, lay strewn with the bodies of men and horses and dappled with streams of blood, deepening the dread of the faint-hearted.
Hewn again and again by swords, pikes, and spears, neither your men nor the Pāṇḍavas turned back, O Bhārata.
Striking with all their might so long as breath held within them, the warriors fell, vomiting blood from their wounds.
A headless trunk was seen, gripping a head by its hair and raising a keen sword drenched in blood.
And as many headless trunks rose up, O ruler of men, and from the reek of blood, the warriors sank into a swoon.
Then, as the clamor died down, Saubala, with the few horses that remained to him, advanced against the great host of the Pāṇḍavas.
Thereupon the Pāṇḍavas, greedy for victory, rushed swiftly upon him—footmen and elephants and horsemen with weapons upraised.
Hemming him in within an enclosure and surrounding him on every side, they struck at him with weapons of every kind, eager to reach the farther shore of the war.
But your men, seeing them charging in from every quarter, rushed against the Pāṇḍavas with horse, foot, elephants, and chariots.
Some footmen, brave men with their weapons spent, struck at one another in the fray with feet and fists, and so fell.
Charioteers fell from their chariots and elephant-riders from their elephants, like Siddhas cast down from their celestial cars when their merit is exhausted.
Thus, straining against one another in the great battle, the warriors slew—fathers, brothers, comrades, and others their very sons.
So lawless was that battle, O best of the Bhāratas, as the dreadful welter of javelins, swords, and arrows raged on.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: When the clamor had grown faint and the host lay slaughtered by the Pāṇḍavas, Saubala turned about with the seven hundred horses that remained.
Riding swiftly to the army, that tamer of foes urged it on, crying again and again to the joyous men, "Fight on!"—and he asked the warriors there, "Where now is the king, the great chariot-hero?"
Hearing Śakuni's words, they answered, O bull of the Bhāratas: "Yonder stands the Kaurava, the great chariot-hero, in the midst of the battle—
there where that vast parasol shines bright as the full moon, where these armored chariots stand with their guards and finger-shields ready.
Where this tumultuous roar resounds like the thundering of a storm-cloud, go thither swiftly, O king, and there you shall behold the Kaurava."
Thus addressed by those brave men, Śakuni Saubala then set forth to where your son stood, O ruler of men, encircled on all sides by heroes who never turned back in battle.
Then, beholding Duryodhana stationed amid the array of chariots, Śakuni heartened all your chariot-warriors,
and with a joyful air, O lord of peoples, deeming his task all but accomplished, spoke this word to King Duryodhana:
"Slay the chariot-host, O king! All the horsemen have been vanquished by me. Yet Yudhiṣṭhira cannot be conquered in battle without staking one's very life.
When that chariot-host guarded by the Pāṇḍava is destroyed, we shall slay these elephants and the footmen and the rest as well."
Hearing his words, your men, greedy for victory, fell joyfully and at speed upon the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
All with quivers thrown open and bows seized fast, brandishing their bows, they raised a lion's roar.
Then once more, O lord of peoples, arose the din of bowstrings and palm-guards, and a most terrible noise of well-loosed arrows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing them drawn near at speed with bows upraised, Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, said to the son of Devakī:
"Urge on the horses without fear and plunge into this ocean of armies. Today I shall make an end of my enemies with sharpened arrows.
Eighteen days, O Janārdana, has this great war now lasted, as the hosts have closed against each other.
The banner-host of these great-souled men, once seeming endless, has come to destruction in the battle this day—behold how fate works its will!
The army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, vast as the sea, O Mādhava, on meeting us has become like the print of a cow's hoof, O undecaying one.
Had he made peace when Bhīṣma fell, well would it have been, O Mādhava; but that fool, the witless son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, did not do so.
The word that Bhīṣma spoke, salutary and wholesome, O Mādhava, that too senseless Suyodhana did not heed.
When Bhīṣma had fallen, struck down upon the face of the earth, I know not what cause it was for which the war went on.
Wholly deluded and utterly foolish I deem the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who, when the son of Śaṃtanu had fallen, yet renewed the battle.
And thereafter, when Droṇa, best of those versed in the Veda, was slain, and Rādheya and Vikarṇa, still the slaughter did not cease.
When this army had but little left, and the son of the charioteer, that tiger among men, was struck down together with his son, still the slaughter did not cease.
When the hero Śrutāyus was slain, and Jalasaṃdha of the Pauravas, and King Śrutāyudha, still the slaughter did not cease.
When Bhūriśravas and Śalya and Śālva too, O Janārdana, and the heroes of the Avantis fell, still the slaughter did not cease.
When Jayadratha was slain, and the rākṣasa Alāyudha, and Bāhlika and Somadatta, still the slaughter did not cease.
When the brave Bhagadatta was slain, and Sudakṣiṇa of the Kāmbojas, and Duḥśāsana laid low, still the slaughter did not cease.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And though he saw brave warriors slain, the kings of many provinces one by one, and the mighty fallen in battle, O Kṛṣṇa, still the slaughter did not cease.
Seeing the commanders of whole armies struck down by Bhīmasena, whether from delusion or from greed, still the slaughter did not cease.
What other man born in a royal house, a Kaurava above all, would wage so great and so fruitless a feud, save Suyodhana?
Knowing his foe the greater in worth, in strength, and in valor, what man not deluded, what wise man who discerns his good from his harm, would still make war?
Since his mind would not bend even when you spoke the salutary word of peace with the Pāṇḍavas, how should he hearken to any other?
He by whom Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu, and Droṇa, and Vidura too were rebuffed when they pleaded for peace—what cure is there for him today?
He who in his folly, O Janārdana, spurned his aged father, and who slighted and rejected his mother as she spoke the salutary word out of love for his welfare—to whose counsel would such a man ever incline?
Plainly this man was born to be the ruin of his line, O Janārdana; so do his conduct and his policy appear, O lord of peoples. He will never yield us our kingdom—such is my conviction, O undecaying one.
Many a time, my friend, the great-souled Vidura told me: while he lives, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will in no wise grant you your portion.
"So long as breath stirs within the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O giver of honor, so long will he work his wickedness against you who are sinless."
"He cannot be overcome by any means save war," O Mādhava—thus Vidura, the seer of truth, said to me ever again.
All that resolve of the wicked one I now perceive this day to be true, even as it was spoken by the great-souled Vidura.
For that fool who, having heard the wholesome and faithful counsel of the son of Jamadagni, made light of it, stands surely at the threshold of his ruin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For it was foretold by many Siddhas at the very birth of Suyodhana: "On this wicked one's coming, the warrior race shall go to its destruction."
And that word of theirs has now come true, O Janārdana, for kings in multitudes have gone to their destruction for Duryodhana's sake.
This day, O Mādhava, I shall slay all his warriors in battle; and when the warriors are swiftly slain and his camp left empty,
he will choose, to his own undoing, to do battle with us; and so, by my reckoning, this feud shall come to its end, O Mādhava.
Thus do I see it, O Vārṣṇeya, reflecting with my own understanding, by the word of Vidura and by the conduct of that wicked one.
Drive on into the Bhārata host, O hero, that I may slay with sharpened arrows the wicked Duryodhana and his army in the fray.
This day I shall secure the welfare of the Dharma King, O Mādhava, by destroying this feeble army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son before his very eyes."
Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed by Savyasācin, the Dāśārha, reins in hand, fearlessly entered amid the flood of the enemy's host in battle.
That dreadful army—where the choicest bows were thorny thickets bristling with lances, its pathways maces and iron clubs, its great trees the chariots and elephants—
strewn over with creepers of horse and foot—Govinda of great renown, plunging into it, ranged through it there on his banner-decked chariot.
Those white horses, O king, bearing Arjuna into battle and urged on by the Dāśārha, were seen ranging in all directions.
Then Savyasācin, scorcher of foes, advanced on his chariot into the fight, scattering keen arrows by the hundred like a cloud pouring down its torrents of rain.
A great noise arose from the smooth-jointed arrows as the field was covered over with shafts by Savyasācin.
Without lodging in the armor, the floods of arrows fell to the ground—shafts loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, whose touch was like the thunderbolt of Indra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Striking down men, elephants, and horses too, O lord of peoples, the arrows fell upon the field like swarms of humming locusts.
All was overspread with the shafts loosed from the Gāṇḍīva, and in the battle neither the quarters nor the intermediate quarters could be discerned.
The whole world seemed filled with arrows graven with Pārtha's name—gold-feathered, washed in oil, and burnished by the smith.
Scorched by Pārtha as elephants are scorched by fire, the Kauravas, struck down by his whetted arrows, sank to the ground.
Bearing his bow and arrows, Pārtha, blazing as it were, O Bhārata, burned up the warriors in battle as a flaming fire consumes dry brushwood.
As at the forest's edge a roaring blaze, set loose by the woodsmen and leaving a black trail, would burn the thicket thick with trees and canopied with withered creepers—a fierce conflagration grown mightily in strength—
even so did he, blazing with his volleys of iron shafts, his arrows for flames and his fierce radiance flaring high and low, in his impetuous fury, brooking nothing, the swift one, burn up the whole army of your sons.
His life-taking arrows, well loosed and golden-feathered, were not stayed by any armor; nor did he loose a second shaft upon a man, a horse, or a mighty elephant.
For with arrows of many shapes and forms he penetrated the host of great chariot-warriors, and he alone slew the army of your sons as the Wielder of the Thunderbolt slew the Daityas.
Saṃjaya said: Of those heroes who hurled their weapons and strove and would not turn back, Dhanaṃjaya with the Gāṇḍīva made every resolve come to nothing.
He was seen loosing arrows whose touch was like Indra's thunderbolt, unbearable and of vast power, as a thundercloud pours down its torrents.
That army, O best of the Bhāratas, being slaughtered by the Diademed One, fled from the battle before the very eyes of your son.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some chariots had their draught-horses slain, others their charioteers killed, and some, O lord of peoples, had their axles, yokes, wheels, and poles shattered.
Others had their arrows spent, and others were tormented by shafts; and some, though unwounded, fled all together, oppressed by fear.
Some, taking up their sons, their mounts for the most part slain, cried aloud; others called upon their fathers, and yet others upon their comrades.
And some, O tiger among men, abandoning their kinsmen, their brothers and their relations here and there, took to flight, O lord of peoples.
Many great chariot-warriors there, grievously pierced and swooning, were seen groaning—men struck down by Pārtha's arrows.
Others, mounting them upon a chariot and reviving them for a while, once rested and their thirst quenched, went again to the fight.
Some, having set them aside and gone, returned once more eager to fight, frenzied for battle, carrying out the command of your son.
Others, having drunk water and refreshed their mounts and donned their armor again, O best of the Bhāratas—
and others, having revived their brothers and set them down in the camp—some their sons and some their fathers—once more longed for battle.
Some, having made ready their chariots each in due order, O lord of peoples, and charging upon the Pāṇḍava host, once more longed for battle.
Those heroes, covered over with nets of little bells, shone forth like the Daityas and Dānavas bent upon the conquest of the three worlds.
Some, coming on suddenly in chariots adorned with gold, fought against Dhṛṣṭadyumna amid the ranks of the Pāṇḍavas.
And Dhṛṣṭadyumna the Pāñcāla, and Śikhaṇḍin the great chariot-warrior, and Śatānīka the son of Nakula did battle against that host of chariots.
Then the Pāñcāla, enraged and surrounded by a great force, charged in fury, eager to slay your men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, as he rushed on, your son, O ruler of men, sent forth against him many a volley of arrows, O Bhārata.
Then, O king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna was swiftly struck in the arms and the breast by your son the archer with many iron shafts.
That mighty archer, deeply pierced like an elephant goaded by the hook, sent his four horses to their death with his arrows, and with a broad-headed shaft swept the head of his charioteer from its body.
Then King Duryodhana, his chariot destroyed, mounted upon the back of a horse and withdrew a little way, that subduer of foes.
But seeing his own host broken in prowess, your mighty son, O great king, went to where the son of Subala was.
Then, when the chariots were broken, three thousand great elephants surrounded on every side the five Pāṇḍava chariot-warriors.
Those five, encircled in battle by the host of elephants, O Bhārata, those tigers among men shone like planets veiled in clouds.
Then Arjuna, O great king, the mighty-armed, a sure marksman, with his white horses and Kṛṣṇa for his charioteer, sallied forth in his chariot.
Surrounded on all sides by those elephants like mountains, he crushed that host of elephants with his bright, sharp iron shafts.
There we saw great elephants slain each by a single arrow, fallen and falling and torn asunder by Savyasācin.
But Bhīmasena, beholding those elephants—he, the mighty one, like a maddened elephant himself—seized his great mace in his hand and, leaping swiftly down from his chariot, fell upon them like Death with his rod in hand.
Seeing that great chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas with his mace upraised, your soldiers trembled and voided their dung and urine; and the whole host was thrown into terror when Vṛkodara held his mace in hand.
We saw elephants like mountains, their frontal globes split by Bhīmasena's mace, covered with dust and running wildly.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those elephants, having charged forth and been struck by Bhīmasena's mace, fell with a cry of anguish like mountains whose wings had been clipped.
Beholding those many elephants with their temples split, fleeing this way and that and falling, your soldiers were seized with terror.
Yudhiṣṭhira too, in great wrath, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī slew the elephant-fighters with their whetted, vulture-feathered arrows.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, having vanquished the king in battle—when your son had withdrawn and taken refuge upon the back of a horse—
and seeing all the Pāṇḍavas surrounded by the elephants, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O great king, the son of the Pāñcāla king, together with all the Prabhadrakas, went forth eager to slay those elephants.
But not seeing Duryodhana the subduer of foes among the host of chariots, Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata asked the warriors there: "Where now has Duryodhana gone?"
Not seeing the king while the slaughter of men went on, those great chariot-warriors, thinking your son slain there, with downcast faces asked after your son.
Some said, "His charioteer being slain, he has gone where the son of Subala is"; but others among the sorely wounded warriors said otherwise.
"What need have you of Duryodhana? You shall see him if he lives. Fight, all of you together! What will the king do for you?"
Those warriors, their limbs wounded and their mounts for the most part slain, and themselves tormented by arrows, spoke as it were indistinctly.
"Let us slay this whole force by which we have been surrounded. These Pāṇḍavas, having slain our elephants, are all advancing upon us."
But hearing their words, the mighty Aśvatthāman, leaving behind that irresistible host of the Pāñcāla king—
and Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman—those heroes of the firmest bows, abandoning the host of chariots, went to where the son of Subala was.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, when they had gone, the Pāṇḍavas, with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at their head, came on, O king, slaughtering your men.
Seeing those great chariot-warriors rushing on, exultant and bold, those heroes who had then given up all hope of life, your host became for the most part pale of face.
Seeing them surrounded, their weapons spent, I, O king, with a force of two divisions, having staked my own life—
myself the fifth, fought against the host of the Pāñcāla, taking my stand in that place where the son of Śaradvat stood.
We five joined battle, tormented by the arrows of the Diademed One, against Dhṛṣṭadyumna and his great host; there was a mighty struggle there for us. Vanquished by him, we all withdrew thereupon from the fight.
Then I saw Sātyaki, that great chariot-warrior, coming on with four hundred chariots, and the hero charged at me in the battle.
Hardly escaped from Dhṛṣṭadyumna, my mounts wearied, I fell upon the host of the Mādhava as an evildoer falls into hell. There the battle was dreadful for a while, exceedingly terrible.
But the mighty-armed Sātyaki, having slain my retinue, took me captive alive as I lay swooning, fallen upon the ground.
Then in but a moment that host of elephants was destroyed—by the mace of Bhīmasena and by the iron shafts of Arjuna.
With the great elephants like mountains crushed all around, the passage of the Pāṇḍavas became, as it were, not easily made.
Then the mighty Bhīmasena cleared paths for the chariots of the Pāṇḍavas, O great king, by dragging away the great elephants.
Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata, not seeing Duryodhana the subduer of foes among the host of chariots, went searching for the king, your son, that great chariot-warrior.
And leaving the Pāñcāla behind, they went to where the son of Subala was, distraught at not seeing the king while the slaughter of men went on.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: When that host of elephants had been destroyed by the son of Pāṇḍu, O Bhārata, and the army was being slaughtered by Bhīmasena in the battle,
and seeing Bhīmasena the subduer of foes ranging thus, like wrathful, life-taking Death with his rod in hand—
