the surviving sons of yours, O king, gathering together in the battle—since the Kaurava, your son Duryodhana, was nowhere to be seen—those brothers of one womb, joining as one, rushed upon Bhīmasena.
Durmarṣaṇa, O great king, Jaitra, Bhūribala, and Ravi—these your sons, joining as one, charged upon Bhīmasena from every side and hemmed him in on all quarters.
Then Bhīma, O great king, mounting once more upon his own chariot, loosed whetted arrows into the vital parts of your sons.
Your sons, overwhelmed by Bhīma in that great battle, sought to drive Bhīmasena back as one might turn an elephant back from a slope.
Then Bhīma, enraged in the fight, swiftly struck off the head of Durmarṣaṇa with a razor-edged arrow and brought it down to the ground.
Then with another broad-headed shaft that pierced through every armor, Bhīma the great chariot-warrior slew your son Śrutānta.
Then, piercing Jayatsena with an iron shaft as if in mirth, the subduer of foes felled that Kaurava from the floor of his chariot; and he fell from the car, O king, to the earth, and swiftly died.
Then Śrutarvan, in wrath, pierced Bhīma, O honored one, with a hundred straight-jointed arrows fledged with vulture feathers.
Then Bhīma, enraged in the fight, struck these three—Jaitra, Bhūribala, and Ravi—with three arrows like poison and fire.
Those great chariot-warriors, slain, fell from their chariots to the ground like kiṃśuka trees in springtime, dappled with blossoms, cut down.
Then that scorcher of foes, striking Durvimocana with another sharp iron shaft, sent him to his death.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Slain, that foremost of chariot-warriors fell to the ground from his own car, like a tree growing on a mountain peak broken by the wind.
Then he slew Duṣpradharṣa and Sujāta, two of your sons, each with two arrows apiece in the battle, at the head of the host; and those two foremost of chariot-warriors fell, their limbs pierced by his shafts.
Then, marking another of your sons striving in the fight, Bhīma, hard to withstand in battle, pierced him with a broad-headed shaft; and he fell slain from his mount before the eyes of all the archers.
But seeing his many brothers slain by one man in the battle, Śrutarvan, overcome with indignation, advanced upon Bhīma.
Drawing his very great bow adorned with gold and loosing many arrows like poison and fire,
But he, O king, having cut apart the bow of the Pāṇḍava in that great battle, then covered him, now bowless, with twenty arrows.
Then, taking up another bow, Bhīmasena the mighty chariot-warrior overwhelmed your son with shafts and cried, "Stand! Stand!"
Great was the combat between those two, wondrous in form and terrible, such as once raged in olden days between Jambha and Vāsava.
By the bright arrows loosed by those two, arrows like the rod of Yama, the whole earth was veiled, and the sky, and all the quarters likewise.
Then Śrutarvan, swollen with wrath, drawing his bow, struck Bhīmasena in battle, O king, upon the arms and the breast with his shafts.
Pierced deep, O great king, by your bow-wielding son, Bhīma, enraged, heaved like the great ocean at the turning of the moon.
Then Bhīma, seized by fury, O lord, sent your son's charioteer and his four horses with his arrows to the abode of Yama.
Marking him robbed of his chariot, that hero of measureless spirit covered him with feathered shafts, displaying the swiftness of his hand.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śrutarvan, his chariot lost, O king, took up sword and shield; but even as he seized the sword and the gleaming shield bright with a hundred moons, the Pāṇḍava with a razor-edged shaft struck his head from his body.
Then, his head severed by the razor-shaft, the body of that great-souled warrior fell from the chariot, making the earth resound.
When that hero had fallen, your warriors, bewildered with fear yet eager to fight, rushed upon Bhīmasena in the battle.
As they swiftly charged from that ocean of host left over from the slain, the mailed and valiant Bhīmasena received them; and they, closing upon him, encircled him on every side.
Then Bhīma, hemmed in by your men with their whetted arrows, harried them all as the thousand-eyed one harried the Asuras.
Then, having slain five hundred great chariot-warriors with their car-guards, he struck down in the fight a host of elephants, seven hundred more.
Having slain ten thousand foot-soldiers with his supreme shafts, and eight hundred horse, the Pāṇḍava shone resplendent.
And Bhīmasena, son of Kuntī, having slain your sons in battle, deemed his purpose fulfilled and his birth made fruitful, O lord.
As he thus fought on, cutting down your men, your troops could not bear even to look upon him, O Bhārata.
Having routed all the Kurus and slain their foot-followers, he made a din with his two arms, terrifying the great elephants.
With the greater part of its warriors slain, your army, O lord of peoples, was reduced to a wretched remnant, O great king.
Saṃjaya said: Duryodhana, O great king, and Sudarśana too, your son, the survivors then of the slaughter, stood firm amid their horsemen on the field.
Then, beholding Duryodhana posted among his horse, the son of Devakī spoke to Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī.
"The foes are slain for the most part, our kinsmen are kept safe; and yonder bull of Śini's line has turned back, having taken Saṃjaya captive."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And Nakula is worn out, and Sahadeva too, O Bhārata, having fought in battle against the wicked retainers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son."
"Forsaking Suyodhana, these three stand apart: Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman, and Droṇa's son, the great chariot-warrior."
"Yonder stands the prince of Pāñcāla, endowed with surpassing splendor, having slain Duryodhana's host together with all the Prabhadrakas."
"Yonder is Duryodhana, O Pārtha, posted amid his horsemen, the parasol held above him, gazing about again and again."
"Having marshalled his whole force, he stands in the midst of the field; slay him with your whetted arrows, and you shall have accomplished your end."
"Seeing the elephant-host destroyed and you come upon them, O subduer of foes, slay Suyodhana before these others scatter in flight."
"Let someone go to the prince of Pāñcāla, bidding him come at once; for with his force worn out, this sinful one shall not escape, my friend."
"Having slain your whole force in the battle, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, deeming the sons of Pāṇḍu vanquished, bears himself with a great show of pride."
"Seeing his own host slain and hard-pressed by the Pāṇḍavas, the king will surely come into the battle, even unto his own destruction."
Thus addressed, Phalguna spoke this word to Kṛṣṇa: "All the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been slain by Bhīma, O giver of honor; and these two who yet stand, O Kṛṣṇa, this day shall be no more."
"Bhīṣma is slain, Droṇa is slain, Karṇa son of Vikartana is slain; the king of the Madras is slain, Śalya is slain, and Jayadratha is slain, O Kṛṣṇa."
"Five hundred horse remain to Śakuni, son of Subala; and of chariots but two hundred remain, O Janārdana, and a full hundred of tusked elephants, and three thousand foot-soldiers."
"Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa, and the lord of the Trigartas likewise, Ulūka and Śakuni, and Kṛtavarman of the Sātvatas—"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"—this is the force left to Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, O Mādhava; for surely from Time there is no deliverance upon the earth for any one."
"His army thus destroyed, behold Duryodhana standing firm; this very day shall the great king be left without a friend."
"For none of the foe shall escape me, so I resolve; and those fierce in battle, O Kṛṣṇa, who this day shall not abandon the fight—all of them I shall slay, even were they more than human."
"This day in battle, sore enraged, I shall take away the long sleeplessness of the king, by felling the Gāndhāra prince with my whetted arrows."
"Those jewels which the evil-doing son of Subala, by his cheating, won from us at the dicing in the assembly hall—those I shall this day win back."
"This day too shall all the women of the City of the Elephant learn, hearing that their husbands and their sons have been slain by the Pāṇḍavas in the fight."
"This day shall all the work be brought to its end, O Kṛṣṇa; this day shall Duryodhana give up his blazing fortune and his life together."
"If, O Kṛṣṇa, he does not flee from the battle in fear of me, then know the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that great fool, as already slain, O Vārṣṇeya."
"For this throng of horses cannot bear the twang of my bowstring and the slap of my palm-guard, O subduer of foes; drive on, that I may slay them."
Thus addressed by the illustrious Pāṇḍava, the Dāśārha urged on the horses, O king, toward Duryodhana's host.
Beholding that array, three great chariot-warriors ready for battle—Bhīmasena and Arjuna and Sahadeva, O lord—advanced with a lion's roar, eager to slay Duryodhana.
Seeing them all together, sweeping on at speed with bows uplifted, the son of Subala charged in battle against the Pāṇḍavas, those bringers of doom.
Sudarśana, your son, advanced against Bhīmasena; Suśarman and Śakuni did battle with the Diademed One; and your son, mounted upon a horse's back, advanced against Sahadeva.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then swiftly and without effort, your son, O lord of men, smote Sahadeva hard upon the head with a javelin.
Struck down by your son, he sank upon the floor of his chariot, all his limbs bathed in blood, hissing like a venomous serpent.
Then, regaining his senses, Sahadeva, O lord of peoples, in his wrath covered Duryodhana with sharp arrows.
Pārtha too, displaying his prowess in the fight—Dhanaṃjaya, son of Kuntī—struck the heads of the brave warriors from off their horses' backs.
Then Pārtha scattered that array with his many arrows, and felling all the horses, drove against the chariots of the Trigartas.
Then the great chariot-warriors of the Trigartas, joining together, overwhelmed Arjuna and Vāsudeva with showers of arrows.
Assailing Satyakarman, the greatly renowned son of Pāṇḍu cut apart with a razor-shaft the pole of his chariot.
And with a razor-shaft honed upon stone, O lord, that greatly renowned one, smiling, severed his head, adorned with burnished earrings.
Then, before the very eyes of the warriors, he seized upon Satyeṣu, as a lion in the forest, O king, seizes a deer in its hunger.
Having slain him, Pārtha then pierced Suśarman with three arrows, and struck down all those chariots adorned with gold.
Then, pressing swiftly on, Pārtha loosed the keen venom of a wrath long gathered up against the lord of Prasthala.
Arjuna, O bull of the Bhāratas, having filled him with a hundred shafts, then slew the horses of that bowman.
Then, taking up a whetted arrow like the rod of Yama, he aimed at Suśarman and loosed it swiftly, as though in mirth.
That arrow, sped by that bowman blazing with wrath, reached Suśarman and clove his heart in the battle.
Lifeless, O great king, he fell upon the surface of the earth, gladdening all the Pāṇḍavas and grieving your men.
Having slain Suśarman in battle, he brought to destruction with his shafts the sons of that warrior, great chariot-fighters, five and forty in number.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, having slain all his foot-followers with his whetted arrows, that great chariot-warrior advanced upon the remnant of the Bhārata host.
But Bhīma, wrathful in the battle, made your son Sudarśana invisible with his arrows, O lord of men, as though smiling the while.
Then, smiling in his wrath, he struck his head from his body with a keen razor-shaft; slain, he fell to the earth.
When that hero had been slain, his foot-followers then encircled Bhīma in the battle, scattering their whetted shafts.
Then Vṛkodara with his whetted arrows, whose touch was like the thunderbolt of Indra, covered that array on every side; and in a moment, O bull of the Bhāratas, Bhīma cut it down.
As these were being destroyed, the mighty captains of the host closed with Bhīmasena and gave battle, O Bhārata; and the Pāṇḍava covered them all with his terrible arrows.
In like manner your men, O king, hemmed in on every side the great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas with a mighty rain of arrows.
All was thrown into confusion—the Pāṇḍavas locked with the foe, and your men in the battle striving against the followers of Pāṇḍu.
There the warriors then fell, smiting one another down, in both the armies, O king, grieving for their kinsmen.
Saṃjaya said: As that battle, the destroyer of men and horses and elephants, raged on, Śakuni, son of Subala, O king, advanced against Sahadeva.
Then, as he charged swiftly on, the valiant Sahadeva sent forth floods of arrows, swift-flying like locusts; and Ulūka in the battle pierced Bhīma with ten shafts.
And Śakuni, O great king, having pierced Bhīma with three arrows, then covered Sahadeva with ninety shafts.
Those heroes, O king, closing with one another in the battle, pierced each other with whetted arrows fledged with heron and peacock feathers, golden-nocked, honed upon stone, and drawn back to the ear before they were loosed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The shower of arrows loosed from their bow-arms, O lord of peoples, veiled all the quarters, as a rain-cloud veils them with its torrents.
Then Bhīma, wrathful in the battle, and Sahadeva, O Bhārata, those two of exceeding might, ranged the field, working havoc in the fray.
Shrouded by their hundreds of arrows, that host of yours, O Bhārata, became here and there as dark as a sky filled with gloom.
By horses galloping wildly in every direction, riddled with arrows, O lord of the people, paths were carved here and there as they dragged along the many slain.
With slaughtered horses together with their riders, with shattered coats of mail and broken lances, O venerable one, the earth became so covered that it seemed dappled, as if strewn with blossoms.
The warriors there, O great king, closing upon one another, ranged across the battlefield in fury, striking each other down.
With faces whose eyes were rolled upward in rage and whose lips were bitten through, still wearing their earrings and resembling the filaments of lotuses, the earth was covered over.
With severed arms, O great king, that resembled the trunks of lordly elephants, still bearing their armlets and gauntlets and still grasping sword, lance, and battle-axe,
with headless trunks that had risen up though severed, and others dancing on the field, thronged with hosts of carrion-eaters, the earth became a thing of horror, O lord.
When the army was reduced to a remnant, the Pāṇḍavas, grown exultant in that great battle, dispatched the Kauravas to the abode of Yama.
In that interval the valiant, mighty son of Subala struck Sahadeva hard upon the head with a lance; and he, O great king, reeling and stunned, sank down upon the floor of his chariot.
Seeing Sahadeva thus, the mighty Bhīmasena, blazing with wrath, held back all the enemy hosts, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He pierced them through with iron shafts by the hundreds and the thousands, and having pierced them, he sent up a lion's roar, O subduer of foes.
Terrified by that sound, the followers of Śakuni, together with their horses and elephants, all at once fled in sudden fear.
Seeing them broken in rout, King Duryodhana cried out: "Turn back, you who know not righteousness! Fight! What good is your flight to you?
The hero who wins renown here and yields up his life in battle without showing his back attains the higher worlds after death."
Thus addressed by the king, the followers of the son of Subala turned again upon the Pāṇḍavas, making death itself their refuge from retreat.
By those rushing onward, O lord of kings, a most terrible roar was raised, like the tumult of a churning ocean, and it surged up on every side.
Beholding the followers of the son of Subala bearing down upon them, the Pāṇḍavas, intent upon victory, advanced to meet them, O great king.
And the unassailable Sahadeva, having regained his breath, O lord of the people, pierced Śakuni with ten shafts and his horses with three, and as if smiling cut through the bow of the son of Subala with his arrows.
Then taking up another bow, Śakuni, drunk with the frenzy of battle, pierced Nakula with sixty shafts and Bhīmasena with seven.
Ulūka too, O great king, seeking to shield his father in the fight, pierced Bhīma with seven shafts and Sahadeva with seventy.
Bhīmasena in that combat pierced him with sharpened shafts, and Śakuni with sixty-four, and those who stood at their flanks with three apiece.
Though struck by Bhīma with oil-tempered iron shafts, they in their wrath covered Sahadeva in battle with showers of arrows, as lightning-charged clouds drench a mountain with torrents of rain.
Then, as Ulūka bore down upon him, the valiant and mighty Sahadeva struck off his head with a broad-headed shaft, O great king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Cast down by Sahadeva, he fell from his chariot to the ground, his every limb bathed in blood, gladdening the Pāṇḍavas in the battle.
But seeing his son slain there, O Bhārata, Śakuni, his throat choked with tears, sighed deeply, recalling the words of Vidura.
Having brooded a moment, his eyes brimming with tears and sighing, he closed upon Sahadeva and pierced him with three arrows.
Warding off those loosed shafts with volleys of his own arrows, the mighty Sahadeva, O great king, cut through his bow in the encounter.
His bow being severed, O lord of kings, Śakuni the son of Subala then seized a broad sword and hurled it at Sahadeva.
As that sword of dreadful form came rushing upon him, O lord of the people, he cut the weapon of the son of Subala in two in the fray, as if in mockery.
Seeing his sword cleft in two, he took up a great mace and hurled it at Sahadeva; but it fell vainly to the ground.
Then the son of Subala, blazing with rage, flung at the Pāṇḍava a most fearful spear, upraised like the Night of Doom.
As it came hurtling upon him, Sahadeva, as if smiling, cut it in three with gold-adorned shafts upon the field.
Severed in three, that gold-wrought spear fell to the earth, crumbling as it dropped, like a blazing flash of lightning falling from the sky.
Seeing the spear struck down and the son of Subala stricken with fear, all your men, the son of Subala among them, fled as terror seized them.
Then a great shout went up from the Pāṇḍavas, radiant with the look of victory, and thereupon the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra for the most part turned their faces away.
Seeing them downcast, the valiant son of Mādrī held them back in the battle with many thousands of arrows.
Then Sahadeva fell upon the son of Subala in the fight as he rode away, guarded by the Gāndhāras and seated upon swift, fine-backed horses, bent upon victory.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Recalling that Śakuni remained as the share allotted to him, O king, Sahadeva bore down upon him in his gold-bodied chariot, having strung and drawn back his great bow with main force.
Rushing upon the son of Subala, he struck him hard in his wrath with stone-whetted, vulture-feathered shafts, as one goads a great elephant with hooks.
And the wise one, checking him as though to remind him, said: "Standing firm in the duty of a warrior, fight! Be a man!
That gladness you felt then, you fool, when you cast the dice in the assembly hall — receive now the fruit of that deed, O evil-minded one!
Slain are those wicked men who once mocked us; Duryodhana, the firebrand of his line, remains, and you, his maternal uncle.
Today I will strike off your head, churned from your shoulders by a razor-shaft, as one plucks down a fruit from a tree with a crushing cudgel."
Having spoken thus, O great king, the mighty Sahadeva, that tiger among men, blazing with wrath, advanced upon him with a rush.
Closing in, the unassailable Sahadeva, that lord of warriors, drew his bow with might, as if laughing in his anger,
and having pierced Śakuni with ten shafts and his horses with four, and cut down his parasol, his banner, and his bow, he roared like a lion.
His banner, bow, and parasol cut away by Sahadeva, the son of Subala was then pierced in all his vital points by many arrows.
Then once more, O great king, the valiant Sahadeva sent against Śakuni an irresistible shower of arrows.
Then the son of Subala, in his fury, single-handed and seeking to slay Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī, swiftly rushed upon him in the press of battle with a gold-decked lance.
At the forefront of the fight the son of Mādrī, with three broad-headed shafts at a single stroke, severed that upraised lance together with both his shapely arms, and shouted aloud, sweeping through the middle of the field.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, acting in an instant, with a well-aimed broad shaft of hard iron, gold-feathered and able to pierce every guard, he wrenched the head from his body.
His head struck off in battle by the Pāṇḍava with that gold-adorned, keen-whetted shaft bright as the sun, the son of Subala fell to the earth.
That head, which was the very root of the ruin of the Kurus, the son of Pāṇḍu in his wrath sent flying with a swift, gold-feathered, stone-whetted shaft.
Beholding Śakuni with his head struck off, lying upon the earth, his limbs drenched with blood, your warriors, their spirit shattered by terror, fled in every direction, still grasping their weapons.
Routed, their mouths dry, their senses gone, stunned by the twang of Gāṇḍīva and tormented by fear, their chariots, horses, and elephants broken, the foot-soldiers too, along with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, fled away.
Then, having cast Śakuni down from his chariot, the sons of Pāṇḍu, filled with joy, O Bhārata, blew their conches in the battle in their exultation, gladdening their soldiers, with Keśava among them.
And all of them, doing honor to Sahadeva, said to him in their gladness upon the field: "By good fortune, O hero, the deceitful and wicked one, together with his son, has been slain by you in battle."
Saṃjaya said: Then, O great king, the followers of the son of Subala, enraged and giving up their lives amid the wailing, hemmed in the Pāṇḍavas on every side.
Them Arjuna received in battle, bent upon Sahadeva's victory, and Bhīmasena too, blazing with energy, his aspect like that of an enraged venomous serpent.
The resolve of those who, spear, pike, and lance in hand, sought to slay Sahadeva, Dhanaṃjaya rendered vain with Gāṇḍīva.
The arms that grasped weapons, of the warriors who rushed forward, Bībhatsu cut away with broad-headed shafts, and their heads as well, and their horses too.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Struck down and bereft of life, they sank to the earth, swiftly smitten by Savyasācin, that hero of the world.
Then King Duryodhana, beholding the destruction of his host, in his wrath, O lord, gathered together the hundreds of chariots that survived the slaughter,
and the elephants and horses and foot-soldiers, O scorcher of foes; and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke to them all assembled these words:
"Closing upon all the Pāṇḍavas in battle, together with their bands of friends, and the Pāñcāla prince too with his force, slay them and swiftly turn back."
Receiving his word upon their heads, those drunk with the frenzy of battle advanced to meet the sons of Pṛthā in the fight, at your son's command.
As they who had survived the slaughter rushed swiftly forward in that great battle, the Pāṇḍavas covered them over with shafts shaped like venomous serpents.
That army, O best of the Bhāratas, was in a moment slain by those great-souled ones once it joined the battle, and found no protector; yet though it sought to stand firm, for fear it could not hold its ground, armored though it was.
With horses galloping wildly and the host wrapped in dust, neither the quarters nor the intermediate quarters could be discerned in the battle.
Then many men, sallying forth from the Pāṇḍava ranks, struck down your men in the fight in but a moment, O Bhārata; and so that army of yours was left without a remnant, O Bhārata.
The eleven full armies assembled for your son, O Bhārata — those, O lord, were slain in battle by the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas.
Amid those thousands of great-souled kings of your side, Duryodhana alone, O king, was seen, sorely wounded.
Then, gazing about him in all directions and seeing the earth made empty, bereft of all his warriors, and beholding the Pāṇḍavas in the field —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
exultant, all their aims fulfilled, roaring on every side — and hearing too the sound and clamor of the arrows of those great-souled ones,
Duryodhana, O great king, overcome by despair, his forces and his mount gone, set his mind upon flight.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: My army slain and left without remnant, my camp made desolate — what then, O charioteer, was the strength of the Pāṇḍavas that remained? Tell me this, who ask it of you, for you are skilled, Saṃjaya.
And what did my dull-witted son Duryodhana do, that lord of the earth, alone, having beheld the ruin of his host in this way?
Saṃjaya said: Two thousand chariots, and seven hundred elephants, and five thousand horse, and ten thousand foot —
this was the great force of the Pāṇḍavas that remained, O king, having taken command of which Dhṛṣṭadyumna stood arrayed in the battle.
Then King Duryodhana, alone, O best of the Bhāratas, that foremost of chariot-warriors, saw no comrade anywhere in the battle.
Beholding the foes roaring and the destruction of his own host, he abandoned his slain horse and fled eastward in fear.
Your son Duryodhana, lord of eleven armies, blazing with energy, took up his mace and set out on foot toward the lake.
When the king had gone but a little way on foot, he remembered the words of Vidura, that wise man of righteous conduct.
"Surely the deeply wise Vidura foresaw this long ago—this great slaughter of ours and of the kṣatriyas in battle."
Brooding thus, his heart scorched with grief at the sight of his army's destruction, O king, the lord wished to enter the lake.
And the Pāṇḍavas, great king, with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at their head, enraged, rushed against your forces, O king.
As the host roared, brandishing spears, swords, and lances in their hands, Dhanaṃjaya with his Gāṇḍīva brought their resolve to nothing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Slaying them with his keen shafts, together with their counselors and kinsmen, Arjuna, standing in his chariot drawn by white horses, shone in great splendor.
When Subala's son fell with his horses, chariots, and elephants, your army became like a vast forest hewn down.
In the host of Duryodhana, many hundreds of thousands strong, no other great warrior, O king, was seen to be left alive—
save the heroic son of Droṇa, and likewise Kṛtavarman, and Kṛpa of Gautama's line, O king, and your son the prince.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, seeing me, laughed and said to Sātyaki: "Why take this man captive? There is no use in his living."
Hearing Dhṛṣṭadyumna's words, Śini's grandson, that mighty warrior, raised his sharp sword and made ready to slay me then.
But the deeply wise Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana came up and said: "Let Saṃjaya be released alive; he must by no means be slain."
Hearing Dvaipāyana's words, Śini's grandson joined his palms, then released me and said: "Fare well, Saṃjaya; go your way."
Dismissed by him, I laid aside my armor and weapons and set out toward the city at evening, drenched in blood.
Having withdrawn about a krośa, I saw, O king, Duryodhana standing alone, mace in hand, grievously wounded.
His eyes brimming with tears, he could not gaze upon me; yet, seeing me standing there wretched, he looked toward me.
And I too, seeing him grieving and alone upon the field, was so overwhelmed with sorrow that for a moment I could say nothing.
Then I told him all of it—how I had been taken captive, and how by the grace of Dvaipāyana I had been released alive from the battle.
After brooding for a moment and recovering his senses, he then asked me about his brothers and all his armies.
To him I, who had seen it with my own eyes, told everything: that all his brothers were slain and his army cut down.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Three warriors of your host are left, it is said, O lord of men"—so Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana had told me at the time of my departure.
Sighing as if from the depths, and gazing about him again and again, your son touched me on the shoulder with his hand and spoke.
"Save you, Saṃjaya, no one else here lives through this battle; I see no second man—while the Pāṇḍavas have their allies still."
"Tell the king, Saṃjaya—the lord whose eye is wisdom—that your son Duryodhana has entered the lake."
"Bereft of such friends, of sons and of brothers, and with the kingdom seized by the Pāṇḍavas, what man like me would go on living?"
"Tell him all of this—and that I, escaped from the great battle, lie sleeping alive in this lake of water, sorely wounded."
Having spoken thus, great king, the lord entered that lake, and by his magic power the king of men froze its waters firm.
When he had entered the lake, I, alone, saw three warriors with their teams worn out coming together to that place—
Kṛpa, the hero of Śaradvat's line, and Droṇa's son, best of warriors, and Kṛtavarman of the Bhojas, together, all torn by arrows.
All of them, catching sight of me, swiftly urged on their horses, and drawing near they said: "By good fortune you live, Saṃjaya!"
And they all asked me about your son, the lord of men: "Does our king Duryodhana yet live, Saṃjaya?"
I told them then that the king was unharmed, and I recounted all that Duryodhana had said to me, and I pointed out the lake into which the king of men had entered.
But Aśvatthāman, O king, hearing my words and gazing upon that broad lake, lamented piteously.
"Alas, shame! The king does not know that we still live—for together with him we are enough to fight the foe."
Those great warriors, foremost of charioteers, lamented there a long while, then fled away, having seen Pāṇḍu's sons upon the field.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Mounting me on Kṛpa's well-furnished chariot, those three warriors, the survivors of the slaughter, came to the army's encampment.
There the terror-stricken guard-posts, as the sun went down, all cried aloud when they heard of the destruction of your sons.
Then the aged men who guarded the women, great king, taking up the royal consorts, set out toward the city.
There arose on every side a mighty clamor of women shrieking and weeping, when they heard of that destruction of the army.
Then those women, O king, wailing again and again, made the earth resound with their cries like ospreys.
They beat their heads with their nails and with their hands, and tore their hair, crying out here and there.
Wailing their cries of woe and beating their breasts, they shrieked and wept there, lamenting, O lord of peoples.
Then Duryodhana's counselors, their throats choked with tears and sorely stricken, taking up the royal women, set out toward the city.
And the gatekeepers, O lord of peoples, with worn canes in their hands, the guardians of the women, gathered up the gleaming couches with their costly coverlets and went swiftly toward the city.
Other men, mounting chariots yoked with she-mules, taking up each his own womenfolk, set out toward the city.
Those women whom even the sun had never before beheld within their chambers, men now saw, great king, as they went toward the city.
Those tender, delicate women, O best of the Bhāratas, their own kinsmen and relations slain, hastened toward the city.
Down to the very cowherds and shepherds, the people fled in confusion toward the city, tormented by fear of Bhīmasena.
And a fierce, most dreadful fear of the Pārthas was upon them; gazing at one another, they ran toward the city.
While that most terrible rout was taking place, Yuyutsu, bewildered with grief, pondered what the hour demanded.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Duryodhana, lord of eleven armies, is vanquished in battle by the Pāṇḍavas of fearsome valor; his brothers are slain, and all the Kurus, with Bhīṣma and Droṇa at their head, are dead."
"I alone have escaped, by the working of fortune and by chance, while all the camps are scattered on every side."
"Whatever of Duryodhana's ministers are left, they have taken up the royal women and are running toward the city."
"I think the hour has come for me to enter the city along with them, O lord—once I have taken leave of Yudhiṣṭhira and of Bhīmasena as well."
The mighty-armed one set this matter before the two of them; the king, ever moved by compassion, was pleased with him, and the strong-armed one, embracing the son of the vaiśya woman, gave him leave to go.
Then, mounting his chariot, he swiftly urged on his horses, and, overtaking the royal women unlooked-for, set off toward the city.
Together with them he swiftly entered Hāstinapura as the sun was setting, his throat choked with tears and his eyes streaming.
He saw the deeply wise Vidura, his eyes too wet with tears, coming out from the king's presence, his mind stricken with grief.
To him, who stood bowing before him, the steadfast-in-truth one said: "Now that this destruction of the Kurus has come to pass, by good fortune, my son, you are alive."
"Yet without the king's own entry, how is it that you have come here? Tell me the whole reason of this in full."
Yuyutsu said: "When Śakuni was slain, dear sir, with his kinsmen, sons, and relations, then King Duryodhana, with but the remnant of his retinue left, abandoned his own horse and, turning eastward, fled in fear."
"When the king had withdrawn from the encampment of the host, all the people, distraught with fear, fled toward the city."
"Then the keepers of the women, mounting upon the carriages the consorts of the king and of all his brothers, fled in fear."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Then I, having taken leave of the king together with Keśava, entered Hāstinapura, to guard against the world's reproach."
Hearing these words spoken by the son of the vaiśya woman, and knowing them timely, Vidura, knower of all that is right, of immeasurable soul, honored the eloquent Yuyutsu.
"All this of yours is timely amid the ruin of the Bhāratas; today rest here, and tomorrow you shall go to Yudhiṣṭhira."
Having spoken these words, Vidura, knower of all that is right, dismissed Yuyutsu and entered the king's dwelling; and Yuyutsu too passed that night in his own house.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When all my armies had been slain by Pāṇḍu's sons on the field of battle, what did those survivors of my host do, Saṃjaya?
Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa, and the valiant son of Droṇa—and King Duryodhana of feeble mind—what did he do then?
Saṃjaya said: When the women of the great-souled kṣatriyas had fled away and the camp lay empty and abandoned, the three warriors, deeply distraught,
hearing the shouts of the victorious sons of Pāṇḍu and seeing the camp deserted at evening, longing for their king, found that place no longer to their liking, and so they went toward the lake.
Yudhiṣṭhira too, the righteous-souled, together with his brothers, ranged exultant over the field, O king, eager to slay Duryodhana.
Enraged and bent on victory, they searched for your son, seeking him out with all their effort, yet nowhere did they see the lord of men.
For he, mace in hand, had withdrawn with swift speed and had entered that lake, holding back its waters by his own magic.
When at last all the Pāṇḍavas found their teams quite spent, they returned to their own camp and halted there with their soldiers.
Then Kṛpa and Droṇa's son and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata, while the Pārthas were encamped, set out slowly toward that lake.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Reaching the lake where the lord of men lay, they addressed the unassailable king as he slept within the waters.
"Rise, O king, and fight beside us! Conquer Yudhiṣṭhira and enjoy the earth, or, slain, attain to heaven."
"Their whole force too, Duryodhana, has been struck down by you, and most of those soldiers who remain there are sorely beset."
They will not be able to withstand your onslaught, O lord of peoples, when you are shielded by us. Therefore rise, O Bhārata.
Duryodhana said: By good fortune I see you delivered from such a slaughter of men, surviving still, O bulls among men, from the deadly clash of Pāṇḍava and Kaurava.
We shall conquer them all once we are rested and our weariness has passed. But you are exhausted, and I am gravely wounded, while their force is at its height; for that reason I do not favor battle now.
It is no marvel, O heroes, that your spirit is so great and your devotion to us so supreme; yet this is not the hour for valor.
Having rested this one night, I shall tomorrow give battle to the enemy at your side; of this I have no doubt.
Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed, the son of Droṇa spoke to the king, frenzied for battle: Rise, O king—good fortune to you—we shall conquer the foe in war.
By my sacrifices and pious works, by charity, by truth, and by my prayers I swear, O king, that this very day I shall slay the Somakas.
May I never attain the joy fitting for the virtuous that belongs to those who have performed sacrifices, if, when this night has passed, I do not slay the enemy in battle.
Until I have slain all the Pāñcālas I shall not loosen my armor, O lord; this I declare as truth—hear it from me, O ruler of men.
While they were thus conversing, certain hunters came by chance to that place, weary beneath their loads of meat, seeking water.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For these hunters, O great king, were ever in Bhīmasena's service, bringing him their loads of meat with the deepest devotion, O lord.
Halting there, gathered together among themselves, they overheard in secret all that the warriors said, and Duryodhana's words as well.
And all those mighty bowmen, longing for battle, pressed the Kaurava with the utmost insistence, though he had no wish to fight.
Watching thus those great chariot-warriors of the Kauravas, and the king who lingered in the waters with no mind for battle—
having heard their conversation and the words of the king who lay within the water, the hunters came to know, O lord of kings, that Suyodhana was hidden in the lake.
These men had earlier been questioned by the son of Pāṇḍu about your son; coming there by chance, they had been seeking the king.
Then, recalling what the son of Pāṇḍu had said, the deer-hunters spoke softly to one another, O king, in this wise:
"Let us reveal Duryodhana; the Pāṇḍava will give us wealth. Plainly enough, King Duryodhana has been disclosed to us in the lake."
"Therefore let us all go to where King Yudhiṣṭhira is, to tell him that the wrathful Duryodhana lies asleep in the water."
"Let us all tell the wise Bhīmasena, the wielder of the bow, that the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra lies hidden in the water."
"Well pleased, he will give us abundant riches. What use to us is this dry, withered, shriveled meat?"
Having spoken thus, the hunters, greatly delighted and eager for wealth, took up their loads of meat and set out toward the camp.
And the Pāṇḍavas, O great king, sure-aimed and hard-striking warriors, not seeing Duryodhana standing on the field of battle,
and longing to reach the end of that wicked deceiver's trickery, sent out scouts in every direction across the field of war.
Returning, all the soldiers together reported to the Dharma-king that King Duryodhana had vanished.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing those words of the scouts, O bull of the Bhāratas, the king fell into bitter brooding and drew a heavy sigh.
Then, O bull of the Bhāratas, while the Pāṇḍavas stood there dejected, the hunters, hastening away from that place, O lord,
came joyfully to the camp, having seen King Duryodhana; and though held back, they pressed in within sight of Bhīmasena.
Coming before the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena of mighty strength, they told him all that had happened and all that they had heard.
Then Vṛkodara, O king, the scorcher of foes, having given them abundant wealth, related the whole matter to the Dharma-king.
"That Duryodhana, O king, has been discovered for me by the hunters; he for whose sake you grieve lies asleep, having stilled the waters about him."
Hearing those welcome words of Bhīmasena, O lord of peoples, Ajātaśatru, the son of Kuntī, rejoiced together with his brothers.
And learning that the great bowman had entered the watery lake, he set out at once, placing Janārdana at the fore.
Then there arose a tumult of glad shouting, O lord of peoples, from the exultant Pāṇḍavas and Pāñcālas on every side.
They raised lion-roars and battle-cries, O bull of the Bhāratas; and the warriors hastened, O king, to the lake of Dvaipāyana.
"The wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is found, he is seen!"—again and again in the fray the Somakas cried out there on all sides, their faces glad.
From their swift-moving, speeding chariots there arose a tumultuous din that touched the heavens, O lord of the earth.
Eager to lay hold of Duryodhana, they followed King Yudhiṣṭhira here and there in haste, their mounts worn out.
Arjuna and Bhīmasena, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the Pāñcāla, and the unvanquished Śikhaṇḍin,
Uttamaujas, Yudhāmanyu, and the unconquered Sātyaki, and those Pāñcālas who remained, and the sons of Draupadī, O Bhārata, and all the horses and elephants, and foot-soldiers by the hundred—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
then, O great king, the son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, reached the famed lake of Dvaipāyana, where Duryodhana was.
Its waters cool and clear and pleasing, like a second ocean—there your son had taken his stand, having stilled the waters by his magic.
By a most wondrous device, through the working of fate, O Bhārata, he lay sunk within the water, hard for any man to behold, O lord—the ruler of men, club in hand, O sovereign of men.
Then King Duryodhana, dwelling sunk within the water, heard the tumultuous din, loud as a thundercloud's roar.
And Yudhiṣṭhira, O lord of kings, came to that lake with his brothers, O great king, to slay your son.
With the great blast of conch-shells and the rumble of chariot-wheels, raising up a vast cloud of dust and making the earth tremble,
the great chariot-warriors Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa, hearing the din of Yudhiṣṭhira's army, spoke thus to the king:
"Here come the Pāṇḍavas, exultant and flushed with victory. We shall withdraw for now—give us leave, O lord."
Duryodhana, hearing this from those glorious men, said "So be it," and by his magic stilled that lake, O lord.
Having taken leave of the king, deeply sunk in grief, those chariot-warriors led by Kṛpa went far off, O great king.
Having traveled a long way, they spied a banyan tree, O venerable one, and sat down, sorely wearied, brooding upon the king.
The mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra slept, having stilled the water; and the Pāṇḍavas too had reached that place, eager for battle.
"How then will the battle come about? What will become of the king? How, O king, will the Pāṇḍavas deal with the Kaurava?"
Brooding thus, those chariot-warriors led by Kṛpa unyoked their horses from the chariots and took their rest there, O king.
Saṃjaya said: Then, when those three chariot-warriors had departed, the Pāṇḍavas drew near to the lake where Duryodhana was.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Reaching the lake of Dvaipāyana, O best of the Kurus, and seeing that body of water held fast by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the delight of the Kurus spoke these words to Vāsudeva:
"Behold this magic the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra has worked upon the waters! Having stilled the water, he lies there; he has no fear of any man."
"Having wrought this divine illusion, he has sunk himself within the water; yet that knower of trickery shall not escape me alive through his deceit."
"Even if the wielder of the thunderbolt himself should lend him aid in battle, still the world shall see him slain in war, O Mādhava."
The illustrious Vāsudeva said: Destroy this illusion of the illusionist by illusion, O Bhārata. The trickster must be slain by trickery—this is the truth, Yudhiṣṭhira.
By many ways and means working an illusion upon the waters, slay the wicked-souled Suyodhana, O best of the Bhāratas.
By ways and means Indra slew the Daityas and Dānavas; by manifold ways and means the great-souled one bound Bali.
By ways and means of old the great Asura Hiraṇyākṣa, and Hiraṇyakaśipu too, were destroyed by stratagem; and Vṛtra was slain, O king, by stratagem alone—of this there is no doubt.
So too the rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, son of Pulastya's line, was slain by Rāma, O king, together with his kin and his followers, through resort to a contrived design; therefore do you also show your prowess thus.
By ways and means, O king, in olden time were slain by me the great Daitya Tāraka and the valorous Vipracitti.
Vātāpi and Ilvala, and Triśiras as well, O lord, and the asuras Sunda and Upasunda—all were destroyed by stratagem alone.
By ways and means does Indra enjoy the threefold heaven, O lord. Stratagem is mighty, O king; there is nothing else like it, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Daityas and Dānavas, rākṣasas and kings alike, have been slain by ways and means; therefore put a stratagem into practice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, the Pāṇḍava of firm vows, the son of Kuntī, O great king, spoke to your mighty son who stood within the water, smiling as it were, O Bhārata:
"Suyodhana, to what end is this resort to the waters made by you, after you have brought to ruin all the warrior-folk and your own kin as well, O lord of peoples?"
"Today you have entered the water, craving your own life. Rise, O king, and do battle with us, Suyodhana!"
"Where, O best of men, has that pride of yours gone, and where that arrogance—you who, having stilled the water, stand there in fear, O king?"
"All men proclaim you a hero in the assembly; but I deem that valor of yours, who lie hidden in the water, to be in vain."
"Rise, O king, and fight! You are a warrior, born of noble line, a Kaurava above all—remember your birth in that house."
"How is it that you, vaunting your birth in the Kaurava line, now in terror of battle have entered the water and there take your stand?"
"To refuse battle and to abandon one's post—this is not the eternal law. Flight from the field, O king, is the practice of the ignoble and bars the way to heaven."
"How, without having reached the far shore of battle, can you wish to live, having seen these fallen—sons and brothers and fathers alike?"
"Having brought to death your kinsmen and your comrades, your uncles and your relations, how, my friend, do you now linger in this lake?"
"You fancy yourself a hero, but a hero you are not. Falsely you speak, O Bhārata—'I am a hero!'—you fool, in the hearing of all the world."
"For heroes never flee, in any wise, at the sight of foes. Tell us, then, O hero, by what resolve you forsake the fray."
So rise up, you, and fight, casting off the fear within you—having destroyed your whole army and your brothers too, O Suyodhana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It is no time now to set your mind on life out of a wish to act righteously, O Suyodhana; rather, one of your kind should hold fast to the warrior's duty.
Leaning upon Karṇa and upon Śakuni the son of Subala, you understood not your own self, deluded as though you were immortal.
Having wrought that exceedingly great evil, fight back, O Bhārata; for how should one of your kind, out of folly, find flight pleasing?
Where has that manhood of yours gone, and where your pride, O Suyodhana? Where has your valor gone, and where your great thundering boast?
Where has your skill in arms gone, and why do you lie down in this pool of water? Rise up, you, and fight by the warrior's duty, O Bhārata.
Either conquer us and rule this earth, or, slain by us, you shall sleep upon the ground, O Bhārata.
This is your foremost duty, ordained by the great-souled Creator; fulfill it truly and become a king, O mighty chariot-warrior.
Duryodhana said: It is no wonder, great king, that fear should enter a living being; yet it is not from fear for my life, O Bhārata, that I withdrew in dread.
Without a chariot and without a quiver, my flanking driver slain, alone and without a host in the battle, I chose to take a moment's rest.
Not for the sake of my life, nor from fear, nor from despair, O lord of peoples, have I entered these waters; this I have done out of exhaustion.
Take rest yourself, O son of Kuntī, and those who follow you; I shall rise and fight you all in the battle.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: We are all well rested indeed, and long have we been seeking you; so rise up now and fight here, O Suyodhana.
Either slay the sons of Pṛthā in battle and win a flourishing kingdom, or, slain by us in the fight, you shall attain the world of heroes.
Duryodhana said: Those for whose sake I desired the kingdom of the Kurus, O delight of the Kurus—they, all my brothers, lie slain, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This earth, stripped of her jewels, her bull-like warriors slain, I have no heart to enjoy—as one would not a widowed woman.
Yet even now I hope to vanquish you, Yudhiṣṭhira, breaking the spirit of the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, O bull of the Bhāratas.
But now I think there is no longer any purpose at all in fighting, with Droṇa and Karṇa stilled in death and the grandsire slain.
Let this whole earth be yours alone now, O king; for what king, bereft of helpers, would wish to rule a kingdom?
Having lost such friends, sons, brothers, and fathers, with the kingdom seized by you, who like me would care to live?
I shall go to the forest, clothed in deerskins; for I, whose side has been slain, take no joy in a kingdom, O Bhārata.
Her kinsmen for the most part slain, her horses slain, her elephants slain—this earth is yours, O king; enjoy her, your fever gone.
To the forest I shall go, clad in two deerskins; for I, vanquished, have no longing for life this day, O mighty one.
Go, you, and enjoy the earth at your ease, O lord of kings—her rulers slain, her warriors slain, her jewels lost, her ramparts crumbled.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Do not, dear sir, standing there in the water, utter the wailings of one in distress; this prattle of yours, like Śakuni's, finds no place in my mind, O king.
And even were you able to make a gift of it, O Suyodhana, I would not wish to rule an earth bestowed by you.
By unrighteousness I would not take this earth given by you; for the acceptance of gifts is not held to be the duty of a warrior, O king.
I would not desire the whole earth given by you; rather, having vanquished you in battle, I shall enjoy this realm.
And being no longer her lord, how do you wish to give the earth away? Why, O king, did you not give this earth even then?
When we sought it rightfully, for the sake of peace within our line, you first rebuffed the mighty scion of the Vṛṣṇis, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What now do you give? What madness has seized your mind? For what king, once assailed, would wish to give away the earth?
You have no power today to give the earth, O delight of the Kurus, nor to wrest her away by force, O king; so how do you wish to give? Vanquish me in battle, then rule this earth.
Even so much of the land as could be held on the tip of a needle—not even that much would you give us before, O Bhārata.
How then do you give away this whole earth, O lord of peoples? You who once would not yield a needle's point, how do you now relinquish the land?
Having attained such lordship and ruled this earth, what fool would resolve to give the realm to his enemy?
But you, deluded by sheer folly, do not understand: though you wish to give the earth, this day you shall be parted from your life.
Either conquer us and rule this earth, or, slain by us, go to the most exalted worlds.
While the two of us yet live, O king—both I and you—a doubt about the victory of either will surely remain among all beings.
Your life, O evil-minded one, rests now in my hands; I could, if I wished, let you live—but you are not fit to live.
For you made every effort to burn us, above all, and with venomous serpents, with poisons, and with drownings in water; you wronged us, O king, by the seizure of our kingdom too.
For this reason, O wicked one, there is no life left for you; rise up, rise up and fight—that shall be the better course for you.
Saṃjaya said: Thus did those heroes proclaim, again and again, manifold words ringing with victory, here and there, O lord of men.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Thus reviled, my son, the lord of the earth, a hero wrathful by nature, a scorcher of foes—how did he bear it?
For never before had he heard such reviling, and through his kingly state he had been honored by all the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And this entire earth, thronged with barbarians and forest dwellers, was upheld by his grace, as you yourself witnessed, Saṃjaya.
He, thus reviled in particular by the sons of Pāṇḍu, bereft of his own servants and wholly hemmed in a desolate place—
hearing those bitter words ringing with victory again and again, what did he say to the Pāṇḍavas? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Reviled then, O king, your son standing in the water—reviled by Yudhiṣṭhira together with his brothers, O lord of kings—
hearing those bitter words, the lord of men in his dire plight sighed long and hot, again and again, as he stood there in the water.
Submerged within the water, the king, wringing his hands again and again, set his mind upon battle and addressed the king.
You, the sons of Pṛthā, are all with your friends, all with your chariots and mounts; I am but one, worn down, chariotless, my mounts slain.
Surrounded by many who bear their weapons and ride their chariots—how, being one man on foot and unarmed, can I dare to fight?
But let each of you fight me one by one, O Yudhiṣṭhira; for it is not just that one man should be made to fight against many heroes in battle.
all the more so when I am without armor, exhausted, taking refuge in the water, my limbs sorely wounded, my mounts and men worn out.
I have no fear of you, O king, nor of Pārtha, nor of Vṛkodara, nor of Phalguna, nor of Vāsudeva, nor again of the Pāñcālas;
nor of the twins, nor of Yuyudhāna, nor of whatever other warriors you have; alone and enraged, I could well dare to fight them all here.
The fame of the good among men is rooted in righteousness, O lord of men; guarding both righteousness and renown here, I declare it.
I shall rise and fight you all in the battle, meeting each in turn as the year meets all the seasons that come round one after another.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Today, though unarmed and chariotless, I shall destroy you with your chariots and steeds by my splendor, as the sun at the ebbing of night destroys all the stars; stand firm, O Pāṇḍavas.
Today I shall discharge my debt to the illustrious warriors—to Bāhlika, Droṇa, and Bhīṣma, and to the great-souled Karṇa,
to brave Jayadratha and to Bhagadatta, to both of them, to Śalya the king of the Madras, and to Bhūriśravas as well,
to my sons, O best of the Bhāratas, and to Śakuni the son of Subala, to my allies and friends and kinsmen likewise.
Today I shall discharge my debt by slaying you together with your brothers. Having spoken this much, the lord of men fell silent.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By good fortune you too know the warrior's duty, O Suyodhana; by good fortune your mind turns toward battle alone, O mighty-armed one.
By good fortune you are a hero, O Kaurava; by good fortune you know warfare, you who, alone, wish to fight us all in the battle.
Meeting one against one, whatever weapon is approved by you, take that up and fight; we will stand as your onlookers.
And this, your cherished wish, O hero, I grant you further: slay any one of us and the kingdom is yours, or, slain, attain heaven.
Duryodhana said: If the choice is granted me this day to fight one in single combat, then of weapons this mace is the one I choose, with your consent.
Whichever one of your brothers thinks he can withstand me, let him fight me in battle on foot with the mace.
Chariot-battles, wondrous at every step, have run their course; let this one great and marvelous mace-duel come to pass today.
Even with their foods do men wish to make a change in turn; let there be a change of battles too, with your assent.
With the mace, O mighty-armed one, I shall vanquish you together with your younger brothers, the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas, and whatever other warriors are yours.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Rise up, rise up, O son of Gāndhārī, and do battle with me, O Suyodhana, meeting one against one in the fight, mace to mace, you mighty one.
Be a man, O son of Gāndhārī, and fight with full resolve; this day there is no life left for you, even were you swift as thought.
Saṃjaya said: This your son, that tiger among men, could not endure, submerged within the water and hissing like a great serpent in its hole.
Thus goaded again and again by the lash of those words, the wise one could not brook that speech, as a noble steed cannot brook the whip.
Churning the water with force, the valorous one took up his mace—heavy, wrought of mountain-iron, adorned with golden bands—and rose up from beneath the water, hissing like the lord of serpents.
Cleaving the spellbound water and laying the iron mace upon his shoulder, your son rose up, blazing like the radiant sun.
Then the wise and mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra grasped the heavy mace of tempered iron, embellished with gold.
Beholding him mace in hand, like a peaked mountain, standing there like the trident-bearer enraged against his creatures, the Bhārata with his mace shone, blazing like the sun.
As that mighty-armed subduer of foes rose up from the water, mace in hand, all beings beheld him as Death himself, the rod of doom in his grasp.
Like Śakra with the thunderbolt in his hand, like Hara with the trident in his, all the Pāñcālas, O lord of men, gazed upon your son.
But seeing him risen from the water, the Pāñcālas and the sons of Pāṇḍu thrilled with joy on every side and struck their palms against one another.
But taking that for mockery, your son Duryodhana, enraged, rolled his eyes wide as though he would burn the Pāṇḍavas to ash.
Knitting his brow into a threefold furrow and biting his lip, he then made answer to the Pāṇḍavas and Keśava among them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This mockery of yours I shall answer this very day, O Pāṇḍavas. Slain on the instant, you and the Pāñcālas with you shall go to the abode of Yama."
Risen from those waters, your son Duryodhana stood firm, mace in hand, drenched and bespattered with blood.
His body, smeared with gore and sprinkled with water, shone then like a mountain streaming with red ochre.
Beholding that hero with mace upraised, the Pāṇḍavas there took him for the wrathful son of Vivasvat, his attendants standing with weapons lifted.
Roaring like a thundercloud, bellowing in his joy like a mighty bull, that valiant one then summoned the Pārthas to battle with his mace.
Duryodhana said: Come against me one by one, O Yudhiṣṭhira; for it is not right, O hero, that one should be made to fight against many in battle.
And the more so when one has laid aside his armour, is weary and drenched in the waters, his limbs sorely gashed, his mounts and soldiers slain.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Where was this wisdom of yours, Suyodhana, when many great chariot-warriors together slew Abhimanyu in the fight?
Put on your armour, O hero, and bind up your hair; and whatever else you lack, take that too, O Bhārata. This one wish besides, O hero, I now grant you.
Of the five sons of Pāṇḍu, choose whomever you wish to fight here; having slain him you shall be king, or being slain attain heaven. What, O hero, save your life itself, can we do to please you in this combat?
Saṃjaya said: Then your son, O king, took up his golden armour and a wondrous helmet adorned with the gold of the Jambū river.
With his helmet fastened on and wearing his fair golden mail, your son shone, O king, like a golden mountain-king.
Armed and mace in hand, made ready at the forefront of battle, your son Duryodhana spoke, O king, to all the Pāṇḍavas:
"Let one of you brothers fight with me, mace to mace. I will fight with Sahadeva, or with Bhīma, or with Nakula,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
or with Phalguna this day, or with you yourself, O bull of the Bhāratas. Joining battle, I shall conquer on the field of war.
This day, O tiger among men, I shall reach the far and hardly-won end of this enmity, with my mace bound about with bands of gold.
Be sure of this: in mace-combat there is none my equal. With my mace I shall slay you all, even should you come together. Let him who will fight with me this day take up his mace."
Saṃjaya said: As Duryodhana roared thus again and again, O king, Vāsudeva, wroth with Yudhiṣṭhira, spoke these words:
"If indeed, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he should choose for combat you, or Arjuna, or Nakula, or even Sahadeva—
what is this rashness, O king, that you have uttered, saying, 'Slay but one of us in the fight and be king among the Kurus'?
For thirteen years has he practised here, O king, upon a man of iron, in his longing to slay Bhīmasena.
How then shall our purpose be accomplished, O bull of the Bhāratas? Out of compassion, O best of kings, you have done a rash thing.
I see no other fit to meet him in battle save Vṛkodara, son of Pṛthā—and even he is not greatly practised.
So this gambling-match is begun again as of old, the same crooked game of Śakuni's and of yours, O lord of peoples.
Bhīma is strong and able, but King Suyodhana is skilled. Between strength and skill, O king, the skilled man prevails.
Thus, O king, you have set the enemy upon even ground and staked yourself upon a perilous one; you have brought us into sore distress.
What man, having vanquished all his foes, would choose to gamble it all on a single throw with one remaining adversary, and so take pleasure in such a fight?
For I see not in the world that best of men, mace in hand, who could fight Duryodhana in battle and by his skill surpass him—
neither Phalguna, nor yourself, nor the two sons of Mādrī do I deem a match for that mace-wielder in the fray.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
How then, O Bhārata, do you tell the foe, 'Fight with the mace, and having slain but one of us in battle be king'?
Even when Vṛkodara meets him, our victory is in doubt should they fight by the rules; for this man is skilled and of great might."
Bhīma said: O slayer of Madhu, give way to no despair, O joy of the Yadus. This day I shall reach the farther shore of this enmity, so hard to cross.
I shall slay Suyodhana in battle, of that there is no doubt. Victory for the King of Righteousness, O Kṛṣṇa, is seen for certain.
This mace of mine is heavier by half again than that of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son. Be not troubled, O Mādhava.
The three worlds with the gods themselves, bearing weapons of every kind, would I gladly fight in battle—how much more, this day, Suyodhana!
Saṃjaya said: As Vṛkodara spoke thus, Vāsudeva, rejoicing, honoured him and spoke these words:
"Leaning upon you, O mighty-armed one, the King of Righteousness Yudhiṣṭhira, his foes slain, shall surely regain his own resplendent fortune, of that there is no doubt.
By you have all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra been laid low in battle, and kings and princes and elephants struck down.
The Kaliṅgas, the Māgadhas, the Easterners, the Gāndhāras, and the Kurus, meeting you in the great battle, were slain, O joy of Pāṇḍu.
Having slain Duryodhana too, O son of Kuntī, give over the sea-girt earth to the King of Righteousness, as Viṣṇu gave it to the lord of Śacī.
Meeting you in battle, the wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall perish; breaking both his thighs, you shall fulfil your vow.
Yet the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra must ever be fought with care, O Pārtha; he is skilled and strong, and at all times a connoisseur of battle."
Then Sātyaki, O king, honoured the son of Pāṇḍu, and with words of many kinds Mādhava too honoured him.
The Pāñcālas and the sons of Pāṇḍu, with the King of Righteousness at their head, all alike applauded those words of Bhīmasena.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Bhīma of terrible strength spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, who stood amid the Sṛñjayas, blazing like the sun:
"Joining with him, I am eager to fight in this combat. This basest of men is not able to vanquish me in battle.
This day I shall loose upon Suyodhana, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the wrath long pent and brooding in my heart, as Arjuna loosed the fire upon the Khāṇḍava forest.
This day I shall draw forth the dart that lies in your heart, O son of Pāṇḍu. Having slain the wicked one with my mace, be happy this day, O king.
This day I shall set upon you a garland woven of glory, O sinless one; this day Suyodhana shall let go of his life, his fortune, and his kingdom.
And King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, hearing this day that his son is slain by me, shall remember that evil deed which was born of Śakuni's counsel."
Having spoken thus, that best and most valiant of the Bhāratas raised his mace and rose up for the fight, as Śakra rose to challenge Vṛtra.
Coming upon the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who stood alone like an elephant strayed from its herd, the Pāṇḍavas thrilled with joy.
Seeing him with mace upraised, peaked like Kailāsa, Bhīmasena then, O king, spoke to Duryodhana:
"Recall that evil deed which King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and you wrought against us—what came to pass at Vāraṇāvata.
Recall how Draupadī, in her courses, was tormented in the midst of the assembly, when the king was won at dice by the settled cunning of Śakuni.
And whatever other sins, O evil-souled one, you have wrought against the blameless sons of Pṛthā—behold now the great fruit thereof.
For your sake the son of Gaṅgā, the glorious best of the Bhāratas, the grandsire of us all, lies slain upon a bed of arrows.
Slain is Droṇa, and Karṇa, and slain is the mighty Śalya; and Śakuni, the first author of this enmity, has been slain in battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Slain are your valiant brothers, and your sons together with their soldiers; slain too are the brave kings who never turned back in battle.
These and many other bulls among the kṣatriyas have been slain; and the wicked Prātikāmin too, who wrought Draupadī's affliction, has been slain.
You alone are left, destroyer of your line, basest of men; and you too this day shall I slay with my mace—herein is no doubt.
This day, O king, in battle I shall destroy all your pride, and your vast hope of kingdom, and the wrong you did the Pāṇḍavas."
Duryodhana said: What use this boasting in so many ways? Fight with me now. This day, O Vṛkodara, I shall take from you all appetite for battle.
Do you not see me, O sinner, standing ready for the mace-fight, gripping a mighty mace shaped like a Himālayan peak?
What foe, O sinner, dares this day hope to vanquish me, mace in hand and fighting by the rules—not even Purandara among the gods?
Roar not in vain, O son of Kuntī, like a rainless autumn cloud. Show in battle what strength is yours this day.
Hearing those words of his, the Pāñcālas together with the Sṛñjayas, all longing for victory, applauded that speech.
As one rouses a maddened elephant, the men, O king, with the clapping of their hands urged King Duryodhana on yet more.
There the elephants trumpeted, the horses neighed again and again, and the weapons of the victory-seeking Pāṇḍavas blazed forth.
Saṃjaya said: When that most terrible combat had begun, O great king, and all the high-souled Pāṇḍavas had taken their seats,
then Rāma of the palm-tree banner, the bearer of the plough, hearing that combat between his two pupils was at hand, came near, O king.
Seeing him, the kings, well pleased, did him honour and said, "Behold, O Rāma, the skill of your two pupils in battle."
And then Rāma, beholding Kṛṣṇa and the son of Pāṇḍu, and Duryodhana of the Kuru line standing with mace in hand, spoke:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Forty days and two are gone this day since I set forth; I departed under the asterism Puṣya and am returned under Śravaṇa. I long, O Mādhava, to see the mace-combat of my two pupils."
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, embracing the bearer of the plough, bade him welcome and duly enquired after his well-being.
The two Kṛṣṇas as well, those mighty archers, saluted Halāyudha; greatly delighted and full of affection, the two glorious ones embraced him.
The two valiant sons of Mādrī, and the five sons of Draupadī, having saluted the mighty son of Rohiṇī, stood waiting, O king.
Then the powerful Bhīmasena, and your son too, O lord of men, both with maces upraised, paid honour to the strong one.
Honouring him there again and again with words of welcome, the kings said to Rāma, "Behold the combat, O mighty-armed one!" — thus did the rulers of men address the great-souled son of Rohiṇī.
Then Rāma, embracing the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas as well, asked after the welfare of all those Pāṇḍavas of measureless might; and they in turn, approaching him, inquired after his good health.
The plough-bearer, great of mind, returned the honour to all the kṣatriyas, exchanging cordial greetings of welfare each according to his age.
Janārdana and Sātyaki he embraced with love, and kissing the two upon the head, he inquired after their welfare.
And those two, O king, honoured him in due form as their elder, as Indra and Upendra, filled with joy, would honour Brahmā, the lord of the gods.
Then the son of Dharma said to the son of Rohiṇī, that tamer of foes, "Behold this great combat of the two brothers, O Rāma!" — so he spoke, O Bhārata.
In their midst the mighty-armed and illustrious elder brother of Keśava took his seat, supremely pleased, honoured by the great chariot-warriors.
Seated amid the kings, clad in dark blue and of fair complexion, he shone like the moon in the sky, ringed about by the hosts of stars.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the clash of those two grew tumultuous and hair-raising, O king — a clash that would put an end to the enmity of your sons.
Janamejaya said: Earlier, when that war was at hand, the lord Rāma, having taken leave of Keśava, departed together with the Vṛṣṇis.
"I shall give no aid to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Keśava, nor to the sons of Pāṇḍu; I shall go my way as I came."
Having said this, Rāma, the crusher of foes, departed then. Of his return now, O brāhmaṇa, you should tell me once more.
Recount to me in full how Rāma came to be present, and how he beheld the combat; for you are skilled, O most excellent one.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the great-souled Pāṇḍavas were encamped at Upaplavya, the slayer of Madhu was sent to the presence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, in the cause of peace, O mighty-armed one, for the good of all living beings.
Having gone to Hāstinapura and met with Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he spoke words that were true and especially salutary; but the king did not act upon them, just as has been told you before.
Failing to win peace there, Kṛṣṇa, that best of men, the mighty-armed one, came back to Upaplavya, O lord of men.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having returned, dismissed by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with nothing accomplished, O tiger among men, said this to the Pāṇḍavas:
"The Kurus, driven on by fate, will not heed my word. March forth, O Pāṇḍavas, together with me, under the constellation Puṣya."
Then, as the forces were being marshalled, the best of the mighty, the great-souled son of Rohiṇī, spoke to his brother Kṛṣṇa:
"To those others too, O mighty-armed slayer of Madhu, let aid be given"; but Kṛṣṇa did not then act upon that word of his.
Then, his heart overcome with displeasure, the delight of the Yadus, the plough-bearer of great renown, set out on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords along the Sarasvatī, under the conjunction of the Maitra constellation, accompanied by all the Yādavas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Bhoja, that tamer of foes, gave his allegiance to Duryodhana, while Vāsudeva, together with Yuyudhāna, supported the Pāṇḍavas.
When the valiant son of Rohiṇī had departed, the slayer of Madhu, under the star Puṣya, placing the Pāṇḍavas at the fore, marched forth to face the Kurus.
As he journeyed, while still upon the road, Rāma said to his attendants: "Bring from Dvārakā the provisions for the pilgrimage and all the requisites — the sacred fires and the officiating priests as well."
"Gold and silver, milch cows, garments, horses, elephants and chariots, mules and camels and beasts of burden — let all the equipage for the sake of the pilgrimage be brought quickly."
"Travel swiftly, upstream along the Sarasvatī; and bring the officiating priests and bulls among the twice-born by the hundred."
Having thus instructed his attendants, the mighty Baladeva set forth on the pilgrimage, O king, during the slaughter of the Kurus, journeying upstream along the Sarasvatī from the sea.
Surrounded by officiating priests and friends and other most excellent of the twice-born, by chariots, elephants and horses and attendants, O bull of the Bharatas, and by many conveyances drawn by oxen, mules and camels.
For the weary and worn of body, for children and for the long-lived, those conveyances waited in their several places, O Bhārata; and food was made ready on every side for the sake of the hungry.
Whatever twice-born one wished, wherever, to take his food, to that very one, just there, they brought it then, O king.
The men stationed there, O king, by the command of the son of Rohiṇī, made heaps of food and drink everywhere about.
And costly garments, couches and spreadings were arranged there for the honouring of the brāhmaṇas who sought comfort.
Wherever a brāhmaṇa, or a kṣatriya too, lay down to sleep, O Bhārata, there for that very one was everything seen ready prepared.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All the folk then rested or journeyed at their ease — conveyances for one who wished to travel, and drink for one who thirsted,
and savoury foods for one who hungered, O bull of the Bhāratas; there the men brought garments and ornaments besides.
That road shone forth, O king, bringing comfort to every one; it was then like heaven, O hero, for the men who travelled there.
Filled with unending joy, abounding in delicacies, attended by auspicious things, thronged with hundreds of diverse folk trading their wares in shops and markets, set about with many trees and creepers, and adorned with jewels of every kind.
Then the great-souled one, his self set firm in vows, at the holy fords, O king, gave wealth to the twice-born and the sacrificial fees — that foremost hero of the Yadus, the renowned plough-bearer.
Milk-giving cows by the thousand, draped in fine cloth, their horns bound with gold, and horses born in lands of many kinds, conveyances and serving-women — these he gave to the twice-born.
Jewels — pearls, gems and coral — and horned gold and bright silver, and vessels of iron and of copper, Rāma bestowed upon the foremost of the twice-born.
Thus did the great-souled one bestow abundant wealth at the excellent fords of the Sarasvatī; then he of incomparable might and noble conduct came by stages to Kurukṣetra.
Janamejaya said: Tell me of the origin of the virtues of the fords along the Sarasvatī, and their fruit, O best of two-footed beings, and the accomplishment of rites there.
And in due order, O blessed one, of the fords one after another, O brāhmaṇa, O best of the knowers of brahman; for great is my curiosity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hear, O king, the full account of the fords and the origin of their virtues in every part, the holy tale told by me, O lord of kings, in its entirety.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
First, O great king, that foremost hero of the Yadus, together with hosts of officiating priests, friends and brāhmaṇas, came to the holy Prabhāsa — where the lord of the stars was being afflicted by consumption.
There, freed from the curse and regaining his splendour, he lights up the whole world, O lord of men. Thus this foremost ford upon the earth, from his shining forth, is therefore called Prabhāsa.
Janamejaya said: For what reason was the blessed Soma seized by consumption? And how did the moon plunge himself into that foremost of fords?
And how, having bathed therein, was the hare-marked moon replenished once more? Tell me all of this in full, O great sage.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Those who were the daughters of Dakṣa came into being, O lord of peoples; and Dakṣa gave twenty-seven maidens to Soma.
Devoted to the conjunctions of the constellations and serving for the reckoning of time, O Bhārata, they were the wives of that Soma, O lord of kings, marked with auspicious signs.
All of them were wide-eyed and unequalled in beauty upon the earth; yet among them Rohiṇī surpassed the rest in the fullness of her beauty.
Therefore the blessed maker of the night set his love upon her; she became dear to his heart, and so he ever resorted to her.
For in olden time, O lord of kings, Soma dwelt long with Rohiṇī; and at this the constellations, wives of the great-souled one, grew wroth.
They went to their father, the Lord of Creatures, and without delay declared: "Soma dwells not with us; he resorts ever to Rohiṇī."
"We all, gathered together, will dwell in your presence, O lord of creatures, with restricted food, intent upon the practice of austerities."
Having heard their words, Dakṣa then said to Soma: "Behave equally toward your wives, lest a great unrighteousness touch you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And to all of them Dakṣa said: "Go to Soma's side; by my command the moon shall dwell equally with all of you."
Dismissed, they then went to the dwelling of the cool-rayed one; yet even so the blessed Soma, O lord of the earth, dwelt still with Rohiṇī, delighting in her again and again.
Then all of them together spoke again to their father: "Engaged in serving you, we shall dwell in your hermitage; Soma dwells not with us, he has not done your bidding."
Having heard those words of theirs, Dakṣa then said to Soma: "Behave equally toward your wives, lest I curse you, O shining one."
But disregarding that word of Dakṣa, the blessed hare-marked one dwelt with Rohiṇī; then once more those wives grew wroth.
And going to their father, bowing then with their heads, they said: "Soma dwells not with us; therefore be you our refuge."
"With Rohiṇī alone, O blessed one, the moon dwells ever; therefore protect us all, that Soma may come to us."
Hearing this, the blessed one, wrathful, O lord of the earth, in his anger let loose consumption against Soma; and it entered the lord of the stars.
His being overcome by the consumption, the hare-marked one waned day by day; and he made effort, O king, to be freed of that consumption.
Though the maker of the night performed sacrifices of many kinds, O great king, he was not released from the curse, and indeed came to wasting away.
Then, as Soma wasted away, the herbs no longer grew; all of them were robbed of savour and wholly stripped of their potency.
When the wasting of the herbs had come about, there was wasting of living beings too; and all creatures grew gaunt as the maker of the night waned away.
Then the gods, having assembled, said to Soma, O lord of the earth: "What is this? Your form does not shine forth as it once did."
"Tell us all the cause, whereby this great peril has come upon you; and having heard the word from you, we shall then provide a remedy."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed, the hare-marked one answered all of them — the curse, and its cause, and the consumption that had come upon himself.
The gods, hearing his words, went to Dakṣa and said: "Be gracious, O blessed one, toward Soma, and let this curse be turned back."
"For yonder moon is wasted, and but a little of him is seen remaining; and through his wasting, O lord of the gods, the creatures too have come to ruin."
"The plants and herbs and the seeds of many kinds, and we ourselves, O teacher of the world — you should show us grace."
Thus addressed, the Lord of Creatures pondered and spoke this word: "This word of mine cannot be turned otherwise; yet, O illustrious ones, by some means it shall be reversed."
