"Let the hare-marked one behave equally toward all his wives evermore; and emerging at the excellent ford of the Sarasvatī, the hare-marked one shall grow full again, O gods — that word of mine is true."
"For half a month Soma shall ever pass to waning, and for half a month always to waxing — this word of mine is true."
Then, by the seer's command, Soma went to the Sarasvatī; he came indeed to Prabhāsa, the supreme tīrtha upon the Sarasvatī.
On the new-moon day the mighty-splendored one, rising up there in great brilliance, illumined the worlds and regained his cool-rayed nature.
And all the gods, O lord of kings, having reached abundant Prabhāsa and joined together with Soma, stood before Dakṣa.
Then the Lord of Creatures dismissed all the deities, and the blessed one, pleased, spoke once more to Soma these words:
"Despise not women, my son, nor ever the brāhmaṇas. Go now, and being ever diligent, carry out my command."
Dismissed thus, O great king, he went to his own abode, and the creatures grew glad, partaking of nourishment as before.
All this I have told you—how the night-maker was cursed, and how Prabhāsa came to be the foremost among tīrthas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
On every new-moon day, O great king, the hare-marked one, the glorious Moon, bathing at the supreme tīrtha of Prabhāsa, is replenished.
Therefore men know it as Prabhāsa, O lord of the earth; for the Moon, rising up there, attained his supreme radiance (prabhā).
Then the unfallen, mighty one went on to Camasodbheda—that which men speak of as Camasodbheda.
There Halāyudha, having bestowed choice gifts, stayed a single night and bathed according to the prescribed rite.
Then the elder brother of Keśava went swiftly to Udapāna, gaining there too the foremost benediction and great reward.
For by the moistness of the herbs and of the earth, O Janamejaya, the perfected ones, O lord of kings, discern the Sarasvatī even where she has vanished.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: From there Halāyudha went on, O great king, to the Udapāna—the river-sunk well of the illustrious Trita.
There the wielder of the pestle, well pleased, bestowed much wealth and honored the brāhmaṇas, and touched the water in that very place.
There it was that Trita dwelt, devoted to dharma, of mighty austerity; and that great soul, while abiding in the well, drank the soma.
And there, abandoning him, his two brothers went home; whereupon Trita, that best of brāhmaṇas, laid a curse upon them both.
Janamejaya said: How came the well to be, O brāhmaṇa, and how did that one of great austerity, that best of the twice-born, fall in, and why was he forsaken by his brothers?
And how, leaving him in the well, did the two brothers go home? Tell me this, O brāhmaṇa, if you think it fit to be heard.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: In a former age, O king, there were three brother-sages, Ekata, Dvita, and Trita, resembling the sun.
All were like Prajāpati, blessed with offspring, all winners of the world of Brahman by austerity, all expounders of the Veda.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Their father Gautama, ever devoted to dharma, was always pleased by their austerity, their discipline, and their self-restraint.
And in the course of long time, having gained their devotion, the blessed one departed to the abode befitting himself.
Those kings who before had been the patrons of that great soul, when he had gone to heaven, all honored his sons.
By his works and by his study, O king, Trita attained pre-eminence, even as his father had done.
All the blessed sages of holy mark honored that illustrious one for his learning as well.
Now once, O king, the two brothers Ekata and Dvita set their minds upon a sacrifice, and especially upon gaining wealth thereby.
This thought arose in the two, O scorcher of foes: to take Trita with them, to gather all their patrons, and to receive cattle from them.
"Joyfully we shall drink the soma, having gained a sacrifice of great fruit." And so, O great king, the three brothers performed it.
Going about thus among all their patrons for the sake of cattle, they performed sacrifices for them, and so obtained from those patrons very many beasts.
Having received their due by that priestly office according to rule, those great-souled seers came toward the eastern quarter.
Trita walked before them, O great king, gladly, while Ekata and Dvita came behind, driving the cattle.
Seeing the great herd of cattle, a thought arose in the two: "How might these cows be ours, the two of us, without Trita?"
Conferring with one another, Ekata and Dvita—the two sinners—spoke together; hear what they said, O lord of men.
"Trita is skilled in sacrifices, Trita is grounded in the Vedas; Trita will obtain still other and far more numerous cows."
"Therefore let the two of us, joined together, drive off the cows and go; and let Trita too go where he will, parted from us."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As they came on by night, a wolf appeared in their path; and not far off, on the bank of the Sarasvatī, there was a great well.
Then Trita, seeing the wolf standing before him in the path, recoiled in fear of it and fell into that well—bottomless, most terrible, dreadful to all beings.
Then the illustrious Trita, that best of sages, fallen within the well, raised a cry of distress, and the two sages heard it.
Knowing him fallen into the well, the brothers Ekata and Dvita, out of fear of the wolf and out of greed, abandoned him and went on.
Forsaken by his two brothers, greedy for cattle, that one of great austerity lay, O great king, in the well, waterless and choked with dust.
Trita beheld himself sunk in the well overgrown with creepers and grass, O best of Bhāratas, as a sinner sunk in hell.
Wise as he was, fearing death and yet undrinker of soma, he reckoned in his mind: "How might the soma be drunk by me, while I bide here?"
Pondering thus in that well, the one of great austerity saw a creeper hanging there by chance.
Then in that dust-clogged well the sage, imagining the water, conceived the sacrificial fires, and himself as the hotṛ-priest.
Then, conceiving that creeper to be the soma, the sage of mighty austerity, calling to mind in thought the Ṛcs, the Yajuses, and the Sāmans, and making the pebbles into the pressing-stones, performed the pressing, O king.
He made the water into clarified butter and the portions for the dwellers of the threefold heaven; and having pressed the soma, he raised a tumultuous sound.
And that trained, well-pitched chant of Trita pierced heaven, O king; and he accomplished that sacrifice as it is prescribed by the expounders of the Veda.
As the sacrifice of the great-souled Trita went forward, all the threefold heaven was thrown into agitation, and none could fathom the cause.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Bṛhaspati heard that most tumultuous sound, and hearing it, the chaplain of the gods spoke to all the deities:
"The sacrifice of Trita is in progress; let us go thither, O gods. For that one of great austerity, if angered, might create other gods as well."
Hearing that word of his, all the deities together set forth to the place where that sacrifice of Trita was being performed.
The gods, having gone there to the well where Trita was, beheld that great soul consecrated for the sacrificial rites.
And seeing that great soul endowed with surpassing splendor, they said to the illustrious one: "We have come, seeking our portions."
Then the seer said to the gods: "Behold me, O dwellers of heaven, sunk in this fearful well and well-nigh out of my senses."
Then Trita, O great king, gave them their portions according to rule, accompanied by the sacred formulas; and they were well pleased thereat.
Then the dwellers of heaven, having received the portions duly obtained, glad at heart, granted him the boons that he desired in his mind.
And he chose this boon: "You ought to deliver me from here; and whoever touches the water in this well, let him attain the state of the soma-drinkers."
Thereupon, O king, the Sarasvatī surged up there full of waves, and Trita, lifted by her, stood honoring the dwellers of heaven.
Saying "So be it," the gods went, O king, as they had come; and Trita too, well pleased, then went to his own abode.
But that one of great austerity, having reached his two brother-sages, then in anger spoke harsh words to them and cursed them:
"Since the two of you, greedy for cattle, forsook me and ran away, therefore in the form of fanged beasts you shall roam about,
cursed by me for this evil deed; and your offspring shall be langurs, bears, and monkeys."
And when this was spoken by him, that very instant, O lord of peoples, the two were seen so transformed by the word of the truth-speaker.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There too Halāyudha of boundless valor touched the water, bestowed gifts of many kinds, and honored the brāhmaṇas.
And having seen that river-sunk well and praised it again and again, the undaunted one then reached Vinaśana.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O king, Halāyudha came to Vinaśana, where the Sarasvatī vanished out of loathing for the Śūdras and the Ābhīras.
Because she, the Sarasvatī, O best of Bhāratas, vanished out of loathing, therefore the seers ever call that place Vinaśana.
And there too Bala of mighty strength touched the waters of the Sarasvatī, and then went on to Subhūmika upon the fair bank of the Sarasvatī.
There the radiant apsarases, ever unwearied, of unblemished countenance, sport at all times with pure and lovely games.
There, O lord of men, the gods together with the gandharvas come month after month to that holy tīrtha frequented by brāhmaṇas.
There the gandharvas and likewise the throngs of apsarases were seen, gathered and joined together, O king, each as it chanced and at their ease.
There the gods and the ancestors rejoice amid the herbs, ever showered again and again with holy, heavenly blossoms.
That fair playground of those apsarases, O king, is renowned as Subhūmika, upon the lovely bank of the Sarasvatī.
There the Mādhava, having bathed and bestowed wealth upon the brāhmaṇas, and having heard that heavenly song and the sound of the instruments—
and having seen the broad shadows of the gods, gandharvas, and rākṣasas—the son of Rohiṇī then came to the tīrtha of the gandharvas.
There the gandharvas led by Viśvāvasu, endowed with austerity, make most delightful dance, music, and song.
There the plough-bearer bestowed upon the brāhmaṇas manifold wealth—goats and sheep, cattle, asses and camels, gold and silver as well—
and having fed the twice-born with all they desired and gratified them with great riches, the Mādhava went onward in the company of the brāhmaṇas, being praised by them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And from that gandharva-tīrtha the mighty-armed subduer of foes, wearing a single earring, came to the great tīrtha of Gargasrotas.
There it was that the aged Garga, his soul refined by austerity, attained the science of the reckoning of time and of the courses and transits of the heavenly bodies.
There too, O Janamejaya, the dread and the auspicious portents were determined by that great soul at the holy ford of the Sarasvatī; and after his name that ford is remembered as Gargasrotas.
There, O king, the sages of firm vows constantly waited upon the illustrious Garga, O lord, to learn from him the science of time.
Having gone there, O great king, Bala, anointed with white sandal paste, duly bestowed wealth upon the sages whose souls were refined.
And having given to the brāhmaṇas foods of every kind, high and humble, that hero of great renown, clad in dark blue, then proceeded to the Śaṅkha ford.
There the mighty Bala, the palmyra-bannered, beheld a great conch-tree, lofty as Mount Meru, resembling a white mountain, frequented by hosts of sages, a tree grown upon the bank of the Sarasvatī.
There were yakṣas and vidyādharas and rākṣasas of boundless energy, and piśācas of measureless strength, and siddhas by the thousand.
All of them, forsaking other food, would from time to time eat only the fruit of that lord of the forest, observing their vows and restraints.
Keeping each his own appointed observances, they roamed about apart, one and all, and ranged there unseen by men, O bull among men.
Thus famed in this world, O ruler of men, was that lord of the forest; and there upon the Sarasvatī is a purifying ford renowned throughout the world.
At that ford the tiger of the Yadus bestowed upon the renowned sages vessels of copper and of iron and garments of every kind.
Having honored the brāhmaṇas and being himself honored by those rich in austerity, Halāyudha came, O king, to the holy Dvaitavana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having gone there and beheld the sages wearing garbs of many kinds, Bala bathed in the water and paid honor to the brāhmaṇas.
And having likewise given the brāhmaṇas ample objects of enjoyment, Bala then set forth, O king, along the southern bank of the Sarasvatī.
And that mighty-armed one of great renown, righteous of soul and unfailing, having gone no great distance, came to the ford named Nāgadhanvan.
There, O great king, was the abode of Vāsuki, king of serpents, of mighty splendor, surrounded by many serpents; and there dwelt fourteen thousand sages who had attained perfection.
There the gods, having assembled, duly consecrated Vāsuki, foremost of serpents, as king over all the serpents; and there, O Kaurava, no fear of serpents is to be found.
There too, having duly bestowed heaps of jewels upon the brāhmaṇas, he proceeded toward the east, O king, blazing with his own splendor.
Bathing again and again with delight in those fords, the plough-bearer gave wealth to the twice-born and passed on, surpassingly given to austerity.
Having saluted the hosts of sages who abode there, Halāyudha—Rāma—then went to a great ford frequented by sages.
There the Sarasvatī once again turned back and flowed eastward, for the sake of the great-souled sages of the Naimiṣa forest.
Beholding that best of rivers there turned back upon her course, Bala the plough-bearer, anointed with white sandal, was filled with wonder, O king.
Janamejaya said: Why, O brāhmaṇa, did the Sarasvatī turn back and flow eastward? I wish to hear all this explained, O best of priests.
And for what cause was the joy of the Yadus filled with wonder there, and how did that best of rivers turn back? Tell me this, O most excellent of the twice-born.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Of old, in the Kṛta age, O king, the ascetics of the Naimiṣa forest were holding a vast sacrificial session lasting twelve years; and many sages, O king, assembled there together.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And when those illustrious ones had dwelt at that session according to the ordinance, and the twelve-year session of the Naimiṣa sages had come to its close, many sages came thither for the sake of the holy fords.
And by reason of the multitude of sages, O lord of peoples, the fords along the southern bank of the Sarasvatī then took on the likeness of cities.
As far as Samantapañcaka, O tiger among men, those most excellent of the twice-born, longing for the holy fords, took their stand along the river's shore.
As those sages of refined souls offered their oblations, the quarters of the sky were filled with the mighty sound of their study of the sacred texts.
Then, with the fire-oblations of those great souls being offered and blazing on every side, the best of rivers shone resplendent.
There were the Vālakhilyas, O great king, and ascetics who ground their food with stones, and others who used their teeth for a mortar, and still others who washed clean all they ate.
And ascetics who fed on air, who took only water, who ate but leaves, who kept observances of many kinds, and who lay upon the bare ground.
Such sages dwelt there beside the Sarasvatī, gracing that best of rivers as the dwellers of heaven grace the Gaṅgā.
Thereafter came other sages, performers of sacrificial sessions; but those keepers of mighty vows found no open room for them in Kurukṣetra.
Then with their sacred threads they measured out a ford for themselves, offered their fire-oblations, and performed rites of many kinds.
Then, O lord of kings, the Sarasvatī showed herself for their sake to that company of sages who were dejected and sunk in anxious thought.
Then, out of compassion for the sages of holy austerities, the best of rivers turned back her course, forming many bowers, O Janamejaya.
Then, having turned back for their sake, O lord of kings, the Sarasvatī, best of rivers, flowed once more toward the west.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Not in vain shall my coming be: for their sake I flow back again,"—and so, O king, the great river wrought a great marvel.
Thus, O lord of kings, that bower in Kurukṣetra is remembered as Naimiṣeya; there, O best of the Kurus, perform great rites.
Beholding there the many bowers and that river turned back upon her course, wonder then came over the great-souled Rāma.
There too the joy of the Yadus touched the water according to the rite, and bestowed gifts upon the twice-born—vessels of many kinds and food and drink of every sort he supplied to the brāhmaṇas.
Then Bala set forth, O king, honored by the twice-born, to an excellent ford of the Sarasvatī thronged with hosts of birds of many kinds.
It was adorned with jujube and iṅguda, kāśmarya and plakṣa, fig-tree and vibhītaka, with breadfruit and palāśa, with karīra and pīlu trees.
And with trees grown on the Sarasvatī's bank—the bandhana and the syandana, with groves of parūṣaka, and with bilva and āmrātaka trees.
It was graced with thickets of atimuktaka and with pārijāta trees, abounding most in groves of plantain—a place beloved, lovely, and delightful to the heart.
It was peopled by many forest sages who fed on air, on water, on fruit, and on leaves, who used their teeth for a mortar, and who ground their food with stones.
It resounded with the chant of sacred study, was thronged with hundreds of herds of deer, and was much frequented by men who did no harm and held righteousness supreme.
To the ford named Saptasārasvata Halāyudha came, where the great sage Maṅkaṇaka, who had won perfection, had performed his austerities.
Janamejaya said: Why is it called Saptasārasvata, and who was the sage Maṅkaṇaka? How did the venerable one win perfection, and what was the observance he kept?
In whose lineage was he born, and what did he learn, O most excellent of the twice-born? All this I wish to hear in due order, O best of brāhmaṇas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: O king, there are seven Sarasvatīs, by whom this world is pervaded; for, summoned by the mighty here and there, the Sarasvatī came.
They are Suprabhā and Kāñcanākṣī, Viśālā and Mānasahradā, the Sarasvatī known as Oghavatī, Suveṇu, and Vimalodakā.
While a sacrifice of the mighty Grandsire was in progress upon the earth, the sacrificial enclosure spread wide and the twice-born assembled there—
with the pure proclamations of the holy day and the resounding of the Vedas, while the gods themselves were intent upon that sacrificial rite—
there, O great king, when the great-grandsire had been consecrated and was offering a session that fulfilled every desire,
whatever things the twice-born, skilled in righteousness and worldly gain, conceived in their minds, those things, O lord of kings, came to them there of their own accord.
There the gandharvas sang, and the troops of apsarases danced, and divine instruments of music were straightway sounded.
At the perfection of that sacrifice even the gods were delighted and fell into the utmost wonder—how much more, then, those of mortal birth?
As the sacrifice went forward thus, with the Grandsire abiding at Puṣkara, the sages said, O king: "This sacrifice cannot bear great fruit, since the best of rivers, the Sarasvatī, is nowhere seen here."
Hearing this, the venerable one was pleased and called the Sarasvatī to mind; and being summoned by the sacrificing Grandsire, the Sarasvatī came to Puṣkara, there bearing the name Suprabhā, O lord of kings.
Beholding the swift-flowing Sarasvatī, who came to do honor to the Grandsire, the sages were gladdened and held that sacrifice in high esteem.
Thus this best of rivers, the Sarasvatī, came into being at Puṣkara for the Grandsire's sake and for the delight of the wise.
At the Naimiṣa forest, O king, the sages assembled and sat together; and there, O lord of peoples, wondrous discourses arose concerning the Veda.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There were sages versed in the recitation of various branches of sacred lore; and those sages, having gathered, called the Sarasvatī to mind.
Thus meditated upon, O great king, by the sages who were performing the session, the illustrious and holy Sarasvatī came thither, O lord of kings, to aid those great souls who had assembled.
At the Naimiṣa forest the best of rivers came as Kāñcanākṣī, and there, O Bhārata, she was worshipped by the sages who performed the session.
When Gaya was offering a great sacrifice at Gayā, the best of rivers, the Sarasvatī, was summoned to the sacrifice of Gaya.
At Gayā the sages of strict vows call her Viśālā—that swift-flowing river, born from the side of Himavat.
And at the sacrifice of Auddālaka, when he was offering it, O Bhārata, with a great circle of sages assembled there from every side,
in the northern region of Kosala, O king, the holy place of that great soul, the Sarasvatī was first called to mind by the sacrificing Auddālaka.
The best of rivers came to that country for the sages' sake, honored by hosts of sages clad in bark and deerskin; and because she was drawn thither by their minds, she became famed as Mānasahradā.
As Suveṇu the illustrious best of rivers, the Sarasvatī, came to the holy isle of Ṛṣabha, frequented by royal sages, and to Kurukṣetra when the great-souled Kuru was sacrificing there.
As Oghavatī too, O lord of kings, the Sarasvatī of divine waters was summoned at Kurukṣetra by the great soul Vasiṣṭha.
And summoned by Dakṣa when he sacrificed at Gaṅgādvāra, the divine Sarasvatī came as Vimalodā; and again, summoned by Brahmā at his sacrifice, she went thither to the holy mountain of Himavat.
Then those seven, gathered together at that ford, became one; and thus that ford became renowned upon the earth as Saptasārasvata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus the seven Sarasvatīs have been proclaimed by name, and thus too the holy ford of Saptasārasvata is remembered.
Hear now of the great sport of Maṅkaṇaka also, who had kept the vow of celibacy from his boyhood, when he had plunged into the river, O king.
Beholding by chance there in the water, O Bhārata, a woman bathing—fair of glance, clad only in the quarters of the sky, and blameless—his seed, O great king, fell into the waters of the Sarasvatī.
That seed the great ascetic gathered into a jar; and there within the jar it split into seven parts, and from it were born seven sages, the hosts of the Maruts.
Vāyuvega and Vāyubala, Vāyuha and Vāyumaṇḍala, Vāyujvāla, Vāyuretas, and the valiant Vāyucakra — thus were these born, the begetters of the hosts of the Maruts.
And hear now, O lord of kings, another wonder more marvellous still upon this earth — such a deed of that great seer as is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Of old, Maṅkaṇaka the perfected one — so we have heard — wounded his hand upon the tip of a kuśa-blade, O king, and from it flowed a sap like vegetable juice; and beholding that sap, he was seized with joy and fell to dancing.
Then as he danced, all that was unmoving and all that moves — both alike, O hero — fell to dancing, bewildered by the force of his power.
Then the gods led by Brahmā, O king, and the seers rich in penance besought Mahādeva on the seer's behalf, O lord of men: 'Bring it to pass, O god, that this one dance no longer.'
Then the god, seeing the sage utterly transported with joy, Mahādeva, desiring the welfare of the gods, addressed him thus:
'Ho there, Brāhmaṇa, knower of dharma, why do you dance on so? What cause for joy is this of yours, O best of sages — for one given to penance and set upon the path of dharma, O best of the twice-born?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The seer said: 'Do you not see, O brahman, the sap that has flowed from my hand? Beholding it I fell to dancing in great joy, O mighty one.'
Laughing, the god said to the sage thus bewildered by passion: 'I, O brahman, am not moved to wonder by such a thing — look upon me.'
Having so spoken to the best of sages, the wise Mahādeva, O lord of kings, struck his own thumb with the tip of his finger.
Then from the cut, O king, came forth ash white as snow; and seeing it, O king, the sage was abashed and fell at his feet.
The seer said: 'I deem none greater, none mightier, than the god Rudra; you, wielder of the trident, are the refuge of the world of gods and demons alike.'
'By you was this universe created, so the wise declare here; and into you alone does all enter again at the ending of the age.'
'Not even by the gods can you be fully known — how then by me? In you are all the gods beheld, beginning with Brahmā, O sinless one.'
'You are all things; you are of the gods the doer and the cause of doing; by your grace all the gods rejoice here, freed from every fear.'
Having thus praised Mahādeva, the seer bowed low and said: 'O Lord, by your grace may my penance never wane.'
Then the god, well pleased in heart, spoke again to that seer: 'May your penance increase a thousandfold by my grace, O brahman; and here in this hermitage I shall ever dwell together with you.'
'And whatever man shall worship me here at this Seven-Sarasvatī, nothing shall be hard for him to win, in this world or the next; and they shall go to the Sārasvata world, of this there is no doubt.'
Such was the deed of Maṅkaṇaka of abundant splendour; for he was a son begotten upon Sajanyā by Mātariśvan, the Wind.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having dwelt there and honoured the dwellers of the hermitage, Rāma the plough-wielder showed too his gracious favour toward Maṅkaṇaka.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having given gifts to the twice-born and passed that night in fasting, honoured by the throngs of sages, the plough-bearer rose at dawn.
Having taken leave of all the sages and touched water, O Bhārata, mighty Rāma set forth in haste for the sake of the sacred fords.
Then the plough-wielder came to the ford of Uśanas, called Kapālamocana, the Skull-Release, where the great sage was set free.
There, O king, Mahodara had had his leg gripped by a great head — the head of a rākṣasa hurled of old by Rāma, O mighty monarch.
There of old the great-souled Kāvya practised penance, and there the whole of his statecraft came forth for that high-souled one; abiding there he pondered the warfare of the Daityas and Dānavas.
And having reached that most excellent of fords, O king, Bala duly bestowed wealth upon the great-souled Brāhmaṇas.
Janamejaya said: How, O brahman, came it to be the Skull-Release, where the great sage was freed? How did the head cleave to him, and for what cause?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Of old, in the Daṇḍaka forest, by the great-souled Rāghava dwelling there, O tiger among kings, were the rākṣasas slain.
At Janasthāna the head of an evil-souled rākṣasa was severed with a keen-edged shaft, and it fell within the great forest.
That head, by chance, fastened upon the shin of Mahodara as he wandered in the forest, O king, piercing the bone and there it stuck fast.
With that thing clinging to him the twice-born one, wise though he was, could no longer make his way to the fords and holy places.
Tormented with pain by the foul stuff that oozed from it, the great sage went, so we have heard, to all the sacred fords upon the earth.
Having gone to all the rivers and to the seas, that great ascetic told all this to the seers of purified souls.
Bathing in all the fords, he yet won no release; but that lord of brahmans heard a weighty word of the sages.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That on the Sarasvatī there was a renowned excellent ford of Uśanas, dispeller of all sins, an unsurpassed field of the perfected ones.
And the twice-born one, going thither to the ford of Uśanas, as he touched the water at the ford of Uśanas, that head let go his foot and fell down into the depths of the water.
Then Mahodara, freed of pain, O king, his soul made pure and his stain gone, came back glad to his hermitage, his purpose fulfilled.
And the great ascetic, set free and come to the holy hermitage, told all this to the seers of purified souls.
Hearing his words, O giver of honour, the assembled sages gave to that ford the name Kapālamocana, the Skull-Release.
There Mādhava, the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, having given many gifts and honoured the brahmans, went then to the hermitage of Ruṣaṅgu.
Where Ārṣṭiṣeṇa had practised dread penance, O Bhārata, and where the great sage Viśvāmitra had won the estate of a brāhmaṇa.
Thence the glorious plough-bearer, surrounded by brahmans, went, O lord of kings, to the place where Ruṣaṅgu had laid down his body.
Ruṣaṅgu, an aged brāhmaṇa ever devoted to penance, O Bhārata, set his mind upon laying down his body, having pondered the matter long and in many ways.
Then the great ascetic Ruṣaṅgu, gathering all his sons, said to them: 'Lead me to Pṛthūdaka.'
Knowing Ruṣaṅgu, rich in penance, to be far advanced in years, those ascetics led him to that ford of the Sarasvatī.
Brought then by his sons, that wise one came to the Sarasvatī, holy, endowed with a hundred fords, frequented by throngs of brahmans.
There, O king, having bathed according to rite, that great ascetic, knowing the virtues of the ford, the best of seers, well pleased, O tiger among men, spoke thus to all his sons who attended upon him:
'Whoever on the northern bank of the Sarasvatī, at Pṛthūdaka, intent upon prayer, lays down his body — him the morrow's death shall not afflict.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There the righteous plough-bearer bathed and touched the water, and gave many gifts, fond as he was of the brahmans.
Where the Lord, the Grandsire of the worlds, brought forth the worlds; where, O Kaurava, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa of firm vows, the best of seers, attained brāhmaṇa-hood through mighty penance, O king.
And where the royal seer Sindhudvīpa, and Devāpi of great penance, and the great sage Viśvāmitra — that mighty ascetic, the lord of fierce splendour and great penance — won brāhmaṇa-hood.
Thither came the mighty and majestic Balabhadra.
Janamejaya said: How did the lord Ārṣṭiṣeṇa practise his vast penance, and how too did Sindhudvīpa then win brāhmaṇa-hood?
And how Devāpi, O brahman, and how Viśvāmitra, O best of men? Tell me this, O lord, for great is my curiosity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Of old, in the Kṛta age, O king, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, best of the twice-born, dwelling ever in his teacher's house, was ever devoted to study.
Yet for him, O king, dwelling ever in his teacher's house, his learning came to no completion, nor did the Vedas, O lord of peoples.
Then, grown weary, O king, that great ascetic practised penance; and by that penance he won the supreme Vedas.
Learned and endowed with the Vedas and perfected, the best of seers, that great ascetic bestowed three boons there at the ford.
'At this ford of the great river, from this day forth, the man who bathes shall win the abundant fruit of the horse-sacrifice.'
'From this day forth there shall be here no fear from beasts of prey, and even with little effort one shall win abundant fruit.'
Having so spoken, the sage of great splendour went to the third heaven; thus did the majestic lord Ārṣṭiṣeṇa attain perfection.
At that very ford then the majestic Sindhudvīpa, and Devāpi, O mighty king, attained the high estate of brāhmaṇa-hood.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And likewise Kauśika, my son, ever devoted to penance, his senses subdued, attained brāhmaṇa-hood through well-practised penance.
There was a great kṣatriya named Gādhi, renowned upon the earth; his son, O king, was the majestic Viśvāmitra.
That king Kauśika, my son, became a great yogin, it is said; and the great ascetic, having consecrated his son Viśvāmitra,
set his mind upon laying down his body; but his subjects, bowing low, said to him: 'You must not go, O wise one; save us from this great peril.'
Thus addressed, Gādhi then answered his subjects: 'My son shall be the protector of the whole world.'
Having so spoken, Gādhi, having established Viśvāmitra in his place, went to the third heaven, O king; and Viśvāmitra became king, yet for all his effort he could not protect the earth.
Then that king heard of a great peril from the rākṣasas, and went forth from the city attended by his fourfold army.
Having gone a long road, he came upon the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha; and his soldiers, O king, wrought there many wrongs.
Then the lordly brahman Vasiṣṭha came to his hermitage and saw the whole great forest being broken to pieces.
Wrathful at this, O mighty king, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, said to his cow: 'Bring forth dread Śabaras.'
Thus bidden, the cow brought forth men of terrible aspect; and they, falling upon that army, scattered it in every direction.
Seeing his army put to flight, Viśvāmitra the son of Gādhi, deeming penance the higher power, set his mind upon penance alone.
At this excellent ford of the Sarasvatī, O king, with mind composed, he wasted his own body with vows and fasts.
He became one who fed on water, who fed on air, who fed on leaves; one who lay upon the bare ground, and observed whatever other separate vows there are.
Again and again the gods set obstacles to his vow, yet the resolve of that great soul would not turn aside from his observance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, having practised manifold penance with the utmost effort, the son of Gādhi grew in splendour like unto the sun.
Viśvāmitra being thus endowed with penance, the Grandsire of mighty splendour, the giver of boons, deemed him worthy of that boon.
And he chose his boon, O king, saying: 'May I become a brāhmaṇa'; and Brahmā, the Grandsire of all the worlds, said, 'So be it.'
Having won brahminhood by fierce austerity, that man of great renown, his desire fulfilled and god-like in his splendour, roamed across the whole earth.
At that excellent sacred ford Rāma bestowed wealth of many kinds — milk-giving cows, draught animals, and couches —
and garments too, and ornaments, and fine food and drink. Gladly, O king, he gave these gifts, having honoured the foremost of the twice-born.
Then, O king, Rāma went on from there to the hermitage of Baka close by, where, as tradition tells, Baka the son of Dalbha had performed fierce austerity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The delight of the Yadus went to that place thronged with men of brahmin lineage, where, O king, Baka the son of Dalbha, of mighty austerity, for the sake of cattle once offered up into the fire the kingdom of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Vicitravīrya.
Wasting his own body with austerity of dreadful aspect, that righteous and mighty sage was seized by a great anger.
For long ago, when the twelve-year sacrificial session of the seers of Naimiṣa had been completed, at the close of the Viśvajit rite the sages went to the Pāñcālas.
There those wise men asked the lord of that land for a sacrificial fee: twenty-one strong young calves, free of disease.
To them aged Baka said: 'Divide these cattle among yourselves; for my part, leaving these beasts aside, I shall beg of the best of kings.'
Having spoken thus to all the seers, O king, that mighty and foremost of brahmins went to the dwelling of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Drawing near to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, the son of Dalbha begged him for cattle; but that king answered him in anger:
'Look on these cows that have died of their own accord, O best of kings' — so the king said — 'take these beasts at once, you wretched excuse for a brahmin, if you wish.'
The seer, knower of dharma, hearing these words, fell to thinking: 'Alas, cruel indeed is the speech with which I have been addressed in the assembly!'
Having pondered a while, that foremost of the twice-born, seized by wrath, set his mind upon the destruction of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
That best of the twice-born, cutting the flesh from the dead cattle, then offered up into the fire the kingdom of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
At a secluded ford of the Sarasvatī, having kindled the sacred fire, Baka the son of Dalbha, O great king, took up a most rigorous vow; and that sage of mighty austerity offered up his kingdom with those very pieces of flesh.
When that most terrible sacrificial session had been duly begun, the kingdom of Dhṛtarāṣṭra began to waste away, O king.
Like a boundless forest hewn down by the axe, O lord, that kingdom became ruined, scattered, and bereft of sense.
Seeing his kingdom so laid waste, that lord of men grew downcast, O king, and the sovereign fell to brooding.
He strove together with his brahmins to win release from it; yet that king remained distressed, O king, and so too were those learned men.
And when he could not free his kingdom, O king, he then questioned the readers of omens there, O Janamejaya.
Then the readers of omens declared: 'The sage Baka, slighted by you in the matter of cattle, is offering up your kingdom with flesh as oblation.'
'By his oblation this great ruin has come upon your kingdom; this is the working of his austerity, by which this great calamity has fallen upon you. In a watery thicket of the Sarasvatī, O king, win his favour.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the king went to the Sarasvatī and, prostrating with his head to the ground, his palms joined, said to Baka, O bull of the Bhāratas:
'I beseech your favour, O holy one; forgive my offence — wretched, greedy, and bereft of sense through my own folly that I am. You are my refuge, you are my protector; deign to show me grace.'
Seeing him lamenting thus, his mind overwhelmed with grief, the sage was moved to pity, and he set that kingdom free.
The seer became gracious toward him and, laying aside his fury, offered up another oblation for the release of that kingdom.
Having freed the kingdom and received many head of cattle, with a glad heart he went back once more to the Naimiṣa forest.
And the righteous, high-minded king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, now easy in mind, returned to his own most prosperous city.
At that ford, O great king, Bṛhaspati of noble intellect — for the undoing of the Asuras and the flourishing of the dwellers in heaven —
performed a sacrifice with offerings of flesh as well; and thereupon the Asuras began to waste away, shattered too in battle by the gods, who shone with the look of victors.
There too that man of great renown duly gave to the brahmins horses and elephants and chariots yoked with mules,
and gems of great worth, and wealth and abundant grain; then that mighty-armed one went to the ford of Yayāti, O lord of the earth.
There, O great king, at the sacrifice of Yayāti, the great-souled son of Nahuṣa, the Sarasvatī flowed forth with ghee and milk.
Having there performed sacrifice, Yayāti, tiger among men and lord of the earth, ascended on high rejoicing, and won abundant worlds.
Where, O king, for Yayāti as he sacrificed, the Sarasvatī streamed forth and granted the desires of the great-souled brahmins —
for wherever any brahmin wished for whatever he desired, there and there that best of rivers poured forth manifold flavours.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There the gods along with the Gandharvas were delighted at the splendour of the sacrifice, and the mortals too were amazed to behold that perfection of the rite.
Then he of the palm-tree banner, a great bulwark of dharma, high-souled and perfected in spirit, ever devoted to lavish giving, steadfast and self-mastered, came to the place of Vasiṣṭha's carrying-off, where the river had run with mighty and terrible force.
Janamejaya said: How came that carrying-off of Vasiṣṭha, of fearful swiftness, to be? And why did that best of rivers bear the seer away?
And with whom did he have this enmity, and what was its cause, O lord? Being asked, O most wise one, tell it; for I am not sated — let it be told.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Between the seer Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha, O Bhārata, there arose a fierce and mighty enmity, O king, born of their rivalry in austerity.
The great hermitage of Vasiṣṭha stood at the ford of Sthāṇu on the eastern side, while that of the wise Viśvāmitra lay to the west.
There, O great king, Sthāṇu performed exceedingly great austerity, and there, as the wise relate, he wrought that dreadful deed.
Where the lord Sthāṇu, having sacrificed and worshipped the Sarasvatī, established that ford, which is therefore called Sthāṇutīrtha, O lord.
There, O ruler of men, all the gods consecrated Skanda, slayer of the foes of the gods, with the great office of commander of their host.
At that ford of the Sarasvatī, the great sage Viśvāmitra unsettled Vasiṣṭha by fierce austerity — hear how it was.
Day after day, O Bhārata, those two — Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha, both rich in austerity — carried on their fierce contest born of penance.
There the great sage Viśvāmitra, burning all the more, seeing the splendour of Vasiṣṭha, fell into deep thought; and this was the resolve that came to that ever-righteous one, O Bhārata:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'This Sarasvatī shall swiftly bring near to me, by the force of her current, Vasiṣṭha rich in austerity, that best of those who chant the sacred words; and when that foremost of the twice-born is brought hither, I shall slay him — of this there is no doubt.'
Having so resolved, the lord Viśvāmitra, that great sage, his eyes red with anger, called to mind the best of rivers.
Summoned by the sage's thought, she fell into agitation, for the fair one knew him to be of great might and great wrath.
Then, trembling and pale, her palms joined, the Sarasvatī came and stood before that best of sages, Viśvāmitra.
Like a woman whose husband has been slain, she was sorely grieved, and she said to that best of sages: 'Tell me — what shall I do?'
The angry sage said to her: 'Bring Vasiṣṭha quickly, that I may slay him this very day.' Hearing this, the river was stricken with dread.
Then she, whose eyes were like lotus-petals, joining her palms, trembled like a well-grown creeper shaken by the wind.
Seeing her come thus, trembling, with palms joined, Viśvāmitra in anger said: 'Bring Vasiṣṭha quickly!'
Then that best of rivers, afraid, fell to thinking, O Bhārata, dreading the curse of both: 'How shall this come about?'
And going to Vasiṣṭha, she set forth this matter — all that the best of rivers had been told by the wise Viśvāmitra —
trembling again and again in fear of the curse of both, brooding upon the dread curse, sorely terrified by the seers.
Seeing her wasted and pale and filled with anxiety, the righteous Vasiṣṭha, best of men, O king, said to her:
'Save yourself, O best of rivers; swift-flowing one, carry me away — for else Viśvāmitra will curse you. Do not hesitate.'
Hearing that word of the compassionate sage, the river pondered, O Kaurava: 'What course, if taken, would be well done?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This thought arose in her: 'Vasiṣṭha has ever shown me great kindness; surely his good must be wrought by me.'
Then, O king, beholding upon her own bank the son of Kuśika, that best of seers, as he chanted and offered oblation, the Sarasvatī reflected:
'This is the moment.' And so that best of rivers tore away her own bank with the force of her current.
By that carrying-away of the bank the son of Mitra and Varuṇa was borne off; and as he was borne along, O king, he then praised the Sarasvatī:
'From the lake of the Grandsire have you sprung forth, O Sarasvatī, and all this world is pervaded by your most excellent waters.'
'You, O goddess, moving through the sky, release your waters in the clouds; you alone are all the waters, and from you do we draw our sustenance.'
'You are nourishment, radiance, and renown, attainment, increase, and Umā; you alone are Speech, you are Svāhā; upon you this world depends, and you dwell here in all beings in your fourfold form.'
Thus praised by the great seer, O king, the Sarasvatī bore that brahmin swiftly toward the hermitage of Viśvāmitra, and again and again she presented the sage to Viśvāmitra.
Seeing him brought by the Sarasvatī, filled with rage, Viśvāmitra then sought out a weapon to make an end of Vasiṣṭha.
But seeing him enraged, the river, from fear of the slaying of a brahmin, carried Vasiṣṭha off untiringly toward the eastern quarter — thus obeying the word of both, yet outwitting the son of Gādhi.
Then, seeing Vasiṣṭha, that best of seers, borne away, the wrathful and unforgiving Viśvāmitra said:
'Since you, O best of rivers, having deceived me, have slipped away again — flow with blood, fair one, the kind that demon-chiefs delight in!'
Then the Sarasvatī, cursed by the wise Viśvāmitra, carried water mingled with blood for a whole year thereafter.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the seers and the gods, the Gandharvas and the Apsarases, seeing the Sarasvatī in such a state, were sorely grieved.
Thus came the carrying-off of Vasiṣṭha to be famed in the world, O ruler of men; and that best of rivers came again to her own course.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: She, cursed by the wrathful and wise Viśvāmitra, carried blood at that bright and excellent ford.
Then, O king, the Rākṣasas came thither, O Bhārata, and there they all dwelt at ease, drinking the blood.
Sated to the full by that blood, contented and freed of fever, they danced and laughed like those who had conquered heaven.
After some time, O lord of earth, the sages rich in austerity came together on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords along the Sarasvatī.
Bathing at all those fords, those bulls among sages—learned men eager for further penance—won the highest joy; and then, O king, they proceeded onward to that very ford.
Then, O best of kings, when those greatly blessed ones reached that dreadful ford, they beheld the water of the Sarasvatī flooded with blood and being drunk by a host of rākṣasas.
Seeing those rākṣasas, O king, the sages of firm vows made the utmost effort to rescue the Sarasvatī.
Those greatly blessed ones, men of mighty vows, all gathered together, and summoning the best of rivers, they spoke these words.
"Tell us the cause, O blessed one: why has this pool of yours fallen into such a troubled state? When we have heard it, we shall set it right."
Then, trembling, she told them all that had come to pass; and beholding her in her grief, those sages rich in penance spoke.
"We have heard the cause, O sinless one, and we have heard of the curse as well; now all these sages rich in penance shall do what is needful."
Having spoken thus to the best of rivers, they said one to another, "Let us all release this Sarasvatī from the curse."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At their word alone the Sarasvatī was restored to her natural state, her waters grown clear as before; and freed, that best of rivers shone forth as she had of old.
Beholding the water of the Sarasvatī thus made pure by those sages, the rākṣasas, tormented by hunger, O king, with hands joined in reverence, spoke again and again to all those merciful sages.
"We are famished, and fallen away from the eternal law; yet this is no doing of our own desire, that we have become workers of evil."
"It is through your displeasure and through evil deeds that our number swells; for from such causes do we become brahma-rākṣasas."
"For thus it is: among vaiśyas and śūdras, and among kṣatriyas likewise, those who hate the brāhmaṇas become rākṣasas here."
"Those creatures who slight the teacher, the officiating priest, the elder, and the aged become rākṣasas here; and the breed grows too through the taint in the wombs of sinful women."
"Therefore show us your compassion here, O best of the twice-born; you have the power to deliver even all the worlds."
Hearing their plea, those sages praised that great river; and for the deliverance of those rākṣasas they spoke, their minds intent.
"Food into which an insect has fallen, or that is left as another's leavings, into which a hair has dropped, or that is shaken about, or sickened, or touched by dogs—that is the portion of the rākṣasas here."
"Therefore the wise man, knowing this, should ever shun such food; for whoever eats food of that kind eats the food of rākṣasas."
Then, having purified that ford, those sages rich in penance urged the river onward for the deliverance of the rākṣasas.
Knowing the will of the great sages, that best of rivers, O bull among men, brought forth her own stream as the Aruṇā.
Bathing in her, those rākṣasas cast off their bodies and went to heaven; for the Aruṇā, O great king, washes away the slaying of a brāhmaṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Knowing this virtue of it, the king of the gods, Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices, bathed at that excellent ford and was freed, indeed, from his sin.
Janamejaya said: For what cause did the blessed Śakra incur the guilt of slaying a brāhmaṇa, and how, by bathing at this ford, did he become free of stain?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hear this tale as it came to pass, O lord of men—how of old Vāsava broke his compact with Namuci.
Namuci, in dread of Vāsava, entered into a ray of the sun; with him Indra made friendship, and spoke this compact.
"Not with anything wet nor dry, not by night nor yet by day shall I slay you, O best of asuras; I swear it to you, my friend, in truth."
Having made this compact, the Lord conjured up a mist, and with the foam of the waters, O king, Vāsava severed his head.
That severed head of Namuci followed close behind Śakra, crying out hard upon him, "O slayer of a friend! O sinner!"
Thus driven on again and again by that head, sorely tormented, he laid the matter before the Grandsire.
The Teacher of the worlds said to him: "At the Aruṇā, O lord of gods, offer sacrifice according to rule and touch its waters; for it washes away the slaying of a brāhmaṇa."
Thus addressed, O Janamejaya, the Slayer of Bala, in a bower of the Sarasvatī, sacrificed as ordained and touched the waters of the Aruṇā.
Freed of that sin wrought by the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, the lord of the thirty gods went to heaven with gladdened heart.
And that head of Namuci too, bathing there, O Bhārata, attained the worlds that grant every wish and never wane, O best of kings.
There too the great-souled Bala touched the waters, and bestowing gifts of many kinds, that doer of noble deeds won the highest merit; then he went on to the great ford of Soma.
There, O lord of kings, Soma himself had of old performed the Rājasūya sacrifice duly; and at that foremost of rites the wise Atri, chief of brāhmaṇas, that great soul, served as the invoking priest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At whose close there arose a tremendous battle—the gods against the dānavas, the daityas, and the rākṣasas—the fierce war called Tāraka's, wherein Skanda slew the asura named Tāraka.
There Mahāsena, slayer of the daityas, won the command of the armies of the gods; and there in person dwelt Kārttikeya—where the youth Kumāra abides forever, that lord of the Plakṣa king.
Janamejaya said: This glory of the Sarasvatī you have told, O best of the twice-born; but now, O brāhmaṇa, you ought to relate the consecration of Kumāra.
At what time and in what place, and in what manner, O best of speakers, and by whom and by what rite the blessed lord was consecrated—
and how Skanda wrought the great slaughter of the daityas—tell me all of it, for my curiosity is very great.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: This curiosity of yours is worthy of the line of Kuru; this word of yours gives me joy, O Janamejaya.
Come then, I shall tell you, as you listen, O ruler of men, the consecration of Kumāra and the glory of that great soul.
Of old, the seed of Maheśvara, spilled and fallen into the fire—that imperishable splendour the blessed All-devourer could not consume.
By it the bearer of oblations grew exceedingly bright and blazing; yet he could not hold that embryo made of splendour.
Then the lord, at the command of Brahmā, drew near to Gaṅgā and placed in her the divine embryo, splendid as the sun.
But Gaṅgā too, unable to bear the burden of that embryo, cast it off upon the lovely mountain Himavat, honoured by the immortals.
There the son of the Fire grew, filling the worlds; and then the Kṛttikās beheld that embryo in the likeness of flame.
That great soul, the son of Fire, the lord, lying in a thicket of reeds—they all approached him, each longing for a son, crying, "He is mine!"
Knowing that longing of those mothers, the blessed lord then drank with six mouths the milk that flowed from them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beholding that power of the child, the Kṛttikās, goddesses bearing forms divine, fell into the utmost amazement.
There, on the mountain's crest, where the blessed one was cast off by Gaṅgā, that whole peak turned to gold and shone, O best of the Kurus.
By that growing embryo the earth itself was made radiant, and thus all the mountains became mines of gold.
And Kumāra of mighty valour came to be known as Kārttikeya; first he was Gāṅgeya, the son of Gaṅgā, endowed with the great power of yoga.
That god, possessed of penance and of valour, grew exceedingly, O lord of kings, fair to look upon as the moon.
There in that golden, divine thicket of reeds, wrapped in splendour, he lay while gandharvas and sages sang his praises.
And so before him danced the daughters of the gods by the thousand—skilled in heavenly music and dance, lovely to behold, hymning his praise.
The river Gaṅgā, best of streams, waited upon the god, and the earth, taking on her fairest form, bore him up.
Bṛhaspati performed for him the birth-rite and the rest of the ceremonies; and the Veda in fourfold form attended him with hands joined in reverence.
The science of archery in its four divisions, the whole array of weapons with their lore, and Speech herself, all alone, in person stood there to serve him.
He beheld the god of mighty valour, the god of gods, the lord of Umā, seated together with the Daughter of the Mountain and surrounded by hundreds of throngs of spirits.
The hosts of those spirit-throngs were most wondrous to look upon—misshapen, of distorted form, with distorted ornaments and banners.
Some had the faces of tigers, lions, and bears; some the visages of cats and crocodiles; others bore the muzzles of bulls and rats, and yet others the faces of elephants and camels.
Some had the faces of owls, some the look of vultures and jackals, and some with faces like the krauñca and the dove, or like the antelope.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Others, here and there, bore bodies resembling those of porcupines, hedgehogs, and monitor lizards, of asses, rams, and cattle.
Some were like mountains or rain-clouds, armed with discus, firebrand, and mace; some shone like heaps of collyrium, and some gleamed like a white mountain.
The bands of the Seven Mothers too came together, O lord of peoples, and the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Vasus, and the fathers as well.
The Rudras and Ādityas, the siddhas, serpents, dānavas, and birds; and the blessed self-born Brahmā with his sons, together with Viṣṇu.
Śakra too came to look upon that noblest and imperishable Kumāra, as did the best of the divine gandharvas, led by Nārada.
The divine sages and the siddhas, led by Bṛhaspati, and the boon-giving ones called Ṛbhus, gods even of the gods—they too gathered there, the Yāmas and the Dhāmas, all of them.
And the blessed one, though but a child, endowed with the great power of yoga, drew near to the lord of gods, the trident-bearer, the wielder of the Pināka.
As they marked him drawing near, a thought arose at one and the same moment in the minds of Śiva, of the Daughter of the Mountain, of Gaṅgā, and of the Fire.
"To which of us first will this child come out of reverence—will it be to me?"—such was the thought in the mind of each of them.
Perceiving this intent of those four, he at once resorted to yoga and put forth bodies of various kinds.
Then in an instant the blessed lord became fourfold in form: Skanda, Śākha, and Viśākha, and Naigameṣa behind them.
Thus having made himself fourfold, the blessed lord—as Skanda, wondrous to behold—went to where Rudra was.
Viśākha went to where the goddess, daughter of the best of mountains, was; and the blessed Śākha, in the form of the Wind, went to the Fire; while Naigameṣa, the youth bright as flame, went to Gaṅgā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All four of them, with shining bodies and alike in form, drew near them unhurried; and this was as a wonder to behold.
A great cry of wonder arose from the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas as they beheld that mighty marvel, wondrous and hair-raising.
Then Rudra, and the Goddess, and Pāvaka, together with Gaṅgā—all of them bowed down before the Grandsire, the Lord of the world.
Having made their obeisance in due form, O bull among kings, they then spoke these words, O king, in their wish to secure a boon for Kārttikeya:
"For this boy, O Lord, for our gratification, O Lord of the gods, it is fitting that you grant a sovereignty befitting him, such as he may desire."
Then that wise and blessed Grandsire of all the worlds pondered in his mind: "What should be bestowed upon him?"
For all the lordships of the gods, the gandharvas and the rākṣasas, of the spirits, the yakṣas, and the birds, and of the serpents in their entirety,
he had already ordained among the hosts of the great-souled ones; yet that one of vast wisdom deemed the boy fit for sovereignty.
Then, having reflected for a moment, intent upon the welfare of the gods, he bestowed upon him the office of commander over all beings, O Bhārata.
All those who were renowned as kings among the several hosts of the gods—the Grandsire of all beings appointed them, every one, to his command.
Then the gods, led by Brahmā, taking the prince with them, came together to the king of mountains for the consecration.
They came to the holy goddess sprung from Himavat, Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, who at Samantapañcaka is renowned throughout the three worlds.
There upon the holy bank of the Sarasvatī, endowed with every excellence, the gods and gandharvas all took their seats, their hearts filled with contentment.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having gathered together all the materials of the consecration according to scripture, Bṛhaspati poured clarified butter into the kindled fire as the rite ordained.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, seated upon a divine throne supreme, given by Himavat, gleaming with the choicest gems and studded with celestial jewels,
the hosts of the gods, taking up the materials of the consecration with all auspicious appurtenances, attended by the proper rites and sacred formulas,
Indra and Viṣṇu of mighty valour, the Sun and the Moon, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ likewise, and Anila and Anala,
with Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Aryaman, with Aṃśa and Vivasvat, and the wise Rudra together with Mitra and Varuṇa—
the Lord surrounded by the Rudras, the Vasus, the Ādityas, and the two Aśvins, by the Viśvedevas and the Maruts, and by the Sādhyas together with the Fathers,
by gandharvas and apsarases, by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and serpents, by countless divine sages and by the foremost brahmin sages,
by the Vaikhānasas and the Vālakhilyas, by those who feed on air and those who drink the rays of the sun, by the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases and the great-souled ascetics, and surrounded by all the holy vidyādharas perfected in yoga,
the Grandsire, and Pulastya, and Pulaha of great austerity, Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, and Atri, Marīci and Bhṛgu,
Kratu, Hara, and Pracetas, Manu and Dakṣa likewise, and the seasons, the planets, and the heavenly luminaries, O lord of peoples,
the rivers in embodied form, and the eternal Vedas, the seas and the lakes and the various sacred fords, the Earth, the Sky, and the quarters, and the trees, O ruler of men,
Aditi the mother of the gods, and Hrī, Śrī, Svāhā, and Sarasvatī, Umā, Śacī, Sinīvālī, and Anumati, Kuhū, and Rākā, and Dhiṣaṇā, and the other wives of the dwellers of heaven,
Himavat, and Vindhya, and Meru of many peaks, Airāvata with his followers, the moments and the divisions of time, the months and half-months, the seasons, and Night and Day, O king,
Uccaiḥśravas, the best of horses, and Vāmana, the king of elephants, Aruṇa and Garuḍa, and the trees together with the healing herbs,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and the divine Lord Dharma—all these assembled and came together, and Time, and Yama, and Death, and those who are Yama's followers.
And the manifold hosts of deities not named here on account of their multitude came together from this place and that for the prince's consecration.
Then, O king, all those dwellers of heaven took up the vessels of consecration and every auspicious object.
With golden jars filled with divine appurtenances, O king, and with the holy waters of the Sarasvatī, waters indeed celestial,
the dwellers of heaven, greatly rejoicing, consecrated the prince, the great-souled commander, the terror of the asuras.
As of old, O great king, Varuṇa the lord of waters was consecrated, even so did the blessed Brahmā, the Grandsire of the world, consecrate him, and Kaśyapa of great splendour, and the others not here recounted.
To him Brahmā, well pleased, the Lord gave mighty attendants swift as the wind, perfected beings who bore valour at will, great companions of his retinue:
Nandiṣeṇa, Lohitākṣa, and the esteemed Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and as his fourth follower, the renowned Kumudamālin.
Then, O lord of kings, Sthāṇu gave to Skanda the great companion Kratu of mighty force, and Kāma, wielder of a hundred illusions, endowed with strength and valour at will, the destroyer of the foes of the gods.
For he, in the war of the gods and the asuras, in his wrath slew with his two arms fourteen million of the daityas of dreadful deeds.
Likewise the gods gave him an army teeming with rākṣasas, that wrought the destruction of the gods' enemies, unconquerable and of every shape.
Then all the gods together with Vāsava raised the cry of victory, and the gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, the sages, and the Fathers as well.
Yama gave two followers, both like Yama and Time themselves, Unmātha and Pramātha, of mighty valour and great splendour.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Subhrāja and Bhāskara, the two who attend upon the Sun—those the glorious Sūrya, well pleased, gave to Kārttikeya.
Resembling the peak of Kailāsa, garlanded and anointed with white, Soma too gave two followers, Maṇi and Sumaṇi.
Jvālājihva and Jyoti—these the Fire-god gave to his own son as followers, two heroes who crushed the armies of the foe.
Parigha and Vaṭa, and the mighty Bhīma, and Dahati and Dahana, fierce and esteemed for valour—these five followers Aṃśa too gave to the wise Skanda.
Utkrośa and Paṅkaja, both bearing the thunderbolt and the rod, Vāsava the slayer of enemy heroes gave to the son of Agni; for these two had slain in battle many of great Indra's foes.
Cakra and Vikramaka, and the mighty Saṃkrama—these three followers Viṣṇu of great renown gave to Skanda.
Vardhana and Nandana, both skilled in all the sciences, the two Aśvins, well pleased, gave to Skanda, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Kundana and Kusuma and Kumuda, and Ḍambara and Āḍambara—these the illustrious Dhātṛ gave to the great-souled one.
Vakra and Anuvakra, two mighty ones with ram-faces, swollen with strength and full of great illusion—Tvaṣṭṛ gave these excellent followers to Skanda.
Suvrata and Satyasaṃdha, two great-souled bearers of austerity and sacred knowledge—the Lord Mitra gave to the great-souled prince.
Fair to look upon, granters of boons, renowned throughout the three worlds—the great-souled Suprabhā and Śubhakarman, famed in the worlds, Vidhātṛ bestowed upon Kārttikeya.
Pālitaka and Kālika, both masters of great illusion—these two attendants Pūṣan gave to Kārttikeya, O Bhārata.
Bala and Atibala, both great of mouth and great of strength, Vāyu gave to Kārttikeya, O best of the Bhāratas.
Ghasa and Atighasa, two of mighty strength with the faces of sea-monsters, Varuṇa, true to his pledge, gave to Kārttikeya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The great-souled Suvarcas, and likewise Ativarcas, Himavat gave, O king, to the son of the Fire-god.
The great-souled Kāñcana and Meghamālin—these two followers Meru gave to the son of Agni, O Bhārata.
Sthira and Atisthira—two more Meru gave likewise to the great-souled son of Agni, both of great strength and prowess.
Ucchrita and Atiśṛṅga, two warriors who fought with great boulders, Vindhya gave to the son of Agni as his attendants.
Saṃgraha and Vigraha, both bearers of the mace, the Ocean too gave to the son of Agni, two great companions of his retinue.
Unmāda, Puṣpadanta, and Śaṅkukarṇa likewise—these Pārvatī, fair of aspect, gave to the son of Agni.
Jaya and Mahājaya, two serpents, O tiger among men, Vāsuki the lord of serpents gave to the son of Fire.
Thus the Sādhyas and the Rudras, the Vasus and the Fathers, the seas and the rivers, and the mighty mountains,
gave him captains over the hosts of his army, bearers of the lance and the spear, furnished with divine weapons and adorned in manifold guise.
Hear now the names of the others, those who were Skanda's soldiers, furnished with manifold weapons and bright ornaments and armour:
Śaṅkukarṇa and Nikumbha, Padma and Kumuda, Ananta of twelve arms, and Kṛṣṇa and Upakṛṣṇaka,
Droṇaśravas, Kapiskandha, Kāñcanākṣa, Jalaṃdhama, Akṣasaṃtarjana, O king, Kunadīka, and Tamobhrakṛt,
Ekākṣa and Dvādaśākṣa, and Ekajaṭa the lordly, Sahasrabāhu, Vikaṭa, Vyāghrākṣa, and Kṣitikampana,
Puṇyanāman and Sunāman, Suvaktra and Priyadarśana, Pariśruta, Kokanada, and Priyamālyānulepana,
Ajodara, Gajaśiras, Skandhākṣa, Śatalocana, Jvālājihva, Karāla, Sitakeśa, Jaṭin, and Hari,
Caturdaṃṣṭra and Aṣṭajihva, Meghanāda, Pṛthuśravas, Vidyudakṣa, Dhanurvaktra, Jaṭhara, and Mārutāśana,
Udarākṣa and Jhaṣākṣa, Vajranābha, Vasuprabha, Samudravega, O lord of kings, and Śailakampin likewise,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Putrameṣa and Pravāha, and Nanda and Upanandaka, Dhūmra, Śveta, and Kaliṅga, Siddhārtha, and Varada,
Priyaka and Nanda, and the valorous Gonanda, Ānanda and Pramoda, Svastika, and Dhruvaka likewise,
Kṣemavāpa and Sujāta, and Siddhayātra, O Bhārata, Govraja, Kanakāpīḍa, the great lord of the retinue,
Gāyana and Hasana, Bāṇa and the valiant Khaḍga, Vaitālin and Atitālin, and Katika and Vātika,
Haṃsaja, Paṅkadigdhāṅga, and Samudronmādana, Raṇotkaṭa and Prahāsa, Śvetaśīrṣa, and Nandaka,
Kālakaṇṭha and Prabhāsa, and the other Kumbhāṇḍaka, Kālakākṣa and Sītā, and Bhūtalonmathana likewise,
Yajñavāha and Pravāha, Devayājin and Somapa, the mighty Sajāla, and Krātha and Krātha, O Bhārata,
Tuhana and Tuhāna, and the valiant Citradeva, Madhura and Suprasāda, and the mighty Kirīṭin,
Vasana and Madhuvarṇa, and Kalaśodara, Dhamanta, Manmathakara, and the valiant Sūcīvaktra,
Śvetavaktra and Suvaktra, and Cāruvaktra, Pāṇḍura, Daṇḍabāhu and Subāhu, Rajas, and Kokilaka likewise,
Acala and Kanakākṣa, and the lordly protector of children, Saṃcāraka, Kokanada, Gṛdhravaktra, and Jambuka.
Iron-horse-faced Jaṭhara, and Kuṇḍaka with a face like a pot, and Madgugrīva the diver-necked, and Kṛṣṇaujas of dark might, and goose-faced Candrabhās of moonlike sheen.
And Śambūka with hands like a tortoise, and Śikṣaka the five-faced, and Jambūka with the face of a blue jay, and Kuṇḍaka of the herb-leaf countenance.
Yoked in yoga, great of soul, ever dear to the brāhmaṇas, descended from the Grandsire, lofty-spirited, mighty attendants — youths in their prime, and children, and the aged too, O Janamejaya.
By the thousand the attendants drew near to wait upon the Prince; and those who bore faces of every kind — hear of them now, O Janamejaya.
With faces of tortoise and cock, and others with the muzzles of hare and owl, and some with the faces of ass and camel, and others with the snouts of boars.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With the faces of men and rams, and others with the muzzles of jackals, and terrible ones with the maws of sea-monsters, and faces like the river-dolphin's.
With the faces of cat and hare, and long-faced ones, O Bhārata, with the faces of mongoose and owl, and yet others dog-faced.
With the faces of mouse and ichneumon, and the countenances of peacocks, and others fish-faced and ram-faced, and some bearing the faces of goat, sheep, and buffalo.
With the faces of bear and tiger, and the countenances of leopard and lion, and terrible ones with the faces of elephants, and others with the maws of crocodiles.
With the faces of the eagle and the rhinoceros, and the faces of wolf and crow, and others with the faces of ox, ass, and camel, and some with the muzzles of the wildcat.
With huge bellies, feet, and limbs, and eyes like stars, O Bhārata, and others with the faces of doves, and yet others with the faces of bulls.
And others with the faces of cuckoos, and countenances of hawk and partridge, and some with the faces of chameleons, clad in spotless garments.
Serpent-faced, with faces like spear-points, fierce-faced, hundred-faced, venomous as fanged snakes, clad in bark, and shrouded like the bull-nosed cobra.
With swollen bellies yet slender limbs, and bulky limbs yet lean bellies, short-necked, large-eared, adorned with serpents of every kind.
Robed in the hides of lordly elephants, and clad in black antelope-skins, some with faces set in their shoulders, O great king, and some with faces set in their bellies.
Some with faces in their backs, some with faces upon their jaws, and some with faces upon their shanks, and many with faces in their flanks, with faces set in every region of the body.
And there were troop-lords with mouths like those of worms and winged insects, and others with the faces of sundry beasts of prey, bearing many arms and heads.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some with arms like the branches of various trees, others with heads set at their hips, with faces like the coils of serpents, dwelling among the many thickets.
With bodies wrapped in bark, and clothed in plates of wood, wearing garb of every fashion, and some clad only in hides.
Wearing turbans and diadems, with necks ringed like the conch, of radiant splendor, crowned, some with five locks of hair, and others with stiff, bristling hair.
With three locks, with two locks, and others with seven locks, some with crests, some crowned, some shaven bald, and others with matted hair.
Some bearing wreaths of many hues, and some with hairy faces, wearing divine garlands and raiment, ever pleasing in their forms.
Dark of hue, with fleshless faces, long-backed and belly-less, some thick-backed, some short-backed, with dangling bellies and pendulous parts.
Great-armed and short-armed, with stunted bodies, dwarfish, hunchbacked, with long shanks, and bearing the ears and heads of elephants.
With the noses of elephants, of tortoises, and others with the noses of wolves, with long lips and long tongues, ghastly, and downward-faced.
With great tusks and small tusks, and others with four tusks, some like lordly elephants, terrible, O king, by the thousand.
With shapely, well-proportioned bodies, blazing, finely adorned, tawny-eyed, with pointed ears and crooked noses, O Bhārata.
With broad fangs and great tusks, thick-lipped, with tawny lion-hair, having feet, lips, and tusks of every kind, and hands and heads of every kind, sheathed in armor of every sort, and speaking tongues of every kind, O Bhārata.
Skilled in the speech of every land, these lordly ones chattered to one another; and so the mighty attendants leapt about in their delight.
Long-necked, long-nailed, with long feet, heads, and arms, tawny-eyed and blue-throated, and with drooping ears, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some with bellies like wolves', some dark as collyrium, with white bodies and crimson necks, others tawny-eyed, and many of mottled and motley hue, O king, of dappled colors, O Bhārata.
Resembling clusters of yak-tail plumes, streaked with white and crimson, of varied hues and of single hue, with a luster like the peacock's.
Hear now once more as I tell of their weapons; for the remaining attendants had taken up arms as their own.
Some with hands raised aloft bearing nooses, with gaping maws and ass-faces, broad-eyed and blue-throated, and with arms like iron clubs.
Bearing in their hands the śataghnī and the discus, and grasping pestles, holding spears and swords, of huge frame and mighty strength.
Bearing maces and the bhuśuṇḍi in their hands, and grasping lances, holding swords and mallets, and wielding staves, O Bhārata.
With dread weapons of every kind, lofty of spirit, swift of pace, mighty in strength and impetus — such were these great attendants.
Beholding the consecration of the Prince, those lovers of battle rejoiced, and with their limbs bound about with nets of bells, those puissant ones fell to dancing.
These and many other mighty attendants, O king, drew near to wait upon the great-souled and glorious Kārttikeya.
Heavenly and aerial and earthly, swift as the wind, those heroes, appointed by the gods, became the followers of Skanda.
Of such as these, by the thousands, the millions, and the hundred-millions, they surrounded the consecrated great-souled one and stood in attendance upon him.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hear now, O king, of these troops of mothers, the followers of the Prince, whom I shall celebrate, O hero — destroyers of the hosts of his foes.
Hear the names of the glorious mothers, O Bhārata, by whom — auspicious ones — the three worlds, with all that moves and is unmoving, are pervaded.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Prabhāvatī, Viśālākṣī, Palitā, and Gonasī, Śrīmatī, and Bahulā, and likewise Bahuputrikā.
And Apsujātā and Gopālī, and Bṛhadambālikā, Jayāvatī, Mālatikā, Dhruvaratnā, Bhayaṃkarī.
Vasudāmā and Sudāmā, Viśokā, and Nandinī, Ekacūḍā, Mahācūḍā, and Cakranemi, O Bhārata.
Uttejanī, Jayatsenā, then Kamalākṣī and Śobhanā, and Śatruṃjaya likewise, Krodhanā, Śalabhī, Kharī.
Mādhavī and Śubhavaktrā, and Tīrthanemi, O Bhārata, Gītapriyā and Kalyāṇī, Kadrulā, and Amitāśanā.
Meghasvanā, Bhogavatī, and Subhrū, and Kanakāvatī, Alātākṣī, Vīryavatī, and Vidyujjihvā, O Bhārata.
Padmāvatī, Sunakṣatrā, Kaṇḍarā, Bahuyojanā, and Saṃtānikā, O Kaurava, and Kamalā the mighty.
Sudāmā and Bahudāmā, and Suprabhā the glorious, and Nṛtyapriyā, O lord of kings, and Śatolūkhalamekhalā, girt with a hundred mortars.
Śataghaṇṭā, Śatānandā, and Bhaganandā the comely, Vapuṣmatī, Candraśītā, and Bhadrakālī, O Bhārata.
Saṃkārikā, Niṣkuṭikā, Brahmā, Catvaravāsinī, Sumaṅgalā, Svastimatī, Vṛddhikāmā, Jayapriyā.
Dhanadā and Suprasādā, and Bhavadā, and Jaleśvarī, Eḍī, Bheḍī, and Sameḍī, and Vetālajananī, mother of the ghoul, and Kaṇḍūti, and Kālikā, and Devamitrā, O Bhārata.
Lambasī and Ketakī, and Citrasenā, and Balā, Kukkuṭikā, Śaṅkhanikā, and Jarjarikā, O king.
Kuṇḍārikā, Kokalikā, and Kaṇḍarā, and Śatodarī, Utkrāthinī, and Jareṇā, and Mahāvegā, and Kaṅkaṇā.
Manojavā, Kaṇṭakinī, Praghasā, and Pūtanā, Khaśayā, Curvyuṭi, Vāmā, Krośanā, and Taḍitprabhā, bright as the lightning.
Mandodarī and Tuṇḍā, and Koṭarā, Meghavāsinī, Subhagā, Lambinī, Lambā, Vasucūḍā, Vikatthanī.
And Ūrdhvaveṇīdharā, who wears her braid upturned, tawny-eyed Lohamekhalā girt with iron, broad-faced Pṛthuvaktrā, Madhurikā, and Madhukumbhā likewise.
Pakṣālikā, Manthanikā, Jarāyu, Jarjarānanā, and she renowned as Dahadahā, and likewise Dhamadhamā, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Khaṇḍakhaṇḍā, O lord of kings, Pūṣaṇā, Maṇikuṇḍalā, and Amocā, O Kaurava, and Lambapayodharā with pendulous breasts.
And Veṇuvīṇādharā, bearing flute and lute, tawny-eyed Lohamekhalā girt with iron, hare-and-owl-faced, dark of hue, with ass's shanks, and very swift.
Śiśumāramukhī with the face of a river-dolphin, Śvetā the white, Lohitākṣī the red-eyed, Vibhīṣaṇā the terrible, Jaṭālikā, Kāmacarī who roves at will, Dīrghajihvā the long-tongued, and Balotkaṭā of surpassing strength.
Kāleḍikā, Vāmanikā, and Mukuṭā, O Bhārata, Lohitākṣī the red-eyed, Mahākāyā of huge frame, and Haripiṇḍī, O lord of the earth.
Ekākṣarā, Sukusumā, and Kṛṣṇakarṇī the dark-eared, O Bhārata, Kṣurakarṇī the razor-eared, Catuṣkarṇī the four-eared, and Karṇaprāvaraṇā who is mantled in her ears.
Catuṣpathaniketā who dwells at the crossroads, Gokarṇī the cow-eared, Mahiṣānanā the buffalo-faced, Kharakarṇī the ass-eared, Mahākarṇī the great-eared, and she whose voice resounds like the kettledrum.
And she whose voice is like conch and pot, Bhaṅgadā the mighty, Gaṇā and Sugaṇā, and Abhīti the fearless, and Kāmadā the granter of desires.
And Catuṣpatharatā who delights in the crossways, Bhūtitīrthā, Anyagocarā, Paśudā giver of cattle, and Vittadā giver of wealth, and Sukhadā of great fame, giver of joy, Payodā giver of milk, Gomahiṣadā giver of cow and buffalo, and Suviṣāṇā the fair-horned, O Bhārata.
Pratiṣṭhā and Supratiṣṭhā, Rocamāna, Surocanā, Gokarṇī and Sukarṇī, Sasirā, and Stherikā likewise, Ekacakrā, Megharavā whose roar is the thundercloud, Meghamālā garlanded with clouds, and Virocanā.
These and many other mothers, O bull of the Bhāratas, followers of Kārttikeya, of every form, by the thousand.
Long-nailed, long-toothed, and long-snouted, O Bhārata, yet upright and sweet, in the bloom of youth and finely adorned.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Endowed with grandeur of soul, able to take any shape at will, some with fleshless bodies and white of hue, and others gleaming like gold.
Others like the black thundercloud, and some smoke-gray, O bull of the Bhāratas, some glowing like the dawn, the highly blessed, long-haired and white-robed.
And some wearing their braids upturned, tawny-eyed, with pendant girdles, with hanging bellies, with drooping ears, and likewise with pendulous breasts.
With copper-red eyes and copper hue, and others tawny-eyed, granters of boons, roving at will, and ever joyous.
Some belonging to Yama, some to Rudra, and some to Soma, those of Kubera, and the mighty, those of Varuṇa, and those of great Indra, and those of Agni, O scorcher of foes.
And those of Vāyu, and those of Kumāra, and those of Brahmā, O bull of the Bhāratas, equal to the apsarases in beauty, and like the wind in swiftness.
In speech like the cuckoo, and in abundance like Kubera the lord of wealth, in valor the equals of Śakra, and in radiance like the fire.
Dwelling among trees and at the crossroads, making their abodes at the meeting of four ways, dwelling in caverns and burning-grounds, and lodging by mountains and waterfalls.
Wearing ornaments of every kind, garlanded and robed in every fashion, in garb of manifold and wondrous sorts, and speaking tongues of every kind as well.
These and many other hosts, terror to their foes, followed the great-souled one, with the consent of Indra, lord of the thirty gods.
Then the blessed Pākaśāsana bestowed the spear-weapon upon Guha, O tiger among kings, for the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
And a banner, loud-resounding, hung with a great bell, blazing, of white radiance and the hue of the young sun, O bull of the Bhāratas—
Paśupati gave him that, and a mighty army of all the spirits, fierce, bearing weapons of every kind, endowed with the power of austerity, valor, and strength.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Viṣṇu gave the Vaijayantī garland that swells one's strength; Umā gave two spotless garments, gleaming bright as the sun.
Gaṅgā with love gave the prince a divine, supreme water-pot born of the nectar, and Bṛhaspati gave a staff.
Garuḍa gave his beloved son the peacock with its dappled plumage, and Aruṇa gave the red-crested cock, that creature whose weapons are its feet.
King Varuṇa gave a noose endowed with strength and valor; and Brahmā the Lord, maker of the worlds, gave a black antelope skin to the devout one, and bestowed victory in battles as well.
Having attained command over the host of the gods, Skanda shone forth, blazing and flaming like a second fire, surrounded then by his attendants and by the Mothers.
