That dreadful army of spirits, with bells and uplifted banners, with kettledrums, conches, and tabors, with weapons and standards, shone like the autumn sky adorned with its stars.
Then those companies of the gods and the throngs of the spirit-army, unhurried, sounded their drums and abundant conches,
war-drums and rattles, saws and ox-horns, kettledrums and cow-faced trumpets, and tabors of mighty sound.
All the gods with Vāsava praised the prince, the celestial gandharvas sang, and the troops of apsarases danced.
Then the great-armied one, well pleased, granted a boon to the thirty gods: "I shall slay in battle those foes who seek your destruction."
Receiving the boon from that best of the wise, the great-souled gods, glad at heart, counted their foes as already slain.
When the boon was granted by the great-souled one, a roar of joy arose from all the assembled spirits and filled the three worlds.
Then the great-armied one set forth, encircled by his vast army, to slay the daityas in battle and to protect the dwellers of heaven.
Resolve, Victory, Righteousness, Success, Fortune, Constancy, and Memory marched before the armies of the great-armied one, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With that terrible host—weapons of pike and mace, of club and pestle, of iron shaft, spear, and lance in its hands—roaring like a proud lion, the god Guha bellowed and went forth.
Seeing him, all the daiteyas, rākṣasas, and dānavas fled in every direction, agitated with fear on every side; and the gods, weapons of every kind in hand, rushed upon them.
And the blessed Skanda, beholding this, was enraged; endowed with splendor and strength, he hurled the dreadful spear-weapon again and again, kindling his own brilliance like a fire fed with oblation.
As the spear-weapon was being hurled by Skanda of measureless brilliance, blazing meteors fell, O great king, upon the surface of the earth.
And crashing thunderbolts fell upon the ground, as fearsome as those at the hour of the world's end, O king.
A single spear was hurled by the dread son of fire, and from it sprang forth tens of millions of spears, O bull of the Bhāratas.
With that spear-weapon the blessed Lord slew in battle the daitya-king named Tāraka, of mighty strength and prowess, surrounded by a hundred thousand valiant daityas and by ten mighty warriors, O king.
He smote down Mahiṣa, encircled in battle by eight hundred billion, and slew Tripāda, surrounded by ten times a million times a hundred thousand.
And the Lord slew Hradodara, encircled by ten hundred billion, together with his followers bearing weapons of every kind.
There, as the foes were being slain, the prince's followers raised a mighty roar, O king, filling the ten directions.
By the flames of the spear-weapon on every side, O lord of kings, the daityas were burned by the thousand, and others by the war-cries of Skanda.
Some enemies of the gods, struck down by the lashing of the banner, were slain; some, terrified by the clang of the bell, fell upon the earth; and some, cleft by weapons, dropped down lifeless.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus the heroic Kārttikeya, mighty and strong, slew in battle many a powerful and aggressive foe of the gods.
Now a daiteya named Bāṇa, the son of Bali, of mighty strength, took to Mount Krauñca and harassed the hosts of the gods.
The great-armied one, lofty of mind, advanced upon that enemy of the gods; and out of fear of Kārttikeya he took refuge in Krauñca.
Then the blessed Kārttikeya, full of great wrath, clove Krauñca—resounding with the cry of the krauñca-bird—with the spear given by Agni.
With its sāl trunks and pines, with elephants of the forest in panic, with birds startled from its riverbanks and serpents tumbling forth,
echoing with troops of fleeing langurs and bears, loud with the rush of running deer, thronged with bewildered wild oxen,
with śarabhas and lions suddenly bursting forth and fleeing—though fallen into a pitiable state, that mountain still shone in splendor.
The vidyādharas who dwelt upon its peaks flew up, and the kiṃnaras too, terrified and startled by the roar of the falling spear.
Then the daityas, in their hundreds and thousands, decked in gleaming ornaments and garlands, rushed forth from that blazing best of mountains.
The prince's followers overtook and slew them in the fray, and the son of fire, slayer of hostile heroes, clove Krauñca with his spear.
Making itself now manifold, now single, the spear hurled in battle by the great-souled one returned to his hand again and again.
Of such power was the blessed son of fire, and greater still: by him Krauñca was riven asunder and the daityas were slain by the hundred.
Then the blessed god, having slain the enemies of the gods, honored by the gods, attained the highest joy.
Then the kettledrums sounded, O king, and the conches, O Bhārata, and the women of the gods let fall an incomparable rain of flowers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A holy breeze blew, bearing a celestial fragrance, and the gandharvas praised him, as did the sacrificing great seers.
Some declare him to be the Lord, the son of the Grandsire, Sanatkumāra, the first-born of all, sprung from Brahman;
some the son of Maheśvara, some the son of Vibhāvasu; and they speak of him also as the son of Umā, of the Kṛttikās, and of Gaṅgā.
The mighty one, lord of yogins, that god—one and twofold and fourfold, and in his hundreds and thousands of forms.
Thus has the consecration of Kārttikeya been told to you, O king; now hear the holiness of the lineage of fords of the Sarasvatī.
When the enemies of the gods had been slain by the prince, there arose a most excellent ford, O great king, like a second heaven.
And dwelling there, the Lord, the son of fire, then bestowed dominions, each in turn, upon the chief spirits throughout the three worlds.
Thus was the blessed one, the ender of the daitya race, consecrated at that ford by the gods as commander of the host of heaven, O great king.
That ford is named Aujasa, where of old the lord of waters, Varuṇa, was consecrated by the hosts of the gods, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Having bathed at that most excellent ford and worshipped Skanda, the Plough-bearer gave gold, garments, and ornaments to the brāhmaṇas.
Having passed the night there, Mādhava, slayer of hostile heroes, the Plough-bearer, worshipped that excellent ford and touched its waters; and that best of the Mādhavas became glad and joyful at heart.
All this has been told to you, that which you asked of me—how the blessed Skanda was consecrated by the assembled gods.
Janamejaya said: Most wondrous is this, O brāhmaṇa; I have heard truly and in full detail the consecration of the prince, just as it was ordained.
Hearing it, I know my very self to be purified, O treasury of austerity; the hairs of my body stand thrilled, and my mind is serene.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At hearing the consecration of the prince and the slaying of the daityas, my joy is supreme—and my curiosity is greater still.
How was the lord of waters consecrated here by gods and asuras? Tell me that, O greatly wise one, for you are skilled, O best of men.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hear, O king, this marvel just as it was in a former age. Of old, while that first age, the Kṛtayuga, ran its course in due order, all the deities came together and spoke thus to Varuṇa:
"As Śakra, king of the gods, ever guards us from dangers, so do you too become the lord of all the rivers.
And your dwelling shall ever be, O god, in the ocean, abode of the sea-monsters; this sea, lord of streams, shall be under your sway.
And with Soma your waning and waxing shall come to pass." "So be it," said Varuṇa in answer to those gods.
Then all of them, coming together, made Varuṇa, dweller in the ocean, the lord of waters, by rites prescribed in the ordinance.
Having consecrated Varuṇa as lord of the water-creatures and honored the lord of waters, the gods then went each to his own abode.
Consecrated by the gods, the greatly glorious Varuṇa governed the rivers and seas, the streams and the lakes, by rule, even as the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices governs the gods.
Then, having touched the water there too and given wealth of many kinds, the greatly wise slayer of Pralamba went to the Agni-tīrtha, where the oblation-eater, hidden in the heart of the śamī tree, had vanished and could not be seen.
And when the destruction of light and darkness throughout the worlds had come to pass, O sinless one, the gods drew near the great-souled Grandsire of all the worlds.
"The blessed fire has vanished, and we do not know the cause; let there be no destruction of all the worlds—restore the fire to us."
Janamejaya said: Why did the blessed fire, sustainer of the worlds, vanish, and how was it found out by the gods? Tell me that truly.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Sorely afraid by reason of the curse of Bhṛgu, the mighty Jātavedas, entering the heart of the śamī tree, the blessed one thereupon vanished.
When the fire had thus vanished, all the gods with Vāsava, sorely grieved, then searched for the lost flame.
Then, reaching the Agni-tīrtha, they beheld the flame there dwelling, after its own manner, within the heart of the śamī tree.
All the gods, O tiger among men, with Bṛhaspati at their head and with Vāsava, drew near that flame and were gladdened; they returned each as they had come, and that fire became the devourer of all.
By the curse of Bhṛgu, O guardian of the earth, that which was spoken by the knower of Brahman came to pass; and having bathed there too, the wise one went to the source of Brahman.
There, where the blessed Grandsire of all the worlds had brought forth creation, having bathed, the Lord Brahmā with the gods of old created the foods of the deities, each in due order.
Having bathed there and bestowed wealth of many kinds, he went on to the tīrtha of Kubera, where, having performed great austerity, the Lord, son of Ilabilā, attained the sovereignty over riches, O king.
Even as he abode there, O king, riches and treasures waited upon him, O best of men; and the Plough-bearer, having gone to that tīrtha and bathed according to rule, gave wealth to the brāhmaṇas.
There in Kubera's domain, in that loveliest of forests, he beheld that place where of old great austerity had been performed by the exalted one.
There it was that King Kubera obtained abundant boons, and from Rudra of measureless splendour he won lordship over wealth and friendship besides.
There, O mighty-armed one, the lord of riches readily gained godhood, the office of world-guardian, and a son, Nalakūbara.
There too he was consecrated, having assembled with the hosts of the Maruts; and to him was given that lovely conveyance yoked with swans, the celestial Puṣpaka chariot, and the sovereignty over the Nairṛtas as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having bathed there, O king, and bestowed lavish gifts, Bala — Rāma, smeared with white unguents — went on in haste to the next holy ford.
It was frequented by all living beings, Badarapācana by name, graced with groves of every season, ever blossoming and fruitful and fair.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Rāma proceeded to the excellent ford named Badarapācana, hallowed by the deeds of ascetics and adepts, where a maiden, firm in her vows, once dwelt.
She was the daughter of Bharadvāja, peerless in beauty upon the earth, O lord, a maiden named Srucāvatī, who lived in chastity.
She practised the fiercest austerity through many observances, O king, that lovely woman, having resolved within herself, 'May the king of the gods become my husband.'
Many years passed over her, O upholder of the Kuru line, as she kept those several vows, severe and most hard for women to fulfil.
By that conduct of hers, by her austerity, O lord of peoples, and by her supreme devotion, the divine Punisher of Pāka was well pleased.
The lord and sovereign of the thirty gods came to her hermitage, having assumed the form of the brahmin sage, the great-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Seeing him of dread austerity, Vasiṣṭha, foremost among those who do penance, she honoured him with the rites prescribed by the sages, O Bhārata.
And that auspicious maiden, versed in observances and sweet of speech, said: 'Reverend one, tiger among sages, what do you command, O lord?'
'All that lies in my power I will give you this day, O firm in vows; yet out of my devotion to Śakra I will in no wise give you my hand.'
'By vows and observances and by austerity, O wealth of penance, it is Śakra, lord of the three worlds, whom I must satisfy.'
Thus addressed, the divine lord, gazing upon her as though with a smile, spoke to her who knew the observances, soothing her as it were, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Fierce is the austerity you practise; well do I know you, O firm in vows. The purpose for which this endeavour lies in your heart, O auspicious one —'
'— all that shall come to pass even as it is, O fair-faced one. By austerity all things are won; all things rest upon austerity.'
'Those celestial realms that belong to the gods, O fair of face, are to be attained by austerity; great bliss is rooted in austerity.'
'Having performed dread austerity here and laid aside the body, mortals attain godhood, O auspicious one. Now hear this word of mine.'
'Cook these jujubes, O fortunate one, O fair in vows — cook them,' said that divine slayer of Bala, and departed.
Having taken leave of that auspicious maiden, he then murmured his sacred recitation not far from that hermitage, at the excellent ford, the Indratīrtha, O great king, renowned throughout the three worlds.
To put her to the test, the divine Punisher of Pāka, lord of the gods, caused the jujubes not to cook.
Then, O king, with self restrained, speech curbed, and weariness gone, intent upon her task and clad in spotless raiment, she set them on the fire; she of mighty vows cooked the jujubes, O tiger among kings.
As she cooked, a very long while passed, O bull among men, yet the fruits would not soften, and the day drew toward its close.
When the fire had consumed her store of firewood, seeing the flame bereft of fuel, she then set her own body to burn.
Casting first her two feet into the flame, that fair maiden, the blameless one, turned her feet back ever again into it as they burned and burned.
Though her feet were being consumed, the irreproachable one, lotus-petal-eyed, gave no thought to her pain, longing only to please the great sage.
Then, beholding this deed of hers, the lord of the three worlds was well pleased, and thereupon revealed to the maiden his own true form.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the foremost of the gods said to that maiden of unbending vows: 'I am pleased with you, O fair one, by your devotion, your austerity, and your observance.'
'Therefore whatever desire is dear to you shall be fulfilled, O fair one; and laying aside your body, O greatly blessed, you shall dwell with me in heaven.'
'And this excellent ford of yours shall stand abiding in the world, washing away all sins, O fair-browed one — Badarapācana by name, renowned throughout the three worlds, frequented by brahmin sages.'
'For at this excellent and auspicious ford, O greatly blessed one, the Seven Sages of old once departed and went to the Himālaya, leaving Arundhatī behind.'
'Then those greatly blessed and well-disciplined sages, having gone thither, set forth, it is said, to gather fruits and roots for their sustenance.'
'As they dwelt there seeking their livelihood in the Himālayan forest, a drought set in then that lasted twelve years.'
'Those ascetics, having made a hermitage there, took up their abode; and the auspicious Arundhatī too was at that time ever steadfast in austerity.'
'Then beholding Arundhatī engaged in fierce observance, the three-eyed god, bestower of boons, came to her, greatly pleased.'
'Then Mahādeva of great renown, having assumed the form of a brahmin, approached her and said: "I wish for alms, O fair one."'
'Then that fair maiden answered the brahmin: "Our store of food is spent, O brahmin; eat these jujubes here." Thereupon Mahādeva said: "Cook these, O firm in vows."'
'Thus addressed, that illustrious woman, wishing to please the brahmin, set the jujubes upon the kindled fire and cooked them.'
'Meanwhile she listened to divine, delightful, and holy tales; and so passed away that dreadful drought of twelve years.'
'As she fasted and cooked and hearkened to those auspicious tales, that most grievous span of time passed for her as though it were a single day.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Then those sages arrived, bringing fruits from the mountain; and thereupon the pleased lord spoke to Arundhatī.'
'"Draw near, O knower of duty, to these sages as before. I am pleased with you, O knower of duty, by your austerity and your observance."'
'Then the lord Hara revealed his own true form, and thereupon recounted to them that great deed of hers.'
'"The austerity that you gained upon the slopes of the Himālaya, O brahmins, and the austerity of this woman — these I deem not equal."'
'"For by this ascetic woman austerity most hard to perform was practised; fasting and cooking, she has carried through twelve full years."'
'Then the lord again spoke to that same Arundhatī: "Choose a boon, O auspicious one, whatever you desire in your heart."'
'She of wide coppery eyes said to the god in the assembly of the Seven Sages: "If, O lord, you are pleased with me, may this become an excellent ford, dear to the Siddhas, gods, and sages, Badarapācana by name."'
'"And, O lord of the lords of gods, may one who dwells here in purity for three nights gain by his fasting the fruit of twelve years." Saying to her, "So be it," Hara then departed to heaven.'
'The sages were filled with wonder, beholding Arundhatī unwearied and unfaded, the chaste one who had borne hunger and thirst.'
'Thus did the pure Arundhatī attain supreme perfection — even as you, O greatly blessed one of unbending vows, have done for my sake.'
'For a still greater devotion, O gentle one, have you given to this vow; and so this day, well pleased by your observance, I grant you this.'
'A special boon I grant you, O auspicious and excellent one, beyond that boon which the great-souled god bestowed upon Arundhatī.'
'And by his grace and by your own splendour, O auspicious one, I shall now declare here yet another boon in due form.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Whoever shall dwell at this ford for a single night with mind well composed, having bathed, shall upon the laying aside of his body attain worlds hard to win.'
Having so spoken to the holy Srucāvatī, the mighty thousand-eyed god then returned again to heaven.
When the wielder of the thunderbolt had gone, O king, a rain of celestial flowers fell there, sweet with celestial fragrance, O best of the Bhāratas.
Kettledrums of mighty sound resounded on every side, and a fragrant, gentle breeze blew fittingly, O lord of peoples.
And casting off her fair body, she passed to the state of Indra's consort, having won it by fierce austerity, and rejoiced together with that imperishable lord.
Janamejaya said: Who, O reverend one, was her mother, and where was that lovely maiden reared? I wish to hear, O brahmin, for great is my curiosity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the great-souled brahmin sage Bharadvāja beheld the wide-eyed apsaras Ghṛtācī approaching, his seed was shed.
That foremost of those who murmur prayers caught the seed in his hand and cast it into a cup of leaves; and therein that fair maiden came into being.
Having performed for her all the birth-rites and the rest, the great sage Bharadvāja, that wealth of penance, bestowed upon her a name.
'Srucāvatī' — so the righteous one named her in the assembly of the sages; and leaving her in the hermitage, he went to the Himālayan forest.
There too the high-souled foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, having touched the waters and given wealth to the great brahmins, went with well-composed soul to the ford of Śakra at that time.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having then gone to the Indratīrtha, the mighty foremost of the Yadus, after bathing in due form, gave wealth and jewels to the brahmins.
For there that king of the immortals worshipped with a hundred sacrifices, and the lord of the gods bestowed abundant wealth upon Bṛhaspati.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Unhindered rites, attended by the jārūthya offerings, all with manifold sacrificial fees, he performed there as prescribed, with priests deeply versed in the Vedas.
Those sacrifices, O best of the Bhāratas, the one of great splendour duly accomplished a hundred times over, and thence became renowned as Śatakratu, 'lord of a hundred rites.'
And by his name that ford, blessed, holy, and eternal, became famed as the Indratīrtha, the deliverer from all sins.
Having there too touched the waters in due form, the wielder of the pestle honoured the brahmins with drink, raiment, and food, and from that excellent and auspicious ford went on to Rāmatīrtha.
There the greatly blessed Rāma, scion of Bhṛgu, of mighty austerity, again and again rid the whole earth of its foremost warriors of the Kṣatriya race.
Setting at the fore his preceptor Kaśyapa, best of sages, he worshipped with the Vājapeya rite and with a hundred horse-sacrifices, and gave away as the sacrificial fee the whole earth with its seas.
Rāma, having given wealth there to the brahmins, O Janamejaya, touched the waters according to rule and likewise honoured the twice-born,
and at that holy ford, in that auspicious place, the fair-faced one bestowed wealth and saluted the sages, and then came to the Yamunātīrtha.
There it was that the greatly blessed son of Aditi, Varuṇa of white radiance, once conducted the Rājasūya sacrifice, O lord of the earth.
There, having vanquished in battle both men and gods, Varuṇa, slayer of hostile heroes, performed that excellent sacrifice.
When that excellent sacrifice was concluded, a war arose between the gods and the dānavas, bringing destruction upon the three worlds.
When the Rājasūya, that foremost of sacrifices, is brought to its close, O Janamejaya, a most terrible war arises that falls upon the Kṣatriyas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Rāma, the plough-armed, the Mādhava, having bathed at that finest of fords and bestowed wealth upon the twice-born,
the lotus-eyed one, garlanded with woodland flowers, gladdened then and praised by the twice-born, went on from there to the Āditya ford.
There, O best of kings, the radiant Lord Bhāskara, the maker of light, by sacrificing won lordship over the luminaries and his splendor.
On the bank of that river, all the gods with Vāsava, the Viśvedevas together with the Maruts, the Gandharvas and Apsarases,
Dvaipāyana and Śuka too, and Kṛṣṇa the slayer of Madhu, the Yakṣas and the Rākṣasas and the Piśācas, O lord of peoples,
these and many others, perfected in yoga by the thousands, abode at that holy and auspicious ford of the Sarasvatī, O scorcher of foes.
There, O best of the Bhāratas, Viṣṇu of old, having slain the Asuras Madhu and Kaiṭabha, bathed at that highest and most excellent of fords.
And the righteous-souled Dvaipāyana, O Bhārata, having bathed there, attained the supreme yoga and reached the highest perfection.
And Asita Devala too, of great austerities, taking his stand there in supreme yoga, that sage attained the yoga.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There indeed of old dwelt the righteous-souled Asita Devala, rich in austerities, holding to the householder's duty.
Ever devoted to dharma, pure, self-controlled, one who had laid down the rod of punishment, of great austerities, even toward all creatures in deed, in mind, and in word;
free of anger, O great king, regarding alike blame and what is dear and not dear, of great austerities, looking with even eye upon gold and upon a clod of earth;
ever worshipping the gods and his guests together with the twice-born, ever delighting in chastity, always devoted to dharma.
Then, O great king, having drawn near and taken his stand in yoga, the mendicant, the wise sage Jaigīṣavya, came composed to that ford.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the hermitage of Devala, O king, that one of great splendor dwelt, ever steadfast in yoga, O great king, who had attained perfection through his great austerities.
Yet Devala, though he beheld the great sage Jaigīṣavya dwelling there, did not address him in the manner that righteousness required.
Thus, O great king, a long time passed for the two of them, and Devala did not see the sage Jaigīṣavya.
At mealtime, O Janamejaya, the wise wandering ascetic, knower of dharma, would present himself before Devala at the hour of begging.
Seeing the great sage come there in the guise of a beggar, Devala showed him the highest reverence and great affection.
And Devala, O Bhārata, honored him to the best of his power according to the rite as seen by the seers, attentively, for many years.
Once, O king, a very great wonder arose in the great-souled Devala as he beheld that sage of great splendor.
"Many years have passed while I have honored him, yet this listless mendicant has never spoken a word to me."
Pondering thus, the illustrious Devala, a traveler through the sky, took up his water-jar and set out for the great ocean.
As that righteous-souled one was going toward the ocean, lord of rivers, he then saw Jaigīṣavya, who had already arrived there before him, O Bhārata.
Then the powerful Asita, filled with amazement, fell to wondering: "How has this mendicant arrived at the ocean and already bathed?"
Thus did the great seer Asita ponder; and then, having bathed in the ocean according to rule and being pure, he murmured his prayer.
His muttered prayer and daily rites performed, the illustrious one went back to his hermitage, taking up his jar filled with water, O Janamejaya.
Then, as he was entering his own hermitage-ground, the sage saw Jaigīṣavya seated there within the hermitage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Jaigīṣavya did not speak to him in any way at all; like a block of wood that one of great austerities dwelt upon the hermitage-ground.
He had seen him bathed in the waters of the ocean—that one like the ocean itself—and now he saw him already entered into the hermitage before him.
Asita Devala, O king, the wise one, fell to pondering, having seen the power of Jaigīṣavya's austerity born of yoga.
That best of sages pondered, O lord of kings: "How is it that I have seen this one both at the ocean and in the hermitage?"
Pondering thus, that sage who had mastered the sacred formulas rose up from the hermitage into the sky, O lord of peoples—Devala then, to learn the truth about the mendicant Jaigīṣavya.
He beheld the Siddhas who traverse the sky, composed in meditation, and he saw Jaigīṣavya being honored by those Siddhas.
Then Asita Devala, deeply intent, resolute, firm in his vows, saw Jaigīṣavya passing on into heaven.
And from there he saw him going to the world of the ancestors; and from the world of the ancestors he saw him passing on to the world of Yama.
And rising up even from there, he watched the great sage Jaigīṣavya going on to the much-praised world of Soma.
He watched him rise to the blessed worlds of those who sacrifice in solitary devotion, and thence to the worlds of those who keep the fire-oblation, and from those too he rose.
The wise one beheld him pass beyond the worlds of those rich in austerity who offer the new-moon and full-moon sacrifices, and beyond the worlds of those who sacrifice with animals; and he saw him going to a spotless world honored by the gods.
He saw him passing likewise to the station of those rich in austerity who sacrifice with the manifold four-monthly rites, and so to that of those who offer the Agniṣṭoma.
And Devala watched him reach the station of those rich in austerity who sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He saw him in the worlds of those very wise ones who perform the Vājapeya, the finest of rites, abounding in gold.
And Devala saw Jaigīṣavya in the worlds of those who sacrifice with the Puṇḍarīka and with the Rājasūya.
He saw him in the worlds of those best of men who perform the Aśvamedha, the finest of rites, and the Naramedha as well.
And Devala saw Jaigīṣavya in the worlds of those who perform the hard-to-attain Sarvamedha and the Sautrāmaṇī.
And in the worlds of those who sacrifice with the various twelve-day sacrificial sessions, O king, Devala saw Jaigīṣavya.
Then Asita saw him having attained shared dwelling in the worlds of Mitra and Varuṇa, and so too of the Ādityas.
And then Asita saw him having passed beyond the station of the Rudras and of the Vasus, and that of Bṛhaspati—all of them.
And having ascended the world of cattle, Asita then saw Jaigīṣavya going on to the worlds of those who keep the Brahmā-session.
He watched that brāhmaṇa rise by his own splendor to three further worlds, and pass on to the worlds of women faithful to their husbands.
Then Asita no longer saw that best of sages, Jaigīṣavya, fixed in yoga and vanished from sight, O subduer of foes.
The greatly fortunate Devala reflected upon the power of Jaigīṣavya, his excellence in vows, and the matchless perfection of his yoga.
Then Asita, steadfast and self-restrained, with palms joined, asked the most excellent Siddhas in those worlds, those keepers of the Brahmā-session:
"I do not see Jaigīṣavya; tell me of that mighty one. This I wish to hear, for my curiosity is very great."
The Siddhas said: "Hear, O Devala, firm in your vows, the truth of the matter as we tell it. Jaigīṣavya has gone to the eternal, imperishable world of Brahmā."
Hearing the words of those Siddhas, keepers of the Brahmā-session, Asita Devala swiftly soared upward—and then fell back down.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then those Siddhas spoke again to Devala: "You have no power to go there, O Devala, rich in austerity—to reach, O brāhmaṇa, the abode of Brahmā that Jaigīṣavya has attained."
Hearing those words of the Siddhas, Devala descended again, in due order, through all those worlds.
He came to his own holy hermitage-ground like a bird alighting, and as he entered Devala saw Jaigīṣavya there.
Then Devala reckoned with a mind grounded in righteousness, having beheld the power of Jaigīṣavya's austerity, born of yoga.
Then Devala, O king, bowed in humility, drew near the great sage and said to the great-souled Jaigīṣavya: "I would wish, O blessed one, to take up the dharma of liberation."
Hearing those words of his, the other gave instruction—the supreme method of yoga, and what should and should not be done according to scripture.
Then, seeing that one whose mind was set upon renunciation, the great ascetic performed all his rites for him with the rite as ordained.
Seeing him with his mind set upon renunciation, the beings together with the ancestors wept aloud: "Who now will share his portion with us?"
But Devala, hearing the piteous words of the beings as they cried out through the ten directions, set his mind upon abandoning liberation.
And then, O Bhārata, the fruits and roots, the sacred grasses, the flowers and the herbs cried out aloud by the thousands:
"Surely the base, ill-minded Devala will cut us down again—he who, having granted safety to all beings, takes no heed of it!"
Then once more that best of sages reckoned with his own mind: "In liberation or in the householder's dharma—which would bring the greater good?"
Having so resolved in mind, O best of kings, Devala abandoned the householder's dharma and chose the dharma of liberation.
Reflecting upon these things and the like, Devala by his resolve then attained the supreme perfection and the highest yoga, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the gods, the ascetics led by Bṛhaspati, came together and praised Jaigīṣavya and his austerity.
Then the best of seers, Nārada, said to the gods: "There is no austerity in Jaigīṣavya, who only astonishes Asita."
To that steadfast one who spoke thus the dwellers of heaven replied, "Not so!"—and they praised the great sage Jaigīṣavya.
There too the great-souled plough-bearer touched the water, and having bestowed wealth upon the twice-born and gained the highest merit, that doer of noble deeds went on to the great ford of Soma.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Where Soma, lord of the stars, sacrificed of old with the Rājasūya, O Bhārata—when that was done, there arose the great battle called Tārakāmaya.
There too Bala touched the water, and the self-possessed, righteous-souled one, having given gifts, went on to the ford of the sage Sārasvata.
There, in a twelve-year drought of old, the sage Sārasvata taught the Vedas to the best of the twice-born.
Janamejaya said: How was it that in a twelve-year drought of old the ascetic sage Sārasvata taught the Vedas?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was of old, O great king, a wise sage of great austerities, renowned as Dadhīca, a celibate who had conquered his senses.
Of him and his surpassing austerity Śakra was ever afraid, O lord; nor could he be tempted by rewards of every kind.
Then, to tempt him, the Chastiser of Pāka sent forth a celestial apsaras, holy and fair to behold, named Alambusā.
As that great-souled one was offering libations to the gods upon the Sarasvatī, O great king, the lovely woman drew near and stood close beside him.
Beholding her of celestial form, the seed of that contemplative sage spilled forth into the Sarasvatī, and the river took it up.
Seeing that seed, O bull among men, she received it into her womb; and that great river bore the embryo for the sake of a son.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In due time that best of rivers gave birth to a son, and taking the child she went to that sage, O lord.
Seeing that most excellent of sages in the assembly of seers, the river, O lord of kings, spoke thus as she handed over his son: 'O brahmā-seer, this is your son, borne by me out of devotion to you.'
'When at the sight of the apsaras Alambusā your seed was once spilled, that, O brahmā-seer, I held within my womb out of devotion to you.'
'Resolved that this radiance of yours should not perish, I bore it; receive now your own blameless son, given to you by me.'
Thus addressed, that best of twice-born accepted him and felt the highest delight; with mantras and with love he kissed the boy upon the head.
Embracing him a long while, O best of the Bhāratas, the great sage, well pleased, then granted a boon to the Sarasvatī.
'The Viśvedevas together with the fathers, and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, shall attain satisfaction, O fortunate one, when honored with libations of your waters.'
Having spoken thus, pleased and supremely joyful in heart, he praised the great river with these words; hear them duly, O king.
'O greatly blessed one, you flowed forth of old from the lake of Brahmā; the sages of strict vows know you, O best of rivers.'
'And you have ever done me kindness, O lovely to behold; therefore great shall be your son Sārasvata, O fair-complexioned one.'
'Renowned by your very name, your son, a benefactor of the worlds, shall become famed as Sārasvata, great in austerity.'
'During a drought of twelve years, O greatly blessed one, this Sārasvata shall teach the Vedas to the bulls among the twice-born.'
'And of all holy rivers you shall ever be the most holy, O auspicious one, O greatly blessed Sarasvatī, by my grace.'
Thus praised by him, the great river, having received her boon, took her son and went away rejoicing, O bull of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At that very time, in the strife between the gods and the dānavas, Śakra, seeking a weapon, ranged through the three worlds.
Yet the lord Śakra found then no weapon that would be fit to slay those foes of the gods.
Then Śakra said to the gods: 'These mighty asuras, foes of the thirty, cannot be slain by me save with the bones of Dadhīca.'
'Therefore go, O best of gods, and let that foremost of sages be entreated: "Give the bones of Dadhīca"—with them we shall slay our enemies.'
Earnestly entreated by the gods to give up his bones—to lay down his very life—that best of sages did so without a moment's hesitation; and having done the gods this kindness, he won then the imperishable worlds.
From his bones, then, Śakra, with greatly delighted heart, had fashioned divine weapons of many kinds—thunderbolts, discuses, maces, and ample heavy staves.
For he, the benefactor of the worlds, had been begotten through fierce austerity by the supreme sage Bhṛgu, son of Prajāpati.
Vast of body, full of splendor, fashioned from the essence of the worlds, he was born—heavy as a mountain, towering, renowned for his might, a lord; ever did the Chastiser of Pāka tremble at his radiance.
With that thunderbolt, charged with mantras, O Bhārata, hurled in furious wrath and sprung from the power of brahman, the lord slew nine times ninety of the daitya and dānava heroes.
Then, when a long and most terrible span of time had passed, a drought of twelve years came on, O king.
In that twelve-year drought the great seers, afflicted by hunger, fled in every direction in search of livelihood, O king.
Seeing them scattered to the quarters, the sage Sārasvata then made up his mind to depart; but the Sarasvatī spoke to him.
'You must not go from here, my son; I shall always give you food—the choicest of fishes; dwell here, O Bhārata.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed, he made offering to the fathers and to the gods, took his food daily, and so preserved both his life and the Vedas.
Then, when that drought had passed, the great seers questioned one another concerning the recitation of their sacred study once more.
For all of them, gripped by hunger and wandering about, the Vedas had been lost, O lord of kings; not one of them had any recollection left.
Then a certain one of the seers came upon Sārasvata, that most excellent and disciplined of sages, engaged in his sacred recitation.
Going back, he told them of the brilliant Sārasvata, godlike in his luster, performing his sacred recitation in a solitary place.
Then all the great seers gathered there, O king, and, assembled before Sārasvata, that best of sages, said this:
'Teach us,' they said; and the sage replied to them: 'Become my pupils duly, sirs, according to the rule.'
Then the company of seers said: 'You are but a boy, dear child.' He answered the sages again: 'So that my dharma not be lost.'
'He who teaches against right, or who receives teaching against right—let both of them swiftly perish, or both become foes to each other.'
'Not by years, nor by grey hairs, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers determine eminence in dharma: he who is learned in the sacred lore is great among us.'
Hearing these words of his, those sages duly received the Vedas from him and re-established their dharma anew.
Sixty thousand sages became the pupils of the brahmā-seer Sārasvata for the sake of recovering the recitation of the Vedas.
Then each of them brought handful upon handful of darbha grass for the seat of that brahmā-seer; though he was but a boy, they remained obedient to him.
There too the son of Rohiṇī, the mighty elder brother of Keśava, having bestowed wealth, then went on rejoicing, in due course, to that great and famed sacred ford where the Aged Maiden once dwelt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Janamejaya said: How, O reverend one, did that maiden of old come to be devoted to austerity? For what purpose did she practice penance, and what was her vow?
Most arduous and unsurpassed is this that I have heard from you, O brāhmaṇa; tell me the whole truth, how she stood firm in austerity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was a sage of great vigor and great fame, Kuṇi of the line of Garga; having performed vast austerity, O king, that best of ascetics, the mighty one, brought forth from his mind a fair-browed daughter.
And beholding her, Kuṇi of Garga's line, of great fame, was exceedingly pleased; then, O king, casting off his body here, he went to heaven.
That fair-browed and lovely maiden, blameless, with eyes like lotus-petals, having built a hermitage, gave herself to fierce and mighty austerity.
Honoring with fasts the fathers and the gods of old, she passed a great span of time in fierce austerity, O king.
Though offered by her father to a husband, that blameless one would not consent, for she saw no husband worthy of herself.
Then, mortifying her own body with fierce austerity, she remained intent upon the worship of the fathers and the gods in a solitary forest.
Though she deemed herself to have fulfilled her purpose, she grew worn with toil, O lord of kings, wasted by old age and by penance alike.
When she could no longer walk even a single step by herself, she then set her mind upon passing to the other world.
But seeing her wishing to release her body, Nārada said: 'Whence are there worlds for you, O sinless maiden, when you are unconsecrated by marriage?'
'For thus have we heard in the world of the gods, O woman of great vows: supreme austerity you have attained, but the worlds you have not won.'
Hearing those words of Nārada, she said in the assembly of seers: 'I will give half of my austerity to him who takes my hand, O most excellent ones.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When she had thus spoken, a sage sprung from Gālava, named Śṛṅgavān, took her hand and laid down this condition:
'On this condition shall I touch your hand today, O fair one: that you must dwell with me for a single night.'
'So be it,' she promised, and gave her hand to him then; and the son of Gālava took her hand and wedded her.
In the night she became, O king, a young woman of godlike complexion, adorned with celestial ornaments and raiment, with celestial garlands and unguents.
Beholding her, who seemed to shine with her own radiance, the son of Gālava was delighted, and dwelt with her one night; at dawn she said to him:
'The condition you made with me, O brāhmaṇa, best of ascetics—by it I have dwelt with you; blessings upon you, may all be well with you; now I depart.'
Granted leave, she spoke once more: 'Whoever, intent in spirit, shall dwell one night at this ford, having made offering to the dwellers of heaven—'
'—he shall obtain the fruit of one who duly observes chastity for eight-and-forty and for two-and-eight years.' Having spoken thus, the virtuous woman then cast off her body and went to heaven.
The sage too grew downcast, brooding on her beauty; and by the terms of the pact he had with difficulty received half her austerity.
Then, having perfected himself, he followed in her course, grief-stricken, O best of the Bhāratas, overpowered by her beauty. This great tale of the Aged Maiden has now been told to you.
While he abode there, the Plough-armed one heard that Śalya had been slain; and there too, having bestowed gifts upon the twice-born, O scorcher of foes, he grieved for Śalya, then slain in battle by the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, passing out from the gate of Samantapañcaka, Rāma the Mādhava asked the company of seers what was the fruit of Kurukṣetra.
Questioned by the lion of the Yadus about the fruit of Kurukṣetra, O lord, those great-souled ones recounted it all to him exactly as it was.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The seers said: Samantapañcaka is called, O Rāma, the eternal northern altar of Prajāpati, where of old the gods of heaven, the great bestowers of boons, worshipped with an excellent sacrifice.
And of old this field was ploughed through many years by the wise and best of royal seers, the great-souled Kuru of measureless splendor; thence it became famed in the world as Kurukṣetra.
Rāma said: For what purpose was this field ploughed by the great-souled Kuru? This I wish to hear told, O you whose wealth is austerity.
The seers said: Of old, O Rāma, as Kuru was ploughing, ever unwearied, Śakra came down from heaven, approached him, and asked the reason.
'What is this you are about, O king, with such utmost effort? O royal seer, what is your aim, that you plough this earth?'
Kuru said: 'Those men who die upon this field, O Hundred-Sacrificer, shall go to the worlds of the virtuous, free from all sin.'
Then, laughing in derision, the lord Śakra went back to heaven; but the royal seer, undaunted, kept on ploughing the earth.
Coming again and again, and mocking him again and again, the Hundred-Sacrificer, questioning him over and over, would each time depart, while Kuru remained undaunted.
But when the king ploughed the earth with fierce austerity, then Śakra told the gods what the royal seer was minded to do.
Hearing this, the gods spoke these words to the thousand-eyed one: "Let the royal sage be appeased with a boon, O Śakra, if it can be done."
"For if men who die in this place go straight to heaven without honoring us through sacrifices, then no share of the offerings will be left for us."
So Śakra came and spoke then to the royal sage: "Enough of your toil! Let my word be carried out."
"Those men who, forgoing food, untiringly cast off the body, or who are duly slain in battle, even those gone to the state of beasts, O king—"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"—let them become partakers of heaven, O lord of kings, O great-minded one." "So be it," said King Kuru then to Śakra in reply.
Then, having taken his leave, the slayer of Bala, his inmost soul rejoicing, swiftly returned once more to the realm of heaven.
Thus it was, O best of the Yadus, that this field was plowed of old by the royal sage, and Śakra too granted that it should be holy for those who release their breath here.
And here Śakra himself, the lord of the gods, sang a verse composed about Kurukṣetra; hear it, O wielder of the plow.
"Even the dust-grains from Kurukṣetra, stirred up by the wind, lead even the doer of evil deeds to the supreme goal."
Bulls among the gods and the most excellent of brāhmaṇas, and Nṛga and other chiefs among god-like kings, O lion among men, having worshiped with costly sacrifices and laid down their bodies, attained the blessed goal.
That which lies between Tarantuka and Arantuka, and between the lakes of Rāma and Macakruka—this Samantapañcaka of Kurukṣetra is called the upper altar of Prajāpati.
Auspicious, great, and holy is this place, honored by the dwellers of heaven, endowed with the virtues of the celestial realm; and therefore all the lords of the earth, when slain here, shall go to the goal of great souls.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having then beheld Kurukṣetra and bestowed gifts, the Sātvata went on to a very great and divine hermitage, O Janamejaya.
It was furnished with groves of madhūka and mango, thick with plakṣa and banyan trees, holy, set about with ciribilva, and crowded with panasa and arjuna trees.
Beholding it, foremost in holy marks, the best of the Yādavas asked all those sages: "Whose excellent hermitage is this?"
And they all said to the great-souled wielder of the plow, O king: "Hear in full, O Rāma, whose hermitage this was of old."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Here in days past the god Viṣṇu performed supreme austerity; here all his eternal sacrifices were duly carried out."
"Here too a brāhmaṇa woman, perfected, chaste from girlhood, joined to yoga and accomplished in austerity, the ascetic went to heaven."
"She was the illustrious daughter of the great-souled Śāṇḍilya, O king—firm in her vows, virtuous, disciplined, and chaste."
"Having attained the highest yoga, she went to the supreme heaven; the blessed one, having enjoyed in that hermitage the fruit of the horse-sacrifice among those who reap reward, the highly fortunate one went to heaven, honored by the self-controlled."
Having approached and beheld the holy hermitage, the bull of the Yadus, that unfailing one, then saluting those sages, sent back all his encampments and ascended the mountain on the slope of the Himavat.
Going not far thence up the mountain, the mighty one whose banner bears the palm beheld a holy and excellent ford, and was filled with utmost wonder.
And Bala reached the source of the Sarasvatī, the spring of the plakṣa tree, and Kārapacana, the foremost and most excellent of fords.
There too the mighty wielder of the plow bestowed gifts, bathed in the cold water, and thence, greatly pleased, went on to the hermitage of Mitra and Varuṇa.
To that region where Indra, Agni, and Aryaman of old found their delight, on the Yamunā, he went from Kārapacana.
Bathing there too, the righteous one attained supreme contentment; and the mighty bull of the Yadus, seated together with sages and perfected ones, listened to glorious tales.
And while they were tarrying thus, the blessed sage Nārada came to that region where Rāma was stationed.
Wrapped in a coil of matted locks, clad in golden bark, of great austerity, bearing a golden staff, O king, and carrying a water-pot as well,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
holding that lovely lute named Kacchapī of sweet sound, skilled in dance and song, honored by gods and brāhmaṇas,
a stirrer-up of quarrels and ever fond of strife, he came to that region where the illustrious Rāma was stationed.
Rising up, they all paid honor to that one of restrained vows, and questioned the divine sage about what had befallen the Kurus.
Then, O king, Nārada, knower of all dharmas, recounted to him all just as it had happened—the past destruction of the Kurus.
Then the son of Rohiṇī said to Nārada in a sorrowful voice: "In what state now is that warrior caste, and the kings who were there?"
"All this I have heard before, O wealth of austerity, yet a great eagerness has arisen in me to hear it in full."
Nārada said: Bhīṣma was slain at the very first, and Droṇa, and the lord of the Sindhus likewise; Karṇa, son of Vikartana, was slain, and his sons, the great chariot-warriors.
Bhūriśravas, O son of Rohiṇī, and the valiant king of the Madras—these and many other mighty ones, here and there,
kings and princes who never turned back in battles, laid down their own dear lives for the sake of the Kaurava's pleasure.
But hear from me, O mighty-armed Mādhava, who there are not slain: those remaining in the host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son—Kṛpa, the valiant Bhoja, and the mighty Aśvatthāman—their army broken, have scattered to the directions.
His army slain, and Kṛpa and the others fled, Duryodhana, sorely grieved, entered the lake named Dvaipāyana.
As the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra lay there, the waters frozen still, the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇa, tormented him with fierce words.
Goaded on every side by their words, O Rāma, the mighty hero rose up at last from the lake, seizing his great mace.
And even now he has come to combat with Bhīma; and forthwith, O Rāma, a most terrible fight between the two shall take place.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If you have any curiosity, go, O Mādhava, without delay; behold the most dreadful fight of your two pupils, if you are so inclined.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard Nārada's words and honored those bulls among brāhmaṇas, he dismissed all who had come there with him, and commanded his followers, "Let us go to Dvārakā."
Descending from the best of mountains, from the auspicious spring of the plakṣa tree, then Rāma, glad of heart, having heard of the great fruit of the ford, sang in the presence of the brāhmaṇas this verse, that unfailing one:
"Where is delight to equal dwelling by the Sarasvatī? Where are virtues to equal dwelling by the Sarasvatī? Men who have gained the Sarasvatī and gone to heaven shall ever remember the river Sarasvatī."
"The Sarasvatī is holy among all rivers; the Sarasvatī ever brings happiness to the world. Men, even doers of grievous deeds, having gained the Sarasvatī, never grieve, in the world beyond or here."
Then, gazing again and again with affection upon the Sarasvatī, the scorcher of foes mounted his gleaming chariot yoked with horses.
With that swift-going chariot the bull of the Yadus, eager to see, arrived where the combat of his pupils was at hand.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus did that tumultuous combat come about, O Janamejaya, concerning which the grief-stricken King Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words.
"When the mace-combat was at hand and Rāma seen present, how did my son fight back against Bhīma, O Saṃjaya?"
Saṃjaya said: Coming into Rāma's presence, your son Duryodhana, mighty-armed and valiant, eager for combat, rejoiced greatly.
Beholding the plow-bearer, the king rose up, O descendant of Bharata, and, filled with utmost joy, then said to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Let us go swiftly from here to Samantapañcaka, O lord of peoples—that renowned upper altar of Prajāpati in the world of the gods."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In that most holy and eternal place of the three worlds, one who meets his death in battle shall surely attain heaven."
Saying "So be it," O great king, the heroic lord Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, set out facing toward Samantapañcaka.
Then King Duryodhana, the resplendent one, seizing his great mace, went on foot in his wrath along with the Pāṇḍavas.
As he went thus, mace in hand and clad in armor, the gods who move in the sky honored him crying "Well done! Well done!"; and what men of the air there were, beholding him, were filled with joy.
Surrounded by the Pāṇḍavas, the Kuru king, your son, went forward, assuming the gait of a rutting lordly elephant.
Then with the blare of conches, the great din of kettledrums, and the lion-roars of the heroes, all the directions were filled.
Having gone to the westward-facing region as designated by your son, it was encircled by them on every side, in all directions.
To the south of the Sarasvatī lay an excellent ford named Samanta; in that region, on ground free of barren salt, they resolved to do battle.
Then Bhīma, clad in armor, taking up his mace of vast bulk, bore a form, O great king, like unto Garutmat.
His helm bound on, wearing golden armor in the fray, your son shone forth, O king, like a golden king of mountains.
Both heroes, Bhīma and Duryodhana, encased in their armor, shone in the combat like two enraged elephants.
Standing in the midst of the battle-circle, those two bulls among men, the kinsmen, shone, O great king, like the risen moon and sun.
They glared at each other like two angry mighty elephants, burning each other with their eyes, O king, each seeking the other's death.
With exultant heart, O king, the Kaurava took up his mace, licking the corners of his mouth, his eyes red with wrath, breathing hard.
Then the valiant King Duryodhana, taking up his mace and looking toward Bhīmasena, challenged him as one elephant challenges another.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Likewise the valiant Bhīma, taking up his mace forged of the essence of the mountains, challenged the king as one lion challenges another in the forest.
With maces raised in their hands, Duryodhana and Wolf-belly shone in the fray like two mountains crowned with peaks.
Both were exceedingly enraged, both of terrible prowess, both pupils in mace-combat of the wise son of Rohiṇī.
Both were alike in their deeds, like Yama and Vāsava, and likewise the two mighty ones matched the deeds of Varuṇa.
Those two, O great king, were the equals of Vāsudeva, of Rāma, and of Vaiśravaṇa, and of Madhu and Kaiṭabha in combat.
Both were alike in their deeds in battle to Sunda and Upasunda, and the two scorchers of foes were equal as well to Time and to Death.
They rushed upon each other like two great elephants in rut, frenzied as in autumn, proud at the meeting over a she-elephant.
Those two bulls of the Bhāratas, eager for victory like two maddened elephants, spat forth the blazing venom of their wrath like two serpents.
Furious at each other, those two tamers of foes glared, both tigers among the Bhāratas, endowed with valor.
Unassailable as two lions, those scorchers of foes in mace-combat, the heroes were hard to withstand as two tigers armed with claws and fangs.
They were like two oceans hard to cross, churned at the destruction of all creatures; and the two great chariot-warriors blazed in their fury like two angry red-bodied planets of Mars.
Radiant and great-souled, blazing and of mighty strength, the two foremost of the Kurus were beheld, like twin suns of doom risen at once.
Furious as two tigers, roaring like rain-clouds, the mighty-armed pair bristled with delight like a pair of maned lions.
Enraged like two elephants, ablaze like two fires, those great-souled ones were beheld like two peaked mountains.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Their lips quivering with wrath, gazing upon each other, the two great-souled best of men came together, maces in hand.
Both supremely exultant, both held in highest honor, neighing like two fine stallions, trumpeting like two elephants—
bellowing like two bulls, Duryodhana and Vṛkodara, drunk with strength like two Daityas, those best of men shone forth.
Then, O king, Duryodhana spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira, who stood among the Sṛñjayas blazing like the sun:
"This combat between us two, between Bhīma and myself, is resolved upon. Be seated, O best of kings, and watch the clash."
Then that vast circle of kings, seated all around and resplendent, appeared like the orb of the sun shining in the sky.
In their midst, O great king, the mighty-armed and glorious elder brother of Keśava sat, honored on every side.
Clad in dark blue and of fair radiance, set amid the kings, he shone like the full moon ringed by the stars at night.
And so those two, O great king, maces in hand and hard to assail, stood facing each other, hewing one another with fierce words.
Having spoken bitter taunts to each other, those two bulls of the Kurus stood glaring, like Vṛtra and Śakra upon the field of battle.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then arose a tumultuous war of words, O Janamejaya, whereupon the grief-stricken king Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke thus:
"Fie indeed upon mortal life, whose end is such as this—where my son, master of eleven armies, was the overlord!"
"Having commanded all the kings and enjoyed this earth, taking up his mace he now sets out on foot, in haste, to battle."
"Having been lord of the world, my son now goes forth like one bereft of a protector, mace raised aloft—what is this but the working of fate?"
"Ah, great is the sorrow my son has come to, Saṃjaya!" Having spoken thus, the lord of men, stricken with grief, fell silent.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: With a voice like thunder, roaring in his joy like a great bull, the valiant one then summoned Pārtha to combat in the fray.
As the great-souled king of the Kurus called forth Bhīma, manifold and most fearful portents appeared.
Winds blew with crashing thunderbolts, a rain of dust fell down, and all the quarters became veiled in darkness.
Loud-roaring, thunderous, tumultuous, and hair-raising, meteors then fell by the hundreds, splitting open the vault of heaven.
And Rāhu swallowed the sun though it was no eclipse-time, O lord of peoples, and the earth with its forests and trees shook with a mighty trembling.
Harsh winds blew low, raining down gravel, and the very peaks of mountains crashed down upon the surface of the earth.
Beasts of manifold forms came rushing from the ten directions, and blazing jackals of dreadful aspect, most terrible, set up their howling.
Most fearful, hair-raising thunder-crashes resounded, and in the blazing quarter, O lord of kings, beasts cried out their ill-boding cries.
The waters in the wells swelled up on every side, and great bodiless voices were heard then, O king.
Having beheld these and like portents, Vṛkodara spoke to his eldest brother, Yudhiṣṭhira the King of Righteousness:
"This dull-witted Suyodhana cannot vanquish me in battle. Today I shall loose upon Suyodhana, lord of the Kauravas, the wrath long hidden in my heart—as the fire upon the Khāṇḍava forest."
"This day, O Pāṇḍava, I shall draw out the dart lodged in your heart, slaying with my mace this wicked one, the basest of the Kuru line."
"This day I shall fasten a garland woven of glory upon you, when I have slain this doer of evil deeds with my mace at the forefront of battle."
"This day I shall shatter his body into a hundred pieces with this mace; never again shall he enter the city called Vāraṇasāhvaya."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For the loosing of serpents upon my bed, for the giving of poison in my food, for the hurling down at Pramāṇakoṭi, for the burning in the house of lac;"
"for the mockery in the assembly-hall, for the seizing of all our wealth, for the year spent in hidden exile and the years dwelt in the forest, O sinless one—"
"this day, O best of the Bhāratas, I shall reach the end of all these sorrows; slaying him in a single day, I shall be free of my debt to myself."
"This day, O best of the Bhāratas, the life-span of the evil-minded, unrestrained son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is at an end—and the sight of his mother and father with it."
"This day this disgrace of the line of the Kuru king Śaṃtanu, abandoning life and fortune and kingdom, shall lie stretched upon the ground."
"And King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, hearing this day that his son has been slain by me, will recall that inauspicious deed born of Śakuni's counsel."
Having spoken thus, O tiger among kings, the valiant one took up his mace and stood ready for battle, like Śakra challenging Vṛtra.
Seeing him with mace upraised, peaked like Mount Kailāsa, Bhīmasena, wrathful once more, spoke thus to Duryodhana:
"Call to mind, then, that evil deed of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra's, and of yourself as well—what was done at Vāraṇāvata."
"And how Draupadī was tormented in the assembly-hall, though she was in her season; and how the king was cheated at dice by you and by the son of Subala."
"And the great grief we suffered in the forest through your doing, and in the city of Virāṭa, as though we had entered the wombs of others—for all of that I take requital this day. By good fortune you are now in my sight, O evil-minded one!"
"Through your doing the majestic son of Gaṅgā, foremost of chariot-warriors, lies slain upon a bed of arrows, struck down by the son of Yajñasena."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Droṇa is slain, and Karṇa, and the majestic Śalya too; and Śakuni, son of Subala, the kindler of the fire of this enmity, lies slain."
"The wicked herald who wrought Draupadī's torment is slain; and all your brothers, heroes and valiant fighters, are slain."
"These and many other kings have been slain because of you; and you too I shall slay this day with my mace—of this there is no doubt."
As Vṛkodara spoke thus aloud, O lord of kings, your son of unfailing prowess answered him without fear, O king:
"What use is all this boasting? Fight, Vṛkodara! This day I shall drive out of you your appetite for battle, O disgrace of your line!"
"Duryodhana, O base one, is not to be frightened with words by any of your sort, as some common man might be."
"By good fortune the gods have brought to pass this thing long desired and set in my heart—this mace-combat with you."
"What use is much talk and boasting, O evil-minded one? Let this speech of yours be made good by deeds—do not delay any longer."
Hearing those words of his, all the kings and the Somakas who had gathered and were present there acclaimed him.
Then, honored by all, his body-hairs bristling with delight, the delight of the Kurus once more set his mind, resolute, upon battle.
With clapping of palms the lords of men spurred on once more that wrathful Duryodhana, like a maddened elephant.
Then the great-souled Pāṇḍava Vṛkodara, raising his mace, rushed with great speed upon the great-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
There the elephants trumpeted and the horses neighed again and again, and the weapons of the Pāṇḍavas, eager for victory, blazed forth.
Saṃjaya said: Then Duryodhana, seeing Bhīmasena come on in this wise, undismayed in spirit, rushed to meet him with great speed, roaring aloud.
Bellowing, the two closed upon each other like a pair of horned bulls, and their clash arose with the din of a great thunderbolt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And there arose between them a tumultuous, hair-raising combat, each seeking to vanquish the other in battle, like Indra and Prahrāda of old.
Their every limb drenched in blood, maces in hand, those resolute and great-souled ones appeared like two kiṃśuka trees in full bloom.
As that great and most terrible combat went on, the field shone lovely to behold, as though the sky were thronged with fireflies.
As that fierce and tumultuous melee raged on, both of those tamers of foes, fighting hard, grew weary.
Having rested for a moment, those two scorchers of foes, gripping fast their gleaming maces, once again fell to striking each other there.
Beholding those two bulls among men of mighty valor, rested and rejoined, like two powerful elephants frenzied with rut for the sake of a cow-elephant—
gazing upon those two of boundless valor, both with maces upraised, the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas fell into utmost wonder.
Seeing Duryodhana and Vṛkodara with maces upraised, doubt arose in all beings as to which should win.
Closing once more, those two kinsmen, the foremost of the strong, each seeking an opening in the other, maneuvered for an opening against the other.
The onlookers beheld, O king, the heavy mace, like the staff of Yama, raised on high like the thunderbolt of Indra—fierce and death-dealing.
As Bhīmasena whirled his mace in the encounter, a most tumultuous and dreadful sound arose for a moment.
Watching the Pāṇḍava as he whirled that mace of no slight force, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was filled with wonder.
And weaving through manifold movements and circling figures, O Bhārata, the hero Vṛkodara then shone forth all the more.
Closing with one another, each warding off the other, those two hacked away again and again, like two cats fighting over a morsel.
And Bhīmasena ranged through movements of many kinds, and varied circlings, and stances of every sort.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the zigzag steps, the varied passes, the advance and retreat, the parrying of blows, the evasion, and the circling run;
the charge, the feint, the firm stand with its grapple, the wheeling and the closing, the leap aside and the leap forward, the laying on of the mace and the drawing of it back—so skilled were the two in mace-combat.
Thus ranging about, those two best of the Kurus struck at each other, and feinting again, the two moved on.
Disporting themselves, the two mighty ones wheeled through their circling figures; then those two strong ones, maces in hand, took their stand in the circle.
To the rightward circle, O king, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra moved, while Bhīmasena there moved to the leftward circle.
And as Bhīma moved thus at the forefront of battle, Duryodhana, O great king, struck him upon the region of his flank.
Struck thus by your son, O Bhārata, Bhīma, heedless of the blow, whirled his heavy mace aloft.
Terrible as Indra's thunderbolt, lifted like the rod of Yama, that mace of Bhīmasena, O great king, the onlookers beheld.
Seeing Bhīmasena whirling his mace, your son, that tamer of foes, raised his own dreadful mace and whirled it back in answer.
From the wind-swift sweep of your son's mace, O Bhārata, a tremendous roar arose, and a blaze of splendor was kindled.
Ranging through manifold paths and tracing his circling figures one by one, the radiant Suyodhana shone forth even more brilliantly than Bhīma.
Whirled with all his might by Bhīma, that great and fearsome mace, loud-roaring, shot forth fire wreathed in smoke and flame.
Seeing the mace brandished by Bhīmasena, Suyodhana, whirling his own heavy mace hard as the heart of a mountain, shone resplendent.
Beholding the wind-swift speed of that great soul's mace, fear entered all the Pāṇḍavas together with the Somakas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Displaying on every side their battle-sport upon the field, those two tamers of foes struck at each other all at once with their maces.
Closing upon each other like two tuskers clashing with their tusks, the pair, O great king, drenched in blood, shone splendidly.
Thus did that battle rage, dreadful of aspect and unrestrained, savage as the day declined, like the war of Vṛtra and Vāsava.
Seeing Bhīma standing firm, your mighty son, ranging through ever more wondrous paths, rushed upon the son of Kuntī.
As that furious one charged, the enraged Bhīma struck down his mace, swift-driven and adorned with gold.
From the clash of the two there arose a roar shot through with sparks, O great king, as of two thunderbolts hurled together.
As that swift mace, loosed by Bhīmasena, came hurtling down, O great king, the earth itself trembled.
The Kaurava brooked not the parrying of his mace in battle, enraged like a maddened elephant at the sight of a rival bull.
Wheeling to the left, O king, his purpose set, he smote the son of Kuntī upon the head with his fearsomely swift mace.
Yet struck by it, the Pāṇḍava Bhīma, smitten by your son, did not waver, O great king — a thing well-nigh marvelous.
And all the armies, O king, applauded that wonder — that Bhīma, struck by the mace, did not stir a single step.
Then Bhīma of terrible prowess hurled at Duryodhana his blazing, gold-wrought mace, heavier still.
Unflustered, the mighty Duryodhana by his nimbleness made that blow miss its mark, and great was the wonder thereat.
That mace, O king, gone wide as it fell, driven by Bhīma, shook the earth with a sound like a mighty thunderclap.
Taking to the Kauśika maneuvers, leaping up again and again, and foreseeing the descent of the mace, he eluded Bhīmasena.
Having thus baffled Bhīma, that best of the Kurus, mighty and enraged, struck him with his mace upon the chest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Struck by the mace and reeling in that great battle, Bhīma, smitten by your son, could not for the moment think what next to do.
As things so stood, O king, the Somakas and the Pāṇḍavas, their hopes sorely shaken, grew downcast at heart.
But he, goaded by that blow like a maddened elephant, rushed elephant-like upon your son, himself like an elephant.
Then the impetuous Bhīma, with his mace, charged your son at full speed, as a lion charges a wild forest elephant.
Closing in upon the king, skilled in the casting of the mace, he whirled it, O king, aiming straight at your son.
Bhīmasena struck Duryodhana then upon the flank, and he, staggered by the blow, sank to the earth upon his knees.
When that best of the Bhāratas had sunk to the ground upon his knees, a great shout went up from the Sṛñjayas, O lord of the world.
Hearing that roar of the Sṛñjayas, that bull among men, your son, O best of the Bhāratas, blazed up in fury.
Rising up, the mighty-armed one, enraged and hissing like a serpent, gazed upon Bhīmasena as though to burn him with his eyes.
Then that best of the Bhāratas, mace in hand, rushed forward as if to crush Bhīmasena's head in the fray.
That great soul, of terrible prowess, struck the great-souled Bhīma upon the temple, yet, mountain-like, Bhīma only swayed.
Struck by the mace in battle, the son of Pṛthā shone all the more, O king, his blood gushing forth, like a rutting elephant whose temples flow.
Then, seizing his hero-slaying mace of iron, roaring like the thunderbolt, the elder brother of Dhanaṃjaya, grinder of foes, sprang forth with all his might and smote his enemy.
Struck by Bhīmasena, your son fell, the very knitting of his frame shaken loose, like a great flowering sāla tree in a vast forest, reeling under the force of the storm-wind.
Then the Pāṇḍavas roared and rejoiced, beholding your son fallen to the earth; but your son, regaining his senses, sprang up again like an elephant rising from a lake.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That king, ever brooking no defeat, the great chariot-warrior, wheeling about with the grace of one well-schooled, struck the Pāṇḍava who stood before him; and Bhīma, his limbs faltering, touched the ground.
The Kaurava raised a lion's roar, having felled Bhīma to the ground in battle by his might, and with a mace-blow blazing like the thunderbolt he split asunder Bhīma's body-armor.
Then in the sky a great clamor arose from the dwellers of heaven and the apsarases as they cried out, and from on high, sent down by the immortals, there fell a glorious rain, a shower of heaped and wondrous blossoms.
Then the utmost fear seized the foe, beholding that best of men fallen to the ground, and the Kaurava in no wise diminished in his strength, and hearing how the stout armor had been cloven.
Then in a moment Vṛkodara recovered his senses, wiped his own face wet with blood, gathered his resolve, and, his eyes rolling, steadied himself by main strength and stood firm.
Saṃjaya said: Then, beholding the battle of the two foremost Kurus swelling to its height, Arjuna spoke to the illustrious Vāsudeva.
"Of these two heroes in combat, which do you deem the greater? And in which is the larger merit? Tell me this, Janārdana."
Vāsudeva said: "The training of the two is equal, yet Bhīma is the stronger; but this son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is more practiced in his art than Vṛkodara."
"Bhīmasena, fighting by the rules, will not prevail; but fighting by unfair means, he may yet slay Suyodhana."
"By guile the gods overcame the asuras — so have we heard; and Virocana too was overcome by Śakra through guile, my friend. By guile, moreover, the slayer of Bala wrested away the energy of Vṛtra."
"And Bhīma vowed at the time of the dicing, O Dhanaṃjaya, saying to Suyodhana: 'In battle I will shatter your thighs with the mace.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let this grinder of foes, then, make good that vow, and cut down by guile this guileful king."
"For if, relying on his strength, he strikes by fair means, then King Yudhiṣṭhira will be left in dire straits."
"And once more I tell you, O Pāṇḍava — mark this from me: through the fault of the Dharma-king, peril has come upon us again."
"Having wrought a most mighty deed, having slain the Kurus led by Bhīṣma, you have won victory and foremost fame, and the feud is requited; yet now that very victory, once gained, has been cast again into doubt."
"This was a great folly of the Dharma-king, O Pāṇḍava — that he staked the whole on a single combat of this kind; for Suyodhana is skilled and valiant, a man with nothing to lose, brought to his last resort."
"Moreover, there is heard an ancient verse sung by Uśanas, freighted with the truth of things — hear it as I recite it to you."
"Of broken foes who turn back again, clinging to life, the last remnant must be feared, for they are come to their final stand."
"This Suyodhana — broken, his army slain, gone to take refuge in the lake, defeated, longing for the forest, despairing of regaining his kingdom —"
"what man of sense would summon him afresh to single combat in battle? Might not Suyodhana yet snatch back from you the kingdom already won?"
"For thirteen years has he labored with the mace, and he ranges high and crosswise in his eagerness to slay Bhīmasena."
"And so, if the mighty-armed one slay him not by unfair means, this Kaurava, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, will yet become your king."
And Dhanaṃjaya, hearing this from the great-souled Keśava, struck his own thigh with his hand within Bhīmasena's sight.
Taking the sign, Bhīma then ranged the battlefield with his mace, tracing wondrous circling figures, both paired and single.
The rightward circle, the leftward, and the zigzag course as well, the Pāṇḍava traced, O king, as though to bewilder his foe.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In like manner your son too, skilled in the ways of the mace, ranged nimbly and intricately in his eagerness to slay Bhīmasena.
Brandishing their dreadful maces, smeared with sandal and aloe, seeking to make an end of their enmity, the two were in battle like Death himself enraged.
Seeking each the other's death, those two foremost heroes, bulls among men, fought like two Garuḍas striving after the flesh of serpents.
As the king and Bhīma traced their wondrous circling figures, there sprang up from the clashing of their maces tongues of fire.
As the two valiant and mighty ones struck alike in the fray, they were, O king, like two oceans churned up by the wind.
As the two struck evenly, like a pair of rutting elephants, there arose a crashing thunder of mace-strokes from their blows.
In that fierce and tumultuous combat, both those tamers of foes, fighting on, grew sorely spent.
Resting a moment, those two scorchers of foes, enraged once more, gripped their great maces and fell upon each other again.
There arose between them a battle dreadful of aspect and unrestrained, O lord of kings, as with falling maces they hewed at one another.
Hurtling forward in their exertion, those two swift and bull-eyed heroes smote at each other like buffaloes mired in the mud.
Their every limb battered and bruised, drenched all over in blood, the two appeared like a pair of kiṃśuka trees in bloom upon the Himālaya.
When Duryodhana had laid open an opening, the son of Pṛthā, smiling a little, all at once sprang forward.
Seeing him come within reach in the battle, the wise and mighty Vṛkodara hurled his mace down at him with tremendous force.
But seeing that descending stroke, your son, O lord of peoples, slipped aside from his place, and the mace fell wide upon the ground.
Having made that blow miss in his swift recovery, your son, that best of the Kurus, struck Bhīmasena in turn with his mace.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With the blood streaming from him and from the heavy fall of that blow, a swoon, as it were, came over the immeasurably mighty Bhīma.
Duryodhana knew that the Pāṇḍava had been wounded in the battle; yet Bhīma too held up his sorely battered body.
Your son thought him to be standing ready and about to strike in the fray, and for that reason he did not smite him again.
Then, after recovering for a moment, O king, the valiant Bhīmasena rushed with great speed upon Duryodhana, who stood his ground.
Seeing him of measureless might charging in fury, O bull of the Bhāratas, your son wished to make that blow of his fall in vain.
Setting his mind firmly in his stance, your high-souled son resolved to leap upward, O king, meaning to outwit Vṛkodara.
Bhīmasena perceived the king's intent, and so, rushing upon him and bounding forward like a lion,
as the king deceived him by his footwork and was again about to spring up, the Pāṇḍava hurled his mace with great force at his thighs, O king.
Cast by him of dreadful deeds, that mace, like the crash of a thunderbolt, shattered both the comely thighs of Duryodhana.
That tiger among men fell, making the earth resound, his thighs broken by Bhīmasena—your son, O lord of the earth.
Winds blew with thunderclaps, a rain of dust fell, and the earth trembled with its trees, shrubs, and mountains.
When that hero fell, the lord of all earthly kings, a great blazing meteor, loud-roaring, attended by thunderclaps and terrible to behold, fell as the master of the earth went down.
So too, O Bhārata, Maghavan rained down a rain of blood and a rain of dust there, when your son was struck down.
A great roar of Yakṣas, of Rākṣasas, and of Piśācas as well was heard in the sky, O bull of the Bhāratas.
At that dreadful sound there arose from many beasts and birds a still more dreadful cry on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those horses and elephants that remained there, together with the men, let loose a mighty clamor when your son fell.
And a great sound of kettledrums, conches, and tabors arose, even from beneath the earth, when your son was struck down.
The quarters were then filled, O king, with headless trunks—many-footed, many-armed, fearful to behold—that danced about and spread terror.
Those bearing standards, those bearing missiles, and those bearing weapons all began to tremble then, O king, when your son was struck down.
Lakes and wells vomited forth blood, O best of kings, and rivers of mighty current began to flow backward against their streams.
Women took on, as it were, the marks of men, and men the marks of women, when your son Duryodhana fell, O king.
Beholding those wondrous portents, the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas all became troubled in mind, O bull of the Bhāratas.
The gods departed at their pleasure, and the Gandharvas and Apsarases likewise, recounting the wondrous combat of your sons, O Bhārata.
