So too the Siddhas, O king of kings, and the wandering Cāraṇas, praising those two lions among men, departed each the way he had come.
Saṃjaya said: Seeing him laid low, like a towering sāla tree felled, all the Pāṇḍavas there became glad at heart.
Like a maddened elephant struck down by a lion they beheld him; and all those Somakas too, their hair bristling with joy, looked on.
Then, having struck down Duryodhana, the valiant Bhīmasena drew near to the fallen lord of the Kauravas and spoke these words:
"'Cow! Cow!'—O fool, when of old in the assembly you laughed and mocked us and Draupadī clad in a single garment, O wicked-minded one: of that mockery receive this day the fruit!"
Having spoken thus, with his left foot he touched the diadem, and with that foot he spurned the head of the lion among kings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And then, red with wrath, Bhīma the crusher of hostile hosts spoke once more these words; hear them, O ruler of men.
"Those who once danced before us crying again and again 'Cow! Cow!'—those we now dance against, crying once more 'Cow! Cow!'"
"In us there is no treachery, no fire of arson, no dicing, no deceit; relying on the strength of our own arms, we crush our foes."
Having reached the far shore of his supreme enmity, Vṛkodara, laughing softly, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, to Keśava and the Sṛñjayas, to Dhanaṃjaya, and to the two sons of Mādrī:
"Those who dragged Draupadī in while she was in her courses, and those who in the assembly stripped her of her garment—behold those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, slain in battle by the Pāṇḍavas through the ascetic merit of the daughter of Yajñasena!"
"Those cruel sons of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra who once called us barren sesame seeds—they are slain by us with their followers and kin; now let us go, if it must be, to heaven or to hell."
And again, as the king lay fallen on the ground, he—gazing at the mace resting on his shoulder, and crushing the head with his left foot—called Duryodhana a worker of deceit.
But when, O king, they saw the foot set upon the head of the Kuru king by the exultant, base-minded Bhīmasena, the righteous chiefs of the Somakas did not rejoice.
As Vṛkodara, having thus slain your son, boasted and danced about again and again, the Dharma King spoke these words:
"Crush not his head with your foot, lest your great righteousness pass away. He is a king and a kinsman, and now slain; this is not seemly for you, O blameless one."
"He is undone, his counselors slain, his brothers slain, his offspring slain, his line's oblations cut off—and he is our brother; this you have done is not seemly."
"'This Bhīmasena is a righteous man,' so people once spoke of you. Why then, Bhīmasena, do you set your foot upon a king?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing Duryodhana brought to such a state, King Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, with eyes brimming with tears spoke these words:
"Surely this was ordained by the mighty, high-souled Ordainer—that we should seek to slay you, and you us, O best of the Kurus."
"For through your own fault you have met with so great a calamity, born of greed, of pride, and of folly, O Bhārata."
"Having caused the death of your companions, your brothers, your fathers, your sons, your grandsons, and your teachers, you have come at last to your own destruction."
"Through your fault we have slain your brothers, those great chariot-warriors, and your other kinsmen too; I deem destiny hard to overcome."
"The daughters-in-law and granddaughters-in-law of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, distraught and widowed, wasted with grief, will surely reproach us."
Having spoken thus, that king, sore afflicted with grief, sighed deeply; and Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, lamented long.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Seeing the king slain by unrighteous means, what then, O bard, did the foremost of the Mādhavas, the mighty Baladeva, say?
He who knew the finer points of mace-combat, skilled in mace-combat—the son of Rohiṇī—what he did, that recount to me, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Seeing your son struck on the head by Bhīmasena, Rāma, the strongest of strikers and mighty himself, blazed up in great wrath.
Then in the midst of the kings, the plough-wielder, raising his arms aloft and uttering a fierce cry of anguish, said: "Shame, shame upon you, Bhīma!"
"Alas, shame, that a blow was struck below the navel in a contest of pure valor! Never has it been seen in mace-combat, this which Vṛkodara has done."
"'One must not strike below the navel'—such is the ruling of the treatises; but this fool, ignorant of the treatises, acts after his own willful pleasure."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As he spoke thus again and again, a great fury arose in him; then, raising his plough, the mighty one rushed upon Bhīma.
With his arms raised aloft, the form of that high-souled one was like a great white mountain, gleaming with manifold mineral hues.
As he sprang forward, Keśava, bowed in humility yet powerful and strong, caught hold of him with effort in his round, brawny arms.
The two best of the Yādavas, the fair one and the dark, shone forth then exceedingly, O king, like the moon and the sun risen together in the sky at the day's end.
And Keśava, as if to calm that infuriated one, said to him: "One's own increase, the increase of one's friend, and the rising of one's friend's friend—and the reverse of these among one's foes: such is the sixfold increase of one's own self."
"When in oneself and in one's friends the contrary should come to pass, one should recognize the decline of one's purpose and quickly become a maker of peace."
"The Pāṇḍavas, of pure manhood, are our natural friends; they are our own, the sons of our father's sister, and they have been grievously wronged by their foes."
"The fulfillment of a vow is the duty of a Kṣatriya—this you know. 'I shall shatter Suyodhana's thighs with my mace in the great battle'—this was vowed of old by Bhīma upon the floor of the assembly."
"And he was cursed long before by the great seer Maitreya: 'Bhīma shall break your thighs with his mace,' O scorcher of foes. Therefore I see no fault here; be not wroth, O slayer of Pralamba."
"By ties of marriage and of the heart we are bound here to the Pāṇḍavas; in their prosperity is our own prosperity. Be not wroth, O bull among men."
Rāma said: "Righteousness, well practiced by the good, keeps in check the other two—wealth in the case of one too greedy for gain, and pleasure in the case of one too much addicted to it."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"He who pursues righteousness and wealth, righteousness and pleasure, pleasure and wealth—nay, righteousness, wealth, and pleasure together—without letting one injure another, attains supreme happiness."
"But all this has been thrown into disorder by the injury done to righteousness by Bhīmasena, O Govinda—however much you may speak to me as you do."
Vāsudeva said: "Free from anger, righteous of soul, ever cherishing righteousness—so are you renowned in the world. Therefore grow calm; be not wroth."
"Know that the Kali age has come, and remember the Pāṇḍava's vow; let the Pāṇḍava be quit of his debt of enmity and of his vow alike."
Saṃjaya said: Hearing even this quibble upon righteousness from Keśava, O lord of peoples, Rāma, his mind not at all pleased, spoke these words in the assembly:
"Having slain by unrighteousness the king Suyodhana, a man of righteous soul, the Pāṇḍava will gain renown in this world as a crooked fighter."
"Duryodhana too, a righteous soul, will attain the everlasting goal—a king who fought straight, slain though he was, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, ruler of men."
"Having entered upon the consecration of battle, having spread out the sacrifice of war, and having offered himself as oblation in the fire of his foes, he has won the glory of the final ablution."
Having spoken thus, the valiant son of Rohiṇī, in form like the peak of a white cloud, mounted his chariot and set out toward Dvārakā.
And the Pāñcālas with the Vārṣṇeyas, and the Pāṇḍavas, O lord of peoples, when Rāma had departed for Dvāravatī, were not greatly pleased at heart.
Then Vāsudeva spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira, who was downcast, sunk in thought, his face bent low, his resolve stricken by grief:
"O Dharma King, why do you countenance this unrighteousness—done to this man whose kin are slain, who lies fallen and bereft of sense?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Why do you look on, knowing righteousness as you do, O ruler of men, while Duryodhana's head is crushed by Bhīma's foot?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "This is not pleasing to me, Kṛṣṇa, that Vṛkodara in his wrath touched a king's head with his foot; nor do I rejoice in the ruin of our house."
"By deceit were we ever deceived by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; with many a harsh word spoken, we were sent away into the forest."
"That grief of Bhīmasena's dwells exceedingly in his heart; reflecting upon this, O Vārṣṇeya, I overlooked this deed."
Therefore, now that this man of feeble wits, greedy and a slave to his desires, has been slain, let the Pāṇḍava have his heart's wish—whether what was done was righteous or unrighteous.
Saṃjaya said: When the King of Righteousness had spoken thus, Vāsudeva, the upholder of the Yadu line, said only with difficulty, "So be it; let it be as you wish."
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, who sought Bhīma's welfare and delight, Yudhiṣṭhira approved of all that Bhīma had done in the battle.
And Bhīmasena, the wrathful one, having slain your son in battle, stood before Yudhiṣṭhira, saluted him, and, filled with joy, folded his palms in reverence.
O lord of peoples, that hero of mighty splendour, his eyes wide with gladness and wearing the look of a victor, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Righteousness.
"Today the earth is yours, O king, made secure and freed of every thorn. Govern it, O great king, upholding your own sacred duty."
"He who was the author of this enmity, the lover of deceit who delighted in treachery—he now lies slain upon the earth, O lord of the earth."
"Duḥśāsana and all the rest, those harsh of speech, Rādheya too, and Śakuni—all your foes have been struck down."
"This earth, strewn with jewels, with its forests and its mountains, has this day returned to you, O great king, now that your enemies are slain."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The end of the feud has come; King Suyodhana is slain. Following the counsel of Kṛṣṇa, this earth has been won.
By good fortune you have discharged your debt both to our mother and to her wrath; by good fortune you are victorious, O unassailable one; by good fortune the enemy has been cast down.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When they beheld Duryodhana slain by Bhīmasena in the combat, what did the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas do, O Saṃjaya?
Saṃjaya said: When they beheld Duryodhana slain by Bhīmasena in the combat, O great king, as a lion slays a rutting wild elephant in the forest—
there, with their hearts rejoicing, the Pāṇḍavas together with Kṛṣṇa, and the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas, when the joy of the Kurus had been slain—
whirled their upper garments and roared their lion-roars; so filled with joy were they that the earth itself could scarcely bear them.
Some brandished their bows, and others twanged their bowstrings; some blew their great conches, and others beat their kettledrums.
Still others sported and laughed, those foes of yours, and again and again the heroes spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"A hard deed, a very great deed, have you accomplished in battle this day, slaying with your mace the lord of the Kauravas, worn out as he was by his exertions."
As Indra slew Vṛtra in the supreme combat, so the people deemed this slaying of the foe to have been wrought by you.
"This brave Duryodhana, who ranged through manifold paths and wheeled in every circling movement—who other than Vṛkodara could have slain him?"
"You have reached the far shore of this enmity, a shore beyond the reach of others here; such a feat as this no other could have brought to pass."
"As by a rutting tusker, O hero, at the head of the fray, by good fortune Duryodhana's head has been crushed by your foot."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"As a lion does with a buffalo, having waged a wondrous battle, by good fortune the blood of Duḥśāsana was drunk by you, O blameless one."
"Those who wronged King Yudhiṣṭhira, the soul of righteousness—upon their heads, by your own deeds and by good fortune, your foot has been set."
"By the overthrow of your enemies and by the slaying of Duryodhana, O Bhīma, by good fortune your vast renown is spread abroad over the earth."
"Surely, as the bards rejoiced over Śakra when Vṛtra was slain, so we rejoice over you, your foe destroyed, O descendant of Bharata."
"The hairs upon our bodies that bristled with joy at the slaying of Duryodhana—know, O descendant of Bharata, that even now they will not lie down again." So the praise-singers gathered there spoke to Bhīmasena.
To those exultant tigers among men, the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas, who spoke words befitting the moment, Madhusūdana then said:
"It is not fitting, O lords of men, to slay again and again an enemy already slain. This dullard has indeed already been struck down by your harsh words."
"This wicked man was slain at that very moment when, shameless, greedy, the companion of the wicked, he transgressed the counsel of his friends."
"Though urged again and again by Vidura, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Gaṅgā, and the Sṛñjayas, he would not grant the Pāṇḍavas their ancestral share."
"This basest of men is no longer fit to be reckoned friend or foe. What use is it to keep reviling with words one who has become as a senseless log of wood?"
"Mount your chariots swiftly; let us depart, O lords of the earth. By good fortune this evil-souled one is slain, together with his counsellors, his kinsmen, and his allies."
But hearing this reproach from Kṛṣṇa, King Duryodhana, overcome with indignation, raised himself up, O lord of peoples.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seated upon his haunches, propping himself against the earth with both arms, he knit his brows into a frown and cast his gaze upon Vāsudeva.
The form of the king, his body half upraised, was then like that of an angered venomous serpent whose tail had been severed, O descendant of Bharata.
Heedless of the dreadful, life-ending agony, Duryodhana assailed Vāsudeva with savage words:
"O heir of the slave of Kaṃsa, have you no shame for this, that by unrighteous means I have been brought down in the mace-duel?"
"Do you think I did not perceive how, treacherously prompting Bhīma's memory, you said to Arjuna, 'Smash his thighs'?"
"Having caused thousands of kings who fought fairly to be slain by many crooked devices—have you no shame, no remorse?"
"Day after day, as he wrought great slaughter among heroes, your grandsire was made to be slain by you, with Śikhaṇḍin set in the forefront."
"By slaying the elephant that bore the same name as Aśvatthāman, O most wicked one, the preceptor was made to lay down his weapons—do you think this is unknown to me?"
"And when that valiant one was being struck down by this cruel Dhṛṣṭadyumna, you looked on and did not restrain him."
"The very spear that was begged for, meant for the slaying of the son of Pāṇḍu, you caused to be wasted upon Ghaṭotkaca. Who is a greater doer of evil than you?"
"His arm severed, set upon the vow of fasting unto death, the mighty Bhūriśravas was slain at your bidding by the vile descendant of Śini."
"And Karṇa, performing a deed of the highest valour in his longing to vanquish Pārtha, was thwarted through the wasting of the arrow that was Aśvasena, son of the lord of serpents—"
"and again, when his chariot wheel sank down, that foremost of men, Karṇa, struck by calamity and overcome, distracted with his wheel, was cast down in the combat."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Had you fought fairly against me and against Karṇa, against Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle, victory would surely never have been yours."
"But by you, ignoble one, through crooked ways were we and other kings, who kept to our own sacred duty, brought to destruction."
Vāsudeva said: O son of Gāndhārī, you have been slain together with your brothers, your sons, and your kinsmen, your followers and your friends, because you trod the path of wickedness.
It was by your own misdeeds that the heroes Bhīṣma and Droṇa were laid low, and Karṇa too, who followed your ways, was slain in the encounter.
Though entreated by me, O fool, you would not give the Pāṇḍavas their ancestral share, the half of their own kingdom, out of greed and at Śakuni's resolve.
You administered poison to Bhīmasena, and all the Pāṇḍavas, together with their mother, you sought to burn in the house of lac, O most wicked one.
And the daughter of Yajñasena, in her courses, was dragged into the assembly hall at the dicing—even then, O evil-souled and shameless one, you deserved to be killed.
Because, with the dice-cunning son of Subala, you by treachery defeated one who knew righteousness but knew nothing of the dice—for that you have been slain in battle.
Because, when they had gone hunting, Kṛṣṇā was tormented in the forest by the wicked Jayadratha at the hermitage of Tṛṇabindu—
and because Abhimanyu, a mere boy, alone amid many in the fray, was slain through your misdeeds, O wicked one—for that you have been slain in battle.
Duryodhana said: I have studied as the rule prescribes, I have given gifts duly, I have ruled the earth with its girdling seas, I have stood upon the heads of my enemies—who then has come to a happier end than I?
That very death which is the wish of warriors who keep their own sacred duty in view—that death I have now attained. Who then has come to a happier end than I?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Pleasures worthy of the gods, such mortal joys as kings can scarcely win, I have enjoyed; sovereignty supreme I have attained. Who then has come to a happier end than I?
With my friends and my followers I shall go to heaven, O Acyuta; while you, your purposes shattered, shall live on in grief.
Saṃjaya said: At the close of this speech of the king of the Kurus, O descendant of Bharata, a great shower of sweet-scented flowers fell down.
The Gandharvas made music and the throngs of Apsarases sang, and the Siddhas uttered their voices, crying "Well done! Well done!", O descendant of Bharata.
And a fragrant breeze blew, holy-scented, gentle and pleasant, and the spotless sky shone forth, gleaming like a sapphire.
Beholding these wondrous portents, and seeing the honour shown to Duryodhana, those led by Vāsudeva were overcome with shame.
And hearing that they had been slain unrighteously, they grieved, stricken with sorrow, for Bhīṣma and Droṇa, for Karṇa, and for Bhūriśravas.
But seeing the Pāṇḍavas sunk in thought and downcast in spirit, Kṛṣṇa, whose voice was as the thunder of the clouds, spoke these words:
"This swift-handed warrior, and all those great chariot-heroes, valiant as they were, could not have been slain by you in fair fight upon the field."
"These stratagems were therefore devised by me, O lords of men; otherwise the sons of Pāṇḍu would never anywhere have won the victory."
"For those four great-souled warriors, mightiest of charioteers upon the earth, could not by righteous means have been slain even by the guardians of the worlds themselves."
"And likewise this son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, mace in hand and unwearied, could not by righteous means have been slain even by Death himself, the wielder of the rod."
"Nor should you take it to heart that this king was struck down. When the enemies are many and overpowering, they must be slain by stratagem and craft."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This is the path followed of old by the gods who slew the Asuras; the road that the good have trodden is the road that all men follow."
"Our task is accomplished; let us settle upon our lodging now in the evening. Let us all rest, O lords of men, with our horses, elephants, and chariots."
Hearing the words of Vāsudeva, the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas, exceedingly gladdened, then roared like a pride of lions.
Then those bulls among men, rejoicing to see Duryodhana slain, blew their conches, and Mādhava blew the Pāñcajanya.
Saṃjaya said: Then all those rulers of the earth set forth toward their lodging, blowing their conches in their joy, their arms like iron bludgeons.
And as the Pāṇḍavas were going to our camp, O lord of peoples, the great archer Yuyutsu followed behind them, and Sātyaki as well.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, and the sons of Draupadī, one and all, and all the other great archers, went each to his own encampment.
Then the sons of Pṛthā entered the camp of Duryodhana, its splendour quenched and its lord slain, like a theatre when the people have dispersed.
It was like a city whose festival had ended, like a pool from which the elephant had been carried off—thronged for the most part with women, and watched over by aged ministers.
There, O king, those who had once gone before Duryodhana waited upon them, their palms joined in supplication, clad in soiled ochre garments.
Having reached the camp of the Kuru king, the Pāṇḍavas, those foremost of chariot-warriors, descended from their chariots, O great king.
Then Keśava, ever devoted to his welfare and his good, addressed the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, O bull of the Bhāratas.
"Lay down the Gāṇḍīva and the two inexhaustible great quivers; afterward I too shall descend, O best of the Bhāratas."
"And do you yourself dismount; this is for your good, O blameless one." And so the hero Dhanaṃjaya, son of Pāṇḍu, did just that.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then afterward the wise Kṛṣṇa, releasing the reins of the horses, descended from the chariot of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva.
And when the lord of beings, that great-souled one, had stepped down, the divine ape-banner of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva vanished from sight.
That mighty chariot, scorched by Droṇa and Karṇa with their divine weapons, then, kindled by fire, blazed up at once, O lord of the earth.
With its quivers, its reins, its horses, its yoke and chariot-pole, the chariot of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, reduced to ashes, fell to the ground.
Seeing it thus turned to ashes, the sons of Pāṇḍu were filled with wonder, O lord; and Arjuna, O king, spoke these words.
With joined palms, affectionately bowing down and saluting him: "Govinda, blessed lord, why was this chariot consumed by fire?"
"What is this great marvel that has come to pass, O delight of the Yadus? Tell me of it, mighty-armed one, if you deem it fit for me to hear."
Vāsudeva said: This chariot had already been burned by weapons of many kinds, O Arjuna; yet because I occupied it, it did not break apart in battle, O scorcher of foes.
But now, scorched by the fiery power of the Brahmā-weapon, it has crumbled, for I have released it today, O son of Kuntī, now that your task is accomplished.
Saṃjaya said: And the blessed Keśava, slayer of foes, smiling faintly, embraced King Yudhiṣṭhira and spoke to him.
"By good fortune you are victorious, O son of Kuntī; by good fortune your foes are conquered; by good fortune the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava are well."
"And you too are safe, O king, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī; delivered from this slaughter of heroes, your enemies slain, swiftly perform the rites that now remain to be done, O Bhārata."
"When I came to Upaplavya together with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, and you brought me the honey-offering, what you then said to me—"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'This Dhanaṃjaya is your brother and your friend, O Kṛṣṇa; he is to be guarded, mighty-armed one, in every peril, O lord'—and to you who spoke thus I answered, 'So be it.'"
"That ambidextrous archer has been guarded for you and is victorious, O lord of men; together with his brothers, O king of kings, that valiant one of truthful prowess is delivered from this slaughter of heroes, from this hair-raising battle."
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, the Dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira, the hair of his body bristling with joy, O great king, replied to Janārdana.
"The Brahmā-weapon let loose by Droṇa and by Karṇa, O crusher of foes—who other than you could withstand it, even Purandara the wielder of the thunderbolt in person?"
"By your grace many have been conquered in battle, and Pārtha, plunged into the great fray, never turned his face away."
"And likewise, mighty-armed one, through many turns of fortune I have seen the unbroken succession of deeds and the auspicious course of your splendor."
"At Upaplavya the great sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana said to me: 'Where there is righteousness, there is Kṛṣṇa; where Kṛṣṇa is, there is victory.'"
When this had been said, those heroes, having entered your camp, O Bhārata, took possession of the stores of treasure, jewels, and riches.
Silver and gold, gems and pearls, the finest ornaments, woolen blankets and deerskins, slave-women and slaves beyond counting, and the appurtenances of kingship.
Having obtained your inexhaustible wealth, O bull of the Bhāratas, those great archers, their foes conquered, raised a shout of triumph, O lord of men.
Then those heroes, having taken rest and unyoked their mounts, halted there awhile—all the Pāṇḍavas, and Sātyaki likewise.
Then, O great king, the illustrious Vāsudeva said: "For the sake of auspiciousness we must lodge outside the camp."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saying "So be it," all the Pāṇḍavas, and Sātyaki as well, together with Vāsudeva, went outside for the sake of auspiciousness.
Reaching the holy river Oghavatī, O king, the Pāṇḍavas, their enemies slain, passed that night there.
Then they dispatched the Yādava to the city named after the elephant; and the mighty Vāsudeva, mounting Dāruka upon his chariot, set out swiftly with all speed toward where the king, son of Ambikā, was.
As he was about to set forth, his steeds Sainya and Sugrīva yoked, they said to him: "Console Gāndhārī, the illustrious lady whose sons are slain."
Bidden by the Pāṇḍavas, that best of the Sātvatas set out for that city, eager to reach without delay Gāndhārī, whose sons had been slain.
Janamejaya said: For what reason did that tiger among kings, the Dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira, send Vāsudeva, scorcher of foes, to Gāndhārī?
When Kṛṣṇa had earlier gone for the sake of peace to the Kauravas and had not won that desire, then this war came to pass.
But now that the warriors were slain and Duryodhana likewise killed, and the earth made rivalless for the son of Pāṇḍu by the war,
the camp scattered and emptied, and the highest glory attained—what then was the reason, O brāhmaṇa, for which Kṛṣṇa went forth once more?
And this reason does not seem to me a small one, O brāhmaṇa, since the immeasurable Janārdana himself went there in person.
Recount it all to me truly, O best of officiating priests—the reason, O brāhmaṇa, that determined this undertaking.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: This further question that you ask of me is worthy of you, O prince; I shall declare it to you duly, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Seeing Duryodhana, the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, slain by Bhīmasena in the duel in transgression of the agreed rule, O king—
seeing him slain unfairly in the mace-combat, O Bhārata, a great fear then entered Yudhiṣṭhira, O great king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For he thought of the illustrious Gāndhārī, endowed with austerity—armed with dreadful penance, she could burn even the three worlds.
As he pondered, this thought then arose in him: the wrath of Gāndhārī, blazing with anger, must first be pacified.
"For she, hearing of such a slaying of her sons as we have wrought, will in her wrath reduce us to ashes with the fire of her mind."
"How will Gāndhārī endure this fierce grief, when she hears that her son, who fought without guile, was killed by a trick?"
Having pondered thus in many ways, filled with fear and grief, the Dharma-king addressed these words to Vāsudeva.
"By your grace, Govinda, the kingdom, its thorns destroyed—a thing unattainable even in thought—has here been won by us, O imperishable one."
"Before my own eyes, mighty-armed one, in that hair-raising battle, a most mighty struggle was undertaken by you, O delight of the Yādavas."
"As of old in the war of the gods and demons you lent your aid for the slaying of the foes of the immortals, and the enemies of the gods were destroyed,"
"so too, mighty-armed and imperishable one, you lent your aid to us; and by your charioteering, O Vārṣṇeya, we were upheld."
"Had you not been Phalguna's protector in the great battle, how could this ocean of armies have been conquered in the fray?"
"Vast blows of maces, and battering with iron bludgeons, with lances, slings, javelins, and battle-axes—"
"and harsh words too were endured by you who sought our good; and all these have borne fruit for you, now that Duryodhana is slain, O imperishable one."
"Be mindful, mighty-armed Mādhava, of the wrath of Gāndhārī; for that illustrious lady is ever wasted thin by fierce austerity."
"Hearing of the slaughter of her sons and grandsons, she will surely burn us up; her appeasement, O hero, is in my judgment now timely."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And what man, save you, O best of men, is able even to look upon her, her eyes blazing with anger, worn thin by the calamity of her sons?"
"To me it seems fitting that you go there, O Mādhava, if it please you, to pacify Gāndhārī, who is ablaze with wrath, O subduer of foes."
"For you are the maker and unmaker of the worlds, their origin and dissolution; with words joined to motive and cause and fitted to the occasion,"
"swiftly, O greatly wise one, will you calm Gāndhārī; and the venerable grandfather Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana too will be there."
"By every means, mighty-armed best of the Sātvatas, the quelling of Gāndhārī's wrath must be accomplished by you who seek the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas."
Hearing the words of the Dharma-king, the upholder of the Yadu line summoned Dāruka and said: "Let the chariot be made ready."
Hearing the words of Keśava, Dāruka then in haste reported to the great-souled Keśava that the chariot was ready.
Mounting that chariot, the best of the Yādavas, the scorcher of foes, the all-pervading Keśava, set out in haste for Hāstinapura.
Then, O great king, the blessed Mādhava, that chariot-warrior, set forth; and reaching the city named after the elephant, the valiant one entered it.
Entering the city, the hero, making it resound with the thunder of his chariot, and announced to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, descended from his splendid chariot.
With undejected spirit he approached the dwelling of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and there he saw the best of sages, who had come before.
Clasping the feet of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana and of the king as well, Janārdana, unperturbed, paid his respects; and Keśava saluted Gāndhārī too.
Then the best of the Yādavas, Adhokṣaja, taking hold of the king Dhṛtarāṣṭra's hand, wept aloud.
After shedding for a moment the tears born of grief, washing his eyes with water and sipping water as enjoined, the subduer of foes spoke humble words to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"There is nothing of past or future unknown to you, O Bhārata; and how the working of time has come to pass is well known to you, O lord."
"This was the very thing all the Pāṇḍavas, deferring to your wishes, strove for—that there might be no destruction of the lineage, nor of the warrior class, O Bhārata."
"Making a compact with his brothers, that lover of righteousness forbore; defeated by the trickery of the dice though they were able men, he submitted to dwelling in the forest."
"And the practice of living in concealment, cloaked in various disguises, and many other hardships besides, were borne ever, as though by men without power."
"And by me, coming in person when the hour of war was at hand, in the presence of all the world, you were asked for five villages."
"By you, smitten by time, out of greed they were not granted; and through your fault, O king, the whole warrior race has gone to destruction."
"By Bhīṣma, by Somadatta, by Bāhlika and Kṛpa, by Droṇa together with his son, and by the wise Vidura, you were ever entreated for peace; yet you did not make it."
For every man whose mind is overthrown by Time grows bewildered, O Bhārata, even as you yourself, deluded before, rose up in this very matter.
What else is there but the working of Time? Destiny alone is the final refuge. Lay not the blame, O great king, upon the Pāṇḍavas.
Not the slightest transgression is there in the great-souled Pāṇḍavas, neither in righteousness, nor in justice, nor in affection, O scorcher of foes.
Knowing all this to be the fruit wrought by your own fault, you ought not to harbor resentment against the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Your lineage, your line of descent, the funeral offering, and the fruit that a son procures — for both you and Gāndhārī all of these now rest upon the Pāṇḍavas.
Reflecting upon all this, and upon your own offense, turn your thoughts toward the Pāṇḍavas with goodwill. Homage to you, O bull of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You know full well, O mighty-armed one, O tiger of the Bhāratas, what devotion the Dharmarāja bears toward you, and what natural affection too.
Even having wrought this slaughter of the offending foe, he burns with grief day and night, and finds no peace at all.
Grieving for you, O tiger among men, and for the renowned Gāndhārī, O best of the Bhāratas, he finds no calm.
Overcome by the deepest shame, he dares not approach you — you who are consumed by sorrow for your sons, your senses confounded in mind.
Having spoken thus to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O great king, the foremost of the Yadus addressed these supreme words to Gāndhārī, wasted with grief.
O daughter of Subala, hear what I shall say to you, O woman of noble vows. There is no woman equal to you this day in all this world, O auspicious one.
I know, O queen, how in the assembly, in my presence, you spoke a word fraught with righteousness and gain, beneficial to both parties, O gracious lady — yet it was not heeded by your sons.
To Duryodhana, hungry for victory, you spoke a stern word: 'Hear my word, O fool — where righteousness is, there is victory.'
That word of yours, O daughter of a king, has now come wholly true. Knowing this, O gracious one, set not your mind upon grief, and let your thought never turn to the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas.
For you are able, O greatly blessed one, by the power of your austerities, to burn up the earth with all that moves and is unmoving, with an eye kindled by wrath.
Hearing the words of Vāsudeva, Gāndhārī spoke: 'It is even so, O mighty-armed one, as you say, O Keśava.'
My mind, scorched by anguish, had been set trembling; but now, hearing your word, O Janārdana, it has grown steadfast.
For this old, blind king, bereft of his sons, O Keśava, you are now the refuge, together with those heroes, the Pāṇḍavas, O best of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken only this much, covering her face with her garment, Gāndhārī, consumed with sorrow for her sons, broke into loud weeping.
Then the mighty-armed lord Keśava consoled her, wasted with grief, with words fraught with reason and argument.
And having comforted Gāndhārī and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Mādhava, Keśava, perceived the resolve that the son of Droṇa had conceived.
Then, rising in haste and bowing his head to the feet of Dvaipāyana, O lord of kings, he spoke thus to the Kaurava:
'I take my leave of you, O best of the Kurus; do not set your mind on grief. The son of Droṇa harbors an evil purpose, and for that reason have I risen up in haste; this night his mind has shown itself bent on the slaughter of the Pāṇḍavas.'
Hearing this word, the mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with Gāndhārī, spoke to Keśava, the slayer of Keśin:
'Go swiftly, O mighty-armed one, and guard the Pāṇḍavas; I shall meet with you again right soon, O Janārdana.' Then Acyuta set forth in haste, together with Dāruka.
When Vāsudeva had departed, O king, Vyāsa of measureless soul, revered by all the worlds, consoled Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men.
And Vāsudeva too, the righteous-souled, his purpose accomplished, set out from Hāstinapura toward the camp, desiring to behold the Pāṇḍavas, O king.
Reaching the camp by night, he came to the Pāṇḍavas, and having reported all to them, he settled down in their company.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: My son, his thighs shattered, fallen to the earth, his head trodden under foot, proud of his might — what words did he utter, O Saṃjaya?
That king, exceedingly prone to wrath and bearing inveterate enmity against the sons of Pāṇḍu, having met with utter ruin in that supreme combat — what did he say?
Saṃjaya said: Hear, O king; I shall relate it as it befell, O ruler of men — what was spoken by the broken king when that calamity had come upon him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With his thighs shattered, the king, O monarch, was covered over with dust; gathering up his hair, and gazing about at the ten directions,
binding up his hair with effort, hissing like a serpent, with eyes brimming with tears of fury he looked upon me,
and pounding his arms upon the ground again and again, like an elephant in rut, shaking his scattered locks, grinding tooth against tooth, reviling the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, he sighed and then spoke thus:
'With Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, as my protector, with Karṇa, foremost of those who bear arms, with Gautama and Śakuni too, and with Droṇa, foremost of those who bear arms —
with Aśvatthāman likewise, and Śalya, and the valiant Kṛtavarman — yet to this state have I come; for Time is hard indeed to overpass.'
'I, the lord of eleven armies, have come to this plight! When Time comes upon him, O mighty-armed one, no one prevails against it.'
'It must be told to those of my own who yet live in this battle — how I was slain by Bhīmasena in violation of the rules of fair fight.'
'Many most cruel deeds have indeed been done by the Pāṇḍavas — against Bhūriśravas, against Karṇa, against Bhīṣma, and against the illustrious Droṇa.'
'And this infamous deed too has been wrought by the cruel Pāṇḍavas, whereby, among the good, they shall come to be despised — such is my conviction.'
'What joy can there be for a man of true worth in a victory won by trickery? And what wise man would deign to commend the breaker of compacts?'
'What learned man would rejoice at a victory gained by unrighteousness, as that wicked son of Pāṇḍu, Vṛkodara, rejoices?'
'And what wonder is there in this — that today, my thighs being broken, my head was crushed with his foot by the enraged Bhīmasena?'
'Against one resplendent, blessed with fortune, and moving honorably among his kin — the man who would act thus, O Saṃjaya, is he then to be esteemed?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'My mother and my father both know well the duty of the warrior caste; those two, O Saṃjaya, stricken with grief, are to be informed in my words.'
'Sacrifices have I performed, my servants well maintained, the sea-girt earth duly ruled; while my foes yet lived, I stood upon their heads, O Saṃjaya.'
'Gifts have I bestowed according to my power, and kindness done to friends; all my enemies have been crushed — who then has come to a better end than I?'
'The realms of others have I overrun, and kings I have made to serve me like slaves; good have I done to those dear to me — who then has come to a better end than I?'
'All my kinsmen have I honored, every worthy person duly revered; the threefold ends of life have all been pursued — who then has come to a better end than I?'
'My command has held sway over the chief among kings, and honor most hard to win was mine; borne I was by steeds of noble breed — who then has come to a better end than I?'
'The Veda I have studied, gifts duly bestowed, a span of life free from disease attained; by my own duty I have won the higher worlds — who then has come to a better end than I?'
'By good fortune I was not vanquished in battle so as to depend upon foes like a menial; by good fortune my ample royal splendor has passed, at my death, to another, O lord.'
'That death which is the desire of warriors who hold fast to their own duty — that very death I have attained; who then has come to a better end than I?'
'By good fortune I never turned back from enmity to be vanquished like a common man; by good fortune I was overthrown without ever stooping to any baseness.'
'As one might slay a man asleep, or off his guard, or by poison — even so, by one who had cast off righteousness, was I slain through the breaking of the compact.'
'The greatly blessed Aśvatthāman, and Kṛtavarman of the Sātvata clan, and Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat — these are to be told in my words:'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'In the Pāṇḍavas, who have so many times acted by unrighteousness and broken their compacts, you must place no trust.'
And the king, your son of truthful valor, spoke also to the messengers: 'Tell them how I was slain in battle by Bhīmasena through unrighteousness.'
'I shall follow after Droṇa, gone to heaven, and both Śalya and Karṇa likewise, and the mighty Vṛṣasena, and Śakuni too, the son of Subala,'
'Jalasaṃdha of great valor, and king Bhagadatta, the son of Somadatta, mighty archer, and Jayadratha the lord of the Sindhus,'
'and my brothers, with Duḥśāsana at their head, equal to my very self, and the valiant son of Duḥśāsana, and Lakṣmaṇa — my own two sons —'
'these and very many others of mine by the thousand I shall follow from behind, like a traveler bereft of his caravan.'
'How, on hearing of her slain brothers and her slain husband, will my sister Duḥśalā fare, wailing aloud, stricken with grief?'
'And my aged father the king, together with Gāndhārī, with his daughters-in-law and their daughters-in-law, lamenting — what refuge shall he find?'
'Surely Lakṣmaṇa's mother too, her son slain and her lord slain, the gracious, large-eyed lady, will swiftly go to her destruction.'
'If Cārvāka the wandering ascetic, that master of speech, comes to know of this, the greatly blessed one will surely exact requital for me.'
'At holy Samantapañcaka, renowned throughout the three worlds, having met my death, I shall attain the everlasting worlds.'
Then thousands of people, their eyes brimming with tears, O honored one, hearing the lament of the king, fled away in all ten directions.
The dread earth, with its seas and forests, with all that moves and is unmoving, then trembled with a roar, and the quarters of the sky grew turbid.
They, coming to the son of Droṇa, reported all as it had befallen — the manner of the mace-duel and the slaying of the king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having related this to the son of Droṇa, O Bhārata, they all, brooding for a long while, departed grief-stricken by the way they had come.
Saṃjaya said: Having heard from the messengers that Duryodhana was slain, the great chariot-warriors of the Kauravas who survived the slaughter, O king —
pierced through by sharp arrows, by maces, javelins, and spears — Aśvatthāman, and Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman of the Sātvatas — came in haste upon swift horses to the field of battle.
There they beheld the great-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra struck down, broken as a mighty sāla tree in the forest is broken by the force of the wind.
writhing upon the ground, drenched with blood, like a great elephant in the wild brought down by a hunter,
rolling about again and again, awash in a flood of blood, fallen as if by chance — like the disk of the sun cast down from the sky,
like an ocean dried up by a mighty gale, like the full moon in the heavens with its orb veiled in mist,
begrimed with dust, long-armed, of prowess equal to an elephant's, that best of kings encircled on every side by dreadful hosts of spirits and flesh-eating beasts, as though by servants greedy to seize his wealth,
his brows knit at the corners of his face, his eyes rolled upward in wrath — that tiger among men still full of fury, like a tiger struck down.
But when those great archers saw the king fallen to the earth, all the chariot-warriors, Kṛpa and the rest, were overcome with a swoon.
Descending from their chariots, they ran to where the king lay, and gazing upon Duryodhana, they all sank down upon the ground.
Then, O great king, the son of Droṇa, his eyes brimming with tears and breathing hard, spoke to that foremost of the Bhāratas, the lord of all the lords of the world.
Surely there is nothing unendurable in the lot of mortals, when you, O tiger among men, lie here smeared with dust.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having once been a king, having ruled over the whole earth, how is it, O lord of kings, that today you lie alone in a desolate wood?
I do not see Duḥśāsana, nor Karṇa the mighty charioteer, nor all those dear friends—what does this mean, O bull of the Bhāratas?
Hard indeed it is, by any means, to know the course of fate, when you, the lord of the worlds, lie here smeared with dust.
This scorcher of foes, who marched at the head of the anointed kings, now swallows dust along with grass—behold the reversal wrought by time!
Where is that spotless parasol of yours, where the fan, O prince? Where has that mighty army of yours gone, O best of kings?
Hard to fathom, surely, is the course of events when the cause is otherwise than it seems, for you, who were once the teacher of the world, have come to this pass.
Among all mortals fortune is shown to be unstable indeed, now that we behold the grievous calamity of you who once rivalled Indra himself.
Hearing that speech of the deeply grieving man, O king, your son spoke these words befitting the hour.
Wiping his eyes with both hands and shedding the tears born of sorrow, that ruler of men then addressed all those heroes, Kṛpa and the rest:
"Such, men say, is this law of mortals ordained by the Creator: the destruction of all beings, brought about by the turning of time.
This destruction has now overtaken me before your very eyes—I who once protected the earth have come to this end.
By good fortune I never turned my back in battle in any peril; by good fortune I have been slain by the wicked, and that especially through treachery.
By good fortune I, ever eager to fight, kept my resolve unflagging; by good fortune I am slain in battle, my kinsmen and friends already fallen.
And by good fortune I see you delivered from this slaughter of men, safe and sound and whole—that is to me a joy beyond all others.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let none of you grieve out of affection at my death; if the Vedas are an authority for you, then the imperishable worlds have been won by me.
Though I knew well the might of Kṛṣṇa of boundless splendour, not even by him was I made to fall away from the warrior's law well observed.
That end has been attained by me, and in no way am I to be mourned. You have acted in a manner worthy of yourselves and true to your nature; you strove ever for victory—but fate is hard to overcome."
Having spoken thus far, his eyes troubled with tears, he fell silent, O lord of kings, overwhelmed grievously by his pain.
But seeing the king thus filled with tears and grief, the son of Droṇa blazed up with wrath, like the fire at the dissolution of the world.
And he, possessed by anger, wringing one hand within the other, spoke to the king in a voice broken by tears:
"My father was slain by base men through a most cruel deed; yet I do not grieve so much for that, O king, as I grieve this day for you.
Hear now this word of mine, O lord, as I speak in truth—by my sacrifices and works of merit, by my gifts, by my righteousness, and by my good deeds:
This very day, before the eyes of Vāsudeva himself, I will by every means lead all the Pāñcālas to the dwelling-place of the king of the dead. But you, O great king, must grant me your leave."
Hearing this speech of Droṇa's son, which gladdened his heart, the Kaurava spoke this word to Kṛpa: "Teacher, bring quickly a pitcher filled with water."
Understanding that command of the king, the best of brāhmaṇas took up a brimming pitcher and drew near to the king.
Then your son spoke to him, O great king, O lord of peoples: "By my command, O foremost of the twice-born, let the son of Droṇa be consecrated to the office of commander-in-chief—blessings upon you—if you wish to do what pleases me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At the king's command a brāhmaṇa too must fight, and especially one who walks in the law of the warriors—so the knowers of dharma have declared.
Hearing then the king's word, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, by the king's command consecrated the son of Droṇa to the command of the army.
Once consecrated, O great king, he embraced that best of kings and set forth, making all the quarters resound with his lion's roar.
And Duryodhana too, O lord of kings, drenched in a flood of blood, then passed into that night which struck terror into all beings.
Then, withdrawing swiftly from that field of battle, O king, their minds shaken with grief, they sank into the helplessness of brooding thought.
Saṃjaya said: Then those heroes, banded together, set out facing southward, and as the hour of sunset drew near they came to the neighborhood of the camp.
Hastily unyoking their mounts, they grew afraid; and reaching a dense thicket, they settled there, hidden from view.
They halted not far off, near the army's encampment, hacked by sharp weapons and gashed with wounds on every side.
Breathing long, hot sighs, they brooded upon the Pāṇḍavas, having heard the terrible uproar of the Pāṇḍavas hungry for victory.
Afraid of pursuit, in terror they fled again, this time turned eastward; and after going on for a short while, their mounts spent and themselves athirst,
those mighty archers could bear it no longer, falling under the sway of wrath and indignation; tormented by the slaying of their king, they halted for a moment.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Unbelievable is this deed wrought by Bhīma, Saṃjaya—that my son, whose strength was that of ten thousand elephants, has been struck down.
Unslayable by all beings, his frame hard as the thunderbolt, my son in his youth has been killed in battle by the Pāṇḍavas, Saṃjaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It is not possible, O son of Gavalgaṇa, for men to overstep what fate decrees—since, having closed with the sons of Pṛthā in battle, my son has been brought down.
Surely my heart is made of the very substance of stone, Saṃjaya, for on hearing that a hundred sons are slain it has not burst into a thousand shards.
How shall an aged couple endure the loss of their sons? For I have no heart to dwell within the realm of the son of Pāṇḍu.
How, having been father of a king and myself a king, Saṃjaya, am I to live on as a servant, at the command of the son of Pāṇḍu?
Having commanded the whole earth and stood at its very summit, Saṃjaya, how shall I now become a servant, I who once wrought deeds past all bounds?
How, Saṃjaya, shall I be able to hear the words of Bhīma, by whom alone my full hundred sons have been slain?
True has been made the word of that great-souled Vidura, for that son of mine, Saṃjaya, would not act upon his counsel.
When my son Duryodhana had been slain by foul means, dear Saṃjaya, what then did Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa do?
Saṃjaya said: Having gone on, O king, your men halted not far away, and beheld a terrible forest thick with manifold trees and creepers.
Resting a while, with their fine horses now watered, at the hour of the sun's setting they reached a vast forest—
frequented by herds of varied beasts, alive with birds of every kind, mantled in diverse trees and creepers, haunted by manifold serpents,
strewn with many waters and graced with ponds, covered over with a hundred lotus-beds and bright with blue lilies.
Entering that fearsome forest and gazing about on every side, they then beheld a banyan veiled in a thousand boughs.
Approaching that banyan, O king, those great chariot-warriors, foremost among men, looked upon that finest of forest-lords.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dismounting from their chariots and unharnessing their horses, they sipped water as the rite ordains, O lord, and sat in worship of the twilight.
Then, when the day-maker had passed to the foremost of mountains in the west, night came on, the sustainer of the whole world.
Adorned with planets, lunar mansions, and stars scattered abroad, the sky shone like a fair garment, lovely to behold on every side.
The creatures that roam by night began faintly to stir abroad, while the creatures that move by day passed into the power of sleep.
Dreadful grew the cry of the night-roaming creatures, the eaters of raw flesh rejoiced, and the terrible night had come.
In that fearful onset of night, filled with anguish and grief, Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa sat down together side by side.
Seated there, grieving all about the banyan, they brooded on that very matter now past undoing—the ruin of Kurus and Pāṇḍavas alike.
Their limbs overcome by sleep, they sank to the surface of the earth, bound fast by weariness and torn with arrows of every kind.
Then the two great chariot-warriors, Kṛpa and the Bhoja, fell under the sway of sleep—men used to ease and undeserving of pain—and lay down upon the bare earth; and those two slept, O great king, worn out with toil and sorrow.
But the son of Droṇa, O Bhārata, fallen under the sway of wrath and indignation, could in no way win his way to sleep, hissing like a serpent.
Sleep he gained not at all, burning with measureless fury; and the mighty-armed one let his gaze wander over that forest, terrible to behold.
Surveying that quarter of the wood, haunted by manifold creatures, the mighty-armed one beheld the banyan thronged with crows.
There thousands of crows were passing that night, sleeping at ease, O scion of Kuru, each roosting apart in its own place.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While those crows slept untroubled all about, he beheld of a sudden an owl come gliding in, dreadful to behold—
loud of voice and huge of body, tawny-eyed, of dun and ruddy hue, with a very long beak and talons, swift as a fine-winged eagle.
That bird, uttering a soft cry, as if stealing in unseen, made then for a bough of the banyan, O Bhārata.
Alighting upon that bough of the banyan, that bird, the bane of crows, slew the sleeping crows in great numbers.
From some it sheared the wings, and the heads of some it lopped away; and the feet of others it broke off—that creature whose weapons were its claws.
In an instant the strong bird slew all that stood within the path of its sight; and with their severed limbs and bodies, O lord of peoples, the whole compass of the banyan was strewn over on every side.
Having slain those crows, the owl rejoiced, that slayer of foes, taking its vengeance upon its enemies according to its heart's desire.
Beholding that stealthy deed wrought by the owl in the night, the son of Droṇa, his resolve shaped to that very mind, pondered alone:
"A lesson has this bird taught me for my own warfare, fit for the destruction of foes; and I deem the moment for it has come.
The Pāṇḍavas, flushed with the show of victory, cannot be slain by me this day—they are strong, full of zeal, sure of their aim, and fierce in the strike; yet I have sworn their slaughter in the presence of my king.
To take up a course like the moth's rush into the fire, that ends in one's own undoing—for one who fights by fair rule, the loss of life is beyond doubt; but by stratagem success may come, and a great destruction of the foe.
In such a case, the course that proves certain, set against the course of doubtful issue—that men hold in high esteem, those who are versed in the science of statecraft.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And whatever in this would be blameworthy, censured, and condemned by the world—that too must a man do who walks in the warrior's law.
And all manner of blameworthy, contemptible, and crooked deeds have been done at every step by the Pāṇḍavas, men of unmastered souls.
On this matter two verses sung of old are heard, framed by ponderers of the law, who looked to right reason—seers of the truth of things, who grasped its inmost sense:
"When the enemy's host is spent, when it is scattered, when it is taking food, at its setting out and at its entering in—then is the foe's force to be struck.
Spent with sleep at the dead of night, and likewise when its leaders are lost, when its warriors are broken, and when the force is split in two—"
Thus did the valorous son of Droṇa form his resolve—to slay in the night, while they slept, the sons of Pāṇḍu together with the Pāñcālas.
Fixing his mind upon that cruel purpose, and resolving on it again and again, he roused those two as they slept—his maternal uncle and the Bhoja.
He could find there no fitting answer, held back by shame; and after musing as it were a moment, choked with tears, he spoke:
"Slain is King Duryodhana, the matchless hero of mighty strength, for whose sake this feud of ours with the Pāṇḍavas was joined.
Alone, by many base men, that lord of eleven armies, whose valor was pure, was brought down in battle by Bhīmasena.
By base Vṛkodara this most cruel thing was done—that he ground with his foot the head of a king consecrated with the royal anointing.
The Pāñcālas roared aloud, they shouted and they laughed; in their hundreds, exultant, they blew their conches and beat their kettledrums.
The tumultuous din of their instruments, mingled with the blare of conches and borne upon the wind, dreadful, seems to fill all the quarters of the sky.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of horses neighing and of elephants trumpeting, and the lions' roar of warriors—this mighty clamor is heard.
From the eastern quarter, where the exultant ones roar fiercely, the very clatter of chariot-rims is heard, making the hair stand on end.
This slaughter of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra has been wrought by the Pāṇḍavas; and we three alone are left in that great carnage.
Some who had the strength of a hundred elephants, some skilled in every weapon, have been slain by the sons of Pāṇḍu—I deem it the turning of Time.
Surely this end was fated to be, in very truth, by the working of that deed—seeing that such was its issue, even when the hard task had been accomplished.
But if the wisdom of you both has not, through bewilderment, been diminished, now that this great cause is undone, let that which is our welfare be spoken."
Kṛpa said: All your words, well grounded in reason, have I heard, O lord; yet hear now some word of mine also, O mighty-armed one.
All men are bound, held fast, by two kinds of working—by fate and by human effort; beyond these two there is nothing.
For deeds are not brought to fulfillment by fate alone, O noblest one, nor yet by effort alone; success comes only from the joining of the two.
By these two together are all undertakings bound, the lowest and the highest alike; and they are seen both set in motion and held back in every way.
The rain-cloud, pouring upon a mountain, what fruit does it bring to pass? And withholding its rain from a ploughed field, what fruit does it then bring to pass?
The exertion that lacks fate's favor, and fate that lacks exertion—each is everywhere in vain; which of them, then, comes first, who can decide?
As, when the god of rain has poured well and the field is rightly ploughed, the seed yields a rich abundance—even so is success that is wrought by man.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of these two, fate ordains its course wholly by its own will; but the wise, taking their stand on diligence, strive on through human effort.
For by these two are all the aims of men's undertakings governed, O bull among men; and they are seen both striving forward and likewise held back.
Even human effort, once made, comes to its fulfillment by fate; and so for the doer of that deed the fruit is brought to pass.
But the exertion of able men, when fate is wanting, is seen in the world to bear no fruit, even though rightly carried through.
Thereupon the slothful among men, those who are dull of spirit, decry exertion; but to the wise that thinking is not pleasing.
For most often a deed once done is seen to bear no fruit on earth; and again, a deed not done is, to one's sorrow, seen to have borne great fruit.
If one who makes no effort yet gains something by mere chance, or one who, having made his effort, gains nothing—both these are in sorry case alike.
The capable man is able to live; the slothful man does not prosper in ease. Here in the world of the living it is the capable, for the most part, who are seen to be the friends of their own welfare.
If a capable man, for all his undertaking of deeds, does not reap their fruit, no blame whatever can fall upon him, and he yet arrives at the truth of things.
But he who in the world wins a reward without having done the work, sitting idle, makes himself liable to censure and for the most part becomes an object of hatred.
He who, disregarding this truth, conducts himself otherwise brings ruin upon himself; this is not the way of the wise.
When effort is wanting in human exertion, or again in destiny, or in both these causes together, then endeavor proves fruitless; and a deed that lacks human exertion does not succeed here.
But he who, having paid homage to the gods, rightly strives after his aims—capable and endowed with skill—is not struck down in vain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And this, again, is right striving: that a man attends upon his elders, asks them what is best, and acts upon their salutary counsel.
Rising up again and again, one should always question those honored by the aged; they are the supreme root of his enterprise, and success is said to be rooted in them.
He who, having heard the word of the elders, then applies himself to exertion, soon obtains in full measure the fruit of that exertion.
The man who strives after his ends out of passion, anger, fear, or greed—without self-mastery and full of arrogance—swiftly falls away from prosperity.
This very aim was begun by Duryodhana—greedy, short-sighted—without due preparation, undertaken in folly and without reflection.
Disregarding those of benevolent counsel, taking counsel instead with the wicked, and though dissuaded, he wrought enmity with the Pāṇḍavas, who were the worthier in virtue.
Of exceedingly evil character even before, he ought not now to give way to despair; for when an undertaking has come to ruin, it is the unheeded word of friends that scorches the heart.
But because we followed in the train of that wicked man, this great and terrible calamity has now come upon us as well.
And my mind, even now tormented by this disaster, though it ponders, cannot in any way discern what is for its own good.
A man bewildered should question his wise and well-wishing friends; and whatever they, being asked, may say, that should be done accordingly.
Let us, then, go and approach Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, and the great-minded Vidura too, and inquire of them.
And whatever they, being asked, may declare to be best for us in the time at hand, that we should thereupon do—such is my settled conviction.
From the non-undertaking of tasks no end is ever accomplished; and those whose task does not succeed though human exertion has been made are stricken down by destiny—about them there need be no debate.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saṃjaya said: Having heard the auspicious words of Kṛpa, joined with righteousness and reason, Aśvatthāman, O great king, was filled with grief and sorrow.
Burning with grief as though by blazing fire, he then hardened his mind to cruelty and addressed those two in reply.
In each and every man his own particular understanding seems fair to him, and all alike take satisfaction, each in his own wisdom.
For every man in the world deems himself the wiser; to each his own self is held in high regard, and each man praises his own self.
For every man's own wisdom is fixed in self-approval; men blame another's understanding and praise their own again and again.
Those whose judgment, through the play of differing causes, happens to agree in an undertaking take satisfaction in one another and esteem each other highly, again and again.
Yet in one and the same man this or that understanding, from time to time, undergoes a reversal as circumstances change, and one judgment falls out of accord with another.
For because the minds of men are unfathomable, and especially so, it is upon coming into some derangement of mind that this or that understanding is born in them.
Just as a skilled physician, having duly diagnosed a disease, prepares a remedy by sound method for the sake of its cure, O lord—
so do men form a judgment for the accomplishment of a task; yet though endowed with their own wisdom, men afterward find fault with that very judgment.
In youth a mortal is beguiled by one cast of mind, in middle life by another, and in old age he comes to favor yet another judgment.
And again, upon meeting with terrible adversity, or with prosperity of like measure, a man, O Bhoja, undergoes a transformation of his understanding.
In one and the same man this or that understanding arises from time to time, and because his wisdom is impermanent, that very judgment ceases to please him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the resolve which, having decided according to his wisdom, a man sees to be sound—upon that he fixes his intent, and it becomes the spur to his exertion.
For every man, O Bhoja, once he has resolved "this is right," sets about gladly to perform it, even in deeds that lead to death and the like.
For all men, having grasped a course of action and their own wisdom too, exert themselves in manifold endeavors, deeming each one to be for their good.
This resolve of mine that has arisen today, born of calamity, I shall declare to you both—a resolve that is the destroyer of my grief.
The Lord of Creatures, having created beings and ordained their tasks, established in each several class one special excellence above the rest.
In the Brāhmaṇa, unwavering self-restraint; in the Kṣatriya, the highest valor; in the Vaiśya, skill; and in the Śūdra, willing service to all the classes.
An unrestrained Brāhmaṇa is no true man; a Kṣatriya without valor is base; a Vaiśya is blamed if he lacks skill, and a Śūdra if he is contrary.
I am born in the most excellent and honored lineage of Brāhmaṇas; yet through ill fortune I have taken up this duty of the Kṣatriya.
If, while knowing the Kṣatriya's duty, I were to perform some very great deed grounded instead in the Brāhmaṇa's way, that would not be thought becoming in me.
Having borne the celestial bow and celestial weapons in battle, yet having seen my father slain, what shall I say in the assembly of men?
Therefore today, embracing that Kṣatriya's duty according to my will, I shall go upon the path of the king, and of my father too, of mighty splendor.
This night the Pāñcālas will sleep, trusting and wearing the look of victors, their yokes and armor cast off and filled with joy, holding that we are beaten and worn out by our exertion.
Upon them, as they sleep at ease in the night within their own camp, I shall this day make a hard onslaught upon the encampment.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Falling upon them in the camp, senseless and as good as corpses, I shall strike them down by my valor, as Maghavat struck down the Dānavas.
This day I shall strike down by my valor all of them gathered together, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, as a blazing fire consumes dry grass; and having slain the Pāñcālas, I shall win peace, O best of men.
I shall range among the Pāñcālas this day, slaying them in battle, as Rudra himself, the Pināka in hand, in fury ranges among the beasts.
This day, having slain and cut down all the Pāñcālas, I shall in my fury crush in battle the sons of Pāṇḍu as well.
This day, having strewn the earth with the bodies of all the Pāñcālas, smiting them down one by one, I shall become free of my debt to my father.
This day I shall send the Pāñcālas upon that hard road traveled by Duryodhana, by Karṇa, by Bhīṣma, and by the lord of the Saindhavas as well.
This day, in the dead of night, I shall by main force crush the head of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the king of the Pāñcālas, as one crushes the head of a sacrificial beast.
This day, in the night, I shall crush in combat with my whetted sword the sleeping sons of the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, O Gautama.
This day, having slain that host of the Pāñcālas in their sleep by night, I shall be a man whose purpose is fulfilled and who is content, O great-minded one.
Kṛpa said: By good fortune this resolve to requite the foe has arisen in you, O undecaying one; not even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself were able to turn you back.
But we two together shall follow you at dawn; tonight take your rest, your armor and banner laid aside.
I shall follow you, and Kṛtavarman of the Sātvatas as well, both mounting our chariots and clad in mail, as you advance to face the enemy.
United with us two, tomorrow in the encounter you shall slay the foe, displaying your valor, O best of chariot-warriors—the Pāñcālas together with their followers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You are well able to display your valor; rest this night. Long have you kept awake, dear son; sleep, then, for this one night.
Rested, your sleep taken, and your mind at ease, O bestower of honor, you shall meet the foe in battle and slay them—of that there is no doubt.
For when you, O best of chariot-warriors, son of the Fire, have taken up your choicest weapons, none even among the gods has the power to conquer you.
As the son of Droṇa advances, joined with Kṛpa and arrayed beside Kṛtavarman, who—even the king of the gods—could do battle with him, raging in the fight?
We, well rested, our sleep taken, and our fever of grief gone, will slay our enemies when the night has given way to dawn.
For yours are celestial weapons, and mine too, beyond doubt; and the Sātvata also is a mighty archer, ever skilled in battles.
We three together, dear son, having by main force slain in battle all the foes assembled, shall win abundant joy. Rest, then, untroubled, and sleep this night in comfort.
I and Kṛtavarman, both bowmen and scorchers of the foe, mounting our chariots and clad in mail, shall together follow you, O best of men, as you set forth—a chariot-warrior advancing in haste.
Having gone to their camp and proclaimed your name aloud in the battle, you shall then work great slaughter among the enemies as they fight.
And when you have wrought their slaughter, you shall in the clear light of dawn disport yourself as Śakra did when he had struck down the great Asuras.
For you are able to conquer in battle the host of the Pāñcālas, as the slayer of all the Dānavas, in his wrath, conquered the army of the Daityas.
When you are joined with me in the fray and guarded by Kṛtavarman, not even the mighty wielder of the thunderbolt himself, in person, could withstand you.
And neither I in battle, dear son, nor Kṛtavarman likewise, will ever withdraw from the fight until we have conquered the Pāṇḍavas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having slain in battle the base Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas, we shall all return—or else, slain, we shall go to heaven.
At dawn we ourselves shall be your helpers by every means; this I declare to you truly, O mighty-armed and sinless one.
Thus addressed in salutary words by his maternal uncle, the son of Droṇa then answered his uncle, O king, his eyes rolling with wrath.
Whence comes sleep to a man who is anguished, and who is consumed with rage, who broods over his purposes, or who again is filled with longing?
See how all four of these have come upon me today; any one quarter of them would in a moment destroy my sleep.
What grief in this world can equal the remembrance of my father's slaying? It burns my heart, and today, by night and by day, it gives me no rest.
And the manner in which my father, above all, was slain by those wicked men—you yourself witnessed it all—that cuts me to the very vitals.
How indeed can one like me live in this world even for a moment, when I hear the words of the Pāñcālas: "Droṇa is slain"?
Without slaying Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle I have no wish to live; he, for the murder of my father, must die, and so must the Pāñcālas who were leagued with him.
And that lament of the king whose thighs were shattered, which I heard — whose heart, even the heart of a cruel man, would it not consume with grief?
From whose eyes, even a pitiless man's, would tears not flow, on hearing again such words as those of the king whose thighs were broken?
And the cause of my friends, vanquished while I yet live, swells my sorrow as the rush of waters swells the sea. With my mind fixed on one thing alone this day, whence should sleep come to me, whence any ease?
Guarded as they are by Vāsudeva and Arjuna, I hold them, uncle, to be utterly unassailable, even by mighty Indra himself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nor can I in any way be restrained from this deed; I see no one in this world who could turn me back from my purpose. This is my settled resolve, and I deem it right.
The ruin of my friends, told to me by the messengers, and the victory of the Pāṇḍavas — these all but burn my heart away.
But once I have wrought slaughter among my foes this night while they sleep, then I shall take my rest, and sleep at last, my fever gone.
Kṛpa said: A man dull of wit and unrestrained in his senses, though eager to learn, is not able to grasp duty and gain in their fullness — such is my thought.
Likewise the keen-witted man who is not schooled in discipline knows nothing whatever of the sure judgment of duty and gain.
But the keen-witted man, eager to learn and restrained in his senses, would understand all the sacred teachings and would not contend against what ought to be accepted.
But the ungovernable man, scornful, evil-souled and base, casting aside the blessed path ordained, performs deeds heavy with sin.
Friends restrain from wrongdoing the man who heeds them; the man of good fortune turns back, but the luckless man turns not back.
As a man whose mind is troubled is steadied by words now stern, now gentle, so too the tractable man can be guided by a friend; but the untractable comes to ruin.
Even so, when a wise friend sets about an evil deed, the wise restrain him with all their power, again and again.
Set your mind, then, upon the good, restraining yourself by yourself; heed my word, my son, that you may not grieve hereafter.
The slaying of those who sleep is not honored in this world by the law of righteousness, nor the slaying of those who have laid down their weapons and unyoked their chariots and steeds.
Nor of those who would say, 'I am yours,' nor of those who have come for refuge, nor of those whose hair has come loose, nor of those whose mounts are slain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This night the Pāñcālas will sleep, lord, their armor cast off, all of them trusting and unwary through the night, like the senseless dead.
The crooked man who should do them violence while they are in such a state would surely sink into a hell bottomless, vast, and without a raft to bear him.
In all the world you are renowned as the foremost of those skilled in every weapon, and never in this world has even the slightest stain clung to you.
You, again, are like the sun: when the dawn comes and the sun has risen, in the sight of all beings you shall conquer your foes in open battle.
A blameworthy deed would be a thing unthinkable in you — like a stain of red set upon white cloth: such is my thought.
Aśvatthāman said: It is so, even as you instruct me here, uncle. But by them was this dyke of righteousness first shattered into a hundred pieces.
Before the very eyes of the lords of earth, and in your presence too, my father, having laid down his weapon, was struck down by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
And Karṇa, foremost of chariot-warriors, when the wheel of his chariot had sunk down, caught in dire distress, was slain by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva.
So too Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, his weapon laid down and unarmed, was slain by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, who set Śikhaṇḍin before him.
Bhūriśravas, the great archer, having sat down in the rite of fasting unto death upon the field, was struck down by Yuyudhāna while the lords of earth cried out against it.
And Duryodhana, meeting Bhīma with the mace in combat, was felled by foul means in the sight of the lords of earth.
Alone, hemmed in there by many great chariot-warriors, that tiger among men was felled unrighteously by Bhīmasena.
The lament of my king whose thighs were shattered, which I have heard from the telling of the messengers, cuts me to the quick.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus lawless and sinful are the Pāñcālas, breakers of the dyke of right. Why does your honor not condemn them, who have so broken every bound?
Having slain in the night, as they sleep, the Pāñcālas who killed my father, I am content, even if I be reborn as a worm or a moth.
And I make haste this day toward this that I am resolved to do; for me who hasten so, whence should sleep come, whence any ease?
There is born in this world no man, nor shall there ever be, who could turn me from this resolve I have set upon their slaying.
Saṃjaya said: Having so spoken, great king, the valiant son of Droṇa yoked his horses apart and set forth straight toward his foes.
To him the two great-souled ones, the Bhoja and the son of Śaradvat, said: Why is this chariot yoked, and what deed do you intend to do?
We two have set out together with you on one road, O bull among men, sharing alike your grief and joy; you should not mistrust us.
Then Aśvatthāman, kindled to wrath as he recalled his father's slaying, told them truly what he was resolved within himself to do.
When he had slain warriors by the hundred thousand with his keen arrows, my father, his weapon laid down, was struck down by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Just so will I slay this very day, with his armor cast off, that sinful son of the Pāñcāla king — by a deed as foul as his own.
And how should that wicked Pāñcāla, slain by me like a beast, attain the worlds won by the valor of arms in battle? Such is my thought.
Quickly, then, your armor girt on, swords at your sides and bows in hand, mount your noble chariots, you scorchers of foes, and wait for me.
Having spoken thus, he mounted his chariot and set forth straight toward his foes; and Kṛpa, O king, and Kṛtavarman of the Sātvatas followed him.
As they went forth, the three of them, facing their foes, shone like three blazing sacrificial fires being fed with oblations at a sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And they came to the camp of their foes, where the folk lay deep in sleep, lord; and reaching the place of the gate, the son of Droṇa halted upon his splendid chariot.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: When they beheld the son of Droṇa halted there at the place of the gate, what did those two, the Bhoja and Kṛpa, do? Tell me, Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said: Bidding Kṛtavarman and the great chariot-warrior Kṛpa await him, the son of Droṇa, his soul possessed by fury, drew near the gate of the camp.
There he beheld a being of vast body, of splendor like the moon and the sun, standing and barring the gate, terrible enough to make the hair stand on end.
He was clad in a tiger's skin streaming with great gouts of blood, a black antelope-hide for his upper garment, and a serpent for his sacred thread.
With his long, massive arms raised aloft bearing weapons of every kind, great serpents bound about him for armlets, his face wreathed in garlands of flame —
his mouth dreadful with fangs and gaping wide, a thing of terror, adorned with thousands of wondrous eyes of many hues.
Neither his form nor his very garb could be told in words; and at the sight of it, the very mountains might burst asunder.
From his mouth, from his nostrils, from his ears on every side, and from those thousands of eyes, there blazed forth mighty tongues of flame.
And from those rays of blazing light there appeared, by the hundred and the thousand, forms of Hṛṣīkeśa, each bearing conch and discus and mace.
Beholding that most wondrous being, terror of the worlds, the son of Droṇa, unshaken, overwhelmed it with showers of celestial weapons.
