"By fortune, great king, you do not look upon this terrible destruction of the Bharatas, this dreadful wailing of the Kurus, this ending of an age."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"By fortune you do not this day behold slain your heroic son, whose banner bore the sacrificial post, giver of many thousands, performer of many sacrifices."
"By fortune, great king, you do not hear amid the outcry of your daughters-in-law their many dreadful laments, like the cries of cranes upon the ocean."
Wrapped in a single garment, their dark hair flying loose, your daughters-in-law run about, their children slain and their lords slain.
Ah, by fortune you do not see him devoured by beasts of prey, that tiger among men, his arm severed, struck down by Arjuna.
Śala slain in battle, and Bhūriśravas too, and all your daughters-in-law made widows: by fortune you do not behold them here this day.
By fortune you do not see that golden parasol of the high-souled one whose banner bore the sacrificial post, flung down upon the chariot-seat of Somadatta's son.
And there the dark-eyed wives of Bhūriśravas, gathered round their husband slain by Sātyaki, grieve over him.
Wailing long and wasted with grief for their husband, they fall forward upon the earth, piteously, alas, O Keśava.
How did Bībhatsu do this most loathsome deed, that he should sever the arm of an unguarded hero, a man of sacrifice?
And Sātyaki wrought a deed yet more wicked than that, in that he struck down one who, his soul resolved, had sat himself down to die by abstention.
"One, you who were righteous, were slain by two through unrighteousness, and so you lie": thus, O Mādhava, do the women of him whose banner bore the sacrificial post cry out.
This wife of him whose banner bore the sacrificial post, her waist no wider than a hand may span, laying her husband's arm upon her lap, piteously lamented:
"This is that hand which would loosen my girdle, which would press my full breasts, which would touch my navel, my thighs, my hips, and slip away the knot of my robe."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In the very presence of Vāsudeva, by Pārtha of untiring deeds, was he struck down while he fought another in the field, off his guard."
"What now, O Janārdana, will you tell in the assemblies and the tales of Arjuna's great deed, or what will the diademed one himself say of it?"
Having thus reproached him, that fair-limbed woman falls silent; and her co-wives grieve for her as for their own daughter-in-law.
Śakuni, king of Gāndhāra, mighty and true in valor, has been slain by his sister's son Sahadeva — the uncle by the nephew.
He who once was fanned with two fans on golden staves now lies there and is fanned by the wings of birds.
He who would take on shapes by the hundred and by the thousand — the illusions of that master of illusion have been burned away by the splendor of the Pāṇḍavas.
He whose cunning skill in deceit won from Yudhiṣṭhira his vast kingdom in the assembly hall through trickery has now in turn been won out of his very life.
The birds, O Kṛṣṇa, gather all about Śakuni, that gambler schooled for the destruction of my sons.
By him was this great enmity kindled with the Pāṇḍavas, for the slaying of my sons, and of himself, and of all his kin.
As the worlds were won by the sword for my sons, O lord, so too for this evil-minded one have the worlds been won by the sword.
And how, O slayer of Madhu, may this crooked one not even there set my straight-minded sons at strife with their brothers?
Gāndhārī said: Behold the unassailable Kāmboja, accustomed to coverlets of Kāmboja make, lying slain in the dust, his shoulders broad as a bull's, O Mādhava.
Gazing upon his two arms, smeared with blood and anointed with sandal, his wife, stricken with utmost grief, laments piteously.
"These are those two arms, like iron bars, their palms and fingers fair, in whose embrace, when I came to it, delight never of old forsook me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"To what refuge shall I go now, bereft of you, O lord of men?" — so cries she of voice exceedingly sweet, her kinsfolk far away, like one without a protector.
Like garlands of many kinds wilting in the heat, the women too are wearied; yet even so their beauty does not forsake their bodies.
Behold the hero of Kaliṅga lying near at hand, O slayer of Madhu, his great arms clasped with a pair of gleaming armlets.
Behold the women of Magadha, O Janārdana, gathered weeping round Jayatsena, the lord of the Māgadhas.
The wail of these wide-eyed, sweet-voiced women, O Janārdana, ravishing both heart and hearing, seems to bewilder my very mind.
Their every ornament scattered, weeping, wasted with grief, the women of Magadha, who once had well-spread couches, now lie upon the bare ground.
Round Bṛhadbala, the prince and lord of the Kosalas, their husband, these women stand and weep, each apart.
Filled with anguish, they draw forth the arrows lodged in his limbs, driven there by the might of Kṛṣṇa's son's arm, swooning again and again.
The faces of these wholly faultless women, weary with the heat and toil, shine like faded lotuses, O Mādhava.
Slain by Droṇa, the heroes lie there with their splendid armlets, all five Kekaya brothers, fallen facing Droṇa.
Clad in mail of refined gold, with banners of copper hue and chariot-garlands, they light up the earth with their radiance, like blazing fires.
Behold Drupada struck down by Droṇa in the battle, O Mādhava, like a great elephant of the forest slain by a mighty lion.
The broad white parasol of the Pāñcāla king, O lotus-eyed one, shines forth like the sun in the autumn sky.
And these grieving daughters-in-law and wives, having burned aged Drupada, the Pāñcāla king, go round him keeping him on their left.
The women, their senses bereft, bear away the hero Dhṛṣṭaketu, the great archer, that bull of the Cedis, slain by Droṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having struck back against Droṇa's weapon in the press of battle, O slayer of Madhu, this great archer lies slain, like a tree carried away by a river.
This brave lord of the Cedis, Dhṛṣṭaketu, the mighty chariot-warrior, lies slain in the battle, having slain his foes by the thousand.
Around him, his body torn by birds, his wives stand gathered, O Hṛṣīkeśa — round the king of the Cedis, slain together with his forces and his kinsmen.
These fair women of the Cedi king's household, taking upon their laps the hero born of the Dāśārha woman's son, true in valor, as he lies there, weep aloud.
Behold his son, O Hṛṣīkeśa, fair of face and wearing lovely earrings, cut to pieces in the battle by Droṇa's arrows.
Surely, even to this day, O slayer of Madhu, the brave youth did not forsake the rear of his father, who stood in the fray fighting against his foes.
So too, O mighty-armed one, the son of my son followed his father: Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, went after Duryodhana.
Behold, O Mādhava, Vinda and Anuvinda, the two princes of Avanti, fallen — like a pair of sāla trees in bloom at winter's end, brought down by the wind.
Armored, with golden armlets, bearers of arrow, sword, and bow, their eyes like a bull's, they lie there still, their garlands yet unstained.
Unslayable were the Pāṇḍavas, O Kṛṣṇa, every one of them, with you beside them — they who escaped Droṇa and Bhīṣma, Karṇa son of the Sun, and Kṛpa,
Duryodhana, the son of Droṇa, the lord of Sindhu, that great chariot-warrior, Somadatta, Vikarṇa, and the valiant Kṛtavarman — those bulls among men who by the force of their weapons could have struck down even the gods.
Yet here they lie, slain in battle — behold the turning of Time. Surely, O Mādhava, no burden is too heavy for fate, since these heroes, these bulls among the Kṣatriyas, have been slain by Kṣatriyas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
My swift and valiant sons were as good as slain, O Kṛṣṇa, on that very day when you returned to Upaplavya with your purpose unachieved.
On that day Śaṃtanu's son and wise Vidura both told me: 'Do not set your love upon your own sons.'
Their foresight, my child, could not prove false: in but a little while my sons have been reduced to ashes, O Janārdana.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, Gāndhārī, wasted by grief, her senses shattered by sorrow, abandoned her composure and fell to the ground, O Bhārata.
Then Gāndhārī, her whole body seized by anger, drowned in grief for her sons, her senses tormented, turned in reproach upon the scion of the Śūras.
Gāndhārī said: The Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra wronged one another, O Kṛṣṇa. Why then, O Janārdana, did you stand by and let them destroy themselves?
You were able, with many retainers, standing amid a vast host, with power over both sides, and your word was heeded —
yet the ruin of the Kurus you let pass by, willingly, O slayer of Madhu. Since you did so, O mighty-armed one, reap now its fruit.
By whatever austerity I have gathered through devotion to my husband, by that, O you whose self is so hard to win, I will curse you, O bearer of discus and mace.
Because you stood by, O Govinda, while the kinsmen — Kurus and Pāṇḍavas alike — slew one another, you yourself shall slay your kinsmen.
You too, O slayer of Madhu, when the thirty-sixth year arrives — your kinsmen slain, your counselors slain, your sons slain — wandering in the forest, shall meet your death by a contemptible means.
And your women too, their sons slain, their kinsmen and friends struck down, shall fall about in just this way, as these women of the Bharatas do now.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing those dreadful words, the great-minded Vāsudeva spoke to the lady Gāndhārī, smiling faintly:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
None other than I is the destroyer of the host of the Vṛṣṇis, O gracious lady. This I already know; yet you do but accomplish what is fated, O Kṣatriya woman.
They cannot be slain by any other men, nor by gods nor demons; therefore the Yādavas shall meet a ruin wrought by their own hands upon one another.
When the lord of the Dāśārhas had spoken thus, the Pāṇḍavas grew sick at heart, deeply shaken, and despaired even of life.
Vāsudeva said: Rise, rise up, Gāndhārī, and do not set your mind on grief. For it was through your own fault that the Kurus went to their destruction.
You who, setting your evil-souled, envious, overweening son Duryodhana before all, deemed wrongdoing to be right —
he who was cruel, harsh in his enmity, defiant of the counsel of his elders — how can you wish to lay upon me the fault of your own making?
Whoever grieves over what is past — the dead or the lost — gains but sorrow through sorrow, and falls into a twofold misfortune.
A Brāhmaṇa woman bears her child for austerity, a cow her calf to bear burdens, a mare hers to run, a Śūdra woman bears a servant and a Vaiśya woman a herdsman — but a king's daughter such as you bears her son for slaughter.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing again these unwelcome words of Vāsudeva, Gāndhārī fell silent, her eyes troubled with grief.
But Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the royal sage, righteous of soul, having restrained the darkness born of unwisdom, questioned Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of righteousness:
You know the count of the living among the armies, O Pāṇḍava. If you know the count of the slain as well, tell it to me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: One billion six hundred and sixty million and twenty thousand are they who have been slain in this battle of kings.
And of the heroes whose fate is unknown, there are twenty-four thousand, O lord of kings, and one hundred and sixty-five besides.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Yudhiṣṭhira, to what state have those best of men gone? Tell me, O mighty-armed one, for I hold you to be all-knowing.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Those who, exulting, offered up their bodies in that supreme conflict — those of true valor have gone to worlds equal to the realm of the king of the gods.
But those who fought thinking gloomily, 'I must die,' O Bhārata, and so were slain in battle — they have joined the company of the Gandharvas.
Those who, standing on the field of battle, met their death by the weapon while begging or turning their backs in flight — they have gone among the Guhyakas.
Those great souls who, hard pressed by the foe, deserted and weaponless, yet restrained by shame, faced their enemies in the fray —
those heroes of bright splendor, hewn by sharp weapons, devoted to the law of the warrior, when slain have gone to the abode of Brahmā.
Those who were slain there, O king, somewhere in the midst of the battle — they, O king, have attained the Northern Kurus.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: By what power of knowledge, my son, do you see all this as one perfected? Tell me, O mighty-armed one, if it may be heard by me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Long ago, at your command, as I wandered through the forest on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, this grace was won by me.
There I beheld the divine sage Lomaśa, and through him I gained the power of recollection; and the divine eye too I obtained long ago through the discipline of knowledge.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Among these people, O Bhārata, are those who have kinsmen and those who have none. Will their bodies be burned according to rite?
For those who have none to perform the rites, and those who tended no sacred fire — for whom among such a multitude shall we perform them, my son, so great is the work?
Those whom the great birds and the vultures drag this way and that — even for them, by their own deeds, the worlds shall be won, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the deeply wise Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, gave command to Sudharman, to Dhaumya, to the charioteer Saṃjaya,
and to Vidura of great wisdom, and to Yuyutsu the Kaurava, and to the servants and charioteers headed by Indrasena, all of them together:
Let your honors have the funeral rites of these performed in full, so that no body shall perish unattended, as though it had no kin.
At the command of the king of righteousness, the steward Vidura, the charioteer Saṃjaya, Sudharman together with Dhaumya, and Indrasena and the rest,
gathering sandalwood and aloeswood and fragrant timber, clarified butter and oil and perfumes, and garments of fine linen,
and costly heaps of firewood, and the shattered chariots there, and weapons of every kind,
made the pyres with care and, calmly, by the rite prescribed in scripture, had the foremost of the kings cremated.
King Duryodhana and his brothers, more than a hundred of them, Śalya and King Śala, and Bhūriśravas as well,
and King Jayadratha and Abhimanyu, O Bhārata, the son of Duḥśāsana, and Lakṣmaṇa, and King Dhṛṣṭaketu,
Bṛhanta and Somadatta and more than a hundred of the Sṛñjayas, King Kṣemadhanvan, and Virāṭa and Drupada too,
Śikhaṇḍin the Pāñcāla and Dhṛṣṭadyumna son of Pṛṣata, and the valiant Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas as well,
the prince of Kosala and the sons of Draupadī, and Śakuni son of Subala, Acala and Vṛṣaka, and King Bhagadatta,
and the wrathful Karṇa, son of the Sun, together with his sons, and the Kekayas, those mighty archers, and the Trigartas, those great chariot-warriors,
and Ghaṭotkaca, lord of the Rākṣasas, the brother of Baka, and King Alambusa, and King Jalasaṃdha,
and other kings, O king, by the hundreds and the thousands — all these they had burned with blazing fires fed by streams of clarified butter.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For some of those great souls the rites for the fathers were performed; some were chanted over with hymns of the Sāman, and over others the mourners lamented.
With the sound of the Sāman and the Ṛc verses, and the weeping cries of the women, a swooning faintness came upon all beings in the night.
Those fires, smokeless, kindled and blazing, appeared as planets in the sky veiled by a thin haze of cloud.
And those who were without kin there, come together from many lands — gathering them all and heaping them in piles by the thousands,
Vidura, unhurried, having stacked them with abundant wood soaked in oil, had them burned at the command of the king of righteousness.
When he had had their rites performed, Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus, set Dhṛtarāṣṭra before him and went toward the Gaṅgā.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: They came to the Gaṅgā, auspicious, frequented by holy folk, full of pools, rich in banks, with broad marshlands and great forests,
and casting off their ornaments, their upper garments, and their headcloths, then for their fathers, grandsons, brothers, and kindred,
for their sons and elders and husbands, all the women of the Kurus, weeping and sorely afflicted, made the water-offering; and the knowers of the law performed the libation rites for their friends as well.
As the water-offering was made by the wives of the heroes for the heroes, the Gaṅgā came to have easy fords, and spread her waters wide again.
That bank of the Gaṅgā, vast as the great ocean, joyless and without festival, thronged with the wives of the heroes, shone in its mournful splendor.
Then Kuntī, O great king, suddenly worn by grief, weeping, spoke to her sons in a faltering voice:
That hero, the mighty archer, the leader of leaders of chariot-bands, who was slain in battle by Arjuna, marked with every sign of a hero —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
he whom you, O Pāṇḍavas, thought a charioteer's son, Rādheya — he who shone in the midst of the host like the radiant lord of day,
who once fought against you all and your followers, who, leading on the whole army of Duryodhana, shone in his splendor,
to whose valor there is none equal on all the earth — true to his word, valiant, never fleeing in battle —
make the water-offering for that brother of yours, untiring in his deeds. For he was your elder brother, born to me of the Sun, that hero with earrings and armor, whose splendor was like the maker of day.
Hearing this unwelcome word of their mother, all the Pāṇḍavas grieved now for Karṇa, and became more stricken than before.
Then that tiger among men, the heroic Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, said to his mother, hissing like a serpent:
He within whose arrow's flight none but Dhanaṃjaya could stand his ground — how was that god-begotten one of old a son of yours?
He by the might of whose arms we were scorched on every side—how could you have kept him concealed, like a fire wrapped in a garment? He whose terrible strength of arm the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra leaned upon for support—
No other chariot-warrior among warriors could withstand Karṇa, the son of Kuntī. He was our first-born brother, the foremost of all who bear weapons. How is it, lady, that you bore him first, him of wondrous valor?
Alas, by the concealing of this counsel of yours we are undone; for by the slaying of Karṇa we have been crushed, together with our kinsmen.
By the destruction of Abhimanyu, by the slaughter of the sons of Draupadī, by the ruin of the Pāñcālas, and by the fall of the Kurus—
this grief, a hundredfold greater than all of that, has touched me to the quick; for grieving over Karṇa I burn as though cast into a fire.
Nothing whatever would have been beyond our reach, even were it set in heaven, nor would this terrible carnage, which has brought the Kauravas to their end, ever have come to pass.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having lamented thus at great length, O king, the King of Righteousness, Yudhiṣṭhira, wailing softly, the lord performed the water-offering for him.
Then on all sides the women and men who stood about there, gathered for that water-rite, suddenly broke into wailing.
Then the wise lord of the Kurus, Yudhiṣṭhira, out of love for his brother, had Karṇa's women brought forth with their retinue.
Then, together with them, that righteous-souled one performed the funeral rites; and having done so, his senses overwhelmed, he came up out of the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the sons of Pāṇḍu, together with Vidura and Dhṛtarāṣṭra and all the women of the Bharatas, had made the water-offerings for all their kinsmen,
those great-souled delights of the Kurus dwelt there for one full month outside the city, to complete the rites of purification.
And to the righteous-souled king Yudhiṣṭhira, who had performed the water-rite, there came great souls, perfected ones, the most excellent of brahmin-sages.
Dvaipāyana and Nārada and Devala that mighty seer, Devasthāna and Kaṇva, and the most excellent of their disciples;
and other twice-born ones, learned in the Vedas, of perfected wisdom, householders and graduates all alike, came to behold the best of the Kurus.
Having approached and been honored according to custom, those great-souled mighty seers took their places upon seats of great worth.
Then, having received the homage suited to that hour, they sat in attendance, encircling Yudhiṣṭhira as was fitting.
On the holy bank of the Bhāgīrathī the brahmins, in their hundreds of thousands, sought to console the king whose mind was distraught with grief.
And Nārada, in due time, having taken counsel with the sages, addressed the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira in words befitting that hour:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"By the might of your arm, by the grace of Mādhava, and by righteousness, this whole earth has been won, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
By good fortune you have come safe through this battle that struck terror into the world. Devoted as you are to the duty of the warrior, do you now rejoice, O son of Pāṇḍu?
Having slain your foes, do you gladden your friends, O king? And having attained this sovereign fortune, does grief no longer torment you?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This whole earth has been conquered, resting upon the strength of Kṛṣṇa's arm, by the grace of the brahmins, and by the might of Bhīma and Arjuna.
Yet this great sorrow abides in my heart unceasingly: that I have wrought this vast destruction of my own kinsmen, all of it born of greed.
Having caused the deaths of Subhadrā's son and the sons of Draupadī, my dear children, this victory, O blessed one, appears to me to wear the face of defeat.
What will the Vṛṣṇi-maiden, my daughter-in-law, say to Madhusūdana — to Kṛṣṇa, to Hari, the dweller in Dvārakā — when he returns hence to her?
This Draupadī, her sons slain, her kinsmen slain, wretched, ever devoted to our love and welfare, torments me yet the more.
And there is this other thing, O blessed Nārada, of which I shall speak to you: by the keeping-secret of a counsel, I have been yoked to sorrow by Kuntī.
He who had the strength of ten thousand elephants, in this world a warrior without an equal in battle, who moved with the sporting gait of a lion, wise, compassionate, self-controlled, firm in his vows;
the refuge of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, proud, fierce in valor, impatient of insult, ever ardent for the fray, our reviler in battle after battle;
swift with his weapons, a varied fighter, accomplished, of wondrous prowess — he was Kuntī's son, born in secret, and our own brother, of the same womb.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whom Kuntī, at the water-rite, declared to be the son of Sūrya — her own son, endowed with every virtue, cast away of old upon the waters.
He whom all this world deemed the charioteer's son and called Rādheya — he was Kuntī's eldest son, and our brother, born of the same mother.
By me, not knowing, greedy for the kingdom, he was brought to his death in battle. That burns my limbs as fire burns a heap of cotton.
For not even Pārtha of the white steeds knew him for his brother, nor I, nor Bhīma, nor the twins — yet he, true to his vows, knew us.
We have heard that Pṛthā went to him, desiring peace between us, and said, 'You too are my son.'
But Pṛthā's wish was not granted by that great-souled one; rather, at the very last, he said this to his mother, so we have heard:
'I cannot forsake King Duryodhana in battle; that would be ignoble in me, cruel, and an act of ingratitude.'
'If, by your will, I were to make peace with Yudhiṣṭhira, men would think me afraid of him of the white steeds in battle.'
'When I have conquered in the field Vijaya together with Keśava, then afterward I shall make peace with the son of Dharma' — so he said.
Then Pṛthā, it is said, spoke again to that broad-chested one: 'Grant safety to four of them; fight Phalguna if you will.'
And the wise one answered his mother, trembling, with folded hands: 'Even when I have them in my power and can withstand them, I will not slay those four sons of yours.
Five sons, O mother, shall surely remain to you in any case: either with Karṇa if Pārtha falls, or with Arjuna if I fall.'"
Then his mother, longing for her sons, spoke to her son once more: 'Do good to your brothers, you who wish to do them good.'
Having spoken thus to him, Pṛthā took her leave and went home; and that hero was slain by Arjuna — brother by brother, born of the same womb.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Neither Pṛthā's secret nor his own was ever disclosed, O sage; and so that valiant great archer was struck down by Pārtha.
Only afterward did I learn, O best of the twice-born, from Pṛthā's own words, O lord, that Karṇa was my elder brother, born of the same womb.
By this my heart is sorely pained, a slayer of my brother; for with Karṇa and Arjuna for my helpers I could have vanquished even Vāsava himself.
When I was being tormented in the assembly hall by the evil-souled sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the anger that suddenly rose in me would grow calm at the mere sight of Karṇa.
For even when I heard his harsh words, bitter in their import, spoken in the assembly at the gambling-match, he desiring Duryodhana's good —
even then my anger would vanish when I gazed upon his feet; for Karṇa's feet were like Kuntī's — such was my thought.
Seeking the cause of that likeness between him and Pṛthā, I could find no reason for it, however much I pondered.
How was it that in battle the earth swallowed his chariot-wheel? And how was my brother cursed? This you ought to tell me here.
I wish to hear from you, O blessed one, the whole of it exactly as it was; for you, all-knowing and learned, know in this world what has been done and what has not.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the sage Nārada, best of speakers, related the whole of it — how that son of the charioteer had been cursed.
"It is even so, O mighty-armed Bhārata, as you say: for Karṇa and Arjuna there was nothing in battle that could not be borne or overcome.
But this is a secret of the gods, which I shall tell you, O king. Hear it then, O great king, as it came to pass of old.
'How may the warrior caste go to heaven, purified by the sword?' — with this purpose, O lord, one who would breed strife was fashioned, conceived in the womb of a maiden.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That child, endowed with splendor, came to the state of a charioteer's son, and learned the science of archery under your teacher, the best of the Āṅgirasas.
The strength of Bhīmasena, and the deftness of Phalguna, and your wisdom, O lord of kings, and the discipline of the twins —
and the friendship of the wielder of Gāṇḍīva with Vāsudeva from boyhood, and the affection of the people — brooding on all these, he was consumed inwardly.
In his boyhood he formed a friendship with King Duryodhana, ever at enmity with you — both by destiny and by his own nature.
Then, perceiving that Dhanaṃjaya surpassed him in learning in the science of arms, Karṇa came in secret to Droṇa and spoke these words:
'I wish to learn the brahma-weapon, together with its secret and its withdrawal; it is my desire to become Arjuna's equal in battle.
Surely your affection for your sons and your disciples is equal; by your grace, let not the discerning call me unaccomplished in arms.'
Droṇa, thus addressed by Karṇa, mindful of Phalguna and knowing too the evil bent of Karṇa, said to him:
'A brahmin who has duly fulfilled his vows may know the brahma-weapon, or a warrior who is an ascetic; no other may know it on any account.'
Thus addressed, he took leave of the best of the Āṅgirasas and, paying him reverence, went straightway to Rāma upon Mount Mahendra.
Approaching Rāma and bowing with his head, he came to him with reverence, saying, 'I am a brahmin of the Bhārgava line.'
Rāma received him, having asked him fully of his lineage and the rest, and said, 'Be welcome; dwell here.' And he was exceedingly pleased with him.
While Karṇa dwelt there upon Mahendra, the best of mountains, there was for him fellowship with gandharvas and rākṣasas, yakṣas and gods.
There he gained mastery over weapons, in due form, from the best of the Bhṛgus, and became exceedingly dear to the gods, the gandharvas, and the rākṣasas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Once, wandering by the seashore near the hermitage, alone, with sword and bow in hand, the son of the charioteer roamed about.
And there, O Pārtha, unknowingly and by mere chance, he killed the sacrificial cow of a certain brahmin given to the fire-oblation, a knower of the Veda.
Reckoning the deed to have been done in ignorance, Karṇa confessed it to the brahmin, and seeking to appease him, spoke these words:
'Without intent, O blessed one, this cow of yours has been slain by me; in this, grant me your grace' — so he said again and again.
But that brahmin, enraged, said to him, reviling him as it were with his speech: 'You wretch of evil conduct, you deserve death; reap your fruit, you of evil mind!
With that very one whom you ceaselessly seek to rival, for whose sake you strive day and night — when you fight with him, O sinful one, the earth shall swallow your chariot-wheel.
And when your wheel is swallowed by the earth, your foe shall surge forward and strike off the head of you, bewildered. Go, basest of men!
As this cow of mine was slain by you in your heedlessness, O fool, even so shall another strike off your head when you are heedless.'
Then he sought again to appease that best of the twice-born with cows and wealth and jewels; but the brahmin spoke to him once more:
'Not even the whole world could make this utterance of mine false. Go or stay, or whatever you must do, do it.'
Thus told by the brahmin, Karṇa, his face cast down in misery, came to Rāma in fear, brooding upon that very curse in his heart.
Nārada said: By the might of Karṇa's arm, by his modesty and self-restraint, and by his service to his teacher, the tiger of the Bhṛgus was well pleased.
To him that ascetic, calmly and in full, taught the entire brahma-weapon, complete with its withdrawal, in due form — to that ardent striver.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Karṇa, accomplished in arms and taking his ease in the hermitage of the Bhṛgu, applied himself to the science of archery, he of wondrous prowess.
Then one day the wise Rāma, walking near the hermitage in Karṇa's company, worn thin by fasting,
the son of Jamadagni lay down to sleep — that teacher, weary of mind, his affection grown from trust — resting his head upon Karṇa's lap.
Then a worm, born of phlegm, a feeder upon flesh and blood, dreadful and dreadful to the touch, came near to Karṇa.
Reaching his thigh, that drinker of blood pierced it through; yet Karṇa could neither cast it off nor slay it, for fear of waking his teacher.
Though he was being gnawed in this way by that worm, O Bhārata, the son of the charioteer, fearing to wake his teacher, simply endured it.
But Karṇa, by his steadfastness, suppressed that unbearable pain, and without flinching, without showing distress, held the descendant of Bhṛgu upon his lap.
But when the bearer of the Bhṛgu line felt his body touched by the blood, the radiant one awoke, and, distressed, he spoke these words:
"Alas, I have been rendered impure! What is this that is being done to you? Set fear aside and tell me the truth of this matter."
Then Karṇa told him of the worm's devouring, and Rāma beheld that worm, which resembled a boar,
eight-footed, with sharp fangs, bristling as if covered with needles, its body all hedged with hairs, Alarka by name.
No sooner was that worm seen by Rāma than it gave up its life there, drenched in blood; and this seemed a marvel.
Then in the sky there appeared a rākṣasa of every form and terrible aspect, red of throat, dark of limb, borne upon a cloud.
With palms joined, his heart fulfilled, he addressed Rāma: "Blessings upon you, O tiger of the Bhṛgus! I shall now depart whence I came.
I have been delivered from hell by you, O best of sages. May good fortune be yours, and joy; you have done me a great kindness."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The mighty-armed and majestic son of Jamadagni said to him: "Who are you, and why did you fall into hell? Tell me that."
He replied: "In an earlier time I was a great asura named Gṛtsa, in the age of the gods, dear one—a contemporary, as it were, of Bhṛgu himself.
I carried off by force the beloved wife of Bhṛgu, and by the curse of the great sage I became a worm and fell to the earth.
Your forefather said to me in his wrath: 'Feeding on urine and phlegm, O wicked one, you shall pass into hell.'
'Let there be an end to the curse, O brahman,' I said to him then; and Bhṛgu answered me: 'It shall come when Rāma appears in the line of Bhṛgu.'
So I came to this state, ill-fated as it was; but by meeting with you, O virtuous one, I am freed from that sinful birth."
Having spoken thus and bowed to Rāma, the great asura departed; but Rāma in anger spoke these words to Karṇa:
"This pain was extreme, O fool; no brahman could ever endure it. Yours is the steadfastness of a kṣatriya. Speak the truth, by your desire."
Then Karṇa, afraid of a curse, said to him, seeking to appease him: "Know me, O descendant of Bhṛgu, to be born a sūta, between brahman and kṣatriya.
People on earth call me Karṇa, the son of Rādhā. Be gracious to me, O brahman, O descendant of Bhṛgu, who longed only for weapons.
A teacher who imparts the knowledge of the Veda is, beyond doubt, a father and a lord; therefore in your presence I claimed the Bhārgava lineage."
The best of the Bhṛgus, angry yet half-smiling, said to him as he lay fallen on the ground, wretched and trembling, with palms joined:
"Because out of greed for weapons you have deceived me here, therefore, O fool, this Brahmā-weapon shall not appear to you in your memory—
except at the hour of your death, when you face one who is your equal. For in one who is no brahman, the brahman power can never abide secure.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Go now! Here there is no place for falsehood. Yet no kṣatriya on earth shall ever be your equal in battle."
Thus addressed by Rāma, he duly departed; and coming to Duryodhana, he declared, "I am now accomplished in arms."
Nārada said: Having gained this weapon from the son of Bhṛgu, Karṇa, together with Duryodhana, rejoiced, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then once, O king, the kings gathered together at the bride-choosing of Citrāṅgada, the king in the Kaliṅga country.
There, O Bhārata, was a splendid city named Rājapura; thither the kings came by the hundreds, seeking the maiden's hand.
Hearing that all the princes were assembled there, Duryodhana went, accompanied by Karṇa, in a chariot adorned with gold.
Then, O best of kings, when that bride-choosing, a great festival, was under way, the rulers came together for the maiden's sake:
Śiśupāla, Jarāsaṃdha, Bhīṣmaka and Vakra, Kapotaroman and Nīla, and Rukmī of firm valor,
and Sṛgāla, O great king, and he who was lord of the women's realm, Aśoka and Śatadhanvan, and the hero called Bhoja by name,
these and many others who dwell in the southern quarter, and kings who were teachers of the mlecchas, and those of the east and north, O Bhārata.
All wore golden armlets, all bore wreaths of fine gold, all with shining bodies, fierce in their pride like tigers.
Then, O Bhārata, when those kings had taken their seats, the maiden entered the arena, attended by her nurse and her chamberlain.
Then, O Bhārata, as the names of the kings were being proclaimed, that maiden of lovely complexion passed by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
But Duryodhana of the Kuru line did not brook being passed over; he stopped the maiden, slighting the assembled rulers.
Drunk with the pride of his strength, relying on Bhīṣma and Droṇa, he mounted the maiden upon his chariot and challenged the kings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Behind him followed, O bull among men, the charioteer Karṇa, best of those who bear arms, sword in hand and fitted with leather guard and finger-thongs.
Then there arose a mighty tumult among the kings, O Yudhiṣṭhira, as they donned their armor and yoked their chariots.
Enraged, they rushed upon both Karṇa and Duryodhana, loosing showers of arrows like clouds upon two mountains.
As they charged, Karṇa with a single razor-arrow each struck down their bows, with their quivers, upon the ground.
Then some he left without bows, some with bows still upraised, and some still drawing their arrows, their lances and clubs and chariot-spears,
all thrown into disorder by his swiftness. Karṇa, foremost of warriors, vanquished most of those rulers, their charioteers slain.
Urging on their own horses, crying "Drive! Drive!", those kings, their spirits broken, abandoned the field and fled away.
Then Duryodhana, guarded by Karṇa, went on his way, and joyfully bore the maiden to the city named for the elephant.
Nārada said: Learning that Karṇa had revealed his might, the king of Magadha, the lord of earth Jarāsaṃdha, challenged him to single combat between chariots in battle.
A battle arose between the two, both versed in celestial weapons, as in combat they rained upon each other with weapons of every kind.
Their arrows spent, their bows undone, their swords broken, they came down to the earth, and both, endowed with strength, grappled with their arms.
Then, fighting with the thorn-like strokes of the arms, Karṇa rent apart the joint of his body which Jarā had once knit together.
Seeing the alteration of his own body, the king said to Karṇa, "I am pleased," and laid aside his enmity, O Bhārata.
Out of affection he then gave to Karṇa the city of Mālinī; and so, O tiger among men, that vanquisher of foes became king among the Aṅgas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Karṇa, crusher of enemy hosts, ruled over Campā with Duryodhana's consent, as is known to you as well.
Thus by the splendor of his arms he became renowned upon the earth; and for your benefit the lord of the gods begged of him his armor and his earrings.
Bewildered by the god's illusion, he gave away his celestial, inborn earrings, most cherished, and his inborn coat of mail as well.
Stripped of his two earrings and of his inborn armor, he was slain in battle by Vijaya, before the very eyes of Vāsudeva—
by the curse of a brahman and of the great-souled Rāma, by the boon Kuntī had granted, and by the wiles of him of a hundred sacrifices,
by Bhīṣma's slighting of him, who reckoned him but half a chariot-warrior in the count, by Śalya's draining of his spirit, and by the counsel of Vāsudeva,
and by the weapons of Rudra, of the king of the gods, of Yama and of Varuṇa, of Kubera and Droṇa, and of the great-souled Kṛpa—
taking up these celestial weapons, the wielder of Gāṇḍīva slew in battle Karṇa, son of Vikartana, radiant as the day-making sun.
Thus cursed was your brother, and deceived by many; yet that tiger among men is not to be mourned, for he met his death in battle.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus far, the divine sage Nārada fell silent; but the royal sage Yudhiṣṭhira, drowned in grief, sank into brooding.
To that hero, downcast in spirit, his face bowed low, anguished, sighing like a serpent, his eyes brimming with tears—
to him Kuntī, her body wrung with grief, her mind stricken with sorrow, sweet of speech, spoke in season these words full of meaning:
"Yudhiṣṭhira, mighty-armed one, you should not grieve for him. Cast off your sorrow, O most wise, and hear these words of mine.
Long ago I strove to make known to him his brotherhood with you, O best of the upholders of dharma, and so did the god Bhāskara, his father.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All that a friend desiring his welfare and wishing him prosperity might say—so was he told by the day-maker at the close of a dream, and in my presence as well.
Yet neither could the Sun, nor I, by any motives of affection, win him over of old, nor bring him to union with you.
Then, overtaken by fate, bent on kindling the fire of enmity, set on working against you—so I let him be.
Thus addressed by his mother, the Dharma-king, his eyes clouded with tears, the righteous one, his mind distraught with grief, spoke these words:
"Because of your keeping the secret hidden, I am stricken," he said to her; and that one of great splendor, overcome with deep sorrow, laid a curse: that throughout all the worlds women should hold no secret concealed.
That king, remembering his sons and grandsons, his kinsmen and his friends, became troubled at heart and sick in mind.
Then, his soul wrapped in grief like a fire wrapped in smoke, the wise king, tormented by anguish, gave himself over to despair.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: But Yudhiṣṭhira, righteous of soul, his mind distraught with grief, mourned, burning with sorrow, as he remembered Karṇa, the great chariot-warrior.
Possessed by pain and grief, sighing again and again, looking upon Arjuna, worn down by sorrow he spoke these words:
"Had we lived by begging in the city of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, rather than leaving our kinsmen bereft of their men, we would not have come to this misery.
Our enemies, the Kurus, had their wealth and their ends fulfilled, it seems; but having slain ourselves by our own hands, what fruit of dharma do we gain?
A curse upon the kṣatriya way of life! A curse upon strength of breast! A curse upon the wrath by which we have been brought to this calamity!
Good are forbearance, self-restraint, purity, freedom from enmity, freedom from envy, non-injury, and truthful speech—these are the constant virtues of those who dwell in the forest."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But we, out of greed and delusion, clinging to arrogance and pride, have fallen into this plight from craving for a mere shred of kingship.
Not with the sovereignty of all three worlds could anyone gladden us, who have looked upon our kinsmen slain upon the earth—we who hungered after spoils.
For the sake of the earth we forsook men who ought never to have been killed, men equal to the earth itself, and now we live on, bereft of purpose, our kinsmen slain.
We greedy for the flesh, like dogs—nay, not even dogs—both the flesh is lost to us, and lost too are those who would have eaten it.
Not for the whole earth, not for heaps of gold, not for all the cattle and horses, ought those to have been given up who now lie slain.
Yoked to desire and wrath, filled with anger and intolerance, they mounted the chariot of death and went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Wishing much good fortune, fathers strive for sons through austerity, through chastity, through worship, and through forbearance.
Through fasts and through offerings, through vows and auspicious rites, mothers conceive their children and bear them for ten months.
"If only they be born in safety; if only, once born, they live; if only, grown strong and esteemed, they grant us happiness here and hereafter"—so the wretched ones hope, intent upon their fruit.
For those mothers this whole endeavour has come to nothing, utterly fruitless, in that their sons—young men with polished earrings—have been slain.
Without having tasted a king's enjoyments, without having discharged their debts to the ancestors and the gods, they have gone to the abode of Vaivasvata.
When, dear friend, the parents of these princes were as if made of love for them, in their very prime of strength and beauty those kings were struck down.
Yoked to desire and wrath, unsteadied by anger and elation, never at any time will they taste the least fruit of their birth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of the Pāñcālas and the Kurus, even those who are unslain are as good as slain; while we, by our own deeds, must come to the lowest worlds.
We ourselves are accounted the cause of the destruction of this world; through the treachery of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son we were brought to this pass.
Ever skilled in deceit, a hater, living by guile, he behaved falsely toward us at all times, though we had done him no wrong.
We desired our share, and so did they; yet neither did we win, nor did they: by them this earth was not enjoyed, nor its women, nor its song and music.
Neither counsel in the assembly of ministers, nor the learning of the learned, nor jewels beyond price, nor land, nor any gaining of wealth.
Seeing that prosperity of ours, he grew pale, sallow, and gaunt; and so he was reported by the son of Subala to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
His father, out of fondness for his son, consented to him though he stood in unrighteousness, without ever heeding the patriarch, the son of Gaṅgā, or Vidura. Without a doubt Dhṛtarāṣṭra has come to the same pass as I.
By failing to restrain his impure, greedy son, who followed the bidding of his lusts, he has fallen from his blazing fame, and has caused brothers to slay one another.
And that Suyodhana, ever bent on hatred of us, ever evil-minded, has cast these two aged ones into the fire of grief.
What kinsman of noble birth would speak to those who wish him well as that base man, eager for war, spoke in the presence of the Vṛṣṇis?
For through our own fault we are ruined for endless years, we who once burned across all the quarters with our splendour, like suns.
That man of enmity toward us came under the sway of evil counsellors; for Duryodhana's sake this whole lineage of ours has been brought down. Having slain those who should never have been slain, we have earned the world's reproach.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having made that wicked-minded, evil-doing destroyer of this lineage the lord of the realm, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra now grieves.
The heroes are slain, the sin is done, our own domain laid waste; having killed, our wrath has departed, and this grief now hems me in.
Dhanaṃjaya, sin once committed is undone by righteous deeds; and the man given to renunciation, the scripture says, has no power to commit sin again.
Since the scripture holds that the man of renunciation incurs neither birth nor death, then, having found the path and settled his mind, he attains to Brahman.
And so, Dhanaṃjaya, free of the pairs of opposites, a sage endowed with knowledge, I shall take leave of you all and go to the forest, O scorcher of foes.
For the scripture declares that the most perfect dharma cannot be attained by one who holds possessions; this, O slayer of foes, is plain to my own sight.
By me, who craved possessions, sin was set loose; and the scripture says that what causes the ending of birth can indeed be attained.
So, casting off possessions and the whole kingdom as well, I shall go forth wholly released, freed of sorrow, freed of fever.
Do you rule this earth, made secure, its thorns cut away; I have no need of kingship nor of enjoyments, O foremost of the Kurus.
Having spoken these words, the Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira fell silent; and then the younger son of Pṛthā made answer.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Arjuna spoke, as if stung past endurance, in measured and well-composed words, firm in argument and bold in speech.
Showing himself fierce, the son of Indra, fierce in his prowess, that man of great splendour smiled and again and again licked the corners of his mouth.
Alas, what sorrow, what distress, what utmost faintness of heart, that after performing superhuman deeds you would forsake the highest fortune!

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having slain your foes and won the earth, gained by your own proper duty, your enemies destroyed—how could you give it all up out of a lightness of mind?
For whence should kingship come to a coward, or again to a dawdler? And why then did you slay those guardians of the earth, blind with wrath?
He who would choose to live by begging, attempting no undertaking by any work at all, stripped of well-being and owning nothing, becomes notorious in all the worlds, joined neither to sons nor to cattle.
O king, if you abandon your prosperous kingdom and take up the most wretched way of life of a skull-bearing mendicant, what will this world say of you?
Renouncing all undertakings, stripped of well-being and owning nothing—why, my lord, do you long to go about begging like a common man?
Born in this royal house, having conquered the whole earth, you would forsake dharma and artha entire and set out for the forest in your folly!
If the wicked should make havoc here of these oblations, abandoned by you, then upon you alone the sin will fall.
"Possessing nothing is not to be wished for," thus did Nahuṣa declare; for in poverty deeds turn cruel. Fie upon poverty in this world!
The life of the seers that takes no thought for the morrow exists indeed—this you know; but that which men call dharma proceeds from wealth.
Whoever steals a man's wealth steals his dharma along with it; and when our wealth is borne away, O king, to whom shall we show forbearance?
Men look upon the poor man standing at their side as though he were a condemned criminal; poverty is a grievous fault in the world—who could ever praise it?
The fallen man is pitied, O king, and the man without wealth is pitied too; I find no difference between the outcast and the destitute.
From riches grown abundant, gathered from this source and that, all undertakings spring forth, as rivers spring from the mountains.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From wealth come dharma and pleasure and heaven too, O lord of men; for the very sustenance of life in the world is not secured without wealth.
For the man bereft of wealth and of little wit, all undertakings dry up, as the little streams in the summer's heat.
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen; he who has wealth is a man in the world, and he who has wealth is also accounted learned.
By a poor man, however much he desires wealth and seeks to gain it, wealth cannot be won; wealth is bound fast by wealth, as great elephants are caught by elephants.
Dharma and pleasure and heaven, joy, anger, learning, and self-control—all these proceed from wealth, O lord of men.
From wealth lineage arises, from wealth dharma proceeds; for the man without wealth there is neither this world nor the next, O best of men.
The man without wealth cannot duly perform the works of dharma; for dharma flows forth from wealth as a mountain stream from the rock.
He whose horses are lean, whose cattle are lean, whose servants and guests are lean—he, O king, is the truly lean man; not he who is lean of body.
Reflect as is right; consider how it was between gods and asuras. O king, by what else than the slaughter of their kinsmen do the very gods prosper?
If another's property were not to be seized, how could one undertake that as dharma? This very conclusion has been fixed by the sages in the Vedas.
The threefold knowledge is to be studied, and one must become wise; by every means wealth is to be acquired, and sacrifice performed with diligence.
By hostility the gods won their stations in heaven on every side—so the gods determined, and so run the eternal pronouncements of the Veda.
They study, they perform austerities, they sacrifice and make others sacrifice; and all that is the highest good—even what they take from another.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nowhere do we see any wealth that has not been taken by force from some other; and even thus do kings conquer this earth.
Having conquered, they claim ownership, like sons over a father's wealth; the royal sages who have won heaven—theirs, it is declared, is dharma.
Just as the waters flow from the full ocean to the ten directions, even so does wealth go forth from the royal house and establish itself over the earth.
This earth was Dilīpa's, and Nṛga's, and Nahuṣa's, and Ambarīṣa's, and Māndhātṛ's; that same earth now rests in you.
A sacrifice rich in goods, with all its sacrificial fees, has come to you; if you do not offer it, O king, you incur sin against the gods.
Those for whom a king offers the horse-sacrifice, attended with its fees—drawing near to its concluding ablution, they all become purified.
The great god of universal form, in the great rite of the all-sacrifice, offered up all beings, and himself as well, by his own self.
Eternal is this path of prosperity; we have never heard of its end. Great is the road that the son of Daśaratha trod: do not, O king, go by a crooked path.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For but a moment, holding mind and hearing steady within your inmost self, listen; and then let my words find favour with you.
Never again, for your sake, would I tread the road travelled by the common throng; that road I shall now go, forsaking the pleasures of the village.
Ask of me, "What safe road is there to be walked alone?" Or, if you do not wish to ask, then hear me even unasked.
Forsaking the ways and comforts of the village, performing great austerity, eating fruits and roots, I shall wander in the forest among the deer.
Offering into the fire at its due season, touching water at both the twilights, lean, of measured fare, clad in deerskin and bark and wearing matted locks.

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
At life's end, when he casts off this all-but-wasted body, that sin lays hold of its doer; for it is the fruit of the deed that belongs to him who did it.
Thus, in this wheel of transmigration whirling round like a chariot-wheel, this throng of beings, driven by its tasks, comes together with another throng of beings.
For him who forsakes this round of rebirth—pithless and ill-ending, beset by birth, death, old age, sickness, and pain—there is happiness.
When even gods fall from heaven and great seers from their stations, who indeed that knows the truth of causes would still be a seeker after worldly existence?
For having done manifold deeds, each marked by its own diverse character, a king is bound fast by other princes upon the slenderest of pretexts.
Therefore, this nectar of wisdom has at long last come to me; and having gained it, I seek that state which is imperishable, eternal, and fixed.
Wandering ever by this manner of life, in this very fashion, I shall sustain my body, having set foot upon the path that is free of fear.
Bhīma said: Like that of some dull, unlettered reciter of scripture, O king, your understanding is deadened by recitations and does not perceive the true meaning of things.
You who have set your heart upon idleness and who spurn the duty of kings—in the destruction of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, what fruit will there be, O bull of the Bhāratas?
For one who treads the warrior's path, no forbearance, pity, compassion, or gentleness toward a kinsman has any place in the moment between you and him.
Had we known this mind of yours to be of such a sort, we would never have taken up the weapon, nor would we have slain any man at all.
We would have gone about for alms until the release of the body, and this terrible war of the kings of the earth would never have come to be.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All this is the food of life—so the wise have known; the unmoving and the moving alike, all of it is the nourishment of the breath of life.
Whoever stand in the way of one who is taking a kingdom—those, the wise who know the duty of warriors have declared, must be slain.
Those guilty men, the obstructers of your kingdom, have been slain by us; having slain them, enjoy this earth in righteousness, Yudhiṣṭhira.
As a man, having dug a well but reached no water, should turn back smeared with mud—just like that is this work of ours.
As one, having climbed a great tree and taken the honey from it, should go to his death without tasting it—just like that is this work of ours.
As a man, falling along a long road in hope, should turn back hopeless—just like that is this work of ours.
As a man, O best of the Kurus, having had his enemies slain, should afterward destroy himself—of just such a kind is this work of ours.
As a hungry man, having got food, should by some whim not eat it, or a lover, having won the woman he desires, should let her go—of just such a kind is this work of ours.
We ourselves are the ones to be blamed in this, we who are dull of wit and who follow you, O king, merely because you are the eldest, O Bhārata.
For we, mighty of arm, accomplished in learning, and high of spirit, stand obedient to the word of a weakling, as though we were powerless ourselves.
Bereft of all recourse, our purpose ruined just when our aim was to be fulfilled—how should men not look upon us as such men are looked upon?
It is taught that renunciation is to be undertaken in a time of calamity—by one overtaken by old age, or one outwitted and undone by his foes.
Therefore those of ripened wisdom do not commend renunciation here and now; the keen-sighted hold this very thing to be a transgression of dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
How should one who is sprung from it, founded upon it, and sheltered by it, sit there reviling that very thing? Or is one's trust to be placed elsewhere?
It is set going by men bereft of fortune, by the poor, by unbelievers—this doctrine that decries the teaching of the Veda, falsehood wearing the semblance of truth.
One may, by taking to a shaven head and maintaining oneself by oneself, putting on dharma as a disguise, manage to subsist—but not truly to live.
And again, one may live easily and alone in the forests, supporting neither sons nor grandsons, neither the divine seers, nor guests, nor the ancestors.
These deer are not winners of heaven, nor the boars, nor the birds; yet if it were by this manner of life, men would have declared them holy—and they do not.
If, O king, anyone could win perfection by mere renunciation, then the mountains and the trees would swiftly attain to perfection.
For these are seen to be ever in renunciation, free of all affliction, owning nothing, and forever moving by their own nature alone.
But if a man attains perfection by his own destiny and not by that of others, then it is action alone that must be performed; there is no perfection for the man without action.
Then creatures of the water and the rest of created things would attain perfection—they who have only themselves to maintain and no other being whatever.
Behold how the world is busied, each thing with its own several deeds; therefore it is action alone that must be performed; there is no perfection for the man without action.
Arjuna said: On this very matter they tell this ancient tale, the colloquy of Śakra with certain ascetics, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Certain brāhmaṇas, forsaking their homes, went away to the forest—dull-witted, their beards not yet grown, born of good family, they took to the wandering life.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Deeming this to be dharma, they took their stand in chastity, having abandoned their homes and their fathers; and Indra took pity upon them.
The Lord, becoming a bird of gold, addressed them: "A thing most hard to do is this that men have done, men who eat the leavings of others' meals.
Holy, indeed, is the deed of these, and praiseworthy their manner of life; perfected, devoted to dharma, they have reached the foremost goal."
The seers said: "Ah! this bird praises the eaters of leavings! Surely he is instructing us—for we too are eaters of leavings."
The bird said: "I do not praise you, smeared with mud, soiled with dust, eaters of refuse, dull of wit; quite other are the true eaters of leavings.
The seers said: "This we have honored as the supreme good. O bird, tell us what is the higher good; truly we put great faith in you."
The bird said: "If you do not mistrust me, having tested your own selves by your own selves, then I shall declare to you a word salutary and according to the truth.
The seers said: "We hearken to your word, dear one; well known to us are your ways. We wish to stand by your command, O righteous one; instruct us."
The bird said: "Among four-footed creatures the cow is foremost; among metals gold is best; among sounds the sacred mantra is foremost; and the brāhmaṇa is the best of two-footed beings.
This mantra, the rite of birth and the rest, is ordained for the brāhmaṇa, for him who lives—each in its due season—until his laying to rest in the burning-ground.
His are the Vedic rites; the path to heaven is the unsurpassed one; and they declare that all rites are made effectual by the mantra.
Those founded firmly upon the sacred tradition—so is fulfillment held to be attained herein. Months and half-months and seasons, the sun, the moon, and the stars,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and all beings strive on—that is the cosmic order for those bound to action. This is the holy field of fulfillment; this very order is the great stage of life.
But those men who, decrying action, have gone upon the wrong road—of those deluded ones, bereft of all good, there is found only sin.
Forsaking the lineages of the gods, the lineages of the ancestors, and the eternal lineages of brahman, the deluded carry on, and thereby pass onto a path not sanctioned by the scriptures.
Let this be your fitting austerity—the giving prompted by the seer's word, 'I bestow.' Therefore, for one who is intent upon it, the austerity of the austere man is so named.
Apportioning their due to the lineages of the gods, the lineages of the ancestors, and the eternal lineages of brahman, and serving one's teacher—that, truly, is called the hard thing to do.
The very gods, by doing the hard thing, attained to supreme dominion; therefore I declare to you that to bear up the householder's life is hard to do.
This is the highest austerity, and the root of all creatures—of that there is no doubt—this ordinance of the household, wherein all things have their ground.
This the brāhmaṇas, gone beyond the pairs of opposites and free of envy, have known as austerity; and so the forest life is reckoned only a middling austerity among the worlds.
And to the unassailable state go the true eaters of leavings, who at evening and at morning apportion the food within their own household according to the ordinance."
Those who eat what remains after they have first given to guests, to the gods, to the ancestors, and to their own kin—these are called the eaters of the leavings, the vighasāśins.
Therefore, abiding in their own duty, firm in their vows and truthful in speech, having become the teachers of the world, they remain unblemished and undefiled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Reaching the third heaven, the celestial realm of Śakra, free from all envy, those who perform deeds hard to perform dwell there for everlasting years.
Then, having heard his words fraught with righteousness and worldly gain, they abandoned the path of the unbelievers and took refuge in the duty of the householder's life.
Therefore you too, O unassailable one, taking hold of an unwavering steadiness, govern the whole earth now that her enemies are slain, O best of men.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of Arjuna, Nakula spoke, gazing upon the king, that foremost of all upholders of duty.
Deferring to his brother's mind, that subduer of foes, deeply wise, broad-chested and mighty-armed, his face coppery and his speech measured, spoke thus.
At the sacrificial post of Viśākhayūpa the fires of all the gods were kindled; know therefore, O great king, that the gods themselves abide on the path of ritual action.
The ancestors, the givers of life to the faithful, are themselves no unbelievers; they too perform action alone—behold this ordinance, O lord of the earth. But those who reject the teachings of the Veda, know them to be unbelievers in the extreme.
For the brāhmaṇa who casts aside what the Veda has declared in all his works does not attain the summit of heaven by the path of the gods, O descendant of Bharata.
There are those who transcend all the orders of life, so say the brāhmaṇas learned in scripture and certain in their grasp of the Veda; mark them well, O ruler of men.
He who pours forth his wealth righteously gained upon the foremost of sacrifices and upon men of disciplined soul—that man, O great king, is remembered as a true renouncer.
But he who, heedless of his own well-being and grounded only in what lies beyond, casts away his very self—that self-renouncer, O great king, is a renouncer steeped in dark inertia, O lord.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The sage who is homeless and wandering, taking shelter at the roots of trees, kindling no cooking fire, ever absorbed in yoga—that mendicant, O Pārtha, is a renouncer.
The brāhmaṇa who, disregarding anger and elation and slander alike, O lord of peoples, studies the Vedas and honours his teacher—he is a renouncer.
The wise declare that all the orders of life are held even upon a balance: on one side, O king, stand the three orders together, and on the other the household life alone.
He who keeps in view worldly gain, desire, and heaven alike, O descendant of Bharata—this is the path of the great sages, this the course of those who know the worlds.
He who shapes his disposition thus is the true renouncer, O bull of the Bhāratas—not he who abandons his home and goes to the forest like one bewildered.
When the crooked man who hunts the snare of righteousness merely to gratify his desires looks upon those desires, then the king of death binds him by the throat with the noose of death.
Action done out of pride is said to bear no fruit; but joined with renunciation, O great king, every deed yields a mighty fruit.
Tranquillity, restraint, austerity, giving, truth, purity, and uprightness, sacrifice, fortitude, and righteousness—this is remembered as the eternal ordinance of the sages.
Herein the undertaking made for the sake of the ancestors, the gods, and guests is praised; for here alone, O great king, the threefold aim of life is the entire fruit.
For the renouncer who treads this ordinance practised by the brāhmaṇas, who goes forward upon it, there is found no ruin anywhere at all.
For Prajāpati, the stainless one of tranquil soul, brought forth creatures, O king, thinking, 'They shall worship me with sacrifices of manifold gifts.'
And the creepers and the trees, and likewise the healing herbs for the sake of sacrifice, and the beasts fit for offering, and the oblations meant for sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the work of sacrifice falls hard upon the one who dwells in the householder's order; therefore the household life here is difficult to perform and difficult to attain.
Those householders who, having gained that state and being well supplied with cattle and grain, yet do not sacrifice—upon them, O great king, rests an everlasting guilt.
Some sages make their sacrifice of sacred study, others their sacrifice of knowledge, and yet others perform the great sacrifices by the mind alone.
For the twice-born one who thus treads the path of giving and inward composure, who has become one with Brahman, O king, even the dwellers in heaven yearn.
Without bestowing in sacrifices the varied jewels gathered from here and there, you prattle of unbelief; in one who clings to his household I see no renunciation, O ruler of men.
With the Rājasūya and the Aśvamedha, or again with the Sarvamedha and whatever other rites are honoured by the brāhmaṇas, my dear—worship with these, O great king, as Śakra the lord of the gods once did.
That king who, through the fault of his own negligence, offers no refuge to his subjects while they are plundered by brigands—he is called a very embodiment of strife, a Kali among kings.
Horses and cattle and serving-women, and richly adorned she-elephants, and villages and provinces, and fields and houses—
if we do not bestow these upon the twice-born, our minds possessed by selfish envy, we shall become the very dregs and strife of kings, O lord of peoples.
Those who give nothing and afford no refuge, who partake of the guilt that stains kings, are the enjoyers of sorrows alone and never of joys.
If, without having worshipped with the great sacrifices, without having offered the libation to the ancestors, and without having bestowed gifts at the holy fords, you shall then go forth as a wanderer—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
you will go to your dissolution like a sundered cloud driven by the wind, fallen from both worlds and left suspended in the void between them.
Whatever, within or without, breeds attachment in the mind—by relinquishing that does one become a renouncer, not by merely forsaking his place and going elsewhere.
For the brāhmaṇa who treads this ordinance practised by the wise, O great king, there is found no ruin anywhere at all.
Having swiftly struck down his flourishing foes, as Śakra struck the hosts of the Daityas in battle—who, O Pārtha, devoted to his own duty, should grieve over a path remembered by the ancients and cherished by the virtuous, O lord of the earth?
Having conquered the earth by the kṣatriya's law and by your valour, and bestowed it upon those who know the sacred verses, you shall go to the summit of heaven, O lord of men; there is nothing for you to grieve over this day, O Pārtha.
Sahadeva said: Perfection does not come by casting away outward possessions, O descendant of Bharata; by casting away the possession that is the body, perfection may come, or it may not.
Whatever merit or whatever happiness belongs to one who is free of outward possessions yet still craves the things of the body—let that fall to the lot of those who hate us.
Whatever merit or whatever happiness belongs to one who casts away even the possession that is the body while he governs the earth—let that fall to the lot of our friends.
Of two syllables is Death, mṛtyu; of three syllables is the eternal Brahman, śāśvatam. 'Mine' is Death; 'not mine' is the eternal.
Both Brahman and Death, O king, abide together within the self alone; unseen, they wage war over all beings—of this there is no doubt.
If the indestructibility of this living essence is a fixed truth, O descendant of Bharata, then in cleaving the bodies of beings no real injury is incurred.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But if, on the other hand, the essence arises together with the body and so too dissolves with it, then when the body perishes it would perish as well, and the whole path of ritual action would be in vain.
Therefore, casting aside this extreme view, the path that was followed by the ancients and by those still earlier, by the good—that path should be followed by the one who truly knows.
The king who, even having won the whole earth with all that stands still and all that moves, does not rightly enjoy it—his life is fruitless.
And on the other hand, O king, of one who dwells in the forest and lives upon its wild fare, if he still feels the sense of 'mine' toward possessions, he abides within the very jaws of death.
Behold the true nature of things both outward and inward, O descendant of Bharata; those who perceive that nature are released from the great fear.
You are my father, you my mother, you my brother, you my teacher; therefore you should forgive me, a man in distress, the grief-stricken lamentations I have uttered.
Whether what I have here spoken be true or untrue, know it to be spoken out of devotion, O protector of the earth, O best of the Bhāratas.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, the king of righteousness, kept silent, and his brothers were declaring their various certainties drawn from the Veda—
Draupadī, sprung from a great lineage, radiant and large-eyed, the foremost of women, addressed that lord of kings.
He sat there, a bull among kings, encircled by his brothers who were like lions and tigers—even as the leader of a herd is encircled by elephants.
Ever proud, and most of all toward Yudhiṣṭhira, forever cherished by the king, she who knew righteousness and beheld righteousness—
the broad-hipped one, addressing her lord with words exceedingly gentle and conciliatory, and gazing upon him, then spoke.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
These brothers of yours, O Pārtha, stand here parched like the cātaka birds, crying out again and again, yet you give them no answering gladness.
Gladden them, O great king, who like great rutting elephants have long been partakers of sorrow, with words that befit the occasion.
How is it, O king, that in the Dvaita forest you once spoke such words to these your brothers, gathered together and tormented by cold, wind, and heat—
'Having slain Duryodhana in battle, we shall enjoy the earth, full of all that the heart desires'—we who longed for victory in the fray?
'Having unhorsed the chariot-warriors and slain the great elephants, and strewn the earth with chariots and their riders, O subduers of foes—'
'We shall worship with manifold sacrifices, abundant and supplied with fitting gifts; and the sorrow wrought by our forest-dwelling shall turn to our joy.'
Having yourself spoken to them in this very wise, O foremost of the upholders of duty, how is it, O hero, that today you crush their spirits again?
No weakling enjoys the earth, no weakling partakes of wealth; in the weakling's house no sons abide—they perish like fish in the mud.
The kṣatriya who wields no rod of chastisement does not shine; without the rod he gains no prosperity; without the rod of the king, his subjects do not thrive in happiness, O descendant of Bharata.
Friendliness toward all beings, giving, sacred study, and austerity—this would be the duty of the brāhmaṇa, not of the king, O best of kings.
The restraint of the wicked and the protection of the good—this is the supreme duty of kings, and not to flee in battle.
He in whom dwell forbearance and anger, giving and withholding, fear and fearlessness, and both punishment and grace—he indeed is called one who knows what is right.
Not by learning, nor by giving, nor by conciliation, nor by sacrifice, nor yet by bribery was this earth won by you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That mighty host of your enemies, raised up by heroes, abounding in elephants, horses, and chariots, the greater for its three divisions—
guarded by Droṇa and Karṇa, by Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa—that host you struck down, O hero; therefore enjoy the earth.
Jambūdvīpa, O great king, thronged with its many provinces, was crushed by you, O tiger among men, by the rod of chastisement, O lord.
Krauñcadvīpa, the equal of Jambūdvīpa, O ruler of men, lying to the west of the great Meru, was crushed by you with the rod.
Śākadvīpa, the equal of Krauñcadvīpa, O ruler of men, lying to the east of the great Meru, was crushed by you with the rod.
Bhadrāśva, equal in measure to Śākadvīpa and lying to the north of the great Meru, O tiger among men, was crushed by you with the rod.
And the continents together with their lesser islands, the dwelling-places of many peoples—plunging across the ocean, O hero, you crushed them with the rod.
Having wrought these matchless deeds, O descendant of Bharata, you take no joy, O great king, though you are honoured by the twice-born.
So you, O Bhārata, looking upon these your brothers, greet them with gladness—like bulls in their prime, like mighty lordly elephants in rut.
All of them are the equals of the immortals, able to withstand any foe, scorchers of their enemies; and even one of them, I think, would suffice to bring you happiness.
How much more, then, these tigers among men, my husbands, bulls among men—who are to you as all the senses together are to the body in its every action.
My mother-in-law, who knew all and saw all, told me no falsehood when she said: 'O Pāñcālī, Yudhiṣṭhira shall establish you in happiness beyond compare.'
You of swift valour, having slain many thousands of kings—yet all of that I now see made vain through your bewilderment, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those whose eldest is crazed all follow in his train; and so, O lord of kings, through your madness all the Pāṇḍavas are stricken with madness too.
For if your brothers were not maddened, O lord of men, they would bind you and, together with the unbelievers, would themselves rule the earth.
For he who acts thus foolishly and does not attain his good is to be treated with fumigations, salves, nasal remedies, and drugs—he who walks upon a wayward path is one to be healed.
And so I, O best of the Bhāratas, am the basest of all women in the world—I who, though our foes have been brought low, still wish to go on living.
To these men who strive, prosperity comes of its own accord; but you, having won the whole earth, fashion calamity for yourself.
As Māndhātṛ and Ambarīṣa, those best of kings, were honoured of kings upon the earth—so, O king, do you shine forth.
Rule the goddess Earth with her mountains, forests, and islands, guarding your subjects according to dharma; do not, O king, be downcast in spirit.
Offer sacrifice with manifold rites, pouring oblations into the fires; and bestow cities, enjoyments, and garments upon the twice-born, O foremost of kings.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of Yājñasenī, Arjuna again spoke, after paying due deference to his mighty-armed eldest brother, his lord.
The Rod of governance chastises all subjects; the Rod alone protects them; the Rod keeps watch while they sleep—the wise know the Rod to be dharma itself.
The Rod safeguards dharma, and likewise wealth, O lord of men; the Rod safeguards desire as well—the Rod is said to be the threefold aim of life.
By the Rod is grain protected, by the Rod is wealth protected; grasp this, O learned one, and behold the very nature of the world.
Through fear of the king's Rod some evildoers commit no evil; some refrain through fear of Yama's rod, and some through fear of the world to come.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Through fear of one another some evildoers commit no evil; thus, in this established world, all things rest upon the Rod.
Through fear of the Rod alone some do not devour one another; men would sink into blind darkness were the Rod not to protect them.
Because it subdues the unsubdued and punishes the untaught—through this subduing and this punishing the wise call it the Rod, daṇḍa.
For the brāhmaṇas the rod lies in speech, for the kṣatriyas in the strength of the arm; the vaiśya's rod is reckoned to be giving, while the śūdra is said to wield no rod at all.
That mortals might not be confounded, and that their wealth might be preserved, the bound called the Rod was established in the world, O lord of the people.
Where the dark, red-eyed Rod moves abroad in truth and justice, there the subjects are not led astray—provided the ruler sees rightly.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—all these men keep to their proper path through fear of the Rod alone.
No man without fear offers sacrifice, O king; no fearless man wishes to give; nor does any fearless man wish to keep to his covenant.
Without cutting into the foe's vital points, without doing terrible deeds, without slaying like a fisherman killing fish, no man wins great fortune.
For one who does not slay there is here no glory, no wealth, nor again any subjects; it was by the killing of Vṛtra alone that Indra became the great Indra.
Those very gods who are slayers the world worships most ardently: the slayer Rudra, and Skanda, Śakra, Agni, Varuṇa, and Yama;
the slayer Kāla, and Vāyu, Mṛtyu, Vaiśravaṇa, and the Sun; the Vasus, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, and the Viśvedevas, O Bhārata.
To these gods the people bow, bent low before their fierce power; but to Brahmā, to Dhātṛ, to Pūṣan, never in any wise.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Only a few men, themselves tranquil in all their works, worship those gods who are indifferent toward all beings, self-restrained, and devoted to peace.
For I see no creature in the world that lives by non-injury; living beings live upon living beings, the stronger upon the weaker.
The mongoose eats mice, and the cat eats the mongoose; the dog devours the cat, O king, and the beast of prey the dog.
And man eats all of these—behold how dharma has come to be! All this, both moving and unmoving, is food for the breath of life.
In this ordinance, decreed by the gods, the wise man is not bewildered; as you were created, O lord of kings, so must you consent to be.
