The protector, the giver, ever devoted to dharma and unwearied, free from passion and spite—him men come to love.
Do not seek the increase of wealth through gain won by unrighteousness; for him who follows wrong precepts, both dharma and wealth are unstable.
A king who follows wrong precepts attains no store of wealth; and that wealth of his, ill-placed, all perishes utterly.
Driven by greed for wealth, he works his own undoing, for in his folly he oppresses the people with levies that the scriptures nowhere sanction.
For he who, craving milk, should cut away the cow's udder would get no milk at all; just so a realm afflicted by misrule does not thrive.
But he who tends the milch cow with care wins milk continually; even so, the king who draws upon his realm with prudent means reaps its fruit.
A realm well guarded and enjoyed by skilful means, Yudhiṣṭhira, ever brings forth an unmatched increase of the treasury.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The people, well protected by the king, yield him grain and gold, as a contented mother yields her milk freely to her own and to others alike.
Be like the gardener, O king, not like the charcoal-burner; so disposed, you will be able, by protecting your realm, to enjoy it long.
If, through a campaign against a hostile power, your wealth should be exhausted, then by conciliation alone should you seek to gather what wealth lies among men who are not brāhmaṇas.
Let not your mind waver at the sight of a brāhmaṇa possessed of wealth, not even in the direst extremity, O Bhārata, and how much less when you are prosperous?
Rather should you give wealth to them according to your power and their desert; consoling and protecting them, you will attain heaven, hard though it be to win.
Thus, by conduct grounded in dharma, protecting the people, you will attain an end that is good, meritorious, and crowned with renown, O joy of the Kurus.
Protect the people through righteous administration, O Pāṇḍava; so engaged, Yudhiṣṭhira, you will not be bound by the fetters of sorrow.
This indeed is the supreme dharma, that the king protect his people; for the protection of beings in accordance with dharma is the highest compassion.
Therefore those skilled in dharma hold this to be the supreme dharma: that the king, devoted to protection, shows compassion toward all beings.
The sin a king commits in a single day by failing to guard the people from fear—only after a thousand years does he reach the end of its consequence.
The merit a king earns in a single day by protecting the people righteously—its fruit he enjoys in heaven for ten thousand years.
Whatever worlds are won by him who has sacrificed well, studied well, and practised austerity—those a king attains in a moment by protecting the people righteously.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus diligently upholding dharma, O son of Kuntī, having gained the fruit of merit here, you will not be bound by the fetters of sorrow.
And in the world of heaven you will attain great splendour, O Pāṇḍava. Duties such as these are impossible for those who are not kings; therefore it is the king alone, and no other, who can win so vast a reward.
Having won a flourishing kingdom and ruling it righteously, gratify Indra with the soma offering, and your friends and people with the fulfilment of their desires.
Bhīṣma said: He who would protect the good and root out the wicked—he alone, O king, is the man the king should appoint as his royal chaplain.
On this point too they recite an ancient tale: the dialogue between Purūravas, son of Ilā, and Mātariśvan, the Wind.
The son of Ilā said: Whence was the brāhmaṇa born, and whence the other three classes? And by what cause is one superior to the rest? Explain this to me, O Wind.
The Wind said: From the mouth of Brahmā was the brāhmaṇa created, O best of kings; from his arms the kṣatriya was brought forth, and from his thighs, they say, the vaiśya.
To serve these three classes, O bull among men, the fourth class was fashioned thereafter: the śūdra, made from his feet.
The brāhmaṇa, the very moment he was born, came into being upon the earth as lord over all creatures, for the safekeeping of the treasury of dharma.
Then he made the kṣatriya, the second class, as the protector of the earth and the wielder of the rod, for the guarding of the people.
The vaiśya should sustain these three classes with wealth and grain, and the śūdra should serve them—such is the ordinance of Brahmā.
The son of Ilā said: To whom does this earth, together with its wealth, rightfully belong—to the twice-born or to the kṣatriya? Tell me this truly, O Wind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Wind said: All this, whatever exists upon the earth, belongs to the brāhmaṇa; by reason of his birth as the eldest, those skilled in dharma know it to be his.
The brāhmaṇa enjoys only what is his own, wears what is his own, and gives away what is his own; for the twice-born is the guru of all the classes, eldest and most excellent.
As a woman, in the absence of her husband, takes the husband's brother as her lord, so the earth, by reason of succession, takes the kṣatriya as her lord.
This is the first rule for you; another is meant for times of distress—if, by way of dharma, you seek the highest place in heaven.
Whoever should conquer territory should make it over to a brāhmaṇa—one endowed with sacred learning and good conduct, knowing dharma and given to austerity—
to one content in his own duty, who is not greedy for wealth, who could guide the king by an understanding complete in every respect.
For a brāhmaṇa born in a good family, of ripened wisdom and disciplined speech, leads the king toward what is good, his eloquence flowing in wondrous strains.
Whatever dharma the king practises as shown to him by the brāhmaṇa—being attentive, free of arrogant speech, and steadfast in the vow of kṣatriya duty—
by that very measure he, grown wise, abides long in renown; and of all that dharma the royal chaplain is a sharer.
In just this way, all the people who take refuge in the king, conducting themselves well and abiding in their own duties, are beset by no fear from any quarter.
Whatever dharma they practise within the realm, well protected by the king—of that dharma the king obtains a fourth share.
Gods, men, ancestors, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas all live upon sacrifice—and there is no sacrifice where there is no king.
By what is offered from here the gods and likewise the ancestors live; and upon the king alone rests the securing and preserving of this dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the heat one finds comfort in shade, in water, and in the breeze; in the cold one finds comfort in fire, in clothing, and in the sun.
The mind delights in sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; yet in all these enjoyments it is the man free of fear who finds true happiness.
He who is the giver of freedom from fear, his is the very greatest reward; for in the three worlds there is no gift equal to the gift of life.
The king is Indra, the king is Yama, the king is Dharma himself; the king bears all these forms, and by the king is all this upheld.
Bhīṣma said: The king should appoint as his chaplain one who is learned and deeply versed in scripture, who has weighed well both dharma and artha—both immeasurable—each in close relation to the other.
Those kings whose chaplain is righteous of soul and knowing of dharma, and who are themselves endowed with such virtues—with them, O king, all is well in every way.
Both together cause the people, the gods, and the ancestors near and far to flourish—the two who, joined together and steadfast in dharma, are worthy of trust and rich in austerity.
Friends to each other, in mutual accord and of one mind—through the honour paid to brahman and kṣatra the people would attain happiness.
But by the dishonouring of these two the people would surely perish; for brahman and kṣatra together are called the root of all duties.
On this point too they recite an ancient tale: the dialogue between the son of Ilā and Kaśyapa—mark it well, Yudhiṣṭhira.
The son of Ilā said: When brahman forsakes kṣatra, or when kṣatra in turn forsakes brahman, which of the two then enjoys the stronger power, and through which of them does the weakness set in?
Kaśyapa said: Ruined becomes the realm of the kṣatriya wherein brahman and kṣatra fall into discord; there the brigands come to enjoy the power, and there the good men waste away into weakness.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Their bulls do not thrive, nor their cows; no churning-stick stirs the curds, nor do they sacrifice; nor do their sons study the Veda—when the kṣatriyas abandon brahman.
No bull thrives in their household ever; they do not study with their offspring, nor do they sacrifice; degraded, they become as brigands—those brāhmaṇas who abandon the kṣatriyas.
For these two are ever bound together in upholding each other: kṣatra is the womb of brahman, and the twice-born are the womb of kṣatra.
When these two are ever devoted to each other, they attain a great and firmly seated splendour; but if their ancient union is broken, then all falls into utter confusion.
Then he who would cross over finds no raft, like a boat cast adrift upon fathomless depths; the four-fold order falls into confusion, and thereupon the people are set on the path to ruin.
The tree of brahman, when guarded, rains down honey and gold; but left unguarded, it rains down only tears and evil without end.
When one who is no celibate, fallen away from right discipline, yet a brāhmaṇa, seeks protection within the brahman order, there the god rains only by rare chance, and there calamities hard to bear assail again and again.
Where a sinner who has slain a woman or a brāhmaṇa finds approval in the assembly, and feels no fear even in the king's presence—from that does danger arise for the kṣatriya.
When sin is wrought by sinners beyond all measure, then is this god Rudra born; the wicked by their wickedness bring forth Rudra, and then he destroys all alike, the good and the wicked.
The son of Ilā said: Whence is Rudra, and of what nature is this Rudra? By living beings the living are seen to be destroyed. Explain this to me, learned Kaśyapa—whence is this god Rudra born?
Kaśyapa said: Rudra is the self within the hearts of men; he slays both one's own body and the body of another. They call Rudra like the onslaughts of the wind; his form is like forest fires and like thunderclouds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The son of Ilā said: No one can wrap up the wind, nor does the thundercloud rain, nor the forest fire blaze, in the same fashion as is seen among men; for it is through desire and hatred that a man is bound and is set free.
Kaśyapa said: As a fire blazing in a single house may swiftly burn down the whole village, so this god works delusion, and thereupon all are touched by merit and demerit together.
The son of Ilā said: If the rod of punishment touches the man of merit without distinction, when sin is wrought by sinners, then for what reason should one do good, and for what reason should one refrain from evil?
Kaśyapa said: Because the evildoers are not cast off, the same punishment touches the innocent through their commingling; the green is burned together with the dry by reason of their mingling. Let one therefore never mingle in any way with those who do evil.
The son of Ilā said: Here the earth bears up the good and the wicked alike; here the sun warms the good and the wicked alike; here the wind blows upon the good and the wicked alike, and the waters likewise carry the good and the wicked alike.
Kaśyapa said: Thus indeed it is in this world, but not so in the world beyond, O prince; after death there is a wide difference between the two—him who does good and him who does evil.
The world of merit flows with honey, its flame is clarified butter, its light is gold, and it is the very navel of immortality; there, after death, the man of holy conduct rejoices—there is no death, no old age, and no sorrow.
The world of evil is hell, devoid of light, ever full of pain and abounding in grief; there the evildoer laments over himself, falling through many years without any foothold.
Through mutual discord between brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas the people enter into pain hard to bear; knowing this, the king should indeed here appoint as chaplain a learned man, not one of meagre knowledge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And he should consecrate such a one along with himself; so is the dharma ordained, for the brāhmaṇa is declared foremost of all here, by the law of dharma.
For first of all were the brāhmaṇas created, so those who know dharma understand; and by reason of his birth as the eldest, all that is highest has come to him.
Therefore the brāhmaṇa is to be honoured and worshipped, the first to partake of the offered food; whatever is best and most excellent should, by dharma, be presented to him.
This must without fail be done by the king, however mighty he may be; for brahman makes kṣatra to flourish, and from kṣatra brahman flourishes in turn.
Bhīṣma said: The securing and preserving of the realm is said to rest upon the king; and the securing and preserving of the king himself rests upon the chaplain.
Where brahman quells the unseen dangers of the people, and the king with his two arms quells the seen, that realm thrives in happiness.
On this point too they recite an ancient tale: the dialogue between King Mucukunda and Vaiśravaṇa.
Mucukunda, lord of the earth, having conquered this whole earth, and wishing to test his own might, marched against the lord of Alakā.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa loosed his Rākṣasas upon him, and those night-roving demons advanced, crushing his armies.
As his host was being slaughtered, Mucukunda, that subduer of foes and ruler of men, reproached his learned house-priest.
Then Vasiṣṭha, the foremost knower of Brahman, having performed fierce austerity, struck down the Rākṣasas there and so found a way through.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa showed himself to Mucukunda, and, as the armies were being slain, spoke these words.
"Mightier than you were the kings of old, together with their house-priests; yet they did not conduct themselves as you do here.
Those lords of the earth too, skilled in arms and mighty as they were, came and waited humbly upon me, the dispenser of joy and sorrow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If there is strength in your arms, it is that you should display. Why do you presume so far by the power of a Brāhmaṇa?"
Then Mucukunda, though angered, answered the lord of wealth with these words, grounded in reason, unflustered and unperturbed.
"This Brahman and Kṣatra were created of a single origin by the Self-existent One, yet with their distinct allotments of power; together they guard the world.
The power of austerity and sacred formula is ever established in the Brāhmaṇas; the power of weapons and arms is ever established in the Kṣatriyas.
By the union of these two the protection of the people must be carried out; and yet, O lord of Alakā, you reproach me for acting in just this way."
Then Vaiśravaṇa said to the king and his house-priest: "I do not bestow a kingdom upon anyone unless it has been ordained for him.
Nor do I wrest away what has been ordained — know this, O lord of the earth. Rule, O hero, this whole earth, given by me to you."
Mucukunda said: "I do not wish to enjoy a kingdom given by you, O lord of the earth. It is my desire to possess a kingdom won by the might of my own arms."
Bhīṣma said: Then King Vaiśravaṇa was struck with the utmost wonder, beholding Mucukunda standing firm and unshaken in the Kṣatriya's duty.
Then King Mucukunda governed the earth, rightly won by the might of his arms, holding faithfully to the Kṣatriya's duty.
Thus the king who knows Brahman and acts with Brahman foremost conquers the earth as yet unconquered, and attains great glory.
The Brāhmaṇa should ever keep his sacred libations, and the Kṣatriya his weapons ever ready; for upon these two depends everything that exists in the world.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By what manner of life does a guardian of the earth make his people prosper, and conquer the holy worlds? Tell me this, O grandsire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: The king should be given to charity and to sacrifice, O Bhārata, devoted to fasting and austerity, and intent upon the protection of his people.
And the king should ever guard all his subjects by dharma, with diligence and vigilance, and should honor the righteous.
For when dharma is honored by the king, it is thereupon honored everywhere; whatever the king practices, that is pleasing to the people.
And he should ever hold the rod of punishment raised, like Death itself toward his enemies; he should slay robbers on every side, and should not from mere caprice spare anyone.
For whatever dharma the people, well guarded by the king, here practice — of that dharma, O Bhārata, the king obtains a fourth part.
In what they study, what they sacrifice, what they give, what they worship — of all this the king, guarding the people with dharma, is partaker of a fourth.
But whatever evil is done in the realm when the king fails to protect his people — of that sin too, O Bhārata, the king obtains a fourth part.
Some say he bears the whole of it; the settled view is that he bears the greater half of the deed, O guardian of the earth — for he is then deemed cruel and a speaker of untruth. Hear by what means the king is freed from such a defilement.
If wealth carried off by thieves cannot be recovered, it should be made good from his own treasury — even by one who is poor and lives in want.
The property of Brahman and the Brāhmaṇas alike must ever be guarded by all the classes; whoever does injury to the twice-born should not be suffered to remain in the realm.
For when the property of Brahman is guarded, all is guarded; and when their favor has been gained, the king has accomplished his task.
As living creatures depend upon the rain-cloud, and as birds upon a great tree, so men depend for their living upon that king who is the accomplisher of all their aims.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For a king who is slave to his desires, ever crooked of mind, cruel and overgreedy, can never protect his people.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I am no seeker after the pleasures of kingship; I do not desire the kingdom even for a moment. It is for the sake of dharma that I welcome sovereignty — yet here no dharma is to be found.
Enough, then, for me of a kingdom in which dharma is not found. I shall go away to the forest, out of my longing to practice dharma.
There, in the holy forests, laying down the rod, my senses subdued, I shall worship dharma as a sage, feeding on roots and fruits.
Bhīṣma said: I know that mind of yours — it is born wholly of the virtue of mercy; yet by pure mercilessness toward self alone one cannot attain to greatness.
Rather, finding you gentle, self-controlled, exceedingly noble and exceedingly righteous, the world will think you weak, a man unmanned by squeamish piety, and will hold you in little esteem.
Look to the duties of kings, befitting your fathers and forefathers. This conduct in which you wish to stand is not the way of kings.
For not by resorting to a mercy tainted with faint-heartedness — but by the protection of your people — have you indeed attained the fruit of dharma.
For neither Pāṇḍu nor Kuntī ever prayed for such a blessing as this for you, my child — nor for the kind of cleverness by which you now act with such subtlety.
Valor, strength, and resolve your father ever invoked for you; greatness of soul, strength, and magnanimity Kuntī prayed for on your behalf.
Ever do the gods through Svāhā and the fathers through Svadhā — both, the human offerings and the divine — ever do fathers and deities desire such blessings in their sons.
Charity, study, sacrifice, and the protection of the people — for this dharma, and against its opposite, you were born into the very station of your birth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O son of Kuntī, of those who are yoked in due season to the burden, who bear the load laid upon them — even though they sink beneath it, their fame does not sink.
He who, fully self-restrained on every side, bears the burden without faltering — from his blameless deed and word comes that perfection which belongs to action itself.
No one here has ever passed his life by an utter and undivided abstention from action — be he a righteous man, a householder, a king, or again a student of sacred lore.
That deed which is mostly good, though small, is itself noble; what is done is better than what is left undone, and there is nothing more sinful than inaction.
When a man of good lineage, knowing dharma, attains the highest lordship, then, O king, the welfare and security of all conduce to their good.
One man by gifts, another by force, another by gracious and truthful speech — thus, having gained a kingdom, the righteous king should win men over on every side.
That king through whom learned men, born in good families and afflicted by the fear of want, find satisfaction and stability — what dharma is higher than this?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What is more conducive to heaven than this? What joy is higher than this? What is the supreme lordship beyond this? Tell me, if you think fit.
Bhīṣma said: He in whom men, rightly established, find security on the instant — he, in our view, is the foremost conqueror of heaven; this truth I tell you.
Be you, then, O best of the Kurus, the one who gladdens the Kurus. Be king, conquer heaven; protect the good and destroy the wicked.
May your friends, together with the good, live in dependence upon you, my child — as living creatures upon the rain-cloud, as birds upon a sweet-fruited tree.
Bold, brave, a smiter of foes, yet merciful and master of your senses, tender and openhanded in sharing — so may the people live in dependence upon you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Some are engaged in their own proper duty, and others likewise in unfitting work. Declare to me, O grandsire, the distinctions among such Brāhmaṇas.
Bhīṣma said: Those endowed with learning and its marks, who everywhere perceive the sacred tradition — these Brāhmaṇas, O king, are proclaimed equal to Brahman itself.
Those accomplished as officiating priests and teachers, steadfast in their own duties — these, O king, become as gods among the Brāhmaṇas.
The sacrificial priest, the house-priest, the counsellor, the envoy, and the overseer of affairs — these, O king, become as Kṣatriyas among the Brāhmaṇas.
Riders of horses, riders of elephants, charioteers, and foot-soldiers — these, O king, become as Vaiśyas among the Brāhmaṇas.
Those who are devoid of the deeds befitting their birth, sordid, mere kinsmen of Brāhmaṇas in name — these, O king, become as Śūdras among the Brāhmaṇas.
All who are unlearned in the Veda, and all who have not kindled the sacred fire — upon all of these the righteous king should levy tribute and forced labor.
Hired summoners, keepers of temple-idols, casters of horoscopes, and priests for whole villages — these are the outcaste Brāhmaṇas, with the highway-wanderer as the fifth.
From these the lord of the earth, when his treasury is depleted, may take tribute — save only from those who are equal to Brahman and those who are godlike.
The king is the owner of the wealth of non-Brāhmaṇas — so declares the sacred Veda — and likewise of those Brāhmaṇas, whoever they be, who take to unfitting work.
But those given to unfitting work should never be neglected by the king in any way; out of a desire to uphold dharma they should be restrained and provided for.
In whatever king's realm a twice-born man turns thief, those who understand such matters reckon that fault to be the king's alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who, learned in the Veda and a graduate of his studies, becomes a thief for want of livelihood — that man, O king, must be maintained by the king: so the knowers of dharma understand.
But if, once his livelihood has been provided, he does not mend his ways, O scorcher of foes, then he should be banished from that land, together with his kinsmen.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Over whose wealth has the king mastery, O bull of the Bhāratas, and by what manner of life should he conduct himself? Tell me this, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: The king is the owner of the wealth of non-Brāhmaṇas — so declares the sacred Veda — and likewise of those Brāhmaṇas, whoever they be, who take to unfitting work.
And Brāhmaṇas given to unfitting work should never in any way be neglected by the king — so the good recount the ancient practice of kings.
In whatever king's realm a twice-born man turns thief, they reckon that fault, that defilement, to be the king's alone, O king.
By that deed they deem themselves as if accused of a crime; therefore all the royal sages devoted themselves to protecting the Brāhmaṇas.
On this, too, they relate this ancient tale — the words sung by the king of the Kekayas as he was being carried off by a Rākṣasa.
A dreadful Rākṣasa seized the lord of the Kekayas, O king — a man given to sacred study and of firm-held vows, who dwelt in the forest.
The king said: In my realm is no thief, no miser, no drunkard, none who has neglected the sacred fire, none who has failed to sacrifice — yet you have entered into me, into my inmost being.
Nor in my realm is there a Brāhmaṇa unlearned, or without vows, or who drinks not the Soma, or who has not kindled the sacred fire — yet you have entered into my inmost being.
In my realm none sacrifice with rites whose priestly fees are unpaid, and none who is without vows pursues sacred study — yet you have entered into my inmost being.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They study and they teach, they sacrifice and they officiate at sacrifice, they give and they receive — firmly established in the six prescribed duties.
Honored and provided for, gentle and truthful in speech — my Brāhmaṇas abide in their own duty: enter into my inmost self.
They do not beg but bestow, skilled in truth and in dharma; they do not teach for hire nor study as pupils, they sacrifice but do not officiate as priests.
They protect the Brāhmaṇas and never flee from battles — my Kṣatriyas abide in their own duty: enter into my inmost self.
By farming, cattle-tending, and trade they earn their living without deceit — vigilant, performing their rites, true to their vows, truthful in speech.
Devoted to sharing, self-restraint, purity, and goodwill — my Vaiśyas abide in their own duty: enter into my inmost self.
They serve the three higher orders duly and without envy — my Śūdras abide in their own duty: enter into my inmost self.
To the wretched, the helpless, the aged, the weak, the sick, and to women — to all of these I have given a share: enter into my inmost self.
Of the established duties of family and region and the rest, I am one who, as prescribed, lets none of them lapse: enter into my inmost self.
The ascetics in my realm are honored and protected, given their share and treated with respect: enter into my inmost self.
I never eat without first sharing, I never approach another man's wife, I never sport as one wholly self-willed: enter into my inmost self.
In my realm no mendicant lives uncontinent, no continent man is left to beg; no offering is poured save through a proper priest: enter into my inmost self.
I despise neither the aged nor the learned nor the ascetics; I keep watch while my kingdom sleeps: enter into my inmost self.
Accomplished in the study of the Veda, an ascetic, knower of all dharma, master of the whole kingdom — such is my illustrious household priest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By giving I long for the celestial worlds; by truth, and by guarding the Brāhmaṇas, and by attendance I draw near to my elders — I have no fear of the Rākṣasas.
In my realm there is no widow, no Brāhmaṇa in name only, no Brāhmaṇa fallen to poverty, nor any thief, no adulterer, no doer of evil — I have no fear of the Rākṣasas.
On my body, as I fight for the sake of dharma, there is no span of two fingers' breadth unbroken by weapons: enter into my inmost self.
For cattle and Brāhmaṇas and for sacrifice the people of my realm forever pray my well-being: enter into my inmost self.
The Rākṣasa said: Since in every circumstance you look only to dharma, therefore reach your home in safety, O Kaikeya — and I depart in peace.
They who guard their cattle and Brāhmaṇas and protect their subjects, O Kekaya, have nothing to fear from the Rākṣasas — how much less from any man?
Those whose leaders are the learned, whose strength is the strength of brahman, whose wives hold guests dear — those men have surely won heaven.
Bhīṣma said: Therefore let the king protect the twice-born, for they, when protected, protect in return; their blessing falls upon kings, and the kingdom flourishes aright.
Therefore the king must especially restrain those twice-born who stray into wrongful acts, and must provide for them, for the welfare of the people.
The king who conducts himself thus toward townsfolk and country folk, having enjoyed blessings here, attains to dwelling in the world of Indra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The livelihood proper in times of distress has been expounded by way of the Kṣatriya's dharma, O Bhārata; but may a Brāhmaṇa somehow live by the dharma of a Vaiśya, or may he not?
Bhīṣma said: One unable to subsist by the Kṣatriya's dharma may live by the Vaiśya's dharma, taking up farming and cattle-tending in calamity, when his livelihood has failed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Selling which wares does a Brāhmaṇa, living by the Vaiśya's dharma, not fall from the heavenly worlds, O bull of the Bhāratas?
Bhīṣma said: Liquor and salt, sesame, lions and other beasts, bulls, honey and flesh, and cooked food, O Yudhiṣṭhira —
in all conditions a Brāhmaṇa should avoid these; for from selling them, my son, a Brāhmaṇa goes to hell.
The goat is Agni, the ram is Varuṇa, the horse is Sūrya, the earth is Virāṭ; the milch-cow, the sacrifice, and the Soma — these are never to be sold by any means.
The good do not commend the barter of raw for cooked; yet one may exchange cooked for raw for the sake of food, O Bhārata.
"We shall eat what is already cooked; let your honor prepare this raw food" — exchanging with such an understanding, there is never any unrighteousness.
On this I shall set forth for you what the ancient dharma was for those engaged in commerce; learn it, Yudhiṣṭhira.
"I give this to your honor; let your honor in turn grant that" — dharma proceeds by mutual consent, never by force.
Thus did the dealings of old proceed, among the seers and among others alike; and this, beyond doubt, is good.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: But, father, when all the people take up arms and depart from their own duties, and the strength of the Kṣatriya order wanes —
when there is no king to be a protector in the world, what then would be the refuge? Resolve this doubt of mine in full, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: By giving, by austerity, by sacrifices, by freedom from malice, and by self-restraint, the orders headed by the Brāhmaṇas should seek their own security.
Among them, those strong in the Veda, rising up on every side, should increase the king's strength, as the gods increase the strength of great Indra.
For when a king is failing, they say that brahman alone is his refuge; therefore one who knows should rise up by the power of brahman itself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But when a victorious king has secured the kingdom's safety, then let the orders enter again, each according to its dharma, upon their own tasks.
But when all bounds are overthrown and confusion is wrought by brigands, then all the orders, though bearing arms, incur no fault, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: But if the Kṣatriya order should everywhere turn evil against the Brāhmaṇas, who then is the Brāhmaṇa's protector, what is his dharma, what his refuge?
Bhīṣma said: By austerity, by chastity, by the weapon and by force, by honest means and by stratagem, it must then be brought under control.
When the Kṣatriya power has grown overweening, especially against the Brāhmaṇas, brahman alone should be its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya order springs from brahman.
From water arose fire, from brahman the Kṣatriya, from stone iron; the all-pervading fierce energy of these is quenched in its own source.
When iron cleaves the stone, when fire assails the waters, and when the Kṣatriya hates the Brāhmaṇa — then these three are quelled.
Therefore in brahman, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the surging, unconquerable fiery energies and forces of the Kṣatriyas are quelled.
When the might of brahman has grown soft and the might of the Kṣatriya weak, and all the orders have turned wholly evil against the Brāhmaṇas —
those who then make war, surrendering their own lives, guarding the Brāhmaṇas, and dharma, and their own souls —
those high-minded and wrathful men win the worlds of the meritorious; for the taking up of arms by all is sanctioned for the Brāhmaṇas' sake.
Beyond the worlds of those who have sacrificed well and studied well, beyond those of ascetics and of those who enter into fasting unto death or into the fire — the heroes go to the highest goal; thus, through the surrender of self, men know no higher dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Homage and benediction to them who offer up their bodies, restraining the haters of brahman; may we share their world. Manu declared those heroes winners of the world of brahman and worthy of heaven.
As those who have bathed in the final ablution of the horse-sacrifice are purified, so too, both the evildoer and the doer of good, are those slain by the sword in battle.
What is unrighteous becomes righteous; both righteousness and unrighteousness, by reason of place and time — and such is that place and time.
The friendly, doing cruel deeds, win the highest heaven; the righteous, doing what seem sinful deeds, reach the supreme goal.
On three occasions a Brāhmaṇa, taking up the weapon, incurs no fault: in defense of his own life, in a confounding of the orders, and amid the constraints of a besieged stronghold.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When a host of brigands has risen up, in the cause of the Kṣatriya order, amid a confusion of castes, when the orders are utterly bewildered — if another, a strong man, should prevail,
a Brāhmaṇa or a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, O best of kings, and he should protect the people from the brigands, wielding the rod of punishment in accordance with dharma —
should this be done or not done? Should he be restrained or not? Or is the weapon never to be taken up by any save those of Kṣatriya kin?
Bhīṣma said: Whoever proves a farther shore where there is none, a raft where there is no boat — be he a Śūdra or any other — by all means deserves honor.
He under whose shelter men may live at their ease, O king — men once helpless, now protected, who had been afflicted by brigands —
him let those men honor with affection as their own kinsman; for one who does great service again and again, O Kaurava, deserves esteem.
What use is an ox that bears no burden, what use a cow that yields no milk? What good is a barren wife? And what good is a king who does not protect?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As an elephant made of wood, as a deer made of leather, as a cart without a driver, as a barren field beside the road —
so a Brāhmaṇa who does not study his Veda, a king who does not protect, and a cloud that does not rain — all these are without purpose.
But he who ever protects the good and strikes down the wicked — he alone should be made king; by him is all this world upheld.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what origin, of what character, and of what kind should the officiating priests be, O grandfather, O lord of kings? Tell me that, O best of speakers.
Bhīṣma said: For each rite the ancient usage of the officiating priests is prescribed: first, having ascertained the metres and the sacred learning of the twice-born.
Those who are ever single-minded, steadfast, who speak no unkind word, friends to one another, respected, and even-sighted toward all;
in whom dwell kindness and truth, harmlessness, austerity, uprightness, freedom from malice and from pride, modesty, forbearance, self-restraint, and calm;
the man of modesty, firm in truth, self-controlled, who does no harm to living beings, free from desire and hatred, endowed with the three pure qualities;
harmless and satisfied in knowledge — he is worthy of the seat of brahman. These are the great officiating priests, my son, all to be honored according to their worth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This word of the Veda that is laid down concerning sacrificial fees — "this is to be given, this is to be given" — nowhere comes to a fixed limit.
This teaching takes no account of one's wealth, nor of the dharma of distress, which lies outside the rule; this dread command of the scripture regards not a man's capacity.
"One should sacrifice beginning with faith" — such is the Vedic revelation; but for a sacrifice tainted with falsehood, what then will faith accomplish?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Not by contempt of the Vedas, not by guile, not by deceit does anyone attain to greatness; let no such notion be yours.
The fees, my son, are a limb of the sacrifice, the strengthening of the Vedas; mantras bereft of fees can in no way carry one across.
One's capacity, measured by a brimming vessel, becomes not the least defective; for surely, my son, by the three orders the sacrifice must be performed as prescribed.
"Soma is the king of the Brāhmaṇas" — such is the Vedic revelation; and though they wish to sell him, no worthless livelihood is sanctioned. When he has been duly purchased according to dharma, the sacrifice is thereupon set in motion.
Thus has it been proclaimed in accordance with dharma by the seers who expound the dharma: the man, and the sacrifice, and the Soma should all be conducted by lawful means; for the man who proceeds by unlawful means is of no use to another, nor even to himself.
"The body is the vessel of the sacrifice" — so runs this scriptural saying; and in the case of great-souled brāhmaṇas these vessels are rightly consecrated.
"Austerity is higher even than sacrifice" — this is the supreme scriptural truth. I shall now declare that austerity to you, O learned one; hear it from me as well.
Non-injury, truthful speech, freedom from cruelty, self-restraint, and compassion — this the wise know to be austerity, and not the wasting away of the body.
To deny the authority of the Vedas, to transgress the scriptures, and to live everywhere without rule and order — that, indeed, is the ruin of the self.
Learn, O Pārtha, the nature of the ordinance of the ten priests of inward sacrifice: understanding is the ladle, the mind is the clarified butter, and supreme knowledge is the purifying strainer.
All that is crooked is the road to death; uprightness is the road to Brahman. Such is the whole scope of knowledge — what will idle babbling accomplish?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Even a slighter task is hard for a single man to accomplish without a helper — how much more, then, the rule of a kingdom, O grandsire?
Of what character and what conduct should a king's minister of affairs be? In what sort of man should a king place his trust, and in what sort should he place none?
Bhīṣma said: Kings, O king, have friends of four kinds: the ally bound by a shared interest, the loyal partisan, the friend by birth, and the friend made by contrivance.
The righteous-souled man is a fifth kind of friend; but he belongs neither to one party nor to two — he stands on whichever side dharma stands, or else he remains neutral.
Whatever design of his own may not please that righteous one, the king should not disclose to him; for kings bent on conquest move now by right means and now by wrong.
Of the four, the two middle kinds are the best; the other two are ever to be suspected. Indeed all are ever to be watched with caution, and the king's own business must be seen to before his very eyes.
For the king must never be negligent in the safeguarding of his friends; a negligent king the people surely come to despise.
The bad man turns to goodness, the good man becomes harsh; the foe becomes a friend, and the friend in turn grows corrupt.
A man's mind is ever changeable — who could ever wholly trust him? Therefore whatever business is of chief importance, that the king should carry out under his own eye.
Trust placed wholly and without reserve is the destroyer of both dharma and material gain; yet distrust of everyone everywhere is no better than death itself.
Trust is an untimely death, for he who trusts comes to ruin; he survives only at the pleasure of the man in whom he has placed his trust.
Therefore in some men one should trust, and in some one should be wary — this is the course of statecraft, my child, and the everlasting way of Fortune herself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The man of whom one thinks, "By my downfall this gain would come to him" — of him one must ever be wary; the wise know such a one to be an enemy.
From whose field the water flows down into another's field — there, against his will, all his dykes are liable to be broken through.
And so too the man below, afraid of the excess of water, wishes to break those dykes; whomever one perceives to bear such a mark, him one should mark out as a foe.
He who is not gladdened by your prosperity, and who grows more wretched at your decline — this they declare to be the sign of the highest friend.
The man of whom one thinks, "By my downfall his own downfall would follow" — in him one should place trust, even as one would in a father.
Him, as one prospers, one should foster to the utmost by every means — the friend who ever guards one from harm, both in matters of dharma and in one's undertakings.
One should know fear of one's harm to be the highest mark of a friend; those who desire one's harm are reckoned one's enemies.
He who is ever fearful of one's misfortune and contented only in one's prosperity — such a friend, when one is found, is said to be as one's own self.
Endowed with fair form, complexion, and bearing, patient and free from envy, well-born and rich in good character — such a man may be your nearest confidant.
Intelligent, of good memory, capable, and by nature free from cruelty, one who, whether honored or unhonored, would never turn malicious — such a man is fit.
Be he a priest, or a preceptor, or a comrade greatly esteemed — such a minister should dwell in your house, one who is held in the highest honor.
He may know your most secret counsel and the very ground of your interests and your dharma; in him your trust may rest, even as it would in a father.
Neither two nor three such should be appointed, lest they fail to bear with one another; for it is from a single shared interest that strife among beings ever arises.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who holds fame above all, who stands firm to his agreement, who does not hate the able but rather makes men able —
who would not abandon dharma out of desire, fear, greed, or anger, and who is capable and weighty in his counsel — such a man may be your nearest confidant.
Brave and noble, learned and skilled in resolve, well-born and of upright character, patient and free from envy —
these are the men to be made ministers, set over all affairs, honored and given their due share, well-supported and well-established.
When such men are wholly assigned to the tasks that befit them, and set to weighty undertakings, they bring forth the greatest goods.
These men perform their tasks, ever vying with one another, and they accomplish their objects, reporting them each to each.
And of your kinsmen you should be ever afraid, as of death itself; for as a rival king cannot endure a king's prosperity, so a kinsman never can.
Of the upright, the gentle, the generous, the modest, the truthful man — none, O mighty-armed one, rejoices in his ruin so much as a kinsman.
Yet to be without kinsmen is no great happiness either; and beyond that they are not to be despised, for the man who has no kinsmen, strangers indeed hold in contempt.
For the man wronged by others, his kinsman alone is his refuge; never does one kinsman endure to see another humiliated by outsiders.
Even when wronged by his own kin, a man knows it as a wound to himself; in them there are virtues, and in them too defects are seen.
One who is no kinsman neither shows favor nor hurls the poisoned shaft; but in the world of kinsmen both are seen — the good and the bad alike.
Them one should honor and ever revere, in word and in deed, and do what is pleasing to them, and never do anything displeasing.
Toward them one should always conduct oneself as though trusting, yet untrusting; for there is no man free of fault or of virtue to be found among them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the man who conducts himself thus and is never negligent, even his enemies grow well-disposed, and they too become his friends.
He who ever conducts himself thus, within the circle of his kinsmen and connections, among friends and foes alike, abides long in sovereignty and in glory.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When that circle of kinsmen and connections is thus not to be grasped, how is one's true disposition to be made plain, among friends and foes alike?
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount an ancient tale — the dialogue of Vāsudeva and the divine sage Nārada.
Vāsudeva said: One who is no true friend does not deserve to know one's deepest counsel, O Nārada, nor does a friend who is foolish, nor even a wise man who lacks self-command.
Relying upon your friendship, I shall tell you something, O Nārada; and beholding the whole of your understanding, I ask of you, O traveler of the triple heaven.
I render service to my kinsmen under the mere name of lordship; I am but a half-sharer in enjoyments, and I bear with their harsh words besides.
As one desiring fire churns the fire-stick, so do their harsh words churn my heart; that ill-spoken speech, O divine sage, burns me without end.
Strength dwells ever in Saṃkarṣaṇa, and softness again in Gada; Pradyumna is intoxicated with his own beauty — and so I am without a helper, O Nārada.
And the other Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, O Nārada, are men of great fortune, mighty and hard to assail, and endowed with unceasing energy.
He who lacks them would be as nothing; yet for him who has them it is sheer distress. Held back forever between two factions, I cannot choose either one.
For him who has both Āhuka and Akrūra, what could be more grievous than that? And for him who has neither of those two, what could be more grievous than that?
I am like the mother of two gamblers, O great sage: for the one I wish victory, and for the other no defeat.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As I am thus ever afflicted on both sides, O Nārada, you ought to tell me what is best, both for my kinsmen and for myself.
Nārada said: Calamities are of two kinds, O Kṛṣṇa — outer and inner, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis — and they arise whether self-wrought or sprung from another.
This grievous calamity of yours is the inner kind, born of your own deeds; for all these troubles spring from Akrūra and the Bhojas and follow in their train.
For the sake of gain, or out of desire, or through Dvāravatī, or even from loathing, the sovereignty you yourself had won was made over to others.
Now that lordship has struck root, has gained renown, and has won its supporters; it cannot be taken back again by you, any more than food once vomited up.
The kingdom of Babhru and Ugrasena can in no way be regained — out of fear of a split among the kinsmen, O Kṛṣṇa, and least of all by you.
And if it should be accomplished by great effort, after performing a most arduous deed, it would bring vast ruin and expense, or else destruction would come once again.
With a weapon not of iron, soft, yet cleaving to the very heart, draw out the tongue of all of them, stroking and soothing them again and again.
Vāsudeva said: How, O sage, am I to know that weapon — not of iron, and soft — by which I may draw out their tongue, stroking and soothing them again and again?
Nārada said: The constant giving of food to the best of one's power, forbearance, self-restraint, uprightness, and honoring each according to his due — this is the weapon not of iron.
When your kinsmen are minded to speak words bitter and slighting, do you with gentle speech quiet their hearts, their words, and their minds.
No one who is not a great man, none lacking self-command, none without helpers, takes up the mighty yoke; lift it up and bear it upon your breast.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Any ox at all bears a heavy load on level ground; but on rough roads it is the well-made, sturdy bullock that bears the burden hard to carry.
From division comes the ruin of confederacies; you are the chief of your confederacy, O Keśava. So act that this confederacy, having you, may not be brought to ruin.
By nothing but wisdom and patience, by nothing but mastery of the senses, by nothing but the giving up of wealth, does a community hold together in a wise leader.
So act, O Kṛṣṇa, that the destruction of your kinsmen may be averted — a thing fortunate, glorious, life-giving, and auspicious, which exalts your own party.
For the future and for the present alike, nothing is unknown to you, O lord — neither the ordering of the six measures of policy, nor the manner of march and of march against the foe.
The Mādhavas, the Kukuras, the Bhojas, and all the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis depend upon you, O mighty-armed one — yes, and the worlds too, and those who are lords of the worlds.
The seers too wait upon your wisdom, O Mādhava; you are the teacher of all beings, you know the going and the coming of all things; and having you, O best of the Yadus, your kinsmen thrive in happiness.
Bhīṣma said: This is the first mode of conduct; now hear the second, O Bhārata. Whatsoever man brings forth wealth for the king, that man the king should protect.
Whoever — whether in the king's pay or not — should report that the royal treasury is being plundered by a minister and brought to ruin, O Yudhiṣṭhira —
He must be heard in private, and he must be guarded from the ministers; for the ministers, O Bhārata, most often slay the man who would expose them.
The plunderers of the royal treasury band together and harass the guardian of that treasury; left unprotected, he perishes.
On this point men recount an ancient tale: what the sage Kālakavṛkṣīya once said to the king of Kosala.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When Kṣemadarśin had attained the sovereignty over the Kosalas, the sage Kālakavṛkṣīya came to him — so we have heard.
Having confined a crow in a cage, he first went diligently about the realm of Kṣemadarśin, again and again, seeking out intelligence.
"I have mastered the lore of crows; the crows declare to me what is to come, what is past, and what is happening now."
Roaming thus through the kingdom in the company of many men, he inquired into the misdeeds of all the king's officers.
And when he had learned the whole working of that kingdom in every part, and had learned, here and there, all the offences of the king's officers,
Then, taking that very crow, the sage of stern vows came to see the king, proclaiming, "I am all-knowing."
Coming to the king of Kosala, he would say to the adorned royal minister, "By the word of the crow, this deed of yours was done in such-and-such a place;
"This man and that man know that the royal treasury was robbed by you. So this crow declares; let it be swiftly looked into."
And so too he denounced the others who were always pilfering the royal treasury; nor was any word of his ever found anywhere to be untrue.
Thus thwarted, all the king's officers, O foremost of the Kurus, went past him by night while he slept and crushed the crow.
But seeing the crow in the cage pierced through with an arrow, in the forenoon the brāhmaṇa spoke these words to Kṣemadarśin:
"O king, I beg of you safety — you, the lord and master of my life and wealth; with your leave I would speak words for your good, set before you.
"He who, sore distressed for a friend's sake and gone to him with whole-hearted devotion, should say in vexation, 'This man is robbing your wealth' —
"Wishing to rouse his friend to awareness, as a charioteer rouses a good horse, even if, in his earnestness for the other's good, he grows over-zealous —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In such a friend his fault must be forgiven by the discerning man who would prosper, who desires lasting sovereignty."
The king answered him thus: "Whatever you may say to me, why should I not forgive it, seeking as I do my own good?
"O brāhmaṇa, give me your assurance, and speak out if you wish; for I shall do whatever you tell me, O sage."
The sage said: Having learned the courses of policy, the dangers, and the perils that come from your servants, out of devotion I have come into your presence to set forth a rule of conduct.
This fault of those who serve kings was declared long ago by the teachers: that a livelihood spent at a king's side is the last resort of the man who has no other resort.
They say that he who keeps company with kings keeps company with venomous serpents; for kings have many friends, and just as surely many foes.
From all of these, they say, danger comes to the king's attendants; and from these on the one side, O king, fear may arise in but a moment.
Toward a king one cannot keep watchfulness wholly unbroken; yet by no means must the man who desires prosperity ever be careless.
For through one's carelessness a king may stumble, and once he has stumbled there is no surviving him; the well-schooled man should approach a king as he would a blazing fire.
As though he were an angry venomous serpent, a man should always wait with care upon his lord, the master of his life and wealth, thinking, "I am as good as nothing."
Wary of an ill-spoken word, of a misdeed, of a thing badly managed, of sitting wrongly, of walking wrongly, of a gesture, of a movement of the limbs —
For a king, when pleased, like a god grants every object of desire; but enraged, like the all-consuming fire, he may burn one up root and all. Thus, O king, did Maya declare, and so indeed it stands.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Now I shall make the matter still plainer, again and again: a counsellor such as I lends the aid of his wisdom in time of peril.
My crow too, O king, was marked out for death; in this I do not blame you, nor those to whom you are dear. But discern who wish you well and who do not; do not let your judgement be a thing kept in the dark.
As for those who dwell in your house bent only on grasping, who wish no welfare to living beings — it was by such as these that my crow was struck down.
Or those who, plotting through hidden agents, desire the kingdom for themselves the moment you are destroyed — they succeed, O king, in no other way than this.
For fear of them, O king, I shall depart to another hermitage; for it was they who aimed the arrow that fell upon the crow, O lord.
By a stealthy stroke my crow was sent to the abode of Yama; for this I have seen, O king, with the far-seeing eye that austerity has given me.
Teeming with crocodiles and fish and water-monsters, thronged with shoals of timiṅgilas — that river which is yourself I have crossed, using the crow for a hook.
Beset with stumps and stones and thorns, swarming with tigers and lions and elephants, hard to approach, hard to enter, like a Himālayan cavern —
A fastness of darkness is passed by fire, a watery one by boats; but for crossing the stronghold that is a king, the learned know no sure means.
Your kingdom is an impenetrable thicket, wrapped in murk and gloom; here trust is impossible even for you — how much less for me?
Therefore no dwelling here is auspicious, where good and evil are reckoned alike; for here, doubtless, death falls upon the well-doer and the ill-doer the same.
By justice destruction falls upon the evildoer; but how should death come to the well-doer? It is not fitting to stay here long; the wise man should hasten away from here at once.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There is a river called Sītā, O king, in which the very raft sinks; like to that, I deem, is this all-destroying snare.
You are like a downpour of honey, like food laced with poison; your disposition runs as the wicked's does, not the good's; you are like a well, O king, ringed about with venomous serpents.
As a river of sweet water, but with treacherous fords and high banks, hedged with karīra and cane — even so, O king, are you; and though haunted by dogs and vultures and jackals, you are yet the equal of a royal swan.
As, taking root beside a great tree, the dense brushwood grows mighty, and then closes over it and, overtopping it, grows on —
And fed by that very fuel, the dreadful forest-fire surely burns — like to this are your ministers, O king; purge them away.
Made by you yourself, O king, and cherished by you, they hold you in contempt and seek to slay the one who is dear to you.
I have dwelt here suspicious, on my guard against carelessness — like a serpent within the house, like a hero's wife in his hall — wishing to test the character of the king while living at his side.
Has the king mastered his senses? Are his intimates won over? Is the king dear to them? Are the subjects dear to the king?
Wishing to learn these things I have come here to you, O best of kings; and you please me, O king, as food pleases a hungry man.
But your ministers please me not, as water pleases not one whose thirst is quenched; for the very reason that I serve your interest, they have laid a fault upon me — no other cause exists, of this I have no doubt.
For I have done them no injury; that has turned into a grievance with them. One should fear an enemy ill-struck, as one fears a serpent with its back but broken.
The king said: With greater retinue and greater honour, held in greater esteem, O best of brāhmaṇas, dwell yet again in my house.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who do not want you, O brāhmaṇa, shall not dwell in my house; and you yourself shall determine what is now to be done forthwith.
How the evildoer should be punished, and how the good deed should be rewarded — having considered these, O reverend one, appoint me to whatever is best.
The sage said: Without revealing this design, weaken them one by one; then, having found out the cause, do away with each man in turn.
For many men, banded together by a common grievance, may crush even thorns; from fear that your counsel be betrayed, O king, I tell you this.
But we who are called brāhmaṇas are mild in punishment and full of compassion; and I wish well to you, and to others, as to my own self.
O king, I declare myself to you — for I am a kinsman of yours; I am the sage known by the name Kālakavṛkṣīya.
I was your father's friend, esteemed by him, true to my word. When your kingdom had fallen into ruin, O king, and your father had passed away,
Renouncing every desire, I then practised austerity. Out of affection I tell you this, that you may not go astray again.
Having seen both sorrow and joy, and having won a kingdom by good fortune, how, O king, can you be heedless of a realm that rests in the hands of its ministers?
Bhīṣma said: Thereupon, when that bull among brāhmaṇas had been received into the house of the royal chaplain, great rejoicing once more arose in the royal family.
Having made the earth subject to a single parasol for the renowned king of Kosala, the sage Kālakavṛkṣīya performed sacrifices with the highest rites.
Having heard that salutary counsel, the king of Kosala ruled the earth; and the king did, O Bhārata, even as the sage had told him.
Bhīṣma said: Men ever good, restrained by modesty, endowed with truth and rectitude, able to speak rightly — let such be your members of council.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Men of great wealth and great valour, and brāhmaṇas of wide learning, well contented, O son of Kuntī, and of great energy in their tasks —
Seek such men as helpers in all calamities, O Bhārata; for a man of good family, ever honoured, does not conceal his strength.
For whether pleased or displeased, whether oppressed or despoiled, he most often turns the matter back to good — when such a one, even single, is cherished.
Men of good birth, native to the land, wise, comely, of wide learning, bold and devoted — let such be your retinue.
But the base-born, the greedy, the cruel, the shameless — these, my son, will wait upon you only so long as their palms are still moist.
With wealth and honour and homage and esteem, and with enjoyments high and low, whomever among your favourites you judge deserving of substance — let them have their share of comfort.
The learned of unbroken conduct, of good ways, who have kept their vows — such men, never mean and ever truthful, will not forsake you, though they look constantly to your bounty.
The ignoble, dull of mind, who do not know what is fitting — guard yourself against these, and mark out those who have fallen from their covenants.
One should not, forsaking a whole body of men, set one's heart on a single man, were a choice to be made between them; but if one man be better than many, then by all means let him give up the many for that one.
For this is the mark of a superior man: in whom valour is seen, who holds renown foremost, and who stands fast by his covenant.
Who honours the capable, who does not contend with those past contending, and who, from desire, fear, anger, or greed, never casts off dharma —
Free of pride, truthful, capable, master of himself, honouring those worthy of honour — such a man, tested in every condition, may be your companion in counsel.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Well-born, possessed of truth, enduring, capable, self-possessed, brave, grateful, and honest — this, O Pārtha, is the mark of a superior man.
When such a man, discerning, conducts himself in this way, even his enemies grow well-disposed and thereafter become his friends.
Thereafter the king, self-restrained, mature in wisdom, and desirous of prosperity, should examine the merits and faults of his ministers.
He should bind to himself trustworthy men of good birth, native to his own land, incorruptible, never wavering in loyalty, and well tested in every respect.
Warriors, hereditary retainers, and others duly equipped should be enlisted by a man who desires prosperity and seeks to flourish.
Those whose minds are schooled in discipline and whose nature is excellent, who possess energy, steadiness, forbearance, purity, devotion, constancy, and firmness—
those of tested virtues, of seasoned character, able to bear the yoke of office, and proven against the five temptations—these the king should make the agents of his affairs.
Men ample in speech, valiant, skilled in resolve, well-born, endowed with truth, able to read intentions, and free from harshness;
who know the disposition of place and time and seek the welfare of their master's work—such men the king should ever make his counselors in all matters.
For a man wanting in energy and joyless never reaches a firm decision, but inevitably breeds doubts in all undertakings.
Likewise a counselor of little learning, though of auspicious birth and versed in dharma, artha, and kāma, is not competent to weigh counsel.
And so one not nobly born, though he be ever so widely learned, falters in matters that call for reasoning, like a leaderless man without eyes.
And he who is unsteady of purpose, though intelligent, learned in tradition, and skilled in expedients, is unable to carry an undertaking through to its end.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From mere routine conduct, again, no discernment of the finer points of an affair can arise in the unlearned man of poor understanding.
In a counselor who lacks devotion there can be no trust; therefore one should never disclose counsel to a man who is not devoted.
For a crooked man, joined with other counselors, would torment the king, as fire entering through the fissures opened by the wind consumes a tree.
A master grows wroth at times and casts a man down from his post; in his fury he assails him with words, yet afterward he is appeased.
All such things can be endured by a devoted man; but a counselor's wrath would burst forth like the crash of a thunderbolt.
But the man who restrains such resentments, wishing only to please his master, and who shares alike in his joys and sorrows—him the king should consult in his affairs.
But a crooked man, though devoted and endowed with all other virtues and gifted with discernment of the king's mind, does not deserve to hear his counsel.
He who is bound up with the king's enemies and holds the townsfolk in little regard—such a friend of the king does not deserve to hear his counsel.
The ignorant, the impure, the arrogant, the server of foes, the boaster, the irascible, the greedy friend—he does not deserve to hear the counsel.
And a stranger, though devoted and ever so learned, though honored or made a sharer in fortune, does not deserve to hear the counsel.
And he who, even over some trifling matter, has once been reproached, though afterward endowed with other virtues, does not deserve to hear the counsel.
The man mature in wisdom, intelligent, wise, native to the realm, pure, and unblemished in all his dealings—he deserves to hear the counsel.
Endowed with knowledge and discernment, knowing the nature of foe and self alike, a friend who is the king's very equal—he deserves to hear the counsel.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Truthful in speech, endowed with good character, deep, modest, and gentle, one who is a servant from his fathers and forefathers—he deserves to hear the counsel.
Content, esteemed, truthful, high-spirited, holder of evil-doers in hatred, knower of counsel and of the right time, and valiant—he deserves to hear the counsel.
To one able to bring all people equally under his sway by conciliation, O king, the counsel should be entrusted by him who would wield the rod of punishment.
He in whom the townsfolk and country-folk place their trust by virtue of his righteousness, a warrior and one wise in statecraft—he deserves to hear the counsel.
Therefore the counselors, well honored and endowed with all these virtues and knowing the affairs of state, should number at least three, if one aspires to greatness.
They should mark the weak points in their own constituents and in those of the foe; for it is upon counsel as its root that the king's realm grows and prospers.
Let no enemy see his weak point; let him watch for the foe's weak points; let him hide his limbs like a tortoise and guard his own openings.
The wise counselors are the holders of the kingdom's counsel; the king is the very frame that binds the counsel together, and the rest of the people are its limbs.
They declare that the kingdom is rooted in espionage and has counsel for its essence; and here the counselors follow their master for the sake of their livelihood.
Having subdued pride and anger, conceit and envy, and grown serene, he should ever take counsel together with ministers proven against the five temptations.
Fixing his mind upon it, he should grasp the manifold deliberation of those three; and at the time of further counsel he should set forth both his own conclusion and that of the others.
Composed, he should approach and consult a venerable brāhmaṇa learned in dharma, artha, and kāma upon the highest matter; and when a firm resolve has been reached with him, he should pursue that course without attachment.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus, they say—those who know how to determine the true meaning of counsel—should one ever take counsel; therefore you too should always so frame counsel fit to win and hold the people.
Let no dwarf, hunchback, or emaciated man, no cripple, no blind or witless person, no woman or eunuch be there; let no animal, and let no one move about in front or behind, above or below.
Having ascended to an empty terrace, open and bright, free of kuśa and kāśa grass, and avoiding all faults of speech and gesture, he should deliberate his counsel on the matter at no untimely hour.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Bṛhaspati and Śakra, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Śakra said: What is that one word, O brāhmaṇa, which a man, practicing rightly, may become the standard for all beings and win great renown?
Bṛhaspati said: Conciliation is that one word, O Śakra, by practicing which rightly a man may become the standard for all beings and win great renown.
This one word, O Śakra, brings happiness to the whole world; practicing it toward all beings, a man becomes dear to them forever.
For he who never speaks a word, his face forever knit in a frown, becomes hateful to all beings, since he practices no conciliation here.
But he who first looks kindly upon a man and is the first to address him, speaking with a smile—toward him the world is well disposed.
For even a gift, given everywhere without kindly words, does not please beings—like food served without seasoning.
For even a man who gives nothing, by uttering sweet speech to beings, brings this whole world under his sway through conciliation, O Śakra.
Therefore conciliation should be practiced by those who would wield the rod here; thus it bears fruit, and the people do not shrink from him in dread.
For to conciliation well wrought, smooth and sweet and rightly employed, there is never found an equal.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Thus instructed by his preceptor, Śakra did all accordingly; and you too, son of Kuntī, should practice this rightly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How, O lord of kings, does a sovereign, while protecting his subjects in accordance with dharma, win in particular an everlasting fame?
Bhīṣma said: By pure administration of justice, devoted to the protection of his subjects, the upright king attains both dharma and fame, and wins both worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What sort of justice, and with whose aid, should the king administer? Being asked this, O greatly wise one, you ought to declare it duly.
And those virtues that were earlier spoken of concerning a man—these are not found in any single man, such is my view.
Bhīṣma said: It is so, O greatly wise one, as you say, O intelligent one: hard to find is any man endowed with all these manifold virtues.
Yet good character, in brief, is not hard to find here for one who strives; I shall tell you how, and what manner of ministers you should appoint.
Four brāhmaṇas, learned, bold, of sattvic temper, and pure; and three śūdras, disciplined and pure, of proven service in their former duties;
and one sūta versed in the ancient lore, endowed with eight virtues, fifty years of age, bold, and free from envy, he should employ;
possessed of intelligence and memory, disciplined, even-handed, competent among litigants disputing a case, and ungreedy of gain.
In the midst of these eight counselors, wholly free from the seven dreadful vices, the king should take his counsel.
Then he should send them forth into the realm, and make it known to the realm: 'By this administration of justice are your subjects ever to be overseen.'
Nor should any hidden affair, ruinous to the business of state, be entertained by you; for should the affair miscarry, that unrighteousness would afflict both you and them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And your realm would scatter, like flocks of birds fleeing a hawk, and would forever leak away like a shattered boat upon the sea.
For a king who protects his subjects wrongly and unrighteously here, a fear arises within his very heart, and heaven is barred against him.
And whoever rules unrighteously—be he king, minister, or king's son—when appointed to the seat of justice that is rooted in dharma, O bull among men—
the king's followers, appointed over affairs but not discharging them aright, go down to ruin, putting themselves at the head, together with the king.
Of those oppressed by the powerful and crying out piteously in their misery, the king is ever the protector—the protector of men who have no other lord.
In a dispute, then, the weight of good witnesses must decide the matter; but a case without witnesses, or one unsupported, must be examined with particular care.
He should lay upon evildoers a punishment befitting the offense: the wealthy he should chasten with fines, the poor with flogging and imprisonment.
The wicked the king may discipline, even with corrective measures and with blows; and the well-behaved he should cherish with conciliation and with gifts.
Whoever should seek to slay the king—for him let the death be exemplary; so too for the assassin, the thief, and the corrupter of the social order.
For a king who duly metes out punishment, O lord of the people, or for one fit to do so, there is no unrighteousness; here it is righteousness everlasting.
But the unwise man who inflicts punishment at the prompting of caprice becomes joined to infamy here, and when dead attains hell.
He should not inflict punishment upon others merely on another's word; having pursued the proper inquiry, he should then either imprison or release them.
But a king should never slay an envoy in any extremity; the slayer of an envoy enters into hell together with his ministers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A king devoted to the kṣatriya's dharma who slays an envoy for delivering his message as told—the forefathers of such a king incur the guilt of slaying an embryo.
Well-born, endowed with good character, eloquent, skillful, agreeable in speech, faithful in delivering his message, and of good memory—an envoy should possess these seven virtues.
Endowed with these same virtues, his door-warden becomes his protector; and possessed of these same virtues, one becomes the guardian of his very head.
One who knows the true import of the treatises on dharma and artha should be the minister of peace and war—intelligent, resolute, wise, and a keeper of secrets.
Well-born, endowed with truth, capable—such is the praiseworthy minister; and endowed with these same virtues, so too should the commander of the army be.
Let him be one who truly knows battle-arrays, engines, and weapons, endowed with valor, enduring of rain and cold and heat and wind, and skilled at detecting the weak points of his foes.
Let him inspire confidence in others, yet himself trust no one; for even in one's sons, O lord of kings, trust is not to be commended.
This essence of the meaning of the treatises I have declared to you, O sinless one; mistrust is said to be the supreme secret of kings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In what kind of city ought a king himself to dwell — one already built, or one he has caused to be built? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Where one must dwell, O son of Kuntī, together with sons and brothers and kinsmen, it is right there to inquire into its defenses and its means of livelihood, O Bhārata.
Therefore I shall set forth for you the matter of fortifications in particular; having heard it, you should so dispose things and carry them out with care.
Resorting to fortification of six kinds, let him establish cities — whichever abounds chiefly in all resources, or wherever such abundance may be possible.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A desert-fort, an earthwork-fort, a hill-fort, likewise a fort of men, a water-fort, and a forest-fort — these are the six.
That city which is well provided with defenses, furnished with grain and weapons, with stout ramparts and moats, and thronged with elephants, horses, and chariots —
where there are learned men and craftsmen, and stores well laid up, and where the people are righteous and have attained the highest skill;
vigorous in its men, elephants, and horses, graced with crossroads and markets, of well-established commerce, tranquil, and with nothing to fear from any quarter;
radiant, resounding, with well-ordered dwellings, filled with people who are brave and wealthy, and made to echo with the chanting of the Veda —
abounding in assemblies and festivals, where the gods are ever worshipped: in such a city let the king, with ministers and army obedient to him, himself dwell.
There let him increase his treasury, his army, his allies, and his commerce, and let him do away with every defect in city and countryside alike.
With diligence let him enlarge his storehouses and armories, and increase all his stores, his engines of war, his maces, and his medicines.
Timber, iron, chaff, charcoal, planks, horn, bone, and bamboo; marrow, oil, fat, and honey, and a whole supply of medicinal herbs —
hemp, resin, grain, weapons and arrows, hides and sinews, and cane, and muñja and balbaja grasses and the wood of the dhanvana tree.
Reservoirs and wells, excellent and abounding in water, should ever be kept secure by the king, and so too the trees that yield sap.
And with care let him honor teachers, officiating priests, and chaplains; mighty archers, architects, astrologers, and physicians;
the wise, the intelligent, the self-controlled, the able, the brave, the deeply learned, the well-born, the men of great spirit, fit for every task.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let the king honor the righteous and restrain the unrighteous, and with diligence set all the classes to their proper tasks.
Having made well known through his spies the people of city and country, both without and within, let him then set his measures in motion.
To his spies, his counsel, and his treasury — and to his counsel above all — let the king himself attend; for upon these everything rests.
Whatever the neutral, the foe, and the ally intend to do, in city and country alike, is to be known through the eye of his spies.
Thereupon let everything be so ordered without negligence, the king ever honoring the loyal and restraining the hostile.
He should ever sacrifice with sacrifices, and give gifts without oppression; the protection of the people is to be done, and no blameworthy deed is to be done.
For the wretched, the helpless, and the aged, and for widowed women, let him ever provide both welfare and livelihood.
To the hermitages, at the proper seasons, let the king ever bring clothing, vessels, and food, doing them honor and never holding them in contempt.
Himself, all his affairs, and even his kingdom let him diligently lay before the ascetic, and ever stand before him in humility.
One who has renounced all possessions, born of good family and deeply learned — seeing such a one, let the king honor him with bed, seat, and food.
In him let the king place his trust in any time of distress; for even robbers place their trust in ascetics.
With him let him deposit his treasures and from him gather wisdom; yet let him not wait upon him too constantly, nor honor him to excess.
One such man should be employed within his own realm, another in foreign realms, another in the forests, and another in the cities of bordering princes.
To those stationed in foreign realms and forests let him render the same honors, attentions, and shares as to those within his own domain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In any such circumstance, those ascetics of rigorous vows will, at his wish, grant refuge to the king who seeks refuge.
This, in brief, is the summary of the marks I have declared to you — of the kind of city in which a king ought himself to dwell.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: To me who would rightly understand it, O king, declare the protection of the realm and likewise the gathering-in of the realm, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Bhīṣma said: The protection of the realm and the gathering-in of the realm — come, I shall declare it all to you rightly; listen with single-minded attention to the truth.
A headman should be appointed for a village, another over ten villages, another over twice that number, and so over a hundred, and over a thousand let him likewise appoint one.
Whatever faults of the village the village-headman has to keep watch over, let him report to the lord of ten; and he in turn to the lord of twenty.
