And that lord of twenty should report all the doings among the country-folk to the protector of a hundred villages.
Whatever the village affords for enjoyment, the village-headman may partake of; by him the lord of ten is to be maintained, and by the latter the lord of twenty.
The overseer of a hundred villages, held in honor, is entitled to enjoy a village — a great one, O best of the Bhāratas, thronged with prosperous people; for therein much that belongs to the king is at stake, O Bhārata.
But the lord of a thousand deserves a great market-town as his portion; that high officer of the realm is entitled to enjoy it through the revenue of grain and gold.
And whatever pertains to the village's business and the headman's duty, some minister versed in dharma should himself oversee, unwearied.
In every city there should be one superintendent of all affairs, set on high and of awesome aspect, like a planet among the stars; let him ever make his rounds over them all himself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Considering the selling, the buying, the road-tolls, the provisioning together with its costs, and the safe conduct of goods, let him levy the taxes upon the merchants.
Considering again and again the output, the cost of materials, and the craft itself, let him impose upon the artisans dues proportioned to their craft.
The taxes, high and low, were justly fixed by the kings of old, Yudhiṣṭhira; the lord of earth should so act that they suffer no diminution.
Considering both the yield and the labor, let him then apportion everything; for no one undertakes either yield or labor without a motive.
So that both the king and the laborer may be sharers in the work — considering this, the taxes should ever be levied by the king.
Out of greed let him not cut off his own root, nor that of others, by blocking the avenues of their enterprise; rather let the king be of gracious aspect.
Men come to hate a king notorious as a devourer of too much; whence comes good to one who is hated? The well-loved obtains what is dear to him.
The realm should be milked, as it were a calf, by a king of undiminished judgment; for the calf, once nourished and grown strong, can bear the strain, O Bhārata.
A calf milked too hard does no work, Yudhiṣṭhira; and a realm too heavily milked likewise performs no great labor.
That king who, having taken the realm in hand, cherishes it, and lives upon what it brings forth, obtains a very great fruit.
For against a time of distress do kings here heap up their stores; the realm itself should be as a treasury, and the treasury kept within the palace.
Upon all the townsfolk and country-folk, and those who have sought his shelter or come near it, and upon all his intimates as well, let him have compassion as far as he is able.
Having divided off the outer folk, the middling sort may be drawn upon at ease; thus the people, whether well-off or hard-pressed, do not grow wrathful.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But before levying the tax, having spoken of it again and again, let him assemble the people in his domain and set before the realm the danger that threatens it:
"This calamity has arisen, a great peril of an invading host; it may well end in destruction, as the bamboo's bearing of fruit ends in its death."
"My foes have risen up together with many bandits, and seek to crush this realm to its very ruin."
"In this dread calamity now come upon us, in this terrible peril, for your own deliverance I shall ask of you your wealth."
"And when the danger is past I shall repay it all to you; but the foes, should they carry it off by force from here, will make no repayment."
"Putting one's wife and family first of all, a man's wealth perishes of itself — even though wealth be hoarded for the very sake of children and wife."
"I rejoice in your prosperity as in the rising fortune of my own sons; and as far as I am able, I favor you, without oppressing the realm."
"In times of distress alone is the burden to be borne by you, like good oxen; in no calamity is there anything you hold dearer than wealth."
With words sweet, gentle, and courteous like these, let the king, knowing the proper season, take up the yoke and slacken his own reins.
Considering the pasturage, the keeping of servants, the expense, the danger to herds and villages, and their welfare and safety, let him levy the taxes upon the herdsmen.
For if neglected, the herdsmen who dwell in the wilds would be ruined; therefore toward them in particular let him act with gentleness foremost.
Conciliation, protection, gifts, and steady care — these are ever to be shown to the herdsmen, O Pārtha, with fair shares and kindnesses.
The fruit to be drawn from the herdsmen is to be used unceasingly on every side; it enriches the realm, and commerce, and tillage too.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore the discerning king should with diligence foster the goodwill of the herdsmen, being compassionate and vigilant, and levying upon them only gentle taxes.
Everywhere, my son, security of movement is easily had through the herdsmen; for there is no wealth, Yudhiṣṭhira, to compare with this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When a king, though capable, finds himself in need of treasure, O great-minded one, how should he then proceed? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: According to place, according to time, and according to their capacity, let the king, seeking dharma and devoted to their welfare, direct his subjects.
In such wise as he judges to be for their good and for his own, let the king set in motion all righteous works throughout the realm.
Let him milk the realm as one gathers honey, without destroying the bees; let him milk it with regard for the calf, and not lacerate the teats.
Let him drink from the realm gently, as a leech does, O lord of men; and let him carry it as a tigress carries her cub — without biting, lest it fall.
By little and little of what is owed, let him cause the increasing yield to be paid; then more and more, at will, let him bring about its growth.
As one who tames steeds yet to be broken, let him steadily increase their burden, and gently, with patient effort, draw the harness over them.
Once entangled in the harness, they will no longer be hard to govern; treated as is fitting, with care, they will become amenable.
Therefore, since a throng of men is hard to set in motion all at once, having first conciliated the chief among them, let him then draw revenue from the rest of the people.
Then, having set at variance those inclined to dispute among themselves, and having won them over, let him draw upon them at ease, without strain.
Let him not levy taxes upon them in the wrong place or at the wrong time, but in due order, with gentleness, at the proper season, and according to rule.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
These I declare to be skillful means; no deceit is what I intend. He who tames by the wrong means only provokes his horses to fury.
Drinking-houses and brothels, and those who keep procuresses, actors and gamblers, and whatever others are of this kind—
all these must be restrained, for they are the bane of the realm; abiding within it, they oppress the honest folk.
"By no one shall anything be begged of another save in distress"—such was the ordinance laid down of old for all beings by Manu.
For if all men were to live thus and did no labor here, then without doubt all the three worlds would cease to be.
The king is master to restrain them; he who does not restrain such men shares a fourth part of their guilt, so says the sacred lore—just as, when righteousness is done, he partakes of a fourth part of its merit.
Frequenting these haunts and given over to their allure, a man bent on his welfare's ruin, enslaved to desire—what wicked deed would he forbear?
Yet in distress alone may those who have no possessions beg; to them gift should be made righteously, out of compassion, by one who is moved to mercy.
Let there be no beggars in your realm, and let there be no robbers; both alike are mere takers of what is desired, neither of them nurturers of living beings.
Those who favor living beings and those who make the people thrive—let such men flourish in your realm, and not those who fail to nurture creatures.
And those whose aim is to seize wealth deserve punishment, O great king; let him set them to honest occupation, even as he sets tribute-payers to theirs.
Agriculture, cattle-keeping, and trade, and whatever else is of this kind—let him have such work done by men together with many laborers.
If a man engaged in farming, cattle-rearing, or trade should fall into any peril through it, the king is held blameworthy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let him always honor the wealthy with carriages, raiment, and food, and they should be told: "Receive these honors along with me."
This is a mighty limb of kings—the wealthy man, O Bhārata; the man of means is the very summit of all beings, of this there is no doubt.
The wise man, the hero, the man of wealth, the righteous, the ascetic, the truthful, and the man of understanding—each guards his own.
Therefore be well-disposed toward all of these, O prince, and uphold truth, uprightness, freedom from wrath, and absence of cruelty.
Thus shall you gain the power to punish, a treasury, allies, and land; devoted to truth and uprightness, O king, you will be furnished with friends and treasure.
Bhīṣma said: Let them not fell, within your domain, trees that bear edible fruit; for the wise declare that roots and fruit are the rightful portion of the brāhmaṇas.
Let other folk consume only what is left over after the brāhmaṇas; never may another take so as to deprive a brāhmaṇa in any way.
If a brāhmaṇa, worn thin by want of livelihood, should make this known and take to renunciation, a means of support should be provided for him together with his wife, O lord of men.
If he does not turn back from it, he is to be admonished in the assembly of brāhmaṇas: "In whom, then, will this world now find its bound of right conduct?"
Without doubt he will desist, if he says nothing further; but this correction, O son of Kuntī, should first be done out of his hearing.
"People say this, O brahman, yet I do not put faith in it; and he should be won over with enjoyments, should he act so for want of livelihood."
Agriculture, cattle-keeping, and trade are the livelihood of folk here below; and higher still is the threefold lore—it is that which sustains all beings.
When that lore is being striven after, those who become its adversaries are robbers; for their slaying here below, Brahmā then created the warrior order.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Slay your foes, protect the people, perform the sacrifices, O king; fight in battle, having become a hero, O delight of the Kurus.
The king who guards those to be protected is the noblest doer of kingly deeds; whoever fail to protect them are of no use whatever.
Ever must the king keep watch over all the people, O Yudhiṣṭhira; for that very reason should the ruler of men draw his sustenance from men.
Guarding outsiders from those within, and again those within from outsiders, outsiders from outsiders and your own from your own—protect them all without ceasing.
Guarding himself on every side, let the king guard the earth; for the learned declare that all this has its root in the self.
"What is my weak point? What entanglement is mine? What lies undone? From what quarter may some flaw flow in upon me?"—thus let him reflect continually.
With trusted spies, well-approved, let him keep watch over the land: "Is my conduct rightly ordered—do they praise it or not? Do I find favor in the countryside? Does my fame stand bright in the realm?"
Of those who know the law, who are steadfast, who do not flee in battle, of those who live by the realm and those who live by the king,
and of all the ministers and all the neutral parties everywhere, and of those who praise you or who blame you—make them all well-governed, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
For it is not possible, my son, to please all utterly; among all beings there is friend, foe, and the neutral, O Bhārata.
Among men equal in the strength of their arms and alike attended by virtues, how should any one be superior? Yet it is he who shall draw revenue from men.
For the moving devour the unmoving, and the fanged devour the fangless, like venomous serpents enraged, like snakes devouring snakes.
Against these be ever heedful and on guard, O Yudhiṣṭhira; for these are like the bhāruṇḍa birds—they swoop down upon the careless.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I trust the merchants in your realm are not driven to despair, afflicted by taxes—those who buy much for little and toil through the wilderness ways?
I trust the tillers, when too sorely oppressed, do not abandon the realm—they who bear the yoke for kings and sustain all the rest besides?
By what is given from their hands live the gods and the hosts of ancestors, men, serpents, and rākṣasas, the birds, and the beasts as well.
This is the conduct of the realm for you and the safeguarding of the realm, O Bhārata; resting upon this very theme, I shall speak yet further, O Pāṇḍava.
Bhīṣma said: Those duties of the warrior caste which Utathya, the Āṅgirasa, foremost knower of the Veda, spoke with goodwill to Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva—
even as Utathya, foremost knower of the Veda, instructed him, all that I shall declare to you in full, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Utathya said: A king exists for the sake of righteousness, not for the working of his own desire; know it thus, O Māndhātṛ—the king is the protector of the world.
If a king practices righteousness, he goes indeed unto godhood; but if he does not practice righteousness, he goes straight to hell.
Upon righteousness all beings rest; righteousness rests upon the king; the king who governs that righteousness well—he is a king, a lord of the earth.
When a king of the highest righteous soul, endowed with fortune, is yet called wicked, then the gods too fall into reproach, and it is said, "There is no righteousness."
When the prosperity of those who dwell in unrighteousness is seen, the world takes that for the whole of blessedness and follows after it.
Righteous conduct is cut away, and great unrighteousness prevails; men say there is dread by day and night when the wicked man is not restrained.
The twice-born who keep their vows no longer follow the Vedas, and the brāhmaṇas spread out no sacrifices, when the wicked man is not restrained.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The minds of all men grow distraught, as of those condemned to death, O great king, when the wicked man is not restrained.
Looking to both worlds, the seers themselves brought forth the king, that mighty being: "This shall be righteousness incarnate."
In whom righteousness shines forth, him they proclaim a king; in whom righteousness dissolves away, him the gods know for a base outcaste.
For the blessed Dharma is the Bull; whoever cuts that Bull short, him the gods know as the bull-mangler, the outcaste—therefore let none destroy righteousness.
When righteousness waxes, all beings ever wax with it; when it wanes, they wane away—therefore let him cause righteousness to flourish.
Righteousness flows from wealth, or else, it is held, from sustaining; it is remembered, O lord of men, as the setter of the bound against forbidden deeds.
For the welfare of beings was righteousness created by the Self-existent; therefore let him make righteousness flourish, for the sake of grace toward the people.
For that reason, O tiger among kings, righteousness is remembered as supreme; he is a king who governs the people, a doer of good, a bull among men.
Disregarding desire and wrath, let him uphold righteousness alone; righteousness is the surest bringer of welfare to kings, O best of the Bhāratas.
The brāhmaṇas are the womb of righteousness; therefore let him ever honor them, and let him, free of grudging, O Māndhātṛ, fulfill the desires of the brāhmaṇas.
For from not fulfilling their desires there arises danger to the king; his friends increase not, and they even turn to enemies.
When Bali, son of Virocana, came to bear ill will toward the brāhmaṇas, then majestic Fortune, who had dwelt in him, departed from him.
Then, having gone forth from him, she passed to Indra, the chastiser of Pāka; and afterward Bali grieved sorely, beholding Fortune now in Purandara.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This is the fruit of envy and of pride, O mighty one; therefore take heed, O Māndhātṛ, lest majestic Fortune forsake you.
Insolence by name, the son of Fortune, was born of unrighteousness, so says the sacred lore; by him, O king, gods and asuras alike were again and again brought under sway.
And many royal seers as well; therefore take heed, O prince. Conquering him, one becomes a king; vanquished by him, one becomes a slave.
So conduct yourself, O Māndhātṛ, that you cleave not to unrighteousness joined with insolence, if you wish to endure for long.
From the drunken, the heedless, the half-grown boy, and above all from the madman, from the practice of their ways, from association with them, and from the company of the ill-disposed—
from a minister who has been disgraced, and above all from women, from mountain and ravine and fastness, from elephant, horse, and creeping thing—
against all these let him be ever on guard, and let him shun roaming by night; let him shun excessive spending, overweening pride, hypocrisy, and wrath.
With women unknown to him, with the unsexed, with wanton women, with the wives of others, and with maidens, let the king not engage in union.
From the confusion of castes there are born into families wicked, demon-like beings—the unmanly, the maimed of limb, the thick-tongued, and the witless.
These and others are born when the king grows negligent; therefore the king must conduct himself with especial care for the welfare of the people.
When a kṣatriya grows heedless, a great fault is born of it: lawless deeds break loose that throw the people into confusion and ruin.
Cold sets in when it should be warm, and in the cold season the cold fails; drought comes, then flood, and sickness invades the people.
The lunar mansions turn baleful, and dread planets likewise rise against him; and many portents are seen abroad that spell a king's undoing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The king who does not guard himself, and does not guard his people either—his subjects waste away, and he in turn perishes after them.
Two men seize what belongs to one, and many others seize from those two; maidens are carried off by force—this, they say, is the defilement of a king.
'This is mine'—such a claim holds firm for no single man, when the king forsakes dharma and follows the path of heedlessness.
Utathya said: When the rain-cloud pours in its season and the king walks in dharma—when this fortune comes to pass, it sustains the people in happiness.
A washerman who does not know how to strip the soil from garments, nor how to cleanse the dyed cloth, is as good as no washerman at all.
Just so the foremost brāhmaṇas, the kṣatriyas, the vaiśyas, and the śūdras—the four varṇas—are each set to their several appointed tasks.
Service belongs to the śūdra, husbandry to the vaiśya, and the rule of the rod to the king; chastity, austerity, the sacred verses, and truth belong to the twice-born.
That kṣatriya among them who knows how to scour away faults of conduct, as one scours soiled garments clean, is a father to his people—he is their Prajāpati.
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali, O bull of the Bhāratas, are all the workings of the king; the king himself is called the very age.
The fourfold order of varṇas, the Vedas, and the four stages of life—all this falls into confusion when the king grows heedless.
The king alone is the maker of all creatures, and the king alone their destroyer; he whose soul is set on dharma is their maker, and he whose soul is lawless, their destroyer.
The king's wives and sons, his kinsmen and his friends, all gather together and grieve when the king grows heedless.
Elephants and horses and cattle, camels, mules, and donkeys—all sink into ruin, O prince, when the king's conduct is lawless.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the sake of the weak, O Māndhātṛ, the ordaining Creator brought strength into being—so it is said; for the weak are that great power on which all else rests.
Whatever creature he cherishes, and the creatures that follow in its train—all of them sink into ruin, O prince, when the king stands on the side of unrighteousness.
The eye of the weak man, like the eye of a sage or of a venomous serpent, I hold to be the hardest of all to withstand: never give offense to the weak.
Take heed of the weak, my son, and let them never be despised, lest the eyes of the weak burn you to ashes together with your kinsmen.
In the house of one burned by the weak nothing ever springs up again; the fire consumes it down to the very root—so never give offense to the weak.
The weak is mightier than the strong, even than strength that is overwhelming in its might; for of strength once burned by the weak, nothing whatever remains.
If one who is scorned, struck down, and crying out finds no protector, then a chastisement not wrought by human hand falls there and destroys the king of men.
Do not, my son, take your stand upon mere force, nor oppress the weak, lest the eyes of the weak consume you as fire consumes the dwelling that gives it shelter.
The tears that fall from those falsely accused as they weep—those tears slay the sons and the cattle of the men who lay false charges upon them.
If not upon a man himself, then upon his sons, and if not upon his sons, then upon his grandsons and their offspring; for a sinful deed once done does not ripen at once, like a cow whose calf takes time to grow.
Where a weak man, set upon and slain, finds no protector, there a great and terrible chastisement, wrought by fate, comes down.
When the country folk, hard-pressed, take to begging like brāhmaṇas, then again and again, by the taint of their beggary, such men bring destruction on the king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When in a king's domain many of the king's officers conduct themselves by misrule, that is a great sin laid upon the king.
When the appointed officers carry off the goods of those who beg piteously, whether out of lust or in greed for gain, that is a great slaughter charged against the king.
A great tree springs up and grows, and creatures take their shelter beneath it; but when the tree is cut down or burned, those that sheltered there are left without a home.
When men in the realm practice what they proclaim to be the highest dharma, or the rite, or the royal virtue, and yet through delusion as to dharma practice unrighteousness in its very name, one should swiftly abandon such deeds, both well done and ill.
Where the wicked, known for what they are, go about freely, there strife befalls the king's good men; when a king chastises men who are not deserving of it, that kingdom does not prosper, O lord of the earth.
But the king who honors his minister as he deserves and sets him to his task in counsel and in war—that king's realm grows great, and he enjoys the whole earth for a long age.
Here too the king who discerns a deed well done and a word well spoken, and honors them, attains the highest dharma.
When he shares before he himself enjoys, and despises no man, and strikes down the strong man grown insolent—that is called the dharma of a king.
When he protects all by word, by body, and by deed, and will not condone a wrong even in his own son—that is called the dharma of a king.
When the king guards those who have sought his refuge as though they were his sons, and never breaks the bounds of right—that is called the dharma of a king.
When, filled with faith, he sacrifices with rites whose priestly fees are duly paid, heedless of desire and hatred—that is called the dharma of a king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When he wipes away the tears of the wretched, the helpless, and the aged, and kindles gladness in his people—that is called the dharma of a king.
When he increases his friends and draws down his foes, and pays honor to the good—that is called the dharma of a king.
When he keeps his word faithfully, ever bestows land in due measure, and honors guests and dependents—that is called the dharma of a king.
Where both restraint and favor are firmly established, the king gains the fruit thereof in this world and in the next.
Yama, the supreme lord, O Māndhātṛ, is the king of the righteous when he holds living beings in due restraint; but when he restrains them not, he turns to evil.
When he honors the officiating priests, the family chaplain, and the teachers, and never slights them but rightly upholds them—that is called the dharma of a king.
Yama holds all beings in check without distinction; the king should do as he does, and govern his people according to the ordinance.
Every king is likened to the thousand-eyed Indra; for whatever dharma he beholds, that, O bull among men, is dharma.
With unwavering care learn forbearance, understanding, steadfastness, and judgment, and the discernment of the true nature of creatures, of good and evil, always.
The winning of all creatures, generosity, and gentle speech—and the townsfolk and the country folk are to be protected as one's own people.
Never can an unskilled king protect his subjects; for it is a very great burden, my son—kingship, so they call it, is exceedingly hard to bear.
A king who is wise, valiant, and versed in the rod can protect them; it cannot be done by one who lacks the rod, who is unmanly, or who is without understanding.
With men of fitting bearing, well born, skilled, devoted, and deeply learned, you should test out all counsels—even those of the ascetics in their hermitages.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then you will come to know the highest dharma of all beings; and whether in your own land or another's, your dharma will not be lost.
Of dharma, artha, and kāma, let dharma ever be the highest; for in this world and the next, the one who knows dharma flourishes in happiness.
Men, when they are duly honored, will give up wife and life itself; the winning of creatures lies in generosity and in gentle speech.
Vigilance and purity, my son, work great prosperity; and from these, O Māndhātṛ, never at any time fall away into heedlessness.
Let the king be ever watchful, marking the weak points of his foe and of himself; let no enemy spy out a weak point in him, while he himself seeks out his enemy's weak points.
Such was the conduct of Vāsava, of Yama, and of Varuṇa, and of all the royal sages: do you too uphold it.
Do that, O great king—that course which the royal sages have followed; set your feet without delay upon the heavenly path, O bull of the Bhāratas.
For a king of righteous conduct, O Bhārata, in the world hereafter and in this one, the gods, the sages, the fathers, and the gandharvas, boundless in might, sing his praise.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by Utathya, O Bhārata, Māndhātṛ acted on it without a doubt, and he alone won the whole earth.
You too, like Māndhātṛ the lord of the earth, by rightly practicing dharma and guarding the earth, will gain a place in heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How should a righteous king, wishing to stand firm in dharma, conduct himself? This I ask you, O best of the Kurus; tell it to me, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this they tell an ancient tale, sung by the wise Vāmadeva, who had perceived the very truth of things.
A king named Vasumanas, ruler of the Kosalas, mighty and pure, questioned the great sage, the renowned Vāmadeva.
'Instruct me, blessed one, with words that hold both dharma and artha—by what conduct, standing firm, I may not fall away from my own dharma.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
To him spoke Vāmadeva, that ascetic, foremost of those who murmur the sacred prayers, as the king sat attending upon him, golden-hued, like Yayāti the son of Nahuṣa.
Follow dharma alone, for nothing higher than dharma is known; for it is kings established in dharma who conquer this earth.
The king who holds dharma higher than the winning of wealth, and makes his understanding true, shines forth by his dharma.
The king whose vision is set on unrighteousness, who acts by sheer force, swiftly falls away from this world, losing both the first end and the middle.
The slayer of dharma, with wicked and basest counselors, fit for the world to put to death, swiftly sinks to ruin together with his whole retinue.
He who attends not to his proper aims, who follows his own whim and boasts loudly, though he win the whole earth, swiftly comes to destruction.
But the wise king who takes hold of what is good, free of malice and master of his senses, grows great, as the ocean grows by its inflowing streams.
Let the lord of the earth never think, 'I am full'—neither in dharma, nor in desire, nor in wealth, nor in understanding, nor in friends—at any time.
For upon all these the course of the world is founded; and one who gives ear to these gains glory, renown, fortunes, and subjects.
Thus the king who is zealous for dharma, who ponders well both dharma and artha, and who undertakes his ventures after due reflection, surely attains greatness.
The king who gives nothing, who shows no warmth, who drives his people on with the rod and is rash by nature, swiftly comes to destruction.
And the fool who does evil knowingly yet does not see it, burdened with infamy besides, when dead attains to hell.
But of the king who honors others, who gives, who is upright and knows the savor of things, when calamity befalls him men long to ward it off as though it were their own.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who has no teacher in dharma and asks no counsel of others, who is given over to ease in his pursuit of gain, does not long enjoy greatness.
He who holds his teacher foremost in matters of dharma, yet examines questions of profit for himself, and who keeps dharma foremost among the worlds — he long enjoys greatness.
Vāmadeva said: Where the stronger man works injustice upon the weaker, those who follow in his train take up that same way of life and live by it.
They follow that king who sets evil in motion, that ill-disciplined man — and swiftly does such a realm perish.
The very conduct by which men live under a king who keeps his proper course, even his own kin will not endure in one who has gone astray.
Where a king of reckless temper does some monstrous deed, a king who bears not the mark of the scriptures swiftly comes to ruin.
The Kṣatriya who does not follow the conduct long established toward the conquered and the unconquered falls away from the dharma of warriors.
The king who, having captured in battle a hostile foe who has done his deeds well, fails out of malice to honor him, falls away from the dharma of warriors.
Let the king, though powerful, be of gracious countenance, and show compassion in distress; thus he becomes dear to all beings and does not fall from his fortune.
To one whom he has wronged, let him afterward do a greater kindness; for in a little while he becomes dear who, having displeased, then renders a pleasing deed.
Let him shun all false speech and do kindness unasked; neither from desire, nor from fury, nor from hatred let him cast off dharma.
Let him not be shamed by questions, nor utter a word that can be assailed; let him not be hasty, nor envious — thus is another won over.
In what is pleasant let him not rejoice overmuch, and in the unpleasant let him not be inflamed; let him not lose his bearings in straits of policy, ever mindful of the welfare of his people.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The lord of the earth who, by his virtues, ever does what is pleasing — his undertakings prosper, and fortune does not forsake him.
Let the king favor the devoted man who has turned from hostile courses and walks in ways agreeable to him — for that, here, is the conduct of the good.
The man of well-governed senses, wise, wholly loyal, pure, capable and devoted — him let the king employ in a great office.
But even one so endowed with virtues, who feels no attachment to the king and who grudges his master's interests — such a man let him not employ in any office.
The dullard, the slave of his senses, the greedy, the ignoble in conduct, the deceitful, one who has not passed the tests of integrity, the cruel, the ill-minded, the unlearned —
the man who abandons what he has taken up, who is given to drink, addicted to dice, women, and the hunt — the king who employs such a one in a great task is cut off from his fortune.
But the king who guards himself and protects those who are to be protected — his subjects flourish, and he surely attains greatness.
Let him keep watch upon all the lords of the earth, whoever they may be, through trusted friends who go unrecognized; thus the king comes to no harm.
Having injured one who is strong, let him not feel secure thinking, "I am far away"; for such men, ranging like hawks, swoop down upon him who grows heedless.
Firmly rooted and of unblemished soul, having gauged his own strength, let him march against the weak — but not against those who are stronger than he.
Having won the earth by valor and protecting his subjects by dharma, let the king, devoted to dharma, meet his end in battle.
All this ends in death; nothing here is free from decay. Therefore let the king, established in dharma, protect his subjects by dharma.
The office of protection, warfare, the administration of dharma, deliberation upon counsel, and timely ease — by these five the realm increases.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He for whom these are kept secure — that king, O best of kings, ever abiding in them, enjoys this earth.
These cannot be watched over unremittingly by one man alone; setting trustworthy men over them, the king enjoys the earth for long.
The giver, the one who shares fairly, the man of gentle bearing, the pure, who does not abandon his people — him the people make their beloved.
But he who, recognizing the highest good, takes up that knowledge, casting aside his own opinion — him the world follows.
He who, out of contrariness, will not bear the word of one who seeks his good, shall before long, dejected, hear words contrary to his wishes.
He who fails utterly to grasp the wisdom of a conduct above the common — toward the conquered and the unconquered alike — falls away from the dharma of warriors.
He who, forsaking his chief ministers, takes base men for his favorites, when calamity befalls him finds no firm ground in his deep distress.
He who out of hatred holds in no esteem his kinsmen of excellent qualities — irresolute in soul, yet fixed in wrath — his fortune does not delight to dwell near him.
But he who, by kindness, makes obedient to him men endowed with virtues, even though they be unpleasing to his heart, abides long in renown.
Let him not press his interests out of season, nor ever be inflamed at what displeases him, nor rejoice overmuch at what pleases him; let him keep to wholesome action.
Which kings are attached to me in love, which have taken refuge with me out of fear, and which among them are tainted by neutrality — this let him ever ponder.
Having grown strong, let him never trust a weaker man in any matter; for these, like the bhāruṇḍa birds, swoop down upon him who grows heedless.
Even a master endowed with all virtues and gentle of speech the evil-souled man will betray; therefore let him stand in wary dread of such people.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This secret science of kings Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, proclaimed; intent upon the conquest of men, the king destroys even his most matchless foes.
Vāmadeva said: Let the lord of the earth enlarge his victory without war; for the victory won through war, O ruler of men, they call the lowest kind.
Nor let him seek to gain what he has not gained while his foundation is not yet firm; for to a king whose base is weak no gain is ordained.
He whose realm is thriving and prosperous, whose people love their king, whose ministers are contented and well-nourished — that prince is firmly rooted.
He whose warriors are well content, conciliated, and proven loyal under tests of integrity — that king conquers the earth with even a small army.
He whose townsfolk and countryfolk are well affected and well honored, rich in wealth and grain — that prince is firmly rooted.
When the wise king judges both his power and the season to be in his favor, then let him seek to gain another's land and wealth.
For him who spares not himself in indulgence yet is compassionate to all beings, who is diligent and self-controlled, the dominion grows.
He hews at his own self, as one hews a forest with an axe, who deals falsely with his own people when they conduct themselves rightly.
The enemies of a king who slays them perpetually are nonetheless never exhausted; but he who knows how to curb his wrath has no enemy at all.
Let the wise man not do that deed which the noble hold in hatred; whatever is good, let him set his mind upon it and bend himself to it.
That king whom others do not despise, who is not consumed by self-reproach, and who seeks his pleasures only with what remains after duty is done —
the lord of the earth who walks in such conduct among men, having conquered both worlds, is firmly established in victory.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Thus counseled by Vāmadeva, the king did all of it; and you too, by acting so, shall conquer both these worlds — there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Now when one Kṣatriya seeks to conquer another in battle, what victory of his is righteous? Being asked this, tell it to me.
Bhīṣma said: With aid or without aid, a king, having entered a realm, should declare: "I am your king, and I shall ever protect you."
"Render unto me the tribute that is lawful — or how will you receive me?" If they then choose him who has come, it shall be well.
But if those who are not Kṣatriyas should oppose him in any way, O ruler of men, they who stand in wrongful action must be restrained by every means.
Then another, deeming the Kṣatriya powerless, takes up arms, judging him utterly unable even to protect himself.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Now when a Kṣatriya king marches against another Kṣatriya, how is he to be fought against? Tell me that, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: A Kṣatriya not arrayed for battle and without armor must not be fought in war; one is to be matched with one, and he should be told, "Loose your weapon, and I shall loose mine."
If he comes arrayed for battle, then one must array oneself; if he comes with an army, then with an army let one challenge him.
If he fights with treachery, with counter-stratagem let one fight him; but if he fights by dharma, then by dharma alone let one ward him off.
Let him not assail a chariot-warrior with cavalry; a chariot-warrior should advance against a chariot-warrior. One must not strike at a man in distress, nor at one who is afraid, nor at one already vanquished.
Let no arrow be smeared with poison, nor be barbed — such is the weapon of the wicked. One must fight only for victory; let him not rage against one who seeks not to slay.
But if, through a falling-out among the good, a good man should come to grief, he must not be struck if he is wounded, nor in any case if he is without offspring.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The man whose weapon is broken, whose horse is fallen, whose bowstring is cut, whose mount is slain — he should be tended in one's own domain, or be enabled to reach his own home; and even if unwounded he must be set free. This is the eternal dharma.
Therefore one must fight by dharma, so Manu the self-born declared; the dharma of the good is ever upheld among the good — abiding in it, let him not bring it to ruin.
The Kṣatriya, waxing in power, who conquers by unrighteousness, slays himself by himself — a wicked man, living by treachery.
This is the way of the wicked; let one conquer the wicked by good means. Better is death in righteousness than victory by an evil deed.
Unrighteousness, once done, O king, does not bear fruit at once, like the earth; but, burning, it comes after its doer's roots and branches alike.
Having gained wealth by an evil deed, the wicked man rejoices; and that wicked man, waxing by theft, clings ever more to evil.
Thinking, "There is no such thing as dharma," mocking, as it were, the pure-hearted, through his unbelieving disposition he comes to destruction.
Bound by the nooses of Varuṇa, he yet fancies himself immortal; swollen like a great leather bag, he keeps puffing himself up by his own doing.
Then he is swept away root and all, like a tree from a river's bank; and men revile him, like a pot shattered upon a stone. Therefore let the king, if he would, seek his victory by dharma.
Bhīṣma said: Let not the lord of the world seek to conquer the earth by unrighteousness; what king, having won a victory by unrighteousness, would approve of it?
A victory bound up with unrighteousness is fleeting and bars the way to heaven; it brings down both the king and his realm, O bull of the Bhāratas.
The man whose armor is shattered, who says, "I am yours," who folds his hands in supplication and has laid down his weapon — having captured him, one must not do him harm.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who has been overcome by force — the king must not fight him further; let him keep him in custody for a year, and thereafter he becomes as one reborn.
A maiden carried off by force must not be touched before a year is out; and even so all wealth and whatever else has been seized by violence.
Yet the wealth should not stand idle and barren; let the Brāhmaṇas drink the milk, or let the oxen be yoked to labor — or else forbearance may then be shown.
By a king a king alone is to be fought — thus is the dharma ordained; no other, who is not of royal blood, should in any way assail a king.
If, when two armies stand arrayed against each other, a brāhmaṇa should pass between them desiring peace from both sides, then there must be no fighting; whoever transgresses against that brāhmaṇa breaks an eternal bound.
And if one who merely calls himself a kṣatriya should overstep this bound, he shall thereafter be without honor, and his word shall carry no weight in the assembly.
The king who would conquer should not pursue any course that destroys dharma and shatters the bounds; for what gain could be greater than a victory won in accord with dharma?
Having swiftly bent the people to his will, he should quickly win them over with conciliation and the granting of enjoyments: this is the highest policy of kings.
For those who are exploited without justice, scorched within their own realm, will turn to attend upon his enemies, awaiting the flood of his misfortunes.
And in his hour of distress they would swiftly side with the foe, O king—wholly disaffected and longing for the king's ruin.
An enemy must never be utterly mutilated nor pressed past all bearing; for a man pressed too far will one day cast away his very life.
Even the wrongdoer, granted some little thing, is content; and one in such straits prizes even his bare life highly.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whose realm is thriving and prosperous, whose king is beloved, whose servants and ministers are content—that ruler stands firm-rooted.
He by whom the officiating priests, the household chaplain, the teachers, and all others esteemed for sacred learning—those worthy of honor—are duly honored, he indeed is called a conqueror of the worlds.
By this very conduct the foremost of the gods won the earth; and following Indra's victory, kings too have sought to conquer.
Having vanquished a king in battle, Pratardana seized the conquered city but spared its land, and carried off again and again its life-giving healing herbs.
Divodāsa carried off the sacred fires, the remnants of the fire, the oblations, and the very sacrificial vessels; therefore he came to be reviled.
Nābhāga gave away whole kingdoms together with their kings as sacrificial fee, save only the property of vedic scholars and of ascetics, O Bhārata.
Manifold and varied, O Yudhiṣṭhira, were the ways of the ancient kings who knew dharma; and all of it is approved by me.
Or let the king who desires his own prosperity seek victory through surpassing mastery of every branch of knowledge—never through deceit, never through fraud.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: There is no dharma more grievous than the dharma of the kṣatriya, O bull of the Bhāratas, for in marching forth and in battle the king destroys a great multitude of people.
Then tell me, O learned one, O bull of the Bhāratas, to me who longs to know: by what deed does a king win the higher worlds?
Bhīṣma said: By the restraint of the wicked and the support of the good, by sacrifices and by gifts, kings become pure and free of stain.
Kings bent on conquest press hard upon living beings; yet those same kings, once victory is won, make their subjects flourish again.
They cast off their sins by the power of gift, sacrifice, and austerity; and through their grace toward living beings their merit grows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Just as a weeder of a field, weeding it once, destroys the brush together with the grain, yet the grain itself is not lost—
so those who loose their weapons slay, on one occasion, those fit to be slain; and the full atonement for that is the fostering of living beings thereafter.
He who protects living beings from loss of wealth, from slaughter, and from affliction, and saves their lives from robbers—he is a giver of wealth, a giver of happiness, a sovereign in splendor.
That king, having sacrificed with all the sacrifices whose fee is the gift of fearlessness, enjoys blessings here and attains to dwelling in the same world as Indra.
When a cause arises for the sake of the brāhmaṇas, he who marches forth and fights, raising his own self as the sacrificial post—his is a sacrifice of boundless fee.
Fearless, scattering his foes and likewise receiving their arrows—the gods behold nothing on earth more excellent than such a man.
As many weapons as pierce his skin in the fray, so many imperishable worlds does he enjoy, yielding every desire.
The blood that flows from the wounds of his body is no defilement; rather, by that very blood he is released from all his sins.
Whatever pains he endures in the searing of his wounds—there is no austerity greater than that, so the knowers of dharma have understood.
In the rear of the battle linger the cowards, the basest of men, seeking shelter from the brave man as one seeks life-giving rain from the cloud.
If the brave man would shield them in safety as he does in danger, men would render him fitting honor—yet it does not work out so.
If they, knowing what he has done, would always bow to him and act toward him with fitness and justice—but it does not work out so.
Among men seemingly equal a great difference is seen in battle, at the hour when the ranks clash, amid the war-cries and the charging onset.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The brave man falls facing the foe; the coward flees, taking a road that leads not to heaven, abandoning his comrades in the moment of peril.
Never beget such men, my son—those basest of men who, abandoning their comrades in battle, went home unscathed and pleased with themselves.
The gods, with Indra at their head, work woe upon them—those who by deserting their comrades seek to save their own lives.
Such a man the kṣatriyas should strike down with sticks and clods, or burn with a fire of straw, or slaughter like a beast—those kṣatriyas who are of true worth.
This is the kṣatriya's disgrace: that his death should come upon a bed, spilling phlegm and bile, wailing piteously.
The kṣatriya who meets his dissolution with body unwounded—those who know the ancient lore do not praise that act of his.
Death at home, my son, is not commended for kṣatriyas; for the proud, that is ignoble, contrary to dharma, and wretched.
"Ah, this is pain, this is anguish, this is the bitterest of woes"—so groaning, his face wasted away, his body foul, causing much grief to his ministers—
he envies the healthy and again and again longs even for death; the hero, proud and high of spirit, deserves no such death as this.
Having wrought havoc in battle, ringed by his kinsmen, sorely torn by keen weapons—such a death the kṣatriya deserves.
For the brave man, possessed by truth and righteous wrath, fights fiercely, and does not even feel his limbs being hewn apart by his foes.
Meeting his end in battle—an end lauded and honored by the world—having fulfilled his own ample dharma, he attains to dwelling in the world of Śakra.
Every warrior, resolved to strike down the foe and ready to cast away his life—the brave man who never shows his back—attains to dwelling in the world of Indra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What worlds belong to brave warriors who fight without ever turning back, once they have met their end? Tell me that, O grandfather.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue of Ambarīṣa and Indra, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
For Ambarīṣa, son of Nābhāga, having reached that heaven so hard to win, beheld dwelling in the world of the gods, alongside Śakra, his own minister—
his own lord and commander-in-chief, formed all of radiance, seated in a splendid celestial chariot, rising higher and higher.
Seeing his commander rising above him, that noble-minded one, beholding the glory of Sudeva, spoke in wonder to Vāsava:
"Having ruled the whole earth bounded by the sea, in due order, governing the four orders according to scripture, devoted out of love for dharma;
having through stern chastity and service in the teacher's house studied the Vedas in the way of dharma, and the science of kingship complete;
having honored guests with food and drink, the ancestors with offerings, the seers with private study and consecrations, and the gods with unsurpassed sacrifices;
and standing firm in the dharma of the kṣatriya, as scripture and rule prescribe, surveying the host I conquer in battle, O Vāsava—
O king of the gods, this Sudeva, who was once my commander, a warrior of serene spirit—why does he so far surpass me?
He sacrificed not with the foremost rites, nor were the twice-born duly satisfied by him, O Śakra—why then does he so far surpass me?"
Indra said: Of this Sudeva, my son, a mighty battle-sacrifice was spread out—as it is for any other man who fights.
It is settled doctrine that every warrior, armored and consecrated, having reached the front of the host, stands invested with the office of the battle-sacrifice.
Ambarīṣa said: What are the oblations in this sacrifice, what the clarified butter, and what the fee? And who are called the officiating priests here? Tell me that, O Śatakratu.
Indra said: There the elephants are the officiating priests, the horses the adhvaryu priests; the choicest flesh is the oblation, and the blood is the clarified butter.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The jackals, vultures, and ravens are the assessors and partakers of the session; these drink the remnant of the butter and consume the oblation in that sacrifice.
The clusters of barbed darts and lances, the swords, spears, and battle-axes, blazing, sharpened, and burnished—these are the sacrificial ladles of him who holds the session.
The arrow, sped by the force of the bow, keen, cleaving the bodies of the foe, straight, well-whetted, and burnished—that is his great offering-spoon.
The sword bound with leopard-hide, its hilt wrought of ivory, grasped in a hand strong as an elephant's trunk—that becomes his wooden sword of the rite in the battle.
The smiting with the blazing, whetted, burnished darts, spears, and axes, keen and forged of well-tempered iron—that is his wealth of oblation.
And the blood that, by the rush of onset, streams upon the ground in battle—that is his full and abundant final oblation poured into the fire, yielding every desire.
He at the front of whose host this cry is heard, "Cut! Cleave!"—for him the chanters sing the Sāman hymns in the abode of Yama.
They call the front of the enemy's host his oblation-shed; the massed array of elephants, horses, and armored men—that is the fire named Śyenacit, ordained in his sacrifice.
And the headless trunk that rises up here when a thousand have been slain—that is called the eight-cornered sacrificial post of khadira-wood for that hero.
The elephants, goaded by the hook, trumpet the call of the Iḍā invocation; with the resounding clap of palms and the cry of Vaṣaṭ, O king, the war-drum sounding its triple Sāman is held to be the chanting priest in that battle.
He who, when the property of brāhmaṇas is being carried off, gives up his beloved body in battle, raising his own self as the sacrificial post—his is a sacrifice of boundless fee.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The brave man who, for his lord's sake, would show his prowess at the front of the host and would not turn back through fear—his worlds are even as mine.
He whose sacrificial altar is strewn over with swords shaped like the dark moon and with arms like iron clubs—his worlds are even as mine.
He who, bent on victory, looks to no comrade for aid and plunges into the very midst of the host—his worlds are even as mine.
He for whom the clustered lances are the rafts, the kettle-drums the frogs and turtles, the bones of heroes the gravel, hard to ford, its mire flesh and blood—
a river whose rafts are swords and shields, whose moss and water-grass is human hair, bridged over with shattered horses, elephants, and chariots;
its reeds and rushes banners and standards, its current a stream of slain mounts, its waters blood, brimful, hard to cross even for men who would reach the farther shore;
with slain elephants for its great crocodiles, dreadful, bearing men to the other world, its sandbanks heaped with pikes, swords, and standards, with vultures and herons floating upon it—
Haunted by flesh-eating creatures, breeding faintness in cowards—such is the river. In the great sacrifice of war that is held to be the warrior's final ablution.
He whose altar is strewn with the heads of his foes, with the shoulders of horses and the shoulders of elephants—his are worlds such as mine.
He for whom the vanguard of the enemy's host serves as the wife's pavilion, and his own troops as the oblation-shed—so the wise declare.
The assembly-hall is the fire amid the contending warriors, and the priest's fire-shed lies toward the north—the consort of the enemy's army has all the worlds close at hand.
When the array is drawn up on both sides with open ground in front, that is his altar; and in this sacrifice the three Vedas are ever the three fires.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the warrior who turns away and, panic-stricken, is slain by his foes goes to a bottomless hell—of this there is no doubt.
He by whose surging blood a river is made to overflow, thick with hair and flesh and bone, attains the supreme state.
He who slays the enemy's commander and mounts his chariot strides with the stride of Viṣṇu; his is a sacrifice equal to that of Bṛhaspati.
He who takes captive alive a leader, or a chief authority, or whoever is honored there—his are worlds such as mine.
For the hero slain in battle one should never grieve; the slain hero is beyond mourning—he is exalted in the world of heaven.
For the slain hero men perform no rite of food, no water-offering, no bath, no observance of impurity—hear from me the worlds that are his.
Thousands of choice apsarases rush headlong toward the hero slain in battle, each crying, 'Let him be my husband!'
This is austerity, this is merit, this is the eternal dharma, and these are the four stages of life—for the man who does not flee in battle.
The aged force is not to be killed, nor a woman, nor a brāhmaṇa, nor one who takes a blade of grass in his mouth and says, 'I am yours.'
I slew Vṛtra, Bala, Pāka, Virocana of the hundred wiles, the irresistible Namuci, and Śambara of manifold deceits;
and the Daitya Vipracitti, and all the sons of Danu, and Prahrāda—having slain them in battle, I then became lord of the gods.
Bhīṣma said: Having heard and taken to heart this speech of Śakra, Ambarīṣa came to understand the perfection attainable by warriors and by himself.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale—the battle that Pratardana and the king of Mithilā waged together.
Hear, Yudhiṣṭhira, how Janaka of Mithilā, wearing the sacred thread, roused his warriors to ardor upon the field of battle.
King Janaka of Mithilā, the great-souled one who knew all truths, revealed to his warriors both heaven and hell.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Behold! These shining worlds belong to the fearless—filled with the daughters of the gandharvas, granting every desire, and imperishable.
And these hells stand ready for those who flee—everlasting infamy, and a fall to follow at once.'
'Seeing those foes, conquer them, your minds resolved upon self-surrender; do not fall under the sway of the bottomless hell.
For self-sacrifice is the root of heroes' unsurpassed gateway to heaven.' So addressed by the king, O conqueror of enemy cities, those warriors—
—vanquished their foes in the fray, gladdening their lord of men. Therefore the self-possessed man should ever stand firm at the head of battle.
Amid the elephants the chariot-warriors, behind the chariots the horsemen, and between the horsemen the mailed foot-soldiers should be stationed.
The king who arrays his forces thus ever conquers his enemies; therefore it should always be ordered in this way, Yudhiṣṭhira.
All, desiring merit, full of fierce wrath through good fighting, would shake the enemy ranks as sea-monsters churn the ocean.
They should cheer the dejected and steady one another; one should guard the ground that has been won, and not pursue the routed too far.
The onset of men who turn back to fight and have despaired of life cannot easily be withstood, O king; therefore do not pursue too far.
For heroes have no wish to strike those who run off in fear; therefore one should not press the pursuit of those who flee.
The motionless are food for the moving, the fangless for the fanged, the handless for those who have hands—and cowards are food for the hero.
Though equal in back and belly, in hand and foot, cowards follow the hero from behind; and so, tormented by fear, bowing low and folding their hands, they wait upon the brave.
Upon the arms of heroes this world ever leans, as a child upon its parent; therefore in every circumstance the hero deserves honor.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For in the three worlds there is nothing higher than valor; the hero protects all, and upon the hero all things rest.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How those who seek victory lead an army, even by straining dharma a little—tell me that, O grandfather, bull of the Bhāratas.
Bhīṣma said: Some duties rest upon truth, others upon sound reasoning, some upon the conduct of the good, and some upon expediency. I shall expound the duties of expedient means, which fulfill the aims of both profit and dharma.
Lawless brigands become highway-robbers; to counter them I shall set forth the established usage. Learn from me those expedients for the accomplishment of one's ends.
Two kinds of wisdom must be known, O Bhārata—the straight and the crooked. Knowing the crooked, one should not practice it, yet should repel it when it comes.
Enemies indeed approach a king through the sowing of dissension; knowing that deceit, the king beats them back as he would foes.
The flank-hides of elephants, of bulls and great serpents, porcupine-quill plate and iron—these are reckoned as body-armor.
The weapons should be sharpened and burnished, the coats of mail tawny-red, and the pennants and standards dyed in many colors.
Swords, lances, blades, and whetted battle-axes, shields and bucklers—these are to be prepared in great numbers; the weapons well-tempered, and the warriors well-trained.
The mustering of the army is commended in the month of Caitra or of Mārgaśīrṣa, for then the earth bears ripened grain and abundant water.
The season then is neither too cold nor too hot, O Bhārata; therefore one should mobilize at that time, or in the seasons of the enemy's distress—such occasions for marshaling an army are commended for harrying the foe.
A road with water and grass, level and passable, is to be preferred—one well reconnoitered beforehand by skilled scouts versed in the forests.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Through fresh wildwoods it would be no more possible to march than for herds of deer; therefore those who seek victory employ scouts in every army.
A camp that has water, is hard of access, and has open ground around it is commended, for thereby the enemy's infiltrators are repulsed.
But open ground near a forest is held more advantageous, on account of its many merits, by men skilled in war.
The posting of spies, the concealment of foot-soldiers, the repelling of the enemy, and a refuge against calamity—
—placing the Seven Sages at their back, they would fight unshaken as mountains. By this method, O king, one may seek to conquer even the unconquerable.
Where the wind is, where the sun is, where Śukra is—there is victory; and of these, each former is the more important when they meet, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Free of mire, free of water, unbounded, free of clods—such ground for cavalry men skilled in war commend.
Level, waterless, and open ground is commended for chariots; ground with low trees, tall grass, and water is for those who fight on elephants.
Ground full of fastnesses, great trees, overspread with reeds and bamboo, and the mountains and groves—such terrain is fit for foot-soldiers.
An army rich in foot-soldiers is steadfast, O Bhārata; an army rich in chariots and horses is commended in fair weather.
One rich in foot-soldiers and elephants is commended in the rainy season. Weighing these qualities, one should make use of place and time.
He who, having pondered thus, marches forth, honoring the lunar day and the asterism, ever wins victory, marshaling his army aright.
One should not strike those asleep, thirsty, weary, or scattered, nor at the time of release, of march, of movement, or of drinking and eating.
Those flung far off, those scattered apart, those struck down, those reduced to small numbers, those grown over-confident, those engaged in some undertaking, those inflamed by intrigue—having set spies abroad as agents who follow them to their dwellings—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
—at the gate that has come down by tradition, whoever are the attendants, the warders of service, and whatever bold and dashing men there are—
—those who break the enemy's ranks and those who close up a broken line—these are to be given equal food and drink and double wages.
Captains over ten should be appointed, and likewise captains over a hundred; and over them one should set as captain of a thousand a hero who is never slothful.
Assembling them by rank of precedence, one should say: 'Let us swear that for the sake of victory in battle we shall not forsake one another.
Let any cowards among us turn back here and now, lest by making a breach in the uproar of battle they get us killed.
He who flees in combat destroys both himself and his own side; in flight there is loss of property, slaughter, infamy, and disgrace.
Ugly and joyless are the words of the man who flees, his lips and teeth quivering, all his weapons cast aside.
As for him who flees, abandoning his comrades when their lives hang in the balance, hemmed in by his foes—let such a fate be our enemies', not ours.
For those who turn their backs are the dregs of men; they merely swell the heap of the dead, gaining nothing here or hereafter.
With glad hearts the enemies go out to meet the man who flees; but friends, my son, greet the victor with salutations and with blessings.
He at whose misfortune, O king, his enemies rejoice—that, I deem, is a sorrow harder to bear even than death.'
'Know prosperity to be the root of dharma and of all happiness; from cowards she passes to others, but the hero attains her.
We, then, longing for heaven, our lives laid down in battle, whether conquering or being slain, deserve to win the goodly path.'
Thus having sworn their oath together, having wholly given up their lives, the fearless heroes plunge into the enemy's host.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In front should be a phalanx of men bearing sword and shield, behind a line of wagons, and the noncombatants in the middle.
For repelling the enemy and concealing the foot-soldiers; for upon this the foe would grow greedy—those of them who advance in the van.
Those esteemed for the front rank, courageous and high-spirited, should advance first, and the rest of the men close behind them.
And even the cowards should be roused to ardor with effort; or let them at least stand close by, merely showing their shoulders.
A small force one should make fight in close formation, but a large one may be spread out at will; against a numerous foe, a small force's array should be needle-pointed.
When the battle is joined, or when spirits are high, whether it be true or false, one should raise his arms and cry aloud, 'The enemy are broken, broken!'
"Our ally's host has come—strike, and have no fear!" Raising a fearsome din, they should rush forward with their war-cries.
Let them sound their roars and shrill cries, their conches, krakaca-rattles and cow-horns, their kettledrums, tabors and small drums—and make the war-elephants trumpet.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what character, O Bhārata, of what bearing and of what aspect, what armor and what weapons should the men be who are to stand in battle, O king?
Bhīṣma said: A man's weapon and his armor are assigned here according to his custom, for it is according to his upbringing that a man conducts himself in his deeds.
The Gāndhāras, the Sindhus and the Sauvīras fight with claw-blades and lances; the Ābhīras are very strong, and their force is one that prevails everywhere.
The Uśīnaras are skilled in every weapon and full of mettle; the men of the east are skilled in elephant-warfare, though they fight by guile.
So too the Yavanas and the Kāmbojas, and those who dwell about Mathurā, are skilled in close combat; the southerners are men of sword and shield.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Heroes of great spirit and great strength are born everywhere. This much has been told in the main; now hear from me the marks of a warrior.
Those whose voice and eyes are like a lion's or a tiger's, whose gait is like a lion's or a tiger's, whose eyes are like a dove's or a sparrow's—all such are heroes, crushers of their foes.
Others with a wild beast's voice and a leopard's eyes, with a bull's eyes, loud of speech, exceedingly fierce, wrathful, with a voice like a kiṃnarī's—
some with a voice like thunder and an angry face, some with a young-camel's bellow; with crooked noses and slender shanks, who range far and strike at a distance—
hunched like a cat, lean, with thin hair and thin skin, brave and restless of mind—such men prove hard to withstand.
Some whose eyes are half-closed like an iguana's, and mild by nature, who in motion sound like the tramp of horses—these men are capable of carrying a thing through.
Well-knit, slender, broad-chested and well-formed, they dance when the drums sound and rejoice in quarrels.
Deep-eyed or with protruding eyes, tawny-hued, knit-browed of face, or with eyes like a mongoose's—all such are heroes ready to give up their bodies.
Squint-eyed, with jutting foreheads, with fleshless jaws, with crooked arms and clenched fingers, gaunt and laced over with veins—
when the clash is at hand they plunge in with great speed; like elephants in rut they prove hard to withstand.
With blazing, bristling hair, with thick flanks, jaws and faces, with high shoulders and broad necks, grim of look and with thick calves—
with prominent eyes yet handsome necks, and stooped like birds; round-headed, with a serpent's mouth, or faces like a cat's—
fierce-voiced, full of fury, who go forward in battle with a roar, ignorant of dharma and arrogant, dreadful and terrible to behold—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
all these, careless of their lives, lowborn and never turning back, should always be set in the van of the army: they are slain, and they slay.
Lawless and of broken conduct, their ruin is itself a good thing; for in just this way they rise up again and again in rage even against their own king.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What, O bull among men, are the auspicious signs of an army destined to win victory? These I wish to learn here.
Bhīṣma said: The auspicious signs that mark an army destined to win victory, O bull among men, all of these I shall tell you in full.
When the appointed time has summoned a human venture, fate first sets to work upon it; this the wise perceive with the far-reaching eye of knowledge.
And those who know such things, performing here the rites of expiation, their mutterings and oblations and acts of blessing, lay to rest even the ill-omened.
The army in which the warriors and the mounts alike are high of heart—of that army, O Bhārata, one may surely foretell victory.
When the winds blow at its back, and the rainbows of Indra, and the clouds and the sun's rays follow behind it—
and when jackals, crows and vultures move along with the host on the favorable side, then its success is unsurpassed.
When the sacred fire is bright of flame, its rays mounting upward, its tongue curling to the right and free of smoke, and the holy fragrances of the oblations waft abroad—this, they say, is the sign of victory to come.
Where the conches and kettledrums sound deep and resounding, and where the men are eager to fight and not set against it—this, they say, is the sign of victory to come.
For those who have set out or are about to set out, deer behind and on the left are auspicious; for those who mean to strike, deer on the right betoken success; but those that cross in front forbid it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the birds cry with auspicious voices—geese, curlews, woodpeckers and blue jays—and the warriors are glad and full of spirit—this, they say, is the sign of victory to come.
Those whose host is radiant and hard to look upon for the bright gleam of weapons, armor, banners and standards and for the fair faces and the bright complexions of its young men—they overcome their enemies.
Those whose warriors are obedient and free of vanity, who hold to friendship with one another and keep themselves pure—this, they say, is the sign of victory to come.
When the sounds, the touches and the scents that move about are pleasing to the mind, and firmness enters into the warriors—that is the face of victory.
For one who has entered, the omen on the left is favorable; for one about to enter, the right; an omen behind accomplishes the aim, while one in front forbids it.
Having gathered a great army of the four arms, O Yudhiṣṭhira, you should first strive to turn the foe back by conciliation, and only then by war.
This victory which is won by war is the lowest kind, O Bhārata, for in battle victory is a doubtful thing—whether it comes by chance or by fate is a matter of question.
Like the great rush of waters, like herds of deer in panic, a great host once broken is most impossible to check.
At the mere cry "It is broken!" even the wise break apart for no cause—a great host of noble strength, like a herd of ruru-deer.
Heroes who know one another, joyful, careless of their lives and resolute—even fifty such can crush the army of the foe.
Or even five, six, or seven, joined together and firm of resolve, wellborn and rightly honored, will conquer their enemies here.
Pitched battle should by no means be entered upon while another way is possible; war is said to be the last resort after conciliation, sowing dissension, and gifts.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For at the advance of an army fear afflicts the timid: "Where, like a blazing thunderbolt, will this thing fall?"
When men learn that a host has marched forth and go out to meet it, the limbs of the warriors quiver, and so does the whole country.
The whole land is shaken, O king, with all that stands and moves within it; the very marrow sinks in the bodies of men scorched by the heat of arms.
To them conciliation, mixed with sternness, should be applied again and again; for when hard pressed, the enemy will come round to terms in every way.
To divide those within the enemy's ranks one should send forth spies; and with the king who lies beyond him, a treaty is to be commended.
For no other pressure of such a kind can be brought upon him as the assault from every side made together with his own enemy.
Forbearance is indeed a good thing, and impatience is never good; yet know, O Pārtha, the proper use of both forbearance and its opposite.
The fame of a king who, having conquered, shows forbearance grows great, for then even those who have gravely offended come to trust in him.
Śambara held that forbearance is good only after one has first worn the foe down; for wood that has not been heated returns again to its natural shape.
This the teachers do not commend, nor is it a good example; rather, men should be governed without harshness and without destruction, as one would govern one's own son.
A harsh king becomes hateful to all creatures, O Yudhiṣṭhira, yet a mild one men despise; therefore he should partake of both.
When about to strike, he should speak kindly, and kindly too while striking, O Bhārata; and having struck, he should show pity, as one grieving, as one in tears.
"It gives me no pleasure that he was slain"—thus he should say openly before others—"yet you did not heed my word though I told you again and again."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Alas, how I longed that he should live! A man like this did not deserve to die. Hard indeed to find are good men who do not flee from battles."
"He who slew this man in the fray has done me a hurt"—saying this aloud, in secret he should yet honor the slayers.
And whatever wrong the slayers or those struck down may have done, he may even cry out with arms uplifted, wishing to win the people to himself.
Thus acting in all conditions with conciliation foremost, the king who knows dharma and is free of fear becomes dear to all creatures.
And in him all creatures come to place their trust, O Bhārata; and one who is trusted, and so attended upon, can be enjoyed at will.
Therefore the king who wishes to enjoy the earth should win the trust of all creatures without guile, and guard them on every side.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How should a king conduct himself toward an enemy who is mild, how toward one who is fierce, and how toward one with a great following, O lord of the earth? Tell me that, grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue of Bṛhaspati and Indra, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Saluting Bṛhaspati and approaching him with joined palms, Vāsava, lord of the gods and slayer of enemy heroes, put this question to him:
"How, O holy one, should I bear myself toward my foes, ever vigilant, and how, without wholly destroying them, may I yet restrain them by stratagem?
"At the clashing of two armies victory is shared in common; doing what may I keep my blazing, glorious fortune from forsaking me?"
Then he who was skilled in dharma, profit and desire, ready of wit and learned in the ordinances of kingly duty, answered Puraṃdara:
"Never should one seek to restrain wrongdoers by open strife, for fury and impatience are the resort of fools; nor should one openly show himself an enemy if one means his death.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Curbing within himself the anger, the force and the impatience born of his own nature, he should wait upon his enemy as though trusting him, while trusting him not at all.
"He should always speak kindly and do nothing unkind; he should desist from barren feuds and spare himself empty straining of the throat.
"As a skilled fowler, mimicking the cry of the birds, brings those birds under his power, so let the skilled king bring his enemies under his sway and then destroy them, O Puraṃdara.
"One who forever scorns his foes does not sleep at ease, O Vāsava; the evil-minded man stays wakeful, like fire risen amid a heap of fuel.
"No pitched battle should be joined when victory is doubtful; rather, the enemy, once trusted and won, should be brought under control and so disposed of, O lord.
"Having taken counsel with his great-souled ministers versed in policy, he should look on as if indifferent though he be despised, unconquered in his heart;
"and then, when the time comes and his foe's footing has somewhat faltered, he should strike, and corrupt his army through trusted agents.
"Knowing the beginning, middle and end, he should plot in secret, and corrupt his enemy's forces, having learned their full measure.
"By sowing dissension, by bribes, and by employing drugs as well; but he should never enter into close fellowship with his foes.
"Though he must wait even a long while, biding his time, he should yet destroy his enemies; and he should keep them in check until they come to trust him."
Let him not strike down his foes in haste; the victory of the watchful comes without fever. He who does not jar the embedded barb, nor opens up a fresh wound, prospers.
But when the appointed time has come, let him strike; for the moment does not return again to the man who longs, O lord of the gods, to slay his enemy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the occasion that slips past the man who awaits his occasion is hard for him to regain, though he would act in accord with the law of timeliness.
Thus let him master his own vigor, winning over the men whom the good esteem; let him always accomplish his ends in their season, and not press hard before the time has come.
Setting aside desire and wrath, and pride as well, the disciplined king should watch for the opening in his foes, O Puraṃdara.
Softness, harshness, sloth, and heedlessness, O best of gods, and manifold deceits, O Śakra — these overcome the man who lacks discernment.
Having destroyed these four, and having warded off deceit, he is then able to strike his enemies without hesitation.
Whenever a secret design can be carried out by one alone, let him do it so; for ministers let secrets slip among themselves, and even betray them.
Or, judging a thing beyond his single power, let him then make common counsel with others — the rod of brahman against unseen foes, the fourfold army against those in sight.
Let him first employ division, and likewise silent chastisement; the king should apply each of these in its proper season, this one now and that one then.
And he should bow in submission, in due season, before an enemy stronger than himself; yet, disciplined and unheedful of nothing, let him seek that foe's destruction when the foe grows careless.
With homage, with gifts, and speaking in honeyed words, let him attend upon his enemy, yet never let the enemy grow suspicious of him.
Let him ever shun the haunts of men who are wary of him, and place no trust in them; for once injured, those who have been spurned remain watchful here.
For there is no task harder than this, O best of gods, than to hold sovereignty over men of manifold conduct, O lord of the immortals.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
So too is it called the very nature of men of varied dispositions. Let him strive, taking his stand upon strategy, holding off both friend and foe.
The gentle man they despise, yet from the harsh the people shrink. Be neither too harsh nor too gentle: be harsh, be gentle, each in its turn.
As an embankment, when the rushing waters flood it on every side, is breached forever once a gap appears, so is the kingdom of the heedless king.
Let him not assail many foes at once, O Puraṃdara, but by conciliation, by gift, by division, and by force.
Crushing them one by one, let him deal skillfully with those that remain; for even when able, the wise king should not take on all of them together.
