But after a moment, regaining his composure, the bird said to the slayer of birds: "I shall satisfy you; wait but a moment."
Having said this, the pigeon, kindling the fire to a blaze with dry leaves, filled with great joy, spoke again:
"From the gods, from the sages, and from the great-souled ancestors I have heard before of the supreme dharma that lies in honoring a guest."
"Grant me this favor today—truly I tell you this: my resolve is fixed upon honoring my guest."
Then the bird, true to his vow, as if smiling, circumambulated that fire three times and entered into it, O lord of the earth.
Seeing the bird enter into the midst of the fire, the fowler reflected in his mind: "What is this I have brought about?"
"Alas, for me, a cruel man, contemptible by reason of my own deeds, a most great and terrible sin will surely come—there is no doubt."
In many ways and at great length the fowler lamented thus, reproaching his own deeds, as he beheld the twice-born bird come to such an end.
Bhīṣma said: Then the fowler, watching the pigeon fallen into the fire and overwhelmed with pity, spoke again these words:
"What a thing have I, a cruel and witless man, done! For as long as I live this sin will dwell forever in my heart."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Reviling himself, he said again and again: "Shame upon me, the dull-witted, ever bent upon treachery, who, abandoning every good deed, became a hunter of birds!"
"This is, beyond doubt, a rebuke to me, a cruel man—delivered by the great-souled pigeon who gave his own flesh."
"I shall give up my own dear life and forsake my children and wife, for dharma has been taught to me by that supremely righteous pigeon."
"From this day forth I shall dry up my own body, stripped of all enjoyments, as the scant water of summer is dried away."
"Enduring hunger, thirst, and heat, grown gaunt with veins drawn taut, I shall pursue, through fasts of many kinds, the way to the world beyond."
"Lo, by the offering of his body, the honoring of a guest has been shown! Therefore I shall practice dharma, for dharma is the supreme goal—I have seen what dharma is, such as the righteous practice it, in that best of birds."
Having spoken thus and made his resolve, the fowler of cruel deeds, taking up the Great Departure, set forth with a vow firmly fixed.
Then his staff, his sticks, his snare, and his cage—and the pigeons he had bound—he loosed and set free.
Bhīṣma said: When the fowler had gone, the grieving hen-pigeon, remembering her husband and weeping, fainting with sorrow, spoke:
"I cannot recall, beloved, that I ever once did anything to displease you. Every widowed woman, O sky-ranger, even one with many sons, becomes an object of pity to her kin—a noble-hearted woman bereft of her husband."
"Ever was I cherished by you and soothed with great regard, again and again, with words sweet, tender, and most delightful."
"In the caverns of the mountains, by the cascades of the rivers, and on the lovely crowns of the trees, I was made happy by you, my beloved."
"In our flights through the sky I knew happiness with you, my love; I sported with you—but now none of that is left to me at all."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"A father gives but a measured portion, a mother a measured portion, a son a measured portion; but a husband, who gives without measure—what woman would not honor him?"
"There is no protector like a husband, and no happiness like a husband; renouncing all her wealth and possessions, a woman's refuge is her husband alone."
"I have no use, my lord, for life in this world without you. What virtuous woman bereft of her husband could bring herself to live?"
Having lamented thus in many a piteous way, the deeply grieving, devoted wife entered the blazing fire.
Then she beheld her husband, clad in shining garments, seated in a celestial chariot, honored by the great-souled doers of good deeds.
He wore bright garlands and garments and was adorned with every ornament, surrounded by a hundred million celestial cars belonging to those of holy renown.
Then the bird, gone to heaven, was reunited with his wife; honored for that deed of his, he rejoiced there together with her.
Bhīṣma said: The fowler, O king, saw the pair seated in the celestial chariot; and seeing the husband and wife, he reflected, out of his grief, upon the good path.
"By what manner of austerity might I attain the supreme goal?" Having resolved this in his mind, he set out upon his journey.
Taking up the Great Departure, the fowler who had lived by killing birds became still, living on air alone, free of all sense of "mine," in longing for heaven.
Then he saw a broad and lovely lake, adorned with lotuses, thronged with flocks of many birds, its cool waters fair—a sight at which even one tormented by thirst would be satisfied, of this there is no doubt.
But the fowler, O king, grown exceedingly gaunt with fasting, gladly approached a forest inhabited by beasts of prey.
Having made his great resolve, the fowler entered in; and even as he entered the forest, he was caught fast by thorns.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His limbs torn by the thorns, his skin made wet with blood, he wandered through that desolate place teeming with all manner of wild beasts.
Then in that forest, from the friction of great trees driven by the wind, there arose a mighty fire, bearer of oblations.
That forest, dense with trees and tangled with creepers and boughs, the fire consumed in fury, blazing like the flame at the end of an age.
Attended by flaming sparks fanned up by the wind, it burned that dreadful forest thronged with beasts and birds.
Then, with a heart full of gladness, seeking the release of his body, the fowler ran toward that swelling fire.
Then, consumed by that fire, the fowler, his sins destroyed, attained the supreme perfection, O best of the Bhāratas.
Then, his anguish gone, he beheld himself established in heaven, shining like Indra amid the yakṣas, gandharvas, and siddhas.
Thus indeed the pigeon and the devoted hen-pigeon, together with the fowler, went to heaven through their meritorious deeds.
And whatever woman of such a kind follows after her husband, she too shines forth at once, dwelling in heaven like that hen-pigeon.
Thus did this come to pass of old: the righteous destiny, won through meritorious deeds, of the great-souled fowler and of the pigeon.
Whoever should ever hear this, and whoever should recite it, no misfortune befalls him, even should his mind grow heedless.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, great is this dharma, O best of the upholders of dharma. Even for slayers of cattle there may be expiation of their sinful deed; but there is no expiation for him who would slay one who has come to him for refuge.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: One who commits a sin unknowingly, O best of the Bhāratas—how is he freed from that wrong? Tell me this.
Bhīṣma said: On this matter I shall relate to you an ancient tale—what Indrota the brāhmaṇa, son of Śunaka, said to Janamejaya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There was a king of great valor, Janamejaya, son of Parīkṣit; unwittingly, the slaying of a brāhmaṇa came upon that lord of the earth.
All the brāhmaṇas, together with his household priests, forsook him; and the king, burning day and night, went off to the forest.
Abandoned by his subjects, he did great works of merit; he practiced austerity beyond all measure, burning the while with remorse.
On this I shall tell a tale that confirms and amplifies this dharma: burning with his evil deed, Janamejaya set forth.
Wishing to choose him as priest, he came to Indrota, son of Śunaka, of firm-fixed vows, and clasped him, pressing hard upon his feet.
Then the great sage, afraid, rebuked him most severely: "You who have wrought a great sin, slayer of an unborn child—why have you come here?"
"What is there for you to do with us? Touch me not, by any means whatever! Go, go—your presence here surely gives us no pleasure."
Your odor is as of blood, and the sight of you is as of a corpse; though resembling one who is wholesome, you are inauspicious, and you wander about, dead, as though alive.
Inwardly dead, your soul unpurified, brooding upon evil alone, you wake, you sleep, you live, you move about at ease.
Vain is your life, O king, and in torment you live; it is for evil that you were created, for the basest of deeds.
Desiring much good, fathers strive for sons through austerity, through sacrifices to the gods, through worship and through forbearance.
Behold this line of your fathers, gone to hell on your account; fruitless are all the bonds of hope they had set upon you.
Toward those Brāhmaṇas, by honoring whom men obtain heaven, long life, fame, and happiness, your hatred is ceaseless and without purpose.
Quitting this world, you will fall headlong, through your sinful deeds, for years uncounted and years without end.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Devoured there by creatures and vultures, white-necked and iron-beaked; and even thence, returning once more, you will pass into a sinful womb.
As for your thought, O king, that there is no world beyond this—whence then?—the messengers of Yama, in Yama's abode, shall make you remember it well.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Janamejaya answered that sage: 'What is blameworthy, you blame; what is censurable, you censure—do not so reproach me.'
You reproach me as one deserving reproach; therefore I seek your favor, for all this is my own doing, and I burn as though cast into the fire.
Looking back upon my own deeds, my mind takes no delight; surely a terror dreadful even beyond the son of Vivasvat has come upon me.
Without drawing out that barb, how shall I be able to live? Laying aside all your wrath, speak to me, O Śaunaka.
I shall again become the cook-house of the Brāhmaṇas, rich in offerings; let there be a remnant of this house, let not this line be undone.
For of us, cursed by the Brāhmaṇas, no remnant ought to remain—of us who cannot grasp the sacred texts, nor the knowledge that comes from sure certainty of the Veda.
Sorely afflicted, I shall speak yet again of what is fitting now; for again and again they perish, as men without dharma and without prayer.
And they sink down low, like the Pulindas and Śabaras; for those who offer no sacrifice can in no way attain that world beyond.
Without yet knowing my understanding, which is as a child's before the learned, O Brāhmaṇa, look kindly upon me, O Śaunaka, as a father upon his sons.
Śaunaka said: What wonder is it that a wise man should do much of what is fitting? Having become learned, he is not tormented on account of living beings.
Mounting the palace of wisdom, himself beyond sorrow, he grieves for the multitude, and with his wisdom looks down upon them as one upon a mountain looks upon those who stand upon the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yet he does not grasp it there, nor does he see the things that ought to be done—being weary of soul, or remote, or held in reproach among all the good.
Having known the power that lies on both sides, he knows the greatness that is in the scripture: attain here the great peace, and let Brahman be your refuge.
Fair indeed is that other-worldly reward for those who do not anger the Brāhmaṇas—if you grieve for your sins, and if you look toward dharma.
Janamejaya said: I grieve for my sin, and I practice no unrighteousness; and I in turn desire one who wishes me well and who serves me, O Śaunaka.
Śaunaka said: Cutting away both stubbornness and pride, I desire your gladness, O king; abide in the welfare of all beings, and keep dharma in remembrance.
Not from fear, nor from meanness, nor from greed do I call upon you; let the gods, together with the Brāhmaṇas, hear that my word is true.
I, who seek nothing from anyone, call upon you and upon dharma, while all beings cry out, 'Alas! Shame!'
Those who know not dharma will speak against me, and men who are no friends will speak against me; and my friends, hearing those words, will burn with great distress for me.
Only some, of great wisdom, will understand what must be done; know what I have done, dear one, toward the Brāhmaṇas, O descendant of Bharata.
So act that on my account they may obtain security; and promise that you will do no harm to the Brāhmaṇas, O lord of men.
Janamejaya said: Neither by word, nor by thought, nor ever again by deed shall I do harm to the Brāhmaṇas, O sage; I touch your very feet.
Śaunaka said: Therefore I shall declare to you, whose mind is turned back to it, the dharma—you who, prosperous, mighty, and content, now look toward dharma; and that, having first been harsh, is the more wondrous still.
Living beings show favor through their own conduct, O king; surely the whole world resolves what is good and what is bad accordingly—wherein you, having become such as you were, today look toward dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That, forsaking most delicious food and enjoyments, one should take his stand in austerity—this too is a marvel among beings, O Janamejaya.
That a weak man should be a giver, or a wretched one rich in austerity—this they call no wonder, for it stands not far off.
For this very thing, when done wholly without reflection, is mere wretchedness; therefore let it be done with discernment, and thereby virtue will arise in it.
Sacrifice, giving, compassion, the Vedas, and truth, O lord of the earth—these five are purifiers, and well-performed austerity is the sixth.
That very thing is the supreme purifier of kings, O Janamejaya; by rightly laying hold of it, you shall attain the more excellent dharma.
Going to holy places is remembered as the supreme purifier; and indeed they recite these verses that were sung by Yayāti.
The mortal who would set out, or would live out his span of life once more—let him, having performed sacrifice with single devotion, then renounce it and practice austerity.
They call Kurukṣetra holy, and Pṛthūdaka upon the Sarasvatī, where, having bathed or drunk, one need not grieve over death on the morrow.
To Mahāsaras, to the Puṣkaras, to Prabhāsa and Uttaramānasa, and to Kālodaka indeed you shall go, having gained your span, to live again.
Resorting to the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, you should wander along them; devoted to the recitation of scripture, you should perform your ablutions at all the sacred sites.
He declared renunciation, the dharma of giving up, to be the highest of purifiers; and here too they recite these verses made by Satyavat.
Even as a child, in truth, is neither doer of merit nor doer of sin—for in all beings there is no abiding sorrow, whence then could there be happiness?
So it is for those who are by nature thus, who go through every kind of contact, and who for the most part give up life, when merit and sin alike lie open before them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But that which is the greater among the duties of a king, that I declare to you: by strength and by sharing out gifts, conquer heaven and purify yourself.
The man who has such strength and vigor is the lord of dharma; for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas, do you traverse this earth.
Even as you once cast them down, so now win their favor, though you be reproached, though you be forsaken in many ways.
Knowing the vision of the self, O learned one, be not angered with the thought 'I am not'; striving in your own duties, achieve the highest good.
One king there is who becomes dreadful as frost or fire; and another becomes like the plough or the thunderbolt, O scorcher of foes.
One must not think a man wholly lost, nor again as past all cure; nor should one ever cling, among the wicked, to the thought 'I am undone.'
Grieving over a wrong deed, one is freed from a quarter of the sin; resolving 'I shall not do this again,' he is freed from a second; resolving 'I shall practice dharma alone,' he is freed from a third.
The good is to be approved by a man who wishes to prosper: those who frequent fragrant things become fragrant accordingly, and those who frequent foul-smelling things become foul accordingly.
One devoted to the practice of austerity is at once freed from sin; tending the fire for a year, the accused man is released; tending the fire for three years, even the slayer of an embryo is wholly freed.
By delivering from death as many living beings of that same kind, by their own nature perishing, as he had slain, the slayer of an embryo is wholly freed.
Or he should plunge into the waters, reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa thrice; that is even as the final bath of the horse-sacrifice—so Manu declared.
Swiftly he drives away his sin, and likewise obtains honor; and toward him living beings grow gracious, even those dull and dumb.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The gods and demons all together, O king, came to Bṛhaspati, the teacher of the gods, and questioned him: 'You know the fruit in dharma, when done, O great sage, and likewise in the other, in hell, the world of sin.'
'But for one in whom both good deeds should be present, which of the two would there prevail in victory? Tell us, O great sage, the fruit of works: how does one of virtuous conduct drive away sin?'
Bṛhaspati said: Having first committed sin unwittingly, he who then performs meritorious deeds with deliberate purpose—such a one of virtuous conduct drives away that sin, as a soiled garment is cleansed by the use of lye.
Having done a sin, a man should not think 'I am undone'; rather, faithful and free of malice, he should ever wish to do good.
As one repairs the holes of a garment with good thread, so does the man who, having done a sin, takes up the doing of good.
As the sun, rising again, drives away all darkness, so one who practices good drives away all his sin.
Bhīṣma said: Having thus addressed king Janamejaya, Śaunaka of Indrota's line had him perform, according to rule, the horse-sacrifice.
Then that king, his stain removed, endowed with majesty in the likeness of blazing fire, entered his own kingdom, that wearer-down of foes, as the full-bodied moon enters the sky.
Bhīṣma said: Hear, O Pārtha, as it befell, an ancient tale—the dialogue of the vulture and the jackal that took place long ago at Vidiśā.
Certain grief-stricken people, taking up a child who had not yet reached his youth—the very all-in-all of their family—wept, overwhelmed with sorrow.
Having taken up the dead child, they stood facing the cremation-ground, and passing him from lap to lap, they wept then upon the ground.
At the sound of their weeping a vulture drew near and spoke these words: 'Leave this one whose single self has passed, and depart from the world of the living without delay.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Here thousands of men, and thousands of women too, have been brought together by Time; how then could these ever be without kinsmen?'
'Look upon the whole world, beset with pleasures and pains; union and separation are met with by turns.'
'Those creatures who take up the dead and carry them, and those who follow after them, they too depart, each according to the measure of his own life-span.'
'Enough of lingering in this cremation-ground, thronged with vultures and jackals, heaped with skeletons, dreadful, terrifying to all living beings.'
'No one who has met the law of Time lives again, whether dear or hated; such is the course of living beings.'
'Everyone who is born into the world of mortals must surely die; upon the path ordained by the Ender, who shall bring the dead to life?'
'In a world where labor draws to its close, and as the sun is going down, let each go to his own abode, casting off his love for the son.'
Then, having heard the vulture's words, those kinsmen, crying aloud, O king, set forth, abandoning the son upon the ground.
And then, having made their resolve, forsaking their own offspring, despairing of his life, they set out upon the road and went their way.
But a jackal, colored like a crow or a storm-cloud, coming forth from his hole, called out to them as they departed: 'Pitiless indeed are these mortals!'
"The sun yet stands in the sky, you fools — show your love and do not be afraid. The hour takes many forms; perhaps even now the child may yet revive."
"Having laid him upon the ground, stripped of all love for your son, why do you abandon the boy at the cremation ground and go away so pitilessly?"
"Have you no tenderness for this son, this sweet-spoken child, by the mere sound of whose speech you would melt into delight?"
"Do you not see how strong is the love for offspring even among beasts and birds, though from rearing them no profit ever comes to them?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For four-footed creatures, for birds and insects, for all beings bound by affection, this love is, in its bearing on the world beyond, like the sacrificial rites of sages."
"For these creatures that delight in their young, no advantage is seen either in this world or the next — and yet they go on sustaining their offspring."
"When they no longer behold their beloved young, no grief abides in them; nor, once grown, do those offspring ever nourish their mother and father in return."
"Whence then this love among men, in whom grief is destined to dwell? How will you forsake this son, the very perpetuator of your line, and go your way?"
"Long shed your tears, long gaze upon him with love; for things dear as these are, above all, hard to give up."
"Of one fallen low, hard-pressed, and facing the cremation ground, where the kinsmen take their stand, no stranger will stand beside him."
"To every creature its own life is dear, and every creature comes to know love; behold how strong is the love of the good even among the beasts of the wild."
"How can you abandon and go from this boy, with his long, lotus-restless eyes, adorned as for a fresh wedding, bathed and decked with garlands?"
Bhīṣma said: Having heard the jackal's words of piteous lamentation, all those people then turned back for the corpse's sake.
The vulture said: Ah, shame! Addressed by this cruel, dull-witted, base little jackal, O men of feeble resolve, why do you turn back?
"Forsaken by the five elements, empty, reduced to the state of a mere log and devoid of motion — why do you grieve for him? Why do you not rather grieve for your own selves?"
"Practice fierce austerity, by which you may be freed from sin. By austerity all things are won; what will lamentation accomplish?"
"Know that fortunes, with their embodied forms, are unwelcome too, whereby this world passes on, bequeathing grief that has no end."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Wealth and cattle and gold, gems and jewels too, and offspring — all are rooted in austerity, and through the practice of austerity are won."
"As it has been wrought, so among beings is their measure of joy and sorrow attained; a creature is born already having taken up its sorrows and its joys."
"Not by the father's deeds does the son fare, nor the father by the son's; by separate paths they go, each leaving behind his own good and evil works."
"Practice righteousness with diligence, and likewise turn back from unrighteousness; and conduct yourselves, each in due season, toward the gods and toward the twice-born."
"Cast off grief and wretchedness, and turn back from love of your son. Let him be abandoned to the open air, and then return at once."
"Whatever good deed a man does, and whatever dreadful unrighteous deed, the doer alone reaps it; what part have kinsmen in this?"
"Having abandoned him here, the kinsmen do not remain beside their beloved kinsman; casting off their love, they go away, their eyes brimming and clouded with tears."
"Wise man or fool, rich man or poor — every one, endowed with his good and his evil, passes into the power of Time."
"What will you gain by grieving? Why do you mourn the dead? For Time is the lord of all, looking upon all alike according to the law."
"Those in the prime of youth, and children, and the aged, and even those yet in the womb — all of them death enters. Such is this world."
The jackal said: Ah, by this dull-witted vulture the love of you, who are overcome by tenderness for your son and grieve so sorely, has been made to grow cold!
"By words measured and well-marshalled, couched in courtesy, has he persuaded you to depart at the setting of the sun, casting off a love so hard to cast off?"
"Ah, in the loss of a son, in the tending of the dead and desolate, how grievous is the anguish of those who cry aloud — like cows bereft of their calves!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"This day I learn the grief of men upon the earth; for beholding their piteous love, tears come even to my eyes."
"Effort must ever be made; once made, it is brought to fulfillment by destiny. Destiny and human exertion alike are wrought together by Fate."
"One must never yield to despair, for from despair whence comes happiness? By striving the object is attained; why then do you go away so heartlessly?"
"This body, sprung from your own flesh, formed of half your own frame, the continuer of the line of your fathers — having forsaken it in the forest, where will you go?"
"When the sun has set and twilight is come, then you may bear away your son, or else remain here."
The vulture said: Now a full thousand years and more have passed since I was born, O men, yet I have never seen one — woman, man, or eunuch — once dead come back to life.
"Some die in the womb; some are born and die the moment they are born; others die while striding forth in their strength, and yet others in the bloom of youth."
"Fortunes here are fleeting, for four-footed creatures and for birds; and for things that move and things that move not, life-span stands ever at its very end."
"Sundered from beloved wives, and stricken with grief for sons, men, ever burning with sorrow, go home day after day."
"Thousands of things unwished, and hundreds of things wished-for, the kinsmen here forsake and go their way, plunged in deep sorrow."
"Let this lifeless thing be abandoned, empty, reduced to the state of a log. For one whose self has passed into another body, the corpse is but a log to wait upon."
"For him whose life has wandered away, why do you not lay aside your tears and go? For this love is fruitless, and fruitless too is this clinging."
"Not with eyes, not with ears, does he hear or behold any longer; therefore abandon him and go quickly to your own homes."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"By words grounded in the law of liberation, well-reasoned and not unkind, I have spoken to you: go quickly, each to his own dwelling."
"With words endowed with wisdom and discernment, words that bring back understanding and reason, you, O men, have been told this hard truth: turn back!"
The jackal said: This boy, hued like burnished gold, adorned with ornaments — how, at a vulture's word, will you abandon a son who would offer the funeral rice to your fathers?
"There is no resisting the love that weeps and wails aloud; from abandoning this dead one, anguish will surely come to you."
"It is heard that when Śambūka, the Śūdra, was slain, a Brāhmaṇa's child was restored to life through righteousness, by Rāma whose valor is truth."
"And so too the child of the royal sage Śveta, who had reached his appointed end — at break of day, dead though he was, he was restored to life again by one ever devoted to righteousness."
"Even so, some perfected sage, or holy man, or even a deity, might take pity on you wretched ones weeping here."
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the grieving folk, tender toward their son, turned back, and laying his head upon their laps, they wept long and without restraint.
The vulture said: Drenched with the fall of your tears, pressed by the touch of your hands, and by the working of the King of Righteousness, he has been led into a long sleep.
"Even one joined with austerity is not, before his time, struck down. This is that place where all loves come to their end — the city of the dead."
"Forsaking always thousands of children and aged ones, the kinsmen abide in sorrow upon the earth, through the days and through the nights."
"Enough of this stubbornness! Let the hindrance of grief be put away. There is no warrant for it: whence should this child have life again here today?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Not by the jackal's words will this one regain his life; for the dead, whose body has been cast off, there is no body again."
"Neither by the giving of a body, nor even by a hundred jackals, can this child be made to live — no, not in a hundred years."
"Were Rudra, or Kumāra, or Brahmā, or Viṣṇu himself to grant him a boon — then might this infant live."
"Not by the shedding of tears, not by any comforting, not by long weeping here, will he come to life again."
"I, and this jackal too, and you, his kinsmen — all of us, having taken up our righteousness and unrighteousness, are journeying here upon the road."
"From what is unkind and harsh, from injury to others and from another's wife, from unrighteousness and falsehood, let the wise man hold himself far aloof."
"Truth, righteousness, goodness, what is just, great compassion for living beings, uprightness and freedom from guile — seek these out with diligence."
"Those who, while their mother and father, their kinsmen and friends, are still alive, take no heed of them — for such men there is a perversion of duty."
"For one who no longer sees with his eyes, nor stirs in any way at all, who has reached the end of his appointed course — what will you accomplish by weeping?"
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the kinsmen, leaving that son upon the ground, overwhelmed with grief and burning with love for their child, set out for their homes.
The jackal said: Dreadful is this world of mortals, the destroyer of all living things, with its parting from beloved kin, and life withal so brief.
"Full of falsehood and untruth, of contradiction and unwelcome speech — beholding this state of recurring birth, which swells the tide of pain and grief —"
"this world of men pleases me not even for a moment. Ah, shame, that at a vulture's word you turn away, O men!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Ablaze with grief for your son as you are, you are likewise become senseless. How can you, with your tenderness, go away, casting off love for your son, having heeded the words of that wicked, unrefined vulture?"
"Hard upon joy follows sorrow, and hard upon sorrow follows joy; in a world compounded of joy and sorrow, no single thing here is without an end."
"Having laid this comely child upon the ground — a son whose loss would be the wellspring of grief to your line — where, you fools, will you go, abandoning him?"
"Endowed with beauty and youth, as though shining with splendor — I see him living, with my mind's eye; of this there is no doubt."
"Destruction is not his desert; you shall yet find happiness, O men. For you, consumed by the fire of grief for your son, that he should even be dead would today be a mercy to you."
"Having brought sorrow upon yourselves, and holding fast to your own ease, where will you go this day, abandoning him, forsaking him like men of little wit?"
Bhīṣma said: And so, by the jackal — opposed to righteousness, brooding upon false endearments, a dweller in the cremation ground, ever ranging by night —
the kinsmen were brought to wavering irresolution by words that seemed like nectar; by the jackal, for his own ends, were they held fast there.
The vulture said: This dreadful tract of forest is thronged with ghosts, haunted by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, and made to resound with the cries of owls.
"Fearful and most terrible it is, dark as a blue-black cloud. Lay down the corpse in this place and perform the rites for the dead."
"While the sun has not yet gone to its setting, and while the quarters of the sky are still clear, lay him down and attend to the funeral rites."
"Harshly the hawks are screaming, the dreadful jackals howl, the lions of the wild answer back in chorus — and the sun is going down to its setting."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The trees here are stained dark by the smoke of the pyres, and in this charnel-ground the creatures that haunt it, foodless and lean, rejoice at the prospect of a corpse.
All of them are bold in their might and most terrible in this place; misshapen flesh-eaters, they will fall upon you and overpower you.
This stretch of wilderness lies far off, and here danger will arise. Abandon this body that has become mere wood; do not heed the jackal's words.
If, with your judgment fallen away, you listen to the jackal's words, which are barren and false, then you will all be undone.
The jackal said: Stay here, and do not be afraid. So long as the sun still burns, abide here for love of your son, without despair.
Weep your fill, untroubled; gaze your fill with love upon him. Stay while the sun yet stands—what are the words of a flesh-eater to you?
If, your minds bewildered, you accept the vulture's words—harsh and headlong as they are—your son will be no more to you.
Bhīṣma said: The vulture said the sun had not yet set; the jackal said it had gone down. So those two, driven by hunger, spoke to the dead child's kin.
O king, both the vulture and the jackal, each shrewd in his own cause, worn out by hunger and thirst, kept arguing, each leaning upon scripture for support.
At the words—sweet as nectar—of those two learned in cunning, the jackal and the winged one, the people now made to set out, now turned to go.
Sunk in grief and misery, weeping, they then stood still, kept whirling this way and that by the practiced skill of those two who each pursued his own ends.
While those two cunning ones thus wrangled on, and the kinsmen stood there waiting, Śaṃkara drew near.
Then the Trident-bearer, granter of boons, said to those men, 'I am here to grant a boon.' Grieving, bowed low, they stood and answered him these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'We have all lost our only son and long to go on living; by giving life back to our son, you would be giving life to us.'
Thus addressed, the blessed Lord, with a palm full of water, granted that boy his life, to last a hundred years.
And to the jackal and the vulture the blessed bearer of the Pināka, ever devoted to the welfare of all beings, gave the boon of the ending of their hunger.
Then, O lord, bowing to that god, filled with joy at their good fortune, their purpose fulfilled, glad and at ease, they set out for home.
By unwavering, long-sustained perseverance, by firm resolve, and by the grace of the God of gods, the fruit is swiftly won.
See how the god's coming and the kinsmen's resolve together wiped away the tears of those wretched mourners.
And see how in a short time, through resolve and persistent seeking, those grieving ones, having won Śaṃkara's grace, attained their joy.
Amazed and overjoyed at the bringing back to life of their son, O best of the Bhāratas, they were made glad once more by the grace of Śaṃkara.
Then, O king, having known a grief born of calamity, they made haste and, taking up their son, entered the city with glad hearts. Such is the wisdom set forth for all men within the four orders of society.
By hearing this auspicious tale, bound up with dharma, worldly gain, and liberation, a man rejoices forever, both here and after death.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they tell an ancient tale, O best of the Bhāratas—the dialogue between the silk-cotton tree and the Wind.
On the slopes of the Himālaya there stood a mighty forest-lord, grown great over a host of years, rich in branches, trunk, and foliage.
There, O mighty-armed one, rutting elephants, oppressed by the heat and worn out with toil, would rest, and so too the other tribes of wild creatures.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A bowshot in girth, with dense shade, the forest-lord was loud with parrots and mynahs, laden with fruit and laden with flowers.
Caravan-folk and merchants, ascetics and forest-dwellers, travelers upon the road, would take their lodging in that loveliest, most excellent of trees.
Seeing its broad branches and its trunks on every side, Nārada drew near and addressed it, O bull of the Bhāratas.
'Ah, how delightful you are, and ah, how you charm the heart! We take everlasting joy in you, O silk-cotton tree, foremost of trees.'
'Forever, dear one, the birds, and below the deer and the elephants, dwell about you full of delight, and grow the more charming for it.'
'Your branches, O great-branched one, and your broad trunk as well—nowhere do I see them broken by the wind in any way.'
'Is the wind, then, dear one, fond of you, or your friend, that the Breeze should always protect you so surely here in this forest?'
'For the wind, blowing in its force, shakes trees great and small from their place, and the very peaks of mountains.'
'The pure bearer of scents, blowing on, dries up the very netherworld—the deep pools, the rivers, and the seas as well.'
'Surely the wind protects you out of friendship, no doubt of it; and so you are thick with branches, full of leaves and full of flowers.'
'And this seems delightful in you, O forest-lord—that these birds, dear one, take their joy in you, glad at heart.'
'Sweet is the voice heard of them, each apart and all together, as they cry out most charmingly in the season of the rejoicing of the flowers.'
'And these glad elephants, the pride of their own herds and lineages, when reaching you in the torment of the heat, find their ease, O silk-cotton tree.'
'And likewise you are adorned by other tribes of wild creatures, and adorned by the dwelling of caravans, O tree—so that you shine like Meru.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'With brahmins perfected in austerity, with ascetics and with wandering mendicants, I deem your abode the very equal of heaven.'
'Out of kinship or out of friendship, O silk-cotton tree—of this there is no doubt—the terrible, all-pervading wind ever protects you.'
'You have come, O silk-cotton tree, into the deepest submission to the wind, so that the wind, as though saying "I am yours," forever protects you.'
'I see no tree, nor any mountain however firm, that has not been broken upon the earth by the force of the wind—such is my conviction.'
'You, then, O silk-cotton tree, are surely protected for some cause; by the wind, with all your retinue, you stand secure beyond doubt.'
The silk-cotton tree said: The wind is no friend of mine, O brahmin, nor my kinsman, nor my well-wisher, nor my supreme lord, that the wind should protect me out of such regard.
My fiery strength, O Nārada—the wind, terrible though it is, does not by its blasts attain even an eighteenth part of mine.
When the mighty wind comes rushing on—shattering trees and mountains and whatever else there may be—I check it by my force.
That breaker of all things, the storm-wind itself, has often been broken by me; and so, O divine sage, I do not fear the wind, even in its wrath.
Nārada said: O silk-cotton tree, your view is perverse, of this there is no doubt; for in strength there is nowhere any being equal to the wind.
Indra, Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, and Varuṇa the lord of waters—not even they are equal to the wind; how much less you, O forest-lord?
Whatever living thing stirs here upon the earth, O silk-cotton tree—everywhere it is the blessed wind, the lord, that grants both motion and breath.
When rightly disposed, it sets living beings rightly in motion; when ill-disposed, it stirs again, working disorder, in men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That you do not honor such a wind—best of all that sustains living things, worthy of honor as it is—what is this but lightness of wit?
You are without substance, O fool, and merely babble much; clouded over by anger and the like, you speak falsely, O silk-cotton tree.
Anger has risen in me at you, while you talk on like this; I shall myself report to the wind much of your evil speech.
By sandal and spandana trees, by śāla, by sarala and deodar, by reed and bandhana, and by others yet stronger still—
not even by these, O fool, those disciplined ones, is the wind thus reviled; for they know both the wind's strength and their own.
Therefore those best of trees do homage to the wind; but you, out of delusion, do not know the wind's strength, which has no end.
Bhīṣma said: Having thus spoken to the silk-cotton tree, O lord of kings, Nārada, best of the knowers of brahman, reported to the wind every word the tree had said.
'A certain silk-cotton tree, sprung on the slopes of the Himālaya, with a great following, of mighty root and mighty branch—he, O Wind, holds you in contempt.'
'Many insulting words he spoke of you, O Wind; yet it is not fitting for me to repeat them to you, O lord.'
'I know you, O Wind, to be the best of all that bears the breath of life, most excellent and most weighty, and in wrath like the son of Vivasvat himself.'
Hearing Nārada's words thus, the wind, drawing near to that silk-cotton tree, spoke in anger these words.
'O silk-cotton tree, as for that reviling of me which you uttered before Nārada—I, the Wind, shall show you my power, my own strength.'
'It is not that I do not know you—you are well known to me, O tree. At the creation of beings, the Grandfather, the lord, took his rest in you.'
'It is by that resting of his that the grace shown to you was granted; by that you are protected, O fool—not by your own valor, O basest of trees.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Since you despise me as though I were some common thing, I shall now show you myself, so that you shall come to know me for what I am.'
Thus addressed, the silk-cotton tree then said, as though laughing: 'O Wind, angered here in the forest, show your self by your own self.'
'Let your anger at me be set aside—what will you do to me in your wrath? I do not fear you, O Wind, even though you are your own master.'
So addressed, the wind spoke just this word—'Tomorrow'—'I shall show you my might'; and then the night drew on.
Then the silk-cotton tree, considering in its mind what the wind could do, and seeing that its own self was no match for Mātariśvan,
thought: 'What I declared to Nārada concerning the wind was false; for I am no match for the wind in strength—strong indeed is he.
The wind is forever strong, just as Nārada declared him; and I am weaker than the other trees, of this there is no doubt.
Yet in wit no forest-tree is my equal; so, resorting to wit, I shall free myself from the danger of the wind.
If the leaf-bearing trees of the forest were to act with that same wit, they would forever be unharmed by the angry wind, of this there is no doubt.
But here those foolish ones do not know, as I know, how the wind, when greatly enraged, may toss them about.
Then, having so resolved in its mind, the silk-cotton tree, deeply agitated, of its own accord cast down its branches, its boughs, and its lesser limbs.
Having shed its branches, its leaves, and its blossoms, the forest-lord awaited the coming of the wind at dawn.
Then the angry wind, roaring and casting down great trees, came on to that place where the silk-cotton tree stood.
Beholding it stripped of its leaves, its topmost branches fallen, its blossoms scattered, the Wind spoke this word, smiling, to the silk-cotton tree, its boughs now broken, that had once stood there flush with joy:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I too, O silk-cotton tree, would have done to you in my wrath exactly this — the wholesale stripping away of your branches that you have now wrought upon yourself."
"Bereft now of blossoms and topmost boughs, your buds and foliage withered, by your own ill counsel you have here fallen under the sway of my might."
Hearing this speech of the Wind, the silk-cotton tree was then put to shame and tormented with regret, recalling the words that Nārada had once spoken to it.
Thus, O tiger among kings, the fool who, being weak, fastens enmity upon one stronger than himself comes to grief, even as the silk-cotton tree did.
Therefore let the weak man form no enmity with those of greater strength; for one who provokes such enmity will surely grieve, just as the silk-cotton tree grieved.
For the great-souled do not openly proclaim their enmity against those who wrong them; rather, O great king, little by little they reveal their power.
Let not the dull-witted man pick a quarrel with one who lives by his wits; the intellect of the wise man advances upon him as fire advances through cotton.
Nothing in a man, O king, is found to equal intellect; nor, O lord of kings, should one imagine that anything equals strength.
Therefore, O lord of kings, one should bear with the foolish, the dull, the deaf, and even with one of superior strength; that, O slayer of foes, has been seen in you.
Eleven akṣauhiṇīs, O you of great splendour, together with seven more, were not, O king, a match in strength for the great-souled Arjuna.
And they were slain and shattered by the illustrious son of Pāṇḍu, the son of Indra, slayer of Pāka's foe, as he ranged the field relying upon his might in battle.
The duties of kings and the duties for times of distress have been told you at length, O Bhārata; what more, O great king, shall I declare to you?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That which is the seat of sin, the source from which sin springs forth — this I wish to know in its very truth, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Bhīṣma said: Hear, O ruler of men, what the seat of sin is. Greed alone is the great devourer; from greed all sin proceeds.
From it come sin and unrighteousness and unsurpassed sorrow; this indeed is, through deceit, the very root whereby men become workers of evil.
From greed arises wrath; from greed desire is set in motion; from greed come delusion and guile, arrogant pride, and the destruction of others' lives.
Intolerance, the casting off of shame, the loss of prosperity, the ruin of righteousness, covetous brooding, and want of wisdom — all proceed from greed.
Injustice and want of discernment, and those deeds done amid forbidden acts, fraudulent learning and the like, and the intoxication of beauty and dominion —
distrust of all creatures, crookedness toward all creatures, malice toward all creatures, faithlessness toward all creatures, the seizing of others' wealth, and the violation of others' wives —
the urge of speech and the urge of the mind, and likewise the urge to slander, the urge of the loins and the belly, and the dread urge that drives toward death —
the mighty urge of envy, the urge to falsehood so hard to renounce, the urge of taste that none can ward off, and the urge of hearing so hard to bear —
contempt, boastfulness, jealousy, sin, the doing of what ought not to be done, and the commission of all rash and improper deeds —
In infancy, in childhood, in boyhood, and in youth alike, man does not abandon this conduct of his own — that which does not grow old even as he grows old.
This greed, O scion of Kuru, can never be filled by any gain, even as the ocean is never filled by ever-flowing rivers of deep waters; it rejoices not in acquisitions, and is sated by no enjoyments.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That greed, which is known in its true nature, O king, neither by the gods nor by the gandharvas, nor by the asuras nor by the great serpents, nor by all the hosts of beings — that greed, together with delusion, must be conquered by one who has mastered himself.
Hypocrisy, malice, slander, talebearing, and jealousy — these, O Kaurava, arise in the greedy whose souls are uncultivated.
The deeply learned bear in mind even the vastest treatises and resolve the doubts of others, yet here in this world the small-minded among them are tormented all the same.
Given over to hatred and wrath, cast out from the conduct of the cultured, knives within yet honeyed of speech, like wells hidden over with grass, these base men, snaring the world under the banner of righteousness, plunder it.
Relying on the force of specious reasonings, they devise many a path of their own, and so they tear up every righteous path, fixed as they are in greed and ignorance.
When righteousness is carried off by the wicked seized with greed, whatever established order is thereby corrupted, that corruption goes on spreading from it.
Insolence, wrath, intoxication, sloth, exultation, grief, and excessive pride — these, O Kaurava, are seen for that very reason in those whose minds are greedy. Know such men to be ill-bred and forever possessed of greed.
But of the cultured, of pure vows, whom I shall now describe to you, you should make inquiry — those in whom there is no fear concerning livelihood, nor fear concerning the next world,
in whom there is no clinging to sensual baits, nor to things pleasant or unpleasant, to whom the conduct of the cultured is dear, and in whom self-restraint is firmly established;
to whom the happiness and sorrow of others are their own, whose sole refuge is truth, who are givers and not takers, and who are likewise full of compassion;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
who are devoted to ancestors, gods, and guests, and ever steadfast in exertion, doers of good to all, firm of mind, and upholders of every duty;
who seek the welfare of all beings and bestow on all, O Bhārata — such men, having reached the far shore of the practice of righteousness, cannot be swerved from their course.
The conduct laid down of old by the good is never broken in them; they are not given to terror, nor fickle, nor cruel, but stand firm upon the path of the righteous.
They are ever to be attended upon by the good — those in whom non-injury is firmly set, who are free from desire and wrath, free from possessiveness and from egotism, of excellent vows and steadfast bounds. Wait upon such men and question them.
Their righteousness, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is not for the sake of cattle nor for fame; and the offices of the body they perform only as things that must needs be done.
In them is found no fear, no rashness of wrath, no grief; they bear no false banner of righteousness, and they keep nothing hidden.
In those in whom there is freedom from greed and delusion, who delight in truth and uprightness, in whom the mind is made free of sloth — in such men, O son of Kuntī, may you find your joy.
Those who rejoice not in gains nor are troubled by their absence, who are without possessiveness, without egotism, established in goodness, and equal-eyed toward all —
those of steadfast valour, of awakened souls, abiding in goodness, to whom gain and loss, joy and sorrow, dear friend, the pleasant and the unpleasant, death and life are all alike —
such men of mighty splendour you should, with care and watchfulness, win over by what is pleasant and agreeable; for by destiny all become endowed with their qualities, even as utterances of speech turn out good or ill.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Greed has been declared the seat of all calamities, O grandsire. Now of ignorance also, dear sire, I wish to hear the truth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: He who does sin out of ignorance, who knows not what is fitting for himself, and who hates those of virtuous conduct — such a man becomes a thing of reproach in the world.
Through ignorance a man goes to hell, and through ignorance to an evil state; through ignorance he meets with affliction, and so sinks down into calamities.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The arising of ignorance, its seat, its growth, its decline and its increase, its root, its means, its course, its time, its occasion, and its cause —
all this, O king, I wish to hear truly and just as it is; for this sorrow that is met with here springs from ignorance.
Bhīṣma said: Passion, hatred, and delusion, exultation, grief, and conceit, desire and wrath and insolence, drowsiness and sloth as well,
longing and aversion, and torment, the distress born of another's prosperity — this is declared to be ignorance, together with all the deeds of the sinful.
The activity that comes of this, and the growth and the rest about which you ask — hear that too at length, O mighty-armed lord of the people.
These two, O Bhārata, are alike in their fruit and alike in their fault; ignorance and excessive greed — know them, O king, to be in truth but one.
Ignorance, springing from greed, once grown waxes greater still; in stability it gains stability, in decline it meets with diminution, and so it follows many a course.
The root of great greed is the workings of time and of the self; whether greed be cut off or uncut, time alone is the cause thereof.
From its ignorance comes greed, and from greed comes ignorance again; thus all faults arise from greed, and therefore one should renounce greed.
Janaka and Yuvanāśva, Vṛṣādarbhi and Prasenajit, by the destruction of greed attained heaven, and so likewise did other lords of men.
Plainly, then, O best of the Kurus, renounce greed here and now by your own resolve; having renounced greed, you shall dwell in happiness in this world and after death as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For a brāhmaṇa who has striven hard in the study of the Veda and who longs for righteousness, O righteous-souled grandsire, what is said to be the highest good here?
In a world where views are manifold, that which you hold to be the highest good, both in this world and in the next — that tell me, O grandsire.
Great is this path of righteousness, O Bhārata, and many are its branches; which then, among all the duties, is held to be the most worthy of being practised?
Of righteousness, O king, which is vast and many-branched, that which in truth is its supreme root — all that, dear sire, declare to me untiringly.
Bhīṣma said: Come then, I shall tell you that by which you shall attain the highest good; and like a wise man who has drunk of the nectar of immortality, you shall be sated with knowledge.
The ordinances of righteousness are not few; they have been declared, this one and that, by the great seers, each relying upon his own understanding — yet self-restraint is the highest aim of them all.
The elders, who see things with certainty, have called self-restraint the supreme good; and for a brāhmaṇa in particular self-restraint is the eternal duty.
For one who is unrestrained no proper accomplishment of works is found; self-restraint surpasses charity, and sacrifices, and the study of the Veda.
Self-restraint increases a man's spiritual energy; self-restraint is the supreme purifier; and the man who is free from sin and endowed with such energy attains the great goal.
We have heard of no other duty in the worlds that is the equal of self-restraint; for self-restraint is the supreme thing in the world, praised by all who follow righteousness.
And after death too, O lord of men, the self-restrained man attains supreme happiness; for joined with self-restraint he wins to the great reward of righteousness.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The self-restrained man sleeps in happiness and in happiness awakes; in happiness he ranges through the worlds, and his mind is serene.
The unrestrained man meets again and again with affliction, and brings upon himself many other calamities born of his own faults.
In all the four stages of life they call self-restraint the highest vow; and I shall declare its marks, whose sum and union is self-restraint.
Forbearance, steadfastness, non-injury, evenness of mind, truth, uprightness, mastery over the senses, skill, gentleness, modesty, and freedom from fickleness;
absence of meanness, freedom from agitation, contentment, kindly speech, freedom from craving, and freedom from spite — the union of all these is self-restraint.
Reverence for elders, O Kaurava, compassion toward all beings, freedom from talebearing, courteous discourse, truthful speech, and the shunning alike of flattery and of slander —
desire and wrath and greed, insolence, stubborn pride, and boastfulness, delusion, envy, and contempt — these the self-restrained man does not indulge.
Blameless, free of desire in soul, of few wants, and untouched by spite — such a man is like the ocean, and is never to be filled.
"I am yours, and you are mine; you are theirs, and I am theirs" — such attachments, born of former bonds of kinship and union, the self-restrained man does not cherish.
All the pursuits of the world, whether of the village or of the forest, and likewise both blame and praise — he who clings to none of these is set free.
The man who is friendly, endowed with good character, devoted to worthy companions, and freed from attachments of every kind—great is his reward in the world beyond.
Of good conduct, endowed with virtue, serene of soul, knower of the self, and wise—he wins honor here in this world and attains a happy course hereafter.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever auspicious deed is practiced here by the good—that very dharma of the sage endowed with knowledge never fails him.
Having gone forth and taken up the forest, possessed of knowledge, his senses conquered, awaiting his hour and wandering thus, he becomes fit for union with Brahman.
He from whom no creature has anything to fear, and from whom creatures themselves have no fear—when he is released from the body, he has nothing whatever to dread.
He neither gathers up deeds nor heaps them together; impartial toward all beings, let him walk the path of universal friendship.
As the track of birds in the sky or of creatures that move through water cannot be seen, so too is his course—of this there is no doubt.
He who, O king, casts off his household and attains to liberation alone—for him radiant worlds are made ready for everlasting years.
Having renounced all works, having renounced austerity duly performed, having renounced the manifold branches of knowledge—having renounced, indeed, everything—
and turning back no more toward the objects of desire, serene of soul, knower of the self, and pure—he wins honor here in this world and attains to heaven.
And that station of the Grandsire, sprung from the mass of Brahman, hidden forever in the secret cave of the heart—that is reached through self-restraint.
For one whose delight is in knowledge, who is awakened, at enmity with no living being, there is no fear of return to birth here—whence then any fear in the world beyond?
In self-restraint there is but a single flaw; a second is not to be found: that people take a man endowed with forbearance to be weak.
Yet from this very flaw, O greatly wise one, springs a far greater merit: by forbearance vast worlds are easily won by the patient man.
What need has the self-restrained man of the forest, and what use is it to the unrestrained, O Bhārata? Wherever the self-restrained may dwell, that very place is forest and hermitage to him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this speech of Bhīṣma, King Yudhiṣṭhira, as though sated with the nectar of immortality, became filled with joy.
And once more he questioned Bhīṣma, best of the upholders of dharma, concerning austerity; and he, O pride of the Kurus, told him all of it.
Bhīṣma said: All this, the seers declare, is rooted in austerity; for the fool who has practiced no austerity wins not the fruit of action.
By austerity alone the Lord Prajāpati brought forth all this creation, and even so did the seers attain the Vedas through austerity.
By the gradual course of austerity, those who feed on fruit, root, and air, perfected by austerity and deeply composed, behold the three worlds.
Healing herbs, antidotes and the rest, and the three refined branches of knowledge—all succeed through austerity alone, for austerity is the root of every means.
Whatever is hard to win, hard to learn, hard to overcome, hard to endure—all of it can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is not to be surpassed.
The drinker of liquor, the taker of what is not given, the slayer of an embryo, the defiler of his teacher's bed—by austerity well performed a man is freed even from such sin.
Austerity is of many forms, proceeding through this gate and that; yet for one who lives by withdrawal, there is no austerity higher than fasting.
Non-injury, truthful speech, generosity, and the curbing of the senses—even beyond these, O great king, there is no austerity higher than fasting.
There is nothing harder to do than giving, no order of life surpassing the householder's; beyond the threefold knowledge nothing is higher, and renunciation is the supreme austerity.
Men here guard the senses for the safeguarding of wealth and grain; therefore, for both prosperity and dharma, there is no austerity higher than fasting.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seers, ancestors, gods, men, the best of beasts, and whatever other beings there are, unmoving or moving—
all of them, devoted to austerity, attain perfection through austerity; and thus by austerity the very gods won their greatness.
These cherished portions of reward are ever won through austerity; by austerity, assuredly, even godhood can be attained.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Brahmins, seers, ancestors, and gods praise truth as the foundation of dharma. I wish to hear of truth; tell me of it, O Grandsire.
What are the marks of truth, O king, and how is it attained? Having attained truth, what comes of it, and how is it spoken of?
Bhīṣma said: The confounding of the duties of the four orders is not commended; truth, most unchanging of all, holds good among all the orders, O Bhārata.
Truth is ever the dharma of the good; truth is the eternal dharma. To truth alone should one bow, for truth is the supreme goal.
Truth is dharma, austerity, and yoga; truth is the eternal Brahman; truth is declared the highest sacrifice; in truth all things rest.
I shall set forth here the observances of truth duly and in order, and the marks of truth as well, each in its turn.
How truth is attained, that too you deserve to hear; truth is of thirteen kinds throughout all the worlds, O Bhārata.
Truthfulness, impartiality, self-restraint—of this there is no doubt—freedom from envy, forbearance, modesty, endurance, absence of malice,
renunciation, meditation, nobility, steadfastness ever firm, and non-injury, O lord of kings—these are the thirteen forms of truth.
Truth is imperishable, eternal, and likewise unchanging, and at variance with no dharma; this is attained through yoga.
Impartiality toward what is dear to oneself, toward what is hateful, and toward an enemy alike—this is gained by reaching the extinction of liking and loathing, and likewise the extinction of desire and wrath.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Self-restraint is the perpetual absence of craving for another's goods, together with constancy, depth of character, fearlessness, and the stilling of anger; this is attained through knowledge.
The wise call freedom from envy giving, and self-control in matters of dharma; by truth steadfastly maintained one becomes free from envy.
Between the pleasant and the unpleasant fruits of impatience and of forbearance, the good man forbears in every case; and the truthful man attains what is good.
The modest man does deep good yet never boasts of it; with speech and mind ever at peace—and modesty is won through dharma.
To forbear for the sake of dharma and gain is called endurance, which is patience; undertaken for the holding together of the world, it is won through steadfastness.
Renunciation is the giving up of affection and likewise of the objects of sense; for one who has cast off passion and aversion such renunciation comes about, and not otherwise.
Nobility is that whereby a man strives diligently to do auspicious works for living beings, without thought of self, and to attain freedom from passion.
Steadfastness is that by which one is not thrown into agitation in pleasure or in pain; let the wise man who desires his own welfare ever cultivate it.
In every way one should be forbearing, and likewise devoted to truth; freed from elation, fear, and wrath, the learned man attains steadfastness.
Doing no harm to any creature in deed, in thought, or in word, together with kindness and giving—this is the eternal dharma of the good.
These thirteen forms, though severally bearing the single mark of truth, partake of truth here and make it grow, O Bhārata.
No end can be told of the virtues of truth, O Bhārata; therefore the brahmins, with the ancestors and the gods, praise truth.
There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood; truth is the very ground on which dharma stands—therefore one should never break truth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From truth proceed giving, and sacrifices duly furnished with their fees, the vows and the fire-oblation and the Vedas, and whatever other determinations of dharma there are.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once weighed in the balance; and truth outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Whence arise anger and desire, O bull of the Bharatas, grief and delusion, the craving to know, the wish to take another's life, and pride,
greed, envy, and jealousy, contempt, malice, and likewise pity—all this, O greatly wise one, tell me as it truly is.
Bhīṣma said: These thirteen are remembered as the most powerful enemies of living beings; all together they wait upon men here, O great king.
Themselves never heedless, they assail the heedless man; like wolves they fall upon and rend men less than men the moment they spy them out.
From these springs suffering, from these springs sin—so let the mortal ever understand, O bull of the Bharatas.
Their rising, their seat, and their destruction, O best of men—come, I shall expound to you; listen as I declare it.
From greed arises anger; it is roused by the faults of others; through forbearance it is held in check, O king, and in a man of dignity it turns away.
From resolve is born desire; indulged, it grows; it departs at the sight of its baseness, and through knowledge of reality it departs from the wise.
Men of little understanding see the scriptures here at variance with one another; thereupon the craving to know is born, which turns back through knowledge of reality.
From love springs grief, at the parting from its object for the embodied one; when he knows it to be empty of purpose, then at once it perishes.
The wish to take another's life proceeds from anger and greed and from habit; through compassion toward all beings and through detachment it turns away.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From the abandonment of goodness springs envy, and it courts what is harmful; but this, dear son, is worn away by attendance upon the good.
From high birth, from learning, and from lordship comes the pride of embodied beings; but when these very things are rightly understood, pride at once perishes.
Jealousy arises from desire and from rivalry, O Bhārata; but in mortals of another sort it perishes through wisdom.
From the wanderings of those who stand outside the world, and from hateful, ill-fitting words, contempt is born, O king; through indifference it is stilled.
Toward a wrongdoer entrenched in power, against whom one is unable to retaliate, fierce malice is born; through compassion it turns away.
Seeing the wretched again and again, thereupon pity is born; but when one knows their steadfastness in dharma, then that pity is stilled.
These thirteen, they say, are conquered through tranquility; and these same thirteen faults were all those of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. By you, with your whole soul and ever, they have been conquered, and you shall conquer them still.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I know gentleness by the constant sight of the good; the cruel I do not know, nor their deeds, O Bhārata.
As men shun thorns, a pit, and fire, so do men shun the man whose deeds are cruel.
For the cruel man is ever the lowest, both hereafter and here, O Bhārata; therefore, O Kaurava, tell me the settled judgment of dharma concerning him.
Bhīṣma said: He whose craving is hidden away yet betrayed by his deeds; who reviles and is reviled in turn, who binds others and is himself bound;
who proclaims his own gifts, who is crooked, mean, deceitful, treacherous; who shares nothing, is proud, attached, and boastful;
who suspects everyone, is harsh, foolish, and miserly; who forever flatters his own faction, who hates and confounds the orders of life—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who takes his pleasure forever in cruelty, who draws no distinction between virtue and vice, who is full of falsehood, headstrong, exceedingly greedy, and a doer of pitiless deeds—such a one is known as cruel.
He takes a man of righteous conduct, endowed with virtues, to be wicked; judging others by the measure of his own disposition, he trusts no one at all.
Wherever there is a fault in others, that secret he makes public; and though their faults be no greater than his own, he ruins them for his own advantage.
He reckons one who has done him a kindness to be merely a dupe; and even after giving wealth in time of need, he grieves over it toward his benefactor.
He who would eat the things to be chewed, the things to be swallowed, the things to be licked, and whatever other goodly food, while others look on hungry—him they know to be cruel.
But he who first gives the choicest portion to the brāhmaṇas and then eats together with his friends—he gains heaven hereafter, and even here enjoys an unending abundance.
Thus, O best of the Bhāratas, has the cruel man been described to you; he is ever to be shunned by any man who wishes to fare well.
Bhīṣma said: One whose purpose is accomplished, who is about to perform sacrifice, who has mastered the whole of the Vedānta, and who seeks alms for the sake of his teacher, his ancestors, his wife, or for the sake of his own recitation of the sacred texts—
these are seen to be worthy brāhmaṇas who beg for the sake of righteousness; to them a gift should be given even from what is not one's own surplus, in proportion to their special learning.
Apart from these, O best of the Bhāratas, the sacrificial fee that is to be given is given to others outside the altar; but uncooked food is not ordained for them.
The king should bestow all manner of precious things, each as is fitting; and the brāhmaṇas and the sacrifices alike should be furnished with food and with sacrificial fees.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whose store of food is sufficient for three years to maintain his dependents, or even more than that, is fit to drink the soma.
If the sacrifice of a sacrificer—especially of a brāhmaṇa—should be hindered in but a single one of its parts, while the king is a righteous one,
then, if there be a vaiśya rich in cattle who performs no rites and drinks no soma, the king may take from that man's household the wealth needed for the sacrifice.
He may take somewhat, if he wishes, from the dwelling and the goods of a śūdra; for in a śūdra's house there exists no possession that may not be taken.
From one who has not set up the sacred fires though he owns a hundred cattle, and from one who performs no sacrifices though he owns a thousand—from the households of both of these the king may take without hesitation.
From those who will not give, the king may ever take, O lord, after making his purpose known; for by acting thus the whole duty of a king is fulfilled.
Likewise one who, fasting through six meals, must eat at the seventh, may, by the rule of one who lays up no store for the morrow, take from the niggard who neglects his rites—from his field, from his house, or from wherever it may be had.
This should be declared to the king, whether he asks or asks not; and the king who knows the law should not, in accordance with righteousness, lay any punishment upon such a one.
If through the folly of a kṣatriya a brāhmaṇa is afflicted by hunger, the king, having learned of the man's learning and conduct, should provide him a livelihood, and should thereafter protect him as a father protects his own begotten son.
At the close of each year he should ever offer the Vaiśvānara oblation; the ancient law admits of no alternative, save only in the disputations of those who debate the law.
Yet by the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the brāhmaṇas, and the great sages, in seasons of distress, fearing death, a substitute that bears only the outward sign was sanctioned.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But he who, though capable of the primary rule, conducts himself by the secondary expedient—for that man of evil mind there is found no reward in the world to come.
No man should denounce brāhmaṇas before the king; one of little power, by such denouncing, would learn his own weakness, and one of great power his still greater strength.
Therefore the king must hold the splendor of those who expound the sacred word to be unbearable; the brāhmaṇa is called the deviser, the chastiser, and the ordainer—a very god; to him one should speak no unkind word, nor utter any bitter speech.
The kṣatriya crosses over his own calamity by the strength of his arms; the vaiśya and the śūdra by their wealth; and the twice-born by his sacred formulas and his oblations.
Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one ignorant of the sacred formulas, nor a fool, nor an uninitiated man should be the server at the Agnihotra; for those who make the offering thus fall into hell, together with him whose rite it is.
He who, at the establishing of the fires, has not given a horse as the Prājāpatya sacrificial fee is declared by those who perceive the law to be one who has not set up the fires.
Faithful and master of his senses, let him perform other meritorious acts; but with sacrifices whose fees are not fully rendered let him by no means sacrifice.
A sacrifice without its fee destroys offspring, cattle, and heaven; it cuts away the senses, the renown, the fame, and the very life of him who offers it.
Those households where the women dwell in their courses unregarded, those that keep no sacred fires, and those families in which the Veda is not studied—all these follow the law of śūdras.
A brāhmaṇa who becomes the husband of a śūdra woman, dwelling for twelve years in a village whose only water is from a well, sinks here into the condition of a śūdra in his works.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who keeps an ignoble woman in his bed, casting off and forsaking his brāhmaṇa wife, should, no longer accounting himself a brāhmaṇa, sit behind the others upon the grass; thus, O king, is he purified—and hear in this matter my words.
The sin which a brāhmaṇa commits in a single night by consorting with a woman of the black caste, he should expiate in three years, passing his time standing and seated by turns and bound by his vow, and so quell the sin of his soul.
A word spoken in jest does no harm, O king, nor one spoken to women, nor at the time of a marriage, nor for a teacher's sake, nor to save one's own life: these five untruths the wise declare to be no sins.
With faith one may receive auspicious knowledge even from a man of low birth, and gold even from filth—such is the settled doctrine.
A jewel of a woman may be taken even from a base family, and the nectar of immortality may be drunk even out of poison; for women undefiled are jewels, pure as water—so it is by the law.
For the welfare of cattle and brāhmaṇas, and when the castes are thrown into confusion, and for the saving of his own life, even a vaiśya may take up the bow.
The drinking of liquor, the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, and the defiling of a teacher's bed are deemed beyond all enumeration, and the doctrine holds them to be sins that endure to the very end of life.
The theft of gold, robbery, and the seduction of a brāhmaṇa's wife are grievous sins; so too is the open drinking of strong drink, and intercourse with women forbidden to a man.
And through union with brāhmaṇas who have fallen, and through alliance by marriage with them, O great king, a man very soon becomes such as they are.
By a year's association with a fallen man one becomes fallen—through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or marriage ties with him, but not merely through riding, sitting, or eating with him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
These sins, and others besides, are held to be of the kind that can be defined and atoned; by the prescribed rule, in due time, and free from addiction to them, a man becomes purified.
Food should not be offered crosswise to the fire, nor at a funeral rite for one not yet fallen; but in those three former cases one should make no debate.
A righteous man may, in accordance with the law, forsake even ministers or teachers; with such men, who perform no expiation, he ought to hold no compact.
A doer of wrong destroys his guilt by righteousness and austerity; and he who calls a thief a thief incurs but so much guilt, while he who calls one who is no thief a thief incurs twice the sin.
A maiden who lets herself be defiled incurs a third part of the guilt of slaying a brāhmaṇa; but he who defiles her incurs the remaining portion of the sin.
To raise a weapon against a brāhmaṇa here is a sin, and to touch him with it is heavier still; for a hundred years the sinner finds no firm standing.
And he who actually strikes him down must dwell a thousand years in hell; therefore one should never even raise a weapon against him, nor ever strike him down.
As many specks of dust as the blood from a brāhmaṇa's wound takes up, for so many years, O king, does the offender turn round and round in hell.
The slayer of an embryo is purified by falling beneath weapons in the midst of battle; or he may offer himself up in the kindled fire, and by that he is cleansed.
The drinker of liquor is freed from his sin by drinking boiling spirituous liquor; his body burned away thereby, he is purified through death in the world beyond, and the brāhmaṇa thus wins the higher worlds, which otherwise he would not win.
The evil-souled, wicked-minded man who has defiled his teacher's bed is purified through death by embracing a blazing iron image of a woman.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Or else, taking his own organ and testicles in his cupped hands, let him face toward the southwest quarter and fall straight onward, never swerving, until he dies.
Or he may lay down his life for a brāhmaṇa's sake, and by that he is purified; or by duly performing the Horse Sacrifice, or the Cow Sacrifice, or the Agniṣṭoma, he is cleansed both here and hereafter.
Likewise the slayer of a brāhmaṇa may for twelve years bear a skull, and as a chaste and silent sage go begging his food, proclaiming aloud his own deed.
Thus, joined to austerity, the slayer of a brāhmaṇa may become fit for the sacrifice. And he who, unknowingly, approaches a woman of the line of Atri who is with child incurs twice the guilt of brāhmaṇa-slaying in the ruin of that Ātreyī.
The drinker of liquor, eating sparingly, chaste, and given to forbearance, may after three years sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut as the supreme rite; and by giving a thousand cows together with a bull he attains to blessedness.
For slaying a vaiśya, two years of penance and a gift of a hundred cows with a bull; for slaying a śūdra, but a single year, and eleven cows with a bull.
Having killed a dog, a barbarian, or an ass, he should perform the same vow as for a śūdra; and likewise for a cat, a blue jay, a frog, a crow, a vulture, or a mouse.
Thus has the rule been told, O king, for the killing of creatures, reckoning them as on a level with cattle; now I shall declare the other expiations in their order.
For approaching another's bed and for theft he should perform a year's penance for each; for the wife of a Veda-learned man three years are enjoined, and for another man's wife two.
Eating only at the fourth mealtime, let him become chaste and bound by his vow, passing his time standing and seated, and bathing thrice a day from sunrise on; so too is it for one who, having failed to rinse his mouth, casts away his sacred fires.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And he who, without cause, forsakes his father or his mother becomes a fallen man, O Kaurava; such is the settled rule in matters of law.
The teaching is that to a wife who has gone astray—and especially to one kept in confinement—he should grant ample food and clothing; and the same vow that men perform for going to others' wives, that vow he should cause her to perform.
The woman who, abandoning a worthier man in her bed, resorts to a baser one—her the king should have devoured by dogs in a public place thronged with people.
