The wise king should bind the man upon a bed of heated iron, and should heap on logs beneath, so that the evildoer may be burned away thereon.
This, O great king, is the punishment for women who transgress against their husbands; for the wicked man so denounced for a year, it shall be doubled.
Two years for him, three years for one who has consorted thrice, four for him who has long kept such company; and the man of evil ways should beg his food for five years, bound by the vow of a silent sage.
The elder brother passed over in marriage, the younger who marries before him, she through whom he is so passed over, and the priest who joins their hands—all these, by the law, are accounted fallen.
All of these should perform the same vow as the slayer of a hero performs; for a month he should observe the lunar penance, or the kṛcchra, for the cleansing of his sin.
The younger brother who has married before should give over that bride to the elder who was passed over; but a younger brother who, with the elder's leave, marries next in turn gains release from the sin—both he and she and the elder alike, in accordance with the law.
As regards beasts other than the human kind—save only the cow—mere defilement entails no sin; for man is known to be the master and consumer of the animals.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Clad in a skin with the hair turned outward, and bearing a vessel of clay, let him go begging through seven houses, proclaiming aloud his own deed.
Eating only what is gained in that begging, he is purified after twelve days; or he may perform that vow for a full year, which is the rite of one cast out.
Thus among human cases the highest expiation comes to be; and for those given to liberality he may ordain a gift of any kind whatever; but for unbelievers the loss of even a single cow's life they reckon as enough.
He who has eaten the flesh, the urine, or the dung of a dog, a boar, a man, a cock, or an ass deserves the rite of purification.
A soma-drinking brāhmaṇa who has smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor should drink hot water for three days, hot milk for three days, and hot clarified butter for three days, and then for three days more live upon air alone.
Thus has the eternal rule of expiation been set forth, especially for the brāhmaṇa; yet true purification arises from the knowledge of the truth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, finding a pause in the discourse, Nakula, who was skilled in combat with the sword, spoke thus to the grandsire as he lay upon his bed of arrows.
There is a saying, grandfather, that the bow is the finest of weapons; yet my own view, O knower of dharma, is that the keen-honed sword is best of all.
When the bow has been shattered, O king, and the horses have all been spent, with the sword a warrior may still guard himself well in battle.
Bearers of the bow, and those who wield mace and spear alike — a single hero armed with the sword is able to hold them all at bay.
On this point I have both a doubt and the keenest curiosity: which weapon, O king, is the finest in every kind of combat?
And how was the sword brought into being, for whose sake, and by whom? Tell me too, great-grandfather, who was the first teacher of the sword.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When he had heard this speech of the wise son of Mādrī — a speech full of all skill, fair, and rich with subtle and striking meaning —
then, in reply to the disciple of Droṇa who had asked, he framed an answer well-formed in accent and articulation, perfect in learning and reasoning.
Bhīṣma, knower of all dharma and master of the science of arms, lying upon his bed of arrows, spoke to the great-souled Nakula.
"Hear the truth, son of Mādrī, concerning all that you ask; by you I am roused, as a mountain rich in ore is wakened to its veins."
"Of old, dear child, all this was a single ocean of water, unstirred, without sky, its floor of earth beyond all designation."
"Wrapped in darkness, untouchable, fathomless to the gaze, soundless and immeasurable — and within it the Grandsire was born."
"He, the mighty one, created wind and fire and the radiant sun; he created the sky above, and below the earth in its southwestern quarter."
"The heavens with their moon and stars, the lunar mansions and the planets, the years, the days and nights, the seasons, the moments and the instants —"
"then, having set his own body within the world, the blessed Grandsire begot sons of surpassing splendour."
"The seer Marīci, and Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, both Vasiṣṭha and Aṅgiras, and Rudra the mighty lord —"
"and Dakṣa, son of Pracetas, who begot sixty daughters; and all those brahmin-seers received them for the sake of progeny."
"From them sprang all beings: the gods and the hosts of the ancestors, the gandharvas and apsarases, and demons of many kinds —"
"birds, beasts and fishes, monkeys and great serpents, and others of varied form and strength that move through water and over the land."
"Sprung from the soil, born of sweat, born of eggs and born of the womb — thus, dear child, came forth the whole world, moving and unmoving alike."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Having wrought this creation of beings, the Grandsire of all the worlds then ordained as well the eternal dharma that the Vedas proclaim."
"Established in that dharma stood the gods together with their teachers and priests: the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Sādhyas, the Maruts and the Aśvins —"
"Bhṛgu, Atri and Aṅgiras, the Siddhas, and Kaśyapa rich in austerity, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama and Agastya, and Nārada and Parvata too."
"The seers, the Vālakhilyas, the Prabhāsas and the Sikatās, the Ghṛtācas, those born of Soma and of the wind, the Vaikhānasas and the Marīcipas —"
"the Akṛṣṭas and the Haṃsas, the seers born of the womb of fire, the forest hermits and the Pṛśnis — all abode within the rule of Brahmā."
"But the lords of the dānavas, transgressing that ordinance of the Grandsire, wrought the decay of dharma, possessed by wrath and greed."
"Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa, Virocana, Śambara and Vipracitti, Prahrāda, Namuci and Bali —"
"these and many others, daityas and dānavas with their hordes, broke through the dyke of dharma and revelled, resolved upon unrighteousness."
"'We are all of one birth: as the gods are, so are we' — taking their stand on such a claim, they contended with the gods and the seers."
"They showed neither kindness nor compassion toward living beings, O Bhārata; passing over the three milder means, they oppressed the people with the rod alone, and in their arrogance those foremost of asuras would make no compact with them."
"Then the blessed Brahmā, attended by the brahmin-seers, upon the most lovely ridge of Himavat, jewelled with lotuses and stars,"
"a hundred yojanas in breadth, heaped with gems and pearls — upon that noblest of mountains, my son, with its forests of flowering trees, Brahmā, foremost of the wise, took his stand to accomplish the welfare of the worlds."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Then, at the close of a thousand years, the Lord spread out the sacrificial canopy, ordered by the rite revealed in the scriptures and furnished just as enjoined."
"By seers skilled in sacrifice, who duly performed each rite, by the Maruts spread all about, and by the blazing fires,"
"adorned with shining golden vessels of sacrifice, and ringed about by the hosts of gods, the sacrificial enclosure shone resplendent."
"Graced too by brahmin-seers serving as members of the assembly — and there, so I have heard from the seers, a most dreadful thing took place."
"As the moon and the rising stars adorn the cloudless sky, so, it is told, a being then rose up, rending the fire of the altar."
"Of hue like the blue lotus, with sharp fangs and lean of belly, tall and terrible to behold, and of surpassing brilliance withal —"
"as that being sprang forth, the earth trembled, and the great ocean was churned into a turmoil of waves and whirlpools."
"Meteors fell as great portents, the trees shed their boughs, all the quarters grew overcast, an evil wind blew, and again and again living creatures trembled with terror."
"Then, beholding that wondrous and tumultuous thing arisen before him, the Grandsire spoke thus to the great seers, the gods and the gandharvas:"
"'This being have I conceived; it is the Sword, mighty by name and nature, fashioned for the protection of the world and the slaying of the foes of the gods.'"
"Then, casting off that form, it shone forth as a sword indeed — bright, keen-edged, and uplifted like Death, the ender of time."
"Then to the blue-throated Rudra, whose banner bears the bull, Brahmā gave that blazing sword, the warding-off of unrighteousness."
"Then the blessed Rudra, praised by the hosts of brahmin-seers, the immeasurable one, grasped the sword and took on another form."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Four-armed, though standing upon the earth he touched the vault of heaven with his head, his gaze turned upward, of mighty emblem, casting forth flames from his mouth and shifting his colour through many hues — blue, pale, and red."
"Wearing a black antelope-skin as his garment, starred with choice gold, with one great eye set in his forehead like the sun, while his two other eyes shone clear, black and tawny."
"Then the god Mahādeva, the trident-bearer, who once struck out Bhaga's eye, taking up that sword, bright as the fire of doomsday's sun,"
"and raising his three-pointed shield like a lightning-laced cloud, that one of mighty strength and prowess ranged through manifold movements, brandishing the sword in the air, eager to make an end of the dānavas."
"As he roared his war-cry and loosed a mighty laugh, the form of Rudra grew terrible to behold, O Bhārata."
"Seeing Rudra in that form and themselves bent on dreadful deeds, all the dānavas, exulting, rushed upon him together."
"They rained down stones, and blazing firebrands, and other dreadful weapons, sharp-edged and iron-tipped."
"Then that host of dānavas and its unfaltering leader, scattered by the might of Rudra's sword, reeled and swooned away."
"So wondrous and so swift was the sword-bearer's movement that all the asuras took that single one to be a thousand."
"Cleaving, piercing, crushing, slashing, rending and grinding, Rudra ranged through the throngs of daityas like fire amid dry grass."
"Broken by the rush of the sword, their arms and thighs and breasts hewn through, their heads sheared off, the great asuras fell upon the earth."
"Other dānavas, shattered and crushed by Rudra's blows, roaring at one another, fled to all the quarters."
"Some plunged into the earth, others into the mountains, some fled to the sky, and others entered the waters."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"When that great and most fearful battle had run its course, the earth, miry with blood, looked terrible to behold."
"Strewn with the huge bodies of the dānavas, drenched in gore, O mighty-armed one, it seemed like a range of hills clothed in flowering kiṃśuka trees."
"Soaked through with blood, the earth then shone like a dark woman, faint with drink, her garments soaked in red."
"Rudra, having slain the dānavas and set the world once more under the sway of dharma, swiftly cast off that terrible shape, and the Auspicious One assumed his gracious form.
"Then all the great seers and all the hosts of gods worshipped the God of gods with a hymn of victory of wondrous fashioning."
"Then the blessed Rudra, with all honour, gave the sword — still wet with the dānavas' blood, the guardian of dharma — into the keeping of Viṣṇu."
"Viṣṇu gave it to Marīci, and the blessed Marīci to the great seers, and the seers in turn gave the sword to Vāsava."
"Mahendra gave it to the guardians of the world, and the world-guardians, my son, gave the broad sword to Manu, the son of the Sun."
"And they said to him, who was the first lord of men: 'You are the ruler of mankind; with this sword, dharma's very womb, protect the people.'"
"'Those who overstep the dyke of dharma, for causes great or small, are to be kept in check by punishment apportioned according to dharma, never at random.'"
"'Reproof, restraint, fines heavy with gold, mutilation of the body, and — for no slight cause — death itself:'"
"'these, beginning with reproof, are to be reckoned the forms of the sword; and the very measures of the sword arise from the gravity of the offence.'"
"Then, having appointed his own son lord over the people, Manu, for the protection of the people, gave the sword to Kṣupa."
"From Kṣupa, Ikṣvāku received it, and from Ikṣvāku, Purūravas; from him Āyus obtained it, and then Nahuṣa upon the earth."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"From Nahuṣa, Yayāti, and from him Pūru obtained it; from him Āmūrtarayas, and after him King Bhūmiśaya."
"And Bharata, the son of Duḥṣanta, received the sword from Bhūmiśaya; and from him, O king, it passed to the dharma-knowing son of Iḍaviḍā."
"Then from the son of Iḍaviḍā, the king Dhundhumāra obtained it; from Dhundhumāra it passed to the Kāmboja, and thence Mucukunda received it."
"From Mucukunda, Marutta, and from Marutta, Raivata; from Raivata, Yuvanāśva, and from Yuvanāśva, then Raghu."
"From him, born of Ikṣvāku's line, the valiant Hariṇāśva; from Hariṇāśva, Śunaka received the sword, and from Śunaka in turn —"
"Uśīnara, the righteous-souled; from him the Bhojas together with the Yādavas; and from the Yadus, Śibi received it, and from Śibi, Pratardana."
"From Pratardana, Aṣṭaka, and from Aṣṭaka, Ruśadaśva; from Ruśadaśva, Bharadvāja, from him Droṇa, and after him Kṛpa; and then you, together with your brothers, have obtained that supreme sword."
"The Kṛttikās are the sword's lunar mansion, Agni is its presiding deity, Rohiṇī its lineage, and Rudra its supreme teacher."
"Now learn from me the eight secret names of the sword, O son of Pāṇḍu, by ever proclaiming which a man wins victory."
Sword, Slayer, Blade, Keen-edged, Hard-to-withstand, Womb-of-Fortune, Victory, and likewise Guardian-of-Dharma —
the sword, O son of Mādravatī, is foremost among weapons, fashioned by Maheśvara, and so established by decree in the ancient lore.
It was Pṛthu who brought forth the first bow, O subduer of foes; and by him, the son of Vena, this earth was protected of old.
This teaching of the seers, O son of Mādrī, you should hold as authoritative; and the sword must ever be honored by those skilled in war.
Thus this first rite has been expounded to you at full length, O bull of the Bhāratas — the origin and tradition of the sword, just as it is.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hearing in every way this supreme discipline of the sword, a man attains fame in this world and, after death, partakes of the eternal.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Bhīṣma had spoken thus and fallen silent, Yudhiṣṭhira, finding the moment, drew aside and questioned his brothers, with Vidura the fifth among them.
"The conduct of the world rests upon dharma, artha, and kāma. Of these, which is the weightiest, which the middling, and which the least?
And in which of them should the self be governed, so as to master the threefold aim? Of one accord, you ought to speak the decisive word, just as it is."
Then Vidura, who knew the true workings of worldly gain and was ready of wit, spoke first, calling to mind the treatises of dharma.
"Wide learning, austerity, renunciation, faith, the performance of sacrifice, forbearance, purity of intent, compassion, truth, and self-restraint — these are the riches of the soul.
To this alone hold fast; let not your mind waver. On this dharma and artha are rooted; this is the one sure path to good.
By dharma the seers crossed beyond; on dharma the worlds are established; by dharma the gods reached heaven; and in dharma is artha contained.
Dharma, O king, is highest in worth; artha is called the middling; and kāma the least — so the wise declare. Therefore one should be self-controlled, holding dharma foremost."
When his speech was done, Pārtha — versed in the science of statecraft and knowing the true meaning of words — spoke without weariness:
"This is the field of action, O king, and here livelihood is praised — farming, trade, the herding of cattle, and the various crafts.
It is wealth that underlies all undertakings without exception. Without wealth neither dharma nor kāma can be pursued — so says the sacred word.
For the man of wealth, victorious, is able to honor the highest dharma and to pursue desire — both beyond the reach of those who have not mastered themselves.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dharma and kāma are but the limbs of artha — so says the sacred word; for once wealth is secured, these two are brought to their fulfillment.
For the man whose fortune has risen, even those of nobler birth attend upon him without ceasing, as living creatures attend upon Brahmā.
Bearing matted locks and deerskins, self-disciplined, smeared with mud, their senses conquered, shaven, casting off the sacred thread — even such men dwell apart, each a seeker of gain.
Others, robed in ochre, bearded, well-cloaked in modesty, learned and serene, freed of all possessions —
some among them seek gain, others long for heaven, and some uphold the customs of their line — each following his own road.
Believers and unbelievers alike, bound and intent upon self-restraint — ignorance is a thing of darkness, but knowledge is light.
He who plies his servants with enjoyments and his foes with chastisement — he is the man of substance. This, O best of the wise, is my view, just as it stands. But now mark the words of these two whose speech is poised upon the throat."
Then, next in turn, the sons of Mādrī — Nakula and Sahadeva, skilled in dharma and artha — spoke their excellent word:
"Sitting, lying, moving about, or standing still, a man should pursue gain steadfastly, by means high and low alike.
For when this wealth — hard to win, most dear — is well secured, one attains all desires in this very world, plainly; of this there is no doubt.
Wealth joined to dharma, and dharma joined to wealth, are like honey blended with nectar; therefore both of these are esteemed in this world.
For the man without wealth there is no kāma; and whence comes wealth to him who lacks dharma? Therefore the world shrinks from one who is cast out from dharma and artha.
Therefore wealth should be sought by one who is self-controlled, holding dharma foremost; for among trusting creatures everything alike comes to fruition.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let a man first practice dharma, then wealth conjoined with dharma, and only afterward pursue desire; for that is the fruit reserved for one whose purpose is accomplished."
When the two sons of the Aśvins had spoken these words and fallen silent, Bhīmasena then set himself to say this:
"Without desire none longs for wealth; without desire none wishes for dharma; without desire there is no one who craves at all — therefore kāma is supreme.
It is moved by desire that the seers are intent upon their austerities, feeding on leaves, fruits, and roots, living on air, well-restrained.
Others give themselves to the recitation of the Veda, masters of private study, and to the rites of śrāddha and sacrifice, and to giving and receiving gifts.
Merchants, farmers, herdsmen, craftsmen, artisans, and those who perform rites for the gods — all are driven by desire in their labors.
Still other men, urged by desire, plunge into the sea. For desire takes manifold forms; all things are strung through with desire.
There is not, was not, nor shall ever be a being greater than one whose essence is desire. This is the very pith of it, O great king; dharma and artha both rest within it.
As butter is the best of curds, so is kāma the best of wealth and dharma. Oil is better than oil-cake, and clarified butter better than buttermilk.
Flower and fruit are better than mere wood; so is kāma the choicest of dharma and artha. As nectar's sweetness is born from the flower, so from desire is happiness born.
With women fairly adorned, lavishly decked, flushed with passion and sweet of speech, draw near and take your pleasure at will; for desire, O king, swoops down with sudden force.
Such is my thought, set forth here in this assembly. Let there be no hesitation in you, O son of Dharma. May the word agreed upon, framed by the good and of no hollow substance, prove in the end the highest of all — compassion."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Dharma, artha, and kāma should be cultivated equally. The man who serves but one of them is the lowest; him who is adept in two they call the middling; but he is highest who is devoted to all three."
Wise and kindly, anointed with sandal essence, decked in fair garlands and ornaments, Bhīma the younger, having spoken his word both in sum and in detail, then fell silent.
Then after a moment the Dharma King, having pondered well their words, spoke with a smile, in speech that was free of falsehood — he, the widely learned, the foremost of the upholders of dharma:
"Beyond doubt, you are all sure in the science of dharma and well versed in its standards. The decisive word you have spoken to me, who wished to understand — that I have heard. Yet now hear without distraction the word that I, in turn, must needs declare.
The man who clings neither to sin nor to merit, neither to wealth nor to dharma nor to desire, freed of all faults, to whom a clod and gold are alike — he is released from the whole pursuit of pleasure and pain.
All beings are bound up with birth and death, beset by age and decay, and roused again and again by these afflictions; they extol release — yet that release we do not know.
"For him who is not bound by attachment, these afflictions exist not" — so the Self-Existent Lord declared. And the wise, intent upon nirvāṇa, say the same; therefore one should make for oneself neither the dear nor the hateful.
This is the principal thing — not the willful following of desire. As I am ordained, so do I act. Ordinance appoints all beings to their tasks; know all of you that ordinance is the stronger.
By action one cannot win what is not to be won; whatever is to be, all of it comes to pass — know this. Even one bereft of the threefold aim may yet find his gain; therefore this mystery is set forth for the welfare of the world.

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
Trusted and tender toward kin, they show no faults of greed and delusion and the like toward their friends, whether in matters of wealth or of women.
To whom a clod and gold are of equal worth, guileless of mind toward friends, who walk without conceit, freely lavishing wealth and adornments, sustaining their retinue, ever devoted to their master's good —
the king who makes alliance with such excellent men sees his realm spread wide, as the moonlight of the lord of planets spreads abroad.
Steadfast in the scriptures, masters of their anger, mighty, loving battle, patient, endowed with character and virtue — such are the best of men, fit for alliance.
And of those men endowed with faults whom I have named, O sinless one, the basest, O king, is the ingrate, the slayer of friends; that man of evil conduct must be forsaken by all — such is the settled conclusion.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I wish to hear in full, O king, the matter and its connection. Tell me too of that man whom you have called a betrayer of friends and ungrateful.
Bhīṣma said: Come, I shall recount to you an ancient tale of what once came to pass in the northern region, among the barbarian peoples, O lord of men.
A brāhmaṇa from the Middle Country, dark of limb and devoid of sacred learning, spying a village thronged with people, entered it in hope of alms.
There dwelt a robber, rich in wealth, knowing well the distinctions of all the classes, devoted to brāhmaṇas, true to his word, and given to charity.
Coming to his dwelling, the brāhmaṇa then begged of him: a shelter to live in, and alms enough to last the year.
To that brāhmaṇa he gave fresh garments, fitting and fine, and also a woman in the bloom of her years, who was then bereft of her husband.
Having received all this from the robber, the twice-born one, glad at heart, then dwelt in that fine house, O king, and took his pleasure with her — this Gautama.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He even lent his aid to the robber in the affairs of his household, and so he dwelt there through the rains in that prosperous abode of the Śabaras; and Gautama applied himself with the utmost effort to piercing the mark with arrows.
And the crooked-limbed birds that came within range of his arrows, on every side, this Gautama slew without ceasing, O king, just as the robber band would do.
Bent on violence, void of pity, ever delighting in the slaughter of living things, Gautama, through his close company with the robbers, grew to be the equal of them.
As he dwelt thus at ease in the robbers' village, many months went by while he killed great numbers of birds.
Then on a certain day another twice-born one came to that country: matted of hair, clad in bark-cloth and deerskin, supreme in the study of the Veda, and pure.
Humble, restrained in his eating, devoted to the brāhmaṇas, master of the Veda to its far shore — a fellow student of Gautama, born of that same land, and his very dear friend — he came to that robbers' village where Gautama had settled.
Seeking out the house of a brāhmaṇa, shunning the food of Śūdras, he wandered in every direction through that village crowded with robber folk.
Then that best of the twice-born entered Gautama's house, and Gautama too returned, and the two were brought together once more.
He saw Gautama come to the door of the house, his hands laden with crooked-limbed birds, his bow in his grip, a doer of sinful deeds, his limbs spattered with blood —
and seeing him, like a man-eating fiend, fallen and ruined as he came to his dwelling, the twice-born one knew him, and was overcome with shame, and spoke these words:
"What is this you do in your folly? You are a brāhmaṇa, sprung of a noble line, well known in the Middle Country. How have you sunk to the ways of a robber?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Remember those foremost of brāhmaṇas, your forebears, renowned, masters of the Veda, in whose line you were born — you, such a disgrace to your family!
Come to know your own self by yourself, and calling to mind truth, good conduct, sacred learning, self-restraint, and compassion, abandon this dwelling, O twice-born one."
Thus addressed by his friend, who sought his good, he then answered, O king, having made up his mind, and as one in distress:
"I am without wealth, O best of the twice-born, nor am I a knower of the Veda. Know me, O finest of brāhmaṇas, to have come here for the sake of a livelihood.
But by the sight of you, O sage among brāhmaṇas, I count my purpose fulfilled, O twice-born one. We shall go forth together; only stay here this night, and tomorrow we depart."
Bhīṣma said: When that night had passed away and the best of the twice-born had gone, Gautama set out and made his way toward the sea, O descendant of Bharata.
Then he saw seafaring merchants halted along the road, and with that caravan he journeyed on toward the ocean.
But that caravan, O great king, in a certain mountain ravine was set upon by a rutting elephant and very nearly destroyed.
The brāhmaṇa, freed somehow from that caravan, bewildered and clinging to his life, fled away to the north.
Cut off on every side — from caravan, from the country, and from his goods — he ran on there alone through the forest, like a wild Kiṃpuruṣa.
Then, lighting upon a path that ran down toward the sea, he came at last to a lovely, vast forest with trees in flower.
It was made beautiful by groves of mango trees blossoming in every season — like a tract of Nandana itself, haunted by Yakṣas and Kiṃnaras.
It was graced with woods of śāla and tāla, of dhava and aśvattha, of cinnamon-bark and aloe, and with trees of the finest sandalwood, upon lovely, fair, and sweetly fragrant mountain slopes.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
On every side the noblest of birds sang there sweetly; and others, with the faces of men, were known as Bhāruṇḍas; and still others, the Bhūliṅga birds, were all about the sea.
Listening to those most charming and delightful songs of the birds, the brāhmaṇa Gautama went onward.
Then he beheld, in a most lovely spot — a level, varied stretch of land strewn with golden sand, bright as a region of heaven —
a great tree endowed with splendor, a banyan, perfectly rounded, adorned with shapely branches, and shaped like a parasol.
Its root was well sprinkled with water scented by the finest sandal, decked with divine flowers, glorious — like the very court of the Grandsire.
Seeing that tree — peerless, dear to the sages, holy, like the dwelling of a god, and ringed by flowering trees — Gautama was glad, and coming up to it with joy, he sat down beneath it.
As Gautama sat there, O Kaurava, a pure breeze, soft and kindly, having touched the flowers, blew gently, refreshing all the limbs of Gautama, O king.
And the brāhmaṇa, weary and touched by that hallowed wind, finding ease, fell asleep; and the sun went down to its setting.
Then, when the sun had set and the hour of twilight had come, the best of birds came home to his own abode from the world of Brahmā.
He was renowned as Nāḍījaṅgha, the beloved friend of Brahmā, a king among cranes, vast in wisdom, sprung from the very being of Kaśyapa.
Famed as Rājadharma, he was without equal upon the earth — the son of a daughter of the gods, glorious, learned, and radiant as the lord of the gods.
Covered with burnished gold, adorned upon all his limbs with ornaments bright as the sun, born of divine seed, he blazed with splendor.
Seeing that bird arrive, Gautama was filled with wonder; yet, his spirit overcome by hunger and thirst, he looked upon him with intent to kill.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Rājadharma said: Welcome to you, O brāhmaṇa! By good fortune you have come to my home. The sun has gone to its setting, and this twilight is now upon us.
You have come to my dwelling, a welcome and blameless guest; honored with rites as the ordinance prescribes, you shall go your way in the morning.
Bhīṣma said: Hearing that sweet speech, Gautama then was amazed, and filled with curiosity, O king, he gazed upon Rājadharma.
Rājadharma said: Sir, I am the son of Kaśyapa, and my mother is a daughter of Dakṣa. You are my guest, endowed with virtues — welcome to you, O bull among the twice-born!
Bhīṣma said: Having paid him honor with rites as the ordinance prescribes, he made ready for him a divine seat fashioned of śāla blossoms.
And he procured for him great fishes — such as range the regions watered by the Gaṅgā, the tracts once traversed by Bhagīratha's chariot.
A well-kindled fire, too, and fishes good and plump did the son of Kaśyapa set before Gautama, his guest.
And when the brāhmaṇa had eaten and was content at heart, the great-souled bird, to take away his weariness, fanned him with his two wings.
Then, as the brāhmaṇa sat rested, the bird asked him the question of his lineage; and he said only, "I am of the Gautama gotra," and gave no other account of himself.
For him he made ready a divine couch of leaves, perfumed with heavenly flowers and rich with fragrance; and there indeed he lay at ease.
Then, as Gautama sat upon the couch, the king of cranes, the eloquent son of Kaśyapa, asked him the reason for his coming.
Then Gautama answered him: "I am a poor man, O great-minded one. I long to go to the sea for the sake of wealth, O descendant of Bharata."
The son of Kaśyapa, well pleased, said to him: "You ought not to be troubled. Your end accomplished, O best of the twice-born, and laden with wealth, you shall return to your home.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the winning of wealth is fourfold, according to the teaching of Bṛhaspati: by inheritance, by fate, by one's own effort, and by a friend, O lord.
I have shown myself to be your friend, and my heart is friendly toward you. I shall so strive that you will come to be a man of wealth."
Then, at the hour of dawn, having asked after his rest, the bird spoke thus: "Go, gentle sir, by this path, and you shall attain your purpose.
Go three yojanas from here, and you will find a great lord of the Rākṣasas, renowned as Virūpākṣa, my friend, of mighty strength.
Go to him, O chief of the twice-born, prompted by my word; he will grant you the desires of your heart — of this there is no doubt."
Thus addressed, Gautama set forth, O king, his weariness gone, eating at his pleasure fruits that were like the nectar of immortality.
Passing along that road, O great king, amid groves of sandal and aloe and the choicest cinnamon-bark and leaf, he went swiftly on.
Then he came to a city named Meruvraja, with gateways of rock, with ramparts and bulwarks of rock, and barred with engines and bolts of rock.
And he became known to that wise lord of the Rākṣasas — sent by a friend, O king, a welcome guest to be cherished.
Then that lord of the Rākṣasas said to his own servants, O Yudhiṣṭhira: "Let Gautama be brought in swiftly from the city gate."
Then from that fair city men with white turbans came to the city gate, calling out, "Gautama! Gautama!"
Those servants of the Rākṣasa lord said to the brāhmaṇa, O great king: "Make haste, come quickly, the king wishes to see you.
The lord of the Rākṣasas, the hero known as Virūpākṣa, is eager to see you; therefore let it be done at once."
Then the brāhmaṇa hurried forward, his weariness gone in his wonder, gazing in utter amazement upon the splendor of that city.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In their company he hastened swiftly to the king's palace, that brāhmaṇa then longing for the sight of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Bhīṣma said: Then, announced to the king, he entered that noble palace and, honored by the lord of the Rākṣasas, sat down upon an excellent seat.
And being asked of his lineage and observance, his Vedic study and his life of chastity, the brāhmaṇa there said nothing beyond his gotra alone.
Of him who was bereft of the lustre of sacred learning and had ceased from Vedic study, who knew only his gotra, the king then inquired about his dwelling-place.
"Where is your dwelling, good sir? And of what gotra is your brāhmaṇa wife? Tell me the truth, you need have no fear; rest at your ease."
Gautama said: "I was born in the Middle Country; my dwelling is in an abode of the Śabaras. My wife is a Śūdra woman, once wedded before — this truth I tell you."
Bhīṣma said: Then the king pondered: "How is this matter to be handled? And how may a good deed be wrought by me?" — so he considered in his mind.
"This man is a brāhmaṇa by birth, the friend of that great-souled one, and he has been sent to my presence by that son of Kaśyapa.
I shall do what is dear to him, for he has ever leaned upon me; he is my brother, my kinsman, and a friend who has won my heart."
"On this day of the full moon of Kārttika a thousand of the finest twice-born shall dine with me; among them this man too shall eat, and to him I shall give wealth."
Then a thousand brāhmaṇas, learned and finely adorned, freshly bathed and clad in unworn linen garments, arrived together.
As those foremost of the twice-born came, O lord of peoples, Virūpākṣa received each according to his due with rites prescribed by ordinance.
By command of the lord of the rākṣasas seats of grass were laid out for them, spread with choice coverlets upon the ground by his servants, O best of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Honored by the king and seated upon them, those most excellent of the twice-born shone forth, O great king, like the lords of the constellations.
Then he gave to the brāhmaṇas vessels of fine gold, marked with diamonds, spotless and lovely, brimming with choice food drenched in honey and clarified butter.
At his court, ever on the full moon of Āṣāḍha and of Māgha, many twice-born regularly received the choicest fare they desired, always with honor.
But on the full moon of Kārttika in particular, at the close of autumn, he bestowed jewels upon the twice-born—so the sacred report has it—on that day of the full moon.
Gold and silver, gems and pearls, and diamonds of great worth, lapis lazuli, hides, and woolen rugs—
having heaped up these masses of treasure to serve as priestly gifts, O Bhārata, the far-famed Virūpākṣa then spoke to those foremost of the twice-born:
"Take these jewels, according to your wish and as much as your eagerness allows; and whatever vessels you have eaten from, O most excellent of the twice-born, take those very vessels too and depart to your own homes," O Bhārata.
When that high-souled lord of the rākṣasas had spoken these words, those bulls among brāhmaṇas took up the jewels as they pleased.
Then, all honored with those costly and beautiful jewels, the brāhmaṇas in their spotless garments became greatly content.
Then the lord of the rākṣasas, having restrained the rākṣasas who had come from every quarter, O king, again addressed those twice-born with these words:
"For this one day, O brāhmaṇas, you have nothing whatever to fear here from the rākṣasas. Rejoice, and go where you please without delay."
Then all the throngs of brāhmaṇas hastened away in every direction; and Gautama too, taking up a load of gold, set out in haste.
Bearing it with much labor, O hero, he came to a banyan tree and sat down, worn out, weary, and hungry.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, O king, Rājadharman, that finest of birds, came up to him and, fond of his friend, welcomed Gautama with greetings of "You are welcome."
By the fanning of his wing-tips the bird drove away his fatigue; and the wise one paid him honor and made ready food for him as well.
Having eaten and well rested, Gautama then reflected: "This is a very great load of fine gold that I have taken up out of greed and delusion, and my journey is far.
And there is nothing on the road to eat that might sustain my life. By what means, then, might I keep my life going?"—so he pondered.
Then, seeing nothing whatever along the road to eat, that ingrate, O tiger among men, thought this within his mind:
"This lord of cranes stands at my side, a very heap of flesh. Having killed him and taken him, I shall go on my way in all haste."
Bhīṣma said: Now a great blazing fire, with the wind for its charioteer, had been kindled there nearby by the lord of birds for his protection.
And the king of cranes too slept trustingly at his side; but that ingrate, the wicked-souled one, eager to slay him, lay awake.
Then with a blazing firebrand he struck down the trusting bird; and having slain him, filled with glee, he did not foresee the consequence.
Having plucked him bare of feathers, he cooked him then upon the fire; and taking both the bird and the gold, the brāhmaṇa went away in greater haste.
Then, when the next day had come, Virūpākṣa said to his son: "I do not see Rājadharman today, my son, that finest of birds.
He always goes at the morning twilight to pay homage to Brahmā, and never once does that bird go to his home without first seeing me.
For two nights now, at both twilights, he has not come to my dwelling; therefore my heart is not at ease. Let it be learned how that friend fares.
That basest of the twice-born, bereft of his sacred recitation and void of brahmanic luster—I fear that, having gone to him there, he may have slain him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of evil conduct and evil mind, I marked him by his gestures—idle, of cruel aspect, swarthy, base as a marauding outlaw.
That Gautama has gone there, and at that my mind is troubled. My son, go swiftly from here to Rājadharman's abode, and let it be learned whether that pure-souled one yet lives—and waste no time."
Thus addressed, he went in haste, accompanied by rākṣasas, and there at the banyan tree he beheld the skeleton of Rājadharman.
Weeping, the son of the wise lord of the rākṣasas went on, hastening with all his might to seize Gautama.
Then, not far off, the rākṣasas seized Gautama, and with him the body of Rājadharman, stripped of its wings, bones, and feet.
Taking him up, the rākṣasas went swiftly to the dwelling on Meru and showed the king the body of Rājadharman, and that ungrateful man Gautama of sinful mind.
At the sight the king wept, together with his ministers and his household priest, and a very great cry of anguish arose in his dwelling.
The whole city, with its women and children, grew sick at heart; and the king said to his son, "Let this evildoer be put to death."
"Let all these feast upon his flesh at their pleasure. Of evil conduct, evil deeds, evil soul, and evil resolve, this man is to be slain—such is my judgment, O rākṣasas; let it be carried out by you."
Thus addressed by the lord of the rākṣasas, the rākṣasas of dreadful prowess did not wish to devour him, saying, "This man is a doer of evil."
"It were well that this basest of men be given over to the outlaws this very day"—so, O great king, the night-roamers said to the lord of the rākṣasas.
And touching the ground with their heads, they said to the lord of the rākṣasa hosts: "You ought not to give us this sinner to eat."
"So be it," the lord of the rākṣasas said to those night-roamers; "let this ingrate be given over to the outlaws this very day, O rākṣasas."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When this was said, his servants, spears and maces in hand, cut that sinner into pieces and then gave him over to the outlaws.
But the outlaws too did not wish to eat that doer of evil; even flesh-eating beasts, O lord of kings, do not feed upon an ingrate.
For the slayer of a brāhmaṇa, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the breaker of vows, an expiation is ordained, O king; but for the ingrate there is no expiation.
The betrayer of a friend, the cruel man, and the ingrate—basest of men—such men are not fed upon even by carrion-beasts, by worms, or by any other creatures.
Bhīṣma said: Then the rākṣasa had a funeral pyre made ready for the lord of cranes, adorned with jewels, with many perfumes, and with garments.
Having there set the king of cranes ablaze, O king, the mighty lord of the rākṣasas performed the funeral rites in due form.
At that very moment the goddess Surabhī, lovely daughter of Dakṣa, appeared above him, abounding in milk.
From her mouth there fell foam mingled with milk, O sinless one, and it dropped upon that pyre of Rājadharman.
By this the king of cranes was restored to life, O sinless one, and the lord of cranes, springing up, came to meet Virūpākṣa.
Then the king of the gods came to Virūpākṣa's city and said this to Virūpākṣa: "By good fortune this one lives!"
And Indra made known to Virūpākṣa the ancient tale—how a curse had once been laid upon Rājadharman by Brahmā:
When once, O king, the lord of cranes failed to approach Brahmā, the Grandsire in anger spoke this to the lord of cranes:
"Since that base crane in his folly has not come to my assembly, therefore that wicked-souled one shall meet his death before long."
So it was that, by that word, this crane was slain by Gautama; and by that same word, sprinkled with the nectar, he was restored to life again.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Rājadharman, bowing before Purandara, said: "If your mind is set on showing me favor, O Purandara, then restore to life my dear, beloved friend Gautama."
Heeding his words, Vāsava, O bull among men, brought Gautama back to life and gave him then to his friend.
O king, the lord of cranes, coming upon him with his vessels and his goods, embraced his friend, filled with the highest affection.
Then Rājadharman, lord of cranes, having sent away that doer of evil deeds together with his wealth, entered his own abode.
And the crane, as was fitting, then went to the assembly of Brahmā; and Brahmā honored that high-souled one with the rites of hospitality.
And Gautama too, returning again to that dwelling of the Śabaras, begot upon his Śūdra woman sons who became doers of evil.
And a most grievous curse was then laid upon him by the hosts of the gods: "Having begotten sons after long delay in the womb of his remarried wife, this ingrate shall at last attain a great hell," O lord.
All this Nārada told me long ago, O Bhārata, recalling that very great tale; and I too, O bull among men, have recounted the whole of it to you just as it was.
Whence is there glory for an ingrate, whence a standing, whence happiness? For the ingrate is not to be trusted; for the ingrate there is no expiation.
The betrayal of a friend should never be done by any man; the betrayer of a friend attains a dreadful and endless hell.
One should ever be grateful and desirous of friends, O sinless one; from a friend springs truth, from a friend springs strength. The discerning man should honor a friend with the highest marks of respect.
The wise should wholly forsake the sinful ingrate, the shameless one, the betrayer of friends—a disgrace to his line, a doer of evil deeds, basest of men.
Thus, O best of the upholders of dharma, I have declared to you this sinner, the betrayer of friends, the ingrate. What more do you wish to hear?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing these words then spoken by the high-souled Bhīṣma, Yudhiṣṭhira became glad at heart, O Janamejaya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The auspicious duties pertaining to the dharma of kings have been declared by the Grandsire. Now, O lord, be pleased to speak of the highest dharma of those who dwell in the orders of life.
Bhīṣma said: Dharma is ordained everywhere, and leads to heaven; austerity has truth for its fruit. Of dharma, which has many gateways, no act here is fruitless.
Whatever discipline a man comes to settle upon, that very one he acknowledges and no other, O best of the Bhāratas.
And the more one comes to grasp how the fabric of the world is without substance, the more does dispassion toward it arise—of this there is no doubt.
Since the world is found to be thus full of faults, O Yudhiṣṭhira, a man of understanding should strive for the sake of the liberation of his self.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When wealth is lost, or a wife, or when a son or a father has died, by what understanding may one drive away grief? Tell me that, O Grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: When wealth is lost, or a wife, or when a son or a father has died, brooding "Ah, the sorrow of it!"—thus one should work toward the wearing away of grief.
On this point too they relate this ancient tale of how a certain brāhmaṇa spoke these words to Senajit.
Seeing the king scorched by grief for his son, overwhelmed by sorrow, his face downcast, the brāhmaṇa spoke these words.
Why are you so deluded? You yourself are a thing to be grieved for—why do you grieve? For those who mourn you, themselves to be mourned, will pass to that same destination.
You and I, O king, and all the others who attend upon you—all of us shall go there, to the very place from which we came.
Senajit said: What is your wisdom, O brāhmaṇa, what is your austerity, what your contemplation, O you whose wealth is penance? What knowledge, what scripture have you attained, that you do not despair?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The brāhmaṇa said: Behold all beings, bound up with suffering on every side. This self even is not mine—or else the whole earth is mine.
"As it is mine, so it is others'"—with this understanding I feel no anguish. Having attained this insight, I neither rejoice nor grieve.
As two logs of driftwood come together upon the great ocean, and having met, drift apart again—just so is the meeting of beings.
So it is with sons and grandsons, with kinsmen and relations: no attachment should be formed toward them, for separation from them is certain.
From the unseen he came forth, and to the unseen he has returned again. He does not know you, nor do you know him—being who, do you grieve for whom?
Suffering springs from the torment of craving; pleasure springs from the torment of suffering. From pleasure is suffering born again and again; suffering follows hard upon pleasure, and pleasure hard upon suffering.
From pleasure you have fallen into suffering; again you will come upon pleasure. None attains suffering forever, nor does any attain pleasure forever.
Friends do not suffice for happiness, nor do enemies suffice for sorrow; wisdom does not suffice to win wealth, nor does wealth suffice for happiness.
Intelligence does not secure the gaining of wealth, nor does dullness ensure poverty. The wise man alone knows the turning course of the world's affairs—not the other.
The wise and the foolish, the brave and the timid, the dull and the learned, the weak and the strong—happiness attends upon whoever is destined for it.
A milk-cow may belong to its calf, to the herdsman, to the owner, or to a thief; but the certainty is this: the cow belongs to whoever drinks her milk.
Those who are most deluded in the world, and those who have passed beyond intellect—these men prosper in happiness; it is the people in between who suffer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The steadfast take their delight in the extremes; they do not delight in the middle states. They call the attainment of an extreme a happy thing, and the region between the two extremes a misery.
But those who have attained the happiness of wisdom, who have passed beyond the dualities and are free of envy—neither gains nor losses ever trouble them.
But those who have not attained wisdom, yet have passed beyond utter folly—they rejoice beyond all measure, and likewise fall into anguish.
The deluded are ever exultant, like the hosts of gods in heaven, swollen with great conceit and bereft of understanding.
Idleness is a pleasure that ends in pain; diligence is a pain whose outcome is pleasure. Prosperity, together with fortune, dwells in the diligent man and not in the slothful.
Whether it be pleasure or pain, the hateful or the dear, let a man meet each thing as it comes, with a heart that is never overcome.
Thousands of occasions for grief and hundreds of occasions for joy assail the fool day after day, but not the wise man.
Sorrow does not touch the man who is wise, of ripened understanding, eager to learn and free of malice, self-controlled and master of his senses.
Holding fast to this understanding, with a guarded mind let the wise man go his way; for sorrow has no right to touch one who knows the rising and the setting of all things.
Whatever is the cause of grief, of terror, of pain itself, or of toil—from whatever root these spring, let a man renounce it, though it be a very limb of himself.
Whatever of his desires a man renounces, by just so much is he filled with happiness. The man who runs after his desires perishes in the wake of those desires.
Whatever pleasure of desire there is in this world, and whatever great pleasure there is in heaven—these are not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes from the extinction of craving.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The deed done in a former body, whether good or evil, attends upon the wise man, the fool, and the brave alike, according to the nature of what was done.
Even so do these things—the dear and the unwelcome, the sorrows and the joys—revolve and recur among living beings.
Therefore, taking his stand on this understanding, let the man of virtue live in happiness. Let him shun all desires and put attachments behind him; for this swelling tide within the heart is Death himself, fashioned of the mind.
When a man draws in his desires from every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, then the self, become its own light, finds peace within the self alone.
Whenever anything at all is appropriated with the thought "this is mine," that very thing then becomes, in its entirety, an occasion for torment.
When a man fears nothing, and nothing fears him, when he neither craves nor hates—then he attains to brahman.
Casting off both truth and falsehood, both sorrow and joy, both fear and fearlessness, and abandoning the dear and the hateful, you shall become a soul wholly at peace.
When the steadfast man works no evil toward any living being, in deed, in thought, or in word, then he attains to brahman.
That craving which the foolish-minded find so hard to abandon, which does not age though the body ages, that disease which ends only with life's breath—happy is he who casts it off.
On this matter, O king, are heard the verses sung by Piṅgalā, telling how she, even in her hour of distress, attained the eternal dharma.
At the appointed trysting-place the courtesan Piṅgalā was left bereft by her lover; then, fallen into distress, she fixed her mind upon a serene resolve.
Piṅgalā said: I, a madwoman, long pursued a lover who was no madman. Though my true beloved was near at hand, until now I never found him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This little house with its single pillar and nine doors I shall now bolt shut. What woman, when a lover comes to her, would still think, "this is my beloved"?
Loveless rogues in the guise of lovers, hell-shaped deceivers—they shall cheat me no more. I am awakened now; I am awake.
Even calamity becomes a blessing, by fate or by deeds done before. I am awakened, free of all longing; no longer am I one whose senses are unmastered.
He who is without hope sleeps in peace; hopelessness is the highest happiness. Having turned hope into the absence of hope, Piṅgalā sleeps in peace.
Bhīṣma said: By these and other reasoned utterances of the brāhmaṇa King Senajit was set firmly at rest, and he rejoiced in happiness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: As this time slips away, bringing destruction to all beings, what good should a man pursue? Tell me that, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, a dialogue of a son with his father. Mark it well, Yudhiṣṭhira.
To a certain brāhmaṇa, O Pārtha, who was devoted to the recitation of the Veda, there was born a son of keen mind, Medhāvin by name.
That son, skilled in the meaning of the dharma of liberation and discerning in the true nature of the world, spoke to his father, who was absorbed in the recitation of the Veda.
What should a steadfast and discerning man do, dear father, seeing that the lifespan of men slips swiftly away? Tell me this in accord with the truth, father, so that, in due order, I may practise the dharma.
The father said: Having studied the Vedas in chastity, my son, let a man desire sons for the purifying of his ancestors; then, having duly established the sacred fires and offered sacrifice, let him enter the forest and seek to become a sage.
The son said: When the world is thus stricken and beset on every side, when the unerring shafts are falling, how can you speak as though you were a man of calm wisdom?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The father said: How is the world stricken? By what is it beset? What unerring shafts are falling here? Why do you seek, as it were, to frighten me?
The son said: The world is stricken by death and beset by old age; these days and nights are the falling shafts. How is it you do not understand?
When I know this—that death never stands still—how, then, shall I wait, moving about as I am with the net cast over me?
When with every passing night the span of life grows ever shorter, who could find any joy, like a fish in shallowing water? Let the discerning man know that very day to be barren and lost.
While his desires are yet unfulfilled, death comes upon a man as he gathers his pleasures like tender shoots, his mind set elsewhere; like a she-wolf seizing a lamb, death takes him and departs.
This very day do what is good; let not this moment slip past you. For while one's tasks are still undone, death drags a man away.
Let a man do tomorrow's task today, and the afternoon's work in the morning; for death does not wait to ask whether one's work is done or undone. Who knows upon whom the army of death will descend this very day?
While still young let a man be devoted to dharma, for life is uncertain and without warning. When dharma is practised, there is renown here and, after death, happiness as well.
For a man possessed by delusion, toiling for the sake of wife and children, doing what ought and what ought not to be done, devotes himself to their nourishment.
That man, intoxicated with sons and cattle, his mind ensnared—death takes him and departs, as a great flood carries off a sleeping tiger.
While he is still heaping up the objects of his desire, unsated, all alone, death takes him and departs, as a tiger seizes its prey.
"This is done, this remains to be done, this other thing is half-finished"—the man so caught up in the pleasure of striving, fate brings under its sway.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Before he has gained the fruit of deeds already done, while he still clings to that fruit, attached to field and shop and house, death takes him and departs.
Death and old age and disease, and suffering with its many causes, cling fast to the body—why, then, do you stand as though you were safe and at ease?
From the very moment of its birth, the destroyer pursues the embodied being toward its end, and old age follows after it. By this pair are all things bound, the moving and the unmoving alike.
The delight a man takes in dwelling in the village is nothing but the very house of death; the wilderness, says the sacred tradition, is the meeting-ground of the gods.
The delight a man takes in dwelling in the village is the rope that binds him fast. The doers of good cut it through and go free; the doers of evil do not cut it.
He who does no harm to living creatures by thought, word, or body, nor by deeds that would strip another of life and livelihood—that man is not bound.
None can ever turn back the oncoming army of death, save by truth, which must never be forsaken; for in truth the immortal abides.
Therefore let a man, keeping the vow and practice of truth, devoted to the discipline of truth, taking his delight in truth, even-minded and self-controlled, conquer the destroyer by truth alone.
Both the immortal and death are established within the body. Through delusion one comes upon death; through truth one comes upon the immortal.
And so I, harmless, seeking truth, having cast out desire and anger, the same in suffering and in pleasure, secure in peace, shall leave death behind me like one who is immortal.
Delighting in the sacrifice of peace, self-controlled, a sage established in the sacrifice of brahman, performing the sacrifice of word, mind, and deed, I shall become such a one in the northward course of the sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
How could a wise man such as I fittingly worship with cruel animal sacrifices, whose fruit is perishable—or, like a flesh-eating demon, with the sacrifices of warriors?
He whose speech and mind are always rightly composed, who has austerity, renunciation, and yoga—he indeed shall attain everything.
There is no eye equal to knowledge; there is no strength equal to knowledge. There is no suffering equal to passion; there is no happiness equal to renunciation.
Born of the self by the self alone, established in the self, even though I be without offspring, I shall abide in the self alone; no offspring delivers me.
No wealth such as this belongs to a brāhmaṇa—oneness, even-mindedness, and truthfulness, steadfastness in good conduct, the laying down of the rod of violence, uprightness, and, beyond all these, withdrawal from action.
What use to you are riches, what use your kinsmen? What use to you a wife, O brāhmaṇa, you who must die? Seek out the Self that has entered the cave of the heart. Where has your grandfather gone, and where your father?
Bhīṣma said: Having heard these words of his son, the father did accordingly, O king. So should you too conduct yourself, devoted wholly to truth and dharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Those who live as their own masters, whether rich or poor — how does happiness and sorrow come upon them, and in what manner, O grandfather?
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite an ancient tale — what was sung by Śamyāka, a man set free, who had attained tranquillity.
A certain brāhmaṇa, established in renunciation, once spoke to me — a man afflicted by a poor wife, by ragged clothing, and by hunger.
Once a man is born into this world, from the very moment of birth manifold sorrows and joys come crowding upon him.
If either of these two should lead him onto its road, let him not exult on gaining happiness, nor burn with anguish on meeting sorrow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You do not pursue what is truly best for the Self, nor what you strive after; yet even desireless you forever take up the yoke and bear it.
Owning nothing, wandering free, you shall taste happiness; the man who owns nothing sleeps in peace and rises in peace as well.
Possessionlessness is happiness in this world — wholesome, blessed, free of disease, and free of enemies; hard for most to win, yet easily won by the good.
Surveying the three worlds, I see nothing to equal the man who owns nothing, who is pure and complete in every way.
I weighed possessionlessness and kingship together in the balance, and poverty outweighed kingship, richer still in virtue.
Between possessionlessness and kingship the difference is vast indeed: the wealthy man is forever in dread, like one held in the very jaws of death.
Neither fire nor the sun, neither death nor robbers can prevail against the man who is free of the ruin that wealth brings and free of all craving.
Him the dwellers in heaven ever praise — the man who roams at will, who lies down on no spread bed, his arm for a pillow, abiding in stillness.
The wealthy man, possessed by anger and greed, his wits undone, looks askance with a dry mouth, malign, his face contorted in a scowl.
Biting his lower lip in his rage, harsh in his speech — who would wish even to look upon such a man, though he offered to grant the whole earth?
Constant fellowship with Fortune deludes the man without discernment; she carries off his mind as the wind sweeps away an autumn cloud.
Then pride of beauty and pride of wealth take hold of him: "I am nobly born, I am accomplished, I am no mere mortal" — by these three causes his mind is overflowed and swept away.
His mind thus carried off, he squanders the enjoyments his fathers had heaped up, and once reduced to want, he thinks it fitting to seize the goods of others.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As he oversteps all bounds, snatching from this side and that, the kings hold him back, the greedy man, as huntsmen check a beast with their arrows.
Thus do these sorrows, and those, of many kinds, come upon a man in this life, and with them too the pains born of the body's contact with things.
For those supreme sorrows let a man apply the remedy of wisdom, having well understood the way of the world — that the lasting goes mingled with the fleeting.
Without renouncing, one wins no happiness; without renouncing, one attains not the highest; without renouncing, one sleeps not free of fear — so renounce all and be happy.
Thus was this set forth to me long ago in Hāstinapura by the brāhmaṇa Śamyāka; and therefore renunciation is held by me to be supreme.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: If a man, straining at his ventures, fails to gain wealth, and is overborne by the thirst for wealth — by what conduct might he yet find happiness?
Bhīṣma said: Even-mindedness toward all, freedom from striving, truthful speech, O Bhārata, dispassion and the absence of craving to know — the man who has these is the happy one.
These five steps, the elders say, lead to tranquillity; and this is heaven, this is dharma, and this the unsurpassed happiness of the good.
On this too they recite an ancient tale — what Maṅki sang out of his dispassion; hear it now, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Maṅki, striving after wealth, his efforts broken again and again, with the last remnant of his money bought a pair of young oxen for the yoke.
The two untrained beasts, well harnessed, set out to be broken in, and all at once they rushed straight past a camel that sat in their path.
As the two reached its shoulders, the camel, enraged, sprang up, hoisted the pair of young oxen aloft, and bolted away at great speed.
Seeing his two young oxen carried off by that furious camel, and dying as they were carried, Maṅki spoke these words then and there:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Wealth that fate has not ordained cannot be won even by the able man — even by one diligent, full of faith, pursuing his effort rightly.
Though I labored beforehand, beset by misfortunes, and toiled on still, behold by what chance my fate has overtaken me with calamity!
Heaving up my two young beasts again and again, it makes off as over rough ground, tossing them by sheer chance — as a jackal is crushed by a falling palm-fruit.
My two dear young bullocks dangle like the two pendants at a camel's neck. This is fate, pure and simple; here there is no human effort at all.
And even if what is called human effort should somewhere come to bear, when one searches it out, that too rests upon fate alone.
Therefore the man who longs for happiness must come to dispassion in this world; the dispassionate sleeps in peace, having given up hope of gaining gain.
Ah, how rightly it was spoken by Śuka, who set himself free from everything, departing from Janaka's dwelling into the great forest!
Of him who might obtain all desires and him who would utterly renounce them, the renunciation of all desires surpasses the gaining of them all.
No one has ever yet reached the end of all his cravings to know; for the dull-witted man, thirst only swells — thirst for the body and for life itself.
Turn back, O my own self, from your cravings to know; grow calm, grow weary of them. Time and again you have been thwarted, and still, my dear body, you take no disgust at it.
If I am not to be your ruin, if you would still take your delight in me, then do not yoke me to greed in vain, you craver of riches!
Heaped up and heaped up, your goods have been lost again and again. When will you let go, you fool, your longing for wealth, you craver of wealth?
Ah, what folly is mine, that I have been your plaything! Should a man ever sink into bondage as the servant of others?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Neither those of old nor those of later times have ever reached the end of desires. Forsaking all my ventures, I am awakened now — I am awake!
Surely your heart, O Desire, is hard and made of the very essence of adamant, that, beset by a hundred miseries, it is not split into a hundred shards.
I renounce you, Desire, and all that is dear to you. Seeking your happiness, I now find happiness instead within my own Self.
Desire, I know your root: it is from willful imagining that you are born. I shall imagine you no longer, and so, root and all, you shall cease to be.
The striving for wealth is no happiness; once gained, the anxiety only grows. To lose what is gained is like death, and whether it stays gained or not remains uncertain.
For him who exerts himself and gains nothing — what is more painful than that? And he who gains is not content with what he has gained, but only seeks for more.
Wealth only breeds fresh thirst, sweet as the water of the Gaṅgā; yet this is what undoes me. I am awakened now — let it go!
Whatever throng of elements has taken shelter in this body of mine — let it depart hence as it pleases, or dwell on as it finds ease.
I take no delight in you here, you that run after desire and greed; therefore, casting you all off, I take refuge in truth alone.
Beholding all beings within my body and within the mind of the Self, fixing my intellect on yoga, my being on sacred lore, and my mind on Brahman —
I shall wander free of attachment, happy and untroubled through the worlds, so that you, Desire, may never again plunge me thus into sorrows.
For driven on by you, I find no other course; for you, O Desire, are forever the wellspring of thirst, of grief, and of toil.
The loss of wealth I count the greater grief, greatest of all; for kinsmen and friends alike despise the man fallen from his riches.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In poverty the troubles are harsher, with a thousand humiliations; and what little fraction of happiness lies in wealth, that too is meted out only through sorrows.
"This man has wealth" — and at once robbers strike him down, torment him with manifold punishments, and harry him without end.
That the dull man's covetousness is misery I have understood at long last: whatever you fasten upon, O Desire, to that very thing you bind yourself.
You know not the truth of things, you are a child, hard to satisfy, a fire never to be filled. You know not what is easy to win, nor what is hard.
Hard to fill as the netherworld, you wish to yoke me to sorrows; but no longer, Desire, can you wrap me round again.
Having come, by the chance loss of my goods, to dispassion, and having reached the highest peace, I no longer give a thought to desires.
I have borne extreme afflictions here, witless and unawakened; brought low by the loss of wealth, I lay with every limb burning with fever.
I cast you off entirely, O Desire, abandoning every wandering of the mind. No more, Desire, will you make sport with me as with a beast led by a nose-rope.
I shall forgive those who do not forgive; though injured, I shall do no injury; spoken to with hatred, I shall answer kindly, paying no heed to that unkindness.
Content, my senses ever at rest within themselves, living on whatever comes to hand, I will not let you have your way, you who are the enemy of my Self.
Know that I have taken refuge in dispassion, in repose, in contentment, in peace, in truth, in self-restraint, in forbearance, and in compassion for all beings.
Therefore let desire and greed, thirst and wretchedness, all forsake me as I take my stand; for now I am established in pure being.
Having cast away desire and greed, anger and harshness, no longer fallen under the sway of greed shall I, an undisciplined man, come to grief.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Each desire that a man renounces, by just so much is he filled with happiness; but he who is forever in thrall to desire walks straight into sorrow.
Casting aside desires, a man shakes off whatever passion clings to him — the sorrow born of desire and anger, and shamelessness, and discontent as well.
Here am I, entered into Brahman as into a cool lake in the heat of summer; I grow still, I am wholly quenched, and I abide in pure happiness alone.
Whatever happiness of desire there is in the world, and whatever great happiness is divine — these are not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness that is the extinction of thirst.
Having slain Desire — the seventh enemy, counting the Self — as one slays a foremost foe, and reached the unassailable city of Brahman, I shall be happy as a king.
Taking his stand upon this insight, Maṅki came to dispassion, and forsaking all desires, attained Brahman, the great happiness.
Through the loss of his young oxen, it is said, Maṅki attained immortality; he cut away the root of desire, and thereby won the great happiness.
On this too they recite an ancient tale — what was sung by Janaka, king of the Videhas, as he attained tranquillity.
Boundless indeed is my wealth, I who possess nothing at all! Though Mithilā burn, nothing of mine is consumed in the fire.
On this very point they recite this collection of sayings of Bodhya, set forth concerning detachment. Heed it well, Yudhiṣṭhira.
King Nahuṣa questioned the seer Bodhya, the self-restrained, who through detachment had attained peace—serene and contented in wisdom.
"O greatly wise one, teach me the instruction in tranquility. Reflecting upon what insight do you wander serene and at rest?"
Bodhya said: I live by instruction, yet I instruct no one here. I will declare its mark; let it be pondered for oneself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Piṅgalā, the osprey, the serpent, the questing bee in the forest, the arrow-maker, and the maiden—these six are my teachers.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By what conduct, O knower of conduct, may one wander the earth free of sorrow? And by doing what does a man in the world attain the supreme goal?
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Prahrāda and the sage of the python's vow.
O king, a certain brāhmaṇa was wandering, sound of mind and free of ailment, when the intelligent Prahrāda, honored among the wise, questioned him.
"At ease, capable, gentle, self-restrained, without craving to know, free of malice, fair of speech, highly esteemed in the world and wise—yet you wander like a child.
You do not seek after gain, nor do you grieve at not gaining; as though ever content, O brāhmaṇa, you despise nothing at all.
While creatures are swept along by the current, you seem untroubled; amid the affairs of dharma, desire, and gain you appear immovable as an anvil.
You pursue neither dharma nor wealth, nor do you occupy yourself with desire; disregarding the objects of the senses, you wander free, like a mere witness.
What then is your wisdom, what your learning, what your way of life, O sage? Tell me quickly, O brāhmaṇa, what you here hold to be the highest good."
Thus questioned, that sagacious one, knower of the world's ways and ordinances, replied to Prahrāda in gentle speech that did not stray from its purpose.
Seeing, O Prahrāda, the arising of beings without apparent cause, and their decline, growth, and destruction, I neither rejoice nor am I distressed.
Seeing that all activities proceed by their own nature and are bound up wholly with their own nature, I am tormented by nothing.
Seeing, O Prahrāda, that unions end in separations and that accumulations end in ruin, I fix my mind upon nothing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For one who sees that beings, endowed with their qualities, are perishable, and who knows their origin and their end—what task remains to be done?
For even of the creatures born of the water I perceive the end in due succession—of great bodies and of small alike within the great ocean.
And of beings moving and unmoving, O lord of the asuras, and of those of the earth as well, I plainly behold death on every side.
And of the birds that move through the sky, O foremost of the dānavas, death arises in its due time, even for the strong.
And the lights that move across the heavens, both small and great, I observe falling in their due time.
Thus seeing all beings pursued by death, knowing it the common lot of all, I, my task fulfilled, sleep at ease.
A very great mouthful, if it comes to me by chance, I swallow; and again, eating nothing, I lie down for many days together.
Food flows to me sometimes abundant and of many kinds, sometimes meager and of few, and sometimes it does not come at all.
Sometimes I eat broken grains, and sometimes I swallow oil-cake; again I partake of fine rice and meat, and of foods of every degree.
Sometimes I lie on a couch, and again I lie on the bare ground; and sometimes a bed in a palace is mine.
I wear rags, hempen cloth, linen, and hides; and at another time I wear garments of great worth.
What lawful enjoyment falls to me by chance I do not refuse; yet neither do I cling to it, however hard it be to obtain.
Unshakable, deathless, blessed, free of grief, pure, unequalled, established in the esteem of the wise—not approved, not practiced by the foolish: this python's vow I follow in purity.
Steadfast of mind, never fallen from my own dharma, restrained in my wanderings, knower of the high and the low, freed of fear, taint, greed, and delusion: this python's vow I follow in purity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With fruit, food, fare, and drink unfixed, with place and time apportioned by the turning of fate, a delight to the heart, unpracticed by the miserly: this python's vow I follow in purity.
Having keenly observed, with insight into truth, mankind overwhelmed by craving—"this, and this"—failing to win wealth and sinking in despair: this python's vow I follow in purity.
Having seen in many ways how, for the sake of gain, the noble man here resorts wretchedly to the ignoble—taking delight in calm, self-possessed and serene: this python's vow I follow in purity.
Pleasure and pain, loss and the winning of gain, delight and aversion, death and life—seeing all of these in truth ordained by fate: this python's vow I follow in purity.
Freed of fear, passion, delusion, and pride, endowed with steadfastness, judgment, and intellect, serene—having marked those given over to the enjoyment of results: this python's vow I follow in purity.
My couch and seat unfixed by nature, possessed of restraint, observance, vow, truth, and purity, freed of the hoarding of results, and glad: this python's vow I follow in purity.
Having come to understand, and seeing how striving for gain brings on misery, abiding in the self, to rein in the thirsting, unsteady mind: this python's vow I follow in purity.
Neither heart nor mind clings, as I keep in view the rareness of what is dear and pleasant and its impermanence—observing both of these together: this python's vow I follow in purity.
Much indeed has this been told by intelligent seers, by poets seeking to spread their own renown—"this, and this," here and there, that and that—who reasoned out a thicket of their own and others' doctrines.
Having observed all this—divided, severally embraced here by men of no understanding, unsettled, its shore a boundlessness of faults—I move among men, my anger and craving subdued.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: That great-souled man who here would follow the python's vow and course, with passion subdued, freed of fear, wrath, greed, and delusion—he indeed would pass through this sojourn in happiness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Kinsmen, action, wealth, or wisdom—which here, O grandsire, is a man's true foundation? Being asked this, tell it to me.
Bhīṣma said: Wisdom is the foundation of beings; wisdom is held the highest gain. Wisdom leads to the supreme good in the world; wisdom is reckoned heaven by the good.
For by wisdom Bali attained his end even at the ruin of his sovereignty, as did Prahrāda, Namuci, and Maṅki. What is found that surpasses it?
On this too they recite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Indra and Kāśyapa. Learn it, Yudhiṣṭhira.
A certain vaiśya, my son, prosperous and arrogant, struck down with his chariot the seer Kāśyapa, an ascetic firm in his vows.
Struck down, suffering and enraged, ready to renounce his own life, he then said: "I shall die. For one without wealth here, there is no purpose in living."
As he sat thus wishing to die, uttering no sound and senseless, his mind full of wrath, Indra in the form of a jackal addressed him.
"All beings everywhere long for birth in the human womb; and within humanity, all rejoice at the state of a brāhmaṇa.
You are a human, and a brāhmaṇa, and learned in the Veda, O Kāśyapa. Having won this most rare estate, free of blemish, you wish to die?
"All gains breed conceit"—true indeed is that saying! You are one whose lot ought to content you, yet out of greed you set such store by more.
Ah, how fulfilled are they who have hands in this world! We long for those who possess hands, just as you long for wealth.
No gain whatever is greater than the gaining of hands. Lacking hands, O brāhmaṇa, we cannot even pull out the thorns from our flesh.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But those to whom the gods have given two hands with ten fingers pull worms from their bodies and scratch the spots that itch.
They contrive their protection against cold, rain, and heat, and enjoy clothing, food, comfort, a bed, and shelter from the wind.
Mastering the ox in the world they live off it and make it draw their loads, and by many devices they bring others under their sway.
Those wretched ones who are tongueless, weak of breath, and without hands endure such miseries; by good fortune, O sage, you are not so.
By good fortune you are no jackal, no worm, no mouse, no serpent, no frog, nor any other born of a wretched womb.
With even so much for your portion you ought to be content, O Kāśyapa—how much more, you who are, among all creatures, the foremost of brāhmaṇas!
These worms here are devouring me, and to pull them off I have no power, for I lack hands. Behold this plight of mine!
