Bhīṣma said: Then the son of Vivasvat, and Kāla, and Mṛtyu—these three, O lord—approaching that illustrious brāhmaṇa, spoke thus:
"Of this austerity, well performed and well conducted, the attainment of fruit is supreme for you. I am Yama, and I speak to you.
Duly have you attained the highest fruit of this recitation; the time has come for you to ascend to heaven. I am Kāla, and I have come to you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Know me to be Mṛtyu, O knower of dharma, come in person in embodied form, urged on by Kāla, O brāhmaṇa, to lead you hence this very day."
The brāhmaṇa said: Welcome to the son of the Sun, and to the great-souled Kāla, and to Mṛtyu, and to Dharma. What service shall I render you?
Bhīṣma said: Having offered them the welcome-water and water for the feet at that meeting, he, exceedingly pleased, said: "By my own power, what may I do for you?"
At that very time, O lord, having undertaken a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, Ikṣvāku came there, to the place where those sages were assembled.
That royal sage, the best of kings, honored them all and bowed before them, and inquired after the welfare of every one of them.
Then the brāhmaṇa, having offered him a seat, water for his feet, and the guest-offering, and having exchanged greetings of welfare, spoke these words.
"Welcome to you, great king. Tell me whatever you desire here. What may I do for you according to my power? Let your honor declare it to me."
The king said: "I am a king, and you are a brāhmaṇa, established in the six prescribed duties. I shall give you some wealth; tell me what you would ask of me."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Brāhmaṇas, O king, are of two kinds, and dharma too is held to be twofold—the path of engagement and the path of withdrawal. I have withdrawn from the acceptance of gifts."
"Give your gifts, O ruler of men, to those who follow the path of engagement; I do not accept them. What is your wish? What may I give you? Tell me, O best of kings—what shall I accomplish for you by my austerity?"
The king said: "I am a kṣatriya; I know not anywhere the word 'give to me.' 'Grant me battle'—such is the speech we are wont to utter, O best of the twice-born."
The brāhmaṇa said: "You are content with your own dharma, and so, O king, are we content with ours. Neither has the upper hand over the other; do then as you wish."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The king said: "You said before, 'I shall give according to my power.' I beg of you: let the fruit of this japa of yours be given to me, O twice-born one."
The brāhmaṇa said: "You boasted that your speech ever asks only for battle. Yet there is no battle between you and me—why, then, do you now ask of me at all?"
The king said: "Brāhmaṇas are said to be armed with the thunderbolt of speech, while kṣatriyas live by the strength of their arms. This, O sage, is a fierce war of words between you and me."
The brāhmaṇa said: "That same pledge of mine still stands even now. What shall I give you according to my power? Tell me, O lord of kings, and I shall give it without delay, so far as my means allow."
The king said: "That fruit which you have won by reciting your prayer through a full hundred years—give that to me, if your honor is minded to give."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Then let the highest fruit of what I have recited be taken. Receive, without hesitation, half the fruit thereof."
"Or rather, O king, take the whole fruit of my recitation as you wish, if it is everything that you desire here."
The king said: "I have no need of the whole—blessings upon you. I asked only for the prayer's fruit. May it be well with you; I shall go. But tell me, what is that fruit?"
The brāhmaṇa said: "I know not what fruit I have won; I have given what I recited. Let Dharma here, and Time, and Yama, and Death be witnesses to this."
The king said: "What use to me is the fruit of this merit, when its measure is unknown? Let the sage keep that fruit; I do not wish for what is uncertain."
The brāhmaṇa said: "I shall not take back what I have given; the fruit has been given by my word, and a word once given may not be gainsaid. The spoken word is binding, O royal sage—upon me and upon you alike."
"Never in any way did I make a calculation of gain in my recitation. O tiger among kings, how then should I know its fruit?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'Give to me,' was said by you, and 'I give,' was said by me in answer. I shall not falsify my word; guard the truth, and stand firm."
"If now you will not honor my word, spoken thus, a great unrighteousness will fall upon you, O king, wrought by your own falsehood."
"It is not fitting for you to utter a false word, O subduer of foes; and still less can I bring myself to speak falsely."
"I promised before, without reservation, 'I shall give.' Take it, then, without hesitation, if your honor stands in truth."
"For having come here, O king, you begged of me the fruit of my recitation. Take, then, what I have surrendered, and stand firm in truth."
"For the man addicted to falsehood there is neither this world nor the next; he cannot deliver his forefathers—how much less, O king, his descendants?"
"Neither sacrifice, nor Vedic study, nor giving, nor the vows can deliver a man in the world beyond, O bull among men, as truth can."
"The austerities you have already performed, and the austerity you shall yet perform through hundreds and thousands of years—none of it surpasses truth."
"Truth is the single-syllabled brahman; truth is the single-syllabled austerity; truth is the single-syllabled sacrifice; truth is the single-syllabled sacred lore."
"Truth keeps watch within the Vedas; the highest fruit is held to lie in truth. From truth come dharma and self-restraint; all things rest upon truth."
"Truth is the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; truth is the sacrifice and its ordinance; truth too is the practice of vows; and truth is the very syllable Oṃ."
"Truth is the birth of living beings, and truth is their continuance. By truth the wind blows on its course; by truth the sun gives forth its heat."
"By truth the fire burns; heaven is established upon truth. Truth is the sacrifice, the austerity, the Vedas, the chants, the sacred verses, and the goddess Sarasvatī."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Dharma and truth, so we have heard, were once set upon a balance; and while the two held the scale even, truth proved the weightier."
"Where there is dharma, there is truth; all things grow by truth. Why, then, O king, do you wish to do an act of untruth?"
"Set your heart firmly upon truth; commit no falsehood, O king. Why do you make of your inauspicious word, 'give to me,' a thing of untruth?"
"If you will not receive the fruit of the recitation given by me, O king, then, fallen from your own duties, you will wander through the worlds in misery."
"He who, having promised, will not give, and he who, having begged, will not receive—both these are men of untruth. You ought not to make yourself false."
The king said: "To fight and to protect—such, indeed, is the dharma of the kṣatriya, O twice-born one. Kṣatriyas are called givers; how, then, should I take from you?"
The brāhmaṇa said: "I did not solicit you, O king, nor did I come to your house. You it was who came here and begged of me; how, then, will you now refuse to receive?"
Dharma said: "Let there be no dispute between you two. Know me to be Dharma, come hither in person. The brāhmaṇa is endowed with the fruit of giving, and the king with the fruit of truth."
Heaven said: "Know me, O lord of kings, to be Heaven, come here in embodied form. Let there be no dispute between you two; you both are equal in the fruit you have earned."
The king said: "I have no business with heaven; go, O Heaven, as you please. If the sage wishes to give, then let him in turn accept my wealth."
The brāhmaṇa said: "If in my childhood, through ignorance, I once stretched out my hand to receive, yet now I follow the dharma marked by withdrawal, reciting the sacred text."
"Me, a brāhmaṇa long withdrawn from the world, why, O king, do you seek to tempt? I shall accomplish my purpose by my own means; I desire no fruit from you, O king. Devoted to austerity and to sacred study, I have ceased from the acceptance of gifts."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The king said: "If, O sage, the highest fruit of your recitation has been surrendered by you, then whatever fruit belongs to us two, let it here be held by us together."
"The twice-born are appointed to receive, and those born of royal lineage to give. If dharma has been truly heard by us, O sage, then let the fruit be shared by us both."
"Or else, let there be no sharing between us: take then the fruit that is mine. Accept the merit I have wrought, if you would show me your grace."
Bhīṣma said: Then two men of strange demeanor appeared, ill-clad, clutching and clinging to each other, and spoke these words.
"You owe me nothing," said the one; "I do owe you," said the other. "This is the dispute between us; let this king be our judge."
"I speak the truth in this: you owe me nothing." "It is you who speak falsely here; I do owe a debt to you."
The two of them, both sorely troubled, said this to the king: "Let the matter be examined, so that we two may not stand here in disgrace."
Virūpa said: "O tiger among men, I owe to Vikṛta here the fruit of a cow; yet though I would pay it, Vikṛta will not accept it from me, O lord of earth."
Vikṛta said: "This Virūpa owes me nothing at all, O ruler of men. He speaks falsely, and it is to you, O king, that he makes this false appearance."
The king said: "Virūpa, what is it that you owe to him? Tell me, and having heard it I shall act accordingly—such is the resolve of my mind."
Virūpa said: "Listen attentively, O king, how it is that I owe this to Vikṛta here, in its entirety, O royal sage, O bull among men."
"Long ago, O sinless one, this man, for the sake of gaining merit, gave a fine milk-cow, O royal sage, to a brāhmaṇa devoted to austerity and sacred study."
"And I, O king, came to Vikṛta and begged of him the fruit of that gift; and Vikṛta gave it to me with a wholly purified inner heart."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Thereafter I did a meritorious deed for my own purification: I bought two tawny cows, fond of their calves and abundant in milk."
"And those two, O king, I bestowed, as was prescribed and with full faith, upon one who lived by gleaning. That same merit, O lord, I would now once more render back to him."
"Having received that, I would now repay it here twofold for the one cow. O tiger among men, who in this matter is in the right, and who at fault?"
"Thus disputing, we two have come before you here, O king. Do what is right or what is wrong, but settle us in due conduct and resolve our quarrel."
"If he will not accept my gift, even as this man once gave to me, then let your honor, standing firm in this, set us upon the right path, O lord."
The king said: "Why do you not accept the debt now offered to you? Even as it has been granted to you, so receive it without delay."
Vikṛta said: "'Let it be given,' was said by him, and 'I give,' was said by me. He owes me nothing in this matter; let him go wherever he wishes."
The king said: "You do not accept it though he offers—this seems to me unjust. You, I judge, deserve punishment; of that there is surely no doubt."
Vikṛta said: "I gave it to him, O royal sage; how then should I take it back again? If herein lies my offense, decree my punishment, O lord."
Virūpa said: "If you will in no wise accept what is offered by me, then this king, the upholder of dharma, will restrain and chastise you."
Vikṛta said: "What was my own I gave here when begged of me; how should I take it back again today? Go, your honor—I grant you leave to depart."
The brāhmaṇa said: "You have heard, O king, what these two have related. Take, then, without hesitation, what I promised to you."
The king said: "A weighty matter is here laid before us two, deep as a thicket. How shall this firm resolve of the reciter be carried through?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"If, then, I do not accept what the brāhmaṇa has surrendered, how shall I not today be tainted with a grievous fault?"
Bhīṣma said: And that royal sage said to the two: "Your purpose accomplished, you may now depart. Let it not be, now that you have come to me, that the dharma of kings should prove false."
"One's own dharma must be upheld—such is the firm conclusion for kings. Yet the dharma of the brāhmaṇa weighs heavy; it has entered me, who am no longer master of myself."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Take it; I owe it to you. I have heard your request. If you will not receive it, O king, I shall surely curse you—of that there is no doubt."
The king said: "Shame upon the dharma of kings, which decides such a matter thus! For this reason I must accept it—how else might the scales be made even?"
"Behold, O sir, this hand of mine is stretched out as never before, to receive the deposit. What you owe me, O sage, let it now be given."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Whatever merit I have gained by reciting the sacred text—receive it all, if indeed any merit of mine exists."
The king said: "This water has fallen upon my palm, O best of the twice-born. Let it be shared, let it be held in common—and let your honor too accept it."
Virūpa said: Know us two to be Desire and Wrath; it was by us that you were made to act. And as for the equality of which you spoke, your worlds and his are indeed equal.
This brāhmaṇa holds nothing back from you; this testing was done for your sake. Time, Dharma, and Death, Desire and Wrath — such are you two.
All has been rubbed together upon the touchstone of mutual proof, as you have seen. Go now to the worlds you have won by your own deeds, wherever you wish.
Bhīṣma said: I have fully proclaimed to you the attainment of fruit by the reciters — the course, the abode, and the worlds, and how they are won by the reciter.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who studies the saṃhitā goes forth to Brahmā the Supreme; or else he draws near to Agni, or enters into the Sun.
If, through his fiery nature, he takes delight there, then, deluded by attachment, he assumes the qualities of those realms.
So too in Soma and in Vāyu; clothed in the body of earth and ether, still bound by attachment, he dwells there, partaking of their qualities.
But if there he becomes free of attachment, he passes beyond all uncertainty; longing for the supreme and imperishable, he enters into That alone once more.
Having passed from the immortal to the immortal, grown cool, freed of self-clinging, become Brahman, beyond all pairs of opposites — he is happy, at peace, and untouched by ill.
He attains that abode of Brahman from which there is no returning, the One named the Imperishable — that station free from sorrow, free from age, and serene.
Transcending the Puruṣa that is marked off by four signs, by six, and by sixteen, he attains the ether-like Absolute.
But if, his nature still passionate, he desires, he presides over all that; and whatever he prays for, that he attains by the mind alone.
Or else, free of craving and released from all things, he looks upon all the worlds set forth before him as in a hall, and rejoices there in happiness.
Such, great king, is the course of the reciter. All this I have declared to you. What further do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When that had been spoken, what answer did the two then make — the brāhmaṇa, or else the king? Tell me that, grandfather.
Or did the two then depart to that place of which you have spoken? What dialogue passed between them, and what did they do there?
Bhīṣma said: Having assented, saying "So be it," and having honored Dharma, O lord, and reverenced the worthy ones — Yama, Time, Death, and Heaven —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and having bowed his head to all the bulls among brāhmaṇas, those of old and the others assembled there, the brāhmaṇa spoke these words to the king:
"Endowed with this fruit, O royal sage, go to your holy reward; and with your leave I would recite once more."
"For long ago, O mighty one, the goddess granted me a boon, O lord of peoples: 'Faith shall be ever yours as you recite.'"
The king said: "If thus your perfection bears no fruit, yet you have faith to recite, then come, brāhmaṇa, along with me, and obtain the reciter's reward."
The brāhmaṇa said: "A very great effort has been made here in the presence of all. Equal in fruit, let us two go together to wherever our course leads."
Bhīṣma said: Knowing the resolve of the two, the lord of the thirty gods drew near, together with the gods and likewise with the guardians of the worlds.
The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, and the mighty luminaries, the rivers, mountains, and oceans, and the many places of pilgrimage —
the austerities, the rule of ritual conjunction, the Vedas, the chanted syllables, Sarasvatī, Nārada, and Parvata, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā and Hūhū —
the gandharva Citrasena with his retinue of attendants, the nāgas, the siddhas, and the sages; the God of gods, Prajāpati; and Viṣṇu the thousand-headed, the inconceivable deity — all came together.
In the midspace, O lord, kettledrums and trumpets sounded; divine showers of blossoms fell upon those great souls, and troops of apsarases danced everywhere on every side.
Then Heaven himself, in visible form, spoke these words to the brāhmaṇa: "You are perfected, O blessed one; and you too are perfected, O king."
Then, O king, the two together, each in due order, both performed the withdrawal of the senses from their objects.
Prāṇa and apāna, udāna, samāna, and vyāna — having fixed these breaths in the mind, they then placed the mind upon the vital breaths.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Steady in their posture there, the two slowly held the mind, with eyes upon the tip of the nose, below the brows, fixed upon the seat within.
With bodies wholly motionless, gaze unwavering, deep in concentration, masters of their seat, they fixed the very self within the crown of the head.
Then, bursting through the region of the palate of the great-souled brāhmaṇa, a vast flame of light went up to the third heaven.
Then a great cry of wonder arose in all the quarters; and that light, hymned with praise, entered then into Brahmā.
Then the Grandfather, rising to meet that radiance — the Puruṣa no larger than a span — said "Welcome," O lord of peoples.
And further he spoke another word, a sweet one: "The yogins have a fruit equal to that of the reciters — herein is no doubt."
"For yoga the fruit, in comparison with these, is direct vision; but for the reciters the rising-up to meet them is a greater distinction still."
Saying "Let him dwell in me," he then restored him to awareness once more; and the brāhmaṇa, his fever of passion gone, entered into His mouth.
The king too, by this same method, entered then into the blessed Grandfather, just as the tiger among brāhmaṇas had done.
Then the gods, having saluted the Self-Existent, spoke: "This effort was for the reciter's sake, and for that we have come."
"These two have been honored alike by you, and alike in their fruit. The fruit of the yogin and of the reciter has this day been seen to be very great. Let these two pass beyond all the worlds and go wherever they wish."
Brahmā said: "Whoever recites the Mahāsmṛti, and likewise the auspicious Anusmṛti — those two also, by this method, would attain to a shared world with me."
"And whoever is devoted to yoga — he too, of this there is no doubt, would by this method attain my worlds at the body's end. Let it be so; I shall bring it about, that each may reach his proper station for perfection."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, the god then vanished on the spot; and the gods, taking their leave of him, departed each to his own dwelling.
And all those great souls, having honored Dharma there, followed after, O king, all of them with hearts well pleased.
This is the fruit of the reciters, and their course has been proclaimed, just as I have heard it, great king. What further do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What is the fruit of the yoga of knowledge, of the Vedas, and of self-restraint? And how is the Self of beings to be known? Tell me that, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite an ancient story — the discourse between Manu the Lord of creatures and the great sage Bṛhaspati.
Bṛhaspati, the great sage, foremost of the host of divine seers, bowing as a disciple to his teacher, asked this ancient question of Prajāpati, the most excellent upon the earth:
"For what cause is the rite of sacred formulas set in motion? What fruit do the brāhmaṇas declare to lie in knowledge? And that which is not made manifest by the words of the formulas — let it be told to me truly, O blessed one."
"That great fruit which is sought by those versed in the treatises, the scriptures, and the formulas, through many sacrifices and gifts of choice cattle — what is it, and how, and where shall it come to be?"
"The earth and earth-born things, the wind and the midspace, the water-dwellers and the water, the heaven and the heaven-dwellers — that ancient source from which they sprang, let it be told to me, O blessed one."
"Since a man longs for knowledge, his striving is directed to that end. Yet I do not know the supreme and ancient One — and how then should I undertake a striving that is false?"
"Though I have studied the Ṛc and the bodies of Sāman and the Yajus chants, the meters, the course of the constellations, etymology, grammar with the ritual codes, and phonetics — still I do not know the primordial nature of beings."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let your honor declare to me all this: what fruit there is in knowledge or in action; and how the embodied one falls away from the body, and how it comes again to a body."
Manu said: Whatever is dear to a man they call his pleasure; that very same thing, when unwished-for, they call his pain. "May the wished-for be mine, and may the other not be" — for this the rule of action is set in motion. "May neither the wished-for nor the unwished-for come upon me" — for this the rule of knowledge is set in motion.
The works of ritual action in the Vedas are rooted in desire; freed from these, a man may attain the Supreme. The man who, seeking happiness, has set out upon the manifold path of action does not reach the Supreme; for the Supreme stands apart from the path of action — free of all petition, given over wholly to Brahman.
Creatures are brought forth by mind and by action; both these are good paths, frequented by the world. Seeing that action is everlasting yet also has an end, the renunciation of the mind is the cause of release — there is no other.
At the passing of night, the self enveloped in darkness is its own guide, as the eye is a guide; but knowledge, joined with the quality of discernment, sees that evil action is to be shunned.
Knowing them for what they are, men avoid serpents, the sharp points of kuśa grass, and the open well; but the deluded, through ignorance, fall into them. See how distinguished is the fruit that lies in knowledge.
The whole formula duly employed, the sacrifices as prescribed, the priestly fees, the giving of food, and the concentration of the mind — fivefold, they say, is the fruit of action.
The Vedas declare action to consist of the qualities; therefore the formulas, and the formula is the root of action; the rule is to be carried out, and its fulfillment is by the mind. But the enjoyer of the fruit is the embodied self.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sounds and forms and pleasant tastes, touches and fragrances likewise auspicious — and a man may become a lord, dwelling among them: this is the fruit that is won in the world of action.
Whatever action one does with the body, being joined to a body one enjoys it; the body is the very seat of pleasure, and the body is the seat of pain as well.
Whatever action one does by speech, by speech one fully enjoys it all; and whatever action one does by the mind, abiding in the mind one enjoys that.
As, seeking fruit, this self performs its host of deeds according to the qualities, intent upon the fruit of action, so, conjoined with those very qualities, it enjoys the good and evil fruit of action.
As a fish darts along, following the current, so one comes upon the action one did before. In the good deed the embodied one is content, but in the ill-done deed the supreme embodied one finds no content.
That from which this whole world is brought forth, which the masters of self come to know and pass beyond, that which is not made manifest by the words of the formulas — hear from me as I tell it, the Supreme:
Devoid of tastes and of the various fragrances, soundless, touchless, and without form, ungraspable, unmanifest, colorless, One — it brought forth the fivefold creation of beings.
It is neither woman, nor man, nor neuter; neither being nor non-being, nor yet both being and non-being. That which the men who know Brahman behold — know it to be the Imperishable, for it does not perish.
Manu said: From the Imperishable comes ether, from ether wind, from wind fire, and from fire water; from water the earth is brought forth, and upon the earth the world is born.
These, with their bodies, pass into water, and from water into fire, into wind, into the midspace; those not destined for the Supreme turn back from the ether, but those who are destined attain the Supreme.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Neither hot nor cold, neither soft nor sharp, neither sour, astringent, sweet, nor bitter; neither possessed of sound nor of fragrance, nor of form — such is That, the supreme essence.
The body knows touch, the tongue taste, the nose fragrances, the ears sounds, the eye forms; but that which is supreme beyond these — the men who do not know the inner Self cannot grasp it.
Having drawn back the tongue from tastes, the nose from fragrance, the ears from sound, the body from touch, and the eye from the quality of form — beyond that he beholds his own essence.
That from which one takes hold and acts, and that in which one begins one's activity; that in which, that which, that by which, and the one who is the doer — that they call the cause and the means.
That which is sovereign, effecting and all-pervading, which is hymned in the world as in the formulas; He who is the cause of all and works the highest end — that is the Cause; whatever is other than it is effect.
As a man, by his good deeds, attains the good and the ill without conflict, so within bodies good and ill this knowledge is bound fast, born of one's own deeds.
As a lamp kindled before one, blazing, gives light to another, so here the five senses, lamp-trees set ablaze by knowledge, are yet dependent on another.
For just as the many ministers of a king, each in his appointed office, pronounce their judgment separately, so within bodies are the five senses; but the supreme one, the single seat of knowledge, stands above them all.
As the flames of fire, the gusts of the wind, the rays of the sun, and the waters in the rivers come forth and pass away, ever streaming on, even so do the bodies of embodied beings come and go.
And as a man who takes up an axe sees neither smoke nor fire within the wood, so when they cleave open the body—its trunk, hands, and feet—they do not perceive that other thing which dwells within.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But as one who churns those very logs together would, by the proper means, see both smoke and flame, so the man of keen and disciplined intellect, gathering the senses into equipoise, perceives the Supreme, his own true nature.
As in dream a man, while his own limbs lie fallen upon the earth, beholds another self of his own, so the man of clear mind and disciplined intellect, endowed with hearing and the other faculties, passes from one subtle body to another subtle body.
That supreme embodied one is not touched by birth, growth, decay, or dissolution; yet by this subtle body, unseen, he passes to another subtle body through the working of rebirth's bond.
With the eye he does not behold the form of the Self, nor does he come into any contact with it; nor does he accomplish his ends through the senses. They do not perceive him, yet he perceives them.
As in a burning lamp the flame takes on some form born of its own heat, yet bears within no inner quality of visible form, even so is the form of this Self beheld.
As a man, casting off his body, enters another, unseen body, so the embodied one, surrendering the body into the great elements, takes on a form that rests upon them.
Space, wind, fire, water, and earth—the embodied one enters into them on every side; and abiding in their several seats, engaged in their works, the five faculties beginning with hearing take hold of the five sense-qualities.
Hearing arises from space, smell from earth; form is made of light, and so too is digestion; sweat and taste are declared to rest upon water; and the quality born of touch is of the nature of wind.
The five sense-objects dwell within the great elements, and the senses within those objects; all of these follow the mind, the mind follows the intellect, and the intellect follows its own essential nature.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever deed, good or evil, has been done by him, that very deed he takes back upon himself in his own body; and high and low alike follow after the mind, as a creature of the water follows the favoring current.
As a moving thing, though minute, enters the path of sight and appears like some great form, and the eye discerns its own proper shape, so the Supreme passes into the path of the intellect.
Manu said: That which long remembers the sense-qualities once gathered and presented by the faculties before, even after those faculties have afterward been destroyed—that is the Supreme, whose nature is intellect.
Since one does not apprehend all the sense-objects together at once, in their entirety and in equal time, but the knowing one moves among them according to his capacity, therefore the supreme embodied one is one alone.
He passes through rajas, tamas, and sattva as the third—the varied qualities pertaining to knowledge; and the embodied one enters into the senses as the wind enters the fire lodged in fuel.
With the eye he does not behold the form of the Self, nor does the inner sense of the senses perceive touch, nor is the mark of hearing found within the act of hearing; whatever is so apprehended perishes.
The faculties beginning with hearing do not perceive their own selves by themselves; but the all-knowing, all-seeing Knower of the Field perceives them all.
As the far side of the Himālaya, or the hidden face of the moon, has never been seen before by men—yet it does not therefore cease to exist—
so too the Self of beings, dwelling within all beings, subtle and possessed of the nature of knowledge, though never before seen by the eyes, does not therefore cease to exist.
As the world, though it sees the mark upon the moon, does not comprehend it, so the question whether this Self is or is not cannot be settled—yet it is not for that reason no refuge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The wise, intent upon it, though it is formless, behold with the understanding as endowed with form, at rising and at setting, the course of the sun.
Even so, by the lamp of the intellect, the truly discerning seek to bring near that which stands afar—the object of knowledge, fully gathered up within knowledge itself.
For surely no end is attained without the proper means, as men net the fish, those creatures of the water, with snares of corded mesh.
As deer are caught by deer, and birds by birds, and elephants by elephants, so the object of knowledge is grasped by knowledge.
It is shown by the saying that only a serpent can see the feet of a serpent; even so, by knowledge one perceives the knowable that abides within embodied forms.
As the senses cannot, even with the senses, contrive to know one another, so here the higher intellect does not behold the Supreme by intellect alone.
As the moon, on the night of its dark phase, is not seen because it shows no mark, and yet suffers no destruction—so know the embodied Self to be.
On the night of the dark moon, its sheath worn away, the moon does not shine forth; even so the embodied one, when parted from his bodily form, is not apprehended.
As the moon, gaining a fresh sheath, shines forth once more, so the embodied one, gaining another subtle body, shines forth again.
Birth, waxing, and waning of it are apprehended by direct perception; but that is the manifest appearance of the moon, not of the embodied Self.
As, through its arising, waxing, and waning, it is grasped as 'the moon,' so the moon, even on the dark night, remains the same possessor of form.
The darkness, whether creeping upon or releasing the moon, is not seen as it withdraws or as it approaches; behold the embodied Self in just this way.
As that darkness is apprehended when joined to moon or sun, so the Self, when joined to a body, is apprehended as 'the embodied one.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As Rāhu, once released from moon and sun, is no longer apprehended, so the embodied one, once freed from the body, is no longer apprehended.
As the moon, gone into its dark phase, is still joined with the constellations, so the Self, though freed from one body, is joined with the fruits of its deeds.
Manu said: As in sleep this manifest body lies still while the conscious knower roves abroad in dream, so, after death, knowledge joined with the senses passes through being and non-being.
As in clear water one beholds a reflection with the eye, so he whose senses are serene perceives the knowable through knowledge.
But as that same man, when the water is troubled, does not behold the reflection, so when the senses are agitated, one does not perceive the knowable within knowledge.
Want of understanding is wrought by ignorance; by want of understanding the mind is defiled; and when the mind is defiled, the five mental faculties are wholly corrupted.
He who is sated with ignorance, plunged deep in the objects of sense, does not behold the Self; but the man of purified soul turns back from those objects without having beheld it.
No cutting-off of thirst comes to a man here so long as his defilement remains; but when his sin has come to its end, then his thirst likewise ceases.
Through clinging to the objects of sense, and through failing to take refuge in the Eternal, and through hankering with the mind after something other, a man does not attain the Supreme.
Knowledge arises in men through the wearing-away of sinful deeds; and then, as in the surface of a mirror, one beholds the Self within the self.
With the senses let loose a man is wretched; with those same senses restrained he is happy. Therefore let him, by the self, draw the self back from the forms presented to the senses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than that is the intellect; higher than the intellect is knowledge; and higher than knowledge is the Supreme.
From the Unmanifest knowledge streams forth; from it the intellect, and from that the mind; and the mind, joined with hearing and the other faculties, rightly perceives sound and the rest.
He who forsakes sound and the rest, and likewise all manifest things, and lets go the whole host of forms—he, once freed of them, partakes of the immortal.
As the sun, rising, sends forth its orb of rays, and that same sun, going to its setting, withdraws them back into itself,
so the inner Self, entering the body with the rays of the senses, and laying hold of the five sense-qualities, withdrawing them, goes to its own setting.
Led again and again along the path laid out by his deeds, this self-possessed one attains the fruit of his works—dharma grown abundant.
For the embodied one who abstains, the objects of sense turn away, save for the relish of them; but even that relish departs once he has beheld the Supreme.
When the intellect, stripped of the qualities born of action, abides within the mind, then Brahman is attained, dissolved into that very state.
Touching nothing, hearing nothing, tasting nothing, seeing nothing, smelling nothing, and without deliberation—thus the being enters the Supreme.
Forms are merged into the mind; the mind has passed beyond into the understanding; the understanding has passed beyond into knowledge; and knowledge has gone over into the Supreme.
Through the senses the mind achieves its work, yet the mind does not know the intellect; the intellect does not know the Unmanifest; but the Subtle One perceives them all.
Manu said: Know that knowledge is brought to completion by the knowable; the mind has knowledge for its quality; and from the mind, joined with the instrument of wisdom, the intellect proceeds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the intellect, endowed with the qualities of action, abides within the mind, then Brahman is discerned through the deep absorption of meditative yoga.
This intellect, possessed of the qualities, moves ever among the qualities, as water streaming down in descent from a mountain peak.
When the meditation that arose first within the mind attains the quality-less state, then Brahman is discerned, as gold is tested upon the touchstone.
But the mind, which has carried off the intellect and which is fixed upon the objects of sense, intent upon the qualities, cannot directly behold that which is without qualities.
Closing fast all these gates, and standing firm within the mind, having made the mind one-pointed, one attains that Supreme.
As the great elements turn back when their qualities are spent, so the intellect, taking up the senses, abides within the mind.
When that intellect, moving within, abides in the mind, endowed with the quality of resolve, then the mind is fully formed.
When the mind, endowed with the qualities through the qualified faculties and possessing the quality of meditation, then forsakes all qualities, it attains the quality-less.
For the discernment of the Unmanifest there is here no comparable illustration; where there is no setting down of a foot, who could reach that domain?
By austerity and by inference, by good qualities, by birth, and by sacred learning, let a man, with wholly purified inner self, seek to draw near that supreme Brahman.
He who lacks the qualities follows that path only from without; for through the absence of qualities and through nature itself, the knowable is beyond reasoning, measured only against itself.
Through quality-lessness one attains Brahman; through having qualities one is turned back; for the intellect spreads out among the qualities as fire spreads through fuel.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As the five senses are released from their own functions, so that supreme Brahman stands released, beyond Nature.
Thus from Nature all embodied beings arise; and when they turn back at the cessation, they no longer come into creation.
The Spirit, Nature, the intellect, the particulars and the senses, the ego-sense and self-conceit—all this, come into being, bears the name of the elemental world.
The first activity of the One proceeds forth from Primal Matter; the second governs the manifestation of pairs out of the undifferentiated.
From dharma the good is drawn forth, and likewise the ill from unrighteousness; the man of passion goes back to Nature, while the dispassionate becomes possessed of knowledge.
Manu said: When your five faculties, together with the mind, are released by the five, then you shall behold that Brahman, like a thread strung through a gem.
And as that same thread runs again through gold, through pearls, through corals, through what is made of clay, and through what is made of silver,
so it runs through cattle and through men, through elephants, deer, and the rest, through worms and moths—the Self bound fast by its own deeds.
By whatever body this one performs whatever deed, by that very body he reaps that very fruit.
For as the earth, single in its savor, conforms itself to the nature of each plant, so the intellect follows after one's deeds, attentive to the inner Self.
Desire arises preceded by knowledge; intention is preceded by desire; action is preceded by intention; and the fruit, in turn, has action for its root.
Let one know that fruit has the nature of action, and that action in turn has the nature of the knowable; let one know that the knowable has the nature of knowledge, and that knowledge has the nature of both being and non-being.
When knowledges, fruits, knowables, and actions have all come to their end, that fruit which remains is the divine knowledge, firmly grounded in the knowable.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That supreme Great Being the disciplined yogins behold; but the unwise do not see it, dwelling within themselves yet bound by an understanding ruled by the qualities.
Greater than the form of earth is the form of the waters here; greater than the waters is fire, and greater than fire is the wind.
Greater than the wind is ether, and beyond that is mind; greater than mind is the intellect, and greater than the intellect, it is taught, is Time.
Greater than Time is the Lord Viṣṇu, to whom belongs all this world; of that God no beginning, no middle, and no end can be known.
Because he is without beginning, without middle, and without end, he is imperishable; he transcends all sorrows, for sorrow is said to be that which has an end.
That is declared the supreme Brahman, that is remembered as the supreme abode; reaching it, men are freed from the domain of Time and find their refuge in liberation.
By these qualities things are made manifest; beyond that is the qualityless, which transcends them. The dharma marked by withdrawal likewise leads to the infinite.
The Ṛc verses, the Yajus formulas, and the Sāman chants, taking refuge in bodies, issue forth upon the tips of tongues—achieved by effort, and perishable.
But Brahman is not held to be of such a kind, arising from dependence on a body; that Brahman is not to be won by effort, has no beginning nor middle, nor is it subject to an end.
A beginning of the Ṛc verses, of the Sāmans, and of the Yajus is spoken of; and an end is seen for whatever has a beginning. But no beginning of Brahman is taught.
Because it is without beginning and without end, it is infinite and imperishable; and because it is imperishable it is free of all pairs of opposites, and through the absence of opposites it is the Supreme beyond.
Because it cannot be seen, because there is no means to it, and because of their deliberate intent upon action, mortals do not behold that by which they might reach the Supreme.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Through contact with sense-objects, and through gazing upon the eternal while yet longing in his mind for something else, a man does not attain the Supreme.
Whatever men perceive here in the realm of the qualities, that other people desire; they do not long for the Supreme at all, for, being seekers of the qualities, they shun its qualityless nature.
But how shall one who is bound by the lower qualities come to know these very qualities? Only by inference are they to be approached, together with the qualities as their constituent parts.
By a subtle mind we know it, but by speech we are unable to utter it; for mind is grasped only by mind, and sight only by sight.
Having purified the intellect by knowledge, and the mind by the intellect, and the host of the senses by the mind, one attains the Infinite.
He who is bereft of intellect, ill-endowed in mind, and devoid of all desire enters into the state of the qualities; lured astray, such men abandon the Supreme here, as the wind abandons the fire that lies within the fuel.
In the taking up of the qualities and in the parting from them, the mind is ever drawn by the higher and lower workings of the intellect; set in motion by this very ordinance, in taking up the qualities it comes to embodiment in Brahman.
The Person whose self is unmanifest and whose actions are unmanifest passes into the unmanifest at the time of the end; clad in the form of his deeds, he abides among these very senses, whether they wax in strength or wither away.
Joined with all the senses, this body, once attained, comes to rest upon the five elements; through its incapacity it does not pass on here by action alone, deprived of that supreme imperishable One.
A man does not see the end of this earth, yet know that an end of it there shall be; the lures of the world carry the man who is enticed astray, as the wind drives a raft adrift upon the sea.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As the maker of day, though qualityless, takes on a quality, and may then become an orb stripped of its rays, so too that sage here, having become free of all distinctions, enters the qualityless and imperishable Brahman.
The state of no-return, the supreme goal of those rich in good deeds, the self-existent, the imperishable source and resting-place of all that arises—the eternal, deathless, imperishable abode: meditating upon it, one attains peace and immortality.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O grandsire of vast wisdom, of the lotus-eyed, unfallen Acyuta—Viṣṇu, the maker who is himself unmade, the origin and dissolution of all beings—
of Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Govinda the unconquered—O best of the Bhāratas, I wish to hear of Keśava in his very truth.
Bhīṣma said: This matter I have heard as it was spoken by Rāma, son of Jamadagni, and by the divine sage Nārada, and by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana,
and by Asita Devala, my child, and by Vālmīki of great austerities, and by Mārkaṇḍeya, who tells of Govinda a great and wondrous tale.
Keśava, O best of the Bhāratas, is the Lord, the sovereign, the master; that he is the Person who is all, the all-pervading One, is heard told in many ways.
Yet hear now, O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, those greatnesses of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow which the brāhmaṇas in the world know of.
And those things which the men learned in the ancient lore declare, O lord of men—all of them concerning Govinda I shall recount in full.
The great-souled Supreme Person, the very Self of beings, fashioned the great elements—wind, fire, and likewise water, ether, and earth.
And beholding the earth, that lord and sovereign of all beings, the great-souled Supreme Person, made his couch upon the waters.
Composed wholly of radiance, reclining there upon that fair couch, he meditated upon Saṃkarṣaṇa, the firstborn of all beings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
We have heard that the Self of beings holds within his mind the refuge of all creatures, and bears up both that which has been and that which is to come.
Then, O mighty-armed one, when that great-souled being had manifested, a divine lotus, rivaling the sun, was born from his navel.
There upon that lotus, my child, the divine Lord, illumining the quarters, came into being as Brahmā, the grandsire of all beings.
And when that great-souled one too had been made manifest, O mighty-armed one, there was born of the darkness, before all others, a great demon named Madhu.
That fierce one, fierce in his deeds, set upon a fierce intent, the Supreme Person slew, thereby rendering a service to Brahmā.
Because of his slaying, my child, all the gods, demons, and men called him Madhusūdana, the bull among all the Sātvatas.
And Brahmā created sons born of his mind, seven with Dakṣa: Marīci, Atri and Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Marīci, my child, brought forth Kaśyapa as his eldest son, a mind-born and radiant one, most excellent in sacred knowledge.
From his thumb Brahmā created one even prior to Marīci; he became, O best of the Bhāratas, the lord of creatures named Dakṣa.
To that lord of creatures, O Bhārata, there were first born thirteen daughters; the eldest among them was Diti.
Kaśyapa, son of Marīci, knower of all the particulars of dharma, of holy renown and great fame, my child, became the husband of them all.
Having begotten ten more daughters younger than those, the illustrious Dakṣa, lord of creatures and knower of dharma, gave them to Dharma.
The sons of Dharma are the Vasus and the Rudras of measureless splendor, and the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas and the Marutvats, O Bhārata.
And there were other daughters, twenty-seven younger than these; the illustrious Soma became the husband of them all.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And other daughters brought forth the gandharvas, horses, birds, cattle, the kiṃpuruṣas, fishes, and the sprouting plants and forest trees.
Aditi gave birth to the Ādityas, foremost of gods and of great strength; among them Viṣṇu became the Dwarf, and the Lord Govinda came to be.
By that very striding of his the fortune of the gods increased, and the dānavas were overthrown, along with the demonic offspring of Diti.
Danu brought forth the dānavas led by Vipracitti, while Diti gave birth to all the asuras, beings of great might.
Day and night, and Time, and the seasons in their turn, the forenoon and the afternoon—all of it Madhusūdana fashioned.
By his intelligence he created the waters and the clouds, and likewise things moving and unmoving; he created the whole earth, joined together, by his abundant splendor.
Then the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Lord, brought forth once more from his mouth a hundred excellent brāhmaṇas.
From his arms a hundred kṣatriyas, from his thighs a hundred vaiśyas, and from his feet a hundred śūdras did Keśava bring forth, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Having thus brought forth the four classes, that Lord of great fame made the Ordainer the overseer of all beings.
For just so long as men had the will to sustain their bodies, just so long did they live; and there was no fear wrought by Yama.
Nor was there among them the custom of sexual union, O bull of the Bhāratas; their offspring came into being by mere will.
There in the age of the Tretā, offspring were born by will; nor was there among them either the custom of sexual union, O ruler of men.
In the Dvāpara the custom of sexual union arose among creatures, O king; and so in the Kali age, O monarch, people came under the sway of the pairs of opposites.
Thus is proclaimed this lord of beings, his own overseer, my child; but now, O son of Kuntī, I shall recount those peoples who are without an overseer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Born in the southern region are all the Talavaras and Āndhrakas, the Utsas, the Pulindas, the Śabaras, and the Cūcupas, together with the Maṇḍapas.
Now I shall recount also those born in the northern region: the Yaunas, the Kāmbojas, the Gāndhāras, and the Kirātas, together with the Barbaras.
These evildoers, my child, roam this earth, sharing the nature of dogs, crows, vultures, and the strong birds of prey, O ruler of men.
These did not roam this earth in the Kṛta age, my child; only from the Tretā onward do those peoples exist, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then in that most terrible twilight time at the ending of an age, kings clashed together, falling each upon the other.
Thus, O best of the Kurus, did the divine sage Nārada, beholder of all worlds, declare this manifestation of the great-souled one.
And Nārada too, O ruler of men, deemed the eternity of Kṛṣṇa supreme, rightly so, O mighty-armed bull of the Bhāratas.
Thus is this mighty-armed Keśava, of true valor, the inconceivable, the lotus-eyed one; he is no mere mortal man.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who were the lords of creatures in former times, O bull of the Bhāratas? And who are the illustrious sages remembered for each of the several quarters of the sky?
Bhīṣma said: Hear, O best of the Bhāratas, that which you ask of me—who were the lords of creatures remembered for each of the several quarters.
There is one self-existent Lord, the primeval and eternal Brahmā; and of that self-existent Brahmā there are seven great-souled sons.
Marīci, Atri and Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and the illustrious Vasiṣṭha—they are indeed the equals of the Self-existent One.
"The seven Brahmās"—such is the settled conclusion arrived at in the ancient lore. Beyond this I shall now declare all the lords of creatures.
Sprung from the line of Atri, born of Brahman, eternal, was the Lord Prācīnabarhis; and from him came the ten Prācetasas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of those ten there was a single son, the lord of creatures named Dakṣa; he has two names in the world—he is called Dakṣa, and also Ka.
Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci; of him two names are heard—one is Ariṣṭanemi, and the other they know as Kaśyapa.
And there was Aṅga, the glorious son begotten of his own loins, and the valiant king Bhauma, who attended through a thousand divine ages.
And the lord Aryaman too, and whatever other sons there were, O mighty one — these have been declared the regions and the fashioners of the worlds.
And of Śaśabindu there were ten thousand wives, O undecaying one, and from each one of them there were then a thousand sons.
Thus that great-souled one had a hundred times a hundred thousand sons, and they would acknowledge no other as Lord of Creatures.
The wise call that ancient progeny the Śāśabindava line; that great lineage of the Lord of Creatures became the source of the Vṛṣṇi race.
These illustrious ones have been recounted as the Lords of Creatures; now hereafter I shall declare the gods, the sovereigns of the three worlds.
Bhaga and Aṃśa, and Aryaman, and Mitra, and Varuṇa likewise, and Savitṛ, and Dhātṛ, and the mighty Vivasvant —
Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise Indra — and Viṣṇu is called the twelfth: these are the twelve Ādityas, sprung from the very self of Kaśyapa.
Nāsatya and Dasra too are remembered as the two Aśvins; these two are the sons of Mārtāṇḍa, the eighth Lord of Creatures.
And the glorious, far-famed Viśvarūpa was the son of Tvaṣṭṛ; then Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata —
And Hara, and Bahurūpa, and Tryambaka the lord of gods, and Sāvitra, and Jayanta, and the bow-bearing Aparājita: these are the Rudras. And earlier the eight illustrious Vasus were proclaimed.
These gods of such a kind are sprung from Manu, the Lord of Creatures; and the Ancestors are remembered as twofold — the former ones, and the gods as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some others delight in virtue and beauty, and others belong to the Siddhas and Sādhyas; and the Ṛbhus and the Maruts too are reckoned hosts of the gods.
Thus have these been enumerated — the Viśvedevas and likewise the Aśvins. Among them the Ādityas are the warriors, and the Maruts the commoners.
The two Aśvins are held to be Śūdras, intent upon fierce austerity; and the Āṅgirasa gods are remembered, by settled judgment, to be Brāhmaṇas. Thus the fourfold order of all the gods has been proclaimed.
Whoever, rising at dawn, glorifies these gods is released from every sin — both that done by himself and that done by another.
Yavakrīta, and Raibhya, and Arvāvasu and Parāvasu, and Auśija, and Kakṣīvant, and Nala — these are sons of Aṅgiras.
Kaṇva, the son of the sage Medhātithi, and likewise Barhiṣad — these, my son, are fashioners of the three worlds, the seven seers in the eastern quarter.
Unmuca and Vimuca, and the valiant Svastyātreya, and Pramuca, and Idhmavāha, and the lord of firm vows —
And the majestic Agastya, son of Mitra and Varuṇa — these are the Brahman-seers, forever stationed in the southern quarter.
Ruṣadgu, Kavaṣa, Dhaumya, and the valiant Parivyādha, and Ekata, and Dvita, and Trita — these are the great seers.
And the lord, the son of Atri, and likewise the mighty Sārasvata — these nine great-souled ones are stationed in the western quarter.
Ātreya, and Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa the great seer, and Gautama, with Bharadvāja, and Viśvāmitra the Kauśika —
And likewise the lord Jamadagni, son of the great-souled Ṛcīka — these seven are stationed in the northern quarter.
All these, of keen splendour, have been recounted in each quarter — great-souled ones who stand as witnesses and as fashioners of the worlds.
Thus these great-souled ones are stationed, each in their several quarters; by uttering praise of them a man is released from all his sins.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In whatever quarter these dwell, the man who takes refuge in that quarter is freed from all his sins, and may go home in safety and well-being.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O grandsire, deeply wise, whose valour in battle is unfailing as truth, I wish to hear in full of Kṛṣṇa, the undecaying Lord.
His most vast splendour, and his deeds of old — tell me all of that as it truly is, O bull of the Bhāratas.
How did Hari come to bear a form born in the animal womb, and for the accomplishing of what task? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Long ago, having gone out hunting, I halted at the hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya; there I beheld hosts of sages seated by the thousand.
Then they did me honour with the madhuparka offering; and having accepted that honour, I in turn greeted the seers with gladness.
There this tale was told by the great seer Kaśyapa — a divine tale that gladdens the heart; hear it now with single mind.
In olden times the foremost of the Dānavas, filled with wrath and greed, drunk with might by the hundred — great Asuras led by Naraka —
and likewise many other Dānavas, mad for battle, could not endure that unsurpassed prosperity of the gods.
Tormented by the Dānavas, the gods and the divine seers found no refuge, O king, but scattered hither and thither.
And the dwellers of heaven beheld the earth in the very shape of anguish — overrun by mighty Dānavas of dreadful form, oppressed by her burden, dragged down, suffering, and sinking away.
Then the sons of Aditi, sore afraid, spoke thus to Brahmā: How, O Brahman, can we endure this crushing by the Dānavas?
The Self-Born said this to them: The ordinance has been set forth here by me. They are drunk with their boon, with their might, and with their arrogance;
in their utter delusion they will not perceive Viṣṇu, whose vision is hidden — the god in the form of a boar, unassailable even by the immortals.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Going swiftly to where those vilest of Dānavas, dreadful ones, dwell by the thousand deep within the earth, he will quell them. Hearing this, those best of the gods rejoiced.
Then Viṣṇu, of vast splendour, assuming the form of a boar, entered deep within the earth and went forth against the sons of Diti.
And beholding that more-than-mortal being, all the Daityas together, bewildered by destiny, rose up at once with sudden force and made their stand.
And all together they rushed upon the boar and seized him as one, and in their fury they dragged that boar this way and that on every side.
Those lords of the Dānavas, of huge frame, mighty valour, and towering strength, were yet unable to do him any harm at all, O mighty one.
Then those lords of the Dānavas fell into wonder, and then, from fear, by the thousand they deemed their own selves brought to peril.
Then that foremost god of gods, whose self is yoga, the charioteer of yoga, the Lord, taking his stand in yoga, O best of the Bhāratas —
roared out a mighty roar, throwing the Daityas and Dānavas into turmoil — a roar by which all the worlds and all the ten quarters were made to resound.
By the sound of that roar the worlds were thrown into commotion, and all the quarters were confounded, and the gods with Śakra at their head.
And the whole universe then became utterly without motion, all that is fixed and all that moves alike, stupefied by that roar.
Then all those Dānavas, terrified by that sound and overwhelmed by the splendour of Viṣṇu, fell down with their breath gone out of them.
And those foes of the gods who had fled to the nether world the boar tore apart with his hooves — their heaped-up mass of flesh and fat and bone.
By that mighty roar he came to be remembered as the Eternal — the lotus-naveled, the great yogin, the teacher of beings, the king of beings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all the hosts of gods spoke to the grandsire: What manner of roar is this, O god? We do not know it, O mighty one. Who is he, or whose is this roar, by which the universe is thrown into distress?
In that very interval Viṣṇu, abiding in his boar-form — the great god — rose up, being praised by the great seers.
The grandsire said: Having slain the lords of the Dānavas, this god of vast frame and mighty strength — the great yogin, the Self of beings, the begetter of beings —
is the lord of all beings, the yogin, the womb and the Self even of the Self. Be steadfast: this is Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of all sin.
Having done this most excellent deed that none could do, he of boundless radiance, illustrious and of great brilliance, has returned into his own Self — the lotus-naveled, the great yogin, the Self of beings, the begetter of beings.
No grief, no fear, no sorrow should be felt, O best of the gods; this is the ordinance and the power, and Time the worker of dissolution. By this great-souled one, who upholds the worlds, the roar was let forth.
For he indeed is the illustrious one, adored by all the worlds — the undecaying, the lotus-eyed, the origin of all beings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me, my father, the supreme yoga of liberation, O scion of Bharata; I wish to know it in its truth, O best of those who speak.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount this ancient tale — a dialogue concerning liberation between a pupil and his teacher.
A certain pupil, of supreme intelligence, seeking the highest good and fully composed, having clasped the feet of a Brāhmaṇa, his teacher and the best of seers, who sat there, stood with joined palms and spoke.
If, O lord, you are pleased with my service, there is a certain great doubt of mine; this you ought to explain to me.
Whence am I, and whence are you? Tell me rightly that which is highest; and how, O best of the twice-born, among all beings that are alike, do their rightly-ordered courses turn back, and their decline and rise prove contrary?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the word that is in the Vedas, and that which is worldly and all-pervading — all this, O learned one, you ought to expound as it truly is.
The teacher said: Hear, O pupil of great wisdom, this supreme mystery of Brahman — the inmost Self of all beings, and that which is the treasure of the scriptures.
Vāsudeva is all this; he is the mouth of Brahman, the universe. Truth, giving, and sacrifice, forbearance, self-restraint, and uprightness —
That which the knowers of the Veda know as the eternal Person, Viṣṇu — the maker of creation and dissolution, the unmanifest, the everlasting Brahman — this Brahman is of the Vṛṣṇi; hear from me the tale of it.
The greatness of Viṣṇu, the god of gods, of measureless splendour, should be made to be heard by Brāhmaṇas for a Brāhmaṇa, and by Kṣatriyas for one of royal birth. You, O blessed one, are worthy of it; hear that which is supreme, the tale of the Vṛṣṇi.
The wheel of Time, without beginning or end, marked by being and non-being, turns round like a wheel through the three worlds among all beings.
That which is the imperishable, the unmanifest, the immortal, the everlasting Brahman — that they declare to be Keśava, the tiger among men, the bull among men.
The supreme, the undecaying, creates the Ancestors, the gods, and the seers, and likewise the Yakṣas and Dānavas, the Nāgas, Asuras, and human beings.
And likewise the Vedas and the sciences, and the everlasting laws of the world — these, at the dissolution, having reached primordial Nature, the Lord creates again at the dawn of the age.
As in the seasons the marks of the seasons, in their various forms, are seen — those very same ones again in their turning — so it is in the days and nights of Brahmā.
Now whatever is to come to be, by the conjunction of Time, at the beginnings of the ages — that very knowledge arises, born of the ordering of the world's course.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Vedas, vanished at the age's end, together with the histories, the great seers regained of old through austerity, permitted thereto by the Self-Born.
The lord, the knower of the Veda, knows the Veda; Bṛhaspati declared the limbs of the Veda; and the Bhārgava declared the science of statecraft, for the good of the world.
Nārada declared the lore of the Gandharvas, Bharadvāja the wielding of the bow, Gārgya the deeds of the divine seers, and Kṛṣṇātreya the art of healing.
Many systems of reasoning were set forth by various disputants; what is propounded in accordance with logic, scripture, and right conduct — that is held in honour.
That supreme Brahman, which is without beginning, neither the gods nor the seers comprehend; the Lord Nārāyaṇa alone, the Ordainer, the Sovereign, knows it.
From Nārāyaṇa the hosts of seers, the foremost gods and demons, and the royal sages of old received that supreme remedy for sorrow.
Presided over by the Person, Nature ever brings forth existence; bound up with cause, the whole world thereby revolves on.
As from one lamp other lamps are kindled by the thousands, so Nature creates, yet, being infinite, is never diminished.
From the Unmanifest, born of action, arises the intellect; the intellect brings forth the I-sense; from the I-sense comes ether, and from ether arises wind.
From wind comes fire, from fire the waters, and from the waters the earth springs up; these are the eight root-natures, and in them the world abides.
From these come the five organs of knowledge, the five organs of action, and the five objects of sense; and the mind is the one and sixteenth among the modifications.
Ear, skin, the two eyes, tongue, and nose—these are the five sense-organs; and the feet, the anus, the generative organ, the two hands, and speech are the organs of action.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sound, touch, then form, taste, and likewise smell—these are to be known; and the pervading consciousness, the mind, is present in all of them.
In the knowledge of taste it is the tongue, and likewise speech in utterance; joined with the manifold organs, the mind is distributed throughout them all.
One should know these sixteen divinities each in its own division; in the bodies they wait upon and worship the Knower, the maker of knowledge, seated within.
Thus the tongue has the quality of Soma, and smell is the quality of earth; the ear has sound for its quality, and the eye is the quality of fire; and touch one should know as the quality of wind, in all beings and at all times.
The mind, they say, has goodness for its quality, and goodness too is born of the Unmanifest, abiding as the self in all beings; therefore let the wise man understand it so.
These existences bear up the whole world with all that moves and is unmoving, resting upon that passionless God whom they call the supreme abode.
The holy city of nine gates, furnished with these existences, the great Self pervades and there reposes; and therefore is it called the Person who dwells in the city (puruṣa).
Ageless is He and deathless, expounded as both manifest and unmanifest, all-pervading, endowed with qualities, subtle, the support of the qualities of all beings.
As a lamp is luminous by nature, whether it be small or great, so should one know the Person, whose essence is knowledge, present in all creatures.
It is He who here knows what is to be known, He who hears, He who sees; this body is His instrument, and He is the doer of all actions.
As the fire latent in wood is not seen until the wood is split, so the Self abiding in the body is perceived here only through yoga.
As the waters are bound up in rivers, as the rays belong to the sun, streaming forth as they flow on, so are the bodies of embodied beings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As in the state of dream the Self, gathered together with the five senses, casts off the body and wanders forth, even so is it to be apprehended here.
By action it is first overspread, by action it comes into being, and by action—by the deeds it has wrought, mightier than all else—it is led elsewhere.
And how, abandoning one body, it passes from body to body and takes on another—of this aggregate of beings, born of their own action, I shall now fully speak to you.
The teacher said: Beings are of four kinds, both unmoving and moving; they have the Unmanifest for their source and the Unmanifest for their dissolution, they say. Let one know that the mind, whose nature is dissolution into the Unmanifest, has the Unmanifest for its very self.
As the mighty fig-tree, lying hidden within the tiny seed of the aśvattha, is seen to come forth full-grown, so does the manifest arise from the unmanifest.
The lodestone draws the iron toward itself, though both are without consciousness; even so existences arise from causes inherent in their own nature, and so too is it with whatever else is of this kind.
Even so the existences born of the Unmanifest, marked as the instruments of the doer, though themselves unconscious, are bound together by cause for the sake of the conscious one.
Neither earth nor space nor heaven, neither the elements nor the seers, neither gods nor demons, nor anything else existed apart from the living soul; nor had they yet come together in combination.
By every reckoning it is all-pervading, having mind for its cause and bearing its own mark; the action of ignorance is what is pointed to here—this is the character of the cause.
Conjoined with its causes, it is the gatherer-together of effects, by which this great wheel, without beginning or end, turns on.
The wheel whose hub is the Unmanifest, whose spokes are the manifest, whose rim is the round of modifications, presided over by the Knower of the field, turning upon a well-oiled axle, revolves unceasingly.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Because of its oiliness the whole world is crushed in this wheel like sesame, pressed down, as it were, by oil-pressers, by enjoyments born of ignorance.
Out of craving, action lays hold of the I-sense as its possession; in the conjunction of cause and effect that craving has been shown to be the determining ground.
The effect does not surpass its cause, nor the cause its effect; but in the bringing-about of effects, time becomes the operative ground.
Joined to their causes, the primary natures and the modifications move toward one another, each upon each, ever presided over by the Person.
Fallen away through existences full of passion and darkness, driven on by the force of causes, it follows after the Knower of the field, as dust is borne along by the wind; yet that essence is not touched by them, nor are they touched by that great Self.
As the wind may be either laden with dust or free of dust, so let the wise man know the difference between the field and the Knower of the field; and being thus disciplined through practice, he would not return again to Nature.
This doubt, once it arose, the blessed seer cut away; and so let one regard the matter, weighed by the marks already established.
As seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again, so, with its afflictions burnt away by knowledge, the Self is not bound again.
The teacher said: As for the dharma marked by engagement in action, how it comes to be observed—to those steadfast in true knowledge no other principle is pleasing than this.
Rare are the knowers of the Veda who stand firm in what the Veda enjoins; and so, with an end in view, men here desire the path that is held in honor.
Because it has been practiced by the good, this conduct is beyond reproach; this is the one understanding, and there is that other by which one reaches the supreme goal.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The embodied being, out of delusion, takes on all possessions, beset by the impulses of desire, anger, and the rest, born of passion and darkness.
Therefore let him who seeks to sustain the body do nothing impure; for one who leaves an opening in his conduct would not attain the auspicious worlds.
As gold alloyed with base metal, even when refined, does not shine forth, so knowledge whose dross is unburnt away does not shine.
And he who, drifting after desire and greed, practices unrighteousness through delusion, though he has set foot upon the path of dharma, perishes together with all his kin.
Therefore let him pass through the objects of sense—sound and the rest—without attachment; for anger, elation, and dejection arise one from another.
In this body made of the five elements, compounded of goodness, passion, and darkness, whom does one praise, at whom does one rail, and what is there to say?
In touch, form, taste, and the rest the foolish form attachment; through want of discernment they do not grasp that the earthy quality is sprung from their own selves.
As a dwelling made of clay is plastered over with clay itself, so this earthen body is smeared over with the modifications of clay.
Honey, oil, milk, clarified butter, flesh, salt, jaggery, grains, fruits and roots—these, together with water, are modifications of clay.
As one who is crossing a wilderness should give way to no longing, but in his weariness take food merely to sustain himself, though it be unsavory—
even so, crossing the wilderness of worldly existence, intent on his labor, let him take food only for the journey's sake, as a sick man takes medicine.
By truth, purity, uprightness, and renunciation, by good repute and by valor, by patience, by steadfastness, by understanding, by the mind, and by austerity—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
let him dwell among all states of being as they come, each in its due order; and desiring peace, with undejected soul, let him also restrain the senses.
Bewildered by goodness, by passion, and by darkness, creatures turn round and round as on a wheel, sorely, through ignorance.
Therefore let him rightly examine the faults that spring from ignorance, and ever cast off the I-sense, which has ignorance for its source.
The great elements, the senses, the qualities—goodness, passion, and darkness—and the threefold world with its Lord: all this is established upon the I-sense.
As here time, in its fixed course, displays the marks of the seasons, so let one know the I-sense within beings to be the impeller of beings.
Let one know darkness, the bewilderer, as black and sprung from ignorance; and learn now these three qualities together, bound up with pleasure and pain—those of goodness, of passion, and of darkness.
Lack of confusion, joy-born delight, freedom from doubt, steadfastness, and memory—these one should know as the qualities of goodness; and these others as belonging to passion and darkness:
desire and anger, heedlessness, greed and delusion, fear and weariness, dejection and grief, discontent, pride and arrogance, and ignobility.
Having examined the gravity and lightness of such faults as these, which abide within the self, let him reflect on each one in turn, continuously.
The pupil said: Which faults are cast off by the mind, which are loosened by the understanding, which return again and again, and which, through delusion, are as if without fruit?
Of which should the wise man weigh the strength and weakness with the understanding, by reasoned grounds? Declare all this to me, O master, so that I may know it.
The teacher said: When the faults are cut off at the root, the purified soul is set free; as a thing of iron destroys what is brought against it, so too the unperfected soul perishes through the inborn faults that spring from passion.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That which is of passion and that which is of darkness, arising from action—for the pure soul, all this is the seed of embodied beings, and for one who is master of himself it is all alike.
Therefore by the self-possessed man both passion and darkness are to be shunned; goodness, set free from passion and darkness, would attain to stainlessness.
Or else they might declare, in the manner of sacred formula, that the taking of flesh is sanctioned by the Yajus; that same ground holds also for not taking it, in the keeping of the pure dharma.
Through passion one may accomplish even works conjoined with dharma and bound up exceedingly with gain; and one pursues all desires as well.
Through darkness one pursues deeds joined to greed and born of anger, delighting in the sport of violence, beset by sloth and sleep.
He who abides in goodness, taking refuge therein, beholds the pure states of goodness; that embodied one is stainless, glorious, pure, and endowed with knowledge.
The teacher said: By passion and by darkness, O bull among men, delusion is wrought, and anger, greed, fear, and arrogance; by the conquering of these one becomes pure.
They enter into the supreme One, the Supreme Self, the imperishable, undecaying God, Viṣṇu, who abides in the Unmanifest, the best of the gods.
But men whose limbs are scorched by His illusion, fallen from knowledge, bereft of hope, through the bewildering of their knowledge thereupon pass on indeed to desire.
From desire men attain to anger, and to greed and delusion; from pride and arrogance comes the I-sense, and from the I-sense thereupon come actions.
From actions comes the bond of affection, and from affection follows sorrow forthwith; from the undertaking of pleasure and pain men are made fit for birth and rebirth.
And from birth comes the dwelling in the womb, arising from seed and blood, foul with the oozings of dung and urine, sprung from blood.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Overcome by craving, bound by these things and drifting after them, let one there understand women to be the bearers of the loom of worldly existence.
By their nature they are as the field, while men bear the mark of the Knower of the field; therefore let the discerning man pass beyond these in particular.
For these women are dread enchantments that bewilder the undiscerning; the eternal embodiment of the senses lies hidden within passion (rajas).
From craving-natured desire, as from a seed, creatures are born. As a man casts off the worms bred from his own body, knowing them as no part of himself, so should he renounce those worms called 'sons'—deeming them his own yet truly not his own.
Creatures are born from seed, from sap, and from affection, whether by nature or by the conjunction of past deeds; the wise man should regard them with detachment.
Passion (rajas) is overlaid upon darkness (tamas), and goodness (sattva) too abides in darkness; ignorance, founded upon knowledge, is marked by intellect and the sense of 'I.'
This, they declare, is the seed of embodied beings; this seed is named the living self (jīva), which, through action joined to time, keeps the wheel of saṃsāra turning.
As one disports in a dream by the mind alone, as though possessed of a body, so the embodied self, through the qualities that hold the germ of his deeds, comes to be lodged within a womb.
Whatever sense is impelled by deed grown into a seed, that sense arises out of the sense of 'I,' through a mind charged with desire.
From his craving for sound, the ear of this self that has been shaped by desire is born; from craving for form, the eye; and the nose, from the wish to seize upon scent.
From the cravings for touch arises the vital air, resting upon prāṇa and apāna; and vyāna, udāna, and samāna—fivefold, sustaining the body in its course.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With limbs thus born, sprung from deeds and enveloped by Brahman, the man comes into being—amid sufferings of body and mind, sorrowful at their beginning, their middle, and their end.
Let him know that suffering arises from grasping, and grows through self-conceit; by renouncing these there comes its cessation, and he who knows that cessation is set free.
Both the rising and the dissolution of the senses lie within passion alone; having examined this, let the wise man move through the world rightly, with the eye of scripture.
The organs of knowledge do not draw their objects toward the man free of craving; and once their causes are understood, the embodied self need take on a body no more.
The teacher said: Herein I shall declare the means, rightly, with the eye of scripture; the wise man who walks by that understanding may attain the supreme goal.
