Having spoken thus, those high-souled ones, all beholders of the true meaning—the seers and the tranquil ascetics—at once made their declaration.
Such inauspicious and dreadful customs as these, O Jājali, you do not, for all your skill, perceive, simply because they are universally practiced.
One should seek dharma upon principle, and not merely follow the way of the world. As for him who would strike me and him who praises me—hear of this too, O Jājali:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
those two would be alike to me, for I have neither liked nor disliked. Such a dharma as this the wise extol.
For, furnished with sound reasoning, it is honored by ascetics and by those ever devoted to dharma, and it is marked out by its subtlety.
Jājali said: By the dharma you have set forth, you who hold the scale, the gate of heaven and the very livelihood of creatures will be barred.
For from agriculture food arises, and thereby you yourself live; and by cattle and by herbs do mortals live, O trader.
From these too sacrifice arises—yet you prate of the denier's creed; for this world could never go on if it abandoned husbandry altogether.
Tulādhāra said: I shall expound the right way of life, O Jājali; I am no denier, O brāhmaṇa, nor do I condemn sacrifice—yet one who truly knows sacrifice is very hard to find.
Homage to the brāhmaṇa's sacrifice and to those who know sacrifice; for the brāhmaṇas have forsaken their own sacrifice and taken up here the kṣatriya's sacrifice.
It has been set in motion, O brāhmaṇa, by the greedy, by those bent on wealth, by deniers who, not understanding the words of the Veda, take what is false for what merely wears the semblance of truth.
'This must be given, this must be given'—and he seeks no end to it; hence arise theft and forbidden deeds, O Jājali. That oblation alone is well made by which the gods are gladdened.
By reverence, by oblation, by recitation of the Veda, and by herbs let the worship of the gods be performed, as the scriptures show.
From the rites and works of the wicked is born a crooked offspring; from the greedy is born the greedy, from the impartial the impartial.
As is the sacrificer in himself, so too are his priests, and so his offspring; from sacrifice offspring arises, as pure water from the sky.
The oblation cast into the fire, O brāhmaṇa, attends upon the sun; from the sun is born rain, from rain food, and from food creatures.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore, from sacrifice well performed, the men of old won all their desires; the earth ripened her harvests untilled, and the plants grew at their blessings—yet they looked for no reward in their sacrifices or in themselves at all.
But those who, anxious for reward, would sacrifice in any selfish fashion are born again as wicked men, as cheats, as the greedy whose end is gain.
By his unholy deeds such a one goes to the worlds of the doers of evil. The man who would make right out of wrong and do the unholy is of evil soul, of undeveloped wisdom, ever so here, O best of the twice-born.
The brāhmaṇa who knows both kinds of duty—what is to be done as that which is to be done—dwells as Brahman itself in the world, and falls back no more into the bondage of obligation.
And action shorn of its qualities is the higher, so we have heard; that is, to forbear from harming any being, and to be restrained as to its fruit.
Those whose sacrifice is truth, whose sacrifice is self-restraint, who are free of greed and content within themselves, renouncers of whatever arises—all such folk have set envy at a distance.
Knowing the truth of the field and the knower of the field, perfected in their own sacrifice, studying the holy Veda, they gladden even the immortals.
All divinity entire, all Brahman, rests upon the brāhmaṇa; when he is satisfied the gods are satisfied, and they are content when the contented man is content, O Jājali.
As one sated with every flavor takes joy in nothing more, so for him who is content in wisdom there is a contentment, perpetual, that gives rise to bliss.
Delighting in dharma, finding their joy in dharma, wholly resolved, the seekers after wisdom say: 'There is yet more for us, beyond, in very truth.'
Some, possessed of knowledge and discernment, longing to cross to the farthest shore beyond—that shore is supremely holy ever, joined with a holy lineage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Going whither men neither grieve nor fall away nor suffer pain—those of pure nature attain here to that abode of Brahman.
They desire not heaven, nor do they sacrifice with wealth got for renown; they follow the path of the good, according to their power, through non-violence.
Trees and herbs and fruit and root—these they know for their offerings; greedy priests, set on gain, do not conduct their sacrifices for them.
Pursuing only their own true purpose, the twice-born, perfected in their works, performed sacrifice once again, out of a wish to bless the people.
That they might lead the people to heaven by the practice of their own dharma—such is the conviction that abides in me, impartial in all things, O Jājali.
By those rites which the wise ever employ in sacrifice, O bull among the twice-born, they journey along that path of the gods, O great sage.
For one kind there is return to rebirth, but for the wise there is no returning; both these, O Jājali, travel by the path of the gods.
For such men the oxen yoke and draw of their own accord, and the cows give milk of themselves, by the mere fulfilment of their mind's resolve.
Of themselves they take up the sacrificial posts and worship with their own well-earned offerings; he whose self is so refined is worthy to lay hold of a cow for sacrifice.
But men not of that stature, O brāhmaṇa, should sacrifice with herbs and plants alone; setting the renunciation born of wisdom foremost, such is the path I declare to you.
Free of craving, undertaking nothing, offering no obeisance and no praise, undiminished yet spent of all works — him the gods know as the true brāhmaṇa.
Neither reciting the scriptures aloud, nor sacrificing, nor giving among brāhmaṇas, yet seeking a worldly livelihood — to what goal does such a man come, O Jājali? Tell me how, making this his deity, he may attain the fruit of sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Jājali said: We have not heard the very truth of the sages; I ask you, O merchant — this is a hard matter. Not heeding what went ever before, the seers set down no doctrine higher than this.
In this holy ford of the self the beasts could not find their happiness; then by which deed of his own, O merchant, may a man attain happiness? Tell me this, O greatly wise one — deeply indeed do I trust your word.
Tulādhāra said: Whether they offer sacrifices or none, those rites are nowhere worthy of the true offering. With clarified butter, with milk and curds, above all with the full oblation — yes, by her hair, her horn, her hoof, the cow herself brings the sacrifice to be.
And by this rule a man appoints his wife to her office and so performs it; for the sacrificial cake is declared the pure oblation that stands for all the beasts.
All rivers are as the Sarasvatī, all mountains holy; the self alone, O Jājali, is the sacred ford — do not be a stranger wandering from land to land.
Practising such duties as these in this world, O Jājali, while seeking righteousness through outward means, a man does not attain the blessed realms.
Bhīṣma said: Such duties as these does Tulādhāra extol — duties accomplished by sound reasoning and ever followed by the good.
Tulādhāra said: Whether by the good or by the wicked this path has been resorted to, let it be made plain before your eyes, and then you shall know how the matter truly stands.
These many birds wander all about you — hawks and creatures of other kinds, hatched and reared upon your very head.
Call to them, O great brāhmaṇa, as they settle here and there; behold them clinging to your hands and feet and over all your body.
The birds, cherished by you, honour you as their father; beyond doubt you are their father — call to your children, O Jājali.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Then, summoned by that Jājali, the winged ones uttered divine speech, speaking, so it is said, the word of dharma.
The work founded upon non-injury and the rest bears fruit both here and beyond; but rivalry destroys it, O brāhmaṇa, and that rivalry, once roused, destroys the man himself.
Sacrifice cannot save the speech and mind that grow only through faith; here those versed in old lore recite the verses sung by Brahmā.
The mind of the pure man without faith and of the impure man possessed of faith — the gods deemed these alike in the work of sacrifice.
Of the learned but stingy man and of the generous usurer the gods weighed both, and reckoned their food as of equal worth.
Prajāpati said to them: This judgement is unequal. The generous man's food is hallowed by faith; the other's is spoiled by faithlessness. The generous man's food may be eaten, but not the stingy man's, nor the usurer's.
He alone who lacks faith is unworthy of the gods' oblation; his food, and his alone, is not to be eaten — so know those learned in dharma.
Faithlessness is the highest sin; faith is the deliverer from sin. The man of faith casts off his sin as a serpent its worn-out skin.
Greatest among purifying things is renunciation joined with faith; he who has turned away from the faults of conduct and holds fast to faith is verily pure.
What need has such a one of austerity, of observance, of any further discipline of self? This man is made of faith; whatever his faith is, that very thing is he.
Thus has dharma been declared by the good who perceive its meaning and aim; we, desiring knowledge, have come to you out of our vision of dharma.
Cast off rivalry, O greatly wise one, and then you shall attain the highest. Faithful and full of faith, fixed in his own path of duty, this merchant here is the worthier man, O Jājali.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus was the matter of high import set forth by Tulādhāra, and rightly was the eternal dharma grasped and declared.
Having heard the words of that Tulādhāra of renowned power, the twice-born one, O son of Kuntī, won his way to peace.
Then before long that Tulādhāra and he, both greatly wise, having gone to heaven, dwelt there in ease, each attaining his own station won by the fruit of his deeds.
For those who are even-minded, faithful, restrained, and pure of heart, when they perform what is called sacrifice, the sacrifice is never found wanting.
Faith indeed is the goddess of the quality of goodness, daughter of Sūrya, O king — Sāvitrī, the bringer-forth, and the giver of trust to all living things.
Faith preserves what is grown through speech and grown through mind, O Bhārata. This has been taught you by way of parable — what more do you wish to hear?
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they tell this ancient tale, sung by King Vicakhnu out of compassion for living creatures.
Seeing a bull with its post struck down and hearing the loud bellowing of the cattle at the cow-pen of the sacrificial ground, that king looked on.
"May it be well with the cattle in all the worlds!" — thus he made his pronouncement; for once slaughter had begun, this blessing was devised.
It was by men of no fixed bounds, deluded, denying the scriptures, of doubting and unsettled mind, that the killing of beasts came to be praised.
In all works non-injury is the law — so spoke Manu whose very self was righteousness; it is from lust and passion that men slaughter beasts outside the altar.
Therefore the subtle dharma should be discharged by the discerning man according to right measure; for non-injury is held greater than all other duties.
Having fasted and become rigorous in vows, yet abandoning the revealed truths the Veda ordains — calling it 'observance,' these are no observances at all, but the wretched practices of men set on reward.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If men, on the pretext of sacrifices, of sacred trees, and of sacrificial posts, eat flesh in vain, this is no dharma to be commended.
Flesh, honey, liquor, fish, strong drink, and rice cooked with sesame — all this was set going by cheats; it is nowhere ordained in the Vedas.
Out of lust, delusion, and greed was this craving set in motion; in all sacrifices the brāhmaṇas recognize Viṣṇu alone, and his worship is held to be with milk-rice and with flowers.
And the trees fit for sacrifice that are appointed in the Vedas, and whatever else is to be done, when well prepared in purity by the great-souled and pure of heart — all that is worthy of the gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For one who does no injury, the body and its distresses are at strife; how shall the body's sustenance be secured for one who undertakes nothing?
Bhīṣma said: So that the body does not waste away, so that it does not fall under the sway of death, in such measure should one engage in works; the able man should practise dharma so.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How should one examine a deed to be done — swiftly, or with long deliberation? In this stronghold of hard choices you are in every way our highest teacher.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they tell this ancient tale of what befell long ago to Cirakārin in the line of Aṅgiras.
O Cirakārin, blessings on you, blessings on you, O Cirakārin! For the man who acts deliberately is wise, and offends not in his deeds.
Cirakārin, the greatly wise, was the son of Gautama; for he undertook all his tasks long and with careful regard.
Long pondering his aims, long waking, long sleeping, because he carried out his tasks only after long delay, he was therefore called Cirakārin, 'the Slow-Doer.'
He earned the name of sluggard and was called dull-witted by people of nimble but shallow understanding, who see not far ahead.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Now, upon some transgression, passing over his other sons, he was bidden by his enraged father: "Slay this mother of yours!"
Having slowly answered "So be it," by his very nature the Slow-Doer, reflecting in his deliberate way, fell long to pondering.
How shall I carry out my father's command, and how shall I not slay my mother? How shall I keep from sinking, like a wicked man, into this snare disguised as dharma?
A father's command is the highest dharma; yet a son's own duty is the protection of his mother, and sonship is bound and not its own master — how should this not torment me?
Who, having slain a woman, and his mother at that, could ever know happiness? And who, by slighting his father, could ever win a firm standing?
Not to slight the father is fitting; to uphold and protect the mother is fitting too. Both these claims deserve forbearance — how shall I overstep either of them?
For the father places his own self within the wife, that a child be born, for the sustaining of character, conduct, lineage, and family.
I myself am that very self, brought forth again by my father into the state of a son; how then should I lack understanding? — and so he came to know his own origin.
What the father pronounces at the birth-rite and at the rite of initiation — that firm confirmation suffices to establish the reverence due to the father.
The father is the foremost teacher, the highest dharma, a benefactor through nurture and the gift of learning; whatever the father declares is dharma, and that too is firmly settled in the Vedas.
A son is to his father but a source of joy, whereas the father is everything to the son; all things — body and the rest, the gifts that are to be given — the father alone bestows.
Therefore the father's word must be done, and in no way questioned; even his sins are cleansed away for the man who carries out his father's word.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In enjoyment, in fortune, in childbearing, in the witness of all the world, in union with a husband, and in the parting of the bride's hair —
The father is heaven, the father is dharma, the father is the highest austerity; when the father is brought to delight, all the gods are delighted.
Whatever blessings the father pronounces, those come to that man; the father is the expiation of all sins, in whatever he gives his glad approval.
The blossom is loosed from its stalk, the fruit is loosed from its stem; but the father, though wearied by his love for his sons, never lets his love go.
Thus far has the son's reverence for the father been pondered; but the father is the lesser station — now I shall reflect upon the mother.
This frame of mine, formed of the five elements in mortal life — of it my mother is the cause, as the fire-stick is of the fire; the mother is the kindling-block of men's bodies, the soothing of all who suffer.
He grieves not, nor does old age drag him down, who, even bereft of fortune, comes home and finds one to call 'Mother.'
He who, surrounded by sons and grandsons, still takes refuge with his mother, moves about like a child of two years even at the close of a hundred years.
Able or unable, lean or full of flesh — the mother guards her son all the same; no other is his sustainer by ordained right.
Then a man grows old when he grows sorrowful; then the world becomes empty for him, when he is parted from his mother.
There is no shade like a mother's, no refuge like a mother's, no protection like a mother's, no fountain of comfort like a mother's.
For bearing him in her womb she is the sustainer; for giving him birth she is called the mother; for the nourishing of his limbs she is 'Ambā'; and for bringing forth a hero she is the hero's mother.
For tending the infant she is 'Śuśrū'; the mother is the body's own nearest source. The man of sense would slay her only if his head were no hollow vessel — that is, if he had lost all reason.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What compact was made in the joining of the husband's and wife's life-breath, that the mother knows, or the father; but the truth of the matter rests with the mother.
The mother knows the lineage; the mother knows whose son he is. For her mere act of bearing him there is love, while the father's affection toward his offspring rests on trust alone.
Having of their own will taken her hand in marriage and entered upon a shared duty with her, if men then drive their women away, those women do not deserve to be cast off.
For a man is a woman's bhartṛ because he supports her, and her pati because he protects her; but when these virtues fail in him, he is neither her supporter nor her protector nor her lord.
Thus the woman commits no offense; it is the man alone who offends; and in committing a grave transgression, it is the man alone who is at fault.
For a woman's husband is her highest lord, declared to be her supreme deity; and she has given her very self, a self equal to his own, as the highest gift. Since in all matters the fault falls upon the man, women themselves commit no offense.
And as for any command not spoken yet pressed upon a woman for the sating of lust, in him who would so remind her there is plainly unrighteousness; of this there is no doubt.
That a woman, and above all a mother set in the highest reverence, is not to be slain—this even brute beasts, lacking all discernment, understand.
They know the father to be the gathering of all the gods made one; yet out of the affection that belongs to mortals and to gods alike, one turns toward the mother.
As Cirakārin pondered thus at length, in keeping with his slow-acting nature, a long stretch of time passed by; and then his father came to him.
Medhātithi, the deeply wise Gautama, steadfast in austerity, had in that interval reflected upon the breach of his wife's conduct.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Scorched by grief, shedding tears in plenty, and brought through the calm grace of learning and fortitude to remorse, he spoke.
"Purandara, lord of the three worlds, came to my hermitage; taking up the guise of a guest, he assumed the form of a brāhmaṇa.
He was soothed with fitting and gracious words, honored with a welcome, and by her, in due form, was offered the guest-water and the water for his feet.
Told, 'I am subject to another,' yet he said, 'I shall press my suit by craft.' In the misfortune that arose from this, the woman bears no transgression.
Thus neither the woman, nor I, nor that wandering lord of the gods has sinned against dharma; it is heedlessness alone that has done the wrong.
The seers who have raised their seed on high call jealousy a born vice; and I, hurled down by jealousy, am sunk in the ocean of evil deeds.
Should I slay a virtuous woman, and a wife condemned only out of my own vice, a wife who is mine to cherish and sustain—who then will carry me across?"
"Cirakārin, whom I commanded in a moment's haste, is noble of mind; if today he be true to his slow-acting way, he will save me from this sin.
O Cirakārika, blessings on you—blessings on you, O Cirakārika! If today you are still slow to act, then you are truly Cirakārika.
Save me, and your mother too, and the austerity I have amassed, and your own self from sins—be this day Cirakārika!
Slow-acting is your inborn way, joined to a wisdom that takes its time; let it bear fruit for you today—be this day Cirakārika!
Long were you longed for by your mother, long carried in her womb; make your slow-acting nature bear fruit, O Cirakārika!
Out of anguish he lingers long; restrained, he sleeps long—consider the long anguish of us both, O Cirakārika!"
Thus grieving, O king, the great seer Gautama then beheld his son Cirakārin standing close at hand.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Cirakārin, seeing his father in deepest grief, cast aside his weapon and, bowing his head, set about winning his father's favor.
And Gautama, seeing his son fallen with his head upon the ground, and his wife unharmed, came to the highest joy.
For that great-souled one had not driven his wife to ruin, dwelling as he did in the solitude of the hermitage; and his son too had been composed.
He might have slain her without reproach, with his son standing weapon in hand; yet, the boy having humbly asked his counsel, he could now resolve upon his own course of action.
And seeing his son bowed at his feet, the thought came to him: 'Out of fear he is concealing the rashness of having taken up the weapon.'
Then the father praised him long, long kissed him upon the head, long held him in both arms, and uttered, 'Live long!'
Thus that deeply wise Gautama, filled with love and gladness, embraced his son and spoke these words.
"O Cirakārika, blessings on you—be ever slow to act, and live long! Yet while you tarried, I was long and grievously stricken with sorrow."
And the learned Gautama, best of sages, also spoke these verses, founded on the recital of the virtues of the steadfast slow-acting ones.
"Slowly should one bind a friend, and slowly cast off a friendship once made; for a friend made slowly deserves to be kept long.
In passion, in arrogance, in pride, in enmity, in sinful deeds, and in any unkind act that must be done, the slow-acting man is praised.
In the unproven offenses of kinsmen, of friends, of servants, and of womenfolk, the slow-acting man is praised."
Thus, O Bhārata, that Gautama was pleased with his son for that deed, O Kaurava—pleased by that very slowness to act.
So a man who reflects in all his undertakings, and after long deliberation comes to a decision, does not grieve for long thereafter.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He holds his anger long in check, long restrains his action, and no deed that breeds remorse befalls him.
Long let him wait upon his elders, long attend and honor them; long let him practice the duties of dharma, and long pursue his inquiry.
Long attending upon the wise, long serving the cultured, and long disciplining himself, a man comes in time to a state beyond contempt.
Even when another utters words bound up with dharma, let him question long and answer long; thus he is never long despised.
Having dwelt for many years in that hermitage, the brāhmaṇa of mighty austerities then went to heaven, together with his son.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How should a king protect his subjects and yet cause no one distress? I ask you, best of the good; tell me that, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite an ancient tale—the dialogue of Dyumatsena with King Satyavat.
Satyavat spoke what had not been spoken before—so we have heard—when, by his own father's order, certain men were being led away to execution.
"Righteousness passes into unrighteousness, and unrighteousness into righteousness, if killing were to be called a duty—this ought not to be."
Dyumatsena said: If non-killing were the law, then what could ever count as duty at all? If robbers were never slain, O Satyavat, a ruinous confusion would arise.
'This is mine'—such a claim would have no force in the age of Kali, and the very course of worldly life could not go on. If you know otherwise, declare it to us.
Satyavat said: All three of the lower orders should be made to hold fast to the brāhmaṇas; and of those bound by the cords of dharma, only a few will go astray.
Whichever of them should transgress, let the twice-born point him out, saying, 'This man will not heed me'; upon such a one let the king sit in judgment.
What the scripture lays down in accord with the truth of each case—that must be carried out; killing is not to be ordered otherwise, nor deeds done without examining them by the science of statecraft as ordained.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When a king slays robbers, more often than not he destroys the guiltless along with them; for when a man is killed, his wife, mother, father, and son are killed in him. Therefore, where one man has wronged another, let the king judge with care.
An evil man may one day come to good character; and even from the good, born of those who are evil, there may spring an unworthy offspring.
No root-and-branch slaughter should be carried out; that is not the eternal law. Indeed, even without killing, expiation may be prescribed.
By rebuke, by imprisonment, by disfigurement, and by the punishment of death are such men to be afflicted, but not at once with the full measure of harm.
When, seeking refuge, they come round to the royal chaplain, saying, 'Brāhmaṇa, we shall do no sin again,'
then they deserve to be released—such is the king's ordinance. A brāhmaṇa, shaven and bearing the staff and deerskin, is worthy to receive a fresh garment of pardon.
For graver and graver offenses, repeated again and again, men deserve release—but not in the same measure as at the first.
Dyumatsena said: Wherever the people can be held within their bounds by a compact, that is called dharma—but only so long as it is not overstepped.
But if no one were ever put to death, everything would fall into ruin. In the earlier ages, and in those still earlier, the people were easy to govern.
Gentle they were, abounding in truth, with little malice and little wrath. Of old the only chastisement was a word of reproach; next came rebuke by speech.
Then there came also the penalty of confiscation; and today the penalty of death prevails. Yet there are some men who cannot be restrained even by death.
There is no robber of men alone, says the sacred lore, nor of the gods alone, nor of the gandharvas and the ancestors alone; for here in the world, who is anything to anyone, and who is no one at all?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One takes a lotus even from a cremation ground, and a deity's emblem even from a demon. As for those who are ignorant and bereft of sense—who could make a binding compact with such men?
Satyavat said: If you cannot bring such men to goodness without violence, then make an end of them—but in such a way that there is some gain for someone, present or yet to come.
Dyumatsena said: For the sake of the world's order kings undergo the highest austerity; they feel shame before such righteous men and so come to act righteously themselves.
Holding evildoers in dread, the well-doers do not slay them from mere desire; for the most part kings govern their subjects by virtue alone.
Thus the world follows the better conduct of the better man; for men ever follow the conduct of their superior.
Him who, without composing himself, would set others in order, while he is yet a slave to his senses amid objects of desire—at such a man men laugh.
Whoever, out of pride and delusion, does anything unfitting toward the king, is to be restrained by every means; thus does he turn back from sin.
He who would curb wrongdoing must first curb his own self; and he should chastise with heavy punishments even his nearest kinsmen.
Where the doer of evil who deserves affliction meets no great suffering, there sins multiply and dharma surely dwindles—so the learned brāhmaṇa, of compassionate nature, gave his instruction.
In just this way, my son, I have been instructed by my forefathers and grandsires, who out of tenderness reassured me again and again.
This rule the king observed in its full first form in the Kṛta age; with dharma diminished by a quarter he proceeded so in the Tretā age, with dharma upon two feet in the Dvāpara, and upon a single foot in the latter age.
And so, when the Kali age has come, through the misconduct of kings and by the peculiar working of time, only a sixteenth part of dharma may remain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Now if one were to follow the first rule in full, O Satyavat, confusion would arise; therefore, marking out a man's span of life, his strength, and the times, the king should prescribe his penance.
For the sake of truth, that one might not here forsake the great fruit of dharma, and out of compassion for living beings, Manu, son of the Self-Existent, declared this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That renunciation which, without doing harm to living beings, fosters the sixfold policy—the dharma that partakes of both worldly life and renunciation—tell me of that, grandfather.
Of the duty of the householder and the duty of renunciation, both of which set out toward a goal not far apart—which, grandfather, is the more excellent?
Bhīṣma said: Both ways of duty, my son, are exalted, both exceedingly hard to tread, both bear great fruit, and both have been practised by the good.
On this I shall set forth for you the authority of them both. Listen with single-minded attention, Pārtha, and your doubts about duty and its purpose will be cut away.
On this point too they relate an ancient tale, the dialogue of Kapila and the Cow. Mark it well, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Beholding the ancient, eternal, abiding tradition, Nahuṣa long ago took a cow belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ — so we have heard.
That cow, made ready for sacrifice, the sage Kapila then beheld — he of undejected spirit, steadfast in goodness, delighting in righteous custom, possessed of knowledge, restrained in his eating.
Having attained the highest understanding, perfected and fearless from every side, he said but once: "I recall it but faintly — the truth is loose-held: 'the Vedas,' indeed!"
Then the seer Syūmaraśmi, entering into that cow, spoke to the ascetic: "Ho there! If the Vedas are held to be authoritative, by what are other duties to be held authoritative?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For of the ascetic, the resolute, who has the eye of scriptural discernment and has come to know the Self, men hold that all his utterance is of the seers.
For one whose craving has thus departed, who is freed of fever and of every longing, undertaking nothing at all — what desire to expound the Vedas can remain to him?
Kapila said: I do not revile the Vedas, nor do I ever wish to dispute them. We have heard that the works of those in the several stages of life, though distinct, have one and the same aim.
The renouncer surely reaches the goal, and the forest-dweller reaches it; the householder and the celibate student — both of these too reach it.
Four are the eternal paths held to lead toward the gods; among them their greater and lesser standing, their strength and weakness, is told in terms of their fruits.
Having thus understood all these aims, "let him undertake works" — so runs the Vedic injunction; and elsewhere "let him not undertake them" — so is heard the scripture of final renunciation.
In non-action there may be freedom from fault; in action there is the highest faultlessness. Of scripture standing thus, the relative strength is hard indeed to discern.
If there is here anything immediately evident, held higher than non-injury yet apart from the scriptures of tradition — declare it, if you can see it.
Syūmaraśmi said: "Let him who desires heaven offer sacrifice" — so the scripture is ever heard. For first the fruit is set forth, and only thereupon is the sacrifice extended.
The goat and the horse and the ram, the cow, and the flocks of birds, and the plants of village and of wilderness — "all these are the food of life" — so says the scripture.
Just so is food day by day apportioned, at evening and at dawn; and the cattle and the grain are members of the sacrifice — so says the scripture.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
These together with the sacrifice did Prajāpati ordain; and with that sacrifice the Lord Prajāpati worshipped the gods.
All these living beings, moving each upon the other, are sevenfold and sevenfold; and the whole world, brought to bear within sacrifices, men call the thing named Highest.
This too was sanctioned by the ancients and by those still more ancient. What wise man would ever fail to weigh well his own capacity?
Beasts and men and trees together with the plants all long for heaven alone; yet heaven there is none apart from sacrifice.
Plants, cattle, trees, creeper, clarified butter, milk, curds, oblation, earth, the quarters, faith, and time — these are the twelve.
The Ṛc verses, the Yajus, the Sāman, and the sacrificer as the sixteenth; the fire is to be known as the householder, and that is called the seventeenth. These are the members of the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is the root — so says the scripture.
With its clarified butter, its milk, its curds, its dung, its curd-and-milk mixture, its hide, its hairs, its horn, its hoof — the cow becomes the very sacrifice; thus each single part of it serves whatever purpose is ordained for it.
Joined together with the priests and with the sacrificial fees, they bear the sacrifice onward; and all these things, brought together, bring the sacrifice to its completion.
For they were created for the sake of sacrifice, even as the scripture is heard to declare; and thus the ancients and the still more ancient among men engaged in works.
He does no harm, though he acts; he bears malice toward nothing — he who sacrifices thinking only "the sacrifice is to be offered," with no craving for its fruit.
And these members of the sacrifice, as has been told, beyond doubt, when joined to one another by the prescribed rule, carry one another across.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I behold the tradition of the seers, in which the Vedas are established; the wise perceive it through their contemplation of the Brahman.
The sacrifice springs from the Brahman and is offered up into the Brahman; the whole world follows after the sacrifice, and the sacrifice ever follows after the world.
"Oṃ" is the womb of the Brahman; "Namaḥ," "Svāhā," "Svadhā," "Vaṣaṭ" — he by whom these are employed, performed according to his power, however slight —
of him they know no fear of the world beyond, throughout the three worlds — so the Vedas declare here, and the perfected ones and the supreme seers.
The Ṛc verses, the Yajus, the Sāman, and the chant-syllables impelled by the rule — he in whom all these dwell outwardly, he indeed is the twice-born.
What comes to be in the kindling of the sacred fire, and in the pressed Soma, twice-born one, and what comes by the other great sacrifices — all that the venerable one knows of his own self.
Therefore, brahmin, let him surely sacrifice and cause sacrifice to be made, without hesitation; for one who sacrifices by the rite that wins heaven, the fruit of heaven hereafter is great.
For those who do not sacrifice there is neither this world nor the next — so is the settled judgement; and those versed in the doctrine of the Veda are then the authority for both.
Kapila said: Beholding only thus much, the ascetics go forward as travellers of the path; for them, throughout all the worlds, there is no transgression at all.
Beyond the pairs of opposites, free of homage, unbound by any longing, the wise ones, released from all sins, wander pure and stainless.
Resolved upon final release, upon renunciation, and upon true understanding, most devoted to the Brahman, having become the Brahman, they have made their dwelling in the Brahman alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Free of grief, with passion destroyed, theirs are the everlasting worlds. When one has attained their supreme goal, what need has he of the householder's life?
Syūmaraśmi said: Even if this be the highest consummation, even if this be the supreme goal, no other stage of life can proceed without depending upon the householders.
As all creatures live by depending upon their mother, so the other stages of life subsist by depending upon the householder.
It is the householder who sacrifices, the householder who practises austerity; the householder's estate is the root of this whole order of duty, of whatever stirs and lives.
For all bearers of breath, O sage, are brought forth through procreation; and procreation, moreover, is in no wise to be found elsewhere.
Whatever plants there be without, and the many of the wilderness too, O twice-born — since beyond the plants no living being is to be found, for whom could this saying hold true, that "there is no release outside the household"?
By the faithless, the unwise, bereft of subtle insight, the despairing, the slothful, the weary, tormented by their own works, the cessation of toil — that which is called renunciation — has been devised, while passing for learned men.
For the very cause of the three worlds is the eternal, abiding bound of order; and he who is named the brahmin, the venerable one, is honoured from his birth onward.
For among the twice-born the sacred formulas begin even before the implanting of the embryo; they attend, beyond doubt, both upon the unconfiding rites and upon the confiding ones.
And again the cremation upon his death, the eating from the vessel when he is laid out, the gift of cows or of cattle, and the sinking of the rice-balls in the waters —
The fathers, the flame-possessing, the seated-on-sacred-grass, the eaters of the offerings, are remembered in the rites; the sacred formulas give their sanction even to the dead, and the formulas are the cause.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While the Vedas thus cry aloud, whence is there release for anyone, since mortals stand in debt to the fathers, the gods, and the twice-born?
It is by men bereft of glory, slothful, calling themselves learned, that the ignorance of the Veda's doctrine is talked away as though it were knowledge — falsehood wearing the semblance of truth.
He is not carried off by sins nor dragged down — the brahmin who sacrifices according to the Veda's ordinances; his sacrifice goes upward together with the beasts, and, being sated, it sates him with the objects of desire.
Not by contempt of the Vedas, not by guile, not by deceit, does a man attain the great; he finds the Brahman within the Brahman.
Kapila said: The new-moon and the full-moon rites, the fire-oblation of the wise, and the four-monthly observances — in these abode the everlasting sacrifice.
Undertaking no works, well-steadied, pure, given over to the Brahman, those seekers after the immortal sate the gods by the Brahman alone.
For him who has become the Self of all beings, who beholds all beings, who is without a track yet seeks the track — upon his road even the gods grow bewildered.
The man is a city of four gates, four-faced; and fourfold does blame come upon him — from his two arms, from his speech, from his belly, from his loins. Of these gates one should wish to be the gatekeeper.
Let him not gamble with the dice, nor take another's wealth, nor receive the cooked food of a man of unworthy birth; and the wise one, when angered, should never strike — thus are his hand and foot well guarded.
Let him not give way to reviling, nor speak falsely, nor practise slander or idle gossip among men; vowed to truth, sparing of speech, ever heedful — thus is the gate of his speech well guarded.
Let him not be a glutton, nor a great eater; let him be free of greed, and take his food as brought to him by the good; let him receive here only such food as serves to sustain his journey — thus is his belly's gate kept guarded.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let him not dally with a woman who is a hero's wife, nor summon a woman to him out of season; let him hold to himself the vow of fidelity to his wife — thus would the guarding of his loins' gate be kept.
The wise man whose gates are all well guarded — the loins, the belly, the arms, and the speech as the fourth — he indeed is the twice-born.
For him whose gates are unguarded, all his deeds become vain; what use to him is austerity, what use the sacrifice, what use his very self?
Him who wears no upper garment, who lies down on no spread couch, whose pillow is his own arm, who has grown still — him the gods know for a brahmin.
The sage who, alone, takes delight amid all those who delight in the pairs of opposites, brooding upon no thoughts of others — him the gods know for a brahmin.
He by whom all this is understood, both nature and its modification, who knows the course of all beings — him the gods know for a brahmin.
From whom there is safety for all beings, since from him all are without fear, who has become the Self of all beings — him the gods know for a brahmin.
They do not deny the fruit of action that belongs to the Vedas as a thing apart; yet having granted all that, they find their pleasure in another thing that bears no fruit.
And they see that works are fruitful, yielding their reward, and abiding; yet also that they are flawed and not unfailing in their issue.
And here the merits are most hard to know, and even when known, most hard to perform; and once performed, they have an end — so do you perceive.
Syūmaraśmi said: How the authority of the Veda stands, and how renunciation bears its fruit, and how both these paths are made manifest — declare that to me, O venerable one.
Kapila said: You who stand upon the true path behold here what is immediately evident; yet what is there here, immediately evident, that you reverently attend upon?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Syūmaraśmi said: I am Syūmaraśmi, brahmin, come here for the sake of knowledge; desiring the highest good, I have answered you out of sincerity and not out of any wish to dispute. Let the venerable one resolve for me this terrible doubt.
You who stand upon the true path, beholding here what is immediately evident — what is here most evident of all, that you reverently attend upon, apart from the sciences of reasoning and from tradition followed each according to its tradition?
Tradition is the doctrine of the Veda, and the sciences of reasoning too are tradition; let one attend upon it each according to his tradition, and there tradition is made effective; and perfection in the form of the immediately evident is seen to arise from the certainty of tradition.
As one boat bound fast to another, both swept along together by the current — how, O brahmin, shall it carry the dull-witted across? Let the venerable one declare this; I have come fittingly to you — teach me, sir.
There is none who is truly a renouncer, none truly content, none free of grief, none free of ill, none free of curiosity, none turned away, none turned wholly back.
You too rejoice and grieve, even as we do; and the objects of your senses are the same as those of all living creatures.
Among the prescribed observances of the four orders and the four stages of life, when men hold fast to a single one of them, what in the final determination is flawless and free of ill?
Kapila said: Whatever course the scripture enjoins amid all undertakings—wherever a man's practice falls, there and there alone lies that which is flawless and free of ill.
Knowledge purifies all things for one who follows after knowledge; but the way of life that departs from knowledge destroys its creatures.
You who are ever possessed of knowledge are, in every respect, beyond the bounds of scripture; yet only some rare man, only at some rare moment, attains that oneness of the self.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For some men, who have not grasped the scripture in its truth and rely only on the force of argument, fall under the sway of egoism, overpowered as they are by desire and hatred.
Not having understood the scriptures as they truly are, they become robbers of scripture, thieves of the sacred word—men who undertake nothing, whose minds are unripe and whose ways are inauspicious.
They see only fault and do not seek out the virtues; for such men, whose very bodies are made of darkness, darkness alone is their final refuge.
Whatever a creature's inborn nature, if he remains subject to that nature's sway, then hatred and desire, anger, deceit, falsehood, and pride—the strands of being born of his nature—ever rise up and overwhelm him.
Perceiving this with the understanding, the ascetics who delight in self-restraint and long for the supreme goal should renounce alike the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Syūmaraśmi said: All this, O brahman, has been proclaimed by me on the authority of scripture; for no undertakings are set in motion without one's having understood the purport of scripture.
Whatever conduct is righteous is in its entirety scripture—so declares the sacred tradition; and whatever is unrighteous is contrary to scripture—this too is the tradition that is heard.
It is settled that no activity whatsoever exists apart from scripture; and whatever is other than the teachings of the Veda is contrary to scripture—so runs the tradition.
Many who fancy themselves clear-sighted look upon things as set apart from scripture; while others, here and in the world beyond, fail to see the faults that come of forsaking it—men whose discernment is slain by ignorance, of meager wit and shrouded in darkness.
It is indeed possible for one man, set free, who has wholly accomplished his task, to wander in every direction relying on no more than a morsel of food; and leaning upon the teaching of the Veda, to declare that liberation exists.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But this is hard work that the householder takes upon himself, bound to family and home: gift-giving, the study of the sacred texts, sacrifice, the continuance of offspring, and uprightness.
If, even after a man has done all this, there is no liberation for anyone, then fie upon the doer and the deed alike, and all this toil is to no purpose.
Otherwise there would be denial of the divine and a casting of the Vedas behind one's back. Of this, O blessed one, I wish to hear the unending truth, plainly and at once.
Tell me the truth, O brahman; I have come to you as a suppliant—teach me, sir. As liberation is known to you, even so I wish to be instructed in it.
Kapila said: The Vedas are the measure of all the worlds, and the Vedas are not cast behind one's back. Two Absolutes are to be known: the Absolute that is sound, and that which is supreme; and one who is well-versed in the Absolute that is sound attains the supreme Absolute.
That which a man fashions in accordance with the Veda fashions his body and gives it form; for only when his body has been made pure does the brahman become a fit vessel.
Of him who, through his action, pursues the infinite, I now speak to you—a truth needing no scriptural support, no hearsay, but plain to perception and witnessed by all the world.
Those who spread out their sacrifices solely for the sake of righteousness, free of craving for reward, given to renunciation as it arises, untouched by greed, and devoid of pity-seeking and spite—for them this is the true path of wealth: its bestowal upon worthy recipients at the holy fords.
Resting on nothing, they are never given to evil deeds, even from the source whence action springs; they are perfected by the resolve of their own minds, settled in the certitude of utterly pure knowledge.
Free of anger, free of malice, without egoism or envy, fixed in knowledge, threefold pure, they delight in the welfare of all beings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the most part they were householders, never swerving from their own duties; and likewise the kings were yoked to their tasks, and the brahmans too, each according to rule.
Even-minded, endowed with uprightness, content, settled in knowledge, with righteousness made manifest before them, pure and full of faith in the higher and the lower alike.
From the first their souls were refined, their vows duly fulfilled; and even in hardship and dire straits, banded firmly together, they walk in the way of righteousness.
For those who in former times walked together in righteousness, that itself was happiness; for them there was never any penance that needed to be ordained.
For, taking their stand upon truth and righteousness, they were held to be most unassailable; they yielded not even to a hair's breadth of compromise, nor in the end to any sham of righteousness.
Whatever was the foremost rule, that very rule they all practiced together; for those who stand firm in this state, no penance is to be found. Penance arose for the weak of soul—so runs the tradition.
For brahmans of this kind in olden days were the bearers of sacrifice, grown old in the threefold lore, pure, of good conduct and great renown, offering sacrifices day after day—wise men freed from the bonds of craving.
Their sacrifices, their Vedas, and their rites were all according to scripture; their sacred recitations were according to the appointed seasons, and their resolves according to their vows.
For men who had cast off desire and anger, whose selves were by nature keen and disciplined, upright, ever tranquil, steadfast in their own duties—all was the infinite itself: so runs the eternal tradition handed down to us.
For those of undaunted spirit, whose conduct and works were hard to pursue, who were wholly compassed by their own duties, their austerity attained a fearsome intensity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That conduct of the virtuous—wondrous, ancient, everlasting, and fixed—has been but faintly indicated among the duties, for those who cannot practice it in full.
Their conduct was a righteousness free of calamity, free of negligence, free of defeat; and among them, in all the orders, there was never any transgression.
Those bulls among men held fast to the one righteousness of four feet; and the good, attaining it duly, go to the supreme goal.
Some, going forth from their homes, betook themselves to the forest; others, abiding in the household itself, were thereafter chaste students of the sacred lore.
This righteousness of four feet the brahmans know as the system of life-stages; the infinite is the abode of the Absolute—the brahmans, in truth, are its certitude.
And so those brahmans of olden days, of this kind, walkers in the way of righteousness—these very twice-born ones are seen in heaven, become lights in the sky.
Like the constellations in their stations, like the manifold hosts of stars, they have attained the infinite through contentment—so the Vedic teaching declares.
And if such men come again into the round of rebirths, into the wombs once more, they are never stained by evil deeds, even from the source whence action springs.
A brahman thus disciplined is a brahman indeed; another is but a brahman in name only. It is a man's action alone that proclaims him, whether for good or for ill.
Thus for those whose impurities have been ripened away, through the infinite and through sacred learning, all was the infinite itself: such is the eternal tradition handed down to us.
For those who have put away thirst, who are washed clean, of auspicious soul, the fourth duty—that of the Upaniṣads—is remembered as common to all.
It is ever brought to perfection by the perfected, by brahmans of disciplined self; rooted in contentment, its essence renunciation, it is called the very seat of knowledge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The way of final release, eternal, is the everlasting duty of the ascetic; whether held in common or kept alone, it is practiced according to one's strength.
As one goes ever onward toward security, the weak man here sinks down by the way; but he who, seeking the station of the Absolute and remaining pure, is freed from the round of rebirths.
Syūmaraśmi said: Those who enjoy, those who give, those who sacrifice and who study, who do so with the means righteously obtained, or those who have taken to renunciation—
of these, in the life after death, which is the most victorious in winning heaven? Tell me this, O brahman, in its very truth, for I ask it.
Kapila said: All possessions are good, and so are the prosperities that come of merit; yet they do not attain the happiness of renunciation—this too you can see for yourself.
Syūmaraśmi said: You are firmly grounded in knowledge, while householders are settled in action; yet in their consummation a oneness is said to belong to all the life-stages.
As to their oneness and their distinctness, no other difference is spoken of. Let the blessed one declare this to me duly and according to reason.
Kapila said: Rites are the ripening of the body, but knowledge is the supreme goal. When the impurity has been ripened away through the purgings, one no longer abides in the mere savoring of relish.
Freedom from cruelty, forbearance, peace, non-injury, truth, uprightness, freedom from malice and from arrogance, modesty, endurance, and tranquility—
these are the paths to the Absolute; by these a man attains what is supreme. Knowing this, let the wise man comprehend in his mind the true ground of action.
That goal to which the brahmans, tranquil in every way, utterly pure, settled in knowledge and content, attain—that they call the supreme goal.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having known the Vedas and that which is to be known, each in its proper standing—such a man they call a knower of the Veda; one other than this is but a windbag.
The knowers of the Veda know all; in the Veda all is established. For in the Veda is the ground of everything, whatever exists and whatever does not.
This is the very ground of everything, whatever exists and whatever does not; this is the end and the middle, the real and the unreal, for one who truly discerns.
It rests in total renunciation, and in tranquility; here the good lies in contentment, and it is established in final release.
It is the cosmic order, the truth, the known and the yet-to-be-known; the Self of all, both the moving and the unmoving; it is all happiness, and that which is auspicious and supreme—the Absolute, the unmanifest, the source and the imperishable.
It is splendor, forbearance, peace, the flawless, the auspicious; even such is that eternal, fixed expanse. By these words, with the understanding for one's eye, It is approached: to that Absolute, to that holy Power, be homage.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Righteousness, wealth, and pleasure—these the Vedas commend, O Bhārata. Of which is the gaining most excellent? Tell me that, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall relate to you an ancient tale, of the kindness that Kuṇḍadhāra long ago, out of affection, did for his devotee.
A certain penniless brahman, out of desire, looked toward righteousness; and then, longing for the means to sacrifice, he performed a terrible austerity in his craving for wealth.
Then, having made his resolve, he worshiped the gods with devotion; yet even after worshiping the gods, he did not come upon any wealth.
Then he fell again to brooding: 'Which deity might that be, who would be swiftly gracious to me—one not made dull by the worship of men?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, in gentle form, he beheld close at hand an attendant of the gods, the cloud-spirit Kuṇḍadhāra, standing near.
The moment he saw that great being, devotion was born in him: 'This one will grant me good fortune, for such indeed is his form.'
'And he is close to the god, and not beset by other men's worship; this one will give me wealth in abundance, and that swiftly too.'
Then with incense and perfumes and garlands of every sort, and with manifold offerings, the twice-born one worshiped him.
Then in a little while the cloud-spirit was pleased, and intent on doing him a kindness, he spoke this measured word.
'For the slayer of a brahman, for the drinker of liquor, for the thief, and for the breaker of vows, an expiation has been ordained by the good; but for the ingrate there is no expiation.'
'Unrighteousness is the son of hope; anger is remembered as the son of envy; greed is the son of deceit—but the ingrate deserves no offspring at all.'
Then that brahman, lying upon the kuśa grass, beheld in a dream, through Kuṇḍadhāra's power, all created beings.
By tranquility, by austerity, and by devotion made unadorned and undefiled, the pure-souled brahman beheld in the night a revelation.
He beheld there, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Maṇibhadra, of great splendor among the gods, that great-souled one, issuing his commands.
There the gods bestow kingdoms and wealth; moved by auspicious deeds they grant, and in the case of inauspicious ones they cut these off.
Then, while the yakṣas looked on, Kuṇḍadhāra of great splendor flung himself down and fell to the ground before the gods, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then, at the bidding of the gods, the greatly renowned Maṇibhadra spoke to Kuṇḍadhāra, who had fallen to the ground: "What is it that you desire?"
Kuṇḍadhāra said: "If the gods are gracious to me, this brāhmaṇa is my devotee. I wish that some favor be granted him from which his happiness may arise."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Then Maṇibhadra, at the very word of the gods, spoke once more to the radiant Kuṇḍadhāra.
"Rise up, rise up, good fortune to you! Your purpose is accomplished; be happy. However much wealth this brāhmaṇa, your friend, may ask for, that much—beyond counting—I shall give him, by the command of the gods."
But Kuṇḍadhāra, reflecting that the human estate is unsteady and impermanent, turned his mind toward austerity for the illustrious brāhmaṇa.
Kuṇḍadhāra said: "I do not ask riches for the brāhmaṇa, O giver of wealth. Quite another favor is what I wish to have granted to my devotee."
"Not the earth filled with jewels, nor a vast hoard of wealth, do I wish for my devotee—rather, that he may become a man devoted to dharma."
"Let his mind delight in dharma; let him live by dharma; let him hold dharma foremost. This is the favor I have in mind."
Maṇibhadra said: "Since sovereignty and manifold joys are the fruit of dharma, let him too partake of these fruits, freed from bodily affliction."
Bhīṣma said: Then the greatly renowned Kuṇḍadhāra applied himself again and again to this very thing—the practice of dharma—and thereupon the gods were pleased with him.
Maṇibhadra said: "All those gods are pleased with you, and likewise with this brāhmaṇa. He shall become a man whose very self is dharma, and he shall fix his mind upon dharma."
Bhīṣma said: Then Kuṇḍadhāra the cloud-bearer was glad, his purpose accomplished, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having obtained the boon his heart desired—one most hard for others to win.
Then that best of brāhmaṇas saw fine bark garments laid down at his side, brought to him there; and he was overcome with world-weariness.
The brāhmaṇa said: "This one does not know a good deed done him—who else, then, will recognize what is done for him? I shall go to the forest; better to live by dharma."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Out of world-weariness, and by the grace of the gods, that best of brāhmaṇas entered the forest and there began a mighty austerity.
Living on fruits and roots—on what was left after the gods and guests were served—that brāhmaṇa, O great king, came to find his delight in dharma.
Giving up all roots and fruits, that brāhmaṇa became one who fed on leaves; and giving up leaves, that best of brāhmaṇas then subsisted on water alone.
Thereafter, for many gatherings of years, he lived on air alone; and yet his life-breath did not waste away—and this was as a wonder.
As he held faith in dharma and abided in fierce austerity, after a long span of time divine sight arose in him.
This thought arose in him: "Were I, well pleased, to bestow great wealth on anyone, my word would not prove false."
Then, his face joyful, he took up austerity once more; and the perfected one pondered again, and attained that which is higher still.
"Were I, well pleased, to bestow a kingdom upon anyone whatsoever, he would shortly become a king, and my word would not prove false."
To him, O Bhārata, Kuṇḍadhāra showed himself in person, drawn by the power of the brāhmaṇa's austerity and moved by friendship.
Having met with him, the brāhmaṇa then did honor to Kuṇḍadhāra according to rite, and he was filled with wonder, O king.
Then Kuṇḍadhāra said: "Yours is the supreme divine eye. Behold the destiny of kings, O wise one, and survey the worlds with that eye."
Then that wise one, from afar, with the eye endowed with divine power, saw thousands of kings sunk down in hell.
Kuṇḍadhāra said: "If, having honored me with true feeling, you were to come to grief, what would I have done for you, and what favor would have been yours?"
"Look, look once more: how should a man crave the objects of desire? For the gate of heaven is barred shut—above all to mortals."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Then he beheld desire and anger, greed, fear, and intoxication, sleep, languor, and sloth standing there, enveloping men.
Kuṇḍadhāra said: "By these the worlds are tightly hemmed in. The gods fear mankind, and so, at the gods' word, these obstacles work hindrance in every way."
"No one becomes righteous unless the gods permit it. Yet you, by your austerity, are now able to bestow a kingdom and riches."
Bhīṣma said: Then the brāhmaṇa, whose self was dharma, fell head-bowed before the cloud-bearer and said: "A great favor has been done me."
"For the grudging I once bore you, bound up with desire and greed, not knowing your affection—for that you ought to forgive me."
Saying "It is already forgiven by me," Kuṇḍadhāra embraced that bull among brāhmaṇas with both his arms and there and then vanished.
Then the brāhmaṇa wandered through all these worlds, joined to such power of austerity, by the grace of Kuṇḍadhāra of old.
Travel through the sky, and the fulfillment of whatever he resolved upon—such power came to him from dharma and from yoga, and that supreme goal as well.
Gods, brāhmaṇas, the good, yakṣas, men, and cāraṇas honor here the righteous—not the rich in wealth, nor the slaves of desire.
Truly the gods are well pleased that your mind delights in dharma. In wealth there is but some small fraction of joy, but in dharma is the supreme happiness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of the many sacrifices and austerities that have one and the same aim, O grandfather, how was a sacrifice performed for the sake of dharma and not for the sake of pleasure?
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall relate to you what was recounted by Nārada—an ancient tale of a gleaner-brāhmaṇa, concerning the matter of sacrifice.
In a most excellent realm rich in dharma, among the Vidarbhas, there once lived a brāhmaṇa, a certain sage who lived by gleaning, and he set about a sacrifice within his sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His food there was wild śyāmāka grain and suvarcalā, the consort of the Sun; and bitter, savorless greens, which by his austerity had turned sweet.
Resorting to the earth in the forest, without harm to any living being, a sacrifice offered even with roots and fruits leads to heaven, O scorcher of foes.
His wife, gaunt with vows, pure, who moved among the lotus-pools, had been brought to the office of sacrificer's wife; by truth she was made to comply—yet she, terrified of a curse, did not act according to her own nature.
A garment of peacock-feathers and worn leaves was made for her, leaf-clad as she was and unwilling, there at the sacrifice, in accordance with the office of the hotṛ.
Now a rebirth of Śukra, fallen through wrong meditation and unversed in dharma, had become in that forest a deer dwelling nearby, a companion; and with words it spoke the truth: "An ill deed has been done by you."
"If this sacrifice is marred, lacking in mantras and ritual limbs—then cast me, sir, into the offering, and go untiring to heaven."
Then at the sacrifice Sāvitrī in person summoned him; but when she invited him, he answered: "I will not slay one who dwells beside me."
Thus answered, she turned back and entered the sacrificial fire—wishing to see what wrong there might be in the sacrifice, even down to the nether world.
Then she, with hands joined in entreaty, again besought the deer by truth; and embracing it with truth, she enjoined: "Let it be permitted to go."
Then that deer, having gone eight steps, turned back: "Slay me freely, O truthful one; slain, I shall go to a good destiny."
"Behold the divine apsarases—with the eye I have given you—and the wondrous chariots of the great-souled gandharvas."
Then, beholding that lovely sight with an eye fixed in longing, and gazing upon the deer, he deemed dwelling in heaven worth the act of killing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But it was Dharma who, having become a deer, dwelt many years in the forest; he set in train the man's expiation—for that was no proper rule of sacrifice.
By that very intent—his mind bent on slaying the deer—his great austerity was then cut off; therefore killing is not fit for sacrifice.
Then the lord Dharma himself caused him to perform the sacrifice; and by his austerity he gained the supreme reconciliation of his wife.
Non-injury is the whole of dharma; injury in sacrifice is unfitting. I shall declare to you the truth—what is the dharma of those who speak the truth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How does a man become evil-souled, and how does he do what is righteous? By what does he take up world-weariness, and by what does he attain liberation?
Bhīṣma said: All the dharmas are known to you; you ask for the sake of confirming them. Hear of liberation together with world-weariness, and of evil and of dharma, from their very root.
For the sake of perceiving the objects of the five senses, desire first sets to work; and on attaining them, craving or aversion is born, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then for the sake of that he strives, and undertakes action anew, and seeks to make a habit of the pleasing forms and scents he loves.
From that, passion arises, and aversion straight after; from that, greed arises, and delusion straight after.
In one overwhelmed by greed and delusion, beset by passion and aversion, no true mind for dharma is born; and he practices dharma only as a pretext.
To one who practices dharma as a mere pretext, the pretext of gain too becomes pleasing, as riches are won through such pretense, O joy of the Kurus.
On that very thing he sets his mind, and then he seeks to do evil, even though restrained by his friends and by the wise, O Bhārata.
He gives a rejoinder cloaked in reason and dressed up in scripture; and his unrighteousness, born of passion and delusion, grows threefold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He thinks evil, and speaks it, and does it; and the good perceive the faults of him who is bent upon unrighteousness.
Only those of like character take up friendship with the evildoer. He gains no happiness here—how then could he hereafter?
Thus a man becomes evil-souled. Now hear from me of the righteous-souled—how one whose dharma is wholesome attains to the wholesome.
He who, with discernment, foresees these faults beforehand—skilled in the ways of pleasure and pain—attends as well upon the good.
From his good conduct and from constant practice his wisdom grows; he delights in dharma and lives by dharma.
Then, upon the riches won through dharma, he sets his mind; he waters the very root of that whence he sees virtues arise.
Thus he becomes righteous-souled and gains a worthy friend; and through the gaining of friends and wealth he rejoices both hereafter and here.
In sound and touch, in form, taste, and scent, O Bhārata, the creature gains mastery; this they know to be the fruit of dharma.
Having won the fruit of dharma, he is not sated, O Yudhiṣṭhira; and unsated, with the eye of knowledge, he takes up world-weariness.
When, with the eye of wisdom, he perceives the fault in desire, then he turns away from desires, yet does not let go of dharma.
Seeing the world to be of the nature of decay, he strives for total renunciation; thereafter he strives for liberation—not by wrong means, but by right ones.
Little by little he takes up world-weariness and casts off evil deeds; he becomes righteous-souled and attains the supreme liberation.
This I have told you, my son, that which you asked of me—evil, and dharma, and liberation, and world-weariness, O Bhārata.
Therefore set yourself to dharma in every condition, O Yudhiṣṭhira; for those who stand firm in dharma, O son of Kuntī, attainment is everlasting.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Liberation, O grandsire, has been declared by you as attainable through right means, not without means. That means, just as it truly is, I wish to hear, O descendant of Bharata.
Bhīṣma said: In you alone, O greatly wise one, this keen insight is fitting, that by right means you ever seek out all your ends, O sinless one.
The knowledge that goes into the making of a pot is not the same as what brings the pot into being, O sinless one. So too with the means to righteousness: for the duties themselves there is no other cause than these.
The road that leads to the eastern sea does not lead to the western. But the path of liberation is one alone; hear it from me in full.
By forbearance let one root out anger; desire, by renouncing the will that craves; and the steadfast man, by cultivating goodness, is fit to root out sloth.
By vigilance let him ward off fear, and the breath by the discipline of the knower of the field; longing, aversion, and desire let him turn back by firmness.
Confusion, delusion, and the whirling of the mind let him turn back by practice; and sleep too, and idle fancy, the knower of truth turns back by the practice of knowledge.
Afflictions and diseases he conquers by eating what is wholesome, well-digested, and measured; greed and delusion by contentment; the objects of sense by the vision of truth.
By compassion let him conquer unrighteousness, and righteousness by detachment; hope he conquers by looking to the future, and gain by renouncing attachment.
By reflecting on impermanence the wise man conquers fondness, and hunger by yoga; by compassion he conquers his own pride, and thirst by full contentment.
By exertion let him conquer drowsiness, and doubt by resolve; idle talk he conquers by silence, and fear by valor.
Let him restrain speech and mind by the intellect, and restrain the intellect by the eye of knowledge; the great Self restrains knowledge, and that Self the peace of the soul restrains.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This is to be understood by one who has grown calm, whose actions are pure, having rooted out the five flaws of yoga that the seers have known.
Desire, anger, greed, fear, and sleep as the fifth—having abandoned these, let him cultivate the following aids to yoga:
Meditation, study, giving, truth, modesty, uprightness, forbearance, purity, cleanness in food, and restraint of the senses.
By these his inner radiance grows and his sin is dispelled; his purposes are accomplished, and true discernment arises in him.
With his sins shaken off, radiant, eating sparingly, his senses mastered, having brought desire and anger under his sway, let him seek to reach the abode of Brahman.
Freedom from delusion, freedom from attachment, the renouncing of desire and anger, absence of meanness, absence of arrogance, freedom from agitation, and steadiness—
this is the path of liberation, serene, spotless, and pure; and so too the restraint of speech, body, and mind. To act from desire is the contrary way.
Bhīṣma said: On this very matter they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue between Nārada and Asita Devala.
Seeing the aged Devala seated, Nārada, the best of the wise, questioned him about the origin and dissolution of beings.
From what was this universe of moving and unmoving things created, O brahman? And into what does it pass at the dissolution? Of this may your honor instruct me.
Asita said: Those from which Time, impelled by the inner nature of things, brings forth beings—the five great elements—these the contemplators of being declare them to be.
From these Time, impelled by itself, brings forth beings; and whoever should speak of anything beyond these would, beyond doubt, be speaking of what is not.
Know, Nārada, these five to be eternal, unmoving, fixed, vast masses of energy, with Time as the sixth, such by their own nature.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Water, the atmosphere, earth, wind, and fire—beyond these elements there is no establishment of anything else; of this be free from doubt.
Neither by argument nor by reasoning could one, beyond doubt, affirm what is not. Know these to be wholly manifested—he of whom these six are the masses.
Those five, and Time, and pure being and non-being—these are the eight that constitute the eternal coming-to-be and passing-away of beings.
From non-being into the things brought into being, and from these they arise again; and even when destroyed, the creature becomes again just these same, fivefold.
Its body is made of earth; its hearing arises from space; the sun is its eye, the wind its vital breath, and its blood, indeed, comes from the waters.
The two eyes, the nose, the ears, the skin, and the tongue as the fifth—these the seers know to be the senses, the faculties of knowing the objects of sense.
Seeing, hearing, smelling, touching, and likewise tasting—by reasoning know the five qualities in the five, fivefold.
Form, smell, taste, touch, and sound—these are their qualities; they are apprehended by the senses, the five by the five in fivefold ways.
Form, smell, taste, touch, and sound—these qualities the senses themselves do not perceive; it is the knower of the field who perceives them through the senses.
Beyond the aggregate of the senses is thought; beyond that is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; and the knower of the field is higher than the intellect.
First the creature becomes aware, through the senses, of objects severally; then, having pondered them with the mind, it determines them with the intellect—it is the intellect that resolves upon all the objects grasped by the senses.
Thought, the aggregate of the senses, the mind, and the intellect as the eighth—these eight they call the organs of knowledge, the contemplators of the inner self.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The hands and feet, the anus, the organ of generation, and the mouth as the fifth—hear now these, named in order, the organs of action.
For the sake of speaking and of eating, the mouth is called an organ; the feet are the organ of motion, and the hands are the instruments of action.
The anus and the genital are two organs of like function, both serving discharge—the one in the voiding of excrement, the other in the discharge of desire.
Strength is the sixth—these six have I named in speech rightly, according to tradition; all the faculties of knowledge, of action, and their qualities have I declared.
When, through weariness, the senses cease from their own functions, then by the withdrawal of the senses a man falls asleep.
When, the senses having ceased, the mind has not ceased but still dwells upon the objects of sense—that one should know to be the seeing of dreams.
As for the states that are of goodness, of passion, and of darkness—men praise the sattvic ones as bound up with right action, and the others likewise according to their kind.
Joy, the accomplishment of deeds, attainment, and the highest goal—these are the marks of the sattvic man; memory takes refuge in his states of being.
In each several creature the states that abide by their ordinance—of the two states, the constant desired aim is the direct attaining of both.
The senses and the states of being are reckoned as seventeen qualities; the eighteenth of them is the embodied one, who within the body is eternal.
Or else all those qualities are bodied together with the embodied beings, dwelling in them; for at their separation from the body those bodied qualities are no more.
Or else this body is a conjunction made of the five elements; and the qualities, nineteen together with the embodied ones, or with the bodily heat as the twentieth, form the aggregate made of the five elements.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Great One, together with the breath, sustains this body; and of this being, joined with its states, there is a cause for the body's breaking apart.
Even as a thing comes into being, so too it dissolves into the five elements; at the ending of the exhaustion of merit and demerit, impelled by merit and demerit, in due time it enters a body—and thence is it born of its own deeds.
Forsaking body after body, this one passes on, taking a new support; the lord of the field, urged on by Time, moves from one dwelling to another, as from a worn-out house to a new home.
At this the wise, whose conclusions are firmly settled, do not grieve; but the wretched grieve—folk who fancy themselves bound by kinship.
For this one belongs to no one, and to it no one belongs; it remains ever alone within the body, the partaker of pleasure and pain.
The creature is never truly born, nor does it ever perish; this one passes from body to body, and, having had its enjoyment, attains at last the highest goal.
Wearing away the body made of merit and demerit through the spending of its store of deeds, the embodied one, his body exhausted, attains again to the state of Brahman.
For the spending away of merit and demerit the knowledge of Sāṃkhya is enjoined; for at its exhaustion they behold his supreme goal in the state of Brahman.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Brothers, fathers, sons, kinsmen, and friends—for the sake of wealth they were slain by us, cruel men of sinful mind.
This thirst that springs from wealth—how, O grandsire, are we to turn it back? For it was by thirst that we were made to do the sin.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, sung by the king of Videha to Māṇḍavya, who had questioned him.
Most happily, indeed, do I live, I who possess nothing at all; though Mithilā be ablaze, nothing of mine is burned.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Riches, indeed, when abundant, are surely a sore grief to those who understand; yet even when not abundant they ever delude those without discernment.
Whatever pleasure of desire there is in the world, and whatever great pleasure there is of heaven—these are not worth a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the destruction of thirst.
Even as the horn of an ox grows as the beast grows in time, so does thirst grow along with growing wealth.
Whatever has once been claimed as 'mine' through the sense of possession—that very thing, when it is lost, becomes again a cause of torment.
Let one not give way to desires; for delight in desires is suffering. Having gained wealth, let him employ it in righteousness, and abandon desire.
The wise man should be toward all creatures as one is toward tiger's flesh; having done what is to be done, his self made pure, he forsakes all things together.
Forsaking both truth and falsehood, sorrow and joy, the pleasant and the unpleasant, and casting away both fear and security, he becomes wholly tranquil and free of affliction.
