The man who has cast off pride and serves his elders, who though learned looks upon them with the meekness of one without power, out of pure affection — not lacking in diligence, yoked to dharma and self-restrained — such a noble one is honored in this world by the good.
Parāśara said: The livelihood of the lowliest, drawn from the three higher orders, is honorable; offered with goodwill and prescribed by rule, it ever makes men most righteous.
If a śūdra has no fixed livelihood handed down from father and grandfather, he should not seek a calling from another, but should set himself to the service of others.
Fellowship with the good, who perceive dharma, is becoming at all times and in every condition; never fellowship with the wicked — such is my conviction.
As an object glows by its nearness to the mountain of sunrise, so even a man of low birth shines by nearness to the good.
With whatever hue a white cloth is steeped, just that color it takes on — understand the matter from me to be exactly so.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore take your delight in virtues, never in vices; for the life of mortals here is impermanent, ever shifting and unsteady.
The wise man who, whether placed in happiness or in sorrow, gathers up only good deeds — he comes to behold blessings here.
A deed that has fallen away from dharma, though it might bring great reward, the man of insight should not pursue; it is not called wholesome here.
A king who, failing to protect his people, plunders thousands of cattle only to give them away, reaps as his fruit no more than empty repute — such a king becomes a thief.
The Self-existent first created the Ordainer, honored by the worlds; and the Ordainer created a single son, devoted to the upholding of all creatures.
Having worshiped him, the vaiśya should make his wealth abound exceedingly; it is then to be protected by the men of royal blood and put to use by the twice-born.
By śūdras who are honest, free from guile and from anger, and who furnish the means for offerings to the gods and to the ancestors, the cleansing service should be done — thus dharma does not perish.
When dharma is thus kept from perishing, the people become happy; and by their happiness, O lord of kings, the gods rejoice in heaven.
Therefore the king who protects his people is honored through dharma; so too the brāhmaṇa who studies, the vaiśya who is intent on earning,
and the śūdra who renders service, constantly and with senses controlled. Acting otherwise than this, O lord of men, a man falls away from his own dharma.
Even a few small coins, wrung from one's own life's hardship, earned by lawful means and given away, bear great fruit — how much more so other sums by the thousand.
He who, doing them honor, gives to the twice-born, O lord of men, ever reaps a mighty fruit, each according to the manner of his giving.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What is given gladly, the giver himself approaching the recipient, the wise call the most blessed and most praised; but what is given upon being asked, the learned call middling.
What is given with contempt, and likewise without faith, that the truth-speaking sages call the lowest of gifts.
A man, ever sinking in transgression of many kinds, should so exert himself that he may be delivered from the peril.
The brāhmaṇa shines by self-restraint, the kṣatriya by victory, the vaiśya by wealth, and the śūdra ever shines by diligence.
Parāśara said: Goods that come to the brāhmaṇa through acceptance of gifts, to the kṣatriya as won by the sword, to the vaiśya as earned by lawful means, and to the śūdra as gained by service — even when slight, such goods are praised, and bear great fruit when used for the sake of dharma.
The śūdra is declared the perpetual servant of the three orders. A twice-born man who follows the duty of a kṣatriya or of a vaiśya, when no other livelihood remains, does not fall; but when he takes up the work of a śūdra, then indeed the twice-born man falls.
Trade, the keeping of cattle, and a living gained by craftsmanship are ordained even for the śūdra, when no other livelihood arises for him.
Taking to the stage, a living gained by one's looks, subsisting upon liquor and meat, and the sale of iron and of leather —
a deed the world reviles should not be taken up by one who has not done it before; but for one who has done it before and now forsakes it, there is great dharma — so says the sacred tradition.
Whatever evil a man, however accomplished, commits in the world with a mind flooded by intoxicating pride — that too is declared not to be taken as a precedent.
For in the lore of old we hear of peoples who were governed by the rod of reproach alone — self-restrained, holding dharma foremost, and following the path of justice and right.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It is dharma alone, O king, that is ever praised among men here; for men who have grown great in dharma cultivate the virtues upon the earth.
That dharma, my son, the asuras could not endure, O lord of peoples; growing ever stronger, step by step they entered into those creatures.
Then arrogance, the destroyer of dharma, arose in those creatures; and out of their arrogance, wrath in turn was born within them.
Then, in those overpowered by wrath, all conduct accompanied by decency perished, and modesty itself perished, O king; and from this delusion was born.
Then, beset by delusion, they no longer saw, as before, how they might live with one another at ease, without crushing each the other.
When that rod of mere reproach reached such men, it became of no avail against them; and so they went on to despise both the gods and the brāhmaṇas.
At this very time the gods went for refuge to Śiva, foremost of the gods, the hero of many forms, the lord of the hosts.
By him those sky-dwellers, together with their cities — all three — were cast down to the earth with a single arrow, whose splendor the gods had swelled.
Their overlord was the dreadful Bhīma of dreadful prowess, a terror to the gods; he was slain by the Bearer of the Trident.
When he was slain, men returned to their own true nature, and the Vedas and the scriptures were set going once more, as in the days of old.
Then they consecrated Vāsava to the kingship of the gods in heaven, and the Seven Seers appointed men to the wielding of the rod of chastisement.
After the Seven Seers there was a king named Vipṛthu, and kings and kṣatriyas each ruling separately in their several realms.
In those born of great lineages, and in those who lived in former ages, the asura nature does not slip away from the heart.
Therefore, through that very nature clinging persistently to them, kings of dreadful might took to performing asura-like deeds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They held firm to those very deeds and continue to establish them; and even to this day those men who are most foolish cling to them.
Therefore I tell you, O king, after pondering it in the light of the scriptures: one should pursue what leads to true perfection, and forsake every deed whose essence is harm.
The discerning man should not gather wealth by confusion of duties; to abandon the right way for the sake of dharma is not called auspicious.
Such a one as you are—self-controlled, a kṣatriya dear to your kinsmen—cherish your subjects, your dependents, and your sons in accordance with your own dharma.
Union with the pleasant and the unpleasant, enmity and likewise friendship—through many thousands of births these revolve again and again.
Therefore take delight in virtues, never in faults; for the man devoid of virtue and of evil mind is called his own enemy.
Among human beings, O great king, dharma and adharma have their course; not so among the other creatures here that are devoid of human nature.
The learned man of righteous disposition, whether active in worldly effort or free from it, should always move through the world as one with all, harming no living being.
When his mind has become free of all inner scruple and falsehood no longer dwells in him, then he attains the auspicious state.
Parāśara said: This rule of dharma for the householder, my son, has now been declared; but I shall expound the rule of austerity—listen to me as I speak it.
For in the householder, O best of men, there generally arises what is called "the sense of mine," born of attachment through states of tamas and rajas.
Resting upon his house, a man comes to possess cattle, fields, and wealth, a wife, sons, and servants in this world.
As he goes on thus, ever fixing his gaze upon these things and never perceiving their impermanence, his attraction and aversion grow and grow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And upon the man overwhelmed by attraction and aversion, enslaved to his possessions, there comes, O ruler of men, what is called delight, born of delusion.
Deeming himself fulfilled by enjoyment and wholly devoted to pleasure, he sees no gain from delight beyond that of vulgar comforts.
Then, his soul overcome by greed, through attachment he increases his household, and he strives in this world to provide for the nourishment and welfare of that household.
Though he knows it ought not to be done, the man pursues it for the sake of gain; his soul wrapped in fondness for his children, he grieves when that wealth is lost.
Then, filled with pride and guarding himself against defeat, he does whatever he thinks will make him an enjoyer of pleasures—and by this he comes to ruin.
For austerity is the eternal vision of Brahman for those who are joined to wisdom—men who seek the auspicious work and renounce mere pleasure.
Through the loss of the objects of his affection, through the loss of wealth, O prince, and through the torment of mental and bodily afflictions, a man attains to disgust with the world.
From world-weariness comes awakening to the self; from awakening, insight into scripture; and from perceiving the meaning of scripture, O king, he comes to behold austerity itself.
Rare indeed, O lord of men, is the reflective man who, when his cherished happiness has waned, resolves to undertake austerity.
Austerity, my son, is open to all, and is ordained even for the lowly; for one who has conquered his senses and is self-restrained, it points out the path to heaven.
In the beginning the lord Prajāpati created living beings through austerity, intent here and there upon vows, undertaking his observances, O prince.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and likewise Agni, the Aśvins, and the Maruts, the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas, the ancestors, and the host of the Maruts—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, and the other dwellers in heaven—all were perfected through austerity, my son, as were the others who abide in heaven.
And the brāhmaṇas who were created at the beginning by Brahmā through austerity in days of old—they wander, sustaining the earth and likewise the heavens.
And the kings in the world of mortals, and the other householders who are seen in great families—all that is the fruit of austerity.
Silken garments and lovely ornaments, mounts and seats and conveyances—all that is the fruit of austerity.
Lovely women, pleasing to the heart, by the thousands, and a dwelling upon the heights of a palace—all that is the fruit of austerity.
Choice couches and foods of many kinds—all things desired come to those who have performed the deed of austerity.
There is nothing in these three worlds unattainable by austerity, O scorcher of foes; but the renunciation of all enjoyment is the only fruit of those who have done no such deed.
Whether happy or sorrowful, a man should forsake greed, looking with his mind upon scripture and with his intellect, O best of kings.
Discontent leads only to misery; from greed comes the bewilderment of the senses; and thereby his wisdom perishes, like learning bereft of practice.
When a man's wisdom is destroyed, then he no longer perceives the right; therefore, when the loss of happiness has befallen him, let him practice fierce austerity.
What is desired they call happiness; what is hated is here called sorrow. Behold what kind the fruit is, of austerity done and undone.
Those who have performed stainless austerity ever look upon blessings and enjoy the objects of sense, and they attain to renown.
But the seeker of reward who has forsaken the path of the good wins only what belongs to the senses—unpleasant things and dishonors and sorrow of many forms.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In him there arises doubt concerning dharma, austerity, and almsgiving; and having done only evil deeds, he attains to hell.
But whether dwelling in happiness or in sorrow, O best of men, the man who does not swerve from his own conduct—he is one whose eye is scripture.
In the union with touch, the delight lasts but the moment of an arrow's flight, and likewise in taste, in sight, in smell, and in hearing, O lord of the people.
Thereupon, when that delight has waned, sharp pain is born in him again—for which reason the wise extol liberation as the unsurpassed happiness.
Then he acts for the sake of the fruit, and his virtues grow ever greater; and through righteous conduct he is never deprived of pleasure and prosperity.
The objects of sense, when they come without effort, may be enjoyed by householders; but it is one's own dharma that is to be sought with striving—such is my conviction.
For the proud, the high-born, those whose eye is ever upon the meaning of scripture, who are cut off from the performance of dharma and whose selves are hemmed in by helplessness—
when the human deed they undertake comes to naught, for them there is in this world no recourse but the work of austerity.
With his whole soul let the householder hold firm to his resolve in works; with diligence, for the sake of offerings to gods and ancestors, let him follow his own dharma, O king.
As all rivers and streams come to their rest in the ocean, so all who follow the orders of life come to their rest in the householder.
Janaka said: From what, O great sage, does the class of the mixed classes arise? This I wish to hear; tell it to me, O best of speakers.
The scripture says that whatever offspring is born is the same as that from which it springs; how then has one born of a brāhmaṇa come to take on a distinct class?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Parāśara said: It is even so, O great king: one is the same as that from which he is born; but through the falling away of austerity he has come to assume a separate caste.
From a good field and from good seed a meritorious birth comes to be; but when either of the two is deficient, an inferior offspring is born.
From the mouth, from the two arms, from the thighs, and from the feet they were born, as Prajāpati created the worlds—so the knowers of dharma understand.
Born of the mouth are the brāhmaṇas, my son; born of the arms, the kindred of the kṣatriyas; born of the thighs, the men of wealth, O king; and born of the feet, the servants.
There is a scriptural origin only for the four classes, O bull among men; those others who are over and above these are held to be born of intermixture.
The Kṣatrajātis, the Ambaṣṭhas, the Ugras, and likewise the Vaidehakas, the Śvapākas, the Pulkasas, the Stenas, the Niṣādas, the Sūtas, and the Māgadhas—
the Āyogas, the Karaṇas, the Vrātyas, and the Caṇḍālas, O ruler of men—these are born from the four classes in mutual intermixture.
Janaka said: How can there be diversity of lineage among those born of the one Brahman? For there are indeed many lineages in this world, O best of sages.
How is it that the sages, born here and there—some sprung from a śūdra womb, and others from a womb other than their own—came to attain their own proper origin?
Parāśara said: O king, this is not to be taken as if the origin of the great-souled, whose selves are perfected by austerity, were defiled by a lowly birth.
Having begotten sons here and there, O king, the sages, by their own austerity, conferred upon them once again the state of being seers.
My grandfather of old, and Ṛśyaśṛṅga, and Kaśyapa, Vaṭa, Tāṇḍya, and Kṛpa, Kakṣīvān, Kamaṭha, and the rest—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and Yavakrīta, O king, and Droṇa, best of speakers, Āyu, Mataṅga, Datta, Drupada, and Matsya as well—
these, O Vaideha, attained their own true nature through reliance upon austerity; knowers of the Veda, they stood firm in self-restraint and in austerity.
Four root-lineages came into being, O prince: Aṅgiras and Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha and Bhṛgu.
The other lineages arose from works, O prince—they are but names, and through austerity they too win acceptance among the good.
Janaka said: Declare to me, O blessed one, the particular duties of the classes, and likewise their common duties; for you are skilled in all things.
Parāśara said: Receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and likewise teaching, O king, are the particular duties of the brāhmaṇas; protection is the glory of the kṣatriya.
Tillage, the herding of cattle, and trade belong to the vaiśyas; and the service of the twice-born is the work of the śūdra, O ruler of men.
The particular duties of the classes have now been proclaimed, O king; now hear from me at length, my son, the duties common to all.
Freedom from cruelty, non-injury, vigilance, the sharing of one's goods, the rites for the ancestors, hospitality, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—
contentment with one's own wife, purity, constant freedom from envy, knowledge of the self, and forbearance—these are the common duties, O king.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas—these three classes are the twice-born; among these their entitlement lies in the sacred duties, O best of two-footed beings.
The three classes, when settled in forbidden works, fall low, O king; but they rise up by resorting, as is fitting, to their own proper works here.
And it is settled that the śūdra does not fall low, nor is he entitled here to the sacraments; he does not attain to the dharma that proceeds from scripture, yet no prohibition of dharma has been laid upon him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The twice-born who are versed in scripture cite the example of the Vaidehaka śūdra, O great king; for I behold, O lord of men, the god Viṣṇu, the foremost principle of the whole universe.
By following the conduct of the good, the lowly who long to lift themselves up are not defiled when they perform the rites of prosperity, save for the use of the sacred mantras.
In just the measure that other folk take hold of the conduct of the good, in that same measure do they win happiness and repose at ease, both here and after death.
Janaka said: Is it conduct that defiles a man, or birth, O great sage? A doubt has arisen in me; this you should explain to me.
Parāśara said: Without doubt, O great king, both are makers of defilement—both conduct and birth; but mark the distinction.
He who, by birth and by conduct alike, pursues defiled deeds is corrupt; but he who, though base by birth, does no evil—he is the true man.
When a man eminent by birth performs a deed that is to be condemned, that deed defiles him; therefore it is the deed that is not fair.
Janaka said: O best of the twice-born, which deeds are in keeping with dharma, such that, when performed in this world, they never bring harm to living beings at any time?
Parāśara said: Hear from me, O great king, the answer to what you ask of me — those deeds free of harm, which always deliver a man to safety.
Having laid aside the sacred fires and sitting in devotion, freed of feverish care, they behold — step by step ascending the dharma-path that leads to the highest good.
Humble, endowed with discipline, ever devoted to self-restraint and well-tempered, they go forth to the ageless abode, having renounced all works.
All the varṇas, O king, having rightly performed the works of dharma and spoken words of truth, having cast off cruel unrighteousness while in the world of the living, attain to heaven — of this there can be no doubt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Parāśara said: A father, friends, elders, and wives are never, in this world, devoid of worth, O king — they are single-hearted in devotion, kindly in speech, well-wishing, and obedient alike.
The father is the supreme deity of men; greater even than the mother do they call the father. They declare the gaining of knowledge to be the highest gain, and those who have conquered the objects of the senses attain the supreme.
On the battlefield, where the strewn bed is the fire of arrows, the prince who meets his slaying is consumed there; he passes to worlds scarce won even by the immortals, and enjoys the fruit of heaven at his ease.
The weary man, the frightened, the one whose weapon has fallen, the weeping, the one who has turned his back, the one stripped of attendants, the unresisting, the sick, the suppliant — these one must not strike, O king, nor the child nor the aged.
Only one well-furnished with attendants, ready for combat, and come to an equal footing — such a son of the kṣatriyas may the king assail in battle.
Death at the hands of an equal, or of a superior, is the better lot — such is the settled view; but the slaying of the lowly and the timid is, for kings, a blameworthy deed.
To slay one who is wicked, of wicked conduct, and base, O lord of men, is itself declared a sin that leads to hell — so it is determined.
No one, O king, can save the man who has come under the power of his appointed end; yet one whose span of life still has a remainder, someone may indeed drag back from death.
Deeds being done by those who are dear should here be turned away from harm; one should not, by deeds whose nature is violence, seek long life at the cost of another's life.
But for all householders who long for the dissolution of self, the death is a fair one, dear son, when, performing their rites, they die upon the sandbanks of holy rivers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When one's span comes to its wasting, he attains dissolution into the five elements; this does not happen without cause — it is brought about by causes.
Thus a body comes to be, brought into being from a former body; this one has gone along the road, and this one has passed from house to house.
There is no second cause to be found in this, none other whatsoever; that body, joined to the embodied, abides among the things subject to release.
A frame of veins, sinews, and bones, crowded with what is loathsome and impure, a meeting-place of the elements, the senses, and the qualities —
this, bounded by the skin, the learned who ponder the inner Self call the body; the body, worn away even of its qualities, has come to its mortal end.
Abandoned by the embodied Self, motionless and devoid of consciousness, with its elements returned to their native source, it then sinks down into the earth.
Shaped by the working of past deeds, it is born here and there; this body, O prince of Videha, dies here and there; another such nature is seen, and likewise the casting-off that is the fruit of action.
Yet for a certain time, O king, this elemental self is not born again; it wanders about, like a great rain-cloud across the sky.
Then he is born again, O king, having gained here an abode; for the Self is higher than the mind, and the mind is higher than the senses.
Of beings, which are of two kinds, the moving are held supreme, O king; among the moving, the two-footed are deemed supreme; and among the two-footed, the twice-born are remembered as supreme.
Among the twice-born too, O lord of kings, the wise are deemed supreme; among the wise, those awakened to the Self; and among the awakened, those free of pride.
Death follows close upon the born — this is the settled truth for men; for deeds have their end, and the creatures pursue them according to their qualities.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the sun has reached its northern course, he who comes to his death under an auspicious constellation and at an auspicious hour, O king, is a doer of merit.
Without burdening folk with affliction, and having washed away his ill deeds, he dies here by a death that is not common, having performed his works according to his own power.
Poison, hanging, burning, slaying at the hand of robbers, and death by fanged beasts and by cattle — such a death is called a common one.
And the doers of meritorious deeds are not joined to these, nor to such as spring from violent intent, nor to many others of like common sort.
Departing upward, the life-breaths take their station, O king, for the doers of merit; from the middle for those of middling merit; and downward for those whose deeds were ill.
There is but one foe, and no second foe, O king, equal to a man's own ignorance; veiled by it and set upon by it, he performs deeds dreadful and most cruel.
He whose path to awakening lies through the dharma of sacred lore and the service of his elders — that foe, O prince, is to be conquered only by effort, and, churned away by the arrow of wisdom, it departs.
Having studied the Vedas in austerity as a celibate, and having here offered the five sacrifices as he is able, the man who desires dharma should go to the forest — having gathered up the higher good and established his lineage.
Even when forsaken by every enjoyment, one should not let the self sink into despair; for human birth, even in the state of an outcaste, is in every way hard to win, dear son.
For this is the foremost birth, O lord of the earth, on attaining which the self can be saved through deeds marked by auspiciousness.
"How may we not fall away from this birth?" — with this thought, O lord, men practise dharma, guided by their regard for the authority of sacred revelation.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The man who, having won this human state so very hard to attain, becomes a despiser of dharma and a slave to desire — he, surely, is deceived of his gain.
But he who, with an eye that goes before in loving-kindness, beholds living beings as lamps — for just so long as the flame does not die out, dear son —
by gentleness, by giving, and by kindly speech, becoming one to whom the sorrow and joy of others are as his own — he is exalted in the world beyond.
Giving, renunciation, and a fair form arise from the waters; the body, moreover, is to be cleansed by austerity — at the Sarasvatī, at Naimiṣa, at Puṣkara, and at whatever other holy places there are upon the earth.
For those whose life-breaths fall away within their homes, the bearing-out is then commended, and the conveying upon a bier to the cremation ground; and surely the burning, performed with purity and according to rule.
Sacrifice and nurture, offering for oneself and officiating for others, giving, and the practice of meritorious works; whatever rite to the fathers is commended, as one is able — all these a man performs for the sake of his own self.
The treatises on dharma, the Vedas, and the six auxiliary sciences, O lord of men, are ordained for the highest good of the man whose deeds are untainted.
Bhīṣma said: Thus indeed was all this declared of old by that sage of mighty soul to the king of the Videhas, for the sake of the highest good, O lord of men.
Bhīṣma said: And once again Janaka, lord of Mithilā, questioned the great-souled Parāśara, supremely resolved in the knowledge of dharma.
What is the highest good? What is the goal? O brāhmaṇa, what deed, once done, does not perish? Gone where, does one not return? Tell me this, O great sage.
Parāśara said: Non-attachment is the root of the highest good; knowledge is the supreme goal of knowing. Austerity rightly practised does not perish, as water does not perish in a field.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When, having cut the noose made of unrighteousness, one delights in dharma, and bestows the gift of fearlessness, then one would attain perfection.
Though a man give thousands of cattle and hundreds of horses, the gift of fearlessness to all beings surpasses that giving.
The wise man, though he dwell amid the objects of sense, dwells not in them at all; while the dull-witted dwells fast in them, even among objects that are unreal.
Unrighteousness clings not to the wise, as water clings not to the lotus-leaf; but to the unwise sin clings the more, as lac clings to wood.
Unrighteousness, awaiting its occasion, does not release the doer; the doer surely, in due time, meets with all of it. But those of perfected self, who behold the Self by direct conviction, are not broken by it.
He who, heedless of his mind, his deeds, and his senses, does not awaken, and whose self is clinging to things good and evil, attains to a very great fear.
He who is free of passion, has conquered anger, and is ever rightly poised — even while moving among the objects of sense, he is not joined to sin.
The dyke of dharma, bound firmly within its bounds, never gives way; and held in check like a swelling current, the store of merit grows abundant.
As a pure gem takes up, by its fixed disposition, the brilliance that comes from the sun, O tiger among kings, so does yoga come into operation.
As the essence of sesame seeds, from their resort to flowers, passes severally into a surpassing sweetness, so among men upon the earth whose selves are refined, the quality of goodness unfolds according to that on which it rests.
He forsakes his wife, and longs no more for fortunes, for fine horses and chariots and the manifold rites; when a man's mind is born toward the heaven of the gods, then his understanding parts from the objects of sense.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The man whose understanding is fastened upon the objects of sense, who never once awakens to his own true welfare — with a mind running after every passing state, he is dragged off like a fish by the bait, O king.
The world of mortals is a thing held together, each leaning upon the other, hollow at the core like the trunk of a plantain; it sinks down like a boat upon the waters.
No fixed time for dharma is appointed to a man, nor does death await a man's leisure; the practice of dharma is at all times fair — for a man stands ever within the very mouth of death.
As a blind man, well-acquainted with his own house, goes about by mere practice, so, with a mind made steadfast, the wise man goes to that goal.
Death is declared to lie within birth, and birth indeed rests upon death; the man unlearned in the laws of release, being bound, wanders round and round like a wheel.
As the lotus-stalk swiftly sheds the mire that clung to it, so the self of a man is here released by the mind; the mind leads the self onward, and it yokes the self to that course.
But he who, while toiling for another's ends, fancies it to be his own true task — clinging to the objects of the senses, he falls away from his own true task.
A downward course, a course athwart, or else the supreme course in heaven — the self attains by its own deeds, whether the man be wise here or otherwise.
As liquid is poured into a vessel of clay that has been fired, so the body, tempered by austerity, comes to enjoy its object.
He who devours the objects of sense shall, without doubt, not truly enjoy; but the self that renounces its enjoyments — that one is resolved upon the true enjoying.
Wrapped about as if in fog, given over to the cravings of sex and belly, his self veiled, he does not perceive the path, like one blind from birth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As a merchant gains wealth from the sea according to his purpose, so, upon the ocean of mortal existence, a creature's course follows from the knowledge of its deeds.
Roaming through this world made of day and night, in the form of old age, Death devours living beings, as the serpent swallows the wind.
The deeds it has itself done, the creature, once born, comes to meet; no one here obtains anything, pleasant or unpleasant, that was not first done by him.
Lying down, going forth, seated, or set upon the objects of sense — deeds good and evil come to meet a man at all times.
For having reached the farther shore, one does not resolve to cross back again; rare indeed is seen any falling of his into the great ocean once more.
As a laden boat upon the great waters is held by its cable, so the mind, by its exertion, draws the body back toward itself.
As, on every side, the several rivers are sewn fast unto the sea, so the primal nature is, by yoga, ever sewn fast and made one.
Men whose minds are caught by the manifold cords of affection, abiding within nature, sink down in despair, like a house of sand within the water.
For the embodied one who dwells within the house of the body, whose holy ford is purity, and who has set forth upon the path of wisdom — there is happiness, both here and in the world beyond.
Elaborate undertakings are bound up with toil, while the simple ones bring ease; all elaborate striving is for the sake of others, but the wise know renunciation to be one's own true good.
The circle of friends is born of intention, and kinsmen are bound by self-interest; wife, servants, and sons alike pursue each their own advantage.
Neither mother nor father can take on aught for another; the creature, whose only provision for the road is what it has given, feeds on the fruit of its own deeds alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Mother, son, father, brother, wife, and friends are set down upon the squares of life's board like dice cast at their stations on the gaming-cloth.
All the deeds a creature has wrought of old, good and evil, follow after the self; and the inner soul, perceiving that the fruit of deeds has come upon it, accordingly spurs the intellect to act.
He who, taking his stand upon resolve, gains himself helpers—no enterprise of his ever sinks into failure.
The man of undivided mind, steadfast, brave, resolute, and wise—prosperity never forsakes him, even as its rays never forsake the sun.
What the man of blameless soul undertakes with faith and resolve, with skillful means, with wonder, and with wisdom—that aim of his never comes to ruin.
Every creature, fixed by destiny, takes up of itself from the womb its own deeds, both fair and foul—both that which it has formerly wrought; and death, not to be escaped, walking evenly toward all, severed at the appointed time, brings the creature to the end of its deeds, as iron tools reduce a log to dust.
His native form, his own self-wrought course of life, his lineage and descent, his hoarded store of wealth—every man obtains all this as he has made it, by the good or evil deeds himself has done.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed in accordance with truth by that sage, O king, Janaka, foremost among those who know dharma, hearing it, attained the highest joy.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Truth, forbearance, self-restraint, and wisdom—these the learned among men extol in the world, O grandsire. What is your judgment in this matter?
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall relate to you an ancient tale, the dialogue here between the Sādhyas and the Swan, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Becoming a golden swan, the Unborn, the Eternal, Prajāpati went his rounds through the three worlds, and so he came to the Sādhyas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Sādhyas said: O bird, we are gods, the Sādhyas, and we entreat you; we ask of you the dharma of liberation, for you, it is said, are a knower of liberation.
We have heard you are learned and a speaker of steady wisdom; the fame of your good name flies abroad, O winged one. What do you deem the highest, O twice-born? In what does your mind take its delight, O great-souled one?
Teach us then our task, O best of birds—that one work which you deem foremost of all works, by doing which a man is here set free, and swiftly, from all bonds, O king of birds.
The Swan said: This is the task, O you who hope for immortality, as I have learned it—austerity, self-restraint, truth, and guarding of the self; loosing all the knots of the heart, one should bring the pleasant and the unpleasant alike under one's own control.
Let a man not be a stinger to the quick, nor a speaker of cruel words; let him not snatch from another by base means. That speech by which another would be made to shudder—galling and leading to evil worlds—let him not utter it.
Arrows of speech fly forth from the mouth, struck by which a man grieves through nights and days; they fall upon another's tender places—those the wise man should never loose against others.
If another should pierce him sorely with the arrows of abusive speech, calm alone should be his course here below; he who, being provoked to wrath, yet endures it, takes to himself the very merit of the other.
He who, when stung by insult and pride and the falseness of assault, restrains his blazing anger—untainted in mind, cheerful, free of malice—he takes to himself the merit of others.
Though reviled, I say nothing; though struck, I ever forbear; for the noble declare forbearance to be the best, and likewise truth, uprightness, and freedom from cruelty.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The secret essence of the Veda is truth; the secret essence of truth is self-restraint; the secret essence of self-restraint is liberation—this is the whole of the teaching.
The urge of speech, the urge of the mind, the urge of anger, the urge of craving, the urges of belly and loins—he who withstands these urges when they rise up, him I deem truly a brāhmaṇa and a sage.
The man free of anger is superior to the angry; the patient is superior to the impatient; the truly human is superior to the brutish; and the man of knowledge is foremost above the ignorant.
Though reviled, let him not revile in return; the very anger of the patient man burns up the reviler, and the patient one wins the merit that was his.
He who, though heavily abused, speaks neither harsh word nor flattering one; who, though struck, strikes not back out of steadfastness; and who wishes no evil to him that smites him—for such a man the gods ever yearn.
Let one forbear toward the worse, the better, and the equal alike; slighted, struck, and reviled, thus shall he attain perfection.
Ever, though lowly, I wait upon the noble; I have no craving, nor is there any anger in me; nor do I go about grasping after gain, nor do I tread any crooked path at all.
Though cursed, I curse not back at all; for I know self-restraint to be the very gate of immortality here. This secret brahman I declare to you: there is nothing higher than the truly human.
Freeing himself from sins as the moon emerges from the clouds, the steadfast man, stainless and awaiting his time, attains perfection through steadfastness.
He who is worthy of all men's worship, like a well-set pillar at a consecration; he of whom men speak words of high praise—he, his self subdued, goes indeed to the gods.
Men do not so wish to speak of the good qualities in a man as carping fault-finders wish to speak of his lack of worth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whose speech and mind are guarded, ever rightly composed—the Vedas, austerity, and renunciation are his; he would attain all this.
By the reviling and contempt of the foolish, the wise man grows; therefore let him not magnify another in retort, nor do violence to his own self.
Let the twice-born be content with contempt as though with nectar; for he who is despised sleeps in peace, while he who despises perishes.
Whatever sacrifice the angry man offers, whatever he gives, whatever austerity he practices, whatever he pours in oblation—Yama, son of Vivasvat, carries it all away from him; the toil of the angry man is in vain.
He whose four gates are well guarded, O best of immortals—the loins, the belly, the hands, and speech as the fourth—he is a knower of dharma.
Devoted to truth, self-restraint, uprightness, and freedom from cruelty, to firmness and to patience; ever given to sacred study, coveting nothing of others, fond of solitude—such a man attains the upward path.
Pursuing all these as a calf pursues the four teats, nowhere have I ever found anything more purifying than truth.
Moving to and fro among men and gods, I declare it: truth is the stairway to heaven, even as a boat for crossing from shore to shore.
With what sort of men a man dwells, what sort he attends upon, and what sort he wishes to become—of that sort the man becomes.
Whether he serves the good or the wicked, whether the ascetic or the thief, as a cloth takes on the color of its dye, so he passes under the sway of those he keeps.
The gods ever converse with the good; they do not come to look upon the realm of men. Let one be like the moon, even and serene, not like the restless wind—he who knows the realm of high and low.
When the inner person within the heart abides untainted, by that very thing are the gods pleased—by one who stands firm upon the path of the good.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those men who are ever given over to the loins and belly, thieves, and harsh of speech without cease—knowing them to be devoid of virtue, the gods shun them from afar.
The gods are not to be pleased by the man of base nature, who eats all things and does evil deeds; but with those men vowed to truth, grateful, and delighting in dharma, they hold communion.
Silence, they say, is better than speech; if one must speak, let him speak the truth—that is the second; let him speak what is in keeping with dharma—that is the third; let him speak what is pleasant—that is the fourth.
The Sādhyas said: By what is this world enveloped? By what does it fail to shine forth? By what does a man forsake his friends? By what does he fail to reach heaven?
The Swan said: By ignorance is the world enveloped; through envy it fails to shine forth; through greed a man forsakes his friends; through attachment he fails to reach heaven.
The Sādhyas said: Who, then, among brāhmaṇas takes delight alone? Who, alone, sits content amid many? Who, alone, is strong even though weak? And who among them does not pursue a quarrel?
The Swan said: The wise man among brāhmaṇas takes delight alone; the wise man, alone, sits content amid many; the wise man, alone, is strong even though weak; the wise man among them does not pursue a quarrel.
The Sādhyas said: What is the godhood of brāhmaṇas, and what is called their goodness? What is their badness, and what is held to be the merely human in them?
The Swan said: Sacred study is their godhood; the keeping of vows is called their goodness; slander is their badness; and death is said to be the merely human in them.
Bhīṣma said: Thus has this excellent dialogue of the Sādhyas been recounted. The field is verily the womb of deeds; goodness of being is called truth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, dear sire, you should tell me the distinction; for to you, the all-knowing, all is known, O best of the Kurus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: The followers of Sāṃkhya extol Sāṃkhya, and the twice-born adherents of Yoga extol Yoga; each declares the superiority of his own by reasons, to exalt his own side.
"How could one without a Lord be liberated?"—thus, O harrier of foes, the followers of Yoga, well-reasoning sages, declare their superiority by their arguments.
And this reasoning the twice-born followers of Sāṃkhya rightly declare: he who, having understood here all the conditions of being, has grown detached from the objects of sense—
—he, upon rising above the body, is most surely liberated, and not otherwise. This the greatly wise declare to be the Sāṃkhya, the very vision of liberation.
In support of one's own position the reasoning to be accepted is that which is cogent, sound, and salutary; for the judgment of the learned is to be accepted by such as you, esteemed among the learned.
The Yogas rest upon direct perception as their ground, the Sāṃkhyas upon the conclusions of scripture; both these doctrines are, in my view, truth, dear Yudhiṣṭhira.
Both these doctrines, O king, are held to be true knowledge, approved by the learned; practiced according to scripture, they lead to the supreme goal.
Equal in both is the purity enjoined, and equal the compassion toward all beings, O sinless one; equal is the upholding of vows—but their doctrines of how to see are not the same.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: If vow, purity, and compassion are equal in both here, O grandsire, then why is their doctrine of seeing not the same? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Passion, delusion, attachment, desire, and anger alone—cutting off from the very start these five faults by means of Yoga, the yogins attain that goal.
As great fishes, breaking the net, win the water again, so the yogins, freed of taint, attain that abode.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And just as strong beasts, breaking through the snare, would gain the open road, set free from every bond—
—so, O king, the yogins, endowed with strength, breaking the bonds born of greed, go stainless along the supreme and blessed path.
But weak beasts, O king, and others caught in the snares perish, beyond doubt; just so do men perish who are without the strength of Yoga.
And as feeble fishes caught in the net, O son of Kuntī, come to their end, O lord of kings, so do the very weak among yogins.
And as small birds, falling upon a net, O subduer of foes, caught fast therein come to ruin, while the strong win free—
—so, bound by the bonds born of deeds, O scorcher of foes, the weak among yogins perish, while the strong are set free.
And as a small, feeble fire dies out, O king, overlaid with great logs of fuel, so does the weak yogin, O lord.
And when that same fire, O king, gathering strength again and joined with the wind, may swiftly burn up the whole earth itself—
—so the yogin grown strong, blazing with splendor and of mighty power, like the sun at the hour of doom, may parch up the whole world.
And as a weak man, O king, is swept away by the current, so the feeble yogin is carried off, helpless, by the objects of sense.
But as an elephant holds back that very current, so, having gained the strength of Yoga, the yogin marshals and sets at naught the many objects of sense.
And the yogins, endowed with the strength of Yoga and become lords, enter at will, O Pārtha, into the Prajāpatis, the seers, the gods, and the great elements.
Neither Yama, nor the wrathful Ender, nor Death of terrible prowess hold sway, O king, over the yogin whose splendor is measureless.
Having attained power, O bull of the Bhāratas, yoga can fashion many thousands of selves, and with all of these the yogin may roam the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He may take possession of objects of sense, and again practice fierce austerity, and again draw them back in, O Pārtha, as the sun draws back the rays of its splendor.
For the yoga that is established in power and is lord over its own bondage, O ruler of the earth, the capacity to bring about liberation is assured beyond all doubt.
These powers in yoga have been declared by me, O lord of peoples; and by way of illustration I shall now further expound to you its subtle aspects.
Concerning the concentration of the self and concerning steady fixation, O sovereign lord, hear from me the subtle illustrations, O bull of the Bhāratas.
As the unwavering archer, fully composed, strikes the mark, so the yogin, rightly disciplined, attains liberation beyond all doubt.
As a man, with mind fixed motionless upon a vessel brimming with oil, would mount the stair, vigilant and disciplined in thought—
so yoga, having yoked the self in that motionless way, O ruler of the earth, renders the self stainless and radiant as the sun to behold.
And as a composed helmsman, O son of Kuntī, would swiftly steer a ship adrift upon the great ocean to the harbor, O ruler of the earth—
so the knower of truth, having yoked the concentration of the self through yoga, attains that station hard to reach, abandoning this body, O king.
And as a charioteer, well composed, having yoked his fine steeds, swiftly bears the bowman to the desired place, O bull among men—
so too, O king, the yogin, composed in his fixations, swiftly attains the supreme station, as a loosed arrow reaches its mark.
The yogin who, having entered the self into the Self, stands unmoving—as the slayer of fish destroys evil—attains the ageless abode.
In the navel, in the throat, in the head, in the heart, in the breast, in the two sides, and likewise in sight, in touch, and in smell, O man of measureless valor—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the yogin who, in these stations, composed in the great vow, rightly yokes by the self the subtle Self, O lord of peoples—
he, swiftly of stainless wisdom, having burned away action both good and ill, taking his stand on the highest yoga, is liberated, if he so wishes.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Taking what kind of food, and conquering what things, O descendant of Bharata, does the yogin attain power? This you ought to tell me.
Bhīṣma said: Devoted to eating broken grains and oil-cake, and devoted to abstaining from oily foods, the yogin would attain power.
Eating coarse barley-gruel for a long time, O subduer of foes, delighting in solitude, his self wholly purified, the yogin would attain power.
Passing through fortnights, months, and the varied seasons, and roaming through caves, drinking water mingled with milk, the yogin would attain power.
Or, fasting unbrokenly for a whole month continuously, O lord of men, his self rightly purified, the yogin would attain power.
Conquering desire and likewise anger, cold and heat, and the rains, fear, sleep, and breath, manly pride and the objects of sense—
discontent hard to conquer, and dreadful craving, O ruler of the earth, all sensations of touch, and torpor hard to conquer, O best of kings—
the great-souled ones, free from passion, of vast wisdom, kindle the subtle Self by the self through the riches of meditation and study.
But this is held to be a hard road, that of the learned brāhmaṇas; for none travels upon it in safety, O bull of the Bhāratas.
As some young man might safely make his way through a dreadful forest, full of many snakes and creeping things, pitted with holes, devoid of water, hard to pass, thick with thorns—
a road untrodden, wilderness-like, its trees scorched by forest fire, infested with robbers—safely traversing it,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
so when any twice-born one, having reached the path of yoga, practices it, should he safely turn back from that road, he is held to be greatly at fault.
It is easier to stand firm upon the sharpened edges of razors, O lord of the earth, than to stand firm in the fixations of yoga for those whose selves are unperfected.
Fixations gone awry, my son, lead one to an unhappy state, as ships without a pilot lead men astray upon the ocean, O king.
But he who stands firm, O son of Kuntī, in the fixations as prescribed, casts off death and birth, sorrow and joy alike.
This, perfected in the various treatises, has been set forth among the yogas; but the supreme yoga in its entirety is determined among the twice-born.
For that is the supreme, the great Brahman, O great-souled one—Brahmā the lord, and Viṣṇu the boon-giver, and Bhava, and Dharma, and the six-faced one, and the six mighty sons of Brahmā—
and grievous, vast darkness, and passion, and pure goodness, and the supreme primordial nature, and the goddess Siddhi, the wife of Varuṇa, and splendor entire, and great steadfastness—
the stainless lord of stars with its constellations, and all the gods, the serpents and the ancestors, all the mountains and the dreadful oceans, all the rivers, the woodlands, and the clouds—
the serpents, the mountains, the hosts of yakṣas and the quarters of space, the throngs of gandharvas, men and women—reaching each in turn, the great and great-souled yogin would enter in, liberated ere long.
And this auspicious discourse, O king, which has dwelt upon the god of mighty valor and wisdom—the great-souled one, his soul become Nārāyaṇa, surpasses all the yogas of mortals.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Rightly have you described, O king, the path of yoga approved by the cultivated, in due order, to a disciple, as one desiring his good.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But now, of the Sāṃkhya teaching, declare to me who ask the doctrine in its entirety; for whatever knowledge is in the three worlds, all of it is known to you.
Bhīṣma said: Hear from me this pure doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas, the knowers of the Self, ordained by enlightened ascetics, by sovereign sages such as Kapila and the rest.
In which no confusions whatever are to be seen, O bull among men, in which there are many virtues and the utter removal of faults.
Having reckoned up by knowledge the faulty objects of sense, O king—the human objects, hard to conquer, in their entirety, and the objects of the piśācas likewise—
having known the objects of the rākṣasas and likewise the objects of the yakṣas, having known the objects of the serpents and likewise the objects of the gandharvas—
having known the objects of the ancestors and of creatures that move as beasts, O king, having known the objects of the suparṇas and likewise the objects of the Maruts—
having known the objects of the royal sages and likewise of the brahmā sages, having known the objects of the asuras and likewise of the Viśvedevas—
having known the objects of the divine sages, and the lords of the yogas, and the objects of the lords of creatures, and likewise the objects of Brahmā—
and having truly understood the utmost span of life in the world, and having understood the highest truth of happiness, O best of speakers—
and the suffering that comes, when the time is at hand, to those who fall, the seekers of sense-objects—the suffering of those who fall into the state of beasts, and that of those who fall into hell—
and all the virtues of heaven and all its faults, O descendant of Bharata, and what faults there are in Vedic disputation, and what Vedic virtues there are—
and what faults there are in the yoga of knowledge and what virtues in yoga, O king, and what faults there are in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya and likewise its virtues, O king—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
having known goodness as tenfold in quality, passion as ninefold likewise, having known darkness as eightfold and the intellect as sevenfold likewise—
having known space as sixfold and mind as fivefold likewise, having known intellect as fourfold and great darkness as threefold—
and having known passion as twofold and goodness, again, as onefold, having understood truly the path and likewise the beholding of things at the dissolution—
those endowed with knowledge and discernment, refined by auspicious causes, attain blessed liberation—subtle, here passing beyond into space supreme.
Sight conjoined with form, and smell with the quality of odor, hearing thus attached to sound, and the tongue to the qualities of taste—
the body thus attached to touch, the wind resting in space, delusion clinging to darkness, greed resting upon objects—
Viṣṇu in stride, Śakra in strength, fire abiding thus in the belly, the goddess thus resting in the waters, and the waters resting upon heat—
heat clinging to the wind, the wind resting in space, space conjoined with the great principle, and the great principle resting in intellect—
intellect clinging to darkness, darkness resting upon passion, passion thus attached to goodness, goodness attached thus to the Self—
the Self attached to the Lord, and thus to the god Nārāyaṇa, the god clinging to liberation, but liberation attached to nothing whatsoever.
Having known the body joined with goodness, enveloped by the sixteen qualities, having known the inherent nature and the consciousness resident within the body—
having known the one Self standing in the midst, in which no evil is found, and as a second, the action of those who seek sense-objects, O king—
having truly known the senses and all the objects of the senses as resting in the Self, and the prāṇa and apāna and samāna, and the vyāna and udāna—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
having known the downward-coursing wind and again the onward-bearing wind, and likewise the remaining seven winds, sevenfold, again as prescribed—
having known the lords of creatures and the seers, and the many excellent paths, and the many groups of seven seers, and the royal sages, O scorcher of foes—
having known the divine seers and other great ones, the great seers resembling the sun, fallen from their sovereignty in the course of vast time, O king—
having heard of the destruction of great hosts of beings, O ruler of the earth, and having known the unhappy course of those who do evil deeds, O king—
and the suffering that there is in the Vaitaraṇī for those fallen in Yama's realm, and the inauspicious transmigrations through manifold wombs—
and the dwelling in the foul belly, a vessel of blood and water, amid phlegm, urine, and excrement, attended by a pungent stench—
in the conglomeration of seed and blood, encompassed by marrow and sinew, strewn with a hundred veins, the impure city of nine gates—
having understood the Self thus lodged, and the various yogas, O king, and of creatures sunk in darkness, their selves enveloped by what seems pleasant—
and of creatures of the quality of goodness—what is despicable, O bull of the Bhāratas, and what is censured in the estimation of the great, the Sāṃkhyas who know the Self—
having beheld the dread eclipses of the moon and likewise of the sun, the falling of the stars, and the wheeling round of the constellations—
and having understood the pitiful sundering of paired ones, O king, and having beheld the inauspicious devouring of one another among living beings—
and having understood the delusion of childhood and the inauspicious decay of the body, and goodness somewhere taking refuge when passion and delusion have come upon one—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
among thousands some one man takes refuge in the resolve for liberation; and having understood, on the authority of scripture, the difficulty of attaining liberation—
the high regard for things unattained, and again indifference once they are attained, and having understood, again, the wickedness of the objects of sense, O king—
and having beheld the inauspicious bodies of those whose breath has gone, O son of Kuntī, and having understood the suffering of dwelling among the families of creatures, O descendant of Bharata—
having known the dreadful destiny of the slayers of brāhmaṇas, the fallen, and of evil-souled brāhmaṇas addicted to the drinking of liquor, and having known the inauspicious destiny of those given over to the wives of their teachers—
And there are those, Yudhiṣṭhira, who do not conduct themselves rightly toward their mothers, and men who do not walk uprightly in the worlds together with their gods.
By that knowledge having discerned the destiny of those whose deeds are evil, and having discerned, one by one, the courses of those fallen into the wombs of beasts—
the manifold doctrines of the Vedas, and likewise the rotations of the seasons, the wasting away of the years, and the wearing down of the months,
having beheld the passing of the fortnights and the dwindling of the days, and having seen with his own eyes the waning and the waxing of the moon,
having seen the rising of the seas and again their ebbing, and the loss of riches and again likewise their increase,
having beheld the dissolution of unions and, above all, of the ages, and having seen the crumbling of the mountains and likewise the drying of the rivers,
having seen the decline of the orders and, again and again, the end that decay leads to, and having beheld old age and death and birth and all sorrows,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
having known the body's defects and their suffering as it truly is, and having rightly understood the body's frailty, O Bhārata,
and having discerned all the faults of the self that lodge within the self, and having understood the foul odors that rise from one's own body—
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What faults arising from one's own limbs do you see, O man of measureless valor? This whole doubt of mine you ought to resolve for me truly.
Bhīṣma said: Five faults in the body, O lord, the wise declare—the Sāṃkhyas, followers of Kapila, who know the path. Hear of them, O slayer of foes.
Desire and anger, fear, sleep, and breath as the fifth—so it is called. These faults are seen in the bodies of all embodied beings.
By forbearance they cut off anger, desire by the renouncing of resolve, sleep by the cultivation of purity, and fear by vigilance; and the fifth, breath, they cut off by lightness of diet, O king.
Knowing the virtues by hundreds of virtues, and the faults too by hundreds of faults, having truly discerned the manifold causes by their hundreds of varied causes,
having seen this world as like the foam upon the waters, wrapped in the hundredfold illusions of Viṣṇu, resembling a painting on the wall of the mind, hollow as a reed's pith and devoid of worth,
having seen it like a pit of darkness, like a bubble of the rain, all but perishing, void of happiness, ending in ruin, sunk in nonbeing, with rajas drowned in tamas, helpless as an elephant mired in mud,
the Sāṃkhyas, O king, of vast wisdom, casting off the body fashioned for procreation, by the all-pervading and mighty Sāṃkhya whose object is knowledge and the knowable, O king—
the impure odors born of rajas, those of like kind born of tamas, and the holy odors born of sattva, all sprung from contact and lodged in the body—these they swiftly sever with the sword of knowledge and the rod of austerity, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then this fearful flood whose water is sorrow, whose great pools are anxiety and grief, whose mighty crocodiles are disease and death, whose great serpent is terror,
whose tortoise is darkness, whose fish is passion, whose mire is affection, whose fastness is old age, whose island is the sense of touch—they cross over by wisdom, O subduer of foes.
whose abyss is action, whose shore is truth, whose firmness is steadfast vows, O king, whose swift mighty current is violence, whose great mines are the manifold tastes,
whose great jewels are the manifold delights, whose driving wind is the fever of sorrow, whose great whirlpool is grief and craving, whose great elephant is keen disease,
whose raft is the frame of joined bones, whose foam is phlegm, O subduer of foes, whose pearl-mine is charity, fearful, whose coral is the pool of blood,
whose roar is laughter and outcry, hard to cross by reason of its manifold lore, whose brine is the impurity of weeping and tears, whose haven is the renunciation of attachments,
whose surging tide is the round of births again and again, whose cities are sons and kinsfolk, whose bounding shore is non-violence and truth, whose great billow is the giving up of life,
whose isle of refuge is the attainment of the Vedānta, whose ocean is compassion for all beings, whose hard-won goal is liberation, vast as the sea that holds the mare's-mouth fire—
this the perfected sages cross by the discipline of knowledge, O Bhārata, and having crossed the hard passage of birth they enter the stainless firmament.
Then the Sun bears those well-doing Sāṃkhyas upward by his rays, entering them as through the fibre of a lotus stalk and bearing them past the realms of sense, O king.
There the bearing wind, Pravaha, receives them, O Bhārata—those ascetics free from passion, perfected, endowed with vigor, rich in austerity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Subtle, cool, sweet-scented, and pleasant to the touch, O Bhārata, the best of the seven winds, which travels to the blessed worlds—that wind bears them, O son of Kuntī, to the supreme goal beyond the sky.
The sky bears them, O lord of the world, to the supreme goal that is rajas; rajas bears them, O king of kings, to the supreme goal that is sattva;
sattva bears them, O pure of soul, to the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa; and the Lord, pure-souled, bears them by his own self to the Supreme Self.
Having reached the Supreme Self, become stainless with their abode in that Being, they are fitted for immortality and do not return, O mighty one. That is the supreme goal, O Pārtha, of the great souls who are beyond the pairs of opposites.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Having reached that highest station, the Blessed One, do those of steadfast vows remember their births and deaths, or do they not, O sinless one?
What herein is the truth, that you ought to tell me as it is; for apart from you there is no other man whom I should ask, O Kaurava.
This would be a grave flaw in liberation—if the seers who have won perfection, and the highest ascetics, still dwell upon that very knowledge.
I deem the dharma marked by active engagement the highest, O king; for to one immersed in the supreme knowledge, what could be more painful than such remembering?
Bhīṣma said: Rightly, my son, have you asked a most difficult question; even the awakened are bewildered in this matter, O bull of the Bhāratas. Yet hear herein the supreme truth, well set forth by me.
There where the supreme understanding of the great-souled followers of Kapila abides, even the senses come to awareness, O king, of the embodied one's own body; those are the instruments of the self, and the subtle one perceives through them.
But once forsaken by the self, like wood and like a wall, they perish—of this there is no doubt—even as foam upon the great ocean.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While the embodied one sleeps together with the senses, O tormentor of foes, the subtle self moves everywhere, like the wind moving through the sky.
He sees aright and feels the touches, O mighty one, perceiving as before, in their entirety, even here, O Bhārata.
Here all the senses, each in its own station and as ordained, dissolve through their want of mastery, like serpents whose venom has been drawn.
But overmastering, in their very own stations and on every side, the subtle motions of all the senses, the self ranges abroad—of this there is no doubt.
All the qualities of sattva, and again the qualities of rajas, and all the qualities of tamas, and the qualities of the intellect, O Bhārata,
and likewise the qualities of the mind, and so the qualities of ether, and the qualities of wind, O righteous one, and again the qualities of fire,
and the qualities of water, O Pārtha, and the qualities of earth as well—pervading all these qualities with his whole being, he is the Knower of the Field, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
And the self proceeds to the Knower of the Field, and the two kinds of action, good and ill, and the senses too proceed to him, O lord, as disciples to a great-souled master.
And transcending even Nature, he goes to the imperishable Self, the supreme one whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, beyond the pairs of opposites and beyond Nature.
Freed from merit and demerit, having entered that flawless, attributeless Supreme Self, he does not return, O Bhārata.
But what remains here—the mind, my son, and the senses, O Bhārata—come back in due season, doing the bidding of their teacher.
And it is possible in a short time to attain peace for one who seeks the qualities, thus disciplined, O son of Kuntī, joined to right knowledge and bent on liberation.
The Sāṃkhyas, O king, of vast wisdom, go to the supreme goal; with this knowledge, O son of Kuntī, no knowledge is to be found equal.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let there be no doubt of yours herein: the Sāṃkhya is held to be the supreme knowledge—imperishable, fixed, unmanifest, the primeval, eternal Brahman.
That which is without beginning, middle, or end, beyond the pairs of opposites, the agent, everlasting, unmoving at the summit, and eternal—so the men of tranquil soul declare it.
That from which proceed all the transformations of creation and dissolution, and which they extol in the scriptures and the supreme seers proclaim,
and all the brāhmaṇas and the gods and the people learned in scripture—as the supreme God devoted to Brahman, infinite, beyond all, undecaying,
the brāhmaṇas longing for him proclaim him, their minds set on the qualities—rightly disciplined the followers of Yoga, and the Sāṃkhyas of boundless vision.
Of him who is without form, O son of Kuntī, the Sāṃkhya is his form—so runs the sacred tradition; these, they say, are the marks by which he is known, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Twofold are the beings here upon the earth, O lord of the earth, named the moving and the unmoving; but the moving is the more excellent.
Whatever great knowledge is found among the great, O king—in the Vedas, in the Sāṃkhya systems, and likewise in Yoga, and whatever manifold ancient lore is seen—all of that is comprised within the Sāṃkhya, O lord of men.
And whatever is seen in the great chronicles, and whatever is in the science of statecraft honored by the wise, O king, and whatever knowledge there is in the world here—all that great wisdom too is comprised within the Sāṃkhya, O great-souled one.
Tranquility and supreme strength, and subtle knowledge, are duly set forth therein; subtle austerities and joys as well are duly ordained in the Sāṃkhya, O king.
For when it falls short, O Pārtha, the Sāṃkhyas go ever and easily to the gods; and having ranged through those worlds, then, their purpose fulfilled, they descend again among devout brāhmaṇas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And casting off the body, the Sāṃkhyas enter liberation, O Pārtha, as the dwellers of heaven enter the sky; thereafter those twice-born ones are devoted, beyond all else, to the precious Sāṃkhya honored by the wise, O king.
For no going to the brute wombs is seen for them, nor a downward course, the abode of evildoers; nor are those twice-born ones among the unwise—they who are devoted to this knowledge, O king.
The Sāṃkhya, vast, supreme, ancient, a great ocean, stainless, of noble beauty—the whole Sāṃkhya, O king, the great-souled Nārāyaṇa upholds, immeasurable.
This truth I have declared to you, O lord of men: Nārāyaṇa is this whole ancient universe; at the time of creation he makes the creation, and at the time of dissolution he devours it again.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What is that which is called the imperishable, from which one does not return again? And what is that which is called the perishable, from which one returns again?
I wish to grasp clearly the distinction between the imperishable and the perishable, O slayer of foes, in its very truth, O mighty-armed delight of the Kurus.
For you are called a treasury of knowledge by the brāhmaṇas versed to the end of the Vedas, by the highly blessed seers, and by the great-souled ascetics.
Few are the days remaining to you while the sun keeps its southern course; once the blessed sun has turned, you will go to the supreme goal.
Once you have departed, from whom shall we hear of the good? You are the lamp of the Kuru line, shining with the substance of knowledge.
Therefore this I wish to hear from you, O upholder of the Kuru race; I am not sated here, O king of kings, listening to such nectar as this.
Bhīṣma said: Upon this I shall recount to you an ancient tale, the dialogue of Vasiṣṭha and Janaka the Terrible.
Of Vasiṣṭha, foremost of seers, seated there with the radiance of the sun, King Janaka inquired concerning the supreme knowledge that leads to the highest good.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Saluting the son of Mitra and Varuṇa as he sat there—skilled in the supreme science of the self and sure in the knowledge of the soul's destiny—with hands joined in reverence,
in well-articulated, humble, sweet, and unobtrusive speech, King Karāla-Janaka of old questioned that best of seers.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear of the supreme, eternal Brahman, from which the wise attain to no return again.
And that which is called the perishable, wherein this world melts away, and that which is declared the imperishable—auspicious, secure, and free from ill.
Vasiṣṭha said: Hear, O lord of the earth, how this world perishes, and what it is that does not perish, and through how vast a span of time it endures.
Know that an age is twelve thousand years, and a kalpa four times that; a thousand kalpas turning round make up what is called the Day of Brahmā, and the Night, O king, is of equal length—at whose end He awakens.
Then the formless Self, Śambhu, the source of all good, brings forth the Great One, the firstborn being of endless action, embodied and all-pervading—endowed with the powers of minuteness, lightness, and attainment, the lordly, imperishable Light.
With hands and feet on every side, with eyes, heads, and faces turned in every direction, with ears in every quarter, it stands enveloping all things in the world.
This blessed one is Hiraṇyagarbha; he is remembered as Intellect (buddhi), and among the Yogins as the Great (mahat), and likewise as Viriñca.
In the Sāṃkhya treatise too he is recited under many names, manifold in nature, varied in form, the Soul of the Universe, remembered as the One Imperishable Syllable.
Since by him the whole threefold world, manifold in essence, is enveloped through his own self, and because of his many forms, he is remembered as the All-formed (Viśvarūpa).

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This one, having undergone transformation, brings forth from himself by himself the Ego-principle (ahaṃkāra)—he of great splendor begets the self-conscious Lord of Creatures.
From the Unmanifest the Manifest arises; this they call the creation born of Knowledge—namely the Great One; while the Ego-principle they call the creation born of Ignorance.
The lawless and the lawful alike arose together from one source; they are proclaimed as Knowledge and Ignorance by those who ponder the meaning of scripture and treatise.
Know, O son of Pṛthā, that the creation of the elements from the Ego-principle is the third; and within the Ego and the elements know the fourth, the modified creation.
Air, fire, then ether, water, and earth likewise; sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as well.
Thus this group of ten arose all at once, beyond doubt; know it, O king of kings, as the fifth, the elemental creation, full of purpose.
Ear, skin, the two eyes, tongue, and smell as the fifth; and speech, the two hands, the two feet, the anus, and the organ of generation as well—
these are the organs of perception and the organs of action; they all came into being here at once, together with the mind, O son of Pṛthā.
This set of twenty-four principles abides in all forms; knowing which, the Brāhmaṇas who perceive truth grieve no more.
This is declared to be the body in all embodied beings throughout the three worlds; it is to be understood so, O best of men, among gods, men, and Dānavas alike,
among Yakṣas, spirits, and Gandharvas, among Kiṃnaras and great serpents, among Cāraṇas and Piśācas, among celestial sages and night-roaming demons,
among gnats, insects, and mosquitoes, among foul worms and mice, in the dog and the dog-cooker, the basket-weaver, the Caṇḍāla, and the Pulkasa,
in elephant, horse, ass, and tiger, in tree and in cow as well—whatever possesses bodily form anywhere, this same teaching applies.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In water, on earth, and in the sky—nowhere else: such is the settled conclusion that there is an abode for embodied beings; thus have we heard it handed down.
All of this much, my son, that bears the name of the Manifest, perishes; day after day the elemental self decays, and therefore it is remembered as the Perishable (kṣara).
This too has been called Imperishable—even as this world perishes; they declare the world, whose essence is delusion, to be the Unmanifest bearing the name of the Manifest.
The Great One too, the firstborn, is eternal: this is the exposition of the Perishable, told to you, O great king—from which one does not return again.
The twenty-fifth is Viṣṇu, beyond the principles yet named a principle; because it is the refuge of the principles, the wise call it the True (tattva).
Whatever the formless created as the Manifest, that very form it presides over; the twenty-fourth is the Manifest, while the formless is the twenty-fifth.
That very Self abides in the heart within all forms—the conscious one, ever giving consciousness, eternal, taking on all forms yet itself formless.
Subject to a Nature whose law is creation and dissolution, it is itself without creation or dissolution; it ever ranges within her domain, free of the qualities yet called by their name.
Thus this Great Soul, skilled in creation and dissolution, undergoing transformation and possessed of Nature, in its want of wisdom takes these to be its own.
Yoked to darkness, goodness, and passion, it dissolves into one womb after another here below, through its failure to awaken and its keeping company with the unawakened.
Its very nature being to dwell in fellowship, it thinks, 'I am no other than this'; and saying, 'What I am, that I am,' it turns and follows after the qualities.
Through darkness it attains to manifold states marked by darkness, through passion to those marked by passion, and through resort to goodness to those that are good.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
White, red, and black—these are the three colors; know that all these colors belong to Nature.
Those of darkness go to hell, those of passion to the human estate, while the partakers of goodness, sharing in happiness, go to the world of the gods.
By unmixed sin one reaches the animal womb, by merit and sin together the human state, and by merit alone the rank of the gods.
Thus the wise call that whose sphere is the Unmanifest the Perishable; but this twenty-fifth one comes forth into action through knowledge alone.
Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, through its failure to awaken, the unawakened one follows along, and so passes from one body into thousands of bodies.
Now into thousands of animal wombs, now even among the gods, it is born—through its conjunction with the qualities and, again, through the wasting of those qualities.
From manhood it goes to heaven, and from heaven back to manhood; from manhood it attains the place of hell, in endless succession.
As the cocoon-spinning worm binds itself fast forever with the threads and strands it spins, so does this one, though itself qualityless, bind itself with the qualities.
Though beyond all pairs of opposites, it meets with them in womb after womb here below—in headache and eye-disease, in toothache and quinsy,
in dropsy and the disease of piles, in fever, swellings, and cholera, in leucoderma, leprosy, and burning fever, and in skin-eruption and epilepsy too,
and whatever other manifold pairs of opposites, born of Nature, arise in embodied beings—these too this one claims as its own; out of conceit it claims them, and its good deeds likewise.
Clad in a single garment, or ill-clad; sleeping ever upon the bare ground; lying crouched like a frog; or seated in the hero's posture;
wearing rags; sleeping or standing under the open sky; lying upon a bed of bricks, or upon a bed of thorns;

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
all this it claims as its own through want of true understanding; and so too the threefold qualities—goodness, passion, and darkness—and righteousness, wealth, and desire. Thus does the self, which is but Nature, divide up its own self in this way.
The cries of svadhā and vaṣaṭ, of svāhā and the acts of homage; officiating at sacrifices and teaching, giving and—so they say—receiving gifts, sacrificing and studying, and whatever else there is besides—
and in birth and death, in dispute, and in slaughter too—all this, made up of good and evil, they call the path of action.
It is Nature, the goddess, who brings about the great dissolution as well; at the day's end she gathers in these qualities, and the One alone abides.
As the sun draws in its net of rays at the appointed time, so does this one, again and again, claim all things as its own for the sake of sport.
These manifold qualities, in the likeness of its own self and dear to its heart, it transforms in just this way, performing the works of creation and dissolution.
Attached to the path of action and inaction, it becomes endowed with the three qualities though it transcends them; engaged upon the path of action and inaction, it thinks, 'This is indeed I.'
