It thinks: 'Thus these pairs of opposites are ever present with me; these arise for me alone, and these afflict me.'
'And all these are to be surmounted by me'—so it thinks, O lord of men, in its want of wisdom; and it thinks the like of its good deeds as well.
'These fruits are to be enjoyed by me when I have gone to the world of the gods; and here itself I shall enjoy this harvest of good and evil that ripens.'
'And happiness alone is to be pursued; once I have secured my happiness, my felicity shall endure to the very end, birth after birth.'
'Yet sorrow without end shall also be mine here, through what I have done; for the human state is great suffering, and so too is the plunge into hell.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'And from hell I shall in time come again to the human state.' From manhood to godhood, from godhood back to manhood, and from manhood to hell it passes by turns.
He who thinks thus, forever selfless yet enveloped by the qualities of the self, by reason of that is born again among gods and men and in hell.
Forever wrapped in the sense of 'mine,' it revolves there alone, through thousands upon millions of creations, in forms that all end in death.
Whoever performs action whose nature is fruit good and evil, he himself, embodied, eats of that fruit throughout the three worlds.
It is Nature that performs the action whose nature is fruit good and evil, and it is Nature, roaming where she wills, that eats of it throughout the three worlds.
In the animal womb, in the human state, and likewise in the world of the gods—these three stations one should know to belong to Nature.
Nature they declare to be without distinguishing mark, yet by its marks we infer it; and the mark of the Spirit too one perceives only by inference.
Having taken on another mark—the wound-free mark of Nature—and presiding over the gateways of the wounds, it imagines the actions to be in the self.
All the organs beginning with the ear, and the five organs of action beginning with speech, function only amid the qualities, together with the qualities; yet it thinks, 'It is I who do these, and these senses are mine.'
Though devoid of the senses, he imagines, "I am wounded," though he is woundless; though without attribute, he conceives the marked self as his own, and the self that is beyond time he takes for one bound by time.
The unreal he takes for the real self, the untrue for the true; deathless, he conceives the self as subject to death; unmoving, he takes the self to be in motion.
Fieldless, he takes the field to be the self; uncreated, he conceives himself as created; though beyond austerity, he thinks the self performs austerities; though without going, he imagines the self to have a course.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Free of becoming, he takes the self as caught in becoming; free of fear, as fearful; imperishable, he conceives the self as perishable — thus, lacking awakened insight, he misconceives.
Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, through being unawakened and through keeping company with the unawakened, he passes through thousands of millions of creations, each ending in a fall.
From abode to abode he passes through thousands of dwellings, each ending in death — in the wombs of beasts, in the human state, and likewise in the world of the gods.
As the moon dissolves within its sheaths, so this man, lacking insight, dissolves there again and again by the thousand, all through being unawakened.
The womb is the fifteen digits, and that, it is taught, is the abode; know this for certain — the moon is the sixteenth digit.
In the digit the man without insight is born ceaselessly, again and again; they consume his dwelling, and yet once more he is born.
But the sixteenth digit is subtle — let that be understood as the moon; it is not consumed by the gods, rather it is that which sustains the gods.
Thus, having wasted away that digit, he is born again, O best of kings; for this is seen to be his very nature, and from the wasting of it release is declared to come.
So, taking this sixteen-digit body, which bears the name of the Unmanifest, to be "mine," he keeps revolving within that very round.
So too the twenty-fifth principle, the Self — through its failure to awaken, though it is stainless and wholly pure and frequents the pure breath of liberation —
the pure Self becomes as if impure, O lord of earth; and even one awakened, by keeping company with the unawakened, may sink back into unawakening.
In that very way the unawakened one is to be understood, O best of kings; through resorting to threefold-strained Nature he becomes a creature of Nature.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Karāla-Janaka said: This union of the two, the Imperishable and the perishable, is held to exist; and the union of woman and man too, O blessed one, is said to be of just that kind.
Without the man no woman here conceives a child, and without the woman no man can bring a form into being.
By their mutual union, by their resting one upon the other's qualities, form is brought forth — and so it is in all the wombs.
Through the union sought for pleasure, by their resting on one another's qualities, in due season form is brought forth — and I shall set out the proof of this.
What qualities are the man's here, and what the mother's qualities — bone, sinew, and marrow we know to come from the father, O brāhmaṇa,
while skin, flesh, and blood are mother-born — so we have heard; thus, O best of the twice-born, it is taught in the Vedas and the treatises.
What the Veda declares is authority, and what the treatise declares and is recited; and the authority of Veda and treatise is the eternal standard.
Just so I see Nature and Spirit forever bound together, O blessed one; and therefore no path of release exists, it seems to me.
Or if there be some other proof drawn from a different ground, declare it to me truly, for you are in every way one of direct vision.
We too long for release, and we yearn for that which is free of affliction — bodiless, ageless, divine, beyond the senses, owning no master.
Vasiṣṭha said: This proof from Veda and treatise that you have stated is indeed so — but you have not grasped it as it truly is.
You hold the text of both the Veda and the treatise in your memory, O lord of men, but you do not know the truth of the text as it really is.
For one bent on retaining the text in Veda and treatise, yet who does not know the truth of the text's meaning — his retaining of it is in vain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He merely carries a burden who does not know the meaning of the text; but for one who knows the truth of the text's meaning, his learning of the text is not in vain.
Such a man, when asked the meaning of the text, is fit to declare it; for by approaching its truth he attains the meaning of that text.
But one of coarse understanding who would expound the text's meaning in assemblies — how, being dull of discernment, shall he expound the text with sure conclusion?
A flawed mind cannot state the conclusion truly; and even a man of some self-command thereby falls into a state of ridicule.
Therefore listen, O lord of kings, to how this is rightly seen as it is, among the great souls who follow Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
What the followers of Yoga see is followed also by the Sāṃkhyas; and he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one — he is the man of true insight.
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, bile, marrow, bone, and sinew — all this belongs to the senses, dear one, this of which you have just spoken.
From substance arises substance, and likewise sense from sense; one obtains body from body, and seed from seed in the same way.
But for this embodied Self, which is without sense, without seed, without substance, how shall there be qualities, since the great Self is free of qualities?
Qualities arise within qualities and there too they subside; thus qualities are born of Nature, and yet in themselves they have no being.
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, bile, marrow, bone, and sinew — know these eight, together with semen, to be of Nature indeed.
Male and not-male and the threefold-marked — this is held to belong to Nature; he who is neither truly male nor not male is called the one possessed of marks.
Nature, herself without mark, is apprehended through the marks born of her, just as the seasons are ever made manifest in form by their flowers and fruits.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the same way, even the markless is apprehended through inference; the twenty-fifth, dear one, is of unbound nature amid the marks.
Without beginning or end, infinite, all-seeing, free of affliction — yet merely through self-conceit it is called, amid the qualities, the qualityless one.
Qualities belong to one possessed of qualities; whence should there be qualities for the qualityless? Thus do those people understand it who discern the qualities.
But when this Self conceives all the qualities of Nature as its own, then it appears as one possessed of qualities — though by the highest view it is otherwise.
That which the Sāṃkhyas and the Yogins everywhere declare to be beyond the intellect — the awakening, the supremely wise — comes through the forsaking of the unawakened state.
The unawakened Unmanifest, endowed with qualities, they call the Lord; and the qualityless Lord too, eternal and the abiding overseer.
The twenty-fifth, beyond Nature and the qualities, the wise ones understand — they who are skilled in Sāṃkhya and Yoga and who seek the highest.
When the awakened ones, fearful of the births that come with worldly states, fully comprehend the awakening one beyond the Unmanifest, then they bring it to that selfsame oneness.
This is the right discernment and that the wrong discernment, drawn severally from the awakening one and the unawakened, O subduer of foes.
Thus, set one against the other, is told the proof of the perishable and the Imperishable: oneness they call the Imperishable, and manifoldness is called the perishable.
When this one, grounded in the twenty-fifth, proceeds wrongly, then his vision is of oneness, and yet there is also a failure to see, in manifoldness.
This is the distinct proof of the principled and the unprincipled; but the creation that ends in the twenty-fifth the wise call the principled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That which is beyond the twenty-fifth they call the proof of the unprincipled; class upon class, and discipline, and principle beyond principle — eternal.
Karāla-Janaka said: Manifoldness and oneness — this you have declared, O best of seers; yet I see the proof of these two as still beset with doubt.
So too of the unawakened and the awakened and of the awakening one, O sinless one, with my coarse understanding I do not see the truth of this — there is no doubt.
And the cause you declared concerning the Imperishable and the perishable — that too, through my unsteady understanding, has all but slipped away from me, O sinless one.
This I wish to hear: the vision of manifoldness and oneness, and the awakened, the unawakened, and the awakening one, in their truth.
And knowledge and ignorance, O blessed one, the Imperishable and the perishable, and Sāṃkhya and Yoga in their fullness — both severally and together.
Vasiṣṭha said: Come then, I shall set forth for you that which you ask — the practice of Yoga, O great king; hear it from me first, by itself.
The chief practice of the followers of Yoga is meditation, their supreme strength; and that meditation, those versed in the Veda declare to be of two kinds.
Single-pointedness of mind, and likewise the restraint of breath: the restraint of breath belongs to the qualified, while the stilling of the mind belongs to the unqualified.
In passing water, in voiding the bowels, and in eating, O ruler of men — at these three times let him not yoke himself; the rest of the time, intent, let him practice the yoga.
Withdrawing the senses from the objects of sense by the mind, the sage — by tens or by twelves, and then beyond the twenty-fourth —
with urgings the wise man should urge on that Self, the ageless one abiding there, of which the thoughtful have spoken.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And by these the Self is ever to be known — so we have heard in succession; it is a thing graspable only by one whose mind is undiminished, and not otherwise — this is the settled truth.
Freed from all attachments, light in his eating, his senses conquered, in the first watch of the night and in the last let him fix the mind upon the Self.
Having steadied the host of the senses by the mind, O lord of Mithilā, and having made the mind firm by the intellect, let him be unmoving like a stone,
unshaken as a post, immovable as a mountain; then the wise, who know the ordinances of the rule, declare him to be yoked.
He hears not, nor smells, nor tastes, nor sees, nor is aware of touch, nor does the mind form any intention;
he conceives nothing, nor is he aware of aught, like a log of wood — then the thoughtful call him yoked, returned to his own Nature.
As a lamp burning in a windless place — so is he seen: steady and unmoving, rising upward, taking no sideways course.
Then let him behold that Self, on whose being seen it is said — "the inner Self that dwells in the heart" — the Knower to be known, dear one, by such as I am.
Like the seven-tongued fire without smoke, like the sun bright with rays, like the fire of lightning in the sky — so is the Self seen within the self.
Whom the great souls behold, the steadfast and the thoughtful, the brāhmaṇas grounded in the womb of Brahman — the wombless one, immortal in essence.
That very one they call subtler than the subtle, greater than the great; it abides within, fixed in all beings, yet is not seen.
By the instrument of the intellect, by the lamp of the mind, the maker of the world may be seen — dwelling beyond the great darkness, dear one, himself untouched by darkness.
He is called the dispeller of darkness by those who know the truth and have crossed to the far shore of the Veda — stainless, free of gloom, without mark, known by the name of the markless.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This indeed I deem the Yoga of those who practice Yoga, the very mark of Yoga; seeing thus, they behold the Self, the ageless and supreme.
Thus far have I declared to you, in truth, the vision of Yoga; now I shall set forth the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, the proof by full enumeration.
The expounders of primal nature call the Unmanifest the supreme Prakṛti; and from it, O best of kings, there arose the Great Principle (mahat), which is the second.
From the Great Principle comes the I-sense (ahaṃkāra), the third, so we have heard; and from the I-sense, the followers of Sāṃkhya declare, arise the five elements.
These are the eight sources of evolution; and the modifications are sixteen — the five gross particulars together with the five senses.
Just this is the enumeration of the principles, say the wise ones learned in the rules and ordinances of Sāṃkhya, ever devoted to the Sāṃkhya path.
Whatever is born from a given source dissolves again into that very source; in reverse order they are reabsorbed, and they are sent forth by the inner Self.
In forward order they come to be, and in reverse order they dissolve; constantly the qualities merge into the qualities, as the waves of the ocean into the sea.
Such is the creation and dissolution of Prakṛti, O best of kings: oneness in dissolution, and multiplicity when it sends forth creation. Thus, O lord of kings, is it to be understood by those who ponder what is to be known.
The Unmanifest is its presiding ground — this too is the illustration. The knower of truth sees the oneness and the multiplicity that follow upon Prakṛti: oneness in dissolution, and multiplicity in active unfolding.
Making itself manifold, it brings forth Prakṛti, whose nature is to generate; and over that Field the Great Self, the twenty-fifth principle, presides.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is called the Presider, O lord of kings, by the best of ascetics; because he presides over the Fields, he is the Presider — so we have heard.
He knows the Field, the Unmanifest, and so is called the Knower of the Field; and because he lies within the city of the Unmanifest, he is also called the Puruṣa, the indwelling Person.
The Field is one thing, and the Knower of the Field is said to be another; the Field is declared to be the Unmanifest, while the Knower is the twenty-fifth principle.
Knowledge is one thing, and the object of knowledge is said to be another; the knowledge is declared to be the Unmanifest, while the object to be known is the twenty-fifth principle.
The Unmanifest is called the Field, and likewise sattva, and likewise the Lord; it is without lordship and without selfhood, while the twenty-fifth is the true principle endowed with selfhood.
So much is the Sāṃkhya doctrine, the teaching of full enumeration; it carries out the reckoning, and it declares the nature of Prakṛti.
The followers of Sāṃkhya, reckoning truly the twenty-four principles together with Prakṛti, hold that the twenty-fifth is free of those principles and stands beyond them.
As long as the twenty-fifth has not awakened its self, it is called the one who is awakening; but when it knows the Self, then it becomes the Absolute, alone and unconditioned.
Thus has the right vision been truly expounded to you; and they who know it in this way attain to oneness and equality.
This is rightly named the demonstration, the direct apprehension of Prakṛti; these are the principles bound up with the qualities, while the Other, devoid of qualities, stands apart.
For those who abide thus there is no returning again; because of their imperishable being there is for them an undecaying state, free of mutual involvement.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those of single-minded fixity may see, yet their vision is not perfect; again and again, O subduer of foes, they fall back into the Unmanifest.
Though they know all this, yet for want of full awakening to the whole they will become manifest once more, falling under the sway of the manifest.
All this has been called the Unmanifest, the All; but the twenty-fifth is not the All. For those who know him truly, no fear is to be found.
Vasiṣṭha said: So much of the Sāṃkhya doctrine has been told to you, O best of kings; now learn from me, in due order, of Knowledge and Ignorance.
The Unmanifest, subject to creation and dissolution, they call Ignorance; and the twenty-fifth, free from creation and dissolution, they call Knowledge.
Learn, in due order, of their mutual relation in ignorance, my son, as the seers have expounded the teaching of this Sāṃkhya.
For all the organs of action, the organs of perception are reckoned their knowledge; and for the organs of perception, the gross particulars are their knowledge — so we have heard.
For those gross particulars, the wise declare the mind to be their knowledge; and for the mind, they call the five elements its knowledge.
For the five elements, the I-sense is their knowledge — herein is no doubt; and for the I-sense, the intellect is its knowledge, O lord of men.
For the intellect, Prakṛti, the Unmanifest, the supreme lord of the principles, is to be known as its knowledge, O best of men; and it is reckoned the highest ordinance.
Of the Unmanifest, they declare the twenty-fifth to be the supreme Knowledge; the All of all has been called the object to be known of knowledge, O king.
Knowledge is called the Unmanifest, while the object to be known is the twenty-fifth; and so again the Unmanifest is the knowledge, while the knower is the twenty-fifth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the truth of the meaning of Knowledge and Ignorance I have told you in detail; now learn from me what is meant by the Imperishable and the Perishable.
Both these have been called perishable, and both these also imperishable; but I shall declare the reason why they are so set forth in truth.
Both these are held to be without beginning and without end, both indeed lords; both are spoken of as bearing the name of true principle by those who ponder knowledge.
Because it is subject to creation and dissolution, they call the Unmanifest perishable; for it transforms itself again and again for the creation of the qualities.
It gives rise, one from another, to the qualities beginning with the Great Principle; and because it presides over them, this twenty-fifth is called the Field.
But when it draws that net of qualities back into the Unmanifest as its self, then together with those qualities the twenty-fifth dissolves away.
The qualities merge into the qualities, and then Prakṛti alone remains; and when, my son, even the Knower of the Field dissolves into that Field —
then Prakṛti, named after the qualities, attains imperishability; and from the withdrawal of the qualities, O prince of Videha, it attains the state of being without qualities.
And just so the Knower of the Field, when the knowledge of the Field is exhausted, becomes through Prakṛti free of qualities — thus have we heard it taught.
When this one becomes perishable, it then comes to recognize Prakṛti as endowed with qualities, and likewise the quality-less nature of its own Self.
Then he becomes wholly pure through the abandonment of Prakṛti, when the wise one knows, 'I am one thing, and she is another.'
Then he attains to separateness and no longer falls into commingling; and with Prakṛti, O lord of kings, he is seen as unmingled and other.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But when he comes to loathe that net of qualities born of Prakṛti, and beholds the Other as the seer, then, seeing, he is no longer consumed by fever.
'What have I done all this while, I who through all this time have followed birth after birth, as a fish, through want of knowledge, follows the net!'
'For I myself, through delusion, have pursued one birth after another from birth to birth, as a fish, mistaking the net for water, follows after it here.'
'As a fish, through ignorance, does not perceive its distinctness from the water, so I, through ignorance, fail to know my own Self and its separateness.'
'Shame upon me, the unawakened, who, sunk again in this, have through delusion pursued one birth after another, from birth to birth!'
'This other here shall be my kinsman; with this one comes my liberation. Having come to equality and oneness, I am of the same nature as he.'
'I see here an equality: I am indeed like unto him; for he is stainless and manifest, and I too am even such as he.'
'I, who through the delusion of ignorance entered into activity with the unknowing one — I, unattached, have dwelt all this time with her who is attached.'
'Brought under her power, I did not awaken all this time. How shall I dwell with her any longer, the cause of high, middling, and low estates?'
'How could I, in my unawakened condition, have come into this dwelling-together with her? Now at last let me be steadfast.'
'No longer will I enter into dwelling with her; for all this time I have been deceived. I, the changeless, have been deceived by her who is full of change.'
'Yet this is no fault of hers; the fault herein is mine, who became attached here and turned my face away from the truth.'
'Hence, formless, I have dwelt within manifold embodied forms; and though formless, I have taken on a bodied self, overpowered by the sense of "mine."'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Through the leadership of Prakṛti, dwelling in this womb and that, what has been done to me — to one free of "mine" — by the sense of "mine," as I passed through womb after womb with a mind whose awareness was lost!'
'I have no further business here with her, whose very self is made of the I-sense, who, making herself manifold, would yoke me to herself again and again. Now have I awakened, free of "mine," free of the I-sense.'
'Casting off the sense of "mine" ever wrought by her through the I-sense, and forsaking her, I shall take refuge in the One free of all affliction.'
'With him I shall attain equality, not with this unconscious one; fitting for me is union with him, not oneness with her.' Thus, through supreme awakening, the twenty-fifth comes to enlightenment.
He attains imperishability, the unafflicted, abandoning the perishable — the Unmanifest, whose nature is to become manifest, both with qualities and without. Having first beheld the Quality-less, he becomes such as It, O prince of Mithilā.
This demonstration of the Imperishable and the Perishable, replete with knowledge, has been told to you by me here, according to the testimony of sacred tradition.
What is free of doubt, subtle, enlightened, and stainless I shall declare to you yet further; learn it as it has been heard.
Sāṃkhya and Yoga have been expounded by me from the testimony of the two scriptures; and that very teaching declared in Sāṃkhya is itself the doctrine of Yoga.
The awakening knowledge of the followers of Sāṃkhya, O lord of the earth, is therein set forth with full clarity, out of desire for the good of disciples.
And the skilled declare that scripture to be vast; yet in this scripture of the followers of Yoga it is, as it were, curds again and arrow again — set forth ever afresh.
Beyond the twenty-fifth they see no further principle, O ruler of men; for the followers of Sāṃkhya, the supreme has been there described just as it is.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Awakened, the Unawakened, and the one in the act of awakening, truly considered — the one in the act of awakening and the Awakened — such, they declare, is the teaching of Yoga.
Vasiṣṭha said: Now hear of the Unmanifest, the Unawakened, and this ordering of the qualities; for she upholds the qualities, sends them forth, and withdraws them again.
Ceaselessly here, for the sake of play, transforming herself, O ruler of men, and making her self manifold, she beholds those very forms.
Her, thus transforming herself, the one in the act of awakening does not yet comprehend; and because of his awareness of the Unmanifest, they call him the one in the act of awakening.
Yet he does not comprehend the Unmanifest, whether with qualities or without; and therefore at times indeed they call this Unmanifest the Unawakened.
If the twenty-fifth comes to comprehend this Unmanifest, he becomes the one in the act of awakening, yet still of the nature of attachment — so runs the sacred word.
On this account they call the unfailing Unmanifest the Unawakened; and because of his awareness of the Unmanifest, they call him the one in the act of awakening.
And that twenty-fifth, the great Self, does not yet comprehend the twenty-sixth — the stainless, the Awakened, the immeasurable, the eternal.
But the twenty-sixth ever comprehends both the twenty-fifth and the twenty-fourth; for he pervades both the seen and the unseen — both, those of great splendor.
But the Unmanifest does not comprehend that Brahman, the Absolute, my son; the twenty-fifth alone does not behold the twenty-fourth as the Absolute.
As long as the one awakening thinks of himself, 'I am other,' so long is he still possessed of Prakṛti, with his vision fixed upon the Unmanifest.
But when he comes to know the supreme Intelligence, wholly pure and stainless — the twenty-sixth — then, O tiger among kings, he attains to the state of the Awakened.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then he forsakes the Unmanifest, whose nature is creation and dissolution; free of the qualities, he knows Nature to be bound up with the qualities and devoid of consciousness.
Thereupon, through his vision of the Unmanifest, he becomes one whose nature is absolute; uniting with the Absolute and liberated, he attains the Self.
This, they say, is that Reality, itself beyond the principles, ageless and deathless; through its dependence on the principles it seems to possess them, yet it does not, O bestower of honor. The wise declare that the principles are twenty-five.
This one, my son, does not possess the principles; rather, the wise one is beyond the principles. He swiftly relinquishes the principles, for that is the mark of the awakened.
"I am the twenty-sixth"—when the wise man is grasped by this knowledge, ageless and deathless, by the power of the Absolute alone he attains identity with it, beyond all doubt.
Awakened by the twenty-sixth yet still in the act of awakening, he is not yet fully wise: this is what is called their difference, taught from the testimony of the Sāṃkhya scriptures.
For the twenty-fifth principle, joined with the conscious one, there arises oneness with it, so long as it does not awaken through the intellect to the distinction.
Awakening, it attains identity with the unawakened, O Maithila; this Self, free of attachment by nature, thus comes to bear the character of attachment, O lord of men.
But on reaching the Self that is free of attachment, they know the twenty-sixth, the unborn; the all-pervading one forsakes the Unmanifest when it awakens to this, and through the awakening of the twenty-sixth it forsakes also the unfathomable twenty-fourth.
This, O sinless one, has been explained to you as the unawakened, the awakening, and the truly awakened, according to the testimony of scripture; just so much of their difference and oneness is to be discerned by those whose sight is the teaching.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As the gnat is other than the fig in which it dwells, so are these two distinct; as a fish in water is other than the water, so is their difference perceived.
Just so is the difference and the oneness of these two to be understood; this, bound up with the knowledge of the Unmanifest, is declared to be liberation.
This twenty-fifth principle, which abides within bodies, is the one that must be set free—so they declare—out from the domain of the Unmanifest.
Thus and not otherwise is it freed: such is the settled conclusion. Uniting with the Supreme, it takes on the nature of the Supreme.
Uniting with the pure, it becomes pure in nature; with the awakened, it becomes wise; with the liberated, its nature becomes that of the liberated, O bull among men.
Uniting with one bound to duty, it takes on the character of duty; and uniting with the liberator, it likewise becomes liberation itself here.
Of pure deeds and pure it becomes, of measureless radiance; and uniting with the stainless Self, it too becomes stainless of soul.
So too, uniting with the Absolute, it becomes absolute in soul; and uniting with the independent, it attains independence.
This much have I told you truly, O great king, in its real and very essence; receive this teaching without envy—the eternal Brahman, pure and primordial.
To a man merely devoted to the letter of the Veda, O king, this supreme teaching should not be given by you; but to one who longs to know, this enlightening instruction—for the sake of awakening—should be given to him who bows in reverence.
Nor is it to be given to the man of false soul, to the deceitful, to the coward, to the crooked of mind, nor to one who flaunts learning to torment others; learn now to whom you should give it.
To one endowed with faith and with virtues, ever turned away from slandering others, to one of pure discipline and wise, active in rites, forbearing, and benevolent.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
To one of solitary conduct who loves the sacred rule, free of contention, deeply learned and discerning, who does not condone what is harmful, and is capable of restraint and of the inner peace of embodied beings.
To one most destitute of these virtues it must not be given—this supreme Brahman, which they call utterly pure; what is bestowed on such a one will not be joined with blessing, and by giving to the unworthy the teacher of dharma himself loses his merit.
Even though one offered this whole earth filled with jewels, this is not to be given to a man without vows; but to one who has mastered his senses, this supreme teaching should without doubt be imparted by you, O lord of men.
Karāla, let no fear of any kind be yours; today you have heard this supreme Brahman, declared just as it is—most sacred, sorrowless, utterly without beginning or middle.
Unfathomable in birth, deathless, O king, free of disease, fear gone, and auspicious—looking upon it, cast off now all delusion, having understood this, the very essence of knowledge.
This was obtained of old from the eternal Hiraṇyagarbha as he spoke it, O lord of men, when by earnest effort that one of fierce splendor had been won over—just as the eternal Brahman has now been won by you.
As you have questioned me, O lord of men, so have I declared this to you today; thus did I obtain from Brahman that great and ancient knowledge of those who know liberation, O lord of men.
Bhīṣma said: This has been declared the supreme Brahman, from which the twenty-fifth returns no more, O great king, according to the testimony of the highest seers.
He who, even after attaining supreme knowledge, does not truly awaken, though awakening, undergoes return again; but the one who knows it as it is becomes ageless and deathless.
This highest of all knowledges, which brings the supreme good, I have told you truly, my son, having myself heard it from the divine seer, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From Hiraṇyagarbha the great-souled seer Vasiṣṭha received it, and from Vasiṣṭha, tiger among seers, Nārada obtained this.
From Nārada this eternal Brahman became known to me. Grieve not, O lord of the Kurus, now that you have heard this supreme state.
For him by whom the perishable and the imperishable are known, no fear exists; but fear does exist for him who does not know this, O son of Pṛthā.
And the deluded soul, through ignorance, suffering torment again and again, undergoes after death thousands of births, each ending in death.
He passes through the world of the gods, the animal realm, and the human state as well, if in time he is purified out of that ocean of ignorance.
The dreadful ocean of ignorance is called the Unmanifest, the unfathomable, wherein day after day living beings are submerged, O Bhārata.
Since you have crossed beyond that unfathomable, eternal Unmanifest, therefore you are free of passion and free of darkness, O son of Pṛthā.
Bhīṣma said: A certain son of Janaka, while roaming in the hunt through a lonely place, beheld in the forest a lord of brahmins, a seer who carried on the lineage of Bhṛgu.
Seating himself near that seated sage and bowing his head in reverence, then with the seer's leave, the prince Vasumat asked him this.
"Holy one, what is that good which avails a man, here or hereafter, when his body is impermanent and he is in the grip of desire?"
Thus honored and questioned, the great-souled one of mighty austerity then spoke to him this word that brings about the good.
"If you desire what is not contrary to the mind, here and hereafter, then with senses restrained turn away from whatever is hurtful to living beings.
Dharma is the welfare of good men; dharma is the refuge of the good. From dharma, my son, the three worlds with all that moves and is unmoving have come forth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
O craver of sweet things, why do you not reach freedom from thirst for desires? You see the honey, dull-witted one, but you do not see the precipice beneath.
Just as familiarity with knowledge must be cultivated by one who seeks its fruit, so too familiarity with dharma must be cultivated by one who seeks its fruit.
For a bad man who desires dharma, pure action is hard to accomplish; but for a good man who desires dharma, even hard action is easily done.
He who in the forest pursues the pleasures of the village is no better than a villager; while he who in the village lives by the conduct of the forest is as one who dwells in the wild.
In the dharma of thought, word, and deed place your faith with a collected mind, having weighed the merits and demerits of withdrawal or of action.
And one should ever give abundantly to good men, free of envy, what has been sought with vows and purity and offered with honor at the proper place and time.
What has been gained by righteous means one should bestow upon the worthy, casting off anger; and having given, one should neither regret it nor boast of it.
Free of cruelty, pure, self-controlled, truthful of speech, established in uprightness, pure in birth and conduct, and learned in the Veda—such a brahmin is a worthy recipient.
A wife honored and devoted to one husband is desired here for the purity of lineage in birth; and the learned one who chants Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman and performs the six rites is called a worthy recipient.
The very same act may be dharma or adharma with respect to each particular man, according to the distinction of recipient and deed, and with regard to place and time.
As a man wipes a little dust from his limb with ease, so the removal of sin is accomplished only by great and strenuous effort.
As clarified butter becomes a wholesome medicine for one who has been duly purged, so the dharma that bears on the hereafter brings happiness to one whose faults have been expelled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The mind moves among all beings, toward the good and toward the evil; drawing it away from the evil, one should set it down upon the good alone.
Honor all that is done, by all, everywhere; and wherever your inclination lies within your own dharma, there let dharma be ordained at your pleasure.
O man of unsteady soul, stand firm in resolve; dull-witted one, become wise; O unquiet one, grow calm; O foolish one, conduct yourself as the wise do.
The good, here and hereafter, can be attained by inner energy accompanied by right means; and the root of that is supreme steadfastness.
The royal seer Mahābhiṣa, lacking steadfastness, fell from heaven; while Yayāti, his merit spent, regained the worlds through steadfastness.
By attending upon ascetics, the righteous, and the learned, you will gain abundant understanding, and so will you come to the good."
And he, endowed with a noble nature, having heard the words spoken by the sage, turned his mind away from desire and set his understanding upon dharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That which is freed from dharma and adharma, freed from all dependence, freed from birth and death, and freed from merit and demerit—
that which is auspicious, eternal, fearless, ever imperishable and undecaying, pure, eternal, and effortless—of that you ought to speak.
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall relate to you an ancient tale, the dialogue of Yājñavalkya with Janaka, O Bhārata.
The illustrious Janaka, son of Daivarāti, foremost among those skilled in questioning, put a question to Yājñavalkya, the best of seers.
"How many are the senses, O brahmin-seer? How many are the primary natures held to be? What is the Unmanifest, what the supreme Brahman, and what lies beyond even that?
Of the origin and the dissolution, and likewise of the reckoning of time, you ought to speak, O lord of brahmins, to me who longs for your grace.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Out of ignorance I question you, for you are a treasury made wholly of knowledge; I wish to hear all of this beyond any doubt."
Yājñavalkya said: Hear, O guardian of the earth, what you ask after—the supreme knowledge of the followers of Yoga, and of the followers of Sāṃkhya especially.
There is nothing unknown to you; yet you wish to test me. Still, when questioned one must answer—this is the eternal law.
Eight are the primary natures declared, and sixteen the modifications; and the contemplators of the inner self say there are seven that are manifest.
The Unmanifest, the Great One, and the I-maker; earth, wind, ether, water, and fire as the fifth—
these are the eight primary natures; now hear from me also the modifications: hearing, skin, eye, tongue, and smell as the fifth—
sound and touch, form, taste, and likewise smell; speech, the two hands, the two feet, the organ of excretion, and the organ of generation as well—
these are the particulars within the five great elements, O lord of kings; and these, the organs of cognition together with their particulars, O Maithila—
the mind they declare to be the sixteenth—they who contemplate the course of the inner self, both you and other learned men skilled in the discernment of the principles.
From the Unmanifest the Great Self arises, O son of Pṛthā; this the wise call the first creation, born of the primordial Nature.
From the Great Principle, O lord of men, arises the I-sense; this they call the second creation, and it is remembered as having the nature of intellect.
From the I-sense comes into being the mind, whose nature is the qualities of the elements; this third creation is called that which springs from the I-sense.
From the mind, O lord of men, arise the great elements; this fourth creation they designate as the mental one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as well — this the contemplators of the elements call the fifth creation, the elemental one.
Ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose as the fifth — this they call the sixth creation, remembered as the seat of manifold reflection.
Below arises the host of organs of action, O lord of men; this they call the seventh creation, remembered as that pertaining to the lower organs.
The upward-flowing and the crosswise-flowing then arise, O lord of men; this the wise call the eighth creation, the natural one.
The crosswise-flowing and the downward-flowing then arise, O lord of men; this the wise call the ninth creation, the natural one.
These nine creations, and the four-and-twenty principles, O lord of men, have been declared according to scripture and tradition.
Now hereafter, O great king, learn from me, in truth, the reckoning of time for this quality, as it has been declared by the great-souled ones.
Yājñavalkya said: Learn from me, O best of men, the reckoning of time for the Unmanifest. Five thousand kalpas, doubled, are called its day.
Its night, too, is of the same length, O lord of men; and when awakened, it first creates the herbs, the sustenance of all embodied beings.
Then it created Brahmā, born from the golden egg; that form is the embodiment of all beings — thus have we heard.
Having dwelt a year within the egg and come forth, the great sage, the Prajāpati, formed of half the whole earth and of half the heaven.
This is recited in the Vedas, O king, concerning heaven and earth; and between those two halves the Lord made the sky.
And for this one too the reckoning, declared by those versed in the Vedas and their auxiliaries, is: ten thousand kalpas less a quarter are called its day; and the contemplators of the inner self declare its night to be of the same length.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The sage creates the I-sense, a being of divine nature, and four other sons; before his body, the Great Sage. These, it is heard, are the fathers of the very forefathers, O best of kings.
The gods are the sons of the forefathers, and by the gods the worlds, moving and unmoving, are pervaded, O best of men — thus have we heard.
The I-sense, the supreme abode, created the elements in five ways: earth, air, sky, water, and light as the fifth.
For this one too, while it performs the third stage, they declare its night to be five thousand kalpas, and its day is said to be just as long.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth — these are the particular qualities, O king of kings, in the five great elements, by which beings are pervaded day after day, O lord of the earth.
These long for one another, delight in one another's welfare, esteem one another, and likewise contend with one another.
Slain by one another through their alluring qualities, yet imperishable, they revolve here in this very world, entering the wombs of beasts.
Three thousand kalpas are called the day of these, and the night is of the same length — and so too for the mind, O lord of men.
The mind ranges, O king of kings, over all that is experienced by the senses; yet the senses do not see — here it is the mind alone that sees.
The eye sees forms, but through the mind, not through the eye alone; when the mind is distracted, the eye, though looking, does not see. So it is said that all the senses perceive only thus.
When the mind is stilled, O king, the senses too come to rest; but when the senses are stilled, the mind does not come to rest. Thus one should recognize that the senses have the mind as their chief.
For the mind is called the lord of all the senses; into it all beings here enter, O greatly renowned one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yājñavalkya said: The reckoning of the creation of the principles, and likewise the reckoning of time, have been declared by me in order; now hear from me the dissolution as well.
How Brahmā — without beginning or end, eternal and imperishable — withdraws creatures and creates them again and again.
Then, perceiving the waning of his day, his mind turned to slumber as the night comes on, the blessed Unmanifest urged onward the I-sensed Person.
Then the sun of a hundred thousand rays, urged on by the Unmanifest, made himself twelvefold, blazing like fire.
Swiftly with his blaze he burns up the fourfold web of creatures — the womb-born, the egg-born, the sweat-born, and the sprout-born, O lord of men.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, all that is fixed and moving is destroyed, and the earth becomes everywhere level like the back of a tortoise.
Having burnt the world, he of boundless might leaves the earth alone; then swiftly it is filled on every side with mighty waters.
Then, encountering the fire of Time, that water passes to destruction; and when the water is gone, O king of kings, the great fire blazes forth.
That immeasurable, exceedingly mighty, blazing fire, the warmth of all beings, the seven-flamed — straightway then,
the mighty wind, eightfold and powerful, of boundless breath, ranging crosswise, upward, and downward, devoured it.
That irresistible and terrible wind the sky swallows into itself; and roaring beyond the sky, the mind swallows up the ranging sky.
The I-sense, the Prajāpati, the Self of all, swallows the mind; and the Great Self, knower of past, present, and future, swallows the I-sense.
And even that incomparable Self, the universe — Śambhu the Prajāpati, possessed of minuteness, lightness, and attainment, the Lord, the imperishable light —
with hands and feet on every side, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side, with ears on every side, abides in the world, enveloping all.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The heart of all beings, of the measure of a thumb at the joint, the infinite great-souled Lord swallows up the universe.
Then all became imperishable, undecaying, and flawless — the sinless creator of beings past, future, and present.
This dissolution has been duly expounded to you, O king of kings; now let the relation to the self, to the elements, and to the deities be heard.
Yājñavalkya said: The feet, say the Brāhmaṇas who perceive the truth, are the inner principle; that which is to be traversed is the elemental aspect; and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity there.
The organ of excretion, say those who see the true meaning, is the inner principle; voiding is the elemental aspect; and Mitra is the presiding deity there.
The organ of generation, they say according to the teaching of yoga, is the inner principle; pleasure is the elemental aspect; and Prajāpati is the deity.
The hands, they say according to the teaching of Sāṃkhya, are the inner principle; the deed to be done is the elemental aspect; and Indra is the presiding deity there.
Speech, they declare according to the teaching of scripture, is the inner principle; what is to be spoken is the elemental aspect; and Fire is the presiding deity there.
The eye, they say according to the teaching of scripture, is the inner principle; form here is the elemental aspect; and Sūrya is the presiding deity there.
The ear, they say according to the teaching of scripture, is the inner principle; sound there is the elemental aspect; and the quarters of space are the presiding deity there.
The tongue, they say according to the teaching of the principles, is the inner principle; taste alone is the elemental aspect; and the Waters are the presiding deity there.
The nose, they say according to the teaching of scripture, is the inner principle; smell alone is the elemental aspect; and Earth is the presiding deity.

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
He who is joined with passion and darkness is born in the wombs of beasts; and he who is joined with passion, darkness, and goodness attains the human state.
The wise declare that, for those freed from both merit and demerit, there is an abode that is everlasting, imperishable, indestructible, and without fear.
It is the highest origin of the knowers — a station flawless and unfailing, beyond the senses, without seed, the dispeller of birth, death, and darkness.
That supreme thing seated in the Unmanifest, about which you have questioned me, O lord of men — this very one, abiding in primordial Nature, is called the Stationary.
And this one, O king, is held to be without consciousness and seated in Nature; yet, presided over by the conscious Self, it both creates and withdraws the world.
Janaka said: Both of these, O great sage, are without beginning or end, formless, unmoving, unshakable, and without flaw.
Both are imperceptible, O tiger among sages — how then is the one said to be without consciousness, while the other, possessed of consciousness, is called the Knower of the Field?
For you, O chief of brāhmaṇas, cultivate the doctrine of liberation in its entirety; I wish to hear, in truth, the whole of the law of liberation.
Its existence, its solitary state, and likewise its separateness — and also the station of departure for the embodied soul when it is loosed from the body.
Tell me, O twice-born, what station it reaches in due time, and the knowledge of Sāṃkhya in its essence, and Yoga as well, each apart.
And you ought to declare, in truth, the omens of death, O best of men; for all this is known to you as clearly as an āmalaka fruit upon the palm.
Yājñavalkya said: The qualityless one cannot be made to possess qualities, my friend, O lord of peoples; and how the qualified one is also unqualified — learn that from me as it truly is.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For it is by reason of the qualities that one is called qualified, and the qualityless one is without qualities — thus have the great-souled sages, the seers of truth, declared.
The Unmanifest, whose nature is the qualities, abides amid the very qualities and makes use of those same qualities; and by its very nature it is unknowing.
The Unmanifest does not know, while the Spirit by its very nature is the knower; yet it forever imagines, 'There is nothing higher than I.'
For this reason the Unmanifest must be without consciousness; and by its eternity and imperishability it is, in truth, otherwise than the perishable things.
When, through unknowing, it brings forth the creation of the qualities again and again, and when it does not know itself, then it is here called the Unmanifest.
Because it is the maker of the elemental principles, it is called the bearer of the nature of those principles; and because it is the maker of the wombs, it is called the bearer of the nature of the womb.
Because it is the maker of the primal natures, it bears the nature of primal Nature; and because it is the maker of seeds, it is called the bearer of the nature of the seed.
And because it gives birth to the qualities, it bears the nature of bringing-forth; and because it is the maker of dissolutions, it bears the nature of dissolution.
By its being seed, by its being Nature, and by its being dissolution as well, by its indifference, its otherness, and its self-conceit — it is the Sole.
The pure ascetics, whose fever is gone through the science of the Self, deem the Unmanifest now transient, now eternal — thus indeed have we heard.
They declare the Unmanifest to be a oneness, and the Spirit likewise to be a manyness — those who, full of compassion for all beings, abide in pure knowledge alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Spirit is one thing, and the Unmanifest another — the latter unsteady yet bearing the name of steady; for just as the muñja reed is drawn from its inner stalk, so does this come to be.
One should know the gnat to be one thing and the fig-tree another; the gnat is not stained there by its contact with the fig.
Likewise the fish is one thing, and the water is held to be another; and the fish is in no way stained by the touch of the water.
For the fire is one thing and the cauldron another — know it ever thus, good sir; and that fire is not defiled by its contact with the cauldron.
And here the lotus-leaf is one thing, while the water is held to be another; the lotus-leaf is not stained there by the touch of the water.
The dwelling-together and the parting of these pairs are perpetual; but common folk do not always see it as it truly is.
But those who see it otherwise have no right vision; they enter manifestly into dreadful hell, again and again.
This supreme vision of the Sāṃkhyas has been fully reckoned out for you; for having reckoned it thus, the Sāṃkhyas have attained to absolute solitude.
And for those others skilled in the principles, this is the teaching; hereafter I shall expound the vision of the Yogins as well.
Yājñavalkya said: The knowledge of Sāṃkhya has been declared by me; now learn from me the knowledge of Yoga, as heard and as seen, in its truth, O best of kings.
There is no knowledge equal to Sāṃkhya, no power equal to Yoga; both walk a single path, and both are held to be without end.
Men of little understanding see them as separate, each apart; but we, O king, with certainty see them as one and the same.
That very thing which the Yogins behold is also seen by the followers of Sāṃkhya; he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one is the knower of truth.
Know the other Yogins to have Rudra as their chief, O scorcher of foes; and in that very body they roam through the ten directions.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Until the dissolution of the world, my friend, by means of the subtle eightfold Yoga he roams happily through the worlds, having renounced all, O sinless one.
In the Vedas, too, the wise call Yoga eightfold; they declare the subtle eightfold Yoga, and no other, O best of kings.
They declare the highest practice of the Yogins to be twofold — with qualities and without qualities — even as the scriptures teach.
There is the fixing of the mind and the restraint of the breath, O king: the restraint of breath is with quality, while the fixing of the mind is without quality.
Where one would be seen letting go of the vital breaths, O best of the Maithilas, there an excess of wind arises; therefore one should not practise it so.
In the first watch of the night twelve exercises are enjoined; and having slept at midnight, in the last watch likewise twelve exercises.
Thus, by one grown calm, self-controlled, given to solitude, delighting in the Self, and awakened, the Self must be yoked — of this there is no doubt.
Having cast off the fivefold faults of the five senses — sound, touch, and form, taste, and smell as well —
and having drawn back imagination and its surrender, O Maithila, having settled the whole host of the senses within the mind,
and having established the mind likewise in the I-sense, O lord of men, the I-sense in the intellect, and the intellect too in primal Nature,
having thus reckoned it out, one should then meditate upon the Sole alone — stainless and spotless, eternal, infinite, pure, and without flaw,
the abiding Spirit, the Real, indivisible, free from age and death, everlasting and imperishable, the Lord, the unfailing brahman.
One should mark the signs of the man who is yoked, O great king: the mark of his serenity is that, like one who is sated, he sleeps in ease.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As a lamp fed with oil burns in a windless place, its flame steady and upright, so the wise describe the man who is yoked.
As a stone struck by the raindrops born of the clouds cannot be made to stir, such is the mark of the man who is yoked.
By the blare of conch and kettledrum, by manifold songs and instruments being played, he would not be shaken — this is the token of the man who is yoked.
As a man, grasping a brimful vessel of oil in both his hands, would mount a stairway, fearful, threatened by men with swords in hand,
and, his self controlled, would not for fear of them spill a drop from the vessel — even so is it with one who is ascending, his mind made single-pointed.
By the steadiness of his senses and likewise by their stillness, one should thus mark the signs of the sage who is yoked.
That yoked one beholds the brahman, which is supreme and imperishable, set in the midst of the great darkness, blazing like fire.
By this he attains the Absolute, having cast aside the unwitnessed body, after a great length of time, O king — this is the eternal revelation.
This indeed is the Yoga of the Yogins — what other mark of Yoga could there be? Having known it, the wise hold themselves to have done all that is to be done.
Yājñavalkya said: Hear now attentively of the soul's departing, O king. For one departing through the feet, the station of Viṣṇu is declared.
Through the shanks he would attain the Vasu gods — so have we heard — and through the knees he would reach the greatly blessed Sādhya gods.
Departing through the fundament, he would attain the station of Mitra; through the hips, the Earth; and through the thighs, Prajāpati.
Through the two flanks the Marut gods, and through the nostrils the Moon; through the arms, they say, Indra; and through the breast, Rudra.
Through the neck he attains that best of seers, the unsurpassed Nara; through the mouth, the All-Gods; and through the ear, the quarters of space.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Through the sense of smell, the bearer of fragrance, the Wind; through the eyes, Sūrya; through the brows, the two Aśvin gods; and through the forehead, the Fathers.
Through the crown of the head he attains the all-pervading Brahmā, foremost of the gods. These are the stations of departure, O lord of Mithilā.
Now I shall declare the omens of death, set forth by the wise, which would arise in an embodied one a year before his parting.
He who can no longer see Arundhatī, though he has seen her before, and likewise the Pole-star, the full moon, and a lamp — or who sees them broken in appearance on the right — such men too have but a year to live.
And those who do not see themselves in another's eye, formed as the image of their own shadow, O king — they too have but a year to live.
Excess of splendor, excess of insight, loss of insight, and loss of splendor — this change-and-disorder of one's nature is a sign of death within six months.
He who scorns the gods and quarrels with the brāhmaṇas, whose hue grows dark, dusky, and corpse-like — that is a sign of death within six months.
He who sees the moon pierced like a wheel with a worn-out nave, and likewise the thousand-rayed sun, is doomed to die within seven nights.
The man who smells the stench of a corpse though a sweet fragrance is at hand, while standing in the temple of a god, is doomed to die within six nights.
A drooping of the ears and nose, a fading of the teeth and the sight, a loss of awareness, and a lack of warmth — these are tokens of immediate death.
And he whose left eye streams without cause, O lord of men, and from whose head smoke seems to rise — these are tokens of immediate death.
Having known these many omens, the self-possessed man should, by night and by day, yoke his own self to the Supreme Self.
Awaiting that hour, whatever the hour against which it is to come — but if death is not desired by him and he wishes to remain, let him perform this practice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Composed, let him hold fast all scents and tastes; for in this way, with the inmost self intent upon That, he conquers death.
And having learned the practice of fixation together with Sāṃkhya, O bull among men, he may conquer death by Yoga, with the inmost self intent upon That.
He would attain and pass on to the imperishable Whole — unborn, blessed, and unfailing — the everlasting, unmoving station, hard to win for those whose selves are unperfected.
Yājñavalkya said: That supreme thing seated in the Unmanifest, about which you have questioned me, O lord of men — hear attentively this most secret question, O king.
By following here the ancient seers' ordinance, even one held in disregard, I obtained the Yajus verses from the Sun himself, O lord of Mithilā.
With great austerity I served the god of fiercest heat; and well pleased, the all-pervading Sūrya then spoke to me, O sinless one.
"Choose a boon, O sage among brāhmaṇas, whatever you desire, however hard to win; that I shall grant you with a gladdened heart, for my favor is hard to obtain."
Then, bowing my head, I said to the best of those who give heat: "The Yajus verses not yet possessed — these I wish to learn quickly."
Then the Blessed One said to me: "I shall impart them to you, O brāhmaṇa; Sarasvatī, become speech, will enter into your body."
Then the Blessed One said to me: "Open wide your mouth." And when I had opened my mouth, Sarasvatī entered it.
Then, burning, I plunged into the water, O sinless one, out of ignorance and impatience toward the great-souled maker of light.
Then, as I burned, the Blessed Sun said to me: "Bear the burning for a moment, and thereafter you shall become cool."
And seeing me grown cool, the Blessed maker of light said: "The Veda, with its supplements and its appendices, shall be established in you, O brāhmaṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And you shall set forth the whole of the Śatapatha, O bull among brāhmaṇas; and at its end your mind shall be set upon nonrebirth.
And you shall attain what you desire, that state sought by the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga." Having said only this much, the Blessed One went to his setting.
Then, having heard what was declared, when the radiant god had departed, I returned home and, full of joy, I meditated upon Sarasvatī.
Then the goddess Sarasvatī came forth in me, most auspicious, adorned with vowels and consonants, making the syllable Oṃ at the beginning.
Then I duly offered the guest-water to Sarasvatī and to the most excellent of those who give heat, seated and wholly devoted to them.
Then I composed the whole Śatapatha, with its esoteric portions, its compendium, and its appendices, with the utmost delight.
And having taught it, I produced a hundred excellent disciples — to the displeasure of my great-souled maternal uncle and his pupils.
Then by me together with my disciples, as the Sun pervades with his rays, the sacrifice of your great-souled father was overspread, O great king.
Then, even as Devala looked on, I carried off half the sacrificial fee due to my own Veda, in contest with my maternal uncle.
Then by Sumantu, by Paila, by Jaimini, by your father, and by the sages, I was honored and acknowledged.
Fifteen Yajus recensions I obtained from the Sun, O sinless one; and likewise from Lomaharṣaṇa the Purāṇa lore was ascertained.
Placing this seed before me, and the goddess Sarasvatī, and by the power of the Sun, I set to work, O ruler of men,
to compose the Śatapatha Veda, never before made; and it was brought about by me, accomplished in the manner I had wished.
To my disciples the whole of it entire, together with its compendium, was imparted; and all the disciples, pure, departed in supreme delight.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having established at will these fifteen branches of lore shown by the maker of light, I then pondered upon that which is to be known:
"What here is the holy truth, and what is the supreme object of knowledge?" As I was reflecting on this, a gandharva came and questioned me —
Viśvāvasu, O king, skilled in the knowledge of the Vedānta; having asked twenty-four questions about the Veda, O lord of the earth, he asked a twenty-fifth question, concerning the science of reasoning.
The universal and the non-universal; the pervading and the unpervading; Mitra and Varuṇa; knowledge and the knowable; the unknowing and the knowing; who is the warm and the not-warm; the devourer of the Sun and the Sun; knowledge and ignorance, likewise;
the knowable and the unknowable, O king; the unmoving and the moving; the unprecedented, the imperishable, and the perishable — this was that incomparable question.
Then I addressed him, O king — that king among gandharvas — who had asked, in due order, a question lofty and full of meaning:
"Let it be borne with for a moment, until I reflect upon it." Saying "So be it," the gandharva remained silent.
Then once more I called to mind the goddess Sarasvatī; and in my mind that question was churned out, as clarified butter is drawn from curds.
There I churned, in my mind, both the Upaniṣad and the appendix, O son, having beheld the supreme science of reasoning.
This, O tiger among kings, is the fourth science, that which avails for the world beyond; it was declared by me to you, founded upon the twenty-fifth principle.
Then I addressed him, O king — King Viśvāvasu — at that time: "Hear now the answer to the question you have here asked of me."
"As for this universal and non-universal about which you inquire, O lord of gandharvas, let one know the supreme Unmanifest as the universal, the dread of all that has been and shall be.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It is threefold through the agency of the qualities; the non-universal, again, is the partless one. The 'pervading' is likewise seen as a pair, even so.
They call the Unmanifest Prakṛti, and the quality-less they call Puruṣa; likewise Mitra is the Puruṣa, and Varuṇa is Prakṛti.
Knowledge they call Prakṛti, and the knowable is the partless one; the Puruṣa is both unknowing and knowing, and therefore he is called partless.
Who is the warm, who is called the not-warm, and who is he said to be the Puruṣa? The warm, they say, is Prakṛti; the not-warm is held to be the partless one.
So too the Unmanifest is the unknowable, while the Puruṣa is called the knowable. As for the 'moving and unmoving' you have spoken of, hear that also from me.
They call Prakṛti the moving, the cause of casting forth and creation; the Puruṣa, who neither casts forth nor creates, is held to be the unmoving.
Both are unborn and offspringless, and both also imperishable; both, they say, are unborn and eternal — those who are firm in the knowledge of the higher Self.
Because it is imperishable in begetting, they call it here unborn and undecaying; the Puruṣa they call imperishable, for no decay is found in him.
Because of the perishing of its qualities it is Prakṛti; yet because it is the agent, the wise call it imperishable. This is for you the science of reasoning, the fourth, which avails for the world beyond.
Having made wealth endowed with knowledge by action in the perpetual rite — all the Vedas are held to be of single, definite vision, O Viśvāvasu.
They who do not know the purpose of the Veda — that wherein these beings are born and die, and whence they have fallen — they do not know the knowable, O best of gandharvas.
Even if one studies the five Vedas with all their limbs and sub-limbs, yet does not know what the Veda is to make known, he is but a bearer of the Veda's burden.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who, desiring butter, should churn the milk of a she-ass, O best of gandharvas, would find there only dung — neither cream nor butter.
Even so, one who knows the Veda's letter does not find the knowable and the unknowable; he, of merely deluded mind, is held a bearer of the burden of knowledge.
These two are ever to be discerned, by the inner Self devoted to that supreme end, so that for him birth and death may not be, again and again.
Having pondered the ceaseless round of birth and death, and abandoning this triple Veda — which is here perishable — one takes his stand upon the imperishable dharma.
But when, O Kāśyapa, he sees utterly, day after day, then, become wholly isolated, he beholds the twenty-sixth.
One is the ever-Unmanifest, and other is the twenty-fifth; though there be these two of his, the good behold him as one alone.
For this reason they do not recognize the twenty-fifth as imperishable — the followers of Yoga and Sāṃkhya, seekers of the highest, dreading birth and death.
Viśvāvasu said: As for this twenty-fifth that has been declared by you, O best of brāhmaṇas — whether it is so or not so, it behooves you to tell.
I have heard the teaching of Jaigīṣavya, of Asita, and of Devala; of the sage Parāśara, and of the wise Vārṣagaṇya;
of the mendicant Pañcaśikha, of Kapila and Śuka, of Gautama, of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and of the great-souled Garga;
of Nārada and of Āsuri, and of the wise Pulastya; of Sanatkumāra, then, and of the great-souled Śukra;
of Kaśyapa and of my own father, all this I heard long ago; and thereafter of Rudra of universal form, the wise one,
and from the gods, the ancestors, and the daityas, here and there; all this has been gained by me — what they ever call the knowable, the eternal.
Therefore I wish to hear it through your understanding, O brāhmaṇa; you are the foremost of the treatises, bold and of surpassing intellect.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nothing is unknown to you; you are held to be a treasury of sacred lore, O brāhmaṇa — so it is told in the world of the gods and in the world of the ancestors.
The great sages who have gone to the world of Brahmā recount it, and the lord of those who give heat, the Sun himself, ever speaks of you.
The knowledge of Sāṃkhya has been obtained by you whole and entire, O brāhmaṇa, and likewise the knowledge of Yoga in particular, O Yājñavalkya.
Beyond all doubt you are awakened, comprehending the moving and the unmoving; I wish to hear that knowledge, even as one would the cream-rich butter.
Yājñavalkya said: I deem you to be one who has grasped the whole, O best of gandharvas; yet you would test me, O king. Learn it, then, as I have heard it.
The twenty-fifth knows Prakṛti, who herself does not know; but Prakṛti, O gandharva, does not know the twenty-fifth.
Because of this non-awareness they call her the Pradhāna — both the Sāṃkhyas and the Yogas, knowers of the truth, according to the testimony of scripture.
Seeing and likewise not-seeing, yet another one sees, O sinless one: the twenty-sixth sees both the twenty-fifth and the twenty-fourth; but, though seeing, the one he sees does not see him in return.
The twenty-fifth would imagine: "There is no other higher than I" — yet the twenty-fourth is not ungraspable to men who behold by knowledge.
As a fish follows the water and moves by reason of its movement, even as the fish has awareness, so too does this one come to awareness — bound by affection, by shared dwelling, and ever by self-conceit.
He sinks in time when he does not comprehend his oneness; and he rises in time, enveloped by the sense of "mine."
But when the twice-born thinks, "I am other, and this is other," then, become wholly isolated, he beholds the twenty-sixth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One, O king, is the lower, and other is the twenty-fifth; yet because the one abides within the other, the good behold them as one alone.
For this reason they do not delight in the twenty-fifth as imperishable; afraid of the dread of birth and death, the Yogas and the Sāṃkhyas, O Kāśyapa, the pure and wholly devoted, behold the twenty-sixth.
When, become wholly isolated, he beholds the twenty-sixth, then that learned one, all-knowing, does not undergo birth again.
Thus the unawakened, the awakening, and the awakened have been declared to you, O sinless one, according to their truth, by me, from the testimony of scripture.
Whoever should behold the seen and the unseen, O Kāśyapa, and the blissful Reality — the isolated and the non-isolated, the primal, and that which is beyond the twenty-fifth —
Viśvāvasu said: True and auspicious is this that has been spoken by you, sir — rightly, bringing peace, beginning with the deity, exactly so. May there be welfare imperishable to you for ever; ever joined with wisdom through your wisdom — homage to you!
Yājñavalkya said: Having spoken thus, he set forth to heaven, shining indeed with a glorious aspect; and well content, with the highest contentment, that great-souled one rejoiced and made his rightward circuit around me.
To Brahmā and the rest, to the sky-faring ones, O lord of men, and to those who dwell upon the earth and in the realms below — to all of them he revealed this very vision, that auspicious vision granted to those who have taken to the path that leads aright.
All the followers of Sāṃkhya who delight in the Sāṃkhya discipline, and likewise the Yogins who delight in the discipline of Yoga, and whatever other men there are who long for liberation — for them this vision is the one seen through knowledge.
From knowledge is liberation born for men; from ignorance there is none — so they declare, O lord of men. Therefore knowledge is to be sought in its very truth, by which one may free the self from birth and death.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having gained knowledge from a brāhmaṇa or a kṣatriya, from a vaiśya or a śūdra, even from a lowly man, the believer must ever and constantly hold it in faith; into the man of faith birth and death shall not enter.
All the classes are brāhmaṇas, all are sprung from Brahman, and all forever utter Brahman. The truth, the teaching, I declare with a mind fixed on Brahman: this whole universe, in its entirety, is Brahman.
From the mouth of Brahman the brāhmaṇas were brought forth, from the arms the kṣatriyas were brought forth, from the navel the vaiśyas, and from the feet the śūdras; all the classes are to be understood thus and not otherwise.
Out of ignorance they resort, O king, to this or that womb whose source is karma, and so pass into nothingness; even so the classes, bereft of knowledge, fall — out of dread ignorance into the natural web of wombs.
Therefore knowledge is to be sought on every side; it abides everywhere, as I have told you. Brahman stands fast, and that other one who likewise stands fast — for him the chief of the twice-born declare eternal liberation.
What you asked, that I have taught according to its very truth; be free of sorrow, O king. Reach the far shore of this matter. It has been rightly declared — may all be well with you herein for ever.
Bhīṣma said: Thus instructed by the wise Yājñavalkya, the king, the lord of Mithilā, was then filled with joy.
When that best of sages had departed, after the circumambulation had been performed, the king Daivarāti, knower of liberation, sat there.
He caused ten million cows to be touched in gift, and likewise gold, and a single handful of gems besides he then bestowed upon the brāhmaṇas.
And having established the kingdom of Videha upon his son, the lord of Mithilā lived on, devoting himself to the discipline of the renunciant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Studying the knowledge of Sāṃkhya and the science of Yoga in its entirety, and condemning, O lord of kings, both dharma and adharma as belonging to mere nature,
holding the eternal and the absolute alone to be endless, he reckoned dharma and adharma, merit and demerit, the true and the false alike,
and birth and death too, O lord of kings, as belonging to nature; thus he meditated ever, O ruler of men: this is the work of the Unmanifest, of Brahman.
The Yogins and the Sāṃkhyas, defined each by their own teaching, behold it thus: severed from the welcome and the unwelcome, Brahman stands, higher than the highest. The wise call it eternal and pure; therefore be pure.
Whatever is given and whatever is received, what is bestowed and what is approved, and what a man gives, O best of men, and what he accepts — it is the Unmanifest alone that gives this, and the Unmanifest that receives it.
For the Self alone is the one Self; who other than yourself could be greater than you? Think thus continually; do not ponder it otherwise.
He by whom the Unmanifest is not known — whether with its qualities or beyond all qualities — by that unwise man holy fords and sacrifices must be frequented.
Not by recitations, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices, O joy of the Kurus, does one attain abidance in the Unmanifest; only by knowing the Unmanifest, O lord of the earth.
Likewise one may attain the station of the Great Principle, and the station born of egoity, and the stations that lie even beyond egoity.
But those, devoted to the scriptures, who know the eternal that is beyond the Unmanifest — that which is free of birth and death, and free of both being and non-being —
This I obtained of old from Janaka, and he in turn obtained it, O king, from Yājñavalkya. Knowledge is supreme; sacrifices are not its equal. By knowledge one crosses the hard passage, not by sacrifices.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Birth and death are a hard passage, O king, and yield no abiding good — so say the knowers of knowledge. By sacrifices, austerities, observances, and vows men reach heaven, only to fall again to earth.
Therefore worship that which is supreme, great, pure, gracious, the spotless and hallowed liberation, O knower of the field-knower. Worshipping, O king, the sacrifice of knowledge and the truth, you shall become a seer.
This secret doctrine Yājñavalkya then imparted of old to King Janaka — that by which, when the eternal and imperishable is reckoned and known, one attains the auspicious, sorrowless state of immortality.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Having won great lordship, O bull of the Bhāratas, or wealth, or having gained a long span of life — how then may one pass beyond death?
By great austerity, by action, by sacred learning, or by the application of elixirs — by what means does one escape old age and death?
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale — the dialogue here of the mendicant Pañcaśikha with Janaka.
Janaka, king of Videha, questioned the great seer Pañcaśikha, foremost knower of the Vedas, who had cut away every doubt concerning dharma and the goal of life.
By what course of conduct, O blessed one, might one pass beyond old age and death — by austerity, by understanding, by action, or by sacred learning?
Thus addressed, the knower of the unseen replied to the king of Videha: there is no halting these two, nor is there any way to keep them from halting all else.
For the days do not turn back, nor the months, nor again the nights; this fleeting creature sets out upon the long, unending road.
The destruction of all beings is borne along forever as if by a current; and as he is swept along and sinks in the boatless ocean of time, where old age and death are the great sea-monster, no one comes to his aid.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
No one shall belong to him, nor does he belong to anyone; this gathering with wife and other kinsfolk is but a meeting upon the road. No lasting companionship has ever yet been won by anyone.
Begotten by time, born again and again, they are flung this way and that, groaning over and over — like masses of cloud driven by the wind.
For old age and death are the devourers of beings, like two wolves — of the strong and the weak, of the small and the great alike.
When beings are of such a nature, ever coming to be yet never enduring, how should one rejoice when they are born, and how burn with grief when they die?
Whence have I come, who am I, where shall I go, and to whom do I belong? In what do I abide, where shall I be? Wherefore, and over what, do you grieve?
For there is no one who has beheld heaven, nor likewise hell; yet without transgressing the sacred tradition one should give gifts and offer sacrifice.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O best of the royal seers of the Kurus, without forsaking the householder's life, who has attained, by his understanding, the discipline of restraint? Tell me the truth of liberation.
How is this self renounced, and what is he who has renounced the self, and what is the supreme goal of liberation — tell me that, O grandfather.
