Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale — the dialogue of Janaka and Sulabhā, O Bhārata.
There once was a certain king who had won the fruit of renunciation, a man of Mithilā, Janaka by name, known as Dharmadhvaja.
Versed in the Veda, in the science of liberation, and in his own kingly science, he held his senses in check and ruled this earth.
Hearing of that virtuous conduct of his, the wise who know the Veda, and other men throughout the worlds, looked upon him with longing, O lord of men.
Now in that righteous age a certain wandering mendicant woman named Sulabhā, who practised the discipline of Yoga, was roaming over the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As she wandered through all this world, she heard the lord of Mithilā spoken of, here and there, by the triple-staffed ascetics in their discourse on liberation.
Having heard the most subtle account, but in doubt whether it was true or not, she conceived a resolve to behold Janaka in person.
Then, casting off her former shape by the power of Yoga, the faultless-limbed one took on another, surpassing form.
In the mere blink of an eye, moving with the swiftness of a flying arrow, the fair-browed, lotus-eyed woman came to the city of the Videhas.
Reaching lovely Mithilā, thronged with prosperous folk, on the pretext of seeking alms she came to behold the lord of Mithilā.
Beholding her surpassing delicacy and her form, the king was struck with wonder: Who is this, whose is she, and whence?
Then, bidding her welcome and assigning her an excellent seat, he honoured her with water for her feet and gratified her with choice food.
Then, having eaten and well pleased, the mendicant woman challenged the king — surrounded by his ministers, in the midst of all who were skilled in disputation.
But Sulabhā, in doubt whether he was truly liberated in his observances or not, being skilled in Yoga, entered his being with her own being, O lord of the earth.
Joining the rays of her eyes to the rays of his eyes, she bound him, as he was about to challenge her, with the bonds of Yoga.
And King Janaka, smiling, discerning her intent, the best of kings, met her purpose with his own purpose.
Let this dialogue now be heard, set within one and the same seat — between him who, though amid parasol and the rest, was liberated, and her who was liberated within the triple staff.
"Where, lady, has this wandering of yours been undertaken, and where will you go? Whose are you, and whence?" — thus the lord of the earth questioned her.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In learning, in age, and in birth, true worth is not discerned; therefore in these matters an answer must be made known when the good come together.
Know me to be wholly liberated, despite the parasol and such distinctions. I wish to take counsel with you, for you are deemed by me worthy of honour.
From whom of old I gained this distinctive knowledge, of whose teaching on liberation there is no other expounder — hear of him too from me.
Of the aged, great-souled mendicant Pañcaśikha, of the lineage of Parāśara, I am the most esteemed disciple.
In the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, in Yoga, and in the rule of kings, and in this threefold law of liberation, he had traversed the whole path and cut away every doubt.
Wandering forth by the path laid down in the scriptures, he once dwelt happily with me for the four months of the rainy season.
By that foremost of Sāṃkhyas, who had clearly seen the truth, I was instructed in the threefold liberation according to its very essence, yet was not swayed from my kingdom.
So I, freed of passion, follow that whole threefold way joined to liberation, moving alone, established in the supreme station.
Dispassion, again, is the supreme rule of this liberation; and dispassion is born of knowledge alone, by which one is set free.
By knowledge one makes the effort, and by effort the great is attained; the great leads to release from the pairs of opposites — that perfection which transcends the passing of age.
This supreme wisdom, this freedom from the pairs of opposites, has been won by me even here, as I move with delusion gone and attachment cast off.
As a field made soft and flooded with water brings forth the sprout, so does the action of men bring forth rebirth.
And as a seed scorched in a potsherd, set down anywhere, though it has the capacity to sprout, is no longer seed and does not sprout,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
even so, by that blessed mendicant whom Pañcaśikha taught, my knowledge has been made seedless, and amid the objects of sense it sprouts no more.
It clings to nothing — neither to harm nor to possession — nor does it take delight in these, since passion and its faults are seen to be in vain.
He who should anoint my right arm with sandal, and he who should hack at my left with an axe — these two are alike to me.
Happy am I, my purpose accomplished, regarding clod and stone and gold alike; free of attachment, seated upon my throne, I surpass the other triple-staffed ascetics.
For in liberation a threefold ground has been seen by the great seers of old: knowledge that transcends the world, and the utter renunciation of all actions —
Some men, versed in the science of liberation, declare it grounded in knowledge; while others, ascetics of subtle vision, declare it grounded in action.
Renouncing both of these alike—pure knowledge and action—that great-souled one has declared this third as the firm ground of consummation.
In restraint and observance, in hatred, desire, and possession, in pride, hypocrisy, and likewise affection, those ascetics are no different from householders.
If liberation comes through some knowledge while one yet holds the triple staff and the rest, why should it not come amid parasols and such, the cause of attachment being equal?
For whatever object serves a man's purpose, for whatever reason, that very thing he clings to—each to his own possessions.
He who, seeing fault in the householder's life, passes to another stage—renouncing one thing while grasping another—he too is not freed from attachments.
When their sovereignty is alike, its essence the power to punish and to favor, by what cause are royal sage, mendicant, and teacher set free?
And if even amid real lordship men are freed here by knowledge alone, why should those who abide established in the supreme state not be freed?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The wearing of ochre robes, the shaven head, the triple staff held upright, the water-pot—these outward signs serve excessively little for liberation: such is my view.
If, even when this badge is present, knowledge alone is the cause here of release from suffering, then the mere badge is without purpose.
Or if, seeing some slackening of suffering, one's mind is set upon the badge—why is that same common benefit not to be discerned amid parasols and the rest?
In utter destitution there is no liberation; in having something there is no bondage; whether having something or not, the creature is freed by knowledge.
Therefore, amid dharma, wealth, and desire, and likewise the holding of a kingdom—in these abodes of bondage—know me to stand established in the state where no bond is.
The noose made of royal dominion, the fetter that is the abode of affection—here I have cut it with the sword of renunciation, whetted upon the stone of liberation.
I, having come to this state, am free; yet I have grown wary of you, O mendicant woman, for your guise is false—I shall tell you why; hear that from me.
Your delicacy, your beauty, your superb body, and your youth—all these together, set beside your ascetic discipline, breed doubt.
And since your conduct ill befits this badge you wear, my retinue has been thrown into agitation, wondering whether this one be liberated or not.
In one yoked to desire there is no triple staff, even were such a one freed; and you do not keep this discipline—yet for the liberated there is nothing to conceal.
And hear too this transgression of yours, arising from your resort to my side—you who by your own nature have entered into what is already mine.
By whom was your entry made into my realm and my city? And by whose leave have you entered into my very heart?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You are foremost of the highest class, a brāhmaṇa woman, while I am a kṣatriya; there is no joining of us two—do not work a confusion of the orders.
You dwell in the duties of liberation, while I am in the householder's stage; this is your second grievous fault—a confounding of the stages of life.
Whether of my lineage or of another, I do not know you, nor do you know me; in entering one of the same lineage lies your third fault—a confounding of clans.
And if your husband yet lives, though abroad or somewhere away—another man's wife is not to be approached: this is the fourth, a confounding of right.
You, then, with an eye to some end, undertake these things that ought not be done—whether possessed of mere ignorance, or again of false knowledge.
Or else you act on your own authority, through some fault of your own; and if you possess any learning at all, you have rendered it wholly useless.
This is yet a third thing of yours, frustrating the touch of true intent: the badge of a corrupt woman is plain to see, and must be openly declared.
Your design, in your longing for victory, was not set upon conquering me alone; this whole assembly of mine too you wish to conquer.
For thus, again and again, you let loose your own doctrine—to strike down my position and to set up your own.
You, bewildered by the delusion born of your own impatience for mastery, again loose the weapon of yoga, like poison and nectar mingled into one.
For when both desire it, the union of woman and man is like nectar; but the failure of it, for one who feels no passion, is here a flaw like poison.
Touch me not; know rightly; keep faithful to your own teaching. This examination has been made by you—whether I am liberated or not—and all this, concealed within me, you ought not to hide from me.
Whether you act for your own purpose or for that of some other king, the truth—disguised under a pious pretext—you ought not to hide from me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
None should approach a king with falsehood, nor a brāhmaṇa in any wise, nor a woman endowed with womanly virtues; for these, falsely approached, can destroy.
For the strength of kings is their dominion; the strength of those who know the sacred is the sacred itself; beauty, youth, and good fortune are the unsurpassed strength of women.
Mighty therefore by these strengths, such ones must be approached with straightforwardness by him who seeks his own good; for crookedness leads to ruin.
You, then, ought to tell me truly your birth, your learning, your conduct, your intent, your nature, and your errand in coming.
Thus rebuked by the king with these unpleasant, unjust, and ill-ordered words, Sulabhā was not shaken.
When the king had finished speaking, the fair-faced Sulabhā then set herself to utter words still fairer.
Free from the eighteen faults—nine and nine again—that vitiate speech and understanding, well furnished with meaning and endowed with the eighteen merits:
Subtlety, enumeration, and sequence—these two—decision, and purpose: these five orders of meaning together are called a true utterance, O king.
Hear the proper mark of each one of these meanings—subtlety and the rest—as they are set forth in due order through the senses of words, word by word and sentence by sentence.
When, among distinct objects of knowledge, cognition proceeds according to their distinctions, there the surpassing keenness of the intellect operates as what is called subtlety.
The measuring out of faults and merits, severally and apart, with some particular aim in view—that is to be understood as enumeration.
"This is to be said first, this afterward"—the ordering of what one means to express: that too those who know speech call the conjunction of sequence within an utterance.
Having made a particular proposition concerning dharma, wealth, desire, or liberation, that which is declared at the close of the speech as "this is that" is the decision.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Where, through the sufferings born of desire and aversion, some impulse arises, the activity that follows there, O king, is held to be the purpose.
These, then, just as stated—subtlety and the rest, O lord of men—joined together upon a single meaning: mark well my utterance.
Furnished with meaning, undivided in meaning, neither digressive nor excessive, not rough, not doubtful—such supreme speech shall I utter to you.
Not cumbered with heavy syllables, nor turned away from its subject, not false, not opposed to the three aims, nor uncultivated;
not deficient, nor of harsh words, nor uttered out of order, not left incomplete, nor by way of mere makeshift, not causeless nor without ground.
Out of desire, anger, fear, greed, abjectness, or baseness, out of shame, pity, or pride—from none of these shall I speak in any wise.
When speaker, listener, and speech, O king, come together unimpaired and matched in the intent to convey, then that meaning shines forth.
But when, in what is to be spoken, the speaker holds the listener in contempt, declaring his own meaning or another's, then the speech does not take root.
And when a man, abandoning his own meaning, declares another's, mistrust arises toward him, and that speech too is faulty.
But the speaker who declares a meaning unopposed to both—to the listener's and to his own—he is the true speaker, no other, O king.
This speech of mine, then, full of meaning and endowed with the perfections of utterance, you ought to hear, O king, with mind undistracted and intent.
"Who are you, whose, and whence?"—thus you have challenged me; to that, hear this answer of mine, O king, with single mind.
As lac and wood and grains of dust are closely held together by drops of water, even so, O king, is the coming-to-be of living creatures here.
Sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; the five sense-faculties; and the self apart—these ten realities are bound together like lac and wood.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Among these there is no prompting of one by another—this is the settled conclusion; here no single one has cognition of itself or of another.
The eye does not know its own eye-hood, nor does hearing turn upon itself; and likewise they do not act upon one another by deviation; though bound together, they do not arise from one another, as grains of dust do not from water here.
They depend on other, external factors—hear those too from me: form, the eye, and light are the three causes of seeing; and just as here, so in the other cases the causes of cognition and its objects hold.
In that interval between cognition and its object there is another factor named mind, by which this being deliberates, in deciding, upon what is right and what is wrong.
And there a twelfth, another factor named intellect, is remembered, by which one comes to resolution upon things to be understood that were first beset with doubt.
Then, beyond that twelfth, another factor named disposition, by which a creature is inferred to be of great spirit or of little.
And the knower-of-the-field is yet another, the fourteenth factor there, by which one thinks "this is mine," and again thinks it not.
Then a fifteenth, O king, another factor there is remembered: the gathering into wholeness of the aggregate of parts otherwise separate—that is here so called.
And yet another factor there, the combination, is the sixteenth, in which these two factors—shape and manifest form—are conjoined.
Pleasure and pain, old age and death, gain and loss, the pleasant and the unpleasant—this, the nineteenth, is remembered as the conjunction of opposites.
Above the nineteen there is another factor named time; know thereby, in these twenty, the arising and passing-away of beings.
This combination of twenty, and the five great elements, and the conjunction of being and non-being—these are two further illuminating factors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus the twenty-seven factors that are remembered; and ordinance, generative seed, and force—these three are yet further factors.
Thirty parts in all are remembered by enumeration; that wherein they all together subsist is remembered as the body.
As the unmanifest source of these parts some hold their nature to be; while another, of grosser sight, beholds their manifest form alone.
Whether unmanifest or manifest, twofold or fourfold, the nature of all beings—so the meditators on the inmost self behold it.
This very nature, unmanifest, comes through its parts to manifestation—I and you, O lord of kings, and all others that are embodied.
The states beginning with the deposit of the drop, arising from seed and blood—by the very falling-together of which there comes to be what is called the embryonic film.
From the film arises the swelling mass, and from the mass the fleshy lump; from the lump the formation of limbs, and from the limbs the nails and hairs.
When the ninth month is full and the creature is born, O king of Mithilā, name-and-form comes to be, marked as woman or man by its sign.
But that form just newly born, seen with its copper-hued nails and fingers, once it has assumed the form of childhood, is no longer recognized by its earlier shape.
From childhood comes youth, and from youth comes old age; by this sequence of stages the earlier condition can never be regained.
The transformation of the constituent parts, each with its own function, proceeds moment by moment in all beings; but because it is so subtle it is not perceived.
Neither their passing away nor their arising can be marked, O king, from one state to the next—it is like the motion of a lamp's flame.
And of this whole world, possessed of such power and ceaselessly running like a fine horse, who is it, and whence, or who is not, and from where?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whose is this, or whose is it not, whence is this, or whence is it not? What connection have living beings here even with their own bodily parts?
As fire arises from the sun, from the crystal, and from kindling-plants, so too do living creatures arise from the assemblage of constituent parts.
Just as you behold the self in the self by the self, why do you not likewise behold the self by the self in another—if you hold to the sameness of the self in yourself and in another?
Then why do you keep asking me, 'Who are you, whose are you?' For one freed from the pairs of opposites—'this is mine, this is not'—O king of Mithilā, what purpose has the question, 'Who are you, whose, and whence?'
In one who still acts toward foe, friend, and the neutral party, toward conquest, peace, and war, O ruler of the earth—what mark of the liberated is there in him?
In one who does not clearly know the sevenfold division within the threefold aim amid his deeds, and who is still attached to that triad of aims—what mark of the liberated is there in him?
In one whose eye is not equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, toward the weak and the strong—what mark of the liberated is there in him?
Therefore, O king, that conceit of yours regarding liberation, while you are yet unliberated, ought to be checked by your friends, as a madman's delusion is checked by remedies.
Reviewing one by one these many seats of attachment, O subduer of foes, one should examine the self within the self—what mark of the liberated is there in him?
Hear from me these and certain other subtle seats of attachment, bearing on liberation, that pertain to the fourfold array of kingship.
He who rules this whole earth beneath a single parasol—that one king, after all, dwells in but a single city.
And in that city he occupies but a single house; in that house but a single bed, where at night he sinks to rest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And of that bed too only half is his, the other side first taken by a woman; thus, by this reasoning, he is joined here only to that much fruit.
Just so it is with his enjoyments, with his food and clothing, with his measurable pleasures, and with regard to punishment and favor.
The king is ever dependent on others; even in trifling matters he is entangled. In the affairs of peace and war, where then is the king's independence?
In matters of women, sport, and recreation his lack of freedom is constant; and in counsel and in the assembly of ministers, where then is there independence?
It is only when he commands others that he is called independent; yet there too he is made to act against his will, bound to each particular obligation.
Wishing to sleep, he is not allowed to sleep by people seeking his judgment on their affairs; even when granted leave to lie down and asleep, he is roused up against his will.
'Bathe! Touch this in consecration! Drink! Eat! Pour the oblations into the fires! Sacrifice! Speak! And listen!'—thus is he made to act, powerless, by others.
Coming to him again and again, people constantly beg of him; yet, guarding his wealth, he cannot bring himself to give freely, fearing the multitude.
For in giving there is loss to his treasury, and in withholding there is enmity; in a moment there crowd upon him faults that breed disaffection.
The wise, the brave, and the wealthy—even gathered in one place—he distrusts; even in safety the king feels fear of the very men by whom he is constantly attended.
And when those whom I have named turn corrupt, O king, then fear of them is born in him—behold of what kind it is.
Every man is a king in his own house, every man a householder in his own house; in dealing out punishment and favor he is the equal of kings, O Janaka.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sons, wife, and even his own self, treasury, friends, and his stores—all these he shares in common with others, through this cause or that.
'The land is ravaged, the city burned, the chief elephant is dead'—over these things, which he holds in common with all the world, he grieves through false understanding.
Unliberated, he is afflicted by mental sorrows born of desire, hatred, and affection, and likewise by diseases such as headache and the rest that strike him down.
Smitten by these various pairs of opposites, suspicious on every side, he tends a kingdom beset with many adversaries, counting out the nights.
Who would take up a kingship of such scant happiness, exceeding sorrow, and no substance—and, having gained it, find peace thereby?
This city and realm that you think 'this is mine,' this army, treasury, and ministers—whose are they, or are they no one's, O king?
Allies and ministers, city and realm, the rod of punishment, treasury, and sovereign—this seven-limbed assemblage, this wheel, is what is called the kingdom, O king.
In this seven-limbed kingdom, standing firm like a tripod, its parts bound to one another in mutual benefit, which is superior to which in worth?
For in each particular circumstance, this or that limb becomes preeminent; whichever accomplishes the task at hand is fit to be reckoned the foremost.
The seven-limbed aggregate, with three others besides, O best of kings, together make this tenfold group, which enjoys the kingdom even as the king himself does.
And the king who is of great energy and devoted to the duty of the warrior should be content with a tenth share; another, however, with less than a tenth.
There is no king who possesses anything not held in common, nor any kingdom without a king. Without a kingdom, whence dharma? Without dharma, whence the supreme goal?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And even that supreme dharma which is the purifier of king and kingdom—the horse-sacrifice whose sacrificial fee is the whole earth—does not exist for me.
I am able, O king of Mithilā, to recount these deeds and the sorrows of kingship by the hundreds, or even by the thousands.
I have no clinging even to my own body; how then to another's possessions? You ought not to speak so to me, who am liberated in this way.
Surely you have heard the whole doctrine of liberation from Pañcaśikha—with its means, its esoteric teachings, its disciplines, and its settled conclusions.
How then, O king, do you, who are free of attachment yet stand trampling upon its very bonds, have attachment once more to such distinctions as the royal parasol and the rest?
What you have heard, I think, you have not truly heard; or else what you heard you heard wrongly; or what merely resembled the teaching you heard; or you heard something else than the teaching.
And if you still take your stand upon these worldly notions, then, bound by clinging and by restraint, you are judged by me to be but an ordinary man.
As for this entering into you that I have effected by the power of mind—what harm has been done to you thereby, if you are indeed liberated in every respect?
For this is the rule among the disciplines of ascetics—that they should dwell as in a void; and by me, dwelling thus within a void, what has been defiled, and whose?
Not with hands, not with arms, not with feet or thighs, O sinless one, nor with any other limb of the body do I touch you, O ruler of men.
By one born in a great family, possessed of modesty and far-sighted wisdom, what is done privately between two people, whether proper or improper, ought not to be spoken of in the assembly.
These Brāhmaṇas are venerable, and these ministers most worthy of honor; and you, moreover, are venerable even to them—thus there is mutual reverence among you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore, reflecting in this way and examining what should and should not be said, you ought not to speak of this meeting of a woman and a man in the assembly.
As water resting on a lotus-leaf abides upon that leaf without touching it, so shall I dwell within you, O king of Mithilā.
And if you fancy any contact in me, who touch nothing at all, then how, by this mendicant woman, has your seedless knowledge been rendered fruitful here?
Fallen from the householder's life, yet not having attained that liberation so hard to know, you remain in the middle between the two, a mere pretender to release.
For between one liberated and a liberated knower, in the matter of oneness and separateness, in the conjunction of being and non-being, no confusion of classes can arise.
And though the classes and orders be distinct, for one who has seen the truth and is himself undivided, knowing that the one is not the other, the one does not pass over into the other.
The bowl in the hand, the milk in the bowl, the flies in the milk—by the relation of the supported to its support, we abide each one separately upon our support.
But the milk has no part in the nature of the bowl, nor the flies in the milk; these things rest each upon its own support, not by merging with another.
Since the orders of life are distinct, and the classes likewise are diverse, and since all stand separate from one another, how can there be any confusion of classes for you?
I am not of the highest class by birth, nor a Vaiśyā, nor of a lower order; I am, O king, of your own class, of pure lineage and unsullied.
There was a royal sage named Pradhāna—surely his name has reached your ears; know me to be born in his line, Sulabhā by name.
Droṇa, Śataśṛṅga, and the mountain Vakradvāra—these were heaped up at the sacrifices of my forebears, together with Maghavat.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Born in that lineage, and finding no husband fit for one like me, schooled in the disciplines of liberation, I wander alone, keeping the vow of a sage.
I am no one concealed under a deceitful guise, nor one who lays false claim to others' goods, nor one who causes confusion of dharma; I am steadfast in my vow within my own dharma.
I am not unsteady in my own resolve, nor one who speaks without consideration; nor have I come into your presence, O ruler of men, without due reflection.
Having heard that your mind was set upon liberation, and wishing you well, I have come here desiring to know the truth of this liberation of yours.
I do not say this as a partisan of either side, my own or another's: whether one is liberated or not liberated, whether one is at peace or not at peace.
As a mendicant might lodge a single night in an empty house in the city, so shall I dwell this one night within this body of yours.
Honored thus with the gift of a seat and the hospitality of speech, having slept well sheltered and content, tomorrow I shall depart, O king of Mithilā.
Having heard these words, well-reasoned and full of meaning, the king could find nothing further to say in answer beyond this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How did Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, come of old to detachment from the world? This I wish to hear, O Kaurava, for great is my curiosity.
Bhīṣma said: When his son, of fair conduct and fearing nothing, was going his natural way, the father, having taught him the whole of sacred study, instructed him thus.
Cleave to dharma, my son, for sharp indeed are cold and heat; conquer hunger and thirst and the wind, ever having mastered your senses.
Truth, uprightness, freedom from anger, freedom from envy, self-restraint, austerity, non-injury, and gentleness—observe these duly.
Stand fast in truth, delighting in dharma, casting off all crookedness; sustain the journey of your life on what remains after the gods and guests are served.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
While the body is like a vessel of foam and the soul perches in it like a bird, and the company of loved ones is impermanent—how can you sleep, my child?
While the foes are watchful, awake, ever intent, and seeking an opening, you, in your childishness, do not awaken to it.
As the years are being counted off, as your life-span dwindles and the time left to live grows ever less, why do you not rise up and run?
Those hardened unbelievers strive only after worldly things that nourish flesh and blood, while toward the works that bear upon the world beyond they lie fast asleep.
As for the men, deluded in mind, who cavil at dharma, of those who walk the wrong road even one who merely follows after them comes to grief.
But those who are content, well-controlled, devoted to the scripture of truth, who have mounted the path of dharma — attend upon them and question them.
Having marked well the counsel of those elders who behold dharma, restrain with the highest understanding your mind that strays onto wrong paths.
With a mind fixed on the present hour, thinking "tomorrow is far off," fearless and devouring all things, the senseless do not see the field of works.
Mounting the ladder of dharma, climb it rung by little rung. Like the silkworm that wraps itself round, you do not awaken to your own confinement.
The unbeliever, who has broken every bound, unsteady as a collapsing riverbank, set him at your left without misgiving — a man arrogant as a reed shooting up.
Across the river whose waters are desire, anger, and death, fed by the five senses, make for yourself a boat of steadfastness and cross over the strongholds of birth.
In a world struck down by death and oppressed by old age, while the unerring arrows fall, cross over by the vehicle of dharma.
Since death seeks out the man who stands and the man who lies down alike, from where will you find ease, when without warning you are undone by death?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Even while he goes on heaping up, still unsated in his desires, death comes upon him as a she-wolf upon a lamb, seizes him, and is gone.
Let the great lamp whose flame is gathered step by step, fashioned of the resolve toward dharma, be held with care against the darkness that must be entered.
Falling through the meshes of body after body, only now and then in the human state does a creature attain brahminhood; guard it well, my son.
For this body of the brahmin is not born for the sake of pleasure: here it is for hardship and austerity, but beyond, for happiness beyond compare.
Brahminhood is won by many austerities; having gained it, one must not make light of it for any wage. Ever yoked to recitation, to austerity, and to self-restraint, seeking your welfare and intent on the good, strive always.
Unmanifest in its nature, bodied in fractions, subtle of self, made of moments and instants, its hairs the blinks of an eye, its mouth the seasons, its eyes the bright and dark halves equal in force, its limbs of flesh — the horse of men's lifetime gallops on.
Seeing it loosed, unceasing, fierce in its speed, going on forever here without a backward glance — if your eye is not one to be led by another's leading, then, having grasped the highest, let your mind rest upon dharma.
But those whose conduct has slipped from dharma into craving, forever crying out, yoked to what they would not have, are afflicted, their bodies wholly encompassed by pain, harried sorely by the many residues of unrighteousness.
The king devoted to dharma, ever the guardian of good, after due regard bestows their worlds upon the doers of good; and to one who fares in manifold ways he allots a happiness unattained before, and blameless.
Dogs with dread iron jaws, and birds, and the flocking hosts of herons and vultures, drinkers of blood, in the slaughter of men tear apart the one who, ceasing to heed, has spurned his teacher's word.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who, following the bent of his mind, shatters tenfold these bounds laid down here by the Self-Born — that sinner dwells in deep misery, plunged into the wilderness of the realm of the fathers.
The man who is wholly greedy and loves falsehood, who takes ceaseless delight in cheating and deceit, who works misery with deposits entrusted to him — that doer of evil deeds goes to the deepest hell and there suffers misery without end.
Plunged into the scalding Vaitaraṇī, that great river, his limbs torn in the forest of sword-leaf trees, fallen to lie in the forest of axes, he dwells in the great hell, sore-stricken.
You boast of mighty exploits, yet you do not look to what lies beyond; you do not perceive the long-deferred summoner, death, until it has come.
For those who must depart, why this sitting still? A great terror has risen up, crushing and dreadful: see to your own well-being.
Before, struck dead, you are led away by Yama's death-decree, against that drawing-near make harsh effort toward uprightness.
Before the Lord who knows no sorrow carries off your life here together with kin and root — and there is none to hold him back — act.
Before the wind that is Yama's herald blows, before you are led off, you alone — make provision for the journey beyond.
Before the wind of the Ender blows upon you with the death-rattle, and before, at the coming of the great terror, the quarters reel about you — act.
Before your memory is choked off here, my son, and you depart in utter confusion — achieve the highest concentration.
Before you grieve, recalling the good and evil done and left undone, ruined by the works of heedlessness — lay up the one true treasure.
Before old age, robber of strength and limb and form, wears your frame to ruin — lay up the one true treasure.
Before the Ender, with the arrows of disease, by main force splits your body at the wasting of life — practice great austerity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Before the dread wolves whose range is the human body rush upon you from every side — strive in the cultivation of merit.
Before, alone, you behold the darkness, make haste indeed; before you gaze upon the golden trees on the mountain's crest — act.
Before bad company and foes wearing the faces of friends shake you from your vision — strive, my son, for what is highest.
That wealth which fears nothing from the king nor from the thief, and which does not forsake even the dead — gather that wealth.
There no man shares with another out of his own deeds; whatever is each one's own portion, that alone he enjoys there.
That by which one lives in the world beyond — that, my son, is what should be given. Gather for yourself, with your own hand, the wealth that is imperishable and sure.
As long as the gruel of the great host is not yet cooked — while that gruel is still raw — before you are led away, make haste.
Neither mother, father, and kin, nor any well-known and beloved person follow after him who passes through the strait, going down alone.
Whatever deed, good or evil, one has done by oneself alone — that, and that only, becomes his portion as he goes to the world beyond.
Hoards of gold and jewels, amassed by fair means or foul, do not, at the dissolution of his body, serve to accomplish his purpose.
Of your deeds done and left undone that travel with you to the world beyond, there is among men here no witness equal to your own self.
For him who goes to the world beyond, the human body becomes void and empty; behold this with the eye of understanding, for so it is shown on every side.
Here three — Agni, Sūrya, and Vāyu — dwell within the body; these very ones become his witnesses, the beholders of his dharma.
While they pass through every night, touching all things, rending all things, working now openly and now in secret — guard your own dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
On a road beset by many highwaymen, watched over by misshapen and terrible guards, let one's own deed be one's safeguard, for it is one's own deed that goes thither.
There no man shares with another out of his own deed; the fruit, born of one's own deed and shaped just as the deed was done — that alone is tasted.
As the throngs of apsarases, together with the great sages, attain their fruit and their joy, so men, by their deeds, attain it — borne in flying chariots at their will.
Whatever good is done here by the sinless and the perfected of soul, that the men of purified birth likewise attain.
By the causeways of the householder's dharma they go to the supreme goal — to a shared world with Prajāpati, with Bṛhaspati, and with the Hundred-Sacrificer.
A thousandfold, in manifold ways, I am eager to declare it; yet without the Lord, the gruel of folly that deludes the mind is not undone.
Your twice-eight years are gone; soon, surely, you will be twenty-five. Make your store of dharma, for your lifetime slips past you.
Before that Ender lays his curb, whose mouth gapes upon the heedless — even as it was grasped, so it has risen up — make haste in the keeping of dharma.
When you yourself shall go behind, and you yourself before, what use are self or other to one bound on that road?
That which serves the good who go down alone to the world beyond — that great treasure for the journey amid its terrors — lay it up.
The Lord, unhindered, carries off a man with his line, his root, and his kin, and there are none who can stop him; therefore lay up a store of dharma.
This teaching, my son, that I hold fitting for you here, set forth from my own insight and inference — act upon it.
He who by his own deed bestows his wealth on this man or that, through qualities born of folly and delusion, finds but one reward in a hundred.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let your sacred learning be made to bear fruit as you perform good works; that alone is the wisdom there which knows its debts and is joined to true aim.
This delight in dwelling in the village is the tethering rope; the doers of good cut it and depart, but the doers of evil cannot cut it.
What is your wealth to you, what your kinsmen, what your sons, my son, you who must die? Seek out the Self that has entered into the cave of the heart. And your grandfathers — where have they all gone?
Let tomorrow's task be done today, and the afternoon's in the morning; for who knows whose, and on what day, the army of death will come knocking?
Having followed as far as the edge of the burning ground, the kinsmen here turn back, casting the man into the fire — both kin and friends alike.
The unbelievers, the pitiless, men fixed in evil intent — set them at your left without misgiving, you who, untiring, seek what is highest.
While the world is thus struck down and pressed hard by Time, lay hold of a very great steadfastness and practice dharma with your whole soul.
And the man who rightly knows this way of insight, having here done dharma aright, thrives in happiness in the world beyond.
For those who truly know, the breaking of the body is not death, nor is there annihilation when the path is well kept; he who makes dharma grow is the wise one, while he who falls away from dharma is the deluded.
Of one's own two kinds of deed set going upon the road of action, the doer reaps the fruit according to law: the man of base deeds comes to hell, while he who has crossed to the far shore of dharma goes to the triple heaven.
Having gained the hard-won human state, which is the stairway to heaven, one should so compose oneself that one does not fall away again.
He whose mind, faithful to the path to heaven, does not stray from it — him they call a doer of meritorious deeds, one not to be mourned by friends and kin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whose unmarred understanding rests firm in its resolves, who has made his place secure in heaven — for him there is no great terror.
Those who are born in the groves of austerity and there meet their death — their dharma is the lesser, since they have never known the enjoyment of desire.
But he who, having renounced pleasures, practices austerity with his body — by him there is nothing that is not attained; that, in my judgment, is the high fruit.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, are yet to come and have already passed away. Whose are they, and whose are we?
You have no business with them, nor they any with you; they have gone, each by his own deeds, and you too shall go.
For in this world even a stranger acts as kin to the rich man, while the very kinsmen of the poor desert them while they yet live.
A man heaps up evil deeds out of regard for wife and household, and thereby comes to suffering, both in the world beyond and here as well.
See for yourself how the world of the living is riddled with holes by one's own deeds; therefore, my son, do in full all that has been declared.
Seeing all this clearly, one who longs for the world beyond should enter this realm of action and there perform what is holy and good.
By the fire of the sun, which turns the round of months and seasons, fed with the fuel of night and day, witness to the fruit that follows upon each being's own works, Time ripens all creatures by main force.
What is the use of wealth from which one neither gives nor enjoys? Of strength by which one does not subdue one's foes? Of learning by which one does not practice the dharma? Of a self that has not mastered and made obedient the senses?
Having heard this wholesome counsel spoken by Dvaipāyana, Śuka departed, leaving behind his father, the teacher of liberation.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How was Śuka, righteous of soul and of great austerity, born to Vyāsa, and how did he attain the supreme perfection? Tell me this, grandsire.
And upon whom did Vyāsa, rich in austerity, beget Śuka? For we do not know the mother of that great soul, nor his surpassing birth.
And how, while still a child, did his mind reach into subtle knowledge, such as the mind of no other, no second, in this whole world has done?
This I wish to hear at length, O most radiant one, for there is no satiety for me here as I listen to this supreme nectar.
Tell me, grandsire, faithfully and in due order, the greatness of Śuka, his union with the Self, and his deep wisdom.
Bhīṣma said: Not by years, not by grey hairs, not by wealth, not by kinsmen did the sages measure dharma: he who is learned in the Veda, he is great among us.
All this about which you ask me, son of Pāṇḍu, has austerity for its root; and only by restraining the senses does austerity arise, and in no other way.
By attachment to the senses a man surely meets with ruin; but by subduing those very senses he attains perfection.
The fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and of a hundred Vājapeyas, my son, is found not to equal even a fraction of yoga's reward.
On this I shall relate to you the fruit of Śuka's birth and of his yoga, and that supreme course of his, hard to be known by the unperfected.
Of old, they say, upon the peak of Meru, thick with groves of karṇikāra trees, the Great God roamed, surrounded by his terrible hosts of spirits.
There too of old was the goddess, daughter of the king of mountains; and there the lord Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana performed his divine austerity.
Entering into his own self through yoga, wholly devoted to the discipline of yoga, holding fast, he wrought austerity for the sake of a son, O best of the Kurus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"May a son be born to me, O mighty one, equal in power to fire, to earth, to water, to wind, and to the firmament" — so he prayed.
With this resolve, hard to be reached by the unperfected, established in the highest austerity, he sought a boon of the Lord of the gods.
Feeding only on air, the lord stood firm, they say, for a hundred years, worshipping the Great God of many forms, the consort of Umā.
There gathered all the brahmin-sages and the divine sages too, the guardians of the worlds before the Lord of the worlds, and the Sādhyas together with the Vasus.
The Ādityas and the Rudras, the maker of day and the maker of night, the Maruts and the Wind, the oceans and the rivers as well.
The two Aśvins, the celestial gandharvas, and the pair Nārada and Parvata, Viśvāvasu the gandharva, the Siddhas, and the hosts of apsarases.
There Rudra, the Great God, wearing a fair garland wrought of karṇikāra blossoms, shone like the moon clothed in its moonlight.
In that lovely divine forest, thronged with gods and divine sages, the seer, established in the supreme yoga, stood intent upon his desire for a son.
His radiance did not fade, nor did any weariness arise in him; and to all three worlds this seemed a wonder.
And the matted locks of that yoked one of measureless splendor were seen ablaze with his fiery power, like tongues of the all-consuming fire.
For the blessed Mārkaṇḍeya it was who told me this; he it was who ever recounted to me the deeds of the gods.
Even to this day, my son, those matted locks of the great-souled Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, kindled by that austerity and fire-hued, shine forth.
By austerity of such a kind and by his devotion, O Bhārata, the Great Lord, his heart made gracious, formed a resolve within his mind.
And the blessed three-eyed god spoke to him, as though smiling: "A son of just such a kind shall be yours, O Dvaipāyana."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Pure as fire, pure as wind, pure as earth, pure as water, and pure as space — so shall your great son be."
"Sharing that nature, that understanding, that very self, taking refuge in that alone, enveloping the three worlds with his splendor, he shall win unrivalled glory."
Bhīṣma said: Having won this supreme boon from the god, the son of Satyavatī took up the fire-drilling wood and churned it, wishing to kindle the sacred fire.
Then, O king, the blessed seer beheld an apsaras named Ghṛtācī, bearing a surpassing beauty radiant with her own glow.
Beholding the apsaras, the blessed seer Vyāsa was on the instant overpowered by desire there in that forest, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
And she, having made Vyāsa's mind tremble with longing, then became a parrot-hen, O great king, and so Ghṛtācī drew near.
Seeing that apsaras cloaked in another form, he was followed close by the body-born god of love that surged through all his limbs.
Though with great firmness the sage strove to hold down the desire lodged in his heart, Vyāsa could not restrain his mind once it had streamed forth; for, the passion being destined to be, he was carried away by the form of Ghṛtācī.
As the sage labored to restrain himself in his wish to kindle the fire, his seed fell suddenly upon the very drilling-wood.
With a mind untroubled, that best of the twice-born, the brahmin-sage, churned the drilling-wood even so; and therein was Śuka born, O king.
As the seed was being churned forth, Śuka was born, of great austerity, a supreme seer, a mighty yogin, sprung from the womb of the drilling-wood.
As the kindled fire at the sacrifice shines forth when it has received the oblation, so was Śuka born in that very likeness, blazing as it were with splendor.
Bearing his father's matchless form and hue, O Kaurava, that perfected soul then shone like a smokeless flame ablaze.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, taking her own embodied shape, came to him on Meru's height, O lord of men, and bathed him in her waters.
And from the sky, O Kaurava, a staff and a black antelope-skin fell to earth, O sovereign of kings, for the sake of the great-souled Śuka.
The gandharvas sang again and again, the hosts of apsarases danced, and the kettledrums of the gods sounded forth with mighty peals.
And Viśvāvasu the gandharva, and Tumburu and Nārada, and the gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū extolled the birth of Śuka.
There assembled the guardians of the worlds, with Śakra at their head, the gods and the divine sages, and the brahmin-sages too.
The Wind rained down there every kind of celestial flower, and the whole world, moving and unmoving, was filled with joy.
The great-souled god of mighty splendor, together with the goddess, then with affection himself performed in due rite the investiture of the sage's son, scarcely born.
To him Śakra, lord of the gods, gave with affection a water-pot of marvellous, divine appearance, and celestial garments, O mighty one.
Geese and hundred-petalled cranes and sārasa birds by the thousand, and parrots and blue jays, O Bhārata, circled him in reverence.
Thus the son of the drilling-wood, of great splendor, having gained his divine birth, dwelt there, wise, a keeper of vows, and inwardly composed.
No sooner was he born than the Vedas, with their mysteries and their compendia, came and waited upon him, O great king, even as they had upon his father.
Knower of the Vedas, their auxiliaries, and their commentaries, he chose Bṛhaspati for his teacher, O great king, meditating ever upon dharma alone.
Having studied all the Vedas with their mysteries and compendia, and the ancient lore in its entirety, and the sciences of statecraft, O mighty one,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the great sage gave his teacher the closing fee, returned home, and, a chaste student inwardly composed, undertook a fierce austerity.
Even in childhood, that one of great austerity was fit to be consulted by gods and seers, and honored by them for his knowledge and his penance.
Yet his mind, O lord of men, looking ever toward the discipline of liberation, took no delight in the three orders of life that have the householder's state for their root.
Bhīṣma said: Brooding upon liberation alone, Śuka went to his father, and, seeking the highest good, full of humility, he saluted his teacher and spoke:
"You, blessed one, are skilled in the laws of liberation: instruct me, lord, in such a way that the supreme peace of mind may arise in me."
Hearing his son's words, the supreme seer said to him: "Study, my son, both liberation and the manifold dharmas as well."
At his father's bidding Śuka, best of those who know the Brahman, mastered the whole science of yoga and also the Kāpila teaching, O Bhārata.
When Vyāsa saw his son endowed with the splendor of the Brahman, his prowess equal to Brahmā's, and accomplished in the lore of liberation,
he said: "Go now to Janaka, the lord of Mithilā; he will expound to you the whole matter of liberation, fully and in detail."
At his father's bidding he set out toward Janaka, king of Mithilā, to ask of him the consummation of dharma and the highest goal of liberation.
And he was told, unsurprised: "You are to go by a human road; you must not travel by your power, coursing through the sky."
"You must go by the straight way, not by a path that seeks comfort; nor must distinctions be sought after, for distinctions breed attachment."
"No pride is to be shown before that king for whom we serve as priests; you must remain subject to him, and he will cut away your doubt."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"That king is skilled in dharma and accomplished in the science of liberation; he is one for whom I officiate, and whatever he says is to be done without misgiving."
Thus addressed, that righteous sage went on foot to Mithilā, though he was able to traverse the sea-girt earth through the air.
Crossing over mountains, fording rivers and lakes, and the manifold forests thronged with many serpents and beasts of prey,
passing in turn beyond the two regions of Meru and Hari and the region of Himavat, he reached the land of Bhārata.
Beholding various lands inhabited by the Cīnas and the Hūṇas, the great sage came at last to this land of Āryāvarta.
Mindful of his father's word and pondering that very purpose, he passed along the road, a sky-farer faring as it were through the sky.
Lovely market-towns and prosperous cities and jewels of varied kinds — Śuka, though he saw them, saw them not.
Lovely gardens, and temples, and holy fording-places too he passed by upon his road,
and in no long while he came to the land of the Videhas, guarded by the great-souled Janaka, that righteous king.
There he saw many villages where food and savory fare abounded, and thriving hamlets and herdsmen's settlements teeming with many a cattle-fold.
He passed teeming lands rich with rice and barley, frequented by swans and cranes, and adorned by the hundreds with stately, beautiful lotus-pools.
Having crossed through the Videha country, thronged with prosperous folk, he reached the lovely, richly endowed pleasure-grove of Mithilā.
Crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, thronging with men and women — the steadfast one passed through it, seeing it yet as though he saw it not.
Bearing that burden in his mind and pondering that single aim, delighting in the Self, serene of spirit, he came at last to Mithilā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Reaching her gate, he was barred by the gatekeepers; rapt in meditation he stood, the liberated one, and only when recognized did he enter.
Coming to the royal highway, crowded with prosperous people, and reaching the king's palace, without hesitation he entered in.
There too the gatekeepers with harsh words forbade him, and Śuka, free of all anger, simply stood his ground.
Though scorched by sun and road, beset by hunger, thirst, and weariness, he neither grew faint nor wilted, nor did he withdraw from that heat.
But one of those gatekeepers, filled with compassion, beheld Śuka standing there like the sun arrived at its zenith.
Having honored him as was fitting and saluted him with folded hands, he led him then into the second court of the king's palace.
Seated there, my child, Śuka of great splendor pondered liberation alone, looking with equal eye upon shade and upon sun.
After but a moment the king's minister came to him with folded hands and led him into the third court of the king's palace.
There, adjoining the inner apartments, was a great park like Citraratha's own, with well-laid bathing-pools, lovely, its trees in flower.
Having shown Śuka that finest of groves and appointed him a worthy seat, the minister then withdrew once more.
Then young women, fair to behold, in graceful attire, shapely of hip, clad in fine red garments and decked in refined gold ornaments,
skilled in converse and witty repartee, accomplished in dance and song, speaking always with a smile, in beauty the equals of the apsarases —
adept in the arts of love, reading every mood, accomplished in all things — these chief courtesans, more than fifty women, came hastening near.
Receiving him with water for his feet and the rest, honoring him with the highest reverence, they refreshed him too with wholesome food befitting the place and the hour.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When he had eaten, my child, they showed him that delightful garden of the inner court, O Bhārata, one part after another.
Sporting and laughing and singing, those women, all skilled in the ways of the heart, then waited upon Śuka of noble spirit.
But the son of the fire-sticks, pure of soul, free of the three doubts, performer of the threefold rite, his senses mastered and his anger conquered, neither rejoiced nor grew wroth.
To him those choice women gave a divine couch and seat, worthy of the best, jeweled and spread with coverlets such as men contend to own.
Having washed his feet and worshiped at the twilight hour, Śuka sat down upon that holy seat, pondering still that single aim.
In the first watch of the night he gave himself wholly to meditation; at midnight, as was proper, that self-possessed one took his sleep.
Then, rising after a brief while and at once performing his ablutions, the wise one, though surrounded by women, betook himself again to meditation alone.
In this manner the steadfast son of Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana passed the remainder of that day and that night within the royal household, O Bhārata.
Bhīṣma said: Then, O Bhārata, that king Janaka, together with his ministers, putting his household priest at the fore and all the women of the inner apartments,
and bearing before him a seat, and jewels of many kinds, and carrying the welcome-offering upon his head, drew near to the teacher's son.
Taking up that seat, adorned with many jewels, spread with enviable coverlets, auspicious on every side and richly wrought,
which the priest held ready — the king, touching it with his hand, gave it, most reverently honored, to the teacher's son Śuka.
When the son of Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana had taken his seat there, the king honored him according to the scriptures: offering first water for his feet, then the welcome-draught and a cow; and Śuka received that worship with its sacred verses in due form.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And having accepted that worship from Janaka, the best of the twice-born gave leave for the cow to be spared, and showing honor to the king,
Śuka of great brilliance inquired, O lord of kings, after the king's welfare, his unfailing prosperity and his health, and that of his retinue as well.
Then, granted leave by him, the king of noble nature and high lineage sat down upon the ground with his attendants, his hands folded in reverence.
And the king, having inquired after the welfare and well-being of Vyāsa's son, then asked him this: 'What is the purpose of your coming?'
Śuka said: My father told me — blessings upon you — 'The king of Videha, renowned as Janaka, is one for whom I have officiated, and he is versed in the law and aim of liberation.
Go to him at once, if any doubt lingers in your heart, whether concerning action or withdrawal from action; he will cut your doubt away.'
So I, at my father's bidding, have come here to question you; therefore, O best of those who uphold the law, you should tell me truly:
What ought a brāhmaṇa to do in this world, and of what nature is the aim of liberation? And how is liberation to be attained — by knowledge, or by austerity?
Janaka said: Hear, then, what a brāhmaṇa ought to do in this world from his birth onward. Once invested with the sacred thread, my child, he should be wholly devoted to the Veda;
by austerity, by service to his teacher, and by chastity, O mighty one, he becomes free of debt to the gods and to the ancestors, and free of all envy.
Having studied the Vedas, self-controlled, and having bestowed the teacher's fee, and then obtaining leave, the twice-born one should return home from his studentship.
Having returned, he should dwell in the householder's state, self-restrained and with a wife, free of envy, and, as is proper, keeping the sacred fires kindled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And having begotten sons and grandsons, he should dwell in the abode of the forest hermitage, tending those same fires as the scriptures prescribe, and welcoming guests gladly.
Then in the forest, the knower of dharma, having in due form laid those fires within his own self, beyond the pairs of opposites and freed of passion, should dwell in the abode of the renunciant devoted to Brahman.
Śuka said: When knowledge and discernment have arisen, immediate and abiding within the heart, must one then perforce dwell through the orders of life and in the forests?
This I ask of you, and you should answer it; tell me, O ruler of men, in accord with the very truth of the Veda's meaning.
Janaka said: Without knowledge and discernment there can be no attaining of liberation; and without the bond with a teacher, no attaining of knowledge is taught.
The teacher is the ferryman, and knowledge is here called the raft; but once he has understood and accomplished his task, having crossed over, he should let both go.
For the unbroken continuance of the worlds and the unbroken continuance of rites, the dharma told of in the teaching of the four orders of life was practiced by the ancients.
By this disciplined sequence, through many births, having performed both good and ill deeds, what is called liberation is here attained.
Through causes ripened in many wombs of recurring existence, this man of purified soul reaches liberation even in the first order of life.
But for one who has attained it — liberated, having seen the truth, wise, and longing for the supreme — what need is there of the three remaining orders of life?
Let him ever shun the faults born of passion and of darkness; treading the path of purity, let him behold the Self by the self.
Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings within the Self, he is not tainted, as the water-creature is not wetted by the water.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Like a bird soaring up in flight, he wins endlessness in the world beyond; casting off the body, released, beyond the pairs of opposites, he attains to perfect peace.
On this, hear the verses sung of old by King Yayāti, which, my child, are held in memory by the twice-born skilled in the science of liberation.
The light is within the Self, nowhere else, and it delights in that alone; and it can be seen of oneself by a mind well composed.
He of whom no other is afraid, and who fears no other, and who neither craves nor hates — then he becomes Brahman.
When he harbors no evil intent toward any being, in deed, in thought, or in word — then he becomes Brahman.
Yoking the self by austerity, casting off bewildering envy, and abandoning desire and greed — thereupon he attains to the state of Brahman.
When toward all that is heard and seen, and toward all beings and their dissolution, he becomes the same, beyond the pairs of opposites — then he becomes Brahman.
When he looks with equal eye upon praise and blame alike, upon gold and upon iron, and upon pleasure and pain the same,
upon cold and heat, upon gain and loss, the dear and the unwelcome, upon life and death alike — then he becomes Brahman.
As a tortoise, having stretched forth its limbs here, draws them in again, so should the mendicant restrain the senses by the mind.
As a house enveloped in darkness is made visible by a lamp, so by the lamp of the intellect can the Self be perceived.
All this I see in you, O best of the wise; and whatever else there is to be known, that too you know in its very truth.
O brāhmaṇa-sage, you are known to me as one who has reached the end of all objects of sense, by the grace of your teacher and by your own diligent learning.
And by that same grace, O great sage, this divine knowledge has arisen in me also; therefore are you known to me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Greater is your discernment, and higher your attainment, and greater your sovereign power — yet of this you yourself are not aware.
Whether through immaturity, or doubt, or fear born of not yet being released, a man may fail to reach that goal even when discernment has arisen.
But with pure resolve, his doubt severed by such as I am, loosing the knots of the heart, he attains that goal.
And you, in whom discernment has arisen, steadfast of mind and free of craving — even without such resolve, O brāhmaṇa, you attain that supreme state.
For you there is no distinction in pleasures and pains, there is no craving; no eagerness for dance and song, and no passion arises in you.
You have no bondage to kinsmen, and amid terrors there is no fear in you; I see you, O greatly blessed one, holding a clod, a stone, and gold as all alike.
I, and the other thinkers as well, behold you as having entered upon the supreme path, the imperishable and the free of all affliction.
That which is the fruit of a brāhmaṇa's life here, and of what nature is the aim of liberation — in that very state you abide, O brāhmaṇa; what more do you ask?
Bhīṣma said: Having heard this counsel, the perfected one, his resolve now firm, taking his stand upon the Self by the self, and beholding the Self by the self,
his purpose accomplished, happy and at peace, set forth in silence facing the north, making for the snow-clad mountain, of a nature like unto the Wind.
And at that very time the divine sage Nārada was on his way to behold the Himavat, frequented by the perfected ones and the celestial wanderers.
That mountain was thronged with troops of apsarases and resounded with the strains of song; it teemed with bands of kiṃnaras and with kingfishers as well,
with cormorants and wagtails, with bright-hued jīvajīvaka birds, with peacocks of brilliant plumage radiant with a hundred cries, with flocks of royal swans, and with joyous cuckoos.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There the king of birds, Garutmān, comes ever and again; and there the four guardians of the world, the gods together with their hosts of sages, repair continually, desiring the welfare of the world.
There the great-souled Viṣṇu once performed austerities for the sake of a son; and there in his childhood Kumāra hurled defiance at the dwellers in heaven,
when Skanda, scorning the three worlds, planted his spear upon the surface of the earth, and the lord of the world spoke these challenging words:
"If there be another mightier than I, O brāhmaṇas, one dearer to you and more devoted to brahman, a second hero of valor in the three worlds—
let him lift up this spear, or even make it tremble!" Hearing this, the worlds were thrown into dismay, wondering, "Who could lift this up?"
Then the blessed Viṣṇu beheld the whole host of gods, with senses and minds bewildered, dismayed together with the asuras and rākṣasas, and he pondered, "What deed well done would here be fitting?"
He would not brook that challenge, and he looked upon the son of Fire. Then the Supreme Person, pure of soul, laughed, and with his left hand made the blazing spear tremble.
And when the spear was set trembling by the mighty Viṣṇu, the whole earth was shaken, with its mountains, woods, and forests.
Though able to wrench it up, the lord Viṣṇu only made it tremble and did not draw it forth, sparing thereby the glory of King Skanda's challenge.
Having made it tremble, the blessed one said this to Prahrāda: "Behold the valor of Kumāra—no other could do this deed."
Unable to bear those words, Prahrāda, resolved to wrench it up, seized the spear of Skanda—yet he could not so much as make it tremble.
Letting forth a mighty cry, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, swooning and overcome, fell to the ground upon the summit of the mountain.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There, my son, having gone to the northern quarter beside the king of mountains, the unassailable god whose banner bears the bull performed his austerities without ceasing.
His hermitage was encircled by blazing fire—a place named Ādityabandhana, unapproachable by those who have not subdued themselves.
There no yakṣas, rākṣasas, or dānavas can pass; ten yojanas in extent, it is wholly wrapped in flames of fire.
There the blessed and valorous Fire-god himself abides, quelling every obstacle for the wise Mahādeva.
For a thousand divine years Mahādeva, firm in his vow, stood there upon a single foot, scorching the gods with the heat of his penance.
But upon the eastern quarter of the wise king of mountains, on a secluded slope, the son of Parāśara, the great ascetic Vyāsa, of mighty penance, instructed his disciples in the Vedas.
He taught the illustrious Sumantu, and Vaiśaṃpāyana, and the deeply wise Jaimini, and Paila too, the ascetic—
surrounded by these disciples sat Vyāsa of great penance. There the son sprung from the kindling-sticks, pure of soul, beheld his father's holy and excellent hermitage, shining like the sun in the sky.
Then Vyāsa beheld his son drawing near—encircled with radiance, blazing like fire, splendid as the sun itself.
Unimpeded by trees, by crags, or by rugged ground, the great-souled one, yoked in yoga, came like an arrow loosed from the bowstring.
Approaching, the son born of the kindling-sticks clasped his father's feet; and the great sage greeted those disciples too, each according to his pleasure.
Then Śuka, his heart full of joy, reported to his father in full and without omission his colloquy with King Janaka.
Thus instructing his disciples and his son, the valorous son of Parāśara, the great sage Vyāsa, dwelt upon the flank of the Himavat.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then on a certain day the disciples gathered round him and stood before him—accomplished in the study of the Vedas, tranquil of soul, their senses conquered.
Having attained mastery in the Vedas with their auxiliary sciences, those disciples of surpassing austerity then spoke to Vyāsa, their teacher, with hands joined in reverence:
"Blessed with great good fortune and enriched with renown are we; yet now we desire one favor to be granted us by our teacher."
Hearing their words, the brahmarṣi said to them, "Speak it, my children—whatever you would have done, that is dear to me."
Hearing this word of their teacher, the disciples, glad at heart, again folded their hands and, bowing their heads to their guru,
spoke together, O king, this excellent word: "If our preceptor is pleased with us, then blessed are we, O best of sages.
We all crave one boon granted by the great sage: that no sixth disciple of yours should attain renown in this lore. Be gracious to us in this."
"We four are your disciples, and the teacher's son is the fifth; let the Vedas be established here in us alone—this is the boon we crave."
Hearing the disciples' words, Vyāsa, knower of the truth of the Vedas' meaning, the wise son of Parāśara, mindful of the good of the world beyond, righteous of soul, spoke to his disciples a word in accord with dharma and conducing to the highest weal:
"The sacred lore must ever be imparted to a brāhmaṇa who is eager to learn, by one who steadfastly desires a dwelling in the world of brahman.
Let your numbers grow many; let this Veda be spread abroad. Yet it must not be bestowed upon one who is no true disciple, nor upon one without vows, nor upon one whose soul is unperfected.
All these marks of a true disciple are to be known according to their truth; to one whose conduct has not been tested, knowledge must in no wise be given.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For as pure gold is tested by heating, cutting, and rubbing, so should one examine disciples by their lineage, their virtues, and the rest.
And your disciples must not be set to a task that is no fit task and that is fraught with great peril. According to one's understanding and one's recitation, so will the knowledge bear its fruit.
Let every man cross over hardships; let every man behold good fortune. One may cause the four varṇas to hear the lore, placing the brāhmaṇa foremost.
This study of the Veda is indeed a great duty, so it is held; for the praise of the gods were the Vedas created by the Self-Existent.
Whoever out of delusion should revile a brāhmaṇa versed to the end in the Vedas, that man, through the brāhmaṇa's ill-wishing, will without doubt come to ruin.
He who expounds against dharma and he who questions against dharma—one or the other of the two perishes, or else incurs enmity.
All this has been declared to you concerning the rule of sacred recitation. One should do good to his disciples, and let this abide within your hearts."
Bhīṣma said: Hearing this word of their teacher, the mighty disciples of Vyāsa, glad of heart, then embraced one another.
"What the blessed one has spoken to us, joined to the present and to the future, is firmly rooted in our minds, and we shall do even so."
Thus honoring one another, their hearts well pleased, they—skilled in speech—again made their request to their teacher:
"We desire, O great sage, to go from this mountain down to the earth, to multiply the Vedas in their many forms—if it be your pleasure, O lord."
Hearing the disciples' words, the lord, the son of Parāśara, then replied with a word joined to dharma and to wealth, and conducing to their good:
"Go to the earth or to the world of the gods, whichever pleases you; but you must be ever vigilant, for the sacred lore abounds in pitfalls."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all of them, granted leave by their truth-speaking teacher, departed, having circled Vyāsa from the right and saluted him with their heads bowed.
Descending to the earth, they then ordained the office of the four priests, conducting sacrifices for brāhmaṇas, for kṣatriyas, and for vaiśyas alike.
Ever honored by the twice-born, rejoicing and content in the householder's life, devoted to officiating at sacrifice and to teaching, they were prosperous and renowned throughout the world.
When his disciples had gone down to the earth, the wise Vyāsa, with only his son for company, sat down in solitude, silent and absorbed in meditation.
Nārada, of exceeding great penance, beheld him at the hermitage, and in due season addressed him in a voice of honeyed syllables:
"Ho there, great sage, descendant of Vāsiṣṭha! The chant of the Veda is heard no more. Why do you sit alone, silent and absorbed in thought, as though brooding?"
"Bereft of the chant of the Veda, this mountain has no splendor, even as the moon, when eclipsed, is dimmed by dust and darkness.
Though frequented by hosts of divine sages, yet emptied of the sound of the Veda, it shines no longer as before, but is like a dwelling-place of niṣādas.
And the sages, the gods, and the mighty gandharvas, forsaken by the chant of the Veda, shine not as they did of old."
Hearing Nārada's words, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana said: "Great sage, skilled in the discourse of the Veda, what you have spoken—
this is wholly agreeable to my mind, and you are worthy to declare it, being all-knowing, all-seeing, and ever curious in all things.
Whatever has come to pass in the three worlds rests entire within your knowledge. Command me then, O brāhmaṇa sage; tell me, what shall I do for you?"
"Declare, O brahmarṣi, what I am to perform; for parted now from my disciples, my mind here is not greatly glad."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nārada said: The Vedas are sullied by neglect of recitation; the lack of vows is the brāhmaṇa's stain; the Vāhīkas are the stain of the earth, and idle curiosity the stain of women.
Let your honor recite the Vedas together with your wise son, dispelling by the chant of the Veda the darkness wrought by the terror of the rākṣasas.
Bhīṣma said: Hearing Nārada's words, Vyāsa, supreme knower of dharma, said "So be it," rejoicing, and firm of vow in the practice of the Veda.
Then with his son Śuka he set about the recitation of the Veda, with a loud voice trained in the science of accent, as though filling the worlds with sound.
As the two recited thus, expounding the manifold doctrines of dharma, a wind blew beyond all measure, driven by the gale off the ocean.
Thereupon Vyāsa checked his son, saying, "This is a time when study must cease." But Śuka, no sooner checked, was filled with curiosity,
and asked his father: "O holy one, whence has this wind arisen? Be pleased to tell me all the workings of the wind."
Hearing this word of Śuka, Vyāsa, exceedingly amazed, spoke this word concerning the occasion of the suspension of study:
"A divine eye has arisen in you; your mind is steady and unsullied. Free from darkness and from passion, you are established in goodness.
As one beholds his own reflection in a mirror, so do you behold the Self by the self. Laying the Vedas within yourself, ponder them well with your intellect.
The path of the gods belongs to Viṣṇu; the path of the fathers is of the dark quality. These are the two roads beyond death—the one leading upward to heaven, the other downward.
Upon the earth and in the firmament, where the winds blow together, there are these seven paths of the wind. Learn them now from me in their order.
There the troops of gods, the Sādhyas, came into being, of mighty strength; and their son too was born, Samāna by name, hard to conquer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Udāna was his son; Vyāna was Udāna's offspring; and after him is to be known Apāna, and Prāṇa beyond him.
Prāṇa was without offspring, unassailable, the scorcher of foes. But the several functions of these winds I shall now declare to you according to the truth.
In all living beings the wind sustains, severally, the diverse motions of life; and because it makes creatures breathe, it is called prāṇa, the breath of life.
That wind which drives onward the massed banks of cloud, those born of smoke and those born of heat, is the first, moving upon the first path; it is the wind named Pravaha.
That of surpassing splendour which gathers the moisture in the sky from the clouds and from the lightnings is the second; named Āvaha, it blows roaring as it breathes.
That which ceaselessly brings about the rising of the luminaries, of the moon and the rest, and which within the bodies of beings the great seers call by the name of udāna,
that wind which holds up the waters drawn from the four oceans, and which, lifting them, draws the waters from the rain-clouds into the sky,
that which, charging the rain-clouds with water, delivers them to Parjanya, the rain-god — most abundant in showers, the third, ever in motion, is named Udvaha.
By it the dark clouds, borne along in many directions and gathered apart, set themselves to release their rain and become massed thunderheads piled cloud on cloud.
Welded together and pierced through by it, the clouds become the rivers of the thundering sky; gathered for the protection of the world, they take on the form of clouds.
That which bears the celestial cars of the gods through the firmament is the fourth, the wind named Saṃvaha, the crusher of mountains.
That swift and parching wind which shatters the clouds and dries up their savour — struck by it, the clouds break apart and form no thunderheads.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Coursing on with dreadful portents, carrying the thunder of the heavens, of mighty speed, is the fifth wind, named Vivaha.
Upon it, as upon a floating raft, the celestial waters are borne through the sky, and the holy water of the heavenly Gaṅgā is held up and abides.
Within it the maker of day, the sun, whose single ray is turned back from afar, becomes the source of a thousand beams by which the earth is made to shine.
By it the moon, that celestial treasury of nectar, is replenished; the sixth, named Parivaha, is that wind, foremost among the swift.
That which at the hour of the end casts forth the life-breaths of all that breathe, in whose track both Death and the son of Vivasvat — Yama — follow after,
that which, for those who look rightly with the understanding by an ever-spiritual peace and who delight in the practice of meditation, conduces to immortality —
reaching which with its swiftness, the ten thousand sons of Dakṣa, the lord of creatures, attained to the ends of the quarters,
that which, once it has cast a thing forth, vanquished, it goes on and never returns — that highest wind, hard to withstand, is named Parāvaha.
Thus these sons of Aditi, the most wondrous Maruts, never resting, blow on every side, pervading all, upholding all.
And here is the great marvel: that this noblest of mountains was suddenly set trembling by that wind as it blew full against it.
This wind is the breath of Viṣṇu, my son; when, driven by its own force, it is suddenly stirred up, the whole world quakes in distress.
