Therefore the knowers of the Veda do not recite the sacred word while the wind blows too strongly; for fear of the wind is enjoined, and that recitation would be marred.
Having spoken these words, the lord, the son of Parāśara, and having bidden his son, "Resume thy study," then betook himself to the heavenly Gaṅgā of the sky.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: In this interval, when the place was empty, Nārada drew near to Śuka, who was absorbed in his recitation, intending to expound the meanings of the Vedas that he longed to hear.
Beholding the divine sage Nārada come before him, Śuka honoured him with the rite ordained in the Veda, offering first the welcome-water.
Then Nārada said, well pleased and joyful, "Speak, O best of those who know the Absolute; with what blessing, my son, shall I unite thee?"
Hearing Nārada's words, Śuka replied, O descendant of Bharata: "With that which would be of benefit in this world it is fitting that thou shouldst unite me."
Nārada said: In olden days, to the seers of disciplined souls who sought to know the truth, the blessed Sanatkumāra spoke these words.
There is no eye like knowledge, there is no austerity like knowledge; there is no sorrow like passion, there is no happiness like renunciation.
To turn away from sinful action, to be ever of meritorious disposition, good conduct and right behaviour — this is the unsurpassed good.
He who, having attained this joyless human state, clings to it is deluded; he is unequal to release from sorrow, for attachment is the very mark of sorrow.
The mind of the man who clings wavers, swelling the net of delusion; wrapped in the net of delusion, he reaps sorrow both here and hereafter.
By every means the man who seeks the good must subdue desire and anger; for these two stand ready to destroy the good.
Let a man ever guard his austerity from anger, his prosperity from envy, his learning from honour and dishonour, and his own self from heedlessness.
Freedom from cruelty is the highest dharma, and forbearance the highest strength; knowledge of the self is the highest knowledge, and nothing is found higher than truth.
To speak the truth is good, yet even better than truth may be that which benefits; that which is of utmost benefit to living beings — this, in my view, is truth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who renounces the fruit of all his undertakings, free of desire and free of possessions, he by whom all has been wholly let go — he is the wise, he is the learned man.
With senses subject to the self he moves here among the objects of sense without cleaving to them, his soul at peace, unaltered, composed.
Himself not bound to them, whether among those who are like himself or apart from them, he, being freed, before long attains the highest good.
He who, O sage, keeps ever without seeing, without touching, and without converse together with living beings — he finds the highest good.
Let him do no harm to any living being, and let him walk in the way of friendliness; having attained this birth, let him bear enmity toward none.
Possessing nothing, perfect contentment, freedom from craving, and steadiness — this, they say, is the highest good for the self-knower who has conquered himself.
Renouncing possessions, become, my son, the conqueror of thy senses; take thy stand in the sorrowless state, free from fear both here and hereafter.
They who are without craving do not grieve; cast away the lure of the senses from thyself. Having renounced that lure, gentle one, thou shalt be freed from the burning of sorrow.
The sage ever fixed in austerity, self-controlled, with disciplined soul, who longs to conquer the unconquered, must remain unattached amid all attachments.
Unattached to the bonds of the qualities, ever delighting in the solitary life, the brāhmaṇa before long attains unsurpassed happiness.
Among beings that take their pleasure in pairs of opposites, the sage who delights alone — know him to be content in true wisdom; the one content in knowledge does not grieve.
By good deeds one wins godhood, by mixed deeds a human birth, and by evil deeds, helpless, one wins a lowly birth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therein, ceaselessly assailed by the sorrows of death and old age, the creature is cooked in the round of rebirth: how is it that thou dost not perceive this?
In the harmful thou takest the harmful for the good, in the unstable for the stable, in the worthless for the worthwhile: why dost thou not awaken?
Wrapping thyself round, like a silkworm spinning its cocoon, with the many threads of delusion that are thine own offspring, thou dost not awaken.
Enough of possessions here, for possession is a thing of fault; the silkworm, that little spinner, is bound by the very cocoon it makes its own.
Clinging to sons, wives, and household, creatures sink down, foundering like aged forest elephants drowned in the mire of a pool.
Behold these creatures, sorely afflicted, dragged in by the net of affection, like fish drawn in by a great net and cast up upon dry land.
Household, sons and wife, the body, hoards of wealth — all belongs to others and is unstable; what is truly thine own save the good and ill that thou hast wrought?
When, abandoning all, thou must depart helpless, why art thou bent upon the worthless and dost not pursue thine own true good?
How wilt thou travel alone that road which is the wilderness of darkness — without rest, without support, without provisions, without a guide?
For when thou hast set forth, none will follow at thy back; only thy good and ill deeds will go after thee as thou departest.
Learning, action, valour, and far-reaching knowledge are pursued for the sake of gain; but he whose end is achieved is set free.
That delight of one who dwells in the village is the binding rope; cutting it, the doers of good go free, but the doers of evil cut it not.
Whose banks are forms, whose current is the mind, whose island is touch, that bears along taste; whose mud is smell, whose water is sound, hard to ferry on the road to heaven —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
that swift river, whose oar is forbearance, whose substance is truth, whose harbour-banyan is steadfastness in dharma, traversed by the wind of renunciation — let him cross it by the boat of the understanding.
Renounce dharma and unrighteousness, renounce both truth and falsehood; and having renounced both truth and falsehood, renounce that by which thou renouncest.
Renounce dharma by ceasing to will, and unrighteousness by non-harming; renounce both truth and falsehood by the understanding, and the understanding itself by the highest resolve.
Its pillars are bones, knit together by sinews, plastered over with flesh and blood, bound round with skin, foul-smelling, filled with urine and dung —
beset by age and grief, the abode of disease, ailing, defiled with passion and impermanent — cast off this dwelling-place of the elements.
This whole moving universe and whatever is unmoving — all that is great and all that is the minutest atom — is in essence composed of the great elements.
The five senses, and tamas, sattva, and rajas — thus this aggregate of seventeen is named the Unmanifest.
Joined here with all the objects of sense, both manifest and unmanifest, this becomes the group of twenty-five, the principle made up of the manifest and the unmanifest.
United with all these, it is called the Person; herein lie the triad of aims, pleasure and pain, life and likewise death.
He who knows this in truth knows the origin and the dissolution of things; here, O son of Parāśara's line, is what is to be understood, and whatever else there is of all the kinds of knowledge.
Whatever is grasped by the senses, that stands as the manifest; what lies beyond the senses, apprehended only by its marks, is to be known as the unmanifest.
The embodied one is nourished by the restrained senses, as if by streams of water; he beholds the self spread through the world, and the world within the self.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The power of one who sees the higher and the lower beholds no shore of knowledge, even as he sees all beings in every condition and at all times.
For one who has become the Absolute no contact with evil arises; for him who by knowledge has transcended the manifold afflictions born of delusion, the path of the world is not lost in the light of his understanding.
The creature without beginning or end, abiding in the self, imperishable, the non-doer and the formless — so the blessed knower of the sacred fords has declared.
The creature ever made wretched by those very deeds he himself has done, in order to ward off his own pain, slays other creatures in manifold ways.
Thereupon he takes on yet again much fresh deeds, and again is tormented by them, like a sick man who has eaten what is harmful to him.
Stricken with delusion without cease, taking his sorrows for happiness, he is bound and churned forever by his deeds, as butter is churned by the churning-stick.
Then, even when freed from one bond of his own, through the rising up of fresh deeds here below, he wanders round the round of rebirth like a wheel, suffering many pains.
And so you, having turned away from bondage and turned away likewise from action, become one who knows all, conquers all, and is perfected — wholly free of clinging to existence.
By self-restraint and through the power of austerity, having warded off any new bondage, many have attained perfection — unhindered and dawning into bliss.
Nārada said: There is a sorrowless teaching, made to destroy sorrow, peace-bestowing and benign; hearing it, one gains wisdom, and gaining that wisdom one flourishes in happiness.
Thousands of occasions for grief and hundreds of occasions for fear, day after day, beset the fool — but never the wise.
Therefore, for the destruction of all that is unwelcome, mark well this ancient tale of mine; if the mind is held under control, it attains the undoing of sorrow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From union with what is unwelcome and from separation from what is dear, men of meager understanding are yoked to the sufferings of the mind.
When possessions have passed away, one should not dwell upon the merits they had; for him who ceases to prize them, the bond of affection is loosed.
Wherever passion arises, there one should become a discerner of faults; one should regard even what is cherished as if unwelcome, and so quickly grow dispassionate.
He who grieves over what is past gains thereby no profit, no merit, no renown; he may even be brought to ruin, and yet the lost thing does not return to him.
By the strands of nature all beings are joined together, and just so are they parted; this is no ground for the grief of any single one.
He who grieves over the past — whether one dead or one lost — gains only sorrow upon sorrow, and falls into a twofold misfortune.
Those who, beholding through wisdom the unbroken succession in the worlds, shed no tears — for one who sees all things rightly, no occasion for weeping arises.
When an affliction of suffering befalls, whether of the body or of the mind, and nothing can be done against it, one should not brood upon it.
This is the medicine for sorrow: that one should not dwell upon it; for sorrow brooded over does not depart, but rather grows the greater.
Mental suffering one should slay with wisdom, and bodily suffering with remedies; this is the power of discernment — let him not sink to the level of the foolish.
Youth, beauty, life, the hoarding of wealth, health, the company of loved ones — all are impermanent; in these the wise man does not grasp with greed.
A man ought not, by himself alone, to grieve over a calamity that has befallen a whole land; without grieving he should act against it, if he sees a course of remedy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In life there is far more suffering than happiness — of this there is no doubt; through delusion comes attachment to the objects of sense, and death is held unwelcome.
The man who utterly renounces both pain and pleasure alike attains absolutely to Brahman; for him the wise do not grieve.
Riches are won with pain and given up with pain; in their keeping there is no happiness, and with pain are they gained — at their loss one should not grieve.
Attaining one greater state of wealth after another, men remain unsatisfied and go to their destruction; the wise, however, attain contentment.
All hoards end in depletion, all risings end in falling, all unions end in separation, and life itself ends in death.
There is no end to thirst, but contentment is the supreme happiness; therefore the wise look upon contentment itself as wealth in this world.
Not even for the space of an eyeblink does the passing of one's years stand still; when one's own body is impermanent, why brood as though anything were eternal?
Reflecting on the non-being inherent in all beings, those who have come to know what lies beyond darkness do not grieve; their journey is accomplished, and they behold the supreme goal.
This man, still gathering and never sated in his desires — death, falling upon him as a tiger upon its prey, seizes him and is gone.
Yet should one see a means for the release from suffering, without grieving he should set to work upon it, steadfast and free of vice.
In sound, in touch, in form, in smells, and in tastes, there is nothing more than their enjoyment — for the rich man or the poor alike.
Before beings come together there is no suffering, but only well-being; at the separation of all things, however, let him not grieve who abides in his own nature.
By firmness one should guard the loins and the belly, the hands and the feet by the eye, the eye and the ear by the mind, the mind by speech, and speech by knowledge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Withdrawing affection from both the familiar and the stranger, he who moves through the world unpuffed by pride — he is happy, and he is wise.
Seated and rejoicing in the inner Self, free of expectation, free of craving, he who goes through the world with the Self alone for his companion becomes happy.
Nārada said: When the reversal of happiness and sorrow comes to pass, neither wisdom, nor sound policy, nor manly effort can save a man from it.
By his very nature a man should persist in effort, for the diligent man does not sink down; from old age, death, and disease he should rescue the self that is dear to him.
For diseases, of the body and of the mind, torment the bodies of men like sharp-pointed arrows loosed by mighty bowmen.
The body of the sick man — anxious in his cravings, trembling, longing to live yet helpless — is dragged away to its destruction.
The nights and days flow on and never return, like the currents of rivers, bearing away the lifespan of mortals again and again.
This unceasing alternation of the bright and the dark fortnights ages the mortal who is born, and does not pause even for the blink of an eye.
That sun, ageless yet aging the joys and sorrows of beings, goes down to its setting and rises again, again and again.
Taking up the never-before-seen, unsuspected conditions of men — the welcome and the unwelcome alike — the nights pass on to their setting.
Whatever a man might wish, according to his desire, that very thing among objects of longing he would attain — if only the fruit of a man's action were not subject to another power.
For men who are self-controlled, capable, and wise are seen to come to nothing, deprived of the fruit of their own labors.
While others, foolish, devoid of merit, the basest of men, though joined to no blessings, are seen to have every desire fulfilled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yet another, ever bent upon doing harm to creatures and upon deceiving the world, grows old amid nothing but pleasures.
Upon one man, idle and sitting still, Fortune comes to wait; while another, for all his pursuit of action, does not attain what he seeks.
Declare, then, what the fault of a man is, given his own nature: the seed conceived in one place goes again to another.
When that seed has lodged in the womb, an embryo may form or may not; its failure to develop is found to be like the falling of the mango's blossom.
For some who long for sons, who desire continuance of their line and strive with all their power for success, no fertile seed comes to be at all.
And for those who recoil from offspring as from an enraged venomous serpent, a long-lived son is nonetheless born — how is it that the father himself becomes, in him, but a ghost made manifest?
Having worshipped the gods and performed austerities, by wretched men greedy for sons, and borne in the womb ten months — there are born defilers of the family.
Others are born to wealth and grain and enjoyments amassed by their fathers in abundance, obtained through those very auspicious rites.
When two come together, drawn to one another in the union of intercourse, the embryo enters the womb as though it were a calamity taking possession.
Worn away within another's body, stripped of its skin, the embodied thing — amid the obstruction of the living creature's breath, a stirring of flesh and phlegm —
scorched by another's body, itself a wavering further body, perishing at the term of its perishing, like one boat made fast to another.
A drop of seed, lifeless, set by chance within the belly — by what striving do you behold it here as a living embryo?
In that very belly where food and drink are digested and what is eaten is consumed — why is the embryo not digested like food?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The course of the embryo, of urine, and of excrement is fixed by their own nature; in their retention or their release, the agent has no power.
For some embryos flow out from the belly even as they are being born; and of others the destruction comes about along with their very coming-to-be.
He who escapes alive from this entanglement of the womb, and gains some offspring, sinks once more into the play of opposites.
Of a hundred born together, some reach the seventieth and some the hundredth stage of life — yet of these, five do not attain a hundred years.
There are, beyond doubt, no fixed means by which men may rise up again; they are churned and crushed by diseases, as small beasts by serpents.
For those devoured by diseases, who give up vast wealth, the physicians, for all their striving, cannot draw off the pain.
And even those skilled physicians, expert and well-stocked with remedies, are themselves dragged off by diseases, like deer harried by hunters.
They too, drinking decoctions and clarified butters of many kinds, are seen broken by old age, like elephants overthrown by mightier elephants.
And who on earth tends the beasts and birds afflicted by disease, the wild creatures and the destitute? Yet for the most part they are not so tormented.
Even kings, terrible, unassailable, and of fierce splendor, disease overpowers and carries off, as a herdsman takes his cattle.
So is this world, none coming to its aid, overwhelmed by delusion and grief, hurled all at once into the current and swept away by that mightier force.
Not by wealth, nor by kingdom, nor by fierce austerity, do those innate natures, appointed to embodied beings, ever be set aside.
They would not die, they would not grow old, all would have every desire fulfilled, and none would meet with anything unwelcome as the fruit of their striving — were it otherwise.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Higher and ever higher above the world each man wishes to be, and strives to the limit of his power — and yet it does not come to pass so.
And upon men drunk with the intoxication of power, and drunk with the intoxication of liquor, the vigilant, the crafty, the cruel, the bold dance attendance — biding their time.
For some, troubles turn back unforeseen of their own accord; while for others, strive as they will, nothing whatever is attained.
And a great disparity of reward is seen in the conjunctions of action: some bear the palanquin, while others ride within it.
Though all alike long for prosperity, some go forth with chariots leading the way; and there are men with a hundred wives, and women widowed by the hundred.
Among beings that take their delight in the pairs of opposites, men go their way one by one, each alone; behold now this other, higher truth — do not give yourself over to delusion.
Renounce both righteousness and unrighteousness, renounce both truth and falsehood; and having renounced both truth and falsehood, renounce that by which you renounce.
This supreme secret has been declared to you, O best of seers — that by which the gods, abandoning the world of mortals, went to heaven.
Bhīṣma said: Having heard the words of Nārada, Śuka, supreme in wisdom and steadfast, pondered them in his mind, yet could not arrive at a settled resolve.
"In sons and wives there is great affliction, in the recitation of sacred lore great toil — what then might be the everlasting abode, of little affliction and great fruition?"
Then, pondering for a moment, he who knew the higher and the lower of righteousness fixed upon the goal determined for himself — the supreme path that leads to highest beatitude.
How then, untainted, might I reach the supreme goal, so that I never again return into the ocean of birth and transmigration?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For I long for that highest state from which there is no returning, abandoning all attachments and the resolute course of the mind.
There I shall go, where my self will attain peace, where, imperishable and undecaying, I shall abide everlasting.
But that supreme goal cannot be reached without yoga, for no bondage through deeds can befall the one who is liberated.
Therefore, taking my stand in yoga and casting off this dwelling that is the body, becoming wind itself I shall enter the mass of radiance, the sun, maker of day.
For this does not meet with the waning that the moon, Soma, suffers among the host of gods: shaken, it falls toward the earth and rises up again, for Soma ever wanes and is filled full once more.
The sun, however, scorches the worlds with its fierce rays and draws in radiance from every side, its orb forever undiminished.
Therefore it pleases me to go to the Āditya of blazing splendor; there I shall dwell, unassailable, with an inner self free of all attachment.
And in the abode of Sūrya I shall lay down this body and, together with the seers, pass into the solar radiance that none can scarcely bear.
I take my leave of the trees and the serpents, of the mountains, the earth, the quarters and the sky, of the gods, the Dānavas and Gandharvas, of Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Free of doubt, I shall enter into all beings throughout the worlds; let all the gods, together with the seers, behold the power of my yoga.
Then, asking leave of that seer Nārada, renowned throughout the worlds, and having received his leave, he went toward his father.
Saluting the great-souled seer, the sage Dvaipāyana, and circling Kṛṣṇa reverently, the sage Śuka took his leave of him.
Hearing those words of Śuka, the great-souled seer, well pleased, spoke to him once more: "O my son, my son, stay yet this one day, so that I may gladden my eyes for your sake."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Śuka, become indifferent, free of affection, his bonds undone, fixing his thought on liberation alone, set his mind on departure; and that best of the twice-born, taking leave of his father, went his way.
Bhīṣma said: Ascending the mountain's ridge, O descendant of Bharata, the son of Vyāsa sat down in a level and secluded spot, wholly free of thorns and distractions.
And that great sage, skilled in the graded discipline, held his self in restraint according to the scriptures, fixing it limb by limb, beginning from the feet, in due order.
Then the learned one, facing east while the sun had risen but a little while, composing hands and feet, sat down with humble bearing.
There where the wise son of Vyāsa set himself to enter into yoga, there was no flock of birds, no sound, and nothing to be seen.
He then beheld his own self released from every attachment; and gazing upon the sun, Śuka broke into laughter.
Again taking his stand in yoga to win the path of liberation, and becoming a great lord of yogins, he soared up into the sky.
Then, circling reverently the divine seer Nārada, he made known his yoga to that supreme seer.
"The path is seen, and I have set forth. May it be well with you, O treasury of austerity. By your grace I shall go, O greatly resplendent one, to the goal I desire."
Granted leave by Nārada, the son of Dvaipāyana then, saluting him, took his stand once more in yoga and entered the sky.
Springing up from the ridge of Kailāsa, he then flew into the heavens, the glorious son of Vyāsa, mover through the firmament, wholly resolved.
As that best of the twice-born rose up, splendid as the son of Vinatā and swift as mind and wind, all beings beheld him.
By his resolve contemplating all the three worlds entire, he held to the divine course, his radiance equal to fire and sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All beings, both the moving and the unmoving, beheld him as he went, single of mind, untroubled, and fearing nothing from any quarter.
Then, each as best they could and as was fitting, they worshipped him; and the dwellers of heaven covered him with showers of divine flowers.
Beholding him, all the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases were amazed, and the seers who had attained perfection fell into utter wonder.
"Who is this that travels the firmament, come to perfection through austerity, his body downward and his face turned up, borne onward by the eyes of all?"
Then that supremely steadfast one, renowned throughout the three worlds, gazing upon the sun, went onward facing east with speech restrained, as though filling the whole of space with sound on every side.
Seeing him suddenly approaching, all the hosts of Apsarases, O king, were bewildered in mind and seized with the greatest wonder—Pañcacūḍā and the rest, their eyes opened wide.
"Which deity is this, set upon the highest goal, who comes here so wholly resolved, like one liberated and without desire?"
Then he passed beyond the mountain named Malaya, which Urvaśī and Pūrvacitti ever frequent; and they came to the utmost wonder at the son of the brahman-seer.
"Ah, the steadiness of mind in this brahman devoted to the study of the Vedas! In so short a time he ranges the sky like the moon. Through obedient service to his father he has attained perfection beyond compare."
"Devoted to his father, firm in austerity, a son most dear to his father—how was he forsaken by that father whose mind was set on nothing else?"
Hearing the words of Urvaśī, Śuka, supreme knower of dharma, looked out upon all the quarters, his mind intent upon their speech.
He gazed then upon the firmament and the earth with its mountains, woods, and forests, and likewise upon the lakes and the rivers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all the deities, their palms joined in reverence, gazed upon the son of Dvaipāyana with the highest honor.
Then Śuka, supreme knower of dharma, spoke these words to them: "If my father should come after me, crying out 'Śuka! Śuka!'—
"then an answer should be given by all of you, with one accord. Out of affection for me, may you all see fit to do as I say."
Hearing the words of Śuka, the quarters with their groves and forests, the oceans, the rivers, and the mountains answered him from every side:
"As you command, O brahman, so verily shall it be. When the seer utters his words, we shall make answer."
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken these words, the brahman-seer Śuka of mighty austerity set forth to perfection, leaving behind the fourfold worlds.
Casting off the eightfold darkness and forsaking the fivefold passion, the wise one then forsook even goodness; and it was as if a marvel.
Then in that eternal state, free of the qualities and bereft of all mark, in Brahman he stood firm, blazing like a smokeless fire.
Falling meteors, burnings of the quarters, and earthquakes too broke forth in that instant; and it was as if a marvel.
The trees let fall their branches and the mountains their peaks, and Himavān, with the sound of thunderclaps, seemed as though it were splitting apart.
The thousand-rayed sun shone no more, and the fire blazed no more; the pools and the rivers, and the oceans likewise, were thrown into turmoil.
Vāsava rained down water savory and sweet of scent, and the wind too blew, pure and bearing the fragrance of heaven.
There were two peerless, divine peaks, born of Himavān and Meru, joined together, the one white and the other golden, made of silver and of gold, both fair—
a hundred yojanas in breadth, across and upward, O descendant of Bharata; and resting toward the northern quarter, those two resplendent peaks he beheld.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With a mind free of all hesitation Śuka flew straight at them; whereupon the two mountain peaks, O great king, all at once appeared cleft in twain; and it was as if a marvel.
Then he passed out from between the two mountain peaks all at once, and that best of mountains did not hinder his passage.
Then a great cry arose in heaven from all the dwellers of the sky, from the Gandharvas and the seers, and from those who dwell upon the mountains.
Beholding Śuka passed beyond and the mountain cleft in twain, there arose on every side the cry "Well done! Well done!", O descendant of Bharata.
He was honored by the gods and the Gandharvas and the seers, and by the hosts of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas and the throngs of Vidyādharas.
The firmament was strewn on every side with divine flowers, O great king, at the soaring of Śuka in that hour.
Then, passing above the lovely Mandākinī, the righteous Śuka beheld it with its forests of trees in flower.
In its waters the hosts of Apsarases sport with delight and bathe; unclothed, and themselves heedless of form, they beheld Śuka who was empty of all form.
Aware that he was departing, his father, filled with affection, took to the highest course and followed after him from behind.
But Śuka, having made his course through the firmament swifter than the wind and shown forth his own power, then became one with all beings.
And Vyāsa of great austerity, rising up by the foremost course of mighty yoga, in the mere space between two blinks went after Śuka's flight.
He beheld where Śuka had passed, having cleft the mountain's summit in twain; and the seers then recounted to him that deed of his son.
Then "Śuka!" with a long and trained call was the cry his father himself raised aloud, his voice resounding through the three worlds.
Śuka, become all-pervading, the self of all, facing every way, the righteous one answered back, making all resound with the sound "Bhoḥ!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, sounding forth the single-syllabled cry "Bhoḥ!", the whole world, moving and unmoving, gave it back aloud.
And from that time even to this day, in the caverns and ridges of the mountains, sounds severally uttered have echoed back in answer to "Śuka."
But having shown forth his power, Śuka then vanished from sight, and forsaking the qualities, sound and the rest, he attained the supreme state.
But beholding that greatness of his son of boundless splendor, he sat down upon the mountain's tableland, brooding upon his son alone.
Then the hosts of Apsarases, sporting on the bank of the Mandākinī, all came upon that seer and were bewildered, their senses fled.
Some hid themselves in the water, some took refuge in the thickets, and some, beholding that best of sages, snatched up their garments.
But the sage, perceiving that liberation of his son and his own attachment, was at once gladdened and ashamed.
To him, surrounded by gods and Gandharvas and honored by the hosts of great seers, came the blessed Śaṃkara, the Pināka in his hand.
To Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, then scorched with grief for his son, Mahādeva spoke these words, with consolation foremost:
"A son equal in power to fire, to earth, to the waters, to wind, and to the firmament itself you once asked of me long ago.
"Such, marked with those very signs, was the son born to you, nurtured by your austerity and by my power—pure, made wholly of the splendor of Brahman.
"He has attained the supreme goal, hard to win even for the gods whose senses are unconquered, O brahman-seer. Why then do you grieve for him?
"As long as the mountains shall stand, as long as the oceans shall endure, so long shall your fame, together with your son's, remain imperishable."
A shadow resembling your own son, never departing from you on any side, you shall behold always in this world, O great sage, by my grace.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus consoled by the blessed Lord Rudra himself, O descendant of Bharata, that sage, beholding the shadow, returned home with the highest joy.
Thus the birth and the destiny of Śuka, O bull of the Bhāratas, have I recounted to you in full, even as you questioned me.
This the divine seer Nārada related to me of old, O king, and so too the great yogin Vyāsa, again and again in our converse.
Whoever, devoted to inward peace, holds fast to this holy narrative, fraught with the law and aim of liberation, attains the supreme goal.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: A householder, a student of sacred lore, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant — whoever should desire to attain perfection, which deity is he to worship?
Whence comes to him an enduring heaven, whence the highest beatitude? By what rite should he make oblation to the gods and likewise to the fathers?
To what goal does the liberated man go, and of what nature is liberation itself? And one who has reached heaven, what should he do so that he does not fall from that realm?
Who is the god of the gods, and who the father of the fathers, and what is higher still than these — that tell me, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: A hidden question you put to me here, O sinless one, you who know how to question; for this cannot be answered by reasoning, not even in a hundred years.
Save by the grace of the god, O king, or by the coming of true knowledge — for profound is this teaching that must be expounded to you, O scourge of foes.
On this point too they relate an ancient tale: the colloquy of Nārada and of the seer Nārāyaṇa.
For Nārāyaṇa, the Self of all, fourfold in form, eternal, came to be born as the son of Dharma — thus did my father declare to me.
In the Kṛta age of old, O great king, in the epoch of Svāyaṃbhuva, there were Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and Hari and Kṛṣṇa as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of these, the imperishable Nara and Nārāyaṇa practised austerity, having reached the hermitage of Badarī, seated in a chariot wrought of gold.
Eight-wheeled was that conveyance, yoked with living powers and delightful; there those two primordial lords of the worlds sat, lean, their veins standing forth.
By their austerity and their splendour hard to look upon even for the gods — he upon whom the two bestow their grace is fit to behold those divinities.
Surely by their leave, urged in his heart by the longing that dwells in the heart, Nārada slipped from the peak of the great mountain Meru toward Gandhamādana.
Nārada, that mighty being, who had ranged through all the worlds, came swift as the wind to that region, O king, the hermitage of Badarī.
At the hour of their daily rites a wonder arose in him: This is the whole foundation upon which the worlds are established.
With its gods, asuras, and gandharvas, with its seers, kiṃnaras, and serpents — this was at first a single form, then became fourfold.
The great lineage of Dharma has been increased by these. Ah, today is Dharma graced here by these gods — by Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and by Kṛṣṇa and Hari likewise.
There Kṛṣṇa and Hari, abiding upon some other occasion, intent upon righteousness, were thus established in austerity.
These two are the supreme abode — what then is their daily rite? Fathers of all beings, themselves divine and glorious, what deity do these two of great mind worship, or what fathers?
Reflecting thus in his mind, through devotion to Nārāyaṇa, he at once appeared near the two gods at that moment.
When the rites to the gods and to the fathers had been performed, he was then beheld by the two and honoured with the rite as prescribed by scripture.
Beholding that great marvel, that unprecedented fullness of ritual, the blessed seer Nārada, well pleased, took his seat beside them.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Gazing upon Nārāyaṇa with a serene inmost soul, having bowed to the Great God, he spoke these words.
In the Vedas together with the Purāṇas, with their limbs and sub-limbs, you are sung: you the unborn, the eternal, the ordainer, held to be the imperishable beyond which there is none higher; in you stands all that has been and is to be, this whole world.
The four orders of life, O god, all rooted in the householder's state, worship you day after day, you who abide established in manifold forms.
Father and mother and eternal teacher of the whole world are you — yet whom do you today worship as god, and whom as father? We do not know.
The blessed Lord said: This is the unspeakable that must be spoken, the eternal mystery of the Self; yet to you who are full of devotion, O brāhmaṇa, I shall declare it as it truly is.
That which is subtle, unknowable, unmanifest, unmoving, abiding, devoid of the senses and the objects of the senses and of all elements —
That is the inner Self of beings, and it is called the Knower of the Field; transcending the three strands, it is conceived as the Spirit. From it arose the Unmanifest, made of the three strands, O best of the twice-born.
The Unmanifest, abiding in the state of the manifest, that is imperishable Nature; know her to be the womb of us two — and that which is of the nature of being and non-being is worshipped by us both in the rites ordained for gods and for fathers.
There is no other higher than That, no father or god, O brāhmaṇa; that is to be known as the very Self of us two, and therefore we worship it.
By That, O brāhmaṇa, has this bound been laid down, that shapes the worlds: the rite to the gods and to the fathers is to be performed — such is its ordinance.
Brahmā, Sthāṇu, Manu, Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, Dharma, Tapas, Dama, Marīci, Aṅgiras and Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vasiṣṭha and Parameṣṭhin, Vivasvat and Soma, he who is called Kardama, and Krodha and Vikrīta —
twenty-one in number arose, and these are remembered as the Lords of Creatures; they honour the eternal bound of that god.
Knowing truly the rites to the gods and to the fathers as ever belonging to That, the best of the twice-born thereby come to know the things that are attained within the Self.
Whatever embodied beings, even those dwelling in heaven, bow down to That, they by its grace go to the goal whose fruit has been appointed by it.
Those who are freed of the seventeen attributes and of works as well, and have cast off the fifteen parts — these, it is determined, are the liberated.
But the goal of the liberated, O brāhmaṇa, is conceived as the Knower of the Field; for he is declared to be all-pervading and devoid of attributes.
He is seen through the discipline of knowledge, and from him we two have issued forth; so, having known that Self, we worship the Eternal.
Him the Vedas and the orders of life, abiding in their manifold forms, worship with devotion as the Primeval One, and he grants them their goal.
But those who, filled with the thought of That, have taken their stand in single-minded devotion — this is the surpassing portion of theirs: that they indeed enter into Him.
Thus the exposition of the mystery has been declared to you, Nārada; through devotion and love, O sage among brāhmaṇas, and through your devotion to us, you have heard it.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, that noblest of two-footed beings spoke this word to Nārāyaṇa, the noblest of two-footed beings, the dwelling-place of the welfare of the worlds:
For whatever purpose, O self-originated one, your supreme fourfold birth has come to be here in the house of Dharma — let that be accomplished today for the good of the worlds. I go to behold your primal Nature.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Vedas I have well studied, O Lord of the worlds; austerity I have practised; never before have I spoken falsehood; I render worship to my teachers without ceasing, and never before have I betrayed another's secret.
The four are guarded by me according to scripture; toward foe and friend I am ever the same; taking refuge unceasingly in that Primal God, I choose Him without ceasing in single-minded spirit. With my being made wholly pure by these excellences, why should I not behold the infinite Lord?
Hearing that word of the son of the Supreme One, Nārāyaṇa, the guardian of the Sātvata law, having honoured Nārada with the rites prescribed for himself, said to him, "Go."
Then, dismissed, the son of the Supreme One, having reverenced that ancient seer, sprang up into the sky with the highest speed, and thereupon swiftly came to rest upon Meru's height.
And there the sage halted for a moment, having gained a solitary spot upon the mountain's peak; gazing toward the northwest, he beheld a region endowed with a most wondrous form.
To the north of the Ocean of Milk lies an island, vast, renowned by the name of Śveta, the White; thirty-two thousand leagues beyond Meru it is reckoned by the wise.
There the men are beyond the senses, without need of food, free of all motionlessness, and most fragrant — white men, with all sin departed, who rob the very sight of evil-doing men.
Their bodies are of adamantine bone, equal in measure and proportion, of celestial lineage and form, endowed with auspicious strength; their heads shaped like parasols, their voices like a mass of thunderclouds, with four fair lotus-marks, and a hundred lotuses upon their feet.
Furnished with sixty white teeth and with eight tusks, they are such as lick on every side, with their tongues, a face that shines like the sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With devotion they worship the god, the source of all, from whom all the worlds are brought forth; the Vedas, the laws, the tranquil sages, and all the gods are his emanations.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Beyond the senses, without food, unmoving, fragrant — how were these men born, and what is their highest goal?
This indeed is the mark of those men who become liberated here, O best of the Bhāratas — the mark of the dwellers of Śvetadvīpa.
Therefore cut away my doubt, for great is my curiosity; for you are the pleasure-garden of all tales, and upon you we have taken our stand.
Bhīṣma said: This is a far-reaching tale, O king, heard by me in my father's presence; and it must be told to you, for it is remembered as the very essence of narratives.
There was a sovereign of the earth named Uparicara, a renowned friend of Indra the Cleaver, devoted to Nārāyaṇa Hari.
Righteous, ever devout, and unwearied in his constant service to the fathers, he had obtained imperial sway of old through a boon of Nārāyaṇa.
Following the Sātvata rite, which issued forth of old from the mouth of the Sun, he worshipped the Lord of the gods, and with the remnant of that worship he honoured his forefathers.
And with what remained from the fathers he shared among the brāhmaṇas and among his dependants; eating only the leavings, devoted to truth, harming no creature, he worshipped with his whole being the God of gods, Janārdana.
As he bore this devotion to Nārāyaṇa, O harrier of foes, Śakra the king of the gods himself granted him a shared couch and seat.
Himself, his kingdom and his wealth, his wife and his mounts — all this is the blessed Lord's: thus was it ever regarded by him.
The voluntary, the occasional, and the perpetual sacrificial acts, the highest rites — all of them he performed with collected mind, following the Sātvata ordinance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The foremost knowers of the Pañcarātra in the house of that great-souled king observed the discipline taught by the Lord and partook of the first-offered food.
While that slayer of foes ruled his kingdom by righteousness, no false word arose from him, nor did his mind grow corrupt, nor did he commit by his body any sin, not even the most minute.
Those seven sages renowned as the Citraśikhaṇḍins — being of one mind, they proclaimed the supreme scripture.
Marīci, Atri, and Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha of great splendour — these are the Citraśikhaṇḍins.
These are the seven primary principles, and Svāyaṃbhuva is the eighth; by these the world is upheld, and from them the scripture has issued forth.
Single-minded, self-controlled, the sages delighting in restraint — "This is the good, this is the Absolute, this is the highest welfare" — pondering the worlds in their minds, they then composed the scripture.
Therein righteousness, gain, and desire, and liberation thereafter, are proclaimed; and manifold bounds besides, established in heaven and upon earth.
Having propitiated by austerity the god Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, for a thousand celestial years, all of them together with the seers —
then the goddess Sarasvatī, instructed by Nārāyaṇa, entered into all those seers, out of desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Then this teaching was rightly set in motion by the twice-born who knew austerity, perfect in word, in meaning, and in reasoning—born of the first creation.
At the very beginning that scripture, adorned with the sound of Oṃ, was meditated upon by the seers in that place where the Compassionate One dwells.
Then the Blessed One, well pleased, his body undisclosed, unseen, the Supreme Person, spoke to all those seers.
This supreme work of a hundred thousand verses has been composed, from which proceeds the dharma of the whole order of the world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This shall be the source of both engagement and renunciation, honored by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, and by the Atharva-Āṅgirasa hymns as well.
As it is authoritative, so too by me was Brahmā made, born of my grace, and Rudra, born of my wrath, O brahmins, and you yourselves as the primal natures.
The sun and moon, the wind, the earth, the waters, and fire too, and all the hosts of stars, and whatever is named as a created being—
all abide within their offices, each according to its own; and as the expounders of Brahman are each authoritative, so is this supreme scripture.
This my teaching shall be authoritative, and from it Manu, the self-existent one's son, shall himself proclaim the dharmas.
And when Uśanas and Bṛhaspati shall come into being, then they shall expound the scripture drawn forth from your own minds.
When the dharmas of Svāyaṃbhuva, the scripture composed by Uśanas, and the doctrine of Bṛhaspati have been pondered throughout the worlds,
this scripture, made by you, shall the protector of his people, Vasu, then receive from Bṛhaspati, O best of the twice-born.
For that king shall be devoted in thought to me and shall be my worshipper, and by that scripture he shall perform all rites throughout the worlds.
For this, of all scriptures, is the one named supreme; this is rich in meaning, conformable to dharma, and conducive to glory—this is the highest.
And by setting this in motion you shall be blessed with offspring, and that king, the great Vasu, shall be endowed with majesty.
But when that king has passed away, this eternal scripture shall vanish from sight. This is the truth I have declared to you.
Having spoken these words, the unseen Supreme Person dismissed all those seers and departed for some quarter unknown.
Then those fathers of the world, who meditate on the welfare of all worlds, set in motion that eternal scripture, the womb of dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And when the son of Aṅgiras had come to be, in the first-ordained age, they established the scripture, with its limbs and Upaniṣads, in Bṛhaspati,
and went, resolved upon austerity, to the region of their desire—they who sustain all the worlds and set in motion all the dharmas.
Bhīṣma said: Then, when the great aeon had passed and the son of Aṅgiras had been born, the gods were content, for the chaplain of the gods had come into being.
"Vast," "Brahman," "great"—these are words that signify the same; endowed with these qualities, O king, was the learned Bṛhaspati.
His foremost pupil was the king Uparicara Vasu, who then studied thoroughly the scripture born of the Citraśikhaṇḍins.
That king Vasu, ordained beforehand by divine decree, ruled the earth as Indra, the Render-asunder, rules heaven.
That great-souled king held a great sacrifice, a horse-sacrifice, and Bṛhaspati, his preceptor, served there as the hotṛ priest.
And there the three sons of Prajāpati were the assessors—Ekata, Dvita, and Trita, those great seers.
Dhanuṣākṣa and Raibhya, Arvāvasu and Parāvasu, the seer Medhātithi too, and Tāṇḍya, the great seer,
the illustrious seer Śakti, and he who was Vedaśiras, and Kapila, best of seers, grandsire of Śālihotra,
the first Kaṭha, and Taittiri, the forerunner of Vaiśaṃpāyana, Kaṇva, and Devahotra—these sixteen are renowned. All the appurtenances were gathered, O king, for that great rite.
There was no slaying of any animal there; the king stood firm in this way—free of harm, pure, free of meanness, free of craving, lauded for his deeds—and the shares were apportioned there as chanted in the verses of the Āraṇyaka.
Then the Blessed One, the ancient God of gods, well pleased with him, showed himself to him in person, though he was unseen by any other.
He himself, smelling the share, took up the sacrificial cake; by the unseen God, whose intent is Hari, the share was carried off.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Bṛhaspati, enraged, swiftly raised the ladle, and striking at the sky with blows of the ladle, in his fury he let his tears flow.
And he said to Uparicara: "This share offered up by me was taken by the God himself, before my very eyes—of this there is no doubt.
For when sacrificial shares are offered up, the gods receive them here in person; why then has the all-pervading Hari not granted his appearance here?"
Then the great lord of earth, Vasu, and all the assessors together, soothed that agitated sage.
And, unperturbed, they said to him: "You ought not to give way to anger; it is no part of dharma in the Kṛta age that you should have stirred up such wrath.
For that God, to whom this share was offered, is free of anger; he cannot be seen by you, nor by us, O Bṛhaspati. He upon whom He bestows His grace—he alone is worthy to behold Him."
Ekata, Dvita, and Trita said: "We are renowned as the mind-born sons of Brahmā; once, for the sake of the highest good, we journeyed to the northern quarter.
For four thousand years we practiced the highest austerity, standing perfectly upon one foot, motionless as logs, our minds composed,
in the northern part of Meru, along the shore of the Ocean of Milk—that region where we performed our most terrible austerity, thinking, 'How might we behold the God Nārāyaṇa?'
Then, at the final ablution of our vow, a bodiless voice spoke: 'Well practiced is your austerity, O brahmins, with an inmost self made serene.
You are seekers, devoted—how shall you behold that Lord? North of the Ocean of Milk lies the White Island of great splendor.
There dwell men devoted to Nārāyaṇa, radiant as the moon, who have attained single-minded devotion, worshippers of the Supreme Person.
They enter into the eternal God of a thousand rays—beyond the senses, taking no food, motionless, sweetly fragrant.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those single-hearted men dwell on the White Island; go there, O sages, for there my Self is made manifest.'
Then, having all heard that bodiless voice, we made our way to that region by the path that had been told.
Reaching the great White Island, our hearts set upon Him, longing to behold Him—then the very range of our sight was struck back.
And we could not see the Person, our vision carried off by His radiance; then there arose in us a knowledge born of union with the God.
Truly He cannot readily be beheld by one whose austerity is unperformed; so once more we practiced for a hundred years a great austerity suited to the hour.
At the close of our vow we beheld men most fair, white, resembling the moon, marked with every auspicious sign,
with hands ever folded, murmuring Brahman, facing the east and north. That muttered prayer, called the Mental, is murmured by those great-souled ones, and by that single-mindedness of theirs Hari is well pleased.
What the radiance of the sun would be at the dissolution of an age, O tiger among sages, such was the splendor of each single one of those men.
'That island is the abode of splendor,' so indeed we deemed; none there was greater than another, for all were equal in their radiance.
Then suddenly we beheld, O Bṛhaspati, the splendor of a thousand suns risen all at once, once again.
And those men ran swiftly forward together, their hands folded in cupped reverence, rejoicing, crying out only, 'Homage!'
Then, as they uttered their praise, we heard a vast sound; an offering, it seemed, was being presented to that God by those men.
But we, our minds suddenly carried away by His radiance, could see nothing at all, our sight, strength, and senses borne away.
But one sound, unceasing, we heard uttered: 'Victory to You, lotus-eyed One! Homage to You, maker of the universe!

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Homage be to You, Hṛṣīkeśa, firstborn of the great Person!'—such was the sound we heard, sounded forth in the syllables of correct articulation.
In that interval a pure wind, bearing every fragrance, wafted divine flowers and herbs fit for the rite.
By those single-hearted men, knowers of the five sacred times, Hari was worshipped; surely the God had come there, as their utterance declared—yet we did not see Him, bewildered by His māyā.
And when the wind had ceased and the offering had been made, we became troubled in mind with anxious thought, O best of the Āṅgirasas.
Among those thousands of men of pure birth, not one honored us with so much as a thought or a glance.
Those hosts of sages too, self-possessed, vowed to the one Being, set no regard upon us, abiding in the state of Brahman.
Then, as we were sorely wearied and wasted by our austerity, some being there, abiding in the sky, bodiless, addressed us:
'You have seen the white men, devoid of all sensory cravings; when these have been seen, the Lord of gods is seen, O best of the twice-born.
Go, all you sages, soon and the way you came; that God can in no way be seen by one without devotion.
In the fullness of a long time, by those who have attained single-heartedness, that Blessed One may indeed be seen—He who is hard to behold for His orb of radiance.
But a great task is to be accomplished by you, O best of the twice-born, when this Kṛta age has passed and the reversal of things has come.
In the age of Vaivasvata, O brahmins, when the Tretā age has come, you shall be helpers for accomplishing the task of the gods.'
Then, having heard that wondrous speech, O drinker of soma, by His grace we readily reached the region of our desire.
Thus, even with our high austerity and with offerings to gods and ancestors, that God was not seen by us; how then could you be fit to see Him? Nārāyaṇa is the great Being, the maker of the universe, the eater of oblations to gods and ancestors."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Thus, conciliated by the speech of Ekata and by the counsel of Dvita and Trita, and by the assessors, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati then brought the sacrifice to completion and worshipped the deity.
His sacrifice ended, King Vasu too protected his people; but, fallen from heaven by a brahmin's curse, he thereafter entered the earth.
And though gone within the earth, ever cherishing dharma, becoming wholly devoted to Nārāyaṇa, he chanted the word of Nārāyaṇa.
And by His grace alone he rose up once more, and passing from the surface of the earth he went straightway to the abode of Brahmā, attaining the supreme goal—such, truly, was his final consummation.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When King Mahāvasu was a devotee of the Blessed One, why did he fall and enter a crevice of the earth?
Bhīṣma said: On this too they tell this ancient tale, the dispute between the seers and the gods, O descendant of Bharata.
"One must sacrifice with an aja," the gods told the best of the twice-born; "and by aja the goat is to be understood, no other beast"—such was their position.
The seers said: The Vedic revelation declares that one should sacrifice in the rites with seed-grains; the grains themselves are called 'aja' — therefore you ought not to slay a goat.
O gods, that is no dharma of the virtuous wherein a living creature is slain. This is the most excellent Kṛta age — how then should a beast be killed?
Bhīṣma said: While the seers were disputing thus with the gods, the foremost of kings, Vasu, came upon that place along his path — that glorious one who roamed the sky, with all his forces and chariots about him.
Seeing Vasu come suddenly, coursing through the air, the twice-born said to the gods: 'This one will resolve the doubt.'
'A performer of sacrifices, the foremost of lords of giving, devoted to the welfare of all beings — how could this great Vasu speak a word that is otherwise than true?'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having thus made their agreement, the gods and the seers alike approached King Vasu at once and questioned him at close hand.
'Ho, King! With what should one sacrifice — with a goat, or rather with the herbs? Resolve this doubt of ours; you are held to be our authority.'
Vasu, joining his palms in reverence, questioned them in turn: 'Which view does each of you hold? Speak the truth, you who are assembled here.'
The seers said: 'That one should sacrifice with grains — this is our position, O ruler of men; but the gods' position favors the beast. Pronounce for us, O King.'
Bhīṣma said: Then Vasu, knowing the opinion of the gods and inclining to their side, spoke these words: 'One should sacrifice with a goat — with the aja.'
At this all those sages, radiant as the sun, grew angry and said to Vasu, seated upon his flying chariot, who had spoken in support of the gods' cause:
'Since you have taken the gods' side, therefore fall from heaven! From this day on, O King, your course through the sky is severed; struck by our curse, you shall cleave the earth and sink into it.'
Then in that very moment King Uparicara at once sank downward, the monarch passing into a cleft of the earth; yet by the command of Nārāyaṇa his memory did not desert him then.
But all the gods together, unperturbed, took thought for Vasu's release from the curse, for that deed of the king had been a meritorious one.
'On our account this great-souled king has incurred a curse. We dwellers in heaven must together render him a kindness in return.'
Having resolved thus in their minds and swiftly reached their decision, the lords, glad of heart, then said to King Uparicara:
'You are devoted to Hari, the god who befriends the brāhmaṇas, the teacher of gods and demons; well-pleased of soul, he may at will work your deliverance from the curse.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Yet honor must be shown to the high-souled twice-born; their austerity must inevitably bear its fruit, O best of kings.'
'Since you have fallen suddenly from the sky to the surface of the earth, this one favor we grant you, O most excellent of kings.'
'For as long a time as you must dwell through the fault of the curse, O sinless one, sunk in the cleft of the earth, for just so long you shall receive the well-offered stream of Vasu's draught, poured by the high-souled brāhmaṇas in their sacrifices.'
'By our favoring thought you shall obtain it; let no weariness touch you, nor hunger and thirst, O lord of kings, while you abide in the fissure of the earth.'
'Nourished by drinking the stream of Vasu and replenished in your splendor, that god, pleased by our boon, shall lead you to the world of Brahmā.'
Having thus granted the boon to the king, all the dwellers in heaven there — the gods and the seers rich in austerity — departed to their own abodes.
And ever, O descendant of Bharata, he paid worship to Viṣvaksena, and ceaselessly chanted the prayer that had issued from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
Even there, O subduer of foes, sunk in the cleft of the earth though he was, he worshipped Hari, the lord of the gods, with five sacrifices at the five appointed times.
Then the Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, was pleased by the devotion of that virtuous man — one whose devotion was undivided, who was wholly given to him, master of himself.
The Lord Viṣṇu, the granter of boons, spoke as if smiling to the foremost of the twice-born who stood near him — Garutmān of mighty speed:
'O best of the twice-born, greatly blessed one, go at my word: the sovereign king named Vasu, a soul devoted to dharma, has taken refuge in me.'
'By the wrath of the brāhmaṇas he entered the floor of the earth; yet those foremost of brāhmaṇas have been honored. Go now, O best of the twice-born.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'O Garuḍa, by my command make that foremost of kings, hidden in the cleft of the earth and now moving below, a sky-rover once more — and do it without delay.'
Then Garutmān, swift as the wind, spreading wide his wings, entered the cleft of the earth where Vasu abode in restrained speech.
Then the son of Vinatā, lifting him up at once, sprang swiftly into the sky and there released him.
In that very moment King Uparicara came to be again, and that best of kings went, in his own body, to the world of Brahmā.
Thus, O son of Kuntī, even by him, that high-souled one, through a fault of speech and the curse of the brāhmaṇas, a destiny befitting one who offers no sacrifice was incurred — and reversed by the gods' command.
Solely because he had served the Supreme Person, Hari the Lord, he swiftly cast off the curse and attained the world of Brahmā.
All this I have related to you — how the mortals came to be. And how the seer Nārada too went to the White Island, all of that I shall now declare to you; listen with single mind, O King.
Bhīṣma said: Having reached the great White Island, the venerable seer Nārada beheld those very men — white, radiant as the moon, and fair.
He honored them with his bowed head and with his mind, and was honored by them in turn; longing for the vision, supremely given to silent prayer, bearing every austerity, he abode there.
With mind made single-pointed, the brāhmaṇa, that great sage, his arms upraised, chanted a hymn to the Universal One, the One free of qualities, the Great Soul.
Nārada said: Homage to you, God of gods [1], Actionless [2], Free of qualities [3], Witness of the worlds [4], Knower of the field [5], Endless [6], Spirit [7], Great Spirit [8], the One of three strands [9], Primordial nature [10], Deathless [11], Sky [12], Eternal [13], the Being and Non-being, Manifest and Unmanifest [14], whose dwelling is cosmic order [15], the First and Foremost god [16], Bestower of wealth [17], Lord of creatures [18], Best Lord of creatures [19], Lord of the woodland [20], Great Lord of creatures [21], Lord of vigor [22], Lord of speech [23], Lord of mind [24], Lord of the world [25], Lord of heaven [26], Lord of the Maruts [27], Lord of the waters [28], Lord of the earth [29], Lord of the quarters [30], the First-dwelling [31], Brahmā's chaplain [32], the Brahmā-bodied [33], the Great-bodied [34], the Mahārājika [35], the Fourfold-Mahārājika [36], the Radiant [37], the Greatly-radiant [38], the Sevenfold-greatly-radiant [39], the Yāmya [40], the Great Yāmya [41], the Named-and-Nameless [42], the Tuṣita [43], the Great Tuṣita [44], Pratardana [45], the Wholly-fashioned [46], the One whose will prevails [47], the Un-fashioned [48], Sacrifice [49], Great Sacrifice [50], Origin of sacrifice [51], Womb of sacrifice [52], Embryo of sacrifice [53], Heart of sacrifice [54], Praised in sacrifice [55], Receiver of the sacrificial portion [56], Upholder of the five sacrifices [57], Goal of those who perform the five rites at their times [58], the Pāñcarātrika [59], Vaikuṇṭha [60], Unconquered [61], the Mental One [62], Supreme Master [63], the Well-purified [64], the Swan [65], the Supreme Swan [66], the Supreme Sacrificer [67], Sāṃkhya-and-Yoga [68], the One who reposes in the deathless [69], the One who reposes in gold [70].

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Praised thus with secret and true names, that Lord, bearer of the universal form, revealed himself to the sage Nārada.
In part pure of self as the moon, in part surpassing even the moon; in part of the color of fire, and in part the Lord shaped like a blazing altar-hearth.
In part the color of a parrot's wing, and in part with the luster of crystal; like a heap of dark collyrium, and somewhere with the radiance of pure-born gold.
And of the hue of a coral shoot, and white in places he shone; somewhere with the gleam of gold, and somewhere like a beryl gem.
Like a blue beryl, and somewhere like the sapphire of Indra; with the sheen of a peacock's neck, and somewhere like a necklace of pearls.
Bearing these manifold colors in his form, the Eternal One — thousand-eyed, glorious, hundred-headed, thousand-footed.
Thousand-bellied and thousand-armed, and somewhere the Unmanifest — uttering from his mouth the syllable Oṃ, and the Sāvitrī that follows upon it.
And from his remaining mouths the god Hari Nārāyaṇa, the self-controlled, chanted the wealth that springs from the four Vedas, the Āraṇyaka.
An altar, a water-pot, darbha-grass, gem-like stones, a deerskin, a staff of wood, and the blazing fire that devours oblations — these the Lord of gods, the master of sacrifice, then held in his hands.
Nārada, that best of the twice-born, his own self serene, with restrained speech and purified, did homage to the gracious Supreme Lord; and to him, bowed in head, the imperishable First of the gods spoke:
'The great seers Ekata, Dvita, and Trita came to this place, longing to behold me.'
'But they did not see me, nor shall anyone see me, save the best of the single-minded devotees — and you are accounted single-minded.'
'These excellent embodiments of mine were born in the house of Dharma, O brāhmaṇa; worship them ever, and accomplish your purpose as you have come to do.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'And choose a boon from me, O brāhmaṇa, whatever you desire here; I, of universal form and imperishable, am pleased with you this day.'
Nārada said: 'This day, O god, the fruit of my austerity, my restraints and my observances, has been at once obtained — in that I have beheld you, Lord.'
'This is my utmost boon — that I have seen you, the Eternal: the Lord, the all-seeing, the lion, of every form, the great sovereign.'
Bhīṣma said: Having thus revealed himself to Nārada, son of the Supreme One, he spoke again these words: 'Go, Nārada, without delay.'
'For these devotees of mine, moon-bright, who take no food through the senses, would meditate upon me single-mindedly — let no hindrance arise for them.'
'These greatly blessed ones are perfected; long ago they became single-minded. Freed from darkness and passion, they shall enter into me beyond all doubt.'
'He who is not to be seen by the eye, nor touched by the sense of touch, nor smelled by way of scent, and is void of taste —'
'whom the qualities — goodness, passion, and darkness — do not attend; who is all-pervading, the witness, and is called the Self of the world —'
'when the bodies of the host of beings perish, he does not perish: unborn, eternal, everlasting, free of qualities, and without parts.'
'Beyond the twice-twelve principles, he who is renowned as the twenty-fifth is the Spirit, the actionless, and is said to be perceived through knowledge.'
'Having entered into whom men become liberated here, O best of the twice-born — he is to be known as Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self, the Eternal.'
'Behold the greatness and the majesty of the god, O Nārada, who is never tainted by deeds, whether pure or impure.'
'Goodness, passion, and darkness — these they declare to be the qualities; these abide in all bodies and move within them.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'These qualities the Knower of the field enjoys, yet by them he is not enjoyed: free of qualities, yet the enjoyer of qualities, their creator, and surpassing them.'
'O divine seer, earth is the foundation of the world; earth dissolves into the waters, the waters dissolve into fire, and fire dissolves into wind.'
'Wind passes into dissolution in space, and space into mind; for mind is the highest element, and that dissolves into the Unmanifest.'
'The Unmanifest, O brāhmaṇa, dissolves wholly into the Spirit, the actionless; there is nothing higher than that Spirit, the Eternal.'
'For in the world there is no eternal being, moving or unmoving, save that one Spirit, Vāsudeva the Eternal; for Vāsudeva of great might has become the Self of all beings.'
'Earth, wind, space, water, and fire as the fifth — these great elements, when joined together, are designated a body.'
'He who enters into that, O brāhmaṇa — unseen, of swift action — comes into being therein at once, the Lord who sets the body in motion.'
'Nowhere does a body come to be without the assemblage of elements; nor, O brāhmaṇa, do the elements stir without the living self.'
'That living self is reckoned to be Śeṣa, the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa; from him one may attain, by his own works, the state of Sanatkumāra.'
'And he into whom all beings pass at the dissolution — he, the mind of all creatures, is proclaimed to be Pradyumna.'
'From him is born the doer who is both the effect and the cause, and from whom springs the whole world, moving and unmoving — he is Aniruddha, he is the Lord, the manifestation present in all works.'
'He who is the Lord Vāsudeva, the Knower of the field, of nature free from qualities — that very Lord is to be known as the living self, the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa.'
'From Saṃkarṣaṇa comes Pradyumna, who is said to be of the nature of mind; and the Aniruddha who comes from Pradyumna is the principle of ego, the Great Lord.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'From me arises the whole world, moving and unmoving — the imperishable and the perishable, the being and the non-being alike, O Nārada.'
Those devotees of mine who are liberated enter into me and abide here. For I am to be known as the Puruṣa, actionless, the twenty-fifth principle.
Devoid of qualities, without parts, free from the pairs of opposites, without possessions am I. This you cannot fully grasp — though I am seen to possess a form. Should I so wish, I could vanish in an instant, for I am the Lord, the teacher of the world.
For this is māyā, fashioned by me, that you behold me, O Nārada, as endowed with the qualities of all beings; thus you ought not to know me. By me has been rightly told to you my fourfold manifestation.
For these greatly blessed men have become perfected, single-minded ones; freed from darkness and passion they shall enter into me, O sage.
I am the doer, the deed, and the cause as well, O Nārada; I indeed am that which bears the name of the living soul, and in me the living soul is gathered up. Let not this thought arise in you here: 'the living soul has been seen by me.'
I am all-pervading, O brahmin, the inner self of the host of beings; though the bodies in the host of beings perish, I do not perish.
Hiraṇyagarbha, the origin of the worlds, the four-faced one, versed in etymology, Brahmā the eternal god, is the ponderer of my manifold purposes.
Behold my eleven Rudras stationed at my right side, and likewise the twelve Ādityas standing together at my left.
And before me behold the eight Vasus, foremost of the gods; and behind me behold the two physicians, Nāsatya and Dasra.
Behold all the Prajāpatis, behold too the seven seers, the Vedas, and the sacrifices by the hundreds; behold the nectar of immortality and the healing herbs.
Behold the austerities and the observances, and the restraints of various kinds, and the eightfold lordly power gathered in one place, embodied in form.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Behold Śrī, and Lakṣmī, and Kīrti, and the Earth bearing her summits, and the goddess Sarasvatī, mother of the Vedas, abiding in me.
And behold Dhruva, best of the heavenly lights, the sky-traveler, O Nārada; the rain-bearing clouds, the oceans, the lakes, and the rivers as well.
Behold the four hosts of the fathers in embodied form, O most excellent one; and behold these three qualities, abiding in me yet devoid of form.
More distinguished even than rites for the gods, O sage, is the rite for the fathers; for of both the gods and the fathers I alone am the one father from the beginning.
Becoming Hayaśiras, the horse-headed one, in the northwestern ocean, I drink the well-offered oblation and the offering to the fathers, both attended with faith.
Of old Brahmā was created by me, and he himself offered sacrifice to me; then, well pleased, I granted him boons beyond compare.
Sonship to me at the dawn of each aeon, and overlordship of the worlds, and a name born of self-consciousness that designates him by his synonyms.
'No one shall transgress the boundary that you have set, and you yourself, O brahmin, shall be the bestower of boons to those who desire boons.'
'Of the hosts of gods and demons, and of the seers, O wealthy in austerity, and of the fathers, O greatly blessed one of rigorously kept vows, and of the manifold beings, you shall ever be the worshipful one.'
'And I, having come into manifestation in the affairs of the gods, am ever to be instructed by you, O brahmin, and to be set to my task, as a son is.'
Having granted these and other splendid boons to Brahmā of measureless splendor, I, well pleased, became wholly devoted to withdrawal.
The extinction of all duties — withdrawal — is remembered as the supreme state; therefore, having attained withdrawal, let one move through the world with every faculty at rest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Me, accompanied by knowledge, abiding in the sun, the eternal one, the teachers whose convictions are settled by Sāṃkhya call Kapila.
This blessed Hiraṇyagarbha, well praised in the Vedic hymns — that am I, named in the Yoga treatises as the goal of yoga, O brahmin.
Having come into manifestation, I abide everlasting in heaven; then, at the end of a thousand ages, I shall withdraw the world again, having drawn into myself the beings, both the unmoving and the moving.
Alone, together with knowledge, I shall sport, O best of the twice-born; then once more I shall fashion the whole world here through knowledge.
That fourth form of mine created the imperishable Śeṣa; he indeed is called Saṃkarṣaṇa, and he too begot Pradyumna.
From Pradyumna I am Aniruddha — my creation recurs again and again; and from Aniruddha comes Brahmā, born from the primal lotus there.
From Brahmā arise all beings, both the moving and the unmoving. Know this to be the creation that recurs again and again at the dawn of each aeon.
As Time of measureless brilliance forcibly brings back again the sun's rising and setting once they have vanished from the sky here, so by my power do I, for the welfare of all beings, restore the Earth —
— her whole body overrun by creatures, sunk away, girded by the ocean, I shall bring back to her own place, having taken on the boar's form.
I shall slay Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, drunk with his strength; and again, taking on the man-lion form, for the gods' sake I shall slay Hiraṇyakaśipu, that destroyer of sacrifice, the son of Diti.
Bali, the mighty son of Virocana, a great demon, shall come to be, and he shall cast Śakra down from his own sovereignty.
When the three worlds have been carried off by him, and the lord of Śacī is turned away helpless, I shall be born as the twelfth son in Aditi, from Kaśyapa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then I shall restore the kingdom to Śakra of measureless splendor; I shall establish the gods in their own stations, O Nārada, and Bali I shall make a dweller in the depths of the netherworld.
In the Tretā age I shall become Rāma, upholder of the lineage of Bhṛgu, and I shall root out the warrior order, abounding in forces and mounts.
And when the juncture of the Tretā and the Dvāpara has arrived, becoming Rāma the son of Daśaratha, I shall be the lord of the world.
Through harm done to Trita, the two seers, sons of Prajāpati — Ekata and likewise Dvita — incurring disfigurement, shall attain the condition of monkeys.
Those forest-dwellers who shall be born in their line shall become my helpers in the gods' undertaking, O twice-born.
Then in battle I shall slay the terrible lord of the rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa, the defiler of Pulastya's line, that thorn in the world's side, together with his host.
At the final juncture of the Dvāpara and the Kali ages, my manifestation, for the sake of Kaṃsa, shall come to be in Mathurā.
There, having slain very many dānavas, those thorns in the gods' side, I shall make Kuśasthalī, the city of Dvārakā, my dwelling.
Dwelling there in that city, I shall slay Naraka the son of the Earth, doer of displeasure to Aditi, and Mura, and the dānava Pīṭha.
The lovely city of Prāgjyotiṣa, filled with manifold treasures, I shall carry off to Kuśasthalī, having slain the foremost of the dānavas.
And Śaṃkara and Mahāsena, who seek the welfare and pleasure of Bāṇa, both girded for the fight and honored by the world of the gods — these I shall vanquish.
Then, having conquered Bali's son Bāṇa of the thousand arms, I shall destroy thereafter all the dwellers in Saubha.
He who shall be known as Kālayavana, enveloped in the splendor of Garga — his slaying shall come from me alone, O best of the twice-born.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the mighty Jarāsaṃdha, opposer of all kings, shall come to be a swollen demon, a ruler of the earth in Girivraja; his slaying shall come about through the working of my design.
When the powerful ones, all the kings upon the earth, are gathered together, the son of Vāsava alone shall be my good helper.
Thus the worlds shall say: 'The two seers Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the two lords, girded for the work, are consuming the warrior order for the sake of the world's purpose.'
Having relieved the Earth of her burden as I desired, O most excellent one, I shall bring about a terrible dissolution of all the chief Sātvatas and of Dvārakā, destroying my own kinsmen.
For I, bearer of the fourfold form, having performed deeds beyond all measure, shall go to my own worlds, honored by Brahman.
The Swan and the Horse-headed one too were manifestations, O best of the twice-born; when the sacred utterance of the Veda was lost, then it was recovered by me — and with their Vedas and revealed texts restored, men were set aright of old in the Kṛta age.
These have passed away in ages gone by, whether heard of in the ancient lore or somewhere else; and many of my surpassing manifestations have passed away, having done the works of the world and then returned to their own essential nature.
For not even by Brahmā has such a vision of me been gained as you have gained today here, your mind set upon the single-pointed path.
All this has been declared to you, O brahmin, devoted as you are, by me — the past and the future, together with its secret, O most excellent one.
Thus that blessed god, bearer of the universal form, the imperishable one, having spoken just so much speech, vanished there and then.
And Nārada of great splendor, having received the grace he longed for, hastened to the hermitage of Badarī to behold Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This great Upaniṣad, conjoined with the four Vedas, wrought of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, named in keeping with the Pañcarātra —
— sung forth from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, Nārada recited again in the abode of Brahmā, my son, just as he had seen and just as he had heard.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Wondrous indeed is the greatness of that wise one; does Brahmā not know it, that he had to hear of it from Nārada?
