That is called Aniruddha; that they declare to be the Primordial Nature. It is to be known as the Unmanifest, composed of the three qualities, O best of kings.
The god Viṣvaksena, the lord Hari, accompanied by his power of wisdom, made his couch upon the waters and entered the yoga of sleep, pondering the creation of the world—a wondrous creation arising from manifold qualities.
As he pondered creation, the Great Principle, called the quality of the Self, arose; from it was born self-consciousness, and thence Brahmā of the four auspicious faces, the blessed Hiraṇyagarbha, grandfather of all the worlds.
Sprung then from Aniruddha upon a lotus, lotus-eyed and radiant, the eternal one sat upon the thousand-petalled flower.
In that wondrous expanse the lord beheld the worlds made wholly of water; abiding in goodness, the supreme one then brought forth the hosts of beings.
And even before that, upon the petal of the lotus, bright as the sun's rays, there were two drops of water made by Nārāyaṇa, surpassing in their qualities.
The blessed one, without beginning or end, the unfallen, beheld those two; one drop there was the color of honey, of lovely radiance.
That one, born of darkness, became Madhu by the command of Nārāyaṇa; the other drop, hard, born of passion, became Kaiṭabha.
Those two mighty foremost ones, endowed with the qualities of darkness and passion, maces in hand, rushed forth, making their way along the stalk of the lotus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
They beheld Brahmā of immeasurable splendor, seated upon the lotus, first bringing forth the four Vedas of lovely form.
Then those two foremost of demons, having taken bodily form, seeing the Vedas, suddenly seized them as Brahmā looked on.
Then those two foremost of the Dānavas, having seized the eternal Vedas, swiftly entered the netherworld in the great ocean to the north-east.
Then, when the Vedas had been stolen, Brahmā fell into despair; bereft of the Vedas, he spoke these words to the Lord.
"The Vedas are my supreme eye, the Vedas are my supreme strength; the Vedas are my supreme abode, the Vedas are my highest Brahman."
"All my Vedas have been carried off from here by force by the two Dānavas; bereft of the Vedas, my worlds have become wrapped in darkness. What can I do without the Vedas, intent as I am upon creating the worlds?"
"Alas, a great sorrow born of the loss of the Vedas has come upon me; it torments my heart, rending it open to fierce grief."
"Who shall today lift me, sunk in this ocean of grief, out of it, and bring back those lost Vedas? To whom shall I become dear?"
As Brahmā spoke thus, O best of kings, O foremost of the wise, the thought arose in him to praise Hari; then the lord, with hands joined in reverence, intoned a supreme hymn.
"Homage to you, O heart of Brahman; homage to you, my forefather; O first of the worlds, best of all beings, treasury of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, O all-pervading one."
"O inconceivable maker of the manifest and unmanifest, you who abide upon the path of well-being, devourer of the universe, inner Self of all beings, O you who are born of no womb!"
"I am born of your grace, to you the abode of the worlds, the self-existent. From you came my first birth, born of the mind, honored by the twice-born."
"My second birth of old was from the eye; and by your grace my third great birth was from speech."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"From you, too, came my fourth birth, born of the ear, O all-pervading one; and my birth from the nose is called the fifth, again from you."
"And my birth from the egg, the sixth, was fashioned by you; and this is my seventh birth, born of the lotus, O you of measureless splendor."
"In creation after creation I am your son, free of the three qualities, renowned, O lotus-eyed one, fashioned from the qualities of Primordial Nature."
"You are the very nature of the Lord, the self-existent, the supreme Person; by you was I fashioned, having the Vedas for my eye, surpassing all age."
"Those Vedas, my eye, have been stolen; I have become blind. Awake! Restore to me my two eyes. I am dear to you, and you are dear to me."
Thus praised, the blessed Person, facing in every direction, then forsook his sleep, intent upon the task of the Vedas, and by his sovereign power took on a second body.
With a body finely formed and fair as the moon, the lord then made the white horse's head, the abode of the Vedas.
His head became the heavens with their constellations and stars, and his long hairs became bright as the rays of the sun.
His two ears were the sky and the nether regions, his brow the earth that bears all beings; the holy Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, the great rivers, were his two eyebrows.
His two eyes were the moon and the sun; his nose was held to be the twilight; the syllable Oṃ was his ritual consecration, and lightning was made his tongue.
His teeth, O king, were the ancestors known as the drinkers of soma; the world of cows and the world of Brahmā were the lips of the great one; and his neck, O king, was the Night of Time, surpassing in its qualities.
Having made this horse's head, wrapped about with manifold forms, the lord of all, the sovereign, vanished and entered the netherworld.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having entered the netherworld once more and taken up the supreme yoga, he, assuming the disciplined tone of the science of recitation, sent forth the sound Oṃ.
That sound, resonant and far-reaching, all-pervading and tender, became hidden within the earth, arising from the qualities of all beings.
Then those two Asuras, having bound the Vedas by a pact and laid them down in the netherworld, rushed toward the place from which the sound came.
In that interval, O king, the god Hari, bearing the horse's head, seized all the Vedas that had been left in the netherworld and gave them back to Brahmā, then returned to his own nature.
Having set the horse's head in the great ocean to the north-east, the Horse-Headed one thus became the abode of the Vedas.
Then the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, seeing nothing, came rushing back to that place; and they beheld that the spot where the Vedas had been laid was empty.
Then, taking on their utmost speed, those two foremost of the strong rose up swiftly again from the abode of the waters and beheld that very Person, the lord, the first maker.
White, gleaming pure as the moon, abiding in the body of Aniruddha, of immeasurable valor, he had once more entered the yoga of sleep.
He lay upon a couch fashioned to his own measure, set above the waters, made rich with the coils of the serpent and wreathed about with garlands of flame.
Endowed with stainless goodness and of lovely radiance—seeing him, those two lords of the Dānavas burst into great laughter.
And those two, possessed by passion and darkness, said: "This is that white Person who lies here sunk in sleep."
"Surely it is by him that the Vedas were carried off from the netherworld. Whose is he? Who indeed is this? And why does he sleep in such luxury?"
Having uttered these words, the two roused Hari; and the supreme Person, awaking, perceived that they sought battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And gazing upon those two lords of the Asuras, he set his mind upon battle; then there arose a war between the two of them and Nārāyaṇa.
Those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, their bodies possessed by passion and darkness—the slayer of Madhu killed them, doing a service of recompense to Brahmā.
Then, by the slaying of those two and by the recovery of the Vedas, the supreme Person swiftly dispelled the grief of Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, his foes slain and honored by the restoring of the Vedas, attended by his retinue, created all the worlds, both the moving and the unmoving.
Having granted to the Grandfather the foremost wisdom for the bringing-forth of the worlds, the god Hari vanished thereupon into the very place from which he had come.
Having slain those two Dānavas and made the horse-headed body, Hari, for the sake of the dharma of activity, again established that very body.
Thus did this greatly blessed Hari become the Horse-Headed one; this ancient form, boon-granting and sovereign, has now been told.
For that brāhmaṇa who should ever hear this or hold it in memory—his learning would never come to ruin at any time.
Having propitiated by fierce austerity the god who bears the horse's head, the Pāñcāla attained the method, and Rāma along the path that was pointed out.
This tale of the Horse-Head, O king, has been recounted to you—the ancient story equal in worth to the Veda, about which you questioned me.
Whatever body the god might wish to make at any time in the ordering of his work, that body he would make, transforming his very self by himself.
This glorious one is the treasury of the Vedas; this indeed is the treasury of austerity; this is Yoga and Sāṃkhya and the foremost Brahman—Hari, the all-pervading lord.
The Vedas have Nārāyaṇa for their goal; the sacrifices have Nārāyaṇa for their essence; austerity has Nārāyaṇa as its highest aim; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme destination.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Truth has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground; the cosmic order is of Nārāyaṇa's very essence. Dharma too is grounded in Nārāyaṇa, that dharma by which return to rebirth is hard to come by.
The dharma marked by active engagement in the world is likewise of Nārāyaṇa's essence. Scent itself, the foremost quality residing in earth, is taught to be of Nārāyaṇa's essence.
And the quality of the waters, O king—taste—is of Nārāyaṇa's essence; the quality of the luminous bodies—form—is taught to be of Nārāyaṇa's essence.
Touch as well, the quality of wind, is taught to be of Nārāyaṇa's essence; and sound, which arises from space, is likewise of Nārāyaṇa's essence.
And mind too, which has come to be from that, marked by the quality of the Unmanifest—time has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground, as does the course of the heavenly lights.
Fame has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground, and the goddesses Śrī and Lakṣmī. Sāṃkhya has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground, and Yoga is of Nārāyaṇa's essence.
For those who hold the Puruṣa to be the cause, and likewise the primordial Nature as cause, and inherent disposition, and deeds, and fate as cause—
reckoned by these five causes, Hari is verily the final ground in every case—for those who seek to know the truth through reasonings that face in every direction.
The one Reality is the great yogin, Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord—of the worlds together with Brahmā, and of the great-souled seers,
of the followers of Sāṃkhya and the yogins, and of the ascetics who know the Self—the inmost thought of all these Keśava knows, but they do not know his.
Whoever in all the worlds perform rites for the gods and for the ancestors, and bestow gifts, and practice great austerity—
the refuge of them all is Viṣṇu, who abides in lordly ordinance; because he has made his dwelling in all beings, he is called Vāsudeva.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For he is the eternal, supreme Great Seer, of vast might, possessed of qualities yet called free of qualities; he swiftly enters into union with the qualities, as time, in its season, joins itself to the seasons.
None can find the going of this great-souled one, nor does anyone here perceive his coming. Only the great seers, made of knowledge and self-restrained, behold forever the Puruṣa who transcends the qualities.
Janamejaya said: Ah, the Lord Hari gives delight to all the single-minded devotees, and the Lord himself receives the worship offered according to ordinance.
But for those in the world whose fuel of karma is burnt away, who are free of merit and demerit, you have set forth the goal that is reached by the unbroken succession of the tradition.
By the fourth course they go to the Supreme Person; the single-minded ones indeed go to the highest abode.
Surely this dharma of single-minded devotion is the most excellent, dear to Nārāyaṇa, since its followers, without passing through the three other courses, go straight to the imperishable Hari.
Those brahmins who, abiding rightly, recite the Vedas together with the Upaniṣads, holding fast to ordinance, and those too who follow the dharma of ascetics—
I know that the goal of the single-minded men is more distinguished than theirs. By whom was this dharma declared—by a god, or by a seer?
And what is the practice of the single-minded ones, and when was it brought forth, O mighty one? Cut through this doubt of mine, for great is my curiosity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas had been drawn up for battle, and Arjuna was dispirited, it was sung by the Lord himself.
The coming and the going I have already related to you. For this dharma is profound, hard to comprehend for those who have not perfected the self.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It is measured by the Sāmaveda, established of old in the first age; it is upheld, O king, by the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
On this matter, O great king, the highly blessed Nārada, questioned by Pārtha amid the seers, while Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma listened—
and this was related by my teacher to me as well, O best of kings. Hear it now just as it was related there by Nārada.
When there was the mind-born birth of Brahmā, sprung from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, O protector of the earth, then Nārāyaṇa himself, by that dharma, performed the rites for the gods and for the ancestors, O Bhārata.
The Phenapa seers received that dharma; the Vaikhānasas received this dharma from the Phenapas, and from the Vaikhānasas Soma received it; thereafter that god vanished once more.
When there was the second birth of Brahmā, the eye-born one, O king, then from the grandsire Soma he came to know this dharma, of Nārāyaṇa's essence, O king, and he gave it over to Rudra.
Then Rudra, established in yoga, of old in the Kṛta age, O king, taught this dharma to all the Vālakhilya seers; thereafter it vanished once more by the magic power of that god.
When there was the third, the great speech-born birth of Brahmā, then this dharma came forth from Nārāyaṇa himself, O king.
The seer named Suparṇa obtained it from the Supreme Person, through austerity well practiced, through self-control and discipline.
Suparṇa traversed this supreme dharma three times over; for that reason this observance is here called the Trisauparṇa.
This observance, recited in the recitation of the Ṛgveda, is indeed hard to fulfill; and this eternal dharma was obtained from Suparṇa as well.
By Vāyu, O best of bipeds, it was made known—Vāyu, the life-breath of the world; and from the presence of Vāyu it was obtained by the seers who eat the remnants of offerings.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
From them the great Ocean obtained this supreme dharma; thereafter it vanished once more, gathered back into Nārāyaṇa.
When once again there was the ear-born creation of the great-souled Brahmā, O tiger among men, listen as I relate it.
The god Hari Nārāyaṇa himself, intent on creating the world, the Lord, brought to mind a Person who would make the creation of the world.
Then, as he was pondering, a Person issued from his two ears—Brahmā, the maker of creatures' generation; and the Lord of the world addressed him:
"Create all the creatures, my son, from the mouth and likewise from the feet; I shall ordain your welfare, your strength and your splendor, O you of good vows."
"And receive from me the dharma named Sātvata by name; by it, establish the whole Kṛta age according to ordinance."
Then Brahmā made obeisance to the god Harimedhas, and he took up the foremost dharma, together with its mystery and its summary, accompanied by the Āraṇyaka, sprung from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
Having then imparted to Brahmā of measureless splendor that dharma proper to the Kṛta age, known as action free of desire, he went beyond the darkness, where the Unmanifest abides.
Then the boon-granting god, the grandsire of the world of Brahmā, created at that time all the worlds entire, the unmoving and the moving.
Then at the beginning the auspicious Kṛta age set in; and thereupon the Sātvata dharma, pervading the worlds, stood established.
By that very first dharma, Brahmā, the maker of the worlds' outpouring, worshipped the Lord of gods, Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Master.
And for the sake of establishing dharma, he then taught it to Manu Svārociṣa, out of his desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Then Svārociṣa, undistracted of old, the lord and master of all worlds, himself taught it to his son Śaṅkhapada, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Śaṅkhapada too taught it to his own son, born of his body, Sudharman the guardian of a quarter, O Bhārata; thereafter it vanished once more, when the Tretā age had come again.
At the nostril-born birth of Brahmā of old, O best of kings, the god Hari Nārāyaṇa himself, the lotus-eyed Lord, brought forth this dharma while Brahmā looked on.
Then the blessed Sanatkumāra learned it, O king; and from Sanatkumāra the lord of creatures Vīraṇa, at the dawn of the Kṛta age, O tiger of the Kurus, learned this dharma.
And Vīraṇa, having studied it, gave it to Manu Raucya; Raucya gave it to his son, the pure, devout, and wise Suvrata—
that is, he bestowed it upon the righteous guardian of the quarters named Kukṣi; thereafter it vanished once more, the dharma sprung from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
At the egg-born birth, again, of Brahmā whose source is Hari, this dharma arose once more from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
It was received by Brahmā, O king, and applied according to ordinance; and the sages named the Barhiṣads were instructed in it, O king.
And from the Barhiṣads, Hari—keeper of the observance of the eldest Sāman—passed it on to the twice-born one who had reached the end of the Sāmaveda, renowned by the name Jyeṣṭha.
And from Jyeṣṭha it passed on to King Avikampana; thereafter, O king, this dharma of the Lord Hari vanished away.
This which is the seventh birth of Brahmā, the lotus-born, O king—there this dharma was declared by Nārāyaṇa himself.
To the pure grandsire, the upholder of the worlds at the age's dawn, and the grandsire gave this dharma of old to Dakṣa.
Then Dakṣa bestowed it upon his eldest grandson, O best of kings; and from him Vivasvat received it, the eldest son of Savitṛ among the Ādityas.
And at the dawn of the Tretā age, again, Vivasvat gave it to Manu; and Manu, for the welfare of the worlds, gave it to his son Ikṣvāku.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And declared by Ikṣvāku, it stood pervading the worlds; and at the end of the cosmic dissolution it shall go back again to Nārāyaṇa, O king.
And the dharma which belongs to those who keep the vows, that, O best of kings, was related to you before in the Songs of Hari, set forth in summary form.
By Nārada this dharma was obtained, with its mystery and its summary, directly from the Lord of the world, from Nārāyaṇa, O king.
Thus this great dharma, primordial and eternal, O king, hard to comprehend and hard to practice, is upheld at all times by the Sātvatas.
By this knowledge of dharma, and by action well applied and joined with the dharma of non-injury, the Lord Hari is well pleased.
In one place his distribution is of a single array; somewhere it is called a twofold array; he is reckoned as a threefold array, and a fourfold array too is seen.
For Hari alone is the Knower of the field, free of self-claiming and without parts, and the living soul in all beings, transcending the qualities of the five elements.
He is the renowned mind too, O king, that sets the five senses in motion; he is the wise treasure-house of the worlds, he is the maker of the worlds' outpouring.
He is both the non-doer and the doer, the effect and the cause as well; just as he wishes, O king, so does the imperishable Person play.
This dharma of single-minded devotion has been recounted to you, O best of kings, by me through the grace of my teacher—hard to comprehend for those who have not perfected the self; for single-minded men, O king, are not to be found in great numbers.
If the world were thronged with the single-minded, O joy of the Kurus—men who do no harm, who know the Self, who delight in the welfare of all beings and have renounced action done with desire—then the Kṛta age would be regained.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus did the blessed Vyāsa, my teacher, O lord of peoples, the knower of dharma, the best of the twice-born, relate it to the Dharma King.
In the presence of the seers, O king, while Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma listened—and to him too, before, Nārada of mighty austerity had related it—
the supreme god, the highest Brahman, white, with the luster of the moon, the unfallen, to whom the single-minded ones go, wholly devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Janamejaya said: This dharma of many kinds, practiced by the awakened—why do other brahmins, established in their various observances, not follow it?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Three natures, O king, are fashioned within the bonds of the body—the sāttvika, the rājasa, and the tāmasa, O Bhārata.
Among those bound in the body, the best of men, O upholder of the Kuru line, is the sāttvika one, O tiger among men—he it is who would be resolved upon the goal of liberation.
And here too he discerns the Person abiding in Brahman; since liberation has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground, the sāttvika one is verily so esteemed.
And he attains the object of his heart's desire, meditating on the Supreme Person—single-minded in devotion forever, wholly given over to Nārāyaṇa.
For all those wise ascetics who long for liberation, who have severed every craving, it is Hari who bears their welfare and their gain.
Whatever man, at his very birth, Madhusūdana looks upon, that man is to be known as endowed with sattva and assured of liberation.
This dharma practised with single-minded devotion is equal in worth to Sāṃkhya and Yoga; through it men attain the supreme goal, the liberation whose very self is Nārāyaṇa.
The man whom Nārāyaṇa beholds is awakened to truth; but one awakened by his own will alone, O king, is not so awakened.
The rājasic and tāmasic natures are remembered to be intermingled; and the man whose self is composed of these, O lord of peoples, born marked by the signs of worldly engagement, Hari himself does not regard.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It is Brahmā, the grandsire of the worlds, who looks upon such a man at his birth—the mortal flooded over by rajas and tamas.
True, the gods and the sages abide in sattva, O best of kings; yet, lacking that subtle sattva, they are accordingly remembered as belonging to the modified order.
Janamejaya said: How can a man of the modified order attain the Supreme Person?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Joined to the most subtle sattva, joined to the three syllables, the man, ceasing from action, attains that Person, the twenty-fifth principle.
Thus Sāṃkhya and Yoga are one, and so too the Veda and the Āraṇyaka; these, together with the Pañcarātra, are declared to be limbs of one another. This is the dharma of the single-minded devotees, whose supreme Self is Nārāyaṇa.
As the floods of water gone forth from the ocean enter again, O king, that very ocean, so the great floods of knowledge enter again into Nārāyaṇa.
This Sātvata dharma has been told to you, O kinsman of the Yadus; observe it as is fitting, if you are able, O descendant of Bharata.
For thus did the greatly blessed Nārada declare to my teacher the imperishable, single-minded goal of the white-robed ascetics.
And Vyāsa, out of affection, recounted it to the wise son of Dharma; that very teaching, descended from my teacher, I have now set forth to you.
Hard to follow, indeed, is this dharma, O best of kings; even as you do, so others do not embrace it, for they are bewildered.
For Kṛṣṇa alone is the creator of the worlds, their bewilderer, and their destroyer too, and their very cause, O lord of peoples.
Janamejaya said: Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the Pañcarātra, and the Veda with its Āraṇyaka—these bodies of knowledge, O brahmin sage, are current among the worlds.
Do these rest upon a single foundation, or upon separate foundations, O sage? Being asked by me, declare it, and their origin in due order.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: To that great sage, knowing many things, supreme and most noble, the self-possessed son whom Gandhavatī bore to Parāśara on the island—to him, dispeller of the darkness of ignorance, be salutation.
They declare him the sixth, counting from the Grandsire, the great sage endowed with the glory of the seers, born of a portion of Nārāyaṇa, the only son, Dvaipāyana, the great treasure-house of the Veda.
Him, in the primal ages, did Nārāyaṇa of mighty majesty, the great treasure-house of the Brahman, create for the sake of a son—the unborn, the ancient one of lofty splendour, brought forth the great-souled Vyāsa.
Janamejaya said: By you yourself was his lineage told before, O best of the twice-born: Śakti was the son of Vasiṣṭha, and Parāśara the son of Śakti.
The heir of Parāśara was the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana; yet now you speak of this same one as the son of Nārāyaṇa.
What, then, is the earlier birth of Vyāsa of measureless splendour? Tell me, O man of excellent mind, of his birth that sprang from Nārāyaṇa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While my teacher, most righteous, a treasury of austerity, fixed upon knowledge, longing to understand the meanings of the Vedas, was dwelling at the foot of the Himālaya—
having composed the tale of the Bhārata, the wise one was wearied with austerity; and we, O king, intent upon it, rendered him our devoted service in those days.
Sumantu, and Jaimini, and Paila of firm vows, I myself the fourth disciple, and Śuka, the son of Vyāsa—
surrounded by these five excellent disciples, Vyāsa shone at the foot of the Himālaya like the Lord of beings amid his attendant spirits.
As he recited the Vedas together with their auxiliaries, and the meanings of the Bhārata in every part, we, attentive, waited upon him, the single-minded, the self-controlled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, in the course of some discourse, that best of the twice-born was asked by us about the meanings of the Vedas, the meanings of the Bhārata, and his birth from Nārāyaṇa.
He, the knower of truth, having first spoken of the meanings of the Vedas and of the Bhārata, then set about to relate this birth of his from Nārāyaṇa.
Hear this excellent tale, supreme, belonging to the seers, arising in primal time, O brahmins, attained by me through austerity.
When the time of the creation of creatures had come, in the seventh, the birth from the lotus, Nārāyaṇa, the great yogin, free of good and evil alike—
created from his navel a son, Brahmā of boundless radiance; thereupon that one came forth, and to him he spoke these words:
"You are born from my navel, the lord and maker of the creation of creatures; create manifold beings, O Brahman, both the dull and the wise."
Thus addressed, he turned away, his mind troubled with anxious thought; and bowing to the boon-granting god, he said to Hari, the Lord:
"What power have I, O Lord of the gods, to create creatures? Homage be to you. I am without the requisite wisdom, O god; ordain what is to follow."
Thus addressed, the Blessed One then vanished from sight, and the Lord of the gods, the foremost of the wise, called to mind Buddhi, the faculty of intellect.
Then Buddhi, having taken visible form, presented herself before the Lord Hari; and he, the unattached, himself joined her by his power of yoga.
To that Buddhi, established in the yoga of sovereign power, mighty and true, the imperishable Lord, the god, spoke these words:
"Enter into Brahmā, for the accomplishing of the world's creation." Then, commanded by the Lord, Buddhi swiftly entered into him.
Then Hari beheld him once more, now joined with Buddhi, and again spoke to him this word: "Create these manifold beings."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished there itself, and in a single moment attained his own abode, named after the gods.
And reaching that very nature, Brahmā came to be one with it; thereupon, it is said, another thought arose within him again.
All these creatures were created by Brahmā the supreme one, thronged with hosts of Daityas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas; and this earth, the bearer of wealth, was born, pressed down by the burden and made to suffer.
"Many mighty Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas shall arise upon the earth, and engaged in austerity they shall obtain the highest boons."
"Inevitably, by all those grown arrogant through the granting of boons, the hosts of gods and the sages rich in austerity shall be oppressed; therefore it is fitting that I should there bring about the lifting of this burden."
"Then, by my various manifestations upon the earth, in due succession, by the curbing of the wicked and the upholding of the good—
I shall sustain this suffering, faithful earth; for by me, in the form of the serpent abiding in the nether world, is she upheld.
Upheld by me, she in turn bears the world with all that moves and is unmoving; therefore, taking birth, I shall accomplish the deliverance of the earth."
Having pondered thus, the Blessed Madhusūdana brought forth many forms, for the sake of his manifestations.
"The boar-form, the man-lion, the dwarf, and the human likewise—by these the unruly foes of the gods are to be destroyed by me."
Then again the creator of the world, making the regions resound with the sound "Bhoḥ!", uttered forth the goddess Sarasvatī; and thereupon arose the Sārasvata one.
Apāntaratamas by name, the son sprung from the speech of the Lord, knower of past, present, and future, a speaker of truth, firm in his vows.
To him, bowed with his head, the imperishable first of the gods said: "By you, O best of the wise, the śruti must be set in order in the expounding of the Vedas; therefore do this my word as it has been commanded, O sage."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By him, in the age of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, the Vedas were then divided; and thereafter the Blessed Hari was well pleased by that work of his, and by his austerity well practised, by restraint and by observance.
The glorious Lord said: "Through the ages of the Manus, my son, you shall thus be the setter-in-motion of the worlds—unshaken, O Brahman, and forever unassailable.
And again, when the Tiṣya age has come, there shall be the Bhāratas called the Kurus, great-souled kings renowned upon the earth.
Among those descended from you a splitting of the line shall come to pass, ending in their mutual destruction—save for you alone, O best of the twice-born.
There too, endowed with austerity, you shall divide the Vedas in many ways; and when the Kṛṣṇa age has come, you shall be of dark hue.
You shall be the author of manifold dharmas and likewise a maker of knowledge, possessed of austerity; yet you shall not be freed from attachment.
And a son of yours, free of all passion, shall be the Supreme Self, by the grace of Maheśvara; this word shall not prove otherwise."
He whom they call the mind-born son of the Grandsire, endowed with the highest understanding—Vasiṣṭha, the foremost, the treasure-house of austerity, who shines surpassing even the sun—
and in his line, thereafter, the great sage named Parāśara, of mighty power—he, your father, the most excellent treasury of the Veda, of great austerity, the very dwelling-place of penance, born of a maiden upon his father's daughter; of that seer you shall be the son.
You, in whom every doubt about all matters of past, present, and future is severed—those thousand-yuga cycles that have passed away before,
all those pointed out by me you shall behold, endowed with austerity; and again you shall behold the many thousand-yuga cycles to come.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And me, without beginning or end in the world, bearing the discus in my hand, O sage—through meditation upon me, O sage, this word shall not prove otherwise."
"Śanaiścara, the son of Sūrya, shall become the great Manu; and in that age of the Manu, foremost among the host of the Seven Seers, you yourself shall be, my dear child, by my grace—of this there is no doubt."
Vyāsa said: Having spoken thus to the Sārasvata sage Apāntaratamas, the Lord then said, "Go now and accomplish it."
And I, by the grace of that god of Hari's own wisdom, was thus born by the name Apāntaratamas at the command of Hari; and again I was born, renowned, the joy of Vasiṣṭha's line.
Thus has this former birth of my own been told by me, brought about by the grace of Nārāyaṇa, and born of a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
For I performed a most mighty austerity, exceedingly severe, in days of old, O best of the wise, with the highest concentration.
All this has been told to you that you asked of me, my children—my former birth and what is to come—out of affection for the devoted.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: This lineage of our teacher has now been told to you, O king—of Vyāsa of untroubled mind. Now hear once more what you have asked.
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the Pañcarātra, the Vedas, and the Pāśupata likewise—know these bodies of knowledge, O royal sage, to be of differing doctrines indeed.
The expounder of Sāṃkhya, it is said, is Kapila, the supreme sage; the ancient knower of Yoga is Hiraṇyagarbha, and no other.
And Apāntaratamas, it is said, is the teacher of the Vedas; some here declare that sage to be Prācīnagarbha.
Umā's consort, the Lord of beings, Śrīkaṇṭha, the son of Brahmā—Śiva, undisturbed, declared this knowledge, the Pāśupata.
But the knower of the whole Pañcarātra is the Blessed One himself; and in all these bodies of knowledge, O best of kings, he is to be seen.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
According to the tradition and according to the knowledge, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the final ground; yet those become darkness do not know him thus, O lord of peoples.
Him alone the wise declare to be the author of the scriptures, and they proclaim that the seer Nārāyaṇa is the final ground, that no other exists beside him.
In all those who are free of doubt Hari dwells forever; but in those still beset by doubt, who lean upon mere argument, Mādhava does not abide.
But those, O king, who know the Pañcarātra and follow its order step by step, who have attained single-minded devotion—they truly enter into Hari.
Sāṃkhya and Yoga are the two eternal paths, O king, and the Vedas entire in all their fullness; by all the seers together it has been declared that Nārāyaṇa is this whole ancient universe.
Whatever deed, good or evil, is set in motion and proceeds in all the worlds—let it be known that it issues from that seer alone, whether in heaven, in the mid-air, on earth, or in the waters.
Janamejaya said: Are the puruṣas many, O brahmin, or is there but one? Who here is the supreme Puruṣa, and what is said to be the source in this matter?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: For those who reason after the manner of Sāṃkhya and Yoga the puruṣas in the world are many; these do not hold that the Puruṣa is one, O upholder of the Kuru line.
But just as a single source is spoken of for the many puruṣas, so shall I expound that all-pervading Puruṣa who transcends the strands of nature.
Having paid homage to the teacher Vyāsa of measureless splendour, devoted to austerity, self-controlled, worthy of worship, the supreme seer—
This Hymn of the Puruṣa, O lord of the earth, is renowned in all the Vedas as the cosmic order and as truth, pondered by that lion among seers.
By way of general rule and exception, the seers led by Kapila, taking their stand on inquiry into the inner Self, have set forth the scriptures, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In brief I shall declare to you, by the grace of that one of boundless might, the unity of the Puruṣa even as Vyāsa has proclaimed it.
On this point too they recite this ancient tale, the dialogue between the three-eyed god and Brahmā, O lord of peoples.
In the midst of the Ocean of Milk there stands, gleaming like gold, the foremost of mountains renowned as Vaijayanta, O king.
There the god, dwelling alone and meditating upon the course of the inner Self, ever frequents Vaijayanta from his abode of Virāj.
Now as that wise four-faced one sat there, his son Śiva, born from his brow, came of his own accord—long ago, the lord of yogins, the three-eyed master, gliding through the very sky.
Then he descended swiftly from the heavens upon the summit of that mountain, and stood before him well pleased, and bowed at his feet.
Seeing him fallen at his feet, the lord, the sole Prajāpati, then raised him up with his left hand.
And the Blessed One spoke to his son, come after so long: "Welcome to you, mighty-armed one; by good fortune you have come into my presence."
"Is it well with you, my son, in your study and your austerity always? For you are ever fierce in penance—therefore I ask you again."
Rudra said: By your grace, Blessed One, it is well and undiminished with me in study and austerity, and so it is with the whole world.
Long had I not beheld you, Blessed One, in your abode of Virāj; therefore have I come to this mountain that is hallowed by the service of your feet.
And I am moved with wonder at your going apart into solitude; for the cause of this can be no small one, O grandsire.
What of that supreme dwelling, free from hunger and thirst, inhabited by gods and demons and by seers of measureless lustre—
—forever frequented by gandharvas and apsarases, that you have forsaken to come alone to this best of mountains?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Brahmā said: This best of mountains, Vaijayanta, is ever frequented by me; here, with mind one-pointed, the cosmic Puruṣa, Virāṭ, is meditated upon.
Rudra said: Many puruṣas, O Brahmā, have been created by you the Self-born, and others, O Brahmā, are being created—yet that Puruṣa, Virāṭ, is one.
Who then is he, O Brahmā, the Supreme Puruṣa upon whom you meditate? Resolve me this doubt, for great is my wonder.
Brahmā said: The many puruṣas you have named, my son—this view, though it goes past the mark, is yet to be regarded, and so is the view that it is not so; but I shall declare to you the ground of the one Puruṣa.
As a single source is spoken of for the many puruṣas, so into that all-pervading Puruṣa, supreme and greatest of the great, free of all qualities, men become free of qualities and enter—the eternal one.
Brahmā said: Hear, my son, how this Puruṣa is declared to be everlasting and imperishable, undecaying, immeasurable, and all-pervading.
He cannot be seen by you, nor by me, nor by any other, O best one; with qualities yet without qualities, all-pervading, he is remembered to be visible only to knowledge.
Bodiless, he dwells within all bodies; and though he dwells within bodies, he is not stained by their deeds.
He is the inner Self of me and of you and of all others who bear the name of body; the witness of them all, he cannot be grasped by anyone anywhere.
His head is all heads, his arms all arms, his feet, eyes, and nostrils all of these; alone he moves through the fields, ranging at will and at his ease.
The fields are the bodies, and the seeds are the good and evil deeds; these he, whose essence is yoga, knows—therefore is he called the Knower of the Field.
Neither his coming nor his going can be known by any being, neither by the method of Sāṃkhya nor by Yoga, however step by step pursued.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I ponder his course, yet I do not know that supreme course; but as far as my knowledge reaches I shall speak of that eternal Puruṣa.
His is oneness and greatness, and he is remembered as the one Puruṣa; he alone, the eternal one, bears the name Great Puruṣa.
One fire is kindled in manifold ways; one is the sun, and one the source of all heats; one wind blows in many ways through the world; the great ocean is the one source of all waters; and one is the Puruṣa, without qualities, of universal form—into that quality-less Puruṣa men enter.
Forsaking all that is made of the qualities, abandoning deeds good and evil, casting off both truth and untruth—thus one becomes free of qualities.
And the ascetic who, having known that unthinkable fourfold subtlety of being, ranges ever vigilant—he shall attain the lordly Puruṣa.
Thus some learned men hold him to be the Supreme Self; others, the inquirers into the inner Self, hold him to be the one Self, and the Self of all.
Among these, he who is the Supreme Self is remembered as eternally free of qualities; he is to be known as Nārāyaṇa, the Self of all, the very Puruṣa; nor is he stained by the fruits of deeds, as the lotus-leaf is untouched by the water.
But that other, whose essence is action, is bound up with bondage and release; he is joined too with the aggregate of seventeen and one. Thus has the Puruṣa been declared to you in manifold ways, in due order.
That which is the whole abode of the world's fabric, the supreme to be known, to be awakened to, together with the awakener—he is the thinker and the thing thought, the taster and the thing to be tasted, the smeller and the thing to be smelt, the toucher and the thing to be touched;
—the seer and the thing seen, the hearer and the thing to be heard, the knower and the thing known, with qualities and without; that which is declared to be the equipoise of the strands, the Primordial Nature—this is eternal, everlasting, and imperishable.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That which the Ordainer first brings forth, the primal treasure-house, the brahmins call Aniruddha; and whatever Vedic rite is rightly performed in the world, joined with its blessing, is indeed his to enjoy.
All the gods and the well-disciplined sages worship him first with sacrifices as the receiver of the sacrificial share. I am Brahmā, the first lord of creatures; from him am I born, and you from me; from me the world, moving and unmoving, and all the Vedas with their secret lore, O son.
Divided fourfold, that Puruṣa sports as he wills; thus is the Blessed One himself awakened to through knowledge.
This has been told to you, my son, as you asked, in due form, and described as it is both in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya and in Yoga.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The auspicious duties grounded in the law of liberation have been declared by the grandsire; now may you tell me the highest duty of those who dwell in the orders of life.
Bhīṣma said: Everywhere duty is ordained that leads to heaven and yields the fruit of truth; of duty, which has many doors, no act here is barren.
But in whatever sphere a man arrives at his settled conviction, that alone he comes to know, and no other, O best of the Bhāratas.
And moreover, O tiger among men, you should hear from me a tale told long ago to Śakra by the divine seer Nārada.
The divine seer Nārada, O king, a perfected one honoured throughout the three worlds, ranges in turn through the worlds, like the wind that none can obstruct.
Once, O mighty archer, he went to the abode of the king of the gods, and being honoured by great Indra, he came and seated himself near at hand.
As he sat there at his ease, the lord of Śacī questioned him: "O brahmin-seer, is there any wonder that you have seen, O sinless one?
"For you, O brahmin-seer, ever moved by curiosity, range as a perfected one through the three worlds with all that moves and is still, like a witness."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For there is nothing in the world unknown to you, O divine seer; tell me, then, whatever you have heard, or experienced, or seen."
To that king of the gods, O king, as he sat and made his fitting request, Nārada, best of speakers, related a far-reaching tale.
In what manner and by what fashion that best of the twice-born, being asked, told him the tale—even so do you now hear it from me.
Bhīṣma said: There was once, O best of the Kurus, in the noblest of cities, Mahāpadma, upon the southern bank of the Gaṅgā, a certain brahmin of composed mind.
Gentle, of the lineage of Soma, accomplished in the Veda's course, with all doubts severed, ever devoted to duty, master of his anger, ever content, his senses subdued—
—ever delighting in non-harming, truthful, honoured by the good, endowed with wealth rightfully gained and with his own virtuous conduct;
In a great and renowned family, rich in kinsmen and connections, esteemed as a refuge by its friends, he kept to a distinguished course of life.
Seeing his many sons, established in his abundant rites, abiding by the duty of his line, O king, he became wholly devoted to the practice of dharma.
Then, pondering in his mind the threefold dharma—that declared in the Veda, that declared in the treatises, and that practised by the cultured—
"What good might come to me from acting? What is fitting? What is the highest refuge?" Thus he was ever troubled, yet came to no certainty.
As he was thus troubled, while abiding in the highest dharma, there came on a certain day a guest, a brahmin of well-composed mind.
He showed him hospitality with the rite due to such an occasion, and when the guest had rested and was seated, he spoke to him these words.
The brahmin said: A bond of name has arisen between us through the sweetness of your speech, O sinless one; having come to friendship with you, I shall say something to you—hear it.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having fulfilled the householder's duty, O lord of brahmins, and that which concerns my sons, I would now perform the highest dharma; what then, O brahmin, should be my path?
Standing alone within the Self, I long to make the Self abide in the Self; I no longer wish to be bound by the common strands of nature.
So long as the season of my life, given over to the fruit of sons, has not yet wholly passed, so long do I wish to gather provision for the world beyond.
For in this unending stream of worldly existence, as I yearn for the farther shore, this thought has arisen in me: where is the raft made of dharma?
Hearing how in the world good things are swept away and carried off, and seeing the garland of pennon and banner of dharma scattered above the heads of creatures—
—my mind takes no delight in the season of enjoyment, seeing the ascetics who strive after the world beyond. Therefore, O guest, with the support of your strength of understanding, set me to the truth of dharma and its purpose.
Bhīṣma said: That guest, hearing the words of the man who longed for dharma, being wise, spoke gentle words in a sweet voice.
In this matter I too am bewildered; this same longing is mine as well, and I come to no certainty regarding heaven with its many doors.
Some praise liberation, O brāhmaṇas, and some the fruit of sacrifice; some cleave to the forest-hermit's order, and some to the life of the householder.
Some take refuge in the duty of kings, and some in the fruit that pertains to the self; some rest in service to a teacher, and some in this saying or that as their support.
Some, by waiting in service upon mother and father, have gone to heaven; others have reached heaven through non-injury, and yet others through truth.
Some, struck down while facing the foe in battle, have gone to heaven; others, perfected by the vow of gleaning, have taken the road that leads to heaven.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some, devoted to study and intent on the Vedic vows, the pure and the wise, content in spirit and masters of their senses, have gone to heaven.
Others, joined to uprightness though slain by men who walked crookedly, the upright and pure of soul, are established upon the vault of heaven.
Thus, by the many and unbarred gateways of dharma in the world, my own mind too is set astir, like a streak of cloud scattered by the wind.
The guest said: I shall give you instruction, O brāhmaṇa, in keeping with tradition, even as it was expounded to me by my teacher; hear it from me in its true meaning.
There, where in a former creation the wheel of dharma was set in motion, in Naimiṣa on the bank of the Gomatī, stands a city named after the Nāga.
There, O bull among the twice-born, sacrifice was offered by all the gods together, there where Māndhātā, best of kings, surpassed even Indra.
There has taken up his dwelling a righteous soul, the great Cakṣuḥśravas, the lotus-naveled and greatly blessed one, renowned simply as Padma.
He, O bull among the twice-born, by speech and by deed and by mind, gladdens living beings, standing firm upon the threefold path.
By conciliation, by gift, by sowing division, and by force—these four means—he guards both the people set against him and his own folk, watching over them with the meditation of his eye.
Approaching him in due form, you may ask what you desire; and he, without falsehood, will reveal to you the highest dharma.
For that Nāga is a host to all, deeply versed in wisdom and the sacred lore, endowed with every excellence that one could wish, none of them deficient.
By nature ever pure as water, ever delighting in study, joined with austerity and self-restraint, and of conduct in no way wanting.
A performer of sacrifice, delighting in giving, patient, established in the highest conduct, truthful in speech, free from envy, virtuous, and a sure refuge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He eats only the food that is left over, and is agreeable in his speech; eminent in benevolence and uprightness, he knows what has been done and what is left undone. He bears no enmity, is devoted to the welfare of all beings, and is endowed with lineage pure as the waters of Gaṅgā's deep pools.
The brāhmaṇa said: Like the lifting of a great burden from one who labors beneath too heavy a load, this consoling word of yours have I heard.
As a bed to one weary from the road, as a seat to one weary of standing, as water to the thirsty and food to one afflicted with hunger;
as the gaining of a thing long desired, as food coming to a guest at the proper season, as a son born to an aged man who has yearned for him in his time;
as the sight of a dear and loving one whom the mind had been longing for—so does the word you have spoken gladden me to the heart.
As one to whom sight has been given, I now look upon the open sky and ponder it. Since this instruction has been given me out of words of wisdom, I shall indeed do exactly as you tell me.
Stay here this night with me, O good one; at daybreak you shall go your way, refreshed and well rested. For yonder the blessed Sūrya, his rays grown faint, sinks with his face turned downward.
Bhīṣma said: Then, having received that hospitality, the guest, O slayer of foes, passed that night, so it is told, together with that brāhmaṇa.
And as the two of them conversed on this and that matter touching dharma, the whole of that night passed pleasantly away, like a day.
Then at the hour of dawn the guest was honored, to the best of his power, by that brāhmaṇa who longed to accomplish his own purpose.
Then that brāhmaṇa, knower of dharma, his resolve in dharma now fixed, taking leave of his kinsfolk, set out in due time toward the abode of the lord of serpents, as he had been directed, single in his resolve upon the good.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: As he journeyed on by stages, passing through wondrous forests and sacred fords and lakes, he came at length upon a certain sage.
Of him the brāhmaṇa duly inquired after the Nāga, as that other brāhmaṇa had directed; and having heard, he went on his way.
Reaching the Nāga's dwelling as it had been described, that man of discernment uttered, adorned with a courteous greeting, the words: "Here I am."
Then, hearing his words, the wife of the Nāga, fair of form, cherishing dharma and faithful to her lord, showed herself to that brāhmaṇa.
Devoted to dharma, she paid him honor in due form, and having welcomed the newcomer with words of welcome, she said: "What may I do for you?"
The brāhmaṇa said: I am rested, and I have been honored by you with gentle speech, gracious lady. I wish to behold that godlike one, the most excellent of Nāgas.
This indeed is my highest errand, this the fruit I desire; and for this purpose have I today come to the abode of the serpent.
The Nāga's wife said: Noble sir, he has gone to draw the chariot of Sūrya for his month-long term of service; in seven or eight days, O brāhmaṇa, he will without doubt show himself to you.
Let this be known to your noble self—the cause of my husband's absence. Whatever else there may be to be done, tell me, and let it be done.
The brāhmaṇa said: With this very resolve, O virtuous one, have I come here; awaiting his return, O lady, I shall dwell within this great forest.
And when he has duly arrived, you are calmly to announce that I have come here; my arrival should be made known, and these my words spoken to him by you.
I too shall dwell here, on the fair bank of the Gomatī, awaiting the appointed time, eating but sparingly, abiding as has been said.
Bhīṣma said: Then that brāhmaṇa, having reassured the Nāga's wife again and again, that bull among the twice-born went away to that very bank of the river.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Now, O best of men, those serpents grew distressed because that ascetic brāhmaṇa was dwelling there without taking any food.
All the kinsmen of that Nāga, gathering together—his brothers, his sons, and his wife—went up to that brāhmaṇa.
They beheld him on a lonely stretch of the bank, that brāhmaṇa of steadfast vow, seated and fasting, intent upon his recitation of prayer.
They all came forward and, honoring the brāhmaṇa again and again, the kinsmen of their host spoke these unequivocal words.
This is now the sixth day since you came here, O treasury of austerity, and yet you crave no food at all, O cherisher of dharma.
You have come to us, and we have presented ourselves before you; the duty of hospitality must be fulfilled by us, for we are all householders.
A root, or a fruit, or a leaf, or milk, O best of the twice-born, or grain to sustain you—deign to eat something, O brāhmaṇa.
Because you, who have forsaken food, dwell here in the forest, all of us, young and old alike, are tormented by this strait of conscience.
For there is none among us who has slain an embryo, none disloyal to the king, none false of word, nor any who eats before the gods, guests, and kinsmen are served in this our house.
The brāhmaṇa said: By your own counsel I have undertaken this manner of fasting, until the return of the Nāga, for ten nights less two.
If, when the eight nights have passed, the serpent should not come, then I shall take food; for his sake alone is this my vow.
You ought not to grieve; go your way as you came. This vow of mine is for his sake, and you should not break it here.
Bhīṣma said: Thus dismissed by the brāhmaṇa, those serpents went back to their own dwelling, their errand unaccomplished, O bull among men.
Bhīṣma said: Then, when many days were fulfilled, the serpent arrived, having been given leave, his service to Vivasvat done, and came to his own abode.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His wife came forward to attend him with the rites of washing his feet and the rest; and the serpent questioned that virtuous lady so endowed with merits.
Have you, O gracious one, in the worship of gods and guests, kept faithfully to the rule laid down of old, fitting and worthy of me?
Surely you have not, with a woman's softness of mind, grown lax through any unfulfilled task, O fair-hipped one, nor, through separation from me, fallen away from the bridge of dharma?
The Nāga's wife said: For pupils, service to the teacher; for brāhmaṇas, the completion of the Veda; for servants, the word of their master; for kings, the protection of the world;
the deliverance of all beings is here declared to be the duty of the kṣatriya; for the vaiśyas, the carrying out of sacrifice, conjoined with hospitality;
service to brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas is the work of the śūdra; and the householder's duty, O lord of serpents, is the seeking of the welfare of all beings.
Restraint in food at all times, the practice of vows each in its order—for dharma, by its very kinship with dharma, is the disciplining of the senses.
"Whose am I? Whence am I? Who am I? Who here could be mine?"—he whose mind is ever bent on this inquiry into purpose becomes thereby one set upon the path of liberation.
Fidelity to her husband is declared the highest dharma of a wife; and that, O lord of serpents, I know in its very truth, from your own teaching.
How, then, should I—who know dharma, while you who are ever constant in dharma still stand by me—forsake the good road and walk upon a crooked path?
The observance of dharma toward the gods, O greatly blessed one, has not been neglected; and in the welcoming of guests I have been ever diligent and unwearied.
For it is now seven or eight days since a brāhmaṇa came here; nor does he disclose his errand to me, but only longs for the sight of you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
On the bank of the Gomatī he sits, eager for the sight of you, that brāhmaṇa of stern vow, reciting the sacred word.
By him, O lord of serpents, I was earnestly told, with gentle and conciliatory words: "He, the best of serpents, when he has returned, is to be sent to my presence."
Having heard this, O greatly wise one, you ought to go to him there; or grant him the sight of you, O you whose very seeing is renowned.
The Nāga said: Now then, what manner of one in a brāhmaṇa's form do you take him to be—a mere mortal brāhmaṇa, or perhaps a god, O you of pure smile?
For what mortal, O illustrious one, desiring to behold me and longing for my sight, would be able to speak words framed almost as a command?
Among the hosts of gods and demons, and among the divine seers too, O lovely one, surely we Nāgas, sprung from Surasā, are mighty in valor and swift in strength;
and we are worthy of homage and bestowers of boons, even when we follow in another's train; over men in particular we are lords of wealth—so runs the sacred saying.
The Nāga's wife said: In all candor I judge that he is no god, O eater of the wind; one thing only do I perceive of him—he is full of devotion, though quick to wrath.
For he, desiring nothing but his one errand, like the cātaka-bird that craves water and longs for rain, that bird in love with rain, so longs for the sight of you.
For no divine being, troubled at heart, would wait thus upon you; one born of equal lineage does not pay court to another.
Therefore, casting off your inborn anger, you ought to grant him sight of you; by cutting off his hope this day, you ought not to scorch your own self.
A king, or a king's son, who fails to wipe away the tears of those who come to him in hope, is bound by the guilt of slaying an embryo itself.
From silence comes the winning of the fruit of knowledge, and from giving, great renown; by truthful speech one gains eloquence, and is exalted in the world beyond.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By the gift of land one attains a destiny equal to that of the hermitages of asceticism; and by restoring to a man wealth that was lost, one reaps the fruit thereof.
He who performs a desired deed without grudging and free of self-interest goes not to hell — so the knowers of dharma have understood.
The Nāga said: My pride was born of arrogance, and through the flaw of my birth a great wrath sprang up from my own resolve, O virtuous one — but you have burned it away with the fire of your words.
And I see no greater darkness than wrath, O virtuous one — a fault to which serpents above all others are held accountable.
For having fallen under the sway of this fault, the mighty ten-necked one, who dared to rival Śakra, was slain by Rāma in battle.
And hearing that Rāma had carried off the calf kept within their inner chambers, the sons of Kārtavīrya, agitated with wrath at the affront, were slain.
By Rāma the son of Jamadagni, the mighty Kārtavīrya, peer of the thousand-eyed one, was struck down in battle through his own wrath.
And so this wrath, the foe of austerities and the destroyer of all that is good, I have now subdued in myself the moment I heard your words.
And I count myself especially blessed, O steadfast one, that you, large-eyed lady endowed with every virtue, are my wife.
I go now to that very place where the brāhmaṇa abides; and since he has indeed spoken his word, he shall not depart with his purpose unfulfilled.
Bhīṣma said: That lord of serpents set out toward the brāhmaṇa, pondering him in his mind and weighing the purpose at hand.
Approaching him, that wise lord of Nāgas, O ruler of men, devoted by nature to dharma, spoke these honeyed words.
Sir, I beg your pardon as I address you; you should bear me no anger. For whose sake have you come here, and to what end?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Coming straight up to you out of affection, I ask you, O twice-born: upon this solitary bank of the Gomatī, what is it that you worship?
The brāhmaṇa said: Know that I have come to this Dharma-forest to see the Nāga, the lotus-naveled chief of the twice-born; in him my purpose is fixed.
But I have heard that he is absent, that he has gone away; and I await him, my own kinsman, as a farmer awaits the rain-cloud.
To work him no trouble, intent on his welfare, I recite the sacred word ten thousand times, joined in yoga and free of affliction.
The Nāga said: Ah, you are of blessed conduct, truly devoted to the good; rich in sacred learning, O illustrious one, you look upon me with the highest affection.
I am that very Nāga, O sage among brāhmaṇas, whom you would find; command me freely as you wish — what kindness may I do for you?
I have heard from my kinsfolk that you had come here, and so I myself have come forth to see you, O twice-born.
And now that you have come, today you shall return with your purpose accomplished; with full confidence, O best of the twice-born, you may set me to any task within my domain.
For we are all bought over by your virtues, and above all you, who, setting aside your own advantage, are devoted here to me alone.
The brāhmaṇa said: I have come, O illustrious one, longing for the sight of you, wishing to ask, in my ignorance, about a certain matter, O serpent.
Established in the Self and seeking my own welfare, I approach you, O greatly wise and mighty one, as one in search of a refuge.
You are made radiant by your own virtues, whose rays are pregnant with glory, soothing as the touch of the moon's beams, delightful, shining from within.
Resolve, then, the question that has arisen in me, O eater of wind; afterward I shall tell you my errand, and you should hear me out.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The brāhmaṇa said: Since you in your turn go forth to bear that single-wheeled, wondrous chariot of Vivasvat — if you have seen anything remarkable there, you should relate it.
The Nāga said: Upon whose thousand rays, as birds upon branches, perfected sages dwell, taking refuge there together with the gods —
From whom the mighty wind, issuing forth and resting upon the sun's rays, spreads wide across the sky, O brāhmaṇa — what is more wondrous than that?
Whose dark ray, named Śukra, becomes a cloud-bearer in the sky and pours forth water in the rains — what is more wondrous than that?
Who for eight months draws up the waters shed by his radiant beam, and again gives them back in their season — what is more wondrous than that?
In whose particular splendors the Self is forever established, and from whom the seed of life and this earth with all that moves and is still are upheld —
In whom abides the mighty-armed god, eternal, supreme, imperishable, without beginning or end, O brāhmaṇa — what is more wondrous than that?
Yet hear from me this one thing, a wonder among wonders, which I beheld in the clear sky while attending upon the Sun.
Once at the hour of noon, while the maker of light was scorching the worlds, there appeared from every side a being resembling a second sun set against the sun.
Lighting up all the worlds with his radiance, with his own splendor, he advanced toward the sun, as if cleaving the heavens apart.
Like a flame fed with offered oblation, pervading all with the rays of his brilliance, in a form beyond describing, he seemed a second sun.
As he drew near and arrived, Vivasvat extended his hand to him, and he too, seeking to return the homage, extended his right hand.
Then, cleaving the very sky, he entered the orb of the sun; and that splendor, made one, in an instant attained the nature of the sun itself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thereupon a doubt arose in us at the meeting of those two splendors: which of the two is the Sun — this one stationed in the chariot, or that one who has come?
And we, our doubt thus arisen, questioned the Sun: who is this that has mounted the heavens and passed on, like a second sun?
The Sun said: This is no god, no friend of the wind, no Asura, nor any serpent; it is a sage, perfected in the vow of gleaning his livelihood, who has thus ascended to heaven.
This brāhmaṇa, living on roots and fruits, eating fallen leaves, feeding on water and on air, abode in deep self-restraint.
By this brāhmaṇa were the sacred verses chanted, hidden within their collected texts; by such effort, with heaven's gate as his goal, he has gone to the triple heaven.
Steadfast and without craving, ever subsisting on gleaned and gathered grain, devoted to the welfare of all beings — such is this brāhmaṇa, O serpent.
For neither gods nor Gandharvas, neither Asuras nor serpents, prevail here over those beings who have attained the supreme goal.
The Nāga said: Such was the wonder I beheld there, O twice-born — a man's body made perfect, which, having reached the goal of the perfected, now circles the earth in company with the Sun, O brāhmaṇa.
The brāhmaṇa said: It is a wonder, no doubt of it; I am well pleased, O serpent, and by your words, fitting and to the point, I have been shown the path.
May it be well with you; I shall depart, O good one, best of serpents. Keep me in remembrance, with errands and commands to fulfill.
The Nāga said: Without telling the errand you had with me, where do you set out for now? Speak, O twice-born, what is your business, and for what purpose you have come here.
Whether your errand, spoken or unspoken, be done, take leave of me, O bull among the twice-born; then, with my consent given, you shall go, O brāhmaṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For having merely looked upon me, you should not, affectionate as you are, leave me and go, O sage among brāhmaṇas, as one passes by a tree at whose foot one has rested.
In you am I, O best of the twice-born, and you are in me — there is no doubt; all this world is yours. What anxiety, then, can you have concerning me, O sinless one?
The brāhmaṇa said: So it is, O greatly wise one, who has understood the truth, O serpent; not in any respect have you set the gods above what is just so.
He who is I is the very one who is you — even so it is, O serpent; I and you and all beings are forever all-pervading.
But I had a doubt, O lord of serpents, concerning the gathering of merit; and so I, O good one, shall practice the vow of gleaning, having now seen its purpose.
This is my resolve, O good one, now firmly grounded in its reason. I take my leave of you — may it be well with you; my purpose is accomplished, O serpent.
Bhīṣma said: And that brāhmaṇa, having taken leave of the best of serpents, his resolve now firm and longing for consecration, then betook himself, O king, to Cyavana of Bhṛgu's line.
By him the sacraments were performed for him, and he devoted himself wholly to dharma; and even so, O king, he related this very tale at that time.
And by the Bhārgava too, O lord of kings, in the dwelling of Janaka, this holy tale was told to the great-souled Nārada.
And by Nārada too, O lord of kings, in the dwelling of the lord of the gods, it was told when he was asked, O best of the Bhāratas, he of untiring deeds.
And by the king of the gods of old, this auspicious tale was told to all the renowned Vasus together, O lord of the earth.
And when I had that most terrible battle with Rāma, then, O king, this tale was told to me by the Vasus.
And to you, who ask of it in truth, O lord of peoples, I have told this holy tale, in accord with dharma, O best of the upholders of dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This, then, is the highest dharma about which you ask me, O Bhārata: to be steadfast and without craving in the working out of dharma and its ends, O king.
And that foremost of the twice-born, his resolve made firm, his course of action pointed out to him by the lord of serpents, composed in restraint and observance, subsisting on measured gleanings of gathered grain, entered the depths of the forest.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tranquillity, grandfather, you have called manifold in form and subtle; yet there is no peace in my heart, having done such a deed as this.
On this matter, O sinless one, you have spoken of peace in its many kinds; but for one's own deed, what peace could there be, even through tranquillity of every manifold sort?
Beholding your body studded with arrows and its grievous wounds, O hero, I find no peace, brooding only upon my evil deeds.
Seeing you, O tiger among men, your limbs drenched in blood and streaming like a mountain, I wither as a lotus withers in the rains.
What can be more grievous than this — that on my account the grandfather has been brought by his foes to such a state on the field of battle, and likewise other kings, together with their sons and kinsmen?
For we and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra alike, in thrall to time and to wrath, having wrought this blameworthy deed — what destiny shall we attain, O king?
I am the cause of your end and the slayer of my own kinsmen; I can find no peace, beholding you stricken upon the ground.
Bhīṣma said: How do you regard yourself, who are subject to another's will, as the cause in this deed, O greatly fortunate one? Subtle indeed is this matter, and beyond the senses.
On this they recite this ancient tale — the colloquy between Death and Gautamī, together with Time, the fowler, and the serpent.
An aged woman named Gautamī, O son of Kuntī, endowed with tranquillity, beheld her own son, bitten by a serpent, lying senseless.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then a fowler named Arjunaka, full of indignation, bound that serpent with a sinew-snare and brought it before Gautamī.
And he said to her: This vile serpent is the slayer of your son. Tell me quickly, O greatly fortunate one, by what means it shall be put to death.
Let it be cast into the fire, or else be cut to pieces; for this wicked killer of a child does not deserve to live long.
Gautamī said: Release it, Arjunaka; you are without understanding. It is not for you to slay it. Who, reflecting on what is yet to be attained, would burden his own soul with such a grievous weight?
Those made light by righteousness float in the world, as rafts float upon the water; but those made heavy by sin sink, as a weapon dropped into water.
Nor will my son be freed from death by the slaying of this creature; and what harm would befall the people were it left unslain? By the destroying of this living, breathing thing, who could pass into the endless realm of Death?
The fowler said: I know that here in this world not all who are enjoined to such tasks discern merit from demerit; the elders are reverend indeed. But these counsels are for one at ease; therefore I shall slay this base serpent.
Those who seek their end await the working of time; but the wise, who know the truth, cast off grief at once. Constant sorrowing brings only decay of one's good; therefore grief is to be abandoned. Cast off your sorrow when this creature is slain.
Gautamī said: No such anguish is found in such as we, for the virtuous ever take their delight in righteousness. The childish, by contrast, are forever vexed; but this is righteousness, and I have no power over this serpent's life.
Brāhmaṇas know no wrath; and whence, then, should torment proceed from wrath? Out of gentleness let it be forgiven, O good man; let this serpent go free.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The fowler said: From the slaying a gain would come, an imperishable good; an immediate gain is praised by the mighty. The gain that springs at once is better than one drawn out in time; and in slaying so contemptible a thing, there is surely benefit.
Gautamī said: What end is gained by seizing and slaying an enemy? And what peace, by holding a captured foe and not releasing him? Why, gentle one, should I not forgive the serpent? For what reason should I not grant it release?
The fowler said: From this single creature the many must be protected; one is not to be protected at the cost of many, Gautamī. Those who know righteousness abandon the offender; so slay this wicked, crawling thing.
Gautamī said: By the slaying of this serpent my little son will not regain his life, O fowler; nor do I see any other good in its killing. Therefore, fowler, set the serpent free, alive.
The fowler said: By slaying Vṛtra the king of the gods won the foremost portion; and the trident-bearing god, by destroying the sacrifice, gained his share. Act, then, as the gods act: slay the serpent at once, and let there be no hesitation.
Bhīṣma said: Though urged again and again by the fowler concerning the serpent, the greatly fortunate Gautamī set not her mind upon the sinful deed.
Then the serpent, breathing faintly and with difficulty steadying itself, oppressed by its bonds, uttered slow words in a human voice.
What fault is there in me here, foolish Arjunaka? For it was Death who, having me powerless and not my own master, drove me to it.
It was at his bidding that this child was bitten, not out of my own wrath nor out of desire; if any guilt there be, O fowler, that guilt is his.
The fowler said: If this evil deed of yours was done while subject to another, O serpent, still you too are a cause in it; therefore you too bear the guilt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For in the making of an earthen pot, just as the rod and the wheel and the rest are reckoned among the causes, so too are you, O serpent.
The guilty one is to be slain by me, and guilty you are, O serpent; for you yourself, O snake, declare yourself a cause in this.
The serpent said: All these — the rod, the wheel, and the rest — are not their own masters; and so am I. Therefore this is no fault of mine, as you suppose.
Or if this be your view — that these too are mutually each other's instigators — then a doubt about effect and cause arises from their mutual impelling.
This being so, there is no fault in me; I am neither to be slain nor guilty. The guilt, if you reckon there to be guilt, would lie in the concurrence of them all.
The fowler said: If you were not a cause, then you would not be a doer either; but you are indeed a cause in this destruction, and therefore I hold that you are to be slain.
Even when the effect is not yet wrought, the cause is not thereby tainted here, O serpent; yet you are to be slain — why speak so much?
The serpent said: When there is no effect, there can be no action, whether the cause be present or absent. Therefore, of the causes in this matter, you above all are to be charged as the cause.
If, in truth, I am held to be a cause, O fowler, then another is the agent who applied it, and his is the guilt in the slaying of this living thing.
The fowler said: You are to be slain by me, O fool, killer of a child and doer of cruelty. Why speak so much, when you are doomed to die, O vile serpent?
The serpent said: As officiating priests who, greedy at a sacrifice, pour out the oblations gain no fruit thereby in the world beyond, so it is with me.
Bhīṣma said: While the serpent, impelled by Death, was speaking thus, Death himself came forth, and spoke this word to the serpent.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Impelled by Time, O serpent, I urged you on; neither you nor I am the cause of the destruction of this living child.
As the wind drives the rain-clouds hither and thither, so, like a cloud, O serpent, am I obedient to the will of Time.
All states of being whatsoever — those of sattva, those of rajas, and those of tamas — have Time for their essence, and arise in living creatures.
The moving and the unmoving, whether in heaven or upon the earth — all have Time for their essence, O serpent; this whole world has Time for its essence.
Whatever activities there are in the world, and likewise the cessations from them, and whatever transformations of these — all is held to have Time for its essence.
The sun, the moon, Viṣṇu, the waters, the wind, the lord of a hundred sacrifices, fire, the sky, the earth, Mitra, the healing herbs, and likewise the Vasus —
the rivers and the oceans, and being and non-being too, O serpent — all are by Time created, and by Time again drawn away.
Knowing this, how can you deem me at fault, O serpent? And if, things being so, the fault were mine, then you too would share in the fault.
The serpent said: I do not call you faultless or at fault, O Death; I say only this much — that I was impelled by you.
Whether the fault lies in Time, or whether it be held to lie not even there — the fault is not for me to examine, for in this we hold no authority.
Yet the absolving of this fault must somehow be wrought by me, O Death, so that I may be free of fault; that is my whole purpose.
Bhīṣma said: Then the serpent said to Arjunaka: You have heard the words of Death. It is not fitting for you to torment me, the innocent, with your snare.
The fowler said: I have heard the word of Death, and yours as well, O serpent; yet this does not establish your freedom from fault, O snake.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Both Death and you are causes in the destruction of this creature; I deem both to be the cause. A non-cause cannot be the cause.
A curse upon Death, that evil-souled, cruel one who brings grief upon the good; and you too I shall slay — the wicked cause of a wicked deed.
Death said: Both of us are helpless, subject to the power of Time, doers of what is ordained; we two are not to be charged with the fault, if you see the matter rightly.
The fowler said: If you both, Death and serpent, are subject to the power of Time, then how can there be joy and wrath in you? This I wish to understand.
Death said: Whatever activities there are in this world are all impelled by Time; this very thing I have already declared to you, O fowler — that it proceeds from Time.
Therefore we two are both subject to the power of Time, doers of what is ordained; we are never to be charged by you with the fault, O fowler.
Bhīṣma said: Then Time himself drew near, in that doubt concerning righteousness and its meaning, and spoke to the serpent, to Death, and to that fowler Arjunaka.
Time said: Neither I, nor this Death, nor this serpent, O fowler, is guilty in the dying of the creature; for we are not the instigators.
The deed that this child himself performed — that, Arjunaka, was our impeller. No other was the cause of his ruin; he is slain by his own deed.
By the deed that he himself wrought he has come to his end; his own deed is the cause of his destruction. We are all subject to the power of deeds.
The world inherits its deeds; it is marked by the bond of deeds. As deeds impel one another here, so too are we impelled.
As from a lump of clay the maker fashions whatever he desires, so does a man come to receive the deed that he himself has wrought.
As shadow and sunlight are ever closely bound together without interval, so are the deed and the doer bound by the doer's own deeds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus neither I, nor Death, nor the serpent, nor you, nor this aged brāhmaṇa woman — the child alone is the cause here.
When Time had spoken thus, O king, the brāhmaṇa woman Gautamī, deeming the worlds to rest upon one's own deeds, said to Arjunaka:
Neither Time, nor the serpent, nor Death is the cause here; by his own deeds, in the course of time, this child has come to his end.
And I too wrought that deed by which this son of mine has died. Let Time depart, and Death likewise; release the serpent, Arjunaka.
Bhīṣma said: Then Death, Time, and the serpent went each the way it had come; Arjunaka was freed of his anger, and Gautamī of her grief.
