Having heard this, attain tranquillity; be not given over to brooding, O king. Know that the three worlds rest upon one's own deeds, O bull among men.
It was not done by you, O Pārtha, nor indeed by Duryodhana; know that it was done by Time, by which the kings were brought down.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard these words, the mighty-splendored Yudhiṣṭhira, knower of righteousness, became freed of his fever and asked this further:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Grandfather, greatly wise, versed in all the scriptures — I have heard this noble tale, O best of the discerning.
Yet I wish to hear still more, something joined with righteousness and its meaning, told by you, O king; deign to expound it to me.
By what householder was Death conquered, through resort to righteousness? Tell me all this truly, O king.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite this ancient tale — how Death was conquered by a householder through resort to righteousness.
O king, of Manu the Prajāpati was born a son named Ikṣvāku; and to that king, radiant as the sun, a hundred sons were born.
His tenth son, O descendant of Bharata, was named Daśāśva; righteous of soul and true in valour, he became king in Māhiṣmatī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Daśāśva had a son who was a most righteous king, one whose mind was ever devoted to truth, to austerity, and to giving.
Renowned upon the earth as Madirāśva, lord of the earth, he was ever absorbed in the science of archery and in the Veda.
Madirāśva's son was a king named Dyutimān, greatly fortunate, of great splendour, great courage, and great strength.
Dyutimān had a son, a king named Suvīra, righteous of soul and rich in treasure, like a second king of the gods.
Suvīra's son, unconquerable in every battle, was famed by the name Durjaya and skilled in all the sciences.
Durjaya, who had the form of Indra, had a son with the splendour of fire, a great king named Duryodhana, O best of kings.
For him, equal to Indra in might and never turning back in battle, his dominion and his power advanced together in equal measure.
With jewels, with wealth, with cattle, and with grains of every kind, his city and his realm then became full to overflowing.
In his realm there was no wretched man, nor any fallen on hard times; not anywhere in it was there a man sick or wasted away.
Generous with gifts, sweet of speech, free from envy, master of his senses, righteous of soul, gentle, valiant, yet given to no boasting,
a performer of sacrifices, liberal, wise, devoted to the brahmins, true to his word, despising none and ever giving, and one who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Him, the best of men, the divine river Narmadā—holy, cool-watered, and auspicious—desired of her own accord, O descendant of Bharata.
To him then upon that river was born a lotus-eyed daughter, named Sudarśanā, O king, and Sudarśanā—fair to behold—indeed in beauty.
Never before among women, O Yudhiṣṭhira, had there been one of such beauty as this daughter of Duryodhana proved to be, that lady of fairest hue.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Her, the princess Sudarśanā, Agni himself desired; and taking the very form of a brahmin, he sought her hand of that king.
"This man is poor and not of my caste"—so thinking, the king was unwilling to give his daughter Sudarśanā to that brahmin.
Thereupon, while his sacrifice was being performed, the bearer of oblations vanished; and then King Duryodhana spoke these words to the priests:
"What evil deed can there be of mine, or of yours, O bulls among the twice-born, by which the fire has gone to ruin, as though a service were rendered to base men?"
"For no small misdeed is this by which the fire has come to ruin—whether yours or mine; let this be pondered in its very truth."
Hearing this speech of the king, those brahmins, O bull of the Bhāratas, restrained and controlled in speech, took refuge with the Purifier, the fire.
Then the blessed bearer of oblations showed himself to them, assuming his own blazing form, radiant as the autumn sun.
Then the great-souled Consumer addressed those bulls among brahmins: "For my own sake I seek the hand of Duryodhana's daughter."
Then, rising at daybreak, those brahmins, all of them astonished, made known to the king what had been said by the One of Wondrous Rays.
Then that king, hearing this speech of the expounders of the Veda, attained the highest joy, and the wise one said, "So be it."
The king asked of the blessed Vibhāvasu a bride-price: "Let your perpetual presence be here, O One of Wondrous Rays." And the blessed Agni answered the king, "So be it."
Thus even now the presence of Vibhāvasu abides in Māhiṣmatī; for it was seen by Sahadeva when he was conquering the quarters in that day.
Then King Duryodhana, having adorned the maiden in unworn garments, gave her to the great-souled Purifier.
And Agni received that princess Sudarśanā by the rite ordained in the Veda, as he receives the stream of wealth in the sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Pleased with her beauty, her conduct, her lineage, her form, and her grace, Agni was filled with delight and placed an embryo within her.
In her was born a son, by name Sudarśana, son of Agni; while still a child he mastered all the eternal sacred lore.
Now there was a king named Oghavān, grandfather of Nṛga; and to him belonged a daughter, Oghavatī, and a son named Ogharatha.
That daughter Oghavatī, of divine beauty, Oghavān himself gave in marriage to the learned Sudarśana, to be his wife.
Sudarśana, devoted to the householder's order of life, dwelt with her in Kurukṣetra, O king, together with Oghavatī.
"As a householder I shall conquer Death"—so, O lord, that wise one of blazing splendour made his vow, O ruler of men.
Then, O king, the son of the Purifier said to that Oghavatī: "Nothing contrary to a guest's wish must ever be done by you."
"By whatever means a guest may be satisfied, by that you must always satisfy him—even by the giving of your own self; let there be no hesitation in you."
"This vow forever turns within my heart; for householders, O fair-hipped one, there is nothing higher than the guest."
"If my word is your standard, O fair-thighed and lovely one, then hold this saying ever in your heart with a steady mind."
"Whether I have gone forth, O auspicious one, or am near at hand, O blameless lady, no guest of yours must be slighted—if indeed I am your standard."
To him Oghavatī, with restrained mind and palms joined at her brow, replied: "There is nothing whatsoever, set by your word, that I will leave undone."
But Death, O king, ever seeking a weak point, then followed close behind Sudarśana as he strove to conquer him there within his house.
Now when that son of Agni, Sudarśana, had gone out for firewood, a guest, a glorious brahmin, then said to Oghavatī:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I wish hospitality given me by you this day, O lady of fairest hue, if the dharma approved for the householder's order is your standard."
Thus addressed by that brahmin, the renowned princess received him by the rite ordained in the Veda, O ruler of men.
Having given a seat and water for the feet to that twice-born one, Oghavatī said to the brahmin: "What is your need? What shall I give you?"
Then the brahmin said to her, the princess Sudarśanā: "My need is of you yourself, O auspicious one; do this without any misgiving."
"If the dharma approved for the householder's order is your standard, O queen, then by the giving of your own self you ought to do me this pleasure."
Though pressed by the princess with other desirable offerings, that brahmin chose from her no boon but the giving of her own self.
But the princess, recalling from the first her husband's word, said to that bull among the twice-born, abashed, "So be it."
Then that brahmin sage and she, remembering the word of her husband, who longed to keep the householder's order, withdrew together into privacy.
Then the son of the Purifier, having gathered the firewood, drew near, attended ever by Death of fearsome aspect, as though by a kinsman.
Then, having come to the hermitage, the son of the Purifier called out to Oghavatī again and again, "Where are you? Where have you gone?"
But she gave no answer then to her husband, that faithful wife, devoted to her lord, having been touched by the two hands of that brahmin.
Thinking "I am defiled," and ashamed before her husband, the virtuous one kept silent and said nothing at all.
Then Sudarśana spoke this to her once more: "Where is that virtuous one? Where has she gone? What is dearer to me than she?"
"Devoted to her lord, truthful in nature, ever delighting in uprightness—why does she not come forth to meet me today, smiling as of old?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the brahmin, standing within the leaf-hut, answered Sudarśana: "Know that a guest has arrived, O son of the Purifier, and that I am a brahmin."
"I was entreated by this wife of yours, O excellent one, with this and that mark of honour due to a guest; firm is her mind in uprightness."
"By this observance does this fair-faced one honour me; what is fitting here today, that you ought now to declare."
And Death, a heavy mallet in his hand, attended close upon him, thinking, "Should he here fall short of his vow, I shall slay him."
But Sudarśana, in mind, in deed, in glance, and in word free of jealousy and free of wrath, smiling, spoke thus:
"Let your union be a joy, O foremost of brahmins, for my delight is supreme; the householder's highest dharma is the honouring of a guest who has come."
"The householder from whose house an honoured guest departs satisfied—no dharma higher than this, so the wise declare."
"My life-breaths, my wife, and whatever other wealth there is—all this is to be given by me to guests: such is the vow I have taken."
"Without any doubt has this word of mine been uttered to you; by that truth, O brahmin, I myself take hold of my own self."
"Earth, air, ether, the waters, and fire as the fifth; intellect, self, mind, time, and the quarters of space—these are the ten witnesses."
"For these, abiding within the bodies of embodied beings, ever behold the deeds of men, both good and ill, O best of the upholders of dharma."
"As surely as this speech uttered by me this day is no falsehood, by that truth let the gods either protect me or consume me."
Then a sound arose in all the quarters, O descendant of Bharata, again and again: "It is true! This is no falsehood!"—on every side.
Then from that leaf-hut the brahmin came forth, filling sky and earth with his form, like the wind upraised.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With a voice schooled in the sacred chants, the brahmin made the three worlds resound, and, addressing that knower of dharma first by name, said to him:
"I am Dharma—blessing upon you! I have come to test you, O blameless one; and knowing your truth, my delight in you is supreme."
"And Death, who follows you—ever seeking a weak point in you—has been conquered by you and brought under your sway by your steadfastness."
"And there is no power in the three worlds in anyone, O best of men, even to look upon this virtuous wife of yours, devoted to her lord."
"Guarded by your virtues and by her own virtues as a faithful wife, she is inviolable; whatever she should declare, that shall come to pass and not otherwise."
"For she, endowed with her own austerity and an expounder of the sacred lore, shall become the noblest of rivers, for the purification of the world."
"With one half she shall be the river named Oghavatī, and with the other half, in body, the greatly fortunate one shall follow you; for the power of yoga stands within her command."
"And together with her you shall go to the worlds won by austerity, those everlasting and eternal worlds whence one returns no more."
With this very body you shall win the worlds; Death has been conquered by you, and supreme is the sovereignty that is yours.
By your own valor you have transcended the five elements and the mind-born one; and by this dharma of the householder both desire and anger have been conquered by you.
Attachment and passion, sloth, delusion, and sheer malice—all these, O king, have been wholly vanquished through the devoted service of your princess-wife.
Bhīṣma said: Then the lord Resolve, taking hold of a most excellent chariot yoked with a thousand white steeds, departed to that place.
Death and the self and the worlds were conquered, and the five elements, intellect, time, mind, and ether, and likewise desire and anger as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Therefore, for one established in the householder's order, there is verily no other deity than the guest, O tiger among men—ponder this in your mind.
When a guest, having been honored, dwells in his mind upon a man's welfare, the wise declare that not even by a hundred sacrifices is its equal attained.
But whoever, on receiving a worthy guest rich in virtue, fails to honor him—that unhonored guest, by departing, makes away with the host's store of merit.
This unsurpassed tale has been told to you by me, my son—how Death was vanquished of old by a householder.
This excellent tale brings prosperity, fame, and long life; it should be reflected upon by one who wishes for well-being, for it wipes away all evil conduct.
That learned man who would recite this day after day, O Bhārata—the deeds of Sudarśana—would attain the holy worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: If brahmanhood is hard to attain by the three varṇas, O lord of men, how was it attained, O great king, by a great-souled kṣatriya?
By Viśvāmitra, O righteous one, brahmanhood was attained, O bull among men; I wish to hear of this truly—tell it to me, grandsire.
For by him of boundless valor the hundred sons of the great-souled Vasiṣṭha were slain in an instant by the power of his austerity, O great-grandsire.
And many sorcerers and rākṣasas of fierce energy, like Time the destroyer, were created by him whose body was possessed by wrath.
And the great lineage of Kuśika, thronged with a hundred brahmin-sages, was established in this world of men by the learned one praised among brahmins.
And Śunaḥśepa, the son of Ṛcīka, of great austerity, who had been reduced to the state of a sacrificial victim, was set free from the great sacrifice.
At the sacrifice of Hariścandra, having gratified the gods by his own splendor, he came to be a son of the wise Viśvāmitra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When the five hundred sons did not salute their eldest, Devarāta, O lord of men, they were cursed and reduced to the condition of dog-cookers.
Triśaṅku the Ikṣvāku, forsaken by his kinsmen, was borne lovingly to heaven head-downward, abiding in the southern quarter.
The broad river of Viśvāmitra, frequented by royal sages, the auspicious and holy Kauśikī, is resorted to by hosts of brahmin-sages.
And the apsaras named Rambhā of the five tresses, highly esteemed, who came to obstruct his austerity, was by his curse turned into stone.
And likewise, in fear of him of old, Vasiṣṭha bound himself and plunged into the water, but, his fetters undone, he rose up again.
From that time onward the holy great river became known as Vipāśā, by reason of that deed of the great-souled Vasiṣṭha.
And by whom the lord Skanda, leader of the host of the gods, was praised with hymns and became glad of heart, and released him from a curse.
And he who blazes ever in the midst of Dhruva, son of Uttānapāda, and of the brahmin-sages, abiding in the northern quarter.
These deeds of his, and others too, O Kaurava—done by a kṣatriya—it is from this that my curiosity has arisen.
What is this? Tell me truly, O bull of the Bhāratas: without taking on another body, how did he become a brahmin?
All this you ought to recount to me truly, O king; and as the truth of Mataṅga was, so too tell me this.
With reason did Mataṅga fail to attain brahmanhood, O bull of the Bhāratas; for, born in the womb of a caṇḍāla, how could he attain brahmanhood?
Bhīṣma said: Let it be heard truly, O Pārtha, how of old Viśvāmitra attained to brahmanhood, my son, and likewise to the state of a brahmin-sage.
In the lineage of Bharata there was a king named Ajamīḍha, O best of the Bhāratas, a performer of sacrifices, foremost among upholders of dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His son was the great lord of men named Jahnu, whose daughter the great-souled Gaṅgā became.
His son, of equal virtues, was the greatly renowned Sindhudvīpa; and from Sindhudvīpa came the royal sage Balākāśva of great might.
His son was Vallabha, like another Dharma made manifest; his son was Kuśika, equal in splendor to the thousand-eyed Indra.
The illustrious son of Kuśika was the lord of men named Gādhi; that mighty-armed one, being without a son, went to dwell in the forest.
To him as he dwelt in the forest a daughter was born, a maiden named Satyavatī, unmatched in beauty upon the earth.
Her the illustrious lord of the Bhṛgu line, the son of Cyavana, renowned as Ṛcīka, established in vast austerity, sought in marriage.
But Gādhi, crusher of foes, did not give her to that great-souled Ṛcīka, deeming him to be poor.
Having refused him, that best of kings said to him as he was departing again: "Let a bride-price be given to me; then shall you wed my daughter."
Ṛcīka said: What bride-price shall I give to you, O lord of kings, O sovereign, for your daughter? Speak freely; let there be no hesitation of reckoning in you.
Gādhi said: Of horses bright as the moon's rays, swift as the wind, dark in one ear, give me a thousand, O Bhārgava.
Bhīṣma said: Then that tiger of the Bhṛgus, the lord, son of Cyavana, addressed the god Varuṇa, the Āditya, lord of the waters:
"Of horses dark in one ear, with the luster of the moon, swift as the wind—a thousand I beg of you, O best of the gods."
"So be it," said the god Varuṇa, the Āditya, to that best of the Bhṛgus: "Wherever you desire, there shall the steeds arise."
No sooner had Ṛcīka meditated upon them than a thousand horses with the luster of the moon, of vast vigor, rose up from the waters of the Gaṅgā.
That excellent bank of the Gaṅgā, not far from Kānyakubja, men call even to this day the Ford of Horses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, my son, Ṛcīka, foremost among those who murmur prayers, gladly gave that fair thousand of horses to Gādhi as the bride-price.
Then king Gādhi, astonished and also fearful of a curse, adorned the maiden and gave her to the son of Bhṛgu.
That best of brahmin-sages took her hand according to the rite, and she, having gained him for her husband, attained the highest joy.
And the brahmin-sage was well pleased with her conduct, O Bhārata, and offered that fair-complexioned woman the granting of a boon.
That maiden told all of it to her mother, O best of kings; then the mother said to her daughter, whose face was somewhat downcast:
"To me also, my daughter, your husband ought to show favor; that one of great austerity is able to grant offspring."
Then she went in haste and reported it all—what her mother wished to be done, O king—and Ṛcīka thereupon said to her:
"You and she shall each bring forth virtuous offspring, O blessed one; let not the wish of your mother turn out otherwise."
"And to you, O fair one, shall be born a son praised for his virtues, illustrious, the continuer of our line; and your brother too shall be the founder of a line."
"And bathed after your season, she shall embrace an aśvattha tree and you an udumbara tree, O blessed one; thereby you both shall obtain what you desire."
"And these two oblations of rice, hallowed by sacred formulas, O you of bright smile—you and she shall partake of them, and then you both shall obtain sons."
Then Satyavatī, gladdened, spoke in reply to her mother and told her what Ṛcīka had said, and of the two oblations.
Then the mother spoke thus to her daughter Satyavatī: "My daughter, since I take refuge with bowed head, do as I bid you."
"This oblation, hallowed with sacred formulas, which has been given to you by your husband—give it to me, and take you mine."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And let us two also make an exchange of the trees, O you of bright smile, if the word of your mother is of any authority, O blameless one."
"Surely whatever the holy one has appointed in this matter shall come to pass; therefore my desire is set upon your oblation and upon your tree, O slender-waisted one. Consider only thus: how may your brother prove the more excellent."
And thus the mother and Satyavatī both did, and then both of them conceived, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
And that great sage, the best of the Bhṛgus, seeing his wife with child, said to Satyavatī, troubled in mind:
"Plainly the oblation has been partaken of by you in exchange, and plainly an exchange has been made by you with regard to the tree as well, O fair one."
"For all the brahmin power I had placed in your oblation, and the whole of the kṣatriya might I had placed in hers."
"You were to bring forth a brahmin of virtues renowned throughout the three worlds, and she a kṣatriya of surpassing kind; for this end was this done by me."
"But since the exchange has been made by you and likewise by your mother, therefore your mother shall bring forth the best of brahmins."
"But you, O gentle one, shall bring forth a kṣatriya of fierce deeds; for what you did out of love for your mother was not well done, O proud lady."
Hearing this, the fair-complexioned Satyavatī, scorched with grief, fell to the ground, O king, like a lovely creeper cut through.
And regaining her senses and bowing down with her head, the wife, the daughter of Gādhi, said to her husband, that bull among brahmins:
"As your wife implores you, O best of the knowers of Brahman, show favor, O brahmin-sage: let no kṣatriya be my son."
"Let my grandson, if you will, be one of fierce deeds, but let not my son be such, O brahmin: let this boon be granted to me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"So be it," said the one of mighty austerity to his wife; and then she brought forth a fair son, Jamadagni.
And the renowned wife of Gādhi brought forth Viśvāmitra, by the power of the sage, O lord of kings—a brahmin-sage, an expounder of Brahman.
Thus Viśvāmitra of great austerity, though a kṣatriya, attained to brahmanhood, and so became the founder of a brahmin lineage.
His sons were great-souled, increasers of the brahmin line, ascetics, knowers of Brahman, and founders of gotras as well.
The lord Madhucchandas, and the valiant Devarāta, and Akṣīṇa, and Śakunta, Babhru, and Kālapatha likewise;
And the renowned Yājñavalkya, and Sthūṇa of great vows, Ulūka and Yamadūta, and likewise the sage Saindhavāyana.
There was the venerable Karṇajaṅgha, and Gālava the great sage, the seer renowned as Vajra, and Śālaṅkāyana too.
Lālāṭya and Nārada, and likewise Kūrcamukha as he is remembered, Vāduli and Musala, and Rakṣogrīva as well.
Aṅghrika and Naikabhṛt, Śilāyūpa, Sītā, Śuci, Cakraka, Mārutantavya, Vātaghna, and then Aśvalāyana.
Śyāmāyana, and Gārgya, Jābāli, and Suśruta likewise, then Kārīṣi and Saṃśrutya, and the Parapauravatantavas.
The great sage Kapila, and the seer Tārakāyana, and likewise Upagahana, and the seer Arjunāyana.
Mārgamitri, Hiraṇyākṣa, Jaṅghāri, Babhruvāhana, Sūti, Vibhūti, and Sūta, and Suraṅga too, indeed.
Ārāddhi and Nāmaya, and Cāmpeya and Ujjayana likewise, Navatantu, Bakanakha, and Śayonarati as well.
Śayoruha, Cārumatsya, Śirīṣī, and then Gārdabhi, Ujjayoni, Adāpekṣī, and Nāradī the great sage — all these are the sons of Viśvāmitra, sages and expounders of the Veda.
Therefore, O king, this Viśvāmitra of mighty austerities is no kṣatriya; this supreme brahminhood was implanted in him by Ṛcīka, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
All this I have told you in truth, O bull of the Bhāratas — the birth of Viśvāmitra, whose splendor was that of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And wherever a doubt may yet arise in you, O best of kings, there ask of me, and I shall sever your uncertainties.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I wish to hear in full the virtues of the dharma of compassion and of the devoted person; tell me that, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: In the realm of the king of Kāśi, a hunter, having set out from the villages and taken a poisoned arrow, went hunting for game.
There in the great forest, the hunter, greedy for meat, having seen a deer not far off, fitted his arrow to the bow.
By that man of irresistible weapon, whose shaft swerved from its mark, a great forest tree was struck as he sought to slay the deer there.
That tree, overborne by the arrow smeared with keen poison, shed its fruits and leaves and withered away.
In that tree, brought to such a state, a parrot long dwelling in its hollows did not abandon his abode, out of devotion to that lord of the forest.
Going nowhere, taking no food, weary, his voice grown faint, that grateful and righteous bird withered away together with the tree.
Learning of that noble bird of great spirit, whose conduct surpassed the human and who shared alike in joy and sorrow with the tree, the Chastiser of Pāka was amazed.
Then Śakra fell to pondering: How is it that this bird, born in the brute creation, has taken his stand on a compassion scarcely to be conceived of there?
Yet, thought Vāsava, there is nothing strange in this; for among all living beings here, everything may be seen everywhere.
Then Śakra, having assumed a human form in the guise of a brāhmaṇa, descended to the earth and spoke to that bird.
O parrot, best of birds, the daughter of Dakṣa has been blessed with worthy offspring through you; I ask you — why do you not forsake this withered tree?
Thus questioned, the parrot, bowing to him with his head, replied: Welcome to the king of the gods, whom I have recognized through my austerity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then by the Thousand-eyed one it was said, "Well done, well done! Ah, what discernment!" — and thus was the bird honored for his austerity.
Though he well knew the bird's attainment, the Slayer of Bala questioned that parrot of holy deeds and supreme righteousness.
"Leafless, fruitless, withered, no refuge for birds — why do you cling to this tree, when this forest is so vast?
Many other trees, their hollows shaded with leaves, fair and offering ample range, are to be found in this great forest.
Reflect with wisdom, O steadfast one: this tree's life is spent, its strength is gone, its sap is drained, its splendor destroyed — forsake this perishing tree."
Hearing this spoken by Śakra, the righteous parrot, sighing long and deeply, in distress uttered these words:
"The decrees of the gods are not to be transgressed, O lord of Śacī; where one came to be, there one abides — understand this, O sovereign of the gods.
In this tree I was born, and endowed with good qualities; in my infancy I was sheltered here and never assailed by enemies.
Why, O sinless one, do you make my compassion come to nothing — mine, who am devoted to kindness, attached and faithful to this tree?
For compassion is the great mark of the dharma of the good, and the compassion of the good ever bestows delight.
You yourself are asked by all the gods to resolve their doubts about dharma; therefore, O god, you stand established in sovereignty over the gods.
You ought not, O Thousand-eyed one, to make me abandon this out of my devotion; how should I now forsake this tree on which I have lived and which once sustained me?"
Gladdened by his gentle words and pleased by his compassion, the Chastiser of Pāka spoke to that parrot who knew dharma:
"Choose a boon!" — and then the parrot, ever devoted to compassion, chose as his boon the restoration of that tree.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Śakra, knowing that firm wealth of character in the parrot, was pleased, and at once sprinkled the tree with the nectar of immortality.
Then, through the parrot's steadfast devotion, that tree regained its fruits, its leaves, its lovely branches, and its splendor.
And the parrot, by that deed wrought of compassion, O great king, at the end of his life attained to the same world as Śakra.
Even so, O lord of men, one who takes refuge with a devoted being attains the fulfillment of all his aims, as the tree did by gaining the parrot.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O grandfather, greatly wise, versed in all the scriptures — between fate and human effort, which would be the more excellent?
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount this ancient tale, the dialogue of Vasiṣṭha and Brahmā, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
"Of the two works, the divine and the human, which is the better?" — thus, of old, the venerable Vasiṣṭha questioned the Grandfather.
Then, O king, the lotus-born Grandfather, god of gods, spoke a sweet utterance, weighty in meaning and adorned with reasons:
"Nothing is born without a seed, nor is there fruit apart from the seed; from seed springs seed, and from seed alone, it is taught, comes fruit.
Whatever seed the farmer sows when he comes upon a field, whether in good soil or bad, just such a fruit does he obtain.
As a field sown without seed proves fruitless, so without human effort fate does not bear fruit.
Human effort is declared to be the field, and fate the seed; from the union of field and seed the crop thereby flourishes.
The doer himself reaps the ripening fruit of his deed; this is plainly seen in the world, both of what is done and of what is left undone.
From a good deed comes happiness, from an evil deed sorrow; what is done is everywhere obtained, what is not done is nowhere enjoyed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The man of action everywhere wins standing, even when fortune has wounded him; the idle and fallen man earns only a sprinkling of salt upon his wound.
By austerity beauty and good fortune, and jewels of many kinds — all is gained by effort, not by fate, by one whose self is unprepared.
Likewise heaven, and enjoyment, and whatever consummation is desired — all this is attained here through human effort exerted.
The luminaries, the gods, the nāgas, the yakṣas, the moon, the sun, the winds — all, through human effort, have passed from the human state to godhood.
Wealth, or a circle of friends, or lordship attended by noble birth, and even prosperity — all are hard for the idle to come by and enjoy.
By purity the brāhmaṇa wins prosperity, the kṣatriya by valor, the vaiśya by effort, and the śūdra by service.
Riches do not resort to the ungiving, nor to the impotent, nor to the inactive, nor to the slothful, nor to the cowardly, nor to one without austerity.
He by whom the three worlds were created, the daityas and all the gods — that very lord Viṣṇu performs austerity upon the ocean.
If the fruit of one's own deed did not exist, all action would be fruitless; the world, leaning upon fate alone, would grow indifferent — but it is not so.
He who, without doing the human work, follows after fate, toils in vain, like a woman who has gained an impotent husband.
There is not so much peril in the human world, in things good and ill, as there is in the world of the gods, where peril arises from a small cause.
When human effort is made, fate follows after it; fate, where nothing is done, can give nothing to anyone.
When even among the gods their stations are seen to be impermanent, how shall fate, without action, endure or make anything endure?
The gods in this world do not engage in anyone's affairs; rather, fearing their own overthrow, they breed fierce contention.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Between the seers and the gods there is ever strife; for by whose word could there be a no-fate, since from these does fate proceed?
And how does its origin come about, in the manner that fate sets in motion? Thus even in the world of the gods many deceptions are met with.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, the self alone the foe of the self; and the self alone is the witness of the self, of what is done and what is left undone.
Something done and something marred alike comes to fruition when the deed is performed; but an evil deed laid upon a good one does not come duly to pass.
Merit is the refuge of the gods; all is won through meritorious acts. Against a man whose nature is meritorious, what will fate avail to do?
Of old Yayāti, undone, cast down, fallen to the earth, was raised again to heaven by his daughters' sons through their meritorious deeds.
And the royal sage Purūravas, addressed of old by the brāhmaṇas, renowned as Aila, that lord of the earth attained to heaven.
The lord of Kosala, honored by sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice — Saudāsa, by the curse of a great seer, came to the state of a man-eater.
Aśvatthāman and Rāma, sons of sages and bearers of the bow, do not go to the world of heaven, even by their good deeds done here.
Vasu, having sacrificed with a hundred sacrifices, like a second Vāsava, by a single false utterance descended to the floor of the netherworld.
Bali, son of Virocana, bound by the gods with the noose of dharma, was made to lie in Pātāla through the effort of Viṣṇu.
Janamejaya, setting Śakra's foot aside, set forth — having wrought the slaying of brāhmaṇa women, why was he not restrained by fate?
The brāhmaṇa sage Vaiśaṃpāyana, having unknowingly slain a brāhmaṇa and been touched by the killing of a child — why was he not held back by fate?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the royal sage Nṛga, of old, by a false gift of a cow to brāhmaṇas at a great sacrifice, came to the state of a lizard.
And the royal sage Dhundhumāra grew old amid his very sacrifices; abandoning the gifts of his affection, he slept on at Girivraja.
The kingdom of the Pāṇḍavas was wrested away by the mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and won back again — not by fate, but by the strength of their own arms.
The sages, devoted to austerity and self-restraint, firm in their vows — do they hurl their curses by the power of fate, or rather by their own deeds?
A man may attain in this world all that is most hard to win, yet cast it away through sin; once fallen into greed and delusion, fate cannot save him.
As fire, though small, when fanned by the wind grows great, so fate, when joined to action, prospers and increases well.
As a lamp, when its oil is spent, fades and dies away, so fate, when one's works are exhausted, fades and dies away.
Though a man here win a vast flood of wealth, enjoyments, and women, if he is bereft of action he has not the power to enjoy them; and even riches well-secured and guarded by the gods, ample and ready to be spent, men gain hold of only through their own deeds.
The world of the gods surpasses the world of men by its far greater abundance; beside the dwellings of the immortals, the houses of mortals seem like haunts of the burial-ground — yet for the man of evil deeds fate bears no fruit in the world of the living.
Human effort leads astray a man who goes the wrong path — fate has no sovereign power; like a weighty teacher, foremost action carries fate along. Unharmed and unbowed, fate is steered at will by accumulated human effort, here and everywhere.
All this I have now declared to you, O best of sages — the fruit of human effort, ever beheld and known in its truth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By rousing fate through action duly undertaken, and by deeds performed according to the ordinance, a man may attain the road to heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O bull of the Bhāratas, of all good deeds, O foremost of the great, declare to me, who ask of you, their fruits.
Bhīṣma said: Hear, Yudhiṣṭhira, the secret of the seers — by what means is attained, in the life after death, the long-desired goal.
With whatever body a man performs whatever deed, with that same body he enjoys its several fruits.
In whatever state a man does good or evil, in that same state he tastes it, birth after birth.
The deed once done is never lost; here the five senses are ever its witnesses, and the self is the sixth, likewise eternal.
Let a man give his eye, give his mind, and give kindly truthful speech; let him walk behind his guest and wait upon him — that is a sacrifice with fivefold offering.
He who, without grudging, gives food upon the road to a weary stranger never seen before — great is the fruit of his merit.
For those who lie upon the bare ground there shall be houses and couches; for those clad in rags and bark-cloth, garments and ornaments.
For the man of disciplined soul, rich in austerity, who sleeps beside his sacred fires, there shall be mounts, seats, and chariots, and the estate of royalty, it is said.
From the renouncing of savory tastes good fortune follows; from the renouncing of meat a man gains cattle and sons.
He who hangs head downward, who dwells immersed in water, and who ever sleeps alone — he shall attain the goal of his desire.
Water for the feet, a seat, a lamp, food, and shelter — let him give these in honor of his guest: that too is a sacrifice with fivefold offering.
For him who keeps the hero's posture, the hero's bed, and the hero's station, the worlds are imperishable and lead to every desire fulfilled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By giving a man wins wealth, by silence command, O lord of peoples; by austerity enjoyments, and by chastity long life.
Beauty, sovereignty, and health are the fruit that non-violence brings; for those who eat fruits and roots, a kingdom; and heaven for those who eat but leaves.
From fasting unto death comes a kingdom, and happiness everywhere, it is said; by truth a man wins heaven, and by consecration a noble birth.
By the vow of eating only herbs a man becomes rich in cattle; eating only grass, he goes to heaven. Women who bathe at the three pressings and drink only the wind win the merit of a sacrifice.
The twice-born who lives on water alone, ever tending his sacred fire and duly consecrated, who masters the desert wilderness, gains a kingdom; and by total fasting, the summit of heaven.
He who keeps fasting, consecration, and the ritual bathing, O king, for twelve years, surpasses even the reward of the hero's station.
Having studied all the Vedas, a man is at once released from sorrow; practicing the dharma of the mind, he attains the world of heaven.
That craving which the foolish cannot abandon, which does not age though the man ages, that disease which lasts until the breath departs — happy is he who casts it off.
As among a thousand cows the calf finds its own mother, so the deed once done in the past follows after its doer.
As flowers and fruits, unbidden, do not pass beyond their season, so the deed done in the past comes at its appointed time.
As a man grows old, his hair grows old; his teeth grow old as he grows old; his eyes and ears grow old — yet craving alone never grows old.
By that whereby he pleases his father, Prajāpati is pleased; by that whereby he pleases his mother, the Earth is honored; by that whereby he pleases his teacher, the Brahman itself is worshipped.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who honors these three has honored all his duties; but he who honors them not — all his rites are without fruit.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing those words of Bhīṣma, the bulls of the Kurus were filled with wonder, their hearts gladdened, and they were then well content.
What is lost when the sacred verse is uttered in vain, what is lost when the Soma is pressed in vain, what is lost when the oblation is poured into the fire in vain — all that is lost when speech itself is spoken in vain.
Thus what was declared by the seer I have now told, O mighty one, concerning the gaining of the fruits of good and evil. What more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who are to be worshipped, who are to be saluted, to whom do you bow, O Bhārata? Tell me all this, O king — those for whom you yearn.
Even in the midst of the gravest peril, where your mind ever turns — in all this world of men, and there beyond as well as here.
Bhīṣma said: I yearn for those twice-born ones whose highest wealth is the sacred Brahman, whose heaven rests on their own faith, won by austerity and the study of scripture.
Those whose elders and whose young alike bear up the yoke of their fathers and forefathers and do not falter — for them indeed I yearn.
Of those well-trained in the branches of knowledge, self-controlled, gentle of speech, endowed with learning and good conduct, ever knowing the sacred syllable, the virtuous —
As they speak in the assemblies, their voices, like the gathered calls of swans, are auspicious in form, lovely, and resonant as the celestial thunderclouds —
Their well-uttered words are heard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, by the attentive king, bringing happiness both here and in the world hereafter.
And those who are their listeners, ever honored in the assembly, endowed with the virtue of discernment — for them too I yearn.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who, pure and diligent, give well-prepared, clean, and wholesome food to the brāhmaṇas for their full satisfaction, O Yudhiṣṭhira — and who do so unceasingly, O king — for them too I yearn.
It is possible to fight in battle, but not to give without grudging; the brave and valiant exist by the hundreds in this world, Yudhiṣṭhira; but among them all, when they are counted, the hero of giving stands supreme.
Blessed should I be, O gentle one, were I born again even as a humble brāhmaṇa, sprung from a noble line, set upon the path of dharma, devoted to austerity and learning.
There is none in this world dearer to me than you, O joy of Pāṇḍu; yet dearer to me than you are the brāhmaṇas, O bull of the Bhāratas.
As the brāhmaṇas are dearer to me than you, O foremost of the Kurus — by that truth may I go to those worlds where Śaṃtanu dwells.
Not my own father was dearer to me than the brāhmaṇas, nor my father's father, nor any of my other kinsmen and friends.
For no offense of mine against the brāhmaṇas is known here, be it small or great — as is known to those of righteous deeds.
By deed, by thought, or by word, O scorcher of foes, whatever I have done toward the brāhmaṇas — for that I feel no torment today.
"Devoted to the brāhmaṇas" — so they call me, and by those words I am made content; this very thing is held the highest of all things that purify.
I behold the stainless, pure worlds attained by those devoted to the brāhmaṇas; thither, my son, must I go, whether soon or after long.
As the dharma of women in the world rests upon the husband, O Yudhiṣṭhira — he their god, he their refuge, and no other — so for the kṣatriya are the twice-born.
A kṣatriya of a hundred years and a brāhmaṇa of ten are to be regarded as father and son — and of the two, the brāhmaṇa is the father.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As a woman, in the absence of a husband, takes her husband's brother for husband, so the Earth, lacking a brāhmaṇa, takes the kṣatriya for her lord.
And so the brāhmaṇas are to be protected as one's sons, waited upon as one's teachers, and tended as the sacred fire, O best of the Kurus.
Upright, virtuous, true in their conduct, devoted to the good of all beings — yet, when angered, like venomous serpents — such twice-born ones a man should ever serve with care.
One should ever stand in dread of their fiery energy and their austerity, O Yudhiṣṭhira; both of these are to be guarded against — their splendor and likewise their penance.
In both of these the resolve to act is swift indeed; for when angered, O great king, the brāhmaṇas who are rich in austerity can slay.
Whatever is given to a brāhmaṇa who is free of anger returns in twofold measure; let a man, when giving, keep no remainder back, but give without leaving a remnant on either side.
As a herdsman, staff in hand, stands ever steadfast over his cattle, so should the kṣatriya guard the brāhmaṇas and the sacred Brahman.
As a father guards his sons, so should you guard the brāhmaṇas radiant with the splendor of the Brahman; and look into their households, whether their livelihood holds here.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Those in the world who, having promised a gift to the brāhmaṇas, give it not through delusion, O grandsire — what do they become, O most wise?
Tell me this truly, the law of it, O best of the upholders of dharma — those evil-souled men who, having promised, do not give.
Bhīṣma said: He who, having promised little or much, does not give — all his hopes are destroyed, like the fruit of offspring in a eunuch.
From the night that wretch is born to the night that he perishes, whatever good he has done in that interval, O Bhārata, and whatever oblation he has offered — all of it is undone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
On this the people learned in the law-books have spoken this saying — hear it, O best of the Bhāratas, with a mind most attentive.
And the people learned in the law-books cite this also: by a thousand horses with dark ears that man is released.
On this very matter they relate an ancient tale, the converse of the jackal and the monkey, O Bhārata.
The two had once been friends in their state as men, O scorcher of foes, but had passed into other births — the one a jackal, the other a monkey.
Then, seeing the jackal devouring the dead in the midst of the burning-ground, the monkey, recalling their former birth, spoke to him.
What grievous and most terrible deed did you commit of old, that here in the burning-ground you eat the rotting, loathsome corpses?
Thus addressed, the jackal answered the monkey then: "Having made a promise to a brāhmaṇa, I did not fulfill it."
"For that I have come into this sinful birth, O leaping one; therefore, hungering, I eat such food as this."
Thus, O king, I heard this from the brāhmaṇa as he spoke, that knower of dharma reciting the holy and ancient tale.
And moreover, O lord of peoples, O Pāṇḍava, I once heard this too from Kṛṣṇa, who long ago recited it concerning a brāhmaṇa.
And just so the brāhmaṇas ever instruct me: once a promise is made, the gift must be given; never should the brāhmaṇas' hope be left unfulfilled.
For a brāhmaṇa, O lord of the earth, once his hope has been kindled, is reckoned to be like a well-fed, blazing fire.
Whomever he, enraged, fixes his gaze upon—his hope once roused—him, O king, he would consume utterly, as an inexhaustible fire devours dry brushwood.
Yet that same brāhmaṇa, when contented, gives thanks with his words, and becomes for that man's realm like a healing medicine, O Bhārata.
Sons and grandsons, cattle and kinsmen, ministers too, the city and the countryside—all these he causes to flourish, like a peace devoutly sought.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For this supreme splendor of the brāhmaṇa is seen here on earth, like that of the thousand-rayed Sun upon the face of the world.
Therefore, once a promise is made, the gift must indeed be given, Yudhiṣṭhira, if one wishes to attain a fair birth, O best of the Bhāratas.
For by what is given to a brāhmaṇa, the unsurpassed heaven can surely be won, and won abundantly; for giving is a mighty act.
By what is given here the gods live, and the ancestors likewise; therefore the wise man should bestow his gifts upon the brāhmaṇas.
For the brāhmaṇa, O best of the Bhāratas, is called a great holy ford; at no fitting hour should a brāhmaṇa depart unhonored.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When one, out of the goodwill of friendship, gives instruction to a man of lower birth, O royal sage—does fault arise for him or not?
This I wish to have explained in truth, O grandfather; for subtle is the course of dharma, wherein men go astray.
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall relate to you, O king; listen as it has come down to us, even as I heard it long ago from the speech of the sages.
Instruction should not be given to any man of base birth; a grave fault is declared to fall upon the teacher for such instruction.
Hear from me this illustration, O king, O bull of the Bhāratas—of the offense of ill-spoken words, Yudhiṣṭhira—of what came to pass of old at a brahmanic hermitage upon the fair flank of the Himavat.
There stood a holy hermitage, set amid clusters of many kinds of trees, thick with shrubs and creepers, frequented by deer and birds.
Resounding with siddhas and cāraṇas, lovely, its groves in flower, thronged with many keepers of vows and graced by ascetics.
Crowded too with brāhmaṇas of great fortune, resplendent as the sun and fire, perfect in restraints and vows—with ascetics, O best of the Bhāratas, consecrated, sparing in food, their selves perfected.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Filled with the murmur of Vedic recitation, O bull of the Bhāratas, and frequented by many Vālakhilyas and by men of strict discipline.
There a certain śūdra, summoning his resolve, full of compassion, came to that hermitage and was honored by the ascetics.
And seeing those hosts of sages, godlike and of great might, bearing their manifold vows, he was filled with joy, O Bhārata.
Then his mind turned toward asceticism, O bull of the Bhāratas; and so, clasping his feet, he addressed the head of the community, O Bhārata.
By your grace I wish to practice dharma, O bull among the twice-born; therefore, O blessed one, you ought to instruct me and to set me upon the ascetic's path.
I am of a lower order, O blessed one—a śūdra by birth, O most excellent; I wish to render service. Be gracious to me, who have come to you for refuge.
The head of the community said: It is not possible here for a śūdra to live having taken up the ascetic's emblem. Stay, if such is your mind, and devote yourself to service.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by the sage, that śūdra reflected, O king: "What am I to do in this? My faith in dharma is supreme. So be it—I shall do what is dear to my own soul."
Going far from the hermitage, he built himself a hut of leaves; and there, having set in place an altar, a hallowed ground, and shrines for the deities, O best of the Bhāratas, he abode happily, firm in his vows.
Performing ablutions and observances, and offering the bali-oblation at the shrines, and pouring oblations into the fire, he worshiped the deities as well.
Endowed with resolve and restraint, living on fruit, his senses subdued, ever furnished with the herbs and fruits that lay close at hand.
He honored, in due form, the guests who came to him; and thus a very long span of time passed by for him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then a sage came by chance to his hermitage; and welcoming the seer with words of greeting, he gratified him fully according to rule.
Having exchanged agreeable converse, the seer—of supreme splendor, righteous of soul, his senses controlled—questioned him duly.
Thus, O bull of the Bhāratas, that seer went many times to the śūdra's hermitage, O bull among men, to see the śūdra.
Then the śūdra said to that ascetic, O bull of the Bhāratas: "I shall perform a rite for the ancestors; in this grant me your favor."
"So be it," the brāhmaṇa said to him, O bull of the Bhāratas; and the śūdra, having purified himself, brought water for that seer's feet.
Then darbha grass and wild herbs, O bull of the Bhāratas, and a purifying strainer, a seat, and a grass cushion he brought near.
Then, turning it to the south, when the seer saw the cushion's head laid out the wrong way, contrary to rule, he spoke to him.
"Set its head toward the east, and face the north, being purified." And the śūdra did all that the seer had told him.
As instructed, the discerning man arranged the darbha grass and the rest just so; and the whole rule of offerings to gods and ancestors was told to him by that ascetic.
By the seer he was thus guided in the rite for the ancestors, and he himself stayed firm upon the path of dharma; and when the rite was done, the seer, taking his leave, departed.
Then after a long time that śūdra-ascetic, performing his austerities, met dissolution in the forest; and by that good deed he was reborn, of great radiance, O great king, in a royal lineage of kings.
And likewise that seer, my child, having met his appointed end, was reborn as a brāhmaṇa in the family of a royal chaplain, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Thus the two of them—the śūdra and the sage—were both born there; and growing up in due course, both became skilled in the branches of learning.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the Atharvaveda and the other Veda the seer became well-grounded, accomplished in the practice of ritual and in astronomy he attained the highest mastery; and between the two of them a supreme delight in friendship grew apace.
And when his father had passed away, the prince, having completed the rites of purification, O Bhārata, was anointed king by the subjects; and by the anointed king that seer was anointed as chaplain.
Placing him at his head, the king dwelt happily, O bull of the Bhāratas, ruling his kingdom by dharma and guarding his subjects well.
At the proclaiming of auspicious days, and repeatedly in the rites of dharma, the king, on seeing the chaplain, would smile and even laugh; and thus, O king, many times did he laugh at the chaplain.
But the chaplain, having marked the lord of men do so many times, and seeing him forever smiling, grew filled with resentment.
Then in a solitary place the chaplain, meeting with the king, delighted him with agreeable conversation.
Then that chaplain said to the lord of men, O bull of the Bhāratas: "One boon I desire, to be granted by you, O greatly radiant one."
The king said: A hundred boons would I grant you, how much more a single one, O best of the twice-born; for out of affection and high regard there is nothing I would withhold from you.
The chaplain said: One boon indeed I desire, if you are pleased, O lord of the earth; what you grant, O great king, speak it truly, and let it be no falsehood.
Bhīṣma said: "So be it," the king replied to him, O Yudhiṣṭhira; "if I shall know the answer, I will tell it; but not knowing, I will not speak."
The chaplain said: At the proclaiming of auspicious days, ever in the rites of dharma, and always at the homas for peace—why is it that, looking upon me, you laugh?
My mind is filled with shame at your laughing; adjured by my wish, O king, you ought not to speak otherwise than the truth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There must surely be a cause in this; your laughter is not without reason. My curiosity is very keen—tell me the truth of it.
The king said: Since you have spoken thus, O brāhmaṇa, even what ought not to be told must now of necessity be told. Listen with single mind, O twice-born one.
Learn what came to pass in a former body, O best of the twice-born; I remember my birth, O brāhmaṇa—listen to me attentively.
A śūdra I was of old, an ascetic strictly self-disciplined; and you, O most excellent of the twice-born, were then a seer of fierce austerity.
For then, O brāhmaṇa, out of love and a mind to favor me, you of old gave me instruction in the rite for the ancestors, O sinless one—concerning the grass cushion, the darbha grass, the offering to the gods and the offering to the ancestors, O best of sages.
By this fault of action you were born a chaplain, and I a king, O chief of brāhmaṇas; behold the turning of time! For through the instruction you gave on my account, this fruit has fallen to you.
For this reason, O brāhmaṇa, I laugh at you, O best of the twice-born; not in scorn of you do I laugh, O brāhmaṇa—you are my elder.
At this reversal my heart is grieved, and my mind is sorely pained thereby. I remember our births—for you—and therefore it is that I laugh.
Thus your fierce austerity was undone by the giving of instruction; cast off the office of chaplain and strive again toward a future birth.
Lest from here you fall into another, baser womb, O twice-born; take this wealth, O brāhmaṇa, and become purified in soul, O excellent one.
Bhīṣma said: Then, dismissed by the king, the brāhmaṇa bestowed gifts of many kinds—wealth, land, and villages—upon the brāhmaṇas in every way.
And that best of the twice-born, having performed the penances as prescribed, and having visited the holy fords, and made manifold gifts—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and having given cattle to the brāhmaṇas, that twice-born one became purified in soul; and going back to that very hermitage, he practiced abundant austerity.
Then the brāhmaṇa attained supreme perfection, O best of kings, and became honored among those dwellers of the hermitage.
Thus that seer came to great distress, O best of kings; therefore a brāhmaṇa should not speak instruction to a person of lower order.
A brāhmaṇa should ever shun the giving of such instruction, O king; for in giving instruction the twice-born one would come to distress.
The king should ever seek knowledge by his speech from the best of the twice-born; but to a person of lower order nothing whatever should here be expounded.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas—these three orders are the twice-born; speaking among these, O king, a brāhmaṇa incurs no fault.
Therefore the good should not speak anything in the presence of anyone heedlessly; for subtle is the course of dharma, hard to discern by those whose souls are unperfected.
For this reason the sages, with reverence, undertake vows of silence; from fear of ill-spoken words, O king, they answer nothing at all.
The righteous, endowed with virtues, devoted to truth and uprightness, when stricken by an ill-spoken word, come thereby to evil-doing here.
Instruction should never be given at any time to anyone; for from instruction a brāhmaṇa would incur that sin.
Therefore the wise man who desires dharma should speak only after reflection; for instruction given through truth mixed with falsehood surely brings harm.
When questioned, one should answer only after first weighing the matter and its contrary; and such instruction alone is to be given as leads to the attainment of dharma.
All this I have now declared to you: when instruction is given amiss, great affliction follows; therefore let no one give such instruction anywhere.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In what kind of man, dear sire, or in what kind of women, O bull of the Bhāratas, does Śrī, the lotus-goddess, ever abide? Tell me that, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall relate to you, as I have seen and as I have heard, how Rukmiṇī once questioned Śrī in the presence of the son of Devakī.
Beholding radiant Śrī, lotus-faced, seated in the lap of Nārāyaṇa, the mother of Makaradhvaja, her lovely eyes wide with wonder, questioned her out of curiosity.
Which beings here do you attend upon, and beside which do you abide; and which do you not serve? O beloved of the Lord of the three worlds' creatures, O daughter of the great sage, tell me this truly.
Thus addressed by the goddess in the presence of him whose banner bears Garuḍa, Śrī, moon-faced and serene, spoke these words, sweet in utterance and ravishing to the mind.
I dwell, O fair one, in the man who is truthful, bold, and capable, ever active in his work; I dwell not in the indolent man, nor in the unbeliever, the corrupter of castes, the ingrate, nor in him of broken conduct or cruel conduct, nor in the thief, nor in him who is envious of his teachers.
And those poor in energy, strength, and inner worth, who rejoice and rage at the merest trifle—in such men, O goddess, whose aspirations lie asleep, I do not abide.
He who craves nothing for himself, and he whose inner self is corrupted by his own nature—in such men, O goddess, ever content with little, I never make my dwelling.
I dwell in the righteous of conduct, in the knowers of dharma, in the great-souled, in those who serve their elders, in the self-controlled, in the noble who understand goodness.
Among women I dwell in the patient and the self-controlled, devoted to gods and brāhmaṇas, truthful in conduct, and steadfast in their own nature.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The woman who scatters her household vessels, who acts without reflection, who ever speaks against her husband, who delights in another's house and is without shame—such a woman I forsake.
The fickle, the unclean, the greedy gobbler, her devoid of steadiness, fond of quarrels, overcome by sleep and forever lying abed—such a woman I forsake.
I dwell in women ever truthful, fair to look upon, blessed with good fortune and rich in virtues, faithful to their husbands, of auspicious character and well adorned.
In chariots, in maidens, in ornaments, in sacrifices, in rain-bearing clouds, in blossoming lotus-pools, and in the autumn pathways of the stars, I make my dwelling.
In mountains, in cattle-pens, and in forests, in lakes bright with open water-lilies and lotuses, in rivers loud with the calls of swans and adorned by the cries of cranes.
In rivers graced with broad-banked pools, frequented by ascetics, perfected ones, and brāhmaṇas, abundant in waters churned by lions and elephants, I ever dwell; and ever in the rutting elephant, in the bull, in the king, in the lion-throne, and in the good man.
In that house where the fire-bearer of oblations is fed, where cattle, brāhmaṇas, and the gods are honored, and offerings of flowers are made in due season—in that house I ever take up my dwelling.
In the twice-born ever devoted to their sacred study, in the kṣatriya forever delighting in dharma, in the vaiśya intent on husbandry, and in the śūdra faithfully given to service, I dwell.
But in Nārāyaṇa I dwell single-minded, with my whole being, made as it were his very body; for in him is set the mighty dharma, and there too are devotion to the brāhmaṇas and all that is dear.
It is not with my body that I dwell, O goddess—that I cannot here declare; but the man in whom I dwell in spirit prospers in dharma, in fame, in wealth, and in desire fulfilled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In the union of woman and man, whose pleasure of touch is the greater? This doubt of mine, O king, you ought to resolve aright.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite an ancient tale—how of old enmity arose between Bhaṅgāśvana and Śakra.
Long ago there was a royal sage named Bhaṅgāśvana, exceedingly righteous. Being without a son, O tiger among men, he undertook a sacrifice to obtain offspring.
That mighty royal sage performed the rite called Agniṣṭu, hateful to Indra, which is enjoined among the expiations of mortals for one who desires a son.
But Indra, the glorious lord of the gods, learning of that sacrifice, sought for an opening against that royal sage of disciplined soul.
And after some time, as the king roved out on the hunt, Śakra, judging "this is the opening," cast a bewilderment upon him.
Wandering on a single horse, deluded by Indra, the royal sage could no longer make out the quarters of the sky, and was tormented by hunger and thirst.
Galloping this way and that, afflicted by weariness and thirst, the king beheld a most lovely lake brimming with excellent water; and plunging into the lake, dear son, he let his horse drink.
Then, when the horse had drunk, that best of kings tied it to a tree, and entering the water to bathe, the king attained womanhood.
Seeing himself turned into a woman, that best of kings was abashed, his whole being given over to anxious thought, his senses and mind confounded.
"How shall I mount the horse, how shall I return to the city? I performed the rite called Agniṣṭu, and a hundred sons of my own loins were granted me—
sons born of great strength. What shall I now say of them to my wives, and to the people of city and countryside?"
Softness, slenderness, and timidity—these the sages, who behold the truth and meaning of dharma, have declared the qualities of woman; while exertion, hardness, and valor are the qualities of man.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"My manhood is utterly lost, and womanhood has come upon me by some agency; in this state of womanhood, how can I bring myself to mount the horse again?"
Then with great distress that lord of men mounted the horse and, turned into a woman, returned to the city, dear son—that best of kings.
His sons and wives and servants, and the folk of city and countryside, perceiving "what then is this?", were struck with the utmost amazement.
Then that royal sage, now a woman, best of speakers, said: "I had set out to hunt, firmly surrounded by my forces; but, deluded by fate, I strayed and entered a fearsome wilderness.
And in that most terrible wilderness, parched with thirst and bereft of my wits, I beheld a lake of most lovely aspect, thronged with birds.
Having plunged therein, I was made a woman—plainly by fate, there is no doubt—as though I had not yet had my fill of sons, of wives, and of wealth."
Then that best of kings, now a woman, said to his sons: "In harmony enjoy this kingdom; I shall go to the forest, my dear ones." And having consecrated his hundred sons, the king departed to the forest.
In the hermitage, dear son, an ascetic took that woman to wife; and by that ascetic a hundred sons were born to her in the hermitage as well.
Then taking these sons, she said to her former sons: "You are my sons begotten in manhood, and these hundred are my sons in womanhood.
Enjoy the kingdom together, as brothers, my dear ones." And those brothers, united, then enjoyed the kingdom together.
Seeing them enjoy that excellent kingdom in brotherly accord, Indra, lord of the gods, overwhelmed with wrath, reflected: "I have done that royal sage a service, not an injury."
Then in the guise of a brāhmaṇa, the king of the gods, lord of a hundred sacrifices, went to the city and sowed dissension among those sons of the king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"There is no brotherhood among brothers, even among the sons of one father: for the sake of the kingdom the gods and demons, sons of Kaśyapa, fell to strife.
You are the offspring of Bhaṅgāśvana, while the others are the sons of an ascetic—just as the gods and the demons were the sons of Kaśyapa; yet your paternal kingdom is being enjoyed by the ascetic's sons."
Set at variance by Indra, they struck one another down in battle; and hearing this, the ascetic-woman, sore stricken, broke into weeping.
Approaching her in the disguise of a brāhmaṇa, Indra then inquired: "With what grief are you tormented, that you weep, O fair-faced one?"
Seeing the brāhmaṇa, that woman piteously replied: "My two hundred sons, O brāhmaṇa, have been laid low by time.
I was once a king, O brāhmaṇa, and there a hundred sons were begotten by me, handsome and valiant, O best of the twice-born.
Once, gone out to the hunt, I strayed in a dense forest and, plunging into a lake, was made a woman, O best of brāhmaṇas; and having established my sons in the kingdom, I then withdrew to the forest.
And to me as a woman a hundred sons were begotten by a great-souled ascetic in the hermitage, O brāhmaṇa; these too I brought to the city.
And by the working of time enmity arose among them, O brāhmaṇa; this I lament, O best of brāhmaṇas, overwhelmed by fate."
Seeing her in her grief, Indra spoke harsh words: "Of old, O lady, you wrought me grief most hard to bear,
by performing a sacrifice hateful to Indra, slighting me, O perverse one. I am Indra, O foolish one, and the enmity I have requited upon you."
But seeing Indra, the royal sage fell with bowed head at his feet: "Be gracious, O best of the gods; that sacrifice was performed by me in longing for sons, O tiger among the gods; in this you ought to forgive me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Well pleased by her obeisance, Indra granted a boon: "Which of your sons, O king, shall live? Tell me—those born to you as a woman, or those who came to you as a man?"
Then the ascetic-woman, with reverently folded hands, said to Śakra: "Let those who were born to me as a woman live, O Vāsava."
But Indra, astonished and delighted, questioned that woman again: "How are the sons you begot as a man become hateful to you?
How is it that your love is greater for those born when you were a woman? I wish to hear the reason; this you ought to tell me here."
The woman said: A woman's love is the greater—not so a man's; therefore, O Śakra, let those live who were born to me when I was made a woman.
Bhīṣma said: When she had spoken thus, Indra, well pleased, replied: "Let all your sons live here, O truthful one.
And choose a boon, O lord of kings, whatever you desire, O steadfast in vows—manhood or womanhood, whichever you crave from me."
The woman said: I choose womanhood itself, O Śakra, since you are gracious, O Vāsava.
Thus addressed, Indra, lord of the gods, replied to that woman: "How is it that, forsaking manhood, you prefer womanhood, O mighty one?"
Thus addressed, that best of kings, now a woman, replied: "In the union of woman and man, the pleasure of the woman is ever the greater; for this reason, O Śakra, I choose womanhood itself."
"And I take greater delight in womanhood—truly, O best of gods; I am content in my woman's state. Go now, O lord of the gods."
Saying "So be it," and taking leave of her, Indra departed to heaven. Thus, O great king, is the woman's pleasure declared the greater.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What ought a man to do who seeks the welfare that sustains worldly life? And of what conduct should he be as he carries on the course of the world?
Bhīṣma said: Of action by the body there are three kinds, by speech four kinds, and by the mind three; these ten paths of evil action one should renounce.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The slaying of living beings, theft, and intercourse with another's wife—these three sins of the body one should utterly shun.
Idle babble, harshness, slander, and falsehood likewise—these four sins of speech, O lord of kings, one should neither utter nor even ponder.
Freedom from coveting another's goods, good will toward all beings, and the conviction that actions bear fruit—this threefold course one should practice with the mind.
Therefore let a man do no evil by speech, body, or mind; for doing deeds good or evil, he tastes the fruit of each in turn.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O mighty one, declare to me the names of the grandsire-lord, of Śambhu, of Babhru, of him who is the māyā of the universe, and his exalted majesty in truth.
Bhīṣma said: O preceptor of gods and demons, O divine Viṣṇu, it is you who ought to speak that which Yudhiṣṭhira asks of me concerning Śiva, who has the universe for his form.
The thousand names of the god, which were proclaimed of old by Taṇḍin, sprung from Brahmā, and were once set forth before Brahmā in the world of Brahmā.
Let these sages too, rich in austerity—Dvaipāyana foremost among them—men of noble vows and self-restraint, listen as you speak.
Tell us, O mighty one, of the high glory of him who is the Unmoving, the Giver of joy, the Sacrificer, the Protector, the Creator of all, who is Fire itself—of the Shaven-headed and the Matted-locked one.
Vāsudeva said: The course of the Lord's deeds cannot be known in its truth.
The gods, led by Hiraṇyagarbha and Indra, and the great sages of subtle vision, do not know his end nor his beginning. How then could he, the goal of the good, be known by a mere man?
Yet of that blessed Lord, the slayer of the asuras, the master of all vows, I shall recount to you some of his attributes, as faithfully as I am able.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa sipped water, made himself pure, and began to relate the attributes of that great-souled and wise one.
Vāsudeva said: Listen, O foremost of brāhmaṇas, and you too, dear Yudhiṣṭhira; and you, son of the River, attend to the names of the Lord of the world.
How in time past I gained, for the sake of Sāmba, that which is most hard to win, and how the blessed Lord was once beheld by me through deep meditation—
After Śambara had been slain of old by the wise son of Rukmiṇī, when the twelfth year had passed, Jāmbavatī said to me—
Beholding the little sons of Rukmiṇī—Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa and the rest—and herself longing for a son, she came to me and spoke, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
"Grant me without delay, O Acyuta, a son who is valiant, foremost among the strong, lovely in form, free of all blemish, the equal of yourself."
"For there is nothing in the three worlds beyond your reach; should you wish it, you could create other worlds, O upholder of the Yadu line."
"Living on air and wasting away for twelve years, by propitiating the Lord of creatures, you begot upon Rukmiṇī her sons."
"Cārudeṣṇa and Sucāru, Cāruveṣa and Yaśodhara, Cāruśravas and Cāruyaśas, Pradyumna, and Śambhu as well—"
"Even as those sons of fair prowess were begotten of Rukmiṇī, so grant to me also a son endowed with strength."
Urged in this way by the lady, I said to the fair-waisted one: "Give me leave, O queen; I shall do as you ask." And she said to me: "Go, for victory and for blessing."
"May Brahmā, Śiva, and Kāśyapa, the rivers, the gods who follow the mind, the fields and the herbs, the bearers of the sacrifice, the sacred metres, the hosts of sages, and the Earth—"
"the oceans, the sacrificial fees, the chants, the constellations, the ancestors, the planets, the wives of the gods, the daughters of the gods, and the mothers of the gods—"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"the cosmic ages of the Manus, the cattle, the Moon, Savitṛ, Hari, Sāvitrī and the knowledge of Brahman, the seasons, the years, the nights—"
"the moments, the instants, the hours, the wink-spans of time, and the turning of the ages—may they guard you wherever you go, O Yādava, bringer of joy. Go your way unharmed and watchful, O sinless one."
Thus blessed by her with rites of well-being, having taken leave of that daughter of the lord of the apes, I went to her father, that best of men, to her mother, and to King Āhuka—
and laid before them what the deeply grieving daughter of the lord of the Vidyādharas had asked of me; then, sore at heart, I took leave of them, and of Gada and of mighty Rāma as well.
Having obtained the leave of my elders, I called to mind Tārkṣya; he bore me to Himavat, and upon reaching it I dismissed him.
There upon that noblest of mountains I beheld wondrous sights, and I saw a holy ground supreme among the seats of austerity, a most excellent hermitage—
the divine hermitage of the great-souled Upamanyu, son of Vyāghrapad, honoured by gods and gandharvas, endowed with a sacred and Brahmic splendour.
It was rich with dhava, kakubha, kadamba and coconut trees; with kurabaka, ketaka, jambu and pāṭala; with banyan, varuṇaka, vatsanābha and bilva; with sarala, kapittha, priyāla, sāla and palm;
with jujube, kunda and punnāga, with aśoka, mango and atimukta, with bhallātaka, madhūka, campaka and breadfruit;
graced with woodland trees of many kinds bearing fruit and flower, strewn with blossoming shrubs and creepers, made lovely with thickets of plantain.
It was adorned with trees whose fruits gave food to birds of many sorts, and beautified with rows of woodland set each in its fitting place.
It teemed with deer, elephants, tigers, lions and panthers; was thronged with antelope and peacocks, beset with wildcats and serpents, frequented by herds of beasts of many breeds, by buffaloes and bears.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There a pleasant breeze blew, laden with the pollen of many flowers, perfumed with the ichor of elephants, and filled with the songs of celestial women.
With the murmur of cascades and the cries of birds, with the auspicious trumpeting of elephants, with the lofty songs of the kiṃnaras, and the holy sounds of those who chant the Sāman, O hero—
—it was such as others could not so much as conceive in the mind; adorned with lakes, beautified with broad fire-shelters, and carpeted with kuśa grass.
Adorned, O king, by the daughter of Jahnu with her holy and purifying waters, ever-frequented by her, it was graced by great-souled seers, foremost among upholders of dharma, who blazed like fire.
It was adorned all around by foremost brāhmaṇas—ascetics who lived on air, who drank only water, who were ever at their muttered prayers, who scoured their vessels clean, who were ever in meditation, who fed on smoke, who drank only warmth, and who lived upon milk alone.
There were those who grazed like cattle, those who ground their grain on stones, those whose mortar was their own teeth, those who lived on the sun's rays, those who drank only foam, and those who roamed like the wild deer.
Beholding these men who upheld their grievous vows in the rigour of austerity, with wide-open eyes I set myself to enter in.
Well honoured by the hosts of gods, the great-souled ones, Śiva and the rest, doers of holy deeds, O Bhārata, that circle of hermitage ever shone, O king, like the orb of the sun in the heavens.
There the mongooses sported with the serpents, and the tigers with the deer, as friends—through the power and the virtue of nearness to those whose austerity blazed forth.
In that supreme hermitage, delightful to all beings, frequented by tigers among the twice-born who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliaries—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
—and by great-souled sages renowned for their manifold vows, even as I entered I beheld the Lord, wearing matted locks and bark-cloth garments.
Blazing like fire with splendour and with austerity, seated amid his pupils, serene, youthful, a bull among brāhmaṇas—Upamanyu spoke to me as I bowed my head before him.
"Welcome, O lotus-eyed one. Our austerities have borne their fruit, since you who are worthy of worship pay us honour, and you who are worthy to be beheld desire to behold us."
Then, with palms joined together, I asked after the welfare of his beasts and birds, of his sacred fires, of his observance of dharma, and of the band of his pupils.
Then the blessed sage said to me with words most gentle and kind: "You shall surely obtain, O Kṛṣṇa, a son who is your own equal—of this there is no doubt."
"Undertaking a most mighty austerity, propitiate the Lord, the Ruler; for here, O Adhokṣaja, the god disports himself together with his consort."
"In this very place, O Janārdana, the gods together with the hosts of sages, in days of old, having gratified that best of deities by austerity, by chastity, by truth and by self-restraint, obtained their fair desires."
"That blessed Lord, the treasure-house of all splendours and austerities, dwells here together with the Goddess—he, the inconceivable one, who sends forth and withdraws all states of being, both fair and foul—the very one whom you entreat, O slayer of foes."
"Hiraṇyakaśipu, the dānava who once shook Mount Meru, obtained from Śarva the lordship over all the immortals for a full ten million years."
"His foremost son, renowned as Mandara, by a boon of Mahādeva did battle with Śakra for ten million years."
"Even the dread discus of Viṣṇu and the thunderbolt of Ākhaṇḍala, O dear Keśava, were of old shattered upon the limbs of that demon Graha."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And the gods, sorely oppressed by that mighty Graha, slew in their turn many a lord of the asuras who had been granted boons by Śiva."
"Well pleased with Vidyutprabha too, he gave him the sovereignty of the three worlds; for a hundred thousand years he became the lord of all worlds, and the god said: 'You shall ever be my attendant.'"
"Likewise the Lord granted him ten thousand sons, and the blessed Unborn one gave him the island of Kuśa to rule as a kingdom."
"So too there was a great asura named Śatamukha, fashioned by the Creator, who for a full hundred years offered up the fire with his own flesh; and the blessed Śaṃkara, well pleased, said to him: 'What shall I do for you?'"
"And Śatamukha answered him: 'Let mine be a wondrous power of yoga, and grant me, O best of the gods, strength that endures forever.'"
"And Kratu, son of the Self-existent, of old, longing for offspring, entered into himself through yoga for three hundred years."
"To him the god granted a thousand sons, each the equal of Kratu himself. You know, O Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of yoga who is sung of by the gods—of this there is no doubt."
"The Vālakhilyas, it is said, were once slighted by Maghavat; and they in their wrath gratified the blessed Rudra by their austerities."
"And to them the best of gods, the Lord of the world, well pleased, declared: 'By your austerity you shall bring forth Suparṇa, the carrier-off of the soma.'"
"Through the wrath of Mahādeva the waters of old were destroyed, and the gods brought other waters into being by means of the seven-skulled rite."
