"The wife of Atri too, a speaker of sacred truth, forsook her husband, saying: 'Never again shall I be subject to the will of that sage'; and so saying she went, it is said, for refuge to Mahādeva."
"Taking no food, in fear of Atri, she lay even upon pestles for three hundred years, to win the grace of Bhava."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"To her the god said, smiling: 'A son shall surely be born to you, and in your own line he shall attain the renown you desire, bearing your name.'"
"Śākalya, a man of disciplined soul, propitiated Bhava for nine hundred years with the sacrifice of the mind, O Keśava."
"And the blessed Lord, well pleased, said to him: 'You shall become an author of treatises, my child; your fame shall be imperishable throughout the three worlds, and let your lineage be undying, adorned with great sages.'"
"There was too a renowned sage named Sāvarṇi in the Kṛta age; here he practised austerity for six thousand years."
"To him the blessed Rudra appeared in person and said: 'I am pleased with you, O sinless one. You shall become a maker of treatises, renowned throughout the world, free of age and death.'"
"And how I too of old beheld in person the God of gods, the all-pervading Lord, Paśupati himself, of that also hear, dear Mādhava."
"And for what purpose I once, with strenuous effort, propitiated the mighty Mahādeva of great splendour—that too hear in full."
"And whatever I formerly gained from the God of gods, from Maheśvara, all of that, entire and without omission, I shall now relate to you, O sinless one."
"Long ago, in the Kṛta age, my dear one, there lived a sage of great renown, known as Vyāghrapad, master of the Vedas and their auxiliaries. I was his son, and Dhaumya was my younger brother."
"Now once upon a time, O Mādhava, I came at play, together with Dhaumya, to the hermitage of sages whose souls were purified."
"And there I saw a milk-cow being milked, and I marked that its milk was sweet to the taste, like the very nectar of immortality."
"Now flour, O Mādhava, stirred together with water, used to be brought to the two of us to drink, under the name of 'milk.'"
"Then once, my dear one, I tasted the milk of a cow, and thereafter the flour-water, O dear one, no longer gave me any pleasure."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Then in my childish way I said to my own mother: 'Give me food made with milk-porridge to eat.'"
"Then my mother, filled with grief and sorrow, embracing me out of a mother's love and kissing me upon the head, O Mādhava, said to me:"
"'Whence is milk-porridge to come, my child, for sages of purified souls who dwell ever in the forest and feed upon roots, bulbs and fruits?'"
"'Without first winning the grace of the three-eyed Virūpākṣa, the giver of boons, the unmoving and undecaying Sthāṇu—whence, my child, is milk-porridge to come, or comforts, or fine raiment?'"
Take refuge always in Śaṃkara, my child, with your whole being; by his grace, little son, you shall win from your desires their fruit.
Having heard those words of my mother, O slayer of foes, from that day onward an unwavering devotion to Mahādeva took root in me.
Then, undertaking austerity, I set myself to please Śaṃkara, standing for a thousand divine years poised upon the tips of my toes.
For one hundred years I lived then on fruit alone; for a second hundred I ate withered leaves; for a third I subsisted on water; and for seven hundred years more I fed upon air alone.
Then Mahādeva, the Lord and Master of all worlds, was pleased; assuming the form of Śakra and encircled by all the hosts of the gods, he became the thousand-eyed one, thunderbolt-handed and of great renown.
He mounted a mighty elephant, white as nectar, with red eyes, ears held stiffly erect, fierce in its rut, its trunk coiled, terrible to behold, and armed with four tusks.
Mounted upon it, the Lord came on, blazing with his own splendour, crowned with a diadem and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
A white parasol was held above his head, the Apsarases waited upon him, and the music of celestial Gandharvas resounded around him.
Then the lord of the gods spoke to me: 'I am pleased with you, O best of the twice-born; choose from me whatever boon dwells in your heart.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But hearing Śakra's words, O Kṛṣṇa, my heart was not gladdened, and I then spoke to the king of the gods these words.
'I desire no boon from you, nor from any other deity save Mahādeva, O gentle one; this truth I tell you.'
'At a word from Paśupati I would gladly become at once a worm, or a tree with countless branches; but the sovereignty and splendour even of the three worlds, if not born of Paśupati's gracious boon, is unwelcome to me.'
'Even an insect or a moth I would gladly become at Śaṃkara's command; but the dominion over the three worlds, were it given by you, O Śakra, I do not desire.'
'So long as Paśupati, my Lord and God, whose locks are bound with the pure crescent fragment of the moon, is not pleased with me, so long shall I bear the sorrows ordained for the body, smitten by a hundred old ages, deaths, and births.'
'Without winning the favour of Rudra—radiant as sun, moon, and fire, the essence of the three worlds, boundless, primordial, unique, unaging, undying—what man in this world could ever attain peace?'
Śakra said: 'And what is your reason concerning the Lord, the Cause of all causes, that you should seek favour from no god other than him?'
Upamanyu said: 'What need have you of other reasons? The Lord is the Cause of all causes. We have never heard that the emblem of any other is worshipped by the gods.'
'Whose emblem, save that of Maheśvara, is worshipped by all the gods, or has been worshipped of old? Tell me, if you have heard of any such.'
'He whose emblem Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and you too together with the gods, forever worship—he therefore is the most supreme of all.'
'From him alone do I desire a boon, or even death itself, O Kauśika. Go or stay as you please, O Śakra, slayer of Bala.'
'Let it be, then—whether a boon be mine from Maheśvara, or even a curse; I desire no other deity, not though it bring me the fruit of all my wishes.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having thus spoken to the lord of the gods, my senses troubled with grief and brooding, 'Why is it that Rudra is not gracious to me?'—in that very instant I beheld once again that same Airāvata.
It had taken the form of a bull, like a swan, like jasmine, like the moon, gleaming as the lotus-stalk and the white water-lily, vast as the very Ocean of Milk before my eyes.
Huge of body, with a black tail and eyes tawny as honey, adorned on every side with a girth of pure gold.
Red-eyed, with a great muzzle, fine ears, fine flanks at the haunch, well-formed sides, broad shoulders—shapely and lovely to behold.
Its hump shone, rising full upon its shoulder, like the peak of a snow-clad mountain, like the crest of a white cloud.
Mounted upon it together with Umā, the Lord, God of gods, the great Mahādeva, shone like the lord of the stars on the night of the full moon.
The fire born of his radiance, charged with clouds and thunder, stood enveloping all things like a thousand suns at once.
The Lord, of vast and mighty splendour, was like the all-consuming fire, poised as if to burn up every being at the ending of an age.
When that splendour, hard to gaze upon, had spread on every side, my heart was troubled once more, and I pondered, 'What is this?'
That splendour, having filled all the ten directions for but a moment, was in an instant stilled again by the power of the God of gods.
Then I beheld the Lord Maheśvara, the Steadfast One, standing there—gentle, seated upon the bull, like a smokeless flame—the Supreme Lord together with Pārvatī, fair in every limb.
The blue-throated, great-souled, unattached one, treasury of all splendours, the Steadfast, with eighteen arms, adorned with every ornament.
The God clad in white garments, garlanded and anointed in white, bearing a white banner, unassailable, wearing the white sacred thread.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He was surrounded by his celestial attendants—singing, dancing, leaping here and there—each equal to himself in valour.
Crowned with the crescent moon, pale-bright as the autumn moon newly risen, blazing with his three eyes like three suns risen at once.
And upon the God's body, fair of hue, there shone a garland woven of golden lotuses and set with jewels.
And the weapons of Bhava, of measureless splendour—embodied and wholly made of radiance—these I beheld, O Govinda.
The bow of that great-souled one, gleaming like a thousand rainbows, renowned by the name of Pināka—and that bow was itself a mighty serpent.
Seven-headed, vast of body, with sharp fangs and abounding in venom, its great neck wound about as the bowstring, it stood there in the shape of a man.
And the arrow, resembling the sun, of a brilliance like the fire of doom—that great and most terrible divine weapon, the mighty Pāśupata.
Without a peer, beyond all describing, striking terror into every being, huge of frame and scattering sparks, as though shedding forth fire.
One-footed, with great fangs, with a thousand heads and bellies, with a thousand arms, tongues, and eyes, as though belching forth fire.
Surpassing the weapons of Brahmā, of Nārāyaṇa, of Indra, of Agni, and of Varuṇa, O mighty-armed one, and the destroyer of every other weapon.
By which, in days of old, Mahādeva burned Tripura and reduced it to ashes in an instant, with a single arrow and as if in sport, O Govinda.
Loosed from Maheśvara's arm, it would consume the whole universe, the three worlds with all that moves and is unmoving, in half the blink of an eye—of this there is no doubt.
In this world there is none it cannot slay, not even among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods. That weapon, supremely wondrous and marvellous, did I behold, my friend.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And another supreme and secret weapon, equal to it or even greater—that which is renowned throughout all the worlds as the trident of the Trident-bearer.
Hurled by the Trident-handed one, it could cleave the whole earth asunder, or dry up the great ocean, or destroy the entire universe.
By it, in olden times, was Māndhātṛ slain, the son of Yuvanāśva, together with his army—a sovereign emperor of vast splendour, the king who had conquered the three worlds.
Mighty in strength and valour, in prowess the equal of Śakra, he was slain, O Govinda, by that trident here held in the hand of the demon Lavaṇa.
That trident, exceedingly sharp of point, most dreadful and hair-raising, stood as though it had drawn its three prongs into a frown and was threatening all before it.
Smokeless yet flaming, dark, risen like the sun of doom, serpent in hand, beyond describing, like Death with his noose in hand—that weapon I beheld, O Govinda, in the presence of Rudra.
And the keen-edged axe that of old was given to Rāma by the well-pleased Mahādeva, bringer of destruction to the Kṣatriyas—by which, in a mighty battle, the emperor Kārtavīrya was slain.
By which the earth was made bereft of Kṣatriyas thrice seven times over, O Govinda, by Rāma the son of Jamadagni, of unwearied deeds.
With blazing edge and most fearsome face, wound about at the throat and tip with serpents, it stood beside the Trident-bearer like a tongue of flaming fire.
Numberless are the divine weapons of that wise one; these, the chief among them, have I recounted to you, O sinless one.
On the God's left side stood Brahmā, the Grandsire of the worlds, mounted upon a celestial car yoked with swans and swift as thought.
And likewise Nārāyaṇa stood upon his left flank, mounted upon the son of Vinatā, bearing conch, discus, and mace.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Skanda, mounted upon his peacock, stood near the Goddess, his spear held aslant his shoulder, like a second fire.
And before the God I saw Nandin stationed, standing braced upon his trident, like a second Śaṃkara.
The Manus, beginning with Svāyaṃbhuva, the sages, beginning with Bhṛgu, and the gods, beginning with Śakra—all alike drew near.
Saluting the great-souled one and encircling him on every side, the gods then praised Mahādeva with hymns of many kinds.
Brahmā, praising Bhava, intoned the Rathantara hymn; and Nārāyaṇa then sang to the Lord of gods with the Jyeṣṭha Sāman; while Śakra chanted the supreme Brahman, the excellent Śatarudrīya.
Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa and Kauśika the king of the gods—those three great-souled ones shone like three sacred fires.
In their midst the Lord God Śiva shone resplendent, like the sun freed from the autumn clouds yet still wreathed in a halo. Then I too praised that God of holy vows with this hymn.
Homage to the God of gods, homage indeed to Mahādeva; to Śakra, to him whose form is Śakra's, to him who wore the garb of Śakra.
Homage to you, thunderbolt in hand, tawny and ruddy of hue; to the Pināka-bearer evermore, to him who bears the sword and the trident.
Homage to you, clad in black, with dark curling locks, mantled in a black antelope hide, and delighting in the eighth of the dark fortnight.
To the white of hue, to the white one, to him clad in white garments, smeared with white ashes, and delighting in pure deeds.
You are Brahmā among all the gods, the blue-and-red Nīlalohita among the Rudras, the Self of all beings, and in the Sāṃkhya you are called the Puruṣa.
You are the bull among holy things, the partless and auspicious one among the Yogins; among the stages of life you are the householder, among lords you are Maheśvara, among all the Yakṣas you are Kubera, and among sacrifices you are called Viṣṇu.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Among mountains you are the great Meru, among the lunar mansions the Moon; among the sages you are Vasiṣṭha, and among the planets you are called the Sun.
Among the beasts of the forest you are the lion, O Supreme Lord; among the beasts of the village you are the bull, O Lord, worshipped by all the world.
Among the Ādityas you are Viṣṇu, among the Vasus the Fire-god, among birds the son of Vinatā, and among serpents you are Ananta.
Among the Vedas you are the Sāmaveda, among the Yajus formulas the Śatarudrīya, among the Yogins Sanatkumāra, and among the followers of Sāṃkhya you are Kapila.
Among the Maruts you are Śakra, O God; among the ancestral fathers you are the king of dharma; among the worlds you are the world of Brahmā, and among the goals you are called liberation.
Among the oceans you are the Ocean of Milk, among mountains the Himavat; among the social orders you are the Brāhmaṇa, and among the learned the consecrated twice-born. You are the beginning of the worlds, and you are likewise their destroyer, even Time itself.
And whatever other being in the worlds is held to surpass the rest in splendour—all that is the Lord himself: such is my settled conviction.
Homage to you, O Lord and God; homage to you, tender to your devotees; homage be to you, O Lord of Yoga; homage to you, O source of the universe.
Be gracious to me, your devotee, wretched and forlorn, beset by helplessness; be my refuge, O eternal one.
Whatever offense I have committed in ignorance, O supreme lord, deign to forgive it all, O lord of gods, for I am your devotee.
I was deluded, O lord of gods, by the disguise of your form, and so I offered you neither the welcome-water nor the water for your feet, O lord of the celestials.
Having thus praised Īśāna, with hands folded in reverence I offered him in devotion the water for his feet, the water of welcome, and all the rites.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, O dear one, a gracious shower of flowers, cool with water and fragrant with celestial scents, fell upon my head.
Then a celestial kettledrum was sounded by the servants of the gods, and a holy breeze blew, pure-scented and bringing delight.
Then Mahādeva, the bull-bannered one, well pleased and accompanied by his consort, spoke to the gods, gladdening me as it were.
Behold, all you gods, the supreme and celestial devotion of the great-souled Upamanyu toward me, established in singleness of heart.
Thus addressed by the trident-bearer, O Kṛṣṇa, all those gods, with folded hands and bowing to the bull-bannered one, replied:
O lord, O god of gods and ruler of gods, O protector of worlds, master of the universe, let this best of the twice-born obtain from you the fruit of all his desires.
Thus addressed by the gods led by Brahmā, Śarva—the lord, Śaṃkara—spoke to me as though smiling:
My child Upamanyu, I am pleased; behold me, O bull among sages. You are firm in devotion, O brahmin seer, and I have tested you.
By this devotion of yours I am exceedingly delighted; therefore I grant you this day all the desires you wish for.
When Mahādeva had thus spoken to me, O mighty one, tears flowed from joy, and my hair stood on end.
And then, touching the earth with my knees and bowing again and again, I addressed the god in a voice faltering with joy:
Today indeed am I born, O god; today my austerity has borne fruit, in that Mahādeva himself stands graciously before me.
That god of boundless might, whom even the gods cannot behold for all their worship, I have now beheld; who is more blessed than I?
Thus do the wise meditate upon him as the supreme eternal principle, known as the twenty-sixth, the imperishable, higher than the highest.
This same lord, the imperishable god, is the source of all principles, knower of the ordering of all principles, the master of Primal Nature and Spirit.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It was the lord who created from his right side Brahmā, the origin of the worlds, and from his left side Viṣṇu for the protection of the worlds; and when the age's end arrives, the master brings forth Rudra from his body.
That Rudra, of great splendor, withdrawing the whole world of things moving and unmoving, becomes Time itself, like the all-consuming fire of dissolution.
This god, Mahādeva, having created the world of things moving and unmoving, at the end of the aeon withdraws the consciousness of all and abides alone.
All-pervading, the self of all beings, the source from which all beings arise, he abides forever present everywhere, unseen even by all the gods.
If a boon is to be granted to me, and if my lord is pleased with me, then let my devotion to you, O Śaṃkara, be everlasting and eternal.
And that I may know what is past, what is to come, and what is present, O mighty one—such is my wish—by your grace, O best of the gods.
And that I may eat of inexhaustible milk-rice together with my kinsmen, and that your supreme presence may ever abide for me in my hermitage.
Thus addressed, the lord—Maheśvara, worshiped by all the worlds, of great splendor, the master and teacher of all things moving and unmoving—said to me:
Be free from age and free from death, released from sorrow, virtuous, endowed with every excellence, all-knowing, and fair to look upon.
Let your youth be unfading and your splendor like fire, and let the ocean of milk be present wherever you wish, O sage.
There the presence of the ocean of milk shall be yours at will, and you shall eat milk-rice mingled with the nectar of immortality.
Together with your kinsmen you shall live through the aeon and then come to me; and I will make my presence abide forever in your hermitage, O best of the twice-born.
Abide as you wish, my child; you need not grieve. Whenever you remember me, O brahmin, I will ever grant you my sight.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus, that lord Īśāna, radiant as ten million suns, granted me the boon and vanished on the spot.
Thus, O Kṛṣṇa, did I behold the god of gods through deep contemplation, and all that was promised by that wise one came to pass for me.
And behold here before your very eyes, O Kṛṣṇa, the perfected ones gathered—seers, vidyādharas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and apsarases.
Behold these enchanting trees, ever laden with flowers and fruit, bearing the blossoms of every season, with glossy leaves and fair branches—all this, O mighty-armed one, is filled with a celestial presence.
Upamanyu said: These and thousands of others Hara has favored with his thought; why then, O Mādhava, should the lord not show his grace to you?
For communion with the gods is praiseworthy through one like you—devoted to brahmins, free of cruelty, and full of faith; and I will impart to you the prayer by which you shall behold Śaṃkara.
Kṛṣṇa said: I answered him, O brahmin, great sage: By your grace I shall behold the lord of the gods, the crusher of the hosts of Diti's sons.
And on the eighth day I was duly consecrated by the brahmin—bearing a staff, with shaven head, holding kuśa grass, clad in rags, anointed with ghee, and girded with a sash.
For one month I lived on fruit, for the second on water alone, and through the third, the fourth, and the fifth I subsisted on air.
Standing on one foot, with arms upraised and never slackening, I beheld in the sky, O Bhārata, a radiance like that of a thousand suns.
And in the midst of that radiance, O son of Pāṇḍu, I saw a cloud-mass like a heap of dark mountains, its form wreathed with rainbows, its lattice-windows of lightning-garlands, adorned with cranes.
And upon it stood the lord of great brilliance, together with the goddess, his consort, blazing with austerity, splendor, and radiant beauty.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There Maheśvara, the lord, shone forth with the goddess, even as the sun joined with the moon shines when resting amid the clouds.
With my hair bristling, O son of Kuntī, and my eyes wide with wonder, I beheld Hara, the refuge of the hosts of gods, the remover of distress.
Crowned, mace-bearing, trident in hand, clothed in a tiger's skin, with matted locks and staff in hand, wielder of the Pināka bow and the thunderbolt, with sharp tusks, fair-armleted, wearing a serpent for his sacred thread—
bearing upon his breast a celestial garland of many hues, hanging down to his ankles—him I beheld like the moon ringed with a twilit halo at the passing of the rains.
He was surrounded on every side by the troops of the pramathas, hard to gaze upon, like the sun ringed with a halo in autumn.
And the eleven Rudras, self-controlled, praised him, the bull-riding one, of auspicious deeds, with their rites.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the two Aśvins praised the god, the god of all, with hymns of every kind.
And the lord of a hundred sacrifices and Viṣṇu, both sons of Aditi, and Brahmā chanted the Rathantara sāman in the presence of Bhava.
Many lords of yoga praised him, the giver of yoga, the father and teacher, as did the brahmin seers with their sons and the divine seers.
The earth and the firmament, the constellations and the planets, the months and fortnights, the seasons, the nights, the years, and the moments—
the hours and the instants, and likewise the revolutions of the ages—all these, O king, made obeisance, as did the celestial sciences and all the quarters of space.
Sanatkumāra, the Vedas, and the ancient legends as well; Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu—
the Manus, Soma, Atharvan with Bṛhaspati, Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Kāśya as well—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the metres, the consecration, the sacrifices and their priestly fees, the fire and the oblation, and all the materials that go to a sacrifice, embodied in form, O Yudhiṣṭhira—
all the lords of creatures, the rivers, the serpents and the mountains, all the mothers of the gods, and the wives of the gods together with their maidens—
sages by the thousands, by the tens of thousands and the millions, made obeisance to the serene lord, as did the mountains, the oceans, and the quarters of space.
And the gandharvas and apsarases, skilled in song and instrument, singing in celestial measures, praised the wondrous Bhava, as did the vidyādharas, the dānavas, the guhyakas, and the rākṣasas.
And all beings, unmoving and moving, made obeisance, O great king, to the all-pervading lord with word, mind, and deed; and Śarva, the lord of the gods, stood before me.
And when the whole world, with the Lords of Creatures and Śakra, saw my Īśāna standing before me, O Bhārata, it gazed up at me.
And I had then no power to look upon Mahādeva; thereupon the god said to me: Behold, Kṛṣṇa, and speak.
When I had bowed my head to the god, the goddess Umā was well pleased; then I praised Sthāṇu, who is praised by the gods led by Brahmā:
Homage to you, O eternal one, source of all; the seers call you the sovereign of Brahmā; and the holy ones declare that austerity, and goodness, passion, and darkness, and truth itself are none but you.
You indeed are Brahmā and Rudra, Varuṇa, Agni, Manu, and Bhava; you are Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Vidhātṛ; you are the lord whose faces are turned in every direction.
From you are born all beings, unmoving and moving; you are the origin of all beings, and you alone are their dissolution.
The objects of the senses and the whole of the mind, the seven winds and the fire, and the deities that dwell in heaven among men—beyond all these the seers declare you to be.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Vedas and the sacrifices, the soma and the priestly fee, the fire and the oblation, and whatever else pertains to the sacrifice—all that, O lord, are you, beyond doubt.
Sacrifice offered, gifts bestowed, scripture studied, and the vows and observances; modesty, renown, prosperity, splendor, contentment, and attainment—all are offered up to you.
Desire, anger, fear, greed, pride, arrogance, and envy, and afflictions of mind and body—these too, O lord, are your offspring.
Creation, transformation, dissolution, Primal Nature, the imperishable source; the supreme womb of the mind and inherent nature, eternal; the unmanifest, O purifier, O all-pervading one of a thousand rays and golden hue.
You are the origin of all the qualities, the refuge of life; the Great Self, intelligence, Brahmā, the Universe, Śambhu, the self-existent one.
Intellect, wisdom, perception, awareness, fame, steadfastness, and memory—by these synonymous words you, the Great Self, are conceived.
Having known you, the learned brahmin falls into no delusion; you are the heart of all beings, the Knower of the Field, praised by the seers.
With hands and feet on every side, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side, with ears on every side, you abide in the world, enveloping all.
You are the fruit of every act, from the blink of an eye onward, O fierce-rayed one; you are the radiant-flamed Spirit seated in the heart of all; you are minuteness, lightness, and attainment, the lord, the imperishable light.
In you abide intellect, thought, and the worlds; and those who take refuge and rely upon you are the meditators, the ever-yoked, the true to their word, the conquerors of the senses.
He who knows you as the changeless one, dwelling in the cave of the heart—the lord, the ancient Spirit, the all-formed, the golden one, the supreme goal of the wise—he, the wise one, transcends the intellect and abides.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having known the seven subtle principles and you who are six-membered in your embodied form, the wise one, established in the discipline of the ordering of primal matter, enters into you alone.
When I had spoken thus, O Pārtha, to Bhava the destroyer of affliction, the whole world, moving and unmoving, raised up a lion's roar.
The hosts of brāhmaṇas, the gods and the asuras, the nāgas, the piśācas, the ancestral fathers and the birds, the throngs of rākṣasas and all the bands of spirits, and the great seers as well, then bowed down in reverence.
Upon my head heaps of fragrant celestial flowers came showering down, and a most pleasant breeze blew.
The Lord, the benefactor of the world, having looked upon the goddess Umā and upon me, and having gazed at Śatakratu, Śaṃkara himself spoke to me.
We know, O Kṛṣṇa, your supreme devotion to us, O slayer of foes; let your own welfare be secured, for our love for you is supreme.
Choose eight boons, O Kṛṣṇa; I shall grant them to you, O most excellent one. Speak, O tiger among the Yādavas, of whatever boons, however hard to obtain, you desire.
Kṛṣṇa said: Falling down with my head upon that mass of splendor, self-controlled, and then attaining the highest joy, I addressed the Lord.
Firmness in dharma, the slaying of foes in battle, foremost renown and supreme strength, devotion to yoga, nearness to you, and a hundred times a hundred sons — these I choose.
"So be it" — these words Śaṃkara spoke, having been addressed by me.
Then the mother of the world, Umā the all-purifying Earth, intent and composed — Śarvāṇī, the treasury of austerities — spoke to me.
"A son named Sāmba has been granted to you by the Lord, O sinless one; from me too receive eight cherished boons, which I give to you." And bowing my head, I addressed her, O delight of Pāṇḍu's line.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Freedom from anger toward the twice-born, my father's favor, a hundred sons and the highest enjoyment, affection within my kindred and my mother's grace, the attainment of peace, and skillfulness too — these I chose.
The goddess said: "So shall it be, O you of immortal majesty; never at any time do I speak falsely. Sixteen thousand wives shall be yours, and beloved standing among them, and likewise undecaying vigor."
"Foremost affection from your kinsmen I grant you, and the loveliness of your form; and seven hundred guests shall ever feast in your house."
Vāsudeva said: Having thus granted me boons, the god and the goddess, O Bhārata, vanished in that instant together with their attendant hosts, O elder brother of Bhīma.
All this exceedingly wondrous matter I recounted in full to the brāhmaṇa Upamanyu of surpassing splendor, O best of the Kurus.
And having made obeisance to the god of gods, he of firm vows declared: "There is none equal to Śarva in giving, none equal to Śarva in battle, no god equal to Śarva, no refuge equal to Śarva."
There was a seer in the Kṛta age, my son, renowned by the name of Taṇḍi; for ten thousand years the god was worshipped by him, devoted, with deep meditation. Hear now the outcome that came to him.
He beheld Mahādeva and praised the Lord with hymns: "You are the purifier of the pure, the goal of those who seek a goal, O most excellent one; the fiercely blazing splendor of splendors, the supreme austerity of austerities."
"O you to whom Viśvāvasu, Hiraṇyākṣa, and Puruhūta bow down, bestower of abundant blessings, O all-pervading Lord, O ancient truth — homage be to you!"
"For the ascetics striving in their endeavor, who dread birth and death, O all-pervading Lord, you are the giver of nirvāṇa, O thousand-rayed one; homage be to you, O abode of bliss!"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Brahmā, Śatakratu, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and the great seers do not know you in your true essence; how then shall we come to know you?"
"From you time proceeds, and in you time dissolves; you alone are that which is called Time, that which is called Puruṣa, and that which is called Brahman."
"Three forms of yours are recounted by the divine seers learned in ancient lore: that pertaining to the cosmic Person, to the self, and to beings and deities; and pertaining to the worlds, to higher knowledge, and to sacrifice — you alone are all these."
"Having known you, who dwell within the body of the self, hard to know even by the gods, the wise, set free, attain the supreme, disease-free state."
"For you, O all-pervading Lord, who desire it not, there is no birth or death in any manifold way; you are the gateway to heaven and to liberation — you both withhold and bestow."
"You alone are liberation and heaven; you indeed are desire and wrath; you alone are sattva, rajas, and tamas, and the below and the above."
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, Skanda and Indra, Savitṛ, Yama, Varuṇa and the Moon, Manu, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ — you are the lord of wealth, Kubera."
"Earth, wind, light, and the waters, speech, intellect — you are thought and mind, action, and both truth and untruth; you alone are being and non-being."
"The senses and the objects of the senses, and that abiding reality beyond primal nature — you alone are the existence transcending both the manifest and the unmanifest universe, the thinkable and the unthinkable."
"That which is the supreme Brahman, that which is the supreme abode, and the goal of the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga — that are you, O Lord; herein there is no doubt."
"Surely this day we have achieved our purpose; surely we have attained the goal of the good — that goal which here is reached by those whose minds are made pure through knowledge."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Alas, for a very long time we have been deluded, devoid of understanding, in that we knew not the supreme, eternal God whom the wise know."
"This very god, the bestower of grace upon his devotees, has now been reached by me in person through many births — the god whom, once known, one tastes immortality."
"That which is the eternal secret of gods, asuras, and men — the Brahman hidden in the cave of the heart, hard to be known even by the gods —"
"This very one is the blessed God, the maker of all, facing in every direction, the Self of all, the all-seeing, the all-pervading, the knower of all."
"Maker of breath, sustainer of breath, the breathing one, giver of breath, the goal of all that breathe; maker of bodies, sustainer of bodies, the embodied one, enjoyer of bodies, the goal of all the embodied."
"For those steadfast in the path of the inner self, for meditators and knowers of the Self, for those who desire no second death — the goal that is theirs, that is this Lord."
"And this one bestows upon all beings their auspicious or inauspicious destinies; and this one ordains the birth and death of all creatures."
"And this Lord is the giver of perfection to the seers who desire perfection; and this Lord is the giver of liberation to the twice-born who desire liberation."
"Having brought forth all the worlds beginning with the earth, along with the dwellers in heaven, the god sustains them with his eight bodily forms, and grants their boons."
"From him everything proceeds; in him everything is established; and in him it goes to dissolution — he is the one eternal."
"This is the supreme world of truth for the good who desire truth; he is the final release of the liberated and the absolute solitude of those who proclaim the Self."
"This Lord is kept hidden in the cave of the heart by the perfected beings beginning with Brahmā, so that he might not be manifest to gods, asuras, and men."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"You, that Bhava, the gods, asuras, and men do not truly know, deluded indeed and led astray by this very one who dwells within the heart."
"But to those who take refuge in him through the discipline of devotion, O Bhārata, this dweller in the heart reveals the Self to them by the Self."
"Whom having known, there is no birth nor death again; whom having understood as the supreme object of knowledge, nothing further remains to be known."
"Whom having gained as the supreme gain, one deems nothing greater thereafter; one comes to that highest attainment, subtle as the breath of life, which brings the undecaying."
"Whom the followers of Sāṃkhya, knowers of the truth of the guṇas, versed in the Sāṃkhya teaching, delighting in subtle knowledge, having first known, are freed from their bonds."
"Whom the knowers of the Veda know as the object of knowledge, established in the Vedānta, and whom those ever intent on breath-control enter into and ceaselessly recite."
"He, as the Sun, is called the gateway of those who travel the path of the gods; and he, as the Moon, is called the gateway of those who travel the path of the fathers."
"He is the varied course of time in years, ages, and the rest, and presence and absence in the present moment, and the southern and northern courses of the sun."
"Thus did Prajāpati of old, having worshipped him with many hymns, choose for his son the one named the Blue-and-Red."
"Whom the reciters of many ṛc-verses extol with the Ṛg verses in the ritual act, and whom, threefold to be known, the adhvaryu priests offer oblation to with the Yajus formulas in the sacrifice."
"And whom the singers of the Sāman, pure of mind, hymn with the Sāman chants — he is remembered as the supreme womb of sacrifice and its supreme lord."
"Night and day are his ears and eyes, the fortnights and months his head and arms; the seasons are his potency, austerity his firmness, the year his hidden secret, with thighs and feet of vast measure."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Death, Yama, and the fire-god, Time impetuous in destruction — he is the supreme source of time, and he is this eternal Time itself."
"The moon and the sun with the constellations, with the planets and the wind, the Pole Star and the seven seers, and the seven worlds as well —"
"Primal matter, the great principle, the unmanifest, ending in the particularized, together with its modifications, all from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, the elements and whatever is being and non-being —"
"The eight constituent natures, and that which is beyond the natures — the whole of this revolves as a portion of this god."
"This is the supreme bliss, which is also the eternal; this is the goal of the dispassionate, this the highest state of the good."
"This is the abode free from agitation, this the eternal Brahman; for those learned in the scriptures, the Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas, this is the supreme object of meditation and the highest abode."
"This is that supreme limit, this that supreme part; this is that supreme perfection, this that supreme goal."
"This is that supreme peace, this the highest beatitude, attaining which the creators thought, 'We have accomplished all that is to be done.'"
"This is contentment, this is perfection, this is revelation, this is tradition; for the wise who are steadfast in the path of the inner self, this is the undecaying attainment."
"For those who sacrifice, desiring sacrifice, with rites of abundant priestly fees, the divine goal won together with the gods — that goal are you, O eternal one."
"For those who practice austerity through recitation, oblation, vows, penances, restraints, and the mortifying of the body, O god — the goal that lies in the Vairāja world, that goal are you."
"For those who have renounced action and the dispassionate, here and there — the goal that lies in the abode of Brahmā, that goal are you, O eternal one."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"For those who desire no second death, who abide in the highest dispassion, and for the modifications dissolved back into their source — that goal are you, O eternal one."
"For those steadfast in knowledge and discernment, the goal that is indescribable, stainless, the absolute solitude, the supreme — that goal, O god, are you."
"These five goals, declared in the Vedas, the śāstras, and the Purāṇas, are recounted; they are won only by your grace, and otherwise are not won, O all-pervading Lord."
Thus Taṇḍi, through the power of his austerity, praised the imperishable Lord, and sang the supreme Brahman which the maker of the world had sung of old.
"Brahmā, Śatakratu, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and the great seers know you not" — and at this Śiva, well pleased, then spoke to him.
"He shall be undecaying and imperishable, free of sorrow, renowned, endowed with splendor, and possessed of divine knowledge."
"Approachable by the seers and a composer of aphorisms, your son shall be, by my grace, O best of the twice-born; of this there is no doubt."
"What desire, then, shall I grant you this day? Speak, my child, of what you wish." With folded hands he said this: "Let my devotion to you be firm."
Having thus granted the boon, the god, revered by the divine seers and praised by the wise, vanished then and there.
When the Lord with his attendants had vanished, O lord of the Yādavas, the seer, having returned to his hermitage, recounted all this to me here.
And those names, renowned from the first, which Taṇḍi declared to me, O best of men, hear them now for your perfection.
In the Vedas the Grandsire proclaimed ten thousand names of Śarva, and in the scriptures, likewise, a thousand names.
These secret names of the Blessed One, O Acyuta, O lord of the gods, the sage Taṇḍi declared of old, by the grace of the deity, to that great-souled one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vāsudeva said: Then, my dear Yudhiṣṭhira, that brahmin-sage, having purified himself, with palms joined in reverence, recited to me the litany of names from the beginning.
Upamanyu said: With names declared by Brahmā, declared by the seers, born of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, renowned throughout all the worlds, I shall praise Sthāṇu.
With names ordained by the great ones, true, perfected, accomplishing every aim, fashioned in devotion by the sage Taṇḍi, whose self was made one with the god.
With names handed down as spoken, famed throughout the world, given by sages who see the truth — supreme, primordial, leading to heaven, the welfare of all beings, auspicious, heard everywhere in the universe, brought down from the world of Brahmā.
That supreme mystery, eternal, declared by Brahmā, I shall now speak, O best of the Yadu line; listen to me with full attention.
As one devoted, you hold the god Bhava to be the Supreme, the highest Lord; therefore I shall cause you to hear that eternal Absolute.
No one is able to tell in full detail the glories of Śarva — not even one wholly absorbed in yoga, not even in a hundred years.
He whose beginning, middle, and end not even the gods can reach — who, O Mādhava, could tell his attributes in their entirety?
Yet of the mighty god, in words and syllables compressed in meaning, I shall recount his deeds as best I can, and by his grace alone.
Without first obtaining his sanction, the Lord cannot here be praised; only when granted leave by him may one ever praise Bhava.
Of him without beginning or end, the source of all, the great-souled one whose origin is unmanifest, I shall set forth some portion of his names.
Of the giver of boons, the most excellent, the cosmic-formed, the wise one — hear the enumeration of names that was spoken by the Lotus-born.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The ten thousand names that the great Grandsire declared — churning these in his mind, he drew them forth as clarified butter is drawn from curds.
As gold is the essence of the mountain, as honey is the essence of the flower, as cream is the essence of clarified butter, so this essence was drawn forth.
This litany, which removes all sin and is joined with the four Vedas, is to be mastered with effort and held fast by one of disciplined soul — bringing peace, fostering prosperity, slaying demons, purifying, and great.
This is to be given to one who is devoted, faithful, and a believer — never to one without faith, to an unbeliever, or to one whose self is unconquered.
And whoever reviles the god, the Self of all beings, the wielder of the Pināka bow — he, O Kṛṣṇa, goes to hell together with his forebears and his followers.
This is meditation, this is yoga, this is the unsurpassed object of contemplation; this is the prayer to be murmured, this is knowledge, this the supreme mystery; knowing this, even at the hour of death one attains the highest goal.
Pure, auspicious, meritorious, blessed, and supreme — this I shall now recite, O mighty-armed one: the highest of all hymns of praise.
Brahmā, the Grandsire of all the worlds, having composed this of old, appointed it to sovereignty over all the celestial hymns.
From that time onward this hymn of the great-souled Lord has been renowned in the world as the King of Hymns, honored by the immortals; and this King of Hymns was brought down from the world of Brahmā.
Because Taṇḍi proclaimed it of old, it came to be called the work of Taṇḍi; and from heaven to this earthly world it was indeed brought down by Taṇḍi.
Auspicious among all auspicious things, destroying every sin — this I shall recite, O mighty-armed one: the highest of all hymns.

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
The Path of moon and sun, the Comet, the Seizing Planet, the Lord of planets, the Excellent; the Mountain, the Mountain-dweller, the Maker, He who loosed the arrow at the deer-form, the Sinless.
Of great austerity, of terrible austerity, the Undejected, the Helper of the wretched; the Maker of the year, the Sacred Formula, the Measure, the Supreme Austerity.
The Yogin, the One to be united with, the Great Seed, the Great-seeded, of great austerity; He of golden seed, the All-knowing, of goodly seed, the Bull-borne.
The Ten-armed, the Unblinking, the Blue-throated, the Husband of Umā; the Cosmic-formed, the Self-supreme, the Mighty Hero, the Strong, the Host.
The Maker of hosts, the Lord of hosts, the Sky-clad, and the Desirable; the Pure, the Supreme, the Sacred Formula, Hara who brings every state of being to pass.
Bearer of the water-pot, the Bowman, the Arrow-handed, He who holds a skull; armed with the thunderbolt, the śataghnī, the sword, and the spear — the Weaponed, the Great.
The Ladle-handed, the Fair-formed, Radiance, the Maker of radiance, the Treasure-store; the Turbaned, the Fair-faced, the Lofty, and likewise the Bowed.
The Tall, the Tawny-haired, the Goodly Ford, and the Dark One; the Jackal-formed, the All-purposed, the Shaven-headed, the Ringed, He of the water-pot.
The Unborn, the Deer-formed, the Bearer of fragrance, He of the matted braid; of upward-flowing seed, with phallus raised, lying on high, the very vault of heaven.
The Triple-braided, the Rag-clad, Rudra, the Army-commander, the All-pervading; the Day-rover and the Night-rover, of fierce wrath, of brilliant splendor.
Slayer of the elephant, slayer of demons, the World itself, the Upholder of the world, the Mine of virtues; of the form of lion and tiger, wrapped in a garment of fresh hide.
The Yogin of Time, the Great Roar, the Dwelling-place of all, the Crossroads; the Night-rover, the Wanderer among ghosts, the Wanderer among spirits, the Great Lord.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of many forms, of many treasures, the Support of all, of boundless course; Lover of the dance, ever-dancing, the Dancer, the Sporter of all.
The Terrible, of great austerity, the Noose, the Eternal, the Mountain-rover, the Sky; the Thousand-handed, the Victorious, Resolve itself, the Blameless.
The Unforbearing, the Forbearing-souled, the Destroyer of the sacrifice, the Slayer of desire; the Despoiler of Dakṣa's sacrifice, the All-enduring, and the Mean between extremes.
Robber of radiance, slayer of might, the Joyful, the Aim, the Conquered, the Best; of deep voice, the Profound, He whose strength and mount are profound.
Of the banyan's form, the Banyan, abiding in the tree's hollow, the All-pervading; of sharp heat, the Tawny-horsed, the Companion, the Knower of the time of action.
Propitiated by Viṣṇu, the Sacrifice, the Ocean, the Mare's-mouth fire; the Ally of the fire that eats oblations, the Tranquil-souled, the Oblation-eater himself.
Of fierce radiance, of great radiance, the Victory, the Knower of the hour of triumph; the Pathway of the lights, Attainment, Union, and also Strife.
The Crested, the Staff-bearer, the Matted-haired, the Flaming; Born of form, Crowning the head, the Strong; the Flute-player, the Drummer, the Cymbalist, Time itself, the Kālakaṭaṃkaṭa.
The Ordainer of the array of stars, the Increase of qualities, Dissolution, the Inaccessible; the Lord of creatures, He whose arms are the quarters, the Apportioning, the Face-turned-everywhere.
The Liberator, the Host of the gods, Sprung from golden armor; Born of the loins, the Wanderer in strength, the Great Wanderer, and likewise the Praised.
Sounding all the trumpets, the Possessor of every instrument; of serpent form, dwelling in caverns, the Gold-garlanded, the Knower of the waves.
The Thrice-ten gods, the Holder of the three times, the Looser of every bond of action; yet the Binding of the chiefs of the asuras, the Destroyer of foes in battle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Grace of Sāṃkhya, the Ill-clad, the Served by all the good; the Onrushing, the Apportioning, the Incomparable, the Knower of the sacrificial share.
The Dwelling of all, the Wanderer everywhere, the Ill-clad, the Wealth-giver, the Immortal; the Golden, the Maker of gold, the Sacrifice, the Upholder of all, the Supreme Sustainer.
The Red-eyed, the Great-eyed, the Eye of victory, the Skilled; the Gathering-up, the Restraint, the Maker, Clothed in the slough of serpents.
The Foremost and the Not-foremost, the Body and the Body's increase, the Granter of every desire; Gracious at all times, of goodly strength, bearing the form of strength.
Of the form of the treasure-store that is space, the Down-striker, the Serpent, the Sky-goer; of fierce form, the Ray, the Sun, He whose beams are wealth, of brilliant splendor.
Swift as wealth, of mighty speed, swift as thought, the Night-rover; Dwelling in all, dwelling with Fortune, Hara the giver of instruction.
The Sage, the Lord of his own self in the world, the One to be feasted, the Thousandfold giver; the Bird and the Bird-formed, the Surpassingly radiant, the Lord of peoples.
Frenzy, of the form of passion, the Maker of wealth from wealth, the Hairy one; Vāmadeva and the Lovely, He who faces east and south, the Dwarf.
The Withdrawer of perfected yoga, the Perfected, the Accomplisher of every aim; the Mendicant and the Mendicant-formed, the Horned, the Gentle, the Imperishable.
The Great-armied, and Viśākha, He of the sixtyfold portion, the Lord of cattle; the Thunderbolt-handed, the Prop, and the Stayer of armies.
The Season, the Maker of seasons, Time, the Sweet, the Maker of sweetness, the Unmoving; Sprung from the lord of trees, He of the array of strength, ever honored in the hermitages.
The Chaste student, the World-rover, the Wanderer everywhere, the Knower of good conduct; the Ruler, the Lord, Time, the Night-wanderer, the Bearer of the Pināka bow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nandīśvara and Nandin, the Gladdening, the Increaser of joy; the Slayer of Bhaga's eye, Time, the best of those who know the Absolute.
The Four-faced, of mighty emblem, and likewise of fair emblem; the Overseer of the emblem, the Overseer of the gods, the Overseer of the worlds, the Bearer of the yoke of the ages.
The Overseer of the seed, the Maker of the seed, He who attends upon the inmost Self, the Strong; the Maker of legend, the Aeon, Gautama, and the Lord of waters.
Pride and the Prideless, the Conqueror of pride, the Subdued, the Subduer, the Seer; the Maker of the world, the Lord of beasts, the Great Maker, the Mighty Herb.
The Imperishable, the Supreme Absolute, the Mighty, and Śakra himself; Right conduct and Misconduct, the Pure-souled, the Pure, the Honored, the Course of the mind.
Abundant in grace, the Dreamer, the Mirror, and the Vanquisher of foes; the Maker of the Vedas, the Maker of the aphorisms, the Learned, the Crusher in battle.
He who dwells in the great cloud, the awesome one, the subduer; flame of fire, mighty blaze, the deeply smoke-hued, the oblation offered and the offering itself.
The virile one, Śaṃkara the bestower of peace, the eternal, the radiant, he whose banner is smoke; the dark-blue one, eager in his limbs, the resplendent, the unrestrained.
Giver of blessing and the very state of blessing; the partaker, the apportioner, the swift; the embrace, the great-limbed, of mighty womb, supreme, ever young.
Of dark hue and of golden hue, he who is the senses of all embodied beings; great of foot, great of hand, of mighty frame, of vast renown.
Great of head, of great measure, great of eye, whose dwelling is the quarters of space; great of tooth, great of ear, mightily endowed, great of jaw.
Great of nose, great-throated as a conch, great of neck, haunter of the cremation-ground; broad of chest, mighty-breasted, the inmost Self, whose abode is among the deer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The pendant one, with hanging lip, master of great illusion, the ocean of waters; great of tooth, great of fang, great of tongue, great of mouth.
Great of nail, great of hair, of great locks, with mighty matted braids; without a rival, the gracious one, the ground of all conviction, accomplished upon the mountain.
He who shows tenderness and he who is without attachment, the unconquered, the great sage; in form like a tree, whose emblem is the tree, the fire, borne upon the wind.
The ringed one, whose seat is Meru, breaker of the pride of gods and Dānavas; he whose head is the Atharva, whose face is the Sāman, whose unbounded gaze is the thousand verses of the Ṛk.
He whose feet and arms are the Yajus, the hidden one, the manifest, and likewise the moving; of unfailing purpose, the gracious, the approachable, fair to behold.
Lover of offerings, Śarva, the golden, the gold-bright, the steadfast; the navel, maker of joy, he who is to be meditated upon, lord enthroned upon the lotus, the unmoving.
The twelvefold, the terrifier, the primal; the sacrifice and he who is composed within the sacrifice; the night, the age of strife, and Time itself, the sea-monster, worshipped through all time.
He who is with his hosts and maker of hosts, the charioteer who fosters all beings; couched upon ashes, guardian of ashes, become as ash, the tree, the troop.
He without host, and the dissolution, the great-souled, worshipped by all; the stake, the triple-staked, the perfected, the pure, attended by the spirits.
Abiding in the hermitage, seated as a dove, maker of the universe, the choicest lord; the Branch and Viśākha, copper-lipped, a net of lotuses, the firmly resolved.
The tawny and the non-tawny, the hero, and life itself, the higher and the lower; the Gandharva, indeed Aditi, Tārkṣya, the easily known, the skilled charioteer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whose weapon is the battle-axe, the god, doer of all purpose, the good kinsman; bearer of the gourd-lute, of mighty wrath, of upward-drawn seed, who couches upon the waters.
The fierce, the maker of lineage, the lineage, the sound of the flute, the blameless; whose form is in every limb, the wielder of illusion, the true friend, the wind and the fire.
The binder and maker of bonds, and the loosener of the close-drawn fetter; he is the foe of the sacrifice, he the foe of desire, great of fang, mighty in arms.
The arm indeed, the blameless, Śarva, Śaṃkara, the bestower of peace who is without possession; lord of the immortals, the Great God, the All-god, slayer of the foes of the gods.
Ahirbudhnya and Nirṛti, Cekitāna, and likewise Hari; Ajaikapād and the bearer of the skull, the triple-staked, the unconquered, the auspicious one, Śiva.
Dhanvantari, he whose banner is smoke, Skanda, and likewise Vaiśravaṇa; Dhātṛ and Śakra and Viṣṇu, Mitra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhruva, the upholder.
The source of power, the all-pervading, the wind, Aryaman, Savitṛ, the sun; the lofty, and Vidhātṛ, Māndhātṛ, the fosterer of beings.
The sacred ford of delight and the eloquent, bearer of every desire and quality; lotus-wombed, of mighty womb, moon-faced, the ravisher of the mind.
The mighty and the wholly tranquil, the ancient, skilled in what is meritorious; doer of deeds, whose form is Time, become the Kurus, the Great Lord, Maheśvara.
The refuge of all, who couches upon darbha grass, lord of all that breathes; foremost among god of gods, the unattached, the existent and the non-existent, knower of every jewel.
Dweller on the peak of Kailāsa, who has his refuge on the Himavat mountain; sweeper-away of banks and maker of banks, of manifold lore, giver of much.
The merchant, the increaser, the tree, the mongoose, the sandal, the leaf-shelter; firm of neck, of mighty collarbone, the unwavering, and the great healing herb.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Accomplisher of true ends and the one whose end is accomplished, supreme in metre and grammar; the lion's roar, lion-fanged, lion-gaited, lion-borne.
His own self the source of power, the Time of the world, the rhythm, the good of the worlds, the tree; the dappled one, whose body is the nine wheels, garlanded with banners, the well-disposed.
The dwelling of beings, lord of beings, blameless as day and night; the bearer of all beings, their resting-place, the all-pervading, the existent, Bhava.
The unerring, the restrained, indeed the horse, the sustenance, the upholder of life-breath; steadfast, wise, skilful, honoured, lord of the aeons.
The herder, lord of cattle, the village, clad in a hide of leather, Hara; golden-armed, and likewise the guardian of the cave for those who enter.
The well-established, of great joy, conqueror of desire, conqueror of the senses; Gāndhāra and Surāla, who delights in the works of austerity, the bow.
Of great song, of mighty dance, attended by the hosts of Apsarases; the great-bannered, the bow, the upholder, follower of many ridges, the ever-moving.
He to whom all is to be made known, the indwelling presence, bearer of every fragrance and joy; the gateway, the deliverer, the wind, who courses about from one place alone.
The union, the increaser, the aged, the mightily aged, lord of the hosts; the eternal, his own self his only helper, lord of gods and Asuras, the master.
The yoked and the strong-armed, the twofold and the well-jointed; Āṣāḍha and Suṣāḍha, the fixed one, slayer of Hari's foes, Hara.
The body for those caught in the turning round of birth, best of the Vasus, the great path; bearer of heads, the deliberating one, adorned with every auspicious mark.
The axle and he yoked to the chariot, the master of all yoga, of mighty strength; the sacred tradition and what lies beyond tradition, god of the holy fords, the great charioteer.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The lifeless and the life-giving, the sacred word, fair of eye, of many a rough place; rich in jewels, red of limb, who knows the drinking-down of the great ocean.
The root, the vast, indeed the immortal, the manifest and unmanifest, the treasury of austerity; the ascent and the descent, sweeper-away of mountains, of mighty penance.
Marshalled like an army, the great cosmic age, maker of age upon age, Hari; whose form is the aeon, of mighty form, the purifier, the unfathomable, the mountain.
He who quenches all by right reasoning, the foot, the learned, indeed like the unmoving mountain; many-garlanded, of great garland, of fair garland, of many eyes.
The expanse, the salt, the well, the blossom, whose rising bears fruit; the bull, whose limb is marked with the bull, the bearer of jewel and bilva, wearer of matted locks.
The moon, the emanation, fair of face, the god, armed with every weapon, the forbearing; the surrender, born of nectar, of sweet fragrance, the great bow.
Garlanded with fragrance, the Blessed One, the rousing of all works; the churner, the abundant, the arm, the whole, the all-seeing.
He who beats time swiftly, who beats time with his hand, of upward-knit frame, the bearing one; the parasol, the well-sheltering, the renowned, the refuge of all worlds, the great.
The shaven-headed, the formless, the misshapen, the staff-bearing and bald, the transforming one; tawny-eyed, the eminence, the wielder of the thunderbolt, of blazing tongue, thousand-footed.
Thousand-headed, lord of the gods, made of all gods, the teacher; thousand-armed, present in every limb, the refuge-giving, maker of all worlds.
The pure, the threefold sweetness, the sacred word, the youngest, the dark and tawny; fashioner of the staff of Brahman, the hundred-slayer, holder of a hundred nooses.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Lotus-wombed, of mighty womb, womb of the Brahman, sprung from the waters; the ray of light, maker of the sacred word, Brahmā, knower of the Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa, the goal.
Of endless forms, not of a single self, of keen splendour, the self-existent; whose self moves ever upward, lord of cattle, swift as the wind, fleet as thought.
Sandal-anointed, foremost in his garland of lotuses, who delivers across by fragrance, the Man; great-wreathed with karṇikāra blossoms, blue-crested, bearer of the Pināka bow.
Lord of Umā, beloved of Umā, who upholds the Jāhnavī, consort of Umā; the boon, the boar, the giver of boons, lord of boons, of mighty resounding voice.
Of great grace, the subduer, slayer of foes, white and tawny; glad of soul, of disciplined soul, of restrained soul, upholder of primal nature.
Born at every side, Tārkṣya, the common ground of dharma, the choicest; the self of all that moves and is still, of subtle soul, the good bull, lord of the cattle-bull.
Seer of the Sādhyas, the Vasu, the Āditya, Vivasvān, Savitṛ, the gracious; Vyāsa, the gathering-together of all, the expanse, the turning round, the guiding course.
The season, the year, the month, the fortnight, the completion of reckoning; the moment-fraction, the instant, the particle, the measure, the muhūrta, the day, the nights, the breaths of time.
The field of the universe, the seed of all creatures, the sign, the primal, indeed the blameless; the existent and the non-existent, the manifest and the unmanifest, father, mother, grandsire.
The gate of heaven, the gate of creatures, the gate of release, the triple heaven; extinction and gladdening too, the world of Brahman, the supreme goal.
Fashioner of gods and Asuras, the refuge of gods and Asuras; teacher of gods and Asuras, the god, saluted by gods and Asuras.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The chief minister of gods and Asuras, the resort of the hosts of gods and Asuras; overseer of the hosts of gods and Asuras, foremost leader of the hosts of gods and Asuras.
The god beyond the gods, the divine seer, giver of boons to gods and Asuras; lord of gods and Asuras, the god, the Great Lord of gods and Asuras.
Made of all gods, the inconceivable, whose self is the deities, self-arisen; the sprouting forth, the thrice-striding, the healer, the stainless, clad in stainless raiment.
The praiseworthy, the elephant, the tiger among gods, the lion among gods, the bull among men; foremost and choicest of the wise, the best, the highest of the high among all gods.
The well-applied, the resplendent, the thunderbolt, Īśāna the ruler, the lord, the imperishable; the teacher, the beloved, the innate, the creation, the pure, who bears all upon him.
The horned, lover of the peak, the tawny, king of kings, the unailing; the delightful, the host of gods, the ceasing, the means of all attainment.
Eyed upon the brow, his body the universe, the fawn-hued, possessed of the lustre of the Brahman; and lord too of all things unmoving, increaser of restraint and the senses.
He whose aim is accomplished, the welfare of all beings, the inconceivable, true to his vow, the pure; lord of vows, the supreme Brahman, the highest goal of the liberated.
The wholly released, of unfettered splendour, the glorious, the increaser of glory, the world itself: thus, as each was foremost, has the Blessed One been hymned by me in devotion.
Him whom the gods, with Brahmā at their head, do not know, whom the great seers do not know, that one worthy to be praised, worshipped, and revered, the Lord of the world — who shall hymn him?
Setting devotion alone before me, having first obtained his leave, I have hymned the lord of sacrifice, the Vasu, the best of the wise.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who praises Śiva the god with these names that increase well-being, ever steadfast and grown pure, attains the Self by the self.
For this is the supreme Brahman, sung by the Self-existent himself; and with it the seers and the gods praise that which is beyond.
The Great God, when praised, is gladdened by the names of his own self; the Blessed One, compassionate to his devotees, establishes them within himself.
And likewise among men, those who are foremost among men, the faithful and the believing, through many births and many hymns of praise,
waking and sleeping, walking or halted upon the road, they praise him and are themselves extolled, and they are content and rejoice, through thousands of millions of births in the manifold wombs of transmigration.
In the creature whose sin is wholly cleansed there is born devotion to Bhava; and once arisen, devotion to Bhava becomes undivided, with the whole of one's being.
The cause of such devotion has been ordained for him who is wholly liberated in every way; this is hard to attain even among the gods, and is not to be had among men.
Unobstructed, unwavering, and unswerving is devotion to Rudra; and it is by his grace alone that such devotion arises in men, by which those whose minds are fixed upon his being attain the supreme perfection.
Those men who have come to him with their whole being, taking him as the Supreme, the god who cherishes those who take refuge in him would lift up out of the round of existence.
Thus the other gods do not accomplish the release of men from the cycle of birth, not even by the power of austerity, as does Mahādeva.
Thus, O Kṛṣṇa, was the Blessed One, lord of the existent and the nonexistent, clad in his hide, praised by Taṇḍi—one like unto Indra and of purified understanding.
This hymn to the Blessed One Brahmā himself bore in memory; Brahmā declared it to Śakra, and Śakra declared it to Death.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Death declared it to the Rudras, and from the Rudras it came to Taṇḍi; by mighty austerity it was won by Taṇḍi in the abode of Brahmā.
Taṇḍi declared it to Śukra; the descendant of Bhṛgu spoke it to Gautama; and Gautama spoke it, O Mādhava, to Manu the son of Vivasvat.
Manu spoke it to Nārāyaṇa the Sādhya, his beloved and wise one; and the blessed Sādhya, the imperishable Nārāyaṇa, spoke it to Yama.
The blessed Yama, son of Vivasvat, spoke it to Nāciketas; and Nāciketas, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis, spoke it to Mārkaṇḍeya.
From Mārkaṇḍeya I received it through self-discipline, O Janārdana; and to you too, O slayer of foes, I now give this renowned hymn—conferring heaven, health, long life, prosperity, and strength as well.
No hindrance do the Dānavas work upon him, nor the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, the Piśācas and the demons that devour, the Guhyakas, nor even the serpents.
He who, having become pure, chaste, and master of his senses, recites it for a year with unbroken discipline obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the great yogin, the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, spoke: "Recite it, my son—blessings upon you; may Maheśvara be pleased with you.
Of old, my son, while I performed the highest austerity upon Meru for the sake of offspring, O great king, this hymn was recited by me.
I obtained those desires of mine, O delight of Pāṇḍu's line; and you too shall obtain all your desires from Śarva."
Then the Four-headed one spoke, the beloved friend of Śakra, renowned by the name Ālambāyana, whose nature was compassion:
"Having reached Gokarṇa and performed austerity there for a hundred years, I won—of sons not born of any womb, self-controlled, knowers of dharma, and radiant,
of the ageless, the sorrowless, who live a hundred thousand years—a hundred sons from Śarva of old, O son of King Pāṇḍu."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The blessed Vālmīki too addressed Yudhiṣṭhira: "In a dispute over a Sāman chant I was told by the sages, 'You are a slayer of a brāhmaṇa,' and in an instant, O Bhārata, I was possessed by that unrighteousness.
Then I, taking refuge, praised the sinless Lord Īśāna, and helpless though I was, I was freed from that sin; and he, the destroyer of suffering, the slayer of Tripura, said to me, 'Your glory shall be foremost.'"
And the son of Jamadagni, foremost of the upholders of dharma, addressed the son of Kuntī, standing amid the seers like blazing fire, dear child:
"Tormented by the slaying of my father and of brāhmaṇas, O eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, having made myself pure, I went for refuge to Mahādeva, O king.
With his names I praised the god, and thereupon Bhava was pleased; and the god gave me the axe and divine weapons as well.
'No sin shall be yours this day, and you shall be unconquerable; death shall have no power over you, and you shall be full of glory.'"
"Thus the Blessed One, the crested one whose very form is Śiva, spoke to me; and all that I have attained is by the grace of that wise god."
And Asita Devala addressed the king, the son of Pāṇḍu: "By a curse of Śakra, O son of Kuntī, my accumulated merit was perishing; but Bhava restored to me that merit, my foremost glory, and my life as well."
The seer named Gṛtsamada, the beloved friend of Śakra, blessed and radiant as Bṛhaspati, addressed the descendant of Ajamīḍha:
"The blessed one named Vasiṣṭha, son of Manu Cākṣuṣa, while the inconceivable Śatakratu's sacrificial session of a thousand years was in progress, spoke these words when a Sāman had been chanted by me:
'O best of the twice-born, the Rathantara is not rightly rendered; consider it again with your mind, casting off your excitement, O foremost of the twice-born. You have committed a sin that bears no sacrifice, O most wicked-minded one.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus, in great wrath he angrily uttered these further words: 'Bereft of wisdom, wretched, forever fearful, a wanderer of the woods shall you become—for ten thousand years and ten and eight hundred more,
in a region without water or pasture, shunned by deer and other beasts, with no trees fit for sacrifice, haunted by antelope and lion—there you shall become a savage beast beset with great suffering.'
At the close of that utterance, O Pārtha, I was indeed born a beast; then, when I had come to him for refuge, the yogin Maheśvara said to me:
'Ageless and deathless shall you become, free of sorrow; even and equable shall your happiness be—and may the sacrificial rite of you both prosper.'"
"Thus does this Blessed and all-pervading Lord bestow his favors—the supreme Ordainer and Disposer, and ever the giver of pleasure and pain.
Inconceivable is this Blessed One in deed, in thought, and in speech; not even one learned in knowledge, dear child, O best of warriors, is his equal."
Jaigīṣavya said: "The eightfold lordly power was given to me of old by the mighty Blessed One, with but little effort, at Vārāṇasī, O Yudhiṣṭhira."
Gārgya said: "The wondrous knowledge of time, with its sixty-four branches, he gave to me, well pleased by a sacrifice of the mind, upon the bank of the Sarasvatī, O Pāṇḍava.
And he gave me a thousand sons, all alike, expounders of the sacred word, and a lifespan—for me together with my sons—of a hundred and ten thousand years."
Parāśara said: "Having propitiated Śarva of old, O king, I pondered in my mind—desiring a son of great austerity, great splendor, great yoga, and great fame, a Vedavyāsa, an abode of glory, devoted to brahman, and compassionate of nature:
'Might there be granted to me from Maheśvara the son I desire?' Knowing this resolve in my heart, the best of the gods spoke to me:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'As the fruit of his being born of me, he shall be Kṛṣṇa, and in the creation of Manu Sāvarṇa he shall be one of the seven seers.
He shall be the divider of the Vedas and the continuer of the Kuru line, and the author of the epic history; your son shall be a benefactor of the world.
That great sage shall become beloved of Mahendra, ageless and deathless, O Parāśara—he, your son.'
Having spoken thus, that Blessed One vanished then and there, O Yudhiṣṭhira—the great yogin, the valiant, the imperishable, the undecaying."
Māṇḍavya said: "When, though no thief, on suspicion of theft I was impaled upon the stake, I praised the god while fixed there, and Maheśvara said to me:
'You shall be freed from the stake, and you shall live a hundred million years; nor shall the pain caused by the stake be yours, O brāhmaṇa, and free of mental and bodily afflictions shall you be.
Since your self, O sage, has come forth from the fourth quarter, you shall be without compare; make your birth bear fruit indeed.
The fruitful bathing in sacred fords you shall attain without hindrance, and an imperishable heaven, mighty and exalted, I bestow upon you, O brāhmaṇa.'
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the most excellent, borne upon the bull, Maheśvara, O great king, clad in his hide and of mighty radiance, foremost of the gods together with his hosts, vanished then and there."
Gālava said: "Dismissed with leave by Viśvāmitra, I came to my father; then my mother, sorrowing and weeping bitterly, said to me:
'Your father does not behold you, dear child—his son adorned with the Vedas, dismissed with leave by Kauśika, young, self-controlled, and sinless.'
Hearing my mother's words, despairing of seeing my father, with self subdued I beheld Mahādeva, and he said to me:
'Your father and your mother and you yourself, my son, shall be free of death; enter quickly, and you shall behold your father in his dwelling.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dismissed with leave by the Blessed One, having gone home, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I beheld my father, dear lord, just come forth from completing his offering.
Having touched water and taken up the fuel-sticks and the kuśa grass, and having set down those holy implements within the dwelling, my father, his eyes brimming with tears, said to me—
embracing me as I bowed and smelling my head, O Pāṇḍava: 'By good fortune are you seen by me, my son, accomplished in learning and come here at last.'"
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard these most wondrous deeds of the great-souled one recounted by the sages, the Pāṇḍava was filled with amazement.
Then Kṛṣṇa, foremost of the wise, spoke again to Yudhiṣṭhira, ever devoted to dharma, as the Lord might speak to Indra of the many invocations:
"The sun and moon, the wind and fire, the sky, the earth, the waters, the Vasus, the All-gods, the Ordainer, Aryaman, Śukra and Bṛhaspati, the Rudras together with the Sādhyas, Varuṇa the guardian of wealth,
Brahmā, Śakra, the Wind, the sacred word, truth, the Vedas, the sacrifices, the priestly fee, the bearers of the Vedas, Soma, the sacrificer, and whatever is offered and the oblation itself, protection, consecration, and whatever observances there are,
the cries Svāhā and Vaṣaṭ, the brāhmaṇas, the offspring of the divine cow, dharma, the wheel and the moving wheel of time, glory, self-restraint, intelligent steadfastness, the auspicious and the inauspicious, and the seven sages—
the foremost intellect, perception by mind and sight, attainment in touch, and the attainment that crowns deeds, the hosts of the gods—the drinkers of warm vapor and the drinkers of Soma, the Lekhas, the Suyāmas, the Tuṣitas, the Brahmakāyas,
the Ābhāsvaras, the drinkers of fragrance, the sustainers of sight, those opposed in speech and those opposed in mind, the pure gods and those who delight in extinction, those who feed on touch, the beholders, and the drinkers of clarified butter—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
those who abide in thought and are chief among the gods, and whatever other deities there are, O descendant of Ajamīḍha, the Suparṇas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, and Dānavas, the Yakṣas, the serpents, and the Cāraṇas—
the subtle, the gross, the soft, and what is not subtle, pleasure, pain, and what lies between pleasure and pain, Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and what is highest of the high—know all that I have named to be sprung from Śarva.
Sprung from him are the makers of beings, the most excellent; all the gods are guardians of this world, who, entering this earth, have protected the ancient creation of that god.
Searching with my mind, I would praise some truth for the sake of life; I am bowed down. May that god grant the boons desired here; may the undecaying Lord, ever praised by us, bestow them."
That man who, restraining his senses and having become pure, recites this hymn with unbroken discipline, self-controlled, for one year—he would obtain the fruit that lies in the horse sacrifice.
A brāhmaṇa would gain all the Vedas, a king would conquer the whole earth, a vaiśya would gain profit and skill, and a śūdra would win a good course after death and happiness as well.
Having made this king of hymns, they fixed their minds upon Rudra—the hymn that removes all faults, meritorious, purifying, and glory-bestowing.
As many as are the pores of the hair upon his body, O Bhārata, for so many thousands of years does that man dwell in heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "This thing that is called 'shared dharma,' O bull of the Bhāratas—how has it come to be enjoined for women at the time of the taking of the hand in marriage?
Is this the law of the seers, or of Prajāpati, or indeed of the asuras—this 'shared dharma' that was declared of old by the great sages?
A very great doubt is this, and a contradiction, in my view: the shared dharma that holds here in this life—where, then, is it ordained to hold in the world beyond?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Does shared dharma belong to the dead in heaven, O grandsire? Yet one dies first while the other remains—tell me, where then is it?"
"When men are many, endowed with the fruits of diverse deeds, dwelling in diverse states of action, ending in diverse hells,
and when the author of the aphorisms lays down that 'women are untruthful'—since women are untruthful, dear lord, whence is shared dharma enjoined for them?
'Women are untruthful'—even in the Vedas this is so recited. This dharma, this ancient designation, this customary usage, this rule of rites—
all this appears to me an impenetrable thicket as I ponder it day and night; make all of this free of doubt for me, O grandsire, as the sacred revelation has it."
Of what nature this is, and just how it came to be ordained — let your honored self declare all of it to me in full, O profoundly wise one.
Bhīṣma said: On this matter too they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue of Aṣṭāvakra with the Quarter of Space, O descendant of Bharata.
In days of old, Aṣṭāvakra of great austerities, wishing to marry, sought the daughter of the high-souled sage Vadānya.
Suprabhā she was named, peerless in beauty upon the earth, foremost in virtues, of upright conduct, radiant in character.
That fair-eyed maiden, merely by the sight of her, stole away his heart, as a glorious belt of forest does in spring, heaped with blossoms.
The sage said to him: My daughter shall be given to you — hear me out. Go first to the holy northern quarter, and there you shall behold a sight.
Aṣṭāvakra said: What is it I am to behold there? Be pleased to tell me, sir; and even so shall I act now, just as your honored self shall instruct me.
Vadānya said: Passing beyond the realm of Kubera the Wealth-giver, and likewise beyond Himavat, having looked upon the abode of Rudra, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
thronged by his joyful attendants dancing with manifold faces, by Piśācas anointed with divine unguents, by woodland beings of every kind,
and with hand-claps for cymbals and rhythm beaten on wooden bars in even measure — by these, exultant and dancing, is Śarva there attended.
That divine abode upon the mountain is beloved of him, so we have heard recounted; ever present there is the god, and with him his auspicious attendants.
There the Goddess performed austerity most hard to bear for Śaṃkara's sake; therefore that place is dear to the god and to Umā alike — so runs the tradition.
There, on the northern side beside the god, is a great well; and the seasons, and Kālarātri the Night of Doom, both those that are divine and those that are mortal —
all of them, taking embodied form, there wait upon the god, so it is told. Passing beyond that dwelling, you must journey on.
Then you shall see a tract of dark-blue forest, resembling a rain-cloud, lovely and heart-captivating; and there you shall behold a woman.
An ascetic woman, greatly blessed, aged, established in her vows — her you must behold there, and reverence with all care.
Having seen her, you shall return, and then take my daughter's hand in marriage. If this compact be acceptable, let it be fulfilled — go thither.
Aṣṭāvakra said: So be it; I shall accomplish this. Without doubt I will go there where you bid me, O virtuous one; let your honored self prove true to his word.
