Bhīṣma said: Then that reverend one set out toward the supreme northern quarter, toward Himavat, best of mountains, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
That tiger among the twice-born, journeying to the great mountain Himavat, came upon the holy river Bāhudā, bestower of righteousness.
At the pure ford of Aśoka he bathed and made offerings to the gods, and there, settling for the night upon a couch of kuśa grass, he rested at ease.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, when the night had passed, the twice-born one rose at dawn, bathed, kindled the sacred fire, and made oblation according to the rite.
Coming to the Well of Rudrāṇī, he refreshed himself in the pool there; and when rested he arose and went on toward Kailāsa.
He beheld a golden gateway, blazing as it were with splendor, and the Mandākinī, and the lotus-pond of the high-souled Wealth-giver.
Then all those Rākṣasas who guard the lotus-pool rose up before the reverend one, with Maṇibhadra at their head.
He greeted those Rākṣasas of fearsome valor in turn, and said: Announce me at once to the Wealth-giver.
Then those Rākṣasas, O king, said to the reverend one: Yonder King Vaiśravaṇa comes himself into your presence.
The reverend one is known to him, and the purpose of his coming; behold him now, that greatly blessed lord, blazing as if with radiance.
Then Vaiśravaṇa, approaching the blameless Aṣṭāvakra and inquiring after his welfare as the rite prescribes, said to that sage among brahmans:
Have you come in comfort, sir? And what would you have of me? Speak — whatever you shall ask of me, twice-born one, all that I will do.
Enter my dwelling at your pleasure, O best of the twice-born; honored and with your purpose fulfilled, you shall depart unhindered.
He entered his own dwelling, having taken that best of the twice-born by the hand, and gave him his own seat, and water for his feet, and the welcome-offering as well.
When the two were seated there, Kubera's own folk — Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas, led by Maṇibhadra — took their places there.
Then, when they were seated, the Wealth-giver spoke this word: Learning your honored one's pleasure, let the troops of Apsarases dance.
"Supreme hospitality must be shown, and service rendered to you — so let it be," said he. And the sage replied in a sweet voice, "Let it proceed."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Urvarā and Miśrakeśī, Rambhā and Urvaśī too, Alambusā and Ghṛtācī, Citrā, Citrāṅgadā, Ruci,
Manoharā and Sukeśī, Sumukhī, Hāsinī, Prabhā, Vidyutā, Praśamā, Dāntā, Vidyotā, and Rati as well —
these and many other fair Apsarases fell to dancing, and the Gandharvas sounded their instruments of every kind.
And when the divine Gandharva music had begun, the sage of mighty austerities tarried there, delighting, a full celestial year.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa said to the reverend one: A full year and more has passed for you here, O brahman, while you watched.
Enchanting is this pleasure, O brahman, Gandharva music by name; let it continue at your pleasure, sir, or as your honored self may bid.
You are a guest to be honored, and this house is yours; command all of it at once — we are wholly subject to you.
Then the reverend one, well pleased, replied to Vaiśravaṇa: I have been honored as is fitting; I shall now depart, O lord of wealth.
I am pleased, and all things here befit you, O lord of riches. By your grace, my lord, and by the charge of the high-souled great sage, I depart today; may you flourish and prosper.
Then the reverend one, going forth, journeyed on facing northward, and traversed all the golden heights — Kailāsa and Mandara.
Passing beyond those great mountains, he made reverent circuit of the supreme abode of the Kirātas, bowing with his head; and descending to the earth, he became then purified in soul.
Having circled the mountain thrice and turned to face north, he went on over level ground, gladness leading him onward.
Then he beheld another lovely tract of forest, furnished with roots and fruits of every season and with birds, adorned here and there with delightful woodland glades.
There the reverend one beheld a divine hermitage-ground, and golden crags of manifold form, jewel-bedecked, and lotus-pools set into a soil of gems.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Many other charming things besides he beheld; and the mind of the great sage, his soul refined, took deep delight.
There he saw a divine golden mansion, wrought all of jewels, of wondrous aspect, surpassing even the dwelling of the Wealth-giver.
There stood great palaces of many kinds, like mountains, and lovely sky-borne chariots, and gems of every sort.
The river Mandākinī was strewn with mandāra blossoms, and there were self-luminous jewels, and the ground was adorned with diamonds.
On every side it was encompassed by mansions of many kinds, with archways of variegated gems, festooned with nets of pearls and decked with jewels and precious stones, ravishing to mind and eye, lovely and auspicious.
The sage looked all about and saw delight on every hand; then a thought arose in him: Where might my lodging be?
Then, going up close to the gateway and standing there, he said: Let those who are within grant leave to me, a guest who has arrived.
Then forth from that house came maidens, attended one upon another — seven maidens, O lord, of varied form, all of them ravishing.
Whichever maiden he looked upon, that one stole away his heart; he could not hold his mind steady, and it began to sink within him.
Then resolve arose in that wise brahman; and the fair women said to him: Let the reverend one enter.
And filled with wonder both at those lovely women and at the mansion itself, the twice-born one entered the house.
There he beheld a woman bowed with age, clad in spotless garments, aged, seated upon a couch, and decked with every ornament.
And when he had greeted her with "Hail," that woman answered him then, and rising before the brahman, she said: Be seated.
Aṣṭāvakra said: Let all of them go to their own quarters; let one well-discerning and well-composed attend upon me; let the rest depart at their pleasure.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then those maidens, having circled the sage in reverence, went forth from that house; but the aged one remained behind.
Then, lying down upon the shining bed, he said to her: Do you too take your rest, good lady, for the night is wearing away.
Being thus addressed by the brahman in talk, she lay down upon a second bed there, divine and of great splendor.
Then she, her limbs trembling, pleading the cold as her pretext, climbed up onto the great sage's bed.
"Welcome — let welcome be yours," the reverend one said to her; and she clasped the sage in her two arms with affection, O bull among men.
But seeing the sage unmoved, like a post or a wall, she grew distressed, and entered into talk with the sage.
Brahman, women have no power over desire, nor restraint before a man; bewildered with longing am I — accept me who seek you in love.
Be glad, O sage among brahmans; unite yourself with me; embrace me, brahman — I am sorely afflicted with desire for you.
For this, O righteous one, is honored as the fruit of your austerity, sought from the mere sight of you — accept me who give myself to you.
This mansion and this forest, and whatever else you see — over all of it your lordship extends, and over me as well, beyond doubt.
I shall fulfill every desire; take your delight together with me, O brahman, in this lovely forest that yields the fruit of all desires.
I shall be wholly yours, and you shall take delight with me, enjoying all the pleasures, both those that are divine and those that are mortal.
For there is no higher aim for women than union with a man; this indeed is our supreme fruit.
Women act by their own will, driven on by the god of love; even going their way over coals of well-heated dust, they are not burned.
Aṣṭāvakra said: I would never, good lady, approach another man's wife; the touching of another's wife is condemned in the treatises of dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Know me, good lady, to be one who wishes to marry — by truth I swear it; I am untutored in the pleasures of sense, for offspring is begotten for the sake of dharma.
Thus, through sons, shall I attain the higher worlds — of this there is no doubt. Understand righteousness, good lady, and understanding it, desist.
The woman said: Not the Wind, not Fire, not Varuṇa, nor any of the other gods, O brāhmaṇa, are as dear to women as is desire; for women are creatures given over to pleasure.
Scarcely one woman in a thousand is found here who is restrained; and among a hundred thousand, only here and there is one devoted to her husband.
They heed neither father nor lineage nor mother, neither brothers nor husband, neither sons nor brothers-in-law.
Sporting in their wantonness, they destroy their families as the great rivers wear away their banks; and Prajāpati declared that such failings dwell within women of weak mind.
Bhīṣma said: Then the sage, with collected mind, answered that woman: "As you please, be seated; or tell me—what is the task you would have done?"
The woman replied: "Lord, in due place and time you shall see. Dwell here a while, O greatly wise one; when your purpose is accomplished, you shall depart."
The brāhmaṇa-seer then said to her, "So be it," O Yudhiṣṭhira—"I shall dwell here as long as it pleases you; of that there is no doubt."
Then the seer, gazing upon that woman bowed down with age, fell into deep reflection and became as one consumed with care.
Whatever limb of hers that bull among brāhmaṇas looked upon, there his gaze found no delight, overcome by her ruined form.
"Surely this is the deity of this house, disfigured by some curse; yet it would not be fitting for me to seek out the cause of it in haste."
As he was thus absorbed in thought, longing to know the truth of the matter, the remainder of that day passed away while his mind was troubled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then that woman said: "Lord, behold the form of the sun joined with the clouds of twilight. What shall be made ready for you?"
He then said to that woman: "Bring water here for bathing; then, restrained in speech and with senses controlled, I shall attend upon the twilight rite."
Bhīṣma said: Then that woman, saying to the brāhmaṇa, "So be it," took up celestial oil and brought to him a bathing-cloth.
And, granted leave by that great-souled sage, the woman anointed all his limbs with the oil.
Gently rubbed down, he went into the bathing-chamber; and the seer then took his place upon a fine new seat richly adorned.
And when he was seated upon that goodly seat, she bathed the seer slowly, with a gentle hand, and performed for the sage the celestial rite duly, with every attendance.
By that pleasantly warm water and by the soothing touch of her hand, that man of great vows did not perceive that the whole night had passed away.
Then the sage, rising up in utter amazement, beheld the sun risen in the sky in the eastern quarter.
This thought came to him: "Is this a delusion, or is it the truth?" Then, having worshipped the thousand-rayed one, he said to her, "What shall I do?"
She set before the seer food that was like the taste of nectar; and by reason of the sweetness of that food he could not make an end of it. So the rest of the day passed away, and the twilight came again.
Then that woman urged the lord, saying, "Let us sleep," upon celestial couches there made ready, one for him and one for her.
Aṣṭāvakra said: "No, good lady; my mind does not cling to another man's wife. Rise up, good lady—blessings upon you—go to sleep, and desist."
Bhīṣma said: She, thus turned back by the brāhmaṇa's firmness, said to him, "I am my own mistress; there is no deceiving of dharma in this for you."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Aṣṭāvakra said: "Women have no independence; a woman is never her own mistress. This is the doctrine of Prajāpati: a woman is not entitled to independence."
The woman said: "Desire torments me, O brāhmaṇa; behold too my devotion. You will incur unrighteousness, O brāhmaṇa, in that you will not welcome me."
Aṣṭāvakra said: "Faults that are born within carry a man off wherever they will once they arise; but I am ever master of myself through firmness. Go, good lady, to your own couch."
The woman said: "With my head I bow, O brāhmaṇa; deign to show me grace. To me who am falling to the ground, be my refuge, O sinless one."
"But if you see a fault arising in approaching another man's wife, then this day I make a gift of myself: take my hand, O brāhmaṇa."
"And no fault shall there be—this I tell you in truth. Know me to be my own mistress; whatever unrighteousness there be, let it rest upon me."
Aṣṭāvakra said: "How are you your own mistress, good lady? Tell me the reason for this. There is no woman in the world who is entitled to independence."
"In childhood the father protects her, in youth the husband, and in old age the sons; a woman is not entitled to independence."
The woman said: "Mine is the chastity of girlhood; I am yet a maiden, without doubt. Harbor no misgiving, O brāhmaṇa; do not cast away your faith in me."
Aṣṭāvakra said: "As it is for me, so it is for you; as it is for you, so for me. Let me probe this: is this hindrance to the seer real, or what?
"For this is a thing of the utmost wonder. What course would be best for me? This maiden, decked in celestial ornaments and garments, has come before me."
"But how was her surpassing beauty aged before, and how again has she now this very day the form of a maiden? What can be the answer to this?"
"Yet so far as my strength of resolve avails, I shall in no wise swerve; for swerving I deem not good. By steadfastness thus do I prevail."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How was it that the woman did not fear the curse of one so resplendent? And how did the venerable one desist? Tell me this, I pray.
Bhīṣma said: Aṣṭāvakra questioned her: "How is it that you change your form? You must speak no falsehood; tell me, out of regard for a brāhmaṇa."
The woman said: "This desire of mine is as boundless as heaven and earth, O best of brāhmaṇas. Listen attentively to all of it, O you of truthful valor."
"Know me to be the Northern Quarter. The fickleness of women has been shown to you; and by your not swerving, the heavenly worlds have been won by you, O you whose valor is truth."
"This testing was set in motion by me to make you steadfast, O sinless one—for even in aged women the fever of desire still torments."
"The Grandsire is pleased with you this day, and so are the gods together with Vāsava. And as for the purpose for which you, venerable one, have come here—
"sent by that brāhmaṇa, the father of the maiden, O bull among the twice-born, to make the instruction known to you—all of that has been accomplished by me."
"Safe shall you go to your home, and weariness shall not come upon you. You shall win that maiden, O brāhmaṇa, and she shall bear you sons."
"You questioned me out of desire, and so the answer was uttered—an answer that can never be gainsaid by all the three worlds together."
"Go now, your good work done. Or is there aught else you wish to hear, that I may tell it truly, O seer among brāhmaṇas, Aṣṭāvakra?"
"I have been entreated by the seer on your behalf, O bull among the twice-born; and to do him honor these words of mine were spoken to you."
Having heard her words, the brāhmaṇa stood with palms joined; and, taking leave of her, he made his way back to his own home.
Having come home and rested, and having honored his kinsfolk, he went duly to that brāhmaṇa, O delight of the Kurus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And being questioned by that brāhmaṇa, "Has this token been seen?", the brāhmaṇa then spoke to the brāhmaṇa with a heart well pleased:
"Granted leave by you, I set out for Gandhamādana; and in the region to the north of it I beheld that mighty deity."
"And, granted leave by her, with you too made known to her, and having been told her saying, I have come home, my lord."
Then the brāhmaṇa said to him: "Receive my daughter, when star and lunar day are in conjunction; for you are a most worthy recipient."
Bhīṣma said: Aṣṭāvakra, saying "So be it," and accepting that maiden, O lord—he of the highest righteousness—was then filled with joy.
Having received that maiden as his most beautiful wife, he dwelt there gladly in his own hermitage, his fever of doubt now gone.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Whom, O best of the Bhāratas, do the brāhmaṇas declare to be from of old a worthy recipient—the brāhmaṇa who bears the outward marks, or the brāhmaṇa without them?
Bhīṣma said: To one who keeps to his proper conduct, whether he bears the marks or not, a gift should be given, O great king; for both of these are men of austerity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When a man, purified by the highest faith, presents to a twice-born the offering to the gods, the offering to the ancestors, and gifts, what fault could there be, O Grandsire?
Bhīṣma said: A man purified by faith, my son, even though he be hard to discipline, becomes pure in every way, without doubt—how much more, then, do you, O lord of the earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: In rites to the gods a man should never examine the brāhmaṇa; but in the giving of offerings to the ancestors, the wise hold that the brāhmaṇa is to be examined.
Bhīṣma said: It is not the brāhmaṇa who brings the offering to fulfillment; it succeeds by the gods' ordinance. By the grace of the gods the sacrificers obtain their fruit, without doubt.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The brāhmaṇas, O best of the Bhāratas, are ever expounders of the sacred word; thus did the wise Mārkaṇḍeya declare of old here among the worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Whether a man be a stranger or a learned one, or a kinsman, or an ascetic, or one given to sacrifice—how is it that such a one becomes a worthy recipient?
Bhīṣma said: Wellborn, performing his rites, learned in the Veda, compassionate, modest, upright, truthful—such a one is a worthy recipient; and the first three among these qualities are foremost.
On this point hear from me, O Pārtha, the judgment of four glorious beings—of the Earth, of Kāśyapa, of Agni, and of Mārkaṇḍeya.
The Earth said: As a clod of earth cast into the great ocean swiftly dissolves away, so all ill conduct is dissolved away by the recitation of the threefold Veda.
Kāśyapa said: All the Vedas together with their six limbs, the Sāṃkhya, the Purāṇa, and birth in a noble line—none of these, all of them together, become a refuge for the man who is bereft of good character, O king.
Agni said: He who, learned in the texts and accounting himself a sage, destroys the renown of others by his learning—by that, O brāhmaṇa, he commits the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, and his heavenly worlds come to an end.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were weighed in the balance; and I do not find that the one would attain even to half of that truth.
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, those four of boundless splendor swiftly departed—the Earth, Kāśyapa, Agni, and the long-lived scion of Bhṛgu.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When brāhmaṇas in the world who keep their vows eat the sacrificial offering, that offering eaten for the sake of a brāhmaṇa—how does it become a meritorious deed?
Bhīṣma said: Those brāhmaṇas, O king of kings, learned to the end of the Veda, who, being invited, eat for the sake of a brāhmaṇa—they become fallen from their vows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The wise call dharma many-sided and of many doors. What in it may be held as certain? Tell me that, O Grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Non-injury, truth, freedom from anger, compassion, self-restraint, and uprightness—this, O king of kings, is the certain mark of dharma.
But those who go about this earth praising dharma while not practicing that dharma, devoted to confusion of duties, O lord—
he who gives to them a jewel, or gold, or a cow, or horses—for ten years he feeds upon filth, lodged in hell.
Of the meda outcastes, of the pulkasas, and likewise of those who dwell at the cremation-ground, the rite performed is as good as unperformed, since they babble out of passion and delusion.
And those fools who give the Vaiśvadeva offering to a brāhmaṇa who is a student of the sacred word—nay, O king of kings, they go to enjoy worlds of ill.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What is the highest form of chastity, what the highest mark of dharma, and what the most excellent purity? Tell me that, O Grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Chastity is the highest course, dear son, and the renunciation of honey and meat; dharma abides within bounds, and tranquillity is the mark of purity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: At what time should one pursue dharma, at what time pursue wealth, and at what time enjoy pleasure? Tell me this, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: In the early hours let him attend to wealth, then immediately after to dharma; afterward let him attend to pleasure, yet never give himself over to attachment.
Let him hold the brāhmaṇas in honour and revere his elders; gentle toward all beings, soft of nature, and kindly in speech.
Falsehood in the exercise of office, slander carried to the king, and deceit practised against one's teacher—each of these is equal to the slaying of a brāhmaṇa.
Let him not strike at kings, nor likewise slay a cow; he who indulges in either of these does what is equal to the killing of an embryo.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let him never abandon the sacred fire, nor forsake the Vedas, nor revile a brāhmaṇa—for that too is equal to the slaying of a brāhmaṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What kind of brāhmaṇas are the virtuous ones, gifts to whom bear great fruit, and of what kind are those whose food may be eaten? Tell me this, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: Free from anger, devoted to dharma, ever truthful, delighting in self-restraint—such are the virtuous brāhmaṇas; a gift given to them bears great fruit.
Free from conceit, all-enduring, having perceived the truth, their senses subdued, friendly and devoted to the welfare of all beings—a gift given to them bears great fruit.
Free from greed, pure, learned, modest, truthful in speech, and intent upon their own duty—a gift given to such men bears great fruit.
That bull among the twice-born who has studied the four Vedas with their auxiliary sciences, and who has turned away from the six base occupations—him the seers know to be a worthy recipient.
Those who are endowed with such qualities—a gift given to them bears great fruit; the giver to one worthy by his merits gains a thousandfold reward.
Endowed with wisdom and sacred learning, with right conduct and good character, a single bull among the twice-born can in this world deliver an entire lineage.
Let him bestow upon such a one a cow, a horse, wealth, or food, and other goods besides; then in the life beyond he shall not grieve.
Even one foremost among the twice-born can in this world deliver a whole lineage—how much more, then, a single soul? Therefore let one seek out a worthy recipient.
And having heard of a brāhmaṇa endowed with virtue and esteemed by the good, let him summon him from afar for the rite and honour him in every way.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Concerning the time of the śrāddha, concerning the offering to the gods, and concerning dharma as well, grandfather, I wish to hear from you what has been ordained by the divine seers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Let him perform the offering to the gods in the forenoon, but the rite for the ancestors in the afternoon, accomplished in auspicious observances, having performed his purifications, and diligent.
But to men he should give at midday, as is fitting; a gift bestowed out of its proper time—that portion they know to belong to the rākṣasas.
What has been stepped over, what has been licked, what has been done amid strife, and what has been looked upon by women in their courses—that portion they know to belong to the rākṣasas.
What is eaten amid clamour, and what is eaten by one who keeps no vows, O Bhārata, and what has been touched by a dog—that portion they know to belong to the rākṣasas.
Food into which a hair or an insect has fallen, upon which one has sneezed, which dogs have gazed upon, over which there has been weeping, or which has been shaken about—that portion they know to belong to the rākṣasas.
What is eaten without the sacred syllable Oṃ, and what is eaten with a weapon at hand, O Bhārata, and what is eaten by an evil-souled man—that portion they know to belong to the rākṣasas.
What is eaten that has been left over by another, and what may have already been partaken of—at the rite for the gods or for the ancestors alike, that portion they ever know to belong to the rākṣasas.
What is reviled and condemned, what is served amid wrath, whether at the rite for the gods or for the ancestors—that portion they know to belong to the rākṣasas.
A śrāddha that is served wanting in sacred chants and wanting in proper rites by the three varṇas, O best of men—that portion they know to belong to the rākṣasas.
Whatever is served without the oblation of clarified butter, and what is eaten by men of evil conduct—that portion they know to belong to the rākṣasas.
Those portions that are declared to belong to the rākṣasas have now been told, O bull of the Bhāratas; henceforth hear the examination of the brāhmaṇa upon the giving away of the gift.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All those brāhmaṇas who are fallen, and likewise the dull-witted and the mad—at the rite for the gods or for the ancestors, O king, they deserve no invitation.
The man afflicted with white leprosy, the leper, the eunuch, he who is wasted by consumption, the epileptic, and the blind, O king, deserve no such honour.
Physicians, temple priests who serve images for hire, those who keep vows to no purpose, and sellers of the soma—at a śrāddha they deserve no invitation.
Singers and dancers, acrobats and players of instruments, reciters of tales and prize-fighters, O king, deserve no invitation.
Those who officiate at the sacrifices of the base-born, and those who instruct the base-born, and likewise the pupils of the base-born, O king, deserve no invitation.
The brāhmaṇa who hires another's sacred service and he who is so hired, O Bhārata—neither of these two deserves the śrāddha, for both are sellers of sacred knowledge.
A brāhmaṇa who has been made the leader at the marriage of a man of lower varṇa—though he be versed in all the sciences, O king, he deserves no invitation.
Those brāhmaṇas who keep no sacred fires, and those who bear forth the dead for hire, and thieves and the fallen, O king, deserve no invitation.
Those of unknown ancestry, and those born of a guild's promiscuous union, O Bhārata, and the sons born of an appointed daughter—at a śrāddha they deserve no invitation.
The maker of debts, O king, and the twice-born who lives by usury, and he whose livelihood is the selling of living creatures, O king, deserve no invitation.
Those who were once women, and the makers of arrow-shafts, all of them, O bull of the Bhāratas, and brāhmaṇas who do not chant the sāvitrī—at a śrāddha they deserve no invitation.
The brāhmaṇas who are debarred from the śrāddha and the offering to the gods have been named, O bull of the Bhāratas; now hear again, of giver and receiver alike, who are worthy of favour.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who have fulfilled their vows and are endowed with virtues—even if they be tillers of the soil—if they know the sāvitrī and perform the rites, they, O king, are fit to be invited.
Even a well-born twice-born who follows the kṣatriya's dharma in battle one may invite; but a trader, dear son, one should never appoint at the śrāddhas.
The brāhmaṇa who maintains the agnihotra fire, who dwells in the village, who is no thief and is mindful of guests—he, O king, is fit to be invited.
He who chants the sāvitrī at the three junctures of the day, O bull of the Bhāratas, who lives by alms and performs the rites—he, O king, is fit to be invited.
He who rises with the sun and rests at its setting, and likewise rests at its setting and rises with it, who does no harm and has but few faults—he, O king, is fit to be invited.
The brāhmaṇa free from guile and free from idle cavil, O bull of the Bhāratas, possessed of full awareness and living by alms—he, O king, is fit to be invited.
One who was vowless, a gambler, a thief, a seller of living creatures, and a trader, but who afterward has drunk the soma—he, O king, is fit to be invited.
One who first earned his wealth by the harsh labours of tillage, and who afterward becomes hospitable to all guests—he, O king, is fit to be invited.
Wealth got by the selling of sacred knowledge, wealth earned by a woman, and wealth gained through unmanliness—these are not to be given to the ancestors and the gods.
When the concluding rite is being performed, the twice-born who does not utter what is fitting, O bull of the Bhāratas—his transgression is as the falsehood that loses a cow.
The brāhmaṇa is the right occasion for the śrāddha; fit also are curds and clarified butter when they come to hand, the waning of the moon, and the flesh of forest game, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At the conclusion of a brāhmaṇa's śrāddha, let the word svadhā be well pronounced; for a kṣatriya, too, let him then say, "May the ancestors be pleased."
At the conclusion of a vaiśya's śrāddha rite, O Bhārata, the word "imperishable" is to be spoken; and for a śūdra, "well-being," O Bhārata.
In the offering to the gods, the proclamation of an auspicious day is ordained for the brāhmaṇa; this same proclamation, without the syllable Oṃ, is ordained for the kṣatriya; and for the vaiśya it is to be spoken thus: "May the deities be pleased."
Hear now the due sequence of the rites and their prescribed performance—all the sacraments beginning with the birth-rite among the three varṇas, O Bhārata; for the brāhmaṇa and the kṣatriya they are enjoined with sacred chants, and so too for the vaiśya, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
For the brāhmaṇa the girdle is of muñja grass, for the kṣatriya it is of bowstring fibre, and for the vaiśya it is of balbaja grass—such is the law, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Hear now, of the giver and the receiver alike, these their dharma and their transgression: for the brāhmaṇa, the sin in falsehood is declared to bear the name of a grievous fault; for the kṣatriya it is held to be fourfold, and for the vaiśya eightfold.
A brāhmaṇa, if invited beforehand by another brāhmaṇa, should not eat elsewhere; for the younger man who does so incurs a guilt equal to the slaughter of an animal.
But if, being invited, he should eat at the homes of a kṣatriya or a vaiśya, the younger man thereby incurs half the share of the guilt of slaying an animal.
The brāhmaṇa who eats at the rite for the gods or for the ancestors, in the houses of brāhmaṇas and the rest, while yet unbathed, O king—his transgression is as the falsehood that loses a cow.
The brāhmaṇa who, while in a state of impurity, eats in the houses of brāhmaṇas and the rest, knowingly and out of greed, O king—his transgression is as the falsehood that loses a cow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who would seek food in return for food, and who invites another merely for the sake of his own rite, O Bhārata, O lord of kings—his transgression is reckoned to be a falsehood.
Those wanting in the Vedas, in vows, and in good conduct, who are served as if entitled to the sacred chants by the three varṇas, O Yudhiṣṭhira—in their case the transgression is as the falsehood that loses a cow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of that which is given at the rite for the ancestors or for the gods, grandfather, I wish to hear in whom a gift bestowed bears great fruit.
Bhīṣma said: Those whose wives await the leavings and remnants of the meal as tillers await a good rain—feed them, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Those steadfast in good conduct, O king, who are lean and whose means are meagre, and who come as suppliants—a gift given to them bears great fruit.
Those who are devoted to you, who dwell in your house, O king, whose wealth and whose refuge lie in you, and who come as suppliants in their need—a gift given to them bears great fruit.
Those who, distressed by fear of thieves or of enemies, O Yudhiṣṭhira, come as suppliants desiring to eat—a gift given to them bears great fruit.
The young students who beg on behalf of a guileless brāhmaṇa, one who has shaped his soul by living on gleaned alms—a gift given to them bears great fruit.
Those brāhmaṇas who, robbed of their goods and bereft of their wives in the ruin of a land, come seeking aid—a gift given to them bears great fruit.
Those brāhmaṇas observing vows and firm in their restraints, esteemed for their sacred learning, who desire help for the completion of those vows—a gift given to them bears great fruit.
Those who have never strayed from the dharmas into the doctrines of heretics, whose vital strength is wasted and whose wealth is meagre—a gift given to them bears great fruit.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who, though blameless, have been stripped of all their possessions by the powerful, and who long for a meal of food—a gift given to them bears great fruit.
The ascetics steadfast in austerity, and those of them who wander seeking alms, who as suppliants desire some little thing—a gift given to them bears great fruit.
The rule of great fruit in giving you have now heard, O bull of the Bhāratas; now hear that by which men go to hell, and likewise to heaven.
Save for the sake of one's teacher or to save a life, O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who utter falsehood—they indeed are bound for hell.
Those who carry off the wives of others, who lay hands upon the wives of others, and who procure the wives of others—they indeed are bound for hell.
Those who seize away the goods of others, who destroy the goods of others, and who are informers against others—they indeed are bound for hell.
The men who are destroyers of watering-sheds, of assembly halls, of bridges and causeways, and of houses, O Bhārata—they are bound for hell.
Those men who deceive a helpless woman, a child, an old person, one in fear, or one given to austerity — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those who cut off a man's livelihood, his home, his wife, his friend, or his very hope, O Bhārata — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Informers, breakers of alliances, those who live by another's labor, and the ungrateful toward their friends — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Heretics, defilers, those who violate covenants, and those who have fallen back from their vows — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those who, by sowing discord, draw away one who has placed his hope in them, who has served them, given his devotion, and spent his toil for them — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those who eat before their wives, their servants, and their guests have eaten, and who have let the worship of the fathers and the gods lapse — they, indeed, are bound for hell.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sellers of the Vedas, defilers of the Vedas, and those who commit the Vedas to writing — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those men who stand outside the four stages of life, outside the revealed scripture, and who live by forbidden acts — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Dealers in hair, O king, dealers in poison, and dealers in milk — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those who, O Yudhiṣṭhira, slip in to obstruct the affairs of brāhmaṇas, of cattle, and of maidens — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Sellers of weapons, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and the makers of barbed darts and of bows — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those who block the road with spikes, with stakes, or with pits, O bull of the Bhāratas — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those who abandon their teachers, their servants, and their devoted dependents when these are helpless, O bull of the Bhāratas — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those who break in beasts before their time, who pierce their noses, and who keep cattle in bondage — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those who fail to protect, who gain their wealth by fraud, who are intent on exacting the sixth-part tribute, and who, though able, give nothing — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those who, once their purpose is served, abandon the patient, the self-controlled, and the wise who have long dwelt with them — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
Those men who eat first, without first giving to the young, the old, and the servants — they, indeed, are bound for hell.
These the ancient seers beheld and declared to be bound for hell. Now I shall tell you, O bull of the Bhāratas, of those who share in the world of heaven.
In all undertakings that begin with rites to the gods, O Bhārata, an affront committed against a brāhmaṇa destroys one's sons and all one's cattle entirely.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those men who, O Yudhiṣṭhira, follow the way of dharma through giving, through austerity, and through truth — they are bound for heaven.
Those who, having gained sacred learning through service and austerity, O Bhārata, feel no craving to accept gifts — they are bound for heaven.
Those for whose sake others are delivered from fear, from sin, from oppression, from poverty, and from the ravages of disease — they are bound for heaven.
The forbearing and the steadfast, those ever roused to acts of dharma, and those devoted to auspicious conduct — they are bound for heaven.
Those who have turned away from honey and flesh, from the wives of others, and from intoxicating drink — they are bound for heaven.
The founders of hermitages, of families, of regions, and of cities, O Bhārata — they are bound for heaven.
Those who give garments and ornaments, food, drink, and victuals, and who provide for whole households — they are bound for heaven.
Those who have ceased from all harm, who endure all things, and who become a refuge for all — they are bound for heaven.
Those who, masters of their senses, serve their mother and father, and bear affection toward their brothers — they are bound for heaven.
Those who, though wealthy, strong, and in the bloom of youth, O Bhārata, yet remain steadfast and masters of their senses — they are bound for heaven.
Those who remain affectionate even toward offenders, who are gentle, fond of their friends, and easy to win over — they are bound for heaven.
Those men who feast thousands, who give to thousands, and who are the protectors of thousands — they are bound for heaven.
The givers of gold and of cattle, O bull of the Bhāratas, and of carriages and draught-animals — they are bound for heaven.
Those who give maidens in marriage, who give attendants and garments, O Yudhiṣṭhira — they are bound for heaven.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who provide pleasure-grounds, resting-houses, gardens, wells, groves, and assembly-halls, and who build embankments — they are bound for heaven.
Those who give dwellings, fields, and lodgings, O Bhārata, and whatever is asked of them — they are bound for heaven.
Those men who, having themselves raised juices, seeds, and grain, O Yudhiṣṭhira, then give them away — they are bound for heaven.
In whatever family they are born, men blessed with many sons and a span of a hundred years, full of compassion and having conquered their wrath — they are bound for heaven.
Thus has it been told, for the sake of the world beyond, regarding the rites to the gods and to the fathers, O Bhārata, and the dharma and adharma of giving, even as the ancient seers ordained them.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This, O king, you ought to tell me truly, O Bhārata — by what act here, even without slaying, is the guilt of brahmin-murder incurred?
Bhīṣma said: That which I once asked of Vyāsa, having addressed him, O lord of kings, I shall now relate to you in full — listen here with single-minded attention.
You who are the fourth in descent from Vasiṣṭha — declare to me the truth, O sage: by what act here, even without slaying, is the guilt of brahmin-murder incurred?
Thus questioned, O great king, the son born of Parāśara's body, skilled in dharma, spoke without doubt and beyond all dispute.
He who himself summons a brāhmaṇa of meager livelihood to receive alms, and afterward says, 'There is nothing' — know that man to be a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
The man of evil mind who robs of his livelihood a learned and impartial brāhmaṇa here, O Bhārata — know that man to be a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
He who, O lord of the earth, raises an obstacle to the water sought by a herd of cattle tormented by thirst — know that man to be a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who, in his ignorance, reviles the established sacred lore or the scripture rightly composed by the sages — know that man to be a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
He who does not bestow his own daughter, endowed with beauty and grown to maturity, upon a worthy suitor — know that man to be a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
The deluded man, devoted to unrighteousness, who falsely inflicts upon the twice-born a grief that pierces to the quick — know that man to be a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
He who carries off the whole property of one bereft of sight, of a cripple, or of a simpleton — know that man to be a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
He who in his folly sets loose fire upon a hermitage, a forest, a village, or a town — know that man to be a slayer of a brāhmaṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The sight of the sacred fords is a blessing, and bathing in them too, O bull of the Bhāratas; and hearing of them as well, O greatly wise one — I wish to hear of them truly.
Those holy fords that are upon the earth, O bull of the Bhāratas, you ought to tell me of them; I shall listen, intent and self-restrained, O lord.
Bhīṣma said: This lineage of the sacred fords, declared by Aṅgiras, O one of great splendor, you ought to hear — blessings be upon you; you shall attain the highest dharma.
Approaching the brāhmaṇa, the great sage Aṅgiras, who had gone to the grove of austerities, Gautama of rigid vows questioned him, O hero.
I have, O blessed one, a certain doubt concerning the dharma of the sacred fords. All of it I wish to hear; declare it to me, O great sage.
What fruit accrues from touching the waters at those fords, O sage, in the life beyond, O greatly wise one? Tell it to me just as it is.
Aṅgiras said: He who for seven days plunges into the Candrabhāgā and the wave-garlanded Vitastā, fasting and free of all sense of possession, becomes like unto a sage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The rivers that, in the region of Kāśmīra, fall into the great river — coming to those streams of the Sindhu, the man of virtuous conduct attains heaven.
Having plunged into Puṣkara, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, the ocean-waters, the Devikā, the Indramārga, and the Svarṇabindu, a man is awakened set upon a celestial chariot, hymned by the apsarases.
Having stirred the waters of Hiraṇyabindu and, self-controlled, reverently saluted the Kuśeśaya, he attains godhead, and his sin is washed away.
Reaching the Indratoyā near Gandhamādana, and the Karatoyā among the Kuraṅgas, the man who has fasted three nights and plunges in, restrained and pure, gains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
Having bathed at the Gate of the Gaṅgā, at Kuśāvarta, at Bilvaka, at Mount Nemi, and at Kanakhala, a man, his sins shaken off, goes to heaven.
Touching the waters at the lake Apāṃ Hrada, a chaste man who has conquered wrath, true to his word and harmless to all, gains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Where the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā turns toward the northern quarter, at the abode of Maheśvara, the man who is consecrated there, fasting for a whole month, beholds the gods themselves.
At Saptagaṅga, at Trigaṅga, and at the Indramārga, the man who offers libations to the fathers gains the nectar of immortality to taste, when he is born again.
Touching the waters at Mahāśrama, the pure man devoted to the fire-offering, fasting for a whole month, attains perfection in that month.
Touching the waters at the Great Lake on Bhṛgutuṅga, the man free of greed, having fasted three nights, is released from the guilt of brahmin-murder.
Touching the waters at the Kanyākūpa and making his offering of water in the Balākā, a man wins renown among the gods and shines forth in glory.
Touching the waters at Deśakāla and likewise in the lake Sundarikā, a man gains from the Aśvins beauty and brilliance of form when he passes to the other world.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Touching the waters of the Mahāgaṅgā, and likewise at Kṛttikā and Aṅgāraka, a man who fasts for a single fortnight, made spotless, attains heaven.
Touching the waters at Vaimānika and likewise at the hermitage of Kiṅkiṇīkā, in the celestial dwelling of the apsarases, a man is honored and roams there at will.
Reaching the hermitage of Kālikā and making his offering of water in the Vipāśā, a chaste man who has conquered wrath is freed, after three nights, from the round of rebirth.
He who bathes at the hermitage of the Kṛttikās and offers libations to the fathers, having gladdened Mahādeva, made spotless, attains heaven.
Touching the waters at Mahāpura, a man who has fasted three nights casts off all fear of moving creatures, of unmoving things, and of men.
Having bathed in the Devadāru grove, his sins shaken off, and made his offering of water, the pure man who has fasted seven nights attains the world of the gods.
At Kauśanta, at Kuśastamba, at Droṇaśarmapada, and bathing at Āpaḥprapatana, a man is waited upon by the throngs of apsarases.
Plunging, while fasting, into Citrakūṭa, into Janasthāna, and into the waters of the Mandākinī, a man attains the royal fortune of a king.
Having gone to the hermitage of Śyāmā, and dwelling there and bathing, after spending three sets of three nights in succession, a man may dwell in the city of the gandharvas.
Touching the waters at Ramaṇyā and likewise at Gandhatārikā, a man who fasts for a whole month gains the power of vanishing from sight.
Reaching the Gate of the Kauśikī, a man free of greed who feeds on air alone ascends to heaven after twenty-one nights.
He who bathes in the Mataṅga pool attains perfection in a single night; for he passes through the eternal, supportless, blinding darkness.
He who, with senses subdued, touches the waters at Naimiṣa and at the Svargatīrtha, and offers libations there for a month, wins the fruit of the Puruṣamedha sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Touching the waters of the Gaṅgā-pool and likewise of the Utpalāvana, and offering libations there for a month, a man obtains the merit of the Horse Sacrifice.
At the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, and upon Mount Kālaṃjara, touching the Ṣaṣṭi pool—no other gift surpasses what is gained there.
Ten thousand sacred fords, and thirty million others besides, all gather at Prayāga in the month of Māgha, O bull of the Bhāratas.
He who, restrained and firm in his vows, bathes at Prayāga during the month of Māgha, O best of the Bhāratas, becomes spotless and attains heaven.
Touching the waters at the Marudgaṇa, pure at the hermitage of the Fathers, and at the ford of Vaivasvata, a man himself becomes as holy as a sacred ford.
So too, having gone to Brahmaśiras and offered libations in the Bhāgīrathī, fasting for one month, a man attains the world of Soma.
A man who bathes at Kapotaka and offers libations at Aṣṭāvakra, fasting for twelve days, wins the fruit of the Naramedha sacrifice.
By visiting Muñjapṛṣṭha and Gayā, Nirṛti and the mountain of the gods, and thirdly the Krauñcapādī, even the slaying of a brāhmaṇa is purged away.
Touching the waters at Kalaśī, and often at the Vedī, bathing at the city of Agni and offering libations at Viśālā, and touching the waters of the Devahrada, a man shines forth, having become one with Brahman.
Having resorted to Purāpavartana, the Nandā, and the Mahānandā, the self-controlled and harmless man is waited upon by the apsarases in the grove of Nandana.
He who, well-composed, goes there at the conjunction of Urvaśī and the Kṛttikā stars, and bathes in due form in the Lauhitya, wins the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Touching the waters of the Rāma-pool and offering libations at Viśālā, fasting for twelve days, a man is wholly freed from defilement.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Touching the waters of the Mahāhrada with a purified mind, fasting for one month, a man attains the realm reached by Jamadagni.
Mortifying himself on the Vindhya, true to his word and harmless, standing on one spot for six months, he is purified in but a single month thereafter.
Touching the waters of the Narmadā and likewise the waters of Śūrpāraka, fasting for a fortnight, a man is ordained to be born a king's son.
At Jambūmārga, restrained and well-composed for three months, a man wins perfection in but a single day and night.
Plunging into the waters at Kokāmukha and going to the hermitage of Caṇḍālikā, living on herbs and clad in bark, a man obtains ten maidens.
He whose dwelling is at the Kanyā-pool never goes to the abode of Vaivasvata; rather, he attains the world of the gods.
At Prabhāsa, in a single night on the new moon, the composed man attains perfection here, O mighty-armed one—the man who is born again.
Touching the waters at Ujjānaka, at the hermitage of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and bathing at the hermitage of Piṅgā, a man is released from all sins.
Touching the waters at Kulyā and reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, fasting three nights and pure, a man obtains the merit of the Horse Sacrifice.
Touching the waters at Piṇḍāraka and fasting for one night, a man, pure when the night brightens into dawn, obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
So too, having gone to the Brahmā-lake, adorned by the Dharma forest, a man, pure when the night brightens into dawn, obtains the merit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Bathing on Mount Maināka and worshipping at the twilight hours, and conquering desire for a month, a man wins the fruit of the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
Renowned and holy is the Himavat, the mountain that is Śaṃkara's father-in-law, the mine of all gems, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There the twice-born man who has reached the end of the Veda, knowing life to be impermanent, may lay down his body according to the rite, fasting unto death.
Having there worshipped the deities and bowed to the sages, he then, made perfect, goes to heaven, to the eternal world of Brahman.
He who, having conquered desire, anger, and greed, dwells at a sacred ford—there is nothing he has not gained by his pilgrimage to that ford.
Those sacred fords that are unreachable, hard of access, and perilous may be reached in the mind, by gathering together all the fords within oneself.
This is holy, this brings prosperity, this leads to heaven, this gives happiness; this is the secret of the gods, and the purifier of those who bathe.
This one should impart to the twice-born, to the virtuous, or to one's own son; and one may whisper it in the ear of friends, or of a devoted disciple.
This Aṅgiras of great austerity gave to Gautama, with the sanction of his teachers and of the wise Kaśyapa.
This is the supreme prayer of the great purifying sages; reciting it, ever risen from sleep, a man becomes spotless and attains heaven.
And whoever hears this secret, the teaching of Aṅgiras, wins birth in an exalted family and remembers his former lives.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: His equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom, like Brahmā in forbearance, equal to Śakra in valour, and matching the Sun in splendour—
upon the son of Gaṅgā of abundant lustre, struck down by Arjuna in battle, Yudhiṣṭhira waited in attendance, together with his brothers and others.
To that best of the Bhāratas, the unshaken one lying upon his hero's bed and awaiting his appointed hour, the great sages came, desiring to behold him.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Gautama, Agastya, Sumati, Svāyu the self-possessed,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Viśvāmitra, Sthūlaśiras, Saṃvarta, Pramati, Dama, Uśanas, Bṛhaspati, Vyāsa, Cyavana, Kaśyapa, Dhruva,
Durvāsas and Jamadagni, Mārkaṇḍeya and Gālava, Bharadvāja and Raibhya, Yavakrīta and likewise Trita,
Sthūlākṣa and Śakalākṣa, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, Kṛśa, Nārada and Parvata, Sudhanvan, and then Ekata and Dvita,
Nitaṃbhū, Bhuvana, Dhaumya, Śatānanda, Akṛtavraṇa, and Rāma the son of Jamadagni, and Kāmya, and others such as these—great-souled sages all, gathered to behold Bhīṣma.
To those great-souled ones who had come, Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers, paid homage in due form, one after another.
Thus honoured and seated at ease, the great sages held discourse—discourse centred upon Bhīṣma, most sweet, and delighting every sense.
Bhīṣma, hearing the discourse of those sages of disciplined soul, deemed himself already dwelling in heaven, filled with the highest contentment.
Then those great sages, taking leave of Bhīṣma and the Pāṇḍavas, all vanished from sight while everyone looked on.
Those most blessed sages, though they had vanished, the Pāṇḍavas all praised, and bowed to them again and again.
With serene minds, those best of the Kurus, skilled in sacred verses, attended upon the son of Gaṅgā as upon the rising Sun.
Beholding, through the power of their austerities, those sages illumining all the quarters of the sky, the Pāṇḍavas were filled with the utmost wonder.
Reflecting upon the supreme greatness of those sages, the Pāṇḍavas, together with Bhīṣma, made them the subject of their discourse.
At the close of the talk, the son of Dharma, touching Bhīṣma's feet with his head, put to him a question concerning dharma—Yudhiṣṭhira, the Pāṇḍava.
Which lands, which realms, which hermitages, and which mountains are most excellent in holiness; and which rivers should be known as such, O grandsire?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: On this point, too, they tell an ancient tale, the dialogue between one who lived by gleaning ears of grain and a Siddha, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
A certain man, best among bipeds, having wandered again and again over this earth adorned with mountains, came to the house of an excellent householder—
he reached the home of the gleaner, who, having fulfilled his duty, honoured him in due form and then attended upon that Siddha as his guest.
Those two great souls, meeting and seated at ease, held auspicious discourse bound up with the Veda and marked by what completes its purport.
At the close of the talk, the gleaner, an intelligent man, earnestly addressed the Siddha and asked him the very question that you now ask of me:
The gleaner said: Which lands, which realms, which hermitages, and which mountains are most excellent in holiness; and which rivers should be known as such—let that be told.
The Siddha said: Those lands, those realms, those hermitages, and those mountains are most excellent through whose midst the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, best of rivers, flows.
That goal which a creature attains by resorting to the Gaṅgā, he could not win even by austerity, by chastity, by sacrifices, or again by renunciation.
Those embodied beings whose limbs have been touched and laid to rest by the waters of the Gaṅgā—for them no expulsion from heaven is ever ordained.
Those men all of whose rites have been performed with the waters of the Gaṅgā, O brāhmaṇa, having left the earth, abide unshaken in heaven.
Those men who, having done evil deeds in their earlier years, afterward resort to the Gaṅgā—they too attain the highest goal.
The fruit that comes to men of disciplined soul who have bathed in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā—that comes not even from a hundred sacrifices.
For as many thousands of years as a man's bone rests in the waters of the Gaṅgā, so long does he, having attained heaven, abide there in honour.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As the sun, scattering the dense darkness at its rising, shines forth, so, scattering his sin, shines the man sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
As nights are without the moon, as trees are without blossom, so are the lands and the regions that are bereft of the holy waters of the Gaṅgā.
As all the castes and stages of life would be, were they stripped of the knowledge of their own duty, and as sacrifices would be without the Soma—so is the world without the Gaṅgā.
As the sky would be without the sun, the earth without mountains, and space without wind, so are the lands and regions that lack the Gaṅgā—of this there is no doubt.
Whatever living beings there are in the three worlds, all of them, when refreshed with the holy waters of the Gaṅgā, attain the highest satisfaction.
He who drinks the water of the Gaṅgā warmed by the sun gains more than from barley-gruel freed of the cattle's dung-fuel.
Whether a man perform for a thousand lunar fasts the cleansing of the body, or whether he drink the water of the Gaṅgā—whether these two be equal or not equal, who can say?
Whether a man stand for a thousand ages upon a single foot, or whether he dwell but one month by the Gaṅgā—whether these two be equal or not equal, who can say?
Though a man hang head-downward for ten thousand ages, yet he who dwells at the Gaṅgā as he pleases surpasses him.
As cotton cast into the fire is burnt utterly away, O best of the twice-born, so all the sin of one who plunges into the Gaṅgā is burnt away.
For all beings here whose minds are stricken with sorrow and who seek a refuge, there is no refuge like the Gaṅgā.
As serpents are rendered venomless at the sight of Tārkṣya, so by the sight of the Gaṅgā a man is released from all his sins.
To whatever beings are without support, and to whatever beings take refuge in unrighteousness, the Gaṅgā here is their support, their refuge, their comfort, and their armour.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Men of the lowest sort, seized by manifold and grievous evils and falling into hell — if they have taken refuge in the Gaṅgā, she will carry them across once they have passed beyond death.
Those who continually resort to the Gaṅgā — to whom the gods themselves resort — surely share fellowship with the sages and with the gods, Vāsava at their head.
Even those basest of men, devoid of discipline and right conduct and inauspicious in nature — O brāhmaṇa, they become auspicious if they take refuge in the Gaṅgā.
As nectar is to the gods, as the funerary oblation is to the ancestors, as ambrosia is to the serpents, so is the water of the Gaṅgā to mortals.
As children tormented by hunger attend upon their mother, so do embodied beings here, longing for what is highest, attend upon the Gaṅgā.
As the abode of the Self-born is declared the highest of all stations, so the Gaṅgā is here declared, for those who bathe, the foremost of rivers.
As the cow is held the sustainer of those who live by her, and the earth of the gods and the rest, so is the Gaṅgā the sustainer here of all that draws breath and lives by her.
As the gods live upon the nectars that abide in soma and the sun, won through the satra and other sacrifices, so do men live upon the water of the Gaṅgā.
Sprinkled with the sands that rise from the banks of the Jāhnavī, a man deems himself made radiant, as though dwelling in heaven.
He who bears upon his head the clay born of the Jāhnavī's bank bears a form pure and stainless as the sun's, for it destroys all darkness.
And when the wind, anointed by the waves of the Gaṅgā, touches a man, it wipes away his sin that very instant.
For a man scorched by calamities and on the verge of ruin, the joy born of beholding the Gaṅgā draws those calamities away.
With the cries of swans, the calls of the cakravāka, and the songs of other birds the Gaṅgā vies with the gandharvas, and with her sandbanks she rivals the mountains.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beholding the Gaṅgā thronged with swans and a great many varied birds, and crowded with herds of cattle, one forgets even heaven.
Not even for one dwelling in heaven and enjoying every desire is there such joy as the supreme joy of men upon the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Even a man here seized by sins born of word, mind, and deed becomes purified by beholding the Gaṅgā — of this I have no doubt.
By beholding, touching, and plunging into the Gaṅgā, a man delivers seven generations of ancestors below, seven above, and those still beyond them.
Heard of, longed for, seen, touched, drunk, and bathed in, the Gaṅgā carries across both lineages of men in full measure.
By the sight of her, the touch of her, the drinking of her, and the mere uttering of the name 'Gaṅgā,' she purifies men of no merit by hundreds and by thousands.
He who would have his birth, his life, and his learning bear fruit should go to the Gaṅgā and there satisfy the ancestors and the gods.
Not by sons, nor by wealth, nor by ritual works could a man ever win that utmost fruit which he attains on reaching the Gaṅgā.
Those who, though able, do not look upon the Gaṅgā with her holy and auspicious waters are here the equals of the blind from birth, of the dead, and of cripples.
What man would not wait upon the Gaṅgā, attended as she is by the great sages who know past, present, and future, and by the gods with Indra at their head?
What man would fail to take refuge in the Gaṅgā, to whom forest hermits, householders, ascetics, celibate students, and the learned have resorted?
He who, self-controlled and honored by the wise, with his life-breaths departing fixes his mind in thought upon the Gaṅgā, attains the supreme goal.
The man here who waits upon the Gaṅgā until his body falls away has no fear of any terrors, nor of sins, nor of the king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That most holy goddess whom Maheśvara, as she fell from the sky, upheld upon his head — her very self he honors in heaven.
The three worlds are adorned by her three pure courses; and the man who resorts to her water becomes one whose every purpose is fulfilled.
As the sun is the light in heaven, and the moon the light of the ancestors, and the lord of the gods supreme among men, so is the Gaṅgā here among rivers.
The grief of one parted from mother, father, sons, wife, or wealth is not so great as the grief born of separation from the Gaṅgā.
Not from forests, nor from beloved objects of sense, nor from sons, nor from the gaining of wealth comes such serenity to men as comes from beholding the Gaṅgā.
As the sight of men grows serene at beholding the full moon, so does their sight grow serene at beholding the Gaṅgā, who flows along three paths.
He whose being is in her, whose mind is set upon her, who is established in her and devoted to her, and who follows the Gaṅgā with devotion, comes to be dear to her.
By beings high and low — those that dwell on earth, those in the air, and those in heaven — the Gaṅgā is ever to be entered; this is the foremost duty of the good.
Throughout the three worlds the fame of the Gaṅgā is renowned for her holiness, in that she led the sons of Sagara, reduced to ashes, up to heaven.
Kindled by the gleaming waves of the Gaṅgā — driven by the wind, swift, mightily resounding, and reared up exceedingly high — he shines like the thousand-rayed sun.
Those steadfast ones who, having gone to the Gaṅgā — rich in waters, rich in butter, exceedingly bountiful, abounding, swift, and hard to ford — have given up their bodies there, have attained equality with the gods.
The glorious, mighty, all-formed Gaṅgā, served by the gods with Indra, by sages, and by men, joins the blind, the dull, and the destitute to every desire fulfilled.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who have taken refuge in the Gaṅgā — full of vigor, full of sweetness, most holy, flowing along three courses, the guardian of the three worlds — have gone to heaven.
To the mortal who shall dwell beside her or even behold her, the gods grant joys; and to him whose heart is fixed upon her touch and sight, the gods appoint the goal he desires.
Those who have gone to the Gaṅgā — skillful, broad, mighty, far-extending, auspicious, true, sweet-watered, most serene, radiant, and the foundation of all beings — have gone to the third heaven.
She whose renown of old stood firm forever throughout the sky, heaven, and earth, and through the quarters and the intermediate quarters — by resorting to the water of that best of rivers, all mortals attain their every purpose.
'This is the Gaṅgā' — she is the steadfast support, the bearer in her womb of Guha and of the golden one; at dawn she runs along three paths, carrying butter, free of all sin, descended from the firmament, her waters poured forth on every side.
The consort of Hara, who bears the mountains, befitting the girdle alike of heaven and of earth, gracious, the destiny of the earth — she shines, O king: the Gaṅgā, bestower of merit upon the three worlds.
Her stream is sweet as honey, adorned by great waves uplifted with the hue of butter and by brāhmaṇas as well; fallen from heaven and borne upon Bhava's head, the Gaṅgā, upholder of the earth, is the garland of the third heaven.
The most excellent womb, stainless, far-spreading, mighty, the nourishing draught, the bearer of waters, the giver of fame, all-containing, very form itself, the sacrifice, kindled — the Gaṅgā is the path of the world for those whom she has sprinkled.
In forbearance the equal of the earth, in protecting and upholding, and in radiance the equal of fire and of the sun, the Gaṅgā is ever honored by the brāhmaṇas and by Guha's devotion to the brahman.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who in this world have taken refuge with their whole being — even in mind — in the Jāhnavī, praised by sages, sprung from Viṣṇu's foot, ancient, of most holy waters, have gone forth to the abode of Brahmā.
She who leads these worlds onward as a mother leads her sons, endowed in her whole being with every excellence — the Gaṅgā is ever to be honored by the self-controlled who here seek their own desired and holy station, the abode of Brahmā.
The self-controlled man who longs for perfection should take refuge in the Gaṅgā — radiant, beloved, ever-watchful, watered on every side, the nourishing draught, armed with the thunderbolt, abounding, the refuge of the mountains, the refuge of the wise, immortal, beloved of Brahmā.
Bhagīratha, having propitiated all the gods together with their lords, by fierce austerity brought the Gaṅgā down to earth; and the man who resorts to her unceasingly knows no fear, neither here nor hereafter.
Of her virtues I have, having pondered with my understanding, set forth before you but a single portion in every way; I have no power here to tell, or likewise to measure out, all her virtues.
The whole hoard of jewels of Meru and the ocean, the number of the pebbles, or even of the drops of water, might be told — but here the recital of the virtues of the Gaṅgā's waters can neither be told nor measured out.
Therefore let a man, joined with supreme devotion and possessed of the highest faith, honor by speech, by mind, and by deed all these virtues of the Jāhnavī, which I have spoken with supreme faith.
Spreading your fame across these three worlds, and winning that great and hard-won perfection, you shall ere long roam at will through the desired worlds that the Gaṅgā bestows.
May the mind of you and of me, exalted in spirit, ever delight in the virtues that belong to our own dharma; for the Gaṅgā, tender toward those who come to her, cherishes the devout one and joins him to every joy.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Having thus in manifold ways instructed Śilaratin in the many true virtues that pertain to the discourse on the threefold-pathed river, that radiant siddha of supreme wisdom entered the vault of heaven.
And Śilavṛtti, then enlightened by the words of the siddha, having honored the Gaṅgā according to the rule, attained that perfection most hard to win.
Therefore you too, son of Kuntī, joined with supreme devotion, resort unceasingly to the Gaṅgā, and you shall attain the highest perfection.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this tale told by Bhīṣma, joined with the praise of the Gaṅgā, Yudhiṣṭhira together with his brothers attained the highest joy.
Whoever should hear or recite this holy tale, joined with the praise of the Gaṅgā, would be released from all his sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Since you, O best of the upholders of dharma, are endowed with wisdom and learning, with conduct and character, with all the virtues, and with the fullness of years, therefore I ask you concerning dharma.
By what means, O best of kings, might a kṣatriya, or a vaiśya, or a śūdra attain brāhmaṇahood? This you ought to explain to me.
If one should desire brāhmaṇahood, whether by very great austerity, or by ritual works, or by sacred learning — tell me this, grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Brāhmaṇahood, dear son, is hard for the three orders headed by the kṣatriyas to attain; for this, Yudhiṣṭhira, is the highest station of all beings.
Passing through many wombs, being born again and again, only in some turn of the cycle, dear son, is one born as a brāhmaṇa.
On this point too they tell this ancient tale, Yudhiṣṭhira: the dialogue of Mataṅga and the she-ass.
There was, dear son, a mighty son of a certain twice-born man, of like color to his father, Mataṅga by name, endowed with every virtue.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That performer of sacrifice, O son of Kuntī, scorcher of foes, sent forth by his father, set out upon a swift-going chariot yoked with asses.
He, O king, with his goad pierced again and again upon the nose a young ass that was drawing the chariot beside its mother.
But the she-ass, yearning for her offspring, seeing him grievously wounded, said: 'Grieve not, my child; it is a caṇḍāla who sits over you.'
'In a brāhmaṇa there is no cruelty; a brāhmaṇa is called the friend of all. He is the teacher and chastiser of all beings — why would he strike?'
'But this one, of evil nature, shows no mercy to a young creature; he does but honor his own origin — a nature passes on to its like.'
Hearing this harsh speech of the she-ass, Mataṅga quickly stepped down from the chariot and answered her.
'Tell me, gracious she-ass, by whom was my mother defiled? How do you know me to be a caṇḍāla? Quickly, she-ass, declare it to me.'
'By whom was I born a caṇḍāla, so that my brāhmaṇahood is lost to me? Tell me this truly, O most wise one, all of it without reserve.'
The she-ass said: 'You were begotten by a śūdra, a barber, upon a brāhmaṇa woman maddened with drink; therefore you are a caṇḍāla, and therefore your brāhmaṇahood is lost.'
Thus addressed, Mataṅga turned back homeward; and seeing him return, his father then spoke these words.
'By me you were appointed to the weighty task of the completion of the sacrifice; why have you turned back? Is it that all is not well with you?'
Mataṅga said: 'He may be well whose birth is from no womb, or from the highest womb; but whence can there be well-being for him whose mother is such as this, O father?'
Father, this she-donkey, no mere beast but more than human, declares me born of a brāhmaṇa woman by a man of the lowest sort; therefore I shall practice a mighty austerity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken thus to his father, his resolve fixed, he set out; and going to the great forest, he practiced a mighty austerity.
Then Mataṅga, endowed with austerity, scorched the gods with the heat of his penance, seeking to win a blissful station beyond even that gained by right conduct.
To him, thus engaged in austerity, the bearer of the bay steeds said: "Mataṅga, why do you mortify yourself, casting aside the pleasures of men?"
"Come, I grant you a boon; choose whatever you desire. And whatever else may be obtained, declare it all to me without delay."
Mataṅga said: "Longing for brāhmaṇahood, I have undertaken this austerity. May I attain it and reach that state here; this is the boon I have chosen."
Hearing these words, Puraṃdara said to him: "You crave brāhmaṇahood, which is unattainable by those whose selves are unperfected."
"Craving that supreme thing, the foremost among all beings, which no austerity can surpass, you will soon perish."
"That which is held the highest purity among gods, asuras, and mortals can in no way be attained by one born in the womb of a caṇḍāla."
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Mataṅga, his soul resolute and his vows controlled, stood upon one foot for a hundred years, O unfaltering one.
Then the greatly renowned Śakra spoke to him once again: "Mataṅga, you seek that highest station, which is most hard to win."
"Do not act so rashly, my son; this is not the path of dharma for you. Craving what cannot be attained, you will soon perish."
"Mataṅga, though restrained by me once, you still strive by austerity for the highest station; by no means will you attain it."
"If any creature fallen into the womb of beasts comes at last to human birth, it is born now and then as a pulkasa or a caṇḍāla."
"Whoever here is marked as a son of a wanton woman or of a sinful womb, Mataṅga, revolves in that very condition for a very long time."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Then, after a tenfold span of time, he attains even the state of a śūdra; and in the śūdra womb thereafter he revolves many times."
"Then, after a thirtyfold span of time, he attains even the state of a vaiśya; and in that vaiśya condition he revolves for a long time."
"Then, after a sixtyfold span of time, he is born one called a rājanya; and in that kṣatriya estate he revolves for a long time."
"Then, after a sixtyfold span of time, he attains kinship with brāhmaṇas; and as such a brahma-kinsman he revolves for a long time."
"Then, after twice a hundred such spans, he attains the state of a kāṇḍapṛṣṭha; and as a kāṇḍapṛṣṭha he revolves for a long time."
"Then, after thrice a hundred such spans, he attains even the state of a twice-born; and having reached it, he revolves there for a long time."
"Then, after four hundred such spans, he is born one called a śrotriya, learned in the Veda; and in that śrotriya estate he revolves for a long time."
"And even then anger and elation, desire and hatred, excessive pride and harsh speech, my son, enter that lowest of the twice-born."
"If he conquers those enemies, he then attains the good path; but if they conquer him, he is cast down as from the top of a palm tree."
"Mataṅga, having weighed this, on account of which I have urged you, choose some other desire; for brāhmaṇahood is very hard to win."
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Mataṅga, sunk deep in grief, went to Gayā and stood there poised upon his great toe for a hundred years.
Sustaining a most difficult discipline, grown gaunt with his veins standing forth, reduced to skin and bone, that righteous soul fell down at last—so we have heard.
As he fell, Vāsava rushed forward and caught him—the lord and bestower of boons, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Śakra said: "Mataṅga, your attaining of brāhmaṇahood is hedged about by obstacles. He who honors the brāhmaṇa wins happiness; he who fails to honor him wins sorrow."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"In the brāhmaṇa the welfare and security of all beings rests secure; through brāhmaṇas the ancestors and the gods alike are satisfied."
"The brāhmaṇa, Mataṅga, is declared the highest of all beings; for the brāhmaṇa accomplishes whatever and however he wishes."
"Passing through many wombs, being born again and again, only at some turn in the round, my son, does one here come upon brāhmaṇahood."
Mataṅga said: "Why do you torment me, stricken with grief, and slay me who am already dead? But I grieve for that man who, having gained brāhmaṇahood, cares not to be a brāhmaṇa."
"If brāhmaṇahood is hard to win for the three other varṇas, O lord of a hundred sacrifices, yet having gained that thing so hard to win, men do not live up to it."
"He is the most sinful of the sinful, the basest among them, who slights his brāhmaṇahood as a man might slight a hard-won treasure he has gained."
"Hard indeed to attain is the brāhmaṇa's estate, and once attained, hard to maintain; yet having won this thing so hard to win, men do not live up to it."
"I delight in solitude, O Śakra, free from the pairs of opposites, owning nothing, established in non-violence, self-restraint, and giving—how am I not worthy of the brāhmaṇa's estate?"
"Grant then that I may roam at will, a bird that takes what form it wishes; that I may receive honor without offense to brāhmaṇa or kṣatriya; and that my fame, O Puraṃdara, may become imperishable."
Indra said: "Renowned as Chandodeva, you shall become an object of worship among women."
Bhīṣma said: Having granted him this boon, Vāsava vanished; and Mataṅga too, giving up his life-breaths, attained that highest station.
So this highest station, called brāhmaṇahood, O Bhārata, is hard to win in this world, even as the words of great Indra declared.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard this great tale, O upholder of the Kuru line; you declare brāhmaṇahood most hard to win, O best of speakers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yet it is heard that long ago Viśvāmitra attained brāhmaṇahood; and still you say it is hard to win, O most virtuous one.
And I have heard that the royal sage Vītahavya passed into the brāhmaṇa's estate; that very story, son of Gaṅgā, I wish to hear, O mighty one.
By what deed did he attain brāhmaṇahood, O best of kings—by a boon, or by austerity? That you should be pleased to explain to me.
Bhīṣma said: Hear, O king, how the greatly renowned king Vītahavya, though a kṣatriya, came to attain the brāhmaṇahood that the world reveres.
Of the great-souled Manu, who ruled by the dharma of a guardian of his people, there was a righteous son, renowned by the name of Śaryāti.
In his line, O king, there arose two kings, Haihaya and Tālajaṅgha, among the Vatsas, O best of the victorious.
Of Haihaya's sons by ten wives, O Bhārata, there came to be a famed hundred, heroes who never turned back in battle.
Equal in form and power, learned and skilled in war, they had labored diligently in every branch of the science of archery and of the Veda.
Among the Kāśis too, O king, there was a ruler, the grandfather of Divodāsa, renowned as Haryaśva, best of the victorious.
The heirs of Vītahavya came against him, O bull among men, and in the land between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā he was struck down in battle.
Having slain that finest of men, those Haihaya great chariot-warriors returned, free from all fear, to the lovely city of the Vatsas.
Then Haryaśva's heir Sudeva, godlike in his splendor, like Dharma himself made manifest, was consecrated king of Kāśi.
As the righteous joy of the Kāśis was ruling the earth, those sons of Vītahavya came once more and in battle utterly defeated him.
Having defeated him too in the fray, they returned as they had come; and then Sudeva's son Divodāsa was consecrated lord of Kāśi.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Divodāsa, knowing well the prowess of those great-souled foes, in his great splendor built the city of Vārāṇasī at Śakra's command.
It was thronged with brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas, teeming with vaiśyas and śūdras, heaped with goods of every kind, rich in its markets and its stalls.
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, by the edge of the rampart, O best of kings, and on the southern side of the Gomatī—like Śakra's own Amarāvatī.
There, as that tiger among kings, the lord of the earth, was dwelling, the Hehayas came once again and assailed him on every side, O Bhārata.
That mighty king of great radiance, Divodāsa, sallied forth and gave them battle, dreadful as the clash of gods and asuras.
In that battle, O great king, for a thousand days, with the most of his mounts slain, he was at last brought to wretchedness.
His warriors slain and his treasury drained, O king, the lord of the earth Divodāsa abandoned his city and gave himself over to flight.
Coming to the hermitage of the wise Bharadvāja, the king sought refuge with folded hands, O subduer of foes.
The king said: "Holy one, the sons of Vītahavya have destroyed my line in battle; I alone, utterly afflicted, have come to you for refuge."
"By your affection for a pupil, holy one, you ought to protect me; for my line has been left without remnant by those doers of evil deeds."
To him the blessed and mighty Bharadvāja said: "Fear not, fear not, son of Sudeva; let your dread depart."
