"This very day I shall perform a sacrifice for a son for you, O lord of the people, that you may overcome the thousands of Vītahavya's kin."
Then the sage performed for him that sacrifice for the gaining of a son; and there was born to him a boy renowned as Pratardana.
No sooner was he born than he grew, on the instant, to a youth of thirteen years, and mastered the whole Veda and the science of archery, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Pervaded by the yoga of the wise Bharadvāja, he gathered into himself the splendor of the world and entered into that prince.
Then, mailed, bow in hand and arrows ready, blazing like fire, he marched forth, brandishing his bow like a rain-cloud about to pour.
Beholding him, Sudeva's son was filled with the highest joy, and that king reckoned in his mind that the sons of Vītahavya were already consumed.
Then, having installed Pratardana in the office of heir-apparent, the king rejoiced, accounting himself to have accomplished his purpose.
Then for the slaying of the sons of Vītahavya that lord of the earth sent forth his son, Pratardana, the subduer of foes.
Swiftly that valiant one, conqueror of hostile cities, crossed the Gaṅgā with his chariot and marched upon the city of the sons of Vītahavya.
But the sons of Vītahavya, hearing the swelling thunder of his chariot, sallied forth on chariots vast as fortresses, crushers of the chariots of their foes.
Sallying forth, those tigers among men, mailed and skilled in varied fighting, weapons raised, struck at Pratardana with showers of arrows.
With missiles of every kind and floods of chariots, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they rained upon the king as rain-clouds upon the Himālaya.
Warding off their missiles with his own, king Pratardana of great splendor slew them with arrows that were like the thunderbolt and like fire.
Their heads severed by his broad-headed arrows, O king, they fell in their hundreds and thousands, their limbs drenched in blood, like kiṃśuka trees cut down.
When all those sons were slain, Vītahavya fled, abandoning his city, and made his way even to the hermitage of Bhṛgu.
The king Vītahavya went to Bhṛgu for refuge, and Bhṛgu, O king, granted that king his protection; then, becoming Bhṛgu's disciple, he was offered a seat as well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, hard upon his heels, Pratardana swiftly arrived there; and reaching the precincts of the hermitage, the son of Divodāsa spoke.
"Ho there! Who are present in this hermitage as disciples of the great-souled Bhṛgu? I wish to see the sage; announce me to him."
When Bhṛgu learned of him, he came forth from the hermitage and honored him then with the highest ceremony.
And he said to that prince, O lord of kings, "What is your purpose?" And the king told him the reason for his coming.
"This king Vītahavya, O brahman, let him be given up from here; for by his sons, O brahman, my whole lineage was destroyed, and the realm of the Kāśis with its store of treasures was laid waste."
"The hundred sons of this man, drunk with his might, were slain by me; now by his death, O brahman, I shall become free of my debt to my father."
To him Bhṛgu, foremost of the upholders of dharma, filled with compassion, said: "There is no kṣatriya here at all; for all these are brahmans."
Hearing this truthful word of Bhṛgu, Pratardana gently touched his feet and, smiling, spoke these words:
"Even so, O blessed one, I have accomplished my purpose, without doubt, since by my prowess this king has been made to forsake his own caste."
"Give me leave, O brahman, and think of me with kindly intent; for by me this king has been made to lose his caste, O scion of Bhṛgu."
Then, granted leave by him, King Pratardana departed as he had come, O great king, like a serpent that has discharged its venom.
And by the mere word of Bhṛgu, Vītahavya attained, O great king, the state of a brahman seer and the mastery of brahman-lore.
His son was Gṛtsamada, in beauty like a second Indra, who was once seized by the Daityas with the cry, "You are Śakra!"
And there is a foremost sacred text in this regard in the Ṛgveda, O lord of peoples, wherein that Gṛtsamada, O brahman, is exalted by the brahmans.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That Gṛtsamada became a celibate brahman seer, illustrious; and Gṛtsamada's son too was a brahman named Sucetas.
Varcas was the son of the mighty-splendored one, and Vihavya was his offspring; Vihavya's son was Vitatya, and his offspring in turn.
Vitatya's son was Satya, and Santa was Satya's offspring; his son was the seer Śravas, and from Śravas came Tamas.
And from Tamas was born a son, Prakāśa, best of the twice-born; and from Prakāśa came Vāgindra, foremost of the victorious.
His son was Pramati, master of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; and to him by Ghṛtācī was born a son named Ruru.
And to Ruru by Pramadvarā was born a son, a brahman seer named Śunaka, whose son in turn was Śaunaka.
Thus did the king Vītahavya attain to brahman-hood, by the grace of Bhṛgu, O lord of kings, though a kṣatriya, O bull among kṣatriyas.
So too has the lineage of Gṛtsamada been recounted by me to you in full, O great king. What else do you ask?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who are to be honored, who are to be reverenced by men, O bull of the Bhāratas? Tell me this in full, for I am not sated; let it be told.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount this ancient tale, the dialogue of the two, Nārada and Vāsudeva.
Seeing Nārada with joined palms doing honor to the bulls among the twice-born, Keśava asked him: "Blessed one, whom do you reverence?"
"Toward whom is your highest regard, those whom you reverence? If it may be heard, I wish to know; tell me this, O best of the knowers of dharma."
Nārada said: Hear, O Govinda, those whom I honor, O crusher of foes; for what man in the world other than you is worthy to hear this here?
Varuṇa, Vāyu, the Sun, Parjanya, the fire-born Jātavedas, Sthāṇu, Skanda, and Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu and Brahmā too—
Vācaspati, the Moon, the Waters, the Earth, and Sarasvatī—those who reverence these unceasingly, them do I reverence, O mighty one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those rich in austerity, knowers of the Veda, ever devoted to the Veda, most worthy—O tiger of the Vṛṣṇis, them I always honor.
Those who, before eating, perform the rites of the gods, free of boastfulness, content and endowed with forbearance—them I reverence, O mighty one.
Those who give rightly to the worthy—patient, self-controlled, masters of their senses—grain, wealth, land, and cattle, them I reverence, O Yādava.
Those who dwell in austerity in the forest, feeding on roots and fruits, hoarding nothing, performing their rites—them I reverence, O Yādava.
Those intent upon supporting their dependents, ever fond of guests, who eat what remains after offering to the gods—them I reverence, O Yādava.
Those who, having mastered the Veda, are unassailable, eloquent, expounders of the brahman, ever engaged in performing sacrifices and in teaching—them I honor.
And those of serene heart toward all beings always, devoted to their study even to the point of bodily exhaustion—them I honor.
Those who strive for the favor of their teacher and for their study, steadfast in their vows, eager to serve and free of envy—them I reverence, O Yādava.
Those sages of good vows, devoted to the brahman, true to their pledges, bearers of offerings to gods and ancestors—them I reverence, O Yādava.
Those devoted to the practice of begging, lean, sheltering in the teacher's house, without comfort and without wealth—them I reverence, O Yādava.
Free of possessiveness, free of rivalry, free of false shame, free of selfish ends, devoted to non-injury, and those men vowed to truth, self-controlled and intent on tranquillity—them I reverence, O Keśava.
Householders devoted to the worship of gods and guests, who live always like the dove, gleaning only what suffices—them I reverence, O Yādava.
Those in whose deeds the three aims of life abide and are not diminished, who follow the conduct of the cultivated—them I reverence always.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those brahmans in the three worlds who pursue the three aims of life, free of greed, of holy character—them I reverence, O Keśava.
Those who feed always on water, on air, or on nectar, and who are bound by various vows—them I reverence, O Mādhava.
Those of no womb, those born of fire, those born of the brahman, and those born of the self that is the source of all beings—those twice-born I reverence.
These I reverence always, O Kṛṣṇa—the seers who make the worlds, eldest of the worlds, fixed in knowledge, destroyers of darkness, lights of the world.
Therefore you too, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis, honor the twice-born always; for when honored, those worthy of honor will grant you happiness, O sinless one.
For in this world and in the next these are ever givers of happiness; honored as they deserve, they will indeed bestow happiness upon you.
Those who are ever hospitable to all, devoted always to cattle and to brahmans and to truth—they pass beyond all hardships.
Those ever intent on tranquillity, and those free of envy, and those ever devoted to their study—they pass beyond all hardships.
Those who reverence all the gods while relying upon a single god, full of faith and self-controlled—they pass beyond all hardships.
And likewise those who, having reverenced the foremost brahmans of disciplined vows, become devoted to giving—they pass beyond all hardships.
Those who, having established the sacred fires according to rule, maintain them with care and have attained the soma-offering—they pass beyond all hardships.
Those who always conduct themselves rightly toward mother and father and teachers, just as you do, O tiger of the Vṛṣṇis—so saying, he fell silent.
Therefore you too, O son of Kuntī, rightly honor ancestors, gods, the twice-born, and guests, by which you shall attain the goal you desire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of all a king's duties, which is the weightiest, O grandsire? By doing what deed does a king win both worlds?
Bhīṣma said: This is the foremost duty of a consecrated king, O Bhārata: the serving of brahmans. One who desires the highest happiness should ever honor the learned, the brahmans, and the aged.
And the brahmans of city and countryside, deeply learned, he should honor with conciliating words, with gifts of enjoyments, and with marks of reverence.
He should mark this as ever the foremost duty of a king; he should cherish them as he would himself, as he would his own sons.
And those among them who are most worthy of honor he should honor steadfastly; when they are at peace, the whole realm shines forth.
They are to be honored, they to be reverenced, they to be guarded like one's own fathers; upon them rests the world's course, as upon Vāsava that of beings.
By sorceries and by stratagems, even by their own fiery power, they could consume; when angered, the fierce ones, whose valor is truth, could leave nothing remaining.
I see no limit to their power, nor any quarter left uncovered; when angered they blaze up like flames of fire in a forest conflagration.
There are found in them daring qualities in the extreme; some are like wells covered over with grass, while others are pure as the sky.
Some among them act by force, others are soft as cotton; some of them are exceedingly crafty, while still others are exceeding ascetics.
Some practice farming and the tending of cattle, others live by begging; some are thieves, others liars, and yet others actors and dancers.
They are seen in all occupations, the peaceful and the other kind, and endowed with manifold ways of life are the brahmans, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Engaged though they are in diverse occupations and living by many trades, they are knowers of dharma and good men; their praise one should ever proclaim.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of ancestors and of gods, of men, serpents, and rākṣasas, the brahmans, O lord of men, are the highly blessed household priests.
These twice-born cannot be conquered by gods, nor by ancestors, nor by gandharvas, nor by rākṣasas, nor by asuras, nor by piśācas.
They could make a non-god into a god, and a god into a non-god; whomever they wish, he becomes king, and whomever they hate, he comes to ruin.
And those senseless ones who utter reproach against the brahmans—the twice-born, skilled in blame and praise, who dispense fame and infamy, high and low, grow ever wrathful, O king, toward those who hate them.
The man whom the brahmans praise, that man prospers; but he who is reviled by the brahmans comes to ruin in an instant.
The Śakas, Yavanas, and Kāmbojas, and those various kṣatriya races, have fallen into the condition of degraded men through the absence of brahmans.
The Dramiḷas and Kaliṅgas, the Pulindas and Uśīnaras, the Kaulas, Sarpas, and Māhiṣakas—those various kṣatriya races—
have fallen into the condition of degraded men through the absence of brahmans. Better is defeat at their hands than victory, O best of the victorious.
Even one who should slay all this world—there is nothing equal to slaying a brahman; the killing of a brahman is a grievous sin, so say the supreme seers.
Reviling of the twice-born must never be listened to under any circumstance. Either let a man sit silent with face bowed down, or let him rise and walk away.
There is none born, nor to be born, upon this earth, who by setting himself against the brāhmaṇas could dare to live in ease.
Hard to seize with the fist is the wind, hard to touch with the hand is the moon, hard to bear upon the head is the earth—and hard to conquer upon this world are the brāhmaṇas.
Bhīṣma said: The brāhmaṇas, ever and always, one should honor with the utmost zeal, for they have Soma for their king and are the masters of joy and sorrow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With enjoyments, with adornments, and with whatever else they may desire, they are ever to be honored, saluted, and protected by kings as one's own fathers; for from this comes the peace of the realm, as the peace of all beings comes from Vāsava.
Let there be born in the realm a pure brāhmaṇa radiant with sacred lore; and a mighty-chariot warrior of the royal line, a scorcher of foes, is to be wished for.
A brāhmaṇa endowed with noble birth, knowing dharma, of well-honed vows—him, O king, let one settle in one's house; truly there is nothing higher than that.
The oblation given to brāhmaṇas the gods receive, and the fathers of all beings; than these there is known nothing higher.
The sun, the moon, the wind, the earth, the waters, the sky, the quarters—all of these, entering into the brāhmaṇa, partake of the good food offered.
The fathers do not eat of the man whose brāhmaṇas do not eat; nor do the gods partake of that sinner who hates the brāhmaṇas.
But when the brāhmaṇas are content, the fathers too are ever pleased, and likewise the gods, O king; in this no doubt need be entertained.
Likewise are those pleased to whom that oblation comes; and they do not perish after death, but attain the supreme goal.
By whatever oblation a man satisfies the brāhmaṇas, by that very same the fathers are pleased, and the gods as well.
From the brāhmaṇa alone arises that being whence creatures spring, whence this world comes forth, and whither it goes after death.
He knows the path of heaven and likewise of hell, both what has come and what has not yet come—the brāhmaṇa, best of two-footed beings. The brāhmaṇa, O finest of the Bhāratas, knows his own dharma by his wisdom.
And those who follow him go not to ruin; they do not perish after death, nor do they come to downfall.
Those who accept the word received from the brāhmaṇa's mouth—the perfected of soul, the great-spirited—they go not to downfall.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Of the kṣatriyas who blaze forth with energy and with might, their splendors and their powers find their quenching in the brāhmaṇas alone.
The Bhṛgus conquered the Tālajaṅghas, the Aṅgirases conquered the Nīpas, and Bharadvāja conquered the Vaitahavyas and the Ailas, O bull of the Bhāratas.
These, with the black antelope-skin for their banner, conquered even the Citrāyudhas; and having cast away the water-jars, one should set out upon him who would carry men across.
Whatever is told in the world, whatever is heard or seen, all of that abides in the brāhmaṇas, as fire lies hidden in wood.
On this point, too, they recite this ancient tale, the dialogue between Vāsudeva and the Earth, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Vāsudeva said: O auspicious one, mother of all beings, I ask you my doubt: by what deed does a householder put away his sin?
The Earth said: Let him serve the brāhmaṇas, for this is the highest purifier; for one who serves the brāhmaṇas, all his impurity is destroyed.
From this comes prosperity, from this glory, from this is wisdom born—for those below, for those above, and for those still beyond the highest.
The man whom the brāhmaṇas praise, he flourishes; but he who is reviled by the brāhmaṇas comes to ruin before long.
As a lump of unbaked clay cast into the great ocean dissolves away, so an ill-doing deed conduces to one's downfall.
Behold the mark set upon the moon, the salt water in the ocean, and great Indra branded with the thousand marks.
By their very power he became the thousand-eyed one, the lord of a hundred sacrifices—behold, O Mādhava, of what kind that was.
Desiring prosperity and glory and the higher worlds, O slayer of Madhu, let a man abide pure and self-possessed by the consent of the brāhmaṇas.
Having heard this word of the Earth, the slayer of Madhu, saying "Well said, well said, so be it," did reverence to the Earth in return.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having heard this parable, O Pārtha, with diligence honor the bulls among brāhmaṇas continually; thereby you shall attain to good.
Bhīṣma said: By his very birth the one called brāhmaṇa is born greatly blessed, to be saluted by all beings, a guest who eats the first portion set forth.
All the brāhmaṇas are our well-wishers, my son, kindly of face; when honored, they wish us well with words laden with blessing.
But all the brāhmaṇas become our foes, my son, their wrath aroused, and when slighted they would strike with words laden with menace.
On this point those who know the past recite verses sung by Brahmā; for the Ordainer, having created the twice-born, addressed them as of old.
Nothing else here, nothing beyond, need be done by you according to rule: guarded yourselves, guard the sacred lore—therein lies your fair and excellent good.
As you perform your own proper work, the splendor of Brahman shall be yours; you shall become the measure of all beings, and shall attain to mastery over them.
No śūdra's work should be done by a learned brāhmaṇa, for when one performs a śūdra's work, his dharma is obstructed.
Splendor and wisdom and energy and majestic dominion—and through self-study alone you shall attain a stainless greatness of soul.
Having offered into the fire set in the āhavanīya hearth, established in high blessedness, you are the first to be fed among created beings, fashioned with the splendor of Brahman.
Endowed with supreme faith, gained without malice, devoted to self-restraint and self-study, you shall attain all your desires.
Whatever there is in the world of men, and whatever among the gods, all of that is attainable by austerity, by knowledge, and by discipline.
Thus have these verses sung by Brahmā been recounted to you by me, O sinless one; for this was uttered by that wise one out of compassion for the brāhmaṇas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Greater still I deem the power of those ascetics than even that of a king: unapproachable, fierce, impetuous, swift to act.
Among them are some of lion-nature and others of tiger-nature, some of boar-and-deer nature and others of elephant-nature.
Some are soft as cotton, while others strike like the makara; some slay by mere speech, and others slay with a glance.
There are those like venomous serpents, and there are others mild; manifold are the ways of the brāhmaṇas here, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Mekalas, the Dramiḍas, the Kāśas, the Pauṇḍras, and the Kollagiras, the Śauṇḍikas, the Daradas, the Darvas, the Cauras, the Śabaras and Barbaras—
the Kirātas and the Yavanas too—those various kṣatriya races sank into the state of low-born men through failing to behold the brāhmaṇas.
Through their contempt for the brāhmaṇas, the asuras lie sunk in the waters; and through the grace of the brāhmaṇas, the gods are dwellers in heaven.
The sky cannot be touched, the Himavān mountain cannot be moved, the Gaṅgā cannot be dammed by any dike—and the brāhmaṇas cannot be conquered upon this earth.
By setting oneself against the brāhmaṇas, the earth cannot be ruled; for the brāhmaṇas, the great-souled, are deities even of the gods.
Honor them continually with gifts and with service, if you wish to enjoy this earth that is girdled by the sea.
By the receiving of gifts the energy of the brāhmaṇas is quieted, O sinless one; and those who would not wish to receive gifts—they too are to be protected by you, O sinless one.
Bhīṣma said: On this point, too, they recite this ancient tale, the dialogue between Śakra and Śambara; mark it well, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Śakra, in a form unrecognized, having become a matted-haired ascetic ruddy with dust, and taking on an ugly shape, put a question to Śambara.
By what conduct, O Śambara, do you stand above those of your own race? For what reason do they hold you to be the best? Tell me that, who ask you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Śambara said: I never spurn the brāhmaṇas, nor Brahmā the grandfather; the brāhmaṇas, as they expound the sacred texts, I honor to their full content.
And having heard them, I do not despise them, nor do I ever offend; the worshipful I question with deference, and I clasp the feet of the wise.
Trustful, they speak freely and ever restrain me from error; among the heedless I am heedful, and among the sleeping I keep ever awake.
Those teachers pour upon me—set on the path of the scriptures, devoted to the brāhmaṇas, free of envy—their instruction, as bees pour out their honey.
And whatever they, well-pleased, declare, that I receive with my understanding, ever keeping the composure of my soul attuned and undisturbed in thought.
Thus I, the licker of the savors poured forth from the tip of their speech, stand above those of my own race, as the moon above the constellations.
This is the nectar upon the earth, this the unsurpassed eye—the teaching which, heard here from the brāhmaṇa's mouth, sets one upon his way.
Having learned this cause, and having beheld of old the war between the gods and the asuras, my father, glad of heart and amazed, came to acknowledge it.
And having beheld the greatness of the great-souled brāhmaṇas, he asked the moon, the night-maker, "How is it that these have attained perfection?"
Soma said: The brāhmaṇas all attain perfection through austerity, their strength ever in their speech; for kings have their valor in their arms, but the twice-born have speech for their weapon.
Even while abroad let him study, dwelling through many hard sojournings; free of wrath and free of pride, an ascetic let him be, looking on all alike.
Even if one of noble birth should study all the Vedas in his father's house, yet study as if boasting of it, him they call a vulgar man.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The earth swallows up these two, as a serpent swallows creatures that lie in their holes: the king who will not fight, and the brāhmaṇa who will not go abroad.
Excessive pride destroys the fortune of a man of little understanding; a maiden is spoiled by an untimely conceiving, and a brāhmaṇa by mere staying at home.
Having heard this from Soma of wondrous aspect, my father honored the brāhmaṇas of great vows—and even so do I.
Bhīṣma said: Having heard this word fallen from the mouth of the lord of the dānavas, Śakra honored the twice-born, and attained the sovereignty of great Indra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: A worthy recipient may be one newly come, or one who has dwelt long with us, or one arrived from afar; who, O grandfather, is a fit recipient?
Bhīṣma said: For some, the rite is this—a vow kept in silence is the highest: "Whoever begs whatever it may be, all of it let us give."
Yet without oppressing one's dependants—thus have we heard it taught; for he who oppresses his dependants drags himself down.
Whether the recipient be newly come, or one who has dwelt long, or one arrived from afar—the wise know him too to be a fit recipient.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Without oppressing our dependants, and without harm to dharma, let us know in truth that recipient to whom a gift, once given, brings no regret.
Bhīṣma said: The officiating priest, the family priest, the teacher, disciples, kinsmen, and relations—all are to be honored and revered, provided they are endowed with sacred learning and good conduct.
Those who conduct themselves otherwise than this are none of them worthy of honor; therefore one should ever examine men, observing them closely with care.
Freedom from anger, truthful speech, non-injury, self-restraint, uprightness, freedom from malice, absence of pride, modesty, forbearance, austerity, tranquillity—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the man in whom these are seen, firmly settled by their very nature, O Bhārata, and who does no forbidden deeds—that one is a worthy vessel, deserving of honor.
So too one long abiding here, or one but newly arrived, whether a stranger never seen before or an old acquaintance—such a vessel deserves honor.
To deny the authority of the Vedas, to overstep the sacred treatises, and to lack steadfastness in all things—this is the ruin of one's own self.
The brāhmaṇa who fancies himself learned, who reviles the Vedas, who is devoted to the science of logic and to fruitless disputation,
who utters arguments of mere reasoning amid the good, a refuter who confounds those who do not so reason, and who is forever a reviler and abuser of brāhmaṇas—
suspicious of all, deluded, childish, and harsh of tongue—such a one, my son, is to be recognized for what he is, for they call him a dog among men.
As a dog is let loose to bark and to bite, so are such men loosed for wrangling and for the slaughter of all the scriptures; men of little learning, given to crooked logic—such false scholars are seen and met with everywhere.
One should seek out the learned—those versed in śruti, smṛti, the chronicles, the purāṇas, and the forest-treatises, men of wide knowledge who grasp the essence of things.
The course of worldly life must be observed, and dharma, and what is for one's own good; the man who so conducts himself flourishes through everlasting years.
Having discharged his debt to the gods, and likewise to the seers, to the ancestors, to the brāhmaṇas, and as the fifth, to guests,
in due order, with pure and well-cleansed action—thus the householder, performing his works, falls not away from his sacred duties.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I wish to hear of the nature of women, O best of the Bhāratas; for women are the root of faults, and light of mind, O grandsire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: On this they relate an ancient tale of old—the dialogue between Nārada and the wanton apsaras Pañcacūḍā.
Of old, as the wise divine seer Nārada wandered through the worlds, he beheld the blameless apsaras Pañcacūḍā, born of Brahmā.
Seeing her, lovely in every limb, the sage questioned the apsaras: 'A certain doubt stirs within my heart; tell me of it, O slender-waisted one.'
Thus addressed, she answered the brāhmaṇa Nārada: 'If it lie within my province I shall speak of it, and if you deem me equal to the task.'
Nārada said: I shall in no way set you, gentle lady, to a matter beyond your province; I wish to hear from you, O fair-faced one, the nature of women.
Bhīṣma said: Hearing this word of the divine seer, the foremost of apsarases replied: 'I shall not be able, being myself a woman, to censure women.'
'Women are known to you, both who they are and of what nature they are; you ought not, O divine seer, to set me to a question such as this.'
To her the divine seer said: 'Speak the truth, O slender-waisted one; in false speech there is fault, but in truth no fault is found.'
Thus addressed, the sweetly smiling one made up her mind, and set herself to declare the everlasting and true faults of women.
Pañcacūḍā said: Women of good family, beautiful, and possessed of protectors do not abide within the bounds of propriety; that, Nārada, is the fault in women.
There is indeed nothing else more given to wickedness than women, for women are the root of faults; this too you yourself well know.
Though their husbands be renowned, prosperous, comely, and wholly devoted, women, finding an opening, are unable to remain faithful.
This is the wicked way of us women, O lord—that, casting off shame, we consort with men more base than our own.
For whoever woos a woman, draws near to her, and renders her but a little service—him the women desire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Only because men do not solicit them, and out of fear of their kinsfolk, do women—unrestrained though they are—abide within bounds and stay with their husbands.
For them no man is forbidden, nor have they any fixed regard for age; be he ugly or handsome, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Not from fear, nor from compassion, nor for the sake of wealth in any way, nor from the bond of kindred and family do women remain with their husbands.
Women of good families yearn after those women who, being in the flush of youth, adorned with bright ornaments and raiment, live as they please.
Even those women who are forever highly esteemed, cherished, and guarded—even they cleave to hunchbacks, the blind, the dull-witted, and dwarfs.
Even to the lame, O divine seer, and to other men despised—in this world, O great sage, there is no man forbidden to women.
If, O holy one, access to men in no way befalls them, they will resort even to one another, for they cannot abide content with their husbands.
For want of men, from fear of their household, and from dread of slaying and bondage, they keep themselves guarded of their own accord.
Fickle by nature, hard to serve, and by their disposition hard to grasp—women are even as the speech of a wise man here below.
As fire is never sated with fuel, nor the great ocean with rivers, nor Death with all beings, so are the fair-eyed ones never sated with men.
And here is another secret of all womankind, O divine seer: at the mere sight of a pleasing man, a woman's loins grow moist with desire.
Even a husband who grants their every desire, who shows them honor and tender words, who is their guardian—even such a peerless husband women do not patiently endure.
They do not prize abundant enjoyments, nor heaps of ornaments and wealth, so highly as they prize the favor of the act of love.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Ender, the Subduer, Death, the netherworld, the submarine fire, the razor's edge, poison, the serpent, and flame on the one side—and women on the other.
From whatever source the five great elements arose, and the worlds were ordained by the Creator, from that same source men and women were fashioned—and from that very moment, O Nārada, the faults were set in women.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: These men in the world cleave again and again to women, possessed utterly by a delusion ordained by fate, O king; and women too, plainly and with the world for witness, cleave to men.
Herein a keen doubt revolves within my heart: how do men form attachment to these women, O delight of the Kurus, and how do women take pleasure in them, or again grow weary of them?
Such being so, O tiger among men, how are women able to be guarded by a man in this world? That you ought to explain to me.
For these women beguile men here with the wiles of Maya, and no man once come into their hands escapes them; like cattle to fresh grass, they seize on ever-new men.
All the sorcery that was Śambara's, and the sorcery of Namuci, of Bali, and of Kumbhīnasī—all of it women know.
At one who laughs they laugh, and at one who weeps they weep; and one who is unwelcome to them they take captive with sweet words, as the moment requires.
The science that Uśanas knows, and that which Bṛhaspati knows, are not superior to the cunning of women—how then are they to be guarded by men?
They call falsehood truth, and likewise truth they call falsehood; how, O hero, are such women to be guarded by men in this world?
By drawing forth the very cunning of women, O slayer of foes, the treatises on statecraft, I think, were composed by the good—by Bṛhaspati and the rest.
When honored by men, women turn their minds away from those men; and when cast off as well, O king, women turn their minds away likewise.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Who could be able to guard them?—this is my great doubt. Tell me of it, O mighty-armed one, increaser of the line of the Kurus.
If their guarding can in any way be accomplished, O best of the Kurus, or has ever been accomplished of old, that you ought to explain to me.
Bhīṣma said: So it is, O mighty-armed one; in this there is nothing false, even as you say concerning woman, O Kaurava, O lord of men.
On this I shall relate to you an ancient tale—how of old a guarding was accomplished by the great-souled Vipula.
And how women were created by Brahmā, O bull of the Bhāratas, and to what end—that too I shall declare to you, my son, O lord of the earth.
For there is nothing, my son, more given to wickedness than women; a woman is blazing fire, and the wiles born of Maya, O lord; the razor's edge, poison, the serpent, and Death on the one side—and women on the other.
These creatures, O mighty-armed one—being righteous, so we have heard—were attaining godhood of their own accord; and thereupon fear came upon the gods.
Then those gods came to the Grandsire, O subduer of foes; and having laid bare what was in their minds, they stood silent, their faces downcast.
Knowing what lay hidden within those gods, the Grandsire, the lord, for the deluding of men, created women as instruments of bewitchment.
In the first creation, O son of Kuntī, women here were virtuous; but the unvirtuous, the instruments of bewitchment, arose from the later creation of Prajāpati.
To them the Grandsire granted desires according to their wish; and those women, greedy for pleasure, then set to tormenting men.
The lord of gods created Anger as the helper of Desire; and all creatures, fallen under the sway of desire and anger, grew enthralled.
And no sacred rite belongs to women—so the law is established; women are without sacred rites and without mantras, untruth itself—so says the śruti.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Couch and seat, adornment, food and drink, ignobleness, foul-tongued speech, and the pleasure of love—these Prajāpati gave to women.
Their guarding cannot in any way be accomplished by a man—not even by the Maker of All, my son; how much less by mortal men here?
Neither by word, nor by slaying and bonds, nor by manifold torments can women be guarded; for they are ever unrestrained.
But this, O tiger among men, I have heard in former times: how of old a guarding was wrought by Vipula over his preceptor's wife.
There was a seer of great fortune, renowned by the name of Devaśarman; his wife was named Ruci, unmatched in beauty upon the earth.
By her beauty were maddened the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas, and most of all, O king of kings, the slayer of Vṛtra, the chastiser of Pāka.
Now Devaśarman, the great sage, knew well the ways of women, and he guarded that wife of his to the utmost of his power and resolve.
And he knew Puraṃdara to be one who lusted after other men's wives; therefore he kept watch over his wife with diligent care.
Once, my son, that seer, minded to perform a sacrifice, fell to pondering how the guarding of his wife might be accomplished.
Having devised in his mind the manner of her guarding, that great ascetic summoned his beloved disciple, Vipula of Bhṛgu's line, and spoke to him.
'I shall go to perform a sacrifice; and this Ruci the lord of the gods forever woos. My son, guard her to the best of your power.'
'You must remain ever vigilant against Puraṃdara, for he assumes shapes of many kinds, O scion of Bhṛgu.'
Thus addressed by him, Vipula the ascetic—his senses subdued, ever fierce in penance, O king, radiant like fire and the sun,
knower of dharma and speaker of truth—answered, 'So be it'; and then, O great king, he further questioned his renowned preceptor in these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What forms does Śakra assume when he comes, O sage? Of what kind is his body and his splendor? This you ought to expound to me.
Then that blessed one, O Bhārata, declared to the great-souled Vipula, according to the truth, the magic art of Śakra.
Rich in illusions, O brahmin-seer, is the slayer of Bala, the chastiser of Pāka; this form and that he conjures, manifold, again and again.
Diademed, wielder of the thunderbolt, bearing a bow, crowned, with fastened earrings he appears; and in a moment he looks like a caṇḍāla.
With a topknot, with matted locks, clad in bark, he becomes again, my son; now huge of body, now stout, now lean.
Fair, dusky, and dark of hue he becomes by turns; misshapen and again comely, young and likewise old.
Wise and dull and mute, short and likewise tall; a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, and likewise a śūdra, born against the grain and with it—so does the lord of a hundred sacrifices become.
In the form of a parrot and a crow, in the form of a goose and a cuckoo, and again he takes on the shape of lions, tigers, and elephants.
The body of a god, of a daitya, and of kings he bears as well; very lean, his limbs broken by the wind, a misshapen bird likewise.
Four-footed and of many forms he again becomes a fool; and he takes on too the body of flies, gnats, and the like.
None can lay hold of him, O Vipula—not even by the Maker of all, dear son, by whom this world was created.
Now Śakra, hidden, is seen only by the eye of wisdom; and having become wind, that king of the gods becomes himself once more.
Thus does the chastiser of Pāka ceaselessly take on these forms; therefore, Vipula, guard with all effort this slender-waisted one.
See that the king of the gods does not lap up Ruci, O best of the Bhṛgus, as an evil-natured dog laps the oblation set down and placed at the sacrifice.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having thus spoken, that sage, the performer of the sacrifice, then departed—the greatly fortunate Devaśarman, O best of the Bhāratas.
But Vipula, having heard his teacher's word, fell to brooding, and devised the utmost guard against the king of the gods of great might.
"What can I do to guard my teacher's wife? For that lord of the gods is a master of illusion, unassailable, and mighty in valor.
Not by shutting up the hermitage can the chastiser of Pāka be warded off, nor the leaf-hut, for his forms are of every kind.
In the form of the wind Śakra might assail my teacher's wife; therefore, entering into this Ruci, I shall this very day take my station within her.
Or else by mere manly strength she cannot be guarded by me, for the blessed one borne by bays is heard to be of many forms.
Therefore by the power of yoga I shall guard her from the chastiser of Pāka; I shall enter limb by limb into her limbs to keep her safe.
Yet if my teacher should see this wife Ruci defiled, then beyond doubt he, of divine knowledge and great austerity, will curse me in his wrath.
And she cannot be guarded as other women are guarded by men, for that lord of the gods is a master of illusion—alas, I have come into peril!"
"The teacher's command must surely be carried out; yet if I were to do this, a marvel would be wrought by me.
Entering by yoga here into the body of my teacher's wife, free from any form of passion, no fault would be mine.
As a wayfarer upon the road might lodge in an empty hall, so this day shall I lodge within my teacher's wife's body.
As a drop of water resting on a lotus leaf clings not, but trembles free, even so, composed, shall I dwell within her body."
Thus having looked upon dharma and upon the Vedas and their lore in every part, and having regarded the abundant austerity of his teacher and of himself,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
having so resolved in his mind concerning the guarding, that descendant of Bhṛgu set himself to the utmost effort—hear how, O lord of earth.
Seated beside his teacher's wife, Vipula of great austerity beguiled with stories that seated one of faultless limbs.
Joining with his two eyes the beams of her eyes, beam to beam, Vipula entered her body as the wind enters the sky.
Mark upon mark, face within face, the sage stood unmoving, gone within her like a shadow.
Then Vipula, holding fast the body of his teacher's wife, abode there intent on guarding, and she was not aware of him.
For all the while, O king, that the great-souled teacher had not returned to his own house, his sacrifice concluded, for all that while did he keep watch.
Bhīṣma said: Then on a certain day the king of the gods, bearing a body of divine form, thinking "this is the moment," came thereupon to the hermitage.
Having made for himself a peerless, alluring form, O ruler of men, becoming most fair to behold, he entered that hermitage.
He beheld there, seated, the body of Vipula, motionless, with fixed and staring eyes, like a figure set down in a painting.
And Ruci of lovely sidelong glance, full of hip and breast, wide-eyed as the petals of a lotus, her face like the full moon.
Seeing him, she suddenly sought to rise to greet him, amazed at his beauty, wishing then to ask, "Who are you?"
Though she wished to rise, she stayed still, held fast by Vipula, O lord of men, and could not stir.
The king of the gods addressed her with words most soft and winning: "Know that I, the king of the gods, have come for your sake, O bright-smiling one.
Tormented by the bodiless god of love, born of longing for you—therefore accept me, fair-browed one, before the time slips away."
Vipula the sage, dwelling within the body of his teacher's wife, heard Śakra speaking thus, and beheld the lord of the gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the blameless one could not rise, O king, nor could she speak, O king, held fast as she was by Vipula.
But that scion of Bhṛgu, perceiving the bearing of his teacher's wife, restrained her—he of great splendor—forcefully by yoga, O lord, and with the bonds of yoga he bound all her senses.
Seeing her unmoved, the lord of Śacī once again, abashed, O king, spoke to her who was overcome by the power of yoga.
"Come, come," he said; and then she sought to answer him, but Vipula turned aside that speech of his teacher's wife.
"Sir, what is the purpose of your coming?"—thus from her mouth, like unto the moon, came forth speech adorned with refinement.
Abashed, having spoken that word against her own will, she fell silent; and Puraṃdara then grew alarmed and dismayed.
Marking that strangeness, the king of the gods, O lord of peoples, the thousand-eyed one, then looked with his divine eye.
And he beheld the sage moving within her body, lodged in his teacher's wife's frame like a reflection in a mirror.
Seeing him endowed with terrible austerity, Puraṃdara trembled, sorely afraid, fearing a curse then, O mighty one.
Then Vipula of great austerity, releasing his teacher's wife, entered his own body and spoke to the frightened Śakra:
"O you of unconquered senses, evil-souled, lustful Puraṃdara! Not for long shall the gods, nor men likewise, honor you.
Have you forgotten this, Śakra? Does it not stand in your mind—how by Gautama you were marked over with the signs of a woman's parts?
I know you to be childish of mind, undisciplined of self, and fickle. By me is she guarded, O fool; go, O wicked one, as you came.
I would this day burn you to ashes by my own splendor, O dull-souled one; yet out of compassion I do not wish to burn you, Vāsava.
And that wise teacher of mine, of terrible austerity, seeing you of wicked heart, would this day burn you utterly with an eye blazing with wrath.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Never act thus again, Śakra; the twice-born are to be honored by you. Go not, with your sons and ministers, to ruin, stricken by the might of brahman.
Holding to the thought, 'I am immortal,' you conduct yourself so; do not despise it—there is nothing whatsoever unattainable by austerities.
Hearing that speech of the great-souled Vipula, Śakra, saying nothing, ashamed, vanished then and there.
When but a moment had passed since Śakra's going, Devaśarman of great austerity, having performed his sacrifice as he wished, came home to his hermitage.
When the teacher had come, O king, Vipula, doer of welcome deeds, presented to him the blameless wife he had guarded.
And having saluted him, that tranquil-souled Vipula, devoted to his teacher, attended upon his teacher as before, untroubled.
Then to him, rested and seated together with his wife, Vipula reported that deed of Śakra.
Hearing this, that majestic sage grew pleased with Vipula for his character and conduct, his austerity and his self-restraint.
Seeing Vipula's conduct toward his teacher, his devotion to him, and his steadfastness in dharma, the lord said, "Well done, well done!"
And the righteous one, applauding his disciple who was devoted to dharma, offered to gratify him with a boon; and he, devoted to his teacher and so permitted by him, practiced unsurpassed austerity.
So too Devaśarman of great austerity, together with his wife, fearless of the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, roamed in the lonely forest.
Bhīṣma said: But Vipula, having done his teacher's bidding, performed fierce austerity; and the valiant one then deemed himself accomplished in austerity.
Vying through that deed with the earth itself, O lord of earth, he roamed fearless and content, having won renown, foremost among men.
And the lord deemed that both worlds had been won by him likewise, O Kaurava, through that deed and through his abundant austerity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then when some time had passed, O delight of the Kurus, there was a giving in marriage of Ruci's sister, with wealth and grain.
At that very time a certain divine and lovely woman, bearing surpassing beauty, passed through the air.
From her body flowers fell to the earth, not far from that hermitage, fragrant with a divine scent, O Bhārata.
These then Ruci of lotus eyes gathered up, O king; and just then a summoner came swiftly on her sister's behalf.
For her elder sister, dear son, Prabhāvatī by name, had become the wife of Citraratha, the lord of the Aṅgas.
Having bound those flowers in her hair, the fair-complexioned one, being invited, then went, that Ruci, to the house of the lord of the Aṅgas.
Seeing those flowers, the lovely consort of the Aṅga lord, the fair-eyed one, then urged her sister to obtain such flowers.
Ruci of most lovely face told all to her husband; and the sage approved of all that had been spoken by her sister.
Then, O Bhārata, Devaśarman of great austerity summoned Vipula and urged him on for the sake of the flowers, saying, "Go, go."
And Vipula, of great austerity, without questioning his teacher's word, said "So be it," O king, and went to that region.
In the region where those blossoms had fallen from the vault of the sky, other unwithered flowers also lay there.
Then he gathered up those flowers, celestial and lovely, won by his own austerity and divine in fragrance, O Bhārata.
Having obtained them, glad of heart and obedient to his teacher's word, he then swiftly set out for Campā, garlanded with campaka trees.
In a deserted forest, my son, he saw a pair of beings turning round and round like a wheel, each grasping the other's hand.
There one of them moved swiftly, wheeling about in step, but the other did not do so likewise, O king; and thereupon the two fell to quarrelling.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"You go too fast," said the one; "No," said the other; and "No, no!" the two of them, my son, then said to each other.
As the two thus contended, this oath then arose; fixing their minds upon Vipula, they spoke these words:
"Whichever of us two has spoken falsely, may his lot in the world beyond be that of the brahmin Vipula!"
Hearing this, Vipula grew downcast of face, thinking: "I, of such fierce austerity—and yet this fate they invoke is a grievous burden."
"What sin of mine toward this pair could there be, that a destiny abhorred by all creatures has today been proclaimed for me by them?"
Pondering thus, O best of kings, Vipula, his face downcast and his head bowed, brooded upon his own misdeed.
Then he saw six other men gambling with dice of gold and silver, filled with greed and glee.
As they swore that very oath which the pair had sworn, they too, with Vipula in mind, then spoke these words:
"Whoever among us, yielding to greed, should venture to play foul, may he attain that lot which in the world beyond is Vipula's!"
Hearing this, Vipula could find no breach of dharma committed by himself before, from his very birth onward, O scion of the Kurus.
He brooded then, O king, like fire laid upon fire, his mind consumed with burning at having heard such a curse.
While he brooded, my son, many days and nights passed by; and this lay upon his mind—the guarding he had done in the matter of Ruci.
"By matching feature with feature and face with face I wrought the deed, and I did not then tell my teacher the truth of it."
This, O Kaurava, Vipula then reckoned a misdeed in himself, O illustrious one—and so indeed it was, beyond doubt.
Reaching the city of Campā, he gave the flowers to his teacher and, dear to his teacher as he was, honored him duly according to rite.
Bhīṣma said: Looking upon his disciple who had returned, Devaśarman of great splendor then spoke these words—hear them, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Devaśarman said: What did you see today, Vipula, in that great forest? They know you, O skillful one—your own self too, and Ruci as well.
Vipula said: O brahmin-sage, what was that pair, and who were those men, O mighty one, who know me in truth? You ought to tell me of them.
Devaśarman said: That pair, O brahmin, know to be day and night; wheeling round like a wheel, they know your misdeed.
And those men, O brahmin, who gamble joyously with dice—know them to be the seasons; they too know your misdeed.
Let no man of evil soul trust, thinking "None knows me," when he does a sinful deed in secret, O brahmin.
For the seasons forever behold a man doing a sinful deed in secret, and so too do day and night.
Seeing you smiling with joy yet not disclosing your deed to your teacher, they spoke thus to remind you, as you have heard.
Day and night know, and the seasons too know forever, the sinful deed in a man, or the auspicious deed of him who acts auspiciously.
Knowing that you did not declare to me that deed of yours, born of transgression and full of fear, they spoke to you thus, O brahmin.
And those worlds would befall you, as they befall the doer of sin, had you done that deed of yours and not disclosed it to me.
And thus an ill-conducted woman can be guarded, O brahmin; but you committed no offense at all—therein I am pleased with you.
But had I seen you ill-conducted, O best of brahmins, I would have cursed you in anger—of that I have no doubt.
Women cling to a man, and great is men's desire for them; had you guarded her otherwise, the curse and that fate would have been yours.
She was guarded by you, my son, and reported to me as well. I am pleased with you, dear child; blessings upon you—you shall go to heaven.
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus to Vipula, the pleased and great sage Devaśarman rejoiced, attaining heaven together with his wife and his disciple.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This tale, O king, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya once told me long ago, in the course of a discourse on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Therefore I tell you, O Pārtha, concerning all women: in them both are ever to be seen, the good and the bad alike.
Virtuous women, illustrious, esteemed as the mothers of the world, uphold this earth, O king, with its forests and groves.
But the unvirtuous, ill-conducted, ruinous to their families and bent on evil, are to be known by the evil marks inborn in their own bodies, O king.
Thus by great souls women can be guarded; otherwise, O tiger among kings, women cannot be guarded at all.
For these, O tiger among men, are fierce and of fierce vigor; there is none truly dear to them in union and intercourse with men.
These are to be wooed and to be won and to be possessed, O bull of the Bhāratas; yet these find no lasting delight in any single man, O joy of the Pāṇḍus.
No fondness, and likewise no jealousy, should be shown toward them by men, O lord of people; resting in patience and resting in dharma, let a man enjoy his lot.
A man who acts otherwise comes to ruin, O joy of the Kurus; in every case, O tiger among kings, sound judgment is everywhere to be honored.
By Vipula alone was the guarding of a woman accomplished; no other in this world of men, O king, has been able to guard women.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That which is the root of all duties, of offspring and of the household, and of the rites to ancestors, gods, and guests—of this tell me, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: This indeed, of all duties, is held the most to be pondered, O lord of the earth—namely, to what kind of man a maiden should be given.
Having well examined his character and conduct, his learning, his lineage, and his deeds, a maiden should be given, with the pouring of water, to a worthy suitor of good qualities. This, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is the eternal duty of righteous brahmins.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He should take in marriage from one fit to give in marriage, and he who gives should give willingly—this is the eternal duty of cultivated kṣatriyas.
Setting aside his own preference, when a man is the maiden's own choice, and she who is desired by him is given to him, O Yudhiṣṭhira—that rite those versed in dharma call the gāndharva.
Buying her with much wealth and enticing her kinsmen—this, O king, the wise declare to be the rite of the asuras.
Slaying and cleaving the heads of those who weep, and carrying off by force the weeping maiden from her home, my son—that is the mark of the rākṣasa rite.
Of the five, three are lawful and two unlawful, O Yudhiṣṭhira; the paiśāca and the āsura should never be practiced in any way.
The brāhma, the kṣātra, and the gāndharva—these are lawful, O bull among men; whether singly or combined, they may be practiced, herein is no doubt.
Three wives may a brahmin have, but two wives a kṣatriya; a vaiśya should take a wife of his own caste; among these the offspring rank equal.
The brahmin wife should be foremost, and the kṣatriya wife of a kṣatriya; a śūdra wife may be taken for pleasure—though others say, "No."
The good do not approve the begetting of offspring upon a śūdra woman; a brahmin who begets children upon a śūdra woman is enjoined to perform expiation.
A man of thirty years should take to wife a girl of ten, still a maiden; or one of twenty-one should win one of seven years.
But her who has neither brother nor father, O bull of the Bhāratas, one should never marry, for she is bound by the law of the appointed daughter.
A maiden who has reached her courses should wait three years; but when the fourth has come, she may herself win a husband.
Her chance of offspring is lost, and her pleasure too, O bull of the Bhāratas; one who acts otherwise becomes blameworthy before Prajāpati.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One who is not a sapiṇḍa of his mother and not of the same gotra as his father—such a one should he take; that law Manu has declared.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: One man may have paid the bride-price; another may say, "I shall pay it"; another may speak with force; and another may display his wealth.
And yet another may be the one who takes her hand—whose, then, is the maiden, O grandfather? For us who seek to know the truth, may you be our eye.
Bhīṣma said: Whatever human act is carried forward to its conclusion, its sealing with sacred words is as with a binding formula; but a false utterance therein is a sin.
Wife, offspring, officiating priest, and teacher, and disciple and instructor too, deserve punishment when falsely addressed—though others say, "No."
For Manu does not commend an agreement made unwillingly; what is false is inglorious and unlawful and provokes the wrath of dharma.
There is no fault wholly fixed upon any one man, where such a gift is not properly obtained—she whom they bestow according to dharma, and she whom they buy, O Bhārata.
With the kinsmen's consent, let him perform the sacred words and the oblation; thus those formulas avail—never in the case of one not duly given.
That compact of sacred words which is made mutually between wife and husband—that, and the one made with the kinsmen, they declare the weightier.
By the ordinance of dharma a husband knows his wife as given by the gods; she casts off as false all other speech, divine or human.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When a maiden's bride-price has been received, if a better suitor should come, endowed with dharma, desire, and wealth—should an untruth be spoken here, or not?
When fault lies on both sides in that matter, let a man do and practice the better course. This, of all our duties, we hold the most to be pondered.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For us who seek to know the truth, may you be our eye; tell us all of this, for I am not sated—let it be told.
Bhīṣma said: Knowing that bride-price is not what makes the marriage final, no good man ever exacted it; for the good, intent on a bride-price, never give a maiden at all.
But the kinsmen ask, as it were, a bride-price consisting of other good qualities—"Adorn her and take her away," says he who gives willingly.
He gives both that gift and her as well; it is no bride-price, and that is no sale. What is received in turn should be given back—this is the eternal law.
"I shall give the maiden to you" — when this has not been declared beforehand, there are some who say it, some who do not, and some who must say it of necessity.
Therefore, up until the taking of the hand, the two parties make request of one another. We have heard it told that in ancient times the bridegroom for a maiden was bestowed by the Maruts.
"A maiden is not to be given to one undesired" — so the sages have enjoined. That, in my judgment, is the root of procreation, which itself is rooted in desire.
Having weighed well the many evils that arise from the cohabitation of two who hate each other, hear now how the bride-price never came to be a thing that settles the matter.
For Vicitravīrya I brought home two maidens, after I had vanquished all the Māgadhas, the Kāśis, and the Kosalas. One had already had her hand taken in pledge, and being thus claimed, she met with rebuff.
"She whose hand has been taken must there and then be released," so my father said; and that scion of the Kurus took home only the other maiden.
He inquired further about the other as well, being uncertain of his father's word; for his longing after dharma was exceedingly great — greater even than my father's.
Then I myself, O king, desiring to know the right usage, spoke these words again and again: "I wish to understand the established practice in its very truth."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When I had spoken thus, O great king, my father Bāhlika, foremost of those who uphold dharma, made this reply.
"If for you the matter is settled by the bride-price and not by the taking of the hand, then let her for whom the price has been received attend upon the husband she has chosen, even up to the parched-grain rite."
"For those who know dharma do not declare that to be authoritative which rests on mere words alone — those, that is, for whom the matter is settled by the bride-price and not by the taking of the hand."
"What is openly spoken at the giving away is their rejoinder besides; but those who reckon the bride-price as a purchase — those folk do not know dharma."
"To such men a maiden is not to be given, nor by them is one of that sort to be wedded; for a wife is in no wise to be bought, nor ever to be sold."
"Those folk who buy a woman as one buys a slave-girl, and those who sell — for such greedy men of sinful mind let the matter be settled in that fashion."
On this point of dharma the people questioned Satyavān: "In the case of a maiden for whom the price has been received, the one who paid the price has died."
"And another would be the one to take her hand — herein lies our doubt concerning dharma. Resolve it for us, O greatly wise one, for you are esteemed among the wise; be you the eye for us who seek to know the truth."
To all of them speaking thus Satyavān made reply: "She is to be given where it is desired; herein no debate need be made. Men act so even while the man yet lives; when he is dead, there is no doubt at all."
"Let the maiden go in unto the husband's brother, or else let her practice great austerity; remaining ever faithful to him alone, she bears the name of the one who took her hand."
"For some it is set down plainly in writing, for others only by degrees" — those who hold discourse together on this matter know this to be the settled conclusion.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Where a reply is given before the taking of the hand, that is indeed the all-auspicious sacred formula; but a false utterance is a cause of downfall.
The consummation of the hand-taking formulas comes at the seventh step; she becomes the wife of the man who takes her hand, the man to whom she is given with the pouring of water.
Having circled the fire according to rule, the foremost of the twice-born wins as his wife one who is compliant, of suitable lineage, given by her brother, and led before the sacred fire.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: If, for a maiden whose price has been received, there is no husband at all, what then should be the right procedure? Tell me that, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: She would then have the standing of one without a son and without inheritance.
But if she should take the bride-price, she becomes, being bought, the woman of the one who paid it; for his sake let her seek to bear offspring by whatever lawful means she can.
For her let no one perform any rite whatsoever with sacred formulas.
"She chose for herself" — thus Sāvitrī was accepted by her father; this some who know dharma commend, but other folk do not.
Yet others did not do this, nor ever did the good men of old; and the conduct of the good is, moreover, the weightier mark of dharma.
On this very topic Sukratu spoke his word — the grandson of the great-souled Janaka, king of Videha.
"Upon a course of conduct that is wrong, how should there be praise, or further inquiry, or doubt? This the good would censure."
"A lapse from dharma is itself a thing unworthy — a demonic dharma. Never have we heard of this manner of thing among men of bygone births."
"For the bond of wife and husband, of woman and man, is one of equals; their delight is a dharma shared in common" — so spoke that prince.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Now by what rule is the wealth of men inherited? For a daughter ought to be to her father even as a son.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: As is one's own self, so is the son; and equal to the son is the daughter. While she, who is one's very self, yet stands, how should another carry off the wealth?
Whatever was the mother's marriage gift, that is the unmarried daughter's portion; or else the daughter's son may take the inheritance of a maternal grandfather who has no son.
For he offers the funeral rice-ball both to his own father and to his maternal grandfather; between a son and a daughter's son no distinction is here declared in point of dharma.
For by offspring born elsewhere a man seeks as it were a son; and a daughter, through a son born elsewhere of her, is even more distinguished.
By the rule of the daughter's son I see herein no cause for distinction; and the sons born of women who have been sold belong to the father alone.
But envious, most unrighteous, seizers of others' goods, and deceitful are they — sprung from the demonic mode of marriage, crooked of conduct in matters of dharma.
On this point those versed in ancient lore, knowers of dharma, recite the verses chanted by Yama, set down in the treatises of dharma, in the bulwarks of dharma.
Whatever man sells his own son and desires wealth thereby, or who for the sake of a livelihood gives away his daughter for a price —
in the seventh and lowest, most terrible hell called Kāla, that departed one feeds, in that place, on sweat, urine, and dung.
In the sage's marriage some call the pair of cattle a bride-price; but that is false. Whether little or much, O king, such a thing is just so much a sale.
Even though it has been practiced by some, this is in no wise dharma; and the practices of still others too are seen to spring from greed.
And those who enjoy a maiden who is set apart as their dependent — these are doers of sin, and they lie thereafter in blind darkness.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nay, any other human being too is not to be sold — how much less one's own offspring! For of wealth rooted in unrighteousness there is no profit whatsoever.
Bhīṣma said: Those versed in ancient lore recite the saying of Pracetas' son: where the kinsmen take nothing for a maiden, that is no sale.
That is the honoring due to maidens, and that the most free from cruelty; and all of it should be given back to the maiden, without remainder.
By fathers and brothers, by fathers-in-law and husbands' brothers, women should be honored and cherished by those who desire great welfare.
If a woman take no pleasure and do not gladden the man, then from the man's lack of gladness procreation does not increase.
Women are ever to be honored and cherished, O ruler of men; and where they go unhonored, there all rites are fruitless. That house ceases to be a house in the very hour when its women grieve.
Houses cursed by their women, as though cut down by a sorcerer's spell, neither shine nor prosper, being bereft of fortune, O prince.
Manu, when about to depart for heaven, entrusted women to the keeping of men — the weak ones, scant in covering, kindly, ever winning by their truth.
Jealous, eager for honor, fierce, unfriendly, and unknowing though they be — women deserve honor; honor them, O men.
For your dharma rests upon women, and your delights and enjoyments wholly so; let the service, the food, and the consecrations be dependent upon them for you.
The begetting of offspring, the rearing of what is born, and the daily course of the world for the sake of joy — behold, all this is bound up with women.
And by these, when they are duly honored, you shall attain all your aims. On this the daughter of the king of Videha sang a verse.
"For a woman there is no sacrifice, no rite for the ancestors, no fasting; her dharma is service to her husband, and by that she wins heaven."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The father protects her in girlhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons in old age; a woman is not fit for independence."
These women are very Fortune herself; they are to be well treated by one who desires prosperity. A woman, when cherished and yet held in check, becomes Śrī, O Bhārata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O you who know the ordinances of all the treatises, best knower of the duties and aims of kings, you are renowned throughout the earth as one who cuts away doubt utterly.
A certain doubt is mine; tell me of it, O grandfather. In this grievous time of distress, whom else should we ask?
What a man ought to do, and what is the eternal dharma — all this, O mighty-armed one, you are able to expound.
Four wives are ordained for a brāhmaṇa, O grandfather, if he desires their company — a brāhmaṇī, a kṣatriyā, a vaiśyā, and a śūdrā.
Among the sons born of all these, O best of the Kurus, which of them, in due order, is entitled to the paternal inheritance?
And by which of them, and how much, is to be taken from the father's wealth, O grandfather? I wish this to be told — what division among them is laid down.
Bhīṣma said: The brāhmaṇa, the kṣatriya, and the vaiśya — these three varṇas are the twice-born; among these is the rule ordained for the brāhmaṇa, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Through irregularity, or through greed, or through desire, O scorcher of foes, a brāhmaṇa may come to have a śūdra wife; but she is not approved by any sound precedent.
A brāhmaṇa who raises a śūdra woman to his bed becomes thereby defiled, and must perform expiation by a means prescribed in the rules.
And if children are born of her, the expiation would be twofold, O Yudhiṣṭhira. Hence I shall now declare to you the rule concerning the wealth, O Bhārata.
An auspicious bull marked with good signs, and whatever conveyance is most excellent — these the son of the brāhmaṇī shall take as a single share, over and above, from the father's wealth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the remainder of the brāhmaṇa's property is to be made into ten parts, O Yudhiṣṭhira; and of these the same son shall take four shares of the father's wealth.
The son of the kṣatriyā wife is also a brāhmaṇa, beyond all doubt; but by reason of the difference in his mother he is entitled to take three shares.
And he who is born in the third varṇa, of a vaiśyā by a brāhmaṇa, shall take two shares of the brāhmaṇa's property, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The one born of a śūdra woman by a brāhmaṇa is declared to be one whose share of wealth is not fixed by right; yet at least a little is to be given to the son of the śūdra woman, O Bhārata.
This would be the order for wealth divided into ten parts. But for sons born of wives of the same varṇa one should allot equal shares.
The son of a śūdra woman they reckon, owing to his lack of fitness, as no brāhmaṇa; for one born of a brāhmaṇa in the three varṇas becomes a brāhmaṇa.
Four varṇas are declared, and no fifth is recognized; yet the son of a śūdra woman may take a tenth part of the father's wealth.
But that he may take only if it has been given by the father; what is not given he is not entitled to take. Yet of necessity some wealth must be given to the son of the śūdra woman, O Bhārata.
"Freedom from cruelty is the highest dharma" — therefore it is given to him; and wherever he may have been born, it serves only to his benefit.
Even if he have but a single son, O Bhārata, or no son at all, to the son born of a Śūdra woman let him give no more than a tenth share.
When a twice-born man has a store of food beyond three years' sustenance, with that wealth let him perform sacrifice; he should not amass riches to no purpose.
To a woman a portion of wealth amounting to at most three thousand may be given; and that wealth which is bestowed upon her by her husband she may enjoy, but not what is not so given.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What women receive as their husband's gift is held to be theirs for enjoyment as its fruit; yet women must in no wise make off with anything from their husband's substance.
But whatever wealth has been given by her father to a woman, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the unmarried daughter of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall inherit it; for she is even as a son, O king. She indeed is ordained to be the equal of a son, O delight of the Kurus.
Thus has this been set forth among the laws, O bull of the Bhāratas. Mindful of this law, a man should not amass wealth to no purpose.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: If the son born of a Brāhmaṇa upon a Śūdra woman is declared to have no claim to inheritance, on what distinction is even a tenth share assigned to him?
A son begotten by a Brāhmaṇa upon a Brāhmaṇa woman is, beyond doubt, a Brāhmaṇa; and so too is the son begotten upon a Kṣatriya woman, and likewise upon a Vaiśya woman.
Why then should they receive unequal shares, O best of kings, when all three of these classes have been declared by you to be Brāhmaṇas?
Bhīṣma said: Though by one and the same name 'wife' is wives spoken of in the world, O scorcher of foes, even under that single name there exists a very great distinction.
Should a man, having first taken three wives, afterward wed a Brāhmaṇa woman, she shall be the foremost, she the one to be honored, and she the worthiest of them all.
The husband's bathing and adorning, the cleansing of his teeth and the anointing of his eyes, the offerings to gods and to the ancestors, and whatever else of sacred duty may arise in the house—
so long as she is present, no other wife may ever perform these; the Brāhmaṇa woman alone shall do them for the Brāhmaṇa, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Food and drink, garlands, garments, and ornaments—these should be given by the husband to the Brāhmaṇa wife, for she is the worthiest of all.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And in the treatise declared by Manu, O delight of the Kurus, there too, O great king, this eternal law is seen to hold.
But should a man act otherwise, out of mere desire, O Yudhiṣṭhira, then he becomes like that Brāhmaṇa-Caṇḍāla seen of old—even so does he become.
The son who is of equal standing born of a Brāhmaṇa woman and the son born of a Kṣatriya woman—between these, O king, there is no difference of class, in respect of either.
Yet by birth the Kṣatriya woman is not in the world the equal of the Brāhmaṇa woman. The eldest son of the Brāhmaṇa woman shall receive the greater portion, O best of kings; and a yet greater portion shall be taken by him out of the father's wealth, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
As the Kṣatriya woman can never be the equal of the Brāhmaṇa woman, so the Vaiśya woman can never be the equal of the Kṣatriya woman.
Prosperity and sovereignty and the treasury are ordained for the Kṣatriyas, O Yudhiṣṭhira; and to them, O king, is the earth seen allotted, bounded by the sea.
For the Kṣatriya, by his own proper duty, attains abundant prosperity. The king is the wielder of the rod of justice, O king; protection lies nowhere but with the Kṣatriya.
For the Brāhmaṇas are most blessed, the very deities of the gods themselves. Toward them let the king conduct himself with worship, as the ordinance prescribes.
Knowing the everlasting, imperishable law laid down by the sages, the Kṣatriya, by his own proper duty, protects the people when their rights are being violated.
When wealth and wives are being carried off on every side by robbers, the king becomes the deliverer of all the classes alike.
The son of the Kṣatriya woman shall be the greater, without doubt, over the son of the Vaiśya woman; and by him too a greater share is to be taken out of the father's wealth, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have duly spoken, O king, concerning the property of a Brāhmaṇa, O grandsire; but for the other classes, how is the division ordained?
Bhīṣma said: For a Kṣatriya too, two wives are ordained, O delight of the Kurus; a third may be a Śūdra woman, though she is not held to be such by the rule of precedent.
This same order shall hold for the Kṣatriyas, O Yudhiṣṭhira; the property of a Kṣatriya is to be divided in eight parts, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The son of the Kṣatriya woman shall take four shares of the father's wealth; and whatever of the father's belongs to the spoils of war, that too he shall take.
The son of the Vaiśya woman shall take three shares, and the son of the Śūdra woman the eighth; he too may take what was given by the father, but he is not entitled to take what was not given.
For a Vaiśya there shall be but one wife, O delight of the Kurus; or a second may be a Śūdra woman, though she is not held to be such by the rule of precedent.
For a Vaiśya who lives with a Vaiśya woman, O bull of the Bhāratas, and with a Śūdra woman as well, O son of Kuntī, the division between their offspring is thus declared.
The property of a Vaiśya is to be divided fivefold, O bull of the Bhāratas; and the apportionment among the offspring of those two I shall declare, O lord of men.
By the son of the Vaiśya woman four shares of the father's wealth are to be taken; the fifth share shall fall to the son of the Śūdra woman, O Bhārata.
He too may take what was given by the father, but he is not entitled to take what was not given. Thus a Śūdra born of the three higher classes becomes one to whom wealth must be apportioned.
For a Śūdra the wife shall be of his own class alone, and none other in any wise. For a Śūdra the shares shall be equal, even were there a hundred sons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Among sons born of wives of the same class, without distinction, in every one of the classes an equal share in the wealth is ordained.
The eldest's portion shall be the foremost—the one share that is preeminent. This is the rule of inheritance, O Pārtha, declared of old by the Self-existent One.
Among sons born of wives of the same class there is yet another distinction, O king, arising from the precedence of the marriage: the earlier-born, the earlier, is held the superior.
Even among sons of equal standing the eldest shall take the one preeminent share, the middle son a middling portion, and the youngest the least.
Thus, in all the births, those of the same class as the father have attained the foremost rank. This too the great sage Kaśyapa, son of Marīci, declared.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Whether from the pursuit of gain, or from desire, or from uncertainty regarding the classes, or even from ignorance of the classes, there arises a confusion of classes.
For those born in this manner in the confusion of classes, what is their duty, what their occupations? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: In the very beginning, for the sake of sacrifice, Prajāpati brought forth the four classes alone, and the occupations belonging to those four classes.
Four are the wives of a Brāhmaṇa; of two of them a son of his own self is born, while of the two lower, in order of rank, are born sons taking the class of the mother.
This son of the Brāhmaṇa, sprung as it were from a living corpse, the son of the Śūdra woman, they call a Pāraśava. Let him be a servant of his own family, and let him never forsake his own proper conduct.
Weighing well every means, he should uphold the lineage of his own family—whether elder or younger, whoever of the twice-born be devoted to service and given to charity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By a Kṣatriya's union there are three wives; of two of them a son of his own self is born, while of the third, a lower-class son is begotten, a Śūdra known as the Ugra.
And of a Vaiśya there are two wives; of both of them a son of his own self is born. The Śūdra has but one wife, a Śūdra woman, and of her a Śūdra alone is born.
But baser than these is the lowest, the violator of his elders' wives, who begets an outcast class, despised by the four classes.
A degraded Kṣatriya, fallen from his sacraments, begets the Sūta, intent on the chanting of hymns, who is unfit to have sacrifices offered for him; a degraded Vaiśya begets the Vaidehaka, a discarded Maudgalya.
A Śūdra begets upon a Brāhmaṇa woman the Caṇḍāla, exceedingly fierce, the slayer of the condemned, who dwells beyond the village—such are these defilers of their lineage. These, O best of the wise, O lord, are born of the confusion of classes.
From a Vaiśya is born of a Kṣatriya woman, through transgression, the Māgadha, a bard who lives by his words; from a Śūdra is born the Niṣāda, a slayer of fish.
From a Śūdra upon a Vaiśya woman is born the Āyogava, of village calling, a carpenter who lives in the forest, from whom no Brāhmaṇa may accept a gift.
These too beget, within their own kind, offspring of like class; but upon women of lower womb the higher beget offspring taking the mother's class.
As among the four classes a son of one's own self is born of two of the wives, so the outcast classes too are chiefly born from union with the class next adjoining.
They too beget, within their own kind, offspring of like class; but consorting one with another, they beget the despised.
