And as a Śūdra begets upon a Brāhmaṇa woman an outcast creature, so from one more outcast still is an outcast born, sprung from beyond the four classes.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Living thus against the grain, from the outcast is begotten the yet more outcast; from the low are born the lower classes, fifteen in number are they.
And by union with the forbidden the confusion of classes proceeds. Among the fallen here are born the Sairandhras and, among the Māgadhas, one skilled in adorning and attendance, no slave yet living by a slave's labor.
From this is begotten the Āyogava, living in the forest by snares; and the Vaidehaka begets the Maireyaka, a brewer, and likewise the Mādhuka.
The Niṣāda begets the Mudgara and the Dāśa, who lives by the boat; and the Caṇḍāla begets the Mṛtapa and the Śvapāka, exceedingly abhorred.
The Māgadhī bears four sons, cruel ones living by deceit; and a cook who makes flesh savory, called the Saugandha.
From the Vaidehaka is born one most sinful, cruel, who lives off his wife; and from the Niṣāda the Madranābha, who journeys in carts drawn by asses.
And from the Caṇḍāla is born the Pulkasa, who feeds on asses, horses, and elephants, who is clad in the garments of the dead, and who eats from broken vessels.
Upon women of the Āyogava and other lower classes are born those three; from the Vaidehaka, the Kṣudra and the Āndhra, whose dwelling lies outside the village.
The Kārāvara is begotten by a Carmakāra upon a Niṣāda woman; and from a Caṇḍāla is born the Pāṇḍusaupāka, who deals in hides and pith.
The Āhiṇḍika is begotten by a Niṣāda upon a Vaidehī woman; and by a Caṇḍāla the Saupāka, whose mode of living is like the Maudgalya's.
And a Niṣāda woman bears by a Caṇḍāla a son, the Antāvasāyin, who haunts the cremation ground, cast out even by the outcasts.
Thus these are the castes born of confusion, through the transgression of father and mother; whether concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their own deeds.
There is a law for the four classes alone, and for no other; among those of the classes who are devoid of law, there exists here no settled name for any.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By chance unions, with those excluded from sacrifice and from the company of the good, outcasts are begotten of outcasts, according to their occupation and their station.
Crossroads and cremation grounds, mountains and other great trees, they make their own, and ornaments too, and the implements of their craft.
Rendering their help, beyond doubt, for the sake of cows and Brāhmaṇas—freedom from cruelty, compassion, truthful speech, and forbearance,
and the protection of others with their own bodies—these bring fulfillment even to the outcasts, O tiger among men; of this I have no doubt.
A man of understanding should beget offspring only upon women duly proclaimed, according to the teaching, after careful reflection; for a son of base womb drags a man down, as a stone drags down one who would cross the water.
Whether a man be unlearned, or again though he be learned, women in this world surely lead astray onto the wrong path him who is the slave of desire and wrath.
And the very nature of women is, in this world, a corrupter of men; for this reason the wise do not cleave attached to women.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: A man fallen from his class, unrecognized, born of a tainted womb, ignoble though noble in seeming—how, O king, are we to know him?
Bhīṣma said: Though one be born of a tainted womb and beset by manifold conduct, purity of birth is to be discerned by his deeds—by the practices observed among the good.
Ignobility, lack of right conduct, cruelty, and a nature averse to duty—these reveal, here in the world, the man born of a tainted womb.
He takes up either the disposition derived from his father, or that from his mother, or both alike; but one of mixed origin can in no way hold his own true nature in check.
Just as a tiger is born resembling its mother and father in form, with its markings, so too a man conforms to his own womb of origin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Though the lineage's stream be concealed, the man whose origin is of mixed birth still cleaves to that disposition, whether in small measure or great.
Even of one who walks a counterfeit path, bearing the appearance and conduct of the noble, his own innate character determines for certain whether he belongs to his own class or another.
Among beings of varied conduct, devoted to varied works, that which is well-joined in the world—where birth and conduct match—does not fall away.
Here a man's body is drawn along by its inner nature—be that nature highest, middling, or lowest; and like delights in like nature.
One should not honor even a person of higher standing who is wanting in good character; but a Śūdra of virtuous conduct, knowing dharma, one should indeed honor.
A man proclaims himself by his deeds, good and ill, wrought by his own disposition and conduct; and so a man, though his own lineage be lost to sight, brings it again to light by his own actions.
Among all these wombs of origin, both the mixed and the others, the wise man should shun those in which he ought not to beget himself.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me, O best of the Kurus, of the sons of the several classes, each apart—from what kind of woman, and of what kind, are the sons of whom, and who are they?
Many conflicting opinions are heard concerning the matter of sons; here, O king, you must cut away the doubt of those who are bewildered.
Bhīṣma said: The son born of oneself is to be known, and he who is born next after him; and the son begotten under appointment is to be known, and likewise the son born of one cast off.
And the son born to the wife of a fallen man, lawfully united by a husband; and the two sons, the given and the made; and yet another, the son brought with a married bride.
And the six born of degradation, and the son of an unwed maiden, and the lowborn—these have thus been declared to you; know them, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who are the six born of degradation, and who again are the lowborn? All this, in accordance with the truth, you must expound to me.
Bhīṣma said: The sons whom a Brāhmaṇa begets upon the three other classes, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and the two whom a Kṣatriya begets upon the two classes, O Bhārata—
and the one whom the man of two classes begets—thus reckoned here, these are the six born of degradation. Now hear likewise of the lowborn.
The Caṇḍāla, and the Vrātya and the Vena—the three lowborn of a Śūdra are marked out, born respectively upon a Brāhmaṇa woman, upon a Kṣatriya woman, and upon a Vaiśya woman.
The Māgadha and the Vāmaka, the two reckoned as a Vaiśya's, born upon a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman; and the Kṣatriya's is but one—
the Sūta, marked out as born upon a Brāhmaṇa woman. These are remembered as the lowborn; for the seed that makes a son cannot be made false, O ruler of men.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Some declare the son to be the field-born, others the seed-born; of which of the two are these equally sons? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: A son may be born of the seed, or, being abandoned, may be field-born; or he may be the adhyūḍha, born when a compact is broken—learn this from me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The son born of the seed we know; but how comes the field-born to be? And how do we know the adhyūḍha son, born when a compact has been set aside?
Bhīṣma said: When a man, having begotten his own son, abandons him for some other cause, the seed is no longer the deciding factor there; that son belongs to the lord of the field.
For when a man desiring a son, for a son's sake, takes a woman, O lord of peoples, there the field is the measure, and the son is not reckoned as begotten of his own seed.
In another case the son is marked as field-born, O bull of the Bhāratas; for one's own self cannot be slain—this is borne out by the established example.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And some son is the made one, recognized merely by adoption; there neither seed nor field is the measure, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what kind is the made son, recognized merely by adoption, where neither seed nor field is found to be the measure, O Bhārata?
Bhīṣma said: One whom a man finds abandoned by mother and father upon the road, and whose mother and father are not known—he is the made son.
In whom one establishes ownership over the ownerless, and a man of the same class rears him, that son becomes of the same class as his rearer.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How is the sacrament to be performed for him, and after whose manner, and how? And how is a maiden to be given to him? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: One should perform the sacrament for him as for one's own son, and so according to the rearer's standing.
He who, abandoned by mother and father, comes to a man of the same class—for him one should perform the sacrament according to that man's lineage and class, O unfaltering one.
Then the maiden is to be given according to that man's class, O Yudhiṣṭhira; and where the mother's class is determined, the rites are to be done by the mother's lineage.
The son of an unwed maiden and the son brought with a married bride are likewise to be known as flawed sons; yet the settled rule is that these two also are to be consecrated as though they were one's own sons.
And whether field-born or lowborn, those who are the adhyūḍhas—for these too the Brāhmaṇas and the rest should perform the sacrament as for their own sons.
This is the settled rule concerning the classes as shown in the books of dharma. All this has been declared to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What sort of affection arises in the seeing of cattle and in dwelling with them, O grandsire, and what is the great blessedness of cows? Tell me that, O grandsire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Come then, I shall relate to you an event of olden days, O greatly radiant one—the colloquy between Nahuṣa and the great sage Cyavana.
Of old, O bull of the Bhāratas, the great sage Cyavana of Bhṛgu's line, having undertaken a dwelling in the waters, became one of mighty vow.
Having slain pride and anger, and elation and grief as well, the sage held fast to his vow of dwelling in the water for twelve years.
He bestowed upon all beings the highest, most blessed trust, even upon the creatures that move in the water, like the cool-rayed lord the moon.
Becoming still as a post, and pure, and bowing to the gods, he entered the water between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
The most terrible current of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, with its dreadful roar and a swiftness like the rush of the wind, he received upon his head.
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, and the streams that follow after them, made their reverent circuit around the sage and did not afflict him.
Beneath the water the great sage slept, become like a log of wood; and thereafter the wise one stood upright, O bull of the Bhāratas.
He became a delight to behold for the creatures that dwell in the water, and the fishes, joyful in heart, came then and nuzzled him; and as he abode there a great span of time passed by.
Then, at one time, on a certain occasion, men who lived by fishing came to that region, nets in hand, O greatly radiant one.
Many Niṣādas, resolved upon hauling up fish, tall, strong, and bold, never turning back in the waters, came to that region, set upon the work of the net.
And they fastened together their net with special care, O lord of men, having reached the fish-filled water, O best of the Bhāratas.
Then those fishermen, craving fish, by many contrivances cast their nets over the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Their net was well-spread, made of new cord, and so fashioned in breadth and length as to be fit for that water.
Then, having cast it out on every side—that net so very great, so strong, and so well-woven—they all hauled it in together.
Fearless in aspect and full of joy, working in concert one with another, they ensnared therein the fishes and other water-roving creatures as well.
And Cyavana, the delight of Bhṛgu's line, surrounded by the fishes, they drew up by chance in their net, O great king.
His limbs smeared with the river's moss, wearing a tawny beard and matted locks, his body clung about with clusters of shells, as if covered with strange chambered casings.
Seeing him drawn up in the net, that master of the Vedas, all the fishermen then, with joined palms, fell to the ground with their heads bowed.
From exhaustion and terror, and from the dragging of the net, and from being hauled onto dry land, the fishes perished.
That sage, beholding the slaughter wrought of the fishes, was overcome with compassion and sighed again and again.
The Niṣādas said: For the sin that we have done in ignorance, grant us your grace therein. What may we do to please you? Tell us that, O great sage.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Cyavana, standing amid the fishes, spoke these words: Hear with attentive minds what is now my highest wish.
Either to the giving up of life, or to being sold, will I go along with these fishes; for I cannot bear to forsake my companionship with these dwellers in the water.
Thus addressed, those Niṣādas, trembling exceedingly with fear, all of them with downcast faces, made it known to Nahuṣa.
Bhīṣma said: And Nahuṣa, hearing then that Cyavana had come to such a pass, set out thither in haste, together with his ministers and his household priest.
Having performed his purification as the rule requires, with palms joined and self subdued, the king announced himself to the great-souled Cyavana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And that king's household priest also honored him—true to his vow, greatly blessed, and godlike, O lord of peoples.
Nahuṣa said: What may I do to please you? That you must explain to me. I shall do it all, O blessed one, even though it be most hard to accomplish.
Cyavana said: The fishermen who live by fish are joined to great toil; pay them my price, together with the price of the fishes.
Nahuṣa said: Let a thousand be given as the price to the Niṣādas, O priest, for the ransom of the blessed one, even as the delight of Bhṛgu's line has said.
Cyavana said: I am not worth a thousand—or how do you reckon it, O king? Let a fitting price be given; make your determination by your own judgment.
Nahuṣa said: Let a hundred thousand be given at once to the Niṣādas. Might this then be the price? Or does your honor reckon otherwise?
Cyavana said: I am not to be valued at a hundred thousand, O bull among rulers. Let a fitting price be given; consider it together with your ministers.
Nahuṣa said: Let a crore be given as the price to the Niṣādas, O priest; and if even this is no fit measure for you, let yet more than this be given.
Cyavana said: O king, I am not worth a crore, nor even more, O greatly radiant one. Let a fitting price be given; consider it together with the Brāhmaṇas.
Nahuṣa said: Let half the kingdom, or the whole of it, be given to the Niṣādas. This I deem to be the price—or do you reckon otherwise, O twice-born?
Cyavana said: I am not worth half the kingdom, nor the whole, O ruler. Let a fitting price be given; let it be pondered together with the sages.
Bhīṣma said: Hearing the great sage's words, Nahuṣa, worn with distress, then fell to pondering, together with his ministers and his household priest.
But there a certain other forest-dweller, who lived on roots and fruits, came to stand near Nahuṣa—a sage born of a cow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That best of the twice-born, addressing the king, said: I shall satisfy the Brāhmaṇa, so that he shall be content.
"I would not speak a false word even in jest, much less in a grave matter. Whatever I shall say to you must be carried out without any hesitation."
Nahuṣa said: "Let the holy one name a price befitting the great sage, the son of Bhṛgu. Deliver me from this peril, and my kingdom, and my lineage."
"For the holy one, when angered, could destroy even the entire threefold world—how much more easily me, who am devoid of austerity and rely only on the strength of my arms."
"To one sunk in fathomless waters, together with his ministers and his priests, be you a raft, O great sage. Determine the price."
Bhīṣma said: Having heard the words of Nahuṣa, the majestic sage born of a cow spoke, gladdening all the ministers and that king as well.
"Beyond all price, O great king, are the twice-born, highest among the social orders, and so too are cows, O protector of the earth. Let a cow be reckoned as the price."
And then, O king, hearing the great sage's word, Nahuṣa was filled with great joy, together with his ministers and his household priest.
Approaching Cyavana, the son of Bhṛgu, firm in his vows, he spoke these words, O lord of men, as if soothing him with his speech.
"Rise, rise, O sage among brahmins! With a cow you have been purchased, O scion of Bhṛgu. This I deem your price, O best of the upholders of dharma."
Cyavana said: "I rise, O lord of kings; rightly have I been bought by you, O sinless one. No wealth do I see in this world that is equal to cows, O unfailing one."
"To celebrate cows, to hear of them, to give them, and even to behold them, O king—all this is praised, O hero, as auspicious and the remover of every sin."
"Cows are ever the root of prosperity; in cows no evil is found. Cows are always food itself, and the highest oblation of the gods."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The sacred utterances svāhā and vaṣaṭ are eternally established in cows. Cows are the very bearers of the sacrifice, and they are the mouth of the sacrifice."
"They yield and they bear the nectar, imperishable and divine; they are the abode of immortality, revered by all the worlds."
"In radiance and in form, cows are like fire upon the earth; cows are a great splendor indeed, and bestowers of happiness upon living beings."
"Wherever a herd of cattle, settled and at ease, breathes freely without fear, it makes that land shine and draws away its evil."
"Cows are the stairway to heaven; cows are honored even in heaven. Cows are goddesses who yield every desire; nothing else is held to be higher."
"Thus has the glory of cows been proclaimed by me, O bull among kings—yet this is but the telling of a portion of their virtues; their full account cannot be exhausted."
The Niṣādas said: "A meeting and a converse with us you have had, O sage; among the good, seven steps together make friendship. Show us your favor, O lord."
"As the fire devours all oblations, so are you too, O righteous soul, a fire in the form of a man, blazing with power."
"We seek to win your favor, O learned one; bowed low are we. For the sake of grace toward us, let this cow be accepted."
Cyavana said: "The glance of one who is wretched, of a sage, and of a venomous serpent burns a man down to the root, as a blazing fire consumes the dry brushwood."
"I accept your milch-cow, O fishermen; freed from your sins are you. Go swiftly to heaven, together with the fish drawn up in your net."
Bhīṣma said: Then, by the grace of that great sage of purified soul, the Niṣādas, through that word, ascended to heaven together with the fish.
Then King Nahuṣa was struck with wonder, beholding the fishermen, and the fish too, ascending to the threefold heaven, O bull of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then both the one born of a cow and Cyavana, the upholder of Bhṛgu's line, offered the king his choice of two fitting boons.
Then the mighty King Nahuṣa, lord of the earth, well pleased, said "It is excellent," O best of the Bhāratas.
Then that king, equal to Indra, took up a firm standing in dharma; urged "So be it," he, well pleased, paid honor to those two sages in return.
Then Cyavana, his consecration completed, went to his own hermitage, and the one born of a cow, of great splendor, returned to the site of his own hermitage.
And the Niṣādas went to heaven, and so did the fish, O lord of men; and Nahuṣa too, having obtained his boon, entered his own city.
"This has been told to you, my son, that which you asked of me: what kind of affection arises in beholding one, and in dwelling together, O Yudhiṣṭhira."
"And the great blessedness of cows, and likewise the determination of dharma. What more shall be told, O hero? What is it that you wish to ask in your heart?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "A doubt I have, O greatly wise one, vast as the ocean. Hear it from me, O mighty-armed one, and having heard, be pleased to explain it."
"Great is my curiosity, O lord, concerning the son of Jamadagni—Rāma, the foremost of the upholders of dharma. Be pleased to explain it to me."
"How was this Rāma, whose valor is truth, brought forth? And how, in a line of brahmin-sages, was he born with the dharma of a kṣatriya?"
"Recount his origin in full, O king; and how it was that from the Kauśika line, a kṣatriya line, there came to be a brahmin."
"Ah, how very great was the power of those two great souls—of Rāma, O tiger among men, and of Viśvāmitra indeed."
"How was it that, passing over their sons, this defect arose among their grandsons, leaving the sons aside? Be pleased to explain this to me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale—the dialogue of Cyavana and of Kuśika, O Bhārata.
Foreseeing this defect of old as it was to come upon his own line, Cyavana the son of Bhṛgu, that bull among sages of great wisdom—
—pondering in his mind the whole of it, its merits and defects, its strength and weakness, that ascetic resolved to burn down the entire family of the Kuśikas.
Cyavana, coming to that Kuśika, spoke these words: "A wish has arisen in me to dwell together with you, O sinless one."
Kuśika said: "Holy one, this is a duty to be shared in marriage, upheld here by the learned; it is spoken of by the wise always at the time of the giving of maidens."
"But as for that door of duty which has so far been passed by, O ascetic, that task I shall perform; be pleased to grant me leave for it."
Bhīṣma said: Then, taking up a seat for Cyavana the great sage, Kuśika, together with his wife, came to where the sage was.
Taking up a water-vessel, the king offered him water for his feet, and performed all the rites of welcome for that great soul.
Then that king, the great-souled one, steadfast in his vows and unperturbed, had Cyavana receive the honey-and-curd offering according to rule.
Having thus honored the brahmin, he spoke these words: "Holy one, the two of us are at your command. Tell us, what shall we do?"
"Whether the kingdom, whether wealth, whether cows, O you of stern vows, and likewise sacrifices and gifts—say the word, and I shall give you all."
"This house, this kingdom, and this seat of dharma are yours. You are the king; govern the earth. I am your servant, dependent upon you."
When these words were spoken, then Cyavana the son of Bhṛgu, filled with the highest gladness, replied thus to Kuśika:
"I desire not the kingdom, O king, nor wealth, nor women, nor cows, nor your lands, nor sacrifices. Let this be heard:"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"I shall undertake a certain observance, if it pleases the two of you; and that you both should attend upon me without hesitation."
When this was spoken by him, the wedded pair rejoiced, and they answered that sage, "So be it," O Bhārata.
Then Kuśika, delighted, led him into a most excellent quarter of the house, and there showed him a beautiful spot.
"This is your couch, holy one; dwell here as you please. We two shall strive to bring you delight, O ascetic."
Now the sun passed onward while they were thus conversing, and the sage then called for drink and likewise for food.
Then King Kuśika, bowing low, asked him: "What kind of food is desired by you? What shall I set before you?"
Then he, with the utmost pleasure, replied to the lord of men: "Give me whatever food comes ready to hand," O Bhārata.
Honoring that word, the king said "So be it," and the lord of men gave him such food as was at hand.
Then that holy one, knower of dharma, having eaten, said to the wedded pair: "I wish to sleep; drowsiness oppresses me, O lord."
Then, reaching the sleeping-chamber, the holy one, best of sages, lay down; but the king, together with his wife, remained standing.
"I am not to be wakened once asleep," said the son of Bhṛgu then; "my feet are to be massaged, and you two must keep watch through the night."
And Kuśika, the knower of dharma, without hesitation said "So be it," and the two did not waken him even at the closing of the night.
According to the great sage's command, the wedded pair, intent on his service and self-restrained, then remained so, O great king.
Then that holy brahmin, having so instructed the king, slept upon a single side for twenty-one days.
But that king, taking no food, together with his wife, O delight of the Kurus, attended upon him with gladness, devoted to the propitiation of Cyavana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But the son of Bhṛgu, the ascetic, rose up of his own accord, and saying nothing at all, that great ascetic walked out of the house.
The two of them followed after him, hungry and worn with toil, husband and wife; but the best of sages did not so much as look upon them.
Even as the two of them looked on, the upholder of the line of the Bhārgavas vanished, O lord of kings; thereupon the king fell to the ground.
After resting a moment, that king of great splendor, together with his queen, then made the utmost effort to search for him once again.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "When that brahmin had vanished, what did the king do then, and his greatly blessed wife? Tell me that, O grandsire."
Bhīṣma said: Not finding that sage, the protector of the earth, together with his wife, utterly spent, turned back, abashed and bereft of his senses.
Entering the city, downcast, he spoke not a single word; he brooded only upon that conduct of Cyavana.
Then with a vacant mind the king entered his house, and he beheld, upon that very couch, the son of Bhṛgu lying asleep.
The two of them, astonished, beholding him and pondering that marvel, became refreshed at the very sight of that sage.
Taking their proper places, the two once more massaged him; and then that great sage slept upon his other side.
And after that same span of time the mighty one awoke; yet the two, anxious with fear, showed no change of countenance at all.
Now the sage, having awakened, said to the two, O lord of peoples: "Let an anointing with oil be given me; I shall bathe," O Bhārata.
Promising "So be it," the two, hungry and worn with toil, attended upon him with hundred-times-refined oil of great value.
Then, holding their speech in check, the two attended upon the sage as he sat at his ease; yet Bhārgava, of mighty austerities, said it was not enough.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When Bhārgava observed that the two remained unmoved, he rose all at once and entered the bathing-chamber; there the bathing appointments, befitting a king, stood already made ready.
But the sage, scorning all that, vanished from the very spot once more before the king's eyes; and the royal couple, O bull of the Bhāratas, harbored no resentment.
Then, having bathed, the venerable lord, the delight of the Bhṛgus, seated upon a lion-throne, showed himself to Kuśika and his wife.
With a glad countenance, King Kuśika, together with his wife, bowed low and unperturbed announced to the sage that the meal was prepared.
"Let it be brought," the sage said to that lord of men; and the king, together with his wife, fetched forth that food.
Many kinds of meat dishes, and vegetables of many kinds, and preparations richly spiced, and light beverages,
varied sweet cakes, and sweetmeats, and the six-flavored relishes, and juices of every sort, and the wild forest fare fit for a sage.
And fruits of many kinds, and other foods in abundance—jujubes, iṅgudas, kāśmarya berries, marking-nuts, and banyan figs—
whatever food belongs to householders and whatever belongs to forest-dwellers—the king had all of it brought, in dread of the sage's curse.
Then all of it was set out before Cyavana; whereupon the sage gathered up the whole of it, along with the couch and the seat,
and, having covered it over with fine garments together with the vessels of the meal, Cyavana, the delight of the Bhṛgus, set the whole of it ablaze.
Yet the couple, steadfast in their great vow, gave way to no anger; and even as the two looked on, he vanished once again.
And in that very place the royal sage stood through that night, with his wife, silent and glorious; nor did anger enter into him.
Day after day the dressed food of many kinds, and the finest couches, and lavish baths were furnished in the royal dwelling,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and garments of every fashion were procured; and Cyavana could find no flaw therein to seize upon.
Then once more the brahman-sage said to King Kuśika: "With your wife, convey me swiftly by chariot to wherever I direct."
"So be it," said the king, without misgiving, to that ascetic rich in penance. "Shall it be a pleasure-chariot, O venerable one, or a war-chariot?"
Thus addressed by that gladdened king, the sage Cyavana, well pleased, made this reply to the conqueror of hostile cities:
"Make ready at once the chariot that you reckon a war-chariot—furnished with weapons, with banners, with a lance, and with a barbed javelin,
resounding with a hundred bells, fitted with arrays of pikes, bound about with mace and sword, and supplied with hundreds of choice arrows."
Then he, saying "So be it," made ready the great chariot, and set his wife at the left of the yoke and himself at the right,
and took up there a goad three-pronged and sharp as an adamant needle at its point. Having given all this over, the king then spoke these words:
"Venerable one, where shall the chariot go? Let the delight of the Bhṛgus declare it. Wherever you shall say, O brahman-sage, there shall your chariot go."
Thus addressed, the venerable one replied to that king: "From here onward you must go step by step, slowly,
so that no fatigue may come to me. Move at my pleasure, you two; I am to be drawn in comfort, and let all the people look on."
"No traveler is to be thrust aside; to them I shall give wealth—to the brahmans too who shall beg of me their desires along the way.
I shall give it all without remainder, the wealth and the jewels alike. Let this be done in full; do not deliberate, O king."
Hearing that word of his, the king then said to his servants: "Whatever the sage may ask, all of it is to be given without hesitation."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then jewels beyond number, women, draught-teams, goats and sheep, gold both wrought and unwrought, and lordly elephants like mountains,
and the king's ministers, all of them, followed after that sage; and the whole city became a tumult of grief, struck with anguish.
Goaded all at once by the sharp-pointed prod, pierced upon the back and on the hip, the two, unmoved, drew him along.
Trembling, gone without food, wasted by fifty nights, the heroic couple drew that surpassing chariot with utmost difficulty.
Pierced again and again and grievously, oozing the blood sprung from their wounds, they appeared, O great king, like two kiṃśuka trees in flower.
Beholding the two, the townsfolk were utterly given over to grief; yet, terrified by the dread of his curse, they said nothing at all.
And all of them said, two by two: "Behold the power of penance! Though wrathful, we cannot so much as look upon this best of sages."
"Ah, the might of the venerable great sage of perfected soul! And behold too what fortitude the king, with his wife, displays!"
For though spent, with great hardship they drew this chariot onward; yet the delight of the Bhṛgus saw in the two no change of heart.
Bhīṣma said: Then, seeing the two unmoved, the upholder of the Bhṛgu line dispensed wealth as Vaiśravaṇa himself might do.
In that too the king, glad of heart, did as he was bidden; whereupon the venerable one, that best of sages, grew pleased with him.
Descending from that finest of chariots, he released the couple; and having freed them duly, he then spoke these words.
In a voice tender, deep, and most serene, Bhārgava said: "Let me grant the two of you a choicest boon; name it," O Bhārata.
And that best of sages, the knowing one, touched the two tender ones with his hands, hands like ambrosia, out of affection, O best of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the king spoke: "There is no weariness in us two here; by your power, O Bhārgava, by your very meditation, we are wholly rested."
Then the venerable Cyavana, greatly delighted, said to the two: "What I declared before was not spoken in vain; it shall come to pass.
Delightful is this spot, this fair bank of the Gaṅgā; for some time, intent upon my vow, I shall dwell here, O king.
Go to your own city, my son; rested, you shall return. Tomorrow, with your wife, you shall behold me abiding here, O lord of men.
Nor should you give way to wrath: a blessing has drawn near to you. Whatever is wished for, set in your heart, all of it shall come to be."
Thus addressed, Kuśika, with inmost soul rejoicing, spoke to that tiger among sages this word fraught with meaning:
"I bear no wrath, O greatly fortunate one; by you, venerable lord, I am made pure. We two have become young again, full of beauty and of strength.
The wounds you made upon me and my wife with the goad—I see them no longer upon our limbs; I am whole again, together with my wife.
And this lady I behold, O sage, like a celestial apsaras, endowed with surpassing beauty, even as I saw her of old.
By your grace has all this come to pass, O great sage; yet this is no wonder in you, O venerable one whose valor is truth."
Thus addressed, Cyavana then replied to Kuśika: "You shall come here, and with your wife," O lord of men.
Thus addressed and given leave, the royal sage saluted him and set forth, endowed with beauty, toward the city, like the king of the gods.
Then there came forth to meet him the ministers with the household priests, the men of the army, the courtesans, and all the orders of the realm as well.
Encircled by them, King Kuśika, blazing with surpassing splendor, entered the city, gladdened, honored by the bards.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, having entered the city and performed all the rites of the day, that lord of earth, with his wife, dined and passed the night.
Then the two, beholding their renewed youth in each other, rejoiced like immortals freed of age, beautiful of form upon their couch, endowed with that splendor bestowed by the best of brahmans.
And that sage too, the increaser of the Bhṛgu line's renown, rich in penance, fashioned by the power of his mind a delightful, flourishing forest, adorned with jewels of many kinds, such as is not found even with the lord of a hundred sacrifices.
Bhīṣma said: Then that high-minded king, awakened at the close of night, having performed the morning rites, set out with his wife toward that forest.
Then the king beheld a palace all of gold, rich with a thousand jeweled pillars, like a city of the gandharvas; and there Kuśika beheld marvels of celestial design.
Mountains with lovely peaks, and lotus-pools bearing their blossoms, and picture-galleries of many kinds, and gateways, O Bhārata, and ground heaped with fresh turf, paved too with gold.
Mango trees in full bloom, ketakas, uddālakas, dhavas, aśokas, and mucukundas, and atimuktakas all flowering,
campakas, splendid tilakas, jackfruit trees, and vañjulas too, and karṇikāras in flower—these he beheld here and there.
The śyāmā creeper, the vāraṇapuṣpī, and the aṣṭāpadikā vine, set out here and there—these that lord of earth beheld.
Trees bearing lotuses and water-lilies, and others blossoming in every season, and palaces shaped like celestial cars, mansions resembling lotuses,
and waters cool, and in some places warm, O Bhārata, and seats of varied work, and couches of the choicest kind,
divans all of gold, spread over with coverlets of priceless worth, and food to be eaten and to be enjoyed without end, made ready here and there.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Sweet-voiced parrots too, and śārikā mynas and bhṛṅgarāja birds, cuckoos and woodpeckers, sandpipers and jungle-fowl,
peacocks and wild-cocks, putraka birds and jīvaṃjīvakas, cakora partridges, monkeys, swans, sārasa cranes, and the birds named after the cakravāka,
crying out on every side, most charming—these he beheld, and in some places throngs of apsarases and of gandharvas, O king.
Others he beheld there embraced by their beloved ones; and then he saw them no more, and again the king saw them once more.
The sweet sound of song, and likewise the sound of recitation, and the swans most sweet of voice—these the king heard there.
Beholding that exceeding marvel, the king then pondered within his mind: "Is this a dream, a derangement of the mind, or is it truly real?
Ah, in this very body have I reached the supreme abode—the holy Northern Kurus, or else Amarāvatī itself!
Yet what is this great wonder that I behold?"—so he mused. And even as he mused thus, he beheld the bull among sages,
the delight of the Bhṛgus, reclining in that golden car thronged with jeweled pillars, upon a precious, celestial couch.
Toward him the lord of men, with his wife, drew near in great joy; whereupon Cyavana vanished once again, and that couch as well.
Then in another quarter of the forest he beheld him once more, seated upon a couch of kuśa grass, murmuring his prayers, steadfast in his great vow. Thus, by the power of yoga, the brahman bewildered the king.
In an instant that forest, and the throngs of Apsarases, and the Gandharvas, and the trees as well—all of it vanished away.
The bank of the Gaṅgā fell silent once more, O king, and became thick with kuśa-grass and anthills, just as it had been before.
Then king Kuśika, together with his wife, beholding that great marvel, was struck by that deed with the utmost astonishment.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Kuśika, filled with delight, said to his wife: "Behold, good lady, what wondrous, exceedingly rare splendors we have seen!
By the grace of the foremost of the Bhṛgus—whence else but from the power of austerity? For by austerity is attained that which cannot be won by mere wishing.
Austerity surpasses even the sovereignty of the three worlds; for through austerity well practiced this man, whose wealth is austerity, sports as he pleases.
Ah, the might of the great-souled Brahmā-sage Cyavana! Should he so wish, by the force of his austerity he could even create other worlds.
Brāhmaṇas alone would be born—holy in speech, in thought, and in deed; for who else but Cyavana could here have the power to do such a thing?
Brāhmaṇhood is hard to attain in this world, while sovereignty is easily gained by men; for through the power of his Brāhmaṇhood we two were yoked to his chariot like well-matched draught-horses.
As the king mused thus, he became known to Cyavana, who, looking upon him, said to him: "Come hither at once."
Thus addressed, the king together with his wife approached the great sage, and bowed with his head to that one worthy of reverence.
Then the wise sage, having pronounced his blessings upon the lord of men, said to him, "Be seated," speaking gently to him, O bull among men.
Then the descendant of Bhṛgu, returned to his natural calm, O king, addressed the monarch in smooth speech, as if refreshing him, O Bhārata.
"O king, since you have here rightly conquered the five senses among the five objects, with the mind as the sixth, by that very feat you are released from peril.
You have rightly propitiated me, my son, O best of speakers; not the slightest fault, however subtle, is found in you.
Give me leave, O king; I shall depart as I came. I am pleased with you, O lord of kings; let a boon be accepted from me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kuśika said: O blessed one, it was as one standing amid fire that I conducted myself in your presence, O tiger of the Bhṛgus; that I was not burned up—that is boon enough.
This is the chief boon I have gained, O joy of the Bhṛgus: that you are pleased with my conduct, and my line is made pure, O sinless one.
This is grace enough for me, O brāhmaṇa, and the very purpose of my life; this is the fruit of my kingship, and this my highest austerity.
But if you are well pleased with me, O brāhmaṇa, joy of the Bhṛgus, there is a certain doubt in me; that you ought to explain to me.
Cyavana said: Let a boon be taken from me; and whatever doubt is in your heart, declare it, O best of men—all of it I shall resolve for you.
Kuśika said: If you are pleased, O blessed one, then tell me, O descendant of Bhṛgu—I wish to hear the reason for the dwelling you made in my house:
your lying on one side for twenty-one days, your going outside without saying a word, O bull among sages,
your sudden disappearance and again your reappearance, and once more your lying down, O brāhmaṇa, for twenty-one days;
your departure when anointed with oil, and your eating in my house; and how, when manifold food had been brought together, it was burned by Jātavedas the fire; and how you suddenly set out swiftly in the chariot;
and the squandering of my riches, and the apparition of the forest, and of the many golden palaces, O great sage,
and the sight of couches with legs of gem and coral, and then again the vanishing of all that—I wish to hear the reason.
For in this I am utterly bewildered, brooding day and night, and I cannot arrive at any certainty about all of it; this I wish to hear in full and truly, O you whose wealth is austerity.
Cyavana said: Hear all of it without remainder—this thing, and the reason for it; for being so questioned, O king, I cannot leave it untold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What I once heard the Grandsire say at an assembly of the gods, that, O king, hear from me as I relate it.
"Through the strife of Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya there shall come a mingling of lines; a grandson shall be born to you, O king, endowed with brilliance and might.
Therefore, to safeguard my own line, I came to you, O Kuśika, seeking to bring about your extinction, longing to burn up your house.
So, having come to you then, O lord of the earth, I said: "I shall undertake a certain observance; let attendance be rendered to me."
But I found no fault whatever in your house; by that you live, O royal sage—otherwise it would have been far otherwise with you.
With this intent I slept for twenty-one days, thinking, "If anyone should wake me…," O king.
When neither you nor your wife roused me from sleep, at that very moment I was pleased with you in my heart, O best of kings.
And I rose and went out, thinking, "If you, O lord of the earth, should ask me, 'Where are you going?'—then I would curse you," O lord.
And I made myself vanish, and again and again, in your house, taking up yoga, I lay down for twenty-one days.
Thinking, "Perhaps, hungry or worn with toil, he will resent me," O lord of men—with this intent I wasted you both with hunger.
Yet not the slightest anger arose in your mind, O king, nor in your wife's, O best of men; therefore I am pleased with you.
And when I gathered the food and set it ablaze—thinking, "Perhaps out of resentment he will grow wrathful"—that too you endured.
Then I mounted the chariot and said to you, O lord of men, "Together with your wife, draw me along"—and that too you did.
Without misgiving, O lord of men—and by that too I was pleased with you; even when the squandering of your wealth was done, no anger overcame you.
Then, being pleased, O king, I did this once more for you and your wife—that forest; know it for what it was, O ruler of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And for your delight this showing of heaven was made by me—that divine vision which you beheld in this forest, O king.
That region of heaven, O king, you experienced in your own body for a moment, together with your wife, O best of kings.
It was to give a glimpse of austerity and of dharma, O lord of men; the longing that arose in you there, O king, that too is known to me.
For you long for Brāhmaṇhood and for austerity, O lord of the earth, disdaining the rank of a king and even the rank of Indra of the gods, O monarch.
It is as you say, my son: Brāhmaṇhood is hard to attain; where there is Brāhmaṇhood there comes seerhood, and in seerhood the life of austerity.
This desire of yours shall be fulfilled: from Kuśika a Kauśika brāhmaṇa shall arise, who, reaching the third generation, shall attain Brāhmaṇhood.
Your line, O best of kings, shall through the very brilliance of the Bhṛgus—your grandson shall become a brāhmaṇa, an ascetic, with the splendor of fire,
who shall strike fear into gods and men and into the three worlds alike—this I tell you in truth.
Take the boon, O royal sage, that lies in your heart; I shall set out on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, for the time slips by.
Kuśika said: This is my very boon today—that you are pleased, O great sage. May it be as you have said: let there be austerity in my grandson, O sinless one, and Brāhmaṇhood for my line, O blessed one; this is the boon I ask.
And again I wish you to explain in full, O blessed one: how shall my line come to brāhmaṇa-hood, O joy of the Bhṛgus? And who shall be that kinsman of mine, and who the one esteemed among them?
Cyavana said: This must surely be told to you, O bull among men—the very reason for which I came to destroy you, O ruler of men.
The Kṣatriyas are ever the patrons whose sacrifices the Bhṛgus perform, O lord of men; yet they shall fall into discord through a cause ordained by fate.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the Kṣatriyas shall slay all the Bhṛgus, O lord of men, cutting them down even to the embryo in the womb, driven by the rod of destiny.
Then in our line shall be born one who shall increase the lineage, named Aurva, of great brilliance, with a radiance like blazing fire and sun.
He shall give birth to a fire of wrath to destroy the three worlds—a fire that would reduce the earth, with its mountains and forests, to ashes.
But after some time that best of sages shall himself quell that fire, casting it into the ocean within the mare's mouth.
Upon his illustrious son Ṛcīka, joy of the Bhṛgus, the whole science of archery shall present itself in visible form, O sinless one,
for the undoing of the Kṣatriyas, through a cause ordained by fate; and he, having received it, shall pass it on to his son.
To Jamadagni, the illustrious, his soul refined by austerity; and that tiger of the Bhṛgus too shall hold that science.
And from your line, O righteous one, he shall obtain a maiden, for the raising up of your house, O best of kings.
Gaining the daughter of Gādhi, your granddaughter, that great ascetic shall beget Rāma, a brāhmaṇa with the ways of a Kṣatriya.
And in your line he shall bring forth Viśvāmitra, son of Gādhi—a Kṣatriya with the works of a brāhmaṇa, in might like Bṛhaspati, deeply righteous, endowed with great austerity, O you of great splendor.
Two women shall be the cause of this exchange; by the ordinance of the Grandsire it shall not be otherwise.
In the third generation Brāhmaṇhood shall come to you, and you shall become a kinsman of the Bhṛgus, whose souls are refined.
Bhīṣma said: When king Kuśika heard the words of the great-souled sage Cyavana, he was filled with joy, and that righteous one spoke this word: "So be it," O best of the Bhāratas.
But Cyavana of great brilliance again urged the lord of men to take a boon; and the king said to him:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Surely, even so I shall gladly accept it from you, O great sage: let my line become brahman-like, and let its mind be set upon dharma."
Thus addressed, the sage Cyavana answered, "So be it," and, taking leave of the king, then set out upon his pilgrimage to the sacred fords.
All this I have told you without remainder, O king—the cause of the kinship between the Bhṛgus and the Kuśikas.
And just as it was foretold by the sage, so it came to pass, O king—the birth of the sage Rāma and of Viśvāmitra as well.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I seem to swoon today as I hear, brooding again and again over this earth bereft of its bands of glorious kings.
Having gained kingdoms by the hundred and conquered the earth, O Bhārata, having slain men by the tens of millions, I am consumed with anguish, O grandfather.
What shall now be the lot of those noble women who are bereft of husbands, of sons, of maternal uncles, and of brothers?
For we, having slain our elders and kinsmen and friends as well, shall surely fall headlong into hell; of this there is no doubt.
I wish to yoke this body to fierce austerity, O Bhārata; I wish to be instructed herein according to the truth, O lord of men.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of Yudhiṣṭhira, the great-souled Bhīṣma, after examining Yudhiṣṭhira keenly with his discerning mind, spoke to him.
Hear the secret and the wondrous thing that I shall declare to you, O descendant of Bharata—by what means a man attains his destined state in the conditions that follow death.
By austerity heaven is won, by austerity fame is won; length of life and enjoyments too are gained by austerity, O mighty one.
Knowledge, discernment, health, beauty, prosperity, and good fortune as well—all these are attained by austerity, O bull of the Bhāratas.
By austerity one obtains wealth; silence bestows knowledge; enjoyments come through giving, and long life through chastity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Beauty is the fruit of non-injury; birth in a noble lineage the fruit of sacred vows; a kingdom befalls those who feed on fruits and roots, and heaven those who feed on leaves.
He who lives on milk goes to heaven; by ritual bathing one grows rich in possessions; by service to the teacher comes learning, and by constant offerings to the ancestors comes progeny.
By vows of eating only herbs a man becomes rich in cattle; from feeding on grass, they say, comes heaven; from bathing at the three pressings come women, and by drinking only air one gains the merit of a sacrifice.
By bathing daily one becomes capable; the twice-born who murmurs his prayers at the two twilights wins a kingdom by mastering the desert wilds, and the vault of heaven by total fasting.
For those who sleep upon the bare ground there come houses and couches; through garments of rags and bark come fine robes and ornaments.
For the ascetic rich in penance and joined to discipline come beds, seats, and chariots; for one who enters the fire, the world of Brahmā is surely ordained.
By renouncing savory delicacies one finds good fortune here; by abstaining from flesh one's offspring become long-lived.
He who dwells standing in water becomes a lord of men; the truth-speaker, O best of men, rejoices in the company of the gods.
Renown comes through giving, and health through non-injury; by service to the twice-born comes a kingdom, or else abundant twice-born status itself.
By the gift of water one's fame becomes everlasting; by the gift of food and drink one is sated to the full in the enjoyment of one's desires.
He who speaks gently to all beings is freed from every sorrow; service to the gods bestows a kingdom and a celestial beauty.
By the gift of lamplight a man becomes endowed with keen sight; by the gift of fair spectacles he attains memory and intelligence.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By abstaining from perfumes and garlands one's renown grows abundant; for those who let their hair and beard grow there comes excellent progeny.
He who keeps fasting, the sacred vow, and ablution for twelve years, O king, surpasses even the abode of heroes.
By giving a daughter in righteous marriage—along with maidservants and menservants, ornaments, fields, and houses—a man obtains them all in turn, O bull among men.
By sacrifices and fasts a man goes to the triple heaven, O descendant of Bharata; and the man who offers oblations and flowers gains an enduring station.
The man who bestows a thousand cows adorned with golden horns attains the blessed world of the gods in heaven—so declare the assembled sages and deities.
To him who gives a tawny cow draped in cloth, with a bronze milking-vessel and gold-tipped horns, that cow—becoming for him a fulfiller of every wish by all those virtues—returns to the man who gave her.
As many as are the hairs upon the cow, so great is the reward the giver of cattle obtains; and he delivers his sons, his grandsons, and his whole line down to the seventh generation in the world beyond.
For one who gives to a twice-born a cow of sesame, complete with priestly fee, with fair golden horns, a bronze milking-vessel, and a covering of wealth, the worlds of the Vasus become easy to win.
As a ship driven by the wind across the great ocean, so the gift of cattle carries a man across to the world beyond—a man bound fast by his own deeds and falling into a hell of dense darkness.
He who gives a maiden in righteous marriage, who bestows land upon a brāhmaṇa, and who gives food according to the rite—he attains the world of Puraṃdara.
The man who gives a dwelling endowed with every comfort to a twice-born adorned with the virtues of sacred study and good conduct—for him too the worlds in the northern Kurus are won.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By the gift of draught-oxen and likewise of cattle and horses, a man attains the worlds of the Vasus; and they say the gift of silver leads to heaven, while the gift of gold is more excellent still.
By the gift of a parasol comes an excellent house; by the gift of footwear, a chariot; by the gift of garments, the fruit of beauty; and by the gift of perfumes a man becomes fragrant.
He who bestows upon a twice-born a tree laden with flowers or with fruit gains, without effort, a house rich in women and filled with many jewels.
The giver of food, drink, water, and savory dishes obtains all delights to his heart's content; and the giver of shelter and clothing obtains those very same—of this there is no doubt.
The man who gives to the twice-born wreaths, incense, perfumes, unguents, bathing-materials, and garlands becomes free from disease, and likewise comely, in the world of kings.
The man who gives to a twice-born a house not empty of seed and furnished with couches gains, O king, an excellent abode, holy and delightful and filled with many jewels.
The man who gives to a twice-born a bed furnished with fragrant and richly patterned coverings gains, without effort, a wife endowed with beauty, well-supported by kin, and pleasing to the heart.
The man who lies down to die as a hero becomes a follower of the Grandsire; than this there is nothing higher—so declare the supreme seers.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard those words of his, the delighted son of the Kurus no longer favored dwelling in a hermitage, longing instead for the path of the hero.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the bull of the Bhāratas, that lord addressed the Pāṇḍavas: "Let the words of the Grandsire find favor with you."
Thereupon all the Pāṇḍavas, and the illustrious Draupadī, honored those words of Yudhiṣṭhira, saying, "So be it."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Among those gifts that are reckoned as made outside the sacrificial altar, which gift do you hold to be the most excellent, O foremost of the Kurus?
For my curiosity in this matter is very great, O lord: declare to me that gift whose merit follows after the giver.
Bhīṣma said: Freedom from fear granted to all beings, and aid given in time of distress; and that which one gives, the very thing he longs for, to a thirsting suppliant who begs—
that gift, after giving which one feels he has truly given, is called the best; for it is the gift whose merit follows after the giver, O bull of the Bhāratas.
The gift of gold, the gift of cattle, and the gift of land—these indeed are purifying, and they carry across even the doer of evil.
Give these always to the virtuous, O tiger among men; for gifts release a man from sin—of this there is no doubt.
Whatever is most cherished in the world, and whatever is most beloved in one's own house—that should be given to a worthy man by one who desires it to become imperishable.
He who gives what is dear and does what is dear obtains dear things in the world, and becomes beloved of all beings both here and hereafter.
He who, out of pride, does not honor to the best of his power a suppliant who begs—one full of hope and possessing nothing—that man is cruel, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
He who shows favor in time of distress even to an enemy who comes wretched and seeking refuge—he indeed is the best of men.
To the gaunt and modest man, my son, ruined in his livelihood and sinking down—he who drives away that man's hunger, no other man is his equal.
The virtuous who are held back by modesty, worn thin with the care of wives and children, and who do not beg—these, O son of Kuntī, invite by every means.
Those who make no entreaty either to the gods or to mortals—worthy men, ever fixed in goodness, living on whatever they happen to obtain—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
guard yourself against such men, who are like venomous serpents, O descendant of Bharata; sound out those most excellent of the twice-born with respectful words.
Invite them ever, O scion of Kuru, with dwellings made ready, complete with servants and furnishings, that bring every desire and comfort.
If those righteous men of holy deeds should accept what is hallowed by faith, O Yudhiṣṭhira, deeming it merely a duty to be done—
those brāhmaṇas accomplished in learning, accomplished in vows, who live without dependence on others, whose private study and austerity are hidden, and whose vows are firmly held—
whatever good you do to them—the pure, the self-controlled, devoted to their own wives—that will establish you in the higher worlds.
As the fire-oblation well offered evening and morning by the twice-born, so does the gift given to the twice-born by a man of disciplined soul become.
This is your sacrifice spread out, hallowed by faith and furnished with priestly fees—surpassing all other sacrifices. Let it proceed, my son, as you give.
An offering to the ancestors is like a gift when made to such men, O Yudhiṣṭhira; by making such offerings and honoring them, one is freed of his debt to them.
Those who are never angry with us and never covet even so much as a blade of grass—they are the most worthy of our reverence, and likewise the others who speak kindly.
Those others who do not think much of us and do not press themselves forward—they too are to be cherished like one's own sons; reverence to them, and to them freedom from fear.
The officiating priest, the household chaplain, and the teacher—these bear the sacred power gently; for even the splendor mingled with kṣatriya might is quenched in the twice-born.
Thinking "I have wealth, I am mighty, I am king," do not, O Yudhiṣṭhira, slight the brāhmaṇas in the matter of garments and of food.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever wealth you have for the sake of splendor or of strength, O sinless one, with it the brāhmaṇas are to be honored by you who follow your own duty.
The brāhmaṇas, living rightly according to truth, are to be saluted by you; let them take their pleasure in you to their ease and to their delight, as sons do with a father.
For who else but you, O best of the Kurus, is fit to provide the maintenance of these gracious friends who are content with little?
As the duty of women in the world is eternally to take refuge in their husband—he is their god, he their sole recourse and no other—so are the twice-born to us.
If the brāhmaṇas, dishonored, should forsake us, my son—seeing the cruel deeds that ever attend the kṣatriya—
then, bereft of the Veda, of fame, of the higher worlds, and of sacrifice, what use is life to us? For that all rests upon our recourse to the brāhmaṇas.
On this I shall expound to you what the eternal law is. In olden days the kṣatriya waited upon the brāhmaṇa, O king, the vaiśya upon the kṣatriya, and the śūdra upon the vaiśya—so runs the sacred tradition.
The brāhmaṇa, blazing like fire, is to be served by the śūdra from a distance, but he may be served with touch by the vaiśya and by the kṣatriya.
Attend upon those twice-born, who are gentle of nature, truthful in conduct, and guardians of the law of truth, yet who when angered are like venomous serpents.
The fiery energies and austerities of the kṣatriyas who burn with splendor and might—surpassing some, surpassing others, surpassing even those beyond the rest—are quelled in the brāhmaṇas alone.
Not my father is dearer to me, nor are you, my son, so dear, nor my father's father, O king, nor my own self, nor my life—
and though there is none on earth dearer to me than you, yet even dearer to me than you, O bull of the Bhāratas, are the brāhmaṇas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This truth I speak, O joy of Pāṇḍu, just as it is; and by that truth may I go to those worlds where Śaṃtanu dwells.
And may I behold the pure worlds of the good, with the sacred power set foremost; thither, my son, I must go, both soon and for long to come.
And I, having beheld such worlds, O best of the Bhāratas, do not repent of what I have done for the brāhmaṇas, O son of Pṛthā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of two men who are alike endowed with good conduct, and equal in learning and in birth—to which of these is the gift more excellent, to the one who does not beg or to the one who begs?
Bhīṣma said: A gift bestowed upon one who does not beg is held more meritorious than one given to a beggar, O Pārtha; for the steadfast man is far worthier of honor than the wretch whose soul lacks self-command.
The kṣatriya is steadfast in protection, the brāhmaṇa steadfast in not soliciting; the learned and contented brāhmaṇa, firm of resolve, gives delight to the gods.
Begging, O Bhārata, they call the resort of the powerless, a kind of seizing; for he who begs ever distresses living beings, like a robber.
The one who begs is as good as dead, and the giver dies along with him if he refuses; but by giving, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he keeps that suppliant alive, and himself as well.
Freedom from cruelty is the supreme dharma, which is fulfilled in what is given to one who begs; but those who suffer in silence and do not ask, invite them by every means.
If such foremost of the twice-born should dwell within your realm, take pains to recognize them, like fires hidden beneath their ashes.
Blazing with their austerity, they could consume even the earth; for they are worthy of worship, endowed with knowledge, discernment, austerity, and yoga.
Offer worship to those brāhmaṇas, O scorcher of foes, bestowing gifts of many kinds, and coaxing forth those who do not ask.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever fruit accrues from the agnihotra well-offered at evening and at dawn, that same fruit is declared to belong to a gift made to one possessed of learning, Veda, and vows.
Those brāhmaṇas who have bathed in the close of learning, Veda, and vows, who live without dependence on others, whose private study and austerity are hidden, who are firm in their vows—
with pleasing dwellings built for them, furnished with servants and appointments, you should invite those foremost of the twice-born, O son of Kuntī, and with other things they desire.
Perhaps they will accept what is hallowed by faith, O Yudhiṣṭhira, thinking only that it must be done—knowers of dharma, seers of the subtle.
Perhaps those brāhmaṇas, having eaten, will return to homes with stores laid by, whose wives await them as farmers await the rain-cloud.
Let the brāhmaṇas, disciplined celibates, partaking of food at the morning pressing, my child, give delight thereby to your three sacred fires.
Let your midday pressing proceed, my child, as you give cattle, gold, and garments; by that may Indra be pleased with you.
That is your third, the Vaiśvadeva pressing, O Yudhiṣṭhira, in what you bestow upon the gods, the ancestors, and the brāhmaṇas.
Non-injury toward all beings, sharing in every way, self-restraint, renunciation, steadfastness, and truth—let these serve as your concluding bath of the sacrifice.
This is your sacrifice spread wide, hallowed by faith, attended with its offerings, surpassing all sacrifices; may it ever go forward, my child.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of giving and the rite of sacrifice here, which yields the greater fruit hereafter? Whose fruit is declared the loftier—and to what kind of recipients, how, and when?
This I wish to know truly as it is, O Bhārata; learned one, to me who seeks to understand, expound the laws of giving.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What is given within the altar-ground, with faith and without cruelty—which of these brings the highest good, my father? Tell me that, grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: The work of the kṣatriya is forever fierce, my child; for him the rite of the sacred fires and giving are the purifiers in this world.
But the good do not accept gifts from kings who do evil; for this reason a king should worship with sacrifices furnished with well-earned offerings.
But if they do accept, let the king give day after day, taking his stand on the highest faith; for this is the supreme purification.
Let him, his vows controlled, satisfy with gifts the brāhmaṇas at the sacrifice—the friendly, the good, the knowers of the Veda, endowed with character, conduct, and austerity.
Whatever they shall accomplish thereby will become an accomplished deed for you; bring sacrifices to fulfillment for the good, with savory food and ample offerings.
Deem yourself to have sacrificed and given; by the act of giving honor those constant in sacrifice, that a share thereof may be yours as well.
Support too the brāhmaṇas blessed with offspring and burdened with many to feed; by this one becomes rich in progeny, even as the begetter himself.
As many righteous observances as the good keep alive, so many of those men who bear heavy burdens of dependents must likewise be maintained.
Prosperous as you are, bestow upon the brāhmaṇas, O Yudhiṣṭhira, milch-cows, oxen, food, a parasol, garments, and sandals.
Clarified butter to the sacrificers, and food and viands, O Bhārata, and conveyances drawn by horses, dwellings, and beds.
These are to be given—fruitful and easily come by, O Bhārata—once you have marked out the blameless brāhmaṇas worn thin by want of livelihood.
Whether in secret or in the open, provide them with a livelihood; for a kṣatriya that is more excellent than the Rājasūya and the Aśvamedha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus freed from your sins and made pure, you shall attain heaven, when, having loosed your treasury again, you shall protect your realm.
And thereafter you shall attain oneness with Brahman, and wealth besides; guard well the livelihood of yourself and of others, O Bhārata.
Cherish your servants and your subjects as you would your sons; and let your care for their welfare and security ever rest upon the brāhmaṇas, O Bhārata.
A king who does not protect but seizes, who plunders and gives nothing—that disgrace among kings, that pitiless one, the people, banding together, would do well to slay.
The lord of earth who says 'I am your protector' yet does not protect—him should the people unite to kill, like a mad and rabid dog.
Whatever evil the subjects commit when left unprotected by the king, a fourth part of that evil the king incurs, O Bhārata.
Some say it is the whole; others fix it firmly at a half; but a fourth is our own view, having heard the teaching of Manu.
And whatever good the subjects do when well protected by the king, a fourth part of that merit the king obtains, O Bhārata.
May all your subjects live in dependence on your life, O Yudhiṣṭhira, as living beings on the rain-cloud, as birds upon a mighty tree.
As the rākṣasas live in dependence on Kubera, as the immortals on Indra of the hundred sacrifices, so may your kinsmen and friends live in dependence on you, O scorcher of foes.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: 'This is to be given, this is to be given'—so runs the injunction of scripture, and kings have many things to give; but what gift is the most excellent of all?
Bhīṣma said: Surpassing all gifts, the gift of land is proclaimed supreme; for the earth is unmoving and imperishable, yielding desires that have no equal.
She yields garments, gems, cattle, rice, and barley; the giver of land flourishes among all beings for everlasting years.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As long as the life of the earth endures, so long does the giver of land flourish; there is nothing here higher than the gift of land, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Even a little of the earth the ancients gave, so we have heard; all those people who enjoy the use of land have in truth given land.
By their own deeds alone do men live, here and hereafter; the earth, prosperity itself, the great goddess, makes the giver dear to her.
That lord of earth who bestows this imperishable gift, on attaining human birth once more, shall himself become a lord of earth.
As the gift, so the enjoyment—such is the settled rule in the codes of dharma; let a man either yield up his body in battle or give away this earth.
This they declare to be the highest blessing of the warrior kinsmen; the earth, once given, purifies the giver—so have we heard.
Even him whose conduct is sinful, even a slayer of a brāhmaṇa or a speaker of falsehood—she alone cleanses of that sin, she alone can release from sin.
Even from kings who do evil the good accept the earth, and desire nothing else; for she purifies like a mother.
'Priyadattā'—'Dear when given'—is the secret, eternal name of this goddess; either gift or knowledge is dearest to that name of hers. Therefore, no sooner has a king won the earth than he should give it to a brāhmaṇa.
By no means may the earth be held by one who is not a lord of the soil; nor should one conceal it through a worthy proxy, nor proceed by stealth. And whoever else might covet land should act in this same way, beyond all doubt.
He who takes away a good man's land—he wins no land at all; but he who gives land to the good wins land indeed, and that righteous soul gains great renown both here and hereafter.
He whose land the brāhmaṇas, being good, ever govern—his enemies, O king, never come to rule the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever sin a man commits, worn thin by want of livelihood, he is cleansed of it by the gift of land—even of land no larger than a cowhide.
Even for those kings whose deeds are mixed and whose works are cruel, the supreme gift of land is to be proclaimed a means of purity.
That the difference is ever but slight, the men of old held: between one who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha and one who gives the earth to a good man.
Even when they have done a good deed, the wise may yet harbor misgiving; this one thing alone is beyond such doubt—the supreme, irreproachable gift of land.
Gold, silver, garments, jewels, pearls, and riches—all this, O greatly wise one, the giver of the earth bestows in giving it.
Austerity, sacrifice, sacred learning, character, freedom from greed, truthfulness, and worship of teachers and gods—none of these surpasses the giver of land.
Those who, devoted to their lord's highest good, give up their lives and are slain in battle, the perfected who have gone to the world of Brahman—even they do not outstrip the giver of land.
As a mother ever nourishes her own son with her milk, so does the earth favor the giver with all her savors.
The rod that is Death's servant, the most dreadful burning of fire, and the terrible nooses of Varuṇa—none of these draws near the giver of land.
The ancestors abiding in the world of the fathers and the gods in the world of the gods—both does that serene soul satisfy who gives away the earth.
To the gaunt, the dying, the man wasted in his livelihood and sinking down, a man who gives sustaining land becomes as one who has performed a sacrificial session.
As a cow runs to her calf, letting her milk flow freely, so, O highly blessed one, does the earth come to the giver of land.
By giving land plowed and sown, bearing seed and yielding fruit, or by giving a noble refuge, a man becomes a granter of desires.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The man who makes a brāhmaṇa accept land—one perfect in conduct, who has set up his sacred fires, pure in his vows—does not go to the abode of Yama.
As the waxing of the moon comes day by day, so does the gift made of land increase with every crop.
On this the knowers of old recite the songs sung by the Earth herself, on hearing which the son of Jamadagni gave the earth to Kaśyapa.
'Receive me, give me; having given me, you shall win me again—in this world and in the next, and thereafter once more in birthlessness.'
The brāhmaṇa, devoted to Brahman, who knows this utterance, at a śrāddha whose oblations are being offered attains oneness with Brahman.
'A mighty quelling am I of malign rites and curses, the calmer of ill-offered sacrifices; once a man has performed the expiation that I am, it purifies ten on either side.'
'Whoever knows this is purified, and I myself am likewise the Veda; the source of all beings, the everlasting earth—so am I held.'
As soon as a king is consecrated, let this sacred lore be recited to him, that on hearing it he may give the earth and not take it from the good.
This, then, is the whole matter, both of the brāhmaṇa and of the king, beyond all doubt; for a king skilled in dharma is the foremost mark of prosperity.
Now those whose king is ignorant of dharma and a denier of the sacred order—they neither wake in comfort nor sleep in peace.
The people are forever distressed by his misdeeds; and many who would have brought security and prosperity refuse to enter his realm.
But those whose king is wise and righteous—they wake in happiness and sleep in deep contentment.
Contented by that king's auspicious and noble deeds, his subjects flourish through their own labors, through prosperity and through the rains.
He is well-born, he is a true man, he is a kinsman, he is a doer of merit, he is a giver and he is valorous—the one who gives away the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Like the Ādityas, those mortals blaze with splendor upon the earth who bestow rich land upon a brāhmaṇa learned in the Veda.
As seeds scattered upon the ground spring up, so do desires sprout forth when they are won by the gift of land.
Āditya, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Soma, the fire-eater Agni, and the blessed Lord who bears the trident—all rejoice in the giver of land.
Upon the earth men are born, and upon the earth they come to their end; for this fourfold world is constituted of the qualities of the earth.
She is the mother and the father of the world, O lord of the earth; there exists no being equal to her, O ruler of men.
And on this matter they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having sacrificed with a hundred great rites richly endowed with priestly fees, Maghavat questioned Bṛhaspati, foremost of those skilled in speech, on this very matter.
O blessed one, by which gift does a man who has gone to heaven thrive in happiness? Tell me that gift which is imperishable and of great worth, O best of speakers.
Thus addressed by the lord of the gods, the priest of the celestials, the mightily resplendent Bṛhaspati, replied to him of the hundred sacrifices.
The gift of gold, the gift of cattle, and the gift of land, O slayer of Vṛtra—the man of great wisdom who bestows these is released from all his sins.
There is nothing higher than the gift of land, O lord of the gods, O master; I hold it to be the most excellent, even as the wise have declared.
Those heroes slain in battle who, eager for giving, have gone to heaven—not one of them, O best of the gods, surpasses the giver of land.
The heroes devoted to their lord's supreme good, who lay down their lives and are slain in battle and attain the world of Brahmā—even they do not surpass the giver of land.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Five forefathers and six who have gone before—the man who gives land delivers all eleven of his line here in this world.
He who gives away land strewn with jewels, O Puraṃdara, is freed from all his impurities and is honored in the world of heaven.
A king who gives away a flourishing land endowed with all that the heart desires becomes a king of kings; that indeed is the gift unsurpassed.
He who bestows the earth of Kaśyapa, furnished with every object of desire—all beings think, 'It is to me that he gives,' O Vāsava.
The mortal who gives a cow that yields every wish and grants every desire, O thousand-eyed one, goes to heaven.
Rivers that flow with honey and clarified butter, and that bear milk and curds, refresh here, O lord of the gods, the giver of land.
By the gift of land a king is freed from the guilt that clings to kingship; for no other gift surpasses the gift of land.
He who gives away the earth bounded by the oceans, won by the sword—men tell of him here for as long as this earth shall endure.
He who gives a holy land rich in sap, O Puraṃdara—the worlds he has won by the merit of the gift of land never wane for him.
By every means should a ruler who ever desires prosperity, who longs for happiness, O Śakra, give land according to the prescribed rite to a worthy recipient.
Even a man who has committed a sin, by giving land to a twice-born, casts off that sin as a serpent casts off its worn-out skin.
Oceans, rivers, mountains, and forests in their entirety—all this a man gives, O Śakra, when he gives away the earth.
Ponds and wells, streams and lakes, oils and every kind of sap—all these he gives when he gives away the earth.
Herbs abounding in milky sap, trees laden with flowers and fruit, and forests, stones, and crags—all these he gives when he gives away the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Though one sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma and other rites, complete with their proper priestly fees, he does not attain the fruit that he enjoys from the gift of land.
The giver favors ten generations; he who reviles a gift destroys ten; and he who takes back land once given goes down to hell.
He who, having promised, does not give, or who takes back what he has given, is bound in the nooses of Varuṇa and tormented by the decree of death.
Those who support a brāhmaṇa of the highest order—one who has kindled the sacred fire, ever offers sacrifice, keeps but scant retinue, and loves his guests—do not come near Yama.
It should be regarded as a debt owed by the king to the brāhmaṇas, O Puraṃdara; but of the other castes too he should rescue the lean and the feeble.
Let no one wrest away land once made over by another, O lord of the thirty gods, to a brāhmaṇa of scant means, O best of the celestials.
And the tears that fall from those wretched, sinking brāhmaṇas when their field is seized destroy three generations of the despoiler's line.
But he who restores once more a ruler fallen from his realm—his dwelling, O thousand-eyed one, is honored upon the vault of heaven.
Land covered over with sugarcane, thick with barley and wheat, abounding in cattle, horses, and beasts of burden, won by the strength of his own arm—
—land whose womb holds treasures and which is adorned with every jewel: the man who gives it attains imperishable worlds, for that is to him a very sacrifice of land.
Having shaken off all his impurity, cleansed of passion and esteemed by the good, he who gives away the earth is honored in the world by the virtuous.
As a drop of oil fallen upon water spreads, O Śakra, so does a gift made in land spread out in crop after crop.
Those kings, heroes resplendent in the assembly of battle, who are slain facing the foe at the front of combat, O Śakra—they go to the world of Brahmā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Women given to dance and song, adorned with celestial garlands, attend forever upon the giver of land in heaven, O lord of the gods.
He who duly, by the prescribed rite, gives land here to a twice-born rejoices in happiness in heaven, honored by gods and gandharvas.
