A hundred apsarases, adorned with celestial garlands, attend forever upon the man who is a giver of land, O lord of the gods.
The conch, the throne of state, the parasol, fine horses and noble elephants, and heaps of gold—these are the blossoms that spring from the gift of land.
Command forever unopposed and the cry of victory besides—these are the flowers of the gift of land; its fruit is heaven, O Puraṃdara.
Herbs with blossoms of gold, and lawns of kuśa grass and gold—the man who gives land attains a land that brings forth ambrosia.
There is no gift like the gift of land, no elder like a mother, no dharma like truth, and no treasure like giving.
Having heard this from the son of Aṅgiras, Vāsava then gave to that son of Aṅgiras this very earth strewn with wealth and jewels.
He who recites this hymn in praise of the gift of land at a śrāddha rite—no portion of his offering falls to the rākṣasas or to the asuras.
And what is given to the ancestors becomes imperishable—of this there is no doubt; therefore at śrāddhas let a brāhmaṇa recite this to the twice-born as they dine.
Thus have I declared to you, O sinless one, that which is the foremost of all gifts, O tiger of the Bhāratas; what more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What gifts in this world should a king desirous of giving bestow upon brāhmaṇas of surpassing merit, O best of the Bhāratas?
By what are they at once made content, and what, when content, do they grant in return? Tell me this, O mighty-armed one—the great and holy fruit of such merit.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What gift, O king, bears fruit both in this world and in the next? I wish to hear it from you; tell me that in full detail.
Bhīṣma said: On this very matter Nārada, who beholds the gods, was once questioned; hear from me as I tell what he then declared, O descendant of Bharata.
Nārada said: It is food above all that the gods, together with the hosts of sages, praised of old; for the order of the world and the sacrifices—all rest upon food.
No gift equal to food has been or shall ever be; therefore men desire above all to give food.
Food gives strength in the world, and the vital breaths are established in food; by food this whole universe is upheld, O lord.
From food the householders in this world subsist, and the mendicants likewise; from food springs the breath of life—this is plain to see, and herein is no doubt.
Even at the cost of straitening his own household, a man who desires his own welfare should give food to a great-souled brāhmaṇa and to a mendicant.
He who gives food to a worthy brāhmaṇa in need lays up for himself the finest of treasures, a treasure for the world beyond.
The householder who desires prosperity should honor the weary traveler on the road, the aged and worthy man who has come to his door.
Casting off rising anger, well-conducted and free from grudging, the giver of food attains, O king, whatever happiness there is both in heaven and here.
Let him never slight one who has come, nor turn him away by any means; even when given to an outcaste or to a dog, a gift is never lost.
He who ungrudgingly gives food to a weary man upon the road, one never seen before, attains a great measure of dharma.
The man who gratifies with food the ancestors, the gods, the sages, the brāhmaṇas, and his guests, O ruler of men—great is the fruit of his merit.
Even one who has done an evil deed, if he gives food to a needy man—and above all to a brāhmaṇa—is not bound by his sin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A gift to brāhmaṇas is imperishable; food given to a śūdra bears great fruit; the giving of food, whether to a śūdra or to a brāhmaṇa, is preeminent.
When food is begged of him here by a brāhmaṇa, let him not inquire into the lineage, the conduct, the sacred study, the homeland, or the birth of the one who asks.
For the giver of food there grow trees of food laden with the fruit of every desire, whether here or in the world beyond, O king; herein is no doubt.
For the ancestors yearn, as farmers yearn for good rain: 'Will our son too, or our grandson, give food on our behalf?'
For the brāhmaṇa is a great being who himself begs, saying 'Give'; and whether one gives unwillingly or willingly, by giving one attains merit.
The brāhmaṇa is the guest of all beings, the one who eats the first portion offered; he it is to whose house the twice-born come ever, begging alms.
And when they depart honored, that household prospers exceedingly; and after death one attains birth in a family of great abundance, O descendant of Bharata.
Having given food, a man attains in this world an unsurpassed station; and he who gives the most delicate of foods dwells honored in heaven.
Food is the very life-breath of men, for all things rest upon food. The giver of food becomes rich in cattle, blessed with sons, abounding in wealth, and full of enjoyments.
He becomes vigorous in life and comely in form as well, O king. The giver of food is in this world a giver of life, and he is called the giver of all things.
For when one bestows food, according to the ordinance, upon a guest who is a brāhmaṇa, the giver attains happiness and is honored even by the gods.
The brāhmaṇa is indeed a great being who roams about as a field on foot; and whatever seed is sown therein yields a mighty fruit of merit.
The gift of food brings joy at once, plainly visible, both to him who eats and to him who gives; whereas all other gifts bear their fruit only out of sight.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Know that procreation springs from food, and from food too comes delight, O Bhārata. Know that dharma and prosperity arise from food, and likewise from food comes the destruction of disease.
In the ancient age Prajāpati declared that food is verily ambrosia. Food is the earth, the heaven, and the sky; all things rest upon food.
When food is wanting, the five elements within the body fall asunder; and the strength even of the strong perishes in this world through lack of food.
Receptions and weddings and sacrifices cannot proceed without food, O best of men, and the recitation of the Veda too dissolves away for want of it.
For all this, whatever is fixed or moving, arises from food. Therefore, throughout the three worlds, food should be given by the wise for the sake of dharma.
For the man who gives food, his strength, vigor, glory, happiness, and renown grow forever throughout the three worlds, O lord of the earth.
The auspicious wind, the very breath of living things, gathers water in the clouds; and that water lodged within the clouds Śakra rains down, O Bhārata.
And Āditya, the sun, draws up the moisture of the earth with his own rays; and from the sun the wind, the god Prajāpati, draws those essences.
And when the water has fallen from the cloud upon the ground, then the goddess Earth, bearer of treasures, grows moist and rich, O Bhārata.
Thereupon the crops spring up, by which the world is sustained; and from that, in turn, arises the production of flesh, fat, bone, and seed.
Then from that seed living creatures come into being, O lord of the earth; for Agni and Soma are that generative seed, and they nourish the begetting of offspring.
Thus food, and the sun, and the wind, and the seed are remembered as one single mass, from which all beings have been born.
He who promptly gives food to a needy one come to his house bestows life-breath upon living beings, and splendor as well, O bull of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by Nārada, I gave food always, O king. Do you too, free of envy and freed of all fever of heart, give food therefore.
Having given food according to the ordinance, O king, to brāhmaṇas worthy of it and as is fitting, O lord, you too shall thereby attain heaven.
Now hear of those worlds that belong to the givers of food, O ruler of men. In heaven there shine the mansions of those great-souled ones, of manifold shapes and forms and furnished with manifold pillars.
White as the orb of the moon, hung with nets of little bells, of the hue of the young rising sun, some standing fixed and some that move.
Rising in many hundreds of storeys, having within them pools of water and groves, gleaming like beryl and the sun, and wrought of silver and gold.
And trees yielding the fruit of every desire stand set within those mansions, with tanks, avenues, halls, wells, and long ponds on every side.
And resounding chariots stand ready harnessed by the thousand; there are mountains made of dainties and viands, and garments and ornaments too.
There are rivers streaming with milk, and mountains of food, palaces gleaming like pale white clouds, and couches bright with gold. To these the givers of food attain; therefore be a giver of food.
These are the worlds of those great-souled doers of meritorious deeds, the givers of food. Therefore food above all should be given by men upon the earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard your words on the rule for the giving of food. Now tell me of the manner of giving according to the conjunction of the lunar mansions.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount this ancient tale, the dialogue between Devakī and the divine sage Nārada.
When Nārada, who beheld the gods, had come to Dvārakā, Devakī, who looked upon dharma, then put this question to him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
To her as she questioned, the divine sage Nārada then expounded all duly, according to the ordinance. Hear that, O lord of peoples.
Nārada said: Under the asterism Kṛttikā, O blessed lady, by satisfying worthy brāhmaṇas with milk-rice mixed with ghee, one attains worlds most excellent.
Under Rohiṇī one should give to a twice-born, for the sake of discharging one's debt, choice meats, beans, cooked food, and ghee, with milk to drink afterward.
Having given a milch cow together with her calf under the asterism whose deity is Soma, men pass from the world of men to the most excellent world of heaven.
Having fasted and given, under Ārdrā, a dish of rice and sesame mingled with oil, a man crosses over difficult straits and mountains sharp as razors' edges.
Having given cakes and likewise foods under the fair asterism Punarvasu, one is born renowned and endowed with beauty in a house abounding in food.
Having given gold under Puṣya, whether wrought or unwrought, he shines like the moon in worlds that are otherwise without light.
He who under Āśleṣā gives silver or a bull becomes freed from every fear and stands triumphant over his foes.
Having presented under Maghā vessels filled with sesame, brimming over, a man, blessed with sons and cattle, rejoices both here and in the world to come.
At the season of the Pūrvā Phālgunī, having fasted and given to brāhmaṇas dainties prepared with raw sugar, one attains good fortune.
Having given duly, in the domain of the Uttarā asterism, rice of the sixty-day kind dressed with ghee and milk, one is exalted in the world of heaven.
Whatever gift is bestowed by men in the domain of the Uttarā asterism becomes of great and endless fruit: such is the settled truth.
Having fasted and given under Hasta an elephant-chariot drawn by four, one attains the highest worlds, fulfilled in merit and in desire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having given under Citrā a bull and holy perfumes, O Bhārata, one roams in the world of the apsarases and takes delight in the grove of Nandana.
And having given under Svāti the wealth that is dearest to himself, he attains auspicious worlds, and great renown even here.
Under Viśākhā, having given an ox and a milch cow yielding milk, and a cart with its yoke-pole, laden with grain and furnished with cloth—
—he gladdens the ancestors and the gods, and after death enjoys the endless; he meets with no hard straits and goes to the world of heaven.
Having given to brāhmaṇas as prescribed, he obtains the livelihood he desires, and does not meet with hell and other torments: such is the settled truth.
Having fasted and given under Anurādhā an outer wrap and another garment, a man is exalted in heaven for even a hundred ages.
A mortal who under Jyeṣṭhā gives to brāhmaṇas dark pot-herbs together with their roots gains the prosperity he wishes for and the destiny he desires.
Having given roots and fruits to brāhmaṇas under Mūla with a composed mind, he gladdens the ancestors and goes to the destiny he desires.
And under the Pūrvā Aṣāḍhā, having fasted, by presenting bowls of curds to a brāhmaṇa endowed with good family conduct and versed to the end in the Veda, one is born after death into a house rich in herds of cattle.
Having given under the Uttarā Aṣāḍhā a barley-and-water gruel with ghee and abundant honey and raw sugar, one would attain all desires.
And one ever devoted to dharma who, under the conjunction of Abhijit, gives to the wise milk drenched with honey and ghee is exalted in the world of heaven.
Having given under Śravaṇa a woolen blanket together with another garment, one journeys in a white chariot through all the unobstructed worlds.
Having given under Dhaniṣṭhā with composed mind an ox-drawn carriage fitted with cloth and reins, he straightway attains sovereignty after death.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having given under the conjunction of Śatabhiṣaj perfumes together with aloe-wood and sandal, one attains after death the worlds of the apsarases and fragrances everlasting.
And having presented kidney-beans under the conjunction of Pūrvā Bhādrapadā, endowed with the fruit of every kind of food, he is verily happy after death.
He who under the conjunction of Uttarā Bhādrapadā gives the flesh of a ram gladdens the ancestors and after death enjoys the endless.
He who under Revatī gives a milch cow milked into a bronze vessel—after death she comes, bearing his desires, and waits upon the giver.
Having given under Aśvinī a chariot yoked with horses, the best of men is born radiant in a house rich in elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having presented under Bharaṇī to twice-born ones a cow made of sesame, a man obtains cattle in great abundance, and renown likewise, after death.
Bhīṣma said: Thus was this summary of the marks declared, according to the conjunction of the lunar mansions, by Nārada to Devakī; and she spoke this to her daughters-in-law.
Bhīṣma said: Those who give gold give all desires—thus spoke the venerable Atri, the son of the Grandsire.
Gold is purifying, pure, life-giving, and, for the ancestors, imperishable—so it was extolled by Hariścandra, the lord of men.
The gift of water is the highest of gifts, Manu declared. Therefore one should have tanks and wells and pools dug out.
A well whose water flows freely and ever flows well carries away here half the sin of a man's deeds.
He whose dug-out reservoir is one where cattle and brāhmaṇas and good men ever drink saves his whole lineage.
He at whose place water stands unstinted in the season of summer's heat never meets with hardship, peril, or distress.
By the gift of ghee there comes the favor of the venerable Bṛhaspati, of Pūṣan, of Bhaga, of the two Aśvins, and of the Fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For this ghee is the supreme medicine; this is the best of offerings in sacrifice; this is the best of savory things and the best of fruits.
He who desires fruit, who desires fame, and who desires thriving—such a man, pure and self-possessed, should ever give ghee to the twice-born.
For him who gives ghee to brāhmaṇas in the month of Āśvayuja, the two Aśvin gods, well pleased, bestow beauty in this world.
He who gives to the twice-born milk-rice mixed with ghee—his house the rākṣasas never assail at any time.
He who gives waterpots does not die of thirst, is seen to be pleasing of speech, and meets with no calamity.
The man who, self-restrained and filled with supreme faith, gives to the foremost of brāhmaṇas obtains ever a sixth share of the merit of their ritual sippings of water.
The man who, for the sake of their rites and for warmth, ever gives firewood to brāhmaṇas of good conduct, O king of kings—
—for him his aims ever prosper and his manifold undertakings as well; and he blazes in splendor of form higher and higher above his foes.
And the venerable Fire is ever well pleased with him; the herds do not forsake him, and in battle too he is victorious.
He who gives a parasol obtains sons and prosperity; he contracts no disease of the eyes, and he partakes of a share in the sacrifice.
Whoever bestows an umbrella in the hot season or in the rains, no anguish of mind ever arises in him; and from hardship and from peril, O brāhmaṇa, he wins deliverance.
Of all gifts, the gift of a cart is the most excellent—thus declared the greatly blessed and venerable seer Śāṇḍilya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When a man gives a pair of sandals to a brāhmaṇa whose feet are scorched, what fruit accrues to him—tell me that, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: He who, with collected mind, bestows a pair of sandals upon brāhmaṇas tramples down all thorns and crosses over every rough place; and he stands triumphant above his foes, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
A gleaming carriage yoked with she-mules, adorned with silver and gold, attends upon him, O lord of peoples, O son of Kuntī; and it is as though he had given a cart yoked with trained oxen.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The fruit that is proclaimed in the gift of sesame and the gift of land, in the gift of a cow and the gift of food—tell me of that once more, O Kaurava.
Bhīṣma said: Hear from me, O son of Kuntī, what fruit the gift of sesame yields; and having heard it, bestow it duly, O best of the Kurus.
Sesame seeds were created by the Self-Existent as the foremost food of the ancestors; therefore by the gift of sesame the company of the fathers rejoices.
He who in the month of Māgha gives sesame to brāhmaṇas does not behold the hell thronged with every kind of creature.
He who honors the ancestors with sesame worships them with all desired things fulfilled; yet the sesame śrāddha must never be offered grudgingly, against one's will.
These sesame seeds sprang forth from the limbs of the great seer Kaśyapa; thence, O lord, sesame attained a divine nature among the offerings of gifts.
They give nourishment, they bestow beauty, and they are destroyers of sin; therefore, of all gifts, the gift of sesame is the most excellent.
The sagacious Āpastamba, and Śaṅkha, and Likhita, and the great seer Gautama too—all went to heaven by gifts of sesame.
Brāhmaṇas devoted to the sesame oblation, all restrained in their pleasures, are reckoned the equals of those who offer the oblation of cow's products and who abide steadfast in their observances.
Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of sesame is held to be supreme; among all gifts, the gift of sesame is here declared imperishable.
And of old, when the oblation had been produced, the seer Kuśika, O scorcher of foes, having offered into the three fires with sesame, attained the highest goal.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus has the unsurpassed gift of sesame been declared, O foremost of the Kurus, together with the rite by which the offering of sesame is here commended.
Hereafter learn of this, O great king—how the gods, desiring to perform a sacrifice, came together with the Self-Existent Brahmā.
The gods, having assembled before Brahmā and wishing to sacrifice, begged for a portion of earth, an auspicious tract: "Let us perform the sacrifice," O son of Pṛthā.
The gods said: O Blessed One, you are the lord of all the earth and of the threefold heaven; with your leave, O greatly blessed one, let us perform the sacrifice, for on unsanctioned ground no one wins the fruit of a sacrifice.
For you are the lord of the whole world, both the moving and the unmoving; therefore it is fitting that you grant us your sanction.
Brahmā said: I give you a portion of the earth, O bulls among the gods, the tract whereon you shall perform your sacrifice, O sons of Kaśyapa.
The gods said: O Blessed One, our wish is fulfilled; we shall sacrifice with the prescribed fees duly rendered—and this very tract the sages have ever frequented and revered.
Bhīṣma said: Then Agastya and Kaṇva, Bhṛgu, Atri, Vṛṣākapi, and Asita Devala came to the gods' sacrifice.
Then the high-souled gods performed the sacrifice, O unfailing one, and the bulls among the gods brought it to its completion in due season.
Having performed their sacrifice, the thirty gods upon Himavat, that loftiest of mountains, made the gift of land a sixth part of that rite.
Whoever gives even a span's measure of land, unencumbered, does not sink in times of hardship nor fall into straits.
Having given a well-prepared plot for a dwelling, proof against cold, wind, and heat, a man dwells in the world of the gods and is not dislodged even when his merit is spent.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The wise man dwells in joy together with Śakra, O son of Pṛthā; and the giver of shelter, he too is exalted in heaven.
He in whose house a man born in a line of teachers, learned in the Vedas and of subdued senses, dwells contented—that giver attains the foremost world.
Likewise, a great shelter for the sake of cattle, proof against cold and rain, redeems one's line down to the seventh generation, O best of the Bhāratas.
By giving farmland in this world, my son, a man would gain prosperity; and by bestowing a tract rich in gems, he would cause his family line to flourish.
But one should never give land that is barren and salt, nor land scorched and burnt, nor land bordered by a cremation ground, nor land used for wicked deeds.
When a man makes an offering to the ancestors upon a tract of land belonging to another, that funerary rite is despoiled by the fathers of the land's owner.
Therefore let the discerning man first buy the land, even a little, and then give it; for the rice-ball offered to the fathers upon such ground becomes everlasting.
Forests and mountains, and whatever river-fords there be—all these, they say, are ownerless, for there is no private possession of them.
Thus has the fruit of the gift of land been told, O lord of peoples; and now, after this, I shall proclaim to you the gift of a cow, O sinless one.
Since cows are higher than all ascetics whatsoever, therefore the god Maheśvara undertook his austerity in their company.
These cows dwell in the world of Brahmā together with Soma, O Bhārata; from their midst the perfected brahman-seers seek the supreme goal.
With milk, with the clarified offering, with curd, and even with their dung, with their hide, with their bones, with their horns and their hair do they render service, O Bhārata.
Neither cold nor heat afflicts them; ever do they do their work; neither rain nor rough weather brings them any distress.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
United with the brāhmaṇas they go to the highest station; therefore the wise speak of cow and brāhmaṇa as one.
At the sacrifice of Rantideva they were appointed as sacrificial victims; thence, O king, the river Carmaṇvatī came to flow from the hides of the cattle.
Released thereafter from the state of sacrificial victims, they were ordained for giving away; and whoever gives these to the foremost of brāhmaṇas, O lord of earth, would cross over grievous calamity, even though set in dire straits, O son of Pṛthā.
He who gives a thousand cows beholds no hell after death and wins victory everywhere, O ruler of men.
"The milk of cows is verily the nectar of immortality," so said the lord of the thirty gods; therefore he who gives a milch-cow gives the nectar itself.
The knowers of the Veda know this to be the imperishable oblation-stuff of the fires; therefore he who gives a milch-cow bestows the very means of the offering.
This bull, the lord of the cows, is heaven in bodily form; whoever gives him to a brāhmaṇa endowed with virtues is himself exalted in heaven.
These are declared to be the very life-breaths of living beings, O bull of the Bhāratas; therefore he who gives a milch-cow gives life-breath itself.
"Cows are the refuge of creatures," thus the knowers of the Veda know; therefore he who gives a milch-cow bestows refuge itself.
A cow must not be given to be slaughtered, nor to a miser, nor to an unbeliever; nor should a cow be given to one who lives by trafficking in cattle, O bull among men.
The man who gives cows to such evildoers goes to the imperishable hell—so the wise have declared.
One should not give to a brāhmaṇa a cow that is emaciated, or one whose calf has come to harm, or one that is barren or diseased, or one that is maimed or worn out.
He who duly gives ten thousand cows rejoices together with Śakra; the man who gives a hundred thousand wins imperishable worlds.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus the gift of cattle, the gift of sesame, and the gift of land have been proclaimed; now hear concerning the gift of food, O Bhārata.
The gift of food they declare to be foremost, O son of Kuntī; for by the gift of food Rantideva went to heaven.
He who gives food to one weary and hungry, O lord of earth, beholds the greatly blessed son of the Self-Existent, O ruler of men.
Not by gifts of gold, nor of garments, nor by the gift of horses, O Bhārata, do men win such welfare as the givers of food win here, O lord.
Food is verily the supreme substance, and food is deemed the highest prosperity; from food springs life-breath, and likewise vigor, valor, and strength.
The man who gives food to the good, ever single-minded, does not fall into straits—thus declared Parāśara.
Having duly worshipped, one should present the food to the gods; for whatever food a man eats, O king, that same food belongs to his deities.
He who makes a gift of food on the full-moon day of Kārttika, in the bright fortnight, crosses over all straits and, after death, partakes of the infinite.
He who, with collected mind, gives food to a guest before he himself has eaten, would surely attain the worlds of those who know Brahman, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Though fallen into the direst calamity, the giver of food crosses over; he crosses beyond sin even here, and casts off his ill deeds.
Thus has the fruit of the gift of food, and of the gift of sesame, and of the gift of land, and of the gift of cattle been proclaimed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard the fruit of giving that you have proclaimed, dear father; but food, in your account, is here especially praised, O Bhārata.
And how is the gift of water supreme here, and of great fruit? This I wish to hear in full, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: Come, I shall recount it to you faithfully, O bull of the Bhāratas; hearken now as I tell it, O you whose valor is truth; beginning with the gift of water, I shall declare it all to you, O sinless one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
When a man, having given food and water, then enjoys their fruit—there is, in my judgment, no gift higher than this.
From food, dear son, all that bear life come forth in every way; therefore food is called supreme in the world among all gifts.
From food the strength and the vital fire of living beings ever increase; therefore Prajāpati has declared the gift of food to be the best.
For from Sāvitrī herself, O son of Kuntī, you have heard the auspicious word, whence this is and how this is, at the sacrificial session of the gods, O greatly wise one.
When food is given by a man in this world, life-breaths too are given thereby; and than the gift of life-breath no higher gift is known here.
For you have heard, O mighty-armed one, that word of Lomaśa as well—what Śibi of old attained when he gave up his own life for the sake of a dove.
That same goal one wins by giving food to a brāhmaṇa, O lord of peoples; the givers of life-breath go to a most exalted goal—so have we heard.
And food itself arises from water, O best of the Kurus; for without that which is born of water, nothing whatsoever comes to be.
Water-born too is the blessed Soma, lord of the host of planets, and the nectar of immortality, and ambrosia, and Svāhā, and Vaṣaṭ as well.
Grains and healing herbs, O great king, and the creeping plants are sprung from water—whence the life-breaths of all that bear life come into being, O lord of peoples.
The food of the gods is the nectar of immortality, and that of the nāgas is ambrosia; the food of the fathers is declared to be svadhā, and that of the beasts the creeping plants.
Food, the wise declare, is the very life-breath of human beings; and all of this, O tiger among men, arises from water.
Therefore nowhere is there a gift higher than the giving of water; and the man who would seek his own well-being should give it without ceasing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The giving of water brings fortune, fame, and length of days, O lord of peoples; and the giver of water, O son of Kuntī, stands ever superior even to his enemies.
He gains all his desires and undying renown in this world; after death he attains the endless realms and is set free from his sins.
The giver of water, O tiger among men, O greatly resplendent one, having gone to heaven, attains the imperishable worlds — so said Manu.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what kind is the gift of sesame seeds, and of lamps as well, and of food and of garments? Tell me of these once again.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue of a brāhmaṇa and Yama, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
In the Middle Country there was once a great village of brāhmaṇas, set between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, below the Yamunā mountain.
It was renowned as Parṇaśālā and was a place of delight, O ruler of men; and learned brāhmaṇas in great numbers dwelt there in those days.
Then Yama spoke to a certain man clad in black garments, red-eyed, with hair standing on end, with the shanks, eyes, and nose of a crow.
"Go you to the village of the brāhmaṇas, and going there bring back the one of the Agastya line by gotra, and Śarman by name.
He is settled in tranquillity, learned, a teacher, yet little honored; and do not bring back another of his same gotra dwelling beside him.
For that other one is of like qualities, equal to him in study and in birth, in offspring, and in conduct — wholly his match in wisdom. Bring back the one I have appointed, for I must do him honor."
He went and did the contrary to Yama's command: he seized and brought back the very one whom Yama had forbidden.
To him the mighty Yama rose up and did honor, then declared, "Let this man be taken back, and let that other be brought instead."
When the King of Righteousness had spoken thus, that twice-born one, weary of his studies, said to the Dharmarāja: "Whatever span of life remains to me, let me dwell it out here, O imperishable one."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yama said: "In no way can I overstep what Time has ordained; I only know who it is that practices righteousness.
Go, brāhmaṇa, this very day to your own home, O greatly resplendent one; or speak as you freely wish — what shall I do for you?"
The brāhmaṇa said: "Tell me that deed which, done back there, would bring the greatest merit; for you are the standard of all, even of the three worlds, O most excellent one."
Yama said: "Hear truly, O sage among brāhmaṇas, the supreme rule of giving. Sesame seeds are the highest gift, and their merit here is everlasting.
Sesame seeds should be given according to one's power, O bull among the twice-born; given without ceasing, sesame fulfills every desire.
They praise sesame at the rites for the ancestors, for this gift is unsurpassed; bestow it upon the brāhmaṇas with rites performed as the ordinance directs.
Sesame should be eaten always, and with it the touching of the body should be performed without fail by those who, with their whole heart, desire well-being in the home.
So too water should ever be given and offered to drink — of this there is no doubt; and here one should have lotus-pools, tanks, and wells dug out.
This is the rarest of all in the world, O best of the twice-born; water should ever be given by you, for this merit is unsurpassed.
And watering-sheds should ever be built by you for men to drink, O most excellent of the twice-born; and even after a meal you should especially offer water to drink."
When this had been spoken, he was then led home by that messenger of Yama, and he carried out in full all that command of Yama.
Having brought that man home, the messenger of Yama then took Śarman and went, and presented him to the King of Righteousness.
The majestic King of Righteousness honored that knower of dharma, and having made his compact with him, sent him back as he had come.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
To him too Yama gave the whole instruction; and returning, that man did all that Yama had told.
Likewise Yama praises lamps, desiring the welfare of the ancestors; therefore the giver of lamps forever carries the fathers across.
Lamps should be given always, O most excellent of the Bhāratas; for they are held to abide in the eyes of the gods and of the fathers, O lord.
The gift of gems too is declared a very great merit, O ruler of men; for selling them, the brāhmaṇa, the giver of safety, performs sacrifice.
Whatever a brāhmaṇa, having himself received, gives to other brāhmaṇas becomes imperishable for both — for the giver and for the receiver alike.
He who, abiding in right conduct, gives a gift to be received by such a man — this Manu, the knower of dharma, declared an imperishable merit for both.
By the gift of garments, a man devoted to his own wife becomes well-clothed and well-adorned — so have we heard in turn.
Cows, and gold, and sesame too have been extolled again and again, O tiger among men, on the strength of the Vedas' authority.
And one should make marriages and beget sons; for the gaining of a son, O descendant of Kuru, surpasses every other gain.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Once again, O best of the Kurus, recount the supreme rule of gifts, O greatly wise one, and the gift of land in particular.
A kṣatriya should give land, and a brāhmaṇa by his own proper office should duly receive it; but no other has the right to give it.
What may be given by all the varṇas who long for its fruit, or what is enjoined in the Veda — that you ought to expound to me.
Bhīṣma said: Three things to be given bear like names and like fruit, yielding here every desired reward — cows, the earth, and Sarasvatī (sacred speech).
And he who would impart to a pupil the righteous, sacred speech of Brahman enjoys a fruit equal to the giving of land and cows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Likewise they praise cows, and nothing is to be given higher than they; for their fruit is close at hand and easily had, O Yudhiṣṭhira. Cows are the mothers of all beings, the bestowers of every happiness.
He who longs for increase should ever keep cows and circle them to the right; these goddesses are the abode of auspiciousness, and therefore are ever to be revered.
For those engaged in the work of tending cows, a god-given impulse is at hand; only that first imperishable syllable, and nothing else, should ever be uttered over them.
Whether at pasture or at the watering-trough, the wise man should not vex the cows; for thirsting and gazing upon him, they might destroy a man together with his kin.
The dwellings of the fathers and the temples of the gods are forever purified by their dung — what is purer than that?
He who for a full year gives a handful of fodder to another's cow before he has taken his own food — that vow grants every desire.
For he gains sons, and glory, and prosperity besides; he destroys what is inauspicious and drives away evil dreams.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what marks are the cows that should be given, and which should one avoid? To what kind of man should they be given, and to what kind not?
Bhīṣma said: To a man of evil conduct, a sinner, a greedy man, a speaker of falsehood, one who has forsaken the offerings to gods and ancestors — to such a one a cow should never in any way be given.
But the giver who bestows ten cows upon a mendicant of many sons, a knower of the Veda who has kindled the sacred fire, attains the highest worlds.
And of whatever dharma that man performs, and whatever the meritorious fruit thereof, the giver shares a portion of it all; for through him these undertakings come to be.
He who begets a man, he who saves him from danger, and he who provides his livelihood — these three are all his fathers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Service to one's elders destroys defilement; honor wins great fame; three sons remove childlessness, and ten milch-cows remove want of livelihood.
To one steadfast in the end of the Veda, deeply learned, content in wisdom, his senses conquered, refined, self-restrained and disciplined, who speaks ever kindly to all beings —
who out of fear of hunger would do no forbidden deed, who is gentle, self-controlled, and ever hospitable — to such a brāhmaṇa, of like virtue and with his sons and wife, one should grant a livelihood.
As great as are the merits of giving a cow to a worthy recipient, so great is the sin in stealing a brāhmaṇa's property; in every circumstance the seizing of a brāhmaṇa's goods, and their wives as well, must be shunned from afar.
Bhīṣma said: On this very matter the good recount how, in laying hands upon a brāhmaṇa's property, the great distress was met by Nṛga, O foremost of the Kurus.
Long ago, as Dvāravatī was being settled, O Pārtha — so the tradition runs — a great well was found, overgrown with grass and creepers.
Men in want of water, laboring there with great effort upon that well whose water was well concealed,
saw a lizard of huge body lodged within; and they strove by the thousands to draw it out.
Binding it with ropes and straps of leather — that creature like a mountain — they could not haul it up; then they went to Janārdana.
"A great lizard sits blocking the mouth of the well, and there is no drawing it out" — so they reported to Kṛṣṇa.
Drawn up by Vāsudeva, and asked of his desires, the king Nṛga then made himself known, declaring of old that he had offered a thousand sacrifices.
To him speaking thus Mādhava said: "Pure was the deed you did, and not sinful; how then did you come to so wretched a state, O lord of men? Tell me — what is this thing of such a kind?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"A hundred thousand cows, a hundred again and again, eight hundred myriads — so we have heard that you of old gave to the twice-born, O king. Where then has that merit of yours gone?"
Then Nṛga said to Kṛṣṇa: "A single cow belonging to a brāhmaṇa, a keeper of the sacred fire who was away from home, had strayed into my herd of cattle.
Counted then by my herdsmen among a thousand cows, she was given by me to a brāhmaṇa, for I sought reward in the world beyond.
And the brāhmaṇa whose she had been, searching, spied her in another's house, and said, 'This cow is mine.'
The two of them came before me, disputing in great heat, and they said to me then: 'You are the giver — you are the thief!'
With an exchange of a hundred cows by the hundred I begged the one who had received her; but he said this to me:
'She is suited to time and place, a good milker, gentle, most loving, a giver of sweet milk, auspicious, and ever in my home.
And this cow nourishes my frail, unweaned son; her I cannot give up.' Having spoken thus, he went away.
Then I begged that other brāhmaṇa in exchange: 'Let a hundred thousand cows be taken in her stead.'
The brāhmaṇa said: 'I accept nothing from kings; I am able to seek out my own. Let that very cow be given back to me at once' — so he said, O slayer of Madhu.
Though I offered gold and horses, silver and chariots too, that bull among brāhmaṇas would take none of it, and then went his way.
At that very time, urged on by the law of Time, I reached the world of the fathers and came before the King of Righteousness.
Yama, having honored me, then spoke these words: 'No end can be reckoned, O king, to your meritorious deeds.
And yet a sin too has been committed — and that by you in ignorance. Undergo the penalty for that sin either afterward or before, as you please.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'I shall be protected'—so it was promised you, yet your pledge proved false; and you took what belonged to a brāhmaṇa: thus your transgression is threefold."
"'First I shall undergo the hardship, and the bliss thereafter'—O lord, even as I was saying this to the King of Dharma, I fell upon the surface of the earth."
"And as I was tumbling down I heard Yama proclaiming aloud: 'Vāsudeva, Janārdana, shall be your deliverer.'"
"'When a full thousand years are ended and your evil deed is exhausted, you shall attain the eternal worlds, won by your own action.'"
"I beheld myself fallen headlong into the well, sunk into the womb of a beast; yet memory did not forsake me."
"Today I have been ferried across by you—by what else than the power of austerity? Give me leave, O Kṛṣṇa, that I may go this very day to heaven."
Granted leave by Kṛṣṇa, having bowed to Janārdana, he mounted a celestial chariot and went to heaven, O subduer of foes.
Then, when Nṛga had reached heaven, O best of the Bhāratas, Vāsudeva uttered this verse, O joy of the Kurus:
"A discerning man must never seize a brāhmaṇa's property; a brāhmaṇa's property, once seized, destroys, as the brāhmaṇa's cow destroyed Nṛga."
"Communion with the good, O Pārtha, is never fruitless for the good: behold how Nṛga was released from hell through fellowship with the holy."
"In this matter giving bears fruit, and so too does wrongdoing bear its fruit; therefore, Yudhiṣṭhira, one should shun any offence against cows."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me, O sinless one, of the fruit that comes from cows that are given away; tell it at length, O mighty-armed—let it be told, for I am not yet sated.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, the words of both the seer Uddālaka and of Nāciketa.
The seer Uddālaka, having undertaken a consecration, said to his son Nāciketa, "Attend upon me"; and when that observance was completed, the great seer spoke to his son.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"While I was intent on my ablutions and absorbed in my recitation, I forgot the kindling, the darbha grass, the flowers, the water-pot, and the water all about. Fetch them and come here from the riverbank."
Going there, the young ascetic could not recover any of it, for it had been swept away by the river's current; and so he said to his father, "I do not see it."
Then the sage Uddālaka, overcome by hunger, thirst, and weariness—he of great austerity—cursed his son, saying, "Go behold Yama!"
Struck thus by his father with the thunderbolt of speech, with hands joined and saying only "Be gracious," the boy fell to the ground, his life gone out of him.
Seeing Nāciketa fallen, the father, swooning with grief and crying, "What have I done!", sank down upon the earth.
For him, encompassed by sorrow as he held his own son in his embrace, the remainder of that day passed, and a grim night came over him there.
By the falling of his father's tears, O foremost of the Kurus, Nāciketa stirred upon the bed of kuśa grass, like a crop revived when steeped in rain.
He questioned that worthy son returned to him once more, anointed with celestial fragrances, risen as if from a fading dream.
"Have you, my son, won the blessed worlds by your own deeds? By good fortune you are restored to me again—surely your form is no longer that of a mortal."
He who had beheld all with his own eyes, when questioned by his great-souled father, recounted it truthfully to that father in the midst of the great seers.
"Carrying out your command, I went swiftly forth, and reaching the vast and radiantly lustrous hall of Vaivasvata, I beheld it, its golden floor stretching for thousands of leagues."
"The moment he saw me hastening toward him, the son of Vivasvat showed me to his abode and assigned me a seat; and for your sake he honoured me with the welcome-offering and other tokens of reverence."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Then softly I said to him, surrounded by his assessors and receiving their homage: 'O King of Dharma, I have come into your realm; ordain for me those worlds which I deserve.'"
"Yama said to me: 'You are not dead, gentle one; yet your father the ascetic, in splendour like a blazing fire, bade you behold Yama—and that, O brāhmaṇa, cannot be made false.'"
"'You have beheld me—go back, my child; he who gave you your body is grieving. And I grant whatever your heart desires: choose your wishes, O welcome guest.'"
"Thus addressed by him, I answered him: 'I have reached your realm, hard to come back from; I wish to behold the abounding worlds of those who have done good, if I am worthy of a boon from you.'"
"Then that god, setting me upon a radiant, sun-bright chariot yoked with steeds, showed me at that time all the worlds of those who have done good, O foremost of brāhmaṇas."
"There I beheld the gleaming mansions of the disciplined souls, of manifold shapes and forms and wrought all of jewels."
"White as the disc of the moon, festooned with networks of little bells, of many hundred storeys, set amid waters and groves within."
"Shining like beryl and the sun, fashioned of silver and gold, of the hue of the young morning sun, some fixed and some that moved at will."
"Mountains made of food hard and soft, and garments and couches, and trees bearing the fruit of every desire, standing about the dwellings."
"Rivers, avenues, assembly-halls, ponds, and long pools on every side, and chiming chariots ready-yoked by the thousand."
"Rivers flowing with milk, and mountains, and clarified butter, and water utterly clear; many regions sanctioned by Vaivasvata, never seen before, did I behold."
"Having seen all this, I said to the King of Dharma, the ancient and almighty one: 'These rivers of milk and of clarified butter, ever-flowing—for whose enjoyment are they ordained?'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Yama said: 'Know that these are to be enjoyed by those good men who are givers of the products of the cow; and there are still other worlds, eternal and free from sorrow, thronged with those devoted to the gift of cows.'"
"'Yet the mere giving of them is not what is praised; the worthy recipient, the time, the particular cow, and the rite all matter. Knowing these, O brāhmaṇa, should one give—for the true worth of a cow is as hard to discern as the nature of fire and the sun.'"
"'A brāhmaṇa rich in sacred recitation, exceedingly austere, established in the sacrificial fires, is the worthy recipient of these. Cows released in time of hardship, or come for their nurture—by such avenues are particular cows esteemed.'"
"'Having fasted three nights on water and lying on the bare ground, contented cows should be given to those who have been satisfied—cows glad with their calves, rich in offspring, attended with all due rites; and having given them, for three days one should live upon the cow's own products.'"
"'Having given a milch-cow of gentle ways, milked into bronze, with a fair calf and not given to straying—for as many hairs as are upon her, for so many years does the giver enjoy the world of heaven.'"
"'So too, having given to a brāhmaṇa an ox—tamed, fit for the yoke, strong and young, sustaining its lineage, vigorous and great—one enjoys worlds equal to those of the giver of a milch-cow.'"
"'One forbearing toward cows, a refuge to cows, grateful, and worn down in his livelihood—such a man they call a worthy recipient; whether in failing livelihood, in some great emergency, for the sake of ploughing, for an oblation, or at a birth—'"
"'—or for a teacher's sake, or out of concern for the nourishment of children: no particular place or time is required for giving cows. Such cows may be born among one's own herd, gained by fair purchase, acquired by sacrifice or knowledge, bought at the price of one's own life, won in battle, or received as a libation of water.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nāciketa said: "Having heard the words of Vaivasvata, I asked him again: 'How does one who has no cow attain the worlds of the givers of cows?'"
"Then the wise Yama said: 'The gift of a cow leads to the highest goal; yet there are substitutes for the gift of a cow, and even without a cow there are those who count as cow-givers.'"
"'He who, lacking cows, gives a cow made of clarified butter, firm in his vow—for him these rivers of butter flow as tenderly as loving cows yielding their milk.'"
"'And he who, wanting butter, gives a cow made of sesame, firm in his vow, is borne across distress by that cow and rejoices in the river of milk.'"
"'And he who, wanting sesame, gives a cow made of water, firm in his vow, comes to enjoy this cool river that flows at his desire.'"
"Such things and more did the King of Dharma show me there; and beholding them I attained the highest joy, O Acyuta."
"And I announce to you a glad tiding: a great sacrifice, requiring but small wealth to perform, has come to me, dear father, sprung from me; conducted by the rule of the Veda, it shall come to fruition."
"For this curse of yours came to me as a grace, in which I beheld Yama; and having there seen the great reward of giving, I shall practise the duties of gift-giving beyond all doubt."
"And this the King of Dharma told me again and again, greatly pleased, O seer among brāhmaṇas: 'Be ever assiduous in giving, my child, and above all perform the gift of cows.'"
"'For wealth honestly come by must not be scorned: in accord with your own duty, it should be given to a worthy recipient at a fitting place and time. Therefore cows should ever be given by you; let no doubt of any kind arise in you here.'"
"'These men of old, of tranquil soul, set upon the path of giving, gave cows unceasingly; undertaking fierce austerities without misgiving, they too bestowed gifts to the full measure of their power.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'Giving in due time according to their power, casting envy aside—pure of soul, faithful, of virtuous conduct—having given and having done penance, they have attained yonder world, and these men of virtuous conduct shine resplendent in heaven.'"
"'This gift, won by lawful means and given to brāhmaṇas, should be conferred upon a worthy recipient after due scrutiny; and on the desired eighth day one should pass ten days living on the products of the cow—its milk, its dung, or its yield.'"
"'The giver of a bull keeps the vow of the Veda; the gift of a yoke of cattle yields the attainment of the Veda; the gift of a yoked team yields the attainment of holy fords; and the gift of a tawny cow yields the casting-off of sin.'"
"'By bestowing even a single tawny cow, lawfully come by, one is wholly freed from defilement. Than the milk of cows there is nothing higher; the gift of cows, they declare, is a very great thing.'"
"'Cows, yielding their milk, sustain the worlds; cows bring forth food in the world. The man who, knowing this, does not give his heart to cows—that man of evil mind shall surely go to hell.'"
"'Whether you have a thousand cows to give, or a hundred, or fifty, or ten with goodly calves, or even one to a worthy brāhmaṇa—she shall be for that man a river of holy fords in the world beyond.'"
"'In their bounty, their nourishment, and their guarding of the world, cows on earth are the equals of the sun's rays: the name is the same, the lineage is the same, and the enjoyment is the same; therefore the giver of cows shines forth like the sun.'"
"'In the gift of cows the disciple should choose a teacher; he, the reciter of the rite, is assuredly the bestower of heaven. Great among those who know the rites is this duty; for all rites have recourse to that first ordinance.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'This gift, won by lawful means, you should confer upon brāhmaṇas, giving it to a worthy recipient after due scrutiny. Upon you the immortals and men alike set their hopes, and we too, men of virtuous conduct, when the gift goes forth.'"
"Thus addressed by the King of Dharma, O great seer, bowing my head to that righteous one, and given leave by Vaivasvata, I came back to the feet of your reverence."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have spoken of the gift of cows in connection with the seer Nāciketa, and you have also told, by way of summary, the greatness of cows, O lord.
And how the great-souled Nṛga underwent suffering through a single offence committed in ignorance, O grandsire of mighty mind;
and how he was raised up at Dvāravatī while it was being settled, Kṛṣṇa becoming the cause of his deliverance—this too I have grasped.
But a doubt remains in me concerning the world of cows, O lord; I wish to hear truly into what region the givers of cows enter.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, how Śatakratu put this very question to the Lotus-born.
Śakra said: Outshining by their own radiance the splendour of those who dwell in heaven, I behold the dwellers of the cow-world faring on; herein lies my doubt.
Of what nature, O blessed one, are the worlds of cows? Tell me that, O sinless one—those that the givers inhabit; this I wish to know.
Of what kind are they, what fruit do they bear, and what is the supreme excellence there? And how do men come thither, freed from all affliction?
For how long does the giver enjoy the fruit of his gift? And how is a gift made manifold, or how even a small one?
What is the giving of many cows like, and what the giving of few? And by what means are there those reckoned cow-givers who have given none? Tell me that as well.
And how may the giver of many be the equal of the giver of few, O lord? And how may the giver of little rank as a giver of much, O master here?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And what kind of sacrificial fee is esteemed highest in the gift of cows? All this, O blessed one, you ought to declare to me in truth.
Brahmā said: This question that you have asked, bearing upon the worthiness for the gift of cows—there is in this world no questioner of it other than you, O Śatakratu.
There exist worlds of many kinds, O Śakra, which you do not behold — worlds that I behold, and likewise the women who are faithful to a single husband.
By their wholly auspicious deeds the seers of firm vows, and the Brāhmaṇas of pure conduct, attain those worlds in their very bodies.
And those of firm vows, by laying down the body in release and through a mind made spotless, behold even here those worlds that are like a dream.
And those worlds, O thousand-eyed one — hear with what qualities they are endowed. There time does not advance, nor old age, nor any evil; nor anything else inauspicious, no disease there, and no fatigue.
And whatever the cattle there desire in their minds, O Vāsava, all that they obtain by beholding me directly; going where they wish, roaming where they please, at will they enjoy their every wish.
Tanks, lakes, rivers, and forests of many kinds, dwellings and mountains too, and whatever substance there may be —
all that is pleasing to every being is seen there. Know those worlds to be of such a kind; there is no world higher than that.
To that place go, O Śakra, the best of men — all-enduring, patient, affectionate, devoted to their elders, and wholly free of egotism.
The man who never eats flesh of any kind, ever devoted until his end, who honors his mother and father, joined to truth, a server of the Brāhmaṇas, blameless —
free of anger toward cattle and toward the twice-born, delighting in dharma, a servant of his elders, devoted lifelong to the practice of truth, given to charity, and forgiving of offense —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
gentle, self-controlled, devoted to the gods, hospitable to all guests and full of compassion — a man endowed with such qualities proceeds to the world of cattle, eternal and imperishable.
No adulterer beholds this world, nor the slayer of a teacher, nor the babbler of falsehood, nor the forever-slandering Brāhmaṇa who has let his Vedic learning lapse, nor the evil-souled one yoked to other faults.
No betrayer of a friend, no deceiver, no ingrate, no rogue, no crooked man, no hater of dharma, no slayer of a Brāhmaṇa may even in his mind behold the world of cattle, the dwelling of those who have done meritorious deeds.
All this has been told you with precision, O lord of the gods; now hear the fruit that belongs to those devoted to the gift of cattle, O performer of a hundred rites.
He who, having bought cattle with wealth obtained as his rightful inheritance, gives them away, attains imperishable worlds purchased with righteously gained riches.
He who, having won wealth at dice, buys cattle and gives them away, enjoys, O Śakra, a divine reward lasting ten thousand years.
Cattle that are a man's inheritance, gained by lawful means and then bestowed, become for their givers imperishable and enduring.
And he who, having received cattle, gives them away with a wholly purified heart — know, O husband of Śacī, that for him too the worlds here are imperishable and enduring.
He who from birth speaks truth, his senses restrained, forbearing toward elders and the twice-born and patient — his attainment is equal to that won by the gift of cattle.
Never should a Brāhmaṇa be addressed with what ought not be spoken, O husband of Śacī; one should not even in mind do harm to cattle, but live by their ways and be compassionate to them.
For one devoted to truth and dharma — hear, O Śakra, his reward: his single cow becomes equal to a thousand.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Hear the reward of a Kṣatriya endowed with these same qualities: for him too one cow becomes equal to a hundred — such is the firm conclusion.
If these qualities belong to a Vaiśya, for him it becomes equal to fifty; and for a disciplined Śūdra too the reward is reckoned as a quarter of that.
And he who carries this out, ever devoted — joined to truth and to service of his elders, self-controlled, forbearing, a worshipper of the gods, serene, pure, awakened, of righteous disposition, free of self-assertion in speech —
that man attains a great reward by giving to a twice-born, according to this rule, a milch cow yielding milk. Let him give ever, taking but one meal a day, established in truth and a servant of his elders.
He who recites the Veda and is devoted to cattle, who ever rejoices at the sight of cows, and who bows to cattle from his very birth — mark, O Śakra, the reward that is his.
Whatever reward there is from performing the Rājasūya, whatever from sacrificing with abundant gold — equal and foremost to this, they declare his reward to be, all the holy ones and the seers and the perfected.
He who, without first tasting any morsel of his food, always offers the first portion to cattle — vowed to the cow, truth-speaking, serene, awakened — that man of meritorious character attains within a year the merit of a thousand cows.
He who eats but one meal a day and gives even one share to cattle — vowed to the cow and compassionate to it — gains ten endless years of merit.
And he who, taking but a single meal a day, buys a cow and gives it away — for as many days as are reckoned to him, O performer of a hundred rites, so many hundreds of cows' eternal reward does he obtain.
This is the reward of the Brāhmaṇa; now hear what is declared for the Kṣatriya. The Kṣatriya's reward is reckoned at five years' worth; the Vaiśya's at half of that, and the Śūdra's at half the Vaiśya's.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And he who, having even sold himself, buys cattle and gives them away, enjoys reward for as many cows as he can touch; for each hair upon them, O greatly blessed one, his worlds are reckoned imperishable.
But he who, having won cattle in battle, gives them away — know those gifts to be equal to selling oneself, and eternal, O Kauśika.
He who, when no cattle can be had, gives a cow made of sesame, his vows controlled, is carried by that cow across the hard passage and rejoices upon a river of milk.
Yet the mere giving of them is not praised; the worthy recipient, the time, the particular kind of cow, and the rite all matter. Knowledge of the right time, O Brāhmaṇa, and the differences among cattle are hard to know, being of the very nature of fire and the sun.
Rich in Vedic recitation, of pure birth, serene, settled in the sacrificial fires, fearful of sin, grateful, forbearing toward cattle, not over-harsh, a refuge for others, yet worn by want of livelihood — such a one they call a worthy recipient.
When a man is sorely worn by want and sinking utterly, whether for the sake of tillage, or for the oblation, at a birthing, for an elder's need, or for the raising of a child — let one give a cow at a fitting place and time.
Born within one's own herd, gained by a good purchase, bought at the cost of one's life, won in battle, born together as a single litter, released from peril, or come to one for their nurture — by these means the choicest cattle are approved.
Strong, of good temper and fit age, sweet-smelling — all such are praised; for as the Gaṅgā is the best among rivers, so the tawny cow is the best among the white.
Having fasted three nights upon water and lain upon the ground, well-satisfied cattle should be given to satisfied recipients — cows with well-fed, milk-drinking calves, good in pasture; and for three days after the gift one should live on their milk-products alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having given a cow of gentle disposition, with a fine calf, of auspicious habits and not given to straying, for as many hairs as are upon her, so many years does one dwell in the world beyond.
Likewise, having given to a Brāhmaṇa a draught-ox fit for the yoke — young, strong, well-broken, a bearer of the plough, of boundless vigor — one attains the worlds of a giver of ten milch cows.
He who in the wilderness rescues Brāhmaṇas and cattle, O Kauśika, and brings them safely free — hear the fruit of his merit: his reward becomes eternal and equal to that of the horse-sacrifice.
At the hour of death, O thousand-eyed one, whatever state of being he longs for, whatever manifold heavenly worlds, or whatever dwells within his heart —
all that the man attains by that deed, and, granted favor by the cattle, he is everywhere held in honor.
And he who by this very rite follows the cattle into the forests, eating grass, cow-dung, and leaves, free of craving, restrained and pure —
that man, desireless and glad, O performer of a hundred rites, must dwell in my world together with the gods, in whatever world he may also wish.
Indra said: He who knowingly carries off a cow, or sells it for the sake of gain — this I wish to understand: what indeed is his destiny?
Brahmā said: As for those who carry off a cow — whether to eat it, to sell it, or to give it to a Brāhmaṇa — hear in this matter what the fruit shall be.
He who, unbridled, would slay a cow to sell it or to eat it, and those self-seeking men who would consent to the one who has it killed —
the slayer, the eater, and likewise he who gives his consent — for as many hairs as are upon that cow, so many years does he sink in hell.
Whatever faults, and of whatever kind, attach to one who ruins a twice-born's sacrifice, those very faults are declared to attach to the selling and the carrying off of a cow, O lord.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But he who carries off a cow and then gives it to a Brāhmaṇa — for as long as the reward of that gift would last, so long does he descend into hell.
Gold, they say, is the sacrificial fee in the gift of a cow, O greatly resplendent one; gold is declared the supreme thing for the purpose of the fee, beyond all doubt.
The gift of a cow carries across seven ancestors and seven descendants; and when gold is given as the fee, the deliverance is said to be twofold.
Gold is the supreme gift, gold is the highest fee; gold is purifying, O Śakra, and is reckoned the foremost among purifiers.
Gold they declare to be the purifier of lineages, O performer of a hundred rites; thus has the matter of the fee been told by me in brief, O greatly resplendent one.
Bhīṣma said: This was spoken by the Grandsire to Indra, O bull of the Bhāratas; Indra told it to Daśaratha, and the father then told it to Rāma.
Rāghava in turn told it to his dear brother, the glorious Lakṣmaṇa; and by Lakṣmaṇa, dwelling in the forest, it was told to the seers, O lord.
And this, come down through the succession, the seers of strict vows held fast though it is hard to hold, and the righteous kings likewise; and this was told to me too by my teacher, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The Brāhmaṇa who would ever recite this in an assembly of Brāhmaṇas, at sacrifices, at the giving of cattle, and at the meeting of the two —
for him, they say, the worlds are imperishable forever, together with the gods — thus spoke the blessed Brahmā, the supreme lord.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have been given confidence by you as you declare the dharmas, O lord; yet I shall set forth a doubt — resolve it for me, O Grandsire.
What reward is declared for vows, and of what kind, O greatly resplendent one? What is the reward of restraints, and what the reward of diligent study?

title: Mahābhārata
text:
What here is the reward of self-restraint, and what in the retention of the Vedas? What is the reward in teaching them? All this I wish to know.
And what reward in the world is there for one who accepts no gifts, O Grandsire? And what reward, seen or heard of, for one who bestows them?
And what is the reward of those devoted to their own duty, and of the heroes as well? What reward is declared for truth, and what for chastity?
And what in the service of one's father, and likewise in the service of one's mother, in the service of preceptor and elder, in mercy and in compassion?
All this in full and exactly as it is, O Grandsire, I wish to know, O knower of dharma; for great is my curiosity.
Bhīṣma said: He who undertakes a vow exactly as it has been prescribed, unbroken and rightly begun — for him the worlds are everlasting.
The reward of the restraints, O king, is seen plainly here in this world; and this reward of the restraints and of the sacrifices has been won by you.
And the reward of diligent study too is seen both there and here; in this world he is ever possessed of substance, and in the world of Brahmā he rejoices.
But hear from me at length, O king, the reward of self-restraint: the self-restrained are happy everywhere, the self-restrained are everywhere at peace.
The self-restrained go wherever they wish and are slayers of all foes; and whatever the self-restrained seek, that they obtain — there is no doubt of it.
For the self-restrained are united with all desired things everywhere, O Pāṇḍava, and they rejoice in heaven through their austerity and their valor.
Just as the self-restrained, endowed with forbearance, prosper by gifts and by sacrifices of many kinds — yet the giver may grow angry, the self-restrained never does; therefore self-restraint is higher than giving.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But he who gives without growing angry — for him the worlds are everlasting; for anger destroys the gift, and therefore self-restraint is higher than giving.
There are unseen abodes by the tens of thousands in heaven, O great king — the abodes of the seers, to which the gods proceed throughout all the worlds.
To these, O lord of men, the supreme seers proceed through self-restraint, longing for that great abode; therefore self-restraint is higher than giving.
The teacher, through his toil, enjoys an imperishable reward, having duly offered oblation into the fire, in the world of Brahmā, O ruler of men.
And he who, having mastered the Vedas, imparts them to those versed in right reasoning, and who extols the duty owed to a teacher—he too is exalted in heaven.
The kṣatriya devoted to study, to sacrifice, and to the work of giving, who is a protector in battle—he too is exalted in heaven.
The vaiśya intent upon his own duty gains a great reward through giving; the śūdra intent upon his own duty attains heaven through dutiful service.
Heroes have been declared to be of many kinds; hear from me their meanings, and the reward set forth for those of heroic lineage and for the hero himself.
There are heroes in sacrifice, heroes in self-restraint, and others who are heroes in truth; men called heroes in battle, and likewise heroes in giving.
Others again are heroes in wisdom, and some heroes in forbearance; and there are men who are heroes in uprightness and who abide in tranquillity.
By this or that observance there are many other heroes besides: heroes in the study of the Vedas, and heroes devoted to teaching them.
Heroes in serving the teacher, others in serving the father, heroes in serving the mother, and others again heroes in the life of mendicancy.
Many are heroes in Sāṃkhya and others heroes in Yoga; heroes in the forest, in the household life, and in the honouring of guests—all of them attain the highest worlds, won by the fruit of their own works.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The retaining of all the Vedas, the bathing at every sacred ford—whether for him who ever speaks the truth these be equal or not equal.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were weighed in the balance: truth alone outweighs a thousand horse-sacrifices.
By truth the Sūrya gives heat, by truth Agni blazes, by truth the wind blows; all things are established upon truth.
By truth one gladdens the gods, the ancestors, and the brāhmaṇas alike. Truth, they say, is the supreme dharma; therefore one should never transgress the truth.
The sages are devoted to truth, the sages have truth for their valour, the sages have truth for their vow; therefore truth is supreme. The truthful rejoice in the world of heaven, O bull of the Bhāratas.
The attainment of the fruit of self-restraint and of truth has been told by me with all my heart. Beyond doubt, every man of disciplined self is exalted in heaven.
Now hear from me the virtues of chastity, O lord of the earth. He who in this world remains a celibate from birth until death—know, O lord of men, that for him there is nothing unattainable.
Many tens of millions of seers dwell in the world of Brahmā—those ever delighting in truth, the self-restrained, the keepers of upward-flowing seed.
Chastity, when cultivated, burns away all sins, O king—especially when cultivated by a brāhmaṇa; for the brāhmaṇa is called a very fire.
This too is plain to your own eyes among the brāhmaṇas and the ascetics: how Śakra trembles when assailed by a celibate. Such is the fruit of chastity seen here among the seers.
Hear from me too the duty that lies in honouring mother and father. He who serves his father and never in any way speaks ill of his mother, who utters no proud word against his elder or his teacher—
—know, O king, that his reward is the highest station in the world of heaven; the self-possessed man who serves his elders shall never behold hell.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I wish to hear truly the supreme ordinance concerning cows, by which we may attain in their entirety those everlasting worlds.
Bhīṣma said: There is nothing higher than the gift of a cow, O lord of the earth; for a cow righteously obtained and given away delivers one's whole line at once.
That which was rightly created for the good, fashioned aright and consecrated for the welfare of creatures—since the gift of cows has been in practice from the very first beginning, hear from me, O king, its ordinance.
Of old, when cows had been brought near, Bṛhaspati answered the question put to him by Māndhātṛ, who was in doubt as to what he should behold.
Having honoured the twice-born and having announced the time on the morrow, the man of steadfast vow should set apart a red cow for the purpose of the gift.
He should employ the call, 'O perfect-limbed one, O abundant one,' and entering into the midst of the cows he should recite this sacred utterance:
'The cow is my mother, the bull is my father; heaven is my shelter, the earth my support.' Taking refuge thus and passing the night among the cows, the silent one should let forth this speech at the giving of cows.
That man, for that one night a fellow and a vow-sharer of the cows, by reaching oneness with them is at once wholly freed from sin.
A cow whose bull and calf have been set free is to be given at the sight of the sun; and a threefold formula is to be observed—the explanatory praise, the benediction, and the hymns of laud.
'Rich in vigour and full of nourishing strength, they are the sacrifice, the womb of the nectar, and the support of the world; the source of prosperity upon the earth forever, born of Prajāpati'—such is the explanatory praise, comprising all.
'May these cows of the Sun drive away my sin, and may those of the Moon be for my journey to heaven; let those that are named grant me their shelter, and let all those unnamed be a blessing upon me.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'At the giving away of all that remains, at the releasing of the body through rites, you Sarasvatī-cows are ever set toward the highest good; ever to be carried forth by holy works, grant me, you that have come, the goal I desire.'
'What you are, that am I—today of one single being; in giving you away I give my very self. Released from the mind yet endowed with mind, kindle me, O you of gentle form and terrible form.'
Thus, before him, the giver of cows should first speak the former half according to ordinance, as seen of old; and the twice-born one who knows the rite, in receiving at the gift of cows, should answer with the remaining half.
'I give the cow'—so should it be said by him who bestows the welcome-offering, garments, and wealth; the udder is to be kept filled, and he should declare her sacred to Viṣṇu.
He should proclaim her name, and reward upon reward accrues in order of number—twenty-six, and eight, and twenty thousand.
Thus the giver of cows wins all these growing merits of cows and the rest, in due order, complete at the eighth stage.
The giver of cows becomes virtuous; the giver of the welcome-offering becomes fearless; the giver of wealth ceases to be sorrowful and gains his desires; and the learned man who has borne the filled udder, O Bhārata—for all these the worlds of Viṣṇu and of the Moon are declared.
Having given cows, one should keep the cow-vow for three nights, and dwell here for one night among them; on the eighth day, sought of desire, one should pass three nights subsisting on the cow's juices, or on its dung, or on its milk.
The giver of a bull becomes a keeper of the Veda-vow; in the gift of a yoke of oxen lies the attainment of the Veda. So the sacrificer who follows the ordinance of cows wins the foremost worlds—but not he who knows not the rite.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who gives away all earthly desires gathered into one, and a milch-cow that yields every wish—rightly do such cows abound in streams of offerings to gods and ancestors; and greater still is the bestowal of the bulls among them.
One should not impart this to a non-pupil, to one without vows, nor to the unbelieving, nor to the crooked of mind; for this is the secret dharma of all the world, and one should not babble this dharma here and there.
There are believing men in the world, and there are mean ones, very demons among men, to whom the giving of a gift is hateful; the unholy take refuge even in disbelief.
Hearing this counsel of Bṛhaspati, those kings who, having made gifts of cows, attained the worlds—holy in conduct and of good ways—hear of them, O king, as I recount them.
Uśīnara, Viṣvagaśva, and Nṛga; Bhagīratha, and the renowned son of Yuvanāśva; Māndhātṛ indeed, and King Mucukunda; Bhūridyumna, the lord of Niṣadha, and Somaka—
Purūravas, and Bharata the universal emperor, in whose line are all the Bhāratas; and the hero Rāma, son of Daśaratha; and whatever others renowned and glorious there were.
So too King Dilīpa of mighty deeds, knowing the ordinance of the gift of cows, attained heaven; and Māndhātṛ became great through sacrifices, gifts, austerity, the duties of kings, and through gifts of cows.
Therefore, O Pārtha, do you too hold fast to this teaching of Bṛhaspati that I have spoken; and gladly, having gained the kingdom of the Kurus, bestow holy cows upon the foremost of the twice-born.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: So the King of Righteousness did all this, as Bhīṣma had told him, duly in the gift of cows; that king rightly upheld the dharma of Māndhātṛ, which had been taught by the god of gods.
Thus, O king, ever intent upon the giving of cows, drinking barley-grains together with cow-dung, sleeping upon the bare ground, wearing the tuft, self-controlled—that bull among kings became then as a bull itself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That king was ever devoted to them, with mind made pure, glorifying the cows; and he yoked no cow again to the burden of royal service, but went here and there with his choicest steeds.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira the wise, O king, full of humility, asked the son of Śaṃtanu yet further about the gift of cows in its fullness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me once more, O Bhārata, the merits in the gift of cows, fully; for I am not sated, O hero, listening to such nectar as this.
Thus addressed by the King of Righteousness, the son of Śaṃtanu, O king, then duly recounted to him the unmixed merits of the gift of cows.
Bhīṣma said: Giving to a brāhmaṇa such a cow—affectionate, endowed with good qualities, young, and draped with cloth—a man is freed from all his sins.
There are worlds called 'sunless'; into them one goes who gives a cow whose water is drunk dry, whose grass is eaten up, whose milk has failed, and whose powers are spent—
—worn out with age, her usefulness already taken, decrepit like a waterless well; giving such a one, he enters darkness, for he would yoke the twice-born to mere trouble.
A cow that is vicious, ill-tempered, diseased, or feeble, and those for which the price has not been paid, are not to be given; he who yokes a brāhmaṇa to troubles that bear no fruit—his worlds too shall be without vigour and without fruit.
All praise cows that are strong, endowed with good temper and right age, and sweet of scent; for as the Gaṅgā is the best of rivers, so among the white cows the tawny one is the best.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When the gift of a many-coloured cow is the same, why is the gift of a tawny one extolled by the good? I wish to hear the distinction, O great-souled one; for you are able to declare it.
Bhīṣma said: What I have heard from the elders as they spoke, that, my son, of which you ask, I shall tell you in full—how the red cows were fashioned.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Commanded of old by the Self-existent, 'Create creatures,' Dakṣa first of all created their very sustenance, desiring the welfare of beings.
For as the dwellers in heaven subsist depending on the nectar, even so do creatures subsist depending upon their sustenance, O mighty one.
Than motionless beings the moving are better, and than these, men; and than these, the brāhmaṇas are best; in them the sacrifices are established.
By sacrifices the Soma is nourished, and that is established in the cows; all the gods rejoice, and thence creatures fare as of old.
Now these very beings cried aloud in longing for sustenance, and athirst they came after the giver of sustenance as toward a father and mother.
Pondering this in his mind, Prajāpati then, for the sake of his own creation of beings, drank the nectar that bestows strength.
Having come to the contentment thereof, belching forth a fragrant odour, he beheld Surabhī, the daughter born from his mouth, brought forth from his eructation.
And Surabhī brought forth the daughters of Surabhī, the mothers of the world—tawny cows of golden hue, the milch-cows that are the sustenance of creatures.
As those of nectar-hue flowed forth on every side, there arose from them a foam born of the nectar, even as the wave-born foam of streaming rivers.
That foam, fallen from the mouth of a calf, lighted upon the head of Bhava as he stood upon the earth; thereat the Lord, enraged, gazed upon the red cows with the eye sprung from his forehead, as though to burn them up.
That fierce splendour, O lord of peoples, brought the tawny cows to many-coloured hues, as the sun colours the clouds.
