But those that drew away from it and took refuge in the Soma, abiding in their own hue as they were born, were not brought to any other colour.
Then Prajāpati spoke to the angry Mahādeva: 'You have been besprinkled with nectar; there is no defilement among the cows.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For as the Soma, having taken up the nectar, flows forth again, so do these red cows, sprung from the nectar, pour forth their milk.
The wind is not defiled, nor fire, nor gold, nor the ocean; nectar drunk by nectar is no defilement, and the loving cow, drunk of by her calf, is not made impure.
These cows shall sustain the worlds with their oblation and their milk; partake of their sovereignty, auspicious and made wholly of nectar.'
And Prajāpati gave him a bull together with those cows, and by that he won over the mind of Rudra, O Bhārata.
And Mahādeva, well pleased, then made the bull both his banner and his mount; therefore is he the Bull-bannered one.
Then by the gods was Mahādeva made the Lord of Beasts, Paśupati; and he, the Sovereign, is called among the cattle Vṛṣāṅka, the one whose emblem is the bull.
Thus the first and foremost rite in the giving of tawny cows of unblemished hue and mighty splendour is proclaimed for all of them.
Eldest in the worlds, set in motion to sustain the life of the worlds, joined with Rudra, born of the overflowing of Soma, gentle, holy, granters of desires and givers of life — by bestowing such cows a man becomes a giver of every wish.
This supreme account of the origin of cattle, the man who recites it ever pure and devoted to the highest auspiciousness is freed from the taint of the Kali age, and obtains dear sons and wealth in cattle besides.
Oblations to the gods, offerings to the ancestors, the libation of refreshment, rites of peace, the means of conveyance, raiment, and the nourishing of the aged and the young — all these merits of the gift of cattle, O king, the giver attains forever.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of the grandsire, the king of Ajamīḍha's line together with his brothers — Pārtha — then gave cattle whose milk was drawn into vessels of gold and bronze to the most excellent of brāhmaṇas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In the same way he bestowed upon those twice-born thousands and hundreds of cattle, intending them as sacrificial gifts at the sacrifices, in order to conquer the worlds and the highest renown.
Bhīṣma said: At that very time, King Saudāsa, born of the line of Ikṣvāku, the best of givers, approached Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent of seers.
Having saluted his household priest — the perfected one who ranges through all the worlds, the eternal treasury of sacred knowledge — he began to put this question to him.
Saudāsa said: In the three worlds, O blessed and sinless one, what is declared to be purifying, by ever proclaiming which a mortal might obtain the highest merit?
Bhīṣma said: To him who bowed before him the learned sage then spoke a wholesome word — the secret doctrine of cattle — being pure and having made obeisance to the cattle.
Cattle are fragrant with sweet scent and breathe the perfume of guggulu; cattle are the support of all creatures, cattle are a great means of blessing.
Cattle are what has been and what shall be; cattle are nourishment eternal; cattle are the root of prosperity; what is given to cattle is never lost; cattle are ever food itself, and the highest oblation of the gods.
The utterances svāhā and vaṣaṭ are forever established in cattle; cattle are indeed the fruit of sacrifice, and in cattle the sacrifices are grounded.
At evening and at dawn, constantly at the hour of oblation, O great-minded one, the cattle yield what is to be offered to the seers, O bull among men.
Whatever hard straits there be, and whatever evil deeds have been done, those who bestow a milch-cow cross beyond them and beyond sin itself, O lord.
Let the owner of ten cows give one, the owner of a hundred give ten, and the owner of a thousand give a hundred — for all of these reap an equal fruit.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who keeps no sacred fire though he owns a hundred cows, he who offers no sacrifice though he owns a thousand, and the wealthy man who is yet a miser — these three deserve no offering of honour.
Those who bestow a tawny cow together with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, conquer both worlds.
A young and vigorous bull, lord of the herd, leading a hundred cows, a chief among cattle with broad horns and richly adorned, given to a foremost brāhmaṇa —
those who bestow such a bull upon a learned reciter of the Veda, O scorcher of foes, are born to lordship again and again with each rebirth.
Let one not lie down to sleep without praising the cattle, nor rise again without calling them to mind; let one make obeisance to the cattle at evening and at dawn, and thereby attain prosperity.
Let one never feel disgust at the urine and dung of cattle, nor eat their flesh; thus does one enjoy the abundance that flows from cattle.
Let one ever extol the cattle and never hold them in contempt; and upon beholding an ill-omened dream, let a man at once invoke the cow.
Let one ever bathe with cow-dung and rest upon dried cow-dung; and let one avoid casting phlegm, urine, and ordure where cattle are, and any act of injury to them.
Let one eat upon a fresh hide, gazing toward the western quarter, restrained in speech, with clarified butter upon the ground; thus does one enjoy the abundance that flows from cattle.
Let one offer oblation to the fire with clarified butter, pronounce the benediction with clarified butter, give clarified butter and partake of clarified butter; thus does one enjoy the abundance that flows from cattle.
He who, having consecrated with the Gomatī hymn a cow fashioned of sesame, rich in flavour and precious as a jewel, bestows it — that man shall not grieve over what he has done or left undone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
May the cattle, golden-horned and pouring forth milk, the fragrant ones and the offspring of Surabhī, attend upon me as the rivers attend upon the sea.
May the cattle ever look upon me, and I in turn look upon the cattle; the cattle are ours and we are theirs; where the cattle are, there are we.
Thus by night and by day, in smooth straits and in rough, and in great perils, the man who utters this prayer is delivered from fear.
Vasiṣṭha said: Austerity most arduous was practised for a hundred thousand years by the cattle created of old, with the thought, "May we attain to pre-eminence."
"In this world may we be the highest of all sacrificial gifts, and may we not be stained by any fault" — so they resolved, O scorcher of foes.
He whose mind harbours an injurious intent toward them is ever defiled thereby; and with their dung let gods and men perform their rites of purification.
"And so may all beings, whether unmoving or moving, and those who bestow us, attain to the worlds of cattle" — thus they wished, O bestower of honour.
To them Brahmā himself, the Lord, at the end of their austerity granted a boon: "So be it," said the mighty one, "and may you carry beings across the worlds."
They rose up, seeking perfection, the mothers of all that has been and shall be — the cattle, refuge of the worlds, at the close of their austerity, O great king.
Therefore the cattle are most blessed and are declared the supreme means of purification; and likewise the cattle stand upon the head of all beings.
Having given a tawny milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Brahmā.
Having given a red milch-cow with a calf of matching hue, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Sūrya.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having given a dappled milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Soma.
Having given a white milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Indra.
Having given a black milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Agni.
Having given a smoke-grey milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Yama.
Having given a cow the colour of water's foam, with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
Having given a cow the colour of wind-blown dust, with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of Vāyu.
Having given a golden-hued, tawny-eyed cow with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one attains the world of Kubera.
Having given a cow the smoky colour of straw, with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one is honoured in the world of the ancestors.
Having given a plump cow with her calf, white-throated and adorned, one attains the excellent and unconfined abode of the All-Gods.
Having given a fair-white milch-cow with a like-coloured calf, rich in milk, gentle of nature and draped with cloth, one attains the world of the Vasus.
Having given a cow the colour of a pale woollen blanket, with her calf, milked into a bronze vessel and draped with cloth, one attains the world of the Sādhyas.
Having given a bull with a broad, sapphire-dark back, adorned with every jewel, one attains the ageless worlds of the Maruts.
Having given a dark-bodied cow furnished with a calf and decked with every jewel, a man attains the worlds of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having given a white-throated ox adorned with every jewel, one attains the worlds of Prajāpati, free from sorrow.
The man devoted to the giving of cattle, cleaving through the gathered banks of clouds, journeys in a celestial chariot of the sun's hue, shining radiant in the sky, O king.
A thousand fair women of comely raiment and lovely hips delight that man, O best of men, who is devoted to the giving of cattle.
By the strains of vīṇās and lutes, by the tinkling of anklets, and by the laughter of doe-eyed maidens, he is awakened when he sleeps.
For as many hairs as there are upon the milch-cow, for so many years is he honoured in heaven; and even when he falls from heaven, he is then born again in the world of men in a family rich in cattle.
Vasiṣṭha said: The cattle that yield clarified butter and milk, that are the womb of butter and the source of butter, that are rivers of butter and whirlpools of butter — may they ever dwell in my house.
May butter be ever in my heart, may butter be established in my navel, may butter be in all my limbs, and may butter abide in my mind.
May the cattle be ever before me, may the cattle be behind me, may the cattle be on every side of me; in the midst of cattle do I dwell.
Having sipped water, let a man recite this ever at evening and at dawn; from whatever sin he commits by day, from that he is wholly freed.
Where there are golden palaces, where flows that Stream of Wealth, where dwell the Gandharvas and Apsarases — thither go those who give a thousand cows.
Where rivers flow with mire of fresh butter, with milk for their waters, thick with curds for moss — thither go those who give a thousand cows.
He who, according to the ordinance, bestows a hundred thousand cattle, having attained the highest prosperity, is honoured in the world of cattle.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
After death he upholds ten ancestors on either side, of his mother's and his father's line, in the worlds of the virtuous, and that man sanctifies his whole family.
He who gives a cow of sesame, equal in measure to a milch-cow, and likewise gives water to drink, comes to no torment whatever in the realm of Yama.
The foremost means of purification, the support of the world, the immeasurable mothers of the dwellers in heaven — let one touch them reverently, walk about them keeping them on the right, and give to a worthy recipient, having regarded the fitting time.
Having given a tawny milch-cow with her calf, with broad horns, milked into bronze and draped with an upper garment, a man passes free from fear through that hall of Yama which is otherwise so hard to traverse.
"The fair-formed, the many-formed, and the all-formed mothers — may the cattle attend upon me" — thus let one ever proclaim.
There is no gift more holy than this, no fruit more holy than this; nor can any being arise in the worlds more excellent than this.
With hide, with hair, with horns and tail, with milk and with fat, all together they sustain the sacrifice — what is there greater than they?
That milch-cow by whom all this world of moving and unmoving things is pervaded — her I revere with bowed head, the mother of what has been and what shall be.
This, O best of men, is but one portion of the gathered recital of the cattle's virtues, proclaimed by me to thee; for there is here no gift higher than cattle, nor any other refuge like to them.
Bhīṣma said: Reflecting that the seer's choice words were the highest truth, that great-souled king, his self subdued, then bestowed upon the twice-born very many herds of cattle, and won the worlds thereby.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That which is the purest of pure things, and which is supreme in the world, and the highest sanctifier of all — tell me of that, O grandsire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Cattle are of great worth and are holy, and they carry men across; and these creatures they sustain with their milk and with the oblation.
There is nothing more holy than cattle, O best of the Bhāratas; they are pure and holy, unsurpassed throughout the three worlds.
And above even the gods the cattle have their dwelling; and by bestowing them, O lord of men, the wise go forth to heaven.
Māndhātṛ son of Yuvanāśva, and Yayāti, and Nahuṣa — these, ever giving cattle measured by hundreds of thousands, attained the supreme abode that is hard to win even for the gods.
And on this matter I shall recount to you a tale of olden days, O sinless one.
The wise Śuka, having saluted Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, foremost among the sages, and having performed the daily rites, pure and earnest of mind, questioned his father, who had beheld the higher and lower worlds.
Which sacrifice is held to be the most excellent of all sacrifices? And by doing what do the wise attain the highest heaven?
By what purifying thing, O mighty one, do the gods enjoy heaven? And wherein lies the sacrificial essence of a sacrifice, and upon what is sacrifice established?
What is the highest of gifts, and what beyond that is the supreme rite of offering? And what is the purest of pure things — tell me that, O sinless one.
Hearing these words, Vyāsa, supreme knower of dharma, told his son all of it truly, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Vyāsa said: The cows are the foundation of all beings, and the cows are their refuge; the cows are holy and pure, the very means of purification and dharma itself.
In ancient times the cows were hornless, so we have heard; and to gain horns they worshipped the imperishable Lord.
Then Brahmā, beholding the cows seated in fasting devotion, the Lord granted to each of those cows, one by one, the boon they desired.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Horns arose upon them, for each according to her heart's wish; and bearing horns of varied hues, they shone resplendent, O dear son.
Blessed by Brahmā with boons, those auspicious cows became the givers of oblations to gods and ancestors — holy, pure, fortunate, marked with divine form and feature. The cows possess a great and divine splendour, and the gift of cows is extolled.
Those righteous men, free of envy, who bestow these cows are called doers of merit and givers of every gift; and they attain the holy world of the cows, O sinless one.
There the trees bear honeyed fruit and are laden with divine blossoms and fruit, and there are fragrant celestial flowers, O best of the twice-born.
The whole ground is wrought of gems, its sand fine gold; everywhere soft to the touch, free of mire, free of dust, and lovely.
There the pools shine, set about with groves of red lotuses and with golden, jewel-stemmed stalks, gleaming like the newly-risen sun.
And with lakes thick with many lotuses, their leaves of priceless gems, their filaments gleaming like gold, mingled with blue water-lilies.
They are adorned with blossoming oleander groves girdled by a thousand eddies, with flowering saṃtānaka groves, and with fair trees.
And there the rivers cast up sand-banks heaped with spotless pearls, with gems of great worth, and with pure gold.
They are studded with wondrous peaks of every jewel, with lofty mountains, and with others of pure gold radiant as fire.
There are golden mountains, masses of rock of gems and jewels, that shine with lovely upraised peaks made of every precious stone.
There the trees, ever in flower and fruit, throng with birds, bearing blossoms and fruits of divine fragrance and savour, O bull of the Bhāratas.
There the doers of holy deeds disport themselves forever, O Yudhiṣṭhira, every desire fulfilled, free of sorrow, their wrath departed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In gorgeous and delightful aerial cars, O Bhārata, the glorious doers of holy deeds rejoice, roaming at their pleasure.
And fair throngs of apsarases sport before them, O king. Such worlds does one attain by the gift of a cow, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
May those cows, of whom Pūṣan is lord, and the mighty, powerful Wind, and king Varuṇa over their abundance, the bearers of the yoke, protect me.
"The mothers, fair of form, of many forms, of every form, born of Prajāpati" — thus, O brāhmaṇa, let one of disciplined vows recite daily.
And to him who serves the cows and waits upon them in every way, they, well pleased, grant boons even hard to obtain.
Let one bear no malice toward cows even in thought, for they are the givers of happiness; let one ever revere them and honour them with salutations. Self-controlled and glad of heart, one thus enjoys the rich reward of the cows.
That purifier by which the gods enjoy the highest world, the purest of pure things — that clarified butter let one bear upon one's head.
With clarified butter let one offer to the fire, with clarified butter pronounce the blessing; let one taste it and bestow it — thus one enjoys the rich reward of the cows.
For three days let one drink the warm urine of cows, for three days drink their warm milk; having drunk the warm milk for three days, let one drink the warm clarified butter for three days; and having drunk the warm butter for three days, let one live for three days on air alone.
And living for a month on a handful of barley-gruel made from barley trodden out by cows, one is cleansed of every sin, even one equal to the slaying of a brāhmaṇa.
This rite of purification was performed by the gods for the undoing of the daityas; and thereby the mighty ones attained godhood and were made perfect.
The cows are pure and holy, the supreme and mighty means of purification; and by bestowing them upon the twice-born, a man attains heaven.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Made pure, in the midst of cows let one recite the Gomatī hymn in mind; having sipped purified water, he becomes pure and spotless.
In the midst of the fire, in the midst of cows, and in the assembly of brāhmaṇas — the brāhmaṇas, accomplished in knowledge, the Veda, and vows, doers of holy deeds —
should teach their pupils the Gomatī hymn, deemed equal to a sacrifice. Having fasted for three nights and heard the Gomatī, one obtains a boon.
He who longs for a son obtains a son, and wealth besides; she who longs for a husband obtains a husband; and a man obtains all his desires. The cows, when served, well pleased, bestow these things — there is no doubt.
Thus know these glorious ones, fit for sacrifice, granters of every desire, to be the Rohiṇīs; there is nothing higher than they.
Thus addressed by his great-souled father, Śuka of mighty splendour ever honoured the cows; therefore do you too honour them.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard that the dung of cows is graced by Śrī. This I wish to hear, for herein my doubt is great.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, O king — a colloquy between the cows and Śrī, O best of the Bhāratas.
Śrī, having assumed a lovely form, entered into the midst of the cows; and the cows, beholding the perfection of her beauty, were amazed.
The cows said: Who are you, O goddess, and whence have you come, peerless in beauty upon the earth? We are amazed, O glorious one, at the perfection of your beauty.
We wish to know you: who are you, and whither will you go? Tell us all this truly, O you of golden lustre.
Śrī said: I am the beloved of the worlds, blessings upon you; I am renowned here by the name of Śrī. The daityas, forsaken by me, have perished for everlasting years.
Indra, Vivasvat, Soma, and Viṣṇu, the waters and Agni too, the sages and the gods — all whom I attend upon prosper.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And those whom I hate, O cows, perish utterly; bereft of dharma, wealth, and pleasure, they become beset with misery.
Know me, O cows, to be of such power, the bestower of happiness; and I desire to dwell within you all forever. I have come beseeching: be graced with Śrī, O sinless ones.
The cows said: You are unsteady and fickle, shared in common with many; we do not desire you. Blessings upon you — go where it pleases you.
We are all comely of body; what need have we of you today? Go wherever you wish; we are well content without you.
Śrī said: Is this seemly of you, O cows, that you do not welcome me here? Why do you not now receive me, hard to win as I am?
And there is a true saying current in the world, O you of good vows, which holds for certain: "What comes of itself is held in contempt."
Having wrought great and fierce austerity, men attend upon me — gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, piśācas, serpents, and rākṣasas.
It is fitting for you, O cows: receive me here. For I am not to be slighted, O gentle ones, throughout the three worlds with all that moves and is still.
The cows said: We do not slight you, O goddess, nor do we hold you in contempt; you are unsteady and fickle of mind, and for that reason we shun you.
What need of many words here? Go where you will. We are all comely of body; what need have we of you, O sinless one?
Śrī said: I shall be despised in all the worlds, O bestowers of honour, if I am refused by you. Show me your grace.
Glorious are you and worthy refuges; deliver me, who have come for shelter, who devote myself to you forever and am blameless. I desire your regard always, O auspicious ones.
I wish to dwell even in some one part of you, however lowly. Yet there is nothing lowly to be seen in your limbs, O sinless ones.
Holy, pure, and fortunate ones, grant me your bidding; in which part I am to dwell, that you should declare to me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, those auspicious cows, tender with compassion, having taken counsel together, all spoke to Śrī, O lord of men.
You must surely be honoured by us, O glorious one; dwell within our dung and urine, for this is holy in us, O auspicious one.
Śrī said: Happily have you shown me grace, full of favour. So be it; blessings upon you. I am honoured, O bestowers of happiness.
Bhīṣma said: Having thus made her compact with the cows, O Bhārata, Śrī vanished then and there, even as they looked on.
Thus, my son, has the greatness of cow-dung been recounted to you; and now hear further of the greatness of the cows as I tell it.
Bhīṣma said: Those who bestow cows, and those who eat only what remains after the oblation, possess the merit of sacrificial rites and sacrifices perpetually, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Without curds and clarified butter no sacrifice can proceed; therein lies the sacrificial essence of a sacrifice, and herein its very root is seen.
Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of cows is extolled; the cows are most excellent and pure, and this is the supreme means of purification.
For prosperity let one serve them, and for peace as well — those whose milk, curds, and clarified butter release one from all sin.
The cows are declared the supreme splendour in this world and the next; there is nothing more purifying than cows, O bull among men.
On this too they recount an ancient tale — a colloquy between the Grandsire and Indra, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
When the daityas had been vanquished and Śakra was lord of the three worlds, all creatures throve, devoted to truth and dharma.
Then the sages with the gandharvas, the kiṃnaras, serpents, and rākṣasas, the gods, asuras, and suparṇas, and the lords of creatures — once upon a time, O Kauravya, they waited upon the Grandsire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nārada and Parvata, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū, singing in divine melodies, waited upon that Lord.
There the wind wafted celestial flowers, and the seasons too brought fragrant blossoms each in turn.
In that gathering of the gods, that assembly of all beings, resounding with celestial instruments and thronged with divine women and cāraṇas, Indra, having saluted and bowed to the Lord of gods, asked him:
O blessed Grandsire, wherefore is the world of cows set above that of the gods, the lords of the worlds? This I wish to know.
What austerity or chastity, O Lord, was performed by the cows here, that they dwell in joy, free of passion, above the gods?
Then Brahmā said to Śakra, the slayer of Bala: The cows have ever been slighted by you, O slayer of Bala.
Because of this you do not know the greatness of these cows; hear it, O lord. Learn the supreme power and majesty of cattle, O bull among the gods.
Cows are declared to be a limb of sacrifice, indeed the very sacrifice itself, O Vāsava; and without them no sacrifice could ever proceed at all.
They sustain living beings with their milk and with the oblation; and their offspring too apply themselves to the labor of the plow.
They bring forth grains and seeds of many kinds; from these the sacrifices proceed, and the offerings to the gods and to the ancestors in every form.
Milk, curds, and clarified butter—holy are these cows, O lord of the gods; and tormented by hunger and thirst they bear burdens of every kind.
By their toil they sustain the sages here and all living beings as well, O Vāsava; drawing their loads with guileless hearts, and by their meritorious deeds, they dwell forever above even us.
This, O Śakra, is the reason I have now told you why the abode of cattle lies above even the gods, O lord of a hundred sacrifices.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For these cows are both granted by boon and themselves bestowers of boons, O Vāsava—daughters of Surabhī, doers of holy deeds, purifying, and marked with auspicious signs.
And for what reason the daughters of Surabhī attained the rank of cattle, O best of the gods—hear that too in full as I tell it, O slayer of Bala.
Of old, in the age of the gods, dear one, when the great-souled lords of the Daityas were ruling the three worlds, Viṣṇu entered the womb.
While Aditi was practicing fearsome and most difficult austerity, standing ever upon a single foot for the sake of a son, O best of the immortals—
and seeing that great goddess engaged in mighty austerity, the goddess who was Dakṣa's daughter, Surabhī by name,
in gladness, devoted to dharma, performed a fearsome austerity upon the lovely peak of Kailāsa, frequented by gods and Gandharvas.
Established in supreme yoga, she stood upon a single foot for ten thousand years and ten hundred years besides.
Scorched by the heat of her austerity, the gods together with the sages and the great serpents went there with me and waited upon that auspicious one.
Then I spoke there to that goddess girt with austerity: 'For what purpose, O goddess, do you practice this fearsome austerity, O blameless one?'
'I am pleased with you, O fortunate one, by this austerity, O lovely one; choose a boon, O goddess, for I am ready to grant it'—so said Brahmā, O Purandara.
Surabhī said: By a boon, O blessed one, my purpose is fulfilled, O grandsire of the worlds; this very thing is my boon today—that you are pleased with me, O sinless one.
Brahmā said: To the goddess Surabhī, who spoke thus, O lord of the thirty gods, I made reply—learn now what I said, O king of the gods, O consort of Śacī.
'By your freedom from greed and desire, O goddess, and by your holy austerity, I am well pleased; therefore I grant you the boon of immortality.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Above even the three worlds shall you dwell, and by my favor that place shall become renowned as the World of Cattle, Goloka.'
'And your sons, doing their work among men, and all your daughters too shall dwell there, O fortunate one.'
'Whatever enjoyments, divine and human, you conceive in your mind, and whatever happiness of heaven there is, O goddess—all that shall be yours, O auspicious one.'
Her worlds, O thousand-eyed one, are furnished with every desire; there death does not advance, nor old age, nor fire; no misery and nothing inauspicious is found there, O Vāsava.
There are divine forests there, and divine dwellings, and well-appointed celestial chariots that go where one wishes, O Vāsava.
By holy vows of many kinds, by frequenting sacred fords, by great austerity, and by good works, Goloka can be attained, O lotus-eyed one.
All this I have declared to you, O Śakra, who asked of it; you must show no contempt for cattle, O slayer of foes.
Bhīṣma said: Having heard this, the thousand-eyed one ever honored cattle and always held them in high esteem, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
All this I have told you, purifying and of great splendor; the supremely holy and highest greatness of cattle has been proclaimed, O tiger among men—a thing that destroys all sins.
Whoever, with collected mind, recounts this always to the brāhmaṇas—at the offerings to gods and ancestors, at sacrifices, and at the rites for the fathers—an imperishable reward fulfilling every desire awaits his ancestors.
The man devoted to cattle obtains whatever he desires; and women too who are devoted to cattle attain their wishes.
He who longs for a son obtains a son; the maiden gains a husband; he who seeks wealth gains riches; he who seeks dharma attains dharma.
He who seeks knowledge attains knowledge; he who seeks happiness attains happiness; for him who is devoted to cattle nothing is hard to win, O descendant of Bharata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The grandsire has declared this—that the gift of cattle is unsurpassed, and especially so for kings who keep their gaze upon dharma.
For kingship is unceasing sorrow, and the orders of life are very hard to know; with a great retinue comes grief, hard to bear for those whose souls are unperfected; and most often no auspicious destiny is found for kings.
They are surely purified herein who bestow the gift of land; and the duties you have already related to me before, O joy of the Kurus.
Just so the gift of cattle was extolled by you, as it was shown of old by King Nṛga and by the sage Nāciketa.
And in the Vedas and the Upaniṣads, in all rites the sacrificial fee is enjoined, and in all sacrifices: land, cattle, and gold.
Therein the supreme scriptural teaching is that gold is the fitting fee; this I wish to hear, O grandsire, exactly as it is.
What is gold, how did it come to be, in what age, and of what nature? What is its gift, what is its fruit, and why is it called the highest?
Why do the wise honor the gift of gold, and why is it commended as the fee in the rites of sacrifice?
And why is gold the most purifying—above land and above cattle—and supreme as a sacrificial fee? Tell me this, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Listen attentively, O king, to the full account of its many causes—the origin of gold and what I myself have experienced.
My father, the greatly resplendent Śaṃtanu, had passed away; wishing to perform his śrāddha rite, I came to the Gate of Gaṅgā.
Having arrived there, my son, I began the śrāddha rite for my father, and my mother Jāhnavī then lent me her aid.
Then, having seated before me many sages perfected in austerity, I began the rites, beginning with the offering of water.
Having completed that preliminary rite as prescribed, with collected mind I set about offering the funeral oblation rightly, in due order.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, breaking through that arrangement of darbha grass, an arm rose up, adorned with a lovely armlet and with pendent ornaments, O lord of peoples.
Seeing it risen up, I fell into utter astonishment, thinking, 'It is my father in person, come to receive the offering,' O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then my reason returned to me, and reflecting upon the scriptures I thought: 'This rule is not enjoined in the Vedas—that the offering be placed into a hand'; and this conviction arose in me, O lord.
'A man's fathers, being hidden from sight, do not anywhere receive it directly; it is thus enjoined that the rice-ball be offered upon the kuśa grass.'
Then, disregarding the appearance of my father's hand, mindful of the subtle rule on the authority of scripture, O king—
I offered all of it upon the darbha grass, O bull of the Bhāratas, following the path of scripture; know this, O bull among men.
Thereupon that arm of my father vanished, O ruler of men; and then the fathers showed themselves to me at the close of a dream.
And being well pleased they said to me: 'We are pleased, O bull of the Bhāratas, by this discernment of yours, in that you are not led astray from dharma.'
'For by making scripture your authority herein, O king, you have honored—as the great sages do—the self, dharma, sacred learning, the Vedas, and the fathers.'
'The grandsire Brahmā himself, the teachers, and Prajāpati have been upheld as authority, and the established order has not been shaken.'
'This rite has been rightly begun by you today, O bull of the Bhāratas; but for the sake of land and cattle, let gold be given.'
'Thus shall we, and dharma, and all our forefathers be purified; for that is the highest purification.'
'Those who bestow gold carry across ten ancestors before them and ten descendants after'—thus did my fathers speak to me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, awakened in astonishment, O king, O lord of peoples, I set my mind upon the gift of gold, O best of the Bhāratas.
Hear too this ancient tale, O king, concerning the son of Jamadagni, O mighty one—a tale that bestows fortune and long life.
By Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, filled with fierce wrath, the earth was made bereft of warriors thrice seven times of old.
Then, having conquered the whole earth, the lotus-eyed hero Rāma performed a sacrifice honored by brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas alike.
A horse-sacrifice, O great king, furnished with every desired thing, purifying to all beings and enhancing splendor and luster.
Though already free of sin, that resplendent son of Jamadagni did not, even by the fruit of that sacrifice, reach lightness in his own esteem.
Having worshipped with that most excellent, fee-laden sacrifice, the great-souled scion of Bhṛgu questioned the sages and the gods, who were learned in scripture.
'Let it be told, O greatly fortunate ones, what is the supreme purification for men engaged in dread and violent deeds'—so spoke he in whom compassion had arisen.
Vasiṣṭha said: They who give gold bestow the very gods; for Agni is all the gods, and gold is of that same essence.
Therefore by him who gives gold all the gods are given, O tiger among men; for they know of nothing higher than this.
And learn yet further the greatness of gold as I tell it, O sage among brāhmaṇas, O best of all who bear weapons.
This I heard of old in the ancient lore, O joy of the Bhṛgus, as the Prajāpati Manu, the self-existent, related it.
It concerns the trident-bearing lord, the great-souled Rudra, upon the most excellent mountain Himavat, O upholder of the Bhṛgu line.
When the wedding of the goddess Rudrāṇī had been accomplished, O joy of the Bhṛgus, and the great-souled lord came together with the goddess, then all the gods, deeply agitated, approached the lord.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having propitiated with bowed heads the seated Mahādeva and the boon-granting goddess Umā, they all spoke to Rudra, O upholder of the Bhṛgus.
'This union of yours with the goddess, O sinless god—of you, an ascetic, with her, an ascetic; of you, supremely fiery, with her, the fiery one—O god, your fire is unfailing, and so too is this goddess Umā.'
'The offspring of you two, O god, will be mighty, O lord; surely it will leave nothing remaining in the three worlds.'
'Therefore to these gods who bow before you, O broad-eyed one, grant a boon, O lord of the worlds, out of desire for the welfare of the three worlds: for the sake of progeny, restrain your blazing, supreme seed.'
As they spoke thus, the blessed lord whose banner bears the bull replied to those gods, O sage among brāhmaṇas: 'So be it.'
Having said this, the bull-borne lord drew his seed upward; and from that time forth he became one whose seed flows upward.
Then Rudrāṇī, enraged that the begetting of offspring had thus been cut off, spoke to the gods, in her womanly nature, harsh words.
"Because my husband, who longed for offspring, has been turned from his purpose, therefore all of you gods shall be without progeny.
Since the cutting off of my offspring has been wrought by you this day, therefore, O sky-rangers, none of you shall have progeny."
But Pāvaka was not present there at the time of the curse, O scion of Bhṛgu; and so, by the goddess's curse, the gods became without offspring.
Rudra, meanwhile, held back that incomparable seed; yet something of it spilled forth from him and fell there upon the earth.
That fell then into the fire and grew, a thing of wondrous likeness; radiance mingled with radiance, and so came to share a single source.
At this very time the gods, with Śakra at their head, were grievously tormented by an asura named Tāraka.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Maruts, and the two Aśvins, and all the Sādhyas, were terrified by the prowess of that descendant of Diti.
For the abodes of the gods, their celestial chariots and cities, and the hermitages of the sages too were seized by the asuras.
All of them, downcast in heart—the gods and the sages alike—went for refuge to the god Brahmā, the undecaying lord.
The gods said: "An asura named Tāraka, to whom you granted a boon, O Lord, afflicts the gods and the sages; let his slaying be ordained.
From him terror has arisen for us, O Grandsire; save us, O god, for we have no other refuge."
Brahmā said: "I am equal toward all beings, and I take no pleasure in unrighteousness; let Tāraka, the oppressor of the hosts of gods and sages, be slain swiftly.
The Vedas and the laws of dharma must not go to ruin, O best of gods; this matter has already been provided for by me—let your fever pass away.
The gods said: "By the granting of your boon, O blessed one, the son of Diti is proud of his strength; he cannot be slain by the gods—how then shall he be brought to an end?
For he obtained from you, O Grandsire, the boon: 'May I be slayable neither by the gods, nor by the asuras, nor by the rākṣasas.'
And the gods were cursed by Rudrāṇī, when the cutting off of her offspring was wrought of old: 'You shall have no progeny,' O lord of all the worlds."
Brahmā said: "Hutāśana was not present there at the time of the curse, O best of gods; he shall beget offspring for the slaying of the foes of the Thirty.
That offspring, surpassing all—gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas, men and gandharvas, nāgas and birds—
with a weapon of unfailing aim, with his spear, shall slay him from whom your terror has arisen, and whatever other foes of the gods there be.
For the eternal Resolve is named Kāma; and the seed of Rudra spilled forth and fell into the fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That radiance, become a mighty being, like a second Fire, Agni shall bring to birth in the Gaṅgā for the slaying of the foes of the gods.
He, the eater of oblations, did not incur that curse, for he had vanished at the time; therefore, O gods, the son of Pāvaka shall arise as the remover of your fear.
Let the Burning One be sought out, then, and appointed this day to the task; the means of Tāraka's slaying has been told you by me, O sinless ones.
For curses do not prevail over the radiance of the radiant; lesser powers, when they meet a greater power, become powerless indeed.
Kāma, who is delight in resolve, the most ancient Fire, could slay even the unslayable, the granters of boons, and the ascetics.
He is the lord of the world, indefinable, all-pervading, the source of all being, the one who dwells in the hearts of all creatures, the eldest, a lord mightier even than Rudra.
Let him be sought out swiftly, Hutāśana, that mass of radiance; that god shall fulfill the desire that lies in your hearts."
Having heard this speech of the great-souled one, the gods then went forth, their resolve made firm, searching for Vibhāvasu.
Then the sages, together with the gods, searched through the three worlds, longing for the sight of Vahni, all with their minds fixed upon him.
Endowed with the highest austerity, glorious, renowned throughout the worlds, the perfected ones all ranged across the worlds, O scion of Bhṛgu; yet they did not find Hutāśana, who had vanished, withdrawn into himself.
Then to those who were stricken with terror and yearning for the sight of Agni, a frog, a water-dweller, weary in spirit and scorched by the radiance of Agni, rose up from the depths of the nether region and spoke to the gods:
"In the depths of the nether region, O gods, dwells Agni, O lord; I have come here driven by the burning that springs from Pāvaka.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He, the blessed Havyavāhana, lies asleep in the water, O gods; mingling the waters with his radiance, he has scorched us by it.
If the sight of him, of Vibhāvasu, is your wish, O gods, go to him there, if you have business with Vahni.
Let it be gone to; as for us, we shall make our escape from the fear of Agni, O gods." Having said only this, the frog hastily entered the water.
But Hutāśana perceived the frog's treachery, and, coming upon him, cursed him: "You shall know no flavors."
Having bound the frog with that curse, the all-pervading Pāvaka went elsewhere to dwell, and did not show himself to the gods.
But the gods bestowed a favor upon the frogs, O scion of Bhṛgu; hear it all from me as I tell it, O mighty-armed one.
The gods said: "Though tongueless and cut off from the knowledge of flavors by Agni's curse, you shall utter speech of many kinds.
Even when you dwell in holes, foodless and senseless, even when lifeless and dried up, the earth shall sustain you; and you shall roam abroad even in the darkness-shrouded night."
Having spoken thus to them, the gods then ranged once more over this earth for the sake of the Burning One, yet they did not find Hutāśana.
Then a certain elephant, like unto the elephant of the king of the gods, said this to them, O scion of Bhṛgu: "Agni dwells within the aśvattha tree."
The Burning One, overcome with wrath, cursed all the elephants: "Your tongue shall be turned backward," O scion of Bhṛgu.
Having said this, Agni, betrayed by the elephant, came forth from the aśvattha; then Vahni entered the womb of the śamī tree, desiring to sleep.
Hear now the favor that the gods, whose valor is truth, bestowed, well pleased, upon the elephants, O lord, O best of Bhṛgu's line.
The gods said: "Even with your backward-turned tongue you shall take all your food, and you shall utter a voice aloud, with unarticulated sound." Having said this, the dwellers of heaven once more went in pursuit of Agni.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Agni, having come forth from the aśvattha, had then entered the womb of the śamī; betrayed by a parrot, O brāhmaṇa, the gods rushed upon him.
But Agni cursed the parrot: "You shall be bereft of speech"; and the eater of oblations then turned that one's tongue backward too.
But the gods, seeing the Burning One, spoke to the parrot, filled with compassion: "You shall not, O bird, be wholly deprived of speech.
Though your tongue is turned backward, your speech shall be lovely—soft, indistinct, and wondrous, like that of a grown person who yet speaks as a child."
Having said this, and beholding Vahni within the womb of the śamī, the gods made that very tree his holy abode for all sacred rites.
From that time forth Agni is found within the wombs of the śamī, and men too followed this means for the kindling of fire.
Those waters in the nether region that were mingled with Citrabhānu, O Bhārgava, release their heat through the springs of the mountains, scorched as they were by the radiance of Pāvaka, who lay couched within them.
Then Agni, seeing the gods, became troubled, and Pāvaka asked them thus: "What is the purpose of your coming?"
All the wise ones and those supreme sages said to him: "We would appoint you to a task; you ought to perform it; and when it is done, a great benefit shall accrue to you as well."
Agni said: "Tell me what your task is; I shall do it all, O gods; for I am yours to command—let there be no hesitation in you over this."
The gods said: "An asura named Tāraka, made proud by Brahmā's boon, oppresses us by his might; let his slaying be ordained.
Save these hosts of gods, dear one, and the hosts of the Prajāpatis, and the greatly blessed sages too, O Pāvaka.
Beget an offspring endowed with radiance, a great hero, O lord, who shall destroy the fear we have from that asura, O Havyavāhana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For us, cursed by the great Goddess, there is no other refuge than your valor; therefore deliver us from this peril."
Thus addressed, the blessed bearer of oblations to gods and ancestors said "So be it," and that one hard to assail went then toward the Gaṅgā, the daughter of Bhagīratha.
He mingled with her, and an embryo formed within her then; and that embryo grew, as the fire whose path is black grows in dry brushwood.
By the radiance of that embryo Gaṅgā, her senses overwhelmed, came to a fierce burning, and she could not endure it.
When the embryo, charged with radiance, had been placed by the Burning One in Gaṅgā, a certain asura let loose a terrible roar.
At that vast roar, fallen upon her unawares, Gaṅgā—her eyes wide with terror and rolling, her gaze swimming, her senses gone—was unable to hold the embryo within herself.
Then Jāhnavī, her limbs encompassed by radiance and trembling, overborne by the embryo, spoke these words, O brāhmaṇa: "I am not able, O blessed one, to bear up this radiance of yours.
I am bewildered, and by it I have been made most ill at ease; I am overwhelmed, O blessed one, and my own radiance is lost, O sinless one.
I am not able to hold this embryo, O best of those that burn; I shall release it out of distress, and in no wise out of any wish to do so.
There is no touch of inclination in my heart, O god Vibhāvasu; for a bond formed in time of distress, even the subtlest, is no true bond, O greatly resplendent one.
Whatever here is endowed with merit, or otherwise, O Hutāśana, I deem that to rest in you alone, and the merit and demerit of it to be wholly yours."
Then Vahni said to her: "Let it be borne, let this embryo be borne, charged with my radiance, the source of great and meritorious fruit.
For you are able to bear and to sustain the whole earth; there is nothing beyond your power, save the holding of my seed."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Though held back by Vahni and by the gods, that best of rivers then cast off the embryo upon Meru, the noblest of mountains.
Though capable of bearing it, overborne by the radiance of Rudra, she was then unable to sustain that embryo by her strength.
Having cast off in distress that embryo, bright as the blazing Vaiśvānara, Agni then showed himself to Gaṅgā, O scion of Bhṛgu, and asked that best of rivers: "Is the embryo a happy birth?
Of what hue, O goddess, and of what form does it appear? And with what radiance is it endowed? Tell me all of this."
Gaṅgā said: "That embryo is of golden form, in radiance like to yourself, O Anala—of fair gold, spotless, blazing; and it lit up the mountain.
It is cool as pools intermingled with lotuses and blue water-lilies; and its fragrance is equal to that of the kadamba blossoms, O best of those that burn.
By the radiance of that embryo, as by the rays of the sun-maker, whatever substance was touched, upon the earth or in the mountains, all of that was seen on every side to have turned to gold.
He coursed over the mountains, the rivers, and the springs, and with his radiance he set ablaze the three worlds, all that moves and all that is still.
Of such a form, O bearer of oblations, is that lordly son of yours, equal to the sun and to Vaiśvānara, and in his loveliness like a second moon. Having spoken thus, the goddess vanished then and there.
And the radiant Pāvaka too, having accomplished the purpose of the dwellers in heaven, then went to the region he desired, O delight of Bhṛgu's line.
For these qualities of his deeds, the name of Agni is sung throughout the world as Hiraṇyaretas, 'he whose seed is gold,' by the seers and by the wise; and the goddess Earth from that time was renowned as Vasumatī, 'she who holds the treasure.'
But that embryo of mighty splendor, son of Gaṅgā and offspring of Pāvaka, having reached the celestial thicket of reeds, grew up, a wonder to behold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Kṛttikās beheld him, his luster like the newly risen sun, and conceiving tenderness for that child, they nourished him with the flowing of their breasts.
Thereupon that one of supreme radiance attained the name Kārttikeya; from his having been let fall he gained the name Skanda, and from his dwelling in a hidden place he became Guha.
Thus did gold come to be, the offspring of Jātavedas; and of it the Jāmbūnada gold is the finest, an ornament even of the gods.
And from that time onward this gold has been called jātarūpa, 'born of his form'; for the gold itself is the lord Agni, the master, the Lord of Creatures.
For gold is the purest of all pure things, O best of the twice-born; and jātarūpa is declared to have the very nature of Agni and Soma.
It is the most excellent of jewels, the most excellent of ornaments, the purest of pure things, and the most auspicious of all that is auspicious.
Vasiṣṭha said: Moreover, O Rāma, of old I heard this revelation of Brahman, what befell concerning the Grandsire Brahmā, the Supreme Self.
My son, of the great god who bore the form of Varuṇa, in the sovereign domain of Varuṇa, O Rāma, in the lordship of Rudra the Ruler, O mighty one—
there came all the sages, and the gods with Agni at their head, and all the members of the sacrifice, and the Vaṣaṭ-call itself embodied.
And the Sāman chants embodied, and the Yajus verses by the thousand, and the Ṛgveda came there, adorned with its word-order and its sequence of recitation.
The marks of grammar, the accents, the chant-syllables, the etymology, and the divisions of tone, and the syllable Oṃ dwelt there, and likewise restraint and free recitation as his two eyes.
The Vedas with their Upaniṣads, the sacred lore, and the Sāvitrī as well—the past, the present, and the future the lord Śiva upheld, himself then offering the self into the self, O mighty one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the wives of the gods, and the maidens, and the mothers of the gods came there together at that time, O upholder of the line of Bhṛgu.
Delighted, they came to the sacrifice of the great-souled Paśupati, of Varuṇa; but when the Self-existent beheld them, his seed fell upon the earth.
From the spilling of that seed Pūṣan gathered up the dust from the ground and cast it with both his hands into that very oblation-eating fire.
Then, when that long sacrificial session was under way with its fire ablaze, as Brahmā was offering oblation, a manifestation came forth there.
And taking up with the offering-ladle that seed the moment it was shed, he offered it as one offers clarified butter, and with sacred formulas, O delight of Bhṛgu.
Thereupon that mighty one brought forth the host of beings; and from that fiery essence there was born in the worlds all that is fiery in nature.
From darkness come the states marked by darkness; goodness too is pervasive, and both alike; the fiery essence is forever endowed with quality, and within darkness lies the ether.
And so in all beings there is goodness, fiery energy, and darkness; but when the seed was offered into that fire, three beings came forth, O mighty one.
They were men endowed with bodily form, endowed with the qualities arising at their birth: from the very crackling 'bhṛg' came Bhṛgu first, and from the embers came Aṅgiras into being.
And from his dwelling upon the embers another came to be, named Kavi; since Bhṛgu arose together with the flames, he is therefore remembered as Bhṛgu.
From the rays of light arose Marīci, and from Marīci came Kaśyapa; from the embers came Aṅgiras, my son, and the Vālakhilyas from the heap of stones; and they say, O mighty one, that Atri was born here, and so he is called Atri, 'born just here.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Likewise from the scatterings of ash arose the Vaikhānasas, equal to the host of Brahman-seers, longing for the merits of austerity and sacred learning; and from his unheard-of essence arose the two Aśvins, esteemed for their beauty.
The remaining Lords of Creatures were born from his channels; the seers were born from the pores of his skin, and from his sweat came the meters, which have the nature of his impurity.
For this reason the seers, endowed with sacred learning, declare on the authority of the Vedas that all the deities are Agni.
The kinds of kindling-wood are his months; the exudations are called his fortnights; the days and nights and moments are his bile, and the light is that of Varuṇa.
The red they call Raudra, Rudra's own; from the red, gold is held to arise; this is to be understood as belonging to Mitra, and from the smoke the Vasus are remembered to spring.
His flames are the Rudras and likewise the Ādityas of great splendor; and so too are his embers declared to be those that stand upon the fire-altars set in the sky.
He is the primeval Lord of the world, that supreme Brahman, that abiding one; they call it the granter of every desire, and there he bore the oblation aloft.
Then the great god Varuṇa, the Supreme Self, spoke: 'This celestial sacrificial session is mine, and here I am the householder.'
'Those three first offspring are mine, of that there is no doubt—know this, O sky-goers; for they are the fruit of my sacrifice.'
Agni said: Born from my limbs and brought forth by resort to me, those offspring are mine alone; for Varuṇa is one who has lost mastery of himself.
Then spoke Brahmā, the teacher of the worlds, the Grandsire of the worlds: 'Those offspring are mine alone, for it was my seed that was offered.'
'I am the utterer of the sacred formula and the offerer of the seed; his is the fruit whose seed it is, if the seed be held the cause.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then the hosts of gods, approaching the Grandsire, spoke, all of them with palms joined together and bowing low with their heads in salutation.
'We all, O lord, and the world with all that moves and is still, are entirely your offspring; therefore let Agni Vibhāvasu and the lord god Varuṇa each obtain the desire he longs for.'
And Varuṇa, by his nature the lord of the water-creatures, born of Brahmā, took first as his offspring Bhṛgu, who shone with the splendor of the sun.
The Lord assigned Aṅgiras to Agni for the sake of his offspring; and the Grandsire, knower of the truth, took Kavi for his own offspring.
Thus Bhṛgu was renowned as Varuṇa's, a doer of the work of begetting; the glorious Aṅgiras as Agni's; and Kavi, of great renown, as Brahmā's. The lines of Bhṛgu and of Aṅgiras in the world bear the mark of the world's continuance.
These three are all foremost among the twice-born, Lords of Creatures; understand that all this lineage is theirs.
Bhṛgu had seven sons, equal to Bhṛgu in their qualities: Cyavana and Vajraśīrṣa, and Śuci, and Aurva likewise.
Śukra and Vareṇya the mighty, and Savana—these are the seven, all Bhārgavas, all of Varuṇa's line, in whose lineage you too belong.
And Aṅgiras had eight sons; they too are declared to be of Varuṇa's line: Bṛhaspati and Utathya, and Vayasya, and Śānti.
Ghora, Virūpa, Saṃvarta, and Sudhanvan, remembered as the eighth—these eight, all born of Agni, are devoted to knowledge and free from affliction.
The sons of Kavi, who is Brahmā's, are also declared to be of Varuṇa's line: eight of them, endowed with the qualities arising at their birth, knowers of Brahman, blessed.
Kavi and Kāvya and Viṣṇu, and the wise Uśanas likewise, and Bhṛgu, and Virajās, and Kāśi, and Ugra the knower of dharma.
These are the eight sons of Kavi; by them the whole world is spread out; for these are Lords of Creatures, by whom these creatures came to be.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus the world is forever filled by the offspring and descendants of Aṅgiras and of Kavi, and by those born in the line of Bhṛgu, O tiger among Bhṛgu's race.
And Varuṇa, the mighty Lord, took first, O brāhmaṇa—Kavi, my son, and Bhṛgu as well; therefore those two are remembered as belonging to Varuṇa.
The crested god, the oblation-eater, took Aṅgiras; therefore all who are of his line are to be known as descendants of Aṅgiras.
Brahmā the Grandsire was of old propitiated by the deities, who said: 'These lords of the world will carry us across through their progeny.'
'All of them are Lords of Creatures, all of them are surpassing ascetics; by your grace they will carry this everlasting world across.'
'And likewise may they be founders of lineages, enhancers of your splendor, all knowers of the Veda, and masters of speech.'
'Holding to the side of the gods, gentle, sprung from the Lord of Creatures, these great seers attain austerity and the highest practice of chastity.'
'For all of us, and these too, are your offspring alone, O lord; for you are the maker of the gods and of the brāhmaṇas, O Grandsire.'
'Setting Marīci at the head, and all the Bhārgavas too—regarding them as our offspring, we ask your pardon, O Grandsire.'
'In this very form they will beget creatures, and will establish themselves anew at the beginning and the end of each age.'
Thus did this come to pass of old at the sacrifice of that great-souled one, the best of the gods, at the world's beginning, as he bore the form of Varuṇa.
Agni, Brahmā, Paśupati, Śarva, Rudra, the Lord of Creatures—this is the settled tradition: that gold is indeed the offspring of Agni.
And in the absence of fire, those who know the authorities place gold in the stead of fire upon the altars, O son of Jamadagni, on the showing of the Vedic revelation.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
One offers oblation to the fire in a tuft of kuśa grass, with gold set there; and when the oblation is made, the Lord deems delight-giving prosperity to abide therein.
Therefore we have heard that all the deities have Agni as their highest; for Agni was brought forth from Brahmā, and from Agni in turn came gold.
Therefore those who, beholding dharma, give gold—they give all the deities together: so have we heard.
And for him, free of darkness, going to the supreme goal, there are worlds; in the world of heaven he would be consecrated to the kingship over kings, O Bhārgava.
He who, when the rising of the sun has come, gives gold accompanied by rite and sacred formula—he wards off the evil dream.
He who gives the moment the sun has risen, his evil is shaken off; for one who gives gold at midday, it destroys the evil that is yet to come.
He of steadfast vow who gives gold at the evening twilight attains to dwelling in the same world as Brahmā, Vāyu, Agni, and Soma.
And in the worlds where Indra dwells he gains a blessed standing; having won renown in this world, his evil stilled, he rejoices.
Thereafter he comes to be peerless forever in the other worlds; his movement is unobstructed, and he becomes one who goes wherever he wills.
And he does not fall away from those worlds, but enjoys the great reward forever; having given imperishable gold, he attains the most abundant worlds.
But he who, having kindled the fire toward the rising of the sun, should give with a vow in view—he attains all his desires.
That gift they call Agni himself, the bringer of happiness; endowed with whatever excellence is desired, it is remembered as setting all good things in motion.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, the valorous son of Jamadagni gave gold to the brāhmaṇas and was released from his sin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
All this have I declared to you, O lord of the earth—the fruit of the giving of gold, and its peerless origin from Agni.
Therefore do you too bestow abundant gold upon the brāhmaṇas; by giving gold, O king, you shall be released from all sin.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The grandsire has set forth here at length, according to the ordinances, the virtues of the gift of gold as attested by the scriptures.
But touching the cause of the origin of gold that has been declared here—how did Tāraka meet his death? That tell me.
He was said to be unslayable by the gods, O lord of the earth; yet his death has not been recounted by you here in full.
This I wish to hear from you, O upholder of the Kuru line—the slaying of Tāraka in its entirety; for great is my curiosity.
Bhīṣma said: Their endeavour having failed, O king of kings, the gods and the sages alike urged the Kṛttikās to undertake the rearing of the child.
For not one among the goddesses was able by her own might to bear that embryo of Agni, the knower of all that is born.
Then Pāvaka, the purifier, was pleased with those six for their bearing of the embryo, by reason of his own outpoured splendour and supreme potency.
Those six Kṛttikās nourished the embryo of Jātavedas; into their six channels was the whole splendour of Agni deposited, O lord.
Then, their limbs wholly compassed about by the splendour of that growing and high-souled boy, they could find ease nowhere.
Then, their limbs encompassed by that splendour, when the appointed time was come, all those Kṛttikās gave birth to the embryo together, O bull among men.
Then the Earth received that embryo, which from its six seats had come into oneness, near the city of Kāntī.
That embryo, of celestial form, blazing, bright as Pāvaka, having reached a divine thicket of reeds, grew up, fair to behold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Kṛttikās beheld that child, splendid as fire; and tenderness arising, out of affection they nourished him with the flowing of their milk.
He became Kārttikeya throughout the three worlds, with all that moves and is unmoving; from his being poured forth he attained the state of Skanda, and from dwelling in a covert he became Guha.
Then the three-and-thirty gods, and the quarters with their guardian lords, Rudra and Dhātṛ and Viṣṇu, Yajña, Pūṣan, Aryaman, Bhaga,
Aṃśa and Mitra and the Sādhyas, the Vasus, Vāsava, the two Aśvins, the Waters, Vāyu, the Sky, the Moon, the lunar mansions, the planets, the Sun—
and other separate beings, those that are offered in oblation to the gods, came there to behold that prince, the son of the flaming one; and the sages praised him, and the Gandharvas likewise sang.
That prince of six faces and twice-six eyes, dear to the twice-born, broad-shouldered, twelve-armed, with the lustre of Fire and the Sun,
as he lay couched within the reed-clump—beholding him, the gods together with the sages won the highest joy, and deemed the Asura already slain.
Then the gods, every one of them, did all that was pleasing to him, and to him at his play they gave playthings and flocks of birds.
Suparṇa gave him for his vehicle a peacock with bright-hued plumage, and the Rākṣasas gave him both a boar and a buffalo.
Varuṇa himself bestowed a cock resembling fire; the Moon gave a ram, and the Sun a radiant splendour.
And the goddess, mother of cattle, gave kine by hundreds of thousands; Agni gave a goat endowed with good qualities, and Ilā much fruit and flower.
Sudhanvan gave a cart and a chariot with measureless pole; Varuṇa gave auspicious celestial serpents of his own kind; and Surendra gave lions and tigers and panthers and other fanged beasts.
and many fearsome beasts of prey, and parasols of various kinds; and hosts of Rākṣasas and Asuras there were who followed that lord.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But beholding him as he grew, Tāraka sought by many devices to slay him, yet he could not slay that mighty one.
The gods, having honoured the dweller in the covert with the office of commander, told him of that outrage which Tāraka had wrought.
Then Guha, grown to full strength, of mighty valour, the lordly commander of the divine host, slew the Dānava Tāraka with his unfailing spear.
When the Asura had been slain by that prince as though in sport, Surendra was once more established as lord upon the kingdom of the gods.
Then valorous Skanda shone forth as commander, the lord and protector of the gods, and a doer of what was dear to Śaṃkara.
This same blessed one of golden form, the son of Pāvaka, ever a youth, attained to the generalship of the gods.
Therefore gold is held auspicious, an imperishable and excellent jewel, born together with Kārttikeya, deemed the supreme splendour of Fire.
Thus did Vasiṣṭha relate to Rāma of old, O Kaurava; therefore strive after the giving of gold, O ruler of men.
For Rāma, having given gold, was freed of all his sins, and won in heaven a high place hard for men to attain.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The duty of the four orders, O righteous one, has been declared by you, O sinless lord; even so now declare to me in full the rite of the śrāddha, O king.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu then set about to expound this whole rite of the śrāddha.
Bhīṣma said: Hearken attentively, O king, to this auspicious ordinance of the śrāddha—wealth-giving, fame-bestowing, conducive to offspring, the sacrifice to the fathers, O scorcher of foes.
By gods, Asuras, and men, by Gandharvas, serpents, and Rākṣasas, by Piśācas and Kiṃnaras, the fathers are ever to be honoured.
Having first honoured the fathers, men afterward satisfy the gods; therefore with all endeavour should a man honour them ever.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The śrāddha of the fathers, O great king, is called the anvāhārya; and its performance with flesh, by ordinance, was the rite first appointed.
On all days are the fathers gladdened by the śrāddhas performed; yet I shall declare to you, for each lunar day, the merits and demerits of each.
On whatsoever days the śrāddhas, when performed, yield what fruit, O sinless one—all this I shall duly recount; learn it of me.
Worshipping the fathers on the first lunar day, a man obtains in his own house women fair-formed, bearing comely offspring, lovely to look upon, and rich in children.
On the second are born daughters; on the third, panegyrists; on the fourth there come to be in the house many small cattle.
On the fifth, to those who perform it, O king, are born many sons; and men who perform it on the sixth come to share in radiance.
He who performs the śrāddha on the seventh becomes a sharer in the harvest, O king; performing it on the eighth, a man obtains gain in trade.
To him who performs the śrāddha on the ninth come single-hooved beasts in plenty; and to him who performs the śrāddhas on the tenth, the kine increase.
A man who performs it on the eleventh becomes a sharer in base metals, O king; and sons radiant with sacred lore are born within his house.
To him who strives at the rite on the twelfth there is ever seen abundant silver of varied kind, and gold delightful to the mind.
Performing the śrāddha on the thirteenth, a man becomes foremost among his kinsmen; yet inevitably the young men of his house come to die.
A man who performs the śrāddha on the fourteenth becomes a partaker in battle; but offering on the new-moon day, he obtains all his desires.
In the dark fortnight, beginning with the tenth and excepting the fourteenth, the lunar days are commended for the rite of the śrāddha—not so are the others.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And even as the latter fortnight is held superior to the former, so for the śrāddha is the afternoon superior to the forenoon.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What gift made to the fathers becomes imperishable, O lord? What oblation avails for a long season, and what conduces to endlessness?
Bhīṣma said: The oblations in the rite of the śrāddha that the knowers of the śrāddha know—hear of me those that fulfil desire, and their fruit, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
With sesame, with rice and barley, with beans, with water, and with roots and fruits—by the śrāddha so offered the fathers are gladdened for a month, O king.
A śrāddha abounding in sesame is imperishable, Manu declared; and among all things that may be eaten, sesame is held to hold the foremost place.
With fishes the satisfaction of the host of fathers lasts two months; with mutton, men say, three months; and with hare's flesh, four months.
With goat's flesh the fathers are gladdened five months, O king; with boar's flesh six months; and seven months with the flesh of fowl.
Eight months with the flesh of the spotted deer, and nine indeed with that of the ruru deer; and with the flesh of the gavaya the satisfaction lasts ten months.
With buffalo's flesh the fathers' contentment lasts eleven months; but when the śrāddha is offered with cow's milk and the like, it is said here to last a full year.
As with the produce of the cow, so likewise is it with milk-rice joined with clarified butter; and with the flesh of the vādhrīṇasa the satisfaction lasts twelve years.
Rhinoceros-flesh given at the offering to the fathers avails for endlessness; and the kālaśāka herb, and red goat, are said likewise to conduce to endlessness.
And here too they sing verses sung by the fathers, O Yudhiṣṭhira; the blessed Sanatkumāra of old spoke them unto me.
"May there be born in our line one who would offer us, on the thirteenth day, under the asterism Maghā, in the sun's southern course, milk-rice joined with clarified butter;

title: Mahābhārata
text:
or with goat's flesh, or with red goat, under those very Maghās, one of steadfast vows, duly fanned with the ear-fan amid the shadows of elephants."
Many sons should be desired, that even one of them might journey to Gayā, where stands renowned throughout the worlds that fig-tree which makes the offering imperishable.
Water, root, fruit, flesh, or food given at the offering to the fathers—whatsoever is mingled with honey conduces to endlessness.
Bhīṣma said: The śrāddhas that Yama declared to Śaśabindu—hear of me those that fulfil desire, severally under each lunar mansion.
The man who should ever perform the śrāddha under the conjunction of the Kṛttikās, having set up the sacred fires, would sacrifice with offspring and free of fever.
He who longs for offspring should offer under Rohiṇī; he who longs for vigour, under the lordly deer-mansion; but a man giving the śrāddha under Ārdrā becomes one of cruel deeds.
A man performing the śrāddha under Punarvasu becomes a sharer in the harvest; and one who longs for nourishment should strive at the śrāddha under Puṣya.
Giving the śrāddha under Āśleṣā, a man begets heroic sons; and offering the śrāddha under the Maghās, he becomes foremost among his kinsmen.
Giving the śrāddha under the Phalgunīs, the giver becomes blessed with fortune; under the Uttaras he becomes a sharer in offspring, and under Hasta a sharer in fruit.
Giving the śrāddha under Citrā, he obtains comely sons; worshipping the fathers under the conjunction of Svāti, he lives by trade.
A man striving at the rite to the fathers under the Viśākhās becomes rich in sons; and performing it under the Anurādhās, he sets in motion the wheel of empire.
A man, O foremost of the Kuru line, going with faith and self-restraint before him, attains to sovereignty by making the offering under Jyeṣṭhā.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Under Mūla he should attain health, and under the Aṣāḍhās fame unsurpassed; and under the Uttarāṣāḍhās, freed of sorrow, he would range the earth.
Performing the śrāddha under Abhijit, he would obtain the highest knowledge; and giving the śrāddha under Śravaṇa, he would go after death to the supreme course.
He who performs the śrāddha under Dhaniṣṭhā becomes a sharer in kingdoms and meets with no calamity; performing it under the lunar mansion of Varuṇa, a man attains success in the healing art.
Performing it under the Pūrva-Proṣṭhapadā stars, he gains goats and sheep in abundance; performing it under the Uttarā stars, he gains cattle by the thousand.
Resorting to Revatī, he gains wealth wrought of much silver; under Aśvayuj he obtains horses, and under the Bharaṇī stars the highest length of life.
Having heard this ordinance of the śrāddha, Śaśabindu acted accordingly; without hardship he conquered the earth, and he ruled it.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: To brāhmaṇas of what sort should the śrāddha-offering be given, O grandsire? O tiger of the Kurus, you ought to expound this to me.
Bhīṣma said: A kṣatriya versed in the law of giving should not scrutinize brāhmaṇas in rites for the gods; but in the rite for the ancestors, scrutiny is held to be proper.
The deities here honor the offering by their divine splendor when they draw near; therefore a man should have the offering given to all the gods alike.
But at the śrāddha, O great king, the wise man should examine the brāhmaṇas by their family, character, age, and form, by their learning and noble birth.
Of these, some are defilers of the row and others are sanctifiers of the row; those who are unworthy of the row, O king, I shall now name—hear of them.
The gambler, the slayer of an embryo, the consumptive, the cattle-herder, the misshapen, the village drudge, the usurer, the professional singer, the seller of every kind of ware,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
the house-burner, the poisoner, the eater of food in a vessel of adultery's child, the seller of soma, the seafarer, the king's servant, the oil-presser, the forger of false coin,
he who quarrels with his father, he in whose house there is a paramour, the man falsely accused, the thief, and he who lives by a manual craft,
the maker of festival days, the informer, the betrayer of friends, the adulterer, the teacher of those without vows, and likewise the renegade who turns his back on his own kindred,
he who roams about with dogs, he who has been bitten by a dog, he who marries before an elder brother, the man of diseased skin, the defiler of his teacher's bed, the actor-dancer, the temple-priest who lives off idols, and he who lives by reading the stars—
these one should know to be unworthy of the row, the basest of the twice-born, together with those of little wit who give instruction to śūdras.
A one-eyed man defiles sixty, a eunuch a hundred, O king; and a man with white leprosy, when seated in the row, defiles as far as his eye can reach.
What is eaten with the head wrapped, what is eaten facing south, and what is eaten while still shod—all this one should know to belong to the demons.
What is given grudgingly and what is given without faith—all this Brahmā has apportioned as the share of the lord of the asuras.
Dogs and defilers of the row should by no means look upon the offering; therefore one should give it in an enclosed place and scatter sesame seeds around it.
When the sesame offering is omitted, the flesh-eating fiends, the hosts driven by wrath, the yātudhānas, and the piśācas plunder that oblation.
For as long as one unfit for the row gazes upon those eating in the row, so long does he strip the foolish giver of his reward.
But these, O best of the Bhāratas, are to be known as sanctifiers of the row; those who are such I shall now declare—examine these brāhmaṇas here.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Brāhmaṇas who have completed their study of the Veda and their vows of the bath are, every one, worthy of the row; and those whom I shall name as worthy should be known as sanctifiers of the row.
He who has thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire, the keeper of the five fires, the knower of the Trisuparṇa hymn, the master of the six Vedāṅgas, he born of a line of brahma-given marriages, the chanter of the Sāman, the singer of the Jyeṣṭha-sāman,
he who is obedient to his mother and father, the learned man of ten generations of Veda-knowers, and he who always approaches his lawful wives only in their season—such a brāhmaṇa, accomplished in Veda, learning, and vow, indeed purifies the row.
The student of the Atharvaśiras, the chaste one of restrained vows, the speaker of truth, he of righteous conduct, and he who is devoted to his own appointed duty—
and those who have toiled in ritual bathing at holy fords, and who have been bathed in the final ablution of sacrifices accompanied by their proper mantras—
those free of anger, free of fickleness, patient, self-controlled, masters of their senses, and devoted to the welfare of all beings—these one should invite to the śrāddhas; what is given to them is imperishable, for these indeed are sanctifiers of the row.
These others too, O great king, are to be known as sanctifiers of the row: the ascetics who know the law of liberation, the men of yoga of well-practiced vows,
those who, intent and pure, recite the ancient lore to the best of the twice-born, those who are versed in commentary, and those who delight in grammar,
those who study the Purāṇa and the treatises on dharma as well, and who, having studied them duly and rightly, act according to their precepts,
he who has dwelt completely in his teacher's household, the speaker of truth, the giver of a thousand gifts, the foremost in all the Vedas and in all the recitations—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
as far as these gaze upon the row, so far do they purify it; and because of this purifying of the row, each is called a sanctifier of the row.
Even a single such man, born of a line of brahma-given marriages, can sanctify the offering from a distance of two and a half krośas—so the knowers of Brahman declare.
If one who is neither officiating priest nor teacher takes the foremost seat unauthorized by the officiants, he carries off, along with the row, only ill-deserved demerit.
But if he is a knower of the Veda, free of all the faults of the row, and is not a fallen man, O king, then he is indeed a sanctifier of the row.
Therefore with all care one should examine and invite brāhmaṇas devoted to their own duties, self-controlled, well-born, and deeply learned.
He whose śrāddhas and oblations are devoted chiefly to friends gratifies neither the ancestors nor the gods, and he does not attain to heaven.
He who turns the śrāddha into a gathering of friends does not travel by the path of the gods; like a fig loosed from its stalk, the man who befriends at the śrāddha falls away from the world of heaven.
Therefore the performer of the śrāddha should not honor a friend with it; let him give his friends wealth to win their goodwill instead. Whom he regards as neither foe nor friend, that neutral man let him feed at the rites for gods and ancestors.
As seed sown in barren ground does not sprout, and the sower of it gains no return on his seed, so the śrāddha eaten by the unworthy yields its fruit neither here nor hereafter.
For a brāhmaṇa who has not studied dies down like a fire of straw; to him the śrāddha should not be given, for no oblation is poured upon ashes.
The mere feeding of friends is a fee fit for piśācas; it reaches neither the gods nor the ancestors. Drained of merit, it wanders here below, like a cow within the stable that has lost its calf.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
