As clarified butter poured upon a fire that has died reaches neither the gods nor the ancestors, so too is what is given to dancing and to singing, and the fee one bestows upon one who knows no sacred verse.
The fee given to one who knows no sacred verse destroys them both and nourishes neither; deadly and contemptible, in its falling it casts the departed of such men down from the path of the gods.
Those who ever observe the discipline of the seers, O Yudhiṣṭhira, steadfast and knowers of all dharma—the gods know such brāhmaṇas to be true.
The seers are to be understood as devoted to recitation, devoted to knowledge, devoted to austerity, and devoted to ritual action, O Bhārata.
The ancestral offerings are to be entrusted to those devoted to knowledge, O Bhārata; and among them, whatever brāhmaṇas there be who revile no one—those are the most excellent.
But those who revile others in their chatter—one should not feed them at the śrāddhas; for brāhmaṇas reviled, O king, can destroy a family through three generations.
The word of the Vaikhānasa seers is heard, O king: from afar should one examine the brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Veda, and whether they be dear or hateful, in them should one set the śrāddha.
Though a man should feed a thousand thousands of men who know no sacred verse, a single knower of the mantras, when pleased, outweighs them all, O Bhārata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By whom was the śrāddha first conceived, at what time, and of what nature? In the age of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras, by which of the two sages was it ordained?
What things are to be shunned in the śrāddhas, and what roots and fruits, and what kind of grain is to be avoided? Tell me this, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: How the śrāddha came into being, at what time, of what nature, and by whom it was conceived—hear this from me, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There was Atri, son of the Self-existent, O Kauravya, a supreme seer of mighty splendor; in his line, O great king, was born he remembered as Dattātreya.
Dattātreya had a son named Nimi, rich in austerity; and to Nimi there was born a son named Śrīmān, endowed with glory.
At the close of a full thousand years, having performed hard austerities, his being overtaken by the law of time, he came to his death.
But Nimi, having performed the purifications by the rite ordained, fell into bitter grief, wholly given over to sorrow for his son.
Then, having made the funeral offerings on the fourteenth day, the great-minded one, brooding upon that very grief, awoke at the close of night.
As he awoke, his self veiled by grief, having drawn his mind back from the objects of sense, his understanding ranged far and wide.
Then, composed in mind, he pondered the ordinance of the śrāddha—what foods, what roots, and what fruits had been dear to his son,
and whatever others were prescribed, and whatever were beloved of him—all these the man rich in austerity determined in his mind.
On the night of the new moon, O greatly wise one, having summoned brāhmaṇas and honored them, he himself fashioned all the seats of grass coiled toward the right.
Then he brought forward seven brāhmaṇas together to the meal, and the lord gave them food of wild millet, with everything save salt.
Then darbha grasses, their tips pointing south, were laid upon the seats and at the feet of the brāhmaṇas who were partaking of the food.
And having set the darbhas with their tips toward the south, well-disciplined and pure, he offered the rice-ball to Śrīmān, pronouncing his name and lineage.
Having done this, that best of sages, tormented by great remorse at the confounding of dharma he had wrought, fell to thinking:
"What is this I have performed, never done by the sages before? How may the brāhmaṇas not consume me with their curse?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then he called to mind the founder of his own line; and no sooner was he thought upon than Atri, rich in austerity, came near.
Then Atri, seeing him so wasted with sorrow for his son, the imperishable one comforted him deeply with kindly words:
"O Nimi, this rite for the ancestors has been conceived by you, O man of austerity. Let no fear be yours: this dharma was foreseen of old by Brahmā himself.
This dharma, ordained by the Self-existent, has been conceived by you; for save the Self-existent, who else could have set forth this ordinance of the śrāddha?
And I shall declare to you further the most excellent ordinance of the śrāddha, ordained by the Self-existent, O son; perform it, and mark my words.
Having first performed the fire-rite with its proper mantras, O man of austerity, then ever offer to Aryaman, to Soma, and to Varuṇa;
and to those All-gods who ever range together with the ancestors—for them the shares were appointed by the Self-existent himself.
And here the Earth is to be praised, she who upholds the offering—called the Vaiṣṇavī, the Kāśyapī, and likewise the Imperishable.
And at the bringing of water, the all-pervading Varuṇa is to be praised; thereafter Agni and Soma are here to be gratified, O sinless one.
The gods named the Fathers were indeed fashioned by the Self-existent, those drinkers of vapor of exceeding blessedness; for them the shares were apportioned.
Honored by the śrāddha, they are released from sin; the ancestral line is sevenfold, as foreseen of old by the Self-existent.
And the All-gods, fire-faced, were reckoned of old; I shall declare the names of those great-souled ones who are worthy of a share.
Sahas, Kṛti, Vipāpman, Puṇyakṛt, and Pāvana likewise; Grāmaṇi, Kṣema, Samūha, and Divyasānu as well.
Vivasvat, Vīryavat, Hrīmat, Kīrtimat, and Kṛta; Vipūrva, Somapūrva, and Sūryaśrī — so they are named.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Somapa, Sūryasāvitra, Dattātman, Puṣkarīyaka; Uṣṇīnābha, Nabhoda, Viśvāyu, and Dīpti too.
Camūhara and Suveṣa, Vyomāri, Śaṃkara, Bhava; Īśa, Kartṛ, Kṛti, Dakṣa, Bhuvana, and Divyakarmakṛt.
Gaṇita and Pañcavīrya, Āditya, and Raśmimat; Saptakṛt, Somavarcas, Viśvakṛt, and Kavi too.
Anugoptṛ and Sugoptṛ, Naptṛ, and Īśvara; Jitātman, Munivīrya, Dīptaloman, and Bhayaṃkara.
Atikarman and Pratīta, Pradātṛ, and Aṃśumat; Śailābha, Paramakrodhin, Dhīroṣṇi, and Bhūpati.
Srajin, Vajrin, and Varin — these are the eternal Viśvedevas, the greatly blessed ones, now celebrated, who move within the range of time's course.
Among grains, kodrava and pulaka are unfit for the śrāddha rite; among condiments, asafoetida; among vegetables, the onion and the garlic.
The onion, the drumstick plant, the carrot and their kind, the gourd-fruit and the bottle-gourd, and black salt as well.
The flesh of the domestic boar, and whatever has not been consecrated, black cumin, biḍa salt, and the slow-ripening melon, sprouted shoots and the like, and water-chestnuts — these too are to be shunned here.
One should avoid all manufactured salt, and likewise the fruit of the rose-apple; and at śrāddha rites one should reject whatever has been sneezed or wept upon.
At an offering of food, of oblations to the gods or to the fathers, the sight of a dog is to be deplored; neither the fathers nor the gods take pleasure in such an oblation.
When the offering of food is set forth, the Caṇḍāla and the dog-eater must be kept away, as must the wearer of ochre robes, the leper, the outcaste, and even the slayer of a brahmin.
A brahmin of mixed birth, and a kinsman who has fallen from his estate — these the wise must exclude when the offering of food is set forth.
Having thus spoken of old to the sage born of his own line, the venerable Atri, rich in austerity, departed to the divine assembly hall of the Grandfather.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: When the rite had been set in motion in this manner, all the great sages performed the sacrifices to the fathers with action prescribed by ordinance.
The sages, ever devoted to dharma, having made their food-offerings, performed too the libation of water from sacred fords, steadfast in their vows.
Gratified by the offerings of food given by the four orders, O Bhārata, the fathers and the gods could not, however, digest the food.
Stricken by indigestion, those gods together with the fathers, oppressed by the offered food, betook themselves to Soma.
Reaching Soma, the fathers, afflicted with indigestion, said: "We are tormented by the offered food; let some remedy be devised for us in this matter."
Then Soma answered them: "If you desire a remedy, O gods, go to the abode of the Self-Existent; he will ordain what is best for you."
At Soma's word, those gods together with the fathers, O Bhārata, approached the Grandfather, who was seated upon the peak of Meru.
The fathers said: "By the offered food, O Lord, we are sorely tormented. Show us your grace, O God; let some remedy be ordained for us."
Hearing these words of theirs, the Self-Existent spoke thus: "Here at my side is Fire; he will ordain what is best for you."
Agni said: "Together, dear ones, we shall eat when the offering of food is set forth, and along with me you shall digest the food — of this there is no doubt."
Hearing this, the fathers were thereupon freed of their distress; and for this very reason, O king, the foremost portion is given to Agni.
When the offering is made with Agni first, O bull among men, the brahma-rākṣasas do not defile that offering, and the demons turn away when the god of radiant light is present.
First one should offer the rice-ball to the father, then to the grandfather, and then to the great-grandfather: this is held to be the ordinance of the śrāddha.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At the śrāddha, with collected mind, one should recite the Sāvitrī over each rice-ball; one should say "to Soma," and likewise "to him attended by the fathers."
A woman in her courses, or one maimed in her ears, should not attend at the offering; nor are those of another lineage to be admitted.
While crossing a body of water, one should call to mind the grandfathers; and upon reaching a river, one should perform the rice-ball offering and libation to the fathers.
First having made the water-libation to those born of one's own line, one should then offer a handful of water to the company of friends and kinsmen.
When one crosses the water yoked to a pair of dappled oxen, the fathers indeed long for him, and as he climbs aboard the boat; ever upon the boat those who know offer the water-libation with collected minds.
In the half-month of the dark fortnight one should make the food-offerings; for nourishment, long life, vigor, and prosperity attend upon him who is devoted to the fathers.
The Grandfather, Pulastya, Vasiṣṭha, and Pulaha, Aṅgiras, Kratu, and the great sage Kaśyapa — these, O best of the Kuru line, are remembered as the mighty lords of yoga.
These too are the fathers, O king; this is the supreme ordinance of the śrāddha. The departed, bound to the rice-ball offerings, are by that act set free.
Thus, O best of men, has the origin of the śrāddha, as it was first set forth, been declared to you according to tradition. Of the gift of charity I shall now speak hereafter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: If the twice-born, bound by their vows, eat the oblation — food given out of desire to please the brahmins — how can this be, O grandfather?
Bhīṣma said: Those bound by vows not enjoined in the Veda, if they eat, are merely doers of their duty; but those who eat while under vows enjoined in the Veda, O Yudhiṣṭhira, have broken their vow.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That fasting which the common folk here call austerity — is this indeed austerity, or might true austerity be something else?
Bhīṣma said: The fasting for a month or half a month that people deem austerity — he who thereby injures his own constitution is neither an ascetic nor a knower of dharma.
The very perfection of renunciation is taught to be the highest austerity; one may be ever a faster and likewise ever a celibate.
A brahmin may be ever a sage, and ever may he sacrifice to the gods, though he be a householder devoted to dharma, and ever wakeful, O Bhārata.
He may be ever an eater of ambrosia, and ever may he be pure; ever a speaker of truth he may be, and ever may he be self-restrained.
He may be ever an eater of the remnants, and ever loving toward his guests; ever an abstainer from flesh he may be, and ever may he be pure.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How may one be ever a faster and a celibate, O king? And how may one be an eater of the remnants, and how a lover of guests?
Bhīṣma said: He who does not eat again in between the evening meal and the morning meal becomes ever a faster.
Approaching his wife only in her season, a man becomes ever a celibate; and a man given to charity becomes ever a speaker of truth.
By not eating flesh in vain, one becomes an abstainer from flesh; by giving in charity, one becomes pure; and even sleeping by day, one remains free of sleep.
The man who ever eats only after his dependents and guests have eaten — know, O Yudhiṣṭhira, that he eats nothing but ambrosia.
The man who does not eat while the brahmins have not yet eaten — by that very abstinence heaven is won by him.
He who eats what is left over after the gods, the fathers, his dependents, and his guests — him they call an eater of the remnants.
For such men, boundless worlds in the abode of Brahmā are remembered, attended by Apsarases and Gandharvas, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Together with the deities, the guests, and the fathers they feast, and they take delight with their sons and grandsons; theirs is a course beyond all surpassing.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Men bestow various gifts upon the brahmins; between the giver and the receiver, which is the more excellent, O grandfather?
Bhīṣma said: The twice-born who accepts a gift from a virtuous man, or likewise from one who is not virtuous, incurs little fault if the giver is endowed with merit, but he sinks down if the giver is devoid of it.
On this point, too, they recount this ancient tale, the dialogue between Vṛṣādarbhi and the Seven Sages, O Bhārata.
Kaśyapa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha, then Bharadvāja and Gautama, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, and the virtuous Arundhatī as well.
Now Gaṇḍā was the serving-maid of all of them, and the Śūdra Paśusakha was her husband.
All of them, performing austerities, of old wandered over this earth, striving through meditation toward the eternal world of Brahmā.
Then there came a great drought, O delight of the Kurus, in which this world was reduced to a hard struggle for life and gripped by hunger.
And once, of old, at a certain sacrifice, the son of Śibi, the patron of the rite, gave his own son to the officiating priests as a sacrificial fee.
At that time, O lord, that short-lived boy came to the end ordained by fate; and they, scorched by hunger, surrounded him and stood near.
Then, seeing the patron's son bereft of life, those most excellent sages, tormented by hunger, set to cooking him in a pot, O Bhārata.
In this world of mortals where there was nothing to eat, those ascetics, seeking to preserve their own lives, fell into a wretched mode of living for the sake of food.
Now the lord of the earth, the Śaibya king Vṛṣādarbhi, roaming along the road, beheld them cooking, sorely afflicted.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vṛṣādarbhi said: Accepting a gift brings deliverance; it is indeed a nourishment for those who receive. Hear, O you rich in austerity, what wealth is to be found with me.
Dear to me indeed is the brahmin who asks; I would give you a thousand she-mules, each one with its sire and brought to birth, all of them swift-going and white of coat.
Bulls that sustain a family, by the hundred upon hundred, draught-oxen fair and fit for the yoke I would give you wholly, broad and well-fed bearers of the earth, and as many milch-cows, choice young heifers, gentle of disposition.
Choice villages, rice and barley and savory things, and other jewels hard to obtain — what shall I give? Do not turn your minds to forbidden food; for your nourishment, what shall I bestow upon you?
The sages said: O king, a gift from a king is sweet to the taste as honey, yet like poison. Knowing this, why do you set temptation before us?
The warrior-order leans upon the brahmin as upon a deity; for this brahmin, made spotless by austerity and well pleased, gives pleasure to the gods themselves.
Sometimes the austerity of a brahmin is born here in but a single day; and a king's gift, once received, would burn that away as a forest fire consumes.
"May welfare, along with your giving, be ever yours, O king; let all be given to those who seek it" — having so spoken, they then departed.
That flesh of theirs, wise as they were, remained even yet uncooked; and so, abandoning it, they all went off into the forest, still longing for food.
Then, urged on by the king, his ministers went into the forest and, gathering wild figs, set about giving them as a gift.
Now they brought up other wild figs, gold-laden within, and the king's servants then ran forward to press these upon the sages to accept.
Knowing them to be heavy, Atri declared they were not to be taken: "We are no men of deluded understanding, ho! We are no dullards of feeble wit! We know these are made of gold; we are awake, we keep watch."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For this, taken up here, would yield a bitter fruit hereafter; by one who longs for happiness in the world beyond and in this one, it is simply not to be accepted.
Vasiṣṭha said: A gold coin counted by hundreds, reckoned by thousands — the man who accepts ever more of it surely wins the most sinful destiny.
Kaśyapa said: All the rice and barley, the gold, the cattle, and the women upon this earth — even all of it is not enough for one man; therefore let the wise go to tranquility.
Bharadvāja said: As the horn of the ruru deer, once sprung up, keeps growing as the creature grows, so a man's craving grows; of it no measure can be found.
Gautama said: There is no substance in the world that could fill the world; a man is like the ocean — he is never, ever filled.
Viśvāmitra said: When the desire of a man who desires some object is fulfilled, then yet another desire, a thirst, pierces him like an arrow.
Jamadagni said: Restraint in accepting gifts is austerity; it surely upholds him firmly. That wealth of a brahmin who grows greedy here flows away and is lost.
Arundhatī said: Though the gathering of goods for the sake of dharma is approved by some, here the gathering of austerity is far superior to the gathering of goods.
Gaṇḍā said: From that fierce peril for which these my masters, mighty though they are, tremble like the weak, I too tremble all the more from this time on.
Paśusakha said: That beyond which there is nothing higher in dharma — that the brahmins know to be true wealth. For the sake of discipline I would duly wait upon a man of deep learning.
The sages said: Well-being, together with the gift, to him whose subjects these are! But fruits laden with a hidden snare — such as these you offer us in this way.
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus and cast aside those fruits stuffed with gold within, the sages, every one of them firm in their vows, went elsewhere.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The ministers said: Suspecting a hidden snare, they have cast these fruits aside and now go off by another route altogether. Let this be known to you, O king.
Thus addressed by those servants, Vṛṣādarbhi grew enraged; and to take revenge upon them all, he went into his house.
Going there, the king took up a severe observance and, in the consecrated fire, offered one by one the oblations sanctified with sacred formulas.
Out of that fire there arose a Kṛtyā, a sorcery-fiend who struck terror into the world; and Vṛṣādarbhi gave her the name Yātudhānī.
That Kṛtyā, like Kālarātri the Night of Doom, stood before him with hands joined in reverence and said to King Vṛṣādarbhi, "What shall I do?"
Vṛṣādarbhi said: Go to the seven sages, and to Arundhatī as well, and to the husband of the slave-woman and to the slave-woman herself; fix their names firmly in your mind.
Once you have learned their names, destroy them all; and when they are destroyed, go freely as you please, wherever you wish.
Promising "So be it," Yātudhānī, taking on a form of her own, went to that forest in which those great sages were wandering.
Bhīṣma said: Now, O king, the great sages led by Atri were wandering in that forest, living upon roots and fruits.
Then they saw a wandering mendicant, Śunaḥsakha, roaming about — a man of stout limbs, with well-fleshed shoulders, hands, feet, face, and belly.
But the lovely Arundhatī, seeing him grown full in every limb, said to the sages, "You yourselves will surely come to be like this — yet it is not so."
Vasiṣṭha said: This man does not, as we do, have an agnihotra left unoffered, to be made evening and morning; that is why Śunaḥsakha is so plump.
Atri said: This man's vigor is not, as ours is, struck down by hunger, nor is what he learned with hardship now lost; that is why Śunaḥsakha is so plump.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Viśvāmitra said: This man has not, as we do, the sacred lore ever upon him like an old ox at its yoke; he is idle, given over to hunger, a dullard — that is why Śunaḥsakha is so plump.
Jamadagni said: This man has not, as we do, any rainy-season store of food and firewood to fret over and lay by; that is why Śunaḥsakha is so plump.
Kaśyapa said: This man does not, as we do, have four brothers born of one womb who beg, "Give, give!"; that is why Śunaḥsakha is so plump.
Bharadvāja said: This man has not, as has a witless wretch of a brahmin like us, grief from a wife's reproaches; that is why Śunaḥsakha is so plump.
Gautama said: This man has not, as we do, three woolen rāṅkava blankets, each one to last three years; that is why Śunaḥsakha is so plump.
Bhīṣma said: Then the wandering mendicant Śunaḥsakha, seeing those great sages, drew near and duly greeted them with a touch of the hand.
And telling one another of their forest livelihood, which served to ward off hunger, they then set out together.
United in a single resolve and purpose, they roamed the woods, digging up and gathering roots and fruits.
Once, as they wandered, they came upon a lovely lotus pond, ringed by close-set trees, its water pure, bright, and clear.
It was adorned with blossoms shining like the body of the newly risen sun, and covered over with lotus leaves the color of beryl.
It was thronged with birds of many kinds that haunt the spreading waters, having but a single approach, no one to claim it, with fair landings and free of mud.
But the Kṛtyā set to her task by Vṛṣādarbhi, hideous of aspect and known as Yātudhānī, was guarding that lotus pond.
With Śunaḥsakha for their companion, those great sages went up to the pond, seeking lotus stalks — all of them, to that pond guarded by the Kṛtyā.
Then the great sages, seeing that Yātudhānī, the Kṛtyā of hideous aspect, standing on the bank of the lotus pond, spoke to her.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You stand here alone — who indeed are you? For whose sake, and with what purpose? Keeping to the bank of the lotus pond, tell us, what is it you mean to do?
Yātudhānī said: I am whoever I am; no questioning of me is to be made, by any means. Know me, all you whose wealth is austerity, to be the guardian of this pond.
The sages said: We are all tormented by hunger, and we have nothing else at all. So with your leave, we shall every one of us gather the lotus stalks.
Yātudhānī said: Take the lotus stalks from here on a condition, as you please: let each one of you first declare his name to me, and then gather them without delay.
Bhīṣma said: Recognizing that Yātudhānī to be a Kṛtyā bent on the sages' destruction, Atri, his very self overwhelmed by hunger, then spoke these words.
"A-rātri" is the night that for Atri is no-night, the night he does not study thrice in a day; therefore, fair one, know my name to be Atri, the "no-night."
Yātudhānī said: This name of yours, great sage, as you have explained it to me, is hard to hold in the mind; go on, then — go down into the pond.
Vasiṣṭha said: I am Vasiṣṭha, I am the most excellent (variṣṭha); I dwell (vase) even in houses my dwelling (vāsam). From being most excellent and from dwelling, know me as Vasiṣṭha.
Yātudhānī said: This etymology of your name has syllables hard to pronounce; it cannot be held in mind. Go on — go down into the pond.
Kaśyapa said: "Lineage upon lineage," a guardian of the wicked, a protector — Kaśyapa the twice-born, of Kāśi, from his resemblance to a shining radiance (kāśa): hold this name of mine.
Yātudhānī said: This name of yours, great sage, as you have explained it to me, is hard to hold in the mind; go on, then — go down into the pond.
Bharadvāja said: I support (bhare) my sons, I support my pupils, I support the gods, I support the twice-born, I support my wife, doing so without pretense — I am Bharadvāja, the upholder, O fair one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yātudhānī said: This etymology of your name has syllables hard to pronounce; it cannot be held in mind. Go on — go down into the pond.
Gautama said: "Tamer of cattle," "tamer-goer," the smokeless one, restraint, the one hard to look upon — know me, O Kṛtyā, as Gautama; mark me well, Yātudhānī.
Yātudhānī said: This name of yours, great sage, as you have explained it to me, cannot be held in mind. Go on — go down into the pond.
Viśvāmitra said: The All-Gods (Viśvedevas) are my friends, and I too am a friend (mitra) to the cattle; mark me, O Yātudhānī, renowned as Viśvāmitra, friend of all.
Yātudhānī said: This etymology of your name has syllables hard to pronounce; it cannot be held in mind. Go on — go down into the pond.
Jamadagni said: Born of sacrifice and offering, by name "the purifier," she said, "you wish to be born" — renowned as Jamadagni; from this know me, O fair one.
Yātudhānī said: This name of yours, great sage, as you have explained it to me, cannot be held in mind. Go on — go down into the pond.
Arundhatī said: Like the earth, the sustainer, the bearer of wealth, I stand ever close behind my husband, holding my mind faithful to him (anurundhatī) — by this know me as Arundhatī.
Yātudhānī said: This etymology of your name has syllables hard to pronounce; it cannot be held in mind. Go on — go down into the pond.
Gaṇḍā said: Going cheek by cheek (gaṇḍa by gaṇḍa), I am called Gaṇḍa-gaṇḍā; know me as Gaṇḍā, as it were "cheek upon cheek," O daughter of fire.
Yātudhānī said: This etymology of your name has syllables hard to pronounce; it cannot be held in mind. Go on — go down into the pond.
Paśusakha said: A friend, in friendship, one fit to be befriended, and ever a friend (sakhā) to the cattle (paśus) — by this secondary derivation know me thus as Paśusakha, O you born of fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yātudhānī said: This etymology of your name has syllables hard to pronounce; it cannot be held in mind. Go on — go down into the pond.
Śunaḥsakha said: A name such as these have spoken I do not care to utter here; mark me, O Yātudhānī, as the companion of Śunaḥsakha, the dog's friend.
Yātudhānī said: Your name has been spoken indistinctly, in words of doubtful sound; so now, O twice-born, tell me once and clearly what your name is.
Śunaḥsakha said: My name was uttered once, and since you did not grasp it, therefore, struck down by the triple staff, go to ashes without delay!
Bhīṣma said: Struck then upon the head by that staff, which was like the rod of Brahmā, the Kṛtyā fell to the earth and was reduced to ashes.
And Śunaḥsakha, having slain that mighty Yātudhānī, planted his triple staff in the ground and sat down upon the grassy turf.
Then all the sages, taking lotus blossoms and stalks as they pleased, rose up filled with joy.
Wearied with great toil, they laid the lotus stalks in bundles on the bank of the pond and made the water-offering with its waters.
Then, rising up from that water, they all came together — and yet, O bull among men, they could not see those lotus stalks.
The sages said: By what evildoer, what cruel wretch, have the lotus stalks been carried off from us — overcome by hunger and longing for food?
Suspecting one another, those best of the twice-born questioned each other; and they all said, "Let us swear an oath," O scourge of your foes.
Saying "Yes, indeed," all of them, together with Śunaḥsakha, tormented by hunger and utterly worn out, set about taking the oath.
Atri said: Let him touch a cow with his foot and pass water facing the sun, and study on the forbidden days — whoever it is that has stolen the lotus stalks.
Vasiṣṭha said: Let him in this world be one who shuns sacred study and instead drags a dog about, a wandering mendicant given to his own desires — whoever it is that has stolen the lotus stalks.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let him slay one who has come to him for refuge, betray a friend, live off his own daughter, and crave wealth from a miser — whoever it is that has stolen the lotus stalks.
Kaśyapa said: Let him gamble everything away on everything, embezzle what is left in trust, and become a false witness — whoever it is that has stolen the lotus stalks.
Let him eat meat offered in vain, make gifts in vain, and go in to a woman by day — whoever it is that has stolen the lotus stalks.
Bharadvāja said: Let him be cruel and abandoned by dharma toward women, kinsmen, and cattle, and let him even win out over a brahmin — whoever it is that has stolen the lotus stalks.
Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—let him recite the verses of the Ṛc and the Yajus while degrading his own teacher beneath him, and let him offer oblation while consumed in a brushwood fire.
Jamadagni said: Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—let him void his excrement into the waters, let him slay even a milch-cow, and let him go to coupling out of season.
Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—let him be a hateful man living off his wife, his kinsmen estranged, surrounded by enmity, and let such men be guests of one another.
Gautama said: Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—having studied the Vedas let him cast them off, let him let his three sacred fires die out, and let him sell the soma.
Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—let him attain the same world as that brāhmaṇa who, in a village flooded by a broken well, is the husband of a low-caste woman.
Viśvāmitra said: Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—while his elders and dependents yet live, let strangers maintain them; let him be destitute though burdened with many sons.
Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—let him be impure, a counterfeit of a brāhmaṇa, made arrogant by his very prosperity, a ploughman, and grudging.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—let him toil for years as a hireling, let him be a king's house-priest, and let him serve as ritual officiant for a man unfit to sacrifice.
Arundhatī said: Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—let her forever revile her mother-in-law, let her be ill-disposed toward her husband, and let her eat the dainty food alone.
Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—dwelling amid the houses of her kin, let her eat parched meal at day's end; let her be luckless and bear no living son.
Gaṇḍū said: Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—let her speak falsehood always, let her quarrel with the good, and let her give her daughter away for a bride-price.
Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—having cooked the food, let her eat it herself first; let her live in servitude, and let her perish through forbidden deeds.
Paśusakha said: Whoever steals the lotus-stalks—let him be born only of a slave-woman, childless and possessing nothing, paying no homage to the gods.
Śunaḥsakha said: Whoever it is that steals the lotus-stalks—let that brāhmaṇa, who has studied the Atharva Veda, give his daughter to an Adhvaryu priest, or to a Chāndoga who has fulfilled his vow of chastity, and then perform his ritual ablution.
The seers said: O Śunaḥsakha, this oath you have sworn is the very thing desired by the twice-born; yet it is you who have committed the theft of the lotus-stalks against us all.
Śunaḥsakha said: What was spoken by you, men of accomplished rites who did not see where the stalks were first laid aside—this is true, this is no falsehood: the theft of the lotus-stalks was done by me.
For it was I who hid away these very lotus-stalks—behold them here! O sinless ones, I did this to test you reverend sages, and I have come for the protection of you all.
O you whose wealth is austerity, this was a fierce demoness, a deadly enchantment seeking your destruction, sent against you by Vṛṣādarbhi—and she has been slain by me.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This wicked, sinful thing, born of fire, would have done you harm; therefore I have come, O brāhmaṇas—know me to be Vāsava.
By your freedom from greed you have won imperishable worlds where every desire is fulfilled. Rise up from here at once, O twice-born, and attain them.
Bhīṣma said: Then the great seers, well pleased, said "So be it" to Puraṃdara, and together with Indra, lord of the thirty gods, they all went to heaven.
Thus these great-souled ones, though oppressed by the keenest hunger and tempted with enjoyments of every kind by exalted beings, gave way to no greed at all, and so they won heaven.
Therefore in all conditions of life a man should renounce greed. This, O king, is the highest dharma, renowned by the name of freedom from greed.
Let a man recite this noble tale in assemblies; he comes to share in happiness and meets with no calamities.
His ancestors are pleased, and so too the seers and the gods; and after death the man comes to share in glory, dharma, and wealth.
Bhīṣma said: On this very matter they recount an ancient tale—what came to pass on a pilgrimage to the holy fords, concerning an oath. Hear it.
O best of the Bhāratas, in olden days, O great king, a theft was committed over a lotus by royal seers and likewise by brāhmaṇa seers.
The seers, gathered together in the west at Prabhāsa, took counsel among themselves: "Let us all roam the earth and its holy fords—that is our task; come now, let us all set out."
O king, Śukra and Aṅgiras, and the learned Kavi, and Agastya, and Nārada and Parvata, Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Gautama, Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni—
and the seer Gālava, and Aṣṭaka, Bharadvāja, Arundhatī, the Vālakhilyas, Śibi, Dilīpa, Nahuṣa, Ambarīṣa, King Yayāti, Dhundhumāra, and Pūru—
O lord of men, setting at their head the mighty Śatakratu, slayer of Vṛtra, they journeyed; circling round all the holy fords, in the month of Māgha they came to the sacred Kauśikī ford.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Their sins washed away in all the fords, they went then to the most holy Lake of Brahmā; and those sages, splendid as fire, plunging into the water at the god's ford, fed upon lotus-stalks and lotus-blossoms.
There, O king, some dug up lotus-stalks, and other brāhmaṇas dug up lotus-fibres; then they saw a lotus being carried off, drawn up from the pool by Agastya.
Agastya said to all those foremost seers: "By whom was my fair-grown lotus taken? I suspect you. Let my lotus be returned to me—surely you ought not to steal the flower."
"I hear that the age destroys the strength of dharma; this oppression of dharma has now come and grows apace. Before unrighteousness here increases further, I shall depart for the other world for a long while."
"Before brāhmaṇas, with loud-proclaimed voice, recite the Vedas in the midst of villages for low-caste men to hear, before the king looks on at unrighteous lawsuits, I shall go to the other world."
"Before all men come to despise their betters, their elders, and the worthier—while this rule of the worse-over-the-better does not yet prevail—until then I shall depart for the other world for a long while."
"Before I see weak mortals devoured by the stronger, by the more powerful—for that reason I shall go to the other world for a long while, for I cannot bear to witness such things in the world of men."
Distressed, the seers said to that great sage: "We have not stolen your lotus. You ought not to lay a false charge upon us; we shall swear fierce oaths, O great seer."
Then those great seers, resolved and reverencing dharma in this manner, O lord of men, swore oaths each in turn, O king, together with their sons and grandsons.
Bhṛgu said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him, when reviled, revile back, when struck, strike back, and let him devour the flesh of others' backs through slander.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vasiṣṭha said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him be one given over to the neglect of Vedic study, let him drag a dog about, and let him become a beggar in the town.
Kaśyapa said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him trade in everything everywhere, let him grasp at goods left in his trust, and let him take up the office of false witness.
Gautama said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him live made arrogant by his own cleverness, let him trade in the basest of wares, and let him be a ploughman and grudging.
Aṅgiras said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him be impure, a counterfeit of a brāhmaṇa, let him drag a dog about, and let him be a destroyer of sacred knowledge.
Dhundhumāra said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him be ungrateful to his friends, let him beget offspring upon a śūdra woman, and let him eat the finest food alone.
Pūru said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him ply the trade of medicine, let him grow rich through his wife, and let his livelihood come from his father-in-law.
Dilīpa said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him go to the worlds of that brāhmaṇa who, in a village flooded by a broken well, is the husband of a low-caste woman.
Śukra said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him feed on backbiting slander, let him resort to coupling by day, and let him be a king's menial servant.
Jamadagni said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him study on days when study is forbidden, let him feed a mere friend at the funeral rite, and let him eat at a śūdra's funeral feast.
Śibi said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him die without having kindled the sacred fires, let him work obstruction at a sacrifice, and let him quarrel with ascetics.
Yayāti said: Whoever steals your lotus—wearing matted locks, let him beget offspring out of season upon a wife bound by a vow, and let him cast aside the Vedas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Nahuṣa said: Whoever steals your lotus—as a householder let him drive away the guest, as a consecrated man let him follow his lusts, and let him sell his learning for hire.
Ambarīṣa said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him be cruel and forsworn of dharma toward women, kinsmen, and cattle, and let him forsake even the brāhmaṇa.
Nārada said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him be ignorant within while reciting scripture outwardly with discordant, faulty verse, and let him despise his betters.
Nābhāga said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him speak falsehood always, let him quarrel with the good, and let him give his daughter away for a bride-price.
Kavi said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him kick a cow with his foot, let him make water facing the sun, and let him abandon one who has come to him for refuge.
Viśvāmitra said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him toil for years as a hireling, let him be a king's house-priest, and let him serve as ritual officiant for one unfit to sacrifice.
Parvata said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him be set as an officer over a village, let him travel in a donkey-cart, and let him drag dogs about to earn his living.
Bharadvāja said: Whoever steals your lotus—let there cling to him forever the sin that is the gathering-up of all sins, the sin that lies in cruelty and in falsehood.
Aṣṭaka said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him be a king devoid of wisdom, a lustful evildoer, and let him rule the earth by unrighteousness.
Gālava said: Whoever steals your lotus—let that man be worth less than the vilest of the wicked, a worker of his own sin, and let him boast aloud of the gift he has given.
Arundhatī said: Whoever steals your lotus—let her speak ill of her mother-in-law, let her be ill-disposed toward her husband, and let her eat the dainty food alone.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The Vālakhilyas said: Whoever steals your lotus—let him stand on one foot at the village gate to earn his bread, and though he knows dharma, let him be forsworn of dharma.
Paśusakha said: Whoever steals your lotus—let that twice-born man sleep at ease, neglecting the fire-oblation, and as a wandering renunciant let him follow his lusts.
Surabhī said: Whoever steals your lotus—let her tether the cow with a halter of coarse grass, let her milking-pail be of bronze, and let her milk with another's calf at the udder.
Bhīṣma said: Then, O lord of the Kurus, as they swore those many and various oaths, the thousand-eyed sovereign of the gods rejoiced greatly, gazing upon that wrathful chief of brāhmaṇas.
Then Maghavat, addressing that seer who had grown enraged, declared his own avowal in the midst of the brāhmaṇa-seers, the divine seers, and the royal seers—mark now, O king, what I tell you here today.
Śakra said: Whoever it is that takes your lotus—let that brāhmaṇa, having studied the Atharva Veda, give his daughter to an Adhvaryu priest, or to a Chāndoga who has fulfilled his vow of chastity, and then perform his ablution.
Whoever steals your lotus—let him study all the Vedas, let him be of holy character and righteous, and let him go to the abode of Brahmā.
Agastya said: What you have uttered, O slayer of Bala, is a blessing, not an oath of cursing. Let my lotus be returned to me—that is the eternal dharma.
Indra said: Reverend one, I did not take this lotus today out of greed; I took it from a wish to hear an exposition of dharma. You ought not to be angry.
This dharma I have now heard—the exaltation of sacred lore, the flawless dike of righteousness—belonging to the seers, everlasting, eternal, and imperishable.
So take back this lotus, O learned one, O best of sages; reverend and blameless one, you ought to forgive my transgression.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed by great Indra, that ascetic, sorely wrathful though he was, took back the lotus; and the wise sage became serene.
Then those forest-dwelling sages went on once more to the holy fords, and at the sacred fords they bathed their limbs.
Whoever, devout, reads this tale at every change of the moon will beget no foolish son, nor will he himself be cast out.
No calamity will touch him, nor fever, nor disease; freed of impurity and endowed with blessedness, after death he will attain heaven.
And whoever meditates upon this scripture, guarded by the seers, will go, O best of men, to the imperishable world of Brahmā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O bull of the Bhāratas, the umbrella and the pair of sandals that are given away in the rites of the funeral offering—by whom was this first set in motion? How did it come to be, and for what purpose is it given?
Not only in the rite of the śrāddha, but in works of merit as well, is this given. I wish to hear of it in full and in truth, O king.
Bhīṣma said: Listen attentively, O king, to the full account of the parasol and the sandals—how this became renowned in the world, and by whom it was first set in motion.
And how it attained imperishability, and how it came to be accounted meritorious—all of this, without remainder, I shall declare to you, O lord of men.
Hear this ancient tale of what came to pass of old, O ruler of men—the colloquy of Jamadagni with the great-souled Sūrya.
In olden days that blessed one in person sported with his bow, O lord; nocking arrow after arrow, the scion of Bhṛgu, it is said, loosed them forth.
All those arrows of his, blazing with splendor, that he had loosed, Reṇukā fetched and brought back, and gave them to him again and again, O unfailing one.
Then, delighted by the sound of the bowstring against the wrist-guard and of the arrow, he kept loosing them, and she kept bringing them back.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, when the sun had climbed to noon at the foot of the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, that brāhmaṇa, having loosed his shafts, said this to Reṇukā:
"Go, O wide-eyed one, fetch these arrows fallen from the bow, that I may loose them once again, O fair-browed one"—so he spoke, O lord of men.
As that lovely woman went, she took refuge midway in the shade of a tree and halted, for her head was scorched, and her feet likewise.
Having paused but a moment, the fair one, in dread of her husband's curse, the dark-eyed lady set out once more to fetch the arrows, and the illustrious woman returned, taking up those shafts.
Drenched in sweat, that fair-limbed one, bearing the pain in her feet, approached her husband, trembling out of fear of him.
Then the sage, wrathful, spoke these words to the fair-faced woman: "Reṇukā, why have you come so late?"—again and again.
Reṇukā said: My head was aflame, and my feet as well, O treasury of austerity. Held back by the sun's fierce heat, I took refuge in the shade of a tree.
For this reason, O brāhmaṇa, was this delay caused by me. Knowing this of me, O mighty one, be not wrathful, O treasury of austerity.
Jamadagni said: This very day, Reṇukā, this sun of blazing rays, the giver of your pain, I shall bring down with my arrows by the fiery power of my weapons.
Bhīṣma said: Drawing taut his celestial bow and taking up many shafts, he stood facing the sun, turning toward whatever quarter it moved.
Then, as he was about to strike, Sūrya, drawing near in the form of a brāhmaṇa, spoke these words, O son of Kuntī: "What wrong has the sun done you?
With his rays the sun in heaven, O learned one, draws up moisture from here and there; and that essence the day-maker pours down again in the rains.
Thence is born food, O brāhmaṇa, that brings well-being to men—for 'food is the breath of life,' as it is recited in the Vedas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, hidden within the clouds and girt about by his own rays, he rains down with showers upon these seven continents, O brāhmaṇa.
Thence, born of the leaves and flowers of herbs and creepers, all food, brought forth by the rains, comes into being, O lord.
All the birth-rites, the vows and the initiations, the gifts of cows and the marriages, and likewise the abundance of sacrifices—
the sacrificial sessions and the gifts, the unions and the heapings-up of wealth—all proceed from food, as you well know, O scion of Bhṛgu.
Whatever delightful things there are, and whatever undertakings—all arise from food; what is well known I now recount to you.
For all this that I have recounted you yourself know, O brāhmaṇa. I entreat your favor, O brāhmaṇa-sage: why should the sun be struck down by you?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When the light-maker thus pleaded with him, what course did Jamadagni, the best of sages, of great splendor, resolve upon?
Bhīṣma said: Though the sun pleaded thus, the sage Jamadagni, radiant as fire, did not come to peace at all, O joy of the Kurus.
Then Sūrya, in the guise of a brāhmaṇa, with hands joined and bowing low, addressed him in honeyed speech, O lord of peoples:
"Moving is the mark, O brāhmaṇa-sage, of the ever-traveling sun. How will you take aim at the moving day-maker, who is forever in motion?"
Jamadagni said: Whether still or moving, I know you with the eye of knowledge. Without fail, today, the imparting of discipline must be wrought upon you by me.
In the afternoon you pause for half the blink of an eye, O day-maker; there I shall mark you, O Sūrya. Of this I have no doubt.
Sūrya said: Without a doubt you will mark me, O brāhmaṇa-sage, O best of bowmen. Yet though I have done you injury, know me, blessed one, as one who has come to you for refuge.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma said: Then the blessed Jamadagni laughed and said to him: "No fear need be felt by you, O Sūrya, for you have come to me in submission.
The uprightness that is in brāhmaṇas, and the steadfastness in the surface of the earth, the gentleness of the moon, and the depth of Varuṇa,
the blaze of Agni, the radiance of Meru, and the scorching might of the burning sun—whoever would transgress these, he might slay one who has sought refuge.
He who slays one who has sought refuge would be as a defiler of his teacher's bed, and would be as a slayer of a brāhmaṇa, and would be as one who drinks strong liquor.
But, my friend, devise a remedy for this misfortune, so that the path, scorched by your rays, may become easy to travel."
Bhīṣma said: Having said only this much, the upholder of the Bhṛgus then fell silent; whereupon Sūrya at once gave him a parasol and a pair of sandals.
Sūrya said: O great sage, accept this parasol, a shelter for the head that wards off my rays, and these leather sandals for the protection of the feet.
And from this day forth this shall pass current in the world, and in all meritorious gifts it shall be supreme and imperishable.
Bhīṣma said: Thus were the sandals and the parasol set in motion here by Sūrya; this meritorious thing is renowned throughout the three worlds, O Bhārata.
Therefore bestow upon brāhmaṇas the finest parasol and sandals; great indeed shall be your merit. Of this I have no doubt.
For whoever, O best of the Bhāratas, should give to a brāhmaṇa a parasol, white and of a hundred ribs, he, when he has departed, flourishes in happiness.
He dwells in the world of Śakra, ever honored by brāhmaṇas and by the apsarases and by the gods, O bull of the Bhāratas.
He who gives a pair of sandals to a brāhmaṇa scorched by the heat, to a snātaka, O mighty-armed one, to a brāhmaṇa firm in his vows—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
he too attains worlds honored by the gods, and in the world of cows, filled with joy, he dwells when he has departed, O Bhārata.
This, O best of the Bhāratas, has been told by me in full—the fruit of the gift of parasol and sandals, O most excellent of the Bhāratas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O delight of the Kurus, the fruit that comes from groves and from reservoirs of water—that I wish to hear from you this day, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Bhīṣma said: Fair to behold, clothed in forest, adorned with bright mineral ores, and furnished with all seeds—such land is here said to be the best.
Of its choice tracts, and of the establishing of tanks, and of all matters concerning water, I shall speak in due order.
I shall tell, too, what virtues belong to tanks once they are made; throughout the three worlds, everywhere honored is he who possesses a tank.
The establishing of tanks is a dwelling-place of friends, friendly, an increaser of friends, a begetter of fame, and most excellent.
The wise declare a tank well made in a fitting region to be the fruit of dharma, of artha, and of kāma—a very field that is a great refuge.
One should regard a tank as belonging to creatures of the four kinds, and all tanks bestow the highest prosperity.
Gods, men, gandharvas, ancestors, serpents and rākṣasas, and the unmoving creatures too, all resort to a reservoir of water.
Therefore I shall declare to you those virtues that are remembered as belonging to a tank, and the winning of fruit therein, as proclaimed by the sages.
When in a tank the water of a single rainy season abides for a man, the wise declare his fruit to be the fruit of the agnihotra.
When in his tank the water abides through the autumn season, he, when he has departed, gains the supreme fruit of a thousand cows.
When the water abides in his tank through the season of early winter, he gains the fruit of a sacrifice rich in gold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For him in whose tank there is water in the cold season, the wise declare the fruit to be that of the agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
He whose well-made tank is a great refuge in the spring enjoys the fruit of the atirātra sacrifice.
When in the hot season the drinking-water abides in his tank, the sages know his fruit to be equal to that of the vājapeya.
He delivers his whole lineage, in whose excavated reservoir cows drink water, and good men always.
He in whose tank thirsting cows drink the water, and deer and birds and men, gains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice.
Whatever water they drink there, and where they bathe and rest—all this avails the giver of the tank, when he has departed, for eternity.
Water is hard to come by, my friend, and especially so in the world beyond; through the gift of drinking-water, lasting contentment arises.
Give sesame, give drinking-water, give lamps, and keep watchful; rejoice together with your kinsmen—for among the departed these things are hard to come by.
Heavier than all gifts, and distinguished above all gifts, is drinking-water, O tiger among men; therefore it must surely be given.
Thus has the supreme fruit that lies in tanks been told; hereafter I shall speak of the planting of trees as well.
Of unmoving beings six kinds are proclaimed: trees, shrubs, climbers, creepers, those whose pith lies in the bark, and the grasses.
These are the kinds of trees; in the planting of them these are the virtues—fame in the world of men, and after death a blessed fruit as well.
He wins renown in the world and is honored by the ancestors; even when he has gone to the world of the gods, his name does not perish.
The planter of trees delivers both his line of ancestors, past and yet to come, O Bhārata; therefore let one plant trees.
These trees become his sons—of this there is no doubt; and when he has passed to the other world, he attains heaven and imperishable realms.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
With their blossoms the trees honor the hosts of the gods, and with their fruits the ancestors, and with their shade the guests, my friend—these earth-born ones.
Kinnaras, serpents, and rākṣasas, gods, gandharvas, and men, and the hosts of sages too, all take refuge in the trees.
Blossoming and bearing fruit, they gratify men here; and as sons do, the trees deliver the giver of trees in the world beyond.
Therefore by one who seeks the good, trees should ever be planted beside a tank, and should be tended as one's sons; for in the law they are accounted his sons.
The maker of a tank, the planter of trees, and the brāhmaṇa who has offered sacrifice—these are exalted in heaven, and so are others who speak the truth.
Therefore let a man dig a reservoir, and let him plant pleasure-gardens; let him worship with sacrifices of many kinds, and let him speak the truth unfailingly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Declare to me the whole duty of the householder, O bull of the Bhāratas; by doing what, O king, does a man attain prosperity in this world?
Bhīṣma said: On this matter I shall relate to you an ancient happening, O lord of men, the dialogue of Vāsudeva and the Earth, O descendant of Bharata.
Having praised the goddess Earth, the mighty Vāsudeva questioned her, O best of the Bhāratas, on the very thing you now ask of me.
Vāsudeva said: For one who has taken up the householder's life, by me or by one of my kind, what, O Earth, must of necessity be done, and by doing what does a man become happy?
The Earth said: The seers, the ancestors, the gods, and men as well, O Mādhava, are to be worshipped with sacrifice and honored with reverence; learn from me how this is done.
Ever the gods with sacrifice, and men with hospitality, and the worthy ones day after day according to their wish—let him serve them constantly; thereby the hosts of seers are made glad, O slayer of Madhu.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Let him tend the sacred fire daily, and before eating perform the offering of bali; thus indeed are the gods pleased, O slayer of Madhu.
Day by day let him perform the śrāddha with food, or with water, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.
From cooked food let him make the Vaiśvadeva offering in the fire according to rule—to Agni and Soma, to the All-Gods, and thereafter to Dhanvantari.
To the Lord of Creatures too a separate oblation is ordained; and in the same order let him carry out the rite of the bali-offering.
In the south to Yama, in the west to Varuṇa, and in the north to Soma, and in the center of the dwelling to the twice-born.
To Dhanvantari in the northeast, and in the east to Śakra, O Mādhava; and to Manu, they say, the bali is offered at the door of the house; while to the Maruts and the deities he should offer the bali within the house.
Likewise to the All-Gods let him offer the bali into the open air, and to the spirits that roam by night let him offer the bali in the nighttime.
Having duly made the bali in this way, let him give alms to the twice-born; and if no brāhmaṇa is to be found, let him take up the choicest portion and cast it into the fire.
When a man wishes to offer a śrāddha to the ancestors, let him perform these other rites afterward, once the śrāddha-rite is concluded.
Having gratified the ancestors, let him perform the bali according to rule; then let him make the Vaiśvadeva offering, and after that the formal address of the brāhmaṇas.
Then with the food that remains let him feed his guests as well, with worship first, O great king; thereby he gives satisfaction to men.
Because he abides only for a fleeting while, he is called atithi, the guest who keeps no fixed day.
To his teacher, to his father, to a friend, and to a trusted guest, let him always announce, "This much is in my house, mine to give."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever they may say, that let him do—so the law is laid down; and the householder, O Kṛṣṇa, should ever eat only what remains after others are served.
A king, a priest, a snātaka, a teacher, and a father-in-law—if they have stayed away a full year—let him honor with the madhuparka offering.
And for the dogs, for the outcastes, and for the birds let him scatter food upon the ground; this indeed is called the Vaiśvadeva rite, ordained for both evening and morning.
Whoever, free of grudging spirit, performs these duties of the householder, having attained the highest prosperity here, is exalted in heaven hereafter.
Bhīṣma said: Having heard these words of the Earth, the mighty Vāsudeva did accordingly ever after; do you too conduct yourself in this same way.
Thus mindful of the householder's duty, O ruler of men, you shall win fame in this world and, departing, shall attain heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This thing called the giving of light—of what nature is it, O bull of the Bhāratas? How did it arise, and what is its fruit? Tell me of it.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they cite an ancient tale, the discourse of Manu the Lord of Creatures and of Suvarṇa, O descendant of Bharata.
There was once an ascetic, Suvarṇa by name; golden of hue in color, he was renowned as Suvarṇa, "the gold-colored one."
Endowed with high birth, character, and virtue, and grown supreme in the study of sacred texts, he surpassed by his own merits many who had sprung from his lineage.
On a certain day that brāhmaṇa beheld Manu and approached him, and there the two of them exchanged inquiries after one another's welfare.
Then those two, whose every resolve was fulfilled, sat down together upon a delightful slab of rock on Meru, the golden mountain.
There the two conversed in tales of many a theme, concerning the brāhmaṇa-seers, the gods, and the daityas, the great-souled ones of ancient days.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then Suvarṇa spoke these words to the lord Manu, the self-born: "For the good of all beings, be pleased to answer a question of mine."
"The deities are worshipped with flowers, O Lord of Creatures—what is this, and how did it come about? Declare to me too the fruit that attends it."
Manu said: On this too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Śukra and Bali at their meeting.
To Bali, son of Virocana, while he ruled over the three worlds, there came in haste Śukra, the upholder of Bhṛgu's line.
Having honored that scion of Bhṛgu with the arghya and the rest, that lord of the asuras, lavish in his largesse, afterward took his seat according to rule.
There arose this very topic which you have now recounted, concerning the fruit that lies in the giving of flowers, incense, and lamps.
Then the lord of the daityas put this excellent question to the chief of seers: "What is the fruit of giving flowers, incense, and lamps, O best knower of the Brahman? That, O foremost of the twice-born, be pleased to tell."
Śukra said: Austerity arose first; from it, immediately after, came the Law; and in this same interval came the creepers and the healing herbs as well.
And the essence of Soma came to be in manifold forms upon the face of the earth—the nectar and the poison, and those other things of like kinds.
Nectar gives the mind delight and at once bestows nourishment; sharp poison wholly wearies the mind by its very smell.
Know nectar to be auspicious, and grievous poison to be inauspicious; all healing herbs are nectar, while poison is a fiery power born of fire.
Because they gladden the mind (manas) and also bestow splendor, they are called sumanasaḥ, "flowers," by men who do righteous deeds.
The pure man who gives flowers to the deities—because of him too they are called sumanasaḥ, since by them the deities are well pleased.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
To whatever god, O lord, the flowers are offered for the sake of blessing, by that gift is that god made gracious to the giver, O ruler of the daityas.
But the healing herbs are to be known severally—the fierce, the gentle, and the radiant—of many potencies and of many forms as well.
Of the trees fit for sacrifice and of those unfit, learn from me, and of the garlands proper to the asuras and of those wholesome for the gods.
And which are dear to the rākṣasas, the gods, and the yakṣas, and which are beloved of the ancestors and of men—all in their due order.
Wild and cultivated alike, sown in tilled ground or mountain-dwelling, thornless or thorn-bearing, possessed of fragrance, form, and savor.
Twofold is the fragrance held to be that is born of flowers, the pleasant and the unpleasant; let him understand that flowers of pleasant fragrance are for the gods.
Of thornless trees, and those mostly white in color—their flowers are ever pleasing to the gods, O lord.
And the water-born garlands, the lotuses and the like, and whatever others there are—those let the discerning man give to the gandharvas, the nāgas, and the yakṣas.
Herbs with red flowers, pungent and beset with thorns, are shown in the Atharvan texts to be for the working of sorcery against foes.
But those of sharp potency, hard to grasp and thorny, of color mostly red, and the black ones too—let him offer to the spirits.
Those flowers that gladden the mind and heart, sweet when crushed and fair of form, are held to be for men, O lord.
But let him not bring such as have grown in cremation-grounds, nor such as have sprung up in temples of the gods, into rites of prosperity, into weddings, or into private chambers.
The gentle flowers that grow on mountain-slopes let him present to the gods, gentle and sprinkled and besprinkled with water, as is fitting and as tradition prescribes.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By fragrance the gods are pleased, by the sight the yakṣas and rākṣasas, the nāgas by actual enjoyment; but men by all three of these.
At once he gladdens the gods, and they, being gladdened, foster mortals, fulfilling their resolves and the longings of their hearts.
The gods are ever pleased when honored, and they honor in return; but when slighted and spurned, they burn up the basest of men.
Hereafter I shall declare the fruit in the rite of giving incense; and the manifold incenses, the good and the bad alike, learn from me.
The resinous, the simple, and the compounded—these are the three; their fragrance may be pleasant or unpleasant; hear this from me in detail.
The resins, save that of the sallakī tree, are dear to the gods; and of them all guggulu is the choicest—so it is settled.
Aloe-wood is the best of the simple kinds for the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and serpents; while the sallakī-born resin, and whatever is of that sort, is coveted by the daityas.
Then with the fragrances of sarja-resin and the like, of earthy and woody substances, combined with treacle and fermented liquor, is the incense ordained for men.
It is held to give instant satisfaction to gods, dānavas, and spirits; but those others that serve for pleasure are reckoned to be for men.
Those very grounds of merit that were named in the giving of flowers are to be understood in the matter of incense too; these same are what increase favor.
In the giving of lamps I shall declare the unsurpassed fruit that attends it—how, with what, and when they should be given, and of what kind they are.
Light, splendor, and radiance are described as ever upward-moving; therefore the giving of lights increases the splendor of men.
Blind darkness and the gloom of night, and the sun's southward course; from this is the northward course; and on this account the giving of light is praised.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Because this light moves upward and is the very remedy for darkness, therefore the giver becomes one of upward course—so it is determined.
Because the gods are radiant, mighty, and luminous, while the rākṣasas are of darkness, therefore the lamp is given.
By the giving of light a man becomes keen-eyed and endowed with radiance; having given such lamps, let him not damage them, nor steal them, nor cause them to perish.
The stealer of a lamp becomes blind, doomed to a dark course and of dim luster; but the giver of lamps shines forth, garlanded with lamps, in the world of heaven.
With clarified butter is the first manner of lighting, and the second with the saps of herbs; but with fat, marrow, bone, or resinous gum it must not be done by one who desires prosperity.
At a mountain precipice, in a thicket, at a shrine, or at a crossroads, let him ever be a giver of lamps who desires his own welfare.
The man who gives lamps becomes ever the lamp of his lineage, pure of soul; he attains to radiance and to dwelling in the same sphere as the luminaries.
In the rites of bali-offering I shall declare the merits and the rising fruits of the act—for gods, yakṣas, serpents, and men, and for spirits and rākṣasas.
Those whose Brāhmaṇas, gods, guests, and children eat no portion offered first—know them to be very rākṣasas, devoid of the auspicious vaṣaṭ-call.
Therefore one should offer the first portion, duly honored, to the gods, and bowing his head should present the oblation untiringly.
For the household deities ever look in hope toward the home, and so too the outer comers, the other beings—Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and serpents.
By what is given from here the gods and the ancestors live, and being pleased they gratify these givers with long life, with fame, and with wealth.
To the gods one should present oblations together with flowers—holy ones graced with drops of curds, sweet-scented and fair to behold.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas the oblations should be rich in blood and flesh, set forth with wine and liquor and adorned with parched grain and unguents.
For the serpents, ever dear to them, oblations mingled with lotuses and water-lilies; and to the spirits one should present sesame well supplied with molasses.
He who gives the first portion shall himself enjoy the first portion, endowed with strength and beauty; therefore let him offer the first portion, duly honored, to the gods.
Day after day his dwelling blazes with light; and those household deities of his are to be worshipped by one who desires welfare, by him who offers the foremost portion outstretched.
Thus did the descendant of Bhṛgu, Kāvya, declare this to the lord of the Asuras; Manu told it to Suvarṇa, and Suvarṇa to Nārada.
And Nārada too told these virtues to me, O greatly resplendent one; do you also, having understood all this here, act upon it, my son.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard, O best of the Bhāratas, the fruit of those who offer flowers and incense, and the rule of oblation; you should tell me more of it.
What is the fruit of giving incense, and likewise of the lamp, and for what purpose are oblations cast forth by householders?
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale—the colloquy of Agastya and of Bhṛgu concerning Nahuṣa.
For Nahuṣa, O great king, a royal sage of mighty austerity, had attained the sovereignty of the gods by his good deeds here.
There too, O king, Nahuṣa, dwelling in the third heaven, remained devout, performing manifold rites both human and divine.
All those human rites of that great-souled one continued in the third heaven, O king, as did the eternal divine ones.
Fire-rites, kindling-sticks, kuśa grass and flowers, oblations with food and parched grain, the burning of incense and the offering of lamps—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
all this went on in the house of that great-souled king; and even in the third heaven he performed sacrifices of muttered prayer and sacrifices of the mind.
And that lord of the gods worshipped all the deities according to rule, each in its proper manner as of old, O subduer of foes.
Then, through his having become Indra, pride entered into him, and all his rites began to fall away, O ruler of the earth.
Drunk with the boon that had been granted him, he made the sages bear him as draught-animals; and lapsing from his rites, he came into weakness.
As he, overcome by pride, made the foremost sages rich in austerity bear him, a very long time passed by.
Then he began to yoke the sages by turns to draw him, and the turn of Agastya too came round, O Bhārata.
Then Bhṛgu of great splendor, best of the knowers of Brahman, came and, approaching Agastya who was in his hermitage, spoke thus.
Why, O great sage, should we endure this insolence of Nahuṣa, this evil-minded lord of the gods?
Agastya said: How can this one be cursed by me, O great sage, to whom a boon was granted by the boon-giver—a boon known to you?
"Whoever shall come within the path of my gaze, let him fall under my power"—such was the boon this one begged of the god as he went up to heaven.
So he has not been burned by me, nor, beyond doubt, by you; nor has he been cursed or cast down by any other foremost sage.
And of old the nectar was given him to drink, O mighty one; for that reason this great-souled one is not cast down by us.
The god granted a boon that brings sorrow to creatures; that basest of men commits deeds of unrighteousness against the twice-born.
Tell us what is fitting for the occasion in this matter, O best of speakers; and as you may direct, so shall we act.
Bhṛgu said: By the command of the Grandsire I have come to you, that we may retaliate now that mighty Nahuṣa is set upon his arrogance.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This very day that most evil-minded king of the gods will yoke you to his chariot; this very day, by my power, I shall make the upstart no longer Indra.
This day, before your eyes, I shall set Indra of the hundred sacrifices in his place, dislodging the evil-doing, most wicked-minded one from the station of Indra.
And this day that false lord of the gods will strike you with his foot—dull-witted, his mind smitten by fate, working his own ruin.
Him who has transgressed dharma, that sinner and enemy of the twice-born, I—made wrathful past bearing by his outrage—shall curse in fury, saying, "Become a serpent!"
Then that most evil-minded one, his radiance struck down by the word of shame, I shall hurl to the earth before your eyes, O great sage—
Nahuṣa, the evil-doer, deluded by lordship and might; and as it pleases you, so shall I do it, O sage.
Thus addressed by Bhṛgu, the imperishable son of Mitra and Varuṇa, Agastya, became greatly pleased and freed of his distress.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How was he undone, and how was he cast down upon the earth, and how did he come to lose his Indra-hood? This you should tell me.
Bhīṣma said: While the two were thus conversing, all the rites of that great-souled one were going forward—those that were divine and those that were human.
Likewise the gifts of lamps and all the appurtenances, the rite of oblation and whatever else, and libations of various kinds—all these arose for that great-souled king of the gods.
In the world of the gods and the world of men, good observances are taught by the wise; if these are kept, O king of kings, householders prosper—through gifts of incense and of lamps, and likewise through acts of homage.
As the first portion of cooked food is given to a Brāhmaṇa, and as oblations are set within the precincts of the house—by this the deities are pleased.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And as great as is the householder's own satisfaction in the rite of oblation, a delight a hundredfold greater arises among the deities.
Thus the good praise the giving of incense and the giving of lamps, joined with acts of homage, as bringing virtue to the self.
By the rite that the wise man performs with bathing and with water, joined with acts of homage, the deities are pleased; and all the household deities, worshipped according to rule, are gratified.
Holding to this understanding, that lord of men, Nahuṣa, having attained the great lordship of the gods, accomplished this marvel.
But after some while, when the wasting of his fortune drew near, he scorned all this and no longer did such as this.
Then that lord of the gods fell away from the rite of oblation; he no longer performed the observance of incense, lamp, and water as was fitting; and thereupon the sphere of his sacrifice was beset by Rākṣasas.
Then that mighty one, as if smiling, summoned in haste Agastya, the best of sages, from the bank of the Sarasvatī, to draw his vehicle.
Then Bhṛgu of great splendor said to the son of Mitra and Varuṇa: "Close your eyes, while I enter into your matted locks."
Then, while Agastya stood motionless as a post, the unfailing Bhṛgu of mighty splendor entered into his matted locks, to bring about the king's downfall.
Then that king of the gods came up to the sage to make him draw his car; and thereupon Agastya spoke this word to the lord of the gods, O lord of peoples.
"Yoke me quickly, O Indra; and to what region shall I bear you? Wherever you shall bid, there will I carry you, O lord of the gods."
Thus addressed by him, Nahuṣa yoked that sage; and Bhṛgu, lodged within his matted locks, was exceedingly glad.
Nor then did Bhṛgu let himself be seen, knowing the power of the boon granted to the great-souled Nahuṣa.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Agastya, though yoked by Nahuṣa, did not grow angry; yet the king goaded him with the whip, O Bhārata.
That righteous one did not grow angry; then the king of the gods, in wrath, struck Agastya's head with his left foot.
When that head was struck, Bhṛgu, hidden within the matted locks, sorely enraged, cursed the evil-hearted Nahuṣa.
Bhṛgu said: Since in wrath you struck this great sage upon the head with your foot, therefore become a serpent and go swiftly to the earth, O most wicked-minded one!
Thus addressed by him, by Bhṛgu unseen, he then became a serpent and fell to the surface of the earth, O bull of the Bhāratas.
For had Nahuṣa beheld Bhṛgu, O lord of the earth, he would not have had the power to cast him down by his splendor.
But by those various gifts and austerities and observances, though fallen to the earth, O great king, he remained possessed of his memory and besought Bhṛgu's grace, saying, "Let there be an end to my curse."
Then Agastya, moved by compassion, entreated Bhṛgu for the ending of the curse, O great king; and he, filled with pity, granted it.
Bhṛgu said: A king named Yudhiṣṭhira, upholder of the Kurus, shall arise; he will release you from the curse. So saying, he vanished.
And Agastya of great splendor, having accomplished the purpose of Indra of the hundred sacrifices, went to his own hermitage, honored by the twice-born.
And Nahuṣa too, O king, delivered by you from that curse, went to the abode of Brahmā before your very eyes, O ruler of men.
But then, having cast Nahuṣa down to the earth, Bhṛgu went to the abode of Brahmā and reported the matter to Brahmā.
Then the Grandsire, having brought Śakra back, said to the gods: "O gods, through a boon of mine Nahuṣa won the kingship, and he, cast down by the wrathful Agastya, has gone to the surface of the earth."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And the gods can in no wise abide without a king; therefore let this Śakra again be consecrated to the sovereignty of the gods."
As the Grandsire spoke thus, O Pārtha, the gods, rejoicing, answered the Grandsire, "So be it."
Consecrated to the sovereignty of the gods by the blessed Brahmā, Vāsava, O tiger among kings, shone forth as before.
Thus did this come to pass of old, through Nahuṣa's transgression; and by those very deeds was Nahuṣa once more made perfect.
Therefore lamps should be offered at evening by householders; the giver of lamps obtains the divine eye after death, and those who give lamps come to be radiant as the full moon.
For as many twinklings of the eye as the lamp burns, for so many years does the giver of the lamp become a man of beauty and of wealth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Those dull men who steal the property of Brāhmaṇas, O bull of the Bhāratas—the cruel-doing, deluded—whither do such men go?
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale—the colloquy of a Caṇḍāla and a base-born Kṣatriya, O Bhārata.
The man of royal birth said: You are of aged aspect, O Caṇḍāla, yet you behave like a child; you who haunt the dust of dogs and donkeys—why do you shrink from cattle?
"The work assigned to a Caṇḍāla is condemned by the virtuous. Why do you pour into a vessel of water that which has been defiled by the dust raised by cattle?"
The Caṇḍāla said: O king, in a former age the dust raised by a Brahmin's cattle, as they were being driven off, defiled the Soma; and the twice-born who then drank that Soma—
And that consecrated king too, together with all his officiating priests, swiftly entered hell, for they had lived off that property belonging to a Brahmin.
And those men who there drank the milk, the clarified butter, and the curds—Brahmins together with the Kṣatriyas—all of them entered hell.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By that milk the husband and wife, watching over their cattle in righteous conduct, struck down their own sons and grandsons as the cows tossed and shook themselves.
I dwelt there, O king, a celibate student with my senses subdued; and the alms I had gathered, O lord of men, were defiled by the dust of those cows.
Having eaten that, O king, I became a Caṇḍāla when I died; and that king who stole a Brahmin's property came to a state without any foundation.
Therefore let no one ever take anything whatever of a Brahmin's wealth. Look upon me—what I have become—for having eaten what was defiled by the dust of a Brahmin's property.
Therefore even the Soma must not be sold by a discerning man, for the wise here condemn the sale of Soma.
Those people who buy it, O king, and those who sell it, all alike, on reaching the abode of the son of Vivasvat, go to the hell Raurava.
But should a learned reciter of the Veda knowingly sell Soma that has been defiled by dust, becoming a usurer he is ruined for a long night of time; reaching the thirty hells, he subsists upon the dung of dogs.
The life of a dog, excessive pride, and transgression against the wives of friends—Dharma weighed these in the balance, and excessive pride proved the heaviest of all.
Look upon this sinful dog, discolored, tawny, and lean, who through excessive pride toward living beings has come to this condition.
In another birth, O mighty one, I was born into a great family endowed with wealth, having mastered both knowledge and discernment.
Although I knew these faults, I yet acted out of arrogance then; in my fury I devoured the flesh from the backs of living creatures.
And so, by that conduct and by that eating, I have come to this state. Behold the turning of time!
Behold me, as if my garment's hem were ablaze, as if tormented by bees, running about in a frenzy, covered with dust.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By recitation of the sacred texts householders cross over great sin, and likewise by gifts of many kinds, even as the wise have declared.
