Maheśvara said: Brahmā created Surabhī, the cow of nectar, the giver of milk; once created, she multiplied manifold, streaming forth milk like nectar.
The foam dropped from the mouth of her calf fell upon my body; then in anger I scorched the cows, and they took on their many colours.
Then I was brought to peace by the world's teacher, who knew what was fitting; and he gave me this bull for my banner and for my mount.
Umā said: Your dwellings are of many forms, endowed with every kind of quality; forsaking these, O blessed one, how is it that you delight in the cremation-ground?
Terrible, strewn with hair and bones, crowded with skulls like potsherds, teeming with vultures and jackals, thronged with the fires of a hundred pyres;
Unclean, strewn with flesh, miry with marrow and blood, littered with heaps of carrion, resounding with the howls of jackals.
Maheśvara said: Seeking the pure, I roam the whole earth by night, and nothing more pure than the cremation-ground is to be found here.
Therefore, of all dwellings, my mind delights in the cremation-ground, shaded by the branches of the banyan, adorned with cast-off garlands.
And there too my hosts of spirits take their delight, O fair-faced one; nor can I, O goddess, bear to dwell apart from my spirit-troops.
This dwelling I hold to be pure and heavenly; holy and supreme, it is frequented by those who seek purity.
Umā said: O blessed lord of all beings, foremost of all upholders of dharma, Pināka-handed giver of boons, this great doubt is mine.
This whole host of sages, O lord, crying "Austerity! Austerity!", wanders through the world seeking austerity in manifold forms.
For the sake of this assembly of seers, and to please me, O subduer of foes, deign to resolve this doubt of mine here.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By what marks is dharma declared? And how can it be practised by men who have not found dharma? O knower of dharma, tell me, O lord.
Nārada said: Then the whole host of sages honoured the goddess in return with words adorned by the meaning of Ṛc-verses and with hymns, O best of those who know the truth.
Maheśvara said: Non-injury, truthful speech, compassion for all beings, self-control, and giving according to one's power—this is the highest dharma of the householder.
No thought toward another's wife, protection of women left in trust, abstaining from taking what is not given, and shunning honey-wine and meat;
This fivefold dharma, of many branches, yielding happiness, is the store of merit to be heaped up by embodied beings devoted to dharma.
Umā said: O Lord, having been asked of my doubt, you should explain it to me — the dharma proper to the four orders, that which brings merit to each in its own order.
What kind of dharma belongs to the brāhmaṇa, what kind to the kṣatriya? What is the mark of dharma for the vaiśya, and what its mark for the śūdra?
Maheśvara said: Justly, O greatly blessed one, has your doubt been raised. The twice-born in this world are ever the highly honored gods upon earth.
Fasting is ever the dharma of the brāhmaṇa — of this there is no doubt; for he is born for the sake of dharma and is fit to attain unto Brahman.
For him, O goddess, the performance of dharmic rites, the observance of vows according to rule, and likewise the sacred initiation — these befit the twice-born alone.
For the honoring of teacher and deity, consisting in the practice of self-study — this wellspring of dharma must be observed by embodied beings devoted to dharma.
Umā said: O Lord, herein lies my doubt; you should explain it to me. Proclaim with precision the dharma of the four orders.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Maheśvara said: The hearing of the secret teachings is dharma, and the keeping of the Vedic vows; devotion to the observance of vows is dharma, and the gracious service of the teacher's feet.
Devotion to the gathering of alms is dharma; constant fasting is dharma; constant self-study is dharma, and likewise the stage of chaste studentship.
And when permitted by his teacher, the twice-born should return home; thereafter he should take a fitting wife according to the rule.
The shunning of a śūdra's food is dharma, and the following of the good path; constant fasting is dharma, and likewise continence.
Having kindled the sacred fires, studying, offering oblation, with senses restrained, eating the remnants of sacrifice, moderate in food, truthful of speech and pure — such is the householder.
Devotion to the vow of hospitality is dharma, and the maintaining of the three fires is dharma; the iṣṭi-rites and the animal sacrifices he should perform in due order.
Sacrifice is the highest dharma, and likewise non-injury toward embodied beings; not to eat before others is dharma, and the eating of the sacrificial remnants.
To eat afterward, once the household has eaten, is declared to be dharma — especially for the brāhmaṇa householder learned in the Veda.
Harmony of character between husband and wife is the dharma of householders, and the constant offering of flowers and oblations to the household deities.
Daily anointing of the dwelling is dharma, and likewise constant fasting — in a house well-swept and freshly smeared, where the smoke of ghee rises up.
This is the householder's dharma among the twice-born, the sustainer of the world; among the good twice-born it ever holds sway, always.
But that dharma pertaining to the kṣatriya, which you have raised, O goddess — that I shall declare to you; hear it from me with attentive mind.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The dharma of the kṣatriya is held to be, first of all, the protection of the people; for the king who enjoys his appointed reward is thereby joined with dharma.
The lord of men who protects his people in accordance with dharma — for him there are worlds won by dharma, accumulated through the protection of his people.
Therein the king's foremost dharma is self-restraint and self-study, the busy tending of the sacred fire, and likewise giving and learning.
The wearing of the sacred thread, sacrifice, and the performance of dharmic rites; the maintenance of his dependents is dharma, and unfailingness when a deed is to be done.
Standing firm in just punishment is dharma; the performance of Vedic sacrifices is dharma; abiding by lawful judgment is dharma, and likewise delight in truthful speech.
The king who lends a hand to the distressed is exalted both here and hereafter; and one who, valiant for the sake of cattle and brāhmaṇas, meets his death in battle, attains the worlds won by the horse-sacrifice, in the abode of the third heaven.
The constant dharma of the vaiśya is the tending of cattle and tillage, the busy tending of the sacred fire, and likewise giving and learning.
Trade conducted upon the honest path, hospitality, tranquility, self-restraint, the welcoming of brāhmaṇas, and liberality — this is the eternal dharma of the vaiśya.
Sesame, perfumes, and liquids he should never sell anywhere; following the merchant's calling, the vaiśya keeps to the honest path.
Full hospitality to the three orders, according to his means and as is fitting — and the highest constant dharma of the śūdra is service rendered to the twice-born.
That śūdra, steadfast in austerity, true to his word, with senses conquered, who serves the guest that has arrived, accumulates great austerity.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having abandoned violence, of pure conduct, a worshipper of the deities and the twice-born — such a wise śūdra is united with the cherished fruits of dharma.
All this has been told to you, O lovely one, concerning each of the four orders here. What else, O blessed one, do you wish to hear?
Umā said: You have told the separate, auspicious dharmas befitting the four orders. But that dharma which is all-pervading, O Lord — that one tell me.
Maheśvara said: The brāhmaṇas were created by the Maker, seeking virtue, out of the very essence of the world, to ferry all the worlds across — gods upon earth among mortals.
Of them I shall declare this arising of the fruit of dharmic deeds; for the dharma that is among the brāhmaṇas is held to be the supreme dharma.
But these three were created by the Self-Born for the sake of the world's dharma, ever created for the bringing forth of the earth; hear of them too from me.
The supreme dharma is that declared in the Veda; another is that found in the smṛti-treatises; another, it is said, is that practiced by the cultured — these three are the eternal dharmas.
A brāhmaṇa learned in the three Vedas, yet not living merely by recitation, performing the three duties, having gone through the three stages, friendly toward all — such a one is held to be a true twice-born.
These six duties the Lord of the world declared for the livelihood of the brāhmaṇas; hear them, O attentive one.
Sacrificing and officiating at sacrifice, likewise giving and receiving gifts, teaching and being taught — the twice-born of the six duties is a sharer in dharma.
Constant self-study is dharma; sacrifice is the eternal dharma; and giving, according to his means and according to rule, is praised in him.
But this is the supreme dharma, ever practiced among the good: the householder's life of the wholly pure is a great treasury of dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His self purified by the five sacrifices, truthful of speech, free of malice, a giver, an honorer of brāhmaṇas, his dwelling well-swept —
free of pride and ever upright, speaking words made gentle, delighting in the guest who has come, making his meal of the remnants of food —
who offers, as is right, water for the feet, the welcome-offering, a seat, a bed, a lamp, and shelter too — he is the righteous one.
Rising at dawn and sipping water for purification, inviting the guest with food, and who, having honored him, walks after him a way in farewell — his is the eternal dharma.
Full hospitality to the three orders, according to means, by day and night — the dharma of the śūdra has been declared to be service to the three orders.
The dharma marked by active engagement is ordained among householders; that one I shall proclaim — auspicious and for the welfare of all beings.
Gifts should be given again and again, according to one's power, and likewise sacrifice should be offered again and again; and the rites that bring increase should be performed by one who desires prosperity.
Wealth should be gathered by dharma; the riches gained through dharma are threefold; a man should make dharma supreme with diligent effort.
With one portion the aim of dharma should be served by one who desires prosperity; with one portion the aim of pleasure; and one portion he should make to grow.
But another dharma, marked by withdrawal, is remembered as liberation; its way of life I shall declare — hear it from me, O goddess, in its truth.
Compassion for all beings is dharma, and not dwelling in a single village; and release from the bonds of craving is praised for those who long for liberation.
No attachment to a water-pot, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to a seat, nor to the triple staff, nor to a bed, nor to fire, nor to a place of shelter.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He whose mind is fixed on the Supreme Self, whose thought is on That, devoted to That, ever intent upon yoga and likewise upon discriminating reflection —
sleeping ever at the root of a tree, dwelling in an empty house, lying upon the sandbanks of a river, and delighting on a river's bank —
the twice-born freed from all attachments and from the bonds of affection — fixing the being of the self in the Self alone, the twice-born wanders.
Become motionless as a post, fasting, by deeds directed toward liberation — he who, disciplined, goes forth as a wandering mendicant, his is the eternal dharma.
Not long attached in any one place, nor ranging within a single village, disciplined and released he wanders, not sleeping always on one sandbank.
This is the dharma of those who know liberation, the good path of the good, declared in the Veda; for one who follows this road, no further state of rebirth exists.
The mendicants are of four kinds: the kuṭīcara, the kṛtodaka, the haṃsa, and the paramahaṃsa; and whichever comes later, that one is the higher.
Beyond this there is nothing higher, nothing lower, nothing aside or in front — that which is without sorrow, without pleasure, gentle, free of age, deathless, and imperishable.
Umā said: The dharma of the householder and the dharma of liberation, practiced by the good, you have set forth — the great and beneficial road for the world of mortals.
But the dharma of the seers, O knower of dharma, I wish to hear — that unsurpassed dharma; for I have a constant longing toward those who dwell in the groves of austerity.
The fragrance arising from the smoke of ghee seems to fill the whole grove of austerity; beholding it, my mind, O Maheśvara, would ever be glad.
This doubt of mine concerning the dharma of the sages, O God, O mighty one, O knower of the truth of all dharma and its aims, O God of gods, tell me in full — O Mahādeva, as I have asked, just as it is.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Maheśvara said: Behold, I shall declare to you the unsurpassed dharma of the sages, by following which the sages attain perfection through their own austerity, O lovely one.
The dharma that belongs ever to the foam-drinking seers, the knowers of dharma — hear it from me, O greatly blessed one, O knower of dharma, that dharma from the beginning.
Therein they ever glean the holy, auspicious mass of foam — that sweet nectar drunk by Brahmā, spread abroad in heaven.
This is the road wrought by the practice of dharma for those wholly pure foam-drinkers, O you whose wealth is austerity; now hear of the host of the Vālakhilyas.
The Vālakhilyas, sages perfected in austerity, within the orb of the sun — knowers of dharma, they glean the gleanings, abiding by the way of life of the birds.
Clothed in deerskins, garbed in rags and bark, beyond the pairs of opposites, having reached the good path — such are the Vālakhilyas, whose wealth is austerity.
No larger than a thumb-joint, settled firmly within their own bodies, they strive at the practice of austerity; great is the fruit of their dharma.
They attain equality with the gods, for the accomplishing of the gods' purposes, illumining all the quarters, their sins burned away by austerity.
And those others, pure of mind, devoted to compassion and dharma, the good who move in companies, the holy ones who range the world of Soma —
dwelling near the world of the fathers, they glean according to rule — the saṃprakṣālas and the aśmakuṭṭas, and likewise the dantolūkhalins.
And those who, dwelling near the soma-drinking gods and likewise the vapor-drinking ones, glean their food, their senses restrained by their very nature —
for them the tending of the sacred fire, the worship of the fathers and the gods, and likewise the offering of the five sacrifices is declared to be dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This is the dharma of the seers, O goddess, ever practiced by the twice-born who move in companies and range the world of the gods; now hear from me that other dharma as well.
In all the dharmas of the seers, the self is first to be conquered, the senses subdued; and thereafter desire and anger are to be conquered — such is my conviction.
Diligent tending of the sacred fire-offering, the keeping of the holy night-vigil, sanction for the soma-sacrifice, and the sacrificial fee as the fifth duty—
the constant performance of sacrifice is dharma, delight in the worship of the ancestors and the gods, and hospitality to all must be offered with food gathered by gleaning.
Abstention from enjoyment of pleasures, contentment with the milk of the cow, sleeping upon the bare ground, the practice of yoga, and subsisting on herbs and leaves;
eating fruits and roots, living on air and water, and feeding on moss—these indeed are the observances of the sages, by which they win the goal that none else attains.
When the smoke has cleared, the pestle is laid aside, the embers are gone, the household has finished eating, the round of the serving-vessels is past, and the hour for begging is over—
awaiting a guest, taking his meal of what food remains, delighting in truth and dharma, patient and serene—such a man is joined to the law of the sage.
He who is neither stiff with pride nor vain, neither heedless nor bewildered, friendly and the same toward friend and foe alike—he is the highest knower of dharma.
Umā said: In delightful regions, by the cascades of the mountains, in the bowers along the flowing streams, and in the groves upon the hills,
and in varied lands abounding in fruit and rich in roots, there dwell those of steadfast vows, their minds collected.
I wish to hear, O Śaṃkara, the holy rule of these too—of the forest-dwellers, O lord of gods, who live by the labor of their own bodies.

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
Devotion to the sacrifice on the eighth day, the observance of the four-monthly rites, the sacrifice performed at the full moon, and likewise the perpetual sacrifice—
freed from union with wives, freed from all defilement, and freed from every sin, the sages wander in the forest.
Holding the sacrificial ladle and vessels as their highest treasure, ever taking refuge in the three sacred fires, the good who keep always to the path of the good—they attain the supreme goal.
To the world of Brahmā, of great merit, and to the eternal world of Soma the perfected sages go, by their reliance upon the dharma of the seers.
This auspicious dharma resting upon the forest-hermits, O goddess, rich in meaning, I have set forth to you at length in its broad outline.
Umā said: O blessed one, lord of the lords of gods, to whom all beings bow, tell me the dharma of the company of sages who dwell amid the teachings of perfection.
Those perfected in the teachings of perfection and likewise dwelling in the forest, who live freely and yet keep the company of wives—how is their dharma declared?
Maheśvara said: Those ascetics who live freely, O goddess, all of whom take their pleasure with wives—for them the shaven head, the ochre robe, and the measured division of day and night are the means.
Bathing at the three times of day, the great oblation performed as the seers ordained, deep meditation, standing fast upon the path of the good, and observance as has been declared;
and those duties of the forest-dwellers spoken of before—if they observe these duties, they obtain the fruit of austerity.
And those who keep the dharma of the married pair, their senses restrained to their own wives, who approach them only in the fertile season as the ordinance prescribes,
for them, righteous as they are, the dharma laid down by the seers is fulfilled; for no other desire arising from mere lust is to be indulged by those who behold dharma.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who rightly grants to all beings the gift of fearlessness, his self freed from violence and anger—he indeed is joined with dharma.
He who is compassionate toward all beings, vowed to uprightness toward all beings, and who has become one in spirit with all beings—he indeed is joined with dharma.
Bathing at all the sacred waters, and uprightness toward all beings—these two might be held equal, or else uprightness is the greater.
Uprightness, they say, is dharma; crookedness is called unrighteousness. A man here endowed with uprightness is joined with dharma.
The upright man dwells forever in the world near the immortals; therefore let him be constant in uprightness who desires dharma for himself.
Patient, self-controlled, having conquered anger, become the very embodiment of dharma, doing no harm, his mind ever delighting in dharma—such a man is joined with dharma.
Free of sloth, righteous in soul, capable, holding to the path of the good, supreme in conduct and awakened, he becomes fit for union with Brahman.
Umā said: O god, the ascetics who delight in the hermitage, those rich in austerity and radiant with splendor—by what observance do they become so?
Kings and the sons of kings, the poor or the greatly wealthy—by what deed, O blessed one, do they obtain the great fruit?
Having reached the eternal abode, anointed with celestial sandal—by what deed, O god, do they become rangers of the forest?
Resolve for me this doubt of mine, O god, concerning the holy practice of austerity; declare it all without remainder, O three-eyed one, destroyer of the Three Cities.
Maheśvara said: Tamed by vows of fasting, doing no harm, speaking the truth, and made perfect, after death they rejoice free of all ill in the company of the gandharvas.
He of righteous soul who, lying in the frog-posture of yoga, keeps his consecration according to place and ordinance, rejoices in the company of the serpent-nāgas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who, consecrated and filled with joy, feeds among the deer on the grass cast off from their mouths, goes to Amarāvatī, the city of the immortals.
He who, bound to that vow, feeds on moss or on fallen leaves, ever bearing the discipline of cold, may attain the supreme goal.
He who lives on air or on water, or who eats fruits and roots, attains lordship among the yakṣas and rejoices amid the troops of apsarases.
He who in summer bears the discipline of fire, performing for twelve years the rite seen in the ordinance, becomes a king who rules the earth.
The sage who, observing restraint of food for twelve years and with effort mastering the desert wastes, becomes a king who rules the earth.
He who, upon the bare ground, taking the pure open sky as his shelter on every side, and entering with joy upon the twelve-year consecration—
the fruits of this couch on the bare ground, they say, O lovely one, are chariots and couches and houses of great worth, white as the moon.
He who, living by his own self, restrained and restrained in food, casts off his body by fasting, attains to heaven.
He who, living by his own self through the twelve-year consecration, casts off his body in the great ocean, attains the world of Varuṇa.
He who, living by his own self through the twelve-year consecration, breaks his feet upon a stone, rejoices among the guhyakas.
Having perfected the self by the self, beyond the pairs of opposites and free of possessions, having kept for twelve years the one consecration fixed in his mind, he attains the world of heaven and rejoices in the company of the gods.
He who, living by his own self through the twelve-year consecration, offers himself in the fire and casts off his body, is exalted in the world of Agni.
But the twice-born who, O goddess, consecrated as the ordinance requires and restrained, having set the self within the self, beyond the pairs of opposites and free of possessions,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
having kept for twelve years the one consecration fixed in his mind, and bound the fire-sticks upon his shoulder, wanders forth uncovered—
his mind ever set on the hero's road, delighting in the hero's posture, and standing fast in the hero's place—he attains the goal of heroes.
Gone forever to the world of Śakra, attended by every desire fulfilled, strewn with celestial flowers and adorned with celestial sandal, the righteous one dwells in bliss in heaven among the hosts of the gods.
The hero gone to the world of heroes, ever bearing the hero's discipline, steadfast in goodness, who renounces all and, consecrated, restrained, and pure, takes up the hero's road—for him the worlds are everlasting.
In a sky-chariot that goes where it wills he ranges at his pleasure, and gone to the world of Śakra, glorious and free of all ill, he rejoices.
Umā said: O blessed one, slayer of Bhaga's eye, who struck out the teeth of Pūṣan, who ruined the sacrifice of Dakṣa, O three-eyed god, great is this doubt of mine.
The four orders were of old created by the blessed Self-Existent One; by what ripening of deeds does a vaiśya pass into the state of a śūdra?
By what means does a vaiśya become a kṣatriya, or a twice-born become a kṣatriya? And how, O god, can dharma be observed against the natural order?
By what deed is a brāhmaṇa born in the womb of a śūdra, and by what deed, O mighty one, does a kṣatriya pass into the state of a śūdra?
Resolve for me this doubt, O god, lord of beings, sinless one: how may the three orders by their very nature attain to brāhmaṇa-hood?
Maheśvara said: Brāhmaṇa-hood, O goddess, is hard to win. By his very nature, O fair one, a brāhmaṇa is a brāhmaṇa; so too the kṣatriya, the vaiśya, and the śūdra are such by nature—this is my judgment.
By an evil deed here the twice-born falls from his station; therefore, having attained the highest order, let the twice-born guard it well.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whether a kṣatriya or a vaiśya, he who stands firm in the brāhmaṇa's dharma and lives by brāhmaṇa-hood goes toward union with Brahman.
But he who, abandoning his brāhmaṇa-state, practices the dharma of the warrior, falls from brāhmaṇa-hood and is born in the womb of a kṣatriya.
And the brāhmaṇa of little understanding who, given over to greed and delusion, having attained brāhmaṇa-hood so hard to win, ever does the work of a vaiśya—
that twice-born passes into the state of a vaiśya, and a vaiśya likewise into the state of a śūdra; the brāhmaṇa fallen from his own dharma thereby attains the state of a śūdra.
Then, fallen from his order and cast out, he comes to hell; fallen from the world of Brahman, he is born again as a śūdra.
And the kṣatriya, O greatly blessed one, or the vaiśya, O practiser of dharma, who casts aside his own duties and follows the works of a śūdra—
fallen from his own station, he sinks into the confusion of the orders; such a brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, or vaiśya passes into the state of a śūdra.
But he who is purified by his own dharma, possessed of knowledge and discernment, pure, knowing dharma and devoted to it—he enjoys the fruit of dharma.
And there is this further teaching, O goddess, proclaimed by Brahmā: the highest spiritual doctrine, observed by the good who long for dharma.
The food of a cruel man is condemned, O goddess, as is the food of a horde, the food connected with a śrāddha or a birth-impurity. Food announced by a public crier must never be eaten, and a Śūdra's food never at all.
The food of a Śūdra is condemned, O goddess, by the great-souled gods of gods; uttered from the mouth of the Grandsire himself, this is authoritative — such is my conviction.
He in whose belly a remnant of a Śūdra's food remains when he dies — though he be one who has kindled the sacred fires and offered sacrifices — shares the destiny of a Śūdra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
By that remnant of a Śūdra's food a Brāhmaṇa is cast down from the station of Brahman and becomes a Śūdra — of this there is no question.
A Brāhmaṇa in whose belly a remnant of another's food remains when he dies, whose food he has lived upon, passes into that very womb.
He who, having attained the auspicious and hard-won state of a Brāhmaṇa, holds it in contempt and eats forbidden food, surely falls from his twice-born estate.
The drinker of liquor, the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, the base man, the thief, the breaker of vows, the impure, he who has abandoned his sacred study, the sinful, the greedy, the deceitful, the crooked —
the man without vows, the keeper of a Śūdra woman, the eater of an adulterer's food, the seller of Soma, the servant of the lowly — such a Brāhmaṇa falls from his Brahman-born nature.
He who defiles his teacher's bed, who hates his teacher, who delights in reviling his teacher, and who hates Brahman — such a Brāhmaṇa, too, falls from his Brahman-born nature.
But by these auspicious deeds duly performed, O goddess, a Śūdra may attain Brāhmaṇahood, and a Vaiśya may attain Kṣatriyahood.
All the duties of a Śūdra, rightly and according to rule, with service and attendance upon the highest class — these let the Śūdra perform diligently and ungrudgingly, standing ever upon the good path.
Honouring the gods and the twice-born, holding to the vow of hospitality toward all, approaching his wife only in season, self-restrained and temperate in food —
clean and seeking the company of the clean, making his meal of the food that remains, never eating meat got in vain — such a Śūdra attains to Vaiśyahood.
Truthful in speech, free of self-assertion, beyond the pairs of opposites, skilled in tranquillity, performing the daily sacrifices, devoted above all to sacred study, and pure —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
self-controlled, honouring Brāhmaṇas, wishing well to all the classes, holding to the householder's vow, taking food at the two appointed times —
eating the remnant, having conquered his appetite, free of craving, free of self-assertion, tending the sacred fire and making oblations according to rule —
showing hospitality to all, making his meal of the food that remains, ordained to the three fires and their mantras — if a Vaiśya lives thus, he is born into a pure and great Kṣatriya family.
That Vaiśya, born now a Kṣatriya, sanctified from birth, invested with the sacred thread and devoted to his vows, becomes an honoured twice-born man.
He gives, he sacrifices with consecrated rites and ample fees, he studies, ever seeking heaven, taking refuge in the three fires.
Ever stretching out a giving hand to the afflicted, protecting his subjects by dharma, truthful, fulfilling his promises, and ever pleasant to behold —
wielding the rod for justice and yet not without restraint, directing the works of dharma, governed in the discharge of his duties, taking the sixth part as his appointed due —
let him not indulge the ways of carnal pleasure at his own whim, though skilled in worldly gain; rather, righteous in soul, let him approach his wife only in season.
Practising all the fasts, self-restrained, devoted above all to sacred study, pure, ever sleeping upon the strewn sacrificial grass within the fire-chamber —
showing hospitality to the three classes with a gracious mind always, and ever saying to Śūdras who desire food, 'It is ready' —
who notices nothing for his own gain or for his own desire, and who makes his every effort for the sake of the ancestors, the gods, and his guests —
who in his own house duly partakes even of alms, and who offers the fire-oblation thrice a day according to rule —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and who, for the good of cows and Brāhmaṇas, is slain facing the foe in battle — or one purified by the three fires and their mantras — enters and becomes a twice-born man.
Endowed with knowledge and discernment, sanctified, having mastered the Vedas, a righteous-souled Kṣatriya becomes a Brāhmaṇa by his own deeds.
By these fruits of action, O goddess, even a Śūdra sprung from a lowly birth and family, if endowed with sacred learning and sanctified, becomes a twice-born man.
And a Brāhmaṇa, too, of evil conduct, who eats every defiled mixture of food, casting off his holy Brāhmaṇahood, becomes such a one — a Śūdra.
By pure deeds, O goddess, even a Śūdra of cleansed soul, his senses conquered, is to be honoured like a twice-born man — so Brahmā himself declared.
Where an auspicious nature and conduct dwell even in a Śūdra, that purified man is to be known indeed as twice-born — such is my conviction.
Neither birth, nor the sacraments, nor learning, nor lineage are the causes of being twice-born; conduct alone is the cause.
Every Brāhmaṇa in this world is ordained such by his conduct; and one who stands firm in good conduct, O fair-hipped lady, attains to Brāhmaṇahood.
The Brahman-nature, O blessed one, is the same everywhere — such is my conviction; where the qualityless, stainless Brahman abides, there is the twice-born man.
These are the fruits of birth, O goddess, indicating one's portion and station, declared by the boon-granting Brahmā himself as he created creatures.
The Brāhmaṇa is a great field that moves about in the world on foot; the seed he sows there is the tillage that bears fruit in the world beyond.
He must ever be moderate in eating and ever cleave to the good path; one who wishes to flourish must not transgress, but conduct himself upon the way of Brahman.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As a householder in his home he must be a reciter of the sacred texts, ever given to study, living by giving and learning.
A Brāhmaṇa who is thus, standing ever upon the good path, having kindled the sacred fire and ever studying, becomes fit to be one with Brahman.
Having attained Brāhmaṇahood, it must be guarded by the self-restrained — guarded in marriage, in the acceptance of gifts, and in deeds, O lady of the bright smile.
All this I have told you — how a Śūdra may become twice-born, and how a Brāhmaṇa, fallen from dharma, comes to the state of a Śūdra.
Umā said: O Lord, ruler of all beings, worshipped by gods and demons, regarding the right and the wrong conduct of men, O god, resolve my doubt for me, O all-pervading one.
By deed, by thought, and by word — threefold — a man is ever bound by fetters and snares, or else is set free again.
By what character, O god, or by what kind of deed, by what conduct, what virtues, what words, do men attain heaven here?
Maheśvara said: O goddess, knower of the truth of dharma and artha, ever devoted to truth and to self-restraint — your question is for the welfare of all living beings; let it be heard, for it increases wisdom.
The good, devoted to truth and dharma, free of all craving, their doubts cut away, are bound neither by unrighteousness nor by righteousness.
Those who know the truth of dissolution and origination, the all-knowing, the even-eyed, free of passion — such men are released from all bonds.
Those who by deed, thought, or word injure nothing whatever, who cling to nothing — they are not bound by their actions.
Refraining from the destruction of life, virtuous, full of compassion, regarding the hated and the loved alike, self-controlled — they are freed from the bonds of action.
Compassionate toward all beings, trusted by every creature, who have renounced all violent conduct — those men go to heaven.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Free of all greed for another's wealth, ever shunning another's wife, enjoying only riches gained by righteous means — those men go to heaven.
Those who ever look upon other men's wives as upon a mother, a sister, or a daughter — those men go to heaven.
Those who refrain ever from theft, content with their own wealth, and who live upon their own portion — those men go to heaven.
Those who are devoted to their own wives, approaching them only in season, and who do not give themselves to vulgar pleasures — those men go to heaven.
Those whose eyes are ever veiled by virtue in the presence of other men's wives, restrained in their senses, devoted to good character — those men go to heaven.
This is the path made by the gods, always to be followed by men; and the path freed of the taints of passion is ever to be followed by the wise.
Endowed with charity, righteousness, and austerity, made of good character, purity, and compassion — this path, whether for one's livelihood or for the sake of dharma, must ever be followed by men who long to dwell in heaven; but that which is beyond it should not be followed.
Umā said: Those deeds of speech by which a man is bound, or again is set free — tell me of them, O god, lord of beings, O sinless one.
Maheśvara said: Those who, whether for their own sake or another's, or out of jest and laughter, never speak falsehood here — those men go to heaven.
Those who, whether for livelihood or for the sake of dharma, or even at the bidding of desire, do not utter untruth — those men go to heaven.
Those who address others with a smooth speech, free of harm, sweet, free of evil, and with words of welcome — those men go to heaven.
Those who never speak a bitter, harsh, or cruel word, the good who delight in the absence of slander — those men go to heaven.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who never speak a slanderous word that sets friends at variance, but utter true and friendly speech — those men go to heaven.
Those men who ever shun tale-bearing and treachery against others, even toward all beings and self-controlled — those men go to heaven.
Those who refrain from deceitful prattle, who shun what is hostile, and who ever speak gently — those men go to heaven.
Those who, even in anger, do not utter a speech that tears the heart, but speak conciliating words though provoked — those men go to heaven.
This dharma wrought of speech, O goddess, auspicious and ever endowed with the quality of truth, is always to be followed by men; falsehood must ever be shunned by the wise.
Umā said: By what deed of the mind a man is ever bound — tell me that, O greatly blessed one, god of gods, wielder of the Pināka bow.
Maheśvara said: Men ever joined with the dharma of the mind go to heaven, O blessed one; hear it as I recount it to you.
By a mind ill-directed a man becomes of even more ill-directed form, and is bound by it; hear, moreover, of the other side, O fair-faced one.
Those men who, beholding another's wealth left in a forest or a lonely place, do not lay hold of it even in thought — those men go to heaven.
Whatever goods of another are left unguarded in a village or a house, those who never covet them — those men go to heaven.
And those who, even toward another's wife given to passion and met in a secret place, do no harm even in thought — those men go to heaven.
Those men who ever regard foe and friend with an equal mind, and meeting them deal with both in friendship — those men go to heaven.
Learned, compassionate, pure, true to their pledges, fully content with their own wealth — those men go to heaven.
Those who bear no enmity, are free of agitation, ever devoted to a friendly mind, compassionate toward all beings — those men go to heaven.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Full of faith, compassionate, clean and dear to clean folk, ever knowing right from wrong — those men go to heaven.
And those who know the ripening of the gathered fruits of deeds both good and evil, O goddess — those men go to heaven.
Endowed with justice, endowed with virtue, ever devoted to the gods and the twice-born, having attained to equanimity — those men go to heaven.
By the fruits of their good deeds, O goddess, these have been proclaimed by me as travellers upon the road to heaven. What else do you wish to hear?
Umā said: A great doubt of mine concerns mortals, O Maheśvara; therefore it behoves you to expound it to me today with precision.
By what deed does a man obtain long life, O Lord? By what austerity, O Lord of the gods, does he obtain a great span of years?
By what deed does a man on earth become short-lived? Be pleased to declare the ripening of deeds, O blameless god.
Some men enjoy great wealth, while others enjoy but little; some are of low birth, and yet others are of noble birth.
Some men appear ill-favoured to look upon, as though carved of wood, while other men are pleasing at the very first sight.
Some appear dull of wit, some appear learned, and others again are of great wisdom, perceivers of knowledge and discernment.
Some men are seen to suffer little affliction and others great affliction, O god; it behoves you to explain this to me.
Maheśvara said: Come then, I shall declare to you, O goddess, the arising of the fruit of deeds, whereby all men in the world of mortals reap each his own reward.
The man who is a slayer of living things, cruel, ever with rod uplifted in hand, and ever ready to strike, who kills the hosts of creatures—
merciless toward all beings, ever a maker of terror, offering no refuge even to worms and ants, utterly without pity—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
such a man, O goddess, comes to hell; but his opposite, the righteous-souled, is born handsome of form.
The cruel-souled goes to hell, the harmless goes to heaven; and in hell that man obtains fierce and grievous torment.
And if at length he rises up out of that hell and obtains human birth, even then he is born there short-lived.
Bound by his sinful deed, O goddess, the man who delighted in violence is born hateful to all beings and short of life.
But he who is of pure nature, abstaining from the slaying of living things, who has laid down the rod and bears no rod, who never does harm—
who neither causes slaughter nor slays, nor approves of one who slays, but is loving toward all beings, regarding others as he regards himself—
such an excellent man, O goddess, attains to godhood, and joyfully enjoys the happy delights that fall to his lot.
And if at some time he is reborn in the world of men, that man, born long-lived, flourishes there in happiness.
Thus the path of the long-lived, of those of good conduct and good deeds, lies through the renunciation of harm to living things—so it was declared by Brahmā.
Umā said: Of what character, of what conduct, and by what deeds do men attain to heaven, and by what kind of giving?
Maheśvara said: The giver, the honourer of brāhmaṇas, the bestower of foods to be chewed and eaten, of grain, of drink, and of garments upon the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the like—
who gives shelters, assembly-halls, wells, watering-stations, and lotus-pools, and all the daily necessaries, and abundantly whatever is desired—
seats, beds, vehicles, wealth, jewels, and houses, all kinds of crops, cattle, fields, and even women—
the man who gives these ever with a glad and trusting heart—such a one, O goddess, when he dies is born in the world of the gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dwelling there a very long time, enjoying delights unsurpassed, rejoicing and sporting with the apsarases in Nandana and the other groves,
and fallen from that heaven, he is reborn among the worlds of men, O goddess, in a family of great wealth, well furnished with riches and grain.
There, endowed with every quality that the heart desires and filled with joy, the man becomes one of great enjoyment, of great treasure, and rich.
These beings of great enjoyment, O goddess, given to charity, were declared of old by Brahmā to be pleasing to the sight of all.
Other men, O goddess, are miserly in giving, and though they possess the means, when entreated by the twice-born they do not give, being foolish.
Seeing the poor, the blind, the wretched, beggars, and even guests entreating them, they turn away, possessed by greed of the palate.
Neither wealth nor garments nor enjoyments nor gold, neither cattle nor any dish of food do they ever give.
Those who are inactive in good, greedy, unbelieving, and devoid of charity—such men, O goddess, the foolish, go to hell.
And if in the course of time they come again to human birth, those of little understanding obtain birth in a family empty of wealth.
Beset by hunger and thirst, cast out from all enjoyments, hopeless of every pleasure, they live the meanest of lives.
Born in a family of meagre means, men content with meagre enjoyments—by this deed, O goddess, men become destitute of wealth.
Others, ever stiff with pride, vain, delighting in sin, the senseless who do not offer a seat to one who deserves a seat—
who, of little wit, do not yield the way to one who deserves the way, and who, of little wit, do not offer water for the feet to one who deserves it—
who do not honour with due rites those worthy of honour, and who, of little wit, do not offer the welcome-offering or water for rinsing the mouth—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
who do not wish to honour as a teacher the teacher come in love, but are settled in greed driven by arrogance—
who slight those worthy of respect and despise their elders—such men, O goddess, all go to hell.
And if those men rise up at last from that hell, then after a long succession of years they obtain birth in a despised family.
In the families of the despised and senseless—dog-cookers, pulkasas, and the like—are born those who had slighted their teachers and elders.
He who is neither stiff with pride nor vain, a worshipper of gods and brāhmaṇas, honoured by the world, a maker of reverence, modest, sweet of speech,
who does what is pleasing to all the varṇas, ever intent on the welfare of all beings, free from malice, of pleasant countenance, gentle, ever uttering affectionate words,
who harms no being and greets all with welcome, and who waits upon them, honouring each with the courtesy he deserves,
yielding the way to one who deserves the way, honouring the teacher as a teacher, delighting to receive guests, and a worshipper of those who come—
such a man, O goddess, attains to heaven, and thereafter, gaining human birth, is born in a distinguished family.
There, possessed of ample enjoyments and furnished with every jewel, he becomes a giver to the worthy according to their deserts and devoted to the practice of dharma.
Esteemed by all beings and honoured by all the world, the man himself ever obtains the fruit of his own deeds.
Born of an exalted family and ever of exalted lineage—this is the law I have declared, the very law set forth by the Ordainer himself.
But he who is of cruel conduct, a terror to all creatures, who with his hands or his feet, or again with rope or rod,
with clods or posts or by other devices torments living beings, O lovely one—who, with a mind bent on cunning and cruelty, terrifies them,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and assails creatures, ever a maker of terror—such a one, of such character and conduct, comes to hell.
And if in the course of time he should come to human birth, he is born in a low family, sorely afflicted with many ailments.
Hated by the world, the lowest of men through the fruits wrought by his own deeds—this, O goddess, is to be understood among men and among kinsmen and relations.
Another, full of compassion, looks upon all beings with a friendly eye, like a father, free from enmity, with senses restrained;
he neither frightens beings nor does them harm, and with hands and feet well controlled he is trusted among all creatures.
Neither with rope nor with rod, nor with clods nor with weapon does he terrify beings—gentle in his deeds and given to compassion.
One of such character and conduct is born in heaven, and there in a divine mansion he dwells in joy, like a god.
And if, when his merit is spent, the mortal is reborn among men, he, born free from ailment and from calamity, flourishes in happiness.
A partaker of happiness, untoiling, and ever free from agitation is that man. This, O goddess, is the path of the good, where no affliction is found.
Umā said: These men are seen skilled in reasoning for and against, endowed with knowledge and discernment, wise and versed in affairs; while others, O god, are dull of wit, devoid of knowledge and discernment.
By the ripening of what deed does a man become wise? How does a man come to be of little wisdom, O three-eyed one? Cut away this doubt of mine, O best of all who know dharma.
And some men, O god, are seen blind from birth, others afflicted with disease, and others impotent; tell me the cause therein.
Maheśvara said: Those who day by day inquire of brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas, of the perfected, and of those who know dharma, concerning what is right and wrong,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
who shun the unwholesome deed and cleave to the wholesome, ever obtain heaven and happiness here in this world.
And if such a one comes to human birth, he is born there of keen intellect, and learning, attended by wisdom and blessedness, arises in him.
Those fools who cast a wicked eye upon the wives of others—by that wicked disposition they become blind from birth.
And those who with corrupted mind gaze upon a naked woman—such men, doers of evil deeds, become afflicted with disease here.
But those deluded, ill-conducted, very foolish men who delight in unnatural intercourse with men come to impotence.
Those who couple beasts, those who defile the bed of their teacher, and those of promiscuous intercourse—such men are born impotent.
Umā said: What deed is blameworthy, and what is blameless, and what is the higher good that a man obtains by doing it, O best of the gods?
Maheśvara said: He who, keeping ever to the better path, inquires of the twice-born, a seeker of dharma and a yearner after virtue, attains to heaven.
And if at some time, O goddess, he comes to human birth, he is born there of keen intellect, endowed with retentive memory, and wise.
This, O goddess, is the law of the good, to be deemed a maker of prosperity; for the welfare of men it has been declared by me to you.
Umā said: Other men, of scant understanding and haters of dharma, do not wish to wait attentively upon brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas.
Some men hold to vows, devoted to faith and self-restraint; others are without vows, fallen from the rules, and like rākṣasas.
Some, again, are performers of sacrifice, and others offer no oblations; by the ripening of what deed do they become so here? Tell me.
Maheśvara said: From the tradition of the laws of the world, the bounds were established of old; through their authority men follow them, and so the firm in vows are seen.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those who, fallen under the sway of delusion, call unrighteousness righteousness — men devoid of vows, who have cast off all bounds of conduct — they are declared to be brahma-rākṣasas.
And if, through the working of time, such ones are born here as human beings, they become the lowest of men, performing no oblations and uttering no sacred vaṣaṭ-calls.
Thus, O goddess, to resolve your doubt I have expounded to you in full this ocean of dharma — the good and the evil deeds of men.
Maheśvara said: O knower of high and low, O knower of dharma, O dweller in the penance-grove, O virtuous one of lovely brows and beautiful tresses, O daughter of the Himavat mountain —
O skillful one, endowed with calm and self-restraint, free of selfishness, walker in the path of dharma — I ask you, O fair-hipped one; being asked, tell me what I desire to know.
Sāvitrī is the chaste wife of Brahmā, Śacī the faithful wife of Kauśika (Indra), Dhūmorṇā of Yama the son of Mārtaṇḍa, and Ṛddhi of Vaiśravaṇa (Kubera);
Gaurī is the wife of Varuṇa, Suvarcalā of Sūrya, the faithful Rohiṇī of the Moon, and Svāhā of Agni the radiant;
and Aditi of Kaśyapa — all of these revere their husbands as gods, and all of them, O goddess, you have ever questioned and waited upon.
Therefore I question you, O knower of dharma, O speaker of dharma: I wish to hear the duty of women, expounded by you from the beginning.
You are my partner in dharma, equal to me in conduct, equal in vows, equal in essence and might, and fierce penance has been performed by you; therefore what is spoken by you in particular will attain the standing of authority.
And women in particular are ever the refuge of womankind: as a cow goes after a cow, O fair-hipped one, such is forever the way of things in the worlds.
You are half of my body, and from my half you came forth; you are the doer of the gods' work and the continuer of the world's lineage.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The whole of the eternal duty of women is well known to you, O auspicious one; therefore declare to me the duty of women fully and in detail.
Umā said: O Lord, O sovereign of all beings, O source of what has been, what shall be, and what is — by your power alone, O god, does this speech rise up within me.
But these rivers, O lord of gods, charged with the waters of all sacred fords, stand near and wait upon you for the sake of their cleansing touch.
Having taken counsel together with these, I shall declare it in due order; for he who, though powerful, speaks without egotism — he indeed is called a true man.
And a woman, O lord of beings, ever follows after a woman; moreover these foremost rivers will be honored by my doing so.
This holy Sarasvatī is the highest of rivers, first among all streams, a river that flows to the sea;
and the Vipāśā, the Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, the Irāvatī, the Śatadru, the Devikā, the Sindhu, the Kauśikī, and the Gomatī as well;
and this divine river too, encompassed by all sacred fords, the goddess Gaṅgā who descended from heaven to earth, the foremost of all streams.
Having spoken thus, the consort of the God of gods, foremost of the upholders of dharma, then addressed all those rivers as if with a smile,
and the queen of the god, devoted to dharma, asked them of the duty of women — those foremost streams, Gaṅgā and the rest, who were skilled in the duty of women.
"This question concerning the duty of women has been put by the Lord; having taken counsel with you, I wish to answer it to Śaṃkara."
"For I see that perfect knowledge is to be attained by no single being's effort alone, on earth or in heaven, O ocean-going ones; therefore do I honor you."
Bhīṣma said: When all those most holy and auspicious rivers, foremost of streams, had thus been questioned, the divine river Gaṅgā, being charged with the answer, after honoring the goddess,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
abounding in many insights, knowing the duty of women, of pure smile — that holy one, remover of sin, auspicious — addressed the goddess, daughter of the king of mountains;
endowed with intellect and modesty, accomplished in all branches of knowledge, rich in much wisdom, Gaṅgā spoke these words with a smile.
"Blessed are we, favored are we, O goddess devoted to dharma, that you, honored by the whole world, should honor mere rivers, O sinless one."
"He who, though powerful, questions others or shows them honor — such a one, surely of untainted heart, attains the name of a wise man."
"He who questions others — men endowed with knowledge and discernment, skilled in reasoning and refutation, fit to expound — he indeed attains the highest station."
"In one way the man rich in much wisdom speaks his word in the assembly; in quite another the egotist utters feeble speech."
"O you of divine knowledge, supreme in heaven, of divine merit, ever exalted — you alone, O goddess, are fit to instruct us in the duty of women."
Bhīṣma said: Then the goddess, propitiated by Gaṅgā with her many virtues — that fairest of the celestials — declared in full and without omission the whole duty of women.
"As the duty of women appears to me according to the ordinance, that I shall proclaim, that it may be made widely known just so."
"This duty of a woman is first laid upon her by her kinsmen at the wedding: in the presence of the sacred fire she becomes her husband's partner in dharma."
"Of good nature, gentle of speech, of good conduct, pleasant to behold, with mind fixed on none but her husband, fair of face — such a one is a woman walking in dharma."
"She becomes supreme in dharma, she becomes a partaker of dharma — that virtuous one who ever looks upon her husband as upon a god."
"She who renders service and attendance to him as to a god, with no other feeling, untroubled in mind, steadfast in her vows, pleasant to behold —"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"she who gazes upon her husband's face again and again as upon the face of her son, virtuous and disciplined in conduct — she is a woman walking in dharma."
"Having heard the auspicious duty of husband and wife, ordained as their shared dharma, she who is single-minded and fair of face toward her husband is a woman walking in dharma."
"The woman who, even when addressed with harsh words or looked upon with a cruel eye, keeps a serene face toward her husband — she is devoted to her lord."
"She who, save her husband, gazes not upon the moon, the sun, or a tree bearing a masculine name — that fair-hipped one is a woman walking in dharma."
"The woman who tends a husband poor, sick, wretched, or worn out by the road, as though he were her son — she is a partaker of dharma."
"The woman who is pure and capable, the woman who bears sons, who holds her husband dear and makes him her very life — she is a partaker of dharma."
"She who renders service and attendance ever with untroubled mind, of good cheer and modest bearing — she is a partaker of dharma."
"She whose longing is set not on pleasures, nor on enjoyments, nor on lordship, nor on comfort, but upon her husband alone — she is a partaker of dharma."
"Devoted ever to rising at dawn, intent upon the service of her elders, keeping her dwelling well swept and plastered with cow-dung,"
"ever intent upon the fire-rite, always offering flowers and oblations, and having set apart, together with her husband, food for the gods, guests, and dependents,"
"the woman who eats what remains, as is right and ordained, keeping her household ever content and well-nourished — she is joined with dharma."
"The woman endowed with virtue who gladdens the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, and is ever devoted to mother and father — she is rich in penance."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"The woman who nourishes with food the brāhmaṇas, the weak and helpless, the wretched, the blind and the destitute — she partakes of the merit of a faithful wife."
"She who ever keeps a vow hard for the frail of nature to perform, her thoughts upon her husband and devoted to his welfare — she partakes of the merit of a faithful wife."
"This is merit, this is penance, and this is the eternal heaven — for the woman who holds her husband supreme, vowed to her husband, and auspicious."
"For the husband is the god of women, the husband their kinsman, the husband their refuge; there is no refuge equal to the husband, nor any deity like unto him."
"For a woman the favor of her husband and heaven itself may be of equal worth — or rather, I would not even desire heaven if you were displeased, O Maheśvara."
"Should a husband, whether poor or sick, ever in any wise command what ought not be done, or what is contrary to dharma, or even what would destroy life —"
"or if he be in distress, fallen into enemy hands, or even afflicted by a brāhmaṇa's curse — then, regarding the duties proper to times of calamity, that is to be done without hesitation."
"Thus, O god, at your bidding I have declared the duty of women; and the woman who is of such a disposition becomes a partaker of dharma."
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the lord of gods, having honored the daughter of the mountain, dismissed the worlds together with all their attendants.
Then the hosts of beings and the rivers departed as they had come, and the gandharvas and apsarases too, bowing their heads to Bhava (Śiva).
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the duties in full and all the means of purification, Yudhiṣṭhira spoke once again to the son of Śaṃtanu.
"What is the one deity in the world? What too is the one supreme refuge? By praising whom, by worshipping whom, may men attain blessedness?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"What dharma, of all dharmas, do you hold to be the highest? By murmuring what may a creature be freed from the bondage of birth and the round of existence?"
Bhīṣma said: The Lord of the universe, the God of gods, the infinite, the Supreme Person — praising him with his thousand names, a man ever vigilant,
and worshipping that same imperishable Person constantly with devotion, meditating, praising, bowing down, and offering sacrifice to him alone —
praising forever Viṣṇu, without beginning or end, the great Lord of all worlds, the overseer of the worlds — he passes beyond all sorrow.
He who is devoted to the brahman, who knows all dharmas, the increaser of the renown of the worlds, the Lord of the worlds, the Great Being, the origin of the becoming of all beings —
this I hold to be the highest of all dharmas — that a man should ever worship with hymns, in devotion, the lotus-eyed one.
He who is the supreme great splendor, who is the supreme great penance, who is the supreme great brahman, who is the supreme refuge;
who is the purifier of things pure and the auspiciousness of things auspicious, the deity of deities, and the imperishable father of all beings;
from whom all beings come into being at the dawn of the first age, and into whom they pass to their dissolution again at the ending of the age —
hear from me, O lord of the earth, the thousand names of that Viṣṇu, the foremost of the worlds, the Lord of the universe — names that drive away sin and fear.
Those descriptive names of the great-souled one that are renowned and have been sung by the seers — those I shall declare for your welfare.
The Universe; Viṣṇu; the Vaṣaṭ-utterance; Lord of what has been, shall be, and now is; Maker of beings; Sustainer of beings; pure Being; the Self of beings; the Nurturer of beings;

title: Mahābhārata
Mahābhārata
text:
He is Aja, the unborn; Sarveśvara, lord of all; Siddha, the perfected; Siddhi, attainment itself; Sarvādi, the beginning of all; Acyuta, the unfallen; Vṛṣākapi, the boar of righteousness; Ameyātmā, of immeasurable being; and Sarvayogaviniḥsṛta, who issues forth from all union.
He is Vasu, the abode of all; Vasumanas, of generous mind; Satya, the truth; Samātmā, even-souled; Saṃmita, well-measured; Sama, the impartial; Amogha, whose deeds are never in vain; Puṇḍarīkākṣa, the lotus-eyed; Vṛṣakarmā, whose deeds are righteous; and Vṛṣākṛti, the very form of dharma.
He is Rudra, the terrible; Bahuśiras, the many-headed; Babhru, the upholder; Viśvayoni, the womb of the universe; Śuciśravas, of pure renown; Amṛta, the immortal; Śāśvata, the everlasting; Sthāṇu, the firm and unmoving; Varāroha, the supreme ascent; and Mahātapas, of mighty austerity.
He is Sarvaga, the all-pervading; Sarvavid, the all-knowing; Bhānu, the radiant; Viṣvaksena, before whose marshalled hosts the foe scatters; Janārdana, who afflicts the wicked; Veda, the sacred knowledge; Vedavid, the knower of the Vedas; Avyaṅga, the flawless; Vedāṅga, whose limbs are the Vedas; Vedavit, the knower of the Veda; and Kavi, the seer-poet.
He is Lokādhyakṣa, overseer of the worlds; Surādhyakṣa, overseer of the gods; Dharmādhyakṣa, overseer of dharma; Kṛtākṛta, both the effect and its cause; Caturātmā, of fourfold self; Caturvyūha, of fourfold manifestation; Caturdaṃṣṭra, the four-tusked; and Caturbhuja, the four-armed.
He is Bhrājiṣṇu, the ever-shining; Bhojana, the object of enjoyment; Bhoktā, the enjoyer; Sahiṣṇu, the all-enduring; Jagadādija, born at the beginning of the world; Anagha, the sinless; Vijaya, victory itself; Jetā, the conqueror; Viśvayoni, the womb of the universe; and Punarvasu, who dwells again and again within all.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is Upendra, the younger of Indra; Vāmana, the dwarf; Prāṃśu, the towering; Amogha, the unerring; Śuci, the pure; Ūrjita, of mighty strength; Atīndra, who surpasses Indra; Saṃgraha, the gatherer of all; Sarga, creation itself; Dhṛtātmā, the self-sustained; Niyama, the appointing power; and Yama, the restrainer.
He is Vedya, the one to be known; Vaidya, the wise physician; Sadāyogī, ever united in yoga; Vīrahā, slayer of mighty foes; Mādhava, lord of knowledge; Madhu, the sweetness of nectar; Atīndriya, beyond the senses; Mahāmāya, of great wondrous power; Mahotsāha, of mighty energy; and Mahābala, of great strength.
He is Mahābuddhi, of great intelligence; Mahāvīrya, of great virility; Mahāśakti, of great power; Mahādyuti, of great splendor; Anirdeśyavapus, whose form cannot be defined; Śrīmān, the glorious; Ameyātmā, of immeasurable being; and Mahādridhṛk, who upheld the great mountain.
He is Maheṣvāsa, the mighty archer; Mahībhartā, the upholder of the earth; Śrīnivāsa, the abode of Śrī; Satāṃ gati, the refuge of the good; Aniruddha, the unobstructed; Surānanda, the joy of the gods; Govinda, the keeper of cows and finder of the earth; and Govidāṃ pati, lord of those who know the words of wisdom.
He is Marīci, the ray of light; Damana, the subduer; Haṃsa, the swan of the soul; Suparṇa, the fair-winged; Bhujagottama, best of serpents; Hiraṇyanābha, the golden-naveled; Sutapas, of perfect austerity; Padmanābha, the lotus-naveled; and Prajāpati, lord of creatures.
He is Amṛtyu, the deathless; Sarvadṛk, the all-seeing; Siṃha, the lion; Saṃdhātā, who joins and ordains; Saṃdhimān, who abides by his bonds; Sthira, the steadfast; Aja, the unborn; Durmarṣaṇa, who cannot be borne by foes; Śāstā, the chastiser and teacher; Viśrutātmā, of famed renown; and Surārihā, slayer of the enemies of the gods.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is Guru, the teacher; Gurutama, the highest of teachers; Dhāma, the supreme abode; Satya, the true; Satyaparākrama, of true and tireless valor; Nimiṣa, who closes his eyes in cosmic sleep; Animiṣa, the ever-wakeful; Sragvī, garlanded; Vācaspati, lord of speech; and Udāradhī, of noble intellect.
He is Agraṇī, the foremost leader; Grāmaṇī, the guide of the multitude; Śrīmān, the glorious; Nyāya, justice itself; Netā, the leader; Samīraṇa, the moving wind; Sahasramūrdhā, the thousand-headed; Viśvātmā, the soul of the universe; Sahasrākṣa, the thousand-eyed; and Sahasrapāt, the thousand-footed.
He is Āvartana, who turns the wheel of being; Nivṛttātmā, the soul turned away from the world; Saṃvṛta, the enveloped and hidden; Saṃpramardana, the great crusher of foes; Ahassaṃvartaka, who sets the days revolving; Vahni, the bearer of oblations as fire; Anila, the wind; and Dharaṇīdhara, the upholder of the earth.
He is Suprasāda, the gracious; Prasannātmā, of serene soul; Viśvadhṛk, who upholds the universe; Viśvabhuk, who enjoys all worlds; Vibhu, the omnipresent; Satkartā, the honorer of the good; Satkṛta, who is honored; Sādhu, the righteous; Jahnu, who withdraws all beings; Nārāyaṇa, who dwells upon the waters; and Nara, the eternal Man.
He is Asaṃkhyeya, the innumerable; Aprameyātmā, of immeasurable being; Viśiṣṭa, the most excellent; Śiṣṭakṛt, who lays down the law for the righteous; Śuci, the pure; Siddhārtha, whose every purpose is fulfilled; Siddhasaṃkalpa, whose resolves come to pass; Siddhida, the giver of perfection; and Siddhisādhana, the means to all attainment.
He is Vṛṣāhī, whose days are righteousness; Vṛṣabha, the bull of dharma; Viṣṇu, the all-pervading; Vṛṣaparvā, the ladder of righteousness; Vṛṣodara, from whose belly all beings spring; Vardhana, who makes all flourish; Vardhamāna, the ever-increasing; Vivikta, the unmingled and aloof; and Śrutisāgara, the ocean of sacred scripture.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is Subhuja, the fair-armed; Durdhara, hard to hold or bear; Vāgmī, the eloquent; Mahendra, the great lord; Vasuda, the giver of wealth; Vasu, wealth itself; Naikarūpa, of manifold forms; Bṛhadrūpa, of vast form; Śipiviṣṭa, who dwells within the rays; and Prakāśana, the illuminator.
He is Ojastejodyutidhara, who holds vital force, splendor, and brilliance; Prakāśātmā, of luminous self; Pratāpana, who blazes forth heat; Ṛddha, the abounding; Spaṣṭākṣara, made manifest in the syllable Oṃ; Mantra, the sacred utterance; Candrāṃśu, ray of the moon; and Bhāskaradyuti, with the radiance of the sun.
He is Amṛtāṃśūdbhava, from whom the nectar-rayed moon arose; Bhānu, the shining; Śaśabindu, the hare-marked moon; Sureśvara, lord of the gods; Auṣadha, the healing herb; Jagataḥsetu, the bridge across the world; and Satyadharmaparākrama, whose valor is truth and righteousness.
He is Bhūtabhavyabhavannātha, lord of past, future, and present; Pavana, the wind; Pāvana, the purifier; Anila, the breath that needs no support; Kāmahā, destroyer of desire; Kāmakṛt, fulfiller of desire; Kānta, the beautiful and beloved; Kāma, desire itself; Kāmaprada, the granter of wishes; and Prabhu, the lord.
He is Yugādikṛt, the maker of the ages' beginning; Yugāvarta, who turns the cycle of yugas; Naikamāya, of manifold illusion; Mahāśana, the great devourer; Adṛśya, the invisible; Vyaktarūpa, of manifest form; Sahasrajit, conqueror of thousands; and Anantajit, the ever-victorious.
He is Iṣṭa, the beloved; Viśiṣṭa, the most excellent; Śiṣṭeṣṭa, dear to the righteous; Śikhaṇḍī, the crested one; Nahuṣa, who binds all beings; Vṛṣa, the embodiment of dharma; Krodhahā, slayer of wrath; Krodhakṛt, who rouses wrath against the wicked; Kartā, the doer; Viśvabāhu, of universal arms; and Mahīdhara, the upholder of the earth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is Acyuta, the unfallen; Prathita, the renowned; Prāṇa, the breath of life; Prāṇada, giver of life; Vāsavānuja, the younger brother of Indra; Apāṃ nidhi, the treasure-house of the waters; Adhiṣṭhāna, the foundation of all; Apramatta, the ever-vigilant; and Pratiṣṭhita, the self-established.
He is Skanda, who flows forth as nectar; Skandadhara, upholder of the path of dharma; Dhurya, who bears the yoke of creation; Varada, the granter of boons; Vāyuvāhana, who drives the winds; Vāsudeva, the indwelling and all-pervading; Bṛhadbhānu, of vast radiance; Ādideva, the primeval god; and Puraṃdara, the breaker of strongholds.
He is Aśoka, the sorrowless; Tāraṇa, who ferries beings across; Tāra, the deliverer; Śūra, the hero; Śauri, born in the line of Śūra; Janeśvara, lord of men; Anukūla, the ever-favorable; Śatāvarta, of a hundred manifestations; Padmī, the lotus-holder; and Padmanibhekṣaṇa, whose eyes resemble lotuses.
He is Padmanābha, the lotus-naveled; Aravindākṣa, the lotus-eyed; Padmagarbha, who is contemplated in the lotus of the heart; Śarīrabhṛt, the sustainer of bodies; Maharddhi, of great prosperity; Ṛddha, the abounding; Vṛddhātmā, the ancient soul; Mahākṣa, the great-eyed; and Garuḍadhvaja, who bears Garuḍa on his banner.
He is Atula, the incomparable; Śarabha, who dwells within the body; Bhīma, the terrible; Samayajña, knower of the proper occasions; Havis, the oblation; Hari, the tawny and the remover of sin; Sarvalakṣaṇalakṣaṇya, known by every auspicious mark; Lakṣmīvān, the consort of Lakṣmī; and Samitiṃjaya, the victor in battle.
He is Vikṣara, the imperishable; Rohita, the assumer of forms like the fish; Mārga, the path; Hetu, the cause; Dāmodara, bound at the waist with a cord; Saha, the all-enduring; Mahīdhara, upholder of the earth; Mahābhāga, of great fortune; Vegavān, the swift; and Amitāśana, of boundless appetite.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is Udbhava, the source of all; Kṣobhaṇa, who stirred creation into being; Deva, the resplendent; Śrīgarbha, in whose womb all glory abides; Parameśvara, the supreme lord; Karaṇa, the instrument; Kāraṇa, the cause; Kartā, the doer; Vikartā, the maker of manifold worlds; Gahana, the unfathomable; and Guha, the hidden one.
He is Vyavasāya, resolute knowledge; Vyavasthāna, the ordainer of order; Saṃsthāna, the final dissolution; Sthānada, the giver of abodes; Dhruva, the immovable; Pararddhi, of supreme prosperity; Parama, the highest; Spaṣṭa, the manifest; Tuṣṭa, the contented; Puṣṭa, the full; and Śubhekṣaṇa, of auspicious gaze.
He is Rāma, the delightful; Virāma, the end and cessation; Virāṭa, the desireless; Mārga, the path; Neya, who is to be guided to by wisdom; Naya, the guide; Anaya, who needs no guide; Vīra, the hero; Śaktimatāṃ śreṣṭha, foremost of the powerful; Dharma, righteousness; Dharmavid uttama, the highest knower of dharma.
He is Vaikuṇṭha, who unites the scattered worlds; Puruṣa, the cosmic Person; Prāṇa, the breath of life; Prāṇada, the giver of life; Praṇava, the sacred Oṃ; Pṛthu, the vast and expanded; Hiraṇyagarbha, the golden womb; Śatrughna, slayer of foes; Vyāpta, the all-pervading; Vāyu, the wind; and Adhokṣaja, who never declines from his own nature.
He is Ṛtu, the season; Sudarśana, of fair vision; Kāla, time itself; Parameṣṭhī, established on high; Parigraha, the receiver and embracer of all; Ugra, the formidable; Saṃvatsara, the year; Dakṣa, the able and swift; Viśrāma, the place of rest; and Viśvadakṣiṇa, skillful in all things and most liberal.
He is Vistāra, the expanse in which all worlds abide; Sthāvarasthāṇu, the firm and unmoving ground; Pramāṇa, the measure and proof of all; Bīja avyaya, the imperishable seed; Artha, the goal of all desire; Anartha, who has no want of his own; Mahākośa, the great treasury; Mahābhoga, of great enjoyment; and Mahādhana, of great wealth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is Anirviṇṇa, the never-despondent; Sthaviṣṭha, the most massive; Bhū, the abode of being; Dharmayūpa, the sacrificial post of righteousness; Mahāmakha, the great sacrifice; Nakṣatranemi, the hub of the stars; Nakṣatrī, the lord of constellations; Kṣama, the all-capable; Kṣāma, who abides when all is dissolved; and Samīhana, who wills the good of all.
He is Yajña, the sacrifice; Ijya, the one to be worshipped; Mahejya, supremely worshipped; Kratu, the rite; Satra, the prolonged offering; Satāṃ gati, the refuge of the good; Sarvadarśī, the all-seeing; Vimuktātmā, the ever-liberated soul; Sarvajña, the omniscient; and Jñānam uttamam, the highest knowledge.
He is Suvrata, of holy vows; Sumukha, of fair countenance; Sūkṣma, the subtle; Sughoṣa, of auspicious sound; Sukhada, the giver of joy; Suhṛt, the true friend; Manohara, the captivator of the mind; Jitakrodha, conqueror of wrath; Vīrabāhu, of heroic arms; and Vidāraṇa, the render of the wicked.
He is Svāpana, who casts beings into the sleep of ignorance; Svavaśa, subject to none but himself; Vyāpī, the all-pervading; Naikātmā, of manifold selves; Naikakarmakṛt, the doer of countless deeds; Vatsara, the abode of all; Vatsala, the affectionate; Vatsī, the loving father; Ratnagarbha, in whose womb lie all jewels; and Dhaneśvara, lord of wealth.
He is Dharmagub, the protector of dharma; Dharmakṛt, the doer of righteousness; Dharmī, the upholder of dharma; Sat, the existent; Asat, the non-existent; Kṣara, the perishable; Akṣara, the imperishable; Avijñātā, who is beyond all knowing; Sahasrāṃśu, the thousand-rayed; Vidhātā, the ordainer; and Kṛtalakṣaṇa, who has fixed the marks of all.
He is Gabhastinemi, the hub at the center of the rays; Sattvastha, abiding in the heart of all beings; Siṃha, the lion; Bhūtamaheśvara, the great lord of beings; Ādideva, the primeval god; Mahādeva, the great god; Deveśa, lord of the gods; Devabhṛt, the upholder of the gods; and Guru, the teacher.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is Uttara, who lifts beings out of the ocean of being; Gopati, lord of the earth and of cows; Goptā, the protector; Jñānagamya, to be reached by wisdom; Purātana, the ancient; Śarīrabhūtabhṛt, who upholds the elements of the body; Bhoktā, the enjoyer; Kapīndra, lord of monkeys as Rāma; and Bhūridakṣiṇa, of abundant sacrificial gifts.
He is Somapa, the drinker of soma; Amṛtapa, the drinker of nectar; Soma, the moon that nourishes the herbs; Purujit, conqueror of many; Purusattama, supreme among beings; Vinaya, who humbles the proud; Jaya, victory; Satyasaṃdha, true to his word; Dāśārha, worthy of all offerings; and Sātvatāṃ pati, lord of the Sātvatas.
He is Jīva, the living soul; Vinayitā, the bestower of discipline; Sākṣī, the witness; Mukunda, the giver of liberation; Amitavikrama, of measureless valor; Ambhonidhi, the treasure-house of waters; Anantātmā, of infinite being; Mahodadhiśaya, who reposes upon the great ocean; and Antaka, the maker of the end.
He is Aja, the unborn; Mahārha, supremely worthy of worship; Svābhāvya, established in his own nature; Jitāmitra, conqueror of foes; Pramodana, the giver of joy; Ānanda, bliss itself; Nandana, the delighter; Nanda, the abounding in joy; Satyadharmā, whose dharma is truth; and Trivikrama, who strode across the three worlds.
He is Maharṣi Kapilācārya, the great seer who taught as Kapila; Kṛtajña, knower of all that is wrought; Medinīpati, lord of the earth; Tripada, the three-stepped; Tridaśādhyakṣa, overseer of the thirty gods; Mahāśṛṅga, the great-horned who saved the Vedas; and Kṛtāntakṛt, the maker of all ends.
He is Mahāvarāha, the great boar; Govinda, the finder of the earth; Suṣeṇa, of goodly hosts; Kanakāṅgadī, adorned with golden armlets; Guhya, the secret one; Gabhīra, the profound; Gahana, the unfathomable; Gupta, the hidden; and Cakragadādhara, the bearer of discus and mace.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is Vedhā, the creator; Svāṅga, who is his own instrument; Ajita, the unconquered; Kṛṣṇa, the dark and all-attracting; Dṛḍha, the firm; Saṃkarṣaṇa, who draws all beings into himself; Acyuta, the unfallen; Varuṇa, who gathers his rays at evening; Varuṇa, son of Varuṇa as Vasiṣṭha; Vṛkṣa, the tree that stands unshaken; Puṣkarākṣa, the lotus-eyed; and Mahāmanas, of vast mind.
He is Bhagavān, the blessed lord of the six excellences; Bhagahā, who withdraws those powers at dissolution; Nandī, ever joyful; Vanamālī, wearer of the forest garland; Halāyudha, who wields the plow as Balarāma; Āditya, the son of Aditi; Jyotirāditya, the radiance within the orb of the sun; Sahiṣṇu, the all-enduring; and Gatisattama, the supreme refuge.
He is Sudhanvā, of the goodly bow; Khaṇḍaparaśu, who bore the battle-axe as Rāma Jāmadagnya; Dāruṇa, the merciless to the wicked; Draviṇaprada, the giver of riches; Divaḥspṛk, who touches the heavens; Sarvadṛk, the all-seeing; Vyāsa, the arranger of the Vedas; Vācaspati, lord of speech; and Ayonija, who is born of no womb.
He is Trisāmā, hymned by the three Sāmans; Sāmaga, the singer of the Sāman; Sāma, the chant itself; Nirvāṇa, supreme extinction in bliss; Bheṣaja, the medicine; Bhiṣak, the physician; Saṃnyāsakṛt, who ordained renunciation; Śama, tranquility; Śānta, the peaceful; Niṣṭhā, the final ground; Śānti, peace itself; and Parāyaṇa, the supreme goal.
He is Śubhāṅga, of beautiful form; Śāntida, the giver of peace; Sraṣṭā, the creator; Kumuda, who delights in the earth; Kuvaleśaya, who reposes upon the waters; Gohita, the well-doer of the earth and cattle; Gopati, lord of the earth; Goptā, the protector; Vṛṣabhākṣa, whose eyes rain down all desires; and Vṛṣapriya, the lover of righteousness.
He is Anivartī, who never turns back from righteousness; Nivṛttātmā, the soul withdrawn from the world; Saṃkṣeptā, who draws the vast worlds together; Kṣemakṛt, the bestower of welfare; Śiva, the auspicious; Śrīvatsavakṣas, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark upon his breast; Śrīvāsa, the dwelling-place of Śrī; Śrīpati, lord of Śrī; and Śrīmatāṃ vara, foremost of the glorious.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He is Śrīda, the giver of fortune; Śrīśa, lord of Śrī; Śrīnivāsa, the abode of Śrī; Śrīnidhi, the treasury of glory; Śrīvibhāvana, the dispenser of fortune to all; Śrīdhara, who bears Śrī upon his breast; Śrīkara, the maker of prosperity; Śreyas, the highest good; Śrīmān, the glorious; and Lokatrayāśraya, the refuge of the three worlds.
He is Svakṣa, of beautiful eyes; Svaṅga, of fair limbs; Śatānanda, of a hundred joys; Nandī, supreme bliss; Jyotirgaṇeśvara, lord of the host of luminaries; Vijitātmā, who has conquered the self; Vidheyātmā, ever at his own command; Satkīrti, of true renown; and Chinnasaṃśaya, in whom all doubt is severed.
He is Udīrṇa, who transcends all beings; Sarvataścakṣus, whose eyes are turned in every direction; Anīśa, over whom there is no lord; Śāśvata, the everlasting; Sthira, the steadfast; Bhūśaya, who reposes upon the earth and the waters; Bhūṣaṇa, the ornament of the worlds; Bhūti, pure existence and prosperity; Viśoka, the sorrowless; and Śokanāśana, the destroyer of grief.
He is Arciṣmān, the effulgent; Arcita, the worshipped; Kumbha, the vessel in which all abides; Viśuddhātmā, of utterly pure self; Viśodhana, the purifier; Aniruddha, the unobstructed; Apratiratha, who has no equal foe; Pradyumna, of surpassing wealth; and Amitavikrama, of measureless valor.
He is Kālaneminihā, slayer of the demon Kālanemi; Vīra, the hero; Śūra, the valiant; Śauri, born in the line of Śūra; Janeśvara, lord of men; Trilokātmā, the soul of the three worlds; Trilokeśa, lord of the three worlds; Keśava, of beautiful locks and lord of Brahmā and Śiva; Keśihā, slayer of the demon Keśin; and Hari, the remover of sin.
He is Kāmadeva, the god of love and the object of all desire; Kāmapāla, the guardian of desires fulfilled; Kāmī, in whom all wishes are complete; Kānta, the beautiful; Kṛtāgama, the author of the sacred scriptures; Anirdeśyavapus, of indefinable form; Viṣṇu, the all-pervading; Vīra, the hero; Ananta, the infinite; and Dhanaṃjaya, the winner of wealth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
