"The son said: 'I am your offspring, your son; and a son is so named because he saves. The son is held to be one's very self; therefore by your self save your self here.'"
"The father said: 'In form you are like me, and in character and in self-restraint; and I have tested you many times. Therefore I will take your meal.'"
"So saying, that best of the twice-born, glad of soul, took the meal and, almost smiling, gave it then to the brāhmaṇa."
"Yet even after eating that meal he was not satisfied; and the gleaner, that excellent brāhmaṇa, was overcome with shame."
"Then the virtuous daughter-in-law, standing by, desiring to please the brāhmaṇa, gladly took up her meal and spoke this word to her elder:"
"'Through your line my line shall continue, O brāhmaṇa. Take this meal of mine and give it to the guest.'"
"'By the continuance of your progeny, imperishable worlds will surely be mine; through a grandson one attains those worlds, going whither one grieves no more.'"
"'As the triad headed by righteousness, and likewise the triad of sacred fires, so too the triad of sons and grandsons is, in heaven, surely imperishable.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'A son delivers the ancestors because he saves them — so we have heard. And through sons and grandsons one assuredly enjoys the worlds of the righteous.'"
"The father-in-law said: 'Seeing you with your limbs wasted by wind and sun, pale and emaciated, O you of pious conduct, your mind distraught with hunger —'"
"'how shall I take your meal and so become a destroyer of righteousness? O auspicious one of blessed conduct, you ought not to speak thus.'"
"'You who keep your vow until the sixth mealtime, endowed with good conduct and purity, living a hard life, without food — how could I bear to look upon you so?'"
"'Young, hunger-stricken, and a woman, you are ever to be protected by me; for you, worn out by fasting, are the delight of our kin.'"
"The daughter-in-law said: 'You are the elder of my elder, the deity of deities, the god beyond gods; therefore take my meal, O lord.'"
"'My body, my life-breath, and my merit — all this is for the service of my elder. By your grace, O brāhmaṇa, I shall attain the worlds I long for.'"
"'Thinking either "she is to be regarded" or "she is of firm devotion," or else "she is one for whom I must provide," you ought, O brāhmaṇa, to take this meal.'"
"The father-in-law said: 'By this ever-virtuous conduct of yours you shine, O good woman — you who, endowed with righteous vows, look to the service of your elders.'"
"'Therefore I will take your meal, O daughter-in-law; you do not deserve to be cheated of your due. Reckoned among them, O blessed one, you are the foremost of the upholders of righteousness.'"
"So saying, he took up that meal and gave it to the brāhmaṇa; and then that brāhmaṇa was at last contented by the gift of that great-souled and righteous man."
"Glad of soul, that eloquent best of the twice-born — who was Dharma himself in human form — then spoke this word to the bull among brāhmaṇas:"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'By your pure gift, righteously obtained with effort and given freely to the best of your power, I am well pleased, O excellent brāhmaṇa.'"
"'Behold! Your gift is being proclaimed in heaven by the dwellers there; and see the rain of flowers falling from the sky upon the earth.'"
"'The divine sages, gods, and gandharvas, and those who go before the gods, and the messengers of the gods, stand here singing your praises, amazed at your gift.'"
"'The brahmic sages seated in their celestial cars, and those who have gone to the world of Brahmā, long to behold you. Go to heaven, O bull among brāhmaṇas.'"
"'All your ancestors who have gone to the world of the fathers are delivered by you, and many more who are yet to come, through many ages hence.'"
"'By chastity, by sacrifice, by giving, and likewise by austerity, and by guileless righteousness — therefore go to heaven, O brāhmaṇa.'"
"'Because you, O man of firm vows, practise austerity with supreme faith, the gods are pleased with you for this, O most excellent of brāhmaṇas.'"
"'Since all this, your every possession, was given up with a pure heart in a time of dire need, by that deed of yours this heaven has been won.'"
"'Hunger drives away wisdom and dispels the righteous mind; and one whose understanding is gripped by hunger forsakes even his firmness.'"
"'But whoever conquers the craving to eat surely conquers heaven; and when one delights in giving, then righteousness does not falter.'"
"'Disregarding love for your son and love for your wife, and knowing righteousness alone to be your true elder, you reckoned not your own craving.'"
"'Slender is the acquiring of goods by men; greater than that is a gift to a worthy recipient; greater than the gift is the right time; and greater still than that is faith.'"
"'The gate of heaven is exceeding subtle, and through delusion men do not see it. The bolt that bars heaven is the seed of greed, hidden by passion, hard to overcome.'"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'But those men perceive that gate who have conquered anger and subdued their senses — brāhmaṇas yoked to austerity, who give according to their power.'"
"'He who can give a thousand and gives a hundred, he who can give a hundred and gives ten, and he who gives but water according to his power — all are held to reap an equal fruit.'"
"'For King Rantideva, having nothing, gave only water with a pure mind, O brāhmaṇa, and thereby went to the summit of heaven.'"
"'Righteousness is not so well pleased, my dear one, by gifts of great fruit that are given, as it is contented by slender gifts righteously obtained and hallowed by faith.'"
"'King Nṛga gave thousands of cows to brāhmaṇas, yet by giving away a single cow that belonged to another he came to hell.'"
"'By the gift of his own flesh, King Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, attained the worlds of those who have done meritorious deeds, and that man of firm vows rejoices in heaven.'"
In sheer abundance there is no merit for men; for the good, what is earned righteously by one's own power outweighs, O brāhmaṇa, the fruit gathered through manifold sacrifices.
Anger destroys the fruit of giving, and through greed one does not reach heaven; but the man of righteous conduct, knowing how to give, attains heaven through his austerity.
Not by many Rājasūya sacrifices offered with lavish gifts, nor by many Aśvamedhas, could a fruit be won equal to this of yours.
By a measure of barley-meal the world of Brahmā has been won by you, O sinless one; go, O brāhmaṇa, to the stainless abode of Brahmā as you wish.
For all of you, O best of the twice-born, a celestial chariot now stands ready; mount it at your pleasure. I am Dharma, O brāhmaṇa—behold me.
By you the body has been purified, and your fame stands firm in the world; with your wife, with your son, and with your daughter-in-law, go to heaven.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Thus addressed by Dharma, that brāhmaṇa mounted the chariot and, with his wife, his son, and his daughter-in-law, went up to heaven.
When that brāhmaṇa, knower of dharma, had gone to heaven with his son, his daughter-in-law, and his wife as the fourth, I then came forth from my burrow.
And then, by the scent of that barley-meal, by the moisture of the water, by the crushing of celestial flowers, by those very fragments of the good man's gift, and by that brāhmaṇa's austerity, my head was turned to gold.
And by the slender gift of that man true to his word, half my body too, O brāhmaṇas, was made of gold. Behold this vast transformation, wrought by the austerity of that wise one.
'How might my other side too become like this?'—so thinking, O twice-born, eagerly I visit again and again the groves of penance and the sites of sacrifice.
Hearing of this sacrifice of the wise king of the Kurus, I came with the highest hope—yet I have not been turned to gold.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, laughing, I spoke these words: this sacrifice is by no means the equal of that measure of barley-meal.
For by those fragments of the barley-meal I was then turned to gold; this great sacrifice, in my judgment, is not their equal.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having thus spoken to all the foremost brāhmaṇas at the sacrifice, the mongoose vanished from sight, O king, and those brāhmaṇas went to their homes.
All this I have related to you, O conqueror of hostile cities—the wonder that came to pass at that great horse-sacrifice.
You should feel no astonishment at all, O king, at the sacrifice; for thousands upon tens of millions of sages have gone to heaven through their austerities.
Harmlessness toward all beings, contentment, good conduct, uprightness, austerity, self-restraint, truth, and giving—these are held to be of equal worth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Janamejaya said: Kings are devoted to sacrifice, the great sages devoted to austerity, and the brāhmaṇas set upon peace—'tranquillity and self-restraint,' so they say, O lord.
'Therefore nothing here is found to equal the fruits of sacrifice'—so my mind has held, and so without doubt it seemed to me.
For many kings, O best of the twice-born, having worshipped with sacrifices and won the highest fame here, departed hence to heaven after death.
The thousand-eyed king of the gods, mighty in splendour, the all-powerful one, attained by sacrifices with abundant gifts the entire sovereignty over the gods.
Just as King Yudhiṣṭhira, with Bhīma and Arjuna at his head, was the equal of the king of the gods in prosperity and in valour.
Then why did that mongoose disparage that rite, the Aśvamedha, the great sacrifice of that high-souled king?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The foremost rule of sacrifice and its fruit, O bull among men, hear from me as I tell it truly here, O king, O Bhārata.
Long ago, while Śakra was sacrificing, all the great sages spoke out, when the priests were busy with their tasks and the rite of sacrifice was under way.
As the oblation was poured into the fire, the office of the hotṛ priest being richly endowed, the gods being summoned, and the supreme sages standing by.
By the brāhmaṇas then well assured, versed in their own scriptures and clear of voice, O king, and by the foremost adhvaryu priests, tireless and deft.
At that moment of immolation, when the sacrificial animals had been seized, the great sages, O mighty king, were filled with compassion.
Then, seeing the wretched animals, those sages rich in austerity came up to Śakra and said: 'This rule of sacrifice is not auspicious.'
'This is a misunderstanding on your part, who desire the great dharma; for herds of animals at a sacrifice are not what is sanctioned by the rule, O Purandara.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'This undertaking of yours, O lord, is a destroyer of dharma; this is no dharma born of righteousness—violence is not called dharma.'
'Let them perform your sacrifice by scripture alone, if you wish it; by a sacrifice sanctioned by the rule your dharma would be very great.'
'Sacrifice with seeds, O thousand-eyed one, kept stored at most for three years; this is great dharma, O Śakra, attained when rightly pondered.'
But Śatakratu did not accept that counsel spoken by the sages who perceive the truth, for he was in thrall to pride and delusion.
A very great dispute arose between Śakra and the great sages—whether sacrifice should be made with moving creatures or with things that do not move, O Bhārata.
But those sages who perceive the truth, weary of the dispute, then, by agreement with Śakra, put the question to King Vasu.
'O greatly blessed king, what is the scriptural tradition handed down for sacrifices? Should one sacrifice with sacred animals, or rather with seeds and with that which is unborn?'
Hearing that question of theirs, without weighing its strength and weakness, the king declared: 'One should sacrifice with whatever is brought to hand.'
Having spoken thus, that king sank into the nether world; for he had uttered a falsehood here, O king—that lord and master of the Cedis.
Whoever, being unwise, though longing for dharma, sacrifices with wealth obtained by unrighteous means, gains no fruit of dharma.
And the man of evil soul who makes a snare of dharma, who gives gifts to brāhmaṇas merely to win the world's trust—
Such an unbridled twice-born, having gained wealth by sinful deed and possessed by passion and delusion, attains in the end a foul course.
The gifts bestowed by that sinful man of ruined judgment, however vast, find no firm ground and perish.
For that wicked-minded man given to unrighteousness, the cruel one of evil soul, there is no glory in his giving—neither here nor after death.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Indeed, the man bent on hoarding, in thrall to greed and delusion, of sinful mind, torments living beings with his violence.
He who, having gained wealth thus through greed, sacrifices and gives—by that deed he does not succeed, for it springs from ill-gotten means.
Gleaned grain, root, fruit, herb, or a vessel of water, O you rich in austerity—righteous men who give such a gift according to their means go to heaven.
This is great dharma: renunciation, giving, and compassion for living beings; chastity, truth, mercy, steadfastness, and forbearance—this is the eternal root of the eternal dharma.
For we hear, O brāhmaṇas, of kings of old, Viśvāmitra and the rest—Viśvāmitra and Asita, Janaka the lord of earth, Kakṣasena and Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and Sindhudvīpa the king.
These and many other kings, rich in austerity, attained the highest perfection through truth and through gifts gained by righteous means.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras who have taken to austerity—purified by the fire of giving and dharma, they go to heaven, O Bhārata.
Janamejaya said: If, O reverend one, all is attainable through renunciation that comes by righteous means, then declare all this to me, for you are skilled in speaking.
The great fruit that came of the gift of barley-meal by one living on gleaned grain has been told me as great, O brāhmaṇa; this is true beyond doubt.
How then, among all sacrifices, would the supreme certainty be reached? This you ought to tell me in full, O bull among the twice-born.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: On this they recount too this ancient tale, of what came to pass long ago at the great sacrifice of Agastya, O subduer of foes.
Long ago, Agastya of great splendour, devoted to the welfare of all beings, entered upon a consecration of twelve years, O mighty king.
At the rite of that high-souled one the officiating priests were like fire itself—living on roots, or taking no food at all, grinding grain with stones, or drinking only the rays of the sun.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Some ate only what was ground fine, some only the leavings of others, some kept naught for the morrow; and ascetics and mendicants too were there, stationed all about.
All of them had dharma made manifest in them, had conquered anger and subdued their senses; all were established in self-restraint, free of hypocrisy and delusion.
Ever fixed in pure conduct, untroubled by the senses, those great sages attended upon that sacrifice and partook of its food.
That food the reverend one had procured according to his power; and at that rite nothing whatever was unfit, for great sacrifices have been performed thus by many sages.
But while the great sacrifice of Agastya, of such a kind, was going on, the thousand-eyed one did not send rain, O best of the Bhāratas.
Then, in an interval of the rite of the high-souled Agastya, O king, this discourse arose among the sages of disciplined souls.
'Agastya, the sacrificer, gives food without grudging; yet the rain-cloud sends no rain—how will there be food?'
'And this great rite of the sage, O brāhmaṇas, lasts twelve years; and the god will not send rain for these twelve years.'
'Considering this, you ought to do a kindness for this wise great sage, Agastya of surpassing austerity.'
When these words had been thus spoken, Agastya the mighty, eloquent of speech, won the sages over with a bow of his head and said this:
'If for twelve years Vāsava sends no rain, I shall perform the sacrifice of thought; this is the eternal rule.'
'If for twelve years Vāsava sends no rain, by my own exertion I shall accomplish other sacrifices of surpassing rigour.'
'This sacrifice of mine with seeds, gathered over many years—I shall carry it out with prepared seeds, and here there will be no hindrance.'
'This rite of mine cannot be made vain by any means, whether the god sends rain here or whether he does not.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Or else Indra may grant my entreaty—but not by his mere pleasure; I myself shall become Indra and give life to the creatures.'
'Whatever each being was born to feed upon, that it shall have just so; and beyond this I shall make abundance, again and again, exceedingly.'
'This day let gold come hither, and whatever other wealth is hard to win; whatever exists in the three worlds, let it come here of its own accord.'
'And the celestial throngs of apsarases, with the gandharvas and the kiṃnaras, Viśvāvasu and the others too—let them ever wait upon you.'
'And whatever wealth there is among the Northern Kurus, let it all present itself here of its own accord at my sacrifice—heaven, and the dwellers in heaven, and Dharma himself as well.'
When he had spoken thus, all this came to pass for that wise one. Then those sages, beholding the power of that sage's austerity, were amazed and all spoke this word of deep meaning:
'We are pleased by your word, yet we do not wish for this expenditure of austerity; we are content with our own sacrifices, and we desire only what comes by righteous means.'
'Sacrifices, consecrations, oblations, and whatever else we seek—let that be ours through sacrifices of our own making; we do not seek it from elsewhere.'
We win our food by lawful means, devoted to our own duties, and we seek to master the Vedas through chastity, in accordance with right law.
And in due course, having lawfully gone forth from our homes, we shall practice austerity by the prescribed gateways that are sanctioned by righteousness.
This resolve of yours is wholly right, free from all violence; proclaim this non-injury at sacrifices forever, O lord.
Then we shall be well pleased, O best of the twice-born; and being released at the conclusion, we shall depart from this sacrificial session.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Even as they were speaking thus, the king of the gods, Puraṃdara of mighty splendor, beholding the power of his austerity, sent down rain.
And before the sacrifice was concluded, O Janamejaya, Indra, lord of the gods, of measureless valor, became a rainer of showers at will.
And the lord of the thirty gods himself came forth, O royal sage, and, placing Bṛhaspati before him, conciliated that Agastya.
Then, at the close of the sacrifice, Agastya, supremely pleased, honored those great sages according to rule and dismissed them.
Janamejaya said: Who was that, in the form of a mongoose with a golden head, who spoke in a human voice? Tell me this, for I ask you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Of this I was not asked before, nor was it told by us. Let it be heard who that mongoose was, and how his speech was human.
In olden days, it is said, Jamadagni resolved to perform a śrāddha; the cow of oblations came to him, and he himself milked her.
He set that milk in a new vessel, firm and clean; and Anger, in his own embodied shape, overturned the pot.
Wishing to test that best of sages—what would he do when an offense was given—that evil-minded one, so reflecting, defiled the milk.
But the sage, recognizing him as Anger, was not in the least angered at him; whereupon that Anger, taking embodied form and standing with joined palms, said this to him:
"I am conquered, O best of the Bhṛgus! It is a false report in the world that the Bhṛgus are exceedingly prone to wrath, for I have been vanquished by you."
"Now today I stand at your mercy, who are forbearing and great of soul; I dread your austerity, O virtuous one. Show me your grace, O mighty lord."
Jamadagni said: "You have been seen by me face to face, O Anger. Go, with your fever gone. You have done me no wrong this day, and there is no resentment in me."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"But those for whose sake this resolve concerning the milk was made by me—they are your forefathers, the greatly blessed; turn to them for understanding, and let you go."
Thus addressed, struck with terror, he vanished there; and through the curse-like contact of the forefathers he attained the state of a mongoose.
He propitiated them, that there might be an end to the curse; and he was told by them: "When you shall revile Dharma, then you shall be released."
So bidden by them, scorning the regions sacred to sacrifice and the forests of righteousness, ranging about, he came at last to that sacrifice.
Then, having reviled the son of Dharma over that measure of barley-meal, he, that Anger, was freed from the curse; for Dharma himself was Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thus did this come to pass at the sacrifice of that great-souled one; and there, even as we looked on, the mongoose vanished away.
Janamejaya said: When my illustrious grandsires the Pāṇḍavas had won the kingdom, how did they conduct themselves toward the great-souled king Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
That king, his counsellors slain, his sons slain, left without support and stripped of sovereignty—how did he fare, and how the renowned Gāndhārī?
And for how long did those great-souled forefathers of mine remain in possession of the kingdom? This you ought to expound to me.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having won the kingdom, their foes slain, the great-souled Pāṇḍavas governed the earth, keeping Dhṛtarāṣṭra at their head.
Upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra waited Vidura and Saṃjaya, and the wise Yuyutsu too, that Kaurava born of a vaiśya woman.
In all affairs the Pāṇḍavas consulted that king, and with his sanction they carried them out for fifteen years.
Daily those heroes would go and attend upon that king, doing homage at his feet and abiding by the Dharma-king's will; and when he had kissed their heads, they went about all their tasks.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Kuntī, daughter of Kuntibhoja, deferred to Gāndhārī; and Draupadī and Subhadrā and the other wives of the Pāṇḍavas behaved with equal devotion toward both mothers-in-law, as was due.
Costly couches, garments, and ornaments, and all things befitting a king, and foods and dainties in great abundance—all these, O great king, Yudhiṣṭhira presented to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Likewise Kuntī behaved toward Gāndhārī as toward an elder; and Vidura, Saṃjaya, and Yuyutsu the Kaurava waited upon that aged lord of men whose sons were slain.
And Droṇa's brother-in-law, that one beloved and mighty brāhmaṇa, the great archer Kṛpa, was likewise at his side then.
And the blessed Vyāsa, that sage of old, ever dwelt with the king, telling tales of gods, divine seers, kings, and rākṣasas.
Matters in accord with dharma and bound up with civil dealings, Vidura, sanctioned by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, caused to be carried out.
Even weighty favors sought of him by the neighboring chiefs were obtained at trifling cost, through the influence of Vidura.
He effected releases of prisoners and the freeing of those condemned to death, and the king, son of Dharma, never said anything against it.
And on outings and excursions the Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira of great splendor granted every desire to the son of Ambikā.
Cooks, broth-makers, and confectioners of sweets waited upon king Dhṛtarāṣṭra as in former days.
And costly garments and garlands of many kinds the Pāṇḍavas duly brought to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Maireya liquor, mead, meats, and light beverages, and varied preparations of dainties, they made for him as before.
And those guardians of the earth who came together from all quarters all waited upon the Kaurava lord as in former days.
And Kuntī and Draupadī, and the lovely Sātvatī woman, and Ulūpī the serpent-maiden, and the lady Citrāṅgadā as well—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
and the sister of Dhṛṣṭaketu, and the daughter of Jarāsaṃdha—all of these waited like handmaids upon the daughter of Subala.
"Bereft of his sons though he is, let him suffer no grief whatever"—thus did Yudhiṣṭhira ever instruct his brothers, the king commanding them.
And so, having heard the weighty word of the Dharma-king, they conducted themselves with special care—all save Bhīma alone.
For that which had been wrought through the dicing by evil-minded Dhṛtarāṣṭra never slipped from the heart of that hero.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus honored by the Pāṇḍavas, the king, son of Ambikā, disported himself as of old, attended by sages.
And that scion of the Kurus made grants of land in gift to brāhmaṇas, and the king, son of Kuntī, approved of it all.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, devoted to gentleness and full of affection, then spoke thus to his brothers and his counsellors, that lord of the earth:
"By me and by you this lord of men is to be honored. Whoever abides by Dhṛtarāṣṭra's command is my friend; the man who acts contrary is my foe, and shall be cast out."
"And on the appointed days, in the funeral rites for his sons, let the king bestow upon all whatever he is minded to give."
Then that great-minded Kaurava king Dhṛtarāṣṭra gave riches without stint to brāhmaṇas worthy of high honor.
And the Dharma-king, and Bhīma, and Savyasācin, and the twins too, all followed in this out of regard for Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"How may the aged king, smitten with grief for his sons, not perish from any sorrow brought upon him by us?"—thus did they take thought.
"Whatever happiness was the chief of the Kurus' when his sons were living, let him attain that and its enjoyments"—thus were they resolved.
Then all the five Pāṇḍava brothers together, of such disposition, stood obedient to the rule of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
And Dhṛtarāṣṭra looked upon those heroes—well-disciplined, steadfast in good conduct, ever bearing themselves as pupils—as a teacher upon his own.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Gāndhārī, through manifold funeral rites for her sons, discharged her debt to them, bestowing their desires upon the brāhmaṇas.
Thus the foremost of the upholders of dharma, the wise Dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers, did honor to that king.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: That king of mighty splendor, the aged upholder of the Kuru line, saw then nothing displeasing in the son of Pāṇḍu.
While the great-souled Pāṇḍavas held to good conduct, king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, son of Ambikā, grew full of contentment.
And Gāndhārī, daughter of Subala, casting off her grief for her sons, was ever well-pleased with them, as with her own children.
Toward the king, son of Vicitravīrya, the Kaurava ever did only what was pleasing and nothing displeasing, O scion of the Kurus.
Whatever task, weighty or slight, that lord of men Dhṛtarāṣṭra would name, and the renowned Gāndhārī as well—
that, O great king, the king, the foremost burden-bearer of the Pāṇḍavas, the slayer of hostile heroes, honored the word and carried out.
With such conduct that lord of men was pleased with him, yet he grieved, remembering his dull and witless son.
And ever, rising at dawn, the king, having said his prayers and purified himself, would invoke for the sons of Pāṇḍu unconquerableness in battle.
And having had the brāhmaṇas recite their blessings and having made oblation to the fire, that lord of men would invoke long life for the sons of Pāṇḍu.
That lord of the earth had not attained from his own sons such supreme joy as the king then attained from the sons of Pāṇḍu.
And to the brāhmaṇas and the elders and the kṣatriyas, O Bhārata, and to the assembled vaiśyas and śūdras, he then became most dear.
And whatever wrong had formerly been done by Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, the king, not keeping it in his heart, deferred to that king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And whatever man did anything displeasing to the son of Ambikā incurred the hatred of the wise son of Kuntī.
For fear of Yudhiṣṭhira no man would speak any ill deed of king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, nor indeed of Duryodhana.
Pleased with the firmness of the king of men, and with his purity, were Gāndhārī and Vidura too—of him whose foe was never born; but not with Bhīma, O slayer of foes.
Bhīma too complied, though grumbling, with the king born of Dharma; yet looking upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra he was ever ill at heart.
That Kaurava complied with the great-minded son of Dharma, the king, who deferred to Dhṛtarāṣṭra—but with his heart turned away.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Between king Yudhiṣṭhira and the father of Duryodhana, O king, men saw no difference in regard to affection.
But whenever the Kaurava king remembered his foolish son, then, O king, that lord brooded ill in his heart against Bhīma.
And likewise Bhīmasena could not endure king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O lord of kings, being ever as it were discontented in his heart.
In secret Vṛkodara did things displeasing to him, and ever, through suborned men, he would countermand his commands.
Then Bhīma, the wrathful one, amid his friends would clap his arms within the hearing of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and of Gāndhārī as well.
Recalling his foe Duryodhana, and Karṇa and Duḥśāsana too, Bhīma, much enraged, then spoke these harsh words:
"The sons of the blind king were all sent by me, of the mace-like arms, to yonder world, their lives taken by sundry weapons."
"These are those two arms of mine, like iron bludgeons, unassailable, coming within whose reach the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra went to their destruction."
"These two arms of mine, anointed with sandal and worthy of worship, by which Duryodhana was brought to ruin with his sons and kinsmen."
These and other manifold words of Vṛkodara, sharp as barbs, the lord of men heard, and was overcome with despair.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And that wise lady, who knew the turning of the times, Gāndhārī, versed in all dharma, heard those bitter taunts.
Then, when the fifteenth year had passed, the lord of men, the king, fell into despair, tormented by the arrows of Bhīma's speech.
Of this the king, Yudhiṣṭhira son of Kuntī, was unaware, nor was Arjuna of the white steeds, nor Kuntī, nor the renowned Draupadī.
But the two sons of Mādrī, who knew Bhīma's mind, gave their assent; yet, guarding the king's feelings, they uttered nothing displeasing.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra gathered together his friends, and choked exceedingly with tears, he spoke this word with great force:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: It is known to you how the destruction of the Kurus came to pass; and all of it, O Kauravas, must be understood to have sprung from my fault.
For it was I who consecrated to the sovereignty of the Kauravas that evil-minded, deluded Duryodhana, the increaser of his kinsmen's terror.
And in that I, dull of mind, did not heed the weighty word of Vāsudeva—"It is well that this sinner be slain along with his counsellors"—
and that, overcome by love of my son, though counselled for my good by the wise—by Vidura, by Bhīṣma, by Droṇa, and by Kṛpa—
and at every step by the blessed great-souled Vyāsa, by Saṃjaya, and by Gāndhārī—for this it is that I am tormented today.
And in that I did not bestow upon the virtuous, great-souled sons of Pāṇḍu this blazing splendor, the heritage of fathers and forefathers—
for, foreseeing the destruction of all the kings, Janārdana the elder brother of Gada deemed this the supreme good.
And so I bear within my heart, forever, these falsehoods that have rebounded upon myself, lodged there like a thousand barbs.
And especially do I burn now in this fifteenth year; and for the purifying of this sin I, most ill-witted, hold myself under vows of restraint.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
At the appointed fourth watch, and sometimes only at the eighth, I take but what quells my thirst; Gāndhārī knows this of me.
All my attendants always suppose that I take food, for they fear Yudhiṣṭhira; yet the son of Pāṇḍu knows it well, and grieves exceedingly.
I lie upon the ground, given over to silent prayer, on a bed of darbha grass and wrapped in deerskin; and the illustrious Gāndhārī too, under the same vow of discipline.
My hundred sons, heroes who never fled from battle, were slain; yet for that I do not mourn, for men know that to be the law of the warrior. Having said this to the King of Righteousness, the Kaurava spoke again.
Blessings upon you, son of the Yādava mother; hear now these words of mine. Happily have I dwelt here, my son, well cared for by you.
Great gifts have been given, and again and again the rites for the dead performed; my years are far advanced, my son, and I have practiced merit as my strength allowed. This Gāndhārī, who has lost her sons, looks upon me with fortitude.
Those who wronged Draupadī and who robbed you of your sovereignty are no more; those cruel men were lawfully slain in battle.
I see nothing further to be requited against them, O joy of the Kurus; all of them, slain while facing the foe, have gone to the worlds won by the sword.
But now the chief thing to be done is what is good for my own self and for Gāndhārī, O lord of kings; this you ought to grant me leave to do.
For you are the best of those who uphold righteousness, ever cherishing the law; you are king and elder to all living beings, and therefore I speak this to you.
With your leave, O hero, I would resort to the forests, clad in rags and bark, O king, together with this Gāndhārī; uttering blessings upon you, I shall become a dweller in the woods.
It is the custom in our line, my son, O bull of the Bhāratas, for all to lay sovereignty upon their sons and at the close of their years to go to the forest, O king.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There, living on air alone or even wholly without food, O hero, I shall practice supreme austerity together with this my wife.
And you too, my son, shall share the fruit of that austerity, for you are the king; for kings partake of the fruit, whether of good or of its opposite.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This kingdom gives me no joy while you are thus afflicted, O king. Shame upon me, dull of mind, heedless, and clinging to the throne!
I who, with my brothers, never perceived that you were stricken with grief, O king, wasted with fasting, sparing of food, and sleeping on the bare ground!
Alas, fool that I am, I have been deceived by you who concealed your mind; having first won my trust, you all the while endured this suffering.
What is a kingdom to me, what enjoyments, what sacrifices, what pleasure, when you, O ruler of the earth, have endured such sorrows for my sake?
By these words of yours, O lord of men, in your affliction, I know my kingdom to be a torment, and my very self as well.
You are our father, you our mother, you our highest elder; deprived of you, where indeed shall we stand?
Let Yuyutsu, your own begotten son, O best of kings, be king, O great king, or whomever else you may deem fit.
I shall go to the forest, and you shall rule this kingdom; already scorched by infamy, I do not deserve to be scorched by you again.
I am not the king; you are the king. I am subject to you. How then could I presume to grant leave to you, my elder and knower of the law?
No anger is in our hearts for what Duryodhana did, O sinless one; what was destined to be, came to pass, for both we and they were deluded.
For we are your sons, even as Duryodhana and the others were; and Gāndhārī and Kuntī are, in my regard, without distinction.
If you, O lord of kings, forsaking me, shall depart, I will follow at your back; by truth I swear it upon myself.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
This earth, full of riches and girded by the sea, would bring me no delight were I bereft of you.
All this is yours; with bowed head I entreat you. We are subject to you, O lord of kings; let the fever of your mind depart.
I deem that what was destined has overtaken you, O lord of men; by good fortune, in serving you, I shall be freed of the fever of my mind.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: My mind, my son, is set upon the ascetic life, O joy of the Kurus; for going to the forest is the custom of our house, O lord.
Long have I dwelt here, my son, and long have you served me; you ought now to grant me, an old man, your leave, O lord of men.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to the King of Righteousness, who stood trembling with palms joined, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, said these words.
I wish that Saṃjaya the high counselor, and Kṛpa the great chariot-warrior, together with you, should prevail upon the lord of the earth.
For my mind grows faint and my mouth is parched, both from my advanced age and from the exertion of speaking.
Having spoken thus, the righteous old king, the upholder of the Kurus, wise as he was, leaned all at once upon Gāndhārī like one whose life had fled.
Seeing the Kuru king sitting thus motionless, the king, the son of Kuntī, slayer of hostile heroes, was swiftly seized with anguish.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: He whose strength equaled ten thousand elephants—this king now lies, leaning upon a woman, as though his life had fled!
He who of old, in his might, ground to powder the iron statue of Bhīmasena—he, seeking support in his weakness, leans upon a woman.
Shame upon me who know not the law, shame upon my understanding, and shame upon my learning, for whose sake this guardian of the earth lies in a state so unbefitting him!
I too shall fast, even as this my elder does, if this king will not eat, nor the illustrious Gāndhārī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, knower of the law, gently stroked his chest and face with a hand cooled by water.
By that touch of the hand, holy and fragrant, graced with gems and healing herbs, the king regained his senses.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Touch me again with your hand and embrace me, son of Pāṇḍu, for from your touch I seem to live again, O lotus-eyed one.
I wish to smell your head, O lord of men, and to touch you all over with my hands; for my life-breaths have not yet forsaken me.
This is now the eighth period since I took food, O tiger of the Kurus, by reason of which I am unable to stir.
And this excessive exertion I made in entreating you; thereby, my son, faint of mind, I became as one bereft of sense.
Having received this touch of your hand, O mighty one, a touch like nectar itself, I feel myself revived, O upholder of the Kuru line.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by his eldest father, O Bhārata, the son of Kuntī, out of affection, gently touched him then upon all his limbs.
Then King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having regained his breath, clasped the son of Pāṇḍu in both arms and smelled his head.
And Vidura and all the others wept, grievously stricken; and out of their excess of sorrow the sons of Pāṇḍu said nothing at all to the king.
But Gāndhārī, knower of the law, bearing her grief intensely within her mind, held back her sorrows, O king, and said only, "Not so."
The other women, all of them, together with Kuntī, in deep sorrow, with eyes brimming over with tears, stood gathered around him.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke again to Yudhiṣṭhira: Grant me leave, O king, for the ascetic life, O bull of the Bhāratas.
My mind grows faint, my son, as I keep on speaking again and again; you ought not, my son, to distress me further than this.
As that lord of the Kauravas spoke thus to the son of Pāṇḍu, a great cry of grief arose from all the women of the inner apartments.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Seeing the king, wasted and pale, in a state so unbefitting him, worn out with fasting, reduced to skin and bone—
the mighty-armed son of Dharma, embracing his father and shedding tears born of grief, spoke these words again.
I do not desire life, O best of men, nor the earth, so much as I wish to do what is pleasing to you, O king, scorcher of foes.
But if I am worthy of your favor, or am dear to you, then let food be taken; thereafter we shall know our course.
Then that king of great splendor said to the son of Dharma: With your leave, my son, I would eat; that is my wish.
As the lord of kings, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, was speaking thus to Yudhiṣṭhira, the sage Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, drew near and spoke these words.
Vyāsa said: O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, what the great-souled Dhṛtarāṣṭra, joy of the Kurus, has said to you—do that without hesitation.
For this king is old, and has moreover lost his sons; that he should endure this hardship much longer is, in my judgment, beyond him.
And the greatly blessed Gāndhārī, wise and full of compassion, bears her grief for her sons, O great king, with steadfast fortitude.
I too say to you this very thing: do as I bid. Let the king obtain his leave, lest he die here in vain.
Let the king follow the path of the royal sages of old; for the final refuge of all royal sages is the forest.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Vyāsa of wondrous deeds, the king, the King of Righteousness Yudhiṣṭhira of great splendor, replied.
Your reverence is the one we honor, your reverence is our elder; your reverence is the support of this kingdom and of our line.
I am but a son; your reverence is a father; the king too is my elder; and a son who carries out his father's command is, by the law, truly a son.
Thus addressed, Vyāsa, the best of the upholders of righteousness, of great splendor, spoke again to Yudhiṣṭhira, O lord of peoples.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
It is even so, O mighty-armed Bhārata, as you say; but this king has reached old age and stands at the utmost limit of his span.
He, granted leave by me and by you, O lord of the earth, let him fulfill his own intent; do not become an obstacle to him.
This is the highest law of the royal sages, Yudhiṣṭhira: that death should come either in battle or in the forest by the prescribed observances.
By your father Pāṇḍu, O lord of kings, who ruled the earth, this king was attended like a teacher, as though he were a disciple.
He has worshiped with great sacrifices, rich in priestly gifts and graced with mountains of food; he has tasted enjoyments, and reared his sons.
For thirteen years, while you were in exile, he enjoyed the vast kingdom held in trust for his sons, and gave away wealth of many kinds.
And by you, O tiger among men, with your attendants and through service to your elders, this king has been gratified, and the illustrious Gāndhārī as well.
Grant your father leave; the time has come for him to take up the observances of austerity; and there dwells in him not the least anger, Yudhiṣṭhira, however slight.
Having spoken these words and obtained leave from the king, and being answered by the son of Kuntī, "So be it," he departed for the forest.
When the reverend Vyāsa had gone, the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, then spoke to his aged father, bowing very low, very slowly.
What the reverend Vyāsa has said, and what is your own resolve, and what the great archer Kṛpa has said, and Vidura too—
Yuyutsu and Saṃjaya too — what they advise I shall do at once; for all of these are worthy of my regard, well-wishers of this our line.
But this one thing I beg of you, O king, my head bowed low: first let a meal be taken, and then set out for the hermitage.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, with the king's leave, the majestic Dhṛtarāṣṭra went to his own dwelling, followed by Gāndhārī.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Slow of breath and step, the wise lord of the earth went on foot, hauling himself along as if with effort, like an aged lordly elephant.
Behind him walked the learned Vidura and the bard Saṃjaya, and likewise that great archer Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat.
Having entered his house and performed the morning rites, the king satisfied the foremost of the twice-born and then took his meal.
And Gāndhārī, knower of dharma and high of mind, together with Kuntī, honored with attentive service by the daughters-in-law, also ate, O Bhārata.
When the meal was done, all of them — Vidura and the rest, and the Pāṇḍavas as well — having eaten, attended upon that king, the best of the Kurus.
Then, O great king, the son of Ambikā spoke to Kuntī's son seated near at hand, touching his back with his hand.
"You must be ever vigilant, O joy of the Kurus, in every way, O tiger among kings, over the kingdom of eight limbs, with dharma set foremost."
"How the kingdom and dharma may be guarded, dear son of Pāṇḍu, O son of Kuntī — learned though you are, hear this from me."
"Wait ever upon those ripe in learning, Yudhiṣṭhira; listen to what they say, and act on it without hesitation."
"Rising at dawn, O king, and honoring them in due form, when the time for action comes you should ask them about your own affairs."
"Honored by you who seek the kingdom's good, O king, they will tell you all that is beneficial, dear joy of the Kurus."
"And guard all your senses as one guards horses; rightly kept, they will turn to your good, even as wealth that is well guarded."
"Ministers proven beyond temptation, serving since your fathers' and grandfathers' days, pure and self-controlled — appoint the chief of them to the chief of all your tasks."
"And keep your foes ever under watch through spies unknown to them and well tested, in manifold fashion, both in your own realm and in others'."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Let your city be well defended, with stout ramparts and gateways, thick-set with watchtowers, opening on six roads to every quarter."
"Its gates should be made ample and broad, well disposed on every side and guarded by engines of war."
"By men who understand their charge, known for their family and character; and your own person too must ever be guarded, in eating and the rest, O Bhārata."
"At times of pastime and of food, in garlands, bed, and seats; and let your women be well protected, set under elders trustworthy, virtuous, well-born, and wise, O Yudhiṣṭhira."
"For counselors take twice-born men skilled in learning, well-disciplined and well-born, adept in dharma and artha, and upright."
"With them you should take counsel — but not with too many together, sometimes with all, sometimes with each apart, under some pretext or other."
"Take counsel in a well-enclosed council chamber, or having climbed to high ground, or in a forest free of reeds — but never by night, in any wise."
"Monkeys and birds that mimic men, and all who are dull-witted or crippled, are to be barred from the council chamber."
"For the ills that befall lords of the earth when counsel is betrayed can in no way be set right again — such is my conviction."
"And in the circle of counselors you should declare the harms of betraying counsel, and the merits of keeping it, again and again, O king, subduer of foes."
"And the honesty and dishonesty of townsmen and countryfolk, Yudhiṣṭhira — see that it becomes known to you, O king, and act accordingly, subduer of foes."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "And your legal affairs, dear son, should ever be set under trustworthy men — men contented and devoted, O king — and constantly watched over by spies."
"Knowing the due measure, O Bhārata, your men should impose punishment upon the punishable according to law, Yudhiṣṭhira."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Those given to plunder, violators of others' wives, those foremost in cruel oppression, and speakers of falsehood;"
"revilers and the greedy, murderers fond of reckless deeds, breakers of assembly and pastime, and corrupters of the social orders — these are to be fined in gold or put to death, according to place and time."
"At dawn you should review those who manage expenditure; thereafter attend to your adornment and your food."
"Then you should review your warriors, ever cheering them on; and for envoys and spies let the early evening always be your time."
"Let the last watch of the night always be yours for settling the business of state; at midnight your repose, and at midday too your rest."
"Yet all hours are urgent when affairs press, O bull of the Bhāratas; so, adorned and lavish in gifts, hold yourself ready at the proper time — for the round of duties, dear son, turns ceaselessly like a wheel."
"Make effort always, by lawful means, to gather your treasury of both kinds, O great king, and shun whatever is contrary to law."
"Learning through spies of those enemies who would obstruct your rule, you should have them slain from afar by trusty men, one against another."
"Then, judging by their work, choose your servants, O scion of the Kurus, and have tasks carried out under men suited and unsuited each to their place."
"And let the leader of your army, dear son, be a man firm in his vows, brave, enduring of hardship, and dear to you."
"And let all your country-officers, O Pāṇḍava, your stewards and assessors, attend to your affairs — they who conduct the dealings of state."
"Your own weak points and the enemy's, among your own people and among others' — these you must mark always, Yudhiṣṭhira."
"And men dwelling in other lands, valiant in every kind of work, should be won over by you with fitting favors, to your benefit."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Esteem must be shown to those learned men who prize merit, O lord of men; and let each of them stand unshakable as the great mountain Meru."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "And you should understand the circles of states — those of your foes, and of yourself, and likewise of the neutrals and of the middle powers."
"Of the four kinds of enemies, all of them aggressors, you must discern friend and the friend of an enemy, O harrier of foes."
"And ministers, territories, fortresses, difficult terrain, and armies, O best of the Kurus, belong to these powers at their pleasure."
"These powers of kings, O son of Kuntī, are twelve, of varied nature; and the constituents headed by the ministers are sixty and twelve, O lord."
"This the masters skilled in statecraft call the circle of states; upon it rest the six measures of policy, Yudhiṣṭhira — learn that."
"Increase and decline, and stability too, must be discerned, O joy of the Kurus; by these seventy-two, mighty-armed one, follow then the six measures of policy."
"When one's own side is strong and the enemy's side weak, then, having made open war upon his foes, the lord of earth should march, O son of Kuntī; but when one's own side is weak, then he should resort to peace."
"And a great store of goods should likewise be amassed, so that one becomes fit to march out before long, O Bhārata."
"Then let all be made ready, and let him not partition his ground; land of little yield may be ceded to one in the opposite case, O Bhārata."
"Gold abounding in base metal, an ally enfeebled and without a treasury — such inferior things one skilled in treaties should not himself accept."
"For the sake of a treaty you may seek to obtain a prince, O bull of the Bhāratas; but in any emergency you should not surrender your own son in turn — rather, knowing the means and counsels, strive for his release."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"And a king should weigh the strength and weakness of his afflicted subjects' calamities, O son of Kuntī — in turn, all at once, or two by two."
"The harassing, the crippling, and the breaking of the treasury of his foes should be wrought with effort by one who himself guards his own realm."
"A neighboring lord who has submitted should not be harmed by one who desires increase, O son of Kuntī; he who seeks to conquer the earth should do him no injury."
"You should, with your counselors, contrive the dividing of confederacies — likewise by gathering the good to you and by restraining the wicked."
"And the weak should never be oppressed unceasingly by the stronger; stand firm, O tiger among kings, adopting the way of the reed."
"And if a mighty king should thus march against the weak, the latter should turn him back step by step by the expedients beginning with conciliation."
"But if unable to give battle, let him sally forth together with his counselors, his treasury, his townsfolk, his army, and whatever others wish him well."
"And if all this be impossible, let him escape with what is most precious; by this gradual course deliverance may be had — even of the bare body alone."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "Herein too you should regard peace and war, O best of kings — twofold in origin, threefold in means, and of many forms, Yudhiṣṭhira."
"O lord of kings, having resolved your own duality, you should bide your time; and remember that the enemy too is self-possessed, with contented and well-nourished forces."
"At a time for biding, the opposite is enjoined; at a time of crushing assault, O lord of kings, withdrawal is then the better course."
"He should then bring upon his foes calamity and division, wasting and terror, and in battle too great destruction."
"A king about to march, well versed in the treatises, should ponder threefold the power both of himself and of his foe."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Furnished with the power of energy, the power of sovereignty, and the power of counsel, O Bhārata, a man may march; otherwise, the opposite."
"A king should muster his hereditary force, the force of allies, the force of forest tribes, the hired force, and whatever force of the guilds there is."
"Of these, O king, the force of allies is not superior to the hereditary force; and the force of guilds and the hired force are equal — such is my view."
"Likewise the force of forest tribes is to be reckoned equal to these, O king, by a ruler in times of mustering, when the hour is at hand."
"And the calamities of many forms that befall kings must also be understood, O lord of men, O Kaurava — hear of them now severally."
"Many are the varieties of calamities, O king, joy of the Pāṇḍus; by employing conciliation and the rest, a king should ever quell them."
"A king should set out on his march furnished with the six forces, O scorcher of foes, joined with the right place and time, with his troops and his own virtues."
"With contented and well-nourished forces a king bent on rising prosperity should march; and when summoned, a ruler should march even out of season."
"For the ruin of his rivals a king should march forth like one crossing a river whose stones are the pillars, whose chief current is horses and chariots, whose banks and bluffs are screened by tree-like banners, made miry by foot-soldiers and elephants."
"Then, as occasion fits, the cart array, the lotus, and the thunderbolt array, O Bhārata — the science that Uśanas knows, therein all this is ordained, O lord."
"Having crushed the enemy's force and roused the ardor of his own, he should join battle on his own ground and likewise on the enemy's."
"What he has won the king should pacify, and settle wealthy men there; and recognizing that land as his own domain, he should approach it with conciliation and the rest."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In every way, great king, one should sustain the body here below; for both this world and the next, the highest good of the self is to be pursued.
Acting thus, the king hears words of praise in this world, and in the next attains heaven by guarding his subjects with righteousness.
Thus, O best of the Kurus, you must ever conduct yourself for the welfare of your subjects, my son, so as to win both worlds.
You were instructed before by Bhīṣma, by Kṛṣṇa, and by Vidura; and I too must needs speak, out of love for you, O best of kings.
Do all this according to right, O giver of abundant gifts; thus, dear to your subjects, you shall win happiness in heaven.
Whether a lord of the earth offers a thousand horse-sacrifices or guards his subjects with righteousness, he reaps an equal fruit.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I shall do all this just as you have spoken, O lord of the earth; and I am ever to be further instructed by you, O bull among kings.
Now that Bhīṣma has gone to heaven, that the Slayer of Madhu has departed, and Vidura and Saṃjaya as well, who else is fit to counsel me?
Whatever you, set upon my good, instruct me here this day, that I shall do, O guardian of the earth; be at ease, O Bhārata.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the wise King of Righteousness, that royal sage wished to take his leave of the son of Kuntī, O bull of the Bhāratas.
"My son, let there be rest awhile; my weariness too is great" — so saying, the king then entered the chamber of Gāndhārī.
When he had taken his seat, the queen Gāndhārī, faithful to her duty and knowing the fitting moment, addressed her husband, who was the equal of Prajāpati.
"Granted leave by the great sage Vyāsa himself, and with Yudhiṣṭhira's consent, when will you depart to the forest?"
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Gāndhārī, granted leave by my great-souled father himself, and with Yudhiṣṭhira's consent, I shall go to the forest before long.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For I wish, in the presence of all my subjects gathered in my house, to bestow upon all those sons of mine who gamed at the wicked dice the wealth that follows them into the life beyond.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the king sent word to the King of Righteousness; and at his word the lord of the earth had everything brought together.
Then the king came forth from that inner apartment, and gathered all his kinsfolk and friends, all his subjects, and all the assembled people of the city and the countryside.
And to the brāhmaṇas and to the rulers gathered from many lands, the mighty-splendored Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the earth, then spoke.
"Listen with single-minded attention, you brāhmaṇas of Kurujāṅgala, and you kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras here assembled."
"You and the Kurus have dwelt together for a long time, friends to one another and devoted to one another's good."
"Whatever I now say, this hour being come, that you must do without questioning my word."
"My mind, together with Gāndhārī's, is set upon going to the forest, with the consent of Vyāsa, of the king, and of the son of Kuntī. Do you too grant me leave; let no other doubt arise in you."
"The love that is between us and you is everlasting; nowhere else among the kingdoms, I think, does such a bond between kings exist."
"I am wearied by old age and bereft of my sons; I am wasted by fasting, together with Gāndhārī, O sinless ones."
"With the kingdom passed to Yudhiṣṭhira, I have attained great happiness — greater, I deem, than under Duryodhana's sovereignty, O most excellent men."
"But for me, blind and aged and bereft of my sons, what refuge is there save the forest, O blessed ones? Therefore grant me leave."
Hearing those words of his, all the people of Kurujāṅgala wept, their voices choked with tears, O bull of the Bhāratas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
To them, who could utter nothing, sunk in grief and sorrow, the mighty-splendored Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke once again these words.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Śaṃtanu duly guarded this earth, and Vicitravīrya too, sheltered by Bhīṣma, ruled over you as a father — this you know beyond all doubt.
And how my brother Pāṇḍu was beloved of you, and how he too ruled rightly — that too you well know.
And whatever service I rendered you, well done or ill done, O sinless and blessed ones, that you must forgive, being free of resentment.
And in the kingdom that Duryodhana enjoyed unopposed, even there that dull-witted, evil-minded one did you no wrong.
Through the offense of that evil-minded one, through the arrogance of the rulers of the earth, and through the misdeeds wrought by me, there arose a most terrible carnage.
Whether what was done by me was well or ill, you must not hold it in your hearts; grant me your leave.
"This man is old, bereft of his sons, this lord of men is stricken with grief, and he is the son of the kings of old" — bearing this in mind, grant me leave.
And this poor aged Gāndhārī, bereft of her sons, ascetic and wretched, tormented by grief for her children, entreats you together with me.
Knowing us two to be old and bereft of our sons and afflicted, grant us leave — blessings upon you — that we may depart; and you are our refuge.
And this Kaurava king, Yudhiṣṭhira son of Kuntī, is to be regarded by you all in fair fortune and in foul; nor will he ever at any time turn to wrong.
His four brothers, of vast might, are his counselors; like the guardians of the world are they all, beholders of righteousness and gain.
Like the lord Brahmā, master of all beings and of the world, the mighty-splendored Yudhiṣṭhira will protect you.
Because it must needs be said, I say it to you: as a trust I give Yudhiṣṭhira to you all, and you I make a trust given over to that hero.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
If any wrong was done by them, my sons, or by any other of mine, that too you must forgive.
For you have never in any way before stirred my wrath; to you, ever most devoted to your elders, are these folded hands, this salutation.
For the sake of those fickle-minded, greedy ones who followed their own desires, I beseech you all, together with Gāndhārī, O sinless ones.
Thus addressed by that king, the people of the city and countryside, faltering with tears, said nothing, but looked upon one another.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the aged king, the people of the city and countryside became, O Kaurava, as though robbed of their senses.
Then to them, fallen silent with throats choked by tears, the lord of the earth, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, spoke yet again.
"Old am I, and bereft of my sons, lamenting in many ways and pitiably, together with this my lawful wife, O most excellent men."
"Granted leave for life in the forest by my father Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana himself, and by the righteous king who knows the law, O knowers of righteousness —"
"— I, bowing my head, beseech you again and again, O sinless ones: grant leave to me, together with Gāndhārī."
Hearing these piteous words of the Kuru king, the gathered people of Kurujāṅgala wept on every side, O king.
Covering their faces with their upper garments and with their hands, they wept awhile, scorched with sorrow, as for a father and a mother.
With hearts grown empty, bearing the grief born of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's departure, they became as though bereft of their senses.
Having mastered that anguish born of parting from the Kuru king, little by little they then spoke their minds to one another.
Then, having all composed their words together in brief and entrusted them to a single brāhmaṇa, O king, they addressed the lord of men.
Then an aged man, honored in his own conduct, skilled in matters of policy, learned in the Ṛgveda and named Sāmba, O king, began to speak.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having paid honor to the great king and addressed that assembly, the bold and wise brāhmaṇa spoke thus to the king.
"O king, the word of all this people has been wholly entrusted to me; that I shall speak, O hero — receive it kindly, O lord of men."
"As you say, O king of kings, so is all this, O mighty one; there is in it no false word at all. You are our friend, and we yours, each to each."
"Never at any time has there been among the kings of this line one who, as a guardian of his people, became hateful to his subjects."
"As a father and as a brother you have guarded us; nor did Duryodhana do anything unbefitting, O king."
"As the righteous sage, son of Satyavatī, directs, so do, O great king; for he is our supreme preceptor."
"But forsaken by you, we shall long be given over to grief and sorrow, O king, captivated by your hundred virtues."
"As we were sheltered by King Śaṃtanu and by Citrāṅgada, and by your father, screened by the valor of Bhīṣma, O lord of the earth —"
"— and by Pāṇḍu, ruler of the earth, who shared your wisdom, and by King Duryodhana too, we were well protected."
"Not even a little wrong did your son do us, O king; in that lord of men too we trusted utterly as in a father — even as you well know."
"And now, guarded for a thousand years by the wise and steadfast son of Kuntī, we shall find happiness, O king."
"Of the royal sages of old, the upholders of your line — Kuru, Saṃvaraṇa and the rest, and the wise Bharata —"
"— their conduct does this righteous-souled one, giver of abundant gifts, follow faithfully; herein, O great king, there is not even the subtlest fault to be found."
"Guarded by you, we have ever dwelt in happiness; not the subtlest wrong is to be found in you or in your son."
"But concerning what you have said of Duryodhana in this destruction of kinsmen, in that matter too I shall console you, O delight of the Kurus."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The brāhmaṇa said: That the Kurus went to ruin was not Duryodhana's doing, nor yours, nor that of Karṇa and the son of Subala.
That, we know, was fate, which cannot be turned aside; fate cannot be overcome by human effort.
Eighteen akṣauhiṇīs, great king, came together, and in eighteen days were slain by ten foremost warriors.
By Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa and the rest, by the great-souled Karṇa, by the hero Yuyudhāna, and by Dhṛṣṭadyumna —
— and by the four sons of Pāṇḍu, by Bhīma, Arjuna and the twins, O king — this slaughter of people was wrought by men compelled by the power of fate.
In the world, a kṣatriya — and above all a man of the warrior breed — must of necessity meet his death in battle, by the weapon.
By those tigers among men, endowed with knowledge and strength of arm, this whole earth was struck down, together with its horses, chariots, and elephants.
That king, your high-minded son, does no wrong; nor do you, nor your servants, nor Karṇa, nor the son of Subala.
That the foremost of the Kurus and kings by the thousand perished — all that, in truth, was wrought by fate; who here is fit to say anything of it?
You are accounted the elder of this whole world, its lord. Therefore to you we give our assent concerning your righteous-souled son.
Let that ruler of men, together with his companions, attain the worlds of heroes; sanctioned by the foremost of the twice-born, let him rejoice in happiness in the third heaven.
And you, O best of the Bhāratas, will obtain merit and a supreme standing in righteousness; you know fully and rightly what is meritorious.
We have seen the exploits of the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men; they are capable of governing even heaven, how much more the earth.
And these subjects will follow the Pāṇḍavas, adorned with good character, O best of the Kuru line, in fair times and foul alike.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The grants of land bestowed upon brahmins, the exemptions, O king, and the endowments made by former kings—the Pāṇḍava upholds them all.
Far-seeing and accomplished in wisdom, ever like Vaiśravaṇa, this high-minded son of Kuntī has no petty counsellors.
Compassionate even toward a foe, and pure, O bull of the Bhāratas, the wise one looks upon things with uprightness and ever protects us as if we were his children.
And through their fellowship with the son of Dharma, O royal sage, neither Bhīma nor Arjuna nor the rest will do anything displeasing to these people.
Gentle toward the gentle are these Kauravyas, but like venomous serpents toward the harsh; valiant, great-souled, and devoted to the welfare of the citizens.
Neither Kuntī, nor the Pāñcāla princess, nor Ulūpī, nor the Sātvatī woman will ever do anything contrary to the good of these people.
The affection you have shown, which Yudhiṣṭhira has nurtured, the people of city and countryside will not cast behind their backs.
Even men given to unrighteousness the sons of Kuntī, those mighty charioteers, will protect, themselves remaining wholly devoted to righteousness.
Therefore, O king, putting away from yourself any grief of mind concerning Yudhiṣṭhira, perform your righteous duties; homage to you, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: That righteous speech of his, excellent in its bearing upon the matter at hand, all that assembly received with cries of "Well said, well said!"
And Dhṛtarāṣṭra, honoring that speech again and again, then gently dismissed all his subjects.
That king, honored by them and regarded with kindly eyes, then with joined palms honored that people in turn, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then the king entered his dwelling together with Gāndhārī; and learn now what he did when the night had passed.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the night had passed, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, sent Vidura to the dwelling of Yudhiṣṭhira.
He, the greatly lustrous one, foremost of all the wise, having gone at the king's bidding, addressed the unfailing sovereign Yudhiṣṭhira.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O great king, has resolved upon dwelling in the forest; he will go to the forest, O king, now that this full-moon of Kārttika has come.
He desires of you a certain thing, O best of the Kuru line; he wishes to offer a śrāddha for the great-souled son of Gaṅgā,
and for Droṇa, for Somadatta, and for the wise Bāhlika, and for all his sons and for those friends of his who were slain—and, if you grant leave, for that vile Saindhava as well.
Hearing this speech of Vidura, Yudhiṣṭhira was gladdened and paid him honor, as did the Pāṇḍava Guḍākeśa.
But Bhīma of firm wrath and great lustre did not then accept that speech of Vidura, remembering what Duryodhana had done.
But Phalguna, the diademed one, knowing Bhīmasena's intent, bowing a little, spoke these words to Bhīma:
"Bhīma, the aged king our father, resolved upon dwelling in the forest, wishes to make the funeral offerings for all his friends.
With the wealth won by you, O mighty-armed one, the Kaurava wishes to make gifts on behalf of Bhīṣma and the rest; it is fitting that you grant leave for this."
"By good fortune, O mighty-armed one, Dhṛtarāṣṭra now entreats us—he whom we once entreated. Behold the turning of time!
He who was lord of the whole earth, a ruler of men, his offspring slain by his foes, now longs to go to the forest.
Let your view, O tiger among men, be of nothing but giving; anything other than this would be inglorious and unrighteous, O mighty-armed one.
Attend upon the king, your eldest brother and lord; it is for you to give, not to withhold, O bull of the Bhāratas." As the son of Kuntī spoke thus, the King of Righteousness honored him.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But Bhīmasena, full of wrath, then spoke these words: "It is we who should perform the funeral rites for Bhīṣma here, O Phalguna,
for King Somadatta, and for Bhūriśravas, and for the royal sage Bāhlika, and for the great-souled Droṇa,
and for the other kinsmen; and Kuntī shall make the śrāddha offerings for Karṇa, O tiger among men—let not the Kaurava king bestow them.
Such is my mind. Let not our enemies rejoice; let Duryodhana and all the rest go from misery to misery still greater—those defilers of their line by whom this whole earth was brought to slaughter.
How can you today forget the enmity of those twelve years, the going into hidden exile that swelled Draupadī's grief? Where then was Dhṛtarāṣṭra's affection for us in that hour?
Clad in a black antelope's hide, stripped of your ornaments and finery, you went before the king together with the daughter of Pāñcāla. Where then were those two, Droṇa and Bhīṣma, or Somadatta?
During the thirteen years in which you lived in the forest on its wild produce, the elder who is our father did not then regard you with a father's eyes.
Have you forgotten, O Pārtha, how this defiler of the line, that wicked one, said to Vidura at the dicing, 'What has been won?'
To his brother speaking thus, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the wise son of Kuntī, said in rebuke, "Hold your peace and be still."
Arjuna said: Bhīma, you are my elder and my teacher; beyond this I dare not speak. But Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that royal sage, deserves honor in every way.
The good, those best of men who never breach the bounds of duty, do not remember wrongs done to them, but remember the kindnesses.
Say this from me, O Kṣattṛ, to the Kaurava king: 'However much you wish to give on behalf of your sons, so much do I give.'
'For Bhīṣma and all the rest, those friends who did us good service, let it be from my treasury,' O lord—and let Bhīma not be sore at heart.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When this had been spoken, the King of Righteousness honored Arjuna in return, while Bhīmasena cast a sidelong glance at Dhanaṃjaya.
Then the wise Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these words to Vidura: "That king ought not to feel anger toward Bhīmasena.
For this Bhīma was sorely afflicted by snow, rain, sun, and the like—by manifold sufferings in the forest, as you well know.
But say this from me to the king, that bull of the Bhāratas: 'Whatever you wish, and however much, let it be taken from my house.'
'The grudge that this Bhīma harbors, being grievously pained, ought not to be taken to heart'—so the king is to be told.
'Whatever wealth there is of mine and in Arjuna's house, of that the great king is the master'—so the king is to be told.
Let the king give to the brahmins as he pleases; let the expenditure be made for his sons and his friends; let him this day pass free of his debt to them.
'This body of mine too is at your disposal, O ruler of men, and so is my wealth'—know this, O Kṣattṛ; herein is no doubt.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the king, Vidura, best of the wise, approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra and spoke these words full of weighty meaning:
"King Yudhiṣṭhira was told your message from the first, and that one of great lustre, having heard your words, praised them.
And Bībhatsu of great lustre offers you his houses, the wealth that is in his house, and even his very life.
And the King of Righteousness, your son, grants you the kingdom, his life, his wealth, O royal sage, and whatever else there may be.
But Bhīma, the mighty-armed, recalling his many and manifold sorrows, gave his assent as if with difficulty, sighing deeply.
He, the mighty-armed, was won over by his righteous brother the king and by Bībhatsu, and was set firm in friendship.
And the King of Righteousness says to you: 'You ought to feel no anger if Bhīma, remembering that enmity, should act unjustly.'

title: Mahābhārata
text:
For such is by and large the duty of the kṣatriyas, O ruler of men; and this Vṛkodara is devoted to war and to the kṣatriya's code.
For Vṛkodara's sake, both I and Arjuna again and again entreat you, O king; in this matter you are the lord.
Let your honor bestow as much wealth as you wish, O king; you are the master of our kingdom and of our lives, O Bhārata.
Grants of land to brahmins, and the funeral offerings for your sons, and from here jewels and cattle, maidservants and menservants, goats and sheep—
let the best of the Kurus have these brought and bestow them upon the brahmins, and upon the wretched, the blind, and the destitute, here and there at the king's command.
'Cause halls richly furnished with abundant food, savory dishes, and drink to be built, Vidura, and watering-troughs for cattle, and whatever other various works of merit there are.'
Thus the king spoke to me, and Pārtha Dhanaṃjaya likewise. Whatever next is to be done in this, it is for you to declare."
Thus addressed by Vidura, Dhṛtarāṣṭra rejoiced at it and set his mind upon a great gift-giving on the full-moon of Kārttika, O Janamejaya.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Vidura, the king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that ruler of men, was made glad by the conduct of the king Yudhiṣṭhira and of Jiṣṇu.
Then, on behalf of Bhīṣma, for his sons, and for his friends, he selected by the thousand suitable brahmins, those best of sages.
Having had prepared food and drink, conveyances and garments, gold, gems, and jewels, maidservants, menservants, and furnishings,
woolen blankets, hides and jewels, villages and fields, goats and sheep, ornaments, elephants and horses, and maidens, the choicest of women—pointing out each in turn, that best of kings gave them to the brahmins.
Naming Droṇa and Bhīṣma, Somadatta and Bāhlika, and King Duryodhana, and his sons each one by one, and those headed by Jayadratha, and all his friends without exception,

title: Mahābhārata
text:
that śrāddha-sacrifice grew great, rich in fees of cattle and wealth, a flood of manifold riches and jewels, then carried out at Yudhiṣṭhira's pleasure.
There, ceaselessly, the men, the accountants, and the scribes, at the word of Yudhiṣṭhira, kept asking that king,
"Command us: what is to be given to these? Let it be given"—and the very thing was shown ready to hand at the end of the speech.
Where a hundred was to be given, a thousand was given, and where a thousand, then ten thousand, at the word of the wise king, the son of Kuntī.
Thus that king, a rain-cloud raining showers of wealth, satisfied those brahmins, even as a cloud pouring rain upon the earth.
Then immediately thereafter the lord of the earth, that king, flooded men of all the castes with a deluge of food, drink, and savory dishes.
With its foam of garments and its flood of jewels, its roar the sound of drums, its whirlpools the cattle and horses for sea-monsters, and women, those jewels, for its great mass of waters—
That ocean of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's compassion, rich with streams of villages and rent-free estates, its waters jewels and gold, flooded the whole world.
Thus, O great king, on behalf of his sons and grandsons, of his ancestors, of himself, and of Gāndhārī, he gave the funerary offerings for the departed.
When he had grown weary from bestowing gifts of every kind, the upholder of the Kurus brought his sacrifice of giving to its close.
In this way the Kaurava king held a great festival of giving, abounding in actors, dancers and mimes, lavish with food, drink and priestly fees.
Having thus bestowed gifts for ten days, the king, the son of Ambikā, became free of debt to his sons and grandsons, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then at daybreak King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, having fixed his hour for departing to the forest, summoned the heroic Pāṇḍavas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Wise, with Gāndhārī beside him, after greeting them in due form, on the full-moon day of Kārttika he had the sacrifice performed by Brāhmaṇas versed in the Vedas.
Setting the sacred fire before him, clad in bark and deerskin, surrounded by the women of his household, the king then went forth from the palace.
Then, as the king, the son of Vicitravīrya, set forth, a great wail arose from the women of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, and from the other ladies of the royal house of the Kurus.
Then the king, having honored that house with parched grain and many-hued flowers, and having provided for all his servants with wealth, dismissed them and departed.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, his palms joined and trembling, his throat choked with tears, cried aloud, 'Alas, great king, virtuous one, whither do you go, father!' and fell to the earth.
And Arjuna too, foremost of the Bhāratas, scorched by keen grief, sighing again and again, said to Yudhiṣṭhira, 'Not so,' and grasping him as he sank, lifted him up.
The heroes Vṛkodara and Phalguna, the two sons of Mādrī, Vidura and Saṃjaya, the son of the Vaiśya woman together with Gautama, Dhaumya and the Brāhmaṇas followed after, their throats choked with tears.
Kuntī supported the hand of Gāndhārī, her eyes bound, as she walked, holding it laid upon her shoulder; and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, resting his hand upon Gāndhārī's shoulder, went on serenely.
So too Kṛṣṇā Draupadī and the Yādava lady, Uttarā of the Kurus with her infant child, Citrāṅgadā, and whatever other women there were—all set forth together with the king and his daughters-in-law.
The wail of those weeping women rose up loud then, O king, like the cry of ospreys in their grief; and from every side poured forth the women of the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, of the Vaiśyas and Śūdras as well.
At his going forth the townsfolk of Hāstinapura grieved exceedingly, O king, as they had once grieved before, when the Pāṇḍavas departed after the dice-game in the assembly hall of the Kurus.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those women whom neither moon nor sun had ever beheld, now, when that lord of men, the chief of the Kurus, set out for the great forest, came forth into the royal highway, stricken with grief.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O king, upon the palaces and mansions and upon the ground, there arose a very great clamor of women and of men.
With difficulty the wise king made his way out along the royal road thronged with men and women, trembling, his palms joined in reverence.
He went out from Hāstinapura through the Vardhamāna gate, and again and again he bade the throng of people turn back.
