That king, son of a sage and thoughtful, did as he bade; restraining the whole host of his senses, he became then like a log of wood.
And the greatly blessed Gāndhārī, and Pṛthā your mother, and that king your father—all were joined with the forest fire.
But the high-minded Saṃjaya escaped from that conflagration; I saw him on the bank of the Gaṅgā, surrounded by ascetics.
That radiant one, taking leave of them and reporting all this in full, the charioteer Saṃjaya set out for the mountain Himavat.
Thus did the high-minded Kuru king meet his end, and so too Gāndhārī and Pṛthā, your two mothers, O ruler of men.
Wandering there by chance, I beheld the king's body and the bodies of both those queens, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then into that penance-grove gathered the ascetics, having heard of the king's end; yet they did not grieve, knowing the goal he and they had attained.
There I heard all of this, O best of men: how the king was burned, and the two queens as well, O Pāṇḍava.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
You should not grieve, O lord of kings; that ruler of the earth came to a good end, attaining union with the fire, as did Gāndhārī and your mother.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing of the passing of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, great grief arose among all the great-souled Pāṇḍavas.
And then a great cry of anguish went up from the inner apartments and from the townsfolk, O great king, when they heard of the king's end.
"Alas! Shame!" cried King Yudhiṣṭhira, sore stricken with grief; with arms upraised, remembering his mother, he wept aloud, and so did all his brothers, led by Bhīmasena.
And then a very great sound of weeping arose in the inner apartments, O great king, when they heard that Pṛthā had so passed away.
And all of them mourned that aged king, burned thus, whose sons had been slain, and the ascetic Gāndhārī as well.
When that clamor had subsided, after a moment, O Bhārata, Dharmarāja, restraining his tears by firmness, spoke these words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That such a great-souled one, engaged in fierce penance, should perish as if helpless, while we his kinsmen yet lived—
hard indeed to fathom, I think, are the destinies of men, when that son of Vicitravīrya was thus burned by the forest fire.
He whose splendid hundred sons were born to him, the strong-armed king with the might of ten thousand elephants—he it is who was burned by the forest fire.
He whom of old the loveliest women fanned with palm-leaf fans—him, scorched by the forest fire, the vultures fanned with their wings.
He who as he lay was wakened by throngs of bards and minstrels—that king now lies upon the bare earth, through the deeds of my own sin.
Yet I do not grieve for the illustrious Gāndhārī, her sons slain, who has reached her husband's world, so steadfast in her vow of devotion to her lord.
But for Pṛthā alone do I grieve, who, casting aside the great and shining sovereignty of her sons, chose instead to dwell in the forest.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Fie on this kingdom of ours, fie on our strength, fie on our valor, and fie on the warrior's code, since we live on while she is dead!
Most subtle indeed is the course of Time, O most excellent of the twice-born, in that she gave up the kingdom and chose to dwell in the forest.
The mother of Yudhiṣṭhira, of Bhīma, and of Vijaya—how could she have been burned as though she had no protector? Thinking on it I am bewildered.
In vain, it seems, was the fire gratified at Khāṇḍava by the ambidextrous Arjuna; ungrateful is that fire, heedless of the kindness done it—so I think.
For there that lord burned the mother of the ambidextrous one—the same who, in the guise of a brāhmaṇa, had once come begging for alms. Fie on that fire, and fie on the renowned fidelity to truth of Pārtha!
And this other thing seems to me more grievous still, O blessed one: that the lord of the earth met his end through a fire kindled in vain.
For that ascetic Kaurava royal sage—how could a death of such a kind befall him, who had ruled over this whole earth?
Though his fires sanctified by sacred mantras stood there in the great forest, my father met his end joined to a fire kindled in vain.
I imagine Pṛthā, trembling, gaunt, her veins standing out, crying aloud in that great terror, "Alas, my son, O Dharmarāja!"
And wailing too, "Bhīma, save me from this peril!"—my mother was encircled on every side by the forest fire.
Sahadeva was dear to her, dearer even than her own sons; yet that hero, the son of Mādrī, could not deliver her.
Hearing this, the five Pāṇḍavas all wept, embracing one another, stricken with grief, like beings at the dissolution of an age.
And the sound of those lords of men weeping, pent up within the vast expanse of the palace, made heaven and earth resound in answer.
Nārada said: That king, the son of Vicitravīrya, was not burned by a fire kindled in vain, as I heard there; this I shall tell you, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As that wise one entered the forest, feeding on air alone, he had a sacrifice performed and then released his fires—so we have heard.
His officiating priests then let those fires loose in the lonely forest and went their way as they pleased, O best of the Bhāratas.
That fire then grew great in that forest, and by it, they say, the wood was set ablaze—so the ascetics told me.
Thus that king, on the bank of the Jāhnavī, as I have told you, was joined with that fire—his own very fire, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Thus did the sages report to me, O sinless one—those whom I beheld upon the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thus, O lord of the earth, the king was united with his own sacred fire. Do not grieve: that monarch has gone to the highest goal.
And through her devoted service to her elders, your mother too, O son of Pāṇḍu, has attained a most exalted perfection—of this I have no doubt.
It is fitting, O scion of Kuru, that you perform the water-rites for them, together with all your brothers; let this now be ordained here.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then that guardian of the earth, the foremost bearer of the Pāṇḍavas' burden, set forth together with his brothers and his wife, O bull of the Bhāratas.
And the city-folk and the country-folk, moved foremost by their devotion to the king, went down all around to the Gaṅgā, each clad in a single garment.
Then, plunging into the water, all those bulls among the Kurus, with Yuyutsu placed at their head, offered the libation to the great-souled one.
And for Gāndhārī and for Pṛthā, duly by name and lineage, they performed the rites; and completing the period of mourning, they dwelt there outside the city.
That best of the Kurus dispatched men who knew the rites and were faithful in their duties to Gaṅgādvāra, the place where the king had been consumed by fire.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There at Gaṅgādvāra the lord of the earth then instructed those men, on whom gifts had been bestowed, that the funerary water-offerings for them were to be performed.
On the twelfth day, his mourning ended, that ruler of men, the son of Pāṇḍu, duly offered for them the śrāddha rites, attended with sacrificial fees.
Designating the offering for Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that lord of the earth gave gold, silver, cattle, and couches of very great worth.
And for Gāndhārī and for Pṛthā, each in turn, the splendid king, proclaiming their names, bestowed gifts beyond compare.
Whatever a brahmin desired, and however much, that much he received—bedding, food, a carriage, jewels and gems, and wealth besides.
Carriages, garments, comforts, and serving-maids as attendants—all these the king, that lord of the earth, gave, designating the offerings for those two mothers.
Then that guardian of the earth, having offered the śrāddha rites many times over, the wise one entered once more the city called after the elephant.
And those men who had gone forth at the king's command, having duly performed the water-offerings for them, came back again from there.
Having honored them according to rule with garlands and divers perfumes, and having duly performed the water-rites for them, they then reported it to the lord of the earth.
And having consoled the king, the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira, Nārada too, that supreme sage, departed, O king, as he wished.
Thus passed the years of the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra—three then in dwelling in the forest, and fifteen within the city.
His sons slain in battle, he ever bestowed gifts in memory of his kinsmen, his relations by marriage, his friends, his brothers, and his own people.
But King Yudhiṣṭhira, his heart far from glad, his kinsmen and relatives slain, upheld that kingdom even then.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the thirty-sixth year had come, Yudhiṣṭhira, joy of the Kurus, beheld portents of an evil and contrary kind.
Harsh winds blew, attended by thunderclaps and showers of gravel, and the birds wheeled in their circling flights from the left.
The great rivers ran backward against their course, the quarters of the sky were wrapped in mist, and meteors raining live coals fell from the heavens upon the earth.
O king, the sun's orb was veiled with dust; rayless at its rising day after day, it was seen ringed about by headless trunks.
Dreadful halos appeared about both the moon and the sun, of three colors, dark and rough at their edges, and glowing with an ashen-red light.
These and many other portents foretelling terror were seen day after day, O king, casting the heart into agitation.
Then, after some time had passed, Yudhiṣṭhira, king of the Kurus, heard that the host of the Vṛṣṇis had been destroyed in the slaughter of the iron clubs.
And hearing that Vāsudeva and Rāma had departed from their bodies, the son of Pāṇḍu gathered his brothers and said to them, "What now shall we do?"
When they heard how the Vṛṣṇis, driven on by the force of a brahmin's curse, had fallen upon one another and perished, the Pāṇḍavas were stricken with grief.
The death of Vāsudeva was like the drying up of the ocean; those heroes could not believe in the destruction of him who bore the Śārṅga bow.
Having heard of the affair of the clubs, the Pāṇḍavas, filled with grief and sorrow, despondent and bereft of all resolve, sat down together.
Janamejaya said: How, holy one, did the Andhakas perish together with the Vṛṣṇis, and the Bhojas, those great chariot-warriors, while Vāsudeva looked on?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: In the thirty-sixth year a great calamity befell the Vṛṣṇis, and, driven on by Time, they slew one another with iron clubs.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Janamejaya said: By whom were those heroes cursed, that the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas met their ruin, and the Bhojas too? Best of the twice-born, tell me this in full.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The heroes, with Sāraṇa at their head, saw Viśvāmitra, Kaṇva, and Nārada, that treasury of austerities, who had come to Dvārakā.
Then, putting Sāmba forward, decked out like a woman, they approached the sages and, oppressed by the rod of destiny, addressed them thus:
"This woman is the wife of Babhru of boundless splendor, who longs for a son. O seers, divine it truly: what will she bring forth?"
Thus addressed, O king, the sages, outraged at being so deceived, answered them; hear what they said, lord of men.
"For the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, this Sāmba, heir of Vāsudeva, will bring forth a terrible iron club,
by which you, vicious, cruel, and full of wrath, will utterly root out your whole race, save only Rāma and Janārdana.
The glorious Halāyudha, casting off his body, will go to the sea; and one named Jara will pierce the great-souled Kṛṣṇa as he lies upon the ground."
So spoke the sages, O king, mocked by those evil-minded men, their eyes red with anger as they glanced at one another.
Having spoken thus, the sages then went to Keśava.
Then the slayer of Madhu, hearing of this, spoke to the Vṛṣṇis; wise and knowing the end, he told them, "What is fated must be so."
Having said this, Hṛṣīkeśa went again into his house; for the lord of the world had no wish to turn fate to another course.
On the morrow Sāmba indeed brought forth that club, great as a death-dealing servant of Yama, for the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
They reported to the king the birth of that dread thing, the offspring of the curse; and the king, downcast of face, had it ground to fine powder.
By the king's command men cast it into the sea, and at the word of Āhuka they proclaimed throughout the city:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"From this day forward, in all the houses of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, no spirituous drink shall be made by any dweller of this city.
And whatever man shall make strong drink anywhere unknown to us, he shall be impaled alive upon a stake of his own making, together with his kinsmen."
Then, out of fear of the king, all men bound themselves to this rule, having learned the command of that great-souled monarch.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While the Vṛṣṇis, together with the Andhakas, strove thus, Time prowled about the houses of them all, day after day.
A man hideous, misshapen, and bald, dark and tawny of hue, would peer into the houses of the Vṛṣṇis and then be seen no more anywhere.
Day after day great and terrible winds arose, hair-raising and many in number, for the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
The streets swarmed with rats, the earthen pots cracked apart, and the mynah birds cried "cīcī-kūcī" in the dwellings of the Vṛṣṇis; nor did that clamor cease either by day or by night.
The cranes mimicked the hooting of owls, and the goats, O Bhārata, took up the howling of jackals.
Pale birds with red feet, driven on by Time—pigeons—then roamed about within the houses of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
Asses were born of cattle, and camels of she-mules; cats were born of bitches, and rats of mongooses.
The Vṛṣṇis, working evil, then knew no shame; they came to hate even the brahmins, the ancestors, and the gods alike.
They scorned their elders too—though not Rāma and Janārdana; wives wronged their husbands, and husbands their wives.
The blazing fire, when kindled, turned to the left, sending forth its flames apart in hues of blue, blood-red, and madder.
At rising and at setting, day after day in that city, the sun was seen by men again and again ringed about by headless trunks.
In the kitchens, when the food was cooked and most carefully prepared, worms were seen in it as it was being served, O lord of men.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And while the blessing of the auspicious day was being recited and the high-souled ones were murmuring their prayers, the sound of feet rushing about was heard, yet no one could be seen.
They all saw the constellations being struck again and again by the planets, one against another, yet not one of them could perceive his own.
And when the conch Pāñcajanya sounded within the dwellings of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, the asses brayed back at it on every side with hideous voices.
Seeing thus that the turning of Time had come, Hṛṣīkeśa, when he beheld the new moon fall upon the thirteenth day, spoke these words:
"The fourteenth has been made the fifteenth once more by Rāhu; just so it befell in the war of the Bhāratas, and now it has come again for our destruction."
Reflecting upon that hour and pondering it, Janārdana, the slayer of Keśin, judged that the thirty-sixth year had indeed arrived.
"That which Gāndhārī, scorched by grief for her sons and bereft of her kinsmen, uttered in her anguish—this has now come to pass.
And this too has come about which Yudhiṣṭhira foretold of old, when, the armies drawn up in array, he beheld the dire portents."
Having said this, Vāsudeva, wishing that very thing to be fulfilled, then gave command for a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, O subduer of foes.
By Keśava's order men proclaimed there, "You bulls among men shall make a pilgrimage to the sea."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: A black woman with pale teeth, entering by night and laughing, ran about through Dvārakā, snatching away the women in their dreams.
The ornaments, the parasol, the banners, and the coats of mail were seen being carried off by demons most terrible to behold.
And that iron discus of Kṛṣṇa, given by Agni, its hub hard as the thunderbolt, mounted up into the sky as the Vṛṣṇis looked on.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
His divine chariot, yoked and bright as the sun, the horses bore away as Dāruka looked on; those four chief steeds, swift as thought, wheeled away over the surface of the sea.
The two great banners, the palmyra and the Garuḍa, well honored by Rāma and Janārdana, were borne aloft by the apsarases day and night, and they cried out, "Let the pilgrimage to the sacred fords be made!"
Then those great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, those bulls among men, eager to set out, desired the pilgrimage, taking the women of their households with them.
Then the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis prepared food and dainties and drink in abundance and of many kinds, with much wine and flesh of every sort.
Then, given over to their liquors, those glorious men of fierce splendor went forth from the city by carriages, on horses, and on elephants.
Then the Yādavas encamped at Prabhāsa, each in his appointed place and as in his own home, with their wives and with abundance of food and drink.
When he perceived that they had encamped there by the shore of the sea, Uddhava, skilled in yoga and wise in matters, took his leave of those heroes and departed.
As that great soul set forth, saluting him with folded hands, Hari, knowing the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis to be at hand, had no wish to hold him back.
Then those great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, encompassed by Time, beheld Uddhava departing, covering heaven and earth with his radiance.
The food that had been prepared for the brahmins' sake by those high-souled men, reeking of wine, they gave instead to the monkeys.
Then the great carousal of those men of fierce splendor began at Prabhāsa, filled with the sound of a hundred instruments and thronged with players and dancers.
In Kṛṣṇa's presence Rāma drank, together with Kṛtavarman, and so too did Yuyudhāna, Gada, and Babhru.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then, in the midst of the assembly, Yuyudhāna, made arrogant by drink, addressed Kṛtavarman, mocking and despising him:
"What man who counts himself a kṣatriya would slay sleeping men as though they were already dead? That deed of yours, O son of Hṛdika, the Yādavas will not forgive."
When Yuyudhāna had thus spoken, Pradyumna, best of chariot-warriors, applauded those words, himself also scorning the son of Hṛdika.
Then Kṛtavarman, kindled to the height of fury, spoke to him, pointing as it were in contempt with his left hand:
"Bhūriśravas, his arm cut off, sitting fasting unto death upon the field—how was that hero felled by you, by a slaughter most cruel?"
Hearing these words of his, Keśava, slayer of enemy heroes, full of wrath, cast at him a sidelong glance heavy with anger.
And Sātyaki reminded the slayer of Madhu of the tale of that jewel, the Syamantaka, which had once belonged to Satrājit.
Hearing this, Satyabhāmā, weeping and enraged, went to Keśava's lap, herself rousing Janārdana to anger.
Then Sātyaki rose up in his wrath and spoke—in the name of the five sons of Draupadī, of Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin:
"I go now upon the road they took, and thus I swear by the truth: those who were slain in their sleep in the night attack by this evil-souled man—
by the wicked Kṛtavarman, the ally of Droṇa's son—this very day, O fair-waisted one, his life and his glory shall both be ended!"
Having spoken thus, there in Keśava's very presence, the enraged Sātyaki rushed upon Kṛtavarman with his sword and struck off his head.
As Yuyudhāna went on slaying others all around him, Hṛṣīkeśa rushed up to him, wishing then to hold him back.
Then, O great king, the Bhojas and Andhakas, all banded together and goaded on by the turning of Time, surrounded Śaineya.
Seeing them swiftly falling upon him in fury, Janārdana of great splendor did not grow wrathful, for he knew the turning of Time.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
But they, possessed by the frenzy of drink and driven on by rage, then struck at Yuyudhāna with the leftover drinking vessels.
As Śaineya was being struck down, the wrathful son of Rukmiṇī rushed into the fray, seeking to rescue the grandson of Śini.
There, locked in combat — the one with the Bhojas, and Sātyaki with the Andhakas — both were slain by sheer numbers before the very eyes of Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing Śaineya and his own son slain, Keśava, the delight of the Yadus, in his wrath seized then a fistful of eraka reeds.
That became a fearsome iron pestle, hard as a thunderbolt, and with it Kṛṣṇa struck down those who stood before him.
Then the Andhakas and Bhojas, the Śaineyas and the Vṛṣṇis alike, goaded by Time, struck one another down with pestles amid the uproar.
Whoever among them in fury laid hold of an eraka reed, O king — that reed appeared then, O lord, as though it had become a thunderbolt.
Even a blade of grass was seen there to turn into a pestle. Know, O king, that all this was wrought by the curse of the Brahmins' rod.
Whatever blade of grass they whirled and hurled, O king, that was seen then as a hard pestle, become a thunderbolt.
Son slew father, and father son, O Bhārata; drunken, they fell upon one another, crushing each other.
Like moths into fire the Kukuras and Andhakas fell; in not one of them being slaughtered was there any thought of flight.
Beholding this, the mighty-armed slayer of Madhu, knowing the turning of Time, stood firm, leaning upon his pestle.
Seeing Sāmba slain, and Cārudeṣṇa, and Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, Mādhava then grew wrathful, O Bhārata.
And catching sight of Gada lying slain, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the mace, filled with violent wrath, then made a clean end of them all.
As he of great splendor was slaying them, Babhru the conqueror of hostile cities, and Dāruka too, spoke to the Dāśārha — hear what they said.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"O blessed one, O Acyuta, by you nearly all have now been destroyed. Seek out the place of Rāma; let us go there, where he is."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Dāruka and Keśava, and Babhru too, set out, hastening, toward the place of Rāma; and they beheld Rāma of boundless valor seated beneath a tree in a solitary spot, lost in thought.
Then the great-souled Kṛṣṇa, having reached him, gave this command to Dāruka: "Go swiftly to the Kurus, and tell Pārtha of this great slaughter of the Yadus.
Let Arjuna come here at once, on hearing that the Yādavas have perished by the Brahmins' curse." Thus addressed, Dāruka, his senses bewildered, set off by chariot then toward the Kurus.
Then, when Dāruka had gone, Keśava, seeing Babhru nearby, spoke these words: "Let your honor go quickly and guard the women, lest robbers harm them out of greed for wealth."
He set out, instructed by Keśava, sick with drink and stricken by the slaughter of his kin; and as Babhru hurried on alone in Keśava's very presence, a great pestle — flung from the snare of a hunter and itself cursed by the Brahmins — struck him dead all at once.
Then, seeing Babhru slain, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to his elder brother: "Wait for me here, Rāma, while I see to the women, the wards of our kinsmen."
Then, entering the city of Dvāravatī, Janārdana spoke these words to his father: "Let your honor guard all our women, awaiting the coming of Dhanaṃjaya. Rāma sits at the forest's edge today, waiting for me; with him shall I now unite."
"I have witnessed this destruction of the Yadus, as before I witnessed that of the kings, the bulls of the Kurus. Without the Yadus I am not able today to look upon this city of the Yādavas."
"I shall practice austerities — mark this from me — withdrawing to the forest together with Rāma." Having said this and touched his father's feet with his head, Kṛṣṇa departed in haste.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then a great wail arose from that city with its women and children; and Keśava, turning back when he heard the cry of the women lamenting, spoke.
"Savyasācin will come to this city — that foremost of men shall free you from sorrow." Then Keśava, going on, beheld Rāma, seated alone in a solitary part of the forest.
Then he saw a great white serpent issuing from the mouth of Rāma, who was rapt in yoga; and the noble one departed, watched by all, going toward the great ocean.
Thousand-headed, vast in girth as a mountain, red-mouthed, he cast off that body of his; and the ocean duly received him, as did the divine serpents and the holy rivers.
Karkoṭaka and Vāsuki and Takṣaka, Pṛthuśravas, Varuṇa, and Kuñjara, Miśrī, Śaṅkha, Kumuda, and Puṇḍarīka, and likewise the great-souled serpent Dhṛtarāṣṭra —
Hrāda, Krātha, Śitikaṇṭha of foremost splendor, and the two serpents Cakramanda and Atiṣaṇḍa, the best of serpents Durmukha, and Ambarīṣa, and King Varuṇa himself, O king — these came forth to meet him, greeted him with welcome, and honored him with offerings of arghya and water for his feet.
Then, when his brother had departed, Vāsudeva — who with divine vision knew all the courses of things — wandering in the empty forest, deep in thought, that one of supreme splendor lay down upon the ground.
For all of this had already been known to him beforehand: the words Gāndhārī had spoken to him long ago, and what Durvāsas had said about the spot smeared with the remnants of the milk-rice — all this Kṛṣṇa called to mind.
Reflecting on the destruction of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis and on the ruin of the Kurus, the noble one judged that the time of his passing-over had come; and thereupon he set about the restraint of his senses.
With his senses, speech, and mind reined in, Kṛṣṇa entered into the great yoga and lay still; and just then a fierce hunter named Jara, greedy for game, came to that region.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
That hunter Jara, mistaking the yoga-rapt Keśava as he lay for a deer, swiftly pierced him in the sole of the foot with an arrow; and going up to seize his quarry, the hunter beheld a man rapt in yoga, clad in yellow, with many arms.
Believing himself to have wronged him, stricken with grief, he clasped Kṛṣṇa's feet with his head; and the great-souled one consoled him at that moment, even as he ascended on high, filling heaven and earth with his glory.
As he reached the heavens, Vāsava and the Aśvins, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Viśvedevas, and the sages and the Siddhas too, and the chief Gandharvas together with the Apsarases, came forth to meet him.
Then, O king, the blessed Nārāyaṇa of fierce splendor, the source of all and the imperishable, the master of yoga, filling heaven and earth with his glory, that immeasurable great soul attained to his own abode.
Then Kṛṣṇa was met by the gods and the seers and the Cāraṇas, O king, and honored by the foremost Gandharvas, by lovely Apsarases, and by the Siddhas and Sādhyas bowing low.
Those gods welcomed him, O king; the best of sages worshipped the Lord with hymns; the Gandharvas too attended upon him, singing his praise; and Puruhūta greeted him with joy.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Dāruka too, having gone to the Kurus and seen the Pārthas, those great chariot-warriors, told them how the Vṛṣṇis had destroyed one another in the affray of the pestles.
On hearing that the Vārṣṇeyas, together with the Bhojas, Kukuras, and Andhakas, had perished, the Pāṇḍavas were consumed with grief and their minds were stricken with dismay.
Then Arjuna, the dear friend of Keśava, taking leave of them, set out to see his maternal uncle, saying, "This is the end of all this."
Going to the dwelling-place of the Vṛṣṇis together with Dāruka, the hero beheld Dvārakā, O lord, like a woman whose husband is dead.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Those women who once had a protector in the Lord of the world now, bereft of protection, cried aloud when they saw Pārtha as their protector.
There were sixteen thousand women, the wives of Vāsudeva; a great wail arose from them at the very sight of Arjuna come among them.
At the mere sight of them, the Kaurava Arjuna, his eyes veiled with tears, was unable to look upon them, bereft as they were of Kṛṣṇa and of their sons.
That city, whose waters were the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, whose fish were the horses, whose boats were the chariots, whose flood of sound was the din of instruments and cars, whose great whirlpools were its mansions and bathing-ghāts —
with gems for its rafts of waterweed, garlanded with ramparts hard as diamond, with its streets for currents and eddies of water, and its squares for still, deep pools —
with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa for its mighty crocodiles — that river-like Dvārakā, now seized by the noose of Time, dreadful, like the river Vaitaraṇī —
such did the wise Arjuna behold her, bereft of the bulls of the Vṛṣṇis, her splendor gone and her joy departed, like a lotus-pond in the cold of winter.
Seeing that Dvārakā and those wives of Kṛṣṇa, Pārtha gave way to loud weeping and fell to the ground.
Then Satyā, the daughter of Satrājit, and Rukmiṇī, O lord of peoples, ran up, and surrounding Dhanaṃjaya, they wept aloud.
Then, raising the great-souled one up and seating him upon a golden seat, they, speaking to him, stood about him in attendance.
Then, having praised Govinda and spoken with them, and having consoled those women too, the Pāṇḍava went on to see his maternal uncle.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The bull of the Kurus beheld that great-souled hero Ānakadundubhi lying down, consumed with grief for his sons.
More stricken than the stricken man himself, the broad-chested, mighty-armed Pārtha, his eyes brimming with tears, clasped his feet, O Bhārata.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
The aged, mighty-armed one embraced Arjuna with both arms, and weeping, remembering all his sons, utterly overcome, he lamented — for his brothers and sons and grandsons, for his daughters' sons and his friends as well.
Vāsudeva said: "Those by whom kings of the earth and demons were conquered by the hundreds, O Arjuna — having seen them, I see them here no longer; yet I live on, Arjuna, hard to kill that I am."
"Those two pupils of yours, Arjuna, ever dear to you and held in high esteem — through their misconduct, O Pārtha, the Vṛṣṇis have gone to their destruction."
"Those two who alone among the foremost heroes of the Vṛṣṇis were reckoned supreme chariot-warriors — Pradyumna and Yuyudhāna — of whom you would speak in pride —"
"of whom you, O tiger of the Kurus, and my dear son Kṛṣṇa would ever speak — those two, O Dhanaṃjaya, became the very forefront of the Vṛṣṇis' ruin."
"Yet I do not blame Śaineya, nor Hārdikya, nor Akrūra, nor the son of Rukmiṇī, O Arjuna; for the curse alone was the cause of this."
"He, the Lord of the world, who by his might struck down Keśin and Kaṃsa, and who, O Pārtha, made an end of the Caidya proud of his strength —"
"and Ekalavya, son of the Niṣāda, and who subdued the Kaliṅgas and Māgadhas, the Gāndhāras and the king of Kāśi, and the princes of the desert lands —"
"and the kings of the East and of the South and of the hill-country alike — that slayer of Madhu suffered this calamity to come to pass."
"Then, seeing his sons and grandsons and brothers and friends lying slain, he spoke this to me:"
"'Now, O bull among men, this end of our house has come. Bībhatsu will come to this city of Dvāravatī."
"'Tell him what has happened, the great slaughter of the Vṛṣṇis. He of great splendor, on hearing of the ruin of the Yadus, O lord, will come here at once — of this I have no doubt."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"'Know that I am that Arjuna, and that Arjuna is none other than I; whatever he says, that must be done so — understand this, Mādhava."
"'That Pāṇḍava Bībhatsu will do what is timely for your women and your children, and will perform your funeral rites as well."
"'And this city, with its ramparts and watchtowers, the ocean will flood the moment Dhanaṃjaya has departed."
"'For I, taking up a vow in some holy place, will at once make my end together with the wise Rāma.'"
"Having spoken thus, Hṛṣīkeśa of inconceivable prowess, the Lord, leaving me behind with the children, departed in some direction or other."
"And I, brooding on those two great-souled brothers of yours and on the terrible slaughter of my kin, take no food, wasted away with grief."
"I shall neither eat nor live on. By good fortune you have come, O Pāṇḍava. Whatever Kṛṣṇa said, O Pārtha — do all of that, every bit."
This kingdom is yours, O Pārtha, and the women, and the jewels too; for I, O slayer of foes, shall now give up this dear life of mine.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by his maternal uncle, Bībhatsu, the scorcher of foes, with a heavy heart spoke these words to the despairing Vāsudeva.
O my uncle, O lord, I cannot long endure to look upon an earth bereft of that foremost hero of the Vṛṣṇis and of the Madhus.
The king, and Bhīmasena, and Sahadeva the Pāṇḍava, and Nakula, and the daughter of Yajñasena — we six are of one mind.
The hour has surely come for the king's own departure as well. Know that this time has arrived, O best of those who know the seasons of time.
By all means, O tamer of foes, I shall take the wives of the Vṛṣṇis, the young and the old alike, into my charge and lead them to Indraprastha.
Having said this, Dhanaṃjaya spoke these words to Dāruka: I wish to see the counsellors of the Vṛṣṇi heroes without delay.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having spoken these words, the heroic Arjuna, mourning for those great car-warriors, entered the Yādava assembly hall, Sudharmā.
When he had taken his seat there, all the subjects, and the Brāhmaṇas, and the townsmen gathered round and stood before him.
To all of them, dejected in mind, subdued, and bereft of their senses, Pārtha — himself more dejected still — then spoke these words.
I shall myself lead the people of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas to Śakraprastha; but this whole city the ocean shall overwhelm.
Make ready your conveyances and your jewels of every kind. This Vajra shall be your king at Śakraprastha.
On the seventh day, when the spotless sun has risen, we shall all dwell beyond these walls. Make ready without delay.
Thus addressed by Pārtha of untiring deeds, the townsfolk swiftly made themselves ready, eager for their own welfare.
That night Pārtha passed in the dwelling of Keśava, suddenly overwhelmed by a vast bewilderment of grief.
When the morrow came, the glorious Vāsudeva, scion of Śūra, of great splendour, composed himself in yoga and passed to the highest goal.
Then there arose a great and terrible clamour in Vāsudeva's house, of women crying aloud and weeping.
With dishevelled hair, their ornaments and garlands cast aside, beating their breasts with their hands, the women wailed piteously.
Devakī and Bhadrā and Rohiṇī and Madirā, those foremost of women, resolved to follow their lord upon the pyre.
Then, O Bhārata, upon a great bier borne by men and decked with many garlands, Pārtha carried the scion of Śūra forth from the city.
And after him there followed, smitten with pain and grief, all the townsmen who dwelt in Dvārakā, O bull among men.
His parasol from the horse sacrifice, and the blazing sacred fires, and the priests went on before that bier.
And those queens, beautifully adorned, followed that hero, surrounded by thousands of women and by daughters-in-law by the thousand.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
In that place which had been dear to the great-souled one while he lived, they laid him out and performed the funeral rites for the dead.
Then the four wives, fair-limbed and seeking the world of their lord, ascended the pyre after that hero, the son of Śūra, when he had been placed upon the fire.
And the son of Pāṇḍu had him, attended by those four women, burned with sandalwood and with fragrances of every kind.
Then there arose the sound of the kindled fire, and the chanting of the Sāman singers, and the weeping of men as well.
Then the young sons of the Vṛṣṇi heroes, with Vajra at their head, and the women too, all offered the water-libations to the great-souled one.
Having had this rite duly performed without omitting any sacred duty, Phalguna went, O bull of the Bhāratas, to the place where the Vṛṣṇis had perished.
Beholding them fallen in that slaughter, the descendant of Kuru was sorely grieved, and he performed for them the rites due at such a time.
He then performed all the rites in due order of rank for those who had been slain by the Brāhmaṇa's curse with the clubs sprung from the eraka grass.
Then, having sought out the bodies of both Rāma and Vāsudeva, he had them cremated by trusted men.
Having duly performed the funeral rites for them, the Pāṇḍava set out in haste on the seventh day, mounting his car, with chariots yoked to horses and others drawn by oxen, mules, and camels.
The women of the Vṛṣṇi heroes, weeping and wasted with grief, followed after the great-souled son of Pāṇḍu, Dhanaṃjaya.
The servants of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, the horsemen and the car-warriors, and the townsmen and country-folk, bereft of their heroes, old and young, went surrounding the women at Pārtha's command.
The elephant-riders went mounted on elephants like unto mountains, attended by their foot-guards and equipped with their upper weapons.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the sons of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, all devoted to Pārtha, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras of great wealth, went with him.
Sixteen thousand women of Vāsudeva's inner apartments went forth, placing at their head Vajra, the grandson of the wise Kṛṣṇa.
And many thousands, millions, and tens of millions of women of the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, their lords slain, went forth.
That host of the Vṛṣṇis, vast as the ocean and of great prosperity, Pārtha — best of car-warriors, conqueror of hostile cities — led onward.
When that people had gone forth, the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, overwhelmed with its waters Dvārakā, that city filled with jewels.
Beholding that wonder, the people who dwelt in Dvārakā hastened on ever more swiftly, crying, 'Ah, this is fate!'
Halting amid lovely forests, mountains, and rivers, Dhanaṃjaya led the women of the Vṛṣṇis along the way.
Reaching the Land of the Five Rivers, prosperous and abounding in cattle, livestock, and grain, the wise lord made his encampment there.
Then greed arose in the robbers, O Bhārata, when they saw the women, their protectors slain, being led on by Pārtha alone.
Then those Ābhīras of evil deeds, their minds corrupted by greed and ill-favoured to look upon, gathered together and took counsel.
'This Arjuna, a single warrior, leads on past us this throng of old men and children, their lords slain, and these fighters too have lost their vigour.'
Then those robbers, armed with cudgels, in their thousands rushed upon that people of the Vṛṣṇis, bent on seizing plunder.
With a mighty lion's roar, driving the common folk before them, they fell upon them for the sake of wealth, impelled by the turning of time.
Then the son of Kuntī turned back at once, his followers behind him, and the mighty-armed Arjuna spoke to them, almost laughing.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Turn back, you who know not righteousness, if you have no wish to die — lest, pierced through by my arrows and slain by me, you grieve in vain.'
Though thus addressed by that hero, the fools made light of his words and, though warned again and again, fell upon the people.
Then Arjuna began, only with effort and scarcely at all, to string that great, undecaying, celestial bow, the Gāṇḍīva.
He strung it with difficulty amid the tumultuous confusion, and he called to mind his celestial weapons, yet he could not remember them.
Seeing that great failing in the strength of his arms in battle, and the loss of his great celestial weapons, he was filled with shame.
And all those Vṛṣṇi warriors, riding on elephants, horses, and chariots, were unable to turn back that people who were being carried off.
But because the women were so many, scattering this way and that, Pārtha made every effort to protect the people.
While all the warriors looked on, those fairest of women were dragged away on every side, and others went off of their own will.
Then Pārtha, Dhanaṃjaya the lord, in great agitation, slew the robbers with arrows shot from the Gāṇḍīva, together with the servants of the Vṛṣṇis.
In a moment, O king, his straight-flying arrows were spent: those shafts, once inexhaustible, were exhausted, having fed upon blood.
His arrows spent, smitten with pain and grief, the son of the chastiser of Pāka then slew the robbers with the very tip of his bow.
Yet even as Pārtha looked on, those barbarians carried off the choicest women of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas on every side, O Janamejaya.
The lord Dhanaṃjaya pondered that working of fate in his mind, and, overcome with pain and grief, fell to deep sighing.
By the loss of his weapons, the ebbing of the strength of his arms, the unruliness of his bow, and the exhaustion of his arrows —

title: Mahābhārata
text:
— Pārtha grew dejected, reflecting that it was fate; then he desisted, O king, saying, 'This is no longer what it was.'
Then the great-minded one, taking what remained of the women, the most of whose jewels had been carried off, came down to Kurukṣetra.
Having thus brought the women of the Vṛṣṇis, what was left of them after the plunder, the Kaurava Dhanaṃjaya settled them here and there.
Pārtha, best of men, settled the son of Hṛdika in the city of Mārtikāvata, together with the remaining women of the Bhoja king.
Then the Pāṇḍava, taking the old men, the children, and the women, all bereft of their heroes, settled them at Śakraprastha.
The righteous one settled the son of Yuyudhāna, the beloved son of Sātyaki, on the banks of the Sarasvatī, with the old and young at his head.
The slayer of hostile heroes gave the kingdom at Indraprastha to Vajra; but the wives of Akrūra, though restrained by Vajra, departed.
Then Rukmiṇī, and Gāndhārī, and Śaibyā, and Haimavatī, and queen Jāmbavatī entered the fire.
And Satyabhāmā and the other queens cherished by Kṛṣṇa entered the forest, O king, resolved upon the life of asceticism.
As for those men of Dvārakā who had followed Pārtha, the victorious one divided them as was fitting and entrusted them to Vajra.
Having done what the hour required, Arjuna, his eyes veiled with tears, beheld Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, O king, seated in his hermitage.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As he entered the hermitage of the truthful sage, O king, Arjuna beheld the son of Satyavatī seated apart in solitude.
Approaching that knower of righteousness of great vows, he stood before him, and announcing his name, 'I am Arjuna,' he then addressed him.
'Welcome to you,' said the sage, the son of Satyavatī, and the great sage, serene of soul, added, 'Be seated.'
Seeing Pārtha downcast in mind, sighing again and again, and despondent of heart, Vyāsa spoke these words.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
'Has some stain that comes not from valour befallen you? Or has a Brāhmaṇa been slain by you? Or have you been vanquished in battle? You seem like one whose splendour has departed.'
I do not recognize you as the man you were. What has happened, O bull of the Bhāratas? If it is fit for me to hear, O Pārtha, you should tell it to me at once.
Arjuna said: He whose body was the very form of wisdom, the glorious one with great lotus eyes—that Kṛṣṇa, together with Rāma, has cast off his body and gone to heaven.
At the battle of the iron clubs, born of a brahmin's curse, the destruction of the Vṛṣṇi heroes came to pass at Prabhāsa—a slaughter of warriors that made the hair stand on end.
Those valiant, great-souled men, proud as lions and mighty in strength, the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, O brahmin—by one another they were slain in battle.
Men who could withstand maces, iron bars, and spears, whose arms were like iron clubs—they were struck down by mere blades of eraka grass. Behold the turning of Time!
Five hundred thousand of those strong-armed warriors were slain; they met their end by falling upon one another.
Again and again I cannot bear it, brooding upon the destruction of those of immeasurable might—of the Yadus and of the glorious Kṛṣṇa.
It is like the drying up of the ocean, the shaking of a mountain, the falling of the sky, and the cold of fire.
Unbelievable I hold the destruction of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; and I have no wish to remain here in this world, parted from Kṛṣṇa.
And hear of another thing more grievous still than this, O you whose wealth is austerity—a thing by which, as I brood on it again and again, my heart is torn asunder.
Before my very eyes, O brahmin, the women of the Vṛṣṇis, by the thousands, were carried off in a fight—pursued and seized by the Ābhīras who dwell in the land of the Five Rivers.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Taking up my bow there, I could not even bend it to string it, and the strength of my arms was not as it once had been.
My weapons of many kinds had vanished from me, O great sage, and my arrows ran out on every side in but an instant.
And that Person of immeasurable soul, bearing conch, discus, and mace, four-armed, clad in yellow, dark of hue, with eyes long as lotus petals—
he who used to go before my chariot, of exceedingly great splendor, burning up the armies of the foe—him I see no longer today.
He by whose splendor the enemy hosts were first scorched—those I then destroyed afterward with the arrows loosed from the Gāṇḍīva.
Not seeing him, I sink in despair and reel as if dizzy, O best of men; and with a heart utterly weary, I cannot find any peace at all.
Without the hero Janārdana I have no will to live; for at the mere hearing that Viṣṇu was gone, the very quarters of the sky grew bewildered before me.
To me, whose kinsmen and whose strength are utterly lost, empty and wandering aimlessly, you should counsel what is best, O best of men.
Vyāsa said: Burned up by a brahmin's curse, the great warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas have perished, O tiger of the Kurus; you ought not to grieve for them.
For it was bound to be so; this was the fate ordained for those great souls, and Kṛṣṇa, though able to turn it aside, let it be.
For Kṛṣṇa could have made the whole threefold world, with all that moves and stands still, to be otherwise—how much more the curse of the wise!
He who went before your chariot, bearer of discus and mace—that ancient seer, the four-armed Vāsudeva—did so out of love for you.
Having lifted the burden from the earth, the large-eyed one, having delivered the whole world, has gone to his own supreme abode.
By you, O bull among men, a great work for the gods has here been accomplished, with Bhīma as your helper and with the twins, O mighty-armed one.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I deem you to have fulfilled your purpose and attained your end, O foremost of the Kurus; the time for your departure has come, and that I hold to be the best course for you.
Strength, intellect, splendor, and resolve, O Bhārata, arise in the times of their flourishing and fail when the time turns adverse.
All this has Time for its root; Time is the seed of the world, O Dhanaṃjaya. Time alone gathers it back again at its own will.
That same man, having grown strong, becomes weak again; and he, having become a lord here, is once more commanded by others.
Your weapons, their work accomplished, have today gone the way by which they came; they will return again to your hand when the time shall be.
It is time for you too to go upon the highest path, O Bhārata; this I hold to be your supreme good, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Heeding this counsel of Vyāsa of boundless splendor, and granted leave, Pārtha set out for the city named after the elephant.
And the hero, entering the city and coming to Yudhiṣṭhira, related all that had happened concerning the people of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, just as it had occurred.
Janamejaya said: Having thus heard of the slaughter at the iron clubs among the houses of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, what did the Pāṇḍavas do when Kṛṣṇa too had gone to heaven?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: The moment the Kaurava king heard of the great destruction of the Vṛṣṇis, he set his mind upon departure and spoke these words to Arjuna.
Time ripens all created beings, O greatly wise one. I deem it fit that we lay down our deeds, and you too should recognize this.
So addressed, the valiant son of Kuntī, murmuring "Time, it is Time," assented to the words of his eldest brother.
Learning Arjuna's resolve, Bhīmasena and the twins also assented to the words that Savyasācin had spoken.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, summoning Yuyutsu and desiring to set forth in pursuit of dharma, made over the whole kingdom to that son born of a vaiśya woman.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Having consecrated Parīkṣit as king over his own realm, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, the king, sorely grieved, spoke to Subhadrā.
This son of your son shall be the king of the Kurus; and Vajra, the survivor of the Yadus, has been made king.
Parīkṣit shall reign at Hāstinapura and the Yādava at Śakraprastha; Vajra the king is to be guarded by you. Set not your mind upon unrighteousness.
Having spoken thus, the Dharma King performed, for the wise Vāsudeva, for his aged maternal uncle, and likewise for Rāma and the others,
together with the mothers, the righteous one, unwearied, offered the water-libations, and then duly performed the funerary rites in honour of them all.
He gave to the foremost of the twice-born jewels, garments, villages, horses, chariots, and women, and cows by the hundreds of thousands.
Honouring the preceptor Kṛpa with wealth and high regard, the best of the Bhāratas entrusted Parīkṣit to him as his pupil.
Then the royal sage Yudhiṣṭhira, having assembled all his subjects, declared to them his whole intended purpose.
The people of the city and countryside, hearing his words, were sorely troubled in mind and did not welcome that speech.
"This ought not to be done," they said then to the lord of men; but the king, who knew the law of the turning of Time, did not act otherwise.
Then the righteous one, having taken leave of the people of city and country, set his mind upon departure, and so too did his brothers.
Then that Kaurava king, Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma, casting the ornaments from his limbs, took up garments of bark.
Bhīma and Arjuna, the twins, and the illustrious Draupadī—all of them likewise took up the bark garments, O lord of men.
Having duly performed the final sacrifice, O bull of the Bhāratas, and cast their sacred fires into the waters, those bulls among men set forth.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Then all the women wept aloud, seeing those bulls among men setting forth with Draupadī as the sixth, as of old when they had been beaten at the dice.
But joy arose in all the brothers at the prospect of departure, knowing Yudhiṣṭhira's resolve and beholding the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis.
The five brothers, with Kṛṣṇā as the sixth and a dog as the seventh—the king himself thus the seventh—set out from the City named for the Elephant, followed far by the citizens and by all the women of the inner apartments.
None could bring himself to say to him, "Turn back"; and then all the men dwelling in the city returned.
Kṛpa and the others gathered about Yuyutsu; and Ulūpī, the daughter of the serpent, entered the Gaṅgā, O Kaurava.
Citrāṅgadā too went away towards the city of Maṇipūra, while the other mothers who remained gathered about Parīkṣit.
And the great-souled Pāṇḍavas and the illustrious Draupadī, having undertaken their fasts, O Kaurava, then set forth facing the east.
Yoked in yoga, those great-souled ones who had embraced the dharma of renunciation traversed many lands, rivers, and mountains.
Yudhiṣṭhira went in front, Bhīma next after him, Arjuna following him, and the twins in their order.
And behind them went Draupadī, the fair-hipped, dark-hued, lotus-petal-eyed, best of women, O best of the Bhāratas.
And a single dog followed the Pāṇḍavas as they set forth into the forest. Step by step those heroes journeyed to the Lauhitya, the watery ocean.
Dhanaṃjaya did not relinquish the divine bow Gāṇḍīva, nor, out of attachment to those treasures, the two inexhaustible great quivers, O great king.
There they beheld Agni standing before them like a mountain, barring their path, present in bodily human form.
Then that god of the seven flames spoke this to the Pāṇḍavas: "Ho, ho, heroic sons of Pāṇḍu! Know me to be Pāvaka, the Fire."

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena scorcher of foes, Arjuna, and you two heroic sons of the Aśvins—heed my words."
"I am Agni, O best of the Kurus, and by me was the Khāṇḍava forest consumed, through the might of Arjuna and likewise of Nārāyaṇa."
"Let this your brother Phalguna give up the supreme weapon Gāṇḍīva and proceed into the forest; there is no longer any need of it."
"That jewel of a discus which rested in the hand of the great-souled Kṛṣṇa has departed, and in time it shall come again into his grasp."
"This Gāṇḍīva, best of bows, was formerly brought by me from Varuṇa for Pārtha's sake; let it now be given back to Varuṇa."
Then all the brothers urged Dhanaṃjaya, and he cast into the water both the bow and the two inexhaustible great quivers.
Then Agni, O best of the Bhāratas, vanished on the very spot; and the heroic Pāṇḍavas went on thereafter, facing southward.
Then, along the northern shore of the salt sea, O tiger of the Bhāratas, they journeyed towards the south-western quarter.
Then, turning again, they came to the western quarter, and there they saw Dvārakā engulfed by the ocean.
Turning once more to the north, those best of the Bhāratas, devoted to the discipline of yoga, journeyed on, desiring to make their circumambulation of the earth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then those self-controlled ones, holding to the northern quarter and yoked in yoga, beheld the great mountain Himavat.
And as they crossed beyond it, they beheld a sea of sand, and they gazed upon the great mountain Meru, best of all peaks.
As all of them, devoted to the discipline of yoga, were going swiftly on, Yājñasenī, her yoga fallen away, dropped down upon the earth.
Seeing her fallen, the mighty Bhīmasena, looking upon Yājñasenī, spoke to the Dharma King.
"No unrighteousness has been done by the princess, O scorcher of foes. What then is the cause, O king, that Kṛṣṇā has fallen to the ground?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Great was her partiality, especially towards Dhanaṃjaya. The fruit of that she now reaps today, O best of men.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the king, the son of Dharma, went on without looking back at her—the wise, righteous bull among men, his mind firmly fixed.
Then the wise Sahadeva fell down upon the earth; and seeing him too fallen, Bhīma spoke to the king.
"He who was ever attentive in serving us all, and free of pride—this son of Mādravatī, why has he fallen to the ground?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said: He thought none so wise as himself. By that fault has this prince fallen.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus and left Sahadeva behind, the son of Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira, then went on together with his brothers and the dog.
Seeing Kṛṣṇā fallen and the Pāṇḍava Sahadeva likewise, the heroic Nakula, who loved his kinsmen, sank down stricken with grief.
When that hero Nakula of fair aspect had fallen, Bhīma once more spoke this to the king.
"This brother of unblemished righteousness, ever obedient to our word, unmatched in beauty in the world—Nakula has fallen to the ground."
Thus addressed by Bhīmasena, the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, best of all the wise, replied concerning Nakula.
"'In beauty none is equal to me'—such was his view; and 'I alone am surpassing'—this stood fixed in his mind."
"For that reason has Nakula fallen. Come on, O Vṛkodara. Whatever is ordained for a man, that he must surely undergo, O hero."
Seeing them fallen, the Pāṇḍava of the white steeds, the slayer of hostile heroes, then in his turn sank down, consumed with grief.
When that tiger among men, of Indra's splendour, the unassailable one, had fallen and lay dying, Bhīma spoke to the king.
"I do not recall a single falsehood of this great-souled one, not even in jest. What then is the fault by which he has fallen to the ground?"

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "In a single day I shall burn up my foes," so Arjuna said; yet he did not accomplish it. Proud of his prowess, he therefore fell.
And this Phalguna held in contempt all other bowmen. One who desires prosperity should do even as he has said.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the king went on; and then Bhīma fell down. Fallen, Bhīma spoke to the Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira.
"Ho, ho, O king! Look back—I, your beloved, have fallen. And tell me the cause of my fall, if you know it."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You ate to excess, and you boasted of your strength; and you took no heed of others, O Pārtha. For that you have fallen to the earth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to him, the mighty-armed one went on without looking back; and only the dog followed him—that dog whom I have so often mentioned to you.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Śakra, making heaven and earth resound on every side, came near to Pārtha with his chariot and said to him, "Mount up."
Seeing his brothers fallen, the Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira, consumed with grief, spoke this word to the Thousand-eyed one.
"My brothers have fallen here; let them come with me. Without my brothers I do not wish to go to heaven, O lord of the gods."
"The princess too, so delicate and worthy of every comfort, O Purandara—let her come with us; may you grant this."
Indra said: Your brothers and your sons, who have gone before to the third heaven, you shall behold—all of them, together with Kṛṣṇā. Grieve not, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Having laid aside their human bodies, they have gone there, O bull of the Bhāratas; but you shall go to heaven in this very body—of that there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This dog, O lord of what is and what shall be, has been devoted to me always. Let him go along with me, for my mind is set on freedom from cruelty.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Indra said: Immortality and equality with myself, O king, and prosperity entire and vast, and renown, and the joys of heaven you have now attained today. Abandon the dog; in this there is no cruelty.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: An ignoble deed is hard for a noble man to do, O thousand-eyed and noble one. Let me have no union with that prosperity for whose sake I must forsake one who is devoted to me.
Indra said: In the world of heaven there is no abode for those who keep a dog; the Krodhavaśas carry off the merit of sacrifice and pious works. Therefore, having considered, do as is fitting, O Dharma King: abandon the dog; in this there is no cruelty.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: They declare the abandonment of one who is devoted to be a most grievous sin, equal in the world to the crime of slaying a brahmin. Therefore, O great Indra, never, in any way, will I today forsake this one for the sake of my own happiness.
Indra said: Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, set forth openly, or poured into the fire — the Krodhavaśas carry it off if it has been looked upon by a dog. Therefore make this abandonment of the dog; by abandoning the dog you shall attain the world of the gods.
Having forsaken your brothers and even your beloved Kṛṣṇā, O hero, you have won this world by your own deeds. How then do you not forsake this dog? Established in renunciation entire, why are you bewildered now?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: With mortals who are dead there can be neither alliance nor enmity — such is the settled truth among men in the world. I had no power to bring them back to life; therefore my forsaking of them was the forsaking of the dead, not of the living.
The surrendering back of one who has come for refuge, the slaying of a woman, the seizing of a brahmin's wealth, the betrayal of a friend — these four, O Śakra, and the abandonment of one devoted, I hold to be equal.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard that speech of the King of Righteousness, the blessed one — Dharma himself in bodily form — spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, lord of men, filled with affection, in gentle words joined with praise.
You are nobly born, O king of kings, in the conduct of your father and in wisdom, and in this compassion of yours toward all beings, O Bhārata.
Once before, in the Dvaita forest, you were tested by me, my son, where your brothers, striving for the sake of water, were struck down.
There, setting aside both your brothers Bhīma and Arjuna, desiring equity between your two mothers, you wished that Nakula should live.
"This dog is devoted to me" — for this very reason you have refused the celestial chariot. Therefore, O ruler of men, there is none in heaven equal to you.
Hence imperishable worlds are yours in your own body, O Bhārata; you have attained, O best of the Bhāratas, a divine and unsurpassed destiny.
Then Dharma and Śakra, the Maruts too and the Aśvins, the gods and the divine sages, having set the son of Pāṇḍu upon the chariot —
— set forth in their own celestial cars, those perfected ones who move at will, all free from passion, holy, pure in speech and thought and deed.
Mounting that chariot, the king who upheld the line of the Kurus rose swiftly upward, enveloping heaven and earth with his splendor.
Then Nārada, knower of all worlds, standing amid the host of the gods, eloquent of speech and mighty in austerity, spoke aloud these words:
Even all those royal sages who are gathered here — the king of the Kurus surpasses them, eclipsing their renown.
Having pervaded the worlds with his fame, his splendor, and the richness of his conduct, having come hither in his own body — of none other than the son of Pāṇḍu have we ever heard such a thing.
Hearing the words of Nārada, the king of righteous soul addressed the gods, and the kings of his own party as well, and spoke this speech:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Be it good or be it evil, whatever the abode of my brothers, that alone do I now wish to attain; other worlds I do not desire.
Hearing the king's speech, so full of compassion, the king of the gods, Puraṃdara, replied to Yudhiṣṭhira:
Dwell in this abode, O king of kings, won by your auspicious deeds. Why do you still drag along with you this human attachment?
You have attained the supreme perfection, as no other man has ever anywhere attained it. Your brothers have not reached this abode, O delight of the Kurus.
Even now the human condition clings to you, O ruler of men. This is heaven — behold the divine sages and the perfected ones who dwell in the third heaven.
But the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, to the lord Indra of the gods who spoke thus, again spoke these meaningful words:
Without them I have no will to dwell here, O slayer of the Daityas. I wish to go there, to where my brothers have gone,
and to where that stately dark-hued lady, endowed with wisdom and goodness and every virtue, Draupadī, best of women, my beloved, has gone.
Janamejaya said: Having reached heaven, the threefold celestial realm, what abodes did my forefathers attain—the Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra alike?
This I wish to hear, for I hold you to be one who knows all things, sanctioned as you are by the great sage Vyāsa of wondrous deeds.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hear, then, what your forefathers did—Yudhiṣṭhira and the rest—once they had reached heaven, the threefold celestial realm.
Having reached heaven, the threefold celestial realm, the Dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira beheld Duryodhana seated upon a throne, attended by splendor.
Blazing like the sun, encompassed by the glory of heroes, surrounded by the radiant gods and the Sādhyas of holy deeds.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing Duryodhana, grew indignant, and at once turned back when he beheld such splendor upon Suyodhana.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Speaking aloud to them, he said: I have no wish to share these worlds in the company of Duryodhana, that greedy and short-sighted man.
For whose sake the whole earth, and our friends and kinsmen too, were slain by us in furious battle—we who had first been tormented in the great forest.
And Draupadī, the Pāñcāla princess, devoted to righteousness, our blameless-limbed wife, was sorely abused in the midst of the assembly, in the presence of our elders.
Farewell, O gods! I have no desire to look upon Suyodhana. I wish to go to where my brothers are.
Not so, said Nārada to him, smiling as it were: In heaven, O lord of kings, where one dwells, all enmity perishes.
Mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, speak not so by any means concerning King Duryodhana; and hear these words of mine.
This King Duryodhana is honored together with the thirty gods and with those virtuous, foremost kings who dwell here in heaven.
He has attained the realm of heroes, having offered up his own body in battle—that battle in which all of you, godlike men, were arrayed against him.
By the law of the warrior he has won this station, this lord of the earth who remained fearless in the midst of great peril.
You must not take to heart, my son, what was brought about by the dicing; nor ought you to dwell upon the abuse of Draupadī.
And whatever other torments were inflicted upon you through the dicing, whether in battles or elsewhere, you ought not to recall them.
Meet King Duryodhana in due courtesy. This is heaven, O lord of men; here no enmities exist.
Thus addressed by Nārada, the Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira, wise as he was, asked after his brothers and spoke these words.
If these are the eternal worlds of heroes for Duryodhana—a wicked man, ignorant of righteousness, a betrayer of the earth and of his friends—
for whose sake the earth was laid waste with its horses, chariots, and elephants, and we ourselves were burned by wrath, seeking to repay our feud—

title: Mahābhārata
text:
then where are those heroes, those great-souled brothers of mine, men of mighty vows, true to their pledges, the world's brave and truthful champions?
What worlds are theirs now? I wish to behold them—and the great-souled Karṇa, the son of Kuntī, true to his battle-pledge.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Sātyaki, and the sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and those kings who met their death by weapons according to the warrior's law.
Where then are those kings, O brāhmaṇa? I do not see them here, Nārada—Virāṭa and Drupada, and those led by Dhṛṣṭaketu.
And Śikhaṇḍin the Pāñcāla, and all the sons of Draupadī, and the unassailable Abhimanyu—these I wish to behold, Nārada.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Here, O gods, I do not see Rādheya of measureless might, nor the two great-souled brothers Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas.
those great warriors who offered their bodies into the fire of battle—the kings and princes who were slain in war for my sake.
Where are all those great warriors, valiant as tigers? Has this world been won by them too, those most excellent of men?
If all those great warriors have attained these worlds, then know, O gods, that I shall abide here only in the company of those great-souled ones.
Surely this imperishable, blessed world has been gained by those kings? Without them—my kinsmen and brothers—I will not dwell here.
For having heard my mother's words at the time of the water-rites—'Let the libation of water be made for Karṇa'—it is by that I am tormented even now.
And this too torments me again and again, O gods: that his feet were like my mother's, that man of measureless might.
Yet even on seeing this I did not go over to Karṇa, the crusher of enemy hosts—for with Karṇa at our side not even Śakra could have vanquished us in battle.
Wherever he may be, I long to see him, the son of Sūrya—he who, unknown to me, was slain by Savyasācin.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And Bhīma of terrible prowess, dearer to me than life itself; and Arjuna, like unto Indra; and those two twins, the equals of the Aśvins.
And I wish to behold the Pāñcāla princess, devoted to righteousness. I do not wish to remain here—this truth I tell you.
What is heaven to me, bereft of my brothers, O best of the gods? Where they are, there is my heaven; this is no heaven in my eyes.
The gods said: If your heart is set on going there, then go, my son, without delay; for we act to please you, by command of the king of the gods.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to him, the gods then instructed a divine messenger: Show Yudhiṣṭhira his friends, O scorcher of foes.
Then the king, the son of Kuntī, and the divine messenger went forth together, O tiger among kings, to where those bulls among men were.
The divine messenger went in front and the king behind, along a foul and difficult path frequented by evildoers.
shrouded in darkness, terrible, its grass and moss made of hair, reeking with the stench of those who had done evil, a mire of flesh and blood;
swarming with gadflies and crickets, covered with flies and gnats, hemmed in on every side, here and there, with corpses;
strewn with bones and hair, teeming with worms and insects, and on all sides girdled with blazing fire;
overrun by iron-beaked ravens and vultures, and beset by needle-mouthed ghosts as huge as the Vindhya mountains;
and with severed arms, thighs, and hands smeared with marrow and blood, and bellies and feet cut off, flung about here and there.
Through the midst of that corpse-stinking place, inauspicious and hair-raising, the righteous king passed, pondering much.
He saw a river filled with scalding water and hard to cross, and a forest whose leaves were swords, hedged about with sharp razors.
He saw burning sands of gravel, and slabs of iron set apart, and cauldrons of iron with oil seething on every side.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the son of Kuntī beheld the thorny śālmali tree, untouchable with its sharp spikes, and the torments of those who had done evil.
Marking that foul stench, he spoke to the divine messenger: How far must we travel along such a road as this?
And where are my brothers? This you ought to tell me. And what region of the gods is this? This I wish to know.
Hearing the words of the Dharma-king, the divine messenger turned back and said to him: Thus far does your journey go.
For I must turn back, so I was told by the dwellers in heaven. If you are weary, O lord of kings, then you may return.
But Yudhiṣṭhira, sickened and faint from that stench, set his mind on returning and turned back, O Bhārata.
As the righteous one turned back, filled with grief and sorrow, he heard piteous voices speaking all around him there.
O son of Dharma, royal sage, Pāṇḍava of holy lineage! For our sake, in mercy, stay but a moment longer.
As you, unassailable one, draw near, a holy breeze blows, bearing your fragrance, dear lord, by which ease has come to us.
We, O Pārtha, bull among men, after so long a time shall find relief at the sight of you, O best of kings.
Stay, mighty-armed one, even for a moment, O Bhārata; for while you remain, O Kaurava, the torment does not afflict us.
Such manifold pitiful voices of those in agony did he hear, O king, as they cried out on every side in that place.
Hearing those words of the wretched speakers, the compassionate Yudhiṣṭhira cried, Alas, what misery! and halted where he stood.
Those voices of the faint and the suffering, heard before now again and again, the Pāṇḍava could not recognize.
Not understanding those voices, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, said: Who are you, and why do you remain here?
Thus addressed, they all then cried out from every side: I am Karṇa, I am Bhīmasena, I am Arjuna, O lord!

title: Mahābhārata
text:
I am Nakula, I am Sahadeva, I am Dhṛṣṭadyumna; I am Draupadī, and we are the sons of Draupadī—thus they cried aloud.
Hearing those voices, fitting to that place, O king, the king then reflected: What is this, brought about by fate?
What sinful deed can have been done by these great-souled ones—by Karṇa, or by the sons of Draupadī, or by the fair-waisted Pāñcāla princess—
that they should be in this dreadful, evil-smelling region? For I know of no misdeed in all these doers of holy works.
What has the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra done, King Suyodhana, the wicked one, that he should be endowed with such splendor, together with all his followers,
and sit there glorious as great Indra, supremely honored? Whose doing now is this perversion, that these have gone to hell?
They who knew every law, brave men devoted to truth and scripture, intent on the warrior's duty, wise, performers of sacrifice with abundant gifts—
Am I asleep or awake? I am conscious, yet I do not comprehend. Ah, this must be some disorder of my mind, or some delusion of my senses.
In such manifold ways did King Yudhiṣṭhira reflect, overcome with grief and sorrow, his senses confounded by anguished thought.
And King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, gave way to fierce anger, and reproached both the gods and Dharma himself.
Tormented by that pungent stench, he said to the divine messenger: Go, good sir, into the presence of those whose messenger you are.
For I shall not go there; let it be made known that I remain here. For through my presence, O messenger, these my brothers find ease.
Thus addressed by the wise son of Pāṇḍu, the messenger then went to where the king of the gods, Śatakratu, abode.
And he reported the Dharma-king's resolve, all of it just as the son of Dharma had spoken it, O lord of men.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Pārtha, Yudhiṣṭhira the king of righteousness, had stood there a moment, O Kauravya, the gods came to that place, led by Śakra.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Dharma himself, embodied in form, came there to behold the king, to the very spot where the Kuru lord Yudhiṣṭhira stood.
When those gods of radiant bodies, of holy birth and holy deeds, had assembled, that darkness vanished, O king.
And there the torments of the evildoers were no longer to be seen, neither the river Vaitaraṇī nor the spiked silk-cotton tree.
The iron cauldrons and the dreadful rocks were seen no more; and those mangled bodies which the son of Kuntī had beheld everywhere about him—these too became invisible.
Then a wind, soft to the touch, bearing holy fragrances, auspicious and most cool, blew there near the gods, O Bhārata.
The Maruts with Śakra, the Vasus together with the two Aśvins, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and whatever other dwellers of heaven there were—
all of them assembled there, together with the Siddhas and the supreme sages, where the king of great splendour, the son of Dharma, was standing.
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, endowed with supreme majesty, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira these soothing words:
"Yudhiṣṭhira, mighty-armed one, the hosts of the gods are pleased with you. Come, come, O tiger among men; enough has been done, O lord. Perfection has been attained by you, O king, and yours are the imperishable worlds.
You should harbour no anger; and hear these words of mine. Hell must of necessity be seen, dear son, by every king.
There are two heaps, O bull among men, of good deeds and of evil. He who first enjoys the fruit of his good deeds goes afterward to hell; but he whose lot is hell first attains heaven afterward.
He whose deeds are mostly evil enjoys heaven first; and therefore, O king, I, seeking your good, led you there in this manner.
For by a deception you deceived Droṇa concerning his son; and so by a deception, O king, hell was shown to you.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
As you did, so did Bhīma, so Pārtha, so the twins, and so too Kṛṣṇā Draupadī—through deception they went to hell.
Come, O tiger among men; they are freed from their sin. And those kings of your own side who were slain in battle for you have all attained heaven—behold them, O bull among men.
And Karṇa, the great archer, the foremost of all who bear weapons—he for whose sake you grieve has gone to the supreme perfection.
Behold him, that tiger among men, the son of the Sun, O lord, established in his own station, mighty-armed one; cast off your grief, O bull among men.
Behold too your brothers and the other kings of your own side, each arrived at his own proper station; let the fever of your mind depart.
Having endured hardship before, from this point onward, O Kaurava, sport with me, free of grief and free of affliction.
Reap now, dear son, the fruit of your holy deeds, won by your own austerity, and of your gifts, O mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu.
This day let the gods and Gandharvas and the celestial Apsarases, clad in spotless garments, attend upon you in your blessedness in heaven.
Attain, O mighty-armed one, the worlds won by your Rājasūya and increased by the Aśvamedha, and the great fruit of your austerity.
Far above the worlds of other kings are your worlds, Yudhiṣṭhira—equal to those of Hariścandra, O Pārtha—in which you shall take your delight.
Where the royal sage Māndhātṛ is, where King Bhagīratha is, where Bharata the son of Duḥṣanta is—there shall you take your delight.
This is the holy river of the gods, O Pārtha, that purifies the three worlds—the heavenly Gaṅgā, O lord of kings; bathing therein you shall go forward.
When you have bathed here your human nature will pass away; rid of grief and of toil, freed from enmity you shall become."
While the lord of the gods was thus speaking to Yudhiṣṭhira, lord of the Kurus, Dharma, visibly embodied in form, addressed his own son:

title: Mahābhārata
text:
"Ho, O king of great wisdom, I am pleased with you, my son, by your devotion to me, by your truthful speech, by your forbearance and your self-restraint.
This is the third test of you, O king, that I have made; you cannot be moved from your nature by any inducements, O Pārtha.
Earlier you were tested in the Dvaita forest, over the matter of the fire-drill and its kindling-stick, and you passed that trial.
When your own brothers had fallen, and Draupadī too, there, O Bhārata, you were tested by me again, my son, in the form of a dog.
This is the third—that you wished to remain here for your brothers' sake. You are wholly pure, O greatly fortunate one, happy and free from all stain.
And your brothers, O Pārtha, are not in hell, O lord of peoples; this was an illusion employed by the king of the gods, the great Indra.
Hell must of necessity be seen, dear son, by all kings; and so for this brief moment you received this extreme of suffering.
Neither Savyasācin nor Bhīma, nor the twins, those bulls among men, nor the truthful, heroic Karṇa deserve to remain long in hell, O king.
Nor does the princess Kṛṣṇā deserve hell, Yudhiṣṭhira. Come, come, O best of the Bhāratas; behold the Gaṅgā that flows through the three worlds."
Thus addressed, that royal sage, your forefather of old, went on together with Dharma and with all the dwellers of the threefold heaven.
And having plunged into the Gaṅgā, the holy river of the gods, the purifier praised by the sages, the king cast off his human body.
Then, becoming of celestial form, Yudhiṣṭhira the king of righteousness, free of enmity and free of sorrow, was bathed in that water.
Then the wise Yudhiṣṭhira, king of the Kurus, surrounded by the gods and accompanied by Dharma, went on, being praised by the great sages.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, honoured by the gods together with the hosts of sages and Maruts, went on to where those bulls of the Kurus were.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
There he beheld Govinda invested with a brahmic form, recognizable by that very likeness he had seen before.
Blazing with his own splendour, attended by celestial weapons—the dread divine ones, the discus and the rest, in human form—and waited upon by the hero Phalguna of fair radiance.
Then in another place the joy of the Kurus beheld Karṇa, the foremost of weapon-bearers, in the company of the twelve Ādityas.
And in yet another place he saw the lordly Bhīmasena, surrounded by the host of the Maruts, invested with that very form.
And in the station of the two Aśvins the joy of the Kurus beheld Nakula and Sahadeva, blazing with their own splendour.
And so he beheld the Pāñcāla princess, garlanded with lotuses and blue lilies, standing with her form filling heaven, radiant as the sun.
