Then King Yudhiṣṭhira at once wished to question her; whereupon the lord Indra, king of the gods, told him:
"This is Śrī, in the form of Draupadī, who came into the mortal world for your sake—born of no womb, beloved of the worlds, of holy fragrance, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Born in the line of Drupada, and shared as your wife, she was fashioned by the trident-bearer for your delight.
These five greatly fortunate ones, Gandharvas radiant as fire, are the sons of Draupadī, O king—yours, of measureless might.
Behold the king of the Gandharvas, the sagacious Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and know him to be the elder brother of your father.
This is your elder brother, the son of Kuntī, of fire-like brilliance, the son of the Sun, your firstborn and foremost, renowned as Rādheya; he goes in the company of the Ādityas—behold him, O bull among men.
Among the hosts of the Sādhyas, the gods, the Vasus, and the Maruts, behold, O lord of kings, the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, the heroes led by Sātyaki, and the Bhojas, the mighty car-warriors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Behold, in the company of Soma, the unconquered son of Subhadrā—Abhimanyu, the great archer, of splendour like the moon.
This is Pāṇḍu, the great archer, reunited with Kuntī and Mādrī; your father comes ever to my presence by his celestial car.
Behold King Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, in the company of the Vasus; and mark this Droṇa, your teacher, at the side of Bṛhaspati.
These and other lords of the earth, and your warriors too, O son of Pāṇḍu, go in the company of the Gandharvas and the Yakṣas, those holy beings.
And some of those best of men have attained the state of the Guhyakas, having cast off the body and won heaven by holy speech, thought, and deeds."
Janamejaya said: The high-souled Bhīṣma and Droṇa, and King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and both Virāṭa and Drupada, and Śaṅkha and Uttara as well,
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Jayatsena, and King Satyajit, and the sons of Duryodhana, and Śakuni the son of Subala,
and the valiant sons of Karṇa, and King Jayadratha, and Ghaṭotkaca and the rest, and the others not here named—
and those other kings of radiant form who were named there—for how long a time did they abide in heaven? Tell me that as well.
Or is their station there eternal, O best of the twice-born? Or at the end of their deeds, what destiny did those bulls among men attain? This I wish to hear, told by you, O brahmin.
The Sūta said: Thus addressed, that sage among brahmins, given leave by the high-souled Vyāsa, began to recount it to that king.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: At the end of his deeds everyone must depart, O lord of men. Hear this secret of the gods, O king, O bull of the Bhāratas, which the one of great splendour, of divine sight, the mighty—
the ancient sage, O Kauravya, the son of Parāśara of great vows, of fathomless intellect, omniscient, knowing the destinies of all deeds—declared.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Bhīṣma of great splendour and great brilliance attained the Vasus themselves; for indeed only eight Vasus are now seen, O bull of the Bhāratas.
Then Droṇa entered into Bṛhaspati, the best of the line of Aṅgiras; and Kṛtavarman the son of Hṛdika entered the host of the Maruts.
Pradyumna entered into Sanatkumāra, whence he had come; and Dhṛtarāṣṭra attained the worlds of the lord of wealth, hard to reach.
And the illustrious Gāndhārī went together with Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and Pāṇḍu, together with his two wives, went to the abode of the great Indra.
Both Virāṭa and Drupada, and King Dhṛṣṭaketu, and Niśaṭha, Akrūra, and Sāmba, and Bhānu, Kampa, and Viḍūratha,
Bhūriśravas and Śala, and Bhūri the lord of the earth, and Ugrasena, and Kaṃsa, and the valiant Vāsudeva,
and Uttara, that bull among men, together with his brother Śaṅkha—these best of men entered into the All-Gods, the Viśvedevas.
The son of Soma, named Varcas, of great splendour and might, became Abhimanyu, the son of Phalguna, that lion among men.
Having fought by the law of the warrior as no other man anywhere had done, that righteous great car-warrior, at the end of his deeds, entered into Soma.
Karṇa entered the Sun, his father, O bull among men; Śakuni attained Dvāpara, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the fire-god.
All the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, fierce in might, were Rākṣasas; prosperous and high-souled, purified by the weapon, they went to heaven. And the Kṣattṛ (Vidura) entered into Dharma himself, as did King Yudhiṣṭhira.
The blessed god Ananta entered the nether region, Rasātala—he who, by the command of the Grandsire, by his yoga upheld the earth.
The sixteen thousand women who were the consorts of Vāsudeva, O Janamejaya, in time plunged into the Sarasvatī; and they too, becoming apsarases, went to Vāsudeva.
Those heroic mighty warriors who were slain in that great battle—Ghaṭotkaca and all the rest—attained the company of the gods and the yakṣas.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
And the rākṣasas who are celebrated as the allies of Duryodhana, O king, in due order attained the most excellent of all the worlds.
Those bulls among men entered the abode of great Indra, and of wise Kubera, and likewise the worlds of Varuṇa.
All this has been recounted to you in full detail, O greatly radiant one—the entire history of the Kurus and of the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata.
The Sūta said: Having heard this from the foremost of the twice-born, that king Janamejaya was struck with the utmost wonder there in the intervals of the rites of the sacrifice.
Then his officiating priests brought that rite to completion, and Āstīka was well pleased, having delivered the serpents.
Then he gratified all those twice-born ones with sacrificial fees; and, honored by the king, they departed as they had come.
And king Janamejaya too, having dismissed those brāhmaṇas, then returned once more from Takṣaśilā to the city named for the elephant.
All this, proclaimed by Vaiśaṃpāyana, has been recounted to you—told by the command of Vyāsa at the snake sacrifice of the king.
Holy is this work called a history, and supremely purifying, O brāhmaṇa—composed by the sage Kṛṣṇa, the disciplined, the speaker of truth,
by the all-knowing, the knower of ordinance, the possessor of knowledge of dharma, the good, the transcender of the senses, the pure, whose soul was perfected by austerity,
who dwelt in sovereign power, who knew Sāṃkhya and Yoga, awakened in many systems of teaching, having beheld it with the divine eye,
spreading abroad in the world the fame of the great-souled Pāṇḍavas and of other kṣatriyas abounding in wealth and splendor.
The learned man who has this recited at every sacred season, his sins shaken off and heaven won, goes on to become one with Brahman.
And whoever has even a quarter of this recited to brāhmaṇas at a śrāddha, for him imperishable food and drink await his ancestors.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
Whatever sin one commits by day, whether through the senses or even through the mind, by reciting the Mahābhārata one is afterward freed of it at the twilight prayer.
In dharma, in artha, in kāma, and in mokṣa, O bull of the Bhāratas—whatever is here may be found elsewhere; but what is not here is found nowhere at all.
This history is named Jaya, the Victory, and should be heard by one who desires prosperity—by a king, by princes, and even by a woman with child.
He who longs for heaven may gain heaven; he who longs for victory may gain victory; the woman with child obtains a son, or a daughter of great fortune.
The mighty Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, foreseeing things to come, in three years wrought the composition of this Bhārata out of love for dharma.
Nārada recited it to the gods, Asita Devala to the ancestors, Śuka to the rākṣasas and yakṣas, and Vaiśaṃpāyana indeed to mortals.
This holy history, of great import, equal to the Vedas—whoever recites it to the three varṇas, placing a brāhmaṇa at their head,
that man, freed from sin and gaining renown here, O Śaunaka, will attain the supreme perfection—of this I have no doubt.
By the meritorious study of the Bhārata—even of one who studies but a quarter of it with faith—all sins are wholly purged away.
The great sage, the venerable Vyāsa, having of old composed this collection, in four verses the venerable one instructed his son Śuka.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, experienced in the round of births, have passed away, and others yet will pass.
Thousands of occasions for joy and hundreds for fear, day after day, beset the fool, but not the wise.
With arms upraised I cry aloud, yet no one hears me: from dharma flow both artha and kāma—why then is dharma not pursued?
Never out of desire, nor out of fear, nor out of greed should one forsake dharma, even for the sake of life itself. Dharma is eternal, while pleasure and pain are fleeting; the soul is eternal, but its cause is transient.

title: Mahābhārata
text:
He who, rising at dawn, recites this Sāvitrī of the Bhārata, gaining the fruit of the Bhārata attains the supreme Brahman.
As the lordly ocean and as the Himālaya mountain are both renowned as treasuries of jewels, so is the Bhārata declared to be.
Whoever, well-composed in mind, recites the tale of the Mahābhārata will attain the supreme perfection—of this I have no doubt.
For one who attains the Bhārata as it is recited—immeasurable, holy, purifying, sin-removing, and auspicious, sprung from the cradle of Dvaipāyana's lips—what need has he of consecration with the waters of the lotus-pool?
